beijing-institute-of-technology.h: Beijing Institute of Technology in brief

blocks.x: Beijing Institute of Technology, known as BIT, is a state-funded university located in the Haidian district of north-western Beijing. It belongs to the national Project 211, Project 985 and Double First-Class Construction groups of universities, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has overseen it since 2008. Its beginnings lie far from the capital: it grew out of a science academy set up in Yan'an, in Shaanxi, in 1940. For a prospective student, this means BIT combines a long engineering tradition with the resources of one of China's best-supported university groups.

beijing-institute-of-technology.h: How BIT grew from Yan'an to Beijing

blocks.x: The institute's story is a series of moves and mergers across northern China. Dating the very first steps depends on which account you read: one says a Yan'an research academy for the natural sciences was set up in May 1939, while another gives 1 September 1940 as the day teaching opened. Both agree that in January 1940, at one of the toughest moments of the war against Japanese invasion, the Communist Party reorganised the research academy as the Yan'an Academy of Natural Sciences, the first science and engineering university the party founded. In practical terms, it was created to train technical people for the war effort and for building up industry.

The academy's task was to help build industry in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region. Li Fuchun, who was then secretary of the party committee for the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, became the first president, and the educator Xu Teli followed him. In its early days it received help from international organisations and individuals, among them Rewi Alley. A merger followed in March 1943, when the academy was combined with a newly created University of Yan'an and renamed that university's School of Natural Sciences. Towards the end of 1945 the whole University of Yan'an relocated northwards.

The School of Natural Sciences moved to Zhangjiakou in January 1946. Authorities of the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region decided to keep it there and combined it with the region's technical college to create a new industrial college. Later the same year the college moved into Hebei and merged with the border region's railway academy, forming a College of Industry and Transportation. A year after that it moved to Jingxing County and took the name of an industrial bureau technical school. In August 1948 it joined the engineering college of Northern University to become the Institute of Technology of North China University.

beijing-institute-of-technology.h: North China University and the move to Beijing, 1949 to 1952

blocks.x: October 1950 brought another merger: the Institute of Technology of North China University took in Sino-French University's home campus along with that university's mathematics, physics and chemistry departments. Much later, research came almost to a halt during the Cultural Revolution, but it picked up again soon after 1976.

BIT has a long reputation for defence-related technology, with radar, missiles and armoured combat vehicles as the best-known areas. Alongside them it keeps strong research in automation, photonics, computer science and industrial design, and in electrical, mechanical and chemical engineering. As of 2015 it had links with more than 200 universities in 58 countries and ran student exchanges with over 40 of them. Partners include Germany's Technical University of Munich, Russia's Bauman Moscow State Technical University, the Tokyo Institute of Technology, the University of California and the Australian National University. If you are a visiting student, exchange agreements like these are the usual route in, so it is worth asking your home university whether one already exists, and what credits would transfer. Treat the figures above as a snapshot and confirm the current list with the institute.

BIT lists 16 national key disciplines and 25 key disciplines at ministry level. Altogether there are 60 undergraduate majors, 144 master's-level majors and 62 doctoral ones, plus 17 post-doctoral research stations, so there is a wide choice at every level.

The strongest research fields are information engineering, electrical engineering, automation, photonics, vehicle and aerospace engineering, and mechanical and chemical engineering. In recent years new areas have emerged, among them computer science, industrial design and research into higher education itself. The institute operates five national key laboratories or research centres, six national-defence key laboratories, two laboratories under the Ministry of Science and Technology and four Beijing municipal key laboratories, as well as a national key science park. Its research spending in 2004 topped 620 million RMB. The institute is also one of the Seven Sons of National Defence, a nickname for the universities that traditionally supply the defence industry. Foreign applicants should be aware that this defence focus can affect admissions to some programmes, so ask the university directly.

Within China, BIT sits in the top 20 of all universities, and worldwide it is in the top 300. It was one of the first 15 universities named to Project 211 and the tenth to be named to Project 985. Many people list it, with Tsinghua, Peking University, Beihang and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, as one of Beijing's strongest engineering schools. In the 2021 WURI ranking of innovative universities, it sat in the 201 to 300 band.
The Ministry of Education's discipline evaluation places BIT in the national top ten in ten disciplines, out of roughly 20 in which it was assessed:
Information engineering, optical engineering and aerospace science and engineering: each fifth
Mechanical engineering and metallurgical engineering: each seventh
Transportation and traffic engineering: ninth
Instrument science and technology, automation science and engineering, and chemical engineering: each tenth
Positions shift with each evaluation round, so look at the university's own site for the latest results.
BIT is spread over several sites, some in different parts of Beijing and some in other provinces:

The Zhongguancun campus is the oldest of all, with a site of 920,700 square metres and 724,000 square metres of floor space. After Liangxiang opened in 2007, Zhongguancun became mainly the home of senior undergraduates and postgraduates.

Undergraduates have been based at Liangxiang since 2007. It lies in the Liangxiang University Town in Fangshan District, a long way out from central Beijing, so expect some travel if you plan to move between sites.
In Xishan there is a laboratory research centre. A separate Fangshan campus was co-founded by BIT and the district government of Fangshan.

Founded in 1984, the Qinhuangdao campus runs a one-year preparatory course for ethnic-minority students who do not speak Mandarin as their first language. Besides BIT's own future students, it also takes preparatory students heading for six other engineering universities: Beihang, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Engineering University and Northwestern Polytechnical University.

The Zhuhai campus in Guangdong province concentrates on continuing education, distance learning and special courses linked to local industry. It also hosts a graduate school, a science park and many research institutions, among them a joint optomechatronic engineering research centre with the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a city and public security centre run with Hong Kong Polytechnic University.

Renovation of the main library finished in 2006. It is a modern building of 25,509 square metres with wireless coverage throughout, and its collection tops three million items, of which 1.13 million are electronic. BIT Press was founded in 1985 and has published over 3,000 books.

The football team is regarded as one of the best in Chinese university football. It has won 11 national championships since the Chinese University Football League began in 2000, represented Chinese football at the 2003 and 2005 Summer Universiade games, and remains the only university side ever promoted into the professional Chinese Football Association Jia League, so football is a real part of campus life. Beijing Institute of Technology FC plays its home games at the Eastern Athletic Field.

About 100,000 people have graduated from BIT. Among them are academicians of the two national academies (sciences and engineering), generals in the armed forces and officials ranking above provincial governor.
Li Peng, who served as Premier and later chaired the National People's Congress
Zeng Qinghong, formerly vice-president of China
Zou Jiahua, formerly a vice-premier
Ni Zhifu, formerly a vice chairman of the legislature
Ye Xuanping, a former governor of Guangdong who became a vice-president of the CPPCC advisory body
Peng Shilu, often called the father of China's nuclear submarine
Huang Chunping, who directed the rocket system used for the Shenzhou 5 spacecraft

Wang Xiaomo, who won China's top science award, the State Preeminent Science and Technology Award; up to 2014 he was the only winner who had gone to college after 1949, and he is known as the father of China's airborne early warning systems
A good picture of the capital helps you imagine daily life as a BIT student. Here is what to expect from its buildings, landscape, weather and air.

Three architectural styles dominate Beijing. The first is imperial: Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City all belong here. The second group is the so-called Sino-Soviet style of the 1950s to 1970s, whose buildings tend to be boxy and are sometimes poorly built. The third is the modern style, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east, with landmarks such as the new CCTV Headquarters, the National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the early 21st century the city has put up a great many new buildings by international designers, especially in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s industrial design with neofuturistic touches, and the tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. Two Beijing buildings have been named best tall building of the year by the CTBUH (Linked Hybrid in 2009, CCTV Headquarters in 2013); only a single building worldwide receives that award annually.

Older housing is organised as siheyuan, courtyards ringed by buildings, linked by alleys called hutongs. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the residence of Soong Ching-ling. Most hutongs are straight and aligned east to west, which puts doorways on the north and south sides, a choice made for good feng shui. Their width varies, and the narrowest allow only a few pedestrians through together. They were once everywhere but are fast vanishing as city blocks are cleared for tall buildings. Residents may move into new flats at least as large as their former homes, yet many complain that the community spirit and street life of the lanes are lost, and the properties tend to be state-owned.

Beijing sits at the northern edge of the triangular North China Plain, which spreads out to the south and east. Mountains to the north, north-west and west protect the city and the farmland behind it from the desert steppe. In the north-west, Yanqing and Huairou districts are dominated by the Jundu Mountains, and the west is framed by Xishan, the Western Hills. The Great Wall runs along the rugged northern part of the municipality, built to defend against raiders from the steppe. The highest point, Mount Dongling in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, reaches 2,303 metres (7,556 feet).

The main rivers, the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, all belong to the Hai River system and flow south-east. The Miyun Reservoir on the upper Chaobai is the largest reservoir in the municipality. The Grand Canal, built more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route, begins in Beijing and runs south to Hangzhou. The South-North Water Transfer Project, finished in the last decade or so, ends here too and carries Yangtze basin water to the city.

The built-up area sits on the plain in the south-centre of the municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and it is small relative to the whole but growing. The city spreads in concentric ring roads, of which the Second follows the course of the old city walls and the Sixth ties together satellite towns in the suburbs. At the centre are Tian'anmen and the Square, directly south of the Forbidden City where the emperors lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, home of the country's present leaders, and Chang'an Avenue, between Tian'anmen and the Square, is the main east-west axis. Beijing's outward growth is often compared to a spreading pancake (tan da bing), a pattern often blamed for the city's urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (BSk). Summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon, while winters are brief, cold and dry under the Siberian anticyclone. Spring can bring sandstorms from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe, together with quickly rising and generally dry conditions, and autumn is a transitional season with little rain. Early August has been the hottest period and early January the coldest. The national seasonal calendar puts the start of spring at 26 March, of summer at 20 May, of autumn at 13 September and of winter at 31 October. Faster warming in March and September and slower warming in May and October mean autumn is generally shorter than spring.

Numbers worth knowing, based on 1991 to 2020 data: the urban annual mean temperature is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F), with daily minimums of 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily maximums of 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). The low-lying suburbs average 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with daily minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). Mountain areas sit between 0 and 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), getting colder with altitude. January averages -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Yearly precipitation is about 528 millimetres (20.79 inches), or 584.2 millimetres in Haidian and Chaoyang, with close to three-quarters of it from June to August. Possible sunshine runs from 42 percent in July to 62 percent in January and February, adding up to 2,490.5 hours. Since 1951 the coldest reading was -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966 and the hottest 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.

Beijing has a long record of environmental trouble, and anyone moving there should know the background. In the decade 2000 to 2009 the built-up area grew to four times its earlier size. That raised emissions and changed the local weather as well: reflectivity of the surface, wind speed and humidity near the ground dropped, whereas ground and air temperatures, ozone and vertical mixing of the air increased. Urban growth and fossil-fuel burning have caused serious problems and health effects for many residents. In 2013, heavy smog hit Beijing and much of northern China, affecting around 600 million people. That event made air pollution a major economic and social concern, and the city's government announced measures, including reducing coal's share from 24 percent in 2012 to 10 percent in 2017. Nationally, vehicles that pollute heavily were ordered off the road between 2015 and 2017, and the push toward clean energy sources was stepped up.
#### Where the pollution comes from

Joint American and Chinese research in 2006 found that much of Beijing's pollution is blown in from neighbouring cities and provinces: between 35 and 60 percent of the ozone comes from outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin have a significant effect, partly because summer winds blow mostly from the south and south-east and mountains lie to the north and north-west. Coal burning is behind about 40 percent of PM 2.5 and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 the city has been switching its coal-fired power stations to natural gas, with a goal of holding annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 Beijing used 26.3 million tons, of which 73 percent went to heating and power generation and the rest to industry. Neighbouring regions burn far more. Tianjin's use was forecast to climb from 48 to 63 million tons over 2011 to 2015, and in 2011 Hebei burned more than 300 million tons, a total above that of the whole of Germany, with only 30 percent going to power and much of the rest to steel and cement. Power plants in the coal-mining areas of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (where consumption has tripled since 2000) and in Shandong add to the problem. Ranked by coal use, the leading provinces are Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, in that order. Beijing had four major coal-fired power plants that supplied electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant shut in 2014, two others in March 2015, and the last, the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to close in 2016. The city also planned to cut 13 million tons of coal use between 2013 and 2017 and to limit consumption to 15 million tons in 2015.
#### Olympic and event measures

Before the 2008 Summer Olympics the city spent nearly US$17 billion to keep its promise to clean the air. During the Games it stopped work on all construction sites, closed many factories for good, shut industry in neighbouring regions for a time, closed some petrol stations and halved motor traffic with odd-and-even licence plate days, cut bus and metro fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It also assembled 3,800 natural-gas buses, one of the world's largest fleets, and became the first Chinese city to require the equivalent of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

For big events the government has also used cloud seeding to bring rain and clear the air, for example before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. More recently it has temporarily closed factories and tightened vehicle limits, producing the short spells known as APEC blue and parade blue around the 2014 APEC meeting and the 2015 Victory Day Parade. In both cases the air improved dramatically, then returned to unhealthy levels soon after.
#### Alerts and recent improvement

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, which shut most industry and commerce in the city, and a red alert followed later that month. From 2017, highly polluting older cars were to be banned from the road whenever red alerts are issued in the city or nearby regions, as announced by the environmental protection bureau in November 2016. Following the declaration of a war on pollution in 2014, pollutants fell measurably. Fine particulates were 35 percent lower in 2017 and fell further by 2020, mostly because gas replaced coal power and polluting factories were cleaned up. The yearly average of PM2.5 fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013, and in 2024 there were only two heavy-pollution days, the lowest on record and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days of 2013.
#### Checking the readings

Different sources report pollution differently, which can be confusing for newcomers. Daily data from 27 monitoring stations appears on the website of the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau, while the American Embassy publishes hourly PM2.5 and ozone readings. Because they measure different pollutants by different standards, the bureau's figures and reported health impact are often lower than the embassy's. Polluted air is linked to higher rates of heart and respiratory disease, hospital visits and, in extreme cases, death, so it is sensible to check an air-quality app each morning and wear a mask on bad days, as many residents do.
#### Dust storms

Dust from eroding deserts in northern and north-western China causes seasonal dust storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain to counter them. There were at least eight in the first four months of 2006, and one in April 2002 dropped nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it moved on toward Japan and Korea.

BIT is a defence and engineering university with roots in wartime Yan'an and several campuses in and beyond Beijing. Studying there means living in a vast, historic capital with hot summers, very cold winters and an air-quality record that has improved a great deal in the last decade. For current admissions rules, fees and which campus you would attend, always consult the university's own website.
Beijing Institute of Technology lists 280 programs for international students on this site: 56 bachelor, 74 master's, 68 doctoral, 82 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 192 taught in Chinese, 88 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 23,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 23,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 32,000 to CNY 49,000 (median CNY 32,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 44,400 to CNY 44,400 (median CNY 44,400), according to the university's published fee table.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

beijing-institute-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beijing Institute of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Beijing Institute of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

The Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology (南京信息工程大学), commonly shortened to NUIST, is a public university run by Jiangsu Province and located in Nanjing. It belongs to the Double First-Class Construction programme, which gives selected subjects national priority status. Its strongest identity is in meteorology, both in research and in teaching.

Prospective students should also know about two points of reputation. The university's position in international rankings has gone down in four consecutive years, 2021 to 2024. It has also been a party to several lawsuits, in one of which a local court ordered it to pay a penalty. Neither point tells you about a particular programme, but they are reasons to look at the university's own website and at independent reviews before you apply.

nanjing-university-of-information-scienc.h: From meteorology college to information university

blocks.x: The university's roots go back to 1960, when the China Meteorological Administration set up a Meteorology College of Nanjing University. In May 1963 the school was renamed the Nanjing Institute of Meteorology. It is regarded as China's oldest institution of higher education devoted to the science of weather and climate.

Control passed in February 2000 from the China Meteorological Administration to the Jiangsu provincial government. The present name, Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, was adopted in May 2004 with approval from the Jiangsu government and the Ministry of Education.

The university has been criticised in China for giving fashionable new names to established departments. After Facebook rebranded as Meta, interest in the metaverse surged in China. In 2022 NUIST renamed its Department of Information Engineering as the Department of Metaverse, presenting itself as China's "first metaverse institution", although it had no known strength in the metaverse or in 3D games. Critics saw the move as an attempt to profit from hype. China Daily, the country's leading English-language newspaper, said that education and research in departments with trendy names were no different from before. If a department's name is unfamiliar, ask which courses and staff sit behind it.

NUIST awards associate, bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees. The subject range runs from atmospheric and environmental science through engineering and management to literature, economics, law and agriculture. Double First-Class status applies to certain disciplines only. Before 2004 some students paid no tuition if they agreed on entry to work for the China Meteorological Administration (CMA); they would start work with the CMA during their fourth year and might receive credentials as well. That arrangement dates from before the current name was adopted, so do not assume it applies today.

International students already come in numbers. A count taken in autumn 2013 found more than 200 foreign students at NUIST, drawn from 43 different countries, so you would not be the first overseas student on campus. The number is dated, and the current figure may be much larger.
The units listed below include general colleges, professional and adult-education arms, and departments by subject.
Colleges and schools: Binjiang College, the College of Adult Education, the Technical College for Professional Training, the School of Business, Yue Jiang Academy and Reading Academy
Languages and international study: the College of English, the Foreign Languages Department, and the College of International Education (CIE), which is meant for foreign students
Atmosphere and environment: Atmospheric Science, Applied Meteorological Science, Environmental Science and Engineering, and Resource, Environment and City-rural Planning

Science and computing: Mathematics and Statistics, Physics and Optoelectronic Engineering, Computer Science and Technology, Electronic Engineering, Spatial Information Science, Information Management, and Information and Communications Technologies
Humanities and social sciences: Law, Public Administration, Economics and Trade, and Chinese Language and Literature
If you are an international student, the CIE is the first office to contact.

The university offers a number of scholarships to local and international students. One stands out: NUIST is one of just two universities that offer the Chinese Government Scholarship-WMO Program, a specialised award for students of meteorology or related subjects. The other institution that offers it is Hohai University.

nanjing-university-of-information-scienc.h: Things the university points to with pride

blocks.x: In 1972 three NUIST students climbed Mount Everest, and one of the three made a record by standing on the north summit on three separate climbs.

In 2020 a joint Chinese and Nepalese team produced the most accurate measurement yet of Everest's height. Two NUIST alumni supplied weather forecasts and other key support, and the university provided technical help as well.
In 2021 a team of NUIST researchers published the first academic study of "dual circulation".

Students recruited by the university can draw on scholarships from the Chinese government, from Hanban and from Jiangsu Province. In 2009 the university set up a "Confucius class" in the Bahamas, the fourth that Jiangsu Province had founded at an overseas university, and in 2011 it was upgraded to a Confucius Institute.

The university is home to a regional training centre of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Over 1,600 meteorological technicians and managers from 134 countries and regions have been trained there. The WMO's tenth conference on education and training took place at NUIST, as did the third international conference on quantitative precipitation estimation and forecasting. In 2010 the WMO Executive Council, at its 62nd session, issued certificates recognising the university's major contribution to international meteorological training.
A UK link followed in 2015, when NUIST and the University of Reading jointly created the NUIST-Reading Academy, which teaches both pure sciences and social sciences.

What a student needs to know about daily life largely concerns the city around the campus: how to travel, what the weather brings and what the surroundings are like. The sections below introduce Nanjing, where NUIST is based.

Nanjing is the main transport centre of eastern China and of the region downstream on the Yangtze. Land, water and air links form a three-dimensional system. As in most Chinese cities, most people get around by public transport. In October 2014 four bridges and two tunnels crossed the Yangtze, joining the districts on the north bank with the city centre on the south.

The first Yangtze bridge at Nanjing was finished in the 1960s, and for years it was the only crossing of the lower Yangtze in eastern China. It carries great symbolic value as a source of pride and a symbol of modern China, since Chinese engineers designed and built it after other countries' surveys failed and after the project first relied on Soviet expertise and then dropped it. Building started in 1960 and the bridge opened to traffic in 1968. It has two levels, one for road traffic and one for rail; the upper deck runs 4,600 metres (15,100 ft), of which around 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) are over the water.

Four more bridges and four tunnels followed. Together they make up ten crossings listed in the downstream direction. The bridges among them are Dashengguan (the Third Bridge), the Fifth Bridge, the First Bridge, Baguazhou and Qixiashan. The tunnels are the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel and the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), with the Line 10 metro tunnel counted too. A map is the easiest way to place them. The numbered bridges are:
Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (First Bridge), opened 1968, longest span 160 m
Baguazhou Bridge (Second Bridge), opened 1997, longest span 628 m
Dashengguan Bridge (Third Bridge), opened 2005, longest span 648 m
Qixiashan Bridge (Fourth Bridge), opened 2012, longest span 1,418 m
Jiangxinzhou Bridge (Fifth Bridge), opened 2020, longest span 600 m
Xianxin Bridge, opened 2023, longest span 1,760 m

The 2010 census put Nanjing's population at 8.005 million. At that time the OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 11.7 million. An official 2011 estimate gave the city 8.11 million, of whom 6.47 million lived in the urban area. Births ran at 8.86 percent and deaths at 6.88 percent, with 107.31 men for every 100 women.

Ethnically, Nanjing resembles most of eastern China. Han people make up 98.56 percent, and there are 50 other official groups. A 1999 count found 77,394 residents from minority groups, of whom 64,832 were Hui (83.76 percent of all minority residents). Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) were the next largest. Jianye District had the largest share of minority residents, who made up 9.13 percent of its population.

The city is an important base for grain and commercial crops. Money crops include rice and cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea and bamboo, along with fruit and medicinal materials. The fertile waters along both banks of the Yangtze also make Nanjing one of the key freshwater fishing centres in China.

In 2019 agriculture, forestry, livestock and fishing together produced 47.250 billion yuan, which was 4.8% more than in 2018. Crops accounted for 24.077 billion yuan, fishing 15.389 billion, services to these sectors 3.333 billion, livestock 2.435 billion and forestry 2.017 billion.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), shaped by the East Asian monsoon. Damp conditions last all year, and the four seasons are well defined. Summer is very hot and sticky, winter cold and wet, while spring and autumn are each reasonably long. Nanjing, Chongqing and Wuhan are traditionally the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze because of their constant summer heat. From mid-June to the end of July the plum trees blossom and the meiyu, East Asia's rainy season, arrives; the word means "plum rain", and it brings steady light rain and humidity. In winter the wind mostly blows from the northeast.

Even so, the winters are cold for a city at this latitude. They are similar to London's or colder: January in Nanjing, at 32°04'N, is about 2 °C colder than January in London, at 51°30'N. Set against Savannah, Georgia, on the American East Coast (a place with the same climate type), Nanjing's winter is 7 °C colder. Bring proper winter clothes.

January temperatures average 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the record low of −14.0 °C (6.8 °F) was recorded on 6 January 1955. In summer, southeast winds prevail, July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), and one record gives the hottest day as 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on 13 July 1934. Another list of extremes since 1951 puts the high at 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959. The two do not agree, so treat the very top figure with care. Annual mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F).

Precipitation exceeds 0.1 mm on 112.9 days in an average year (roughly 113), and the most ever recorded was 160 days, in 1957. Rainfall over a year averages 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in). Late summer and early autumn bring a small chance of typhoons. June has the least sunshine, at 37 percent of the possible total, while August and October have the most, at 48 percent; over twelve months Nanjing sees 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine.

A heavy smog began on 2 December 2013 across central and eastern China, over a stretch of about 1,200 kilometres (750 miles). The affected provinces and cities ranged from Tianjin and Hebei to Shandong, Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang. Cold air failed to move in, and slow air masses carrying industrial emissions let pollutants collect in a thick layer. Central and southern Jiangsu suffered most, especially Nanjing, where the air quality index was "severely polluted" for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to windless conditions, vehicle exhaust under low pressure and coal-fired district heating in northern China. Prevailing winds carried low air masses of factory emissions, mostly sulfur dioxide, towards the east coast. That was a single event, but it is a reminder to check the air quality when you plan trips and outdoor activities.

The Yangtze runs diagonally through Nanjing from southwest to northeast over about 93 kilometres, and the sea is more than 300 kilometres away. The Qinhuai River, which Nanjing calls its "mother river", rushes northwards through the central urban districts before it merges with the Yangtze. Two city-centre lakes, Xuanwu and Mochou, are likened to a pair of pearls in the urban fabric. Water covers about 11% of the city today.

Nearly everything drains into the Yangtze system; the only exception is the streams of northern Liuhe District, which reach the Huai River system by way of Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake. The Yangtze system comprises the Qinhuai system south of the river and the Chuhe system north of it, small streams entering from both sides, a pair of lakes (Shijiu and Gucheng) and the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun. Groundwater is abundant and of excellent quality, and the Pukou Pearl Spring is particularly well known. Two districts, Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou, have been famous hot-spring areas for a very long time.

Nanjing has China's biggest inland port, whose cargo handling reached 191,970,000 tonnes in 2012. The port area stretches for 98 kilometres (61 miles) and has 64 berths, of which 16 handle ships larger than 10,000 tonnes. It is the largest container port on the Yangtze, too: a base able to hold one million containers, the Longtan Containers Port Area, opened in March 2004. In 2010 the port ran six public ports and three industrial ones. A waterway 12.5 metres deep lets ocean ships of 50,000 tons sail directly to the port, and ships of 100,000 tons or more can also reach it after lightening their loads during the Yangtze's high tide. CSC Jinling has a large shipyard here.

Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are open to the public in the heart of the city. Purple Mountain is forested with deciduous and coniferous trees and protects a number of historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel on the Yangtze was being built to bring 50,000 DWT ships from the East China Sea to Nanjing.

Nanjing covers 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 square miles). The city occupies the core of the lower Yangtze drainage area, and also lies within the Yangtze River Delta, which is among the largest economic zones in the country. The river passes the city's west side and then its north, and the Ningzheng Ridge rings the north, east and south.

Distances help to picture the location: Luoyang is 650 kilometres (400 miles) northwest of the city, Beijing 900 kilometres (560 miles) to the north-northwest, Shanghai 270 kilometres (170 miles) to the east-southeast and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) to the west-southwest. Having started its journey downstream at Jiujiang in Jiangxi, the Yangtze crosses Anhui and Jiangsu and then enters the East China Sea. In its lower basin the Huai River basin is on the north side and the Zhe River basin on the south, and the Grand Canal east of Nanjing joins them. The wider area is known as the Xiajiang (下江, "downstream river") region; Jianghuai dominates its northern half and Jiangzhe the southern. It is also widely known as Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, "south of the river").

Neighbouring cities inside Jiangsu are Yangzhou in the northeast, Zhenjiang due east and Changzhou in the southeast. To the west, Nanjing meets the province of Anhui, and five Anhui cities of prefecture level share its border: Chuzhou lies northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan west, and Xuancheng southwest.

Two principal kinds of soil occur: zonal and cultivated. Yellow-brown zonal soil covers the north and centre, while red soil lies in the south near the Anhui border. Cultivated soil, shaped by farming, is chiefly paddy soil, with some yellow Gang soil and vegetable-garden soil. Distribution follows the relief and water conditions and can be sorted into low mountain and hill areas, hills and plains. The second national soil survey of 1980 to 1987 divided the city's soils into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species over 416,300 hectares.

Plant life in Nanjing is rich and varied, with complex vegetation. Seven kinds of natural vegetation are recognised: conifer woodland, broadleaf woodland that sheds its leaves, mixed woods of leaf-shedding and evergreen broadleaf trees, then bamboo, scrub, grass and water plants. Man-made vegetation covers field crops, vegetables, commercial forests, orchards and green belts. Seven plants are protected nationally as rare or endangered. Pterocarpus sinensis and Ming Codonopsis are two of them, and the others include Chinese Allium chinense and Sphaerocarpus sinensis.

Wild animals include 795 insect species (125 families, 11 orders), 99 fish species (22 families, 12 orders) and 327 land vertebrates (29 orders, 90 families). Birds account for 243 of those species (56 families, 17 orders) and mammals for 47 (22 families, 8 orders). Nine animals receive the highest national protection, among them the Oriental white crane and the white-shouldered eagle. Another 65 are in the second category, for instance the little swan, the Chinese tiger, the swallowtail and the finless porpoise. The province also names 125 key protected animal species and 35 endangered ones.

Underground, the city holds more than 40 kinds of minerals; its iron and sulfur stocks make up 40 percent of Jiangsu's total, and its strontium reserves are the largest in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Exploration has identified 49 mineral types (iron, copper, lead and zinc, then strontium and ferrosulfide, then dolomite, limestone, gypsum and clay), and 31 of these have proven reserves. They cluster in four metallogenic belts, including the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen belt of iron, copper and sulfur, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt. Water resources are plentiful from both the Yangtze and underground, and natural hot springs such as Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou add to them.

nanjing-university-of-information-scienc.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.

Travel to Nanjing, register at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

zhejiang-university-of-science-and-techn.h: Zhejiang University of Science and Technology at a glance

blocks.x: Zhejiang University of Science and Technology (浙江科技大学), abbreviated ZUST, is a full-time undergraduate university run by Zhejiang Province. It describes itself as a distinctive, application-oriented provincial university: the emphasis is on practical skills as well as theory. Bachelor's and master's degrees are both on offer, and the university has authority to take in overseas applicants, as well as those from Taiwan, Macao and Hong Kong.

Hangzhou's Xihu District holds the main campus, inside Xiaoheshan Higher Education Park, while the branch campus lies further out in the new Science, Education, and Culture area of Anji. National recognition has come from the Ministry of Education more than once. The university was in the first group to put the "Excellent Engineer Education and Training Program" into practice, and in the first group picked for the "New Engineering Research and Practice Projects". It additionally counts as a construction unit in the provincial "Internationalization Characteristic Universities" plan for Zhejiang.
The university's story is a series of name changes and steps toward independence, and the dates help you see how it grew:
1980: an industrial college attached to Zhejiang University (ZJU) in Hangzhou is set up.
1983: it gains independence as Hangzhou Industrial College.
1984: it is again placed under ZJU, now as a junior college.
1987: independence returns, and the name is Hangzhou Junior College.
1992: the name changes to Hangzhou Institute of Applied Engineering.
2001: the institution becomes Zhejiang University of Science and Technology, rendered in Chinese as Zhejiang Science and Technology College.
2009: it is accepted as a project construction unit working towards authority to award master's degrees.

2023: the provincial education department proposes a small change to the English name, to "Zhejiang University of Science & Technology". The Ministry of Education gave formal agreement on 14 December 2023.

The payroll has 1,620 regular staff, of whom 1,240 are full-time teachers, and over 520 of those hold senior professional titles. About 56% of teachers have doctorates, and 85% hold a master's degree or higher. More than 30% have spent over six months on academic work overseas. Over 40% combine theoretical and practical teaching ability, and more than 40% have experience in enterprise practice, which fits the university's applied character.
Honours at provincial level go to individuals and teams alike:
Two experts whose contributions are outstanding, in the young and middle-aged group
Sixty-one participants in the provincial "151 Talent Project"
Fourteen academic leaders, young or middle-aged, in the province's universities
Four research or teaching teams

Six disciplines are rated first-class by the province. Fifteen platforms for disciplines and research, provincial key laboratories among them, are rated at provincial or ministerial level or higher. Over the past few years staff have taken on upwards of 100 projects under national science and technology plans or the National Natural Science Foundation, and the university has collected more than 30 research prizes at provincial or ministerial level or above, including 2 national science and technology awards.

Teaching infrastructure is also substantial. Eight platforms are national-level, notably a National Engineering Practice Education Center, and another 16 are provincial or ministerial, such as an innovation experimental zone for talent training models. Three provincial teaching teams exist. Five majors have national-level status (this includes national first-class undergraduate majors), and the province recognises 28 more. Eight majors have passed professional accreditation.

On the curriculum side, 45 courses reach provincial or ministerial level or higher, some being national excellent courses, and 29 textbooks or textbook projects are part of national and provincial plans. Prizes for teaching include 2 national teaching achievement awards and 4 first prizes at provincial level.

zhejiang-university-of-science-and-techn.h: A German connection and other international ties

blocks.x: ZUST has been active in foreign cooperation for several decades, and internationalised education is part of its character. The Ministry of Education has designated it a pilot institution for Sino-German cooperation in training higher applied talents.
The partnership with Germany unfolded in clear steps:
1985: the province of Zhejiang agreed with Lower Saxony, a German state, to build the university jointly.
1990: the two national governments exchanged notes formally, which launched a project at government level.
From 2000: joint undergraduate programmes in the "2+3" pattern, designed with seven German universities of applied sciences (Hochschule Hannover is one of them).

ZUST also started a "Sino-German Forum" on cultivating high-level applied talents, which many Chinese and German universities take seriously, and the Ministry of Education chose the university to build the forum's base. Confucius Institutes were established with two partners: Erfurt University of Applied Sciences in Germany, and Babes-Bolyai University, which is in Cluj in Romania. When Hangzhou hosted the G20 summit, Chancellor Merkel of Germany spoke warmly of the results of the Sino-German cooperation run by ZUST.
Day-to-day life for a student depends on the surrounding city: its weather, its transport and the things to do. This part of the profile introduces Hangzhou, where ZUST is located.

Northwestern Zhejiang is where Hangzhou lies, in the south-central Yangtze River Delta. The Grand Canal, which runs all the way to Beijing, ends here in the south. As a sub-provincial city its territory reaches from the mountainous edge of Anhui in the west to the coastal plain by Hangzhou Bay in the east. Houses and offices cluster around the east and north shores of West Lake, slightly north of the Qiantang River.

Zhejiang's biggest river is the Qiantang, and it produces a natural show. Between the 15th and 18th days of the eighth lunar month every year comes the Qiantang Tide, nicknamed "the Biggest Tide in the World". The largest tidal bore anywhere rushes upstream past Hangzhou and can reach 12 m (39 ft) high.
Hangzhou has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), and the four seasons are clearly distinct. Summers are long, very hot and humid. Winters are chilly, cloudy and drier, with snow on some days.
Key figures:
Over a year the temperature averages 17.0 °C (62.6 °F). January is coolest at 5 °C (41.0 °F) on average, and July warmest at 29.3 °C (84.7 °F).
Rainfall averages 1,438 mm (56.6 in) per year. In June the city is touched by the Asian monsoon's plum rains.

Typhoon storms hit in late summer, from August to September, but typhoons seldom strike directly. They usually come ashore on Zhejiang's southern coast, and Hangzhou feels strong winds and stormy rain.

Since 1951 the lowest official reading is −9.6 °C (15 °F), on 6 February 1969, and the highest 41.9 °C (107 °F), on 3 August 2024. Unofficial figures go further at both ends: down to −10.5 °C (13 °F) in both December 1912 and January 1916 (on the 29th and the 24th respectively), and up to 42.1 °C (108 °F) on 10 August 1930.
Possible sunshine varies between 30% in March and 51% in August, adding up to 1,709.4 hours of sunshine a year.

Counting Xiaoshan and Yuhang, Hangzhou had a permanent population of 12.522 million in 2023, with 10.543 million (84.2%) living in urban areas. For the wider metropolitan area the OECD gave an estimate of 13.4 million as of 2010, though other sources go above 21 million, and it includes Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou. Among people on the city's register, life expectancy stood at 83.18 years in 2021, among the highest figures in China.

Hangzhou has long been a religiously diverse city. A description from 1848, in the Qing period, called it the "stronghold" of Islam in China, noting several mosques with Arabic inscriptions. A Hui man from Ningbo told an Englishman something similar about Zhejiang, comparing Hangzhou's multiple mosques with his own congregation of around 30 families. Notable mosques that you can find in the city today include the Phoenix Mosque and the New Hangzhou Great Mosque.

Chinese Jewish life had an important centre here around the end of the 1500s and start of the 1600s, and Hangzhou may be where the Kaifeng Jewish community first came from. Synagogues once stood in both Hangzhou and Ningbo, though nothing of them can now be found, and only Kaifeng still had known Jews in China. Catholic history is long as well. Hangzhou produced two members of the group called the Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism, and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, some 400 years old and from the Ming dynasty, ranks among the oldest Catholic churches in the country. Christians were persecuted in the city in the early 21st century.
Many temples stand near West Lake:

Lingyin Temple, whose name means Soul's Retreat, is about 2 km (1.2 mi) to the lake's west. Its founding dates to AD 326, which was the first year of Xianhe under the Eastern Jin Dynasty. At about 1,700 years old, it is thought to be the oldest Buddhist temple in the city and the earliest famous one, and it has been wrecked and rebuilt repeatedly.
Yue Fei Temple was built in 1221, under the Song Dynasty, on the northwest shore of the lake. It honours General Yue Fei, who died as a result of political persecution.
You can also see the Jingci Temple and two pagodas, the Baochu and the Leifeng.
North of the Qiantang, Yuelun Hill carries the Liuhe Pagoda. A further temple is the Hupao Temple (虎跑寺).

Fast growth has marked Hangzhou's economy ever since the city opened up in 1992. Its industries are varied, among them light industry, farming and textiles, and it counts as an important logistics hub and manufacturing base on China's coast. E-commerce and technology are also centred here.

In 2001 the city's GDP was RMB 156.8 billion, second only to Guangzhou among provincial capitals. Output more than tripled over the next 17 years, to RMB 1.3509 trillion in 2018, while per capita GDP went from US$3,020 up to $21,184. An estimate for 2019 put gross metropolitan product for the whole metropolitan area at 3.2 trillion yuan ($486.53 billion). That is bigger than Argentina's economy ($452 billion, 26th in the world) and Nigeria's ($448 billion, Africa's biggest).

Rankings reflect this. A study by PwC and the China Development Research Foundation placed Hangzhou first among "Chinese Cities of Opportunity". GaWC classes it as a World City at "Beta+" level, and the Global Financial Centres Index of 2018 put it 89th. The Economist Intelligence Unit ranked it first in its China Emerging City Rankings, which assess growth potential, in 2021 and 2022. By number of billionaires, the Hurun Global Rich List 2020 put it 11th in the world and 6th in China, after Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou. As of August 2023, within its city limits it hosted more Fortune Global 500 headquarters than any city except nine others worldwide. In China only Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen host more. The city also pursues a smart city initiative, aiming to digitise the economy and become a cashless city.

Several technology companies have their headquarters in Hangzhou: Alibaba Group, Ant Group, NetEase, DeepSeek, Geely and HikVision. Alibaba's new global headquarters opened in May 2024. It has seven buildings with a floor area of around one million square metres, and room for 30,000 employees. Programmers have moved to Hangzhou from Beijing, Shanghai and other cities because of its internet industry.

The city has also nurtured new industries. These range from medicine and information technology to heavy equipment, car parts, home appliances, electronics, telecommunications, fine chemicals, chemical fibre and food processing. Officials talk about "1 + 6" industrial clusters. The single "1" is the digital economy. The "6" refer to cultural and creative industries, finance, tourism, fashion manufacturing and top-end equipment manufacturing, among others. Since at least 2023, the digital and creative or cultural sectors have driven growth.

One study found that Alibaba's total revenue has a positive effect on the city's economic growth, but that the causal link runs only one way, from the company to the city. A 1% rise in Alibaba's revenue can lead to 0.272% growth in the city's economy in the long run.

In March 2013 the Hangzhou Tourism Commission began an online "Modern Marco Polo" campaign on Facebook. Within a year nearly 26,000 people from around the globe applied to become Hangzhou's first foreign tourism ambassador. The winner, Liam Bates, was announced at a press conference in Hangzhou on 20 May 2014. His prize was a $55,000 contract, and he was the first foreigner to be given such an official post by China's government.
Three development zones shape the city's economy.

In 1993 the State Council approved the Hangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone as a national zone. Its area is 104.7 km2 (40.4 sq mi), and it promotes industries such as food processing, biological medicine, electronic information, and the manufacture of machinery and appliances for the home.

Approval from the State Council led to the creation of the Hangzhou Export Processing Zone on 27 April 2000. Of its type it is the only one that Zhejiang has, and it was among the first in the country. The zone is planned to cover 2.92 km2 (1.13 sq mi) and is near both the airport (Hangzhou Xiaoshan International) and the port of Hangzhou.

March 1991 saw the State Council approve the Hangzhou Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (HHTZ) at state level. It is in three parts, and the main ones are the Xiasha Sci-Tech Industrial Park and the Zhijiang Sci-Tech Industrial Park. The HHTZ is now among Zhejiang's most influential bases for innovation and industry in high technology. It housed over 1,100 software developers and BPO enterprises in 2013, and Siemens, Nokia and Motorola are among the firms with research and development centres there. In 2011 the zone's GDP rose 13.1 percent to RMB 41.63 billion, 5.9 percent of Hangzhou's total. The zone presents itself as China's "Silicon Valley" and is home to Alibaba's headquarters. In 2023 Alibaba accelerated work on its global headquarters in Hangzhou with local government support, after signing a new cooperation pact with local authorities.

Recent development has changed Hangzhou a great deal, but the city has kept its historical, cultural and natural character, and tourism is still an important part of the economy. With numerous skyscrapers, it is the world's 19th city and China's 9th for skyscraper numbers.

One of the best-loved attractions is West Lake, which UNESCO has inscribed as a World Heritage Site. Its Cultural Landscape extends across about 3,323 ha (8,210 acres) and takes in many of the city's finest historic and scenic spots. Around the lake are cultural sites, historic pagodas, hills and tea fields, such as Phoenix Mountain, and two big causeways run across the water. Dreaming of the Tiger Spring is found on the western side of the lake. It is known for its natural spring and lies close to the celebrated longjing tea plantations.

Parts of the Grand Canal run through Hangzhou. The Jiangnan Canal, which joined Suzhou to Hangzhou, was built in 610 CE by dredging and widening a channel that already existed. The Grand Canal as a whole became a World Heritage Site in 2014. Metro Line 5 from The Grand Canal station or from East Gongchen Bridge station is the way to reach historic places around Gongchen Bridge.

Xiacheng District contains West Lake Cultural Square, where the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology and the Zhejiang Natural History Museum are located. So is the Zhejiang Global Center, which at about 160 m (520 ft) is one of the tallest buildings downtown.

The Xixi National Wetland Park was created to protect the area's wetland ecosystem and extends to around 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi). Work to bring back reed beds and to restore fish ponds has helped attract many kinds of birds. A temple and several historic houses from the countryside lie inside it.

Chun'an County, which is part of Hangzhou, contains Qiandao Lake. This artificial reservoir has more islands than any other lake in China, and they differ greatly in size and form, with scenery that is distinctive to each. The Hangzhou Zoo and the Hangzhou Botanical Garden are both in Xihu District.

Natives of Hangzhou speak the Hangzhou dialect, a Wu dialect that is unique to the area, and the same goes for parts of the rest of Zhejiang and of southern Jiangsu. It is not the same as dialects in southern Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu. Mandarin is the official language set by the central government and the dominant spoken language, but it cannot be understood by speakers of the Hangzhou dialect without learning it. An estimated 1.2 to 1.5 million people speak the dialect.

Museums in the city include the China National Silk Museum, the world's largest silk museum, the China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆) and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum, which combines the study of human history with exhibition and research and holds over 100,000 cultural relics. Opera, for example Yue opera, is staged in many theatres. There are also big productions on the history and culture of Hangzhou, such as the Romance of Song Dynasty and Impression West Lake. The city's landscapes link the stories of famous figures from Chinese history with the feelings of ordinary visitors.

The China Academy of Art is based in Hangzhou, and so were noted painters like Fang Ganmin and Lin Fengmian. The city government puts a great deal of money into tourism and the arts, and it particularly promotes silk, umbrellas and Chinese folding fans held in the hand.

A part of the Zhejiang Library, the Hangzhou Ancient Book Restoration and Display Center, offers the public regular demonstrations. Visitors see how traditional restoration of paper and binding methods help to preserve ancient Chinese texts. The centre has a major role in the conservation of Jiangnan cultural documents.

ZUST is a practical, engineering-minded provincial university with strong German links, and it is set in Hangzhou, a city that blends a UNESCO-listed lake and canal heritage with one of China's most active technology economies.

Dalian Medical University (大连医科大学, Dàlián Yīkē Dàxué) is a provincially run university in Dalian, in Liaoning province, and it opened in 1947. In October 2007 it moved to a new campus in Lushunkou District, on the opposite side of Lushun South Road from the new campus of Dalian University of Foreign Languages.

One unusual detail about the university: its subsidiary, Dalian Medical University Plastination Co., supplies the plastinated specimens that have appeared around the world in the exhibition Bodies: The Exhibition.
The university has developed with medicine as its focus and is a key construction university for first-class university status in Liaoning Province. These are its official credentials:

dalian-medical-university.h: Dalian: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Dalian is a seaside industrial and tourist city, so a student here experiences both the sea and heavy industry. The sections below describe its setting, weather, economy, attractions and transport.

Dalian is one of China's most heavily industrialised areas. The municipality today combines two main parts. One is Dalian itself; the other, smaller and farther along the Liaodong Peninsula, is Lüshunkou, once the city of Lüshun, which Western and Russian writers called Port Arthur. Historical accounts say that the Russian-designed city of Dalniy (also spelled Dalney), on the southern side of Dalian Bay, lay 40 kilometres (25 miles) from Port Arthur, known today as Lüshunkou, literally "Lüshun Port".

Dalian looks out over Korea Bay, which lies north of the Yellow Sea, and occupies about the midpoint of the Liaodong Peninsula, at the narrowest stretch of its neck. It has a 1,906 km (1,184 mi) coastline and governs most of the peninsula and about 260 islands and reefs in the sea nearby. It lies south-south-west of the Yalu River, and the harbour entrance forms a small bay called Dalian Bay.

The climate is humid continental with a monsoon influence (Köppen Dwa). The East Asian monsoon makes summers warm and wet, and the huge Siberian anticyclone makes winters cold, windy and dry. Apart from winter, the seasons here arrive about a month late, a result of the peninsula location. In January the daily mean is -3.3 °C (26.1 °F), while August averages 24.8 °C (76.6 °F); across the full year the mean is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F).

Rainfall averages 580 millimetres (22.8 in) a year but is concentrated in the summer and varies a lot between years. The coast keeps the difference between day and night temperatures small, with a yearly average of 6.66 °C (12.0 °F). Possible sunshine is 45% in July and 66% in March, for 2,625 hours of bright sunshine a year. The record low since 1951 is -21.1 °C (-6 °F), set on 4 January 1970, and the record high is 37.3 °C (99 °F), recorded on 7 August 2026.
At the 2010 census Dalian had 6.69 million people. By the end of 2014 the registered household population was 5.943 million, which was 29,000 more than a year earlier.

The city's GDP has grown by double digits each year since 1992. The growth rate in 2014 was lower, at 5.8%, but GDP still reached RMB 765.56 billion, or RMB 109,939 per person. In the National Bureau of Statistics' nationwide appraisal of overall strength, Dalian comes eighth among Chinese cities. Electronics, petrochemicals, oil refining and machine manufacturing lead its industries.

The area started out based on agriculture and aquaculture. In the early twentieth century a ferry opened between Yantai and Lüshun, and farmers and fishers from Shandong, across the Yellow Sea, began to settle here during the Chuang Guandong migration era.

Heavy engineering has deep roots here. Shipbuilders and locomotive makers were already working in the city through the Second Sino-Japanese War, and their successors are Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and the Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (DLoco). The postwar decades made the city a centre for heavy and light industry, with names like Wafangdian Bearing Co., Dalian Chemical Group and Dalian Heavy Industry Co., and also for distribution, where the Dashang Group is prominent.

The port is at the heart of all this. A major gateway for foreign trade, it is connected with over 300 ports across 160 countries and regions, and more than 100 container routes, domestic and international, run from it. In 1976 an oil-tanker harbour was finished where the pipeline from the Daqing oilfields ends; it is the biggest of its kind in China by tonnage. Dalian is the sixth-largest port in China, and the AAPA's world port ranking placed it eighth by cargo tonnage in 2012 and twelfth by TEUs of containers in 2013. That helps explain why diesel engineering, chemicals and oil refining are so important locally.

A second port, Dayaowan Port (大窑湾港, Dàyáowān Gǎng), opened in 1993 on the Dagushan (大孤山) Peninsula in the northern suburbs and specialises in importing and exporting mining and oil products. Transport links add to this: two railway stations (Dalian and Dalian North), the international airport, three northern expressways to Shenyang (Shenda), Changchun (Changda) and Harbin (Hada), and another road to Dandong in the east. With the ports, they make the city a key distribution point.

The central government has given Dalian many advantages. A 1984 designation as an "open city" lets Dalian take in a lot of foreign investment (see also Special Economic Zones). The Development Zone in Jinzhou District attracted Japanese firms first, among them Toshiba, Sanyo Electric, Nidec, Mitsubishi Electric and Canon, and then South Korean, American and European companies, including Pfizer.

Intel announced in 2007 that it would build a chip factory (a "fab") in the zone; it was the firm's first fab on a brand-new site since 1992. Called Fab 68, it was announced on 26 March 2007, started up on 26 October 2010, and is Intel's first chip fab in East Asia. Car manufacturers are also present: BYD Automobile makes its K9 electric bus here, and Chery and Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company have plants too.
Four further zones exist: the Hi-Tech Industrial Zone, the Free Trade Zone, the Export Processing Zone and an Economic and Technological Development Zone, each with "Dalian" in its name.

Dalian is the financial centre of Northeast China. Branches of China's five biggest banks are found here: Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, Industrial & Commercial Bank of China and Bank of China. The former Dalian City Commercial Bank is now the Bank of Dalian, which also handles the processing for the Mingzhu IC Card used on public transport, and which has opened branches in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenyang and five further cities.

Northeast China's only futures exchange is the Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE), set up in 1993, and futures trading has expanded quickly since. It has 19 futures products that the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has approved. Farm goods include eggs, soybeans and their meal and oil, corn and its starch, RBD palm olein, and polished round-grained rice. Industrial products include coking coal, metallurgical coke and iron ore, plastics and chemicals (LLDPE, PVC, PP, EG and EB) and building boards (fibreboard and blockboard). Options on three of these are traded: corn, soybean meal and iron ore. For 2019 the DCE recorded 1,331 million lots and RMB 68.92 trillion of turnover, and the Futures Industry Association in the US ranked it 11th in the world by trading volume.

Since the 1990s the city has stressed the IT industry, particularly in the Dalian Hi-Tech Zone and the Dalian Software Park, both in the western suburbs close to Dalian University of Technology. The High-Tech Zone houses more than 4,700 enterprises, 80 of them Fortune Global 500 companies. Companies from China (Neusoft Group, Hisoft and DHC) share the zone with firms from the US, Europe, India and Japan: Cisco, Hitachi, Oracle, Accenture, Sony, Panasonic, Ericsson, HP, Dell, IBM, Infosys and Wipro. Nine professional business incubators, including a hi-tech one and others for animation and software, have helped over 400 companies get started. Work continues on the "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" plan, whose projects include Phase 3 of Dalian Software Park.

Tourists from China and abroad, above all from Japan, South Korea and Russia, come to Dalian for its beaches, its mild weather and its role in modern Chinese history. Famous beaches include Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸), Fujiazhuang (付家庄), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Xinghai Bay (星海湾) and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子). Hangzhou and Chengdu shared with Dalian the title "China's best tourist city" in 2007, an award from the National Tourism Administration and the United Nations World Tourism Organization.
Zhongshan Square (中山广场): Russians drew up the plan in the 19th century, and the classical buildings around it were put up by the Japanese in the early twentieth century

Laohutan Ocean Park: a Coral Aquarium, a World of Birds, and the Polar Region Marine Animals World, where a show with white whales and dolphins is the main draw. The Tigers Sculpture Square close by has the tiger that stands for Tiger Beach (老虎滩, Lǎohǔtān), and visitors can go aboard the Taiyuan, a decommissioned Anshan-class destroyer
Xinghai Square (星海广场, "Square of the Sea of Stars"), on Xinghai Bay, built for the city's centennial in 1998 and the largest city square in the world
Heishijiao Geological Park and Dalian Natural History Museum
Sunasia Ocean World
Dalian Forest Zoo

Bangchuidao Scenic Area: a carefully kept park, State Guesthouse from 1960 on, now opened to visitors, with lush greenery, villas in Chinese and Western styles, a hot spring, a golf course, a recreation centre, tennis and badminton courts and a beach. Off the beach you can see Bangchui Island (棒棰岛, Bàngchuí Dǎo), whose name refers to an islet shaped like a bangchui, an old washing implement. Guests at the guesthouse have included Juan Antonio Samaranch, Gerhard Schröder, Boris Yeltsin, Henry Kissinger, Kim Jong Un, Xi Jinping, Hu Jintao, Jiang Zemin, Deng Xiaoping and Zhou Enlai
Dalian Sightseeing Tower, a viewpoint over the city
Donggang Music Fountain, a show of water and music
Fujiazhuang Beach, one of the city's famous beaches

blocks.x: Dahei Mountain

Jinshitan National Holiday Resort and Discoveryland (金石滩, Jīnshítān, meaning "Golden Pebble Beach"), which comprises two peninsulas, east and west, the open ground in between, and the Golden Coast beach, 16 kilometres (10 mi) long

Jinshitan has plenty to see and do. Museums include a waxworks, a geological museum, a hall of Mao Zedong badges, and the Model Movie & TV Art Center, and there is a coastal national geopark. Outdoor and leisure venues include Golden Rock Park, Wanfuding Park, a martial arts hall, an international vehicle campsite, a hunting club and an equestrian base, with the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort for relaxing. Two golf courses, the Golden Gulf Golf Course and the Golden Pebble Golf Club, and an international convention centre with a resort complete the picture, along with the Discoveryland Theme Park. Annual events held here include a beach carnival, a winter swimming festival and a grape festival, each with international participants.
The Discoveryland Theme Park (发现王国, or "Discovery Kingdom") opened in 2006 and was designed by Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, who had worked on Disney parks.
History is richest in Lüshunkou, where several sites relate to the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05:
Lüshun Museum, a good starting point
Lüshun Railway Station, an old station that is itself a landmark
East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山) and Hill 203, where the most violent fighting of the Battle of Lüshun took place, and the Shuishiying Meeting Place, where the ceasefire treaty was signed

The Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum: Russians built the prison in 1902, and the Japanese later enlarged it. During World War II it was used to hold people of various nationalities who resisted the Japanese invasion. Among the prisoners who were killed there was An Jung-geun, the Korean independence activist who assassinated Itō Hirobumi
Lüshun Snake Museum, together with a nature reserve on Snake Island and the Lüshun Bird Port
Hengshan Temple (横山寺), a Han dynasty foundation rebuilt in 2003 that stands near the Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库), and the nearby Longwangtang Cherry Blossom Park
In Pulandian District: the Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场)
In Wafangdian: the golf course on Changxing Island (Changxing Island International Golf Course)
In Zhuanghe: Bingyu Valley Scenic Area, and a hot spring on Buyun Mountain (步云山温泉)
In Changhai County: a group of islands

Hot spring hotels are numerous. In Lüshunkou District you will find the Laotieshan and Tianmu hot spring hotels, in Jinshitan the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, in Wafangdian the Minghu Hot Spring Hotel, and in Ganjingzi District the Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa.

More and more people ski in Dalian. Two resorts are in Ganjingzi District (Linhai, and Dalian Happy Snow World, which is near the airport), one is in Pulandian District (Anbo), and Wafangdian has Minghu, with its Minghu International Skiing Holiday Village.
Cycling is less popular here than elsewhere in China because the roads are hilly. As in a number of Chinese cities, local law forbids motorcycles in the downtown core, so you will see few of them.

The city has an extensive bus network and an efficient metro. As of March 2023 the metro included underground Lines 1, 2 and 5, and overground Lines 3, 12 and 13. Extensions and new lines such as Line 4 and Line 7 are under way, designed over time to link all parts of the city. Only one other Chinese city has an older tram system than Dalian's. Most public transport can be paid for with the Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡).

For quality of life, China Daily named Dalian the most liveable city in China in 2006. Among its theatres, Beijing Opera is staged at the Hongji Grand Stage, music mainly at the Dalian People's Culture Club, and Errenzhuan mainly at the Working People's Theater-Doudou Grand Stage (工人剧院/豆豆大舞台); another venue is the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院). The Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, is the city's best-known research centre.
