Xinjiang Medical University (新疆医科大学; Uyghur: شىنجاڭ تىببىي ئۇنىۋېرسىتېت) used to be known as Xinjiang Medical College. The campus is in Ürümqi, the regional capital of Xinjiang (the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region) in China's northwest. The National Ministry of Education ratified its university status in 1998, and the university's name was inscribed by Jiang Zemin.

Medicine is the core of the curriculum, with management and linguistics also given particular weight. The university has 25 specialties at undergraduate level and 17 for academic study at higher levels. More than 50,000 students have studied there. As of 2010 the university enrolled 13,100 students, and 5,405 people worked in teaching positions.
Carp Hill rises behind the campus, which lies in the northeast of Ürümqi and extends over more than 3 million square feet.

Top national leaders were involved in the founding. Mao Zedong, then Chairman, and Zhou Enlai, then Premier, told the Ministry of Health to cooperate with the Soviet Union's foreign ministry on a new medical centre for Dihua, which is the present-day city of Ürümqi. Instructions from Saifuddin Azizi lay behind that decision.

The university was formed by combining two bodies, a traditional Chinese medicine college within Xinjiang and the Xinjiang Medical College. Before that merger, the medical college had been one of the 156 key projects supported by the former Soviet Union under the First Five-Year Plan, and it began taking new students in 1956. In its more than 60 years the university has received visits and interest from national and international leaders, among them Party officials and figures from other provinces and cities across the country.
The university seal dates from 1956 and authenticates official paperwork produced by staff. The administration supervises its use, and the university's constitution governs how it is kept safe.
There are eight colleges in the medical and related fields: Medical, Public Health, Traditional Medicine, Basic Medical Sciences, Pharmacy, Nurses Training, Continuing Education and Vocational.
A seven-year course leads to the degree of Doctor of Medicine (MD).

Every hospital in the region is affiliated with the university, and by 2010 it managed 40 clinical posts spread among these hospitals. The leading affiliated hospital provides clinical teaching and internship places for PhD students, runs a seven-year training programme for postgraduates and supervises international students.

The teaching faculty in 2010 consisted of 1163 professors and assistant professors, and 4290 staff worked in other capacities. The university has set up 400 supervisory posts for doctoral and master's students.

Some buildings on the existing campus date back to the Russian period in late Xinjiang history. The grounds have been totally renewed and modernised, and they now have a library, canteens, hospitals and training centres. The experimental laboratories have modern bioinformation-processing systems and models.

Construction of a new campus was expected to begin in 2020. The first stage consists of two new medical buildings with about 134,838 square metres of floor area, costing 390.5 million yuan ($56.25 million). Overall, the new campus will cover 126.67 hectares and offer 739,000 square metres of floor space. Investment of 4.08 billion yuan is planned, and the site will accommodate about 24,000 teachers and students. These are plans reported at the time, so check the university for progress.

A new library building went up in 1995. It now covers 16,000 m2 and holds more than 1.07 million books, and readers can consult over 1,300 periodicals and journals, in Chinese as well as other languages. The library has introduced six book databases and is connected to the database of Partners Harvard Medical International. The reading area seats over 2,500 and the electronic access area over 350.
Every floor has a central reading area for daily users. Doctoral students have their own thesis areas on the fifth and sixth floors.

The International Education College (新疆医科大学国际教育学院) has recruited international medical students since 1982. As of December 2018 the college had over 700 international students, both undergraduate and postgraduate, with more than 450 faculty members. The college says it recruits from countries including Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Gulf states and some African countries, but you should apply directly through the university and check the official channels, not simply rely on an agent.

A scholarship programme announced by the Chinese government in January 2009 rewards students with strong results in the Pre-Medical programme of the Faculty of Sciences (FSc). Holders spend six years studying clinical medicine taught in Chinese, and within a year of admission they must reach HSK band 3 or above.

The early part of the course, in years one and two, is basic theory. Subjects include chemistry (organic and inorganic), biochemistry, embryology, histology, physiology and anatomy. Clinical teaching starts in year three, and it covers surgery, internal medicine, gynecology, pediatrics, neurology, dermatology, psychiatry and ear, nose and throat (E.N.T.).
In 2012 Li Bin was Party Secretary and Muhammad Yasen was president. Posts like these change, so look up the current officeholders.

Research awards have accumulated since 1998: 58 at provincial and ministerial level. Within the Autonomous Region, the university is among the leading research institutions. No other institution in China has won the "Chinese Medical Academic Award" in four successive years, and among the universities tracked by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, it was at the top.

The university was recognised by the Pakistan Medical & Dental Council as of 22 July 2009, one of seven such institutions in China, and it already had recognition from the Medical Council of India. Check current recognition if you plan to practise in another country.
Several ranking positions are reported, from different years and methods:
It ranks first among medical universities in Xinjiang.
It was 37th among the "Top Chinese Universities in Medicine" in 2011.
In the 2012 China Medical Universities Rankings, an annual list from China University Assessment, it held 49th place.
Webometrics put it 388th in China overall, and 236th among Chinese universities with a score of 20.00; its world rank was 2944 on 24 April 2020.
Much of student life depends on the city, including its weather, transport and attractions. The sections below describe Ürümqi, where the university is located.

No other city in western China is as big as Ürümqi, which also holds a Guinness World Record: it is the world's most distant city from any sea, with the nearest coastline roughly 2,500 kilometres (1,600 miles) off. Karamay and Altay, both in Xinjiang, are in fact even nearer to the Eurasian pole of inaccessibility, but Ürümqi is the closest major city to it. Its administrative area covers 10,989 square kilometres (4,243 sq mi) and its mean elevation is 800 metres (2,600 ft).

A point in the southwestern suburbs (Ürümqi County), at coordinates 43°40′52″N, 87°19′52″E, was declared the "center point of Asia" by local geography experts in 1992. A monument followed in the 1990s, and visitors from the region come to see it.

Deserts surround the city, the Gurbantünggüt to the north and the Taklamakan to the south, but small rivers from the snow-capped Tian Shan water the Ürümqi area. The main Tian Shan range lies south of the city in Ürümqi County, and the Bogda Shan is east of the city in Dabancheng District.

Xinjiang holds 20,000 glaciers, nearly half of China's total. Since the 1950s they have shrunk by between 21 and 27 percent as the climate has warmed. Tianshan Glacier No. 1 (一号冰川) feeds the Ürümqi River. It is the biggest glacier close to any major Chinese city, though it has already broken into two smaller ones.

Because population and the economy are growing, demand for water has passed the natural supply. To ease shortages, the Irtysh–Ürümqi Canal was built in the 2000s. The canal's trunk finishes at "Reservoir 500" ("500"水库), at 44°12′00″N, 87°49′00″E, in the north-eastern outskirts where Midong District meets Fukang City. West of this reservoir a new industrial area was under development in 2009, called Ganquanbao Industrial Park (甘泉堡工业园) or Industrial New City 500 (500工业新城), and it relies on the reservoir for water. Further canals take water on from there across the lower Midong District.

Ürümqi falls between two climate types, humid continental (Köppen Dfa, Trewartha Dcac) and cool semi-arid (Köppen BSk, Trewartha BSac). The gap between summer and winter is very large. July averages 24.2 °C (75.6 °F) in very warm to hot summers, while January averages −12.2 °C (10.0 °F) in frigid winters, and the annual average is 7.8 °C (46.0 °F).

The summer months are slightly wetter than winter ones, yet they are far more likely to be sunny, and humidity is lowest then. December gets the least sunshine (33 percent of possible hours) and September the most (75 percent), and altogether the city sees 2,643 hours of bright sun in a year. Precipitation totals roughly 365 millimetres (14.4 in) annually. The coldest day since 1951 was 27 February 1951 at −41.5 °C (−42.7 °F), and the hottest was 1 August 1973 at 42.1 °C (107.8 °F). Winter clothing needs to be serious.

Ürümqi's air has drawn international criticism. In 2007 the Blacksmith Institute listed Ürümqi among the most polluted places in the world because of air pollution, along with two other Chinese cities, Linfen and Lanzhou. The Toronto Star named it one of the ten worst places to live worldwide the next year, citing sulphurous pollution. Heavy winter haze is very common and often disrupts air traffic. Officials thought that energy-intensive industry and an outdated coal-fired winter heating system were the main causes of the severe winter pollution.

Researchers in Fudan University's Department of Environmental Science and Engineering reported that winter 2007 averages for PM2.5 were twelve times the American standard, while total suspended particles (TSP) were three times the limit in China's National Ambient Air Quality Standard. Sulfur dioxide from industry mixed with local aerosol and with soil dust carried in from outside the city, and the main result was a high concentration of sulfate, a leading cause of the pollution. These are figures from earlier years, so look up current readings before you go.

China keeps a single time zone, which puts far-western Ürümqi's solar time 2 hours 10 minutes behind China Standard Time (CST, UTC+8). Early January sunrise comes at 09:45, with sunset between 18:45 and 19:10. In March and September the sun comes up at about 08:00 and goes down near 19:45, and in June it rises at about 06:25 and stays up until 21:45. Expect late mornings and long summer evenings.

Since the Qing conquest, Ürümqi has been home to several peoples. At first the Manchus were based in Gongning Cheng and the Han in Dihua, and groups such as the Hui and Uyghurs lived in suburban districts. Muslim settlement lay to the south of the walled city of Dihua; the walls are gone, but Muslim residents are still mostly found in that area.

In 1787 a census recorded 114,348 Hui and Han across the prefectures of Zhenxi, which included Barköl and Hami, and Ürümqi. In the city proper, the population was 39,000 in the 1880s and had reached 50,000 early in the 20th century. A 1908 account described the inhabitants as Uyghurs (called Turkis in those days), Chinese, Manchus and a few Mongols, estimating that Uyghurs made up about a quarter.
After the People's Republic was founded, an active programme moved Han people into Xinjiang. By 1960 Ürümqi counted 477,321 Han Chinese and 76,496 Uyghurs.
The 2000 census found 2,081,834 inhabitants, a density of 174.53 per km2 (452.3 per sq. mi.). A 2021 estimate put the population at 4.544 million.

Ürümqi is a major industrial centre for Xinjiang. Together with Karamay and Korla it accounts for 64.5 percent of Xinjiang's industrial output. It is also the region's largest consumer market, with retail sales of consumer goods of ¥41.9 billion in 2008, 26 percent more than in 2007. For 2025 the city reported GDP of CN¥465.8 billion, or US$65.2 billion, and about CN¥112,485 (US$15,748) per person. The Central Government has made Ürümqi a central target of the China Western Development project.

Every year since 1991 the city has staged a trade fair (the Urumqi Foreign Economic Relations and Trade Fair), which became the first China-Eurasia Expo in 2011. It promotes domestic and overseas markets. The 17th edition drew participants from the Ministry of Commerce and from the China Council for Promotion of International Trade.

Among local businesses, Xinjiang Guanghui Industry Investment Group is Xinjiang's largest real-estate enterprise and its strongest private company, with current interests in energy and automobiles. Its headquarters, China CITIC Bank Mansion, rises 229 metres (751 feet) in a business district on North Xinhua Road. That makes it the highest building in Ürümqi and in Xinjiang, and also in Central Asia and northwestern China.

Since 2005 Zhongshan Road (Sun Yat-sen Road, 中山路) has been listed as one of the ten best-known shopping streets in China. It is also where the city buys electronics. Xinjiang's biggest market for computers, phones and gadgets is found here, in complexes such as Baihuacun, Cyber Digital Plaza and Fountain Plaza.

Since the 1990s the urban area has expanded as the economic centre of Xinjiang. Business districts have multiplied around all major districts. The old city lies mainly in the south, but the north began to develop in the late 1980s. The city centre moved north with the completion in 2003 of the new office tower of the Ürümqi Municipal Government, at Nanhu Square (南湖广场) on Nanhu Road. The city has no subway on that scale, so it began building viaducts for the Outer Ring Road (外环路) in 2003, which has made travel considerably easier.

Youhao Road (友好路) and its neighbourhood form the commercial centre for business, shopping and entertainment, and the local firm Youhao Group (友好集团) owns a large share of retail. One of the few prominent stores for luxury merchandise is Maison Mode Ürümqi (乌鲁木齐美美百货), which opened in 2008. In the northern Toutunhe District, the Ürümqi Economic and Technological Development Zone (UETD) leads in steel, machinery manufacturing and biochemistry, among other industrial innovations.
The city's airport is Ürümqi Tianshan International Airport, the biggest in Xinjiang and a hub of China Southern Airlines. It is China's only airport with flights from Afghanistan and Tajikistan.

Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) began in August 2011, backed by 930 million yuan of investment to improve urban traffic. Nine routes are in service now: BRT 1 to 5, BRT 6 and its branch 61, and BRT 7 and its branch 71.

The first part of the Ürümqi Metro opened on 25 October 2018 (the northern section of Line 1), and the southern section opened on 28 June 2019. Line 1 is entirely underground. It links the airport with Santunbei in the centre, with 21 stations along 27.615 km (17.2 mi).
Plans call for seven lines, totalling 211 km (131 mi). The first stage is Lines 1 and 2, with a cost estimate of 31.24 billion yuan.

Ürümqi is the main rail hub of Xinjiang, with two primary stations: the older Ürümqi South (formerly Ürümqi railway station) and Ürümqi railway station, which opened in July 2016. Both are served by the Lanzhou–Xinjiang High Speed Railway, which connects Ürümqi with Lanzhou railway station and has operated since late 2014.

Conventional railways also call at Ürümqi. Two lines, the Lanzhou–Xinjiang (Lanxin) and the Ürümqi–Dzungaria (Wuzhun), end there from the east, and the Northern Xinjiang (Beijiang) and second Ürümqi–Jinghe lines come in from the west. Lanxin and Beijiang are sections of the Trans-Eurasian Continental Railway. That route starts in Rotterdam, enters China at the Alataw Pass on the Kazakhstan border, reaches Ürümqi, and carries on through Lanzhou to Lianyungang.

The city is reached by China National Highways 216, 312 and 314. Roads heading north and west often shut by early October and do not reopen until winter ends; remember this when planning winter travel.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Jilin City, where Jilin Medical University is located.
Jilin City, which is located in central Jilin Province spanning from 125° 40' to 127° 56' E longitude and 42° 31' to 44° 40' N latitude. Neighbouring prefectures are:
Harbin, Heilongjiang (N)
Changchun (W)
Siping (W)
Yanbian (E)
Liaoyuan (S)
Tonghua (S)
Baishan (S)

Jilin City is situated in a hilly area near the Songhua River. There are four famous mountains surrounding Jilin City, which is North Mountain in the west, Long Tan Mountain in the east, Zhuque Mountain in the North, and Turtle Mountain in the south, plus Songhua River, it forms a bagua in the Taiji pattern. North Mountain, called Beishan, is the most famous mountain in Jilin City and is home to several Buddhist Temples. The Qianlong Emperor reportedly visited the mountain.

Jilin City has a four-season, monsoon-influenced, humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa). Winters are long (lasting from November to March), cold, and windy, but dry, due to the influence of the Siberian anticyclone, with a January mean temperature of −15.4 °C (4.3 °F). Spring and autumn are somewhat short transitional periods, with some precipitation, but are usually dry and windy. Summers are hot and humid, with a prevailing southeasterly wind due to the East Asian monsoon; July averages 23.3 °C (73.9 °F). Snow is usually light during the winter, and annual rainfall is heavily concentrated from June to August.

The Jilin chemical plant explosions were a series of explosions which occurred on November 13, 2005, in the No.101 Petrochemical Plant in Jilin City, killing six. The explosion severely polluted the Songhua River, with an estimated 100 tons of pollutants containing benzene and nitrobenzene entering the river. The benzene level recorded was at one point 108 times above national safety levels. This caused downstream major cities, including Harbin, Songyuan and Khabarovsk suspending their water supply for almost one week. Chinese leaders later had to apologize to the Russian government over its handling of the incident as the pollutants finally flowed into the Amur (Heilong) River, the major boundary river between China and Russia.

Jilin was one of the worst-hit regions in China by rain and landslides in the 2010 summer China floods. On July 28, 2010, several thousand barrels, which contained toxic chemicals including trimethylsilyl chloride and hexamethyldisiloxane, about 170 kg of a poisonous substance in each, were washed into the Songhua River by the floods from two chemical plants based in Jilin. There were reports that some barrels exploded on contact with water. By late afternoon on August 1, 6,387 barrels had been retrieved from the river. Officials stated that tests show the water in the river remains safe to drink. Three soldiers of the People's Liberation Army in Jilin drowned after working to remove the barrels and control the flooding. The Dahe Dam in Changshan Township was breached on July 28, spilling 4 million m3 of water, destroying five villages downstream and leaving 40 people dead or missing. Over 100 were dead or missing after floods devastated Jilin prefecture. Workers started repairing fifty-one damaged small reservoirs and fortifying riverbanks in the province after the Songhua River surged to levels twice as high as normal.

Jilin City is a popular destination for tourists to come each winter to view the magnificent rime ice (雾凇; 霧凇) on trees along the banks of the Songhua River, the only river in the region that does not freeze in winter. The rime ice is a natural phenomenon that occurs every year during January and February. It is a result of water vapor rising from the warm Songhua River to meet the cold −20 °C (−4 °F) night air, causing the crystallisation of water vapour on willow branches.

The place was the center for the collection of local products to the imperial court during the Qing dynasty. In 1682, when, according to Ferdinand Verbiest, Wulajie (Ula) was "the most illustrious city of the whole province"—the Kangxi Emperor himself visited the place to enjoy sturgeon fishing. These days, a public school nearby is one of the few schools in the country where some Manchu is taught.

The airport is located about 76 km (47 mi) away from Jilin City and has flights to many cities from the airport. China Southern Airlines also provides some international connections directly from Changchun.

Jilin Medical University is in Jilin, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Jilin.
In ancient times, Jilin was inhabited by the Xianbei, Sushen, the Mohe, Jurchens, and the Wùjí (勿吉). The kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo ruled parts of this area.

The region then fell successively under the domination of the Xiongnu, Xianbei state, Goguryeo, Balhae, Khitan Liao Dynasty, the Jurchen Jin Dynasty, and the Mongol Yuan dynasty. During the Qing dynasty, much of the area was under the control of the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose area of control extended to encompass much of what is Russia's Primorsky Krai today.

After the Primorsky Krai area was ceded to Russia in 1860, the government began to open the area up to Han Chinese migrants, most of whom came from Shandong. By the beginning of the 20th century, Han Chinese had become the dominant ethnic group of the region. In 1932, the area was incorporated into Manchukuo, a puppet state set up by Japan. Changchun (then called Xinjing), capital of Jilin today, was made the capital of Manchukuo. After the defeat of Japan in 1945, the Red Army captured Jilin after Operation August Storm. The region, with the rest of northeastern China, was ceded to the Communists by the Soviet Union. Manchuria was the staging ground from which the communists eventually conquered the rest of China in the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949, Jilin province was smaller, encompassing only the environs of Changchun and Jilin City, and the capital was at Jilin City, while Changchun was a municipality independent from the province. In the 1950s, Jilin was expanded to its present borders. During the Cultural Revolution, Jilin was expanded again to include a part of Inner Mongolia, giving it a border with the independent state of Mongolia, though this was later reversed.

In recent times Jilin has, with the rest of heavy industry-based Northeast China, been facing economic difficulties with privatization. This prompted the central government to undertake a campaign called "Revitalize the Northeast".

Jilin lies in the central part of northeastern China, bordering Russia and North Korea in the east and southeast respectively. Jilin has an area of 190,000 km2 (73,000 sq mi) and a population of 24 million. Its capital is Changchun, which lies 113 km (70 mi) west of Jilin City. Jilin is rich in natural mineral deposits with 136 types of minerals, of which 70 have been extracted. Jilin has an abundance of Traditional Chinese medicine resources, with approximately 27,000 kinds of wild plants and 9,000 kinds of medicinal herbs.
The province is rich in large reserves of oil, gas, coal, iron, nickel, molybdenum, talc, graphite, gypsum, cement rock, gold and silver; its reserves of oil shale are the largest in the country.

Jilin is highest in altitude in the southeast and drops gently towards the northwest. The Changbai Mountains run through its southeastern regions and contains the highest peak of the province, Paektu Mountain at 2,744 m (9,003 ft). Other ranges include the Jilinhada Mountains, Zhang Guangcai Mountains, and Longgang Mountains.

Jilin is drained by the Yalu and Tumen rivers in the extreme southeast (which together form parts of the border between the People's Republic of China and North Korea), by tributaries of the Liao River in the southwest, and by the Songhua and Nen rivers in the north, both eventually flowing into the Amur.

Jilin has a northerly continental monsoon climate, with long, cold winters and short, warm summers. Average January temperatures range from −20 to −14 °C (−4 to 7 °F). Rainfall averages at 350 to 1,000 mm (13.8 to 39.4 in).
Major cities in this province include Changchun, Jilin City, Baishan, Baicheng, Siping, Yanji, Songyuan, Tonghua and Liaoyuan.

In 2025, the nominal GDP of Jilin province totaled RMB 1,497.4 billion (US$209.6 billion). Its GDP has been rising at a double-digit rate since 2003, growing 51 percent from 2003 to 2007. Per capita nominal GDP increased to RMB 64,618 (US$9,046) in 2025. Meanwhile, the incremental value and profit of large enterprises witnessed an increase of 19 percent and 30 percent respectively, compared with 2005 figures.

Jilin's agricultural production is centered upon rice, wheat, maize, and sorghum. Rice is mostly cultivated in the eastern parts, such as Yanbian Prefecture. The Changbai Mountains are an important source of lumber. Sheep herding is an important activity in the western parts, such as Baicheng.

Among its natural resources, Jilin has the largest reserves of shale oil and one of the top five largest mineral reserves in China. Compared to other provinces of China, Jilin has extensive deposits of Kieselguhr, wollastonite, floatstone, and molybdenum.
Industry in Jilin is concentrated on automobiles, train carriages, and iron alloy.
Jilin is one of the most important commodity grain bases in China and ranks 6th in timber production.
Traditionally, Jilin has been known as a major pharmaceutical center, with yields of ginseng and deer antlers among the largest in China, being used extensively in the field of Chinese medicine.

jilin-medical-university.h: Jilin New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone

blocks.x: The zone was founded in 1992 and is in Jilin city, covering 818 km2 (316 sq mi) of planned area with 242 km2 (93 sq mi) established. The leading industries in the zone are new materials, refined chemical products, integration of photoelectron and mechanism, electronics, medicine and bioengineering. A mere 14 km (8.7 mi) from Songhua Lake, the nearest bus and train stations are within 3 km (1.9 mi).

The Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone was founded in May 1998 and is in the northeast of Jilin city. The zone has a total planned area of 28 km2 (11 sq mi). It is 90 km (56 mi) from Changchun, 5 km (3.1 mi) from Jilin Airport, and 8 km (5.0 mi)from Jilin Railway Station.

Major industries include refined chemicals, bioengineering, fine processing of chemical fiber, and farm products. It is divided into four parts: the Chemical Industrial Park, the Food Industrial Park, the Textile Industrial Park, and the Medical Industrial Park. The latter specializes in the development of traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals, mini molecule medicine, bio-pharmaceuticals and health products.

jilin-medical-university.h: State-level ETDZs Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone

blocks.x: In 1993, with the approval of the state, Changchun Economic & Technological Development Zone (CETDZ) became a state-level economic and technological development zone. The total area of CETDZ is 112.72 km2 (43.52 sq mi), of which 30 km2 (12 sq mi) has been set aside for development and use. By the end of 2006, the total fixed assets investment of the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone reached 38.4 billion yuan. There were 1656 registered enterprises in this zone including 179 foreign-funded enterprises. The regional gross product of the zone reached 101.8 billion yuan; industrial output value reached 233.0 billion Yuan; overall financial revenue reached 15.7 billion yuan.

Changchun is also the location of one of the largest factories where CRRC manufactures bullet trains. In November 2016, CRCC Changchun unveiled the first bullet train carriages in the world that would have sleeper berths, and would be capable of running in ultra low temperature environments. Nicknamed Panda, they are capable of running at 250 kmph, operate at −40 degrees Celsius, have Wi-Fi hubs and contain sleeper berths that fold into seats during the day.
State-level HIDZs Changchun High-Tech Industrial Development Area

Changchun High-Tech Industrial Development Area is connected by four roads and one light-rail line to the downtown area. The nearest train station, Changchun Station, is twenty minutes away by light rail. In 2002, Changchun HDA became the first area in Northeast China to qualify for the environmental certification of ISO14001. Its landscaping ratio reaches 38%.
Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone

Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone was approved to be national-level border economic cooperation zone in 1992, with a planning area of 24 km2 (9.3 sq mi). In 2002 and 2001, the Hunchun Export Processing Zone and Hunchun Sino-Russia Trade Zone were set up in it. It has a strategic location at the junction of the borders of China, Russia and Korea. It focuses on the development of sea food processing, electronic product manufacture, bio-pharmaceuticals, textile industry and other industries.
Hunchun Export Processing Zone

The Hunchun Export Processing Zone is in 5 km2 (1.93 sq mi) area is in the Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone. Its planned area is 2.44 km2 (0.94 sq mi). It relies on the same infrastructure and policies as its parent zone.

Jilin is inhabited by Han Chinese, Manchus, Hui, Mongols and Xibe. Most ethnic Koreans live in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture. The Manchu people were once the majority in the area of Jilin, making it part of their historical region. With the adoption of Han culture and the Chinese languages by the Manchu people, the Manchu language is considered a critically endangered language. Koreans comprise about 4% of the population, owing to its proximity to the Korean Peninsula. The majority of the province speaks Mandarin.
Excludes members of the People's Liberation Army in active service.

Jilin is part of Northeast China and shares many similarities in culture to neighbouring regions, such as Errenzhuan and Yangge. Among its music, Jiju, or Jilin Opera, is a form of traditional entertainment that Jilin has innovated over its short migrant history.
The ethnic Koreans of Jilin have a distinct culture, closely tied to Korea.
The majority of the province speaks Mandarin, the official language of China. Closer to the east, many people speak Korean. Some people of Qian Gorlos autonomous county speak Mongolian.

The Goguryeo sites and tombs found in Ji'an, Jilin, including Hwando Mountain City, Gungnae City, and the pyramidal Tomb of the General, have been listed as part of the Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom, a World Heritage Site.
Paektu Mountain, especially Heaven Lake on the border with North Korea, are popular tourist destinations due to their natural scenery.
The Ancient Tombs at Longtou Mountain, including the Mausoleum of Princess Jeonghyo, are royal tombs of Balhae found in Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture.

wuhan-university-of-technology.h: Wuhan University of Technology in brief

blocks.x: Wuhan University of Technology, known as WHUT or WUT (武汉理工大学), is a state-funded research university in Wuhan, the provincial capital of Hubei. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and it is included in the Double First-Class Construction scheme and in Project 211, two national support programmes for leading universities.

The present university came into being in 2000 when three separate institutions were combined. They were Wuhan Automotive Industrial University (武汉汽车工业大学), Wuhan Industrial University (武汉工业大学) and Wuhan Transportation Technology University (武汉交通科技大学). For that reason, WUT is unusually broad for a technical university, with deep roots in building materials, shipping and transport, and the automotive industry.

Some accounts trace the beginnings back to 1898, when Zhang Zhidong, the Huguang governor, asked the Qing court to set up a technical institution in Hubei. The university in its current form was founded on 27 May 2000. Each of the three partners had a long record of its own, summarised below.

This was the largest strand, and it had three starting points: the Zhongnan Construction Engineering College (1952), the Shenyang Building Materials Industry College (1958) and the Beijing Institute of Building Engineering (also 1958). In 1971 the Beijing institute joined with the Wuhan Construction Engineering School to become Hubei Construction Industry College. A national key-university title followed in 1978, together with a new name, Wuhan Institute of Building Materials. The institution took the name Wuhan University of Technology in 1985, passed the national Project 211 evaluation in 1996, and in 1998 moved under the direct management of the Ministry of Education. It remained in that form until the May 2000 merger.

wuhan-university-of-technology.h: Wuhan Transportation University: shipping and water transport

blocks.x: The transport branch began as the National Maritime Vocational School in 1946. It became Wuhan Transportation College in 1949 and, in 1952, Wuhan River Transportation College. By 1957 it was called Wuhan University of Water Transportation Engineering. In 1963 the Ministry of Transportation reorganised its subject areas and merged it with a Wuhan river transportation school. In 1993 the ministry formally gave it the name Wuhan Transportation University, which it kept until the merger of May 2000.

wuhan-university-of-technology.h: Wuhan Automotive Polytechnic University: vehicles and machinery

blocks.x: This branch started from a Wuhan Institute of Technology established in 1958. It was absorbed by Hubei Chemical Engineering College in 1959. Then, in 1961, a union with two further colleges (Hubei Industry College and another Wuhan Institute of Technology) produced an institution that again carried the Wuhan Institute of Technology name. The Cultural Revolution forced a change of name during the following fifteen years, and the original name returned in 1979. The institute grew quickly between 1983 and 1994, became Wuhan Automotive Polytechnic University in 1995, and in 1999 absorbed two vocational schools, one for mechanical industry (Hubei No.1) and one for energy economy. In May 2000 it joined the other two to create WUT.

The university lists 23 academic schools and 9 state key disciplines, offering 74 doctoral, 135 master's and 82 bachelor's programmes. It employs about 5,570 staff. Among them are 650 professors, plus three academicians from each of the two national academies, the Chinese Academy of Engineering and the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Student numbers are given as over 36,000 undergraduates, 16000 postgraduates (master's and PhD together) and 327 international students. These are approximate and change each year, so look at the university's site for the latest totals.
The list below sets out the main teaching units. Engineering clearly dominates, and a few units serve special audiences such as distance learners and international students.

Engineering and technology: Materials Science and Engineering; Automotive Engineering; Transportation; Mechanical and Electronic Engineering; Energy and Power Engineering; Naval Architecture, Ocean and Energy Power Engineering (a single school); Navigation; Logistics Engineering; Civil Engineering and Architecture; Resources and Environmental Engineering.
Information and automation: Information Engineering; Computer Science and Technology; Automation.
Sciences: Chemistry, Chemical Engineering and Life Science; Sciences.
Business, law and the humanities: Management; Economics; Law, Humanities and Sociology; Art and Design; Foreign Languages.

Other units: the Department of Physical Education, the School of On-line and Continuing Education (for distance and adult learners), the School of International Education (the unit set up for international students), the School of Vocational Technology and the Institute of Higher Education. In short, the university is overwhelmingly engineering-led, with business, law, arts and language schools alongside, so prospective international students should check carefully which school teaches their chosen subject.

Research is organised through 27 centres. These include two State Key Laboratories, one State Engineering Laboratory and several provincial or ministerial laboratories, whose fields are information technology, resources and environmental technology, automobiles and mechatronics, logistics and transport, new energy and new materials. Over the past ten years it has won nearly RMB 3 billion in government and industry funding for high-tech research, and it describes many significant technological results from that work.

There is also a university Science Park inside Wuhan·China Optical Valley, covering 58.7 hectares. The park has nurtured more than 6 high-tech firms in fields such as new materials, fibre-optic sensors, high-speed shipping, new energy and advanced manufacturing. In 2010 the park's total revenue reached RMB1.58 billion.

Industry links are formal. WUT partners with 167 large enterprises spread across building materials and construction, transport and the automotive industry. A board for each of those three sectors meets every year to discuss how the university and the sector can develop together.

Several national approvals show where the university's research is recognised. During 2006 and 2007, two national bodies (the foreign experts administration and the education ministry) jointly authorised a base at WUT for discipline innovation and attracting overseas talent, focused on advanced materials and high-speed shipping technology. The science ministry then approved an international joint research centre for advanced materials in 2008. In 2010, WUT's Thermoelectric Materials Research Team became part of the China-US Clean Energy Joint Research Centre.

More than sixty outside universities and institutions have academic links with WUT. Over one hundred well-known foreign scholars serve as concurrent or honorary professors, and the university often hosts visiting experts from other countries and regions. Each year it also sends teachers, professors and researchers abroad for study and conferences, and some have been appointed as guest professors, special professors or lecturers by their hosts. Exchange and research cooperation covers more than 100 universities and institutes overseas, in places such as Russia, the Netherlands, Australia, France, Japan, the UK and the USA, and over 200 scholars of international reputation have been invited as guest or honorary professors.

WUT began admitting foreign students in 1950 and has since awarded bachelor's degrees, master's degrees or further-study certificates to students from more than ten countries. A further partnership links WUT with Wales' University of Wales Trinity Saint David. Which agreements apply to a particular programme differs, so ask the school you are interested in.

WUT stands in the city of Wuhan, the biggest in Central China, often called a "River City". Three main campuses make up the university: Mafangshan (马房山) with its East and West campus communities, Yujiatou, and the newer South Lake campus. The three together cover 267 hectares. The South Lake campus borders the lake and lies on the south bank of the Yangtze. Mafangshan and Yujiatou are both in Wuchang.

A second figure circulates, of 450 acres (1.8 km2) for the total campus area, so reported sizes differ. The university says its buildings have 1,100,000 square metres of floor space, and its three libraries hold 2,720,000 books. Ask the international office for current campus details and for the site where your own programme is taught, because distances between campuses within a large city can mean a long commute.

All three rankings here are dated, and each ranking uses its own method, so see them as snapshots. In 2008, WUT placed 39th in Wu Shulian's university ranking, one of the best-known Chinese league tables, a position that was third among Wuhan's universities, after Wuhan University and Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Times Higher Education's 2013 world rankings had WUT 58th in Asia, 8th in mainland China and in the 301st to 350th band globally. In the first BRICS & Emerging Economies Rankings of 2014, WUT came 28th overall and 9th in China, which made it the best-placed university in Wuhan in that table.
Student life depends on the city around the campus as much as on the campus itself, so here is what you should know about Wuhan.

wuhan-university-of-technology.h: Where Wuhan is and how it is arranged

blocks.x: The city is in east-central Hubei, at latitudes 29° 58' to 31° 22' N and longitudes 113° 41' to 115° 05' E. Geographically it occupies the junction where the Han River flows into the Yangtze, at the east end of the Jianghan Plain on the middle Yangtze.

The urban area has three parts, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, together called the "Three Towns of Wuhan". The name Wuhan combines "Wu" from Wuchang with "Han" from Hankou and Hanyang. The three were joined administratively in 1927. They face one another over the rivers, and bridges tie them together, among them the "First Bridge", one of China's earliest modern bridges.
Wuchang is on the Yangtze's southeast bank; the river keeps it apart from Hankou and Hanyang.
Hankou is on the northern bank of the Yangtze, across from Wuchang, and north of the Han River, which separates it from Hanyang.
Hanyang is west of the Yangtze, across from Wuchang, and south of the Han River, which separates it from Hankou.

The landscape is uncomplicated, low and level in the middle and hilly toward the south, crossed by the Yangtze and the Han. The She River joins the Yangtze in Huangpi District. The city's land area is 8,494.41 square kilometres, equal to 3,279.71 square miles, and most of it is alluvial plain with scattered hills and a huge number of lakes and ponds. One quarter of the urban territory is water, a higher proportion than in any other large Chinese city.

There are nearly 200 lakes. East Lake, at 33 km2, and Tangxun Lake are the largest lakes lying wholly within a Chinese city. South Lake and Sand Lake are also well known, and Liangzi Lake in the southeast of Jiangxia District is the biggest lake by area in Hubei. The twin peaks where Huangpi District meets Xiaogan City, at 872.5 metres, are the highest points in Wuhan. Several hills stand inside the city limits too. Mount Luojia (珞珈山) is in Wuchang District, while Hongshan District contains the hills called Hong (洪山) and Yujia (喻家山/瑜珈山).

Wuhan is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons and plentiful summer rain. Its summers are famously muggy, with dewpoints often at 26 °C (79 °F) or higher. In the past the trio of Chongqing, Nanjing and Wuhan was nicknamed the "Three Furnacelike Cities" of the Yangtze valley, because summers there are so hot. More recent data suggest that Wuhan has dropped out of the top tier, and a newer set of "Four Furnacelike Cities" is named as Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang.

Spring and autumn are mostly mild. Winter is cool, with little rain and the occasional snow. Monthly means go from 4.1 °C in January (39.4 °F) up to 29.3 °C in July (84.7 °F), and the annual mean is 17.4 °C, or 63.3 °F. Rainfall adds up to slightly under 1,320 mm, about 52 inches, and most arrives between April and July. The frost-free period lasts between 211 and 272 days. Sunshine, measured as a share of what is possible, is 30 percent in January and 53 percent in August, and the city proper gets 1,783 hours of bright sun in a year.

At the extremes, the lowest reading ever recorded was −18.1 °C (−1 °F), logged on January 31, 1977, and the hottest official one is 39.7 °C (103 °F), on both July 27, 2017 and August 18, 2022. One unofficial figure of 41.3 °C (106 °F) was noted on August 10, 1934. For students, that means a hot, sticky summer and a cool winter, so plan your clothing and your accommodation heating and cooling accordingly.

Up to the 21st century Wuhan was mostly agricultural. Starting in 2004, Wuhan became a showcase for a national policy called the Rise of Central China Plan, whose purpose is to turn inland economies with lower incomes into centres for advanced manufacturing. Steel has been the backbone of local industry since 1890. In 2010 the automobile sector for the first time produced more output value than Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO). Five vehicle makers operate locally: SAIC-GM, Dongfeng Renault, DFM Passenger Vehicle, Citroën and Dongfeng Honda. The headquarters of Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd are also in Wuhan.

By 2016, investors from over 80 countries had put money into Wuhan, with 5,973 foreign-invested firms and total capital of $22.45 billion USD. Around 50 French companies operate in the city, including Renault and PSA Group. Together they account for more than a third of all French investment in China, and Wuhan attracts more of it than any other Chinese city.

Put simply, Wuhan is a key centre for the economy, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education, which gives graduates a wide local job market. Leading industries include optoelectronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, bioengineering, new materials and environmental protection. Energy-efficiency technology and renewable energy are listed among its emerging industries. In 2021 the Global Financial Centres Index placed Wuhan among the world's top 100 financial centres.
Wuhan's major zones, in order of founding, are described here.

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone, a national-level zone incorporated in 1993. Its present area is about 10–25 square km, with plans to grow to 25–50 square km. Priority sectors cover telecommunications equipment, heavy industry, chemicals, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, vehicle assembly, and the processing of food and drink.

Wuhan Export Processing Zone, set up in 2000 inside the development zone above. It is planned to cover 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile), of which the first 0.7 square kilometre (0.3 square mile) is built.

Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone (East Lake High-Tech Development Zone), a national high-tech zone whose core industries are optoelectronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, with software outsourcing and electronics also supported. It is China's largest production base for optoelectronic products, with firms such as Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable (the country's largest fibre-optic cable maker) and Fiberhome Telecommunications. It is also the centre of China's laser industry, home to HGTECH and Chutian Laser.

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park, inside the East Lake zone and a joint development with Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. It is planned on 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles), with a total of 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet) of floor space. It lies 8.5 km (5.28 mi) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 mi) from Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Wuhan Biolake, an industrial base an industrial base that dates from 2008, located in the East Lake zone of Optics Valley. It extends over 15 km2, or 5.8 square miles, and is divided into six parks: bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical device and medical health. The aim is to bring together research and everyday living.

No city in Central China has more people than Wuhan, and it is among the biggest in the whole country. The Seventh Census of 2020 counted 12,326,500 residents, up 25.97 percent, or 2.5411 million, on the 2010 census. This was the fastest-growing decade since census records began, an average of 2.34 percent a year, and the first time the population passed 10 million. The OECD put the wider metropolitan area at 19 million in 2010.

A 2019 study that used night-time lighting and land cover data to examine urban development found that Wuhan's social and economic activity is highly concentrated compared with the spread of its built-up area.

A survey published in 2017 found that 79.2% of Wuhan's residents are either non-religious or follow worship of gods and ancestors, and 0.9% of them are Taoists. Of the rest, 14.7% are Buddhist, 2.9% Protestant, 0.3% Catholic and 1.6% Muslim, while another 1.6% follow other religions.

China Railway Wuhan Group runs the Wuhan Railway Hub, one of the four key rail hubs in China. Passengers use three big stations: Hankou and Wuchang stations, in the districts of the same names, and Wuhan station, which stands in newly built-up land to the east of East Lake in Hongshan District. The stations are many miles apart, so always check which one your train uses.

Hankou was the end of the Jinghan line from Beijing and Wuchang the end of the Yuehan line to Guangzhou. Since the First Yangtze Bridge connected the lines into the Jingguang railway, both stations handle trains in all directions, unlike cities such as New York or Moscow, where each station serves one direction.

High-speed rail arrived with the Hefei-Wuhan line, opened on April 1, 2009, which gave Wuhan fast links to Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai. A handful of daily trains cover the way to Shanghai in under six hours, and in early 2010 most of them started at Hankou. Work on the new Wuhan station, with 11 platforms on the north-eastern edge of the city, started in 2006, and it opened in December 2009, when China introduced its second high-speed service, from Guangzhou to Wuhan. At 394 km/h (244.82 mph) it was promoted as the world's fastest train, and it reduced the trip between the two cities from 10.5 hours down to only three. Later the line was lengthened toward Beijing. Around 2011, the new station was used mainly by Guangzhou high-speed trains, and conventional services to other cities continued to use Hankou and Wuchang.

A regional network, the Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity railway, is under construction. Its goal is to tie the three main stations to the outer districts and suburbs, and to neighbouring cities (Huanggang, Huangshi, Xianning and Xiaogan). Passengers could ride the first section, toward Xianning, from late 2013. The Xiaogan section started on December 1, 2016, and on November 29, 2019 the Wuhan–Shiyan high-speed railway extended it as far as Shiyan.

Freight is handled at Wuhan North station in Hengdian Subdistrict, Huangpi District, with 112 tracks and more than 650 switches. The yard is 20 km (12 mi) north of Wuhan station, and 23 km (14 mi) from Hankou station.

Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd owns and runs the system. At the last count the network had 11 lines with 282 stations over 435 km (270 mi). It keeps expanding, so those totals will be out of date. Line 1 began running on July 28, 2004, which made Wuhan the seventh mainland city to have rapid transit; it followed Dalian, Changchun, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Tianjin and Beijing. Line 2, which began on December 28, 2012, was the first subway line to cross the Yangtze underground. Crossing the Yangtze and Han rivers had long been a bottleneck, and the metro greatly eased it. With 1.22 billion passengers in 2019, it is the sixth-busiest metro in mainland China. City officials have pledged to open at least two lines or sections every year. During the COVID-19 outbreak the whole network was shut between January 23 and March 27, 2020.
Trams reappeared on the city's streets on July 28, 2017, when the Auto-city T1 line opened. The tram systems that are running, planned or being built are:
Auto-city trams (T1, T2, T6 and T8), serving the Economic Development Area in the far west of Hanyang; only T1 had opened by 2017.
Optics Valley trams, with two lines (T1 and T2) to the south and east of Guanggu Circle in south-east Wuchang, which started on January 18, 2018.
The Old Hankou Streetcar, a loop around Hankou.

In summary, rail, metro, tram, bus and boat all work together here. Buses, including trolleybuses, provide local transport. The trolleybus network has run since 1958, and its first route, route 1, still operates.

Wuhan is a major port hub for central China, which fits a city built around its rivers, and the Port of Wuhan serves both the local population and shipping. Ferries have a long history on the Yangtze: modern steamboat ferries began in 1900, and a train ferry carried rail cars from Hankou to Wuchang from 1937. Numbered stops let passengers get on and off around the city, and there is a tourist ferry at night. Today the Wuhan Ferry Company runs the service and in 2010 bought ten new ships to replace vessels that had been in use for 29 years.
Wuhan University of Technology lists 568 programs for international students on this site: 104 bachelor, 128 master's, 116 doctoral, 220 non-degree programs.

Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 45,000 (median CNY 33,000), according to the university's published fee table.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

wuhan-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Wuhan University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at Wuhan University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Liaoning Petrochemical University (辽宁石油化工大学; pinyin: Liáoníng Shíyóu Huàgōng Dàxué), found in the city of Fushun, Liaoning, China. Because it is run by the provincial government, it is closely tied to the industries of northeast China.

liaoning-petrochemical-university.h: A pioneer in oil and chemical education

blocks.x: The university was founded in 1950 in Dalian, as the first university in the People's Republic dedicated to petroleum and chemical technology. It moved to Fushun in 1953 and has been there since.

More than 60,000 people have graduated, and most of them went on to become managers and core technical staff in China's petroleum sector and related businesses. Thirteen of its people have become academicians, a title given by the Chinese Academy of Science or the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Its engineering programmes are considered comparatively strong nationwide, above all in subjects connected to petroleum. If you want a career in energy or chemicals, this is exactly the kind of university where the specialism matches the local industry.
Your daily experience as a student will be shaped by Fushun: how it earns its living, how you travel in and out, and what there is to see on weekends. The next sections describe the city.

Fushun is a heavily industrial area, and the nickname "the City of Coal" (also "the capital of coal") fits it well. Fuel, electricity and raw materials form its backbone, and textiles and electronics are offering a growing number of jobs.

The best-known landmark of this history is the West Open Mine, one of the largest open-pit coal mines in the world, south of the city. People have dug coal here since the 12th century, and through the 20th century and into the early 21st it was worked as an open pit. By 2015, however, the pit, about 1,000 feet deep and covering 4.2 square miles, had run out of coal and become unstable. Coal output for the whole of Fushun has dropped under 3 million tons, compared with 18.3 million tons in 1962. Besides mining, the city has a major aluminium-reduction plant and factories making cars, machinery, chemicals, cement and rubber.

For a sense of the city's economic weight, Fushun's total GDP in 2009 was 54.27 billion yuan, fourth among Liaoning's 58 cities and counties. Its GDP per capita that year was 40,391 yuan, which put it 21st of the same 58.

The ground here holds timber plus a long list of minerals: marble, gold, copper, iron, titanium, magnesium, marl, oil shale and coal. The leading producer of coal and oil shale is the Fushun Mining Group, whose 2001 coal output of roughly 6 million tons was mostly a mixture of coking coal and steam coal. Its assets also include coalbed methane of about 8.9 billion cubic meters and high-grade oil shale in the ground totalling some 3.5 billion tons, with 920 million tons of that being recoverable.

Local energy comes from hydroelectric and thermal power. Fushun grew by exploiting these abundant minerals and is now a nationally significant heavy industrial base for petroleum, chemicals, metallurgical machinery and building materials. Newer sectors such as electronics, light industry, weaving and spinning are also gaining ground.
Oil from shale has a particular history here:

1928: shale oil began to be produced on a commercial scale when the South Manchurian Railway built the Fushun Coal Mine Temporary Oil Plant (撫順炭礦臨時製油工場; Fǔshùn Tànkuàng Línshí Zhìyóu Gōngchǎng), nicknamed the Western Refinery (西制油; Xī Zhìyóu), which used Fushun-type retorts.
1949: after the Second World War, shale oil output had stopped, but 100 Fushun-type retorts and the related processing units were brought back into use.
1950: 266 retorts were running, each able to produce 100 to 200 t (98 to 197 long tons; 110 to 220 short tons) of shale oil daily.
1954: "Refinery No. 2" came into production.
1959: annual shale oil production peaked at 780,000 t (770,000 long tons; 860,000 short tons).

After 1965 the use of Fushun's oil shale began to fall, because the Da Qing oil field was discovered in the 1960s. Sinopec, which produced shale oil in that era, closed its oil shale operations in the early 1990s. Meanwhile the Fushun Mining Group created its own Fushun Oil Shale Retorting Plant, which began production in 1992. That was also the year when the China National Oil Shale Association was founded, with its base in Fushun. By the close of 2006 the Mining Group was operating the world's largest shale oil plant: seven retorting units, each with 20 retorts, so 140 Fushun-type retorts in total.
Fushun also has two oil refineries, and a PetroChina subsidiary, Fushun Petrochemical Company, is constructing a new refining and petrochemical complex within the city.

Shenyang Taoxian airport is 40 km (25 mi) from Fushun, which makes arrival simple for international students. The city is joined to Shenyang and to Jilin Province by both rail and road. Two seaports are within reach as well, Dalian at 400 km (250 mi) and Yingkou at 200 km (120 mi), each with good rail and highway connections.

Of the local higher education institutions, the Liaoning University of Petroleum and Chemical Technology ranks highest, 123rd across China. For secondary education, the main names are Fushun No.1 High School and Fushun No.2 High School.

One neighbourhood school gives a snapshot of local education. The No. 44 middle school stands on the second street in Xin Fu District, near Fushun's central business district, with convenient transport, and all its pupils come from the surrounding community. The falling population has reduced numbers: there were over 1,000 students in the 1990s and now there are about 200. Even so, the school has kept up its quality, with a modern building, advanced learning facilities, an indoor gymnasium, large dance and instrument rooms and a synthetic running track in the play yard. Its teaching facilities and equipment have been renewed, and it is a fair example of modern middle-school education in one of China's third-line cities.

The countryside around Fushun has high mountains and thick forest. Around 55 km (34 mi) from downtown lies Houshi National Forest Park, which the central government grades as an AAAA tourist attraction. Another draw is the Saer Hu Scenic Area, which spreads over about 268 km2 (103 sq mi); within it is Dahuofang Reservoir, 110 km2 (42 sq mi) in size and the largest artificial lake in northeast China.

There is plenty of history too. Fushun has applied for two UNESCO World Heritage sites, which should bring more visitors. The first is Xingjing City, where the Qing Dynasty began; it stands within modern Fushun and served as the Late Jin dynasty's initial capital in 1616. The other contains the Yongling tombs, where several royal household members are buried.
Closer to our own time:
Lei Feng, the soldier celebrated across China, was stationed in Fushun and died here. A memorial museum about his life, in Wang Hua District, is a popular stop.
Puyi, the last emperor, was held in Fushun after the end of the Second World War. The Fushun War Criminal Prison became a museum in 1986.

The Pingdingshan Tragedy Memorial Hall Ruins recall the 1931 massacre of Chinese civilians by Japanese forces. Rebuilt and enlarged in 2007, the site includes a pit holding about 800 bodies, mostly infants, adults and elderly victims.
The Ring of Life, opened in 2013, is a circular tower about 157 meters (515 feet) high with an observation deck over the city. It cost over $15 million and is covered in 12,000 LED lights.

Liaoning FC of the Chinese Super League football competition was once based in Fushun at Leifeng Stadium. It could not afford the rent, so it relocated to Beijing and now plays at Chaolai Soccer Base.
A province is the backdrop to student life as much as any campus. Liaoning has a long and layered history, and understanding it helps explain why the northeast looks the way it does.

From the 4th century BC to the 9th century, Liaoning was mostly settled and governed by Han Chinese regimes. Before the 3rd century BC the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived here, and the state of Yan took the area around 300 BC. Yan organised the region into two commanderies. Liaodong meant the land east of the Liao River, and Liaoxi the land to its west. The Yan city of Xiangping, centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today.

When the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family kept up a semi-independent state around Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. This state, also called Yan, sent out many maritime diplomatic and trading missions and left a lasting mark on Northeast Asian culture despite its short life. After the Western Jin dynasty ended, the Murong tribe of the Xianbei ruled Liaoning through three states: Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan. In 436 Northern Wei captured the Yan capital, and Goguryeo took over the Liaodong Peninsula. The Tang dynasty later annexed the region in the Goguryeo-Tang War.

liaoning-petrochemical-university.h: A meeting point of many peoples

blocks.x: In the middle of the 8th century the An Lushan Rebellion drained Tang resources from its borders, and the Bohai gradually moved into Liaodong. The Khitan Liao dynasty eventually conquered Liaoning and split it into four circuits: Eastern Capital (Dongjingdao), Supreme Capital (Shangjingdao), Central Capital (Zhongjingdao) and Lower Capital (Xiajingdao).

The Jurchen Jin dynasty put most of the land into its Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu). What was left went to three other routes: Xianping, Supreme Capital (Shangjinglu) and Northern Capital (Beijinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it later joined the Yuan dynasty. The Yuan administration was intricate. In the east, the Liaoyang and Shenyang routes sat within the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. Xianping Prefecture in the north belonged to the Kaiyuan Route. The western Guangning Route also reported to Liaoyang, whereas Jinzhou and Chaoyang formed part of the Daning Route, which answered directly to the Central Secretariat.

The Ming took control of Liaoning in 1371, three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. Around 1442 they built a defensive wall to shield the province's farmland against a possible threat from the Jurchen-Mongol Oriyanghan, a Ming tributary, to the northwest. In 1467 and 1468 they extended it to cover the northeast against raids by the Jianzhou Jurchens, who would later be called the Manchu. This "Liaodong Wall" had the same purpose as the Great Wall of China but was built more cheaply: stone and tile were used in places, but most of it was just an earth bank with a moat on each side.

The wall did not hold. Early in the 17th century, long before the remainder of China fell to them, the Jurchens took Liaodong, meaning eastern Liaoning. Their dynasty, first styled Later Jin and renamed Qing later, set its capital at Xingjing (兴京) from 1616 to 1621. Xingjing lay outside the Liaodong Wall in the east of modern Liaoning. It next shifted to Dongjing, just east of modern Liaoyang, and in 1625 settled at Shengjing, the city we now call Shenyang. After the Qing took Beijing in 1644 and the main capital moved there, Shengjing stayed an important regional capital for most of the Qing era.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning much of its population. Many local people died in the fighting or escaped to the south side of the Great Wall, and the withdrawing Ming troops razed numerous cities. Zhang Shangxian, Civil Governor (Fuyin) of Fengtian Province, reported as late as 1661 that, apart from Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city east of the Liao River was abandoned or had only a few hundred inhabitants. As he put it, "Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants". Across the river to the west, only three places kept sizeable populations: Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning.

In the second half of the 17th century, beginning with laws in 1651 and 1653, the Qing authorities invited people from the area below the Great Wall, especially Shandong, to settle the sparsely populated Fengtian Province, which roughly matches today's Liaoning. Many present-day Liaoning families trace their roots to those settlers. Officially, though, the remaining Northeast was off limits to Han Chinese through most of Manchu rule. A barrier called the Willow Palisade (c. 1638 to c. 1672) was built to stop them entering today's Jilin, Heilongjiang and nearby Inner Mongolia. It ringed Fengtian's agricultural core, in most places following a line a little beyond the earlier Ming wall, or simply reusing that wall, and separated the farms from Manchu forests in the northeast and from Mongol pastures to the northwest.

Later, the Qing government tried to stop people moving into Fengtian, to send some settlers home, or else to legalise them. An edict of 1704, for example, noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave. It told them to register and join a local defence group (保, bao) or return to their places of origin within ten years. Ten years later another edict appeared, repeating that something had to be done about illegal migrants. The policy never worked as officials in Beijing hoped, and the population of Fengtian still doubled from 1683 to 1734.

Under the Qing, Manchuria was ruled by three generals, most of modern Liaoning fell to the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn). From 1860 the Manchu government started to let people resettle the region again, and Han Chinese soon became its dominant ethnic group.

Fengtian Province was created in the area of today's Liaoning in the 20th century. Liaoning was the scene of many key fights in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905, including Port Arthur and Mukden. The Battle of Mukden was then the biggest land battle in history. In the Warlord Era the Fengtian clique, led by Zhang Zuolin and then his son Zhang Xueliang, controlled Liaoning. The province got its current name on 29 January 1929, and the Zhongdong Railway Incident followed later that year. Japan invaded in 1931 and the region fell under the Japanese-controlled puppet state of Manchukuo. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the first major battles of the Chinese Civil War (the Liaoshen Campaign) took place in and around Liaoning.

When the People's Republic was founded in 1949, there was no Liaoning. Instead the area was divided into Liaodong and Liaoxi provinces plus five municipalities: Shenyang, Lüda (now Dalian), Anshan, Fushun and Benxi. In 1954 they were combined as Liaoning, and in 1955 some territory of the former Rehe province was added. Part of Inner Mongolia was also attached during the Cultural Revolution, but later returned.

Liaoning was one of China's first provinces to industrialise, first under Japanese occupation and then much more in the 1950s and 1960s. Take Anshan, which hosts one of China's largest iron and steel complexes. More recently, that head start in heavy industry has become a weakness, as many large state-owned enterprises have struggled. Because of the particular difficulties in Liaoning and other Northeast provinces with a heavy-industry heritage, the central government launched a "Revitalize the Northeast" campaign.
Think of Liaoning as three bands running across the map, from highland in the west through a plain in the middle to hills in the east.

West: low hills cover the region, and the Nulu'erhu Mountains broadly track the Inner Mongolian border. A thin coastal strip, the Liaoxi Corridor, connects the Liao River Basin with the North China Plain and finishes at the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass.
Centre: a basin drained by the Liao, the Daliao and their tributaries, mostly flat and low.
East: the Changbai and Qianshan ranges, which push on into the sea and create the Liaodong Peninsula. The province's highest point, Mount Huabozi (1,336 m), is in this zone.
Liaoning has a continental monsoon climate. Annual rainfall averages about 440 to 1,130 mm, with rainy summers and dry weather in the other seasons.
Besides Fushun, the main cities of the province are:
Shenyang
Dalian
Anshan
Liaoyang
Dandong
Jinzhou
Yingkou

The main agricultural products are maize, sorghum and soybeans, and cotton is grown too. Dalian's surroundings account for three-quarters of the apples and peaches China exports. Local specialities by place: Dalian and Yingkou for apples, Dalian again for golden peaches, Beizhen (Jinzhou) for pears, Huludao and Suizhong for white pears, and Gushan (Dandong) for apricots and plums.

Anhui Agricultural University (AHAU, 安徽农业大学) is a public university in Hefei, the capital of Anhui. It belongs to the provincial government, and sponsorship is shared with two national bodies, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs and the National Forestry and Grassland Administration, so the Anhui Provincial People's Government is not the only backer. Its main focus is agriculture and forestry.

anhui-agricultural-university.h: A timeline of moves and mergers

blocks.x: The story begins in Anqing, where Anhui University was founded in 1928. A college of agriculture was set up inside it in 1935, and that is where the agricultural side of today's university started. The wider university relocated from Anqing to Wuhu in December 1949, and then went through three adjustments between July 1950 and the summer of 1953, or in July 1950, July 1952, September 1952 and summer 1953. After those changes the university was left with agriculture and forestry as its professional fields, plus two normal-school specialties.

The agricultural college left Anhui University in February 1954 and became the independent Anhui Agricultural College, and that April it moved to Hefei. In December 1968 the college was moved to rural education and divided over three sites, namely the Zilu lake purple campus at Suxian, a campus in Chuxian and another in Fengyang. It admitted its first group of worker-peasant-soldier students in 1970, and between 1970 and 1977 a total of 2,731 peasant and soldier students enrolled. The college returned to Hefei in October 1978, and in 1995 it was renamed Anhui Agricultural University, the name it bears today.
Teaching is split between seventeen schools. They run in reverse of the university's own listing below:
