On the academic side, one national key discipline is currently in progress, and 19 provincial key disciplines exist.

Its labs are one state key laboratory, 37 provincial key laboratories, one national engineering laboratory and one international joint laboratory. Beyond those, there are a provincial key think tank, a provincial research institute of industrial technology and two provincial '2011' collaborative innovation centers.

anhui-agricultural-university.h: Hefei, the city around the campus

blocks.x: The city that surrounds a campus influences daily life as strongly as the university does: the weather, the transport and the entertainment all come with it. Here is Hefei.

Hefei is in south-central Anhui, 130 kilometres, or 81 mi, west of Nanjing. Chao Lake, one of the largest freshwater lakes in China, lies 15 km, or 9 mi, to the south-east. In recent decades nitrogen and phosphorus have polluted it, but both the government and local people are working on it, and the situation is getting better.

The climate of Hefei is humid subtropical, Cfa in the Köppen system, and the four seasons are clearly defined. The annual mean temperature is 16.6 °C, or 61.9 °F, and rainfall just exceeds 1,000 millimetres, or 39 in, a year, with the heaviest falls between May and August.

Winters are damp and cold. January nights fall just under freezing and the month averages 2.8 °C, or 37.0 °F. Snow comes irregularly and is rarely heavy, but cold spells from Siberia can arrive in the winter months, December to February, and sometimes in November and March too, bringing snow and heavier falls. Spring is generally pleasant, if somewhat unpredictable.

Summers are hot and humid, and July averages 28.6 °C, or 83.5 °F. From June through August, and often into September, daily temperatures can reach or pass 37 °C, or 99 °F, and high humidity is normal. Autumn brings a gradual cooling and drying. March is the dullest month, with 35 percent of possible sunshine, and August the brightest at 50 percent, and annual bright sunshine totals around 1,868 hours. The lowest temperature recorded since 1951 was −20.6 °C, or −5 °F, on 6 January 1955, and the highest was 41.1 °C, or 106 °F, on 27 July 2017.
May and June are usually the worst months for the air. The cause is farmers outside the city who burn off their fields to prepare for the next crop, and the resulting smoke covers the city in smog.

Hefei's GDP was CN¥1,141.28 billion in 2021, equal to ¥121,187 per person, or US$18,784, a level in the top 20 among Chinese cities. By 2023 GDP had climbed to CN¥1,267.38 billion, and in 2025 the city built 1.37 million electric vehicles, nearly a twelfth of China's total.
The municipal government takes an active part in business, through investment and through state-owned enterprises. This approach has encouraged growth and reshaped the economic base.

The best-known deal dates from 2008, when the local government paid US$3.5 billion to take a controlling stake in BOE Technology (Jingdongfang). BOE has grown into a leading world maker of semiconductor products for telecommunications, and no company produces more liquid crystal displays, flexible displays or organic light-emitting diodes. It had three production lines in Hefei as of at least 2024, and its presence has helped attract other electronics supply-chain businesses, making Hefei one of China's main optoelectronic centres.
Also in 2008, Hefei put substantial money into iFlytek, a voice-recognition company that grew out of USTC.

Later the local government backed NIO heavily, with the aim of combining it with Hefei Changan Automobile, an established firm dating from the Third Front construction. In 2020, when NIO was close to bankruptcy, Hefei acquired a 25% share for RMB 7 billion. NIO shifted its headquarters to Hefei, and the government helped it get bank loans from local banks to enlarge its supply chains. By 2022 it had become the most successful electric vehicle maker in China. The government has also put money in ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's biggest DRAM maker and the fourth largest in the world.

Two outside assessments are worth noting. In November 2010 the Economist Intelligence Unit's Access China White Paper placed Hefei among the CHAMPS, six cities (Shenyang, Pingdingshan, Ma'anshan, Anshan, Hefei and Chongqing) chosen from its list of China's top 20 emerging cities. A little over two years later, in December 2012, The Economist ranked it first in the world for metropolitan economic growth.
The city has backed its chip industry as well, and it is now one of the largest centres for making memory chips (DRAM).

Hefei became the provincial capital in 1945; before that the capital was Lihuang, which is now Jinzhai. It is naturally a transport centre. Its position suits it for that role: north of Chao Lake, on a low saddle over the north-eastern extension of the Dabie Mountains, which separate the Huai and Yangtze river systems. Water transport is easy too, as boats can cross the lake and reach the Yangtze across from Wuhu.

Two main stations serve the city. Hefei South railway station (Hefeinan station, 合肥火车南站) is the newest, and the one that most high-speed trains pass through. The older and smaller Hefei railway station (合肥火车站) is the alternative.

Several small stations link commuters from nearby towns with the main city: Feidong (肥东火车站), Feixi (肥西火车站), Shuijiahu (水家湖火车站), Chaohu (巢湖火车站), Chaohu East (Chaohudong; 巢湖火车东站), Hefeibeicheng (Hefei Northtown; 合肥北城火车站) and Lujiang (庐江火车站), among others.

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport replaced Hefei Luogang International Airport, starting service at midnight on 30 May 2013. This new domestic hub is in Gaoliu Village, in the north-west of the city. The first plane to land was a China Eastern Airlines flight, MU5172, from Beijing Capital International Airport, and the first to leave was China Eastern's MU5468, bound for Shanghai Pudong International Airport.

Scheduled passenger flights go to China's major airports and a number of foreign cities. In Greater China and nearby: Hong Kong, Macao, Singapore, Taipei (Taoyuan and Songshan airports), Kaohsiung and Taichung. In Korea: Seoul, Cheongju, Yangyang and Jeju. In Japan: Osaka, Nagoya, Shizuoka and Okayama. Further afield: Frankfurt, Siem Reap, Bangkok, and the resort islands of Boracay, Bali, Phuket and Krabi.

Hefei Metro is a rapid transit rail network still under construction that will eventually serve both urban and rural parts of Hefei. Line 1, planned at 24 kilometres, or 15 miles, starts from Hefei Railway Station and opened in December 2016.

Construction of Line 2 began in February 2013. Line 2 is being laid along Changjiang Xi Road, Changjiang Zhong Road and Changjiang Dong Road, which together are a big east-west passenger corridor. It goes through the city centre and meets a transfer point where a shuttle bus runs to Hefei Xinqiao International Airport. Line 2 opened on 26 December 2017.

Line 3 construction started in November 2015, and the line opened on 26 December 2019, and serves the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone and the Economic Technology Development District, running from the vocational education town on to the university town. Work on Line 4 began in 2016 and it opened on 26 December 2021, linking the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone with the High Technology Development District. Line 5 started in 2017; its south part opened on 26 December 2020, connecting Binhu New District with the Beicheng (North city) New District, while the northern part was expected for the end of 2022.

Beyond Lines 1 to 5, the plan includes 12 more metro lines, three tram lines and four intra-metropolitan rail lines, which would go to Lu'an, Huainan, Lujiang and Chaohu, with 2030 as the hoped-for completion date.
The city has an extensive public bus system with eight bus rapid transit lines. A few commuter lines run only at set times or at long intervals.
A province shapes student life nearly as much as the campus does, so here is a brief look at Anhui.

anhui-agricultural-university.h: From the Neolithic to the present

blocks.x: Anhui as a province was created in 1667, under the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty. Its nickname 'Wan' comes from a small state that existed here in the Spring and Autumn period (722-481 BC), and also matches Mount Tianzhu and the Wan state. People lived here as long as 20,000 years ago, as archaeological finds in Fanchang County linked to the Yangshao and Longshan cultural domains of the Neolithic period (8000-2000 BC). A site in Guzhen County, the 4500-year-old Nanchengzi Ruins, was excavated in 2013; archaeologists found a Neolithic wall and moat belonging to a far larger and well-integrated city.

Many historical sites in the province date from before the imperial era. Culturally the province was three regions. The north shared the world of the North China Plain with present-day Henan, southern Shandong and northern Jiangsu. The centre, on the fertile Huai River watershed, had a dense population. The south looked towards Jiangxi and southern Jiangsu, and the hills of the south-east formed a distinctive sphere of their own. When the Qin dynasty united China in 221 BC, the lands were split among several prefectures, including Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang and Sishui; during the Han (202 BC - 220 AD) they were part of the Yang, Yu and Xu prefectures. During the Three Kingdoms era (222-280) Eastern Wu and Cao Wei each dominated it at times. By the Song dynasty (960-1279) economy and culture were thriving. Under the Yuan (1271-1368) Anhui became part of Henan province, and in the Ming period the imperial capital at Nanjing governed it directly.

Under the Qing (1644-1912), Anhui and Jiangsu formed a single province until 1666, in the reign of the Kangxi Emperor. Late in the Qing, the province took a leading role in the Self-Strengthening Movement of Li Hongzhang, when Western weapons, factories and ideas about government came into China. Fifty years on, it was among the most radical and liberal parts of the country, and key figures of the 20th century settled there, including Chen Duxiu, who founded the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and the poet and diplomat Hu Shih.

Disaster struck in 1938. Hoping to hold up the advancing Imperial Japanese Army and keep it from Zhengzhou, President Chiang Kai-shek ordered the demolition of an important dam on the Yellow River, and large parts of northern and central Anhui suffered severe damage. In just ten days, water and sand flooded the whole north and centre of the province; between 500,000 and 900,000 Chinese people died, as did an unknown number of Japanese soldiers. When the Second Sino-Japanese War ended in 1945, the provincial capital was moved to Hefei, at that point a small town, and large sums were invested in building it up. After 1949, projects were launched to repair wartime damage. Anhui was one of the provinces worst hit by the Great Chinese Famine, and it also developed considerably through the Third Front campaign, which built basic and national defence industries in protected locations in case of invasion by the Soviet Union or United States. At the heart of the Shanghai Small Third Front stood a 'rear base' in Anhui, which was described as 'a multi-function manufacturing base for anti-aircraft and anti-tank weaponry'. Growth was rapid from the late 1990s, and Anhui today sits within the China Yangtze River Delta Economic Area, the most developed zone in the country.

The province has a varied landscape. The north belongs to the North China Plain and the north-central part to the Huai River watershed; both are flat and densely populated. Going south, the land grows more uneven, with the Dabie Mountains filling much of the south-west and several hill ranges crossing the south-east, and the Yangtze flowing between them. Lotus Peak, in the Huangshan range of the south-east, is the highest point at 1,873 metres (6,145 feet).

Major rivers are the Huai in the north and the Yangtze in the south. Lake Chaohu, at the centre of the province, is the largest lake, with an area of about 800 km2, or 310 sq mi, and the south-east near the Yangtze has many more lakes.

The weather varies from north to south as well. The north has a more temperate climate with sharper seasonal contrast. In January the mean temperature is roughly −1 to 2 °C above the Huai River and 0 to 3 °C below it, while July averages 27 °C or higher. Plum rains in June and July may bring flooding. Anhui has 16 cities, and the top three economically are Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing.

Farming follows the climate zones: wheat and sweet potatoes north of the Huai River, and rice and wheat to the south. Anhui's nominal GDP for 2022 came to US$670 billion (CN¥ 4.51 trillion), which was about 3.72% of national GDP and placed it tenth among provincial-level units. By sector, primary industry was worth CN¥351.37 billion, or US$52.24 billion, secondary industry CN¥1.8588 trillion, or US$276.36 billion, and tertiary industry CN¥2.29433 trillion, or US$341.1 billion. Per head, nominal GDP of US$10,943 (CN¥73,603) put it fourteenth nationally.

Natural resources include iron at Ma'anshan, coal at Huainan and copper at Tongling, with industries linked to them, such as steel at Ma'anshan. One famous Anhui company is the automaker Chery, based in Wuhu.

Next to its wealthier eastern neighbours, Zhejiang and Jiangsu, Anhui has clearly fallen behind: in 2017 its GDP per capita was about half theirs, an improvement on one third in 2010. Note, however, that provincial GDP per capita is calculated from the population registered in the province (those with a local Hukou), who do not necessarily live there. The disparity within the province is large, with most wealth concentrated in industrial areas near the Yangtze such as Hefei, Wuhu and Ma'anshan. Household appliance makers cluster here in large numbers, among them Meling, Royalstar, Gree, Whirlpool, Hisense and Haier.
The Hefei Economic and Technological Development Zone, established in 1993, is in the south-west of Hefei, close to Hefei Luogang International Airport.

The Hefei Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone was founded in October 1990 and received State Council approval as a state-level zone in March 1991. Later milestones are 1997, when it was ratified as an APEC Science and Technology Industrial Park with special open policies towards APEC and EU members; 2000, when it became a National High Tech Export Base; and 2003, when the Torch Program honoured it as an Advanced High Tech Zone. By now over 100 hi-tech enterprises have moved in. The sectors it welcomes are telecommunications, medical equipment, instruments and industrial equipment, electronics assembly and manufacturing, and chemical production and processing.
The Wuhu Export Processing Zone was approved as a national-level export processing zone, with a planned total area of 2.95 km2, or 1.14 sq mi.

Anhui Medical University (AHMU; Chinese: 安徽医科大学) is a provincial public medical university in Hefei, Anhui, China. It is affiliated with the Anhui Provincial Government, and co-sponsored by the Anhui Provincial Government, the Ministry of Education, and the National Health Commission.

There are 16,673 students at the university, of whom 179 are enrolled in doctoral programs, 2,728 in master's programs, and 8,867 in undergraduate programs, plus 95 international students (including those from Hong Kong and Macao) and 7,187 students enrolled in the School of Extended Education.

The predecessor of Anhui Medical University was Dongnan Medical College, established in 1926 in Shanghai. Moved first to Huaiyuan County, Anhui Province, at the end of 1949, and then to Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, in 1952, Dongnan Medical College changed its name to Anhui Medical College.
In June 1996, approved by the National Committee on Education, Anhui Medical College was renamed Anhui Medical University.

The university has 24 directly affiliated teaching units and ten affiliated hospitals, plus 42 clinical schools and 37 teaching hospitals. Other professional practicing and teaching bases connected to the university are over 100. The university at present offers 29 undergraduate programs and options.

Regarding advanced studies, the university has eight doctoral programs, five first-rate-discipline master's programs, 64 master's programs, and five professional degree programs. The university was authorized to offer an MD degree in clinical medicine and a professional degree in stomatology at master's level. The two degrees, especially that of MD, symbolize a major breakthrough in the advanced professional education in Anhui Province, making it possible for the university to cover in its curricula the full-range professional education at undergraduate, master's, and doctoral levels.

Three post-doctoral programs have been set up in pharmacy, clinical medicine, and public health and preventive medicine. The university owns one national key academic discipline and 22 provincial key academic disciplines, as well as 27 provincial key clinical-medicine disciplines and priorly-supported disciplines. It also owns two key laboratories of the Ministry of Education co-established by Anhui Province and the Ministry of Education, 13 laboratories co-established by the central (the Ministry of Finance) and local authorities, and 19 key laboratories (technological and engineering centers, and public scientific service facilities) at provincial level or above.

Besides, Anhui Medical University is the national base for the study of clinical medicines and chemical reagents. Two courses have been ranked among the National Elite Courses, and two programs approved nationally as the featured ones among the institutions of higher learning.

The university typically has won a national second prize for teaching. Two faculty members of the university hold the directorships on the Committee of Dermatology and Venereology of Chinese Medical Society and on the Committee of Clinical Pharmacology of Chinese Pharmacological Society. Four faculty members have been elected to the international and national status of the project "International-, National-, and Provincial-level Talent." Two faculty members have been specified by the Ministry of Education as "Teaching Cadre" title holders. Five faculty members have been designated by the Ministry of Health as "Young and/or Middle-aged Experts with Spectacular Contributions." Two faculty members hold the title of "Wanjiang Scholar", a specially appointed professorship. Five faculty members have been singled out as experts on the Advisory Board of College-level Medical and Pharmaceutical Disciplines of the Ministry of Education.

Again, Anhui Medical university has launched the organization of "Overseas Legion" for an extensive highest-level talent attraction, specifically, for those from abroad, as indicated by the name of the organization. Its library is the provincial Center Library in Anhui Province, which shares biological and medical literature nationwide via cyber-space or internet.

The university is the owner of 46 research institutes at provincial and university levels. Fifteen national-level learned journals are published and issued nationwide. In the recent five years, the university has taken on a total of 209 scientific research programs, among which are such renowned ones as "863" and "973" Projects, Projects Supported by National Science and Technology, and National Natural Sciences Foundation Project.

The university has won 76 provincial prizes in scientific research and, in 2005 and 2006 consecutively, won the first prizes of Chinese Medical Science and Technology. In 2007, the university won each one of the second prizes of National Science Progress and the first prizes of College-level Science and Technology of the Ministry of Education.

Substantial exchange has been fostered between the university and colleges or universities in Hong Kong and Macao, and other countries. Exchange programs of scholars, students, and technical information have been established for collaboration in scientific research.

The total campus covers an area of 860000 square meters and floor space of about 700 thousand square meters. You can walk through the whole campus in 20 minutes. Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Hefei, where Anhui Medical University is located.

Hefei is located 130 kilometres (81 mi) west of Nanjing in south-central Anhui. Chao Lake, a lake 15 km (9 mi) southeast of the city, is one of the largest fresh water lakes in China. Though the lake has unfortunately been polluted with nitrogen and phosphorus in recent decades, the situation is improving due to efforts by both the government and the people.

Hefei features a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons. Hefei's annual average temperature is 16.6 °C (61.9 °F). Its annual precipitation is just slightly over 1,000 millimetres (39 in), being heavier from May through August. Winters are damp and cold, with January lows dipping just below freezing and January averaging 2.8 °C (37.0 °F). The city sees irregular snowfalls that rarely turn significant. Occasional cold spells from Siberia that usually happen during winter months such as December, January, February. Sometimes November and March which can bring snow and heavier snowfall. (Springs are generally relatively pleasant if somewhat erratic. Summers are hot and humid, with a July average of 28.6 °C (83.5 °F). In the months of June, July, August, and often September, daily temperatures can reach or surpass 37 °C (99 °F) with high humidity levels being the norm. Autumn in Hefei sees a gradual cooling and drying. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 35 percent in March to 50 percent in August, the city receives 1,868 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −20.6 °C (−5 °F) on 6 January 1955, to 41.1 °C (106 °F) on 27 July 2017.

Air quality typically diminishes in May and June when the city is blanketed by smog caused by the smoke generated as farmers outside the city burn their fields in preparation for planting the next crop.
As of 2021, the GDP of Hefei is CN¥1,141.28 billion. The GDP per capita of the city is ¥121,187 (US$18,784), ranking within the top 20 of cities in China.
As of 2023, the GDP of Hefei is CN¥1,267.38 billion.
In 2025, Hefei produced 1.37 million electric vehicles, equivalent to nearly one in every 12 electric vehicles made in China.
Hefei's city government is highly engaged in business, both through state-owned enterprises and investment. This approach has helped drive economic growth and re-structure the cities economic base.

In 2008, the local government spent US$3.5 billion for a controlling ownership stake in BOE Technology (Jingdongfang). BOE Technology subsequently grew to be one of the world's leading manufacturers of semiconductor products for telecommunications. It is also the world's largest manufacturer of liquid crystal displays, organic light-emitting diodes, and flexible displays. As of at least 2024, BOE has three production lines in Hefei, and its presence has helped Hefei attract further business in the electronics supply chain and contributed to Hefei's development as one of the main centers for the optoelectronic industry in China.
In 2008, Hefei invested heavily in iFlytek, a voice-recognition technology firm spun off from USTC.

The local government invested heavily in NIO in order to integrate it with Hefei Changan Automobile, a legacy enterprise from the Third Front construction. NIO was on the brink of bankruptcy in 2020 when Hefei obtained a 25% stake in the company in exchange for RMB 7 billion. NIO moved its headquarters to Hefei, where the government helped it obtain loans from local banks to expand its supply chains. As of 2022, NIO is China's most successful electric vehicle manufacturer. The local government has also invested in the ChangXin Memory Technologies, which is China's largest and the world's fourth-largest DRAM maker.

Hefei has been identified by the Economist Intelligence Unit in the November 2010 Access China White Paper as a member of the CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Ma'anshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), an economic profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China.
Hefei was identified by The Economist in December 2012 as the world's No.1 fastest growing metropolitan economy.
Hefei has supported the growth of the chip industry in the city and has become one of the biggest sites for the manufacture of memory chips (DRAM).

Hefei has been the provincial capital since 1945 (before it was Lihuang, which is today's Jinzhai) and is a natural center of transportation, being situated to the north of Chao Lake and standing on a low saddle crossing the northeastern extension of the Dabie Mountains, which form the divide between the Huai and Yangtze rivers. From Hefei there is easy water transport via the lake to the Yangtze River opposite Wuhu.

There are two main train stations in Hefei. The newest one is Hefei South railway station (Hefeinan station, 合肥火车南站) where most high-speed trains pass through. The alternative station is Hefei railway station (合肥火车站) which is smaller and older.

There are some small stations such as Feidong Station (肥东火车站), Feixi Station (肥西火车站), Shuijiahu Station (水家湖火车站), Chaohu Station (巢湖火车站), Chaohu East railway station (Chaohudong station; 巢湖火车东站), Hefeibeicheng Station (Hefei Northtown Station 合肥北城火车站), Lujiang Station (庐江火车站) and so on. These stations are mostly located in small towns and connect commuters with the main city.

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport replaced the old Hefei Luogang International Airport and started its operation on 30 May 2013, 00:00. This new domestic aviation hub is located in Gaoliu Village situated in the northwestern part of Hefei City. The first arriving flight was China Eastern Airlines flight MU5172 from Beijing Capital International Airport. The first departing flight was China Eastern Airlines MU5468 to Shanghai Pudong International Airport.

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport provides scheduled passenger service to major airports in China and other international cities. Destinations include Hong Kong, Macao, Singapore, Taipei (Taoyuan, Songshan), Kaohsiung, Taichung, Seoul, Cheongju, Yangyang, Jeju, Osaka, Nagoya, Shizuoka, Okayama, Boracay Island, Bali Island, Frankfurt, Siem Reap, Bangkok, Phuket Island and Krabi Island.

Hefei Metro is a rapid transit rail network under construction that will eventually serve both urban and rural areas of Hefei. As planned, Line 1 covers a total distance of 24 kilometres (15 miles) starting from Hefei Railway Station. It was inaugurated in December 2016.

In February 2013, Metro Line 2 also began its construction. It is being built alongside the Changjiang Dong Road, Changjiang Zhong Road and Changjiang Xi Road, which is a major passenger corridor in the east–west direction. It will pass through the city center area and connect to a transit point where passengers will be able to take the shuttle bus to Hefei Xinqiao International Airport. The Line 2 was opened on 26 December 2017.

In November 2015, Metro Line 3 construction began. Line 3 was opened on 26 December 2019. Line 3 connects the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone and the Economic Technology Development District, from the vocational education town to the university town. In 2016, Metro Line 4 construction began and was subsequently opened on 26 December 2021. Line 4 connects the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone and the High Technology Development District. In 2017, Metro Line 5 construction began. The south part of Line 5 was opened on 26 December 2020. Line 5 connects Binhu New District and the Beicheng (North city) New District. The north part of Line 5 is expected to open at the end of 2022.

Alongside Line 1, Line 2, Line 3, Line 4 and Line 5, Hefei is also planning to build other 12 metro lines, 4 lines of intra-metropolitan rail transit (to Lu'an, Huainan, Lujiang and Chaohu) and 3 lines of tram and hopefully accomplish the project by 2030.
There is an extensive public bus system in the city, including eight bus rapid transit lines. There are several commuter lines which only run at designated time or having a large interval.
Anhui Medical University is in Anhui, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Anhui.

Anhui was established 1667, during the reign of the Qing dynasty's Kangxi Emperor. The province's nickname, "Wan", is taken from the name of a small state that existed in the region during the Spring and Autumn period (722–481 BC). The name "Wan" also corresponds to the province's Mount Tianzhu and Wan state. Evidence of human beings inhabiting what is now Anhui 20,000 years before present has been attested by archaeological findings in Fanchang County, related to the cultural domains of Yangshao and Longshan, dated to the Neolithic period (8000–2000 BC). In relation to these cultures, archeologists have discovered through excavation a 4500-year-old city called the Nanchengzi Ruins in Guzhen County, after they discovered a Neolithic city wall and a moat that was part of a much larger and integrated city in the region during their 2013 disinterment.

There are many historical sites located in the province dating to the pre-imperial period. The culture of northern Anhui was associated with that of the North China Plain, together with what is now Henan, northern Jiangsu, and southern Shandong. Central Anhui was densely populated, and consisted of the fertile Huai River watershed. Contrastingly, southern Anhui was closer to Jiangxi and southern Jiangsu; the hills in the southeastern part of the province formed a unique cultural sphere. After the Qin dynasty unified China in 221 BC, the territory of modern Anhui belonged to different prefectures, including Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang, and Sishui. The lands became part of the Yang, Yu, and Xu prefectures during the Han dynasty (202 BC – 220 AD). During the Three Kingdoms era (222–280), Anhui was dominated at various times by Eastern Wu and Cao Wei. By the Song dynasty (960–1279), the economy and culture of area was flourishing. Anhui became part of the province of Henan during the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368); during the Ming dynasty the area was directly administrated by the imperial capital in Nanjing.

Anhui and Jiangsu were merged into one province under the Qing dynasty (1644–1912) until 1666, during the reign of the Kangxi Emperor. It played an important role in the Self-Strengthening Movement led by Li Hongzhang during the later Qing. During this time, western weapons, factories and administrative theories were being introduced into China. Over the next 50 years, Anhui became one of the country's most radically liberal areas, with important 20th-century figures moving to the province, like the poet and diplomat Hu Shih, and Chen Duxiu, the founder of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

In 1938, large areas in north and central Anhui were severely damaged by the decision of President Chiang Kai-shek to demolish a critical dam on the Yellow River, hoping that this would physically impede the ongoing invasion by the Imperial Japanese Army and prevent them from capturing Zhengzhou. Within only ten days of the dam breaking, the water and sands drowned all of north and middle area of this province, resulting in the deaths of between 500,000 and 900,000 Chinese people, as well as an unknown number of Japanese soldiers. Following the end of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1945, the capital city of Anhui moved to Hefei, then a small town. The provincial government made significant investments for its development. After 1949, the government launched projects to repair the damages suffered during World War II. Anhui was one of the worst affected provinces in The Great Chinese Famine. The province underwent significant development via the Third Front campaign to build basic and national defense industries in protected locations, in case of invasion by the Soviet Union or United States. The centerpiece of the Shanghai Small Third Front was the "rear base" in Anhui which served as "a multi-function manufacturing base for anti-aircraft and anti-tank weaponry". During the late 1990s Anhui became one of China's fastest-growing provinces. The province forms part of the China Yangtze River Delta Economic Area, which is the most developed area of China.

Anhui is topographically diverse. The north is part of the North China Plain while the north-central areas are part of the Huai River watershed. Both regions are flat, and densely populated. The land becomes more uneven further south, with the Dabie Mountains occupying much of southwestern Anhui and a series of hills and ranges cutting through southeastern Anhui, between which is the Yangtze River. The highest peak in Anhui is Lotus Peak, part of Huangshan in southeastern Anhui. It has an altitude of 1,873 metres (6,145 feet).

Major rivers include the Huai River in the north and the Yangtze in the south. The largest lake is Lake Chaohu situated in the center of the province, with an area of about 800 km2 (310 sq mi). The southeastern part of the province near the Yangtze River has many lakes as well.

As with topography, the province differs in climate from north to south. The north is more temperate with more distinct seasons. January temperatures average at around −1 to 2 °C north of the Huai River, and 0 to 3 °C south of the Huai River; in July temperatures average 27 °C or above. Plum rains occur in June and July and may cause flooding.
Anhui has 16 cities. In economic terms, the top three cities are: Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing.

Agriculture in Anhui varies according to the climate zones. To the north of the Huai River, wheat and sweet potatoes are grown, while to the south it is rice and wheat instead. As of 2022, Anhui's nominal GDP was US$670 billion (CN¥ 4.51 trilion), about 3.72% of the country's GDP and ranked 10th among province-level administrative units; the province's primary, secondary and tertiary industries were worth CN¥351.37 billion (US$52.24 billion), CN¥1.8588 trillion (US$276.36 billion) and CN¥2.29433 trillion (US$341.1 billion) respectively. Its nominal GDP per capita was US$10,943 (CN¥73,603) and ranked the 14th in the country.

Natural resources of Anhui include iron in Ma'anshan, coal in Huainan, and copper in Tongling. There are industries related to these natural resources (e.g. steel industry at Ma'anshan). One of the famous Anhui-based corporations is the automobile company Chery, which is based in Wuhu.

Compared to its more prosperous neighbours to the east, Zhejiang and Jiangsu, Anhui has lagged markedly behind in economic development, with a GDP per capita around half of those two provinces in 2017 rapidly improved from 1/3 of those two provinces in 2010. However, the provincial GDP per capita is based on the population registered in the province (that is, with local Hukou), but not necessarily residing there. There is significant regional disparity, where much of the wealth is concentrated in industrial regions close to the Yangtze River, such as Hefei, Wuhu, and Ma'anshan. The province is home to a large cluster of white goods manufacture such as Haier, Hisense, Whirlpool, Gree, Royalstar, and Meling.
In 2008, France helped the Anhui Provincial Tourism Bureau develop a rural tourism demonstration project.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

anhui-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Anhui Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hefei, register at Anhui Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

anhui-normal-university.h: Anhui Normal University: a first look

blocks.x: Anhui Normal University (安徽师范大学, pronounced Ānhuī Shīfàn Dàxué) is a higher-education institution in Wuhu, a Yangtze River city in Anhui Province. In 1972 the State Council approved the name it carries today, and the calligraphy of that name was written by Guo Moruo. Its College of International Education (国际教育学院, Guójì Jiàoyù Xuéyuàn) regularly hosts more than 150 foreign students from many countries, including Cuba, Britain, France, Germany, Egypt, Korea, Vietnam, Thailand, Yemen, Japan, Russia and Pakistan. That mix means a newcomer is unlikely to feel isolated, since other international students are always around, and the office there is used to helping people who are new to China.

The university presents itself as the province's earliest higher-education institution and as one of the first national comprehensive universities. It began as Provincial Anhui University in Anqing in 1928, became National Anhui University in 1946, and relocated to Wuhu in December 1949. Several later phases followed under other names: Anhui Teachers College, Hefei Teachers College, Southern Anhui University and Anhui Agricultural and Mechanical University. The State Council approved the present name, Anhui Normal University, in 1972, and a further merger came in 2005, when Wuhu Teachers College joined it.

The current structure includes 16 colleges and offers 56 undergraduate programmes, 72 postgraduate programmes and 7 doctoral programmes. Around 35,000 students from many provinces are enrolled, and the teaching staff numbers over 2600, with more than 580 holding the rank of professor or associate professor. The three campuses together cover over 3300 mu (roughly 230 hectares), and the reported built floor area is about 7.2 million square metres. In the library you will find 2.576 million volumes, including over 600 types of classical collections, as well as electronic databases from China and abroad. Facts like these are reported for a particular year and may have changed since, so the university's own site is the best place to confirm today's totals.

The university puts great weight on exchange in education, both at home and abroad. Long-standing friendly ties link it with several dozen universities, research institutes and academic bodies in the USA, England, Germany, Sweden, Finland, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Canada, as well as Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, and the partners take part in a wide range of academic exchanges.

The state chose it as one of the earliest groups of institutions to host international students on Chinese government scholarships, and it also became one of the first national centres for teaching Chinese language and culture to overseas Chinese. Close to 3000 foreign students from more than 40 countries have come for longer or shorter training courses since 1985.

The university teaches courses to foreign students from many countries; these include refresher study in a chosen major, as well as degree-level study at postgraduate level (three years) and doctoral level (three years). Two practical points are worth noting. Anyone who wants only a refresher course may pick from the majors on the university's list. And since every class is taught in Chinese, a student who is starting from zero can enrol first for a semester or a year of Chinese study.
Daily life revolves around the city, so here is a portrait of Wuhu.

At the 2020 census Wuhu had 3,644,420 inhabitants, and 1,622,799 of them lived in the built-up (metropolitan) area made up of Jiujiang, Jinghu and Yijiang districts. In 2022, 13.75 percent of residents were 14 or younger, 65.60 percent were between 15 and 59, and 20.65 percent were 60 or older; 16.89 percent were 65 or over. The city counts 47 recognised ethnic minorities, the largest being the Hui, Miao and Zhuang. Others with more than 500 people in the city include the Yi, Tujia and Manchu.
In town, the common speech is Wuhu dialect, a Jiang-Huai form of Mandarin. Putonghua, standard Mandarin, is also widely used, while in a few areas the local speech belongs to the Wu Chinese group.

Only the provincial capital, Hefei, has a bigger economy than Wuhu in Anhui. Growth this century has been fast, as in the rest of China: between 2014 and 2022 the city's output almost doubled, and output per person almost doubled between 2012 and 2019.

In 2022 the city's GDP was 450.213 billion renminbi (RMB). The primary sector, mostly farming, contributed 17.925 billion RMB (3.98 percent), the secondary sector 213.558 billion RMB (47.43 percent) and the tertiary sector 218.730 billion RMB (48.58 percent). GDP per capita in 2019 was 96,154 RMB. The statistics bureau reported disposable income per head of 43,145 RMB in 2022, up 6.5 percent from 2021; urban residents averaged 51,481 RMB and rural residents 29,518 RMB. In 2022 Wuhu exported goods and services worth 9.468 billion US dollars and imported 4.142 billion US dollars.

Main industrial products include cars, air conditioning and ventilation equipment, plate glass, cement, steel and copper. In the north of the city, the Economic and Technological Development Area that opened in 1993 was among the first state-level zones of its kind in Anhui, and it contains the only export processing zone in the province. Both the carmaker Chery Automobile and the Anhui Conch Cement Company have their headquarters there. Wuhu is the fifth-largest port on the Yangtze, and Yuxikou Pier is China's biggest inland river coal harbour.
Buses and taxis: Wuhu Bus (芜湖公交, Wúhú Gōngjiāo) provides municipal bus and taxi service, with 157 routes served by more than 1,300 vehicles and about 200,000 passengers a day.
Air: Wuhu Xuanzhou Airport opened on 30 April 2021.
Bridge: the city has one Yangtze crossing, the Wuhu Yangtze River Bridge, which opened in 2000 and carries the G5011 Wuhu-Hefei Expressway and the Huainan Railway.
Train: the Anhui-Jiangxi, Nanjing-Tongling and Huainan railways serve Wuhu, and the high-speed train from Shanghai takes only 2.5 hours.
Rail transit: Wuhu's monorail-style rail transit has two lines, Line 1 opened on 3 November 2021 and Line 2 on 28 December 2021.

anhui-normal-university.h: Culture and history of the city

blocks.x: The renowned poet Li Bai is said to have spent his later years in Wuhu because of its striking scenery. Li Bai's birthplace was Suyab, an old Silk Road city in Central Asia, and he was raised in south-western China. Xie Tiao, a distinctive poet of the Six Dynasties whom Li Bai greatly admired, wrote many poems while holding office here. During the Tang dynasty (619 to 907) another poet, Du Mu, composed a well-known work titled Thoughts on Staying Again at Wuhu.

A local factory continues the craft of wrought-iron pictures, and other local handicrafts include embossed lacquerware and rice-straw pith patchwork. A famous stone tablet recording local events from the Song dynasty, around the year 1000, is regarded as a masterpiece by the celebrated calligrapher Mi Fu.

A second story features Gan Jiang, a smith from the Spring and Autumn era (770 to 476 BC) who was renowned for forging swords. The reddish colour of one hill, Zhe Shan, is blamed on the fire of his furnace, and a nearby hill, Shen Shan, is said to hold his grinding stone and the pool where he tempered blades.

Yanjiang cuisine, the style of the Yangtze riverside, is strongest in Wuhu and Anqing. Cooks there favour river fish and poultry and use particular techniques to cut, shape and colour the food, and sweet or smoked flavours are common.

Western medicine arrived in Wuhu in 1881 with Virgil C. Hart, who led the New York Methodist Mission Society's work and wanted land for a Methodist church and a hospital in Western style. He obtained Yichisan Hill ahead of the British, who hoped to put a consulate and naval base there. The Yichisan Hospital that grew on the site is the oldest Western hospital in Anhui to have run without a break. Hart's eldest son, Dr. Edgerton H. Hart, directed it from 1895 until he died in April 1913. A nurse named Caroline Maddock reached Wuhu in October 1904 to be head nurse of the General Hospital and married Dr. Hart in October 1907. Two years later, in 1909, she and four colleagues established the Nurses Association of China, with her as first president, and it remains the body that represents Chinese nursing.

The province around Wuhu helps explain its character, so here is a wider view.

The Kangxi Emperor of the Qing set up Anhui as a province in 1667. Its short name, Wan, comes from a small state of the Spring and Autumn period (722 to 481 BC) and also corresponds to Mount Tianzhu. Digging in Guzhen County in 2013 exposed a Neolithic city wall and moat, part of a much larger 4500-year-old settlement called the Nanchengzi Ruins.

The province has many sites from before the imperial age. Its northern part shared a culture with the North China Plain, along with today's Henan, northern Jiangsu and southern Shandong, while the middle, in the Huai River basin, was fertile and thickly settled. The south looked toward Jiangxi and southern Jiangsu, and its south-eastern hills formed a culture of their own. When the Qin dynasty united China in 221 BC the land was divided into prefectures such as Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang and Sishui, and the Han (202 BC to 220 AD) placed it within the Yang, Yu and Xu prefectures. Eastern Wu and Cao Wei each controlled it at different moments in the Three Kingdoms era (222 to 280). By the time of the Song (960 to 1279) its economy and culture were thriving. The Yuan (1271 to 1368) attached it to Henan, and the Ming ruled it directly from Nanjing.

Under the Qing (1644 to 1912) the area formed one province with Jiangsu until 1666, in the reign of the Kangxi Emperor. Late in the dynasty it played a big role in the Self-Strengthening Movement of Li Hongzhang, which brought Western arms, factories and administrative ideas to China. In the following 50 years Anhui turned into one of the most liberal-minded parts of the country, and 20th-century figures including the poet and diplomat Hu Shih and the Communist Party founder Chen Duxiu made their homes there.

In 1938 the wartime breaching of Yellow River dams caused disastrous flooding in northern and central Anhui. The water and silt drowned all of the province's north and centre within ten days, and estimates of the death toll range from 500,000 to 900,000 Chinese people. When the Second Sino-Japanese War ended in 1945 the capital was moved to Hefei, which was then only a small town, and the provincial government put substantial investment into building it up. After 1949 projects began to repair wartime damage. Anhui was among the provinces hardest hit by the Great Chinese Famine. It was also transformed by the Third Front campaign, which built basic and defence industries in sheltered locations in case of attack from the Soviet Union or the United States; at the core of the Shanghai Small Third Front was a rear base in Anhui, used as an all-round manufacturing centre for anti-aircraft and anti-tank equipment. Anhui grew into one of China's fastest-growing provinces in the late 1990s, and it is part of the Yangtze River Delta Economic Area, China's most developed region.

Anhui has very varied terrain. In the north lies part of the North China Plain, and north-central areas form the Huai River basin, both flat and heavily populated. Going south the ground becomes rougher: the Dabie Mountains fill a large part of the south-west, and hill ranges cut across the south-east, with the Yangtze running between them. Lotus Peak in the Huangshan range, in the south-east, is the highest summit at 1,873 metres (6,145 feet). Two great rivers shape the map, the Huai to the north and the Yangtze to the south. The biggest lake is Lake Chaohu, in the middle of the province, covering about 800 square kilometres (310 square miles), and the south-east near the Yangtze has many lakes as well.

Climate also varies from north to south, and the northern part is cooler with clearer seasons. January averages run about -1 to 2 °C in the area north of the Huai and 0 to 3 °C south of it, while July is 27 °C or above. Plum rains fall in June and July and can cause floods. Anhui has 16 cities, and the three largest economies are Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing.

Farming follows the climate zones: wheat and sweet potatoes north of the Huai River, rice and wheat to the south. In 2022 the province's nominal GDP came to US$670 billion (CN¥4.51 trillion), roughly 3.72 percent of China's total and tenth among provincial units. By sector, the primary industries produced CN¥351.37 billion (US$52.24 billion), the secondary CN¥1.8588 trillion (US$276.36 billion) and the tertiary CN¥2.29433 trillion (US$341.1 billion). Per-person GDP was US$10,943 (CN¥73,603), ranking 14th.

Natural resources include iron at Ma'anshan, coal at Huainan and copper at Tongling, with related industries such as the steelworks at Ma'anshan. Chery, the car maker, is based in Wuhu. Compared with its richer eastern neighbours Zhejiang and Jiangsu, Anhui has developed more slowly: in 2017 its GDP per head was around half theirs, an improvement from about a third in 2010. Provincial per-capita figures use the registered population, which includes people with local hukou who may not live there, and there is strong regional inequality, with wealth concentrated in industrial areas near the Yangtze such as Hefei, Wuhu and Ma'anshan. A large group of makers of household appliances, among them Haier, Hisense, Whirlpool, Gree, Royalstar and Meling, operates in the province.
In south-west Hefei, near Luogang International Airport, an Economic and Technological Development Zone dates from 1993.

Hefei's Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone was founded in October 1990 and approved as a state-level zone in March 1991. Its special open policies for APEC and EU members came with recognition as an APEC Science and Technology Industrial Park in 1997. It was named a National High Tech Export Base in 2000 and won an Advanced High Tech Zone award under the Torch Program in 2003. Over 100 hi-tech companies have settled there, and it favours electronics assembly, chemicals, instruments, medical equipment and telecommunications.
Wuhu Economic and Technological Development Zone, founded in 1993, was the first state-level zone the central government approved in Anhui, taking advantage of Wuhu's position on the Yangtze delta.
Wuhu Export Processing Zone has national-level status and a planned area of 2.95 square kilometres (1.14 square miles).

Anhui's transport network was long held back by the shortage of bridges over the Yangtze, which divides the province into north and south. The first, the Tongling Yangtze River Bridge, was finished in 1995, and by October 2014 four bridges existed, at Ma'anshan, Wuhu, Tongling and Anqing. The railway network was thin until this century, but high-speed trains now connect most cities, and Hefei South station is the central hub. In 2008 France assisted the Anhui Provincial Tourism Bureau with a pilot project for rural tourism.

Anhui Normal University is a long-established teacher-training and comprehensive university with a welcoming international office, and Wuhu is a mid-sized Yangtze city with a strong industrial economy and good rail links. For current programmes, scholarship rules, fees and Chinese-language courses, consult the university's own website, since figures quoted in this overview are general guides only.
Anhui Normal University lists 35 programs for international students on this site: 7 bachelor, 20 master's, 8 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 23 taught in Chinese, 12 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 15,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

33 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (10):
Biology
Chemistry
Ecology
Education
Foreign Languages and Literatures
Human Resource Management
Journalism
Journalism and Communication
Journalism and Communication Studies
Psychology
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

anhui-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Anhui Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhu, register at Anhui Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Anhui University (often abbreviated AHU) is a provincial public university in Hefei, the capital of Anhui, China. It answers to the Anhui Provincial Government, but its funding is shared with the Ministry of Education and with SASTIND, the national defence science and technology administration. It belongs to the Double First-Class Construction and to Project 211.

More than 34,000 undergraduates and over 15,000 doctoral and master's students currently study here. The share of undergraduate graduates who go on to further study has stayed above 35% on average in recent years, which is a useful signal if you plan to continue to a master's degree. Its 14 colleges offer a wide curriculum: arts subjects such as philosophy, literature and history, social subjects including economics, law and management, and the sciences and engineering.

Anhui University was founded in 1928 in Anqing. In 1952 it moved to Hefei, and there it was split into two separate institutions, Anhui Normal University and Anhui Agricultural College. The Anhui provincial government re-established the university in Hefei in 1958. Government support continues today through the national Double First Class University Plan, the successor to the earlier Project 211.

Altogether there are four campuses: the main campus (55 hectares, or 140 acres), a pair of branch campuses (30 hectares or 74 acres apiece) and a new campus that is much bigger, at about 200 hectares (490 acres).

Teaching is organised into 18 schools and 44 departments. Students can choose from 65 undergraduate programs, 119 master's programs and 16 Ph.D. programs, and there is one post-doctoral research workstation. Two disciplines are recognised at state level and 12 at provincial level. Its staff of 2399 includes 210 professors and 490 associate professors, and the student body totals 28143, including 6466 mature students.

Library holdings exceed 1.75 million books, together with more than 7000 periodicals in Chinese and foreign languages. Libraries are found on the main campus and also on the new campus, two of them in each place.

The university now counts 33 schools and departments. The recognised subject areas are: one Double First-Class discipline, two national key disciplines, fourteen provincial top disciplines (four more are being cultivated for that status) and twenty-five provincial key disciplines.

In research citation data from Essential Science Indicators (ESI), 11 subjects sit among the best 1% worldwide. They are Chemistry, Physics, Mathematics, Engineering, Computer Science, Materials Science, Earth Science, Clinical Medicine, General Social Sciences, Environment/Ecology, and Biology and Biochemistry. A further 4 subjects reach the top 2%. On the national stage, three fields reached China's top 20 in the Best Chinese Subjects table published by Shanghai Ranking in 2024: Applied Economics, Chemistry, and Computer Science and Technology.
It is authorised to grant doctorates across 23 first-level disciplines and professional categories, and master's degrees across 65.

Over its history the university has produced more than 390,000 graduates working in many fields, so in terms of alumni numbers and reach it ranks among Anhui's biggest and most influential. The current community comprises roughly 34,000 full-time undergraduates and 15,000 postgraduates (master's and doctoral), plus about 500 international students.

Materials Science and Engineering

For overseas applicants, this section matters most. Exchange partnerships exist with 74 overseas universities, and foreign students have been enrolled since 1980. The Ministry of Education has authorised the university to take international students holding Chinese government scholarships. The Overseas Chinese Affairs Office of the State Council designated it in 2000 as a base for teaching Chinese language and culture. So far, over 700 international students, drawn from Asia, America and Europe, have joined.
Student life depends on the city around the campus: its weather, its transport and what there is to do. This part introduces Hefei.

Nanjing is 130 kilometres (81 mi) to the east of Hefei, which stands in south-central Anhui. Southeast of the city, at a distance of 15 km (9 mi), is Chao Lake, among China's biggest fresh water lakes. In recent decades nitrogen and phosphorus pollution has hurt the lake, but efforts by government and local people are improving it.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) and each of the four seasons is clearly marked. The mean annual temperature is 16.6 °C (61.9 °F). Rain totals slightly more than 1,000 millimetres (39 in) a year, with the heaviest falls between May and August. Season by season:

Winter: damp and cold. January lows go just under freezing, and the January average is 2.8 °C (37.0 °F). Snowfall is irregular and seldom heavy. Cold spells from Siberia usually arrive in December, January and February, and occasionally in November and March, when they can bring snow and heavier snowfall.
Spring: generally pleasant, though somewhat unpredictable.
Summer: hot and humid, and July averages 28.6 °C (83.5 °F). From June to August, and often into September, daytime highs can hit or pass 37 °C (99 °F), and heavy humidity is normal.
Autumn: a gradual cooling and drying.

Possible sunshine received is 35 percent in March and rises to 50 percent in August, which adds up to 1,868 sunny hours across a year. The record low since 1951 is -20.6 °C (-5 °F), set on 6 January 1955; the record high is 41.1 °C (106 °F), reached on 27 July 2017.
Air quality usually gets worse in May and June. Smog covers the city then, caused by smoke from farmers outside the city burning their fields before the next crop is planted.

Hefei's GDP was CN¥1,141.28 billion in 2021, with GDP per capita of ¥121,187 (US$18,784), placing the city within China's top 20. For 2023 the total grew to CN¥1,267.38 billion. Electric vehicle output in 2025 was 1.37 million, nearly one of every 12 produced in the country.

The municipal government is unusually hands-on with business, running state-owned enterprises and making direct investments. That strategy has driven growth and restructured the local economy. Some examples:

BOE Technology (Jingdongfang): the city paid US$3.5 billion in 2008 to take control. BOE then became a leading semiconductor producer for telecommunications, and the world's largest maker of LCD screens, OLED panels and flexible displays. At least since 2024 it has operated three production lines in Hefei, which helped attract more electronics supply-chain firms and made Hefei a main centre of China's optoelectronic industry.
iFlytek: also in 2008, Hefei invested heavily in this voice-recognition firm, which was spun off from USTC.

NIO: the government invested heavily to combine NIO with Hefei Changan Automobile, an old enterprise from the Third Front construction. By 2020 NIO was nearly bankrupt, and Hefei bought a 25% stake for RMB 7 billion. The company relocated its headquarters here, and the city helped it secure bank loans to widen its supply chains. By 2022 it had become the most successful electric vehicle manufacturer in China.
ChangXin Memory Technologies: a further city investment; it is now the biggest DRAM producer in China and the fourth biggest globally.

In its November 2010 Access China White Paper, the Economist Intelligence Unit listed Hefei in its CHAMPS group, an acronym for six cities, namely Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan and Ma'anshan, as well as Pingdingshan and Shenyang, which it used to describe twenty leading emerging Chinese cities. In December 2012 The Economist called it the fastest-growing metropolitan economy in the world. The city has backed its chip industry and become one of the largest sites for memory chips (DRAM).

Since 1945 Hefei has been the capital of the province, taking over from Lihuang (now Jinzhai). Its geography makes it a natural transport hub. It lies on a low saddle north of Chao Lake, where the Dabie Mountains extend northeast and divide the Huai and Yangtze river basins. Boats can cross the lake from the city and reach the Yangtze across from Wuhu.
Hefei has two main stations. The newest is Hefei South railway station (Hefeinan, 合肥火车南站), through which most high-speed trains pass. The smaller, older one is Hefei railway station (合肥火车站).
Several small stations, mostly in small towns, connect commuters with the main city:
Feidong Station (肥东火车站)
Feixi Station (肥西火车站)
Shuijiahu Station (水家湖火车站)
Chaohu Station (巢湖火车站)
Chaohu East railway station (Chaohudong; 巢湖火车东站)
Hefeibeicheng Station (Hefei Northtown Station, 合肥北城火车站)
Lujiang Station (庐江火车站)

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport opened at midnight on 30 May 2013, replacing the earlier Luogang airport. It is a domestic hub at Gaoliu Village in the city's northwest. The first plane to land came in on a China Eastern Airlines service from Beijing Capital International Airport (MU5172), and the first to leave was China Eastern MU5468, bound for Shanghai Pudong International Airport.
Regular passenger services link it to major airports in China and several overseas cities. Destinations include:
Hong Kong, Macao, Singapore
Taipei (Taoyuan and Songshan), Kaohsiung, Taichung
Seoul, Cheongju, Yangyang, Jeju
Osaka, Nagoya, Shizuoka, Okayama
Boracay Island, Bali Island
Frankfurt, Siem Reap, Bangkok, Phuket Island, Krabi Island
Hefei Metro is still being built and is meant to serve urban and rural areas of Hefei. The plan has 5 lines open or under way:
Line 1: planned to run 24 kilometres (15 miles) from Hefei Railway Station, and inaugurated in December 2016.

Line 2: building started in February 2013, following Changjiang East, Middle and West Roads (Changjiang Dong, Zhong and Xi Roads), the busiest east-west passenger corridor. It passes through the city centre to an interchange with a shuttle bus for Hefei Xinqiao International Airport, and it opened on 26 December 2017.

Line 3: construction began in November 2015 and it opened on 26 December 2019. Its route links the Economic Technology Development District and the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone, and it runs between the vocational education town and the university town.
Line 4: construction began in 2016 and it opened on 26 December 2021, connecting the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone with the High Technology Development District.

Line 5: work started in 2017. The southern part came into service on 26 December 2020, connecting the Binhu and Beicheng (North city) New Districts, while the northern part was expected by the end of 2022.
Further expansion is planned: 12 more metro lines, 3 tram lines and 4 intra-metropolitan rail lines to Lu'an, Huainan, Lujiang and Chaohu, with 2030 as the target date.
The city has a wide public bus network, including eight bus rapid transit lines. Several commuter lines run only at set times or at long intervals.
Student life is influenced by the province as well as the campus, and Anhui is a diverse, fast-growing region with a long history.

Anhui became a province in 1667, under the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty. Its nickname, "Wan", comes from a small state that existed here in the Spring and Autumn period (722-481 BC), and also matches Mount Tianzhu and Wan state. Archaeology in Fanchang County shows that people lived in the area 20,000 years ago, and finds are linked to the Yangshao and Longshan cultures of the Neolithic period (8000-2000 BC). In 2013 excavators uncovered a Neolithic city wall and moat at the Nanchengzi Ruins in Guzhen County. They belong to a city about 4500 years old, which formed a piece of a far bigger, joined-up settlement.
Many sites from before the imperial age survive in the province, and its regions were culturally distinct:
The north shared its culture with the North China Plain, along with today's Henan, southern Shandong and the northern part of Jiangsu.
Central Anhui was densely populated and made up of the fertile Huai River watershed.
The south had closer ties to Jiangxi and the southern end of Jiangsu, while the southeastern hills formed a cultural area of their own.

Once the Qin dynasty united China in 221 BC, the land was divided between prefectures such as Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang and Sishui. Under the Han dynasty (202 BC to 220 AD) the lands were part of Yang, Yu and Xu prefectures. In the Three Kingdoms era (222-280) Eastern Wu and Cao Wei dominated at different times. The economy and culture were thriving by the Song dynasty (960-1279). Anhui joined Henan province under the Yuan (1271-1368), and under the Ming the imperial capital at Nanjing governed it directly.

Under the Qing dynasty (1644-1912), Anhui and Jiangsu were a single province until 1666, in the Kangxi Emperor's reign. Li Hongzhang led the Self-Strengthening Movement of the late Qing, and Anhui played a part in it as Western arms, factories and ideas of administration were arriving in China. During the following 50 years the province turned into a hotbed of radical liberal thinking, among the most so in China. Major 20th-century figures settled there, including Hu Shih (poet and diplomat) and Chen Duxiu, who founded the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

In 1938 President Chiang Kai-shek ordered the demolition of a vital Yellow River dam, intending to block the Imperial Japanese Army's advance and keep it from Zhengzhou. In just ten days, floodwater and sand covered the northern and central parts of Anhui. The death toll among Chinese people was somewhere from 500,000 to 900,000, and an unknown number of Japanese soldiers also died. When the Second Sino-Japanese War ended in 1945, the capital was relocated to Hefei, at that time a small town, and the provincial authorities invested heavily in building it up. After 1949, projects began to repair wartime damage. Anhui was among the provinces worst hit by the Great Chinese Famine.

Large-scale development came with the Third Front campaign, which put basic and defence industries in sheltered locations in case the Soviet Union or the United States invaded. Within the Shanghai Small Third Front, the main project was Anhui's "rear base", summed up as "a multi-function manufacturing base" for anti-aircraft and anti-tank weapons. By the late 1990s the province was growing faster than most of China. It belongs now to the Yangtze River Delta economic area, the most developed in the country.

Anhui has varied terrain. The north belongs to the North China Plain and the north-central part to the Huai River watershed, and both are flat and densely populated. Heading south, the terrain gets rougher: the Dabie Mountains fill most of the southwest, and the southeast is crossed by several chains of hills with the Yangtze running between them. Lotus Peak, in the Huangshan range in the southeast, is the highest point, at 1,873 metres (6,145 feet).

Two major rivers cross the province: the Huai to the north and the Yangtze to the south. Lake Chaohu, about 800 km2 (310 sq mi) in the middle of the province, is the largest lake, but the southeast near the Yangtze contains plenty of others.

Climate also varies from north to south, with a more temperate climate and more distinct seasons in the north. In the north of the province, beyond the Huai River, January averages run at about -1 to 2 °C, and south of that river at 0 to 3 °C. July averages are 27 °C or above. Plum rains fall in June and July and can cause flooding.
Anhui has 16 cities, and economically the top three are Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing.

Farming follows the climate: wheat and sweet potatoes north of the Huai River, and rice and wheat to the south. Mineral wealth includes iron (Ma'anshan), coal (Huainan) and copper (Tongling), and industry has grown up around them, such as the steel works at Ma'anshan. A well-known local company is the automaker Chery, based in Wuhu.

Anhui's nominal GDP for 2022 came to US$670 billion (CN¥ 4.51 trillion). That is about 3.72% of China's total and the tenth highest among provincial-level units. By sector, the primary industry contributed CN¥351.37 billion (US$52.24 billion), the secondary industry CN¥1.8588 trillion (US$276.36 billion), and services (the tertiary industry) CN¥2.29433 trillion (US$341.1 billion). Per head, nominal GDP was US$10,943 (CN¥73,603), which ranked 14th.

Compared with its richer eastern neighbours Zhejiang and Jiangsu, Anhui has lagged in development. In 2017 its GDP per capita was around half of theirs, a rapid improvement on 1/3 in 2010. One caveat is that per-capita GDP uses people registered locally (with a local hukou), who may not actually live there. Wealth is also unevenly spread, concentrated in industrial areas along the Yangtze such as Hefei, Wuhu and Ma'anshan. Anhui is home to a big cluster of home appliance (white goods) makers, such as Haier, Hisense and Whirlpool, plus Gree, Royalstar and Meling.
The Anhui Provincial Tourism Bureau had French help in 2008 to create a rural tourism demonstration project.

Anhui University offers a large, broad-based education in a fast-growing provincial capital with strong science, electric vehicle and display-technology industries, plus rail, metro and international air links. International applicants will find an institution that has welcomed foreign students since 1980.
Anhui University lists 208 programs for international students on this site: 78 bachelor, 81 master's, 48 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 189 taught in Chinese, 19 taught in Chinese and English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 15,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 24,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.

208 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.
