Anshan Normal University (simplified Chinese: 鞍山师范学院; traditional Chinese: 鞍山師範學院; pinyin: Ānshān Shīfàn Xuéyuàn) is a university in the city of Anshan, in Liaoning province. It is under the provincial government. The school was founded in 1958 as a teacher training centre but suspended all operations in 1962 at the dawn of the Chinese Cultural Revolution before it was restarted again in 1978. The campus covers an area of 731,600 square meters. There is a teaching staff of 1207 over various levels from Professor down to post graduate teachers.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Anshan, where Anshan Normal University is located.

Located north of the Liao River plains, Anshan has wide flat lands in the west and central regions that develop into hilly and mountainous terrain on the southeastern fringes, which is bounded by the Qian Mountains and contains the famous Qianshan National Park. The region is rich in minerals including iron ore, coal, magnesite, talcum and jade. The plains of western Anshan have large flat fertile fields ideal for agriculture, with 24,480 hectares (60,500 acres) of arable land accounting for 26.4% of its total land area. One such agricultural product that Anshan has become renowned for is the Nanguo pears (Chinese: 南果梨, Pyrus ussuriensis c.v. Nanguo), nicknamed the "king of pears". Anshan was used as a travel post with motels during the Ming Dynasty (Chinese: 明朝) for travellers who passed by on work duty.

Anshan has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa) characterised by hot, humid summers, due to the monsoon, and rather long, cold, and arid winters, due to the Siberian anticyclone. The four seasons here are distinctive. Nearly half of the annual rainfall occurs in July and August. The monthly 24-hour average temperatures ranges from −7.6 °C (18.3 °F) in January to 25.9 °C (78.6 °F) in July, while the annual mean is 10.6 °C (51.1 °F). Sunshine is generous and amounts to 2,595.4 hours annually, while relative humidity averages 55%, ranging from 44% in April to 71% in July and August. Extreme temperatures have ranged from −26.9 °C (−16.4 °F) up to 38.2 °C (100.8 °F).

The north east of China is a major industrial zone and Anshan is one of the key sites of the north east. Anshan is in the midst of a at least a quarter of China's iron and coal resources. The city is renowned as "China's capital of iron and steel". Prior to the development of the Iron and Steel industries, Anshan was a relatively small city of little importance. As the steel mills expanded, so to did the city. Spin off industries developed alongside the steel plant making the area a centre of heavy industry.

As a joint Sino-Japanese venture, Anshan Zhenzing Iron Ore Company Unlimited was started in Anshan in 1918. When Japan occupied Northeast China in 1931, these mills were turned into a Japanese owned monopoly. Anshan subsequently became part of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo and additional industries developed around the iron and steel mills. Due to its mills, the city became a significant strategic industrial hub during World War II and as such, was subject to constant Allied bombing during the war.

Total production of processed iron in Manchuria reached 1,000,000 tonnes in 1931–32, of which almost half was made by Shōwa Steel in Anshan. Iron production grew to 7,000,000 tonnes in 1938 and by 1941, Shōwa Steel Works had a total capacity production of 1,750,000 tonnes of iron bars and 1,000,000 tonnes of processed steel. By 1942, Anshan's Shōwa Steel Works total production capacity reached 3,600,000 tonnes, making it one of the major iron and steel centers in the world.

In 1945, the steel plant was looted by Soviet forces. The Republic of China government partially repaired the site, but it was destroyed again during the Chinese Civil War that saw the CCP forces victorious. The mills were once again repaired and Anshan Iron and Steel Company (Angang) was founded in 1948. From then to 2001, the company produced 290 million tons of steel, 284 million tons of pig iron and 192 million tons of rolled steel. Until  the opening of a new steel plant in Shanghai, Angang was the largest steel producer in China. Today, Angang consists of three steelworks with 13 rolling mills plus supporting plants which produce coke, refractory materials and machinery for the steel plants. The company has an annual production capacity of 10 million tons of pig iron, 10 million tons of steel and 9.5 million tons of rolled steel. A quarter of China's total iron ore reserves, about 10 billion tons, are located in Anshan, ensuring that the city will remain an important steel producer well into the future.

Anshan is rich in other mineral wealth too. The southern and south eastern areas of Anshan are rich in magnesite, with reserves equivalent to a quarter of all worldwide reserves. Anshan also has the world's largest reserve of talcum, accounting for fully one third of the entire world supply. The Xiuyan area of Anshan is known for the production of jade. The largest single jade stone ever found came from Xiuyan, now carved into the form of a Buddha, it is a major tourist attraction in the area.
Anshan is serviced by Shenyang airport, about 90 kilometres (56 miles) to the north, and by two major highways linking it with Shenyang and Dalian.

The government of Anshan established a five-year plan in 2000 with the aim of turning the city into a strong modern industrial city with plenty of tourism. It also aimed to make the city GDP reach 100 billion RMB by 2005 and to build a modern industrial city by using advances in technology to transform the traditional industries. Attracting foreign investment is also another main idea in the plan. The Anshan government anticipates the foreign investment assets would be around 80 billion RMB by 2005.

Anshan has been identified by the Economist Intelligence Unit in the November 2010 Access China White Paper as a member of the CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), an economic profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China. The opportunities for engaging Anshan's consumers have been documented by the ethnographer and cultural sociologist Michael B. Griffiths.

Out of the 3,584,000 people living in Anshan prefecture, 519,400 are ethnic Manchu, a holdover from northeast China's historical rule by the ethnic group. They are mainly in or around the Xiuyan Man regional ethnic autonomy area which is within Anshan's borders. During the last years of the Qing dynasty, large numbers of Han people migrated to the north east in search of work. This pattern continued into the 20th century. The development of Anshan as a large industrial center during and after World War II caused the city's population to increase rapidly, and the new arrivals began to significantly outnumber the local Man people. As of the last census data, Anshan was home to 48 Chinese ethnic groups. The Han people make up the lion's share at 3,020,500 people. Next, after the Han and Man people, come the Hui and the Chaoxian with 23,400 and 10,000 people respectively. The Hui population is widely dispersed but the Chaoxian population is mostly concentrated in Teixi (West district) and Qianshan district.

Anshan has a population of 3.65 million at the 2010 census. As the city has expanded, the area between Anshan and the neighbouring city of Liaoyang has become urbanised, with little or no farmland visible on route between them. According to the 2010 census, the conurbation of urban Anshan and urban Liaoyang districts contains 2.17 million inhabitants.

The city of Anshan can be divided into districts. The East district, Tiedong has a population of 452,900. The western district, Tiexi has 311,600 people. These two districts are demarcated by the railway lines that run north to south through the city. The north western portion of the city is dominated by the large steel works of Angang. The district of Lishan houses 425,600 people and the suburbs of Qianshan district have 366,200 soles. Within Anshan prefecture lies the subordinate city of Haicheng which accounts for 1,181,100 people. The neighbouring subordinate town of Tai'an has 354,700 people.

Anshan has no river or sea port. The nearby military airport, Anshan Teng'ao Airport (AOG), also accepts commercial domestic flights. Currently there are five routes in operation, Anshan–Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu and Nanjing, with one flight each per day throughout the year. Anshan Teng'ao Airport is 15 km (9 mi) southwest of the city centre. In addition to the small terminal building at the airport, there is also a city terminal situated just off Qianshan Road in Tiexi district. Passengers may buy tickets and check-in at the city terminal, from which they are taken by coach to the main airport terminal. The nearest other major commercial airports are Shenyang Taoxian International Airport (SHE), about 90 km (56 mi) to the north and Dalian Zhoushuizi International Airport about 270 km (170 mi) to the south.

The city is beside the Shenyang–Dalian Expressway (part of the G15 Shenyang–Haikou Expressway), a privately funded eight-lane tolled highway, and was the first road of its kind in mainland China. The Liaozhong Ring Expressway (G91) passes just a few kilometers north of Anshan city. It connects east to Benxi and west onto the Jingshen Expressway (G1). The Panhai and Danxi Expressways (together forming the G16) pass through Anshan's counties of Haicheng and Xiuyan, connecting them to Yingkou and Panjin in the west and Dandong to the east.

Anshan is connected to the Chinese rail network with rail routes to Beijing, Dalian, and to the northeastern provinces of Jilin and Heilongjiang as well as to eastern Inner Mongolia, and even a direct, albeit slow, train to Hong Kong. As of December 2012, the new Harbin–Dalian High-Speed Railway serves Anshan West Railway Station and Haicheng West Railway Station. It connects south to Dalian and north east to Shenyang, Changchun and Harbin. This line was hailed as the world's first alpine high-speed rail line. In summer it runs at its full speed of 300 km/h but in winter speeds are restricted to 200 km/h. High-speed services also run via Anshan to Beijing. Tai'an county of Anshan is served by another high-speed rail line linking Shenyang to Beijing.
Long-distance coaches run to all the main cities of the province as well as to Beijing.

Local transportation is primarily by bus or taxi. Anshan used to have a single tram line—along Zhonghua Avenue, through the city centre and past Angang main gate—but this has been closed and the tracks removed. Due to the flat topography of the city centre, bicycles are popular. Almost all roads have a wide cycle lane on each side. Often this lane is further protected by a traffic island that separates the bikes from larger motor vehicles.
Anshan Normal University is in Liaoning, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Liaoning.

From 4th century BC to 9th century, Liaoning was predominantly settled and administered by Han Chinese regime. Prior to 3rd century BC, Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples inhabited Liaoning and later, the state of Yan conquered the area around 300 BC. Two commanderies, Liaodong ("east of the Liao River") and Liaoxi ("west of the Liao River"), were established within the Liaoning region. The Yan city of Xiangping, the center of Liaodong, was located on the site of the present Liaoyang city. As the Han dynasty fell, warlord Gongsun Du and his family established and maintained a semi-independent state based in Liaodong, until it was defeated by Cao Wei in 238. The state, also known as Yan, conducted numerous maritime diplomatic and trade expeditions, and had a lasting influence on Northeast Asian culture despite being short-lived. After the end of Western Jin dynasty, Liaoning was ruled by Xianbei states of the Murong tribe – Former Yan, Later Yan, and Northern Yan. In 436, as Northern Wei seized the Yan capital, Liaodong Peninsula was taken over by Goguryeo. The Tang dynasty annexed the region during the Goguryeo–Tang War.

In the mid 8th century the An Lushan Rebellion broke out, which greatly drained Tang's resources away from its frontiers, and the Bohai gradually expanded into Liaodong. Eventually, Liaoning was conquered by the Khitan Liao dynasty; during the Liao dynasty, the region was divided among the Eastern Capital Circuit (Dongjingdao), the Supreme Capital Circuit (Shangjingdao), the Central Capital Circuit (Zhongjingdao), and the Lower Capital Circuit (Xiajingdao).

Under the Jurchen Jin dynasty, most of the area was administered by the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu), while the rest was divided among the Xianping Route, the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu), and the Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu). In 1206, Liaoning was conquered by Genghis Khan, and later was incorporated into the Yuan dynasty, during the eastern part of the region belonged to the Liaoyang Route and Shenyang Route under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; the northern area was under the Kaiyuan Route’s Xianping Prefecture; the western area, including Guangning Route, was also subordinate to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; while the Jinzhou and Chaoyang regions were part of the Daning Route under the Central Secretariat.

The Ming Empire took control of Liaoning in 1371, just three years after the expulsion of the Mongols from Beijing. Around 1442, a defense wall was constructed to defend the agricultural heartland of the province from a potential threat from the Jurchen-Mongol Oriyanghan (who were Ming's tributaries) from the northwest. Between 1467 and 1468, the wall was expanded to protect the region from the northeast as well, against attacks from Jianzhou Jurchens (who were later to become known as the Manchu people). Although similar in purpose to the Great Wall of China, this "Liaodong Wall" was of a lower-cost design. While stones and tiles were used in some parts, most of the wall was in fact simply an earth dike with moats on both sides.

Despite the Liaodong Wall, the Jurchens conquered Liaodong, or eastern Liaoning, in the early 17th century, decades before the rest of China fell to them. The Jurchen dynasty, styled "Later Jin" before being renamed to Qing, established its capital in 1616–1621 in Xingjing (兴京), which was located outside of the Liaodong Wall in the eastern part of the modern Liaoning Province. It was moved to Dongjing (east of today's Liaoyang, Liaoning), and finally in 1625 to Shengjing (now, Shenyang, Liaoning). Although the main Qing capital was moved from Shengjing to Beijing after it fell to the Qing in 1644, Shengjing retained its importance as a regional capital throughout most of the Qing era.

The Qing conquest of Liaoning resulted in a significant population loss in the area, as many local Chinese residents were either killed during fighting, or fled south of the Great Wall, many cities being destroyed by the retreating Ming forces themselves. As late as 1661, the Civil Governor (Fuyin) of Fengtian Province, Zhang Shangxian reported that, outside of Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang, and Haicheng, all other cities east of the Liao River were either abandoned, or hardly had a few hundred residents left. In the Governor's words, "Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants". West of the Liao, only Ningyuan, Jinzhou, and Guangning had any significant populations remaining.

In the latter half of the seventeenth century (starting with laws issued in 1651 and 1653), the imperial Qing government recruited migrants from south of the Great Wall (notably, from Shandong) to settle the relatively sparsely populated area of Fengtian Province (roughly corresponding to today's Liaoning). Many of the current residents of Liaoning trace their ancestry to these seventeenth century settlers. The rest of China's Northeast, however, remained officially off-limits to Han Chinese for most of the Manchu era. To prevent the migration of Chinese to those regions (today's Jilin and Heilongjiang, as well as the adjacent parts of Inner Mongolia), the so-called Willow Palisade was constructed (c. 1638 – c. 1672). The Palisade encircled the agricultural heartlands of Fengtian, running in most areas either somewhat outside the old Ming Liaodong Wall, or reusing it, and separating it from the Manchu forests to the northeast and the Mongol grazing lands to the northwest.

Later on, the Qing government tried to stop the migrants flow to Fengtian or even to make some settlers return to their original places of residence – or, failing that, to legalize them. For example, an edict issued in 1704 commented on the recent Han Chinese settlers in Fengtian having failed to comply with earlier orders requiring them to leave, and asked them either to properly register and join a local defense group (保; bao), or to leave the province for their original places within the next ten years. Ten years later, naturally, another edict appeared, reminding of the necessity to do something with illegal migrants ... In any event, the restrictive policy was not as effective as desired by the officials in Beijing, and Fengtian's population doubled between 1683 and 1734.

During the Qing Dynasty, Manchuria was ruled by three generals, one of whom, the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn) ruled much of modern Liaoning. In 1860, the Manchu government began to reopen the region to migration, which quickly resulted in Han Chinese becoming the dominant ethnic group in the region.
Main agricultural products of Liaoning include maize, sorghum, and soybeans. The region around Dalian produces three-quarters of China's exported apples and peaches. Cotton is also produced.

Liaoning's fruits include apples from Dalian and Yingkou, golden peaches from Dalian, pears from Beizhen of Jinzhou, white pears from Huludao and Suizhong, and apricots and plums from Gushan of Dandong.
Anshan Normal University lists 86 programs for international students on this site: 41 bachelor, 13 master's, 32 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 86 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.

13 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

anshan-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Anshan Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Anshan, register at Anshan Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Beihang University lies in Haidian, the northwestern district of Beijing that is home to a cluster of famous campuses. Its official supervisor is the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, not the Education Ministry, and that single fact hints at its character: this is a university created to serve the aircraft and space industries. The central government has placed it in three flagship funding schemes, namely Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction.

The story starts in 1952, when the school opened as Beijing Aeronautics College (北京航空学院). Rather than growing from scratch, it was put together by pulling out the aerospace engineering departments of eight leading universities of the day. Peiyang, Tsinghua, Xiamen, Sichuan and Chongqing universities were among the donors. Four decades later, in April 1988, it was renamed Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics (BUAA). Chinese commentators sometimes group it with the "Seven Sons of National Defence", the universities that work most closely with the military-industrial sector.

What should an applicant take from this? Beihang is a research-intensive engineering school. It has broadened over the years, but flight, space and their supporting technologies still define it. Its research infrastructure includes a national laboratory, nine national key laboratories (four of them in defence technology), six national engineering centres and three Beijing Advanced Innovation Centres. Over 40 of its research results were the first of their type in China, and it has collected top-level national science and technology prizes more than 70 times.

The rest of this profile covers the university's past, the campuses, research and student numbers, symbols and traditions, notable alumni, and then Beijing itself, including its buildings, geography, seasons and air.

beihang-university.h: Why China needed a dedicated school

blocks.x: Beihang calls itself the first higher-education institution of the new China devoted to aerospace, and the training ground for many of the country's early aircraft engineers. The state has treated it as a priority from the beginning. It was in the first group of national key universities in 1959, in the first group admitted to Project 211 in 1997, and in the first batch of "world-class" Class A universities in 2017. One line of the source mentions a national ranking between seventh and tenth, but the sentence is garbled, so please verify rankings on the university's own site. Other schemes that include Beihang are Project 985, Project Everest, Project 111 and the outstanding engineering education programme.

Eight institutions gave up their flight-related teaching units. They were Tsinghua, Peiyang, Northwestern Polytechnic College (now Northwestern Polytechnical University), Xiamen University, the engineering faculty of North China University (which became the Beijing Institute of Technology), Southwest Industrial College (today's Chongqing University), Sichuan University and Yunnan University.

The reason so many were needed goes back to how weak aviation education still was. Feng Ru flew the first Chinese-built aeroplane in 1909, only five years after the Wright brothers, yet the industry never took off because of conservative attitudes and unrest. The invasion crises of the early 1930s (the 18 September Incident and the January 1932 fighting around Shanghai) taught a bitter lesson, and people began to talk of "saving the nation through the air". Young Chinese went abroad to Europe and America to study the field, came home, created departments and began training domestic talent. The earliest aeronautical engineering programme in the country was set up at Tsinghua in 1934, as a department inside the mechanical engineering section of the engineering faculty.

The Japanese war and its aftermath left the field thin. By the mid-1940s only a few schools offered aerospace departments: Tsinghua, Peiyang, Jiaotong, Zhejiang and Xiamen. After 1949 the new government wanted an aviation industry, and the nationwide restructuring of universities that started in 1951 began pooling these small departments.

The first step came in March 1951. The Party Central Committee merged the aeronautics departments of Tsinghua, Peiyang, the Northwestern Engineering Institute and Xiamen into one aeronautical engineering faculty at Tsinghua. Yunnan University's department was folded into Sichuan University's. The former Central Industrial College (renamed Southwest Industrial College) and North China University pooled theirs to create the aeronautics department at the Beijing Institute of Technology.

Later that year, on 10 December, Premier Zhou Enlai called a meeting about shifting aviation from servicing aircraft to building them. Vice Premier Li Fuchun said bluntly that an aviation university was needed urgently, and Zhou accepted and issued the instruction.

The next move was in May 1952. The Ministry of Education drafted a plan to redistribute teaching groups across the country, following a Central Military Commission resolution on building the aviation industry that called for an aviation faculty. By 12 June, the Ministries of Heavy Industry and of Education had agreed to begin formal preparation for a Beijing school of aviation industry, with sign-off from the State Finance and Economic Commission and the military commission.

On 24 October 1952 the Education Ministry issued the licence. That date is why Beihang celebrates its anniversary in late October. Meanwhile, the flight departments of the former Central University, Zhejiang University and Jiaotong University formed the East China Institute of Aviation at Nanjing. It subsequently relocated to Xi'an, joined the Northwest Polytechnic Institute, and after another department was passed to Tsinghua these units became Northwestern Polytechnical University.

A site was picked in May 1953 at Boyanzhuang, in Haidian on the northwestern edge of Beijing. Ground was broken on 1 June, on fields dotted with graves and without roads. Crews worked day and night, and half a year later 60,000 square metres of buildings stood ready. In October, students, a group of professors and staff moved in and normal teaching started.

The planned construction was essentially done in 1957: 135,245 square metres of floor space, 64,160 square metres of paved roads and an outlay of more than 35.6 million yuan. Wu Guang took office in June 1954 as the first president.

beihang-university.h: Aircraft, missiles and a drone in a single year

blocks.x: In 1958 the university adopted a work-study approach, aiming to tie teaching closely to research, design and manufacturing. Teachers and students started building aircraft. A light passenger plane called "Beijing No. 1" was finished in just 100 days and approved by Zhou Enlai in person. It flew its first test on 24 September 1958, and later covered a 2,500 km test route between Beijing and Shanghai.

The same year brought two further firsts. "Beijing-2", described as the first missile of its kind in Asia, was fired successfully on 22 September at the Baichengzi range in the northeast. "Beijing 5" became China's first unmanned aircraft: the team fitted an An-2 with a home-built remote control system and turned it into a drone, which flew a successful test on 25 September, starting the country's drone work.
In May 1959 the Party Central Committee issued its decision naming a group of key universities, and Beihang was one of the first 16. That recognised its first seven years of work.

When the Cultural Revolution came, normal enrolment across China stopped and discipline in teaching collapsed. Beihang was no exception. For a time a Red Guard group, "Red Flag" Beihang, held sway on campus. Yet because of the school's special defence role, it carried less weight than other Beijing universities during the movement and still turned out research results, including unmanned reconnaissance aircraft.
Ignore them. The reliable point is that in April 1988, with the State Education Commission's approval, the Beijing Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics took the title of a university.
1989: named among 14 key universities in the Eighth Five-Year Plan period.
1997: among the first universities in Project 211.

August 2001: Beijing staged the 21st Universiade. Land on the southwest side of the campus was leased for the Universiade Village, which now provides student apartments, and a new gymnasium was built on campus that hosted volleyball.
September 2001: Beihang joined Project 985.

2006: the Beihang Art Museum was completed, permission was granted for the National Aeronautical Science and Technology Laboratory, and the educational and research building (the "new main building") came into use in the second half of the year. It is described as the largest teaching building in Asia.
2007: construction began at the Shahe campus, in Shahe Higher Education Park in Changping District. It was put into use in September 2010.
2008: the university's gymnasium staged the weightlifting events of the 29th Summer Olympics.
2010: Beihang joined the national scheme for training higher-level engineers.
2011: it became a Project Everest university.
2012: it was chosen in the first batch of the "2011 Program".

Beihang started as a narrow school for aviation science. After China's reform and opening-up it widened into a comprehensive institution that offers science, engineering, humanities and social subjects such as law, economics, management, education and philosophy. Its centre of gravity is still engineering, so applicants should expect a technical campus culture.

Thirty faculties and schools cover ten broad fields: engineering, science, management, arts and letters, law, economics, philosophy, education, medicine and art. What links them is a strong aerospace identity combined with engineering technology.
The numbers below date from 2017 and early 2017, so they are a snapshot rather than the current position. Please check recent figures with the university.
Active staff, October 2017: 3,907, of whom 2,147 were full-time teachers.
That last item comes with no explanation, so treat it carefully.

Students, March 2017: 30,642 in total. The breakdown quoted is 4,492 doctoral candidates, 9,336 master's students, 15,466 full-time undergraduate and graduate students, 1,218 international students, plus roughly 11,000 professional master's students.
The categories clearly overlap, but the takeaway is plain: a big university with many postgraduates and a visible international community.

Permission to build the National Laboratory of Aviation Science and Technology was granted in 2006, and the laboratory opened officially at the Shahe campus in 2014. Beihang's other well-known facilities include labs focused on aero-engine aerodynamics and heat, software development environments, virtual reality technology, aircraft control integration, reliability and environmental testing, and computational fluid dynamics.

In total there are 9 national key laboratories, 4 national engineering centres (the opening description gives 6, an inconsistency worth checking on the official site) and 66 provincial or ministerial key laboratories.
Beihang's library is said to be among the best-equipped in the world for aviation and astronautics literature, which matters if you plan to do research in those areas.

On campus grounds in Haidian stands the Beijing Air and Space Museum. The university set it up in 1985, originally as the Beijing Aviation Museum, and it welcomed the public from 1986. Its stated purpose is to back up teaching and to spread knowledge of aviation science and technology among ordinary people.

The exhibition space measures 8,300 square metres. Hetzel Design drew the building, which carries the name Futura Beijing City Air and Space Museum. Inside there are 18 interactive displays, 3 theatres and an astronaut education centre for children. A design puzzle was how to link the surrounding parks with the building. After trying many renderings, the architects made a bridge the heart of the structure and shaped the whole so that it seems to be lifting off like an aircraft.
The university took its present English name in 2002 and is regarded as one of the strongest engineering schools in China and a significant influence on its aviation and space industries.

Beihang's original home lies in northwest Beijing, outside the former Yuan-era city wall line and alongside the west side of Jiu'an Road. Planners split it into a teaching zone, a student residential zone and a staff family zone.

Lectures take place in the northeastern part. A road running through the middle bounds it on the west, and since 2003 the whole zone has been closed to cars. Staff families live along the west, occupying about a third of the campus, with a wall extending south to north and West Campus Road forming the eastern edge of that zone.

Student housing is in the north-central area. A landscaped campus park divides it into northern and southern halves, with 18 student apartment blocks in all. Outside the campus in the southwest corner are the Dayon Village apartments, which include blocks ranging from 1 to 10 floors and from 7 to 17 floors.

Four commercial towers around the perimeter belong to the university. Boyan Tower and Shining Tower stand in the northeast, while Zhizhen Tower and Vision Hotel are in the southeast. The campus's modern buildings have been listed as part of China's 20th Century Architectural Heritage.

Shahe is the newer site, located within Shahe Higher Education Park in Changping District, along the western edge of Bei Shahe Middle Road. It sits roughly 26 kilometres from Xueyuan Road. The mailing address is 9, South Third Street.

The site covers 970,000 square metres, with 620,000 square metres of planned floor area. Plans include 5 linked teaching buildings, 7 linked laboratory buildings and 4 student apartment blocks, plus integrated buildings containing banks and supermarkets. The campus also has a stadium, an engineering training centre, a canteen, key labs and a library. The first part opened in September 2010, and construction was continuing on the remainder when the description was written.

Because the campus lies farther from central Beijing, it is more secluded, with a pleasant setting. The two nearest Changping Line metro stops, Shahe and Shahe Higher Education Park, are each about 2 kilometres away. Getting downtown will take longer than from Xueyuan Road, so think about which campus your programme uses.

During the 2008 Olympics the university's stadium hosted weightlifting. Together with the Universiade of 2001, this means the campus has been a competition venue for two international sporting events.

beihang-university.h: Branches and partner sites outside Beijing

blocks.x: Most of these projects were reported as "under construction" in 2017 or 2018, so opening dates are probably out of date. Look at the university's international admissions pages for what is operating now.

The Hefei campus of the Hefei Innovation Research Institute was conceived as the first campus beyond Beijing. It is beside Shaokan Lake (Laoguchong Reservoir) in the Xinzhan Comprehensive Development Pilot Area of Yaohai District. The area of about 2,500 hectares would hold the research institute and an undergraduate faculty, with an opening targeted for 2018.

Qingdao has two entries. The research institute was Beihang's first institute outside the capital. Its address is No. 393 Songling Road, Laoshan District (postcode 266104). It was founded on 28 May 2016, relying chiefly on the State Key Laboratory of Virtual Reality Technology and Systems, started operating in 2017 and received its first graduate students that year.
Site data are as follows.
Park area: 63,990.6 square metres; total floor area 102,794.05 square metres.
Sports field: 3,600 square metres, with 2 basketball courts, a 5-a-side football pitch, a volleyball court and an equipment field.
Building 1: apartments for teachers and experts. Building 2: student apartments.
Building 3: virtual reality institutes on floors 6 and 7. Building 4: second floor holds the administrative offices of the Qingdao institute.
Building 5: a hub for teaching, student culture events and hands-on innovation.
Building 6: instrumentation and optoelectronics on floor 4, microelectronics on floor 5, new materials on floor 6, and an academic workstation on floor 7.

A larger Qingdao campus was planned in Blue Valley. It would cover 3,000 hectares and house eight schools, among them aerospace, materials science, smart manufacturing and microelectronics, with the first new students expected in 2019.
Suzhou Innovation Research Institute: in the High-Tech Zone of Huqiu District, Jiangsu. A contract was signed on 22 November 2017, an opening was set for 2018, and it may grow into a campus.
Chengdu Research Institute: in Chengdu Science City, Tianfu New District, Sichuan, with graduate training bases at Pengzhou and Luzhou. The opening was also planned for 2018.
Kunming Innovation Research Institute: in Kunming, Yunnan. Yunnan and Beihang signed a cooperation agreement on 22 November 2017.
Hangzhou Innovation Institute: an affiliated research institute in the Hi-Tech Zone, Binjiang District, Zhejiang.

Beihai College is an independent college co-run by Beihang and the Beihai municipal government in Yinhai District, Beihai, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. It started in 2005 and paused admissions in 2013. The Beihai city government reviewed it on 25 August 2017, and recruitment was expected to restart in 2018. A leading group headed by a Beihang vice president handles the college's administration.

Over the decades Beihang has answered to a succession of government departments all linked to aerospace. They were the First Ministry of Machinery Industry first, then the Third Ministry of Machinery and the Ministry of Aviation Industry; after those came the Ministry of Aerospace Industries and then the Commission for Science, Technology and National Defence Industries. The later line-up was the Ministry for Science, Technology and Industry for National Defence, the State Council and today's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

The present arrangement is vice-ministerial in level, with day-to-day management through the national defence science and technology administration. Four partners jointly develop the university: the Industry and Information Technology ministry, the Education ministry, the Academy of Engineering and the Beijing city government.

Funds for running the school have come straight from the state ever since its founding, and, given its research route, those allocations have been protected even when national finances were tight. The Ministry of Education's 2017 statistical compilation on university science and technology, published on 22 May 2018, shows that Beihang's research budget in 2016 was 2.70124 billion yuan, equal to 1.1668 million yuan per teaching and research staff member, the highest in China.

Opening day in 1952 gave the institute the title Beijing Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, already abbreviated "Beihang" in speech. The 1988 renaming produced the present Chinese form, and the English name then read Beijing Aeronautics and Astronautics University with the initials BUAA. The English title switched again in 2002 to "Beihang University", while BUAA stayed as the abbreviation. The calligraphy for today's Chinese name was done by Zhao Pochu in 1988 to mark the renaming.

The logo is based on two nested circles, meant to evoke harmony and an unbounded world, a layered yet unified idea of space and time. On top sits an upward double arrow, an abstract aerospace craft, accompanied by an open book, an elliptical satellite orbit and sparkling constellations. These elements together express the school's inner culture and its high-tech aerospace flavour.

There is deliberate contrast between the Chinese name and the English one. Zhao's brush lettering points to inheritance of a long cultural tradition, while the English wording shows a wish to become more international and modern.
The school colour is "Blue Technology" (#01519A). The university links it with openness, rigour, steadiness, enterprise and an attitude of reaching for the blue sky and exploring boldly.

Introduced in 2002, the flag uses a blue ground with white lettering or the reverse, and shows the logo above the school's name in Chinese and English. Copies have been carried into orbit on the Shenzhou 4 and Shenzhou 9 missions and on the first flights of the C919 airliner. Earlier flags are poorly documented. Footage of Beijing's 2001 Olympic bid shows a red flag with yellow characters, the logo at the upper left and "Beihang University" at the lower right. That lettering can still be found on the nearby office buildings, in a typeface nobody has identified.
On 13 May 2010 the school announced "Looking at the Stars" as its song.
Beihang's spirit is summed up in four ideas: hard work and plain living, diligence, all-round development and bold innovation.
Hard work and plain living means tackling difficult first-time tasks practically, speaking less and doing more.
Diligence is about studying with love for science and truth.
All-round development combines ethics with ability, good character with good marks, and understanding with action.
Bold innovation is perseverance, daring to explore and leading the way in pursuit of top standards.

The motto, "Integrate Virtue with Brilliance and Combine Knowledge with Practice", works as a conduct code for staff and students alike. The first half puts character ahead of skill. The university says it wants to produce talent for the Party and the nation, balanced across moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour education. The second half asks students to look for truth in their studies and have the nerve to turn ideas into action, applying learning to real problems, working for the country in aeronautics and astronautics, filling strategic national needs and helping achieve the "Chinese Dream" of national rejuvenation.
A separate honour: on 25 February 2021 the university's Bureau of Poverty Alleviation received a national "Advanced Collection" title at a national conference summarising poverty-reduction work.

25 October is the school's birthday, the date of its 1952 founding. There is no day off, so students tend to organise a "campus anniversary carnival" during the nearest weekend, with schools and student clubs taking part. The source text breaks off in mid-sentence, so ask current students what actually happens.

beihang-university.h: Beijing as a place to live

blocks.x: A student's daily routine depends heavily on the city outside the campus gate. The sections below move to Beijing: its building styles, terrain, climate and air.

Visitors will see three main kinds of architecture. Imperial buildings include the Tian'anmen gate, the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven, with Tian'anmen the best-known emblem of the People's Republic. Then there is the "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to 1970s, often blocky and not always well built. Finally come contemporary landmarks, with the CCTV Headquarters in the eastern CBD, the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Construction has boomed since the early 2000s, with international designers contributing in many styles, especially in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s industrial design with neo-futurist touches. The tallest tower is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, given once a year to a single tall building worldwide, twice since 2007: the Linked Hybrid (2009) and the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

A siheyuan is a house built around a courtyard, and the better-known ones include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Alleys called hutongs link the courtyards. They usually run east-west so that front doors face north or south, a placement favoured in Feng Shui, and some are narrow enough that only a few people can walk side by side.

They used to be everywhere, but entire blocks are being replaced by high-rises. Hutong residents have the right to new flats no smaller than their old homes, though many say community spirit and street life cannot be rebuilt. Most of these homes are government owned.

Beijing sits at the top of the triangular North China Plain, which spreads out to the south and east. Mountains on three sides protect the city and the farmland of the north from desert steppe. Yanqing and Huairou in the northwest are Jundu Mountain country, and the western boundary is Xishan, the Western Hills. The Great Wall follows the rugged ridges in the north, originally to repel horse-riding raiders. The highest summit, Mount Dongling (2,303 metres, or 7,556 ft), is in the Western Hills on the Hebei border.

Rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma belong to the Hai River system and run southeast. Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the largest reservoir. Beijing also marks the northern end of the 1,400-year-old Grand Canal from Hangzhou, and the terminus of the South-North Water Transfer Project, which has brought Yangtze basin water north over the past decade.

The built-up city occupies the south-central plains at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) elevation, a smallish and growing proportion of the municipality. Ring roads spread outward like ripples. The Second Ring follows the line of the old walls, and the Sixth Ring joins satellite towns. At the heart lie Tian'anmen Square and Tian'anmen, just south of the Forbidden City where emperors lived. Zhongnanhai, the current leadership compound, is just to the west, and Chang'an Avenue slices between the gate and the square to form the main east-west axis.
Locals describe the city's outward growth as "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), a pattern often blamed for Beijing's urban difficulties.

Technically Beijing is classed as humid continental (Köppen Dwa), shading into monsoonal cold semi-arid (BSk). Summers bring heat and humidity from the East Asian monsoon. Winters are short, frigid and dry, thanks to the huge Siberian high. In spring, dust can blow in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe; temperatures climb fast and the days are mostly dry. Autumn is another in-between season with little rain.

Records for 2001 to 2026 put the warmest stretch in early August and the coldest in early January. The official Chinese seasonal calendar starts spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. Recent warming has been faster in March and September and slower in May and October, so autumn usually comes out shorter than spring.

For 1991 to 2020 the average yearly temperature in the built-up area is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Daily lows average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily highs 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).

Suburbs at lower altitude run slightly cooler: yearly mean 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In the mountains the mean sits between 0 and 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), lower with height.

January averages -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Yearly precipitation totals about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), or 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three-quarters of it falls between June and August. Sun is possible for 42% of daylight in July and 62% in January and February, giving 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. The extreme readings since 1951 span from -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), recorded on 22 February 1966, to 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.
Practical advice: bring serious winter clothes, prepare for muggy summers and expect windy, dusty springs.
Air quality comes up constantly in conversations about studying in Beijing, so here is the background.

The city has struggled with environmental trouble for a long time. Its built-up area quadrupled in size between 2000 and 2009. That did more than add emissions; it altered local weather, lowering surface reflectivity, wind speed and ground-level humidity while raising surface and near-surface temperatures, vertical air mixing and ozone. With fossil fuels burned on top of fast urbanisation, serious pollution results, and many residents suffer health problems.

The year 2013 brought a huge smog episode across Beijing and most of northern China, touching 600 million people. The "pollution shock" made air quality a central economic and social concern nationwide. Beijing responded with new measures, such as cutting coal's share of its energy from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, while the central government ordered the removal of the dirtiest vehicles from 2015 to 2017 and pushed harder on clean energy.

Joint American-Chinese research in 2006 found that much of Beijing's pollution is imported from neighbouring cities and provinces. Typically between 35 and 60% of the ozone comes from outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin have a particularly large effect, partly because summer winds blow from the south and southeast and the mountains to the north and northwest trap air.

Coal burning produces about 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and most of its nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been changing its coal-fired power stations to natural gas since 2012 and wants to hold yearly coal use to 20 million tons. It burned 26.3 million tons in 2011; 73% was for heat and electricity and the balance for industry.

Neighbours burn far more. Tianjin's consumption was projected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Hebei burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, which exceeds all of Germany, with only 30% used for power and a large share going into steel and cement. Coal-producing regions (Shanxi, Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi, where use has tripled since 2000) and Shandong power plants also contribute. By coal consumption, the four largest provinces are, in order, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

Four big coal-fired plants once supplied electricity and winter heat. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two others in March 2015, and Huaneng Thermal Power Plant was to follow in 2016. From 2013 to 2017 the city intended to cut 13 million tons of coal use and limit the total to 15 million tons for 2015.

Before the 2008 Summer Olympics, and to deliver on its pledge of clean air, Beijing spent nearly US$17 billion. During the Games it stopped all building-site work, closed many factories for good, shut industry in nearby regions for a time, closed some filling stations and halved traffic by allowing cars on alternate days by licence number. Fares for buses and the subway were lowered, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. The city also gathered 3,800 gas-powered buses, among the largest such fleets anywhere, and was the first Chinese city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

Officials have occasionally seeded clouds to induce rain before big occasions, such as the 60th anniversary parade of 2009, or to counter drought. Lately they favour temporary factory shutdowns and tighter limits on cars, which produced the "APEC blue" of APEC China 2014 and the "parade blue" of the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. The skies cleared dramatically for those events, then returned to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The first-ever smog alert was issued on 8 and 9 December 2015 and shut down most industry and many businesses. Another "red alert" followed later that month. In November 2016 the environmental protection bureau said that from 2017, older high-polluting cars could not be driven when red alerts apply to the city or adjacent regions.

After a "war on pollution" began in 2014, pollutant levels fell. Fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017, with more progress by 2020, mainly from replacing coal with natural gas and cleaning up polluting industry in the area. The annual mean of PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024 the city recorded just two heavy-pollution days, a record low and 96.6 percent below the 58 days of 2013. The air is therefore much improved, but not perfect.

With pollution as a concern, various bodies publish readings. Twenty-seven monitoring stations feed daily figures to the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) website, and the American Embassy posts hourly PM2.5 and ozone readings on Twitter. They measure different things by different standards, so BJEPB's pollution levels and health effects are typically lower than the embassy's. Compare several sources.

Dirty air does damage health: cardiovascular and respiratory illness rates in Beijing are clearly affected, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, emergency visits and even deaths. Anyone with asthma or lung disease should talk to a doctor before choosing the city.

Erosion of deserts in the north and northwest brings seasonal dust storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain artificially to reduce their effects. The first four months of 2006 saw at least eight storms, and one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before blowing on to Japan and Korea.

beihang-university.h: Four things to remember about Beihang

blocks.x: First, its mission. The university was built in 1952 to supply engineers for aviation, and everything from its funding line through the defence-related ministries to its space-flight flags reflects that purpose. If you want to study aerospace, aircraft control, software for complex systems or virtual reality, you are looking at a place with national laboratories in precisely those areas.

Second, its size and resources. With 30 faculties, 66 provincial or ministerial laboratories on top of the national ones, and a 2016 research budget of 2.70124 billion yuan, Beihang is a well-funded institution. Its library is described as among the best equipped in the world for aviation and astronautics.

Third, its geography. Two campuses in Beijing, Xueyuan Road in the city and Shahe about 26 kilometres to the north in Changping, give you very different daily lives. A wider network of institutes in Hefei, Qingdao, Suzhou, Chengdu, Kunming and Hangzhou was being developed when the source information was written.

Fourth, its place in national politics and policy. Beihang has been included, usually in the first group, in every major national excellence programme since 1959, and it is jointly supported by four partners, including the Beijing city government.

beihang-university.h: Which campus will you be on?

blocks.x: The text describes the two Beijing campuses so differently that it is worth asking your programme office early where your classes will be held.

Xueyuan Road is the classic urban campus, with a pedestrian teaching area (no vehicles since 2003), 18 student apartment blocks and nearby commercial towers. It is on the northwest side of the city, close to many other universities in Haidian.

Shahe is newer, larger on paper (970,000 square metres), and quieter. It houses the national aviation laboratory that opened in 2014. Metro stations on the Changping Line are about 2 kilometres away, which means you will probably want to allow for a longer walk or a short ride to the train.

When you read about other places, such as the Hefei or Qingdao sites, remember that they were described as projects. If a programme you are interested in is listed there, confirm with the university that students are actually enrolled and what housing exists.

beihang-university.h: Reading the dated material with care

blocks.x: Several numbers in this profile come from a 2017 snapshot: staff and student counts, the status of branch campuses, and the research budget year of 2016. Some statements are internally inconsistent, such as the number of national engineering centres (6 in one place, 4 in another) and the Cultural Revolution dates. A claim about Nobel Prize winners among the staff is stated without any explanation. Use the figures to understand scale and character, and check Beihang's own English-language pages for anything that affects an application or budget.

beihang-university.h: Living in Beijing: a short checklist

blocks.x: The longer sections above go into detail. Here is how they translate to everyday planning.
Winters are short but sharply cold: the January daily average in the urban area is -2.7 °C, and the all-time low since 1951 is -27.4 °C.
Summers peak in July at about 27.2 °C on average, and three-quarters of the 528 mm yearly rainfall falls between June and August.
Spring dust from the Gobi and occasional dust storms are normal. In the first four months of 2006 alone there were at least eight storms, so it makes sense to be prepared.
Air quality has improved a great deal since 2013, but the city still issues alerts. Compare readings from several sources and follow local rules on car use.

The city is organised in concentric ring roads, with Tian'anmen at the centre and the Second Ring Road following the old walls. Haidian, where Beihang's Xueyuan Road campus stands, is in the northwest of the city. The urban area is flat at 40 to 60 metres, while mountains lie to the north and west, and the Great Wall runs along ridges in the north of the municipality.

Beijing's architecture ranges from the Forbidden City and the Temple of Heaven to the modern CBD and the 798 Art Zone. Wandering a hutong gives a sense of old Beijing, though those alleys are disappearing. Beihang also has its own cultural events: the anniversary carnival on or near 25 October, and the university's art museum, completed in 2006, and air and space museum, open to the public since 1986.

Beihang University offers a serious engineering education tied to national priorities and funded accordingly, in a capital whose weather is demanding and whose air has become much cleaner than it was. Choose it if the subject match is strong, confirm your campus and programme details with the university, and prepare for the climate.
Beihang University lists 596 programs for international students on this site: 72 bachelor, 112 master's, 162 doctoral, 250 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 354 taught in Chinese, 242 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 35,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 35,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 42,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 42,000), according to the university's published fee table.
