International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

beihang-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beihang University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Beihang University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Beihua University (北华大学) is a public university in Jilin City, in the north-east Chinese province of Jilin, and the Jilin provincial government is its supervising authority. Its roots reach back to 1906. In 1999 three colleges were merged to form the present university, which now operates on three campuses. Together the campuses cover 1,263,700 square metres (13,602,000 square feet), with up to 830,300 square metres (8,937,000 square feet) of floor space inside the buildings.

beihua-university.h: Jilin City, where the campus is

blocks.x: Your daily routine as a student will be shaped by the city itself, including the weather, the transport links and the leisure options. This part describes Jilin City, home of Beihua University.

beihua-university.h: Location and the mountains around it

blocks.x: Jilin City is in central Jilin Province, between longitudes 125° 40' and 127° 56' E and latitudes 42° 31' and 44° 40' N. It shares borders with the following prefecture-level areas:
Harbin in Heilongjiang, to the north
Changchun and Siping, to the west
Yanbian, to the east
Liaoyuan, Tonghua and Baishan, to the south

The city lies in hilly country beside the Songhua River. Four well-known mountains ring it: North Mountain (Beishan) on the west, Long Tan Mountain on the east, Zhuque Mountain on the north and Turtle Mountain on the south. Together with the Songhua River they are said to form a bagua within a Taiji pattern. North Mountain is the most celebrated, with several Buddhist temples on it, and it is reported that the Qianlong Emperor once visited.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), affected by the monsoon, with a full cycle of four seasons. Winter lasts five months, from November through March, and brings cold, wind and dryness courtesy of the Siberian anticyclone; in January the mean is −15.4 °C (4.3 °F). The shoulder seasons of spring and autumn are brief and mainly dry and windy, with some precipitation. Summer turns hot and sticky, and the East Asian monsoon sends the wind from the south-east. The mean for July is 23.3 °C (73.9 °F). Winter snow is generally light, and most of the year's rain falls between June and August.
Plan for serious cold from November to March, and expect the heaviest rain in high summer.

A series of blasts at Jilin City's No. 101 Petrochemical Plant on 13 November 2005 left six people dead. They seriously polluted the Songhua River: about 100 tons of pollutants, benzene and nitrobenzene among them, got into the water. At one point the benzene level was 108 times the national safety limit. Major cities downstream, among them Harbin, Songyuan and Khabarovsk, stopped their water supply for almost a week. The pollutants eventually reached the Amur (Heilong) River, which forms much of the border between China and Russia, and Chinese leaders later had to apologise to the Russian government for how the incident was handled.

During the summer 2010 floods in China, Jilin was among the hardest-hit regions for rain and landslides. On 28 July 2010 floodwater swept thousands of barrels of toxic chemicals out of two Jilin chemical plants and into the Songhua River. The barrels held substances such as trimethylsilyl chloride and hexamethyldisiloxane, with about 170 kg of poisonous material in each, and some were reported to have exploded on contact with water. By the late afternoon of 1 August, 6,387 barrels had been pulled out of the river. Officials said tests showed the river water was still safe to drink. Three PLA soldiers stationed in Jilin lost their lives by drowning while they worked on taking out the barrels and holding back the flood.

The Dahe Dam in Changshan Township burst on 28 July, releasing 4 million cubic metres of water that wrecked five villages downstream and left 40 people dead or missing. In all, floods across Jilin prefecture left over a hundred people dead or missing. After the Songhua surged to twice its normal level, workers began repairing 51 damaged small reservoirs and strengthening riverbanks in the province.

Every winter, visitors come to Jilin City to admire the rime ice (雾凇, also written 霧凇) that coats the trees along the Songhua River. No other river in the region stays free of ice in winter, but the Songhua does. The rime ice forms every January and February: water vapour rises from the warm river, meets cold night air of around −20 °C (−4 °F) and crystallises on willow branches.
Places worth a visit include:
The Meteorite Museum, which has the largest stony meteorite from a documented fall
North Hill (Beishan) Park in the north-west of the city
Dragon Pool Mountain Park
Songhua Lake, south-east of the city

Wulajie Old City (乌拉街, once also transcribed Wulakai), at 44°05′N 126°28′E. It is a walled town from the Qing dynasty in Longtan District, on the Sungari River's eastern bank below the main built-up area. Local goods for the imperial court were collected here under the Qing. Ferdinand Verbiest described Wulajie (Ula) in 1682 as the province's most illustrious city, and the Kangxi Emperor visited personally to go sturgeon fishing. Today a nearby public school is one of the few in China that teaches some Manchu.

When it gets cold, locals ski, skate, sledge and snowboard, and winter swimming is a widely popular habit among residents. The ski resorts are Beidahu, Lake Songhua, North Hill (北山滑雪场), Zhuque Hill and Wujiashan, and there is also the Filibiin swimming resort.

Secondary schooling is provided by Ararsame Second High School, Jilin Yuwen High School and Jilin City No. 1 High School. Beyond Beihua University itself, the city has Jilin Medical College, Jilin Agriculture University, Northeast Dianli University and Jilin Institute of Chemical Technology.

The former airport, Ertaizi (IATA: JIL, ICAO: ZYJL), shared its runway between civil and military use. Commercial service there ended on 3 October 2005, when airlines shifted to Changchun Longjia International Airport, newly opened. That airport lies about 76 km (47 miles) from Jilin City, and many destinations are reachable from it. China Southern Airlines also operates some international connections directly from Changchun.

The city's railway station sits on the Changchun-Tumen mainline, which runs east to west, and offers easy journeys to cities such as Beijing, Tianjin, Dalian, Jinan and Hangzhou. For Harbin, Changchun and Shenyang there are frequent, handy services over the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway and the spur that connects Changchun with Jilin.
Main routes are China National Highway 202 and the G12 Hunchun-Ulanhot Expressway.
Student life is influenced by the wider province as well as the campus, so this part turns to Jilin Province.

beihua-university.h: Who lived here and who ruled

blocks.x: In ancient times the area was home to the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and the Wùjí (勿吉). Parts of it fell under the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo. Control then passed from one power to the next: the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo and Balhae, followed by the Khitan Liao, the Jurchen Jin and the Mongol Yuan. Under the Qing most of it was run by an official known as the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose command stretched to cover most of today's Primorsky Krai in Russia.

Primorsky Krai went to Russia in 1860, and from that point the authorities encouraged Han Chinese settlers, the majority from Shandong, into the area. Around 1900 the Han were already its largest ethnic group. In 1932 the area became part of Manchukuo, a puppet state created by Japan, and Changchun (then known as Xinjing), today's provincial capital, became Manchukuo's capital. When Japan was defeated in 1945, the Red Army took Jilin after Operation August Storm. The Soviet Union then handed the region and the rest of north-east China to the Communists, and From Manchuria, the Communists then advanced to win the rest of China during the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949 Jilin province was smaller, taking in only the surroundings of Changchun and Jilin City, with Jilin City as capital while Changchun was a municipality outside the province. It reached its current borders in the 1950s. Another enlargement came in the Cultural Revolution, when a piece of Inner Mongolia was added and Jilin briefly touched Mongolia; this was later undone.

More recently Jilin, like the rest of heavy-industry Northeast China, has faced economic difficulties during privatisation, which led the central government to start a campaign called "Revitalize the Northeast".

Jilin is in the middle of north-eastern China, with Russia to the east and North Korea to the south-east. The province has an area of 190,000 km2 (73,000 sq mi) and 24 million inhabitants. Its capital Changchun is 113 km (70 miles) west of Jilin City. Of 136 mineral types found here, 70 are being extracted. Traditional Chinese medicine materials are plentiful as well: roughly 27,000 wild plant types and 9,000 medicinal herb types.
Large deposits of gold, silver, iron, nickel, molybdenum, talc, graphite, gypsum and cement rock lie underground, along with oil, gas and coal, and no other province has as much oil shale.

The land is highest in the south-east and slopes gently down to the north-west. Crossing the south-east are the Changbai Mountains, where the province's tallest summit, Paektu Mountain, rises to 2,744 m (9,003 ft). The Jilinhada, Zhang Guangcai and Longgang Mountains are other ranges.

In the far south-east the Yalu and Tumen rivers drain the land and together form part of the border between China and North Korea. Tributaries of the Liao River drain the south-west, and the Songhua and Nen rivers drain the north and both finally flow into the Amur.

Jilin has a northerly continental monsoon climate. Winters are cold and drawn out, summers warm but brief, and January temperatures typically sit between −20 and −14 °C (−4 to 7 °F). Rainfall averages from 350 up to 1,000 mm (13.8 to 39.4 inches).
The main cities are Changchun and Jilin City, plus Yanji, Siping, Tonghua, Baishan, Baicheng, Songyuan and Liaoyuan.

Jilin's nominal GDP in 2025 was RMB 1,497.4 billion, or US$209.6 billion. That equals RMB 64,618 (US$9,046) per head. GDP has been growing at double-digit rates since 2003, rising 51 per cent between 2003 and 2007. Compared with 2005 figures, the added value of large enterprises grew 19 per cent and their profits grew 30 per cent.

Farming centres on rice, wheat, maize and sorghum. Eastern areas such as Yanbian Prefecture grow most of the rice. The Changbai Mountains supply significant amounts of lumber. In the west, around Baicheng for example, sheep herding is important.

Jilin has the largest shale oil reserves, and one of the five biggest mineral reserves in China. Several minerals are present in unusually large quantities relative to other provinces: kieselguhr, floatstone, wollastonite and molybdenum. Its industries focus on cars, railway carriages and iron alloy. It is one of China's key commodity grain bases and ranks sixth in timber output. The province has long been a pharmaceutical centre, and its harvests of ginseng and deer antlers, widely used in Chinese medicine, are among China's largest.

Jilin New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone: set up in 1992 in Jilin City. The planned area is 818 km2 (316 sq mi), of which 242 km2 (93 sq mi) has been built. Leading industries are new materials, refined chemicals, photoelectronics integrated with machinery, electronics, medicine and bioengineering. Songhua Lake is only 14 km (8.7 miles) away, and bus and train stations are no more than 3 km (1.9 miles) distant.

Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone: founded in May 1998 in the north-east of Jilin City with a planned total area of 28 km2 (11 sq mi). Changchun is 90 km (56 miles) away. The zone lies 5 km (3.1 miles) from Jilin Airport and 8 km (5.0 miles) from the railway station. Its main industries are refined chemicals, bioengineering and fine processing of chemical fibre and farm products. It has four parts: the Chemical, Food, Textile and Medical Industrial Parks. The Medical Industrial Park concentrates on traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals, small-molecule medicine, biopharmaceuticals and health products.

Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone (CETDZ): the state approved it as a national-level zone in 1993. It spans 112.72 km2 (43.52 sq mi) altogether, and 30 km2 (12 sq mi) of that is allocated for development. By the end of 2006 fixed-asset investment totalled 38.4 billion yuan, and the zone had 1,656 registered enterprises, 179 of them foreign-funded. Regional gross product was 101.8 billion yuan, industrial output 233.0 billion yuan and financial revenue 15.7 billion yuan.

Changchun High-Tech Industrial Development Area: four roads and one light-rail line join it to downtown, with Changchun Station a twenty-minute light-rail ride away. It earned ISO 14001 environmental certification in 2002, the first in Northeast China, and 38 per cent of it is landscaped.

Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone: the zone received national-level border status in 1992 and is planned to cover 24 km2 (9.3 sq mi). It contains the Hunchun Export Processing Zone and the Hunchun Sino-Russia Trade Zone, which were set up in 2002 and 2001. Its location at the meeting point of the Chinese, Russian and Korean borders is strategic, and it focuses on seafood processing, electronics, biopharmaceuticals, textiles and other industries.

Hunchun Export Processing Zone: it lies within the border zone's 5 km2 (1.93 sq mi) area, with a planned size of 2.44 km2 (0.94 sq mi), and it relies on the infrastructure and policy framework of the zone that contains it.

Changchun is also home to one of the biggest CRRC factories for bullet trains. In November 2016 CRRC Changchun showed off the world's first bullet-train carriages with sleeper berths that can also run in ultra-low temperatures. Nicknamed "Panda", they travel at 250 km/h, operate at −40 °C, have Wi-Fi hubs and have sleeping berths that fold into seats in the daytime.

The province is home to Han Chinese, Manchu, Hui, Mongol and Xibe communities. Most ethnic Koreans are in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture, and they make up about 4 per cent of the population because of the closeness of the Korean Peninsula. Manchus were once the majority here, since the area belongs to their historic homeland, but as they have adopted Han culture and Chinese languages the Manchu language is now regarded as critically endangered. The population figures leave out active-service members of the People's Liberation Army.

As a Northeast China province, Jilin has cultural features in common with its neighbours, including Errenzhuan and Yangge. Jilin Opera (Jiju) is its own invention, a traditional entertainment form created during a fairly short history of migration. Jilin's ethnic Koreans, meanwhile, keep a distinctive culture with close ties to Korea.
Most people in the province speak Mandarin, China's official language. Many in the east speak Korean, and some people in Qian Gorlos autonomous county speak Mongolian.

beihua-university.h: Places to visit in the province

blocks.x: At Ji'an, Goguryeo remains such as Hwando Mountain City, Gungnae City and the pyramid-shaped Tomb of the General make up part of a World Heritage Site named Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom.
Paektu Mountain and in particular Heaven Lake, on the border with North Korea, attract visitors for their natural beauty.
Balhae royal tombs lie in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture: these are the Ancient Tombs at Longtou Mountain, which include the Mausoleum of Princess Jeonghyo.

beihua-university.h: Universities and colleges in the province

blocks.x: Jilin has many institutions. In Changchun and elsewhere they include:
Jilin University (吉林大学), Northeast Normal University (东北师范大学), Jilin Normal University (吉林师范大学), Jilin Agricultural University (吉林农业大学) and Jilin Medical College (吉林医药学院)

In Changchun: Changchun University (长春大学), Changchun Normal University (长春师范大学), Changchun Institute of Technology (长春工程学院), Changchun University of Technology (长春工业大学), Changchun University of Science and Technology (长春理工大学), Changchun Taxation College (长春税务学院), Changchun Institute of Post & Telecommunications (长春邮政学院) and the Changchun Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics
Yanbian University (延边大学) and Yanbian University of Science and Technology (延边科技大学)
Other institutions: Beihua University, Jilin Agricultural Science and Technology University, Jilin College of Electrification and the Northeast China Institute of Electric Power Engineering (东北电力学院)
Jilin's teams include the Jilin Northeast Tigers in the Chinese Basketball Association, Changchun Yatai in the Chinese Super League and Yanbian Longding in China League One.
Beihua University lists 132 programs for international students on this site: 64 bachelor, 64 master's, 4 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 132 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 19,000 to CNY 29,000 (median CNY 21,000), according to the university's published fee table.

132 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

Beihua University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

beihua-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beihua University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jilin City, register at Beihua University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

beijing-film-academy.h: Beijing Film Academy at a glance

blocks.x: Beijing Film Academy (BFA, in Chinese 北京电影学院) is a municipal public college in the Chinese capital. It is affiliated with the City of Beijing, and three bodies co-fund it: the municipal government, the National Radio and Television Administration, and the Ministry of Education.

Its roots go back to 1950 and a small body called the Research Institute of Performing Arts of the Central Film Bureau. A series of renamings followed, in 1951 and 1953, and the present name was adopted in 1956 when the school was restructured as an academy.

beijing-film-academy.h: From a small acting institute to a full film academy

blocks.x: The academy opened in May 1950 as an institution for performance art under the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Culture. Thirty-eight students enrolled in that first year. Over the next five years the name changed three times. It was renamed in July 1951 as a film school under the same bureau, became Beijing Film School in March 1953, and received its final title, Beijing Film Academy, on 1 June 1956. Different accounts word the earliest titles slightly differently, so check the academy's own history page if the exact wording matters to you.
At the beginning there were two schools, one for photography and one for animation, each with its own departments and specialties. Screenwriting was among the earliest departments, formed in 1951.

Performing arts came first. On 14 September 1950 the academy launched its first undergraduate course, in acting, for a class of 30 students, many of whom became notable figures in film and television. That success led to the Performance Institute being created in June 1956.

Sound recording followed a similar path. Teaching began in 1952, the sound recording department was officially founded in 1959, and the following year it merged with the School of Engineering. Management also grew from a small start, with a two-year course on managing film and television production that opened in September 1955. Only 28 students graduated from the first class, but its popularity grew and a formal Department of Management came into being in 1987.

The Cultural Revolution, which began in 1966, was hard on schools across China, and BFA was no exception, since many professors left. Faculty began coming back at the start of 1976, after the Cultural Revolution ended. By 1977 the academy had recovered, and in 1978 it was again allowed to admit new students.

The International School was created in 1989, and the Information Research Center followed in October 1999. Individual departments kept building too. Screenwriting started a master's course in 1985, added an undergraduate program in film theory in 1987, and opened doctoral courses in 2004.

BFA offers associate, bachelor's and master's degrees across the film world: script writing, film theory, film directing, film and television production, film acting, film and television art design, advertising, animation, sound art, cinematography, photography and entertainment management. Besides full-time degrees it runs three other kinds of study, namely correspondence courses, night school courses and vocational courses.

Presently the academy is made up of nine schools. They are the Management School, the International Studies School, the Continuing Education School, the Audio-Visual Arts and Communication School, the Animation School, the Photography School, the Fine Arts School, the Sound School and the Performing Arts School.

The curriculum is also organised into departments. The English summary of these is rather muddled, so treat what follows as a rough guide and confirm exact names on the academy's own website. Departments mentioned are Film and TV Technology (also called the Digital Media Institute, covering digital film and television technology), Film Directing, Film Theory (film studies), Management (film production management and distribution), Photography (cinematography), Screenwriting and Cinema Studies (film screenwriting), and Sound Recording. A department for basic education is also listed alongside Sound Recording.

beijing-film-academy.h: Getting in: how competitive it is

blocks.x: Admission to BFA is among the hardest in China and, by common description, globally. More than 40,000 candidates apply each year to sit the entrance exams, and only 400 to 500 are accepted. Most of the admissions process happens in February and March. Candidates sit subject tests and the National Humanities Examination, and acting applicants usually face the stiffest competition of all.

If you are an international applicant, the route in is the International Training Center. In 2013 the academy ran its first undergraduate film production program taught in English. It was delivered by the cinematography department and focused on cinematography, directing and post-production. If English-language study matters to you, ask the international office which programs are currently offered in English.

Put in plain numbers, 400 to 500 places for more than 40,000 applicants means roughly one successful candidate for every 80 to 100 who apply. Because most of the process takes place in February and March, applicants who want to compete seriously should prepare well before the start of the year and confirm current dates and requirements directly with the academy.

Graduates of BFA have earned national and international recognition for more than forty years, as directors, producers, screenwriters, actors and actresses. Among recent graduates, most of the best-known are performers, with a few directors.

Older alumni are chiefly directors of what Chinese film history calls the fourth, fifth and sixth generations. Among fourth-generation directors the best known are Zhang Nuanxin, Teng Wenji, Wu Yigong and Wu Tianming. The fifth generation produced three especially famous names, Zhang Yimou, Chen Kaige and Tian Zhuangzhuang, all graduates of BFA. Other famous Chinese filmmakers from the academy include Teng Congcong, Wei Lian, Huang Jianxin, Cao Cuifen, Li Qiankuan, Ding Yinmeng, Ni Zhen, Zheng Dongtian, Hu Mei, Xie Fei, Huang Shuqin, Chen Qiang and Xie Tian. Turning to the sixth generation, the directors most often named are Zhang Yuan, Wang Xiaoshuai and Jia Zhangke.

The Chinese-American filmmaker Dayyan Eng transferred into the Directing Department, and after graduating he won awards at the Cannes and Venice film festivals. Ai Weiwei, today known as an artist and activist, studied animation here.

A film student's days are shaped by the city outside the classroom: the weather, the air, how the streets are laid out and what the neighbourhoods look like. This part of the profile describes Beijing, where Beijing Film Academy is based.

Beijing's climate is classed as humid continental (Köppen Dwa), sitting close to the edge of the monsoonal cold semi-arid type (BSk). Summers are hot and sticky thanks to the East Asian monsoon, and winters are brief, cold and dry as air from the great Siberian high pressure system settles in. Spring brings fast warming and generally dry days, sometimes with sandstorms carried over from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe. Autumn is another in-between season with hardly any rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the warmest stretch was early August and the coldest early January.

By China's official seasonal calendar, 26 March opens spring, 20 May opens summer, 13 September opens autumn and 31 October opens winter. In recent years March and September have warmed up faster and May and October more slowly, so autumn in Beijing tends to be shorter than spring. Put simply, expect a short, bright autumn and a long, hot, humid summer.

The yearly average for urban Beijing over 1991 to 2020 is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Typical daily minimums run from 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and maximums from 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). Out in the lower suburbs the yearly average is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). Highland areas average between 0 and 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), cooler the higher you go. For a month-by-month picture, the daily mean in January is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F), against 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July.

Annual rainfall comes to about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), though Haidian and Chaoyang districts receive more, around 584.2 mm (23.00 in). Nearly three-quarters of it arrives between June and August. Sunshine, as a share of what is possible, is 42% in July and 62% in January and February, for a yearly total of 2,490.5 hours of bright sun. The coldest day on record since 1951 was 22 February 1966 at -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), and the hottest was 24 July 1999 at 41.9 °C (107.4 °F).

Beijing's air has a long record of problems. From 2000 to 2009 the built-up area grew fourfold, which pushed emissions up sharply and also altered the local meteorology, even apart from human emissions: near-surface wind speed, humidity and albedo fell, while surface and near-surface temperatures, ozone and the vertical dilution of air rose. With urban growth and fossil-fuel burning working together, serious environmental problems follow and many residents suffer health problems.

The turning point was the heavy smog of 2013, which covered Beijing and much of northern China and affected 600 million people. After that so-called pollution shock, air quality became a major economic and social worry nationwide. The Beijing government announced measures, including cutting coal from 24% of its energy mix in 2012 to 10% in 2017. Between 2015 and 2017 Beijing's central authorities also removed the dirtiest vehicles from circulation and intensified the change to clean energy sources.

Where does the pollution come from? A joint American and Chinese study in 2006 found that a large part drifts in from nearby cities and provinces, with 35 to 60% of the ozone originating outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin have a significant influence, partly because summer winds mostly blow from the south and southeast and mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent to keep the promise of cleaner air. During the Games construction sites stopped work, many Beijing factories closed for good, industry in nearby regions paused for a time, some gas stations shut, and traffic was halved by allowing cars on alternate days depending on whether the plate ends in an odd or even number. Bus and subway fares were cut, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. The city put together 3,800 natural-gas buses, one of the largest such fleets anywhere, and became the first Chinese city to require the equivalent of Euro 4 emission standards.

Coal is the biggest single factor, producing about 40% of the PM2.5 and most of the nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Beijing has been converting its coal-fired power stations to natural gas since 2012, with a target of capping yearly coal use at 20 million tons. For comparison, in 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons: 73% went to heating and power generation and the remainder to industry. Much of Beijing's pollution actually comes from its neighbours. Tianjin's coal use was expected to climb from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Hebei burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, with only 30% going to power and a large share to steel and cement. Coal-region power plants in Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (coal use there has tripled since 2000) and in Shandong add to it. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces in coal consumption.

Four large coal-fired plants once supplied the city's electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more shut in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was set to close in 2016. The city planned to cut coal use by 13 million tons between 2013 and 2017 and to hold it to 15 million tons in 2015.

Before major events the government has sometimes seeded clouds to encourage rain and clear the air, for example before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to ease drought. Lately it has relied more on temporary factory closures and tighter traffic limits, which produced the brief 'APEC blue' around APEC China 2014 and the 'parade blue' before the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved dramatically during those periods, then slipped back to unhealthy levels soon afterward.

Beijing's first smog alert was on 8 and 9 December 2015 and it closed most industry and commercial business, and another 'red alert' was issued later that month. The environmental protection bureau announced in November 2016 that from 2017 highly polluting old cars may not be driven whenever a smog red alert is in force in the city or nearby regions.

There has been real improvement since the 'war on pollution' began in 2014. Fine particulates fell 35% in 2017 and dropped further by 2020, chiefly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial facilities were cleaned up. The annual average PM2.5 concentration fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024 there were just two heavy-pollution days, the lowest ever recorded and down 96.6 percent from the 58 heavy days of 2013.

beijing-film-academy.h: Reading the numbers and handling dust

blocks.x: Different sources report different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) publishes daily figures from 27 monitoring stations around the city, while the US Embassy in Beijing tweets hourly ozone and PM2.5 figures. The two measure different pollutants using different criteria, so the bureau's pollution levels and health impact figures often look lower than the embassy's.

Smog is a health hazard. Polluted air has a direct and significant effect on how often people in Beijing suffer cardiovascular and respiratory disease, and heavy exposure can lead to breathing and heart trouble, emergency-room visits and even death.

Seasonal dust storms also plague the city, as dust from eroding deserts in the north and northwest blows in. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rainfall to fight them. At least eight storms struck in the opening four months of 2006, and a single storm in April 2002 dropped nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before heading on to Japan and Korea.

Beijing lies on the northern edge of the triangular North China Plain, which opens out to the south and east. Mountain ranges on three sides (north, northwest and west) protect the city and northern China's farmland from the advancing desert steppe. In the northwest of the municipality, particularly Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, and the Western Hills (Xishan) form the western boundary. The Great Wall was built over this rugged northern terrain to stop nomadic raids from the steppe. The highest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling in the Western Hills, on the border with Hebei, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma rivers are tributaries of the Hai River system and run southeast. The largest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. The Grand Canal to Hangzhou, dug more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route, ends here at its northern terminus, as does the South-North Water Transfer Project, completed in the past decade to bring in Yangtze basin water.

The urban core sits on plains in the south-centre of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and takes up a relatively small but growing fraction of the total area. Ring roads radiate outward in concentric circles. The innermost ring, the Second Ring Road, follows the course of the old city walls, while the outermost Sixth Ring Road links satellite towns in the suburbs. At the heart of the city, directly south of the Forbidden City where the emperors lived, lie Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square. West of the gate is Zhongnanhai, home of China's present leaders, and the main east-west axis is Chang'an Avenue, which passes between Tiananmen and the Square.

What does this mean for a student? Mountains and plain give Beijing a flat, easy-to-navigate centre ringed by hills, and the ring roads give you a simple way to understand where you are in relation to Tian'anmen.
Beijing's growth outward from its old centre is often called 'spreading like a pancake' (tan da bing), a pattern frequently given as a reason for the city's urban problems.

Beijing's architecture falls into three broad families. Imperial-style buildings are the oldest: the imposing Tian'anmen, which is the trademark building of the People's Republic, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. Then come the boxy 'Sino-Sov' structures of the 1950s to 1970s, some of them poorly built. Finally there is the modern generation, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east (the new CCTV Headquarters, for example) and also in places including the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the early 21st century, the city has seen a huge wave of new construction in styles brought by international designers, most strongly in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone is a place where 1950s buildings and neofuturistic design sit together, old beside new. The tallest tower is the 528-metre China Zun. Two Beijing buildings have taken the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which names a single best overall tall building worldwide every year: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

Siheyuan are courtyard homes with buildings around a central yard, and grand examples include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are usually linked by alleys known as hutongs, mostly straight and running east to west so doorways face north and south, which is good feng shui. Their width varies, and in some only a few pedestrians can squeeze through at a time. Once found everywhere in Beijing, siheyuan and hutongs are vanishing quickly as entire blocks are replaced with high-rises. Hutong residents are entitled to apartments in the new buildings at least as large as their old homes, but many complain that the old community feeling and street life cannot be rebuilt. The properties are often owned by the government.
The short version is that Beijing offers everything from imperial monuments to avant-garde towers, and you can see several centuries of building styles in a single afternoon.

Beijing Foreign Studies University, or BFSU (Beijing Waiguoyu Daxue), is a state university in Haidian District, in the north-west of Beijing. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and it is part of both Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction programme. It is best known as the capital's flagship language university.

BFSU is described as a sister institution of Peking University (PKU). Both fall under the Education Working Committee of Haidian District, and that shared affiliation shows up in practice: they cooperate on courses and degree programmes, and a former president of one has been appointed president of the other.

For applicants from abroad, this profile first explains where the university came from, how it is regarded and who has studied there, and then gives a long guide to Beijing, covering weather, air quality, geography and the built environment.

beijing-foreign-studies-university.h: From diplomats' school to broad international studies

blocks.x: BFSU was founded in 1941 and stayed under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs until the early 1980s. In those decades its job was to train diplomats and language specialists for China's foreign service. In the 1980s it widened its offer to include international studies and research. A more recent development is historical scholarship: the Institute for Global History opened in December 2014 to study how different parts of the world have interacted, and in December 2017 a School of History was created under Professor Li Xuetao. It teaches world and Chinese history from a global viewpoint and encourages multilingual, cross-cultural research.

The university's motto is to embrace diversity and pursue broad learning and earnest practice (in Chinese, jianrong bingxu, bo xue du xing). Premier Wen Jiabao suggested it in a letter of congratulations for BFSU's seventieth anniversary. It echoes the ideal of freedom of thought and compatibility associated with Cai Yuanpei during his time as president of Peking University, and it points to three qualities: a global outlook, openness to other cultures, and combining knowledge with practical action.
BFSU has been educating Chinese diplomats and civil servants for decades. Its graduates are a familiar presence in two ministries: Foreign Affairs and State Security.

BFSU is a research university with a speciality in foreign languages and is seen as one of the most distinguished in that field in China. Using Gaokao-based statistics for 2012 to 2023, it ranked 17th out of nearly 3,000 higher education institutions in the country. The Best Chinese Universities Ranking placed it top, in its latest edition, among institutions in China that specialise in languages. In the QS World University Rankings by Subject, it regularly appears in the world top 100 for linguistics, and other world rankings place it high in arts and humanities, modern languages, English language and literature, and education. Its International Business School is accredited by the Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business (AACSB), and that is a helpful quality mark for anyone thinking about studying management.

BFSU has produced many senior diplomatic officials and proudly calls itself the cradle of PRC diplomats. China Foreign Affairs University (CFAU), which has also trained hundreds of Chinese ambassadors, uses a very similar slogan about itself, and the students of both schools still enjoy a rivalry.

Your life outside the lecture hall is spent in Beijing, so this guide covers the city from its seasons to its streets.

Beijing has a humid continental climate (Koppen Dwa) that is close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (BSk). Summer is hot and humid under the East Asian monsoon. Winter is short, cold and dry, shaped by the vast Siberian anticyclone. In spring, dust may blow in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe while temperatures rise quickly and the weather stays dry. Autumn is another transitional season with very little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the warmest part of the year has been early August and the coldest early January.

Under the national calendar, Beijing's spring starts on 26 March, then summer arrives on 20 May, with autumn following on 13 September and winter on 31 October. Recent years have seen quicker warming in March and September and slower warming in May and October, so autumn is normally the shorter of the two shoulder seasons.

For the period 1991 to 2020 the mean annual temperature of the urban area is between 12.9 and 13.3 degrees C. Daily lows average 7.7 to 8.4 degrees C and highs 18.5 to 18.9 degrees C. The lower suburbs average 11.5 to 13.0 degrees C (lows 5.9 to 8.0, highs 18.2 to 18.7), and the mountains stay between 0 and 10 degrees C, getting colder with height. January's daily mean is minus 2.7 degrees C and July's is 27.2 degrees C.

Annual rainfall averages 528.0 millimetres, or 584.2 millimetres in Haidian and Chaoyang, and almost three-quarters falls between June and August. Possible sunshine is 42 per cent in July and 62 per cent in January and February; altogether the city has 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. Since 1951 the extremes have been minus 27.4 degrees C (22 February 1966) and 41.9 degrees C (24 July 1999).
Beijing's smog is the thing visitors worry about, so it is worth being precise.

The problem has deep roots. From 2000 to 2009 the built-up area of the city grew fourfold. That raised emissions, and it also changed the local weather: less surface reflectivity, slower wind and drier air at ground level, but warmer ground and air, weaker vertical mixing of the air and more ozone. Coupled with fossil-fuel burning, this left the city prone to serious pollution and health problems for residents. A heavy smog in 2013 covered Beijing and most of northern China and affected 600 million people. The shock turned air pollution into a major economic and social worry. Beijing responded by cutting coal from 24 per cent of its energy mix in 2012 to 10 per cent in 2017, while the central government told the dirtiest vehicles to leave the roads between 2015 and 2017 and accelerated its move to clean energy.

A 2006 US-China research project showed that much of the pollution drifts in from surrounding regions. On average between 35 and 60 per cent of ozone originates outside Beijing. Shandong and Tianjin exert a notable influence, helped by summer winds from the south and south-east and by the mountains to the north and north-west.

Coal accounts for some 40 per cent of the city's fine particulates (PM2.5) and is the principal source of nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012, power stations have been moving from coal to natural gas, and the city intends to limit annual coal use to 20 million tons. It burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, with 73 per cent going to heat and power and the rest to industry. A good part of Beijing's pollutants arrive from other regions. Tianjin was expected to raise its coal consumption from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million in 2015. Hebei burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, which exceeds the whole of Germany, with just 30 per cent for electricity and a large share for steel and cement. The coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, whose consumption has tripled since 2000, add to it, as does Shandong. Among provinces, coal use is highest in Shandong, then Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, in that order. Beijing used to have four large coal-burning plants for electricity and winter heating: Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two others in March 2015, and the last one, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was set to close in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was to cut coal use by 13 million tons and keep it to 15 million tons in 2015.

When big events approach, the authorities have acted dramatically. For the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly 17 billion US dollars was spent to meet the promise of cleaner air. During the Games, building sites stopped, many factories closed for good, industry in nearby regions was halted for a time, some filling stations shut, car traffic was halved through an odd-even licence plate rule, bus and subway fares were reduced, new subway lines opened, and vehicles with high emissions were banned. Beijing also put together one of the world's largest natural-gas bus fleets, 3,800 vehicles, and was the first Chinese city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 standard.

Cloud seeding is occasionally used to make rain and clear the air before major events, like the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, or to counter drought. More recently the method has been temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, which produced the brief APEC blue and parade blue skies around APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. The air improved dramatically at those times but soon returned to unhealthy levels.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and shut down most industry and commercial activity; a red alert followed later that month. In November 2016 the environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 old, highly polluting cars would be banned from driving when red alerts are in force in the city or surrounding areas.

The situation has become much better since 2014, the year of the declared war on pollution. Fine particles fell 35 per cent in 2017 and fell further by 2020, chiefly through the replacement of coal power with natural gas and the cleaning of polluting industrial sites. The annual average of PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013, and in 2024 only two days of heavy pollution were recorded, a record low and 96.6 per cent fewer than the 58 days of 2013.

Readings differ by source. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily data from 27 stations around the city, and the US Embassy publishes hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures on Twitter. Since the two measure different pollutants against different criteria, the bureau's levels, and the health impact it reports, are often lower than the embassy's. Pollution matters for health: it measurably raises rates of heart and lung disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause respiratory and cardiovascular trouble, hospital visits and even death.

Dust storms add to the picture. Erosion of deserts in northern and north-western China brings seasonal storms, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain deliberately to fight them. In January to April 2006 alone, no fewer than eight storms struck, and a single storm in April 2002 deposited left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before blowing on to Japan and Korea.

beijing-foreign-studies-university.h: Hills, rivers and the shape of the city

blocks.x: The city sits on the northern fringe of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that extends south and east. Ranges to the north, north-west and west guard the capital and the farmland of northern China from the desert steppe. The Jundu Mountains fill the north-west of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou districts, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall follows rough ground across the northern municipality, built to defend against nomad raids. Mount Dongling, on the Hebei border in the Western Hills, is the highest point at 2,303 metres (7,556 feet).

Rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are tributaries of the Hai River system and flow south-east. The Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the municipality's biggest. The Grand Canal to Hangzhou, a transport route more than 1,400 years old, starts in Beijing, and so does the South-North Water Transfer Project, the recent scheme to bring Yangtze water north.

The built-up area lies on the south-central plain at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) and takes up a modest but growing share of the municipality. It is laid out in concentric ring roads. The Second Ring Road runs along the old city wall and the Sixth Ring Road links satellite towns. At the centre are Tian'anmen and the square, just south of the Forbidden City, where emperors once lived; to the west is Zhongnanhai, where today's leaders live, and Chang'an Avenue, running between the gate and the square, is the main east-west axis. The pattern of growth from the old centre to the fringe has a nickname, tan da bing, meaning spreading like a pancake, and many people cite it as a root of the city's urban troubles.

Three kinds of building shape the skyline. First comes the imperial tradition, with Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace, which symbolises the People's Republic), the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City as the leading examples. The second is the Sino-Soviet look of the 1950s to the 1970s, with boxy and sometimes badly built structures. The third is the modern style, found particularly in the eastern CBD, for instance the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the early 2000s Beijing has seen a surge of new building, with international architects contributing many modern styles, most of all in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone is a blend of 1950s architecture and a neofuturist look. China Zun, at 528 metres, is the tallest building. Only one building in the world gets the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best tall building each year. Beijing has won it twice, with the Linked Hybrid (2009) and the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

The old courtyard homes, siheyuan, are built around a central yard; Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are grand examples. Alleys called hutongs connect them. These alleys usually run east-west so that doors face north or south, as feng shui recommends, and widths vary, some being so narrow that only a few people can pass at once. The siheyuan and hutongs, once found everywhere, are vanishing quickly as whole blocks give way to tall buildings. Hutong residents have the right to new flats at least as large as their old homes, yet many say that the old neighbourly feeling and street life cannot be replaced. The properties are often owned by the state.

BFSU's position in Haidian places you in the same district as Peking University, so you will often meet students from many fields. As you plan, remember to pack for a real winter, to consider a mask and air purifier on bad days, to enjoy the contrast between old hutongs and glass towers, and to check the official BFSU site for current programmes and admissions rules, as the ranking figures above come from different editions and years.

beijing-foreign-studies-university.h: A few reminders about the figures

blocks.x: The air-quality numbers in this profile range from 2006 to 2024 and show a clear trend: Beijing was often heavily polluted in 2013 and has had far cleaner air since. Even so, days of poor air still happen, so it is sensible to check daily readings from the municipal bureau or other monitoring services during your stay, and remember that different services can show different levels. The ranking information is also drawn from different years and rankings (Gaokao-based statistics for 2012 to 2023, subject tables from QS and other global lists), so use them as a general sign that BFSU is strong in languages and humanities rather than as precise standings.

Because BFSU and China Foreign Affairs University share both a city and a nickname, applicants sometimes compare them. BFSU is a research university built around languages and has broadened into international studies and history, whereas CFAU is tied to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Both have produced ambassadors, and both enjoy the rivalry described above. Look at the programmes and teaching languages each one offers before you decide.

The urban mean for 1991 to 2020 is 55.2 to 55.9 F, daily lows average 45.9 to 47.1 F and highs 65.3 to 66.0 F. Lower suburbs average 52.7 to 55.4 F, with lows of 42.6 to 46.4 F and highs of 64.8 to 65.7 F. In the mountains the mean runs from 32 to 50 F. January's daily mean is 27.1 F and July's is 81.0 F, annual rainfall is 20.79 inches (23.00 inches in Haidian and Chaoyang), and the extremes are minus 17.3 F and 107.4 F.

Beijing Forestry University (BFU, 北京林业大学) is a public university in Beijing. The Ministry of Education is its supervising body, and it is jointly sponsored by three bodies: the city government of Beijing, the forestry and grassland authority at national level, and the education ministry itself. It has been admitted to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction programme.

The university can trace its roots to 1902, when a forestry section was created within the agricultural faculty of the Imperial University of Peking. Today it teaches far more than trees. Students can choose from a long list: forestry and environmental science of course, but also biology, physics, mathematics, psychology, economics, management, law, languages, electronics, automation, computer science and artificial intelligence. It describes its mission as passing on an environmentally friendly outlook and supplying modern technology to help protect the planet. In 2011 it helped found the Beijing high-tech university alliance, together with 11 other universities that have an industry focus.

beijing-forestry-university.h: From a forestry section to a comprehensive university

blocks.x: The Imperial University of Peking set up a forestry department in 1902, and that is where BFU begins. It became an institute in its own right in 1952, called the Beijing Institute of Forestry, and was given its present name in 1985, Beijing Forestry University, and widened its subject range to include electronics, computer science, psychology and economics. It now has 14 schools, offering more than 60 undergraduate programmes, 120 postgraduate programmes and 40 doctoral programmes.

In the half-century or so since it opened, over 30,000 Chinese and international students have graduated from BFU, and 11 of them have become academicians. There are 956 full-time teachers, among them five academicians and 496 professors. While keeping its traditional subjects, the university has added many new ones to meet social needs. Another way of describing the structure counts 15 units, starting with the graduate school and the schools for forestry, landscape architecture and conservation. Alongside them come biological science and technology, environmental science and engineering, soil and water conservation, industry, information science, materials, pure science, economic management, humanities and social sciences, and foreign languages, with a unit for vocational training and continuing education completing the list.

Its resources include a computer centre, a computer network centre, an educational centre, an audio-visual teaching centre, a biological centre, a micro-technology centre, a forest-organism centre, and a teaching and research tree farm, which is the Jiu Feng National Forest Park. Attached to the university are three further bodies. One is a foreign-language training centre belonging to the State Forestry Administration; the others are a centre for soil control technology on China's Loess Plateau and a centre for training in desertification control. On campus there are laboratories, a gymnasium, a main teaching building (the Central Building of Teaching) and a fast campus network. The library lends books through a computerised system, and the building also serves nationwide as the place where forestry universities and colleges obtain imported teaching materials. In 2001 the university completed a high-rise student apartment building and a new classroom building.

In recent years nearly 200 research discoveries have been given awards by national, provincial and ministry-level bodies, and national and municipal governments have recognised over 20 teaching achievements. Academic exchange and cooperation link BFU to over 150 universities and research institutes in more than 20 countries, which links China with the wider world in forestry and environmental studies.

BFU aims for teaching that combines professional knowledge with all-round skills and a rigorous, creative academic approach. Students can shape their own path through optional courses, subsidiary courses, course exemptions and a bachelor-to-master continuing education route. Student societies and associations run extracurricular activities in science and technology, art, sport, environmental protection and politics. Two groups stand out. Wilderness Survival, formally the Society of Scientific Exploration and Wilderness Survival, received the National Bureau of Environmental Protection's top honour, the Prize of the Earth, and the other is a volunteering body, the Association of Beijing College Volunteers for Environmental Protection. In the landscape gardening architecture design competitions for college students, sponsored by UNESCO together with the International Association of Landscape Gardening Architects, BFU students won prizes four times in a row. They also won a Golden Prize in an international students' architecture design contest, prizes in garden design, and awards in national competitions for scientific inventions, mathematics and art.
The city around BFU shapes daily life, so these sections describe its buildings, landscape, weather and air.

beijing-forestry-university.h: A city of three architectural eras

blocks.x: Beijing's architecture falls into three broad groups. Imperial buildings come first, and include Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), which has become the symbol of the People's Republic, alongside the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City. Then there are the boxy and sometimes poorly built "Sino-Soviet" structures from the 1950s to the 1970s. The third group is modern: the new CCTV Headquarters in the eastern CBD, the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the early 21st century, construction has surged, with international architects contributing a variety of modern styles, above all in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s design and a neofuturistic look sit together. The tallest tower is the 528-metre China Zun. The CTBUH names one best overall tall building in the world annually, and Beijing has produced two winners since 2007, the Linked Hybrid (2009) and then the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

The traditional housing form is the siheyuan, a courtyard enclosed by buildings, and the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are fine examples. Courtyards are joined by hutong alleys, which usually run straight east to west so that doors open north and south, an arrangement meant to bring good feng shui. Some hutongs are so narrow that only a few people can pass at once. Both siheyuans and hutongs, once found across the city, are vanishing quickly as whole blocks give way to high-rises. Residents get apartments in the new buildings at least as large as their old homes, but many say the old neighbourly community and street life cannot be replaced, and the properties are often government owned.

Beijing sits where the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland, begins in the north; the plain extends to the city's south and east. Mountains in the north, northwest and west form a barrier against the desert steppe, protecting both the city and northern China's farmland. The Jundu Mountains dominate the northwest of the municipality (notably Yanqing and Huairou Districts), and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall crosses the north, built on rough terrain to defend against nomadic raids from the steppe. The municipality's highest point, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft), is Mount Dongling in the Western Hills on the Hebei border.

Rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma belong to the Hai River system and flow southeast. Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the biggest in the municipality. Beijing is the northern end of two great waterways: the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built over 1,400 years ago for transport, and the South-North Water Transfer Project, a recent scheme that moves water up from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up city lies on flat ground in the south-central municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and it occupies a small but growing share of the municipality. Ring roads radiate outwards in concentric loops; the innermost, the Second Ring Road, follows where the old walls ran, while the Sixth Ring Road connects satellite towns in the suburbs. At the heart are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, home of China's current leaders, is to the west. The city's main east-west axis is Chang'an Avenue, which passes between Tiananmen and the Square. Beijing's growth outwards from the old core has been nicknamed "pancake spreading" (tan da bing), and it often gets the blame for the city's urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa) and borders on a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid, and the vast Siberian anticyclone makes winters short, cold and dry. In spring, sandstorms may sweep in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe as temperatures climb quickly under mostly dry conditions. Autumn is, like spring, a transitional season with very little rain. Across 2001 to 2026, early August is the hottest part of the year and early January the coldest.

By the official Chinese calendar of seasons, the dates are 26 March for spring, 20 May for summer, 13 September for autumn and 31 October for winter. Recently March and September have warmed faster and May and October more slowly, so autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

Since 1951 the lowest temperature was -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, and the highest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), reached on 24 July 1999.

beijing-forestry-university.h: The air: problems, causes and progress

blocks.x: Prospective students often ask about air quality in Beijing, so the story is told here in some detail.

Beijing has a long record of environmental problems. Its urban area quadrupled in extent between 2000 and 2009, which increased emissions and fundamentally altered the local weather even apart from human emissions: lower surface albedo, wind speed and near-surface humidity, but higher ground and near-surface temperatures, vertical air dilution and ozone. Urban growth and fossil-fuel pollution together create serious environmental trouble and health problems for many inhabitants. Heavy smog in 2013 affected Beijing and much of northern China, 600 million people in all. After that "pollution shock", air pollution became a leading economic and social worry in China. Beijing's government announced measures such as reducing coal from 24% of energy in 2012 to 10% in 2017, and the national government told heavily polluting vehicles to leave the roads between 2015 and 2017 and stepped up the shift to clean energy.

American and Chinese researchers working jointly concluded in 2006 that a large share of the city's pollution originates in nearby cities and provinces, with 35 to 60% of ozone coming from outside. Two neighbours matter most. Tianjin and Shandong, in the researchers' words, have a "significant influence" on air quality in the capital, because summer winds blow mainly from the south and southeast and mountains close off the north and northwest.

About 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5, and most of its nitrogen and sulphur dioxide, comes from burning coal. Power stations in the city have been moving from coal to natural gas since 2012, with a goal of limiting annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73% for heating and power and the rest for industry. Much of its pollution is emitted next door. Tianjin's coal use was forecast to grow from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. In 2011 Hebei burned more than 300 million tons, more than the whole of Germany, and only 30% of it generated power while steel and cement making took much of the rest. The coal-producing regions of Inner Mongolia, Shanxi and Shaanxi, where use has tripled since 2000, add to the burden, as do Shandong's power plants. Among Chinese provinces, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth for coal consumption.

The city had four large coal-fired power plants that supplied electricity and winter heat. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two others in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was to close in 2016. From 2013 to 2017 the plan was to cut coal use by 13 million tons and hold it at 15 million tons in 2015.

Nearly US$17 billion was spent before the 2008 Summer Olympics to meet pledges on cleaner air. For the Games, Beijing stopped work on all construction sites, closed many of its own factories permanently, closed industry in neighbouring regions for a time, shut some gas stations, halved traffic with odd and even licence-plate days, lowered bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It also put together 3,800 natural-gas buses, among the largest such fleets anywhere, and was the first Chinese city to adopt the Chinese counterpart of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

The authorities sometimes use cloud seeding to raise the chance of rain and clear the air before major events, for example ahead of the 2009 parade for the 60th anniversary, and to relieve drought. Lately they prefer temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, which created "APEC blue" and "parade blue", brief clear-sky periods around the 2014 APEC meeting in China and the 2015 Victory Day Parade. In both cases the air improved dramatically, only to return to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing most industrial and commercial operations, and a "red alert" followed later in the month. In November 2016 the city's environmental protection bureau announced that, from 2017, highly polluting old cars would be banned from driving when red alerts are in force in the city or nearby.

Measured pollutants have dropped since the authorities launched a "war on pollution" in 2014: fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017 and fell further by 2020, chiefly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting factories in the area were cleaned up. The annual mean concentration of PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013, and in 2024 the city had just two days of heavy pollution, a record low and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days of 2013.

The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily figures from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the American Embassy publishes hourly readings of ozone and PM2.5 on Twitter. Since the two organisations measure different pollutants against different standards, the BJEPB tends to report lower pollution levels and health effects than the Embassy does.

Smog is a real health risk: it measurably raises rates of cardiovascular and respiratory illness in Beijing, and heavy exposure can lead to respiratory and heart problems, emergency-room visits and death. Anyone with a chronic condition should seek medical advice before coming.

Eroding deserts in the north and northwest send seasonal dust storms to the city, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain to counter them. The first four months of 2006 had at least eight storms. One in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it travelled on to Japan and Korea.

For students interested in forestry, landscape architecture, environmental science, soil and water conservation or nature conservation, BFU offers a specialist base inside a major capital city, with broad international contacts and strong student groups in environmental work. The weather and air notes above are worth reading before you decide when to travel.

beijing-forestry-university.h: Things to check before you apply

blocks.x: Because BFU is a specialist institution with 14 schools, the first decision is which school your programme belongs to: Landscape Architecture, Forestry, Nature Conservation and Soil and Water Conservation are obvious examples of its core subjects, while Information Science and Technology, Economics and Management, Art and Foreign Languages show how far it has broadened since becoming a university in 1985. Ask the admissions office whether your programme is taught in English, and check the optional-course and bachelor-to-master routes if you hope to continue to postgraduate study. Finally, remember that BFU's tree farm, the Jiu Feng National Forest Park, is part of its teaching and research resources, so field-based subjects are well supported.
In short, BFU pairs a century-old specialism with a city that offers both heritage and a lively modern district, and it is worth planning around Beijing's cold, dry winters and hot, humid summers.
Beijing Forestry University lists 206 programs for international students on this site: 26 bachelor, 65 master's, 37 doctoral, 78 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 180 taught in Chinese, 26 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 24,800 to CNY 24,800 (median CNY 24,800), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 29,800 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 29,800), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 33,000 to CNY 39,000 (median CNY 33,000), according to the university's published fee table.

206 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
