International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

beijing-forestry-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beijing Forestry University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Beijing Forestry University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Beijing International Studies University, usually shortened to BISU, is a municipal public university in Chaoyang District, Beijing. Its Chinese name, 北京第二外国语学院, literally means Beijing Second College of Foreign Languages, and that older identity still explains a lot about the place. The university answers to the City of Beijing and is financed from two sources, the municipal government of Beijing and the national culture and tourism ministry.

For an international applicant, the short version is this: BISU is a city-run institution that grew out of a national push to train people who could speak the world's languages, then built a second great strength in tourism and hospitality, and today teaches business, economics, law and politics alongside its languages. The sections below walk through how it got here, what the campuses are like, which research centres and programmes define it, how international students are supported, and what life in Beijing itself will be like.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: A national plan for foreign-language talent

blocks.x: The story begins in the 1950s. The People's Republic was winning wider international recognition, and the country suddenly needed many more people who were properly fluent in foreign languages. In the early 1960s Premier Zhou Enlai returned from a state tour of fourteen countries and launched a seven-year programme to expand foreign language education. As part of that plan he proposed a Beijing Second Foreign Languages Institute, which is the institution we now know as BISU, and he personally oversaw the founding work.

Zhou took his proposal to the State Council, where the new institute was given top priority. A founding report was presented and approved in March 1964, and in August the land on which the main campus still stands was allocated. The first 646 students arrived in September, and a formal Establishment Ceremony took place on 24 October 1964, which the university has treated as its birthday ever since.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: The early curriculum and the changing owners

blocks.x: The first curriculum rested on foreign-language teaching units, supported by Chinese literature, the arts and philosophy, political economy, sport, and the study of both international and domestic affairs. Degree programmes were offered in fourteen languages: Vietnamese, Serbian, Bulgarian, Czech, Polish, Hungarian and Romanian, together with Albanian, Japanese, German, Arabic, Spanish, French and English. The university sat under the Commission for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries, the forerunner of today's Ministry of Culture, and it grew quickly until the Cultural Revolution began in 1966.

After that its supervising body changed several times. The Foreign Ministry took charge in 1968, the Beijing municipal government in 1971, the Ministry of Education in 1978, and the National Tourism Administration in 1983. That last move matters, because by then the university had already started becoming a tourism specialist. In 1981 the university and the foreign trade ministry filed a joint report, the Education Ministry approved it, and a new department for foreign affairs and trade came into being. Within months the tourism authority also introduced a tourism management major at BISU, making the university the earliest shaper of tourism education in China. Through the 1980s and 1990s it carried a second name, China Tourism Institute, and it was recognised as one of the country's leading tertiary institutions for tourism studies, strong in both teaching and research.

For most of its life the English name was Beijing Second Foreign Language University, and that was dropped in 2003 to reflect a wider range of programmes. A multi-disciplinary structure had been taking shape since the 1990s and 2000s, and the university is best known today for its business administration and foreign languages teaching. Language teaching today spans Korean, Arabic, Portuguese, Spanish, Italian, French, Russian, German, Japanese and English, and, for overseas students, Chinese taught as a foreign language. BISU was among the first authorised HSK test centres in Beijing and is considered one of the capital's better universities for studying Chinese. The school colours and visual identity were created in 2003 and refreshed in 2009.

In July 2013 the university reorganised its business and economics disciplines. The old School of Tourism Management was dissolved: Tourism Management and Hotel Management were each raised to full schools, Marketing and Financial Management were combined into a new School of International Business, and the Event Management department moved into Economics and Trade. This was part of the university's Twelfth Five-Year Plan, which aimed to give academic units more autonomy, make use of the university's tourism heritage, and respond to changes in the job market.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: A timeline of the first half-century

blocks.x: Readers who like precise dates will find the main milestones below, grouped by period. Together they show an institution that was founded by the state, shaken by the upheaval of the 1960s and 1970s, and then steadily opened itself to the outside world.

On 7 March 1964 the founding report went to the State Council, and it was approved on 11 March, only a week later. In September 1964 the university was formally established under the Commission for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries. Its first academic units were an English Department, a French Department, a Spanish and Arabic department, a German and Japanese department, a department for Eastern European languages, and a training centre that ran intensive courses for state officials. Most teachers were recruited from the Commission, from Xinhua News Agency and from partner universities, and the first 22 foreign teachers were among them.

The first 646 students began classes on 14 September 1964. On 22 October the foreign minister and vice premier Chen Yi toured the campus and spoke about the principles a foreign-language university should follow. Two days later, at the Establishment Ceremony, the university's name was written out in calligraphy by Guo Moruo, who led the Chinese Academy of Sciences. On 1 March 1965 the fortnightly campus newspaper UniLife was launched.

Classes at every level were suspended on 7 June 1966 because of the Cultural Revolution, and UniLife stopped publishing the next day after 26 issues. From July 1966 Premier Zhou Enlai came to BISU five times in a row, touring the campus, speaking with students and staff, and eating with students in the canteen. Two more vice premiers, Chen Yi and Li Xiannian, came by as well to show their backing.

In 1968 the Commission for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries was abolished and the university came under the Foreign Ministry. Control moved to Beijing's city government in October 1971. For a while the Beijing Language Institute was attached to BISU, but it stood on its own again by October 1972. In 1973 Renmin University was closed, and a number of its foreign teachers were transferred to BISU.

In April 1976, responding to the Tiananmen Incident, staff of the Chinese Teaching and Research Office formed a literary group named Tong Huai Zhou (童怀周), meaning "sharing memories of Premier Zhou". Under that name they compiled poetry selections and photo albums that were issued in millions of copies and had a large impact at home and abroad. The collections went down in history as The Tiananmen Poems.

After the college entrance examination (Gaokao) was restored, the first 226 students of the new era enrolled in February 1978. On 17 February 1978 the State Council passed the university to the Education Ministry, while Beijing's government kept a shared role in running it. In October 1978 the first academic journal, Foreign Language Teaching (外语教学), was founded; it became Paper (学丛) in April 1980 and, in January 1986, the Journal of Beijing International Studies University. In February 1979 a new college was set up as a branch campus, later absorbed by Beijing Union University, which gave it a new title in 1983, Beijing Tourism School. In the winter of 1979 four students (Wang Xinbo, Ma Xiaoyi, Li Shichao and Wan Xing) formed the band Wan Li Ma Wang, which played mostly classic rock and is regarded as the oldest rock band in China.

The year 1981 was a busy one. The joint report mentioned above reached the Education Ministry in April and was approved on 1 July, and the new department admitted 51 students for the first time in September 1982. On 4 June 1981 BISU signed its first formal exchange agreement with a foreign university, Kyoto University of Foreign Studies. In July, 26 students from Kyoto arrived to study Chinese, becoming the first short-term exchange students, while the first long-term foreign students followed that September. UniLife resumed publication on 1 July 1981.

That July the tourism authority also created a Department of Tourism Management, opening two new majors: tourism management, and tourism translation in English, German and Japanese. In 1981 and 1982 a total of 3,100 students enrolled in those two majors. The Center for Foreign Language Teaching opened in September 1981 and handled training schemes started by the United Nations.

Degree-awarding powers followed. Degree-awarding powers came in January 1982, when the State Council Academic Degrees Committee named BISU among the first universities allowed to confer bachelor's degrees, and the 362 graduates that year were the first to receive them. In March 1982 an exchange agreement was signed with the Cornell University School of Hotel Administration. On 29 March 1983 the university formally came under the National Tourism Administration. March 1984 saw the founding of the Research Institute for Tourism Sciences (it became the Research Institute of Tourism Development in 2003), and on 11 April 1984 BISU became one of the first universities permitted to award master's degrees; its first two postgraduate students were admitted that June. In October 1985 China Tourism Institute (中国旅游学院) became an alternative name for the university, used alongside the original name through the 1980s and 1990s. In April 1986 the play Timon of Athens was staged at China's first Shakespeare Festival, one of only two English-language productions, the other being The Merchant of Venice by the People's Liberation Army Art Theatre.

To mark the 30th anniversary in 1994, inscriptions of congratulation were written by Li Lanqing and Qian Qichen, both vice premiers, and by Liu Yi, who headed the tourism administration. That January BISU was also approved as one of Beijing's first HSK test centres. On 17 March 1997 Li Lanqing, by then Vice Premier, visited the campus with National Tourism Administration chairman He Guangwei and gave a speech. On 24 October 1997 the university was named a Model Campus. December 1997 brought its first Internet connection, and electronic payment systems arrived in the dining halls, which ended the era of the paper "meal ticket" (饭票). The official website opened in December 1999 under the domain www.erwai.net.cn.

On 20 June 2001 the National Press Bureau approved renaming UniLife as the Newsletter of Beijing International Studies University, and from September 2001 it became a publicly published news outlet with its own national serial number. In October 2002 BISU was an Outstanding Academic Institution for International Students Education; only 9 of 56 institutions received that rating. On 11 July 2003 the English name officially became Beijing International Studies University (BISU), and the web domain changed to www.bisu.edu.cn. On 5 December 2003 a new logo for the BISU Union, designed by finance student Zhao Ting, came into use.

The Alumni Association was founded on 29 May 2004, and on the same day a statue of Premier Zhou Enlai, donated by alumni and current students, was unveiled on campus. The 40th anniversary ceremony ran from 19 to 24 October 2004, with an inscription from Li Lanqing and messages of congratulation sent by the State Councillors Chen Zhili, Han Qide and Xu Jialu. Japanese graduates founded a BISU Japanese Alumni Association in July 2006, by which time several thousand Japanese students had graduated from the university. The first Confucius Institute linked to BISU opened on 5 November 2007 at the Autonomous University of Chihuahua in Mexico. From 24 to 26 September 2008 the China Tourism Education Committee was formed under the China Tourism Association; BISU was chosen as its president unit, and the then chancellor, Duan Jianguo, became chairman.

On 29 June 2011 the Institute of China Translation Development was inaugurated at BISU. It is the first national research centre devoted to China's translation industry and a strategic alliance between the university and the Translators Association of China, with support from CIUTI and from the publishing administration for foreign languages. Figures from academia and industry attended, and the China Internet Information Center, People's Daily and Xinhuanet all reported on it.

BISU's main site is in Chaoyang District and consists of three connected campuses that are all within walking distance of one another. It holds the main teaching buildings and student services, and it has good public transport, with access to metro Line 6 and Line 8T. The university also has facilities elsewhere in the city: a separately run Hospitality Institute in Daxing, and two branch colleges, one on the boundary of Fengtai and Haidian Districts and another on the outskirts lying between the city proper and Miyun County. A further site was planned for Tongzhou from 2013.

The central campus covers 55.2 acres (about 223,334 square metres) near the Guomao area, roughly 5 miles (8.8 km) due east of the central CBD. The campus sits next to the Communication University of China, which can be reached through the West Gate, and it has two main entrances: the South Entrance on Jianguo Road and the North Entrance on Chaoyang Road, each with bus stops within walking distance.

The architecture blends modern and older styles into a landscaped setting. Even though the campus is in the middle of a city, it has held the title of Garden Campus since 1994, and it was given the Model Campus label for the city in 1997. The facilities include:
five main teaching buildings and four auditoriums
six student residence halls
the university library and a comprehensive learning hub
food options: a pair of dining halls, five specialty restaurants, three corner shops for snacks and drinks, and vending machines on the International Lodge's ground floor
most of the sports venues, namely an indoor gymnasium, an aquatic centre, four tennis courts, and an outdoor stadium that includes six basketball courts and two volleyball courts
a supermarket, two copy shops, a bookshop and a post office

Across the road from the North Entrance, opposite the Tian-Ke-Long shopping mall, you will find a pharmacy and a branch of ICBC bank, and the university's publishing house, Tourism Education Press, has its headquarters nearby. To the north, a separate campus holds the School of Continuing Education along with the Study Abroad Resource Center. In the south is the Yi-Shui-Fang-Yuan campus, developed in 2011 as a residential area, is separated from the central campus by the Jingtong Expressway and lies beside the Tonghui River. It houses most undergraduate and postgraduate students.

A branch campus was expected in Tongzhou District, which is being developed as Beijing's new City Sub-Center, from 2013. President Zhou Lie said in January that the site would be in Lucheng, beside Peking Union Medical College and Renmin University's east campus, only a 20-minute drive from the central campus. By March 2013 the university had held conferences and seminars on the project's feasibility, in light of the 2013 to 2020 national outline for tourism and leisure issued by the State Council in February.

BISU uses the word discipline for a broad administrative grouping of related academic units, and the disciplines usually determine which degrees are awarded. There are four at present. Business Administration, Economic Sciences, and Law and Political Sciences are three of them; the fourth is Arts, which takes in languages, literature, cultural studies and philosophy. Teaching and research are run through departments, schools and institutes. Schools can set up subsidiary departments and other bodies depending on their history or needs. Institutes are graduate-level research units that carry out projects outside the regular course plan, typically with the municipal government or national institutes; otherwise graduate schools sit inside schools and departments themselves. Support is provided by six teaching and research offices for required subjects, plus the University Press and the University Library. About 50 departments, schools and other bodies were running these four disciplines in 2013.

The Research Institute of Tourism Development, founded in 1984, is among the oldest and most respected bodies in China for tourism planning. It has three research affiliates, a Center for Strategic Planning, a Center for Theoretical Research and a Center for Industry Consulting, and it works closely with the National Tourism Administration, local governments and major industry players. It has contributed to around 20 provincial and city development projects, among them the popular tourist destinations Zhangjiagang, Haikou and Sanya. It has also produced over 50 operational and feasibility reports covering national resort zones, reserves and ecotourism areas, for instance Suzhou's Lake Tai resort, Tibet's Pagsum Lake and the Changbai Mountains reserve in Jilin.

The institute joined the National Database for Tourism Management in 1998. Since 1999, with Education Ministry authorisation, it has offered postgraduate coursework and research in Tourism Management, with one direction on theory-based study of how tourism sectors operate and how policy is made, and another on practical planning and development, drawing on business management, science, sociology and architecture. It keeps strong links with the China Tourism Academy and leading companies in the field.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: Transcultural studies, linguistics and applied linguistics

blocks.x: The Institute for Transcultural Studies is a research institution for the arts and humanities. It started out in 2001 under a longer name, the Institute for Comparative Literature and Transcultural Studies. The aim is better intercultural understanding and a stronger global presence for Chinese culture, pursued by reading classic and modern philosophy, art and literature across cultures. It works with leading domestic institutions: the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Foreign Literature Institute helped found the National Center for Foreign Literature Studies, and the Center for Aesthetics and Art Education is a joint scheme with the Chinese Aesthetics Society. Further branches are the Center for Aesthetics and Philosophy, a centre for comparative literature and poetics, and one for Sino-Greek cultural studies, all with good ties to overseas universities and research bodies. BISU also has institutes of linguistics and applied linguistics covering Chinese and foreign languages.

BISU has led in tourism since the early 1980s, when the national tourism authority took over the university and supported its new tourism majors, so it was an early pioneer of this field of teaching in China. Every year since 2004 it has hosted the China Tourism Development, Beijing Dialogue Forum, which the Beijing Tourism Administration strongly supports, and in 2008 it began the Cross-Strait Tourism Seminar.

A research base for Beijing tourism development (北京旅游发展研究基地) was established on the campus in 2004, funded by three city bodies: the Tourism Administration, the Education Commission and the Beijing Planning Office of Philosophy and Social Science. It was one of the first research bases that office accredited, and it acts as a government think tank that supported Beijing's tourism planning during the 2008 Summer Olympics. By 2008 it had built several tourism databases, among them an information platform for China's tourism industry, a language-material portal for Beijing tour guides, and observatories and databases on tourism impact and sustainability. Between 2005 and 2012 it completed around 70 significant research projects, including an annual report on Beijing's tourism development, plus the series China Tourism Studies and International Tourism Studies.

The China Tourism Academy, which is the research arm of the national tourism authority, partnered with BISU in 2009 to found the China Hospitality Industry Research Center (中国饭店产业研究中心), described as a research body chosen from more than 1,000 tourism academies across China. Work published in the International Journal of Hospitality Management showed that, across 1978 to 2008, only two other institutions did more than BISU for research into Chinese tourism and hospitality management, and the centre's director, Professor Gu Huimin, was among the eight most prolific authors in the world.

China's first culture industry institute at state level is the National Institute of Cultural Development (国家文化发展国际战略研究院), created in 2010 by BISU together with the Ministry of Culture. Its roots lie in a 2006 centre for trade in services and cultural trade between countries, and it aims to promote Chinese culture through trade and economics and support national cultural reform. It cooperates domestically and internationally, doubling as a platform for research on cultural trade across borders and as a training base for specialists. Another event is the Annual Forum for International Trade in Services (Beijing), co-hosted by BISU and the China Association of International Trade since 2007 and the only academic forum of this kind in the country; in 2013 it was folded into the second China International Fair for Trade in Services, hosted by the Ministry of Commerce.

A joint venture with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences produced the Global Media and Cultural Soft Power Laboratory (全球影视与文化软实力实验室) in 2012. It studies mass media, cross-platform convergence and cultural diplomacy, looking closely at cultural trends, media flows and consumer behaviour, particularly in film and television. It is the only academic organisation in China focused on soft-power development, and its backers include CCTV and the China Publishing Group.

The Arab Research Center (中国教育部区域和国别研究基地阿拉伯研究中心) was inaugurated at BISU in 2012 as one of just three university-based Arab studies centres chosen for the Ministry of Education's international studies research programme. It studies the Arab world in depth, from politics and economics to history, religion, society, the arts and the humanities. Its researchers come mostly from the Department of Arabic Studies, joined by multidisciplinary specialists and two distinguished experts: Li Shaoxian, Liu Zhentang, a former Chinese ambassador in the Middle East, and Li Shaoxian, a vice president at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations. President Zhou Lie has described it as both a think tank and an intelligence unit for scholarship, talent development, policy advice and international communication.

A second centre arrived that year: the Center for Global Public Opinion and Audience Research (全球舆情与受众研究基地), an academic partnership between BISU and the publishing administration for foreign languages. It uses comparative studies of countries and regions to focus on opinion tracking, public diplomacy and international cultural communication.

The School of Interpreting and Translation is fairly young, with its first students starting in 2007, yet it is one of only four Chinese universities recognised by CIUTI, the international translation studies body. By 2011, 16 BISU professors and staff had been given a lifetime achievement award in translation by the Translators Association of China (TAC). The Institute of China Translation Development, set up in 2011 with TAC, is the first national research centre on the translation industry and concentrates on translation and interpreting theory and professional practice. In 2012 it published the first Annual Report on China's Language Services Industry during the national translation conference, a release the field valued highly. It looks for partners in industry and among international organisations, with CIUTI and the foreign-languages publishing administration in support. A further TAC-affiliated body arrived in 2013, a training centre for China's translation industry (中国翻译行业人才培训基地), set up at BISU.

The university maintains links on every continent, which allow teachers to compare notes on teaching and research and make student exchange possible. By 2013 it had more than 130 international partners, and it is one of 20 Chinese universities chosen for the UNESCO China-Africa collaborative initiative.

The university is well known across China for educating international students, in both scale and quality. In 2002 and 2004 more than 70 countries were represented among its 8,000-plus long-term and 2,000 short-term international students, and on both occasions the Education Commission honoured it as an outstanding institution for educating international students. For the 2013 to 2014 academic year it was one of only two Beijing universities, among eight nationwide, entrusted by the China Scholarship Council with running foundation programmes for international undergraduates.

As an institution that can admit Chinese Government Scholarship students, BISU offers degree programmes to students from around the world: 20 undergraduate and 11 postgraduate programmes, every one of which can be applied for with a Chinese Government Scholarship. In 2007, about 40 percent of international undergraduates and 20 percent of non-degree language students received scholarships each semester, with the top award at CN¥9,000. The university also runs its own merit-based International Scholarships, and every overseas student is entitled to apply.
BISU is linked to a set of Confucius Institutes at partner universities abroad, listed here with their dates.
22 November 2006: Universidad Autónoma de Chihuahua, in Chihuahua, Mexico
11 December 2007: PRES Clermont Université, in Clermont-Ferrand, France
27 March 2008: Université Mohammed V, in Rabat, Morocco
28 April 2008: University of Central Lancashire, in Preston, United Kingdom
Several events punctuate the BISU year, many of them run by language departments or student groups:

First-Year Welcome Party: the BISU Union holds it for all new students, normally on the first Sunday evening before classes, after the military training (jun xun) has ended. Well-known societies perform plays, dubbing, dancing and singing, working in "must-know" tips for freshmen.

German Week: a week-long autumn or winter festival, officially the Cultural Week of German Speaking Countries, organised by the Student Union of the Department of German Studies. The programme starts with an opening ceremony and goes on to a German speech contest between universities, the MoreFun Wednesday Night Show, photo exhibitions and a film night, before a themed costume ball and a closing party. It introduces the cultures of Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Belgium, Luxembourg and Liechtenstein; ambassadors from these countries join the opening, with free German-style snacks and drinks and small fairs on tourist attractions, sports, education, politics, literature and media.

Forums: ongoing talk series put on by different academic units (the Boya Forum, the Career Forum and the Youth Elites Forum), inviting people from the media, politics, literature and the arts to meet students. Speakers have included Li Zhaoxing, Zhang Qiyue and Jin Guihua; the writers Wang Meng and Liang Xiaosheng; Yuan Tengfei, Ji Lianhai and Rao Xueman; Joël Bellassen and Lu Jiande; Sa Beining, Han Qiaosheng, Zhang Shaogang and Chun Ni; and Wang Gengnian and Sun Yusheng.
A week of French and Italian culture, organised by that language department
A Christmas and New Year's Eve party night, organised by the SCA BISU
Kohaku Uta Gassen, run by the School of Japanese Language
Sing Competition, run by the BISU Union
All that music Live Concert, run by RAY Music
Chinese Debating Competition

XiangYu News is the student-run news agency, supported and supervised by University Relations. It brings together BISU Television (BSTV), whose biggest yearly project is the graduation video shown at the ceremony; Voice of Erwai (VOE, Èrwài Zhī Shēng), the campus radio station; and the BISU Press Corps, the student journalists' association behind the BISU Newspaper and the online news service at the BISU Media Center (BMC).

Three student bodies lead campus life. The BISU Student Union, known as the BISU Union, is the official representative body of students. The China Youth League BISU is a student council that runs on party lines. The Students' Community Association (SCA BISU) manages the university's clubs and societies. All three organise inter-university events, including culture festivals, races, flea markets, parties, careers fairs, seminars, volunteering and leadership schemes. The aim is to build community and to draw home and overseas students into what the university calls the BISU family.

Most societies sit under the SCA BISU and begin with individual students who share an interest. Proposals for new societies are accepted at the start of each semester. Many overseas students join groups tied to their own language and culture, and some groups on Chinese culture are open to everyone. There are also academic and career-focused societies, for example the Business Negotiation Club and IIMA, the International Investment & Management Association. Leadership and community groups have multiplied lately, led by AIESEC, Warm Hope Volunteering and the Association for Green Environments.

Sport is strong. The flag football team The Bombers has done well in national leagues, and football and basketball sides hold twice-yearly competitions that draw thousands of spectators. Badminton, tennis and table-tennis tournaments run every year, and outdoor groups include The Runner for running, S-Power for roller skating and The BAMA for martial arts.

The BISU Students Art Troupe was founded in 2009 under the China Youth League BISU as a bridge between students, other universities and the public for Chinese performing arts; it has a choir, a dance group, an orchestra and percussion group, and a drama and recitation group. Arts societies that work independently are among the most popular, such as voice acting group The Charming Voice, dance group The PLUF Crew, the theatre group The Compass and The RAY Music. Others include the BISU Photographic Society, the fashion catwalk group The Modelin, anime and cosplay society The Minor, cycling group The SSS, computing group The September and The Mystery Society.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: Summing up BISU for prospective students

blocks.x: Putting these pieces together, BISU is best understood as a specialist-minded institution. Its founding mission in languages gave it a long record of teaching foreign students, its tourism and hospitality work gave it national influence through research centres and government advisory roles, and its newer institutes in translation, culture and regional studies connect it to national bodies such as the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and the Translators Association of China. Applicants interested in languages, interpreting, tourism, hospitality, international business or Chinese-language study will find the strongest match here, and the scholarship routes described above are worth checking early because they are open to overseas students from all countries.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: Living in Beijing: what to expect

blocks.x: Daily life depends heavily on the city around the campus: its buildings, terrain, weather and air. The sections below describe Beijing as the home city of BISU.

Three architectural styles dominate urban Beijing. The first is classical imperial architecture, best seen in the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple, the Forbidden City and Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace); Tian'anmen is the trademark building of the People's Republic. The second is the so-called Sino-Soviet style of the 1950s to the 1970s, whose buildings tend to be boxy and are sometimes poorly built. The third is the modern style, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east, with the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in landmarks like the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Construction boomed in the early 21st century, bringing designs by international architects, especially in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone mixes 1950s industrial design with a neofuturistic look. The tallest building in Beijing is the 528-metre China Zun. Since 2007 Beijing buildings have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building, an honour given to a single building worldwide each year. The winners were the Linked Hybrid (2009) and the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

Older residential Beijing is made of siheyuan, courtyards enclosed by buildings, joined by lanes called hutongs. Grand examples include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Hutongs generally run straight east to west, which points doorways north and south and is thought to be good feng shui, and their widths vary, with some so narrow that only a few people can pass at a time. Siheyuans and hutongs were once everywhere, but whole blocks are being replaced by high-rises. Residents are entitled to apartments at least as large as their former homes, though many say the old community feeling and street life cannot be rebuilt, and the properties are often owned by the government.

The city lies at the top of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that stretches away to the south and east. Hills and mountains on three sides (north, northwest and west) shield Beijing and the farmland of northern China from the desert steppe. The Jundu Mountains dominate the northwest of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou Districts, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the northern part of the municipality, built along rugged ground to guard against nomadic raids from the steppe. The highest point is Mount Dongling in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The main rivers, including the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, belong to the Hai River system and flow southeast. Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the municipality's largest. Beijing is also the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route, and of the South-North Water Transfer Project, a recent project that carries water north from the Yangtze river basin.

The urban area lies on the plain in the south-central part of the municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and it covers a small but growing share of the municipality. Ring roads spread out from the centre in concentric circles. The innermost one, the Second Ring Road, runs where the old city walls stood, while the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs. Tian'anmen and its Square lie at the centre, just south of the Forbidden City, once the emperors' residence, and Zhongnanhai, where China's current leaders live, is to the west. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tian'anmen and the Square and forms the main east-west axis. The way Beijing has grown outwards from the old centre has a popular nickname, "pancake spreading" (tan da bing), and many people blame it for Beijing's urban difficulties.

The climate is classed as humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen BSk). Expect hot, humid summers, driven by the East Asian monsoon, and short, cold, dry winters shaped by the giant Siberian anticyclone. Spring may bring sandstorms from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, and the weather warms fast and stays mostly dry. Autumn is another season of transition with little rain.

Looking at 2001 to 2026, the hottest period is early August and the coldest is early January. On the Chinese seasonal calendar the seasons begin on these dates: spring 26 March, summer 20 May, autumn 13 September, winter 31 October. Because March and September have been warming faster and May and October more slowly in recent years, autumn tends to be shorter than spring.
The figures for 1991 to 2020 give these averages:
Urban area: annual mean temperature of 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F), with daily minimums of 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily maximums of 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F)
Low-lying suburbs: annual mean of 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with daily minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and daily maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F)
Mountain areas: annual mean between 0 and 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), falling with altitude

The daily average temperature is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) in January and 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July. Annual rainfall averages about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three-quarters of it falls from June to August. Possible sunshine each month varies between 42% (July) and 62% (January and February), and the city gets 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. The coldest reading on record since 1951 was -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966, and the hottest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), recorded on 24 July 1999.
This is the part of Beijing life students ask about most, so it is worth setting out in full, including the improvement of recent years.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: Why the air became a problem

blocks.x: Beijing has a long record of environmental trouble. Between 2000 and 2009 its urban area quadrupled, which raised emissions and altered local weather: surface albedo, wind speed and humidity near the ground dropped, and ground temperatures, air temperatures close to the surface, vertical mixing of air and ozone all went up. Urban growth and fossil-fuel pollution together cause serious problems that harm many residents' health. In 2013 a heavy smog covered Beijing and much of northern China, affecting 600 million people. That "pollution shock" made air quality a major economic and social concern nationally. Beijing responded by announcing coal reductions, bringing coal's share down from 24% (2012) to 10% (2017), and the national government meanwhile removed heavily polluting vehicles between 2015 and 2017 and accelerated the move to clean energy.

American and Chinese researchers working together reported in 2006 that a large part of the pollution in the capital is blown in from nearby cities and provinces; between 35 and 60 percent of ozone comes from outside Beijing. Shandong and Tianjin matter most, partly because summer winds blow from the south and southeast and mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Burning coal produces roughly 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and most of its nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 power stations in the city have been switching from coal to natural gas, and the target is a ceiling of 20 million tons of coal a year. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73% of it for heating and power and the rest for industry. Neighbouring regions emit a great deal of the pollution. Tianjin's coal use was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. In 2011 Hebei burned over 300 million tons, a figure above Germany's total, and just 30% of that fed power generation; steel and cement took a big part. Shaanxi, Shanxi and Inner Mongolia are coal-mining regions whose power plants have tripled consumption since 2000, and Shandong's plants add to the problem too. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces for coal consumption.

Beijing had four major coal-fired power plants providing electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and the last, the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to close in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was a cut of 13 million tons in coal use, and a limit of 15 million tons in 2015.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: The Olympic clean-up and event-driven blue skies

blocks.x: Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, and to keep its promise of cleaner air, Beijing spent nearly US$17 billion. During the Games it stopped work at all construction sites, shut many Beijing factories for good, temporarily closed industry in neighbouring regions, closed some petrol stations, halved motor traffic by allowing odd or even licence-plate numbers on alternate days, cut bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It also assembled 3,800 natural-gas buses, one of the world's largest such fleets, and became the first Chinese city to require the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The government has sometimes used cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air before big events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. More recently it has relied on temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, producing the short-lived "APEC blue" around APEC China 2014 and "parade blue" before the 2015 Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved sharply during those periods and then slipped back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

Beijing's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed most industrial and commercial activity. A second, "red", alert followed before the month ended. In November 2016 the city's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 heavily polluting older cars would be banned from the roads whenever a smog red alert was issued in the city or nearby regions.

After the authorities declared a "war on pollution" in 2014, measured pollutants began falling. Fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017 and fell further by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial plants were cleaned up. By 2022 the yearly average level of PM2.5 was down to 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the cleanest since 2013, and 2024 saw just two heavy-pollution days, a record low that is 96.6 percent below the 58 days of 2013.

Because pollution is such a big issue in Beijing, there are several sources of readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau publishes daily readings from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the American Embassy tweets hourly readings of fine particulates (PM2.5) and ozone. The two measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the Bureau's figures and the health impact it reports are often lower than the Embassy's.

Smog is harmful: air pollution has a direct impact on rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause respiratory and heart problems, emergency-room visits and even death. Students with asthma or other conditions should check the readings and talk to a doctor before arriving.

Dust eroded from the deserts of northern and northwestern China brings seasonal dust storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain artificially to counter them. Between January and April 2006 alone there were at least eight, and in April 2002 a single storm dropped almost 50,000 tons of dust on the city then travelling on towards Japan and Korea.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: Putting Beijing into perspective for a newcomer

blocks.x: In short, Beijing offers a student an unusual mixture: imperial monuments and hutong lanes beside glass towers, a climate of sharp seasonal contrasts with a hot, wet summer and a cold, dry winter, and an air-quality record that was poor for years but has clearly improved since 2013. Because BISU's main site is in Chaoyang, close to the Guomao area and the CBD, you will be living in the modern, eastern part of the city rather than the old centre, with metro Line 6 and Line 8T nearby.
Beijing International Studies University lists 141 programs for international students on this site: 28 bachelor, 41 master's, 5 doctoral, 67 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 124 taught in Chinese, 15 taught in English, 2 taught in Not listed. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 22,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 27,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 27,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 27,000 to CNY 41,300 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.

140 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (7):
Accounting
Business Administration
Chinese-Style Modernization and Urban Development
Financial Management
International Business
Tourism Management
Understanding Contemporary China
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

beijing-international-studies-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beijing International Studies University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Beijing International Studies University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

beijing-jiaotong-university.h: Beijing Jiaotong University in a nutshell

blocks.x: Beijing Jiaotong University, or BJTU (北京交通大学), was formerly known as Northern Jiaotong University. The Chinese name means "Beijing Transport University", and it describes the university's long-standing focus. It is a public university in Haidian District, Beijing. The Ministry of Education is its parent body, but funding is shared among four sponsors: that ministry, the Ministry of Transport, the Beijing city government, and the national rail operator, China State Railway Group Company Limited. BJTU is part of both the Double First-Class Construction scheme and Project 211.

beijing-jiaotong-university.h: From railway school to Jiaotong University

blocks.x: BJTU began as one branch of the older Jiaotong University (also romanised as Chiao Tung University). The first step came in September 1909, when a Qing government postal department opened a Railway Management Institute in Beijing. After the Republic was established the school came under the Ministry of Transportation and Communications and was renamed the "Ministry of Communications Traffic Training Institute". It added subjects at that point, including electrical engineering, cable broadcast and radio.

A merger in 1921 with technical schools from Shanghai and Tangshan produced a single Jiaotong University with campuses in all three places, and the Beijing one was known then as "Jiaotong University Beijing School". Names changed again after 1949: first National Jiaotong University, Beijing (中国交通大学), and then, in 1950, Northern Jiaotong University (北方交通大学). To make its location explicit, the university adopted the name Beijing Jiaotong University (北京交通大学) in September 2003. The Shanghai branch meanwhile went its own way and later split in two, giving rise to Xi'an Jiaotong University (西安交通大学) and to Shanghai Jiaotong University (上海交通大学).

A word of warning: China has five universities with Jiaotong in the name. Besides BJTU there are Southwest Jiaotong University, National Chiao Tung University, and the Shanghai and Xi'an ones above. Make sure you apply to the right one.

BJTU is on the Double First-Class Construction list, was a Project 211 university and was part of the 985 Project Innovation Platform. In 2017 it formally joined the ranks of the double first-class universities.
As of 2009, the university's administration included the following units:
Electronic Information Engineering Institute
Computer and Informational Technology Institute
Economy Management Institute
Communication and Transportation Institute
Civil Engineering and Architecture Institute
Mechanical and Electronic Control Engineering Institute
Electric Power Institute
Physical Sciences Institute
Humanities and Social Sciences Institute
Languages and communication studies Institute
Software Engineering Institute
Architecture and Art Institute
Long-Distance and Continued Education Institute

Research is carried out in 22 institutes and 39 laboratories, among them a transportation system simulation laboratory and a transportation automation laboratory. The library has over a million books and 3000 Chinese and foreign journals, along with numerous microfiche documents and audio and video recordings on up-to-date media. The university also has its own facilities that few campuses can match: a transmitter tower, a hospital, hotels, a TV station, indoor and outdoor swimming pools, a gym, an arboretum, moot courts, a museum, an art gallery, a railway line and a stadium.

In 2017 there were 25,569 full-time students on campus. Of these, 7,527 were postgraduates working toward master's or PhD degrees. There were 500 international students, and 8,767 more were enrolled in correspondence courses, night schools and other programmes. The teaching and research staff number 2844. Within that group, 10 hold academician status in the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering, 286 are full professors, and 588 are associate professors. The faculties of transportation, engineering, law and ICT have a particularly good reputation.

The university's badge is built from an outer ring and a gear ring, which are concentric. The Chinese school name on it is in Mao Zedong's calligraphy ("Beifang Jiaotong University"), and the English name, "BEIJING JIAOTONG UNIVERSITY", is in a different typeface. Symbols on the badge carry meaning: the anvil, hammer, chain and gear represent industry and manufactured goods; the books stand for science and knowledge; and a gear is also used for management. The overall message is that this is a university whose core is science and engineering.
The motto is "知行", a two-character phrase that can be read as "knowing and doing".
The university is a member of an alliance of Beijing science and technology universities.

To promote Chinese culture abroad, BJTU has set up Confucius Institutes in Belgium, Brazil and the United States. It joined OSJD, the international organisation for railway cooperation, in 2017, a step that raised its standing in the global rail sector. Membership of the China-CEEC association of universities, which links China with central and eastern Europe, laid the groundwork for wider exchange with that region. BJTU has also been the host of a rail transit training school run under the Belt and Road Initiative, and of the China-ASEAN rail transit training alliance's annual gathering.

Other agreements include one with Russia, one involving Zhan Tianyou College, and a cooperation agreement between China and Indonesia to build a China-Indonesia high-speed railway research centre together with the Bandung Institute of Technology. A dual degree programme with Universiti Malaysia Pahang in Malaysia is also available.

BJTU was among the first Chinese universities authorised by the government to accept foreign students. Over 3,000 international students and visiting scholars have studied at BJTU, drawn from up to 71 countries on four continents (Asia, Africa, Europe and North America). Partner universities are located in Switzerland, Singapore, Japan, Australia, Germany, the UK, France and the US.

The "Entering China" programme is an international exchange scheme that BJTU sponsors together with a partner, the China Women and Children Development Center. Its aims are to promote cross-border education and cultural contact between Chinese and international students, and the two organisers work together to give international students a full range of educational services. In 2007 BJTU appointed Studypath as strategic technology partner to coordinate student enrolment for it. The online service is a "technological study-path" open worldwide that supports exchange students before and after they arrive in China.
BJTU also works with Shanghai Jiaotong University, so that business and economics students may use both campuses.
Alumni listed below come from politics, engineering, the arts, literature and business. They are given for background only.
Hu Haifeng, a politician and son of Hu Jintao, the former Party General Secretary, President and Central Military Commission chairman.
Mao Yisheng, a structural engineer and bridge-construction expert, who was also a social activist.
Zheng Zhenduo, a journalist, writer, archaeologist and scholar.
Liang Tsai-Ping, a guzheng player.
Li Hejun, who founded Hanergy and chairs it.
Student life depends on the capital around the campus, so the following sections explain the city's buildings, landscape, weather and air.

Three architectural styles stand out in urban Beijing. The first is classical imperial architecture. Its finest examples are the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the most recognisable emblem of the People's Republic. The second is the "Sino-Sov" style, which tends to be boxy and was sometimes poorly built, produced between the 1950s and the 1970s. The third is the far more modern architecture, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east, with the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

New construction has boomed in the early twenty-first century, bringing a range of modern styles by international designers, strongest in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone mixes 1950s design with a neofuturistic look, blending old and new. The tallest building in the city is the 528-metre China Zun. Two Beijing buildings have taken the CTBUH Skyscraper Award since 2007: the Linked Hybrid (2009) and then the CCTV Headquarters (2013). Only a single building in the world wins this prize for best overall tall building each year.

Siheyuans are courtyards enclosed by buildings. Grand examples include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are usually joined by lanes known as hutongs. Most hutongs are straight lanes running east to west, which lets doors face north and south in line with Feng Shui principles. Widths vary, and the narrowest allow only a few people to walk through together. They used to be everywhere, but entire blocks are now giving way to tall buildings and the old courtyards are disappearing fast. Hutong residents are entitled to flats at least as large as their former homes. Even so, many say that the old community spirit and street life cannot be recreated, and the properties are often government-owned.

The city stands where the roughly triangular North China Plain ends in the north; the plain spreads south and east from it. Hills and mountains in the north, northwest and west protect both Beijing and the agricultural heartland of the north from the desert steppes. In the northwest, particularly in Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains rise, and the Western Hills (Xishan) lie along the western side. The Great Wall runs across the north of the municipality, built on rugged ground to keep out nomadic raiders from the steppes. The highest point is Mount Dongling in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Major rivers include the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, all tributaries of the Hai River system that flow to the southeast. The largest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun, on the upper Chaobai. Beijing is also the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, a transport route built over 1,400 years ago, and of the South–North Water Transfer Project, built in the last decade or so to bring water from the Yangtze basin.

Built-up Beijing occupies flat land in the south-central part of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres above sea level (about 130–200 feet). It is a relatively small share of the municipality's area, but a growing one. Concentric ring roads structure the city: the Second Ring Road runs where the old walls stood, and the Sixth Ring Road ties in satellite towns. The middle of the city is Tian'anmen and its Square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, which was the emperors' residence. Zhongnanhai, the residence of today's leaders, is west of Tian'anmen, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between the gate and the square, is the principal east–west axis. Growth outward from the old centre has often been compared to a pancake spreading out (tan da bing in Chinese), and people frequently cite that pattern as a reason for the city's urban problems.

In Köppen terms, Beijing is humid continental (Dwa), verging on cold semi-arid with monsoon influence (BSk). Summers are hot and humid thanks to the East Asian monsoon, and winters are short, cold and dry, shaped by the huge Siberian anticyclone. In spring, sandstorms can blow in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe, while temperatures rise quickly in generally dry weather, and autumn is a transitional season with little rainfall. For 2001 to 2026 the hottest period has been early August and the coldest early January. On China's official seasonal calendar the dates are 26 March for the start of spring, 20 May for summer, 13 September for autumn and 31 October for winter. Because March and September have been warming faster, and May and October slower, in recent years, autumn is usually shorter than spring.

The urban annual mean, measured over 1991 to 2020, is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2–55.9 °F), with average daily lows of 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9–47.1 °F) and average daily highs of 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3–66.0 °F). In low-lying parts of the suburbs the annual average is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7–55.4 °F), with daily lows between 5.9 and 8.0 °C (42.6–46.4 °F) and highs between 18.2 and 18.7 °C (64.8–65.7 °F). In the mountains it falls between 0 and 10 °C (32–50 °F), dropping with altitude. Daily means are −2.7 °C in January (27.1 °F) and 27.2 °C in July (81.0 °F).

The city receives about 528.0 mm of rain a year (20.79 in), although the figure for Haidian and Chaoyang is 584.2 mm (23.00 in), and close to three quarters of it arrives in June, July and August. Sunshine, as a share of the possible, is 42% in July and 62% in both January and February, for a yearly total of 2,490.5 hours of bright sun. The record low since 1951 is −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F) from 22 February 1966, and the record high is 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) from 24 July 1999.

beijing-jiaotong-university.h: Air quality and dust in Beijing

blocks.x: Many prospective students ask about air quality, so this part is a straightforward summary of what is known. It shows long-standing problems, large efforts to fix them and clear improvement in recent years.

Beijing has had environmental problems for a long time. Between 2000 and 2009 its urban area quadrupled, which not only raised emissions but also changed the local weather: wind speed, surface albedo and humidity near the ground went down, while ground and near-surface air temperatures, ozone levels and vertical air dilution went up. Urban growth and pollution from burning fossil fuels together bring serious health problems for many residents. In 2013, a severe smog episode covered Beijing and most of northern China, touching some 600 million people. The event, described as a "pollution shock", made air quality a significant economic and social issue across the country. The Beijing government set out measures including lowering coal's share of energy from 24% (2012) to 10% (2017), and the national government required heavily polluting vehicles to be taken off roads in 2015–2017 while accelerating the move to clean energy.

A 2006 study by American and Chinese researchers working together found that Beijing imports much of its pollution from nearby cities and provinces, with 35–60% of the ozone, on average, traceable to outside sources. They said Shandong and Tianjin matter a great deal for the city's air, because summer winds generally come from the south or southeast and mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Burning coal is behind roughly 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and is also the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been changing its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012, with a target of limiting yearly coal use to 20 million tons. It used 26.3 million tons in 2011, of which 73% went on heating and power and the rest on industry. A lot of the pollution is emitted next door. Tianjin was expected to raise its coal consumption from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million in 2015, and Hebei burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, with only 30% of that going to power generation and a substantial amount to steelmaking and cement. Power plants in coal-producing Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (where coal use has tripled since 2000) and in Shandong add to the problem. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia are, in that order, the first to fourth biggest coal consumers among Chinese provinces.

The city once relied on four major coal-fired power plants for electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed first, in 2014, and two others were closed in March 2015. The fourth, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to follow in 2016. Plans for 2013 to 2017 called for a reduction in coal consumption of 13 million tons and a ceiling of 15 million tons in 2015.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, almost US$17 billion went into cleaning the air. For the Games, Beijing stopped work at every construction site, shut many factories in the city for good and paused industry in nearby regions for a while. Some gas stations were closed. Drivers were allowed on the road only on odd or even days depending on their licence plates, which halved traffic, while bus and subway fares were cut, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles banned. It also assembled 3,800 natural-gas buses, one of the world's largest fleets, and became the first Chinese city to require the equivalent of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

Authorities sometimes use cloud seeding to make rain more likely and so clear the air before major events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to fight drought. In recent years the tools have been temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars instead. These produced the "APEC blue" and "parade blue" skies seen around the 2014 APEC China meeting and around the military parade of 2015 that marked Victory Day. Air quality improved a lot while those events took place but returned to unhealthy levels soon after.

The city's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed most industry and commerce, and a smog "red alert" followed later that same month. In November 2016 the environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017, old high-polluting cars would not be allowed on the road whenever a red alert was in force in the city or neighbouring areas.

Real improvements have followed the declaration of a "war on pollution" in 2014. Fine particulates were 35% lower in 2017 and lower again by 2020, largely thanks to natural gas taking over from coal-fired power and to the clean-up of polluting industrial sites. The 2022 annual average for PM2.5 was 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the cleanest since 2013, and 2024 brought only two days of heavy pollution, a record low and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days of 2013.

Because several organisations publish readings, the numbers you see can differ. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) reports daily levels from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website, while the American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures on Twitter. The two track different pollutants against different standards, which is why the bureau's levels, and the health impact it reports, are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog is harmful. Pollution has a direct effect on how common heart and lung disease are in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, hospital visits and even death. If you have a respiratory condition, look at the daily readings and ask your doctor for advice.

Seasonal dust storms hit the city, carrying dust from the eroding deserts of northern and northwestern China. The Beijing Weather Modification Office at times triggers rainfall to combat them and reduce the damage. January to April 2006 saw at least eight storms, and a single one in April 2002 left almost 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it travelled on, reaching Japan and Korea. Expect some dusty days in spring, and keep a mask handy.

beijing-jiaotong-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beijing Jiaotong University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Beijing Jiaotong University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

BLCU, short for Beijing Language and Culture University (北京语言大学), is a state university devoted to languages and located in the capital's Haidian District. It is a key university run directly by China's Ministry of Education. Its central purpose is to teach Chinese language and culture to students from other countries, and it presents itself as unique: the one international university founded by the People's Republic with 'language' in its title and the dissemination of Chinese language and culture as its chief mission.

It is not only for foreigners. BLCU also enrols Chinese students who specialise in foreign languages and related humanities and social science subjects, and it prepares people to become teachers of Chinese for foreign learners. For many years it was the only institution of this type in China. Since the expansion of higher education that began in the 1990s, similar offerings have appeared in almost every major Chinese city, so the degrees that once made BLCU distinctive, from bachelor's to postdoctoral level in teaching Chinese to foreigners as a second language, and undergraduate and master's study of several foreign languages, are no longer found only here.

The nickname 'Little United Nations' is common in China because so many international students study here. In 2022 there were roughly 9,000 of them on campus, the largest number at any Chinese university. On the 2020 edition of the Best Chinese Universities Ranking, which belongs to the Shanghai Ranking family, BLCU stood fifth in China among institutions specialised in language teaching and research.

The roots lie in the early 1950s, when the field of teaching Chinese as a foreign language had barely started and BLCU's earliest teachers were pioneers in it. That effort led, in June 1962, to the first higher education school designed specially for foreign students, the Higher Preparatory School for Foreign Students. In 1964 it received the official name Beijing Language Institute (北京语言学院, Běijīng yǔyán xuéyuàn).

In June 1996 the name changed to Beijing Language and Culture University (北京语言文化大学, Běijīng yǔyán wénhuà dàxué). In July 2002, with the Ministry of Education's approval, the Chinese name was cut to Beijing Language University, though in English nothing changed. On 6 September 2002 the university marked its 40th anniversary, an event for which Vice-Premier Li Lanqing and General-Secretary Jiang Zemin sent letters of congratulation, while NPC Standing Committee Chairman Li Peng contributed words of encouragement. BLCU gained the authority to confer doctorates in foreign languages and literature in 2011.
Altogether, over 220,000 international students from 189 countries and regions have studied at BLCU. The figure of about 9,000 international students in 2022 is the highest in China.

BLCU's campus is in Haidian District. The site covers about 330,289 m2, with about 427,342 m2 of building floor area. It is divided into two zones. The teaching area holds most of the academic facilities, including the main building, the library and the gym, as well as dormitories for Chinese students. The living area has apartments for staff and families and the special dormitory for foreign students, Building 17. Both zones have a few grocery stores. The largest shopping and market district, Wudaokou, lies by the living area's northern gate, so it is the natural place to find food and everyday supplies.
The program lists below are translated names. Confirm which ones accept international applicants and in which language they are taught on the university's own admissions pages.

Languages form the core of the undergraduate offer. Chinese is studied both as language and literature and as a subject for teaching to non-native speakers. Alongside it come Turkish, Portuguese, Italian, Korean, Japanese, Arabic, Russian, Spanish, German, French and English, each taught as language and literature. Translation and interpretation is a degree in its own right.

Outside languages, BLCU offers programs in finance, accounting, painting, journalism, international politics, international economics and trade, digital media technology, and computing (computer science and technology, plus information management and systems).

At master's level the language subjects are broader and more specialised. Chinese studies options are Chinese linguistics and philology, Chinese ancient literature, contemporary Chinese literature, ancient Chinese philology, and Chinese ethnic languages and literatures. More general options are literary theory, applied linguistics, the linguistics of foreign languages, and comparative and world literature.

Foreign-language programs cover English, French, Japanese, Spanish and Arabic language and literature, plus European languages and literatures and Asian and African languages and literatures. For teaching there are course design and teaching theories, and MTCSOL, the master's program for teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages. The remaining options are special historical studies, international politics, ideological and political education, basic psychology, technology of computer application, and the Master of Translation and Interpreting.

Ten doctoral fields are available. Two are foreign-language fields (Arabic, and English). Five concern Chinese literature or language: Chinese ancient literature, modern and contemporary Chinese literature, Chinese philology, the study of ancient Chinese documents, and the languages and literatures of China's ethnic groups. The rest are linguistics and applied linguistics, comparative and world literature, and the theory of literature and art.

Notable people who have taught at BLCU include Wei-Heng Chen, the novelist and screenwriter Liang Xiaosheng, the English novelist, biographer and literary historian Valerie Grosvenor Myer, and Huang Jing, a Chinese-American political scientist who has been publicly accused of spying.

Graduates have gone on to varied careers. Two former students have led Kazakhstan: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, its President, who earlier headed the United Nations Office at Geneva as Director-General, and Karim Massimov, Prime Minister from 10 January 2007 until 24 September 2012 and again between 2 April 2014 and 8 September 2016. Mulatu Teshome served as President of Ethiopia (the Federal Democratic Republic) from 7 October 2013 until 25 October 2018. Others include the author Da Chen, the diplomat Hong Lei, the actress and rapper Awkwafina, and the language YouTuber Xiaomanyc.

If you study at BLCU, you will spend your time in Beijing, so the city's climate, geography, air and buildings are part of the experience. This section takes them in the order a newcomer is likely to meet them: weather first, then the air, then the shape of the land and the city, and finally the architecture.

Beijing is classed as having a humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa) that edges toward the monsoonal cold semi-arid type (BSk). In summary: hot, muggy summers influenced by the East Asian monsoon, and short but cold, dry winters driven by the big Siberian anticyclone. In spring the air warms quickly and stays dry, and sandstorms may blow across the Mongolian steppe from the Gobi Desert. Autumn also has little rain and acts as a bridge between the seasons. Records for 2001 to 2026 put the hottest period of the year in early August and the coldest in early January.

On China's official calendar of seasons, the first day of spring is 26 March, of summer 20 May, of autumn 13 September and of winter 31 October. In recent years March and September have warmed up faster and May and October more slowly, so Beijing's autumn is generally shorter than its spring.

Here are the figures for 1991 to 2020. Urban Beijing averages 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F) over a year; the daily low averages 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and the daily high 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). The lower-lying suburbs are slightly cooler, at 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F) on average, with lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In the mountains the average falls to somewhere between 0 and 10 °C (32 and 50 °F), dropping with altitude. The coldest month, January, averages -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and the hottest, July, 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

About 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of precipitation falls in a typical year, rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, the districts where many universities sit. Close to three-quarters of it comes in June, July and August. Possible sunshine goes from 42% (July) up to 62% (January and February) and totals 2,490.5 hours annually. The most extreme temperatures recorded since 1951 are -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, and the highest, 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), on 24 July 1999. In practice you need a proper winter coat and light summer clothes, and an umbrella for the summer rains.
