In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, with 73% used for heating and electricity and the rest for industry. A lot of what Beijing breathes comes from elsewhere. Tianjin's coal use was projected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Further sources are power plants in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal use has tripled since 2000, and in Shandong. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces for coal consumption.

Four major coal-fired plants once supplied the city with electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant shut in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to shut in 2016. Between 2013 and 2017 the city planned to reduce its coal use by 13 million tons, limiting it to 15 million tons for 2015.

The government has at times used cloud seeding to raise the odds of rain and clear the sky before big events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to counter drought. beijing-language-and-culture-university.h: Monitoring the air; dust and health

blocks.x: You can follow readings from two main sources. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily pollution data from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the American Embassy publishes hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's pollution and health-impact numbers are often lower than the embassy's.

The health risk is real. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on how common cardiovascular and respiratory diseases are in Beijing, and exposure to heavy concentrations can cause breathing and heart problems, emergency-room visits and even death.

Seasonal dust storms are another nuisance. Desert erosion in northern and northwestern China sends dust toward the city, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain artificially to fight the storms and reduce their effects. No fewer than eight storms struck during January to April 2006, and one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing before travelling on toward Japan and Korea.

beijing-language-and-culture-university.h: The shape of the land and the city

blocks.x: Geographically, Beijing is at the northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that opens to the south and east. Mountains lie to the north, northwest and west, protecting the city and northern China's farmland from the desert steppe. The Jundu Mountains dominate the northwest of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou districts, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the northern part of the municipality on rugged ground chosen to defend against raids from the steppe. The highest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The main rivers (Chaobai, Yongding and Juma) all flow southeast as tributaries of the Hai River system. The largest reservoir is Miyun, on the upper Chaobai. The city is where the Grand Canal to Hangzhou ends in the north (it was built more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route), and it is the destination of the South-North Water Transfer Project, a scheme finished within the last ten years that brings in water from the Yangtze River basin.

The urban area, on plains in the south-central part of the municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) elevation, is a relatively small but expanding share of the total area. Ring roads circle the centre. The Second Ring Road traces the line where the old city walls stood, and the outermost one, the Sixth Ring Road, connects satellite towns out in the suburbs. Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square mark the middle of the city, directly south of the Forbidden City, which was the emperors' residence. Zhongnanhai, where China's present leaders live, lies west of Tian'anmen, and Chang'an Avenue, running between Tiananmen and the Square, is the main east-west axis.

How the city has expanded from its old inner core to its urban edge is often described as 'spreading like a pancake' (tan da bing), and this pattern is regularly named as a cause of Beijing's urban problems.

beijing-language-and-culture-university.h: Old courtyards, imperial gates and new towers

blocks.x: Three architectural styles dominate urban Beijing. The first is the traditional imperial style, best illustrated by Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), which is the trademark building of the People's Republic, along with the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second is the 'Sino-Sov' style of the 1950s to the 1970s, with boxy buildings that are sometimes poorly constructed. The third is modern architecture, seen most clearly in the Beijing CBD in the east, such as the new CCTV Headquarters, as well as at the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Beijing has seen tremendous growth in new buildings in the early 21st century, with modern designs by international architects, particularly in the CBD. In the 798 Art Zone you can see both 1950s design and a neofuturistic style, old and new together. The tallest tower is the China Zun, at 528 metres. Two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which honours one building worldwide each year as the top tall building overall: the Linked Hybrid took it in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

Siheyuan are courtyards enclosed by buildings, and grand examples include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. They are normally linked by alleys called hutongs, which mostly run straight from east to west, so that front doors face north or south as good feng shui requires. Hutongs differ in width, and some are so narrow that only a few pedestrians can pass at a time. Siheyuan and hutongs were once everywhere in Beijing but are fast disappearing as whole blocks give way to high-rises. Hutong residents are entitled to move into apartments at least as large as their old homes, yet many say the old neighbourly community and lively street life can never be recreated. These homes are often government owned.

Beijing Normal University (北京师范大学), widely abbreviated BNU, is a public university in the Haidian district of Beijing. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and the ministry and the Beijing Municipal People's Government share its funding. The university is best known for training teachers and for education science, and it also has solid foundations in both the arts and the natural sciences. Like other leading Chinese universities, it also belongs to Project 211, the Project 985 scheme and the Double First-Class Construction programme.

BNU dates its beginnings to 1902, when a teacher-training department was created inside the Imperial University of Peking (京师大学堂师范馆) on an order from the Qing emperor. Chinese history had not seen an institution devoted mainly to preparing teachers and specialising in education before, so this department set the base for modern higher education in the country. It became independent in 1908 and took the name Supreme Education School of Peking (京师优级师范学堂).

In 1923 the school developed into National Beijing Normal University (国立北京师范大学校), the first time "Normal University" was used as a title in China. In 1931 the university grew considerably: Peking Women's Normal University (北平女子师范大学) came in and joined what was then known as Peking Normal University (北平师范大学). After the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, the institution received its present name, Beijing Normal University.

In 1952, during a nationwide restructuring of higher education, Fu Jen Catholic University was absorbed into BNU as a further consolidation. In 1959, seven years after that, the Ministry of Education named BNU one of the 20 National Key Universities in China.

Around the turn of the 21st century, BNU strengthened its standing by taking part in the major national programmes. It entered Project 211 in 1996, a scheme to raise around 100 universities to a level suitable for the 21st century, and then Project 985 in 2002, which aimed to lift a small group of institutions to world prominence. In 2009 The New York Times described BNU as among China's most progressive institutions, which brought it wider international attention.

In 2017 BNU was among the 36 institutions listed under the Double First-Class Construction initiative, with 11 of its disciplines counted among the country's best. The same year the university worked with the Guangdong provincial government and the Zhuhai municipal government to plan a new campus in Zhuhai, and the Ministry of Education officially approved the BNU Zhuhai Campus in April 2019.

Together with five partner institutions, BNU is part of a consortium that teaches an Erasmus+ joint master's degree as well as a Master in Research and Innovation in Higher Education. Its partners are the University of Tampere, Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology, Hochschule Osnabrück University of Applied Sciences, Eötvös Loránd University and the University for Continuing Education Krems.

It was one of the first Chinese institutions to welcome international students, and it remains especially popular for programmes in Mandarin Chinese. One of its best-regarded programmes is Princeton in Beijing, run jointly with Princeton University in the US. For the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), BNU is a partner in an MA programme in Chinese language and literature, and it hosts the Secretariat of the BRICS Universities League, with BNU acting as a leading university for BRICS higher-education and academic cooperation.

In the 2025 QS World University Rankings by Subject, BNU came 7th in the world, 2nd in the Asia-Pacific and top in China for "Education and Training". That is no surprise, since the Faculty of Education grew out of the normal-university tradition and has always been a historical strength.

In the 2021 WURI (World's Universities with Real Impacts) Ranking, BNU was 36th of the Global Top 100 Innovative Universities. Three major global tables, namely the Academic Ranking of World Universities, the U.S. News & World Report list and the Times Higher Education World University Rankings, all had it within the top 150 as of 2026. Employers like its graduates in China and elsewhere; a 2017 graduate employability ranking placed the university in the global top 200+, among those with high-achieving graduates. For reputation, the THE World Reputation Rankings list BNU among China's most respected universities at #126 worldwide.

Foreign visitors who studied here as language students include three people from Dartmouth College. Timothy Geithner, who became U.S. Treasury Secretary, the 75th person to hold that office, studied Mandarin in 1982 as an undergraduate. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York joined as an undergraduate in Dartmouth's FSP programme, and actress Connie Britton, who took part in the same programme as a language student, was her roommate.
Life outside the classroom depends largely on the city, so these sections describe Beijing: its buildings, its landscape, its weather and the state of its air.

Urban Beijing is dominated by three architectural styles. First comes the traditional architecture of imperial China, best seen in the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the trademark building of the People's Republic, together with the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City. Second is the so-called "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to 1970s, with boxy buildings that were sometimes poorly built. Third are much more modern forms, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, and in other places such as the National Center for the Performing Arts and the Beijing National Stadium.

The early 21st century brought an enormous wave of new construction in many modern styles by international designers, strongest in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone shows how 1950s design and neofuturistic style can be mixed with the old. The tallest building in the city is the 528-meter China Zun. Beijing buildings have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which goes to just one best overall tall building worldwide each year: the CCTV Headquarters in 2013, and the Linked Hybrid before it in 2009.

Then there are the siheyuan, courtyards ringed by buildings, with grand examples such as the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are typically joined by alleys called hutongs, which mostly run east-west, so doorways face north or south, a layout chosen for good Feng Shui. Some are so narrow that only a few pedestrians can pass at a time. Once found everywhere in Beijing, siheyuan and hutongs are vanishing quickly as whole blocks are replaced by high-rises. Hutong residents are entitled to apartments in the new buildings at least as big as their old homes, but many complain that the community spirit and lively street life of the hutongs cannot be recreated, and the properties tend to be government-owned.

Beijing lies on the northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular plain that opens to the south and east. Mountains to the north, north-west and west protect the city and northern China's farming heartland from the desert steppes. The Jundu Mountains cover the north-western part of the municipality, particularly Yanqing and Huairou Districts, and Xishan, the Western Hills, frame the west. Across the north of the municipality runs the Great Wall of China, which follows rugged terrain and was built against nomadic raids from the steppes. The highest point is Mount Dongling at 7,556 ft (2,303 metres), in the Western Hills where Beijing meets Hebei.

The main rivers, including the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, belong to the Hai River system and flow south-east. The Miyun Reservoir on the upper Chaobai is the largest in the municipality. Beijing is also where the Grand Canal to Hangzhou ends in the north; it was built over 1,400 years ago as a transport route. The South-North Water Transfer Project, built within the past decade, ends here too and carries water from the Yangtze River basin.

The urban area sits on the plains in the south-central part of the municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) and covers a relatively small but growing share of its area. Concentric ring roads shape the city's growth: the Second Ring Road traces the old city walls, and the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs. At the centre sit Tian'anmen and its Square, directly south of the Forbidden City where emperors once lived; Zhongnanhai, home of China's current leaders, is to the west. The main east-west axis is Chang'an Avenue, passing between the gate and the Square. People often say Beijing's growth from the old inner city to the fringe "spreads like a pancake" (tan da bing), and that pattern is often blamed for the city's urban problems.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). Summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon, while winters are brief, cold and dry under the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone. Spring can bring sandstorms carried from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, with quick and mostly dry warming. Autumn is another transition season with very little rain. Over 2001 to 2026 the hottest period has been early August and the coldest early January.

By China's seasonal calendar the seasons reach Beijing as follows: spring 26 March, summer 20 May, autumn 13 September, winter 31 October. Because March and September have been warming faster and May and October more slowly lately, autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

For 1991 to 2020 the urban area's annual mean temperature is between 12.9 and 13.3 °C (55.2-55.9 °F). Typical daily lows are 7.7-8.4 °C (45.9-47.1 °F) and daily highs 18.5-18.9 °C (65.3-66.0 °F). In low-lying suburbs the annual mean is 11.5-13.0 °C (52.7-55.4 °F), with lows of 5.9-8.0 °C (42.6-46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2-18.7 °C (64.8-65.7 °F). Mountain areas average from 0 to 10 °C (32-50 °F), cooler the higher you go. January averages -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F), so a student needs clothing for both a real winter and a hot, humid summer.

Annual precipitation is about 20.79 in (528.0 mm), rising to 23.00 in (584.2 mm) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and almost three-quarters of it arrives between June and August. Sunshine is 42% of the possible in July and 62% in January and February, adding up to 2,490.5 hours a year. The record low since 1951 is -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), set on 22 February 1966, and the record high 107.4 °F (41.9 °C), on 24 July 1999.

Environmental trouble has a long history in Beijing. From 2000 to 2009 the urban footprint grew fourfold. This sharply increased human emissions, but it also altered the local meteorology on its own: surface albedo, wind speed and humidity near the ground dropped, while temperatures at the ground and just above it, the vertical mixing of air and ozone levels all went up. Urbanisation and fossil-fuel burning combine to cause frequent serious pollution, with health consequences for many residents. A heavy smog in 2013 hit Beijing and most of northern China, affecting 600 million people altogether, and this "pollution shock" turned air quality into a big economic and social concern nationwide. Beijing's government responded with measures to cut pollution, such as lowering coal's share from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017. Nationally, heavily polluting vehicles had to be taken off the road in 2015-2017 and the transition to clean energy sources was stepped up.

A joint 2006 study by American and Chinese researchers concluded that much of the city's pollution comes from surrounding cities and provinces. On average, between 35 and 60% of the city's ozone comes from outside it. The study pointed to Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality as having a major influence on the city's air, partly because summer winds usually blow from the south or south-east and mountains lie to the north and north-west.

About 40% of the city's PM 2.5 comes from burning coal, which is also the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 Beijing has been switching coal-fired power stations to natural gas, and it wants to cap annual coal use at 20 million tons. The city burned 26.3 million tons in 2011: 73% for heating and power and the remainder for industry. A lot of the pollution is emitted in nearby regions. Coal use in Tianjin was forecast to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, while Hebei Province burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than all of Germany, with only 30% used for power and a large part for making steel and cement. Power stations in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (where coal consumption has tripled since 2000), and in Shandong, add to Beijing's pollution too. Ranked by coal consumption, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia are the first four provinces in China.

Four large coal-fired plants once supplied the city's electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two others shut in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to close in 2016. For 2013 to 2017 the city planned to cut coal use by 13 million tons and hold consumption to 15 million tons in 2015.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent to meet promises about cleaner air. During the Games Beijing halted all construction work, permanently closed many local factories, shut industry in neighbouring regions for a time, closed some gas stations, cut motor traffic by half with an odd-even licence-plate system, lowered bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It also put together 3,800 buses running on natural gas, among the biggest such fleets anywhere, and became the first Chinese city to demand the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Sometimes the authorities use cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air before big events, as before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, or to deal with drought. More recently they have preferred temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, which produced "APEC blue" (APEC China 2014) and "parade blue" (the 2015 China Victory Day Parade), brief spells of clean air around those events. In both cases air quality improved sharply and then fell back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, shutting down most industry and commercial businesses, and later that month a smog "red alert" was declared. In November 2016 the Beijing environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be banned from driving whenever smog "red alerts" were issued in the city or nearby regions.

The recent trend, though, is encouraging, and the situation has clearly improved compared with a decade ago. Pollutant levels have measurably fallen since the "war on pollution" was announced in 2014: fine particulates were down 35% in 2017 and fell further by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial facilities were cleaned up. In 2022 average PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic meter, the cleanest year since 2013, and 2024 brought only two days of heavy pollution, the fewest ever recorded and 96.6 percent below the 58 days counted in 2013. Anyone with asthma or another breathing problem should still talk to a doctor before choosing a city with air this variable.

Because pollution is high, different sources give different readings. Daily readings from 27 monitoring stations are published on the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) website, while the American Embassy in Beijing tweets hourly figures for fine particulates (PM2.5) and ozone. As the two measure different pollutants by different criteria (so it is worth looking at both before outdoor exercise), the BJEPB's pollution and health-impact figures are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog is more than a nuisance: it is dangerous. Air pollution clearly affects rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, hospital emergency visits and even death.

Dust eroded from the deserts of northern and north-western China brings seasonal dust storms to the city, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain artificially to fight them and reduce their effects. The first four months of 2006 alone saw at least eight, and one storm in April 2002 deposited nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city and then travelled on towards Japan and Korea.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

beijing-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Beijing Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Beijing Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Beijing Sport University, known as BSU (北京体育大学), is a public university in the Chinese capital, and its whole focus is sport: sport science, coaching, physical education and everything built around them. It is part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction initiative, and it is run by the General Administration of Sport of China. If you want to study sport at the highest level in China, you will be considering this campus.

The university opened in 1953 under the name Central Institute of Physical Education (中央体育学院). By 1960 it was in the first group of national key universities chosen by the State Council. It is the only university in China that holds the Category I discipline of sport science, which is a national key discipline.

The campus is in Beijing's Haidian District and covers approximately 1,400 acres, with about 600,000 square metres of buildings. BSU has 1,027 faculty and about 14,000 students; the figures given are 8,265 undergraduates and 2,255 postgraduates. As of 2015 its teachers and students together had won 73 gold medals at the Olympic Games, which tells you how closely the university is tied to elite sport.

Undergraduates choose from 39 majors, taught in 20 different colleges. The subject areas include the humanities, sports science, education, the sciences, economic theory and communications, so there is more variety than the university's name might suggest.

Your student life will depend heavily on the city, so the rest of this overview describes Beijing: the air, the weather, the land, and the buildings. We start with the issue that worries many newcomers, air quality, and finish with the architecture.

Beijing has struggled with environmental problems for a long time. Its urban footprint became four times larger between 2000 and 2009. That growth did more than add emissions from people: it changed the local meteorology at a basic level, even before human emissions are counted. Urbanisation plus fossil-fuel pollution means serious environmental trouble is common in Beijing, and it harms the health of many residents.

Beijing itself used to have four large coal-fired power plants providing electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was shut in 2014, and two more closed in March 2015. The health effects are real. Here are the 1991 to 2020 averages. In the urban area the annual mean sits between 12.9 °C and 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F), with night-time minimums around 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daytime maximums of 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). Sunshine, measured as a share of the possible total, is lowest in July (42%) and highest in January and February (62%). Overall the city gets 2,490.5 hours of sun annually. Note that BSU's home district of Haidian is one of the two wetter districts.

beijing-technology-and-business-universi.h: About Beijing Technology and Business University

blocks.x: Beijing Technology and Business University (BTBU; 北京工商大学) is a municipal public university in Beijing, China. It was founded based on the amalgamation of Beijing Light Industry School, Beijing Business School, and the Administration School for Ministry of Machinery Industry.

Under the university, there are 16 schools, 1 department (Research Institute), and 1 education center, within which are 43 undergraduate majors, 35 postgraduate majors, 2 master's degree programs, and some joint doctoral programs that are offered. Among those majors and programs, 16 are awarded the Beijing Municipal and Preferential-construction disciplines or majors. Also at BTBU, there exist 2 national industrial test centers, 1 national experimental center for Practical Teaching, 1 Beijing Municipal Key Lab, and 2 Beijing Municipal Research Bases.
There are three academicians of the Chinese Academy of Engineering in BTBU.

At present, the university has 807 full-time faculty members, 48% of whom have senior professional titles. Eight professors enjoy special research allowance from the State Council; two are awarded as China's Excellent Teachers; three are Famous Teachers of Universities in Beijing; five are Excellent Teachers in Beijing; 53 are Excellent Young Teachers in Beijing; and 11 research teams were selected as Academic Innovation Teams of Beijing.
BTBU now has about 12000 full-time undergraduates, 5700 part-time students, and 1300 postgraduates and doctoral students.
With the prestige of Beijing Institute of Light Industry, currently BTBU has some prestigious scholars like Prof. Baoguo Sun, and has been actively involved in International cooperation.

By the agreement signed by the Irish head of government and the Chinese leader (Brian Cowen and Hu Jintao) in 2008, BTBU exchanges lots students and lectures with University College Cork, UCD Dublin, for combined degree programmes (2+2, and 3+1+1/1.5) and non-degree programmes, and recently, with the University of Oxford.
Many students also are recruited by other universities in North America and European, such as Häme University of Applied Sciences.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Beijing, where Beijing Technology and Business University is located.

Three styles of architecture are predominant in urban Beijing. First, there is the traditional architecture of imperial China, perhaps best exemplified by the massive Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which remains the People's Republic of China's trademark edifice, the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven. Next, there is what is sometimes referred to as the "Sino-Sov" style, with structures tending to be boxy and sometimes poorly constructed, which were built between the 1950s and the 1970s. Finally, there are much more modern architectural forms, most noticeably in the area of the Beijing CBD in east Beijing such as the new CCTV Headquarters, in addition to buildings in other locations around the city such as the Beijing National Stadium and National Center for the Performing Arts.

In the early 21st century, Beijing has witnessed tremendous growth of new building constructions, exhibiting various modern styles from international designers, most pronounced in the CBD region. A mixture of both 1950s design and neofuturistic style of architecture can be seen at the 798 Art Zone, which mixes the old with the new. Beijing's tallest building is the 528-meter China Zun. Since 2007, buildings in Beijing have received the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building twice, for the Linked Hybrid building in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. The CTBUH Skyscraper award for best tall overall building is given to only one building around the world every year.

Siheyuans in Beijing are courtyards surrounding by buildings. Among the more grand examples are the Prince Gong Mansion and Residence of Soong Ching-ling. These courtyards are usually connected by alleys called hutongs. The hutongs are generally straight and run east to west so that doorways face north and south for good Feng Shui. They vary in width; some are so narrow only a few pedestrians can pass through at a time. Once ubiquitous in Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are rapidly disappearing, as entire city blocks of hutongs are replaced by high-rise buildings. Residents of the hutongs are entitled to live in the new buildings in apartments of at least the same size as their former residences. Many complain, however, that the traditional sense of community and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced, and these properties are often government owned.

Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The northwestern part of the municipality, especially Yanqing District and Huairou District, are dominated by the Jundu Mountains, while the western part is framed by Xishan or the Western Hills. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of Beijing Municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills and on the border with Hebei, is the municipality's highest point, with an altitude of 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Major rivers flowing through the municipality, including the Chaobai, Yongding, Juma, are all tributaries in the Hai River system, and flow in a southeasterly direction. The Miyun Reservoir, on the upper reaches of the Chaobai River, is the largest reservoir within the municipality. Beijing is also the northern terminus of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, which was built over 1,400 years ago as a transportation route, and the South–North Water Transfer Project, constructed in the past decade to bring water from the Yangtze River basin.

The urban area of Beijing, on the plains in the south-central of the municipality with elevation of 40 to 60 metres (130–200 feet), occupies a relatively small but expanding portion of the municipality's area. The city spreads out in concentric ring roads. The Second Ring Road traces the old city walls and the Sixth Ring Road connects satellite towns in the surrounding suburbs. Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square are at the center of Beijing, directly to the south of the Forbidden City, the former residence of the emperors of China. To the west of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, the residence of China's current leaders. Chang'an Avenue, which cuts between Tiananmen and the Square, forms the city's main east–west axis.

Beijing's pattern of development from the old inner city to its urban fringe are frequently described as "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing). This pattern of development is frequently cited as a reason for Beijing's urban problems.

Beijing has a humid continental climate (Köppen: Dwa), bordering on a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (Köppen: BSk). The city is characterized by hot, humid summers due to the East Asian monsoon as well as brief but cold, dry winters that reflect the influence of the vast Siberian anticyclone. Spring can bear witness to sandstorms blowing in from the Gobi Desert across the Mongolian steppe, accompanied by rapidly warming, but generally dry, conditions. Autumn, similar to spring, is a season of transition and minimal precipitation. From 2001 to 2026, the hottest period in Beijing is early August, and the coldest period is early January. According to China's seasonal division standard, Beijing enters spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September, and winter on 31 October. Due to the faster warming in March and September and the slower warming in May and October in recent years, Beijing is generally shorter in autumn than in spring. The average annual temperature (From 1991 to 2020) in the urban area of Beijing is 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) to 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), of which the average daily minimum temperature is 7.7 °C (45.9 °F) to 8.4 °C (47.1 °F), and the average daily maximum temperature is 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) to 18.9 °C (66.0 °F). The average annual temperature in the low-altitude part of the suburbs of Beijing is 11.5 °C (52.7 °F) to 13.0 °C (55.4 °F), of which the average daily minimum temperature is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) to 8.0 °C (46.4 °F), and the average daily maximum temperature is 18.2 °C (64.8 °F) to 18.7 °C (65.7 °F). The average annual temperature in mountainous areas is between 0 °C (32 °F) and 10 °C (50 °F), decreasing as the altitude increases. The monthly daily average temperature in January is −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), while in July it is 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Precipitation averages around 528.0 mm (20.79 in) annually (Haidian and Chaoyang has an average annual precipitation of 584.2 mm (23.00 in)), with close to three-quarters of that total falling from June to August. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 42% in July to 62% in January and February, the city receives 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966 to 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.

Beijing had a long history of environmental problems. Between 2000 and 2009 Beijing's urban extent quadrupled, which not only strongly increased the extent of anthropogenic emissions, but also changed the meteorological situation fundamentally, even if emissions of human society are not included. For example, surface albedo, wind speed and humidity near the surface were decreased, whereas ground and near-surface air temperatures, vertical air dilution and ozone levels were increased. Because of the combined factors of urbanization and pollution caused by burning of fossil fuel, Beijing is often affected by serious environmental problems, which lead to health issues of many inhabitants. In 2013 heavy smog struck Beijing and most parts of northern China, impacting a total of 600 million people. After this "pollution shock" air pollution became an important economic and social concern in China. After that the government of Beijing announced measures to reduce air pollution, for example by lowering the share of coal from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, while the national government ordered heavily polluting vehicles to be removed from 2015 to 2017 and increased its efforts to transition the energy system to clean sources.

Joint research between American and Chinese researchers in 2006 concluded that much of the city's pollution comes from surrounding cities and provinces. On average 35–60% of the ozone can be traced to sources outside the city. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality have a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", partly due to the prevailing south/southeasterly flow during the summer and the mountains to the north and northwest.

In preparation for the 2008 Summer Olympics and to fulfill promises to clean up the city's air, nearly US$17 billion was spent. Beijing implemented a number of air improvement schemes for the duration of the Games, including halting work at all construction sites, closing many factories in Beijing permanently, temporarily shutting industry in neighboring regions, closing some gas stations, and cutting motor traffic by half by limiting drivers to odd or even days (based on their license plate numbers), reducing bus and subway fares, opening new subway lines, and banning high-emission vehicles. The city further assembled 3,800 natural gas-powered buses, one of the largest fleets in the world. Beijing became the first city in China to require the Chinese equivalent to the Euro 4 emission standard.

Coal burning accounts for about 40% of the PM 2.5 in Beijing and is also the chief source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012, the city has been converting coal-fired power stations to burn natural gas and aims to cap annual coal consumption at 20 million tons. In 2011, the city burned 26.3 million tons of coal, 73% of which for heating and power generation and the remainder for industry. Much of the city's air pollutants are emitted by neighboring regions. Coal consumption in neighboring Tianjin is expected to increase from 48 to 63 million tons from 2011 to 2015. Hebei Province burned over 300 million tons of coal in 2011, more than all of Germany, of which only 30% were used for power generation and a considerable portion for steel and cement making. Power plants in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal consumption has tripled since 2000, and Shandong also contribute to air pollution in Beijing. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, respectively rank from first to fourth, among Chinese provinces by coal consumption. There were four major coal-fired power plants in the city to provide electricity as well as heating during the winter. The first one (Gaojing Thermal Power Plant) was shut down in 2014. Another two were shut in March 2015. The last one (Huaneng Thermal Power Plant) would be shut in 2016. Between 2013 and 2017, the city planned to reduce 13 million tons of coal consumption and cap coal consumption to 15 million tons in 2015.

The government sometimes uses cloud-seeding measures to increase the likelihood of rain showers in the region to clear the air prior to large events, such as prior to the 60th anniversary parade in 2009 as well as to combat drought conditions in the area. More recently, however, the government has increased its usage of such measures as closing factories temporarily and implementing greater restrictions for cars on the road, as in the case of "APEC blue" and "parade blue", short periods during and immediately preceding the APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, respectively. During and prior to these events, Beijing's air quality improved dramatically, only to fall back to unhealthy levels shortly after.

On 8 and 9 December 2015 Beijing had its first smog alert which shut down a majority of the industry and other commercial businesses in the city. Later in the month another smog "red alert" was issued.

According to Beijing's environmental protection bureau's announcement in November 2016, starting from 2017 highly polluting old cars will be banned from being driven whenever Smog "red alerts" are issued in the city or neighboring regions.

In recent years, there has been measurable reductions in pollutants after the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014, with Beijing seeing a 35% reduction in fine particulates in 2017 and further reduction by 2020. The primary factors behind this reduction were replacing coal power with natural gas and cleaning up polluting industrial facilities in the Beijing area.

Beijing's annual average concentration of major airborne fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, declined to 30 micrograms per cubic meter in 2022, the best air quality for the city since 2013. In 2024, Beijing experienced only two days of heavy pollution, the lowest number on record, which had decreased by 96.6 percent from 58 days in 2013.

Due to Beijing's high level of air pollution, there are various readings by different sources on the subject. Daily pollution readings at 27 monitoring stations around the city are reported on the website of the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB). The American Embassy of Beijing also reports hourly fine particulate (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. Since the BJEPB and US Embassy measure different pollutants according to different criteria, the pollution levels and the impact to human health reported by the BJEPB are often lower than that reported by the US Embassy.

The smog is causing harm and danger to the population. The air pollution does directly result in significant impact on the morbidity rate of cardiovascular disease and respiratory disease in Beijing. Exposure to large concentrations of polluted air can cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems, emergency room visits, and even death.

Dust from the erosion of deserts in northern and northwestern China results in seasonal dust storms that plague the city; the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes artificially induces rainfall to fight such storms and mitigate their effects. In the first four months of 2006 alone, there were no fewer than eight such storms. In April 2002, one dust storm alone dumped nearly 50,000 tons of dust onto the city before moving on to Japan and Korea.

Beijing University of Chemical Technology, known as BUCT (北京化工大学, literally Beijing Chemical Industry University), is a public university in Beijing's Chaoyang District. The university dates from 1958 and reports to China's Ministry of Education. It has a place in two national programmes for leading universities: the Double First-Class Construction and Project 211.
The university's land adds up to 64.4 hectares and is split across three campuses, with a fourth site being developed.
The East campus is the headquarters. It lies along the eastern part of the North Third Ring Road, to the southeast of the Asian Games Village.
The West campus is on the middle stretch of the West Third Ring Road.

The North campus is in Changping, close to Lake Shisanling. Most of it was sold to China University of Petroleum, and what remains will serve as staff dormitories. The reason is that a newer northern site, the Nankou campus, sits farther from the East campus, so staff need extra housing.

The Nankou campus is also in Changping, about 5 km from Changping Xishankou station on the Beijing Subway's Changping line, and it is near the Institute of Nuclear Energy Technology of Tsinghua University.
If you are applying, ask the university which campus your programme and your accommodation will be on, since the distances between sites in Beijing can be considerable.

The university has 14 colleges. The list begins with Chemical Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering, and goes on to cover Life Science and Technology, Mechanical and Electrical Engineering, Information Science and Technology, a general Science college, Economic Management, and Humanities and Law. A further college handles Further Education and Vocational Education, which brings the total to 14. About 1800 staff work on campus, and the student body numbers around 12,000.

BUCT is included among the top 450 universities in a global World University Rankings list. Its strongest reputation is in chemical engineering: it ranks as one of the world's leading research institutions in that field, and in 2022 it took 6th place worldwide for "Chemical Engineering" in ARWU, the Academic Ranking of World Universities. Rankings are revised every year, so check the most recent editions.
Former students who have become widely known include:
Cheng Wei, the founder of Didi Chuxing
Zhou Xiaochuan, who served as governor of the People's Bank of China and was responsible for the country's monetary policy
He Guoqiang, who went on to sit on the Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party's Politburo

Choosing BUCT also means choosing Beijing as a home for several years. The sections below look at what the capital is like: the buildings and neighbourhoods you will see, how the air has changed, the shape of the land, and the seasons.

You will meet three kinds of architecture in the urban area. The oldest is the imperial heritage, with Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace) as the national emblem, as well as the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City. A second layer is the "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to 1970s: blocky, and in some cases not very well built. The newest layer is contemporary, concentrated in the central business district in the east, where the new CCTV Headquarters rises, and visible too in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

At the start of the 21st century, a wave of construction brought international designers and many modern styles, most strongly in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone is a place where 1950s buildings and neofuturistic design sit side by side. China Zun, 528 meters tall, is the highest building in the city. The CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which honours only one building worldwide each year as best overall tall building, has gone to Beijing twice since 2007, in 2009 for the Linked Hybrid and in 2013 for the CCTV Headquarters.

The older domestic form is the siheyuan, a courtyard house ringed by buildings. Impressive examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the home of Soong Ching-ling. Siheyuans open onto lanes called hutongs, and these are mostly straight east-west lines, so that gates face north or south in line with feng shui. Widths differ, and in the narrowest only a few people can walk through together.

Hutongs were once found throughout Beijing, but entire districts have been swept away for high-rise blocks. Residents are entitled to flats at least as large as the homes they leave. Even so, many say that the sense of community and the street life of the old lanes is not replaceable, and the properties involved are frequently state-owned.

beijing-university-of-chemical-technolog.h: How the air got where it is today

blocks.x: Environmental problems have long affected Beijing, and some of the story helps explain why the city talks so much about air quality.

Between 2000 and 2009, the built-up area expanded to four times its former size. More buildings meant more emissions, and the shift also changed local weather in basic ways: less wind and humidity at ground level, a lower surface albedo, warmer ground and air, weaker mixing of air vertically, and more ozone. Together with fossil-fuel pollution, this meant serious health problems for many residents.

A thick smog covered Beijing and most of northern China in 2013 and affected 600 million people. Seen afterwards as a "pollution shock", it made air quality a leading economic and social issue nationally. The city set about reducing coal, lowering coal's share of the energy mix, which stood at 24% in 2012, to 10% by 2017. At national level, heavily polluting vehicles were ordered off the roads between 2015 and 2017, and efforts to move to cleaner energy increased.

Researchers from the United States and China concluded in 2006 that much of Beijing's pollution is brought in from other places: 35 to 60% of the ozone, on average, comes from sources outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin are described as having a major effect on the city's air, helped by southerly and southeasterly summer winds and by the mountains that block the north and northwest.

Coal contributes about 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5, and it is also the leading source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Starting in 2012 the city moved its coal-fired power stations to natural gas, aiming to hold annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 coal consumption was 26.3 million tons, of which 73% went to heating and power generation and the rest to industry.

Neighbouring regions matter a great deal. Tianjin's use was projected to go from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million in 2015. In 2011 Hebei burned more than 300 million tons, a total above Germany's, and only 30% of it fed power plants, with a big share used in steelmaking and cement. Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal use tripled after 2000, and Shandong also send pollution toward Beijing. Among Chinese provinces, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia take the first four places for coal consumption.

The city once had four big coal-fired power plants, supplying electricity and heat in winter. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more shut in March 2015, and Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, the last, was scheduled to close in 2016. Between 2013 and 2017 the plan was to remove 13 million tons of coal use, and to hold the total at 15 million tons by 2015.

Nearly US$17 billion was spent on cleaner air before the 2008 Summer Olympics. For the Games, work stopped on all building sites, many Beijing factories were closed permanently, and industry in neighbouring regions was shut temporarily. Fares for buses and the subway came down, new subway lines opened, and vehicles with high emissions were banned. A fleet of 3,800 natural-gas buses was assembled, among the largest in the world, and Beijing was the first Chinese city to adopt the equivalent of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

Officials have also used cloud seeding to bring on rain and clear the air ahead of major occasions, such as the 60th anniversary parade of 2009, and to deal with drought. More recently, they have preferred temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars. The clear skies that came with the 2014 APEC summit in China and the 2015 Victory Day Parade were called "APEC blue" and "parade blue". Air quality improved a lot in those periods and fell back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

On 8 and 9 December 2015, the first smog alert was issued, closing most industry and commercial business, and a "red alert" followed later in the month. In November 2016 the environmental protection bureau announced that starting in 2017, highly polluting older cars would be barred from the road when a smog red alert was in force in Beijing or nearby regions.

The authorities announced a "war on pollution" in 2014, and pollutant levels then fell in a measurable way. By 2017 fine particulates had dropped 35%, and there were further cuts by 2020, mostly because natural gas took over from coal and polluting industrial sites were cleaned up. The 2022 average for PM2.5 was 30 micrograms per cubic meter, the best since 2013. Heavy pollution occurred on just two days in 2024, the lowest count on record and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days of 2013.

Different sources report different numbers. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) publishes daily readings from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the American Embassy posts hourly fine-particulate (PM2.5) and ozone readings on Twitter. They measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's pollution levels, and the health impact it reports, tend to look lower than the US Embassy's.

The health risk is real. Air pollution directly affects rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure may lead to breathing and heart problems, emergency-room visits and even death. Checking the daily reading is a sensible habit.

Seasonal dust storms are caused by eroding deserts in the north and northwest of the country, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes it rain to counter them. Over January to April 2006 there were at least eight, and one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it blew on toward Japan and Korea.

The city is at the northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that opens out to the south and east. Mountains lie north, northwest and west, protecting the city and northern China's farming heartland against encroaching desert steppes. In the northwest of the municipality, in Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, and to the west the Western Hills (Xishan) form a frame. The Great Wall follows the rugged ground across the north, where it was built to defend against raids by nomads from the steppes. The highest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 ft), in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are the main rivers. All are tributaries of the Hai River system and flow southeast. Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the largest reservoir in the municipality. Beijing is also the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built over 1,400 years ago for transport, and it benefits from the South-North Water Transfer Project, a recent construction that brings water from the Yangtze basin.

The urban area sits on plains in the south-central part of the municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet), and it takes up a small but growing share of the total land. Rings of roads radiate from the centre: the Second Ring Road runs along the line of the old city walls, while the Sixth links satellite towns around the edge. In the middle are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, south of the Forbidden City, former home of the emperors. Zhongnanhai, west of Tian'anmen, is where China's current leaders reside. Chang'an Avenue runs between Tiananmen and the Square and is the main east-west axis.
Locals often say Beijing has spread outward "like a pancake" (tan da bing) from its old inner city. That pattern is often named as one reason for the city's urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), edging toward a monsoonal cold semi-arid one (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid, and the Siberian anticyclone makes winters brief, cold and dry. Sandstorms from the Gobi Desert, crossing the Mongolian steppe, can arrive in spring along with quick warming and dry conditions. Autumn resembles spring, in being a time of transition with little rain.

From 2001 to 2026 the hottest part of the year was early August and the coldest early January. By the official seasonal calendar, spring starts on 26 March and summer on 20 May, followed by autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. Because March and September have warmed faster in recent years, and May and October more slowly, autumn is usually shorter than spring.

For 1991 to 2020, the average annual temperature in the urban area was between 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) and 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Daily minimums averaged 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F), and daily maximums 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). In low-lying suburbs, the annual mean was 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In the mountains the annual mean ranges from 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), falling as altitude rises.

January averages −2.7 °C (27.1 °F) daily, and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Rain and snow add up to about 528.0 mm (20.79 in) a year, rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three-quarters of it arrives between June and August. Possible sunshine is 42% in July but 62% in January and February, so the year totals 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine. The coldest reading since 1951 was −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), recorded on 22 February 1966, and the hottest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), recorded on 24 July 1999.

beijing-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Beijing University of Chinese Medicine: a profile

blocks.x: Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, known as BUCM (北京中医药大学), is a public university in the Chinese capital that specialises in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). It was founded in 1956 and counts as one of the first higher-education institutions in the country devoted to this field. It reports to the Ministry of Education and has been included in the national Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction scheme.

BUCM teaches on three campuses: Heping Street, Wangjing and Liangxiang. Together they cover about 268 acres, which is roughly 108 hectares. Anyone planning to study here should check which campus their programme uses, because the three are in different parts of Beijing.

beijing-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: From a college to a national university

blocks.x: The school opened in 1956 as the Beijing College of Chinese Medicine (BCCM, 北京中医学院) and took its present name, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine (北京中医药大学), in 1963. On 31 July 2000 the university merged with another institution, the earlier Beijing College of Acupuncture, Orthopedics and Traumatology. The combined institution became a priority university supervised directly by the Ministry of Education.

The university's current academic units are listed below. The mix shows how wide traditional medicine education has become, taking in pharmacy, life sciences, nursing, management and the humanities as well as clinical medicine.

beijing-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Research bodies, hospitals and a company

blocks.x: BUCM runs several TCM research organisations and hosts five TCM-related journals. One of them is in English, the Journal of Traditional Chinese Medical Sciences, published by Elsevier. Attached to the university are one clinic and eight hospitals, and five of these hospitals are used for teaching, which gives students a range of places for clinical learning.

The university also used to operate a business that sold TCM preparations. In 2010 this company, which had been owned by the state, was restructured as a limited liability firm with just two shareholders: Yabao Pharmaceutical Group, and Beizhong Asset Management Co, which the university owns.

BUCM students live in China's capital, a huge city with a thousand-year imperial heritage, rapid modern development and a seasonal climate with cold winters. The rest of this profile explains how the city is laid out, what its weather is like and how its air quality has changed, so that you can plan realistically.

Beijing sits on the top edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that opens out to the south and east. Hills form a protective belt around the north, north-west and west, keeping the desert steppe from advancing onto the capital and the farmland of northern China. The north-western districts, especially Yanqing and Huairou, belong largely to the Jundu Mountains, and the western side is bounded by the Western Hills (Xishan). The Great Wall passes through the northern part of the municipality, built along the ridges to resist raids by nomadic peoples from the steppe. The municipality's highest point is Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 feet) tall, which stands in the Western Hills right where Beijing meets Hebei.

Water comes from several rivers, among them the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma. All are tributaries of the Hai River system and run south-east. The biggest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. Two other big water projects connect Beijing to the south: the Grand Canal, whose northern end is here and which runs to Hangzhou, a transport route that is more than 1,400 years old, and the recent South–North Water Transfer Project, which delivers water from the Yangtze basin and was built in the last decade or so.

The urban core is on the plains in the south-central part of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. It takes up a modest part of the whole area, but it keeps growing. Its shape is a set of concentric ring roads. The Second Ring follows the line of the former city walls, and the Sixth Ring reaches satellite towns in the suburbs. At the very middle are Tian'anmen and the square of the same name, just south of the Forbidden City, where China's emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, the residence of the present leaders, is to the west. Chang'an Avenue passes between the gate and the square and serves as the main east–west axis of the city.

The way the city has spread out from the historic centre to the fringe has been compared to a pancake spreading, in Chinese tan da bing. It is often named as a cause of Beijing's urban problems, including congestion.

Urban Beijing is dominated by three kinds of architecture. The imperial layer comes first, with the Tian'anmen gate (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), which has become the symbol of the People's Republic, joined by the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second layer is the so-called Sino-Soviet style of the 1950s to the 1970s, with blocky buildings that were sometimes poorly built. The third layer is the contemporary one, and you see it best in the Beijing CBD in the east, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, as well as in landmarks elsewhere, including the National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the start of the twenty-first century, construction has boomed, bringing various modern designs from foreign architects, above all in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone you will find 1950s industrial design and neofuturistic architecture sharing the same space. China Zun, at 528 metres, is the tallest building in the city. Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, given to only one building worldwide each year, twice since 2007, first for the Linked Hybrid (2009) and then for the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

Another famous feature is the siheyuan, a courtyard house with buildings on all sides. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are among the grandest. Hutongs, the lanes that join the courtyards, mostly run straight from east to west so that front doors can face north or south for good feng shui. They differ in width, and some are so narrow that only a few people can pass at a time. These lanes were once common across the city, but whole blocks are being cleared for high-rise buildings. Residents have the right to a new apartment at least as big as their old home, yet many say that the sense of community and street life is lost for good, and the properties concerned are often owned by the government.
Weather planning is a real part of studying in the capital, because the gap between a January morning and a July afternoon is huge.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa) and close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid one (BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes the summers hot and humid, and winters are short, cold and dry because of the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone. In spring, dust storms blow in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, and temperatures climb rapidly in dry weather. Autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with very little rain. Recent records show that the warmest part of the year is early August and the coldest early January. China's official seasonal calendar starts spring in Beijing on 26 March, then summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and finally winter on 31 October. Warming has been faster in March and September and slower in May and October lately, so autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

Urban area: annual mean 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). The daily minimum averages 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and the daily maximum 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).
Low-lying suburbs: annual mean 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with daily minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F).
Mountains: 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), dropping with height.
January averages −2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).
Annual precipitation is near 528.0 mm (20.79 in), or 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, with almost three-quarters of it falling between June and August.
Bright sunshine totals 2,490.5 hours a year, with possible sunshine at its lowest in July (42%) and its highest in January and February (62%).

Extremes recorded since 1951 are a low of −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), reached on 22 February 1966, and a high of 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), reached on 24 July 1999. Both are rare, but they show how big the range can be.

beijing-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Air quality and what has been done

blocks.x: Air pollution is the most talked-about environmental issue in Beijing. This section explains the causes and the improvements in plain terms, so that you know what to expect.

Pollution has been a serious concern in Beijing for a long time. In the decade from 2000 to 2009 the urban area expanded to four times its size. This not only raised emissions from human activity but also altered local weather: wind speed, humidity and surface reflectivity near the ground fell, while ground and air temperatures, ozone and the lack of vertical mixing increased. Together with fossil-fuel burning, rapid urbanisation produced frequent and serious pollution that affects the health of many residents.

In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and much of northern China, affecting about 600 million people. This pollution shock turned air quality into a major economic and social issue nationally. The Beijing government soon announced measures, among them cutting coal's share of energy from 24% in 2012 to 10% by 2017. At national level, heavy polluting vehicles were ordered off the roads between 2015 and 2017, and the transition to clean energy was accelerated.

Researchers from America and China concluded in 2006 that a large part of Beijing's pollution is imported from nearby cities and provinces. On average, 35 to 60% of the ozone originates outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin have a significant influence on the capital's air, partly because of summer winds from the south and south-east and partly because the mountains to the north and north-west trap pollution.

Burning coal accounts for about 40% of the city's PM2.5, and it also produces most of the nitrogen and sulphur oxides in the air. Since 2012, Beijing has been switching coal-fired power stations to natural gas, with a target of limiting annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, of which 73% went to heating and power and the rest to industry. Much of the pollution comes from elsewhere. Tianjin's coal use was forecast to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, while Hebei burned over 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, with just 30% for power and a sizeable share for steel and cement. Coal-mining regions such as Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where use has tripled since 2000, and Shandong add to Beijing's problem. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia are, in that order, the top four provinces for coal use.

The city once had four large coal-fired plants that supplied power and winter heating: Gaojing closed in 2014, two others in March 2015, and the final one, Huaneng, was scheduled for 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 called for 13 million tons less coal to be burned, with consumption held to 15 million tons in 2015.

Almost US$17 billion was spent before the 2008 Olympics to meet promises of cleaner air. It lowered bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It also put 3,800 natural gas buses into service, one of the world's largest fleets of this type, and became China's first city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 standard.

Officials have sometimes seeded clouds to induce rain and clear the air before important events, as before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. Lately, they rely more on temporary factory closures and tighter limits on road traffic, which produced short spells of clean sky, known as APEC blue and parade blue, during and just before APEC China 2014 and the 2015 Victory Day parade. Air quality improved sharply and then returned to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and shut most of the city's industry and commerce; a red alert followed later that month. Under rules announced in November 2016, older high-polluting cars are banned from the roads whenever a red alert is issued in the city or neighbouring regions, starting in 2017.

Real improvements followed the declaration of a war on pollution in 2014. Fine particulates fell 35% in 2017, with further decreases up to 2020, mostly as a result of replacing coal with gas and cleaning up polluting industrial plants. The annual average PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013, and in 2024 there were just two heavy-pollution days, the fewest on record and 96.6 percent down from 58 days in 2013.

Different organisations publish different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau reports daily data from 27 monitoring stations on its website, while the US Embassy has posted hourly PM2.5 and ozone levels on social media. Because the two measure different pollutants against different criteria, the bureau's levels, and the health effects it reports, are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog is harmful. Polluted air has a direct effect on rates of heart and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can lead to breathing and heart problems, hospital emergency visits and even death. As a student of medicine you will probably find the topic especially interesting, and it makes sense to check air quality before outdoor activities.

Each year dust storms blow in from deserts that are eroding in northern and north-western China. The city's Weather Modification Office sometimes triggers rainfall to fight them and soften their effects. In early 2006 there were at least eight storms in four months, and a single storm in April 2002 dropped almost 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing and then travelled to Japan and Korea. Spring term students should keep a mask and eye drops handy.

Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, widely called BUPT (Beiyou in Chinese), is a state university in the Chinese capital that specialises in information and communications fields. It is under the Ministry of Education, with funding shared between that ministry and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, and it belongs to Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction programme.

The university began in 1955 as the Beijing Institute of Posts and Telecommunications, the name by which it was formerly known. One of its staff, Aidong Men (born 1966), is a professor and doctoral supervisor. BUPT has also been honoured in an unusual way: astronomers of the Beijing Schmidt CCD Asteroid Program found an asteroid, number 101810, and named it Beiyou in the university's honour. The Minor Planet Center published the official naming citation on 24 September 2020 (M.P.C. 125471).

The rest of this profile concentrates on Beijing, because for an international student the city is the setting for nearly everything outside the classroom: its layout, its seasons, its buildings and the story of its air.

beijing-university-of-posts-and-telecomm.h: Between the plain and the mountains

blocks.x: The capital stands at the top of the North China Plain, a lowland shaped roughly like a triangle that widens to the south and east. Hills lie to the north, north-west and west, and they act as a barrier between the city and farmland on one side and the desert steppe on the other. In the municipality's north-west, mostly in Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains rise; to the west are the Western Hills (Xishan). The Great Wall climbs the rough terrain of the northern part of the municipality, where it was intended to hold back raiders from the steppe. The built-up area occupies a low plain in the middle south of the municipality, only 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. It takes up a fairly small but increasing share of the total area. Looked at from above, the city is a set of rings: the Second Ring Road follows the line of the former city walls, and the Sixth Ring Road ties the satellite towns of the outer suburbs together.

The political heart lies at Tian'anmen and its square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, the home of today's national leaders, is just west of Tian'anmen. Chang'an Avenue passes between the gate and the square and is the main axis from east to west. Beijing's outward growth from the old inner city has often been compared to a pancake spreading (tan da bing), and this pattern is frequently named as a source of the city's urban problems, from congestion to pollution.

For a student, this means serious winter clothing, light clothes and an umbrella for the humid summer, and some protection against dust in spring.

beijing-university-of-posts-and-telecomm.h: The old and the new in Beijing's buildings

blocks.x: Three architectural strands coexist. The oldest is imperial: Tian'anmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace and still the symbol of the People's Republic, the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven. The second is the Sino-Soviet manner of the 1950s to the 1970s, known for boxy shapes and sometimes poor construction. The third is the modern look, especially in the Beijing CBD to the east, with the new CCTV Headquarters, and across the city in the National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

During the early 2000s, an immense amount of new construction arrived, as architects from around the world contributed modern designs, most of all in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s industrial-era design and a futuristic style are blended. The tallest building in Beijing is the 528-metre China Zun. From 2007, two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which is given to a single best tall building worldwide each year: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

Then there are the courtyard houses, called siheyuan, in which buildings surround a courtyard. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are grand cases. Courtyards are generally linked by lanes called hutongs, which tend to be straight and to run east-west so that doors face north or south, a layout favoured for feng shui. Their widths vary, and in the narrowest only a few people can walk side by side. Siheyuan and hutongs, once found everywhere, are disappearing fast as whole blocks make way for tall buildings. Residents have the right to move into new flats at least as big as their old homes, but many say that the community feeling and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced; the buildings are often state-owned.

Its built-up area quadrupled between 2000 and 2009, which increased emissions and also altered the local atmosphere: surface reflectivity, near-ground wind speed and humidity fell, while ground temperature, air temperature near the surface, vertical air dilution and ozone rose. beijing-university-of-posts-and-telecomm.h: Where the dirty air comes from

blocks.x: Researchers from the United States and China concluded in 2006 that much of the city's pollution blows in from nearby cities and provinces. Between 35 and 60 per cent of ozone, on average, has sources beyond the city. Much of the pollution comes from the neighbourhood. Tianjin's coal use was forecast to grow from 48 to 63 million tons during 2011 to 2015. The four provinces with the highest coal consumption are Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, in that order.

Beijing used to rely on four large coal-fired plants for electricity and winter heating. The first, Gaojing Thermal Power Plant, closed in 2014; two more shut in March 2015; and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to close in 2016.
