Before the 2008 Summer Olympics, almost 17 billion US dollars went into clean-up promises. For the duration of the Games Beijing halted all building site work, permanently closed many factories, temporarily stopped industry in nearby regions, shut some filling stations, halved car traffic through an odd-even number plate rule, lowered bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It put 3,800 natural-gas buses into service, a fleet among the largest anywhere, and was the first Chinese city to demand the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

Authorities sometimes seed clouds to bring rain that cleans the air before major occasions, as they did before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to deal with drought. Lately they prefer temporary factory closures and tougher car restrictions. That approach produced two short spells nicknamed APEC blue and parade blue, around APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. The air improved dramatically at those times, then returned to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

On 8 and 9 December 2015 Beijing issued its first smog alert, closing most industry and commercial business, and a red alert followed later in the month. The environmental protection bureau announced in November 2016 that from 2017 old vehicles with heavy emissions would not be allowed to drive during red alerts in the city or surrounding regions.

After the war on pollution was declared in 2014, pollutant levels fell. Fine particulates dropped 35 per cent in 2017 and fell again by 2020, thanks mostly to replacing coal power with gas and cleaning up polluting factories. In 2022 the annual average PM2.5 concentration was 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the cleanest since 2013. In 2024 only two days of heavy pollution occurred, the lowest on record and 96.6 per cent fewer than the 58 days of 2013.

Because pollution is a concern, several sources publish readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily data from 27 stations across the city, and the US Embassy reports hourly PM2.5 and ozone on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants by different standards, so the bureau's readings, and the effect on health that it indicates, often look lower than the embassy's. Polluted air raises the number of people with heart and lung disease in Beijing. Heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, hospital emergency visits and even deaths.

Deserts to the north and north-west erode and send dust to the capital in seasonal storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office occasionally brings on rain to counter them. In just the first four months of 2006 there were no fewer than eight storms, and one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before moving to Japan and Korea.

BUPT's core strengths are in posts, telecommunications and related information technology, and it has strong government backing, through two ministries. Check the university website for current programmes, international student arrangements and campus locations, since the city data above come from many different years and some of the university facts here are brief.

beijing-university-of-posts-and-telecomm.h: A student's checklist for the capital

blocks.x: First, plan for extremes: January averages minus 2.7 degrees C and July 27.2 degrees C, and the record range since 1951 runs from minus 27.4 to 41.9 degrees C. Second, allow for the fact that autumn is short, so a warm coat is needed soon after the pleasant weeks of September. Third, on days when the air is poor, use the published pollution readings and remember that the bureau and the US Embassy do not measure in exactly the same way. Fourth, take time to explore the old hutong lanes while they still exist, and enjoy contrasts such as the 798 Art Zone, the Temple of Heaven and the CBD towers. Finally, use the ring-road structure to understand distances: the city grows outward in concentric circles, so a place on the Sixth Ring Road is much farther from Tian'anmen than the map of the centre suggests.

Urban Beijing averages 55.2 to 55.9 F over the year, with daily lows of 45.9 to 47.1 F and daily highs of 65.3 to 66.0 F. The lower suburbs come in at 52.7 to 55.4 F (lows 42.6 to 46.4 F, highs 64.8 to 65.7 F), and mountain areas at 32 to 50 F. The January mean is 27.1 F, the July mean 81.0 F, rainfall is 20.79 inches (23.00 inches in Haidian and Chaoyang), and the record low and high are minus 17.3 F and 107.4 F.

beijing-university-of-technology.h: Beijing University of Technology at a glance

blocks.x: Beijing University of Technology (北京工业大学, literally 'Beijing Industrial University', often shortened to Beijing Tech) is a public university owned by the municipality of Beijing and paid for by the Beijing Municipal People's Government. It stands in the Chaoyang district and teaches more than 20,000 students. It belongs to Project 211 and to the national Double First-Class Construction initiative, two government programmes that single out universities for extra investment.
The university opened in 1960 with five engineering departments. The first intake arrived by transfer, with Beijing Normal University and the Beijing Institute of Technology supplying the students.

Postgraduate education started in 1981, when the graduate school was formed, and in 1985 the university began awarding doctorates to an international standard, among the first universities in China to do so.

Broadening followed in the 1990s. In 1990 the College of Economics and Management came over from Beijing Union University, and in 1993 the Beijing Computer Institute joined as the College of Computer Science. That same year, in cooperation with local business, the university created an Experimental College, which later became independent. As time went on, the social sciences gained ground as well, and results in economics, law and related fields mean the university is, in practice, a comprehensive one with a wide variety of schools and colleges. Even so, its main strengths today lie in engineering research and teaching.
As a key university under the Beijing Municipal Government, Beijing Tech is divided into the colleges and other units below, listed below in the opposite order to the university's own catalogue:
Fan Gongxiu Honors College of Beijing University of Technology

You will find the campus in south-eastern Beijing. The site is roughly 800,000 square metres, and the buildings add up to 4,940,000 square metres of floor space.

The main library is a modern complex with more than 20,000 square metres of floor space. It contains about 700,000 printed items, 60,000 e-books and over 40 database resources, which together form a collection designed to meet teaching and research needs. Partnerships with the Information Centre of the Chinese Academy of Science and with the Capital Library of Beijing bring further specialist help for students and staff.

Sport has a place here too. When Beijing hosted the Olympics in 2008, the campus was picked as the venue for badminton, so a new athletic gymnasium went up for it. It was complete in September 2007 and met the requirements laid down by the International Olympic Committee.

The university treats undergraduate teaching as a steady, carefully run process, reasoning that a supply of educated and trained people is the basis of China's future growth. It therefore arranged undergraduate teaching in three principal groups: management, engineering and science. The current picture is 6,811 undergraduates studying 26 disciplines in 16 departments.

Graduate education is tuned to the needs of economic construction and social development in Beijing and China at large. The stated aim is to raise educational standards and to keep refining the size, structure, efficiency and quality of graduate provision, and the graduate school is the department that carries out both graduate studies and scientific research.

A further branch, the School of Higher Professional Education, dates from July 1996. Its staff exceed 120 people, including five professors and 29 associate professors. It has four departments (Basic Course, Information Technology, Engineering Technology, and Economics and Management) and its subjects range from financial accounting, environmental engineering, architectural technology and concise chemistry to e-business, internet and office automation, applied software, computer science and application, and engineering programmes in information, telecommunication and networks. It runs laboratories and an intern training base, has set up cooperative education programs with Japan, Russia and others, and currently enrols more than 1300 students.

Ranking tables are mixed, so here are several. In 2025 the Academic Ranking of World Universities placed Beijing University of Technology between 201 and 300, while US News & World Report's Best Global University Ranking put it 528th globally and 140th in Asia. The Center for World University Rankings gave it 475th place and the CWTS Leiden Ranking 176th in the world, and the QS World University Rankings listed it 230th in Asia for 2025.

More than 21,000 students study at Beijing Tech. Around 13,000 are undergraduates, over 8,000 are master's students, about 1,000 are doctoral students and 500 are international students; the university also has more than 10,000 continuing education students.
Well-known graduates include Zhang Rongming, who serves as a vice chairwoman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, along with several people in business and research:
Ying Wu, who founded UTStarcom and is its CEO
Yang Shao-Horn, who teaches at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Li Erran Li, a researcher with Amazon Web Services
Xiang Wang, once President of Xiaomi
Xiaodong Zhang, a professor at Ohio State University

beijing-university-of-technology.h: Beijing as a place to live

blocks.x: The city beyond the campus gates shapes everyday student life: the climate, the transport and the leisure options. This part introduces Beijing.

Urban Beijing shows three main architectural styles. One is the traditional architecture of imperial China. Among the finest examples are the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City, as well as the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which is still the best-known symbol of the People's Republic. The second is the 'Sino-Sov' style of the 1950s to 1970s, in which buildings are boxy and sometimes badly built. The third is a far more modern group of forms, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east of the city (the new CCTV Headquarters, for example), though it also appears at other spots, such as the National Center for the Performing Arts and the Beijing National Stadium.

The early 21st century brought a surge of new construction in many modern styles by international designers, most noticeably in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s design and a neofuturistic look sit side by side. The tallest building in the city is the 528-metre China Zun. Since 2007 the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which goes to just one building worldwide each year as the best overall tall building, has gone twice to Beijing: to the CCTV Headquarters in 2013 and, before that, to the Linked Hybrid in 2009.

The traditional housing form is the siheyuan, a courtyard enclosed by buildings. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Alleys known as hutongs usually join the courtyards. Hutongs mostly run straight from east to west, which makes the doorways face north or south, an arrangement thought to be favourable in Feng Shui. Widths vary and some are narrow enough for only a few pedestrians at a time. Siheyuans and hutongs were once everywhere, but they are vanishing quickly as whole blocks are replaced with high-rises. Hutong residents have the right to apartments at least as large as their former homes, though many complain that the old community feeling and street life cannot be replaced, and many of these properties are government owned.

At the northern tip of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens out to the south and east, lies Beijing. Mountains to the north, north-west and west protect the city and northern China's farmland from the advancing desert steppes. In the north-west of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, while the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs over rugged ground across the northern part of the municipality, built to defend against nomadic raids from the steppes. The highest point is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres, or 7,556 ft.

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are among the main rivers, all of them tributaries of the Hai River system flowing south-east. Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the biggest reservoir in the municipality. The city is where the Grand Canal from Hangzhou ends in the north, a waterway built more than 1,400 years ago for transport, and it is likewise the northern terminus of the South-North Water Transfer Project, which brings water from the Yangtze basin and was constructed within the last decade.

The built-up area occupies the plains of south-central Beijing, at 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) above sea level, and, although it is a modest part of the municipality, it keeps expanding. Ring roads spread outward in concentric circles. The innermost, the Second Ring Road, runs along the old city walls, while the Sixth Ring Road connects satellite towns out in the suburbs. At the heart of the city are Tian'anmen and the Square named after it, just south of the Forbidden City, where China's emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, where today's leaders live, is to the west. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tiananmen and the Square and is the main east-west axis.
The way Beijing has grown from the old inner city to the fringe is often described as 'spreading like a pancake' (tan da bing), a pattern commonly blamed for the city's urban problems.

Climatically, Beijing is humid continental (Köppen Dwa) but borders on the monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen BSk). Summers are hot and humid thanks to the East Asian monsoon, and winters are short, cold and dry under the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone. In spring, sandstorms may arrive from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, together with fast warming and mostly dry weather. Autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with little precipitation. Looking at 2001 to 2026, early August is the hottest period and early January the coldest.

The official seasonal calendar used in China starts spring at 26 March, summer at 20 May, autumn at 13 September and winter at 31 October. Because warming has been faster in March and September and slower in May and October lately, autumn is usually shorter than spring.

Averaged over 1991 to 2020, the urban area has a yearly temperature of 12.9 to 13.3 °C, or 55.2 to 55.9 °F. Daily minimums average 7.7 to 8.4 °C, or 45.9 to 47.1 °F, and daily maximums 18.5 to 18.9 °C, or 65.3 to 66.0 °F. In the lower suburbs the annual figure is 11.5 to 13.0 °C, or 52.7 to 55.4 °F, with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C, or 42.6 to 46.4 °F, and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C, or 64.8 to 65.7 °F. Mountain areas range between 0 and 10 °C, or 32 and 50 °F, falling as the altitude rises. The daily mean in January is −2.7 °C, or 27.1 °F, and in July 27.2 °C, or 81.0 °F.

Annual precipitation averages roughly 528.0 mm, or 20.79 in, or 584.2 mm, or 23.00 in, in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three quarters of it falls from June to August. Sunshine as a percentage of the possible total varies from 42% in July to 62% in January and February, so the city has 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. Since 1951 temperatures have ranged from −27.4 °C, or −17.3 °F, on 22 February 1966 to 41.9 °C, or 107.4 °F, on 24 July 1999.

beijing-university-of-technology.h: Pollution and how it has been tackled

blocks.x: Environmental trouble has a long history in Beijing, and you should know the background before you arrive. Between 2000 and 2009 the urban area quadrupled in size, which sharply raised emissions and also altered the local weather. Near the surface, wind speed, humidity and albedo declined, but ground and air temperatures, ozone and vertical mixing of the air all increased. Urbanisation plus the burning of fossil fuels often causes serious environmental problems and health issues for many inhabitants. In 2013, heavy smog covered Beijing and most of northern China and affected 600 million people in all. After that 'pollution shock', air pollution became a major economic and social concern in China. The Beijing government then announced steps to cut it, among them cutting the portion of coal in the energy mix, from 24% in 2012 to 10% by 2017. Nationally, the government required the most polluting vehicles to be withdrawn between 2015 and 2017 and accelerated the move to clean energy sources.

beijing-university-of-technology.h: Where the dirty air comes from

blocks.x: A joint American and Chinese study in 2006 found that much of Beijing's pollution comes from the cities and provinces around it. On average 35-60% of the ozone originates outside the city, and Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality have what the study called a 'significant influence on Beijing's air quality', partly owing to the mountains lying north and north-west and the winds that blow mostly from the south or south-east in summer.

For the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent on cleaning the air. During the Games, measures included stopping work at every construction site, shutting many Beijing factories for good, closing industry in neighbouring regions for a time, closing some gas stations and halving motor traffic by letting drivers on the road only on odd or even days by licence plate number. Bus and subway fares were reduced, new subway lines opened, and high-emission vehicles banned. In addition, 3,800 buses running on natural gas were put together, among the largest fleets of their kind, and Beijing was first in China to demand compliance with the national version of the Euro 4 emissions rules.

About 40% of the PM 2.5 in Beijing's air comes from burning coal, which also produces most of the city's nitrogen dioxide and sulphur dioxide. A programme beginning in 2012 converts coal-fired stations to natural gas, and the target is to hold annual coal use to 20 million tons. It burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, 73% of it for heating and power and the rest for industry. A lot of the pollution comes from nearby regions: coal consumption in neighbouring Tianjin was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, while Hebei Province used more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, of which just 30% went to power generation and a large share to making steel and cement. Smog in Beijing also owes something to power plants in Shandong and in the coal-mining areas of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal use has tripled since 2000. By coal consumption, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces.

Beijing once had four major coal-fired power plants for electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more shut in March 2015, and the last of them, the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to stop in 2016. The city's plan for 2013 to 2017 was to take 13 million tons off coal consumption and to hold the 2015 total at 15 million tons.

Officials sometimes seed clouds to make rain more likely and clear the air before big occasions, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to fight drought. More recently they have preferred temporary factory closures and tougher limits on cars, as with 'APEC blue' and 'parade blue', short spells of clear sky seen around the APEC China 2014 meeting and the China Victory Day Parade of 2015. Air quality improved dramatically during and before these events, then fell back to unhealthy levels soon after.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015, when most industry and commercial business in the city was shut down, and another smog 'red alert' followed later that month. In November 2016, Beijing's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be forbidden to drive whenever red alerts were issued in the city or neighbouring regions.

Since a 'war on pollution' was declared in 2014, measurable improvements have occurred. In 2017 fine particulates fell by 35%, with further falls by 2020, chiefly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial plants were cleaned up. The annual average concentration of PM2.5 dropped to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best figure since 2013, and in 2024 only two days were heavily polluted. That is a record low and a drop of 96.6 percent from 58 such days in 2013.

Because pollution is high, there are many different readings. Beijing's Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) publishes daily readings from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and while the American Embassy publishes hourly levels of fine particulates (PM2.5) and ozone on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's figures for pollution levels and health impact are often lower than the Embassy's.

Smog is harmful. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and long exposure to heavily polluted air can lead to heart and breathing problems, hospital emergency visits and even death. Anyone with asthma or a similar condition should speak to a doctor before coming.

Erosion of the deserts in northern and north-western China brings seasonal dust storms to the city. At times the Beijing Weather Modification Office creates rain by artificial means to fight the storms and soften their impact. During just the first four months of 2006 at least eight storms struck, and one storm in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before passing on towards Korea and Japan.

For an international applicant, Beijing University of Technology offers an engineering-led education in a large municipal university with a broad range of colleges, a well-stocked library and a campus in the south-east of one of the world's biggest cities. The city itself has remarkable historic sights and bold modern architecture, long cold winters, hot humid summers, and an air quality record that has improved markedly but still deserves attention, particularly in winter and spring. Before applying, check current courses, fees and language requirements with the university's own international office, since the figures quoted here come from different years.

Bohai University (渤海大学) belongs to Liaoning Province, which funds and oversees it as a provincial public university, and it is based at Jinzhou in the north-east of China. It came into being in 2003, when Jinzhou Teachers College merged with the Liaoning Commercial Higher Vocational School. The "Bohai" in the name refers to the Bohai Sea, which lies just south of the city.

Bohai is a comprehensive university offering bachelor's degrees, graduate degrees and diplomas. Twenty colleges teach at bachelor's and master's level, and together they cover a wide range of subjects. The colleges are grouped here by field, using the names the university uses.
Humanities and social sciences: literature, politics and history, economy and law, management, tourism, foreign languages, Marxism, arts and communications, and a college of liberal arts and science.

Science and engineering: a college of mathematics and physics; one for chemistry, chemical engineering and food safety; one for engineering; one for new energy; and one for information science and technology, which includes software and service outsourcing.

Education and professional fields: education and P.E.; finance, commerce and trade; adult education; training; and a college of advanced vocation and technology that includes maritime and applied technology.
International: a college of international exchange, focused on South Korea.

That last college deserves a mention for foreign applicants, since it signals a particular link with Korean partners. Ask the university which programmes are open to international students and in what language they are taught.
Jinzhou is a mid-sized industrial city with a strong military-history heritage, a seaside, some quiet temples and a lively night market. This part of the profile explains what to expect.
The city has a broad industrial base. Its main traditional industries are petrochemicals, metallurgy, textiles, pharmaceuticals and building materials.

Established in 1992, the Jinzhou Economic and Technical Development Zone was among the first provincial-level development zones to gain Liaoning's approval. Its good transport links give easy access to Jinzhou Seaport, the airport and several national highways.

Some Western brands have shops in the city. KFC is the best known and has been established in the Chinese market for a long time. RT-Mart, New-Mart and Do-Do Express are the main places to buy food and household goods. The Bank of Jinzhou (Jinzhou Yinhang) was, when the original description was written, the only bank in the city with staff whose first language is English. Western Union and Bank of China are present, along with many other banking services. Visa and MasterCard were not accepted in Jinzhou apart from a few large bank branches that can use those networks. That description is dated, so check current payment options and bring more than one way to pay when you arrive.

Jinzhou Jinzhouwan Airport has flights to major airports in China. The city has two railway stations: one for longer journeys and one for shorter routes. Walking and cycling are the most popular ways to get around. Taxis are plentiful and start at 6 RMB for a trip. Buses cover the whole city and are the cheapest option, but they are not always reliable.

Liaoshen Campaign Memorial (辽沈战役纪念馆, traditional 遼沈戰役紀念館). This large museum commemorates the 1948 Liaoshen Campaign. It displays more than 16,000 pieces of equipment used in the campaign, such as rifles, machine guns, mortars, cannons and tanks, and holds thousands of photographs and documents. The best-known exhibit is the Panoramic Picture Hall, which recreates the whole Battle of Jinzhou on a revolving circular screen.

Yiwulü Mountain. Found in the west of Beizhen City, within Jinzhou, it counts as one of Northeast China's three sacred mountains. Wanghai Mountain, the principal summit, is 867 metres above sea level. Along the range you will come across Beizhen Temple, Shenshui Bridge, a Fish Pool and Lotus Stone, as well as Cloud Pass, Wanghai Temple and the pavilions named Guanyin, Sijiao and Kuangguang.

Mount Bijia. This is an island in the Bohai Sea to the south of Jinzhou, with a Chinese Buddhist temple. For most of the day only a boat can reach it, but when the tide goes out a natural causeway links it to the mainland. People can walk across from the seafront, and the locals call the natural wonder Tian Qiao, or "Sky Bridge". A tall stone pavilion at the summit looks like an enormous pen resting in a pen holder, which explains the name Bijiashan, "Pen Holder Mountain".

Guangji Pagoda (广济寺塔, traditional 廣濟寺塔). It stands in Guta Park in the middle of Jinzhou. The tower is 72 metres high, thirteen levels and octagonal, and it is a fine example of Liao-style architecture. A quiet temple at its foot completes the traditional Chinese scene. In the early morning you will see local people gathering for rituals and exercise. Entering the temple grounds is free.

Winter ice park. A small ice park is set up on the Xiaoling River and lasts as long as the river stays frozen. Visitors can ride ATVs on the ice, skate, use ice-skating chairs and vehicles, and take rubber tyre rides pulled by vehicles.

Night Market. Jinzhou is currently most famous for this market, which usually runs on summer evenings and turns into a morning market in the colder seasons. You can try many snacks and drinks, join in activities and enjoy the busy atmosphere. It is on Nanning Street (南宁路).

"Wild Swans: Three Daughters of China" was one of the bestselling non-fiction books of the 1990s. Its pages describe Jinzhou in detail, in the years before and after what the book calls the 1949 "Liberation of China", and that makes it a readable way to get a human view of the city's past.
Where a university sits in its region matters as much as the campus. Liaoning has a long history of rule by many different peoples, a heavy-industrial economy, and varied terrain.

bohai-university.h: Early peoples and the Han era

blocks.x: From the 4th century BC to the 9th century, Han Chinese governments mostly settled and ran Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived in the area. Around 300 BC the state of Yan took the land and created two administrative districts named after the river: Liaodong, meaning east of the Liao, and Liaoxi, meaning west of it. Xiangping, the Yan city that served as the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today.

When the Han dynasty fell, a warlord named Gongsun Du and his family created a semi-independent state based in Liaodong, which survived until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Although this state, also known as Yan, was short-lived, it conducted many diplomatic and trade voyages by sea and left a lasting mark on the culture of Northeast Asia. Once the Western Jin was over, the Murong branch of the Xianbei ruled Liaoning through three successive states: Former, Later and Northern Yan. In 436 Northern Wei took the Yan capital and Goguryeo took over the Liaodong Peninsula. Later, in the war between Goguryeo and the Tang, the Tang took the region.

In the middle of the 8th century the An Lushan Rebellion drained Tang resources from its frontiers, and the Bohai people gradually spread into Liaodong. Ultimately the Khitan Liao dynasty conquered Liaoning and divided it among four circuits: the Eastern Capital, the Supreme Capital, the Central Capital and the Lower Capital Circuits (Dongjingdao, Shangjingdao, Zhongjingdao and Xiajingdao).

When the Jurchen Jin dynasty held the region, the biggest administrative unit was the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu). Three others shared the remainder: the Xianping Route, plus the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu) and Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it later became part of the Yuan dynasty. Yuan administration was complicated. In the east, the Liaoyang and Shenyang Routes answered to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. In the north, Xianping Prefecture belonged to the Kaiyuan Route. The western districts, among them Guangning Route, were likewise placed under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. Only the Jinzhou and Chaoyang areas, part of Daning Route, reported to the Central Secretariat.

bohai-university.h: Ming rule and the Liaodong Wall

blocks.x: The Ming took control of Liaoning in 1371, only three years after the Mongols had been pushed out of Beijing. Around 1442 they built a defensive wall to guard the province's farmland against a possible threat from the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group that was a Ming tributary, in the north-west. In 1467-1468 they extended it to cover the north-east too, against attacks by the Jianzhou Jurchens, who would later become known as the Manchu. The "Liaodong Wall" served the same purpose as the Great Wall but was cheaper. Some sections used stone and tile, but most of it was just an earth bank with a moat on each side.

The wall did not stop the Jurchens. In the early 17th century they conquered Liaodong, the eastern part of Liaoning, decades before they took the rest of China. This Jurchen dynasty, first called "Later Jin" and later renamed Qing, put its capital at Xingjing (兴京) from 1616 to 1621. Xingjing lay outside the wall in the east of today's Liaoning. The capital then moved to Dongjing, east of present-day Liaoyang, and in 1625 to Shengjing, now Shenyang. After the Qing took Beijing in 1644 the main capital moved there, but Shengjing stayed an important regional capital for most of the Qing era.

Liaoning lost much of its population in the Qing conquest. Some local Chinese died in the fighting, others escaped to the south side of the Great Wall, and the retreating Ming armies themselves wrecked many towns. A report from 1661 by Zhang Shangxian, the civil governor (Fuyin) of Fengtian Province, describes the damage. East of the Liao River he found only Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng still inhabited; every other town was empty or held a few hundred people at most. He wrote that Tieling and Fushun had "only a few vagrants". West of the river the only places with a real population were Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning.

From the second half of the 17th century (starting with laws of 1651 and 1653) the Qing government brought in settlers from south of the Great Wall, mainly from Shandong, to populate the thinly settled Fengtian Province, which roughly matches today's Liaoning. Many of today's residents descend from those 17th-century settlers. The rest of the Northeast stayed officially closed to Han Chinese through most of the Manchu era. To stop migration into what are now Jilin and Heilongjiang and the nearby parts of Inner Mongolia, the government built the Willow Palisade (c. 1638 to c. 1672). It circled the agricultural heartland of Fengtian, running either a little outside the old Ming Liaodong Wall or along it, and separated that heartland from the Manchu forests in the north-east and the Mongol grazing lands in the north-west.

Later the Qing tried to halt the flow of migrants, to send some settlers home or, failing that, to legalise them. An edict of 1704 observed that recent Han settlers had not obeyed earlier orders to leave, and told them either to register and join a local defence group (保, bao) or to leave for their home provinces within ten years. A decade later another edict appeared reminding officials of the need to deal with illegal migrants. The restrictions never worked as well as Beijing wanted, and Fengtian's population doubled between 1683 and 1734.

Three generals ruled Manchuria in the Qing period, and the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn) governed most of what is now Liaoning. In 1860 the Manchu government started to reopen the region to settlement, and Han Chinese soon became the dominant group.

The province of Fengtian was created in the area of today's Liaoning in the 20th century. Several decisive battles of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905 happened in Liaoning, among them Port Arthur and Mukden; the latter was the largest land battle fought anywhere up to that point. During the Warlord Era the Fengtian clique, led by Zhang Zuolin and then by his son Zhang Xueliang, held power. The province got its present name on 29 January 1929, and the Zhongdong Railway Incident followed later that year. Japan invaded in 1931, and the area fell under the Japanese-controlled puppet state of Manchukuo. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the first major battles of the Chinese Civil War, the Liaoshen Campaign, took place in and around Liaoning.

At the moment of the People's Republic's founding in 1949, Liaoning as such did not exist. The area consisted of Liaodong and Liaoxi provinces together with five cities that ran themselves: Shenyang, Lüda (modern Dalian), Anshan, Fushun and Benxi. All seven were combined into "Liaoning" in 1954. A year later, in 1955, pieces of the former Rehe province came in as well. In the Cultural Revolution Liaoning also absorbed a part of Inner Mongolia, but that was undone later.

Liaoning industrialised earlier than most Chinese provinces: the process began while Japan occupied it and went further still in the two decades after 1950. One of China's biggest iron and steel complexes is found at Anshan, to give an example. Lately, though, the early focus on heavy industry has turned into a weakness, since a good many large state-run firms are in difficulty. The central government has recognised that Liaoning and other north-eastern provinces face special difficulties from their heavy-industry heritage, and recently launched a "Revitalize the Northeast" Campaign.
Liaoning can be roughly divided into three regions: highlands in the west, plains in the centre and hills in the east.

West: the Nulu'erhu range, roughly tracing the Inner Mongolia boundary, is the main feature, and low hills are everywhere. A thin band of coastal plain called the Liaoxi Corridor joins the Liao River Basin to the North China Plain, finishing where the Great Wall meets the sea at Shanhai Pass.
Centre: a basin drained by the Liao and Daliao rivers and their tributaries, mostly flat and low.
East: the Changbai and Qianshan Mountains dominate, and they reach into the sea as the Liaodong Peninsula. Mount Huabozi, at 1,336 m, is the highest point of Liaoning and is found here.
The climate is continental monsoon, with average rainfall from about 440 to 1,130 mm a year. Summer is rainy and the other seasons are dry.
The major cities are Shenyang, Dalian, Anshan, Liaoyang, Fushun, Dandong, Jinzhou and Yingkou.

Liaoning has the largest and richest provincial economy in the Northeast. Its nominal GDP in 2017 was 2.39 trillion yuan (about US$354 billion), the 14th largest of China's 31 provinces, and GDP per capita was 54,745 yuan (US$8,108). It leads the three north-eastern provinces on both measures.

In 2008, among the "G8x8" (the eight sub-national units with the highest GDP in the eight top-GDP countries), Liaoning had the fastest GDP growth. Preliminary figures show growth of 13.1 percent in 2009, which kept it first for economic growth. Since then, growth has slowed: the economy expanded by 3% in 2015 and shrank by 1.3% in the first quarter of 2016.

Its leading industries are petrochemicals, metallurgy, electronics and telecommunications, and machinery. On the national stage, the province ranks in the top three for output of pig iron, steel and metal-cutting machine tools. It is also one of China's key raw-material producers: mining and quarrying, ferrous metal smelting and rolling, and the extraction of oil and gas are all highly significant.

It is also an important base for equipment and machinery, with Shenyang and Dalian as the industrial centres. Among the sector leaders are three companies: Shenyang Jinbei, Daxian Group and Shenyang Machine Tool. Light industry is mainly textiles and clothing, including cotton and wool spinning, chemical fibre, knitting, silk, and the making of both garments and textile machinery.

The service (tertiary) sector contributed 34.5 percent of GDP in 2008. Going forward, the province aims to continue reforming its large and mid-sized state enterprises and to concentrate on four mainstay industries: petrochemicals, metallurgy, machinery and electronics. Liaoning is also the birthplace of the Li Keqiang index, an alternative way of measuring economic performance when GDP figures are unreliable.

Maize, sorghum and soybeans are the main crops, and cotton is also grown. The Dalian area supplies three-quarters of China's exported apples and peaches. Local fruit is varied. Dalian and Yingkou are known for apples, and Dalian also for golden peaches. Beizhen (in Jinzhou) produces pears, Huludao and Suizhong are home to white pears, and Gushan in Dandong supplies apricots and plums.

Liaoning holds more iron, magnesite, diamond and boron than any other province-level division in China. It is also an important source of oil and natural gas, and salt is made along the coast. The province has large crude oil deposits too, especially in the Liaohe Oilfield.

capital-medical-university.h: Capital Medical University: who it is

blocks.x: Capital Medical University, often abbreviated CCMU or CMU (首都医科大学), is a public university for medicine owned by the city of Beijing. The money comes from three sources, namely the National Health Commission, the Ministry of Education and the Beijing Municipal People's Government. The university began in 1960 as Beijing Second Medical College, and the present name came later.

In the World University Rankings the university sits within the top 300. At home it is consistently counted among China's leading medical schools. In the Best Chinese Universities Ranking it has held first or second place among Chinese medical universities, a position it shares with Peking Union Medical College.

Subject results reinforce this. As of 2025, the Academic Ranking of World Universities put eight of its subjects among the best 200 in the world. They are clinical medicine, public health, nursing, pharmacy and pharmaceutical sciences, biomedical engineering, medical technology, human biological sciences and dentistry and oral sciences. U.S. News & World Report ranked its clinical medicine 135th in the world.
ARWU, the Academic Ranking of World Universities, is also known as the Shanghai Ranking and comes out every year. It was the world's first university ranking to rely on several different indicators.
The Nature Index tracks which institutions and countries produce high-quality scientific articles, and publishes research output figures monthly.
The Chinese Universities Alumni Association (CUAA, 中国校友会网) issues the Universities Ranking of China, among the leading rankings inside China.
What daily life is like depends on the surrounding city: its weather, its transport and its attractions. The sections below introduce Beijing.

Urban Beijing is dominated by three kinds of architecture. Imperial China supplies the first kind, in the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple, the Forbidden City and above all Tian'anmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace, which is still the trademark building of the People's Republic. Next comes the "Sino-Sov" style, which dates from between the 1950s and the 1970s and gave the city boxy structures, some of them poorly built. Finally there are modern forms, which are most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east, home of the new CCTV Headquarters, and at other sites such as the National Center for the Performing Arts and the Beijing National Stadium.

Since the start of the 21st century Beijing has seen enormous growth in new construction, with many modern styles brought by international designers, strongest in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s design with a neofuturistic style, putting old and new together. The tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing has also taken the CTBUH Skyscraper Award twice since 2007, for the Linked Hybrid (2009) and for the CCTV Headquarters (2013). That prize for the best overall tall building is given to a single building in the world each year, so it is a real distinction.

Traditional homes are siheyuans, courtyards enclosed by buildings. The grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Alleys called hutongs normally link these courtyards. Hutongs generally run straight from east to west, which puts doorways on the north and south sides for good Feng Shui, and their width varies, with some so narrow that only a few pedestrians can pass at once.

Siheyuans and hutongs were once found everywhere in Beijing but are disappearing fast as high-rises replace whole blocks. Hutong residents have the right to move into apartments in the new buildings that are at least as big as their old homes. Even so, many people complain that the neighbourhood spirit and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced by apartment blocks. The properties are often owned by the government. If you want to see this older Beijing, do so while it remains.

Beijing lies on the northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular plain that opens to the south and east. Mountains on the north, north-west and west protect the city, and the farmland of northern China, from the desert steppes that press in from beyond. In the north-west of the municipality, mainly in Yanqing District and Huairou District, the Jundu Mountains dominate, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall, running across the north of the municipality, follows the rugged terrain and was built against raids from nomads of the steppes. The municipality's highest point is Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 ft) high, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The big rivers of Beijing, the Chaobai, the Yongding and the Juma, belong to the Hai River system and flow south-east. On the upper Chaobai, the Miyun Reservoir is the municipality's largest. The city also marks the northern terminus of two waterways. One is the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built more than 1,400 years ago for transport. The other is the South-North Water Transfer Project, built in the last ten years to carry water from the Yangtze basin.

Built-up Beijing takes up a small but expanding share of the municipality. It lies on the plains of the south-central area, 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. Ring roads spread out in concentric circles, and the Second Ring Road follows the line of the old city walls, while the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs. In the middle stand Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, which was the emperors' home. Zhongnanhai, where the country's present leaders live, lies to the west of Tian'anmen. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tian'anmen and the Square and forms the city's main east-west axis.
Commentators often say that Beijing grew outward from its old inner city to the fringes by "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), and they blame this pattern for many of the city's urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen BSk). Summers are hot and humid under the influence of the East Asian monsoon, and winters are short, cold and dry because of the huge Siberian anticyclone. In spring, sandstorms may blow in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, together with fast warming but mostly dry weather. Autumn, like spring, is a transition season with little rain.

Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest period in Beijing has been early August and the coldest early January. By China's seasonal division standard, the seasons begin on these dates: spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September, and winter on 31 October. Recent years have seen quicker warming in March and September and slower warming in May and October, so autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

For 1991 to 2020 the yearly average temperature in the urban area is between 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) and 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Daily minimums average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily maximums 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). Lower suburban areas average 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F) over the year, with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In the mountains the annual average is anywhere from 0 °C (32 °F) to 10 °C (50 °F), falling as the altitude rises.

The coldest month, January, has a daily average of −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), and the warmest, July, one of 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Annual precipitation is roughly 528.0 mm (20.79 in), though the Haidian and Chaoyang districts receive more, 584.2 mm (23.00 in) on average, and close to three-quarters of it falls from June to August. July has the least sunshine (42% of what is possible) and January and February the most (62%), and the yearly total is 2,490.5 hours. The most extreme temperatures since 1951 were a low of −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), recorded on 22 February 1966, and a high of 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999. Winters are cold and dry, so dress for them.

Beijing has long had environmental problems. Its urban extent quadrupled between 2000 and 2009, which greatly increased human emissions and also changed the weather basics, even leaving emissions aside. The surface reflected less light, and wind speed and humidity near the ground dropped. Meanwhile temperatures at the ground and just above it rose, along with ozone levels and the degree of vertical mixing that dilutes air. Urbanisation and the burning of fossil fuel have led to serious environmental problems that harm the health of many residents.

In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and most of northern China and affected 600 million people in all. That "pollution shock" made air pollution a major economic and social concern across China. The Beijing government responded with measures to reduce pollution, including a plan to cut coal's share from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017. At national level, the government told owners of heavily polluting vehicles to take them off the road between 2015 and 2017, and it worked harder to move the energy system towards clean sources.

A 2006 joint study by American and Chinese researchers concluded that a large share of Beijing's pollution blows in from nearby cities and provinces. Between 35 and 60% of the ozone, on average, originates outside the city. Tianjin Municipality and Shandong Province exert what the researchers called a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", partly because of the south and south-east winds that prevail in summer and partly because mountains lie to the north and north-west.

About 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 comes from burning coal, which is also the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 the city has been switching its coal-fired power stations to natural gas, and it wants annual coal use capped at 20 million tons. Beijing burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, of which 73% went on heating and generating power and the remainder on industry. Many pollutants come from neighbouring regions. Tianjin's coal consumption was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. In 2011 Hebei burned over 300 million tons, more than all of Germany, and only 30% went to power generation; a good deal was used to make steel and cement. The power plants of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, coal-mining regions where consumption has tripled since 2000, add to the problem, as do those in Shandong. By coal consumption, the four provinces rank in this order: Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

Four large coal-fired plants in the city once supplied electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant was due to close in 2016. From 2013 to 2017 the city planned to cut 13 million tons of coal use, and to hold consumption at 15 million tons in 2015.

capital-medical-university.h: Clearing the air for big events

blocks.x: Beijing spent nearly US$17 billion before the 2008 Summer Olympics, partly to keep its promise to clean up the city's air. During the Games it put several schemes in place: all construction sites stopped work, many Beijing factories were closed for good, industry in neighbouring regions was shut for a time, and some petrol stations closed. The city also put together 3,800 natural gas buses, one of the biggest fleets in the world, and became the first Chinese city to require the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The government sometimes seeds clouds to make rain more likely and clear the air before large events, as before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to fight drought. More recently it has relied more on other measures, such as temporarily closing factories and restricting road traffic. Examples are "APEC blue" and "parade blue", brief periods around APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. In each case the air improved dramatically, then returned to unhealthy levels soon after.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015, when most industry and commercial business in the city shut down, and a second "red alert" followed later that month. In November 2016 Beijing's environmental protection bureau announced that, from 2017, highly polluting old cars would be banned from the road whenever smog "red alerts" were issued in the city or nearby regions.

The 2014 "war on pollution" has delivered measurable cuts. Fine particulates fell 35% in 2017 and dropped further by 2020. The main reasons were a switch from coal power to natural gas and the clean-up of polluting industrial plants in the Beijing area. The annual average concentration of PM2.5 fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024 Beijing had only two days of heavy pollution, a record low and a 96.6 percent decrease from 58 days in 2013.

Different organisations report different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) publishes daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website, while the American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly figures for ozone and fine particulate (PM2.5) on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's pollution levels and health impact are often lower than the Embassy's. If you are sensitive to air quality, check both.

Smog is harmful to the population. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on how common cardiovascular and respiratory diseases are in Beijing, and exposure to heavily polluted air can lead to breathing and heart problems, hospital emergency visits and even death. Students with asthma or heart conditions should discuss this with a doctor.

Erosion of deserts in northern and north-western China brings seasonal dust storms to the city. At times the Beijing Weather Modification Office causes rain artificially to counter the storms and soften their effects. January to April 2006 saw no fewer than eight, and a single storm in April 2002 deposited almost 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it carried on towards Japan and Korea.

Travel to Beijing, register at Capital Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Capital Normal University, or CNU (首都师范大学), is a public university belonging to the city of Beijing. Its funding comes jointly from the Ministry of Education and the Beijing Municipal People's Government, and it is part of the Double First-Class Construction programme.

The word "Normal" in the name may puzzle newcomers. It marks a type of institution created to train teachers, by teaching them the norms of educational method and curriculum design. Many Chinese normal universities now teach much more than education, but the name stays.
The institution began in 1954 as Beijing Normal College (北京师范学院). In teaching terms it is older: its roots lie in Tongzhou Teachers School (通州师范学校), opened in 1905.

From 1960 a series of other institutions were gradually absorbed. Parts of North China Renmin University (华北人民大学) came first, along with the Beijing Art Normal College (北京艺术师范学院), the Beijing Workers and Peasants Normal College (北京工农师范学院) and the Beijing Normal Vocational School (北京师范专科学校). The branch campus of Beijing Normal University was added in 1992, the year the college adopted the name Capital Normal University. Later mergers brought in the Beijing Preschool Normal School, Tongzhou Normal School, Beijing Third Normal School and the Beijing Union University Foreign Languages Normal School.
Eight campuses make up CNU, and the majority are along Beijing's Third Ring Road. The southern campus serves as headquarters and houses most of the programmes. Other campuses have specific roles.
North 1 campus: the College of International Culture
North 2 campus: the College of Information Engineering
East 1 campus: the College of Education
LiangXiang campus: the Department of Fundamental Education, which teaches first-year students
Confirm the campus for your own programme before you plan accommodation.

Five alumni are named. Bai Jingting is a Chinese actor and singer, and Pu Shu is a well-known ballad singer. Wang Hairong is a grand-niece of Mao Zedong. Xiaoyuan Liu is an academic and author, and Yuan Tengfei is a famous history teacher.

capital-normal-university.h: Beijing, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Because most of what you will do each day happens in the city, the next sections introduce Beijing: its buildings, landscape, weather and, in some depth, its air quality.
You will notice three broad groups of buildings in urban Beijing.

Imperial architecture: the traditional style of imperial China. Its most famous example is Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the trademark building of the People's Republic. The Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple are also in this style.
"Sino-Sov" buildings. These were put up between the 1950s and the 1970s. They tend to be boxy, and some were poorly built.

Modern architecture. The Beijing CBD in the east of the city is the best place to see it, with landmarks such as the new CCTV Headquarters. Elsewhere there are the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Early this century Beijing saw a surge of new building in modern styles by international designers, and the CBD shows it best. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s industrial design with a neofuturistic approach, putting old and new together. Beijing's tallest building is the China Zun, at 528 metres. Twice, a Beijing building has won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building, an honour given to a single building worldwide each year: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

A siheyuan is a courtyard surrounded by buildings. Grand examples include the Residence of Soong Ching-ling and Prince Gong Mansion. A network of alleys, the hutongs, connects them. Most hutongs run straight from east to west, which makes doorways face north or south, thought to be good for feng shui. Some are wide, while others are so narrow that only a few walkers can fit through at once.

Siheyuans and hutongs were once found throughout Beijing, but they are disappearing fast as whole blocks of hutongs are replaced by high-rises. The people who live in the hutongs have a right to flats in the new buildings that are no smaller than their old homes. Even so, many say the community spirit and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced. These properties are often owned by the government.

Beijing is at the northern edge of the North China Plain, a lowland with a roughly triangular shape that opens towards the south and east of the city. To the north, northwest and west there are mountains, which shelter both the city and northern China's farming heartland from the desert steppe. Yanqing District and Huairou District in the northwest are dominated by the Jundu Mountains, and the Western Hills (Xishan) form the western frame. The Great Wall crosses the northern part of the municipality, built on rough terrain to guard against nomadic raiders. The highest point is Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 ft) above sea level, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

Three main rivers, the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, flow southeast as tributaries of the Hai River system. Miyun Reservoir lies on the upper Chaobai and is the biggest reservoir in the municipality. The city also marks the northern end of two great water projects: the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built over 1,400 years ago for transport, and the recent South-North Water Transfer Project, completed in the past decade, which carries water from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up part of Beijing is on plains in the south-central area of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. It is a fairly small part of the municipality's land, though it keeps expanding. The layout is a set of concentric ring roads. The Second Ring Road follows the line of the former city walls, and the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs.

Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square are the centre, just south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, home of China's present leaders. The main east-west axis is Chang'an Avenue, which passes between Tian'anmen and the Square.
The pattern of growth from the old inner city out to the fringe is commonly called "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing). It is often given as one reason for Beijing's urban problems.

Beijing has a humid continental climate (Koppen Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (Koppen BSk). The East Asian monsoon brings hot, humid summers, and the huge Siberian anticyclone brings short, cold, dry winters. In spring, sandstorms may blow in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, together with quickly warming, mostly dry weather. Autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with very little rain.

In the years from 2001 to 2026, early August has been the hottest time of year and early January the coldest. Under China's seasonal standard, the dates are 26 March for the start of spring, 20 May for summer, 13 September for autumn and 31 October for winter. In recent years March and September have warmed faster, and May and October more slowly, so autumn is generally shorter than spring.
For the urban area, 1991 to 2020 averages are as follows.
Annual mean temperature: 12.9 to 13.3 degrees Celsius (55.2 to 55.9 F)
Average daily minimum: 7.7 to 8.4 degrees (45.9 to 47.1 F)
Average daily maximum: 18.5 to 18.9 degrees (65.3 to 66.0 F)

For the low-lying suburbs, the annual mean is 11.5 to 13.0 degrees (52.7 to 55.4 F), the daily minimum is 5.9 to 8.0 degrees (42.6 to 46.4 F) and the daily maximum is 18.2 to 18.7 degrees (64.8 to 65.7 F). In the mountains the annual mean is between 0 and 10 degrees (32 and 50 F) and falls as the altitude rises.

In January the daily average is minus 2.7 degrees (27.1 F), and in July it is 27.2 degrees (81.0 F). Annual rainfall is about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three-quarters falls from June to August. Sunshine ranges from 42 percent of the possible total in July to 62 percent in January and February, and the annual total is 2,490.5 hours. The coldest day since 1951 was 22 February 1966 at minus 27.4 degrees (minus 17.3 F), and the hottest was 24 July 1999 at 41.9 degrees (107.4 F).

Pollution has long been an issue in Beijing, and it is worth understanding before you arrive. Recent trends are much better than the older record. The sections below explain what caused the problems and how they have been tackled.

The built-up area of Beijing grew fourfold in 2000 to 2009. That raised emissions from human activity, and it also changed the local meteorology fundamentally, even when human emissions are left out. Wind speed, humidity near the ground and surface albedo went down, while ground and low-level air temperatures, vertical dilution of air and ozone went up. Urbanisation and the pollution from burning fossil fuels combine to cause serious environmental problems in Beijing, which lead to health problems for many residents.

Heavy smog covered Beijing and most of northern China in 2013, affecting 600 million people altogether. After this "pollution shock", air pollution became a major social and economic concern across the country. Beijing's government responded with measures to cut it, such as reducing coal's share of energy from 24 percent in 2012 to 10 percent in 2017. From 2015 to 2017 the national government ordered the removal of heavily polluting vehicles and stepped up its efforts to move the energy system to clean sources.

A joint study by American and Chinese researchers in 2006 found that a large part of the city's pollution blows in from nearby cities and provinces. Typically 35 to 60 percent of the ozone has an outside origin. The study said Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality have a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", in part because of the prevailing southerly or southeasterly winds in summer and the mountains to the north and northwest.

Coal is a major source: it produces about 40 percent of Beijing's PM 2.5, and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 the city has been changing coal-fired power stations over to natural gas, with the aim of capping coal use at 20 million tons a year. The city used 26.3 million tons in 2011, 73 percent of it for heating and power and the rest for industry.
Neighbouring regions emit a large share of the pollutants too.
Tianjin's coal consumption was expected to rise from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million tons in 2015.
Hebei Province burned more than 300 million tons of coal in 2011, which is more than all of Germany, and only 30 percent went to power generation. A large part went to making steel and cement.
Coal use in the mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi has tripled since 2000, and power plants there and in Shandong add to Beijing's pollution.
Of all Chinese provinces, the biggest coal consumers are Shandong first, then Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

The city itself had four large coal-fired power plants that supplied electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more shut in March 2015, and the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, the last one, was to close in 2016. Beijing planned to cut coal use by 13 million tons from 2013 to 2017, with a cap of 15 million tons in 2015.

The 2008 Summer Olympics brought a clean-up effort that cost nearly US$17 billion, in keeping with promises to improve the city's air. Bus and subway fares were lowered, new subway lines were opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. The city also assembled 3,800 natural gas buses, among the largest fleets anywhere, and it was the first Chinese city to require the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Cloud seeding is sometimes used by the government to make rain more likely before big events, for example before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also against drought. Lately it has turned more to temporary factory closures and tighter limits on road traffic. "APEC blue" and "parade blue" describe the short spells before and during the APEC China 2014 meeting and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, when Beijing's air quality improved dramatically but went back to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed most of the city's industry and commercial business. A smog "red alert" followed later that month. Then, in November 2016, the city's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 old cars that pollute heavily would be banned from driving whenever red alerts were declared in the city or neighbouring regions.

After the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014, there was a measurable fall in pollutants. Fine particulates went down 35 percent in 2017 and dropped further by 2020. The main reasons were replacing coal with natural gas in power generation and cleaning up polluting industrial facilities in the Beijing area.

In 2022 the annual average concentration of PM2.5, the main airborne fine particulate, fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the city's best air quality since 2013. Only two days of heavy pollution occurred in 2024, the lowest number on record and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days in 2013.

Since pollution has been high, several sources publish different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) puts daily readings from 27 monitoring stations on its website. The American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly fine particulate (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. As the two organisations measure different pollutants by different criteria, the pollution levels, and the health effect, reported by the BJEPB are often lower than those from the US Embassy.

Smog harms people. Air pollution directly and significantly affects Beijing's rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease, and heavy exposure can lead to respiratory and cardiovascular trouble, emergency room visits and even death. If you have a health condition, ask a doctor how to prepare for your stay.

Seasonal dust storms trouble the city, caused by dust from eroded deserts in northern and northwestern China. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain artificially to combat the storms and lessen their impact. In just the first four months of 2006 there were at least eight. In April 2002 a single dust storm left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it moved on to Japan and Korea.

In summary, CNU is a teacher-training university in the capital with a long history and several campuses, in a city that offers a great deal of culture and architecture, with cold winters, hot summers and an air-quality record that has improved markedly in recent years.

Capital University of Economics and Business, abbreviated CUEB (首都经济贸易大学), is a public university run by the city of Beijing and located in Fengtai District. The Beijing Municipal People's Government is the body it belongs to and the one that pays for it. CUEB was created in March 1995 by joining two older colleges: Beijing Economics College (北京经济学院) and Beijing Finance and Business College (北京财贸学院). Because the university is a municipal one, its ties with the capital city are close, and a good part of the student experience is simply life in Beijing itself.

capital-university-of-economics-and-busi.h: Beijing, the setting for your studies

blocks.x: What a student needs to know about everyday life largely concerns the city around the campus, meaning the terrain, the weather, the air and the streets. The sections below take these in turn.

Beijing stands at the northern tip of the North China Plain, a plain shaped roughly like a triangle that spreads out to the south and east. Hills and mountains to the north, north-west and west act as a barrier, keeping the encroaching desert steppes away from the city and from the farmland of northern China. In the north-west of the municipality, notably Yanqing and Huairou Districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, and the Western Hills (Xishan) line the western side. The Great Wall of China runs across the north of the municipality, built along rough ground to hold back raiders from the steppes. Dongling Mountain, a peak of the Western Hills right on the Hebei boundary, is the municipality's high point at 7,556 ft (2,303 metres).

Water comes mainly from rivers such as the Chaobai, the Yongding and the Juma. All are tributaries of the Hai River system and flow south-eastward. The Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the largest reservoir in the municipality. Two great engineering works also end in Beijing: the Grand Canal from Hangzhou, a transport channel built more than 1,400 years ago, and the South-North Water Transfer Project, which was built over the past decade to move water from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up city sits on flat ground in the south-central part of the municipality, 130 to 200 feet (40 to 60 metres) above sea level. It makes up a fairly small, though growing, fraction of the municipality's total area. Streets are arranged in concentric ring roads. The Second Ring follows the course of the former city walls, whereas the Sixth Ring joins up satellite towns in the suburbs. Right in the centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where emperors used to live. Zhongnanhai, the home of China's present leaders, is on the western side of Tian'anmen. Chang'an Avenue passes between the Gate and the Square and serves as the main east-west axis.

Observers often say Beijing has expanded "like a pancake" (tan da bing), spreading outward evenly from the old centre to the edges, and that this growth pattern lies behind many of the city's urban difficulties.

capital-university-of-economics-and-busi.h: Four seasons, with a few surprises

blocks.x: In Köppen terms Beijing has a humid continental climate (Dwa) that borders on a monsoonal cold semi-arid one (BSk). Spring may bring sandstorms from the Gobi Desert across the Mongolian steppe together with fast, mostly dry warming, and autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with minimal rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest part of the year was early August and the coldest early January.

China's official seasonal calendar puts the start of spring in Beijing at 26 March, of summer at 20 May, of autumn at 13 September and of winter at 31 October. Recently March and September have warmed up faster while May and October have warmed more slowly, so autumn in Beijing is usually the shorter season of the two.

Typical temperatures for 1991 to 2020 depend on where you are. In the urban area the yearly average is 12.9-13.3 °C (55.2-55.9 °F), with a mean daily low of 7.7-8.4 °C (45.9-47.1 °F) and a mean daily high of 18.5-18.9 °C (65.3-66.0 °F). Lower-lying suburbs average 11.5-13.0 °C (52.7-55.4 °F), with lows of 5.9-8.0 °C (42.6-46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2-18.7 °C (64.8-65.7 °F). In the mountains the yearly average lies between 0 and 10 °C (32-50 °F), falling with height. Over the year the coldest monthly mean is January's -2.7 °C (27.1 °F), and the warmest is July's 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

Rainfall comes to roughly 20.79 in (528.0 mm) per year, rising to 23.00 in (584.2 mm) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and almost three-quarters falls in June, July and August. Sunshine ranges from 42% of the possible in July to 62% in January and February, which gives 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. Records since 1951 show a low of -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966 and a high of 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.
The air deserves a section of its own, because it is the aspect of Beijing that most newcomers worry about, and the story has been improving.

Environmental trouble in Beijing is nothing new. From 2000 to 2009 the urban area expanded to four times its former size. As well as pushing emissions up sharply, this changed the local weather even when human emissions are set aside: albedo at the surface, wind speed and humidity near the ground went down, whereas temperatures at the ground and just above it, vertical dilution of the air and ozone went up. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality have a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", partly because of the south and south-east winds that prevail in summer and the mountains to the north and north-west.

It burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, of which 73% went to heating and power generation and the rest to industry. Neighbouring regions emit much of the air pollution. Tianjin's coal consumption was expected to go from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, and Hebei Province burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than all of Germany; just 30% of that went to power generation, with a large amount used for steel and cement. The power plants of the mining regions Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (where coal use has tripled since 2000), together with Shandong, add to the problem. Among Chinese provinces, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth in coal consumption.

Beijing used to have four big coal-fired plants providing electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, the last, was to close in 2016. For 2013 to 2017 the city planned to cut coal consumption by 13 million tons and to hold it to 15 million tons in 2015.

The 2008 Summer Olympics prompted a large effort: nearly US$17 billion was spent to keep promises about cleaner air. It also put together a fleet of 3,800 buses powered by natural gas, one of the biggest fleets in the world, and it was the first Chinese city to require the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Lately, though, they rely more on temporary factory closures and tighter restrictions on cars. Two examples are "APEC blue" and "parade blue", brief periods of clear air around APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. In each case air quality improved a great deal and then slipped back to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing declared its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, which closed most industry and other businesses, and another smog "red alert" came later in the same month. The city's environmental protection bureau announced in November 2016 that from 2017 highly polluting old vehicles would be barred from the roads whenever a smog "red alert" was in force in the city or its neighbours.

There has been measurable progress since the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014. Fine particulates dropped by 35% in 2017 and fell more by 2020, mostly because natural gas took the place of coal power and polluting industrial plants in the Beijing area were cleaned up. Average PM2.5 in 2022 was 30 micrograms per cubic meter, the best level since 2013, and in 2024 the city recorded only two days of heavy pollution, a record low and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days in 2013.

With pollution this significant, different sources publish different readings. The two organisations measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's figures for pollution and for the health impact tend to come out lower than the Embassy's. Check both if you have a health condition.

Smog is a real hazard. It directly affects rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and breathing heavily polluted air can lead to respiratory and heart problems, emergency room visits and even death.

Erosion of the deserts in northern and north-western China causes seasonal dust storms that trouble the city. Eight or more such storms occurred in just the first four months of 2006, and one storm in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing before continuing to Japan and Korea.

The buildings of urban Beijing fall mostly into three groups. The oldest is the architecture of imperial China, represented by the immense Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the emblem of the People's Republic, as well as the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven. Second comes the "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to the 1970s, whose blocks are boxy and in some cases badly built. The third group is far more modern, concentrated in the Beijing CBD in the east, which has the new CCTV Headquarters, but also seen elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Early in the 21st century Beijing saw a surge of new construction, in many contemporary styles by international designers and strongest in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s design and neofuturistic architecture sit side by side, blending old and new. The tallest building is China Zun, at 528 meters. Since 2007, two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building, which goes to a single building worldwide each year: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

A siheyuan is a courtyard enclosed by buildings, and the grandest examples include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are normally linked by lanes called hutongs, which are generally straight and run east to west, so that doors open to the north and south, which is good Feng Shui. Their widths differ, and some are narrow enough that only a few pedestrians can squeeze through together.
