Hutong residents have the right to apartments in the new buildings that are at least as large as their old homes. Even so, many say that the community feeling and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced, and the properties are often owned by the government.

Check the university's official website for programmes, admission rules and fees before you apply. When you plan for Beijing, prepare for a cold, dry winter, a hot, humid summer, spring dust and the occasional smog alert, and keep an air quality app handy. The air has improved markedly in recent years, as the figures above show.

The home of Capital University of Physical Education and Sports is Beijing, and for an international student the capital will shape daily life as much as the campus does. The sections below cover what the city looks like, how the land lies, what the weather does through the year, and how the air has changed over the past decade.
Three building styles dominate urban Beijing, and you will probably meet all of them in a single week.

The first is the architecture of imperial China. Its best-known examples are Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), which is still the symbol of the People's Republic, and also the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City. The second is the so-called 'Sino-Sov' style from the 1950s to the 1970s, with boxy structures that were sometimes poorly built. The third is the modern look, most visible in the Beijing CBD in the east of the city, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, and also in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts elsewhere.

capital-university-of-physical-education.h: New towers and the 798 Art Zone

blocks.x: Since the early 21st century Beijing has seen an enormous wave of construction, with international designers bringing many modern styles, again strongest in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s industrial design with a neofuturistic look, mixing old and new in one place. The tallest building in the city is the 528-metre China Zun.

Beijing has also won recognition for its towers. Twice since 2007 the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which names the world's best tall building of the year, has gone to a Beijing building: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. Only one building worldwide wins it in any given year.

A very different Beijing survives in the siheyuan, courtyard homes built around an open space. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. The courtyards are normally linked by lanes called hutongs. The lanes are generally straight and run along an east-west line, which makes the doorways face north or south, an arrangement valued for good Feng Shui. Their width varies, and some are so narrow that only a few people can pass at a time.

Siheyuans and hutongs used to be everywhere, but whole blocks of them are now being replaced by high-rises. Residents are entitled to move into new apartments at least as large as their former homes. Even so, many complain that the old sense of community and street life in the hutongs is gone for good, and the properties are often owned by the government. If you want to see this older city, visit it soon and on foot.

Beijing sits at the northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that opens out to the south and east. A mountain barrier curving round the north, northwest and west shields the city, and the farmland of northern China, from the desert steppes beyond.

In the northwest of the municipality, particularly in Yanqing District and Huairou District, the Jundu Mountains dominate, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the northern part of the municipality along the rugged ground, built to hold off nomadic raiders from the steppe. The highest point is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The main rivers, the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, all belong to the Hai River system and run southeast. The largest reservoir in the municipality is the Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. Two great waterworks end here as well. One is the Grand Canal running down to Hangzhou, dug more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route. The other is the South–North Water Transfer Project, built over the last decade to carry water up from the Yangtze basin.

capital-university-of-physical-education.h: How the city is laid out

blocks.x: The urban area occupies the plains of the south-central municipality, lying 40 to 60 metres (130–200 feet) above sea level. It takes up a relatively small share of the municipality but keeps growing. Ring roads radiate outward in concentric circles. The line of the former city walls is followed by the Second Ring Road, whereas the Sixth links the satellite towns out in the suburbs.

At the heart lie Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, directly south of the Forbidden City, which was the home of China's emperors. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, where the country's present leaders live. Chang'an Avenue, which runs through the gap separating Tiananmen from the Square, is the main east–west axis.

The growth from the old centre to the fringe is often compared to a spreading pancake (tan da bing), and this pattern is frequently blamed for the city's urban problems. In practice it means distances are long, so it is worth checking how far your accommodation is from campus.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to the boundary with a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). Summers are hot and humid thanks to the East Asian monsoon, while winters are short, cold and dry, shaped by the vast Siberian anticyclone.

In spring, sandstorms can sweep across the Mongolian steppe from the Gobi Desert, and the weather warms quickly but stays generally dry. Autumn, like spring, is a transition season with little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest period has been early August and the coldest early January.

China's seasonal standard puts the start of Beijing's winter on 31 October, with spring beginning 26 March, summer 20 May and autumn 13 September. Because March and September have warmed faster in recent years, and May and October more slowly, autumn is usually shorter than spring.

capital-university-of-physical-education.h: Temperature, rain and sunshine in numbers

blocks.x: Looking at 1991–2020, the urban area averages between 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) and 13.3 °C (55.9 °F) across the year. The typical daily minimum there is 7.7 °C (45.9 °F) up to 8.4 °C (47.1 °F), and the typical daily maximum is 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) up to 18.9 °C (66.0 °F). Out in the low-lying suburbs the annual figure is 11.5 °C (52.7 °F) to 13.0 °C (55.4 °F); minimums are 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) to 8.0 °C (46.4 °F), and maximums 18.2 °C (64.8 °F) to 18.7 °C (65.7 °F). In the mountains the yearly mean is anywhere from 0 °C (32 °F) to 10 °C (50 °F), falling as the land rises.

January days average −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), while those in July average 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Annual rainfall averages about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three-quarters of it falls from June to August.

Bright sunshine adds up to 2,490.5 hours a year. July is the least sunny month at 42% of the possible total, whereas January and February reach 62%. The record extremes since 1951 are a low of −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), recorded on 22 February 1966, and a high of 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999. In short, you should be ready for a properly cold winter and a hot, wet summer.
Environmental problems have affected Beijing for a long time, and it helps to understand both the causes and the recent progress.

capital-university-of-physical-education.h: Why the air became a problem

blocks.x: Between 2000 and 2009 the built-up area of Beijing grew fourfold. That raised emissions, and it also changed local weather conditions: surface albedo, wind speed and near-surface humidity fell, while ground and near-surface air temperatures, ozone levels and the vertical mixing of air rose. Together with pollution from burning fossil fuels, this has often caused serious environmental trouble and health problems for residents.

In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and much of northern China, affecting 600 million people in total. This 'pollution shock' made air pollution a major economic and social concern across China. Beijing's government then announced measures. One was a cut in coal's share of energy, from 24% in 2012 down to 10% in 2017. Meanwhile national authorities ordered the removal of the dirtiest vehicles between 2015 and 2017 and stepped up the shift to clean energy.

A 2006 study by American and Chinese researchers working together concluded that a good share of Beijing's pollution blows in from surrounding cities and provinces. Between 35% and 60% of the ozone, on average, comes from outside the city boundary. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality exert particular influence, partly through the south and southeasterly flow that prevails in summer and partly because mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Burning coal accounts for roughly 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5, and it is also the chief source of nitrogen dioxide and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012 and wants to hold annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, of which 73% went to heating and power generation and the remainder to industry. Four large coal plants once supplied electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was the first to close, in 2014. Two more followed in March 2015, and the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, the last, was scheduled for closure in 2016. The city's plan for 2013 to 2017 was a reduction of 13 million tons of coal use, with a ceiling of 15 million tons for 2015.

A lot of the pollution is produced next door. Coal use in Tianjin was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Hebei Province alone burned over 300 million tons in 2011, which exceeds the total for the whole of Germany, and just 30% of it fed power generation, while much of the rest went into making steel and cement. The coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where use has tripled since 2000, and Shandong, whose power plants also contribute, add to Beijing's smog. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces for coal consumption.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, and in keeping with promises about cleaner air, close to US$17 billion went on the effort. It cut bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. The city also put together 3,800 natural gas buses, one of the largest fleets anywhere, and Beijing was the first Chinese city to demand the national counterpart of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The authorities have sometimes used cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air before big events, for example before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to tackle drought. More recently they have leaned on temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars. The results were the short spells nicknamed 'APEC blue' and 'parade blue', which surrounded the APEC China 2014 meeting and the China Victory Day Parade of 2015. Air quality improved sharply during and just before those events, and then fell back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The city's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and shut most industry and commercial business; a red alert was issued later the same month. In November 2016 the city's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be banned from driving whenever a smog red alert is in force in the city or nearby regions.

The 'war on pollution' declared in 2014 has produced measurable results. Fine particulates fell 35% in 2017, with further falls by 2020, mainly because coal power was replaced by natural gas and polluting industrial plants were cleaned up. In 2022 the yearly average PM2.5 concentration dropped to 30 micrograms per cubic meter, the best since 2013. Heavy-pollution days in 2024 numbered only two, a record low and a fall of 96.6 percent from the 58 of 2013.

Different sources report different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily figures from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website. Separately, the US Embassy in Beijing reports PM2.5 fine particulates and ozone every hour through Twitter. The two measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's pollution levels and health impact are often lower than the Embassy's. Checking more than one source is sensible if you have asthma or other respiratory concerns.

The smog is harmful. Air pollution directly raises illness rates for cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, hospital emergency visits and even deaths.

Dust eroded from deserts in northern and northwestern China causes seasonal storms in the city. To fight them and soften their effect, the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain artificially. The first four months of 2006 brought at least eight storms, and a single one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it travelled on towards Japan and Korea. Spring is the season to be ready for them.

central-academy-of-fine-arts.h: An art academy with a national reputation

blocks.x: CAFA, short for the Central Academy of Fine Arts, answers directly to China's Ministry of Education. A Philippine newspaper, the Manila Bulletin, once described it as the best-known and most respected art school in the country. Admission is fiercely competitive: over 90% of applicants are rejected each year. For an applicant, that means preparation and a strong portfolio matter a great deal.

central-academy-of-fine-arts.h: From a 1918 school to a modern academy

blocks.x: The roots go back to 1918, when the educator Cai Yuanpei pushed for a national art school in Beijing. That school was the first of its kind in China and the real beginning of modern fine-arts education there. In time it turned into the school then called the Beiping National Art School (国立北平艺术专科学校). CAFA proper dates from April 1950, formed by combining that school with the art department at North China University's third campus.

Past principals read like a who's who: Xu Beihong and Jiang Feng, then Wu Zuoren and Gu Yuan, followed by Jin Shangyi, then Pan Gongkai, and most recently Fan Di'an. The present head is Lin Mao, president from 2023, and the academic commission is directed by Jin Shangyi.

After about four decades without it, design returned to CAFA in 1995 as the Department of Art Design, and in October 2002 that department was upgraded to a School of Design. The goal is to produce design professionals with inventive minds and hands-on skills. Bachelor, master and Ph.D. degrees are offered in fields as varied as photography, fashion, product design, digital media, visual communication and the theory and history of design.

The school is a driving force for design in China. It contributed to designs for the 2008 Beijing Olympics and was involved in founding Tsinghua University's Academy of Arts & Design, which began life as CAFA's Huadong Campus.

Arata Isozaki, the Japanese architect, designed the newer CAFA Art Museum. You will find it on the campus's northeast corner, in Wangjing, at No.8, Huajiadi Nan Street. It occupies 3546 m2 of land with 14,777 m2 of floor space over six storeys, and opened in October 2008 as part of the 90th anniversary celebrations. Its collections include upwards of 2,000 historic scroll paintings from China's Ming Dynasty, and exhibitions rotate through the galleries.

The academy was in the news in 1989, during the Tiananmen Square protests and the crackdown that followed, because its students built the big Goddess of Democracy statue. A statement explaining the sculpture's purpose was signed by every one of the eight art academies.
CAFA's teaching is organised into several schools under the Faculty of Art and Design. The overview below goes school by school.
Chinese Painting is a school of its own.
Fine Art has four departments: oil painting, printmaking, sculpture and mural painting.
Experimental Art is a separate school.
Humanities covers art history and theory and cultural heritage, and it also houses the Non-material Cultural Heritage Research Center and an information center.
Design is split into visual communication, industrial design, digital media design, photography, fashion design and jewelry design.
Architecture teaches architecture proper, landscape design and interior design.

The College of City Design groups its work into an information design department (publishing, communication and commercial information design), a product design department (ceramic, artwork, interior product and jewelry design), a space design department (public art, exhibition design and visual system design) and a video design department (animation, game design and experimental movie).
Arts Administration and Education completes the list of schools.
Beyond the undergraduate schools, the Graduate school offers two levels of study.
Master's Degree Course
Doctoral Degree Course

central-academy-of-fine-arts.h: The collection at the CAFA Museum

blocks.x: The Museum of the Central Academy of Fine Arts, formerly the CAFA Gallery, was set up in the early 1960s. It holds 13,000 works in a wide range of genres and styles, from representative pieces by ancient and modern Chinese masters to fine work by students. Since the academy's founding in 1950 the collection has taken in Chinese painting, oil painting, prints and sculpture, as well as folk art such as New Year pictures, embroidery and the costumes and objects of ethnic minorities, plus Chinese relics in bronze, pottery, engravings and rubbings.

The Best Chinese Universities Ranking has put CAFA first, year after year, among China's arts-focused universities. QS also placed it 15th worldwide for art and design as of 2023, a strong signal for anyone choosing where to build a creative career.
CAFA's former students include many of China's best-known artists, curators and designers.

central-academy-of-fine-arts.h: Living in Beijing: what the city is like

blocks.x: Where you live matters almost as much as where you study. Day to day, a student at the Central Academy of Fine Arts will feel the city's weather, its air, its streets and its skyline long before thinking about its history. The sections below walk through Beijing as a place to live: how it looks, how the land lies, what the seasons do, and how the air quality has changed.

Walk across Beijing and you will meet three architectural layers. The oldest is imperial: the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the best-known symbol of the People's Republic, sits alongside the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second layer is the so-called "Sino-Sov" look of the 1950s to 1970s, when blocky, sometimes badly built structures went up. The third is the modern skyline, concentrated around the Beijing CBD in the east of the city, where you find the new CCTV Headquarters, and also seen at the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the start of the 21st century the city has seen an enormous wave of construction, much of it by international designers and most visible in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone is a good place to see the old and the new side by side, mixing 1950s industrial design with neofuturistic touches. The tallest building in town is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing towers have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which goes to a single best tall building in the whole world each year: first the Linked Hybrid (2009), then the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

Then there are the siheyuans, courtyard homes built around an open yard. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are linked by narrow lanes called hutongs, which usually run east to west so that doors open to the north and south, a layout chosen for good Feng Shui. Some are wide, others so tight that only a few people can squeeze through together. Both used to be everywhere, but entire blocks are being swapped for high-rises. Hutong residents are entitled to new apartments at least as large as their old homes, yet many say the neighbourly street life cannot be rebuilt, and the properties are often owned by the government. If you want to see this old fabric, go sooner rather than later.

Geographically, Beijing is perched where the North China Plain, a rough triangle of flat land, ends in the north; the plain stretches away south and east of the city. To the north, northwest and west, mountains act as a screen, keeping the desert steppes away from the farmland of northern China. In the northwest, notably in Yanqing District and Huairou District, the Jundu Mountains take over, and the Western Hills (Xishan) form the western backdrop. The Great Wall runs along the rugged northern terrain; it was built there to hold off raiders from the steppe. The highest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are the main rivers, all belonging to the Hai River system and all flowing southeast. The largest reservoir is Miyun Reservoir on the upper Chaobai. Two great waterworks end or begin here: Beijing is the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, a transport route more than 1,400 years old, and it receives Yangtze basin water through the South-North Water Transfer Project, built within the last decade.

The built-up city occupies a modest but growing share of the municipality, on flat land 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) above sea level in the south-central part. Its shape is a set of nested ring roads. The innermost, the Second Ring Road, traces where the old walls stood, while the Sixth Ring Road, far out, links the satellite towns around the edge. At the very centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, just south of the Forbidden City, once home to the emperors. West of Tian'anmen lies Zhongnanhai, where China's current leaders live. Chang'an Avenue slips between Tiananmen and the Square and serves as the main east-west axis.

People call this steady outward sprawl from the old core a pancake spreading (tan da bing), and it is often blamed for the city's urban problems, including the long journeys you may face between campus and the centre.

Climatically, the city is classed as humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to the monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). In practice: the East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and sticky, while the huge Siberian anticyclone makes winters brief, cold and dry. Spring can bring sandstorms from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, with fast warming and dry air. Autumn is a transition season with very little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest time was early August and the coldest early January.

Under China's official seasonal definitions, spring starts here on 26 March, followed by summer from 20 May, autumn from 13 September and winter from 31 October. Because March and September have recently warmed faster, and May and October more slowly, autumn is generally the shorter season compared with spring.

Now the numbers, taken over the period 1991-2020. Across the urban area, the yearly mean temperature is 12.9 °C at the low end and 13.3 °C at the high end (55.2 and 55.9 °F). Nights average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 and 47.1 °F), and afternoons 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 and 66.0 °F). Lower suburban land is slightly cooler: yearly means run 11.5-13.0 °C (52.7 and 55.4 °F), with night averages of 5.9-8.0 °C (42.6 and 46.4 °F) and daytime highs of 18.2-18.7 °C (64.8 and 65.7 °F). Up in the mountains the yearly mean sits anywhere from 0 °C (32 °F) to 10 °C (50 °F), falling as the altitude climbs. The average January day sits at -2.7 °C (27.1 °F), while July averages 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

Rainfall is limited. The municipality gets roughly 528.0 mm (20.79 in) in a year, though Haidian and Chaoyang see more, 584.2 mm (23.00 in), and nearly three-quarters of the total arrives between June and August. Skies are often bright: 2,490.5 sunshine hours annually, and the proportion of possible sun is lowest in July (42%) and highest in January and February (62%). Records since 1951 show a low of -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), set on 22 February 1966, and a high of 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), set on 24 July 1999. Pack for real cold in winter and real heat in summer.

Beijing has struggled with pollution for a long time, and prospective students are right to ask about it. The story today is one of clear improvement, but it helps to understand how the problem arose and what has been done.

Among Chinese provinces, coal consumption is highest in Shandong, then Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, in that order.

Inside the city limits there were once four big coal plants supplying power and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was the first to go, in 2014; two others stopped in March 2015; the final one, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to stop in 2016. The plan for 2013-2017 was a cut of 13 million tons in coal burned, with a ceiling of 15 million tons set for 2015.

Beijing's very first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed down most industry and commerce; a second "red alert" was declared later in December. The environmental protection bureau said in November 2016 that from 2017, old high-emission cars may not be driven whenever a smog red alert covers the city or adjoining areas.

If you arrive in spring, expect a few hazy, gritty days.

central-china-normal-university.h: Central China Normal University in outline

blocks.x: Central China Normal University, shortened to CCNU, is a public university in Wuhan, the capital of Hubei province. As a normal university it grew out of the teacher-training tradition, though today it teaches far beyond education. It reports to the Ministry of Education and is jointly funded by the Hubei Provincial People's Government. It belongs to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction programme.

The campus covers more than 330 acres on Guizi Hill, beside South Lake. That is the headline figure for the main site, but the university's own count of its total school area is 1,266,500 square metres, with 896,293 square metres of building floor space.

Three earlier institutions came together to form CCNU: Huachung University, Chunghua University of Wuchang, and the Pedagogical College of Zhongyuan University. Huachung was the senior partner. As a mission university it was the biggest and most influential one in south central China, and it traced its roots to Boone College, which was founded in 1903.

Huazhong University appeared in 1951, when Huachung absorbed the Zhongyuan pedagogical college. A further reorganisation in 1952 produced Huazhong Higher Normal College, which was renamed Central China Normal College in 1953. By then a new campus was being created to the east of Wuchang, on Mount Zhutou.

That hill had a history. More than 700 graves lay on Zhutou, so it was believed to be full of yin qi, the passive force in Chinese cosmology. Builders partly flattened the mountain and gave it a new name, Guizi, after a plant that grew there in quantity and is associated with yang qi, the active force. The name Central China Normal University became official in 1985, written in the calligraphy of Deng Xiaoping, who had been one of the founders of Zhongyuan University. Later, in 1993, Jiang Zemin, the President and Party General Secretary at the time, inscribed a message for the university: "Developing normal education, improving the nation's quality".
Boone College: the earliest forerunner was established in 1903 as the undergraduate Boone College, itself an outgrowth of an earlier Boone College dating from 1871.
Private Huachung University. In 1924 Boone College was renamed Huachung University. In 1929 it took in the Lake College of Yueyang and the Yale College of Changsha.

Public Huazhong University. After the People's Republic was founded, the former private institution became public Huazhong University, and in December 1949 it absorbed the College of Education of Chung Yuan Christian University.

Central China Higher Normal College: in the 1952 national reshuffle of colleges, public Huachung University was combined with private Chunghua University, the Institute of Education of Guangxi University, Nanchang University, South China Normal University, Central Teachers College and Hainan Teachers College. The result was the Central Higher Normal School, also styled Central Ecole Normale Superieure.

Central China Normal College: named in 1953. Part of Hubei University was brought in during 1962, and in 1972 the school absorbed pieces of Hubei Teachers Training College, the Hubei Correspondence School and the South China Institute for Nationalities.

Central China Normal University. The 1985 renaming came with a school motto written by Deng Xiaoping. The university entered the 211 list of key development universities in 2005, received special 985 funds for Innovative Platforms for Key Disciplines in 2007, and joined the Double First-Class Construction in 2017.

From the time of the 7th Five-Year Plan, CCNU staff have carried out national research such as the high-tech 863 project and the "Torch Program". It was among the first Chinese universities allowed to grant doctoral and postgraduate degrees and to award the titles of professor, associate professor and doctoral supervisor. It offers undergraduate, graduate, doctoral and postdoctoral study as well as full-time adult education.
In rankings of national social science research, CCNU stands 10th in China, and the Ministry of Education placed its social science research 6th for four years in a row.

Overseas, CCNU works with over 20 universities, colleges and institutes in eleven countries: America, Germany, Russia, Ukraine, France, Italy, Britain, Japan, Switzerland, Bulgaria and Brazil. It invites foreign experts and teachers to teach, and its own academics travel abroad for joint research.
The figures below come from the university's published profile and may be out of date, so check the official site for the current ones.

Key disciplines: 8 national key disciplines, 1 national key (cultivating) discipline, and 22 provincial and ministerial key disciplines

Teaching staff: 478 professors, 579 associate professors and 269 doctoral supervisors
Staff: 1,834 full-time faculty out of 4,017 faculty and staff in total
Students: 30,000 full-time students, of whom 10,475 are postgraduates, plus 1,341 international students
Library: 39,689 square metres of space and 2,962,000 volumes

The Ministry of Education has designated CCNU a national key university in eight fields, namely Basic Principles of Marxism, Chinese and Foreign Political Systems, Chinese Modern and Contemporary History, Education Theory, Literature and Art Studies, Pesticide Science, Scientific Socialism and International Communist Movement, and Theoretical Physics.

The central government sponsors two national key laboratories on campus, both known to scholars around the world: the Laboratory for Pesticide Science and Chemical Biology and the Laboratory for Quark and Lepton Physics.
Several nationality-based student unions exist. The biggest is the Association of Kazakh Students, which has nearly 100 members.

Food is straightforward. A campus ID card lets you eat in any of the seven canteens. CCNU has introduced electronic student IDs that double as debit cards, and every canteen has service desks and card machines during opening hours.

Oxford University, McGill University and Moscow State University are among its partners. In 2014 it also signed agreements with RMIT University, Macquarie University and the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research.

central-china-normal-university.h: Wuhan, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Day-to-day life depends heavily on the city that surrounds the campus, so the rest of this profile covers Wuhan: its layout, weather, economy, population and transport.

The city lies in east-central Hubei, at 29 degrees 58 minutes to 31 degrees 22 minutes north and 113 degrees 41 minutes to 115 degrees 05 minutes east. At this spot the Han River meets the Yangtze, at the east end of the Jianghan Plain on the Yangtze's middle reaches.

Wuhan is made up of three historic towns: Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, jointly called the "Three Towns of Wuhan". The name is a blend, taking "Wu" from Wuchang and "Han" from Hankou and Hanyang. The towns were merged in 1927 and the city of Wuhan was created. They face each other over the rivers and are linked by bridges, one of which, the "First Bridge", was among the first modern bridges built in China.

As for their positions, Wuchang is to the southeast of the Yangtze, which keeps it apart from both Hankou and Hanyang. Hankou is on the Yangtze's northern side, opposite Wuchang, and north of the Han, opposite Hanyang. Hanyang is on the Yangtze's western side, opposite Wuchang, and south of the Han, opposite Hankou.

The ground is simple, hilly in the south and low and flat through the centre, and the Yangtze and Han both wind through the city. The Sha River enters the Yangtze in Huangpi District. Wuhan covers 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 sq mi), largely alluvial plain dotted with hills, lakes and ponds. One quarter of the urban territory is water, the highest share among China's major cities. The city has close to 200 lakes. Among them East Lake, 33 km2 in area, and Tangxun Lake are the biggest lakes found wholly within a Chinese city.

Further well-known lakes are South Lake, next to the CCNU campus, and Sand Lake. The largest lake in Hubei by surface area, Liangzi Lake, lies in the southeast of Jiangxia District. Wuhan's highest point, at 872.5 metres, is the pair of peaks where Huangpi District meets Xiaogan City. Within the city limits there are also hills, such as Mount Luojia in Wuchang District and Mount Hong and Mount Yujia in Hongshan District.

Wuhan has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen Cfa), with heavy summer rainfall and four distinct seasons. The summers are famously muggy, and dewpoints often rise to 26 degrees Celsius (79 F) or more. Along with Chongqing and Nanjing, the city used to be called one of the Three Furnaces of the Yangtze because of its hot summers. Newer climate data suggest it no longer belongs among the very hottest cities, and the list of the New Four Furnaces now names Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang.

Spring and autumn are mild, and winter is cool and fairly dry, with snow now and then. Averaged over 24 hours, January temperatures are 4.1 degrees Celsius (39.4 F) and July temperatures are 29.3 degrees (84.7 F), and the yearly mean is 17.4 degrees (63.3 F). Frost-free periods run from 211 to 272 days. Annual rain is just under 1,320 mm (52 in), and most of it comes between April and July. Possible sunshine goes from 30 percent in January up to 53 percent in August, adding up to 1,783 hours of bright sun a year in the city proper. The record low is minus 18.1 degrees (minus 1 F) on 31 January 1977. The record high is 39.7 degrees (103 F), reached both on 27 July 2017 and on 18 August 2022, and an unofficial 41.3 degrees (106 F) was noted on 10 August 1934.

Wuhan was largely agricultural until the 21st century. From 2004 it became a key location for the Rise of Central China Plan, an effort to turn less-developed inland economies into advanced manufacturing hubs.

Local industry has rested on steel since 1890. In 2010 car manufacturing for the first time contributed more to output than the Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO). Dongfeng Honda, Citroen, SAIC-GM, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Dongfeng Renault make up the five car makers, and Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd. is headquartered in Wuhan.

Foreign investment had arrived from over 80 countries by 2016. There were 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises in the city, and together they had put in US$22.45 billion. About 50 French firms, Renault and PSA Group among them, are active here, representing over a third of France's investment in China and the highest level in any Chinese city.

The city is an important centre for the economy, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. Main industries are optoelectronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, bioengineering, new materials and environmental protection. Environmental sustainability features in the list of emerging industries, which includes energy-efficiency technology and renewable energy. In 2021 Wuhan was ranked among the top 100 financial centres in the world by the Global Financial Centres Index.
The main zones, in the order in which they were created, are as follows.

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone, a national-level zone established in 1993. It now measures roughly 10-25 square km and plans to grow to 25-50 square km. Industries it encourages include car production and assembly, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, chemicals, food and drink processing, heavy industry and telecommunications equipment.

Wuhan Export Processing Zone, set up in 2000 inside the Development Zone. It is planned to cover 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile), and the first 0.7 square kilometres (0.3 square miles) have been built.

Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone, also known as the East Lake High-Tech Development Zone (ELHTZ), is a national high-tech zone with optoelectronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing at its core, and software outsourcing and electronics are encouraged too. China's biggest production base for optoelectronic products is here, with companies like Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable, the country's largest fibre-optic cable maker, and Fiberhome Telecommunications. It is the centre of China's laser industry as well, hosting HGTECH and Chutian Laser.

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park is inside the East Lake zone, built jointly by that zone and Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. On paper it covers 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles) and offers 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet) of floor space. Distances: 8.5 km (5.28 mi) to National Highway 316, and 46.7 km (29.02 mi) to Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Wuhan Biolake was founded in 2008 within the Optics Valley of China, in the East Lake zone. Its 15 km2 (5.8 sq mi) hold six parks, devoted to bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical devices and medical health, with room for both research and residential life.

At the Seventh Census in 2020 Wuhan had 12,326,500 residents, making it the most populous city in Central China and one of the largest nationwide. That was 2.5411 million, or 25.97 percent, more than in 2010. The ten years from 2010 to 2020 were the fastest-growing in the census's history, at 2.34 percent a year on average, and for the first time the total passed 10 million. The OECD put the surrounding metropolitan area at 19 million as of 2010.

A study of urban development published in November 2019, using night-time lighting and land cover data as stand-ins, found that Wuhan's socioeconomic activity is highly concentrated compared with its physical urban spread.

A survey published in 2017 found that 79.2 percent of Wuhan's population were irreligious or practised worship of gods and ancestors, and 0.9 percent of those were Taoists. Of the other groups, 14.7 percent followed Buddhism, 2.9 percent Protestantism, 0.3 percent Catholicism and 1.6 percent Islam, while 1.6 percent followed other, unspecified religions.

The Wuhan Railway Hub, managed by China Railway Wuhan Group, is one of the four key railway hubs in China. Three major stations serve the city: Hankou, in Hankou; Wuchang, in Wuchang; and Wuhan station, in a newly developed district east of East Lake in Hongshan District. They are many miles apart, so make sure you know which one your train uses.

Originally Hankou Station was the end of the Jinghan line from Beijing, and Wuchang Station was the end of the Yuehan line to Guangzhou. After the First Yangtze Bridge was built and the two lines became the Jingguang railway, trains for every direction began to call at both stations. This is unlike New York or Moscow, where separate stations handle separate directions.

High-speed trains first reached Wuhan when the line from Hefei opened on 1 April 2009, with services to Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai. Several trains daily link Wuhan to Shanghai in under six hours. In early 2010 most of those expresses departed from Hankou.

Construction of the new Wuhan station started in 2006, and it has 11 platforms on the city's northeastern fringe. When it opened in December 2009, China was launching its second high-speed route, with regular Guangzhou-Wuhan services. Promoted as the fastest train anywhere, at up to 394 km/h (244.82 mph), it shortened the journey from ten and a half hours to just three, and it was later extended north to Beijing. As of 2011 the new station mostly handled Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, and ordinary trains for other destinations still ran from Hankou and Wuchang.

An intercity rail network for the Wuhan Metropolitan Area was under construction on several lines. Eventually it will link the three main terminals to stations in the outer districts and suburbs, and to the neighbouring cities of Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang and Xiaogan. Passenger service began on the first line, to Xianning, at the end of 2013. A line to Xiaogan followed on 1 December 2016, and it was extended to Shiyan on 29 November 2019 when the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway opened.

Wuhan North is the main freight station and classification yard for the metropolitan area, with 112 tracks and over 650 switches. You will find it in Hengdian Subdistrict, Huangpi District, 20 km (12 mi) from Wuhan Station and 23 km (14 mi) from Hankou Station.

Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd. owns and operates the metro. It now has 11 lines and 282 stations, with 435 km (270 mi) of track. Line 1 opened on 28 July 2004, making Wuhan the seventh city on the mainland with rapid transit after Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian. Line 2, opened on 28 December 2012, was the first underground metro line to cross the Yangtze.

Getting across the Yangtze and the Han had been the main traffic bottleneck, and the metro has eased it greatly. Annual ridership in 2019 was 1.22 billion, which makes it mainland China's sixth-busiest system. Growth is rapid, with several lines or sections being built, and the city government has pledged to open at least two every year. The whole network was shut from 23 January to 27 March 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Trams came to Wuhan's streets on 28 July 2017, when the first line, the Auto-city T1 Line, opened. Others were under construction or planned.
Auto-city trams: lines T1, T2, T6 and T8, serving the Wuhan Economic Development Area at the western edge of Hanyang. T1 was operating from 2017.
Optics Valley trams: two lines, T1 and T2, running south and east of Guanggu Circle (Guanggu Guangchang) in the southeast of Wuchang, which opened on 18 January 2018.
Old Hankou Streetcar: a loop line round Hankou city.
Buses, including trolleybuses, also carry people around town. The trolleybus system dates from 1958, and its first route, route 1, still runs today.

Wuhan is a major river and maritime transport hub in central China, and the Port of Wuhan provides services to the local population along with shipping. Ferries have a long history on the Yangtze. Modern ferry services were started by steamboat in 1900, and in 1937 a train ferry began carrying railway cars from Hankou to Wuchang. Numbered stops around the city let passengers get on and off, and there is a tourist ferry at night. The Wuhan Ferry Company runs the services at present. In 2010 it bought ten new ships to replace vessels that had been in use for 29 years.

The Central Conservatory of Music (CCOM; in Chinese 中央音乐学院, pinyin Zhōngyāng Yīnyuè Xuéyuàn) serves as China's national academy for music and stands in the capital. The Ministry of Education oversees it. Both Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction, which are national schemes to back top universities, count it among their members.

CCOM was founded in 1950 and teaches both Chinese and international students. Its teaching covers every stage, from primary school to postgraduate level. Undergraduate courses last four or five years and cover musicology, composition, conducting, voice and opera, piano, orchestral instruments and traditional Chinese instruments. For younger musicians there is a six-year middle school teaching music theory as well as piano, orchestral and traditional instruments, plus two primary schools, one for full-time and one for evening pupils. Adults can attend the evening university.

In recent years the conservatory has built close ties with overseas institutions and individual musicians. Visiting foreign performers and scholars are often invited to teach or give lectures, and CCOM in turn sends its staff and students abroad to study, lecture or perform. Performing groups draw on students and teachers: a national youth symphony orchestra, a traditional-instrument ensemble, a chorus of conservatory students, and orchestras and performing groups for the middle and primary school pupils.

The campus covers 53,000 square metres. Its music library holds more than 500,000 volumes and is the biggest music library in China. More than 500 pianos belong to the conservatory, together with a great many other instruments. Teaching spaces include a violin workshop and an electronic music studio fitted with advanced recording and video gear, and in November 2013 it acquired a German-built Oberlinger organ.
Its own journal, the Journal of the Central Conservatory of Music, is widely seen as the top academic periodical for musicology in China.
Programme structures can change, so confirm the exact list and entry requirements with the conservatory. The summary below follows the information available.
Bachelor's degrees are four years long in general, though five years are needed for four subjects:
Musicology, composition (with compositional theory), singing and conducting, each five years
Performance in keyboard instruments

Doctoral study takes three years and is available in musicology and in composition and compositional theory.

central-conservatory-of-music.h: Beijing: the city around the conservatory

blocks.x: Daily life depends on the city, so here is a guide to the capital: first its buildings, then the land and weather, and finally the air you will breathe.

Beijing's urban architecture falls into three broad groups. The first is the imperial heritage: the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which is the best-known emblem of the People's Republic, along with the Forbidden City and two sacred sites, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven. The second is a style from the 1950s to the 1970s, nicknamed Sino-Sov, which tends to be boxy and occasionally poorly built. The third is thoroughly modern, seen above all in the central business district (CBD) in the east, with the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and, for music lovers, the National Center for the Performing Arts.

A building boom in the early twenty-first century brought in international designers and a range of modern styles, most visibly in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s industrial design with neofuturistic elements. The tallest building in the city is China Zun, at 528 metres. Two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH's annual award for the world's best tall building since 2007, which goes to just one building each year: the Linked Hybrid took it in 2009, and the CCTV Headquarters took it in 2013.

A siheyuan is a courtyard house, with buildings arranged around an open yard. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are linked by alleys called hutongs, which generally run in straight east-west lines so that doors face north or south, in keeping with feng shui. Widths differ, and some are so narrow that only a few people can pass at once.

Once found all over Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are vanishing quickly, as entire blocks give way to high-rises. Hutong residents have a right to apartments in the new buildings at least as big as their old homes, but many say the community spirit and street life that the old lanes had cannot be rebuilt. These properties are often owned by the government.

The city lies where the North China Plain, a rough triangle of flat land opening south and east, reaches its northern limit. To the north, north-west and west, mountains protect the city and northern China's farming heartland from the desert steppe. The Jundu Mountains dominate the north-west of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou districts, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the northern part of the municipality on rugged ground, built to keep out raiders from the steppe. The highest point is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei, at 2,303 metres (7,556 feet).

The main rivers, among them the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, all belong to the Hai River system and flow south-east. The largest reservoir in the municipality is the Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. Two major waterworks end here. One is the Grand Canal, which runs to Hangzhou and is over 1,400 years old, built as a transport route. The other is the South-North Water Transfer Project, a recent scheme that brings in water from the Yangtze basin.

The urban area stands on a plain in the south-central part of the municipality, at 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet), and takes up a fairly small but growing share of the total area. Ring roads spread out in concentric circles; the Second Ring marks where the old city walls stood, while the Sixth connects satellite towns in the suburbs. Tian'anmen and its square lie at the centre, directly south of the Forbidden City, the emperors' former residence. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, the government compound. Chang'an Avenue, passing between Tian'anmen and the square, is the main east-west axis.

Because Beijing expanded steadily outward from the old centre to the suburbs, people often say it has spread like a pancake (tan da bing), and this pattern is often blamed for many of the city's urban problems.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Koppen Dwa), bordering on monsoonal cold semi-arid (Koppen BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid, while the huge Siberian high-pressure system brings short, cold, dry winters. In spring, sandstorms may blow in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe, along with fast warming and dry conditions. Autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest period in Beijing has been early August and the coldest early January. China's official seasonal calendar starts spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. In recent years temperatures have risen faster in March and September than in May and October, so autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

Over the 1991-2020 period, the yearly mean temperature in the city proper was between 12.9 and 13.3 degrees Celsius (55.2-55.9 F). Average daily minimums are 7.7 to 8.4 degrees (45.9-47.1 F), and average daily maximums 18.5 to 18.9 degrees (65.3-66.0 F). In low-lying suburbs the annual average is 11.5 to 13.0 degrees (52.7-55.4 F), with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 degrees (42.6-46.4 F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 degrees (64.8-65.7 F). Mountain areas average between 0 degrees (32 F) and 10 degrees (50 F), falling as altitude rises. January's daily mean is minus 2.7 degrees (27.1 F), and July's is 27.2 degrees (81.0 F).

Rainfall averages about 528.0 mm (20.79 inches) a year, or 584.2 mm (23.00 inches) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three-quarters of it falls from June to August. Monthly sunshine ranges from 42 percent of the possible total in July to 62 percent in January and February, adding up to 2,490.5 hours a year. Records since 1951 show a low of minus 27.4 degrees (minus 17.3 F) in February 1966 (the 22nd) and a high of 41.9 degrees (107.4 F) on 24 July 1999. For a student, that means proper winter clothing for the dry cold, light clothes and an umbrella in summer, and a mask or scarf for dusty spring days.

central-conservatory-of-music.h: A history of problems and a long effort to fix them

blocks.x: Beijing has long had environmental problems. Between 2000 and 2009 its built-up area quadrupled, which greatly raised emissions and also changed local weather conditions. The ground-level reflectivity of the surface, wind speed and humidity fell, while ground temperature, air temperature near the surface, vertical dilution of the air and ozone levels all rose. Urban growth and the burning of fossil fuels often combine to cause serious pollution, harming many residents' health.

In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and much of northern China and affected 600 million people in total. Following that shock, air pollution turned into a major economic and social worry. Beijing announced steps to cut it, including lowering the coal share of its energy from 24 percent in 2012 to 10 percent in 2017, while the national government had heavily polluting vehicles removed from 2015 to 2017 and stepped up the switch to clean energy.

A joint study by American and Chinese scientists in 2006 found that much of the city's pollution blows in from nearby cities and provinces. On average, 35 to 60 percent of the ozone comes from outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin strongly affect the capital's air, partly because of the south and south-east winds in summer and the mountains that hem in the city on the north and north-west.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent on cleaning the air. During the Games the city stopped work at all construction sites, closed many Beijing factories for good, temporarily closed industry in neighbouring regions and shut some filling stations. It also put together 3,800 natural-gas buses, one of the world's largest such fleets, and became the first Chinese city to require the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Burning coal produces about 40 percent of Beijing's PM2.5 and also produces most of the nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been changing its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012 and aims to limit annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73 percent for heating and power and the rest for industry. Much of the city's pollution is emitted by neighbouring regions. Tianjin's coal use was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, and Hebei burned over 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, only 30 percent of it for power, with a large part going to steel and cement. Power stations in Shandong and in the coal-mining areas of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (where coal use has tripled since 2000) contribute too; Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia are the four biggest coal-consuming provinces, in that order.

Beijing used to have four big coal-fired power plants that produced electricity and winter heating. The first (Gaojing) closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, with the last (Huaneng) scheduled for 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was a 13-million-ton cut in coal use, and a cap of 15 million tons for 2015.

The authorities have at times used cloud seeding to encourage rain and clear the air before major events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. More recently they have preferred temporary factory closures and stricter limits on cars, which produced what people called APEC blue and parade blue, brief periods of clean air during the 2014 APEC meeting in China and before the 2015 Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved sharply during these events, then returned to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The city's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing much of its industry and commerce, and a second, red alert followed later that month. Under an announcement by the city's environmental protection bureau in November 2016, from 2017 older high-polluting cars could not be driven when red smog alerts were issued in the city or nearby regions.

Pollutant levels have measurably dropped since 2014, when a war on pollution was declared. Fine particulates dropped by 35 percent in 2017 and by more by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal and polluting factories were cleaned up. The yearly average PM2.5 level was down to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. Heavy-pollution days numbered just two in 2024, the lowest ever recorded and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 in 2013.

Because air quality is a concern, there are several sources of readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau publishes daily numbers from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the US Embassy has reported hourly PM2.5 and ozone readings. The two sets differ because they measure different pollutants against different standards, and the bureau's figures and health assessments have often been lower than the embassy's. Polluted air has a direct effect on illness rates for heart and breathing problems in the city, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart trouble, hospital visits and even death, so sensitive people should watch the daily readings.

Dust from the eroding deserts of northern and north-western China brings seasonal dust storms to the city. A local office for weather modification sometimes triggers artificial rain to counter them. January to April 2006 alone saw at least eight storms, and one storm in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing before it carried on towards Japan and Korea.

A conservatory student's days will revolve around practice rooms, ensembles and performances, but your health and comfort depend on the city as well. Plan for a cold, dry winter, a hot, humid summer and a dusty spring, and look at current air-quality figures for the season you arrive. The air numbers above come from various years, so use them to understand the trend rather than today's exact levels. For admissions, current degree options and facilities, the conservatory's own website is the authority.
If you plan to apply, ask the admissions office which audition or entrance requirements apply to your chosen specialism, since these differ between composition, performance and musicology.
Central Conservatory of Music lists 66 programs for international students on this site: 5 bachelor, 23 master's, 19 doctoral, 19 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 66 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,200 to CNY 38,000 (median CNY 38,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 43,000 to CNY 43,000 (median CNY 43,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 48,000 to CNY 48,000 (median CNY 48,000), according to the university's published fee table.

66 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

central-conservatory-of-music.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Central Conservatory of Music may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Central Conservatory of Music by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

central-south-university.h: A snapshot of Central South University

blocks.x: Central South University, usually shortened to CSU (中南大学) is a state-run university based in Changsha, capital of Hunan Province. The central Ministry of Education finances and supervises it, and it belongs to the national Project 985, Project 211 and Double First-Class Construction programmes, which is the shorthand Chinese applicants and employers use for the country's most heavily supported universities.

The university took its present form on 29 April 2000, when three separate institutions were merged into one. Those were Central South University of Technology, Changsha Railway University and Hunan Medical University. That origin explains a great deal about the place today, because medicine, rail and civil engineering, and mining and metallurgy all remain central to its identity.

For a sense of international standing, US News & World Report placed CSU at #131 in its global university list, and the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) put it at #83. Rankings move every year and differ by method, so treat these as a rough guide and check the latest tables before you decide.

Teaching spans twelve academic categories, namely the arts, agriculture, history, education, philosophy, management, economics, law, literature, medicine, science and engineering. The main campus is in Changsha's Yuelu District, and further campuses are spread across the city.

The university reports 33 secondary schools or colleges and 105 undergraduate programmes, of which 90 currently recruit new students. It also counts 72 national first-class undergraduate programme construction sites. For enrolment, the headline figure is 63,919 full-time students: 35,957 undergraduates, 16,587 on master's courses, 9,228 working toward doctorates and 1,999 international students. In-service faculty and staff come to 5,926, not including hospital employees.

Other descriptions of CSU use slightly different totals for colleges and programmes (for example 31 colleges plus a graduate school, or 94 or 83 undergraduate programmes). The differences come from the year of the count and from what is included, so the university's own website has the current numbers.

CSU was created with State Council approval on 29 April 2000. Each of the three founding institutions had a distinct past, and reading about them helps you understand why the university's strengths are so varied.

central-south-university.h: The medical branch and the Xiangya name

blocks.x: Hunan Medical University had been run by the Ministry of Health. Its story starts in 1914, when Xiangya Medical College opened. It grew out of cooperation between the Yale-China Association and the Hunan Yuqun Society, and Yan Fuqing was one of its founders, along with Dr. Edward Hicks Hume. The name "Xiangya" is a blend: "Xiang" is the traditional short name for Hunan, and "ya" echoes the pronunciation of Yale. Even now, the medical school and its hospitals still carry the Xiangya brand.

Changsha Railway University came from the Ministry of Railways system. It was reorganised in 1953 as a civil engineering and architecture college for the Central South region, and the separate university was formally set up in 1960 on the foundation of that earlier college's teaching and research units.

Central South University of Technology had been under the Ministry of Education. It started in 1952, when the nationwide restructuring of higher education began, under the name of the Mining and Metallurgy Institute of Central South China. Its founding departments came from six universities, namely Beijing Institute of Technology, Nanchang University, Hunan University, Guangxi University, Sun Yat-sen University and Wuhan University.
CSU is a national key institution administered directly by the Ministry of Education. Its campuses straddle the Xiang River, below Yuelu Hill and near Hunan University, and total 392.4 hectares.

One count credits it with 83 bachelor's degrees, plus 282 at master's level and 142 at doctoral level. They are delivered by a graduate school and 31 colleges and institutes. Here is the list of academic units, which shows how wide the range is.

In short, engineering and the materials-related sciences are the traditional core, while a full medical complex and a growing set of humanities and social science schools sit alongside them.

Nationally designated strengths include 6 key first-level disciplines, 12 key second-level disciplines and 59 key clinical specialties. It runs 94 undergraduate programmes, 58 master's programmes at first-level discipline level, 33 doctoral programmes at first-level discipline level and 31 postdoctoral research stations.

Seven fields sit in the global top 1 percent of the Essential Science Indicators (ESI) database: neuroscience and behavioral science, biology and biochemistry, pharmacology and toxicology, chemistry, clinical medicine, engineering and materials science. Clinical teaching takes place in 6 affiliated hospitals. Three are the well-known Xiangya hospitals; the rest are Haikou Hospital, Xiangya Stomatology Hospital and the hospital affiliated with the Xiangya School of Medicine.

central-south-university.h: Where you will live and study: the six campuses

blocks.x: CSU is a multi-campus university, and which campus you attend depends on your level and subject. In January 2025 the campuses were renamed, so you may still see old names in older articles and on maps. The main campus is now Yuelushan Campus. The other five are Lunan (once the South Campus), Xiaoxiang (once the New Campus), Xinglin (once the Xiangya New Campus), Kaifu (once the Xiangya Old Campus) and Tianxin (once the Railway Campus).
The roles described for each campus below follow the older arrangement. Allocation of students can change, so confirm with the university before you book accommodation.
Here are the dormitories and classrooms for middle-year undergraduates and postgraduates from most engineering schools, plus offices and two state key laboratories.
Here you find the dormitories for all first-year students and for postgraduates in all the humanities schools, plus office buildings.
This site has teaching buildings used by all first-year students and by humanities and science postgraduates, together with offices and a library.

The old Xiangya site (Kaifu) provides housing and teaching space for medical postgraduates and hosts Xiangya Hospital as well as the national State Key Laboratory of Medical Genetics. The new Xiangya site (Xinglin) is for medical undergraduates and includes the Third Xiangya Hospital and the medical library.

The railway site serves middle-year undergraduates and postgraduates studying architecture, software engineering, traffic engineering and civil engineering, with housing, classrooms, offices and a library.
The School of Life Sciences, previously named the School of Biological Sciences, is a secondary school set up in May 2003.
Graduates and scholars linked with CSU have gone into science, public life and industry. The names below are listed for context only.
Tang Feifan, a medical microbiologist famous for growing the Chlamydia trachomatis agent inside egg yolk sacs, and among the first academicians of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Zhang Xiaoqian, a gastroenterologist seen as the father of the discipline in China. He led Hsiang-Ya Medical College as President, served as Vice President at Peking Union Medical College, and was among the founders of both the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Academia Sinica.
Huang Boyun, a powder metallurgist, academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and former President of Central South University.
Jin Zhanpeng, a materials scientist and academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Wang Dianzuo, a mineral engineering scientist who is an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the Chinese Academy of Engineering and the US National Academy of Engineering, and used to head Central South University of Technology, which is now part of CSU.
Chen Zhiwu, professor of finance at the Yale School of Management and a widely read public commentator in China.
Guo Shengkun, a Politburo member of the Chinese Communist Party who heads its Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission.
Lu Zhangong, a vice chairman of the national political advisory body (the CPPCC), earlier the Party chief in Fujian and then Henan.
Zhao Lijian, who has served as a Foreign Ministry spokesperson and Deputy Director of the ministry's Information Department.
Li Zexiang, who started DJI and runs it as CEO.
Wang Chuanfu, who started BYD and is its CEO.
Liang Wengen, who started Sany Group and chairs it.

CSU says it has long-term cooperation with more than 200 colleges, universities and research institutions in 20 countries and regions. Students from over 80 countries and regions currently study on its campuses, so you will not be the only international face. Partners vary from one department to another, and some links may be limited to particular schools, so ask the relevant college which ones apply to you.
