Daily life as a student depends heavily on the city outside the gates: the climate, the transport and the leisure options. Changsha is the home of CSU, so the sections below describe the city.

Changsha lies in the northeast of Hunan Province, along the lower Xiang River, in the west of the Changliu Basin. Its coordinates run from 111°53' to 114°15' east and from 27°51' to 28°41' north. Neighbouring areas are Yichun and Pingxiang in Jiangxi Province to the east, Zhuzhou and Xiangtan to the south, Loudi and Yiyang to the west, and Yueyang and Yiyang to the north.

From east to west the city stretches about 230 kilometres, and from north to south about 88 kilometres. The whole municipality spans 11,819 square kilometres, equal to 4,563 square miles. Of that, the urban area is 2,150.9 square kilometres (830.5 square miles) and the continuously built-up area is 374.64 square kilometres (144.65 square miles). Elevation ranges from 1,607.9 metres at Mount Qixing (七星岭) in Daweishan Town, which is 5,275 feet, down to 23.5 metres, or 77 feet, at Zhanhu (湛湖) in Qiaokou Town.

central-south-university.h: The Xiang River and the shape of the city

blocks.x: The Xiang is the principal river, flowing north for 74 km (46 mi) through the city's territory. Fifteen tributaries join it, and the four largest are the Liuyang, Laodao, Jinjiang and Wei. The river splits Changsha in two: the eastern side is mainly commercial, while the west bank is mostly cultural and educational, which is where CSU and its neighbour Hunan University are found. On 10 October 2001 the city government moved from Fanzheng Street to Guanshaling, and since then both banks have developed in a more balanced way.

Nearly all of Changsha's rivers are part of the Xiang system. Besides the Xiang itself and the tributaries named above (the Minjiang and Qinshui rivers are also among the main ones), 302 streams are longer than five kilometres, 289 of them in the Xiang basin. Graded by order, they comprise 24 primary tributaries, 128 secondary, 118 third-order and 32 smaller ones, while 13 belong to the Zijiang system. The network is dense and complete, the volume of water is large, the hydropower potential is rich, the rivers do not freeze in winter and they carry little sediment.

The geology is just as varied. Rock layers from every geological period are exposed, granite is widespread and the structure is complicated. The oldest layer formed about a billion years ago. Roughly 600 million years ago the area lay beneath a shallow sea that slowly drew back from the east and west. Much of what is now Changsha, Liuyang and Wangcheng emerged from it and formed the northwestern rim of the ancient Jiangnan landmass. About 140 million years ago the marine phase ended and the area became land, and crustal movement formed the long, mountain-ringed Chang (Sha) Ping (Jiang) Basin. In the most recent geological era the whole Changping Basin rose out of the water. Around 3.5 million years ago, during the third ice age, Liuyang preserved traces of glacial landforms.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Averages run at 17.8 °C over the year, which is 64.0 °F, with January at 5.3 °C (41.5 °F) and July at 29.4 °C (84.9 °F). Although the city lies at 28°N, its January temperatures match those of London or Paris, which are about 20° further from the equator. Yearly rainfall totals 1,499 millimetres, or 59.0 inches, and frost-free days number 275.

Sunshine is limited. Possible sunshine goes from 20% in January up to 53% in July, which adds up to 1,532.8 hours of bright sun annually. The seasons are clear. Summers are long, very hot and rainy. Autumn is comfortable and the driest time of year. Winter is chilly and overcast, with light rain more likely than downpours, and occasional cold snaps that drop below freezing. Spring is notably wet and humid, with sun for less than 30% of the time.

Records from the Wangchengpo Weather Observing Station, kept since 1951, show a low of −11.3 °C (11.7 °F) on 9 February 1972. The high is 40.6 °C (105.1 °F), reached on 13 August 1953 and again on 2 August 2003. An unofficial figure of 43.0 °C, or 109.4 °F, dates from 10 August 1934. In practical terms, pack for damp, cool winters without central heating in many buildings, and for strong summer heat.

Changsha is one of the 15 cities in China described as the most developed and economically advanced. In 2024, GDP per person passed CN¥144,525, which equals US$20,294 in nominal terms or US$42,136 adjusted for purchasing power, and falls in the World Bank's high-income band. Its Human Development Index stood at 0.817, rated very high, in 2016. The city is central to South Central China, to the Yangtze River Economic Belt and to the Belt and Road Initiative. Researchers at the Globalization and World Cities Research Network classify it as a Beta- (second-tier global) city. It is also described as a "new first-tier" city within China, and as a pilot zone for Sino-African trade.

Changsha has been nicknamed the world's capital of construction machinery. It puts construction machinery and new materials at the centre of its industrial chain, backed up by biomedicine, home appliances, electronic information and automobiles.

Expansion accelerated during the 1990s, and in the 2000s the city grew faster than any other major Chinese city. The Xiangjiang New Area, set up in 2015, was the first state-level new area anywhere in Central China. Media and publishing are also prominent, and Changsha was the first Chinese city named a UNESCO City of Media Arts. Hunan Broadcasting System (HBS), the country's most influential provincial TV station, is based here.

A few milestones show the scale. The financial portal Yicai.com issued its first city ranking in 2013, and Changsha was one of 15 cities it labelled new first-tier. In 2017 Changsha became the 13th Chinese city to reach a GDP of one trillion yuan, roughly 154 billion US dollars. By 2020, over 164 Global 500 firms had set up branches in the city, and in 2022 its commercial worth ranked 10th nationwide.

GDP in 2021 topped RMB 1.327 trillion, or US$208 billion nominal and US$318 billion at purchasing power parity. Only Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Wuhan were richer in South Central China, and within Central China only Wuhan was ahead. The nominal figure was bigger than the economies of Ukraine (US$200 billion) and Hungary (US$182 billion), which rank 22nd and 23rd in Europe. Changsha has also pioneered a night-time economy: a 2021-2022 impact report on the subject placed it second nationally, behind only Chongqing.

The Hurun Global Rich List put Changsha among the world's top 35 cities in 2022. By 2024 it held first place in Central China and ninth in Greater China for billionaire residents, trailing Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Hangzhou, Taipei, Guangzhou and Ningbo, in that order. Looking ahead, Oxford Economics expects its nominal GDP to rank among the world's top 50 cities by 2035, with GDP per head reaching US$41,000 by 2030.

The Changsha Economic and Technological Development Zone (ETZ) was founded in 1992 and sits in Xingsha, in eastern Changsha. Both its planned and its present size are 38.6 square kilometres, about 14.9 square miles. National Highways 319 and 107 run nearby, as does the Beijing–Hong Kong and Macau Expressway (G4). It is near the downtown area and the railway station, and only 8 km (5.0 mi) from the airport. Its main sectors are high technology, biotechnology and new materials.

The Liuyang ETZ, in Dongyang Town, opened on 10 January 1998 as a national base for the biological industry. Its main sectors are health food, information technology and biopharmaceuticals. As of 2015 more than 700 enterprises were registered there, with output worth 85.6 billion yuan (about US$13.7 billion) and income of 100.2 billion yuan (about US$16.1 billion), across 16.5 square kilometres of built-up land (6.4 square miles).

central-south-university.h: Things to see and do around Changsha

blocks.x: Tourism is a major industry, and Changsha has repeatedly been ranked as a top tourist city in China. Notable sights include the Yuelu Academy and, beside Meixi Lake, the Meixihu International Culture and Arts Centre in Changsha, a cultural complex by the British practice Zaha Hadid Architects. There are also Kaifu Temple, Changsha IFS Tower, Meixi Lake Park, Window of the World, Changsha Ice World and the statue of the young Mao Zedong on Orange Isle.

The mountain takes its name from the "Nanyue Ji", a text from the Liu Song period of the Southern and Northern dynasties, which says that the area around Nanyue measures eight hundred miles, with Huiyan as its head and Yuelu as its foot. It stands on the west bank of the Xiang River in Yuelu District. Orange Island lies in the middle of the river, looking toward Yuelu on the west and the old city on the east. The scenic area has 977 plant species in 559 genera and 174 families, mostly subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest and warm coniferous forest, with large areas of native secondary forest and many precious endangered and ancient trees.

Orange Island sits in the centre of the Xiang in Yuelu District. The original sandbar covered about 17 hectares, and the whole developed scenic area now covers 91.64 hectares. Of the alluvial sandbars on the lower Xiang, it is the biggest, and it is called "China's First Continent". Attractions include the Mao Zedong youth sculpture and Wen Tiantai. Records say the island formed in 305, the second year of Yongxing under Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, from the build-up of sand and gravel left by rapids.

Huaminglou, in southeastern Ningxiang City, is a well-known visitor site and a nationally protected cultural relic. It was the family home of Liu Shaoqi, a revolutionary leader who later became president of China.

You will find the museum at No. 50 Dongfeng Road in Kaifu District. It belongs to the first group of national first-level museums, is one of eight national key museums co-built by national and local government, and is Hunan's biggest general museum of history and art. The Hunan Provincial Museum first opened in 1897, in the 23rd year of the Guangxu reign, and the current building is its newer home.

The 2020 census counted 10,047,914 residents in Changsha, of whom 7,355,198 lived in the built-up (metropolitan) area, made up of the 6 urban districts plus largely connected Changsha County. Most people are Han Chinese. The three largest minority groups are the Hui, Tujia and Miao. The 2000 census found 48,564 minority residents, 0.7% of the population, and twenty minority groups each have fewer than 1,000 members in the city.

After China Central Television (CCTV), Hunan Broadcasting System is the biggest broadcaster in China. It has its headquarters in Changsha and makes some of the country's most popular programmes, including Super Girl. These shows brought a new entertainment industry to the city, with singing bars, dance clubs, theatre shows and related trades such as hair salons, fashion shops and late-night stalls selling hot, spicy snacks, especially in summer. Changsha has become an entertainment hub and has grown more international, attracting a growing number of foreign residents.

Helong Stadium holds 55,000 and is among the biggest multi-purpose stadiums in China; it takes its name from the military commander He Long. Local football side Hunan Billows F.C., currently in China League Two, play there. The club uses the smaller Hunan Provincial People's Stadium, which seats 6,000, for some matches.

Local technology firms and the Hunan Embroidery Research Institute have opened an AI design lab devoted to Xiang embroidery. Its algorithms study historical patterns and suggest new designs, supporting craftspeople and modernising an intangible cultural tradition.

central-south-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Central South University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.

Travel to Changsha, register at Central South University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

central-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: About Central University of Finance and Economics

blocks.x: The Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) is a public finance and economics university located in Beijing, China. Affiliated with the Ministry of Education of China, the university is co-sponsored by the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Beijing Municipal People's Government. The university is part of the Double First-Class Construction and Project 211.

CUFE is the first economics and management university which was founded by the China Central Government. The university emphasizes the disciplines of economics, management, law, literature, philosophy, science, engineering, pedagogy and art.

In 1949, shortly after the founding of the People's Republic of China, CUFE (then called Central School of Taxation), the first university of finance and economics in the Republic, was created by the China Central Government.
In 1952, the faculties and staffs of economics of Peking University, Tsinghua University, Yenching University, and Fu Jen Catholic University are merged into CUFE.

Formerly known as Central School of Taxation, it went through several stages of development, from Central Institute of Finance, Central Institute of Finance and Economics, to Central Institute of Finance and Banking. In 1996, the institute was officially renamed as Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) under the direct leadership of the Ministry of Education. CUFE upholds "loyalty, unity, truth and innovation" as its motto, adhering to the philosophy of "pursuing truth and excellence". With over 125,000 graduates, CUFE is known as "the Cradle of Giants in the Field of Finance and Management".
In 1999, the Communist Party former general secretary, Jiang Zemin, gave CUFE his autograph to celebrate the 50th birthday of the university.

World-class Discipline honored by the Ministry of Education: Applied Economics, which includes National Economics, Regional Economics, Public Finance, Finance, Industrial Economics, International Trade, Labor Economics, Statistics, Quantitative Economics, Defense Economics, Governmental Economics and Management, Investment, Media Economics, Insurance, Actuarial Science, Security Investment, International Finance, Financial Engineering, Taxation.

National Key Disciplines honored by the Ministry of Education: Applied Economics, National Economics, Regional Economics, Public Finance, Finance, Industrial Economics, International Trade, Labor Economics, Statistics, Quantitative Economics, Defense Economics, Accounting.

According to 2018 China College Rankings By Salary, the average salaries of CUFE graduates is ranked No.9 in China. In the Assessments of Ministry of Education, the Applied Economics of CUFE is ranked as No. 1 in China, tired with the Peking University and the Renmin University of China.

As of 2022, Central University of Finance and Economics ranked the best in Beijing and 2nd nationwide among universities specialized in finance, business, and economics in the recognized Best Chinese Universities Ranking. CUFE ranks in the global top # 33 in "Finance", top # 101 in "Economics", top # 301 in "Business Administration", top # 301 in "Political Science", and top # 301 in "Management" by the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) by Subjects. As of 2024, the U.S. News & World Report Best Global University Ranking ranked CUFE at #108 globally and 24th in Asia in "Economics and Business" subject.
As of 2017, Central University of Finance and Economics has cooperation with 126 universities, governments, international organizations and companies abroad.
Started in 2006, asked to help the China's Central Government, CUFE has trained thousands of senior administration officials from 91 developing countries.

CUFE has cooperation with many universities all over the world, such as University of Waterloo, University of Birmingham, Tilburg University, Stevens Institute of Technology, Victoria University, Academy of Finance of the Russian Federation, St. Petersburg State Economic University, Ukraine Kyiv National University of Economics, Chung-Ang University, Tunghai University, Ming Chuan University, Kyungnam University, Soochow University, University of Pernambuco.

CUFE has cooperation with international organizations as well, such as the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA), the Chartered Insurance Institute, the Australian and New Zealand Institute of Insurance and Finance.
CUFE also has many cooperations with some international companies, such as Zurich Financial Services Group, AXA, National Union Life and Limb Insurance Company.
In 2013, CUFE has launched a Confucius Institute in the University of Pernambuco, Brazil.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Beijing, where Central University of Finance and Economics is located.

Three styles of architecture are predominant in urban Beijing. First, there is the traditional architecture of imperial China, perhaps best exemplified by the massive Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which remains the People's Republic of China's trademark edifice, the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven. Next, there is what is sometimes referred to as the "Sino-Sov" style, with structures tending to be boxy and sometimes poorly constructed, which were built between the 1950s and the 1970s. Finally, there are much more modern architectural forms, most noticeably in the area of the Beijing CBD in east Beijing such as the new CCTV Headquarters, in addition to buildings in other locations around the city such as the Beijing National Stadium and National Center for the Performing Arts.

In the early 21st century, Beijing has witnessed tremendous growth of new building constructions, exhibiting various modern styles from international designers, most pronounced in the CBD region. A mixture of both 1950s design and neofuturistic style of architecture can be seen at the 798 Art Zone, which mixes the old with the new. Beijing's tallest building is the 528-meter China Zun. Since 2007, buildings in Beijing have received the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building twice, for the Linked Hybrid building in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. The CTBUH Skyscraper award for best tall overall building is given to only one building around the world every year.

Siheyuans in Beijing are courtyards surrounding by buildings. Among the more grand examples are the Prince Gong Mansion and Residence of Soong Ching-ling. These courtyards are usually connected by alleys called hutongs. The hutongs are generally straight and run east to west so that doorways face north and south for good Feng Shui. They vary in width; some are so narrow only a few pedestrians can pass through at a time. Once ubiquitous in Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are rapidly disappearing, as entire city blocks of hutongs are replaced by high-rise buildings. Residents of the hutongs are entitled to live in the new buildings in apartments of at least the same size as their former residences. Many complain, however, that the traditional sense of community and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced, and these properties are often government owned.

Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The northwestern part of the municipality, especially Yanqing District and Huairou District, are dominated by the Jundu Mountains, while the western part is framed by Xishan or the Western Hills. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of Beijing Municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills and on the border with Hebei, is the municipality's highest point, with an altitude of 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Major rivers flowing through the municipality, including the Chaobai, Yongding, Juma, are all tributaries in the Hai River system, and flow in a southeasterly direction. The Miyun Reservoir, on the upper reaches of the Chaobai River, is the largest reservoir within the municipality. Beijing is also the northern terminus of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, which was built over 1,400 years ago as a transportation route, and the South–North Water Transfer Project, constructed in the past decade to bring water from the Yangtze River basin.

The urban area of Beijing, on the plains in the south-central of the municipality with elevation of 40 to 60 metres (130–200 feet), occupies a relatively small but expanding portion of the municipality's area. The city spreads out in concentric ring roads. The Second Ring Road traces the old city walls and the Sixth Ring Road connects satellite towns in the surrounding suburbs. Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square are at the center of Beijing, directly to the south of the Forbidden City, the former residence of the emperors of China. To the west of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, the residence of China's current leaders. Chang'an Avenue, which cuts between Tiananmen and the Square, forms the city's main east–west axis.

Beijing's pattern of development from the old inner city to its urban fringe are frequently described as "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing). This pattern of development is frequently cited as a reason for Beijing's urban problems.

Beijing has a humid continental climate (Köppen: Dwa), bordering on a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (Köppen: BSk). The city is characterized by hot, humid summers due to the East Asian monsoon as well as brief but cold, dry winters that reflect the influence of the vast Siberian anticyclone. Spring can bear witness to sandstorms blowing in from the Gobi Desert across the Mongolian steppe, accompanied by rapidly warming, but generally dry, conditions. Autumn, similar to spring, is a season of transition and minimal precipitation. From 2001 to 2026, the hottest period in Beijing is early August, and the coldest period is early January. According to China's seasonal division standard, Beijing enters spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September, and winter on 31 October. Due to the faster warming in March and September and the slower warming in May and October in recent years, Beijing is generally shorter in autumn than in spring. The average annual temperature (From 1991 to 2020) in the urban area of Beijing is 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) to 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), of which the average daily minimum temperature is 7.7 °C (45.9 °F) to 8.4 °C (47.1 °F), and the average daily maximum temperature is 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) to 18.9 °C (66.0 °F). The average annual temperature in the low-altitude part of the suburbs of Beijing is 11.5 °C (52.7 °F) to 13.0 °C (55.4 °F), of which the average daily minimum temperature is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) to 8.0 °C (46.4 °F), and the average daily maximum temperature is 18.2 °C (64.8 °F) to 18.7 °C (65.7 °F). The average annual temperature in mountainous areas is between 0 °C (32 °F) and 10 °C (50 °F), decreasing as the altitude increases. The monthly daily average temperature in January is −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), while in July it is 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Precipitation averages around 528.0 mm (20.79 in) annually (Haidian and Chaoyang has an average annual precipitation of 584.2 mm (23.00 in)), with close to three-quarters of that total falling from June to August. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 42% in July to 62% in January and February, the city receives 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966 to 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.

Beijing had a long history of environmental problems. Between 2000 and 2009 Beijing's urban extent quadrupled, which not only strongly increased the extent of anthropogenic emissions, but also changed the meteorological situation fundamentally, even if emissions of human society are not included. For example, surface albedo, wind speed and humidity near the surface were decreased, whereas ground and near-surface air temperatures, vertical air dilution and ozone levels were increased. Because of the combined factors of urbanization and pollution caused by burning of fossil fuel, Beijing is often affected by serious environmental problems, which lead to health issues of many inhabitants. In 2013 heavy smog struck Beijing and most parts of northern China, impacting a total of 600 million people. After this "pollution shock" air pollution became an important economic and social concern in China. After that the government of Beijing announced measures to reduce air pollution, for example by lowering the share of coal from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, while the national government ordered heavily polluting vehicles to be removed from 2015 to 2017 and increased its efforts to transition the energy system to clean sources.

Joint research between American and Chinese researchers in 2006 concluded that much of the city's pollution comes from surrounding cities and provinces. On average 35–60% of the ozone can be traced to sources outside the city. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality have a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", partly due to the prevailing south/southeasterly flow during the summer and the mountains to the north and northwest.

In preparation for the 2008 Summer Olympics and to fulfill promises to clean up the city's air, nearly US$17 billion was spent. Beijing implemented a number of air improvement schemes for the duration of the Games, including halting work at all construction sites, closing many factories in Beijing permanently, temporarily shutting industry in neighboring regions, closing some gas stations, and cutting motor traffic by half by limiting drivers to odd or even days (based on their license plate numbers), reducing bus and subway fares, opening new subway lines, and banning high-emission vehicles. The city further assembled 3,800 natural gas-powered buses, one of the largest fleets in the world. Beijing became the first city in China to require the Chinese equivalent to the Euro 4 emission standard.

Coal burning accounts for about 40% of the PM 2.5 in Beijing and is also the chief source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012, the city has been converting coal-fired power stations to burn natural gas and aims to cap annual coal consumption at 20 million tons. In 2011, the city burned 26.3 million tons of coal, 73% of which for heating and power generation and the remainder for industry. Much of the city's air pollutants are emitted by neighboring regions. Coal consumption in neighboring Tianjin is expected to increase from 48 to 63 million tons from 2011 to 2015. Hebei Province burned over 300 million tons of coal in 2011, more than all of Germany, of which only 30% were used for power generation and a considerable portion for steel and cement making. Power plants in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal consumption has tripled since 2000, and Shandong also contribute to air pollution in Beijing. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, respectively rank from first to fourth, among Chinese provinces by coal consumption. There were four major coal-fired power plants in the city to provide electricity as well as heating during the winter. The first one (Gaojing Thermal Power Plant) was shut down in 2014. Another two were shut in March 2015. The last one (Huaneng Thermal Power Plant) would be shut in 2016. Between 2013 and 2017, the city planned to reduce 13 million tons of coal consumption and cap coal consumption to 15 million tons in 2015.

The government sometimes uses cloud-seeding measures to increase the likelihood of rain showers in the region to clear the air prior to large events, such as prior to the 60th anniversary parade in 2009 as well as to combat drought conditions in the area. More recently, however, the government has increased its usage of such measures as closing factories temporarily and implementing greater restrictions for cars on the road, as in the case of "APEC blue" and "parade blue", short periods during and immediately preceding the APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, respectively. During and prior to these events, Beijing's air quality improved dramatically, only to fall back to unhealthy levels shortly after.

On 8 and 9 December 2015 Beijing had its first smog alert which shut down a majority of the industry and other commercial businesses in the city. Later in the month another smog "red alert" was issued.

According to Beijing's environmental protection bureau's announcement in November 2016, starting from 2017 highly polluting old cars will be banned from being driven whenever Smog "red alerts" are issued in the city or neighboring regions.

In recent years, there has been measurable reductions in pollutants after the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014, with Beijing seeing a 35% reduction in fine particulates in 2017 and further reduction by 2020. The primary factors behind this reduction were replacing coal power with natural gas and cleaning up polluting industrial facilities in the Beijing area.

Beijing's annual average concentration of major airborne fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, declined to 30 micrograms per cubic meter in 2022, the best air quality for the city since 2013. In 2024, Beijing experienced only two days of heavy pollution, the lowest number on record, which had decreased by 96.6 percent from 58 days in 2013.

Due to Beijing's high level of air pollution, there are various readings by different sources on the subject. Daily pollution readings at 27 monitoring stations around the city are reported on the website of the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB). The American Embassy of Beijing also reports hourly fine particulate (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. Since the BJEPB and US Embassy measure different pollutants according to different criteria, the pollution levels and the impact to human health reported by the BJEPB are often lower than that reported by the US Embassy.

The smog is causing harm and danger to the population. The air pollution does directly result in significant impact on the morbidity rate of cardiovascular disease and respiratory disease in Beijing. Exposure to large concentrations of polluted air can cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems, emergency room visits, and even death.

Dust from the erosion of deserts in northern and northwestern China results in seasonal dust storms that plague the city; the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes artificially induces rainfall to fight such storms and mitigate their effects. In the first four months of 2006 alone, there were no fewer than eight such storms. In April 2002, one dust storm alone dumped nearly 50,000 tons of dust onto the city before moving on to Japan and Korea.

Chang'an University (长安大学 in Chinese; often abbreviated CHD) is a public university in Xi'an, the capital of Shaanxi province in north-west China. It reports to the Ministry of Education, and its funding is shared with the Shaanxi provincial government and with three national ministries: Transport, Natural Resources, and Housing and Urban-Rural Development. It belongs to the national Double First-Class Construction programme and was formerly part of Project 211, two government schemes that single out leading Chinese universities.

The university came into being on 18 April 2000. Three institutions, each founded in the 1950s, were merged to make it. They were a highway and transport university (西安公路交通大学, Xi'an Highway and Transportation University), an engineering college in Xi'an (西安工程学院), and an architecture and building college in the north-west (西北建筑工程学院). The merged university therefore combines strengths in roads and transport, engineering and construction, which is why it is best known for those fields.

The university occupies 199 hectares (490 acres) in Xi'an, a city famous for its long cultural history. Instead of a single site, it runs five campuses within the city: Main, Yanta, Xiaozhai, Weishui and Taibai. They serve different purposes. Undergraduates study at the Weishui Campus, whereas the other four are mainly used by postgraduates and for social practice and fieldwork.
Weishui also has a notable facility: a comprehensive automobile proving ground, the only one of its kind inside a Chinese university.

On the research side, three of its laboratories are key laboratories of the Ministry of Education, and ten more are key laboratories jointly held with ministries and the province. Teaching facilities include six provincial-level experimental teaching demonstration centres, plus two research centres approved under a Ministry of Education engineering construction project, besides the proving ground mentioned above. The ten joint ones are linked to the transport, land and resources, and housing ministries as well as the provincial government. Details of laboratories and centres are updated often, so the university's own website is the place to confirm the current list.

Most of what a student needs to know about everyday life comes down to the city outside the campus gates: the weather, the transport, the work opportunities and the sights. The following sections introduce Xi'an, the home of Chang'an University, and then the province of Shaanxi.

The city sits in the heart of Shaanxi on the Guanzhong Plain, a flood plain built up by eight rivers and streams. Mountains close it off to the south, since the Qin range (Qinling) begins at the city's southern edge, while the Wei River flows along its northern side. Sacred Hua Shan, counted among the five holy mountains of Taoism, is 100 km (62 miles) away to the east, and the Loess Plateau is not far north.

The plain has long been prized. When the Han dynasty began, the adviser Zhang Liang urged Emperor Liu Bang to make Guanzhong his capital, describing it as lying behind Mount Xiao and the Hangu Pass, linking Gansu and Sichuan, and as a fortress of rich farmland stretching for a thousand li (关中左崤函，右陇蜀，沃野千里，此所谓金城千里，天府之国也). From that comes the old nickname for the area, the Nation of Heaven.

Xi'an has a temperate climate affected by the East Asian monsoon. Climate scientists class it as borderline between humid subtropical and hot-summer humid continental (Cwa/Dwa). In the Wei River valley, summers are hot and humid, winters are cold and dry, and spring and autumn are dry. Most of the year's rain falls between July and late October. Snow comes now and then in winter but seldom lies for long. Dust storms are common in March and April as the city warms quickly, and summer brings frequent short thunderstorms.

Monthly mean temperatures go from roughly 0 °C in January to a July peak of 27.0 °C (80.6 °F), with 14.08 °C (57.3 °F) as the annual figure. Records kept since 1951 show a low of -20.6 °C (-5 °F) on 11 January 1955. The high at the current station, in Jinghe, is 42.3 °C (108 °F) from 15 July 2025, although a different station once logged 42.9 °C (109 °F) on 17 June 2006. There is also an unofficial record low of -25.0 °C (-13 °F) from January 1930, taken at another station in the northern suburbs. Bring warm clothes for winter and light, breathable ones for summer, and expect dusty air in spring.

Near Xi'an, in the town of Lintong (临潼), is the National Time Service Center (NTSC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The story begins with the Shaanxi Astronomical Observatory, founded in 1966. In 1975 a geodetic report decided that, to keep measurement bias as low as possible, the national geodetic origin should be in the centre of mainland China, and Lintong was chosen. From 1986 onward, the NTSC has been the body that sets Chinese Standard Time.

The centre researches and provides services for time and frequency. It generates and maintains the national standard time scale and sends out time and frequency signals. During the 1970s and 1980s it built its own universal-time and atomic-time scales and ways of broadcasting them by low-frequency and high-frequency radio, which together met the needs of science, the national economy and other users.

The Seventh National Census in 2020 counted 12,952,907 permanent residents in Xi'an. About 51.07% were men and 48.93% women. By age, 15.65% were between 0 and 14, 68.33% between 15 and 59, and 16.02% were over 60, including 10.9% who were over 65. Another estimate, made by the OECD for 2010, put the whole metropolitan area at 12.9 million people, of whom 5,740,000 lived in urban areas. The two figures are for different years and definitions, so treat them as rough guides rather than exact comparisons.

Many parts of Xi'an are pleasant to cover on foot. In shopping, residential and education districts, above all the lively commercial quarter by the Bell Tower, underpasses and overpasses make walking safer and easier.

A bike-sharing network started in 2013 and now has 52,000 bicycles used by over 200,000 people daily. Taxis are plentiful, but many residents still go to work by one of 270 official municipal bus routes, run with more than 7,800 buses and carrying an average of over 4 million passengers a day. The metro is growing fast and carries over 1.5 million commuters daily. With more than 2 million registered cars in the city, traffic jams are a regular complaint.
#### Metro

Line 2 was the first line to open. It runs north to south, from the North Railway Station to Weiqu Nan, and is 19.9 kilometres (12.4 miles) long with 17 stations. It opened to the public in September 2011 (published dates differ by a few days, and the university or the metro operator can confirm exact ones). Line 1 came next, on 15 September 2013, crossing the city from west to east between Houweizhai and Fangzhicheng and calling at 19 stations. Line 3 opened on 8 November 2016 and links Baoshuiqu in the north-east with Yuhuazhai in the south-west. Line 4 was opened to passengers on 26 December 2018; apart from its northern end it is roughly parallel with Line 2, just to the east, and goes from the North Square of the North Railway Station (Beikezhan or Beiguangchang) to Hangtianxincheng in the south. Line 5, opened on 28 December 2020, has 31 stations over 41.6 kilometres, beginning at Matengkong and ending at Chuangxingang. The newest in this list is Line 16, which started service on 27 June 2023; it has 9 stations along 15.03 kilometres from Qinchuangyuanzhongxin to Shijingli. Four more lines, including an extension of Line 1, are under construction.

The metro reaches several of the city's best-known sights. Banpo Museum is at Banpo Station on Line 1. Take Line 2 for the Bell and Drum Tower and the city walls (Fortifications of Xi'an), Lines 3 and 4 for the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, Line 4 for Daminggong National Heritage Park, and any of Lines 2, 3 and 4 for the Shaanxi History Museum.
For timings, the first trains on Lines 1 to 4 leave at 6:00. The last departures are at 23:00 on Lines 3 and 4, 23:30 on Line 1 and 23:50 on Line 2.
#### Trains

Xi'an North railway station lies a few miles north of the centre and handles high-speed trains on the Zhengzhou-Xi'an High-Speed Railway, which forms part of the Xuzhou-Lanzhou high-speed line. Building of that railway began on 25 September 2005, and it opened on 6 February 2010. It was so quick that flights between Zhengzhou and Xi'an could no longer compete, and all passenger flights between them stopped within 48 days of regular high-speed service starting. The station itself, with 34 platforms, was the largest in north-west China when it opened. Construction began on 19 September 2008 and it opened on 11 January 2011. It is also on the Datong-Xi'an high-speed railway, which links to Beijing North, as well as the Xi'an-Chengdu and Yinchuan-Xi'an high-speed lines.

Xi'an railway station sits just outside the north side of the walled city and is the main hub for ordinary (non-high-speed) trains in Shaanxi. The site is 597,000 square metres (6,430,000 square feet) and has 6 passenger platforms with 11 passenger tracks. Each day it runs 112 services for 80,000 people. You can board direct trains here for Beijing, Zhengzhou, Lanzhou and Baoji, or for Mount Hua.

Two big stations, Xi'an East and Xi'an South, were being built for new high-speed lines such as the Xi'an-Chongqing and Wuhan-Xi'an routes. The city's other stations are Xi'an West, Yinzhen, Sanmincun and Fangzhicheng.
#### Flights

Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (code XIY) is the main airport for the city and the largest in north-west China. It lies 25 miles north-west of the city centre and 8 miles north-east of the middle of Xianyang. The chief airlines are China Eastern, Hainan Airlines and China Southern. Terminal 3 and a second runway opened on 3 May 2012, and Terminal 5 was begun in 2022 and finished in September 2024.
Beyond linking most Chinese cities, the airport has flights to major overseas destinations that include Tokyo, Seoul, London, Paris and Sydney.

The national China Western Development policy made Xi'an a priority for faster growth, with the focus on information technology, new materials, aerospace, energy and chemical engineering. Figures quoted for 1997 to 2006 describe the output of the service sector growing about 13 percent a year on average, compared with 0.74 percent for traditional services, and moving from US$8.113 billion up to US$25.85 billion; the wording of that statistic is unclear, so treat it as a general sign of fast growth.

Two international rankings from 2020 also place Xi'an on the map: the Globalization and World Cities network rates it a Beta- (second-tier global) city, and the Global Financial Centres Index lists it in its world top 100 financial centres.

Key industries are equipment manufacturing, tourism and service outsourcing. Manufacturing produced RMB 36.5 billion a year, equal to 44.5 percent of the city total. Xi'an is also one of China's four ancient capitals, and sites such as the Terracotta Army, the City Wall and the Famen Temple make tourism a major earner. In 2019 more than 300 million tourist visits brought in RMB 314.6 billion. Revenue was said to rise 36.4 percent a year on average, while earnings of foreign currency, at 530 million in 2009, were growing by around 35.8 percent annually.

Xi'an was among the earliest Chinese cities into service outsourcing, and over 800 companies work in the field. Output topped RMB 23 billion in 2008. Between 1997 and 2006, jobs in outsourcing doubled from a starting figure of 60,000, and computer consulting jobs also doubled, from 16,000 to 32,000. Because of this, a Software New Town was planned for completion in 2015 with 30 billion RMB of investment. Lighting equipment and auto parts are other main exports, mechanical and electrical products are the main imports, and the United States is the biggest foreign trade partner.

Freight is another strength. The Xi'an International Trade and Logistics Park, of roughly thirty-five square miles, was planned as a showcase for urban growth built around logistics, and it works as a large inland port and rail container hub. No other city sees more China-Europe freight trains leave or arrive.
#### Software and technology
The city's chief industrial area is the Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone. Jiangcungou, a landfill site that shut in 2019, had been the largest of its type in China.

The strong economy supports a software industry in which Xi'an is a national pioneer. By 2012 the Xi'an Software Park, in the Xi'an Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone (XDZ), had attracted over 1,085 companies and 106,000 workers. A well-known description says the city draws on the 100 or so universities in the area and produces about 3,000 computer graduates a year, with pay at roughly half Beijing's level; the wage figure quoted was around $120 a month, which is dated and now far below actual salaries, so do not rely on it.
#### Aerospace

A partnership between the city and the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation produced the Xi'an Aerospace Science and Technology Industrial Base in November 2006. From the outset it has worked on civilian space activity: manufacturing equipment, software and outsourced services, new materials and solar power cells.

Beyond its core area, the base was meant to cover Xi'an and the Guanzhong region, with an expansion zone reaching parts of north-west and south-west China. The goals set for 2012 were a combined output of 2.8 billion US dollars, between 10 and 20 own-brand products carrying their own intellectual property, and 5 to 8 products able to compete globally.

In 2008, after the first aerospace centre was launched in Shanghai, China began a second civil aerospace centre in Shaanxi. Planning for the Xi'an National Civil Aerospace Industrial Base won approval from the State Development and Reform Commission on 26 December 2007. It is to cover 23 km2 (8.9 square miles) and focus on satellites, new materials, energy, IT and other civil technologies.
Xi'an used to host several professional teams that have since relocated, grouped here by league.
Chinese Jia-A League: Shaanxi National Power, which moved to Ningbo and became Ningbo National Power in 2004
Top-flight football (the Chinese Football Association Super League): Shaanxi Baorong Chanba, which relocated to Guiyang and took the name Guizhou Renhe in 2012
Chinese Basketball Association: Shaanxi Dongsheng, which moved to Foshan and became the Foshan Dralions in 2010
Chang'an University belongs to Shaanxi, and its surroundings colour a student's time as much as the campus. What follows covers the province's past, landscape, economy and culture.

Few places matter more to the story of China than Shaanxi, which is seen as a birthplace of its civilisation. Between the Zhou and Tang dynasties, a span of over 1,100 years, thirteen feudal dynasties chose to base their capitals here. The leading city today, Xi'an, is counted among the four great ancient capitals and was the eastern terminus of the Silk Road, the route that carried goods and ideas toward Europe, Arabia and Africa.

When the Qin dynasty fell, the area was split up for a short time as the Three Qins. This explains one of the province's two short names, 秦 (Qin); the other is 陝 (Shaan). Liu Bang took the region during the struggle between Chu and Han. The Han then extended the Northern Silk Road westward for exploration and for military purposes. This was the most northerly of the Silk Roads, about 2,600 kilometres (1,600 miles) long. It ran from Xi'an across the Wushao Ling Pass to Wuwei and came out at Kashgar, where it met routes to ancient Parthia.

Later events included the Xiongnu-led kingdom of Northern Xia (407 to 431), which had its capital at Tongwancheng, and a border contest between the Northern Song and the Tangut-led Western Xia. Western Xia founded the frontier fort of Luōwùchéng (罗兀城) in 1071, but Song took it in 1081.

Under the Ming, Shaanxi was formally set up in 1376 with the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission, whose territory also included today's Gansu, Ningxia and part of Qinghai. Most travellers from Central and West Asia entered China through Shaanxi in that era. One of the deadliest earthquakes ever recorded hit on 23 January 1556, near Hua Shan in the south-east of the province. An estimated 100,000 people died, and emigration and famine are thought to have reduced the regional population by about 830,000 (it is known as the 1556 Shaanxi earthquake). In the twentieth century, the collapse of the short-lived Jiangxi Soviet set off the Long March, as Mao Zedong and the Communists moved to the Shaanxi Soviet at Yan'an.

Administratively, the Northern Song created a Shaanxi Lu (circuit) in 997, ruled from where Xi'an stands now, and the Yuan founded Shaanxi Province in 1286 under a Branch Secretariat. After the Qing took power, Gansu was split off from Shaanxi, though both were run under the Viceroy of Shaan-Gan.
#### An ancient find

The Lantian Man site in Lantian County, north-west Shaanxi and near Xi'an, yielded hominin fossils about a million years old. Specialists regard Lantian Man as a subspecies of Homo erectus, and the fossils can be seen at the Shaanxi History Museum in Xi'an.

Shaanxi stretches over very different terrain. Desert (the Ordos) lies in the far north by the Inner Mongolia border, the Loess Plateau occupies the middle, and the Qin Mountains (Qinling) cross the south-central area from east to west. South of the Qinling the climate is subtropical. The Wei River Valley, known as Guanzhong, sits between plateau and mountains and was an early cradle of Chinese civilisation.

Going clockwise, Shaanxi borders Shanxi (east and north-east), Henan (east), Hubei (south-east), Chongqing (south), Sichuan (south-west), Gansu (west), Ningxia (north-west) and Inner Mongolia (north). That makes nine neighbours, equal to Inner Mongolia for the most provincial-level neighbours.

Because the province spans a wide range of latitude, it has many climates. Northern areas, the Loess Plateau among them, are classed as cold desert (Köppen BWk) or cold steppe (BSk): winters there are cold and very dry, spring and autumn are dry, and summers are hot and humid. Guanzhong is mostly semi-arid, with a few humid subtropical areas (Cwa), where winters are cool to cold and summers are hot and humid, often with early heatwaves. The south is much more humid, within the humid subtropical zone, with milder winters and long, hot, humid summers. Across the province, yearly mean temperatures are about 8 to 16 °C (46 to 61 °F). In January the averages vary from -11 to 3.5 °C (12.2 to 38.3 °F), and in July they vary from 21 to 28 °C (70 to 82 °F).
Other places of note, apart from Xi'an, are Baoji, Hanzhong, Lintong, Tongchuan, Xianyang, Yan'an and Ankang.

Around the mid-19th century, Shaanxi's exports were animal skins, wine, spirits and musk. Lending was also common, and Shaanxi merchants took part in the Guangzhou loan business. Imports typically included European animal skins, watches, Chinese-language books and cloth. Shaanxi was also a major recipient of industrial investment during the Third Front campaign.

Fossil fuels and high technology are the province's two biggest industries. In 2009 it ranked third in China for coal, natural gas and crude oil production. Because many of western China's top universities and institutes are here, Shaanxi is also a major force in aircraft and aerospace, supplying more than half (over 50%) of the R&D and manufacturing equipment for domestic commercial aviation. The province's nominal GDP for 2011 was 1,239 billion RMB (US$196.7 billion), or 21,729 RMB (US$3,179) per person, which ranked 17th among Chinese provinces.

In the first six months of 2019, Shaanxi's total output value was 1,162.557 billion yuan, up 5.4% on a year earlier. Primary industry added 55.319 billion yuan (up 4.5%), secondary industry 557.935 billion yuan (up 4.2%) and tertiary industry 549.303 billion yuan (up 6.8%).
#### Baoji Hi-Tech Zone

Baoji Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone was set up in 1992 and approved by the State Council as a national hi-tech zone. Its long-term planned area is 40 km2 (15 square miles). The zone is served by Xi'an-Xianyang International Airport and National Highway 310. Firms inside it work in auto parts, electronics, IT, medicines, bioengineering and new materials.
#### Xi'an Export Processing Zone

The State Council approved the Shaanxi Xi'an Export Processing Zone (XEPZ) on 21 June 2002, and it began operating on 5 April 2004. It was the first export processing zone of state level in the north-west, and one of seven pioneers in China to offer bonded logistics. Day-to-day management belongs to the administrative committee of the Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone (XETDZ), to which the city government has delegated economic and administrative authority over the area. It is a special economic zone. More than 40 Chinese and foreign enterprises have settled there, and its main industries are aviation, machinery, electronics and new energy.
Cultural traditions to look for in Shaanxi include the following.
Shaanxi cuisine
Qinqiang, the representative folk opera of the province
Shaanxi shadow play
Xintianyou
Further background on culture and religion appears in the material on Xi'an itself
