Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

changan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Chang'an University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Xi'an, register at Chang'an University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Changchun University (长春大学, Chángchūn Dàxué; traditional form 長春大學) is a multi-disciplinary institution in the Jilin provincial capital. It was founded in 1946, and the number of undergraduates it has trained since then exceeds 40,000. Three campuses share a combined area of 1,129,000 square metres.

The structure is compact: 17 institutions or colleges, 46 undergraduate degree courses and upwards of 13,000 students. The teaching force numbers over 707, among them 110 professors and 318 associate professors. For research, it reports a total of three national-level science centres, a single provincial key discipline, a single provincial key science laboratory, and two provincial key bases devoted to the humanities and social sciences.

For a university of this size the range of subjects is wide: management, medicine, agriculture, engineering, science, history, literature, education, law, economics and philosophy are all covered, so applicants with quite different interests may find a place.

changchun-university.h: What it is like to live in Changchun

blocks.x: Your daily routine will depend on the surrounding city nearly as much as on the campus itself, including the weather, the transport and the things to see. The notes below introduce Changchun first and then the province of Jilin around it.

Changchun sits in the middle of the Northeast China Plain, between latitudes 43° 05′ and 45° 15′ N and longitudes 124° 18′ and 127° 02′ E. The municipality covers 20,571 km2, or 7,943 sq mi, within which the metropolitan area is 2,583 square kilometres, or 997 sq mi, and the city proper only 159 km2, or 61 sq mi. Elevation across the administrative region is moderate, between 250 and 350 metres, or 820 to 1,150 ft. A small belt of low mountains lies to the east, topped by Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres.

The city is also where the third east-west 'Europe-Asia Continental Bridge' crosses another route. The prefecture holds 222 rivers and lakes, and the Yitong River, a minor tributary of the Songhua, flows through the urban centre.

Changchun has a humid continental climate with four seasons and a monsoon influence (Köppen Dwa; Trewartha Dcac). Expect a long winter, running from November until March, that is cold, windy and dry because of the Siberian anticyclone; January averages −14.3 °C, or 6.3 °F. Spring and autumn are short transitional seasons, usually dry and windy with some precipitation. Summers turn hot and humid under a prevailing south-easterly wind from the East Asian monsoon, and July averages 23.7 °C, or 74.7 °F.

Winter snowfall is usually light, and most of the year's rain arrives between June and August. Measured against the possible maximum, sunshine is at its lowest in July (49 percent) and at its highest in February (69 percent), and a normal year adds up to around 2,597 hours. The frost-free period lasts 140 to 150 days. The extremes on record are −36.5 °C, or −34 °F, on 4 January 1970 and 38.0 °C, or 100 °F, on 9 July 1951. Pack seriously warm clothing if you are from a mild climate.

The Sixth China Census counted 7.677 million people in the city of Changchun in 2010, and an estimate for 2011 put the total at 7.59 million. Of these, 3.53 million lived in the urban area. Births ran at 6.08 per thousand and deaths at 5.51 per thousand, and in 2010 there were 102.10 men for every 100 women.
As across most of north-eastern China, the great majority, 96.57 percent, belong to the Han nationality, with a handful of minority groups making up the remainder.

The local speech is Northeastern Mandarin, which grew out of a mixture of languages brought by settlers from Hebei and Shandong. After the People's Republic was founded, fast economic growth drew in large numbers of newcomers from many regions, and since they influenced the urban dialect most, speech in the city sits closer to standard Mandarin than speech in the countryside. That is good news if you have been studying standard Chinese.

Four major religions are present: Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam, with 396 officially approved places of worship. Buddhist and Taoist sites include the Big Buddha Temple, Pumen Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Changchun Temple and Changchun Wanshou Temple; Christians worship at the Changchun West Wuma Road Church and the Changchun Catholic Church, and Muslims at the Changchun City Mosque. Shamanism was widespread in Northeast China in ancient times and was followed by many Manchus; today it and its study are regarded as an important part of the region's cultural heritage.

The Jilin Provincial Museum, rated a national first-grade museum, is found in Changchun. It was transferred from Jilin City after the provincial government moved. Having stood originally in the middle of the old town, it received a new building after nine years of construction, finished in 2016 on the edge of the city in Nanguan District, close to Jingyuetan Park.

Badabu, meaning 'eight ministries', is a group of buildings that once housed the eight ministries of Manchukuo: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs, and Civil Affairs. They have become a sightseeing highlight lately thanks to an unusual blend of Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian architecture.
South-east of the city lies Jingyuetan National Forest Park, one of China's AAAAA-rated tourist attractions. The Vasaloppet China ski event is staged there every year.

Changchun's GDP in 2010 came to RMB332.9 billion, up 15.3 percent on the year before. By sector, the primary industry produced RMB25.27 billion (up 3.3 percent), the secondary industry RMB171.99 billion (up 19.0 percent) and the tertiary industry RMB135.64 billion (up 12.6 percent). In 2012 GDP per person was ¥58,691, or about $9338, and total GDP was RMB445.66 billion, 12.0 percent more than in 2011. In that year the sector figures were RMB31.71 billion for primary industry (growth of 4.3 percent), RMB229.19 billion for secondary industry (13.1 percent) and RMB184.76 billion for tertiary industry (11.8 percent).

The main industries are automobiles, agricultural processing, biopharmaceuticals, photoelectronics, construction materials and energy. Cars are the headline: Changchun is China's largest centre for automobile manufacturing, research and development, and it made 9 percent of the country's vehicles in 2009. The home-town giant is FAW (First Automotive Works) Group, China's biggest vehicle maker, whose first truck, in 1956, and first car, in 1958, were firsts for China. The company's plants, with their housing and services, take up much of the south-west of the city. The Red Flag luxury marque is made here, along with the output of partnerships involving Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. FAW's 2012 results were sales of 2.65 million vehicles and revenue of RMB 408.46 billion, an increase of 10.8%. The city's best-known nickname, 'China's Detroit', reflects its role as the cradle of the auto industry.

Rolling stock and machinery are also big. Half of China's passenger trains and a tenth of its tractors (50 percent and 10 percent) come from Changchun. One CRRC division, Changchun Railway Vehicles, teamed up with Bombardier Transportation in a joint venture making Movia metro cars for the metro systems of Guangzhou, Shanghai and Tianjin. Most of CRRC's bullet-train carriages come from its Changchun factory. In November 2016 it presented the world's first bullet-train carriages with sleeping berths, for overnight journeys across China. Nicknamed Panda, the new trains run at 250 km/h and are designed to operate at −40 degrees Celsius; they offer Wi-Fi hubs, and their berths turn into seats by day.

In 2012 the city drew US$3.68 billion in foreign direct investment, 19.6% more than a year earlier. An example is Coca-Cola's US$20 million bottling plant, opened in 2004 inside the city's ETDZ. Each year the city also hosts an automobile fair, a film festival, an agricultural fair, an education exhibition and a sculpture exhibition, all carrying the Changchun name.

Other large employers include the Yatai Group, which dates from 1993 and has been listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange since 1995; it has become a conglomerate active in property development, cement, securities, coal mining, pharmaceuticals and trading, and Jilin Grain Group, a major grain processor.

The Changchun Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone began in 1993 as the Changchun Automotive Trade Center and took its present form in 1996. In the south-west of the city, next to the FAW Group headquarters and the Changchun Film ThemeCity, it spreads over roughly 300,000 square metres, or 3,229,173 square feet. It contains an exhibition centre and five dedicated industrial centres. The Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center, open since 1994, is China's biggest wholesale market for vehicles and spare parts, and the other centres cover used cars, industrial and commercial vehicles, and tyres.

The Changchun High Technology Development Zone, among the first 27 state-level advanced technology zones, is in the south of the city and occupies 49 km2, or 19 sq mi, Within it are 18 full-time universities and colleges, 11 key national laboratories and 39 research institutions run by the state or the province. Its five target industries are bio-engineering, automobile engineering, new materials, photo-electricity and information technology.

The Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone was created in April 1993 and has the same preferential policies as such zones in coastal open cities. In all it covers 112.72 square kilometres (43.52 square miles); only 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of that has been reserved for development and use. It is 5 kilometres, or 3 miles, from downtown, 2 km, or 1.2 mi, from the freight station and 15 km, or 9 mi, from the international airport. Its five leading industries are automotive parts and components, photoelectric information, bio-pharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials, and high-tech, high-value-added projects deliver over 80 percent of output. In 2006 fixed-asset investment in the zone rose to RMB38.4 billion; of 1656 registered enterprises, 179 are foreign-funded, and total industrial output in 2007 was RMB 277 billion.

The surrounding region is a big grain producer and a regional air and rail hub, and Changchun has used that position to set up an Aviation Food Industrialization Base. It supplies prepared meals to several airlines and carries out food science research for long-haul flights, a niche but distinctive sector.
Transport options in the city range from long-distance rail and air to buses, a historic tram and a growing rapid transit network.

Passenger rail is centred on two big stations. Changchun railway station (长春站) in the centre handles every conventional train and some high-speed trains, on the Beijing-Harbin Railway, the Changchun-Hunchun intercity railway and other lines. From here trains leave every day for destinations within Jilin and the wider north-east, among them Dalian, Shenyang, Harbin, Yanji and Jilin City, and for big cities elsewhere such as Guangzhou, Shanghai and Beijing. Changchun West railway station, at the western edge of the built-up area, mainly serves high-speed trains of the Harbin-Dalian line. Changchun East, a small station in Erdao district, lies on the Changchun-Tumen line.
The bus network has more than 250 routes, and most journeys cost 1-2 yuan.

Changchun is one of the few Chinese cities that still keep a historic tram. It opened in 1941 and at its peak had 6 lines running almost 53 km. After several adjustments only one line has remained since the 2000s. A branch opened in 2014 that reaches the new Changchun West Railway Station, and the whole tram system now falls under the city bus operation.

Changchun Rail Transit combines light-rail and metro lines. The first line began service on 30 October 2002, which put Changchun fifth among Chinese cities to get urban rail transit. By November 2018 there were 5 lines (Lines 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8) covering about 100.17 kilometres. In September 2019 four projects were under construction: Line 6, Line 9, the Line 2 West Extension and the Line 3 East Extension. The plan is for the network to reach 10 lines and 341.62 kilometres in 2025.

Ridership is substantial: average daily passenger volume reached 680,400 in September 2019, the network's peak day was 13 November 2019 with 830,500 passengers, and the estimated total for 2019 was about 168 million.

The national expressway grid reaches Changchun via the Beijing-Harbin Expressway (G1), the Ulanhot-Changchun-Jilin-Hunchun Expressway (G12), the Changchun-Shenzhen Expressway (G25) and the Changchun-Changbaishan Expressway (S1). The busiest section in the province is the Changchun-Jilin North Highway, which joins Jilin's two largest cities and carries the main social and economic traffic between them.
Private cars are increasingly common on congested streets. Compared with other north-eastern Chinese cities, bicycles are relatively rare, while mopeds and pedal cycles are fairly usual.

Changchun Longjia International Airport is 31.2 kilometres, or 19.4 miles, north-east of the urban area. Construction started in 1998, with the aim of replacing the old Changchun Dafangshen Airport, a joint-use field dating from 1941. Passenger service began on 27 August 2005, and Changchun and nearby Jilin City share its operation.

changchun-university.h: The city as a place to study

blocks.x: In the Nature Index 2024 Science Cities, Changchun is placed among the best 30 cities worldwide for scientific research. Its 27 regular institutions of full-time tertiary education enrol roughly 160,000 students. The best known are Jilin University and Northeast Normal University, both designated key universities, and Jilin University, with over 60,000 students, ranks among China's largest. The institutions you may come across include:
Jilin University
Northeast Normal University
Changchun University (the subject of this profile)
Changchun Normal University
Changchun University of Science and Technology
Changchun University of Chinese Medicine
Changchun Institute of Technology
Jilin University of Finance and Economics
Jilin Agricultural University
Jilin Engineering Normal University
Jilin College of the Arts
Also in the city is Jilin Huaqiao Foreign Languages Institute, a private college, offers bachelor's study in foreign languages, international trade management and didactics.

For families moving with a student, the leading secondary schools are Changchun Foreign Languages School, Changchun No.6 Middle School, No.11 High School of Changchun, the Second Experimental School of Jilin Province, No.72 Middle School of Changchun, and the middle and high schools attached to Jilin University and Northeast Normal University.
A university's province also sets the background to student life, so here is a short guide to Jilin.

In ancient times the Jilin area was home to the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and the Wùjí (勿吉), while the kingdoms of Goguryeo and Buyeo governed some of it. Control then passed from one power to the next: first the Xiongnu and the Xianbei state, then Goguryeo and Balhae, and later the Khitan Liao dynasty, the Jurchen Jin dynasty and the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Under the Qing, the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn) controlled much of it, an area that stretched across a great part of today's Russian Primorsky Krai.

After Primorsky Krai was handed to Russia in 1860, the authorities began admitting Han Chinese migrants to the region, mostly from Shandong, and by the early 20th century the Han were the dominant group. In 1932 Japan incorporated the area into Manchukuo, its puppet state, and Changchun, then named Xinjing, became the capital of Manchukuo. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the Red Army took Jilin in Operation August Storm, and the Soviet Union handed the region, along with the rest of the north-east, to the Communists. Manchuria then served as the base from which the Communists went on to win the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949 the province was smaller and covered only the areas around Changchun and Jilin City; Jilin City was the capital, while Changchun stood apart as an independent municipality. In the 1950s Jilin grew to its current borders. During the Cultural Revolution it was enlarged again to include a slice of Inner Mongolia, which gave it a border with Mongolia, though this change was later reversed. More recently, Jilin, like the rest of the heavy-industry north-east, has struggled economically during privatization, which led the central government to launch a 'Revitalize the Northeast' campaign.

Jilin is in the central north-east, bordering Russia to the east and North Korea to the south-east. It covers 190,000 km2, or 73,000 sq mi, has 24 million inhabitants, and has Changchun as its capital, 113 km, or 70 mi, west of Jilin City. Mineral wealth is considerable, with 136 types recorded and 70 already extracted, and the province is also well supplied with traditional Chinese medicine resources, roughly 27,000 wild plant species and 9,000 medicinal herbs. Deposits of silver, gold, cement rock, gypsum, graphite, talc, molybdenum, nickel, iron, coal, gas and oil are large, and nowhere in the country has bigger oil shale reserves.

The land is highest in the south-east and slopes gently towards the north-west. The Changbai Mountains run through the south-east, and there stands the province's highest peak, Paektu Mountain, at 2,744 m, or 9,003 ft. Other ranges are the Jilinhada, Zhang Guangcai and Longgang mountains. The far south-east is drained by the Yalu and Tumen rivers and together mark part of the border with North Korea, tributaries of the Liao River drain the south-west, and the Songhua and Nen rivers drain the north before flowing on into the Amur.

The climate is northern continental and monsoonal: winters are long and cold, summers short and warm. In January the average temperature lies between −20 and −14 °C, or −4 and 7 °F, while annual rainfall averages between 350 and 1,000 mm, or 13.8 and 39.4 in. Beyond Changchun, the principal cities are Liaoyuan, Tonghua, Songyuan, Yanji, Siping, Baicheng, Baishan and Jilin City.

Nominal GDP for the province was RMB 1,497.4 billion, or US$209.6 billion, in 2025, and per capita nominal GDP was RMB 64,618, or US$9,046. It has been growing at a double-digit pace since 2003, 51 percent between 2003 and 2007, while compared with 2005, large enterprises recorded 19 percent more added value and 30 percent more profit.

Crops are rice, wheat, maize and sorghum, with rice concentrated in the east, for example in Yanbian Prefecture. The Changbai Mountains are a key timber source, and in the west, near Baicheng, many people herd sheep. The province is among China's chief commodity grain bases and sixth for timber. Its mineral reserves are among the five largest in China and include the biggest shale oil reserves, with notably large deposits of molybdenum, floatstone, wollastonite and kieselguhr. Heavy industry means cars, train carriages and iron alloy. The province has long been a pharmaceutical centre, with ginseng and deer antler yields among the largest in China, used widely in Chinese medicine.

Two zones in Jilin City are worth knowing. The Jilin New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone was founded in 1992, with 818 km2, or 316 sq mi, planned and 242 km2, or 93 sq mi, established. Leading sectors are new materials, refined chemicals, photoelectron-mechanism integration, electronics, medicine and bioengineering. Songhua Lake is only 14 km away (8.7 mi) and the nearest bus and train stations are within 3 km (1.9 mi).

The Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone opened in May 1998 in the north-east of Jilin City, with a planned area of 28 km2, or 11 sq mi. Distances matter for logistics here: Changchun lies 90 km away (56 mi), the airport 5 km (3.1 mi) and the railway station 8 km (5.0 mi). Main industries include bioengineering, refined chemicals and the fine processing of chemical fibre and farm products, organized in chemical, food, textile and medical parks. The medical park specializes in traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals, small-molecule medicine, bio-pharmaceuticals and health products.

Han Chinese, Manchus, Hui, Mongols and Xibe all live in Jilin. Ethnic Koreans, about 4% of the population because the Korean Peninsula is so near, are mostly found in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture. The Manchu were once the majority here, which makes Jilin part of their historical homeland, but as they adopted Han culture and Chinese, the Manchu language is now seen as critically endangered. Most people speak Mandarin. The provincial population figure leaves out serving soldiers of the People's Liberation Army.

Culturally Jilin belongs to Northeast China and shares traditions with its neighbours, such as Errenzhuan and Yangge. Jiju, also called Jilin Opera, is a musical form of traditional entertainment, and Jilin developed it itself during its fairly brief history of migration. The ethnic Koreans have their own distinct culture, which remains closely tied to Korea.
Changchun University lists 59 programs for international students on this site: 35 bachelor, 23 master's, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 59 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 23,000 (median CNY 16,500), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 19,800), according to the university's published fee table.

58 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

changchun-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Changchun University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Changchun, register at Changchun University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

changchun-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Meet Changchun University of Chinese Medicine

blocks.x: The provincial government of Jilin and the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine have jointly built this institution as a key university. Its home is Changchun, Jilin Province's capital, in northeast China. Its specialty is exactly what its name says, so it is a natural choice if you want to study traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), acupuncture, pharmacy or related health fields.
1950: a training school for traditional Chinese medicine was set up in Changchun, the first medical school of Chinese medicine anywhere in Jilin Province.
1958: on the basis of that school, a college of traditional Chinese medicine was created.
1970: the college was absorbed by Jilin Medical University, which later became the Norman Bethune Health Science Center at Jilin University.
March 1978: the college regained its independence.
1992: the first international students enrolled; the Ministry of Education had approved it as one of the earliest institutions to take them.
2004: Jilin Province designated the college a key educational institution.
2006: renamed Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, it came under the joint direction of the provincial health and education departments.
2020: the Jilin Province project for building characteristic high-level universities included it.
The early enrolment of overseas students is worth noting if you are one: this is a university with roughly three decades of experience in teaching people from abroad.

In short, the school has moved from a 1950 training school to a provincially backed university in about seventy years, and its link to the national traditional medicine administration gives it a clear specialist profile.

Bachelor's, master's and doctoral programmes are offered through a number of schools and departments. Health-related schools are Pharmacy, Nursing, Basic Medical Sciences, Clinical Medicine, Rehabilitation Medicine, Medical Information, Acupuncture and Moxibustion, Traditional Chinese Medicine, and a school that combines traditional and Western medicine. The remaining units cover general subjects and skills: the School of Management, the School of Marxism, the Department of Physical Education, the Department of Foreign Languages, the Innovation and Practice Center, the School for Cultivating Young Marxists and the School of Innovation and Entrepreneurship.

Clinical training takes place at three affiliated hospitals. These are the university's main Affiliated Hospital, a Third Affiliated Clinical Hospital, and a Fourth Affiliated Clinical Hospital, which doubles as Changchun People's Hospital.

The campus occupies 395,000 square metres, and over 30,000 students study here. Cooperation with teaching and research bodies reaches more than 20 countries. ShanghaiRanking's 2026 list of Chinese traditional medicine universities puts it 15th. To find it, go to 1035 Boshuo Road in the Jingyue High-tech Industrial Development Zone of Changchun, Jilin.
The school announced that it would investigate. The source does not report an outcome, so ask the university directly if you want to know its current procedures for handling complaints.
Your daily life will be shaped by the city around the campus, so the sections below cover Changchun's setting, climate, people, sights, economy and transport.

Changchun is in the middle of the Northeast China Plain, in the area bounded by latitudes 43° 05′ to 45° 15′ N and longitudes 124° 18′ to 127° 02′ E. The municipality is 20,571 km2 (7,943 sq mi) in total. Metro areas account for 2,583 square kilometres (997 sq mi), while the city proper is just 159 km2 (61 sq mi). Elevation across the administrative region is moderate: 250-350 m (820-1,150 ft). A small area of low mountains lies in the east, and the highest point there is Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres.

The city also sits at the crossing point of the third east-west "Europe-Asia Continental Bridge". Altogether the prefecture has 222 rivers and lakes. A small Songhua tributary, the Yitong River, flows through the city proper.

Changchun has a humid continental climate with a monsoon influence and four seasons (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). November to March makes up the long, cold, windy but dry winter, a result of the Siberian anticyclone; January averages -14.3 °C, or 6.3 °F. Spring and autumn pass quickly, mostly dry and blustery with the occasional shower. In summer it turns hot and humid and the wind mostly blows from the southeast because of the East Asian monsoon; the July average is 23.7 °C (74.7 °F). Snowfall is generally light, and most of the year's rain falls between June and August.

July has the lowest share of possible sunshine (49 per cent) and February the highest (69 per cent). Over a year that adds up to about 2,597 sunshine hours, and the frost-free period lasts 140 to 150 days. The coldest reading, -36.5 °C (-34 °F), came on 4 January 1970; the hottest, 38.0 °C (100 °F), on 9 July 1951.

In practical terms, pack for a long, dry, windy winter and a warm, humid July; spring and autumn are the short, mild-looking seasons in between, and the frost-free period lasts only about five months.

In the Sixth China Census (2010) the city had 7.677 million residents, and an estimate for 2011 gave 7.59 million. Births ran at 6.08 per thousand and deaths at 5.51 per thousand. 3.53 million people lived in the urban area, and the 2010 sex ratio stood at 102.10 men to 100 women.

Han Chinese predominate (96.57 per cent), as in most of northeast China, with several minority nationalities. Northeastern Mandarin is the most common dialect, a blend of speech brought by settlers from Hebei and Shandong. After the People's Republic was founded, fast economic growth drew huge numbers of newcomers from many places. They strongly affected the dialect in urban areas, so the northeastern speech in the city is closer to standard Mandarin than the speech of the countryside.

Four major religions are present: Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam, with 396 government-approved places for worship and religious activity. Among Buddhist and Taoist sites are Wanshou Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple, Pumen Temple, Big Buddha Temple and Changchun Temple. Christians have the Catholic church and the West Wuma Road Christian church, and Muslims the city mosque. In ancient northeast China, shamanism was widespread and many Manchus believed in it; it, and research into it, now count as important local cultural heritage.
To sum up, Changchun is a mid-sized, mostly Han Chinese northeastern city with a layered religious life and a distinctive local dialect.

A national first-grade museum, the Jilin Provincial Museum, is located in the city; it moved from Jilin City after the provincial government changed its seat. The collections used to be in the middle of the old town. A new building, finished in 2016 after nine years of work, now houses them out on the edge of the city, near Jingyuetan Park in Nanguan District.

Badabu is a group of buildings that once housed eight Manchukuo ministries: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs and Civil Affairs. Their unusual blend of Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian architecture has recently made them a highlight for sightseers.
Southeast of the city, Jingyuetan National Forest Park is one of China's AAAAA Tourist Attractions and hosts Vasaloppet China every year.

Changchun's GDP was RMB 332.9 billion in 2010, up 15.3 per cent on the year before. Primary industry output rose 3.3 per cent to RMB 25.27 billion, secondary industry rose 19.0 per cent to RMB 171.99 billion, and tertiary industry rose 12.6 per cent to RMB 135.64 billion. In 2012 GDP per head was ¥58,691, equal to $9338, and total GDP was RMB 445.66 billion, which is 12.0 per cent more than in 2011. In that year the primary sector grew 4.3 per cent to RMB 31.71 billion, the secondary sector rose by RMB 229.19 billion (up 13.1 per cent), and the tertiary sector grew 11.8 per cent to RMB 184.76 billion.

The leading industries are automobiles, agricultural product processing, biopharmaceuticals, photoelectronics, building materials and energy. Changchun is China's largest centre for car manufacturing and research and development, and it made 9 per cent of the country's cars in 2009. The biggest vehicle maker in China, FAW (First Automotive Works) Group, is based here; it built China's first truck in 1956 and first car in 1958. Its factories, housing and services take up a large part of the city's southwest end. Locally made brands include the luxury Red Flag marque, and there are joint ventures with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. FAW sold 2.65 million vehicles in 2012, with sales revenue of RMB 408.46 billion, up 10.8 per cent. As the birthplace of the auto industry, the city is often nicknamed "China's Detroit".

Transport equipment and machinery are also major industries. The city builds 50 per cent of China's passenger trains and 10 per cent of its tractors. Changchun Railway Vehicles, one of CRRC's main divisions, has teamed up with Bombardier Transportation in a joint venture making Movia metro cars for Guangzhou, Shanghai and Tianjin. Most of CRRC's bullet train carriages are also made in Changchun. A world first came in November 2016: carriages with sleeper berths, which let these trains serve overnight trips across China. They can run in ultra-low temperatures. Nicknamed Panda, the new trains can reach 250 km/h, run at -40 degrees Celsius, have Wi-Fi hubs, and their sleeper berths fold into seats in the daytime.

Foreign direct investment in 2012 was US$3.68 billion, up 19.6 per cent. In 2004 Coca-Cola invested US$20 million in a bottling plant inside the city's ETDZ. Annual events include an International Automobile Fair, a Film Festival, an Agricultural Fair, an Education Exhibition and a Sculpture Exhibition. Other large companies include Jilin Grain Group, a leading grain processor, and the Yatai Group, which dates from 1993 and was listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1995; it has grown into a conglomerate active in property, cement, securities, coal mining, pharmaceuticals and trading.

Starting out in 1993 as the Changchun Automotive Trade Center, the Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone was re-established under its current name in 1996. In the southwest of the city, it adjoins the Changchun Film ThemeCity and the FAW group's works, and its area is roughly 300,000 square metres (3,229,173 square feet). The zone holds an exhibition center and five demarcated industrial centres. The biggest, the Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center (operating since 1994), is China's largest wholesale hub for vehicles and spare parts. Other centres deal with used-vehicle resale, industrial and commercial vehicles, and tires.

The Changchun High Technology Development Zone is among the first 27 state-level advanced technology zones. Located in the city's south, it spans 49 km2 (19 sq mi) and contains 18 full-time higher-education institutions, 11 key national laboratories and 39 research institutions at state or provincial level. It concentrates on five industries: bioengineering, automobile engineering, new materials, photoelectricity and information technology.

The Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone was founded in April 1993 and gets all the preferential policies laid down for such zones in coastal open cities. Its area is 112.72 square kilometres (43.52 square miles); 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of that is earmarked for development. Distances: downtown 5 kilometres (3 miles), the airport 15 km (9 mi), and the freight railway station 2 km (1.2 mi). Its five leading industries are automotive parts, photoelectric information, biopharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials. High-tech, high value-added projects account for over 80 per cent of total output. Fixed-asset investment reached RMB 38.4 billion in 2006, 179 of the 1656 registered enterprises are foreign-funded, and industrial output hit RMB 277 billion in 2007.

Because Changchun is a major grain base and a regional air and rail hub, it has also created a specialised Aviation Food Industrialization Base. The base provides prepared meals for several airlines and carries out food science research for long flights, a niche sector of manufacturing.
The overall picture is a city built around the car and rail industries, with a growing high-tech and food sector that gives graduates in many fields somewhere to work.

Changchun has two main passenger rail stations. Central Changchun railway station (长春站, 長春站) handles all conventional trains and some high-speed ones, on the Beijing-Harbin Railway, the Changchun-Hunchun intercity railway and several other lines. Trains leave many times a day for destinations in the province and the northeast (Jilin City, Yanji, Harbin, Shenyang, Dalian) and for large cities elsewhere, among them Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. A newer station, Changchun West, at the western end of the urbanised area, is mostly for high-speed services on the Harbin-Dalian line. Changchun East, a small station in Erdao District, lies on the Changchun-Tumen line.

Over 250 bus routes make up a comprehensive network, with most rides costing 1 to 2 yuan. The city also keeps a historic tram, a rarity in China. Opening in 1941, the tram once ran 6 lines over almost 53 km, but after various route adjustments just one has remained since the 2000s. In 2014 a new branch connected it to the Changchun West station, and the tram is now operated by the bus system.

Changchun Rail Transit combines light rail and metro lines. Its first line opened on 30 October 2002, which made Changchun the fifth big Chinese city to open rail transit. By November 2018 there were 5 lines (1, 2, 3, 4 and 8) running about 100.17 kilometres. By September 2019 four projects were under construction: Lines 6 and 9, the Line 2 West Extension and the Line 3 East Extension. The plan for 2025 is a network of ten lines, 341.62 kilometres in all.
In September 2019 average daily ridership reached 680,400 passengers, and the maximum daily figure was 830,500 on 13 November 2019. The total expected for 2019 is about 168 million passenger trips.

Expressways tie the city into the national network: the Beijing-Harbin Expressway (G1), the Ulanhot-Changchun-Jilin-Hunchun Expressway (G12), the Changchun-Shenzhen Expressway (G25), the Changchun-Changbaishan Expressway (S1) and the Changchun-Jilin North Highway, the province's busiest section, which joins its two biggest cities and carries their economic and social traffic. Private cars are increasingly common on congested streets. Bicycles are comparatively rare next to other northeast Chinese cities, but mopeds and pedal-assisted bikes are relatively common.

Changchun Longjia International Airport is 31.2 kilometres (19.4 miles) northeast of the urban area. Work began in 1998 so that it could take over from Dafangshen Airport, an older field for both civil and military use that dated from 1941; passenger flights started on 27 August 2005. Changchun and neighbouring Jilin City share its operation.
Altogether, you can reach the rest of Jilin and the northeast easily by rail or road, and the airport handles longer trips.

In the Nature Index 2024 Science Cities, Changchun is one of the world's top 30 cities for research. There are 27 regular full-time tertiary institutions with some 160,000 students. Northeast Normal University and Jilin University count as key national universities, and Jilin is among China's largest with over 60,000 students.

Other institutions in the list: Changchun University of Science and Technology, Changchun University, Changchun Normal University, Changchun Institute of Technology, Jilin College of the Arts, Jilin Agricultural University, Jilin Engineering Normal University, Jilin University of Finance and Economics, and of course Changchun University of Chinese Medicine itself. A private college, Jilin Huaqiao Foreign Languages Institute, teaches bachelor's programmes in languages, international trade management and didactics.

Secondary schools for younger students include Changchun Foreign Languages School, Changchun No. 6 Middle School, No. 11 High School of Changchun, the Second Experimental School of Jilin Province, No. 72 Middle School of Changchun, and the middle schools attached to Jilin University and to Northeast Normal University.

After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Changchun, register at Changchun University of Chinese Medicine by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Changchun University of Science and Technology (CUST) is a public university in Changchun, the capital of Jilin Province in northeast China. It used to be called the Changchun Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics (长春光学精密机械学院), and Wang Daheng founded it in 1958. That earlier name explains the university's character: optics, precision instruments and electronics are still its heartland, even though the range of subjects is now much wider.

Two bodies oversee the university: the Jilin Provincial Education Department, and the national defence science, technology and industry commission (the Commission for Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense).
CUST organises its teaching in fifteen schools, which run from basic science to law and artificial intelligence.
Humanities and social sciences: Law, Chinese Literature, Foreign Languages, and Economics and Management are each a school
Computing: the schools of Artificial Intelligence, Software, and Computer Science and Technology
Chemistry and life sciences: Biological and Medical Engineering, Life Science and Technology, and Chemistry and Environmental Engineering
Science and engineering: Materials Science and Engineering joins Electronics and Information Engineering, Mechatronical Engineering, Photoelectric Engineering and the School of Science

changchun-university-of-science-and-tech.h: The school that started it all

blocks.x: The School of Optical-Electric Engineering dates from 1958, growing out of what was then the department of optical electric engineering. It has five departments: optical engineering, instrumental science and technology, detection and information engineering, photo electronics, and a space technology institute. The school is home to one national key major. Doctoral study is offered in two fields, optical engineering and instrumental science and technology. At master's level there are three: fine instruments, optical engineering, and measuring and testing technology. Four bachelor's programmes complete the picture, namely detection guidance and controlling technology, information confrontation, optical-electric information engineering and controlling technology with instruments.
The university offers a very large range of programmes, listed here by level. Because names can change, check the admissions office for the programmes open to international students in a given year.
Undergraduate subjects fall into groups.
Design and law: Law, Industrial Design and Art Design
Languages and communication: Advertisement, Chinese as a Foreign Language, Chinese Language and Literature, plus Korean, Russian, Japanese and English

Business and economics: Labor and Social Insurance, Accounting, Business Administration, Business Economics with International Economy, Information Management and Information System, Marketing, Financial Engineering and Economics
Biology: Biological and Medical Engineering, Biological Engineering and Biological Technology
Materials, chemistry and environment: Chemical Engineering and Technology, Environmental Science, Material Chemistry, and Inorganic Non-metallic Materials Engineering

Information and communications: Network Engineering, Software Engineering, Computer Science and Technology, then Telecommunication Engineering, Electronic Information Engineering and Electronic Information Science and Technology

Mechanical and electrical engineering: Automation, Electrical Engineering and Automation, Processing Equipment and Control, Mechanical and Electronic Engineering, Mechanical Design Manufacture and Automation, and Measuring and Controlling Technology and Equipment

Physics, optics and electronics: Optical and Electronic Information Engineering, Micro-electronics, Optical-electronics Technology, Optical Information Science and Technology, Electronic Science and Technology, Applied Physics, and Information and Computing Science
At master's level the university offers research degrees in the following areas, many in physics and engineering.
Professional degree: the MBA (Master of Business Administration)

Management and others: Constitution and Administration Law, Chinese Philology, Applied Linguistics with Foreign Languages, Enterprise Management, Industrial Economics, Management Science and Engineering, and Biological and Medical Engineering
Materials and chemistry: Applied Chemistry, Physical Chemistry, Inorganic Chemistry, Material Processing Engineering, Material Science, and Material Physics and Chemistry
Computing: Computer Applied Technology, Computer System Structure, and Computer Software and Theory

Information and electrical engineering: Mode Identification and Intelligent System, Test Technology and Automation Device, Signal and Information Processing, Telecommunication and Information System, Electric Circuit and System, and Electromagnetic Field and Microwave Technology
Mechanical engineering: Mechanical Design and Theory, Mechanical and Electronic Engineering, and Mechanical Manufacture and Automation

Electronics and instruments: Testing and Metrological Technology and Instruments, Precise Instruments and Machinery, Optical Engineering, Micro-electronics with Solid State Electronics, and Physical Electronics
Physics: Optics, Acoustics, Condensed Matter Physics, Radio Physics, Plasma Physics, Atom and Molecule Physics, Particle Physics with Nuclear Physics, and Theoretical Physics

Doctoral study is concentrated in optics and precision engineering. Twelve doctoral programmes are listed. Material Physics and Chemistry and Telecommunication and Information System are two; the mechanical group comprises Mechanical Design and Theory, Mechanical and Electronic Engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Machinery Manufacture and Automation. The rest are Measuring and Controlling Technology and Equipment, Precise Instruments and Machinery, Equipment Science and Technology, Optical Engineering, Physical Electronics and Optics.

The CUST library opened in 1958, the same year as the university, and has grown along with it. Over nearly half a century, it has built two large, modern libraries with distinct collections, one on the east campus and one on the west. Following the university's overall plan, the east-campus library concentrates on science books while the west-campus library mainly holds books in the humanities.
Between them they hold 1,772,000 volumes in Chinese and foreign languages, in a floor area of 32,621 square metres.
The city beyond the campus gates shapes everyday student life: the weather you face, the transport you use and the places you can go. These sections introduce Changchun, the city that hosts CUST.

Changchun sits in the middle of the Northeast China Plain, in the zone between 43°05′ and 45°15′ north latitude and 124°18′ and 127°02′ east longitude. The municipality as a whole spans 20,571 km2 (7,943 sq mi). Inside it the metropolitan area is 2,583 square kilometres (997 sq mi) and the city proper only 159 km2 (61 sq mi). Altitude is modest: the administrative region sits between 250 and 350 metres (820 and 1,150 ft) above sea level. A small area of low mountains rises in the east, and the highest peak there is Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres. The city also lies at the crossing point of the third east-west "Europe-Asia Continental Bridge". The prefecture has 222 rivers and lakes. The one that crosses the city proper is the Yitong River, a minor feeder of the Songhua.

The climate is humid continental, with four seasons and the influence of the monsoon (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). The key fact for newcomers is the winter. It is long, lasting from November to March, and cold and windy but dry, because of the Siberian anticyclone, and January averages −14.3 °C (6.3 °F). Dress seriously for it.
Spring and autumn are short transition seasons, with some rain but mostly dry, windy weather.
Summer is hot and humid; the East Asian monsoon blows in from the southeast. The July average temperature is 23.7 °C (74.7 °F).
Snow is generally light in winter, and most of the year's rain falls between June and August.

Sunshine is greatest in February, at 69 percent of possible hours, and least in July, at 49 percent. In a typical year the city gets about 2,597 sunshine hours, and the stretch free of frost is 140 to 150 days. Records stand at −36.5 °C (−34 °F) for the cold, set on 4 January 1970, and 38.0 °C (100 °F) for the heat, set on 9 July 1951.

The Sixth China Census recorded 7.677 million people in the city in 2010, and an estimate for 2011 put it at 7.59 million. Births numbered 6.08 per thousand people and deaths 5.51 per thousand. 3.53 million lived in the urban area, and in 2010 there were 102.10 men to every 100 women.
As in most of northeast China, Han people dominate, at 96.57 percent, with several minority nationalities making up the rest.

Most residents speak Northeastern Mandarin, a dialect that began as a blend of languages brought by settlers from Hebei and Shandong. After the People's Republic was founded, rapid economic growth drew large numbers of migrants from other regions, and they had a strong effect on speech in the urban areas. As a result, the dialect in the city is closer to standard Mandarin than the dialect in the countryside.

Changchun has four main religions: Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam, with 396 government-approved places of worship and religious activity. The Buddhist and Taoist temples include Changchun Wanshou Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple, Pumen Temple, Big Buddha Temple and Changchun Temple. For Christians there are the Changchun Catholic Church and the Changchun West Wuma Road Christian Church, and Muslims have the Changchun City Mosque.
Shamanism spread through northeast China in ancient times and many Manchus followed it. Today it and its study are an important part of the region's cultural heritage.

Jilin Provincial Museum is a national first-grade museum, and it came to Changchun from Jilin City after the provincial government's seat was moved. It was once in the middle of the old town. A new home for the collections, which took nine years to build, was finished in 2016 out on the edge of the city, in Nanguan District close to Jingyuetan Park.

Badabu is a cluster of buildings that housed eight ministries under the Manchukuo regime: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs and Civil Affairs. It has lately become a sightseeing highlight because of its distinctive architecture that blends Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian styles.
To the southeast of the city lies Jingyuetan National Forest Park, one of China's AAAAA-rated tourist attractions. Vasaloppet China, a cross-country ski event, is held there every year.

Gross domestic product (GDP) in 2010 was RMB332.9 billion, up 15.3 percent from the year before. Farming and related primary output increased by 3.3 percent (to RMB25.27 billion). Secondary industry increased 19.0 percent and reached RMB171.99 billion, while services and other tertiary output grew by 12.6 percent to RMB135.64 billion. For 2012, GDP per head was ¥58,691 (about $9,338), and total GDP was RMB445.66 billion, 12.0 percent higher than in 2011. For that year, secondary industry grew 13.1 percent and reached RMB229.19 billion, and tertiary industry gained 11.8 percent to reach RMB184.76 billion. Primary industry, at RMB31.71 billion, expanded 4.3 percent (the original figures state this as an increase of RMB229.19 billion, which appears to be the sector's value rather than the increase).

The main industries are automobile manufacturing, processing of farm products, biopharmaceuticals, photo electronics, construction materials and energy. Changchun is the biggest centre in China for car manufacturing and research, and in 2009 it produced 9 percent of the country's cars. It is home to FAW (First Automotive Works) Group, China's largest vehicle maker, which built the first Chinese truck in 1956 and the first Chinese car in 1958. FAW's factories, housing and services take up a large part of the city's southwest end. The Red Flag luxury marque is made here, as are cars from joint ventures involving Audi, Volkswagen and Toyota. FAW sold 2.65 million vehicles in 2012, and revenue reached RMB 408.46 billion, up 10.8% on the year before. The city's nickname, "China's Detroit", comes from this role as the cradle of the auto industry.

Transport equipment and machinery are also leading sectors. Half of China's passenger trains come from Changchun, as do one tractor in ten nationally. Changchun Railway Vehicles, a main division of CRRC, works with Bombardier Transportation in a joint venture to build Movia metro cars for the Guangzhou, Shanghai and Tianjin metros.

In 2016 CRRC Changchun showed the world's first bullet train carriages with sleeping berths, so that fast trains can run overnight across China. Nicknamed "Panda", the new trains run at 250 km/h, work at −40 degrees Celsius and have Wi-Fi, and their berths fold into seats during the day. CRRC builds most of its bullet-train carriages at its Changchun factory.

Foreign direct investment reached US$3.68 billion in 2012, a rise of 19.6% on the previous year. Coca-Cola opened a bottling plant in the city's economic and technological development zone in 2004 with an investment of US$20 million. The city also hosts annual events: the Changchun International Automobile Fair, the Changchun Film Festival, the Changchun Agricultural Fair, an education exhibition and a sculpture exhibition.

Two other large companies are worth knowing. Yatai Group started in 1993, and by 1995 its shares were listed in Shanghai. It has become a big conglomerate with interests in property, cement, securities, coal, pharmaceuticals and trade. Jilin Grain Group, by contrast, is a leading processor of grain.

The first is the Changchun Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone. It began in 1993 as the Changchun Automotive Trade Center, and in 1996 it was re-established under its present name. It lies in the southwest, next to the FAW Group and the Changchun Film ThemeCity, and has a footprint of about 300,000 square metres, or 3,229,173 square feet. The zone contains an exhibition centre and five specially marked industrial centres. The Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center, which started work in 1994, is China's largest wholesale centre for vehicles and spare parts. The other centres handle used cars, industrial and commercial vehicles, and tyres.

The second is the Changchun High Technology Development Zone, one of the first 27 national advanced technology zones. It lies in the south of the city and covers 49 km2 (19 sq mi). It is home to 18 full-time universities and colleges, 39 state and provincial research institutions and 11 key national laboratories. It focuses on five industries: bio-engineering, automobile engineering, new materials, photo-electricity and information technology.

The third is the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone, established in April 1993, which has the same preferential policies as the zones in coastal open cities. Its total area is 112.72 square kilometres (43.52 square miles); about 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of that is reserved for development and use. It is 5 kilometres (3 miles) from downtown, the freight rail station 2 km (1.2 mi) and the international airport 15 km (9 mi). Its five lead industries are auto parts and components, photoelectric information, biopharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials. High-tech, high value-added projects make up over 80 percent of output. In 2006 fixed-asset investment in the zone rose to RMB38.4 billion, and of 1656 registered enterprises, 179 are foreign-funded. Industrial output reached RMB 277 billion in 2007.

Because Changchun is a major grain base and a regional air and rail hub, it has also built an Aviation Food Industrialization Base, which supplies prepared meals to several airlines and researches food science for long-haul flights, a niche sector.

Changchun has two major passenger stations. The central Changchun station (长春站) takes all conventional trains and some high-speed ones, and lines such as the Beijing–Harbin Railway and the Changchun–Hunchun intercity railway meet there. Trains leave several times a day for places in Jilin and the northeast (Jilin City, Yanji, Harbin, Shenyang and Dalian) and for large cities across the country, including Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. The newer Changchun West station, at the western edge of the built-up area, mainly serves high-speed trains on the Harbin–Dalian high-speed railway. Changchun East is a small station in Erdao District on the Changchun–Tumen line.
Over 250 bus routes serve the city. A ride usually costs between 1 and 2 yuan.

Changchun is one of the few Chinese cities to keep its historic tram. The system opened in 1941 and at its peak had 6 lines covering almost 53 km. After a number of route changes, one line has remained since the 2000s. In 2014 a new branch line opened, linking the new Changchun West Railway Station, and the whole system now runs as part of the bus network.

Changchun Rail Transit mixes light rail and metro lines. The first line opened on 30 October 2002, which made Changchun the fifth Chinese city to open rail transit. By November 2018 five lines (1, 2, 3, 4 and 8) covered about 100.17 kilometres. In September 2019, four projects were under construction: Lines 6 and 9, the Line 2 west extension and the Line 3 east extension. By 2025 the network is planned to consist of ten lines, which together would run for 341.62 kilometres.
In September 2019 the network carried an average of 680,400 passengers a day, and its busiest day, 13 November 2019, saw 830,500. Total passengers for 2019 were estimated at about 168 million.

The city joins the national highway system through five expressways: the Beijing–Harbin (G1), the Ulanhot–Changchun–Jilin–Hunchun (G12), the Changchun–Shenzhen (G25) and the Changchun–Changbaishan (S1), along with the Changchun–Jilin North Highway, the busiest section in the province. That last link joins Jilin's two biggest cities and carries most of the social and economic traffic between them.
Private cars are increasingly common and city streets are congested. Bicycles are comparatively rare next to other cities in northeast China, but mopeds are quite common, and so are pedal bikes.

Changchun Longjia International Airport lies 31.2 kilometres (19.4 miles) northeast of the urban area. Construction began in 1998 to replace the older Dafangshen Airport, a joint-use field built in 1941. The new airport opened for passengers on 27 August 2005 and is shared by Changchun and neighbouring Jilin City.

The Nature Index 2024 Science Cities ranks Changchun among the top 30 cities in the world for scientific research. It has 27 regular full-time tertiary institutions with roughly 160,000 students in total. Two of them, Jilin University and Northeast Normal University, count among China's key universities, and Jilin University has over 60,000 students, which makes it one of the largest in the country.
Comprehensive and teacher-training universities: Jilin University and Northeast Normal University, along with Changchun Normal University, Changchun University and Jilin Engineering Normal University

Specialist universities: Changchun University of Science and Technology (the subject of this overview), the Changchun Institute of Technology, Jilin Agricultural University, the Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, and arts education at Jilin College of the Arts
A private college, Jilin Huaqiao Foreign Languages Institute, offers bachelor's study in foreign languages, trade management and teaching methods (didactics).
Well-known schools in the city include:
Changchun Foreign Languages School, which may interest families with children
Changchun No. 6 Middle School
No. 11 High School of Changchun
Jilin Province's Second Experimental School
No. 72 Middle School of Changchun
The middle school affiliated to Jilin University
The high school attached to Northeast Normal University
Changchun University of Science and Technology lists 220 programs for international students on this site: 51 bachelor, 48 master's, 36 doctoral, 85 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 157 taught in Chinese, 63 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,200 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 29,000 to CNY 29,000 (median CNY 29,000), according to the university's published fee table.

219 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (23):
Artificial Intelligence
