The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

changchun-university-of-science-and-tech.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Changchun University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Changchun, register at Changchun University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Changsha University of Science and Technology (CSUST, Changsha Ligong Daxue) is a public university in Changsha, the capital of Hunan province in central-southern China. It belongs to the provincial system and is jointly sponsored by the Hunan provincial government and the national Ministry of Transport. In the 2022 edition of the Best Chinese Universities Ranking (often called the Shanghai Ranking) it placed fifth among universities in Hunan.

After about 57 years of development, CSUST presents itself as a comprehensive university whose core is engineering, surrounded by science, law, the arts and humanities, economics and management. Undergraduate teaching is its stronghold, but it also hosts post-doctoral research workstations, awards doctoral degrees and can recommend its graduates for master's study. Official honours it has won include the Hunan Provincial Model Unit of Civility and a national award for its grassroots Party organisation. Nearly 200,000 graduates have come out of the university, and most work in transportation, power, water-related industries and light industry, contributing to regional and national economic development.

CSUST has 16 teaching schools or departments, one independent college and one continuing education college, and recruits students from all 31 provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions of China. There are more than 30,000 registered full-time undergraduates and about 4,700 doctoral and master's candidates. The academic offer includes 30 undergraduate majors, two post-doctoral workstations, three disciplines and 15 sub-disciplines authorised to award doctorates, and, at master's level, 20 disciplines with 105 sub-disciplines plus seven professional degree authorisations.

For research and teaching the university counts 27 natural-science innovation platforms (national engineering laboratories, innovation teams, provincial or ministerial key laboratories and engineering research centres), 10 provincial platforms for philosophy and social sciences, and eleven disciplines designated as key ones by the province or a ministry. It also reports 17 undergraduate teaching projects, among them a national talent-cultivation pilot, teaching teams, experiment and practice centres, characteristic disciplines, elaborate courses and bilingual demonstration courses.

The campuses are Jinpenling and Yuntang, with 210.56 hectares of land and 1,170,000 square metres of floor space. Fixed assets total 2.4 billion yuan, of which teaching and research apparatus is worth 300 million yuan. The library has over 2,960,000 books, 3,192 domestic and foreign periodicals and 4,285 GB of e-books. A gigabit backbone network has been installed, along with part of the core network systems. Altogether the multimedia classrooms and language labs have 16,642 seats. For sport there is a ground of 213,700 square metres, of which 34,500 is under cover.

changsha-university-of-science-and-techn.h: How it is ranked and connected

blocks.x: In 2021 the Academic Ranking of World Universities placed CSUST in the 701 to 800 band. In 2022 U.S. News and World Report, in its Best Global Universities table, listed it at 372 worldwide, 69 in Asia and 36 in China. On the international side, CSUST works with 66 universities and research bodies. They are located in over 40 countries and regions, among them Liberia, South Korea, Russia, Canada, France, Britain, the USA and Hong Kong.

The city occupies north-eastern Hunan, in the western Changliu Basin along the lower Xiang River, and falls between longitudes 111 degrees 53 minutes and 114 degrees 15 minutes east and latitudes 27 degrees 51 minutes and 28 degrees 41 minutes north. Its neighbours are Yichun and Pingxiang (Jiangxi) to the east, Zhuzhou and Xiangtan to the south, Loudi and Yiyang to the west and Yueyang and Yiyang to the north. It is about 230 kilometres wide from east to west and 88 kilometres from north to south, with a total area of 11,819 square kilometres (4,563 square miles); of that, 2,150.9 square kilometres is the urban area and 374.64 square kilometres the built-up urban zone. The highest point is Mount Qixing in Daweishan Town, at 1,607.9 metres (5,275 feet), and the lowest is Zhanhu in Qiaokou Town, at 23.5 metres (77 feet).

changsha-university-of-science-and-techn.h: The river that splits the city

blocks.x: The main river is the Xiang, which flows 74 kilometres north through the territory and is fed by 15 tributaries. Four of them are the biggest: the Liuyang, Laodao, Jinjiang and Wei. The Xiang divides the city: the east bank is mostly commercial and the west bank mostly cultural and educational. On 10 October 2001 the city government moved from Fanzheng Street to Guanshaling, and since then both banks have developed in a more balanced way.

Water statistics show how dense the river system is. Most Changsha rivers belong to the Xiang system, and the Xiang's tributaries include the Liuyang, Laodao, Minjiang and Qinshui. A total of 302 tributaries are longer than five kilometres, 289 of them in the Xiang basin. By grade, there are 24 primary, 128 secondary, 118 third-level and 32 other tributaries, and 13 belong to the Zijiang system. In short, the network is complete and dense, the water volume is large, hydropower potential is rich, the rivers do not freeze in winter and the sediment content is low.

Geologically, strata from every period are exposed in Changsha, granite is widespread and the structure is complicated. The oldest rocks formed about a billion years ago. Some 600 million years ago the area was a shallow sea. The sea withdrew from both east and west, leaving most of the Liuyang, Changsha and Wangcheng areas above water as the north-western fringe of the ancient Jiangnan landmass. About 140 million years ago the marine influence ended and the area turned to land. Crustal movement created a long mountain-ringed depression, the Changping Basin (Chang-Sha and Ping-Jiang), which rose as a whole in the Cenozoic. About 3.5 million years ago, during the third ice age, Liuyang kept traces of glacier landforms.

Changsha has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen Cfa). The yearly average is 17.8 degrees C, with 5.3 degrees C in January and 29.4 degrees C in July. Although the city lies at 28 degrees north, its January temperatures match London and Paris, which are about 20 degrees farther from the equator. Annual rainfall is 1,499 millimetres, with 275 frost-free days. Possible sunshine runs from 20 per cent in January to 53 per cent in July, and the annual total of bright sunshine is 1,532.8 hours.

The four seasons are distinct. Summers are long, very hot and rainy. Autumn is pleasant and the driest season. Winter is cold and overcast, with light rain more likely than downpours, and cold spells sometimes bring temperatures below freezing. Spring is notably wet and humid, with sunshine less than 30 per cent of the time. At the current Wangchengpo observing station the lowest temperature since 1951 was minus 11.3 degrees C (9 February 1972), and the highest 40.6 degrees C (twice: 13 August 1953 and 2 August 2003); an unofficial 43.0 degrees C was set on 10 August 1934. Expect a damp, chilly winter and pack accordingly.

Changsha is listed among the fifteen most advanced and developed cities in China. In 2024 its GDP per person went beyond 144,525 yuan, equal to 20,294 US dollars at nominal rates or 42,136 dollars on a purchasing-power basis, a level the World Bank regards as high income and that international standards treat as a developed city. Its human development index was 0.817 in 2016, which is rated very high. Changsha has a central role in South Central China, in the Yangtze River Economic Belt and in the Belt and Road Initiative; the Globalization and World Cities Research Network gives it Beta-minus status (global second tier); it is classed as a new first-tier city in China, and it leads in trade and economic cooperation with Africa. Nicknamed the world's capital of construction machinery, its industry rests on two pillars, machinery and new materials, with automobiles, electronics and information technology, home appliances and biomedicine as additional sectors.

Growth picked up from the 1990s onward and during the 2000s was the highest among China's big cities. In 2015 the Xiangjiang New Area was established, Central China's first national-level new area. Media and publishing are strong too, and Changsha was named China's first UNESCO City of Media Arts. The city hosts Hunan Broadcasting System (HBS), which is China's most influential provincial television channel.

The financial portal Yicai.com included Changsha among 15 new first-tier cities in the first edition of its ranking in 2013. In 2017 the city joined the one-trillion-yuan GDP club (154 billion US dollars), the 13th Chinese city to do so. By 2020 over 164 Global 500 firms had opened branches in the city, and in 2022 it ranked tenth nationally for commercial worth among new first-tier cities.

In 2021 GDP exceeded 1.327 trillion yuan (208 billion dollars nominal, 318 billion in PPP). With that figure Changsha was fifth in wealth within South Central China, following Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Wuhan, and second in Central China, behind only Wuhan. Its 208 billion dollars of nominal GDP topped that of Ukraine (200 billion) and Hungary (182 billion), which stand 22nd and 23rd among European economies. The city is also strong in nightlife commerce: a 2021-2022 impact report on China's city night economy placed it second, with only Chongqing ahead.

The Hurun Global Rich List placed Changsha among the world's top 35 cities in 2022. In 2024 it was first in Central China and ninth in Greater China for resident billionaires, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Hangzhou, Taipei, Guangzhou and Ningbo. An Oxford Economics study projects that its nominal GDP will be among the world's top 50 cities in 2035 and its GDP per head will reach 41,000 dollars in 2030.

The Changsha Economic and Technological Development Zone dates from 1992 and lies in Xingsha, eastern Changsha. Its planned and current area are both 38.6 square kilometres. National Highways 319 and 107 and the G4 Beijing-Hong Kong and Macau Expressway run nearby, the zone is close to downtown and the railway station, and the airport is only 8 kilometres (5.0 miles) away. Its main industries are high technology, biotechnology and new materials.

Created on 10 January 1998 as a national centre for the biological industry, the Liuyang Economic and Technological Development Zone sits in Dongyang Town. Its pillars are biopharmaceuticals, information technology and health food. By 2015 it had more than 700 registered enterprises, industrial output value of 85.6 billion yuan (13.7 billion dollars), business income of 100.2 billion yuan (16.1 billion dollars) and a built-up area of 16.5 square kilometres (6.4 square miles).

Xiang embroidery now has an artificial-intelligence studio, set up by the Hunan Embroidery Research Institute together with nearby technology firms. Algorithms examine old patterns and suggest new designs, which assists embroiderers and brings this intangible cultural heritage up to date.

Tourism is a major industry, and Changsha has repeatedly been ranked China's top tourist city. Among the places worth visiting is the Yuelu Academy. Overlooking Meixi Lake in Meixihu subdistrict stands a cultural complex, the Changsha Meixihu International Culture and Arts Centre, designed by the British firm Zaha Hadid Architects. Other sites are the young Mao Zedong statue on Orange Isle, Meixi Lake Park, Kaifu Temple, the IFS Tower, Window of the World and the Ice World.

The mountain takes its name from the Nanyue Ji, a work of the Liu Song era in the Southern and Northern Dynasties, which says that Nanyue extends eight hundred miles with Huiyan at the head and Yuelu at the foot. It stands on the west bank of the Xiang in Yuelu District. In the scenic area there are 977 plant species in 559 genera and 174 families, mostly typical subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest and warm-temperate conifer forest, with large patches of native secondary evergreen broad-leaved forest in places and many precious endangered and ancient trees.

Orange Island sits in the middle of the Xiang River in Yuelu District, with Yuelu Mountain to the west and the old city to the east. The island began with only 17 hectares or so; the scenic area as developed is now 91.64 hectares in extent. Of the many sandbars in the lower Xiang, this is the biggest, and it has the nickname China's First Continent. Attractions include the Mao Zedong Youth Art Sculpture and Wen Tiantai. Historical records say the island formed in 305, the second year of Yongxing under Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, as rapids deposited sand and gravel.
Huaminglou, in the south-east of Ningxiang City, is a well-known national key cultural relic site. It was the former home of the revolutionary leader and former president Liu Shaoqi.

The Hunan Museum is at 50 Dongfeng Road, Kaifu District. It belongs to the first group of national first-level museums, is one of eight key national museums built jointly by the central government and localities, and is Hunan's biggest museum of history and art combined. The Hunan Provincial Museum began in 1897 (the 23rd year of the Guangxu reign in the Qing dynasty), and the current building is its new home.

The 2020 census counted 10,047,914 people in Changsha, with 7,355,198 in the built-up area of six urban districts plus Changsha County, which are largely joined together. Most residents are Han Chinese. The largest minority groups are the Hui, Tujia and Miao. In the 2000 census 48,564 people belonged to ethnic minorities, 0.7 per cent of the population, and twenty minorities each had fewer than 1,000 members in the city.

Hunan Broadcasting System, headquartered in Changsha, is China's biggest television broadcaster after CCTV and makes some of the country's most popular shows, such as Super Girl. These programmes helped create an entertainment industry that includes singing bars, dance clubs, theatre shows, hair salons, fashion shops and stalls selling hot spicy snacks at night, especially in summer. Changsha is now an entertainment hub, increasingly westernised, and attracts a growing number of foreigners.

Helong Stadium holds 55,000 and is among the biggest all-purpose stadiums in China; it carries the name of He Long, a Communist military commander. Hunan Billows F.C., who play in China League Two, use it as their home ground. The smaller Hunan Provincial People's Stadium (6,000 seats) is used for the team's lesser games.

CSUST is a mid-sized provincial engineering-led university with strong links to transport and power, in a city that is wealthy, youthful and media-minded. Look for current data on programmes and fees on the university website, because some statistics here are from 2015 to 2022.

changsha-university-of-science-and-techn.h: Practical points for a prospective student

blocks.x: Several details in this profile affect everyday planning. The university's two campuses, Jinpenling and Yuntang, together cover 210.56 hectares, so ask which one your programme uses. The Xiang River divides Changsha into a commercial east and a cultural and educational west, and since the city government moved to Guanshaling in 2001 both banks have developed in step, which means you can expect good facilities on either side. The airport is close to the Changsha Economic and Technological Development Zone (8 kilometres), and the railway station is near downtown, so arrival is simple.

Weather deserves attention. Summers are long, very hot and rainy, spring is damp with little sun, and winter is chilly and overcast with the occasional freeze, even though the city lies much farther south than London or Paris. Autumn is the most comfortable and driest season, and is probably the best time for a first visit.

Finally, keep in mind that rankings and statistics come from different years (2015, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024). The university's own website is the best source for the latest number of programmes, fees, scholarships and the support available for international students.

changsha-university-of-science-and-techn.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Changsha University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Changsha, register at Changsha University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

The Chengdu University of Technology (CDUT; 成都理工大学) is a national public research university located in Chengdu, Sichuan, China. It is a technology-focused institution co-funded by the Ministry of Education of China, the Ministry of Natural Resources of China, and the Sichuan Provincial People's Government. The university is part of the Double First-Class Construction Initiative. CDUT was established in 1956 on the basis of geology-related faculties from Chongqing University, Nanjing University, Northwest University, Beijing Institute of Geology (now China University of Geosciences), Northeast College of Geology (now Jilin University), and Jiao Tong University.

The university covers an area of 1.92 square kilometers. There are 23 colleges, 1 Institute of Sedimentary Geology, and 1 Institute of Geological Survey. The university was recognized as one of China's National Top 50 Universities for Graduate Employment and National Top 50 Universities for Innovation and Entrepreneurship. CDUT ranked within the 601-700 band globally in the 2025 Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU).

Chengdu Institute of Geology, the predecessor of Chengdu University of Technology, was founded in 1956, based on the combination of geology-related faculties of Chongqing University, Nanjing University, Northwest University, former Beijing Institute of Geology (China University of Geosciences), former Northeast College of Geology (Jilin University), former Jiaotong University, etc., with the approval of the State Council of the People's Republic of China.

In 1993, Chengdu Institute of Geology renamed to Chengdu Institute of Technology. Chengdu Institute of Technology (Chengdu Institute of Geology) was a key university under the administration of the Ministry of Land and Resources of China (now the Ministry of Natural Resources of China).

In 2001, Chengdu Institute of Technology renamed to Chengdu University of Technology (CDUT). It is a state key university jointly-administered by the Ministry of Education of China, the Ministry of Natural Resources of China, and the Provincial Government of Sichuan. CDUT is included in the Chinese national Double First-Class Initiative and approved as a Double First Class University.

CDUT is located in Central Chengdu, at the heart of Chenghua District. The main campus occupies an area of approximately 1.92 km2. The campus is served by the Chengdu University of Technology Station on the Line 7 and Line 8 of Chengdu Metro.

In the 2010s, CDUT has invited Nobel Prize laureates and a large number of experts and scholars to give lectures. The university recruits foreign experts to set up courses for undergraduates and postgraduate students on a regular basis and bring them into the talent training system.

CDUT is included in the National Scholarship Council's innovation program and other national projects. The university has established exchanges and cooperation with more than 180 universities and scientific research institutions in Australia, Britain, Canada, Italy, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Russia, the United States, and other countries.

CDUT began to carry out in-depth cooperation with several British universities in 2005, and it is one of the earliest universities in China to set up Sino-foreign dual-degree education programs. In 2013, Chengdu University of Technology and the University of Edinburgh signed a memorandum of cooperation in education. The two universities carry out the '2+2' dual-degree education program in several undergraduate majors, including Geology, Geology and Physical Geography, Geophysics, Geophysics and Meteorology, Geophysics and Geology, Environmental Geoscience, etc. Students study in Chengdu University of Technology for the first two years of undergraduate courses, and then go to the University of Edinburgh for further studies. After completing the rest two years of undergraduate courses, the students can obtain graduation certificate and degree from Chengdu University of Technology and degree from the University of Edinburgh.

CDUT is one of a limited number of universities with both first-level and second-level national key disciplines in China. In 1988, when the first batch of National Key Disciplines were appraised and reviewed, CDUT's two disciplines were rated as first National Key Disciplines. After the merges and restructures of disciplines made by the Chinese Ministry of Education in the following years, the university has 1 first-level National Key Discipline (Geological Resources and Geological Engineering) and 4 second-level National Key Disciplines by 2008.

Approximately 36,000 students are enrolled in the year 2022. By July 2026, the university has 3,550 teaching and administrative staff, including 4 research teams of fellows of Chinese Academy of Science, 731 professors and 869 associate professors.

CDUT has international cooperative relationships and exchanges with more than 60 universities and institutions outside China. More than 2,800 scholars and experts from over 40 countries have visited CDUT to conduct research or to lecture by 2019. Students from the United States, Australia, Germany, Austria, Korea, Japan, Russia and other countries have studied at CDUT in different fields. Over 300 international cooperative research projects have been completed. In recent years, the university has successfully held several international academic conferences.

The CDUT museum, with more than 100,000 specimens, is the largest natural museums in West China. Many world and national class treasures are on display. Among these treasures, the 22 meter long Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis, the world's longest-necked Jurassic dinosaur's fossil, is the highlight of the museum. Another notable treasure is the Chungkingichthys tachuenses, a rare complete fish fossil. The new landmark CDUT Museum, connected with the Shilidian Station of Chengdu Metro Line 8, opened in September 2022.

The CDUT library holds 2,756,000 paper volumes, 2,597,000 electronic books, and over 48,000 electronic-journals. Additionally, the library has subscribed to 90 well-known databases including SCI, Elsevier, CNKI, etc. CDUT's East Library has opened since 2016, providing additional 6000 seats.

By 2025, CDUT has received a total of 1,222 national, provincial and ministerial science and technology awards, including 1 Grand Prize of the National Science and Technology Progress Award, 4 First Prizes of the National Science and Technology Progress Award, 1 China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award, 1 Second Prize of the National Natural Science Award, 9 Second Prizes of the National Science and Technology Progress Award, 1 China Patent Award, 9 National Technological Invention Awards and Third Prizes of the National Science and Technology Progress Award. As of 2019 more than 1920 patents have been granted to CDUT.

The university participates in the key national projects including west-to-east power transmission, west–east gas transmission, south-to-north water diversion, Sichuan-Tibet railway, oil and gas geological exploration, energy development, large-scale hydropower station, regional and urban environment protection, as well as other national large-scale transportation infrastructure projects.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Chengdu, where Chengdu University of Technology is located.
The vast plain on which Chengdu is located has an elevation ranging from 450 to 720 meters (1,480 to 2,360 feet).

Northwest Chengdu is bordered by the high and steep Longmen Mountains in the north-west and in the west by the Qionglai Mountains, the elevation of which exceeds 3,000 m (9,800 ft) and includes Miao Jiling (5,364 m, 17,598 ft) and Xiling Snow Mountain (5,164 m, 16,942 ft). The western mountainous area is also home to a large primitive forest with abundant biological resources and a giant panda habitat. East of Chengdu stands the low Longquan Mountains and the west bordering area of the hilly land of the middle reaches of Min River, an area noted by several converging rivers. Since ancient times, Chengdu has been known as "the Abundant Land" owing to its fertile soil, favorable climate, and novel Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

Chengdu is located at the western edge of the Sichuan Basin and sits on the Chengdu Plain; the dominating terrain is plains. The prefecture ranges in latitude from 30° 05' to 31° 26' N, while its longitude ranges from 102° 54' to 104° 53' E, stretching for 192 kilometers (119 mi) from east to west and 166 km (103 mi) south to north, administering 12,390 km2 (4,780 sq mi) of land. Neighboring prefectures are Deyang (NE), Ziyang (SE), Meishan (S), Ya'an (SW), and the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture (N). The urban area, with an elevation of 500 m (1,600 ft), features a few rivers, three of them being the Jin, Fu, and Sha Rivers. Outside of the immediate urban area, the topography becomes more complex: to the east lies the Longquan Mountains (龙泉山脉) and the Penzhong Hills (Chinese: 盆中丘陵); to the west lie the Qionglai Mountains, which rise to 5,364 m (17,598 ft) in Dayi County. The highest point in Chengdu is Daxuetang (also known as Miaojiling) in Xiling Snow Mountain, Dayi County, at an altitude of 5,364 meters. The lowest point is the riverbank at the exit of the Tuojiang River in Jianyang City, with an altitude of 359 meters.

Chengdu has a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa) and is largely warm, with high relative humidity year-round. It has four distinct seasons, with moderate rainfall concentrated mainly in the warmer months, relieving both sweltering summers and freezing winters. The Qin Mountains (Qinling) to the far north help shield the city from cold Siberian winds in the winter; because of this, the short winter is milder than in the Lower Yangtze. The daily mean temperature in January is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F), and snow is rare, though there are a few periods of frost each winter. The summer is hot and humid, but not to the extent of the "Three Furnaces" cities of Chongqing, Wuhan, and Nanjing, all of which lie in the Yangtze basin. The 24-hour daily mean temperature in July and August is around 25 °C (77 °F), with afternoon highs sometimes reaching 33 °C (91 °F); sustained heat as found in much of eastern China is rare. Rainfall occurs most frequently in July and August, with very little in the cooler months. Chengdu also has one of the lowest annual sunshine totals nationally, with less sunshine annually than much of Northern Europe. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 15 percent in December to 32 percent in August, the city receives 1006 hours of bright sunshine annually. Spring (March–April) tends to be sunnier and warmer in the day than autumn (October–November). The annual mean is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F), and extremes have ranged from −6.5 °C (20 °F) to 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).

In 1988, the Implementation Plan for a Gradual Housing System Reform in Cities and Towns marked the beginning of overall housing reform in China's urban areas. More than 20 real estate companies set up in Chengdu, which was the first step for Chengdu's real estate development.

The comprehensive Funan River renovation project in the 1990s was another step towards promoting Chengdu's environmental development. The Funan River Comprehensive Improvement Project won the UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour Award in 1998, as well as winning the "Local Initiative Award" by the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives in 2000.

Construction of the Five Main Roads & One Bridge project began in 1997. Three roads served the eastern part of the city; the other two led south. It established the foundation of the Eastern and Southern sub-centers of Chengdu. The two major sub-centers determined people's eastward and southward living trends. Large numbers of buildings appeared around the east and south of the 2nd Ring Road. The Shahe River renovation project, along with the Jin River project, also sparked a trend among residents living along both rivers. It was said that the map of Chengdu should be updated every three months.

A speculative housing boom occurred in the late 1990s and early 2000s. In 2000, dozens of commercial real estate projects also appeared. While promoting the real estate market, the Chinese government encouraged citizens to buy their own houses by providing considerable subsidies for a certain period. Houses were included in commodities.

As of February 2026, the world's third-largest building by floor area, the New Century Global Center, is located in the city. The 100-meter-tall (330 ft) structure is 500 by 400 meters (1,600 by 1,300 ft) in size with 1,700,000 square meters (18,000,000 sq ft) of floor area, housing retail outlets, a movie theaters, offices, hotels, a water park with artificial beach and waves and a Mediterranean-style village comprising a large 5-star hotel, a skating rink and a 15,000-spot parking area.

According to the 2020 Chinese census, the municipality had 20,937,757 inhabitants; the metropolitan area itself was home to 16,045,577 inhabitants, including those of the 12 urban districts plus Guanghan City (in Deyang). Chengdu is the largest city in Sichuan and the fourth largest in China. 21,192,000 for 2021, adding more residents than any other city in the country.
As of 2015, the OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) estimated the population of the Chengdu metropolitan area at 18.1 million.
In 2006, China Daily named Chengdu China's fourth-most-livable city.

Some of China's most important literature comes from Chengdu. The city has been home to literary giants, such as Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, two masters of Fu, a mixture of descriptive prose and verse during the Tang dynasty; Li Bai and Du Fu, the most eminent poets of the Tang and Song dynasties respectively; Yang Shen'an, a famous scholar of the Ming dynasty; and Guo Moruo and Ba Jin, two well-known modern writers. Chang Qu, a historian of Chengdu during the Jin dynasty, compiled the earliest local historical records, the Record of Hua Yang State. Zhao Chongzuo, a poet in Chengdu during the Later Shu Kingdom, edited Among the Flowers, the first anthology of Ci in China's history. Meng Chang, the king of Later Shu, wrote the first couplet for the Spring Festival, which says, "A harvest year accepts celebrations, good festivals foreshadow long springs."
In 2023, Chengdu hosted the 81st World Science Fiction Convention, having beat out Winnipeg, Canada, in site-selection voting in 2021.

During the period of the Five Dynasties, Huang Quan, a painter in Chengdu, initiated the Fine-Brush Flower-and-Bird Painting School with other painters. At that time, "Hanlin Painting Academy" was the earliest royal academy in China.
Islam has a long history in Sichuan dating to the Tang dynasty (618–907), 12 mosques are located in Chengdu. Huangcheng Mosque in the center of Chengdu dates from the 16th century.
Chengdu contains official, Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations, some of which are underground churches.

The Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan (now known as Diocese of Chengdu) was established on 15 October 1696. Artus de Lionne, a French missionary of Paris Foreign Missions Society, was appointed as the first Apostolic Vicar.

In 1890, the Canadian Methodist Mission was seeking additional stations in Asia. In February 1891, Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart, who had been Superintendent of the New York Methodist Mission Society of Central China, recommended at a meeting that Chengtu be the site of its first Mission. During the meeting, it was proposed that he lead the contingent to establish it, having built western hospitals as well as boys' and girls' schools at missions he established on the Yangtze and Gan Rivers 1866–88. On 9 May 1891, Hart arrived in Chengtu; two weeks later, he bought a home and had it subdivided into living quarters and a dispensary for the later-arriving Missionary staff to move into.

On 24 June 1892, the doors of Chengtu's first Protestant Mission Headquarters were opened, with over 1,000 people from the community in attendance. The first Methodist religious service was held the following Sunday, with only a few attendants. The first western dispensary in Sichuan was opened on 3 November 1892 with sixteen patients seeking care. The mission site became so popular that a larger space was secured near Chengtu's East Gate in the spring of 1893. This site is where the city's first Methodist church (Sï-Shen-Tsï Methodist Church) and hospital were built. These were later razed by rioting Chinese in 1895, and the Mission staff retreated to Chongqing and later Shanghai to escape the marauders. Dr. Virgil Hart traveled to Peking to demand redress, and full payment of retribution was collected from Sichuan Viceroy Liu Ping Chang. The mission compound was quickly rebuilt, only to be destroyed once more in the riots of 1901. These were rebuilt a second time and later missionaries would relocate and expand the Boys' and Girls' Schools just south of the city, dedicating the Divinity College as Hart College in 1914; a part of the West China Union University, that is now Sichuan University and the West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida). During the Cultural Revolution, the Sï-Shen-Tsï Methodist Church building was no longer in use and the building was entrusted to the nearby Chengdu City Second People's Hospital for management. The hospital used the chapel as a kindergarten and the office of the hospital equipment department. In 1984, the hospital returned the chapel building to the church.

In December 2018, the authorities attempted to close a 500-member underground church, the Early Rain Covenant Church, led by Pastor Wang Yi. Over 100 members of the church were arrested, including the pastor and his wife. The church's kindergarten and theological college were raided, and its media outlets were shut down. Before his arrest, church member Li Yingqiang declared, "Even if we are down to our last five, worship and gatherings will still go on because our faith is real. […] Persecution is a price worth paying for the Lord." Police are said to have told one member that the church had been declared an illegal organization. Chinese media were banned from reporting the events. Video footage, which found its way onto Western social media, showed arrests and photographs alleged to be of injuries inflicted by the police. From a photo of Ms. Jiang's detention warrant it appears that the authorities have charged the church's leaders with "inciting subversion of state power," which carries a maximum sentence of 15 years.
In 2012, a Chabad Jewish Center was established in Chengdu, after moving five times, a permanent location was secured at Wuhou District.

The saying "Shu opera towers above all other performances in the world" reflects the achievement of Sichuan opera and Zaju (an ancient form of comedic drama involving dancing, singing, poetry, and miming). In the city, the first opera, "Bullfighting," was written in the Warring States period. The first detailed opera was staged at the royal court of the Shu Kingdom during the Three Kingdoms period. China's first clearly recorded Zaju was also performed in Chengdu. Tombs of witty Han dynasty poets were excavated in Chengdu. And face-changing masks and fire breathing remain hallmarks of the Sichuan opera.
The native language in Chengdu is Chengdu dialect, a form of Sichuanese. The Chengdu dialect has been influential in Chinese comedy and rap music.

The distinct characteristic of Sichuan cuisine is the use of spicy chilies and peppercorns. Famous local dishes include Mapo doufu, Chengdu Hot pot, and Dan Dan Mien. Both Mapo Doufu and Dan Dan Mien contain Sichuan peppers. An article by the Los Angeles Times (2006) called Chengdu "China's party city" for its carefree lifestyle. Chengdu has more tea houses and bars than Shanghai despite having less than half the population. In 2023, there were more than 30,000 teahouses in Chengdu, and there were 3,566 legally registered bars, nightclubs, and dance halls in the city. A statistical report in 2019 showed that Chengdu had more bars than Shanghai, becoming the city with the most bars in China. Chengdu's tea culture dates back over a thousand years, including its time as the starting point of the Southern Silk Road.
Chengdu is officially recognized and named by UNESCO as the "City of Gastronomy".

Tea houses are ubiquitous in the city, ranging from ornate traditional establishments with bamboo furniture to simple modern ones. Teas on offer include jasmine, longjing and biluochun tea. Tea houses are popular venues for playing mahjong, getting a massage, or having one's ears cleaned. Some larger tea houses offer live entertainment such as Sichuan opera performances.

Chengdu is known for its hot pot. Hot pot is a traditional Sichuanese dish, made by cooking vegetables, fish, and/or meat in boiling spicy broth. A type of food suitable for a gathering of friends, hot pot attracts both locals and tourists. Hot pot restaurants can be found throughout Chengdu.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chengdu, register at Chengdu University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (成都中医药大学, abbreviated CDUTCM) is a public university in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province, with a specialism in traditional Chinese medicine, or TCM. It is part of the Sichuan provincial system, yet three bodies sponsor it together: the Ministry of Education, the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the provincial government. It also takes part in the national Double First-Class Construction scheme.

The starting point was 1956, when it opened under the name Chengdu Traditional Chinese Medicine College (成都中医学院). It was among the four earliest TCM institutions of higher education set up in the People's Republic. In 1995 it was granted university status and took its present name.

The university teaches from undergraduate level up through master's and doctorate, and it offers short-term as well as long-term programmes, for both local and international students. Beyond TCM itself it also teaches engineering, management, literature and agricultural subjects. The campus covers 130 hectares and the university offers more than 50 majors.

Its main aim is to train high-quality TCM professionals for China and for other countries. Specialities range widely. They include Chinese pharmacy for those who want to become pharmacists, pharmaceutical engineering, nursing, management, marketing and Tibetan medicine, and the practice of Chinese medicine in clinics, using herbs and traditional treatments. It is a national base that combines TCM education, research and medical care. A TCM degree therefore does not lock you into one job: graduates can follow specialist paths such as pharmacy.

The materials describing the university give an unclear picture of where graduates go next, saying only that some continue their studies elsewhere, including in Shanghai. If further study matters to you, ask the university for details.

CDUTCM is one of the first universities in China allowed to confer master's and doctoral degrees and to run postdoctoral workstations. It can confer 16 doctoral degrees and 27 master's degrees, and it has 2 postdoctoral workstations, in Chinese pharmacy and in Chinese medicine.

Three national key courses are named: Chinese pharmacy, TCM ear-nose-throat, and acupuncture and moxibustion with tuina. There are 14 provincial key courses. The university also lists 3 key laboratories of the Ministry of Education, 7 grade-three laboratories of the TCM Administration and 5 provincial key laboratories. One figure for provincial key courses is given as 16 in another place, so numbers like these vary between descriptions and may have changed; the university's website has the current figures.

Courses for local students are mainly taught in Chinese, so Chinese ability matters if you want to join a regular programme. Inside the large campus, teaching follows the TCM tradition and is spread over 12 sub-colleges, with students studying their specialised majors in the relevant college rather than all together in one place.

As for staff, the university has more than 500 professors and associate professors, along with 88 supervisors of doctoral students and 283 supervisors of master's students. About 10,000 students are enrolled, including over 1300 working on doctoral or master's degrees and more than 100 from Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan and other countries. Each year, over 200 students come for short-term training programmes.
International students need the right visa to study and stay in China. The university's foreign-affairs office can explain which supporting documents are required.
The university is organised into the following schools and departments:
School of Acupuncture and Moxibustion
School of Administration
School of Basic Medicine
School of Clinical Medicine
School of Continuous Education
School of International Education
School of Nursing
School of Chinese Pharmacy
School of Vocational and Technical Education
School of Cultural and Social Sciences
School of E'mei
Department of Physical Education

The School of International Education is the one most relevant for overseas applicants. International courses are available, and they cover subjects such as acupuncture theory and Chinese herbs and formulas.

The university's teaching hospital is described as one of China's first-class hospitals, using traditional methods and medicines, and it is in Chengdu. Students get the chance to learn in a real hospital setting, which is one of the main attractions of a TCM programme.

CDUTCM carries out TCM-related research and has made contributions to society. Its research is organised through 6 institutes and 37 institutional offices. It hosts a national GCP centre (for clinical trials) as well as a monitoring centre for adverse drug reactions (ADR) and a centre for screening and evaluating Chinese pharmaceuticals.

In recent years it has taken on a state key project from the Tenth Five-Year Plan, projects under the "973 program" and "863 program", and key programmes funded by the National Fund of Nature and Science. It has also been given various prizes. Two museums, the Cultural Museum of TCM and the Museum of Chinese Drug Specimens, hold rich collections that visitors and students can use.

TCM clinics and herbal pharmacies now operate in many countries, and some governments invite skilled TCM practitioners, partly because some people prefer natural herbal treatment. Australia, for example, has TCM schools of its own. The university describes its international exchange and cooperation as leading in western China.

Since 1993 it has enrolled students from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, as well as master's and doctoral students from other countries. It reports information-exchange links with 176 institutions in 31 countries and areas, and it has worked with universities, R&D centres and medical institutes in the United States, Germany, Sweden, Israel, Japan, Korea, Singapore and elsewhere.

The accommodation description is dated and hard to interpret, so check it before you rely on it. It says students can stay in hostels that are separate from teaching buildings, with separate halls by gender, and that rooms hold four people in multi-storey buildings, with some having two telephone lines, and that students were housed separately by year. It also says the hostels and campus are in downtown Chengdu with convenient transport.

For local students the TCM programmes run at several levels, with graduate-level courses taking four years in the usual pattern, and plenty of specialised courses such as pharmacy. For foreign students, the school has facilities and international courses designed for them.
Life outside the university matters, so here is an introduction to Chengdu: its landscape, climate, growth, population, culture and transport.

Chengdu lies on a broad plain at 450 to 720 metres (1,480 to 2,360 feet) above sea level. Steep Longmen Mountains rise in the northwest, and the Qionglai Mountains lie to the west, with heights beyond 3,000 m (9,800 ft). Miao Jiling reaches 5,364 m (17,598 ft) and Xiling Snow Mountain 5,164 m (16,942 ft). The mountainous west also has a large primitive forest rich in wildlife, and giant panda habitat. To the east stand the low Longquan Mountains and, to the west, the hilly land along the middle reaches of the Min River, where several rivers meet. Since ancient times Chengdu has been called "the Abundant Land" because of its fertile soil, favourable climate and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

Chengdu occupies the Chengdu Plain on the western side of the Sichuan Basin, and most of its land is flat. The prefecture lies between 30° 05' and 31° 26' north and between 102° 54' and 104° 53' east. From east to west it stretches 192 kilometres (119 mi); from south to north the distance is 166 km (103 mi). The administered area is 12,390 km2, or 4,780 sq mi. Its neighbours are Deyang to the northeast, Ziyang to the southeast, Meishan to the south and Ya'an to the southwest, and with the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture lying north.

The urban area, at around 500 m (1,600 ft), has several rivers, including the Jin, Fu and Sha. Further out the land becomes more complex. The eastern side has the Penzhong Hills (盆中丘陵) and the Longquan Mountains (龙泉山脉), and in the west the Qionglai Mountains climb as high as 5,364 m in Dayi County. The highest spot is Daxuetang, also called Miaojiling, on Xiling Snow Mountain in Dayi County, at 5,364 meters, and the lowest is the riverbank where the Tuojiang River leaves Jianyang City, at 359 meters.

The climate is humid subtropical with monsoon influence (Köppen Cwa): warm for most of the year, and humid throughout. There are four clear seasons, and moderate rain falls mainly in the warm months. The Qin Mountains, far to the north, hold back the cold winds from Siberia, which means the brief winter is gentler than in the Lower Yangtze area. January's daily mean is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F), snow seldom falls, and there are only a few frosty spells each winter.

Summers are hot and sticky, though less severe than in Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing, the Yangtze basin cities known as the "Three Furnaces". In July and August the average over 24 hours is about 25 °C (77 °F). Afternoons can sometimes reach 33 °C (91 °F), but extended heat of the kind found across much of eastern China is rare. July and August are also the wettest months, and the cooler months get very little rain.

Sunshine is limited. Few places in China get less over a year, and Chengdu has fewer hours than much of Northern Europe: 1006 hours of bright sunshine annually. Possible sunshine is just 15 percent in December and reaches 32 percent in August. Daytime is generally sunnier and warmer in spring (March to April) than in autumn (October to November). The yearly mean temperature is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F), and the range of extremes runs from −6.5 °C (20 °F) up to 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).

The year 1988 saw the start of nationwide urban housing reform, under a plan for gradually reforming the housing system in cities and towns. More than 20 real-estate companies were founded in Chengdu, the first step in the city's property development.

The 1990s renovation of the Funan River was another milestone for the environment. In 1998 the comprehensive improvement project received the UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour Award, and in 2000 it won a "Local Initiative Award", given by an international council for local environmental initiatives.

The Five Main Roads and One Bridge project started in 1997. Three roads served the east and two led south, laying the base for the city's eastern and southern sub-centres, and with them the eastward and southward trends in where people lived. Many buildings went up around the 2nd Ring Road on its eastern and southern sides. Along the Shahe and Jin river projects, living by the rivers also became popular. It was said that Chengdu's map needed updating every three months.

A speculative housing boom followed in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and dozens of commercial property projects appeared in 2000. The government encouraged residents to buy their own homes with considerable subsidies for a period, and houses became commodities.

One landmark is the New Century Global Center, reported to be the third-largest building in the world by floor area. The building stands 100 m (330 ft) high. Its footprint is 500 m by 400 m (1,600 ft by 1,300 ft), and the floor area totals 1,700,000 square meters (18,000,000 sq ft). Inside are shops, cinemas, offices and hotels, a skating rink, parking for 15,000 vehicles, a water park whose beach and waves are artificial, and a village in Mediterranean style that includes a big 5-star hotel.

The 2020 census counted 20,937,757 people in the municipality, with 16,045,577 in the metropolitan area, defined as the 12 urban districts together with Guanghan City, which is in Deyang. It is the biggest city in Sichuan and the fourth biggest in China. A figure of 21,192,000 is reported for 2021, a year in which it added more people than any other city nationwide. In 2015 the OECD estimated the metropolitan population at 18.1 million.
China Daily named Chengdu the country's fourth most livable city in 2006.

Chengdu has produced or hosted many major Chinese writers. They include Yang Xiong and Sima Xiangru, both masters of the fu, a style that blends descriptive prose with verse; the great poets Li Bai and Du Fu; Yang Shen'an, a Ming scholar; and the modern writers Guo Moruo and Ba Jin.

Chang Qu, a historian of the Jin dynasty, compiled the Record of Hua Yang State, which is the oldest surviving local history. Among the Flowers, the first Ci anthology in Chinese history, was edited by Zhao Chongzuo, a poet in Chengdu in the days of the Later Shu Kingdom. The king of Later Shu, Meng Chang, composed the first Spring Festival couplet, which in one translation reads: a bumper year welcomes celebration, and a good festival heralds a long spring.
The 81st World Science Fiction Convention took place in Chengdu in 2023, after the city won the 2021 site-selection vote over Winnipeg, Canada.

During the Five Dynasties period, the Chengdu painter Huang Quan and other painters began the Fine-Brush Flower-and-Bird Painting School. The "Hanlin Painting Academy" of that time was the earliest royal academy in China.

Islam has been present in Sichuan since the Tang dynasty (618 to 907), and Chengdu has 12 mosques. Huangcheng Mosque, in the city centre, dates to the 16th century. The city has official Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations as well.
The Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan, now the Diocese of Chengdu, was set up on 15 October 1696, with Artus de Lionne of the Paris Foreign Missions Society as its first Apostolic Vicar.

Protestant missions came later. The Canadian Methodist Mission was seeking more stations in Asia in 1890, and Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart proposed Chengtu as the first site in February 1891. He arrived on 9 May 1891 and two weeks later bought a house that was divided into living quarters and a dispensary. The first Protestant Mission Headquarters opened on 24 June 1892 with more than 1,000 people attending, and Sichuan's first western dispensary welcomed sixteen patients when it opened on 3 November 1892. A larger site near the East Gate was acquired in spring 1893, and the city's first Methodist church and hospital were built there. These buildings were damaged in riots in 1895 and again in 1901, and rebuilt each time. Later the Boys' and Girls' Schools moved to a new site just south of the city, and the Divinity College was dedicated as Hart College in 1914, within the West China Union University, a forerunner of today's Sichuan University and of the West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida). In the Cultural Revolution the church building passed to the neighbouring Chengdu City Second People's Hospital, which turned the chapel into a kindergarten and an office. The hospital returned it to the church in 1984.
A Chabad Jewish Center was set up in Chengdu in 2012 and, after moving five times, found a permanent home in Wuhou District.

Local pride is expressed in a saying that Shu opera is the best performance in the world. It reflects the achievements of Sichuan opera and of Zaju, an ancient comic art that combines dancing, singing, poetry and mime. The city's first opera, "Bullfighting", dates from the Warring States period, and the Shu Kingdom court staged the first detailed opera during the Three Kingdoms era. The earliest clearly documented Zaju performance in China also took place in Chengdu, and tombs of witty poets from the Han dynasty have been excavated here. Face-changing masks and fire-breathing are still trademarks of Sichuan opera.
People speak Chengdu dialect, a variety of Sichuanese, which has shaped Chinese comedy and rap music. If you studied Mandarin elsewhere, expect some local pronunciation differences.

Sichuan cuisine is known for its spicy chillies and peppercorns. Well-known local dishes are mapo doufu, dan dan noodles and Chengdu hot pot, with Sichuan pepper in both the mapo doufu and the noodles. In 2006 the Los Angeles Times described Chengdu as "China's party city", pointing to its carefree way of life. It has more teahouses and bars than Shanghai even though its population is under half the size. In 2023 the city counted more than 30,000 teahouses, plus 3,566 bars, nightclubs and dance halls that were legally registered. A statistical report in 2019 found more bars in Chengdu than in Shanghai, the highest number in China. Tea culture here is over a thousand years old, and the city was where the Southern Silk Road began. UNESCO has named Chengdu a "City of Gastronomy".

Teahouses are everywhere, from ornate traditional places with bamboo furniture to simple modern ones, serving teas such as jasmine, longjing and biluochun. People go there to play mahjong, have a massage or get their ears cleaned, and some larger teahouses stage live entertainment such as Sichuan opera.

Hot pot is a traditional Sichuan dish of vegetables, fish and meat cooked in a boiling spicy broth. It suits a gathering of friends, attracts locals and tourists alike, and hot pot restaurants can be found all over Chengdu.
Back in 1992 the Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone was founded, and it later became the Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park.

Chengdu is connected to the rest of the country by a set of national expressways, which are worth knowing about if you plan to travel by coach or car during holidays or field trips. Ring roads around the city handle local traffic, and long-distance routes lead to Beijing, Kunming, Shanghai, Xiamen and Chongqing. The main national highways linking Chengdu are:
National Highway G5 Beijing-Kunming
National Highway G42 Shanghai-Chengdu
National Highway G76 Xiamen-Chengdu
National Highway G93 Chengdu-Chongqing Ring
National Highway G4202 Chengdu Ring

chengdu-university-of-traditional-chines.h: Is this the right university for you?

blocks.x: Choosing a university for traditional Chinese medicine is a long-term decision, because programmes can last several years and lead to specialised careers. The summary below pulls the main facts together.
A few points can help you decide whether CDUTCM matches what you want from study in China.
A long-established TCM focus: it was among the first four TCM institutions founded after 1949, and it has held university status since 1995.

National recognition: three national key courses, in Chinese pharmacy, TCM ear-nose-throat, and acupuncture, moxibustion and Tuina, a place in the Double First-Class Construction scheme and a state TCM base for education, research and medical care.
Real clinical exposure through its teaching hospital, plus two specialist museums and research centres for drug screening and monitoring.

An international office and a School of International Education, with courses in acupuncture theory and Chinese herbs and formulas for overseas students, and short-term programmes that bring more than 200 students every year.
Teaching for local students is mainly in Chinese, so ask which programmes and languages are open to you.
Visa requirements and supporting documents come from the university's foreign-affairs office.
Several figures, such as the number of provincial key courses and the hostel details, are described differently in different places, so confirm current facts with the university.

chengdu-university-of-traditional-chines.h: The city you would live in

blocks.x: Chengdu is a very large city, with more than 20 million residents in the municipality, a mild but often cloudy climate, and a reputation for relaxed teahouse and food culture. Winters are shorter and milder than in the lower Yangtze region, summers are warm without the extreme heat of the "Three Furnaces" cities, and light is limited, with about 1006 hours of bright sunshine a year. Together with the hospital and campus described above, this makes the setting a comfortable, food-focused place to spend several years of study.
Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine lists 44 programs for international students on this site: 12 bachelor, 18 master's, 12 doctoral, 2 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 42 taught in Chinese, 2 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,200 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 38,000 to CNY 38,000 (median CNY 38,000), according to the university's published fee table.

44 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (1):
Acupuncture and Tuina
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.
