The China Academy of Art, known as CAA (中国美术学院), is a fine arts college in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang Province. It is a public institution under the Zhejiang provincial government, and it takes part in the Double First-Class Construction, the national scheme that backs selected universities and disciplines. During the 1960s the academy was housed in the Former Residence of Hu Xueyan.

An art school draws much of its character from the place around it, so this overview spends most of its space on Hangzhou and Zhejiang. That is where you would live, walk, sketch and eat, and it helps to know what that place is like before you apply.

china-academy-of-art.h: Hangzhou: the setting for your studies

blocks.x: Daily student life depends on the city beyond the campus gates: the weather, the ways of getting around and what the city offers. The sections below walk through Hangzhou.

Hangzhou lies in the north-west of Zhejiang Province. It marks the southern end of China's Grand Canal, which runs all the way up to Beijing, and sits in the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. As a sub-provincial city its administrative area stretches west into the mountains on the Anhui side and east to the coastal plain around Hangzhou Bay. The urban core curls around the east and north sides of West Lake, with the Qiantang River just to the south.

Zhejiang's biggest river, the Qiantang, is famous for its tide. Each year, in the lunar calendar's period from the 15th to the 18th of the eighth month, the Qiantang Tide arrives. People call it "the Biggest Tide in the World". A tidal bore, the largest anywhere, rushes upriver past Hangzhou and can reach a height of 12 m (39 ft).

Expect a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons. The summer is long, very hot and humid; the winter is cooler, cloudier and a bit drier, with occasional snow. Over a year the mean temperature is 17.0 °C (62.6 °F). Taking each month's daily average, January is the coldest at 5 °C (41.0 °F) and July the warmest at 29.3 °C (84.7 °F). Annual rainfall averages 1,438 mm (56.6 in), and the "plum rains" brought by the Asian monsoon arrive in June.

Typhoon storms reach the region in late summer, from August to September, but direct hits are rare. They tend to come ashore along Zhejiang's southern coast, and Hangzhou feels their strong winds and stormy rain. Since 1951 the coldest recorded day was 6 February 1969 (−9.6 °C, or 15 °F) and the hottest 3 August 2024 (41.9 °C, or 107 °F). Older unofficial figures are more extreme, with −10.5 °C (13 °F) noted twice, in December 1912 and January 1916, and 42.1 °C (108 °F) in August 1930. Sunshine as a share of the possible total falls to 30% in March and peaks at 51% in August, adding up to 1,709.4 hours annually.

In 2023 the permanent population stood at 12.522 million, counting Xiaoshan and Yuhang, and 10.543 million of those (84.2%) lived in urban areas. For the surrounding metropolitan area the OECD gave an estimate of 13.4 million as of 2010, though other sources say it exceeds 21 million. Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou are the big cities within that metropolitan region. Residents with local registration live to 83.18 years on average (2021 figure), one of the highest life expectancies in China.

Religion has a long history here. A writer in 1848, under the Qing, called Hangzhou a "stronghold" of Islam in China because its mosques carried Arabic inscriptions. A Hui man from Ningbo told an Englishman much the same about the whole of Zhejiang, setting Hangzhou's many mosques against the roughly 30 families in his own small Ningbo congregation. Of the mosques today, the Phoenix Mosque and the New Hangzhou Great Mosque stand out.

Other traditions have been present too. The city was also a significant centre of Chinese Jewish life around the late 1500s and early 1600s, and it may be where the Kaifeng Jewish community began. A synagogue once stood in Ningbo as well as Hangzhou, but nothing of either can now be found, and Kaifeng's community is the only one known to have survived in China. Two of the "Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism" came from Hangzhou. The Immaculate Conception Cathedral, 400 years old and dating from the Ming dynasty, is among the oldest Catholic churches in China. Christians in the city faced persecution in the early 21st century.

Buddhist and historical temples crowd the area near West Lake. Lingyin Temple, the "Soul's Retreat", was founded in AD 326, in the first year of Xianhe under the Eastern Jin dynasty. It is about 1,700 years old and is regarded as Hangzhou's earliest famous temple and its oldest Buddhist one. It lies roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the lake's west side and has gone through many cycles of destruction and rebuilding. Yue Fei Temple, on the lake's north-western shore, was first built in 1221, during the Song dynasty, to honour General Yue Fei, who died after political persecution. Also nearby are the Leifeng Pagoda, the Baochu Pagoda and the Jingci Temple.
Elsewhere you will find the Liuhe Pagoda on Yuelun Hill, on the Qiantang River's north bank, and the Hupao Temple (虎跑寺).

Growth took off after the city opened up in 1992. As an industrial city, Hangzhou spans many sectors, including textiles, agriculture and light industry. It is regarded as a significant manufacturing base and logistics centre for the coast of China, as well as an e-commerce and technology hub.

The figures show how fast it grew. In 2001 GDP was RMB 156.8 billion, which put Hangzhou second among provincial capitals, behind only Guangzhou. By 2018 the total was RMB 1.3509 trillion, more than three times as much, and GDP per head grew from US$3,020 to $21,184. In 2019 the metropolitan area produced a nominal gross metropolitan product of around 3.2 trillion yuan (some $486.53 billion), a larger figure than the economy of Argentina ($452 billion, 26th largest in the world) or Nigeria ($448 billion, the biggest in Africa).

Rankings from outside add context. A PwC and China Development Research Foundation study placed Hangzhou first among "Chinese Cities of Opportunity", and GaWC classes it as a "Beta+" world city. In the Global Financial Centres Index of 2018 it was 89th. The Economist Intelligence Unit's China Emerging City Rankings, which judge growth potential, put it first in both 2021 and 2022. For billionaires, the Hurun Global Rich List 2020 ranked it 11th globally and sixth in China; five Chinese cities, Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou, were ahead. As of August 2023 it ranked tenth worldwide for Fortune Global 500 headquarters inside city limits, and fourth in China behind Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.
The city also has a smart-city programme, with efforts to digitise the economy and to become a cashless city.

Hangzhou is the base of many technology companies, for example HikVision, Geely, DeepSeek, Ant Group, NetEase and Alibaba Group. Alibaba opened a new global headquarters in May 2024, covering about one million sqm in seven buildings and designed for 30,000 employees. The internet industry has also drawn programmers from cities like Beijing and Shanghai.

Newer industries have grown up too: medicine, IT, heavy equipment, vehicle components, household electrical goods, electronics, telecommunications, plus fine chemicals, chemical fibre and food processing. The city's own plans talk about "1 + 6" industrial clusters. The "1" is the digital economy. The "6" is described as the cultural and creative economy, finance, tourism, fashion manufacturing and high-end equipment manufacturing (only five items are named for the six, so check the city's official wording). As of at least 2023, the digital sector and the cultural and creative sectors have led growth. For an art student, that creative sector is the most relevant part of the picture.

One study found that Alibaba's total revenue has a positive effect on the city's growth, though the causal link runs only one way, from the company to the city. In the long run a 1% rise in Alibaba's revenue could produce 0.272% growth in the city's economy.

The Hangzhou Tourism Commission ran a "Modern Marco Polo" campaign on Facebook, starting in March 2013. During the following year almost 26,000 people around the world applied to become the city's first foreign tourism ambassador. On 20 May 2014, at a press conference in Hangzhou, Liam Bates was named winner. He received a $55,000 contract and became the first foreigner appointed by China's government to such an official role.

The Hangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone won State Council approval as a national zone in 1993 and extends over 104.7 km² (40.4 sq mi). Its encouraged industries are electronic information, biological medicine, machinery, household appliances and food processing. The Hangzhou Export Processing Zone was set up on 27 April 2000 with State Council approval, as one of the first zones of its kind and the only one in Zhejiang. Planned total area is 2.92 km² (1.13 sq mi), and it is next to both Hangzhou Port and Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport.

The Hangzhou Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (HHTZ) became a state-level high-tech zone in March 1991, with State Council approval. It has three parts, mainly the Zhijiang Sci-Tech Industrial Park and the Xiasha Sci-Tech Industrial Park, and it ranks among Zhejiang's most influential bases for high-tech innovation and industry. In 2013 it housed over 1,100 software developers and BPO companies, and Motorola, Nokia and Siemens had research and development centres there. In 2011 its GDP grew 13.1 percent to RMB 41.63 billion, or 5.9 percent of the city's total. It describes itself as China's "Silicon Valley" and is the home of Alibaba Group. In 2023 Alibaba sped up the building of its global headquarters in Hangzhou, with local government support, after signing a fresh cooperation pact with the authorities.

Despite many recent urban developments, Hangzhou keeps its historical and cultural heritage and its natural setting, and tourism is still important to the economy. It also has plenty of skyscrapers: it is 19th in the world for their number and 9th in China.

Few places in Hangzhou are more popular than West Lake, which UNESCO lists as a World Heritage Site. The West Lake Cultural Landscape spans about 3,323 ha (8,210 acres) and contains many of the city's best-known historic and scenic spots. Cultural sites, historical pagodas, hills, tea fields and Phoenix Mountain ring the water. Two major causeways cross the water.
West of the lake you reach Dreaming of the Tiger Spring, known for its natural spring and for being close to the famed longjing tea plantations.

Stretches of the Grand Canal run through Hangzhou. The Jiangnan Canal, dug out in 610 CE by deepening and widening an older channel, joins Suzhou to Hangzhou. The Grand Canal gained UNESCO World Heritage status in 2014. Hangzhou Metro Line 5 gets you to the historic area around Gongchen Bridge, from either The Grand Canal station or East Gongchen Bridge station.

In the Xiacheng District, the West Lake Cultural Square contains the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology, the Zhejiang Natural History Museum and the Zhejiang Global Center, which at about 160 m (520 ft) is among the tallest buildings downtown.

Xixi National Wetland Park protects the region's wetland ecosystem and covers about 10 km² (3.9 sq mi). Restoration there created reed beds and fish ponds, and the park now supports a variety of birds. A temple and several historically important rural houses are also inside the park.

Qiandao Lake is a man-made reservoir in Chun'an County, part of Hangzhou's jurisdiction, and has more islands than any other lake in China. They differ widely in size and shape, and each has its own scenery. The Xihu District has the Hangzhou Zoo and the Hangzhou Botanical Garden.

The people of Hangzhou have their own dialect, a Wu dialect found only here, and it differs from speech elsewhere in southern Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu. Mandarin, the official language set by the central government, is the main spoken language, but the two are not mutually intelligible. Estimates put the number of speakers at between 1.2 and 1.5 million.

Museums are plentiful. The China National Silk Museum is the biggest silk museum in the world, the China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆) covers the city's tea tradition, and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum combines human studies, exhibition and research, with a collection of more than 100,000 cultural relics.

Theatres across the city stage opera, such as Yue opera, and large shows themed on Hangzhou's history and culture, such as the Romance of Song Dynasty and Impression West Lake. The landscapes tie together stories of famous figures in Chinese history and the feelings of ordinary visitors, who come with enthusiasm and delight.
This city is the home of the China Academy of Art and of well-known painters including Lin Fengmian and Fang Ganmin.
The municipal government spends heavily on promoting tourism and the arts, with special attention to silk, umbrellas and the Chinese folding fan.

The Hangzhou Ancient Book Restoration and Display Center belongs to the Zhejiang Library and runs regular public demonstrations of the traditional paper mending and binding techniques used to keep ancient Chinese texts alive. It is important for the preservation of documents from Jiangnan culture.
What surrounds a university affects student life as much as the campus itself, so here is Zhejiang's story, beginning with the earliest times.

The oldest known settlement in the Hangzhou area belongs to the Kuahuqiao culture, an early Neolithic community that existed between 6000 and 5000 BC. Zhejiang was also home to two other Neolithic cultures, Hemudu (beginning in 5500 BC) and Liangzhu (beginning in 3400 BC).
During the second millennium BC, the Zhejiang area lay outside the main sphere of influence of Shang civilisation. Peoples collectively called the Dongyue lived there instead.

In the chronicles from the Spring and Autumn period, the kingdom of Yue starts to appear, and the records place it in northern Zhejiang. The Shiji states that Yue's leaders descended from Yu the Great, founder of the Xia. Around 528 BC, authors in Hebei and Henan, in north or inland China, wrote down the "Song of the Yue Boatman" (越人歌; Yuèrén Gē), transliterating it into Chinese characters. The song shows that the people of Yue spoke a language the northern and inland dialects could not understand. Other traces of the kingdom include the Sword of Goujian, which carries bird-worm seal script, and the legend of Yuenü (越女; Yuènǚ, "the Lady of Yue"), a swordswoman of the state. The state of Chu, wishing to hold back the growing power of Wu, followed a policy of strengthening Yue.

King Goujian brought Yue back from its early setbacks and, in 473 BC, took over the lands of its rival Wu completely. The kings of Yue then moved their centre of power away from the old home around Mount Kuaiji, in present-day Shaoxing, to the old capital of Wu, now Suzhou. With no southern rival left to use against Yue, Chu turned against it directly and destroyed it in 333 BC. In 222 BC the Qin Empire annexed Yue's former lands and formed a commandery named Kuaiji, which covered Zhejiang but at first had its headquarters in Wu, in what is now Jiangsu.

china-academy-of-art.h: From the Han to the Three Kingdoms

blocks.x: Kuaiji Commandery was where Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu first built their power for the rebellion against Qin. It restored the kingdom of Chu for a time but eventually lost to the Han. Later, under the Later Han, the settlement beneath Mount Kuaiji again controlled the area, but its hold over the Minyue hinterland was weak at best, and the Yue people there largely kept their own political and social structures.

When the Han empire ended, Zhejiang was held by the warlords Wang Lang and Yan Baihu until Sun Ce and Sun Quan defeated them; Sun Quan eventually established the Kingdom of Wu. The Wu court moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (now Nanjing), but the family still developed the region and gained from waves of refugees escaping turmoil in the north. Kilns were set up for industrial production, and trading links stretched to Manchuria and to Funan, in the south of mainland Southeast Asia.

In the Three Kingdoms period (220 to 280), Zhejiang belonged to Wu, often called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu (229 to 280), which was the most developed economy of the three states. The historical novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms credits the Zhejiang region with the best-equipped navy. In it, Shu (蜀) and Wei (魏), both short of material resources, avoided meeting Wu head-on, and in their armed clashes with Wu they relied heavily on camouflage and deception to take Wu's military supplies, including arrows and bows.

Nanjing, then called Jiankang, stayed prominent, but Qiantang, Hangzhou's former name, remained one of three major southern centres that supplied tax revenue to the imperial north. Jiankang and Chengdu were the others. Qiantang was raised in rank in 589 and renamed Hangzhou.

After Wu collapsed and the Wu Hu rose against the Jin dynasty (266 to 420), many elite northern Chinese families had cooperated with non-Chinese rulers and military conquerors. Some may have lost status and fled to land south of the Yangtze, and some of those refugees may have settled near Hangzhou. A case in point is the clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), chancellor of the Shu Han kingdom from the Central Plain. The clan gathered in the outskirts of Hangzhou prefecture and formed a closed village, Zhuge Village (Zhege Cun), where everyone carried the family name "Zhuge". The village has deliberately kept itself apart from its neighbours for centuries and has only recently become known to the public. Such cases suggest that a handful of powerful refugees from the Central Plain may have found shelter south of the Yangtze.

However, Zhejiang is mountainous and has little farmland, so most such refugees probably settled elsewhere in the south, where fertile land and urban resources were available. The likely areas were southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, provinces whose regional governments were less cohesive and less organised. Where a refugee from the north settled may have depended on social status and military power. The remnant Jin state and the Southern dynasties competed against some Han elites, both those from the Central Plain and those from south of the Yangtze.

As the heartland of Jiangnan (the Yangtze River Delta), Zhejiang was the richest area in the Six Dynasties period (220 or 222 to 589), and in the Sui and Tang. When it joined the Sui dynasty, its wealth paid for Sui ambitions to expand north and south, notably into Korea and Vietnam. That plan led the Sui to restore and extend the network that became the Grand Canal of China. Grain and other goods travelled by canal from Zhejiang to the North China Plain. They moved through Hangzhou, the regional centre, whose hinterland lay along the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay's shores, and through Suzhou.

The Korean war went badly, and the failure led to the Sui being overthrown by the Tang, who then oversaw a golden age that lasted for centuries. Within the empire's Jiangnan East Circuit, Zhejiang was a major economic centre, regarded as especially prosperous. All through the Tang, the Grand Canal kept working, carrying grain and materials to the North China Plain and the empire's major cities. When the Tang disintegrated, the regional kingdom of Wuyue took in most of Zhejiang.
Zhejiang is home to several professional sports teams. Here are the clubs by league:
Chinese Basketball Association: the Zhejiang Golden Bulls, plus the Bayi Rockets, who play in Ningbo.
Chinese Super League football: Zhejiang Professional F.C.
For an international student with an interest in sport, these give you a team to follow alongside your studies.

china-academy-of-art.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. China Academy of Art may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hangzhou, register at China Academy of Art by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

CAU (China Agricultural University) is a publicly funded university in Beijing's Haidian District, run under the Ministry of Education. It belongs to three national programmes that pick out China's leading universities: Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction.

CAU was created in 1995 when two Beijing institutions came together. One was Beijing Agricultural Engineering University and the other was Beijing Agricultural University. Their shared ancestry goes back to 1905, which makes the university heir to one of China's earliest agricultural institutions.

In numbers, as of December 2019 CAU offered 66 undergraduate majors, more than 32 master's programmes and 21 doctoral programmes. The student body was around 12,000 undergraduates and 8,900 postgraduates, and 508 of the students came from abroad. A small detail that often interests visitors: its gymnasium hosted the wrestling events at the 2008 Summer Olympics.

The oldest thread starts in 1905, when a College of Agriculture was founded within the Imperial University of Peking. In September 1949 Beijing Agricultural University (BAU) was formed by bringing together the agricultural colleges of Peking University, Tsinghua University and North China University.

A parallel line of development concerned farm machinery. In October 1952, three bodies were combined to form the Beijing Mechanized Agricultural College: the machinery department of BAU, a college of agricultural machinery for North China, and a central school for agricultural mechanisation run by the Ministry of Agriculture. By July 1953 it had become the Beijing Agricultural Mechanization Institute (BAMI). In October 1960 it was one of 64 institutions given National Key University status, and in 1985 it took the name Beijing Agricultural Engineering University (BAEU).

The State Council had already listed BAU in 1954 as one of six top national key universities and one of ten for further construction and improvement. Then, in 1995, BAU and BAEU merged to become China Agricultural University, and since then the university has been seen as the leading academic institution for agriculture in China.

The sport of rugby came back to the People's Republic in 1990, starting with a club at Beijing Agricultural University. Chao Xihuang, a professor there, learned about the game from a Japanese businessman and then organised a couple of teams. Another early development was one of the first bilateral China-Israel collaborations, the Sino-Israeli Agricultural Training Center, which was based at CAU.

china-agricultural-university.h: Where CAU stands in the rankings

blocks.x: Rankings differ in method and are updated every year, so the figures below show a general picture rather than a fixed position. Look at the latest editions before you rely on any of them.
CAU entered the world's top 500 in a global ranking for the first time in 2007. By 2026 it was listed among the top 200 universities in the World University Rankings.

CAU is regarded as one of the leading agricultural research institutions in the world. Since U.S. News & World Report launched its Best Global Universities ranking in 2014, CAU has been in the top 5 for "Agricultural Science".

In 2025 three rankings, namely ARWU (the Academic Ranking of World Universities), the Performance Ranking of Scientific Papers for World Universities and the one by U.S. News & World Report, each placed it first worldwide for agricultural sciences. Separately, the CWTS Leiden Ranking for 2025 put it first globally by number of publications falling in the top 1%, 5% and 10% of "life and earth science". QS ranked it first in Asia and Oceania and fourth in the world for "Agriculture & Forestry".

For "Plant and Animal Science" CAU came first worldwide in 2025 on two lists, the U.S. News & World Report ranking and the Performance Ranking of Scientific Papers. ARWU placed it second globally in "Veterinary Science".
Also in 2025, CAU ranked second in the world in "Food Science and Technology" in both the U.S. News & World Report ranking and ARWU.

china-agricultural-university.h: Beijing: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Where you study affects daily life, so the rest of this profile is an introduction to Beijing: its land and rivers, the weather, the air, and the city's buildings.

Beijing sits at the northern edge of the North China Plain, which is roughly triangular and opens to the south and east. To the north, northwest and west, mountains shield the city, and the farming heartland of northern China, from desert steppes. The Jundu Mountains cover much of the northwest of the municipality, particularly Yanqing and Huairou districts, while the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the north of the municipality along the rugged terrain, built to guard against raiders who came from the steppes. The municipality's top elevation is Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 ft), found in the Western Hills where the border with Hebei runs.

The main rivers, the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, belong to the Hai River system and flow southeast. The largest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. The city is the northern terminus of the Grand Canal that runs to Hangzhou, a transport route more than 1,400 years old. It also receives water through the South-North Water Transfer Project, built within the last decade to bring supplies from the Yangtze basin.

The urban area occupies a modest but growing part of the municipality, on plains in the south-central area at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. Ring roads spread outward in concentric circles. The innermost one that people mention, the Second Ring Road, traces where the old walls stood, while the Sixth connects satellite towns in the suburbs.

At the centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, directly south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, home to China's current leaders, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between Tiananmen and the Square, is the main east-west axis.
The way Beijing has grown outward from its old core to the fringe is often described as "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), and many point to it as one cause of the city's urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to the borderline with a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon produces hot, humid summers, while the huge Siberian anticyclone brings winters that are brief, cold and dry. Sandstorms may sweep in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe in spring, along with rapid warming and mostly dry days, and autumn is another transition period with little rain.

For the period 2001 to 2026 the hottest time is early August and the coldest early January. Under China's seasonal standard, the seasons begin on 26 March (spring), 20 May (summer), 13 September (autumn) and 31 October (winter). Because March and September have been warming faster and May and October slower in recent years, autumn is generally shorter than spring.

Based on 1991 to 2020, the average annual temperature in the urban area is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Daily lows average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily highs average 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). In the low-lying suburbs the annual average is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with daily minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In mountain areas the yearly average falls between 0 and 10 °C (32 to 50 °F) and drops with altitude. The January daily average is −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), against 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July.

Precipitation averages 528.0 mm (20.79 in) a year, or 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three-quarters of it comes between June and August. Possible sunshine is lowest in July at 42% and highest in January and February at 62%, which adds up to 2,490.5 hours of bright sun each year. The lowest temperature on record since 1951 was −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, and the highest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), on 24 July 1999. Pack warm clothes for winter and light ones for the humid summer.

The city has struggled with environmental problems for a long time. Its built-up area grew fourfold between 2000 and 2009, which sharply raised emissions and also changed the local weather. Near the ground, albedo, wind speed and humidity fell, while temperatures, ozone and the stagnation of air layers rose. With urban growth and fossil-fuel pollution together, serious environmental problems have often affected the health of many residents.

Heavy smog hit Beijing and most of northern China in 2013, affecting 600 million people. This "pollution shock" turned air quality into a serious economic and social worry. Afterwards the city announced steps that included bringing coal's share down from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, and the national government ordered the removal of heavily polluting vehicles between 2015 and 2017 while pushing harder toward clean energy.

A 2006 study by American and Chinese researchers working together found that much of the city's pollution originates in neighbouring cities and provinces; between 35 and 60% of ozone, on average, traces back to outside sources. Shandong and Tianjin influence Beijing's air strongly, partly because summer winds usually blow from the south or southeast and the mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Burning coal produces roughly 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide too. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations to natural gas since 2012 and aims to limit coal use to 20 million tons a year. It burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, 73% for heating and electricity and the remainder in industry. Much of the pollution comes from the neighbours. Tianjin was expected to raise its coal use from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, and Hebei burned over 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, with only 30% going to power and a large part to steel and cement. Power plants in the coal-mining areas of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where use has tripled since 2000, add to it, as does Shandong. By coal consumption the four leading provinces are Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, in that order.

Beijing had four major coal-fired power plants for electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to shut in 2016. From 2013 to 2017 the city planned to cut coal use by 13 million tons, with a cap of 15 million tons set for 2015.

For the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent to clean the city's air. During the Games, building sites were halted, many Beijing factories were closed for good, industry in nearby regions was temporarily shut, some petrol stations closed, and traffic was cut by half with odd and even licence-plate days. Bus and subway fares fell, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. It also put together 3,800 natural-gas buses, among the biggest fleets of their kind anywhere, and became the first in China to require the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The authorities also sometimes use cloud seeding to make rain and clear the air before big events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. More recently they have relied on temporary factory closures and traffic limits, as in the "APEC blue" and "parade blue" episodes that surrounded the 2014 APEC meeting in China and the 2015 Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved greatly then and fell back to unhealthy levels soon after.

On 8 and 9 December 2015 Beijing issued its first smog alert, which shut most industry and commerce, and another "red alert" followed later that month. In November 2016 the city's environmental bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be banned from the roads when a red alert is in force in the city or nearby regions.

Pollutants have fallen measurably since a "war on pollution" was declared in 2014. Fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017 and fell further by 2020, and the chief reasons were cleaner industrial plants and natural gas replacing coal power. The annual average for PM2.5 fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013, and in 2024 Beijing recorded only two days of heavy pollution, a record low and 96.6 percent below the 58 days of 2013.

Several sources publish readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) reports daily results from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the American Embassy reports hourly PM2.5 and ozone on Twitter. Because the two measure different pollutants by different criteria, BJEPB figures and their health impact are often lower than the US Embassy's. Smog is harmful: air pollution directly affects the rate of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, emergency visits and even death. It is sensible to check the day's reading, especially in winter.

Erosion of the deserts to the north and northwest sends seasonal dust storms over Beijing, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain to counter them. Eight or more storms struck in just the first four months of 2006, and one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it travelled on to Japan and Korea.

Three architectural styles stand out in urban Beijing. The first is the traditional architecture of the imperial age. Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the national emblem, is the best-known example, along with the Temple of Heaven, the Forbidden City and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second is "Sino-Sov" style, boxy and sometimes poorly built, from the 1950s to the 1970s. The third is modern, most visibly in the CBD in east Beijing, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

In the early 21st century Beijing saw a surge of new construction in many modern styles by international designers, strongest in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s design with neofuturistic styles. The China Zun, at 528 meters, is the tallest. Since 2007, Beijing buildings have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building: the Linked Hybrid took it in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. This award goes to just one building in the world each year.

Siheyuans are courtyard homes surrounded by buildings, and grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. They are linked by alleys called hutongs, which generally run from east to west, so that doorways face north and south, a layout chosen for good feng shui. Some are so narrow that only a few pedestrians can pass at a time. Once everywhere in Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are disappearing as whole blocks give way to high-rises. Residents are entitled to apartments at least as big as their old homes, though many complain that the neighbourly community and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced. These properties are often owned by the government.

china-agricultural-university.h: Putting it together for an international applicant

blocks.x: CAU suits students who want a serious grounding in agriculture and the life sciences. Its programme count (66 undergraduate majors, over 32 master's and 21 doctoral programmes) is broad, and its rankings in agricultural, plant, animal, veterinary and food science are among the strongest anywhere. With 508 international students among about 20,900 in total, it is a university where foreign students are present but a small minority, so you should expect most daily life and many classes to be organised around Chinese students.

Beijing offers the advantages of a capital: rail, ring roads, major museums and old imperial sites, and an active modern district. It also asks for some preparation. Winters are cold and dry, summers hot and humid, spring can bring dust, and air quality, although much better than it was in 2013, is still worth checking each day. Housing and other costs, and the exact programmes and ranking positions quoted above, can change, so use the university's own website for the latest information before you apply.

The China Conservatory of Music, abbreviated CCMusic (中国音乐学院, Zhōngguó Yīnyuè Xuéyuàn), is a music academy owned by the municipality of Beijing and located in the Chaoyang district. The bills are paid jointly by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism and by the Beijing Municipal People's Government. As a higher music education institution, it concentrates on Chinese ethnic music, covering teaching, research, performance and composition. The school gives 1964 as the year it was established, and it belongs to the Double First-Class Construction programme.

The reputation of this conservatory rests mainly on traditional Chinese music. It is generally seen as one of the leading places to study traditional Chinese music and the instruments that go with it, and music education research and other fields are also strong. In company with the Shanghai Conservatory of Music and the Central Conservatory of Music, which is in Beijing as well, it is counted among the three best-known higher music institutions in China.

china-conservatory-of-music.h: A short history of the school

blocks.x: The story begins in 1956, when the art and music departments of Northeast Normal University, East China Normal University and Beijing Normal University, three teacher-training institutions, were put together. The dates are not fully consistent, since the same school is also said to have been founded in 1964, so ask the conservatory which date it uses. In 1964 the Premier of the State Council, Zhou Enlai, made a suggestion that led to a second merger. Three bodies were combined to form the conservatory as it is known now: the China Music Research Institute, the Ethnic Music Program that had been part of the Central Conservatory of Music, and the music department of the Beijing Academy of Fine Arts. The Cultural Revolution interrupted its work in 1969, when the whole school was dispersed, and its original structure was restored in 1980.
Its influence on China's music world is large. Nearly all of the country's famous folk singers and folk instrumentalists are graduates of the conservatory.
Alumni worth looking up are You Hongfei, Wu Fei, Peng Liyuan, Gong Linna and Dadon.

china-conservatory-of-music.h: Living in Beijing: first, the weather

blocks.x: Daily life for a student depends on the capital around the campus. This section begins with the weather and goes on to the terrain, the buildings and the state of the air.

Beijing's climate is classified as humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen BSk). In summer it is hot and humid, thanks to the East Asian monsoon. Winters are brief, cold and dry, and the vast Siberian anticyclone is the cause. Spring can bring sandstorms from the Gobi Desert, carried over the Mongolian steppe; at that time of year temperatures rise rapidly and conditions are mostly dry. Autumn is also a transitional season, with very little precipitation. Between 2001 and 2026, early August has been the hottest time of year and early January the coldest.

The official season dates in China put the start of spring in Beijing at 26 March, summer at 20 May, autumn at 13 September and winter at 31 October. In recent years, because March and September are warming faster and May and October more slowly, autumn is generally the shorter season, and spring is the longer one.

The temperature figures below cover 1991 to 2020. Across the urban area, the mean annual temperature falls between 12.9 and 13.3 °C, or 55.2 and 55.9 °F. Daily lows average between 7.7 and 8.4 °C, or 45.9 and 47.1 °F, and daily highs between 18.5 and 18.9 °C, or 65.3 and 66.0 °F. In the lower-lying suburbs the annual mean runs from 11.5 to 13.0 °C, or 52.7 to 55.4 °F, with lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C, or 42.6 to 46.4 °F, and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C, or 64.8 to 65.7 °F. In the mountains the annual mean is between 0 and 10 °C, or 32 to 50 °F, and drops with height. January's daily mean is −2.7 °C, or 27.1 °F, and July's is 27.2 °C, or 81.0 °F.

Rainfall adds up to about 528.0 mm, or 20.79 in, a year, rising to 584.2 mm, or 23.00 in, in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three quarters of it comes in June, July and August. Monthly possible sunshine goes from 42% in July up to 62% in January and February, and the annual total is 2,490.5 hours. The record low since 1951 was −27.4 °C, or −17.3 °F, on 22 February 1966, and the record high was 41.9 °C, or 107.4 °F, on 24 July 1999.

china-conservatory-of-music.h: The shape of the land and the city

blocks.x: The city sits at the top of the North China Plain, whose rough triangle spreads south and east. Hills and mountains to the north, north-west and west are a barrier keeping the steppe deserts away from the city and from northern China's farming heartland. Yanqing and Huairou districts, in the north-west, are the part of the municipality where the Jundu Mountains dominate, and the Western Hills (Xishan) form the western frame. The Great Wall winds over this rough ground in the north of the municipality, where it was built as a defence against nomad incursions. The highest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling, on the Hebei border in the Western Hills, at 2,303 metres, or 7,556 ft.

Rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma belong to the Hai River system and flow south-east. The largest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. Two great waterworks end here: the Grand Canal from Hangzhou, an old transport route more than 1,400 years old, and the South-North Water Transfer Project, built in the last ten years, which carries Yangtze basin water north.

Beijing's built-up area covers the plains of the south-central municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) above sea level. It is a relatively small share of the municipal area, but it is growing. The shape is a set of concentric ring roads, from the Second Ring Road on the line of the old city wall out to the Sixth Ring Road, which joins the satellite towns in the suburbs. Tian'anmen and the Square are at the centre, south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived, and to Tian'anmen's west is Zhongnanhai, where the present leaders reside. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tiananmen and the Square and is the main east-west line of the city.
People describe Beijing's growth from the old centre to the edge as 'spreading like a pancake' (tan da bing), and this pattern is often named as a source of the city's urban troubles.

Beijing's urban architecture falls into three broad groups. The oldest is imperial: the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), the main symbol of the People's Republic. Then there is the so-called 'Sino-Sov' style from the 1950s to the 1970s, known for boxy and at times poorly built structures. The third group is far more modern, concentrated in the Beijing CBD in the east, with the new CCTV Headquarters, but also seen in the National Center for the Performing Arts and the Beijing National Stadium.

Early in the 21st century a wave of building brought many modern styles from international designers, mostly in the CBD. A blend of 1950s design and neofuturism can be seen in the 798 Art Zone, which puts old and new together. China Zun, at 528 metres, is the tallest building in Beijing. Beijing has won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award twice since 2007, with the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and then the CCTV Headquarters in 2013; each year the prize for the best overall tall building goes to a single building anywhere in the world.

The siheyuan is the courtyard house, with buildings round a central yard; the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are grand examples. Narrow lanes called hutongs usually link such courtyards. Generally they are straight and run from east to west, so doorways point north and south, which is lucky for Feng Shui. Widths vary, and in the narrowest only a few people can pass at a time. Siheyuans and hutongs were everywhere once but are fast disappearing as entire blocks give way to high-rises. People who lived in hutongs may move into new apartments at least as big as their old homes, but many say that the traditional community spirit and street life cannot be replaced, and the properties are often owned by the government.

Beijing has suffered environmental problems for a long time. From 2000 to 2009 the built-up area expanded fourfold. That sharply increased human-made emissions and also changed the local meteorology fundamentally, even leaving the emissions themselves aside: near the ground, albedo, wind speed and humidity all fell, while ground and near-surface air temperatures, vertical dilution of air and ozone concentrations went up. Urbanisation and pollution from burning fossil fuels often cause serious environmental problems, with consequences for the health of many residents. In 2013 heavy smog blanketed Beijing and much of northern China and affected 600 million people. That 'pollution shock' made air pollution a major economic and social concern, and the Beijing government announced steps to cut it, such as shrinking coal's share of the energy supply, from 24% in 2012 to just 10% by 2017. At national level, heavily polluting vehicles were ordered off the road during 2015 to 2017 and the shift towards clean energy sources was stepped up.

A joint study by American and Chinese researchers in 2006 found that a great deal of the city's pollution blows in from nearby cities and provinces, and that on average 35% to 60% of the ozone originates outside Beijing. The study said that Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality 'significantly influence Beijing's air quality', partly because of the usual south or south-easterly flow in summer and the mountains north and north-west of the city.

Nearly US$17 billion was spent before the 2008 Summer Olympics to meet promises to clean the city's air. During the Games a series of schemes was applied: all building sites were stopped, many factories in Beijing were closed for good, industry in nearby regions was shut temporarily, some gas stations were closed, and car traffic was halved by letting drivers use their cars only on odd or even days by licence plate number. Fares on buses and the subway were lowered, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. Furthermore, 3,800 natural-gas buses were put together, making one of the biggest such fleets anywhere. Beijing was also the first Chinese city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Burning coal accounts for around 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 coal-fired power stations in the city have been switched to natural gas, and annual coal use is meant to stay under 20 million tons. In 2011 the city's coal burning came to 26.3 million tons, of which 73% went on heating and power and the rest on industry. Much of the pollutant load comes from neighbouring regions. Tianjin's coal use was expected to climb between 2011 and 2015 from 48 to 63 million tons, and in 2011 Hebei Province used over 300 million tons, a bigger amount than the whole of Germany, with only 30% used to generate power and a large share used in making steel and cement. Beijing's air is also affected by plants in Shandong and in the coal-mining regions of Inner Mongolia, Shanxi and Shaanxi, which have tripled their coal use since 2000. Among Chinese provinces, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth in coal use.

The city had four major coal-fired power plants supplying electricity and winter heat. The first, Gaojing Thermal Power Plant, closed in 2014, another two closed in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was to close in 2016. For the years 2013 to 2017, the plan was to cut coal use by 13 million tons and hold it at 15 million tons in 2015.

Authorities sometimes seed clouds to make rain showers likelier and clear the air before big events, for example before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to deal with drought. Recently, though, they rely more on temporary factory closures and stricter limits on cars. 'APEC blue' and 'parade blue' are the names given to short clear spells around the 2015 China Victory Day Parade and APEC China 2014. In both cases the air improved dramatically, then returned to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing most industry and commercial business in the city, and another smog 'red alert' came later that month. Beijing's environmental protection bureau announced in November 2016 that from 2017, highly polluting old cars would not be allowed to drive whenever red alerts were in force in the city or nearby regions.

The 'war on pollution' declared in 2014 has produced measurable cuts. Fine particulates fell by 35% in 2017, and fell further by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial plants in the Beijing area were cleaned up. The annual average level of PM2.5, the fine airborne particulate matter, fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024, heavy pollution lasted just two days, a record low and 96.6 percent down from 58 days in 2013.

china-conservatory-of-music.h: Checking air quality and staying healthy

blocks.x: With so much pollution, different sources give different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) reports daily pollution figures from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website. The American Embassy in Beijing also posts hourly levels of fine particulates (PM2.5) and ozone on Twitter. The two bodies track different pollutants using different criteria, so the BJEPB's reported pollution levels and health effects tend to come out lower than the Embassy's.

Smog hurts and endangers people. It has a direct and significant effect on the rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and exposure to heavy concentrations can bring respiratory and cardiovascular problems, hospital emergency visits and even death. If you have such a condition, ask your doctor for advice.

Seasonal dust storms trouble the city, carrying dust from eroding deserts in northern and north-western China. At times the Beijing Weather Modification Office artificially induces rain to combat the storms and lessen their effects. Eight storms or more hit during the first four months of 2006, and in April 2002 one storm deposited almost 50,000 tons of dust over the city and then carried on towards Korea and Japan.

For a student of Chinese music, the China Conservatory of Music offers a specialised education in traditional instruments and folk singing at a school with a strong national reputation, set in the capital. Beijing rewards visitors with imperial monuments, hutong alleys and daring new architecture, but expect a cold, dry winter, a hot and humid summer, spring dust, and air quality that has improved a lot but still varies from day to day. Since this overview draws on statistics from different years, confirm course content, fees, language requirements and the date the conservatory itself uses for its founding with the admissions office before you apply.
China Conservatory of Music lists 104 programs for international students on this site: 7 bachelor, 45 master's, 30 doctoral, 22 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 104 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 32,000 to CNY 32,000 (median CNY 32,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 38,000 to CNY 38,000 (median CNY 38,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 42,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 42,000), according to the university's published fee table.

104 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

china-conservatory-of-music.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. China Conservatory of Music may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at China Conservatory of Music by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

China Foreign Affairs University, or CFAU (Waijiao Xueyuan in Chinese, which translates literally as Diplomacy Academy), is a state university in Beijing that trains people for international affairs and foreign service. Its parent body is the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is unusual among Chinese universities, and it has been included in the Double First-Class Construction programme.

Its main claim to fame is its alumni: more than 300 ambassadors and thousands of senior diplomats have studied there, which earned it the nickname cradle of Chinese diplomats. It operates two campuses in Beijing. The original one at Shahe in Changping started work in 1956, and the newer Zhanlanguan Road campus in Xicheng District came into use in 2012.

For overseas applicants, the useful summary is that CFAU is small, specialised and closely tied to the foreign ministry, so its courses lean towards languages, foreign policy, law and international economics rather than a broad general curriculum.

The university was founded in 1955 on the advice of Premier Zhou Enlai at the time. Its forerunner was the Department of Diplomacy at Renmin University of China. (Do not confuse CFAU with the University of International Relations, another Beijing institution.) Chen Yi, who was Vice Premier and Foreign Minister, served as president from 1961 to 1969. The university had to close during the Cultural Revolution and reopened in 1980 with the support of Deng Xiaoping. Many former presidents have been ambassadors. The current president is Wan Fan, a specialist in international relations, and the party secretary is Qi Dayu. Until 2005 the university used the English name Foreign Affairs College.

The curriculum covers three languages (English, French and Japanese) plus foreign policy, international politics, international relations, diplomacy, international law and economics. Degrees are offered at bachelor's, master's and doctoral level, and the university also teaches short programmes for serving Chinese civil servants and visiting foreign diplomats.

In 2001 CFAU and the East Asia Security Centre began to host the East Asia Security Forum and Conference (EASCC). Speakers have included Chinese scholars, officials, ambassadors and senior figures from the Communist Party and the People's Liberation Army, while delegates come from foreign universities, governments, militaries, international bodies and companies.

Model United Nations (MUN) is the university's best-known student activity. CFAU held its first Model UN conference on 3 June 1995, the first of its kind in China to be attended by Chinese students. In 2002, working with the UN Association of China, it organised the first Beijing Model United Nations conference (BMUN, renamed Beijing International Model United Nations, BIMUN, from 2017). It was China's first inter-university MUN and later came to be counted among the three most prestigious university MUNs. In 2004, again with the UN Association of China, CFAU hosted the first China Model United Nations Conference (CNMUN).

CFAU has attracted compliments. On 1 July 2008 the UN Secretary-General of the day, Ban Ki-moon, called it the cradle of Chinese diplomacy and an authoritative forum for discussing China and its growing role in the international community. On 29 April 2009 the former French president Jacques Chirac praised it as a university that nurtures top talent for Chinese diplomacy. Gary Faye Locke, then US ambassador to China, used the phrase incubator of diplomatic talent when he spoke at the launch of a US-China programme to train Afghan diplomats at CFAU.

There is also criticism. A common complaint in recent years is that the university stresses language study at the cost of genuine diplomatic education, so that some people see many Chinese foreign-affairs staff as mere translators or interpreters. In 2013 the National Audit Office carried out a wide-ranging check and found irregularities in procurement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs worth over 52 million yuan, of which around 38 million yuan was linked to building CFAU's new Shahe campus.

Finally, there is friendly rivalry. CFAU proudly calls itself the cradle of Chinese diplomats, but Beijing Foreign Studies University (BFSU), having also trained hundreds of Chinese ambassadors, makes the same claim, and students of the two schools still compete good-naturedly.
Your daily routine will be shaped far more by the city than by the campus, so here is an introduction to Beijing: how it looks, how it is laid out, what the weather does and how clean the air is.

Urban Beijing is dominated by three building styles. The second is the so-called Sino-Soviet style of the 1950s to 1970s, with boxy buildings that were sometimes poorly built. The third is modern architecture, most visible around the Beijing CBD in the east, where you will find the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere, for instance the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

In the early twenty-first century Beijing saw a huge wave of new construction in many modern styles by international designers, strongest in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone mixes 1950s design with a neofuturist look. The tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. Since 2007 Beijing buildings have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which goes to just one tall building a year worldwide: the winners were the Linked Hybrid (2009) and then the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

They are linked by lanes called hutongs, which usually run east to west so that doors face north and south, in line with feng shui. Hutong residents are entitled to flats at least as big as their old homes, but many say the neighbourly community and street life cannot be replaced, and the properties are often state-owned.

The urban core is on the plains in the south-central part, at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and takes up a small but growing part of the municipality. Tian'anmen and its square are in the middle, just south of the Forbidden City, once home to the emperors. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, where China's present leaders live, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between the gate and the square, is the east-west axis. People often say Beijing has spread like a pancake (tan da bing), a pattern blamed for many urban problems.

The summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon, and winters are short, cold and dry under the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone. For 1991 to 2020 the yearly average in the urban area is 12.9 to 13.3 degrees C, with daily minimums averaging 7.7 to 8.4 degrees C and maximums 18.5 to 18.9 degrees C. In low-lying suburbs the mean is 11.5 to 13.0 degrees C (minimums 5.9 to 8.0, maximums 18.2 to 18.7), and in the mountains between 0 and 10 degrees C, falling with altitude. January averages minus 2.7 degrees C and July 27.2 degrees C. Rainfall is about 528.0 millimetres a year (584.2 in Haidian and Chaoyang), with nearly three-quarters falling from June to August. Sunshine is 42 per cent of possible in July and 62 per cent in January and February, 2,490.5 hours a year. Extremes since 1951 run from minus 27.4 degrees C (22 February 1966) to 41.9 degrees C (24 July 1999). Bring a real winter coat and also light summer clothes.

CFAU offers a focused path into international relations and diplomacy, with an alumni network of ambassadors and a lively Model UN tradition. In Beijing you should expect cold dry winters, hot humid summers, dusty spring days and air that is much cleaner than a decade ago but still variable. Check the university website for current admission rules, campus assignments (Zhanlanguan Road or Shahe) and programme languages, as several facts above are dated.

CFAU's two sites give you a choice of settings, so ask which will host your year of study. The original Shahe Campus in Changping District opened in 1956, while the Zhanlanguan Road Campus in Xicheng District has been in use only since 2012. Xicheng lies in the older, central part of Beijing, and Changping is farther out on the northern side, so travel times and neighbourhood character differ. Both are within the Beijing municipality, which means the city information in this profile applies to either.

The comments quoted above, both the praise from international figures and the objections about language training, reflect the fact that CFAU has a very specific role. It is not trying to be a general university. If your aim is a career in diplomacy, international organisations or foreign-affairs research, the alumni network and the Model UN tradition are real advantages; if you are mainly interested in languages or translation, the emphasis on foreign languages will suit you. The 2013 audit finding concerned procurement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, part of which related to the Shahe campus buildings, and it says nothing about teaching quality, but prospective students may want to know about it. For anything that affects your enrolment, rely on the official website and the admissions office.

If you are comparing Beijing universities, note that CFAU is far smaller than the capital's big comprehensive campuses and works under a ministry, not the education authorities. That shapes its character: its activities, from the East Asia Security Forum to the Model UN conferences, revolve around foreign affairs, and its short courses serve officials and foreign diplomats. Contact the admissions office or current students before applying if you can.

For readers who think in Fahrenheit, the urban yearly average of 12.9 to 13.3 degrees C is 55.2 to 55.9 F, with daily lows of 45.9 to 47.1 F and highs of 65.3 to 66.0 F. In the lower suburbs the average is 52.7 to 55.4 F (lows 42.6 to 46.4 F, highs 64.8 to 65.7 F), and in the mountains it lies between 32 and 50 F. January averages 27.1 F and July 81.0 F. Rainfall is 20.79 inches a year, or 23.00 inches in Haidian and Chaoyang, and the recorded extremes are minus 17.3 F and 107.4 F.

china-foreign-affairs-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. China Foreign Affairs University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.
