china-medical-university.h: Which China Medical University is this?

blocks.x: The name China Medical University is shared by two institutions that are easy to confuse. This profile is about the one in Shenyang, Liaoning Province, mainland China (中国医科大学). A different China Medical University (中國醫藥大學) exists in Taichung, Taiwan, and it is a separate institution. If you are comparing programmes, check carefully that you are reading about the right one.

Because details of the campus, programmes and fees are best taken directly from the university, this page concentrates on the place where you would live: Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning, and the province around it. Understanding the weather, the history, the economy and the transport links is a big part of preparing for study there.

china-medical-university.h: Peoples and kingdoms of the early period

blocks.x: Between about the 4th century BC and the 9th century AD, Han Chinese governments were the main authority in the Liaoning area. Before about 300 BC the land belonged to the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples. Then the state of Yan took control and split its new territory in two, naming the halves after the river: Liaodong lay on the eastern side and Liaoxi on the western. Xiangping, Liaodong's centre, stood on the site of modern Liaoyang.

Once the Han dynasty collapsed, Gongsun Du and his family built a semi-independent state around Liaodong, which survived until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. This state also took the name Yan; it was short-lived but organised many sea expeditions for diplomacy and trade, and it left a lasting influence on culture across North-east Asia. Later, following the end of Western Jin, three Xianbei states of the Murong clan (Former, Later and Northern Yan) governed Liaoning. When Northern Wei took the Yan capital in 436, Goguryeo took the Liaodong Peninsula, and eventually Tang forces annexed the area in a war against Goguryeo.

Tang power was weakened by the An Lushan Rebellion in the middle of the 8th century, which pulled resources away from the frontier. The Bohai state spread into Liaodong, and the Khitan Liao dynasty ultimately conquered Liaoning, administering it through four capital circuits: Eastern, Supreme, Central and Lower.

The Jurchen Jin dynasty mostly ruled the land through an Eastern Capital Route, with other parts under the Xianping, Supreme Capital and Northern Capital routes. Genghis Khan took Liaoning in 1206, after which it became part of the Yuan state. Under the Yuan, the east came under the Liaoyang and Shenyang routes of the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat, the north under Kaiyuan Route's Xianping Prefecture, and the west, including Guangning Route, was also supervised by the Liaoyang secretariat, while the Jinzhou and Chaoyang districts formed Daning Route, answering to the Central Secretariat.

The Ming gained control in 1371, only three years after driving the Mongols out of Beijing. About 1442 they built a defensive wall to shield the province's farmland from a possible threat in the north-west, the Oriyanghan Jurchen-Mongols, who were Ming tributaries. An extension in 1467-1468 faced north-east, towards the Jianzhou Jurchens who would later be called Manchus. Though it served much the way the Great Wall did, the Liaodong Wall was cheap: stone and tile were used here and there, but most of it was really an earth bank with ditches on both sides.

The wall failed. In the early 1600s, decades before they won the rest of China, the Jurchens captured Liaodong, the eastern half of Liaoning. Their dynasty, first known as Later Jin and renamed Qing, had its capital at Xingjing between 1616 and 1621. That town lay east of the wall, in today's eastern Liaoning. The capital then went to Dongjing (to the east of present Liaoyang), and in 1625 to Shengjing, today's Shenyang. In 1644 the main imperial court moved to Beijing after taking it, though Shengjing continued to serve as a regional capital for most of the dynasty.

The fighting left the province depleted. Many locals were killed or fled south past the Great Wall, and Ming troops pulling back destroyed numerous towns themselves. In 1661, Zhang Shangxian, the civil governor of Fengtian Province, wrote that outside Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city on the Liao's east bank was either abandoned or down to a few hundred residents; he said Tieling and Fushun contained only vagrants. In the west, only Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning kept notable populations.

The Qing government answered by recruiting settlers from south of the wall, particularly from Shandong, following legislation of 1651 and 1653. The area they settled, Fengtian Province, corresponds roughly to modern Liaoning, and many people living there now descend from these settlers. Elsewhere in the north-east, the government kept the Han away for most of the Manchu period. It built the Willow Palisade (about 1638 to about 1672) around Fengtian's farmland to prevent migration into what is now Jilin, Heilongjiang and neighbouring Inner Mongolia; it often ran just outside the Ming wall or reused it, and it separated the farmland from Manchu forests in the north-east and Mongol grassland in the north-west.

The authorities later tried to halt the flow of migrants, return some of them, or at least make their residence legal. In 1704 an edict complained that recent Han arrivals in Fengtian had ignored earlier orders to depart, and gave them ten years to register and enrol in a local defence group (bao) or leave. Ten years on, another edict raised the matter again. The policy was never as effective as officials in Beijing wanted, and the population of Fengtian doubled between 1683 and 1734.

Manchuria was divided among three generals under the Qing, and the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyun) had authority over much of present-day Liaoning. When the Manchu government started reopening the region to settlement in 1860, the Han Chinese soon became its largest ethnic group.

Maize, sorghum and soybeans are the main field crops, and cotton is also grown. Orchards near Dalian provide three out of every four apples and peaches that China sells abroad. Other regional fruits are apples from Yingkou, pears from Beizhen (Jinzhou) and from Huludao and Suizhong, and Gushan's apricots and plums in Dandong.

Shenyang is a major industrial centre of China and the heart of the Shenyang Economic Zone, which has New Special Reform Zone status. Heavy industry is its backbone, especially planes and space hardware, machine tools, heavy equipment and military production, with software, vehicles and electronics added lately.

The story of the economy has three stages. First, heavy industry took root in the 1920s and was well advanced before the Second World War; in the first five-year plan (1951-1956), many factories rose in the Tiexi district. In the 1970s Shenyang peaked, counted with Shanghai and Tianjin as one of China's three main industrial centres and, at one point, a candidate for direct-controlled municipality status. Second, after the 1980s, planned-economy industry lost ground and many state-owned factories went bankrupt, with hundreds of thousands of workers losing jobs, so Shenyang came to be seen as a rust-belt city. Third, recovery has been marked in recent years because of the national Revitalize Northeast China campaign and expansion in software and car manufacturing, and multinationals that set up offices or headquarters here receive investment subsidies.

The service sector, especially banking, is growing. Foreign banks include Hana Bank (South Korea), Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ (Japan), Bank of East Asia (Hong Kong), United Overseas Bank (Singapore) and HSBC (Britain). The city had 1,063 banks and branches in 2006, along with 144 insurers and related companies. Officials then hoped that by 2010 there would be 30 overseas banks and 60 other kinds of financial institution, so treat all these as older figures. The Economist Intelligence Unit's November 2010 Access China white paper included Shenyang in a six-city set labelled CHAMPS (the others are Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan and Pingdingshan), drawn from a profile of the top 20 emerging Chinese cities. GDP per head in 2009 was 78,490 yuan, which ranked third among the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning.
Business life is organised around three zones, each with its own focus:
The finance and trade zone
The high-tech industrial zone
The economic and technological development zone

Brilliance Auto, a leading Chinese car manufacturer, has most of its plants in Shenyang. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation makes civil aircraft and also supplies the PLA Air Force. Neusoft Group, the largest software firm in China, is based here, and so is Shenyang Machine Tool Group, the largest machine-tool maker. Foreign companies expanding here include Tyco International, General Motors and the Michelin tyre venture. For students in a medical university, the city's size and economic variety mean a broad range of services, plus the practical benefits of a large regional centre.

The population is about 9.07 million, of whom 85.12 percent live in the urban area. Shenyang is culturally varied, with 38 of China's 56 recognised ethnic groups; Han Chinese form 91.26 percent of the total. Besides the Han, there are 37 minority groups, beginning with the larger Manchu, Korean, Hui, Xibo and Mongolian communities and continuing with Zhuang, Miao, Tujia, Dong, Daur, Bai, Uyghur, Tibetan and Yi residents. Smaller numbers include Taiwanese Aboriginal people, Russians, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tatars, Evenks, Oroqen and Nanai, and members of the She, Bouyei, Yao, Akha, Dai, Li, Shui, Nakhi, Jingpo, Tu, Mulao, Qiang, Maonan, Gelao and Lhoba groups. Most are not native to the region, though the Manchu and Xibe are. The city has temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship.

Locals use the Shenyang dialect, which comes from Northeastern Mandarin and took shape in the early Qing. It resembles both other north-eastern varieties and standard Putonghua, but it counts as Dongbeihua and has many words that the standard language does not. Do not be surprised if everyday speech sounds different from your Mandarin classes.

Errenzhuan and Yangge, two north-eastern folk dances, are widely enjoyed. The Big Stage Theatre near Middle Street is known for Errenzhuan and for comic sketches by Zhao Benshan and his pupils, and with so many comedians from the city, Shenyang is seen nationally as a home of Chinese comedy. Arts organisations based here include the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China, Liaoning Ballet and a song-and-dance ensemble. Zimei and Na Ying, both singers, and the pianist Lang Lang are all from Shenyang.

Shenyang is the main transport hub of the north-east. It has an airport, railways, a subway network (five lines in the figures available), a tram network opened in the south in 2013, a web of streets and expressways, and city buses. At the Taoxian International Airport, Terminal 3 is the biggest terminal in north-eastern China.

It is also the north-east's rail hub, with eight lines running to Fushun, Beijing, Dalian, Changchun and Harbin. The Qinhuangdao-Shenyang high-speed railway, which was the first passenger-only line in China, is the main route in and out through the Shanhai Pass. Since early 2007, trains at 200 km/h (120 mph) have shortened Beijing-Shenyang travel by almost two-thirds, to about 4 hours. Late 2012 saw the opening of the Harbin-Dalian high-speed line at up to 300 km/h (190 mph), a service linking Shenyang with Harbin, Changchun and Dalian.
Shenyang North station (Shenhe District) and Shenyang station (Heping District) are the two big stations.

Shenyang North's earlier name was Liaoning General Station (before 1946), and many still call the older site the Old North Station. The first building, now a listed heritage structure, opened as Fengtian City Station in 1927 at the end of the Jingfeng Railway, roughly 1 kilometre (0.62 miles) south-west of the present location. Warlord Zhang Zuolin ordered it built to rival the Shenyang station then under Japanese administration. Work on the current building started in 1986, and it opened in December 1990 as one of the five most significant rail hubs in China, nicknamed Northeast's No. 1 Station. Passenger numbers rose after high-speed trains arrived, and in 2011 a major rebuilding scheme began. It added a three-storey sub-station building and a north square on the Huanggu District side, moved the old waiting hall of the 16-storey main building to a large raised concourse across the tracks, and covered the platforms with a column-free dome roof, the biggest in mainland China. The South Square was remade into a multi-level complex with an elevated, airport-style drop-off, ground-level bus stops and a three-level underground city with shops, parking, taxis and a connection to Subway Line 2, which could quickly become an air-raid shelter if needed.

Shenyang station is more than 100 years old. Russians built it in 1899 on the east of the South Manchurian Railway as Fengtian Station; the Japanese later enlarged it after the Russo-Japanese War and called it Fengtian Yam until the Second World War ended. From 1945 to 1950 it was Shenyang South Station, or just South Station, and local people still use this nickname, even though the actual Shenyang South station now stands where Hunnan meets Sujiatun. These days it focuses on regular passenger services and is undergoing refurbishment with a large archway and a new terminal, with passengers diverted above and below ground in the meantime. A new West Station Building and West Square opened in 2010, and the old East Station Building has provincial heritage protection.
A container train has run direct every day since 2011 from Leipzig, Germany, to Shenyang, carrying car parts about 11,000 km (6,800 miles) through Siberia in 23 days.

The public airport is Taoxian International, in Hunnan District, one of China's eight major airline hubs, ranked 23rd in the country for traffic. The city has three more airfields, none open to the public. East Pagoda Airport in Dadong District, the oldest, opened in the 1920s and was retired in the 1980s, and a 2013 proposal suggested moving and reopening it at Xinmin. Beiling Airport in Huanggu District is used for the aircraft maker's test flights, while Yuhong Airport in Yuhong District serves only the military's local Northern Theater Command units.

Shenyang lies in central Liaoning at 41 degrees 11 minutes to 43 degrees 02 minutes north and 122 degrees 25 minutes to 123 degrees 48 minutes east. In the west, the land is flat river-deposited plain belonging to the Liao River system. The east is forested hill country, the edge of the Changbai Mountains. Elevation goes from 7 metres (23 feet) at the lowest point up to 414 metres (1,358 feet), and the urban area averages 45 metres (148 feet).

North of the Hun River lies the main urban area. The Hun was once the Liao's biggest tributary, and the people of the city call it their mother river. Three man-made rivers surround the city centre and are connected by channels into one continuous water route: the South Canal along the south and south-east, the Xinkai River (formerly the North Canal) to the north and north-east, and the Weigong River, once the Weigong Nullah, in the west. The South Canal, known for its linear parks and gardens, was made out of the old Wanquan River ("ten thousand springs"), historically also the Little Shen River or the Wuli River ("five-li river"), a main source of water for the old city. Smaller rivers at the edges, the Xi, Puhe and Mantang, drain into the Hun at three places: the south-east, due south and south-west of the city. An old canal on the east, the Huishan Nullah, flowed into the lower Xinkai River but has gone, lost to land reclamation for building.

The South Canal Linear Parks are the best-known green spaces, running 14.5 kilometres (9.0 miles) through the south of Dadong, Shenhe and Heping districts. Six large parks and 18 riverside gardens cover approximately 1,400,000 square metres (350 acres) and contain a wide range of plants: roses, scarlet sage, morning glory, natal lily and black-eyed Susan, bladder cherry, apricots and honeylocust, plus large areas of peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, weeping willow, pine and black locust. This is the largest planted open space in the city, which has a greening ratio of 40 percent, and it was a key factor in Shenyang being named a national forest city in 2005.

The city's environmental protection bureau has said that coal burned by boiler stations for district heating in winter produces 30 percent of air pollution; in the winter of 2013-2014, half of the 16 million tonnes of coal the city used went on heating. Other sources were building-site dust at 20 percent, car exhaust at 20 percent, industry at 10 percent and outside dust at 20 percent, mostly yellow dust from the Gobi Desert. The bureau reported that air quality was slowly improving, but these numbers are some years old, so check current readings.

The climate is monsoon-influenced humid continental (Koppen Dwa; Trewartha Dcac), with hot, humid summers brought by the monsoon and dry, cold winters under the Siberian anticyclone. The four seasons are clearly defined, and nearly half of annual rainfall comes in July and August. Mean temperatures run from minus 11.4 degrees Celsius (11.5 F) in the coldest month, January, to 24.9 degrees (76.8 F) in the warmest, July, and average 8.6 degrees (47.5 F) over the year. Frost-free days number 183, a long period considering how severe winters are. There are 2,421 hours of sunshine a year, where the monthly share of possible sunshine ranges between 42 percent in July and 64 percent in February, and extremes from minus 33.1 degrees (minus 28 F) to 38.4 degrees (101 F).

Winters call for proper cold-weather gear, summers for lighter clothes and a rain jacket, and the transport links make it easy to reach Beijing, Dalian, Changchun and Harbin by train. Because many of the facts above (bank counts, subway lines, station works, pollution shares) were recorded in earlier years, and because the university's own information on teaching and admissions is the authoritative source, check the university's website and local sources for current numbers.

Several sets of numbers here belong to particular years, including the population, the bank counts, the GDP per head, the pollution shares, the number of subway lines and the airport rankings. Treat them as a description of scale and character rather than today's exact statistics. Likewise the ethnic-group list simply shows how mixed the city is; it does not mean each community is large. If a figure matters to a decision, confirm it with an official local source.

For a prospective medical student, the most useful points are practical. Shenyang is large enough to offer hospitals, shops, banks and international food, it is a rail hub with fast links to other north-eastern cities and Beijing, and it has a cold winter, so budget for suitable clothing. The local accent is distinctive and the city's humour is well known, which can make the first weeks both challenging and fun.

China Pharmaceutical University, known as CPU (中国药科大学), is a public university devoted to pharmacy and related fields, located in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu Province. The Ministry of Education and Jiangsu Province sponsor it jointly. Its present form dates from 1968, when the National College of Pharmacy was combined with some smaller institutions. Two national schemes that give priority support to leading universities, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction, both include CPU. For a student, that signals that the university sits in the group the state invests in most heavily for its subject.

china-pharmaceutical-university.h: From a pharmacy college to a university

blocks.x: The story starts in September 1936 with the founding of the National Pharmacy College, which ran a four-year course. When the Second Sino-Japanese War came, the college relocated, first to Hankou in Wuhan and then to Chongqing. In June 1950 it took the name East China Pharmacy College (华东药学专科学校).

After that came a series of mergers. In November 1952 the pharmacy departments of Qilu University and Soochow University were joined to the college, and in 1953 it took in a pharmacy class that had belonged to the Wuhan-based College of Hygiene for Central and South China. Postgraduate enrolment started in 1955. A new name, Nanjing Pharmacy College, followed in 1956, and in October 1986 a merger with Nanjing College of Chinese Medicine produced China Pharmaceutical University.
Milestones since then: CPU entered the national Project 211 in 1996, came under the direct management of the Ministry of Education in February 2000, and took in Jiangsu Pharmaceutical School in 2001.

The university is in Nanjing, an ancient capital, and has two campuses. The Xuanwumen campus is downtown, and the Jiangning campus sits in the south-eastern outskirts. Ask which campus your programme uses before you arrange housing.
The academic work is divided between six schools. In the order they are usually listed, these are:
School of Pharmacy
School of Traditional Chinese Pharmacy
School of Life Science and Technology
School of International Pharmaceutical Business
School of Continuing Education
School of Higher Vocational Education

Alongside the schools are four independent departments, which teach basic sciences, foreign languages, social sciences and physical education. In addition, five key laboratories and centres, recognised at state or provincial level, are based at the university.

Degree authority is organised by level. For doctorates, CPU may award degrees in three first-level disciplines, which are biology, pharmacy and traditional Chinese medicine, and it has one professional doctorate point covering biology and medicine. Master's degrees can be awarded in eight first-level disciplines: chemistry, biology, pharmacy, traditional Chinese medicine, basic medical science, biomedical engineering, public administration, and public health and preventive medicine. Five more master's points are professional ones, for pharmacy, traditional Chinese medicine, biology and medicine, applied statistics and public administration. Postdoctoral researchers can work at two mobile stations, pharmacy and traditional Chinese medicine, and the national government rates pharmacy as a key first-level discipline.

There are 530 faculty members. Two of them are academicians, which means they belong to the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering, and more than 40% have advanced academic titles. The staff have completed upwards of 70 projects paid for by the State Key Programs Foundation, and over 300 more paid for by the State Natural Sciences Foundation or the State New Drug Research Foundation. Other national, provincial and municipal departments also provide funds. Plenty of this work has reached international standards, and some of it filled gaps in what China could do in pharmaceuticals.

In 2024 the university had 19,730 full-time students, of whom 448 came from abroad. The Ministry of Education has authorised CPU as the only institution allowed to admit overseas full-time pharmacy students, continuing-education students and senior visiting scholars. The mainland institutions that recruit students from Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao include CPU as well.

International exchange is an active part of the university. CPU has signed exchange agreements with over 30 higher education institutions in countries and regions that include Japan, the United States, Britain, Australia, Italy and Hong Kong. Beyond formal agreements, it has academic contacts with universities and research bodies in over 40 countries and regions.
Most of daily student life depends on the city: the weather, the transport and the things to do. What follows is a guide to Nanjing.

Nanjing has a land area of 6,598 km² (2,548 sq mi). It lies at the centre of the lower Yangtze's drainage area and inside the Yangtze River Delta, which is among the largest economic zones in China. The river passes first the west and then the north of the city, and the Ningzheng Ridge forms an arc around the north, east and south. For distances: the city is 650 km (400 mi) south-east of Luoyang, 900 km (560 mi) south-south-east of Beijing, 270 km (170 mi) west-north-west of Shanghai and 1,200 km (750 mi) east-north-east of Chongqing.

Below Jiujiang in Jiangxi, the Yangtze crosses Anhui and Jiangsu before it reaches the East China Sea. Two basins flank its lower drainage area, the Huai River basin to the north and the Zhe River basin to the south, and the Grand Canal, to the east of Nanjing, links the two. The region round Nanjing goes by the name Xiajiang (下江, "Downstream River"), where Jianghuai culture is dominant in the north and Jiangzhe in the south. It is also called Dongnan (东南, the "South East") and Jiangnan (江南, "South of the River", meaning south of the Yangtze).

To the north-east is Yangzhou, to the east Zhenjiang, and to the south-east Changzhou. The western boundary is shared with Anhui, and five prefecture-level cities are on the other side of it: Chuzhou (north-west), Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan (west), and Xuancheng (south-west).

Nanjing's climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) under the influence of the East Asian monsoon. Seasons are distinct. Dampness persists all year, summers are very hot and muggy, winters are cold and wet, and spring and autumn last a fair length of time. Nanjing, Chongqing and Wuhan are traditionally called the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze because of their hot summers. Between mid-June and the end of July comes the meiyu, East Asia's rainy season, whose name means "plum rain" because it coincides with plum blossom; during it the city gets spells of gentle rain and extra damp. In winter, north-easterly winds are the norm.

The "furnace" label hides the fact that Nanjing is cold for its latitude. Winter temperatures resemble those of London or are lower, and January is 2 °C colder than London's although Nanjing lies at 32°04'N and London at 51°30'N. Another comparison: the US east coast shares this humid subtropical climate type, yet Nanjing's winter is a full 7 °C colder than winter in Savannah, Georgia. In practice, bring proper cold-weather clothing.

January's average is 3.1 °C (37.6 °F). The coldest daily minimum ever recorded was −14.0 °C (6.8 °F), on 6 January 1955. In summer south-easterly winds blow, and July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), with the all-time daily maximum of 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) set on 13 July 1934. Over a year, rain or other precipitation of at least 0.1 mm falls on 112.9 days on average, and the record is 160 such days, in 1957. Mean annual precipitation is 1,144 mm (45.0 in).

Late summer and early autumn can bring typhoons, though they are uncommon. The yearly mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F). Since 1951 the lowest reading has been −14.0 °C (7 °F) on 6 January 1955 and the highest 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959. Possible sunshine ranges between 37 percent (June) and 48 percent (August and October), so there are 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine in a typical year.

The area has plenty of natural resources, including more than 40 kinds of mineral. Iron and sulfur make up 40 percent of Jiangsu's reserves, and strontium reserves rank first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water comes from both the Yangtze and underground sources, and there are natural hot springs at Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou.

In the middle of the city, Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are open to the public. Purple Mountain, with its deciduous and coniferous forests, protects a range of historical and cultural sites. Meanwhile a deep-water channel under construction in the Yangtze will let ships of 50,000 DWT travel upriver from the East China Sea to Nanjing.

On 2 December 2013 a thick wave of smog started over central and eastern China and stretched about 1,200 km (750 mi), passing over Hebei, Tianjin, Shandong, Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang. Stagnant air masses carrying industrial emissions, and too little cold air movement, trapped pollutants in a dense layer. Central and southern Jiangsu were badly affected, especially around Nanjing, where the AQI stood at "severely polluted" for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to weak winds, car exhaust under low air pressure and coal-fired district heating in northern China. Winds pushed low air masses carrying factory emissions, mostly SO2, towards the east coast. Check current air-quality reports before you travel.

Two main soil types occur: zonal soil and cultivated soil. Zonal soil is yellow-brown in the north and centre, and red along the southern border with Anhui. Soil created by farming is mainly paddy soil, plus patches of yellow Gang soil and market-garden soil. Its pattern follows the changes of terrain and hydrology and falls into three groups: low mountains and hills, hills, and plain. The second national soil survey (1980 to 1987) divided Nanjing's soils into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species, over 416,300 hectares.

Nanjing lies in the lower reaches of the Yangtze, which crosses the city diagonally from south-west to north-east. The stretch inside the city is about 93 km long, and it is over 300 km from the river's mouth at the sea. The Qinhuai River flows south to north through the main urban area before joining the Yangtze, and is known as Nanjing's "mother river". Two lakes, Xuanwu and Mochou, are set into the main city like pearls, and in all about 11% of the area is water.

The Yangtze system takes in almost all the local waterways. Just the rivers draining to Baoying Lake and Gaoyou Lake, in northern Liuhe District, belong to the Huai River system instead. The Yangtze system itself has several parts: the Qinhuai River south of the river, the Chuhe River north of it, a riverside network of small streams entering from either bank, the lakes Gucheng and Shijiu, and the West Taihu Lake system in the east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and of excellent quality, with the Pukou Pearl Spring especially famous, and Jiangning's Tangshan and Pukou's Tangquan are long-established hot-spring areas.

The Port of Nanjing is the largest inland port in China, with cargo of 191,970,000 t in 2012. Its 98 km (61 mi) length includes 64 berths, and 16 of them handle ships above 10,000 tons. It is also the largest container port on the Yangtze: in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area, with capacity for one million containers, opened and reinforced the city's lead in the region. As of 2010 it consisted of three industrial ports and six public ones. The Yangtze's 12.5-metre-deep waterway lets ocean ships of 50,000 tons come directly to the port, and vessels of 100,000 tons or more can arrive after unloading part of their cargo during high tide on the river. The CSC Jinling shipyard is also big.

Nanjing has abundant plant life, with great variety. Natural vegetation is of 7 types, running from conifer forest and deciduous broad-leaved forest to mixed broad-leaved forest (part deciduous, part evergreen), bamboo, shrubland, grassland and water plants. Planted vegetation includes field crops, vegetables, commercial forest, fruit orchards and green belts. Seven species are protected nationally as rare or endangered, namely Sphaerocarpus sinensis, Chinese Allium chinense, Ming Codonopsis and Pterocarpus sinensis; the other three are not named in the published text.

Wild animals are plentiful too. There are 795 species of insects from 125 families in 11 orders and 99 species of fish from 22 families in 12 orders. Land vertebrates number 327 species from 29 orders and 90 families, of which birds account for 243 species (in 56 families and 17 orders) and mammals for 47 (in 22 families and 8 orders). Among them, nine wild species receive first-level national protection, for instance the Oriental White Crane and the white-shouldered eagle, and 65 receive second-level protection, such as the finless porpoise, swallowtail, Chinese tiger and little swan. Jiangsu Province also lists 125 key protected animals, and 35 species of endangered animals.

The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge was finished in the 1960s, and at that point it was the sole bridge across the Lower Yangtze in eastern China. Chinese engineers designed and built it themselves, after surveys by other countries had failed and after Soviet expertise was first relied on and then set aside, so it became a source of national pride and a symbol of modern China. Work began in 1960 and traffic opened in 1968. It has two levels, one for road and one for rail, and the upper deck spans 4,600 m (15,100 ft), of which about 1,580 m (5,180 ft) crosses the river itself.

Since then the city has added four more bridges and four tunnels. Going downstream, you meet these crossings in this sequence: the Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Baguazhou Bridge and the Qixiashan Bridge. Another count, for October 2014, gives four bridges and two tunnels, so the totals depend on the date and on how crossings are counted.
The bridges, with opening year and longest span:
First Nanjing Yangtze Bridge (Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge): 1968, longest span 160 m.
Second Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (Baguazhou): 1997, 628 m.
Third Nanjing Yangtze Bridge (Dashengguan): 2005, 648 m.
Fourth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (Qixiashan): 2012, 1,418 m.
Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (Jiangxinzhou): 2020, 600 m.
Nanjing Xianxin Yangtze River Bridge: 2023, 1,760 m.

The mineral wealth is considerable. Discovered deposits include 49 types, among them iron, copper, lead, zinc, strontium, ferrosulfide, dolomite, limestone, gypsum and clay, and 31 have proven reserves. They are concentrated in four metallogenic belts, including the Jiangpu-Liuhe belt for iron and copper and the Ningzhen belt for iron, copper and sulfur polymetals, as well as the Ningwu iron and copper belt. The fourth belt is not named in the published text.

When the census was taken in 2010, Nanjing had 8.005 million residents, while the OECD estimated the surrounding metropolitan area at 11.7 million. Official figures for 2011 suggested 8.11 million. Vital statistics gave a birth rate of 8.86 percent and a death rate of 6.88 percent. Of the total, 6.47 million lived in the urban area, and the sex ratio was 107.31 men to 100 women.

The official breakdown resembles that of most of eastern China: Han people are 98.56 percent, with 50 other recognised ethnic groups making up the rest. In 1999, 77,394 people belonged to those official minorities. Hui were by far the largest group with 64,832 people (83.76 percent of all minority residents), then Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533). Jianye District had the most minority residents, who were 9.13 percent of its population.

The area is a significant agricultural and commercial grain base for China. Its cash crops are rice, cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea, bamboo, fruit and medicinal materials. Water on both banks of the Yangtze is fertile, so the area is also an important freshwater fishing base.

Output from agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishing totalled 47.250 billion yuan in 2019, up 4.8% on the year before. That figure splits into agriculture at 24.077 billion yuan, fishery at 15.389 billion, services for these sectors at 3.333 billion, animal husbandry at 2.435 billion and forestry at 2.017 billion.

Nanjing is a transport hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze region. Land, water and air links form a three-dimensional transport system. As in most Chinese cities, public transport is how most people get around. As of October 2014 the Yangtze was crossed by four bridges and two tunnels, which connected the districts north of the river to the city centre on the south bank.

china-pharmaceutical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. China Pharmaceutical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at China Pharmaceutical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

china-three-gorges-university.h: China Three Gorges University at a glance

blocks.x: China Three Gorges University, abbreviated CTGU (三峡大学), is a public university in Yichang, in central China's Hubei Province, and it answers to the provincial government. It came into existence in 2000, when it was created from two earlier institutions. One was Hubei Sanxia College (湖北三峡学院); the other was the Yichang campus of Wuhan Hydraulic and Electric Power University (武汉水利电力大学宜昌). The sections below explain its identity, the city of Yichang where it is based, and the province of Hubei around it.

CTGU is a comprehensive university with an official founding date of 29 June 2000. Its building blocks were a hydraulic and electric engineering university in Yichang, Hubei Sanxia University, and a medical college that dated from 1946. One source dates the merger of the two main parts to 2002, so use the university's own pages to confirm any date that you need for an application.
The university is best known for hydroelectric and electrical engineering. That reputation fits its setting, because Yichang is next to the Three Gorges Dam and other major dams on the Yangtze.

The campus is 200 hectares in size, with 830,000 m2 (8,934,046 sq ft) of buildings, and 2,000,000 volumes fill its libraries. Enrolment since 2012 has reached more than 24,000 full-time undergraduates, plus 2,336 postgraduates and 1,048 foreign students. It runs a group of key subjects and key laboratories at provincial and national levels, together with doctoral and master's programmes. A different description calls it Hubei's biggest comprehensive university outside Wuhan, with over 20,400 full-time students. These student figures clearly count different things, so ask the admissions office for current numbers.
Where you live shapes your student years as much as the lecture halls do, so this part covers Yichang's geography, weather, transport, people, schools, economy and attractions.

Yichang is a prefecture-level city, which means that it takes in both a central urban area (the part labelled simply "Yichang" on less detailed maps) and the surrounding countryside. It spreads over 21,084 square kilometers (8,141 sq mi) of western Hubei, straddling the Yangtze River. One of the famous Three Gorges, Xiling Gorge, which is the one furthest east, is inside the city's boundaries.
Several tributaries flow into the Yangtze in this area: the Qing River on the right bank and, on the left, the Xiang Xi and Huangbo Rivers.

The city centre is divided between several districts. North of the Yangtze are Xiling District (the heart of the city), Yiling, Wujiagang and Xiaoting. On the south bank is Dianjun District. Each of these except central Xiling also includes a good deal of suburban or rural land outside the built-up area.

Yichang has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa) shaped by the monsoon and with four seasons. Winters are cool, damp and usually overcast, and summers are hot and humid. January is the coolest month, averaging 5.0 °C (41.0 °F) over a full day, and July the warmest at 27.7 °C (81.9 °F); the year as a whole averages 17.08 °C (62.7 °F). Of the 1,160 mm (46 in) of yearly precipitation, close to 70% falls between May and September. Possible sunshine varies between 24% in January and 49% in August; bright sunshine totals 1,568 hours a year, and summer is the sunniest season.

Yichang Sanxia International Airport lies in Xiaoting District, 26 km (16 mi) from the city centre and 55 km (34 mi) from the site of the Three Gorges Dam. It is well placed, with Yihuang Highway on its northern edge, the Long River Golden Waterway on the south and the Jiaozhi Railway on the east. The distance to the Dam site is 55 km (34 mi).

China National Highway 318 crosses most of the prefecture-level city from east to west, passing south of the centre. China National Highway 209 touches only the northwestern corner (Xingshan County). Several provincial highways join the centre of Yichang to most of the counties.
The Yangtze is crossed by several bridges within the city's area. Listed from upstream to downstream, they are as follows.
Xiling Bridge: just a few km downstream of the Three Gorges Dam, it ties the Yiling District communities of Letianxi and Sandouping together
Yiling Bridge: a short way below the Gezhouba Dam, in the middle of Yichang, joining the urban districts of Xiling and Dianjun
Yichang Yangtze Highway Bridge: part of the Hu-Rong Expressway, lower down than the city centre
Yiwan Bridge: a railway bridge almost 5 km (3.1 mi) below Yiling Bridge, used by high-speed trains linking Yichang with Chongqing
Ferries cross the river in several places too.

For a long time Yichang has served as a main port for goods in transit and a distribution centre. It is the economic hub of western Hubei and a go-between for two big cities, Chongqing and Wuhan. Because of its position on the Yangtze, shipping and shipbuilding are its leading industries. The Qing River in the south of the prefecture, with its series of dams, is another important waterway, and Maoping Town, the seat of Zigui County, has a busy passenger wharf.
Several railway lines serve the city. Yichang Railway Station, in the middle of town, opened in 1971 as the first station and closed in 2012 for renovation.

Today the main station is Yichang East, which opened in late 2010 in the eastern suburbs. Two parts of the Shanghai-Wuhan-Chengdu Passenger Dedicated Line, a new east–west trunk route in China's rail network, join here. Going east, the Hanyi Railway (which began running on 29 June 2012) gives frequent service to Wuhan, with certain trains carrying on to Nanjing and Shanghai. Going west, the Yiwan Railway, from Yichang to Wanzhou, began in December 2010 and opens up the southwestern panhandle of Hubei around Enshi; some trains continue to Chongqing and Chengdu.
The Jiaozuo–Liuzhou Railway runs north to south through the east of the prefecture, and its Yangtze crossing is at Zhicheng, in Yidu County-level City.

At the 2020 census the population was 4,017,607. A built-up (metro) area of four urban districts (Yiling, Xiling, Wujiagang and Dianjun) accounted for 1,536,012 of them, as Xiaoting District is not yet urbanised. The Tujia ethnic group is well represented, living mainly in counties in the southwest.

Yichang was also a cultural frontier in ancient times. To its west was the culture of Ba, an old state in the east of what is now Sichuan; to its east was Chu, which covered present-day Hubei and the north of Hunan.

The city has hosted China Three Gorges University since 2002, after the merger of two earlier universities, one for hydraulic and electric engineering and the other Hubei Sanxia University. Outside Wuhan it is the biggest comprehensive university in the province, with more than 20,400 full-time students. Apart from CTGU, the only other higher education institution listed is the Three Gorges Vocational College of Electric Power.

Schooling below that level is as follows: 170 secondary schools take 150,700 pupils, and 53,900 citizens hold a secondary school degree. Primary education is provided by 282 schools with 156,900 pupils, and 27,600 more residents hold secondary school degrees. A total of 383 kindergartens care for 78,500 children.

Yichang has grown quickly of late. In 2023 its GDP was 575.635 billion yuan, or 146,800 yuan per head. Output grew in each sector in 2023: primary by 60.856 billion yuan, secondary by 228.034 billion and tertiary by 286.745 billion. Leading industries are agriculture, fisheries, chemical manufacturing, food and biomedicine, and tourism.

Mineral wealth is considerable. The list covers phosphorus and iron, coal, manganese and vanadium, gold, copper, lead and zinc, then silicon, gypsum, graphite and quartz sand, and finally limestone, marble and barite. Citrus, tea and aquatic products are the key farm resources. The best-known resource is water power: the Three Gorges Dam, the world's biggest hydroelectric station, generates 111.80 billion kWh a year.

Yichang lies where the mountains of western Hubei give way to the Jianghan Plains, which means a mild climate, clear seasons and plenty of rain. These conditions suit citrus and tea, the two main crops. Urbanisation, higher incomes, better supply chains and bigger export markets have widened the customer base, so demand for premium citrus and tea is rising fast. Yichang's citrus is sold abroad mostly to buyers in the United States, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. In 2022 exported citrus sold at 6,700 yuan ($960) a ton. Tea production in 2023 totalled 119,200 tons, with an agricultural output value of 5.984 billion yuan. Between 2000 and 2022 citrus output grew 10.2% a year and tea output 12.8% a year.

Yichang is rich in tourism assets, and its scenery of mountains and rivers draws millions of visitors. Around 79 million people came in 2023. The best-known attractions are the Three Gorges Dam Tourist Area, the Tribe of the Three Gorges, Qingjiang Gallery, the Memorial Temple of Qu Yuan, the Three Gorges Grand Waterfalls and Xiling Gorge. In 2023 tourism brought in 110 billion yuan, 44.5% more than in the previous year. Since the city is the entrance to the Three Gorges Dam, it works as a main tourist hub, and the Yichang Museum displays important relics such as the Zigui Bell.

The prefecture has many large hydroelectric projects. The two best known are huge dams on the Yangtze: Gezhouba, just upstream of central Yichang, and the Three Gorges Dam, 40 kilometers (25 mi) farther upstream. Two dams on the Qing River, Geheyan and Gaobazhou, matter too, and a very large number of medium and small power plants work on smaller rivers and streams.

These projects supply steady, substantial renewable energy and also help control floods, improve navigation and support irrigation in nearby regions. The Three Gorges Dam is among the biggest hydroelectric stations anywhere and stands as a symbol of Chinese engineering. Large dams have also brought problems: ecological change, the relocation of local communities and the need to protect cultural heritage sites. Hydropower in Yichang therefore drives modernisation and remains a subject of continuing debate.
The province around a university affects student life, so here is a short account of Hubei, from ancient states to the present.

Hubei was home to advanced Neolithic cultures. The powerful State of Chu included the area by the Spring and Autumn period (770–476 BC). Chu was nominally a tributary of the Zhou dynasty and grew out of the Chinese civilisation that had arisen in the north several centuries before, but its culture mixed northern and southern elements in a way all its own. It grew mighty, dominating much of the middle and lower Yangtze and pushing its influence north onto the North China Plain.

Chu's chief opponent in the Warring States period (475–221 BC) was Qin, a rising state to the northwest, in present-day Guanzhong in Shaanxi province, which had begun to expand aggressively. Wars between the two cost Chu ground steadily. It lost the Sichuan Basin first and then, in 278 BC, its core territory, roughly modern Hubei. Qin finally pursued the remains of the Chu regime in 223 BC; they had retreated eastwards while Qin was fighting to unite China.

china-three-gorges-university.h: Han, Three Kingdoms and the north–south split

blocks.x: Qin founded China's first unified dynasty in 221 BC, and in 206 BC the Han dynasty took over from it. The Han set up Jingzhou province (zhou) over what is now Hubei and Hunan. Under both dynasties farmland expanded in Hubei, and river dikes were kept up to shield farms from summer floods.

Near the end of the Eastern Han, early in the 3rd century, the warlord Liu Biao ruled Jingzhou. When he died in 208, his heirs gave his realm up to Cao Cao, who by then held almost the whole of north China. Yet in 208 or 209 the Battle of Red Cliffs saw two other warlords, Liu Bei and Sun Quan, force Cao Cao out of Jingzhou. Liu Bei assumed control and sent Guan Yu to Xiangyang (modern Xiangyang in Hubei) as administrator to defend it. Liu Bei then conquered Yizhou, the Sichuan Basin, but Sun Quan took Jingzhou from him; the Wu Kingdom of Sun Quan and his heirs ruled it for several decades.

Northern nomadic peoples moved into the region at the start of the 4th century (the Five Barbarians' rebellion and the Disaster of Yongjia), beginning almost three centuries of division between a nomad-ruled but increasingly Sinicised north and a south ruled by Han Chinese. Hubei stayed under southern rule all that time, until the Sui dynasty unified China in 589.

The Tang dynasty replaced the Sui in 617 and later divided today's Hubei among several circuits: Jiangnanxi in the south, Shannandong in the west and Huainan in the east. After the Tang collapsed in the early 10th century, regional regimes took control: Jingnan in the centre, Yang Wu (later succeeded by Southern Tang) in the east, the Five Dynasties in the north and Shu as far as Shizhou (施州, in modern Enshi, the Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture).

The Song dynasty brought the region back together in 982, placing most of Hubei in Jinghu North Circuit, a longer form of Hubei's present name. The Mongols took the region in 1279 and created the province of Huguang, covering Hubei and Hunan along with sections of Guangdong and Guangxi.

The Ming dynasty (1368–1644) drove the Mongols out in 1368. Its Huguang province was smaller, corresponding almost exactly to modern Hubei and Hunan together. Hubei lay geographically away from the centres of Ming power. In the last years of the Ming, rebel armies under Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng ravaged the area several times. The Manchu Qing, who took charge of much of the region in 1644, split Huguang before long into today's Hubei and Hunan provinces. It still kept a Viceroy of Huguang, though, and one of the best-known, Zhang Zhidong (in office 1889–1907), carried out modernising reforms that made Hubei, and Wuhan in particular, a thriving commercial and industrial hub. Southeast of Wuhan, the Huangshi/Daye district developed into a major centre for mining and metallurgy.

The Wuchang Uprising, in present-day Wuhan in 1911, began the Xinhai Revolution; the Qing fell and the Republic of China was founded. In 1927 left-wing Kuomintang members led by Wang Jingwei set up a government in Wuhan, and it was later absorbed by the Nanjing government of Chiang Kai-shek. In the Second World War, Japan conquered and occupied the east of Hubei, while the west stayed under Chinese control.

Fighting between rival Red Guard factions broke out in Wuhan during the Cultural Revolution of the 1960s. The Wuhan Incident ("July 20th Incident") happened in July 1967, when two hostile groups fought armed battles for the city at the peak of the Cultural Revolution. In the late 1960s, as fears of nuclear war grew during the Sino-Soviet border conflicts, Xianning prefecture in Hubei was picked as the location of Project 131, an underground military command headquarters.

The 1954 Yangtze River Floods badly hit the province, Wuhan most of all. Large dams followed: the Gezhouba Dam on the Yangtze near Yichang, started in 1970 and finished in 1988, and the Three Gorges Dam farther upstream, begun in 1993. Authorities moved millions of people out of western Hubei to make room for it, and smaller dams have been built on the Yangtze's tributaries.

Plans exist for the Xianning Nuclear Power Plant at Dafanzhen, Tongshan County, Xianning, to house at least four AP1000 pressurised-water reactors of 1,250 megawatts (MW) each. Work on the site started in 2010, and the plan was that building of the first reactor would begin in 2011, with grid connection in 2015. As of 2018, however, the first phase was still awaiting a construction start.

The first COVID-19 case of the pandemic was identified in Wuhan on 1 December 2019. The virus, SARS-CoV-2, was formally identified in January 2020, and authorities at local and national level responded with large quarantine zones across Hubei, above all in the provincial capital Wuhan, where the outbreak was centred. Fifteen cities were fully or partly locked down, which directly affected 57 million people. Severe outbreaks followed in many other countries, and in March 2020 the World Health Organization called COVID-19 a pandemic. Lockdowns in most of the province's cities ended after more than eight weeks.

Han Chinese are the largest group. Many Miao and Tujia people live in the southwest, particularly within the Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture. Officials began relocating 330,000 residents of Hubei and Henan on 18 October 2009 because of the Danjiangkou Reservoir on the Han river, a component of the wider South-North Water Transfer Project.

Wuhan Tianhe International is the main airport. For the Three Gorges area, use Yichang Sanxia Airport. Passenger flights also operate from Xiangyang, Enshi and Jingzhou; the last of these is called Shashi Airport after the city's Shashi District.
