Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Yichang, register at China Three Gorges University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

china-university-of-geosciences-beijing.h: What kind of university this is

blocks.x: China University of Geosciences (Beijing), usually shortened to CUGB, is a public university in the Chinese capital. It is affiliated with the Ministry of Education, with funding shared between that ministry and the Ministry of Natural Resources. In national policy terms it belongs to the Double First-Class Construction scheme and to the older Project 211 group of priority universities, which tells you the state treats it as a serious research institution.

One point trips up many applicants: there are two universities with almost the same name. The one in Beijing and the one in Wuhan (CUG) are separate organisations in law and in daily practice. Each has its own charter, its own president and governing board, its own legal registration, its own admissions office, its own finance system, its own web domain and its own logo. When you search for programs, scholarships or application portals, make sure you are on the Beijing institution's pages and not its Wuhan namesake.

china-university-of-geosciences-beijing.h: Study areas, size and international ties

blocks.x: CUGB is a research-oriented university whose centre of gravity is geology, natural resources and environmental science. Around that core it also teaches science, engineering, the humanities, management, economics and law. Geology and geological engineering are both named disciplines under the Double First-Class scheme, and both earned the top A+ grade in the fourth national discipline assessment run by the Ministry of Education.

On the international research-indicator side, six subjects sit in the global top 1 percent of the Essential Science Indicators (ESI) database. They are geology, chemistry, computer science, engineering, materials science, and environment and ecology. Geology stands out further, since it ranks in the top 1 per mille.

By the 2023 count the university was organised into 16 schools. Between them they run 56 undergraduate programs and 16 doctoral programs, and 34 master's programs, of which 18 are research-based and 15 course-based. A further 14 professional degree programs are offered. Around 2021 the roll stood at roughly 17,000 full-time students, split into about 8,000 at undergraduate level, 6,500 working toward a master's and 2,000 at doctoral level (international students are counted among them). The teaching and support staff number about 1,700. Roughly 300 of them are professors, 400 are associate professors and 800 are lecturers or assistant professors. The faculty includes 11 academicians from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, plus a single academician from the Chinese Academy of Engineering.

Former students include Wen Jiabao, who became China's premier, and 44 members of the Chinese academies. It also keeps long-running cooperation agreements with universities and institutes abroad, including the Colorado School of Mines, UCLA, the University of Waterloo, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Birmingham, Moscow State University, the University of Namibia, the University of Southern Queensland, the University of Freiburg, the University of Hanover, the Helmholtz Potsdam Center and the University of Sydney. For a prospective student, this list suggests where exchange or joint research contacts may exist, though you should confirm current arrangements with the international office.

Teaching is spread over sixteen schools, and the roster shows how far beyond pure geology the university reaches. The core earth-science group comprises the Schools of Earth Sciences and Resources, Gemology, Ocean Sciences, Land Science and Technology, Water Resources and Environment, Energy Resources, and Geophysics and Information Technology.

Applied and technical study sits in the Schools of Engineering and Technology, Materials Science and Technology, Artificial Intelligence, and Science. Students interested in business or languages look to the Schools of Economics and Management and of Foreign Languages. The last three are the Schools of Marxism, Physical Education and Continuing Education.

China designates certain fields as national key disciplines, and CUGB holds that status for two first-level fields and eight second-level fields. Most are classic geology territory: geology itself, geochemistry, and paleobiology and stratigraphy, together with structural geology and tectonics and Quaternary geology. Others are applied or technical: mineral exploration and prospecting, geological resources and engineering, earth exploration and information technology, geological engineering, and the combined study of mineralogy, petrology and ore deposits.

A second tier of recognition covers fields that the Beijing municipal government or a national ministry has designated as key. CUGB has 14 research directions of this kind, which shows how widely it works beyond the geosciences proper. The earth and environment group includes geophysics, marine geology, offshore resources and environment, hydrology and water resources, land resources management, and environmental science and engineering. The engineering group covers geotechnical engineering, oil and gas field development engineering, safety science and engineering, and materials science. The remaining directions are computer science, management science, ideological and political education, and demography with resource and environmental economics.

At the top national level, CUGB hosts one State Key Laboratory, the State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources (the national-level lab), and one national platform for sharing rock, mineral and fossil specimen resources. Both matter if your interest is hands-on work with real samples.

Below that, the university runs 15 laboratories and research centres recognised by a ministry or by the Beijing municipality. Those under the Ministry of Education are the laboratories for groundwater cycle and environmental evolution, for how marine reservoirs evolve and how oil and gas become enriched, and for underground information detection technology and instruments. A Ministry of Education key research centre also covers metal mineral exploration and evaluation.

The Ministry of Natural Resources lists four key laboratories here: deep geological drilling technology, strategic evaluation of shale gas resources, resource and environmental carrying capacity evaluation, and land reclamation. It also backs two innovation centres, one on ecological restoration of mining areas and one on natural resources big data.

The Beijing municipality recognises four key laboratories: assessing and developing unconventional natural gas (geological evaluation), water resources and environmental engineering, land resources information research and development, and non-metallic minerals and solid waste resources. The Ministry of Science and Technology lists a cooperation base for machinery and equipment used in deep drilling as a key platform.
Three further research centres focus respectively on geological heritage, on geological microbiology and biogeochemistry, and on environmental science and engineering.

The university also publishes academic journals. The English-language title Geoscience Frontiers is an open-access journal issued with Elsevier. Chinese-language titles are Modern Geology, Resources and Industries, and Chinese Geological Education (given in Chinese on the university's pages).

The next three subsections list what you can actually enrol in. Names are translated from Chinese, so check the university's admissions site for the exact titles and for which programs accept international applicants and teach in English.

The undergraduate catalogue is long and mixes classic earth science with engineering, computing, business and the arts. Geology is offered both as a standard major and as an honours program, and geological engineering likewise has an honours version. Closely related earth-science majors include geochemistry, a dual program in geology and geophysics, tourism geology, solid mineral resources exploration, digital earth and big data, geophysics and intelligent earth exploration, groundwater science, hydrology and water resources, marine science, marine resources, remote sensing, surveying, and natural resources management.

Engineering and energy options include civil engineering, exploration engineering, urban underground space engineering, safety engineering, mechanical engineering with automation, petroleum engineering, energy engineering, new energy science, new energy geology, carbon storage, environmental engineering, ecological engineering, and land reclamation engineering. Materials students can choose materials engineering, materials physics, materials chemistry or new energy materials, and there is also measurement and control technology.

The computing and information side covers software engineering, computer science, data science, artificial intelligence, electrical engineering, information engineering and geographic information systems, with mathematics and applied mathematics among the sciences. Beyond technical subjects there are business and humanities choices: economics, law, accounting, business administration, information management and systems, translation of foreign languages, English studies, product design, gemology, and arts and technology, plus land management.

Research master's programs lean toward the university's strengths, with the earth sciences first, but they also reach into the humanities, sciences and engineering. The geoscience options are geochemistry, tectonics, Quaternary geology, geological engineering, paleobiology with stratigraphy, and mineralogy with petrology and ore deposits. Basic-science options are mathematics, physics, chemistry, geography, atmospheric sciences and biology. Engineering and computing options cover software engineering, mechanical engineering, information and communication engineering, and computer science and technology. The humanities and social side offers business administration, arts, law, education, psychology, kinesiology, journalism and communication, and foreign languages and literature.

The course-based (professional) route groups study into broader fields, several with options inside. Under electronic information you can pick electronics and communication, control engineering, computer science or software engineering. Materials and chemical engineering has two options, material sciences and chemical engineering. The resources and environment field offers petroleum engineering, geological engineering, surveying, environmental engineering and safety engineering. In civil engineering and water resources the options are architecture, hydraulic engineering and civil engineering.

Single-subject course-based programs include mechanical engineering, law, accounting, finance, design, applied statistics, geographic information systems, property evaluation, science history, physical education, public administration, business administration and foreign language translation.

Doctoral study is available in sixteen fields, again leaning toward resources and the environment. Earth and environmental options are geology, geophysics, marine science, geological resources and geological engineering, environmental science and engineering, and surveying and mapping. Engineering options cover petroleum and natural gas engineering, safety engineering, civil engineering, water resources engineering, control engineering, management science and engineering, and materials science and engineering. Applied economics, Marxist theory and public administration complete the list.

china-university-of-geosciences-beijing.h: Life on and around the campus

blocks.x: The campus lies on Xueyuan Road, a name that literally means College Road. This is the education hub of Beijing's Haidian District, and eight universities sit along it. CUGB's grounds cover about 130 acres, and the main road through them is a tree-lined boulevard two kilometres long. Teaching blocks, offices, the library and the halls of residence stand on the north side. The south side holds the sports facilities: two full-size football pitches, nine basketball courts, several badminton and tennis courts and a rock-climbing wall. Close to the east gate you will find the university's Geology Museum, and an international conference centre is on site too.

Your neighbours are other well-known institutions. To the north you will find Beijing Forestry University, China University of Mining and Technology and Beijing Language and Culture University. Beihang University (the Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) is to the south, the University of Science and Technology Beijing is to the east, and Tsinghua University and Peking University are to the west.

A second campus of around 263 acres is being built in Xiong'an and is expected to be finished in late 2025; check with the university for what that means for your intake year. The university also runs field camp stations at Zhoukoudian, Beidaihe and Pingquan, which is where fieldwork teaching takes place.
The history is a little tangled, because the institution moved cities and split in two. Here it is in order.

In 1952 China reorganised its higher education and set up the Beijing Institute of Geology by pulling together geology departments that had belonged to four institutions: Peking University, Tsinghua University, Tianjin University and Tangshan Railway College. It was one of the first 16 key universities in the country in the 1950s.

The Cultural Revolution closed the school from 1966 to 1970. It reopened in 1970 in Jiangling County, Hubei Province, as Hubei College of Geology, then moved to Wuhan in 1975, taking the name Wuhan College of Geology.

In 1978 the graduate school returned to Beijing with the backing of the national leader Deng Xiaoping. By 1986 it had been formally set up as the Beijing Graduate School of Wuhan College of Geology, back on the old Beijing Institute of Geology grounds on Xueyuan Road.

Wuhan College of Geology was renamed China University of Geosciences in 1987, and it ran two campuses with independent legal status, the main one in Wuhan and the graduate school in Beijing. It joined Project 211 key construction in 1997 and came under the Ministry of Education in February 2000.

The two campuses separated into distinct entities in March 2005. Wuhan kept the name China University of Geosciences (CUG), while the Beijing graduate campus became CUGB. CUGB was formally founded in September 2006 under the joint leadership of the Ministry of Education and the then Ministry of Land and Resources. From then on it was no longer a graduate-only school and started undergraduate programs. The same year, it was placed on the list of Project 985 innovation platforms. Together with CUG in Wuhan, it is also included in the national Double First-Class Construction scheme.

The emblem is shaped like the letter U, suggesting a bud about to open and so a promising future. It uses a deep blue (#004e97) known as geology blue, and shows the Chinese and English names, the founding year 1952, the lines of latitude and longitude, and the tools of a field geologist: hammer, compass and hand lens. Although the Beijing and Wuhan universities separated in 2005, the old name China University of Geosciences remains on CUGB's emblem.

The university's anthem is Song of the Exploration Team, borrowed from the old film The Young Generation, with words by Tong Zhixian and music by Xiao He. Students have loved it since the days of the Beijing Institute of Geology. It was formally named the school anthem on 19 June 1990 at the ninth School Affairs Council meeting.
Chinese names below are given with the family name first, which is the custom in China. The university's better-known former students include:
Wen Jiabao, who served as China's Premier at the head of the State Council
Wang Anshun, mayor of Beijing
Zhang Wenyue, former governor of Liaoning Province
Sun Jinlong, a politician linked to the ministry that handles ecology and environment
Jin Yuzhang, who leads the Aisin-Gioro clan, the old imperial house
Ouyang Ziyuan, chief scientist of the Chinese Lunar Project
Zhang Yiwei, a geologist who once presided over China University of Petroleum
Meemann Chang, paleobiologist and winner of a L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science award
Zhao Pengda, mathematical geologist
Liu Baojun, a sedimentary geologist
Fu Jiamo, an environmental geochemist
Wang Shuangming, an engineer in coal prospecting
Gao Shan, also a geologist
Zhang Benren, a geochemist as well
Peng Jianbing, an engineering geologist
Li Zhixin, Wang Fuzhou and Wang Yongfeng, all Chinese mountaineers

china-university-of-geosciences-beijing.h: Living in Beijing: what the city is like

blocks.x: Daily life for a student mostly depends on the surrounding city, meaning its weather, its air, its look and its layout. This part of the profile describes Beijing, the home of China University of Geosciences (Beijing).

Three building traditions dominate central Beijing. The oldest is imperial architecture, best seen at Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), the national emblem of the People's Republic, along with the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second is the so-called Sino-Soviet style of the 1950s to 1970s, with boxy buildings that were sometimes poorly built. The third is the modern style, strongest in the Beijing CBD in the east, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, and also visible at the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the early 2000s construction has boomed, with international architects bringing many modern designs, especially in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s industrial buildings with a neofuturistic look. The tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing towers have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, the prize for the year's best overall tall building worldwide, twice: for the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and for the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

Traditional homes are siheyuan, courtyards ringed by buildings, with grand examples such as Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. They connect through lanes called hutongs, which usually run east to west so that doors face north or south, a choice made for good feng shui. Some are so narrow that only a few people can pass at once. Hutongs and courtyards are vanishing fast as whole blocks give way to high-rises. Residents are entitled to flats at least as large as their old homes, but many say the community spirit and street life cannot be replaced, and the properties are often government owned.

Beijing sits at the northern tip of the triangular North China Plain, which spreads out to the south and east. Mountains on the north, northwest and west protect the city and northern China's farmland from the desert steppe. The Jundu Mountains fill the northwest of the municipality, notably Yanqing and Huairou districts, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall crosses the northern part of the municipality, built along rugged ground to hold off nomadic raiders from the steppe. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, is the highest point at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma rivers all belong to the Hai River system and flow southeast. The Miyun Reservoir on the upper Chaobai is the largest in the municipality. The city is also where the Grand Canal to Hangzhou begins, a transport route dug more than 1,400 years ago, and the northern end of the South-North Water Transfer Project, a recent scheme that carries water up from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up city occupies a modest but growing share of the municipality, on flat ground at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) in the south-centre. Roads circle the centre in rings. The innermost, the Second Ring, runs where the old city walls once stood, while the Sixth Ring ties the outlying satellite towns together. Tian'anmen and its square are at the centre, directly south of the Forbidden City where emperors once lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, home to today's leaders, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between the gate and the square, is the main east-west axis.
Residents joke that the city spreads outward like a pancake (tan da bing), flat and ever wider, and this pattern of growth is often blamed for Beijing's urban problems.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to the borderline with a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (BSk). Summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon. Winters are short, cold and dry under the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone. In spring, sandstorms can blow in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe while temperatures climb fast and the air stays mostly dry. Autumn is another transition season with very little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest time was early August and the coldest was early January.

By China's seasonal calendar, the four seasons begin on 26 March (spring), 20 May (summer), 13 September (autumn) and 31 October (winter). Because March and September have recently warmed faster and May and October more slowly, autumn is now usually shorter than spring.

For 1991 to 2020 the average annual temperature in the urban area is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Daily lows average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily highs 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). In the low-lying suburbs the annual mean is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). Up in the mountains the annual mean ranges from 0 °C (32 °F) to 10 °C (50 °F), dropping as the land rises. January averages -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

Yearly precipitation is about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), or 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, where CUGB's neighbourhood lies. Nearly three-quarters falls from June to August. The share of possible sunshine is lowest in July (42%) and highest in January and February (62%), and the city gets 2,490.5 sunshine hours over a year. The record low since 1951 is -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), set on 22 February 1966, and the record high is 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), recorded on 24 July 1999. Pack for a real winter and a properly hot summer.

Beijing has struggled with environmental problems for a long time. Between 2000 and 2009 its urban area quadrupled, which raised emissions and also changed local weather. Wind speed, humidity near the ground and surface albedo went down, while ground and air temperatures, ozone and vertical mixing of the air went up. Urban growth together with fossil-fuel burning has caused serious pollution and health problems for many residents. In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and most of northern China and affected about 600 million people. This pollution shock made air quality a leading economic and social concern across China. Beijing then announced measures. Coal's share of its energy was to fall from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, and from 2015 to 2017 the national government told the worst-polluting vehicles to leave the roads while pushing clean energy harder.

A 2006 study by American and Chinese researchers working together concluded that a good deal of Beijing's pollution blows in from nearby cities and provinces: between 35 and 60% of its ozone on average comes from outside. Shandong Province and Tianjin weigh heavily on the capital's air, helped by the summer winds from the south and southeast and by the mountains that wall off the north and northwest.

To keep its promise of cleaner air for the 2008 Summer Olympics, the city spent nearly US$17 billion. During the Games it stopped work at construction sites, closed many factories for good, shut industry in neighbouring regions for a time, closed some gas stations and halved motor traffic by letting drivers on the road only on odd or even days by licence plate. It also cut bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines, banned high-emission vehicles and put together 3,800 natural-gas buses, among the largest such fleets in the world. It was also the first city in China to adopt the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Burning coal produces about 40% of Beijing's PM2.5 and most of its nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching, since 2012, coal-fired power stations to natural gas and aims to cap yearly coal use at 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73% for heating and power and the rest for industry. Much of the pollution arrives from neighbours. Coal use in Tianjin was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. In 2011 Hebei burned over 300 million tons, more coal than the whole of Germany, with only 30% going to power and a big share to steel and cement. Power stations in the coal-mining areas of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Shanxi (where coal use has tripled since 2000) and in Shandong add to the problem as well. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among provinces for coal consumption.

Beijing had four big coal-fired plants supplying power and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant shut in 2014 and two others shut in March 2015, with Huaneng Thermal Power Plant due to follow in 2016. For 2013 to 2017 the plan was to trim coal use by 13 million tons, with a ceiling of 15 million tons in 2015.

Before big events the authorities have sometimes seeded clouds to bring rain and clear the air, as before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to fight drought. More recently they have relied on temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, producing the short-lived 'APEC blue' around APEC China 2014 and 'parade blue' before the 2015 Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved sharply during these periods and then returned to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015, which closed most industry and commercial business, and a red alert followed later that month. A November 2016 announcement from the environmental protection bureau said that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be banned from the road during red alerts in the city or nearby areas.

Since the 'war on pollution' began in 2014, pollutants have fallen noticeably. Fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017 and fell more by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial plants were cleaned up. Average PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024 there were only two heavy-pollution days, the fewest on record and 96.6 percent down from 58 in 2013.

china-university-of-geosciences-beijing.h: Checking the air and dust storms

blocks.x: Several sources publish pollution data. Daily readings from 27 monitoring stations appear on the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) website, and the American Embassy posts hourly readings of ozone and fine particulate (PM2.5) on Twitter. Because the two measure different pollutants by different standards, the bureau's figures and the reported health effects are often lower than the embassy's.

The smog is a real health risk. Polluted air directly raises rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, emergency hospital visits and even death.

Dust blown from eroding deserts in the north and northwest brings seasonal dust storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain to fight them and soften their effects. The first four months of 2006 saw at least eight storms, and one storm in April 2002 left close to 50,000 tons of dust on the city before moving on toward Japan and Korea.

Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 26,000 to CNY 39,000 (median CNY 26,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 28,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 28,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 35,000 to CNY 35,000 (median CNY 35,000), according to the university's published fee table.

china-university-of-geosciences-wuhan.h: China University of Geosciences (Wuhan) at a glance

blocks.x: China University of Geosciences (Wuhan), often shortened to CUG, is a public university in Wuhan, the capital of Hubei province. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and the Ministry and the Hubei provincial government jointly provide its funding. It is part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction programme.

china-university-of-geosciences-wuhan.h: Not the same as CUG Beijing

blocks.x: Applicants sometimes confuse this university with China University of Geosciences (Beijing). The two have a shared past that lasted until 2005, but today they are separate institutions. Each has its own constitution, president and governing board, and each is registered as its own legal entity. They also run separate admissions, finance systems, web domains and logos, so make sure you apply to the right one. If you are comparing the two, check the entry requirements and available programmes on each university's own website, because the offerings are not identical.

The Main Campus is called the Nanwangshan Mountain Campus, because it lies at the foot of Nanwangshan. A tunnel running through the mountain links the west campus to the north campus. This is where most students are enrolled each year, and its courses go well beyond the earth sciences. One highlight is the Yifu Museum, a gift of Sir Run Run Shaw, which has some of the best dinosaur fossil displays in China as well as outstanding mineral and rock collections.

A New Campus was built in Wuhan's future technology city and opened in September 2019. Ask the admissions office which campus your own programme uses, since that affects where you will live and how long your commute will be.

The roots of CUG lie in the Beijing Institute of Geology (北京地质学院, Běijīng Dìzhì Xuéyuàn), created in 1952 by merging the geology departments of four institutions: Peking University, Tsinghua University, Tangshan Railway College and Tianjin University. It was in the first group of 16 key universities in China in the 1950s. Operations stopped from 1966 to 1970 because of the Cultural Revolution.

The school restarted in 1970 in Jiangling County, Hubei, with the name Hubei College of Geology (湖北地质学院, Húběi Dìzhì Xuéyuàn). The campus relocated to Wuhan in 1975 and the school was renamed Wuhan College of Geology (WCG; 武汉地质学院, Wǔhàn Dìzhì Xuéyuàn). Back in the capital, Deng Xiaoping's support allowed the Beijing Institute of Geology to reopen in 1978. Then in 1986 the government approved a Beijing Graduate School of WCG, one of just 33 graduate schools created nationwide at that stage.

In 1987 WCG took the name China University of Geosciences, and its Beijing branch became that university's Beijing Graduate School. Then, in 2005, the Wuhan and Beijing campuses were separated into two independent universities: China University of Geosciences (CUG) in Wuhan and China University of Geosciences (Beijing), known as CUGB. CUG belongs to the national Double First Class University Plan.
National-level facilities:
GPMR, the State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources
BGEG, the state key laboratory covering biogeology and environmental geology
A national engineering research centre devoted to geographic information systems
Provincial and ministry-level facilities:
The Ministry of Education's key laboratory for tectonics and petroleum resources
The ministry's Three Gorges research centre on geohazards

Your daily life as a student will be shaped by Wuhan, so here is what it is like.

Wuhan is in east-central Hubei, between latitudes 29°58' and 31°22' N and longitudes 113°41' and 115°05' E. It stands where the Han River joins the Yangtze, at the east end of the Jianghan Plain on the Yangtze's middle reaches.

The city is made up of three historic towns: Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, sometimes called the Three Towns of Wuhan. The name combines Wu from the first with Han from the other two. They were merged in 1927 to create Wuhan, and the rivers that divide them are crossed by bridges, among them the First Bridge, one of China's first modern bridges.
Wuchang is southeast of the Yangtze, which separates it from Hankou and Hanyang.
Hankou is north of the Yangtze, across from Wuchang, and north of the Han River, across from Hanyang.
Hanyang is west of the Yangtze, across from Wuchang, and south of the Han, across from Hankou.

The terrain is simple: flat and low in the middle, with hills in the south, and the Yangtze and Han wind through it. The She River flows into the Yangtze in Huangpi District. The land area is 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 square miles), mostly alluvial plain dotted with hills and a great many lakes and ponds. Water covers a quarter of the urban area, the highest share among China's big cities. Nearly 200 lakes exist, and East Lake (33 square kilometres) and Tangxun Lake are the biggest lakes lying entirely inside any Chinese city.

South Lake and Sand Lake are two more well-known names. The biggest lake in Hubei by surface area is Liangzi Lake, in the southeast of Jiangxia District. The highest ground in Wuhan, at 872.5 metres, is the twin peaks where Huangpi District meets Xiaogan City. Several hills stand within city limits: Mount Luojia (珞珈山) in Wuchang District, plus Hongshan District's Mount Hong (洪山) and Mount Yujia (喻家山, also written 瑜珈山).

Wuhan has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), with plentiful summer rain and four distinct seasons. Summers are famously muggy, with dewpoints frequently at 26 °C (79 °F) or higher. For their hot summers, Wuhan, Chongqing and Nanjing were long called the Three Furnaces of the Yangtze. Modern records, however, indicate that Wuhan no longer belongs among the hottest cities, and the updated four furnace-like cities are Nanchang, Hangzhou, Fuzhou and Chongqing. Spring and autumn are mostly mild, and winter is cool with little rain and occasional snow.

In January the mean is 4.1 °C (39.4 °F) while July reaches 29.3 °C (84.7 °F), and the year as a whole averages 17.4 °C (63.3 °F). Between 211 and 272 days are frost-free. Precipitation totals a little under 1,320 mm (52 in) a year, and most of it falls from April through July. The share of possible sunshine goes from only 30 percent in January up to 53 percent in August, so the city proper gets 1,783 hours of bright sunshine annually. The record low is -18.1 °C (-1 °F) on 31 January 1977, and the record high is 39.7 °C (103 °F), reached on 27 July 2017 and again on 18 August 2022. An unofficial reading of 41.3 °C (106 °F) was noted on 10 August 1934.

Come prepared for steamy summers, cool winters and rain concentrated in spring and early summer. Light, breathable clothing for July and August and a proper coat for January will both be needed, and an umbrella is useful for much of the year.

Wuhan was mainly agricultural until the 21st century. Since 2004 it has been central to the Rise of Central China Plan, a policy to turn less-developed inland economies into advanced manufacturing hubs.

Steel has been the base of local industry since 1890. In 2010 cars overtook the steel of Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO) in contribution to the city's GDP for the first time. Five carmakers operate here (Citroën, Dongfeng Honda, Dongfeng Renault, SAIC-GM and DFM Passenger Vehicle), and the headquarters of Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd are in the city.

As of 2016, investors from over 80 countries had put money into Wuhan, which hosted 5,973 foreign-funded enterprises and a combined 22.45 billion US dollars of capital. About 50 French companies, among them Renault and PSA Group, operate here. Together they represent over a third of French investment in China, the highest level for any Chinese city.

Wuhan is a key centre for economy, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. Its main industries are optoelectronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, bioengineering, new materials and environmental protection. Emerging industries include energy-efficiency technology and renewable energy, which shows an emphasis on sustainability. In 2021, the Global Financial Centres Index ranked Wuhan among the world's top 100 financial centres.
The city's main industrial zones, in order of founding, are as follows.

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone: a national-level zone incorporated in 1993. At the moment it covers about 10 to 25 square km, with plans to grow to 25 to 50 square km. Industries the zone encourages include car assembly, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, chemicals, telecommunications equipment, heavy industry, and the processing of food and drink.

Wuhan Export Processing Zone: set up in 2000 inside the development zone above. It is planned to cover 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile), and the first 0.7 square kilometres (0.3 square miles) have been built.

Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone (East Lake High-Tech Development Zone): a national high-tech zone built around optical electronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, with software outsourcing and electronics also encouraged. It is China's biggest production centre for optoelectronic products, with firms such as Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable (the country's largest fibre-optic cable maker) and Fiberhome Telecommunications. It is also the development centre of the laser industry, home to companies including HGTECH and Chutian Laser.

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park: inside the East Lake zone, a joint project with Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. On a planned site of 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles), it is meant to provide 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet) of floor space. It is 8.5 km (5.28 miles) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 miles) from Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Wuhan Biolake: an industrial base started in 2008 and located within China's Optics Valley, in the East Lake zone. It covers 15 square kilometres (5.8 square miles) and holds six parks, for bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical devices and medical health, to house both research and living.

No city in Central China has more people than Wuhan, which also ranks high nationally. At the Seventh Census in 2020 it had 12,326,500 residents, 25.97 percent or 2.5411 million more than in 2010. Those ten years were the fastest-growing since censuses began, at an average of 2.34 percent a year, and it was the first time the population passed 10 million. The OECD estimated the metropolitan area's population at 19 million in 2010.

Research published in November 2019 used night-time lighting and land-cover data to study urban development. It suggested that socioeconomic activity in Wuhan is highly concentrated compared with how far the city has spread physically.

A 2017 survey found that 79.2 percent of residents are either not religious or worship gods and ancestors, and 0.9 percent of them are Taoists. Buddhists make up 14.7 percent, Protestants 2.9 percent, Catholics 0.3 percent and Muslims 1.6 percent, while another 1.6 percent follow other, unspecified religions.

China Railway Wuhan Group runs the Wuhan Railway Hub, one of China's four key railway hubs. Three main stations serve the city: Hankou railway station in Hankou, Wuchang railway station in Wuchang, and Wuhan railway station in a newly built area east of East Lake, in Hongshan District. They are many miles apart, so check which station your train uses.

The original Hankou Station was the end of the Jinghan line from Beijing, and Wuchang Station was the end of the Yuehan line to Guangzhou. After the First Yangtze Bridge joined these into the Jingguang railway, trains from both stations began to run in all directions. That contrasts with cities like New York or Moscow, where each station serves a different direction.

The Hefei-Wuhan high-speed railway opened on 1 April 2009 and linked Wuhan by fast train with Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai. Today several trains a day get to Shanghai in under six hours; in early 2010 most of these express services left from Hankou.

Construction of the new Wuhan station, with 11 platforms on the northeastern outskirts, began in 2006. It opened in December 2009, when China launched its second high-speed service, running from Guangzhou to Wuhan. The train was billed as the world's fastest, reaching 394 km/h (244.82 mph), and shortened the journey from 10.5 hours to just three. The line has since been extended north to Beijing. For a student, that means a fast rail link from Wuhan to both Guangzhou and the capital. By 2011 the new station served mainly the Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, while regular services to other places continued to use Hankou and Wuchang.

Work has also gone ahead on the Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity railway. When finished it will tie together the city's three main stations, a range of stops in the outer districts and suburbs, and neighbouring cities, namely Huangshi, Xiaogan, Xianning and Huanggang. The Xianning line was first and carried passengers from the end of 2013. A line to Xiaogan followed on 1 December 2016, and it was prolonged to Shiyan on 29 November 2019, the day the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway opened.

The main freight station and marshalling yard is Wuhan North, a huge facility with 112 tracks and over 650 sets of points. It is in Hengdian Subdistrict, Huangpi District, 20 km (12 miles) north of Wuhan Station and 23 km (14 miles) from Hankou Station.

The metro is owned and operated by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd. At present the network is made up of 11 lines and 282 stations, with a route length of 435 km (270 miles). Line 1 opened first, on 28 July 2004, so Wuhan became the seventh mainland Chinese city to have rapid transit. Only Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian were earlier. Line 2 opened on 28 December 2012 as the first underground metro line to pass under the Yangtze River.

Crossing the Yangtze and Han rivers had been the main bottleneck in Wuhan traffic, and the metro has eased that considerably. It carried 1.22 billion passengers in 2019, making it the sixth-busiest system in mainland China. The network is growing quickly, with lines and sections under construction, and the city government has promised at least two new lines or sections every year. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the whole network was closed from 23 January to 27 March 2020.

Trams: the first tram line, the Auto-city T1 Line, opened on 28 July 2017. Further tram systems are built or planned. The Auto-city trams (Lines T1, T2, T6 and T8) are intended for the Wuhan Economic Development Area, at the western edge of Hanyang, and T1 has been operating since 2017. Two Optics Valley lines (T1 and T2) run south and east of Guanggu Circle in southeastern Wuchang and opened on 18 January 2018. The Old Hankou Streetcar is planned as a loop around Hankou.
Buses: local buses include trolleybuses, which have run since 1958. Route 1 was the first and is still in service.
Port: Wuhan is a major centre for shipping in central China, and the Port of Wuhan serves local people and freight.

Ferries: with its location on the Yangtze, Wuhan has a long ferry tradition. Modern service began in 1900 with steamboats, and in 1937 a train ferry started carrying rail cars from Hankou to Wuchang. Numbered stops around the city let passengers get on and off, and there is a tourist ferry at night. The Wuhan Ferry Company runs the service today, and in 2010 it bought ten new ships to replace ones that had been in use for 29 years.

china-university-of-geosciences-wuhan.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. China University of Geosciences (Wuhan) may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at China University of Geosciences (Wuhan) by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

china-university-of-mining-and-technolog.h: China University of Mining and Technology at a glance

blocks.x: CUMT (China University of Mining and Technology, 中国矿业大学) is a state-run university in the city of Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province. It reports to the Ministry of Education and is co-sponsored by the Jiangsu provincial government and by the emergency management ministry. The university takes part in Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction scheme.

The name actually covers two separate institutions. The main one stands in Xuzhou and is simply called CUMT. The other, known as CUMT, Beijing, grew out of what used to be CUMT's graduate school. CUMT presents itself as a leading multi-disciplinary polytechnic with a mining flavour, and applicants should be clear about which of the two they mean.

china-university-of-mining-and-technolog.h: A long journey from Jiaozuo to Xuzhou

blocks.x: The earliest ancestor was a Jiaozuo school for railroads and mines, founded in 1909. The school left Jiaozuo for Tianjin in 1950, and there it was renamed the China Institute of Mining and Technology (CIMT). The 1952 nationwide reorganisation of universities and colleges brought in the mining engineering departments of three bodies: Tsinghua University, the Tangshan Institute of Railroad and the former Beiyang University.

Several relocations followed. In 1953 CIMT relocated to Beijing and became the Beijing Institute of Mining and Technology, and in 1970 it was moved to Sichuan Province and renamed again, as the Sichuan Institute of Mining and Technology. Eight years later, in 1978, it arrived at its current site in Xuzhou, Jiangsu, and took back the original CIMT name. In the same year CIMT also founded a graduate school in Beijing, which began to admit graduate students.

The institute became a university in 1988, when it took the name CUMT. A Beijing branch followed in 1997, built on the Beijing Graduate School and admitting undergraduates from the start. Both in 1960 and in 1978 the government approved the university as one of China's key universities. In February 2000 the university changed supervisor. It had been under the Ministry of Coal Mining, and it passed to the direct supervision of the Ministry of Education, like other state universities in that group.
The division into two universities was approved in 2003. One is CUMT in Xuzhou; the other is CUMTB, based in Beijing.
Daily life, weather and transport all depend on the city around the campus, so the following sections describe Xuzhou.

The city sits at the south-eastern tip of the North China Plain, where the alluvial fan of the Yellow River gives way to the Huai River basin. Its gently undulating plain rests on alluvial deposits 10–60 metres deep (33–197 ft), left by the Yellow River as it wandered over the centuries.

Isolated limestone hills (inselbergs) shoot up from the flat floodplain. Two of them are Yunlong Mountain, 142 metres high (466 ft), and Dadong Mountain, which at 361 metres (1,184 ft) is the top of the region. Geologically, they are part of the Xuzhou–Huaibei fold-thrust belt on the south-eastern edge of the North China Craton.

Along the Tancheng–Lujiang fault zone (Tan-Lu), tectonic movement produced the coalfields of Xuzhou and Feng-Pei. Proven coal reserves had reached 3.94 billion tonnes by the late 1990s, which is more than 93% of everything Jiangsu has. Heavy mining fragmented the landscape and caused subsidence that led to flooding. Closing small mines and restoring the ecology helped, including the conversion of waterlogged subsided land in northern Xuzhou and Jiawang into the artificial wetlands of Jiuli Lake and Pan'an Lake, so the local environment has partly recovered.

Two artificial waterways shape the local water system. One is the Grand Canal between Beijing and Hangzhou. The other is the old channel of the Yellow River, a "perched river", meaning its bed is raised 2–5 metres (6.6–16.4 ft) over the ground beside it, and which now divides the drainage of the Huai system from that of the Yi-Shu-Si rivers. Because of low ground, the elevated riverbed and the city's place on a bend in the channel, flooding was a long-standing hazard. Records list 59 breaches of the embankments close to Xuzhou in the years from 1550 to 1855.

The ancient riverbed runs through the city proper today. Yunlong Lake lies to the south-west, a reservoir used for scenery, with 5.82 square kilometres of water (2.25 square miles). The Kui River drains it and runs southward, covering 35.6 kilometres (22.1 mi) before reaching Anhui Province. For a long time it was among the Huai basin's dirtiest tributaries, and in 2005 a stretch in the city centre was sealed under concrete to hold in the smell. Following extensive ecological repair, those covers were removed in 2021 and the river is an open channel again.

Although the city stands on a fairly stable fault zone separate from the main Tan-Lu system, earthquake risk remains, because loose silt deposits in the ground can liquefy, which makes the soil act like a liquid and increases the damage.

The climate is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence (Köppen Cwa). Winters are cool and dry, springs warm, summers long, hot and humid, and autumns crisp. Mean daily temperatures are 0.7 °C in January (33.3 °F) and 27.3 °C in July (81.1 °F), with a yearly average of 14.9 °C, or 58.8 °F. Snow sometimes falls, but seldom heavily. Winter is dry, and most of the 842.8 millimetres (33.2 in) of annual precipitation falls from June to August. Sunshine is 44% of the possible in July and 54% in three months of the year, and yearly bright sunshine adds up to 2,221 hours.
At the 2020 census Xuzhou had 9,083,900 permanent residents, 5.9% higher than in 2010, and by 2023 the city held roughly 10.6% of Jiangsu's population.

In earlier centuries the numbers were far lower. Xuzhou Prefecture, a bigger unit that then included Dangshan and Xiao counties and the urban districts of Suqian, had 2.95 million people in 1776 and 4.34 million by 1910. Industry and trade were almost absent, and in 1910 only about 32,000 people lived in the prefectural seat. Urbanisation sped up in the twentieth century. The city itself reached 171,903 inhabitants in 1931, then 314,773 in 1947 and 333,190 at the 1953 census.

Xuzhou's GDP in 2023 was RMB 890.04 billion, which is RMB 98,683 per head (c. US$14,000). It is the largest economy in the Huaihai Economic Zone and leads its member cities in GDP, GDP per head and total retail sales, the latter at RMB 444.51 billion.
#### Coal and the energy shift

Industrial coal mining began in 1882 with the Jiawang Coal Mine, and until the 1950s it was the sole industrial-scale coal producer in Jiangsu. Under pressure from the energy crisis of the 1970s, a model of "multi-party development" appeared. The Datun Mining Area, sometimes called a "Shanghai Enclave", operated next to pits run by other regional authorities.

Resources began to run out in the 2000s, and most local mines closed. What remains is concentrated in three groups, namely Shanghai Datun Energy Resources, Xuzhou Mining Group, and the coal and power company China Resources Tianneng Xuzhou. In 2023 the sector's above-scale enterprises had total assets of 41.98 billion RMB.

The move toward renewable energy began in 2006 with the founding of GCL Silicon, which opened its first polysilicon plant in Xuzhou that year. The site grew into a major base for photovoltaic materials. In 2024 BYD started building a sodium-ion battery plant in Xuzhou with a capacity of 30 GWh.
#### Machinery and engineering

Mining created demand for machinery, and that became the anchor of the local equipment industry, which has grown into a modern construction machinery cluster. Headquartered in Xuzhou, XCMG ranked fourth worldwide among construction equipment makers by revenue in 2024. As of 2023 the specialised equipment sector had 225 enterprises above designated size, and annual output of major products included 729,259 tons of cranes and 143,167 tons of mining equipment. Xuzhou is also a production base for two-wheelers, and motorcycles totalled 526,300 units in 2023.

The Yellow Pavilion (黃樓) dates from 1078, when Su Shi was Prefect of Xuzhou, and commemorates the completed fortification of the city wall under his direction. "Yellow" has two meanings. Symbolically it is the colour of the earth element, which overcomes water, and literally it refers to the rammed earth (hangtu) used in the new defences and in the foundation of the pavilion. The building you see today is a reconstruction from 1988.

The city has many urban expressways, among them three Xuzhou 3rd Ring Road sections (east, north and west), the Xuzhou East Ave. expressway (城东大道快速路) and expressways to Pantang, to Jiawang and to Suqian.
Several national expressways serve the city:
G2 Beijing–Shanghai Expressway
G3 Beijing–Taipei Expressway
G30 Lianyungang–Khorgas Expressway
G2513 Huai'an–Xuzhou Expressway
S49 Xinyi–Yangzhou Expressway
S65 Xuzhou–Mingguang Expressway
S69 Jinan–Xuzhou Expressway
The national highways passing through are China National Highway 104, 205, 206 and 311.

Rail is one of Xuzhou's strengths, and the city is among China's major hubs. Xuzhou Railway Station is where the Beijing–Shanghai railway crosses the Longhai (Lianyungang–Lanzhou) railway. Xuzhoudong Railway Station, on the east side, is where high-speed trains on the Beijing–Shanghai line meet those of the Xuzhou–Lanzhou line. Services on three further routes end there, those to Lanzhou, to Yancheng and from Lianyungang. A link known as the Dahu connection line joins the two stations.

In the north, Xuzhoubei Railway Station is the biggest marshalling yard in the China Railway Shanghai Group, with over 20,000 wagons handled each day. The city is one of 14 official assembly centres for China Railway Express and has sea-rail connections to the ports of Qingdao, Yangshan, Lianyungang and Ningbo-Zhoushan. Rail freight in 2023 was 54.53 million tons.

Among Jiangsu's international airports, Xuzhou Guanyin is one of the three busiest, and scheduled flights go to China's main airports. Up to 2019 it had two terminals, a domestic one (Terminal 2) and an international one (Terminal 1). The Grand Canal passes through Xuzhou, with a navigable route from Jining to Hangzhou, and the Luning oil pipeline from Linyi County in Shandong to Nanjing also runs through the city.
Xuzhou opened the first rapid transit system in northern Jiangsu. These are the lines in service:
Line 1 (opened September 2019): from Xuzhoudong Railway Station to Luwo, with interchanges at Pengcheng Square (Line 2) and Xuzhou Railway Station (Line 3).
Line 2 (November 2020): from Keyunbei to Xinchengqudong, serving the Yunlong campus of Jiangsu Normal University (JSNU).
Line 3 (June 2021): from Xiadian to Gaoxinqu'nan, serving CUMT's Wenchang campus as well as JSNU's Quanshan campus.
Line 6 (September 2025): from Xuzhoudong Railway Station to Tongshan Chinese Medical Hospital.
For CUMT students, Line 3 is therefore the line that reaches the Wenchang campus.
Student life is affected by the region as well as by the campus, so here is background on Jiangsu, covering its history and its people.

china-university-of-mining-and-technolog.h: From early kingdoms to the Qing

blocks.x: Jiangsu was a long way from the heart of early Chinese civilisation, which lay in the north-west of today's Henan. In the earliest dynasties the area belonged to an ancient people known as the Huai barbarians (淮夷). Contact grew in the Zhou period, and the state of Wu emerged in southern Jiangsu, one among hundreds of states then scattered across northern and central China. Wu rose to great power toward the close of the Spring and Autumn period, when King Helu beat the northern power Qi (in modern Shandong) in 484 BC while seeking supremacy over all the states. Yue, a new state to the south in modern Zhejiang, conquered Wu in 473 BC, and in 333 BC the western state of Chu subdued Yue. The Qin state then swept away all the others and unified China in 221 BC.

In the Han dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD) Jiangsu was still far from the cultural centres of the North China Plain. Administratively it was split in two, with the north in Xu Province and the south in Yang Province. During the Three Kingdoms, southern Jiangsu was the base of Eastern Wu (222 to 280). Its capital Jianye, renamed Jiankang later, is present-day Nanjing. When nomads overran the north in the 4th century, the Jin court withdrew to Jiankang, so cities in southern and central Jiangsu grew as northern migrants poured in. Four Southern dynasties in turn kept Jiankang as capital, and it became China's biggest commercial and cultural centre.

Once the Sui reunified the country in 581, politics shifted north again, yet the Grand Canal was dug through Jiangsu to connect the Central Plains to the wealthy Yangtze Delta. Every year the Tang (618–907) depended on grain shipped from southern Jiangsu. The Song era (960–1279) saw a rich merchant class and a market economy develop, and Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and surrounding areas) turned into a trade centre. Cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou have stood for luxury ever since, and it is still one of the wealthiest parts of China.

The Jurchen Jin gained North China in 1127 in the Jin-Song wars, and the Huai River, which then crossed northern Jiangsu on its way to the Yellow Sea, marked the frontier between the Jin and the Southern Song. The Mongols took over China in the thirteenth century. After expelling them in 1368, the Ming at first made Nanjing the capital. Territory around Nanjing, roughly modern Jiangsu and Anhui, was called Nanzhili province ("southern directly governed"). A coup led by Zhu Di, afterwards the Yongle Emperor, moved the capital to distant Beijing, although Nanjing remained the southern capital. Jiangnan was still an important trade region in the late Ming, and some historians see early industrialisation and capitalism in its booming textile industry, though that trend was cut short.
Under the Qing, Nanzhili was converted into "Jiangnan province", and in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui were divided into separate provinces. Since then Jiangsu's borders have changed little.

When Western powers began pushing into China in the 1840s, the wealthy trading region of the Yangtze River Delta was exposed to foreign influence early. Shanghai, once an ordinary small Jiangsu town, soon became a cosmopolitan hub of trade and banking and was later made an independent municipality. Jiangnan was also at the heart of the Taiping Rebellion (1851–1864), a vast and deadly revolt that sought to found a Christian theocracy. It started far off in Guangdong and spread through much of the south, and by 1853 the rebels had taken Nanjing and renamed it Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was founded in 1912, and warlords soon split the country. Control of Jiangsu changed hands more than once. Chiang Kai-shek set up a government in Nanjing in April 1927 and went on to unify most of China, and the provincial government went to Zhenjiang in 1928. The full-scale Second Sino-Japanese War of 1937 disrupted that arrangement. Nanjing fell on December 13, 1937, and the atrocities committed by Japanese forces in the next three months are known as the Rape of Nanjing. Japan occupied most of Jiangsu until the war ended in 1945.

After the war Nanjing resumed its role as capital of the Republic of China, but civil war had started between the Kuomintang government and the Communists, whose bases lay mainly in the north-east. The Huaihai Campaign, fought in northern Jiangsu, decided the matter: the Kuomintang lost, and the Communists crossed the Yangtze and entered Nanjing. The Kuomintang moved south and ended up in Taipei, from where the Republic of China government still runs Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands. It also continues, at least in principle, to claim Nanjing as its legal capital. Once Zhenjiang was captured, the provincial government moved to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

With the Communist takeover, Beijing (earlier called Peiping) became the People's Republic's capital and Jiangsu was divided into the Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. Jiangsu was restored as a province on November 15, 1952, though Nanjing was demoted to the provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up first concentrated on the south coast in Guangdong, leaving Jiangsu behind for a while. From the 1990s the policies were applied more evenly. Suzhou and Wuxi, in the south of the province near Shanghai, have become particularly prosperous and are among the top 10 Chinese cities by GDP, ahead of the provincial capital Nanjing. A large income gap still separates northern and southern Jiangsu, and Xuzhou belongs to the north.
Han Chinese are the majority in Jiangsu, and the Hui and Manchus are among the minority groups. In 2021, 73.94 percent of the province lived in urban areas and 26.06 percent in rural ones.

China University of Mining and Technology-Beijing sits inside the capital, so much of your experience will depend on Beijing itself: what the city looks like, how it is laid out, how the seasons feel and what the air is like. The sections below go through each of these in turn.

The northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland, is where Beijing stands, with the plain opening up to the city's south and east. To the north, northwest and west, mountains screen the city, and the farmland of northern China behind it, from the desert steppes beyond. The Jundu Mountains dominate the municipality's northwest, particularly Yanqing District and Huairou District, while the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the northern part of the municipality along rugged ground, built to keep out nomads from the steppes. The municipality's highest point is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The main rivers crossing the municipality, the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma among them, all feed the Hai River system and run southeastward. On the upper Chaobai lies the Miyun Reservoir, the largest in the municipality. Two great water engineering works also end or begin here: The Grand Canal to Hangzhou, a transport route built over 1,400 years ago, ends in Beijing at its northern terminus. A more recent project, the South-North Water Transfer Project, was completed in the past decade to carry water north from the Yangtze River basin.

The built-up area of Beijing occupies a fairly small, but growing, share of the municipality. It lies on the plains in the south-central part, 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) above sea level, and spreads in concentric ring roads. Tracing the line of the old city walls is the Second Ring Road, while the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs.

At the very centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors of China once lived. Zhongnanhai, home of China's present leaders, is to the west of Tian'anmen. The main east-west axis of the city is Chang'an Avenue, which passes between Tiananmen and the Square.
People often say Beijing has developed by "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), from the old inner city out to the fringe, and this pattern is often named as a cause of the city's urban problems.

Beijing's buildings fall mostly into three families. The first is the traditional architecture of imperial China, The massive Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the trademark building of the People's Republic of China, is a leading example. Others are the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City. The second is the so-called "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to the 1970s, whose buildings tend to be boxy and are sometimes badly built. The third consists of far more modern forms, most visibly in the Beijing CBD in the east, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, but modern buildings also stand elsewhere, among them the National Center for the Performing Arts and the Beijing National Stadium.

In the early 21st century the city saw a huge wave of new construction in many modern styles by international designers, strongest in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s design and neofuturistic architecture are blended, so old and new sit together. The tallest building in Beijing is the China Zun, at 528 meters. Two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building since 2007, namely the CCTV Headquarters (2013) and the Linked Hybrid (2009). The award goes to just one building worldwide each year.

A siheyuan is a courtyard surrounded by buildings. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Alleys called hutongs normally link these courtyards. Hutongs mostly run straight from east to west, which puts doorways facing north or south, an arrangement thought to bring good Feng Shui. They come in different widths, and in the narrowest only a few pedestrians fit through together.

Siheyuans and hutongs were once found everywhere in Beijing but are fast disappearing, as whole city blocks of hutongs give way to high-rise buildings. Under the rules, residents of the hutongs may live in new apartments no smaller than their former homes. Even so, many people feel that the community spirit and street life that hutongs once had are irreplaceable. The properties concerned are often government-owned.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to the border with a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon brings hot, humid summers, and the vast Siberian anticyclone gives winters that are brief, cold and dry. In spring, sandstorms can blow in from the Gobi Desert, over the Mongolian steppe, with rapidly warming but usually dry weather. Autumn, like spring, is a season of change with very little precipitation.

Between 2001 and 2026, the hottest time of year in Beijing was early August and the coldest was early January. China's seasonal standard marks the start of spring at 26 March, summer at 20 May, autumn at 13 September and winter at 31 October. In recent years warming has been quicker in March and September than in May and October, so Beijing's autumn tends to be shorter than its spring.

Averages for 1991 to 2020 depend on where you are in the municipality. Mountain districts are the coolest, with a yearly average between 0 °C (32 °F) and 10 °C (50 °F) that drops further as altitude rises. The low-lying suburbs are warmer: the year averages 11.5 °C (52.7 °F) at the low end of the range and 13.0 °C (55.4 °F) at the high end, nights fall to 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) or up to 8.0 °C (46.4 °F), and days reach 18.2 °C (64.8 °F) to 18.7 °C (65.7 °F). The urban area is warmest of all, where the annual mean ranges from 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) up to 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), the typical night-time minimum from 7.7 °C (45.9 °F) to 8.4 °C (47.1 °F), and the typical daytime maximum from 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) to 18.9 °C (66.0 °F).

The daily average for January is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and for July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). About 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of precipitation falls in a year, with a higher 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three-quarters of it falls from June to August. Possible sunshine is 42% in July and 62% in January and February, so the city gets 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. The coldest day on record since 1951 was 22 February 1966, at -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), and the hottest was 24 July 1999, with 41.9 °C (107.4 °F).

Beijing has long had environmental problems. Between 2000 and 2009 its urban extent quadrupled, which raised emissions sharply and also changed the local meteorology in a basic way, even before counting emissions from people. Wind speed, humidity and surface albedo near the ground all dropped, and temperatures at the ground and just above it climbed, as did ozone levels and the dilution of air vertically. Urbanisation and pollution from burning fossil fuel together often cause serious environmental problems in the city, with health consequences for many residents.

Heavy smog hit Beijing and most of northern China in 2013, affecting 600 million people in total. After this "pollution shock", air pollution became a major economic and social concern in China. Beijing's government then announced steps to cut air pollution, for instance, coal's share of the city's energy was to fall from 24% (2012) to 10% (2017). At national level, the government told the worst-polluting vehicles to leave the road across 2015 to 2017 and stepped up its work on shifting to clean energy sources.

A joint study by American and Chinese researchers, reported in 2006, found that a good deal of Beijing's pollution blows in from surrounding cities and provinces. Between 35% and 60% of the ozone comes from outside the city, on average. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality are said to have a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality". One reason is the mountains lying north and northwest of the city; another is the south or southeasterly flow that prevails in summer.

Almost US$17 billion went into cleaning up the air for the 2008 Summer Olympics, in line with promises made. For the Games, Beijing put a series of measures in place. Construction sites all stopped work, many factories in Beijing closed for good, and industry in neighbouring regions shut down temporarily. Bus and subway fares were cut, new subway lines opened, and high-emission vehicles were banned. Beijing also assembled a fleet of 3,800 buses powered by natural gas, among the biggest in the world, and became the first Chinese city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Coal is the culprit behind roughly 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5, and it is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide as well. Starting in 2012, power stations in the city have been switched from coal to natural gas, with a target of keeping yearly coal use under 20 million tons. Beijing used 26.3 million tons in 2011; 73% went into heating and power, and industry took the remainder.

A lot of the pollution is produced next door. Neighbouring Tianjin was expected to see its coal use rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. In 2011 Hebei Province got through over 300 million tons of coal, more than the whole of Germany, with just 30% for generating power and a considerable portion going to steelmaking and cement. Beijing's air is also affected by power plants in Shandong and in the coal-mining regions of Shaanxi, Shanxi and Inner Mongolia, where coal use has tripled since 2000. Four provinces lead China in coal consumption: in order, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

Beijing had four major coal-fired power plants that supplied electricity and winter heating. Closures came one after another: Gaojing Thermal Power Plant in 2014, two more in March 2015, and finally the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, scheduled for 2016. The city's plan for 2013 to 2017 was to cut coal use by 13 million tons, with a ceiling of 15 million tons in 2015.

The government sometimes seeds clouds to make rain more likely and clear the air before big events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to fight drought. More recently it has relied more on temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, as with "APEC blue" and "parade blue", the short periods during and just before the APEC China 2014 meeting and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved dramatically then, but dropped back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, which shut down most industry and other commercial businesses in the city, and another smog "red alert" came later that month. In November 2016 Beijing's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be banned from driving whenever Smog "red alerts" were issued in the city or neighbouring regions.

Pollutants have fallen measurably since the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014: fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017, and the fall continued by 2020. The main drivers were switching from coal power to natural gas and cleaning up polluting industrial sites around Beijing. In 2022 the annual average concentration of PM2.5 fell to 30 micrograms per cubic meter, the best air quality since 2013. In 2024 Beijing saw only two days of heavy pollution, its lowest number on record and a decrease of 96.6 percent from 58 days in 2013.

Pollution readings differ by source. Daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city are reported on the website of the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB), and, on Twitter, the American Embassy of Beijing posts hourly levels of ozone and fine particulate (PM2.5). The two measure different pollutants by different criteria, and BJEPB's pollution levels and health impact are often reported as lower than the US Embassy's.

Health matters here. Smog does real harm, and air pollution has a direct, significant effect on how many people in Beijing fall ill with cardiovascular or respiratory disease. People who breathe heavily polluted air for long may suffer lung and heart problems, need emergency care, or even die.

Seasonal dust storms plague the city, driven by dust from eroding deserts in northern and northwestern China. To fight them and lessen their impact, the Beijing Weather Modification Office at times brings on rain artificially. At least eight such storms struck in January to April 2006 alone. In April 2002 a single storm left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing and then travelled on towards Japan and Korea.

In practical terms, plan for hot summers with most of the rain between June and August, cold dry winters, and spring dust. Check air quality readings from more than one source, and remember that conditions have improved a great deal since 2013.
