The university described here, China University of Petroleum (East China), is based in Qingdao and answers to the Ministry of Education. It has additional sponsors in the shape of five big energy corporations owned by the state and the Shandong provincial government, and it is listed under Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction.

Its near-namesake in the capital, China University of Petroleum (Beijing), is a national public university as well, under the Education Ministry, and it too sits in Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction. The pair were split in 2005 into legally separate bodies with their own constitutions and administrative boards, so take care not to confuse them when you search or apply.

china-university-of-petroleum-east-china.h: A merger of the country's best petroleum teams

blocks.x: The university was established in 1953 as Beijing Petroleum Institute. It was formed by collecting the strongest petroleum-related units from several top institutions:
petroleum research groups from the geology, mining and chemical engineering departments of Tsinghua University;
petroleum research groups from four departments at Peiyang University (today's Tianjin University);
part of the chemical engineering department of Peking University;
part of the mathematics department of Yanching University, which has since merged into Peking University;
students and teachers of the fluid fuel research group in chemical engineering at the Dalian Institute of Technology, today called Dalian University of Technology;
some students and teachers from the mining and chemical engineering departments of Northwestern Polytechnical Institute (now Northwestern Polytechnical University).

In 1969 the institute relocated to Dongying in Shandong Province and was renamed Huadong Petroleum Institute. In 1988 it became The University of Petroleum, with a college section in Dongying and a graduate school section in Beijing. Over time each half developed into a full university teaching undergraduates and graduates. The title China University of Petroleum was adopted in January 2005. The move of the Huadong branch to Qingdao began in 2004 and ended in 2012. Dongying remains a base for continuing and remote education, research laboratories and work with industry.

The university concentrates on petroleum science and engineering across the whole chain from upstream through midstream to downstream, and it describes its overall level as leading in China. It has five national key disciplines at the second level:
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Mineral Resources Prospecting and Exploration
Oil and Gas Well Engineering
Oil and Gas Storage and Transportation Engineering
Oil and Gas Field Development Engineering

china-university-of-petroleum-east-china.h: Qingdao: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Studying here means living in Qingdao, so the sections below describe the city: where it is, its weather, population, economy, transport and culture.

The city occupies the southern coast of the Shandong Peninsula (Schantung-Halbinsel in German). Three prefecture-level cities are its neighbours: Rizhao in the southwest, Weifang in the west and Yantai in the northeast. It covers 10,654 square kilometres (4,114 square miles), between latitudes 35° 35' and 37° 09' north and longitudes 119° 30' and 121° 00' east. Settled areas are fairly flat, but mountains rise within the city limits and nearby, and the highest point is 1,133 metres (3,717 ft) above sea level. By terrain, 15.5% is highland, 25.1% foothills, 37.8% plains and 21.7% lowland. The coastline measures 730.64 kilometres (454.00 mi), and five significant rivers longer than 50 kilometres (31 mi) cross the region.

The climate is temperate with four seasons and a monsoon influence, in the zone where humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa) meets humid continental (Köppen Dwa). Because the ocean regulates it directly, with southeast monsoon winds and sea currents, it also has marked maritime features. From cool to cold, windy and mostly dry: that describes winter, when January averages 0.2 °C (32.4 °F). In summer it is hot and humid, although extremely hot days rarely occur, and August averages 25.6 °C (78.1 °F).

Thanks to the coast and the peninsula, spring arrives a month behind most inland parts of China, and the average daily temperature range over the year is just 6.3 °C (11.3 °F). Autumn feels gentler than in inland Shandong. The sea is warmest in late August, about 25 °C (77 °F), and people can swim for roughly two months before and after that.

The yearly average temperature is 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Records since 1951 include a freeze of -15.9 °C (3 °F) on 7 and 8 January 2021, while on 15 July 2002 the thermometer reached 38.9 °C (102 °F). Colder readings exist: an unofficial -16.9 °C (1.6 °F), and -16.4 °C (2.5 °F) at the official weather station on 10 January 1931. July has the least possible sunshine at 38 percent and October the most at 59 percent, and the year totals 2,261 hours of bright sun.

One summer nuisance: beaches suffer massive algal blooms. Rotting algae release hydrogen sulphide, which smells like rotten eggs. Local officials declared a "large-scale algae disaster" in 2013 when sea lettuce blooms struck, which were partly blamed on seaweed farming in Jiangsu Province.

About 10 million people live in Qingdao, of whom 6.2 million are in the urban area and an estimated 5 million in other cities under its administration. The annual birth rate is about 76,507, which works out at 10.15 per thousand, against a death rate of 6.32 per thousand. Among the leading Chinese cities, Qingdao enjoys some of the best living standards, which stem from the strength of its exports and fairly high household wages.

There is a large Korean community. By 2009 about 100,000 Koreans worked, studied and lived in Qingdao, making it second in China for Korean residents behind Beijing, with around 200,000. The 2021 Qingdao Statistical Yearbook reports 10.1057 million permanent residents in 2020, an increase of 182,700 over 2019.

Shandong is an important province in eastern China, and much of its recent economic change has centred on Qingdao. In 2006 growth hit 18.9 percent and GDP reached 42.3 billion, first in Shandong and tenth among China's top 20 cities. In 2008 GDP per capita was CN¥52,895, or US$7,616; by 2024 it had grown to CN¥161,200, or US$23,000. The World Bank named Qingdao one of six "golden cities" in 2006, out of 120 Chinese cities assessed for factors like investment climate and government effectiveness. GDP reached CN¥1200.15 billion in 2018 but dipped slightly in 2019.

Beyond China the city is probably most associated with Tsingtao beer, brewed by a company that a German-British joint venture started in 1903 and the country's best-known export beer. Two other big names are based here: the household appliance giant Haier and the electronics company Hisense. Epiphone, the guitar maker, opened a factory there in 2002.

In 1984 the government gave one district the status of Special Economic and Technology Development Zone (SETDZ), and the whole city's secondary and tertiary industries then grew on a fast track. Large foreign investment has come in, particularly from South Korea and Japan, and the port is a hub of local and international trade. On the primary side, farmland amounts to about 50,000 acres (200 km2), and the zigzag coastline provides a valuable supply of fish, shrimp and other marine resources. Wind power generation is among the strongest in the region.

Industrial zones include the Qingdao West Coast New District, the Special Economic and Technological Development Area, the Free Trade Zone, the High-tech Industrial Zone and the Qingdao University Industrial Zone.
Roads in the Qingdao area total 1,145 km (711 mi), of which expressways account for nearly 500 km (310 mi). National expressways that pass through the city or start there are:
G15 Shenhai Expressway (Shenyang, Liaoning to Haikou, Hainan)
G18 Rongwu Expressway (Rongcheng, Shandong to Wuhai, Inner Mongolia)
G20 Qingyin Expressway (Qingdao to Yinchuan, Ningxia), which starts in Qingdao
G22 Qinglan Expressway (Qingdao to Lanzhou, Gansu), also starting in Qingdao
G2011 Qingxin Expressway, a spur route from Qingdao to Xinhe in Pingdu

Provincial expressways include S16 Rongwei (Rongcheng to Weifang), S19 Longqing (Longkou to Qingdao), S21 Xinwei (Xinhe to Weifang) and S24 Weiqing (Weihai to Qingdao). National highways include G204 (Yantai to Shanghai), G206 (Yantai to Shantou), G308 (Qingdao to Shijiazhuang) and G309 (Rongcheng to Lanzhou).

china-university-of-petroleum-east-china.h: Bridge and tunnel under the bay

blocks.x: The world's longest bridge over water opened at Qingdao on 30 June 2011. Haiwan Bridge is 42.5 km (26.4 miles) long and ties the city to Huangdao and Hongdao, beating the former record-holder, Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, by nearly 4.8 km (almost three miles). More than 5,000 pillars support it, and the bill was about 10 billion yuan (some 1.5 billion dollars). Shandong Gausu Group was the designer, building took four years, and at least 10,000 workers in two shifts toiled day and night, starting from opposite ends. Commuting between Qingdao proper and sprawling Huangdao now takes 30 minutes less. The Jiaozhou Bay Tunnel opened on the same day, carries public buses and makes travel between the two areas easier.

The Port of Qingdao (officially Qingdao Port International Co. Ltd.) is one of the world's busiest. It has links with 450 ports in 130 countries and is part of the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. In 2003 cargo handled in a year passed 100 million tons for the first time, including 3.41 million twenty-foot equivalent container units (TEU). By 2011 it was the sixth busiest port in the world by total cargo, at 372,000,000 metric tons for that year, and in 2016 it ranked eighth in the world by TEU. The port includes several large neighbouring ports such as Dongjiakou.
Ferries link the city with Japan and South Korea: the Orient Ferry to Shimonoseki, the New Golden Bridge II to Incheon and the Blue Sea Ferry to Gunsan.

Qingdao Jiaodong International Airport is 39 km (24 mi) from the city centre. It opened on 12 August 2021, replacing Qingdao Liuting International Airport, and 13 domestic and international airlines serve it on 94 routes, 12 of them international or regional.

Rail development accelerated in the late 1990s. Qingdao is where the Jinan-Qingdao high-speed railway, the Qingdao-Jinan passenger railway and the original Qingdao-Jinan railway begin. Main stations in the city proper are Qingdao, Cangkou, Dagang and Qingdao North, while Sifang no longer takes passengers. High-speed D and G trains run at up to 300 km/h (190 mph) between Jinan and Qingdao and go on to Tianjin, Hefei, Shanghai, Beijing and Jinan. Beijing's fastest service, G206 or G205, takes 2 hours 58 minutes. Ordinary lines also connect Qingdao with Lanzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Jinan, Jining and Beijing.

In 2012 the public transport system had 5,283 large and medium-sized buses (including CNG buses) and 136 trolleybuses. All can be used with the contactless Qingdao Public Traffic IC Card (青岛卡). Later all public transport companies adopted the Qingdaotong Card, the last being the Zhenqing bus company in the West Coast New Area (the former Huangdao District) in 2019. Non-air-conditioned buses cost 1 yuan (not counting the tunnel bus), and road passenger transport approaches 737 million trips a year. The "Ri-Xin Bus" (日新巴士) public transport brand is well known across China. Taxi firms include Yiqing, Zhongqing, Jiaoyun and Huaqing.

With State Council approval in hand, the city said on 18 August 2009 that it would invest over 29 billion yuan ($4.2 billion) in a subway before 2016. The first line to run was Line 3, opened on 16 December 2015, and 54.7 km (34.0 mi) were built for a total outlay of 29.2 billion yuan ($4.3 billion). Long-term plans then foresaw eight lines for downtown and suburbs, adding 231.5 km (143.8 mi). The system's operating length was recorded as 243 km (151 mi), the lines then running being the Oceantec Valley and West Coast lines together with Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8.

A newer snapshot dates from 24 February 2023. By then the approved network plan included 19 long-term lines of 872 kilometres in total, and the approved third construction phase covered 13 lines of 503 kilometres, ninth among Chinese cities for approved mileage. Seven lines were open, 315 kilometres in all, with the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11 and 13. By March 2023 there were 146 operating stations, tenth in China and second among northern cities. Under construction were ten lines or extensions, adding up to 188 kilometres and expected to be complete by 2028: those are Line 5, both phases of Line 6, Line 7's Phase II, the first phases of Lines 9 and 15, Line 2's Phase II and West Extension, and Line 8's branch and south section. The two figures differ because they come from different dates.

Chengyang District has the Qingdao Tram (formally a modern tram demonstration line), which opened in 2016 and consists of a single line operated by the Rail Bus Co., Ltd. of the Qingdao Public Transport Group.

Many German-style buildings stand in the city centre, which is striking since the German leased-territory period lasted only 16 years (1898 to 1914). The blend of German and Chinese architecture, along with German roots and a large Korean expatriate community, gives Qingdao a distinct atmosphere. An old description of the city runs: red-tiled roofs, green trees, blue sky and blue sea. Many former foreign-style areas are well preserved, and although the new city is being heavily rebuilt, the old city, especially western Shinan District, keeps many traditional buildings.
Writers: Ma Jian (马建), Ma Jun (马军), Gao Fenghan (高凤翰), and the trio Xiao Hong (萧红), Xiao Jun (萧军) and Duanmu Hongliang (端木蕻良)

Academia, business and public life: Zhang Ruimin (张瑞敏), Li Zhaoxing (李肇星), the scientist Zou Chenglu (邹承鲁), the US diplomat James R. Lilley, Erin Pizzey and Malcolm H. Wiener (the last three born in Qingdao, as was Zou)

Every August or September since 1991, Qingdao has held its International Beer Festival. A big international fair, the Qingdao International Horticultural Exposition, was held there too, in 2014.

The city offers a mild maritime climate, a strong port economy, good rail and air links, a growing metro and a distinctive European-influenced look. Qingdao is a port city of about 10 million people, with a mild maritime climate, long coastline and a metro that is still growing. It links to Beijing by a high-speed train in just under three hours, and to Japan and South Korea by ferry. German-era buildings, a beer festival and a strong manufacturing base give it a distinctive character, and the summer algae blooms and cold windy winters are the main drawbacks to prepare for.

china-university-of-petroleum-beijing.h: Two universities with a shared past

blocks.x: China University of Petroleum-Beijing is a national public university in Beijing, run by the Ministry of Education and listed in Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction. It has a sister institution with a similar name, the China University of Petroleum (East China), which is a separate national university in Qingdao, Shandong. The Qingdao university is sponsored jointly by the Ministry of Education, five large state energy companies and Shandong Province. The two share a history but have been separate legal entities, with their own constitutions and governing boards, since 2005, so make sure you are looking at the right one when you compare programmes and read about campuses.
The university began in 1953 as the Beijing Petroleum Institute, built from the strongest petroleum-related teaching in the country. It drew on:
Petroleum research groups from the geology, mining and chemical engineering departments of Tsinghua University
Petroleum research groups from four departments of Peiyang University, which is now Tianjin University
Part of the chemical engineering department at Peking University
Part of the mathematics department at Yanching University, which later merged into Peking University
Some students and staff from a fluid-fuel research group in chemical engineering at the Dalian Institute of Technology, now Dalian University of Technology
Some students and staff from the mining and chemical engineering departments of the Northwestern Polytechnical Institute, now Northwestern Polytechnical University

In 1969 the institute relocated to Dongying in Shandong Province and became the Huadong Petroleum Institute. In 1988 it was renamed the University of Petroleum, with one part in Dongying as the main college and another in Beijing as a graduate school. Both parts gradually grew into full universities with undergraduate and graduate students. In January 2005 the name became China University of Petroleum. The Huadong part began moving to Qingdao in 2004 and finished in 2012, and the Dongying campus now serves for continuing education, distance learning, research laboratories and cooperation with industry.

The university focuses on petroleum science and engineering across the upstream, midstream and downstream sectors, and it is regarded as a leader nationally. It has five national key disciplines at second level:
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Mineral Resources Prospecting and Exploration
Oil and Gas Well Engineering
Oil and Gas Storage and Transportation Engineering
Oil and Gas Field Development Engineering

Not much further detail about the campus, student numbers or course fees is given here, so look at the university's website for the current information, including entry requirements and any programmes taught in English.
A student's daily life depends on the capital, so the sections below describe how it is laid out, what the weather is like, what its buildings are like and how the air has changed.

Beijing is at the top of the North China Plain, a rough triangle of flat land opening towards the south and east. Mountains lie to the north, north-west and west, and they shelter both the city and the farmland of northern China from the desert steppe. In the north-west of the municipality, notably Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, while the Western Hills (Xishan) bound it in the west. The Great Wall crosses the northern part of the municipality along rugged ridges; it was built to stop nomadic raids from the steppe. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, reaches 2,303 metres (7,556 feet) and is the highest point of the municipality.

Rivers such as the Chaobai, the Yongding and the Juma flow south-east and are tributaries of the Hai River system. The biggest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun, on the upper Chaobai. Beijing is the northern terminus of the 1,400-year-old Grand Canal, which was built to carry goods to Hangzhou, and it is the destination of the South-North Water Transfer Project, a scheme of the last decade that brings water from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up core occupies flat ground in the south-centre of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. It makes up a smallish part of the municipality, though it keeps growing, and it is organised as a series of ring roads. The Second Ring Road follows the line of the former city walls; the Sixth Ring Road links the satellite towns in the suburbs. At the very centre are Tian'anmen and its square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived. West of Tian'anmen lies Zhongnanhai, the government compound, and Chang'an Avenue, running between Tian'anmen and the square, forms the main east-west line of the city.

Beijing has grown outward from the old centre in all directions, and this is sometimes called spreading like a pancake (tan da bing). Planners often name that pattern as a cause of the city's urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Koppen Dwa) and edges toward cold semi-arid (Koppen BSk) with a monsoon influence. The East Asian monsoon brings hot, humid summers. Winters are short but cold and dry, thanks to the powerful Siberian high-pressure system. In spring, sandstorms can blow in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe, and the temperature climbs quickly in dry air. Autumn is a transitional, low-rainfall season. Between 2001 and 2026, early August has been the hottest time of year and early January the coldest. The official seasonal calendar puts the start of spring at 26 March, summer at 20 May, autumn at 13 September and winter at 31 October, though in recent years faster warming in March and September and slower warming in May and October have made autumn shorter than spring.

For the period 1991 to 2020 the average yearly temperature in the urban area lies between 12.9 degrees Celsius (55.2 F) and 13.3 degrees (55.9 F), with daily minimums of 7.7 to 8.4 degrees (45.9 to 47.1 F) and daily maximums of 18.5 to 18.9 degrees (65.3 to 66.0 F). The lower suburbs are cooler, at 11.5 to 13.0 degrees (52.7 to 55.4 F), with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 degrees (42.6 to 46.4 F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 degrees (64.8 to 65.7 F), and mountain areas run from 0 degrees (32 F) to 10 degrees (50 F), getting colder with height. The daily average is minus 2.7 degrees (27.1 F) in January and 27.2 degrees (81.0 F) in July.

Annual rainfall is around 528.0 mm (20.79 inches), or 584.2 mm (23.00 inches) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three-quarters falls between June and August. The share of possible sunshine ranges from 42 percent in July to 62 percent in January and February, and the city gets 2,490.5 sunshine hours a year. Since 1951 the extremes have been minus 27.4 degrees (minus 17.3 F), recorded on 22 February 1966, and 41.9 degrees (107.4 F), recorded on 24 July 1999. In plain terms, bring serious winter wear and be ready for a hot, wet summer, with a few dusty days in spring.

Beijing's skyline mixes three architectural traditions. The oldest is the imperial one, best illustrated by the immense Tian'anmen gate, the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven; Tian'anmen is the single most recognisable symbol of the People's Republic. Between the 1950s and the 1970s, the so-called Sino-Sov style produced boxy buildings, some of them poorly constructed. The newest buildings, in contemporary styles, are clustered around the eastern business district (CBD) and include the CCTV Headquarters, as well as the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts elsewhere.

Since the early 2000s the city has seen an enormous amount of construction, with designers from around the world working in many modern styles, above all in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s designs sit alongside neofuturistic ones. The tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, given each year to one outstanding tall building anywhere in the world, twice since 2007: first for the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and then for the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

A siheyuan is a traditional courtyard home, with rooms facing in on an open yard. Among the grander ones are the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Alleys called hutongs connect the courtyards, and these usually run straight from east to west, so that front doors face north or south, which is considered good feng shui. Some are wide, others only wide enough for a few people to walk through at once.

These lanes used to be everywhere. Now, whole blocks are being cleared for high-rises, and siheyuans and hutongs are disappearing quickly. People who lived in the hutongs may move to new apartments at least as large as the old homes, but many say that the closeness of the community and the street life of the lanes are impossible to replace. The properties are often government-owned.

china-university-of-petroleum-beijing.h: Why pollution became a major concern

blocks.x: Beijing's environmental troubles go back a long way. Its built-up area grew fourfold between 2000 and 2009, which raised emissions but also altered the local meteorology. Ground-surface reflectivity, wind speed and humidity close to the surface fell, whereas ground and surface-air temperatures, the vertical mixing of air and ozone levels rose. Together, urban expansion and fossil-fuel burning often lead to serious pollution and health problems for residents.

In 2013, a heavy smog hit Beijing and much of northern China, affecting a total of 600 million people. That episode made air pollution a leading economic and social issue nationwide. Beijing then announced anti-pollution measures, including a cut in the share of coal in its energy mix from 24 percent in 2012 to 10 percent in 2017. At the national level, heavily polluting vehicles were to be taken off the road from 2015 to 2017, and the energy system was moved more quickly towards cleaner sources.

In 2006 American and Chinese researchers working together concluded that much of Beijing's pollution is carried in from neighbouring cities and provinces: on average 35 to 60 percent of the ozone has an external origin. Shandong and Tianjin exert significant influence, partly because of the prevailing south and south-east winds in summer and the mountains to the north and north-west that trap air.

Coal causes about 40 percent of Beijing's PM2.5 and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been converting coal power stations to natural gas since 2012 and wants to cap annual coal use at 20 million tons; in 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, with 73 percent used for heating and power and the rest in industry. Neighbouring areas matter a lot: Tianjin's consumption was forecast to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, and in 2011 Hebei burned more than 300 million tons, which is more than all of Germany, though just 30 percent went to power generation and a large share to steel and cement. In Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal-mining regions have tripled coal use since 2000, and in Shandong, power plants also feed pollution towards Beijing. Among Chinese provinces, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia come first to fourth for coal use.

Beijing itself had four large coal-fired power plants supplying electricity and winter heat. Gaojing was the first to close, in 2014, two more shut in March 2015, and Huaneng, the last, was to close in 2016. From 2013 to 2017 the plan was to reduce coal use by 13 million tons and to hold it at 15 million tons in 2015.

china-university-of-petroleum-beijing.h: The 2008 Olympics and other big events

blocks.x: To fulfil its promises to clean up before the 2008 Summer Olympics, the city spent nearly US$17 billion. During the Games, construction sites stopped work, many Beijing factories were closed for good, industry in nearby regions was suspended temporarily, and some fuel stations closed. The city also assembled 3,800 gas-powered buses, among the world's biggest fleets of this kind, and became the first in China to require a standard equivalent to Euro 4.

The authorities have sometimes seeded clouds to make rain more likely and clear the air before big occasions, such as the 60th-anniversary parade of 2009, and also to fight drought. More recently they have relied on temporary factory closures and stricter limits on cars. The results were known as APEC blue and parade blue: short spells of clean air around the 2014 APEC China meeting and the 2015 Victory Day Parade, which dramatically improved the air but soon gave way to unhealthy readings again.

Beijing's first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing most industry and commercial business in the city, and a red alert followed later in the month. In November 2016 the environmental protection bureau announced that, from 2017, older high-polluting cars would be barred from the road whenever red alerts were declared in the city or surrounding areas.

Pollution has since fallen measurably after the war on pollution declared in 2014. Fine particulates fell 35 percent in 2017 and went down further by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal and polluting industrial plants were cleaned up. In 2022 the annual average concentration of PM2.5 declined to 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the best level since 2013, and in 2024 there were only two days of heavy pollution, the fewest ever and 96.6 percent down on 58 days in 2013.

The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau publishes daily readings from 27 stations around the city on its website, and the American Embassy has posted hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures. Since they measure different pollutants against different standards, the bureau's numbers and its assessment of health effects have often been lower than the embassy's. Smog harms health: polluted air has a direct effect on rates of heart and lung disease in the city, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, emergency visits and even death. If you have asthma or a heart condition, check the day's air quality and keep a good mask handy.

Seasonal dust storms come from the eroding deserts of northern and north-western China. The weather modification office in Beijing sometimes triggers rainfall to reduce their impact. From January to April 2006 alone there were no fewer than eight storms, and a single one in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before travelling on to Japan and Korea.

The city figures above come from different years, and pollution data in particular change often, so use them to understand how Beijing works and how it has changed rather than as today's measurements. china-university-of-political-science-an.h: A law and politics university in the capital

blocks.x: CUPL (中国政法大学), the China University of Political Science and Law, is a state-run national university based in Beijing. It is also called Zhengfa University. The Ministry of Education is its parent body, and it is co-sponsored by the Beijing Municipal People's Government. Both Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme, national programs that single out leading universities, include it.
Its teaching centres on law and politics, along with economics, management, sociology, history and philosophy.

CUPL operates on two sites. The older one is in Haidian, the original home of the university, and the second is in Changping. The two now split the work: the Haidian campus teaches postgraduate students only, whereas undergraduates attend the larger Changping campus. Keep that in mind when you plan where to live.

In 2015 CUPL had 13 schools, 15,833 students and 951 faculty members, 290 of them professors. The university runs a wide range of international exchanges and has about 1,000 foreign students from many countries.

In the QS World University Rankings by Subject, CUPL is among the top 10 universities in Asia for Law and Legal Studies, and it stood 38th in the world for that subject as of 2023. It is also regularly rated number one in China among universities specialising in Political Science and Law in the Best Chinese Universities Ranking.

Life outside the lecture hall depends on the city, so this part of the profile introduces Beijing. It is arranged around questions a newcomer is likely to ask: what the weather is like, how clean the air is, how the land is laid out, and what the buildings and old neighbourhoods look like.

china-university-of-political-science-an.h: How hot, how cold, how wet?

blocks.x: Beijing is classed as humid continental (Köppen Dwa) and sits close to the dividing line with the monsoonal cold semi-arid type (BSk). Expect hot, damp summers, a result of the East Asian monsoon, and winters that are short, cold and dry because of the enormous Siberian anticyclone. In spring the weather warms swiftly and stays mostly dry, though sandstorms from the Gobi Desert can sweep over the Mongolian steppe and into the city. Autumn is a season of change as well, with very little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest period was early August and the coldest was early January.

The national calendar of seasons puts the start of spring at 26 March in Beijing, with summer beginning 20 May, autumn 13 September and winter 31 October. Recent years have brought quicker warming in March and September and slower warming in May and October, which tends to make autumn here shorter than spring.

Now for the numbers. Across the urban area, the 1991 to 2020 yearly mean lies between 12.9 and 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Daily lows average between 7.7 and 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F), and daily highs between 18.5 and 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). Low-altitude suburbs run a little cooler, with a mean of 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). Mountain areas record means of 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F) that decrease as the land gets higher. Monthly averages show the range: -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) in January and 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July.

Beijing's yearly precipitation is about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), though Haidian and Chaoyang, the districts around many campuses, average 584.2 mm (23.00 in). Nearly three-quarters of the rain falls between June and August. Sunshine, as a share of the maximum possible, is lowest in July (42%) and highest in January and February (62%), so the yearly total is 2,490.5 hours of bright sun. The coldest reading since 1951, -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), was taken on 22 February 1966, and the hottest day was 24 July 1999, at 41.9 °C (107.4 °F).

The honest answer is: much better than it was, though still a concern. Environmental problems have a long history in the capital. Between 2000 and 2009 the urban area expanded to four times its size, which raised emissions from human activity and also changed the local weather in basic ways, even leaving human emissions aside. Wind speed, humidity near the ground and surface albedo went down; ground and near-ground air temperatures, ozone and the vertical dilution of air went up. Fossil fuel burning combined with urban growth often leads to serious environmental trouble and health problems among residents.

In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and much of northern China, affecting 600 million people altogether. This 'pollution shock' turned air pollution into a major economic and social issue nationwide. Beijing's government responded with measures such as reducing the share of coal in the city's energy use (24% in 2012) to 10% by 2017. The national government, for its part, ordered heavily polluting vehicles off the road in 2015 to 2017 and stepped up the shift to clean energy.

A study carried out jointly by American and Chinese researchers in 2006 found that surrounding cities and provinces contribute much of Beijing's pollution. About 35 to 60% of the ozone, on average, comes from outside the city. The study called the influence of Shandong Province and of Tianjin on the capital's air quality significant, in part because the summer wind generally blows from the south and southeast and mountains stand to the north and northwest.

Cleaner air was a promise for the 2008 Summer Olympics, and nearly US$17 billion went into keeping it. While the Games lasted, all construction sites stopped, many Beijing factories were closed for good, industry in nearby regions was shut temporarily, some gas stations were closed, and motor traffic was halved by letting drivers out only on odd or even days depending on the licence plate. Bus and subway fares were reduced, new subway lines opened, and vehicles with high emissions were banned. The city built up a fleet of 3,800 natural gas buses, which is one of the largest anywhere, and became the first Chinese city to require China's equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Coal remains the key factor. Burning it is responsible for roughly 40% of the city's PM2.5, and it is also the leading source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. From 2012 the city began switching coal-fired power stations to natural gas, with a goal of limiting yearly coal consumption to 20 million tons. Beijing itself burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, with 73% of that going into heating and electricity and the remainder to industry. Neighbouring regions emit a large share of what Beijing breathes. Tianjin's coal consumption was forecast to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, while Hebei Province burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than Germany as a whole, using only 30% for power and a significant part for steel and cement. Power stations in Shandong and in the coal belt of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000, add to it. In ranking order, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia are the first to fourth provinces by coal use.

The city once had four major coal-fired plants supplying electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant went offline in 2014, two more followed in March 2015, and the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant was to be the last, in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was to cut coal use by 13 million tons and keep it to 15 million tons in 2015.

Before major events, officials have occasionally seeded clouds to make rain more likely and clear the air, as before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and have used the same method against drought. Recently they have relied more on short-term factory shutdowns and tighter limits on cars. The result was 'APEC blue' during and before APEC China 2014 and 'parade blue' before the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, brief periods of dramatically better air that soon gave way to unhealthy levels again.

The first smog alert was issued on 8 and 9 December 2015 and shut down much industry and commercial business. A 'red alert' followed later in the month. A November 2016 announcement by the environmental protection bureau said that from 2017, old, highly polluting cars would be forbidden to drive whenever red alerts were declared in the city or nearby regions.

Measurable improvements have followed the 'war on pollution' declared in 2014. In 2017 fine particulates fell by 35%, with more reduction by 2020, chiefly because gas took the place of coal in power generation and dirty industrial plants nearby were cleaned up. In 2022 the annual average concentration of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the best since 2013. Heavy pollution occurred on just two days of 2024, a record low and a 96.6 percent fall from the 58 days of 2013.

china-university-of-political-science-an.h: Where to check the readings, and why it matters

blocks.x: Several organisations publish figures, which do not always agree. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website, and the American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly ozone and PM2.5 figures on Twitter. The two organisations measure different pollutants using different criteria, so the bureau's pollution levels, and the health impact it reports, are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog harms health. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on the rate of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and breathing very polluted air can bring breathing and heart problems, trips to the emergency room, and even fatalities.

Dust is another seasonal issue. Dust storms that trouble the city come from desert erosion in the north and northwest of the country, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office at times induces rain artificially to fight them and soften their effects. In just the first four months of 2006 there were eight or more storms, and in April 2002 one storm alone deposited almost 50,000 tons of dust on the city before continuing to Japan and Korea.

Start with the map. Beijing lies where the North China Plain, which is roughly triangular, ends in the north; the plain stretches away to the city's south and east. Hills and mountains in the north, northwest and west form a barrier that protects the capital and northern China's farming heartland against the desert steppe. In the municipality's northwest, particularly in Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains rule the landscape, and the Western Hills, known as Xishan, frame the west. The Great Wall, running along the rugged ground of the northern part of the municipality, was built as a defence against nomadic incursions from the steppe. Mount Dongling, a peak in the Western Hills by the Hebei provincial border, is the highest point in the municipality at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Beijing's main rivers, the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, flow southeast and are tributaries of the Hai River system. On the upper Chaobai is the Miyun Reservoir, the biggest in the municipality. Two great waterworks end here: the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, a transport route built more than 1,400 years ago, and the South-North Water Transfer Project, completed in the last ten years to bring in water from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up city occupies the plains of the south-central municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet), taking up a fairly small, though growing, part of the total area. The streets are organised in rings around the middle. The innermost, the Second Ring Road, follows the course of the vanished city walls, and the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs. The centre of Beijing is Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, home to China's current leaders, is to the west of Tian'anmen, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between Tiananmen and the Square, is the main east-west axis of the city.

Local commentators describe the way Beijing has grown, from the old inner city outward, as 'spreading like a pancake' (tan da bing), and they often name that pattern as a reason for the city's urban problems.

Beijing's architecture comes in three main layers. The imperial layer is the oldest and includes the grand Tian'anmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace, which has become the People's Republic's best-known landmark, plus the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. Next comes the 'Sino-Sov' style built from the 1950s to the 1970s, characterised by boxy structures that were sometimes badly built. The latest layer consists of modern forms, clustered in the Beijing CBD in the east, home of the new CCTV Headquarters, but also seen at the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the start of the 21st century the pace of construction has been enormous, with international designers contributing varied modern styles, above all in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s architecture and a neofuturistic look sit side by side. The 528-metre China Zun is the city's tallest building. Twice since 2007 a Beijing tower has won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which names just one best overall tall building in the world each year: for the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and for the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

The traditional home is the siheyuan, a courtyard house surrounded by buildings, and Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are among the more grand. Alleys known as hutongs usually link the courtyards. They mostly run straight from east to west, so doorways face north and south in line with feng shui, and their widths vary, with some so narrow that only a few people can squeeze through at the same time. Courtyards and hutongs used to be everywhere in the city, but they are vanishing rapidly as complete blocks are replaced with tall buildings. People who live in hutongs have the right to apartments in the new buildings at least as large as their previous homes. Still, many residents complain that the traditional community spirit and street life of the hutong cannot be rebuilt, and the properties are frequently government owned.

For a student, the takeaways are simple. Dress for a cold, dry winter and a hot, humid summer; check the air readings on bad days; and enjoy a city where imperial monuments, Soviet-era blocks, courtyard alleys and futuristic towers all share the skyline.

china-youth-university-of-political-stud.h: China Youth University of Political Studies: what it is today

blocks.x: China Youth University of Political Studies (中国青年政治学院, Zhōngguó Qīngnián Zhèngzhì Xuéyuàn) is a Beijing institution that the Communist Youth League of China set up in 1985, and it has stayed linked to the league since. The head of the league (its First Secretary) normally serves as university president too. One former president was Hu Jintao, who went on to become the Party's General Secretary and China's paramount leader. The compact campus covers 12 hectares (30 acres) on Xisanhuan Bei Lu, the West 3rd Ring Northern Road.

One fact matters most to anyone considering an application: in 2017 the institution stopped operating as a public university. What remains is a shared brand name. The league's own training school, the Central School (中央团校, Zhōngyāng Tuán Xiào), uses it as a co-brand. Please read the following history carefully, and check with the school directly before planning any application.

Back in 1948 the league founded a political training school, the Central School, to serve its own needs, and that is where the story starts. Hu Yaobang's reformist administration was at that time changing party organs into public institutions with a public administrative structure. In 1985, as part of those changes, the Youth League School became a public university, taking the name China Youth University of Political Studies. Undergraduates were first admitted in 1986.

Later the direction of policy reversed. With Xi Jinping as general secretary, public institutions were returned to party organs, and in 2017 and 2018 the university came back under Communist Youth League control. The University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences absorbed its undergraduate school. Meanwhile the league revived its Central School under its own control, which keeps using the China Youth University of Political Studies name as a second brand.

While it operated as a public university, CYU was one of China's main institutes for law and politics. Research topics ranged over Marxism and public administration, youth culture and youth development, social work, criminal law and journalism. It opened the country's first department for youth work in 1985. Mainland China's first and biggest social work department, later upgraded to a college, also belonged to it.
Postgraduates could study Marxism, economics, journalism, sociology, and criminal or economic law.
Until 2017 the main emphasis was on undergraduate teaching. Available majors were:
Law and Economics
Mass Communication and Journalism
Sociology, Social Work and Social Security
Public Administration and Youth Work
Chinese Language and Literature
Foreign Languages and Literature
The CYU library was turned into a branch of the National Library of China in 2013.
The office of president goes with the league's First Secretary, so the list of CYUPL presidents is really a list of league leaders over the years:
Hu Yaobang, 1957 to 1978
Han Ying (韩英, Hán Yīng), 1978 to 1982
Wang Zhaoguo, 1982 to 1984
Hu Jintao, 1984 to 1985
Song Defu, 1985 to 1993
Li Keqiang, 1993 to 1998
Zhou Qiang, 1998 to 2006
Hu Chunhua, 2006 to 2008
Lu Hao, 2008 to 2013
Qin Yizhi, from 2013

china-youth-university-of-political-stud.h: Beijing as a place to live

blocks.x: Daily student life is shaped by the city around the campus, including its weather, its transport and what there is to see. This part of the profile describes Beijing, where the university is based.

Three architectural styles stand out in the city. One is the imperial tradition. The best example is the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which has become the People's Republic's signature structure, and the style can also be seen at the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City.

A second style is nicknamed "Sino-Sov". Buildings of this kind date from the 1950s through the 1970s, and are often boxy, with some poorly constructed. A third, far more modern group is concentrated in the Beijing CBD in the east of the city, the new CCTV Headquarters being the most obvious case, but you can find examples across Beijing, such as the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Construction has boomed since the start of the 21st century, with international designers contributing many modern styles, especially in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone a 1950s design and a neofuturistic look sit side by side, blending old and new. China Zun, 528 metres high, is the tallest building in Beijing. Since 2007, two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which names one best overall tall building worldwide each year: the Linked Hybrid (2009) and the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

Traditional Beijing homes are siheyuans, courtyards enclosed by buildings on every side. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are grand examples. Narrow lanes known as hutongs connect them. For good feng shui these lanes mostly run straight, east to west, with doorways facing north and south. Their widths differ, and in some only a few pedestrians can pass at a time.

Everywhere in Beijing hutongs and siheyuans were once the norm, yet they are vanishing quickly as entire city blocks of them are replaced by high-rise buildings. People who live in a hutong may move into new apartments that are no smaller than their former homes. Many complain, however, that the old feeling of community and street life is lost for good. The properties tend to belong to the government.

The North China Plain, a plain roughly triangular in shape and open to the south and east of the capital, ends at Beijing's northern edge. To the north, northwest and west there are mountains that protect both the city and the farmland of northern China from the desert steppes beyond. The Jundu Mountains cover much of the municipality's northwest, particularly Yanqing and Huairou districts, and the Western Hills, known as Xishan, form the western frame. Across the rough terrain of the north runs the Great Wall, built as a defence against raiders from the steppes. On the Hebei border, in the Western Hills, rises Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 ft) high, the highest point in the municipality.

All the main rivers, including the Chaobai, the Yongding and the Juma, run southeast and belong to the Hai River system. The Miyun Reservoir on the Chaobai's upper course is the municipality's largest. Beijing is also the northern end of two major water projects. One is the Grand Canal down to Hangzhou, which was dug more than 1,400 years ago for transport. The other is the South-North Water Transfer Project, which has been built in the last decade to bring in water from the Yangtze basin.

Beijing's urban area occupies plains in the south-central part of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and takes up a fairly small but expanding portion of the municipal territory. Ring roads spread out in concentric circles. The Second Ring Road traces the old city walls, and the Sixth links satellite towns in the suburbs.

At the very centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, directly south of the Forbidden City, once the emperors' residence. Zhongnanhai, where the present leaders of China live, is west of Tian'anmen, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between the gate and the Square, is the main east-west axis of the city.
The way Beijing has grown from the old inner city to the outskirts is often called "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), and many cite that pattern as a reason for the city's urban problems.

Technically Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to the edge of a monsoonal cold semi-arid one (Köppen BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid. Winters are brief, cold and dry, a result of the vast Siberian anticyclone. Spring may bring sandstorms from the Gobi Desert, blown across the Mongolian steppe, as the weather warms quickly and stays mostly dry. Autumn, a lot like spring, is a season of change with minimal rain.
Some further details:
Across 2001 to 2026 the hottest period is early August and the coldest is early January.

The official calendar puts the start of spring on 26 March, of summer on 20 May, of autumn on 13 September and of winter on 31 October. In recent years March and September have warmed up faster, and May and October more slowly, so autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

Averaged over 1991 to 2020, the urban area has a yearly temperature of 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Daily lows average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F), and daily highs 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).
Suburbs at low altitude are slightly cooler: 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F) for the year, with lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F).
Up in the mountains the yearly average is somewhere from 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F) and drops as the land rises.
By month, January is −2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July is 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) on a daily average.
Around 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of precipitation falls each year. For Haidian and Chaoyang the figure is higher, 584.2 mm (23.00 in). Nearly three quarters comes in the three months from June to August.
Sunshine as a share of the possible is 42% in July and 62% in both January and February, so over 12 months there are 2,490.5 hours of bright sun.
Since 1951 the coldest day was 22 February 1966 (−27.4 °C, or −17.3 °F) and the hottest was 24 July 1999 (41.9 °C, or 107.4 °F).

china-youth-university-of-political-stud.h: Air pollution and what has been done

blocks.x: Environmental trouble has a long history in Beijing. Between 2000 and 2009 the built-up area grew fourfold. That raised emissions from people and also altered the local weather in basic ways: wind speed, humidity and surface albedo near the ground went down, whereas temperatures at and near the ground, ozone and vertical air dilution went up. Urban growth plus the burning of fossil fuels has produced serious environmental problems, and many residents suffer health effects.

In 2013 heavy smog struck Beijing and most of northern China, touching 600 million people in all. This "pollution shock" made air pollution a major economic and social concern across China. Beijing's government then announced measures including a drop in coal's share of energy from 24% (2012) to 10% (2017), while from 2015 to 2017 the national government ordered that heavily polluting vehicles be taken off the roads, and worked harder on the shift to clean energy.

A 2006 joint study by American and Chinese researchers found that much pollution reaching Beijing starts in neighbouring cities and provinces: on average, 35% to 60% of its ozone has outside origins. The effect of Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality on local air quality is described as "significant", in part because summer winds mostly blow from the south or southeast and the mountains to the north and northwest hold air in.

Preparing for the 2008 Summer Olympics, and keeping promises to improve the air, Beijing spent nearly US$17 billion. For the period of the Games it brought in many measures. All construction sites stopped work, some factories were closed permanently and industry in nearby regions was shut temporarily, and a few gas stations closed. Cars were allowed on the road only on odd or even days, depending on the licence plate, which halved motor traffic. Fares on buses and the subway were lowered, new subway lines opened, and vehicles with high emissions were banned. A fleet of 3,800 natural gas buses, among the world's largest, was put together, and Beijing became China's first city to require the Chinese counterpart of the Euro 4 standard.

Burning coal accounts for about 40% of PM 2.5 in Beijing, and it is also the biggest source of sulphur dioxide and nitrogen compounds. Since 2012 the city has switched its coal-fired power stations to natural gas, and it wants annual coal use to stay under 20 million tons. In 2011 the total was 26.3 million tons: 73% went to heating and power generation and the remainder to industry.

A lot of the city's pollution is produced elsewhere. Tianjin's coal use was forecast to go up from 48 million tons to 63 million tons over 2011 to 2015. In 2011 Hebei Province consumed more than 300 million tons, a larger amount than Germany as a whole, but only 30% went to electricity, with a large part being used in steel and cement production. Power plants in Shandong and in the coal regions of Inner Mongolia, Shanxi and Shaanxi (the last three have tripled their coal use since 2000) add to Beijing's smog too. Ranked by coal consumption, the provinces in first to fourth place are Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

Within Beijing, four large coal-fired plants once supplied electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was closed in 2014, two others in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to close in 2016. Plans for 2013 to 2017 involved a reduction of 13 million tons in coal use, and a cap of 15 million tons for 2015.

Before big events, officials have at times used cloud seeding to raise the odds of rain and clear the air, for example ahead of the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and the same technique is used against drought. Recently, though, the emphasis has shifted to temporary factory closures and tougher rules for cars. The results are known as "APEC blue" and "parade blue": short periods around APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, when the air improved dramatically, before sliding back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed most of the city's industry and many other businesses. A "red alert" for smog was issued later in the same month. The environmental protection bureau said in November 2016 that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would not be allowed to drive during red alerts in the city or in neighbouring regions.

Things have measurably improved since the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014. Fine particulates went down 35% in 2017, and further still by 2020. The main reasons were that natural gas took the place of coal for power and that polluting industrial sites were cleaned up. Annual average PM2.5 (the fine particulate matter most often tracked) came down to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the cleanest year since 2013. In 2024, Beijing recorded only two days of heavy pollution. That is the lowest ever, and 96.6 percent fewer than the 58 days in 2013.

Because pollution is high, several sources publish readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) reports daily pollution readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website. On Twitter, the American Embassy in Beijing publishes hourly readings of ozone and fine particulate (PM2.5). The two sources differ, because the BJEPB and the embassy track different pollutants using different criteria, and as a result the BJEPB's levels, and the health impact it reports, are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog is harmful. In Beijing, air pollution has a direct effect on how common heart and breathing diseases are, and heavy exposure may bring on respiratory and cardiovascular problems, visits to emergency rooms and even death. Anyone with asthma or a similar condition would be wise to check the readings and plan around them.

Each year dust storms, which come from the erosion of deserts in the north and northwest of China, trouble the city. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes it rain artificially in order to combat these storms and ease their impact. At least eight struck in the first four months of 2006. In April 2002 one storm left nearly 50,000 tons of dust across Beijing and went on to Japan and Korea.

The history of China Youth University of Political Studies is unusual and closely connected to the Communist Youth League. Its status changed in 2017, so it is vital to confirm the current situation before you apply. As a city, Beijing offers famous buildings, traditional courtyards and ancient sites, set against hot summers, cold dry winters, dust in spring and steadily improving air.
