chongqing-jiaotong-university.h: Chongqing Jiaotong University at a glance

blocks.x: Chongqing Jiaotong University, abbreviated CQJTU, is a public university run by the municipality of Chongqing and based in Nan'an District. Its supervising authority is the city government. The word "jiaotong" means transport and communications, which explains the school's long-standing strength in roads, bridges, shipping and related engineering.

The university may award doctorates in three fields, master's degrees in 27 fields and bachelor's degrees in 42 majors. It can also grant master's degrees to people with the same academic background and has the authority to give engineering master's degrees in five fields. Full-time enrolment is above 16,000.

About 1,700 staff work for the university, of whom 1,000 are academic faculty. A further group of 120 talents includes top candidates in a national "thousands and hundreds talents project" run by the Ministry of Communications, scientific and technical experts of that ministry, top academic and technological leaders for the Chongqing Municipality, and specialists at provincial or ministerial level. All receive special allowances from the State Council. More than 140 part-time professors have also been engaged, among them members of the Chinese academies, foreign academics and scholars from China and abroad.

In 2001 the Ministry of Education evaluated the university's undergraduate teaching and rated it "Fine". Graduate supply falls short of demand, and for eight consecutive years more than 90% of its graduates in teacher-training fields have found their first jobs.

Over the most recent five years, research projects have numbered 40 at national level and 250 at provincial or ministerial level. Staff published 100 academic books and 4,000 papers, and 20 invention patents have been granted.

The university issues three public academic journals. Applied Mathematics and Mechanism is edited by Qian Weichang, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, is operated chiefly by the university and is indexed in SCI and EI. It appears in Chinese and English editions and reaches more than 50 countries and regions. A second journal is the natural science edition of the Journal of Chongqing Jiaotong University.

Its earlier national honours were a State invention award (1996) and second and third prizes in the State scientific and technological progress awards (1998). After 2000 it added three: a first and a second prize for scientific and technological progress, and a second prize for teaching achievements.
Students can use a library of 1.4 million books, and a broadband network serves every part of the campus.

Located at No. 66 Xuefu Avenue in Nan'an District, this is the main campus and the seat of administration and major research facilities. It mostly houses third- and fourth-year undergraduates and postgraduate students. Teaching and research take place in the Mingde Building, four numbered teaching buildings and the Language Laboratory Building, while the Huiyuan and Zhiyuan residential areas house students.

This campus is in Shuangfu New District, Jiangjin District. It was largely finished in 2011 and received its first-year students that same year, and it is mainly responsible for first- and second-year undergraduates. The land is gently rolling, and Lizi Lake, at roughly 115 mu (7.7 hectares, or 19 acres), is a feature of the grounds.

The plan reserves 2,500 mu (170 hectares, or 420 acres) for academic use, with total building area of 850,000 m2 (85 ha), and a separate 400 to 500 mu (27 to 33 hectares, or 67 to 82 acres) for staff housing. Already in use are the First Teaching Building, the Experimental Center, the campus library, the Student Activity Center and, for living and services, the Deyuan Residential Area and Deyuan Service Center.
For you, this means a typical undergraduate path starts at Science City and moves to Nan'an for the later years, so check where your programme will be taught and where you will live.

Thirty overseas universities and research units are partners. They include Hannover (Germany), Texas (United States), St. Petersburg (Russia), Burgos (Spain) and Hanoi (Vietnam). It began recruiting overseas students in 2004.

chongqing-jiaotong-university.h: Chongqing: mountain city on two rivers

blocks.x: Everyday life for a student depends heavily on the city. Chongqing is large, hilly and humid, and it is useful to know what to expect before you arrive.

Chongqing is a subtropical city, placed where the Sichuan Basin gives way to the middle and lower Yangtze plain. Monsoon conditions are frequent, and late spring and early summer often bring rain at night. "Night rain in the Ba Mountains" is a poetic image that recurs in Chinese verse, for example in a poem by Li Shangyin titled "Written on a Rainy Night, a Letter to the North". The municipality is at most 470 kilometres (290 mi) from east to west and at its widest 450 kilometres (280 mi) from north to south. Hubei and Hunan are on its eastern side, Sichuan and Shaanxi on the north, and Guizhou on the south.

The area is a patchwork of rivers and mountains. The Daba Mountains stand to the north, Wu Gorge to the east, the Wuling range to the southeast and the Dalou range to the south. Overall the ground falls away from north to south toward the Yangtze valley, a big massif of mountains and hills with steep slopes at different elevations. Karst scenery is widespread, with stone forests, clusters of peaks, limestone caves and valleys. The Longshuixia Gap (龙水峡地缝) and its Three Natural Bridges make it a visitor attraction.

The Yangtze crosses the whole municipality from west to east over 665 kilometres (413 mi) and cuts through the Wu Mountains in three places to form the famous Three Gorges: Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling. The Jialing River comes from the northwest, passes the "Jialing Lesser Three Gorges" (Libi, Wentang and Guanyin), and flows into the Yangtze at Chongqing.

The central urban area, known as Chongqing proper, is built on hills and half-encircled by the Yangtze and Jialing. Its scenery of caves, gorges, waterfalls, springs, forests, rivers and mountains moved the Tang poet Li Bai to write an epigram. Zhongliang Mountain (中梁山) and Tongluo Mountain (铜锣山) roughly mark the western and eastern limits of the urban area. High peaks lie outside the centre, such as Wugong Ling Mountain in Jiangjin, which is 1,709.4 metres (5,608 ft).

Chongqing's climate is monsoonal humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa), bordering on plain humid subtropical (Cfa). Relative humidity is very high through most of the year, above 75% in every month. Together with Wuhan and Nanjing, it is counted as one of the Yangtze's "Three Furnaces". Summers last a long time and rank with the hottest and muggiest in China, reaching urban highs of 34 °C (93 °F) in July and August. Winters are short and fairly mild but damp and grey.

The Sichuan Basin location gives it one of the lowest sunshine totals in China, only 983 hours a year, less than much of northern Europe. Possible sunshine in the city proper is a mere 5% in January and 43% in August. Since 1951 the record low is -1.8 °C (29 °F), set on 11 January 1955, and the record high 43.7 °C (111 °F), set on 18 and 19 August 2022.

With over 100 days of fog every year, the city is nicknamed "Fog City" (雾都). In spring and autumn a thick layer of fog covers it for 68 days a year. The weather may even have helped shield the city from capture by Japanese forces in the Second Sino-Japanese War of 1937 to 1945.

The 2020 census counted 32,054,159 residents, about 2.27% of China's total, a total that makes Chongqing the world's most populous city proper. For 2010 the OECD put the population of the metropolitan area around the central urban zone at 17 million. By urban population, Chongqing passed Shanghai in 2020 to become China's biggest municipality. By 2021 an estimated 70.4% of residents were urban and 29.6% rural, and by 2024 the urban population was 23.01 million.

The census gives 50.55% male and 49.55% female (the figures as printed do not quite add up). By age, 15.91% were 0 to 14, 62.22% were 15 to 64 and 21.87% were 65 or older. For highest education, 15.41% had college, 15.96% high school, 30.58% middle school and 29.89% primary school.

Chinese folk religion, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism are the main faiths. Surveys in 2007 and 2009 found that 26.63% of people follow Chinese ancestral religion and 1.05% are Christian. Those reports gave no figures for other religions, and the other 72.32% could be non-religious or could follow folk sects, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or worship of nature deities. There were 9,056 Muslims in 2010.

Industrial capacity in Chongqing was boosted by heavy investment during the Third Front campaign, and the government has pushed hard to turn it into the economic, trade and financial centre of the region, and to use it as a platform for opening up the western interior. Growth is quick: statistics suggest new construction added about 137,000 square metres (1,470,000 sq ft) of usable floor space each day for housing, commerce and factories. To speed development, and with it the poorer western areas under the China Western Development strategy, Chongqing was separated from Sichuan and was made a municipality on its own account on 14 March 1997. By the 2000s it was an important industrial area.

Nominal GDP came to CN¥2.91 trillion, or US$433 billion, which is about 2.41% of the national figure and 16th among provincial-level units. By sector, the primary industries produced CN¥201.21 billion (US$29.92 billion), the secondary CN¥1.169 trillion (US$173.86 billion) and the tertiary CN¥1.542 trillion (US$229.3 billion). Nominal GDP per person was CN¥90,663 (US$13,479), the tenth highest nationally. The Economist Intelligence Unit's Access China White Paper of November 2010 grouped it with Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang as the CHAMPS, a set of 20 emerging Chinese cities.

Because of its inland, hard-to-reach position, Chongqing and Sichuan have long been military bases for weapons research and development. Industry is diverse, but unlike eastern China the export sector is small. Instead, many factories make goods for domestic buyers, among them electronics, sports equipment, machinery, textiles, chemicals, cars and processed food.

In vehicle production, Chongqing is third in China for motor vehicles and first for motorcycles. A 2007 figure puts annual capacity at 1 million cars and 8.6 million motorcycles. Big names are Changan Automotive Corp (the fourth-largest Chinese car maker), Lifan Hongda Enterprise and Ford, which runs 3 plants there. The municipality also ranks among China's nine largest steel producers and three leading aluminium producers. Key companies are Chongqing Iron and Steel (重庆钢铁股份有限公司) and the Asia's-largest aluminium plant, Southwest Aluminum (西南鋁業). Agriculture also matters, with rice and fruit, especially oranges, as the main crops.

Resources are plentiful: coal, natural gas and over 40 kinds of minerals, for instance strontium and manganese. Estimated coal reserves are roughly 4,800,000,000 metric tons. The Chuandong Natural Gas Field is the country's largest inland gas field, with about 270 billion m3, more than a fifth of China's total. The area holds China's biggest strontium reserve (China has the world's second biggest), and manganese is mined at Xiushan, although the mining sector has been criticised as heavily polluting and unsafe.

A 10 million ton refinery run by CNPC (PetroChina's parent) is planned in Chongqing to process crude from the Sino-Myanmar pipelines. The pipeline was unfinished when the source was written; it will start at Sittwe on Myanmar's west coast, pass through Kunming in Yunnan and end in Chongqing, supplying fuel from Africa, the Middle East and Myanmar.

Recently the city has tried to move up the value chain towards high-technology and knowledge-intensive industry, which has led to new zones such as the Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ). Policies that favour electronics and IT are meant to build a 400 billion RMB hub for high-tech manufacturing, one expected to overtake the car industry and supply a quarter (25%) of exports.

The city has spent heavily on roads and railways that link it to the rest of China, lowering logistics costs. The nearby Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest, supplies power and lets oceangoing ships reach Chongqing's Yangtze port. These improvements brought many foreign investors in industries from cars to finance and retail, with names like Ford and Mazda on the manufacturing side, banks including HSBC, Standard Chartered, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, ANZ and Scotiabank, and retailers such as Wal-Mart, Metro AG and Carrefour.

The city contains several economic and technological development zones: the Chongqing Chemical Industrial Park, Economic and Technological Development Zone, Hi-Tech Industry Development Zone, New North Zone (CNNZ), Export Processing Zone, Jianqiao Industrial Park (in Dadukou District), the Liangjiang New Area, and the Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center, which is China's biggest of its kind. In addition, Chongqing forms the West Triangle Economic Zone with Chengdu and Xi'an.

Since becoming a national-level municipality in 1997, Chongqing has hugely expanded its infrastructure. With railways and expressways built to the east and southeast, it is a major transport hub of southwestern China. By October 2014 there were 31 bridges over the Yangtze, including over a dozen in the urban core. Only the first two (1960 and 1977) are older than 1995.

Getting around means choosing among metro, intercity rail, buses everywhere and what is described as the largest monorail network in the world. In May 2007 the municipal government announced a 150 billion RMB plan over 13 years to build a system mixing underground metro with heavy monorail.

As of 2017 there were four metro lines. Line 1 is a conventional subway of 14 kilometres (8.7 mi). Line 2 is a 19-kilometre (12 mi) heavy monorail. Line 3, also a heavy monorail, connects the airport with the southern part of downtown, and Line 6 links Beibei, a district in the far north, with the centre. Line 5 opened in late 2017. The plan called for six lines and one loop line by 2020, adding 363.5 kilometres (225.9 mi) to the 2012 network and 93 new stations to the 111 in service in 2012, with 18 lines by 2050.

No other Chinese city has retained public aerial tramways as Chongqing has. Of the three it once had (Yangtze River, Jialing River and South Mountain), only the Yangtze River Tramway still runs, now a Class 4A tourist attraction. It is 1,160 metres (3,810 ft) long, joins the south and north banks of the Yangtze and carries about 10,000 passengers a day.
Major stations include these.

Chongqing railway station (Yuzhong): the oldest, near the Jiefangbei CBD, reached via Metro Lines 1 and 3 at Lianglukou. It mainly serves long-distance trains. A big renovation is planned, so many services have moved to Chongqing North.
Chongqing North: completed in 2006 and linked to the metro, with numerous long-distance and high-speed trains running to destinations such as Chengdu and Beijing.
Chongqing West (Shapingba): completed in 2018, with long-distance and high-speed services to many cities.

Shapingba railway station: close to the Shapingba CBD. Passengers reach it from Shapingba metro station (Lines 1 and 9 and the Loop line); local and regional trains stop here, and it was finished in 2018.
Chongqing East: opened in 2025.

Chongqing is also a major rail freight destination. Subsidies and incentives have led many factories to relocate and build in the city, producing a big rise in rail traffic. It is a regional hub, and the lines out of it go to:
Chengdu, Sichuan (Chengdu-Chongqing railway)
Guiyang, Guizhou (Sichuan-Guizhou railway)
Hubei (Xiangyang-Chongqing and Chongqing-Lichuan railways)
Hunan (Chongqing-Huaihua railway)
Sichuan (Suining-Chongqing railway)
Gansu (Lanzhou-Chongqing railway)

For radio, the leading station is the Chongqing People's Broadcast Station. Television is run by Chongqing TV, the only municipal-level network and said to be fourth largest in China; its many local channels can be watched on sets across the country.

CQJTU is a municipal university with a transport engineering heritage, two campuses and international partnerships. Chongqing offers a lively, hilly city with fog, humid summers and great rail, metro and river links, so allow time to get used to the weather and the steep terrain.
Pack for heat and damp. Urban highs reach 34 °C in July and August, humidity stays above 75% in every month, and sunshine totals only 983 hours a year.
Expect fog in spring and autumn: more than 100 days of fog a year earn the city its "Fog City" nickname.
Learn the metro and monorail network, which was expanding quickly; Line 3 connects the airport, and Chongqing North and West stations handle high-speed trains.
Remember that many first- and second-year classes are at the Science City Campus in Jiangjin, whereas third- and fourth-year undergraduates and postgraduates are mainly at Nan'an.
Check the university's own English pages for the current intake of international students, since overseas recruitment only began in 2004.
Chongqing Jiaotong University lists 45 programs for international students on this site: 19 bachelor, 20 master's, 5 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 25 taught in Chinese, 18 taught in English, 2 taught in Chinese and English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 15,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.

39 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (15):
Bridge and Tunnel Engineering
Business Administration
Civil Engineering
Computer Science and Technology
Hydraulic Engineering
Landscape Architecture Studies (Engineering)
Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering
Mechanical Design, Manufacturing and Automation
Mechanical Engineering
Naval Architecture and Ocean Engineering
Network and New Media
Road and Railway Engineering
Transportation Engineering
Transportation Planning and Management
Water Resources and Hydropower Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

chongqing-jiaotong-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Chongqing Jiaotong University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chongqing, register at Chongqing Jiaotong University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Chongqing Medical University (CQMU; Chinese: 重庆医科大学), previously referred to as the Chongqing University of Medical Sciences (CQUMS), was established in 1956 in Chongqing, China. It was originally a branch of the Shanghai First Medical College (now named the Shanghai Medical College of Fudan University).

CQMU is a state key university under the administration of the Chongqing Municipal Government with an integrated educational system of baccalaureate, masters, doctoral, and postdoctoral programs in medicine as well as other health-related fields.

It is one of approximately 30 medical universities in China that are approved by the Chinese Ministry of Education to enroll foreign students into the English-medium MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery) program. It is recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the ECFMG (Educational Committee for Foreign Medical Graduates) in the United States.

Chongqing Medical University currently has 15 affiliated hospitals under its administration. Together, these hospitals provide more than 20,800 beds, accommodate approximately 15.46 million outpatient visits, and manage nearly 660,000 inpatient discharges annually.

Chongqing Medical University comprises 22 schools and departments, offering 36 undergraduate programs. It has been designated with 19 national-level first-class undergraduate program development sites and 28 first-class sites at the Chongqing municipal level. Academic programs such as clinical medicine, stomatology, nursing, traditional Chinese medicine, pediatrics, psychiatry, anesthesiology, medical imaging, pharmacy, and clinical pharmacy have received accreditation from the Ministry of Education.

On the research front, CQMU has three state key laboratories under the Ministry of Education, one state key laboratory under the Chongqing Ministry of Science and Technology, one national engineering research center, 18 municipal key laboratories, 11 research institutes, six research centers, and 22 research laboratories. Since 2020, the university has added more than 4,500 new research projects funded at various levels by the Ministry of Science and Technology and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), taken the lead in 54 national key projects, and published over 10,000 SCI-indexed papers, with an average annual growth rate of 10%. It has also received 38 new scientific and technological awards at the provincial and ministerial levels.

Chongqing Medical University currently has 2,497 full-time faculty members, including 1,690 professionals holding senior academic titles. Among the faculty are 432 doctoral supervisors and 1,598 master's supervisors.

CQMU has a total enrollment of 27,724 full-time students, including 1,601 doctoral candidates, 7,249 master's students, 18,044 undergraduates, and 331 junior college students enrolled under minority support programs. The university also hosts 499 international students.
CQMU offers five postdoctoral programs, 26 doctoral programs, 53 masters programs, and 46 specialities for undergraduates. It has four state key disciplines and 43 municipal key disciplines.

CQMU has accomplished several large-scale research projects including some state-level projects supported by the National Key Technology Research and Development Program in the 6th to 9th Five-year Plan for National Economic and Social Development, Key Program of National Natural Science Foundation, National Basic Research Program (known as '973 Program'), and the National Hi-Tech Research and Development Program (known as '863 Program').

The High-intensity Focused Ultrasonic Therapy System (HIFU), which was initiated by CQMU, is the first large-scale medical equipment system with completely independent intellectual property rights in China. It has been put into use in over 30 major hospitals in China and exported to about ten foreign countries, such as the EU, Russia, Japan, Korea, and Singapore.
The university publishes eight academic journals with international distribution.

Since 2008, CQMU has twice won the National Prize for Progress in Science and Technology, once won the National Award for Technological Invention once, and won over 80 municipal awards. There are many international students from India, Indonesia, Republic of the Congo, Mauritius, Vietnam, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, etc.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Chongqing, where Chongqing Medical University is located.

Chongqing is located in the subtropics, situated in the transitional area between the Sichuan Basin and the plain on the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze. Its climate features frequent monsoon conditions, often raining at night in late spring and early summer. The city's "night rain in the Ba Mountains" features in poems throughout Chinese history, including "Written on a Rainy Night—A Letter to the North" by Li Shangyin. Its territory is 470 kilometers (290 mi) from east to west at its longest, and 450 kilometers (280 mi) from north to south at its widest. It borders Hubei and Hunan to the east, Sichuan and Shaanxi to the north, and Guizhou to the south.

Chongqing covers a large area crisscrossed by rivers and mountains. The Daba Mountains stand in the north, the Wu Gorge in the east, the Wuling Mountains in the southeast, and the Dalou Mountains in the south. The area slopes downward from north to south towards the Yangtze valley, and features a large massif of mountains and hills, with steep sloping areas at different heights. Karst landscape is common in this area, and stone forests, numerous collections of peaks, limestone caves and valleys can be found in many places. The Longshuixia Gap (Chinese: 龙水峡地缝), with its Three Natural Bridges, has made the region a popular tourist attraction. The Yangtze River runs through the whole area from west to east, covering a course of 665 kilometers (413 mi), cutting through the Wu Mountains at three places and forming the well-known Three Gorges: the Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling gorges. Coming from northwest and running through "the Jialing Lesser Three Gorges" of Libi, Wentang and Guanyin, the Jialing River joins the Yangtze in Chongqing.

The central urban area of Chongqing, called Chongqing proper, is built on mountains and partially surrounded by the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. With its special topography, Chongqing's topography includes mountains, rivers, forests, springs, waterfalls, gorges, and caves. The Tang dynasty poet Li Bai was inspired by the natural scenery and wrote this epigram.

The Zhongliang (中梁山) and Tongluo (铜锣山) mountains roughly form the eastern and western boundaries of Chongqing's urban area. Several high mountains are situated outside central Chongqing, including the 1,709.4-meter (5,608 ft)-high Wugong Ling Mountain in Jiangjin.

Chongqing has a monsoonal humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa), bordering on an ordinary humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) and for most of the year experiences very high relative humidity, with all months above 75%. Known as one of the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze River, along with Wuhan and Nanjing, its summers are long and among the hottest and most humid in China, with highs of 34 °C (93 °F) in July and August in the urban area. Winters are short and somewhat mild, but damp and overcast. The city's location in the Sichuan Basin causes it to have one of the lowest annual sunshine totals nationally, at only 983 hours, lower than much of Northern Europe; the monthly percent possible sunshine in the city proper ranges from a mere 5% in January to 43% in August. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −1.8 °C (29 °F) on 11 January 1955 to 43.7 °C (111 °F) on 18 and 19 August 2022

Chongqing, with over 100 days of fog per year, is known as the "Fog City" (Chinese: 雾都); this is because in the spring and fall, a thick layer of fog enshrouds it for 68 days per year. During the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), this special weather possibly played a role in protecting the city from being overrun by the Imperial Japanese Army.

According to the 2020 national census, Chongqing has a population of 32,054,159, accounting for around 2.27% of the national total. This makes it the most populous city proper in the world. As of 2010, the metropolitan area encompassing the central urban area was estimated by the OECD to have, a population of 17 million.

In 2020, Chongqing surpassed Shanghai as China's largest municipality by urban population. As of 2021, 70.4% of Chongqing's population is estimated to be urban, and 29.6% rural. As of 2024, Chongqing had an urban population of 23.01 million.

The Census also lists the male percentage as 50.55% and the female percentage as 49.55%. In terms of age distribution, of the total population, 15.91% were age 0–14, 62.22% were 15–64, and 21.87% were 65 and over. Of the population's highest education level achieved, 15.41% were college, 15.96% were high school, 30.58% were middle school, and 29.89% were elementary school.

The predominant religions in Chongqing are Chinese folk religions, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism. According to surveys conducted in 2007 and 2009, 26.63% of the population practices Chinese ancestral religion, while 1.05% of the population identifies as Christian.

The reports did not give figures for other types of religion; 72.32% of the population may be either irreligious or involved in worship of nature deities, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, or folk religious sects.
In 2010, there were 9,056 Muslims in Chongqing.
Chongqing was a major recipient of China's investment in industrial capacity during the Third Front campaign.

There has been a massive government push to transform Chongqing into the region's economic, trade, and financial center and use the municipality as a platform to open up the country's western interior to further development. Chongqing is facing rapid urbanization. For instance, statistics suggest that new construction added approximately 137,000 square meters (1,470,000 sq ft) daily of usable floor space to satisfy demands for residential, commercial and factory space. Thus, Chongqing was separated from Sichuan province and made into a municipality in its own right on 14 March 1997 in order to accelerate its development and subsequently China's relatively poorer western areas (see China Western Development strategy). By the 2000s the city had become an important industrial area in western China.

As of 2022, Chongqing's nominal GDP was US$433 billion (CN¥ 2.91 trilion), about 2.41% of the country's GDP and ranked 16th among province-level administrative units; the municipality's primary, secondary and tertiary industries were worth CN¥201.21 billion (US$29.92 billion), CN¥1.169 trillion (US$173.86 billion) and CN¥1.542 trillion (US$229.3 billion) respectively. Its nominal GDP per capita was US$13,479 (CN¥90,663) and ranked 10th in the country.

Chongqing has been identified by the Economist Intelligence Unit in the November 2010 Access China White Paper as a member of the CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), an economic profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China.

Traditionally, due to its geographic inaccessibility, Chongqing and Sichuan have both been important military bases in weapons research and development. Even though Chongqing's industries are diversified, unlike eastern China, its export sector is small due to its relatively disadvantageous inland location. Instead, factories producing local-oriented consumer goods such as processed food, cars, chemicals, textiles, machinery, sports equipment and electronics are common.

Chongqing is China's third largest motor vehicle production center and the largest for motorcycles. In 2007, it had an annual output capacity of 1 million cars and 8.6 million motorcycles. Leading makers of cars and motorbikes includes China's fourth biggest automaker; Changan Automotive Corp and Lifan Hongda Enterprise, as well as Ford Motor Company, with the US car giant having 3 plants in Chongqing. The municipality is also one of China's nine largest iron and steel producers in China as well as one of its three major aluminum producers. Important manufacturers include Chongqing Iron and Steel Company (重庆钢铁股份有限公司) and Southwest Aluminum (西南鋁業), which is Asia's largest aluminum plant.
Agriculture remains significant. Rice and fruits, especially oranges, are the area's main produce.

Natural resources are also abundant with large deposits of coal, natural gas, and more than 40 kinds of minerals such as strontium and manganese. Coal reserves total approximately 4,800,000,000 metric tons (4.7×109 long tons; 5.3×109 short tons). Chuandong Natural Gas Field is China's largest inland gas field with deposits of around 270 billion m3 – more than 1/5 of China's total. Has China's largest reserve of strontium (China has the world's 2nd biggest strontium deposit). Manganese is mined in the Xiushan area. Although the mining sector has been denounced as heavily polluting and unsafe. Chongqing is also planned to be the site of a 10 million ton capacity refinery operated by CNPC (parent company of PetroChina) to process imported crude oil from the Sino-Myanmar pipelines. The pipeline itself, though not yet finished, will eventually run from Sittwe (in Myanmar's western coast) through Kunming in Yunnan before reaching Chongqing and it will provide China with fuels sourced from Myanmar, the Middle East and Africa. Recently, there has been a drive to move up the value chain by shifting towards high technology and knowledge intensive industries resulting in new development zones such as the Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ). Chongqing's local government is hoping through the promotion of favorable economic policies for the electronics and information technology sectors, that it can create a 400 billion RMB high technology manufacturing hub which will surpass its car industry and account for 25% of its exports.

The city has also invested heavily in infrastructure to attract investment. The network of roads and railways connecting Chongqing to the rest of China has been expanded and upgraded reducing logistical costs. Furthermore, the nearby Three Gorges Dam, which is the world's largest, supplies Chongqing with power and allows oceangoing ships to reach Chongqing's Yangtze River port. These infrastructure improvements have led to the arrivals of numerous foreign direct investors (FDI) in industries ranging from car to finance and retailing; such as Ford, Mazda, HSBC, Standard Chartered Bank, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, ANZ Bank, Scotiabank, Wal-Mart, Metro AG and Carrefour, among other multinational corporations.
The city includes a number of economic and technological development zones:
Chongqing Chemical Industrial Park
Chongqing Economic & Technological Development Zone
Chongqing Hi-Tech Industry Development Zone
Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ)
Chongqing Export Processing Zone
Jianqiao Industrial Park (located in Dadukou District)
Liangjiang New Area
Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center (the largest of its kind in China)
Chongqing itself is part of the West Triangle Economic Zone, along with Chengdu and Xi'an.

Since its elevation to national-level municipality in 1997, the city has dramatically expanded its infrastructure. With the construction of railways and expressways to the east and southeast, Chongqing is a major transportation hub in southwestern China.

As of October 2014, the municipality had 31 bridges across the Yangtze River including over a dozen in the city's urban core. Aside from the city's first two Yangtze River bridges, which were built, respectively, in 1960 and 1977, all of the other bridges were completed since 1995.
Public transport in Chongqing consists of metro, intercity railway, a ubiquitous bus system and the world's largest monorail network.

According to the Chongqing Municipal Government's ambitious plan in May 2007, Chongqing is investing 150 billion RMB over 13 years to finish a system that combines underground metro lines with heavy monorail.

As of 2017, four metro lines, the 14-kilometer (8.7 mi) long CRT Line 1, a conventional subway, and the 19-kilometer (12 mi) long heavy monorail CRT Line 2 (through Phase II), Line 3, a heavy monorail connects the airport and the southern part of downtown. Line 6, runs between Beibei, a district in the city's far north to downtown. Line 5 opened in late 2017.

It was planned that by 2020, CRT would consist of 6 lines and 1 loop line, adding 363.5 kilometers (225.9 mi) of road and railway to the 2012 transportation infrastructure, and 93 new metro stations would be added to the 111 stations in place in 2012. By 2050 Chongqing would have 18 lines.

Chongqing is the only Chinese city that has kept public aerial tramways. There were three aerial tramways in Chongqing: the Yangtze River Tramway, the Jialing River Tramway and the South Mountain Tramway, of which the Yangtze River Tramway is the only one still operating, now considered a Class 4A tourist attraction. The 1,160-meter (3,810 ft)-long tramway connects the southern and northern banks of the Yangtze River, carrying about 10,000 passengers a day.

The station handles mostly long-distance trains. There are plans for a major renovation and overhaul of this station, thus many services have been transferred to Chongqing North railway station.

chongqing-normal-university.h: Chongqing Normal University at a glance

blocks.x: Chongqing Normal University (重庆师范大学) is one of the leading public research universities in the municipality of Chongqing. Its roots are in East Sichuan Normal School, and it counts as a top university in Chongqing. Seventeen academic faculties offer a wide choice of undergraduate and graduate programmes.

Teaching takes place on three main sites. One is the University City Campus in the Chongqing High-tech Development Zone (Huxi Street). Another is in Beibei District, along Beiquan Road, and the third is in Shapingba District, on Tianchen Road. Check which of them hosts your chosen programme before you arrange accommodation.

Foreign applicants are accepted, as the Ministry of Education has given the university permission to enrol international students. It has a record in Chinese-language teaching too: the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office counted it among the first Chinese-language education centres, and in 2007 the Confucius Institute awarded it a title reserved for a few institutions that promote the language abroad, the National Teaching Base for International Promotion of Chinese.

Politics is a particular strength. The faculty, led by the university's own president, Meng Dongfang, is viewed as one of the foremost political research bodies in the country. It runs three teaching and research platforms: a centre for ideological and political education that belongs to the Ministry of Education, a Chongqing research centre on civic morality and social construction, and a Chongqing centre for theoretical work on socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The institution's story goes back to 1906, when an official school called East Sichuan Normal School was founded. Its first principal was Deng Ken, younger brother of Deng Xiaoping, who later became Vice Mayor of Chongqing and Vice Governor of Hubei. Guo Moruo, who headed the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 1960, wrote out the school's name in his own hand that year. The title Chongqing Normal University became official in 2003. (One of the university's descriptions gives 1954 as the founding year, and another gives 1906. The 1954 date is when the modern institution began under the East Sichuan Normal School name, so if the exact date matters, ask the university.)

The university library began in 1954 and has become a large, comprehensive library for study and research. It works over three campuses with 46,251 square metres of space and 4,529 reading seats. At the end of 2021 its holdings included over 2.73 million printed books, about 1.64 million e-books and more than 900,000 electronic journals, together with access to over 59 databases. A different university description calls this the biggest academic library system in Chongqing, with around 20.4 million items, including 79 e-book databases and about 2.69 million physical items. Since the two accounts count differently, regard all of the numbers as approximate.

A museum was started in 1984 on the Huxi Campus and moved in 2014 to a new building in University Town, with roughly 3,000 square metres of exhibition space. It supports humanities teaching and research by collecting and studying cultural objects, and it has developed its own academic tradition and style of collecting. The displays follow six major themes, such as Three Gorges civilisation, folk culture and archaeological science, and the objects on view include historical relics, Han dynasty pictorial bricks, calligraphy and paintings. Visitors have come from institutions in China and abroad, as well as students and the general public, and the museum is an important cultural venue for University Town and the neighbourhood.
Two graduates are named in the university's profile:
Feng "Franklin" Tao, a chemical engineer born in China who works in the United States
Yin Jiaxu, a former chairman of the defence manufacturer Norinco

chongqing-normal-university.h: Chongqing: the city and its setting

blocks.x: The sections that follow introduce the city where you will study: its geography, weather, people, economy and transport. Chongqing is very hilly, damp and busy, and it is worth knowing in advance that it feels very different from the flat, drier cities of northern China.

Chongqing is a subtropical city where the Sichuan Basin gives way to the plains of the middle and lower Yangtze. The monsoon is a frequent presence, and late spring and early summer often bring rain at night. This "night rain in the Ba Mountains" appears in Chinese poetry through the ages, for example in Li Shangyin's "Written on a Rainy Night - A Letter to the North". At its longest the municipality stretches 470 kilometres (290 mi) from east to west, and at its widest 450 kilometres (280 mi) from north to south. Its neighbours are Hubei and Hunan in the east, Sichuan and Shaanxi in the north, and Guizhou in the south.

Rivers and mountains cross the municipality in every direction. Four ranges frame it: the Daba in the north, the Wuling in the south-east and the Dalou in the south, with the Wu Gorge at the eastern edge. The ground falls from north to south toward the Yangtze valley, in a big mass of hills and mountains whose steep slopes lie at varied heights. Karst features are common: stone forests, clusters of peaks, limestone caves and valleys appear in many places. The Longshuixia Gap (龙水峡地缝), with its Three Natural Bridges, is a popular attraction.

The Yangtze crosses the entire area from west to east over 665 kilometres (413 mi) and cuts through the Wu Mountains in three places, forming the famous Three Gorges: Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling. From the north-west, the Jialing River flows through its own "Lesser Three Gorges" (Libi, Wentang and Guanyin) before meeting the Yangtze at Chongqing.

The urban core, known as Chongqing proper, climbs over hills and is partly wrapped by the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. Its scenery, from forests and springs to waterfalls, gorges and caves, inspired the Tang poet Li Bai to write an epigram. Two ridges, Zhongliang (中梁山) and Tongluo (铜锣山), roughly mark the western and eastern boundaries of the built-up area. A number of higher peaks lie outside the centre, such as Wugong Ling Mountain in Jiangjin, at 1,709.4 metres (5,608 ft).

Chongqing's climate is monsoonal humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa), close to ordinary humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Relative humidity is very high through most of the year, above 75% in every month. Together with Wuhan and Nanjing, the city has earned the label "Three Furnaces" along the Yangtze. Its long summers are among the most oppressive in China, as downtown highs reach 34 °C (93 °F) in July and August. Winters, by contrast, are brief, fairly mild, damp and grey.

Because it sits in the Sichuan Basin, Chongqing gets one of the lowest amounts of sunshine in the country: just 983 hours a year, less than much of Northern Europe. In the city proper, the share of possible sunshine is as low as 5% in January and rises to 43% by August. The coldest day since 1951 was 11 January 1955 (-1.8 °C or 29 °F) and the hottest was 18 and 19 August 2022 (43.7 °C or 111 °F).

Fog is also part of the character of the city. Chongqing has over 100 foggy days a year and is nicknamed the "Fog City" (雾都); in spring and autumn a thick layer covers it for 68 days a year. This unusual weather may have helped protect the city from the Imperial Japanese Army during the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945).

Chongqing's population was 32,054,159 in the 2020 national census, about 2.27% of China's total, a total that makes it the world's biggest city proper by population. The OECD estimated in 2010 that the metropolitan area around the central urban districts had 17 million people.

The year 2020 saw Chongqing pass Shanghai in urban population, becoming the largest municipality in China on that measure. About 70.4% of its people lived in towns and cities in 2021 (29.6% in the countryside), and in 2024 the urban total stood at 23.01 million.

The census gives the male share as 50.55% and the female share as 49.55% (these figures add up to slightly more than 100%, so treat them as approximate). By age, 15.91% were 0 to 14, 62.22% were 15 to 64 and 21.87% were 65 or older. For highest education reached, 15.41% had college, 15.96% high school, 30.58% middle school and 29.89% elementary school.

Chinese folk religion, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism are the leading faiths. Surveys carried out in 2007 and 2009 found that 26.63% of people follow Chinese ancestral religion and 1.05% identify as Christian. No figures were reported for other religions, so the remaining 72.32% could be non-religious or could worship nature deities or practise Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or folk sects. There were 9,056 Muslims in 2010.

During the Third Front campaign, Chongqing was a major recipient of national investment in industrial capacity. Today, the government is pushing hard to make Chongqing the economic, trade and financial centre of its region and a platform for opening the western interior to more development. Urbanisation is fast: statistics suggest that new construction adds about 137,000 square metres (1,470,000 sq ft) of usable floor space each day, to meet demand for homes, business premises and factories.

Administration was part of the plan. Chongqing was cut away from Sichuan province on 14 March 1997 and made a municipality in its own right, so that it could develop faster and pull the poorer west of China along with it, under the China Western Development strategy. The 2000s saw it become a key industrial area of western China.

The 2022 economic output measured US$433 billion nominal (CN¥2.91 trillion), which was about 2.41% of China's GDP and the 16th highest among provincial-level units. Farming and related primary industry produced CN¥201.21 billion (US$29.92 billion), secondary industry CN¥1.169 trillion (US$173.86 billion) and services CN¥1.542 trillion (US$229.3 billion). Per person, nominal GDP reached US$13,479 (CN¥90,663), tenth in the country. A group of cities called CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang) was highlighted in the Economist Intelligence Unit's Access China White Paper of November 2010, as part of a profile of the 20 leading emerging cities.

Because of the difficult geography, Chongqing and Sichuan have long served as military bases for weapons research and development. Industry here is varied, yet exports remain limited because the city lies inland, unlike the east coast. The typical factory makes things for local buyers: cars, chemicals, textiles, machinery, electronics, sports gear and processed food.

For vehicles, Chongqing ranks third in China, and for motorcycles it ranks first. Its 2007 capacity was 1 million cars and 8.6 million motorcycles a year. The biggest names are Changan Automotive Corp (China's fourth-largest carmaker), Lifan Hongda Enterprise and Ford, whose American parent runs 3 plants in the city. Metal is another strength: the municipality is among the nine biggest iron and steel producers in the country and one of three leading aluminium centres. Two important companies are Chongqing Iron and Steel (重庆钢铁股份有限公司) and Southwest Aluminum (西南鋁業), which operates the biggest aluminium plant in Asia. Farming remains important too, with rice and fruit, especially oranges, as the chief crops.

The ground holds a great deal: coal and natural gas in quantity, plus over 40 kinds of minerals including strontium and manganese. Coal reserves are about 4,800,000,000 metric tons, and the Chuandong Natural Gas Field, with around 270 billion m3, is the biggest inland gas field in the country and holds over one fifth of its gas. Strontium deposits in China are the world's second largest, and the country's largest reserve is in Chongqing; manganese comes from the Xiushan area. Critics, though, have called mining heavily polluting and unsafe.

CNPC, the parent of PetroChina, is also expected to build a 10 million ton refinery in the city for crude imported through the Sino-Myanmar pipelines. Those pipelines were unfinished at the time of writing; the finished route will start at Sittwe on the Myanmar coast and pass Kunming in Yunnan on its way to Chongqing, delivering fuel sourced in Myanmar, Africa and the Middle East.

Recently the emphasis has moved towards higher-value work in high technology and knowledge-intensive sectors, which has led to new zones, one being the Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ). Local officials hope that favourable policies for electronics and IT can build a high-tech manufacturing base worth 400 billion RMB, bigger than the car industry, and making up a quarter (25%) of exports.

To attract investment, the city has also spent heavily on infrastructure. Roads and railways linking Chongqing with the rest of China have been expanded and upgraded, lowering logistics costs. The Three Gorges Dam nearby, the biggest in the world, provides electricity and makes the Yangtze river port reachable by oceangoing ships. As a result, foreign companies in fields from motoring to banking and shopping have arrived, among them Ford, Mazda, Carrefour, Wal-Mart, Metro AG and banks such as HSBC, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, Standard Chartered, ANZ and Scotiabank.
Chongqing, together with Chengdu and Xi'an, forms the West Triangle Economic Zone. Inside the city a number of development areas exist:
Chongqing Chemical Industrial Park, for chemicals
Chongqing Economic & Technological Development Zone
Chongqing Hi-Tech Industry Development Zone
Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ)
Chongqing Export Processing Zone, for export goods
Jianqiao Industrial Park, in Dadukou District
Liangjiang New Area
Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center, which is China's biggest cloud computing centre

Since it was made a national-level municipality in 1997, Chongqing has expanded its infrastructure dramatically. With railways and expressways built to the east and south-east, it is now a major transport hub in south-western China.

By October 2014, 31 bridges crossed the Yangtze within the municipality, and over a dozen of those were in the urban core. The first two were built in 1960 and 1977, and all the rest date from 1995 or later.

Chongqing's public transport includes a metro, intercity railway, a ubiquitous bus system and the world's biggest monorail network. A plan the municipal government announced in May 2007 committed 150 billion RMB over 13 years to finish a combined network of underground metro lines and heavy monorail.

As of 2017 there were four metro lines. CRT Line 1 is a conventional subway of 14 kilometres (8.7 mi), and Line 2 is a heavy monorail of 19 kilometres (12 mi) through its second phase. Line 3 is another heavy monorail connecting the airport with the south of downtown, and Line 6 runs from Beibei, a district in the far north, to downtown. A fifth line opened in late 2017.

The plan was for CRT to have 6 lines and one loop line by 2020, adding 363.5 kilometres (225.9 mi) to the 2012 network and 93 new stations to the 111 that existed in 2012. By 2050 the aim is 18 lines.

No other Chinese city has retained public aerial tramways, but Chongqing has. It once had three: over the Yangtze, over the Jialing and the South Mountain Tramway. Only the Yangtze River Tramway still runs, and it is now a Class 4A tourist attraction. It is 1,160 metres (3,810 ft) long, links the south and north banks of the Yangtze, and carries about 10,000 passengers a day.
Chongqing has several main stations, each with a different job, so check which one your ticket uses before you travel. They are:

Chongqing railway station, in Yuzhong, is the oldest; Lianglukou Metro station (Lines 1 and 3) serves it, and it stands close to the Jiefangbei business district. Long-distance trains are its main traffic, and a large renovation is planned, which is why many services now use Chongqing North.
Chongqing North railway station, finished in 2006 and connected to the metro, deals with numerous long-distance and high-speed trains, including those to Chengdu and Beijing
Chongqing West railway station is in Shapingba, opened in 2018, and takes many long-distance and high-speed trains
Shapingba railway station, also finished in 2018, serves mainly local and regional trains; it lies near the Shapingba CBD, and the metro station on Lines 1 and 9 and the Loop line reaches it
Chongqing East railway station opened in 2025.

Freight is an important role of the railways. Subsidies and incentives have moved many factories to Chongqing, so rail traffic has increased greatly, and handling facilities keep improving. The city is a major regional rail hub with these lines:
Chengdu-Chongqing railway (to Chengdu in Sichuan)
Sichuan-Guizhou railway (to Guiyang in Guizhou)
Xiangyang-Chongqing railway (to Hubei)
Chongqing-Huaihua railway (to Hunan)
Suining-Chongqing railway (to Sichuan)
Chongqing-Lichuan railway (to Hubei)
Lanzhou-Chongqing railway (to Gansu)

The largest radio station is Chongqing People's Broadcast Station. For television, the sole municipal network is Chongqing TV, which says it is the fourth biggest station in the country; many of its channels are made for local audiences, though viewers in many parts of China can tune in.

Chongqing University, abbreviated CQU and written 重庆大学 in Chinese, is a state-run institution located in the mountain city of Chongqing in south-west China. It reports to the national Ministry of Education and has been part of the country's flagship funding schemes: Project 211, Project 985 and the current Double First-Class Construction. It is best known for architecture and for engineering fields such as electrical, civil, mechanical and metallurgical, and also for management science. In the Academic Ranking of World Universities for 2024 it was placed in the 151 to 200 band globally. Rankings move from year to year, so check the latest tables and the university's own website.

CQU was born in 1929. A group of professors who were natives of Chongqing and were then teaching at Chengdu University decided that their home city needed a university of its own. General Liu Xiang supported the project, which led to the creation of a preparatory committee. The first term opened on 12 October, and the committee issued a founding declaration stating that talent and education drive the progress of the country and the world.

In 1937 the national capital, Nanjing, fell to Japanese forces, and the government ordered its agencies to relocate to Chongqing so that resistance could continue. National Central University moved to the city as part of this, and Chongqing University gave it 200 mu of land, which started a close working relationship between the two schools. Many distinguished teachers lectured at both institutions during those years. They included the geologist Li Siguang, the painters and art educators Xu Beihong and Wu Guanzhong, the economist and educator Ma Yinchu, the physicist He Lu and the scholar of literature Lu Zuofu. This partnership strengthened both universities and helped keep Chinese education and culture alive through the war.

By 1942 CQU had grown into a national comprehensive university with six colleges, covering arts, science, engineering, law and medicine. The national reorganisation of higher education in 1952 reshaped it into an engineering-oriented, multi-disciplinary university under the Ministry of Education, and in 1960 it was named among the first group of key national universities. After China's reform and opening-up began, CQU placed greater weight on humanities, business management, the arts and physical education, which sped up its transformation into a fully comprehensive institution.

The university runs 28 schools, plus a graduate school and three further colleges for science and technology (the City College), continuing education and online education. Total enrolment is about 50,000, made up of 30,000 undergraduates and 20,000 master's and doctoral students. Its academic offer is wide: 24 mobile postdoctoral research stations, 133 doctoral programmes, 256 master's programmes, 18 professional master's degrees (including the MBA, EMBA, MPA and master of engineering) and 89 bachelor's programmes in eight broad fields, namely sciences, engineering, the liberal arts, economics, management, law, agriculture and education.

Staff numbers are around 5,400, of whom 2,700 are full-time faculty. Their ranks include 3 academicians of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, 12 more who hold contracts from other institutions, 6 people serving on a subject evaluation panel of the State Council's degree committee, 4 chief scientists of national 973 projects and 4 state-level young experts recognised for outstanding contributions. There are 500 doctoral supervisors and 1,700 full and associate professors. These counts come from a past description of the university and may be out of date.

CQU has four campuses that together cover a little over 3.65 square kilometres (another figure puts the site at 367 hectares, about 910 acres, with 1.60 million square metres of buildings). Green hills surround them and the Jialing River runs alongside, which is why Chongqing municipality awarded the university the title Garden University. In 2001 the CQU Technology Park was established, one of only 22 national-level science parks attached to universities across the country.
The academic structure is grouped into faculties, which is a handy way to see where your subject sits.

The Faculty of Arts and Sciences brings together the humanities, social sciences, languages and basic sciences. Its units include an institute for advanced studies in the humanities and social sciences, the Liberal Arts College, schools of economics and business administration, public affairs, foreign languages, arts, and journalism and communication, plus the Law School and the Meishi Film Academy. On the science side it has the schools of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Bioengineering, Physics, Mathematics and Statistics, Physical Education and Life Sciences.

The Faculty of the Built Environment covers the schools of Architecture and Urban Planning and Civil Engineering, the College of Environmental and Ecology and a school for construction management and real estate.

The Faculty of Engineering includes Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Power and Energy Engineering, Material Science and Engineering, Resources and Environmental Science, and Aerospace Engineering. It also hosts the Joint Cooperative Institute (JCI) run with the University of Cincinnati.
The Faculty of Information Science and Technology contains the schools of Computer Science, Automation, Communication Engineering, Opto-Electronic Engineering and Software Engineering.

Beyond the faculties are the International School, which is also called the College of International Education, along with the City College, continuing education and a college delivering networked learning. International applicants should start by asking the International School about teaching languages and application routes.

CQU lists 17 national key subjects, 14 key subjects under the 211 Project and 38 provincial or ministerial key subjects. It has created 14 specially appointed professorships under the Yangtze River Scholar programme and holds three national teaching bases for fundamental courses, plus a national base for quality education of college students. In research infrastructure it counts nine national and ministerial key laboratories, 71 provincial key labs and 130 laboratories in different specialities. For teaching it has built a distance-education centre, large multimedia classrooms and interactive audio-visual classrooms, and it runs labs and training centres with global firms such as Siemens, Microsoft, IBM, Rockwell and Omron. The university also operates a national key publishing house, a first-class architectural design institute and a first-class planning and design institute.

In recent years the university has carried out more than 100 national key science projects. Its trophy cabinet includes 13 national invention awards, 40 scientific and technological advancement awards, 4 natural science awards, 968 ministerial and provincial prizes and 283 prizes for teaching achievement.
The main research bases fall into several groups:

National-level engineering centres and laboratories: mechanical transmission; the safety and new technology of power transmission and distribution equipment; a technology centre for magnesium alloys; micro-nano devices and systems; and an international centre for micro-nano systems and new materials.

Ministry of Education key laboratories: opto-electronic technology and systems; resource exploitation and disaster control in south-west China; the eco-environment of the Three Gorges Reservoir region; and a supervision and testing centre for transgenic biological products. Two more, on upland urban construction and on industrial CT non-destructive testing, were listed as under construction.
Discipline innovation bases under the 111 Project: biomechanics and tissue-repair engineering, and power transformation and transmission equipment safety.

Provincial key laboratories: manufacturing systems, high-voltage technology, biomedical engineering, metallurgy, new electrical engineering technologies, software engineering, automation, thermal engineering, rock and soil engineering, building environment and installation, remote sensing information transmission, new building materials, pollution prevention and waste recycling in construction, municipal and environmental engineering, and mineral resource exploitation and disasters in the Three Gorges region.

The library has 3.90 million printed volumes and subscribes to about 6000 titles of Chinese and foreign periodicals, with a further 2.0 million electronic books. Five digital reading rooms offer 65,000 e-books and journals, and the building also hosts the Chongqing hub of CERNET, China's national education and research network.
International links are part of the university's profile, so it is worth asking about them early.

Partners are found in the USA, the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Japan, South Korea, Russia and other places. If you want to study abroad as part of your degree, or join a joint programme, this network gives you options to ask about.

chongqing-university.h: Chongqing: the city around your campus

blocks.x: A student here will spend as much time getting to know Chongqing as sitting in lectures, so this part explains the geography, the weather, the people and the economy.

chongqing-university.h: Mountains, rivers and the lay of the land

blocks.x: Chongqing is a subtropical city set in the transition zone between the Sichuan Basin and the lowlands along the middle and lower Yangtze. Rain tends to fall after dark from late spring into early summer, and the Tang poet Li Shangyin turned the night rain over the Ba Mountains into a famous literary image in his poem to a friend in the north. The municipality stretches roughly 470 kilometres (290 miles) east to west and about 450 kilometres (280 miles) north to south at its widest. Neighbours are Hubei and Hunan in the east, Sichuan and Shaanxi in the north and Guizhou in the south.

It is a vast territory of rivers and mountains: with the Daba Mountains to the north, Wu Gorge at the eastern end, the Wuling range in the south-east and the Dalou range in the south. The ground tilts from north to south down to the Yangtze valley, with a large mass of mountains and hills in steep steps. Karst scenery is widespread, with stone forests, clusters of peaks, limestone caves and valleys in many places, and the Longshuixia Gap, with its Three Natural Bridges, has become a popular tourist stop. The Yangtze crosses the territory from west to east over 665 kilometres (413 miles), slicing through the Wu range three times to form the celebrated Three Gorges, which are Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling. The Jialing River approaches from the north-west, passing its own smaller gorge trio (Libi, Wentang and Guanyin) before it meets the Yangtze in the city.

The urban core, known as Chongqing proper, rises over hills and is partly enclosed by the two rivers, where mountains, woodland, springs, waterfalls, gorges and caves all sit close together. The poet Li Bai, of the Tang dynasty, found inspiration in this scenery. The Zhongliang and Tongluo mountains roughly mark the western and eastern edges of the urban area, and higher peaks lie outside it, including Wugong Ling in Jiangjin at 1,709.4 metres (5,608 feet).

The climate is monsoonal and humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa, close to Cfa), with relative humidity staying above 75% in every month. It is counted among the three Furnaces of the Yangtze, alongside Wuhan and Nanjing. Summers are long and rank with the hottest and muggiest in China; July and August afternoons in the city reach about 34 °C (93 °F). Winters are brief and fairly mild, but damp and grey. Because the city lies inside the Sichuan Basin, it gets only about 983 hours of sunshine a year, one of the lowest totals in the country and fewer than much of northern Europe; in the city proper the possible-sunshine share climbs from a mere 5% in January to 43% in August. Over the years from 1951, the coldest reading was −1.8 °C (29 °F) on 11 January 1955 and the hottest 43.7 °C (111 °F), seen on 18 and 19 August 2022.

Chongqing is called the Fog City (雾都). Figures for the amount of fog vary: one gives over 100 foggy days a year and another says that thick fog covers the city for 68 days in spring and autumn, so use them as a rough guide. During the Second Sino-Japanese War of 1937 to 1945, the weather is thought to have helped protect the city from capture by the Imperial Japanese Army.

The 2020 national census counted 32,054,159 residents, about 2.27% of China's population, a total that makes Chongqing the largest city proper on the planet by headcount. The OECD estimated in 2010 that the metropolitan area around the central urban districts held about 17 million people. Also in 2020 it overtook Shanghai in urban population among China's municipalities. In 2021 an estimated 70.4% of residents lived in urban areas and 29.6% in rural ones, and by 2024 the urban population had reached 23.01 million.

On age, the census put 15.91% of the population at 0 to 14, 62.22% at 15 to 64 and 21.87% at 65 and over. For highest education level, 15.41% had been to college, 15.96% to high school, 30.58% to middle school and 29.89% to elementary school.

The main belief traditions are Chinese folk religion, Taoism and Chinese Buddhism. Surveys in 2007 and 2009 found that 26.63% practise Chinese ancestral religion and 1.05% are Christian. The remaining 72.32% may be non-religious or involved in nature-deity worship, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or folk sects. There were 9,056 Muslims in 2010.
The job market and industries around the campus shape internships and graduate opportunities, so it helps to know what Chongqing produces and where it is heading.

chongqing-university.h: How Chongqing became an industrial centre

blocks.x: During the Third Front campaign, Chongqing received heavy national investment in industrial capacity. Government policy has pushed the city to become the economic, trade and financial hub of the region and a launch pad for developing the interior of western China. Urbanisation is fast: statistics suggest new construction adds roughly 137,000 square metres (1,470,000 square feet) of usable floor space daily for housing, shops and factories. The aim was to accelerate its growth, and with it the poorer western parts of the country under the China Western Development strategy, so on 14 March 1997 the city was detached from Sichuan province and made a municipality in its own right. By the 2000s it had become a significant industrial area in the west.

In 2022 the nominal GDP was US$433 billion (about CN¥2.91 trillion), roughly 2.41% of the national total, ranking 16th among province-level units. By sector, agriculture and similar primary activity produced CN¥201.21 billion (US$29.92 billion), industry CN¥1.169 trillion (US$173.86 billion) and services CN¥1.542 trillion (US$229.3 billion). Output per person was US$13,479 (CN¥90,663), the 10th highest nationally. In its November 2010 Access China White Paper, the Economist Intelligence Unit named Chongqing as a member of a group labelled CHAMPS, made up of Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang, within a ranking of the 20 leading emerging cities in China.

Thanks to its hard-to-reach position, Chongqing and Sichuan have long been important bases for weapons research and development. Industry is diversified, but unlike the east coast the export sector is small because the city is inland. Factories mostly produce for the domestic market, turning out cars, electronics, chemicals, textiles, machinery, sports gear and processed food.

Chongqing is the number three centre of vehicle production in China and number one for motorcycles; capacity in 2007 reached 1 million cars and 8.6 million motorcycles a year. Leading producers include Changan Automotive (China's fourth-biggest carmaker), Lifan Hongda Enterprise and Ford Motor Company, which had 3 plants there. Iron and steel are also big business, since the municipality is among the nine biggest producers nationally, and it is one of three main aluminium producers too; Chongqing Iron and Steel Company and Southwest Aluminum, Asia's largest aluminium plant, are leading names. Agriculture remains important, with rice and fruit, especially oranges, as the principal crops.

The region has large coal and natural gas reserves and more than 40 types of minerals, including strontium and manganese. Coal reserves are about 4.8 billion metric tons. The Chuandong Natural Gas Field is the largest inland gas field in China, with around 270 billion cubic metres, more than a fifth of the national total. Chongqing also has China's largest strontium reserve (China's deposit is the world's second biggest), and manganese is mined around Xiushan, although the mining industry has been criticised as heavily polluting and unsafe. A 10-million-ton refinery run by CNPC, the parent of PetroChina, was planned to process crude oil brought through the China–Myanmar pipelines, which were designed to run from Sittwe on Myanmar's west coast via Kunming in Yunnan to Chongqing, delivering fuel that originates in Myanmar, the Middle East and Africa. That pipeline was not yet finished at the time of the description.

The city has been trying to move up the value chain towards high-tech and knowledge-intensive industry, and that has led to new districts, the New North Zone among them. Local officials hoped favourable policies for electronics and information technology would create a 400 billion RMB high-technology manufacturing hub that outgrows the car industry and delivers 25% of exports. Investment in roads and railways has cut logistics costs, and the nearby Three Gorges Dam, the largest in the world, supplies power and lets ocean-going ships reach the Chongqing river port. The improvements have drawn foreign direct investment in industries from cars to banking and retail. Companies include Ford, Mazda, HSBC, Standard Chartered, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, ANZ, Scotiabank, Wal-Mart, Metro AG and Carrefour.
Chongqing contains several economic and technological development areas:
Chemical Industrial Park
Economic and Technological Development Zone
High-Tech Industry Development Zone
Export Processing Zone
Jianqiao Industrial Park, found in Dadukou District
The New North Zone
Liangjiang New Area, where the Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center is China's biggest facility of this kind
The city is also one corner of the West Triangle Economic Zone, together with Chengdu and Xi'an.
Chongqing is built on steep hills with rivers in between, so bridges, rail and cable transport matter more than in a flat city. Here is how the main systems fit together.

Since gaining national-level municipality status in 1997, Chongqing has expanded its infrastructure dramatically. With railways and expressways built to the east and south-east, it is a leading transport hub of south-west China. By October 2014 31 bridges crossed the Yangtze in the municipality, including more than a dozen in the urban core. Apart from the first two, from 1960 and 1977, all were finished after 1995.

Public transport combines the metro, intercity rail, a dense bus network and the largest monorail system in the world. In May 2007 the municipal government announced a plan to spend 150 billion RMB across 13 years on a network of underground metro lines and heavy monorail. As of 2017 four lines were running: Line 1, a 14-kilometre (8.7 mile) conventional subway; Line 2, a 19-kilometre (12 mile) heavy monorail; Line 3, a heavy monorail linking the airport with the southern part of downtown; and and Line 6, running from Beibei at the far northern end into downtown. Line 5 followed at the end of 2017. The target was for the system to reach 6 lines and 1 loop line by 2020, adding 363.5 kilometres (225.9 miles) to the 2012 network and 93 new stations to the 111 in place in 2012, and for 18 lines to exist by 2050. The system has changed since, so look up the current map.

Chongqing is the only Chinese city to keep aerial tramways in public service. There were three, over the Yangtze, the Jialing and the South Mountain, and only the Yangtze River Tramway is still in operation. Today it counts as a Class 4A tourist attraction. The cable stretches 1,160 metres (3,810 feet) between the south and north banks and moves roughly 10,000 passengers daily.

Chongqing railway station, in Yuzhong, is the oldest, reached by Metro Lines 1 and 3 at Lianglukou. It sits near the Jiefangbei CBD and mainly handles long-distance trains. A major renovation was planned, so many services moved to the North station.
Chongqing North railway station serves numerous long-distance and high-speed trains, for example to Chengdu and Beijing. It opened in 2006 and connects with the metro.
Chongqing West railway station, in Shapingba, was completed in 2018 and handles long-distance and high-speed services to many cities.

Shapingba railway station, near the Shapingba CBD, is reached through the Shapingba metro station, which has Lines 1 and 9 and the Loop line. Local and regional trains are its specialty, and it too dates from 2018.
Chongqing East railway station is the newest, opened in 2025.
Chongqing is also a big destination for freight by rail, and subsidies and incentives have led factories to move there, greatly increasing rail traffic. Overall it is a major regional rail hub.
