chongqing-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Chongqing University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chongqing, register at Chongqing University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

chongqing-university-of-posts-and-teleco.h: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications in brief

blocks.x: The Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications (重庆邮电大学), known as CQUPT, is a university funded by the city rather than the national government, and its campus is in Nan'an District, Chongqing. Its supervising body is the Chongqing Municipal People's Government. As the name says, its focus is on communications and information technology.

The university was founded in 1950, the same year the People's Republic of China took shape and the Communists took over Chongqing. Its first name was Chongqing Institute of Posts and Telecommunications. By 1965 it had become one of just 10 colleges in what was then Sichuan Province that were allowed to teach at postgraduate level. Chongqing was separated from Sichuan and became a municipality in 1997.

A national reform of universities in 2000 meant that the central government and the Chongqing city authorities would govern and finance the university together. In 2006 a further agreement with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology placed CQUPT among the universities that this central ministry and the city both support.
Daily life as a student is tied to the city around you, so the sections below describe Chongqing, where CQUPT is located.

chongqing-university-of-posts-and-teleco.h: Rail transit and the cable car

CRT Line 1 is a conventional 14 km (8.7 mile) subway; Line 2 is a heavy monorail of 19 km (12 miles) through Phase II; Line 3, also a heavy monorail, connects the airport with the southern part of downtown; and Line 6 links downtown with Beibei, a district at the far northern edge, and Line 5 started service late in 2017. It is 1,160 metres (3,810 feet) long, joins the south and north banks of the Yangtze, and carries about 10,000 passengers a day.
Chongqing is a major regional rail hub. Its main stations are:

Chongqing railway station in Yuzhong, reached by Metro Lines 1 and 3 at Lianglukou, the oldest station and close to the Jiefangbei business district; it mostly handles long-distance trains, and because a big renovation is planned many services have moved to the North station.
Chongqing North, finished in 2006 and linked to the metro, which deals with a lot of long-distance and high-speed trains, for example to Chengdu and Beijing.
Chongqing West, in Shapingba, finished in 2018, with many long-distance and high-speed services to many cities.

Chongqing East, opened in 2025.

Chongqing is a major rail freight destination, with better handling facilities still being developed. Subsidies and incentives have led many factories to move to Chongqing or be built there, which has greatly increased rail traffic.
Regional lines include the following.

The Communication University of China (CUC) is a public university in Chaoyang, Beijing, China. It is affiliated with the Ministry of Education. The university is part of the Double First-Class Construction and Project 211.

CUC developed from what used to be a training center for technicians of the Central Broadcasting Bureau that was founded in 1954. In April 1959, it was upgraded to the Beijing Broadcasting College (Chinese: 北京广播学院; pinyin: Běijīng Guǎngbō Xuéyuàn) approved by the State Council. In August 2004, the Beijing Broadcasting College was renamed the Communication University of China. CUC is located in the eastern part of Beijing near the ancient canal, which occupies 463,700 square meters of land and a total of 499,800 square meters of buildings.

CUC's history dates back to March 3, 1954, when the first training class for broadcasting professionals was held by the then Central Radio Administration. This then led to the founding of Beijing Broadcasting College in 1958. On September 7, 1959, CUC's precursor Beijing Broadcasting Institute (BBI) was established.

Since 2019, CUC hosts the Institute for a Community with Shared Future (ICSF), which serves to promote the concept of "community of a shared future for mankind" internationally. ICSF is overseen directly by the Ministry of Education and manages multiple Research Centers for Community with a Shared Future in several countries.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Beijing, where Communication University of China is located.

Three styles of architecture are predominant in urban Beijing. First, there is the traditional architecture of imperial China, perhaps best exemplified by the massive Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which remains the People's Republic of China's trademark edifice, the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven. Next, there is what is sometimes referred to as the "Sino-Sov" style, with structures tending to be boxy and sometimes poorly constructed, which were built between the 1950s and the 1970s. Finally, there are much more modern architectural forms, most noticeably in the area of the Beijing CBD in east Beijing such as the new CCTV Headquarters, in addition to buildings in other locations around the city such as the Beijing National Stadium and National Center for the Performing Arts.

In the early 21st century, Beijing has witnessed tremendous growth of new building constructions, exhibiting various modern styles from international designers, most pronounced in the CBD region. A mixture of both 1950s design and neofuturistic style of architecture can be seen at the 798 Art Zone, which mixes the old with the new. Beijing's tallest building is the 528-meter China Zun. Since 2007, buildings in Beijing have received the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building twice, for the Linked Hybrid building in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. The CTBUH Skyscraper award for best tall overall building is given to only one building around the world every year.

Siheyuans in Beijing are courtyards surrounding by buildings. Among the more grand examples are the Prince Gong Mansion and Residence of Soong Ching-ling. These courtyards are usually connected by alleys called hutongs. The hutongs are generally straight and run east to west so that doorways face north and south for good Feng Shui. They vary in width; some are so narrow only a few pedestrians can pass through at a time. Once ubiquitous in Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are rapidly disappearing, as entire city blocks of hutongs are replaced by high-rise buildings. Residents of the hutongs are entitled to live in the new buildings in apartments of at least the same size as their former residences. Many complain, however, that the traditional sense of community and street life of the hutongs cannot be replaced, and these properties are often government owned.

Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The northwestern part of the municipality, especially Yanqing District and Huairou District, are dominated by the Jundu Mountains, while the western part is framed by Xishan or the Western Hills. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of Beijing Municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills and on the border with Hebei, is the municipality's highest point, with an altitude of 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Major rivers flowing through the municipality, including the Chaobai, Yongding, Juma, are all tributaries in the Hai River system, and flow in a southeasterly direction. The Miyun Reservoir, on the upper reaches of the Chaobai River, is the largest reservoir within the municipality. Beijing is also the northern terminus of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, which was built over 1,400 years ago as a transportation route, and the South–North Water Transfer Project, constructed in the past decade to bring water from the Yangtze River basin.

The urban area of Beijing, on the plains in the south-central of the municipality with elevation of 40 to 60 metres (130–200 feet), occupies a relatively small but expanding portion of the municipality's area. The city spreads out in concentric ring roads. The Second Ring Road traces the old city walls and the Sixth Ring Road connects satellite towns in the surrounding suburbs. Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square are at the center of Beijing, directly to the south of the Forbidden City, the former residence of the emperors of China. To the west of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, the residence of China's current leaders. Chang'an Avenue, which cuts between Tiananmen and the Square, forms the city's main east–west axis.

Beijing's pattern of development from the old inner city to its urban fringe are frequently described as "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing). This pattern of development is frequently cited as a reason for Beijing's urban problems.

Beijing has a humid continental climate (Köppen: Dwa), bordering on a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (Köppen: BSk). The city is characterized by hot, humid summers due to the East Asian monsoon as well as brief but cold, dry winters that reflect the influence of the vast Siberian anticyclone. Spring can bear witness to sandstorms blowing in from the Gobi Desert across the Mongolian steppe, accompanied by rapidly warming, but generally dry, conditions. Autumn, similar to spring, is a season of transition and minimal precipitation. From 2001 to 2026, the hottest period in Beijing is early August, and the coldest period is early January. According to China's seasonal division standard, Beijing enters spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September, and winter on 31 October. Due to the faster warming in March and September and the slower warming in May and October in recent years, Beijing is generally shorter in autumn than in spring. The average annual temperature (From 1991 to 2020) in the urban area of Beijing is 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) to 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), of which the average daily minimum temperature is 7.7 °C (45.9 °F) to 8.4 °C (47.1 °F), and the average daily maximum temperature is 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) to 18.9 °C (66.0 °F). The average annual temperature in the low-altitude part of the suburbs of Beijing is 11.5 °C (52.7 °F) to 13.0 °C (55.4 °F), of which the average daily minimum temperature is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) to 8.0 °C (46.4 °F), and the average daily maximum temperature is 18.2 °C (64.8 °F) to 18.7 °C (65.7 °F). The average annual temperature in mountainous areas is between 0 °C (32 °F) and 10 °C (50 °F), decreasing as the altitude increases. The monthly daily average temperature in January is −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), while in July it is 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Precipitation averages around 528.0 mm (20.79 in) annually (Haidian and Chaoyang has an average annual precipitation of 584.2 mm (23.00 in)), with close to three-quarters of that total falling from June to August. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 42% in July to 62% in January and February, the city receives 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966 to 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.

Beijing had a long history of environmental problems. Between 2000 and 2009 Beijing's urban extent quadrupled, which not only strongly increased the extent of anthropogenic emissions, but also changed the meteorological situation fundamentally, even if emissions of human society are not included. For example, surface albedo, wind speed and humidity near the surface were decreased, whereas ground and near-surface air temperatures, vertical air dilution and ozone levels were increased. Because of the combined factors of urbanization and pollution caused by burning of fossil fuel, Beijing is often affected by serious environmental problems, which lead to health issues of many inhabitants. In 2013 heavy smog struck Beijing and most parts of northern China, impacting a total of 600 million people. After this "pollution shock" air pollution became an important economic and social concern in China. After that the government of Beijing announced measures to reduce air pollution, for example by lowering the share of coal from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, while the national government ordered heavily polluting vehicles to be removed from 2015 to 2017 and increased its efforts to transition the energy system to clean sources.

Joint research between American and Chinese researchers in 2006 concluded that much of the city's pollution comes from surrounding cities and provinces. On average 35–60% of the ozone can be traced to sources outside the city. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality have a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", partly due to the prevailing south/southeasterly flow during the summer and the mountains to the north and northwest.

In preparation for the 2008 Summer Olympics and to fulfill promises to clean up the city's air, nearly US$17 billion was spent. Beijing implemented a number of air improvement schemes for the duration of the Games, including halting work at all construction sites, closing many factories in Beijing permanently, temporarily shutting industry in neighboring regions, closing some gas stations, and cutting motor traffic by half by limiting drivers to odd or even days (based on their license plate numbers), reducing bus and subway fares, opening new subway lines, and banning high-emission vehicles. The city further assembled 3,800 natural gas-powered buses, one of the largest fleets in the world. Beijing became the first city in China to require the Chinese equivalent to the Euro 4 emission standard.

Coal burning accounts for about 40% of the PM 2.5 in Beijing and is also the chief source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012, the city has been converting coal-fired power stations to burn natural gas and aims to cap annual coal consumption at 20 million tons. In 2011, the city burned 26.3 million tons of coal, 73% of which for heating and power generation and the remainder for industry. Much of the city's air pollutants are emitted by neighboring regions. Coal consumption in neighboring Tianjin is expected to increase from 48 to 63 million tons from 2011 to 2015. Hebei Province burned over 300 million tons of coal in 2011, more than all of Germany, of which only 30% were used for power generation and a considerable portion for steel and cement making. Power plants in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal consumption has tripled since 2000, and Shandong also contribute to air pollution in Beijing. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, respectively rank from first to fourth, among Chinese provinces by coal consumption. There were four major coal-fired power plants in the city to provide electricity as well as heating during the winter. The first one (Gaojing Thermal Power Plant) was shut down in 2014. Another two were shut in March 2015. The last one (Huaneng Thermal Power Plant) would be shut in 2016. Between 2013 and 2017, the city planned to reduce 13 million tons of coal consumption and cap coal consumption to 15 million tons in 2015.

The government sometimes uses cloud-seeding measures to increase the likelihood of rain showers in the region to clear the air prior to large events, such as prior to the 60th anniversary parade in 2009 as well as to combat drought conditions in the area. More recently, however, the government has increased its usage of such measures as closing factories temporarily and implementing greater restrictions for cars on the road, as in the case of "APEC blue" and "parade blue", short periods during and immediately preceding the APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, respectively. During and prior to these events, Beijing's air quality improved dramatically, only to fall back to unhealthy levels shortly after.

On 8 and 9 December 2015 Beijing had its first smog alert which shut down a majority of the industry and other commercial businesses in the city. Later in the month another smog "red alert" was issued.

According to Beijing's environmental protection bureau's announcement in November 2016, starting from 2017 highly polluting old cars will be banned from being driven whenever Smog "red alerts" are issued in the city or neighboring regions.

In recent years, there has been measurable reductions in pollutants after the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014, with Beijing seeing a 35% reduction in fine particulates in 2017 and further reduction by 2020. The primary factors behind this reduction were replacing coal power with natural gas and cleaning up polluting industrial facilities in the Beijing area.

Beijing's annual average concentration of major airborne fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, declined to 30 micrograms per cubic meter in 2022, the best air quality for the city since 2013. In 2024, Beijing experienced only two days of heavy pollution, the lowest number on record, which had decreased by 96.6 percent from 58 days in 2013.

Due to Beijing's high level of air pollution, there are various readings by different sources on the subject. Daily pollution readings at 27 monitoring stations around the city are reported on the website of the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB). The American Embassy of Beijing also reports hourly fine particulate (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. Since the BJEPB and US Embassy measure different pollutants according to different criteria, the pollution levels and the impact to human health reported by the BJEPB are often lower than that reported by the US Embassy.

The smog is causing harm and danger to the population. The air pollution does directly result in significant impact on the morbidity rate of cardiovascular disease and respiratory disease in Beijing. Exposure to large concentrations of polluted air can cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems, emergency room visits, and even death.

Dust from the erosion of deserts in northern and northwestern China results in seasonal dust storms that plague the city; the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes artificially induces rainfall to fight such storms and mitigate their effects. In the first four months of 2006 alone, there were no fewer than eight such storms. In April 2002, one dust storm alone dumped nearly 50,000 tons of dust onto the city before moving on to Japan and Korea.

The city of Dali, in Yunnan in south-west China, is home to Dali University. It is a public university run at provincial level, and the Yunnan Provincial People's Government is its governing authority. Its home is one of the most scenic and historically interesting parts of the province, which is a large part of its appeal to international students.
Two schools started it all in 1978: a medical college and a teachers college, both in Dali. They were merged in 2001 to form Dali College, which later developed into the university we know today.

Dali University sees itself as an international university, with a strong name in Southeast Asia and South Asia. By 2013 more than 5,000 international students had graduated from it, coming from 42 countries and regions. Among their home countries were Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan, South Korea and the USA.
These events and agreements give a flavour of its academic cooperation:
March 2013: an academic symposium bringing together universities from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Chinese universities
December 2012: master's degree courses taught jointly with Deakin University in Australia
September 2012: an academic symposium on geophysics and applied mathematics in China

Several rankings give a rough idea of where Dali University stands:

In 2022 the Best Chinese Universities Ranking listed it 308th nationally and fifth within Yunnan. Four universities were ahead of it in the province: Yunnan University, Yunnan Normal University, Yunnan Agricultural University and Kunming University of Science and Technology. Setting aside the major universities of the provincial capital Kunming, Dali University is the one in Dali City that reaches Yunnan's top five.
Academic performance is the basis of the University Rankings by Academic Performance (2023/24), which put it at 2,082 in the world and 361 in China.

These positions show a regional university, so think of Dali University less as a research powerhouse and more as a place with strong regional links and an exceptional setting.
For a student, daily life depends on the surroundings, so it pays to know the weather, transport and local attractions. This section introduces Dali, where the university is located.

Dali City is in western Yunnan, around 250 km (160 mi) to the northwest of the provincial capital, Kunming. Two landscapes meet here. On one side are the dramatic valleys of the Hengduan ranges, at the eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, and on the other the characteristic mountains of the Yungui Plateau's western section.

Erhai Lake is surrounded by this county-level city. Mount Jizu rises on the eastern side and the Cang Mountains on the western side. The county seat, Xiaguan, stands where the lake empties into the Yangbi River, whereas Dali Old Town is on a fertile plain squeezed between Erhai and the Cang Range. Traditionally, Bai and Yi people have lived on that plain.
Neighbouring counties: Binchuan, Xiangyun and Heqing to the east, Weishan and Midu to the south, Yangbi to the west and Eryuan to the north.

Because Dali is high up, its low latitude does not make it hot, and the result is a mild subtropical highland climate (Köppen Cwb). The winter is short, dry and mild, and the summer warm and wet. Frost can occur in winter, yet afternoons typically still reach 16 °C (61 °F) or more. Most summer days have some rain, with daytime highs of 25 °C (77 °F). Between June and October falls the greater part of the year's rain. Snowfall in December 2013 was unusually heavy.

Nowadays the local economy depends heavily on tourism and on services for visitors. Historically Dali controlled some of the commerce passing between China and India. Skilled woodworkers in the town of Xizhou made it well known, and so did its fine marble, which went into buildings and ornaments. The marble was so central that the modern Chinese word for it, dàlǐshí (大理石), literally means "Dali stone". Tea is grown locally too.
Sanyue Jie, known as the Third Month Fair

Getting about locally means buses, taxis, bicycles or boats on the lake. Buses 4 and 8 take about an hour to go between Xiaguan and the old town. Many visitors hire a bicycle from the numerous shops in the old town and explore that way, perhaps along the dedicated cycle path around Erhai.

Domestic flights use Dali Fengyi Airport (DLU), roughly 13 km (8.1 mi) east of Xiaguan along Weishan or Airport Rd. Taxi fares are around 60 RMB for Xiaguan and 90 RMB for the old town. In 2014 the destinations were Kunming in 20 minutes, Xishuangbanna in 25, Chongqing in 70 and Chengdu Shuangliu in 80, plus Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Guiyuan.

The Hangrui Expressway (G56) connects Dali (strictly, Xiaguan) to Kunming and points east. In the other direction it continues to Ruili, on the Burmese border. A spur, the Dali Expressway (G56₁₁), connects it to Lijiang. China National Highway 214 is the road to the old town, and joins the Lijiang expressway north of the lake. It also goes south from Xiaguan as far as Menghai, near the Burmese border.

From the west gate of the old town, long-distance buses go to Lijiang, Shangri-La and Kunming (around 4½ hours), and each Monday a bus also runs to the market at Shaping. In Xiaguan the long-distance bus stations are on Jianshe Road.

Daily trains to Lijiang and Kunming leave from Dali's own railway station. In the past a single daytime train and two overnight sleeper trains ran to Kunming. Since July 2018 a modern high-speed link has joined Dali and Kunming, with one train every hour. As Yunnan's railway network grows, trains should in future also reach Shangri-La County and Ruili. A standard-gauge railway between Kunming in China and the port of Kyaukphyu in Myanmar opened in 2021, and Dali has a station on it.
Dali is among Yunnan's most visited destinations. Highlights include:
Dali Municipal Museum (大理市博物馆), in a central location, with permanent exhibitions of archaeological finds from the region, paintings and Buddhist sculptures
The Three Pagodas and Chongsheng Temple
A film city built for Demi-Gods and Semi-Devils
Xizhou, a historic town with a reputation for fine architecture and woodwork

Shuang lang, east of the lake. It was a small fishing village, and is now quite a high-class tourist destination, as buildings and businesses have overtaken the village since 2012, and tourism estates fully cover the coast.
Cang Mountain, to the west of both the Old City and the Three Pagodas
A memorial stele for Kublai Khan's conquest of Yunnan (元世祖平云南碑), carried on a big stone tortoise in Sanyue Lane (三月街), on the western side of the Old City at the base of Cang Mountain
What lies around a university colours student life nearly as much as the campus does, which is why this profile also recounts the history of Yunnan.

Railway engineers digging in the 1960s turned up the Yuanmou Man, a Homo erectus fossil. The fossil is thought to be around 1.7 million years old, which makes it the oldest hominid remains known in China. Later, in the Neolithic age, communities settled by Lake Dian, where they made stone tools and put up basic wooden buildings.

Dian was the name given around the 3rd century BC to central Yunnan, the region of present-day Kunming. A general from the state of Chu, Zhuang Qiao (庄蹻), travelled in from the upper Yangtze and declared himself "King of Dian". With his followers came Chinese influence in large amounts, and with them began a long process of migration and cultural spread.

When Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC he pushed imperial authority to the south, creating commanderies and counties in Yunnan. A road already existing in Sichuan, known as the "Five Foot Way", was extended to the south as far as roughly today's Qujing in the east of the province. Dian fell to the Han dynasty in 109 BC. Emperor Wu dispatched General Guo Chang (郭昌), who in the end founded the Yizhou commandery.

Local farming had advanced greatly by then. People worked with bronze tools and ploughs, and their animals included horses, cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and dogs. Anthropologists consider these people ancestors or relatives of today's Tai. They lived in tribal communities, some of which had exiled Chinese as leaders.

Under the Three Kingdoms, one name, Nanzhong, covered modern Yunnan together with western Guizhou and southern Sichuan. As central power in China fell apart, Yunnan became more autonomous and local tribal systems grew stronger. In AD 225 the renowned statesman Zhuge Liang marched three columns into the province to subdue its tribes. Seven times, so the story goes, he captured a local magnate named Meng Huo, a legend recorded in the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Nomadic invaders swept across much of northern China during the 4th century. The Cuan (爨) clan moved into Yunnan in the 320s, and their leader Cuan Chen (爨琛) proclaimed himself king, governing from the area of Lake Dian, called Kunchuan at that time. For more than four centuries the Cuan were the rulers of eastern Yunnan.

Yunnan also lay on routes for foreign trade. Before the Tang period an old overland road went from Yunnan across the Irrawaddy region of Burma to Bengal. People described as barbarians, who were not wholly governed by Tang officials, lived along it, and use of the road stayed limited before the Tang. Later attempts by China to take control of it were upset by the emergence of Nanzhao.

Many tribes, clans and cultures shared Yunnan before the 8th century. Near Lake Erhai, in the Dali area, six political units called zhao developed. They were Mengshe (蒙舍), Mengzi (蒙巂), Yuexi (越析), Langqiong (浪穹), Dengdan (邆赕) and Shilling (施浪). The word zhao (诏), from an indigenous non-Chinese language, meant "king" or "kingdom". As Mengshe was the southernmost of the six, the larger state that grew out of it was named Nanzhao, "Southern Kingdom".

By the 730s the Erhai region was under Nanzhao rule. Piluoge, its fourth king, united western Yunnan in 738, and the Tang court acknowledged him as king of Yunnan. From Dali, thirteen Nanzhao kings reigned for over 200 years, and as a buffer state sitting between the Tang dynasty and the Tibetan Empire, the kingdom helped shape how those two powers dealt with each other.
Nanzhao controlled all of Yunnan by the 750s and so threatened to challenge Tang China. A series of clashes took place:
In 750 Nanzhao seized Yaozhou, which was the biggest Tang settlement in Yunnan.

In 751 the Tang commander of Jiannan (modern Sichuan), Xianyu Zhongtong (鮮于仲通), marched against Nanzhao. Its king, Geluofeng, saw the earlier affair as personal and sent a letter seeking peace. Xianyu held the envoys prisoner and rejected the request. Nanzhao answered by changing sides to the Tibetan Empire: the two powers called each other "fraternal states" and Geluofeng received the title zanpuzhong, meaning "younger brother". The alliance sealed a disaster for Xianyu, whose 80,000 soldiers fell to a quarter of that number.
A further Tang expedition in 753 was beaten as well.
In 754 a Tang army of over 100,000 reached the Dali plain, and again the result was a massacre.
After the 700s were over, the Tang no longer posed a major danger to Nanzhao.

For several decades the kingdom kept growing. A sudden raid into Sichuan in 829 took Nanzhao troops into Chengdu, and they took back hundreds of Sichuan people, skilled craftsmen among them, as they withdrew. By 832 they had taken the Pyu capital in what is now upper Burma, and the Khmer people of Zhenla were also attacked. At that time Nanzhao was the strongest kingdom on the Southeast Asian mainland, and it took an energetic part in the dealings between several states.

Bozhou fell to Nanzhao in 859, sharpening the conflict with the Tang. Next year the Tang governor of Annam recaptured it, so with native allies Nanzhao occupied Hanoi while the Tang army was busy at Bozhou. When Tang troops returned, Nanzhao left Hanoi but raided and plundered Yongzhou. During the winter of 862, along with local groups, a Nanzhao army of over 50,000 invaded Annam again. Across the two Annam campaigns the Tang side reportedly lost over 150,000 men, whether killed or taken prisoner. A Tang victory in Hanoi in the autumn of 866 pushed out the Nanzhao forces, although by then Tang China could no longer mount attacks on Nanzhao.
Even as it lost in Annam, Nanzhao went on raiding Sichuan now and then, led in 869 by Shilong (世隆), its eighth king and its first emperor, and again in 874.

Then came a sequence of coups. In 928 Yang Ganzhen (楊干貞) seized the Dachanghe throne and had Zhao Shanzheng, a qingpingguan, crowned emperor of Datianxing (大天興). The following year, 929, Yang Qianzhen removed Zhao and took the title Emperor of Dayining (大義寧) himself.

The Dayining kingdom was overthrown by Duan Siping in 937, who set up the Dali Kingdom. In 1253, after its king Duan Xingzhi went over to the Mongols, the Mongol Empire conquered it. The Duan family stayed in power as Maharajas within Mongol administration of the new province, although a Mongol prince sent to govern alongside them was killed. Kublai Khan reorganised the province in 1273, naming Ajall Shams al-Din Omar, a semu, as governor.

Parts of Upper Burma became part of Yunnan under the Yuan, following the Mongols' first invasion of Burma during the 1270s and 1280s. In 1303 garrison troops left Burma. That gave local leaders room to enlarge their own bases of power, and by the 1340s it led to Möng Mao's swift rise and rebellion. After the Yuan fell in 1368, the Ming conquest of Yunnan finished off by the early 1380s the loyalists of the Yuan, led by Basalawarmi, and what was left of the House of Duan.

Mu Ying and his family were installed by the Ming as hereditary aristocrats in Yunnan. During both the Ming and Qing periods the native chieftain system governed large parts of the province. In the 1760s the Qing fought a war with Burma, which grew out of efforts on both sides to bring the border areas under the control of local chiefs.

Han Chinese had been coming to Yunnan since the Yuan, and more arrived under the Ming and Qing. Three million of them settled in Yunnan during the Ming, chiefly from Nanjing, some from Shanxi and Hebei. The original population of Nanjing was later mainly replaced by Wu speakers.

The Panthay Rebellion is largely forgotten today, yet it was bloody. Muslim Hui and other local minorities rose up against the Qing dynasty's Manchu rulers, and as many as a million people in Yunnan died. The Manchu official Shuxing'a triggered it by starting an anti-Muslim massacre. A crowd of Muslims had once stripped him and almost lynched him, and from then on he hated Muslims deeply, ordering that several rebels be sliced slowly to death. The writer Tariq Ali used the incident in a novel, claiming that those who attacked Shuxing'a were of another ethnic group rather than Hui, but the official blamed every Muslim regardless. Muslim forces loyal to the Qing assisted in crushing the rebels, and the Qing armies targeted only Muslims who took part in the rebellion or backed it, sparing those who stayed out of it.

Morrison, an Australian correspondent of The Times named George Ernest, travelled through Yunnan from Beijing to British-occupied Burma in 1894 and described the journey in An Australian in China. In 1905, an uprising in Tibet, in which Tibetan Buddhist lamas killed French Catholic missionaries, reached Yunnan too.

Natural history flourished here. French scientists at Paris's National Museum of Natural History described thousands of species of plants, insects and mammals during the 19th century, thanks to the permanent settlements that the Missions étrangères de Paris kept in the north-west of the province. Jean-André Soulié and Felix Biet were prominent among them. In 1916 and 1917 Yvette Borup Andrews and Roy Chapman Andrews led the Asiatic Zoological Expedition for New York's American Museum of Natural History. It crossed much of western and southern Yunnan and other provinces, and their book Camps and Trails in China tells the story.

Other notable explorers were Heinrich Handel-Mazzetti and George Forrest. From 1922 to 1949 Joseph Francis Charles Rock devoted most of his time to studying southwest China's plants, languages and peoples, mostly in Yunnan. Peter Goullart, a White Russian, studied Naxi culture while living in Lijiang from 1940 until 1949.
Two famous fossils come from Yunnan:
Yunnanozoon, a possible chordate from the Lower Cambrian
Jingshanosaurus, a long-necked prosauropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic
Yunnan government statistics suggest about 2.5 million overseas Chinese trace their ancestral homeland to Yunnan.
Yunnan has over 19,000 plant species. Among them are 60 percent of all the plants used in traditional Chinese medicine. Yunnan Baiyao is a well-known product of the province.

Dali University is a modest-ranking regional university with a large number of Asian graduates, set in one of Yunnan's most beautiful and historic places, beside Erhai Lake and below the Cang Mountains. A mild climate, a growing rail network and a rich history make it an interesting place to spend years of study.
Dali University lists 137 programs for international students on this site: 52 bachelor, 44 master's, 41 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 111 taught in Chinese, 26 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 12,000 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 14,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 28,000 to CNY 28,000 (median CNY 28,000), according to the university's published fee table.

137 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (13):
Anesthesiology
Basic Medicine
Clinical Laboratory Diagnostics
Dermatology and Venereology
Ecology
Internal Medicine
Medical Imaging and Nuclear Medicine
Neurology
Obstetrics and Gynecology
Oncology
Ophthalmology
Otolaryngology
Surgery
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

dali-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Dali University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Dali, register at Dali University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Dalian Jiaotong University (Chinese name 大连交通大学) is based in Dalian, a port city in Liaoning Province. The provincial government oversees it today, and before that the national Ministry of Railways did. A smaller second campus sits in Lüshunkou District's Dalian Hi-tech Zone, while the main one stands near the downtown core. The old name, used up to 2004, was Dalian Railway Institute (大连铁道学院, Dàlián Tiědào Xuéyuàn). It is the only university in Northeast China whose curriculum is built around rail transit, which makes it an obvious choice for anyone interested in railways and related engineering.

dalian-jiaotong-university.h: Dalian: the city you will live in

blocks.x: Your day-to-day experience as a student comes down to the surrounding city, meaning the weather, the transport and what there is to do in your free time. The sections below walk through Dalian, where the university is located.

dalian-jiaotong-university.h: Where Dalian is and what it includes

blocks.x: Dalian is among the most heavily developed industrial areas in China. Today the municipality has two main parts: Dalian proper, and Lüshunkou, a smaller area farther along the Liaodong Peninsula. Lüshunkou used to be the city of Lüshun, a name that appears in Western and Russian historical writing as Port Arthur. Older accounts also mention a Russian-planned city called Dalniy (also spelled Dalney) on the south shore of Dalian Bay, which stood 40 kilometres (25 miles) from Port Arthur, today's Lüshunkou (literally "Lüshun Port").

The city faces Korea Bay, at the northern edge of the Yellow Sea, and occupies the narrow neck roughly halfway along the Liaodong Peninsula. The coastline is 1,906 km (1,184 miles) long, and the city administers most of the peninsula along with about 260 islands and reefs. Seen from the Yalu River, it lies south-south-west, and the mouth of its harbour forms a small inlet named Dalian Bay.

Dalian's climate is humid continental, influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa). Summers are warm and wet thanks to the East Asian monsoon. Winters are cold, windy and dry because of the huge Siberian high-pressure system. Apart from winter, the seasons run about a month late, a result of the city's position on the peninsula.
These figures give you a feel for it.
Over 24 hours, January averages −3.3 °C (26.1 °F) and August averages 24.8 °C (76.6 °F). Averaged across the year, the temperature is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F).
Rainfall averages 580 millimetres (22.8 inches) a year, but it is packed into the summer months and can swing a lot from one year to the next.
Because the city is on the coast, daily swings are modest; the yearly mean difference between day and night is only 6.66 °C (12.0 °F).
Possible sunshine ranges from 45 per cent in July to 66 per cent in March, which adds up to 2,625 sunny hours in a year.
The coldest day on record since 1951 was 4 January 1970 at −21.1 °C (−6 °F), and the hottest was 7 August 2026 at 37.3 °C (99 °F).
In practical terms, you will want serious winter clothing, but the summers are comfortable compared with many inland Chinese cities.
In the 2010 census Dalian had 6.69 million residents. At the end of 2014, 5.943 million people were registered as living in households, an increase of 29,000 on the year before.

Dalian's GDP has grown by double digits every year since 1992. In 2014 growth slowed to 5.8 per cent, taking GDP to RMB 765.56 billion, and GDP per head reached RMB 109,939. A national assessment by the National Bureau of Statistics puts Dalian in eighth place among Chinese cities for overall strength. Leading sectors are machinery, petrochemicals with oil refining, and electronics.

Dalian began as a region of farming and fish culture. In the early 20th century a ferry opened between Yantai and Lüshun, and farmers and fishermen from Shandong, across the Yellow Sea, began to settle in the area during the wave of migration known as Chuang Guandong.

dalian-jiaotong-university.h: Heavy industry, light industry and distribution

blocks.x: Ships and locomotives were already being built here around the time of the Second Sino-Japanese War, by the companies that evolved into Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (known as DLoco). When World War II ended, Dalian grew into an important base for heavy and light industry, with Dalian Heavy Industry Co., Dalian Chemical Group and Wafangdian Bearing Co. among its names. Distribution became a strength as well, represented by the Dashang Group.

Dalian Port is an important gateway for international trade. Ships from Dalian connect with over 300 ports across 160 countries and regions, and more than 100 container routes run both overseas and within China. In 1976 the port finished an oil harbour, the biggest in China by tonnage, where a pipeline from the Daqing oilfields ends. Within China only five ports are larger. The AAPA world port ranking put Dalian eighth globally for cargo tonnage in 2012 and twelfth for container volume (total TEUs) in 2013. That strength feeds the city's oil refining, diesel engineering and chemical industries.

Another harbour, Dayaowan Port (大窑湾港), was also finished in 1993 and lies on the Dagushan peninsula (大孤山) in the northern suburbs. Its specialty is the import and export of minerals and oil products. Add the city's two railway stations (Dalian and Dalian North), its international airport, and expressways heading to Shenyang (Shenda), Changchun (Changda), Harbin (Hada) and Dandong, and Dalian is plainly a distribution hub.

The Chinese government has given Dalian many advantages, including the status of "open city" in 1984, which lets it attract large amounts of foreign investment (see Special Economic Zone). A Development Zone was created in Jinzhou District. Japanese companies arrived first (Canon, Mitsubishi Electric, Nidec, Sanyo Electric and Toshiba among them), followed by firms from South Korea, the United States and Europe, such as Pfizer. In 2007 Intel announced a plan for a semiconductor fabrication plant, or fab, in the zone. It was Intel's first fab on an entirely new site since 1992, and it started operating in October 2010. Car manufacturing is also present: Chery, BYD Automobile (where the BYD K9 electric bus is built) and Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company all run plants in Dalian.
The city has further zones, namely an Export Processing Zone, a Free Trade Zone, a Hi-Tech Industrial Zone and an Economic and Technological Development Zone.

Dalian is the financial centre of Northeast China. Five of China's major banks have Dalian branches: Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank and Industrial & Commercial Bank of China. The local lender, formerly Dalian City Commercial Bank and now Bank of Dalian, also processes the Mingzhu IC Card that residents use on public transport. It has expanded to Beijing, Shanghai and Shenyang, plus five more cities.

Dalian also hosts the Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE), opened in 1993, which is Northeast China's sole futures exchange and has expanded rapidly. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has approved 19 products for futures trading. These cover farm goods (corn and corn starch, soybeans with their meal and oil, RBD palm olein, polished round-grained rice, eggs), chemicals and plastics (linear low-density polyethylene or LLDPE, polyvinyl chloride or PVC, polypropylene or PP, ethylene glycol or EG, ethenylbenzene or EB), industrial inputs (metallurgical coke, coking coal and iron ore) and building boards (fibreboard and blockboard). There are three traded options as well, on soybean meal, corn and iron ore. In 2019 trading reached 1,331 million lots, worth RMB 68.92 trillion.

An IT industry has been a priority since the 1990s. Most of it sits in the Dalian Hi-Tech Zone and in the Dalian Software Park, both in the western suburbs close to Dalian University of Technology. The High-Tech Zone is the city's centre for high-tech business, with over 4,700 enterprises, including 80 Fortune Global 500 members. Homegrown IT firms (DHC, Hisoft and Neusoft Group) share the area with foreign names from the US, Europe, India and Japan: IBM, Dell, HP, Oracle, Cisco, Accenture, Wipro, Infosys, Ericsson, Panasonic, Sony and Hitachi. The area has nine specialist business incubators, including hi-tech, animation and software ones, which have nurtured more than 400 companies. A project called the "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" is under way and covers Dalian Software Park Phase 3.
Intel's Fab 68 is in Dalian. The plan was unveiled on 26 March 2007 and operations began on 26 October 2010. This was Intel's first chip factory in East Asia.

Tourists from across China and from abroad, particularly Japan, South Korea and Russia, come to Dalian in large numbers. The mild weather, the many beaches and the city's place in modern Chinese history all help. Among the beaches, the most famous are Xiajiahezi (夏家河子), Xinghai Bay (星海湾), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Fujiazhuang (付家庄) and Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸). The National Tourism Administration and the United Nations World Tourism Organization jointly recognised three cities as "China's best tourist city" in 2007: Dalian, Hangzhou and Chengdu.
The first group of sights is in the inner city.

Zhongshan Square. Planned by the Russians in the 19th century, it is known above all for the classical buildings that the Japanese built around it during the early decades of the 20th century. Its Chinese name is 中山广场.

Laohutan Ocean Park. Inside are a coral aquarium, an aviary called the World of Birds and the Polar Region Marine Animals World, where the beluga and dolphin show is the biggest attraction. Nearby is Tigers Sculpture Square, whose tiger symbolises Tiger Beach (老虎滩). Visitors can also board the Taiyuan, a retired destroyer of the Anshan class.
Xinghai Square (星海广场, "Square of the Sea of Stars"). Built beside Xinghai Bay for the city's hundredth birthday in 1998, it is described as the world's largest city square.
The Dalian Forest Zoo, Sunasia Ocean World, and the Heishijiao Geological Park with the Dalian Natural History Museum.

Bangchuidao Scenic Area. Since 1960 this well-tended park served as a State Guesthouse, and it has now been opened to everyone. It offers green lawns and woods, villas in Chinese and Western styles, a hot spring, tennis and badminton courts, a recreation centre, a golf course and a beach. Offshore you can see Bangchui Island (棒棰岛), named for its islet whose outline resembles a traditional laundry tool, the bangchui. In its guesthouse days the park received a long list of leaders and dignitaries, from Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping to Kim Jong Un, Henry Kissinger, Boris Yeltsin, Gerhard Schröder and Juan Antonio Samaranch.
Dalian Sightseeing Tower
Donggang Music Fountain
Fujiazhuang Beach

dalian-jiaotong-university.h: Jinzhou District and the Development Zone (northern suburbs)

blocks.x: Dahei Mountain is in this district. The biggest attraction is Jinshitan (金石滩, "Golden Pebble Beach"), the Jinshitan National Holiday Resort with Discoveryland. It consists of an eastern and a western peninsula, an open area between them and the 16-kilometre (10-mile) Golden Coast beach. Its main sights are:
Museums: the Golden Pebble Waxworks Museum, the Geological Museum, the China Martial Arts Hall, the Mao Zedong Badge Exhibition Hall and the Model Movie & TV Art Center.
Outdoor spaces: the Coastal National Geopark, Golden Rock Park and Wanfuding Park.
Entertainment: Discoveryland Theme Park, the Golden Pebble Hunting Club and its equestrian base, and two golf venues (Golden Pebble Golf Club and Golden Gulf Golf Course).
Stays and facilities: the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, an International Vehicle Campsite, and the Golden Pebble International Convention Center & Resort.
Each year Jinshitan holds themed events, including the Dalian International Beach Carnival, the International Winter Swimming Festival and the Grape Festival.
The Discoveryland Theme Park (发现王国, also called "the Discovery Kingdom") opened in 2006. Its designer was Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, a firm that worked on the design of Disney's theme parks.
This district is rich in history and is a good place to explore the Russo-Japanese War period.
Lüshun Museum
Lüshun Railway Station

East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山), Hill 203 and the Shuishiying Meeting Place. Here the heaviest fighting of the Russo-Japanese War's Battle of Lüshun (1904 to 1905) took place, and the ceasefire document was signed at this location too.

Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum in Lüshun. The Russians constructed this prison in 1902 and the Japanese expanded it afterwards. Throughout World War II, inmates of various nationalities who resisted Japan's invasion were held inside. The Korean independence activist An Jung-geun, who had killed Itō Hirobumi, was imprisoned and executed at the site.
Lüshun Snake Museum, Lüshun Bird Port and the Snake Island Reservation

Hengshan Temple and Longwangtang Cherry Blossom Park. The temple, Hengshan (横山寺), is next to the Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库); its origins are in the Han dynasty, and a rebuilding took place in 2003.
Beyond the urban core, several areas offer outdoor activities.
Pulandian District: Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场)
Wafangdian: Changxing Island International Golf Course
Zhuanghe: the Bingyu Valley Scenic Area, plus the hot spring at Buyun Mountain (步云山温泉)
Changhai County: the islands of Changhai County

Dalian has numerous hot-spring hotels. In Lüshunkou District you will find Laotieshan and Tianmu Hot Spring Hotels. Others include the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort at Jinshitan, the Minghu Hot Spring Hotel in Wafangdian, and the Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa in Ganjingzi District.

Skiing is increasingly popular. Well-known slopes include Anbo Ski Resort in Pulandian District, Minghu Ski Resort with its Minghu International Skiing Holiday Village in Wafangdian, and, in Ganjingzi District, Linhai Ski Resort and Dalian Happy Snow World (the latter near the airport).
Because the roads are hilly, cycling is less common here than in other Chinese cities. Dalian also bans motorcycles in the downtown core by local law, so few are seen there.

The city has a comprehensive bus network and an efficient metro. In March 2023 the metro network comprised underground Lines 1, 2 and 5, plus overground Lines 3, 12 and 13. Lines 4 and 7 and other extensions are being built, with the goal of eventually linking every part of the city by rail. Dalian also has the second-oldest tram network in China. Most public transport can be paid for with the Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡).
In 2006, China Daily chose Dalian as the most liveable city in the country.

Four theatres stand out. The Hongji Grand Stage specialises in Beijing Opera. The Dalian People's Culture Club is mostly a music venue. The Working People's Theater, also called Doudou Grand Stage (工人剧院/豆豆大舞台), hosts mainly Errenzhuan, and the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院) completes the list.
Scientific research is represented by the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, located in the city.

Where a university sits within its province affects student life nearly as much as the campus itself, so this part looks at the history and farming of Liaoning, the home province of Dalian Jiaotong University.

dalian-jiaotong-university.h: Early rulers, from Yan to Tang

blocks.x: Between the 4th century BC and the 9th century, Han Chinese regimes mostly settled and governed Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the area was home to the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples, and the state of Yan took it over around 300 BC. The area was organised into two commanderies, Liaodong (meaning "east of the Liao River") and Liaoxi ("west of the Liao River"). Liaodong's centre, the Yan city of Xiangping, occupied the site of present-day Liaoyang.

When the Han dynasty collapsed, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family built a semi-independent state centred on Liaodong, which lasted until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. This state, also known as Yan, sent out many sea-going diplomatic and trade missions, and despite its short life it left a lasting mark on Northeast Asian culture. Once the Western Jin dynasty ended, three Xianbei states ruled by the Murong tribe (Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan) held Liaoning in turn. In 436, when Northern Wei took the Yan capital, Goguryeo seized the Liaodong Peninsula, and the Tang dynasty finally annexed the area during the Goguryeo-Tang War.

By the middle of the 8th century, the An Lushan Rebellion was draining Tang strength from its border regions, and the Bohai state slowly moved into Liaodong. The Khitan Liao dynasty then took Liaoning and split it into four circuits named Dongjingdao (Eastern Capital), Shangjingdao (Supreme Capital), Zhongjingdao (Central Capital) and Xiajingdao (Lower Capital).

When the Jurchen Jin dynasty ruled, the larger share of Liaoning was in the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu). Smaller parts went to the Xianping Route, the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu) and the Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu). Genghis Khan conquered the region in 1206 and it passed into the Yuan dynasty, which administered it in several pieces. The east, covering the Liaoyang and Shenyang Routes, along with the west that included Guangning Route, answered to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. The north was Xianping Prefecture within Kaiyuan Route. Jinzhou and Chaoyang, on the other hand, belonged to Daning Route, under the Central Secretariat.

The Ming Empire took Liaoning in 1371, only three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. Around 1442 a defensive wall was built to protect the farming heartland from a possible threat from the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group that was a Ming tributary, in the northwest. In 1467 and 1468 the wall was extended to guard against attacks from the northeast by the Jianzhou Jurchens, who later became known as the Manchu. Its aim matched the Great Wall's, yet this "Liaodong Wall" was built more cheaply: stone and tile were used in places, yet most of it was simply an earth bank with a moat on each side.

The wall did not stop the Jurchens. In the early 1600s they overran Liaodong, the eastern half of Liaoning, long before the remainder of China fell to them. Their dynasty, called "Later Jin" before the name Qing was adopted, made Xingjing (兴京) its capital from 1616 to 1621. Xingjing lay outside the Liaodong Wall in the east of modern Liaoning. The seat then shifted to Dongjing (east of present Liaoyang) and, in 1625, to Shengjing, the city we now call Shenyang. After the Qing took Beijing in 1644, the main capital moved there, but Shengjing stayed important as a regional capital for most of the Qing era.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning many of its people. Some residents died in combat, others escaped beyond the Great Wall, and withdrawing Ming troops razed numerous towns. Even in 1661 the Fengtian civil governor (Fuyin), Zhang Shangxian, wrote that aside from Fengtian City (today's Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city east of the Liao had been deserted or kept just a few hundred people. He said that Tieling and Fushun had only "a few vagrants". Across the Liao to the west, just Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning still had substantial populations.

In the second half of the 17th century, starting with laws of 1651 and 1653, the Qing court sought settlers from the area below the Great Wall, Shandong above all, to populate sparsely settled Fengtian Province, which corresponds roughly to modern Liaoning. Many people in Liaoning today trace their ancestry to these 17th-century newcomers. Elsewhere in the Northeast, Han Chinese were officially barred for most of Manchu rule. To keep them from today's Jilin, Heilongjiang and bordering Inner Mongolia, a barrier called the Willow Palisade was put up between about 1638 and 1672. The palisade encircled Fengtian's farmland, sometimes following the Ming Liaodong Wall and sometimes lying a little outside it, cutting the farmland off from Manchu forests to the northeast and Mongol pastures to the northwest.

Later the Qing tried to halt the flow of migrants into Fengtian, to send some settlers back, or, failing that, to legalise them. An edict of 1704 noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave and told them to register and join a local defence group (保, bao) or return to their home places within ten years. A decade later, naturally, another edict appeared, reminding officials that something had to be done about illegal migrants. The restrictions never worked as well as Beijing wanted, and the population of Fengtian still doubled from 1683 to 1734.

During the Qing dynasty, Manchuria was run by three generals. The one known as the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn) administered much of modern Liaoning. From 1860 the Manchu government started opening the region to migration again, and Han Chinese quickly became the main ethnic group there.
The main crops in Liaoning are maize, sorghum and soybeans, and cotton is grown as well. Around Dalian, farms supply three quarters of the apples and peaches that China exports.

Local fruit varies by area: Dalian and Yingkou for apples, Dalian again for golden peaches, Beizhen (in Jinzhou) for pears, Huludao and Suizhong for white pears, and Gushan (in Dandong) for apricots and plums.

Known as DLMU or DMU (大连海事大学), Dalian Maritime University stands in the port city of Dalian, Liaoning Province. It is a state university under the Ministry of Transport, and it belongs to two national programmes: Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme. For anyone interested in shipping, navigation or marine engineering, it is the best-known name in China.

The earliest roots lie in 1909, when a Shipping Management Section was opened by the Nanyang Institute, in Shanghai. In 1953 three merchant marine institutions were merged to form the present institution, namely Shanghai Nautical College, Fujian Navigation School and the Northeast Navigation College. Its first name was Dalian Marine College, and no other maritime college existed in China at that time. National key status for higher education came in 1960. A major international step followed in 1983: the UNDP (United Nations Development Program) and the IMO placed the Asia-Pacific Region Maritime Training Center here. In 1985 the campus also became home to a branch of the World Maritime University (WMU). The change to the current name happened in 1994.
On 6 June 2009 the university marked its hundredth anniversary. The main guest at the celebration was Chen Zhili, a vice chairman of the standing committee of the 11th National People's Congress.
Project 211 selected only about six percent of China's universities, and DMU is among them. The university has 14 colleges and departments.

Its present programme list is as follows: 42 undergraduate programmes, 2 first-class doctoral programmes and 12 second-class doctoral programmes, and 7 first-class master's programmes plus 59 second-class master's programmes. Transport Engineering, a first-class discipline, has a post-doctoral research and development base. DMU may award the MBA, MPA, J.M. and the Master of Engineering, which is a master's degree taken alongside a job.

Among its international ties, DMU is an active member of the University of the Arctic (UArctic), a cooperative network centred on the circumpolar Arctic. More than 200 universities, colleges and other bodies belong to it, all interested in advancing education and research about the Arctic.
Graduates of note include the following.
Chen Zhenggao
Qian Yongchang
Jin Yan
Your daily life as a student will depend on the city around campus, so this part introduces Dalian: its location, weather, economy, attractions and transport.

Dalian is one of the most heavily industrialised parts of China. The municipality now includes Dalian proper and, farther along the Liaodong Peninsula, the smaller Lüshunkou. This was once the city of Lüshun, which Western and Russian history books call Port Arthur. Records show that Dalniy (sometimes Dalney), a city planned by the Russians on the southern side of Dalian Bay, stood 40 kilometers (25 miles) from that place, which is now called Lüshunkou (literally Lüshun Port).

Dalian faces Korea Bay, to the north of the Yellow Sea, about halfway down the Liaodong Peninsula at the narrow neck of land (the isthmus). Its 1,906 km (1,184 mi) of coastline belongs to a territory covering most of the peninsula and some 260 islands and reefs offshore. The Yalu River is to the north-northeast, and the entrance to the harbour forms a sub-bay called Dalian Bay.

The climate is humid continental, influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa). Summers are warm and wet because of the East Asian monsoon, and winters are cold, windy and dry under the vast Siberian anticyclone. Apart from winter, the seasons arrive about a month late, because the city is on the Liaodong Peninsula.

The coldest month is January, averaging −3.3 °C (26.1 °F) across 24 hours, and the warmest is August, averaging 24.8 °C (76.6 °F). Over the year the mean is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F). Rain and snow total about 580 millimeters (22.8 in) in a typical year, falling mainly in summer and differing greatly from one year to another. Because the city is on the coast, the typical daily swing in temperature is small, 6.66 °C (12.0 °F) over the year. July gets only 45% of possible sunshine and March gets 66%, and the annual total is 2,625 hours of bright sunshine. Records going back to 1951 show a low of −21.1 °C (−6 °F) on 4 January 1970 and a high of 37.3 °C (99 °F) on 7 August 2026.
The 2010 census recorded 6.69 million people in Dalian. By the end of 2014 there were 5.943 million registered in households, a net rise of 29,000 on the year before.

Dalian's GDP had risen by double digits every year since 1992 until recently. In 2014 it increased by 5.8% to RMB 765.56 billion, with GDP per head at RMB 109,939. The National Bureau of Statistics, in a nationwide assessment, put Dalian eighth among Chinese cities for overall strength. Its leading industries are machinery, petrochemicals with oil refining, and electronics.

Dalian was at first an area of farming and aquaculture. After a ferry service began between Yantai and Lüshun in the early 20th century, farmers and fishermen from Shandong, on the far side of the Yellow Sea, began to settle here, in the period known as Chuang Guandong.

dalian-maritime-university.h: Heavy and light industry and distribution

blocks.x: Ships and locomotives were already being built in the city during the Second Sino-Japanese War and before it. Those workshops grew into what later became the Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and the Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (DLoco). When the Second World War ended, Dalian emerged as a major base for heavy and light industry (firms include Dalian Heavy Industry Co., Dalian Chemical Group and Wafangdian Bearing Co.) and for distribution, where the Dashang Group is a leading name.

International trade runs through Dalian Port, which is connected with over 300 ports across 160 countries and regions and has over 100 container shipping routes, both overseas and domestic. In 1976 a harbour for oil tankers was finished at the end of a pipeline from the Daqing oilfields; it is the biggest in China by tonnage. The port is sixth largest in China. As a result the city is a major centre for oil refining, diesel engineering and chemicals.

Another, newer harbour is Dayaowan Port (大窑湾港; pinyin Dàyáowān Gǎng), finished in 1993. Located on the Dagushan peninsula (大孤山) in the northern suburbs, it handles the import and export of mining and oil products. The city's rail stations (Dalian and Dalian North), its international airport and its expressways (Shenda to Shenyang, Changda to Changchun, Hada to Harbin, and a road eastward to Dandong) add to this, and together they make Dalian a significant distribution hub.

The Chinese government has favoured Dalian in several ways, including the title of "open-city" in 1984, which lets it attract considerable foreign investment (compare Special Economic Zone). Jinzhou District holds the Development Zone, which first drew many Japanese companies (Canon, Mitsubishi Electric, Nidec, Sanyo Electric, Toshiba) and was then joined by South Korean, American and European ones such as Pfizer. In 2007 Intel said it would build a semiconductor fabrication facility (a fab) in the Development Zone, its first fab on an entirely new site since 1992; it began operating in October 2010. Car manufacturers have plants here as well: Chery, the Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company, and BYD Automobile, whose Dalian base makes the BYD K9 electric bus.
Further zones include an Economic and Technological Development Zone, an Export Processing Zone, a Free Trade Zone and a Hi-Tech Industrial Zone, all with the Dalian name.

Northeast China's financial centre is Dalian. Branches of the five major Chinese banks operate here: Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, and the Industrial & Commercial Bank of China. A local bank, formerly the Dalian City Commercial Bank and now the Bank of Dalian, processes payments for the Dalian Mingzhu IC Card, the public transport card, among other things, and has branches in Shenyang, Beijing and Shanghai as well as five other cities.

The Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE) began in 1993. No other futures exchange exists in Northeast China, and the futures industry has grown quickly. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has approved 19 futures products for it, including these agricultural goods and industrial materials:
Farm goods: corn and corn starch, soybeans with their meal and oil, polished round-grained rice, RBD palm olein, and eggs
Plastics and chemicals: LLDPE (linear low-density polyethylene), PVC (polyvinyl chloride), PP (polypropylene), EG (ethylene glycol) and EB (ethenylbenzene)
Steel-related materials: metallurgical coke, coking coal and iron ore
Building boards: fiberboard and blockboard

Three options are also traded: on soybean meal, corn and iron ore. In 2019 the DCE traded 1,331 million lots, with turnover of RMB 68.92 trillion. The U.S. Futures Industry Association (FIA) placed it 11th among the world's exchanges by volume that year.

Since the 1990s the city has concentrated on information technology, particularly in the western suburbs near Dalian University of Technology, where the Hi-Tech Zone and the Software Park are located. More than 4,700 enterprises operate in the High-Tech Zone, a base for high technology, and 80 of them are Fortune Global 500 companies. Chinese firms like Neusoft Group, DHC and Hisoft are there beside American, European, Indian and Japanese ones: Wipro and Infosys, IBM and Dell, HP and Cisco, Ericsson, Accenture, Oracle, and Japan's Panasonic, Sony and Hitachi. Nine specialist business incubators, among them ones for hi-tech, animation and software start-ups, have helped over 400 companies. The next stage, the "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt", is being carried out and includes Dalian Software Park Phase 3.
Dalian is also the site of Intel's Fab 68. Announced on 26 March 2007, it began operations on 26 October 2010 and is Intel's first chip manufacturing plant in East Asia.

Dalian is a favourite with Chinese tourists and with visitors from abroad, and the largest groups of foreigners come from Japan, South Korea and Russia. Attractions include the gentle climate, a number of beaches and the role the city played in modern Chinese history. Among the best-known beaches are Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸), Fujiazhuang (付家庄), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Xinghai Bay (星海湾) and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子). In 2007 Dalian shared with Hangzhou and Chengdu the title "China's best tourist city", given by the China National Tourism Administration with the United Nations World Tourism Organization.
Russians first planned Zhongshan Square (中山广场) in the 19th century. It is best known today for the classical buildings around it, which the Japanese built during the earlier part of the 20th century.

Laohutan Ocean Park has a Polar Region Marine Animals World, a Coral Aquarium and a World of Birds, with a white whale and dolphin show as the main draw of the polar section. The Tigers Sculpture Square is close by; its tiger sculpture is the emblem of Tiger Beach (老虎滩; Lǎohǔtān). Visitors can also board a retired Anshan-class destroyer, the Taiyuan.
On Xinghai Bay is Xinghai Square (星海广场, which means 'Square of the Sea of Stars'). It dates from 1998, the centenary of the city, and is said to be the biggest city square anywhere.
Other attractions here include:
A geological park at Heishijiao, together with Dalian Natural History Museum
Sunasia Ocean World and the Dalian Forest Zoo
Dalian Sightseeing Tower
Donggang Music Fountain
The beach at Fujiazhuang

Bangchuidao Scenic Area is a carefully kept park that served as a State Guesthouse from 1960 and is now open to the public. New features include lush greenery, Chinese and Western-style villas, a hot spring, a recreation center, tennis and badminton courts, a golf course and a beach. Looking out from the beach you can see Bangchui Island (棒棰岛; Bàngchuí Dǎo), named for an islet shaped like a bangchui, an ancient washing tool. Many Chinese and foreign leaders and senior officials have stayed in this State Guesthouse. They include Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, as well as Kim Jong Un, Henry Kissinger, Boris Yeltsin, Gerhard Schröder and Juan Antonio Samaranch.

dalian-maritime-university.h: Jinzhou District and the Development Zone

blocks.x: In the northern suburbs, Dahei Mountain is one attraction. The district is also where you find the Jinshitan resort area (金石滩; Jīnshítān; literally 'Golden Pebble Beach'), with its national holiday resort and Discoveryland. The area has two peninsulas (east and west), open ground between them and a Golden Coast beach 16 kilometers (10 mi) long. Visitors can see a waxworks museum, a geological museum, a coastal national geopark, a vehicle campsite, Golden Rock Park, Wanfuding Park, a martial arts hall, a Mao Zedong badge exhibition hall and a model movie and TV art center. Leisure options include the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, a hunting club, an equestrian base, a convention center and resort, and two golf courses (Golden Pebble Golf Club and Golden Gulf Golf Course), as well as the Discoveryland Theme Park. Annual events in Jinshitan include the Dalian International Beach Carnival, the International Winter Swimming Festival and the Grape Festival.

The Discoveryland Theme Park (发现王国, sometimes translated "the Discovery Kingdom") was built in 2006. Its designers were Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, who also worked on the design of a Disney theme park.

Notable places in Lüshunkou include the Lüshun Museum and the old Lüshun Railway Station. History lovers can also visit East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山), Hill 203 and the Shuishiying Meeting Place, which saw the bloodiest fighting of the 1904–05 Battle of Lüshun in the Russo-Japanese War and where the ceasefire treaty was signed.

The prison now preserved as a museum, the Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum, was built by Russians in 1902 and later enlarged by the Japanese. During the Second World War it held people of many nationalities who opposed the Japanese invasion. The Korean independence activist An Jung-geun, who assassinated Itō Hirobumi, was imprisoned there and killed.

Animal lovers can visit the Lüshun Snake Museum, the Lüshun Bird Port and the Snake Island Reservation. Hengshan Temple (横山寺), next to Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库), dates to the Han dynasty and was rebuilt in 2003. Nearby is Longwangtang Cherry Blossom Park.
Pulandian District: Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场)
Wafangdian: Changxing Island International Golf Course
Zhuanghe: the Bingyu Valley Scenic Area, plus Buyun Mountain Hot Spring (步云山温泉)
Changhai County: the islands of Changhai County

Hot spring hotels are plentiful in Dalian. Two are in Lüshunkou District (Laotieshan and Tianmu), one is at Jinshitan (the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort), one is in Wafangdian (the Minghu Hot Spring Hotel) and one is in Ganjingzi District (the Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa).

More and more people ski here. Resorts include Linhai in Ganjingzi District, Anbo in Pulandian District, and the Minghu Ski Resort with its International Skiing Holiday Village in Wafangdian. Also in Ganjingzi District, near the airport, is Dalian Happy Snow World.
Dalian's roads are hilly, so cycling is less common than in other Chinese cities. As in a number of cities in China, local law forbids motorcycles in the downtown core, so you will see few there.

The city has a thorough bus network and an efficient metro. As of March 2023 the metro included underground Lines 1, 2 and 5 and overground Lines 3, 12 and 13; new lines and extensions, among them Lines 4 and 7, are being built. In time the new rail system is meant to connect the entire city. China's second oldest tram system is Dalian's, and the Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡) works on most public transport.
In 2006 China Daily chose Dalian as the most liveable city in China.

Four well-known venues are worth knowing. Music is the main fare at the Dalian People's Culture Club, and Beijing Opera is staged at Hongji Grand Stage. The Working People's Theater (工人剧院), also called Doudou Grand Stage (豆豆大舞台), is mostly for Errenzhuan, and the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院) completes the list.
In the city you also find a Chinese Academy of Sciences institute, the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics.
