Dalian Polytechnic University (大连工业大学, which translates as Dalian Industrial University) is a public institution in Dalian, a port city in Liaoning Province. It is a specialist school rather than a general one, so the sections below explain its history, its focus and the city and province around it.

Shenyang was where it all started: the Shenyang Institute of Light Industry (沈阳轻工业学院) opened there in 1958. Twelve years later, in 1970, the institute relocated to Dalian and was renamed the Dalian Institute of Light Industry (大连轻工业学院). It stayed a college until 2006, when it gained university status and adopted its present name.

Its niche is distinctive. No other higher education institution in northeastern China concentrates on light industry, food science, textiles and art design. Roughly 15,000 students attend, on a campus of 85 acres (340,000 m2). Engineering, science, arts, management and economics are all taught.

A case in 2025 attracted attention beyond the campus. The university expelled a woman student, giving the reasons as improper contact with a foreigner and harm to national dignity. Videos had circulated suggesting that she was intimate with a Ukrainian gamer, and the published notice gave her full name. Prospective international students should note how seriously conduct involving foreigners can be treated, and should read the university's rules closely.

Dalian ranks among the most heavily developed industrial areas in China. The municipality takes in two parts: Dalian proper, and smaller Lüshunkou farther down the Liaodong Peninsula. Lüshunkou was formerly the city of Lüshun, which Western and Russian sources call Port Arthur. Older references describe a Russian-planned town, Dalniy, on the south shore of Dalian Bay, 40 kilometres (25 miles) from Port Arthur, today's Lüshunkou (the name literally means Lüshun Port).

Geographically, the city sits on Korea Bay, which lies to the north of the Yellow Sea, about halfway along the Liaodong peninsula where its neck is narrowest. The shoreline measures 1,906 km (1,184 mi), and the municipality administers most of the peninsula along with some 260 islands and reefs. Its location is south-south-west of the Yalu River. The harbour entrance forms a secondary bay, called Dalian Bay.

Dalian's climate is humid continental, softened by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa). Expect warm, wet summers from the East Asian monsoon, and cold, windy and dry winters under the influence of the Siberian anticyclone. In every season except winter, the peninsula setting delays things by about a month.

The coldest month is January, when the daily mean is −3.3 °C (26.1 °F); the warmest is August, with 24.8 °C (76.6 °F). Averaged over twelve months, the figure is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F). About 580 millimetres (22.8 in) of rain fall in an average year, with most in summer and large swings between years. Because the sea moderates the weather, the average daily swing between highs and lows is only 6.66 °C (12.0 °F). Sunshine ranges from 45% of the possible amount in July to 66% in March, and the city receives 2,625 hours of bright sun annually. Since records began in 1951 the lowest reading was on 4 January 1970 (−21.1 °C, or −6 °F) and the highest on 7 August 2026 (37.3 °C, or 99 °F).
The 2010 census found 6.69 million people in the city. By the end of 2014, 5.943 million were registered in households, a net gain of 29,000 over the year before.

Growth has been quick. The National Bureau of Statistics ranks Dalian eighth among Chinese cities for overall strength. Leading sectors are machinery, petrochemicals with oil refining, and electronics.

The area was farmland and fishing grounds at first. When a ferry link between Yantai and Lüshun opened in the early 1900s, farmers and fishers from Shandong across the Yellow Sea started to move in, in the movement called Chuang Guandong.

Yards and works making ships and locomotives already stood in the city before the Second Sino-Japanese War and during it. Two of those later developed into the Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and the Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (DLoco). When the Second World War ended Dalian turned into a major centre for both heavy and light industry, represented by names like the Dalian Chemical Group, Wafangdian Bearing and Dalian Heavy Industry, and for distribution, led by the Dashang Group.

International trade passes through Dalian Port. It has shipping and trading links with more than 300 ports across 160 countries and regions, and over 100 domestic and international container services. A tanker harbour finished in 1976 is China's biggest by tonnage, and it lies at the end of a pipeline from the Daqing oilfields. The port is the sixth-largest in China. Data from the AAPA place it eighth in the world by cargo tonnage (2012) and twelfth by container volume in TEUs (2013). Refining, diesel engineering and chemicals are therefore major local industries.

A newer harbour, Dayaowan (大窑湾港, Dàyáowān Gǎng), was completed in 1993 on Dagushan (大孤山) Peninsula in the northern suburbs and concentrates on exports and imports of mining and oil products. The city is also a distribution hub through its main railway station, Dalian North station, the international airport, and two major expressways leading north to Shenyang (Shenda), Changchun (Changda) and Harbin (Hada), and east to Dandong.

Beijing has granted Dalian several advantages. It received the title of "open city" in 1984, which meant it could attract large amounts of foreign capital, similar to a Special Economic Zone. The city's Development Zone is located in Jinzhou District. Japanese companies led the way there, among them Toshiba, Sanyo Electric, Canon, Nidec and Mitsubishi Electric, and South Korean, American and European firms came after, Pfizer being one. Intel said in 2007 that it would build a semiconductor fab in the zone, its first on a completely new site since 1992, and it began production in October 2010. Dalian also contains car factories belonging to Chery, BYD Automobile (which builds BYD K9 electric buses) and the Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company.
Several other areas exist too: the Economic and Technological Development Zone, the Export Processing Zone, the Free Trade Zone and the Hi-Tech Industrial Zone.

Northeast China's financial centre is Dalian. Five of the country's largest banks have local branches: Industrial & Commercial Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, Agricultural Bank of China and China Construction Bank. The former Dalian City Commercial Bank is now the Bank of Dalian, which also handles the Dalian Mingzhu IC Card used on public transport and runs branches in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenyang and five further cities.

Since 1993 the city has hosted the Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE), Northeast China's sole futures exchange. Its business has expanded fast. The regulator, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, has approved 19 futures products. Farm and food contracts cover corn, corn starch, soybeans, soybean meal, soybean oil, RBD palm olein, polished round-grained rice and eggs. Plastics and chemicals include linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polypropylene (PP), ethylene glycol (EG) and ethenylbenzene (EB), while raw materials are metallurgical coke, coking coal and iron ore, and building boards are fiberboard and blockboard. Options are listed on soybean meal, corn and iron ore.

Information technology has been a priority for Dalian since the 1990s. The Hi-Tech Zone and the Dalian Software Park, both in the city's west and beside Dalian University of Technology, are the centres. The High-Tech Zone supports high-tech industry and holds more than 4,700 enterprises, of which 80 are in the Fortune Global 500. Chinese IT firms such as Neusoft Group, Hisoft and DHC are located there, together with Japanese, Indian, European and American companies including Cisco, Oracle, IBM, HP, Dell, Accenture, Wipro, Infosys, Ericsson, Panasonic, Sony and Hitachi. There are nine professional business incubators, among them the Hi-tech Business Incubator and some for animation and software, which have incubated over 400 companies. Under way now is the "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" project, which includes Phase 3 of the software park.
Intel's Fab 68 also stands in Dalian. The project was unveiled on 26 March 2007 and went into operation on 26 October 2010, which makes it Intel's first chip fabrication plant in East Asia.

Tourists arrive from across China and from overseas, notably Japan, Russia and South Korea. They are attracted by the mild climate and many beaches and by the city's significance in modern Chinese history. Beaches worth knowing include Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Fujiazhuang (付家庄), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Xinghai Bay (星海湾) and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子). Dalian shared a national and UN World Tourism Organization award in 2007 as one of three "China's best tourist city" choices, the others being Chengdu and Hangzhou.
Zhongshan Square (中山广场) was originally planned by the Russians in the 19th century. Its fame comes from the classical buildings that Japan put up around it in the early decades of the 1900s.

Laohutan Ocean Park has three main parts: a Coral Aquarium, a World of Birds and the Polar Region Marine Animals World. White whale and dolphin shows are the biggest crowd-pleaser in the polar section. Nearby is Tigers Sculpture Square, where a tiger statue represents Tiger Beach (老虎滩; Lǎohǔtān), and a retired Anshan-class destroyer called Taiyuan can be toured.
Xinghai Square (星海广场, "Square of the Sea of Stars") stands on Xinghai Bay. It was built to mark Dalian's 100th anniversary in 1998 and is billed as the biggest city square in the world.

Other places to visit are the Donggang Music Fountain, Fujiazhuang Beach, the Dalian Sightseeing Tower and Sunasia Ocean World, as well as the Dalian Forest Zoo and the Heishijiao Geological Park, where the Dalian Natural History Museum is found.

From 1960 Bangchuidao Scenic Area served as a State Guesthouse, and it has since been opened to the public with improvements. It offers lush gardens, villas in Chinese and Western styles, a hot spring, tennis and badminton courts, a recreation centre, a golf course and its own beach. From the shore you can see Bangchui Island (棒棰岛; Bàngchuí Dǎo), which is named after an islet shaped like an old laundry beater, a bangchui. While it was a guesthouse, its visitors included Chinese leaders (Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao, Xi Jinping) and foreign figures such as Kim Jong Un, Henry Kissinger, Boris Yeltsin, Gerhard Schröder and Juan Antonio Samaranch.

dalian-polytechnic-university.h: Jinzhou District and the Development Zone

blocks.x: Dahei Mountain lies here, and so does Jinshitan (金石滩, "Golden Pebble Beach"), a national holiday resort with the Discoveryland theme park. The resort consists of an east peninsula, a west peninsula, the flat land between them and a 16-kilometre (10 mi) beach called the Golden Coast. Sights include a waxworks museum, a geological museum, a coastal national geopark, an international vehicle campsite, Wanfuding Park, Golden Rock Park, the China Martial Arts Hall, the Mao Zedong Badge Exhibition Hall, a Model Movie & TV Art Center and the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort. For sport and leisure there are a hunting club, an equestrian base, an international convention centre and resort, and two golf courses (the Golden Gulf course and the Golden Pebble club). Each year hosts several themed events, including the Dalian International Beach Carnival, the International Winter Swimming Festival and the Grape Festival.

Discoveryland (发现王国, sometimes "Discovery Kingdom") opened in 2006. The source quotes a figure of 1,217,294 km2 (470,000 sq mi), which is obviously wrong for a theme park, so ask for the real figure. Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, a firm that helped to design a Disney theme park, planned it.

Southwest of the centre, Lüshunkou has the Lüshun Museum and the Lüshun Railway Station. Hill 203, East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山) and the Shuishiying Meeting Place were the scene of the most savage fighting in the Battle of Lüshun in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05), and of the signing of the ceasefire.

A prison museum, the Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum, occupies a building put up by Russia in 1902 and enlarged by Japan. In the Second World War inmates of various nationalities who resisted the Japanese invasion were held there. The Korean independence fighter An Jung-geun, who had assassinated Itō Hirobumi, was jailed and put to death at the prison.

You can also visit the Lüshun Snake Museum and the bird port and Snake Island reservation in Lüshun, and Hengshan Temple (横山寺), set by Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库) near a cherry blossom park. The temple is from the Han dynasty, though it was rebuilt in 2003.

Pulandian District offers the Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场). Wafangdian has the Changxing Island International Golf Course. Zhuanghe has hot springs on Buyun Mountain (步云山温泉) as well as the Bingyu Valley Scenic Area, and the islands of Changhai County are a further attraction.

Hot spring hotels are widespread. Four districts have well-regarded ones. Lüshunkou has the Laotieshan and Tianmu hot spring hotels, Jinshitan has the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, Wafangdian has the Minghu Hot Spring Hotel, and Ganjingzi has Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa.

Skiing is increasingly popular. Ganjingzi District has the Linhai Ski Resort and Dalian Happy Snow World, near the airport. Pulandian has Anbo Ski Resort, and in Wafangdian there are Minghu Ski Resort and its Minghu International Skiing Holiday Village.
Dalian's hilly roads discourage cycling, so it is less common than elsewhere in China. Local law also forbids riding motorcycles in the downtown area, which means few are seen there.

Buses cover the whole city and the metro is efficient. In March 2023 three underground lines (1, 2 and 5) and three overground ones (3, 12 and 13) were running, and extensions, including new Lines 4 and 7, were being built, in an effort to connect the entire city by rail. Dalian's tram network is China's second oldest, and the Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡) works on nearly all public transport.

In 2006 China Daily named Dalian the most liveable Chinese city. Among the main theatres, the Dalian People's Culture Club mostly stages music, Hongji Grand Stage puts on Beijing Opera, the Working People's Theater, also known as the Doudou Grand Stage (工人剧院/豆豆大舞台), mainly shows Errenzhuan, and the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院) completes the list.
A major research body in the city is the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Provinces shape student life as much as campuses do. This is Liaoning's story in order.

Between the 4th century BC and the 9th century AD, Han Chinese regimes mostly ruled Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived there. The state of Yan conquered the region about 300 BC and created two commanderies, Liaodong (the part east of the Liao River) and Liaoxi (the part to its west). Liaodong's centre, the Yan city of Xiangping, occupied the site of Liaoyang today. After the Han dynasty collapsed, a warlord, Gongsun Du, and his family ran a state that was semi-independent from Liaodong, also called Yan, until Cao Wei overthrew it in 238. Though short-lived, it sent out numerous maritime missions for diplomacy and commerce, and its effect on the culture of Northeast Asia endured. When the Western Jin came to an end, Liaoning passed to the Murong Xianbei, whose states were Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan. In 436 the Northern Wei captured Yan's capital and Goguryeo absorbed the Liaodong Peninsula. Later, in the Goguryeo-Tang War, the Tang annexed it.

By the middle of the 8th century the An Lushan Rebellion had pulled Tang resources away from its borderlands, and Bohai steadily advanced into Liaodong. The region was finally taken by the Khitan, whose Liao dynasty split it into the Eastern, Supreme, Central and Lower Capital Circuits, named Dongjingdao, Shangjingdao, Zhongjingdao and Xiajingdao.

Jurchen Jin rule put most of the land in the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu). Other parts went to the Xianping Route, the Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu) and the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it later became part of the Yuan dynasty. Under the Yuan, the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat administered the east (Liaoyang Route and Shenyang Route) and the west including Guangning Route. The north fell within Xianping Prefecture under Kaiyuan Route, whereas Jinzhou and Chaoyang were assigned to the Daning Route, which answered to the Central Secretariat.

The Ming took charge of Liaoning in 1371, three years after Mongol forces had been expelled from Beijing. A wall was erected about 1442 to shield the province's farmland from a possible attack from the northwest by the Oriyanghan, Jurchen-Mongol groups that were Ming tributaries. Between 1467 and 1468 the barrier was extended to the northeast as well, against raids by the Jianzhou Jurchens, who were later known as the Manchu. Although this "Liaodong Wall" served the same purpose as the Great Wall of China, it was built more cheaply: stone and tile were used in places, but mainly it was an earth bank with a moat on either side.

Even so, the Jurchens captured Liaodong, the eastern part of Liaoning, early in the 1600s, several decades ahead of the conquest of the rest of China. Their dynasty was called Later Jin before it became the Qing. Between 1616 and 1621 it was based at Xingjing (兴京), outside the Liaodong Wall in the east of modern Liaoning. The capital then went to Dongjing, east of present-day Liaoyang, and in 1625 to Shengjing, which is Shenyang today. The Qing made Beijing their main capital after taking it in 1644, but for most of their rule Shengjing was still a significant regional capital.

The Qing conquest depopulated Liaoning. Many Chinese residents died in the fighting, others ran south beyond the Great Wall, and the retreating Ming troops themselves destroyed many cities. A report from 1661 by Zhang Shangxian, then Fengtian's civil governor (Fuyin), gives a bleak picture. Apart from Fengtian City, which is Shenyang, plus Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city east of the Liao River was deserted or held a few hundred people at most; he described Tieling and Fushun as home to "a few vagrants". Only three places in the west, Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning, retained noticeable populations.

After laws issued in 1651 and 1653, during the later 17th century, the Qing government brought in settlers from south of the Great Wall, particularly Shandong, to populate Fengtian Province, a sparsely settled area corresponding roughly to modern Liaoning. Many people in Liaoning today descend from these 17th-century settlers. Officially, the rest of the Northeast stayed off limits to the Han for nearly all of the Manchu period. To keep them away from the lands that are now Jilin, Heilongjiang and neighbouring parts of Inner Mongolia, the Willow Palisade was built, around 1638 to 1672. It ran round the farming heartland of Fengtian, mostly just outside the earlier Ming wall or on top of it, dividing that farmland from the Manchu forests in the northeast and the Mongol pastures in the northwest.

Subsequently the Qing government tried to halt migration into Fengtian, to send some settlers home, or else to legalise them. An edict in 1704 observed that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave, and told them to register and join a local defence group (保; bao) or go back to their original homes within ten years. A decade later another edict reminded officials that something had to be done about illegal migrants. The restrictions were less effective than officials in Beijing wanted, and Fengtian's population doubled from 1683 to 1734.

During the Qing, three generals shared the government of Manchuria. One of them, titled General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn), had authority over most of what is now Liaoning. In 1860 the Manchu government started to open the region to migration again, and the Han soon became the dominant ethnic group.

Liaoning grows maize, sorghum, soybeans and some cotton. The area around Dalian is the source of three-quarters of China's apple and peach exports. Local fruit includes apples from Yingkou and Dalian, and Dalian's golden peaches. Pears come from Beizhen (Jinzhou), and white pears from Suizhong and Huludao, while Gushan in Dandong supplies apricots and plums.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

dalian-polytechnic-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Dalian Polytechnic University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Dalian, register at Dalian Polytechnic University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

dalian-university-of-foreign-languages.h: About Dalian University of Foreign Languages

blocks.x: The Dalian University of Foreign Languages (DLUFL; 大连外国语大学) is a provincial public university in Dalian, Liaoning, China. It is affiliated with the Liaoning Provincial People's Government.

Formerly known as Dalian School of Japanese Language, DLUFL was founded in 1964 with the help of the late Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai. It is now under the administration of the Education Commission of Liaoning Province. Through 40 years of development, DLUFL has fledged into a multi-disciplinary foreign language university which also offers programs in other fields like arts, economics, management, engineering and law.

In 2007, the university moved its main campus to Lüshunkou, formerly known as Lüshun Port, which, due to its enviable military harbor, was once the major theater for the Russo-Japanese War during 1904–1905. Lüshunkou or Lüshun／Lvshun, along with its twin sister city Dalian, was also part of the former colony of the Empire of Japan, with Lvshun hosting the headquarters of the Japanese Kwantung Army.

The university's old campus in downtown Dalian remained until 2013, when the School of Chinese Studies was also moved to Lüshunkou District. The Lüshun Campus boasts scenic views, spanning over 1,260,000 square meters (310 acres), with a building area of 500,000 square meters (120 acres).
The library of the university holds 765,000 copies of books and 600,000 electronic books with the electronic reading rooms.
Lüshunkou District, Dalian, No.6 Lüshun South Road (大连市旅顺口区旅顺南路)

With the help of the late Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, DLUFL was founded in 1964 to teach Japanese language, and in the 1970s, the English school and the Russian school were established. Other language departments were then established to meet the needs of the reform and opening up that began in 1978. In the mid-1980s, the university was authorized by Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China to offer postgraduate programs.
Among the 1,000 faculty and staff, 300 hold Professor or Associate Professor titles. Ten prominent professors receive the Special Allowances from the State Council.

DLUFL offers 20 bachelor programs, among which 10 lead to master programs. The 20 bachelor programs include Japanese, English, Russian, French, Korean, German, Spanish, Arabic, Portuguese, Italian, Chinese, Chinese Literature, Teaching Chinese as a Second language, Art Design, Tourism Management, International Economics & Trade, Computer Science & Technology, Information Management and Information Systems, Computer Software Engineering, Journalism and Music Studies are named key disciplines at the provincial level.
DLUFL administers over 20 language tests such as TOEFL, GRE, HSK, JLPT, BJT, KLPT, and WSK.
Liu Xiaoming, former Chinese Ambassador to the United Kingdom.
Chen Naiqing, former Chinese Ambassador to Norway; wife of former Chinese ambassador to the United States Zhang Yesui.
Yu Shayan, Deputy Governor of Heilongjiang Province, China.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Dalian, where Dalian University of Foreign Languages is located.

One of the most heavily developed industrial areas of China, the Dalian municipal area today consists of Dalian proper and the smaller Lüshunkou (formerly Lüshun city, known in Western and Russian historic references as Port Arthur), farther along the Liaodong Peninsula. Historical references note that the Russian-designed city of Dalniy (Alt. Dalney), on the south side of Dalian Bay, was 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Port Arthur/Lüshun (known today as Lüshunkou or literally, Lüshun Port).

Dalian is located on Korea Bay north of the Yellow Sea and roughly in the middle of the Liaodong peninsula at its narrowest neck or isthmus. With a coastline of 1,906 km (1,184 mi), it governs the majority of the Liaodong Peninsula and about 260 surrounding islands and reefs. It is situated at south-south-west of the Yalu River, and its harbor entrance forms a sub-bay known as Dalian Bay.

Dalian has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa), characterized by warm, wet summers due to the East Asian monsoon, and cold, windy, dry winters that reflect the influence of the vast Siberian anticyclone. Except for winter, the city experiences a one-month seasonal lag due to its position on the Liaodong Peninsula. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from −3.3 °C (26.1 °F) in January to 24.8 °C (76.6 °F) in August. Annual precipitation averages 580 millimeters (22.8 in) but is heavily concentrated in the summer months and can vary greatly from year to year. Due to the coastal location, the mean diurnal temperature variation annually is small, at 6.66 °C (12.0 °F). The monthly percent of possible sunshine ranges from 45% in July to 66% in March, with 2,625 hours of bright sunshine annually. The annual mean temperature is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −21.1 °C (−6 °F) on 4 January 1970 to 37.3 °C (99 °F) on 7 August 2026.
See or edit raw graph data.

The population of Dalian according to the 2010 census, totaled 6.69 million. The total registered population in households at year end 2014 was 5.943 million, with a net increase of 29,000 over the previous year.

The city has had a continuous annual double-digit percentage increase in GDP since 1992. In 2014, the city's GDP registered a 5.8% increase, reaching RMB 765.56 billion, while per capita GDP hit RMB 109,939. According to a nationwide appraisal by the National Bureau of Statistics, Dalian ranks eighth among Chinese cities in terms of overall strength. The city's main industries include machine manufacturing, petrochemicals and oil refining, and electronics.

Dalian was originally an agriculture and aquaculture-based area, which, after the opening of the ferry between Yantai and Lüshun during the early 20th century, began to be populated by the farmers and fishers of Shandong, across the Yellow Sea during the Chuang Guandong era.

Even before and during the Second Sino-Japanese War, the shipbuilding and locomotives industries were located in the city, such as the companies which later became Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (DLoco). After WWII, Dalian became an important center of the heavy and light industries, including companies such as Dalian Heavy Industry Co., Dalian Chemical Group, and Wafangdian Bearing Co., and of the distribution industry, such as the Dashang Group.

Dalian Port is an important port for international trade. It has established trading and shipping links with more than 300 ports in 160 countries and regions of the world. There are over 100 international and domestic container shipping routes. A harbor for oil tankers (the largest by tonnage in China), at the terminus of an oil pipeline from the Daqing oilfields, was completed in 1976. Dalian is the 6th largest port in China; and according to AAPA world port ranking data, Dalian is the 8th busiest port in the world by cargo tonnage in 2012, and the 12th busiest container port in the world by total number of TEUs handled in 2013. Accordingly, Dalian is a major center for oil refineries, diesel engineering, and chemical production.

Also completed in 1993 is a newer port called Dayaowan Port (Chinese: 大窑湾港; pinyin: Dàyáowān Gǎng), on Dagushan (大孤山; Dàgūshān) Peninsula in the northern suburbs, specializing in import-export of mining and oil products. Together with the Dalian railway station, Dalian North railway station, Dalian International Airport and two major express roads to Shenyang (Shenda Expressway), Changchun (Changda Expressway), Harbin (Hada Expressway) in the north and to Dandong to the east, Dalian has been an important distribution center.

Dalian has been given many benefits by the Chinese government, including the title of "open-city" (1984), which allows it to receive considerable foreign investment (see Special Economic Zone). The Development Zone was established in Jinzhou District, to which many Japanese companies, such as Canon, Mitsubishi Electric, Nidec, Sanyo Electric and Toshiba, followed by South Korean, American and European companies (such as Pfizer). In 2007, Intel announced plans to build a semiconductor fabrication facility (commonly known as a fab) in the Development Zone, Dalian. It is Intel's first fab to be built at an entirely new site since 1992. The facility began operation in October 2010. Dalian also houses auto-manufacturing plants for Chery, Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company, and BYD Automobile (a production base for BYD K9 electric buses).
Other zones in the city include the Dalian Economic and Technological Development Zone, Dalian Export Processing Zone, Dalian Free Trade Zone, and Dalian Hi-Tech Industrial Zone.

Dalian is the financial center of Northeast China. There are the Dalian branches of China's five major banks: Bank of China, Industrial & Commercial Bank of China, China Construction Bank, Bank of Communications, and Agricultural Bank of China. Dalian City Commercial Bank is now called Bank of Dalian, which, among other things handles processing of the Dalian Mingzhu IC Card for public transportation. Bank of Dalian has opened branches in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenyang, among five other cities.

Founded in 1993, Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE) is the only futures exchange in Northeast China. The futures industry leaped forward in its development. Among its 19 listed futures products approved by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) are corn, corn starch, soybeans, soybean meal, soybean oil, RBD palm olein, polished round-grained rice, linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polypropylene (PP), ethylene glycol (EG), ethenylbenzene (EB), metallurgical coke, coking coal, iron ore, egg, fiberboard and blockboard. 3 options are also listed for trading, which include soybean meal, corn, and iron ore options. In 2019, DCE achieved 1,331 million lots and RMB 68.92 trillion, respectively, in trading volume and turnover. According to the Futures Industry Association (FIA) of the U.S., DCE was the 11th largest exchange in the world by trading volume in 2019.

Since the 1990s, Dalian has emphasized the development of the IT industry, especially in Dalian Hi-Tech Zone and Dalian Software Park in the western suburbs near Dalian University of Technology. Dalian High-Tech Zone is the base of high-tech industries, housing more than 4,700 enterprises, including 80 Fortune Global 500 companies. Not only Chinese IT companies, such as DHC, Hisoft and Neusoft Group, but also American, European, Indian and Japanese IT companies are located there, including Wipro, Infosys, IBM, Dell, HP, Ericsson, Panasonic, Sony, Accenture, Oracle, Hitachi and Cisco. Nine professional business incubators are also located in the area, including the Hi-tech Business Incubator, animation and software incubators, with over 400 companies incubated. Currently, the "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" Plan is proceeding, including Dalian Software Park Phase 3.
Intel's Fab 68 is located in Dalian. The plan was announced on 26 March 2007, and operations started on 26 October 2010. It is Intel's first chip-manufacturing fabrication in East Asia.

Dalian is a popular destination among domestic tourists and foreign visitors, especially from Japan, South Korea, and Russia. Its mild climate and multiple beaches, as well as its importance in the modern history of China, have attracted tourists. Some of the most famous beaches are Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸) beach, Fujiazhuang (付家庄) beach, Bangchuidao (棒棰岛) beach, Xinghai Park (星海公园) beach, Xinghai Bay (星海湾) beach, and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子) beach. In 2007, it was one of the three cities named "China's best tourist city", along with Hangzhou and Chengdu, recognized by the National Tourism Administration and the United Nations World Tourism Organization.
Zhongshan Square

Originally designed by Russians in the 19th century, Zhongshan Square (中山广场) is especially noted for the several classical buildings located around the square built during the first half of the 20th century by the Japanese.

Laohutan Ocean Park: the park contains the Polar Region Marine Animals World, the Coral Aquarium, and the World of Birds. The white whale and dolphin show is a major attraction in the Polar Region Marine Animals World. The Tigers Sculpture Square is nearby, whose tiger sculpture is the symbol of Tiger Beach (老虎滩; Lǎohǔtān). A retired Anshan-class destroyer Taiyuan is open to visitors.
Xinghai Square: situated at the Xinghai Bay, Xinghai Square (星海广场; 'Square of the Sea of Stars') was built at the centennial of the City of Dalian (1998) and is the largest city square in the world.
Heishijiao Geological Park and Dalian Natural History Museum
Sunasia Ocean World
Dalian Forest Zoo

Bangchuidao Scenic Area: a well-maintained park used as a State Guesthouse since 1960, the Bangchuidao Scenic Area is now open to the public with upgraded features including lavish greens, Chinese and Western style villas, hot spring, tennis courts, badminton courts, a recreation center, a golf course and the Bangchuidao beach. The Bangchui Island (棒棰岛; Bàngchuí Dǎo, named for an islet in the shape of an ancient washing tool Bangchui) can be seen from the beach. As a State Guesthouse, the scenic area has received numerous Chinese and foreign leaders and high-profile officials, including Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao, Xi Jinping, Kim Jong Un, Henry Kissinger, Boris Yeltsin, Gerhard Schröder, Juan Antonio Samaranch and so on.

Jinshitan National Holiday Resort and the Discoveryland (Chinese: 金石滩; pinyin: Jīnshítān; lit. 'Golden Pebble Beach') is composed of eastern peninsula, western peninsula, open ground between two peninsulas and the 16-kilometer (10 mi) Golden Coast beach. Major sightseeing points include, Golden Pebble Waxworks Museum, Geological Museum, Coastal National Geopark, International Vehicle Campsite, Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, Golden Rock Park, Wanfuding Park, China Martial Arts Hall, Discoveryland Theme Park, Mao Zedong Badge Exhibition Hall, Model Movie & TV Art Center, Golden Pebble Hunting Club, Golden Pebble Equestrianism Base, Golden Pebble International Convention Center & Resort, Golden Pebble Golf Club, and Golden Gulf Golf Course. Cycling is not as popular in Dalian as in other Chinese cities because of the hilly roads. Dalian is also one of the many cities in China where there are few motorcycles in the downtown core, where motorcycle riding is prohibited by the local law.

The city has a comprehensive bus system and an efficient metro system. As of March 2023, the Dalian Metro consists of the underground Line 1, Line 2, Line 5 and the overground Line 3, Line 12 and Line 13. New lines and expansion of the metro system are under way including Line 4 and Line 7. The new rail traffic system is designed to connect the entire city in the coming future. dalian-university-of-foreign-languages.h: How to apply, step by step

After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.

dalian-university-of-technology.h: Dalian University of Technology in brief

blocks.x: Dalian University of Technology (DLUT, written DUT in some sources) is a public university located in Ganjingzi District, Dalian, in China's Liaoning Province. It answers to the Ministry of Education, and it belongs to the Double First-Class Construction scheme as well as the earlier national programmes, Projects 985 and 211. The university dates from 1949.

Its faculty includes some of the country's most senior scientists. As of August 2021, the full-time staff counted 13 members of the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering, and part-time staff added 38 more. Besides these, the university is linked to one foreign member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, one member of the Swedish Royal Academy of Engineering Sciences, and ten people who sit on the State Council's Academic Degrees Committee review group for disciplines.
This profile first covers a notable partnership with Intel, and then moves outwards to Dalian, the coastal city where you will live, and to Liaoning, the province it belongs to.

In 2007 the Dalian municipal government, Intel and DLUT jointly set up the Dalian Institute of Semiconductor Technology, which DLUT manages. Intel gave the university a production line for 8-inch chips, worth US$36 million altogether. For students interested in microelectronics, a university-run semiconductor institute with an industrial production line is an unusual asset.

dalian-university-of-technology.h: Dalian: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life at DLUT depends on Dalian itself, so the next sections describe its geography, climate, population, economy, tourism, transport and culture.

Dalian is among the most heavily industrialised areas of China. Today's municipal area is made up of Dalian proper and a smaller district further down the Liaodong Peninsula, Lüshunkou, which used to be the city of Lüshun and appears in Western and Russian history as Port Arthur. Older records mention Dalniy (also spelled Dalney), a town the Russians planned on the southern shore of Dalian Bay and which lay 40 kilometres (25 miles) from Port Arthur, the place now called Lüshunkou, literally "Lüshun Port".

Dalian faces Korea Bay, which is to the north of the Yellow Sea, and sits near the centre of the Liaodong Peninsula at the point where the land narrows into an isthmus. Dalian's coastline runs for 1,906 km (1,184 mi), and its jurisdiction takes in most of the peninsula and about 260 nearby islands and reefs. It lies south-south-west of the Yalu River, and the harbour entrance forms a sub-bay called Dalian Bay.

The climate is monsoon-influenced humid continental (Köppen Dwa). Summers are warm and wet because of the East Asian monsoon, while winters are cold, windy and dry under the vast Siberian anticyclone. Apart from winter, the seasons arrive about a month late, a result of the city's position on the Liaodong Peninsula.
Key figures:
January is the coldest month, with a 24-hour average of -3.3 °C (26.1 °F), and August the warmest at 24.8 °C (76.6 °F). The mean for the whole year is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F).
Yearly rainfall averages 580 millimetres (22.8 in), packed into the summer months and varying a lot from one year to the next.
The sea keeps the daily swing between warmest and coolest hours modest: 6.66 °C (12.0 °F) on average across the year.
Possible sunshine is 45% in July and 66% in March, giving 2,625 hours of bright sunshine a year.
Records since 1951 run from -21.1 °C (-6 °F), logged on 4 January 1970, up to 37.3 °C (99 °F), logged on 7 August 2026.
The 2010 census put the population of Dalian at 6.69 million. At the end of 2014 there were 5.943 million registered residents, 29,000 more than the year before.

Since 1992 the city's GDP has grown by double-digit percentages every year. In 2014 growth slowed to 5.8%, bringing GDP to RMB 765.56 billion, or RMB 109,939 per person. In the National Bureau of Statistics' national assessment of overall strength, Dalian comes eighth among Chinese cities. The leading industries are electronics, petrochemicals and refining, and the building of machinery.

Dalian began as a farming and aquaculture area. In the early 20th century a ferry opened between Yantai and Lüshun, and farmers and fishermen from Shandong, across the Yellow Sea, began to settle the area in the migration known as Chuang Guandong.

dalian-university-of-technology.h: Heavy industry, light industry and distribution

blocks.x: The city already built ships and locomotives before and during the Second Sino-Japanese War, through firms that went on to become Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (DLoco). Once the Second World War ended, it turned into a leading centre of both heavy and light industry (Dalian Chemical Group, Wafangdian Bearing Co. and Dalian Heavy Industry Co. are examples) and also of distribution, where the Dashang Group is prominent.

Dalian Port matters for international trade. Shipping and trade connections reach more than 300 ports across 160 countries and regions, and over 100 container routes, domestic and international, start here. An oil-tanker harbour, the biggest in China by tonnage and the end of the pipeline from the Daqing oilfields, was finished in 1976. Dalian is China's sixth-largest port. The AAPA world port rankings listed it as the world's eighth busiest port for cargo tonnage (2012) and twelfth busiest for container volume in TEUs (2013). That is why the city is a big centre for oil refining, diesel engineering and chemicals.

A newer port, Dayaowan Port (大窑湾港, Dàyáowān Gǎng), also opened in 1993 on the Dagushan (大孤山, Dàgūshān) Peninsula in the northern suburbs and specialises in mining and oil products for import and export. Add two railway stations (Dalian and Dalian North), Dalian International Airport and the expressways that lead to Shenyang (Shenda), Changchun (Changda) and Harbin (Hada) in the north and to Dandong in the east, and the ports help make Dalian a significant distribution hub.

The central government has given Dalian many advantages, including the 1984 title of "open city", which lets it receive large amounts of foreign investment (see Special Economic Zone). A Development Zone in Jinzhou District drew in Japanese companies first (Toshiba, Sanyo Electric, Nidec, Mitsubishi Electric and Canon among them) and then South Korean, American and European ones, Pfizer for example. Intel announced in 2007 a semiconductor fabrication plant (a "fab") in the zone, its first fab at a wholly new location since 1992, and it began operating in October 2010. Cars are made here as well, by BYD Automobile (which uses its Dalian base for BYD K9 electric buses), Chery and the Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company.
Four more zones round out the picture: an economic and technological development zone, an export processing zone, a free trade zone and a hi-tech industrial zone.

Dalian is the financial centre of Northeast China. The five big state banks all have Dalian branches (Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, Industrial & Commercial Bank of China and Bank of China). The local lender, formerly Dalian City Commercial Bank and now the Bank of Dalian, also handles processing for the Mingzhu IC Card used on public transport; it has opened branches in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenyang and five further cities.

Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE), founded in 1993, is the one futures exchange in China's northeast, and the futures industry has grown quickly. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has authorised 19 futures products. Agricultural ones include soybeans, soybean meal and soybean oil, corn and corn starch, RBD palm olein, polished round-grained rice and eggs; industrial ones include iron ore, metallurgical coke, coking coal, fibreboard, blockboard, and the plastics and chemicals linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polypropylene (PP), ethylene glycol (EG) and ethenylbenzene (EB). Three options contracts, covering soybean meal, corn and iron ore, are traded too. Trading volume in 2019 was 1,331 million lots, with turnover of RMB 68.92 trillion. The U.S. Futures Industry Association (FIA) ranked it the world's eleventh largest exchange by trading volume that year.

Since the 1990s Dalian has pushed the IT industry, particularly in the Dalian Hi-Tech Zone and Dalian Software Park in the western suburbs close to DLUT. The High-Tech Zone houses more than 4,700 enterprises, among them 80 Fortune Global 500 companies. Chinese IT firms such as DHC, Hisoft and Neusoft Group are based there, as are American, European, Indian and Japanese companies including Wipro, Infosys, IBM, Dell, HP, Ericsson, Panasonic, Sony, Accenture, Oracle, Hitachi and Cisco. Nine professional business incubators operate in the area, among them a hi-tech incubator and animation and software incubators, which have incubated over 400 companies. The "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" plan is in progress and includes Dalian Software Park Phase 3.
Intel's Fab 68 is in Dalian. Announced on 26 March 2007, it started production on 26 October 2010 and was Intel's first chip-making fab in East Asia.

Visitors come from within China and abroad, with Japanese, South Korean and Russian tourists especially common; the draw is a mild climate, plenty of beaches and a significant place in modern Chinese history. Well-known beaches include Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸), Fujiazhuang (付家庄), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Xinghai Bay (星海湾) and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子). Dalian shared the 2007 title of "China's best tourist city" with Hangzhou and Chengdu, an award from the national tourism authority and the UN's tourism body.
Zhongshan Square (中山广场): Russians designed it in the 1800s, and it is noted for several classical-style buildings erected around it by the Japanese in the early 1900s.

Laohutan Ocean Park: its sections include a Coral Aquarium, a World of Birds and the Polar Region Marine Animals World, where a white whale and dolphin show is the biggest attraction. The nearby Tigers Sculpture Square has a tiger that stands for Tiger Beach (老虎滩, Lǎohǔtān), and a retired Anshan-class destroyer, the Taiyuan, can be visited.
Xinghai Square (星海广场, "Square of the Sea of Stars"): beside Xinghai Bay, it was built in 1998 to mark the city's hundredth anniversary and is said to be the world's largest city square.
Heishijiao Geological Park, together with the Dalian Natural History Museum
Sunasia Ocean World
Dalian Forest Zoo

Bangchuidao Scenic Area: a well-kept park used as a State Guesthouse from 1960 that is now open to the public, with greenery, Chinese and Western villas, a hot spring, tennis and badminton courts, a recreation centre, a golf course and the Bangchuidao beach. The offshore Bangchui Island (棒棰岛, Bàngchuí Dǎo) is named for its resemblance to an old laundry tool, the bangchui. In its guesthouse years it received leaders and high officials from China and overseas: Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin; Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping; Kim Jong Un; Henry Kissinger; Boris Yeltsin; Gerhard Schröder; and Juan Antonio Samaranch.
Dalian Sightseeing Tower
Donggang Music Fountain
Fujiazhuang Beach

blocks.x: Dahei Mountain

Jinshitan National Holiday Resort and Discoveryland (金石滩, Jīnshítān, "Golden Pebble Beach"): it has an eastern peninsula, a western peninsula, open ground between the two and the 16-kilometre (10 mi) Golden Coast beach. The sights are varied. For museums and learning there are a waxworks museum, a geological museum, a coastal national geopark, a martial arts hall, a Mao Zedong badge exhibition hall and a model movie and TV art centre. For outdoor leisure there are Golden Rock Park, Wanfuding Park, an international vehicle campsite, the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, the Discoveryland theme park, a hunting club and an equestrian base. Business and golf visitors have the International Convention Center & Resort, the Golden Pebble Golf Club and the Golden Gulf Golf Course. Yearly events include the Dalian International Beach Carnival, the International Winter Swimming Festival and the Grape Festival.
Discoveryland Theme Park (发现王国, or "the Discovery Kingdom"): opened in 2006 and designed by Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, a firm that took part in designing a Disney theme park.
Lüshun Museum
Lüshun Railway Station

Hill 203, East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山) and the Shuishiying Meeting Place: the location of the most intense fighting, and of the ceasefire signing, when the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905 reached Lüshun.

Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum: the Russians built the prison in 1902 and the Japanese enlarged it. During the Second World War it held people of various nationalities who resisted Japan's invasion. The Korean independence activist An Jung-geun, who killed Itō Hirobumi, was held here and put to death.
Lüshun Snake Museum, plus the bird port and the Snake Island nature reserve

Pulandian District: Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场)

Hot spring hotels are plentiful. In Lüshunkou District there are Laotieshan and Tianmu; Jinshitan has the Tang Dynasty resort; Wafangdian has Minghu; and in Ganjingzi District you will find the Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa.

More and more people ski, too. In Ganjingzi District, the Linhai Ski Resort and the Happy Snow World, which is near the airport, are well known. Pulandian District has the Anbo resort, and Wafangdian has Minghu, a ski resort with an international skiing holiday village.
Hilly roads mean cycling is less common than in many Chinese cities. Local law also bans motorcycles in the downtown core, so, as in several other Chinese cities, there are few of them there.

The city has a thorough bus network and an efficient metro. The metro, as it stood in March 2023, has three underground lines (1, 2 and 5) and three overground ones (3, 12 and 13), and builders are working on new lines (4 and 7, among them) and extensions. The new rail system is designed to link the whole city in future. Dalian's tram is China's second oldest. Most public transport can be paid for with the Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡).

China Daily picked Dalian in 2006 as China's most liveable city. The main theatres are the Dalian People's Culture Club (mostly music), Hongji Grand Stage (Beijing Opera), the Working People's Theater, also called the Doudou Grand Stage (工人剧院/豆豆大舞台), mostly for Errenzhuan and the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院). Research is represented by the Chinese Academy of Sciences' institute of chemical physics, located in the city.

dalian-university-of-technology.h: Liaoning: the province beyond the city

blocks.x: A university's region shapes student life as much as its campus does, so here is a brief history and economic picture of Liaoning.

dalian-university-of-technology.h: Early rulers, from Yan to Tang

blocks.x: From the 4th century BC until the 9th century, Han Chinese governments mostly ruled Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived there, and around 300 BC it was taken by the state of Yan. Yan organised the region into Liaodong, meaning "east of the Liao River", and Liaoxi, "west of the Liao River", both commanderies. Its city of Xiangping, the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is now. When the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family kept a semi-independent state, also called Yan, in Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Although short-lived, this state ran many maritime diplomatic and trading missions and left a lasting mark on Northeast Asian culture. After the Western Jin ended, the Murong tribe's Xianbei states governed Liaoning, namely Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan. In 436, after Northern Wei took the Yan capital, Goguryeo took over the Liaodong Peninsula, and the Tang dynasty annexed it during the Goguryeo-Tang War.

The An Lushan Rebellion in the mid 8th century drained Tang resources from the frontiers, and the Bohai state gradually moved into Liaodong. The Khitan Liao dynasty then conquered Liaoning and divided it among four circuits: Eastern Capital (Dongjingdao), Supreme Capital (Shangjingdao), Central Capital (Zhongjingdao) and Lower Capital (Xiajingdao).

The Jurchen Jin dynasty administered most of the land as the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu). Three other routes shared the remainder: Xianping, Shangjinglu (Supreme Capital) and Beijinglu (Northern Capital). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it was later part of the Yuan dynasty. In the east the Liaoyang Route and Shenyang Route came under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; the north was Xianping Prefecture of the Kaiyuan Route; the west, including the Guangning Route, was also under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; while Jinzhou and Chaoyang lay in the Daning Route, answerable to the Central Secretariat.

The Ming Empire took Liaoning in 1371, three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. Around 1442 the Ming built a defensive wall to shield the province's farmland from the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group (and Ming tributaries) who might threaten from the northwest. During 1467 and 1468 it was lengthened to cover the northeast as well, against the Jianzhou Jurchens, who later became the Manchu. The "Liaodong Wall" had the same purpose as the Great Wall of China but was cheaper to build: some stretches used stone and tile, but most of it was an earth dike with a moat on each side.

Even so, the Jurchens captured Liaodong, the eastern part of Liaoning, early in the 17th century, many decades ahead of their conquest of the rest of China. Their dynasty, first styled Later Jin and later renamed Qing, made Xingjing (兴京) its capital from 1616 to 1621. Xingjing lay outside the Liaodong Wall in what is now eastern Liaoning. It then moved to Dongjing (east of present-day Liaoyang) and, in 1625, to Shengjing, which is now Shenyang. Beijing fell to the Qing in 1644 and became the main capital, but Shengjing remained an important regional capital for most of the Qing era.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning much of its population. Some Chinese residents were killed in the fighting and others escaped to the south side of the Great Wall; the withdrawing Ming army itself wrecked many cities. As he put it, "Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants". West of the river, just Guangning, Jinzhou and Ningyuan kept any sizeable population.

In the second half of the 17th century, beginning with laws of 1651 and 1653, the Qing recruited settlers from south of the Great Wall, especially Shandong, for the thinly populated Fengtian Province (roughly today's Liaoning). Many present-day Liaoning residents trace their ancestry to these 17th-century settlers. Elsewhere in the Northeast, Han Chinese were officially barred from settling through most of Manchu rule. A barrier called the Willow Palisade, built from about 1638 to about 1672, was meant to keep them out of what are now Jilin, Heilongjiang and adjoining Inner Mongolia. It circled Fengtian's farmland, sometimes following the line of the Ming Liaodong Wall and sometimes reusing it, and set that land apart from Manchu woodland in the northeast and Mongol pasture in the northwest.

Later the Qing tried to halt the flow of migrants into Fengtian, to send some settlers home, or else to make their presence legal. An edict of 1704 observed that recent Han settlers had not obeyed earlier orders to leave, and told them either to register and join a local defence group (保, bao) or to go back to their original homes within ten years. Ten years on, another edict reminded officials that illegal migrants needed handling. Officials in Beijing never got the results they wanted: from 1683 to 1734 the population of Fengtian actually doubled.

Manchuria was run by three generals in the Qing period, and most of modern Liaoning fell to the one at Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn). Migration was reopened from 1860, and before long Han Chinese were the region's dominant group.

The main crops are maize, sorghum and soybeans, and cotton is also grown. Dalian's surroundings account for three-quarters of the apples and peaches China exports. Named local fruits are apples (Dalian and Yingkou), golden peaches (Dalian), pears (Beizhen in Jinzhou, plus white pears from Huludao and Suizhong), and Gushan in Dandong for apricots and plums.

Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Dalian, register at Dalian University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

DUFE, short for Dongbei University of Finance and Economics (东北财经大学), is a public university run by the province, in the city of Dalian in Liaoning. Over 17,000 students study there, and it counts among Dalian's oldest and largest modern universities. Teaching and research go together, and the main subject areas are economics, management and law, plus arts and sciences. Both full-time and part-time study are available.

The full-time offering is large. Researchers who have already finished a doctorate can work at three first-level mobile stations, covering theoretical economics, applied economics and business administration. Below that level, students choose among 80 master's degree programs and 48 PhD programs (these include the MBA, MPA, MPAcc and J.M.) and 43 undergraduate programs.

The state singles out several disciplines for support. Industrial economics, accounting and public finance (taxation included) are key state-sponsored disciplines, while quantitative economics is a key state-supported discipline. Twenty-five undergraduate majors, among them statistics, finance, accounting and business administration, are part of the state-level first-class construction program.
The university is organised into many units, which can be grouped by theme.
Economics, finance and accounting:
School of Economics

International students will deal first with the School of International Education, which houses the International Students Office.

Students come from all 31 provinces of China, and the international community comes from more than 30 countries. Entry is competitive: the average national college entrance exam (gaokao) result of its new students always ranks in Liaoning's top three. Graduate employment is high too, at over 95%.

DUFE's International Education Center helps students gain an international perspective, including those who stay in China. Partnerships have expanded to 13 exchange programs involving nine universities in six countries. Places mentioned in connection with these links are Korea, Japan, Germany, the UK, Ireland, Austria, Canada and Australia. Examples of joint programs:
DUFE-Curtin University: a 3+1 year Bachelor's program in Accounting
DUFE-Ulster University: a 4+0 year Bachelor's program in Accounting
DUFE-Ulster University: a 4+0 year Bachelor's program in Finance
DUFE-University of Western Ontario (King's University College): a 2+2 year Bachelor's program in Economics
DUFE-Surrey International Institute: master's and undergraduate exchange programs with the University of Surrey, UK
DUFE is proud of its student athletes and is designated a national base for the development of college sport. Some results:

Men's football: four consecutive titles in China's collegiate men's football champions tournament, one win and two runner-up finishes in the "Phillips Cup" of China's men's collegiate champions league, and the championship of the Asia-Pacific University Men's soccer invitational.
Men's basketball: a powerful side in CUBA, the China University Basketball Association, winner of numerous city and provincial titles and a third-place finisher at the national finals.
Track and field: second overall at the Asia University Track and Field Invitational, and first at the ninth China National University Field and Track Games.
Among its alumni are athletes and coaches linked with Olympic gold medalists, world champions, world record holders and numerous national champions.

DUFE is one of China's top schools in its field, and its graduates hold senior positions in government and industry, particularly in banking and finance. It carries real weight across the northeast and nationally. In the 2022 Best Chinese Universities Ranking, it came first in Northeast China and sixth nationwide among universities specialising in finance, business and economics. It also placed among the world's top 400 universities for "Management" and for "Hospitality & Tourism Management".
The alumni network is a strong reason to study here. Many graduates now hold senior posts in public life and finance:
Chen Zhenggao, who serves as Governor of Liaoning Province
Li Wancai, the Mayor of Dalian
Xia Deren, Deputy Party Secretary of Liaoning, formerly both President of DUFE and Mayor of Dalian
Lu Xin, a Deputy Minister at China's Ministry of Education
Dong Dasheng, a deputy director of the National Audit Bureau
Xie Xuezhi, a deputy director at the National Tax Authority
Meng Jianmin, a deputy director of the State Assets Supervision and Administration Commission
Wang Wenyuan, once a vice chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference
Zheng Zhijie, head of the China National Development Bank as its President, with Liu Kegu and Yao Zhongmin both serving as Vice Presidents there
Ma Yongwei, a banker and politician who formerly chaired the China Insurance Regulatory Commission, and Zhou Yanli, who has been one of its vice chairmen
Zhuang Xinyi, vice chairman at the China Securities Regulatory Commission
Wang Hongzhang, chairman of the China Construction Banking Group
Tang Shuangnin, who chairs the China Everbright Banking Group
Wang Xianzhang, chairman of the China Insurance Society and previously Chairman and CEO of the China Life Insurance Group
How you spend your days depends on the city beyond the campus: its weather, its transport and its leisure options. The sections below introduce Dalian.

Few places in China are as industrially developed as Dalian. Today's municipal area covers Dalian itself and the smaller Lüshunkou, further down the Liaodong Peninsula. Lüshunkou used to be Lüshun city, and appears as Port Arthur in Western and Russian history books. Older accounts mention the Russian-planned city of Dalniy (also spelled Dalney) on the south shore of Dalian Bay. Port Arthur, which is Lüshun, lay 40 kilometers (25 miles) away, now called Lüshunkou, a name that literally means Lüshun Port.

The city looks onto Korea Bay, which is north of the Yellow Sea, and stands roughly halfway along the Liaodong Peninsula at its narrowest point, the isthmus. Its coastline stretches for 1,906 km (1,184 mi). Dalian administers most of the peninsula as well as about 260 islands and reefs offshore. The Yalu River is to its north-north-east, and the harbour mouth creates a smaller bay named Dalian Bay.

The climate is humid continental, influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa). Summers are warm and wet because of the East Asian monsoon, and winters are cold, windy and dry under the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone. Outside winter, the seasons run about a month late because of the city's position on the Liaodong Peninsula.
Figures worth noting:
Monthly mean temperatures go from -3.3 °C (26.1 °F) at the coldest, in January, and a warmest month of August at 24.8 °C (76.6 °F). The yearly mean stands at 11.8 °C (53.2 °F).
Annual rainfall averages 580 millimeters (22.8 in), mostly in summer and varying widely from year to year.
The sea keeps day-to-night swings small: on average the daily range is only 6.66 °C (12.0 °F).
Possible sunshine is 45% in July and 66% in March, adding to 2,625 hours of bright sunshine a year.
Extremes recorded since 1951 are a low of -21.1 °C (-6 °F) on 4 January 1970 and the highest reading, 37.3 °C (99 °F), came on 7 August 2026.
Dalian's population was 6.69 million in the 2010 census. By the end of 2014 the registered household population was 5.943 million, up by 29,000 on the year before.

Dalian's GDP has increased by double digits every year since 1992. In 2014 it grew 5.8% to RMB 765.56 billion, and GDP per capita reached RMB 109,939. The National Bureau of Statistics assessed Chinese cities, and Dalian came eighth among Chinese cities for overall strength. Its leading sectors are electronics, machinery, petrochemicals and refining.

Dalian was originally based on farming and aquaculture. In the early 20th century a ferry opened between Yantai and Lüshun, and farmers and fishers from Shandong, across the Yellow Sea, began to settle the area during the Chuang Guandong era.

The city already built ships and locomotives around the time of the Second Sino-Japanese War, in companies that were the forerunners of the Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and of DLoco (Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works). The postwar years made Dalian a significant heavy and light industry centre, with firms such as Wafangdian Bearing Co., Dalian Chemical Group and Dalian Heavy Industry Co. It also became a distribution hub, represented by the Dashang Group.

Dalian Port is a major international trading port. It is connected by trade and shipping to over 300 ports across 160 countries and regions, and runs more than 100 container routes, both international and domestic. In 1976 a harbour for oil tankers, China's biggest by tonnage, was completed where the pipeline from the Daqing oilfields ends. Dalian is the sixth largest port in China. Figures from the AAPA put it eighth in the world for cargo tonnage in 2012, and twelfth for container traffic, measured in TEUs, in 2013. It is, as a result, a major centre for oil refining, diesel engineering and chemical production.

A newer port, Dayaowan Port (大窑湾港; Dàyáowān Gǎng), was completed in 1993 in the northern suburbs, on the Dagushan peninsula (大孤山; Dàgūshān), and handles mining and oil cargo going in and out. Rail stations (Dalian and Dalian North), an international airport and express roads complete the picture. The Shenda Expressway goes to Shenyang, the Changda to Changchun and the Hada to Harbin in the north, and another road goes east to Dandong. All this makes Dalian an important distribution centre.

Beijing has favoured Dalian in many ways, notably by naming it an "open-city" in 1984, which let the city take in a great deal of foreign investment (compare Special Economic Zones). The Development Zone, set up in Jinzhou District, first attracted Japanese firms including Canon, Toshiba, Nidec, Sanyo Electric and Mitsubishi Electric. South Korean, American and European companies followed, Pfizer among them.

In 2007 Intel said it would build a semiconductor fabrication plant (known as a fab) within Dalian's Development Zone, and production began in October 2010. No other Intel fab had been built from scratch on a new site since 1992. Car manufacturing is here too, with plants run by Chery, by BYD Automobile (a base for the BYD K9 electric bus) and by Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company.
More zones exist, namely the Economic and Technological Development Zone, the Export Processing Zone, the Free Trade Zone and the Hi-Tech Industrial Zone.

For a finance and economics student the following is especially relevant. Northeast China's financial centre is Dalian. The five major national banks all have branches here: Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, and Industrial & Commercial Bank of China. The former Dalian City Commercial Bank, renamed Bank of Dalian, also handles the processing for the Dalian Mingzhu IC Card used on public transport, and it has branches in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenyang and five further cities.

The Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE), founded in 1993, is Northeast China's only futures exchange, and the futures business has grown quickly. The CSRC has approved 19 futures products for listing. They fall into groups: farm goods (soybeans, soybean meal, soybean oil, corn, corn starch, eggs, RBD palm olein and polished round-grained rice); plastics and chemicals (linear low-density polyethylene or LLDPE, polyvinyl chloride or PVC, polypropylene or PP, ethylene glycol or EG, and ethenylbenzene or EB); materials for steelmaking (metallurgical coke, coking coal and iron ore); and building boards (fiberboard and blockboard). Options on three of these (soybean meal, corn and iron ore) are traded as well. During 2019 the DCE handled 1,331 million lots with a turnover of RMB 68.92 trillion, and the US-based Futures Industry Association (FIA) placed it 11th worldwide by volume in that year.

Information technology has been a priority since the 1990s, above all in the Hi-Tech Zone and Software Park in the western suburbs, close to Dalian University of Technology. The High-Tech Zone houses more than 4,700 enterprises, 80 of which are Fortune Global 500 companies. Domestic names include Neusoft Group, DHC and Hisoft, and foreign ones come from the USA, Europe, India and Japan: Wipro, Infosys, IBM, Dell, HP, Ericsson, Cisco, Oracle, Accenture, Panasonic, Sony and Hitachi. Nine professional business incubators, among them the Hi-tech Business Incubator and incubators for animation and software, have supported over 400 companies. Meanwhile Phase 3 of Dalian Software Park forms part of the "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" plan, which is going ahead.
Intel's Fab 68 is in Dalian. Announced on 26 March 2007, the fab opened on 26 October 2010 and became Intel's first chip-making plant in East Asia.

Dalian draws many domestic and foreign visitors, particularly from Japan, South Korea and Russia, thanks to its mild climate, many beaches and its place in China's modern history. Well-known beaches include Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸), Fujiazhuang (付家庄), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Xinghai Bay (星海湾) and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子). In 2007 it was one of three cities, with Hangzhou and Chengdu, given the "China's best tourist city" title by two bodies, the National Tourism Administration and the UN's World Tourism Organization.
Zhongshan Square (中山广场): Russians planned it in the 1800s, and it is known for the classical buildings around it, put up by the Japanese early in the 1900s.

Laohutan Ocean Park: its exhibits include a Coral Aquarium, a World of Birds and the Polar Region Marine Animals World, where the shows with white whales and dolphins draw crowds. Next door is Tigers Sculpture Square, with a tiger that stands for Tiger Beach (老虎滩; Lǎohǔtān). Visitors can also board Taiyuan, a decommissioned Anshan-class destroyer.
Xinghai Square (星海广场, "Square of the Sea of Stars"): beside Xinghai Bay, built to mark Dalian's hundredth birthday in 1998, and billed as the biggest urban square anywhere.
Heishijiao Geological Park, with the Dalian Natural History Museum, plus Sunasia Ocean World and the Dalian Forest Zoo

Bangchuidao Scenic Area: a well-kept park that served as a State Guesthouse from 1960 and is now open to the public. It offers lush greenery, villas in Chinese and Western styles, a hot spring, tennis and badminton courts, a golf course, a recreation center and its own beach. Offshore you can see Bangchui Island (棒棰岛; Bàngchuí Dǎo), named after a small islet that resembles the bangchui, an ancient laundry tool. As a State Guesthouse it received a long line of Chinese and foreign leaders and senior figures: Xi Jinping, Hu Jintao, Jiang Zemin, Deng Xiaoping and Zhou Enlai among Chinese leaders, plus foreign guests such as Boris Yeltsin, Henry Kissinger, Kim Jong Un, Gerhard Schröder and Juan Antonio Samaranch.
Fujiazhuang Beach, the Donggang Music Fountain and the Dalian Sightseeing Tower

dongbei-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: Jinzhou District and Development Zone (northern suburbs)

blocks.x: Here you will find Dahei Mountain and also the Jinshitan National Holiday Resort and Discoveryland (金石滩; Jīnshítān, meaning "Golden Pebble Beach"). The resort is laid out as two peninsulas, east and west, with open ground between them and the Golden Coast beach. The attractions are varied: museums (the Golden Pebble Waxworks, a Geological Museum and the Mao Zedong Badge Exhibition Hall), the Coastal National Geopark, Golden Rock Park and Wanfuding Park, the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort, the China Martial Arts Hall, a Model Movie & TV Art Center, an International Vehicle Campsite, and the Discoveryland Theme Park. For leisure there are equestrian and hunting clubs, two golf courses (Golden Gulf Golf Course and the Golden Pebble Golf Club) and the Golden Pebble International Convention Center & Resort. Yearly events include a Beach Carnival (Dalian International), the International Winter Swimming Festival and a Grape Festival.

The Discovery Kingdom, as Discoveryland Theme Park (发现王国) is also called, was built in 2006 to a design by Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, a firm that has also contributed to the design of a Disney park.
Lüshun Railway Station and Lüshun Museum

Hill 203, East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山) and the Shuishiying Meeting Place: these mark where the most intense fighting took place, and where the ceasefire was signed, when Lüshun was contested in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05).

Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum: the prison was built by the Russians in 1902 and enlarged later by the Japanese. During the Second World War it held people of many nationalities who resisted Japan's invasion. The Korean independence activist An Jung-geun, who killed Itō Hirobumi in an assassination, was held and executed here.
Lüshun Snake Museum, and nearby the Snake Island and Bird Port nature reserve
Hengshan Temple (横山寺) and Longwangtang Cherry Blossom Park: the temple stands near Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库). Its origins date to the Han dynasty, and it was rebuilt in 2003.
Pulandian District: Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场)
Wafangdian: Changxing Island International Golf Course
Zhuanghe: the Bingyu Valley Scenic Area and, for hot spring bathing, Buyun Mountain (步云山温泉)
Changhai County: its islands

Hot spring hotels are plentiful around Dalian. In Lüshunkou District you can try Laotieshan Hot Spring Hotel or Tianmu Hot Spring Hotel; others are the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort at Jinshitan, Wafangdian's Minghu Hot Spring Hotel and, in Ganjingzi District, the Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa.

Winter sports are catching on. Popular ski areas include Dalian Happy Snow World, near the airport, and Linhai Ski Resort, both in Ganjingzi District. Pulandian District has the Anbo Ski Resort, and Wafangdian has Minghu Ski Resort together with Minghu International Skiing Holiday Village.
Because of the hilly roads, cycling is less popular in Dalian than in other Chinese cities. Local law also bans motorcycle riding in the downtown core, so there are few of them there.

Buses cover the city thoroughly, and the metro is efficient. In March 2023 the Dalian Metro had three underground lines (1, 2 and 5) and three overground ones (3, 12 and 13). Construction is under way on new lines and extensions such as Line 4 and Line 7, and the planned rail network is meant to join up the whole city in future. The Dalian Tram is the second oldest in China. A single Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡) works on most public transport.

In 2006, China Daily picked Dalian as the best city to live in across China. Its main theatres include the Dalian People's Culture Club (mostly music), the Hongji Grand Stage (Beijing Opera), the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院) and the Working People's Theater, also called Doudou Grand Stage (工人剧院/豆豆大舞台), which mainly stages Errenzhuan. On the research side, the city hosts the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics.

dongbei-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: Why DUFE and Dalian suit many applicants

blocks.x: For applicants to economics, finance, accounting or business, DUFE offers a specialist education, strong employment outcomes and a city that is itself a financial and trading hub.
