Donghua University (DHU, 东华大学) is a public university in Shanghai, China. It is affiliated with the Ministry of Education. The university is part of the Double First-Class Construction and Project 211.
Formerly known as China Textile University, the institution emphasizes not only the original materials science program but also engineering, management, and design disciplines.

Founded in June 1951, Donghua University was originally named the East China Institute of Textile Technology (华东纺织工学院). In September 1985, the institute changed its name to China Textile University (中国纺织大学) and changed it once again to Donghua University in August 1999. The word "Donghua" literally means East China.
It has been a national key university since 1960 and was one of the educational institutions in China authorized to confer all three levels of degree: bachelor's, master's, and doctorate degrees.
Donghua University has two campuses: one in Changning District and the other in Songjiang District in Shanghai. Most bachelor courses are taken in the Songjiang district.
The Changning Campus is the older one, and it has a tunnel under it going along Xinhua Road.

As of 2025, Donghua University is ranked among the world's top 500th universities according to some of the most-widely read university rankings in the world, such as the Academic Ranking of World Universities and the U.S. News & World Report Best Global University Ranking. It is ranked as the top 1 school for Textile Engineering, Fiber Materials Science, and Fashion Design in China in the recognized Best Chinese Universities Ranking.

Being well known as an international university; ranking top 5 in the list of most international-friendly universities in China. Being amongst the first Chinese universities to accept international students, Donghua University is no stranger to the needs of international students like Shanghai Summer School participants. To date, Donghua University has hosted international students from almost 140 countries.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shanghai, where Donghua University is located.

Shanghai is located on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south, and the East China Sea to the east. The land is formed by the Yangtze's natural deposition and modern land reclamation projects. It has sandy soil, and skyscrapers have to be built with deep concrete piles to avoid sinking into the soft ground. The provincial-level Municipality of Shanghai administers the estuary and many of its surrounding islands. It borders the provinces of Zhejiang to the south and Jiangsu to the west and north. The municipality's northernmost point is on Chongming Island, the second-largest island in mainland China after its expansion during the 20th century.

Shanghai is located on an alluvial plain and the vast majority of its 6,340.5-square-kilometre (2,448.1-square-mile) land area is flat, with an average elevation of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flat ecosystems exist around the estuary, but they have been reclaimed for agricultural purposes. The city's few hills, such as She Shan, lie to the southwest; its highest point is the peak of Dajinshan Island (103 metres or 338 feet) in Hangzhou Bay. Shanghai has rivers, canals, streams, and lakes, and it is known for its rich water resources as part of the Lake Tai drainage basin.

Downtown Shanghai is bisected by the Huangpu River, a man-made tributary of the Yangtze created by order of Lord Chunshen during the Warring States period. The historic centre of the city was located on the west bank of the Huangpu (Puxi), near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, connecting it with Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. The central financial district, Lujiazui, was established on the east bank of the Huangpu (Pudong). Along Shanghai's eastern shore, the destruction of local wetlands due to the construction of Pudong International Airport has been partially offset by the protection and expansion of a nearby shoal, Jiuduansha, as a nature preserve.

Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cfa), with an average annual temperature of 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) for downtown areas and 16.2–17.2 °C (61.2–63.0 °F) for suburbs. The city experiences four distinct seasons. Winters are temperate to cold and damp—northwesterly winds from Siberia can cause nighttime temperatures to drop below freezing. Each year, there are an average of 4.7 days with snowfall and 1.6 days with snow cover. Summers are hot and humid, and occasional downpours or thunderstorms can be expected. On average, 21 days meet or exceed 35 °C (95 °F) annually. In summer and the beginning of autumn, the city is susceptible to typhoons.

The most pleasant seasons are generally spring, although changeable and often rainy, and autumn, which is usually sunny and dry. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 28% in June to 46% in August, the city receives 1,754 hours of bright sunshine annually. According to China's seasonal division standard, from 2001 to 2025, Shanghai enters spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October, and winter on 4 December. The average temperature for the three weeks from 19 July to 8 August is above 30 °C (86.0 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977 (unofficial record of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was set on 19 January 1893) to 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022 at a weather station in Xujiahui. It also has 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) as the highest ever daily minimum temperature at Xujiahui on 13 August 2010.

In 2025, the average temperature of Xujiahui was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), which was 1.93 °C higher than the average from 1991 to 2020. The average daily high temperature is 23.66 °C (74.6 °F), and the average daily low temperature is 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund, located by the bank of the Huangpu River, is home to a row of early 20th-century architecture, ranging in style from the neoclassical HSBC Building to the Art Deco Sassoon House (now part of the Peace Hotel). The area has been revitalized several times: the first was in 1986, with a new promenade by the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren. The second was before the 2010 Expo, which includes restoration of the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and reconfiguration of traffic flow.

Much of the city’s development attests to the imperial presence of Western powers, namely Britain, France and the United States.Shanghai's construction boom during the 1920s and 1930s caused the city to have several Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in the city between 1918 and 1947, designed Art Deco buildings such as the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema, and the Paramount. Other prominent Art Deco-style architects are Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, who designed the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel, and the Broadway Mansions; and Austrian architect C.H. Gonda, who designed the Capitol Theatre. One common architectural element is the shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men, "stone storage door") residence, typically two- or three-story gray brick houses with the front yard protected by a heavy wooden door in a stylistic stone arch. Each residence is connected and arranged in straight alleys known as longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). Shanghai also has Soviet neoclassical architecture or Stalinist architecture: most were erected between the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 and the Sino-Soviet Split in the late 1960s when Soviet personnel came to China to aid in the development of a communist state. An example of Soviet neoclassical architecture in Shanghai is the Shanghai Exhibition Center.

Shanghai has 206 buildings 150m+ making it the seventh city in the world with the most skyscrapers. Some of Shanghai's skyscrapers include the Jin Mao Tower, the Shanghai World Financial Center, and the Shanghai Tower, which was completed in 2015 and is currently the tallest building in China and the third tallest in the world. The Oriental Pearl Tower, at 468 m (1,535 ft), is located nearby at the northern tip of Lujiazui. Many areas in the former foreign concessions are well-preserved. Despite rampant redevelopment, the Old City retains traditional architecture and designs, such as the Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan style garden.

The city is a global centre for finance and innovation, and a national centre for commerce, trade, and transportation, with the world's busiest container port—the Port of Shanghai. As of 2022, the Greater Shanghai metropolitan area, which includes Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan, and Huzhou, was estimated to produce a gross metropolitan product (nominal) of nearly 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion). As of 2020, the economy of Shanghai was estimated to be $1 trillion (PPP), ranking the most productive metro area of China and among the top ten largest metropolitan economies in the world. Shanghai's six largest industries—retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing, and automotive manufacturing—comprise about half the city's GDP.

As of 2025, Shanghai had a GDP of CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion in nominal; $1.66 trillion in PPP) that makes up 4% of China's GDP, and a GDP per capita of CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 in nominal; US$66,944 in PPP). In 2022, the average annual disposable income of Shanghai's residents was CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) per capita, while the average annual salary of people employed in urban units in Shanghai was CN¥212,476 (US$31,589), making it one of the wealthiest cities in China, but also the most expensive city in mainland China to live in according to a 2023 study by the Economist Intelligence Unit. According to Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report, Shanghai was the most expensive city in the world for living a luxurious lifestyle in 2021.

In 2023, the city's imports and exports reached CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), accounting for 18.5% of the national total. In 2022, Shanghai was ranked fifth-highest in the number of billionaires by Forbes. Shanghai's nominal GDP was projected to reach US$1.3 trillion in 2035 (ranking first in China), making it one of the world's top 5 major cities in terms of GRP according to a study by Oxford Economics. As of August 2024, Shanghai ranked 4th in the world and 2nd in Greater China (after Beijing) by the largest number of the Fortune Global 500 companies.

In the last two decades, Shanghai has been one of the fastest-developing cities in the world; it has recorded double-digit GDP growth in almost every year between 1992 and 2008, before the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai is a global financial center, ranking third in Asia and eighth globally on the Global Financial Centres Index. Shanghai is also a large hub of the Chinese and global technology industry and home to a large startup ecosystem. As of 2021, the city was ranked as the 2nd Fintech powerhouse in the world after New York City.

As of 2019, the Shanghai Stock Exchange had a market capitalization of US$4.02 trillion, making it the largest stock exchange in China and the fourth-largest stock exchange in the world. In 2009, the trading volume of six key commodities—including rubber, copper, and zinc—on the Shanghai Futures Exchange all ranked first globally. By the end of 2017, Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions, of which 251 were foreign-invested.

As one of the main industrial centres of China, Shanghai plays a key role in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Several industrial zones—including Shanghai Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, and Shanghai Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone—are backbones of Shanghai's secondary sector. Shanghai is home to China's largest steelmaker Baosteel Group, China's largest shipbuilding base Hudong–Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and one of China's oldest shipbuilders, the Jiangnan Shipyard. In auto manufacturing, the Shanghai-based SAIC Motor is one of the three largest automotive corporations in China, and has strategic partnerships with Volkswagen and General Motors. The company ranked 84 on the Fortune Global 500 list in 2023.

In 2017, the number of domestic tourists to the city increased by 7.5% to 318 million, while the number of overseas tourists increased by 2.2% to 8.73 million. In 2017, Shanghai was the highest earning tourist city in the world. According to the International Congress and Convention Association, Shanghai hosted 82 international meetings in 2018, a 34% increase from 61 in 2017. As of 2023, it had 57 five-star hotels, 52 four star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions, and 34 red tourist attractions. In 2023, Shanghai had 3.64 million tourists, a 4.8-fold growth compared to 2022. It generated CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion) in value, a 98.5% increase from the previous year. The number of foreign tourists reached 2.41 million, with a 5.2-fold increase.

In September 2013, the city launched the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone—the first free-trade zone in mainland China. It introduced several reforms to incentivize foreign investment. The Banker reported that Shanghai attracted the highest volumes of financial sector foreign direct investment in the Asia-Pacific region in 2013. As of October 2019, it is the second largest free-trade zone in mainland China in terms of land area (behind Hainan Free Trade Zone) covering an area of 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) and integrating four existing bonded zones—Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, and Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Commodities entering the zone are exempt from duty and customs clearance.

As of 2023, Shanghai had a population of 24,874,500, including 14,801,700 (59.5%) hukou holders (registered locally). As of 2022, 89.3% of Shanghai's population lives in urban areas, and 10.7% live in rural areas. Based on the population of its total administrative area, Shanghai is the second largest of the four municipalities of China, behind Chongqing, but is generally considered the largest Chinese city because the urban population of Chongqing is much smaller. According to the OECD, Shanghai's metropolitan area has an estimated population of 34 million.

According to the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau, about 157,900 residents in Shanghai are foreigners, including 28,900 Japanese, 21,900 Americans, and 20,800 Koreans. The actual number of foreign citizens in the city is probably much higher. Shanghai is also a domestic immigration city—40.3% (9.8 million) of the city's residents are from other regions of China.

Shanghai has a life expectancy of 83.18 years for the city's registered population, the highest life expectancy of all cities in mainland China. This has also caused the city to experience population aging—in 2021, 17.4% (4.3 million) of the city's registered population was aged 65 or above. In 2017, the Chinese government implemented population controls for Shanghai, resulting in a population decline of 10,000 people by the end of the year.
Shanghai has a public transportation system comprising metros, buses, ferries, and taxis, which can be accessed using a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

Shanghai's rapid transit system, the Shanghai Metro, incorporates subway and light metro lines and extends to each core urban district as well as neighboring suburban districts. As of 2025, there are 19 metro lines (excluding the Shanghai maglev train and Jinshan railway), 508 stations, and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of lines in operation, making it the longest network in the world. On 8 March 2019, it set the city's daily metro ridership record with 13.3 million. Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev train is the first and the fastest commercial high-speed maglev in the world, with a maximum operation speed of 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

The first tram line in Shanghai was opened in 1908. By 1925, there were 328 tramcars and 14 routes operated by Chinese, French, and British companies collaboratively, all of which were nationalized in 1949. Since the 1960s, tram lines were either dismantled or replaced by trolleybus or motorbus lines; the last tram line was demolished in 1975. Shanghai reintroduced trams in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram. In 2018, the steel wheeled Songjiang Tram started operating in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the world's most extensive bus network, including the world's oldest continuously operating trolleybus system, with 1,575 lines covering a total length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi) by 2019. The system is operated by multiple companies. As of 2024, 30,900 taxis were in operation in Shanghai, which carried 134 million passengers that year.

donghua-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Donghua University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Donghua University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

East China Normal University, usually shortened to ECNU, is a public institution based in Shanghai. It answers to the Ministry of Education, and the Shanghai municipal government shares the cost of running it. It belongs to three national programmes that signal serious state backing: Double First-Class Construction, Project 985 and Project 211.

The present university dates from 1951, when Great China University (founded in 1924) and Kwang Hua University (founded in 1925) were combined. Its deeper roots go back to St. John's College, set up in 1879. As of 2020 the university was divided into 22 schools, colleges and institutes, spread over two campuses, one in Minhang district and one in Putuo district.

ECNU's family tree begins in 1879, when William Jones Boone and Joseph Schereschewsky, the Bishop of Shanghai, merged two existing Anglican colleges in the city to create St. John's College. The school was upgraded to St. John's University in 1905 and registered in Washington, D.C. Starting in 1907 it awarded bachelor's degrees, the first institution in China to do so, and that legacy shaped modern Chinese higher education well beyond Shanghai.

Two further strands joined the story in the 1920s. In 1924 students at Xiamen University in Fujian staged a protest, and some of their teachers fled north to Shanghai, where they founded the institution that became Great China University, also called Daxia University. A year later, after the May Thirtieth Movement of 1925, some staff and students walked out of St. John's and went on to form the private Kwang Hua University, which backed the labour and anti-imperialist causes of the Republican era.

After the People's Republic of China was founded, Kwang Hua University and Great China University were officially joined together in 1951 to create East China Normal University. Teachers from Fudan University, Tongji University, the University of Shanghai and the East China PE Academy joined at the same moment. The result was the first national teacher-training university of the new republic. Part of the reasoning was practical: the authorities wanted to pull scattered resources into one stronger body, train specialists, and push education forward nationally.

Later in the 1950s the government redrew the map of higher education on the Soviet model. Under that plan, Aurora University, Utopia University, the University of Shanghai, Saint John's University and Zhejiang University all gave up most of their faculties to ECNU, turning it into a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary institution. Some academics from Tongji and Jiaotong universities were also transferred in.

In March 1959 ECNU was named among the 16 earliest National Key Universities, a status confirmed again in 1978. There was one odd interruption: between 1972 and 1980, while the Cultural Revolution was under way, ECNU and four other schools were merged into Shanghai Normal University. In 1980 the old name returned.

Further milestones followed. In June 1986 ECNU was among the first 33 institutions the State Council allowed to set up graduate schools. In 1996 it passed the review that brought it into Project 211. Then in 2006 the Shanghai authorities and the Ministry of Education signed an agreement to co-sponsor the university, which qualified it for Project 985.

Today the university sits directly under the Ministry of Education. It sponsors or oversees over 20 scholarly journals and magazines, its library holds over 4,000,000 volumes, and 25 primary and secondary schools are attached to it, a reminder of its teacher-training identity.

ECNU keeps formal strategic partnerships with well-known universities in several countries. In France these are the Ecole Normale Superieure and its network; in the United States, Cornell University and the University of Pennsylvania; in Japan, Kobe University and Tokyo University; in Australia, the University of Melbourne; and in Britain, the University of Warwick. Beyond those, academic exchanges reach more than 150 universities and institutions in Russia, Korea, Australia, Canada, the United States, Japan, Germany, France and Britain, among others.

For international students, a few details are worth noting. each semester 100 American college students study at a CIEE satellite campus that ECNU hosts. The university also operates an Online College of Chinese in partnership with NOCFL, the National Office for Teaching Chinese as a Foreign Language. It was the first college of its type in the country, and more than 5,800 learners spanning 137 countries and regions are enrolled. In 2008 ECNU added a base for training international teachers of Chinese, named the NOCFL Study and Training Base.

France has a visible presence on campus. In 2002 three French schools, the Ecole Normale Superieure in Paris, the Ecole normale superieure de Cachan and the Ecole normale superieure de Lyon, launched a joint Master's-PhD programme at ECNU. The ENS presence is housed within two ECNU institutes, the Aspiring Researchers Institute and the Franco-Chinese Advanced Studies Institute. The EMLYON Business School opened its official EMLYON Asia Campus in the middle of the ECNU grounds in 2007.

American links run deep too. In 2008 Cornell University and ECNU jointly funded the Cornell-ECNU Center for Comparative Culture. Early in 2011 the Ministry of Education approved New York University Shanghai (NYU Shanghai), China's first Sino-American university, which New York University and ECNU established together.

Two short-term programmes show how ECNU hosts guests. The Study China Programme is organised by the University of Manchester, with funding from UK government departments, Business, Innovation and Skills among them. It brings students from British universities for one to two summer months of Mandarin and Chinese culture. Its aim is to build ties between British students and China, since relatively few British students enroll in full degrees there, and ECNU is one of several Chinese hosts that have taken part for a number of years. The programme has strengthened ECNU's relations with many leading UK universities.

Since 2011 ECNU has also organised the Diplomats' Program, sponsored by the Shanghai Municipal Education Commission and the Shanghai Foreign Affairs Office. Each summer, consular officials from more than 20 countries spend two months studying at the university.

Other measures are more modest but still respectable. The QS Graduate Employability Rankings for 2017 put it in the 151-200 band worldwide, and the World Reputation Rankings from Times Higher Education list it at 151-175, which marks it as a well-regarded Chinese university globally.

east-china-normal-university.h: Shanghai: the city around your campus

blocks.x: Daily life as a student depends heavily on the city you live in: the weather, how you move around and what you can do with your free time. The sections that follow describe Shanghai, home to ECNU.

Shanghai lies where the Yangtze meets the sea on China's east coast. To the north runs the Yangtze, Hangzhou Bay lies south, and the East China Sea forms the eastern edge. The ground itself was built up by silt carried down the Yangtze and by modern land reclamation. The soil is sandy and soft, so tall buildings must stand on deep concrete piles to keep from sinking. The municipality, which has provincial status, administers the estuary and many nearby islands. Zhejiang lies to the south, Jiangsu to the west and north. Its most northerly point is on Chongming Island, which has become the second-largest island in mainland China after growing through the 20th century.

The city occupies an alluvial plain, and nearly all of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land is flat, at an average height of just four metres (13 feet). Around the estuary there were tidal-flat ecosystems, but these have been reclaimed for farming. A handful of hills, such as She Shan, rise in the southwest. The highest spot is the summit of Dajinshan Island, 103 metres (338 feet), out in Hangzhou Bay. Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are everywhere, and Shanghai is famous for abundant water, being within the Lake Tai drainage basin.

The Huangpu River cuts through the middle of the city. It is a man-made tributary of the Yangtze, dug on the orders of Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. The old centre of Shanghai grew on the west bank, called Puxi, close to where Suzhou Creek joins the Huangpu and connects through to the Grand Canal and Lake Tai. The financial district, Lujiazui, was built on the east bank, called Pudong. On the eastern shore, building Pudong International Airport destroyed some local wetland, and this has been partly offset by setting aside and enlarging Jiuduansha, a shoal close by, as a nature reserve.

Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen: Cfa). The average annual temperature is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) in the downtown areas and 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F) in the suburbs. There are four clear seasons. Winters are cool to cold and damp, and northwesterly winds from Siberia can push night temperatures below freezing. In an average year snow falls on 4.7 days and lies on the ground for 1.6 days. Summer, by contrast, is hot and sticky, with occasional downpours and thunderstorms; on average 21 days a year reach or exceed 35 °C (95 °F). Typhoons can hit in summer and early autumn.

Spring and autumn are generally the most comfortable. Spring is changeable and often wet, while autumn tends to be sunny and dry. June is the dullest month at 28% of possible sunshine and August the brightest at 46%, and the city gets 1,754 hours of bright sunshine a year. Using China's seasonal calendar and data from 2001 to 2025, spring arrives 9 March, summer 15 May, autumn 5 October, winter 4 December. From 19 July to 8 August, a three-week stretch, temperatures average over 30 °C (86.0 °F).

Since 1951 the Xujiahui weather station has recorded a wide range. 31 January 1977 saw -10.1 °C (13.8 °F), while both 21 July 2017 and, again, 13 July 2022 reached 40.9 °C (105.6 °F). An unofficial reading from 19 January 1893 was colder still, -12.1 °C (10.2 °F). The highest overnight minimum ever measured at Xujiahui was 32.1 °C (89.8 °F), on 13 August 2010.
The year 2025 averaged 19.43 °C (67.0 °F) at Xujiahui, 1.93 °C above the 1991 to 2020 average. Daily highs average 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and lows 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund runs along the Huangpu and is lined with early 20th-century buildings, ranging from the neoclassical HSBC Building through to Sassoon House in Art Deco style (today part of the Peace Hotel). The waterfront has been renewed more than once. In 1986 came the first renewal, bringing a promenade designed by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren. A second came before the 2010 Expo, including repairs to the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and a rearrangement of traffic.

Much of Shanghai's development reflects the presence of Western powers, above all Britain, France and the United States. A building boom in the 1920s and 1930s left the city with many Art Deco buildings. Laszlo Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in Shanghai between 1918 and 1947, left behind the Paramount, the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner were behind the Broadway Mansions, the Metropole Hotel and the Peace Hotel, and the Austrian architect C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

A typical local home is the shikumen (石库门, meaning "stone storage door"), a two- or three-storey grey-brick house whose front yard is shut off by a heavy wooden door set in a stone arch. These houses are joined together in straight alleys called longtangs (弄堂). There is also Soviet neoclassical, or Stalinist, architecture, mostly put up between 1949 and the Sino-Soviet Split of the late 1960s while Soviet advisers were helping China. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

With 206 buildings of 150 m or more, Shanghai ranks seventh in the world for skyscrapers. Landmarks include the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, along with the Shanghai Tower, completed in 2015, which is the tallest building in China and the world's third tallest. The Oriental Pearl Tower, 468 m (1,535 ft) high, is nearby on Lujiazui's northern tip. Large parts of the old foreign concessions survive in good condition. Even with heavy redevelopment, the Old City keeps traditional architecture, for instance the Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan-style garden.

Shanghai is a global centre of finance and innovation and a national hub for commerce, trade and transport. It has the Port of Shanghai, the world's busiest container port. The wider Shanghai metropolitan region, which also takes in Huzhou, Zhoushan, Jiaxing, Ningbo, Nantong, Wuxi and Suzhou, was estimated in 2022 to generate a nominal gross metropolitan product reaching about 13 trillion RMB, or $1.9 trillion. Around 2020 the city's economy was estimated at $1 trillion (PPP), making it China's most productive metro area and one of the ten largest metropolitan economies globally. Retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing and automotive manufacturing are its six biggest industries and together account for about half of the city's GDP.

In 2025 Shanghai's GDP reached CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion nominal; $1.66 trillion PPP), about 4% of China's total, with per-person GDP of CN¥228,280, which is US$32,840 nominal or US$66,944 PPP. Residents' disposable income in 2022 averaged CN¥79,610 a year (US$11,836), while the average salary for people in urban units reached CN¥212,476 (US$31,589). That makes it one of China's wealthiest cities, but also, in a 2023 Economist Intelligence Unit study, the most expensive place to live in mainland China. For students this is worth budgeting for. Another study, the Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report from Julius Baer, called Shanghai the priciest city on earth for luxury living in 2021.

Trade volumes in 2023, imports and exports combined, added up to CN¥7.73 trillion, or US$1.07 trillion, equal to 18.5% of China's total. In 2022 Forbes ranked Shanghai fifth for number of billionaires. Oxford Economics projected that by 2035 its nominal GDP would be US$1.3 trillion, which would put it first in China and among the world's top five cities by gross regional product. As of August 2024 it stood fourth globally and second in Greater China, behind Beijing, for hosting Fortune Global 500 companies. For twenty years Shanghai has grown faster than almost any other city, recording double-digit GDP growth almost every year from 1992 to 2008, before the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai is a leading financial centre, third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a major hub for Chinese and global technology, with a large startup scene, and in 2021 it was named the world's number two Fintech powerhouse, behind New York City. The Shanghai Stock Exchange's market capitalization was US$4.02 trillion in 2019, which made it China's largest and the world's fourth largest. Six key commodities, among them rubber, copper and zinc, were traded on the Shanghai Futures Exchange in 2009 at volumes that were the highest anywhere. By the end of 2017 Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Shanghai remains one of China's main industrial centres, with an important role in manufacturing and heavy industry. Its manufacturing base rests on several industrial zones: Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone, Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone and Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone. Local companies include Baosteel Group, China's largest steelmaker, Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, the country's largest shipbuilding base, and Jiangnan Shipyard, one of its oldest. In cars, Shanghai-based SAIC Motor is one of China's three largest automotive groups, works with Volkswagen and General Motors, and ranked 84 on the Fortune Global 500 in 2023.

In 2017 domestic tourist numbers rose 7.5% to 318 million, and overseas visitors rose 2.2% to 8.73 million; that year Shanghai was the highest-earning tourist city in the world. The International Congress and Convention Association reported 82 international meetings in 2018, up 34% from 61 in 2017. By 2023 the visitor infrastructure included 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels, plus 1,942 travel agencies; attractions numbered 144 rated sites and 34 red-tourism sites. In 2023, 3.64 million tourists visited, 4.8 times the 2022 figure, worth CN¥177.12 billion, or US$24.53 billion, which was 98.5% more than the year before. Foreign tourists numbered 2.41 million, a 5.2-fold increase.

In September 2013 Shanghai opened the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, the first in mainland China, bringing reforms designed to draw in foreign capital. The Banker reported that Shanghai drew the highest volumes of financial-sector foreign direct investment in Asia-Pacific in 2013. By October 2019 it ranked second among mainland China's free-trade zones for land area, after Hainan, at 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi), merging four bonded zones that already existed: the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park and Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone. Goods entering the zone are exempt from duty and customs clearance.

At the end of 2023 the city had 24,874,500 residents, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) held a local hukou, meaning they were registered in Shanghai. In 2022, 89.3% of people lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. Counting everything inside its administrative boundary, Shanghai ranks second among China's four municipalities, after Chongqing, but it is generally treated as China's biggest city because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller. The OECD estimates the metropolitan population at 34 million.

Official statistics list about 157,900 foreign residents, among them Japanese (28,900), Americans (21,900) and Koreans (20,800), although the true number is probably far higher. Domestic migration is also large, since some 9.8 million people, 40.3% of residents, come from elsewhere in China.

Registered residents can expect to live 83.18 years, the highest of any mainland Chinese city, which has contributed to an ageing population: by 2021, 4.3 million registered residents, or 17.4%, were aged 65 or above. In 2017 the government introduced population controls for Shanghai, and the population fell by 10,000 by the end of that year.
The city's public transport covers metro, buses, ferries and taxis, all of which can be paid for with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

The Shanghai Metro mixes subway and light-metro lines and reaches every core district and nearby suburbs. As of 2025 it runs 19 lines (not counting the maglev or the Jinshan railway). That is the world's longest network, with 808 kilometres (502 mi) of line and 508 stations. On 8 March 2019 it set a daily ridership record of 13.3 million. The Shanghai maglev, opened in 2004, is the first and fastest commercial high-speed maglev anywhere, reaching 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph) at top speed.

Trams date from 1908, when the first line opened; 1925 saw 328 tramcars on 14 routes run jointly by Chinese, French and British companies, all nationalized in 1949. From the 1960s the lines were removed or replaced by trolleybuses and motorbuses, and the final line was torn down in 1975. In 2010 the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram revived the idea, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began running in Songjiang District.

Shanghai's bus network is the largest in the world and includes the oldest trolleybus system still in continuous operation; by 2019 it had 1,575 lines with a total length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi), run by several companies. In 2024, 30,900 taxis were in service and carried 134 million passengers.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

east-china-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. East China Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at East China Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Known as ECUPL for short, East China University of Political Science and Law is a state-run institution located in Shanghai. The state founded it in 1952, and it is one of the small number of Chinese universities whose identity is built around legal education.

Its teaching is spread over three campuses in three Shanghai districts: Songjiang (in the Songjiang University Town), Changning and Putuo. In total they cover 71 hectares (180 acres), with 240,000 square metres of buildings. Students heading for ECUPL should check early which campus their programme uses.

east-china-university-of-political-scien.h: The founding and the legal tradition

blocks.x: Wei Wenbo founded the university in 1952. It was one of the first batch of political and legal institutions set up by the People's Republic and was originally under the Ministry of Justice. Today it is run jointly by the Ministry of Justice and the Shanghai government, with the local government taking priority in management. After several generations of work, the university has broadened from law into a multidisciplinary institution that also covers economics, management, finance and foreign languages, although law remains the centre of gravity.

Law is where ECUPL carries real weight. The university is known as having uncommon influence and prestige in legal education across Shanghai and greater East China, China's most developed region. Its graduates work in nearly every legal setting in the region: law firms, government agencies, courts and schools.

The urban campus occupies the grounds of what used to be St. John's University, an Anglican foundation that had to close in the first years of the People's Republic. The architecture there is protected by the government, and the university has also earned city honours as a Shanghai Model Unit and a Shanghai Garden Unit.

The newer Songjiang campus houses undergraduates. Its neighbours in Songjiang University Town include Donghua University and Shanghai International Studies University. The town also hosts the Shanghai Institute of Foreign Trade, the Shanghai University of Engineering Science, the Shanghai Lixin University of Commerce and the Shanghai Institute of Visual Arts. That is useful to know if you like the idea of a student district with several universities side by side.

At postgraduate level, ECUPL awards doctorates in law (LLD) in four areas: legal history, criminal law, economic law and international law. It offers nine LLM programmes in law, covering theories of law, legal history, constitutional and administrative law, criminal law, civil and commercial law, procedural law, economic law, international law, and environmental and resource protection law. One more LLM programme is a professional law degree. On-the-job students can also enrol for doctoral and master's degrees.

The bachelor's side has 22 majors, ranging well beyond law. Law is the best-known, but the list also includes economics, finance, administration, sociology, journalism, accounting, intellectual property and business administration. Language options are English and Japanese, and Chinese literature and social work are available too. Other majors are international business and trade, public security, labour and social security, frontier defence management, politics and administration, public affairs administration, information science and technology and cultural industry management. A programme in economics investigation (listed as "economics reconnaissance study") completes the 22. The law major also has a track for students who want a second bachelor's degree in law.

The Ministry of Justice has named international economic law and legal history as key subjects, and the Shanghai government has named law in general. Four journals come out of the university. Two have short titles (Law, and Studies of Crime), one is on juvenile delinquency issues, and the fourth carries the university's own name as its Journal. More than 30 research institutions work on topics such as ancient Chinese legal documents and juvenile delinquency. The library holds over 600,000 volumes, and readers can consult more than 1,200 periodicals in Chinese and other languages.

Around 800 faculty members work at ECUPL. More than 400 of them teach and do research, and over 160 are professors or associate professors. The student body exceeds 10,000. These figures are older and may have changed, so confirm current numbers on the university's website.
Cooperation reaches beyond campus: the university reports relationships with more than 100 overseas colleges, research institutions and legal bodies, in addition to institutions inside China.

east-china-university-of-political-scien.h: A controversy to be aware of

blocks.x: In December 2013, ECUPL made international news when a lecturer, Zhang Xuezhong, was dismissed. He had earlier given legal advice to the New Citizens' Movement. State-run media said that he held what they called political views contrary to law. Mentioning this gives you a fuller picture of the context in which Chinese universities operate, and you may want to read more about it independently.

ECUPL pays steady attention to exchanges with overseas institutions. Joint programmes exist with the City University of Hong Kong and with the National University of Singapore, and every year it hosts visiting student groups from the United States and Australia.
It has agreements with around 35 universities abroad, listed in the older profile as including:
In the United States: the law school of Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio; Wisconsin University; Willamette University; and Golden Gate University
In Europe: Ghent University, Vrije Universiteit in the Netherlands and the University of Groningen in the Netherlands
In Australia: Queensland University and Bond University
In Asia: Kyushu University and Kumamoto University in Japan, and Anshan University in South Korea

Each year the university chooses faculty and students to send to partner institutions for further study and research. Graduates and first-year postgraduates are also urged to complete an LLM overseas. It keeps good relations with well-known Shanghai law firms and internationally known companies, which matters for internships and career contacts.

The links have kept growing. As of December 2024, the number of agreements stood at 214 with universities and institutions, plus 9 with international and regional organisations, spread over 48 countries and regions. Two of those organisations are the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization and the UN's training and research institute (UNITAR).
The Office of International Criminal Justice also has an office at the university.

Your daily life as a student will depend heavily on the city, so the sections below look at Shanghai: its land and weather, its buildings, its economy, its people and how to travel around it.

Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary on China's east coast. Water surrounds it on three sides: the Yangtze River lies north, Hangzhou Bay south and the East China Sea east. The ground is made of silt laid down naturally by the Yangtze, plus land won back from the water in modern times. The soil is sandy, which means skyscrapers must stand on deep concrete piles or risk sinking in the soft earth. Shanghai is a provincial-level municipality, administering the estuary and a number of islands around it; its land neighbours are Zhejiang (south) and Jiangsu (west and north). Its northernmost point is on Chongming Island, which grew during the twentieth century into the second-largest island in mainland China.

Most of the city's 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) is flat alluvial plain, at an average height of four metres (13 feet). Tidal-flat ecosystems once surrounded the estuary but have been reclaimed for farming. A few low hills, such as She Shan, rise in the southwest, while the top of Dajinshan Island out in Hangzhou Bay, at 103 metres (338 feet), is the city's highest spot. Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are plentiful, which is why the region is famous for water, being part of the Lake Tai basin.

east-china-university-of-political-scien.h: The two banks of the Huangpu

blocks.x: The Huangpu River divides downtown Shanghai in two. It is an artificial tributary of the Yangtze, dug on the order of Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. Puxi, on the west bank, is where the historic city grew, close to where Suzhou Creek enters; the creek connects the city with the Grand Canal and Lake Tai. The Lujiazui financial district was developed on the east bank (Pudong). Along the east coast, Pudong International Airport destroyed some wetland, and the loss has been partly offset by safeguarding and extending a neighbouring shoal, Jiuduansha, which is now a nature reserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). The mean temperature across the year is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) downtown and 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F) in the suburbs. All four seasons are clear. Winters are mild to cold and damp, and northwesterly winds from Siberia can bring temperatures below freezing at night. On average snow falls on 4.7 days a year and lies on the ground for 1.6. Summer is hot and humid, with the odd downpour or thunderstorm, and about 21 days a year hit 35 °C (95 °F) or more. Typhoons can threaten the city in summer and early autumn.

Spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons. Spring is changeable and often wet, while autumn tends to be sunny and dry. June is the dullest month, with 28% of possible sunshine, and August the brightest at 46%; over twelve months the city gets 1,754 hours of bright sun.

China's official seasonal calendar, applied to 2001 to 2025, gives these start dates for Shanghai: spring on 9 March, then summer from 15 May, autumn from 5 October and winter from 4 December. Mid-summer is intense. Between 19 July and 8 August the mean temperature stays above 30 °C (86.0 °F).

At the Xujiahui weather station, the coldest day since 1951 was 31 January 1977 (−10.1 °C, 13.8 °F), though an unofficial reading of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was taken back on 19 January 1893. The hottest was 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), reached twice, on 21 July 2017 and again on 13 July 2022. Even the lowest overnight temperature on 13 August 2010 was a record 32.1 °C (89.8 °F).
The 2025 mean at Xujiahui was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), which is 1.93 °C warmer than the 1991 to 2020 norm. Typical daily highs average 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and lows 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund runs beside the Huangpu River and has a row of early twentieth-century buildings in different styles. The neoclassical HSBC Building is one; the Art Deco Sassoon House (today part of the Peace Hotel) is another. The district has been revived several times. The first time was in 1986, when Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren designed a new promenade. The second was ahead of the 2010 Expo, which brought restoration work on the Waibaidu Bridge, a century old, and a reorganised traffic flow.

Britain, France and the United States all had a presence here, and a good deal of the city's built heritage reflects that. A building boom in the 1920s and 1930s created many Art Deco buildings. One key designer was the Hungarian-Slovak László Hudec, resident in Shanghai between 1918 and 1947, whose Art Deco work includes the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema and the Paramount. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner were two other notable Art Deco architects, responsible for the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel and Broadway Mansions, and the Austrian C. H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

A typical local building is the shikumen (石库门, "stone storage door") house. Most are two or three storeys of grey brick, and each has a small front yard behind a sturdy wooden door set in a stone arch. The houses link together along straight alleys called longtangs (弄堂). The city also has Soviet neoclassical, or Stalinist, architecture, most of it put up during the two decades after 1949, when the People's Republic was founded, until the Sino-Soviet split of the late 1960s; Soviet staff came during that time to support the development of a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

With 206 buildings reaching 150 m or higher, Shanghai ranks seventh in the world for skyscrapers. Famous ones are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, along with the Shanghai Tower. That last one was finished in 2015, is the tallest building in China and is third tallest anywhere. Close by, at the northern end of Lujiazui, the Oriental Pearl Tower rises 468 m (1,535 ft). Many districts in the former foreign concessions are well preserved, and despite constant redevelopment, the Old City still keeps traditional architecture and design, such as Yu Garden, an elaborate garden in the Jiangnan style.

Internationally the city is a leader in finance and innovation; nationally it is a hub for trade, commerce and transport, and its port handles more containers than any other. A 2022 estimate put the nominal gross metropolitan product of Greater Shanghai (which takes in Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou) at nearly 13 trillion RMB, about $1.9 trillion. For 2020 the city's own economy was put at $1 trillion measured in PPP, giving China's most productive metro area and a place among the ten largest metropolitan economies worldwide. About half of the city's GDP comes from six industries: retail, finance, IT, real estate, machinery and car manufacturing.

In 2025 Shanghai's GDP was CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion nominal; $1.66 trillion PPP), or 4% of the national total, and GDP per head of CN¥228,280, which is US$32,840 nominal or US$66,944 PPP. Money matters for residents in two ways. Average disposable income per person in 2022 was CN¥79,610 (US$11,836), and employees in urban units earned CN¥212,476 (US$31,589) on average that year. Shanghai is among China's wealthiest cities, but a study by the Economist Intelligence Unit in 2023 also found it the priciest in mainland China for everyday living. For a luxury lifestyle, the Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report from Julius Baer said it was the costliest city anywhere in 2021. Budget carefully before you arrive.

Trade in 2023 (imports plus exports) amounted to CN¥7.73 trillion, equal to US$1.07 trillion and 18.5% of China's total. In 2022 Forbes placed the city fifth for billionaires. Oxford Economics expects nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, which would be the highest in China and put Shanghai among the five biggest cities in the world by gross regional product. In August 2024 Shanghai stood fourth in the world, and second in Greater China behind Beijing, for the number of Fortune Global 500 companies.
Few cities have grown as fast over the past twenty years. Between 1992 and 2008 GDP growth reached double digits almost every year, and that run only ended with the financial crisis of 2008.

On the Global Financial Centres Index it comes third in Asia and eighth in the world. It is a major technology hub for China and for the world economy, with a large start-up scene, and a 2021 ranking called it the number-two fintech power, after New York.

By 2019 the Shanghai Stock Exchange's market capitalisation was US$4.02 trillion, the biggest in China and fourth biggest on earth. On the Shanghai Futures Exchange, six main commodities (rubber, copper and zinc are among them) topped global trading volumes in 2009. At the end of 2017 there were 1,491 financial institutions in the city, and 251 had foreign investment.

As a leading industrial centre, Shanghai matters for national heavy industry and manufacturing. Four industrial zones form the backbone of the secondary sector: Hongqiao, Minhang, Jinqiao and Caohejing, the first and the third being economic and technological development zones, the second an export processing zone and the fourth a high-tech zone. Local firms include China's largest steelmaker (Baosteel Group), the country's largest shipbuilding base (Hudong–Zhonghua) and the Jiangnan Shipyard, among the oldest shipbuilders in China. In the car industry, SAIC Motor, based here, is one of China's three biggest groups and works with Volkswagen and General Motors; it came 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

Visitor numbers in 2017 showed 318 million domestic tourists (up 7.5%) and 8.73 million from overseas (up 2.2%), and Shanghai earned more from tourism than any other city. The International Congress and Convention Association counted 82 international meetings held in the city in 2018, 34% above the 61 of 2017. By 2023 it had 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated attractions and 34 "red" tourist sites. Visits in 2023 totalled 3.64 million tourists, 4.8 times the 2022 figure, with a value of CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), up 98.5%, and the 2.41 million foreign visitors were 5.2 times as many as before.

The Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, launched in September 2013, was the first such zone on the mainland and introduced a package of reforms meant to attract foreign investment. The magazine The Banker reported that for 2013, Shanghai pulled in more foreign direct investment in finance than anywhere else in Asia-Pacific. By October 2019 it was the second-largest free-trade zone on the mainland by land area, behind the Hainan Free Trade Zone, covering 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 square miles). It combines four bonded zones that already existed. Two are at Waigaoqiao (the free trade zone and the free trade logistics park), the others are the Yangshan port area and the Pudong Airport comprehensive zone. Goods arriving in the zone avoid duty and customs clearance.

In 2023 the population was 24,874,500, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) held a local hukou, or local registration. In 2022 some 89.3% lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural areas. By total administrative area it is the second largest of China's four municipalities, behind Chongqing, but it is generally treated as China's largest city, since Chongqing's urban population is far smaller. The OECD estimates that the metropolitan area has about 34 million people.

Official figures from the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau show about 157,900 foreign residents. Japanese are the largest group (28,900), followed by Americans (21,900) and Koreans (20,800), and the actual total is probably much higher. The city also draws many migrants from elsewhere in China: 40.3% of residents, or 9.8 million people, come from other regions.

Life expectancy for registered residents is 83.18 years, the highest in any mainland Chinese city, and the flip side is an ageing population: 17.4% of registered residents (4.3 million) were aged 65 or over in 2021. In 2017 the central government introduced population controls for Shanghai, and the population fell by 10,000 by the end of the year.
Public transport includes the metro, buses, ferries and taxis, and a Shanghai Public Transport Card works across them.

The Shanghai Metro combines subway and light-metro lines and reaches every core urban district and neighbouring suburbs. In 2025 the figures stand at 19 lines (not counting the maglev and the Jinshan railway), 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 miles) in service, the longest metro system anywhere. The busiest day was 8 March 2019, with 13.3 million trips. The maglev, in operation since 2004, was the world's first high-speed commercial maglev and remains the fastest, reaching 430 km/h (270 mph).

Tram service started in 1908. In 1925 the network had 328 tramcars on 14 routes, which Chinese, French and British companies operated together, until nationalisation in 1949. From the 1960s onward the lines were dismantled or replaced by trolleybus and motorbus services, and the last tram line was taken out in 1975. The Zhangjiang Tram, a rubber-tyred system, brought trams back in 2010, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began running in Songjiang District, where one of ECUPL's campuses stands.

The bus network is the largest in the world and includes the oldest trolleybus system still in continuous operation. A count for 2019 gave 1,575 lines, adding up to 8,997 kilometres (5,590 miles), run by several different companies. In 2024, 30,900 taxis were in service and carried 134 million passengers.

east-china-university-of-science-and-tec.h: About East China University of Science and Technology

blocks.x: The East China University of Science and Technology (ECUST; Chinese: 华东理工大学; pinyin: Huádōng Lǐgōng Dàxué) is a public university located in Shanghai, China. It is affiliated with the Ministry of Education. The university is part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction.

Established in 1952 as East China Institute of Chemical Technology, it has evolved from an institution with a strong focus on chemical engineering into a university that covers a wide range of academic disciplines.
It was founded in 1952 with chemistry faculty inherited from Jiaotong University, Aurora University, Utopia University, Soochow University, and Jiangnan University.

The main campus is located on Meilong Road in Xuhui District, in the southwest of downtown Shanghai and 17 kilometers from Hongqiao Airport, with an area of approximately 415,000 m2 and 21 dorms capable of accommodating 15,000 students. Most of the departments are easily reached from the Front Gate, behind which Pandeng Road directly leads to the Main Building. Out of the built-up space, classrooms take up 56,000 m2 and laboratories 118,000 m2. The campus houses the administrative offices of the university, Master's as well as PhD students, international exchange and language students, and is home to most of the research facilities.

The Middle School Affiliated To ECUST (华东理工大学附属中学), was established in 1992 and is located in the south of Xuhui District, not far from the main campus. It is attended by 1,200 middle and high school students.

It has a strong tradition of working with industries. The university is now developing into a multi-disciplinary higher educational institution with a balanced curriculum of science, engineering, economics, management, law, humanities and arts spread across 15 academic schools. It is one of Double First Class University Plan, former Project 211 and 985 experiment universities.

The university offers 13 first level and 81 second level doctoral programs, 25 first level and 147 second level master programs and 65 undergraduate programs. The total number of full-time students has reached around 24,140, including 15,460 undergraduates, 7,110 postgraduates studying for master's degrees and 1,570 Ph.D. candidates.

Since 2007 the university has operated an exchange programme with the Technical University of Applied Sciences Lübeck in Germany. ECUST also operates a joint programme with L'École Nationale Supérieure de Chimie in Rennes and a joint business school with Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu in Romania.
