The Library of East China University of Science and Technology (ECUST) was established in 1952 and is placed under direct auspice of the Ministry of Education of People's Republic of China. Starting with the collections of the different departments that initially made up the foundation of the college, it has developed into a research library for multiple disciplines ranging from chemistry and chemical engineering to natural sciences, engineering, management and liberal arts.

The library system of ECUST encompasses three branches among the major campuses. The library in Xuhui, built in 1987, houses most of the book collections, while the new nine-story library in Fengxian marks the center of the new campus and is geared towards undergraduate students. Together, they cover a floor space of almost 46,000 m2 and offer 3,500 seats in the reading rooms. Electronic resources are abundant, with databases shared among several university library systems and access to academic journals. In total, more than 2,600,000 books and publications are available. The university maintains subscriptions for over 2,000 foreign journals in print and over 30,000 in digital form. There is also a library in its Jinshan Campus, storing many books with a low usage.

The library is a member of the Shanghai Library system and one of its main nodes where inter-library loan is possible. It plays an active part in the theory and practice of teaching literature search that have been set up at ECUST. In 2004, with the introduction of a master's degree in Information science, this role was further strengthened. Also on offer are services to students and the wider public, including, but not limited to, a language training center and the provision of teaching material in foreign languages, a center for the distribution of cultural resources and book consulting services both in-person and online.
University Press
The East China University of Technology University Press, founded in 1986, focuses on publications in the technical and social sciences as well as foreign languages and elementary education.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shanghai, where East China University of Science and Technology is located.

Shanghai is located on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south, and the East China Sea to the east. The land is formed by the Yangtze's natural deposition and modern land reclamation projects. It has sandy soil, and skyscrapers have to be built with deep concrete piles to avoid sinking into the soft ground. The provincial-level Municipality of Shanghai administers the estuary and many of its surrounding islands. It borders the provinces of Zhejiang to the south and Jiangsu to the west and north. The municipality's northernmost point is on Chongming Island, the second-largest island in mainland China after its expansion during the 20th century.

Shanghai is located on an alluvial plain and the vast majority of its 6,340.5-square-kilometre (2,448.1-square-mile) land area is flat, with an average elevation of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flat ecosystems exist around the estuary, but they have been reclaimed for agricultural purposes. The city's few hills, such as She Shan, lie to the southwest; its highest point is the peak of Dajinshan Island (103 metres or 338 feet) in Hangzhou Bay. Shanghai has rivers, canals, streams, and lakes, and it is known for its rich water resources as part of the Lake Tai drainage basin.

Downtown Shanghai is bisected by the Huangpu River, a man-made tributary of the Yangtze created by order of Lord Chunshen during the Warring States period. The historic centre of the city was located on the west bank of the Huangpu (Puxi), near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, connecting it with Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. The central financial district, Lujiazui, was established on the east bank of the Huangpu (Pudong). Along Shanghai's eastern shore, the destruction of local wetlands due to the construction of Pudong International Airport has been partially offset by the protection and expansion of a nearby shoal, Jiuduansha, as a nature preserve.

Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cfa), with an average annual temperature of 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) for downtown areas and 16.2–17.2 °C (61.2–63.0 °F) for suburbs. The city experiences four distinct seasons. Winters are temperate to cold and damp—northwesterly winds from Siberia can cause nighttime temperatures to drop below freezing. Each year, there are an average of 4.7 days with snowfall and 1.6 days with snow cover. Summers are hot and humid, and occasional downpours or thunderstorms can be expected. On average, 21 days meet or exceed 35 °C (95 °F) annually. In summer and the beginning of autumn, the city is susceptible to typhoons.

The most pleasant seasons are generally spring, although changeable and often rainy, and autumn, which is usually sunny and dry. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 28% in June to 46% in August, the city receives 1,754 hours of bright sunshine annually. According to China's seasonal division standard, from 2001 to 2025, Shanghai enters spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October, and winter on 4 December. The average temperature for the three weeks from 19 July to 8 August is above 30 °C (86.0 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977 (unofficial record of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was set on 19 January 1893) to 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022 at a weather station in Xujiahui. It also has 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) as the highest ever daily minimum temperature at Xujiahui on 13 August 2010.

In 2025, the average temperature of Xujiahui was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), which was 1.93 °C higher than the average from 1991 to 2020. The average daily high temperature is 23.66 °C (74.6 °F), and the average daily low temperature is 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund, located by the bank of the Huangpu River, is home to a row of early 20th-century architecture, ranging in style from the neoclassical HSBC Building to the Art Deco Sassoon House (now part of the Peace Hotel). The area has been revitalized several times: the first was in 1986, with a new promenade by the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren. The second was before the 2010 Expo, which includes restoration of the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and reconfiguration of traffic flow.

Much of the city’s development attests to the imperial presence of Western powers, namely Britain, France and the United States.Shanghai's construction boom during the 1920s and 1930s caused the city to have several Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in the city between 1918 and 1947, designed Art Deco buildings such as the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema, and the Paramount. Other prominent Art Deco-style architects are Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, who designed the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel, and the Broadway Mansions; and Austrian architect C.H. Gonda, who designed the Capitol Theatre. One common architectural element is the shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men, "stone storage door") residence, typically two- or three-story gray brick houses with the front yard protected by a heavy wooden door in a stylistic stone arch. Each residence is connected and arranged in straight alleys known as longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). Shanghai also has Soviet neoclassical architecture or Stalinist architecture: most were erected between the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 and the Sino-Soviet Split in the late 1960s when Soviet personnel came to China to aid in the development of a communist state. An example of Soviet neoclassical architecture in Shanghai is the Shanghai Exhibition Center.

Shanghai has 206 buildings 150m+ making it the seventh city in the world with the most skyscrapers. Some of Shanghai's skyscrapers include the Jin Mao Tower, the Shanghai World Financial Center, and the Shanghai Tower, which was completed in 2015 and is currently the tallest building in China and the third tallest in the world. The Oriental Pearl Tower, at 468 m (1,535 ft), is located nearby at the northern tip of Lujiazui. Many areas in the former foreign concessions are well-preserved. Despite rampant redevelopment, the Old City retains traditional architecture and designs, such as the Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan style garden.

The city is a global centre for finance and innovation, and a national centre for commerce, trade, and transportation, with the world's busiest container port—the Port of Shanghai. As of 2022, the Greater Shanghai metropolitan area, which includes Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan, and Huzhou, was estimated to produce a gross metropolitan product (nominal) of nearly 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion). As of 2020, the economy of Shanghai was estimated to be $1 trillion (PPP), ranking the most productive metro area of China and among the top ten largest metropolitan economies in the world. Shanghai's six largest industries—retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing, and automotive manufacturing—comprise about half the city's GDP.

As of 2025, Shanghai had a GDP of CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion in nominal; $1.66 trillion in PPP) that makes up 4% of China's GDP, and a GDP per capita of CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 in nominal; US$66,944 in PPP). In 2022, the average annual disposable income of Shanghai's residents was CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) per capita, while the average annual salary of people employed in urban units in Shanghai was CN¥212,476 (US$31,589), making it one of the wealthiest cities in China, but also the most expensive city in mainland China to live in according to a 2023 study by the Economist Intelligence Unit. According to Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report, Shanghai was the most expensive city in the world for living a luxurious lifestyle in 2021.

In 2023, the city's imports and exports reached CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), accounting for 18.5% of the national total. In 2022, Shanghai was ranked fifth-highest in the number of billionaires by Forbes. Shanghai's nominal GDP was projected to reach US$1.3 trillion in 2035 (ranking first in China), making it one of the world's top 5 major cities in terms of GRP according to a study by Oxford Economics. As of August 2024, Shanghai ranked 4th in the world and 2nd in Greater China (after Beijing) by the largest number of the Fortune Global 500 companies.

In the last two decades, Shanghai has been one of the fastest-developing cities in the world; it has recorded double-digit GDP growth in almost every year between 1992 and 2008, before the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai is a global financial center, ranking third in Asia and eighth globally on the Global Financial Centres Index. Shanghai is also a large hub of the Chinese and global technology industry and home to a large startup ecosystem. As of 2021, the city was ranked as the 2nd Fintech powerhouse in the world after New York City.

As of 2019, the Shanghai Stock Exchange had a market capitalization of US$4.02 trillion, making it the largest stock exchange in China and the fourth-largest stock exchange in the world. In 2009, the trading volume of six key commodities—including rubber, copper, and zinc—on the Shanghai Futures Exchange all ranked first globally. By the end of 2017, Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions, of which 251 were foreign-invested.

As one of the main industrial centres of China, Shanghai plays a key role in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Several industrial zones—including Shanghai Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, and Shanghai Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone—are backbones of Shanghai's secondary sector. Shanghai is home to China's largest steelmaker Baosteel Group, China's largest shipbuilding base Hudong–Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and one of China's oldest shipbuilders, the Jiangnan Shipyard. In auto manufacturing, the Shanghai-based SAIC Motor is one of the three largest automotive corporations in China, and has strategic partnerships with Volkswagen and General Motors. The company ranked 84 on the Fortune Global 500 list in 2023.

In 2017, the number of domestic tourists to the city increased by 7.5% to 318 million, while the number of overseas tourists increased by 2.2% to 8.73 million. In 2017, Shanghai was the highest earning tourist city in the world. According to the International Congress and Convention Association, Shanghai hosted 82 international meetings in 2018, a 34% increase from 61 in 2017. As of 2023, it had 57 five-star hotels, 52 four star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions, and 34 red tourist attractions. In 2023, Shanghai had 3.64 million tourists, a 4.8-fold growth compared to 2022. It generated CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion) in value, a 98.5% increase from the previous year. The number of foreign tourists reached 2.41 million, with a 5.2-fold increase.

In September 2013, the city launched the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone—the first free-trade zone in mainland China. It introduced several reforms to incentivize foreign investment. The Banker reported that Shanghai attracted the highest volumes of financial sector foreign direct investment in the Asia-Pacific region in 2013. As of October 2019, it is the second largest free-trade zone in mainland China in terms of land area (behind Hainan Free Trade Zone) covering an area of 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) and integrating four existing bonded zones—Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, and Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Commodities entering the zone are exempt from duty and customs clearance.

As of 2023, Shanghai had a population of 24,874,500, including 14,801,700 (59.5%) hukou holders (registered locally). As of 2022, 89.3% of Shanghai's population lives in urban areas, and 10.7% live in rural areas. Based on the population of its total administrative area, Shanghai is the second largest of the four municipalities of China, behind Chongqing, but is generally considered the largest Chinese city because the urban population of Chongqing is much smaller. According to the OECD, Shanghai's metropolitan area has an estimated population of 34 million.

According to the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau, about 157,900 residents in Shanghai are foreigners, including 28,900 Japanese, 21,900 Americans, and 20,800 Koreans. The actual number of foreign citizens in the city is probably much higher. Shanghai is also a domestic immigration city—40.3% (9.8 million) of the city's residents are from other regions of China.

Shanghai has a life expectancy of 83.18 years for the city's registered population, the highest life expectancy of all cities in mainland China. This has also caused the city to experience population aging—in 2021, 17.4% (4.3 million) of the city's registered population was aged 65 or above. In 2017, the Chinese government implemented population controls for Shanghai, resulting in a population decline of 10,000 people by the end of the year.
Shanghai has a public transportation system comprising metros, buses, ferries, and taxis, which can be accessed using a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

Shanghai's rapid transit system, the Shanghai Metro, incorporates subway and light metro lines and extends to each core urban district as well as neighboring suburban districts. As of 2025, there are 19 metro lines (excluding the Shanghai maglev train and Jinshan railway), 508 stations, and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of lines in operation, making it the longest network in the world. On 8 March 2019, it set the city's daily metro ridership record with 13.3 million. Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev train is the first and the fastest commercial high-speed maglev in the world, with a maximum operation speed of 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

The first tram line in Shanghai was opened in 1908. By 1925, there were 328 tramcars and 14 routes operated by Chinese, French, and British companies collaboratively, all of which were nationalized in 1949. Since the 1960s, tram lines were either dismantled or replaced by trolleybus or motorbus lines; the last tram line was demolished in 1975. Shanghai reintroduced trams in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram. In 2018, the steel wheeled Songjiang Tram started operating in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the world's most extensive bus network, including the world's oldest continuously operating trolleybus system, with 1,575 lines covering a total length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi) by 2019. The system is operated by multiple companies. As of 2024, 30,900 taxis were in operation in Shanghai, which carried 134 million passengers that year.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

east-china-university-of-science-and-tec.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. East China University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at East China University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Fudan University, abbreviated FDU, sits in Shanghai's Yangpu district and is a public research university. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and the Shanghai Municipal Government shares the funding. National schemes that single out the strongest institutions in the country have all included it. Those are Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction, which together mark out the best-supported universities. It is also one of the C9 League, the informal group of China's leading research universities.

A Chinese Jesuit priest, Ma Xiangbo, started the institution in 1905. The way it began, and the way each political era afterwards reshaped it, tells you a good deal about the place you would be joining.

The first form of the university was Fudan College, opened by Ma Xiangbo in 1905. He had previously founded Aurora College, but the Jesuit order often opposed student movements there and interfered with them. Ma wanted something different, so he built a school that prepared students for higher study and that took government money. Its three-year course let students pick a general or a specialised track. After the 1911 Revolution, the college kept offering general instead of specialised teaching.

Fudan turned private in 1917 and added specialised departments. Subjects included psychology, civil engineering, politics, economics, banking, business and administration, foreign literature and Chinese literature. Under a national policy, preparatory teaching came to an end in 1921 and the university adopted a credit-and-elective system modelled on American practice. The new Nationalist government registered it with the Ministry of Education in 1928. A year later it had four faculties: Liberal Arts, Science, Law and Commerce. When the Second Sino-Japanese War broke out, the university relocated to Chongqing in 1937.

Fudan stopped being private in 1941. The Nationalist government agreed to make it a national university, so it could appoint the people holding the leading posts of president, provost and dean. Back in Shanghai from early 1946, the university had a defined purpose under Chiang Kai-shek and the Kuomintang: to give Chinese students an education in the Western style that would help the country rebuild its economy.

After the Communist Party won the civil war against the Kuomintang, its Shanghai Military Control Commission took over Fudan in 1949. By 1952 higher education had been remodelled on the Soviet pattern, and Communist ideology entered what Fudan taught. The university became a Soviet-style comprehensive institution. Arts and science departments from other universities were folded into it, which left it as Shanghai's single university offering basic science and arts. Its job under Mao was to spread socialist values in support of Party goals, and when the Cultural Revolution brought political turmoil, classes at Fudan stopped altogether.

The year 2000 brought a merger with Shanghai Medical University, which dated back to 1927 and had begun as the School of Medicine of the Fourth National Chungshan University. The result is the Fudan University of today.

In December 2019 the university amended its charter. The words "academic independence and freedom of thought" disappeared, and a "pledge to follow the Communist party's leadership" appeared instead. The charter further required Fudan to "equip its teachers and employees" with "Xi Jinping Thought". Students protested against it, and observers worried that academic freedom was shrinking. If this matters to you, read around the topic and ask current students what they experience.

Two newer developments are worth noting. In 2023 Fudan created a fund of funds worth 1 billion yuan to back start-up innovation, and it started CFFF, which it describes as the biggest cloud-based computing platform for scientific research in China.

In 2024 Hungary's government agreed that Fudan's first overseas campus would be built in Budapest. The planned cost was 540 billion HUF, and 450 billion of that would come from Hungarian state funds borrowed from China, with Chinese firms doing most of the construction. Education professionals and politicians in Hungary spoke out against the project, raising economic, higher-education and national-security worries.
Undergraduates are placed in one of five residential-style colleges. They are Xide (希德), Renzhong (任重), Keqing (克卿), Tengfei (腾飞) and Zhide (志德).

The Shanghai base has four campuses, namely Jiangwan (江湾), Zhangjiang (张江), Fenglin (枫林) and the original Handan (邯郸), all governed by one central administration. In addition, 17 hospitals are affiliated with Fudan.
The management school offers several joint MBA programmes (the details below are as of 2024). Each partner awards its own degree, as noted:
MIT Sloan School of Management, United States: running since 1996, with a degree issued by Fudan.
Norway's BI Norwegian Business School: also since 1996, leading to the BI degree.
University of Hong Kong: graduates receive a University of Hong Kong degree.
Washington University in St. Louis, United States: graduates receive a WUSTL degree.

The school also runs an executive MBA with National Taiwan University, and a global master's in management with London Business School that gives graduates degrees from both partners. In Italy, Bocconi University and Luiss University share a double degree in international management that began in 2005; the qualification is a master's in international management, issued by one of the two Italian schools.

Since 2006 Fudan's economics school has teamed up with England's Durham University Business School on a Doctor of Business Administration (DBA), which Durham awards. The first cohort began in 2007. Fudan is still the main base, although parts of the course are taught at Durham and in San Francisco.

There is also the S3 Asia MBA, which Fudan has run since 2008 with Korea University Business School and the National University of Singapore. Students spend six months at every partner, and they graduate with a dual degree from Fudan plus one other member of the group.

Business is not the only field with overseas ties. In 2011 a research tie-up with the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research in the UK produced the Fudan-Tyndall Centre, which studies climate change and sustainable development. Separately, Fudan's institute for global public policy builds academic hubs inside foreign institutions. With the London School of Economics it runs the LSE-Fudan Research Centre for Global Public Policy, and its Arab counterpart focuses on development and governance across the Middle East and North Africa.

For research output in natural and life sciences, the 2024 Nature Index Research Leaders placed Fudan 12th among the world's universities and 9th among those in Asia Pacific. In the 2024 CWTS Leiden Ranking, which counts publications from 2019 to 2022, it comes 11th worldwide.
Fudan has counted 95 academician alumni since 1952. Only Peking University and Tsinghua University have more in China. People who studied there include these:
Chen Yinke (1890-1969): a historian, linguist and orientalist who also worked as a politician and writer.
Chen Wangdao (1891-1977): a scholar and educator, remembered as the first, and so far the only, translator of the whole Communist Manifesto into Chinese.
Chen Zhili, born 1942, a politician.
Chu Coching, geologist and meteorologist.
David Ji (born 1952), a Chinese-American electronics entrepreneur who co-founded Apex Digital. He was detained in China for months, without any charge, during a business dispute.
Kerry Chen: the entrepreneur behind ATRenew, where he is chief executive.
Yan Fu: a translator, newspaper editor, writer and former military officer who introduced Western thought to China in the later 1800s.
Yu Youren, who worked as a politician, scholar, educator and calligrapher.
Wang Huning (b. 1955), a political theorist and senior Communist Party leader.
What a student's daily life is like depends largely on the city around the campus, so here is an overview of Shanghai: its weather, its transport and what it offers.

The city is on the east coast, at the mouth of the Yangtze. To the north runs the Yangtze River, to the south is Hangzhou Bay, and the East China Sea is on the eastern side. Some of the land came from the Yangtze's natural silt, and some from modern reclamation schemes. The ground is soft and sandy, which is why tall buildings rest on deep concrete piles. As a municipality with provincial rank, Shanghai administers the estuary along with many neighbouring islands. Its borders are with Zhejiang (south) and Jiangsu (west and north). At the north end is Chongming Island, which grew during the 20th century into the second-biggest island of mainland China.

The terrain is an alluvial plain, so nearly all of the 6,340.5 km² (2,448.1 sq mi) of land is flat, rising on average just 4 m (13 ft) above sea level. Tidal flats once ringed the estuary but have been turned over to farming. A small number of hills, such as She Shan, rise in the south-west. Highest of all is the summit of Dajinshan Island, out in Hangzhou Bay, which stands 103 m (338 ft) tall. Waterways abound, from rivers and canals to streams and lakes, and the area is part of Lake Tai's drainage basin.

The Huangpu River splits downtown in two. It is a man-made branch of the Yangtze, said to have been created by Lord Chunshen's order in the Warring States era. West of the river lies Puxi, the historic centre, near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, a link to the Grand Canal and Lake Tai. The financial district of Lujiazui was built on the east bank, in Pudong. Building Pudong International Airport destroyed some wetlands along the eastern shore, and that loss has been partly offset by protecting and enlarging a nearby sandbank, Jiuduansha, as a nature reserve.

Shanghai's climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with four clear seasons. Downtown averages 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) over the year, and suburbs between 16.2 and 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F). Winter is cold and damp, ranging from mild to chilly, and Siberian north-westerlies can push night temperatures under freezing. In a normal year, snow falls on about 4.7 days and lies on the ground for 1.6. Summer is humid and hot, with occasional thunderstorms and downpours, and typically 21 days hit 35 °C (95 °F) or more. Typhoons are a risk in summer and early autumn.

Spring is usually pleasant but can turn rainy and unsettled, while autumn tends to be dry and sunny. Between 28% of possible sunshine in June and 46% in August, the city gets 1,754 hours a year. By China's official seasonal rules, using 2001 to 2025 data, spring begins on 9 March and summer on 15 May, with autumn following on 5 October and winter on 4 December. Expect the stretch between 19 July and 8 August to average over 30 °C (86.0 °F).

The Xujiahui weather station has logged the records since 1951. The coldest day, 31 January 1977, reached -10.1 °C (13.8 °F), though an unofficial reading of -12.1 °C (10.2 °F) dates from 19 January 1893. The hottest days, 21 July 2017 and again 13 July 2022, hit 40.9 °C (105.6 °F). Its warmest night was 13 August 2010, when the temperature never dropped below 32.1 °C (89.8 °F). For 2025, Xujiahui had a mean of 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), 1.93 °C warmer than the 1991-2020 norm. The average daily high is 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and the average low 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

Along the Huangpu, the Bund is a row of buildings from the early 20th century whose styles range from neoclassical (the HSBC Building) to Art Deco (Sassoon House, now part of the Peace Hotel). It has been refreshed on more than one occasion. A new promenade designed by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren appeared in 1986, and another round of work came before the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic rerouted.

Britain, France and the United States each held influence in the city, and much of the construction reflects that. A boom in building during the 1920s and 1930s left a number of Art Deco buildings. The Hungarian-Slovak architect László Hudec, resident from 1918 until 1947, designed several, among them the Paramount, the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel. The Broadway Mansions, the Metropole Hotel and the Peace Hotel came from Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, while the Austrian C.H. Gonda created the Capitol Theatre.

You will also meet the shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men), a local house type whose name means "stone storage door". These are grey brick homes of two or three floors, each with a front yard behind a stout wooden door in a stone arch, and they stand side by side along straight lanes called longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). Elsewhere you will find Soviet neoclassical ("Stalinist") buildings, mostly dating from 1949, when the People's Republic was founded, to the late 1960s, when the Sino-Soviet split ended the period of Soviet advisers helping to build a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is a typical example.

By height, Shanghai ranks seventh among the world's cities, with 206 buildings taller than 150 m. The Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center are among them, as is the Shanghai Tower, finished in 2015 and today the tallest building in China (third in the world). Close by, at the tip of Lujiazui to the north, is the Oriental Pearl Tower, 468 m (1,535 ft) high. In spite of rapid redevelopment, many former foreign concession areas are well preserved, and the Old City still has traditional buildings, including the elaborate Jiangnan-style Yu Garden.

As a world centre of finance and innovation, and a national hub for trade, commerce and transport, Shanghai also has the busiest container port on the planet. Its wider metropolitan area, which reaches out to Huzhou, Zhoushan, Jiaxing, Ningbo, Nantong, Wuxi and Suzhou, produced a nominal gross metropolitan product of close to 13 trillion RMB (about $1.9 trillion) in 2022. Measured in PPP terms, the city economy was worth $1 trillion in 2020, the most productive urban area in China and one of the ten biggest in the world. Half of GDP comes from six industries: retail, finance, IT, property, machinery and car manufacturing.

The 2025 GDP figure was CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion nominal, or $1.66 trillion in PPP), or 4% of China's total. Per person that works out as CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 at nominal rates, and US$66,944 on a PPP basis). In 2022 residents had CN¥79,610 each (about US$11,836) in disposable income a year, and urban employees were paid CN¥212,476 (some US$31,589) on average. The city is among China's richest, but the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2023 study also found it to be mainland China's costliest place to live, and the Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report from Julius Baer named it the world's priciest city for a luxurious lifestyle in 2021. For a student budget, plan early.

Foreign trade in 2023 came to 18.5% of the national total, worth CN¥7.73 trillion (that is US$1.07 trillion). In 2022 Forbes counted more billionaires in only four other cities. Oxford Economics forecast a nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, top in China and a place among the five leading cities worldwide by gross regional product. In August 2024 it was fourth in the world, and second after Beijing within Greater China, for the number of Fortune Global 500 companies. Growth has been remarkable: between 1992 and the financial crisis of 2008, GDP rose by double digits nearly every year, so over the past twenty years it has been one of the world's fastest-developing cities.

Shanghai is eighth worldwide, and third in Asia, on the Global Financial Centres Index. It also hosts a big piece of China's technology sector, and of the global one, with a sizeable start-up scene; in 2021 only New York beat it as a fintech powerhouse.

By 2019 the Shanghai Stock Exchange's market capitalisation stood at US$4.02 trillion, the largest in China and fourth in the world. Volume on the Shanghai Futures Exchange led the world in 2009 for six main commodities, rubber, copper and zinc among them. At the end of 2017, 1,491 financial institutions were based in the city, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Shanghai remains one of China's principal industrial centres and a major player in manufacturing and heavy industry. Four zones underpin the secondary sector: Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, and the Hongqiao and Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zones. Names to know: Baosteel Group, the biggest steelmaker in China; Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, the country's largest shipbuilding base; and Jiangnan Shipyard, one of its oldest. SAIC Motor, a Shanghai company, is among China's three largest carmakers and works with both Volkswagen and General Motors. In 2023 it was 84th on the Fortune Global 500.

Visitor numbers have been large. In 2017 domestic tourists rose 7.5% to 318 million, and overseas tourists rose 2.2% to 8.73 million; that year no tourist city in the world earned more. The International Congress and Convention Association counted 82 international meetings in Shanghai in 2018, up 34% from 61 the year before. In 2023 the city had 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels. It also had 144 rated tourist attractions, 34 "red" attractions and 1,942 travel agencies. Its 2023 total was 3.64 million tourists, 4.8 times 2022, worth CN¥177.12 billion (about US$24.53 billion), up 98.5%. Foreign visitors came to 2.41 million, a fivefold-plus rise (5.2 times).

The Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, launched in September 2013, was mainland China's first, with reforms aimed at attracting foreign investment. It currently covers 240.22 km² (92.75 sq mi), as of October 2019, second in area among mainland free-trade zones after Hainan, and merges four earlier bonded zones. Those are Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, and two at Waigaoqiao (a free trade zone and a free trade logistics park). No duty or customs clearance applies to goods entering.

The 2023 population was 24,874,500, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) hold a local hukou, the household registration. Urban areas account for 89.3% of residents and rural areas for 10.7% (2022 figures). Chongqing, whose municipal area is bigger, is the only one of China's four municipalities with a larger administrative population, but because most of Chongqing's people live outside its urban core, Shanghai is normally called the biggest city. The OECD puts the metropolitan population at about 34 million.

Officially, the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau records roughly 157,900 foreign residents: 28,900 from Japan, 21,900 from the United States and 20,800 from Korea. The true total is probably far higher. The city also pulls in migrants from within China, who make up 40.3% of residents (9.8 million).

People live longer here than in any other mainland city: 83.18 years is the life expectancy for registered residents. A consequence is an ageing society, with 4.3 million (17.4%) of the registered population aged 65 or older in 2021. Population controls introduced by the Chinese government in 2017 reduced the city's population by 10,000 by the end of that year.
Local transport combines the metro, buses, ferries and taxis, and one Shanghai Public Transport Card works on all of them.

The Shanghai Metro runs subway and light-metro lines to all core urban districts and several neighbouring suburban ones. At the start of 2025 it had 19 lines, 508 stations and 808 km (502 mi) of track, not counting the maglev or the Jinshan railway, the longest system anywhere. Its daily passenger record, 13.3 million, was set on 8 March 2019. The maglev line opened in 2004 and was the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world, and it remains the fastest, running at up to 430 km/h (270 mph).

Trams first ran in 1908. By 1925 Chinese, French and British companies together operated 328 tramcars on 14 routes, and everything passed into state ownership in 1949. During the 1960s the tracks were taken up or replaced by trolleybus and motorbus services, and the last line vanished in 1975. The Zhangjiang Tram, on rubber tyres, brought trams back in 2010, followed in 2018 by the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram in Songjiang District.

Shanghai's bus system is the biggest in the world and includes the oldest trolleybus network still running without a break. By 2019 it had 1,575 lines totalling 8,997 km (5,590 mi), operated by several companies. Taxis numbered 30,900 in 2024, and they took 134 million passengers that year.
Fudan University lists 515 programs for international students on this site: 61 bachelor, 114 master's, 104 doctoral, 236 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 433 taught in Chinese, 82 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 23,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 23,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 10,000 to CNY 144,000 (median CNY 48,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 120,000 (median CNY 37,000), according to the university's published fee table.

515 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (19):
Biology
Biomedical Engineering
Chinese History

Fudan University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.
Application windows found for Fudan University:
Autumn 2026 English-taught MBBS, phases 1 and 2 (closed): opens 1 Jan 2026, closes 6 Mar 2026
Deadlines can move and seats can fill earlier than the closing date, so apply as soon as your documents are ready.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

fudan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Fudan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Fudan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University, usually shortened to FAFU, is a provincial public university specialising in farming and forestry subjects. It is located in Fuzhou, the capital of Fujian province on China's south-east coast. Because it belongs to the province, the Fujian provincial government is its main sponsor, and two national bodies also contribute: the national agriculture and rural affairs ministry, as well as the national forestry and grassland authority. That joint backing tells a prospective student that the university has links to both provincial and national agricultural policy.

The university's story begins in 1952, when Fujian Agricultural College was created by combining the agricultural colleges of two older institutions, Xiamen University and Fuzhou University. Almost fifty years later, in October 2000, a merger of Fujian Agricultural University (as it was then) with Fujian Forestry College produced the present university. The official site of the university gives a fuller timeline of name changes and reorganisations.

Because daily life depends on where you live, the rest of this overview explains Fuzhou (weather, people, food, travel, economy and research standing) and then the wider province of Fujian, from the earliest settlers to the dynasties that shaped it and its modern tourist appeal.

fujian-agriculture-and-forestry-universi.h: Where the city is and what the weather is like

blocks.x: Fuzhou lies on the north-east coast of Fujian. Its neighbours are Ningde and Nanping to the north, Quanzhou and Putian to the south and Sanming to the west.

The climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa) and shaped by the East Asian monsoon. Expect a lengthy, steamy summer and a brief, gentle, dry winter. Heavy monsoon downpours usually come in the latter half of May, and typhoons can hit in late summer and early autumn, so students should follow weather warnings from August to October. January averages 11.4 degrees C, July 29.4 degrees C, and the year as a whole 20.5 degrees C. Sunshine runs from 26 per cent of the possible total in March to 51 per cent in July, and the city gets 1,607 hours of bright sun a year. Recorded extremes since 1951 are minus 1.9 degrees C (25 January 2016) and 41.9 degrees C (24 July 2022). Snow almost never falls; the last times it settled were in the winters of 1957, 1975 and 1991 (February, December and December respectively).
The culture of Fuzhou differs from that of China's inland heartland and from other parts of the coast. Alongside Mandarin, most local people speak Fuzhounese, the prestige dialect of Eastern Min.

Min opera (also known as Fuzhou drama) ranks among Fujian's principal local operas. Its audience is in Fuzhou itself, in the north-eastern and north-western districts where people speak the Fuzhou dialect, and overseas in Taiwan and the Malay world. The form settled down in the early 1900s. Over a thousand plays exist, mostly based on folk stories, historical fiction or legends, and three of the best known are Making Seal, The Purple Jade Hairpin and the peach-and-litchi tale of Switching Fairy Peach.

Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism are the two traditional mainstream faiths, and many residents follow both at once. The city has many Buddhist monasteries, Taoist temples and monks. Smaller local cults also keep shrines in the streets and lanes. These beliefs go back centuries and absorbed gods, teachings and customs from other religions and cultures, including totem worship and old legends. An example is the Monkey King, who began as an object of monkey worship among early local people and, once the novel Journey to the West appeared in the Ming dynasty, came to be treated in Fuzhou as the God of Wealth.
The worship of Lady Linshui is the most widespread religion in the Min River valley and counts as one of Fujian's three most influential local cults, along with the cults of Mazu and Baosheng Dadi.

Fuzhou cooking is one of four traditional styles within Fujian cuisine, which itself is one of China's eight regional cuisines. Dishes are light yet flavourful. They emphasise umami (xianwei in Chinese) and aim to preserve the natural taste of the main ingredients rather than cover it. Compared with some other Chinese styles the flavours are mild, often a blend of sweet and sour. Soup is an essential part of any meal and is made in many ways from fresh seasonal vegetables and seafood, often with local cooking wine known as Fujian laojiu.

Street food and snacks are a local pride: Fuzhou fish balls, meat-pastry dumplings (bianrouyan), oyster cake (haili bing), rice scroll soup (dingbianhu), guong bian (a lightly savoury pastry), the famous Buddha Jumps over the Wall and pork floss. Many of them come with legends. The oyster cake story tells of a young man in the early Qing who inherited his father's dim sum shop but could barely feed himself, let alone a family. He dreamed of a silver-haired old man who said his fortune was good, and then saw a moon sinking behind the clouds as a golden sun rose in the east. Inspired, he created a cake that is white like the moon until it goes into hot oil and comes out golden like the morning sun. He became wealthy, others copied the recipe, and it has been passed down ever since. Rice scroll soup also has a long history and became popular in the early Qing.

As Fuzhou people settled overseas, their food travelled to Taiwan, Southeast Asia and the United States. You can find guong bian and fish balls in Sitiawan and Ipoh in Malaysia, and a similar trio (rice scroll soup, fish balls and the meat dumplings) in New York's Chinatown. To overseas Fuzhounese these dishes symbolise cultural identity and continuity.

Festival foods follow the calendar: red and white rice cakes at Chinese New Year, tangyuan at the Lantern Festival, zongzi at the Dragon Boat Festival, and plain yuanxiao dipped in sweet soybean powder at the winter solstice. Olive juice (ganlanzhi) is a popular drink, cloudy and pale yellow-green. It is made from the Canarium album tree, grown in Fuzhou since the Tang dynasty, and since 2010 it has had a protected geographical-indication trademark. It is not found elsewhere in China, a reminder of how much food varies from region to region.

Three treasures of traditional Fuzhou art are bodiless lacquerware, paper umbrellas and horn combs. Bodiless lacquerware also forms a trio of superexcellences with cork pictures and Shoushan stone carvings.

Fuzhou Changle International Airport has replaced the old Fuzhou Yixu Airport. Changle is the main international airport and an air hub in south-east China, while Yixu became a PLA airbase after 1997.

Fuzhou is a rail hub for the north of Fujian. The Wenzhou-Fuzhou and Fuzhou-Xiamen lines belong to the Southeast Coast High-Speed Rail Corridor, on which trains may reach 250 km/h (155 mph). The Hefei-Fuzhou High-Speed Railway runs to Beijing through inland Jiangxi province with a top speed of 350 km/h (220 mph). The Nanping-Fuzhou line and the Xiangtang-Putian line reach inland, and the latter takes trains of up to 200 km/h (124 mph). A regional cargo line, the Fuzhou-Mawei line, goes from Fuzhou Railway Station east to the port in Mawei District. The two passenger stations are Fuzhou and Fuzhou South; because of its central location Fuzhou station is often just called the station.

Fujian's earliest rapid transit network is the Fuzhou Metro, which now runs five lines. Line 1 joins the two main stations. Fuzhou station is north of the centre near the North Second Ring Road, while Fuzhou South station, in Cangshan District, is a landmark of the New City scheme (begun in 2007, finished in 2010). Line 1 opened on 18 May 2016, while Line 5 (north-east of the city to Fuzhou South) was finished step by step across 2022 and 2023.

Line 2 crosses the city from east to west. It connects the university city and the Fuzhou High-Tech Zone in Minhou County, the Jinshan Industrial Zone in Cangshan and Gushan mountain in Jin'an District, and it started on 26 April 2019. Line 4 heads southward from the northern part of the city and ends at Difengjian by the Min River. Line 6 intersects it and joins the central districts to the southern areas of Yingqian and Wanshou.

The Matsu Islands, administered by Taiwan, have a regular passenger boat link with Mawei District's port. In addition, a fast ferry leaves Pingtan County, the nearest mainland point to Taiwan, for Taipei and Taichung and takes roughly three hours to cross the strait.

In 1867 the Fuzhou Navy Yard was founded, among the earliest large-scale attempts in China to adopt Western technology. French advisers helped build a shipyard and arsenal and a naval school. The academy at the yard taught English, French, engineering and navigation and became a centre for European languages and technical sciences. It trained a generation of Western-educated officers, among them the scholar-reformer Yan Fu (1854-1921).

The yard was part of a plan to strengthen China after its heavy defeat in the Second Opium War (1856-1860). However, most able students still chose the traditional Confucian route, and by the mid-1870s the government lost interest; funding was hard to find and the yard declined. Until the Second World War Fuzhou remained mainly a trading city and port with little industry, and Japan held the port from 1940 to 1945.

After 1949 the city grew a good deal. The Min River was dredged so medium-sized vessels could sail upstream to Nanping, and in 1956 a railway opened to link Fuzhou with the interior and the national network. Fuzhou itself can no longer be reached by ocean-going ships, but the Luoxingta anchorage and the outer harbour at Guantou on the East China Sea coast have been modernised. Main exports are timber, fruit, paper and food.

Factories draw electricity from the Gutian hydropower scheme in the north-western mountains, delivered over a regional grid. Fuzhou is a centre for commercial banking, designer brands, timber processing, engineering, paper, printing and textiles. A small iron and steel works dates from 1958. In 1984 Fuzhou became one of China's open cities under the open-door policy that invited foreign investment. Handicrafts are still important in the countryside, and the city is known for lacquer and wooden goods. Factories turn out chemicals, silk and cotton cloth, steel and processed food, and exports include fine lacquerware, handmade fans and umbrellas. Trade is chiefly with other Chinese coastal ports, and timber, food and paper leave through Guantou harbour, about 50 kilometres (31 miles) downstream.

Fuzhou is without doubt the political, economic and cultural centre of Fujian, as well as an industrial centre and a seaport on the Min River. Its 2008 GDP was 228.4 billion yuan, up 13 per cent. Exports in 2008 were 13.6 billion US dollars (up 10.4 per cent) and imports 6.8 billion; retail sales came to 113.4 billion yuan, and GDP per head reached 33,615 yuan. The city approved 155 foreign-invested projects, with contracted foreign investment of 1.489 billion dollars and actual investment 1.002 billion, a 43 per cent increase. In 2015 GDP per head was 75,614 yuan (about 12,140 dollars), 52nd among China's 659 cities.

The Fuzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone was created by the State Council in January 1985. It has a planned area of 22 square kilometres, of which 10.1 are built, and is near Changle airport and Fuzhou Port. It welcomes electronics assembly and manufacturing, telecom equipment, trading and distribution, car production and assembly, medical equipment, shipping and logistics and heavy industry.

A third zone, the Fuzhou Export Processing Zone, opened on 3 June 2005 under State Council approval, with the full set of favourable policies. It lies within the Chang'an Investment Zone of the development zone and plans 1.14 square kilometres.

The Fuzhou Free Trade Zone dates from 1992, also approved by the State Council, and plans 1.8 square kilometres. It favours electronics, heavy industry, instruments and industrial equipment, shipping and logistics, telecom equipment, trading and distribution.
Fuzhou is a significant research city, listed among the world's top 50 cities in the Nature Index.

Archaeological finds in 2011 show that Fujian had reached the Neolithic by the middle of the sixth millennium BC. At the Keqiutou site (7450 to 5590 years before present) on Pingtan Island, about 70 kilometres (43 miles) south-east of Fuzhou, diggers found tools of stone, shell, bone, jade and pottery, including wheel-thrown pottery, as well as spinning wheels, firm evidence of weaving. In suburban Fuzhou the Tanshishan site (5500 to 4000 years before present) spans the Neolithic and the Chalcolithic, with semi-underground round buildings in the lower layer. The Huangtulun site, also in suburban Fuzhou and dated to about 1325 BC, belongs to the Bronze Age.

A 2013 study by Tianlong Jiao suggests the Neolithic reached the Fujian coast about 6,000 years ago. Population density was low, and people depended mostly on fishing and hunting with a little farming. Four main cultures grew up on the coast, the earliest ones coming from the north, from coastal Zhejiang:
Keqiutou culture, about 6000 to 5500 years before present (c. 4050 to 3550 BC)
Tanshishan culture, about 5000 to 4300 years before present (c. 3050 to 2350 BC)
Damaoshan culture, about 5000 to 4300 years before present
Huangguashan culture, about 4300 to 3500 years before present (c. 2350 to 1550 BC)
Inland Fujian had two clearly different Neolithic cultures: Niubishan (5000 to 4000 years ago) and Hulushan (2050 to 1550 BC).

Fujian was the home of the kingdom of Minyue. Its name joins Min, probably an ethnic name connected with the word for southern barbarians, to Yue, taken from the State of Yue, a kingdom of the Spring and Autumn period in Zhejiang to the north. The Yue royal house had fled to Fujian after Chu conquered its kingdom in 306 BC. Min is also the name of the area's main river, though the ethnic name is probably older.

The Qin removed the King of Minyue and set up a paramilitary province called Minzhong Commandery, and the kingdom stayed a de facto state until an emperor of the Qin, the first unified imperial state, ended its status.

When the Qin collapsed, the warlords Xiang Yu and Liu Bang fought each other. The Minyue king Wuzhu sent troops to help Liu, a gamble that paid off, for Liu won and founded the Han. In 202 BC he restored Minyue as a tributary but independent kingdom. Wuzhu could build a fortified city in Fuzhou and in a few places in the Wuyi Mountains, all recently excavated. His realm stretched past today's Fujian border to take in parts of Guangdong (east), Jiangxi (east) and Zhejiang (south).

After Wuzhu died, Minyue kept a warlike tradition and launched expeditions against neighbouring kingdoms in Guangdong, Jiangxi and Zhejiang, mainly in the second century BC. The expanding Han stopped this, and the emperor finally decided to end the threat by military force. In 111 BC large armies approached from four directions by land and sea. The Fuzhou leaders surrendered rather than face a hopeless battle and ruin, so Fujian's first kingdom came to a sudden end. Fujian then belonged to the much larger Yang Province, whose capital was at Liyang (today's He County, Anhui). As the Han dynasty fell at the end of the second century AD and the Three Kingdoms period began, The Kingdom of Wu's founder, Sun Quan, needed almost two decades to bring the Shan Yue (the highland Yue people) under control.

Noble families from the north began to arrive early in the fourth century, as Western Jin fell apart and civil wars and tribal uprisings from the north and west tore the north apart. They came mostly from eight central-China families: Chen, Lin, Huang, Zheng, Zhan, Qiu, He and Hu. The first four are still the most common surnames in Fujian.

Even so, rough terrain isolated Fujian from nearby regions and left its economy undeveloped, despite the population boost. Density stayed low compared with the rest of China, and the Western Jin set up only two commanderies and sixteen counties. Like Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou and Yunnan, Fujian was often a place of exile for prisoners and dissidents. During the Southern and Northern Dynasties, four successive southern courts (Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang and Chen) held the lands south of the Yangtze, Fujian among them.

Under the Sui and Tang a large number of new migrants arrived. In the Sui, Fujian again belonged to Yang Province, and in the Tang to the bigger Jiangnan East Circuit, administered from Suzhou, with around five prefectures and 25 counties in modern Fujian. The Tang (618 to 907) was a golden age that boosted Fujian's culture and economy, and Fuzhou's institutions grew. Political unrest in the heartland late in the Tang sent more northerners to settle in northern Fujian.

The name Fujian first appeared for an administrative region in 985, when the area was reorganised as the Fujian Circuit. Under the Yuan, Fujian was part of Jiangzhe province, governed from Hangzhou. Between 1357 and 1366 Muslims of Quanzhou took part in the Ispah Rebellion, moving north and even taking Putian and Fuzhou before the Yuan crushed them. Afterwards Quanzhou lost its foreign trade and its welcoming international character, as the foreigners had been killed or expelled. General Chen Youding, who had suppressed the revolt, continued to rule Fujian even after the Red Turban Rebellion broke out, until forces loyal to Zhu Yuanzhang, the Hongwu Emperor who founded the Ming, defeated him in 1367.
Tourism is well developed, and Fujian has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, a number few Chinese provinces can match.

Some of the dates and economic figures in this profile are older and come from different years, so treat them as background. Confirm programmes, campuses, admissions and visa details with FAFU directly. Prepare for hot, humid summers, a typhoon season in late summer and early autumn, and mild winters, and expect to hear Fuzhounese in everyday life alongside Mandarin.

fujian-agriculture-and-forestry-universi.h: Reading the history of Fujian as a student would

blocks.x: The long list of dynasties may look like trivia, but it explains several things you will notice on arrival. Fujian's mountains kept it apart from the rest of China for centuries, which is why its dialects, operas, shrines and cooking differ so much from northern habits. Repeated migrations from the north brought in family names, such as Chen and Lin, that are still the most common in the province today. Fuzhou's role as a seaport, from the Navy Yard of 1867 to the modern ferries to Taiwan, also helps explain why so many Fuzhou families have relatives abroad and why the city's snacks turn up in Malaysia and New York.

For anyone planning to enrol at FAFU, the most useful points from the city profile are these. Pack for heat and humidity from late spring until autumn. Be aware of typhoon warnings in late summer and early autumn. Use the metro to reach the main railway stations: Line 1 joins Fuzhou and Fuzhou South, and Line 2 passes through the university city area in Minhou County. Allow time to try local dishes such as fish balls, oyster cake and rice scroll soup, and learn a few words of Mandarin since many neighbours speak Fuzhounese among themselves.

Finally, remember that FAFU is a provincial university with national co-funding, so its priorities lie in agriculture and forestry. If you are drawn to those fields, Fuzhou's mix of coastal climate, a long farming and timber trade, and a research-oriented city that ranks among the world's top 50 in the Nature Index makes a sensible base. Ask the admissions office for the latest list of programmes taught in English.

Fujian Medical University (Chinese: 福建医科大学) is a university located in Fuzhou, Fujian, China. Founded in 1937 as Fujian Provincial Medical Vocational School, the school's name was changed to Fujian Provincial Medical College in 1939 and was called Fujian Medical College in 1949. In 1969, after merging with Fujian Chinese Traditional Medical College and the medical department of Huaqiao University, Fujian Medical University was founded and moved to Quanzhou, Fujian. It was moved back to Fuzhou in 1978. The name of the school was changed back to Fujian Medical College in 1982 and then changed back to the present name in April 1996.

Fujian Medical University consist of two main campuses, covering over 876,710 square meters. Currently, the university consists of 17 colleges and departments, 22 undergraduate majors (aspects), 22 doctor-degree locations and 59 master-degree locations. It was conferred the right to recruit Taiwanese students by itself and the students from foreign countries, Hong Kong and Macau. There are more than 1600 postgraduates, 9300 undergraduates and 8700 vocational students. The school was affirmed as the key constructive university by the Fujian provincial government and passed through the teaching evaluation of undergraduate education with good achievements in 2003.

The university library has collection of 1,430,000 volumes, and with the space of 25,600 square meters.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Fuzhou, where Fujian Medical University is located.

Fuzhou has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cfa) influenced by the East Asian monsoon; the summers are long, very hot and humid, and the winters are short, mild and dry. In most years, torrential rain occurs during the monsoon in the second half of May. Fuzhou is also liable to typhoons in late summer and early autumn. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 11.4 °C (52.5 °F) in January to 29.4 °C (84.9 °F) in July, while the annual mean is 20.5 °C (68.9 °F). With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 26% in March to 51% in July, the city receives 1,607 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −1.9 °C (29 °F) on 25 January 2016 to 41.9 °C (107 °F) on 24 July 2022.
Snow is very rare, having covered the ground last times in February 1957, December 1975 and December 1991.
Fuzhou is located in the northeast coast of Fujian province, connects jointly northwards with Ningde and Nanping, southwards with Quanzhou and Putian, westwards with Sanming respectively.
See or edit raw graph data.
The culture of Fuzhou is distinct from the mainstream inland cultures of central China, and in details vary from other areas of the Chinese coast.
Besides Mandarin Chinese, the majority local residents of Fuzhou (Fuzhou people) also speak Fuzhounese (福州話), the prestige form of Eastern Min.

Min opera, also known as Fuzhou drama, is one of the major operas in Fujian Province. It enjoys popularity in the Fuzhou area and in neighboring parts of Fujian such as the northeast and northwest areas where the Fuzhou language is spoken, as well as in Taiwan and the Malay Archipelago. It became a fixed opera in the early 20th century. There are more than 1,000 plays of Min opera, most of which originate from folk tales, historical novels, or ancient legends, including such traditional plays as "Making Seal", "The Purple Jade Hairpin" and "Switching Fairy Peach with Litchi".

The two traditional mainstream religions practiced in Fuzhou are Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism. Traditionally, many people practice both religions simultaneously. The city is also home to many Buddhist monasteries, Taoist temples and Buddhist monks.
Apart from mainstream religions, a number of religious worship sites of various local religions are situated in the streets and lanes of Fuzhou.

The origins of local religion can be dated back centuries. These diverse religions incorporated elements such as gods and doctrines from other religions and cultures, such as totem worship and traditional legends. For example, Monkey King, originated to monkey worship among local ancients, gradually came to embody the God of Wealth in Fuzhou after the novel Journey to the West was issued in Ming dynasty.

As the most popular religion in the Min River Valley, the worship of Lady Linshui is viewed as one of the three most influential local religions in Fujian, the other two being the worship of Mazu and Baosheng Dadi (保生大帝).

Fuzhou cuisine is most notably one of the four traditional cooking styles of Fujian cuisine, which in turn is one of the eight Chinese regional cuisines. Dishes are light but flavorful, with particular emphasis on umami taste, known in Chinese cooking as xianwei (simplified Chinese: 鲜味; traditional Chinese: 鮮味; pinyin: xiānwèi), as well as retaining the original flavor of the main ingredients instead of masking them. In Fuzhou cuisine, the taste is light compared to that of some other Chinese cooking styles, and often have a mixed sweet and sour taste. Soup, served as an indispensable dish in meals, is cooked in various ways with local seasonal fresh vegetables and seafood and often added with local cooking wine (福建老酒).

Fuzhou is famous for its street food and snacks.  Some notable street food dishes include Fuzhou fish balls (魚丸), meat-pastry dumplings (扁肉燕), oyster cake (海蛎饼), rice scroll soup (鼎邊糊), guong bian (光餅; a kind of mildly savory pastry), Buddha Jumps over the Wall (佛跳墙), and pork floss (肉鬆). Many of these street food dishes have a long history and their own local legend; an example would be the oyster cake, according Fuzhou local folklore, in the early Qing dynasty, there was a young man who inherited his father's dim sum business, despite all his hard works, he only managed to earn enough money to feed himself, not enough to raise and feed a family of his own. One night, he dreamt of a silver-haired elderly man, who told him that he has very good fortune, the young man then asked him what he can do to obtain good luck, the elderly man then floated away. That's when the young man notice the setting moon, and after the moon sank under the clouds, rose from the east a golden sun, he was inspired by the dream and invented oyster cake, which is white like the moon before being lowered into hot grease and coming out golden as the morning sun. According to the legend, after the young man made a fortune out of his invention and his oyster cake was imitated by many others, which was passed down till this day. another example of a Fuzhou street food with a long history is rice scroll soup, which became popular in Fuzhou in the early part of the Qing dynasty.  As more Fuzhou residents settled overseas, Fuzhou dishes spread to Taiwan, Southeast Asia and the U.S..  For example, one is able to find guong bian and Fuzhou fish balls in Sitiawan in Ipoh, Malaysia while Fuzhou fish balls, meat-pastry dumplings and rice scroll soup can be found in New York's Chinatown. Fuzhou cuisine has also spread internationally through migration, particularly to Southeast Asia and the United States. Dishes such as fish balls (魚丸), meat-pastry dumplings (扁肉燕), and oyster cake (海蛎饼) are now common in Fujianese communities abroad, including in New York City's Chinatown and in Malaysian cities such as Sitiawan and Ipoh. These dishes are regarded by overseas Fuzhounese as symbols of cultural identity and continuity.

Fuzhou residents also enjoy eating festival foods during traditional Chinese holidays.  For example, red and white rice cakes (年糕) are served over Chinese New Year, tangyuan (汤圆) during the Lantern Festival, zongzi (粽子) during the Dragon Boat Festival, and sweet soy bean powder-covered plain yuanxiao over the winter solstice.

Olive juice is also a much sought-after refreshment. Ganlanzhi (橄榄汁) is cloudy and light yellowish-green in color. Olive trees grown on the Canarium album tree in Fuzhou since the Tang dynasty, it was even approved as a trademark with geographic indication by China in 2010. Not found elsewhere in China, ganlanzhi (橄榄汁) is also a reminder of the many regional differences in China when it comes to food.

Bodiless lacquerware (脫胎漆器), paper umbrellas and horn combs (角梳) are the "Three Treasures" of Fuzhou traditional arts. In addition, bodiless lacquerware, together with cork pictures (軟木畫) and Shoushan stone sculptures (壽山石雕) are called "Three Superexcellences" of Fuzhou.

The city is served by Fuzhou Changle International Airport, which replaces Fuzhou Yixu Airport, the old airfield. The former is its main international airport and an air-hub in southeast China, while the latter was turned into a PLA airbase after 1997.

Fuzhou is a railway hub in northern Fujian.  The Wenzhou–Fuzhou and Fuzhou–Xiamen Railways form part of the Southeast Coast High-Speed Rail Corridor and can accommodate high-speed trains at speeds of up to 250 km/h (155 mph).
The Hefei–Fuzhou High-Speed Railway links the city to Beijing through its nearby inner land province Jiangxi at speeds up to 350 km/h (220 mph).

The Nanping–Fuzhou Railway and Xiangtang–Putian Railway provide rail access inland.  The latter line can carry trains at speeds of 200 km/h (124 mph).  The regional Fuzhou-Mawei Cargo Railway runs from the Fuzhou Railway Station eastward to the port in Mawei District. Fuzhou has two main railway stations, Fuzhou and Fuzhou South. Fuzhou station is often just referred to as Fuzhou station given its central location.
Fuzhou Metro is the first rapid transit system in Fujian province. It has five metro lines in operation.

Line 1 links the two railway stations of the city. The Fuzhou railway station is located north of the city center, near the North Second Ring Road. Fuzhou South Railway Station, located in Cangshan district, is a key landmark of the New City development scheme, begun in 2007 and completed in 2010. Line 1 was opened on May 18, 2016, while Line 5, which runs from the northeast of the city to Fuzhou South, was completed in stages during 2022–2023.

Line 2 runs in the east–west direction of the city, linking the university city and Fuzhou High-Tech Zone in Minhou county, Jinshan Industrial Zone in Cangshan district, and Gushan mountain in Jin'an district. Line 2 was opened on 26 April 2019. Line 4 runs from the north of the city to Difengjian in the south, near the bank of the Min River, the latter being crossed by Line 6 which connects the central areas of the city with Yingqian and Wanshou areas to the south.
Passenger liners regularly sail between ROC's Matsu Islands and the port in Mawei District.
A high-speed ferry sails across Taiwan Strait between the port in Pingtan County, the mainland's closest point to Taiwan, to Taipei and Taichung, a trip that takes about 3 hours.

In 1867 the Fuzhou seaport was the site of one of China's first major experiments with Western technology, when the Fuzhou Navy Yard was established. A shipyard and an arsenal were built under French guidance and a naval school was opened. A naval academy was also established at the shipyard, and it became a center for the study of European languages and technical sciences. The academy, which offered courses in English, French, engineering, and navigation, produced a generation of Western-trained officers, including the famous scholar-reformer Yan Fu (1854–1921).

The yard was established as part of a program to strengthen China in the wake of the country's disastrous defeat in the Second Opium War (1856–1860). Most talented students nonetheless continued to pursue a traditional Confucian education, and by the mid-1870s the government began to lose interest in the shipyard, which had trouble securing funds and declined in importance. Fuzhou remained essentially a commercial center and a port until World War II; it had relatively little industry. The port was occupied by the Japanese during 1940–1945.

Since 1949, Fuzhou has grown considerably. Transportation has been improved by the dredging of the Min River for navigation by medium-sized craft upstream to Nanping. In 1956 the railway linking Fuzhou with the interior of the province and with the main Chinese railway system began operation. The port has also been improved; Fuzhou itself is no longer accessible to seagoing ships, but Luoxingta anchorage and the outer harbor at Guantou on the coast of the East China Sea have been modernized and improved. The chief exports are timber, fruits, paper, and foodstuffs.

Industry is supplied with power by a grid running from the Gutian hydroelectric scheme in the mountains to the northwest. The city is a center for commercial banking, designer brands and timber-working, engineering, papermaking, printing, and textile industries. A small iron and steel plant was built in 1958. In 1984 Fuzhou was designated one of China's "open" cities in the new open-door policy inviting foreign investments. Handicrafts remain important in the rural areas, and the city is famous for its lacquer and wood products.
Its GDP was ¥75,614 (c. US$12,140) per capita in 2015, ranked no. 52 among 659 Chinese cities.

Fuzhou is undoubtedly the province's political, economic and cultural center as well as an industrial center and seaport on the Min River. In 2008, Fuzhou's GDP amounted to ¥228.4 billion, an increase of 13 percent.

Manufactured products include chemicals, silk and cotton textiles, iron and steel, and processed food. Among Fuzhou's exports are fine lacquerware and handcrafted fans and umbrellas. The city's trade is mainly with Chinese coastal ports. Its exports of timber, food products, and paper move through the harbor at Guantou located about 50 kilometres (31 mi) downstream.

In 2008, exports reached US$13.6 billion, a growth of 10.4 percent while imports amounted to US$6.8 billion. Total retail sales for the same period came to ¥113.4 billion and per capita GDP grew to ¥33,615. During the same period, Fuzhou approved 155 foreign-invested projects. Contracted foreign investment amounted to US$1.489 billion, while utilized foreign investment increased by 43 percent to US$1.002 billion.

The Fuzhou Economic & Technological Development Zone was established in January 1985 by the State Council, with a total planning area of 22 square kilometres (8.5 sq mi) and now has 10.1 square kilometres (3.9 sq mi) built. It is located close to Fuzhou Changle International Airport and Fuzhou Port. Industries encouraged in the zone include electronics assembly and manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, trading and distribution, automobile production/assembly, medical equipment and supplies, shipping/warehousing/logistics, and heavy industry.

The Fuzhou Export Processing Zone was founded on June 3, 2005, with the approval of the State Council and enjoys all the preferential policies. It is located inside the Chang'an Investment Zone of the Fuzhou Economic and Technical Development Zone (FETDZ) with a planned land area of 1.14 square kilometres (0.44 sq mi).

The Fuzhou Free Trade Zone was established in 1992 by the State Council, with a planning area of 1.8 square kilometres (0.69 sq mi). Industries encouraged in the free trade zone include electronics assembly and manufacturing, heavy industry, instruments and industrial equipment production, shipping/warehousing/logistics, telecommunications equipment, trading, and distribution.
Fuzhou is also a major city for scientific research, appearing in the global top 50 cities as tracked by the Nature Index.

Fujian Normal University (福建师范大学), usually shortened to FNU, is a state-run institution in Fuzhou, the capital of Fujian Province on China's southeast coast. Locally it has a particular nickname: it is regarded as the province's "cradle of teachers", which tells you what sort of graduates it has traditionally sent out into schools and universities across the region.

FNU traces its roots to the Fujian Superior Normal School, set up in 1907. That makes it the oldest university in Fujian and one of the longest-established teacher-training colleges anywhere in China. The school was later renamed Fujian Provincial Normal College. In 1953, after the People's Republic was founded, it absorbed Hua Nan Women's College and Fukian Christian University, and the result was a larger Fujian Normal College. Fukian Christian University had been founded by the Church Missionary Society as part of its Fukian Mission, with Constance Bryant serving as administrator. The present name, Fujian Normal University, has been used since 1972.
