fujian-normal-university.h: Fuzhou: the city you would live in

blocks.x: A university shapes only part of daily life. The rest is the city, so the sections below explain Fuzhou's weather, language, food, beliefs, transport and economy, followed by a short look at the wider province of Fujian.
Fuzhou lies on the northeast coast of Fujian. Its neighbours in the province are Ningde and Nanping to the north, Quanzhou and Putian to the south and Sanming to the west.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) and shaped by the East Asian monsoon. Expect long, very hot and humid summers and short winters that are mild and dry. Heavy monsoon downpours usually arrive in the second half of May, and late summer and early autumn bring a risk of typhoons.

In January the 24-hour mean temperature is 11.4 °C (52.5 °F); July reaches 29.4 °C (84.9 °F), and across the whole year the mean sits at 20.5 °C (68.9 °F). Sunshine totals 26% of the possible hours in March and 51% in July, which adds up to roughly 1,607 hours annually. Since 1951 the temperature has swung between -1.9 °C (29 °F), logged on 25 January 2016, and 41.9 °C (107 °F), logged on 24 July 2022. Snow is extremely rare: the latest covering fell in December 1991, with earlier ones in December 1975 and February 1957. If you come from a cold climate, winter here will feel gentle, but plan for the heat and humidity of summer.
Fuzhou's culture differs from the inland cultures of central China, and it also differs in many details from other parts of the coast.
Most local people speak Mandarin and also Fuzhounese (福州話), the prestige variety of Eastern Min. You will hear it around the city and it is part of what makes the city feel distinct.

Min opera, also called Fuzhou drama, is among the main opera forms in Fujian. It is popular in the Fuzhou area and in nearby parts of the province where the Fuzhou language is used, in the northeast and northwest, as well as across the water in Taiwan and in the Malay Archipelago. It settled into a fixed form in the early twentieth century. More than 1,000 plays belong to the repertoire, mostly drawn from folk tales, historical novels and ancient legends. Traditional titles include "Switching Fairy Peach with Litchi", "The Purple Jade Hairpin" and "Making Seal".
Two long-standing faiths dominate in Fuzhou: Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism. Many people follow both at once. The city has numerous Buddhist monasteries and Taoist temples, with many Buddhist monks.

Beyond those, shrines to local deities stand in the streets and lanes. Local religion goes back centuries and has absorbed gods and ideas from other traditions, including totem worship and traditional legends. One example is the Monkey King: rooted in ancient monkey worship, over time he became a Wealth God figure in Fuzhou, once the Ming-era novel Journey to the West was published. Another is the cult of Lady Linshui, the most widely followed faith in the Min River Valley, regarded as one of Fujian's three most influential local religions along with the worship of Mazu and of Baosheng Dadi (保生大帝).

Fuzhou cooking is one of four traditional styles within Fujian cuisine, which is itself one of China's eight regional cuisines. Dishes are light but full of flavour, prized for umami, called xianwei (鲜味 / 鮮味) in Chinese, and cooks try to preserve the natural taste of the main ingredient instead of covering it up. Compared with some other Chinese styles the seasoning is mild, and a sweet-and-sour mixture is common. A soup is considered essential at meals, made with seasonal local vegetables and seafood and often finished with local cooking wine (福建老酒).

The city is famous for its snacks. Favourites are pork floss (肉鬆), the banquet dish Buddha Jumps over the Wall (佛跳墙), guong bian (光餅), a lightly savoury pastry, rice scroll soup (鼎邊糊), oyster cake (海蛎饼), meat-pastry dumplings (扁肉燕) and the local fish balls (魚丸). Many come with long histories and folk legends. The tale told about oyster cake is set in the early Qing dynasty: a young man took over his father's dim sum business, but however hard he worked he earned only enough to feed himself. One night he dreamed of a silver-haired old man who told him he was very fortunate, then drifted off before he could ask how to find good luck. The young man noticed the moon setting, and as it slipped behind clouds a golden sun rose in the east. Inspired, he made a cake that is pale like the moon when it goes into hot oil and comes out golden like the morning sun. Legend says he grew rich, others copied the cake, and it has been handed down to the present. Rice scroll soup also has a long past, having become popular in Fuzhou in the early Qing.

As Fuzhou people settled abroad, their food travelled with them to Taiwan, Southeast Asia and the United States. You can find guong bian and fish balls in Sitiawan, near Ipoh in Malaysia, and rice scroll soup, meat-pastry dumplings and fish balls in New York's Chinatown. Overseas Fuzhounese often see these dishes as symbols of their identity and of continuity with home. In short, the same snacks you try in Fuzhou are served in Fujianese communities around the world.

fujian-normal-university.h: Festival foods and a local drink

blocks.x: Seasonal holidays have their own dishes. Red and white rice cakes (年糕) appear at Chinese New Year, tangyuan (汤圆) at the Lantern Festival, zongzi (粽子) at the Dragon Boat Festival, and plain yuanxiao coated with sweet soybean powder at the winter solstice.

Olive juice is a much-loved drink. The cloudy, pale yellowish-green drink called ganlanzhi (橄榄汁) is made from the fruit of the Canarium album tree, which has been grown around Fuzhou since the Tang dynasty. China approved it as a geographical-indication trademark in 2010. Because it is not found elsewhere in the country, it is a reminder of how much food varies from region to region.

Fuzhou's traditional arts have a set of "Three Treasures": horn combs (角梳), paper umbrellas and bodiless lacquerware (脫胎漆器). A second trio, the "Three Superexcellences", pairs that lacquerware with Shoushan stone carving (壽山石雕) and cork pictures (軟木畫).
Fuzhou is well linked by air, rail, metro and sea, which helps when you travel home or explore southeast China.

Fuzhou Changle International Airport is the city's main international airport and an air hub for southeast China. It took over from the old Fuzhou Yixu Airport, which has served as an army airbase since 1997.

Fuzhou is a railway hub for northern Fujian. Trains can run as fast as 250 km/h (155 mph) on the Wenzhou-Fuzhou and Fuzhou-Xiamen lines, both forming sections of the high-speed corridor along the southeast coast. A further link, the Hefei-Fuzhou High-Speed Railway, crosses neighbouring Jiangxi Province on the way to Beijing with speeds as high as 350 km/h (220 mph). The Nanping-Fuzhou Railway and the Xiangtang-Putian Railway open up the inland areas, the latter at up to 200 km/h (124 mph). A regional freight line, the Fuzhou-Mawei Cargo Railway, runs east from Fuzhou Railway Station to the port in Mawei District. The city has two main stations, Fuzhou and Fuzhou South; because of its central position, the first is often simply called Fuzhou station.
Five lines are open on Fuzhou Metro, which was Fujian's earliest rapid transit network.

Line 1 connects the two main railway stations. Fuzhou station is north of the centre near the North Second Ring Road, while Fuzhou South station in Cangshan District is a landmark of the New City development plan, which started in 2007 and was completed in 2010. Line 1 opened on 18 May 2016. Line 5, linking the city's northeast with Fuzhou South, was finished in stages across 2022-2023.

Line 2 runs east to west, joining the university city and the Fuzhou High-Tech Zone in Minhou County with the Jinshan Industrial Zone in Cangshan and Gushan mountain in Jin'an District. Opening day for Line 2 was 26 April 2019. Line 4 joins the northern part of town to Difengjian in the south beside the Min River, and Line 6 crosses that river, connecting the central districts with the Yingqian and Wanshou areas in the south.

Passenger boats sail regularly between the Matsu Islands, administered by the Republic of China, and Mawei District's port. Across the Taiwan Strait, a high-speed ferry sails from Pingtan County, the closest point of the mainland to Taiwan, to Taipei and Taichung in about three hours.

Fuzhou's port hosted an early Chinese trial of Western technology in 1867, when the Fuzhou Navy Yard was founded. French advisers guided the building of a shipyard and arsenal, and a naval school and academy followed. The academy taught English, French, engineering and navigation, became a centre for European languages and technical sciences, and trained a generation of Western-educated officers, among them the scholar-reformer Yan Fu (1854-1921).

The yard was part of an effort to strengthen China after the heavy defeat in the Second Opium War (1856-1860). Yet most able students kept to the traditional Confucian path, and from the mid-1870s official interest faded. The yard struggled for funds and lost importance. Until the Second World War the city stayed mainly a trading centre and port with little industry, and Japanese forces occupied the port from 1940 to 1945.

After 1949 Fuzhou grew considerably. The Min River was dredged so that medium-sized vessels could sail upstream to Nanping, and a railway joining Fuzhou to the province's interior and the national network began running in 1956. The port was upgraded as well. Seagoing ships can no longer reach Fuzhou itself, but the Luoxingta anchorage and the outer harbour at Guantou, on the East China Sea coast, have been modernised. Timber, fruit, paper and foodstuffs are the main exports.

Electricity for industry travels along a grid from the Gutian hydropower project in the northwestern mountains. Commerce-wise, the city is a centre for commercial banking, designer brands, timber processing, engineering, papermaking, printing and textiles. A small iron and steel works opened in 1958. In 1984 Fuzhou became one of China's "open" cities under the new open-door policy that invited foreign investment. Handicrafts remain important in rural areas, and the city is known for lacquer and wood products.

Fuzhou is the political, economic and cultural centre of the province, as well as an industrial centre and a river port on the Min. The factories make processed food, steel, silk and cotton textiles and chemicals. Fine lacquerware, handcrafted fans and umbrellas are among its exports. Trade is mostly with other Chinese coastal ports, and timber, food and paper leave through Guantou harbour, about 50 kilometres (31 miles) downstream.

Some figures are dated, so treat them as snapshots and check current statistics. Per-capita GDP was ¥75,614 (about US$12,140) in 2015, ranking 52nd among 659 Chinese cities. Earlier, in 2008, Fuzhou's GDP was ¥228.4 billion, up 13 percent, and per-capita GDP grew to ¥33,615. That year exports reached US$13.6 billion, up 10.4 percent, and imports reached US$6.8 billion, while retail sales overall came to ¥113.4 billion. Fuzhou approved 155 foreign-invested projects, with contracted foreign investment of US$1.489 billion and utilised foreign investment up 43 percent at US$1.002 billion.

The State Council created the Fuzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone in January 1985. Its planned area is 22 square kilometres (8.5 square miles), of which 10.1 square kilometres (3.9 square miles) is now built. It sits close to Changle International Airport and the port. Encouraged activities range from telecom equipment and electronics assembly to trading, distribution, car assembly, medical supplies, shipping and warehousing logistics, and heavy industry.

The export processing zone opened on 3 June 2005 with State Council approval and carries the full set of preferential policies. It sits within the development zone's Chang'an Investment Zone, and its planned land covers 1.14 square kilometres (0.44 square miles).

The Fuzhou Free Trade Zone dates from 1992 and was also created by the State Council. Covering a planned 1.8 square kilometres (0.69 square miles), it favours heavy industry, instruments and industrial equipment, electronics, telecommunications equipment, logistics and trading.
Fuzhou is also a major centre for scientific research and appears among the world's top 50 cities tracked by the Nature Index.

fujian-normal-university.h: The wider setting: Fujian through history

blocks.x: Where a campus sits within its province matters too, so here is a short history of Fujian. Dating in early periods is approximate, and different studies give different ranges.

Archaeological finds reported in 2011 show that Fujian had entered the Neolithic by the middle of the sixth millennium BC. At the Keqiutou site on Pingtan Island, about 70 kilometres (43 miles) southeast of Fuzhou and dated to roughly 7450-5590 years before present, people left stone, shell, bone, jade and ceramic tools, including wheel-made pottery, and spinning wheels, which are firm evidence of weaving. The Tanshishan site (曇石山), roughly 5500-4000 years old, lies in Fuzhou's suburbs and spans the Neolithic and Chalcolithic. Its lower layer contains round, semi-underground houses. The Huangtulun site (about 1325 BC), also suburban, has a Bronze Age character.

Another reading places the start of the Neolithic on the Fujian coast at about 6,000 years ago. Population was thin and people lived mainly by fishing and hunting, with a little farming. Four main Neolithic cultures are recognised on the coast, the earliest having come from the north, from coastal Zhejiang:
Keqiutou culture (壳丘头文化), about 6000-5500 years ago (roughly 4050-3550 BC)
Tanshishan culture (昙石山文化), about 5000-4300 years ago (roughly 3050-2350 BC)
Damaoshan culture (大帽山文化), about 5000-4300 years ago
Huangguashan culture (黄瓜山文化), about 4300-3500 years ago (roughly 2350-1550 BC)
Inland Fujian had two clearly different Neolithic cultures: the Hulushan culture (葫芦山文化), dated 2050 to 1550 BC, and the Niubishan culture (牛鼻山文化), from about 5000 to 4000 years back.

The first kingdom in Fujian was Minyue. Its name joins "Min" (闽 / 閩, bân), possibly an ethnic label related to 蛮 / 蠻 (mán, bân), with "Yue", from the State of Yue, a kingdom of the Spring and Autumn period in Zhejiang. The link exists because the royal family of Yue fled to Fujian after Chu annexed their kingdom in 306 BC. The main river of the area carries the name Min as well, though the ethnic name is probably older than the river's.

The Qin removed the King of Minyue and set up a paramilitary province, Minzhong Commandery. Minyue remained a kingdom in practice until a Qin emperor, of the dynasty that unified China for the first time, ended its status.

When the Qin fell, the warlords Liu Bang and Xiang Yu fought each other. Minyue's king, Wuzhu, backed Liu with troops, a gamble that paid off when Liu's victory led to the Han dynasty. In 202 BC the new emperor gave Minyue back its position as an independent kingdom paying tribute. Wuzhu was allowed to build a fortified city in Fuzhou and in a few places in the Wuyi Mountains, all excavated in recent years. His kingdom reached beyond today's Fujian across today's provincial border into the east of Guangdong, the east of Jiangxi and the south of Zhejiang.

After Wuzhu died, Minyue stayed militant and launched expeditions against neighbours in Guangdong, Jiangxi and Zhejiang, mostly in the second century BC. The Han, expanding south, stopped this and decided to remove the threat by force. In 111 BC large armies advanced on Minyue from four directions by land and sea. The rulers in Fuzhou surrendered rather than face destruction, and Fujian's first kingdom came to a sudden end. Fujian then belonged to the large Yang Province (Yangzhou), whose capital was at Liyang (歷陽), now He County in Anhui.

The Han collapsed at the end of the second century AD, opening the Three Kingdoms era. It took Sun Quan, who founded the Kingdom of Wu, almost 20 years to subdue the Shan Yue, the mountain-dwelling branch of the Yue.

In the early fourth century the Western Jin dynasty fell and the north was torn by civil wars and risings of tribal peoples. This triggered the first wave of noble-class migration to Fujian, mostly from eight central China families: Hu (胡), He (何), Qiu (邱), Zhan (詹), Zheng (郑), Huang (黄), Lin (林) and Chen (陈). The surnames Chen, Lin, Huang and Zheng remain the four most common in Fujian today.

Even so, rugged terrain kept Fujian cut off from nearby regions and its economy stayed relatively undeveloped despite those population gains. Density remained low next to the rest of China, and the Western Jin set up only two commanderies and sixteen counties. Exiled prisoners and dissidents were frequently sent to Fujian, as to other southern provinces including Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangxi and Guangdong. During the Southern and Northern Dynasties, the Southern Dynasties, meaning the four states of Chen, Liang, Southern Qi and Liu Song, ruled south of the Yangtze, including Fujian.

Under the Sui and Tang, many more migrants settled. Under the Sui, Fujian fell once more within Yang Province. In the Tang it belonged to the Jiangnan East Circuit, governed from Suzhou, and the area held roughly 25 counties grouped into 5 prefectures. The Tang (618-907) is seen as another golden age for China and it boosted culture and the economy in Fujian; Fuzhou's economic and cultural institutions grew. Late in the dynasty upheavals in the heartland pushed even larger waves of northerners into northern Fujian.

In 985 the area was reorganised as the Fujian Circuit, the first time "Fujian" was used as the name of an administrative region. Under the Yuan, Fujian became part of Jiangzhe Province, governed from Hangzhou. Between 1357 and 1366 Muslim communities in Quanzhou joined the Ispah Rebellion, which moved north and captured Putian and Fuzhou before the Yuan crushed it. Quanzhou afterwards lost the foreign trade and open international character it had enjoyed, since foreigners had been killed or expelled. General Chen Youding, who put down the rebellion, continued to govern Fujian even after the Red Turban Rebellion began, until forces loyal to Zhu Yuanzhang (the Hongwu Emperor), the eventual founder of the Ming dynasty, defeated him in 1367.

Fujian draws visitors to many attractions, among them four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, a count that is among the highest in China. Together with Fuzhou's food, temples and coast, that gives students plenty to explore outside class.
Fujian Normal University lists 185 programs for international students on this site: 49 bachelor, 95 master's, 40 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 165 taught in Chinese, 18 taught in English, 2 taught in Chinese and English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 19,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 21,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 37,000 (median CNY 31,000), according to the university's published fee table.

184 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

fujian-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Fujian Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Fuzhou, register at Fujian Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Fujian University of Technology (Chinese: 福建理工大学) is a public university located in Fuzhou, Fujian, China.

The Chinese Ministry of Education established the university in 2002 as a merger of the Fujian College of Architecture and Civil Engineering and the Fujian Institute of Technology. The predecessor of both institutions was the noted "Fujian Gaogong" (Fujian Advanced Technological School) originating from "Canxia Jingshe" (Canxia Elementary Technological School), which was co-founded in 1896 by Lin Shu, an eminent Fujian scholar and translator and Chen Baochen, tutor of the last Chinese emperor Puyi during the Qing dynasty. The university abbreviation is FJUT.
FJUT currently has 24,128 full-time students. There are 18,890 undergraduate students of which 5,238 are collegiates. There are also 4,788 adult students.

The university has 1,350 staff. The faculty members comprise 697 of which 213 are professors and associate professors. The university has 3 campuses, known as Shanxi Campus, Cangshan Campus and Pudong Campus and occupies a total area of 40.5 ha (607 mu). Its new location in Fuzhou University District will occupy an area of 107 ha (1,608 mu). The university is equipped with adequate facilities for teaching and learning with a total of 47 laboratories, the total value of the teaching equipment amounting to 71,420,000 Yuan.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Fuzhou, where Fujian University of Technology is located.

Fuzhou has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cfa) influenced by the East Asian monsoon; the summers are long, very hot and humid, and the winters are short, mild and dry. In most years, torrential rain occurs during the monsoon in the second half of May. Fuzhou is also liable to typhoons in late summer and early autumn. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 11.4 °C (52.5 °F) in January to 29.4 °C (84.9 °F) in July, while the annual mean is 20.5 °C (68.9 °F). With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 26% in March to 51% in July, the city receives 1,607 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −1.9 °C (29 °F) on 25 January 2016 to 41.9 °C (107 °F) on 24 July 2022.
Snow is very rare, having covered the ground last times in February 1957, December 1975 and December 1991.
Fuzhou is located in the northeast coast of Fujian province, connects jointly northwards with Ningde and Nanping, southwards with Quanzhou and Putian, westwards with Sanming respectively.
See or edit raw graph data.
The culture of Fuzhou is distinct from the mainstream inland cultures of central China, and in details vary from other areas of the Chinese coast.
Besides Mandarin Chinese, the majority local residents of Fuzhou (Fuzhou people) also speak Fuzhounese (福州話), the prestige form of Eastern Min.

Min opera, also known as Fuzhou drama, is one of the major operas in Fujian Province. It enjoys popularity in the Fuzhou area and in neighboring parts of Fujian such as the northeast and northwest areas where the Fuzhou language is spoken, as well as in Taiwan and the Malay Archipelago. It became a fixed opera in the early 20th century. There are more than 1,000 plays of Min opera, most of which originate from folk tales, historical novels, or ancient legends, including such traditional plays as "Making Seal", "The Purple Jade Hairpin" and "Switching Fairy Peach with Litchi".

The two traditional mainstream religions practiced in Fuzhou are Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism. Traditionally, many people practice both religions simultaneously. The city is also home to many Buddhist monasteries, Taoist temples and Buddhist monks.
Apart from mainstream religions, a number of religious worship sites of various local religions are situated in the streets and lanes of Fuzhou.

The origins of local religion can be dated back centuries. These diverse religions incorporated elements such as gods and doctrines from other religions and cultures, such as totem worship and traditional legends. For example, Monkey King, originated to monkey worship among local ancients, gradually came to embody the God of Wealth in Fuzhou after the novel Journey to the West was issued in Ming dynasty.

As the most popular religion in the Min River Valley, the worship of Lady Linshui is viewed as one of the three most influential local religions in Fujian, the other two being the worship of Mazu and Baosheng Dadi (保生大帝).

Fuzhou cuisine is most notably one of the four traditional cooking styles of Fujian cuisine, which in turn is one of the eight Chinese regional cuisines. Dishes are light but flavorful, with particular emphasis on umami taste, known in Chinese cooking as xianwei (simplified Chinese: 鲜味; traditional Chinese: 鮮味; pinyin: xiānwèi), as well as retaining the original flavor of the main ingredients instead of masking them. In Fuzhou cuisine, the taste is light compared to that of some other Chinese cooking styles, and often have a mixed sweet and sour taste. Soup, served as an indispensable dish in meals, is cooked in various ways with local seasonal fresh vegetables and seafood and often added with local cooking wine (福建老酒).

Fuzhou is famous for its street food and snacks.  Some notable street food dishes include Fuzhou fish balls (魚丸), meat-pastry dumplings (扁肉燕), oyster cake (海蛎饼), rice scroll soup (鼎邊糊), guong bian (光餅; a kind of mildly savory pastry), Buddha Jumps over the Wall (佛跳墙), and pork floss (肉鬆). Many of these street food dishes have a long history and their own local legend; an example would be the oyster cake, according Fuzhou local folklore, in the early Qing dynasty, there was a young man who inherited his father's dim sum business, despite all his hard works, he only managed to earn enough money to feed himself, not enough to raise and feed a family of his own. One night, he dreamt of a silver-haired elderly man, who told him that he has very good fortune, the young man then asked him what he can do to obtain good luck, the elderly man then floated away. That's when the young man notice the setting moon, and after the moon sank under the clouds, rose from the east a golden sun, he was inspired by the dream and invented oyster cake, which is white like the moon before being lowered into hot grease and coming out golden as the morning sun. According to the legend, after the young man made a fortune out of his invention and his oyster cake was imitated by many others, which was passed down till this day. another example of a Fuzhou street food with a long history is rice scroll soup, which became popular in Fuzhou in the early part of the Qing dynasty.  As more Fuzhou residents settled overseas, Fuzhou dishes spread to Taiwan, Southeast Asia and the U.S..  For example, one is able to find guong bian and Fuzhou fish balls in Sitiawan in Ipoh, Malaysia while Fuzhou fish balls, meat-pastry dumplings and rice scroll soup can be found in New York's Chinatown. Fuzhou cuisine has also spread internationally through migration, particularly to Southeast Asia and the United States. Dishes such as fish balls (魚丸), meat-pastry dumplings (扁肉燕), and oyster cake (海蛎饼) are now common in Fujianese communities abroad, including in New York City's Chinatown and in Malaysian cities such as Sitiawan and Ipoh. These dishes are regarded by overseas Fuzhounese as symbols of cultural identity and continuity.

Fuzhou residents also enjoy eating festival foods during traditional Chinese holidays.  For example, red and white rice cakes (年糕) are served over Chinese New Year, tangyuan (汤圆) during the Lantern Festival, zongzi (粽子) during the Dragon Boat Festival, and sweet soy bean powder-covered plain yuanxiao over the winter solstice.

Olive juice is also a much sought-after refreshment. Ganlanzhi (橄榄汁) is cloudy and light yellowish-green in color. Olive trees grown on the Canarium album tree in Fuzhou since the Tang dynasty, it was even approved as a trademark with geographic indication by China in 2010. Not found elsewhere in China, ganlanzhi (橄榄汁) is also a reminder of the many regional differences in China when it comes to food.

Bodiless lacquerware (脫胎漆器), paper umbrellas and horn combs (角梳) are the "Three Treasures" of Fuzhou traditional arts. In addition, bodiless lacquerware, together with cork pictures (軟木畫) and Shoushan stone sculptures (壽山石雕) are called "Three Superexcellences" of Fuzhou.

The city is served by Fuzhou Changle International Airport, which replaces Fuzhou Yixu Airport, the old airfield. The former is its main international airport and an air-hub in southeast China, while the latter was turned into a PLA airbase after 1997.

Fuzhou is a railway hub in northern Fujian.  The Wenzhou–Fuzhou and Fuzhou–Xiamen Railways form part of the Southeast Coast High-Speed Rail Corridor and can accommodate high-speed trains at speeds of up to 250 km/h (155 mph).
The Hefei–Fuzhou High-Speed Railway links the city to Beijing through its nearby inner land province Jiangxi at speeds up to 350 km/h (220 mph).

The Nanping–Fuzhou Railway and Xiangtang–Putian Railway provide rail access inland.  The latter line can carry trains at speeds of 200 km/h (124 mph).  The regional Fuzhou-Mawei Cargo Railway runs from the Fuzhou Railway Station eastward to the port in Mawei District. Fuzhou has two main railway stations, Fuzhou and Fuzhou South. Fuzhou station is often just referred to as Fuzhou station given its central location.
Fuzhou Metro is the first rapid transit system in Fujian province. It has five metro lines in operation.

Line 1 links the two railway stations of the city. The Fuzhou railway station is located north of the city center, near the North Second Ring Road. Fuzhou South Railway Station, located in Cangshan district, is a key landmark of the New City development scheme, begun in 2007 and completed in 2010. Line 1 was opened on May 18, 2016, while Line 5, which runs from the northeast of the city to Fuzhou South, was completed in stages during 2022–2023.

Line 2 runs in the east–west direction of the city, linking the university city and Fuzhou High-Tech Zone in Minhou county, Jinshan Industrial Zone in Cangshan district, and Gushan mountain in Jin'an district. Line 2 was opened on 26 April 2019. Line 4 runs from the north of the city to Difengjian in the south, near the bank of the Min River, the latter being crossed by Line 6 which connects the central areas of the city with Yingqian and Wanshou areas to the south.
Passenger liners regularly sail between ROC's Matsu Islands and the port in Mawei District.
A high-speed ferry sails across Taiwan Strait between the port in Pingtan County, the mainland's closest point to Taiwan, to Taipei and Taichung, a trip that takes about 3 hours.

In 1867 the Fuzhou seaport was the site of one of China's first major experiments with Western technology, when the Fuzhou Navy Yard was established. A shipyard and an arsenal were built under French guidance and a naval school was opened. A naval academy was also established at the shipyard, and it became a center for the study of European languages and technical sciences. The academy, which offered courses in English, French, engineering, and navigation, produced a generation of Western-trained officers, including the famous scholar-reformer Yan Fu (1854–1921).

The yard was established as part of a program to strengthen China in the wake of the country's disastrous defeat in the Second Opium War (1856–1860). Most talented students nonetheless continued to pursue a traditional Confucian education, and by the mid-1870s the government began to lose interest in the shipyard, which had trouble securing funds and declined in importance. Fuzhou remained essentially a commercial center and a port until World War II; it had relatively little industry. The port was occupied by the Japanese during 1940–1945.

Since 1949, Fuzhou has grown considerably. Transportation has been improved by the dredging of the Min River for navigation by medium-sized craft upstream to Nanping. In 1956 the railway linking Fuzhou with the interior of the province and with the main Chinese railway system began operation. The port has also been improved; Fuzhou itself is no longer accessible to seagoing ships, but Luoxingta anchorage and the outer harbor at Guantou on the coast of the East China Sea have been modernized and improved. The chief exports are timber, fruits, paper, and foodstuffs.

Industry is supplied with power by a grid running from the Gutian hydroelectric scheme in the mountains to the northwest. The city is a center for commercial banking, designer brands and timber-working, engineering, papermaking, printing, and textile industries. A small iron and steel plant was built in 1958. In 1984 Fuzhou was designated one of China's "open" cities in the new open-door policy inviting foreign investments. Handicrafts remain important in the rural areas, and the city is famous for its lacquer and wood products.
Its GDP was ¥75,614 (c. US$12,140) per capita in 2015, ranked no. 52 among 659 Chinese cities.

Fuzhou is undoubtedly the province's political, economic and cultural center as well as an industrial center and seaport on the Min River. In 2008, Fuzhou's GDP amounted to ¥228.4 billion, an increase of 13 percent.

Manufactured products include chemicals, silk and cotton textiles, iron and steel, and processed food. Among Fuzhou's exports are fine lacquerware and handcrafted fans and umbrellas. The city's trade is mainly with Chinese coastal ports. Its exports of timber, food products, and paper move through the harbor at Guantou located about 50 kilometres (31 mi) downstream.

In 2008, exports reached US$13.6 billion, a growth of 10.4 percent while imports amounted to US$6.8 billion. Total retail sales for the same period came to ¥113.4 billion and per capita GDP grew to ¥33,615. During the same period, Fuzhou approved 155 foreign-invested projects. Contracted foreign investment amounted to US$1.489 billion, while utilized foreign investment increased by 43 percent to US$1.002 billion.

The Fuzhou Economic & Technological Development Zone was established in January 1985 by the State Council, with a total planning area of 22 square kilometres (8.5 sq mi) and now has 10.1 square kilometres (3.9 sq mi) built. It is located close to Fuzhou Changle International Airport and Fuzhou Port. Industries encouraged in the zone include electronics assembly and manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, trading and distribution, automobile production/assembly, medical equipment and supplies, shipping/warehousing/logistics, and heavy industry.

The Fuzhou Export Processing Zone was founded on June 3, 2005, with the approval of the State Council and enjoys all the preferential policies. It is located inside the Chang'an Investment Zone of the Fuzhou Economic and Technical Development Zone (FETDZ) with a planned land area of 1.14 square kilometres (0.44 sq mi).

The Fuzhou Free Trade Zone was established in 1992 by the State Council, with a planning area of 1.8 square kilometres (0.69 sq mi). Industries encouraged in the free trade zone include electronics assembly and manufacturing, heavy industry, instruments and industrial equipment production, shipping/warehousing/logistics, telecommunications equipment, trading, and distribution.
Fuzhou is also a major city for scientific research, appearing in the global top 50 cities as tracked by the Nature Index.
Fujian University of Technology is in Fujian, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Fujian.

Recent archaeological discoveries in 2011 demonstrate that Fujian had entered the Neolithic Age by the middle of the 6th millennium BC. From the Keqiutou site (7450–5590 BP), an early Neolithic site in Pingtan Island located about 70 kilometres (43 mi) southeast of Fuzhou, numerous tools made of stones, shells, bones, jades, and ceramics (including wheel-made ceramics) have been unearthed, together with spinning wheels, which is definitive evidence of weaving.

The Tanshishan (曇石山) site (5500–4000 BP) in suburban Fuzhou spans the Neolithic and Chalcolithic Age where semi-underground circular buildings were found in the lower level. The Huangtulun (黃土崙) site (c. 1325 BC), also in suburban Fuzhou, was of the Bronze Age in character.

Tianlong Jiao (2013) notes that the Neolithic appeared on the coast of Fujian around 6,000 B.P. During the Neolithic, the coast of Fujian had a low population density, with the population depending on mostly on fishing and hunting, along with limited agriculture.
There were four major Neolithic cultures in coastal Fujian, with the earliest Neolithic cultures originating from the north in coastal Zhejiang.
Keqiutou culture (壳丘头文化; c. 6000 – c. 5500 BP, or c. 4050 – c. 3550 BC)
Tanshishan culture (昙石山文化; c. 5000 – c. 4300 BP, or c. 3050 – c. 2350 BC)
Damaoshan culture (大帽山文化; c. 5000 – c. 4300 BP)
Huangguashan culture (黄瓜山文化; c. 4300 – c. 3500 BP, or c. 2350 – c. 1550 BC)

There were two major Neolithic cultures in inland Fujian, which were highly distinct from the coastal Fujian Neolithic cultures. These are the Niubishan culture (牛鼻山文化) from 5000 to 4000 years ago, and the Hulushan culture (葫芦山文化) from 2050 to 1550 BC.

Fujian was also where the kingdom of Minyue was located. The word "Mǐnyuè" was derived by combining "Mǐn" (simplified Chinese: 闽; traditional Chinese: 閩; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: bân), which is perhaps an ethnic name (simplified Chinese: 蛮; traditional Chinese: 蠻; pinyin: mán; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: bân), and "Yuè", after the State of Yue, a Spring and Autumn period kingdom in Zhejiang to the north. This is because the royal family of Yuè fled to Fujian after its kingdom was annexed by the State of Chu in 306 BC. Mǐn is also the name of the main river in this area, but the ethnonym is probably older.

The Qin deposed the King of Minyue, establishing instead a paramilitary province there called Minzhong Commandery. Minyue was a de facto kingdom until one of the emperors of the Qin dynasty, the first unified imperial Chinese state, abolished its status.

In the aftermath of the Qin dynasty's fall, civil war broke out between two warlords, Xiang Yu and Liu Bang. The Minyue king Wuzhu sent his troops to fight with Liu and his gamble paid off. Liu was victorious and founded the Han dynasty. In 202 BC, he restored Minyue's status as a tributary independent kingdom. Thus Wuzhu was allowed to construct his fortified city in Fuzhou as well as a few locations in the Wuyi Mountains, which have been excavated in recent years. His kingdom extended beyond the borders of contemporary Fujian into eastern Guangdong, eastern Jiangxi, and southern Zhejiang.

After Wuzhu's death, Minyue maintained its militant tradition and launched several expeditions against its neighboring kingdoms in Guangdong, Jiangxi, and Zhejiang, primarily in the 2nd century BC. This was stopped by the Han dynasty as it expanded southward. The Han emperor eventually decided to get rid of the potential threat by launching a military campaign against Minyue. Large forces approached Minyue simultaneously from four directions via land and sea in 111 BC. The rulers in Fuzhou surrendered to avoid a futile fight and destruction and the first kingdom in Fujian history came to an abrupt end.
Fujian was part of the much larger Yang Province (Yangzhou), whose provincial capital was designated in Liyang (歷陽; present-day He County, Anhui).

The Han dynasty collapsed at the end of the 2nd century AD, paving the way for the Three Kingdoms era. Sun Quan, the founder of the Kingdom of Wu, spent nearly 20 years subduing the Shan Yue people, the branch of the Yue living in mountains.

The first wave of immigration of the noble class arrived in the province in the early 4th century when the Western Jin dynasty collapsed and the north was torn apart by civil wars and rebellions by tribal peoples from the north and west. These immigrants were primarily from eight families in central China: Chen (陈), Lin (林), Huang (黄), Zheng (郑), Zhan (詹), Qiu (邱), He (何), and Hu (胡). To this day, the first four remain the most popular surnames in Fujian.

Nevertheless, isolation from nearby areas owing to rugged terrain contributed to Fujian's relatively undeveloped economy and level of development, despite major population boosts from northern China during the "barbarian" rebellions. The population density in Fujian remained low compared to the rest of China. Only two commanderies and sixteen counties were established by the Western Jin dynasty. Like other southern provinces such as Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, and Yunnan, Fujian often served as a destination for exiled prisoners and dissidents at that time.
During the Southern and Northern Dynasties era, the Southern Dynasties (Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang (Western Liang), and Chen) reigned south of the Yangtze River, including Fujian.
During the Sui and Tang eras a large influx of migrants settled in Fujian.
During the Sui dynasty, Fujian was again part of Yang Province.
During the Tang, Fujian was part of the larger Jiangnan East Circuit, whose capital was at Suzhou. Modern-day Fujian was composed of around 5 prefectures and 25 counties.

The Tang dynasty (618–907) oversaw the next golden age of China, which contributed to a boom in Fujian's culture and economy. Fuzhou's economic and cultural institutions grew and developed. The later years of the Tang dynasty saw several political upheavals in the Chinese heartland, prompting even larger waves of northerners to immigrate to the northern part of Fujian.
The area was reorganized into the Fujian Circuit in 985, which was the first time the name "Fujian" was used for an administrative region.

After the establishment of the Yuan dynasty, Fujian became part of Jiangzhe province, whose capital was at Hangzhou. From 1357 to 1366 Muslims in Quanzhou participated in the Ispah Rebellion, advancing northward and even capturing Putian and Fuzhou before the rebellion was crushed by the Yuan. Afterward, Quanzhou city lost foreign interest in trading and its formerly welcoming international image as the foreigners were all massacred or deported.

Yuan dynasty General Chen Youding, who had put down the Ispah Rebellion, continued to rule over the Fujian area even after the outbreak of the Red Turban Rebellion. Forces loyal to the eventual Ming dynasty founder Zhu Yuanzhang (Hongwu Emperor) defeated Chen in 1367.
Fujian is home to several tourist attractions, including four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, one of the highest in China.
Fujian University of Technology lists 25 programs for international students on this site: 4 bachelor, 20 master's, 1 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 16 taught in Chinese, 9 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 23,000 (median CNY 21,500), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 34,000 (median CNY 29,000), according to the university's published fee table.

fujian-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Fujian University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Fuzhou, register at Fujian University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Fuzhou University (FZU, 福州大学) is a public university in Fuzhou, the capital of Fujian Province, and it is affiliated with the provincial government. Its national status comes from membership in both Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction. The university opened in 1958 and is described as a national key university. The "Double First Class University Plan" and the older "211 Project" are government programmes that back selected universities so they can develop quickly.

The Min River divides the university's two main sites. The old campus is on the north bank, in the western part of Fuzhou. The new one is on the south bank at the edge of the city, at the foot of Qi Mountain. In total the university covers over 333 hectares and consists of several sites. These are Yishan, Qishan and Tongpan, plus the college in Xiamen devoted to arts and design. Day-to-day teaching is concentrated at Qishan, inside the Fuzhou University Town.

Nineteen schools mainly serve undergraduates, and two colleges operate independently: Zhicheng College and Yangguang College. At postgraduate level the university lists 4 post-doctoral research stations; for doctorates, 9 programmes in first-rank disciplines and 54 in second-rank ones; for master's degrees, 29 first-rank and 168 second-rank programmes; and 11 professional degree authorisation stations.

The Ministry of Education has approved the university to teach undergraduate and postgraduate programmes for students from Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan and foreign countries. About 50,000 students currently study there, with over 5,200 of them working on doctoral or master's degrees. Since its start, roughly 200,000 students have graduated, counting full-time doctoral and master's students as well as those with bachelor's and associate degrees.

Fuzhou University works actively on cooperation and exchange. It has hosted international and national academic conferences, which has raised its academic profile, and it has science, teaching and cultural exchanges with Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao. It also promotes dialogue between Chinese and Western civilisations and has set up the "Library of the Western Belvedere", described as China's first centre for Western works, and an Institute of International Sinology. It has built good relations with over 20 universities overseas, for instance in the US, UK, Germany, France, Russia, Japan and South Korea. The university describes itself as an important window for scientific, academic, educational and cultural exchange in Fujian.

The presidents have been, in order: Jia Jiumin (1958 to 1978), Huangfu Lin (1978 to 1983), Huang Jinling (1983 to 1992), Qian Kuangwu (1992 to 1999), Wei Kemei (1999 to 2002), Wu Minsheng (2002 to 2010), Fu Xianzhi (May 2010 to December 2023) and Wu Minghong (December 2023 to the present). Lu Jiaxi served as Honorary President from 1981 to 2001.
Fuzhou is on the northeast coast of Fujian. Ningde and Nanping lie to the north, Quanzhou and Putian to the south, and Sanming to the west.

The Köppen classification for Fuzhou is humid subtropical (Cfa), under the influence of the East Asian monsoon. Summers are long, hot and humid, and winters are short, mild and dry. Torrential monsoon rain normally falls in the second half of May, and typhoons can strike in late summer and early autumn.

January averages 11.4 °C (52.5 °F), July 29.4 °C (84.9 °F), and the whole-year mean is 20.5 °C (68.9 °F). Possible sunshine ranges between 26% in March and 51% in July, and the city gets 1,607 hours of bright sunshine a year. Extremes recorded since 1951: -1.9 °C (29 °F) on 25 January 2016, and 41.9 °C (107 °F) on 24 July 2022. Settled snow is exceptional, having been seen only in February 1957, December 1975 and December 1991.
The local culture stands apart from the mainstream culture of inland central China, and even differs in its details from other stretches of the Chinese coast.

Most local residents use Mandarin and also Fuzhounese (福州話), which is the standard-bearing variety of Eastern Min. Min opera, or Fuzhou drama, is one of Fujian's principal opera forms. Audiences enjoy it in the Fuzhou area, in nearby northeast and northwest parts of Fujian where the Fuzhou language is heard, and in Taiwan and the Malay Archipelago. The genre only settled into a fixed form in the early 20th century. Its repertoire exceeds 1,000 plays, largely based on folk tales, historical novels or ancient legends; classics include "The Purple Jade Hairpin", "Making Seal" and "Switching Fairy Peach with Litchi".

Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism are the two traditional mainstream religions, and many people practise both at once. The city has many Buddhist monasteries, Taoist temples and monks. Alongside them, a number of local cults have shrines in the streets and lanes. Their roots go back centuries, and over time they absorbed gods and doctrines from other traditions, including totem worship and legends. One example is the Monkey King, who began with monkey worship among early locals and, after the Ming-dynasty novel Journey to the West appeared, gradually became the God of Wealth in Fuzhou. The worship of Lady Linshui, most popular in the Min River Valley, ranks among Fujian's three most influential local faiths, together with the cults of Mazu and Baosheng Dadi (保生大帝).

Fujian cuisine, one of the eight regional cuisines of China, has four traditional styles, and Fuzhou's is among them. The food is delicate yet flavourful, with emphasis on umami, known in Chinese as xianwei (鮮味 in traditional characters, 鲜味 in simplified), and they try to keep the original taste of the main ingredients rather than cover it up. Compared with some other Chinese styles, the taste is mild and often mixes sweet and sour. Soup is an essential part of every meal, made in various ways with seasonal vegetables and seafood and often with local cooking wine (福建老酒).

The city is well known for street food and snacks. Typical items are oyster cake (海蛎饼), pork floss (肉鬆), Buddha Jumps over the Wall (佛跳墙), fish balls (魚丸), meat-pastry dumplings (扁肉燕), rice scroll soup (鼎邊糊) and guong bian (光餅), a mildly savoury pastry. Most have long histories and legends. In one, a young man of the early Qing took over his father's dim sum trade yet earned barely enough to feed himself, let alone a family. He dreamed of a silver-haired old man who told him he was very fortunate, then floated away. The young man noticed the moon setting, and as it sank behind clouds a golden sun rose in the east. Inspired, he invented the oyster cake, white like the moon before it goes into hot oil and golden like the morning sun when it comes out. Rice scroll soup has an old history too, having gained popularity in Fuzhou during the early Qing.

As Fuzhou people settled overseas, their dishes travelled to Taiwan, Southeast Asia and the United States. For example, guong bian and fish balls turn up in Sitiawan and Ipoh, Malaysia, and Manhattan's Chinatown sells fish balls, meat-pastry dumplings and rice scroll soup. Fuzhounese abroad treat these dishes as a symbol of who they are and of continuity with home.

Festival foods mark the traditional calendar: red and white rice cakes (年糕) at Chinese New Year, tangyuan (汤圆) at the Lantern Festival, zongzi (粽子) at the Dragon Boat Festival and plain yuanxiao covered in sweet soy bean powder at the winter solstice.

Olive juice is another local favourite. Ganlanzhi (橄榄汁) is a cloudy drink of pale yellowish green. It comes from the Canarium album olive tree, which has been cultivated in Fuzhou since the Tang, and in 2010 it was approved as a geographical-indication trademark. It is not found elsewhere in China, a reminder of how much food differs by region.

Traditional Fuzhou crafts have two famous trios. The "Three Treasures" are paper umbrellas, horn combs (角梳) and bodiless lacquerware (脫胎漆器). The "Three Superexcellences" are bodiless lacquerware again, cork pictures (軟木畫) and Shoushan stone sculptures (壽山石雕).
Fuzhou Changle International Airport is the main international airport and a hub for southeast China. It replaced the old Yixu airfield, which became a PLA airbase after 1997.

Fuzhou is a railway hub for northern Fujian. Two lines, Wenzhou-Fuzhou and Fuzhou-Xiamen, form segments of the Southeast Coast High-Speed Rail Corridor and allow speeds of 250 km/h (155 mph). To the interior, the Hefei-Fuzhou High-Speed Railway gives a route to Beijing across Jiangxi at 350 km/h (220 mph). Inland access comes from the Nanping-Fuzhou Railway and the Xiangtang-Putian Railway, the latter allowing 200 km/h (124 mph). A regional cargo line, the Fuzhou-Mawei Cargo Railway, runs east from Fuzhou Railway Station to the port in Mawei District.
There are two main stations: Fuzhou, which is in the centre and usually just called Fuzhou station, and Fuzhou South in Cangshan district.
Fuzhou Metro is Fujian's first rapid transit system, with five lines running.

Line 1 joins the city's two railway stations. Fuzhou station is north of downtown by the North Second Ring Road; Fuzhou South, in Cangshan district, anchors the New City scheme (begun 2007, finished 2010). Line 1 began service on 18 May 2016.

Line 2 runs east-west and connects the university city, the High-Tech Zone in Minhou county, the Jinshan Industrial Zone in Cangshan and Gushan mountain in Jin'an district. It opened on 26 April 2019.
Line 4 starts in the north and ends at Difengjian beside the Min River in the south, where Line 6 intersects it, connecting the central districts with Yingqian and Wanshou in the south.
Line 5 links the northeastern part of the city with Fuzhou South, and its sections opened in stages between 2022 and 2023.

Regular passenger ships connect Mawei District's port with the Matsu Islands (ROC). Across the Taiwan Strait, a high-speed ferry takes around 3 hours from Pingtan County, the nearest point on the mainland to Taiwan, to Taipei and Taichung.

The Fuzhou Navy Yard, founded in 1867, was among China's earliest big experiments with Western technology. French advisers guided the building of a shipyard and arsenal, and a naval school opened. The academy at the yard taught English, French, engineering and navigation, became a centre for studying European languages and technical sciences, and it produced a cohort of officers with Western training, among them the reformer and scholar Yan Fu (1854 to 1921).

China's heavy loss in the Second Opium War (1856 to 1860) prompted the yard as part of a drive to build national strength. Even so, the most gifted students tended to keep to a classical Confucian schooling, and the government's enthusiasm faded by the mid-1870s. The shipyard struggled for money and declined. Fuzhou stayed essentially a commercial and port city until World War II, with little industry, and Japan occupied the port from 1940 to 1945.

Since 1949 the city has grown a lot. The Min River was dredged so medium-sized boats can sail upstream to Nanping, and in 1956 a railway opened that connected Fuzhou to the interior of Fujian and to China's main rail network. The port has been improved, though seagoing ships can no longer reach Fuzhou itself. The Luoxingta anchorage and the outer harbour at Guantou on the East China Sea coast have been modernised. Timber, fruit, paper and foodstuffs are the chief exports.

Power for industry comes through a grid linked to the Gutian hydroelectric scheme, located in mountains northwest of the city. The city is a centre for commercial banking, designer brands and for timber working, engineering, papermaking, printing and textiles. A small iron and steel works opened in 1958, and in 1984 Fuzhou was named one of China's "open" cities under the new open-door policy that invited foreign investment. Crafts still matter in the countryside, and lacquer and woodwork are what the city is famed for.
2015 GDP per person: ¥75,614 (about US$12,140), ranked 52nd among 659 Chinese cities.
2008 GDP: ¥228.4 billion, up 13 percent. Per-person GDP rose to ¥33,615 and total retail sales reached ¥113.4 billion.
2008 trade: exports of US$13.6 billion (up 10.4 percent) and imports of US$6.8 billion.
2008 investment: 155 foreign-invested projects approved, with contracted foreign investment of US$1.489 billion and utilised investment of US$1.002 billion, up 43 percent.

Fuzhou is the political, economic and cultural centre of Fujian, as well as an industrial centre and a seaport on the Min River. Factories produce processed food, chemicals, iron and steel, and both silk and cotton textiles, while exports include handmade fans and umbrellas as well as fine lacquerware. Its trade is mainly with other Chinese coastal ports, and exports of timber, food and paper move through the harbour at Guantou, about 50 kilometres (31 mi) downstream.

Fuzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone: set up by the State Council in January 1985, planned over 22 square kilometres (8.5 square miles), with 10.1 square kilometres (3.9 square miles) developed so far, and close to Changle International Airport and Fuzhou Port. Sectors it encourages are heavy industry, car production, medical equipment, telecom equipment, electronics, trading and distribution, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.

Fuzhou Export Processing Zone: founded on 3 June 2005 with State Council approval and all the preferential policies, with a planned 1.14 square kilometres (0.44 square miles), located in the Chang'an Investment Zone that is part of the development zone above.

Fuzhou Free Trade Zone: created by the State Council in 1992, over a planned 1.8 square kilometres (0.69 square miles). It favours electronics, heavy industry, instrument and equipment manufacturing, shipping and logistics, telecom equipment and trade.
Fuzhou is a major scientific research city, appearing among the global top 50 cities in the Nature Index.

Fuzhou University has a long reach in Fujian and abroad, with two main sites separated by the Min River, a broad range of schools and an active exchange programme. The city offers a hot, humid climate, famous food, strong rail and metro links, and a long port history. Please confirm campus assignments and programme details with the university.

Weather: expect long, hot, humid summers, with July averaging 29.4 °C. Monsoon downpours usually come in the second half of May, and typhoons are a risk in late summer and early autumn. Winters are short and mild.
Travel: Changle International Airport is the main airport, Fuzhou and Fuzhou South are the main stations, and five metro lines are in service.
Campus: ask which of Yishan, Qishan or Tongpan will host your classes, because the Min River separates the north-bank and south-bank sites.
Food: try oyster cake, fish balls, rice scroll soup and the local olive juice, ganlanzhi.

Several statistics in this profile come from specific years: the economic data are mostly for 2008, the GDP-per-person ranking is for 2015, and the university's headcounts of about 50,000 students and 200,000 graduates are not dated. The source also lists both a College of Foreign Languages and a School of Foreign Languages, so the structure may have changed. For current numbers, programme lists and tuition, rely on the university's own English-language website and its international office.
