gannan-normal-university.h: Ganzhou, the city around Gannan Normal University

blocks.x: Anyone planning to study at Gannan Normal University will spend most of their time in and around Ganzhou, so it helps to know the city before you go: its landscape, its seasons, how its economy works and how to travel in and out. The sections after this one then widen the view to the province of Jiangxi.

The city lies along the upper Ganjiang River at the southern end of Jiangxi, an area known as Gannan ("south Gan"). Its position on the map is 114.93° E, 25.83° N. This is a very large city: its 39,400 km² (15,200 sq mi) cover the southern third of Jiangxi. Forest blankets more than 70% of the area, and over 83% is mountainous. Several important tributaries of the Gan River, which gives the city its name, meet at a confluence in the middle of the urban area.
Neighbouring prefecture-level cities surround it in four directions, grouped by province:
In Jiangxi, to the north: Ji'an and Fuzhou.
In Hunan, to the west: Chenzhou.
In Guangdong, to the south: Meizhou, Heyuan and Shaoguan.
In Fujian, to the east: Sanming and Longyan.

The East Asian monsoon gives Ganzhou a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa). Expect very hot, humid summers that last a long time, and cooler, drier winters that sometimes turn briefly cold. January is the coolest month at 8.2 °C (46.8 °F), averaged over 24 hours; July is the hottest at 29.5 °C (85.1 °F). The annual mean is 19.57 °C (67.2 °F), and rainfall adds up to about 1,450 mm (57 in).

March is the dullest month, with only 20% of possible sunshine, and July is the brightest at 62%, for a yearly total of 1,778 hours. Early winter is fairly sunny and dry, but the weather gets wetter and cloudier as the season goes on. Spring starts especially gloomy: each month from March to June gets more than 170 mm (6.7 in) of rain. In June the heavy rain eases and summer becomes particularly sunny, followed by a warm and relatively dry autumn.

Ganzhou has about 7.94 million inhabitants. Most are Han, with communities of She, Hui, Manchu, Mongolian and Zhuang people, and other groups. A separate figure comes from the 2020 Chinese census, which counted 8,970,014 residents, and 2,588,060 of them lived in the built-up (metro) area formed by Zhanggong, Nankang and Ganxian districts. The birth rate in 2019 was 12.96 per 1,000 people.

gannan-normal-university.h: How the local economy is doing

blocks.x: In 2021 Ganzhou's gross domestic product came to ¥416.9 billion, 9.5% up on the year before. Three sectors make up that total:
Primary sector: ¥37.632 billion, 10.83% of the total.
Secondary sector: ¥136.819 billion, 39.38%.
Tertiary sector: ¥172.983 billion, 49.79%.

GDP per head was ¥35,341.74. As of 2019, urban residents had a disposable income of ¥34,826 per person, while for rural residents the figure was ¥11,941. Ten years before the 2021 figure, in 2011, the city's GDP had been ¥133.598 billion, so it has more than tripled.

The city has two proud nicknames, the "Tungsten Capital of the World" and the "Orange Capital of the World". The city also holds the largest mechanical clock in the world, the Harmony Clock Tower, which was made by the UK clockmakers Smith of Derby Group. Mountain scenery surrounds the city, and other well-known places elsewhere in Jiangxi include Jingdezhen, Nanchang and Lushan.
Natural attractions in the Ganzhou area include:
Mount Jiulian (九连山), in Longnan County
Mei Pass, in Dayu County
Cuiwei Peak (翠微峰), in Ningdu County

Among the area's cultural sites, the walled Hakka houses called "wei" are among the best examples of Hakka architecture. Representative ones are Guanxi Xinwei (关西新围) in Longnan, Yanji Wei (燕翼围) in Yangcun (杨村), Longguang Wei (龙光围) in Taojiang (桃江) and Dongsheng Wei (东生围) in Anyuan, and there are others.

In Zhanggong District you can visit two pavilions, Yugu Pavilion and Bajing Pavilion. The district also has a wall dating from the Song dynasty, plus several Buddhist and Taoist temples and pavilions from the Ming and Qing periods. Zao'er Alley (灶儿巷), 227.3 m (746 ft) long, goes back at least to the Song dynasty.

Since the Song dynasty, floating bridges have spanned the Zhang and Gong rivers, and Dongjin Bridge survives as an example. It is 400 metres long, made of wooden planks laid over around 100 wooden boats that are chained together with iron links. Altogether the area counts about 17 National Cultural Relic Protection Units and 48 at provincial level.
By road, the China National Highways that serve the city are G 105, G 206, G 319 and G 323. Two expressways pass through: the G45 Daqing-Guangzhou Expressway and the G76 Xiamen-Chengdu Expressway.

By rail, the Beijing-Jiulong Railway runs through Ganzhou from north to south. The Ganzhou-Longyan Railway (known as the Ganlong line) joins it at East Ganzhou Railway Station, in Zhanggong District. The Ganzhou-Shenzhen high-speed railway has been open since 10 December 2021 and links Ganzhou with Shenzhen, while the Nanchang-Shenzhen high-speed line was still being built. Stations of note, by line:
Beijing-Jiulong Railway: Dingnan, Longnan, Xinfeng, Nankang, Xingguo and Ganzhou itself.
Ganzhou-Longyan Railway: Ganxian, Yudu, Huichang and Ruijin.

By air, the new Ganzhou Huangjin Airport in Nankang opened on 26 March 2008. The name was inherited from the old Huangjin Airport at Huangjin Town in Zhanggong District, which shut down because the expanding city had grown too close to it. Direct domestic flights go to nine cities: Beijing, Shanghai, Nanjing, Xiamen, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Nanning, Nanchang and Chongqing.
A university's region shapes student life as much as its campus. Gannan Normal University is in Jiangxi, so here is the province's story, setting, economy, people and culture.

Jiangxi is built around the valley of the Gan River, which was historically the main north-south transport route in southern China. The south-eastern mountains are rugged and hard to cross, and the river corridor is one of the few routes that is easy to travel. Merchants and messengers used it to link the North China Plain and the Yangtze valley with the region that is now Guangdong. That explains why Jiangxi has mattered strategically for so much of China's past.

During the Shang dynasty, from the 16th to the 11th century BC, early Chinese civilisation did not reach the area, which was probably home to the peoples known as the Baiyue. In the Spring and Autumn period, the north of today's Jiangxi was Wu's western frontier. When the state of Yue, based in what is now northern Zhejiang, conquered Wu in 473 BC, Chu (based in present-day Hubei) took over the north of Jiangxi, and Yue may have had some influence in the south. Chu then conquered Yue in 333 BC. After Qin defeated Chu in 223 BC, most of Jiangxi was recorded as part of Jiujiang Commandery, centred on Shouchun (壽春), but the commandery did not work well and ended soon after Qin fell.

Yuzhang Commandery (豫章, Gan: Ì-zong) was founded early in the Han dynasty, perhaps before Xiang Yu died in 202 BC, and it was the first commandery a Chinese dynasty set up in Jiangxi. Its name came from the Yuzhang River (豫章江, Gan: Ì-zong Kong), which was the Gan River's first name; "Gan" has since become the province's short form. In 201 BC, eight counties were added to the seven that Qin had set up, and three more came later, so for most of the Han period its eighteen counties covered most of modern Jiangxi. County seats such as Nanchang, Gan, Yudu and Luling were located where major cities stand today, though other counties were later moved or abolished.

Emperor Wu of the Han placed Yuzhang Commandery in Yangzhou Province, as part of a nationwide move to create provinces (zhou). Under the Western Jin, in AD 291, Jiangxi gained its own zhou, named Jiangzhou (江州, Gan: Kong-chiu). Throughout the Southern and Northern Dynasties it was ruled by the southern courts, while the count of zhou crept upwards.

Under the Sui there were seven commanderies and twenty-four counties in Jiangxi. The Tang added one more commandery and fourteen counties, then abolished commanderies and turned them into zhou, a term that from here on is translated as "prefectures" rather than "provinces".

Circuits, a new top-level division, were a Tang invention too. Jiangxi began inside the Jiangnan Circuit, whose name means "the Circuit south of the Yangtze". In 733 this circuit was split in two, an eastern half and a western half. Jiangxi was in the western one, called Jiangnanxi Circuit ("Western circuits south of the Yangtze"), and the name "Jiangxi" derives from it.

The Tang fell in 907, and the era of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms followed. Two states ruled Jiangxi in turn, Wu (吳, Gan: Ng) and after it Southern Tang (南唐, Gan: Nām-thóng), each based in modern Nanjing, downstream on the Yangtze. After the ten kingdoms came to an end, the Jiangnanxi Circuit was revived, with nine prefectures and four army districts covering 68 districts. Later Jiangxi was split into thirteen circuits, and for the first time there was a Jiangxi Province, although it also took in most of today's Guangdong. At this stage Jiangxi had more or less the borders it has now.

gannan-normal-university.h: Revolution and war in the 20th century

blocks.x: After the Qing regime fell, Jiangxi was one of the earliest Communist bases, and many peasants joined the growing revolution. On 1 August 1927, in the middle of the Chinese Civil War, the Nanchang Uprising broke out in the province. Communist leaders went on to shelter in the hills of southern and western Jiangxi, where they evaded the Kuomintang's attempts to wipe them out. In 1931 the government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was set up in Ruijin, a town sometimes known as the "Former Red Capital" (红色故都, Gan: Fūng-set Kū-tu) or the "Red Capital". By 1935 the Nationalist forces had completely surrounded them, but they broke through and set out on the Long March towards Yan'an.

The National Government mounted five military campaigns against the Jiangxi Soviet area from 1930 until 1934. The fighting, along with brutal purges and internal cleansing, killed or drove away so many people that the province's population fell by 40%, leaving 13.8 million in 1936.

Transport changed in the late 1930s. After the Yuehan Railway opened in Hunan in 1936, Jiangxi lost its key position in north-south traffic. The east-west Zhegan Railway opened in 1937 and altered the older traffic patterns considerably, and the port of Jiujiang (九江港) began to decline in importance.

In the Second World War, the Doolittle Raid left American B-25 crews stranded in China. Most reached safety in the end because Jiangxi locals helped them, and those locals paid heavily. The Imperial Japanese Army responded with the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign, meant to scare people out of aiding downed airmen. At least 10,000 civilians died in Jiangxi in connection with the search for Doolittle's men.

The Communist Party took full control of Jiangxi when the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949. The Republican provincial government left for Taichung in Taiwan Province and dissolved itself the same year.

Jiangxi has mountains on three of its four sides: the Mufu, Jiuling and Luoxiao ranges to the west, the Huaiyu and Wuyi Mountains to the east, and the Dayu Mountains and the Jiulian Mountains (九连山) to the south. Hills, ranges and valleys alternate in the southern half, whereas the northern half is lower and flatter. The province's peak is Mount Huanggang (黄岗山), 2,157 metres (7,077 ft) above sea level, in the Wuyi Mountains along the Fujian boundary.

The Gan River is the province's main waterway, flowing from south to north through the entire province into Lake Poyang, China's biggest freshwater lake. From the lake the water drains to the Yangtze, which marks part of the northern boundary. Two important reservoirs are the Zhelin Reservoir on the Xiushui River in the north-west, and the Wan'an Reservoir on the upper Gan.

The provincial climate is humid subtropical (Cfa on the Köppen scale). Winters are cool, damp and brief, and summers are hot and humid. January temperatures average roughly 3 to 9 °C (37 to 48 °F), while July averages 27 to 30 °C (81 to 86 °F). Between 1,200 and 1,900 mm (47 to 75 in) of rain falls each year, much of it during the heavy downpours of late spring and summer.

The provincial capital, Nanchang, is the most densely populated city and one of China's large metropolises. Throughout history it has been the hub of Jiangxi civilisation and has led in commerce, intellectual life, industry and politics. Ganzhou, meanwhile, is the largest subdivision of Jiangxi by area.

During the Third Front campaign, Jiangxi received a large share of China's investment in industrial capacity. Rice is the main crop, with cotton and rapeseed as common cash crops, and Jiangxi leads China in kumquat production, especially in Suichuan County.

Mining matters greatly to the economy. In deposits of copper, tungsten, gold, silver, uranium, thorium, tantalum and niobium, and other minerals, Jiangxi leads all other Chinese provinces. Dexing is a noted centre of copper mining, and Dayu County of tungsten mining.

The province sits right beside some of the richest in China, Guangdong, Zhejiang and Fujian, which people sometimes blame for drawing talent and capital away from Jiangxi. Wages in Jiangxi are the lowest in China, and only two provinces have lower property prices. In 2016 nominal GDP was CNY 1.84 trillion (US$276.48 billion), which works out at CNY 40,400 (US$6,082) per person. For an international student, low prices can mean a cheaper cost of living, but check actual rents and local costs.
Six zones are used to attract industry and investment. Three are in Nanchang and three in Jiujiang:
In Nanchang: an export processing zone, a national high-tech industrial development zone and an economic and technological development zone.
In Jiujiang: a free trade (tariff-free) zone, a national economical and technological development zone and the Gongqingcheng National High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The Nanchang National Export Processing Zone lies inside the Nanchang Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. Approval from the State Council came on 8 May 2006, and the zone cleared the national acceptance inspection on 7 September 2007. Of its planned 1 km² (0.39 sq mi), 0.31 km² (0.12 sq mi) has been built. Customs clearance there is simple and convenient, and special preferential policies apply to both the export zone and the high-tech zone.

The Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone, shortened to NCHDZ, is the only national-grade high-tech zone in Jiangxi and was established in March 1991. It covers 231 km² (89 sq mi), of which 32 km² (12 sq mi) is complete. Its natural conditions and industrial base suit the electronics industry. Using just 0.4% of the city's land, NCHDZ brings Nanchang 25% of its industrial added value and 50% of its industrial benefit and tax.

The 2020 census counted 45.18 million people in Jiangxi, 99.73% of them Han Chinese, mostly Gan and Hakka. Ganzhou, the province's largest city, has an especially large Hakka population. The ethnic minorities include the She people.

Gender ratios are more unbalanced in Jiangxi and Henan than in any other Chinese province. A 2009 British Medical Journal study found over 140 boys for each 100 girls among children aged one to four. In 2019 Liú (刘) was the most common surname in Jiangxi, which was the only province where that held true, although it is the fourth most common surname in the country overall.

The main faiths are Chinese Buddhism, Taoist traditions and Chinese folk religions. Surveys carried out in 2007 and 2009 found 24.05% of people practising ancestor veneration and 2.31% who called themselves Christian. No numbers were given for any other kind of religion, which means the remaining 73.64% could be non-religious, or could follow nature deities, folk religious sects, Confucianism, Taoism or Buddhism.

The Gan group of Chinese varieties is concentrated in Jiangxi and is spoken across most of the northern two-thirds. The Nanchang, Yichun and Ji'an dialects are examples. In the southern third people speak Hakka, and some Mandarin, Huizhou and Wu dialects can be heard near the northern border.

The local style of Chinese opera is Ganju (赣剧, Gan Opera). Jiangxi cuisine is little known outside the province but rich and distinctive, with some of the strongest flavours in China, using chili peppers heavily, along with pickled and fermented foods.

Jingdezhen is widely regarded as the maker of the best porcelain in China and is called its "porcelain capital". The province was also a historical centre of Chan Buddhism, and notable examples of Hakka architecture are found there.

In January 2015 the province had two Yangtze crossings, and both were in Jiujiang. By rail, the Beijing-Kowloon and Shanghai-Kunming railways criss-cross the province and meet at Nanchang, which has a high-speed link to Jiujiang. Connections to neighbours include the Anhui-Jiangxi and Tongling-Jiujiang railways (to Anhui), the Wuhan-Jiujiang Railway (to Hubei), and the Yingtan-Xiamen, Hengfeng-Nanping, Ganzhou-Longyan and Xiangtang-Putian railways (to Fujian).
If you are comparing options or planning a visit, these are other colleges and universities in the province:
Nanchang University
Nanchang Hangkong University
Nanchang Institute of Technology
Jiangxi Agricultural University
Jiangxi Normal University
Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University
East China Jiaotong University
East China University of Technology
Jiangxi Institute of Education
Jiangxi College of Foreign Studies
Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics
Jingdezhen Ceramic Institute
Jinggangshan University
Xinyu University
Yichun University
University of Jiujiang
Gannan Normal University lists 16 programs for international students on this site: 16 master's programs.

By language of instruction: 16 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.

16 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

gannan-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Gannan Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Ganzhou, register at Gannan Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

gansu-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: An introduction to Gansu University of Chinese Medicine

blocks.x: Gansu University of Chinese Medicine is a state-run university located in Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in north-western China. It started life in 1978 under the name Gansu College of Traditional Chinese Medicine and today offers bachelor's, master's and doctoral programmes in traditional Chinese medicine. It is run jointly by the Gansu provincial government and the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Its particular claim is that it stands alone as the sole Chinese-medicine university in the whole of north-western China that is authorised to award doctorates, which matters if you hope to continue to advanced research in this field in the region.

gansu-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: From a provincial college to a full university

blocks.x: The institution's development is easy to follow as a sequence of milestones.
1978: a college of traditional Chinese medicine, named for Gansu, is founded in Lanzhou.
1989: a Tibetan Medicine Department is added.
2014: Dingxi Normal College is merged into the institution.
2015: after the Ministry of Education gives its approval, the college is renamed Gansu University of Chinese Medicine.
2016: it becomes jointly built by the Gansu provincial government and the national traditional medicine administration.
2018: a cooperation agreement is signed with Shanghai University of Chinese Medicine.
2024: it is designated a Gansu provincial base for promoting and teaching traditional Chinese medicine culture.

The pattern is clear: a college that grew by adding a Tibetan medicine department, absorbing a teacher-training college, gaining university status and then building partnerships with both national authorities and a larger sister university in Shanghai.

There are 19,715 full-time students. They include 15,649 bachelor's-level learners, 3,588 master's candidates and 262 doctoral candidates, plus more than 120 international students, so overseas learners are a small but present group. The university is organised into 16 teaching institutions.

Four campuses are in use: Heping, Wulipu, Dingxi and Gannan. Heping Campus is the headquarters, covers 1,050 acres, and looks across toward the Yellow River in the distance. Clinical training is supported by four directly affiliated hospitals and six that are not directly affiliated. The first affiliated hospital is the Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine in Gansu, which holds Grade A tertiary status.

The university also edits and publishes three Chinese-language academic journals: one for the university's own research, one on paediatric Chinese medicine and one on primary health care in Gansu. In the Shanghai Ranking of Chinese universities of Chinese medicine, it was placed 25th in the 2026 edition.
Daily life for a student depends heavily on the city outside the gates: its weather, its transport and what it offers in free time. The following sections describe Lanzhou.

Lanzhou sits at about 1,600 metres (5,200 feet) above sea level in the geographic centre of north-western China. The built-up area, covering over 20 square kilometres (7.7 square miles), stretches along the southern bank of the Yellow River, which here flows from west to east, and mountain ranges lie on both the south and north sides: the Qilian ranges, Mount Pingliang and Mount Kongtong. The city is on the upper stretch of the Yellow River at the point where it leaves the mountains, and it has been an important centre since early times. It marks the southern end of the route that leads across Central Asia through the Hexi Corridor, it controls the western and north-western approaches to the ancient capital district around Chang'an (modern Xi'an), and via the upper river and its tributaries it reaches the Qinghai Lake area.

Lanzhou lies in the temperate zone with a semi-arid climate: hot summers, and winters that are cold and very dry. Based on 1971 to 2000 averages, the monthly mean runs from minus 4.1 degrees Celsius ((24.6 F) at the start of the year and rises to 23.4 degrees (74.1 F) in July, with a yearly mean of 10.9 degrees (51.6 F). Rainfall totals only 309 millimetres (12.2 inches) a year, almost all between May and October, and winters are so dry that snow can be confined to autumn and spring. Sunshine adds up to 2,350 hours a year, with monthly possible sunshine between 47 percent in September and 57 percent in April, which is generous without being abundant. Expect a proper coat in winter and a dry, sunny summer.

Lanzhou's setting has long been a challenge for its air. The city occupies a narrow, curving river valley and the surrounding mountains hold air in, while factories, some of them linked to petroleum processing, and dust blown from the Gobi Desert in winter and spring add to the load. A January 2013 report from Tsinghua University together with the Asian Development Bank listed it among the world's ten most air-polluted cities, and in 2011 the World Health Organization, using Chinese statistics, reported that it found its air the worst of eleven cities in western China, with an annual PM10 level of 150 micrograms per cubic metre, seven times the safe level and worse than Beijing's 121.

The authorities have since taken action, and the effort is generally judged to have been successful. Thirteen polluting enterprises with excess capacity were closed, more than 200 heavily polluting firms were suspended in winter, while 78 factories relocated to an industrial zone beyond the urban area. In 2015 Lanzhou received China's climate progress title and it was cited for cutting its Air Pollution Index faster than any other city in the country. By the 2018 World Health Organization database, of 2,700 towns listed, Lanzhou ranked 158th for PM2.5, at an annual average of 54 micrograms per cubic metre, about twice the figure for Milan. Coarse PM10 remained high at 132 micrograms, partly because of sandstorms. In practice, you should check daily air readings, especially in winter and spring.

The Yellow River reach at Lanzhou carries a heavy load of silt that gives it its muddy look, yet its water quality here is better than the badly polluted outflow reported two hours downstream in 2008. Several endangered Chinese giant salamanders have turned up in and near the river in the city in recent years.

Earthquakes happen regularly in the Lanzhou area, though mostly at low intensity. A large quake in 1920 killed over 100,000 people across Ningxia and eastern Gansu but only 42 in Lanzhou itself, a small number credited to the strong but flexible wooden buildings of the city at that time. The 2008 Sichuan earthquake was also felt in Lanzhou.

In the 2020 census Lanzhou passed four million residents for the first time, with 4,359,446 people overall. About 3,042,863 of them live in the built-up zone covering 1,112.9 square km (429.7 square miles)) that spans four central districts: Chengguan, Qilihe, Anning and Xigu. Lanzhou New Area beside the airport and Honggu District are not yet joined to the built-up area. Growth picked up strongly after a slower period, and the source attributes it to parents seeking better schooling for their children, migrant workers who retired and came back to Gansu, better city services and government policy.

Lanzhou is the main transport and tourist doorway into Gansu and the Hexi Corridor, and it gives access to historic sites such as the Bingling Temple Grottoes. Within the city, the following places are worth knowing.
Five Spring Mountain Park (五泉山公园), on Gaolan Mountain's northern slope, known for its five springs and many Buddhist temples and ancient buildings.
Zhongshan Bridge (中山桥), the first permanent bridge across the Yellow River.
Baita Mountain Park (白塔山公园), built on a hillside at 1,700 metres (5,600 feet), opened in 1958 across from Zhongshan Bridge.
Lanzhou Botanical Garden (兰州植物园) in Anning District, with a wide range of trees, flowers and other plant life.
Xiguan Mosque (西关清真寺), among the larger mosques in China.
Xinglong Mountain (兴隆山), covered in thick pine forest and dotted with colourful temples.
The Lutusi ancient government site (鲁土司衙门旧址), a large complex of historic official buildings.
For rainy days or cultural study, the city has several museums.
Gansu Provincial Museum (甘肃省博物馆), with finds of archaeology and fossils from Gansu, with displays on the province's history.

Lanzhou Museum (兰州市博物馆), an important Silk Road cultural site. As of October 2017 it held over 13,000 items, such as pottery, porcelain, bronzes, calligraphy, coins, jade and stoneware, including 52 first-class, 78 second-class and 682 third-class national cultural relics.
Gansu Art Museum (甘肃艺术馆), a broad display and outreach platform for artists.
Lanzhou City Planning Exhibition Hall (兰州市规划展览馆), presenting the city's Yellow River culture through indoor exhibits, architectural ideas and urban character.
Lanzhou Painted Pottery Museum (兰州彩陶博物馆), with 250 items, 50 of them precious relics, showing the painted pottery civilisation represented by Majiayao ware.
Gansu Science and Technology Museum (甘肃科技博物馆), which uses sound, light, electricity and other high-tech methods so visitors can experience modern science.

Since 1949 Lanzhou has changed from the capital of a poor province into the centre of a significant industrial region. It was among the first Chinese cities to industrialise, as a target of the nation's First and Second Five-Year Plans. Per-person GDP was 25,566 yuan (about 3,681 US dollars) in 2008, ranking 134th of 659 Chinese cities. By 2015 it had grown to 57,191 yuan ((about 9,182.28 dollars)), and the city ranked 100th for total GDP among Chinese cities. UNIDO's International Solar Energy Center is located in Chengguan District.

Deposits found nearby include dolomite, clay, manganese, nickel, zinc, silver, gold and coal. Hydropower is an important resource. There is a coal-fired thermal station supplied from Qinghai coalfields, a hydropower plant at Zhulama Gorge in Gansu, plus a big multipurpose dam on the Yellow River at Liujia Gorge upstream of the city.

The leading industries are textile mills, rubber processing, fertiliser works, an oil refinery, petrochemical output, machinery and metallurgy. Gansu has one of the country's largest oil refineries, Lanzhou is the province's petrochemical centre, and the refinery is connected by pipeline to the Yumen oilfields. The city also makes oil-industry equipment. Its textile sector is known for wool and leather goods, and it builds locomotives and rolling stock for north-western railways, along with machine tools and equipment for mines. Aluminium products, industrial chemicals and fertilisers are produced on a large scale, rubber is a big industry, and copper is mined nearby at Gaolan. Lanzhou has been a centre of China's nuclear industry since the 1960s, when its uranium enrichment plant was completed.

Lanzhou is also a collecting point and market for farm produce and farm animals from a broad area. Typical products are spring wheat, vegetables, beans, oil crops, melons, peaches and tobacco, along with roses and lilies.
Transport links are one of the city's strengths, with an airport, a growing metro, major rail connections and an extensive road network.

Lanzhou Zhongchuan Airport serves as the main air gateway, 70 kilometres (43 miles) north of the city. It opened to the public in 1970 and offers direct connections to more than 70 international and domestic destinations. An intercity railway links Lanzhou Railway Station with the airport.

Lanzhou was the second city in north-western China to announce plans for a subway in August 2012. The planned Lanzhou Metro network has six lines over 207 kilometres (129 miles). Line 1, fully underground, opened in June 2019 and the first stage of Line 2 opened in June 2023. Passengers can change between the two lines at Dongfanghong Square and Wulipu stations.

Lanzhou Railway Station, on Huochezhan Dong Lu, within Chengguan District, is one of western China's major rail hubs. More than 100 passenger trains start from or pass through it each day, and it is a vital connection between the western provinces and the east. Lanzhou West Railway Station is the second main station and handles the high-speed services. The routes from Lanzhou Railway Station run as follows.

Longhai Railway to the east, through Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Lianyungang, connecting with the main eastern network and direct trains to Beijing and Shanghai. It was completed in 1953 and was the earliest line to arrive in Lanzhou.
Lanxin Railway to the west and north-west, carrying direct trains to western Gansu and Urumqi, and onward connections elsewhere in Xinjiang and to Kazakhstan.
Lanqing Railway to the west and south-west, offering direct service to Xining and Lhasa.

A line to the north and north-east, offering direct service to Yinchuan and Baotou.

The Lanhe Railway to Linxia and Hezuo, which is under construction.

New dedicated high-speed passenger lines now run east (Xuzhou to Lanzhou), west (Lanzhou to Xinjiang) and north (Yinchuan to Lanzhou), and these call only at Lanzhou West. The Sichuan to Qinghai railway, designed for 200 to 250 kilometres an hour (120 to 160 mph), is under construction.

Freight matters here too. Lanzhou is a link on one of the Eurasian Land Bridge routes, offers railway links with Qinghai, Xinjiang and Tibet, has a large new freight terminal and has China's fourth-largest marshalling yard. Regular freight services connect it with Chongqing, Hamburg, Almaty and Kathmandu.

The province in which a university sits shapes student life nearly as much as the campus itself, so here is a short portrait of Gansu.

gansu-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: A long history on the Silk Road

blocks.x: The name Gansu was first used under the Song dynasty and joins the names of two earlier prefectures from Sui and Tang times: Gan, near Zhangye, and Su, near Jiuquan. The eastern part of the province forms part of one of the birthplaces of ancient Chinese civilisation.

In prehistory Gansu hosted Neolithic cultures. The Dadiwan culture, which produced important archaeological finds, flourished in the east between roughly 6000 BC and 3000 BC, and the Majiayao and part of the Qijia cultures took root in the province between 3100 and 2700 BC and between 2400 and 1900 BC. The Yuezhi originally lived in the far west of Gansu until the Xiongnu drove them out in about 177 BC. The Qin state, seen as the founder state of the Chinese empire, grew from the south-eastern part of the province around Tianshui, and the Qin name is thought to come partly from this area. Qin tombs and artefacts have been excavated at Fangmatan near Tianshui, including a 2200-year-old map of Guixian County.

In imperial times the Hexi Corridor ran along the province's neck, making Gansu a strategic outpost and communications link. Under the Han dynasty the Great Wall was extended across the corridor and built the fort towns of Yumenguan (the Jade Gate Pass near Dunhuang) together with Yangguan, whose remains can still be seen. The Jiayuguan outpost was a Ming-dynasty construction. Beyond Yumenguan and the Qilian range, at the north-western end, nomads such as the Yuezhi and Wusun lived and occasionally figured in imperial geopolitics. A treaty signed at Qingshui in 823 by the Tibetan Empire and Tang China cost China a large share of western Gansu for a long time. Later, once the Uyghur Khaganate had collapsed, migrating Uyghurs established the Buddhist Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom in part of Gansu, which lasted from 848 to 1036, and the Western Xia dynasty later controlled much of Gansu and Ningxia.

Along the Silk Road, Gansu was both an economic powerhouse and a path for cultural transmission. Temples and Buddhist grottoes such as the Mogao Caves, known as the Caves of the Thousand Buddhas, and the Maijishan Caves hold murals of great artistic and historical value. In August 2006 an early form of paper bearing Chinese characters and dated to about 8 BC was found at a Western Han garrison site near Yumen Pass. The province was also where the Dungan Revolt of 1862 to 1877 began; it had spread from neighbouring Qinghai, and Muslim commanders such as Ma Zhan'ao and Ma Anliang served in the Qing forces that put it down. A second Dungan revolt took place in 1895 and 1896.

Frequent earthquakes, droughts and famines held back Gansu's economic progress compared with other Chinese provinces until recently. Drawing on rich mineral resources, it has now started to develop into an important industrial centre. An earthquake of magnitude 8.6 in 1920 killed about 180,000 people, mostly in what is now Ningxia, and a magnitude 7.6 quake killed 275 in 1932.

The Muslim Conflict in Gansu from 1927 to 1930 was fought against the Guominjun. By 1940 the Muslim general Ma Buqing effectively controlled Gansu, with headquarters at Liangzhou District in Wuwei, from where he controlled 15 million Muslims, while Ma Hongbin served as acting chairman of the province. Xinjiang came under Nationalist control after soldiers entered through Gansu, and Tianshui was the site of a Japanese-Chinese air fight.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War, Gansu was a passage for Soviet supplies reaching the Republic of China through Xinjiang, with a road from Urumqi to Lanzhou as the destination. Gonxingdun Aerodrome was among several bases from which the Chinese Air Force defended the province. From the summer of 1939 Gansu supplied wartime China with most of its its home-produced petrol from the Yumen Laojunmiao wells, producing 250,000 tons of crude in those years. Plans named Lanzhou and Lhasa as the ends of a planned railway. The Kuomintang Islamic insurgency of 1950 to 1958 carried the Chinese Civil War on in several provinces, Gansu included.

gansu-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Land and weather in the province

blocks.x: Gansu covers 454,000 square kilometres (175,000 square miles), and most of it stands over 1,000 metres (3,300 feet) above sea level. Its position is between the Tibetan Plateau on one side and the Loess Plateau on the other, and is neighbour to Mongolia's Govi-Altai Province (north-west), Inner Mongolia and Ningxia (north), Shaanxi (east), Sichuan (south) and Xinjiang (west). The Yellow River crosses the southern part. China's geographic midpoint, indicated by a monument called the Center of the Country, lies at 35 degrees 50 minutes north, 103 degrees 27 minutes east, lies within the province.

Part of the Gobi Desert is in Gansu, along with small sections of the Badain Jaran and Tengger deserts. The Yellow River draws most of its water from Gansu and flows straight through Lanzhou, and the Wuwei area belongs to the Shiyang River basin. The south is mountainous, belonging to the Qilian Mountains, while the north is flat; the top elevation, 5,830 metres (19,130 feet), lies in the far western Altyn-Tagh. The Hexi Corridor, a natural passage roughly 1,000 kilometres (620 miles) in length and linking Lanzhou with the Jade Gate; the Gobi flanks it on the north side and the Qilian Mountains on the south.

The climate is generally semi-arid to arid and continental, bringing warm-to-hot summers and winters that run from cold to very cold, although the day-to-night range is often so large that daytime highs stay above freezing (0 degrees Celsius, 32 F) even in winter. At high altitudes some areas have a subarctic climate, with winter temperatures sometimes falling to minus 40 degrees. Most of the limited rain falls in summer, snow cover is limited to very high ground, and the snow line can reach 5,500 metres (18,040 feet) in the south-west.

Since 2014 services have been the province's largest economic sector, and tourism is growing in importance. In education, Gansu holds the one and only Class A Double First-Class university in China's north-west, Lanzhou University.

gansu-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Reading this profile as an applicant

blocks.x: Taken together, the picture is of a mid-sized provincial university with a clear specialty. Its strengths are the focus on traditional Chinese medicine and Tibetan medicine, the ability to award doctorates in a region where few others can, and the hospital network that supports clinical teaching. International students are present but few, so you should ask the admissions office what support exists for English or other languages and what the language of instruction will be for your programme.

The city shapes the experience as much as the classroom does. Lanzhou has a dry climate, cold winters and a valley setting that has made air quality a long-running concern, although conditions have improved markedly in recent years. It also offers excellent rail and air connections, a young metro system and easy access to the Hexi Corridor and the Silk Road heritage of Gansu. If you plan visits before you commit, spring and autumn visits let you see both the city and the Heping campus in reasonable weather.

graduate-school-of-chinese-academy-of-ag.h: Beijing as a home for graduate study

blocks.x: The Graduate School of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences is in Beijing, so for a postgraduate applicant the capital is more than a backdrop: it sets the weather you live in, the air you breathe, the streets you walk and the pace of daily life. This guide collects the practical facts about the city, from its buildings and layout to its seasons and air quality, so that you can decide what to expect before you arrive.

Walk around Beijing and you will see three kinds of architecture. The oldest is the architecture of imperial China, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple among it, together with the Forbidden City and the huge Tian'anmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace that has become the best-known symbol of the People's Republic. Next come the plain, boxy "Sino-Soviet" buildings of the 1950s to the 1970s, some of which were not built well. Finally there is the contemporary city: the Beijing National Stadium, the National Center for the Performing Arts and, above all, the glass towers of the eastern CBD, such as the new CCTV Headquarters.

The early 21st century brought a building boom, and international designers added a range of modern styles, mainly in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone is a good example of old and new together, blending 1950s industrial design with a neofuturistic look. At 528 metres the China Zun is the city's tallest building. Beijing has been home to two winners of the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building (one winner worldwide per year) since 2007: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013.

Beijing's traditional homes are siheyuan, courtyards with buildings on all sides. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are among the grander ones. A network of alleys known as hutongs joins the courtyards. Most hutongs are straight and run east to west, which means doorways face north or south, an orientation thought to bring good feng shui. Widths differ, and in the narrowest only a few pedestrians can squeeze by at once.

Siheyuan and hutong neighbourhoods used to be everywhere, but they are vanishing fast as whole blocks are demolished for high-rises. People who lived in hutongs may move into the new buildings, into apartments at least as big as their former homes. Many nevertheless complain that the old community spirit and street life cannot be re-created, and the properties tend to be owned by the government.

graduate-school-of-chinese-academy-of-ag.h: How the city is laid out

blocks.x: Beijing lies at the top of a roughly triangular lowland, the North China Plain, which spreads out to the south and east. To the north, northwest and west, mountains act as a screen between the city, with the farming heartland of the north, and the desert steppe. Yanqing and Huairou Districts, in the northwest, are mostly the Jundu Mountains, and to the west stand the Western Hills (Xishan). The Great Wall was built across the municipality's north along the rugged ridges as protection from nomadic raiders from the steppe. The tallest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Rivers here (the Chaobai, the Yongding, the Juma and others) are tributaries of the Hai River system and run toward the southeast. The Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai, is the municipality's biggest. The city also marks the northern end of two long water routes: the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built as a transport route more than 1,400 years ago, and the South-North Water Transfer Project, a project of the last decade that brings Yangtze basin water north.

The urban area sits on the plains in the municipality's south-centre, at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and while it takes up a modest part of the whole municipality, it keeps growing. Beijing is organised in rings: the Second Ring Road follows the line of the old city walls, and the Sixth Ring Road ties the satellite towns of the suburbs together. At the centre are Tian'anmen and the square named after it, immediately south of the Forbidden City, which was the emperors' home. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, where China's present leaders live. Chang'an Avenue runs between Tiananmen and the Square and is the main east-west axis of the city. The way Beijing has expanded from its core to the fringe is often compared to a pancake spreading out (tan da bing), and this pattern is commonly given as one reason for the city's urban problems.
Technically, Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), on the edge of a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (Köppen BSk). In practice, that means:
Summer: hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon.
Winter: short but cold and dry, under the influence of the huge Siberian anticyclone.
Spring: it warms rapidly with little rain, and sandstorms may blow in from the Gobi Desert across the Mongolian steppe.
Autumn: a transitional season like spring, with minimal rainfall.

In the period from 2001 to 2026 the hottest time of year has been early August and the coldest early January. Chinese seasonal convention puts the start of spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. Because March and September have been warming faster, and May and October slower, in recent years, autumn in Beijing now tends to be shorter than spring.

In the urban area the yearly mean temperature is 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). The typical daily low is between 7.7 and 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F), and the typical daily high is between 18.5 and 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).
In the lower suburbs the yearly mean is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with daily lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F).
In mountain areas the mean lies between 0 and 10 °C (32 and 50 °F) and drops as you climb.

January's average daily temperature is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July's 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). About 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of precipitation falls in an average year, although the Haidian and Chaoyang districts average 584.2 mm (23.00 in), and close to three-quarters falls between June and August. The share of possible sunshine is 42% in July and 62% in January and February, so the city gets 2,490.5 hours of bright sun a year. Since 1951 the temperature has gone as low as -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, and as high as 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), on 24 July 1999.

graduate-school-of-chinese-academy-of-ag.h: Why Beijing's air has been a concern

blocks.x: The city has a long history of environmental trouble. From 2000 to 2009 its built-up area grew fourfold, which raised emissions and, even leaving human emissions aside, reshaped its weather: surface albedo, wind speed and near-surface humidity decreased, while ground temperature, near-surface air temperature, vertical air dilution and ozone all increased. Together, urban growth and the burning of fossil fuel cause serious environmental problems that harm many residents' health. A thick smog hit Beijing and most of northern China in 2013, affecting 600 million people altogether, and following this "pollution shock" air pollution became a significant economic and social concern across China. Beijing's government then set out ways to reduce it, such as cutting the share of coal from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017. At national level, heavily polluting vehicles were ordered off the road between 2015 and 2017, and efforts to move the energy system to clean sources intensified.

In 2006 a joint American-Chinese research effort found that much of Beijing's pollution is brought in from the surrounding cities and provinces: on average 35 to 60% of ozone can be traced to sources beyond the city. The influence of Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality on the capital's air quality is described as "significant", partly because the prevailing summer wind is south or southeasterly and partly because of the mountains to the north and northwest.

Burning coal accounts for around 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been converting coal-fired power stations to natural gas since 2012 and seeks to cap annual coal use at 20 million tons. It burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, 73% for heating and power and the rest for industry. A lot of the pollution comes from neighbouring regions. Tianjin's use of coal was expected to rise from 48 million to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Hebei Province's coal burning in 2011, over 300 million tons, was more than all of Germany's, and only 30% of it fed power generation, with a considerable share going to steel and cement. Power plants in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where coal use has tripled since 2000, and in Shandong also add to Beijing's smog. By coal consumption, the provinces rank Shandong first, then Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

The city had four large coal-fired power plants for electricity and winter heating. The first, Gaojing Thermal Power Plant, shut in 2014, two more shut in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to close in 2016. Between 2013 and 2017 the plan was to reduce coal use by 13 million tons and to hold it to 15 million tons in 2015.

Nearly US$17 billion was spent to meet the promise of cleaner air for the 2008 Summer Olympics. During the Games the city stopped work on every construction site, closed many factories in Beijing for good, shut industry in neighbouring regions for a time, closed some gas stations, halved motor traffic with odd and even licence-plate days, cut bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned vehicles with high emissions. It also assembled 3,800 natural-gas buses, which is one of the largest such fleets in the world, and became the first Chinese city to demand the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Sometimes the authorities also seed clouds to make rain more likely and clear the air before big events, for instance before the 2009 parade for the 60th anniversary, and to fight drought. More recently they have turned more to temporary factory closures and tougher limits on cars, which produced the "APEC blue" and "parade blue" of the weeks around APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. In those periods the air improved dramatically, then went back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed most industry and commercial business in the city. Another smog "red alert" followed within the month. In November 2016 Beijing's environmental protection bureau announced that, from 2017, old cars that pollute heavily would be banned from driving whenever red alerts are issued in the city or nearby regions.

A "war on pollution" declared in 2014 has led to measurable cuts. Fine particulates fell 35% in 2017 and fell further by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal for power and polluting industrial facilities in the Beijing area were cleaned up. In 2022 the annual average PM2.5 level was 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the city's best since 2013, and 2024 saw only two days of heavy pollution, a record low and a 96.6 percent decline from the 58 days of 2013.

Because air quality is such a concern, several sources publish readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) puts daily data from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly fine particulate (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. Their pollutants and criteria are different, so BJEPB's pollution levels and health impacts usually come out lower than the Embassy's.

Smog is dangerous for the population. It has a direct and significant effect on illness rates for cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can lead to respiratory and cardiovascular problems, emergency-room visits and even death. Postgraduate students with existing conditions should talk to their doctor first.

Desert erosion in northern and northwestern China sends dust storms to the city each year, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain artificially to fight them and soften their effects. At least eight happened in the first four months of 2006 alone, and in April 2002 a single storm left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing before it moved on towards Japan and Korea.

For anyone planning to study at the Graduate School, the key points are a hot and humid summer, a short and cold dry winter, a quickly warming but dusty spring, an air-quality record that has improved considerably since 2013 but still needs monitoring, and a city whose structure, in ring roads and a central axis, is easy to learn.
