Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, usually shortened to GDUFS, is a provincial public university in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong Province in southern China. Its Chinese name, 广东外语外贸大学, translates literally as Guangdong Foreign Languages and Foreign Trade University, and that double identity (languages plus trade) is the best way to understand what the place is about.

GDUFS has two parents. Guangzhou Foreign Languages College opened in 1964, and Guangzhou Foreign Trade College followed in 1980. Both started life under national bodies: the language college under one ministry-level authority and the trade college under another. In the mid-1990s responsibility for both passed to the Guangdong provincial government, in September 1994 for one and January 1995 for the other.

The provincial government merged the two colleges in May 1995 and gave the new institution its present name. A further addition came in October 2008, when Guangdong Finance and Economics College, which had been set up in April 1996, was folded into the university. In practice this means the university today combines three strands of tradition: foreign languages, international trade, and finance and economics.

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: Where it stands in the rankings

blocks.x: Rankings are a rough guide and every system measures something different, so treat the numbers below as snapshots. They also change from year to year, and the university's own website and the ranking organisations' pages carry the latest positions.
In the 2023 Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), GDUFS appeared in the 901-1000 band.
In the 2025 QS Asian University Rankings it was placed in the 501-520 band.
In the 2025 U.S. News & World Report Best Global Universities list it was placed 996th.

Subject tables tell a more useful story for a languages-and-business university. In the 2024 QS subject rankings, GDUFS was in the 201-250 band for Linguistics. In the 2024-2025 U.S. News subject lists it was 215th for Arts and Humanities, 323rd for Economics and Business, and 609th for Social Sciences and Public Health. In the 2024 Shanghai Ranking subject tables, it fell in the 301-400 band for Education and the 401-500 band for Economics.
The pattern is consistent: the university's strongest international showing is in languages, humanities and business-related fields, which matches its history.

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: Guangzhou: the city around your campus

blocks.x: Daily student life is shaped as much by the city as by the campus, so the rest of this profile looks at Guangzhou, covering its landscape, climate, economy, population and history, and then at the wider province of Guangdong.

Guangzhou grew up near Baiyun Mountain on the eastern bank of the Pearl River, known in Chinese as the Zhujiang. The old town sits roughly 130 kilometres (80 miles) upstream from the point where the river meets the South China Sea, and a very long way below the head of navigation, which lies about 300 miles upriver. From that position the city controlled the rich, silt-built plain of the Pearl River Delta, and the sea approach was guarded at the Humen Strait.

The modern city covers about 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 square miles) on both sides of the river, between roughly 112 degrees 57 minutes and 114 degrees 03 minutes east and 22 degrees 26 minutes and 23 degrees 56 minutes north, in the south-central part of Guangdong. The Pearl is the fourth-longest river in China. Tidal flats once lined the estuary and supported their own ecosystems, though many have since been reclaimed for farming. Baiyun Mountain, meanwhile, is affectionately called the city's lung, a reference to the green space it provides in an otherwise dense urban area.

The land rises from the south-west towards the north-east. Mountains form the city's backbone, and the sea forms its front. The highest point is Tiantang Peak, at 1,210 metres (about 3,970 feet) above sea level.

Water is a defining feature. Rivers and streams account for roughly a tenth of the city's land area; the water surface is given as 74,400 hectares, or 10.05 percent of the land. The main waterways include the Beijiang, the northern main channel of the Dongjiang, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi River, the Baini River, the Guangzhou section of the Pearl River, and the Shiqiao and Shawan waterways. The Beijiang and Dongjiang flow through the city and join the Pearl on their way to the sea. In the south, where the river network is tidal, flows are large and tides strongly influence the water. The Pearl exits into the Lingding sea area and then the South China Sea through three major outlets: Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili.

There is a notable contrast between local water and passing water. The water that actually originates within the city is modest; published figures put the total at 7.979 billion cubic metres a year, though the breakdown given alongside it (7.881 billion of surface water and 1.487 billion of groundwater) does not quite add up, so treat the split as approximate. Divided by the 2010 census population, that is about 1.06 million cubic metres per square kilometre, or roughly 628 cubic metres per person, about half the national average. The water that flows through from upstream rivers is vastly larger: 186.024 billion cubic metres, around 23 times the local supply, concentrated mainly in the southern part of the city and in Zengcheng District. Of that, about 159.15 billion cubic metres is diverted from the Xijiang and Beijiang, 14.203 billion from the Dongjiang, and 2.828 billion arrives from the upper Zengjiang. At the three river mouths, the yearly flood tide is about 271 billion cubic metres and the ebb about 408.8 billion, with an annual runoff of 137.7 billion, so the tide carries a large volume of water, part of it usable fresh water. Different sources give slightly different numbers and they may have been revised, so check the official statistics if you need exact values.

Farming reflects the city's position between the tropics and the subtropics. Guangzhou is regarded as one of the richest areas in China for fruit, with more than 500 varieties in 41 families, 82 genera and 174 species across tropical, subtropical and temperate types, among them 55 major lychee varieties. It is considered a centre of origin for lychee and longan, along with other local fruits such as the yellow-skin fruit and olives. Vegetables are also known for quality and variety, with 15 major categories, 127 species and over 370 varieties. Cut flowers, potted plants, bonsai and ornamental seedlings are grown commercially too, and the Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first local product in the city to gain a protected geographical indication.

Geologically the area is complicated, which has given it a range of minerals, with 47 kinds recorded across 820 sites and 25 medium and large mining areas. Construction granite, cement limestone, ceramic clay, potassium and sodium feldspar, salt, fluorite, marble, mineral water and geothermal water are the main ones. Energy minerals and non-ferrous metals are scarce and scattered. Sources differ on how many oil deposits there are, so this is not a topic to rely on without checking.

Guangzhou lies just south of the Tropic of Cancer and has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen Cwa) shaped by the East Asian monsoon. Summers are hot, wet and muggy, with a high heat index, and winters are mild and relatively dry. The long wet season runs from April to September.

Monthly mean temperatures run from about 13.8 degrees Celsius (56.8 F) in January to 28.9 degrees (84.0 F) in July, with an annual mean of 22.4 degrees (72.3 F). Humidity averages about 76 percent and annual rainfall in the urban area exceeds 1,950 millimetres (77 inches). Sunshine is limited: about 1,559 hours a year, which is noticeably less than in neighbouring Shenzhen or Hong Kong, and monthly sunshine ranges from around 17 percent of the possible total in March to 51 percent in October.

Autumn, from October to December, is usually the most pleasant stretch: mild, cooler and breezy, and often described as the best time to visit. Since 1951 the recorded range has gone from 0 degrees Celsius (seen on two winter dates, in 1957 and 1999) up to 39.1 degrees (102.4 F) on 1 July 2004; the cold records were 0 degrees (32 F) on 11 February 1957 and 23 December 1999. Earlier unofficial readings were lower, including a reported minus 5.0 degrees (23.0 F) on 18 January 1893, which modern meteorologists think was nearer minus 3.0 (26.6 F), and minus 0.3 (31.5 F) at a station opened in 1912 on 8 December 1934. Snow is extremely rare: the most recent fall was on 24 January 2016, the first in 87 years.

For a student, the practical advice is to pack for heat, humidity and rain for much of the year, and to bring a warm layer for the few cooler weeks in winter, as homes and classrooms are often not heated.

Guangzhou is the principal manufacturing hub of the Pearl River Delta, one of China's leading commercial and industrial regions. Its GDP in 2021 was about 2,823 billion yuan, US$444.37 billion at nominal rates, which made it the second-largest economy in South-Central China behind Shenzhen. GDP per head that year was about 151,162 yuan (US$23,794). The city is considered among the most prosperous in the country. By one 2020 wealth listing it ranked tenth in the world and fifth in China for the number of billionaires, and in the 2020 Global Financial Centers Index it placed 21st worldwide and eighth in Asia and Oceania. A forecast by Oxford Economics projected that it would be among the ten largest city economies in the world by 2035, with per-capita GDP above US$42,000 by 2030. Forecasts like these are uncertain, so read them as indications rather than promises.
Rapid industrial growth once left Guangzhou with serious pollution, but green urban planning has since improved conditions and the city is now regarded as one of the more liveable in China.

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: Business districts, trade fair and local products

blocks.x: Zhujiang New Town, in Tianhe District, is the city's twenty-first-century central business district. It covers about 6.44 square kilometres and is home to numerous financial institutions.

The Canton Fair, officially the China Import and Export Fair, takes place each April and October under the national trade ministry. First held in spring 1957, it is the oldest, highest-level and largest trade fair in the country. From its 104th session it moved from the older Liuhua complex to the new Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center in Pazhou. That venue is served by two stations on Metro Line 8, one on Line 11, and three on Tram Line THZ1. The fair now runs in three phases rather than two.

Guangzhou's local specialities include some of the best-known in China. Cantonese food has such a reputation that a local saying advises you to eat in Guangzhou. Craft traditions include Cantonese carving in jade and wood, Canton porcelain (which developed over about three centuries as an export ware and is noted for its bright colours), and Cantonese embroidery, counted among China's four main embroidery styles. Zhujiang Beer, a pale lager, is one of the more successful national brands.
Several zones anchor industry in the city:
GAC Group, a major automobile maker.
The Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone.

The Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone, founded in 2005, with a planned area of about 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 square miles). It lies in Nansha District, about 54 kilometres (34 miles, a 70-minute drive) south of Baiyun International Airport and close to Nansha Port, and Metro Line 4 is being extended towards the Nansha ferry terminal. Car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry are the encouraged sectors.

The Guangzhou Free Trade Zone, founded in 1992 in eastern Huangpu District near the development zone and also close to the airport. It focuses on international trade, logistics, processing and software, and newer sectors such as new energy, artificial intelligence, new mobility, new materials and information technology are being added. The area is now marketed under the Huangpu District name and is also home to the Guangzhou IP Court.
Guangzhou Science City.

The city is a hub for international business. By 2018 more than 30,000 foreign-invested companies had set up there, including projects from 297 Fortune Global 500 firms and regional or global headquarters of 120 of them. For a foreign-languages and trade student, this is a real advantage when looking for internships and early jobs.
At the end of 2024, Guangzhou had a permanent resident population of 18.978 million, and 87.24 percent of people lived in urban areas.

The seventh national census put the permanent population at 18,676,605 on 1 November 2020. That was 5,975,805 more (up 47.05 percent) than the 12,700,800 recorded in 2010. About 86.19 percent, or 16,096,724 people, lived in urban areas and 13.81 percent, or 2,579,881, in rural ones. Migration is central to the story. The census counted 11,522,907 people living somewhere other than where they are registered, including 9,378,825 in the floating population, which makes Guangzhou one of the country's biggest destinations for migrants. An earlier estimate of 13,080,500 for 2014 (with 11,264,800 of them urban residents, and a density of about 1,800 people per square kilometre) is older and not directly comparable, and about five million permanent residents were migrant workers in 2008.

The built-up urban area merges directly into neighbouring cities. The wider Pearl River Delta urban zone covers about 17,573 square kilometres and has been estimated to hold about 22 million people across Guangzhou's nine urban districts, Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890,000) and Huizhou's Huiyang District (760,000). Add Hong Kong and the total exceeds 28 million. The OECD estimated the metropolitan population at 25 million in 2010. Because of the area's labour demand, up to 10 million migrants may live in the region for at least six months of each year. Estimates differ with each source and date, so use the official statistics for current numbers.

Research on land use from 1990 to 2020 shows how the city has spread. In 1990 developed residential districts were mostly squeezed into a small part of western Guangzhou, with farmland and forest around them. From 2005 onwards housing development extended to other parts, and by 2020 built-up residential communities ran from west to east, while the far south and large parts of the north remained mainly farmland and forest.

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: Getting to Hong Kong and Macau, and faith in the city

blocks.x: High-speed catamarans run daily from the Nansha Ferry Terminal and the Lianhua Shan Ferry Terminal in Guangzhou to the Hong Kong China Ferry Terminal, and also from Nansha to the Macau ferry pier in Hong Kong. That is handy for weekend trips and visa runs.

Before modern times Guangzhou had about 124 temples, halls and religious pavilions. Today it has a Buddhist association and a Taoist association, a Jewish community, and a long history with Christianity, which was reintroduced to China through foreign powers.
Because the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does, here is a short history of Guangdong as a whole.

Human settlement here goes back a long way. The Neolithic period began in the Pearl River Delta about 7,000 years ago, with an early phase from about 7000 to 5000 years before present (roughly 5050-3050 BC) and a later one from about 5000 to 3500 (roughly 3050-1550 BC). On the coast, Neolithic practices probably came from the middle Yangtze region. Inland, the Neolithic appeared about 4,600 years ago, and the north is represented by the Shixia culture, dated roughly 4600 to 4200 years before present (about 2650-2250 BC).

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: From the Qin to the Ming

blocks.x: The area was originally home to a mix of peoples whom the Chinese called the Baiyue, or Hundred Yue. It first became part of China under the Qin dynasty, which brought regular administration and, with it, reliable records. After unifying the empire, Qin expanded south and created Nanhai Commandery at Panyu, near present-day Guangzhou. Between the fall of Qin and the reign of Emperor Wu of Han, an independent kingdom called Nanyue ruled the region. The Han then governed Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam as Jiaozhi Province, with its southern end serving as a gateway for merchants from as far away as the Roman Empire. In 226 CE, under the Wu kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period, Guangdong became its own province, Guang Province.

Canton was a prosperous port on a tropical frontier, rich in oranges, bananas, banyan trees and lychees. It traded silk and chinaware with Persian, Indian and Malay merchants, exchanging for medicines and fragrant woods. Muslims and Buddhists lived side by side, each building their own places of worship, and a foreign quarter formed along the river for traders of many backgrounds, including Arabs and Sinhalese. The port lost importance after a raid by Arab and Persian forces in 758.

In 627, under the Tang, Guangdong and Guangxi were joined as the Lingnan Circuit. In 971, under the Song (960-1279), the Guangdong part was renamed Guangnan East Circuit, and the word Guangdong comes from that name, meaning eastern Guang. It was given its present name early in the Ming.

The population gradually became predominantly Han Chinese through trade and state-organised settlement, which moved large numbers of soldiers, civilians and exiles south from the late third century BCE. After the Han fell, waves of migration from the north during periods of upheaval accelerated the change. One example is the unrest in the north around the An Lushan rebellion, which increased the population of Guangzhou prefecture by about 75 percent between the 740s-750s and the 800s-810s. Local peoples were gradually assimilated or moved aside.

In the thirteenth century, as the Mongols conquered China, the Southern Song court retreated south from Hangzhou. The Southern Song fell in 1279 when Mongol naval forces won the Battle of Yamen in Guangdong. During the Mongol Yuan dynasty much of Guangdong belonged to Jiangxi.

From the sixteenth century on, Guangdong had broad trade links overseas. European merchants, particularly Portuguese and British, sailed north via the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea and traded heavily through Guangzhou. Macau, on the southern coast, became the first European settlement in 1557.

In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, pirates, notably the Guangdong Pirate Confederation, plagued the coast around the Pearl River Delta until Portuguese naval forces and Qing forces together suppressed them. Later in the nineteenth century the opium trade through Guangzhou led to the First Opium War, which began an era of Western intervention. Macau was then a Portuguese colony, Hong Kong was ceded to Britain, and Kouang-Tchéou-Wan, in what is now the Zhanjiang area, went to France.

Many people left Guangdong, and emigration from Hong Kong to the wider British Empire was easy, so many overseas Chinese communities trace their roots to Guangdong or to Cantonese culture. Cantonese, Hakka and Teochew are therefore spoken by a larger share of overseas Chinese than Mandarin is. Many Taishanese speakers also went to Western countries, especially the United States, where a large number of Chinese Americans descend from migrants from Taishan, who speak a dialect related to Cantonese. As a result many Western words for Chinese things came through Cantonese rather than Mandarin, such as dim sum, and some foreign loanwords in Mandarin arrived via Cantonese too. The Mandarin word for lemon, níngméng, is one example.

In the 1850s the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, whose leader Hong Xiuquan was born in Guangdong and had come into contact with a Protestant missionary pamphlet there, allied itself with the local Red Turban Rebellion of 1854 to 1856. Direct contact with the West made Guangdong a centre of anti-Manchu and anti-imperialist activity, and Sun Yat-sen, widely regarded as the founder of modern China, was also from the province.

In 2024, Guangdong's population was 75.9 percent urban and 24.1 percent rural. Most people are Han Chinese, but the Han population is so varied that the province has been described as a treasure house of regional languages. The largest group within it are the Cantonese, with significant Hakka and Teoswa populations east of the Pearl River Delta. Small Mien, She, Hmong, Li and Zhuang minorities live there as well.

Studying at GDUFS puts you in a large, warm, humid, trade-minded city with a long history of contact with foreigners, strong food culture, easy links to Hong Kong and Macau, and many international companies. Daily life is likely to involve both Mandarin and Cantonese, so even a little Cantonese will go a long way. For the latest course, fee and campus details, always check the university's own website.

A few notes will help you interpret the figures above. Guangzhou's population is counted as permanent residents, meaning people who have lived in the city for an extended period, whether or not they hold local household registration. The floating population is the portion living away from their registered home, mostly migrant workers and students. Because the group is so large, you will meet people from all over China on campus and in the neighbourhoods around it, and you will hear a mixture of Mandarin, Cantonese and regional speech.

The climate classification Cwa simply means a warm, humid-subtropical zone with a wet summer and a drier winter. Combined with the monsoon months from April to September, it explains why umbrellas, light breathable clothes and dehumidifiers are everyday items in the city.

The economic figures are headline numbers that depend on the exchange rate and the year, and the wealth, financial-centre and forecast rankings come from outside organisations with their own methods. They are best used to judge scale and direction, not exact standing.

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: Planning your time in the region

blocks.x: Guangzhou's position inside the Pearl River Delta is a major benefit for students. The built-up area runs straight into Foshan, Dongguan, Shenzhen and other cities, so trips to nearby centres are easy, and ferries link the Nansha and Lianhua Shan terminals to Hong Kong and Macau. If you are choosing when to arrive, autumn gives the gentlest weather and the city's biggest trade event, the October session of the Canton Fair, is also in that season, though hotels can be busy then, so settle your accommodation early.

Language is part of the experience too. GDUFS is a foreign-languages specialist, so you will be among people who care about other languages, and the city itself has been a gateway for foreign traders for well over a thousand years. Learning a few phrases of Cantonese, the local language of the Cantonese people and of Cantonese food culture, will help you in markets and restaurants.
Guangdong University of Foreign Studies lists 130 programs for international students on this site: 53 bachelor, 44 master's, 9 doctoral, 24 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 127 taught in Chinese, 3 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 23,500 to CNY 35,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.

130 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

guangdong-university-of-foreign-studies.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guangdong University of Foreign Studies may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guangzhou, register at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Guangxi Medical University (GXMU) is located in Nanning, Guangxi, China and is one of the oldest higher education medical institutions in China. In 2010, the university was voted one of the top 20 universities in China for medicine study. Clinical medicine field by the university is categorized as world's top 1%, according to Thomson Reuters Web of Science Essential Science Indicators.

The university was established in Nanning, Guangxi on 21 November 1934 as the Guangxi Provincial Medical School (广西省立医学院), and the campus was moved to Guilin in November 1949, shortly after the establishment of the People's Republic of China.

Established in 1934, the university is one of the first universities in China to accept international students into its English-language medical education program, which is limited only to clinical medicine (临床医学). Foreign students on scholarship are required to study all their courses in Mandarin Chinese

The campus has a total area of 400,000 square meters, which includes teaching buildings and dormitories for Chinese students, international students and teaching staff, a library, food halls, an indoor tennis hall, a swimming pool and laboratories.

The campus is located near the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (广西医科大学一附院), which is the largest hospital in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, and the Institute of Dentistry (口腔学院).

There are nine five-year undergraduate programs offered by the Guangxi Medical University, including clinical medicine, preventive medicine, stomatology, pharmacy, nursing, dentistry, and seven three-year college specialties including nursing, pharmacy, community medical care and cosmetology.

International education has shown a rapid development since the university begin to accept international students, whether for language study or enrolling in clinical medicine program, which offers the MBBS title for undergraduate students. Most international students come from Vietnam, which is a one-hour bus ride from Nanning. Vietnamese students primarily attend Chinese-language classes. International students who attend the English-language classes come from India, Indonesia, Nepal, and Mauritius. Lately there are international students from Somalia, Yemen, Kenya, Nigeria, Namibia, Thailand, and Libya.
In September 2008, the clinical medicine in English program was altered as a six-year programme.

In the research field of Clinical Medicine, Guangxi Medical University ranks top 1% among institutions globally, according to Thomson Reuters Web of Science Essential Science Indicators. Clinical research papers by first or corresponding authors from Guangxi Medical University have been published in The New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Biotechnology, and Nature Genetics.
Temple University
Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Nanning, where Guangxi Medical University is located.

Nanning is home of the 22nd tallest building in the People's Republic of China, the Guangxi China Resources Tower, at 402.7 m (1,321 ft), currently the tallest building in Guangxi and in southwestern China outside of Chongqing.
Nanning has many parks with tropical lush green landscape, it is one of the "greenest" cities in China, and it's known as "Green City"(绿城).

Recently, the government has begun a citywide beautification plan which aimed to further clean up the city and improve its image. This involved curtailing the number of street-side food vendors operating without proper licenses and restricting parking in busy streets. The program has achieved initial success, long-term efforts are still needed to deliver lasting results.

Nanning's GDP in 2015 was 341 billion RMB. The GDP per capita was $7,844. Foreign exports in 2007 were US$10 billion. Foreign fixed asset investment was 34.3 billion RMB. Nanning has six development zones and industrial parks, three of which accounted for 6 billion RMB of Nanning's GDP, more than 8 percent of Nanning's total. Mineral resources include gold, iron, manganese, aluminum, quartz, silver, indium, coal, marble, and granite with a  third of China's different types of mineral resources  found in Nanning.
Nanning Economic & Technological Development Area

Nanning Metro system is known for its Nanning Rail Transit (NNRT), expected to comprise a total of nine lines. The first was completed and put into operation in June 2016, the second began operation in December 2017. Line 3 began operation in 2019, and Line 4 began operation in 2020. Line 1 connects the East and West of Nanning, linking the financial and political center and the academic and research center of Nanning.
Nanning Wuxu International Airport

Nanning has two major railway stations: Nanning railway station and Nanning East railway station. The latter one is newer and also the main destination of high-speed trains. A third, Nanning North railway station, is set to open in 2023 with the Guiyang–Nanning high-speed railway. Nanning railway station is a railway junction for the Nanning–Kunming, Nanning–Guangzhou and Hunan–Guangxi Railways. There are also plans to build a high-speed railway to Pingxiang on the Vietnamese border. The goal is to better integrate Pan-Pearl River Delta and southeast China with members of the ASEAN.

At the end of 2013, some high-speed service has been introduced on the Hunan–Guangxi railway and on the railway line that connects Nanning with Beihai (as well as its branch to Fangchenggang). Guangxi is also a conjunction of Guangzhou-Guiyang Highspeed Rail.
China National Highway 210
China National Highway 322
China National Highway 324
China National Highway 325
G72 Quanzhou–Nanning Expressway
G7201 Nanning Ring Expressway
G7211 Nanning–Youyiguan Expressway
G75 Lanzhou–Haikou Expressway
G80 Guangzhou–Kunming Expressway

Nanning is located in the southern part of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, 160 km (99 mi) from the border with Vietnam. It has an administrative area of 22,293 km2 (8,607 sq mi). Nanning is situated in a hilly basin with elevations between 70 and 500 m (230 and 1,640 ft) above sea-level. Qingxiu Mountain dominates the southern part of town.

Nanning has a warm, humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), It borders the subtropical monsoon climate (Köppen Cwa) with an annual mean temperature of 22.3 °C (72.1 °F). Summers are hot and humid with July, the hottest month, having a 24-hour average temperature of 28.5 °C (83.3 °F). Winters are mild and dry with January, the coolest month, averaging 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). From May to October, rain is most frequent and relative humidity consistently averages above 60 percent; the annual rainfall is 1,286 millimetres (50.6 in). The area is also frost-free for all but 3 or 4 days a year and snowfall is virtually unheard of in the city, with only two exceptions since 1900: in December 1975 and in January 2016 snow fell on the city albeit without sticking to the ground. Extreme temperatures have ranged from −2.1 to 40.4 °C (28 to 105 °F) on 12 January 1955 and May 9, 1958 respectively. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 15 percent in March to 51 percent in September, the city receives 1,579 hours of bright sunshine annually.

Nanning's warm climate gives it a large amount of biodiversity. There are many species of animals and more than 3,000 species of plants. The city flower is the Jaba flower, an evergreen shrub, and the city tree is the almond tree which is regarded as the backbone tree used for greening and landscaping throughout the city.

As of the 2020 Chinese census, Nanning had a population of 8,741,584, of which 5,293,359 live in its built-up (or metro) area made of 6 urban districts, Wuming District not being conurbated yet. Nanning is a city in which Zhuang ethnic group live in compact communities. Thirty-five ethnic groups live in compact communities in Nanning, including people of Zhuang, Han, Yao, Hui, Miao, Dong, and Man minorities.

Nanning is the center of science and technology, education, culture and health in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. There are altogether 54 scientific research institutes subordinate to districts. 10 colleges and 50 trade schools are training specialised personnel of all kinds. Now there are 62 mass cultural organizations, 13 performing groups, 8 cinemas, 285 projecting units, over 70 karaoke halls and over 1000 newsstands. Bookshops and cultural markets can be found everywhere.

Nanning has not only local cuisine but also food from other areas of China and abroad. Traditional food culture can be found around most streets of Nanning. Nanning food shares the style of Cantonese food and of Southeast Asia. Chinese cuisine including Guangdong, Sichuan, Hunan and Jiangsu as well as Japanese, Thai and Western cuisines can be found.

Rice noodles are very popular among the Nanning people. Laoyou rice noodles are the most famous, while other noodle dishes such as Guilin rice noodles and hand made noodles are popular. Laoyou rice noodles (means old friend rice noodles) are made of fry up pepper, sour bamboo shoots, black beans and garlic, then pork, and then soup and rice noodles. The sour-spicy tasting noodles are a very popular and cheap favorite street food for all meals (breakfast, lunch and dinner) in Nanning.
The dish, Lemon duck, is originally from Nanning.

Nanning is close to scenic Guilin, with its world-famous hillscape, northern and western Guangxi and its minority villages, and the border with Vietnam in the south. Tourist attractions in Nanning include Guangxi Museum, People's Park with the Zhenning Fort, Mount Qingxiu, Guangxi Medicinal Herb Botanical Garden, and Yangmei Ancient Town. Other places of interest include Nanhu Park, Shishan Park and Nanning Zoo.
Guangxi Medical University is in Guangxi, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Guangxi.

Originally inhabited by a mixture of tribal groups known to the Chinese as the Baiyue ("Hundred Yue", Vietnamese: Bách Việt), the region first became part of China during the Qin dynasty. In 214 BC, the Han Chinese general Zhao Tuo (Vietnamese: Triệu Đà) claimed most of southern China for Qin Shi Huang before the emperor's death. The ensuing civil war permitted Zhao to establish a separate kingdom at Panyu known as Nanyue ("Southern Yue"). Alternatively submissive to and independent of Han dynasty control, Southern Yue expanded colonization and sinicization under its policy of "Harmonizing and Gathering the Hundred Yue" (和集百越) until its collapse in 111 BC during the southward expansion of the Han dynasty.

The name "Guangxi" can be traced to the "Expansive" or "Wide" province (廣州) of the Eastern Wu, which controlled southeastern China during the Three Kingdoms period. Guilin formed one of its commanderies.

Under the Tang dynasty, the Zhuang moved to support Piluoge's kingdom of Nanzhao in Yunnan, which successfully repulsed imperial armies in 751 and 754. Guangxi was then divided into an area of Zhuang ascendancy west of Nanning and an area of Han ascendancy east of Nanning.

After the collapse of the Southern Zhao, Liu Yan established the Southern Han (Nanhan) in Xingwangfu (modern Guangdong). Although this state gained minimal control over Guangxi, it was plagued by instability and annexed by the Song dynasty in 971. The name "Guangxi" itself can be traced to the Song, who administered the area as the Guangnanxi ("West Southern Expanse") Circuit. Harassed by both Song and the Jiaozhi in modern Vietnam, the Zhuang leader Nong Zhigao led a revolt in 1052 for which he is still remembered by the Zhuang people. His independent kingdom was short-lived, however, and the tattooed Song general Di Qing returned Guangxi to China.

The Yuan dynasty established control over Yunnan during its conquest of the Dali Kingdom in 1253 and eliminated the Southern Song following the Battle of Yamen in 1279. Rather than ruling Lingnan as a subject territory or military district, the Mongolians then established Guangxi ("Western Expanse") as a proper province. The area nonetheless continued to be unruly, leading the Ming dynasty to employ the different local groups against one another. At the Battle of Big Rattan Gorge between the Zhuang and the Yao in 1465, 20,000 deaths were reported.
During the Ming and Qing dynasties, parts of Guangxi were ruled by the powerful Cen (岑) clan. The Cen were of Zhuang ethnicity and were recognized as tusi or local rulers by the Chinese emperors.

The Qing dynasty left the region alone until the imposition of direct rule in 1726, but the 19th century was one of constant unrest. A Yao revolt in 1831 was followed by the Jintian Uprising, the beginning of the Taiping Rebellion, in January 1851 and the Da Cheng Rebellion in April 1854. The execution of St. Auguste Chapdelaine by local officials in Guangxi provoked the Second Opium War in 1858 and the legalization of foreign interference in the interior. Although Louis Brière de l'Isle was unable to invade its depot at Longzhou, the Guangxi Army saw a great deal of action in the 1884 Sino-French War. Largely ineffective within Vietnam, it was still able to repulse the French from China itself at the Battle of Zhennan Pass (modern Friendship Pass) on 23 March 1885.

Following the Wuchang Uprising, Guangxi seceded from the Qing Empire on 6 November 1911. The Qing governor, Shen Bingdan, initially remained in place but was subsequently removed by a mutiny commanded by General Lu Rongting. General Lu's Old Guangxi clique overran Hunan and Guangdong as well and helped lead the National Protection War against Yuan Shikai's attempt to re-establish an imperial government. Zhuang's loyalty made his Self-Government Army cohesive but reluctant to move far beyond its own provinces. Subsequent feuding with Sun Yat-sen led to defeat in the 1920 and 1921 Guangdong–Guangxi War. After a brief occupation by Chen Jiongming's Cantonese forces, Guangxi fell into disunity and profound banditry for several years until Li Zongren's Guangxi Pacification Army established the New Guangxi clique dominated by Li, Huang Shaohong, and Bai Chongxi.

Successful action in Hunan against Wu Peifu led to the Zhuang GPA becoming known as the "Flying Army" and the "Army of Steel". After the death of Sun Yat-sen, Li also repulsed Tang Jiyao's revolt and joined the Northern Expedition establishing control over other warlords by the Republic of China. His was one of the few Kuomintang units free from serious Chinese Communist Party (CCP) influence and was therefore employed by Chiang Kai-shek for the Shanghai massacre of 1927. Within the People's Republic of China, Guangxi is also noted for the Baise Uprising, a failed CCP revolt led by Chen Zhaoli and Deng Xiaoping in 1929.

In 1937, the Guangxi Women's Battalion was founded as a response to Soong Mei-ling's appeal for women to support the Sino-Japanese War. Reports on the size of the battalion vary from 130 students, to 500, to 800.
Being in the far south, Guangxi did not fall during the Chinese Civil War, but joined the People's Republic in December 1949, two months after its founding.

In 1952, a small section of Guangdong's coastline (Qinzhou,  Lianzhou (now Hepu County), Fangchenggang and Beihai) was given to Guangxi, giving it access to the sea. This was reversed in 1955, and then restored in 1965. This made Guangxi the only autonomous region which is not landlocked.
The Guangxi Massacre, during the Cultural Revolution, involved the killing of 100,000 to 150,000 in the region in 1967 and 1968.

While some development of heavy industry occurred in the 1960s and 1970s, the region remained largely a scenic tourist destination. Even the economic growth of the 1990s seemed to leave Guangxi behind. However, in recent years, there has been a growing amount of industrialization and increasing concentration on cash crops. Per capita GDP has risen as industries in Guangdong transfer production to comparatively lower-wage areas in Guangxi.

During the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War, Guangxi communities were important to the Chinese war effort. They supplied logistical support to the People's Liberation Army, including food and housing. Militia members from Guangxi performed tasks including building roads, bridges, trenches, other logistical efforts, and caring for the wounded.

Located in the southern part of the country, Guangxi is bordered by Yunnan to the west, Guizhou to the north, Hunan to the northeast, and Guangdong to the east and southeast. It is also bordered by Vietnam in the southwest and the Gulf of Tonkin in the south. Its proximity to Guangdong is reflected in its name, with "Guang" (simplified Chinese: 广; traditional Chinese: 廣; pinyin: Guǎng) being used in both names.

Large portions of Guangxi are hilly and mountainous. The northwest portion of Guangxi includes part of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, the Jiuwan Mountains and the Fenghuang Mountains both run through the north, the Nanling Mountains form the region's north-east border, and the Yuecheng and Haiyang Mountains both branch from the Nanling Mountains. Also in the north are the Duyao Mountains. The Duyang Mountains run through the west of Guangxi. Near the center of the region are the Da Yao and Da Ming Mountains. On the southeastern border are the Yunkai Mountains. Guangxi's highest point is Kitten Mountain, in the Yuecheng Mountains, at 2,141 metres (7,024 ft).
Karst landforms, characterized by steep mountains and large caverns, are common in Guangxi, accounting for 37.8 percent of its total land area.

Guangxi is also home to several river systems, which flow into several different bodies of water: the Qin River and the Nanliu River both flow into the Gulf of Tonkin, several tributary rivers flow into the larger Xiang River in neighbouring Hunan province, and the Xi River system flows southeast through the autonomous region into the South China Sea.
Along the border with Vietnam there is the Ban Gioc–Detian waterfall (pinyin: Dé Tiān Pùbù), which separates the two countries.
About one-quarter of Guangxi's area is forested.
Guangxi has 7 airports in different cities: Nanning, Guilin, Beihai, Liuzhou, Wuzhou, Baise, and Hechi.

Guangxi is highly linguistically diverse. Aside from Chinese languages such as Guiliu Mandarin and Yue Chinese, Guangxi is also home to significant Zhuang, Kam, Mulam, Maonan, Hmong, Mien, Bunu, Lajia, Sui, Gelao, Nuosu, and Vietnamese (Kinh) speaking populations.

guangxi-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guangxi Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanning, register at Guangxi Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

guangxi-minzu-university.h: A university built for many peoples

blocks.x: Guangxi Minzu University, abbreviated GXMZU, is a provincial research university in Nanning, the capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Its Chinese name is 广西民族大学 (廣西民族大學 in traditional characters), and in the Zhuang language it is Gvangjsih Minzcuz Dayoz. The institution opened in 1952 with a mission of serving the minority populations of Guangxi, and ethnology and foreign languages remain its historic strengths.

Originally a branch of the Central Institute for Nationalities, it grew into a free-standing university. Today it awards bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees and is organised into 26 colleges, departments and professional schools.

The student community is unusually diverse. About half of the roughly 16,000 students belong to an ethnic minority, and 53 of China's 55 officially recognised minority groups are represented, among them the Zhuang, Miao, Yao and Yi. Over 1,000 international students also study here. The College of International Education and partnerships with institutions across Southeast and South Asia help to draw them in, and the number of foreign students is growing.

The beginning was in 1952, when a Guangxi branch of the Central Institute for Nationalities (now called Minzu University of China) opened. In 1953 the branch gained independence as the Guangxi Provincial Institute for Nationalities. Five years later, in 1958, a new name followed: Guangxi College for Nationalities.
In 2006 China's Ministry of Education approved the university's request to take its present name, Guangxi Minzu University.

Doctoral study is newer. Approval to award doctorates came in 2013, covering ethnology, foreign languages and literature, and Chinese language and literature. The first doctoral cohort was admitted a year later, in 2014.
Overall, more than 200,000 students have graduated from the institution. Half of them belong to recognised ethnic minority groups, and the total includes 12,000 international students.

Around 16,000 students are enrolled, and undergraduates choose from 33 majors that run from the arts and economics through to the sciences and engineering. (Some descriptions use the short form "Guangxi Minda" for the university.)

GXMZU has developed into a national research centre for the study of nationalities and their cultures, with particular attention to the ethnic groups of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region and of Southeast Asian countries. It also keeps long-term cooperative ties with local enterprises, so that new research results and technologies can be turned into industrial use.

The university describes its approach as three-sided, summed up in the Chinese phrase "民族性、区域性、国际性": national, regional and international. It has exchange and cooperation partnerships, both academic and cultural, with 137 educational institutions in 17 countries.

Confucius Institutes are an important part of this effort. The university is the host institution for institutes in three neighbouring countries: at Mahasarakham University (Thailand), at the National University of Laos (Vientiane), and at Tanjungpura University (Indonesia).

The university is also one of a group of institutions permitted to receive international students who hold Confucius Institute Scholarships, which are awarded by the Hanban government agency. A further partnership with the Thai Ministry of Education covers training in the Thai language for foreign-language teaching.
For a student, this means a long record of working with Southeast Asia, a good fit if you are interested in the region, in Chinese language, or in the cultures of China's southern borderlands.

guangxi-minzu-university.h: Nanning, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Much of student life depends on the city, so the next sections describe Nanning, then the wider region of Guangxi.

Nanning has the Guangxi China Resources Tower, 402.7 m (1,321 ft) high. That makes it the tallest building in Guangxi and in southwestern China outside Chongqing, and 22nd tallest in the People's Republic.
The city has many parks full of lush tropical greenery. It is counted among China's "greenest" cities and is known as the "Green City" (绿城).

A citywide beautification plan introduced in recent years aims to clean up Nanning and improve its image. It has involved cutting down on street food sellers who work without proper licences and restricting parking in busy streets. Early results are positive, but longer-term effort is still needed.

On the economic side, Nanning's 2015 GDP was 341 billion RMB, equal to $7,844 per head. Exports in 2007 were worth US$10 billion, and 34.3 billion RMB of fixed asset investment came from abroad. There are six development zones and industrial parks, and in three of them output was 6 billion RMB, above 8 percent of the city's GDP. Minerals found locally include marble, granite, quartz, coal, gold, silver, iron, manganese, aluminum and indium, and it is said that a third of the kinds of mineral resource found in China occur here. These figures date from several years ago, so look for more recent data if they matter to you.
The industrial zone most often named is the Nanning Economic and Technological Development Area.
#### Metro

The Nanning Rail Transit (NNRT) is the city's metro, and it was expected to have nine lines in all. Line 1 opened in June 2016 and Line 2 in December 2017, with Line 3 following in 2019 and Line 4 in 2020. Line 1 links the east and west of Nanning, joining the financial and political centre with the academic and research centre. Since these details were written, more of the network may have opened, so check the current map.
#### Air
Nanning Wuxu International Airport serves the city.
#### Trains

Two major railway stations serve the city: Nanning railway station, and the newer Nanning East, where high-speed trains mainly arrive. A third, Nanning North, was due to open in 2023 alongside the Guiyang-Nanning high-speed railway, so confirm whether it is now in service. Nanning railway station connects the Nanning-Kunming, Nanning-Guangzhou and Hunan-Guangxi lines. A high-speed line to Pingxiang, on the Vietnamese border, has also been planned, with the goal of bringing the Pan-Pearl River Delta and southeast China closer to ASEAN countries.

Some high-speed service started at the close of 2013, on the Hunan-Guangxi railway and on the line from Nanning to Beihai (including its branch to Fangchenggang). The region is likewise a junction for the Guangzhou-Guiyang high-speed rail line.
#### Roads
The main roads and expressways include:
G80 Guangzhou-Kunming Expressway
G75 Lanzhou-Haikou Expressway
G72 Quanzhou-Nanning Expressway
G7211 Nanning-Youyiguan Expressway
G7201 Nanning Ring Expressway
China National Highway 210
China National Highway 322
China National Highway 324
China National Highway 325

Nanning is in southern Guangxi, 160 km (99 mi) from the Vietnamese border, and has an administrative area of 22,293 km2 (8,607 sq mi). The land is a hilly basin, rising from 70 to 500 m (230 to 1,640 ft), and Qingxiu Mountain dominates the south of town.

The climate is humid subtropical and warm (Köppen Cfa), bordering on the subtropical monsoon type (Köppen Cwa), and the yearly mean temperature is 22.3 °C (72.1 °F). Hot, humid summers peak in July, when the 24-hour average is 28.5 °C (83.3 °F). January is the coolest month but still mild, averaging 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), and winters are dry.

Rain is heaviest from May to October, when humidity stays above 60 percent, and 1,286 millimetres (50.6 in) falls in a year. Frost occurs on only 3 or 4 days a year. Snow is virtually unheard of: it has fallen just twice since 1900, in December 1975 and January 2016, and it did not settle. Temperature has ranged from −2.1 °C (28 °F), on 12 January 1955, to 40.4 °C (105 °F), on 9 May 1958. Possible sunshine is lowest in March at 15 percent and highest in September at 51 percent, and the city gets 1,579 hours of bright sun each year.

Warm weather gives Nanning rich biodiversity, with many kinds of animals and over 3,000 species of plants. Its official flower is the jaba, an evergreen shrub, and the almond tree is the city tree, used widely as the backbone of greenery and landscaping.

The 2020 census recorded 8,741,584 residents in Nanning, with 5,293,359 of them in the built-up (metro) area covering 6 urban districts; Wuming District has not yet merged into the urban area. Zhuang people live in tight-knit communities in the city, and so do members of 34 other ethnic groups, among them Han, Yao, Hui, Miao, Dong and Man people.

Nanning acts as the regional hub for health, education, culture, and science and technology. Its districts run 54 scientific research institutes, while 10 colleges and 50 trade schools train specialist staff. For leisure there are 62 mass cultural organizations and 13 performing groups, 8 cinemas with 285 projecting units, more than 70 karaoke halls and over 1000 newsstands, and bookshops and cultural markets are everywhere.

The city's food reflects both local traditions and dishes from elsewhere in China and abroad. Nanning cooking is close to Cantonese style and to Southeast Asian styles, and you can find Guangdong, Sichuan, Hunan and Jiangsu cuisines, as well as Japanese, Thai and Western food. Traditional food culture can be found on most streets.

Rice noodles are a firm favourite. Laoyou noodles, whose name means "old friend", are the best known. They are made by frying pepper, sour bamboo shoots, garlic and black beans, adding pork, and then pouring in broth and rice noodles. The flavour is sour and spicy, the price is low, and people eat them at any meal, mostly on the street. Hand-made noodles and Guilin rice noodles are popular too, and lemon duck is a dish that began in Nanning.

Within the city, sights include the Guangxi Museum, People's Park with Zhenning Fort, Mount Qingxiu, Yangmei Ancient Town and the Guangxi Medicinal Herb Botanical Garden, with Nanhu Park, Shishan Park and Nanning Zoo as other places of interest. Guilin, famous for its hill scenery, is close, and so are the minority villages of the north and west of the region; the Vietnamese border is to the south.
The region around a university matters as much as the campus, and Guangxi has a long and eventful past. The next sections cover its history and geography.

Early inhabitants were a mix of tribal peoples whom the Chinese called the Baiyue, or "Hundred Yue". The Qin dynasty brought the area into China. In 214 BC a Han Chinese general, Zhao Tuo, claimed most of the south for Qin Shi Huang, and after the emperor died, civil war allowed Zhao to found his own kingdom, Nanyue ("Southern Yue"), with Panyu as its centre. Nanyue alternately accepted and resisted Han control. Its policy was called "Harmonizing and Gathering the Hundred Yue" (和集百越), and it spread settlement and Chinese culture until Han forces advancing south ended it in 111 BC.

One origin of the name Guangxi is the Eastern Wu, which held southeastern China during the Three Kingdoms and had a province called "Expansive" or "Wide" (廣州); Guilin was a commandery within it. During the Tang dynasty the Zhuang supported Piluoge's kingdom of Nanzhao in Yunnan, which defeated imperial armies in 751 and 754. Guangxi was then divided between a Zhuang-dominated area to the west of Nanning and a Han-dominated area to the east.

After Nanzhao fell, Liu Yan founded the Southern Han, centred on Xingwangfu in modern Guangdong. Its hold over Guangxi was slight and it was unstable, and the Song annexed it in 971. Song officials gave the area its enduring name by organising it as a circuit called Guangnanxi ("West Southern Expanse"). A Zhuang leader, Nong Zhigao, rose in revolt in 1052 and is still remembered by the Zhuang people, but his independent kingdom did not last, and the Song brought Guangxi back under Chinese control.

The Mongol Yuan dynasty took Yunnan by defeating the Dali Kingdom in 1253, and it finished off the Southern Song after the Battle of Yamen in 1279. Instead of governing Lingnan as a dependent territory or a military district, the Mongols created Guangxi ("Western Expanse") as a full province. Even so, unrest continued and the Ming dynasty played local groups off against one another; 20,000 deaths were reported from the 1465 Battle of Big Rattan Gorge, fought between the Zhuang and the Yao.

Through the Ming and Qing periods, the Cen (岑) clan, a powerful Zhuang family recognised by the emperors as local rulers (tusi), governed parts of Guangxi. The Qing mostly left the region alone until they imposed direct rule in 1726.

guangxi-minzu-university.h: The nineteenth and early twentieth centuries

blocks.x: Unrest was constant in 19th-century Guangxi. A Yao revolt broke out in 1831, the Jintian Uprising of January 1851 marked the start of the Taiping Rebellion, and the Da Cheng Rebellion began in April 1854. In 1858 the Second Opium War was provoked in part by local officials executing St. Auguste Chapdelaine, and the war legalised foreign involvement inland. The Guangxi Army fought heavily in the Sino-French War of 1884. It was largely ineffective in Vietnam but drove the French out of China at Zhennan Pass (today's Friendship Pass) on 23 March 1885.

The Wuchang Uprising was followed by a declaration of independence from the Qing Empire, which Guangxi made on 6 November 1911. A mutiny under General Lu Rongting soon removed the governor Shen Bingdan, who had at first stayed on. Lu's Old Guangxi clique extended its reach into Hunan and Guangdong and helped lead the National Protection War, which opposed Yuan Shikai's attempt to restore an imperial government. A quarrel with Sun Yat-sen ended in defeat in the Guangdong-Guangxi War of 1920 and 1921, and Chen Jiongming's Cantonese forces briefly occupied the region. Guangxi then fell into disunity and widespread banditry for some years, until the Guangxi Pacification Army under Li Zongren set up the New Guangxi clique, run by Li together with Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi.

Two other episodes belong to the 20th century. The Baise Uprising of 1929, led by Chen Zhaoli and Deng Xiaoping, was a Chinese Communist Party revolt that failed, and the Guangxi Women's Battalion formed in 1937 after Soong Mei-ling called on women to help in the war with Japan. Reported figures for the battalion's size differ: 130 students, 500 or 800.
As the region lies in the far south, it never fell during the Chinese Civil War. In December 1949, two months after the founding of the People's Republic, Guangxi joined it.

The coast has moved between provinces. A stretch of Guangdong's shoreline covering Qinzhou, Lianzhou (now Hepu County), Fangchenggang and Beihai was handed to Guangxi in 1952, so the region gained a seaport. It was returned in 1955 and restored in 1965, which is why Guangxi is the only autonomous region with a coastline. In 1967 and 1968, during the Cultural Revolution, between 100,000 and 150,000 people in the region were killed in an event known as the Guangxi Massacre.

Some heavy industry developed in the 1960s and 1970s, but the region stayed mostly a scenic destination for tourists, and it appeared to miss out on the growth of the 1990s. Recently there has been more industrialisation and a growing emphasis on cash crops. GDP per person has risen because Guangdong's industries are shifting production to areas of Guangxi where wages are lower.

Guangxi communities played an important part in China's war effort in 1979, during the Sino-Vietnamese War. They gave the People's Liberation Army logistical support such as food and housing, and militia members built roads, bridges and trenches and cared for wounded soldiers.

Guangxi is in the south of the country. It borders Yunnan on the west, Guizhou on the north, Hunan on the northeast, and Guangdong on the east and southeast, with Vietnam to the southwest and the Gulf of Tonkin to the south. The name shares the character "Guang" (广 in simplified form, 廣 in traditional form, pinyin Guǎng) with Guangdong, which reflects how close the two are.

Much of Guangxi is hilly or mountainous. Part of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau lies in the northwest, and the Jiuwan, Fenghuang and Duyao Mountains are in the north. The Nanling Mountains form the northeastern border, with the Yuecheng and Haiyang ranges branching away from them. In the west run the Duyang Mountains, near the middle are the Da Yao and Da Ming ranges, and the Yunkai Mountains sit on the southeastern edge. The top of the region is Kitten Mountain, in the Yuecheng range: 2,141 metres, or 7,024 ft.

Karst scenery, meaning steep hills and big caves, is common here and makes up 37.8 percent of the land. Rivers drain in different directions: the Nanliu and Qin Rivers empty into the Gulf of Tonkin, several tributaries flow to the Xiang River in Hunan, and the Xi River system crosses the region toward the southeast and the South China Sea. On the Vietnamese border, the Ban Gioc-Detian waterfall marks the line between the two countries, and roughly a quarter of the region is forested.
Seven cities have airports: Baise, Beihai, Guilin, Hechi, Liuzhou, Nanning and Wuzhou.
