Guangxi Normal University (广西师范大学, Guǎngxī shīfàn dàxué, often shortened to GXNU) sits in Guilin, in the Guangxi region of southern China. It is a provincial research university which has long been strong in teacher education, the arts and sciences, and international exchange programmes. One of its campuses is built around the Jingjiang Princes' Palace, a Ming Dynasty complex dating from 1372.

Founded in 1932, it was among the first normal schools (teacher-training institutions) in China. It has since grown into a comprehensive university that awards bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees through 21 colleges and departments and offers 75 undergraduate majors. In research terms, its chemistry department ranks in the global top 1% in the 2017 InCites Essential Science Indicators (ESI) from Thomson Reuters, a ranking based on how often published papers are cited.

guangxi-normal-university.h: The first teacher's college and its merger

blocks.x: The story starts in 1932 with the Guangxi Provincial Teacher's College, which was Guangxi's first teacher-training school and one of the earliest in China. Its first president was the well-known educator Yang Dongyu (杨东莼). The original site was in Guilin's Yanshan District, where the university still keeps a branch campus.

Very soon the young school was caught in a tug of war between the Nationalist Ministry of Education and the provincial government of Guangxi. The result was decades of renaming, absorption and re-founding. In 1936 the provincial government ordered it to join National Guangxi University, today's Guangxi University and the flagship public university of the region. It became that university's College of Liberal Arts, concentrating on the humanities and no longer acting purely as a teacher-training school.

guangxi-normal-university.h: Separation, moves and a second merger

blocks.x: By 1941 Guangxi needed more schoolteachers, so the college was split off from Guangxi University and rebuilt as the independent Guangxi Teacher's College. In 1942 it was renamed Guangxi Guilin Teacher's College, and a year later National Guilin Teacher's College. In February 1946 it relocated to Nanning as National Nanning Teacher's College.

In February 1950 it returned to Guilin. This time National Guangxi University absorbed it for a second time, and it was known as the Teacher's College of National Guangxi University, or the College of Culture and Education. It continued to work as a teacher-training school.

In 1953 the People's Republic began reorganising higher education across the country. In July of that year the Ministry of Education ordered the teacher-training school to be re-established on its own as Guangxi Teacher's College. To help the new school start, Guangxi University transferred 53 professors, taken from the Chinese, foreign language, history, mathematics, physics and chemistry departments, along with 256 staff who belonged to the College of Culture and Education and, in many cases, had taught at the original provincial college.

Once it was independent again, Guilin's historic Jingjiang Princes' Palace became its Wangcheng Campus. Up to 1978 no other Guangxi institution of higher education could grant bachelor's degrees in teacher education. In 1981 it received the right to grant master's degrees. On 29 May 1983 it became Guangxi Normal University, and it awarded its first doctoral degrees in 2006.

In 2018 enrolment stood at 26,831 undergraduates, 6,386 graduates and 171 doctoral candidates. More than 1,600 international students are enrolled across all degree levels. On top of that, 16,000 people study through correspondence, online or visiting arrangements.
Colleges and departments run massive open online courses. One of them looks at the lives and work of Tang Dynasty poets connected to the historical Guangxi region.

GXNU has 22 academic disciplines recognised as Guangxi Key Disciplines, which means the programmes are of high quality by the standards of Guangxi universities. It also operates 11 Experimental Teaching Demonstration Centers.

Between 2011 and 2015 the university won 317 national-level research projects. In total it funded 2,122 research projects, with research spending of 403 million yuan, and its staff published 3,919 journal articles. Provincial and municipal prizes numbered 139, covering the Guangxi Social Science Award, the Guangxi Natural Science Award and the Guangxi Science and Technology Progress Award. The university also hosts a State Key Laboratory of Joint Construction, which it established with the Chinese Ministry of Education.

Two journals come from the university. One is the Natural Sciences Edition of the Journal of Guangxi Normal University, which appears in the national Chinese Core Journals Overview; the other is its Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition. In the same 2011 to 2015 period it hosted 9 international and national conferences, on subjects ranging across inorganic chemistry, wildlife ecology and resource conservation.

Three main libraries serve the Wangcheng, Yucai and Yanshan campuses. The Yanshan one is the largest library in the Guangxi autonomous region. As of 2016, printed holdings across the university's libraries topped 3,260,000 books, and 82 databases give access to 2,226,653 e-books and other digital resources.

International exchange is central to GXNU. Within the Guangxi autonomous region, it is the sole university that the Ministry of Education has designated an official "demonstration base" for trial international student programmes, which makes teaching overseas students part of its core mission. Programmes in Chinese language and at undergraduate, graduate and doctoral level bring more than 1,600 international students to the campuses.

Some funding routes are worth knowing about. GXNU is among the Chinese universities that host holders of a Chinese Government Scholarship granted by the Ministry of Education, or a Confucius Institute Scholarship that the agency Hanban funds. It also takes students who hold the ASEAN Scholarship given by the Guangxi provincial government.

The university has cooperation programmes with more than 200 institutions in 40 countries, including Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman in Malaysia. Three Confucius Institutes are run by GXNU abroad: at Hanoi University in neighbouring Vietnam, at Indonesia's State University of Malang, and at Prince of Songkla University in Thailand.

With so many international students, the university marks foreign holidays every year, among them Christmas, Halloween and Songkran, and holds its own International Cultural Festival and a Foreign Language Karaoke Contest. The calendar also has an Indonesia Culture Day in May and an International Student-Parent Conference in June; on 20 November every year the university celebrates Teacher's Day together with Vietnamese Culture Day.

In mid-April comes the International Cultural Festival, featuring cultural shows, student games, parades and food exhibitions built around Burmese, Cambodian, Lao and Thai culture. It centres on the international students, but every student may take part.
GXNU has three campuses within the city of Guilin. Shuttle buses arranged by the university link them, and so does the local number 98 public bus.

Wangcheng is the main campus. It stands on the site of the Jingjiang Princes' Palace, which locals call Wangcheng, a royal complex from the Ming dynasty (roughly 1372 to 1392). Zhu Shouqian, the Prince of Jingjiang, was the original resident of the walled palace. Over the Ming and Qing dynasties it housed 14 kings from 12 generations, and Sun Yat-sen stayed in one of its mansions in 1921.

No other university campus has earned the 5A rating of the China National Tourism Administration. Inside are the old Chengyun gate, opening onto the Prince's Mansion; next the ancient Guoxue Hall, now occupied by the School of Chinese Civilization; and, finally, Solitary Beauty Peak, the tallest rock formation in Guilin, with views across the city and countryside. The best-preserved Ming city wall in China surrounds the complex.

guangxi-normal-university.h: Yucai Campus: parkland near Seven Star Park

blocks.x: The Yucai Campus lies in eastern Guilin beside Seven Star Park. It mixes open green space with teaching buildings and dormitories, and it dates from 1976. Buildings of note are the Shaw Building, used for teacher training and funded by a donation from Hong Kong entertainment figure and philanthropist Run Run Shaw, and the Yucai Campus Library, one of the oldest and biggest in Guangxi. There is also an apartment block for international students and a monument to the friendship between Chinese and Vietnamese students.

guangxi-normal-university.h: Yanshan Campus: sports and the big library

blocks.x: Yanshan opened in 2007. Here you find the university's sports facilities and the Yanshan Campus Library, the largest in the autonomous region. Confucius Square on this campus is the setting for annual events marking Confucius' birthday, ancient Chinese civilisation, Chinese New Year and ethnic food festivals. The canteen specialises in Zhuang and other local dishes.
Alumni include these people:
Wang Yungui, an entrepreneur and businesswoman born in 1992
Liu Dingxin, a major general of the People's Liberation Army (1913 to 1997)
Mo Hua, born 1964, who once served as Party Secretary of Yulin
Peng Xiaochun, born 1961, a one-time vice chairman of the Guangxi CPPCC
Where you study shapes your daily routine as much as the campus, so the next sections look at Guilin, the home of GXNU: its climate, transport and character.

Guilin lies in northern Guangxi. Its neighbours inside Guangxi are Liuzhou (west), Laibin (southwest), Wuzhou (south) and Hezhou (southeast). In Hunan, across the provincial boundary, lie Huaihua in the northwest, Shaoyang in the north and Yongzhou in the east. Its total area is 27,809 square kilometres, or 10,737 sq mi.

The land here is dominated by karst, the dramatic limestone landscape. The karst around Guilin comes from Triassic limestone and dolomite. The Li River is one of the most admired features, flowing 83 km from Guilin to Yangshuo with emerald water and limestone peaks, a stretch that is a concentrated showcase of karst terrain.
Hills and mountains in the area:
Diecai Hill (叠彩山)
Elephant Trunk Hill
Wave-Subduing Hill (伏波山)
Lipu Mountains
Kitten Mountain, the highest peak in Guangxi
Yao Hill (尧山)
Caves worth a visit:
Reed Flute Cave
Seven-star Cave

Guilin has a humid subtropical climate influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Cfa, bordering on Cwa). Winters are brief and mild; summers are long, hot and muggy. Winter begins dry and slowly gets wetter and cloudier. Spring is mostly overcast and often rainy. Summer stays rainy but is also the sunniest season, and autumn is sunny and dry.

January averages 8.1 °C (46.6 °F) and July 28.2 °C (82.8 °F); the year as a whole averages 19.12 °C (66.4 °F). Guilin gets a little under 1,890 mm (74 in) of rain a year,, and roughly half arrives between April and June in the plum rain season, which often brings flood risk. March is the least sunny month with 14% of possible sunshine, and September the sunniest at 53%, giving 1,487 hours of bright sunshine a year. Since 1951 the extremes have been -4.9 °C (23 °F) and 40.3 °C (105 °F), although on 25 January 1940 an unofficial reading went down to -5.0 °C (23 °F).

A population of 4,931,137 was recorded in the 2020 national census. Of those, 2,148,641 were living in the metro area, made up of six urban districts and Lingchuan County, which has now become part of the conurbation. The 2010 census found Han Chinese to be the largest group in the prefecture-level city, with 84.53%, next come the Yao with 7.79% and the Zhuang with 4.81%.

Residents of the urban area speak a Mandarin dialect, but out in the suburbs and surrounding districts Pinghua is the main language. The resident population at the close of 2024 was given as 4,950,700.

GDP per capita was ¥41891 (about US$6569) in 2020, placing Guilin 134th among 659 Chinese cities. Factories and workshops in Guilin make pharmaceutical goods, condoms, tires, machinery and fertilizer, as well as silk, perfume, wine, tea, cinnamon and herbal medicine. Farm products and local foods run from grain, fish and water chestnut to Lipu Taro, moon persimmon, ginkgo, summer orange, Shatian Pomelo and Fructus Momordicae, with pepper sauce, fermented bean curd, Sanhua Alcohol, Guilin Rice Noodle and tightly rolled dried bean milk cream among the prepared items.

guangxi-normal-university.h: From little industry to a mixed economy

blocks.x: Before 1949 Guilin had just a few signs of industry: some small textile mills, a cement works and a thermal power plant. From the 1950s onward the city added electronics, engineering, agricultural equipment, medicine, rubber, buses, textiles and cotton yarn. Food processing, including the handling of local crops, is still the leading industry. Newer enterprises are high-tech, while the services side is built on tourism, trading and other services.
Tourists from ASEAN states can enter Guilin without a visa, provided they travel in a tour group and stay no longer than 144 hours, with the day of arrival not counted.
The city's airport is Guilin Liangjiang International Airport, with the codes ZGKL (ICAO) and KWL (IATA). Airlines serving it include:
China Eastern
Asiana Airlines
China Southern
Air China
Hainan Airlines
Shanghai Airlines
Shandong Airlines
Xiamen Airlines
Tianjin Airlines
EVA Air
Air Asia
Beijing Capital Airlines
Hebei Airlines

High-speed rail serves Guilin through Guilin North, Guilin West and the main Guilin station, and a new station has appeared in Lingui District. The Guiyang-Guangzhou high-speed railway, the Hengyang-Liuzhou intercity railway and the Hunan-Guangxi railway all pass through the main Guilin station and Guilin North, and together they are the principal links between Guangxi and central and southern China.

High-speed trains to Changsha and Beijing began running into North Station in December 2013, and in December 2014 services opened to Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Guiyang and Shanghai, which made travel to Guilin much easier. From Guangzhou the journey is only around 2 or 3 hours, from Shanghai 9 hours and from Beijing 13 hours. A service between Kunming South and West Kowloon, among others, calls at Guilin West.

Buses and taxis make up local public transport. Guilin leads mainland China in regularly operating double-decker buses on major routes; on the main street they pass one after another almost every minute. Sightseeing boats also operate on the city's canals and lakes.

Plans for a Guilin Metro call for 7 lines, 117 stations and 273.2 kilometres of track by 2040. Line 1 was planned to open by 2025, at 29.23 km with 13 stations. As plans like these can slip, check the latest position before relying on the metro.

Local cooking blends Cantonese and Zhuang traditions, and it is known for snacks and for generous use of spices, chili above all. Guilin chili sauce (桂林辣椒酱) is a kitchen staple made from fresh chili, garlic and fermented soybeans. It ranks among the Three Treasures of the city (桂林三宝), together with Guilin pickled tofu and Guilin Sanhua Jiu (桂林三花酒), a baijiu spirit distilled from rice.

Rice noodles have been the usual local breakfast since the Qin dynasty and are famed for their delicate taste. Legend says that when Qin soldiers with stomach trouble marched into the area, a cook invented the noodles for the army because the men struggled with the local food. The local speciality is noodles with horse meat, but you can order them without it. Another popular treat is zongzi, a dumpling wrapped in bamboo or banana leaf and filled with glutinous rice and mung bean paste.
The area surrounding a university affects student life just as much as the campus does, so the next sections give background on Guangxi.

Tribal groups that the Chinese called the Baiyue ("Hundred Yue", Bách Việt in Vietnamese) originally lived here. It was under the Qin dynasty that the region first joined China. The Han Chinese general Zhao Tuo (Triệu Đà in Vietnamese) seized most of southern China in 214 BC for Qin Shi Huang before the emperor died. The civil war that followed let Zhao set up a separate kingdom at Panyu called Nanyue ("Southern Yue"). It was sometimes submissive to the Han dynasty and sometimes independent, and it spread settlement and Chinese culture following its policy of "Harmonizing and Gathering the Hundred Yue" (和集百越) until collapse came in 111 BC, when the Han pushed south.

The Eastern Wu, which held southeastern China in the Three Kingdoms period, had a province called "Expansive" or "Wide" (廣州), and the name "Guangxi" can be traced back to it. Guilin was one of its commanderies.

In Tang times the Zhuang supported Nanzhao, Piluoge's kingdom in Yunnan, whose forces repelled imperial armies in 751 and 754. After that Guangxi divided into a Zhuang-dominated zone west of Nanning and a Han-dominated zone east of it. After Southern Zhao fell, Liu Yan founded the Southern Han (Nanhan) at Xingwangfu (modern Guangdong). It controlled little of Guangxi, was unstable, and in 971 the Song dynasty took it over.

The name comes from the Song, whose Guangnanxi ("West Southern Expanse") Circuit covered the area. With both the Song and the Jiaozhi of modern Vietnam pressing on them, the Zhuang leader Nong Zhigao rose in revolt in 1052, an event the Zhuang still recall. His independent kingdom did not last, after which the tattooed Song general Di Qing brought Guangxi back into Chinese hands.

The Yuan took control of Yunnan by conquering the Dali Kingdom in 1253 and wiped out the Southern Song in 1279 at the Battle of Yamen. Instead of governing Lingnan as a subject territory or a military district, the Mongols made Guangxi ("Western Expanse") a full province. The region stayed restless, and the Ming dynasty set local groups against each other. In 1465 the Battle of Big Rattan Gorge pitted the Zhuang against the Yao, and 20,000 deaths were reported.

Through the Ming and Qing, the powerful Cen (岑) clan ruled parts of Guangxi. The Cen were Zhuang, and the emperors recognised them as tusi, or local rulers. Direct rule was only imposed in 1726; until then the Qing mostly left the region alone. The 19th century was then full of unrest, starting with a Yao revolt in 1831, followed by the Jintian Uprising in January 1851, the start of the Taiping Rebellion, and then the Da Cheng Rebellion of April 1854.

Local officials in Guangxi executed St. Auguste Chapdelaine, an act that helped set off the Second Opium War, which began in 1858, and the legal opening of the interior to foreign interference. In the 1884 Sino-French War the Guangxi Army saw heavy action. Louis Brière de l'Isle could not invade its depot at Longzhou, and although the army was largely ineffective inside Vietnam, it drove the French out of China itself on 23 March 1885, at Zhennan Pass (today's Friendship Pass).

On 6 November 1911, after the Wuchang Uprising, Guangxi broke away from the Qing Empire. The Qing governor, Shen Bingdan, first stayed in office but was later removed by a mutiny led by General Lu Rongting. Lu's Old Guangxi clique took over Hunan and Guangdong too and played a leading part in the National Protection War, which opposed Yuan Shikai's bid to bring back imperial government. Zhuang loyalty kept his Self-Government Army united, but made it unwilling to go far beyond its own provinces. A feud with Sun Yat-sen ended in defeat in the 1920 and 1921 Guangdong-Guangxi War. Chen Jiongming's Cantonese forces briefly occupied Guangxi, and afterwards it slid into disunity, with serious banditry that lasted several years. Eventually Li Zongren's Guangxi Pacification Army formed the New Guangxi clique, in which Li, Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi were the leading figures.

Success in Hunan against Wu Peifu earned the Zhuang-led GPA the nicknames "Flying Army" and "Army of Steel". After Sun Yat-sen died, Li crushed a revolt by Tang Jiyao and took part in the Northern Expedition, through which the Republic of China brought other warlords under control. His army was one of very few Kuomintang units in which the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had no serious influence, and Chiang Kai-shek therefore used it in the Shanghai massacre of 1927. In the People's Republic, Guangxi is also remembered for the Baise Uprising of 1929, a CCP revolt, led by Deng Xiaoping and Chen Zhaoli, that failed.
The Guangxi Women's Battalion was formed in 1937 after Soong Mei-ling called on women to support the Sino-Japanese War. Reported numbers vary from 130 students to 500 or 800.

Lying in the far south, Guangxi was never taken during the Chinese Civil War and became part of the People's Republic two months after its founding, in December 1949. A coastal strip of Guangdong, made up of Beihai, Fangchenggang, Lianzhou (now Hepu County) and Qinzhou, was handed to Guangxi in 1952, so the region gained a sea outlet. This was undone in 1955 and restored in 1965, and as a result Guangxi is the only autonomous region that is not landlocked.

In 1967 and 1968, during the Cultural Revolution, the Guangxi Massacre killed between 100,000 and 150,000 people in the region. Some heavy industry appeared in the 1960s and 1970s, but Guangxi stayed mainly a scenic tourist destination, and even the booming 1990s seemed to pass it by. In recent years industrialisation has grown, with more focus on cash crops, and per capita GDP has risen as Guangdong industries move production to lower-wage parts of Guangxi.

Guangxi communities played an important part in China's effort during the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War. They provided the People's Liberation Army with food and housing and other logistical support. Militia members built roads, bridges and trenches, did other logistical work and cared for the wounded.

guangxi-normal-university.h: Cities, ports and airports in Guangxi

blocks.x: Major cities include Nanning, Liuzhou, Guilin and Beihai, and Longmen, Sanjiang and Yangshuo are towns worth noting. Waterways from the Xi River system connect with the Pearl River Delta. Along Guangxi's short Gulf of Tonkin coast, the important seaports are Beihai, Qinzhou and Fangchenggang, and the Pinglu Canal was built to join the Xi River system to coastal Guangxi.
Seven airports serve Guangxi, located in Hechi, Baise, Wuzhou, Liuzhou, Beihai, Guilin and Nanning.
Guangxi Normal University lists 257 programs for international students on this site: 71 bachelor, 148 master's, 36 doctoral, 2 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 248 taught in Chinese, 9 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 22,000 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

257 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (9):
Analytical Chemistry
Chemical Biology (Science)
English Interpreting
English Translation
Foreign Linguistics and Applied Linguistics
Inorganic Chemistry
Organic Chemistry
Physical Chemistry
Polymer Chemistry and Physics
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

guangxi-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guangxi Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guilin, register at Guangxi Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Based in Nanning, the capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Guangxi University (广西大学) is a public institution. Both the Ministry of Education and the regional authorities provide its funding. It belongs to Project 211 and to the national Double First-Class Construction scheme, and it awards degrees at three levels (bachelor's, master's, doctorate) through 27 colleges and departments with 98 undergraduate majors to choose from.

Its history is unusual. Over the middle decades of the 20th century the university pioneered university education in the centre and southwest of the country, and its teachers, students and assets went into founding over 20 further universities and academic departments. It opened in 1928, was broken up during the national education reforms of the 1950s, and had its departments sent across China to found or strengthen institutions such as what was then Wuhan University, what was then Sun Yat-sen University and what was then Guangxi Normal University. It was later rebuilt.

Planning began as early as 1925, when the Guangxi provincial government started drafting a Guangxi University scheme. Ma Junwu, a scientist and educator born in Guilin, received an invitation from the authorities in the winter of 1927 to return home and help build Guangxi's first modern university. The result opened in October 1928, at Hexi District in Wuzhou on Butterfly Mountain. Armed conflict in Guangxi and the Guizhou region next door forced a short suspension of operations from 1929 to 1931.

The provincial government had founded a separate teacher training school in Guilin in 1932, the Guangxi Provincial Teacher's College. Four years later, in 1936, higher education was reorganised. The Teacher's College was told to merge with Guangxi University, where it joined the colleges of literature and law, and the Guangxi Provincial Medical College was also absorbed and became the university's School of Medicine. At the same time the science and engineering faculties were removed from the university and combined into a separate Guangxi University of Science and Technology. Because of all this adding and shedding, Guangxi University had a hand in shaping many higher education institutions around the region, a role it kept during the 1950s reorganisation.
That same year, 1936, the university itself relocated to Guilin, where it opened a botany institute, a number of agricultural research facilities and an Economic Research Institute.

guangxi-university.h: National Guangxi University and wartime moves (1939-1952)

blocks.x: In 1939 the Nationalist government expanded the university by adding faculties, among them engineering and agriculture, and the new name was National Guangxi University. The following two decades were described as an era of "great contributions and sacrifices", yet they also formed the university's modern identity as a builder of higher education across central and southwestern China.

The war with Japan, which dated from the 1931 invasion of Manchuria in the northeast, had spread to the south of China by the middle of the 1940s. As a Japanese invasion of Guangxi drew close in summer 1944, the university was compelled to abandon its campus in Guilin and head south to Rong County, using eight meeting halls as classrooms. Liuzhou, a nearby city, began wartime preparations by November, which forced a second relocation, this time out of Guangxi entirely and into the neighbouring province of Guizhou.

Even in temporary exile the university carried on teaching, paying special attention to ethnic minority groups living near its location in Guangxi and southwest Guizhou, among them the Zhuang and Miao. Teachers gave talks on farming to local growers while at Rong County, and a cohort of minority students joined the colleges of agriculture, law and business.

Japan surrendered in September 1945 and the university returned to its home province, staying for a time on a campus beside the Lijiang river in Liuzhou. Early in 1946 a student movement brought it back to its original Butterfly Mountain campus in Wuzhou, but in September 1946 it moved again to Guilin.

At the start of the 1950s the university grew by taking in other institutions. In 1950 National Nanning Teacher's College joined and turned into its College of Teacher Education; the undergraduate courses of the provincial Xijiang College were absorbed in 1951; and a separate but affiliated body, the Guangxi Agricultural College, was set up in 1952. Early in 1952 Chairman Mao Zedong wrote the name "Guangxi University" in his own calligraphy, and the university still uses both that name and the calligraphy.

A time of reorganisation, dissolution and eventually suspension started in 1953, when the young People's Republic carried out a nationwide restructuring of higher education on an unprecedented scale. The goal was to widen access by creating new colleges and universities.

Guangxi University was a comparatively well-developed institution, with comprehensive departments, a large student body and substantial equipment, so it was asked to give up a large part of its resources for this national effort. A large share of its faculty, students and equipment was sent to 19 newly created institutions in central and southwestern China, and the university shrank greatly.

The new Guangxi Teacher's College, today's Guangxi Normal University, was formed on 17 October 1953 from 53 professors in the departments of mathematics, physics, chemistry, history and foreign languages together with 256 professors and instructors from the College of Teacher Education. Most of the other departments were then moved elsewhere. Mechanical engineering, among the oldest such departments in China, and electrical engineering were surrendered, with their staff, students and equipment going to the new Huazhong Institute of Technology (today's Huazhong University of Science and Technology) and other schools. The South China University of Technology received chemical engineering. Civil engineering, a highly regarded department, was sent to the Central South Civil Engineering Institute, now part of Hunan University, and Central South University took mining and metallurgy. Agriculture moved to Hubei, where it was renamed Huazhong Agricultural University. Wuhan University and Sun Yat-sen University each took a share of several other departments.

With most of its faculty and students gone, what remained of Guangxi University stopped operating. The depleted institution stayed dormant until 1958, waiting for its teachers and students to be rebuilt.

Reconstruction was approved by the central government in 1958, with a new campus in Nanning, and the first step was to rebuild engineering. Two institutions joined in 1961, the Guangxi Institute of Technology and the Guangxi University of Science and Technology; the latter, ironically, consisted of the engineering departments that had been cut loose some twenty years before. A year later, in 1962, the Guangxi Forestry College was taken in and became the basis of a new agriculture college.

Guangxi Labor University was merged in 1970 into the Guangxi Agricultural College, which was affiliated with but separate from Guangxi University, and the agricultural college was later renamed Guangxi Agricultural University. Guangxi University's first master's degree was conferred in 1978. A decisive step came in March 1997, when the Ministry of Education approved folding Guangxi Agricultural University into it, which substantially strengthened agricultural departments that had been weakened. The first doctorate followed in 1998, along with approval for three more doctoral programmes, and 1999 saw its selection for Project 211, a national programme to raise research standards and support faculty recruitment at a chosen set of rising universities.

The university entered the 21st century helped by two developments: wider improvements funded by the government under Project 211, and the addition of Guangxi Agricultural University, which reinforced its core agricultural departments.

A counterpart agreement in 2001 tied Guangxi University to the South China University of Technology, which had received its chemical engineering department back in 1953, with the aim of supporting innovation. The Ministry of Education gave permission in 2004 for it to found a new university in Guangxi to serve ethnic minorities. Overseas, it co-founded a Confucius Institute at Suphanburi in Thailand with Suan Dusit University in December 2006. A School of International Education followed in September 2007. That school recruits and looks after international students, teaches Chinese as a foreign language, and looks after international partnerships and the overseas Confucius Institutes.

The university describes 26 colleges and schools. Engineering and technology have the largest number: Mechanical Engineering, Electric Engineering, Civil Engineering and Architecture, Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Resources, Environment and Materials, Light Industry and Food Engineering, and Computer, Electronics and Information. For the life sciences and agriculture there are Life Science and Technology, Agriculture, Animal Science and Technology, Forestry, and Marine Sciences, and the Medical College covers medicine. Science colleges are Mathematics and Information Science and Physical Science and Technology.

In the humanities and social sciences, the university has Liberal Arts, Journalism and Communication, Foreign Languages, Arts, Public Policy and Management, a Business School, a Law School, a School of Marxism and a College of Physical Education. Learners who are not full-time undergraduates have the International College and the College of Continuing Education. Among the research institutes is the China-ASEAN Research Institute.

Within the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region it is always ranked first, and it is counted among the highest-ranked universities in South China outside Guangdong and the top 100 across China. Looking at 2025 results, the Performance Ranking of Scientific Papers for World Universities put it 346th globally, and the University Ranking by Academic Performance (URAP) put it 288th. Placement in ShanghaiRanking's Academic Ranking of World Universities is within the 301-400 group. In general, it appears in the global top 500 on several leading international tables, the CWTS Leiden Ranking and the Academic Ranking of World Universities among them.

For research output, the 2025 CWTS Leiden Ranking, which looked at publications from 2020 to 2023, put the university at number 183 in the world. Nature Research's Nature Index Annual Table 2025 counted it in the global top 250 for high-quality natural science papers, and in engineering U.S. News & World Report ranks it among its top 400 global universities.

Nanning has the Guangxi China Resources Tower, 402.7 m (1,321 ft) high, which is China's 22nd tallest building and the tallest in both Guangxi and southwestern China apart from Chongqing. The city is full of lush tropical parks, which make it one of the "greenest" cities in the country and explain its nickname, the "Green City" (绿城). Officials have started a beautification scheme across the city to make it cleaner and improve its reputation. It restricts street-side food sellers who do not hold proper licences and limits parking on busy roads. Early results are good, but lasting improvement will need long-term effort.

The southern part of the region is where Nanning lies, 160 km (99 mi) away from the border with Vietnam. Its administrative area is 22,293 km2 (8,607 sq mi), set within a hilly basin whose height above sea level varies from 70 to 500 m (230 to 1,640 ft). Qingxiu Mountain is the dominant feature of the south of town.

The climate is warm and humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), close to subtropical monsoon (Köppen Cwa). Across a year, the temperature averages 22.3 °C (72.1 °F). July is the hottest month, with a daily mean of 28.5 °C (83.3 °F) in muggy conditions, and January is the coolest and mildly dry, with 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). From May to October rain is at its most frequent, relative humidity never drops below 60 percent on average, and the year's total rainfall is 1,286 millimetres (50.6 in). Frost happens on just three or four days, and snow is practically unknown. Only in December 1975 and January 2016 has it been seen since 1900, and it did not lie on the ground. The extremes recorded are −2.1 °C (28 °F) on 12 January 1955 and 40.4 °C (105 °F) on 9 May 1958. Sunshine runs from 15 percent of the possible total in March up to 51 percent in September, giving 1,579 hours of bright sun annually.

The warm climate supports rich biodiversity, with many animal species and more than 3,000 plant species. The jaba flower, an evergreen shrub, is the city flower, and the almond tree is the city tree, the main tree used for greening and landscaping around the city.

Of these, 5,293,359 are in the built-up (metro) area formed by 6 urban districts, as Wuming District has not yet merged into the urban area. The city's 35 ethnic groups live in tight-knit communities, and the Zhuang are prominent among them, along with the Han, Yao, Hui, Miao, Dong and Man.

In 2015 the city produced 341 billion RMB in GDP, which is $7,844 per person. Foreign exports totalled US$10 billion in 2007 and fixed-asset investment from abroad came to 34.3 billion RMB. There are six development zones and industrial parks; three of them together contributed 6 billion RMB to the city's output, over 8 percent of the total. Mineral resources are varied, covering iron, gold, manganese, aluminum, silver, indium, quartz, coal, marble and granite, and one third of all the mineral types found in China are present around Nanning. One of the industrial zones is the Nanning Economic & Technological Development Area.

Nanning Rail Transit (NNRT) is expected to have nine lines in all. The first opened in June 2016 and the second in December 2017, with Line 3 following in 2019 and Line 4 in 2020. Line 1 runs from east to west, linking the financial and political centre with the academic and research centre.
Nanning Wuxu International Airport serves the city.

The city has two principal railway stations, Nanning and Nanning East. East is newer and the main stop for high-speed trains. A third, Nanning North, was due to open in 2023 with the Guiyang-Nanning high-speed railway. Nanning station is a junction for the Nanning-Kunming, Nanning-Guangzhou and Hunan-Guangxi railways. There are also plans for a high-speed line to Pingxiang on the Vietnamese border, with the aim of connecting the Pan-Pearl River Delta and southeast China more closely with ASEAN members. High-speed services started on the Hunan-Guangxi line and on the line from Nanning to Beihai (and its branch to Fangchenggang) at the end of 2013, and Guangxi is also on the Guangzhou-Guiyang high-speed railway.

China National Highways 210, 322, 324 and 325 serve the city, as do several expressways: G72 Quanzhou-Nanning, G7201 Nanning Ring, G7211 Nanning-Youyiguan, G75 Lanzhou-Haikou and G80 Guangzhou-Kunming.

Science, technology, education, culture and health in the autonomous region are all centred on Nanning. Figures given include 54 research institutes belonging to the districts, 10 colleges and 50 trade schools that train specialised staff, 62 mass cultural organisations, 13 performing groups, 8 cinemas and 285 projecting units. There are over 70 karaoke halls and more than 1000 newsstands too, and bookshops and cultural markets are easy to find.

Eating out in Nanning means both local dishes and food from elsewhere in China and overseas. Along most streets you can see the traditional food culture, and the local style resembles that of Guangdong and Southeast Asia. Restaurants serve Cantonese, Sichuan, Hunan and Jiangsu cuisine as well as Western, Thai and Japanese menus.

Locals love rice noodles. Laoyou noodles, whose name means "old friend", are the best known: the cook fries chilli pepper, black beans, garlic and sour bamboo shoots, adds pork, and then pours on soup over the rice noodles. Guilin rice noodles and hand-made noodles are popular as well. Tangy and spicy, Laoyou noodles are a cheap street food for any meal of the day, breakfast, lunch or dinner. Lemon duck is another dish that comes originally from Nanning.

Nanning is close to the scenic hills of Guilin, to the minority villages of northern and western Guangxi, and to the Vietnamese border in the south. Inside the city, visitors can see the Guangxi Museum, People's Park (where Zhenning Fort stands), Mount Qingxiu, Yangmei Ancient Town and the Guangxi Medicinal Herb Botanical Garden. Nanning Zoo, Nanhu Park and Shishan Park are further options for a day out.

guangxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: A university devoted to traditional Chinese medicine

blocks.x: Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine is a public university in Nanning, the capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China. In the Zhuang language its name is written Gvangjsih Cunghyihyoz Dayoz. Its focus is traditional Chinese medicine, and it combines teaching, research, patient treatment and the production of medicines. Formal establishment came in 1956. Of China's five autonomous regions, only Guangxi has an independently established higher education institution devoted to traditional Chinese medicine, and this is it. It is also recognised as a key university in the national programme to build basic capacity in the Midwest.
1934: a Guangxi provincial medical research institute was set up in Nanning, the seed from which the university later grew.
1956: the institute became the Nanning Chinese Medicine School.
1964: the school started undergraduate programmes and took the name Guangxi College of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
1970: Nanning Jounor Medical College merged into it.
1976: it began to admit international students.
1978: it was among the first institutions in China to start postgraduate programmes.
2012: renamed Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine.
2013: moved to the Xianhu Campus.
2015: became a university supported jointly by the province and the national ministry.
March 2025: inaugurated a research centre for artificial intelligence applied to traditional Chinese medicine.
For a prospective international student, the 1976 date shows a long record of receiving students from abroad.

guangxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: What the university looks like today

blocks.x: The university operates two campuses, Xianhu and Mingxiu, with more than 1,300 acres of land between them. It has 15 affiliated hospitals, 3 of them directly affiliated, plus several bases for research and teaching practice. There are 28 undergraduate majors to choose from; among them are the flagship Traditional Chinese Medicine, a combined course in Chinese and Western medicine, and a major in acupuncture and tui-na. About 14,000 students attend, among them international students from more than 40 countries and regions.

In research terms, it contributed 5 papers to the Nature Index between 1 January and 31 December 2025. Its further roles include acting as a centre for China-ASEAN cooperation in traditional medicine and as a base for training talent. Strategic partners number institutions in over 20 countries, with the United States, Canada and Germany among them.
Xianhu Campus: 13 Wuhe Avenue, in Nanning (Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region).
Mingxiu Campus: 179 East Mingxiu Road, in Nanning (Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region).

Your daily life will take place in Nanning, so it helps to know what the city is like. It is warm and leafy, has a mix of Zhuang and other cultures, and is developing quickly as a gateway to Southeast Asia.

Nanning has the Guangxi China Resources Tower, which is 402.7 m (1,321 ft) high. It ranks 22nd among the tallest buildings in the People's Republic of China, and it is the tallest in Guangxi and in south-western China if Chongqing is left out. The city also has many parks with lush tropical vegetation. It is one of China's greenest cities and is nicknamed the "Green City" (绿城).

In recent years the government has run a citywide beautification plan to tidy up Nanning and improve its image. Among other things, it cut the number of unlicensed street food sellers and limited parking in busy streets. The campaign has had early success, but lasting results will need long-term effort.

The warm climate supports great biodiversity, with many animal species and over 3,000 plant species. As a city symbol it has chosen an evergreen shrub, the Jaba flower, for its flower, and the almond tree for its tree; the latter forms the core of the city's greening and landscaping.

The city is in the southern part of the autonomous region, and the Vietnamese border is 160 km (99 mi) away. Its administrative area is 22,293 km² (8,607 sq mi). The city sits in a hilly basin 70 to 500 m (230 to 1,640 ft) above sea level, and Qingxiu Mountain is the main feature of the southern part of town.

Nanning's climate is warm and humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), bordering on subtropical monsoon (Köppen Cwa). The year averages 22.3 °C (72.1 °F). July brings the hottest, most humid weather at an average of 28.5 °C (83.3 °F) over 24 hours. January is the coolest month, though it averages a mild 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), and winter is dry. Rain is most frequent from May to October, when relative humidity stays above 60 percent on average. Total rainfall is 1,286 millimetres (50.6 in) a year.

The area is frost-free except for three or four days a year, and snow is almost unknown: since 1900, flakes have fallen on the city on only two occasions, in December 1975 and January 2016, and neither time did the snow settle. Recorded extremes run from -2.1 °C (28 °F) on 12 January 1955 to 40.4 °C (105 °F) on 9 May 1958. Sunshine ranges from 15 percent of the possible amount in March to 51 percent in September, giving 1,579 hours of bright sunshine a year. Light clothes and an umbrella are the safe choice most of the year.

In the 2020 census Nanning had 8,741,584 residents. Of these, 5,293,359 live in the built-up (metro) area, which covers 6 urban districts; Wuming District is not yet joined to the urban sprawl. The Zhuang ethnic group lives here in compact communities, and altogether 35 ethnic groups live in such communities in the city, including the Zhuang, Han, Yao, Hui, Miao, Dong and Man.

Official figures show Nanning's GDP in 2015 was 341 billion RMB, equal to a GDP per capita of $7,844. Exports were worth US$10 billion in 2007, and foreign fixed-asset investment came to 34.3 billion RMB. Six development zones and industrial parks exist; just three account for 6 billion RMB of output, which is above 8 percent of the whole city's GDP. Mineral resources include gold, iron, manganese, aluminium, quartz, silver, indium, coal, marble and granite, and a third of the different types of mineral resources in China are found in Nanning. The main industrial area is the Nanning Economic & Technological Development Area.

The Nanning Rail Transit (NNRT) network is meant to have nine lines in all. Line 1 opened in June 2016 and connects the east and west of the city, linking its financial and political centre with its academic and research centre. Line 2 started in December 2017, Line 3 in 2019 and Line 4 in 2020.

Two major stations serve Nanning: Nanning railway station and the newer Nanning East, which is the main stop for high-speed trains. A third, Nanning North, was due to open in 2023 with the Guiyang-Nanning high-speed railway. Nanning station is a junction for the Nanning-Kunming, Nanning-Guangzhou and Hunan-Guangxi lines. A high-speed line to Pingxiang on the Vietnamese border is also planned, aimed at connecting the Pan-Pearl River Delta and south-east China more closely with ASEAN members. High-speed service began at the end of 2013 on the Hunan-Guangxi line and on the line linking Nanning with Beihai and its Fangchenggang branch. Guangxi is also a meeting point for the Guangzhou-Guiyang high-speed rail.
Nanning Wuxu International Airport serves the city. The main roads are:
China National Highways 210, 322, 324 and 325
G72 Quanzhou-Nanning Expressway
G7201 Nanning Ring Expressway
G7211 Nanning-Youyiguan Expressway
G75 Lanzhou-Haikou Expressway
G80 Guangzhou-Kunming Expressway
Elsewhere in Guangxi, seven cities have airports: Nanning, Guilin, Beihai, Liuzhou, Wuzhou, Baise and Hechi.

Nanning is the centre of science and technology, education, culture and health in the autonomous region. It has 54 scientific research institutes under its districts, and 10 colleges and 50 trade schools train specialists of many types. Culture is served by 62 mass cultural organisations and 13 performing groups. Add 8 cinemas with 285 projection units in total, more than 70 karaoke halls and over a thousand newsstands, and note that bookshops and cultural markets are everywhere.

The city has its own cuisine along with dishes from other parts of China and from abroad, and traditional food culture is visible on most streets. Local food shares features with Cantonese cooking and with Southeast Asia. Restaurants also serve regional Chinese dishes (Guangdong, Sichuan, Hunan, Jiangsu) and foreign cuisines such as Japanese, Thai and Western.

Rice noodles are a local favourite. The best known are Laoyou rice noodles, whose name means "old friend rice noodles", although Guilin rice noodles and hand-made noodles are also popular. The Laoyou recipe starts with stir-fried pepper, sour bamboo shoots, black beans and garlic, then adds pork, then soup and rice noodles. The sour-spicy dish is a cheap street-food staple eaten for breakfast, lunch or dinner. Lemon duck is a dish that originated in Nanning.

Nanning is near the scenic Guilin area with its world-famous hills, and also close to northern and western Guangxi with its minority villages and to the Vietnamese border in the south. In the city, look for the Guangxi Museum, People's Park (with Zhenning Fort), Mount Qingxiu, the Guangxi Medicinal Herb Botanical Garden and Yangmei Ancient Town. Nanhu Park, Shishan Park and the Nanning Zoo are further places of interest.

guangxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Guangxi: the region behind the city

blocks.x: The region around a university colours student life nearly as much as the campus. Guangxi has a layered, often turbulent past, and a dramatic landscape. This section covers both.

Guangxi sits in the south of China. On its west is Yunnan, on the north Guizhou, on the north-east Hunan and on the east and south-east Guangdong. Vietnam adjoins it to the south-west and the Gulf of Tonkin gives it a southern shore. The link to Guangdong is built into the name, because both share the character "Guang" (广 in simplified form, 廣 in traditional, Guǎng in pinyin).

Hills and mountains dominate. In the north-west lies a piece of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau. The north holds the Jiuwan, Fenghuang and Duyao ranges, and the Nanling Mountains form the north-eastern boundary, with the Yuecheng and Haiyang ranges branching away from them. The Duyang range runs through the western part, the Da Yao and Da Ming ranges stand near the middle, and the Yunkai range marks the south-east edge. Kitten Mountain, in the Yuecheng range, is the top of the region at 2,141 metres (7,024 ft).

Karst terrain, meaning steep peaks and great caverns, is common: it makes up 37.8 percent of Guangxi's land. Water drains in several directions. Some rivers, such as the Qin and the Nanliu, end in the Gulf of Tonkin; others feed the Xiang River in neighbouring Hunan; and the Xi River system crosses the region towards the south-east and reaches the South China Sea. On the Vietnamese frontier the Ban Gioc-Detian waterfall (Dé Tiān Pùbù in pinyin) marks the line between the two countries. Roughly one quarter of the region is forested.

The first people here were a patchwork of tribal groups that the Chinese lumped together as the Baiyue, "Hundred Yue" (Bách Việt in Vietnamese). Guangxi entered China proper under the Qin. Zhao Tuo (Triệu Đà in Vietnamese), a Han Chinese general, seized the bulk of southern China in 214 BC on behalf of Qin Shi Huang. When the emperor died and civil war followed, Zhao used the chaos to found a separate kingdom, Nanyue ("Southern Yue"), centred on Panyu. Nanyue swung between deference to the Han and independence, and spread Chinese settlement and customs under a policy summed up as "Harmonizing and Gathering the Hundred Yue" (和集百越). It lasted until the Han dynasty's push south destroyed it in 111 BC.

The origin of the word "Guangxi" lies with Eastern Wu, a Three Kingdoms state in the south-east whose "Expansive" or "Wide" province (廣州) included Guilin as a commandery. In Tang times the Zhuang backed Nanzhao, the Yunnan kingdom of Piluoge, which defeated imperial armies in 751 and again in 754. As a result Guangxi split into two zones: Zhuang influence west of Nanning, and Han influence to the east.

Once Nanzhao had collapsed, Liu Yan founded the Southern Han, or Nanhan, from Xingwangfu in what is now Guangdong. His state held little of Guangxi and was unstable, and in 971 the Song annexed it. The Song also gave the region the name it still bears, since they governed it as the Guangnanxi circuit, "West Southern Expanse". Under pressure from both the Song and the Jiaozhi of modern Vietnam, the Zhuang chief Nong Zhigao started a revolt in 1052 that the Zhuang remember to this day. The kingdom he declared did not survive, and the Song general Di Qing, a man with tattoos, brought the area back under Chinese rule.

The Mongol-led Yuan dynasty conquered the Dali Kingdom in 1253 and took Yunnan, then ended the Southern Song in 1279 after the Battle of Yamen. They chose not to run Lingnan as a subject territory or military district, and created Guangxi ("Western Expanse") as a province in its own right. Trouble continued all the same, and the Ming responded by setting local groups against each other. In 1465 the Zhuang and the Yao fought at Big Rattan Gorge, and 20,000 deaths were reported. Parts of Guangxi came under the Cen (岑) clan across the Ming and Qing periods. The Cen were ethnically Zhuang, and the emperors accepted them as tusi, hereditary local rulers.

Direct Qing rule only began in 1726; earlier, the dynasty had mostly left Guangxi alone. The 1800s, however, were restless. A Yao uprising took place in 1831. Then in January 1851 came the Jintian Uprising, which opened the Taiping Rebellion, and in April 1854 the Da Cheng Rebellion. The Second Opium War of 1858 had a Guangxi origin: local officials had put St. Auguste Chapdelaine to death, and the conflict afterwards made foreign interference in the interior legal. In the Sino-French War of 1884 the Guangxi Army fought hard. Louis Brière de l'Isle never managed to attack its depot at Longzhou, and while the army achieved little in Vietnam itself, it drove French forces out of China at the Battle of Zhennan Pass (today's Friendship Pass) on 23 March 1885.

On 6 November 1911, after the Wuchang Uprising, Guangxi declared independence from the Qing. The Qing governor, Shen Bingdan, kept his post for a time, but a mutiny led by General Lu Rongting forced him out. Lu's Old Guangxi clique went on to take Hunan and Guangdong and played a leading role in the National Protection War against Yuan Shikai, who wanted to restore a monarchy. The troops were fiercely loyal to the Zhuang cause, which kept them united but made them unwilling to campaign far from home. A dispute with Sun Yat-sen ended in defeat in the Guangdong-Guangxi War of 1920 and 1921. Chen Jiongming's Cantonese forces occupied the region briefly, after which it broke into disunity and was plagued by banditry for several years. Order returned when Li Zongren's Guangxi Pacification Army created the New Guangxi clique, which Li ran jointly with Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi.

The army won a victory over Wu Peifu in Hunan and was nicknamed the "Flying Army" and "Army of Steel". After Sun Yat-sen's death Li put down a revolt led by Tang Jiyao, then took part in the Northern Expedition, in which the Republic gained authority over other warlords. His forces were among the few Kuomintang units largely clear of Chinese Communist Party influence, so Chiang Kai-shek used them for the Shanghai massacre of 1927. In the story told within the People's Republic, Guangxi is better known for the Baise Uprising of 1929, a failed CCP rising under Chen Zhaoli and Deng Xiaoping. In 1937 a Guangxi Women's Battalion was formed after Soong Mei-ling asked women to support the war with Japan; accounts of its strength vary from 130 students to 500 or 800.

Guangxi lies at the far south, so it escaped being taken in the Chinese Civil War. It joined the People's Republic in December 1949, two months after the republic's founding. A short stretch of Guangdong coast, covering Qinzhou, Lianzhou (now Hepu County), Fangchenggang and Beihai, was transferred to Guangxi in 1952, finally giving it access to the sea. The transfer was reversed in 1955 and restored in 1965. That is why Guangxi is the only autonomous region that has a coastline. A dark chapter came in the Cultural Revolution: the Guangxi Massacre of 1967 and 1968 cost between 100,000 and 150,000 lives.

Heavy industry developed a little in the 1960s and 1970s, yet Guangxi remained mostly a scenic destination for visitors, and even the boom of the 1990s seemed to bypass it. In recent years industry has grown and farmers have turned more to cash crops. Per capita GDP has risen as Guangdong firms shift production to cheaper areas of Guangxi. During the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War, communities in Guangxi were vital to the Chinese war effort, providing the People's Liberation Army with food, housing and other logistical support. Militia members built roads, bridges and trenches, and cared for wounded soldiers.

The city of Guangzhou, in Guangdong Province, owns and pays for GZHMU (广州医科大学), a medical university that has been included in the Double First-Class Construction scheme. It used to be called Guangzhou Medical College. The sections below describe the university, its students and facilities, how its English-taught medical degree works, and then the city of Guangzhou.
The university was founded in 1958. Its international student internship programme began in 2013, and a "Nan Yue Outstanding Graduate Student" campaign has run in Guangdong province since 1993.

The motto, in Chinese, is 诚信务实，自强不息，敢为人先，追求卓越. Translated literally, it says "pragmatic integrity, self-discipline, always to be first, and the pursuit of excellence". The university has used it as its motto since the 1950s.

Each year about 1,500 undergraduates and 550 postgraduates (master's and doctoral students) arrive from the Chinese mainland, Macau and Hong Kong. Full-time enrolment adds up to 23,300: 12,000 on continuing education, 10,000 undergraduates and 1,300 graduate students.

Among international students, 218 full-time undergraduates are taking the MBBS in English, most of them from India and Nepal. Other students are from African countries (Tanzania, Ghana, Cameroon, Comoros, South Africa, Sudan, Uganda, Zambia, Sierra Leone, Equatorial Guinea and Mozambique), South Asia (Bangladesh and Pakistan), and further afield Australia, France, the United States, Saint Vincent, Singapore and the United Kingdom, along with 21 more countries.

There are two campuses, Panyu and Yuexiu, with a land area of 372,300 square metres and 481,900 square metres of building space. The university has 22 colleges, seven directly affiliated hospitals, 11 hospitals that are affiliated indirectly, and 28 research institutions.
Twenty research institutes are named; those listed include:
