Clinical medicine is the centre of the offer, but the list is long. Health-related fields include nursing, anesthesiology, stomatology (dental medicine), preventive medicine, pharmacy, medical imaging, medical examination and therapeutic recreation, plus Chinese and Western integrative medicine. Science and engineering fields are biomedical engineering, biotechnology and psychotechnics. Beyond health there are programmes in law, statistics, public service administration (PSA), marketing management, food quality inspection, and information management and systems.

The degree on offer is the MBBS, which stands for the Bachelor of Medicine and the Bachelor of Surgery. On meeting the requirements, undergraduates receive a medical degree and a certificate of graduation, and graduates can apply to sit the medical licensing examination so that they can practise. Some countries may ask students to complete academic accreditation first, so check the rules of the country where you plan to work.

The physician internship lasts 48 weeks. Students apply for posts at the 8 affiliated hospitals of the university, and a pass at level 3 of the HSK (Han Yu Shui Ping Kao Shi), the Chinese-language test, is needed beforehand.

ARWU, short for Academic Ranking of World Universities and or the "Shanghai Ranking", is published every year as a world league table; it was the first global ranking built on multiple kinds of indicator.
The Nature Index traces which institutions and countries high-quality scientific papers come from, and reports research output by both each month.
The Universities Ranking of China, published by the CUAA (Chinese Universities Alumni Association, 中国校友会网), is among the most important domestic rankings in China.

guangzhou-medical-university.h: Guangzhou: the city around the university

blocks.x: Daily life revolves around the city, so these sections describe Guangzhou's landscape, resources, climate, economy and people.

The original town grew up on the Pearl River's (Zhujiang's) eastern bank beside Baiyun Mountain, around 80 miles (130 kilometres) inland from the South China Sea and some 300 miles downstream of the point where boats can no longer go any farther up. From there it dominated the delta's rich alluvial lowland, and the Humen Strait protected its sea access. The modern city has an area of 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 sq mi), lying on either side of the river between 112° 57′ and 114° 03′ E and 22° 26′ and 23° 56′ N in the centre-south of Guangdong.

The Pearl is the fourth-largest river in China. Tidal flats along the estuary support intertidal ecosystems, although many have been reclaimed for farming. Locals now call Baiyun Mountain the city's "lung" (市肺).
The ground climbs from the southwest toward the northeast, with hills behind and the sea in front. The top of the range is Tiantang Peak, which stands 1,210 metres (3,970 feet) above sea level.

Geologically the area is complicated, which favours the formation of minerals: 47 kinds have been found, in 820 ore fields, among them 18 large or medium oil deposits and, in another count, 25 large or medium mining areas. Building and industrial materials dominate: granite, limestone for cement, ceramic clay, marble, fluorite, nepheline syenite, albite and potassium. There are also salt, mirabilite and manganese, and mineral and geothermal mineral water. Energy and non-ferrous minerals are in short supply, scattered, small in scale and variable in grade.

Local water is scarce but water passing through is abundant. The city's water surface measures 74,400 hectares, which is 10.05% of its land area; the many rivers and streams enhance the landscape and keep the local ecology stable. The main rivers are the Beijiang, the north mainstream of the Dongjiang, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi, the Baini, the Guangzhou reach of the Pearl River, the Shiqiao Waterway and the Shawan Waterway. The Beijiang and Dongjiang flow through the city and join the Pearl River on the way to the sea.

The average local supply is 7.979 billion cubic metres a year (7.881 billion from the surface, 1.487 billion from underground). Divided by the permanent population in the 2010 sixth census, that works out at 1.0601 million cubic metres per square kilometre and 628 per person, half the national per-person average. Water passing through the city is far larger at 186.024 billion cubic metres, 23 times the local total, mostly in the southern Wanghe and Zengcheng Districts. Most of it, 159.15 billion cubic metres, comes in from the Xijiang and Beijiang; the Dongjiang adds 14.203 billion to its north mainstream; and the upper Zengjiang contributes 2.828 billion.

The southern river network lies in the tidal zone, with big flows and strong tides. The Pearl River's three main outlets, Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili, reach the Lingding sea area and the South China Sea south of the city. Over a year, the incoming tide brings 271 billion cubic metres and the ebb takes out 408.8 billion, and the three outlets discharge 137.7 billion of runoff. The tides carry in a good deal of water, some of it usable fresh water.

Farming reflects a transition zone between the tropics and subtropics. Few Chinese regions have more fruit-tree resources: tropical, subtropical and temperate fruits, from 174 species, 82 genera and 41 families, make up over 500 varieties, of which 55 are principal lychee varieties. It is the home of origin and variety for lychee, longan, wampee (yellow skin) and black and white olives. Vegetables are noted for quality and range, with 15 main categories, 127 species and over 370 varieties. The list continues with flowers (cut, potted, bonsai, seedlings, and edible or medicinal kinds), lawns and nursery stock, and with staple grain, cash crops, livestock, poultry, fish and other aquatic products, and wild animals. Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first variety in the city to receive protection as a geographical indication.

Although the city lies just below the Tropic of Cancer, its climate is classed as humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa) under the East Asian monsoon. From April to September the monsoon brings long, wet, hot and humid summers and the heat index is high; winters are mild and relatively dry.
January averages 13.8 °C (56.8 °F) and July 28.9 °C (84.0 °F), and the year as a whole averages 22.4 °C (72.3 °F).
October to December is mild, cool and breezy, and is the best time to travel.
Relative humidity is about 76 percent, and rainfall in the metropolitan area exceeds 1,950 millimetres (77 in) a year.
Sunshine is limited: only 17 percent of the possible total in March and 51 percent in October, adding up to 1,559 hours a year, noticeably less than at Shenzhen and Hong Kong close by.

The official extremes since 1951 are a low of 0 °C (32 °F), which happened twice (23 December 1999 and 11 February 1957), and a high on 1 July 2004 of 39.1 °C (102.4 °F). An unofficial -5.0 °C (23.0 °F) on 18 January 1893, which modern meteorologists think was really -3.0 °C (26.6 °F), and an unofficial -0.3 °C (31.5 °F) on 8 December 1934 at the Huangpu District station (records began 1912) are also mentioned.
The most recent snowfall was on 24 January 2016, 87 years after the one before it.

Manufacturing in the Pearl River Delta, a top commercial and industrial region of China, centres on Guangzhou. Its GDP in 2021, ¥2,823 billion or US$444.37 billion nominal, put it second in South-Central China behind Shenzhen, and GDP per head was ¥151,162 (US$23,794 nominal). It counts as one of China's most prosperous cities.

A few rankings give a sense of scale. For number of billionaires, the 2020 Hurun Global Rich List had Guangzhou tenth worldwide, and fifth in China behind Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Oxford Economics projects that by 2035 it will be among the world's 10 largest cities by nominal GDP, together with Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, and that nominal GDP per person will exceed $42,000 by 2030. The GFCI (Global Financial Centers Index) of 2020 placed it 21st in the world, between Washington, D.C., and Amsterdam; across Asia and Oceania it was eighth, after Dubai, Shenzhen, Beijing, Singapore, Hong Kong, Tokyo and Shanghai. Rapid industrialisation once made it rather polluted, but green urban planning has since made it one of China's most liveable cities.
Zhujiang New Town is Guangzhou's 21st-century central business district. Within Tianhe District it occupies 6.44 km2, and several financial institutions have their headquarters there.

The Canton Fair, officially the "China Import and Export Fair", takes place each April and October, organised by the Ministry of Trade. Starting in the spring of 1957, it matters greatly to the city, being the largest, highest-level and oldest trade fair in China. From the 104th session it moved from the older Liuhua complex to the new Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center (广州国际会展中心) in Pazhou, a site where Line 8 has two stations, Line 11 has one and Tram Line THZ1 has three. Since that session the fair has run in three phases rather than two.
Cantonese cuisine ranks among China's most famous and popular regional cooking, summed up in the saying "Eat in Guangzhou" (食在廣州).
Cantonese sculpture works in jade, wood and, controversially, ivory.
Canton porcelain developed over about three centuries as a major export ware, and is known within China for its very colourful style.
Of China's four principal styles of embroidery, one is Cantonese.
Among the most successful Chinese beer brands is Zhujiang, a pale lager.
GAC Group
Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone

Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone: founded in 2005 with a planned area of 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 sq mi), in Nansha District. The zone favours heavy industry, car assembly and biotechnology. Driving south from Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport takes 70 minutes (54 kilometres or 34 miles) to reach it, and Nansha Port is nearby, and Metro Line 4 is being extended to the Nansha Ferry Terminal.

Guangzhou Free Trade Zone: founded in 1992 in eastern Huangpu District near the Economic and Technological Development Zone and Baiyun Airport. It encourages international trade, logistics, processing and software. It has recently been rebranded under the name Huangpu District, with newer sectors being introduced, such as AI, new energy, new materials, new transport and mobility, and information and communication technology, and it hosts the Guangzhou IP Court.
Guangzhou Science City

Guangzhou is a hub for international business. China Briefing reported that more than 30,000 foreign-invested companies had set up in the city by 2018. Of these, 297 were Fortune Global 500 firms with projects in the city, and 120 more of that group had their headquarters, or a regional headquarters, in Guangzhou.
Permanent residents numbered 18.978 million by late 2024, and the urbanisation rate was 87.24%.

The Seventh National Population Census recorded 18,676,605 permanent residents on 1 November 2020, 5,975,805 (47.05%) more than the 12,700,800 of 2010. Of them, 86.19% (16,096,724) lived in urban areas and 13.81% (2,579,881) in rural ones. Migration is still central to the picture. The census found 11,522,907 residents living away from where they are registered, of whom 9,378,825 were in the floating population, so Guangzhou ranks among the main migrant destinations in China.

guangzhou-medical-university.h: Earlier estimates and the delta region

blocks.x: The 2014 estimate was 13,080,500, including 11,264,800 urban residents, which meant roughly 1,800 people on every square kilometre. The built-up area of Guangzhou proper joins directly with several other cities. The Pearl River Delta Economic Zone's built-up area covers about 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 mi2) and has an estimated 22 million people. Guangzhou's nine urban districts are part of it, with the largest other contributors being Shenzhen at 5.36 million, Dongguan at 3.22 million and Zhongshan at 3.12 million, followed by most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890,000) and the Huiyang District of Huizhou (760,000). Including neighbouring Hong Kong, the agglomeration has over 28 million people. The rapid economic growth and the need for workers have created an enormous floating population of migrants: as many as 10 million live in the area for six months or more annually. In 2008 migrant workers made up around five million of the city's permanent residents.
The OECD estimated that the surrounding metropolitan area had 25 million people in 2010.

A 2018 study by Gong and colleagues traced Guangzhou's development from 1990 to 2020. In 1990 nearly all built-up residential districts were confined to one small corner of the west, with only small pockets elsewhere, mostly surrounded by farm and forest land. From 2005 to 2020 residential development spread, and the 2020 map shows developed residential communities running from west to east across the city, while the far south and large parts of the north are still mostly farmland and forest with very limited housing.

guangzhou-medical-university.h: Getting to Hong Kong and Macau, and religion

blocks.x: There are daily high-speed catamaran services from the Nansha Ferry Terminal and the Lianhua Shan Ferry Terminal in Guangzhou to the Hong Kong China Ferry Terminal, and from Nansha to the Macau Ferry Pier in Hong Kong.

In earlier times the city had about 124 religious sites, including pavilions, halls and temples. Today there are associations for Buddhists and for Taoists, a Jewish community, and a Christian presence with a history that goes back to its reintroduction into China by colonial powers.

Guangzhou Medical University is a city-run medical school with two campuses, a large network of affiliated hospitals, and an English-medium MBBS used mainly by students from South Asia and Africa. Remember the HSK 3 requirement for the internship, check your home country's licensing rules, and plan for a humid subtropical climate with a long wet season from April to September and the most pleasant weather in October to December.

A final practical note: the university's international programme is concentrated on the English-taught MBBS, so applicants should plan their Chinese-language study early to be ready for the hospital internship, and should compare the licensing and accreditation rules of their home country before applying.

Guangzhou Medical University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.
Application windows found for Guangzhou Medical University:
Autumn 2026 MBBS intake (closed): opens 1 Mar 2026, closes 30 Aug 2026
Deadlines can move and seats can fill earlier than the closing date, so apply as soon as your documents are ready.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

guangzhou-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guangzhou Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guangzhou, register at Guangzhou Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, abbreviated GZHTCM (广州中医药大学), is a public university run by the government of Guangdong Province and located in the provincial capital, Guangzhou. It is included in the national Double First-Class Construction programme.

What sets it apart for prospective students is its clinical network. Thirty tertiary hospitals are affiliated with it, four of them directly, which is more than any other university in China has. A student of traditional medicine here is therefore close to a very wide range of teaching hospitals. The faculty list in our source names only one person, Song Jianping, so check the university's own website for staff in the fields that interest you.
The rest of this overview describes Guangzhou, the city you would live in, and then Guangdong, the province around it.

The old town grew up beside Baiyun Mountain on the eastern bank of the Pearl River, known in Chinese as the Zhujiang. It lay about 130 kilometres (80 miles) upstream of the river's meeting with the South China Sea, and roughly 300 miles below the point where boats could no longer go further up. From there it controlled the fertile Pearl River Delta, whose link to the sea was guarded at the Humen Strait.

The modern city straddles the river, reaching from longitude 112° 57′ to 114° 03′ east and from latitude 22° 26′ to 23° 56′ north, in the south-central part of Guangdong. Its area is 7,434.4 square kilometres, or 2,870.4 sq mi. The Pearl is the fourth-largest river in China. Mudflats at the estuary shelter intertidal wildlife, though farmers have reclaimed many of them. Baiyun Mountain is now often called the city's "lung" (市肺), a reminder of how much its greenery matters to a dense urban area.

Ground levels climb gradually from the southwest toward the northeast, so hills form the back of the city while the ocean lies at its front. Tiantang Peak is the summit, standing 3,970 feet (1,210 metres) over sea level.

Guangzhou has little water of its own but a great deal that flows through it. Lakes, rivers and channels take up 74,400 hectares, a little over a tenth (10.05%) of the municipal land. The main watercourses are the Beijiang, the Dongjiang's northern mainstream, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi and Baini rivers, the Guangzhou stretch of the Pearl, and the Shiqiao and Shawan waterways. Both the Beijiang and the Dongjiang run through the city and merge with the Pearl on the way to the ocean.

Locally generated water amounts to 7.979 billion cubic metres a year, with 7.881 billion of it on the surface and 1.487 billion underground. Divided by the population counted in the 2010 census, that is 1.0601 million cubic metres for every square kilometre but only 628 for each resident, which is about half the average for China. Water flowing in from upstream is far larger, at 186.024 billion cubic metres, which is 23 times the local total. Most of it is concentrated in the Wanghe and Zengcheng districts in the south. Of the inflow, 159.15 billion cubic metres come from the Xijiang and Beijiang, 14.203 billion from the Dongjiang's northern mainstream and 2.828 billion from the upper Zengjiang.

Tides strongly affect the southern river network, where flows are large. Three principal mouths of the Pearl, called Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili, empty into the Lingding Ocean and so reach the South China Sea to the south of the city. Over a year the flood tide delivers 271 billion cubic metres and the ebb removes 408.8 billion. River runoff through the three mouths totals 137.7 billion cubic metres a year, and part of the tidal water is fresh enough to use.

Farming around Guangzhou marks the shift from tropical to subtropical conditions, which makes this one of the best fruit-growing regions in China. Tropical, subtropical and temperate fruits are all found, spread over 41 families, 82 genera and 174 species, and totalling above 500 varieties. Lychee alone has 55 principal varieties, and lychee, longan, wampee (called "yellow skin" locally) and black and white olives all originated or diversified here. Vegetables are famous too, both for quality and for the 15 main categories, 127 species and 370-plus varieties on offer. The flower trade is broad. It includes cut flowers, foliage and branches; pot plants, bonsai and bedding plants; ornamental seedlings; edible and medicinal blooms; flowers for industrial uses; and turf. Other output ranges from grain and cash crops to livestock, poultry, fish and wild animals, and Zengcheng Simiao rice became the city's first product to receive protection through a geographical indication.

Guangzhou's geological structure is intricate, and conditions have been good for minerals to form. Surveys have identified 47 mineral types (subspecies included) at 820 sites, with 25 large and medium-sized mining districts, and 18 large and medium-sized oil deposits are reported in the area. Commonly mined materials are granite for construction, limestone for cement, ceramic clay, potassium, sodium feldspar, salt, manganese, nepheline orthoclase, fluorite, marble, mineral water and geothermal water. By contrast, energy minerals and non-ferrous metals are in short supply, found only in scattered pockets, and of small scale and uncertain grade.

For a city only just below the Tropic of Cancer, Guangzhou is classed as humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa) and feels the East Asian monsoon. Hot, humid and rainy summers push the heat index high, while winters are gentle and relatively dry. The monsoon season lasts a long time, April through September, so plan for rain over half the year.

January is the coolest month, averaging 13.8 °C (56.8 °F), and July the warmest at 28.9 °C (84.0 °F); across the whole year the mean is 22.4 °C (72.3 °F). From October through December conditions are very moderate, cool and windy, and that spell is regarded as the best moment to visit. Humidity hovers near 76 percent. Over 1,950 millimetres (77 in) of rain falls each year in the urban area. The sky is often cloudy: March sees only 17 percent of possible sunshine and October 51 percent, totalling 1,559 hours a year, noticeably less than neighbouring Shenzhen and Hong Kong enjoy.

Since 1951 the official range has run from a low of 0 °C (32 °F), reached twice (11 February 1957 and 23 December 1999), up to a high of 39.1 °C (102.4 °F) on 1 July 2004. People also cite an unofficial reading of −5.0 °C (23.0 °F) from 18 January 1893, although today's meteorologists believe the true value was closer to −3.0 °C (26.6 °F). At the Huangpu District station, which began keeping records in 1912, an unofficial −0.3 °C (31.5 °F) was noted on 8 December 1934. The most recent snowfall was on 24 January 2016, the first in 87 years.

Manufacturing in the Pearl River Delta, itself one of China's major commercial and industrial regions, is centred on Guangzhou. In 2021 the city's GDP reached ¥2,823 billion, or US$444.37 billion in nominal terms, placing it second in South-Central China behind Shenzhen. Per capita output was ¥151,162 ($23,794 nominal), and Guangzhou counts as one of the most prosperous Chinese cities. The 2020 Hurun Global Rich List ranked it tenth in the world for billionaires and fifth within China, after Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen.

A study by Oxford Economics expects Guangzhou to be one of the ten biggest cities in the world by nominal GDP in 2035, together with Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, and its nominal GDP per person should be above $42,000 by 2030. As a financial centre it took 21st place worldwide in the 2020 Global Financial Centers Index, between Washington, D.C. and Amsterdam, and 8th in Asia and Oceania, with Shanghai, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, Beijing, Shenzhen and Dubai ahead of it. Fast industrial growth used to leave the city rather polluted, but green urban planning has since made it one of China's more liveable cities.
This is the city's 21st-century central business district, covering 6.44 km2 in Tianhe District and hosting the headquarters of many financial institutions.

The formal name is the China Import and Export Fair. The Ministry of Trade holds it twice a year, in April and October, and it is a major event for the city. First opened in spring 1957, it is the trade fair with the longest history, highest standing and biggest scale in China. From its 104th session it left the older Liuhua complex for the new Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center in Pazhou (广州国际会展中心). Visitors can get there from two Line 8 stations, a Line 11 station or three Tram Line THZ1 stops. Since the 104th session the fair has also been split into three phases in place of the earlier two.

Few Chinese regional cuisines are as famous or as widely loved as Cantonese cooking, and a well-known saying simply tells people to "Eat in Guangzhou" (食在廣州). Crafts here include sculpture worked in jade, wood and, a controversial choice, ivory. Over roughly three centuries Canton porcelain grew into an important export product, and in China today it is known for its bright, colourful decoration. Cantonese embroidery is counted among the four leading embroidery traditions of the country. For a drink, Zhujiang Beer, a pale lager, is among the most successful Chinese brands.
Major industrial names and areas include the GAC Group and the Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone. Three zones are worth describing.

The Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone dates from 2005 and has a planned area of 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 sq mi), in Nansha District. Its priority industries are car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry. It lies 54 kilometres (34 miles) south of Baiyun International Airport, about 70 minutes by road, and close to Nansha Port. Metro Line 4 is being extended to the Nansha Ferry Terminal.

The Guangzhou Free Trade Zone was set up in 1992 in the east of Huangpu District, next to the Economic and Technological Development Zone and very near Baiyun Airport. It favours international trade, logistics, processing and software. The area has recently been rebranded under the name Huangpu District, and new sectors are being brought in, such as new energy, AI, new mobility, new materials, information and communications technology and new transport. It also houses the Guangzhou IP Court.
The list also names Guangzhou Science City.

International business centres on Guangzhou. Reporting from China Briefing put the number of foreign-invested firms that had settled there by 2018 at more than 30,000. Among them were 297 Fortune Global 500 companies running projects in the city, and 120 more that had located a headquarters or regional headquarters there. For a student, that means a large pool of potential internships and graduate jobs, especially for anyone with languages.
At the end of 2024 Guangzhou had 18.978 million permanent residents, and 87.24% of the population was urban.

The Seventh National Population Census recorded 18,676,605 permanent residents on 1 November 2020. That was 5,975,805 more than the 12,700,800 of 2010, a rise of 47.05%. Urban residents numbered 16,096,724 (86.19%) and rural residents 2,579,881 (13.81%).

Newcomers define the city. The 2020 census found 11,522,907 residents living somewhere other than where their household is registered, 9,378,825 of whom belong to the so-called floating population. Few Chinese cities attract more migrants than Guangzhou, so an outsider is far from alone.

For comparison, a 2014 estimate counted 13,080,500 people, with 11,264,800 of them in urban areas, which is a density near 1,800 per km2. Guangzhou's built-up area connects directly with other cities. The continuous urban zone of the Pearl River Delta Economic Zone covers around 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 mi2) and is thought to hold 22 million people. Its parts are Guangzhou's nine urban districts, Shenzhen at 5.36 million, Dongguan at 3.22 million, Zhongshan at 3.12 million, most of Foshan at 2.2 million, Jiangmen at 1.82 million, Zhuhai at 890 thousand and Huiyang District of Huizhou at 760 thousand. Counting adjacent Hong Kong, the cluster passes 28 million. A fast-growing economy that needs plenty of labour has produced an enormous floating population, with as many as 10 million migrant workers staying in the area for at least half of each year. In 2008, roughly five million of Guangzhou's permanent residents were migrant workers.
The OECD estimated that the surrounding metropolitan region had a population of 25 million as of 2010.

A study by Gong and colleagues in 2018 followed Guangzhou's growth from 1990 to 2020. In 1990 developed residential districts were nearly all concentrated in a small area of the west, with other parts having few settlements and being surrounded by farmland and forest. From 2005 to 2020 more areas began to develop, and by the 2020 map housing ran across the city from west to east. The far south and big parts of the north remained largely farmland and forest, with very few housing communities.

High-speed catamarans sail every day linking Guangzhou's Nansha and Lianhua Shan ferry terminals with the China Ferry Terminal in Hong Kong. Nansha also has a service to the Macau Ferry Pier in Hong Kong, so there is a sea route as well as roads and rail.

Before the modern era Guangzhou had around 124 religious pavilions, halls and temples. Besides the Buddhist Association, the city now has a Taoist Association and a Jewish community, and it has a history with Christianity, which was brought back to China by colonial powers.

guangzhou-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Guangdong: the province behind the city

blocks.x: The province around a university shapes daily life as much as the campus, so a short history of Guangdong and its people follows.

Human settlement in the Pearl River Delta (珠江三角洲) goes back a very long way. Archaeologists place the start of its Neolithic era about 7,000 years before present (BP), dividing it into an early period of roughly 7000-5000 BP (about 5050-3050 BC) and a late one of roughly 5000-3500 BP (about 3050-1550 BC). On the coast the Neolithic way of life most likely spread from the middle Yangtze region (Jiao 2013). Farther inland it showed up around 4,600 BP, and in the north of the province the Shixia culture (石峽文化) stands for it, dated 4600-4200 BP (about 2650-2250 BC).

The early inhabitants were a patchwork of tribes whom the Chinese called the Baiyue, meaning "Hundred Yue". The Qin dynasty brought the area into China for the first time, and with Qin rule came organised administration and the first reliable records. Having created the first unified empire, the Qin pushed southward and established Nanhai Commandery at Panyu, close to modern Guangzhou. An independent state, Nanyue, then governed the region in the interval between the end of the Qin and the time of Emperor Wu of Han. The Han ran Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam as a single unit, Jiaozhi Province, and its southern tip became an entry point for merchants arriving from the west, some from as distant as Rome. During the Three Kingdoms period the Wu kingdom turned Guangdong into a province in its own right in 226 CE, called Guang Province.

Canton in those centuries was a thriving harbour town on a tropical frontier. Illness and dangerous animals were a hazard there, but the land produced oranges, bananas, lychees and banyan trees. Traders from Persia, India and the Malay world bought silk and chinaware, and also slaves, and paid with the medicines the place was known for and with scented tropical timber. People of different faiths lived together in the lively town. Shi'a Muslims who escaped persecution in Khorasan and Buddhists from India each built their own houses of worship, and a foreign quarter formed along the river where Arabs, Singhalese and merchants of many other origins settled.
Arab and Persian raiders attacked the port in 758, and its importance declined. In 684, for instance, a merchant ship's captain killed a governor who had abused his position to rob the merchant.

In 627, under the Tang, Guangdong and Guangxi were joined as part of Lingnan Circuit, also called Mountain-South Circuit. In 971, under the Song (960-1279), Guangdong's part was renamed Guangnan East Circuit (廣南東路), and "Guangnan East" (廣南東) is where the name "Guangdong" (廣東; 广东) comes from.

The makeup of the population slowly changed until Han Chinese dominated. Commerce brought the groups into contact, and from about the end of the 3rd century BCE the state also organised colonisation that moved large numbers of northern soldiers, civilians and convicts or exiles south. The pace picked up after the Han fell, as waves of people left the north whenever it was in political turmoil or under attack by nomads. After the rebellion led by An Lushan, for instance, fighting in the north helped to raise the population of Guangzhou prefecture by 75% between the 740s-750s and the 800s-810s. As more settlers came, the local people were either absorbed into Han culture or displaced.

As the Mongols swept across China in the 1200s, the Southern Song court abandoned its capital at Hangzhou and headed south. Its final defeat came at the hands of a Mongol fleet at the Battle of Yamen, in Guangdong, in 1279, ending the Southern Song (960-1279). Under the Yuan, who were Mongol rulers, a large part of what is now Guangdong was administered from Jiangxi. The province received its present name of "Guangdong" in the early Ming period.

From the 1500s onward Guangdong traded widely with the outside world. Merchants from Europe, mainly Portuguese and British, sailed up through the South China Sea after passing the Straits of Malacca, and much of their business went through Guangzhou. The first European settlement in China was Macau, on the province's southern coast, founded in 1557.

In the late 18th and early 19th centuries pirates, notably the Guangdong Pirate Confederation, badly afflicted the coast, especially around the Pearl River delta, until the Portuguese Navy and Qing forces suppressed them together.

During the 19th century the opium trade running through Guangzhou sparked the First Opium War, which began a long period of Western imperialist intrusion in China. Macau was by then Portuguese. Hong Kong passed to Britain, and France obtained Kouang-Tchéou-Wan, the area around present-day Zhanjiang.

Large numbers of people emigrated from Guangdong, and it was easy to travel on from Hong Kong to other territories of the British Empire and later the Commonwealth, so Guangdong or Cantonese roots are found in many overseas Chinese communities. Cantonese, Hakka and Teochew are spoken by a larger share of overseas Chinese than Mandarin. Taishanese speakers also settled in Western countries in numbers. As a result, many Chinese words known in the West, "dim sum" among them, come from Cantonese and not from standard Mandarin. A few Mandarin words borrowed from foreign languages also came via Cantonese: níngméng (simplified 柠檬, traditional 檸檬), the Mandarin for lemon, derives from Cantonese lìng mung. In the United States, a large number of Chinese people descend from emigrants from the county-level city of Taishan, Toisan in Cantonese, whose speech, Taishanese, is a separate dialect related to Cantonese.

Guangdong also played a part in the mid-19th-century upheavals. Hong Xiuquan, who led the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, was born in the province, and it was there that a Protestant missionary gave him a pamphlet. In the 1850s the Taipings joined forces with a local movement, the Red Turban Rebellion (1854-1856). Because it had direct contact with the West, Guangdong became a centre of both anti-Manchu and anti-imperialist activity, and the person usually regarded as the founder of modern China, Sun Yat-sen, was from here too.
Urbanisation is far advanced: as of 2024 the province's population was split 75.9% urban to 24.1% rural.

Han Chinese make up most of the population, yet they are such a varied group that the province has earned the nickname "treasure trove of regional languages" (方言寶庫). The largest Han subgroup is the Cantonese. East of the Pearl River Delta there are sizeable Hakka and Teoswa communities, and the province also has small numbers of Mien, She, Hmong, Li and Zhuang people. Anyone planning life here should expect to hear Mandarin, Cantonese and several other speech forms in daily life.

guangzhou-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.

Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.

guilin-medical-university.h: Guilin Medical University at a glance

blocks.x: Guilin Medical University (GLMU, 桂林医科大学 in simplified Chinese, 桂林醫科大學 in traditional) is a public university in Guilin, in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. It teaches undergraduates and postgraduates through its School of Medicine, its School of Nursing and Midwifery, and its Graduate School.
The Chinese name of the university was changed on February 21, 2025, after approval from the Ministry of Education. If you meet older documents or websites, they may use the earlier Chinese name.

GLMU began in 1935 as the Guilin Senior Nurse Midwifery School. In 1958 it was reorganised and renamed Guilin Medical School. In 1987 the former State Board of Education approved its upgrade to a college for medical undergraduates. It received permission to train foreign students in 1993 and to run graduate programmes in 2006. The Ministry of Education of China recognised it as an "Excellent University" in 2012.

Over a five-year period, the university carried out 945 research projects. Of these, 117 were national projects and 161 were provincial or ministerial projects, and gained 44 science and technology achievement awards of different levels. It won 49 national patents, 12 of them invention patents, and published 4,194 research papers, including 168 indexed in SCI and EI and 1,791 in Chinese core journals. In nearly five years it also completed 134 provincial teaching reform projects. It has received the national teaching award, along with 33 provincial teaching achievement awards. These figures come from the university's own summaries and cover an earlier five-year window, so ask the university for current numbers.

The university has been featured in publications including the "Chinese Medicine" academic journal, "China Journal", the online journal "Articles Digital Periodicals", the American Chemical Abstracts journal, and the Guangxi outstanding scientific journal.
The school's motto is 弘德善医 ("hóng dé shàn yī"). Its philosophy rests on four ideas:
1. A moral education foundation matters, and a medical college must teach the essence of modern education.
2. Medical and teaching staff should show good morals and the value of saving lives.
3. Generations of Guangxi medical students should study hard in search of truth and strive for the peak of medical science and technology.
4. Doctors have a duty to heal the sick, ease pain and unknown illnesses, and show a noble spirit of selfless dedication.
GLMU has three campuses, Lequn (Le Qun), Dongcheng (Dong Cheng) and Lingui, with a combined area of 1,334.27 acres.

Le Qun is the oldest campus. It is in downtown Guilin, across from the Affiliated Hospital of Guilin Medical University, rated among the best hospitals in Guangxi Province, where medical students train and practise. It is also next to the famous Li River and to the Jingjiang Princes' City.

Dong Cheng is the university's main campus, on the Li River's east bank, close to Guilin University of Technology and the Shangri-La Hotels and Resorts. This is where you will find offices like the Foreign Languages Department and the International Education Department, and international medical students take their classes here.

Lingui, in the Lingui District, is the biggest campus. It has enough room for the students enrolled, and with a lake, tall trees and colourful flowers around it, it offers an environmentally friendly setting for teachers, students and guests.
The university has 20 secondary college departments and six affiliated hospitals, as well as 94 classrooms for practical teaching and 23 laboratories for clinical teaching.

GLMU puts clinical medicine first, alongside pharmacy, nursing, medical assay and biotechnology. It describes itself as a multi-major university that has developed harmoniously, with considerable all-round strength and a clear influence both in and beyond the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. It takes an active role in international exchange and cooperation and was one of the earliest higher education institutions recognised by the former State Education Committee.

At present GLMU has both Chinese and international students at undergraduate (majors) and graduate level. The international students come from Thailand, Vietnam, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Nepal, which the source groups as students from Southeast Asia and its neighbours.

College of Nursing
College of Clinical Medicine at Nanxi Shan

Daily life depends on the city: its weather, how you travel and what you can do. The sections below describe Guilin and then the wider region of Guangxi.

Guilin is in northern Guangxi. It borders Liuzhou on the west, Laibin on the southwest, Wuzhou on the south and Hezhou on the southeast, while across the border in Hunan are Huaihua (northwest), Shaoyang (north) and Yongzhou (east). The total area is 27,809 square kilometres (10,737 square miles). The landscape is marked by karst formations, and the karsts around Guilin are made of limestone and dolomite from the Triassic period.

The Li River, which runs from Guilin to Yangshuo over 83 km, is among the city's most celebrated natural sights. It is known for emerald water and limestone peaks, and this stretch of river shows karst terrain in very concentrated form.

Notable hills and mountains include Yao Hill (尧山), Kitten Mountain, which is the highest summit in Guangxi, the Lipu Mountains, Elephant Trunk Hill, Diecai Hill (叠彩山) and Wave-Subduing Hill (伏波山). Notable caves are:
Seven-star Cave
Reed Flute Cave

The climate here is monsoon-influenced and humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa, bordering on Cwa). Winters are brief and mild, while summers are lengthy, hot and humid. Winter opens dry and becomes progressively more damp and cloudy. Spring tends to be grey and frequently wet. Summer continues to be rainy but is the sunniest time of year, and autumn is sunny and dry.

The average temperature over 24 hours is 8.1 °C (46.6 °F) for January, climbing to 28.2 °C (82.8 °F) by July, with an annual mean of 19.12 °C (66.4 °F). Yearly rainfall comes to just below 1,890 mm (74 in), around half of it between April and June, the period of the plum rains, arrive and often bring a risk of flooding. Possible sunshine ranges between 14% in March and 53% in September, giving 1,487 hours of bright sun per year. Temperatures since 1951 have swung between −4.9 °C (23 °F) (an unofficial −5.0 °C, also 23 °F, was noted on 25 January 1940) and 40.3 °C (105 °F).
For a student, the plum rain months of April to June are the ones to prepare for with rain gear.

The 2020 Chinese census counted 4,931,137 people. Within that total, 2,148,641 people lived in the built-up (metro) area, which consists of six urban districts together with Lingchuan County, which has now merged into the built-up zone. For the end of 2024 the resident population of the city was given as 4,950,700.

In the 2010 census Han Chinese made up the biggest ethnic group in this prefecture-level city, at 84.53% of the population, followed by Yao (7.79%) and Zhuang (4.81%). People in the urban area use a Mandarin dialect, whereas Pinghua is mainly spoken in the suburbs and surrounding areas.
GDP per capita was ¥41,891 (about US$6,569) in 2020, ranking 134th among 659 Chinese cities.

Local industries include condoms, pharmaceutical goods, tyres, machinery, fertiliser, silk, perfume, wine, tea, cinnamon and herbal medicine. Local agricultural products include Shatian pomelo, summer orange, Fructus Momordicae (luo han guo), ginkgo and moon persimmon; Lipu taro and water chestnut; grain and fish; and prepared foods such as Sanhua liquor, pepper sauce, fermented bean curd, Guilin rice noodles and rolls of dried bean milk cream.

Until 1949 Guilin had just one thermal power plant, a cement works and a handful of small textile mills as signs of industrialisation. Since the 1950s it has added electronics, engineering, agricultural equipment, medicine, rubber, bus, textile and cotton yarn factories. The most important industry is still food processing, including that of local farm produce, which remains the most important industry. More recent industry features high technology, and the service sector is built around tourism, trading and services.

A visa is not required for ASEAN citizens visiting Guilin when they are part of a tour lasting up to 144 hours, not counting the day of arrival. This rule is for tourist groups, not for study, so students still need the proper study visa.
The city's airport is Guilin Liangjiang International Airport (ICAO: ZGKL, IATA: KWL). The airlines serving it include:

High-speed trains stop at several Guilin stations, named Guilin North, Guilin West and Guilin, with another new station in Lingui District. Guilin and Guilin North stations are on the Hunan-Guangxi railway, the Hengyang-Liuzhou intercity railway and the Guiyang-Guangzhou high-speed railway, the main lines that connect Guangxi with central and southern China.

Fast trains linking Guilin with Changsha and Beijing began running from North Station in December 2013, and in December 2014 high-speed services to Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Guiyang and Shanghai were added, making it easier to reach Guilin. Journey times are about 2 to 3 hours from Guangzhou, 9 hours from Shanghai and 13 hours from Beijing. Trains running from Kunming South to West Kowloon station, for instance, stop at Guilin West railway station.

Public transport consists of bus routes and taxis. Guilin leads mainland China for regular double-decker bus service on major routes, and on its main street the double-deckers run almost every minute, one after another. Boats for sightseers also operate on canals and lakes in the city.

A Guilin Metro has been planned, with 7 lines by 2040, 273.2 kilometres in all and 117 stations. Line 1 was planned to open by 2025, at 29.23 km with 13 stations. As this is a plan, confirm the current status before you rely on it.

Guilin cuisine mixes Cantonese and Zhuang cooking. It is known for snacks and for heavy use of spices, especially chilli. Guilin chilli sauce (桂林辣椒酱), used widely in local cooking, is made from fresh chilli, garlic and fermented soybeans and is counted among what locals call the city's Three Treasures (桂林三宝). Guilin pickled tofu is the second, and the third is Guilin Sanhua Jiu (桂林三花酒), a rice baijiu, a spirit distilled from rice.

Rice noodles, a local breakfast staple ever since the Qin dynasty, are famed for their delicate taste. The local speciality is noodles with horse meat, but the dish can be had without the horse meat. Another popular treat is zongzi, a dumpling of glutinous rice and mung bean paste wrapped in a bamboo or banana leaf.
Guilin Medical University lies in Guangxi, and a university's surrounding region affects student life as strongly as the campus. The sections below describe Guangxi.

guilin-medical-university.h: The earliest rulers: Baiyue and Nanyue

blocks.x: Early Guangxi was home to a patchwork of tribal peoples that the Chinese called the Baiyue ("Hundred Yue"; Vietnamese Bách Việt), and it became a part of China during the Qin dynasty. In 214 BC the general Zhao Tuo (Vietnamese Triệu Đà), a Han Chinese, took most of the south for the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, shortly before the emperor died. In the civil war that followed, Zhao seized his chance and founded his own kingdom at Panyu, named Nanyue ("Southern Yue"). Sometimes it bowed to the Han and sometimes it acted alone. Under a policy of "Harmonizing and Gathering the Hundred Yue" (和集百越), it spread settlement and sinicisation, until Nanyue fell in 111 BC as the Han dynasty pushed south.

The roots of the name "Guangxi" go back to Eastern Wu's "Expansive" or "Wide" province (廣州). That state controlled the southeast of China in the Three Kingdoms period, and Guilin was one of that province's commanderies. In Tang times, the Zhuang threw their weight behind Nanzhao, the kingdom of Piluoge in Yunnan, which beat back imperial armies in 751 and again in 754. After that Guangxi split into two zones: Zhuang influence prevailed in the part west of Nanning, and Han influence in the part east of it.

When Southern Zhao collapsed, Liu Yan set up the Southern Han state (Nanhan), centred on Xingwangfu in modern Guangdong. Its hold on Guangxi was slight, and the unstable state was taken over by the Song dynasty in 971. It was the Song who gave Guangxi its name, governing it as the Guangnanxi ("West Southern Expanse") Circuit. Pressed by both the Song and the Jiaozhi of modern Vietnam, the Zhuang chief Nong Zhigao rose in revolt in 1052, an act the Zhuang still honour. His kingdom was short-lived, though: the Song general Di Qing, who was tattooed, brought Guangxi back under Chinese rule.

The Yuan dynasty gained Yunnan by conquering the Dali Kingdom in 1253, and ended the Southern Song after the Battle of Yamen in 1279. The Mongols did not treat Lingnan as a subject land or a military district; they turned Guangxi ("Western Expanse") into a full province. Even so the area stayed restless, and the Ming dynasty set its various local peoples against each other. In 1465, a clash between the Zhuang and the Yao, the Battle of Big Rattan Gorge, was reported to have killed 20,000.
During the Ming and Qing dynasties the powerful Cen (岑) clan ruled parts of Guangxi. The Cen were Zhuang by ethnicity and were recognised by the emperors as tusi, or local rulers.

Through the 19th century, after the Qing had left the region more or less alone until direct rule came in 1726, unrest was constant. A Yao rising in 1831 came first. In January 1851 the Jintian Uprising began the Taiping Rebellion, and in April 1854 the Da Cheng Rebellion followed. Local officials in Guangxi put St. Auguste Chapdelaine to death, which triggered the 1858 outbreak of the Second Opium War and made foreign meddling in the interior legal. In the Sino-French War of 1884 the Guangxi Army saw heavy fighting; Louis Brière de l'Isle could not capture its depot at Longzhou. The army did little good inside Vietnam, yet on 23 March 1885 it succeeded in expelling the French from Chinese soil itself, at Zhennan Pass (now Friendship Pass).

In the wake of the Wuchang Uprising, Guangxi broke away from the Qing on 6 November 1911. Its Qing governor, Shen Bingdan, stayed in office at first, then a mutiny under General Lu Rongting removed him. Lu's Old Guangxi clique went on to seize Hunan and Guangdong, and it was one of the leaders in the war to protect the republic (National Protection War) against Yuan Shikai's bid to bring back imperial rule. Because the Zhuang were loyal, Lu's Self-Government Army held together but was unwilling to go far from its home provinces. A feud with Sun Yat-sen ended in defeat in the Guangdong-Guangxi War (1920 to 1921). Chen Jiongming's Cantonese forces occupied the region briefly, and then, for years, Guangxi was divided and plagued by banditry. That lasted until Li Zongren's Guangxi Pacification Army created the New Guangxi clique, run by Li with Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi.

Victory over Wu Peifu in Hunan earned the Zhuang pacification force its nicknames, "Flying Army" and "Army of Steel". When Sun Yat-sen died, Li crushed a revolt by Tang Jiyao and took part in the Northern Expedition, which brought other warlords under the control of the Republic of China. Few Kuomintang units were so free of serious influence from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which is why Chiang Kai-shek turned to Li's army for the Shanghai massacre of 1927. In the story of the People's Republic, Guangxi is also remembered for the Baise Uprising of 1929, an unsuccessful CCP uprising led by Chen Zhaoli together with Deng Xiaoping.

Soong Mei-ling called on women to support the war against Japan, and the Guangxi Women's Battalion was raised in 1937 to answer her call. Accounts disagree about how big it was: estimates range between 130 students, 500 and 800.

Located in the far south, Guangxi was not conquered in the Chinese Civil War. It entered the People's Republic in December 1949, two months after the republic was proclaimed. A coastal strip of Guangdong (Beihai, Fangchenggang, Qinzhou and Lianzhou, now Hepu County) was handed to Guangxi in 1952, which gave it a coastline. The transfer was reversed in 1955 and restored in 1965, so Guangxi is the one autonomous region without land on all sides.
During the Cultural Revolution, the Guangxi Massacre killed between 100,000 and 150,000 people across the region in 1967 and 1968.

Some heavy industry came in the 1960s and 1970s, but mostly Guangxi remained a destination for sightseers, and the boom of the 1990s seemed to bypass it. More recently, industrialisation has grown and cash crops have become a bigger focus. As Guangdong's industries move production to cheaper-labour areas in Guangxi, per capita GDP has climbed.

When China fought Vietnam in 1979, communities in Guangxi mattered a great deal to the effort. They fed and housed troops of the People's Liberation Army and supplied other logistical help, while militia members from Guangxi built roads, bridges and trenches, took on other support tasks and looked after the wounded.

Nanning, Liuzhou, Guilin and Beihai are the main cities of Guangxi, and Longmen, Sanjiang and Yangshuo are notable towns. Waterways in the Xi River system lead to the Pearl River Delta. The brief coast along the Gulf of Tonkin holds Guangxi's key seaports, Beihai, Qinzhou and Fangchenggang. The Pinglu Canal was built to join the Xi River system to the coast.

Taiwanese investment in Guangxi was brisk in the mid-2000s. In 2007, seventy-one new Taiwanese ventures opened there, with contracts of up to US$149 million, and gross exports went beyond US$1 billion. The total number of Taiwanese ventures in the region is 1,182, and up to the end of 2006 they had put US$4.27 billion into the autonomous region. In the first half of 2007, Guangxi and Taiwanese investors had contracted 43 projects, valued at RMB 2.6 billion (US$342 million). Their cooperation involves manufacturing, high-tech electronics, farming, energy resources and tourism. These figures are from 2006 and 2007, so they describe the situation of that time.
Seven cities in Guangxi have an airport: Beihai, Baise, Guilin, Hechi, Liuzhou, Nanning and Wuzhou.
