GUET (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) is a provincial university in Guangxi, in the south of China. Founded in 1960, it has become a university built around electronic information technology, with further teaching in business management, literature, law, education and mechanical engineering. A branch research body, the Guilin Electronics Nanning Research Institute, operates in Nanning.

The library shows how large the university has become: its floor area exceeds 45,000 square metres, and the collection includes more than 2.4465 million printed books and over 2.069 million e-books. Readers can search 78 Chinese and foreign databases and over 554,000 electronic journals in Chinese and other languages. Technology is also part of daily campus life, through an advanced network information platform and a smart campus platform.

guilin-university-of-electronic-technolo.h: Founding in the Great Leap era

blocks.x: The origins lie in China's Second Five-Year Plan. In 1958 the First Ministry of Machine-Building Industry drew up a plan for training technical specialists and skilled workers to drive the country's industrialisation. The ministry's order of 12 February 1960 called for two schools, a mechanical college and a trade school, both in Guilin. In April 1960, before they had opened, the ministry decided to combine them: the trade school became part of the college, which then had a Secondary Specialized Division and a Trade Training Division.

The new college took over a former sanatorium in the eastern suburbs of Guilin as its first home, and an opening ceremony took place on 15 September 1960. The six technical subjects offered by this junior college at the start included radio, radar, computing and machine manufacturing.

Economic crisis soon halted this progress. Following the severe hardships after the Great Leap Forward, central authorities ordered educational institutions everywhere to shrink. GUET's predecessor lost its Trade Training Division in June 1961 and, in April 1962, was downgraded to a secondary specialised school with the name Guilin Mechanical Industry School.

No students were recruited at all from 1966 to 1971, during the Cultural Revolution. In spring 1972 teaching resumed under the name Guilin Radio School, taking in junior high school graduates and young people who had been sent to farm in the countryside. From 1973 to 1976 the students were workers, peasants and soldiers selected through political recommendation, not by examination. Admission on merit came back in 1977, when the National College Entrance Examination was reinstated.

As higher education returned to normal after the Cultural Revolution, the Guangxi People's Government suggested in early 1978 that Guilin Radio School be upgraded to a university-level college. Two years of preparation followed, then approval from both the State Council and the Ministry of Education. The Fourth Ministry of Machine-Building Industry gave final authorisation on 20 May 1980 for a new Guilin Institute of Electronic Technology.
The upgraded institute started with three academic departments and six majors:
Electronic and Mechanical Engineering: manufacturing processes and equipment, and the structure of electronic equipment
Radio Engineering: communications engineering, plus electronic instruments and measurement methods
Computer Science: computers and their applications, and automation

To strengthen its teaching, the institute leaned on established universities. Northwest Institute of Telecommunication Engineering transferred 122 employees, among them 87 teachers, and another 28 lecturers came from institutions such as Inner Mongolia University and the Huazhong Institute of Technology.

Its range of courses kept growing. Short training courses and workshops began in October 1982, adult higher education in 1984, and sub-degree diploma courses in 1985. Authority to confer bachelor's degrees was granted on 10 July 1984. For postgraduates, 1985 saw the start of a joint master's course run with Northwest Institute of Telecommunication Engineering and later with further leading universities; full independence in awarding master's degrees came in December 1993.

A reform of administration in Chinese higher education transferred control in February 2000 from a central body, the Ministry of Information Industry, to the Guangxi People's Government. On 24 February 2006 the institution was recognised as a university and took its current name.
Four campuses make up GUET, with 4,700 mu (313 ha) in total. Three are in Guilin itself and the fourth is in the coastal city of Beihai:
Huajiang Campus, also called Yaoshan Campus
Jinjiling Campus, also known as East Campus
Liuhe Road Campus, also known as West Campus
Beihai Campus, in the city of Beihai
As of 2026, eighteen academic schools, colleges and a cooperative institute carry out teaching and research, covering engineering, the natural sciences, management and the humanities.

guilin-university-of-electronic-technolo.h: A note on a past controversy

blocks.x: In November 2018 the university announced plans to inspect mobile phones, computers and external hard drives on campus. The stated purpose was to stop the spread of material inciting violence or terrorism, harmful political information, pornography and other content considered corrupting. After the idea met with disapproval from many quarters, the university reconsidered it. It is a good example of why prospective students should read current campus rules carefully.
The following people are associated with GUET:
Jin Shi, an IEEE Fellow who is a vice president at Southeast University
Gou Ping, who chairs China Satellite Network Group
Ouyang Shan, once a professor at GUET's School of Information and Communication and later one of its vice presidents
Chen Pinghua, who formerly headed discipline inspection for the PLA Rocket Force
The weather, the food and the transport options in Guilin will shape your daily routine. This part introduces the city.

The city occupies 27,809 square kilometres (10,737 sq mi) in northern Guangxi. Its neighbours in Guangxi are Liuzhou (west), Laibin (south-west), Wuzhou (south) and Hezhou (south-east), and in Hunan province it faces Huaihua (north-west), Shaoyang (north) and Yongzhou (east).

The landscape is defined by karst. Around Guilin it is Triassic limestone and dolomite that form the strange peaks. The 83 km of the Li River between Guilin and Yangshuo, with green water running beneath limestone pinnacles, ranks among the city's best-loved natural sights and shows karst terrain at its densest.

Well-known hills include Elephant Trunk Hill, Yao Hill (尧山), Wave-Subduing Hill (伏波山) and Diecai Hill (叠彩山), and the Lipu Mountains also belong to the area. Kitten Mountain is the highest peak in all of Guangxi. For caves, visit the Reed Flute Cave and the Seven-star Cave.

Guilin's climate is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence, classified Köppen Cfa but close to Cwa. Winters are short and mild; summers are long, hot and humid. Winter starts dry but gets wetter and cloudier. Spring is mostly overcast and often wet, while summer stays rainy but is the sunniest season. Autumn is sunny and dry.

January is the coolest month, at a daily average of 8.1 °C (46.6 °F), and July the warmest, at 28.2 °C (82.8 °F); the whole year averages 19.12 °C (66.4 °F). Rainfall totals just under 1,890 mm (74 in) a year, with roughly half falling from April to June, the season of "plum rains", when flooding is a frequent risk. Sunshine ranges from 14% of the possible total in March to 53% in September, for 1,487 hours of bright sunshine over a year. Records from 1951 onward run from a low of -4.9 °C (23 °F) to a high of 40.3 °C (105 °F); a cold reading of -5.0 °C (23 °F), unofficial, dates from 25 January 1940.
A built-up metro area of six urban districts, joined now by Lingchuan County through continuous building, is home to 2,148,641 of them.

The 2010 census showed Han Chinese as the biggest ethnic group in the city (84.53%), with the Yao at 7.79% and the Zhuang at 4.81%. People in the urban area speak a Mandarin dialect, whereas Pinghua is mainly spoken in the suburbs and surrounding areas. The resident population is expected to reach 4,950,700 by the end of 2024.
Per capita GDP in 2020 was ¥41891 (about US$6569), ranking 134th among 659 Chinese cities. Local products are varied. Lists in the available material name these:
Industries: machinery, tires, fertilizer, pharmaceuticals, condoms, silk, perfume, wine, tea, cinnamon and herbal medicine

Agricultural goods: Shatian pomelo, summer orange, luo han guo (Fructus Momordicae), ginkgo, moon persimmon, Lipu taro, Sanhua alcohol, pepper sauce, fermented bean curd, water chestnut, rice noodles, grain, fish and dried bean milk cream rolled tightly

Industrialisation was slow to arrive. Up to 1949 the only signs of it were a thermal power station, a cement works and a handful of small textile mills. The 1950s began a build-up of factories making electronics, engineering and farm equipment, medicines, rubber goods, buses, textiles and cotton yarn. Food processing, which includes handling local farm produce, is still the most important industry. Newer industry includes high technology, and services are marked by tourism, trade and other service businesses.
For visitors from ASEAN countries, a visa is not required to visit Guilin as part of a tour that lasts a maximum of 144 hours, not counting the day of arrival.
The city's airport is Guilin Liangjiang International Airport (codes ZGKL and KWL). Carriers serving it include:
China Eastern
China Southern, among the largest
Air China (a national carrier)
Hainan Airlines
Shanghai Airlines
Shandong Airlines
Xiamen Airlines
Tianjin Airlines
Beijing Capital Airlines
Hebei Airlines
Asiana Airlines
EVA Air
Air Asia

The main rail stations are Guilin, Guilin North and Guilin West, with a further new one in Lingui District; several of them handle high-speed trains. Both Guilin and Guilin North lie on three lines: the Hunan-Guangxi railway, the Hengyang-Liuzhou intercity railway and the Guiyang-Guangzhou high-speed railway, together the chief links between Guangxi and central and southern China.

High-speed trains between Guilin North and both Changsha and Beijing started in December 2013, and in December 2014 services began to Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Guiyang and Shanghai, making the city easier to reach. A journey to Guilin from Guangzhou lasts about 2 or 3 hours, from Shanghai about 9, and from Beijing about 13. Guilin West is also a stop for services that connect Kunming South and West Kowloon.

Buses and taxis make up the public transport network. Guilin runs more regular double-decker services on major routes than any other mainland city, and along its main street one comes by nearly every minute. On the canals and lakes, sightseeing boats also run.

A metro is in the plans, and by 2040 the target is seven lines, 117 stations and 273.2 kilometres of track. The first line, 29.23 km with 13 stations, was due to open by 2025, so check whether it is already running.

The cooking here is a blend of Cantonese and Zhuang traditions, noted for snacks and for heavy use of spices, chilli above all. One of the "Three Treasures" (桂林三宝) of the city is Guilin chilli sauce (桂林辣椒酱), a cooking staple made of fresh chilli, garlic and fermented soybeans. Another is Sanhua Jiu (桂林三花酒), a rice liquor, and the third is pickled tofu.

Breakfast is rice noodles, a habit going back to the Qin dynasty, and they are prized for their delicate taste. The classic version comes with horse meat, though it is possible to leave that out. Zongzi, a parcel of glutinous rice with mung bean paste inside a bamboo or banana leaf, is another popular treat.

guilin-university-of-electronic-technolo.h: Guangxi: the region around the university

blocks.x: GUET belongs to the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Knowing something of its past helps explain why the area has such a mixed population and a frontier character, so here is a short tour of that history, from the first kingdoms to the end of the twentieth century.

Long before Chinese rule, tribal peoples whom the Chinese lumped together as the Baiyue (the "Hundred Yue", Bách Việt in Vietnamese) lived here. The Qin dynasty was the first to bring the region into China. In 214 BC a Han Chinese general, Zhao Tuo (Triệu Đà in Vietnamese), seized most of the south on behalf of Qin Shi Huang, shortly before that emperor died. Civil war broke out afterwards, and Zhao used the chaos to found a separate kingdom with its capital at Panyu, called Nanyue ("Southern Yue"). For some time it alternated between obeying and defying the Han, and it spread settlement and Chinese ways through a policy called "Harmonizing and Gathering the Hundred Yue" (和集百越). The Han marched south and ended it in 111 BC.

The name Guangxi has far older ancestors. One can be traced to a "Wide" or "Expansive" province (廣州) created by the Eastern Wu, a Three Kingdoms power that controlled south-eastern China; Guilin was among its commanderies.

guilin-university-of-electronic-technolo.h: From the Tang to the Ming

blocks.x: In the Tang era the Zhuang sided with Piluoge's Nanzhao kingdom in Yunnan, which defeated imperial armies in both 751 and 754. The result was a split: Zhuang influence prevailed to the west of Nanning, and Han influence to the east.

When Nanzhao collapsed, Liu Yan founded the Southern Han (Nanhan) in Xingwangfu, today's Guangdong. Its hold on Guangxi was slight, and its own instability led to annexation by the Song in 971. It was the Song who supplied the modern name, administering the territory as the Guangnanxi circuit, or "West Southern Expanse". Squeezed by both the Song and the Jiaozhi people of present-day Vietnam, the Zhuang leader Nong Zhigao rebelled in 1052, and he is still honoured among the Zhuang. His kingdom was brief, however: the Song general Di Qing, a man with tattoos, returned Guangxi to Chinese control.

The Mongol Yuan dynasty conquered the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan in 1253 and destroyed the Southern Song after the battle at Yamen in 1279. It chose to turn Guangxi ("Western Expanse") into a regular province, rather than governing Lingnan as a dependent territory or military district. Order was never secure, so the Ming responded by playing local groups off against one another. One result was the Battle of Big Rattan Gorge in 1465, in which the Zhuang and Yao fought and 20,000 deaths were reported.
Across the Ming and Qing periods, the Cen (岑) clan held power in parts of Guangxi. They were Zhuang by ethnicity, and the emperors acknowledged them as tusi, or hereditary local rulers.

guilin-university-of-electronic-technolo.h: Qing rule and the nineteenth century

blocks.x: The Qing largely left the region alone until direct rule was introduced in 1726, and the nineteenth century then brought continuous trouble. There was a Yao revolt in 1831; January 1851 saw the Jintian Uprising, which opened the Taiping Rebellion; and the Da Cheng Rebellion started in April 1854. Local officials in Guangxi executed St. Auguste Chapdelaine, an event that helped trigger the Second Opium War in 1858 and gave legal cover to foreign meddling inside China.

During the Sino-French War of 1884 the Guangxi Army saw heavy action. Louis Brière de l'Isle never managed to invade its supply depot at Longzhou, and although the army achieved little inside Vietnam, it drove the French off Chinese soil at the Battle of Zhennan Pass (today's Friendship Pass) on 23 March 1885.

Guangxi declared independence from the Qing on 6 November 1911, after the Wuchang Uprising. The Qing governor, Shen Bingdan, was at first left in place, but a mutiny led by General Lu Rongting later removed him. Lu headed the Old Guangxi clique, which also took Hunan and Guangdong and was a leader in the National Protection War against Yuan Shikai, who wanted to revive imperial rule. Loyalty among its Zhuang soldiers made the Self-Government Army cohesive, yet unwilling to venture far outside its own provinces. Disputes with Sun Yat-sen ended in defeat in the Guangdong-Guangxi War of 1920-1921. Chen Jiongming's Cantonese forces occupied the region briefly, and then it slipped into disunity and severe banditry for several years. Li Zongren's Guangxi Pacification Army finally created the New Guangxi clique, which was run by Li together with Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi.

The Zhuang soldiers of this army won victories against Wu Peifu in Hunan and gained the nicknames "Flying Army" and "Army of Steel". When Sun Yat-sen died, Li crushed a revolt by Tang Jiyao and joined the Northern Expedition, which placed other warlords under the Republic of China. Few Kuomintang units were as free as his of serious influence by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which is why Chiang Kai-shek used it in the 1927 Shanghai massacre. For the People's Republic, Guangxi's claim to fame is the Baise Uprising of 1929, a failed CCP revolt directed by Chen Zhaoli and Deng Xiaoping.

A women's unit, the Guangxi Women's Battalion, was founded in 1937 to answer Soong Mei-ling's appeal for women to support the war against Japan. Estimates of its strength vary widely, from 130 students to 500 or even 800.
Guangxi's remote southern position meant it was never conquered in the Civil War; it joined the People's Republic in December 1949, two months after the republic was proclaimed.

The question of coastal access has been unsettled. A small stretch of Guangdong's coast, comprising Qinzhou, Lianzhou (now Hepu County), Fangchenggang and Beihai, was assigned to Guangxi in 1952, so it could reach the sea. That was undone in 1955 and put back in 1965, making Guangxi the only autonomous region of China with a coastline.
The darkest episode was the Guangxi Massacre in the Cultural Revolution, when an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 people were killed in the region in 1967 and 1968.

Some heavy industry appeared in the 1960s and 1970s, but Guangxi was mainly known as a scenic destination, and the booming 1990s did not seem to lift it either. In the last few years that has begun to change, with more industry and a growing emphasis on cash crops. Industries in Guangdong are moving production to cheaper-labour parts of Guangxi, and per capita GDP is rising as a result.

The Sino-Vietnamese War of 1979 made Guangxi communities central to China's war effort. Local people provided the People's Liberation Army with food, housing and other logistical help, while militia members built roads, bridges and trenches and looked after the wounded.

Nanning, Liuzhou, Guilin and Beihai are the main cities of Guangxi, and Longmen, Sanjiang and Yangshuo are towns worth knowing. Waterways of the Xi River system run through to the Pearl River Delta. Along the short Gulf of Tonkin coast, the seaports that matter are Beihai, Qinzhou and Fangchenggang, and the Pinglu Canal was built to join the Xi River system to the coast.
Seven airports serve the region: Nanning and Guilin, plus Beihai, Liuzhou, Wuzhou, Baise and Hechi.
Guilin University of Electronic Technology lists 106 programs for international students on this site: 48 bachelor, 47 master's, 11 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 101 taught in Chinese, 5 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 13,000 to CNY 13,000 (median CNY 13,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

106 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (5):
Cyberspace Security
Information and Communication Engineering
Instrument Science and Technology
Mechanical Engineering
Optoelectronic Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

guilin-university-of-electronic-technolo.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guilin University of Electronic Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guilin, register at Guilin University of Electronic Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Guizhou Medical University (贵州医科大学 in simplified Chinese, 貴州醫科大學 in traditional characters) is a public university in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou province in south-west China. It teaches medicine and related health fields, including clinical medicine, nursing, pharmacy, medical laboratory science and preventive medicine, along with some other subjects.

Some materials describe the university as recognised by the World Health Organization and note that students from India can sit the Indian medical screening test after completing the five-year course. Recognition rules and listings change over time and differ by country, so any international applicant should confirm the current position directly with the university and with their own national medical regulator before applying.

guizhou-medical-university.h: From a wartime school to a provincial university

blocks.x: The story starts in 1938, when the central government in Beijing set up and directly ran a school called the National Guiyang Medical University. A change came in 2008, when it was renamed Guiyang Medical University and responsibility passed to the Guizhou provincial government. In June 2015 it was renamed again, this time as Guizhou Medical University, the name it carries now. Over the decades it has gained approval to teach undergraduate medicine, and it has the distinction of being the only provincial university devoted to medical postgraduate education.

Day-to-day life for a student is shaped by the city around the campus: how the weather feels, how people get about, and what there is to do in the evening. What follows introduces Guiyang, the city that hosts this university, and then the province of Guizhou around it.

The middle of Guiyang is organised around two landmarks. One is the Dashizi (大十字), whose name means big cross. The other, Penshuichi (喷水池, which translates as Fountain Pool), is a busy road junction. It once had a big fountain in the middle, but in early 2010 the fountain was covered over so that traffic could move more easily.

Guiyang has a humid subtropical climate with four seasons, shaped by the monsoon (Köppen Cwa), but both its low latitude and its high elevation soften the extremes. Winters are cool and summers are only moderately warm. Of the 1,149 millimetres (45.2 inches) of rain that the city gets in a year, most arrives from May to July. January is the coldest month, averaging 4.6 °C (40.3 °F), and July averages 23.8 °C (74.8 °F); the average across the whole year is 15.2 °C (59.4 °F). Showers are possible in any season, and in winter there are occasional light snow flurries.

Skies are often grey. Possible sunshine runs from 11% of the month in January up to 43% in August, and the whole year gets just 1150 hours, which makes Guiyang one of the least sunny major cities in China. Relative humidity stays above 75% on average in every month, so damp conditions are normal.

Pleasant summers, plus factors such as clean air and wind speed, put Guiyang second on a published list of China's ten best summer capitals. For the extremes, records since 1951 show a coldest day of -7.8 °C (18 °F) on 6 January 1970 (an unofficial -9.5 °C (15 °F) had been noted in January 1925) and a hottest day of 37.5 °C (100 °F) on 5 July 1952.

Guiyang is the commercial and economic centre of Guizhou. In 2017 the city region produced a GDP of 353.8 billion yuan, or 74,493 yuan ($10,720) per person, and the economy was growing at about 10% a year.

Shopping is big business as well, both retail and wholesale. Supermarket and department-store groups from China and abroad trade in the city: Wal-Mart, Carrefour, RT-Mart, Beijing Hualian, Parkson and the local Xingli Group (星力集团), while Gome and Suning sell electronics and appliances. Large wholesale depots deal in regional produce, furniture and heavy machinery for industry and construction. Wal-Mart's vegetable and produce distribution hub for the whole south-west is in Guiyang. Foreign brands have spread fast, with branches of McDonald's, Burger King, H&M and Starbucks, mostly beside shopping centres. The biggest centres are Huaguoyuan Shopping Center (花果园购物中心), Hunter City Plaza (亨特城市广场) and Nanguohuajing (南国花锦).

Energy and heavy industry are part of the picture. Hydro-electric generators sit along the city's main rivers, among them the Wu River, and by 2007 they were providing more than 70% of the electricity the city used. Coal is mined near Guiyang and Anshun, and large thermal power stations at Guiyang and Duyun supply a share of industrial electricity. A large iron and steel plant started production in Guiyang in 1960 to feed the local machinery industry.

The city has a sizeable pharmaceutical sector making both traditional Chinese and Western medicines, which is of obvious relevance to medical students. It has also finished the first stage of a free city-wide WiFi network, D-Guiyang, a joint venture between the city government and technology companies that include Alibaba and Foxconn.

In 2016 the Milken Institute named Guiyang China's Best-Performing City, citing growth in jobs, wages and gross domestic product. In the first half of that year, Guizhou's economy grew 10.5%, the third fastest among China's 31 provincial-level regions, and this was credited to Guiyang's investment in computing and big data. Tax breaks and state backing have drawn in big international names, and offices of Foxconn, Microsoft, Huawei, Hyundai Motor, Tencent, Qualcomm and Alibaba now exist in Guiyang.
Guiyang is home to 49 different minority groups, the largest of which are the Miao, apart from the Han Chinese majority.

The 2020 national census (the seventh) recorded a permanent population of 5,987,018 in the city. The census reports that the city grew by 1,664,407 people (38.5%) since the Sixth National Census in 2010. (One published summary calls this a decrease, but the urban and rural figures below show it was growth.) Of the permanent residents, 4,794,071 (80.07%) live in towns and cities and 1,192,947 (19.93%) in the countryside. Set against 2010, 1,861,786 more people live in urban areas, 197,379 fewer live in rural ones, and the urban share has risen by 12.23 percentage points. An earlier figure, for 2011, put the municipality at 4.3 million people, of whom 2.9 million were urban residents.

Local people speak a variety of Southwestern Mandarin, and some also use minority languages, Miao and Bouyei among them. The dialect lacks the retroflex consonants of standard Mandarin and has just three tones, whereas the standard language has four tones and a neutral one. It preserves many ancient Chinese words, and a few sound rather like Korean or Japanese. Take 去 (to go), pronounced "kèi" in the fourth tone instead of the standard "qù", and 做 (to do), pronounced "zo" in the fourth tone instead of "zuo". If your Mandarin is learned from textbooks, expect to need a few days of listening practice.
Each Chinese province is known for particular specialities, and Guiyang is best known for spicy food and for these dishes.
A sweet dessert called gaoba porridge (糕粑稀饭; Gāobāxīfàn)
Sour soup fish (酸汤鱼; Suāntāngyú), a Miao dish: roasted fish with assorted vegetables
Huangba (黄粑; Huángbā): a sweet rice wrap that can be steamed or fried
Huaxi beef vermicelli (花溪牛肉粉; Huāxī Niúròufěn): rice noodles with beef, commonly eaten for breakfast in Guiyang
Siwawa (丝娃娃; Sīwáwa): thin rice wraps filled with vegetables, either vegetarian or mixed with scraps of pork
Ice jelly (冰粉; Bīngfěn): served with sesame seeds and peanuts, usually in summer and often alongside siwawa or barbecue
Chang-Wang noodles (肠旺面; Chángwàngmiàn): noodles with pig's intestines and pig's blood
Qingyan pig's feet (青岩猪脚; Qīngyán Zhūjiǎo): found mostly in the old town of Qingyan, where pig's feet are a symbol of good luck
Potato cake (洋芋粑; Yángyù bā): mashed potato fried into pancakes and seasoned with chilli powder, a common street snack
Sour soup beef (酸汤牛肉; Suāntāng niúròu): the same tangy broth, used for stewing beef rather than fish, and a refreshing way to whet the appetite
Since the mid-2000s Guiyang has also built up a coffee culture. As of 2025 it has over 3,000 coffee shops, which gives it the highest density of any Chinese city.
As the capital of a province with deep traditions, Guiyang keeps a good number of historic sights that attract tourists.

Jiaxiu Pavilion (甲秀楼; Jiǎxiù Lóu) stands at the southern end of the Nanming River in Guiyang and is regarded as the emblem of the city. It was first built in 1598 in the Ming dynasty, was destroyed several times, and was most recently rebuilt in 1982.
Qingyan Ancient Town (青岩古镇) lies at the southern edge of Guiyang. It dates from 1378, in the Ming dynasty, and is admired for its traditional Chinese architecture.

Xifeng Concentration Camp (息烽集中营; Xīfēng Jízhōngyín) was the biggest and highest-level prison set up by the Nationalist government's military commission during the Second Sino-Japanese War, and the State Council listed it as a major historical and cultural site under state protection in 1988.
Confucian Center (孔学堂; Kǒngxuétáng) is an educational organisation that is not a public body, connected with the Ministry of Education and with the promotion of Chinese culture and language.

Xifeng Hot Spring (息烽温泉) is in the north-east of Xifeng County, in a ring of mountains whose slopes are rich in pine, fir, bamboo and other plants. The setting has made it a good place for sanatoriums, hospitals and villas.

Qianling Park (黔灵公园) is in the north-west of Guiyang. It is named after Mount Qianling, described as the most majestic mountain in southern Guizhou. Dense vegetation covers the park, which holds more than 1,500 species of flowers and trees and at least 1,000 medicinal plants. Hongfu Temple there dates from the end of the Ming and start of the Qing dynasties and is among Guizhou's most famous.

Huaxi National Wetland Park (花溪湿地公园), in the north of the city's Huaxi district, is one of the few urban wetlands in China. It lies in a plateau karst hill region with a humid subtropical climate, and its geology and location give it a rich variety of landscapes.

Nightlife is lively and informal. The busiest street is Qianling East Road (黔灵东路), nicknamed Drinking Street because so many pubs and bars line it. Guizhou is the home of Moutai, a famous Chinese liquor, so drinking is something of a tradition. In Guiyang beer is poured into small cups, and people often play dice or card games while they drink.

When evening comes, street food appears everywhere. On Shaanxi Road (陕西路) you can get roast chicken, baked snails and mutton chops. Bo'ai Road (博爱路) has glutinous rice, rice noodles, mutton patties and dishes that mix western and eastern styles. Many older residents spend the evening on outdoor games such as mahjong, or on square dancing.
Guiyang has a wide network of roads, railways, river routes and air services, and a public transport system of buses and plenty of taxis.

The city is one of the key air hubs of south-west China. Its main airport is Guiyang Longdongbao International Airport (KWE), which opened on 28 May 1997, in the east of the city 11 km (6.8 miles) from the centre. In 2017 it handled over 18 million passengers, three times as many as in 2010.
Building of the Guiyang Metro started in 2011. Line 1 opened in December 2017, Line 2 in April 2021 and Line 3 in December 2023.

Guiyang is a railway hub for the south-west. Four older lines cross at Guiyang Railway Station: the Guizhou-Guangxi Railway (built in 1959 and modified in 2009), the Sichuan-Guizhou Railway (finished 1965), the Guiyang-Kunming Railway (1970) and the Hunan-Guizhou Railway (1975). The station, the city's main southern one, was rebuilt in 2008.

Since 2008 high-speed rail has expanded quickly. The Guiyang-Guangzhou, Shanghai-Kunming and Chongqing-Guiyang high-speed lines opened one after another. Travel times to almost every first-tier city have dropped sharply: about 8 hours to Beijing, 9 to Shanghai, 4.5 to Guangzhou, 4 to Chengdu and roughly 2 to Chongqing. Two rail yards handle fast freight, and passengers use Guiyang North railway station in the Guanshanhu District. Timetables change, so check before booking.

Education in the city covers 224 primary and middle schools and several colleges, including a teacher-training college and a medical school. The Nature Index, which tracks scientific research output, placed Guiyang in the world's top 150 science cities in 2025. Guizhou University, the city's flagship, is a national research university within Project 211 and is supported under the Double First-Class Construction scheme for selected disciplines.
Institutions in the city include the following.
Guizhou University, together with Guizhou Normal University
Guizhou Medical University itself
Guizhou University of Finance and Economics and Guizhou Nationalities University
Guizhou Institute of Technology
Guiyang College and Guiyang College of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Commercial College of Guizhou

Qianming Temple, in the city's Nanming District, goes back to the 17th century and the late Ming. Christianity has a place here too. On 15 October 1696 Guiyang was chosen as the seat of a Catholic body then called the Apostolic Vicariate of Kweichow. That body was shut down in 1715 and revived in 1846; it took the name Apostolic Vicariate of Guiyang in 1924, and in 1946 it was given today's rank, the Archdiocese of Guiyang.
Your university is located in Guizhou, and the surrounding province shapes student life just as much as the campus. The next sections cover Guizhou's past, its landscape and its rivers.

People lived here long ago. Stone tools, including Levallois pieces, found in excavations at Guanyindong Cave show settlement in the Middle Palaeolithic. Optically stimulated luminescence dating places them around 170,000 to 80,000 years ago.

From about 1046 BC until the rise of the State of Qin, the north-west of Guizhou belonged to the State of Shu. Chu seized the area in the Warring States era, and it then passed to the Dian Kingdom. The Dian owed tribute to the Han dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD), in whose time Guizhou was inhabited by a loose group of tribes called the Yelang. They mostly governed themselves until the Han tightened their grip on the south-west and set up the Lingnan province. By the time of the Three Kingdoms, Shu Han (based in Sichuan) ruled parts of Guizhou, followed by Cao Wei (220 to 266) and then the Jin dynasty (266 to 420).

In the 8th and 9th centuries, under the Tang, Chinese soldiers moved into Guizhou (also spelled Kweichow) and married local women. Their descendants are known as Lǎohànrén (老汉人), a name that sets them apart from Chinese who settled later; the group continues to use an old-fashioned dialect. Much of Guizhou's later immigrant population traced its roots to such garrison soldiers and their local wives.

As the Mongols defeated the Song, Möngke Khan and Kublai Khan took the south-west. In the Yuan dynasty (1279 to 1368) they founded, officials and settlers who were Chinese Muslims, many from Bukhara in Central Asia, were brought to the area.

The Ming dynasty, led by Han Chinese again, made Guizhou a province in its own right in 1413. The Ming built many garrisons there to bring the Yao and Miao minorities under control during the Miao Rebellions, and farmers from Sichuan, Hunan and neighbouring provinces brought their expertise, so Chinese-style agriculture flourished. During the Manchu conquest, Wu Sangui drove the Ming out of Guizhou and Yunnan. Later, the Qing nobleman Ortai, as governor-general, ended the tusi system of indirect rule in the south-west. That brought more centralised government but also rebellion from chieftains who lost their position. Taiping rebels held Guizhou for a time before the Qing put them down. Han Chinese soldiers also settled in the Taijiang region, married Miao women and saw their children raised as Miao.

Further Miao rebellions against the Qing failed, in 1735, from 1795 to 1806 and from 1854 to 1873. The Qing fell in 1911, and during the later Civil War the Communists sought shelter in Guizhou on the Long March of 1934 to 1935. The warlord Wang Jialie was the formal ruler, but the Zunyi Conference, held in Guizhou, confirmed Mao Zedong as Communist Party leader. Later, when the Second Sino-Japanese War forced the Nationalist government back to Chongqing in the south-west, Guizhou's transport improved through a link to the Burma Road. After the 1949 revolution, Mao's government shifted heavy industry to inland provinces such as Guizhou so it would be safer from Soviet or American attack. In 1978, reform and opening up began; because of its terrain, Guizhou stayed one of China's poorest provinces, though GDP growth averaged 9 percent a year between 1978 and 1993. Its fortunes have changed a good deal since, as the Guiyang figures above show.
Locals sum up the terrain with a proverb: clear skies seldom last beyond three days, and you will not find level ground that runs on for three miles.

Guizhou lies on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, between 103°36′ and 109°35′ east and 24°37′ and 29°13′ north, at an average height of around 1100 metres. Its neighbours are Hunan (east), Guangxi (south), Yunnan (west), and Sichuan with Chongqing (north). Measured edge to edge it spans around 595 kilometres across and 509 kilometres from top to bottom, and its total area of 176,167 square kilometres makes up 1.8% of China. The most easterly spot is Di Lake Township in Tianzhu County (Qiandongnan Prefecture). In the far west is Yulong Township (玉龙乡) in Weining County, Bijie City. The southern limit is at Luowan Township (洛万乡), part of Xingyi City in Qianxinan Prefecture, and the northern limit at Yangxi Town (阳溪镇) in Daozhen County, Zunyi City.

Guizhou is mountainous, with its higher ground in the west and centre, where the Yungui Plateau ends in the east. The top of the province is Jiucaiping, 2,900 m (9,514 ft) up. Roughly speaking the terrain comes in three kinds, plateau mountains, hills and basins (盆地), and mountains and hills cover 92.5% of the area. Ranges with overlapping ridges and peaks cross the landscape. In the north the Dalou Mountain runs diagonally from west to north-east, and its Loushan Pass sits at 1444 metres. Across the centre and south stretches the Miaoling Range (苗岭), whose main peak, Leigong Mountain (雷公山), reaches 2178 metres. The Wuling Range winds in from Hunan in the north-east, with Fanjing Mountain, at 2572 metres, as its main peak. In the west stands the towering Wumeng Mountain (乌蒙山), and the summit of Jiucaiping (韭菜坪), in Hezhang County's Zhushi Township (珠市乡), reaches 2900.6 metres, the province's highest.

The province's rivers belong to the upper stretches of two great systems, the Yangtze and the Pearl River. As many as 69 counties are part of the Yangtze protective forest conservation area, which makes Guizhou a key ecological shield for the upper courses of both rivers. Following the slope of the land, water runs from the west and middle toward the north, east and south. Miao Ridge is the dividing line. North of it, the Yangtze basin takes up 115,747 square kilometres (65.7% of the province), and its main rivers include the Wu, Chishui, Qingshuijiang, Hongzhou (洪州河), Wuyang, Jinjiang, Songtao (松桃河), Songkan (松坎河), Niulan (牛栏江) and Hengjiang. To the south, the Pearl River basin covers 60,420 square kilometres (34.3%), drained by the Nanpan, Beipan, Hongshui, Duliu and Dagou (打狗河) among others. The province has many rivers that flow all year, and 984 of them are longer than 10 kilometres.

guizhou-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guizhou Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guiyang, register at Guizhou Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

guizhou-minzu-university.h: A university built for the peoples of Guizhou

blocks.x: Guizhou Minzu University (贵州民族大学 in simplified characters, 貴州民族大學 in traditional ones; pinyin Guìzhōu Mínzú Dàxué) is a public university run at provincial level. It stands in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou Province in southwest China. "Minzu" refers to ethnic nationalities, and the name tells you a lot about the institution's purpose.

The university was founded in 1951 as the first higher-education institution in the region created to serve minority peoples, among them the Zhuang, who live in Guizhou. That mission gives it a distinctive place among the universities of a province with many ethnic groups. In April 2014 it took the name Guizhou Minzu University. If you are thinking about studying here, the best source for current programmes and campus information is the university's own website.

Your daily life as a student will be shaped far more by the city than by the campus gate, so this section describes Guiyang: its centre, the weather, the economy, the people, the food, the sights, the nightlife and the transport links.

The middle of Guiyang is organised around two landmarks. One is the Dashizi (大十字), the "big cross"; the other is Penshuichi (喷水池), a name meaning "Fountain Pool", a busy junction where a large fountain stood until early 2010 before being paved over to help traffic flow.

Guiyang has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa) influenced by the monsoon, with four seasons. Its low latitude and high elevation soften the extremes, so winters are cool and summers moderate. Most of the 1,149 millimetres (45.2 inches) of yearly precipitation falls from May to July, though rain is common all year and winter occasionally brings light snow flurries.

January is the coolest month, averaging 4.6 °C (40.3 °F), and July the warmest at 23.8 °C (74.8 °F); across the year the mean stands at 15.2 °C (59.4 °F). Sunshine is limited: only 11% of possible hours are bright in January, and 43% in August at the top of the range, so the city gets only about 1150 hours a year and counts among China's dullest large cities. Relative humidity stays above 75% on average in every month, so damp air is a constant feature of life here.

Thanks to its mild summer temperatures, along with air quality and wind speed, Guiyang placed second in a "Top 10 Summer Capitals of China" ranking. Since 1951 the coldest day was 6 January 1970, at -7.8 °C (18 °F), and the hottest 5 July 1952, at 37.5 °C (100 °F); an unofficial colder reading of -9.5 °C (15 °F) dates from January 1925. In practice, with high humidity all year, expect a cool, damp winter and a comfortable summer, and bring a rain jacket in any season.

Guiyang is Guizhou's economic and commercial centre. In 2017 the Guiyang area's GDP totalled 353.8 billion yuan, or 74,493 yuan ($10,720) per head, and the local economy was growing at about 10% a year.

The city is a major centre for retail and wholesale trade. Domestic and international general retailers operate here, including Parkson, Beijing Hualian, RT-Mart, Carrefour and Wal-Mart, together with the Xingli Group (星力集团) and the electronics and appliance chains Gome and Suning. Large depots sell industrial and construction machinery, furniture and regional farm produce, and Wal-Mart runs its vegetable and produce distribution centre for southwest China from Guiyang. Foreign brands have spread quickly, among them Starbucks, H&M, Burger King and McDonald's, and they are usually found close to the shopping centres. Nanguohuajing (南国花锦), Huaguoyuan Shopping Center (花果园购物中心) and Hunter City Plaza (亨特城市广场) are the largest malls.

Hydroelectric generators sit along the main rivers, including the Wu River, and by 2007 more than 70% of the city's electricity came from hydropower. Coal comes out of the ground around Guiyang and Anshun, and large thermal power stations at Guiyang and Duyun supply part of local industry. A big iron and steel works began production in Guiyang in 1960 and fed the local machinery industry. The city also has a sizeable pharmaceutical sector making both traditional Chinese and Western medicines.

In technology terms, Guiyang has finished the first stage of a city-wide free WiFi network, D-Guiyang, a joint venture between the city government and technology firms including Alibaba and Foxconn. In 2016 the Milken Institute named it China's best-performing city, citing growth in jobs, wages and GDP. In the first half of that year Guizhou Province had the third-quickest expansion of China's 31 provincial-level regions, at 10.5%, which is credited to Guiyang's investment in computing and big data. Tax incentives and state support have drawn multinational companies to open offices here, among them Alibaba, Qualcomm, Tencent, Hyundai Motor, Huawei, Microsoft and Foxconn.

Guiyang is home to 49 different minorities, of which the Miao are the largest, alongside the Han Chinese majority. The 2020 national census counted 5,987,018 permanent residents, of whom 4,794,071 (80.07%) lived in cities and towns and 1,192,947 (19.93%) in rural areas. The census compared with the one in 2010 shows urban numbers up by 1,861,786 and rural numbers down by 197,379, and the urban share rose by 12.23 percentage points. Earlier, as of 2011, the municipality had 4.3 million people, 2.9 million of them urban. Different surveys use different boundaries and definitions, and some published change figures for the ten-year period look inconsistent, so the totals vary; check current official figures. For a student the practical point is that Guiyang is a mid-sized, increasingly urban city with a very mixed population.

Alongside the tongues of minority groups, such as Bouyei and Miao, people in Guiyang use a form of Southwestern Mandarin. It has no retroflex sounds, which sets it apart from standard Mandarin, and it has three tones where standard Mandarin has four plus a neutral one. Many old words and pronunciations from ancient China survive in it, and to Korean or Japanese ears some may sound familiar. Take 去 ("to go"), pronounced "kèi" in the fourth tone rather than "qù", and 做 ("to do") is "zo" in the fourth tone instead of "zuo".
Chinese provinces are known for particular specialities, and Guiyang is best known for spicy food. Dishes worth trying:
Sour soup beef (酸汤牛肉; Suāntāng niúròu): the tangy broth used for fish is often stewed with beef, giving a refreshing, appetising dish.
Potato cake (洋芋粑; Yángyù bā): mashed potato fried into pancakes, a popular street snack dusted with chili powder.
Qingyan pig's feet (青岩猪脚; Qīngyán Zhūjiǎo): found mainly in the old town of Qingyan, where pig's feet stand for good luck.
Chang-Wang noodles (肠旺面; Chángwàngmiàn): noodles served with pig's intestines and pig's blood.
Ice jelly (冰粉; Bīngfěn): a summer treat with sesame seeds and peanuts, eaten alongside siwawa or barbecue.
Siwawa (丝娃娃; Sīwáwa): ingredients wrapped in thin rice wrappers, either vegetarian or with pork scraps and vegetables.
Huaxi beef vermicelli (花溪牛肉粉; Huāxī Niúròufěn): a bowl of beef and rice noodles that locals often have for breakfast.
Huangba (黄粑; Huángbā): a sweet rice wrap, steamed or fried.
Gaoba porridge (糕粑稀饭; Gāobāxīfàn) is served as a sweet dessert.
Suāntāngyú (酸汤鱼), fish in sour soup, is a Miao speciality: roasted fish with assorted vegetables in a sour broth.
There is also a newer food story. Since the mid-2000s Guiyang has built up a coffee culture, and by 2025 it had more than 3,000 coffee shops, the highest density of any Chinese city.
Guiyang is the capital of an old, traditional province, and history is visible in the sights that draw visitors:
On Guiyang's southern edge lies Qingyan Ancient Town (青岩古镇; Qīyán Gǔzhèn). Its origins go back to 1378, also in the Ming dynasty, and it is known for beautiful traditional Chinese architecture.

The Jiaxiu Pavilion (甲秀楼; Jiǎxiù Lóu), at the southern tip of the Nanming River in Guiyang, serves as the city's emblem. It was first built in 1598 under the Ming dynasty, was destroyed several times and was most recently rebuilt in 1982.

The Confucian Center (孔学堂; Kǒngxuétáng) is a non-public educational organisation linked to China's Ministry of Education, concerned with Chinese culture and language. For comparison, the best-known Confucian Temple, in Qufu, was built in 478 BC.

Xifeng Concentration Camp (息烽集中营; Xīfēng Jízhōngyín) was established in 1937, during the second war with Japan, by the military commission of the Kuomintang government and was the largest, highest-level prison among those it ran. In 1988 the State Council put it on its register of key historical and cultural sites protected by the state.

Huaxi National Wetland Park (花溪湿地公园; Huāxī Shīdì Gōngyuán) lies north of central Guiyang in Huaxi district and is among the few urban wetlands of its kind in the country. It occupies a subtropical humid plateau karst hill region, and its karst landforms, location and geology produce a rich variety of landscapes.

In the northwest of Guiyang, Qianling Park (黔灵公园; Qiánlíng Gōngyuán) takes its name from Mount Qianling, regarded as the most majestic mountain in southern Guizhou. It is thickly wooded with old trees and has over 1,500 species of flowers and trees plus no fewer than 1,000 medicinal herbs. Hongfu Temple, built in late Ming to early Qing times, is among Guizhou's best-known temples.

Xifeng Hot Spring (息烽温泉; Xīfēng Wēnquán), in the northeast of Xifeng County, is ringed by mountains whose rich slopes carry pines, firs, bamboo and other plants. The setting is well suited to sanatoriums, hospitals and villas.

The liveliest street is Qianling East Road (黔灵东路), nicknamed "Drinking Street" with no irony because of its many pubs and bars. Guizhou is the home of Moutai, a famous Chinese liquor, so drinking is something of a tradition. In Guiyang beer comes in small cups and people often play dice or card games while they drink.

When evening comes, street food appears everywhere. Shaanxi Road (陕西路) offers roast chicken, baked snails and mutton chops, while Bo'ai Road (博爱路) has rice noodles, glutinous rice, mutton patties and mixed Western and Eastern dishes.
Older residents often prefer outdoor activities such as mahjong or square dancing.
Guiyang is wide-ranging in its connections by road, rail, river and air, and its public transport includes buses and many taxis.

Guiyang is an important air hub for southwest China. The main airport (KWE), Longdongbao International, began operating on 28 May 1997, east of the city and 11 km (6.8 miles) from the centre. In 2017 it handled over 18 million passengers, three times the 2010 figure.
The metro is young, so you will mostly travel on modern trains. Construction on the Guiyang Metro began in 2011. Line 1 opened in December 2017, Line 2 in April 2021 and Line 3 in December 2023.

Guiyang is a rail hub for the southwest. Four older lines meet at Guiyang Railway Station: the Guizhou-Guangxi Railway (built 1959, modified 2009), the Sichuan-Guizhou Railway (completed 1965), the Guiyang-Kunming Railway (completed 1970) and the Hunan-Guizhou Railway (completed 1975). The main southern station was rebuilt in 2008.

High-speed rail has grown quickly since 2008. The Guiyang-Guangzhou, Shanghai-Kunming and Chongqing-Guiyang high-speed lines opened in quick succession and have cut journey times sharply to almost every first-tier Chinese city: about 8 hours to Beijing, 9 to Shanghai, 4.5 to Guangzhou, 4 to Chengdu and roughly 2 to Chongqing. Freight moves rapidly from two rail yards, and passenger trains use Guiyang North station, in Guanshanhu District.

Qianming Temple, in Nanming District of Guiyang, dates from the 17th century, the late Ming dynasty. Catholic history here is long: on 15 October 1696 the city became the seat of a vicariate apostolic called Kweichow. The vicariate was suppressed in 1715, revived in 1846, renamed in 1924 as the Apostolic Vicariate of Guiyang and in 1946 raised to its present rank, the Archdiocese of Guiyang.
The region around a campus influences student life, so here is the province in brief.

guizhou-minzu-university.h: From early settlers to modern times

blocks.x: Stone tools, including Levallois pieces, found at Guanyindong Cave show that people lived in Guizhou in the Middle Palaeolithic; optically stimulated luminescence dating puts them at roughly 170,000 to 80,000 years old.

From about 1046 BC until the rise of Qin, the northwest of the province belonged to the State of Shu. In the Warring States period Chu took the area, and the Dian Kingdom later held control. Under the Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD), to which the Dian paid tribute, Guizhou was home to the Yelang group of tribes, who largely governed themselves until the Han tightened their grip on the southwest and set up Lingnan province. During the Three Kingdoms era some of Guizhou was ruled by Shu Han from Sichuan, then by Cao Wei (220-266) and the Jin dynasty (266-420).

In the 8th and 9th centuries, under the Tang, Chinese soldiers entered Guizhou (Kweichow) and married local women. Their descendants are called Lǎohànrén (老汉人), distinguishing them from Chinese who arrived later, and they continue to use an old-fashioned dialect. Many later immigrants descended from these garrison soldiers and their pre-Chinese wives.

The Mongol rulers Möngke and Kublai took the Chinese southwest while overcoming the Song, and the new Yuan dynasty (1279-1368) brought in settlers and administrators from Bukhara in Central Asia, who were Muslim.

Guizhou became a formal province in 1413, under the Ming, who were again Han-led. The Ming built many garrisons there to suppress the Yao and Miao peoples during the Miao Rebellions, and farmers from Sichuan, Hunan and surrounding provinces brought Chinese-style agriculture. During the Manchu conquest Wu Sangui drove the Ming from Guizhou and Yunnan. Under the Qing governor-general Ortai the tusi system of indirect rule in the southwest was ended, which angered displaced chieftains and led to rebellions and more centralised government. The Second Opium War was followed by criminal gangs in Guangxi and Guizhou selling British opium. The Taiping rebels held Guizhou for a time before the Qing put them down. Meanwhile, Han soldiers who moved to the Taijiang region took Miao wives, and the children grew up as Miao.

More Miao rebellions failed under the Qing, in 1735, from 1795 to 1806 and from 1854 to 1873. After the Qing fell in 1911 and during the Chinese Civil War, the Communists sought refuge in Guizhou on the Long March (1934-1935). The province was formally under the regional leader Wang Jialie, but the Zunyi Conference held there confirmed Mao Zedong as leader of the Communist Party. When the Second Sino-Japanese War pushed the Nationalist government back to its southwest base in Chongqing, transport improved as Guizhou was linked to the Burma Road. After the revolution of 1949 brought Mao to power, heavy industry was moved to inland provinces such as Guizhou for protection from possible Soviet and American attack. The 1957 influenza pandemic is reported to have started in Guizhou, and it killed a million people worldwide. From 1978, once reform and opening up were under way, geographic factors left Guizhou the poorest province in China, even though its GDP grew by an average of 9 percent a year from 1978 to 1993.
A local saying sums up the terrain: sunshine never lasts more than three days, and flat ground never stretches more than three miles.

Guizhou sits on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau and spans 103°36′ to 109°35′ east and 24°37′ to 29°13′ north, at an average altitude of about 1100 metres. Hunan is on its east, Guangxi on the south, Yunnan on the west and Sichuan and Chongqing on the north. The province measures about 595 kilometres from east to west and 509 kilometres from north to south. Its total area is 176,167 square kilometres, 1.8% of China. Its extreme points are Di Lake Township in Tianzhu County, Qiandongnan Prefecture (east), Yulong Township (玉龙乡) in Weining County, Bijie City (west), Luowan Township (洛万乡) in Xingyi City, Qianxinan Prefecture (south) and Yangxi Town (阳溪镇) in Daozhen County, Zunyi City (north).

Guizhou is mountainous, though the highest land is in the west and centre, at the plateau's eastern end, known as the Yungui Plateau. The summit of Jiucaiping, 2,900 m (9,514 ft) up, is its highest point. The terrain falls into three kinds: basins (盆地), hills and plateau mountains, and mountains and hills make up 92.5% of the area. Ranges include Dalou Mountain in the north, running diagonally from west to northeast, with Loushan Pass at 1444 metres; the Miaoling range (苗岭) across the centre and south, whose main peak Leigong Mountain (雷公山) reaches 2178 metres; the Wuling range winding in from Hunan in the northeast, whose main peak Fanjing Mountain is 2572 metres; and the Wumeng Mountain (乌蒙山) in the west, which includes Jiucaiping, at 2900.6 metres, in Zhushi Township (珠市乡), Hezhang County.

Guizhou's rivers belong to the upper Yangtze and Pearl River basins, and 69 counties fall inside the Yangtze protective forest conservation area, making the province an important ecological barrier for both rivers' upper reaches. Water flows from the west and centre toward the north, east and south. Miao Ridge is the watershed. North of it the Yangtze basin covers 115,747 square kilometres, 65.7% of the province, with major rivers including Hengjiang (横江), Niulan River (牛栏江), Songkan River (松坎河), Songtao River (松桃河), Jinjiang, Wuyang River, Hongzhou River (洪州河), Qingshuijiang, Chishui River and the Wu River. South of the ridge the Pearl River basin covers 60,420 square kilometres, 34.3% of the province, with the Nanpan, Beipan, Hongshui, Duliu and Dagou (打狗河) rivers among the major ones. Rivers with continuous flow are numerous: 984 of them are longer than 10 kilometres. Taken together, these facts show a hilly, wet, river-rich province, which is also why the capital's weather is damp and cloudy.
