guizhou-normal-university.h: Guizhou Normal University at a glance

blocks.x: Guizhou Normal University (GZNU for short; 贵州师范大学 in Chinese, pronounced Guìzhōu Shīfàn Dàxué) is a research university run at provincial level, and it stands in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou. Guiyang is nicknamed the "summer capital of China" because of its cool, mild summers. GZNU opened in 1941 and is counted among the original eight normal schools in China, meaning institutions created to train teachers.

Over 36,000 full-time students now study at the university. Bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees are awarded across 24 colleges and departments, and it also serves working adults and other learners through a college of continuing education.

As an adviser's note, "normal" in the name means teacher education. Teacher training is the historical core, although a university of this size teaches many other subjects as well, so check the programme list for the subject you want.

The story begins in 1941 with National Guiyang Normal College (国立贵阳师范学院). The People's Republic of China was proclaimed in 1949, and the college was then renamed Guiyang Normal College. It received its present name, Guizhou Normal University, in 1985, and was accredited as one of Guizhou's provincial key universities in 1996. In 2004 the former Guizhou Vocational Institute of Technology joined the university.
Daily student life depends on the city beyond the campus gates, so here is a guide to Guiyang.

Guiyang's downtown is organised around two landmarks. One is the Dashizi (大十字), a "big cross" of roads. The other is the Penshuichi (喷水池), whose name literally means "Fountain Pool", a busy intersection. It used to have a big fountain in the centre, but in early 2010 that was covered over to make traffic move more easily.

Guiyang's climate is monsoon-influenced humid subtropical (Köppen: Cwa) with four seasons, tempered because the city is far south but also high up. Winters are cool, and summers stay moderate. Annual rainfall is 1,149 millimetres (45.2 in), and most of it falls between May and July. Mean monthly temperatures range from 4.6 °C in January (40.3 °F) to 23.8 °C in July (74.8 °F), with a yearly average of 15.2 °C, or 59.4 °F. Rain can fall in any month, and there are occasional flurries of snow in winter.

It is a grey city. Sunshine is 11% of what is possible in January and 43% in August, which comes to only 1150 hours per year, so Guiyang counts among the least sunny large cities in China. Relative humidity stays above 75% on average every month.

The mild temperatures, together with other factors such as air quality and wind speed, brought Guiyang second place in a "Top 10 Summer Capitals of China" ranking. Since 1951, temperatures have gone as low as −7.8 °C on 6 January 1970 (18 °F) and as high as 37.5 °C on 5 July 1952 (100 °F). An unofficial low of −9.5 °C (15 °F) dates from January 1925.

Commerce and business for the whole province are concentrated in Guiyang. Its regional GDP in 2017 added up to 353.8 billion yuan, or 74,493 yuan per head ($10,720), with growth running near 10% a year. Shopping is a big part of the picture, in both retail and wholesale. Chains operating here include Carrefour, Wal-Mart, RT-Mart, Parkson, Beijing Hualian and the local Xingli Group (星力集团), together with the electronics sellers Gome and Suning. Large wholesale depots deal in farm produce, furniture, and industrial and building machinery, and Wal-Mart's vegetable and produce distribution centre for southwest China is based here.

Foreign brands have arrived rapidly. Starbucks, H&M, Burger King and McDonald's, for example, are mostly near the shopping centres. The biggest of these are Huaguoyuan Shopping Center (花果园购物中心), Hunter city plaza (亨特城市广场) and Nanguohuajing (南国花锦).

Energy is a local strength. Hydro-electric stations stand along the main rivers, such as the Wu River, and by 2007 they were supplying more than 70% of the city's electricity. Coal comes from the area around Guiyang and Anshun, and large thermal power stations at Guiyang and Duyun supply part of local industry. A large iron and steel works began production in Guiyang in 1960 and supplies the machinery-making sector. There is a sizeable pharmaceutical industry, making both traditional Chinese and Western medicines. The first stage of free city-wide WiFi, called D-Guiyang, has been finished as a joint venture between the city government and technology firms including Alibaba and Foxconn.

In 2016 the Milken Institute named Guiyang the Best-Performing City in China, citing growth in jobs, wages and gross domestic product. In the first half of that year Guizhou Province grew by 10.5%, the third-fastest rate among China's 31 provincial-level regions, and the growth is credited to Guiyang's investment in computing and big data. Thanks to tax incentives and state backing, large multinational companies have opened offices in the city. Examples are Alibaba, Qualcomm, Tencent, Hyundai Motor, Huawei, Microsoft and Foxconn.

Guiyang is home to 49 different minorities, and the Miao people are the most numerous of them, alongside the Han majority. The Seventh National Census of 2020 recorded 5,987,018 permanent residents. Of these, 4,794,071 live in towns and cities (80.07%) and 1,192,947 in rural areas (19.93%). Set against the 2010 census, the number of urban residents rose by 1,861,786 while the rural number dropped by 197,379, and the urban share increased by 12.23 percentage points. Population totals from different years (for example 4.3 million in the whole municipality in 2011, of whom 2.9 million were urban) use different definitions and boundaries, so use the city statistics office's current data if you need exact comparisons.

Besides minority languages (Miao and Bouyei, for instance), the usual speech in Guiyang is a variety of Southwestern Mandarin. It lacks the retroflex sounds of standard Mandarin and has three tones, compared with the four tones plus a neutral tone of standard Mandarin. Many old Chinese words survive in it, and some of them are said to sound like Korean or Japanese. As an illustration, 去 ("to go") is said "kèi" in the fourth tone rather than the standard "qù", and 做 ("to do") is "zo" in the fourth tone instead of "zuo". Standard Mandarin is understood, but you will hear the local accent everywhere.
China's provinces are known for their specialities, and Guiyang is best known for spicy food. Dishes to try include:
Gaoba porridge (糕粑稀饭; Gāobāxīfàn), which is a sweet dessert.
Sour soup fish (酸汤鱼; Suāntāngyú), a dish from the Miao people that pairs roasted fish with various vegetables.
Huangba (黄粑; Huángbā), a sweet rice wrap that is either steamed or fried.
Huaxi beef vermicelli (花溪牛肉粉; Huāxī Niúròufěn), beef and rice noodles that locals often eat for breakfast.
Siwawa (丝娃娃; Sīwáwa), rice wraps filled with vegetables, either vegetarian or mixed with pork scraps.
Ice jelly with sesame and peanuts (冰粉; Bīngfěn), normally a summer treat, eaten with siwawa or barbecue.
Chang-Wang noodles (肠旺面; Chángwàngmiàn), made with pig's intestines and pig's blood.
Qingyan pig's feet (青岩猪脚; Qīngyán Zhūjiǎo), found mostly in the old town of Qingyan, where pig's feet stand for good luck.
Potato cake (洋芋粑; Yángyù bā), a common street snack: potato is mashed, fried flat like a pancake and dusted with chilli powder.
Sour soup beef (酸汤牛肉; Suāntāng niúròu). The same sour broth that cooks the fish is also used to stew beef, and it is appetising and refreshing.
Coffee has also taken off. Starting in the mid-2000s Guiyang built up a coffee culture, and by 2025 it had over 3,000 coffee shops, the highest density of any Chinese city.
Guiyang is the capital of a very old and traditional province, and many historic places still attract visitors.

Jiaxiu Pavilion (甲秀楼; Jiǎxiù Lóu) stands at the southern end of the Nanming River in Guiyang and is the emblem of the city. It was first built in 1598, in the Ming Dynasty, was destroyed several times and was most recently rebuilt in 1982.
Qingyan Ancient Town (青岩古镇; Qīngyán Gǔzhèn) is at the southern edge of Guiyang. It dates from 1378, in the Ming Dynasty, and is known for beautiful ancient Chinese architecture.

Xifeng Concentration Camp (息烽集中营; Xīfēng Jízhōngyíng) was a prison run by the Nationalist government's Military Commission. It was the largest and highest-ranking of its prisons in the Second Sino-Japanese War period, which began in 1937. In 1988 the State Council gave it a place among the major historical and cultural sites under state protection.

Confucian Center (孔学堂; Kǒngxuétáng) is a non-public educational organisation linked to China's Ministry of Education, with a focus on promoting Chinese culture. Confucius Institutes teach the language and culture abroad, and the Confucian Temple at the centre of Qufu was built in 478 BC.

Xifeng Hot Spring (息烽温泉; Xīfēng Wēnquán) is in the northeast of Xifeng County, ringed by mountains whose slopes are rich in pine, fir, bamboo and other plants. The setting has made it suitable for sanatoriums, hospitals and villas.

Qianling Park (黔灵公园; Qiánlíng Gōngyuán), in the northwest of the city, is named after Mount Qianling, regarded as the most imposing mountain of southern Guizhou. Thick vegetation and old trees cover it, with over 1,500 species of flowers and trees and a minimum of 1,000 species of medicinal herbs. Hongfu Temple, built at the end of the Ming and the start of the Qing dynasty, is among the most famous temples of Guizhou.

The Huaxi National Wetland Park (花溪湿地公园; Huāxī Shīdì Gōngyuán) occupies the northern part of Huaxi district, close to the heart of Guiyang, and counts among only a few urban wetlands in China. It lies in a subtropical humid, plateau karst hill region, and its location and geology, shaped by karst landforms, create a rich mix of landscapes.
Qianming Temple, in Guiyang's Nanming District, dates back to the seventeenth century, the late Ming era.

Pubs and bars: Qianling East Road (黔灵东路) is the most animated street in the city. Locals call it "Drinking Street", quite literally, because of the huge number and variety of bars along it. Moutai, a well-known Chinese liquor, comes from the province, and drinking is something of a tradition. In Guiyang beer is poured into small cups, and people often play dice or card games as they drink.

Night markets: when darkness falls, street food flourishes across the city. Shaanxi Road (陕西路) is the place for roast chicken, grilled snails and lamb chops, and on Bo'ai Road (博爱路) there are lamb patties, sticky rice and rice noodles, with a mixture of Western and Eastern dishes.
Evening games: older residents often prefer outdoor pastimes such as mahjong or square dancing.

Guiyang has a long Catholic history. On 15 October 1696 it became the seat of the Apostolic Vicariate of Kweichow. The vicariate was suppressed in 1715 and restored in 1846, renamed Apostolic Vicariate of Guiyang in 1924, and in 1946 it was elevated to its present status, the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Guiyang.
Guiyang has a broad transport network of roads, railways, river routes and flights, plus a public transport system of buses and many taxis.

Guiyang is one of the key air hubs of Southwest China. Its main airport is Guiyang Longdongbao International Airport (KWE), which opened on May 28, 1997. It lies in the east of the city, 11 km (6.8 mi) from the centre. In 2017 more than 18 million passengers used the airport, which was triple the 2010 figure.
Construction of the Guiyang Metro began in 2011. Line 1 started running in December 2017, Line 2 in April 2021 and Line 3 in December 2023.

Guiyang is a railway hub for the southwest. Four lines converge at Guiyang Railway Station. They are the Guizhou–Guangxi line (1959, upgraded in 2009), the Sichuan–Guizhou line (completed 1965), the Guiyang–Kunming line (1970) and the Hunan–Guizhou line (1975). The main southern station was rebuilt in 2008.

High-speed rail has grown fast since 2008. The Guiyang–Guangzhou, Shanghai–Kunming and Chongqing–Guiyang high-speed lines opened one after another, and travel times to nearly all the first-tier cities have fallen sharply: Beijing takes about 8 hours, Shanghai 9, Guangzhou 4.5, Chengdu 4 and Chongqing roughly 2. Passengers use Guiyang North railway station in Guanshanhu District, and freight moves through two rail yards.

Older figures describe the city as having one university, one teacher-training college, one medical school and 224 primary and middle schools, though the list below shows how much that has grown. As of 2025 the Nature Index, which tracks research output, placed Guiyang among the top 150 science cities in the world. Guizhou University, a national research university in Project 211 and included in the Double First-Class Construction for some disciplines, is also located here. These institutions are in or around the city.
Guizhou University
Guizhou Normal University
Guizhou Medical University
Guizhou University of Finance and Economics
Guizhou Nationalities University
Guizhou Institute of Technology
Guiyang College
Guiyang College of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Commercial College of Guizhou
With so many universities in one city, student communities are large, and cross-campus events and activities are easier to find than in a smaller place.
The wider region shapes student life as much as the campus does, so the next parts describe Guizhou as a whole.

guizhou-normal-university.h: From early settlement to the Ming

blocks.x: The earliest signs of human settlement go back to the Middle Palaeolithic. Excavations at Guanyindong Cave turned up stone tools, among them Levallois pieces, and luminescence dating suggests they were made some 170,000 to 80,000 years ago.

From around 1046 BC until the Qin state emerged, northwest Guizhou belonged to the State of Shu. Chu conquered the area during the Warring States period, and the Dian Kingdom took over afterwards. The Dian paid tribute to the Han dynasty (206 BC–220 AD), and in that time Guizhou was inhabited by a group of tribes called the Yelang, who mostly ruled themselves until the Han strengthened their hold on the southwest and created the Lingnan province. In the Three Kingdoms era, parts of Guizhou came under Shu Han, which was based in Sichuan, and later under Cao Wei (220–266) and the Jin dynasty (266–420).

During the Tang dynasty, in the 8th and 9th centuries, soldiers from China proper entered Guizhou (Kweichow) and took local wives. Their descendants, called Lǎohànrén (老汉人), are distinguished from the Chinese who arrived later, and they continue to speak an old-fashioned dialect. Many later immigrants descended from these garrison soldiers and their local wives.

As the Mongols defeated the Song, Möngke Khan and Kublai Khan won the Chinese southwest. The Yuan dynasty that followed (1279–1368) brought in Muslim administrators and settlers from Bukhara, in Central Asia.

Guizhou became a formal province in 1413, under the Ming, which was again led by the Han Chinese. The Ming founded numerous garrisons there to subdue the Yao and Miao peoples in the Miao Rebellions, while farmers arriving from Sichuan, Hunan and surrounding provinces helped Chinese-style agriculture to spread.

guizhou-normal-university.h: The Qing dynasty and the twentieth century

blocks.x: Wu Sangui expelled the Ming from Guizhou and Yunnan as the Manchus conquered China. While the Qing nobleman Ortai governed as governor-general, the tusi system of indirect rule in the southwest was ended, which brought rebellions from chieftains who lost their position and led to a more centralised government. Taiping rebels held Guizhou for a time but were eventually put down by the Qing. In the Taijiang area, Han soldiers took Miao wives, and the children grew up as Miao. Further unsuccessful Miao rebellions broke out in 1735, from 1795 to 1806 and from 1854 to 1873.

When the Qing fell in 1911 and civil war later followed, Guizhou became a refuge for the Communists on their Long March (1934–1935). Wang Jialie, a warlord, formally ruled the province, but the Zunyi Conference held there made Mao Zedong leader of the Communist Party. When the Second Sino-Japanese War pushed the Nationalist Government back to its southwest base at Chongqing, transport improved because Guizhou was linked to the Burma Road. After the 1949 revolution, Mao's government promoted the move of heavy industry to inland provinces such as Guizhou, to protect it better against Soviet and American attack. Once reform and opening up started in 1978, Guizhou's geography left it as the poorest province in the country, even though GDP grew by 9 percent a year on average from 1978 to 1993. Conditions have changed a great deal since then, as the Guiyang economy section above shows.
A familiar saying sums up the province's geography: fine weather never lasts beyond three days, and level ground never continues for three miles.

The province sits on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, at longitudes from 103°36′ to 109°35′ east and latitudes from 24°37′ to 29°13′ north, at an average height of around 1100 metres. Its neighbours are Hunan in the east, Guangxi in the south, Yunnan in the west, and Sichuan and Chongqing in the north. Guizhou measures roughly 595 kilometres across and 509 kilometres from top to bottom, and its total area is 176,167 square kilometres, or 1.8% of China. For the record, its extreme points are Di Lake Township in Tianzhu County (Qiandongnan Prefecture) to the east, Yulong Township (玉龙乡) in Weining County (Bijie City) to the west, Luowan Township (洛万乡) in Xingyi City (Qianxinan Prefecture) to the south, and Yangxi Town (阳溪镇) in Daozhen County (Zunyi City) to the north.

Mountains dominate Guizhou, although the highest land lies in the west and centre, where the Yungui Plateau ends toward the east. The top of the province is Jiucaiping, 2,900 m (9,514 ft) above the sea. Three main land types occur, namely plateau mountains, hills and basins, and mountains and hills make up 92.5% of the total area. The ridges and peaks of many ranges overlap across the landscape:
The Dalou Mountain in the north runs diagonally from west to northeast, with the important Loushan Pass at 1444 metres.
The Miaoling Mountain (苗岭) range crosses the central and southern part, and its main peak, Leigong Mountain (雷公山), is 2178 metres high.
The Wuling Mountain Range winds into the northeast from Hunan, with Fanjing Mountain as its main peak at 2572 metres.
The towering Wumeng Mountain (乌蒙山) in the west includes the province's highest point, Jiucaiping (韭菜坪) in Zhushi Township (珠市乡), Hezhang County, at 2900.6 metres.

Guizhou's rivers belong to the upper reaches of the Yangtze and Pearl systems, and 69 counties fall within the Yangtze River protective forest conservation area. That makes the province an important ecological shield for the headwaters of both rivers. Water flows from the west and centre toward the north, east and south, following the land. The Miao Ridge divides the Yangtze basin to the north from the Pearl River basin to the south.

The Yangtze basin covers 115,747 square kilometres (65.7% of the province). Among its main waterways are the Wu, the Chishui, the Qingshuijiang, the Wuyang, the Jinjiang, the Hengjiang, the Hongzhou (洪州河), the Songtao (松桃河), the Songkan (松坎河) and the Niulan (牛栏江). The Pearl River basin covers 60,420 square kilometres (34.3%), with main rivers such as the Nanpan, Beipan, Hongshui, Duliu and Dagou (打狗河). The province has a large number of rivers that run all year round, including 984 that are more than 10 kilometres long.
Guizhou Normal University lists 245 programs for international students on this site: 82 bachelor, 128 master's, 35 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 245 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 15,400), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 19,800), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 22,000 to CNY 24,200 (median CNY 22,000), according to the university's published fee table.

245 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

guizhou-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guizhou Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guiyang, register at Guizhou Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Guizhou University (贵州大学) is a provincial public university located in suburban Guiyang, Guizhou, China. It is affiliated with the Province of Guizhou and is co-funded by the Guizhou Provincial People's Government and the Ministry of Education. The university is part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction.

Founded in 1902, it is the flagship institution of higher learning in Guizhou province. The university was a national key university in the "One Province, One School" project in the Midwest of China. With over 30,000 students, Guizhou University is one of the largest universities by enrollment in Southwestern China.

The predecessor of the modern Guizhou University was known as the Guizhou Institute of Higher Learning (贵州大学堂), which was founded in 1902. The institute evolved into the Provincial Guizhou University (省立贵州大学), National Guizhou College of Agriculture and Engineering (国立贵州农工学院), and finally National Guizhou University (国立贵州大学).
In 1997, the Guizhou Agricultural College, Guizhou Institute of Arts, and Guizhou Agricultural Cadre-Training School were merged into NGU to form Guizhou University.

In 2004, the Guizhou University of Technology merged into Guizhou University to complete the current Guizhou University. In 2005, the university was invited as a member of Project 211 by the Ministry of Education.
The university is included in the Chinese state Double First Class University Plan.

Guizhou University established a sister school relationship with the Presbyterian College in Clinton, South Carolina; the latter offers a Chinese language program for the fifteen American students every year.
The university consists of 39 colleges and offers programs of study in 11 academic divisions leading to associate, baccalaureate, master's, and doctoral degrees. These include:
Agriculture
Administration
Economics
Education
Engineering
History
Law
Liberal arts
Medicine
Philosophy
Sciences

Guizhou University ranked the best in Guizhou Province by several major international university rankings. As of 2025, Guizhou University ranked 86th in China by the Academic Ranking of World Universities.

As of 2024, Guizhou University ranked 803th by SCImago Institutions Rankings among research universities around the world.  The 2024 CWTS Leiden Ranking ranked Guizhou University at 379th in the world based on their publications for the period 2019–2022. The university was ranked 401-500th globally by the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU).  The Nature Index 2025 Annual Tables by Nature Research ranked Guizhou University at 252th among leading academic research institutions in the world for the high quality of research publications in natural science.

guizhou-university.h: International cooperation and Peace Corps involvement

blocks.x: In 1989 Guizhou Agricultural College, then a separate university, began hosting VSO teachers in the Foreign Language Department. The following year, Guizhou University began hosting foreign teachers from the AISH programme in Australia and visiting teacher programmes in both New Zealand and the University of Alabama. Simultaneously, VSO teachers from the UK and the Netherlands were recruited to work in other Guiyang institutes of higher education including the school of fashion and the catering college, both experiencing booms concurrent with Guiyang's emergence from relative obscurity. These teachers taught in both the undergraduate and post-graduate programmes at each institution.

In 2005, eight years after Gui Nong (Guizhou Agricultural College) was merged with Gui Da (Guizhou University), Guizhou University began hosting United States Peace Corps Volunteers. The volunteers teach at both the undergraduate and graduate level in the School of Foreign Languages.

To strengthen educational exchanges and bilateral ties between China and Gambia, Guizhou University in 2018 signed a memorandum of understanding with University of Gambia to establish a Confucius Institute at the University of Gambia.
Guizhou University has three campuses situated in Huaxi District around the city of Guiyang. These campuses are respectively:
East Campus: No. 2708, South Section of Huaxi Avenue, Huaxi District;
South Campus: Xiahui Road, Huaxi District;
West Campus: Jiaxiu South Road, Huaxi District.
The administrative center is located on the West Campus on the Huaxi River, Huaxi District of Guiyang.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Guiyang, where Guizhou University is located.

The city's heart is around the Dashizi (大十字), a "big cross", and Penshuichi (喷水池, literally "Fountain Pool"), a traffic intersection, in the center of which there was a large fountain until early 2010, when it was paved over for better traffic.

Guiyang is the economic and commercial hub of Guizhou Province. In 2016, Guiyang was named as the Best-Performing City in China by the Milken Institute owing to the city's "growth in jobs, wages, gross domestic product (GDP)." Guizhou Province saw the third-fastest growth among China's 31 regional districts in the first half of the year, growing by 10.5%. Guiyang is populated by 49 different minorities, the most populous of which is the Miao people and ethnic Han.

According to the Seventh National Census in 2020, the city's Permanent Population (hukou) was 5,987,018. Compared with the Sixth National Census, the ten-year decrease was 1,664,407, a decrease of 38.5%. Among the permanent residents of the city, 4,794,071 people live in cities and towns, accounting for 80.07%; The rural population was 1,192,947, or 19.93%. Compared with the Sixth national census in 2010, the urban population increased by 1,861,786, the rural population decreased by 197,379, and the proportion of urban population increased by 12.23 percentage points.
As of 2011, the total population of Guiyang municipality was 4.3 million, among which 2.9 million were urban residents.

Besides ethnic minority languages such as Miao and Bouyei, the people of Guiyang speak a variety of Southwestern Mandarin. It differs from common Mandarin for the retroflex sounds it lacks. Compared to Mandarin which has five tones (four and a non-stressed tone), Guiyang's local language only has three tones. Many old characters from ancient China are still used within Guiyang's language, which sound like Korean or Japanese. For example, "去" (to go) is pronounced as "kèi", fourth tone, instead of the Mandarin pronunciation "qù" and 做 (to do) is pronounced as "zo", fourth tone, rather than the Mandarin pronunciation "zuo".
Provinces in China are known for the different specialities they offer, and Guiyang is most known for its spicy food as well as the following dishes:
Gaoba porridge  (糕粑稀饭; Gāobāxīfàn), a sweet dessert.
Fish in sour soup  (酸汤鱼; Suāntāngyú), a Miao dish with roasted fish and various vegetables.
Huangba  (黄粑; Huángbā), a sweet wrap made of rice that can be steamed or fried
Huaxi Vermicelli  (花溪牛肉粉; Huāxī Niúròufěn), a dish that consists of beef vermicelli, that is frequently eaten as a breakfast in Guiyang.
Siwawa  (丝娃娃; Sīwáwa), a dish that can be vegetarian or a mix of pork scraps and vegetables, where the ingredients are enclosed in rice wraps.
Ice jelly with sesame seeds and peanuts  (冰粉; Bīngfěn), usually eaten in summer, with siwawa or barbecue
Chang-Wang noodles  (肠旺面; Chángwàngmiàn), made up with pig's intestines and pig's blood.
Qingyan's pig's feet  (青岩猪脚; Qīngyán Zhūjiǎo), mostly found in the old town of Qingyan, pig's feet symbolize good luck.
Potato cake (洋芋粑; Yángyù bā): Mashed potatoes fried into pancakes, seasoned with chili powder, a common street snack.
Beef in Sour Soup (酸汤牛肉; Suāntāng niúròu): Sour soup is not only used to cook fish, but is also often stewed with beef, which is appetizing and refreshing.
Since the mid-2000s, Guiyang has developed a coffee culture, with as of 2025 over 3,000 coffee shops in the city, the highest density among cities in China.
Being the capital of Guizhou, a very old and traditional province of China, Guiyang is shaped by its history, and still possesses many historical sites that attract many tourists:

The Jiaxiu Pavilion (甲秀楼; Jiǎxiù Lóu): The Jiaxiu Pavilion is located in the southern tip of the Guiyang Nanming River, which is the city's emblem and its symbol. It was initially built in 1598 during the Ming Dynasty and was destroyed multiple times in history. It was being rebuilt most recently in 1982.

Qingyan Ancient Town (青岩古镇; Qīyán Gǔzhèn): Qingyan Ancient Town is located in the southern tip of Guiyang. It was originally built in the year 1378, during the Ming Dynasty. It is known its beautiful Chinese ancient architecture.

Xifeng Concentration Camp (息烽集中营; Xīfēng Jízhōngyín): Xifeng Concentration Camp was the largest, highest-level prison of all the prisons set up by the Military commission of the KMT government during the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, and it was added by the state council to the list of major historical and cultural sites under state protection, in 1988.

Confucian Center (孔学堂; Kǒngxuétáng): the Confucian center is a non-public and educational organization affiliated with the Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China. The Confucius Institute promotes and teaches Chinese culture and language around the world. The Confucian Temple, in the center of Qufu city, was built in 478 BC.

Xifeng Hot Spring (息烽温泉; Xīfēng Wēnquán): Xifeng Hot Spring is located in the northeast of Xifeng County. The hot spring is surrounded by many mountains, upon which rich slopes grow a profusion of pines, firs, bamboos and other plants. This beautiful place has offered its advantages for sanatoriums, hospitals and villas.

Qianling Park (黔灵公园; Qiánlíng Gōngyuán): Qianling Park, in the northwest part of Guiyang, takes its name from Mount Qianling, which is known as southern Guizhou's most majestic mountain. The park is covered with thick vegetation and old trees, with more than 1,500 types of flowers and trees, and at least 1,000 types of Medicinal herbs. The Hongfu Temple, built toward the end of the Ming dynasty and the beginning of the Qing Dynasty, is one of Guizhou's most famous temples.

Huaxi National Wetland Park (花溪湿地公园; Huāxī Shīdì Gōngyuán): Guiyang Huaxi national urban wetland Park is located in the north of downtown Guiyang's Huaxi district. It is one of the only urban Wetlands in the country. On the environmental aspect, it belongs to a subtropical humid climate of the plateau karst hilly region, based on Karst landform characteristics of the urban wetland park, its unique geographical location and geological structure form a rich variety of landscapes resources.
Pubs and bars

The most dynamic street in Guiyang is Qianling East Road (黔灵东路), unironically called "Drinking Street" for the diversity and great number of pubs and bars that occupy it. In the province where Moutai comes from, a well-known liquor in China, drinking tends to be a tradition. In Guiyang, beers are poured in small cups, and games with dice or cards are often played while drinking.
Night markets

When the night comes, street food flourishes everywhere in Guiyang. On Shaanxi Road (陕西路), one can find mutton chops, baked snails, and roast chicken. On Bo'ai Road (博爱路) you can find mutton patties, glutinous rice, rice noodles, and a combination of western and eastern foods.
Night gaming traditions
At night, older people usually prefer to indulge in outdoor games, such as Mahjong or square dancing.
Transportation in Guiyang consists of an extensive network of roads, railways, river and air transport as well as public transportation system with bus system and many taxis.

Guiyang is one of the important air transport hubs in Southwest China. Guiyang's main airport is the Guiyang Longdongbao International Airport (KWE) opened on May 28, 1997. It is located in east of Guiyang, 11 km (6.8 mi) away from the city center. In 2017, the airport handled over 18 million passengers; this is a three-fold increase in passenger traffic from 2010.
Guiyang Metro began construction in 2011. Line 1 began operation in December 2017. Line 2 began operation in April 2021. Line 3 began operation in December 2023.

Guiyang is a railway hub in southwest China. The Guizhou–Guangxi Railway (built in 1959, modified 2009), the Sichuan–Guizhou Railway (completed 1965), the Guiyang–Kunming Railway (completed 1970), and the Hunan–Guizhou Railway (completed 1975) intersect at Guiyang Railway Station. This main southern railway station was rebuilt in 2008.

Since 2008, the city has seen rapid development of high-speed rail. The Guiyang–Guangzhou High-Speed Railway, Shanghai–Kunming high-speed railway and Chongqing–Guiyang high-speed railway began operations in quick succession. The explosion of high-speed rail development has dramatically decreased travel times to nearly all first-tier Chinese cities, including Beijing (8 hours), Shanghai (9 hours), Guangzhou (4.5 hours), Chengdu (4 hours) and Chongqing (~2 hours). The high speed railway lines provide rapid freight service from two rail yards, and passenger service from Guiyang North railway station, in the city's Guanshanhu District.

The city has a university, a teacher-training college, a medical school, and 224 primary and middle schools. As of 2025, Guiyang is ranked one of the top 150 science cities in the world by scientific research outputs, as tracked by the Nature Index. The city is also home to Guizhou University, a national research university under the Project 211 and under the Double First-Class Construction in certain disciplines.

In 1924 it was renamed as the Apostolic Vicariate of Guiyang, and in 1946 it was promoted to its current status as the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Guiyang.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

guizhou-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Guizhou University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guiyang, register at Guizhou University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

guizhou-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: Guizhou University of Finance and Economics: the essentials

blocks.x: GUFE, in full Guizhou University of Finance and Economics (贵州财经大学, Guìzhōu Cáijīng Dàxué), is run by the province and located in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou in south-west China. Locals and students often just call it Gui Cai (贵财). Its main subjects are management and economics, and it also carries out research on big data in finance. Seventeen academic departments teach 62 undergraduate majors and also award master's and doctoral degrees. The university operates the Guiyang Institute for Big Data and Finance, and Professor Hong Yinxing, once Party Secretary of Nanjing University, serves as honorary president.

The main campus is a modern one in the Huaxi University City district, and nearly 20,000 undergraduates are enrolled. That figure includes 300 students at the Western Michigan Institute (西密歇根学院, Xī Mìxiēgēn Xuéyuàn), an undergraduate college set up jointly with Western Michigan University in the United States, and it was only the second Chinese-American educational partnership to be launched in Guizhou.

The university's strategic plan for 2015 to 2020 gave priority to improving undergraduate teaching and the curriculum. It also aimed to recruit first-class faculty, to raise research standards and quality, and to build more international partnerships. Plans of this kind are updated regularly, so ask what the current strategy is.

The university was established on 21 August 1958 when three provincial schools were combined. They had prepared Party cadres with skills such as economics, management, marketing and supply chain management that government work requires. The new body took the name Guizhou College of Finance and Economics (贵州财经学), and its base was Hebin District in Guiyang, where it still has a campus. The Cultural Revolution forced it to stop work. It reopened in 1978 and welcomed its first undergraduate class in the same year.
1992: a provincial training school for Party cadres in economic planning became part of the college.
2002: most of the facilities left Hebin for a fresh campus in the Luchongguan District, and in 2004 it conferred its first master's degree.
15 June 2012: with the Ministry of Education's approval, a ceremony marked the change of name to Guizhou University of Finance and Economics.
2013: students and equipment started to move into a very modern campus in Huaxi University City, a district of Guiyang that was still new, with building work beginning in 2011.
2018: the university gained permission to award its first doctoral degrees.

Foreign partnerships began in 2012, with a joint undergraduate finance course alongside Edinburgh Napier University, a UK public university. Three years later, in 2015, came the Western Michigan Institute, created with Western Michigan University, a state university in the US. Courses in accounting, financial insurance, marketing and logistics management policy are also organised together with Berkeley College, a for-profit college located in New Jersey.
The university works across three campuses in Guiyang.

The headquarters is in Huaxi University City, on a modern campus built from 2011. Buildings there total 1.06 million square metres. Across the library system are 2.21 million printed books, 1.59 million electronic books and 36,000 academic journals from China and abroad. Reported land-area figures for this campus are not consistent, so ask the university for the actual size.
Two older campuses remain in use: the one in Luchongguan District, running since 2002, and the one in Hebin District, the original site of the three Party cadre schools that merged in 1958.

The university has been host of a Confucius Institute in Eritrea since 2013, attached to that country's Commission on Higher Education. Located within the former University of Asmara, it cooperates with state colleges and schools nearby. Teachers and staff from Gui Cai have travelled to Eritrea to teach Chinese and run cultural festivals, and Eritrean students of Chinese have come to study at Gui Cai. Institute staff and Eritrean students have also turned Eritrean textbooks into Chinese and designed a curriculum suited to local learners.
Day-to-day life for a student depends on the city, so the following sections describe Guiyang, from the weather to food, nightlife and getting around.

The centre of Guiyang is around two linked spots: Dashizi (大十字, the Big Cross) and the Penshuichi junction (喷水池, Fountain Pool). A big fountain used to sit in the middle of the junction, but in early 2010 it was covered over to help traffic flow.

The city has four seasons and a humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon (Köppen Cwa), kept mild by the low latitude and the high elevation. Expect cool winters and summers that never get extreme. Annual rainfall is 1,149 millimetres (45.2 inches), mostly between May and July, though it rains at any time of year and there are sometimes flurries in winter. January averages 4.6 °C (40.3 °F) and July 23.8 °C (74.8 °F) over a full day, and the average across the year is 15.2 °C (59.4 °F). Sun is scarce: only about 1150 hours a year, among the lowest for a major Chinese city, with possible sunshine of 11% in January and 43% in August. Humidity does not fall below 75% in any month.

Mild temperatures plus good air quality and moderate wind earned Guiyang second place in a ranking of China's ten best summer capitals. Records since 1951 show a low of −7.8 °C (18 °F) on 6 January 1970, with an unofficial −9.5 °C (15 °F) reported back in January 1925, and a high of 37.5 °C (100 °F) on 5 July 1952. Summer is therefore a pleasant time to be here, but bring an umbrella in any season.

Guiyang is the economic and commercial centre of Guizhou. In 2017 the GDP of the Guiyang region was 353.8 billion yuan, or 74,493 yuan ($10,720) per person, and the local economy was growing at about 10% a year. The city is a big centre for retail and wholesale trade. Domestic and foreign department and grocery chains are present: Wal-Mart, Carrefour, RT-Mart, Beijing Hualian, Parkson and the local Xingli Group (星力集团), along with the appliance and electronics chains Gome and Suning. On the wholesale side there are big regional depots for fresh produce, furniture and heavy industrial and building equipment; the south-west distribution hub for Wal-Mart's vegetables and other produce is also located in the city.

International names such as Starbucks, H&M, McDonald's and Burger King have moved in quickly, mostly next to shopping centres. Three of the biggest malls are Huaguoyuan Shopping Center (花果园购物中心), Hunter City Plaza (亨特城市广场) and Nanguohuajing (南国花锦).

Hydroelectric generators stand along the main rivers, including the Wu River, and by 2007 the city's hydroelectric plants supplied over 70% of its electricity. Coal is mined near Guiyang and Anshun, and big thermal power plants at Guiyang and Duyun power part of local industry. In 1960 a large iron and steel plant opened in Guiyang to supply the local machinery makers. The city also has a sizeable domestic pharmaceutical industry that makes both traditional Chinese and Western medicines. The first phase of free city-wide WiFi has been completed; the scheme, named D-Guiyang, is run jointly by the city authorities and technology firms such as Alibaba and Foxconn.

In 2016 the Milken Institute named Guiyang the best-performing city in China, citing growth in jobs, wages and GDP. Over the first six months of that year Guizhou grew by 10.5%, third fastest among China's 31 regional divisions, a result put down to Guiyang's investment in computing and big data. Tax incentives and state backing have attracted offices of Alibaba, Qualcomm, Tencent, Hyundai Motor, Huawei, Microsoft and Foxconn. For a finance or big-data student, this is a clear benefit of studying here.

Guiyang's population includes 49 different minority groups, and the largest are the Miao people along with the Han. The 2020 national census counted 5,987,018 permanent residents, of whom 4,794,071 (80.07%) live in towns and cities and 1,192,947 (19.93%) in rural areas. Compared with 2010, the number of urban residents grew by 1,861,786 while the rural number dropped by 197,379, lifting the urban share by 12.23 percentage points. An earlier figure from 2011 put the municipality at 4.3 million people, 2.9 million of them in urban areas. Some of the comparisons published for population change are inconsistent, so use the official census tables for exact numbers.

Besides the languages of minorities, such as Miao and Bouyei, the people of the city speak a variety of Southwestern Mandarin. It differs from standard Mandarin because it lacks retroflex sounds, and it has only three tones, where Mandarin has four plus a neutral tone. Many old words from ancient China survive in it, and to some ears they sound like Korean or Japanese. As examples, 去 (go) is said as kèi in the fourth tone rather than the standard qù, and 做 (do) as zo in the fourth tone rather than zuo.
Each Chinese province has its own specialities, and Guiyang is best known for spicy food and the dishes below:
A sweet dessert called gaoba porridge (糕粑稀饭, Gāobāxīfàn).
Fish cooked in sour soup (酸汤鱼, Suāntāngyú), a Miao speciality with roasted fish and vegetables.
A sweet rice parcel, huangba (黄粑, Huángbā), either steamed or fried.
Huaxi beef rice noodles (花溪牛肉粉, Huāxī Niúròufěn), a typical Guiyang breakfast.
Siwawa (丝娃娃, Sīwáwa): rice wrappers around vegetables, or a mix of vegetables and pork scraps.
Bīngfěn (冰粉), an ice jelly topped with sesame and peanuts that people eat in summer, often alongside siwawa or barbecue.
Chángwàngmiàn (肠旺面, Chang-Wang noodles), made with pig's intestines and blood.
Qingyan pig's feet (青岩猪脚, Qīngyán Zhūjiǎo), sold mostly in the old town of Qingyan, where they are a symbol of good luck.
Yángyù bā (洋芋粑), potato cakes made by frying mashed potato and seasoning with chili powder, a popular street snack.
Suāntāng niúròu (酸汤牛肉), beef stewed in the same sour soup used for fish, which is refreshing and whets the appetite.
Since the mid-2000s Guiyang has also built a coffee culture. As of 2025 the city counts over 3,000 cafés, reportedly the densest concentration anywhere in China.

The liveliest street is Qianling East Road (黔灵东路), nicknamed Drinking Street without any irony because of the number and variety of pubs and bars. Guizhou is the home of Moutai, a well-known Chinese liquor, so drinking is something of a tradition. In Guiyang beer is poured into small cups, and people often play dice or card games as they drink.

When night falls, street food appears everywhere. Shaanxi Road (陕西路) is the place for roast chicken, baked snails and mutton chops, while Bo'ai Road (博爱路) offers glutinous rice, mutton patties, rice noodles and dishes that blend Western and Eastern styles. Older residents tend to prefer outdoor games such as mahjong and square dancing in the evening.
Guiyang is the capital of a very old, traditional province, and its history is visible in many sites that attract tourists.

The Jiaxiu Pavilion (甲秀楼, Jiǎxiù Lóu) stands at the southern tip of the Nanming River and is the emblem of the city. A Ming-era building from 1598, it has been destroyed many times, and the latest reconstruction took place in 1982.
Qingyan Ancient Town (青岩古镇) lies at the southern end of Guiyang. It dates from 1378, in the Ming dynasty, and is known for its fine traditional Chinese architecture.

The Xifeng Concentration Camp (息烽集中营) was the biggest and top-ranking prison among those established by the KMT government's military commission in the Second Sino-Japanese War, starting in 1937. The State Council has protected it since 1988 as a major historical and cultural site.

The Confucian Center (孔学堂, Kǒngxuétáng) is a non-public educational organisation tied to China's Ministry of Education. Related to it is the Confucius Institute network that teaches Chinese language and culture around the world, and the Confucian Temple in the middle of Qufu, which dates back to 478 BC.

Xifeng Hot Spring (息烽温泉) is in the north-east of Xifeng County. The hot spring is ringed by mountains whose rich slopes are covered in pine, fir, bamboo and other plants, and this beautiful setting has long been used for sanatoriums, hospitals and villas.

Qianling Park (黔灵公园) in the north-west of the city takes its name from Mount Qianling, known as the most majestic mountain in southern Guizhou. Dense vegetation and ancient trees cover it, including over 1,500 kinds of flowers and trees and at least 1,000 medicinal herbs. Among Guizhou's best-known temples is Hongfu Temple, which dates from the end of the Ming and the start of the Qing.

Huaxi National Wetland Park (花溪湿地公园), in the north of the Huaxi district, is one of the few urban wetlands in the country. It lies in a subtropical humid plateau region of karst hills, and its unusual location and geology give it a rich variety of landscapes.
Transport options include a broad web of roads, rail lines, river routes and flights, plus city buses and a lot of taxis.

Guiyang is one of south-west China's important air hubs. Its main airport, Longdongbao International (KWE), opened on 28 May 1997 in the east of the city, 11 km (6.8 miles) from the centre. In 2017 it handled over 18 million passengers, three times the 2010 traffic.
Metro construction started in 2011. Line 1 began running in December 2017, followed by Line 2 in April 2021 and Line 3 in December 2023.

As a railway hub for the south-west, Guiyang is where four older lines cross at Guiyang Railway Station, the main southern station that was rebuilt in 2008: the Guizhou–Guangxi line (opened in 1959, upgraded in 2009), the Sichuan–Guizhou line (finished in 1965), the Guiyang–Kunming line (1970) and the Hunan–Guizhou line (1975).

High-speed rail has grown fast since 2008. The Guiyang–Guangzhou, Shanghai–Kunming and Chongqing–Guiyang high-speed lines opened in quick succession and have cut journey times to nearly all first-tier cities: about 8 hours to Beijing, 9 to Shanghai, 4.5 to Guangzhou, 4 to Chengdu and about 2 to Chongqing. Passenger service uses Guiyang North station in the Guanshanhu District, and freight service runs from two rail yards.

guizhou-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: Education and faith in the city

blocks.x: Schooling in the city includes a university, a teacher-training college, a medical school and 224 primary and middle schools. Judged by research output in the Nature Index, Guiyang ranked among the top 150 science cities in the world as of 2025. The city is also the home of Guizhou University, a national research university covered by Project 211 and, in some fields, by the Double First-Class Construction. Other institutions are Guizhou Normal University, Guizhou Medical University, Guizhou Nationalities University, Guizhou Institute of Technology, Guiyang College, Guiyang College of Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Commercial College of Guizhou and, of course, this university itself.

On the religious side, Qianming Temple in Nanming District goes back to the 17th century, the late Ming period. The Catholic Church made Guiyang the seat of the Apostolic Vicariate of Kweichow on 15 October 1696; it was suppressed in 1715 and restored in 1846. The name changed to the Apostolic Vicariate of Guiyang in 1924, and in 1946 it was raised to what it is today, the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Guiyang. Students who want to see the city's different traditions can combine temple visits with the historic sites listed above.
