hainan-normal-university.h: A snapshot of Hainan Normal University

blocks.x: Hainan Normal University (海南师范大学) is a public university run by the provincial government in Haikou, the capital of Hainan. It is regarded as the oldest institution of higher learning on the island. Its main role has always been to train teachers, and the campus also hosts the Hainan Secondary School Teachers' Continuing Education Centre and a training centre for staff of higher-education institutions. A new campus opened in 2008 at Guilinyang, a town a few kilometres south-east of Haikou. A published figure for the size of the old campus is obviously wrong, so it is not repeated here; ask the university for current land and building areas.

hainan-normal-university.h: People and programmes at a glance

blocks.x: The university reports the following scale:
Around 800 full-time teachers, among whom 92 are professors and 214 are associate professors.
15 departments and 18 research institutions.
17 graduate programmes and 36 undergraduate programmes.
2 provincial key laboratories.

Elsewhere in this profile you will also read that student numbers exceed 20,000, with about 200 foreign students. Taken together, those numbers describe a mid-sized, teaching-focused university where international students are still a small minority, so you can expect to be noticed and to practise your Chinese.

The university has been spread across more than one site since the Guilinyang campus opened in 2008, a few kilometres south-east of the city. Before you apply, ask the admissions office which campus houses your faculty, because the journey between sites can change your daily routine, your housing choice and your commute. Other local institutions, including Qiongtai Normal University and Haikou College of Economics, also have campuses at Guilinyang, so that area has become something of an education district.
Everything a student needs for daily life depends on the city: where it lies, the weather, the air, and how to move around. This section explains Haikou.

Haikou occupies the island's northern shore, where Haikou Bay opens onto the Qiongzhou Strait and the Leizhou Peninsula lies on the opposite side. The strait runs west toward the Gulf of Tonkin (Beibu Bay) near Vietnam, and east toward the South China Sea. Almost the whole urban area is level ground sitting just a few metres above the sea, covering 2,304.84 square kilometres (889.90 square miles). In the east, the Meishe River winds northward and empties into the Haidian River.

Haidian Island forms the city's northern district. The Haidian River, which is a tributary of the Nandu, separates it from the main built-up area, and four bridges cross the channel. From east to west they are the Renmin, Heping and Xinbu bridges, plus the largest, the Haikou Century Bridge, which joins the Guomao district to the island at the river mouth. Xinbu Island sits just north-east of Haikou, immediately east of Haidian Island.

Haikou is in the northern tropics and is affected by the Intertropical Convergence Zone. Typhoon and tropical-storm season runs from April to October, though most storms arrive in August and September. The rainy season is May to October, and September brings the heaviest falls. The Köppen classification is tropical wet and dry (Aw). Temperatures since 1951 have ranged from a low of 2.8 °C (37 degrees Fahrenheit) on 12 January 1955 to a high of 41.3 °C (106 degrees Fahrenheit) on 30 April 2024. If you arrive during the typhoon months, pay attention to local weather warnings.

By 2018 only Lhasa had better air quality than Haikou among major Chinese cities, although the growing number of cars since about 2009 has made things slightly worse. National Bureau of Statistics data from 2005 had Haikou first among main cities: in 2004 it logged 366 days of air at grade II or better, with the lowest particulate reading of all (0.033 mg per cubic metre), a sulphur dioxide level (0.003) lower only in Lhasa, and the lowest nitrogen dioxide (0.013). The units in those published tables are unclear, so rely on the ranking more than on the individual values.

In 1995 the city government started a quality-of-life programme with the blessing of the World Health Organization and the Ministry of Health. Its ten-point plan covered community health care, vaccination of children, waste recycling, green belts and street trees, environmentally friendly construction, public toilets (reported to be staffed and well kept), sewage treatment, communications and noise.

By 2004, 43 new community health centres were serving 85 percent of the population. Green space reached 2,000 hectares, trees lined 40 percent of the roads, noise dropped from 61.1 to 58.2 decibels, and 300 public toilets had been built. Industrial effluent, solid waste and household sewage are all sent to central treatment plants, and the local groundwater meets international standards and counts as mineral water. Life expectancy has climbed to 78.26 years. Beyond the city proper, 163 model ecological villages have been created, and in 933 villages more than 200,000 people now have running water at home.

Over 2015 and 2016, Haikou carried out large-scale changes as part of a province-wide drive called "double create" (双创), described officially as an effort to make cities cleaner and more civilised. It focused on traffic and commerce, but also improved general appearance, addressed industrial air pollution, aimed to protect drinking-water sources, and improved security at hospitals, schools, shopping centres and tourist sites. Visible changes included:

Traffic: new crossings with signals were installed to help pedestrians and two-wheelers, mostly electric motorbikes. Police stand at major junctions to make sure two-wheel riders obey the rules. Many roads have side lanes for these bikes, while pavements are legally one-way routes for walkers. Riders who go the wrong way or run red lights can be stopped, and some are made to wear a red sash and lecture other offenders.

Commerce: in about August 2015, officers removed nearly all unauthorised business structures, many made of corrugated metal or cinderblock, which were extensions of shops or built on unused space. Street vendors, most of them selling fruit and vegetables, were banned, as were night-time roadside barbecues and restaurant tables placed on pavements. These evening food scenes were once common across the city.

Roads and pavements: many small roads and lanes, including narrow ones in old districts, were resurfaced, and many pavements were rebuilt in brick. Brick is used because the roots of the city's many ficus trees buckle other surfaces.
Demolition and rebuilding: whole neighbourhoods have been or are being knocked down and replaced by new buildings and roads.
From around early 2018, the city government paid for painting and cladding a number of central buildings.

hainan-normal-university.h: What the environmental record means for you

blocks.x: Most international students care about two things in a new city: whether the air is breathable and whether the water is safe. Haikou's record on air is among the best of any large Chinese city, and the local government has invested in sewage treatment, green space and tap water for villages. At the same time, the figures for pollution and for clean-up come from different years, and one of the stated trends is that traffic emissions have been rising since about 2009. The sensible reading is that you will probably find the air pleasant by national standards, but that conditions can change, so look at current readings when you plan your move.

The changes of 2015 and 2016 are worth understanding if you arrive in Haikou today. Crossings, one-way pavements and police at junctions mean that traffic rules are enforced more strictly than a visitor might expect, and the removal of street stalls and pavement tables has changed how the city looks and where people eat out at night. Some neighbourhoods are being rebuilt entirely, so a street you see on an old map may now be a construction site or a new road.

hainan-normal-university.h: Dressing and planning for the climate

blocks.x: With a tropical wet and dry climate, a rainy season from May to October and a storm season from April to October that peaks in August and September, light clothing, a good umbrella and flexible travel plans are more useful than a heavy coat. Winters are warm, and the lowest temperature recorded since 1951 was only 2.8 °C, so you will rarely need serious cold-weather gear.

Water supply and wastewater treatment are run by Veolia Water of France. Under a partial privatisation, Veolia owns 49 percent of a joint venture with Haikou Water Group that lasts 30 years (2012-2042).

The 2010 census recorded 2,046,189 registered residents in the prefecture-level city. That is 537,848 more than in 2000, an average annual rise of 3.1 percent. Han Chinese make up about 97.75 percent of the people.

In 2008 per-person GDP was US$3,573, which placed Haikou 43rd out of 659 Chinese cities, and by 2011 the city's total GDP of 71.3 billion yuan was roughly 30 percent of the whole province. Exports of farm produce and livestock are substantial. Industry is small and includes canning, textiles, rice milling and light engineering.

Plans for an "International Tourism and Central Business District" are under way on the western stretch of Guoxing Avenue, a road that formerly held only government buildings. Beginning about 2011, HNA and other developers built offices there, including the HNA Building, which is the head office of Hainan Airlines. At the southern edge of the city sits the global headquarters of the carmaker Haima Automobile. The Haikou Free Trade Zone covers 1.93 square kilometres between Nanhai Road and Yehai Road; the State Council approved it on 21 October 1992.
Haikou has several higher-education institutions, so campus life here is part of a wider student scene.
Hainan University is based on Haidian Island, and the former South China Tropical Agricultural University, now part of it, occupies the south of the city.
Hainan Normal University, the oldest, now also has the Guilinyang campus, and enrols over 20,000 students, around 200 of them foreign.
Hainan Medical College, set up in 1993, grants medical degrees from its location in the south.
Qiongtai Normal University is found in Qiongshan District and has opened a new Guilinyang campus as well.
Haikou College of Economics sits next to Guoxing Avenue, with its own Guilinyang campus.
Opposite Hainan Medical College stands the Chinese Academy of Tropical Agricultural Sciences.
Hainan Middle School is a respected secondary school in the city.

hainan-normal-university.h: Reading the economy as a student

blocks.x: Haikou is not an industrial giant. Its output is dominated by agriculture, tourism, trade and services, with only a small manufacturing base, plus a few large names such as Hainan Airlines and Haima Automobile. For a graduate, that mix points toward opportunities in education, hospitality, logistics, public administration and trade-related jobs, especially as the free trade port plans develop. Since the numbers quoted above cover different years, check the latest statistics before making long-term plans.

Buses cover the city widely. Every ride costs a flat 1 yuan, and there are no passes, tickets or transfers. Minibuses were withdrawn after 2009. Taxis and electric motorbikes operate everywhere, whereas petrol-powered motorbike taxis were banned and seized at police checkpoints in 2009-2010. Haikou has seen a big rise in car numbers since the early 2000s, so main streets that were once quiet now suffer rush-hour jams like other large cities. The authorities have widened several principal roads and built an elevated road running from the western end of Guoxing Avenue toward new districts west of Holiday Beach.

Many main roads have a separate lane for two-wheelers behind a central divider, and barriers split opposing traffic on numerous two-way roads so that pedestrians cannot cross between junctions. Roundabouts are rare and are used mostly on Hai Xiu Road and one or two other places. Cameras at major junctions record red-light offences, and fines are posted to the owner. There is only one road tunnel in the city, the Qiaozhong Road Tunnel.

The public bicycle scheme has about 20,000 bikes, released with a pre-paid swipe card. On 24 January 2017 privately run, app-based dockless bikes arrived, and by April around 40,000 were available. Ofo, Mobike and "Quick to" each charged 2 yuan an hour. Ofo and "Quick to" bikes had inner tubes in their tyres, so many ended up abandoned with punctures; the public scheme now includes newer puncture-proof models, as does a part of Mobike's fleet.
The airport is Haikou Meilan International (IATA code HAK), 25 km (16 miles) out of town. Haikou became China's first test site for private helicopter flights in January 2011.

A rail link joins Haikou to the mainland, with ferries moving the carriages and other vehicles across the strait. The Hainan East Ring Railway runs from Haikou to Sanya through 15 intermediate stations, some operating and some still being built, on trains designed for 250 km/h (155 mph); the journey takes about 1 hour 22 minutes. Haikou East is the principal station, close to the southern end of Long Quan Road. The Haikou South bus station was moved in 2018 and now stands to the south-east of it. A second high-speed line, the Hainan Western Ring Railway, began operating in 2015 along the west coast and connects with the eastern line. Suburban trains started on 1 July 2019 between Haikou station and Meilan station: up to seven CRH6F-A sets with only four carriages and special liveries, on a route of about 38 km one way with four stops in between.

Three main highways run east, west and south from the city through the middle of the island to the other parts of Hainan, and the Haiwen Expressway heads south-east to Wenchang. The intercity bus terminus is the Haikou Transportation Center beside Haikou East railway station.

The city has four seaports for passengers and cargo. Haikou New Port, formerly the Inner Harbour, is on the south side of the Haidian River mouth. About 7 km (4 miles) west of it is Xiuying Port, much bigger and the main distribution centre for goods entering Hainan and a major gateway for people moving to the island. About 20 km (12 miles) west of downtown are South Port and the Haikou Port New Seaport.

Often called the "Coconut City", Haikou draws a great many visitors. It welcomed 4.11 million tourists in 2002, up 7.99 percent from 2001, and by 2019 the figure had passed 83.11 million. Tourism income was around three billion yuan (US$361 million) in the period quoted, up 11 percent. The sources use different years, so see the figures as a general guide. The city is also developing a meetings and exhibitions business; it founded the Haikou Convention and Exhibition Bureau in June 2012, with a pledge of 35 million yuan (US$5.6 million), and more international hotel groups are arriving. In 2016 China Merchants announced Shenzhen, Haikou and Sanya as the three ports for its South China Sea cruises, and a large cruise terminal opened in Shenzhen in October 2016.

For daily life, the simplest approach is to treat Haikou as a bus-and-bicycle city. The flat 1 yuan bus fare keeps costs low, the public bicycle scheme and app-based bikes cover short trips, and electric motorbikes dominate the side lanes. For longer journeys you have the airport 25 km out of town, a fast rail line to Sanya that takes about 82 minutes, a western ring railway, expressways and four seaports. If you are visiting the mainland, remember that rail cars and vehicles cross the strait by ferry.
Student life reflects the whole region, so here is Hainan in brief.

Some scholars say Hainan was once joined to north-eastern Vietnam and drifted away after volcanic activity, long ago in the Mesozoic. The Baiyue were among the first Kra-Dai groups to arrive. They probably settled between two and six thousand years ago, and genetic evidence points to earlier arrivals from 7,000 to 27,000 years ago.

The island enters Chinese records in 110 BC, when the Western Han founded a garrison after General Lu Bode arrived. Settlement by Han soldiers and officials, alongside territorial expansion, drove the island's gradual sinicisation. Over many centuries emperors also banished criminals and political dissidents to Hainan and northern Vietnam, areas normally ruled through Guangdong. The Song poet and statesman Su Shi is the best-known exile, and he wrote extensively about life on the island in the 11th century. Afterwards many Han people from Fujian and Guangdong moved to the Leizhou Peninsula and Hainan in search of land. The Hlai (Li), one of the Baiyue peoples, stayed in the mountainous south, and the Ming put the island under Guangdong's administration.

Following the founding of the Republic of China in 1912, Hainan was organised as the Qiongya Circuit under Guangdong, and in 1920 Sun Yat-sen suggested a Qiongya Special District. Once the Second World War was over, the ROC's Executive Yuan approved separating Hainan from Guangdong in 1947 and, in 1949, created the Hainan Special Administrative District, made up of Haikou municipality, 16 counties and the South China Sea islands.

Japan invaded in 1939, during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Communist forces and the Hlai people waged a determined guerrilla campaign, so the Japanese held only some of the territory. Feng Baiju commanded the Hainan Independent Column of fighters during the 1930s and 1940s. When Japan surrendered in 1945, the Kuomintang took back control. Hainan was one of the last places to join the People's Republic: its forces attacked in mid-April 1950 (accounts give dates between 10 and 16 April) and controlled the entire island by 1 May. Pratas Island was administered from Hainan until the ROC moved it under Kaohsiung on 13 April 1996.

Under the People's Republic, the territory became the Administrative Region Office, a branch of Guangdong's provincial government, on 1 May 1950, and then, on 1 October 1984, the Hainan Administrative Region with a people's government of its own. When it became a separate province in 1988, it was also named a Special Economic Zone to draw investment. In June 2020 the central government published a master plan for a Hainan Free Trade Port: a basic system by 2025 and a more mature one by 2035. Observers disagree about how the project relates to Hong Kong and whether it meets international trade norms. In July 2025 officials said independent customs operations across the whole island would begin on 18 December 2025. Check official sources for how this policy stands today.
Several small islands lie near the main one, and because they are so close their plants, animals and climate are much the same:
Dazhou Island lies about 5 km (3.1 miles) off Wanning.
Haidian Island, on the northern coast, belongs to Haikou.
Nanwan Monkey Island is in fact a peninsula.
Phoenix Island is a man-made resort island under construction in Sanya Bay.
Wuzhizhou Island sits in Haitang Bay.
Xinbu Island lies just east of Haidian Island.

hainan-normal-university.h: What the island's history adds up to

blocks.x: Hainan has been a frontier, a place of exile, a battleground and, more recently, a showcase for economic experiments. That history helps explain why the island is now treated as a special economic and free-trade area, why its population mixes Han settlers with the Hlai and other groups, and why the local culture feels distinct from both Guangdong and the mainland north. For a student this is useful background: the university sits in a region whose policies and economy are changing quickly, and conditions may differ from the figures given here.

In summary, Hainan Normal University gives international students a teaching-focused education in a tropical, green and fast-changing island capital. For current figures and programmes, consult the university itself.
Hainan Normal University lists 66 programs for international students on this site: 16 bachelor, 16 master's, 3 doctoral, 31 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 59 taught in Chinese, 7 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.

66 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (3):
Biology and Medicine
Chemistry
Materials and Chemical Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hainan-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hainan Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Haikou, register at Hainan Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hainan University (HainanU or HNU) is the flagship public university of China's island province, Hainan, and its main base is in the provincial capital, Haikou. Money comes from three sources working jointly, namely the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Education and the provincial government of Hainan. It belongs to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction programme, two national initiatives that mark out priority universities.

The university in its present shape dates from August 2007, when the original Hainan University joined with the South China University of Tropical Agriculture (华南热带农业大学). The new, merged institution kept the Hainan University name.

The first Hainan University opened in 1983 and was a key university of the province. On 14 August 2007 the Ministry of Education approved a merger of that university with the South China University of Tropical Agriculture (SCUTA).

SCUTA had an unusual origin. It started in 1958 as the South China Institute of Tropical Crops, a creation of the central government at a time when foreign powers were refusing to sell natural rubber to China and enforcing an embargo. Rubber and tropical farming were its specialities. Within Hainan it was the sole higher-education centre with State Key Disciplines and doctoral programmes, which it delivered in partnership with an academy founded even earlier, in 1954, the South China Academy of Tropical Crops (later the China Academy of Tropical Agriculture). Between them, the two bodies had collected over 900 awards in education and scientific research.
2008: the state approved Hainan University as a key university under Project 211.

2012: HNU became part of a national plan for strengthening higher education in the middle and western parts of China. Backing followed from two further central schemes, one building basic capacity and the other raising overall strength in the western and central regions.
2017: it was placed on the national plan for building world-class disciplines.

2018: provincial Party leaders and the provincial government decided strategically to back the university's growth completely. That same year, administration became a joint task for the education ministry and Hainan's government, and HNU was counted among the universities the ministry manages directly.
Five campuses together cover 3.00 km2 (741 acres). This is where you will find each of them.

Haidian Campus, the main one, occupies part of Haidian Island in Haikou and has three principal entrances: the east gate on Renmin Avenue, the north gate on Haidian Wuxi Road, and a newer south gate on Bihai Avenue.
Chengxi Teaching Area is on Xueyuan Road in Haikou's Longhua District.
Mission Hills Campus takes its name from the Mission Hills Group and stands in the Mission Hill Tour Area in Haikou.
Danzhou Campus is in the city of Danzhou.
Yazhou Campus is in the city of Sanya.

hainan-university.h: State Key Laboratory of Marine Resource Utilization in the South China Sea

blocks.x: This laboratory was the first state key laboratory devoted to developing, using and protecting the marine resources of the South China Sea. It is also the only university-based state key laboratory established jointly by Hainan Province and national ministries. Academician Zhang Si currently chairs its Academic Committee, Professor Li Jianbao directs the laboratory, and Professor Wang Ning is deputy director.

hainan-university.h: Hainan Key Laboratory for Sustainable Utilization of Tropical Bioresources

blocks.x: The Ministry of Science and Technology set up this laboratory in 2010 as a national-level key laboratory and cultivation base, co-founded with Hainan province. It responds to the social and economic needs of Hainan and to the building of the university's disciplines. Its research subjects are the distinctive tropical crop resources and tropical microorganisms of Hainan, and it carries out basic research with practical applications in a thorough, systematic way on using tropical bioresources sustainably.
Its research falls into three areas:
Tropical agricultural bioresources: collecting and using tropical crop and microorganism resources, and studying how tropical organisms regulate secondary metabolism and carry out biosynthesis.

Genetic improvement of tropical crops: the molecular basis for regulating important agronomic traits in the main tropical crops, the molecular mechanisms of disease and stress resistance, and molecular breeding.

New ecological farming technology for the tropics: efficient ecological agriculture and recycling of materials, degradation and restoration of tropical agricultural ecosystems, and the efficient use of crop nutrients along with key techniques for better quality.

By building a theoretical system and a technology platform for sustainable use of tropical bioresources, and a leading national centre for tropical agrobiology, the laboratory has earned praise from international colleagues working in the tropics. It also helps advance the university's first-class crop science discipline.
For students, day-to-day experience is shaped mostly by the city beyond the campus gates: the weather, transport and entertainment. The next sections describe Haikou, home of Hainan University.

The city sits beside Haikou Bay on Hainan's northern shore. On the far side of the Qiongzhou Strait is the Leizhou Peninsula; the strait extends westwards from Beibu Bay, close to Vietnam, as far as the James Shoal where the South China Sea begins. Urban land covers 2,304.84 km2 (889.90 sq mi), and the terrain is almost entirely flat, rising just a few metres over sea level. Through the eastern side runs the Meishe River, flowing north into the Haidian River.

Haidian Island, the district in the north of Haikou, is separated from the remainder of the city by the Haidian River, which feeds into the Nandu River. Four bridges link it with the mainland side. The largest is Haikou Century Bridge, which joins the Guomao district to Haidian Island at the mouth of the Haidian River, and the other three road links are the Renmin, Heping and Xinbu bridges, from east to west. Xinbu Island lies to the north-east of Haikou and east of Haidian Island.

Located in the northern tropics and inside the Intertropical Convergence Zone, Haikou has a tropical wet and dry climate (Köppen Aw). Storms and typhoons can occur from April to October, and the peak comes in August and September. Rain falls mainly between May and October, with September the wettest month. Coldest on record since 1951 was 2.8 °C (37 °F), on 12 January 1955; hottest was 41.3 °C (106 °F), on 30 April 2024. In short, typhoon season deserves attention when you plan travel.
In 2018 Haikou had the second-best air quality among major Chinese cities, behind only Lhasa in Tibet. Since about 2009, however, more cars on the road have worsened air pollution somewhat.

Earlier data were even better. The 2005 statistical book from the National Bureau of Statistics gave Haikou the top score among China's main cities for air quality. In 2004 it had 366 days of air at grade II or better, and its readings were the lowest of any main city for particulate matter (0.033 milligrams/m2) and nitrogen dioxide (0.013 milligrams/m2). Only Lhasa had less sulphur dioxide than Haikou's 0.003 milligrams/m2. Groundwater reaches international standard and counts as mineral water.

A city-government initiative in 1995 set out to raise residents' quality of life, approved by both the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization. A ten-point plan dealt with issues such as these:
Community health care
Vaccinations for children
Waste recycling
Green belts and urban trees
Environmentally friendly construction
Public toilets, which are available all over the city, staffed and well maintained
Sewage treatment
Communications
Noise pollution

Results were visible by 2004. Forty-three new community health service centres were opened, serving 85 percent of residents, and green space grew to 2,000 hectares, with trees planted along 40 percent of the roads. Noise dropped from 61.1 dB to 58.2 dB, and 300 public toilets were built. Centralised treatment centres now handle every kind of industrial effluent, wastewater and solid waste, plus all household sewage, so disposal causes no environmental harm. Such improvements helped lift the city's life expectancy to 78.26 years. In the countryside, 163 model ecological villages have been built, and tap water now reaches the homes of more than 200,000 villagers in 933 villages.

In 2015 and 2016 Haikou went through large-scale improvements under a province-wide initiative called 'double create' (双创). Government sources describe it as a drive to create a cleaner and a more civilised city. Its focus was traffic and commerce, but it also changed the city's overall appearance, tackled air pollution from industrial emissions, aimed to protect drinking water sources and raised public security in places such as hospitals, schools, malls and tourist attractions. Specifics included:

Traffic: many new crossings with traffic lights were added to help two-wheeled vehicles, mostly electric motorbikes, and pedestrians. Police were stationed at major junctions to keep riders in line. Bikes have many side lanes, but pavements also work as official one-way routes for them. Officers pull over anyone going the wrong way or jumping a red light, and a rider who offends might be made to put on a red sash, help stop other offenders and give them a talking-to.

Commerce: around August 2015, in a province-wide campaign, teams of officers physically removed almost all illegal business structures, commonly made of corrugated metal or cinderblock, that were shop extensions or built on unused space. Street vendors, mostly selling vegetables or fruit, were banned, as were night-time roadside barbecue sites and restaurant tables on pavements. Such evening food stalls used to be common everywhere in the city.

Roads and pavements: many small roads, including narrow lanes in old neighbourhoods, were repaved, and many pavements were relaid in new brick. Brick is used because the city has many ficus trees whose roots deform other surfaces.
Demolition and rebuilding: whole neighbourhoods have been, and are being, knocked down and replaced with new buildings and roads.
Appearance: from around the start of 2018 the city government paid for painting and cladding a number of buildings in the centre.

Under a partial privatisation, the French firm Veolia Water manages both tap water supply and wastewater treatment in Haikou. It owns 49 percent of a joint venture with Haikou Water Group that lasts 30 years, from 2012 to 2042.

At the 2010 Census, 2,046,189 people were registered in the prefecture-level city, which is 537,848 more than in 2000 and equal to growth of 3.1 percent a year across the decade. About 97.75 percent of them were Han Chinese.
GDP per head was US$3,573 in 2008, which placed Haikou 43rd among 659 Chinese cities, and in 2011 the city's total GDP reached 71.3 billion yuan, around 30 percent of the whole province.

Large volumes of agricultural goods and livestock leave Haikou for other markets, and there is some light industry: textiles, canning, rice hulling and light engineering. At the west end of Guoxing Avenue, which at first had only government buildings, a new International Tourism and Central Business District is going up. Office towers began to appear there about 2011, built by HNA and other groups, and Hainan Airlines has its headquarters in the HNA Building at the same end. Further south, the carmaker Haima Automobile has its global headquarters.
Between Nanhai Road and Yehai Road lies the Haikou Free Trade Zone (海口保税区), a 1.93 km2 zone of state level. The State Council gave its approval on 21 October 1992.

hainan-university.h: Universities and schools in the city

blocks.x: Haikou has several important educational institutions.
Hainan University itself: the main campus is on Haidian Island, while the southern part of the city holds the old South China Tropical Agricultural University, which has since merged into it.
Hainan Normal University is the oldest higher education institution in the city. It has a new campus in Guilinyang and more than 20,000 students, around 200 of them foreigners.
Hainan Medical College was founded in 1993, offers medical degrees and is in the south of the city.
Qiongtai Normal University is based in Qiongshan District and has opened another campus at Guilinyang.
Haikou College of Economics, next to Guoxing Avenue, also has a new Guilinyang campus.
Facing Hainan Medical College from the opposite side of the road is the Chinese Academy of Tropical Agricultural Sciences.
Hainan Middle School is among the secondary schools.

The city has a wide urban bus network. The standard fare is 1 yuan, and there is no pass, ticket or transfer system. Urban minibuses ran until 2009 but have been phased out. Taxis and electric motorbikes work across the city, and between 2009 and 2010 police banned petrol-fuelled motorbike taxis and seized them at many checkpoints.

Since the early 2000s the number of cars has risen sharply. Traffic that was once light on the main streets is now like that of other big cities, with rush-hour congestion. In response, several principal roads have been widened, and an elevated road now runs from the western end of Guoxing Avenue out to the new developments beyond Holiday Beach.
Road layout has some points worth knowing:
Many main roads have a side lane for two-wheeled vehicles, separated by a median.
Barriers divide the lanes on many main two-way streets, installed for safety to stop people crossing anywhere except at junctions.
Roundabouts are rare; you will meet them mostly along Hai Xiu Road and at just a few other spots.
Traffic cameras watch many main junctions, and tickets for red-light offences are sent by post.
The city has one tunnel, the Qiaozhong Road Tunnel.

The public bicycle scheme, which has roughly 20,000 bikes, uses a pre-paid swipe card. Private app-based bikes that need no docking station arrived on 24 January 2017, and some 40,000 were out on the streets by April. Ofo, Mobike and 'Quick to' all charge 2 RMB an hour. Bikes from Ofo and 'Quick to' have inner tubes in their tyres, which means many are abandoned around the city with flats. The public scheme has added newer bikes with tyres that cannot be punctured, and so has part of Mobike's fleet.
Meilan International Airport (IATA code HAK, ICAO code ZJHK) lies 25 km (16 mi) away. A first for China: Haikou became the test site for private helicopter flights in January 2011.
A railway connects Haikou to the mainland, with a ferry service carrying the train wagons, other motor vehicles and so on across the strait.

Between Haikou and Sanya runs the Hainan East Ring Railway, which has 15 intermediate stations, some operating and some still under construction. The trains are built for 250 km/h (155 mph) and cover the Haikou to Sanya route in roughly 1 hour 22 minutes. Haikou East is the principal station, close to the southern end of Long Quan Road. The Haikou South Station, which serves as the main bus station, relocated in 2018 to a spot directly south-east of Haikou East. A second high-speed route, the Hainan western ring line, opened in 2015, follows the west coast and links up with the eastern ring line.

From 1 July 2019 the Haikou Suburban Trains began service. Up to 7 CRH6F-A trains (CRH6F with only 4 carriages) in specially designed colours run between Haikou station and Meilan station, over a longest one-way distance of around 38 kilometres with 4 stations in between.

Three main highways connect Haikou with other parts of Hainan, heading east, west and south through the centre of the province. The Haiwen expressway runs to Wenchang to the south-east. The main bus station is the Haikou Transportation Center, beside Haikou East railway station.

Four seaports handle passengers and freight. Haikou New Port, once known as the Inner Harbour, sits at the Haidian River mouth on its south bank. Xiuying Port, around 7 km (4 mi) further west, is much bigger: it is where most cargo bound for Hainan is distributed, and a main entry point for people settling on the island. The remaining two, South Port and the New Seaport, are about 20 km (12 mi) west of downtown.

Known as the 'Coconut city', Haikou is one of China's important holiday destinations. Visitors numbered 4.11 million in 2002 (7.99 percent more than in 2001), and by 2019 more than 83.11 million tourists came. Earnings from tourism were about three billion yuan (361 million US dollars) in the period mentioned, an 11 percent increase on the year before.

Haikou is also developing business events, known by the initials MICE (meetings, incentives, conferencing and exhibitions). A convention and exhibition bureau was set up by the local government in June 2012, with RMB 35 million (US$5.6 million) committed to support the sector, and international hotel chains are increasingly arriving.

Cruise tourism is another plan. China Merchants, a holding group, revealed in 2016 that its South China Sea passenger cruises would call at three destination ports: Shenzhen, Haikou and Sanya. Shenzhen's large cruise terminal was the first to open, in October 2016.
Hainan University lists 87 programs for international students on this site: 25 bachelor, 43 master's, 18 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 69 taught in Chinese, 12 taught in Chinese and English, 6 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,400 to CNY 20,700 (median CNY 20,700), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,700 to CNY 23,000 (median CNY 23,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 23,000 to CNY 25,300 (median CNY 25,300), according to the university's published fee table.

84 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hainan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hainan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Haikou, register at Hainan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hangzhou Normal University, abbreviated HZNU and written 杭州师范大学 in Chinese, is a public university in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang Province. It is also known in English as Hangzhou Teachers College, which reflects its origins in teacher training. Over time it took in Hangzhou Education College as well as Hangzhou Medical Junior College, and one account counts nine campuses with a combined floor area of 513,590 square metres, though another count mentions five main teaching campuses, so ask the university which sites your course will use.

Student numbers are modest by Chinese standards. There are close to 12,000 full-time students, of whom about 9,000 are undergraduates, and more than 1,000 teachers. Over 100 of the teachers hold or are working towards a doctorate, 283 have a master's degree, and nearly 490 are professors, researchers, associate professors or associate researchers. A later description gives larger figures: 18,597 undergraduates, 1,341 postgraduates and more than 2,100 staff, of whom 700 among 1,388 full-time teachers are professors or associate professors, along with four co-engaged academicians. The two sets of numbers come from different dates, so treat both as approximate.

hangzhou-normal-university.h: A teacher-training school that became a university

blocks.x: The origins go back to 1905, when the governor of Zhejiang founded a school to train teachers for the province's primary and secondary schools. In 1908 it took the name Zhejiang Official Secondary Normal School and occupied the former Zhejiang Gongyuan, the old examination compound. Shen Junru became a supervisor there in 1909.

By 1912, under the Republic of China's Education Department, it was counted among six well-known teacher-training institutions of the day. Students published their own periodicals, such as Baiyang and Zhejiang Trendy, and formed clubs, among them the Music Rock Club, the Lakeside Poetry Club and the Mingyuan Club. Jing Hengyi was principal, and its teachers included Li Shutong and Lu Xun, and its pupils included Feng Zikai, Qian Xuesen and Pan Tianshou.

When Japanese forces invaded Hangzhou in the Second World War, the school was moved to places including Jiande and Lishui, and it returned to Hangzhou after the war. Since 1954 it has been directly under the Hangzhou municipal government. In 1978 the State Council approved the founding of Hangzhou Normal College, and in March 2007 the Ministry of Education approved its present name, Hangzhou Normal University.

The five main campuses are Xiasha, Wenyilu, Yuhuangshan, Gudangwan and Xianghu, covering about 93 hectares (230 acres) in total. The university has acquired a further 37 hectares (91 acres) and is building a sixth site, Cangqian Campus.

Academically it is made up of 18 schools offering 49 majors at undergraduate level and 39 postgraduate disciplines. Three majors have national-level features, 11 majors and six disciplines are designated as key at provincial level, and the university has one national-level and eighteen provincial-level courses. Research facilities include a key laboratory built jointly with Zhejiang Province's Education Department and a group of provincial teaching and demonstration centres, and the university has taken part in national projects such as the 863 Plan, Tenth Five-Year Plan science and technology programmes and National Natural Science and Social Science Funds.

The university publishes periodicals that include a university journal, a university news title and Yuwen Xinpu. The Journal has been earned the title Excellent Magazine in East China, and it appeared for three years in the national list of 100 top liberal arts and social science journals.

One distinctive unit is the Alibaba Business School, formed in 2009 as a joint venture between HZNU and the Alibaba Group, whose founder Jack Ma serves as its chairman. It says it wants to change traditional business education by creating an entrepreneurial college for internet entrepreneurs. In China it offers full-time bachelor's and master's programmes in logistics, e-commerce, international business and marketing, including digital marketing. It also has an ASEAN office in Singapore, which runs an e-commerce certification programme designed to help working adults develop small and medium businesses online or serve as e-commerce specialists in multinational companies.

In cooperation with Singapore's Nanyang International Business College, the school started the ASEAN E-Commerce Executive Training Programme, a series of courses in South-east Asian countries. Since it began in May 2016 it has trained many internet-minded professionals in Singapore and Malaysia, including people in leading enterprises.

To give students intercultural experience, HZNU has academic cooperation programmes with more than 30 universities abroad, in countries in places such as Finland, South Korea, Japan, Australia, the Philippines, the United States and the United Kingdom. The school's eight-character motto lists the qualities it hopes to foster: diligence, caution, honesty, forgiveness, then erudition, refinement, perfection and initiative.
The alumni list spans business, music and academia in China and abroad.

hangzhou-normal-university.h: Hangzhou: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Most of what you need to know about everyday life comes down to the city outside the gates: its weather, how people get about and what there is to do. This part introduces Hangzhou.

Hangzhou lies in the north-west of Zhejiang Province, where the Grand Canal from Beijing reaches its southern end, in the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. As a sub-provincial city its administrative area stretches west to the mountains on the Anhui border and east to the coastal plain by Hangzhou Bay. The city centre wraps around West Lake's eastern and northern shores, a little north of the Qiantang River.

The Qiantang is the largest river in Zhejiang, and every year between the 15th and 18th of the eighth lunar month it produces the Qiantang Tide, nicknamed the greatest tide anywhere. The largest tidal bore on Earth surges up the river through Hangzhou, reaching heights of up to 12 metres (39 feet).

Hangzhou has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons: summers that are long, very hot and humid, and winters that are chilly, cloudy and drier with the occasional snowfall. The annual mean temperature is 17.0 degrees Celsius (62.6 F), with monthly averages that go from 5 degrees (41.0 F) in January up to 29.3 degrees (84.7 F) in July. Average rainfall is 1,438 millimetres (56.6 inches), and June brings the plum rains of the Asian monsoon. Typhoon storms hit in late summer, in August and September, but they seldom strike directly. They normally come ashore on the southern Zhejiang coast and reach Hangzhou as strong winds and rain.

Since 1951 the lowest recorded temperature was minus 9.6 degrees (15 F) on 6 February 1969 and the high was 41.9 degrees (107 F), on 3 August 2024. Unofficial figures have fallen to minus 10.5 degrees (13 F), on 29 December 1912 and again on 24 January 1916, and up to 42.1 degrees (108 F) in August 1930. Sunshine ranges from 30 percent of possible in March to 51 percent in August, and the city gets 1,709.4 hours a year.

In 2023 the permanent population of Hangzhou, counting Xiaoshan and Yuhang, was 12.522 million, and 10.543 million of them (84.2 percent) lived in urban areas. The OECD put the wider metropolitan area at 13.4 million in 2010, although other sources suggest over 21 million. The metropolitan area takes in the cities of Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou. Life expectancy for the city's registered population was 83.18 years in 2021, among the highest in China.

Hangzhou has a layered religious history. In 1848, during the Qing dynasty, it was described as a stronghold of Islam in China, with several mosques bearing Arabic inscriptions, and today two mosques of note are the Phoenix Mosque and the New Hangzhou Great Mosque. In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries the city was an important centre of Chinese Jewish life, possibly the first home of the Kaifeng Jewish community, although no trace of a Hangzhou synagogue can now be found. Two of the so-called Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism came from Hangzhou, and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, about 400 years old and dating to the Ming dynasty, is one of China's oldest Catholic churches.

There are many Buddhist temples near West Lake. Lingyin Temple, meaning Soul's Retreat, lies about 2 kilometres (1.2 miles) west of the lake. Founded in AD 326 in the Eastern Jin dynasty, it has some 1,700 years of history, is believed to be the city's oldest Buddhist temple, and has been destroyed and rebuilt many times. Yue Fei Temple on the north-west shore was built in 1221 to honour General Yue Fei. Other sites include Jingci Temple, Baochu Pagoda, Leifeng Pagoda, Liuhe Pagoda on Yuelun Hill, on the Qiantang's northern bank, and Hupao Temple.

Hangzhou's economy has grown rapidly since the city opened up in 1992. Hangzhou is an industrial city with varied sectors, among them light industry, agriculture and textiles, as well as a major manufacturing base and logistics centre for China's coast, and today it is also a centre of e-commerce and technology. In 2001 its GDP was 156.8 billion yuan, second among provincial capitals after Guangzhou. By 2018 it had more than tripled, to 1.3509 trillion yuan, while GDP per head rose from 3,020 to 21,184 US dollars. The Hangzhou metropolitan area's gross metropolitan product for 2019 was estimated at 3.2 trillion yuan (486.53 billion US dollars nominal)), larger than the economies of Argentina (452 billion dollars, 26th in the world) and Nigeria (448 billion, the biggest in Africa).

Several rankings reflect that success. A study by PwC and the China Development Research Foundation placed Hangzhou first among Chinese Cities of Opportunity. GaWC classifies it as a Beta plus world city, and in 2018 it stood 89th in the Global Financial Centres Index. The Economist Intelligence Unit ranked it first in its China Emerging City Rankings, which measure growth potential, in 2021 and 2022. The Hurun Global Rich List 2020 put it 11th in the world and sixth in China for billionaires, with Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou all ahead of it. As of August 2023, the city limits contained more Fortune Global 500 headquarters than all but nine other cities in the world, and than all but three in China (Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen). A smart-city initiative is digitising the economy, with the aim of a cashless city.

Technology firms with headquarters in Hangzhou include HikVision, Geely, DeepSeek, Ant Group, NetEase and Alibaba Group. Alibaba unveiled a new global headquarters in May 2024, about one million square metres in seven buildings, built for 30,000 staff. Because of the internet industry, many programmers from Shanghai, Beijing and other cities have moved to Hangzhou. New industries have developed in medicine, information technology, heavy equipment, car components, household appliances, electronics, telecommunications, fine chemicals, chemical fibre and food processing. Officials describe the city's key sectors as a 1+6 set of clusters, where the 1 is the digital economy and the 6 are the creative and cultural industries, finance, tourism, fashion production and top-end equipment production, among others. Since at least 2023 expansion has been driven by the digital and creative sectors. One study found that Alibaba's revenue affects the city's growth in one direction only: a 1 percent revenue increase is linked with 0.272 percent long-run growth.

The Hangzhou Tourism Commission launched, in March 2013, an online campaign on Facebook called Modern Marco Polo. Nearly 26,000 people from around the world applied over the following year to become the city's first foreign tourism ambassador. Liam Bates was named the winner at a press conference on 20 May 2014 of a 55,000 dollar contract, the first foreigner appointed to such an official role by China's government.

The Hangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone gained State Council approval as a national zone in 1993, and it covers 104.7 square kilometres (40.4 square miles) and encourages electronic information, biomedicine, machinery, household appliance manufacturing and food processing. Hangzhou's Export Processing Zone was set up on 27 April 2000 after State Council approval; it was among the first of its kind and is the only one in Zhejiang. Its planned area is 2.92 square kilometres (1.13 square miles),, near Xiaoshan International Airport and Hangzhou Port.

The Hangzhou Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone received State Council approval as a national high-tech zone in March 1991. It has three parts, mainly the Zhijiang and Xiasha Sci-Tech Industrial Parks, and it is one of Zhejiang's most influential bases for high-technology innovation and industry. In 2013 it hosted more than 1,100 software and business-process outsourcing firms, and Motorola, Nokia and Siemens have set up research centres there. In 2011 its GDP grew by 13.1 percent to 41.63 billion yuan, 5.9 percent of Hangzhou's total. It calls itself the Silicon Valley of China and is home to Alibaba Group, which sped up construction of its global headquarters in 2023 with local government support after signing a new cooperation pact.

hangzhou-normal-university.h: What the city looks like and what to see

blocks.x: Despite rapid recent development, Hangzhou has kept its historic and cultural heritage and its natural setting, and tourism remains an important part of its economy. It also has many tall buildings, ranking 19th in the world and ninth in China for the number of skyscrapers.

West Lake is among the most popular attractions and holds UNESCO World Heritage status. Its cultural landscape covers about 3,323 hectares (8,210 acres) and takes in notable historic and scenic locations: cultural sites, old pagodas, hills and tea fields, Phoenix Mountain among them, and two major causeways cross the lake. West of it lies Dreaming of the Tiger Spring, known for its spring and its closeness to the famous Longjing tea plantations.

Sections of the Grand Canal run through the city. In 610 CE an existing channel was dredged and widened to become the Jiangnan Canal linking Suzhou with Hangzhou, and the Grand Canal was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. You can reach historic sites around Gongchen Bridge by taking Hangzhou Metro Line 5 to The Grand Canal or East Gongchen Bridge station.

The West Lake Cultural Square in Xiacheng District holds the Zhejiang Natural History Museum and the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology, together with the Zhejiang Global Center, a downtown tower among the city's tallest at about 160 metres (520 feet). Xixi National Wetland Park, about 10 square kilometres (3.9 square miles), protects the region's wetland ecosystem with reed beds and fish ponds restored, and it is now home to many bird species, as well as a temple and several historic rural houses. Qiandao Lake, a man-made reservoir in Chun'an County, which falls under Hangzhou, has more islands than any other lake in China, each with its own scenery. The Hangzhou Botanical Garden and Hangzhou Zoo are in Xihu District.

Native residents, including those from Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu, speak the local Hangzhou dialect, a variety of Wu found only in this area and different from those of southern Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu. Mandarin, China's official language, dominates everyday speech, although it cannot be understood by Hangzhou-dialect speakers who have not learned it. Estimates put its speakers at 1.2 to 1.5 million.

Museums include the China National Silk Museum, which is the world's biggest silk museum, the China National Tea Museum, and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum, which brings together human studies, exhibition and research and holds over 100,000 cultural relics. Theatres stage opera such as Yue opera, and big shows themed on local history and culture include Impression West Lake and Romance of the Song Dynasty. The city's landscapes are tied to the stories of famous figures in Chinese history and to the pleasure of ordinary visitors. The China Academy of Art is based in Hangzhou, as are well-known painters like Lin Fengmian and Fang Ganmin. The local government invests heavily in tourism and the arts, with a focus on silk, umbrellas and Chinese folding fans.

A centre for ancient book restoration and display in Hangzhou, part of the Zhejiang Library, holds regular public demonstrations of the traditional paper restoration and binding methods used to preserve ancient Chinese texts. It plays a key role in conserving documents of the Jiangnan region's culture.

hangzhou-normal-university.h: Hangzhou Normal University: summary for applicants

blocks.x: Pulling the details together gives a clear picture. HZNU is a mid-sized municipal university, closely tied to the city government, with roots in teacher education going back to 1905 but a much wider curriculum today. It is known for a few distinctive features: the Alibaba Business School, which trains students in e-commerce and digital business with a branch for working adults in Singapore, and a network of more than 30 partner universities across Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania.
The key facts to remember are listed here.
Founded in 1905 as a teaching school and renamed Hangzhou Normal University in March 2007.
Five main campuses, a sixth planned at Cangqian, and 18 schools offering 49 undergraduate majors.
Alibaba Business School, formed in 2009, with programmes in e-commerce, international business, digital marketing and logistics.
A city of about 12.5 million people with a humid subtropical climate, long hot summers and chilly, cloudy winters.
An economy driven by digital and creative industries, and a setting that includes West Lake and the Grand Canal, both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Because the figures for campuses, staff and students come from different years and differ between sources, ask the university for its current numbers, and confirm which campus hosts your programme before you arrange housing.
