harbin-engineering-university.h: Harbin Engineering University at a glance

blocks.x: Harbin Engineering University, usually shortened to HEU (Chinese name 哈尔滨工程大学), is a state-funded research institution located in Harbin, the capital city of Heilongjiang Province in China's far northeast. Its identity is built around ships, the sea and nuclear technology. If you are thinking about naval architecture, marine engineering, underwater acoustics or reactor technology, this is one of the first names you will meet in China.

Administratively the university answers to the MIIT. Funding is shared with the Ministry of Education, the province of Heilongjiang, the Harbin municipal authorities and the PLA Navy. In national policy terms, it sits inside the Double First-Class Construction programme (where naval architecture and ocean engineering has been picked out for world-class development) and used to be a Project 211 school. People also know it as one of the "Seven Sons of National Defence", the informal label for defence-minded universities that the MIIT oversees.

The founding date is 1 September 1953. The school grew out of a military engineering academy, passed through a spell as a shipbuilding institute, and took its present name in 1994. Today it offers more than 55 undergraduate programmes, and for marine and ocean engineering the ShanghaiRanking subject table (Global Ranking of Academic Subjects) puts it second worldwide.

harbin-engineering-university.h: A military academy in Harbin (1953 to 1970)

blocks.x: The story starts on 1 September 1953, when a military engineering institute of the People's Liberation Army was set up in Harbin, reporting straight to the Central Military Commission. Its first president was Senior General Chen Geng. The academy followed Soviet military-school models and began with five departments: air force, artillery, navy, armoured forces and engineering corps.

Of those five, the Department of Naval Engineering, also founded in 1953, is the part that matters most for today's university. It trained engineers to design warships, build propulsion systems and develop submarines, and it is the direct ancestor of the subjects HEU is famous for now. In 1961 the institute received national key university status.

Between 1960 and 1962 several departments were sent elsewhere. The artillery department moved to Nanjing and later became Nanjing University of Science and Technology, while the armoured forces department went to Xi'an, among other moves. In April 1966 the Central Military Commission decided to rename the school Harbin Engineering College and take it out of the military system.

harbin-engineering-university.h: Becoming a civilian shipbuilding institute (1970 to 1994)

blocks.x: A 1969 decision to move parts of the old institute away from the border region led, in 1970, to a further split. The naval engineering departments that stayed in Harbin were reorganised as the Harbin Shipbuilding Engineering Institute (HSEI). It now came under civilian management: first the Sixth Ministry of Machine Building, then China State Shipbuilding Corporation. Its task was to serve industrial shipbuilding. Most of the other departments, along with the central administration, had already gone inland to Changsha in Hunan. There they became the Changsha Institute of Technology, known today as the National University of Defense Technology.

Regular enrolment at HSEI began in 1977, and in 1978 it again became a national key institution. In 1981 it won the right to award master's degrees and doctorates, so it was among the earliest Chinese universities with that authority. Over the 1970s and 1980s the staff helped build experimental prototype submarines and hovercraft, moving Chinese underwater vehicle and air-cushion work forward.

In April 1994 HSEI took the name Harbin Engineering University. It cleared the pre-assessment for Project 211 in 1996 and was in the first batch admitted. Then, in 2017, it entered the Double First-Class Construction initiative, which designated naval architecture and ocean engineering as its world-class subject.

The first stage of a new outpost in Qingdao, the Qingdao Innovation and Development Base, was completed in September 2021 and spans 370,000 square metres. It exists for applied research and for working with partners abroad. On the leadership side, Song Yingdong took over as CPC Committee Secretary on 12 September 2025, and Yin Jingwei became president.

One more fact applicants should know: American export rules name the university. The US Commerce Department added it to the Entity List on 23 May 2020, citing support for Chinese military procurement. The scrutiny section further down returns to this.

Like every public university in China, HEU is led through a dual structure in which the CPC Committee has the final say on strategic direction and senior appointments. The committee secretary is Song Yingdong (born 1969, in post since 12 September 2025), who handles party-building and the rollout of major policies. Yin Jingwei (born 1980) took the presidency the same day and doubles as a CPC deputy secretary; the president manages daily operations, academic matters and resources. Among the vice presidents are Han Duanfeng, Yu Zhiwen, Yan Rujian, Zhao Yuxin and Yin Hang.

Membership of the Seven Sons group means the university is expected to rank national defence research and development first. What it knows about shipbuilding, ocean engineering and marine propulsion feeds straight into PLA Navy progress, and it is a leading supplier of graduates to state-owned defence companies. It is also a member of the Sino-Russian Association of Technical Universities (中俄工科大学联盟), a nod to the long Russian connection of this border region.

The academic side is split into over 20 colleges, schools and departments, and almost every one leans toward engineering for naval, marine and nuclear purposes. Key units are Shipbuilding Engineering, Power and Energy Engineering, Intelligent Systems Science and Engineering, Nuclear Science and Technology, Underwater Acoustic Engineering, Materials Science and Chemical Engineering, and Information and Communication Engineering (each is a college in its own right). Outside the main campus, the university also operates the Yantai Research Institute, the South China Sea Research Institute and the Qingdao base mentioned earlier.

In numbers, you can choose among 61 undergraduate majors. Postgraduate study is organised into 32 first-level master's disciplines and 15 first-level doctoral disciplines, backed by 13 post-doctoral research stations. Naval architecture and ocean engineering carries the Double First-Class label. Beyond that, ship and marine engineering is a national key first-level discipline, and navigation, guidance and control counts as a national key second-level discipline.

About 1,793 full-time teachers work here. They include 389 professors, 502 associate professors and 8 academicians drawn from the two national academies (Sciences and Engineering). In the Essential Science Indicators (ESI) tables, engineering reaches the global top 1 per mille. Eight fields in all reach the global top 1 per cent: engineering, materials science, computer science, chemistry, environment and ecology, physics, geosciences and general social sciences.

The 2023 figures put total enrolment at roughly 29,422 students, of whom 27,994 were domestic and 1,428 international. About 8,000 are graduate students, around 35 per cent of the whole body. In that same year, graduates received 4,135 bachelor's degrees, 3,558 master's degrees and 378 doctorates.

Three themes dominate. The first is marine power systems, meaning propulsion and energy technology for both naval and civilian ships. The second is deep-sea engineering, which covers underwater acoustics and robotics. The third is nuclear safety, including simulating reactors and studying heat and fluid flow in sea-going conditions. The university runs more than 40 research organisations and over 150 laboratories.

Some of the physical facilities are impressive. The Ship Model Towing Tank Laboratory has a basin of 108 m by 7 m by 3.5 m for testing hydrodynamic resistance and wave-making. An ocean engineering basin of 50 m by 30 m by 10 m is used for studying vortex-induced vibration. The Nuclear Power Simulation Research Center offers computing and hardware-in-the-loop platforms that let researchers analyse reactor behaviour without needing operating reactors on site.

Two national key laboratories sit on campus, one devoted to underwater acoustic technology and the other to intelligent marine vehicle technology. There is also a national engineering laboratory for e-government modelling and simulation, and a China-Russia joint laboratory on polar technology and equipment that falls under the Belt and Road initiative. Areas of particular skill include submarines, underwater robots, ship stabilisation, dynamic positioning, integrated navigation, acoustic positioning under water, and simulating nuclear power plants. On the quality-management side, HEU was the first Chinese university to pass "dual certification" with ISO 9000.
A few achievements show what this work looks like in practice:
Wukong (悟空号), an autonomous underwater vehicle that dived to 10,896 metres in the Mariana Trench in November 2021, setting a Chinese record for an unmanned submersible with no cable.

Precise positioning technology for deep water that backed the crewed dives of Jiaolong, Shenhai Yongshi and Fendouzhe, earning a National Technological Invention Award (Second Class) and a place in the country's top ten university science and technology advances.
China's first multi-hull search-and-rescue ship.
Major design contributions to 20,000-TEU container ships and to the seventh-generation semi-submersible drilling platform for ultra-deep water.

The World Intellectual Property Organization names HEU as the top patent holder worldwide for efficient ship design in sea transport. Over the 13th Five-Year Plan period and after, it has undertaken more than 6,200 projects and collected upwards of 160 provincial-level or higher science and technology prizes.

The main campus is at 145 Nantong Street in Nangang District, close to the centre of Harbin, and covers about 1.26 million square metres. It occupies what used to be a military compound beside the Heilongjiang Military District. Within reach are the Confucian Temple of Harbin, Jile Temple, Cultural Park and the Guli Orchard.

The library is a six-storey building on the east side of the campus with more than 7.6 million volumes and particular depth in nuclear and marine science. Sport is well catered for: a gym hall with a pool, a stadium, a pair of 400-metre tracks, and grounds for football, rugby, tennis, basketball and volleyball.

HEU also works outside Harbin. The Yantai Research Institute sits in Yantai's Huangbohai New Area and focuses on marine and offshore applications. The Qingdao Innovation and Development Base is in Qingdao's West Coast New Area; its first phase of 370,000 square metres opened in September 2021 for applied research and international cooperation.

Chinese undergraduates are admitted mainly through the Gaokao, the national college entrance examination. In 2024 the minimum admission scores for science-track programmes ran, on average, more than 110 points above provincial first-batch undergraduate lines across 30 provinces. Applicants from the university's own province, Heilongjiang, faced a gap of 144 points. As a sample, Shandong Province's 2024 scores ranged from 607 for ocean engineering to 613 for electronic information and software engineering, against a top score of about 750. These figures tell international applicants that Chinese classmates have been strongly selected.

Overseas students can join certain English-taught programmes in marine subjects. The International Student Scholarship offered by HEU has two tiers: first-class winners get full tuition covered, second-class winners get 50 per cent. Applicants to English-taught programmes generally need a TOEFL score of 79 or an IELTS score of 5.5. Always check the current requirements and scholarship terms on the university's international admissions pages, since these change from year to year.

Exchange and cooperation get real emphasis: partner institutions number over 130 across 30 countries, and visiting scholars and joint research projects are coordinated centrally. In 2023 the roll included more than 1,100 international students from around 90 countries. Looking at the longer run, the International Cooperative Education college has taught 5,600-plus students of more than 100 nationalities.
The rankings tell different stories depending on whether they measure a subject or the whole institution:
ShanghaiRanking subject ranking, 2024 edition: second in the world for marine and ocean engineering.
QS World University Rankings 2026: placed in the 1001 to 1200 group overall; QS Asia 2025: 362nd.
U.S. News and World Report Best Global Universities: 699th worldwide.
ShanghaiRanking Best Chinese Universities Ranking: 45th in China.
EduRank (2025): 81st among Chinese universities.

Domestically, the university holds Double First-Class discipline status and Project 211 key status. Between 2016 and 2020 it was given Outstanding Contribution Awards, one for high-tech weapons equipment and one for aircraft carrier building. The pattern is clear: very strong in its niche, more modest in broad global tables.

A total of 46 alumni have become academicians of the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering. The most famous is Huang Xuhua, who led the design of China's first nuclear submarine. Others are Yang Shi'e in underwater acoustics, Pan Jingfu in naval architecture, Xu Yuru in underwater robotics, and Qian Qihu in protective engineering. Wang Zeshan works on energetic materials, while Ren Xinmin and Liang Shoupan are missile technology specialists, and Ci Yungui and Zhou Xingming are computer scientists.

Other alumni have gone into the military, politics and business. Tang Tianbiao became a general and Jin Mao a deputy commander of the PLA Navy. Yu Zhengsheng once chaired the CPPCC National Committee, China's top political advisory body. In business, Wang Jun chaired CITIC Group and Zhou Huan chaired Datang Group.

The employment link with industry is strong. From 2010 to 2018, HEU supplied over 50 per cent of all the university graduates hired by CSIC (China Shipbuilding Industry Corporation, the defence arm of today's China State Shipbuilding Corporation). Its alumni hold important posts in designing and building PLA Navy surface vessels and submarines. Nuclear-college graduates have contributed to marine nuclear propulsion and floating nuclear platforms, working with the China National Nuclear Corporation.

harbin-engineering-university.h: External scrutiny you should know about

blocks.x: Foreign observers have paid attention to HEU's closeness to the Chinese defence sector. The US listed it under export-control rules in May 2020. In addition, ASPI (the Australian Strategic Policy Institute) includes HEU in its China Defence Universities Tracker as an institution tied to technology-acquisition cases. Concern about China's military-civil fusion strategy has led some Western governments and universities to limit or vet cooperation with the university, EU-funded research consortia among them.

For a prospective student, this may matter if you hope to move on to study, work or research in countries with strict export or security screening. Ask your future host institution early whether any such rules might apply to your chosen field.

Daily life depends heavily on the city around the campus: its weather, how people travel, and what there is to see and do. The sections below describe Harbin, the home of Harbin Engineering University.

The city's land area is 53,068 square kilometres. As capital of Heilongjiang Province, it lies in the province's south. The prefecture sits at the south-eastern margin of the Songnen Plain, part of the great Northeastern Plain, and its centre faces the Songhua River on the south bank of the river's middle section. Heilongjiang's outline looks like a swan, so Harbin is nicknamed "the pearl on the swan's neck". The administrative area is big, running from 44° 04′ to 46° 40′ north and 125° 42′ to 130° 10′ east.

Harbin's neighbours at prefecture level run clockwise from the north: Yichun (north), Jiamusi and Qitaihe (northeast), Mudanjiang (southeast), Daqing (west) and Suihua (northwest). To the southwest, the boundary is with Jilin Province. Most of the urban terrain is flat and low, around 150 metres (490 ft) above sea level on average. The 10 county-level divisions in the eastern part are hills and mountains, and the far east holds large wetlands, especially in Yilan County on the southwestern fringe of the Sanjiang Plain.

Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa). The Siberian high and a position above 45 degrees north explain the cold and long winter, and the city is rightly called the Ice City. Winters are dry and bitterly cold, with a January average over 24 hours of only -17.3 °C (0.9 °F), yet there is little snowfall and often plenty of sun. Spring and autumn are short transitions with changeable wind directions. Summers can turn hot; July averages 23.7 °C, or 74.7 °F.

Most of the year's rain arrives in summer. Of the annual 539 millimetres (21.2 in), more than half falls in July and August. Monthly possible sunshine ranges from 45 per cent in December to 60 per cent in September, giving 2,340 hours of bright sunshine a year, and rain or snow falls on average on 99 days. Across the year the mean temperature is 5.2 °C, or 41.4 °F.

Extremes have been dramatic. The official station recorded -42.6 °C (-45 °F), or -41.1 °C (-42 °F) in January 1931 by another reading, and a high of 39.2 °C (103 °F), most recently reached on 4 June 2001. An unofficial reading of 41.0 °C, or 105.8 °F, came in July 1907. For a new student the practical lesson is to bring or buy serious winter clothing before the first December.
To cope with a changing climate, Harbin's planners have adopted "sponge city" ideas. The Qunli stormwater park is an example: it gathers, filters and stores rain while preserving natural habitat.

No other city in Heilongjiang has a bigger economy. GDP came to RMB 501.08 billion in 2013, up 8.9 per cent year on year, and to RMB 575.12 billion in 2015. The 2012 split between the three sectors was 11.1 : 36.1 : 52.8, and 3.147 million people were in work. Imports and exports at the end of 2012 totalled US$5,330 million.

The soil here is chernozem, among the most fertile in China, which suits food and textile crops. Harbin is therefore a national base for commodity grain and a natural home for agribusiness. It also has a broad industrial base spanning light industry, textiles, medicine, food, aircraft, automobiles, metallurgy, electronics, building materials and chemicals. Leading firms include the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory, Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and Harbin Electric.

Power equipment is a leading industry. Hydro and thermal equipment made in Harbin accounts for one-third of China's total installed capacity. Platts data for 2009 to 2010 placed Harbin Electric second worldwide for steam turbine market share, tied with Dongfang Electric and just behind Shanghai Electric. On the medicine side, Harbin Pharmaceutical Group (research, production and sales of drugs) ranks as the second-largest Chinese pharmaceutical firm by market capitalisation.

The Harbin International Trade and Economic Fair has taken place every year since 1990. Figures to 2013 show it had attracted over 1.9 million exhibitors and visitors from more than 80 countries and regions, with contract volume above US$100 billion. Harbin also ranks among the leading destinations for foreign direct investment in Northeast China (US$980 million actually used in 2013). In October 2013, at the 18th regular meeting of the Chinese and Russian prime ministers, Li Keqiang and Dmitry Medvedev agreed that the fair would become the "China-Russia EXPO". It is now sponsored jointly by China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang government, and Russia's ministries of Economic Development and of Trade and Industry.

Finance and retail are also based here. Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank, among the largest banks in Northeast China, have their headquarters in the city, and In 2011 Harbin Bank was fourth in a competitiveness ranking of Chinese city commercial banks. Qiulin Group runs Harbin's largest department store.
The city's development zones explain where much of its work is concentrated:

Harbin Economic and Technology Development Zone (national level): telecommunications equipment, chemicals, automobile production and assembly, electronics, textiles, and medical equipment and supplies.
Harbin High and New Technological Development Zone: integrated optical, mechanical and electrical products, biology, medicine, electronics and IT.
Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (provincial): car production and assembly, electronics assembly and manufacturing, heavy industry, and instruments and industrial equipment.
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (provincial): trade and distribution, food and beverage processing, medical equipment and supplies, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.
Harbin Port is also part of the economic landscape, and three further zones deserve a closer look.

The Songbei Economic Development Zone, in Songbei District, has a planned area of 5.53 square kilometres. Electronics assembly and manufacturing and food and drink processing are the industries it encourages. Regional and provincial headquarters of big companies, for example China Datang, China Netcom and China Telecom, have moved in, so it is turning into a cluster of regional head offices. Two research centres are based here as well: the Science and Technology Innovation Center and the International Agricultural Science and Technology Innovation Center of Harbin. Thanks to such institutes, a 2006 competitiveness ranking put Harbin ninth among 50 major Chinese cities for ability in scientific and technological innovation, and sixth for volume of scientific and technological achievements.

HETDZ, the Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone, is among China's 90 national economic development zones. It was established in June 1991, and the State Council raised it to national level in April 1993. The dates given for how the hi-tech zone was merged into HETDZ in December 2012 and separated again in 2009 do not fit together, so check local sources on the exact sequence. Today its centralised parks cover 18.5 square kilometres, in two blocks, Nangang and Haping Road. A third park, Yingbin Road Hi-tech (12.2 square kilometres), was once part of HETDZ but has been run by the neighbouring High and New Technology Industry Development Zone since 2009. Nangang Park incubates high-tech projects, hosts research bases for companies, and holds service industries such as finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture and entertainment; the headquarters and branches of famous companies are there. Yingbin Road Park concentrates on high-tech incubation and industrial development. Haping Road Park is a comprehensive industrial base for automobile and parts manufacturing, medicines, food, electronics and textiles, with car production and raw material processing encouraged.

The High and New Technology Industry Development Zone is one of 56 national zones of that type. It started as a provincial zone in 1988 and gained national status from the State Council in 1991. It has 23.9 square kilometres of built-up area, split into the Science and Technology Innovation Town and the High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The 2020 census counted 10,009,854 residents, a fall of 5.62 per cent over the previous ten years. Within the built-up area (every urban district apart from Acheng and Shuangcheng, which are not yet urbanised) there were 5,282,083 people. Of the whole population, 70.61 per cent live in urban areas and 29.39 per cent in rural areas.

The population is fairly old: 10.46 per cent are under 14 and 14.65 per cent are over 65. Males are slightly more numerous (50.02 per cent against 49.98 per cent). The birth rate is 6.95 per 1,000, compared with a Chinese average of 12.13.
Most residents are Han Chinese (93 per cent in 2000), with minorities including Manchu, Hui and Mongol people and a small Russian community.

Catholics are looked after by the Apostolic Administration of Harbin, a missionary jurisdiction that predates a diocese. The city also has the old Eastern Catholic cathedral that belonged to the Russian Catholic Apostolic Exarchate. Another landmark, the heavily damaged Church of the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, once served Russian soldiers from the Outer Amur Military Region who were stationed here. Muslims were a small share (0.4 per cent in 2000), and the Daowai Mosque, the largest in Heilongjiang, stands in the city. Harbin once had a small Jewish community around Zhongyang Main Street, a home to many European Jewish refugees.

Local culture rests on Han Chinese traditions mixed with Manchu and Russian influences, and this shows in architecture, food, music and customs. On 22 June 2010 Harbin was named a UNESCO City of Music within the Creative Cities Network.

Chinese holidaymakers flock here, above all in winter, when big ice sculpture displays go up. Wanda Harbin Mall even contains an indoor ski park with six slopes, the longest 500 metres (1,600 ft). The 2023 to 2024 winter season brought 87 million visitors, mainly from other parts of China. European-style architecture is another draw: Saint Sophia Cathedral, Central Street and the Baroque ensemble of Lao Daowai (Old Town).

Harbin is the northernmost of China's major cities, in northern Northeast China. With the Siberian Anticyclone close by, the winter daily average temperature is -19.7 °C (-3.5 °F), and annual lows below -25.0 °C (-13.0 °F) are not unusual. From December to March, ice and snow sculptures of many styles decorate the city.

The International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival began in 1985. Officially it opens on 5 January each year, though many works can be seen earlier. Sculptures appear all over town, but two areas are the main ones. Giant snow sculptures stand on Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a AAAAA-rated recreation area across the Songhua River from the city. Separately, the "Ice and Snow World" opens each night, lit to show the sculptures from inside and outside. It features full-size buildings made of clear ice blocks 2 to 3 feet thick, taken straight from the Songhua River. Putting the exhibition together takes 15,000 workers 16 days. In early December ice artisans saw about 120,000 cubic metres (4.2 million cubic feet) of ice off the frozen river as raw material.

Parks and main avenues also feature ice buildings, snow sculptures, ice slides, and festival food and drink. Things to do in the season include alpine skiing at Yabuli, snowmobiling, winter swimming in the Songhua, and the old-style ice-lantern show at Zhaolin Garden (first staged in 1963). Visitors from Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore especially know the city's snow carving and ice recreation.

The festival ranks as one of four great ice and snow events worldwide, the others being Sapporo's snow festival in Japan, the Quebec City Winter Carnival in Canada and the Holmenkollen ski festival in Norway. Each November Harbin also exports its art: over 100 artisans make ICE!, a yearly indoor show of Christmas-themed ice carvings, which appears at National Harbor (Maryland), Nashville (Tennessee), Kissimmee (Florida) and Grapevine (Texas).

Heilongjiang Television (HLJTV) is the regional broadcaster, with seven channels plus a satellite channel reaching other provinces. The city's own station, Harbin Television (HRBTV), has five specialist channels. The Long Guang (Dragon Broadcast) radio group, formerly Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, serves the whole province with seven channels, including one in Korean. Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS) carries music, news, traffic, economy and daily-life programmes for Harbin and nearby areas, including Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.
Harbin Engineering University lists 149 programs for international students on this site: 37 bachelor, 45 master's, 30 doctoral, 37 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 102 taught in Chinese, 47 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 45,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 27,000 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 27,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 35,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 35,000), according to the university's published fee table.

149 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (18):
Artificial Intelligence
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Civil Engineering
Computer Science and Technology
Control Science and Engineering
Design and Manufacturing of Ships and Marine Structures
Energy and Power
Information and Communication Engineering
Intelligent Science and Technology
Marine Engineering
Materials Science and Engineering
Mathematics
Mechanical Engineering
Mechanics (Engineering)
Nuclear Science and Technology
Optical Engineering
Power Engineering and Engineering Thermophysics
Underwater Acoustic Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

harbin-engineering-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Harbin Engineering University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Harbin, register at Harbin Engineering University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Where HIT stands in the Chinese system

blocks.x: Harbin Institute of Technology, usually shortened to HIT, is a public university built around science and engineering. Its main campus lies in the Nan'gang area of Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang province in the far northeast of China. It answers to the national Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. That is slightly unusual, because most leading Chinese universities report to the Ministry of Education, and the industry link tells you a lot about HIT's practical, technology-driven character.

HIT carries almost every national label a Chinese university can hold. It is part of Project 211, of Project 985 and of the Double First-Class Construction scheme, and it is one of the nine members of the C9 League, the group often described as China's answer to an elite research alliance. For an international applicant, this means a degree that employers and graduate schools across the country recognise immediately.

The story began in 1920, when the school opened as the Harbin Sino-Russia Industrial School. Today HIT is not a single-site institution. Besides the main campus in Harbin, it runs two satellite campuses: one in Shenzhen, Guangdong, called HIT Shenzhen, and one in Weihai, Shandong, called HIT Weihai. Check carefully which campus teaches your chosen programme before you apply, because climate, city life and course lists differ a great deal between the three.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: A century of growth, decade by decade

blocks.x: HIT's past is tied up with the history of Harbin itself: Russian railway beginnings, wartime occupation and then years of cooperation with the Soviet Union. The timeline below shows how a small technical school turned into a national flagship.

Its original name in 1920 was the Harbin Sino-Russian School for Industry, set up to educate railway engineers. Postgraduate students were first admitted in the spring of 1931. In 1935, while Japan was invading China, the school came under Japanese control. The title Harbin Institute of Technology returned on 1 January 1938, and it is still the official name.

After Japan's defeat in the Second World War and its withdrawal in 1945, the institute came under the Zhongchang Railway Bureau, with China and the Soviet Union sharing management. Then, in 1949, it recruited graduate students from across the whole country, which makes it one of the earliest Chinese institutions to train postgraduates.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Becoming a national key university, 1951 to 1998

blocks.x: In 1951 the central government selected HIT as one of just two institutions of higher learning charged with learning advanced techniques from the USSR. The school earned the nickname 'Cradle for Engineers' during this period. In 1954 it was named one of six national key universities, and it was the only one of the six located outside Beijing.

1984 brought two more steps. The state made HIT one of 15 universities to receive major investment, and HIT was among the first 22 universities allowed to set up a graduate school. In 1996 it was placed among the first-class universities of Project 211, the Ministry of Education's scheme for national key universities. Two years later, in 1998, it was one of the first nine universities invited into Project 985, the funding programme that gives priority to 39 leading research-focused comprehensive universities.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Merger, C9 and the latest elite programmes, 2000 to 2017

blocks.x: In 2000 HIT merged with the Harbin University of Architecture, which shared its roots and counted among China's famous eight old schools, and the combined body became the present Harbin Institute of Technology. The C9 League followed in 2009, when the central government grouped nine leading institutions together. Zhejiang University and Fudan University are in it, as are Peking and Tsinghua. The rest are HIT, Nanjing University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Xi'an Jiao Tong University and the University of Science and Technology of China.

A further national innovation alliance, the so-called Universities and Colleges Innovation Promotion Plan, took HIT in during 2012. A national discipline assessment published in 2013 found 16 first-level disciplines in the country's top five and 25 in its top ten, with mechanics ranked first in China. In 2017 HIT was placed in Class A, the top tier, of the Double First-Class Construction programme, which is the newest scheme for elite Chinese universities.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Study programmes and student numbers on the Harbin campus

blocks.x: On the Harbin campus, HIT teaches through eighteen schools. They award 86 undergraduate degrees and run 41 master's programmes, 29 doctoral programmes and 24 post-doctoral research programmes. That range is wide enough for most engineering and science interests, with a clear lean towards technical fields.

The scale is considerable. As of 2019 the Harbin campus enrolled 15,675 undergraduates, 9,680 master's students and 6,518 doctoral students. Of those, 1,984 were international students, drawn from 128 countries and regions, so a newcomer will not be the only foreigner on campus and will find an established support system for overseas learners.
Rankings never tell the whole story, but they help you place HIT. Here is how the main tables treat it.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Standing in China and in the combined tables

blocks.x: Within China, HIT consistently sits among the top ten research-focused comprehensive universities, and it ranks first in the Northeast, a region covering Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang with more than 100 million people between them. The Aggregate Ranking of Top Universities, which blends the three most widely followed international tables (THE, ARWU and QS), put HIT first in Northeast China, ninth in China and 143rd in the world in 2025.

For 2026, Times Higher Education placed HIT 96th, and the Academic Ranking of World Universities placed it 97th. U.S. News and World Report ranked it 111th, and the Center for World University Rankings ranked it 147th.

On reputation alone, the THE World Reputation Rankings gave HIT 101st place globally, which marks it as one of the best-regarded Chinese universities abroad. Its graduates are also in demand worldwide: the 2021 Global Employability University Ranking from Times Higher Education put HIT at 143rd.

In the 2025 Nature Index, HIT was 27th among Asia Pacific universities and 46th among all universities worldwide. The 2025 CWTS Leiden Ranking placed it 14th in the world for total publications, and 22nd for papers in the top 1% of their fields over 2020 to 2023.

Engineering is where HIT shines. Its research covers a broad range of topics, but the emphasis on engineering sciences is strong. Every year since U.S. News and World Report began its global ranking in 2014, HIT has been placed in the top ten for engineering, and as of 2024 it stood third in the world in that subject.

HIT's staff and students have produced many 'firsts' for China. The list includes an analog computer in 1957, a digital computer in 1958, an intelligent chess-playing computer, an arc welding robot, a world-class new-system radar, an integrated circuit CMOS chip with its own copyright, a computer real-time system for creating three-dimensional images, and a high-performance computer-controlled fibre twister, along with the first superway. Some research at HIT is covered by official secrecy, for example in space science and defence-related technology.

No other university did more to make the Shenzhou and Kuaizhou spacecraft series succeed. The International Astronomical Union recognised this record by naming minor planet number 55838 after the institute, nicknamed the 'Hagongda Star'.

HIT is known for its close relationship with the People's Liberation Army and with China's space programme, and it belongs to the group nicknamed the Seven Sons of National Defence. The Astronautics Innovation Research Center, launched in 2010 jointly with the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, is the largest investment of its kind in the country. One point deserves honest mention for international applicants. The US Bureau of Industry and Security put HIT on its Entity List in May 2020, citing support for the military. If you plan to work with US institutions or companies later, you may want to find out how that listing could affect your plans.

HIT Weihai occupies a site in Weihai's Torch Hi-Tech Science Park. Weihai is a scenic coastal city, found on the Jiaodong Peninsula. The campus has pleasant scenery and a mild climate, adjoins the sea at Golden Beach and is ringed by hills. It ranks among the best 50 universities in China for student satisfaction. It covers 1,560,000 square metres in total, of which 383,000 square metres is built-up floor area.

The Weihai campus is organised into 10 schools and 1 department. Its roll shows 10,466 undergraduates, 542 master's students and 110 doctoral candidates, plus 89 international students. Staff number 861, among them 97 professors and 219 associate professors. It offers 37 bachelor's programmes and shares 22 master's programmes and 18 doctoral programmes with HIT, taught to the same educational standards. It complements Harbin by developing its own characteristic disciplines, namely marine science and ocean engineering and automotive engineering, with strengths in advanced manufacturing, information technology and electrical engineering, computer science and software engineering, and materials science and engineering.

HIT graduates have gone on to lead universities, companies, laboratories and government. The groups below give a sense of the range, though you should remember that some of these careers are in politics and defence.

Besides belonging to that body and to the Chinese Academy of Sciences, he is a foreign member of three overseas academies: the US National Academy of Engineering, the Russian Academy of Sciences and the Royal Swedish Academy of Engineering Sciences.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Living in Harbin: the city behind the campus

blocks.x: A student's everyday experience depends heavily on the surrounding city. The following sections cover Harbin, where the main HIT campus stands, and look at weather, economy, people, culture and leisure.

Harbin, the provincial capital of Heilongjiang, lies in the south of the province. Its prefecture spans 53,068 square kilometres (20,490 square miles) and touches the Songnen Plain, itself a major piece of the wider Northeastern Plain. Downtown, you are on the south side of the Songhua River's middle reaches. Because the outline of Heilongjiang looks like a swan, Harbin has been nicknamed the pearl on the swan's neck.

The administrative area is large: it runs between latitudes 44° 04′ and 46° 40′ north and longitudes 125° 42′ and 130° 10′ east. Around it are six other places, and it helps to know the direction of each.
Yichun lies to the north.
Jiamusi and Qitaihe lie to the northeast.
Mudanjiang lies to the southeast.
Daqing lies to the west.
Suihua lies to the northwest.
Jilin province forms the southwestern border.

Most of the terrain around the city is flat and low, with an average height of roughly 150 metres (490 ft). Hills and mountains are found only in the 10 county-level divisions of the east. Right at the eastern limit of the prefecture, large wetlands spread out, chiefly in Yilan County, where the Sanjiang Plain begins to the southwest.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: Climate: planning for the Ice City

blocks.x: Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa). The Siberian high and a position north of 45 degrees latitude give it cold weather and a long winter. The nickname Ice City is deserved: winters are dry and bitterly cold, and the 24-hour average temperature in January is only -17.3 °C (0.9 °F). There is little precipitation in winter, though, and the skies are often sunny.

Spring and autumn are short transition seasons, with winds that change direction. Summers can get hot: July averages 23.7 °C (74.7 °F). Most of the year's rain falls then, and July and August together bring over half of the 539 millimetres (21.2 in) annual total. Possible sunshine ranges between 45 percent in December and 60 percent in September, which adds up to 2,340 hours of bright sunshine a year, and rain or snow falls on average on 99 days of the year.

Across the whole year the mean temperature is 5.2 °C (41.4 °F). Extremes at the official weather station range from -42.6 °C (-45 °F), with -41.1 °C (-42 °F) recorded in January 1931, up to 39.2 °C (103 °F), most recently reached on 4 June 2001. July 1907 saw an unofficial reading of 41.0 °C (105.8 °F). For students, the practical advice is to arrive with a proper winter coat and thermal layers, because the first months of study can include temperatures far below anything in a temperate country.

To limit the effects of climate change, Harbin's planners have used sponge city ideas. One example is Qunli stormwater park, which gathers, filters and stores rainwater while protecting natural habitat.

No city in Heilongjiang produces more than Harbin. In 2013 its GDP totalled RMB 501.08 billion, up 8.9 percent on the previous year, and by 2015 it had reached RMB 575.12 billion. In 2012 the three sectors of industry stood in the ratio 11.1 to 36.1 to 52.8, so services dominate. Imports and exports were worth US$5,330 million by the end of 2012, and the working population in 2012 was 3.147 million.

The chernozem soil around Harbin is among the most nutrient-rich in China, which suits food and textile crops. That makes Harbin the country's commodity grain base and a natural location for agribusiness.

The city also has light industry, textiles, medicine, food, aircraft, automobiles, metallurgy, electronics, building materials and chemicals, which together form a fairly complete industrial system. Among the key employers are Harbin Electric Company Limited, the Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory. Power equipment is a leading trade: hydro and thermal power equipment made here accounts for one-third of China's total installed capacity. Platts reported that Harbin Electric held second place in world steam turbine market share for 2009 to 2010, level with Dongfang Electric and slightly behind Shanghai Electric. In medicine, Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, active in research, development, production and sales, has the second-highest market value of any Chinese drugmaker.

A trade and investment fair has been held in the city annually from 1990. By 2013's figures, visitors and exhibitors totalled more than 1.9 million, from over 80 countries and regions, and deals worth above US$100 billion had been signed. Harbin also attracts a large share of foreign direct investment into Northeast China: US$980 million was used in 2013. In October 2013, at the 18th regular meeting between Chinese premier Li Keqiang and Russian prime minister Dmitry Medvedev, the two governments agreed that the event would be renamed the China-Russia EXPO. Its co-sponsors are China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang government, and Russia's ministries of economic development and of trade and industry.

Two big regional lenders, Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank, are headquartered in the city. Harbin Bank was fourth in a 2011 ranking of Chinese city commercial banks by competitiveness. For shopping, the Qiulin Group owns the city's largest department store.
Harbin has several zones that concentrate industry and research. The first four below are described briefly, followed by the port and the larger zones in more detail.

Harbin Economic and Technology Development Zone (national level) focuses on telecommunications equipment, chemicals, automobile production and assembly, electronics, textiles, and medical equipment and supplies.
The Harbin High and New Technological Development Zone works on integrated optics, mechanics and electrics, as well as biology, medicine, electronics and information technology.

Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (provincial) specialises in automobile production and assembly, electronics assembly and manufacturing, heavy industry, and instruments and industrial equipment.
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (provincial) centres on trading and distribution, food and beverage processing, medical equipment and supplies, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.
Harbin Port.

Songbei Economic Development Zone sits in Songbei District and was planned to cover 5.53 square kilometres. The government wants electronics assembly and manufacturing and food and drink processing to grow here. Regional and provincial head offices of big firms, among them China Datang, China Netcom and China Telecom, have already settled in, so the area is turning into a hub for local headquarters. Two research centres, the Harbin Science and Technology Innovation Center and the Harbin International Agricultural Science and Technology Innovation Center, are based here too. Thanks to institutes like these, a 2006 comparison of 50 major Chinese cities put Harbin ninth for innovation capacity in science and technology, and sixth for the volume of scientific and technological results.

HETDZ, the economic and technological zone, is one of 90 national-level economic development zones across China. Work began in June 1991, and national status came from the State Council in April 1993. The timeline then gets tangled: a merger with the high-tech zone took place in December 2012, though the hi-tech zone had already been split off in 2009. Today the centralised parks occupy 18.5 square kilometres in two groups, Nangang and Haping Road. A third, the 12.2 square-kilometre Yingbin Road Hi-tech Centralized Park, used to belong to HETDZ but has come under the neighbouring high and new technology zone since 2009.

Nangang Centralized Park is meant for incubating high-tech projects and for company research bases. It also hosts service industries: finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture, recreation and entertainment. Famous companies keep their headquarters or Harbin branches here.
Yingbin Road Centralized Park concentrates on high-tech incubation and industrial development.

Haping Road Centralized Park is intended as a comprehensive industrial base for investment projects in automobile and parts manufacturing, medicines, food, electronics and textiles, with automobile production and assembly and raw material processing encouraged.

Of China's 56 national high and new technology industry zones, one is in Harbin. It began as a provincial-level zone in 1988 and gained national status from the State Council in 1991. Its built-up area totals 23.9 square kilometres and has two parts: the Science and Technology Innovation Town and the High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The 2020 census counted 10,009,854 people in Harbin, a drop of 5.62 percent over the previous ten years. The built-up area, which covers all the urban districts except Acheng and Shuangcheng (not yet urbanised), had 5,282,083 residents. Some 70.61 percent of people lived in urban areas and 29.39 percent in rural areas.

The metropolitan population is on the older side: 10.46 percent are under 14 and 14.65 percent are over 65. Men make up 50.02 percent and women 49.98 percent. Births are fewer than elsewhere in China, with a rate of 6.95 per 1,000 people compared with the national 12.13.

Most residents are Han Chinese (93 percent in 2000). Minorities include Manchu, Hui and Mongol people, and there is a small community of Russians. The 2020 census gives the detailed breakdown by ethnic group.

The city's Catholic minority falls under the Apostolic Administration of Harbin, a missionary jurisdiction that is not yet a full diocese. An earlier Eastern Catholic cathedral also survives, from the Russian Catholic Apostolic Exarchate of Harbin. A badly damaged building, the Church of the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, once housed Russian troops who belonged to the Outer Amur Military Region and were garrisoned in the city. Muslims were a small share of the population (0.4 percent in 2000). The Daowai Mosque, the largest mosque in Heilongjiang, is in Harbin. The city also had a small Jewish community centred on Zhongyang Main Street, which sheltered many European Jewish refugees.

Local culture is rooted in Han traditions, blended with Manchu and Russian influences. This mix shapes the architecture, food, music and customs of the city. On 22 June 2010 Harbin was named a UNESCO City of Music within the Creative Cities Network.

Harbin is a popular domestic destination, especially in winter, when large ice sculpture displays draw crowds. There is even a large indoor ski park inside the Wanda Harbin Mall, with six slopes, the longest reaching 500 metres (1,600 ft). The 2023 to 2024 winter season saw 87 million visitors, mostly from elsewhere in China.
European-style architecture is another draw. Visitors like Saint Sophia Cathedral, Central Street and the Baroque ensemble in Lao Daowai, the Old Town.

Harbin is the northernmost major city in China and falls directly under the Siberian Anticyclone. The average daily winter temperature is -19.7 °C (-3.5 °F), and annual lows below -25.0 °C (-13.0 °F) are not unusual. Because of the freezing season, the city, known as the Ice City, fills with ice and snow sculptures of every style from December to March.

The Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival, an international event, began in 1985. Officially it opens each year on 5 January, yet many works are visible beforehand. Sculptures appear all over the city, but there are two main exhibition areas. One is Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a AAAAA-rated recreation area across the Songhua River from the city, with enormous snow sculptures. The other is Ice and Snow World, which runs each night with the lights on, lighting the sculptures from within and without. It features full-size illuminated buildings made of crystal-clear ice blocks two to three feet thick, taken straight from the Songhua River. Constructing the exhibition takes 15,000 workers 16 days. Early in December, artisans harvest 120,000 cubic metres (4.2 million cubic feet) of ice from the frozen surface of the river as raw material.

Large ice buildings, snow sculptures, ice slides, festival food and drinks also appear in several parks and main avenues. Festival activities include Yabuli alpine skiing, snowmobile driving, winter swimming in the Songhua River and the traditional ice-lantern show at Zhaolin Garden, which started in 1963. Carving in snow and ice enjoys a reputation across Asia, especially in Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore.

Worldwide, only four winter festivals are as large: this one, Japan's Sapporo Snow Festival, the Quebec City Winter Carnival in Canada and Norway's Holmenkollen Ski Festival. Each November Harbin also dispatches ice artists to America to showcase the craft. More than 100 artisans create ICE!, an annual indoor display of Christmas-themed ice carvings, staged in National Harbor in Maryland, Nashville in Tennessee, Kissimmee in Florida and Grapevine in Texas.
Local media are easy to find if you want to practise Chinese listening skills.
Heilongjiang Television (HLJTV), the regional broadcaster, runs seven channels plus a satellite channel for other provinces.
Harbin Television (HRBTV), the municipal station, has five channels for specialised programming.
Long Guang, or Dragon Broadcast, was once the Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station. This radio group covers all of Heilongjiang on seven channels, one of them in Korean.
The city's own radio station, HPBS, carries music, news, traffic, economic and lifestyle programmes to Harbin and neighbouring areas such as Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.

harbin-institute-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Harbin Institute of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Harbin, register at Harbin Institute of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Harbin Medical University (HMU) (Chinese: 哈尔滨医科大学) is a public university located in Harbin, Heilongjiang, China.

HMU is appointed as a national education and training base for biomedical scientists and teaching talents by the National Bureau of Advanced Health Care Education, and a key university of Heilongjiang Province in the national "211 Project".
Harbin Medical University (HMU) is located in Harbin, Heilongjiang province. HMU has a scenic green campus of 2.36 million square meters with buildings of ancient architecture styles.

It has four first-grade doctorate degree programs including basic medical sciences, clinical medicine, public health and preventive medicine, and biology; 41 second-grade doctorate degree programs, and 49 second-grade master's degree programs. The 11 undergraduate programs include basic medical sciences, clinical medicine, preventive medicine, dentistry, anesthesiology, medical imaging, nursing, pharmacy, biotechnology, public affairs management, and medical law. Currently, HMU has five postdoctoral research programs in preventive medicine, clinical medicine, basic medical sciences, biology, and pharmacy, one research program in clinical pharmacy and pharmacology, and the postdoctoral research program in collaboration with Zhonglong Enterprises. HMU has a reasonable discipline structure. Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), also known as the Shanghai Ranking, is one of the annual publications of world university rankings. It's the first global university ranking with multifarious indicators.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Harbin, where Harbin Medical University is located.

Harbin, with a total land area of 53,068 km2 (20,490 sq mi), is located in southern Heilongjiang province and is the provincial capital. The prefecture is also located at the southeastern edge of the Songnen Plain, a major part of China's Northeastern Plain. The city center also sits on the southern bank of the middle Songhua River. Harbin received its nickname The pearl on the swan's neck, since the shape of Heilongjiang resembles a swan. Its administrative area is rather large with latitude spanning 44° 04′−46° 40′ N, and longitude 125° 42′−130° 10' E. Neighbouring prefecture-level cities are Yichun to the north, Jiamusi and Qitaihe to the northeast, Mudanjiang to the southeast, Daqing to the west, and Suihua to the northwest. On its southwestern boundary is Jilin province. The main terrain of the city is generally flat and low lying, with an average elevation of around 150 metres (490 ft). The territory that comprises the 10 county-level divisions in the eastern part of the municipality consists of mountains and uplands. The easternmost part of Harbin prefecture also has extensive wetlands, mainly in Yilan County, which is located at the southwestern edge of the Sanjiang Plain.

Under the Köppen climate classification, Harbin features a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Dwa). Due to the Siberian high and its location above 45 degrees north latitude, the city is known for its cold weather and long winter. Its nickname Ice City is well-earned, as winters in the city are dry and freezing cold, with a 24-hour average in January of only −17.3 °C (0.9 °F), although the city sees little precipitation during the winter and is often sunny. Spring and autumn constitute brief transition periods with variable wind directions. Summers can be hot, with a July mean temperature of 23.7 °C (74.7 °F). Summer is also when most of the year's rainfall occurs, and more than half of the annual precipitation, at 539 millimetres (21.2 in), occurs in July and August alone. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 45 percent in December to 60 percent in September, the city receives 2,340 hours of bright sunshine annually; on average precipitation falls 99 days out of the year. The annual mean temperature is 5.2 °C (41.4 °F), and extreme temperatures have ranged from −42.6 °C (−45 °F) or for the official weather station there, −41.1 °C (−42 °F) in January 1931 to 39.2 °C (103 °F) on which was hit most recently on 4 June 2001, though an unofficial record high temperature of 41.0 °C (105.8 °F) was recorded in July 1907.

To mitigate impacts of climate change, urban planning in Harbin has made use of sponge city concepts, including the Qunli stormwater park which collects, filters, and stores rainwater while conserving natural habitat.

Harbin has the largest economy in Heilongjiang province. In 2013, Harbin's GDP totaled RMB501.08 billion, an increase of 8.9 percent over the previous year. The proportion of the three industries to the aggregate of GDP was 11.1:36.1:52.8 in 2012. The total value for imports and exports by the end of 2012 was US$5,330 million. In 2012, the working population reached 3.147 million. In 2015, Harbin had a GDP of RMB 575.12 billion.

The chernozem soil in Harbin is one of the most nutrient rich in all of China, making it valuable for cultivating food and textile-related crops. As a result, Harbin is China's base for the production of commodity grain and an ideal location for setting up agricultural businesses.

Harbin also has industries such as light industry, textile, medicine, food, aircraft, automobile, metallurgy, electronics, building materials, and chemicals that help to form a fairly comprehensive industrial system. Several major corporations are based in the city. Harbin Electric Company Limited, Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory are some of key enterprises. Power manufacturing is a main industry in Harbin; hydro and thermal power equipment manufactured here makes up one-third of the total installed capacity in China. According to Platts, in 2009–10 Harbin Electric was the second largest manufacturer of steam turbines by worldwide market share, tying Dongfang Electric and slightly behind Shanghai Electric. Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, which mainly focus on research, development, manufacture and sale of medical products, is China's second-biggest pharmaceutical company by market value.

Harbin International Trade and Economic Fair has been held annually since 1990. This investment and trade fair cumulatively attracting more than 1.9 million exhibitors and visitors from more than 80 countries and regions to attend, resulting over US$100 billion contract volume concluded according to the statistics of 2013. Harbin is among major destinations of FDI in Northeast China, with utilized FDI totaling US$980 million in 2013. After the 18th regular meeting between Sino-Russian Prime Ministers between Li Keqiang and Dmitry Anatolyevich Medvedev in October 2013, two sides come to make an agreement that the Harbin International Trade and Economic Fair will be renamed "China-Russia EXPO" and be co-sponsored by the Chinese Ministry of Commerce, Heilongjiang Provincial government, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development and Russia's Ministry of Trade and Industry.

In the financial sector, Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank are some of the largest banks in Northeast China, with headquarters in Harbin. The latter ranks fourth by competitiveness among Chinese city commercial banks in 2011.
In commerce, there is Qiulin Group, which owns Harbin's largest department store.

Harbin Economic & Technology Development Zone (National), mainly focus on telecommunications equipment, chemicals production and processing, automobile production/assembly, electronics, textiles, medical equipment and supplies.
Harbin High and New Technological Development Zone, focus on optical-mechanical-electrical integration, biology, medicine, electronics and information technology.

Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (Provincial), mainly focus on automobile production/assembly, electronics assembly & manufacturing, heavy industry, instruments & industrial equipment production.
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (Provincial), mainly focus on trading and distribution, food/beverage processing, medical equipment and supplies, shipping/warehousing/logistics.

Songbei Economic Development Zone is located in Songbei District of Harbin. The zone has a planned area of 5.53 square kilometers. Electronics assembly & manufacturing, food and beverage processing are the encouraged industries in the zone. Many regional and provincial headquarters of large enterprises such as the China Datang Corporation, China Netcom and China Telecom have joined in this district, preliminary constituting the economy concentration zone of the local headquarters. Regional Scientific research centers including Harbin Science and Technology Innovation Center and Harbin International Agricultural Science and Technology Innovation Center are also located in this development zone. Profit from these major research institutes, Harbin ranked ninth among 50 major Chinese cities in scientific and technological innovation ability in scientific and technological competitiveness ranking in 2006, as well as ranking sixth among Chinese cities in the amount of scientific and technological achievements.
Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone

Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone (HETDZ)  is one of the 90 national economical development zones of China. It was set up in June 1991, and was approved by the State Council as a national development zone in April 1993. In December 2012, Harbin High Technology Development Zone was merged into HETDZ. In 2009, the hi-tech zone was separated from HETDZ again. The area now has a total area of 18.5 square-kilometers in the centralized parks, subdivided into Nangang and Haping Road Centralized Parks. The 12.2 square-kilometers Yingbin Road Hi-tech Centralized Park, which was formerly part of HETDZ, is currently under the administration of Harbin High and New Technology Industry Development Zone since 2009.

Nangang Centralized Park: designated for the incubation of high-tech projects and research and development base of enterprises as well as tertiary industries such as finance, insurance, services, catering, tourism, culture, recreation and entertainment, where the headquarters of large famous companies and their branches in Harbin are located.
Yingbin Road Centralized Park: mainly focus on high-tech incubation projects, high-tech industrial development.

Haping Road Centralized Park: designated for a comprehensive industrial basis for the investment projects of automobile and automobile parts manufacturing, medicines, foodstuffs, electronics, textile; Automobile production and assembly raw material processing are the encouraged industries in this region.
Harbin High and New Technology Industry Development Zone

Harbin High and New Technology Industry Development Zone is one of the 56 national High and New Technology Industry Development Zones of China. The zone was first set up as a provincial level development zone in 1988, and was approved by the State Council as a national development zone in 1991 respectively. It has 23.9 square-kilometers of built-area totally, and subdivided into two parts: Science and Technology Innovation Town and High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The 2020 census revealed total population in Harbin was 10,009,854, representing a 5.62 percent decrease over the previous decade. The built-up area, made up of all urban districts but Acheng and Shuangcheng not urbanized yet, had a population of 5,282,083 people. 70.61 percent lived in urban areas, while 29.39 lived in rural areas.

The demographic profile for the Harbin metropolitan area in general is relatively old: 10.46 percent are under the age of 14, while 14.65 percent are over 65. Harbin has a higher percentage of males (50.02 percent) than females (49.98 percent). Harbin currently has a lower birth rate than other parts of China, with 6.95 births per 1,000 inhabitants, compared to the Chinese average of 12.13 births.

Most of Harbin's residents belong to the Han Chinese majority (93% in 2000). Ethnic minorities include the Manchu, Hui, and Mongol. There is a minor community of Russians. The ethnic composition according to the 2020 census:

The Catholic minority is pastorally served by the Apostolic Administration of Harbin, a missionary pre-diocesan jurisdiction. It also has the Eastern Catholic former cathedral of the Russian Catholic Apostolic Exarchate of Harbin. The badly damaged Church of the Iver Icon of the Mother of God was previously used by Russian soldiers of the Outer Amur Military Region, then garrisoned in Harbin. A small percentage (0.4% in 2000) of the city's population consists of Muslims. Daowai Mosque is located in Harbin and is the largest mosque in Heilongjiang province. Harbin had a small Jewish community centered on Zhongyang Main Street, which was home to many European Jewish refugees.

The Harbin local culture is based on Han culture, combined with Manchu culture and Russian culture. This combination of cultures influences the local architecture style, food, music, and customs. The city of Harbin was appointed a UNESCO City of Music on 22 June 2010 as part of the Creative Cities Network.

Harbin is a popular domestic tourist destination, particularly in the winter, when there are large-scale ice sculpture displays. Harbin also has a large indoor ski park, located inside the Wanda Harbin Mall (counting six ski slants up to 500 metres (1,600 ft) in length). During the 2023–2024 winter season, there were 87 million visitors, mostly coming from other parts of China.
Harbin is also known for its European-style structures and designs, such as the popular Saint Sophia Cathedral, Central Street, and the Baroque compositional complex in Lao Daowai (Old Town).

Located in northern Northeast China, Harbin is the northernmost among major cities in China. Under the direct influence of the Siberian Anticyclone, the average daily temperature is −19.7 °C (−3.5 °F) in winter. Annual low temperatures below −25.0 °C (−13.0 °F) are not uncommon. Nicknamed "Ice City" due to its freezingly cold winter, Harbin is decorated by various styles of ice and snow sculptures from December to March every year.

The annual Harbin International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival has been held since 1985. Although the official start date is 5 January each year, in practice, many of the sculptures can be seen before. While there are ice sculptures throughout the city, there are two main exhibition areas: enormous snow sculptures at Sun Island (Taiyang Dao, a AAAAA-rated recreational area on the opposite side of the Songhua River from the city) and the separate "Ice and Snow World" that operates each night with lights switched on, illuminating the sculptures from both inside and outside. Ice and Snow World features illuminated full-size buildings made from blocks of 2–3 feet thick crystal clear ice directly taken from the Songhua River, which passes through the city. The sculptures inside the exhibition ground takes 15,000 workers to work for 16 days. In early December, ice artisans cut 120,000 cubic metres (4.2 million cubic feet) of ice blocks from Songhua River's frozen surface as raw materials for the ice sculptures' show. Massive ice buildings, large-scale snow sculptures, ice slides, festival food and drinks can also be found in several parks and major avenues in the city. Winter activities in the festival include Yabuli Alpine Skiing, snow mobile driving, winter-swimming in Songhua River, and the traditional ice-lantern exhibition in Zhaolin Garden, which was first held in 1963. Snow carving and ice and snow recreations are famous nationwide, especially among Asian countries including Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore.

The "Harbin International Ice and Snow Festival" is one of the four largest ice and snow festivals in the world, along with Japan's Sapporo Snow Festival, Canada's Quebec City Winter Carnival, and Norway's Holmenkollen Ski Festival.

Every November, the city of Harbin sends teams of ice artisans to the United States to promote their unique art form. It takes more than 100 artisans to create ICE!, the annual display of indoor Christmas-themed ice carvings in National Harbor, Maryland; Nashville, Tennessee; Kissimmee, Florida; and Grapevine, Texas.
Heilongjiang Television (HLJTV) serves as the media outlets of this region, broadcasts on seven channels as well as a satellite channel for other provinces.
Harbin Television (HRBTV) serves as a municipal station, which has five channels for specialized programming.

Long Guang, Dragon Broadcast, formerly Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, the radio station group that serves the whole Heilongjiang region, providing seven channels including a Korean language broadcast station.
Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS), broadcasts music, news, traffic, economy and life in Harbin and adjacent areas including Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.
