International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

harbin-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Harbin Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Harbin, register at Harbin Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Harbin Normal University (HNU; 哈尔滨师范大学, Hā'ěrbīn Shīfàn Dàxué) is a university in Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang province in China's far northeast. It is a teacher-training institution by origin, but today it teaches across many subjects. For an international student, the main things to know are that it sits in one of the coldest large cities in China, that it has a reputation for hosting foreign partners, and that Harbin offers a strongly seasonal, very distinctive student experience.

HNU describes itself as a key university of Heilongjiang. It is run directly by the provincial Department of Education. Teaching is organised in 27 schools and departments, with 77 majors to choose from, and qualifications run from bachelor's through master's to doctorate.

The roots go back to 1946, when the Chinese Communist Party founded Hsing-chih Normal School, named in honour of the educator T'ao Hsing-chih. That school is the direct ancestor of today's university.

The campus covers 3.46 million square metres. Reported fixed assets are worth 2.435 billion yuan, and teaching and research equipment is valued at 2.5 billion yuan. One published floor-area figure for buildings is obviously mistaken, so it is left out here; the university can supply current campus statistics.

HNU promotes what it calls open education and international exchange. It has academic and educational-technology links with more than 70 higher-education institutions in about twenty countries, and it has founded three Confucius Institutes. Daejin University, a private South Korean institution, runs one of its two China campuses inside HNU's grounds, and has its own teaching block plus living quarters there; Daejin's second Chinese site is hosted by Soochow University in Suzhou. That presence means you may share the neighbourhood with Korean students.
Graduates who are publicly known include:
Yu Wenxia, a Miss World titleholder who spent four years at the university studying folk music (sources disagree on the year of her title, so it is not given here).
Wang Beiche, a singer.
Daily life depends on the city around campus: its climate, how people move about, and what there is to do. Harbin is unusual among Chinese cities, so it is worth reading this part closely.

Harbin is the provincial capital and lies in the south of Heilongjiang, with a total administrative area of 53,068 square kilometres (20,490 square miles). It stands at the south-eastern edge of the Songnen Plain, which is a major part of the Northeast China Plain, while the downtown core faces the river from its southern side, along the middle stretch of the Songhua. Because Heilongjiang's outline looks like a swan, Harbin is poetically called the pearl on the swan's neck. The administrative area stretches between 44°04′ and 46°40′ north and between 125°42′ and 130°10′ east. Looking at the map, Yichun lies north of the city. Jiamusi and Qitaihe are to the north-east, Mudanjiang is south-east, Daqing sits west and Suihua north-west. Jilin province forms the south-western edge.

Most of the city is flat and low, at an average height of about 150 metres (490 feet). The ten county-level divisions in the east of the municipality are hilly or mountainous, and the far east includes broad wetlands, chiefly in Yilan County at the south-western edge of the Sanjiang Plain.

By the Köppen system Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Dwa). The Siberian high and a position north of the 45th parallel make for a long, cold winter. The nickname "Ice City" is earned: winters are freezing and dry, and in January the mean over a full day is −17.3 °C, which equals roughly 0.9 degrees Fahrenheit. Snowfall is light, however, and many days are sunny. Spring and autumn are short transitions with changing wind directions. The summer can turn hot: July averages 23.7 °C, or about 74.7 degrees Fahrenheit. This is also the rainy season, and more than half of the 539 millimetres (21.2 inches) of annual precipitation falls in July and August alone. December is the least sunny month at 45 percent of possible sunshine and September the sunniest at 60 percent, giving 2,340 hours of bright sunshine annually.

Harbin also uses green design to cope with climate change. It has adopted "sponge city" ideas, for instance the Qunli stormwater park, which gathers, filters and stores rainwater while protecting natural habitat. For you as a student, the practical lesson is simple: bring serious winter clothing.

Harbin has the biggest economy in Heilongjiang. Its GDP was RMB501.08 billion in 2013, up 8.9 percent on the year before, and RMB575.12 billion in 2015. In 2012 the three sectors (primary, secondary and tertiary) split GDP in the ratio 11.1 to 36.1 to 52.8, so services are the largest. Trade in goods totalled US$5,330 million by the end of 2012, and the working population in that year reached 3.147 million. Figures here are from different years, so check recent statistics if you need current numbers.

The black chernozem soil around Harbin is among the richest in China, which suits grain and textile crops. The city is therefore a base for producing commodity grain and an attractive place for agribusiness.

Industry is wide-ranging: light industry, textiles, pharmaceuticals, food, aircraft, cars, metals, electronics, building materials and chemicals add up to a fairly complete industrial system. Harbin Electric Company, Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory are among the key enterprises. Power equipment is a leading specialty: hydro and thermal generating equipment made here accounts for a third of installed capacity in China. A 2009-10 industry survey by Platts put Harbin Electric second in the world by market share for steam turbines, tied with Dongfang Electric and just behind Shanghai Electric. Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, focused on research, manufacture and sale of medicines, is China's second-biggest pharmaceutical firm by market value.

Since 1990 the city has hosted a yearly investment and trade fair (originally the Harbin International Trade and Economic Fair). Cumulative statistics up to 2013 show more than 1.9 million exhibitors and visitors attending, from over eighty countries and regions, with more than US$100 billion of contracts concluded. Harbin is one of the main destinations for foreign direct investment in the northeast, and actual FDI reached US$980 million in 2013. Following talks in October 2013 between the Chinese and Russian prime ministers (Li Keqiang and Dmitry Medvedev), the two governments agreed to relaunch the event as the "China-Russia EXPO". It is now co-sponsored by China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang government, and two Russian ministries (Economic Development, and Trade and Industry). If you want to study Russian or work with Russian partners, this link is a real advantage.

Finance has local strength: Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank have their head offices here and are among the biggest lenders in the northeast. A 2011 ranking placed Harbin Bank fourth for competitiveness among Chinese city commercial banks. For shopping, the largest department store belongs to the Qiulin Group.
The Harbin Economic and Technology Development Zone (national level) concentrates on telecom equipment, chemicals, car manufacturing and assembly, electronics, textiles and medical supplies.
A separate High and New Technological Development Zone specialises in biology, medicine, electronics, IT and the integration of optics, machinery and electrics.
The Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (provincial level) deals mainly with automobiles, electronics assembly, heavy industry, instruments and industrial equipment.
The Limin Economic Development Zone (provincial level) focuses on trading and distribution, food and drink processing, medical supplies, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.
Harbin Port.

The Songbei Economic Development Zone, in Songbei District, planned for 5.53 square kilometres. Policy favours electronics assembly and food and drink processing. Large enterprises, among them China Telecom, China Netcom and China Datang, have placed regional or provincial head offices in the district, which has become a cluster of such offices. Two research hubs are located inside it as well: one for general science and technology innovation, another devoted to international agricultural technology. Partly because of institutions like these, a 2006 comparison of 50 big Chinese cities gave Harbin ninth place for innovation capacity and sixth place for the quantity of scientific and technological achievements.

HETDZ, the Economic and Technological Development Zone, is one of 90 national zones in China. It opened in June 1991 and won State Council approval as a national zone in April 1993. The hi-tech zone was merged into it in December 2012, having been separated from it earlier, in 2009. Today its centralised parks cover 18.5 square kilometres in two groups, Nangang and Haping Road. A third park, Yingbin Road (12.2 square kilometres), once belonged to HETDZ but has come under the hi-tech industry zone's administration since 2009. Nangang is for incubating high-tech projects and corporate research bases and for service industries such as finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture and entertainment, where large companies keep their headquarters and branches. Yingbin Road targets high-tech incubation and industry. Haping Road is a general industrial base for car and car-parts manufacturing, medicine, food, electronics and textiles, with vehicle assembly and raw-material processing encouraged.

The High and New Technology Industry Development Zone is counted among 56 national hi-tech zones nationwide. Provincial status came in 1988 and national status in 1991. It has 23.9 square kilometres built up, in two parts: Science and Technology Innovation Town and the High-tech Industrial Development Zone proper.

The 2020 census counted 10,009,854 people in Harbin, which is 5.62 percent fewer than a decade earlier. The built-up area, comprising all urban districts except Acheng and Shuangcheng, which are not yet urbanised, held 5,282,083 people. The urban share was 70.61 percent and the rural share 29.39 percent.

The metropolitan area has a relatively old age profile: 10.46 percent of residents are under 14 and 14.65 percent are over 65. Men make up 50.02 percent and women 49.98 percent. The birth rate, at 6.95 per 1,000, is lower than the national figure of 12.13 per 1,000.

Han Chinese form the majority (93 percent in 2000). There are Manchu, Hui and Mongol minorities and a small Russian community. Local Catholics belong to a missionary jurisdiction, the Apostolic Administration of Harbin, and the city holds the former Eastern Catholic cathedral of the Russian exarchate. A heavily damaged church dedicated to the Iver Icon of the Mother of God once housed Russian troops garrisoned here. About 0.4 percent of residents (in 2000) are Muslim, and the Daowai Mosque is the largest mosque in Heilongjiang. Harbin also had a small Jewish community around Zhongyang Main Street, a home to many European Jewish refugees.

harbin-normal-university.h: What the numbers mean for a newcomer

blocks.x: Put together, these facts describe a very large provincial capital of about ten million people whose growth has slowed, with an older-than-average population and a lower birth rate than the national figure. For a student that translates into a city with plenty of space, established services and a calm pace, but also one where much of the economy rests on heavy industry, power equipment, agriculture and cross-border trade with Russia. Graduates who combine a teaching or language qualification with some knowledge of these sectors may find the local labour market easier to read than one that depends on a single trend.

Harbin's local culture rests on Han traditions combined with Manchu and Russian influences, which shows in the architecture, food, music and customs. On 22 June 2010 UNESCO admitted the city to its Creative Cities Network as a City of Music.

Chinese holidaymakers flock here, above all in winter, to see the big ice displays. Inside the Wanda Harbin Mall there is even an indoor ski park with six slopes, the longest reaching 500 metres (1,600 feet). Over the 2023-2024 winter, visitor numbers hit 87 million, the large majority from other parts of China. Architecture is another draw, with European styles on show in St Sophia Cathedral, Central Street and the Baroque group of buildings in Lao Daowai, the old town.

Harbin lies in northern Northeast China and is the northernmost major city in the country. The Siberian anticyclone dominates, so the average winter day is −19.7 °C (that is, −3.5 degrees Fahrenheit), and each year the minimum often falls beneath −25.0 °C, or −13.0 degrees Fahrenheit. From December to March the city is decorated with ice and snow sculptures in many styles.

The big annual event, the International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival, dates from 1985. The official start is 5 January, but many sculptures can be seen earlier. There are two main areas. One is the snow sculpture park on Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a AAAAA-rated recreation area on the opposite bank of the Songhua. The other is "Ice and Snow World", which opens each night with lights inside and outside illuminating full-size buildings made of clear ice blocks 2-3 feet thick, cut straight from the river. Building the exhibition takes 15,000 workers 16 days, and every early December ice workers saw out around 120,000 cubic metres of ice (4.2 million cubic feet) from the frozen Songhua surface for use as raw material. Parks and main avenues in the city also have ice buildings, large snow sculptures, ice slides, and festival food and drink. Winter activities include alpine skiing at Yabuli, snowmobiling, winter swimming in the Songhua, and the traditional ice-lantern show in Zhaolin Garden, first held in 1963. This craft is well known throughout Asia, especially to visitors from Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore.

Harbin's festival is ranked among the world's four biggest winter festivals. The others are Sapporo in Japan, the Quebec City carnival in Canada and the Holmenkollen ski festival in Norway. Each November the city exports its craft: over 100 artisans build ICE!, an indoor display of Christmas-themed carvings that tours National Harbor (Maryland), Nashville (Tennessee), Kissimmee (Florida) and Grapevine (Texas).

Television comes at two levels. The provincial broadcaster, HLJTV, offers seven channels and a satellite service for viewers in other provinces; the city's own station, HRBTV, has five themed channels. Radio is similar: Long Guang (also called Dragon Broadcast), previously the Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, reaches the whole province across seven channels, one of them Korean-language, while the Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS) provides music, news, traffic, economy and daily-life programmes for Harbin and neighbouring Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.

Winter is therefore not just something you endure in Harbin but a part of the city's calendar and identity. Expect many outdoor events to take place in freezing conditions, expect heated indoor spaces everywhere, and plan trips to the sculpture parks for the evening, when the lighting is at its best.

If you are comparing northern cities, Harbin rewards those who arrive in autumn, buy proper boots and a long coat early, and treat the first freezing weeks as part of the adventure rather than a hardship. Most newcomers find that the cold is manageable once they dress in layers and move between heated buildings, trams and cafes.
Because the province surrounding a university colours everyday life nearly as much as the campus itself, a look at Heilongjiang follows.

Early chronicles list the Sushen, the Buyeo, the Mohe and the Khitan among the peoples who lived in the area, while Mongolic Donghu groups occupied the west of the province and neighbouring Inner Mongolia; many place names are Manchu or Mongolian in origin. From the 7th to the 10th century the Bohai Kingdom ruled the east, after which the Khitan Liao dynasty took over. Within the borders of today's province, the Jurchen rose to found the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), which later controlled a big part of northern China.

Heilongjiang became an administrative province in 1683, in the Kangxi reign of the Manchu Qing, when the north-western part of Jilin was separated off. Initially it covered only the western half of the present territory. A military governor, called the General of Heilongjiang, supervised it, and under the Treaty of Nerchinsk his authority stretched north as far as the Stanovoy Mountains. The east remained with the General of Jilin, whose writ ran to the Sea of Japan. Han Chinese were not permitted to settle in these interior Manchurian lands.

The governor's first headquarters stood on the Amur at Heilongjiang City, also known as Aigun or Heihe. It was relocated to Nenjiang (Mergen) on the Nen River in 1690 and again in 1699, farther south, to Qiqihar. Historians today think logistics explain the moves: a convenient waterway, the Nen, joined Nenjiang and Qiqihar with southern Manchuria, whereas supplying Aigun would have meant a long voyage down the Sungari and up the Amur, or a portage over the Lesser Xing'an range. Qiqihar had one more advantage, being where the northbound road to Nenjiang crossed the westbound one to Mongolia, which let its garrison watch for both Russians and Ölöt Mongols.

Few Qing troops were posted beyond Aigun. European writers of the 18th and early 20th centuries, and Russian reports from the 1850s, put the most distant Qing post at Ulusu-Modon (乌鲁苏穆丹), close to the Amur's well-known S-shaped bend. It stood on the left bank, which Russia gained in 1860.

Treaties in 1858 and 1860 forced the Qing to hand the Russian Empire every territory beyond the Amur and Ussuri, which severed the empire's access to the Sea of Japan and fixed the province's northern and eastern frontiers as they are now. Manchuria was thrown open to Han settlers at the same period, and thanks to the mass movement known as Chuang Guandong, the Han were the largest group by the early 1900s.

Japanese forces invaded in 1931 and completed their conquest in 1932, when the province became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. In 1945 the Soviet Army defeated Japanese forces in Manchuria and helped the Chinese communists during the civil war. Heilongjiang became the first province entirely under communist control and Harbin the first major city.

At first, communist-run Heilongjiang covered only the west of the present province and had Qiqihar as its capital; the rest was Songjiang province with its capital at Harbin. In 1954 the two merged into today's Heilongjiang. During the Cultural Revolution the province was enlarged to include Hulunbuir League and other areas formerly in Inner Mongolia, which have mostly since been returned.

Heilongjiang's landscape is varied. Mountain ranges dominate much of it: the Greater and Lesser Khingan, Zhangguangcai, Laoye and Wanda mountains. Datudingzi Mountain, on the border with Jilin, is the top summit at 1,690 metres (5,540 feet). The Greater Khingan contains the largest remaining area of virgin forest in China and matters greatly to forestry. In the lower east and south-west, the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers all feed the Amur, whose valley marks the northern boundary. Xingkai Lake, also called Khanka, sits at the Russian frontier with Primorsky Krai.

Most of the province is humid continental (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), with subarctic conditions (Dwc) in the far north. Long, harsh winters give January means between −31 and −15 °C (that is, −24 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit). July is short and mild to hot, averaging 18 to 23 °C, or 64 to 73 degrees Fahrenheit. Annual rain of 400 to 700 millimetres (16 to 28 inches) falls mostly in summer. Sun shines for about 2,300 to 2,650 hours a year, and in spring the Songnen and Sanjiang plains are rich in wind energy. Cities of note, after Harbin, include Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi, Daqing, Jixi, Shuangyashan, Hegang, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe.

Heilongjiang has an extensive road network, totalling 165,989 km (103,141 miles) of expressways, highways and other roads as of October 2020. The Beijing-Harbin Expressway is the key corridor, running from the Jilin border to the Harbin Ring Expressway. The Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway heads north-east to link remote counties around Harbin, Jiamusi and the north-east, and from it the Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off at Jiansanjiang to serve state farms in the far east until it ends near the Russian border. The Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway runs south-east to north-west through Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar to the Inner Mongolia border. The Hegang-Dalian Expressway moves timber and coal between Hegang and the Jilin border in the east.
The region has hosted or staged:
Harbin hosted the 2009 Winter Universiade.
It staged the Division B tournament of the 2018 Bandy World Championship.
It is a venue for Asia League Ice Hockey.

In short, Harbin Normal University offers a teacher-training heritage, international partnerships and a very distinctive, very cold, very lively city. Check the university's own site for the latest programme and enrolment details.
Harbin Normal University lists 128 programs for international students on this site: 68 bachelor, 50 master's, 9 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

The university known as HRBUST (Harbin University of Science and Technology, 哈尔滨理工大学) is a public institution in Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang Province in northeast China. It is run at provincial level: the Heilongjiang provincial government is its parent authority, and it is co-sponsored by that government and SASTIND (the State Administration for Science, Technology and Industry for National Defence).

It came into being in 1995 when it was formed from three older schools: Harbin Electrical Engineering College, Harbin Industrial Higher Vocational School and Harbin Science and Technology University. The result is an engineering-minded school with roots in industrial training.

The university has four campuses, named East, West, South and North, spread over three city districts: Daoli, Nangang and Xiangfang. Altogether they cover more than 1,275,000 square metres, with over 850,000 square metres of floor space in buildings, and the university's fixed assets are valued at ¥1.032 billion. There is also another campus in Rongcheng, Shandong. The library holds 2.075 million books, and about 4,900 periodicals and journals, Chinese and foreign, are available.
If you plan to enrol, confirm which campus your programme uses, since they are in different parts of the city.

harbin-university-of-science-and-technol.h: Harbin as a place to live

blocks.x: Everyday student life depends heavily on the city: its weather, how people get about, and what you can do in your spare time. Below we introduce Harbin first, then the wider province of Heilongjiang.

Harbin covers 53,068 square kilometres (20,490 square miles) in the south of Heilongjiang and is the provincial capital. Geographically it sits at the south-eastern end of the Songnen Plain (a large piece of China's Northeastern Plain), and the city centre stands on the south bank of the middle Songhua River. People call it "the pearl on the swan's neck", because Heilongjiang is shaped something like a swan. The administrative area is large, running from latitude 44° 04′ to 46° 40′ north and longitude 125° 42′ to 130° 10′ east.

On the map, Yichun lies north of it, with Jiamusi and Qitaihe in the northeast, Mudanjiang southeast, Daqing west and Suihua northwest, all of them prefecture-level cities. Jilin Province marks its southwestern edge.

The main urban area is flat and low, at an average height near 150 metres (490 feet). In the east, the ten county-level divisions are made up of mountains and uplands. In the far east of the prefecture, especially in Yilan County, where the Sanjiang Plain ends in the southwest, there are broad wetlands.

Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa). The Siberian high, together with a position north of 45 degrees latitude, gives the city a cold and lengthy winter, and its nickname Ice City is deserved. Winters are dry and freezing, with a 24-hour January average of just −17.3 °C (0.9 °F), but there is little snow and the skies are often sunny. Spring and autumn are short transition seasons, with winds that change direction. Summers may turn hot, since July averages 23.7 °C (74.7 °F).

The wettest months are in summer: July and August together deliver over half of the 539 millimetres (21.2 inches) of yearly precipitation, which falls on around 99 days. Sunshine, as a share of the possible, runs between 45 percent in December and 60 percent in September, totalling 2,340 hours of bright sun over twelve months. The annual mean temperature is 5.2 °C (41.4 °F). Records show a low of −42.6 °C (−45 °F), or −41.1 °C (−42 °F) at the official station, set in January 1931, and a high of 39.2 °C (103 °F), last reached on 4 June 2001. A further unofficial reading, 41.0 °C (105.8 °F), dates from July 1907.
For anyone arriving from a warmer country, proper winter clothing is a necessity, not a nicety.

Urban planners in Harbin have adopted sponge city ideas to reduce the effects of climate change. The Qunli stormwater park is one example: it collects, filters and stores rainwater while protecting natural habitat.

Harbin has the biggest economy in Heilongjiang. Its GDP was RMB 501.08 billion in 2013, up 8.9 percent on the year before, and reached RMB 575.12 billion in 2015. In 2012 the three sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary) stood in the proportion 11.1 : 36.1 : 52.8. Imports and exports totalled US$5,330 million by the end of 2012, and the working population in that year reached 3.147 million. These figures date from the early 2010s, so look for newer statistics if you need current numbers.

Harbin's chernozem soil is among the most nutrient-rich in China, so it suits food crops and crops used in textiles. The city is China's base for commodity grain and a natural location for agricultural businesses.

Light industry, textiles, medicine, food, aircraft, automobiles, metallurgy, electronics, building materials and chemicals combine into a fairly comprehensive industrial system. Key enterprises include the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory, the Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and Harbin Electric Company Limited. Power equipment is central: hydro and thermal power equipment made here accounts for one-third of the installed capacity in China. Platts reported that in 2009 to 2010 Harbin Electric was the world's second-largest steam turbine maker by market share, level with Dongfang Electric and just behind Shanghai Electric. The Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, which focuses on research, development, production and sales of medical products, is China's second-biggest drug company by market value.

An annual trade and investment event, the Harbin International Trade and Economic Fair, has run since 1990. By the 2013 statistics it had drawn above 1.9 million exhibitors and visitors from over 80 countries and regions, and the deals signed exceeded US$100 billion. Harbin is also a leading magnet for foreign direct investment in Northeast China: US$980 million of FDI was used there in 2013. When Chinese Premier Li Keqiang and Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev held their 18th regular meeting in October 2013, they agreed to rename the fair the "China-Russia EXPO". Its sponsors would be China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang provincial government, and two Russian bodies, the Ministry of Economic Development and the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank are among the largest banks in Northeast China and are headquartered in Harbin. In 2011 Harbin Bank ranked fourth for competitiveness among Chinese city commercial banks. On the retail side, Qiulin Group owns the city's largest department store.
Harbin's economic zones show which industries the city wants to grow. Each has its own focus.

Harbin Economic and Technology Development Zone (national level): its focus is telecommunications equipment, chemicals production and processing, car production and assembly, electronics, textiles, and also medical equipment and supplies.
Harbin High and New Technological Development Zone: the emphasis is on biology, medicine, electronics, information technology, and the combination of optics, mechanics and electrics.

Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone, a provincial-level zone, which works on vehicle production and assembly, electronics assembly and manufacturing, heavy industry, and instruments and industrial equipment.
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (provincial level): trading and distribution, food and beverage processing, medical equipment and supplies, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.
Other places in the list of zones and infrastructure are:
Harbin High and New Technology Industry Development Zone
Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone
Harbin Songbei Economic Development Zone
Harbin Port

You will find this zone in Songbei District, where its planned area is 5.53 sq km. The industries it encourages are electronics assembly and manufacturing and food and beverage processing. Regional and provincial headquarters of large companies, among them China Datang Corporation, China Netcom and China Telecom, have settled there, so the area is starting to work as a hub for corporate headquarters. Two research institutions are also located in the zone: the Harbin Science and Technology Innovation Center, and a separate centre for agricultural innovation, the Harbin International Agricultural Science and Technology Innovation Center. Thanks to these institutes, Harbin took ninth place among 50 major Chinese cities in the 2006 ranking of scientific and technological competitiveness, and sixth among Chinese cities for the volume of scientific and technological achievements.

HETDZ is one of 90 national economic development zones in China. It was set up in June 1991, and in April 1993 the State Council gave it national status. In December 2012 the High Technology Development Zone was folded into it, although that zone had been split off from HETDZ in 2009. The centralised parks now amount to 18.5 square kilometres, in two groups, Nangang and Haping Road. A third park, Yingbin Road Hi-tech (12.2 sq km), once belonged to HETDZ but since 2009 has been managed by the Harbin High and New Technology Industry Development Zone.

Nangang Centralized Park: reserved for incubating high-tech projects and for company research and development bases, together with service industries including finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture, recreation and entertainment. Well-known companies place their headquarters or Harbin branches here.
Yingbin Road Centralized Park: concentrates on incubating high-tech projects and developing high-tech industry.

Haping Road Centralized Park: planned as a broad industrial base to receive investment in cars and car parts, medicines, food, electronics and textiles. Vehicle production and assembly and raw material processing are the favoured industries.

harbin-university-of-science-and-technol.h: High and New Technology Industry Development Zone

blocks.x: This is one of 56 national high and new technology zones in China. It started in 1988 as a provincial-level zone and gained national status from the State Council in 1991. Its built-up area is 23.9 square kilometres, split between Science and Technology Innovation Town and a High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The built-up area, which covers all the urban districts except Acheng and Shuangcheng, which were not yet urbanised, had 5,282,083 residents. Some 70.61 percent live in urban areas and 29.39 percent in rural ones.

The metropolitan area is relatively old: 10.46 percent of residents are under 14, and 14.65 percent are over 65. Men make up 50.02 percent and women 49.98 percent. The birth rate, at 6.95 per 1,000 inhabitants, is lower than elsewhere in China, where the average is 12.13.

Most people in Harbin are Han Chinese (93 percent in 2000). Minorities include Manchu, Hui and Mongol groups, and there is a small Russian community. A breakdown from the 2020 census is published in official statistics.

Harbin's Catholic minority receives pastoral care from the Apostolic Administration of Harbin, a missionary jurisdiction that predates any diocese. The city also has the former cathedral of the Russian Catholic Apostolic Exarchate of Harbin, which was Eastern Catholic. The Church of the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, now badly damaged, once served soldiers of the Outer Amur Military Region who were garrisoned in the city. Muslims made up a small share (0.4 percent in 2000) of residents, and the Daowai Mosque, the largest mosque in Heilongjiang, is in the city. Harbin also had a small Jewish community centred on Zhongyang Main Street, where many European Jewish refugees lived.

Local culture starts from Han tradition and mixes in Manchu and Russian influences, which can be seen in the architecture, food, music and customs. On 22 June 2010 Harbin joined UNESCO's Creative Cities Network as a City of Music.

Harbin is popular with domestic tourists, especially in winter, when large ice sculpture displays appear. There is also a big indoor ski park in the Wanda Harbin Mall, with six slopes up to 500 metres (1,600 feet) long. Over the 2023 to 2024 winter the city received 87 million visitors, mostly from elsewhere in China. Europe-inspired architecture is another draw, notably Saint Sophia Cathedral, Central Street and the Baroque buildings of Lao Daowai (Old Town).

China's northernmost large city, Harbin, feels the Siberian Anticyclone directly. Winter days average −19.7 °C (−3.5 °F), and it is not unusual for the lowest annual temperatures to fall under −25.0 °C (−13.0 °F). Ice and snow sculptures in many styles decorate the city from December to March.

Since 1985 the city has held the Harbin International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival. Its official start is 5 January, but many works can be seen earlier. Ice sculptures are found across the city, and there are two main sites. One is Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a AAAAA-rated recreation area across the Songhua River from the city, which has enormous snow sculptures. The other is the separate Ice and Snow World, which opens each night with lights shining on the sculptures from inside and out. There, full-size illuminated buildings are made from crystal-clear ice blocks two to three feet thick taken straight from the Songhua River. Some 15,000 workers spend 16 days building the exhibition. As raw material, artisans saw 120,000 cubic metres (4.2 million cubic feet) of ice out of the frozen river in early December. Parks and main avenues around the city also show big ice buildings and snow sculptures, and offer ice slides plus festival food and drink.

Other festival activities are Yabuli alpine skiing, snowmobiling, winter swimming in the Songhua River and the traditional ice lantern show in Zhaolin Garden, first held in 1963. Harbin's snow carving and ice recreations are well known across Asia, notably in Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore.
The event ranks as one of the world's four biggest winter festivals, alongside Japan's Sapporo Snow Festival, the Quebec City Winter Carnival in Canada and Norway's Holmenkollen Ski Festival.

The city also exports the craft: each November, ice artisans travel to the United States to promote it. ICE! is an annual indoor show of Christmas-themed ice carvings that takes over 100 artisans to make, and it appears at National Harbor (Maryland), Nashville (Tennessee), Kissimmee (Florida) and Grapevine (Texas).
HLJTV (Heilongjiang Television) is the regional broadcaster, running seven channels plus one satellite channel that reaches other provinces.
HRBTV (Harbin Television) is the city's own station, offering five specialised channels.
The radio group Long Guang, or Dragon Broadcast, was formerly the Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station. It serves the whole province with seven channels, one of them in Korean.
Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS) offers music, news, traffic, economy and local life for Harbin and nearby areas including Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.
The university is in Heilongjiang, and the surrounding province influences student life as strongly as the campus does. The next sections describe it.

Ancient Chinese records and other sources say the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan lived in Heilongjiang. The Mongolic Donghu lived to the west, in Inner Mongolia and western Heilongjiang, and some place names come from Manchu or Mongolian. In the eastern part, the Bohai Kingdom ruled from the 7th to the 10th century, and the Khitan Liao dynasty followed. Within the borders of today's Heilongjiang the Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115 to 1234) emerged, later ruling much of northern China.

Heilongjiang was created as an administrative unit in 1683, during the Manchu Qing dynasty's Kangxi era, carved from the northwest of Jilin Province. Initially only today's western section was included. A military official oversaw it, the General of Heilongjiang (Sahaliyan Ula i Jiyanggiyūn), a title also rendered as Military Governor. Jiyanggiyūn is how Manchu reads the Chinese 將軍 jiāngjūn, "military leader" or "general", a cognate of Japan's shōgun. By the Treaty of Nerchinsk his authority extended north to the Stanovoy Mountains. Today's eastern half remained with a different official, the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose power extended to the Sea of Japan. Han Chinese were not allowed to settle in these remote areas of Manchuria.

In 1683 the Military Governor's seat was at Heilongjiang City on the Amur River (known too as Aigun or Heihe, and in Manchu as Saghalien Ula). Seven years later, in 1690, it relocated to Nenjiang (Mergen), on the Nen River, and in 1699 it went farther south to Qiqihar. Historians today suggest supplies drove these moves. The Nen River is a handy waterway linking Nenjiang and Qiqihar with southern Manchuria. Aigun (Heihe), by contrast, could be reached only by sailing down the Sungari River to where it meets the Amur and then upstream along the Amur, or by portage across the Lesser Xing'an Mountains separating the Nen and Amur valleys. Qiqihar may also have offered the advantage of lying where a northbound road (to Nenjiang) met a westbound one (to Mongolia), which let its garrison defend against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

The Qing military presence north of Aigun was small. European sources from the 18th and early 20th centuries and Russian reports from the 1850s put the farthest Qing advance guard post at Ulusu-Modon (Ulussu-Mudan, 乌鲁苏穆丹 Wūlǔsūmùdān), near the famous S-shaped bend of the Amur. The post stood on the left (north) bank, an area the Russians took in 1860.

The Qing government had to give up, in 1858 and 1860, everything beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers to the Russian Empire. As a result the empire lost its access to the Sea of Japan, and Heilongjiang acquired the northern and eastern borders it has today. Around the same time Manchuria was opened by the Qing to Han Chinese migration, and through the Chuang Guandong movement the Han had become the dominant ethnic group by the early twentieth century.

Japanese forces invaded Heilongjiang in 1931 and completed their conquest of the province in 1932, when it it was incorporated into Manchukuo, the puppet state set up by Japan. The Soviet Army defeated Japan's forces in Manchuria in 1945, and in the Chinese Civil War Soviet troops assisted the Chinese communists. Heilongjiang was the first province to fall wholly into communist hands, and Harbin the first major city.

At the start of communist rule, Heilongjiang covered only the western part of the present province, with Qiqihar as its capital. All the rest formed the province of Songjiang, whose capital was Harbin. These two were combined in 1954 to make the Heilongjiang we know. During the Cultural Revolution the province grew again, taking in Hulunbuir League and certain other areas of Inner Mongolia, though most of that change has since been undone.

Heilongjiang has many kinds of terrain. Much of it is dominated by mountain ranges: the Greater Khingan Range, the Lesser Khingan Range, the Zhangguangcai Mountains, the Laoye Mountains and the Wanda Mountains. Datudingzi Mountain, at 1,690 metres (5,540 feet) on the Jilin border, is the highest peak. China's biggest surviving virgin forest grows in the Greater Khingan Range, which matters greatly for forestry.

In the flatter, lower east and southwest, the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers all flow into the Amur, and part of the Amur valley makes up the northern border. On the frontier with Russia's Primorsky Krai is Xingkai Lake, also called Khanka Lake.

The prevailing climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), except in the far north, which is subarctic (Dwc). Winters are long and bitter; January temperatures average between −31 and −15 °C (−24 and 5 °F). Short summers range from warm to very warm, with a July average of 18 to 23 °C (64 to 73 °F). Rainfall, 400 to 700 millimetres (16 to 28 inches) a year, comes mostly in summer. Sunshine is plentiful, about 2,300 to 2,650 hours a year, and in spring the Songnen Plain and Sanjiang Plain offer abundant wind energy.
Among the biggest cities are Harbin, Qiqihar and Mudanjiang, with Jiamusi, Daqing, Jixi, Shuangyashan, Hegang, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe also in the list.

As of October 2020, the province counted 165,989 kilometres (103,141 miles) of roads, including expressways and highways. The Beijing-Harbin Expressway is the key corridor into the province; it begins at the Heilongjiang-Jilin border and ends inside the Harbin Ring Expressway. The Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway runs northeast and connects far-flung counties under Harbin, Jiamusi and other northeastern areas. Near its end, the Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off at Jiansanjiang and links many state-owned farms in the far east before finishing near the Russian border. The Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway runs southeast to northwest and ties together several of the province's biggest population centres, Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar, ending at the Heilongjiang-Inner Mongolia border. Timber and coal travel along the Hegang-Dalian Expressway, which links Hegang with the eastern Heilongjiang-Jilin border.
Harbin and the province have hosted or staged a number of events:
Asia League Ice Hockey
the 2009 Winter Universiade
the Bandy World Championship of 2018 (Division B)

harbin-university-of-science-and-technol.h: What this means for a prospective student

blocks.x: Putting the pieces together, HRBUST offers an engineering and technology education in a city with a very specific character. The university itself is relatively young as a merged institution, dating from 1995, and it has four urban campuses in Daoli, Nangang and Xiangfang plus another site in Rongcheng, Shandong. Around it is a city of roughly ten million people with a heavy-industry past, a growing set of technology and trade zones, and a strong link to Russia that shows in its buildings, its food and its trade fair.

Three practical points stand out from the facts above. First, the climate: January averages near −17 °C in the city and lower still elsewhere in the province, so winter kit and a plan for the cold months matter. Second, the seasons are not only a challenge, since the long winter produces the ice and snow festival, ski opportunities and the winter sports calendar. Third, the surrounding economy, with its power equipment, aircraft, vehicle, pharmaceutical and food industries, is the setting in which engineering graduates in this region often look for work. For current details about tuition, entry requirements and international student services, consult the university's own website and admissions office directly.

Hebei Medical University (Chinese: 河北医科大学; pinyin: Héběi Yīkē Dàxué) is a university in Shijiazhuang, Hebei, China, under the provincial government. It was established in 1894, making it one of the oldest in China, and is an AAA graded medical school in China.
The staff numbers over 7,100. Of these, 366 are professors, senior researchers and chief physicians. There are 967 associate professors.
There are 25,600 students.

Hebei Medical University has long history of enrolling international students from countries including the United States, Japan, Korea, Philippines, Taiwan, the UK, India, Ghana, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh. Currently there are over 400 international students.

In collaboration with International Education College of Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, a total of more than 300 international students have already completed their Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) from the university in 2010–2011.

After 80 years development and evolution, Hebei Medical University has become a comprehensive medical university composed of western medicine, traditional medicine, pharmacy and other subjects. Now there are 14 colleges, and 15 specialties.

The university has six affiliated hospitals, in which there are 4,566 in-patient beds. Four hospitals have been granted the status of "first-class hospitals in the third category". In addition, it also has 77 teaching hospitals and practice bases providing students with sites of clinical teaching, specialist teaching and practice.
It carried out the first finger transplantation surgery in China, and made the first diagnosis in the world of acute motor axonal neuropathy.

It has 9 subjects and 4 laboratories assessed at advanced provincial  level, and 6 research institutes at provincial level. The Chinese Academy of Preventive Medical Science has set up its Hebei Academic Branch in this university. Each year nearly 200 research projects are undertaken. In addition three national and eight provincial academic periodicals have been compiled and published here.

Hebei Medical University has started the MBBS programme in 2004 and enrolled 200 students successfully from India and Nepal, and in 2005 enrolled 200 more students from India. Both batches have graduated in 2010 and 2011 respectively.

The MBBS programme is taught in English as well as many other courses, something that other universities cannot do, such as Traditional Chinese Medicine, Acupuncture and Massage, Clinical Medicine, Clinical Medicine of Integration of Traditional Chinese Medicine and Western Medicine, Stomatology, Anesthesiology, Preventive Medicine, Medical Imaging, Advanced Nursing Science, Chinese Pharmacology, Pharmacology, Pharmaceutics.

In the past few years, Hebei Medical University has become an important window of cultural and economic exchange with the world. It has established closer cooperation with about ten medical colleges and research institutes in Japan, South Korea, U.S.A and France successively. 24 foreign experts have been invited to take honorary positions in this university. Over 400 experts and professors have been sent abroad to give lectures or attend international academic conferences. Nearly 100 young teachers are studying assiduously abroad for PhD degrees. Its cooperation with the domestic colleges and universities has grown tremendously over the years.

Hebei Medical University is turning on a new look and making great efforts to establish a superior comprehensive medical university with local characteristics to meet the needs of socialist construction.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shijiazhuang, where Hebei Medical University is located.

Shijiazhuang is located in south-central Hebei, and is part of the Bohai Economic Rim. Its administrative area ranges in latitude from 37° 27' to 38° 47' N, and the longitude 113° 30' to 115° 20' E. The prefecture-level city reaches a 148 kilometres (92 mi) north–south extent and a 175 kilometres (109 mi) wide from east to west. The prefecture has borders stretching 760 kilometres (472 mi) long and covers an area of 15,722 square kilometres (6,070 sq mi). Bordering prefecture-level cities in Hebei are Hengshui (E), Xingtai (S), and Baoding (N/NE). To the west lies the province of Shanxi.

The city stands at the edge of the North China Plain, which rises to the Taihang Mountains to the west of the city, and lies south of the Hutuo River. From west to east, the topography can be summarised as moderately high mountains, then low-lying mountains, hills, basin, and finally plains. Out of the eight east–west routes across the Taihang Mountains, the fifth, the Niangzi Pass, connects the city directly with Taiyuan, Shanxi.

The city has a continental, monsoon-influenced semi-arid climate (Köppen BSk / Dwa), characterised by hot, humid summers due to the East Asian monsoon, and generally cold, windy, very dry winters that reflect the influence of the Siberian anticyclone. Spring can see sandstorms blowing in from the Mongolian steppe, accompanied by rapidly warming, but generally dry, conditions. Autumn is similar to spring in temperature and lack of rainfall. January averages −1.4 °C (29.5 °F), while July averages 27.7 °C (81.9 °F); the annual mean is 14.3 °C (57.7 °F). With the monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 38 percent in July to 56 percent in May, the city receives 2,163 hours of sunshine annually. More than half of the annual rainfall occurs in July and August alone. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −26.5 °C (−15.7 °F) on January 12, 1951 to 42.9 °C (109.2 °F) on July 15, 2002.

Shijiazhuang has had a reputation for much-polluted air as part of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, driven by large industries with high levels of energy consumption. In January 2013, analysis released by Tsinghua University and The Asian Development Bank foundin that the city was one of ten most air-polluted cities in the world. Hebei province as a whole has been one of the worst afflicted regions for air pollution in China, and a survey by "Global voices China" in February 2013 showed that the province had seven of the ten cities with the worst air pollution in China, of which one was Shijiazhuang.

In December 2013 Shijiazhuang was blanketed in a dense wave of smog that covered much of the Central and Eastern part of China, across a distance of around 1,200 kilometres (750 mi). A lack of cold air flow, combined with slow-moving air masses carrying industrial emissions, collected airborne pollutants to form a thick layer of smog over the region. Officials blamed the dense pollution on lack of wind, automobile exhaust emissions under low air pressure, and coal-powered district heating system in Northern China . Prevailing winds blew low-hanging air masses of factory emissions (mostly SO2) towards China's east coast.

Air pollution in the city peaked in 2014, when annual average PM2.5 Air Pollution reached 94 μg/m3, almost 19 times the World Health Organization guideline level. The national air pollution action plan issued by the State Council in 2013 highlighted the wider Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region as a focus area for improvement, which gained momentum in the government's "War on pollution". Although air pollution in the city remained well above the guideline level (approx. 8.5 times higher), by 2023 PM2.5 levels in the city had fallen  significantly from their peak, with an annual average of 42 μg/m3 representing a 54.8% reduction from the 2014 record level.

Migrants flowing in from all across China largely contributed to the population growth of Shijiazhuang in recent times. With a population of 120,000 in 1947, Shijiazhuang became the first medium-large city captured by the Chinese Communist Party from the Kuomintang. By the time of the People's Republic of China's founding in 1949, the total urban population increased to more than 270,000 people, more than doubling in a span of two years. In 1953, when China rolled out its first five-year plan, the total population of Shijiazhuang's urban area increased to 320,000. In 1960, the total population of the Shijiazhuang urban area had reached 650,000. In 1968, the city experienced a substantial increase due to it being designated the capital of Hebei to avoid chaos in Baoding amidst the Cultural Revolution. By 1980, the urban population had surpassed the one million mark, joining the ranks of a large city. As of the end of 2017, the urban population of Shijiazhuang exceeded 4.5 million.

In just six decades, the city's population has increased by more than 20 fold. At the end of 2009, the city's total non-migrant population was 9,774,100, an increase of 109,300 over the previous year. The birth rate of the city's population is 14.65%, the death rate is 6.25%, and the natural growth rate is 8.4%.

According to the sixth national census in 2010, the city's total non-migrant population stands at 10,163,788. Compared with the fifth national census a decade prior, there was an increase of 818,365 people, or an increase of 8.76%, and an average annual growth rate of 0.84%. Among them, the male population stood at 5,087,913, accounting for 50.06% of the total population; the female population is 5,075,875, accounting for 49.94% of the total population. The gender ratio of the total population is 100 women per 100.24 men. The population aged between 0 and 14 is 1,548,125, accounting for 15.23% of the total population; the population aged between 15 and 64 is 7,789,753, accounting for 76.64% of the total population; the population aged 65 and over is 825,910, accounting for 8.13% of the total population.
The top 10 surnames of Shijiazhuang are: Zhang (10.27%), Wang (9.25%), Li (9.17%), Liu (6.73%), Zhao (4.28%), Yang (2.82%), Gao (2.08%), Chen (1.92%), Ma (1.77%), and Guo (1.55%).

On May 6, 2011, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences published the "2011 China Urban Competitiveness Blue Book: China Urban Competitiveness Report". In it, the happiness survey sampled 294 cities across China, arriving at the conclusion that the residents of Shijiazhuang were the happiest. This result caused strong doubts from netizens.
In 2014, the GDP of Shijiazhuang reached CN¥510.02 billion (about $80.45 billion in USD), an increase of 12 percent over the previous year, and placing the city 20th in provincial capitals by GDP.

Shijiazhuang has become a major industrial city in North China and is considered to be the economic center of Hebei province, along with Tangshan. The city also located in Beijing-Tianjin-Shijiazhuang Hi-Tech Industrial Belt, which is one of the main Hi-Tech Belts in China. Nicknamed the "medicine hub of China", it is home to major pharmaceutical companies and factories like the North China Pharmaceutical Group Corporation, Shijiazhuang Pharma Group, and Shineway Pharma. The textile industry is also one of the backbones of the city's commerce. Other sectors include machinery and chemicals such as Shijiazhuang Donghua Jinlong, building materials, light industry, and electronics. With abundant agricultural resources, Shijiazhuang has 590,000 hectares of cultivated land and is the main source of cotton, pears, dates and walnuts in Hebei province.
In 2008, total imports reached US$1.393 billion, an increase of 42.1 percent over the previous year. Exports increased by 34.9 percent to US$5.596 billion.
2006 World Bank reported that Shijiazhuang was spending less than RMB400 per capita on education, as opposed to Beijing (RMB1,044) and Weihai (RMB1,631).
Shijiazhuang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone

The zone was established in March 1991 as a state-level development zone and is divided into three districts. National highways 107, 207, 307, 308 pass through the zone. It is 15 km (9.3 mi) away from Shijiazhuang railway station, 105 km (65 mi) away from Tianjin Port. Industries include pharmaceuticals, electronic information, mechanical production, automobile manufacturing, chemicals production and logistics.

The Eastern District, located in the eastern part of Shijiazhuang, covers an area of 5.8 km2 (2.2 sq mi), and serves as the primary section of the New High-tech Industrial Development Zone. The district focuses on the establishment of new high-tech enterprises. There are plans to expand the district into an area of 9.8 km2 (3.8 sq mi). A railway line operated by Shijiazhuang Oil Refinery runs through the zone from north to south, so enterprises in the zone can build lines of their own.

The Western District, located in the southwest of Shijiazhuang, covers an area of 8.2 km2 (3.2 sq mi). It focuses on small- and medium-sized technology enterprises and technology incubation. Liangcun District, which borders the Western District, covers 4 km2 (1.5 sq mi), and focuses on the pharmaceutical industry and the petrochemical industry.

By 2009, some 2,600 enterprises had settled in the zone, of which 185 were foreign-funded enterprises. Firms from Japan, the US, the Republic of Korea, Germany, Italy, Canada, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan had established themselves in the zone.

The city is a center for the dairy trade, being the headquarters of the Sanlu Group. Sanlu became Shijiazhuang's largest taxpayer since it had become the largest formula seller in China for a continuous 15-year period. Richard McGregor, author of The Party: The Secret World of China's Communist Rulers, said that Sanlu became "an invaluable asset for a city otherwise struggling to attract industry and investment on a par with China's premier metropolises."

Both the dairy trade and Sanlu were affected by the 2008 Chinese milk scandal. The chairman and general manager of Sanlu, and several party officials, including the vice-mayor in charge of food and agriculture, Zhang Fawang, were reportedly removed from office. Mayor Ji Chuntang reportedly resigned on September 17, 2008.
The city is served by many expressways, including the Shitai, Beijing–Shenzhen and Taiyuan–Cangzhou Expressways.

Shijiazhuang is a transportation hub at the intersection point of the Beijing–Guangzhou, Taiyuan–Dezhou, and Shuozhou–Huanghua railways. The new Shijiazhuang railway station (opened December 2012) has a rare distinction of being served by both the "conventional" Beijing–Guangzhou Railway and the new Beijing–Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong High-Speed Railway. Such an arrangement is fairly uncommon on China's high-speed rail network, as typically high-speed lines are constructed to bypass city cores, where the older "conventional" train stations are.

In Shijiazhuang's case, to make it possible to bring the new high-speed railway into the central city, a 5 km (3.1 mi) long railway tunnel was constructed under the city. This is the first time a high-speed railway has been run under a Chinese city.
There is also the smaller Shijiazhuang North railway station, used by trains going west toward Taiyuan without the need for passing through downtown.
Line 1, Line 2 and Line 3 of the Shijiazhuang Metro are currently operational. The system is 76.5 km (47.5 mi) in length. The latest metro plan of Shijiazhuang includes 6 lines in total.

The Shijiazhuang Zhengding International Airport is the province's center of air transportation. It is about 30 kilometers northeast of the city. There are 32 domestic routes arriving at and departing from Shijiazhuang, including destinations such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Dalian. The airport serves 12 international destinations including four routes to Russia. The airport is being expanded and will be capable of being an alternate airport to Beijing Capital International Airport.

With the opening of the Beijing–Guangzhou High-Speed Railway at the end of 2012, the airport got its own train station, making available fast, although infrequent, train service between the airport and Shijiazhuang railway station, as well as other stations in the region.

Most large roads in the city feature a separate cycle lane and, combined with the city being flat, make it ideal for cycling. Thousands of cyclists use the city each day and often there are more cyclists waiting at a crossroad than cars.

The city of Shijiazhuang is similar to Beijing in that all roads run from north to south and east to west, making the city easy to navigate. Many roads have cycle paths making it cyclist friendly. In the heart of the city is the Hebei Museum which was refurbished in 2013 and 2014. It holds regular events, mostly showing traditional Chinese art and artifacts. The Yutong International Sports Centre hosts the Shijiazhuang Ever Bright football matches as well as holding pop concerts.

Shijiazhuang Zoo is located on the west side of the city. The zoo has 3,000 animals of 250 species including flamingos, golden monkeys, manchurian tigers, Indian elephants, giraffes, chimpanzees, kangaroos, seals, white tigers, springboks and pandas. Near the Shijiazhuang Zoo are the Botanical Gardens (Chinese: 石家庄植物园), offering a range of exotic and native plants both to view and purchase. The Martyrs Memorial (烈士纪念馆) can be found in the centre of the city, commemorating the soldiers lost in war.

The downtown area of the city contains a range of parks. The largest park is found in the centre of the city known as Chang'an Park (Chinese: 长安公园), the park includes an underground shopping mall, a theatre, a museum, a lake, bars and restaurants. Another park is found on the south east side of the city: Century Park (世纪公园), Century Park contains a lake in the centre with an amusement park to the north side. On the northwest side of the city is Water Park (水上公园) which features a large lake, amusement rides, short walks and various restaurants. As well as these three large parks there are smaller parks scattered across the city.
The 2018 arthouse film An Elephant Sitting Still by Hu Bo was shot and set in Shijiazhuang.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hebei-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hebei Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shijiazhuang, register at Hebei Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hebei Normal University (河北师范大学, HNU) is a publicly funded research university in Shijiazhuang, which is the capital of Hebei province. The province treats it as one of its key universities, and its history stretches back over a century, and it receives support from both the Hebei provincial government and China's national education authorities.

As the name suggests, it grew from teacher education, but the range of subjects today is much wider, covering nine fields from philosophy and law to engineering. Anyone considering the university will find a large, long-established institution rather than a small specialist school.
The university has two starting points. One was the Shuntian School (顺天府学堂), set up in Beijing in 1902. The other was the Beiyang Women Normal School (北洋女师范学堂), opened in Tianjin in 1906.

The modern university was formed in June 1996, when four institutions were combined with approval from the provincial government and given the name Hebei Normal University. Those four were Hebei Teachers University; Hebei Teachers College; a vocational and technological college; and the Hebei Education Institute, which dated from 1952. It counts as one of the early large-scale universities in China.

Among the people who studied here are Tang Yongtong, Zhang Shenfu, Liang Suming, Kang Shien, Yang Xiufeng, Guo Longzhen, Liu Qingyang and Deng Yingchao. The list also includes the academicians Hao Bolin and Yan Luguang, as well as well-known coaches and athletes with international championship titles, such as Cai Zhenhua and Xu Shaofa. More than 200,000 students have been taught at the university since 1949.
The campus covers 1829 mu, which is about 121 hectares, and the library holds 3,300,000 volumes.

Staffing figures show a university of real size. Altogether there are 2,852 faculty and staff, and 1,480 of them teach. The teaching staff includes 974 associate professors and 359 full professors, one academician from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, 871 postgraduate tutors, 138 PhD supervisors and 106 experts honoured as provincial models.

The student numbers are given as 57,658 on-campus students in total, made up of 33,404 in two-year or four-year programmes and 20,388 in further education, plus 3,866 graduate students. These groups are counted differently in different reports and the numbers date from different years, so ask the university for the current breakdown if you need a precise number.

Academic work is organised in 21 colleges, plus one independent college, Huihua College. Students can choose among 81 four-year undergraduate programmes, 91 master's programmes and 24 doctoral programmes. The university also has four post-doctoral research stations and runs two state-level and four provincial-level demonstration centres for experimental teaching.

Nine units come directly under the university's management: the CCP Training School, the Graduate School, a college for further education and teacher training, the College of International Culture Exchange, the Training Centre for Higher Education Teachers, the Further Education Center, the Office for New Campus Construction, the Institute for Education Development and the Office of Development.

Other affiliated bodies include the Computer and Network Center, the Analysis and Test Center, the editorial office of the university journal, the University Logistic Service Group, a publishing house for Chinese philology and a journal on thought and wisdom, the University Hospital, an affiliated middle school, an affiliated primary school, an affiliated experimental middle and primary school and an affiliated minority college for Tibetan students. There are also a computer-teaching department, a provincial centre for modern higher education technology, the Hebei Vocational Education Research Institute, the Hebei Research Institute of Pedagogy, a discipline-education research institute and an institute for selecting and sorting ancient books.
Figures here cover different periods, and they stop some years back, so read them as background on the university's research history.

After the four-institution merger in 1996, the university won two national teaching-achievement awards and 41 provincial ones, and took on eight state teaching-innovation projects and 11 provincial ones. Between 1997 and 2011 it ran 718 research programmes above department level. Of these, 231 were national, including 37 in natural science and 18 in social science, and 199 were provincial, with 123 in natural science and 76 in social science. Some had national influence, such as the national 937 Project, State Natural Science Fund projects and Excellent Youth Scientific Fund projects.

Yearly research funding grew fast, from ¥6 million in 2002 to ¥42.29 million by 2008, and the university took on 143 new state research projects, of which 112 were in the natural sciences and 31 in the social sciences. Significant work has been carried out under the national "973" Plan and the "863" Plan, and under programmes such as key programmes on turning agricultural research into technology, a transgenic industry development programme supported by the National Science Foundation, a key pre-study plan of the Ministry of Science and Technology, key programmes of the National Social Science Foundation and a state key project on Qing-dynasty history. Results from this work have appeared in journals such as Science, The Plant Cell, The Astrophysical Journal and Advances in Mathematics, which the university rates as first-level both at home and abroad.

The university has relationships with more than 30 universities around the world. It is approved by the State Education Committee to enrol international students, as well as applicants from Taiwan, Macau and Hong Kong. If you are applying from abroad, confirm entry requirements and available programmes directly with its international office.

HNU reports a number of good results. Mathematics and Applied Mathematics, and Biological Science, ranked first in Hebei Province. Its law programme was placed in the top 100 among universities in China. Rankings of this kind are old and change with each edition, so compare current ones before deciding.

Its neighbours inside Hebei are Hengshui to the east, Xingtai to the south and Baoding to the north and northeast, while the province of Shanxi lies to the west.

Shijiazhuang lies on the margin of the North China Plain, just south of the Hutuo River, with the Taihang Mountains climbing to its west. Reading the land from west to east, you pass through moderately high mountains, lower mountains, hills and a basin before reaching flat plains. Eight routes cross the Taihang range from east to west, and the fifth of them, the Niangzi Pass, gives the city a direct link to Taiyuan in Shanxi.

The Eastern District, in the east of the city, measures 5.8 km2 (2.2 sq mi) and is the main part of the zone, where new high-tech firms are set up. Plans call for it to expand to 9.8 km2 (3.8 sq mi). A railway line belonging to Shijiazhuang Oil Refinery crosses it from north to south, which lets companies inside build their own branch lines.

The Western District, in the southwest, extends over 8.2 km2, or 3.2 sq mi, and is aimed at small and medium-sized technology firms and at incubation. Beside it lies Liangcun District, with 4 km2 (1.5 sq mi), which specialises in the pharmaceutical and petrochemical industries.

By 2009 about 2,600 enterprises had moved into the zone, 185 of them funded from abroad. Investors came from Japan, the United States, Germany, Italy, Canada, Malaysia and the Republic of Korea, and also from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan.

Shijiazhuang has also been a centre of the dairy trade. The dairy sector and the city's biggest dairy firm were badly hit by the 2008 Chinese milk scandal, and the industry's fortunes have changed since then, so it is best not to assume that this earlier picture still holds.
Many expressways serve the city, including the Shitai, Beijing-Shenzhen and Taiyuan-Cangzhou expressways.

Shijiazhuang is a rail hub where the Beijing-Guangzhou, Taiyuan-Dezhou and Shuozhou-Huanghua railways meet. The new Shijiazhuang railway station, opened in December 2012, is unusual because it is served by both the conventional Beijing-Guangzhou Railway and the Beijing-Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong High-Speed Railway. On most high-speed lines in China, tracks bypass city cores, where the older stations are. To bring the high-speed line to the city centre here, a 5 km (3.1 mi) tunnel was built under the city, the first occasion on which a Chinese city has had a high-speed line passing beneath it. A smaller Shijiazhuang North railway station handles trains going west toward Taiyuan without passing through downtown.
Lines 1, 2 and 3 of the Shijiazhuang Metro are operating, a network of 76.5 km (47.5 mi). The latest plan has six lines in all.

The province's main air hub is Shijiazhuang Zhengding International Airport, roughly 30 kilometres northeast of the city. It has 32 domestic routes, including Shanghai, Shenzhen and Dalian, and 12 international destinations, four of them in Russia. It has been described as being expanded to serve as an alternate airport for Beijing Capital International Airport. When the Beijing-Guangzhou High-Speed Railway began operating in late 2012, the airport gained a rail station of its own, with fast but infrequent trains to Shijiazhuang station and other stations in the region.

Most major roads have a separate cycle lane, and with flat terrain the city suits cycling. Thousands of cyclists are on the road daily, often outnumbering the cars waiting at a crossroads. Like Beijing, the city is laid out on a north-south and east-west grid, so it is easy to find your way around.

In the middle of the city stands the Hebei Museum, refurbished in 2013 and 2014, which stages regular events, mainly displays of traditional Chinese art and artefacts. The Yutong International Sports Centre hosts football matches of Shijiazhuang Ever Bright as well as pop concerts.

Shijiazhuang Zoo, in the west of the city, is home to 3,000 animals from 250 species. Visitors can see pandas, kangaroos, seals, springboks, chimpanzees, giraffes, golden monkeys, flamingos, white tigers, Manchurian tigers and Indian elephants. Close to it are the Botanical Gardens (石家庄植物园), where visitors can see and buy exotic and native plants. The Martyrs Memorial (烈士纪念馆) in the centre commemorates soldiers lost in war.

The biggest park is Chang'an Park (长安公园) in the centre, with a lake, a museum, a theatre, bars, restaurants and an underground shopping mall. In the southeast, Century Park (世纪公园) has a lake in the middle and an amusement park on the north side. In the northwest, Water Park (水上公园) has a large lake, rides, short walks and restaurants. Smaller parks are scattered through the city as well.
Hu Bo's arthouse film An Elephant Sitting Still, from 2018, was both filmed and set in Shijiazhuang.

hebei-normal-university.h: Pulling it together for a prospective student

blocks.x: Hebei Normal University is a large, provincially backed university with roots going back to 1902 and a merger in 1996 that brought four institutions into one. It is strongest in teacher education and the humanities, but its list of 21 colleges also covers life science, physics, chemistry, software, tourism and more, so it can suit students with quite different interests.

The city around it is a flat, grid-like provincial capital with a growing rail and metro network, an airport northeast of town and a good deal of cycling infrastructure. The main practical points to plan for are the climate, which is cold and dry in winter and hot and humid in summer with most rain falling in July and August, and air quality, which has improved markedly since its 2014 peak but still exceeds the World Health Organization guideline. Spring can also bring sandstorms from the Mongolian steppe.

Costs, programme availability, entry requirements and student numbers all change from year to year, and many of the statistics above come from earlier years. For anything that affects your application, such as fees, accommodation or current rankings, rely on the university's own website and its international office.
Hebei Normal University lists 161 programs for international students on this site: 54 bachelor, 62 master's, 43 doctoral, 2 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 145 taught in Chinese, 16 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 19,800 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 29,000 (median CNY 27,000), according to the university's published fee table.

161 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
