International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hebei-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hebei Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shijiazhuang, register at Hebei Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hebei University (河北大学) is a public institution run at provincial level, based in the city of Baoding in northern China's Hebei Province. It is a large institution with about 42,000 full-time students, among them roughly 28,000 undergraduates and more than 6,400 postgraduates. It describes itself as a comprehensive university, so its programmes extend across economics, law, philosophy, literature, history, education, science, engineering, medicine and management.

Its position in the rankings is steady. It is regularly placed in the leading pair of universities in Hebei across a range of measures and is consistently placed within the top 80 in the country. The source mentions the Chinese University Ranking compiled by Wu Shulian, but the year-by-year table is missing here, so look up the latest edition yourself if rankings matter to you.

hebei-university.h: From a French Jesuit institute in Tianjin to Baoding

blocks.x: The university's route to Baoding was indirect. It began in 1921 in Tianjin as the Institut des Hautes Etudes et Commerciales des Tientsin, founded by French Jesuits. Over the following four decades it went through several identities, as Tsin Ku University, then Tianjin Normal College and then Tianjin Normal University. In 1960 it was reorganised as a comprehensive university and given the name Hebei University.

Ten years later, in 1970, it moved to Baoding. The reason was administrative: Tianjin had been made a directly administered municipality three years earlier, which put it outside Hebei Province's jurisdiction, so the provincial university relocated to a city that stayed inside the province.

The campus spans more than 700 acres (2.8 square kilometres). The library holds about 3,900,000 books and 5,000 periodicals, including one of the largest rare-book collections among Chinese universities. The university museum has over 8,000 objects, of which more than 70 are protected by law as national treasures. It also keeps rare animal and plant specimens.

Fifteen colleges offer 85 specialised undergraduate courses leading to a bachelor's degree. At graduate level, master's degrees are available in 140 subjects, and doctorates in 12 fields. The wide spread of subjects means that students from many backgrounds can find a suitable programme, but check the current catalogue and language of instruction with the international office.

The university has a workforce of 3,372 teaching and administrative staff, of whom 1,910 work in teaching and research, including 417 professors and 722 associate professors. Faculty members who are often mentioned include the following.
Yin Xiangchu, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recognised for research into locust habitats
Song Daxiang, an arachnologist and the author of The Arachnids of China
Wei Chunjiang, a microbiologist whose studies of lichens are well known
Qi Xia, an economic historian of the Song dynasty who wrote a major work on that subject
Teng Dachun, a historian of education who wrote on the history of schooling in the United States
Daily life for a student mostly comes down to the city outside the campus: its weather, how you travel and what you can do with your free time. The next sections describe Baoding.

Baoding is in the west-central part of Hebei, on the North China Plain, and the Taihang Mountains are on its west side. Within the province, the adjoining prefecture-level cities are Zhangjiakou (north), Langfang and Cangzhou (east), and Shijiazhuang and Hengshui (south). Beyond the province, it also borders Beijing to the north-east and Shanxi to the west. The city lies between 113 degrees 40 minutes and 116 degrees 20 minutes east and between 38 degrees 10 minutes and 40 degrees north.

The land falls from north-west to south-east. The western part is mountainous and hilly, mostly above 1,000 metres (3,300 feet), and includes parts of Fuping, Tang, Shunping, Mancheng, Yi and Laishui counties and the whole of Laiyuan County, together 30.6 percent of the prefecture. The highest peak is Mount Waitou at 2,286 metres (7,500 feet). Further south-east come low mountains and hills, about 18.9 percent of the area, and then flat ground lying 30 to 100 metres up (98 to 330 feet) in the east, where the main rivers are the Xiaoyi, Fu, Bao, Ping, Juma, Yishui, Tang, Cao, Zhulong, Qingshui and Sha. Baiyangdian, northern China's largest natural lake, is close by.

The climate is continental and monsoon-influenced, between humid continental and semi-arid. Summers are hot and humid under the East Asian monsoon, while winters are generally cold, windy and very dry because of the vast Siberian high-pressure system. Spring can bring sandstorms from the Mongolian steppe, together with fast warming and dry conditions, and autumn resembles spring in its temperatures and dryness.

Rain is variable and unreliable: around 60 percent of it falls in July and August alone, and the city itself averages just 496.1 millimetres (19.5 inches) a year, and annual runoff averages 2.45 billion cubic metres. Monthly mean temperatures rise from minus 2.7 degrees Celsius (27.1 F) in January to 27.1 degrees (80.8 F) in July, with 13.3 degrees (55.9 F). Sunshine totals 2,500 to 2,900 hours a year, and the frost-free period is 165 to 210 days.

The 2010 census counted 11,194,382 residents in the prefecture, up 605,100 (5.71 percent) from 2000, with 101.94 men for every 100 women. About 1,915,800 people (17.11 percent) were aged up to 14, 8,370,600 (74.78 percent) were 15 to 64, and 908,000 (8.11 percent) were 65 or older. The urban area, which has five urban districts, had around 2,739,887 people. The great majority are Han Chinese. People speak Mandarin, in the form of the Baoding variety of Ji-Lu Mandarin. Although the city is close to Beijing, the local speech is not especially similar to the Beijing dialect, being closer to that of Tianjin.

Baoding sits at the middle of the Bohai Rim economic area, a region that takes in Beijing, Tianjin and Shijiazhuang. One of its largest employers is China Lucky Film, the country's largest maker of photosensitive materials and magnetic recording media. The Yingli Group, a 2010 World Cup sponsor and one of the global top ten solar panel makers, is headquartered here, and other known companies include ZhongHang HuiTeng Windpower Equipment (wind turbines), Baoding Tianwei Group (transformers) and Great Wall Motor.

In April 2017 part of the Baoding area was designated the Xiong'an New Area, a development zone beginning at 100 square kilometres and eventually up to 2,000 square kilometres, planned as the site of a future city and the hub of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei development area. The Baoding High-tech Industrial Development Zone is another important location.

Great Wall Motor, founded in 1984 and taking its name from the Great Wall of China, is headquartered in Baoding. It is China's largest maker of sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks, It markets cars and trucks under the Great Wall name and SUVs as Haval and WEY. In 2016 it set a sales record of 1,074,471 vehicles worldwide, 26 percent more than in 2015.
Baoding is well connected because it sits on one of the main routes into and out of Beijing.
Road: the Jingshi Expressway connects Baoding with Beijing, and Baoding is the western end of the Baojin Expressway to Tianjin, which is one of the two nearest ports, the other being Huanghua.

Rail: the Jingguang Railway runs frequent trains to Beijing West railway station. A new Baoding station opened on 30 December 2012 and the old one closed to passengers. Baoding East station lies 9.5 kilometres (5.9 miles) to the east on the Beijing to Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Hong Kong high-speed line. On 1 October 2018 Baoding Railway Station brought its east square into service and opened an east station building too.

Baoding is said to be the origin of Baoding balls, which people use to relax a keyboard hand and strengthen the wrist. The most famous local dish is the donkey burger (驴肉火烧). Anxin County has the Quantou Village Music Association, based on an island in Lake Baiyangdian, which plays traditional music on guan oboes and sheng mouth organs, plus percussion.

The city's streets follow a loose grid, less obvious in the older quarter. Yuhua Road is the traditional main street of old Baoding, and it runs from the centre to the eastern edge, and most historic buildings and some of the bigger shopping centres are along it. Other major streets are Dongfeng Road and Chaoyang Avenue, and a ring road circles the city. Besides Hebei University, Baoding is home to North China Electric Power University, plus three other universities and twelve colleges.

The city proper has an old mansion of a provincial governor and an ancient lotus garden. In the hills north-west of the city near Mancheng lie the Mancheng Han Tombs, the burial place of Prince Liu Sheng and his wife Dou Wan. The wider Baoding area has 16 state-level protected cultural relics.
Yan State Capital Relics (475 to 221 BC), Yixian County
Great Wall at Zijinguan Pass (1368 to 1644), Yixian and Laiyuan counties
Tang-era stele inscribed with Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching (618 to 907)), Yixian County
Western Qing Tombs (1730 to 1915), Yixian County
Geyuan Temple (916 to 1125), Laiyuan County
Ciyun Pavilion (1306), Dingxing County

Kaiyuan Temple (960 to 1127), Dingzhou

The province in which a university sits shapes student life nearly as much as the campus itself, so this part looks at Hebei.

Early humans of the Homo erectus type, known as Peking Man, lived at Zhoukoudian in today's Fangshan District of Beijing, next to Hebei's border, some hundreds of thousands of years ago, and published estimates vary between about 700,000 and 200,000 years. Neolithic finds at the prehistoric Beifudi site go back to 7000 and 8000 BC. The province is the setting for many early Chinese myths: Fuxi, counted among the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, is said to have lived in what is now Xingtai, and the legendary Battle of Zhuolu, in which the Yellow Emperor and Yan Emperor with their Yanhuang tribes defeated the Jiuli tribes led by Chiyou, took place in Zhangjiakou and is held to have started Huaxia civilisation.

In the Spring and Autumn period (722 to 476 BC) Yan ruled the north and Jin the south, and a nomadic people called the Di established Zhongshan in central Hebei. During the Warring States period (403 to 221 BC)) Jin was divided and much of its Hebei territory passed to Zhao. The Qin unified China in 221 BC. Under the Han (206 BC to AD 220) the area belonged to You Prefecture in the north and Ji Province in the south. When the Han ended, the warlords Gongsun Zan (north) and Yuan Shao (south) held most of Hebei, with Yuan Shao the victor until Cao Cao defeated him at the Battle of Guandu in 200, after which Hebei came under the Kingdom of Wei founded by Cao Cao's descendants.

hebei-university.h: From the Jin to the Yuan

blocks.x: After northern peoples invaded when the Western Jin ended, the Sixteen Kingdoms and Northern and Southern dynasties brought chaos. As a frontier region Hebei changed hands often, held at different times by Later Zhao, Former Yan, Former Qin and Later Yan, and the Northern Wei reunified the north in 440 but split in 534, and Hebei went to Eastern Wei and then Northern Qi, whose capital was Ye near modern Linzhang. The Sui reunified China in 589.

Under the Tang (618 to 907) Hebei received its official name for the first time. The Great Yan State existed there between 756 and 763, in the course of the An Lushan Rebellion, and afterwards Lulong remained autonomous from the Tang for most of the ninth century. In the late Five Dynasties period Lulong split among several regimes, until Li Cunxu annexed it in 913 and founded the Later Tang (923 to 936). The Later Jin emperor Gaozu handed over much of northern Hebei to the Khitan Liao. These Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun lay inside the Great Wall and were a weakness in China's defences for the next century.

The sixteen prefectures remained contested between Song China and the Liao in the Northern Song (960 to 1127). Later the Southern Song gave up all of North China, Hebei included, to the Jurchen Jin after the Jingkang Incident of 1127. Hebei suffered from Yellow River flooding, and between 1048 and 1128 the river flowed straight straight through the province instead of south of it. The Mongol Yuan dynasty split China into provinces yet did not make Hebei one, administering it directly from the Secretariat in the capital Dadu.

hebei-university.h: Ming, Qing and the modern era

blocks.x: During the Ming, the area was first set up as Beizhili at a time when the capital was at Nanjing. In 1403 the Yongle Emperor gave Beiping the name Beijing, and in 1421 he formally transferred the capital there from Nanjing. Beizhili comprised parts of modern Hebei, Henan and Shandong, plus Beijing and Tianjin. The Qing took power in 1644 and based the capital in Beijing; Southern Zhili became the province of Jiangnan and Northern Zhili simply became Zhili, meaning Directly Ruled. Its northern borders reached deep into Inner Mongolia, overlapping with Inner Mongolian leagues, and in the eighteenth century they were redrawn to cover Hebei and what is now Beijing, Tianjin, western Liaoning, northern Henan and northern Shandong, as well as Inner Mongolia.

After the Qing collapsed in 1912 and the Republic of China began, regional warlords fought for power. Being so close to Beijing, Zhili was the scene of the Zhiwan War and the First and Second Zhifeng Wars. After the Kuomintang's Northern Expedition in 1926 and 1927 the capital moved from Beijing to Nanjing, parts of northern Zhili were assigned to neighbouring provinces, and the remainder was renamed Hebei. In the Second World War the province was under the Japanese-backed Reorganized National Government of the Republic of China, a puppet state.

When the People's Republic was founded, the Chengde area from Rehe Province and the Zhangjiakou area from Chahar Province were merged into Hebei, pushing the border north beyond the Great Wall, while Puyang was separated, so Hebei lost access to the Yellow River; Puyang joined the short-lived Pingyuan Province and was then added to Henan. The provincial capital was relocated from Baoding to the new city of Shijiazhuang, with a short stay in Tianjin. On 28 July 1976 the Tangshan earthquake, among the deadliest of the twentieth century, killed about 242,000 people by the official count, with some estimates far higher, and smaller quakes followed during the next decade.

Today Hebei, together with the municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin, forms the Jing-Jin-Ji megalopolis. Its 130 million people make it roughly six New York metropolitan areas in size, and one of China's largest urban clusters. Beijing has moved some non-capital functions to the province through the Xiong'an New Area, a zone that ties the three together.

Hebei is the only Chinese province that contains plateaus, mountains, hills, coastline, plains and lakes. Most of the centre and south lies in the North China Plain, the Taihang Mountains rise in the west, and the Yan Mountains cross the north, and the grasslands of Inner Mongolia lie beyond them. The top peak is Mount Xiaowutai, in Yu County in the north-west, at 2,882 metres (9,455 feet). The Bohai Sea borders the east. Most of the centre and south falls within the Hai River watershed, and the Luan River watershed covers the north-east. Leaving aside reservoirs, the largest lake is Baiyangdian in Anxin County, Baoding. Zhangjiakou, Handan, Qinhuangdao, Tangshan, Baoding and Shijiazhuang are the main cities.

The climate is a monsoon-influenced humid continental one, with cold, dry winters and hot, humid summers. January averages run from minus 16 to minus 3 degrees Celsius (3 to 27 F), July from 20 to 27 degrees (68 to 81 F), and annual precipitation is 400 to 800 millimetres (16 to 31 inches), heavily concentrated in summer.

hebei-university.h: Summing up Hebei University for applicants

blocks.x: In short, Hebei University is a large provincial comprehensive university whose history runs from a French Jesuit institute in Tianjin to a campus in Baoding, linked to Beijing by an expressway, the Jingguang Railway and a high-speed line. Its breadth of subjects, large library and rare-book holdings, and museum collection are its main academic assets, and its ranking among the top 80 Chinese universities gives a rough guide to its standing.

For daily life, expect hot humid summers, cold windy winters and spring dust, along with a city that is smaller and calmer than Beijing but well connected to it. Baoding offers local specialities such as the donkey burger, historic sites that range from Han tombs to a Qing-era governor's office, and the neighbouring Xiong'an New Area as a long-term development project. Check programme languages, scholarship rules and accommodation with the university's international office before applying.

hebei-university-of-economics-and-busine.h: Who Hebei University of Economics and Business is

blocks.x: Hebei University of Economics and Business, usually shortened to HUEB (河北经贸大学 in Chinese), is a public university run by the provincial government of Hebei. It sits in Shijiazhuang, the provincial capital in northern China. For an international applicant, the first thing to grasp is that this is a provincial institution rather than a national flagship, with a clear focus on commerce, finance and management. The sections below explain where it came from, what it teaches, how it is organised and what the city around it is like.

HUEB does not have a single starting point. It was formed in 1995 by joining three separate colleges, each with its own long and rather tangled record of name changes. Understanding these three strands helps explain why the university is so strongly rooted in trade, finance and public management.

The oldest thread begins in 1953, when a cooperative school for supply and marketing cooperatives opened in Shijiazhuang. The school was given a new name in 1958: Hebei Province School of Business and Technical Cadres. In 1959 it absorbed the Provincial Grain School and took the title Hebei Province School of Finance and Trade Technical Cadres. A School of Commerce followed in 1960, but it stopped operating after 1965 for reasons the record describes only as historical. It was set up again in 1973 under the same name, and that school then served as the base for a Hebei College of Finance and Trade, which opened in 1978. In 1984 it took the name Hebei Trade and Finance Institute, which it kept until the merger.

The second thread starts in September 1968 with a cadre school on the Hutuo River, set up during the Cultural Revolution period. In 1979 it became the Hebei Provincial Cadre School, and in 1982 a construction institute grew out of it. By 1983 that institute was known as the Hebei Institute of Economic Management Cadres. Over the following years it shared its premises and activities with other bodies: in 1987 a Hebei Provincial Administrative College was created and folded into it, the provincial Socialist College was revived alongside it in 1988, and in 1992 it joined the provincial Township Enterprise Bureau to open a Township Enterprise College. In 1994 the institution was reorganised as Hebei College of Trade and Economics.

The third thread goes back to 1956 and a provincial school for business cadres. After a reorganisation in 1959 it was called the School of Finance and Trade Cadres, then in 1963 it returned to its earlier name. Admissions were paused in 1965. The school reopened in 1982 on the same site as the Provincial School of Commerce, received the name Hebei Business Vocational College in 1984, and turned into the Hebei Commerce College in 1992.

With approval from the State Education Commission, the Trade and Finance Institute, the College of Trade and Economics and the Commerce College were combined in 1995 to create HUEB. On 6 June 1995 Jiang Zemin, who was then General Secretary of the Communist Party and President of China, wrote out the university's name in his own calligraphy. Today HUEB counts among the key universities of Hebei Province and awards degrees at both undergraduate and postgraduate level.

Between 2017 and 2022 the university carried out more than 90 projects financed by the national social science fund, the natural science fund and the Ministry of Education. It also took part in over 1500 other academic projects, and total research funding passed CN¥120 million in that period.

The university's Economic Research Center has produced work with real policy reach. In 2007 its monograph on the competitiveness of the service industry earned a provincial award for outstanding social science achievement. Its yearly Hebei Industrial Competitiveness Report has become an important reference for the province when drawing up the Eleventh Five-Year Plan.

The university's own academic journal, founded in 1980, is a general economics journal that circulates in China and abroad. It now appears every two months, on the 15th. It is listed as a national Chinese core journal, as a source journal (extended edition) of the Chinese Social Sciences Citation Index, and as a core journal in the AMI comprehensive evaluation of Chinese humanities and social sciences. Its editor-in-chief is Peng Jianqiang, who is also a vice president of the university.

The second publication, Economy and Management, began in 1986 and also comes out every two months, mainly carrying research on economics and management. It started life as the journal of the Hebei Economic Management Cadre College. At first the Organization Department of the provincial Party Committee supervised it; later responsibility shifted to HUEB and the provincial Department of Education.

Rankings are a rough guide only, but they show where HUEB sits. In the Wu Shulian ranking of Chinese universities it came 399th nationally. In the Shanghai Ranking's list of Chinese finance universities it held 27th place in 2023, and its reference ranking in the national overall table has stayed steady at 360th in recent years.

Chinese universities must pass a demanding review before they are allowed to award doctorates, and HUEB has not yet gained this right. Several neighbouring finance and economics universities have it: the ones in Shandong, Shanxi and Tianjin, which carry the same type of name. The university teaches only finance, economics and related subjects, with no science or technology disciplines, and that narrow base leaves its overall academic strength modest by comparison with other institutions in the province. Other Hebei universities of comparable standing, for instance North China University of Science and Technology, plus the Hebei University of Science and Technology, either hold such rights or are working towards them. Even Hebei University of Engineering in Handan, which has lower entry requirements, has received a special doctoral programme. If a doctorate in China is part of your plan, this is worth checking directly with the university.

As of 2023 the university has 17 teaching units. The list below gives the main ones with the subjects they cover, so you can see whether your field is available. Here the unit names appear in the form HUEB uses.

The School of Finance dates from 1980 and covers Finance, Fintech, Insurance, Investment as well as Financial Engineering. In 2019 it was named a national first-class undergraduate major construction site.

Business Administration is a school of its own, founded in 1983; its majors are Marketing, Human Resource Management and Cultural Industry Management as well as Business Administration itself, and it too received the first-class designation in 2019.

The School of Accountancy covers Accounting, Financial Management and Auditing. Its accounting major won recognition as a national characteristic major back in 2007, became a national comprehensive reform pilot in 2013 and was chosen as a first-class construction site in 2019.

Public Finance and Taxation has its own college, with majors in Asset Evaluation, Public Finance and Taxation. A separate Business School takes in Economics alongside International Economics and Trade, Trade Economics and E-commerce.
The Public Administration College, established in 1983, has majors in Public Administration, Labor and Social Security, and also Public Utility Administration.

The Law School opened in 1995 and teaches Law. Its law major was named a national characteristic major in 2008, then a national comprehensive reform pilot in 2013, and in 2019 it joined the group of first-class construction sites at undergraduate level.

Management Science and Engineering is another school, covering Information Management and Information Systems, Engineering Management and Logistics Management. Tourism has its own school too, where students can choose Tourism Management, Hotel Management, Exhibition Economy and Management, or Real Estate Development and Management.
Mathematics and Statistics became a college in 2001. Its majors are Mathematics and Applied Mathematics, along with Information and Computational Science, plus Statistics and Applied Statistics.

Computing is taught in the School of Information Technology: Electronic Information Engineering, Computer Science and Technology, Network Engineering, Software Engineering and Data Science and Big Data Technology. Life sciences sit in the School of Biological Science and Engineering, whose subjects are Biotechnology, Food Science and Engineering, and Food Quality and Safety.

Culture and Communication has been a school since 2003. It has six majors: Journalism, Radio and Television, Advertising, Publishing, Chinese Language and Literature, and Chinese International Education. The last of these is the one most relevant to foreign students interested in teaching Chinese.
Languages are handled by the School of Foreign Languages (founded 1998), which covers English, Japanese, Korean and Romanian, plus Business English.

Creative students can look at the School of Arts: Visual Communication Design, Environmental Design and Product Design, then Animation and Painting, and finally the performing options of Music and Dance.
Two further units complete the list.
School of Marxism
International Education School

A joint undergraduate marketing programme with Concordia University Chicago was reported in November 2014. A reporter for the local newspaper was told by the education department of the province that the national ministry had given it approval.

HUEB and Woosuk University (우석대학교) have trained doctoral students together since 2018, with 15 HUEB professors serving as joint doctoral supervisors. In February 2021, under the guidance of supervisors from both universities, all 21 HUEB staff members who had been studying for doctorates in South Korea graduated. It was the university's first overseas joint doctoral training scheme. Note, however, that some people online have questioned the quality of these degrees.
On 13 June 2007 HUEB opened a Confucius Institute together with Kathmandu University. A second one, in Zambia, was set up with that country's national university.

In 2022 the university employed over 1,800 teachers and other staff, most of them full-time teachers. More than 600 hold senior professional titles, and another 600 or so have a PhD or are working towards one.
The charter lists four principles: Party committee leadership, the president's accountability, teaching led by professors, and democratic management.

The main campus is in northern Shijiazhuang, on the Hutuo River's southern bank. It covers 2,600 acres and, before the 21st century, was the largest single-site university campus in Hebei Province. About 40 percent of its area is green space, which is a welcome feature in a city with air quality concerns (more on that below).

Day-to-day life for a student depends heavily on the city beyond the campus gates: the weather, the air, how you travel and what you can do on a free afternoon. The rest of this page introduces Shijiazhuang, the home of HUEB.

Shijiazhuang is found in south-central Hebei, inside the Bohai Economic Rim. Between 37° 27' and 38° 47' N, and between 113° 30' and 115° 20' E, lies its territory. This prefecture-level city extends 148 kilometres (92 mi) north to south and 175 kilometres (109 mi) east to west, with a border running 760 kilometres (472 mi); the total land area is 15,722 square kilometres (6,070 sq mi). Its neighbours in Hebei are Hengshui to the east, Xingtai to the south and Baoding to the north and northeast, while the province of Shanxi lies to the west.

The city stands where the North China Plain meets the foothills of the Taihang Mountains, just south of the Hutuo River. Going from west to east, the landscape changes from fairly high mountains to lower mountains, then hills, a basin and finally open plain. Of the eight routes that cross the Taihang range from east to west, the fifth, the Niangzi Pass, links Shijiazhuang directly to Taiyuan in Shanxi.
The prefecture is made up of several types of area. The mountainous part includes:
Jingxing Mining District
Jingxing County
Zanhuang County
Xingtang County
Lingshou County
Yuanshi County
Luquan District
Further east, the Hutuo River basin takes in:
Xinle City
Wuji County
Shenze County
Jinzhou City
Gaocheng District
Gaoyi County
Zhao County
Luancheng District
Zhengding County
The urban core and its suburbs make up the rest.

The climate is continental and shaped by the monsoon, with semi-arid conditions (Köppen BSk / Dwa). Summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon. Winters are cold, windy and very dry because the Siberian anticyclone dominates. Spring can bring sandstorms from the Mongolian steppe, along with fast warming and dry air, and autumn is much like spring in temperature and in how little rain falls.

The figures give a clearer picture. The January mean is −1.4 °C (29.5 °F), the July mean 27.7 °C (81.9 °F), and over the whole year the mean is 14.3 °C (57.7 °F). Sunshine, as a share of what is possible, varies between 38 percent (July) and 56 percent (May), and 2,163 hours accumulate across a year. More than half of the year's rain falls in July and August alone. Since 1951 the coldest reading has been −26.5 °C (−15.7 °F), on 12 January 1951, and the hottest 42.9 °C (109.2 °F), on 15 July 2002. In practice, pack for real winter cold and for hot summers.

This is a topic every prospective student should read about honestly. Shijiazhuang has long had a name for badly polluted air. It belongs to the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, where heavy industry burns a great deal of energy. Research released in January 2013 by Tsinghua University together with the Asian Development Bank put it among the ten most polluted cities in the world. The province overall ranks among the worst-affected parts of China, and a February 2013 survey by Global Voices China found that seven of the ten worst cities in the country were in Hebei, Shijiazhuang among them.

In December 2013 a dense smog covered much of central and eastern China across roughly 1,200 kilometres (750 mi), and Shijiazhuang lay inside it. Cold air hardly moved, while sluggish air masses full of industrial emissions let pollutants pile up in a thick layer. Officials pointed to the lack of wind, vehicle exhaust under low air pressure and the coal-fired district heating used across northern China. The prevailing winds pushed low-lying air full of factory emissions, mostly SO2, towards the east coast.

Pollution peaked in 2014, when the annual average PM2.5 reading reached 94 μg/m3, almost 19 times what the World Health Organization recommends. The State Council's national air pollution action plan of 2013 singled out the wider Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, and the government's "War on pollution" gave the effort momentum. By 2023 the annual average had dropped to 42 μg/m3, a fall of 54.8% from the 2014 record. That is still roughly 8.5 times the guideline level, so the situation has improved a great deal but has not disappeared.

Shijiazhuang grew mainly because migrants arrived from all over China. In 1947 it had 120,000 residents; the Chinese Communist Party captured it from the Kuomintang that year, making it the first medium-to-large city to change hands in this way. By the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 the urban population had more than doubled, to over 270,000. It reached 320,000 in 1953, when China began its first five-year plan, and 650,000 in 1960. A further jump came in 1968, when the city was made capital of Hebei so as to avoid disorder in Baoding during the Cultural Revolution. One million urban residents were passed by 1980, which made it a large city, and at the end of 2017 it exceeded 4.5 million. In only six decades the city's population has grown more than twenty-fold.
At the end of 2009 the registered (non-migrant) population was 9,774,100, which was 109,300 more than a year earlier. The birth rate stood at 14.65%, deaths at 6.25%, giving 8.4% natural growth.

The sixth national census in 2010 counted 10,163,788 registered residents, up by 818,365 people (8.76%, or 0.84% yearly on average) from the fifth census a decade earlier. Men numbered 5,087,913 (50.06%) and women 5,075,875 (49.94%), a ratio of 100.24 men to 100 women. People aged 0 to 14 totalled 1,548,125 (15.23%), those aged 15 to 64 totalled 7,789,753 (76.64%) and those aged 65 and over totalled 825,910 (8.13%).

Surnames are concentrated: Zhang is the most common at 10.27%, followed by Wang (9.25%), then Li (9.17%) and Liu (6.73%). Next come Zhao at 4.28% and Yang at 2.82%, and the top ten close with Gao (2.08%), Chen (1.92%), Ma (1.77%) and Guo (1.55%).

One curiosity: in May 2011 (the 6th) the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences issued its Blue Book on urban competitiveness in China. A happiness survey of 294 Chinese cities in it concluded that Shijiazhuang's residents were the happiest, a result that many internet users openly doubted.

Shijiazhuang's GDP in 2014 was CN¥510.02 billion (about $80.45 billion), 12 percent more than the year before, which ranked it 20th among provincial capitals. The city is a major industrial centre in North China and, together with Tangshan, is regarded as the economic heart of Hebei. It also lies in the Beijing-Tianjin-Shijiazhuang Hi-Tech Industrial Belt, one of China's main high-technology corridors.

Shijiazhuang is nicknamed the "medicine hub of China" because large pharmaceutical firms and factories are based here, for example the North China Pharmaceutical Group Corporation, plus Shijiazhuang Pharma Group and Shineway Pharma. Textiles are another pillar of local commerce. Machinery, chemicals (Shijiazhuang Donghua Jinlong is one name), building materials, light industry and electronics make up the rest. The surrounding countryside is rich in farmland: 590,000 hectares are cultivated, and the area supplies most of the province's cotton, pears, dates and walnuts.

Trade figures from 2008 show imports of US$1.393 billion, up 42.1 percent on the previous year, and exports rose by 34.9 percent, reaching US$5.596 billion. A 2006 World Bank report noted that the city spent under RMB400 per head on education, compared with RMB1,044 in Beijing and RMB1,631 in Weihai.

The Shijiazhuang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone was founded in March 1991 as a state-level zone and is split into three districts, crossed by national highways 107, 207, 307 and 308. It lies 15 km (9.3 mi) from Shijiazhuang railway station and 105 km (65 mi) from Tianjin Port. Industry here is a mix: pharmaceuticals, electronic information, machine building, cars, chemicals and logistics.

The Eastern District, in the east of the city, has an area of 5.8 km2 (2.2 sq mi) and is the zone's principal section, aimed at starting new high-tech companies. An enlargement to 9.8 km2 (3.8 sq mi) is planned. A railway line run by the Shijiazhuang Oil Refinery crosses it from north to south, so firms there can build their own connecting lines.

The Western District, in the southwest, spans 8.2 km2 (3.2 sq mi) and concentrates on small and medium-sized technology firms and technology incubation. Beside it, Liangcun District has 4 km2 (1.5 sq mi) and specialises in the pharmaceutical and petrochemical industries.

About 2,600 enterprises had moved into the zone by 2009, and 185 had foreign funding. Investors came from Japan and the US, from the Republic of Korea, Germany, Italy and Canada, and from Malaysia, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan.

hebei-university-of-economics-and-busine.h: The dairy trade and the 2008 milk scandal

blocks.x: Shijiazhuang is a centre of the dairy business and was the home of the Sanlu Group. Sanlu led China's infant formula sales for 15 years in a row, which made it the biggest taxpayer in the city. The writer Richard McGregor, in his book on the Communist Party's hidden world, called Sanlu an invaluable asset for a city that otherwise struggled to draw in industry and investment on the scale of China's leading metropolises.

The 2008 Chinese milk scandal hit both the dairy trade and Sanlu hard. Sanlu's chairman and general manager were reportedly removed, as were several Party officials, among them Zhang Fawang, the vice-mayor responsible for food and agriculture. Mayor Ji Chuntang reportedly resigned on 17 September 2008.
The Shitai Expressway passes through the city, as do the Beijing–Shenzhen and Taiyuan–Cangzhou routes.

Three railways cross at Shijiazhuang, which makes it a hub: Beijing–Guangzhou, Taiyuan–Dezhou and Shuozhou–Huanghua. Its new main station, opened in December 2012, is unusual because the old Beijing–Guangzhou line and the new Hong Kong-bound high-speed line (Beijing–Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong) both stop there. This is uncommon in China, where high-speed tracks usually skirt city centres and leave the old stations to conventional trains.

To bring high-speed trains into the middle of Shijiazhuang, builders dug a 5 km (3.1 mi) tunnel beneath the city, the first time a Chinese high-speed railway has run under a city. A smaller station, Shijiazhuang North, handles westbound trains to Taiyuan so they need not pass through downtown.
Three metro lines (1, 2 and 3) run today, with 76.5 km (47.5 mi) of track. The current plan calls for six lines in all.

Shijiazhuang Zhengding International Airport, about 30 kilometres northeast of the city, is Hebei's main air hub. It has 32 domestic routes, to places such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Dalian, and 12 international destinations, four of them in Russia. The airport is being enlarged so that it can act as a back-up to Beijing Capital International Airport. The airport also got a station of its own when the Beijing–Guangzhou High-Speed Railway began operating late in 2012, giving a fast but infrequent train link to Shijiazhuang railway station and other stops in the region.

The city is flat, and most big roads have a separate cycle lane, which makes cycling a natural choice. Thousands of people ride every day, and at many crossroads cyclists outnumber cars. Like Beijing, Shijiazhuang has roads running strictly north–south and east–west, so it is easy to find your way around.

In the heart of the city stands the Hebei Museum, which underwent refurbishment across 2013 and 2014. It runs regular events, mostly on traditional Chinese art and artefacts. The Yutong International Sports Centre hosts matches of the football club Shijiazhuang Ever Bright and also stages pop concerts.

Shijiazhuang Zoo is on the western edge and keeps 3,000 animals from 250 species. Visitors can see pandas, white tigers and Manchurian tigers, golden monkeys and chimpanzees, Indian elephants, giraffes, kangaroos, seals, springboks and flamingos. Close by are the Botanical Gardens (石家庄植物园), where you can see and buy exotic and native plants. In the city centre the Martyrs Memorial (烈士纪念馆) honours soldiers killed in war.

The downtown area has a good range of green space. The biggest park, Chang'an Park (长安公园), is in the centre and contains a lake, a theatre, a museum, bars and restaurants, with a shopping mall underground. Century Park (世纪公园), in the southeast, has a lake at its centre and an amusement park on the northern side. Water Park (水上公园), in the northwest, offers a large lake, rides, short walks and various restaurants. Smaller parks are scattered across the city as well.
Film fans may know the city from An Elephant Sitting Still, an arthouse feature from 2018 directed by Hu Bo, which was both filmed and set here.
Hebei University of Economics and Business lists 17 programs for international students on this site: 10 bachelor, 7 master's programs.

By language of instruction: 17 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 14,000 (median CNY 14,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 22,600 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.

17 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hebei-university-of-economics-and-busine.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hebei University of Economics and Business may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shijiazhuang, register at Hebei University of Economics and Business by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

HEBUT, the Hebei University of Technology (河北工业大学, which translates as 'Hebei Industrial University'), is a public university run at provincial level. One thing to notice immediately is that its home is the city of Tianjin, not Hebei Province itself. Hebei Province is its parent, and the cost is shared by the Hebei Provincial Government, the Tianjin Municipal Government and the Ministry of Education. National programs that include it are Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme.

The student body is about 23,000 undergraduates and 7,500 postgraduates, supported by 1,940 academic staff by one count. Elsewhere the university gives larger staffing figures, covered below, so use its own website for current numbers.

hebei-university-of-technology.h: From an imperial school to a modern university

blocks.x: HEBUT's origins are unusually old. It was Yuan Shikai who founded the school, and in 1903 the Guangxu Emperor approved it by royal charter under the name Peiyang Technological School (sources also write Beiyang Technical School). Zhou Xuexi served as the first president (总办). Designed after well-known universities in Europe and America, the school hoped to revive China by teaching qualified people the new science and technology. A restructuring in 1958 brought the name Hebei Institute of Technology, and the present title, Hebei University of Technology, was adopted in 1995.
The full chain of names is long, so here is the timeline in three periods.

Between 1903 and 1949 there were four names. The first, in 1903, was Beiyang Technical School. After that came Zhili Higher School of Technology (1904), Hebei Provincial Technological Institute (1929) and Hebei Provincial Institute of Technology (1946).

The years from 1949 to 1993 were the most turbulent. In 1950 the name became Hebei Institute of Technology, but a year later the school joined Beiyang University, and together they became Tianjin University. The institute was re-established in 1958 under its Hebei name. Then, in 1962, three other Tianjin schools (Mechanical and Electrical Engineering, Chemical Technology, and Construction and Engineering) were merged with it to make the Tianjin Institute of Technology, until the Hebei Institute of Technology name came back in 1971.

The modern era opened in 1995 with the new name. In 1996 the university was listed among the first key universities of what was then the national Project 211, and it carried out all three stages of that project's construction successfully.

The main campus is in Tianjin, and its areas are called Beichen, Hongqiao South and Hongqiao East. Each offers many amenities and student housing. Equipment for teaching and research is valued at 372 million RMB, and 1.88 million books fill the library on the Beichen campus.

There is a European connection too. In partnership with LUT (Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology) in Finland, HEBUT hosts English-language bachelor's programs at two Finnish campuses, one in Lappeenranta and the other in Lahti.

In all, 69 bachelor's programs are offered, as well as master's and doctoral study. They are generally taught in Chinese, and the main fields are engineering, design and business. There is also a one-semester Chinese language program that leads to no degree, useful if your Chinese needs work first. Chinese law and politics can be studied as well. If you want to study in English, ask the international office what is currently offered, including the Finnish option above.

In another count the university has 2,474 faculty members, with 1,365 of them full-time teachers. Senior professional titles are held by 706 of the teachers and doctorates by 682. The university also runs a national team of technology experts, five provincial teaching teams, three teaching teams at state level, and two innovative research teams in cooperation with the Ministry of Education.

For research, the university has 17 provincial-level institutes along with a laboratory and an engineering research center. A qualification for military research followed the creation of its National Defense and Science Institute. Work is accepted from the Chinese government and from private firms looking for product development or theoretical research.

HEBUT says it takes international cooperation seriously and works to expand and improve educational exchanges and build their reputation. Under a Chinese government project it is qualified to give scholarships to international students. Partner universities are in over 60 countries and regions: examples are Japan, Finland, Great Britain, Australia, Italy, Russia, Germany, the United States and France, as well as Hong Kong and Taiwan. More than 20 exchange programs are currently running. They have hosted 500 international students on non-degree study and have sent over 800 HEBUT students overseas.

Two well-known graduates are Jia Qinglin, who chaired the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, and Wang Xuejun, who governed Anhui Province. Among past teachers is the artist and art teacher Li Shutong.

hebei-university-of-technology.h: Tianjin as a place to study

blocks.x: What daily life looks like depends on the city around the campus. This section covers Tianjin: where it is, the weather, the air, the economy, the people, and what to see.

Tianjin faces the Bohai Gulf from its western shore, with Shandong and Liaoning provinces across the water. The capital, Beijing, is 120 kilometres (75 mi) to the northwest. Hebei Province surrounds the municipality except along the east, where the Bohai Sea is the boundary. Geographically it covers latitudes 38° 34' to 40° 15' N and longitudes 116° 43' to 118° 04' E, and its total area is 11,860.63 square kilometres (4,579.41 sq mi).

The municipality has a coastline of 153 km and land borders totalling 1,137.48 km. It marks the northern end of the Grand Canal of China, a waterway that connects to the Yellow and Yangtze rivers. Most of the land is flat, and swampy near the sea, with tidal flats along the coastal plain beside the city. Hills appear only in the north, where the Yan Mountains extend into the municipality. The summit of Jiuding Peak (九顶山), in Ji County on the Hebei border, is the highest spot at 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft).

Several rivers come together to make the Hai River: the Ziya (子牙河), the Daqing (大清河), the Yongding and the North and South Grand Canals. It runs to the sea inside the municipality, through Tanggu District. There are two large reservoirs: Beidagang, in Dagang District in the south, and Yuqiao, in Ji County in the north.

Tianjin's climate is classed as semi-arid, BSk in the Köppen system, with borders on Dwa and Cwa. Like much of East Asia it follows a monsoon pattern of four seasons. The Siberian anticyclone makes winter cold, dry and windy, and the monsoon season makes summer hot and humid. Spring is dry and windy, and sandstorms that originate in the Gobi Desert sometimes arrive and linger for days.

January's 24-hour average is -2.8 °C and July's is 27.2 °C (27.0 °F and 81.0 °F), and the annual mean is 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). The main weather station in Xiqing District has logged a low of -22.9 °C (-9 °F) and a high of 41.1 °C (106 °F). Sunshine as a percentage of the possible amount is lowest in July (45%) and highest in March and April (61%); in total the city gets 2,460 hours a year.

Yearly rainfall is 521 millimetres (20.5 in), and July and August together bring close to three-fifths of it. Overall this places the city in the semi-arid zone, even if some parts of the municipality count as humid continental.

New laws came in May 2014 to bring pollution down. For days when pollution is severe, the city can halve the number of vehicles on the road, stop construction and manufacturing, close schools and cancel big outdoor events. Flights have been grounded and highways shut in the past as well.

Some foreign professional sportsmen have complained about the air, saying it gets in the way of training and is so thick that you can 'taste' it. If you like to run or play sport outdoors, check the air quality first.

Major industries are petrochemicals, textiles, automobiles, mechanical engineering and metalworking. Airbus (EADS) makes airliners here: its assembly plant for the A320 series has been running since 2009. In 2010 the Tianhe-1A, then the world's fastest supercomputer, was installed at the National Supercomputing Center of Tianjin (rankings change, so this is dated). Tianjin's 2009 GDP was ¥750.1 billion, or RMB ¥62,403 per head.
Several special zones account for much of this activity, and the sections below describe them.

TEDA, the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area, was among the first economic and technological development zones at state level, set up on 6 December 1984 with the State Council's approval. Preferential national policies support its job of attracting domestic and foreign investment into modern, technology-driven industries. Its Administrative Commission is attached to the Tianjin Municipal Government and governs TEDA for it, holding provincial-level powers over administration and economic management.

The Tianjin Export Processing Zone was approved on 27 April 2000 as one of the first 15 such zones in China. It is a special enclosed area where Customs staff continuously supervise whatever goes in or out, and the central government gave it preferential policies to draw in processing and trading firms. It lies northeast of TEDA, with a planned area of 2.54 km2, and a permanent wall divides the zone from the outside. (One published description gives the first-phase area as only one square metre, which is obviously wrong, so check the official figure if it matters to you.)

Tianjin Binhai International Airport and the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone jointly invested in the Airport International Logistics Zone, which is inside the airport's air cargo area. Airfreight companies from China and abroad operate there, sorting, storing, distributing and processing goods and holding exhibitions. The zone is working toward the biggest air cargo hub in northern China.

Northern China's only free trade zone is the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone, approved by the State Council in 1991. It is 30 km from the centre of Tianjin, under 1 km from the wharf and 38 km from the airport.

The Marine High-Tech Development Area at Tanggu began in 1992, and in 1995 the State Council raised it to a national high-tech zone. No other national zone focuses on marine technology. By the end of 2008 it was home to 2,068 corporations in five industries, such as new materials, oil, modern machinery and electronic information.

The Nangang Industrial Zone is a heavy and chemical industry base and port. It forms part of Tianjin's 'dual-city, dual-harbor' strategy and is meant to be a circular-economy area. Of its 200 km2 planned area, 162 km2 is land.

Finally, the Binhai New Area (TBNA) stands where the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt meets the Circum-Bohai City Belt. It is the gateway to North China, Northeast China and Northwest China, in the middle of Northeast Asia, and is the nearest starting point for the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

Farmland covers around 40% of the municipality, and the crops that matter most economically are wheat, rice and maize. Under the ground lie roughly 1 billion tonnes of petroleum, with oilfields in Dagang District, and salt is produced too, notably in the Changlu Yanqu area, one of China's salt regions. Geothermal energy is a further resource, and the manganese and boron deposits here were the first found in China. Tianjin Electric Power Utility builds, delivers and maintains the electricity supply.

Counting the end of 2009, Tianjin had 12.28 million inhabitants. About 9.8 million of them held Tianjin hukou, meaning permanent residence, and lived there; among permanent residents, 5.99 million were urban and 3.81 million rural. Recently the population has started to grow, reaching 14.72 million by the end of 2013, and the OECD put the larger metropolitan area at 15.4 million in 2010. These numbers are dated, so look for current statistics, and note that active-duty People's Liberation Army members are not counted.
Han Chinese are the majority. Tianjin is home to people from 51 of China's 55 minority groups, with the Hui, Koreans, Manchus and Mongols being the larger communities.

Visitors see a blend of European buildings from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and modern Chinese concrete-and-glass structures. Redevelopment is continuing, yet a lot of the colonial architecture enjoys protection.

Tianjin's European flavour has a history. During the nineteenth century foreign powers captured the port city following an argument about a British ship, when armed gunboats overcame Chinese forces. Under the Treaty of Tianjin (1856), nine concession areas on the Hai River were opened to Europeans for trade and the opium business. Each enclave was self-contained, with French châteaus and towers in one and German red-tiled Bavarian villas in another. In 1870 the Tianjin Incident broke out at a French orphanage, and in 1900, during the Boxer Rebellion, foreigners demolished the old city walls to keep an eye on the population.

In 2000 and 2001 most of the old city was pulled down, leaving just a few historic buildings such as the Tianjin Temple of Confucius. Tourists now head for the old concession streets, which lie south of the Hai River and also south and west of the central station. The French châteaus fill the downtown area south of the river, British mansions stand to the east, and German-style buildings survive farther east and south.

The municipality has three national nature reserves. Baxianshan has kept most of its original forest ecosystem because people have hardly disturbed it for a very long time. In Jizhou District, the Middle-Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve is accepted by the International Union of Geological Sciences as a global standard stratigraphic section. The Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve features three typical shell ridges, which show clearly how the plain changed from seabed to dry land as the sea retreated.

There are two World Cultural Heritage sites: a stretch of the Great Wall at Huangyaguan, in the north of Jizhou District, and the Tianjin part of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal. Ancient Culture Street, a national 5A tourist attraction, is built around the Tianhou Temple, the oldest surviving group of historic buildings in the city and a major northern site of Mazu culture. Yangliuqing Town is known for Yangliuqing New Year Paintings and holds the title 'China Historical and Cultural Town'.

In the city centre, the banks of the Haihe River show traditional Chinese, European and modern styles mixed together, which together give the city its own character. The river's 'one bridge, one scene' night lighting has become a landmark and, during major events such as the World Economic Forum, a top attraction for international guests. Time magazine named the Tianjin Binhai Library, in Binhai New Area, number one among its World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018, in August of that year.

The city's museum history starts in the late Qing reform era. A French Jesuit priest and naturalist, Émile Licent, founded the Musée Hoangho Paiho in 1914. It was among the earliest museums in China and made a major contribution to paleontology, geology, archaeology and museology.

Three museums hold national first-class status today. The Tianjin Museum, a general museum of history and art, descends from a Tianjin Museum founded in 1918. The Tianjin Natural History Museum is big and multidisciplinary, covering zoology, botany, paleontology and geology, and it grew out of Licent's Musée Hoangho Paiho. The third is the Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall, at Water Park, which commemorates Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People's Republic, and his wife Deng Yingchao, both of whom studied in Tianjin in their youth.

China's first comprehensive, national maritime museum meant for the public, the National Maritime Museum of China, opened in May 2019 in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City. Other specialised halls include the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall.

Tianjin has been improving its city parks and squares gradually since 2008 and has dropped entrance fees so everyone can walk in freely. In the urban area they include Water Park, the zoo, Nancuiping, Shuixi (which opened officially in October 2018), Meijiang, Ergong, Zhongshan, Hedong and Xigu parks, as well as Beining, Haihe Music, Central, People's and Five Great Avenues parks. Beining Park began as a plantation created in 1906 by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi; it was later renamed 'Ningyuan' after its motto, 'Without tranquility, one cannot reach far.' Parks in Binhai New Area include Haihe Bund, Taifeng, Ziyun, East Embankment, Shell Ridge Wetland, Aircraft Carrier and Haigang parks, together with South Embankment Coastal Trail Park.

A further 16 suburban parks have been planned and built since 2011, spread around the city and Binhai New Area. They have more natural scenery and a rural feel than the city parks. In 2012 construction started on Beiyunhe Suburban Park in the north and Xiqing Suburban Park in the southwest, and by 2014 all 16 fell inside the ecological redline, with a total core area of 66,855 hectares.

Street lighting first appeared in 1902, and the lit-up streets of the 1930s won the city the nickname 'Northern City That Never Sleeps.' Today the night lighting is part of formal urban planning. In central districts it follows a 'fishbone' design, with the Haihe River and its continuations, the North Canal and South Canal, as the spine and smaller roads as the ribs. The Haihe night view is a prime tourist route and has featured in the Summer Davos Forum, the 13th National Games and the SCO Tianjin Summit.
One school is also worth mentioning for local colour: Tianjin No. 7 Middle School.
Hebei University of Technology lists 54 programs for international students on this site: 7 bachelor, 8 master's, 5 doctoral, 34 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 34 taught in English, 20 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 22,000), according to the university's published fee table.

54 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
