Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hebei-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hebei University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Tianjin, register at Hebei University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hefei University (HU, 合肥大学, Héféi Dàxué) is a higher education institution in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province. It began in 1980 as Hefei Union University (合肥联合大学), founded by Yang Chengzong (杨承宗), a nuclear chemist. In 2002 it combined with two other schools, Hefei Normal School and Hefei Education College, and the merged institution took the name Hefei University.

The university has 16 departments, 5 research centres and a further education college, and it offers 40 bachelor's degree programmes. Its full-time student population was 12,527 as of December 2007, which is a dated figure worth checking with the university. Teaching takes place on two campuses: the Downtown Campus (also called the Huangshan Road Campus) and the campus beside Nanyanhu Lake. Engineering, economics and management are its strongest areas, and it also covers literature, science and education are covered as well. The party secretary at the time of the source was Cai Jingming and the president was Wang Qidong.

HU's vision centres on three words: "regionalization, practicability and internationalization". Its purpose is to serve the regional economy, and its guiding idea is to "nurture students with morality through a practical curriculum and teaching methods". It has consistently pushed teaching reform so that graduates leave with practical competence and skills for work.

Two features stand out for a prospective student. The first is the "N+2 Assessment System", introduced in recent years, under which students are judged on their learning during the course as well as on the final exams of each semester. The second is the "9-Semester System", designed so that sophomores spend one full semester on field learning before returning to academic study, to build the problem-solving skills needed in a professional career.

HU has exchange programmes with universities and institutions around the world. Since the early 1980s it has worked with Germany on faculty training, student exchange and joint development of some departments. It now has 9 sister universities in Germany, mostly universities of applied sciences, which matches its practical mission. Student exchange and staff training have expanded, and since 2000 some dual degree programmes have been added. Similar programmes with South Korea began in the late 1990s, and it has 7 sister universities there, with student and faculty exchanges and dual degree programmes covering language, Computer Science, Tourism Management and the teaching of Chinese.

About 50 foreign students are admitted each year to learn Chinese language and culture. Joint workshops, internships and thesis writing are also arranged on campus for international students from sister universities. The university has hosted seminars with an international audience on education, rural development, tourism management and environmental protection, with guests from Germany, Korea, Japan, Singapore and elsewhere. Apart from the German and Korean partners, universities in Austria, Britain, Spain, Thailand and the United States also cooperate with it. Every year the university recruits professors from Australia, Canada, Germany, Japan, Korea and the United States to teach and carry out research on campus.

As an example of China-Germany cooperation, German Chancellor Angela Merkel visited Hefei University on 30 October 2015, during her eighth trip to China. Chinese Premier Li Keqiang, who is from Hefei, accompanied her.

hefei-university.h: Hefei as a place to live

blocks.x: Student life depends on the surrounding city: its weather, how you get around and what you can do. The sections below describe Hefei and then the province of Anhui.

Hefei lies 130 kilometres (81 miles) to the west of Nanjing, in the south-central part of Anhui. Chao Lake, which lies 15 km (9 miles) to the southeast, is among China's biggest freshwater lakes. In recent decades nitrogen and phosphorus pollution has unfortunately affected it, although efforts by both government and residents are improving the situation.

Hefei has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), and its four seasons are clearly distinct. Over a year, the average temperature is 16.6 °C (61.9 °F). Annual precipitation is a little over 1,000 millimetres (39 inches), heaviest from May to August.

Winters are damp and cold. January lows dip just below freezing and the month averages 2.8 °C (37.0 °F). Snow falls irregularly and rarely becomes significant. Cold spells from Siberia usually arrive in December, January and February, and sometimes in November and March, and they can bring snow and heavier snowfall. Spring is generally mostly agreeable, though erratic. Summer is hot and humid: July averages 28.6 °C (83.5 °F), and across June, July and August, and frequently in September too, daytime temperatures may touch or exceed 37 °C (99 °F) while humidity stays high as the norm. Autumn brings gradual cooling and drying.

Possible sunshine runs between 35 percent (March) and 50 percent (August), giving 1,868 hours of bright sun in a year. Since 1951 the temperature has gone from a low of −20.6 °C (−5 °F), logged 6 January 1955, to a high of 41.1 °C (106 °F), logged 27 July 2017.

Air quality usually gets worse in May and June, when smog covers the city. It comes from smoke created by farmers outside the city who burn their fields to prepare for the next crop. If you have respiratory sensitivities, plan for this period.

As of 2021, Hefei's GDP was CN¥1,141.28 billion, and GDP per capita was ¥121,187 (US$18,784), within the top 20 of Chinese cities. In 2023 GDP reached CN¥1,267.38 billion. In 2025 the city produced 1.37 million electric vehicles, nearly one in every 12 made in China.

Hefei's city government takes an active part in business, through state-owned enterprises and direct investment. This approach has helped fuel growth and reshape the city's economic base. Three examples show how it works:

The local government paid US$3.5 billion in 2008 on a controlling stake in BOE Technology (Jingdongfang). BOE later became one of the world's leading makers of semiconductor products for telecommunications, and also the biggest producer of liquid crystal displays, organic light-emitting diodes and flexible displays anywhere. BOE runs three production lines in Hefei (as of at least 2024), and its presence has helped the city draw more of the electronics supply chain and become one of China's main centres of the optoelectronic industry.
Also that year Hefei put large investment into iFlytek, a voice-recognition company spun off from USTC.

The local government invested heavily in NIO to combine it with Hefei Changan Automobile, an older enterprise left over from the Third Front construction. NIO was close to bankruptcy in 2020 when Hefei took a 25% stake in return for RMB 7 billion. NIO then moved its headquarters to Hefei, and the government helped it get local bank loans to grow its supply chains. By 2022 NIO was China's most successful electric vehicle maker. The local government has also invested in ChangXin Memory Technologies, the biggest DRAM maker in China and fourth biggest globally.

hefei-university.h: How others see the city's growth

blocks.x: The Economist Intelligence Unit's November 2010 Access China White Paper listed Hefei among a group called CHAMPS, which consists of Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Ma'anshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang and forms part of a profile of 20 leading emerging Chinese cities. In December 2012 The Economist named Hefei the world's fastest-growing metropolitan economy. The city has also backed the chip industry and has become one of the largest sites for manufacturing memory chips (DRAM).

hefei-university.h: Why it is a transport centre

blocks.x: The provincial capital since 1945 (Lihuang, which is today's Jinzhai, held that role earlier), Hefei. It is a natural transport centre. It lies north of Chao Lake on a low saddle across an extension of the Dabie Mountains running northeast, a range that divides the Huai and Yangtze rivers. Water transport is easy from the city via the lake to the Yangtze opposite Wuhu.

Two main stations serve Hefei. The newest is Hefei South railway station (Hefeinan, 合肥火车南站), through which most high-speed trains pass. The alternative, older and smaller, is Hefei railway station (合肥火车站). Smaller stations include Lujiang Station (庐江火车站), Hefeibeicheng Station (Hefei Northtown Station, 合肥北城火车站), Chaohu East railway station (Chaohudong; 巢湖火车东站), Chaohu Station (巢湖火车站), Shuijiahu Station (水家湖火车站), Feixi Station (肥西火车站) and Feidong Station (肥东火车站) These stations are mostly in small towns and link commuters with the main city.

The old Hefei Luogang International Airport was replaced by Hefei Xinqiao International Airport, which began operating at midnight on 30 May 2013. This domestic aviation hub is in Gaoliu Village, in the northwest of the city. Flight MU5172 of China Eastern Airlines, from Beijing Capital International Airport, was the first to arrive, and China Eastern MU5468 to Shanghai Pudong International Airport was the first to depart.

The airport has scheduled passenger service to major Chinese airports and to other international cities. The destinations listed are Hong Kong and Macao; Singapore; Taiwan (Taipei's Taoyuan and Songshan airports, Kaohsiung and Taichung); South Korea (Seoul, Cheongju, Yangyang and Jeju); Japan (Osaka, Nagoya, Shizuoka and Okayama); Frankfurt; and Southeast Asian leisure destinations including Bangkok, Siem Reap, Phuket, Krabi, Bali and Boracay. Routes change often, so check airline schedules.
The Hefei Metro was a rapid transit network under construction at the time of the source, planned eventually to serve both urban and rural areas.
Line 1: planned at 24 kilometres (15 miles) and starts from Hefei Railway Station. The line opened in December 2016.

Line 2: construction began in February 2013, along Changjiang Xi Road, Changjiang Zhong Road and Changjiang Dong Road, a major east-west passenger corridor. It passes through the city centre and links to a transfer point where passengers can take a shuttle bus to Hefei Xinqiao International Airport. It opened on 26 December 2017.

Line 3: construction began in November 2015, and it opened on 26 December 2019. It links the Economic Technology Development District with the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone, and runs between the vocational education town and the university town.
Line 4: construction began in 2016, and it opened on 26 December 2021. It links the High Technology Development District and the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone.

Line 5: construction began in 2017. The southern part opened on 26 December 2020, linking the Beicheng (North City) New District with Binhu New District. Its northern part was due to open by the end of 2022.

In addition to Lines 1 to 5, Hefei plans another a dozen more metro lines, four intra-metropolitan rail lines (to Lu'an, Huainan, Lujiang and Chaohu) and 3 tram lines, and hopes to finish by 2030. The source is not up to date, so check the current network map.
The public bus system is extensive and includes eight bus rapid transit lines. Some commuter lines run only at set times or with long gaps.
Hefei University sits in Anhui, and the surrounding region influences student life as much as the campus itself does. The sections below describe the province.

Anhui was established in 1667, when the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty was on the throne. Its nickname, "Wan", comes from a minor state that once existed there in the Spring and Autumn period (722 to 481 BC), and it also matches the province's Mount Tianzhu and the Wan state. Archaeological finds in Fanchang County show people living in what is now Anhui 20,000 years ago, linked to the Yangshao and Longshan cultural spheres of the Neolithic period (8000 to 2000 BC). In a 2013 excavation, archaeologists found a Neolithic city wall and moat at the Nanchengzi Ruins in Guzhen County, part of a much larger, integrated city about 4,500 years old.

The province has many historical sites from before imperial times. Northern Anhui's culture resembled that of the North China Plain, as did the cultures of today's Henan, northern Jiangsu and southern Shandong. Central Anhui, which was densely populated, covered the fertile Huai River watershed. In contrast, the south of Anhui lay nearer to Jiangxi and southern Jiangsu, and the hills of the southeast formed a distinct cultural sphere.

The Qin dynasty brought China together in 221 BC, and after that the land of modern Anhui belonged to several prefectures, including Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang and Sishui. During the Han dynasty (202 BC to 220 AD) it became part of Yang, Yu and Xu prefectures. In the Three Kingdoms era (222 to 280) it was dominated at different times by either Eastern Wu or Cao Wei. In the Song dynasty (960 to 1279) its economy and culture were flourishing. In the Yuan dynasty (1271 to 1368) it was part of Henan Province, and in the Ming dynasty it was governed directly from the imperial capital at Nanjing.

Under the Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912), Anhui and Jiangsu were one province until 1666, in the Kangxi Emperor's reign. Li Hongzhang led the Self-Strengthening Movement, in which Anhui had an important part in the later Qing, when Western weapons, factories and ideas about administration were brought into China. Over the next 50 years it became one of the most radically liberal parts of the country, and important figures of the 20th century moved there, such as Chen Duxiu, who founded the Chinese Communist Party, and Hu Shih, a poet and diplomat.

In 1938, President Chiang Kai-shek decided to destroy a vital dam on the Yellow River in the hope to hinder the Imperial Japanese Army's advance and stop it taking Zhengzhou. Large areas of northern and central Anhui were badly damaged. Within ten days of the dam breaking, water and sand drowned all of the north and middle of the province, killing an estimated 500,000 to 900,000 Chinese people, along with an unknown number of Japanese soldiers.

hefei-university.h: From capital move to rapid growth

blocks.x: After the Second Sino-Japanese War ended in 1945, the capital moved to Hefei, then a small town, and the provincial government invested significantly in its development. After 1949 the government started projects to repair wartime damage. Anhui was one of the provinces worst hit by the Great Chinese Famine. Through the Third Front campaign, which aimed to build basic and national defence industries in protected places against a possible invasion from the Soviet Union or the United States, the province developed considerably. The centrepiece of the Shanghai Small Third Front was a "rear base" located in Anhui, characterised as "a multi-function manufacturing base for anti-aircraft and anti-tank weaponry". By the late 1990s Anhui ranked among China's fastest-growing provinces, and it forms part of the Yangtze River Delta Economic Area of China, the most developed region of China.

Anhui has varied terrain. The north belongs to the North China Plain, and the north-central parts to the Huai River watershed. Both are flat and densely populated. Further south the land becomes more uneven, with the Dabie Mountains across much of the southwest and a series of hills and ranges across the southeast, with the Yangtze River running between them. The highest peak is Lotus Peak, part of Huangshan in the southeast, at 1,873 metres (6,145 feet).

The main rivers are the Huai in the north, the Yangtze in the south. Lake Chaohu, in central Anhui, is the largest lake, and measures about 800 km² (310 sq mi). The southeast near the Yangtze also has many lakes.

Climate varies from north to south as well. The northern part is more temperate with sharper seasonal contrasts. In January the average is roughly −1 to 2 °C north of the Huai River and 0 to 3 °C on its south side, while July averages are 27 °C or above. Plum rains in June and July can cause flooding.
The province is divided into 16 cities, and the three leading economically are Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing.

Agriculture depends on the climate zone: wheat and sweet potatoes are grown north of the Huai River, and rice and wheat in the south. In 2022 the nominal GDP of Anhui was US$670 billion (CN¥4.51 trillion), about 3.72% of China's GDP, ranking 10th among province-level units. By sector, primary industry made CN¥351.37 billion (US$52.24 billion), secondary industry CN¥1.8588 trillion (US$276.36 billion) and tertiary industry CN¥2.29433 trillion (US$341.1 billion). GDP per head, nominal, was US$10,943 (CN¥73,603), 14th in the country.

The province has Tongling has copper, Huainan has coal and Ma'anshan has iron, with related industries such as the steel industry at Ma'anshan. A well-known Anhui company is the automaker Chery, based in Wuhu.

Anhui has lagged markedly behind its more prosperous eastern neighbours, Zhejiang and Jiangsu. In 2017 its GDP per capita was around half that of those two provinces, a sharp improvement from one third in 2010. However, provincial GDP per capita is calculated on the population registered in the province (those with a local hukou), not necessarily those who actually live there. There is large regional inequality, and a large part of the wealth sits in industrial areas along the Yangtze, among them Hefei, Wuhu and Ma'anshan. The province also has a large cluster of white goods makers, including Haier, Hisense, Whirlpool, Gree, Royalstar and Meling.
France assisted the Anhui Provincial Tourism Bureau in 2008 with a demonstration project for rural tourism.

hefei-university.h: Putting it together for an applicant

blocks.x: Hefei University is a mid-sized, applied-focus institution with two campuses and a clear emphasis on practical learning, shown by its field-learning semester and its many partnerships with German universities of applied sciences. The city around it is one of China's quickest-growing economies, with strong electric vehicle, display, chip and voice-technology industries that the city government has backed directly. Hefei is a provincial capital with fast trains to Nanjing, Shanghai and beyond, a modern airport and a growing metro.

Points to plan for are the humid summers that can pass 37 °C, a cold, damp winter, and the smoggy spell in May and June. If you are interested in exchange or dual degree routes, the German and Korean links are the ones to ask about. Always check the university's own pages for current enrolment figures, tuition and visa advice.

Hefei University of Technology, usually abbreviated HFUT (合肥工业大学), is a public university in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province. It answers to the Ministry of Education, and the money for it comes jointly from the ministry, the provincial government of Anhui, SASTIND and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. It takes part in the Double First-Class Construction programme and in Project 211.
The student body is large: the university currently enrols 29,480 undergraduates and 11,800 graduate students.

HFUT has four campuses, called Tunxilu, Lu'anlu, Feicuihu and Xuancheng, which together cover about 3,417,390 square metres. Three of them are in Hefei itself. The fourth is in Xuancheng, a city roughly 194 kilometres from Hefei, so it is a separate place rather than a suburb. Photographs of the university usually show the Tunxi Avenue campus and the Lake Emerald campus.
The Hefei campuses together house 19 schools covering many fields, with engineering at the centre of the university's identity. In figures:
82 undergraduate programmes
32 first-level disciplines authorised to award master's degrees
12 first-level disciplines for doctoral programmes, and 12 post-doctoral programmes
4 national key disciplines and 28 provincial key disciplines
1 state key laboratory and 1 national engineering laboratory
46 research centres at ministry or provincial level, and 4 national engineering research centres run jointly with industry
1 architectural design and research institute rated A-level nationally
The Xuancheng campus has 5 departments.

HFUT has a good record in educating students. Its main subject areas, courses, textbooks, experiment and teaching centres and teachers have all won prizes at various levels. In addition, HFUT belonged to the first batch of 61 pilot universities for a Ministry of Education programme called the Education and Development Plan for Outstanding Engineers. About 200 projects by HFUT students have received money from the National University Student Innovation Program.
On the research side, annual funding for scientific work in 2013 exceeded RMB 447 million. That year the university filed 357 applications for invention patents, and 204 had been granted.
The university lists its teaching units as follows. The grouping here is by theme, to make them easier to scan, and the exact English names may vary on the official site.

The daily life of a student depends on the city outside the campus: weather, transport and what is on offer. This part describes Hefei, where HFUT is situated.

hefei-university-of-technology.h: Position and the big lake nearby

blocks.x: Hefei lies in south-central Anhui, 130 kilometres (81 miles) west of Nanjing. About 15 km (9 miles) to the southeast is Chao Lake, among the largest freshwater lakes in China. In recent decades nitrogen and phosphorus have polluted the lake, a problem that is easing thanks to efforts by both the authorities and local people.

Four clear seasons define Hefei's humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa). Over a year the average temperature is 16.6 °C (61.9 °F), and slightly more than 1,000 millimetres (39 inches) of rain falls, with May to August the wettest months.

Winter: damp and cold. January lows fall just below freezing, and the January average is 2.8 °C (37.0 °F). Snowfall is irregular and seldom heavy. Cold spells from Siberia can arrive in December, January and February, and sometimes in November and March, bringing snow and occasionally heavier falls.
Spring: generally pleasant, if somewhat unpredictable.
Summer: sticky and hot. July averages 28.6 °C (83.5 °F), and from June to August, and frequently in September too, afternoons may touch or exceed 37 °C (99 °F) while humidity stays high.
Autumn: a gradual cooling and drying.

Sunshine as a share of possible hours runs from 35 per cent in March to 50 per cent in August, giving 1,868 hours of bright sunshine a year. The coldest reading since 1951 was −20.6 °C (−5 °F), recorded on 6 January 1955, and the hottest reading was 41.1 °C (106 °F), on 27 July 2017.

Air quality typically worsens in May and June. Farmers in the surrounding countryside set fire to their fields to prepare for the next crop, and the smoke settles over the city as smog. If you have asthma or other breathing problems, plan for that period.

Hefei's GDP was CN¥1,141.28 billion in 2021, equal to ¥121,187 (US$18,784) per person, which places the city in the top 20 in China on that measure. GDP then rose to CN¥1,267.38 billion by 2023. Output of electric vehicles in 2025 came to 1.37 million, nearly a twelfth of everything built nationwide.

Hefei's authorities take an unusually active part in business, working through state-owned enterprises and direct investment. This approach has driven growth and helped reshape the city's economic base. Several deals show how it works.

BOE Technology (Jingdongfang): in 2008 the municipal government bought a controlling share for US$3.5 billion. BOE has since become a leading global producer of semiconductor products for telecommunications and the biggest maker of LCD screens, OLED panels and flexible displays. BOE has had at least three production lines in Hefei since at least 2024, which has attracted other firms in the electronics supply chain and helped make Hefei one of China's main optoelectronics centres.
iFlytek: also in 2008 the city invested heavily in this voice-recognition company, which grew out of USTC.

NIO: the government put in large sums so that the electric-car maker could be combined with Hefei Changan Automobile, an older company from the Third Front construction era. In 2020, with NIO close to collapse, Hefei acquired a quarter of the company for RMB 7 billion. The firm then relocated its headquarters to the city, and the government helped it borrow from local banks to widen its supply chains. By 2022 NIO was China's most successful electric vehicle maker.
ChangXin Memory Technologies: the city also backed this DRAM producer, China's largest and the fourth-largest in the world.

hefei-university-of-technology.h: How outsiders have rated Hefei's growth

blocks.x: In its Access China White Paper of November 2010, the Economist Intelligence Unit listed Hefei in a group of six called CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Ma'anshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), part of a portrait of China's 20 leading emerging cities. In December 2012 The Economist described Hefei as the world's fastest-growing metropolitan economy. The city has also supported the chip industry and is now one of the largest centres for memory chip (DRAM) production.

The city became the provincial capital in 1945, replacing Lihuang, which today is Jinzhai. It is a natural crossroads. The city stands north of Chao Lake on a low saddle through the north-eastern extension of the Dabie Mountains, which divide the Huai and Yangtze river basins, and boats can travel easily from Hefei across the lake to the Yangtze opposite Wuhu.

Two main stations serve the city. The newer is Hefei South railway station (Hefeinan, 合肥火车南站), where most high-speed trains stop. The older and smaller one is Hefei railway station (合肥火车站). Smaller stations, mostly in small towns, link commuters to the main city. They include Feidong (肥东火车站), Feixi (肥西火车站), Shuijiahu (水家湖火车站), Chaohu (巢湖火车站), Chaohu East (Chaohudong, 巢湖火车东站), Hefeibeicheng (Hefei Northtown, 合肥北城火车站) and Lujiang (庐江火车站).

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport took over from the old Hefei Luogang International Airport on 30 May 2013 at midnight. The new domestic hub is in Gaoliu Village in the north-west of the city. The first flight to land was China Eastern Airlines MU5172 from Beijing Capital International Airport, and the first to take off was China Eastern MU5468 to Shanghai Pudong International Airport.

The airport has scheduled passenger services to the main airports in China and to some foreign cities. In East Asia the list takes in Hong Kong, Macao, Taipei (Taoyuan and Songshan), Kaohsiung and Taichung, and in Korea and Japan Seoul, Cheongju, Yangyang, Jeju, Osaka, Nagoya, Shizuoka and Okayama. Further afield there are flights to Singapore, Bangkok, Phuket, Krabi, Siem Reap, Bali, Boracay and Frankfurt.

Hefei Metro is a rapid transit network that is still being built and will eventually serve urban and rural parts of Hefei. The details below come from an older description, so check the current network map before you travel.
Line 1: designed to run 24 kilometres (15 miles) from Hefei Railway Station, and opened in December 2016.

Line 2: construction began in February 2013 along Changjiang East, Middle and West Roads, a major east-west passenger corridor. The route crosses the city centre and reaches an interchange, from which a shuttle bus goes to Hefei Xinqiao International Airport. It opened on 26 December 2017.

Line 3: construction began in November 2015 and it opened on 26 December 2019. It links the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone with the Economic Technology Development District, passing from the vocational education town on to the university town.
Line 4: construction began in 2016 and it opened on 26 December 2021, connecting the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone with the High Technology Development District.

Line 5: building started in 2017, and the southern part, which opened on 26 December 2020, joins Binhu New District to the new northern district of Beicheng. The northern section was expected at the end of 2022.
The plan goes well past these five lines: 12 more metro lines, three tram lines and four intra-metropolitan rail routes (serving Lu'an, Huainan, Lujiang and Chaohu), all hoped to be done by 2030.
The city has a wide public bus network, including eight bus rapid transit lines. Several commuter routes run only at set times or at long intervals.
The province in which a university sits has a strong effect on student life, so this part outlines Anhui.

The province dates to 1667, when the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty established it. The short name "Wan" is borrowed from a small state of the Spring and Autumn period (722 to 481 BC), and also matches Mount Tianzhu and the Wan state. Finds in Fanchang County prove that humans were living in the area 20,000 years ago, in cultural spheres connected to Yangshao and Longshan of the Neolithic (8000 to 2000 BC). In 2013 archaeologists dug up a Neolithic wall and moat belonging to a far larger integrated settlement, the 4,500-year-old Nanchengzi Ruins at Guzhen County.

Plenty of historic sites in Anhui come from the era before emperors. Culturally, the north was tied to the North China Plain, as were present-day Henan, northern Jiangsu and southern Shandong. The centre, with its fertile Huai River basin, supported a dense population. The south looked toward Jiangxi and southern Jiangsu, and the southeastern hills had a distinctive culture of their own.

Once Qin unified China in 221 BC, today's Anhui was divided among several prefectures, such as Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang and Sishui. By the Han dynasty (202 BC to 220 AD) it fell under the prefectures of Yang, Yu and Xu. During the Three Kingdoms era (222 to 280) Eastern Wu and Cao Wei each dominated it at various times. By the Song dynasty (960 to 1279) the local economy and culture were flourishing. Under the Yuan dynasty (1271 to 1368) Anhui became part of Henan province, and under the Ming the imperial capital at Nanjing administered it directly.

During the Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912) Anhui and Jiangsu were one province, a union that ended in 1666 under Kangxi. Late in the dynasty Anhui was central to the Self-Strengthening Movement under Li Hongzhang, an effort to import foreign weapons, factories and ideas about administration. In the following half-century the province became one of the most radical and liberal in China. Hu Shih, the poet and diplomat, and Chen Duxiu, who founded the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), were among the major twentieth-century figures who moved there.

In 1938 President Chiang Kai-shek ordered a critical Yellow River dam to be destroyed, hoping to slow the Imperial Japanese Army's advance and keep it from reaching Zhengzhou. Large parts of northern and central Anhui suffered severely. Within ten days, floodwater and silt covered the entire north and centre of the province. Estimates put the Chinese death toll between 500,000 and 900,000, and an unknown number of Japanese soldiers died as well.

After the Second Sino-Japanese War ended in 1945, the provincial capital moved to Hefei, which was then a small town, and the provincial government put substantial money into building it up. Repair projects for wartime damage were started by the government following 1949. The Great Chinese Famine hit Anhui harder than most provinces. Progress came through the Third Front campaign, which put basic and defence industry into sheltered locations as protection against a possible Soviet or American invasion; the heart of the Shanghai Small Third Front was an Anhui "rear base" described as a manufacturing base for anti-aircraft and anti-tank weapons with several functions. Towards the end of the 1990s the province's growth was among the fastest in China. It is today part of the Yangtze River Delta Economic Area, China's most developed zone.

Anhui's terrain is varied. The north belongs to the North China Plain, and the north-central part to the Huai River watershed. Both are flat and densely populated. Heading south, the terrain turns more uneven. The Dabie Mountains take up much of the south-west, while chains of hills cut across the south-east, and the Yangtze flows in between. Lotus Peak, in the Huangshan range of the south-east, is the highest summit at 1,873 metres (6,145 feet).

Of the major rivers, the Huai flows in the north and the Yangtze in the south. The province's largest lake, Lake Chaohu, lies at its centre and covers about 800 km2 (310 sq mi). The south-east, close to the Yangtze, has many lakes as well.

Climate changes from north to south just as the land does. Northern Anhui has a more temperate climate with sharper seasonal contrasts. January temperatures average roughly −1 to 2 °C above the Huai River and 0 to 3 °C below it, while July averages are 27 °C or higher. Plum rains in June and July can cause flooding.
The province has 16 cities, and economically the top three are Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing.

Farming follows the climate zones. North of the Huai River people grow wheat and sweet potatoes, while rice and wheat are grown to the south. For 2022 the province's nominal GDP reached US$670 billion (CN¥4.51 trillion). That was about 3.72 per cent of the national figure and put Anhui tenth among provincial-level units. Divided by sector, primary industry produced CN¥351.37 billion (US$52.24 billion), secondary industry CN¥1.8588 trillion (US$276.36 billion) and tertiary industry CN¥2.29433 trillion (US$341.1 billion). GDP per capita stood at US$10,943 (CN¥73,603), which ranked 14th nationwide.

Natural resources include iron at Ma'anshan, coal at Huainan and copper at Tongling, and related industries have grown up, such as the steel industry at Ma'anshan. A well-known company based in the province is the car maker Chery, which is in Wuhu.

Compared with its richer eastern neighbours, Zhejiang and Jiangsu, Anhui has lagged clearly in development. In 2017 its GDP per head was about half of theirs, up quickly from around a third in 2010. Note, though, that the provincial per-capita figure is based on people registered locally (with a local hukou), who do not always live there. Regional gaps are wide, with most prosperity concentrated in industrial areas along the Yangtze (Hefei, Wuhu and Ma'anshan, for example). A big cluster of household appliance manufacturers is also based here: Haier, Hisense, Whirlpool, Gree, Royalstar and Meling.

hefei-university-of-technology.h: Hefei Economic and Technological Development Zone

blocks.x: This zone lies in the south-west of Hefei and was set up in 1993. It is close to Hefei Luogang International Airport, the old airport that Xinqiao has since replaced.
France lent its support in 2008, assisting the Anhui Provincial Tourism Bureau as it developed a demonstration project for rural tourism.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hefei-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hefei University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hefei, register at Hefei University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

heihe-university.h: Heihe: a border city on the Amur

blocks.x: Heihe University is in the city of Heihe, in the far north of Heilongjiang Province, right on China's border with Russia. A student who comes here is choosing a very particular place: a frontier city with long, bitterly cold winters, a river crossing into another country and a regional economy built on farming, forestry and cross-border trade. This profile concentrates on that setting, since it shapes daily life as much as the classroom. For details of programmes, fees, teaching languages and admissions, consult the university's own website and international office.

Heihe stands on the south bank of the Amur River, directly across from Blagoveshchensk, the capital of Russia's Amur Oblast. The city's jurisdiction covers 54,390 square kilometres (21,000 square miles) between longitudes 124°45′ and 129°18′ east and latitudes 47°42′ and 51°03′ north. Inside China, the neighbouring areas are Da Hinggan Ling Prefecture to the north and Yichun to the south-east. Suihua lies south of Heihe, Qiqihar is south-west, and Hulunbuir, which is part of Inner Mongolia, is to the west.

The river has marked the Sino-Russian frontier since the Aigun Treaty of 1858 and the Treaty of Peking of 1860. The land north of the Amur had earlier belonged to imperial China, a point that explains the historical importance of the old town of Aigun, discussed below.

The climate is humid continental and monsoon-influenced, classed Dwb in Köppen terms, although the south of the prefecture is Dwa. Under the influence of the Siberian high, winters are long, windy and dry as well as bitterly cold, whereas the East Asian monsoon brings warm, wet summers. Figures for 1981 to 2010 show January, the coldest month, at a daily mean of −22.0 °C (−7.6 °F) and July, the warmest, at 21.1 °C (70.0 °F); the whole-year average is +0.92 °C (33.7 °F). Roughly two-thirds of the precipitation arrives from June to August. Recorded temperatures have gone as low as −44.5 °C (−48 °F) and as high as 39.3 °C (103 °F). Anyone arriving from a milder country should plan their winter wardrobe very carefully.
Because the city sits on an international border far from China's big population centres, planning your journey carefully will save time and effort.
The main ways of reaching the city are as follows.

By road: China National Highway 202 starts in Heihe and runs to Dalian, passing through Harbin, Jilin City and Shenyang, and provincial highways join Heihe with Mohe and other towns. A two-lane highway bridge across the Amur between Blagoveshchensk and Heihe was completed at the end of 2019.
By rail: a line from Heihe to Bei'an connects with Harbin, Qiqihar and Daqing.
By air: Heihe Aihui Airport.

Across the river: there has been a proposal for an international cable car to Blagoveshchensk, which would be the first of its kind in the world, with an opening date of around 2022 mentioned. Check whether it exists yet.
Between classes and exams, Heihe offers a few notable places where nature and history meet, and they are good ideas for weekends.

Sights around Heihe include the Amur River and Wudalianchi, a lake and volcanic range where visitors can go on trips to nearby volcanoes. History fans can visit the Old City of Aigun, a well-known scenic and historic spot, where China and Russia signed their nineteenth-century Aigun treaty.

Ancient Chinese records and other sources name the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan among the peoples who lived in the area now called Heilongjiang. The Mongolic Donghu lived in Inner Mongolia and western Heilongjiang, and some place names have Manchu or Mongolian roots. From the 7th to the 10th century the Bohai Kingdom controlled the eastern part, and after it came the Khitan Liao dynasty. The Jurchen Jin dynasty, in power from 1115 to 1234 over much of northern China, started within what are now Heilongjiang's borders.

As an administrative unit, Heilongjiang dates from 1683, under the Kangxi emperor of the Manchu Qing, who separated it from the north-west of Jilin province. This early province covered only the western part of the present one. It was overseen by an official styled the General (or Military Governor) of Heilongjiang, in Manchu Sahaliyan Ula i Jiyanggiyūn; the Manchu title is borrowed from the Chinese 將軍 (jiāngjūn, a general) and is a cousin of the Japanese word shōgun. Meanwhile the General of Jilin, known in Manchu as Girin i Jiyanggiyūn, held the east of today's province, with authority reaching the Sea of Japan. These lands deep in Manchuria were closed to Han Chinese migration.

When the governor's seat was set up in 1683 it was in Heilongjiang City, also called Aigun or Heihe (in Manchu, Saghalien Ula), on the Amur. By 1690 it had already shifted to Nenjiang (Mergen), on the Nen River, and then in 1699 it went further south, to Qiqihar. Modern historians suggest supply was the reason: the Nen River gave Nenjiang and Qiqihar a convenient waterway to southern Manchuria, while reaching Aigun meant sailing down the Sungari to its meeting with the Amur and then upstream, or crossing by portage through the Lesser Xing'an range that separates the two valleys. Qiqihar had a further advantage, standing where a northbound road to Nenjiang met a westbound one to Mongolia, so its garrison could guard against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

The Qing military presence north of Aigun was small. European sources from the 18th and early 20th centuries, and Russian reports from the 1850s, say that the Qing's most distant guard post stood at Ulusu-Modon (乌鲁苏穆丹), close to the famous S-shaped bend in the Amur. That post sat on the north bank and passed to Russia in 1860.

Under pressure in 1858 and 1860, the Qing handed over to the Russian Empire everything beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers. That left the Qing without access to the Sea of Japan and set Heilongjiang's northern and eastern borders where they are today. Around the same time Manchuria was opened to Han settlers, and by the early twentieth century, as a result of the Chuang Guandong movement, Han Chinese were the dominant group.

Japanese forces invaded the province in 1931 and completed its conquest in 1932, when it became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army beat the Japanese in Manchuria in 1945, and in the civil war that followed, Soviet units supported the Chinese communists. Heilongjiang became the first province entirely under communist control, with Harbin the first major city. At the start of communist rule the province covered only the western part of today's territory, with Qiqihar as capital, and the rest formed Songjiang province with its capital at Harbin. In 1954 the two were merged into the present Heilongjiang. During the Cultural Revolution the province was enlarged to include the Hulunbuir League and other areas that had been in Inner Mongolia, though this has mostly been reversed since.

The province has varied terrain. Mountain ranges cover much of it, including the Greater and Lesser Khingan Ranges and the Zhangguangcai, Laoye and Wanda Mountains. On the Jilin border stands the province's highest peak, Datudingzi Mountain, at 1,690 metres (5,540 feet). The Greater Khingan contains the biggest stretch of virgin forest left in China, which makes it a key area for forestry.

The lower, flatter east and south-west are crossed by the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers, which all feed the Amur; the Amur valley itself forms part of the northern edge. Xingkai Lake, also called Khanka Lake, sits on the frontier with Primorsky Krai in Russia.

Most of the province has a humid continental climate (Dwa or Dwb), with subarctic conditions (Dwc) in the extreme north. Long, harsh winters bring January averages of between −31 and −15 °C (−24 to 5 °F). Summers are brief and range from warm to very warm, averaging 18 to 23 °C (64 to 73 °F) in July. Rain amounts to 400 to 700 millimetres (16 to 28 inches) a year and falls mostly in summer. Sunshine totals about 2,300 to 2,650 hours, and in springtime wind energy is plentiful over the Songnen and Sanjiang plains.
Among the province's largest cities are Harbin, Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi and Daqing, followed by Jixi, Shuangyashan, Hegang, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe.

As of October 2020, Heilongjiang's roads, including expressways and highways, add up to 165,989 km (103,141 miles). The key route into the province is the Beijing–Harbin Expressway, which begins at the Jilin border and finishes inside the Harbin Ring Expressway. Heading north-east, the Harbin–Tongjiang Expressway serves far-flung counties belonging to Harbin, Jiamusi and the north-east. At Jiansanjiang a branch road, the Jiansanjiang–Heixiazi Island Expressway, leaves it to reach state farms in the far east and ends close to the Russian border. Another main corridor is the Suifenhe–Manzhouli Expressway, which crosses the province from south-east to north-west past Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar before it ends at the Inner Mongolia border. In the east, the Hegang–Dalian Expressway takes timber and coal from Hegang to the Jilin border.

Sixty railway lines, about 5,300 kilometres (3,300 miles) in total, cross the province, among them part of the Eurasian Land Bridge. In 2012 the high-speed line from Harbin, the provincial capital, to Dalian in Liaoning was completed; it passes through Changchun and Shenyang and has 23 stops. Forecasts were for 37 million passengers a year by 2020, rising to 51 million by 2030.

The major airports are Harbin Taiping International, Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi and Heihe. Harbin's airport can handle six million passengers a year and links with over 70 domestic and international cities.

In 2007 Valery Solomonovich Gurevich, vice-chairman of Russia's Jewish Autonomous Oblast, proposed a railway bridge over the Amur that would join Tongjiang with Nizhneleninskoye, a village in that oblast. The Chinese portion was finished in July 2016 and work on the Russian side began in December 2016. The two halves were physically joined in March 2019. Since then the opening to trains has been postponed repeatedly, with the end of 2020 given as one estimate and then the third quarter of 2021.
Provincial economics determine the jobs and trade networks open to graduates, so here is a brief look at the numbers and industries.

For 2022 the province's GDP was 1.59 trillion RMB, or US$236 billion at nominal rates, which is CN¥51,906 (US$7,717) per head. Farming and other primary activity supplied ¥360 billion (22.7%), industry ¥465 billion (29.2%) and services ¥764 billion (48%).

GDP has risen steadily since 2003, from 443.3 billion yuan to 707.72 billion in 2007, an increase of 60 %. The private economy was worth RMB234 billion in 2006, 37.6 percent of GDP, and private firms paid RMB20.5 billion in taxes that year. Private enterprises have led the province's growth, and many strong private companies have begun to emerge.

Heilongjiang has China's biggest rice, corn and soybean plantations, with 14.37 million hectares (35.5 million acres) of grain, including 4 million hectares (9.9 million acres) of rice and 5.5 million hectares (14 million acres) of corn. Its extensive black soil, or chernozem, is among the most fertile soil types anywhere. Farming across this belt has grown nearly a hundredfold since the early twentieth century, and after the 1960s farming became modern, with heavy mechanisation and more fertiliser. The province is one of Asia's leading regions for japonica rice, known for high-quality brands. Cold-resistant varieties, favourable policies and climate change have raised rice output sharply in recent years. Other commercial crops include beets, flax and sunflowers.

The province is also a key supplier of timber, mainly pine, particularly Korean pine, and larch. Most forests grow in the Greater and Lesser Khingan Mountains, where protected animals such as lynx, the red-crowned crane and the Siberian tiger also live. Herding focuses on horses and cattle, and Heilongjiang has more milk cows than any other province-level division.

Heilongjiang belongs to north-east China, the country's traditional industrial base, with industry built on coal, petroleum, timber, machinery and food. Its location also makes it an important gateway for trade with Russia. After a wave of privatisation closed uncompetitive factories in the 1990s, Manchuria went through stagnation, and the government launched the Revitalize Northeast China campaign, which promotes the private sector as the preferred way to carry out reform and opening up. Petroleum is crucial, with the Daqing oilfields a major national source. Other significant minerals are coal, gold and graphite, and the potential for wind power is large, estimated at 134 gigawatts.
Development zones include:

Daqing New and Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. Construction began in April 1992, and the State Council recognised it as a national high-tech zone later that year. It began with 208.54 km² (80.52 square miles) and has recently grown by a further 32.45 km² (12.53 square miles).
Heihe Border Economic Cooperation Area.
Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone.

Harbin New and Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. Set up in 1988 and approved as a national zone in 1991, it covers 34 km² (13 square miles) in three centralised parks. Nangang is for incubating high-tech projects, corporate R&D and service industries such as finance, insurance, tourism and entertainment, and houses the headquarters of well-known companies. Haping Road is a comprehensive industrial base for cars, parts, medicines, food, electronics and textiles, and Yingbin Road is mainly for high-tech incubation and industry.

Sino-Russia Dongning-Piurtaphca Trade Zone. The State Council gave its approval in 2000 and building was finished in 2005. The planned area is 275.4 hectares; the Chinese side contains a 22-hectare trade centre split into four sub-areas, A to D, where over 6,000 stalls mainly sell clothing, household appliances, food and construction materials.

Suifenhe Border Economic Cooperation Area. In the north of Suifenhe and bordering Russia to the east, it is the biggest of the province's three state-level border-trade zones by number of investors. The Binzhou–Suifenhe Railway connects with the Russian Far East Railway and is an important route for exports. Suifenhe lies 548 km (341 miles) by rail from Harbin, and the Russian port city of Buguranikinai is 21 km (13 miles) away.

By the end of 2022 the permanent resident population of Heilongjiang was 30.99 million, 260,000 fewer than a year earlier. City dwellers numbered 20.52 million against 10.47 million in the countryside, so the urbanisation rate came to 66.2%, half a percentage point higher than before. Children aged 0 to 14 made up 9.3% of the total and people aged 65 and above 17.8%. The 2021 bulletin put the permanent population at 31.25 million, down 460,000 from 2020.

The Seventh National Population Census (2020) recorded 31,850,088 permanent residents. Compared with 38,313,991 in the Sixth Census of 2010, this is a fall of 6,463,903 in ten years (−16.87%), or an average annual rate of −1.83%. The census breakdown is:
Men numbered 15,952,468 (50.09%) and women 15,897,620 (49.91%), a sex ratio of 100.35 when women are set at 100.
By age, 3,286,466 people (10.32%) were under 15, 21,167,932 (66.46%) were between 15 and 59, and 7,395,690 (23.22%) were 60 or older, of whom 4,972,868 (15.61%) were 65 or older.
Urban residents totalled 20,897,694 (65.61%) and rural residents 10,952,394 (34.39%).

The 2020 birth rate was 3.35‰, with a death rate of 8.23‰ and a natural growth rate of −4.48‰. Put simply, births are few, deaths are few, and the population is old, and out-migration has pushed the population down continuously since 2014. Sources give slightly different figures for the same years, so use the official statistical releases for any precise work.

Most residents are non-religious or follow Chinese folk religion, including Taoism. Many Manchu people practise Manchu shamanism, and Chinese and Tibetan Buddhism are important. The culture is part of the north-eastern one known as Dongbei, which is fairly uniform across the region.

Heilongjiang leads China in winter sports and in the winter-sports industry, and has been promoting bandy as an Olympic sport. Past events include the 2009 Winter Universiade, the 2018 Bandy World Championship (Division B) and the Asia League Ice Hockey.

heihe-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Heihe University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Heihe, register at Heihe University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Heilongjiang University, often shortened to HLJU (in Chinese, 黑龙江大学), is a provincial public university in Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang in the far northeast of China. It belongs to the provincial system, but it is not run by the province alone: three bodies back it together: SASTIND (the national defence science and technology authority), the Ministry of Education and the government of the province. For an international applicant this mix of backers is a useful sign that the university has both regional roots and national recognition.

The university traces its beginnings to March 1941 in Yan'an, which was then the key base of the Communist-led revolution. Its earliest ancestor was a Russian-language training unit, the Third Branch School's Russian Language Column of the Chinese People's Anti-Japanese Military and Political University, which existed to train military translators. That language-teaching origin still shapes the character of the place today.

heilongjiang-university.h: From a wartime language school to a provincial university

blocks.x: The early years are easy to summarise. The institution was founded in 1941 and carried several names in its first decade, including the Yan'an School of Foreign Languages. After 1946 the People's Liberation Army's northeastern command moved the foreign language school to Harbin, where it operated as an academic institution under the headquarters of the Northeastern Democratic Army. In 1958 the school was expanded and rebuilt as Heilongjiang University.

So the story runs from a small translators' class in Yan'an, to a language school in Harbin, to a broad provincial university. If you are weighing it up, the Russian-language tradition is the thread that connects every stage.

heilongjiang-university.h: What the university is known for

blocks.x: Heilongjiang University is a provincial key university and one of the institutions that was included in the national 211 programme and is supported by the province. It is best known for languages, civil and commercial law, Marxist philosophy, business studies and water conservancy.
Several of its claims are unusual enough to be worth knowing about before you apply:
It runs the only Manchu language programme in China.
Its Russian language studies are widely regarded as the strongest in the country.
Its Russian centre is one of only three Russian centres that Russia has established in China.
Its library holds about 5.1 million books and is described as the largest in Heilongjiang Province.
The Xuefu bookstore on campus is described as the biggest bookstore in the province.
Together, these facts make HLJU a particularly sensible choice for anyone who wants to study Russian, other Slavic and Asian languages, or northeast Asian affairs.

In national discipline rankings, the highest placings go to Russian philology and Manchu philology. Manchu philology, which exists nowhere else in China, takes first place. Four programmes sit around fourth place: Marxist philosophy, foreign language and literature (discipline code 0502), and Chinese ethnic language and literature. Business English follows at fifth. Both library science and commercial and civil law share seventh place. Arabic philology comes ninth and Japanese philology tenth. Philosophy (discipline code 0101) is placed eleventh and translation twelfth. Rankings change from one evaluation round to the next, so check the university's own website for the current picture.

heilongjiang-university.h: Teaching departments, vocational and adult education

blocks.x: Two teaching departments serve the whole campus: the Applied Foreign Language Teaching Department and the Sports Department. Beyond the main degree colleges there are a College of Vocational and Technical education, a Community College Department, an Adult Education College and the People's Armed College.

Research is organised around four units: the Cultural and Philosophy Research Center, the Russia Research Department, a Manchu Language Culture centre and a Russian Language Literature centre. The university also runs international joint programmes: an economics institute shared with Paris Nanterre University in France, a Chinese-Russian institute with Novosibirsk State University, and a graduate college run with Far Eastern Federal University, both in Russia.

HLJU is spread over several sites. Besides the main and south campuses there is one at Hulan, plus separate sites for the independent Jianqiao College, the People's Armed Forces College and the Heilongjiang Biological Science College. Published figures for the total site area are not consistent and should not be relied on, but the buildings are reported to total about 1.16 million square metres of floor space. The university has more than 34,000 students and organises its teaching through about 30 colleges and independent units, including independent secondary colleges.

In academic capacity, the university reports five post-doctoral research stations. It can award doctorates in 16 subjects and master's degrees in 13 disciplines and 112 secondary-level subjects, and it also offers 6 professional master's degrees. It lists two national key disciplines, a pair of national subject groups and 21 provincial key disciplines, and teaches 75 undergraduate programmes, among them 10 with national characteristics and 21 designated provincial key specialties.

On the practical side, the university reports teaching and research equipment worth about 300 million yuan, a collection of more than five million books and a university-town style campus designed for around 40,000 students. Facilities listed include a modern laboratory building, teaching buildings, two libraries, a gymnasium, two swimming halls and three dining centres, along with campus broadband and multimedia teaching resources. These numbers come from different periods, so treat them as a general guide rather than exact current counts.

The university describes a large and well-qualified teaching body: more than 3,200 staff overall, of whom more than 2,000 are full-time teachers, and over 900 hold senior professional titles. It reports six winners of the national title of renowned teacher, and more than 200 teachers who have received national or provincial honours of various kinds. Other recognitions mentioned include seven national outstanding young experts, several winners of the Ministry of Education's new-century talent programmes, and 73 staff who receive special government allowances. The wording of some of these honours varies between published descriptions, and the staffing numbers have probably changed since they were compiled, so the university's own site is the best place to confirm current figures.

Heilongjiang University says it has substantive cooperation with about 140 universities around the world, including Leeds and Bradford in the United Kingdom, the University of Illinois in the United States, the University of Paris X in France and Niigata University in Japan. Over roughly three decades from 1981, more than 8,500 international students have studied here. Every year learners arrive from Korea, Japan, Russia, Germany, Britain, Africa and America, mostly to study Chinese or international business.

Within Heilongjiang, HLJU is the main provincial base for Chinese as a foreign language. It is an official HSK test centre and one of the institutions designated to receive foreign recipients of the Chinese government scholarship. Its Confucius Institute in Russia was the first one opened in that country, and the joint graduate school mentioned earlier is run with Far Eastern Federal University.

HLJU has teamed up with Yanbian University, Jilin University and Liaoning University to set up a northeastern base for promoting the Chinese language internationally. Visiting students are mainly Russian and Korean, and in recent years some American Fulbright fellows studying Mandarin under the National Security Language Initiative have also studied at HLJU. If you are coming from the English-speaking world, you will find yourself among a diverse international group centred on language study.

Heilongjiang University counts a large number of diplomats, officials, writers and academics among its graduates. Because the university began as a translators' school, many of the best-known names worked in foreign affairs.

A university campus is only part of student life. Everything you will do outside class, from keeping warm to finding something to do on a weekend, depends on the city around it. The sections below describe Harbin, the home of Heilongjiang University.

Harbin is the capital of Heilongjiang province and sits in its southern part. The city's administrative area is large, about 53,068 square kilometres (20,490 square miles), and stretches from about 44°04′ to 46°40′ north and from 125 degrees 42 minutes to 130 degrees 10 minutes east. The urban centre faces the south shore of the central Songhua River, where the south-east fringe of the Songnen Plain (a big part of the Northeast China Plain) begins. Locals call it the pearl on the swan's neck, because the outline of Heilongjiang looks something like a swan.

The main urban terrain is flat and low, at an average of about 150 metres (490 feet) above sea level. In the east, ten county-level divisions are made up of mountains and uplands, and the far east has broad wetlands, mainly in Yilan County, which sits at the south-western edge of the Sanjiang Plain. Going round the compass, the neighbouring prefecture-level cities are Yichun (north), Suihua (north-west), Daqing (west), Jiamusi and Qitaihe (north-east) and Mudanjiang (south-east), and Jilin province runs along the south-west edge.

Harbin is nicknamed Ice City, and the name is earned. The climate is classed as monsoon-influenced humid continental (Köppen Dwa). The Siberian high pressure system and a latitude above 45 degrees north bring long, dry, freezing winters, although snowfall is light and the skies are often sunny. The January average over 24 hours is about -17.3 °C (0.9 °F). Spring and autumn are short transition seasons with changeable winds. Summers can be hot, with a July mean of 23.7 °C (74.7 °F), and this is also when most of the rain falls: of an annual total of 539 millimetres (21.2 inches), more than half arrives in July and August.

Other figures to expect: sunshine runs from 45 percent of possible hours in December up to 60 percent in September, which adds up to about 2,340 hours a year. Precipitation falls on roughly 99 days a year, while the yearly mean temperature comes to 5.2 °C, or 41.4 °F. Records have ranged from around -42.6 °C at the official station (a reading of -41.1 °C in January 1931 is also quoted) to 39.2 °C, most recently reached on 4 June 2001; an unofficial high of 41.0 °C (105.8 °F) was noted in July 1907. Other descriptions put the average winter daily temperature at -19.7 °C (-3.5 °F), and they say winter lows below -25 °C (-13.0 °F) are not unusual. Averages vary slightly with the source and period, but the message is the same: pack seriously warm clothing.
The city has also built sponge-city features to cope with climate change. The Qunli stormwater park, for example, collects, filters and stores rainwater while protecting natural habitat.

Harbin is the largest economy in Heilongjiang. Its GDP was RMB 501.08 billion in 2013, up 8.9 percent on the year before, and RMB 575.12 billion in 2015. The three sectors of the economy were split 11.1 : 36.1 : 52.8 (agriculture, industry, services) in 2012. Imports and exports totalled US$5,330 million by the end of 2012, and the city had 3.147 million people in work that year. These figures are dated, and the university's city authorities publish newer ones.

The city has chernozem, black earth, which is among the most nutrient-rich soil in China. That makes Harbin a national base for commodity grain and a good place for agribusiness. Alongside farming there is a broad industrial base covering light industry, textiles, medicine, food, aircraft, cars, metals, electronics, building materials and chemicals. Among the main employers are the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory, the Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and the Harbin Electric Company Limited. Power equipment is a specialty, and the hydro and thermal power generation equipment made here accounts for about a third of China's installed capacity. One industry ranking for 2009 to 2010 placed Harbin Electric second in the world for steam turbine market share, tied with Dongfang Electric and just below Shanghai Electric. In medicine, Harbin Pharmaceutical Group ranks second among Chinese drugmakers when measured by market value.

A trade and investment show, the Harbin International Trade and Economic Fair, has taken place yearly since 1990. By 2013 the total had passed 1.9 million exhibitors and visitors, coming from more than 80 countries and regions, and deals worth over US$100 billion had been signed. After talks between the Chinese and Russian prime ministers in October 2013, it was agreed that the fair would be renamed the China-Russia EXPO and co-sponsored by China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang government and two Russian ministries. Foreign direct investment reached US$980 million in 2013, making Harbin one of the main destinations for it in the north-east. Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank, both headquartered here, are among the largest banks in the region, and Harbin Bank ranked fourth among Chinese city commercial banks for competitiveness in 2011. The Qiulin Group owns Harbin's biggest department store.
The city has several zones where firms cluster, and graduates sometimes find work in them:
a national Economic and Technology Development Zone, focused on telecommunications equipment, chemicals, automobile assembly, electronics, textiles and medical equipment
the High and New Technological Development Zone, which focuses on biology, medicine, electronics, information technology and optical-mechanical-electrical integration
the provincial Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone, for vehicles, electronics assembly, heavy industry and instruments
the provincial Limin Economic Development Zone, for trading, food and drink processing, medical supplies and logistics
the river port, Harbin Port
the Songbei Economic Development Zone, described next, and the Economic and Technological Development Zone and High-tech Zone covered after it
#### Songbei zone

Songbei District is home to this zone, whose planned area is 5.53 square kilometres. It encourages electronics assembly and food and drink processing. Regional and provincial headquarters of large companies such as China Datang, China Netcom and China Telecom have located there, and research centres for science and technology innovation and for agricultural innovation are based there too. Partly because of such institutes, a 2006 competitiveness ranking put Harbin ninth of 50 major Chinese cities for innovation capacity, and sixth for the volume of scientific and technological results.
#### Economic and Technological Development Zone

HETDZ, the Economic and Technological Development Zone, is counted among China's 90 national economic development zones. It was established in June 1991 and approved as a national zone by the State Council in April 1993. In December 2012 the High Technology Development Zone merged into it, though the hi-tech zone had also been separated from it in 2009. Today its concentrated parks cover 18.5 square kilometres, split between the Nangang and Haping Road parks. The 12.2-square-kilometre Yingbin Road Hi-tech Park, once part of HETDZ, has been under the high-tech zone's administration since 2009.

Nangang Centralized Park is intended for incubating high-tech projects, enterprise research bases and service industries such as finance, insurance, catering, tourism and culture, and it is where headquarters and branches of large known companies are located.
Yingbin Road Centralized Park concentrates on incubating high-tech projects and high-tech industry.
Haping Road Centralized Park is a general industrial base for car and car-parts manufacturing, medicines, food, electronics and textiles.
#### High and New Technology Industry Development Zone

The zone is one of 56 national high-tech zones in China. It began as a provincial zone in 1988 and gained national status from the State Council in 1991. It has 23.9 square kilometres of built area in two parts: a Science and Technology Innovation Town and a High-tech Industrial Development Zone proper.

In the 2020 census the city had 10,009,854 residents, which was 5.62 percent fewer than ten years earlier. Its built-up area (every urban district except Acheng and Shuangcheng, which are not yet urbanised) held 5,282,083 people. About 70.61 percent of the population lives in urban areas and 29.39 percent in rural areas. The population skews older, with 10.46 percent under 14 and 14.65 percent are over 65. There are slightly more men (50.02 percent) than women (49.98 percent), and the birth rate, 6.95 per thousand, is lower than the Chinese average of 12.13.

Most residents are Han Chinese (93 percent in 2000). The minority groups are chiefly the Manchu, Hui and Mongol, and a small Russian community also lives in the city. The census gives a detailed breakdown by ethnic group.

The city's Catholics belong to the Apostolic Administration of Harbin. A former Eastern Catholic cathedral, dedicated to the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, is badly damaged; in earlier years Russian troops garrisoned in Harbin used it. Muslims made up about 0.4 percent of the population in 2000, and the Daowai Mosque is the biggest mosque in Heilongjiang. A small Jewish community once lived around Zhongyang Main Street, which became a home for European Jewish refugees.

Harbin's local culture is built on Han tradition blended with Manchu and Russian influences, and you can see the mix in the architecture, food, music and customs. In June 2010 UNESCO named Harbin a City of Music in its Creative Cities Network.

Harbin is a very popular domestic tourist destination, especially in winter, when huge ice sculpture displays open. It has a large indoor ski park inside the Wanda Harbin Mall, with six slopes up to 500 metres (1,600 feet) long. In the 2023 to 2024 winter season, the city received 87 million visitors, mainly from elsewhere in China. Harbin also stands out for European-style buildings, notably Saint Sophia Cathedral, the pedestrian Central Street and the Baroque complex in the old town, Lao Daowai.

Harbin is the most northerly of China's major cities and sits directly under the influence of the Siberian anticyclone. From December to March, ice and snow sculptures decorate the city in many styles. The big annual event, the International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival, began in 1985 and officially opens on 5 January, though many sculptures are on show earlier. There are two main areas: giant snow sculptures on Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a top-rated AAAAA recreation area across the Songhua River, and Ice and Snow World, which opens each night with the sculptures lit from inside and out. Ice and Snow World has life-size buildings made of crystal-clear ice blocks two to three feet thick, taken from the Songhua River. The work takes 15,000 workers about 16 days, and in early December artisans cut around 120,000 cubic metres of ice from the frozen river (that is about 4.2 million cubic feet). You will also find ice buildings, large snow sculptures, ice slides and festival food and drink in parks and on main avenues.

Other winter activities connected to the festival include alpine skiing at Yabuli, snowmobile driving, winter swimming in the Songhua River, and the ice-lantern show at Zhaolin Garden, which first took place in 1963. The festival is famous across Asia, particularly in Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore, and it is often named as one of the world's four biggest winter festivals, alongside Sapporo in Japan, the Quebec Winter Carnival in Canada and Norway's Holmenkollen skiing event.

Each November the city sends ice artisans to the United States. More than 100 of them create ICE!, an annual indoor display of Christmas-themed ice carvings, in National Harbor in Maryland, Nashville, Tennessee, Kissimmee in Florida and Grapevine in Texas.

Heilongjiang Television (HLJTV) is the main regional broadcaster, with seven channels and a satellite channel for other provinces. The municipal station, Harbin Television (HRBTV), has five specialised channels. On radio, Long Guang (Dragon Broadcast), formerly the Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, serves the whole province on seven channels, one of them in Korean. Harbin People's Broadcasting Station carries music, news, traffic, economic and city-life programmes for Harbin and nearby areas, including Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.

Heilongjiang University offers one of China's best environments for learning Russian and other languages, a wide spread of colleges, and a history that began in wartime Yan'an. Harbin adds a distinctive winter, a lively mix of Chinese, Russian and Manchu culture, and a solid industrial economy. For current admissions rules, programmes and fees, always check the university's own website.
