The Chinese name is 黑龙江中医药大学 (Hēilóngjiāng Zhōngyīyào Dàxué). This is a state-run medical university that was founded in 1959 and sits in Harbin, in the north-east of China. As the name says, its field is traditional Chinese medicine, so students who choose it are joining a specialised institution in a city with a famously cold climate.

Since the university's own description is short, much of what you need to plan a stay comes from the surroundings. The pages below look first at Harbin, where the campus is, and then at Heilongjiang, the province around it. Always compare these general facts with the university's official admissions information, because figures such as population, rankings and road lengths are updated every year and some of the numbers below come from different years.

Harbin is Heilongjiang's capital, in the southern part of the province, and its territory is large: 53,068 km2 (20,490 sq mi). The prefecture occupies the south-eastern fringe of the Songnen Plain, itself a major piece of the Northeastern Plain, and the urban core lies on the south bank of the Songhua River's middle reaches. People sometimes call Harbin "the pearl on the swan's neck", because the outline of Heilongjiang looks like a swan. The administrative area is large, spanning latitudes 44° 04′ to 46° 40′ N and longitudes 125° 42′ to 130° 10′ E.

Several prefecture-level cities border Harbin: Yichun lies north, Jiamusi and Qitaihe north-east, Mudanjiang south-east, Daqing west and Suihua north-west. The south-western boundary is shared with Jilin province. The main terrain is flat and low, at roughly 150 metres (490 ft) above sea level on average. In the east, ten county-level divisions are covered by mountains and uplands, and the far east of the prefecture has large wetlands, mainly in Yilan County at the south-western edge of the Sanjiang Plain.

Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa). It lies above 45 degrees north and is exposed to the Siberian high, so it is known for cold weather and a long winter. The nickname "Ice City" is deserved: winters are dry and bitterly cold, with a 24-hour mean of only -17.3 °C (0.9 °F) in January, although there is little snow and many days are sunny. Spring and autumn are short transition seasons with shifting winds. Summer can be hot, and July averages 23.7 °C (74.7 °F).

Most rain falls in summer. Of the 539 millimetres (21.2 in) that fall in an average year, over half arrives in July and August. The sunniest month is September, when 60 percent of possible sunshine is recorded; December is the dullest at 45 percent. Overall the city gets 2,340 hours of bright sunshine, with rain or snow on 99 days. Averaged over the whole year the temperature is 5.2 °C (41.4 °F).

The extremes are dramatic. A reading of -42.6 °C (-45 °F) is recorded, or -41.1 °C (-42 °F) for the official station in January 1931, and the high is 39.2 °C (103 °F), most recently reached on 4 June 2001; an unofficial 41.0 °C (105.8 °F) was recorded in July 1907. If you are coming from a warm country, plan to buy serious winter clothing before the first cold snap, and expect indoor heating to be strong, so layers that are easy to take off are more useful than one very thick coat.

To limit the effects of climate change, the city has drawn on "sponge city" planning. One example is Qunli stormwater park, which gathers rainwater, filters and stores it, and at the same time protects wildlife habitat.

Harbin is the northernmost major city in China, in the north of the Northeast, and it is directly affected by the Siberian anticyclone. Winter daily temperatures average -19.7 °C (-3.5 °F), and annual lows below -25.0 °C (-13.0 °F) are common. (The January figure given earlier and this winter figure differ because they describe different periods.) Because of this freezing weather the city carries the name "Ice City" and from December to March it is filled with ice and snow sculptures in many styles.

The big annual event is the ice and snow sculpture festival, which has run since 1985. Its official start date is 5 January each year, yet many sculptures are already on view before then. Sculptures appear throughout the city, but two main areas stand out. One is Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a AAAAA-rated recreation area across the Songhua River from the city, with huge snow sculptures. The other is the "Ice and Snow World", which opens every night with lights switched on so the sculptures glow from inside and out.

Inside Ice and Snow World, full-size buildings are lit up and made of clear ice blocks two to three feet thick that come directly from the Songhua River. The work is huge: 15,000 workers spend 16 days building the sculptures in the grounds. Preparation starts in early December, when ice artisans saw 120,000 cubic metres (4.2 million cubic feet) of ice out of the frozen river for raw material. Beyond the main grounds, you will find large ice buildings, snow sculptures, ice slides and festival food and drink in several parks and on major avenues.

Visitors can also try Yabuli alpine skiing, drive snowmobiles, swim in the Songhua in winter, or see the ice-lantern show in Zhaolin Garden, a tradition dating from 1963. Harbin's snow carving and ice recreation have a reputation across China and in Asian countries such as Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore.

Harbin's festival is reckoned one of the world's four biggest of its kind, alongside the Sapporo Snow Festival (Japan), Quebec City's Winter Carnival (Canada) and the Holmenkollen Ski Festival (Norway). Overseas, the city exports the craft each November: it dispatches ice artisans to America, where more than 100 of them build ICE!, a yearly indoor show of Christmas ice carvings held in National Harbor (Maryland), Nashville (Tennessee), Kissimmee (Florida) and Grapevine (Texas).

In short, Harbin offers a student a rare mix of strong winters, Russian-influenced streets and a lively festival calendar. Local culture rests on Han traditions mixed with Manchu and Russian influences, and this blend shows up in architecture, food, music and customs. On 22 June 2010 Harbin was named a UNESCO City of Music, within the Creative Cities Network.

Domestic tourists love Harbin, above all in winter. Beyond the ice sculptures, it has a big indoor ski park inside the Wanda Harbin Mall, with six runs, the longest reaching 500 metres (1,600 ft). In winter 2023-2024 the city welcomed 87 million visitors, mostly from other parts of China. Harbin is equally famous for architecture borrowed from Europe, notably Saint Sophia Cathedral, Central Street and a cluster of Baroque buildings in Lao Daowai, the Old Town.

On television, Heilongjiang Television (HLJTV) is the regional broadcaster, with seven channels plus a satellite channel for other provinces, and Harbin Television (HRBTV) is the municipal station with five specialised channels. On the radio, Long Guang (Dragon Broadcast), formerly the Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, serves the whole province with seven channels, including one in Korean. Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS) covers music, news, traffic, the economy and daily life in Harbin and nearby areas such as Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.

The 2020 census counted 10,009,854 residents in Harbin, which is 5.62 percent fewer than ten years earlier. Counting only the urban districts, apart from Acheng and Shuangcheng (not yet urbanised), the built-up area was home to 5,282,083 people. Overall, 70.61 percent of residents were urban and 29.39 percent rural.

The population is fairly old: 10.46 percent are under 14 and 14.65 percent are over 65. There are slightly more men (50.02 percent) than women (49.98 percent). The birth rate is lower than in most of China, at 6.95 births per 1,000 people against a national average of 12.13.

People from many backgrounds have shaped the city, and its population has been falling slowly in recent years. The great majority are Han Chinese (93% in 2000). Manchu, Hui and Mongol residents form the main minorities, and a small number of Russians also live in the city. (The detailed 2020 ethnic breakdown is not reproduced here.)

Religion reflects the city's mixed history. A missionary jurisdiction that is not yet a diocese, the Apostolic Administration of Harbin, looks after the Catholic minority. The city also contains what used to be the Eastern Catholic cathedral of a Russian Catholic exarchate. Another landmark, the Church of the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, is badly damaged; Russian soldiers from the Outer Amur Military Region, garrisoned in Harbin, once used it. Muslims made up just 0.4% of residents in 2000, and Heilongjiang's biggest mosque, Daowai Mosque, stands in the city. There was also a small Jewish community around Zhongyang Main Street, which sheltered many Jewish refugees from Europe.

For a student, the economy matters because it decides where internships, part-time work and graduate jobs come from. Harbin has the biggest economy in Heilongjiang. GDP in 2013 reached RMB501.08 billion, up 8.9 percent on the previous year, and in 2015 it was RMB 575.12 billion. In 2012 the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors contributed 11.1, 36.1 and 52.8 parts respectively, so services made up over half of the economy. By the end of 2012 imports and exports totalled US$5,330 million, and the working population in 2012 was 3.147 million.

Farming is a strength. Harbin's chernozem soil is among the most nutrient-rich in China and suits food and textile-related crops, so the city is a base for commodity grain and a good place for agribusiness.

The industrial base is broad: light industry, textiles, medicine, food, aircraft, cars, metallurgy, electronics, building materials and chemicals combine into a fairly complete system. Among the leading firms are the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory, Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and Harbin Electric Company Limited. Power equipment is a leading industry, and hydro and thermal equipment made here accounts for a third of all installed capacity in China. By Platts' figures for 2009-10, Harbin Electric was the second-largest steam turbine maker by world market share, level with Dongfang Electric and just behind Shanghai Electric. In pharmaceuticals, the city is home to Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, whose work spans research, development, manufacturing and sales of medical products; by market value it is the second-largest drug company in China, a fact of obvious interest to a medical university's students.

An annual trade and investment fair has been held in Harbin since 1990. Up to 2013 it had drawn more than 1.9 million exhibitors and visitors, from over 80 countries and regions, and contracts signed there were worth more than US$100 billion. The city is also a leading destination in the north-east for foreign direct investment, which reached US$980 million in 2013. In October 2013 the prime ministers of China and Russia, Li Keqiang and Dmitry Medvedev, met for the 18th time and agreed that the fair would become the "China-Russia EXPO"; sponsors are China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang provincial government, and two Russian bodies, the Ministry of Economic Development and the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

Finance and shopping have local champions too. Two of the largest banks in the north-east, Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank, have their headquarters here, and in 2011 Harbin Bank came fourth in a ranking of Chinese city commercial banks by competitiveness. Qiulin Group owns the city's largest department store.
Harbin organises its industry in several zones, each with its own focus:
Harbin Economic & Technology Development Zone (national): telecommunications equipment, chemicals, car production and assembly, electronics, textiles, and medical equipment and supplies
Harbin High and New Technological Development Zone: integrated optical, mechanical and electrical technology, biology, medicine, electronics and IT
Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (provincial): vehicle production and assembly, electronics, heavy industry, and instruments and industrial equipment
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (provincial): trading and distribution, food and beverage processing, medical equipment and supplies, and shipping, warehousing and logistics
Harbin Port
Harbin Songbei Economic Development Zone
Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone (described below as HETDZ)
Harbin High and New Technology Industry Development Zone (the second zone with "High and New" in its name, described below)

Songbei District hosts the Songbei Economic Development Zone, planned to cover 5.53 square kilometres. Authorities encourage electronics assembly and manufacturing and the processing of food and drink here. Big companies, among them China Datang Corporation, China Netcom and China Telecom, have placed regional or provincial headquarters in the district, which is gradually becoming a hub for such offices. Two research bodies, the Harbin Science and Technology Innovation Center and the Harbin International Agricultural Science and Technology Innovation Center, are also located in the zone. Partly because of these institutes, a 2006 competitiveness ranking of 50 major Chinese cities placed Harbin ninth for innovation ability in science and technology, and sixth for the quantity of scientific and technological achievements.

Among China's 90 national economic development zones, HETDZ was launched in June 1991 and received national status from the State Council in April 1993. The material is slightly inconsistent about its later history: it says the hi-tech zone was merged into it in December 2012, yet also says that the two were split in 2009. Either way, its centralised parks now cover 18.5 square kilometres, in the Nangang and Haping Road parks. A third park, the 12.2 square-kilometre Yingbin Road Hi-tech Centralized Park, was part of HETDZ originally but has belonged to the High and New Technology Industry Development Zone since 2009.

Nangang Centralized Park: for incubating high-tech projects and corporate research and development bases, and for services such as finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture and entertainment; large companies' headquarters and branches in Harbin are based here
Yingbin Road Centralized Park: mainly high-tech incubation and high-tech industrial development

Haping Road Centralized Park: a general industrial base for investment in cars and car parts, medicine, food, electronics and textiles; car production and assembly and raw-material processing are encouraged

One of 56 national high-tech zones in China, this zone began as a provincial one in 1988 and was approved by the State Council at national level in 1991. It has 23.9 square kilometres of built-up land, split between a Science and Technology Innovation Town and a High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

Early Chinese records point to a mix of peoples in the area: the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan, with the Mongolic Donghu living further west, in Inner Mongolia and western Heilongjiang. Some place names today come from Manchu or Mongolian. From the 7th to the 10th century the Bohai Kingdom controlled the east, and the Khitan Liao dynasty followed it. Later, the Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115-1234), which came to rule much of northern China, had its origins inside what is now Heilongjiang.

The Qing created Heilongjiang as a separate administrative area in 1683, under the Kangxi emperor, by taking the north-western part of Jilin province. This early province covered just the west of the present one. Its overseer was the General of Heilongjiang (Manchu: Sahaliyan Ula i Jiyanggiyūn), a title also rendered Military Governor; the Manchu word comes from the Chinese 將軍 jiāngjūn, meaning "general", and shares its origin with Japan's shōgun. The Treaty of Nerchinsk gave his authority a northern limit at the Stanovoy Mountains. East of that, the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn) was in charge, and his writ reached to the Sea of Japan. Han Chinese were not allowed to settle in these inner Manchurian lands.

When the post was created in 1683, the governor's seat was Heilongjiang City (known also as Aigun or Heihe, and in Manchu as Saghalien Ula), on the Amur. It moved to Nenjiang (Mergen), on the Nen River, in 1690, and again in 1699 to Qiqihar, farther south. Historians today suspect logistics: Nenjiang and Qiqihar are linked to southern Manchuria by the convenient Nen River waterway, whereas reaching Aigun meant sailing down the whole Sungari to its junction with the Amur and then up the Amur, or crossing the Lesser Xing'an Mountains by portage from the Nen valley. Qiqihar may also have been attractive because a northward road (to Nenjiang) met a westward one (to Mongolia) there, so its garrison could guard against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

Qing military presence north of Aigun was thin. European sources of the 18th and early 20th centuries and Russian reports from the 1850s place the farthest Qing outpost at Ulusu-Modon (Ulussu-Mudan; Chinese 乌鲁苏穆丹 Wūlǔsūmùdān), near the Amur's well-known S-shaped bend, on the left (north) bank, which was lost to Russia in 1860.

Treaties forced on the Qing in 1858 and 1860 transferred everything beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers to the Russian Empire. China lost its access to the Sea of Japan, and Heilongjiang took on the northern and eastern borders it has today. At the same time the Qing opened Manchuria to Han migration, and by the early twentieth century, thanks to Chuang Guandong, the Han had become the main ethnic group.

Japanese forces invaded in 1931 and completed their conquest of the province in 1932, when it became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. In 1945 the Soviet Army defeated the Japanese in Manchuria and, during the Chinese Civil War, helped the communists. Heilongjiang was the first province wholly controlled by the communists, and Harbin was the first major city under their control.

Early in communist rule Heilongjiang covered only the west of the present province, with Qiqihar as capital, while the rest formed Songjiang province, whose capital was Harbin. The two merged in 1954 into the Heilongjiang of today. In the Cultural Revolution the province was enlarged to take in Hulunbuir League and other areas that had belonged to Inner Mongolia, though most of that change has since been undone.

The province offers varied scenery, but mountains dominate: the Greater and Lesser Khingan ranges, along with the Zhangguangcai, Laoye and Wanda mountains. Datudingzi Mountain, on the border with Jilin, is the highest peak, at 1,690 metres (5,540 ft). The Greater Khingan Range holds the largest virgin forest left in China and is an important part of the country's forestry industry.

Flatter, lower land in the east and south-west is watered by the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers; each of these flows into the Amur, and the province's northern edge follows the Amur valley. On the Russian frontier, next to Primorsky Krai, lies Xingkai Lake, also called Khanka Lake.

Most of the province is humid continental (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), apart from the subarctic (Dwc) far north. Expect long, harsh winters, when January temperatures average anywhere from -31 to -15 °C (-24 to 5 °F), then brief summers that are warm or very warm, with July averages of 18 to 23 °C (64 to 73 °F). Between 400 and 700 millimetres (16 to 28 in) of rain falls yearly, mostly in summer. There are roughly 2,300 to 2,650 hours of sunshine a year, and in spring the Songnen and Sanjiang plains are a rich source of wind energy.

The provincial capital is also the largest city, and it is where the university is located. Others of note are Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi and Daqing, followed by Jixi, Shuangyashan, Hegang, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe.
Roads are well developed. Figures from October 2020 give a total of 165,989 km (103,141 mi) covering expressways, highways and other roads. The main corridors are these:
Beijing-Harbin Expressway: the key corridor into the province, starting at the Heilongjiang-Jilin border and ending inside the Harbin Ring Expressway

Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway: runs north-east and connects remote counties under Harbin and Jiamusi and other counties in the north-east; the Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off at Jiansanjiang to serve many state-owned farms in the far east, ending near the Sino-Russian border
Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway: runs south-east to north-west through Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar and ends at the Heilongjiang-Inner Mongolia border
Hegang-Dalian Expressway: carries lumber and coal between Hegang and the Heilongjiang-Jilin border in the east
The region has also hosted notable sporting events and leagues:
2009 Winter Universiade
2018 Bandy World Championship, Division B
Asia League Ice Hockey
Heilongjiang University of Chinese Medicine lists 71 programs for international students on this site: 21 bachelor, 28 master's, 22 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 71 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 21,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 21,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 31,000 to CNY 31,000 (median CNY 31,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 50,000 to CNY 50,000 (median CNY 50,000), according to the university's published fee table.

71 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

heilongjiang-university-of-chinese-medic.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Heilongjiang University of Chinese Medicine may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Harbin, register at Heilongjiang University of Chinese Medicine by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Henan University (河南大学, HENU) is a provincial public university in Henan, operating in both Kaifeng and Zhengzhou. It belongs to Henan Province, is jointly funded with the Ministry of Education, and takes part in the Double First-Class Construction, the national scheme for leading universities. It has three campuses: Minglun and Jinming in Kaifeng, and Longzi Lake in Zhengzhou.

The institution's earliest ancestor was founded in 1912 as a preparatory school in Henan for students heading to Europe and America. In 1942 it was raised to the status of National Henan University. In 1952, after departments were reorganised, it took the name Henan Normal University, and went through further names, including Kaifeng Normal College, before becoming Henan University in 1984. In June 2000 three institutions (the earlier Henan University, Kaifeng Medical College and Kaifeng Normal College) were combined to create the present university. In 2022, its registered legal address was moved from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou.

By December 2023, the university offered 92 undergraduate admission majors across its Longzi Lake, Minglun and Jinming campuses, which together cover more than 5,500 acres. Postgraduate authority includes 45 first-level disciplines and 35 categories for master's degrees, 21 first-level disciplines for doctorates, and 20 postdoctoral research stations. Staff exceed 4,700 and full-time students number more than 50,000. These are figures for one date, so check the university for the latest.

Rankings are a snapshot and different systems measure different things. The 2025 ARWU table (the Academic Ranking of World Universities) places Henan University in the 301-400 band. It was 391st in the CWTS Leiden Ranking, and 763rd in the 2025 U.S. News rankings. The most recent QS edition placed it in the 1201-1400 band. Because the lists are updated every year, consult the ranking bodies for the current positions.

The climate is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence (Koppen Cwa), bordering on humid continental, and each of the four seasons is distinct. Cool, largely dry winters give way to a warm spring with only modest rainfall, then a hot, sticky summer, and finally a crisp, drier autumn. Most rain falls from June to September. Since 1951 temperatures have ranged from minus 16 degrees Celsius (3 F) on 27 December 1971 to 42.9 degrees (109 F) on 19 June 1966. Plan for cool winters and humid summers, and for the most comfortable weather in spring and autumn.

The nearest major airport is Zhengzhou Xinzheng International (IATA code CGO, ICAO code ZHCC), around 55 km (34 miles) from downtown Kaifeng, which in 2017 was the busiest airport in central China for both passengers and cargo. Two intercity railways, the Zhengzhou-Kaifeng line and the Zhengzhou-Xinzheng Airport line, make it quicker to travel between the two. As of August 2018, 12 pairs of intercity trains ran each day between the airport and Songchenglu, taking 53 minutes.

Kaifeng railway station lies on the east-west Longhai Railway and has direct trains to many cities, among them Beijing West, Shanghai and Shanghai Hongqiao, Tianjin, Xi'an, Jinan and Hangzhou. Zhengzhou, Luoyang and Qingdao are served often and conveniently, and long-distance direct trains go as far as Harbin and Urumqi in the north and north-west, Chengdu and Chongqing North in the south-west, Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Fuzhou in the south, and Dalian and Wuhan.

The Zhengzhou-Kaifeng intercity railway has operated since 28 December 2014 between the provincial capital and Kaifeng. It currently ends at Songchenglu, with an extension to Kaifeng railway station planned, and the line is designed for speeds of up to 200 km/h (120 mph). The main high-speed station is Kaifeng North, on the Xuzhou-Lanzhou high-speed line, which opened on 10 September 2016.
Four main coach stations serve Kaifeng:
Kaifeng West Coach Station
Kaifeng Long-Distance Coach Station
Kaifeng Jinming Coach Station
Kaifeng Xiangguosi Coach Station
Buses run often to nearby counties and other cities in the province, and long-distance services reach other provinces. The roads passing through the area include these expressways and highways:
G30 Lianyungang-Khorgas Expressway
G45 Daqing-Guangzhou Expressway
S82 Zhengzhou-Minquan Expressway
S83 Lankao-Nanyang Expressway
China National Highways 106, 220 and 310

Kaifeng is known as the home of the Kaifeng Jews, China's oldest surviving Jewish community. A sizeable Muslim community also lives here and is renowned for its women's mosques (nushi), among them the oldest in China, the Wangjia Hutong Women's Mosque, dating from 1820. Active Christian churches include the Sacred Heart Cathedral.

Kaifeng's cooking is a main ingredient in Henan cuisine. Local specialities include steamed pies and dumplings, and especially famous is the five-spice flatbread (wuxiang shaobing), which can be split open and filled much as pita is. People from Zhengzhou often travel to Kaifeng to see relatives and to eat at the night markets. The Ma Yuxing Bucket Chicken House is regarded by some as the oldest restaurant in the world.

The chrysanthemum is Kaifeng's city flower. Growing different varieties goes back 1,600 years and reached its peak in the Song dynasty, before the Jurchens took the city in 1126. An annual Kaifeng Chrysanthemum Cultural Festival has run each autumn since 1983 (renamed in 1994), when hundreds of varieties go on display and flowers appear everywhere around town. The city has been nicknamed the city of chrysanthemums, so autumn is the time to visit.

The China Zheng-Kai International Marathon is organised each spring by the Chinese Athletic Association with city and provincial governments. It is the leading international sports event in Henan and one of the biggest in central-western China, taking place mainly along Zhengkai Avenue. In 2007, its first year, 5,600 athletes took part, and by 2012 nearly 25,000 runners from 28 countries and regions had joined.

henan-university.h: How many people live in Kaifeng

blocks.x: In the seventh national census of 2020, Kaifeng had a permanent population of 4,824,016. That was 147,857 more than the 4,676,159 counted in 2010, an increase of 3.16 percent over the decade, or an average of 0.31 percent a year.
Student life depends on the wider region as well as the campus, so here is a closer look at Henan.

Chinese tradition treats Henan as a birthplace of its civilisation. The province has a pattern of boom and bust: fertile plains and a position at the centre of the country brought wealth, yet that same strategic spot meant more wars than in many other regions, and the Yellow River has flooded from time to time and caused heavy damage.

Evidence from digs shows that the Yangshao and Longshan peoples lived in what is now northern Henan in Neolithic times. The Erlitou culture that followed has been tied, though not without argument, to the Xia, the traditional first dynasty and one that is mostly legend. Next came the Shang (roughly 1600 to 1046 BC), who took power from the Xia and kept their capitals in Henan. Inscribed oracle bones found at the Yinxu site in Anyang tell us a great deal about Shang writing, religious rites and society.

The Zhou, who arrived from the west in the eleventh century BC, defeated the Shang at Muye. Under the Western Zhou (about 1046 to 771 BC) the centre of power moved out of Henan for the first time. From 721 BC the Spring and Autumn period brought constant rivalry, as many small kingdoms fought for the central plain (a struggle summed up in a Chinese idiom). The Zhou king at Luoyang still held the title of ruler but had lost nearly all real authority over the feudal states. Laozi, who is credited with founding Taoism, was born in the northern Chu territory that lies in today's Henan.

In 221 BC Qin Shi Huang defeated six rival kingdoms and unified China proper. The Han (206 BC to AD 220) set up Henan Commandery and made Luoyang the empire's political and cultural centre. When the Han fell, disorder lasted a long time (220-589) through the Three Kingdoms, the Jin and the Northern and Southern Dynasties, and rival governments took the region in turn. Yet Henan stayed a key source of grain and a meeting ground for many ethnic groups and cultures in the north.

Reunification came with the Sui in 589. The Sui emperor Yang extended the Grand Canal to Luoyang, but the huge labour and cost wore the people out and helped bring the dynasty down. The Tang then ruled for around three hundred years before dying of internal conflict. During the following Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era (907-960), four of the dynasties had their capital at Kaifeng in the east of the province. The Song, who later reunified the country, were based there too, and in this period Kaifeng grew bigger than Luoyang or Chang'an, the largest city in both China and the world.

Jurchen forces from the north-east seized Kaifeng in 1127 and captured the Song emperor. The Yellow River shifted course in 1194, turning south to join the Huai through northern Jiangsu, and millions were forced from their homes. The Mongols overthrew the Jin early in the thirteenth century, took the region, and organised it as the Henan Jiangbei Branch Secretariat.

After so many deaths and so much flight from war and flood, the Ming court in the Hongwu reign ordered compulsory mass resettlement of people from Shanxi to Henan. In 1368 Weihui, Zhangde and Huaiqing prefectures, which lie north of the Yellow River, joined Henan's administration. In 1641 the rebel leader Li Zicheng took Luoyang and, the next year, besieged Kaifeng three times. In the third siege, Ming forces cut the Yellow River's dikes at Zhujiazhai and Majiakou, to the north of the city, to flood out the rebels. Kaifeng was swamped under several zhang of water. Out of 378,000 inhabitants, only 30,000 lived.

The fighting at the end of the Ming and start of the Qing (roughly 1630-1662) ravaged Henan again, but in the Kangxi reign farming recovered and the province regained its role as a populous, grain-producing region.

A dike on the Yellow River burst on 30 September 1887 at Xiayun Shibao, in Zhengzhou (now Shiqiao Village in Huayuankou Town, Huiji District). More than two million died by one common count, and estimates run from 930,000 up to 7 million. A Qing-history specialist, Xia Mingfang, called it the flood with the greatest loss of life in modern Chinese history, and an international-relations professor, Peter Hough, has called it one of history's deadliest natural disasters.

After the 1911 Revolution toppled the Qing, the Republic of China was proclaimed in 1912, and Yuan Shikai, a Henan native, became its first president. During the Second Sino-Japanese War, when Japanese forces took Kaifeng in 1938, the Chinese government breached the dike at Huayuankou near Zhengzhou to slow their advance. Floods hit Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu and caused several hundred thousand deaths. Then in 1942 drought, locusts and war damage produced a famine in Henan.

The People's Republic moved the provincial capital from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou in 1954 because the latter was so important for rail. It had earlier created Pingyuan Province, taking in the northern part of Henan and western Shandong with Xinxiang as capital, but abolished it in 1952.

Suiping County's Yashan became China's first people's commune in 1958, an event that signalled the start of the Great Leap Forward. Famines in the 1960s, blamed on that campaign, killed millions in Henan. Local resistance was mostly through banditry, and a peasant uprising in 1959 was crushed after twenty days.

The Huai River flooded badly in the summer of 1950, which led to dams being built on its tributaries across central and southern Henan. In August 1975 Typhoon Nina dropped more rain than some of them could take, and 62 dams collapsed, the biggest of them the Banqiao Dam in Biyang County. The flooding across Zhumadian Prefecture and farther downstream took at least 26,000 lives; unofficial estimates that include later epidemics and famine run much higher, between 85,600 and 230,000. Heavy rain in July 2021 brought floods that killed 302 people and caused damage worth 82 billion yuan.

The east of Henan is flat floodplain and the west is mountainous. Most of the province belongs to the North China Plain, which is called the breadbasket of China. In the north-west, the Taihang range enters from Shanxi and marks the south-eastern limit of the Loess Plateau. In the west, the Xionger and Funiu ranges make up a network of ridges and plateaus that shelter a surviving patch of the temperate broadleaf forest that used to blanket the entire province. Mount Song, with the Shaolin Temple, stands near Zhengzhou. In the far south the Dabie Mountains divide Hubei from Henan, and beyond them the Nanyang Basin is another farming and population centre whose culture and history are distinct and closer to Hubei's. Desertification is not a problem here, unlike the rest of northern China, though cities near the Yellow River get sandstorms from the river's sand. The highest point, at 2413.8 metres, is Laoyachanao.

The Yellow River enters from the north-west through the Sanmenxia Reservoir and, past Luoyang, leaves the mountains for the plain. The river carries silt from the Loess Plateau, which raised its bed and produced the floods that moulded the landscape; today dams, levees and reduced water supplies have stopped them. In the south, the Huai River is accepted as part of the boundary between northern and southern Chinese climate and culture.

Henan has about 98.2 million people, which puts it third among provinces, after Guangdong and Shandong, and fifth among all sub-national divisions worldwide. Treated as a country, it would rank twelfth, between Mexico and the Philippines. Under the household-registration (hukou) system it counts as the most populous province, with over 103 million people, because migrant workers are counted as residents of Henan; 85.14 million are classed as permanent residents of their registered households.

Demographically Henan is at a late stage of the transition. The birth rate has dropped to 7.06, compared with 9.24 in 2020 and 12.70 in 2015, and the death rate has crept up from 7.05 in 2015 to 8.00, possibly because the population is ageing. Natural growth turned negative, at minus 0.94 percent in 2023, and with steady out-migration this explains slower population growth. Life expectancy is 77.6 years, the same as nationwide. Most households have two to four people, 64.47 percent of residents are of working age (15-64), and the dependency ratio is 54.4 percent, close to the national picture.

There are 57.01 million urban residents, an urbanisation rate of 58 percent, lower than China's national average of 67%, up from 43.45 million in 2014. The shift owes mostly to rural-to-urban movement inside Henan, as the total population grew by under 2 million in the same period. Its per-person GDP ranks 25th out of 31 provinces, and average disposable income is near the national figure of 31.5k yuan.

Government is a major employer. Manufacturing, public administration, education and construction are the biggest sectors, which mirrors national trends, for example the Made in China 2025 plan for keeping manufacturing at the centre of global supply chains. Public administration, which covers jobs like social security and public management, has employed fewer people each year since 2020. In the private part of the urban economy, retail leads employment. The biggest contributions to regional output come from secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services) industries.

Henan runs a high-speed rail network shaped like the Chinese character for rice (a grid with eight directions), centred on Zhengzhou. By 2025 total railway operations reached 6,810 kilometres, including 2,263 kilometres of high-speed line, reaching every prefecture-level city.

henan-university.h: Which campus, and how to get around

blocks.x: Because Henan University operates in both Kaifeng and Zhengzhou, it is worth finding out early which campus your programme uses. The two Kaifeng campuses sit in a historic city that is smaller, quieter and known for its food and flowers, while the Longzi Lake campus is in the provincial capital, a much bigger transport hub. The intercity railway and the airport line shorten the trip between the two cities, so even if you are based in Kaifeng, Zhengzhou's airport and high-speed network are within easy reach.

Several kinds of number in this profile are snapshots: the university's student and staff counts, the rankings, the airport and rail timetables from particular years, and the provincial population and economic figures. Henan's population is reported in more than one way (resident, registered, or including migrant workers), so totals can differ by many millions depending on the definition. Please treat these as general guides, and rely on the university's own website and official statistics for the latest numbers.

For a student, Henan University offers large campuses in two cities, a city with an unusually rich history in Kaifeng, good rail links, and seasons in which autumn and spring are the most pleasant. The university's website holds the current details on admissions, programmes and campus life.
Henan University lists 134 programs for international students on this site: 21 bachelor, 70 master's, 43 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 99 taught in Chinese, 31 taught in Bilingual (Chinese and English), 4 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 24,800 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 22,400 to CNY 25,600 (median CNY 23,200), according to the university's published fee table.

134 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (4):
Foreign Languages and Literatures
Network and Information Security
Pure Mathematics
Software Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

henan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Henan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Kaifeng, register at Henan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

henan-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: About Henan University of Chinese Medicine

blocks.x: Henan University of Chinese Medicine (Chinese: 河南中医药大学; pinyin: Hénán Zhōngyīyào Dàxué) is a public university in Zhengzhou, Henan, China.

One of the earliest of its kind in China, Henan University of Chinese Medicine was established in 1958. It was authorized by the State Academic Council to confer bachelor's and master's degrees, and to collaborate with other universities or colleges in enrolling doctorate students. It was approved by the Ministry of Education to enroll international students as well as students from Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan.

The university offers bachelor's degrees in medicine, management, engineering science, and arts with 14 specialties as Chinese medicine, herbology, pharmaceutical engineering, acupuncture and tuina, integrated Chinese-Western medicine, and public management. It also offers master's degrees in 21 specialties, including Chinese internal medicine, Chinese pediatrics, herbal prescriptions, herbology, acupuncture and Tuina are the key programs of Henan Province.
The university faculty includes 15 doctoral tutors, 94 professors, 425 associate professors, 714 lecturers on campus, and 16 state-nominated and 10 province-nominated distinguished specialists.
There are over 10,000 students including over 150 international students.

It has 20 laboratories and three hospitals besides a central lab, an herbal plantation for quality control, a pharmaceutical factory, and specimen rooms. Institutions have been established in this university in the studies of Zhang Zhong-jing's theories, AIDS, hepatic diseases, gerontology, splenic and gastric diseases, pediatrics, rheumatoid arthritis, and ophthalmology.
The library has a collection of over 500,000 volumes and over 2,000 periodicals from home and abroad.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Zhengzhou, where Henan University of Chinese Medicine is located.

Located just north of the province's centre and south of the Yellow River, Zhengzhou borders Luoyang to the west, Jiaozuo to the northwest, Xinxiang to the northeast, Kaifeng to the east, Xuchang to the southeast, and Pingdingshan to the southwest. With the land within its administrative borders generally sloping down from west to east, Zhengzhou is situated at the transitional zone between the North China Plain to the east and the Song Mountains and Xionger Mountains to the west, which are part of the greater Qinling range. The city centre is situated to the south of the middle reach of the Yellow River, where its valley broadens into the great plain. Zhengzhou is at the crossing point of the north–south route skirting the Taihang Mountains and the mountains of western Henan. The prefecture spans 34° 16' ~ 34° 58 N latitude and 112° 42' ~ 114° 14' E longitude, covering a total area of 7,567 square kilometres (2,922 sq mi), including the metropolitan area, which covers 1,284.89 km2 (496.1 sq mi), and the city centre, which occupies 709.69 square kilometres (274.0 sq mi).

A section of the Yellow River passes by the northern edges of the urban area, extending 150.4 km (93.5 mi) within Zhengzhou prefecture. However, Jialu River, a secondary tributary of the Huai River, is Zhengzhou's main urban river and flood channel. The Jialu enters Zhengzhou from Xinmi to the southwest, and turns to the southeast within the city. Mountains loom over the western counties of Gongyi and Dengfeng while the easternmost county of Zhongmu is a vast, fertile floodplain, with the counties in between being hilly transitions.

Zhengzhou experiences a monsoon-influenced, four-season humid subtropical climate (Köppen climate classification Cwa), with cool, dry winters and hot, humid summers. Spring and autumn are dry and somewhat abbreviated transition periods. The city has an annual mean temperature of 15.4 °C (59.7 °F), with the monthly 24-hour average temperature ranging from 1.0 °C (33.8 °F) in January to 27.8 °C (82.0 °F) in July. The frost-free period lasts on average 220 days. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −17.9 °C (0 °F) on 2 January 1955, 27 December 1971 and 1 February 1990 to 43.0 °C (109 °F) on 19 July 1966.

Rainfall is primarily produced by the monsoonal low during summer; in winter, when the vast Siberian High dominates due to radiative cooling from further north, the area receives little precipitation. During the summer season, the city is also often affected by tropical depressions, which bring additional amounts of rain. The annual precipitation is about 630 millimetres (25 in). With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 37 percent in January to 49 percent in April and May, the city receives 1,905 hours of sunshine per year, which is around 43% of the possible total.
In 2019, there were 177 good days in Zhengzhou, an increase of 9 days year-on-year, and 48.5% of the good days reached the standard. There were 24 days of heavy pollution, 9 days less than last year.

On 20 July 2021, "The heaviest hour of rainfall ever reliably recorded in China crashed like a miles-wide waterfall over the city of Zhengzhou on 20 July, killing at least 300 people, including 14 who drowned in a subway tunnel." Although an emergency alert was issued the day before the flood, businesses and subways remained open. From 4pm to 5pm on 21 July, 7.95 inches of rain fell. A collapsed retaining wall allowed water to pour into subway tunnels. "The Chinese government now appears to be acknowledging missteps by local officials, as well as the possibility that severe weather events will become increasingly common."

Zhengzhou, along with Xi'an, Chengdu, Chongqing and Wuhan, are some of the most economically important cities in inland China. Zhengzhou is the economic center of the province and the surrounding areas such as southeastern Shanxi and southwestern Shandong. Due to its strategic location in one of the most populous areas in the world (nearly 100 million people in Henan alone) and in China's railway, road and aviation transport networks, Zhengzhou is increasingly attracting domestic and international investment as well as migrants from other areas, transforming the city into one of the largest economic centers in China. In 2018, total GDP of Zhengzhou was ¥1020 billion, ranked 17th in China. And in 2021,  total GDP was ¥1269.1 billion, ranked 16th in China. In the first half of 2026, the GDP of city was reached 777.27 billion RMB.

By the end of 2006, Zhengzhou had a total population of over 7 million, of which 2.88 million lived in rural areas. Its main products include apples, paulownia, tobacco, maize, cotton, and wheat. In addition, Zhengzhou also produces Yellow River carp, Zhengzhou watermelons, Xinzheng jujube, Xingyang dried persimmons, Guangwu Pomegranate and Zhongmu garlic, all of which are specialties that are rarely found outside the region.
Zhengzhou and the surrounding area have large reserves of coal and other minerals. Coal mining and electricity generation are traditionally important in the local economy.

Zhengzhou has been one of the major industrial cities in The People's Republic of China since 1949. The city's staple industry is textiles. Others manufactured items include tractors, locomotives, cigarettes, fertilizer, processed meats, agricultural machinery, and electrical equipment. Some high-tech companies in new material, electronics and biotechnology are also growing rapidly during the recently years, especially in the high-tech industrial park in the northwest of the city.
Yutong, China's largest bus producer.
Shaolin Bus, a well-known small-to-medium-sized bus producer.
Dongfeng Nissan, specializing in the manufacture of SUVs and pickup trucks.
Haima Automobile Zhengzhou, an automobile manufacturer specializing in manufacturing microvans and light passenger vehicles.
Zhengzhou Unique Industrial Equipment Co., Ltd., a large tractor and agricultural equipment manufacturer.
Foxconn Zhengzhou, located in Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone, is the largest smartphone production site in the world and is also known as "iPhone City".
Sanquan Food, a frozen food company. With over 20,000 employees, Sanquan produced the first frozen dumplings and rice balls in China.
Synear Food Holdings Limited, along with Sanquan Food, is one of the largest producers of frozen food in China. The market share is over 20% in China
BYD Auto opened one of its largest manufacturing plants in 2023, which by 2025 employed 60,000 workers.

The service industries of Zhengzhou include retail, wholesale, hospitality, finance, exhibition, transport and delivery, tourism, and education. With a number of domestic and international institutions having regional offices in the city, Zhengzhou is becoming the financial center in central China. Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange (ZCE) is one of the only four future exchanges (inc. Shanghai Futures Exchange and Dalian Commodity Exchange and China Financial Futures Exchange) in China and is becoming an important global player specialised in agricultural future exchange. Equipped with newly built facilities such as Zhengzhou International Conference and Exhibition Center. Third party logistics (3PL) in Zhengzhou has also been experiencing industrial boom during the past few years. As a transit and tourist center of Henan Province and central China, Zhengzhou is the center of Henan cuisine.
Dennis, a regional retail chain.
Henan Jianye, a large real estate developer, which owns the China Super League club Henan Jianye F.C.

The Zhengdong New Area (Chinese: 郑东新区), literally Eastern Zhengzhou New Area, similar to Hangzhou Bay New Area in Ningbo and Hangzhou Bay New Area in Ningbo, is one of dozens of major economic zones that are currently developing in various regions of China. Established in 2003 by the provincial and municipal governments, it has become the financial center of Henan province and one of the most rapidly growing areas of China.

Kisho Kurokawa, a Japanese world-renowned planner and architect, was appointed to design the overall planning scheme for Zhengdong New Area. He brought in advanced ideas including ecological city, co-existing city, metabolic city and ring city ideas. The scheme won the "Prominent Award for City Planning Design" at the first session of Annual Meeting of the World Architects Alliance in 2002. Zhengdong New Area is mainly constituted by the CBD area, the Longhu commercial and residential area, the Longzihu college area, and the Zhengzhou East railway station commercial area.
Zhengzhou New & Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone

Zhengzhou High & New Technology Industries Development Zone was established in 1988, and approved by the state Council of PRC to be a state development zone on Mar.6,1991. It was appraised to be advanced high tech zone of China respectively in 1993, 1998 and 2002. The Zone currently covers a total area of 18.6 square kilometres (7.2 square miles). An extension plan was approved by Zhengzhou Municipal Government, the various construction work started in 2004. Under the development strategy of "multiple parks in one zone", the Zone has been making great efforts to promote the development of software, information technologies, new materials, bio-pharmaceutical and photo-machinery-electronic industries.
Zhengzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone

Zhengzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone was approved as state-level development zone on 13 February 2000. The zone has a developed area of 7 square kilometres (3 square miles) Industries encouraged include Electronics Assembly & Manufacturing, Telecommunications Equipment, Trading and Distribution, Biotechnology/Pharmaceuticals, Instruments & Industrial Equipment Production, Medical Equipment and Supplies, Shipping/Warehousing/Logistics and Heavy Industry.
Zhengzhou Export Processing Area

Zhengzhou (Henan) Export Processing Zone was established on 21 June 2002 with approval by the state council. Its planned area is 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile). Zone A is located in Zhengzhou National Economic & technological Development Area and began to operate on 1 June 2004. The area of land developed is 0.893 square kilometres (0.345 square miles) at present. Zone B is located in Zhengzhou Airport Area and is adjacent to Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport on the north and it covers a planned area of 5 square km with bonded logistics zone, bonded processing zone and supporting industry zone, etc.
Zhengzhou is located in the central part of China and is a main national transport hub.

The Zhengzhou Metro is a rapid transit metro rail network serving urban and suburban districts of the Zhengzhou metropolitan area. The system started operation on 28 December 2013. As of 2026, it currently has 13 lines in operation, creating a 450 km (280 mi) long network. The first two lines (Line 1 and Line 2) were approved by the National Development and Reform Commission in Feb. 2009. Construction of the two lines started in 2009 and 2010, and were finished in 2013 and 2015 respectively. The Chengjiao Line (planned to be part of Line 9), which is now in through operations with Line 2, allows the system to serve the Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport. A total of 21 metro lines have been planned to connect all areas in Great Zhengzhou Metropolitan Area.

As of 2026, Zhengzhou Metro operates 13 lines with a total operating length of 450 km, namely Lines 1–8, 10, 12 and 14, the Suburban Line, and the Zhengxu Line. Line 6 Phase I became fully operational on 30 November 2024, when its northeast section entered initial operation, while Line 7 Phase I and Line 8 Phase I opened on 29 December 2024. Zhengzhou's updated rail transit network plan, approved by the municipal government in May 2025, envisions 22 lines totaling about 1,260 km by 2035 and 30 lines totaling about 1,600 km by 2050.

The Zhengzhou subway fares has a segmented pricing system. The starting price is 2 yuan ($0.28) for a ride of up to 6 kilometers. If the mileage exceeds 6 kilometers, the principle of "decreasing for further distances" will apply. Within the mileage of 6 to 13 kilometers, 1 yuan ($0.14) will be added for every 7 kilometers, and for 8 kilometers between 13 and 21 kilometers, 1 yuan ($0.14) will be added. For each additional 9 kilometers above 21 kilometers, an additional 1 yuan ($0.14) is added. Riders can use cash, a physical metro card, or QR code payment available on Alipay or WeChat apps to pay for the ride.
Zhengzhou has a bus system with over 5,700 bus vehicles, operated by the Zhengzhou Bus Communication Corporation (ZZB).

The operations of Zhengzhou Bus Rapid Transit commenced in 2009. The system consists of 5 main routes (B1, B2, B3, B5 and B6) with dedicated bus lanes and dozens of branch routes that serve most areas of the city.

Zhengzhou is the junction of the Longhai Railway (Lianyungang, Jiangsu–Lanzhou, Gansu) and the Beijing–Guangzhou Railway as well as a major national railway hub. The main railway station for these conventional services is Zhengzhou railway station, opened in 1904.

Zhengzhou is also on the Beijing–Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong high-speed railway and the Xuzhou–Lanzhou High-Speed Railway. The high-speed rail network provides fast train services to most major cities in China, including Beijing (2.5 hours), Guangzhou (6 hours), Xi'an (2 hours), Wuhan (2 hours), Shanghai (4 hours), Nanjing (3 hours), Hangzhou (5 hours), and Hong Kong (6.5 hours). Proposed high-speed railways from Zhengzhou to Chongqing, Hefei, Jinan and Taiyuan are under construction.
The completion of the Zhengzhou–Jinan high-speed railway, planned for 2023, will complete a star-shaped (referred to as a "米"-shaped) network of eight high-speed lines radiating out from the city.

Zhengzhou is also the hub of intercity railways in Henan. Currently there are three intercity railways from Zhengzhou: Zhengzhou–Kaifeng intercity railway, Zhengzhou–Jiaozuo intercity railway and Zhengzhou–Xinzheng Airport intercity railway are in operation.

Zhengzhou East railway station is dedicated to high-speed trains and is one of the largest in Asia and Zhengzhou Hangkonggang railway station is a new high-speed railway hub dedicated to Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone.
Zhengzhou North railway station, over 6,000 metres (20,000 ft) long and over 800 metres (2,600 ft) wide, has been described as Asia's largest classification yard.

Henan University of Chinese Medicine is in Henan, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Henan.

Regarded as the cradle of ancient Chinese culture, Henan is known for its historical prosperity and periodic downturns. The economic prosperity resulted from its somewhat fertile plains and its location at the heart of the country. Its strategic location also means that it has undergone more wars compared to certain other regions in China. The floods of the Yellow River have caused damage from time to time.

Archaeological sites reveal that prehistoric cultures such as the Yangshao Culture and Longshan Culture were active in what later is northern Henan since the Neolithic Era. The later Erlitou culture has been controversially identified with the Xia dynasty, the first and mostly legendary Chinese dynasty.

The Shang dynasty (c. 1600 – c. 1046 BC) overthrew the Xia, with their capitals centered in Henan. The discovery of oracle bone scripts at the Yinxu site in Anyang provided invaluable insight into their writing, rituals, and social structure.

In the 11th century BC, the Zhou people arrived from the west and overthrew the Shang dynasty in the Battle of Muye. During the Western Zhou period (c. 1046 – 771 BC), the capital and political and economical center was moved away from Henan for the first time. The Spring and Autumn period, a period of warfare and rivalry, began in 721 BC. What later is Henan and all of China was several kingdoms, which are at war for control of the central plain. (逐鹿中原) While regarded formally as the ruler of China, the control that Zhou king in Luoyang exerted over the feudal kingdoms had virtually disappeared. Laozi, the founder of Taoism, was born in northern Chu, part of what later is Henan.
Qin Shi Huang conquered six kingdoms and unified China proper in 221 BC, and the Han Dynasty (206 BC–220 AD) made Henan Commandery.The empire made Luoyang its political and cultural heart.

Following the Han's fall, Henan entered a period of prolonged turmoil during the Three Kingdoms, Jin, and the Northern and Southern Dynasties (220–589 AD). The region changed hands repeatedly among rival regimes. Despite the destruction, Henan continued to serve as a vital agricultural base and a melting pot of diverse ethnic groups and cultures in northern China.

The Sui dynasty reunified China in 589. Emperor Yang of Sui had the Grand Canal extended to Luoyang, but the massive expenditure of manpower and resources exhausted the populace, which ultimately led to the fall of the Sui empire.

The Tang dynasty lasted for three centuries before it eventually succumbed to internal strife. In the Period of Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms (907–960) that followed, Kaifeng in eastern Henan became the capital of four dynasties. The Song dynasty that reunified China in 982 also had its capital at Kaifeng. Under Song rule, Kaifeng overtook Luoyang and Chang'an as the largest city in China and in the world.

In 1127, the Jurchens, a people from the northeast, captured Kaifeng and took the Song emperor prisoner. In 1194, the Yellow River changed its course, flowing southward into the Huai River through what is now northern Jiangsu, displacing millions of people. In the early 13th century, Mongols destroyed the Jin dynasty and conquered this region, establishing the Henan Jiangbei Branch Secretariat (河南江北行省).

Due to heavy casualties and mass migration caused by warfare and flooding, the Ming court under the Hongwu reign organized large-scale, compulsory resettlement from Shanxi to Henan. In 1368, the prefectures of Weihui (衛輝), Zhangde (彰德), and Huaiqing (懷慶)—areas north of the Yellow River—were placed under Henan's government. In 1641, the peasant rebel leader Li Zicheng captured Luoyang. The following year, Li's forces besieged Kaifeng three times. During the third siege, troops of Ming court breached the Yellow River dikes at Zhujiazhai and Majiakou north of the city in an attempt to flood the rebels. The waters inundated Kaifeng, submerging the entire city under several zhang of water. Of the city's 378,000 residents, only 30,000 survived.

The wars of the late Ming and early Qing (circa 1630–1662) once again devastated Henan. During the Kangxi reign, the province's agricultural economy recovered, and it gradually regained its status as a major population center and grain-producing region.

On 30 September 1887, a major Yellow River dike breach occurred at Xiayun Shibao in Zhengzhou (present-day Shiqiao Village, Huayuankou Town, Huiji District). The disaster claimed over two million lives (with estimates ranging from 930,000 to as high as 7 million). Xia Mingfang, a scholar of Qing history, called it "the most severe flood disaster in terms of population loss in modern Chinese history," while Peter Hough, professor of international relations at Middlesex University, described it as "one of the deadliest natural disasters in human history."

The Qing dynasty was overthrown by the 1911 Revolution and then the Republic of China was established in 1912, during which a man from Henan, Yuan Shikai, played a role and thus became the first president of Republic of China.

In 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, when the Imperial Japanese Army captured Kaifeng, the government led by Chiang Kai-shek bombed the Huayuankou dam in Zhengzhou in order to prevent Japanese forces from advancing further. This caused flooding in Henan, Anhui, and Jiangsu resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths. In 1942 Henan was hit by the Chinese famine of 1942-43 resulting from a mix of drought, locusts and destruction caused by the war.

In 1954, the government of the People's Republic of China moved the capital of Henan from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou, as a result of its railway transportation importance. The PRC had earlier established a Pingyuan Province consisting of what later is northern Henan and western Shandong with Xinxiang as its capital. This province was abolished in 1952.

In 1958, Yashan in Suiping County, Henan, became the first people's commune of China, heralding the beginning of the "Great Leap Forward". In the subsequent famines of the 1960s, which are attributed to the Great Leap Forward, millions of people died in Henan. Suffering under famine and economic chaos caused by the Great Leap, locals in Henan offered resistance mostly through banditry. In 1959, a peasant uprising erupted and was defeated after twenty days of fighting.

A destructive flooding of the Huai River in the summer of 1950 prompted construction of dams on its tributaries in central and southern Henan. Some of the dams were not able to withstand the levels of rainfall caused by Typhoon Nina in August 1975. Sixty-two dams, the largest of which was the Banqiao Dam in Biyang County collapsed; flooding, spread over counties throughout Zhumadian Prefecture and further downstream, killed at least 26,000 people. Unofficial human life loss estimates, including deaths from the ensuing epidemics and famine, range as high as 85,600, 171,000 or 230 000.
In July 2021, rainfall caused flooding, killing 302 and damaging amounting to 82 billion yuan.
