Henan University of Technology (河南工业大学, abbreviated HAUT) is a public university run by the province, located in Zhengzhou, the capital of Henan. Its funding comes from two sources: the National Administration of Grain and the Henan Provincial People's Government. That link that explains much of its academic character.

The present institution was formed in 2004 when two schools were merged. One was the Zhengzhou Industrial Higher Vocational School (郑州工业高等专科学校) and the other was the Zhengzhou Institute of Technology (郑州工程学院); each had been set up back in 1956, so the university traces its roots to that year.

At present it operates from three campuses, located along Lianhua Street, Songshan Road and Zhongyuan Road, with a building area of about 1.013 million square metres, including modern teaching buildings and student apartments. Published figures for the total land area of the campuses are not consistent, so the university's own website is the safest place to confirm how large the campuses are.

henan-university-of-technology.h: What the university is known for

blocks.x: Grain is the thread that runs through HAUT. Food science and technology is one of its signature specialities, and it covers cereal science and technology, cereal-based foods, the storage of grains and grain products, and the chemistry and technology of oils and fats. Two other strengths sit alongside these: the physical distribution of grain (the logistics side) and grain machinery.

For a prospective student, this means that if your interests lie in food, grain processing, storage, or the machinery and logistics around them, the university has a focus that is unusual and clearly defined. If you want something else, check the current list of programmes directly with the admissions office.
Daily life depends on the city around the campus: its geography, climate, economy and transport. The following sections introduce Zhengzhou, and later sections describe the wider province of Henan.

Zhengzhou lies a little north of the centre of the province and south of the Yellow River. The surrounding cities are Luoyang (west), Jiaozuo (northwest), Xinxiang (northeast), Kaifeng (east), Xuchang (southeast) and Pingdingshan (southwest).

The land slopes down from west to east, and the city stands where the North China Plain, to its east, gives way to the Song and Xionger Mountains in the west, ranges that form part of the greater Qinling system. The urban centre is south of the middle stretch of the Yellow River, where the valley opens out onto the plain, and Zhengzhou stands where the north-south route along the Taihang Mountains meets the mountains of western Henan.

The area runs from 34° 16' to 34° 58' north and 112° 42' to 114° 14' east. In total the prefecture spans 7,567 square kilometres (2,922 sq mi). The built-up metropolitan area makes up 1,284.89 km2 (496.1 sq mi) of that, and the core of the city itself measures 709.69 square kilometres (274.0 sq mi).

The Yellow River passes along the northern edge of the urban area, and 150.4 km (93.5 mi) of it runs inside the prefecture. The city's main river and flood channel, however, is the Jialu River, which feeds into the Huai River as a secondary tributary. It comes in from Xinmi in the southwest and turns southeast once inside the city. Mountains dominate the western counties, Gongyi and Dengfeng; Zhongmu, the county furthest east, is wide and fertile floodplain; and the counties in the middle are hilly.

Zhengzhou has a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate with four seasons (Köppen classification Cwa). Winters are cool and dry, and summers are both hot and humid; the two shoulder seasons, spring and autumn, are short and dry.

The annual mean temperature is 15.4 °C (59.7 °F). January is the coolest month, averaging 1.0 °C (33.8 °F), and July the warmest at 27.8 °C (82.0 °F). The frost-free period lasts roughly 220 days. Since 1951 the temperature has fallen as low as −17.9 °C (0 °F), which happened on 2 January 1955, 27 December 1971 and again on 1 February 1990, and has climbed as high as 43.0 °C (109 °F), recorded on 19 July 1966.

Summer rain comes from the monsoon, while winter is dominated by the Siberian High and is very dry. Tropical depressions also often add rain in summer. Yearly precipitation comes to roughly 630 millimetres (25 in). Possible sunshine is lowest in January at 37 percent and highest in April and May at 49 percent, giving 1,905 hours of sunshine a year, about 43% of the possible total.

On air quality, 2019 recorded 177 good days, nine more than the year before, with 48.5% of the days meeting the standard, and 24 days of heavy pollution, nine fewer than the previous year. These are year-specific figures, so look for the latest data if air quality matters to you.

Newcomers should know about the flood of 20 July 2021. It brought the heaviest hourly rainfall ever reliably recorded in China, and at least 300 people died, among them 14 people who drowned inside a subway tunnel. An emergency alert had been issued a day before, yet businesses and the subway were still operating. During the hour from 4pm to 5pm on 21 July, 7.95 inches of rain came down, and a collapsed retaining wall let water into the subway tunnels. Reporting afterwards noted that officials were reviewing how the city responded and that extreme weather events may become more common. It is a reminder to follow weather alerts closely during the rainy season.

Together with Xi'an, Chengdu, Chongqing and Wuhan, Zhengzhou ranks among inland China's most important economic cities. It acts as the commercial centre of Henan and also of neighbouring parts of southeastern Shanxi and southwestern Shandong. Nearly 100 million people live in Henan alone, and the city sits at the heart of the country's rail, road and air networks. These advantages draw domestic and international investment, and migrants from elsewhere, and are turning it into one of the biggest economic centres in China.

Its total GDP was ¥1020 billion in 2018, ranked 17th in the country, and ¥1269.1 billion in 2021, ranked 16th. A figure of 777.27 billion RMB has also been reported for the first half of 2026. Because economic statistics are revised often, treat these as indicators of scale.

At the end of 2006 the population of Zhengzhou stood above 7 million, with 2.88 million of them in rural areas. Farmers grow wheat, maize, cotton, tobacco, apples and paulownia. Local specialities that are seldom found elsewhere include Zhongmu garlic, Guangwu pomegranate, Xingyang dried persimmons, Xinzheng jujube, Zhengzhou watermelons and carp from the Yellow River.
The city and the land around it hold big deposits of coal and other minerals, and coal mining and electricity generation have long been important locally.

The city has been a major industrial centre since 1949, and textiles are its staple industry. It also makes tractors, locomotives, cigarettes, fertiliser, processed meat, agricultural machinery and electrical equipment. In recent years high-tech firms in new materials, electronics and biotechnology have grown quickly, especially in the high-tech park in the northwest.
Some well-known employers:
Yutong, China's largest bus maker.
Shaolin Bus, a well-known producer of small and medium-sized buses.
Dongfeng Nissan, which specialises in SUVs and pickup trucks.
Haima Automobile Zhengzhou, which builds microvans and light passenger vehicles.
Zhengzhou Unique Industrial Equipment Co., Ltd., which makes tractors and other farm equipment on a large scale.
Foxconn Zhengzhou, in the Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone, described as the world's largest smartphone production site and nicknamed "iPhone City".
Sanquan Food, a frozen-food company with over 20,000 employees that produced China's first frozen dumplings and rice balls.
Synear Food Holdings Limited, which together with Sanquan is one of China's largest frozen-food producers, with a market share above 20% nationally.
BYD Auto, which opened one of its largest plants in 2023 and had 60,000 workers there by 2025.

The service sector covers retail, wholesale, hospitality, finance, exhibitions, transport and delivery, tourism and education. Many domestic and foreign institutions have regional offices here, and Zhengzhou is becoming the financial centre of central China.

The Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange is one of only four futures exchanges in China (the others are the Shanghai Futures Exchange, the Dalian Commodity Exchange and the China Financial Futures Exchange), and it is growing into a significant global player in agricultural futures. The city has also built the Zhengzhou International Conference and Exhibition Center, and third-party logistics has boomed. As the transit and tourist centre of Henan and central China, Zhengzhou is also the centre of Henan cuisine, which is good news for anyone who enjoys trying regional food.
Other local names include Dennis, a regional retail chain, and Henan Jianye, a large property developer that also owns a football club in the China Super League.

Zhengdong New Area (郑东新区, "Eastern Zhengzhou New Area") is one of dozens of large economic zones being developed across China. The provincial and municipal governments set it up in 2003, and it has become Henan's financial centre and one of the fastest-growing areas in the country.

The Japanese architect and planner Kisho Kurokawa was appointed to design the overall plan. He introduced the ideas of an ecological city, a co-existing city, a metabolic city and a ring city. At the World Architects Alliance's first annual meeting, in 2002, the plan received a "Prominent Award for City Planning Design". The area comprises the CBD, the Longhu commercial and residential district, the Longzihu college district and the commercial zone around Zhengzhou East railway station.
The city has three main industrial zones. The first is Zhengzhou New and Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone.

The Zhengzhou High and New Technology Industries Development Zone started in 1988 and was approved by the State Council as a national zone on 6 March 1991. It was rated an advanced high-tech zone of China in 1993, 1998 and 2002. Its area today is 18.6 square kilometres (7.2 square miles), and building work on an expansion plan approved by the municipal government began in 2004. Following a "multiple parks in one zone" approach, it concentrates on software, information technology, new materials, bio-pharmaceuticals and photo-machinery-electronic industries.

The second is Zhengzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone. It became a state-level zone on 13 February 2000 with 7 square kilometres (3 square miles) developed so far. Encouraged industries are heavy industry, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, electronics assembly, telecommunications equipment, medical equipment and supplies, instruments and industrial equipment, trading and distribution, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.

The third is Zhengzhou Export Processing Area. It was approved by the State Council and established on 21 June 2002 and was planned to cover 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile). Zone A sits within the economic and technological development area, opened on 1 June 2004, and so far 0.893 square kilometres (0.345 square miles) has been developed. Zone B lies in the airport area, just north of Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport, with 5 square km planned for a bonded logistics zone, a bonded processing zone and a supporting industry zone.
Zhengzhou sits at the centre of the country and serves as a major national transport hub, which is useful if you plan to travel during holidays.

The Zhengzhou Metro serves urban and suburban districts. It began operating on 28 December 2013. These are the Suburban Line, the Zhengxu Line and Lines 1 to 8, 10, 12 and 14. The National Development and Reform Commission signed off on Lines 1 and 2 in February 2009, building started in 2009 and 2010, and the two lines were completed in 2013 and 2015. The Chengjiao Line, planned as part of Line 9, runs through-services with Line 2 and connects the system to Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport. Altogether 21 lines have been planned to link every part of the Greater Zhengzhou metropolitan area.

Recent openings include Line 6 Phase I, fully operating from 30 November 2024, and the first phases of Line 7 and Line 8, both opened on 29 December 2024. In May 2025 the municipal government approved an updated rail plan that aims for 22 lines of about 1,260 km by 2035 and 30 lines totalling roughly 1,600 km by 2050.

Fares are distance-based. A ride up to 6 kilometres costs 2 yuan ($0.28). From 6 to 13 kilometres, 1 yuan ($0.14) is added for every 7 kilometres, between 13 and 21 kilometres 1 yuan ($0.14) is added for the 8 kilometres, and after 21 kilometres 1 yuan ($0.14) is added per extra 9 kilometres. You can pay with cash, a physical metro card, or a QR code through Alipay or WeChat.

The city has more than 5,700 buses, operated by the Zhengzhou Bus Communication Corporation (ZZB). Bus Rapid Transit began in 2009, using dedicated lanes on five trunk routes named B1, B2, B3, B5 and B6, along with dozens of branch routes reaching most parts of the city.

Zhengzhou is where the Longhai Railway (Lianyungang in Jiangsu to Lanzhou in Gansu) meets the Beijing-Guangzhou Railway, making it one of the country's major rail hubs. Conventional services use Zhengzhou railway station, which opened in 1904.

The city is also on the Beijing-Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway and the Xuzhou-Lanzhou High-Speed Railway. High-speed trains reach most major Chinese cities, with approximate journey times of 2.5 hours to Beijing, 6 hours to Guangzhou, 2 hours to Xi'an, 2 hours to Wuhan, 4 hours to Shanghai, 3 hours to Nanjing, 5 hours to Hangzhou and 6.5 hours to Hong Kong. Lines to Chongqing, Hefei, Jinan and Taiyuan have been under construction. The Zhengzhou-Jinan line was planned for completion in 2023 and would finish a star-shaped network of eight high-speed lines radiating from the city, shaped like the character 米; check its current status before relying on it.
Zhengzhou is also the hub for intercity railways in Henan. Three lines run from the city: to Kaifeng, to Jiaozuo and to Xinzheng Airport.

The city has several stations with different roles. Zhengzhou East handles only high-speed trains and ranks among Asia's biggest stations. Zhengzhou Hangkonggang is a recently built high-speed hub serving the Airport Economy Zone. Zhengzhou North is a freight yard more than 6,000 metres (20,000 ft) in length and over 800 metres (2,600 ft) across, described as the largest of its kind in Asia.

henan-university-of-technology.h: Henan, the province around the campus

blocks.x: Student life is shaped by the surrounding province as well as by the campus, and Henan has one of the longest recorded histories in China. The sections below summarise it.

Henan is often called the birthplace of ancient Chinese culture. Its history has been a mix of prosperity and periodic downturns: fairly fertile plains and a position at the heart of the country brought wealth, but that same central position meant it saw more wars than many other regions, and Yellow River floods have caused repeated damage.

Archaeological sites show that prehistoric cultures, namely the Yangshao and Longshan cultures, were active in what is now northern Henan from the Neolithic. The later Erlitou culture has been controversially linked to the Xia dynasty, the first and largely legendary Chinese dynasty.

The Shang dynasty (c. 1600 to c. 1046 BC) overthrew the Xia, and their capitals were in Henan. The discovery of oracle-bone script at Yinxu in Anyang gave valuable insight into their writing, rituals and social order.

The Zhou people arrived from the west in the 11th century BC and beat the Shang at the Battle of Muye. Under the Western Zhou (c. 1046 to 771 BC) power and wealth shifted away from Henan for the first time. Then, from 721 BC, came the Spring and Autumn period, an age of rivalry and war when the area that became Henan, along with the rest of China, was divided among kingdoms that fought over the central plain. The Zhou king in Luoyang was formally ruler but had almost no real control. Laozi, the founder of Taoism, is said to have been born in northern Chu, which lay in what later became Henan.

In 221 BC Qin Shi Huang defeated six kingdoms and brought China proper together. The Han Dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD) then created Henan Commandery, with Luoyang as the political and cultural heart of the empire.

After the Han fell, Henan went through long turmoil in the era of the Three Kingdoms, the Jin and the Northern and Southern Dynasties (220 to 589 AD), passing between rival regimes. Even so, it remained a key farming base and a place where many peoples and cultures of northern China mixed.

China was reunified by the Sui dynasty in 589. Emperor Yang pushed the Grand Canal as far as Luoyang, but the vast demand on labour and resources exhausted the people and ultimately brought the dynasty down.

The Tang lasted three centuries before succumbing to internal conflict. In the period of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms (907 to 960), Kaifeng in eastern Henan became capital of four dynasties. The Song dynasty, which reunified China in 982, also ruled from Kaifeng, and under it the city overtook Luoyang and Chang'an to become the largest in China and in the world.

In 1127 the Jurchens from the northeast took Kaifeng and captured the Song emperor. In 1194 the Yellow River changed course and flowed southward to join the Huai River, passing through what is now northern Jiangsu, and millions were displaced. Early in the 13th century the Mongols brought down the Jin dynasty and took the region, creating the Henan Jiangbei Branch Secretariat (河南江北行省).

War and flooding had cost many lives and driven others away, so under the Hongwu reign the Ming court ordered a large, compulsory resettlement of people from Shanxi into Henan. In 1368 three prefectures lying north of the Yellow River (Weihui, Zhangde and Huaiqing) came under Henan's administration. The rebel leader Li Zicheng took Luoyang in 1641, and in the following year his forces surrounded Kaifeng three times. At the third siege, Ming troops broke the river dikes at Zhujiazhai and Majiakou, to the city's north, hoping to flood the rebels. Kaifeng was submerged under several zhang of water, and only 30,000 of its 378,000 people survived.

Late Ming and early Qing wars (about 1630 to 1662) again devastated Henan. During the Kangxi reign, farming recovered and the province regained its place as a major population centre and grain producer.

On 30 September 1887 a dike on the Yellow River failed at Xiayun Shibao in Zhengzhou, in what is now Shiqiao Village, Huayuankou Town, Huiji District. More than two million people died, although estimates range from 930,000 to as many as 7 million. Historians describe it as the worst flood disaster in modern Chinese history in terms of lives lost, and one of the deadliest natural disasters ever recorded anywhere.
The Qing fell to the 1911 Revolution, and in 1912 the Republic of China was founded. Yuan Shikai, who came from Henan, played a part in this and became the Republic's first president.

In 1938, in the Second Sino-Japanese War, the Japanese army took Kaifeng. The Nationalist government responded by bombing the Huayuankou dam in Zhengzhou to hold back the advance. The flooding hit Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu and killed hundreds of thousands. Then in 1942 Henan suffered the Chinese famine of 1942-43, caused by a mix of drought, locusts and wartime destruction.

The People's Republic moved the capital of Henan from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou in 1954, because Zhengzhou mattered so much for rail transport. Earlier, a Pingyuan Province had been created from northern Henan and western Shandong, with its capital at Xinxiang; it was abolished in 1952.

In 1958 Yashan in Suiping County became China's first people's commune, marking the start of the Great Leap Forward. Famines followed in the 1960s, and these are linked to the campaign; millions of people in Henan died. Hardship and economic disruption led locals to resist mostly through banditry, and a peasant uprising in 1959 was put down after twenty days of fighting.

After a destructive Huai River flood in summer 1950, dams were built along its tributaries across central and southern Henan. Several could not withstand the rain that Typhoon Nina brought in August 1975, and 62 dams collapsed, the biggest being the Banqiao Dam in Biyang County. Floodwater spread over Zhumadian Prefecture and areas downstream, and at least 26,000 people died. Unofficial estimates, which also count deaths from the epidemics and famine that followed, reach 85,600, 171,000 or even 230,000.
In July 2021 heavy rain caused flooding that killed 302 people and caused damage of 82 billion yuan.

Hohai University, abbreviated HHU and written 河海大学 (Héhǎi Dàxué) in Chinese, is a state university in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu Province. The name combines "he" (river) and "hai" (sea), and the subject focus matches: marine and coastal engineering, hydraulic engineering, water resources and hydrology are what the university is best known for. It is a comprehensive institution, but generations of Chinese water-conservancy professionals have come out of its classrooms.

Hohai is overseen by the Ministry of Education and jointly sponsored by four bodies: the Ministry of Water Resources, the State Oceanic Administration, the Jiangsu provincial government and the Ministry of Education itself. It belongs to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction scheme.

The earliest root is the Hohai Civil Engineering School, which opened in 1915. It later joined the engineering department of National Southeastern University, becoming Hohai College of Engineering in 1924, and in 1928 it was absorbed into the Dyisyi Chungshan University as its Department of Water Resources, a university that later became National Central University.

When the People's Republic was founded in 1949 the department continued as the Department of Water Resources at Nanjing University. A major merger followed in 1952: water-related departments from Nanjing University, Jiaotong University, Tongji University and Zhejiang University, along with an engineering school for water resources in East China, came together as the East China Technical University of Water Resources. It received its present name, Hohai University, in 1985.

Hohai has three campuses covering 132 hectares (326 acres) in all. The main campus, 45 hectares (111 acres), sits on the northern slope of Qingliang Hill in Nanjing. Changzhou, which lies between Shanghai and Nanjing, received a second campus in February 1986, occupying 30 hectares in its High-Tech Development Zone. The third, of 57.6 hectares (142 acres), has been operating since September 2001 in the Jiangning Economic Development Zone, within Nanjing's Jiangning District.

The Hohai Library is spread over the three campuses and has a combined area of 47,000 square metres. Its collection comes to over 1.85 million books, among them 120,000 Chinese and English periodicals, and a further 567,000 e-books, with a CD database among them.

the 973 Project, a special fund for major state basic research
the 863 Program, a high-technology R&D scheme
the National Natural Science Foundation of China
It has also contributed to major water conservancy and hydropower undertakings, including:
the Huai River Waterway to Ocean project
dredging and channel regulation on the Yangtze estuary
the Xiaolangdi hydropower station
the Three Gorges Dam
the South-to-North Water Diversion Project

On the transport side it has taken part in large construction schemes such as the Nanjing Railway, the Nanjing-Shanghai Expressway, an expressway project in Guangdong, the Changjiang Second Bridge and the Runyang Yangtze River Bridge.

Since 1995 Hohai has won 262 awards for scientific research, among them 19 at state level and 185 at ministerial or provincial level. More than 11,822 papers have appeared in journals and at meetings in China and overseas, over 245 scientific monographs have been printed and nearly 94 patents have been granted.

hohai-university.h: Ties with industry and with the world

blocks.x: In December 2001 the university set up the Hohai Cooperation and Development Committee. The purpose was to answer the needs of economic construction and social development, to make higher education serve the economy more strongly and to widen the routes by which society can take part in running a university. Ms. Qian Zhengying, who had served as a vice president of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and as the founding president of that technical university, attended the first meeting and was elected honorary president. The committee has 24 prominent figures and scholars as commissioners, plus 120 unit commissioners drawn from enterprises and institutions at every level of government, in fields such as water conservancy, electric power, transport, environmental protection, education, finance and the army.

Hohai was one of the first universities that the State Council authorised to award doctoral, master's and bachelor's degrees to foreign students. Since then it has trained hundreds of doctoral, master's and bachelor's students for other countries and regions and has set up cooperative relationships with nearly 50 universities in more than 20 countries and regions. It is currently also a member of the BRICS Universities League.
Graduates and former students include figures in politics, engineering and science:
Zhang Wentian, who served as General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and later as a vice minister of foreign affairs
Mao Yisheng, a structural engineer often called the father of modern Chinese bridge engineering, who was also a social activist and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering
Xu Zhilun, an engineer and educator who belongs to the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Wen Fubo, a water conservancy engineer and Engineering Academy academician
Mao Zhi, an irrigation and drainage engineer, also an Engineering Academy academician
Wu Zhongru, who designed hydraulic structures and is an Engineering Academy academician
Zheng Shouren, a water conservancy and hydropower engineer and Engineering Academy academician

hohai-university.h: Nanjing: the setting for your studies

blocks.x: Daily life depends heavily on the city, so the sections that follow describe Nanjing's place in the landscape, its weather, rivers, nature, transport and people.

Nanjing covers 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 square miles) in the heart of the lower Yangtze drainage area, inside the Yangtze River Delta, which ranks among the biggest economic regions in China. The Yangtze passes the west side of the city and then turns along its north side, while the Ningzheng Ridge curves around the north, east and south. For orientation, Shanghai lies 270 kilometres (170 miles) to the east-southeast, Beijing 900 kilometres (560 miles) to the north-northwest, Luoyang 650 kilometres (400 miles) to the northwest and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) to the west-southwest.

From Jiujiang in Jiangxi, the Yangtze flows downstream across Anhui and Jiangsu before reaching the East China Sea. The Huai River basin occupies the northern half of the lower Yangtze drainage area and the Zhe River basin the southern half; the Grand Canal, east of Nanjing, links the two. The region is called Xiajiang (下江, "Downstream River"), with the Jianghuai culture strongest in the north and Jiangzhe in the south. It is also known as Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, "south of the river", meaning south of the Yangtze).

Around the city, Changzhou lies to the southeast, Zhenjiang to the east and Yangzhou to the northeast. Anhui borders it on the west, where it shares a boundary with five prefecture-level cities: Chuzhou in the northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan in the west and Xuancheng in the southwest.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), driven by the East Asian monsoon. Seasons are clearly defined, and damp weather is common all year. Summers are very hot and muggy, winters cold and damp, and spring and autumn are of fair length. Nanjing, Chongqing and Wuhan are traditionally counted as the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze because of their relentless summer heat. Between mid-June and late July comes the plum blossom season and the meiyu, the East Asian rainy season whose name means "plum rain", bringing gentle rain and dampness. Northeast winds dominate in winter, and southeast winds in summer.

For a city nicknamed a furnace, winters are surprisingly cold. They match London's or are colder: January is 2 °C colder than in London even though Nanjing lies at 32°04'N and London at 51°30'N, far closer to the equator. Compared with Savannah, Georgia, which has the same climate type on the American east coast, Nanjing's winter is 7 °C colder.

January's mean is 3.1 °C, equal to 37.6 °F, and the lowest daily temperature on record is -14.0 °C (6.8 °F), recorded on 6 January 1955. July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), and the highest daily temperature recorded was 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on 13 July 1934. There are about 112.9 days a year with more than 0.1 mm of precipitation, and the maximum count in one year was 160 days, in 1957. Rain and snow add up to 1,144 millimetres (45.0 inches) in an average year. Typhoons are rare but can occur in late summer and early autumn.

The yearly mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F). Looking only at the period since 1951, extremes ran from -14.0 °C (7 °F) on 6 January 1955 up to a high of 40.7 °C (105 °F), logged on 22 August 1959. Precipitation falls on about 113 days a year, adding up to 1,144 millimetres (45 inches). Sunshine reaches 37 percent of possible hours in June and rises to 48 percent in both August and October, giving 1,932.4 hours of bright sun every year. In practice: bring warm clothes for winter, and prepare for heat and dampness in summer.

Nanjing has abundant natural resources, with more than 40 kinds of minerals. Nanjing holds 40 percent of Jiangsu's iron and sulfur, and its strontium reserves rank first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water is plentiful from both the Yangtze and underground, and several natural hot springs exist, for example Pukou's Tangquan Hot Spring and Jiangning's Tangshan Hot Spring.

Two lakes, Xuanwu and Mochou, lie in the middle of the city and are easy for the public to reach. Purple Mountain, covered in deciduous and coniferous forest, shelters various historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel on the Yangtze is under construction so that Nanjing can handle 50,000 DWT vessels arriving from the East China Sea.

A thick wave of smog hit central and eastern China from 2 December 2013, spreading over roughly 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) and touching Zhejiang, Shanghai, Anhui, Jiangsu, Shandong, Hebei and Tianjin. Little cold air movement and slow air masses carrying industrial emissions let pollutants build into a heavy layer. Central and southern Jiangsu suffered most, especially Nanjing and its surroundings, where the AQI stayed at "severely polluted" for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine more. Officials attributed it to the lack of wind, vehicle exhaust under low air pressure and coal-fired district heating in northern China; the prevailing winds carried low-lying air with factory emissions, mostly SO2, toward the east coast. Episodes like this are mostly a winter issue, so students may want to check air quality forecasts.

Soil in Nanjing falls into two main groups, a zonal group and a cultivated group. Zonal soil is yellow-brown in the north and centre of the city and red in the south near the Anhui border. Cultivated soil, shaped by farming, is mostly paddy soil, with some vegetable garden soil and yellow Gang soil. Distribution follows the shape of the land and the hydrology, and falls into low mountain and hilly areas, hilly areas, and plains. The second national soil survey, run from 1980 to 1987, divided Nanjing's soil into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species over a total of 416,300 hectares.

Nanjing sits on the lower Yangtze, which crosses the city diagonally from southwest to northeast. The stretch within Nanjing is about 93 kilometres long, and the sea entrance is more than 300 kilometres away. The Qinhuai River runs from south to north through the main urban area before joining the Yangtze; it is known as Nanjing's mother river. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are described as two pearls set into the main city. Water now covers about 11% of the city's area.

Nearly all of the rivers and lakes belong to the Yangtze system; only the rivers draining into Baoying and Gaoyou lakes, in the north of Liuhe District, belong to the Huai River system. Within the Yangtze system are the Qinhuai River system south of the river, the Chuhe River system north of it, a riverside system of small streams, a two-lake system formed by Gucheng Lake and Shijiu Lake, and the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and of excellent quality, and Pukou Pearl Spring is especially well known. Hot spring areas with a long history exist at Jiangning's Tangshan and Pukou's Tangquan.

China's biggest inland port is Nanjing's, which handled 191,970,000 t of cargo in 2012. The port area is 98 kilometres (61 miles) long, with 64 berths, 16 of which take ships above 10,000 tons. It is also the biggest container port on the Yangtze: the Longtan Containers Port Area, a base with one million containers of capacity, opened in March 2004. As of 2010 the port ran three industrial ports and six public ones. A 12.5-metre-deep waterway lets 50,000-ton ocean ships reach Nanjing directly, and ships of 100,000 tons or more can also arrive after reducing their load during the Yangtze's high tide. CSC Jinling operates a large shipyard here.

Nanjing is one of the plant-rich areas of China, with many kinds of vegetation. Seven natural vegetation types are recorded: aquatic vegetation, grass, shrub, bamboo forest, mixed deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest and coniferous forest. Cultivated vegetation covers field crops, vegetables, orchards, green belts and economic forests. Seven species are listed as nationally protected rare and endangered plants.

Wildlife counts are detailed. There are 795 insect species in 125 families and 11 orders, and 99 fish species in 22 families and 12 orders. Terrestrial wild vertebrates number 327 species in 29 orders and 90 families, including 243 bird species in 56 families and 17 orders and 47 mammal species in 8 orders and 22 families. Nine species have first-level national protection, among them the Oriental White Crane and the White Shoulder Eagle. In the second protection tier are 65 species, including the little swan, the Chinese tiger, the swallowtail and the finless porpoise. In addition, 125 species are key protected animals of Jiangsu Province and 35 are endangered.

Nanjing's first Yangtze bridge was finished in the 1960s and was then the only bridge across the lower Yangtze in eastern China. It is a source of pride and a symbol of modern China, because the Chinese designed and built it themselves after other countries' surveys failed and after Soviet expertise was relied on and then rejected. Work began in 1960 and traffic started in 1968. The two-level road-and-rail bridge is 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) long on its upper deck, with about 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) over the river itself. Since then more bridges and tunnels have been added, and accounts differ on the exact counts. As of October 2014 the city had four bridges and two tunnels across the river, joining districts on the north bank to the centre on the south bank.

Reading from upstream to downstream, the crossings are the Qixiashan Bridge, Baguazhou Bridge, Yanziji Tunnel, the First Bridge, the Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the Line 10 metro tunnel, the River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Fifth Bridge, the Third Bridge and Dashengguan. The bridges, with opening year and longest span, are:
First Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (1968, longest span 160 m)
Second Bridge at Baguazhou (1997, longest span 628 m)
Third Bridge at Dashengguan (2005, longest span 648 m)
Fourth Bridge at Qixiashan (2012, longest span 1,418 m)
Fifth Bridge at Jiangxinzhou (2020, longest span 600 m)
Xianxin Bridge (2023, longest span 1,760 m)

Nanjing's mineral wealth covers 49 types, including clay, gypsum, limestone, dolomite, ferrosulfide, strontium, zinc, lead, copper and iron, and 31 of these have proven reserves. They are concentrated in four metallogenic belts, among them the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt and the Ningzhen belt, which has iron, copper and sulfur, along with the Ningwu iron and copper belt.

The 2010 census recorded 8.005 million people in the City of Nanjing, while the OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 11.7 million. Official statistics for 2011 gave the city 8.11 million, with an urban area population of 6.47 million. There were 107.31 men for every 100 women. Reported birth and death rates vary between sources, so use the latest official data if you need them.

Like much of eastern China, Nanjing has a Han majority of 98.56 percent, with 50 further official ethnic groups also present. A 1999 count found 77,394 residents from officially defined minorities. Hui people accounted for 64,832 of them, 83.76 percent of the minority total, while Manchu numbered 2,311 and Zhuang 533, the next largest groups. Jianye District housed most minority residents, who were 9.13 percent of that district's population.

Nanjing is an important grain and commercial agriculture base. Main cash crops include bamboo, tea, hemp, silkworm cocoons, cotton, rice, fruit and medicinal materials. The fertile waters on both sides of the Yangtze also make it one of China's key freshwater fishery bases. In 2019 total output from agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishing was 47.250 billion yuan, up 4.8% on the year before. Within that total, crops produced 24.077 billion yuan, forestry 2.017 billion, animal husbandry 2.435 billion, fisheries 15.389 billion and related services 3.333 billion.
Nanjing is a transport hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze. Land, water and air links form a three-dimensional system. As in most Chinese cities, most residents travel by public transport.
Hohai University lists 133 programs for international students on this site: 53 bachelor, 25 master's, 23 doctoral, 32 non-degree programs.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hohai-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hohai University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Hohai University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Huangshan University (黄山学院) is a higher education institution in the city of Huangshan, in Anhui Province, and it is run under the authority of the provincial government. Its roots go back to 1978, when it opened as Huangshan Specialized Normal School. In April 2002 the Ministry of Education approved its upgrade to a university, and it took the name Huangshan University while remaining attached to the Anhui provincial Education Bureau.

The campus covers a large area, recorded as 120,000,0 sq meters. As of July 2014 about 18,000 students were enrolled full time, which makes it a mid-sized provincial university with a settled student community.

huangshan-university.h: The city of Huangshan: what to expect

blocks.x: Daily life for a student depends heavily on the city around the campus, so this section looks at Huangshan itself, starting with what it earns a living from and then how you travel in and out.
Two industries define the local economy, and both are linked to the landscape you will see from campus.

Huangshan is known for tea. Keemun tea comes from Qimen County, and the city is also linked with Maofeng green tea. Tourism is the other big earner. It centres on Mount Huang and also takes in other scenic and historic places such as Xidi and Hongcun, which the city has marketed to overseas visitors in recent years.

For most of its history Huangshan was isolated by steep terrain. Boats on the Xinan River gave a way out to the east, but overland, twisting narrow roads across the Huang Mountains turned any trip towards the Yangtze, Xuancheng, Wuhu or Guichi into a slow ordeal. Over recent decades better infrastructure has made both the city and the nearby attractions far easier to reach.

The local airport is Huangshan Tunxi International Airport (code TXN), which people also call Tunxi Airport, in Tunxi District. Services started in October 1959, and five expansions have followed, one of them in 2000. You can fly on regular routes to Chinese cities as well as Taipei, Hong Kong and Seoul, and charter planes go to Incheon, Nagasaki, Osaka, Fukuoka and similar regional points.

Today you will mostly use Huangshan North station. Fast trains arrive there along three routes, Hefei–Fuzhou, Hangzhou–Nanchang and Chizhou–Huangshan, and connect the city with plenty of destinations.

Up to 2015 the city relied on one line only, the Anhui–Jiangxi Railway, completed in 1982. Its stops were Qimen County, Xiuning County, Tunxi District, She County and Jixi County. From Huangshan Station in Tunxi, trains once ran north to Nanjing, Shanghai, Bengbu, Huaibei, Qingdao, Beijing and other cities, and south to Kunming, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Yingtan and Jingdezhen. Long-distance passenger trains no longer use that route.

Drivers have good options. Expressway G56 (Hangzhou–Ruili), expressway G3 (Beijing–Taipei) and National Route G205 all pass through Huangshan City. Heading north, the Hefei-Tongling-Huangshan Expressway reaches Tongling on the Yangtze and then Hefei, the provincial capital. Two further roads cross the city: the Huangshan-Taling-Taolin Expressway and Provincial Route S326.

Your university stands in Anhui, and the surrounding province touches daily life for students nearly as strongly as the campus itself. What follows explains the history, landscape, economy, people, culture, schools and sights of Anhui.

The province dates from 1667, set up by the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing. People abbreviate it as Wan, borrowed from a small state that existed here between 722 and 481 BC (the Spring and Autumn period); the name also matches Mount Tianzhu and Wan state.

Finds in Fanchang County show humans lived in this land 20,000 years ago. Neolithic remains (8000–2000 BC) relate to the Yangshao and Longshan cultural spheres. Archaeologists have also dug up a 4500-year-old city in Guzhen County called the Nanchengzi Ruins. In 2013 their excavation exposed a moat and a Neolithic city wall, parts of a far larger and coherent urban settlement.

Many sites from before the imperial age survive. Northern Anhui shared a culture with the North China Plain, along with today's Henan, northern Jiangsu and southern Shandong. The centre, on the fertile Huai River basin, was densely populated. The south lay closer to Jiangxi and southern Jiangsu, and the hills of the southeast formed a cultural zone of their own.

Once the Qin united China in 221 BC, the territory was divided into prefectures such as Jiujiang, Zhang, Tang and Sishui. The Han period (202 BC – 220 AD) placed it in the Xu, Yu and Yang prefectures. In the Three Kingdoms years (222–280), the region was ruled at various points by Cao Wei and by Eastern Wu. By the Song dynasty (960–1279) its economy and culture were thriving. The Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) attached Anhui to Henan province, and under the Ming the imperial capital at Nanjing administered it directly.

Through most of the Qing (1644–1912), Anhui was merged with Jiangsu, and the two only parted in 1666 under Kangxi. In the late Qing, Li Hongzhang led the Self-Strengthening Movement, a time when foreign weapons, factories and administrative theory came into China, and Anhui played a major part in it. During the following 50 years the province turned into one of China's most radical liberal areas. Prominent twentieth-century people settled here, including Chen Duxiu, who founded the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Hu Shih, a poet and diplomat.

The year 1938 brought disaster. President Chiang Kai-shek chose to blow up an important Yellow River dam, aiming to hold back the invading Imperial Japanese Army and keep it out of Zhengzhou. In just ten days, floodwater and sand covered northern and central Anhui and drowned 500,000 to 900,000 Chinese people, along with Japanese soldiers whose number is unknown.

When the Second Sino-Japanese War finished in 1945, the capital was relocated to Hefei, which was then only a small town; the authorities poured money into it. After 1949, repair projects tackled the wartime damage. The Great Chinese Famine struck Anhui harder than most provinces. Later, the Third Front campaign set up basic and national defence industries in sheltered locations, as insurance against attack by the Soviet Union or the United States. Anhui hosted the core of the Shanghai Small Third Front, a rear base used to manufacture weapons against aircraft and tanks, in the words of the record a multi-function manufacturing base. By the late 1990s it ranked among China's fastest-growing provinces, and it now sits inside the Yangtze River Delta Economic Area of China, which is the nation's most developed region.

Anhui's terrain varies widely. The north belongs to the North China Plain and the north-centre to the Huai River basin, and both are flat and densely populated. Moving south the ground becomes more uneven: the Dabie Mountains fill much of the southwest, and hill ranges cut across the southeast, where the Yangtze flows among them. The highest point anywhere in Anhui is Lotus Peak, which belongs to Huangshan in the southeast and stands at 1,873 metres (6,145 feet), so the mountain your university is named after is also Anhui's summit.

Two great rivers dominate: the Huai across the north and the Yangtze through the south. Lake Chaohu, in the province's middle and covering about 800 km2 (310 sq mi), is the biggest lake, and many smaller ones lie in the southeast by the Yangtze.

Weather also shifts between north and south. The north is more temperate and has sharper seasons. Winter averages in January sit at −1 to 2 °C above the Huai River and between 0 and 3 °C to its south, while summer in July averages 27 °C or higher. June and July bring the plum rains, which sometimes cause flooding.
Anhui has 16 cities. Economically, the top three are Hefei, Wuhu and Anqing, so these are the places you will hear named most often as centres of business.

What farmers grow depends on where they live. Wheat and sweet potatoes are the crops north of the Huai River; rice and wheat take over in the south. In 2022 the province produced a nominal GDP of 4.51 trilion yuan (US$670 billion), roughly 3.72% of China's total, placing it 10th among province-level units. The primary industries contributed US$52.24 billion (CN¥351.37 billion), the secondary US$276.36 billion (CN¥1.8588 trillion) and the tertiary US$341.1 billion (CN¥2.29433 trillion). Per person, nominal GDP was CN¥73,603 (US$10,943), which put Anhui 14th nationally.

Mineral wealth includes iron at Ma'anshan, coal at Huainan and copper at Tongling, and factories grew around these, for instance the Ma'anshan steel industry. The carmaker Chery, based in Wuhu, is a famous local company. Anhui is also a major centre for appliances, and white goods makers include Meling, Royalstar, Gree, Whirlpool, Hisense and Haier.

Compared with richer eastern neighbours Zhejiang and Jiangsu, Anhui has clearly fallen behind. Its per-person GDP in 2017 was about half of theirs, though that was a quick rise from roughly a third in 2010. One caution: the figure divides output by registered residents (people with a local Hukou), and not all of them actually live in the province. Prosperity is also uneven, and concentrates in industrial cities along the Yangtze such as Hefei, Wuhu and Ma'anshan.
Four zones show how the province attracts industry.
Hefei Economic and Technological Development Zone: set up in 1993 in Hefei's southwest corner, not far from Luogang International Airport.

Hefei Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone: the zone began in October 1990, and the State Council gave it state-level status in March 1991. In 1997 it was ratified as a science and technology industrial park for APEC, with special open policies towards APEC and EU members. It became a National High Tech Export Base in 2000, and the Torch Program gave it an Advanced High Tech Zone award in 2003. Over 100 hi-tech enterprises have settled there, and priority sectors are chemicals, electronics assembly and manufacturing, instruments and industrial equipment, medical equipment and telecommunications.

Wuhu Economic and Technological Development Zone: established in 1993 as the first state-level development zone the central government approved in Anhui, taking advantage of Wuhu's transport position on the Yangtse Delta.
Wuhu Export Processing Zone: approved as a national-level export processing zone with a planned area of 2.95 km2, about 1.14 sq mi, in total.

The Yangtze divides Anhui into a northern and a southern half, and for a long time the lack of bridges held back transport. The first Yangtze bridge in the province, the Tongling Yangtze River Bridge, opened in 1995. By October 2014 there were four, located at Anqing, Tongling, Wuhu and Ma'anshan.
Anhui had no developed rail network until this century, but most cities are now joined by high-speed trains, with Hefei South railway station as the hub.
For roads, the province drew up an ambitious plan for 2015 to 2025 that includes these expressways.
S24, the Changshu-Hefei Expressway
G42, linking Shanghai and Chengdu
G40, linking Shanghai and Xi'an
G3, linking Beijing and Taipei
Hefei and Wuhu both have metro systems. Hefei Metro has 2 finished lines, 3 under construction and another 10 planned, while Wuhu Metro has 2 lines under construction and 3 more planned.

Anhui has 5 major commercial airports in service, with 4 more under construction. Only 2 of them handle international traffic, at Hefei and Huangshan. The airports now operating are these, with their codes.
Hefei: Xinqiao International, codes HFE and ZSOF
Huangshan: Tunxi International, codes TXN and ZSTX
Fuyang: Xiguan, codes FUG and ZSFY
Anqing: Tianzhushan, codes AQG and ZSAQ
Chizhou: Jiuhuashan, codes JUH and ZSJH
The population is overwhelmingly Han Chinese. The two largest minorities are the Huizhou Chinese-speaking Hui and the She.
The gender balance is very uneven. A 2009 study in the British Medical Journal found 138 boys for every 100 girls in the 1–4 age group, among the most skewed ratios of any Chinese province.
Religious life is varied but mostly informal, and the survey figures below help show how people describe themselves.

Chinese folk religion, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism are the main faiths. Surveys from 2007 and 2009 found that 4.64% of people practise ancestor veneration and 5.30% identify as Christian, and a 2010 survey put Muslims at 0.58%. The reports gave no numbers for other beliefs, so the remaining 89.48% could be non-religious, or could worship nature deities or follow Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or folk sects.

Anhui covers several geographic and cultural zones. The flat north, along the Huai River and beyond, resembles neighbouring Henan, Shandong and northern Jiangsu, while the hilly south is closer in culture and dialect to southern hill provinces like Zhejiang and Jiangxi.

Mandarin dialects are spoken north of the Yangtze. Those in the north, such as Bengbu, are Zhongyuan Mandarin, like the dialects of Henan and Shandong, while those in the centre, such as Hefei, are Jianghuai Mandarin, shared with central Jiangsu. South of the Yangtze the dialects are not Mandarin. Wu dialects are spoken in Xuancheng, though Jianghuai Mandarin is rapidly replacing them. Gan dialects are heard in a few southwestern counties bordering Jiangxi, and the Huizhou dialects, a unique and very varied little group, are spoken in roughly ten far-southern counties.

Huangmeixi began around Anqing in the southwest and is a traditional opera popular across China. Huiju, from the Huizhou-speaking south, is one of the main ancestors of Beijing Opera, and was revived in the 1950s after it had disappeared. Luju is a third opera style, heard throughout central Anhui.

Among China's eight great culinary traditions is Anhui cuisine. It blends cooking from the north, the south-centre and the Huizhou-speaking south, and is recognised for wild game and herbs from both land and sea, cooked in fairly simple ways.

Calligraphy materials are another local strength. Traditionally, the finest paper and ink for Chinese calligraphy are Xuan Paper from Xuanzhou (today Xuancheng) and Hui Ink from Huizhou (today Huangshan City). She County is also known for the She Inkstone, a much-preferred type of inkstone.

The province has some of the best-rated universities in China, mostly clustered in Hefei, Wuhu, Bengbu and Maanshan. The national 6th-ranked University of Science & Technology of China (USTC) is based in Hefei.

Further sights include Taiji Cave, East China's longest karst cave, and Anqing City's Zhenfeng Pagoda, built in the Ming dynasty. There is also Zuiweng Pavilion, which is named for the poet Ouyang Xiu (1007–1072 AD).
Tourism planners had foreign help as well: France assisted the Anhui Provincial Tourism Bureau in 2008 with a demonstration project for rural tourism.

huangshan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Huangshan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Huangshan, register at Huangshan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Huaqiao University (HQU) is a public university in Xiamen and Quanzhou, Fujian, China. It is directly under the United Front Work Department of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

Huaqiao University was founded in 1960, with support from the late Chinese premier and historical figure Zhou Enlai, for students of overseas Chinese backgrounds (Hong Kong, Taiwan, Macau, Malaysia, Singapore) to pursue tertiary education in their ancestral homelands. The university has two campuses in the cities of Xiamen and Quanzhou, known for their large numbers of overseas Chinese students who have roots in these cities.

Since its founding, the university has graduated more than 76,000 students, of which 36,000 are from overseas. The university has 28,000 full-time on-campus students, including 3,000 overseas students from 29 countries and regions including Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, Japan, the United States, and Argentina.
The main campus covers an area of 740,000 m2 with a total floor space of 550,000 m2.
The new campus in Xiamen covers 1,320,000 m2. The library has a total collection of 2,040,000 volumes of 1,030,000 titles.

Chinese Language and Culture College is subordinate to Huaqiao University, which used to be Remedial School of Jimei's overseas students (Jimei Chinese Language School), a special school to provide overseas students with Chinese language and cultural knowledge. There are already 320,000 graduates from over 30 countries and areas. Chinese Language and Culture College is the base of the national Chinese education, and the only place for HSK in Fujian Province instituted by the nation's HSK committee. The College offers a short-term Chinese study course, a training course for Chinese teachers, summer and winter camps for overseas students, a symposium of Chinese culture, and a preparatory course for the overseas Chinese students from Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan. It currently has more than 700 postgraduates.

The university has more than 1,700 faculty members, with over 500 holding senior professional titles. There are 900 full-time teachers, 400 professors and associate professors, over 141 PhD holders, and 38 government funded researchers.

The university comprises 19 colleges or departments of science, engineering, economics, management, law, liberal arts, philosophy, and history. It offers 9 PhD programs, 64 masters programs, 6 engineering masters programs, and 52 undergraduate programs, with 12 provincial or ministerial key disciplines.
Chang Li-chi (b. 1984), researcher at the School of International Studies.

Since 1997, the university has enrolled a total of 216 postgraduates from Macau, who pursued such fields as economy, enterprise management, computer science and philosophy.  The university has also offered master's degrees to a total of 30 students from Macau in 2002.
In 2020, the Academic Ranking of World Universities ranked Huaqiao University within the 901-1000 band globally.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Quanzhou, where Huaqiao University is located.

Quanzhou proper lies on a split of land between the estuaries of the Jin River and Luoyang River as they flow into Quanzhou Bay on the Taiwan Strait. Its surrounding prefecture extends west halfway across the province and is hilly and mountainous. Along with Xiamen and Zhangzhou to its south and Putian to its north, it makes up Fujian Province's Southern Coast region. In its mountainous interior, it borders Longyan to the southwest and Sanming to the northwest.

The city features a humid subtropical climate. Quanzhou has four distinct seasons. Its moderate temperature ranges from 0 to 38 degrees Celsius. In summer, there are typhoons that bring rain and some damage to the city.
Major earthquakes have been experienced in 1394 and on 29 December 1604.

As of the 2010 census, Quanzhou has a population of 8,128,530. Its built-up area is home to 6,107,475 inhabitants, encompassing the Licheng, Fengze, and Luojiang urban districts; Jinjiang, Nan'an, and Shishi cities; Hui'an County; and the Quanzhou District for Taiwanese Investment.

Medieval Quanzhou was long one of the most cosmopolitan Chinese cities, with Chinese folk religious temples, Buddhist temples, Taoist temples and Hindu temples; Islamic mosques; and Christian churches, including Nestorian and a cathedral (financed by a rich Armenian lady) and two Franciscan friaries. Andrew of Perugia served as the Roman Catholic bishop of the city from 1322. Odoric of Pordenone was responsible for relocating the relics of the four Franciscans martyred at Thane in India in 1321 to the mission in Quanzhou. English Presbyterian missionaries raised a chapel around 1862. The Qingjing Mosque dates to 1009 but is now preserved as a museum. The Buddhist Kaiyuan Temple has been repeatedly rebuilt but includes two 5-story 13th-century pagodas. Among the most popular folk or Taoist memorial hall is Guan Yue Memorial Hall (通淮關岳廟) that is dedicated to Lord Yue and famous Lord Guan, who is honored for his righteousness and the spirit of brotherhood. Jinjiang also preserves the Cao'an monastery (草庵寺), originally constructed by Manicheans under the Yuan but now used by New Age spiritualists, and a Confucian Memorial Hall (文庙, Wenmiao).

Locals speak the Quanzhou dialect of Hokkien (Min Nan) partly the same as the Amoy dialect spoken in Xiamen, and similar to Malaysian Hokkien, Singaporean Hokkien, Philippine Hokkien, and Quanzhou-descended Taiwanese dialects. It is unintelligible with Mandarin. Many overseas Chinese whose ancestors came from the Quanzhou area, especially those in Southeast Asia, often speak mainly Hokkien at home. Around the "Southern Min triangle area," which includes Quanzhou, Xiamen and Zhangzhou, locals all speak the Hokkien language. The dialects of Hokkien itself that they speak are similar but have different tones and sometimes different pronunciation and vocabulary.

As one of China's best known qiao'xiangs (侨乡, hometown of overseas Chinese), Quanzhou has been a source for Chinese emigration to Southeast Asia and Taiwan. Some of these communities date to Quanzhou's heyday a millennium ago under the Song and Yuan dynasties. About 6 million overseas Chinese trace their ancestry to Quanzhou and Tong'an county. Most of them live in Southeast Asia, including Singapore, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Myanmar, and Thailand.

Historically Quanzhou exported black tea, camphor, sugar, indigo, tobacco, ceramics, cloth made of grass, and minerals. As of 1832 Quanzhou imported, primarily from Guangzhou, wool cloth, wine, and watches. The East India Company was exporting an estimated £150,000 a year in black tea from Quanzhou.

Today Quanzhou is a major exporter of agricultural products such as tea, banana, lychee, and rice. It is also a major producer of quarry granite and ceramics. Other industries include textiles, footwear, fashion and apparel, packaging, machinery, paper and petrochemicals.

Its GDP ranked first in Fujian Province for 20 years from 1991 to 2010. In 2008 Quanzhou's textile and apparel production accounted for 10 percent of China's overall apparel production, stone exports account for 50 percent of Chinese stone exports, resin handicraft exports account for 70 percent of the country's total, ceramic exports account for 67 percent of the country's total, candy production accounts for 20 percent, and the production of sport and tourism shoes accounts for 80% of Chinese, and 20 percent of world production.
Quanzhou is known today as China's shoe city. Quanzhou's 3,000 shoe factories produce 500 million pairs a year, making nearly one in every four pairs of sneakers made in China.

Quanzhou is an important transport hub within southeastern Fujian province. Many export industries in the Fujian interior cities will transport goods to Quanzhou ports. Quanzhou Port was one of the most prosperous port in Tang dynasty and is now still an important Chinese port for exporting.
There is a passenger ferry terminal in Shijing, Nan'an, Fujian, with regular service to the Shuitou Port in the ROC-controlled Kinmen Island.

Quanzhou Jinjiang International Airport is Quanzhou's sole airport, served by passenger flights within mainland China and other regional/international destinations throughout southeast Asia, including Hong Kong, Macau, Manila, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok etc. Major airlines operated in JJN are Xiamen Air, Shenzhen Airlines and West Air.

The Zhangping–Quanzhou–Xiaocuo railway connects several cargo stations within Quanzhou Prefecture with the interior of Fujian and the rest of the country. Until 2014 this line also had passenger service, with fairly slow passenger trains from Beijing.

Passenger trains from China terminated at the Quanzhou East Railway Station, a few kilometers northeast of the center of the city. Passenger service on this line was terminated, and Quanzhou East railway station closed 9 December 2014.

Since 2010, Quanzhou has been served by the high-speed Fuzhou–Xiamen railway, a part of the Hangzhou–Fuzhou–Shenzhen high-speed railway, which runs along China's southeastern sea coast. High-speed trains on this line stop at Quanzhou railway station (in Beifeng Subdistrict of Fengze District, some 10 miles north of Quanzhou city center) and Jinjiang railway station. Trains to Xiamen take under 45 minutes, making it a convenient weekend or day trip. By 2015, direct high-speed service was made available to a number of cities in the country's interior, from Beijing to Chongqing and Guiyang.
The Quanzhou–Xiamen–Zhangzhou Intercity Railway Line, as the name suggests, connecting the cities of Quanzhou, Xiamen, and Zhangzhou is currently conducting on-site surveys.
Long-distance bus services also run daily/nightly to Shenzhen and other major cities. Quanzhou bus station operated from 1990 to 2020.
Quanzhou is listed as one of the 24 famous historic cultural cities first approved by the Chinese government. Notable cultural practices include:
Liyuan Opera (梨园戏)
Puppet Show (提线木偶戏)
Gaojia Opera (高甲戏)
Dacheng Opera (打城戏)
Nanyin (南音), a musical style dating to the Han but performed in the local dialect
Quanzhou Shaolin Five Ancestors Fist (泉州五祖拳)
Yongchun martial arts
The city hosted the Sixth National Peasants' Games in 2008. Signature local dishes include rice dumplings and oyster omelettes.
Notable Historical and cultural sites (the 18 views of Quanzhou as recommended by the Fujian tourism board) include the Ashab Mosque and Kaiyuan Temple mentioned above, as well as:
Qing Yuan mountain (清源山) – The tallest hill within the city limits, which hosts a great view of West lake.
East Lake Park (东湖) – Located in the city center. It is home to a small zoo.
West Lake Park (西湖公园) – The largest body of fresh water within the city limits.
Scholar Street (状元街)  – Champion street about 500 meters long, elegant environment, mainly engaged in tourism and cultural crafts.
Notable Modern cultural sites include:
Fengze Square – Located in the city center and acts as a venue for shows and events.
Dapingshan – The second tallest hill within the city limits, crowned with an enormous equestrian statue of Zheng Chenggong.
The Embassy Lounge – Situated in the "1916 Cultural Ideas Zone" which acts as a platform for mixing traditional Chinese art with modern building techniques and designs

Relics from Quanzhou's past are preserved at the Maritime or Overseas-Relations History Museum. It includes large exhibits on Song-era ships and Yuan-era tombstones. A particularly important exhibit is the so-called Quanzhou ship, a seagoing junk that sunk some time after 1272 and was recovered in 1973–74.
The old city center preserves "balcony buildings" (骑楼; qílóu), a style of southern Chinese architecture from the Republican Era.
Huaqiao University is in Fujian, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Fujian.

Recent archaeological discoveries in 2011 demonstrate that Fujian had entered the Neolithic Age by the middle of the 6th millennium BC. From the Keqiutou site (7450–5590 BP), an early Neolithic site in Pingtan Island located about 70 kilometres (43 mi) southeast of Fuzhou, numerous tools made of stones, shells, bones, jades, and ceramics (including wheel-made ceramics) have been unearthed, together with spinning wheels, which is definitive evidence of weaving.

The Tanshishan (曇石山) site (5500–4000 BP) in suburban Fuzhou spans the Neolithic and Chalcolithic Age where semi-underground circular buildings were found in the lower level. The Huangtulun (黃土崙) site (c. 1325 BC), also in suburban Fuzhou, was of the Bronze Age in character.

Tianlong Jiao (2013) notes that the Neolithic appeared on the coast of Fujian around 6,000 B.P. During the Neolithic, the coast of Fujian had a low population density, with the population depending on mostly on fishing and hunting, along with limited agriculture.
There were four major Neolithic cultures in coastal Fujian, with the earliest Neolithic cultures originating from the north in coastal Zhejiang.
Keqiutou culture (壳丘头文化; c. 6000 – c. 5500 BP, or c. 4050 – c. 3550 BC)
Tanshishan culture (昙石山文化; c. 5000 – c. 4300 BP, or c. 3050 – c. 2350 BC)
Damaoshan culture (大帽山文化; c. 5000 – c. 4300 BP)
Huangguashan culture (黄瓜山文化; c. 4300 – c. 3500 BP, or c. 2350 – c. 1550 BC)

There were two major Neolithic cultures in inland Fujian, which were highly distinct from the coastal Fujian Neolithic cultures. These are the Niubishan culture (牛鼻山文化) from 5000 to 4000 years ago, and the Hulushan culture (葫芦山文化) from 2050 to 1550 BC.

Fujian was also where the kingdom of Minyue was located. The word "Mǐnyuè" was derived by combining "Mǐn" (simplified Chinese: 闽; traditional Chinese: 閩; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: bân), which is perhaps an ethnic name (simplified Chinese: 蛮; traditional Chinese: 蠻; pinyin: mán; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: bân), and "Yuè", after the State of Yue, a Spring and Autumn period kingdom in Zhejiang to the north. This is because the royal family of Yuè fled to Fujian after its kingdom was annexed by the State of Chu in 306 BC. Mǐn is also the name of the main river in this area, but the ethnonym is probably older.

The Qin deposed the King of Minyue, establishing instead a paramilitary province there called Minzhong Commandery. Minyue was a de facto kingdom until one of the emperors of the Qin dynasty, the first unified imperial Chinese state, abolished its status.

In the aftermath of the Qin dynasty's fall, civil war broke out between two warlords, Xiang Yu and Liu Bang. The Minyue king Wuzhu sent his troops to fight with Liu and his gamble paid off. Liu was victorious and founded the Han dynasty. In 202 BC, he restored Minyue's status as a tributary independent kingdom. Thus Wuzhu was allowed to construct his fortified city in Fuzhou as well as a few locations in the Wuyi Mountains, which have been excavated in recent years. His kingdom extended beyond the borders of contemporary Fujian into eastern Guangdong, eastern Jiangxi, and southern Zhejiang.

After Wuzhu's death, Minyue maintained its militant tradition and launched several expeditions against its neighboring kingdoms in Guangdong, Jiangxi, and Zhejiang, primarily in the 2nd century BC. This was stopped by the Han dynasty as it expanded southward. The Han emperor eventually decided to get rid of the potential threat by launching a military campaign against Minyue. Large forces approached Minyue simultaneously from four directions via land and sea in 111 BC. The rulers in Fuzhou surrendered to avoid a futile fight and destruction and the first kingdom in Fujian history came to an abrupt end.
Fujian was part of the much larger Yang Province (Yangzhou), whose provincial capital was designated in Liyang (歷陽; present-day He County, Anhui).

The Han dynasty collapsed at the end of the 2nd century AD, paving the way for the Three Kingdoms era. Sun Quan, the founder of the Kingdom of Wu, spent nearly 20 years subduing the Shan Yue people, the branch of the Yue living in mountains.

The first wave of immigration of the noble class arrived in the province in the early 4th century when the Western Jin dynasty collapsed and the north was torn apart by civil wars and rebellions by tribal peoples from the north and west. These immigrants were primarily from eight families in central China: Chen (陈), Lin (林), Huang (黄), Zheng (郑), Zhan (詹), Qiu (邱), He (何), and Hu (胡). To this day, the first four remain the most popular surnames in Fujian.

Nevertheless, isolation from nearby areas owing to rugged terrain contributed to Fujian's relatively undeveloped economy and level of development, despite major population boosts from northern China during the "barbarian" rebellions. The population density in Fujian remained low compared to the rest of China. Only two commanderies and sixteen counties were established by the Western Jin dynasty. Like other southern provinces such as Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, and Yunnan, Fujian often served as a destination for exiled prisoners and dissidents at that time.
During the Southern and Northern Dynasties era, the Southern Dynasties (Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang (Western Liang), and Chen) reigned south of the Yangtze River, including Fujian.
During the Sui and Tang eras a large influx of migrants settled in Fujian.
During the Sui dynasty, Fujian was again part of Yang Province.
During the Tang, Fujian was part of the larger Jiangnan East Circuit, whose capital was at Suzhou. Modern-day Fujian was composed of around 5 prefectures and 25 counties.

The Tang dynasty (618–907) oversaw the next golden age of China, which contributed to a boom in Fujian's culture and economy. Fuzhou's economic and cultural institutions grew and developed. The later years of the Tang dynasty saw several political upheavals in the Chinese heartland, prompting even larger waves of northerners to immigrate to the northern part of Fujian.
The area was reorganized into the Fujian Circuit in 985, which was the first time the name "Fujian" was used for an administrative region.

After the establishment of the Yuan dynasty, Fujian became part of Jiangzhe province, whose capital was at Hangzhou. From 1357 to 1366 Muslims in Quanzhou participated in the Ispah Rebellion, advancing northward and even capturing Putian and Fuzhou before the rebellion was crushed by the Yuan. Afterward, Quanzhou city lost foreign interest in trading and its formerly welcoming international image as the foreigners were all massacred or deported.

Yuan dynasty General Chen Youding, who had put down the Ispah Rebellion, continued to rule over the Fujian area even after the outbreak of the Red Turban Rebellion. Forces loyal to the eventual Ming dynasty founder Zhu Yuanzhang (Hongwu Emperor) defeated Chen in 1367.
Fujian is home to several tourist attractions, including four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, one of the highest in China.
