Huazhong Agricultural University (HZAU) stands within Wuhan's main urban area, in Hubei Province in central China. It dates back to 1898, in the reign of the Guangxu Emperor (1871 to 1908) of the Qing Dynasty (1644 to 1911), when Zhang Zhidong, then governor of Hubei and Hunan provinces, founded the Hubei Farming School.

In 1979 the State Council designated it a key national university answering directly to China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. The present name dates from 1985. In 2005 the university joined Project 211 as a key institution, and in 2017 it became a national "double first-class" construction university.

The first round of evaluation under the "double first-class" scheme saw the university reach the top grade on seven of nine evaluation indicators. Five disciplines were chosen for the second round of the national "double first-class" initiative: biology, horticulture, animal husbandry and veterinary medicine, as well as the economics of agriculture and forestry. In ESI, it counts in the global top 1% for agronomy, life sciences, science, engineering, medicine and social sciences.

The university's stated aim is to become a world-famous, research-intensive institution with world-class leading subjects and distinctive character. It has achieved notable results in hybrid rapeseed and green rice, breeding pigs of high quality, animal vaccines, premium citrus, test-tube potatoes and cotton, maize and freshwater fish, among other products. It trains many innovative graduates with global competence, and it says it has influenced scientific, technological and industrial development worldwide.

Teaching at HZAU has earned 30 national achievement prizes (one special, four first and 25 second prizes). Its research platforms include three national key laboratories and three national engineering (technology) research centres, one national innovation platform for integrating production and education in biological breeding, and one frontier science centre of the Ministry of Education. There are also four national experimental teaching demonstration centres, six agricultural science and education cooperation training bases run with the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs together with the Ministry of Education. In addition, students can use 11 national practice bases located off campus.
The QS World University Rankings placed HZAU 298th in Asia in 2025 and in the 901 to 950 band in the world for 2026.

Education of international students at HZAU goes to 1960. In 2003 the university was the first pilot unit of experts for developing highly educated foreign students. The programmes it highlights for international students are crop science, horticulture, animal husbandry, veterinary medicine, and food science and engineering. At the time of the source, about 500 international students from 54 countries were enrolled, roughly 70 percent studying for doctorates and 30 percent for master's degrees.
Student life depends on the city: its weather, how you move about and what you can do for fun. The sections below describe Wuhan.

Wuhan is in east-central Hubei, between latitudes 29° 58' and 31° 22' N and longitudes 113° 41' and 115° 05' E. It sits where the Han River flows into the Yangtze, on the east side of the Jianghan Plain along the middle reaches of the Yangtze.

The urban area is made up of three parts, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, together called the "Three Towns of Wuhan". The name Wuhan joins "Wu" from the first with "Han" from the other two. The three cities were consolidated in 1927, and that is when Wuhan was created. They face one another across the rivers and are joined by bridges, among them one of China's first modern bridges, known as the "First Bridge".
Wuchang lies southeast of the Yangtze, a river that divides it from Hankou and Hanyang alike.
Hankou is north of the Yangtze, which divides it from Wuchang, and north of the Han River, which divides it from Hanyang.
Hanyang is west of the Yangtze, which divides it from Wuchang, and south of the Han River, which divides it from Hankou.

Wuhan's terrain is easy to describe. It is flat and low in the centre and hilly to the south, and both the Yangtze and the Han wind their way through the city. In Huangpi District the She River joins the Yangtze. The land area is 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 square miles), most of it alluvial plain with hills, ponds and a huge number of lakes. A quarter of the urban territory is water, the largest share among major Chinese cities. The city has nearly 200 lakes. East Lake (33 km²) and Tangxun Lake are the largest in China that sit entirely within a city.

South Lake and Sand Lake are other well-known lakes. Liangzi Lake, in the southeast of Jiangxia District, is Hubei's largest lake by area. The highest points in Wuhan are the twin peaks at the boundary of Huangpi District and Xiaogan City, at 872.5 metres. Within the city limits there are also several mountains, for example Mount Luojia (珞珈山) in Wuchang District, and in Hongshan District Mount Hong (洪山) and Mount Yujia (喻家山/瑜珈山).

Wuhan has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four clear seasons and heavy summer rainfall. Summers are famously humid, with dew points frequently at or above 26 °C (79 °F). In the past, Wuhan, Chongqing and Nanjing were together labelled the "Three Furnacelike Cities" of the Yangtze because of their scorching summers. Recent climate data, though, suggest that Wuhan has dropped out of the very hottest group; the list now called the "New Four Furnacelike Cities" names Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang.

Mild weather is typical of spring and autumn, while winter is cool with low rainfall and occasional snow. Monthly averages (24-hour) start at 4.1 °C (39.4 °F) in January and peak at 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) in July, while the year's mean is 17.4 °C (63.3 °F). Precipitation totals a little under 1,320 mm (52 in) a year, mostly falling between April and July. Frost-free periods last 211 to 272 days. For possible sunshine, the share ranges from 30 percent (January) to 53 percent (August), giving the city proper 1,783 hours of bright sun every year.

The lowest temperature on record is −18.1 °C (−1 °F), reached on January 31, 1977. The highest is 39.7 °C (103 °F), recorded on both July 27, 2017 and August 18, 2022. An unofficial reading from August 10, 1934, was higher still, at 41.3 °C (106 °F).

Wuhan was mainly agricultural until the 21st century. The Rise of Central China Plan, which seeks to turn less developed inland economies into advanced manufacturing hubs, has made Wuhan one of its focal points since 2004.

Since 1890, steel has formed the backbone of local industry. In 2010 the car industry, for the first time, exceeded the output value of Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO). There are five car makers, namely Citroën, Dongfeng Honda, Dongfeng Renault, DFM Passenger Vehicle and SAIC-GM; the headquarters of Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd is in the city.

By 2016 Wuhan had drawn in foreign investment from more than 80 countries. Some 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises had been established, with total capital of US$22.45 billion. Roughly 50 French companies, Renault and PSA Group among them, operate in Wuhan, which accounts for over a third of French investment in China and is the most French investment in any Chinese city.

Wuhan is an important centre for the economy, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. The main industries are optoelectronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, biological engineering, new materials and environmental protection. Sustainability features in its new industries, such as energy efficiency technology and renewable energy. The Global Financial Centres Index of 2021 placed Wuhan within the top 100 financial centres globally.
The city's major industrial zones, listed from the earliest, are as follows.
Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone

huazhong-agricultural-university.h: Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone

blocks.x: A national-level industrial zone incorporated in 1993. It is currently about 10 to 25 square km, and plans call for expansion to 25 to 50 square km. Encouraged industries are car production and assembly, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, chemicals production and processing, food and drink processing, heavy industry and telecommunications equipment.

Established in 2000 and located inside the Wuhan Economic and Technology Development Zone, it is planned to cover 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile). The first 0.7 square kilometres (0.3 square miles) has already been developed.

huazhong-agricultural-university.h: Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone

blocks.x: This is a national-level high-tech zone. The Wuhan East Lake High-Tech Development Zone (ELHTZ) is built around telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, and also encourages electronics and software outsourcing. It is China's biggest production centre for optoelectronic products, with leading firms such as Fiberhome Telecommunications and Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable, which makes more fibre-optic cable than any other Chinese company. It is also the development centre of China's laser industry, with HGTECH and Chutian Laser based in the zone.

This park lies inside the Donghu zone and is jointly developed by the Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd and the East Lake High-Tech Development Zone. Its planned area is 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles), and the floor area planned in total is 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet). The park lies 8.5 km (5.28 mi) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 mi) from Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Biolake was founded in 2008 in China's Optics Valley, within the East Lake New Technology Development Zone, Biolake is an industrial base covering 15 km² (5.8 sq mi). It has six parks, Bio-innovation, Bio-pharma, Bio-agriculture, Bio-manufacturing, Medical Device and Medical Health, to hold both research activities and living space.

Central China's most populous city is Wuhan, which is also among the most populous in the whole country. China's Seventh Census, taken in 2020, counted 12,326,500 residents, up 25.97% (2.5411 million) from the 2010 census. The decade from 2010 to 2020 was the fastest-growing in the history of the census, averaging 2.34% a year, and the first time Wuhan's population passed 10 million. The OECD estimated that the metropolitan area had 19 million people as of 2010.

A study published in November 2019 used data on night-time lighting and land cover as stand-ins to examine urban development in both spatial and socioeconomic terms. It showed that Wuhan has a high concentration of socioeconomic activity compared with its spatial urban development.

A survey published in 2017 found that 79.2% of Wuhan's population is either non-religious or worships gods and ancestors, of whom 0.9% are Taoists. Among other beliefs, 14.7% follow Buddhism, 2.9% Protestantism, 0.3% Catholicism and 1.6% Islam, and a further 1.6% follow unspecified other religions.

The Wuhan Railway Hub, which China Railway Wuhan Group manages, ranks among the country's four key railway hubs. Three major stations serve the city: Hankou railway station in Hankou, Wuchang railway station in Wuchang, and Wuhan railway station, in a recently developed district east of East Lake (Hongshan District). They are many miles apart, so passengers should check which station their train uses.

The original Hankou Station was the end of the Jinghan railway from Beijing, and Wuchang Station was the end of the Yuehan railway to Guangzhou. After the First Yangtze Bridge was built and the two lines joined into the Jingguang railway, both Hankou and Wuchang can be served by trains in every direction, unlike cities such as New York or Moscow, where each station handles a particular direction.

The Hefei-Wuhan high-speed railway opened on April 1, 2009, and Wuhan became connected by high-speed trains to Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai. A number of daily trains reach Shanghai in under six hours, and at the start of 2010 most of these express trains left from Hankou railway station.

Work on the new Wuhan railway station, which has 11 platforms, started in 2006 on the city's northeastern fringe. The station opened in December 2009, along with China's second high-speed train service, which ran on a schedule between Guangzhou and Wuhan. It was billed as the world's fastest train, able to reach 394 km/h (244.82 mph), and it shortened the journey from ten and a half hours to just three. Service now continues north as far as Beijing. By 2011 the new Wuhan station was used chiefly for the Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, and regular trains to most other places still left from Hankou and Wuchang.

Work has been under way on several lines of the Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity railway, intended eventually to link the three main rail terminals of Wuhan to stations in the outer areas and distant suburbs, and with neighbouring Huangshi, Huanggang, Xianning and Xiaogan. The first to open to passengers was the line to Xianning, at the close of 2013. The Xiaogan line opened on December 1, 2016, and was extended to Shiyan with the opening of the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway on November 29, 2019.

The main freight station and marshalling yard of the metropolitan area is the large Wuhan North, a very large station with 112 tracks and more than 650 switches. It is in Huangpi District's Hengdian Subdistrict, 20 km (12 mi) from Wuhan Station on its north side, and 23 km (14 mi) from Hankou Station.

The Wuhan Metro is run and owned by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd. Today it has 11 lines with 282 stations across 435 km (270 mi). Line 1 was the first, starting service on July 28, 2004, which made Wuhan the seventh mainland Chinese city with rapid transit following Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian. Line 2, opened on December 28, 2012, was the first underground line to cross under the Yangtze River. Getting across the Yangtze and Han rivers had always been the bottleneck of Wuhan's traffic, and the metro greatly eased that problem.

With 1.22 billion passengers in 2019, it is mainland China's sixth-busiest rapid transit network. It keeps growing quickly, and several lines or sections are being built, and the city government has promised at least two lines or sections each year. During the COVID-19 pandemic, between January 23 and March 27, 2020, the entire network was closed.
Trams came to Wuhan's streets on July 28, 2017, with the opening of the first line, the Auto-city T1 Line. Those under construction or planned are:
The Auto-city trams (Lines T1, T2, T6 and T8) serve the Wuhan Economic Development Area, in far western Hanyang. T1 has been operating since 2017.
Optics Valley trams have two lines, T1 and T2, in southeastern Wuchang, south and east of Guanggu Circle (Guanggu Guangchang). This system opened on January 18, 2018.
The Old Hankou Streetcar, which is a loop around Hankou.
Buses, including trolleybuses, also provide local transport. The trolleybus system has run since 1958, and its first route, route 1, still operates.

Wuhan stands on the Yangtze and has a long history of ferries. Steamboats began modern ferry service in 1900, and in 1937 a train ferry started carrying railway cars between Hankou and Wuchang. Passengers can board and leave at numbered stops around the city, and a tourist ferry sails at night. The Wuhan Ferry Company runs the services; in 2010 it purchased ten new ships to take the place of ones that had been working for 29 years.

huazhong-agricultural-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Huazhong Agricultural University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at Huazhong Agricultural University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

huazhong-university-of-science-and-techn.h: About Huazhong University of Science and Technology

blocks.x: The Huazhong University of Science and Technology (HUST; 华中科技大学) is a public university in Wuhan, Hubei, China. The university is part of Project 985, Project 211, and the Double First-Class Construction.

It is a comprehensive key university directly under the Ministry of Education. Its history can be traced back to the original Huazhong Institute of Technology established in Wuhan in 1952, the Shanghai German Medical School (predecessor of Tongji University) founded by German physician Erich Paulun in 1907, and the original Central South School of Architecture and Engineering established in Mount Lu, Jiangxi province in the 1950s. The three schools merged to form Huazhong University of Science and Technology on May 26, 2000.

After the 1949 Revolution, Wuhan was designated the leading city of the Central South region, one of six geographical divisions in China. The Huazhong Institute of Technology, established in 1953, was envisioned as a major national polytechnic institution, akin to Harbin Institute of Technology, Zhejiang University, Jiao Tong University, and Chongqing University within their respective regions. Under the leadership of Zhu Jiusi, the institute rapidly developed into a significant technological university during the 1950s.

In 1958, the institute expanded its scope by introducing programmes in basic and applied sciences, including mathematics, physics, and chemistry. However, these efforts were disrupted by the Cultural Revolution, which began in 1966. When Zhu Jiusi returned to the campus in 1970, he found the university largely abandoned and occupied by local farmers. He initiated efforts to rebuild the institution, recruiting scholars from top universities across China who had been sent to the countryside during the upheaval.

Following the end of the Cultural Revolution in 1976, Deng Xiaoping's return to power in 1978 marked a new era for higher education. That same year, Zhu Jiusi presented a report at a national meeting emphasising the dual importance of universities as centres for both research and teaching. After retiring in 1984, Zhu remained an influential figure in shaping China's higher education.

In 1998, China launched Project 985 to develop world-class universities. Initially, the institution was not selected in the first batch. To improve its prospects, the Wuhan municipal government proposed merging the institute with Wuhan University. Following mediation by Education Minister Chen Zhili, a compromise was reached: Tongji Medical University and Wuhan Urban Construction University were merged into the institution and the institution was renamed as the Huazhong University of Science and Technology, while Wuhan University was consolidated with three other local universities. Both newly merged universities were subsequently included in Project 985.

Since the 1990s, the university has spearheaded the establishment of a state laboratory in opto-electronics, which later evolved into the Optics Valley, a prominent high-tech development zone near its campus.

The consolidation of these cities occurred in 1927 and Wuhan was thereby established. The three former cities face each other across the rivers and are linked by bridges, including one of the first modern bridges in China, known as the "First Bridge".
Wuchang lies south east of the Yangtze River that separates it from both Hankou and Hanyang.

The city of Wuhan is served by three major railway stations: the Hankou railway station in Hankou, the Wuchang railway station in Wuchang, and the Wuhan railway station, located in a newly developed area east of the East Lake (Hongshan District). As the stations are many miles apart, it is important for passengers to be aware of the particular station(s) used by a particular train.

The (original) Hankou Station was the terminus for the Jinghan railway from Beijing, while the Wuchang Station was the terminus for the Yuehan railway to Guangzhou. Since the construction of the First Yangtze Bridge and the linking of the two lines into the Jingguang railway, both Hankou and Wuchang stations have been served by trains going to all directions, which contrasts with the situation in such cities as New York or Moscow, where different stations serve different directions.

With the opening of the Hefei-Wuhan high-speed railway on April 1, 2009, Wuhan became served by high-speed trains with Hefei, Nanjing, and Shanghai; several trains a day now connect the city with Shanghai, getting there in under six hours. As of early 2010, most of these express trains leave from the Hankou railway station.

In 2006, construction began on the new Wuhan railway station with 11 platforms, located on the northeastern outskirts of the city. In December 2009, the station was opened, as China unveiled its second high-speed train with scheduled runs from Guangzhou to Wuhan. Billed as the fastest train in the world, it can reach a speed of 394 km/h (244.82 mph). The travel time between the two cities has been reduced from ten and a half hours to just three. The rail service has been extended north to Beijing.
As of 2011, the new Wuhan railway station is primarily used by the Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, while most regular trains to other destinations continue to use the Hankou and Wuchang stations.

Construction work is carried out on several lines of the new Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity railway, which will eventually connect Wuhan's three main rail terminals with several stations throughout the city's outer areas and farther suburbs, as well as with the nearby cities of Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang, and Xiaogan. The first line of the system, the one to Xianning, opened for passenger operations at the end of 2013. The line to Xiaogen opened on December 1, 2016, and it was extended with the opening of the Wuhan–Shiyan high-speed railway to Shiyan on November 29, 2019.

The main freight railway station and classification yard of the Wuhan metropolitan area is the extensive Wuhan North railway station, with 112 tracks and over 650 switches. It is located in Hengdian Subdistrict of Huangpi District, located 20 km (12 mi) north of the Wuhan Station and 23 km (14 mi) from Hankou Station.

Wuhan Metro is a rapid transit system serving the city of Wuhan. Owned and operated by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd., the network now includes 11 lines, 282 stations, and 435 km (270 mi) of route length. Line 1, the first line in the system, opened on July 28, 2004, making Wuhan the seventh city in mainland China with a rapid transit system, after Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun, and Dalian. Line 2 opened on December 28, 2012, and is the first underground metro line crossing the Yangtze River. Commuting across the Yangtze River and Han River has been the bottleneck of Wuhan traffic. However, the appearance of Wuhan Metro greatly relieved this problem. With 1.22 billion annual passengers in 2019, Wuhan Metro is the sixth-busiest rapid transit system in mainland China. Wuhan Metro is a rapidly developing metro system. There are a number of lines or sections under construction. The government of Wuhan City promised the citizens that at least two lines or sections open every year. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the entire network was out of service from January 23 to March 27, 2020.
Trams were brought to the streets of Wuhan on July 28, 2017, with the first line (Auto-city T1 Line) opened that day. The trams under construction or planning in Wuhan are:
Auto-city trams, with Lines T1, T2, T6, and T8 in the Wuhan Economic Development Area, in the far western reaches on Hanyang. T1 Line is operational as of 2017.
Optics Valley trams, two lines (T1 and T2) south and east of Guanggu Circle (Guanggu Guangchang) in southeastern Wuchang. The system opened on January 18, 2018.
The Old Hankou Streetcar, a loop line around Hankou city.
Local transport is also provided by buses, including trolleybuses. The trolleybus system has been in operation since 1958. Its first route, which remains in operation today, is route 1.
Wuhan is a major hub for maritime transport in central China. The Port of Wuhan provides services for the local population and shipping services.

Located on the banks of the Yangtze River, Wuhan has a long history of ferry services. Modern ferry services were established in 1900 by steam boat. In 1937, a train ferry was established to transport train cars from Hankou to Wuchang. There are numbered stops around Wuhan where people can get on and off the ferry and there is a tourist ferry in the night.
Currently, ferry services are provided by the Wuhan Ferry Company. In 2010, the company bought ten new ships to replace those that had been in service for 29 years.

huazhong-university-of-science-and-techn.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Huazhong University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at Huazhong University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hubei University (湖北大学) is a state-funded institution in Wuhan, the provincial capital of Hubei in central China. It dates back to 1931, when it opened as the Hubei Provincial Education College. Over roughly its first fifty years the institution moved from site to site and was renamed several times. The name Hubei University has been in use since 1984.

The easiest way to follow the university's past is through its successive names. If you come across an older certificate, a research paper or an alumni profile, the institution may appear under one of these earlier titles.
1931 to 1943: Hubei Provincial Education College (湖北省立教育学院)
1944 to 1949: National Hubei Teachers College (国立湖北师范学院)
1949 to 1952: Hubei Education College (湖北省教育学院)
1952 to 1954: Hubei Teachers Vocational College (湖北省教师进修学院)
1954 to 1957: Hubei Teachers Vocational School (湖北师范专科学校)
1957 to 1958: Wuhan Teachers Vocational School (武汉师范专科学校)
1958 to 1984: Wuhan Teachers College (武汉师范学院)
1984 to the present: Hubei University (湖北大学)
So for most of its life this was a teacher-training institution, and the broader university identity only arrived in 1984.
The university's notable names include Andrew Jacobs, who once taught English there, and Wu Chuanxi, who at the time of his appointment was the youngest university president in China.

hubei-university.h: Wuhan, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life as a student depends heavily on the city outside the gates: what the weather is like, how you move around, and what the local economy offers. The sections below introduce Wuhan, where Hubei University is based.

Wuhan lies in east-central Hubei, between latitudes 29° 58' and 31° 22' N and longitudes 113° 41' and 115° 05' E. It stands where the Han River flows into the Yangtze, on the eastern side of the Jianghan Plain and along the middle reaches of the Yangtze.

Wuhan is really three historic towns joined together: Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, often called the "Three Towns of Wuhan". The name is a blend: "Wu" comes from Wuchang, and "Han" from Hankou and Hanyang. The three were merged in 1927, which is the year Wuhan came into being. Rivers run between them, and bridges tie them together; one is the "First Bridge", counted among the earliest modern bridges built in China.
Because the rivers split the city, a quick mental map helps.
Wuchang is on the south-eastern side of the Yangtze, and the river divides it from the other two towns.
Hankou is north of the Yangtze, which divides it from Wuchang, and north of the Han River, which divides it from Hanyang.
Hanyang is west of the Yangtze, which divides it from Wuchang, and south of the Han River, which divides it from Hankou.

The terrain is fairly uncomplicated. The middle of the city is low and flat, the south is hilly, and the Yangtze and the Han wind through it. The She River joins the Yangtze in Huangpi District. Wuhan covers 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 square miles), mostly alluvial plain dotted with hills, ponds and a large number of lakes. A quarter of the urban territory is water, the highest share among China's major cities. There are nearly 200 lakes, including East Lake (33 square kilometres) and Tangxun Lake, which are the biggest lakes lying wholly inside a Chinese city.

South Lake and Sand Lake are also well known. The biggest of all by surface area in Hubei is Liangzi Lake, which lies in the southeast of Jiangxia District. The highest ground in Wuhan is a pair of twin peaks, 872.5 metres tall, where Huangpi District meets Xiaogan City. Several hills also rise inside the built-up area: Mount Luojia (珞珈山) in Wuchang District, and Mount Hong (洪山) and Mount Yujia (喻家山, also written 瑜珈山) in Hongshan District.

Wuhan has four distinct seasons and a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) in which summer brings plenty of rain. The summer air is muggy: dewpoints frequently reach 26 °C (79 °F) or higher. For a long time Wuhan, Chongqing and Nanjing were grouped together as the "Three Furnacelike Cities" of the Yangtze for their hot summers. More recent weather data suggests Wuhan is no longer in the top tier of summer heat, and a "New Four Furnacelike Cities" list names Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang instead.
Here is what to expect through the year.
Spring and autumn are mostly mild. Winter is cool, with little rain and the occasional snowfall.
Averaged over 24 hours, January sits at 4.1 °C (39.4 °F), July reaches 29.3 °C (84.7 °F), and the yearly mean is 17.4 °C (63.3 °F).
Annual precipitation is just under 1,320 mm (52 inches), and most of it falls between April and July.
The frost-free season lasts between 211 and 272 days.
Possible sunshine runs from 30 per cent in January to 53 per cent in August, adding up to 1,783 hours of bright sunshine a year in the city proper.

The coldest recorded reading is −18.1 °C (−1 °F), on 31 January 1977. The hottest is 39.7 °C (103 °F), reached on 27 July 2017 and again on 18 August 2022, although an unofficial figure of 41.3 °C (106 °F) was noted on 10 August 1934.
A practical point for new arrivals: bring clothes for real summer humidity and a proper winter coat, because the cold season, though short, is genuinely chilly.

Until the 21st century Wuhan was mainly an agricultural region. In 2004 it became a focus of the Rise of Central China Plan, a national policy meant to turn less-developed inland economies into centres of advanced manufacturing.

Steel has been the backbone of local industry since 1890. In 2010 the car industry for the first time produced more output than steel from Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO). Five car makers operate in the city (Dongfeng Honda, Citroën, SAIC-GM, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Dongfeng Renault), and the headquarters of Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd is here.

Foreign money matters too. By 2016 Wuhan had drawn investment from more than 80 countries. In all, 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises had been set up, injecting US$22.45 billion in capital. Roughly 50 French companies, among them Renault and PSA Group, operate in the city. Together they account for more than one third of all French investment in China, a level no other Chinese city matches.

In broad terms, Wuhan is a major national centre for commerce, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. Its leading industries include optoelectronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, bioengineering, new materials and environmental protection. Environmental sustainability features among the emerging industries, covering energy-efficiency technology and renewable energy. In 2021 the Global Financial Centres Index placed Wuhan among the world's top 100 financial centres.
Several national-level zones account for much of this activity. They are listed here roughly in the order they were created.

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone. A national industrial zone incorporated in 1993. It currently measures about 10 to 25 square kilometres and plans to grow to 25 to 50. Encouraged industries are vehicle production and assembly, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, chemicals, heavy industry, telecom equipment, and food and drink processing.

Wuhan Export Processing Zone. Set up in 2000 inside the development zone above. It is planned to take up 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile), and the first 0.7 square kilometres (0.3 square miles) have already been developed.

Wuhan Donghu (East Lake) New Technology Development Zone. A national high-tech zone whose core sectors are optoelectronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, and software outsourcing and electronics get official encouragement too. It is the biggest production base for optoelectronic products in China, with companies such as Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable, the country's largest fibre-optic cable maker, and Fiberhome Telecommunications. It is also the centre of the Chinese laser industry, with firms like HGTECH and Chutian Laser based there.

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park. Located inside the East Lake zone and a joint venture between the zone and Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. Its planned area is 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles) and the stated floor area is 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet). It lies 8.5 km (5.28 miles) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 miles) from Wuhan Tianhe Airport. Another description of the same park gives the floor area as 600,000 square metres, so check the current figure on official pages.

Wuhan Biolake. An industrial base founded in 2008 within the Optics Valley of China, in the East Lake zone. It covers 15 square kilometres (5.8 square miles) and has six parks (bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical device and medical health) built to hold both research and living space.

No other city in Central China has more people than Wuhan, and few in the country match it. The Seventh National Census (2020) counted 12,326,500 residents, a 25.97 per cent rise, or 2.5411 million people, over the 2010 census. The decade from 2010 to 2020 was the fastest growth period since census taking began, averaging 2.34 per cent a year, and it was the first time the city's population reached 10 million.
The OECD estimated that the wider metropolitan area held 19 million people in 2010.

A study published in November 2019 looked at Wuhan's urban development with satellite night-light imagery and land cover records standing in for physical and socioeconomic change. It found that socioeconomic activity is highly concentrated compared with how far the city has spread physically.

A 2017 survey found that 79.2 per cent of Wuhan residents are irreligious or follow worship of gods and ancestors, and 0.9 per cent of them are Taoists. Of the rest, 14.7 per cent follow Buddhism, 2.9 per cent Protestantism, 0.3 per cent Catholicism and 1.6 per cent Islam, while another 1.6 per cent follow unspecified other religions.

The Wuhan Railway Hub, run by China Railway Wuhan Group, is among the four key railway hubs in China. Wuhan has three main passenger stations: Hankou station in Hankou, Wuchang station in Wuchang, and Wuhan station in a newly developed district on the east side of East Lake (Hongshan District). The stations are many miles apart, so always check which one your train uses before you set off.

Historically the original Hankou Station was the end of the Jinghan line from Beijing, and Wuchang Station was the end of the Yuehan line to Guangzhou. Once the First Yangtze Bridge tied the two lines together as the Jingguang railway, trains from both stations could head in any direction. That is different from cities such as New York or Moscow, where each station serves its own direction.

The high-speed era began when the Hefei-Wuhan high-speed railway opened on 1 April 2009, connecting Wuhan to Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai by fast train. A number of daily services now make the trip to Shanghai in less than six hours, and in early 2010 the bulk of them departed from Hankou station.

Work on the new Wuhan station, with 11 platforms on the north-eastern edge of the city, began in 2006. It opened in December 2009 together with China's second high-speed line, Guangzhou to Wuhan. That train was promoted as the world's fastest, with a top speed of 394 km/h (244.82 mph), and it brought the trip down from 10.5 hours to just 3. Service now continues north all the way to Beijing. In 2011 the new station was used chiefly for the Wuhan-Guangzhou trains, whereas conventional trains for other destinations still went from Hankou and Wuchang.

A new Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity railway is also under construction on several lines. When complete it will join Wuhan's three main stations to others across the outer districts and distant suburbs, and to the nearby cities of Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang and Xiaogan. Passengers have ridden the first route, to Xianning, since late 2013. The Xiaogan route opened on 1 December 2016, and the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway extended it to Shiyan on 29 November 2019.

Freight is handled mainly at Wuhan North station, a huge classification yard with 112 tracks and more than 650 switches. It sits in Hengdian Subdistrict, Huangpi District, 20 km (12 miles) north of Wuhan Station and 23 km (14 miles) from Hankou Station.

Wuhan Metro, owned and run by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd., now has 11 lines with 282 stations over 435 km (270 miles). Line 1 started service on 28 July 2004. That made Wuhan the seventh mainland Chinese city with rapid transit, following Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian. On 28 December 2012 Line 2 opened, and it was the first underground line to pass beneath the Yangtze.

Crossing the Yangtze and the Han had long been the weak point in the city's traffic, and the metro has eased that considerably. In 2019 it carried 1.22 billion passengers, making it the sixth-busiest system in mainland China. It continues to grow quickly, with several lines or sections under construction, and the city government has pledged to open a minimum of two lines or sections every year. The whole network was shut from 23 January to 27 March 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Trams returned to Wuhan's streets on 28 July 2017, when the first line (Auto-city T1) began running. The planned or under-construction tram routes are:
Auto-city trams: four lines (T1, T2, T6 and T8) serving the Wuhan Economic Development Area at the far western end of Hanyang. Only T1 had begun running as of 2017.
Optics Valley trams: T1 and T2 head south and east from Guanggu Circle (Guanggu Guangchang) in south-eastern Wuchang. This network started running on 18 January 2018.
The Old Hankou Streetcar, which is meant to circle the old centre of Hankou.
Buses also serve the city, including trolleybuses. The trolleybus network has been running since 1958, and its first route, route 1, is still in service.

Wuhan is a major hub for shipping in central China, and the Port of Wuhan serves both local people and commercial shipping. Ferries on the Yangtze have a long history here. Modern ferry service began with steamboats in 1900, and in 1937 a train ferry started carrying railway cars from Hankou to Wuchang. Numbered stops around the city let people get on and off, and a night-time tourist ferry also runs. The Wuhan Ferry Company currently operates the services; in 2010 it bought ten new ships to replace vessels that had served for 29 years.
A university's province shapes student life as much as its campus does, so this section outlines Hubei.

The Jianghan Plain covers most of central and southern Hubei. The west and the edges of the province are more mountainous, with the Wudang, Jing, Daba and Wu Mountains running roughly from north to south. The Dabie Mountains stand northeast of the plain, along the line where Henan meets Anhui. To the north, the Tongbai Mountains sit on the Henan boundary, and in the southeast the Mufu Mountains mark the boundary with Jiangxi. Shennong Peak, in the Daba Mountains within the Shennongjia forestry area, is the highest point in Hubei at 3,105 metres.

Two major rivers cross the province: the Yangtze and its left tributary, the Han. They give the Jianghan Plain its name, with "Jiang" standing for the Yangtze and "han" for the Han River. The Yangtze enters from the west by way of the Three Gorges, whose eastern portion (Xiling Gorge and some of Wu Gorge) is in western Hubei and whose western portion is in Chongqing next door. The Han reaches the province from the northwest. Each river crosses most of Hubei before they join in the middle of Wuhan, the provincial capital.

Several tributaries feed the Yangtze inside Hubei. The Shen Nong Stream is small and lies in the north, and it has been hit hard by the Three Gorges Dam project. The Qing is an important waterway in the southwest. The Huangbo flows near Yichang, and the Fushui River in the southeast.

Thousands of lakes lie across the Jianghan Plain, which is why Hubei is called the "Province of Lakes". The biggest are Liangzi Lake and Hong Lake. Dams have created large reservoirs too, the largest being the Danjiangkou Reservoir, which sits on the Han where Hubei meets Henan.

Hubei is humid subtropical (Cfa or Cwa in the Köppen system) with four distinct seasons. In January, winters are cool to cold at 1 to 6 °C (34 to 43 °F) on average. July is hot and humid, averaging 24 to 30 °C (75 to 86 °F), and the scorching 40 °C (104 °F) days people talk about are mostly associated with Wuhan. The mountains of western Hubei, especially Shennongjia, have cooler summers and attract many weekend visitors from Wuhan and the other lowland cities.

Other important cities besides Wuhan are Jingmen; Shiyan, which is both a car-making centre and the entrance to the Wudang Mountains; Yichang, the base for the huge hydroelectric projects of the southwest; and Shashi.

People often describe Hubei as a "Land of Fish and Rice" (鱼米之乡). The main crops are cotton, rice, wheat and tea. Its industries include cars, metallurgy, machinery, power generation, textiles, food and high-tech goods.

The province holds sizeable deposits of iron, phosphorus, copper, manganese, vanadium, gypsum, rock salt, rutile, garnet, marlstone, wollastonite, borax, hongshiite and gold amalgam. Recoverable coal reserves are 548 million tons, modest next to other Chinese provinces. The province is well known for its fine turquoise and green faustite mines.

During the Third Front campaign, Hubei was a major recipient of national investment in industrial capacity. The Three Gorges Dam, finished in 2012 in western Hubei, generates a great deal of hydroelectricity, about 95 TWh in an average year. Smaller stations also operate at Gezhouba, Danjiangkou, Geheyan, Hanjiang, Duhe, Huanglongtan, Bailianhe, Lushui and Fushui.

In rank terms, Hubei is the seventh-largest provincial economy in China. It is second in Central China after Henan, third in South Central China after Guangdong and Henan, and and it ranks third among landlocked provinces, behind Henan and Sichuan. For 2021, nominal GDP stood at US$787 billion (CNY 5 trillion). GDP per head exceeded US$13,000, which makes Hubei the richest landlocked province and the richest in Central China, and second in South Central China behind Guangdong.

The Jingzhou Chengnan Economic Development Zone in Hubei was founded in 1992 with provincial approval. Its three main industries are textiles, petroleum and chemical processing, and together they produce 90 per cent of its output. Access is easy, with the airport just 6 kilometres (3.7 miles) away and the railway station 4 kilometres (2.5 miles) away.

The East Lake High-Tech Development Zone in Wuhan is a national high-tech zone, again built on optoelectronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing. This second description lists a slightly different set of firms: Changfei Fiber-optical Cables (China's biggest fibre-optic cable producer), Fenghuo Telecommunications, and the Wuhan Research Institute of Post and Telecommunications, which is the country's largest research body for optical telecommunications. HUST Technologies and Chutian Laser are named as laser-industry leaders.
The Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone is a national industrial park incorporated in 1993, with the same size and industry focus described earlier.
Wuhan Export Processing Zone, founded in 2000 inside that zone, plans 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile) of land, of which the first 0.7 square kilometres (0.27 square miles) has been launched.

The Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park lies within the East Lake zone and was developed together with Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. Planned area is 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles) with 600,000 square metres of floor area here, 8.5 km (5.28 miles) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 miles) from Tianhe Airport.
Xiangyang New and Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone

Han Chinese are the main ethnic group in Hubei. A sizeable Miao and Tujia population lives in the southwest, above all in Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture. From 18 October 2009, officials started resettling 330,000 people in Hubei and Henan whose homes were affected by the Danjiangkou Reservoir, a component of the wider South-North Water Transfer Project on the Han.

Wuhan Tianhe International Airport is Hubei's main airport. For the Three Gorges area there is Yichang Sanxia Airport, and Xiangyang, Enshi and Jingzhou also have passenger airports; the one at Jingzhou, Shashi Airport, is named after the city's Shashi District.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

hubei-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hubei University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at Hubei University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

hubei-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: About Hubei University of Chinese Medicine

blocks.x: The Hubei University of Chinese Medicine (湖北中医药大学), formerly known as Hubei Traditional Chinese Medicine College (湖北中医学院), is a provincial public university located in Wuhan, Hubei, China.

The history of Hubei University of Chinese Medicine dates back to 1958 when it was first founded as Hubei Vocational School of Traditional Chinese Medicine. In 2003, the university was renewed by combining with Hubei College of Medical Laboratory Sciences.
The college has three secondary schools, four affiliated hospitals, four State-Level (highest level) Medical Research Centers, and 10 Research Institutions.

The university occupies 161 acres (0.65 km2) with a total construction of about 470,000m2. The university has 15 departments, 28 specialties for bachelor's degrees and 9 specialties for professional training, 28 specialties for master's degrees, and 16 specialties for doctorate degrees; more than 104 bases for clinical practice, including 7 affiliated hospitals, 21 State-Level, Province-Level or College-Level laboratories for teaching. At present the university has 18,000 students.

Since 1986 when it started to enroll foreign students and students from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Africa, Korea, Vietnam, Mongolia, Hong Kong-Macau-Taiwan, the university has successively established such organizations as the Foreign Affairs Department, Overseas Education school and Hong Kong-Macao-Taiwan Affairs’ Office, which serve as a relatively independent facility, providing overseas students with the teaching and the affiliated facilities.

Since 1986, the University has trained over 1,600 overseas students from over 30 countries and regions, has developed the ability to receive about 50 groups of visiting guests per year, and has exchanged and cooperated with over 50 universities, academic institutions and companies from over 25 countries. Up to now, the International Education School has more than 500 resident overseas students from over 30 countries and regions. The new campus started construction in 2004.
The new buildings of the International Education School, consisting of accommodation, canteens, an entertainment center, a fitness center, a gymnasium, conference rooms, and offices.

The university staff has reached the number of 1212 people: among them, 859 are full-time teachers, 385 have the title of Professor or Associated Professor, 300 are tutors for mastership candidates, 40 are for doctorate candidates, 11 nationwide famous tutors for Chinese medicine succession, and more than 30 people enjoy Special Allowance issued by State Council and Provincial Government.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Wuhan, where Hubei University of Chinese Medicine is located.

Wuhan is in east-central Hubei, at latitude 29° 58'–31° 22' N and longitude 113° 41'–115° 05' E. Wuhan sits at the confluence of the Han River flowing into the Yangtze River at the East of the Jianghan Plain along the Yangtze's middle reaches.

The metropolitan area comprises three parts—Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang—commonly called the "Three Towns of Wuhan" (hence the name "Wuhan", combining "Wu" from the first city and "Han" from the other two). The consolidation of these cities occurred in 1927 and Wuhan was thereby established. The three former cities face each other across the rivers and are linked by bridges, including one of the first modern bridges in China, known as the "First Bridge".
Wuchang lies south east of the Yangtze River that separates it from both Hankou and Hanyang.
Hankou sits north of the Yangtze River separating it from Wuchang. Hankou is north of the Han River separating it from Hanyang.
Hanyang lies west of the Yangtze separating it from Wuchang. Hanyang is south of the Han river separating it from Hankou.

It is simple in terrain—low and flat in the middle and hilly in the south, with the Yangtze and Han rivers winding through the city. The She River enters the Yangtze in Huangpi District. Wuhan occupies a land area of 8,494.41 square kilometers (3,279.71 sq mi), most of which is alluvial plain and decorated with hills and a great number of lakes and ponds. Water makes up one quarter of Wuhan's urban territory, which is the highest percentage among major cities in China. Wuhan has nearly 200 lakes, including the East Lake of 33 km2, and Tangxun Lake, which are the largest lakes entirely within a city in China.

Other well-known lakes include South Lake and Sand Lake. Liangzi Lake, the largest lake by surface area in Hubei province, is located in the southeast of Jiangxia District.The twin peaks at the junction of Huangpi District and Xiaogan City, with an altitude of 872.5 meters, are the highest points in Wuhan. There are also several mountains within the city limits of Wuhan including Mount Luojia (珞珈山) in Wuchang District as well as Mount Hong (洪山) and Mount Yujia (喻家山/瑜珈山) in Hongshan District.

Wuhan's climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with abundant rainfall in summer and four distinctive seasons. Wuhan is known for its humid summers, when dewpoints can often reach 26 °C (79 °F) or more. Historically, along with Chongqing and Nanjing, Wuhan is referred to as one of the "Three Furnacelike Cities" along the Yangtze River for their hot summers. However, the climate data of recent years suggests that Wuhan is no longer among the top tier of "The hottest cities in summer" list, the New Four Furnacelike Cities are Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou, and Nanchang. Spring and autumn are generally mild, while winter is cool with quite low rainfall and occasional snow. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 4.1 °C (39.4 °F) in January to 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) in July. Annual precipitation totals just under 1,320 mm (52 in), the majority of which falls from April to July. The annual mean temperature is 17.4 °C (63.3 °F), while the frost-free period lasts 211 to 272 days. With monthly possible sunshine percentage ranging from 30 percent in January to 53 percent in August, the city proper receives 1,783 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extreme low and high temperatures recorded are −18.1 °C (−1 °F) on January 31, 1977, and 39.7 °C (103 °F) on July 27, 2017 / on August 18, 2022 (unofficial record of 41.3 °C (106 °F) on August 10, 1934).

Up until the 21st century, Wuhan was largely an agricultural region. Since 2004 it has been a focal point of the Rise of Central China Plan, which aims to build less-developed inland economies into hubs of advanced manufacturing.

Since 1890, the steel industry has been the backbone of Wuhan's industry. In 2010, automobile industry exceeded GDP for Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO) steel for the first time. There are 5 car manufacturers, including Dongfeng Honda, Citroën, SAIC-GM, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Dongfeng Renault. Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd is headquartered in the city.

As of 2016, Wuhan has attracted foreign investment from over 80 countries, with 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises established in the city with a total capital injection of $22.45 billion USD. Among these, about 50 French companies including Renault and PSA Group have operations in the city, representing over one third of French investment in China, and the highest level of French investment in any Chinese city.

Wuhan is an important center for economy, trade, finance, transportation, information technology, and education in China. Its major industries include optic-electronic, automobile manufacturing, iron and steel manufacturing, new pharmaceutical sector, biology engineering, new materials industry and environmental protection. Environmental sustainability is highlighted in Wuhan's list of emerging industries, which include energy efficiency technology and renewable energy.
As of 2021, Wuhan is ranked among the world's top 100 financial centers, according to the Global Financial Centres Index.
Major industrial zones in Wuhan include in chronological order:
Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone is a national level industrial zone incorporated in 1993. Its current zone size is about 10–25 square km and it plans to expand to 25–50 square km. Industries encouraged in Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone include Auto-mobile Production/Assembly, Biotechnology/Pharmaceuticals, Chemicals Production and Processing, Food/Beverage Processing, Heavy Industry, and Telecommunications Equipment.
Wuhan Export Processing Zone

Wuhan Export Processing Zone was established in 2000. It is located in Wuhan Economic and Technology Development Zone, planned to cover 2.7 square kilometers (1.0 square mile) of land. The first 0.7-square-kilometer (0.3-square-mile) area has already been created.
Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone

Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone is a national level high-tech development zone. Optical-electronics, telecommunications, and equipment manufacturing are the core industries of Wuhan East Lake High-Tech Development Zone (ELHTZ) while software outsourcing and electronics are also encouraged. ELHTZ is China's largest production center for optoelectronic products with key players like Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable, (the largest fiber-optical cable maker in China), and Fiberhome Telecommunications. Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone also represents the development center for China's laser industry with key players such as HGTECH and Chutian Laser being based in the zone.
Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park is located in Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone. Wuhan Optics Valley Software Park is jointly developed by East Lake High-Tech Development Zone and Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. The planned area is 0.67 square kilometers (0.26 square miles) with total floor area of 6,000,000 square meters (65,000,000 square feet). The zone is 8.5 km (5.28 mi) away from the 316 National Highway and is 46.7 km (29.02 mi) away from the Wuhan Tianhe Airport.
Wuhan Biolake

Biolake is an industrial base established in 2008 in the Optics Valley of China. Located in East Lake New Technology Development Zone of Wuhan, Biolake covers 15 km2 (5.8 sq mi), and has six parks including Bio-innovation Park, Bio-pharma Park, Bio-agriculture Park, Bio-manufacturing Park, Medical Device Park and Medical Health Park, to accommodate both research activities and living.

Wuhan is the most populous city in Central China and among the most populous in China. In the Seventh Census of China in 2020, Wuhan was home to 12,326,500 inhabitants, a 25.97% increase by 2.5411 million compared to the last census in 2010. 2010-2020 is the fastest growing 10 years in history since the census was established, averaging 2.34% annually, and it was the first time that Wuhan's population reached 10 million.
The encompassing metropolitan area was estimated by the OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) to have, as of 2010, a population of 19 million.

As of November 2019, urban development status considering both spatial and socioeconomic processes has been examined using Night Time Lighting data and land cover data as proxies; it showed Wuhan's high concentration
of socioeconomic activities compared to its urban spatial development.

According to a survey published in 2017, 79.2% of the population of Wuhan are either irreligious or practice worship of gods and ancestors; among these 0.9% are Taoists. Among other religious doctrines, 14.7% of the population adheres to Buddhism, 2.9% to Protestantism, 0.3% to Catholicism and 1.6% to Islam, and 1.6% of the population adheres to unspecified other religions.

China Railway Wuhan Group manages the Wuhan Railway Hub. Wuhan Railway Hub is considered one of the four key railway hubs of China. The city of Wuhan is served by three major railway stations: the Hankou railway station in Hankou, the Wuchang railway station in Wuchang, and the Wuhan railway station, located in a newly developed area east of the East Lake (Hongshan District). As the stations are many miles apart, it is important for passengers to be aware of the particular station(s) used by a particular train.

The (original) Hankou Station was the terminus for the Jinghan railway from Beijing, while the Wuchang Station was the terminus for the Yuehan railway to Guangzhou. Since the construction of the First Yangtze Bridge and the linking of the two lines into the Jingguang railway, both Hankou and Wuchang stations have been served by trains going to all directions, which contrasts with the situation in such cities as New York or Moscow, where different stations serve different directions.

With the opening of the Hefei-Wuhan high-speed railway on April 1, 2009, Wuhan became served by high-speed trains with Hefei, Nanjing, and Shanghai; several trains a day now connect the city with Shanghai, getting there in under six hours. As of early 2010, most of these express trains leave from the Hankou railway station.

In 2006, construction began on the new Wuhan railway station with 11 platforms, located on the northeastern outskirts of the city. In December 2009, the station was opened, as China unveiled its second high-speed train with scheduled runs from Guangzhou to Wuhan. Billed as the fastest train in the world, it can reach a speed of 394 km/h (244.82 mph). The travel time between the two cities has been reduced from ten and a half hours to just three. The rail service has been extended north to Beijing.
As of 2011, the new Wuhan railway station is primarily used by the Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, while most regular trains to other destinations continue to use the Hankou and Wuchang stations.

Construction work is carried out on several lines of the new Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity railway, which will eventually connect Wuhan's three main rail terminals with several stations throughout the city's outer areas and farther suburbs, as well as with the nearby cities of Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang, and Xiaogan. The first line of the system, the one to Xianning, opened for passenger operations at the end of 2013. The line to Xiaogen opened on December 1, 2016, and it was extended with the opening of the Wuhan–Shiyan high-speed railway to Shiyan on November 29, 2019.

The main freight railway station and classification yard of the Wuhan metropolitan area is the extensive Wuhan North railway station, with 112 tracks and over 650 switches. It is located in Hengdian Subdistrict of Huangpi District, located 20 km (12 mi) north of the Wuhan Station and 23 km (14 mi) from Hankou Station.

Wuhan Metro is a rapid transit system serving the city of Wuhan. Owned and operated by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd., the network now includes 11 lines, 282 stations, and 435 km (270 mi) of route length. Line 1, the first line in the system, opened on July 28, 2004, making Wuhan the seventh city in mainland China with a rapid transit system, after Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun, and Dalian. Line 2 opened on December 28, 2012, and is the first underground metro line crossing the Yangtze River. Commuting across the Yangtze River and Han River has been the bottleneck of Wuhan traffic. However, the appearance of Wuhan Metro greatly relieved this problem. With 1.22 billion annual passengers in 2019, Wuhan Metro is the sixth-busiest rapid transit system in mainland China. Wuhan Metro is a rapidly developing metro system. There are a number of lines or sections under construction. The government of Wuhan City promised the citizens that at least two lines or sections open every year. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the entire network was out of service from January 23 to March 27, 2020.
Trams were brought to the streets of Wuhan on July 28, 2017, with the first line (Auto-city T1 Line) opened that day. The trams under construction or planning in Wuhan are:
Auto-city trams, with Lines T1, T2, T6, and T8 in the Wuhan Economic Development Area, in the far western reaches on Hanyang. T1 Line is operational as of 2017.
Optics Valley trams, two lines (T1 and T2) south and east of Guanggu Circle (Guanggu Guangchang) in southeastern Wuchang. The system opened on January 18, 2018.
The Old Hankou Streetcar, a loop line around Hankou city.
Local transport is also provided by buses, including trolleybuses. The trolleybus system has been in operation since 1958. Its first route, which remains in operation today, is route 1.
Wuhan is a major hub for maritime transport in central China. The Port of Wuhan provides services for the local population and shipping services.

Located on the banks of the Yangtze River, Wuhan has a long history of ferry services. Modern ferry services were established in 1900 by steam boat. In 1937, a train ferry was established to transport train cars from Hankou to Wuchang. There are numbered stops around Wuhan where people can get on and off the ferry and there is a tourist ferry in the night.
Currently, ferry services are provided by the Wuhan Ferry Company. In 2010, the company bought ten new ships to replace those that had been in service for 29 years.
Hubei University of Chinese Medicine lists 61 programs for international students on this site: 33 bachelor, 14 master's, 14 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 61 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 34,000 to CNY 34,000 (median CNY 34,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 40,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.

61 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.
