Hunan Normal University, often shortened to HunNU, is a public university in Changsha, the capital of Hunan province in central China. It is a provincial institution, and the money for it comes from both the Ministry of Education and the Hunan provincial government. Two national schemes include it, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction programme.

hunan-normal-university.h: Roots in the National Normal College

blocks.x: The university grew out of the first independent teacher-training college in China, the National Normal College, founded in 1938. Its history reaches back much further, to Yuelu Academy of the Northern Song dynasty, which is counted among the four most prestigious academies of the past 1,000 years in China. In 1949 the college was merged into Hunan University.

Hunan Normal University has five campuses with a combined area of 1.78 km2 and one million square metres of floor space. Most are near Yuelu Mountain, so students study in one of Changsha's greenest and most scenic districts.

Academically, the university is organised into 23 colleges, 3 teaching departments and 51 research institutions. It offers 74 undergraduate programmes, 147 master's programmes and 55 doctoral programmes. The facilities include 10 postdoctoral research stations and 13 State-level training and research bases or centres. There are also 7 key laboratories on campus, which the Ministry of Education and Hunan Province built together.

Almost 300,000 people have graduated or studied here since the start, including some 4,000 students from abroad and from Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. Today more than 24,000 undergraduates, 8,000 graduate students and 300 international students study there.

The university employs 1091 professors and associate professors. One is an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and another of the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Since 2000 the university has hosted about 600 scholars and experts from more than 20 countries for lectures or research visits, and it has exchange ties with over 80 foreign higher education institutions.

The library holds 3.4 million volumes, 200,000 of them traditional thread-bound books, and takes 4,700 Chinese and foreign periodicals. The university publishes 12 academic journals and has its own publisher, Hunan Normal University Press.
The university is regularly placed third in Hunan province and within the top 100 in China.

On the world stage, the figures are these. ARWU, the Academic Ranking of World Universities, gave it a place at 501 in 2023. The 2025 edition of the Center for World University Rankings had it 759th, and for 2023-2024 the University Ranking by Academic Performance put it 623rd among nearly 30,000 institutions. The 2025 CWTS Leiden Ranking, based on publications from 2020 to 2023, listed it 467th in the world. Positions change each year, so check the newest editions before relying on any one number.

Student life depends heavily on the city outside the campus: how the weather behaves, how you get about, and what you can do in your free time. The sections below introduce Changsha, the home of Hunan Normal University.

The city is in the north-east of Hunan, along the lower course of the Xiang River and in the western Changliu Basin. It lies between longitudes 111°53' and 114°15' east and latitudes 27°51' and 28°41' north. Its neighbours are Yichun and Pingxiang in Jiangxi Province to the east, Zhuzhou and Xiangtan to the south, Loudi and Yiyang to the west, and Yueyang and Yiyang to the north.

Its east-west extent is roughly 230 kilometres and its north-south extent roughly 88 kilometres. The whole municipality has an area of 11,819 km2 (4,563 sq mi). Of that, 2,150.9 km2 (830.5 sq mi) is classed as urban, and the continuously built-up urban core takes up 374.64 km2 (144.65 sq mi). Elevation ranges from 1,607.9 m (5,275 ft) at Mount Qixing (七星岭), in Daweishan Town, down to just 23.5 m (77 ft) at Zhanhu (湛湖) in Qiaokou Town.

The Xiang is the city's main river and flows north through it for 74 km (46 mi), taking in 15 tributaries, the largest four being the Liuyang, Laodao, Jinjiang and Wei. It splits the city into two halves. The eastern bank is mainly commercial and the western bank is mainly cultural and educational, which is where Hunan Normal University and the other major universities are found. On 10 October 2001 the city government moved from Fanzheng Street to Guanshaling, and since then the economies of the two banks have grown in better balance.
#### Rivers and water

Nearly all of Changsha's rivers belong to the Xiang system. Besides the Xiang itself, 15 tributaries join it, mainly the Liuyang, Laodao, Minjiang and Qinshui rivers. A total of 302 tributaries are longer than five kilometres, including 289 within the Xiang basin. By grade there are 24 first-level tributaries, 128 second-level, 118 third-level and 32 fourth-level, and 13 of them belong to the Zijiang system. The result is a nearly complete water system with a dense network of rivers. Its features are abundant water and water energy, rivers that do not freeze in winter, and low sediment content.
#### Geology

Changsha's geology is distinctive: rock layers are widely exposed, granite bodies are spread across the area, and the structure is complex. Rocks from every geological and historical period are visible here, and the oldest layer is roughly a billion years old. Around 600 million years ago this was a shallow sea. Water gradually retreated eastward and westward, and most of what is now Liuyang, Changsha and Wangcheng emerged as the north-western fringe of the ancient Jiangnan land. The sea finally left the Changsha area about 140 million years ago, and it has been land since. Movements of the earth's crust shaped a long, narrow depression, the Chang(sha)-Ping(jiang) Basin. With the dawn of the Cenozoic era the whole Changping Basin was lifted into dry land. The third ice age came about 3.5 million years ago, and Liuyang still preserves some glacial landforms from it.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). The yearly mean is 17.8 °C (64.0 °F); January is cool at 5.3 °C (41.5 °F) and July is hot at 29.4 °C (84.9 °F). Despite its position near 28°N, the city has the same January temperatures as London or Paris, which lie some 20° of latitude farther from the equator. Annual rainfall averages 1,499 millimetres (59.0 in), and there are 275 frost-free days. Sunshine is 20% of possible hours in January and 53% in July, which adds up to 1,532.8 hours a year.

The four seasons are clearly marked. Summers are long, very hot and rainy. Autumn is the pleasant and driest season. In winter the weather is chilly and grey, with light rain rather than downpours, and occasional cold snaps bring the temperature under freezing. Spring is particularly wet and humid, and the sun shines for less than 30% of the time.

At the present Wangchengpo Weather Observing Station, which has recorded since 1951, the lowest temperature was -11.3 °C (11.7 °F), on 9 February 1972, and the highest was 40.6 °C (105.1 °F), on 13 August 1953 and again on 2 August 2003; there is also an unofficial record of 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) from 10 August 1934. In practice that means long humid summers, wet springs and damp, cold winters in which heating may be limited indoors, so warm clothing is worth bringing.

Changsha is among the 15 Chinese cities described as the most developed and economically advanced. GDP per person in 2024 passed CN¥144,525 (US$20,294 at nominal rates, US$42,136 adjusted for purchasing power), which is high-income status by World Bank standards. The city's Human Development Index was 0.817, a very high level, in 2016, similar to a moderately developed country. It is one of the core cities in South Central China, in the Yangtze River Economic Belt and in the Belt and Road Initiative. The Globalization and World Cities Research Network ranks it Beta- (a global second-tier city), it counts as a new first-tier city in China, and it is a pioneer area for China-Africa economic and trade cooperation. Nicknamed the Construction Machinery Capital of the World, it has an industrial chain built mainly around construction machinery and new materials, supported by cars, electronics and information technology, household appliances and biomedicine.

From the 1990s the city's economy began to speed up, and during the 2000s its growth rate was the highest of any major Chinese city. In 2015 the Xiangjiang New Area, Central China's first state-level new area, was established. A strong media and publishing sector led UNESCO to name Changsha a City of Media Arts, the first in China, and the city hosts the Hunan Broadcasting System (HBS), which is the country's most influential provincial TV station.

Yicai.com, a financial news portal, issued its first city ranking in 2013 with Changsha listed among the 15 new first-tier cities. The city reached a GDP of one trillion yuan (about 154 billion US dollars) in 2017 and became the thirteenth in China to do so. As of 2020, over 164 Global 500 companies had opened branches here, and in 2022 it was tenth in the country for commercial value among new first-tier cities.

Changsha's 2021 GDP was above RMB 1.327 trillion (US$208 billion nominal, or US$318 billion by purchasing power). Within South Central China only Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Wuhan were richer, and in Central China only Wuhan was. Set beside European economies, the nominal figure exceeds Ukraine's (US$200 billion) and Hungary's (US$182 billion), which are the 22nd and 23rd largest in Europe. The city is also a leader in the night economy; a 2021-2022 report on city night economies (the China City Night Economy Impact Report) put it second in China for 2021, after Chongqing.

The Hurun Global Rich List placed Changsha among the world's top 35 cities for resident billionaires in 2022. By 2024 it stood first in Central China and ninth across Greater China, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Hangzhou, Taipei, Guangzhou and Ningbo.
Looking ahead, an Oxford Economics study projects that by 2035 its nominal GDP will put it among the 50 largest cities in the world, with nominal GDP per person reaching US$41,000 in 2030.
#### Development zones

The Changsha Economic and Technological Development Zone (ETZ) was founded in 1992 at Xingsha, in the east of the city. The planned area, which is the same as its present area, comes to 38.6 km2 (14.9 sq mi). National Highways 319 and 107 and the G4 Beijing-Hong Kong and Macau Expressway pass close by, and the zone is near downtown Changsha and the railway station. It is only 8 km (5.0 mi) from the airport. Its main industries are high technology, biotechnology and new materials.

In Dongyang Town is the Liuyang ETZ, which was set up as a national biological industry base on 10 January 1998. Biological pharmaceuticals, information technology and health foods are its pillars. At the 2015 count it had more than 700 registered enterprises and an industrial output value of 85.6 billion yuan (US$13.7 billion), and its business income was 100.2 billion yuan (US$16.1 billion). The built-up area measures 16.5 km2 (6.4 sq mi).

Tourism is a major industry, and Changsha has repeatedly been named China's top tourist city. Yuelu Academy is a highlight. So is the Changsha Meixihu International Culture and Arts Centre, a cultural complex by the British firm Zaha Hadid Architects that overlooks Meixi Lake, in the Meixihu subdistrict. The list continues with the statue of the young Mao Zedong on Orange Isle, Meixi Lake Park, Window of the World, Kaifu Temple, Changsha Ice World and the Changsha IFS Tower.
#### Yuelu Mountain

Yuelu Mountain takes its name from the Nanyue Ji, a text from the Liu Song dynasty of the Southern and Northern dynasties, which says that Nanyue extends eight hundred miles, with Huiyan at its head and Yuelu at its foot. It stands on the west bank of the Xiang River in Yuelu District. Orange Island lies in the middle of the river and runs from south to north, with Yuelu to its west and the old city to its east. The scenic area has 977 plant species in 559 genera and 174 families, mostly typical subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest and subtropical warm coniferous forest. In some places large stretches of native secondary evergreen broad-leaved forest remain, and there are many rare, endangered and famous old trees.
#### Orange Island

Orange Island is in the middle of the Xiang River in Yuelu District. Originally the island was about 17 hectares, but the developed scenic area now totals 91.64 hectares. Among the alluvial sandbars of the lower Xiang it is the biggest, and it has the nickname China's First Continent. Attractions include the Mao Zedong Youth Art Sculpture and Wen Tiantai. Historical records say it formed in 305, the second year of Yongxing under Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, from the build-up of sand and gravel carried by rapids.
#### Huaminglou

Huaminglou, in the south-east of Ningxiang City, is a popular tourist site and a key nationally protected cultural relic. It was the family home of Liu Shaoqi, the revolutionary leader who later served as president of China.
#### Hunan Museum

You will find Hunan Museum at No. 50 Dongfeng Road in Kaifu District. It was in the first group of museums in China given national first-level status, is one of eight key national museums that the central and local governments built together, and is the biggest general history and art museum in the province. The museum dates back to 1897 (the 23rd year of the Guangxu reign, Qing dynasty); today's building is a newer home.

The 2020 Chinese census counted 10,047,914 people in Changsha, of whom 7,355,198 lived in the built-up (metro) area made up of the six urban districts and largely joined-up Changsha County. Most are Han Chinese. There is also a sizeable minority population, the three largest groups being the Hui, Tujia and Miao. In the 2000 census, 48,564 members of ethnic minorities lived in the city, or 0.7% of the population, and the other minorities are much smaller, with twenty groups having fewer than 1,000 members in the city.
#### Television and entertainment

After China Central Television (CCTV), Hunan Broadcasting System is the largest television broadcaster in China, and its headquarters are in Changsha. The popular shows it produces include Super Girl. These shows have created a new entertainment industry in the city, with singing bars, dance clubs and theatre shows, along with related businesses such as hair salons, fashion shops and late-night spicy snack stalls (especially in summer). Changsha has become an entertainment hub, and it has also grown more westernised and attracts a growing number of foreign residents.
#### Sport

Helong Stadium, with 55,000 seats, is among the largest multi-purpose stadiums in China, and it takes its name from the Communist military leader He Long. The local football club, Hunan Billows F.C. (who play in China League Two), is based there. Smaller matches are staged at the Hunan Provincial People's Stadium, a more modest 6,000-seat venue that is also in the city.
#### Xiang embroidery and artificial intelligence

Xiang embroidery now has an AI design lab, the product of cooperation between the Hunan Embroidery Research Institute and local technology firms. It uses algorithms to study historic patterns and produce new designs, helping craftspeople with the creative process and bringing this intangible cultural heritage into the modern age.

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Hunan Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.

Travel to Changsha, register at Hunan Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Hunan University (HNU; 湖南大学) is a national public university in Yuelu, Changsha, Hunan, China. It is affiliated with and funded by the Ministry of Education. The university is part of Project 211, Project 985, and the Double First-Class Construction. It is also a member in the BRICS Universities League.
Yuelu Academy was founded in the year 976, during the Song dynasty, as a Confucian shuyuan.
In 1903, during the final years of the Qing dynasty, the Hunan Institute of Higher Education was established.
In 1926, the name of the institution was then changed to Hunan Normal College, and then Hunan Public Polytechnic School, before finally arriving at the name Hunan University.

In 1937, the academy was transformed from a provincial university into a national university, renamed the National Hunan University, and designated by the Ministry of education, becoming the fifteenth national university.

From April 1938 to May 1941, the National Hunan University suffered serious losses and, made it difficult to run the school. During the Battle of Changsha, the National Hunan University was suspended.
In 1949, the name Hunan University was again adopted, and the calligraphy of "Hunan University" was written by Mao Zedong in 1950 as soon as the People's Republic of China was founded.
In 1959, Hunan University was officially restored after the national readjustment of higher education institutions.
In 1963, HNU was subordinated to the First Ministry of Machinery Industry.
In 1978, Hunan University's status as one of the 88 National Key Universities in China was reaffirmed.In 1996, Hunan University became one of the universities sponsored by Project 211.
In 2000, Hunan University was selected as a member of Project 985.

In November 2010, the National Supercomputing Changsha Center was built on the Hunan University campus under the management and operation of Hunan University. It is the first National Supercomputing Center in Central China and the third of its kind apart from other two national centers situated in Tianjin and Shenzhen.
In 2011, HNU participated in the Excellence League, an alliance of 10 Chinese universities with a strong background in engineering.
In 2015, HNU joined the BRICS Universities League, a consortium of leading research universities from BRICS countries.In 2017, Hunan University was listed in the Double First-Class Construction.

For the proportion of their scientific publications that rank among the top 10% and 50% in their fields by citations in the 2024 CWTS Leiden Ranking Open Edition, Hunan University ranks 7th globally (1st in Eurasia) and 1st in the world, respectively.

Hunan University (with a Z-score of 10.2) ranks 2nd only to Tsinghua University (z=11.0), which leads the "High Group of 32 Universities".

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Changsha, where Hunan University is located.

Changsha is in northeast Hunan Province, the lower reaches of the Xiang River and the western part of the Changliu Basin. It lies between 111°53' to 114°15' east longitude and 27°51' to 28°41' north latitude. The city borders Yichun and Pingxiang of Jiangxi Province in the east, Zhuzhou and Xiangtan in the south, Loudi and Yiyang in the west, and Yueyang and Yiyang in the north. It is about 230 kilometres from east to west and about 88 kilometres from north to south. Changsha covers an area of 11,819 km2 (4,563 sq mi), of which the urban area of 2,150.9 km2 (830.5 sq mi), the urban built-up area is 374.64 km2 (144.65 sq mi). Changsha's highest point is Mount Qixing (七星岭) in Daweishan Town, 1,607.9 m (5,275 ft). The lowest point is Zhanhu (湛湖) in Qiaokou Town, 23.5 m (77 ft).

The Xiang is the main river in the city, running 74 km (46 mi) northward through the territory. 15 tributaries flow into the Xiang, of which the Liuyang, Laodao, Jinjiang and Wei are the four largest. The Xiang divides the city into two parts. The eastern part is mainly commercial and the west is mainly cultural and educational. On 10 October 2001, the seat of Changsha City was transferred from Fanzheng Street to Guanshaling. Since then, the economy of both sides of the Xiang River has achieved a balanced development.

Most of the rivers in Changsha belong to the Xiang River system. In addition to the Xiangjiang River, 15 tributaries flow into the Xiang, mainly including Liuyang River, Laodao River, Minjiang River, and Qinshui River. 302 tributaries are more than five kilometers long, including 289 in the Xiang River Basin. According to the tributary grading there are 24 primary tributaries, 128 secondary tributaries, 118 third tributaries, and 32 tributaries; and 13 are Zijiang water systems; a fairly complete water system is formed, and the river network is densely distributed. Hydrological characteristics of Changsha: the water system is complete, the river network dense; the water volume greater, the water energy resources abundant; the winter not frozen, and the sediment content small.

The geological features of Changsha City are: the formation is fully exposed, the granite body is widely distributed, and the geological structure is complex. The strata of each geological and historical period are exposed in Changsha City, and the oldest stratum was formed about one billion years ago. About 600 million years ago, Changsha was a sea, but the sea was not deep. Later, seawater gradually withdrew from the east and west, and most of Liuyang, Changsha, and Wangcheng rose out of the sea and became the northwestern edge of the ancient land of Jiangnan. About 140 million years ago, the sea leaching in the Changsha area ended and it became a land. Due to the influence of crustal movement and geological structure, a long-shaped mountain depression basin, the Chang (Sha) Ping (Jiang) Basin, was formed. Beginning of the new generation, the entire Changping Basin has risen to land. About 3.5 million years ago, the third ice age occurred on the earth, and Liuyang retained the remains of glacier landforms.

Changsha has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), with annual average temperature being at 17.8 °C (64.0 °F), with a mean of 5.3 °C (41.5 °F) in January and 29.4 °C (84.9 °F) in July. Despite locating on 28°N, Changsha has exactly same January temperatures at London or Paris, which are 20° further to the equator than it. Average annual precipitation is 1,499 millimetres (59.0 in), with a 275-day frost-free period. With a monthly possible-sunshine percentage ranging from 20% in January to 53% in July, the city receives 1,532.8 hours of bright sunshine annually. The four seasons are distinct. The summers are long and very hot, with heavy rainfall, and autumn is comfortable and is the driest season. Winter is chilly and overcast with lighter rainfall more likely than downpours; cold snaps occur with temperatures occasionally dropping below freezing. Spring is especially rainy and humid with the sun shining less than 30% of the time. The minimum temperature ever recorded since 1951 at the current Wangchengpo Weather Observing Station was −11.3 °C (11.7 °F), recorded on 9 February 1972. The maximum was 40.6 °C (105.1 °F) on 13 August 1953 and 2 August 2003 [the unofficial record of 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) was set on 10 August 1934].

Changsha is one of China's 15 most "developed and economically advanced" cities. As of 2024, Changsha's GDP per capita exceeded CN¥144,525 ( US$20,294 in nominal or US$42,136 in PPP), which is considered a high-income status by the World Bank and a primary developed city according to the international standard. The HDI of Changsha reached 0.817 (very high) in 2016, which is roughly comparable to a moderately developed country. Changsha is now one of the core cities in the South Central China region, the Yangtze River Economic Belt and the Belt and Road Initiative, a Beta- (global second-tier) city by the Globalization and World Cities Research Network, a new Chinese first-tier city and also a pioneering area for China-Africa economic and trade cooperation. Known as the "Construction Machinery Capital of the world", Changsha has an industrial chain with construction machinery and new materials as the main industries, complemented by automobiles, electronic information, household appliances, and biomedicine.

Since the 1990s, Changsha has begun to accelerate economic development, and then achieved the highest growth rate among China's major cities during the 2000s. The Xiangjiang New Area, the first state-level new area in Central China, was established in 2015. Changsha also has a prominent media and publishing industry, and has been named the first "UNESCO City of Media Arts" in China. Changsha is home to the Hunan Broadcasting System (HBS), the most influential provincial TV station in China.

In 2013, the financial news portal Yicai.com published its first edition of a list of ranking cities in China, with Changsha being included as one of 15 new first-tier cities. In 2017, Changsha made its way into the 1-trillion-yuan GDP club, becoming the 13th city in China with a GDP of one trillion yuan (154 billion US dollars). As of 2020, more than 164 Global 500 companies have established branches in Changsha. As a new first-tier city, Changsha was rated #10 nationwide in terms of its commercial worth in 2022.

As of 2021, Changsha's GDP exceeded RMB 1.327 trillion (US$208 billion in nominal and US$318 billion in PPP), making it the 5th most wealthy city in the South-Central China region after Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Hong Kong, and Wuhan and the 2nd richest city in the Central China region after Wuhan. Changsha's GDP (nominal) was US$208 billion in 2021, exceeding that of Ukraine and Hungary, with  GDPs of US$200 billion and US$182 billion, the 22nd and 23rd largest economies in Europe respectively. Changsha has also led the development of the night economy and as of 2021, it ranked 2nd nationwide after Chongqing in terms of nighttime economic power according to the "China City Night Economy Impact Report 2021-2022".

According to the Hurun Global Rich List, Changsha ranked among the top 35 cities globally as of 2022, and as of 2024, it ranked first in the Central China region and 9th in Greater China (after Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Hangzhou, Taipei, Guangzhou, and Ningbo) in terms of resident billionaires.
Changsha's nominal GDP is projected to be among the world's top 50 largest cities according to a study by Oxford Economics in 2035 and its nominal GDP per capita will reach US$41,000 in 2030.

The Changsha ETZ was founded in 1992. It is located in Xingsha in eastern Changsha. The total planned area is 38.6 km2 (14.9 sq mi) and the current area is 38.6 km2 (14.9 sq mi). Near the zone are National Highways 319 and 107 as well as the G4 Beijing–Hong Kong and Macau Expressway. The zone is also very close to Changsha's downtown area and the railway station, while the distance between the zone and the city's airport is a mere 8 km (5.0 mi). The major industries in the zone include the high-tech industry, the biology project technology industry, and the new material industry.

The Liuyang ETZ is a national biological industry base created on 10 January 1998, located in Dongyang Town. Its pillar industry comprises biological pharmacy, Information technology and Health food. As of 2015, It has more than 700 registered enterprises. The total industrial output value of the zone hits 85.6 billion yuan (US$13.7 billion) and its business income is 100.2 billion yuan (US$16.1 billion). Its builtup area covers 16.5 km2 (6.4 sq mi).

Tourism is a major industry in Changsha. Changsha has been consistently ranked as China's top tourist city. There are several sites in Changsha, notably the Yuelu Academy and the Changsha Meixihu International Culture and Arts Centre, a cultural complex designed by the British firm Zaha Hadid Architects overlooking the Meixi Lake at the Meixihu subdistrict of the city. Others include the Young Mao Zedong statue on Orange Isle, Meixi Lake Park, Changsha IFS Tower, Window of the World, Kaifu Temple and Changsha Ice World.

Yuelu Mountain is named after the "Nanyue Ji" written in the Liu and Song dynasties in the Southern and Northern dynasties, which states that "the surrounding area of Nanyue is eight hundred miles, with Huiyan as the head and Yuelu as the foot." Yuelu Mountain is located on the west bank of the Xiangjiang River in Yuelu District, Changsha City, Hunan Province; Orange Island is located in the middle of the Xiangjiang River, running through the center of the river from south to north, looking at Yuelu to the west and the ancient city to the east. Orange Island has Mao Zedong Youth Art Sculpture, Wen Tiantai and other attractions. It was formed by the alluvial accumulation of rapids and sand and gravel.

Huaminglou is a renowned tourist attraction and a national key cultural relic protection site in China. Located in the southeast of Ningxiang City, it is the former home of Liu Shaoqi, the revolutionary leader and former president of China.

Hunan Museum, located at No. 50 Dongfeng Road, Kaifu District, Changsha City, Hunan Province, is one of the first batch of national first-level museums in China, one of the eight national key museums jointly built by the central and local governments, and the largest comprehensive history and art museum in Hunan Province. The Hunan Provincial Museum was founded in the 23rd year of Guangxu's reign in the Qing dynasty (1897), and the current site is its new museum.

As of the 2020 Chinese census, Changsha was home to 10,047,914 people, whom 7,355,198 lived in its built-up (or metro) area made of the 6 urban Districts plus Changsha County largely conurbated. The majority of people living in Changsha are Han Chinese. A sizeable population of ethnic minority groups also live in Changsha. The three largest are the Hui, Tujia, and Miao peoples. The 2000 census showed that 48,564 members of ethnic minorities live in Changsha, 0.7% of the population. The other minorities make up a significantly smaller part of the population. Twenty ethnic minorities have fewer than 1,000 members living in the city.

These programs have also brought a new entertainment industry into the city, which includes singing bars, dance clubs, theater shows, as well as related businesses including hair salons, fashion stores, and shops for hot spicy snacks at night (especially during summer). While Changsha has developed into an entertainment hub, the city has also become increasingly westernized and has attracted a growing number of foreigners.

Changsha has one of China's largest multi-purpose sports stadiums—Helong Stadium, with 55,000 seats. The stadium was named after the Communist military leader He Long. It is the home ground of local football team Hunan Billows F.C., which plays in China League Two. The more modest 6,000-seat Hunan Provincial People's Stadium, also located in Changsha, is used by the team for their smaller games.

Inner Mongolia Agricultural University, usually shortened to IMAU, is a university in Hohhot, the capital of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in northern China, and it is run under that regional government. Its names are 内蒙古农业大学 in Chinese and ᠥᠪᠥᠷ ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠤᠨ ᠲᠠᠶᠢᠶᠠᠯᠠᠩ ᠤᠨ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠰᠤᠷᠭᠠᠭᠤᠯᠢ in Mongolian script. It was founded in 1952, and today it offers more than 100 undergraduate and postgraduate programmes in agricultural, engineering, scientific, artistic, business and management subjects.
Right from the start the university had a notable link to national leadership: when IMAU opened in 1952, its first president was appointed by Chairman Mao Zedong.

The teaching and research staff number 2,737. Of these, 435 hold doctoral degrees and 653 hold master's degrees, and 101 are supervisors of doctoral students. One professorship comes from the Yangtze River Scholar Award Plan.

IMAU has three campuses: the main campus in Hohhot, the Salaqi branch campus, and the Current Science Park. Together they cover 15,000 hectares, and 10,000 acres of that is used for teaching and research. Sport has four school-standard stadiums, the library has a construction area of 3,000 square meters, and the value of teaching instruments and equipment reaches 412 million RMB.
Over 63 years IMAU has built up a multi-level management system. Undergraduate study is its main objective, yet it also gives serious attention to postgraduate, higher vocational and adult education.

The university is multi-disciplinary, with eight fields of study, among them Education, Social Sciences, Management, Economics, Engineering, Science and Agronomy. It has trained more than 70,000 skilled people across these fields.

Beyond its 19 colleges, which include the College of Animal Science and Medicine, Its other units are the Advanced Educational Research Center and a Department for Physical Education. Its research infrastructure is broad. Laboratories comprise two at ministry level, one for the State Bureau of Forestry, and seven that are regional key laboratories. There is also a state-level open field observation station, and engineering research is supported by three regional technology centers plus one engineering research center backed by the Ministry of Education.

College of Material Science and Art Design
Another group covers management, society and language:
College of Foreign Languages
College of Economics and Management
College of Humanity and Social Science
Last come the colleges designed for particular kinds of student:
College of Continuing Education
College of Vocational Technology
College of International Education

On academic standing, the university counts 22 regional key disciplines, one of the Ministry of Agriculture, three of the State Forestry Administration, and one at state level. Six first-level and 33 second-level disciplines are authorised to award doctorates, and 72 second-level disciplines award master's degrees. Three moving scientific research stations support post-doctorate research.

At undergraduate level the university provides 58 programmes, 13 of them taught in both Mongolian and Chinese. For international and bilingual learners, eighteen undergraduate programmes are offered bilingually in Chinese and English:
Agronomy
Horticulture
Practaculture Science
Animal Quarantine
Biotechnology
Bioscience
Wood Science and Engineering
Landscape Architecture
Furniture Design and International Trade
Food Science and Engineering
Water Resources Engineering
Vehicle Engineering
Computer Science and Technology
Software Engineering
Computer Network Engineering
Finance
Law
Economic Management for Agricultural and Forestry

IMAU's research has produced results in 265 projects, and it has won provincial "Technological Advancement" awards in 18 of them, seven being first-class awards. That work has given wide technical support and service to the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in areas such as reforesting cultivated land, protecting natural forests and the ecology, building the economy, and the ban on open herding in favour of keeping animals in yards.
The regional government has also honoured the university with an award for being an "Excellent collectivity" that made a great contribution to developing the region through technological education.

IMAU has academic ties with roughly 20 universities in countries including the United States, Canada, the UK, France, Australia, Japan, Russia and the Republic of Mongolia. It runs collaborative programmes with foreign educational institutions, and it reports strong achievements in teaching, research, cultural exchange and joint programmes.

inner-mongolia-agricultural-university.h: Hohhot: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Student life depends heavily on the city, so this part of the profile covers Hohhot's setting, weather, people, economy, culture and transport.

Hohhot lies in south-central Inner Mongolia, with the Daqing Shan (大青山, "Great Blue Mountains") to its north, and the Hetao Plateau on its south side. As a curiosity, Argentina is on the far side of the world from Hohhot: the antipode lies 22 kilometres (14 mi) from Los Menucos, a village in Río Negro Province.

inner-mongolia-agricultural-university.h: Climate: cold, dry winters and sunny skies

blocks.x: The climate is cold semi-arid (Köppen BSk). Winters are long, cold and very dry; summers are hot and somewhat humid; spring brings strong winds; and the monsoon has some influence. In January, the coldest month, the daily mean is -10.7 °C (12.7 °F), and The warmest month, July, averages 23.2 °C (73.8 °F), and across the whole year the mean is 7.6 °C (45.7 °F). Rain and snow together total 411 millimetres (16.2 in) a year, with July and August bringing more than half. The figure can swing widely: in 1965 just 155.1 mm (6.11 in) fell, but six years earlier the total was 929.2 mm (36.58 in), over a third of which (338.6 mm, or 13.33 in) came in July alone.

Summer attracts tourists, drawn by the nearby Zhaohe grasslands. In more recent years desertification has meant sandstorms almost every year. Sunshine is plentiful all year, between 54 percent of the possible total in November and 66 percent in September, which adds up to 2,680 hours of bright sunshine annually. The lowest official reading was -32.8 °C (-27 °F), on 6 February 1951, and the highest, 38.9 °C (102 °F), came on 30 July 2010. Although an unofficial low of -36.2 °C (-33 °F) was noted in January 1930.

Hohhot's urban population has grown quickly since the 1990s. The 2010 Census counted 2,866,615 people, which was 428,717 more than in 2000, an average annual growth of 1.63 percent over 2000 to 2010. The built-up (metro) area, covering 4 urban districts, has 1,980,774 residents.

Han Chinese form the majority, with 87.16 percent of the population in 2010. Trace most local Han families back a few decades and the ancestors came from Shanxi, northeast China or Hebei. Mongols in the city mostly speak Chinese: in a 1993 survey, Inner Mongolia University found only 8 percent of Tümed Mongols (the tribe forming the majority in Hohhot) able to speak their own language. A significant share of residents are of mixed ethnic origin. The anthropologist William Jankowiak, in his book of 1993, Sex, Death, and Hierarchy in a Chinese City, wrote that in Hohhot the gap between minority culture and Han culture is "relatively little". Differences gather around lesser matters such as food and art, he found, while similarities are strong on basics like ethics, status, life goals and worldview.

Hohhot is a major industrial centre for Inner Mongolia. With Baotou and Ordos it produces over 60 percent of the region's total industrial output, and it is the third-largest economy in the province after those two. Its GDP reached RMB 247.56 billion in 2012, an 11.0 percent rise on the year before, about 15.5 percent of the provincial total that year. It is also the biggest consumer centre of the region: retail sales of consumer goods were ¥102.2 billion in 2012, up 14.9 percent from 2011. The central government's China Western Development project has treated the city as a central target for development. Famous companies are based here, among them the Inner Mongolia Yili Industrial Group, the biggest Chinese dairy producer measured by sales revenue, as well as the China Mengniu Dairy Co.

As the region's economic centre, Hohhot's urban area has grown a great deal since the 1990s, with CBDs rising fast in all the major districts. A new municipal government office tower in Eastern Hohhot signalled that the city centre was shifting eastward. In the centre stands Hailiang Plaza (海亮广场), a 41-floor tower, and it is now among the very few department stores in town with a luxury focus.
There are two development zones, the Hohhot Economic and Technological Development Zone and the Hohhot Export Processing Zone.

inner-mongolia-agricultural-university.h: A city with a mixed identity

blocks.x: Hohhot is in many ways a mid-sized Chinese industrial city, but its diverse cultural make-up means the streets are full of minority touches. In the old town, Tongdao Road is a major street, and its buildings all carry Islamic and Mongol exterior designs. Recent government initiatives have stressed the city's ties to ethnic minority groups, notably by adding more Mongol-themed architecture around town. Regulations require every street sign and public transport announcement to appear in both Chinese and Mongolian, which is helpful if you want to see the script around you.

Older residents mostly speak the dialect of Hohhot, which is a branch of the Jin language spoken in neighbouring Shanxi province, which can be hard for speakers of other Mandarin dialects to follow. Newer arrivals are concentrated in Saihan and Xincheng Districts and speak Mandarin coloured by Hohhot, usually with a noticeable accent and some vocabulary of its own.

Faiths of many kinds have deep roots here, and religious sites have been built or rebuilt in large numbers since the 2000s. By the 2010s the Old City and Hui district held six mosques, five Protestant churches, a Catholic church, a dozen or so Chinese temples and 12 Buddhist monasteries.

Local specialities lean towards Mongol cooking and dairy products, and commercially the city is the base of two nationally famous dairy giants, Yili and Mengniu. For breakfast, almost everyone in or visiting Hohhot ends up with suutei tsai (Chinese 奶茶, pinyin nǎichá, "milk tea"), the Mongol tea drink. Hot pot and shaomai, a traditional Chinese dumpling served as dim sum, also have rich traditions here.

Baita International Airport (IATA: HET) is about 14.3 km (8.9 mi) by car east of the city centre. It has direct flights to bigger domestic cities such as Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chengdu, and international or regional flights to Taichung, Hong Kong and Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia.

The Jingbao Railway from Beijing to Baotou passes through Hohhot, which has two stations (Hohhot railway station and Hohhot East railway station). Service on the line began in 1921. Beijing trains connect on to places south and northeast. The best-known service is the overnight K90 train, running on the Hohhot-Beijing line since the 1980s and nicknamed the "9-0". Trains heading west go via Baotou and Lanzhou, Other rail routes reach most major Inner Mongolian cities, and one goes to Ulaanbaatar.

Even though Beijing is not far away, the fastest conventional trip takes around six and a half hours. This led to lengthy discussion of high-speed rail before work began in 2008 on a high-speed station, which was finished in 2011 but at first served only ordinary lines. The first D-series (dongchezu) service in Inner Mongolia, operated by CRH, began in January 2015 along the Baotou-Hohhot-Jining corridor, cutting the journey between the region's two largest cities to just 50 minutes. Between Hohhot and Baotou, trains can run at up to 200 km/h (124 mph). A further high-speed line to Zhangjiakou, and the planned Beijing-Zhangjiakou railway, were expected to be ready in 2017 and are designed for 250 km/h (155 mph). In August 2017 the section between Hohhot and Ulanqab (Jining) opened, trimming travel time between those two cities to 40 minutes.

An expressway completed in 1997, then called the Hubao Expressway, joins Hohhot and Baotou. Later it was lengthened eastwards, through Jining and Zhangjiakou and on to Beijing, as a section of the G6 Beijing-Lhasa Expressway (Jingzang Expressway). China National Highway 110 passes through the city on its way from Yinchuan to Beijing, and China National Highway 209 starts in Hohhot and heads south, ending in Guangxi. The Huwu Highway, finished in 2006, connects Hohhot with its northern counties; before it, getting there meant a long detour through mountains. Long-distance buses link Hohhot with outlying counties, with Baotou, Wuhai and Ordos, and with other parts of Inner Mongolia.

Roads (Lu) are the main north-south thoroughfares, and the east-west ones are called streets (Jie). Close to the Drum Tower (Gulou) is the biggest elevated interchange, which takes its name from the tower. Several major streets carry the names of Inner Mongolian leagues and cities. Running east-west are Bayannur, Hailar, Ulaanqab and Erdos, while the north-south ones are Xing'an, Xilin Gol, Ulaanhad (now Chifeng), Jurim (now Tongliao) and Hulun Buir.
The city's public transit relies on close to a hundred bus routes, plus lots of taxis in green or blue. A bus ride costs 1 yuan, and taxi fares start at 8 yuan.
Hohhot Metro is running. The red line, Line 1, measures 21.719 km (13.5 mi), and Line 2, the blue line, measures 27.32 km (17.0 mi).

Inner Mongolia University is the only Project 211 university in the whole of Inner Mongolia, and it is based in Hohhot. The city has plenty of other options, and you can keep the following in mind as neighbours of IMAU. Teacher training is covered by Hohhot College of Education and Inner Mongolia Normal University, with its Honder College. Business and economics are covered by a separate Inner Mongolia College of Finance and Economics and by Inner Mongolia University of Finance and Economics. The specialist ones are:
Inner Mongolia College of Medicine
Inner Mongolia Police Professional College
Inner Mongolia University of Technology
Inner Mongolia University of Agriculture

Families may also care about the high schools. They include the Affiliated Middle School to Inner Mongolia Normal University, the Hohhot experimental middle school, and Hohhot No.2 and No.1 Middle Schools. A final educational note: the city staged the China Adolescents Science & Technology Innovation Contest for the 39th time, after two earlier turns as host.

The city had no professional football team until Shenyang Dongjin F.C. moved there in 2012 and took the name Hohhot Dongjin. The club played at Hohhot City Stadium, newly built in 2007, finished bottom of the league in 2012 and was relegated to League Two. After half a season in Hohhot in 2013, the team moved to Liaoning and made Benxi City Stadium its new home.

Another club, Taiyuan Zhongyou Jiayi F.C., arrived on 14 January 2015 and relocated to Hohhot and was renamed Nei Mongu Zhongyou F.C. Hohhot City Stadium was its 2015 home ground, in China League One. Its origins lie in the establishment of Shanxi Jiayi F.C. on 8 October 2011.
The region around a campus shapes student life as much as the buildings do, so here is a short guide to Inner Mongolia, its past and its landscape.

Much of what we know about the Mongolian Plateau comes from Chinese chronicles and historians. Before the Mongols rose in the 13th century, control of central and western Inner Mongolia, particularly the Hetao region, passed back and forth between Chinese farming communities in the south and northern peoples: the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Khitan, Jurchen, Tujue and nomadic Mongols. In what is now Eastern Inner Mongolia, the story is mostly one of changing Tungusic and Mongol tribes, rather than a contest between nomads and Chinese farmers.

Slab Grave monuments are found across Mongolia (north, centre and east), as well as in Inner Mongolia, north-western China and southern, central-eastern and southern Baikal territory. Mongolian scholars have shown that this culture was related to the Proto-Mongols.

Under the Zhou dynasty, nomads including the Dí, Linhu and Loufan lived in Central and Western Inner Mongolia, in the Hetao region and its surroundings, and the Donghu lived in the east. In the Warring States period King Wuling (340-295 BC) ruled the state of Zhao, which was based in today's Hebei and Shanxi, and he pursued expansion towards this region. After he had destroyed the Dí state of Zhongshan in modern Hebei, the Linhu and Loufan were defeated, and the Yunzhong Commandery was created close to modern Hohhot, and he also built a long wall through the Hetao region. In 221 BC Qin Shi Huang founded the first unified Chinese empire and sent the general Meng Tian to push the Xiongnu out. The old Zhao wall was folded into the Qin dynasty Great Wall of China, two commanderies, Jiuyuan and Yunzhong, were kept in the region, and 30,000 households were moved there to make it secure. After the Qin collapsed in 206 BC, these efforts were given up.

In the Western Han dynasty, in 127 BC, Emperor Wu sent the general Wei Qing to win back the Hetao region from the Xiongnu. He went on building settlements there as a defence, and in the same year set up the commanderies of Shuofang and Wuyuan in Hetao. Meanwhile what is now Eastern Inner Mongolia was held by the Xianbei, who in time became more powerful and influential than the Xiongnu.

During the Eastern Han dynasty (25-220 AD), Xiongnu who had submitted to the Han began to settle in Hetao and mixed with Han immigrants. Later, under the Western Jin, a Xiongnu noble from Hetao, Liu Yuan, founded the Han Zhao kingdom there, which opened the Sixteen Kingdoms period, when northern China broke apart under various Han and non-Han regimes, including Xiongnu and Xianbei ones.

The Sui (581-618) and Tang (618-907) dynasties restored a unified Chinese empire and, like their predecessors, conquered Hetao and settled people there, though again the efforts ended when the Tang began to fall apart. Next the Khitans took over, a nomadic people whose original home was southern Manchuria and Eastern Inner Mongolia. Their Liao dynasty ruled Hetao and the rest of what is now Inner Mongolia. The Western Xia of the Tanguts followed in the western part, including Western Hetao. The Jurchens, forerunners of the modern Manchus, then replaced the Khitans, and their Jin dynasty ruled Manchuria and northern China.

inner-mongolia-agricultural-university.h: The Mongol era and the Ming

blocks.x: In 1206 Genghis Khan brought the Mongol tribes together and founded the Mongol Empire. Its armies conquered the Tangut Western Xia empire in 1227 and Jin, the dynasty of the Jurchens, fell in 1234. His grandson Kublai Khan established the Yuan dynasty in 1271, and its summer capital, Shangdu (also called Xanadu), stood near present-day Dolonnor. Ongud and Khunggirad peoples dominated what is now Inner Mongolia at that time. The Han-led Ming dynasty overthrew the Yuan in 1368 and took parts of Inner Mongolia, including Shangdu and Yingchang. It rebuilt the Great Wall of China where it stands today, following the southern edge of today's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region fairly closely (it departs from that line a good deal at the Hebei-Inner Mongolia border), and it established the Three Guards made up of Mongols. In 1449 came the Tumu incident, in which the Oirat ruler Esen taishi seized the Chinese emperor, and afterwards Mongols poured south from Outer Mongolia into Inner Mongolia. Right up to 1635, during the Northern Yuan period, the political and cultural heart of the Mongols was Inner Mongolia.

Officially a provincial-level subdivision of North China, Inner Mongolia is so long that parts of it belong to Northeast and Northwest China too. Eight provincial-level divisions border it, some in each of those three regions. They are Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning, then Hebei, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia and Gansu. Shaanxi has as many neighbours, so the two share first place for this. Its international border is mainly with Mongolia (sometimes called "Outer Mongolia" in Chinese), and a small part is with Russia's Zabaykalsky Krai.

Geologically, most of Inner Mongolia rests on the North China Craton's northern flank, which is a tilted Precambrian block covered in sediment. Right at the far southwest, the Tibetan Plateau's edge is reached. There stands the highest point in the autonomous region, Main Peak in the Helan Mountains, at 3,556 metres (11,670 ft), and it keeps growing taller in occasional bursts. Most of the region belongs to the Mongolian Plateau, which stands at an average of around 1,200 metres (3,940 ft) and is blanketed with loess and sand. The north holds the Mesozoic-era Khingan Mountains, where the cooler climate supports more forest: chiefly Manchurian elm, ash, birch, Mongolian oak and several pines and spruces. Where discontinuous permafrost occurs north of Hailar District, the forests are almost entirely coniferous. Southward, the natural vegetation is grassland in the east, thinning to very sparse cover in the arid west, and grazing is the main economic activity.

Old, weathered rock lies beneath its deep sedimentary cover, so Inner Mongolia is a major mining district and it holds big deposits of rare-earth minerals, iron ore and coal, which have turned it into a significant industrial region.
Desertification is growing and sandstorms are frequent, which harms agriculture across the region.
Inner Mongolia Agricultural University lists 98 programs for international students on this site: 2 bachelor, 64 master's, 32 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 98 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 13,600 to CNY 13,600 (median CNY 13,600), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,400 to CNY 18,400 (median CNY 18,400), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 20,400 to CNY 22,400 (median CNY 22,400), according to the university's published fee table.

98 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

inner-mongolia-agricultural-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Inner Mongolia Agricultural University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hohhot, register at Inner Mongolia Agricultural University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

inner-mongolia-minzu-university.h: Tongliao: the city around Inner Mongolia Minzu University

blocks.x: The campus of Inner Mongolia Minzu University, also known as the Inner Mongolia University for Nationalities (内蒙古民族大学), is in the city of Tongliao. Student life depends on the surrounding city and region as much as on the university, so this profile covers Tongliao first and then the autonomous region of Inner Mongolia around it.

Among Tongliao's educational institutions are the university itself and the Inner Mongolia College of Farming and Animal Husbandry, an older college that was merged into the university. Another local school is Tongliao Mongolian Middle School (通辽蒙古族中学).

The only demographic material on Tongliao is a caption for the ethnic group figures from the 2010 census, with no numbers attached, so look at the latest census data if the ethnic makeup of the city matters to you.

Tongliao railway station is a hub for rail traffic across Inner Mongolia and the north-east of China. For the capital, the Tongliao-Beijing Railway gives a convenient link, while the Jining-Tongliao railway links the city to other parts of Inner Mongolia, and further lines go to Shenyang and Daqing. Four state highways (111, 303, 304 and 204) pass through the city and carry on to ports such as Dalian, Tianjin and Qinhuangdao. Tongliao Airport handles flights.

Where you study shapes your experience, and Inner Mongolia has a dramatic past. Much of what is known about the Mongolian Plateau comes from the writings of Chinese chroniclers and historians, so keep in mind that this is largely an outside view.

inner-mongolia-minzu-university.h: The long era before the Mongols

blocks.x: Until the Mongols came to power in the thirteenth century, the central and western parts of present Inner Mongolia, above all the Hetao region, were contested. Farming communities of Chinese people pressed from the south, while nomads moved in from the north, including the Xiongnu, the Xianbei, the Khitans, the Jurchens, the Tujue and early nomadic Mongols, and control passed back and forth between them. The east tells a different story: there, the record mostly shows Tungusic and Mongol tribes taking turns, not a contest between nomads and Chinese farmers.

Monuments of the Slab Grave culture lie scattered over a large area: northern, central and eastern Mongolia, Inner Mongolia, north-western China, and parts of the Baikal territory in the south and centre-east. Mongolian scholars have argued that this culture was related to the Proto-Mongols.

By Zhou times, the Hetao area and its neighbours in the centre and west were home to nomads, namely the Loufan, the Linhu and the Dí; in the east lived the Donghu. A turning point came in the Warring States period. King Wuling, who ruled the state of Zhao (in the area of today's Hebei and Shanxi) from 340 to 295 BC, pursued expansion northwards. First he wiped out Zhongshan, a Dí state in modern Hebei. Next he defeated the Linhu and the Loufan, and he founded Yunzhong Commandery close to present Hohhot. He also had a long wall built across Hetao.

In 221 BC, once Qin Shi Huang had united China as its first empire, he sent his general Meng Tian to expel the Xiongnu. The old wall of Zhao became part of the Great Wall of the Qin dynasty. Two commanderies, Jiuyuan and Yunzhong, were maintained there, and 30,000 households were relocated to strengthen the frontier. When the Qin fell in 206 BC, the whole effort was dropped.

The Western Han emperor Wu dispatched General Wei Qing, who retook Hetao from the Xiongnu in 127 BC. Wu went on settling people in Hetao as a defence against the Xiongnu, and in the same year he created two commanderies there, Shuofang and Wuyuan. Meanwhile the Xianbei held the lands of today's eastern Inner Mongolia, and in time they would surpass the Xiongnu in power and influence.

In the Eastern Han era (25-220 AD), Xiongnu groups that submitted to the Han were resettled in Hetao, where they mixed with the Han newcomers. Later, in the Western Jin period, the founder of the Han Zhao kingdom here was a noble from Hetao of Xiongnu descent, Liu Yuan. His kingdom marked the opening of the Sixteen Kingdoms period, when northern China split into many regimes, some Han and others not, among them Xiongnu and Xianbei ones.

With the Sui (581-618) and then the Tang (618-907), a single Chinese empire returned. These dynasties also took Hetao and put settlers there, as earlier ones had, but their efforts ended again as Tang power declined. After that, the Khitans took the region. They were a nomadic people from southern Manchuria and the east of present Inner Mongolia, and their Liao dynasty ruled Hetao and everything else that is now Inner Mongolia. The Tanguts' Western Xia came next in the western areas, western Hetao included, and eventually Jurchens, the ancestors of today's Manchus, replaced the Khitans and built their Jin dynasty across Manchuria and northern China.

inner-mongolia-minzu-university.h: Genghis Khan's empire and the Ming

blocks.x: In 1206 Genghis Khan brought the Mongol tribes together and created the Mongol Empire. Western Xia, the Tangut state, was finally overcome in 1227, and the Jin dynasty of the Jurchens collapsed in 1234. Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis, proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271. Near the site of today's Dolonnor stood his summer capital, Shangdu, which is also known as Xanadu. At the time the Ongud and the Khunggirad were the main peoples of present-day Inner Mongolia.

The Yuan were overthrown in 1368 by the Han-led Ming, who seized portions of Inner Mongolia such as Shangdu and Yingchang. The Ming also rebuilt the Great Wall in its current position. That line roughly traces the southern edge of the modern autonomous region, though with large deviations along the Hebei boundary. There the Ming organised Mongol groups into the Three Guards. In 1449 came the Tumu incident, in which Esen taishi, a ruler of the Oirat, took the Chinese emperor prisoner, and soon afterwards Mongols moved south in great numbers from Outer Mongolia into Inner Mongolia. For the period from then to 1635, Inner Mongolia was the political and cultural heart of the Mongols of the Northern Yuan dynasty.

Near and inside Manchuria, the eastern Mongol tribes (above all the Khorchin and the Southern Khalkha, in what is Inner Mongolia now) intermarried with Jurchen tribes, allied with them and also fought them. This went on until 1593, when Nurhaci, who created the new Jin dynasty, took all of the groups in the area under his control. Far-reaching Manchu control over the Inner Mongolian tribes came in 1635, once the son of Ligden Khan handed the Chakhar Mongol tribes over to the Manchus. Next, in 1644, the Manchus invaded Ming China and brought it under their new Qing dynasty. For the Qing period (1644-1912), the Mongolian Plateau was divided into regions that were each governed differently.

'Outer Mongolia' was the first. It matched the modern state of Mongolia and added to it the Russian-run region of Tannu Uriankhai as well as Bayan-Ölgii, an aimag today, which had been part of northern Xinjiang under the Qing. It comprised four Khalkha Mongol leagues (aimag) north of the Gobi Desert, along with Tannu Uriankhai, for the most part the Tuva Republic of Russia now, and the Khovd regions of north-western Mongolia. The General of Uliastai oversaw these areas from the city of Uliastai.

The second, 'Inner Mongolia', covered the main part of today's autonomous region and bits of Liaoning and Jilin next to it. Its banners and tribes were grouped under six leagues (chuulghan): Jirim, Juuuda, Josutu, Xilingol, Ulanqab and Yekejuu.

The third was 'Taoxi Mongolia'. Its two banners, Alashan Öölüd and Ejine Torghuud, were kept distinct from both the Outer Mongolian aimags and the Inner Mongolian chuulghans, and its territory equals today's Alxa League at the western tip of Inner Mongolia.

There were special cases as well. A military commander at Chahar (modern Zhangjiakou) controlled the Chahar Banners, an area that corresponded to southern Ulanqab and Bayannur plus the Zhangjiakou area of Hebei; border departments of Zhili and Shanxi were part of the same region for jurisdiction. The Guihua Tümed banner answered to the military commander at Suiyuan (now Hohhot), covering the vicinity of modern Hohhot, and some border departments of today's Shanxi also fell under this region. In the north-east, Hulunbuir was part of the jurisdiction of the General of Heilongjiang, one of Manchuria's three generals.

A descendant of Genghis Khan, Ligdan Khan, the Chahar leader, fought the Qing until smallpox killed him in 1634. His son Ejei Khan then surrendered with the Inner Mongols and got the title of Prince (親王; qīn wáng); from there on the Inner Mongolian nobility was closely tied to the Qing imperial family, with many marriages. Ejei Khan died in 1661 and his brother Abunai took over. Abunai showed unhappiness with Manchu rule and was placed under house arrest in Shenyang in 1669, while the Kangxi Emperor gave the title to Abunai's son Borni. Abunai waited, and in 1675, along with his brother Lubuzung, he rose against the Qing in the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, supported by 3,000 Chahar Mongol followers. The Qing put the revolt down within two months, crushing the rebels in a battle on 20 April 1675 where Abunai and every follower died. The title was cancelled; every male of the Chahar Mongol royal line was executed, including sons of Manchu Qing princesses, and every royal woman, except the Manchu Qing princesses, was sold into slavery. The Chahar Mongols were reorganised as the Eight Banners of Chahar and placed directly under the Qing Emperor, in contrast to the other leagues of Inner Mongolia, which retained their autonomy.

inner-mongolia-minzu-university.h: Han settlement and the fate of the steppe

blocks.x: Although Han Chinese were formally barred from settling Manchu and Mongol lands, in the eighteenth century the Qing opted to resettle Han refugees from the north of China, who were suffering through famine, flood and drought, in Manchuria and Inner Mongolia. As a result, by the 1780s Han farmers worked 500,000 hectares in Manchuria and tens of thousands of hectares in Inner Mongolia.

Meanwhile, the Qing kept ordinary Mongols in place: they could not leave their league. Crossing the border of their own banner was prohibited, even to enter another Mongol banner, and so was going into neidi, the eighteen provinces of Han China; violators faced severe punishment. The aim was to keep Mongols divided against each other, which suited the Qing. Anyone wanting to leave a banner for a religious purpose such as a pilgrimage needed a passport.

Despite the ban, more and more Han settlers had been illegally moving onto the Inner Mongolian steppe in the eighteenth century. Settlers in the Front Gorlos Banner were so numerous by 1791 that the jasak asked the Qing government to give legal status to the peasants already living there.

The nineteenth century brought a change in attitude. By then the Manchus had become more and more sinicised and faced a threat from Russia, so they started to encourage Han farmers to settle in Mongolia and Manchuria alike, and the governments after them kept this up. Han settlers benefited especially from new railways in these areas. Some land was sold by Mongol princes, some leased to Han farmers, and some was just taken from the nomads and handed to Han farmers.

A particular group of Han Chinese under the Qing were called 'Mongol followers'. They moved to Inner Mongolia, served Mongols and Mongol princes, and married Mongol women. Their children went on marrying into Mongol families and, as they assimilated, their ethnicity was recorded as Mongol; the forebears of Li Shouxin are an example. These people still set themselves apart from what they called 'true Mongols' (真蒙古).

inner-mongolia-minzu-university.h: The Republic, Japan and the war years

blocks.x: In 1911 Outer Mongolia broke away from the Qing, with the Khalkha's Jebtsundamba Khutugtu proclaimed as Bogd Khan of Mongolia. Most Inner Mongolian banners acknowledged him as supreme ruler of all Mongols, but quarrels within the region stopped them from reuniting fully. Some princes, who hoped to see the Qing restored in Manchuria and Mongolia, counterbalanced the Mongol rebellions in Inner Mongolia, because they believed that the Bogd Khan's theocratic government would be against their plans to modernise Mongolia. In the end the new Republic of China pledged a nation of five races (Han, Manchu, Mongol, Tibetan and Uyghur) and put down the Mongol rebellions of the area.
The Republic then reorganised Inner Mongolia into several provinces:
Rehe province combined the Juuuda and Josutu leagues with the Chengde area, in modern northern Hebei.
Chahar province was made from Xilingol league and a large part of the former Eight Banners territory.
Suiyuan province grouped Ulanqab league, Yekejuu league and the Hetao region, which had been Guihua Tümed territory.
Hulunbuir remained in Heilongjiang, a Manchurian province by that time.
The larger part of Jirim league was given to the new Fengtian province in southern Manchuria.
Taoxi Mongolia, meaning the Alashan and Ejine leagues, was merged into Gansu next door; once Ningxia province was carved out of northern Gansu, Taoxi Mongolia became part of Ningxia.
A few Republic of China maps continue to show this arrangement.

The Second World War brought a complicated period to Inner Mongolia, with Japanese invasion and various forms of resistance. In 1931 the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo took over Manchuria, including Mongol areas in the Manchurian provinces, namely the Hulunbuir and Jirim leagues. Rehe followed in 1933, with the Juu Uda and Josutu leagues, and Manchukuo kept hold of all of this territory until the war ended in 1945.

Japan launched a full, open invasion of the Republic of China in 1937. On 8 December of that year the Mongolian prince Demchugdongrub, known as 'De Wang', announced the independence of the rest of Inner Mongolia, meaning Suiyuan and Chahar provinces, under the name Mengjiang, and made agreements with Japan and Manchukuo. The Mengjiang capital was Zhangbei (today in Hebei), and the puppet government's control stretched west to the area around Hohhot. General Ma Hongbin, a Hui Muslim, stopped the Japanese advance at the Battle of West Suiyuan and the Battle of Wuyuan. After 1945 Inner Mongolia stayed within China.

The Mongol leader Ulanhu was among those who fought the Japanese. Kuomintang Nationalists likewise formed guerrilla units of ethnic Mongols in the late 1930s and early 1940s, based on commissioner's offices in Ejine and Alashaa, and Kuomintang Mongols tried to win Prince Demchugdongrub's Mongols over to the Republic of China. The Nationalists took on 1,700 ethnic minority fighters in Inner Mongolia and set up war zones in the Tumet Banner, Ulanchab League and Ordos Yekejuu League.
Shortly after the Second World War ended, the Inner Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed. It survived for under two months, from 9 September 1945 to 6 November 1945.

Inner Mongolia is officially a provincial-level division of North China, yet it is so extensive that sections of it are in Northeast and Northwest China as well. Eight provincial-level neighbours touch it, in all three of those regions: Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning, Hebei, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia and Gansu. Only Shaanxi matches that count. The greater part of the international border is with Mongolia (called 'Outer Mongolia' in Chinese at times), and a smaller stretch touches Russia's Zabaykalsky Krai.

The foundation is geological: the northern side of the North China Craton, which is a tilted Precambrian block under a layer of sediment. At the far south-west is the margin of the Tibetan Plateau, where the autonomous region's highest summit, Main Peak in the Helan Mountains, reaches 3,556 metres, or 11,670 ft, and keeps rising in short bursts even today. Most of the region forms part of the Mongolian Plateau at an average of about 1,200 metres, or 3,940 ft, covered with thick loess and sand. Cooler weather in the northern Khingan Mountains, a range dating from the Mesozoic era, supports more woodland: Manchurian elm, ash, birch, Mongolian oak, and several kinds of pine and spruce. In the zone north of Hailar District with discontinuous permafrost, forests are almost wholly conifers. To the south the vegetation is natural grassland in the east and very thin in the arid west, and herding is the leading economic activity.

Old, weathered rocks lie beneath the deep sediment, which makes Inner Mongolia a major mining area. Its large reserves of coal, iron ore and rare-earth minerals have helped to turn it into a significant industrial region.
A warning for the future: desertification is spreading across the region and sandstorms are frequent, harming agriculture.
