Inner Mongolia Minzu University lists 65 programs for international students on this site: 6 bachelor, 58 master's, 1 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 65 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 22,600 to CNY 34,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 45,000 to CNY 45,000 (median CNY 45,000), according to the university's published fee table.

65 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

inner-mongolia-minzu-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Inner Mongolia Minzu University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Tongliao, register at Inner Mongolia Minzu University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Inner Mongolia Normal University is a teacher-training-based university whose name appears in Chinese as Nei Menggu Shifan Daxue and in traditional Mongolian script as well. It is run under the government of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region rather than directly from Beijing, and it stands in Hohhot, the regional capital.

The university dates from 1952. It was the first university created in Inner Mongolia after the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, and it was later given the status of a key university within the region. For an international applicant, that history matters: this is the oldest of the modern higher-education institutions in the autonomous region and part of a group of campuses concentrated in the southern part of the city.

inner-mongolia-normal-university.h: The school attached to the university

blocks.x: The university has a related secondary school, the Affiliated Middle School to Inner Mongolia Normal University (known by its short name Fuzhong). It was founded in 1954 and offers senior high school education. It is a key high school of the region that blends Chinese and Mongolian culture, and it counts among the best schools for teaching the history and culture of the area. Three of its key programmes teach in three languages: Mandarin, Mongolian and English. The school sits in the south of the built-up area, in a district full of universities (the other big names there are Inner Mongolia University and Inner Mongolia Agricultural University). Its main campus address is 10 West Daxue Street in Hohhot's Saihan District. Its telephone number is 0471-6293680. Families who relocate with a student may find this school relevant.

Since a student's days are spent in the city and region rather than only on campus, the sections that follow describe Hohhot (setting, climate, people, economy, culture, transport, schools and sport) and then Inner Mongolia as a whole (history, geography and the environment).

Hohhot lies in the south-central part of Inner Mongolia. The Daqing Shan range (Great Blue Mountains) rises to the north and the Hetao Plateau lies to the south. As a curiosity, the point on the opposite side of the Earth is about 22 kilometres (14 miles) from Los Menucos, a village in Rio Negro province, Argentina.

The climate is cold semi-arid (Koppen BSk). Winters are long, cold and very dry, summers are hot and somewhat humid, spring brings strong winds and there is some monsoon influence. The mean in January, the coldest month, is minus 10.7 degrees C, and in July, the warmest, it is 23.2 degrees C; the annual mean is 7.6 degrees C. Yearly rainfall averages 411 millimetres, and over half arrives in July and August. It varies greatly: 155.1 millimetres in 1965 but 929.2 millimetres six years earlier, over a third of which (338.6 millimetres) fell in one month, July.

Summer is a popular time for visitors because the Zhaohe grasslands are nearby. In recent years desertification has meant sandstorms almost every year. Sunshine is generous: monthly possible sunshine ranges from 54 per cent in November to 66 per cent in September, with 2,680 hours of bright sun a year. The official lowest temperature is minus 32.8 degrees C (6 February 1951) and the highest 38.9 degrees C (30 July 2010), while an unofficial minus 36.2 degrees C was reported in January 1930. If you come from a warmer place, plan on serious winter clothing and a lip balm and moisturiser for the dry air.

The city's urban population has grown quickly since the 1990s. The 2010 census counted 2,866,615 residents, which is 428,717 more than in 2000 (average yearly growth of 1.63 per cent over the decade). The built-up area, which has four urban districts, holds 1,980,774 people.

Han Chinese made up 87.16 per cent of the population in 2010. Most Han families trace their roots back a few generations to Shanxi, the north-east or Hebei. Chinese is the everyday language of most Mongols in the city. Inner Mongolia University ran a survey in 1993 and learned that just 8 per cent of the Tumed Mongols (the leading tribe locally) could speak Mongolian. Many residents have mixed origins. The anthropologist William Jankowiak studied the city in the early 1990s (his 1993 book is titled Sex, Death, and Hierarchy in a Chinese City) and concluded that there is hardly any gap between minority and Han culture in Hohhot, with differences mostly in minor matters like food and art and agreement on deeper ideas about ethics, status, life goals and worldview. A detailed breakdown of ethnic groups is not given here, so ask the university or local authorities for current figures.

Older residents mostly use the Hohhot dialect, part of the Jin language group from neighbouring Shanxi, which can be hard for speakers of other Mandarin dialects to follow. Newer residents, concentrated in Xincheng and Saihan districts, speak Hohhot-style Mandarin, generally with a noticeable accent and some distinctive words. Standard Mandarin should serve you well in classrooms and shops.

For a mid-sized industrial city, Hohhot has an unusually strong ethnic minority presence in its street scene. Tongdao Road in the old town has buildings decorated in Islamic and Mongol styles. Recent government policy has stressed the city's minority identity, including more Mongol-themed buildings, and by regulation all street signs and public-transport announcements are given in both Chinese and Mongolian.

Several faiths have been present in Hohhot for a very long time, and from the 2000s onward many religious buildings have been built or rebuilt. By the 2010s the old city and Hui district together contained 12 Buddhist monasteries, roughly a dozen Chinese temples, six mosques, one Catholic church and five Protestant churches.

Local food leans toward Mongol dishes and dairy. Hohhot is home to two nationally famous dairy firms, Yili and Mengniu. Suutei tsai, the Mongol milk tea (nai cha in Chinese), is a standard breakfast drink for residents and visitors alike. The city also has strong traditions of hot pot and of shaomai, a kind of dumpling served as dim sum.

Hohhot is one of Inner Mongolia's main industrial centres. With Baotou and Ordos it produces over 60 per cent of the region's industrial output. Behind Baotou and Ordos, it has the third-largest economy in the region, with a 2012 GDP of 247.56 billion yuan (up 11.0 per cent from a year before), about 15.5 per cent of the regional total. It is also the largest consumer market in the region, with 102.2 billion yuan of retail sales in 2012, 14.9 per cent more than in 2011. National planners have treated the city as a core target of the China Western Development project. Famous firms based here include the country's largest dairy company by sales, the Inner Mongolia Yili Industrial Group, and China Mengniu Dairy Co.

As the economic centre, Hohhot has spread outwards a great deal since the 1990s, and business districts have grown quickly in all major districts. A new municipal government office tower in eastern Hohhot showed that the centre of the city was moving east. Hailiang Plaza, a 41-storey tower in the centre, is one of the few notable luxury department stores in the city.
Two development zones are the main business areas: the Hohhot Economic and Technological Development Zone and the Hohhot Export Processing Zone.

Baita International Airport (HET) is about 14.3 kilometres (8.9 miles) east of the centre by road. There are direct flights to big domestic cities such as Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chengdu, and international or regional services to Taichung, Hong Kong and Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia.

The city is on the Jingbao Railway (Beijing to Baotou), which has been running since 1921. Passengers use either the main Hohhot station or the newer Hohhot East. Trains to Beijing connect onward to the south and the north-east. The best-known service is the overnight K90 train, running since the 1980s and nicknamed the nine-oh. Westbound trains pass Baotou and Lanzhou, and other lines reach most major Inner Mongolian cities and Ulaanbaatar.

The quickest train to Beijing needs about six and a half hours, which seems long for such a short distance, and that is why high-speed rail was widely discussed before work on a high-speed station began in 2008. It was finished in 2011 but at first handled only regular services. In January 2015 China Railway High-speed opened its first D-series route in Inner Mongolia, along the Baotou-Hohhot-Jining corridor, so the ride between the two biggest cities of Inner Mongolia now takes only 50 minutes, at speeds up to 200 km/h (124 mph). A link to Zhangjiakou, joining the planned Beijing-Zhangjiakou line, was due in 2017 and designed for 250 km/h (155 mph). The Hohhot to Ulanqab (Jining) section opened in August 2017, cutting that trip to 40 minutes.

The Hubao Expressway of 1997 joined Hohhot to Baotou. Later it was lengthened eastwards through Jining and Zhangjiakou to reach Beijing, forming part of the G6 Beijing-Lhasa Expressway. China National Highway 110 passes through the city on its way from Yinchuan to Beijing, and National Highway 209 starts in Hohhot and runs south to its end in Guangxi. The Huwu Highway, completed in 2006, links the city with its northern counties; before that, trips north meant a long detour through mountains. Long-distance buses serve nearby counties, Baotou, Wuhai, Ordos and other parts of the region.

The main north-south thoroughfares are called roads (Lu) and the east-west ones streets (Jie). The biggest flyover interchange is by the Drum Tower (Gulou) and is named after it. Many streets take their names from Inner Mongolian leagues and cities. Running north-south you will find Hulun Buir, Xilin Gol, Xing'an, Jurim (the old name of Tongliao) and Ulaanhad (the old name of Chifeng); running east-west are Bayannur, Hailar, Ulaanqab and Erdos.

Public transport consists of close to a hundred bus lines plus plenty of taxis, mostly green or blue. Buses charge 1 yuan and the taxi meter starts at 8 yuan. The metro has also begun operating, with the red Line 1 (21.719 kilometres, 13.5 miles) and the blue Line 2 (27.32 kilometres, 17.0 miles).

The city has also hosted the China Adolescents Science and Technology Innovation Contest, most recently the 39th edition, and two earlier ones.

Hohhot had no professional football club until 2012, when Shenyang Dongjin F.C. moved here and became Hohhot Dongjin. They played in the City Stadium, built in 2007, finished bottom of the league in 2012 and were relegated to League Two. After half a season in 2013 the team moved on to Liaoning and Benxi City Stadium. A second club arrived in 2015: Taiyuan Zhongyou Jiayi F.C., which had been created as Shanxi Jiayi F.C. on 8 October 2011, relocated on 14 January 2015 and was renamed Nei Mongu Zhongyou F.C. It plays in China League One at Hohhot City Stadium.

Inner Mongolia is a provincial-level region in North China, but it is so long that parts of it also lie in the north-east and north-west. It touches eight provincial-level neighbours in the three areas named: Gansu, Ningxia, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Hebei, Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang. Only Shaanxi has the same number. Most of the international border is with Mongolia, sometimes called Outer Mongolia in Chinese, and a short stretch meets Russia's Zabaykalsky Krai.

In geological terms the region is largely the northern flank of the North China Craton, an ancient Precambrian block that has been tilted and buried under sediment. In the far south-west the edge of the Tibetan Plateau rises, and the region's highest point, Main Peak in the Helan Mountains at 3,556 metres (11,670 feet), is still being raised in short bursts. Most of Inner Mongolia belongs to the Mongolian Plateau at about 1,200 metres (3,940 feet), with thick loess and sand deposits. The north is occupied by the Mesozoic Khingan Mountains, where cooler weather supports more forest, chiefly Manchurian elm, ash, birch, Mongolian oak and several pines and spruces. North of Hailar District, where patches of permafrost occur, the forest is nearly all conifers. Further south, natural vegetation is grassland in the east and extremely thin in the dry west, and herding is the main form of livelihood.

Because old, weathered rock lies beneath the thick sediment, the region is a major mining area. It has big deposits of coal, iron ore and rare earths, and these have turned it into an important industrial zone. The environmental downside is increasing desertification and frequent sandstorms, which harm farming.

Much of what we know about the Mongolian Plateau was recorded by Chinese chroniclers. Until the Mongols emerged in the 1200s, control of the centre and west, and above all of Hetao, shifted between southern Chinese farmers and a succession of northern groups: Xiongnu, Xianbei, Khitan, Jurchen, Tujue and nomadic Mongols. In the east the story is mostly a succession of Tungusic and Mongol tribes rather than a contest between nomads and Chinese farmers.

Monuments of the Slab Grave culture have been located over a wide area, from Mongolia itself and Inner Mongolia to north-west China and parts of the Baikal region, and Mongolian scholars link the culture with the Proto-Mongols.

In the Zhou period nomads such as the Loufan, Linhu and Di lived in the centre and west (Hetao and surroundings), while the Donghu lived in the east. In the Warring States period King Wuling of Zhao (340-295 BC), whose state lay in today's Hebei and Shanxi, expanded towards the region. He first wiped out the Di state of Zhongshan in Hebei, then beat the Linhu and Loufan, founded Yunzhong Commandery close to modern Hohhot and had a long wall built through Hetao. In 221 BC the first emperor of a unified China, Qin Shi Huang, dispatched General Meng Tian to expel the Xiongnu. The old Zhao wall was absorbed into the Qin Great Wall, two commanderies (Jiuyuan and Yunzhong) were kept, and 30,000 households were moved in. When the Qin collapsed in 206 BC the effort ended.

Under the Western Han, Emperor Wu sent General Wei Qing to retake Hetao from the Xiongnu in 127 BC, kept settling the area to guard against them and created the commanderies of Shuofang and Wuyuan the same year. Meanwhile the Xianbei controlled eastern Inner Mongolia and later overtook the Xiongnu in power. In the Eastern Han (25-220 AD) surrendered Xiongnu were settled in Hetao and mixed with Han immigrants. Later, in the Western Jin, Liu Yuan, a noble of Xiongnu origin from Hetao, established the Han Zhao kingdom there, which began the Sixteen Kingdoms period in which northern China broke up under Han and non-Han (Xiongnu and Xianbei among them) regimes.

The Sui (581-618) and Tang (618-907) restored a unified empire and, like earlier dynasties, conquered and resettled Hetao, only for the effort to end once again when the Tang declined. The Khitans, nomads from what is now southern Manchuria and eastern Inner Mongolia, founded the Liao dynasty and took over Hetao and the rest of the region. After them came the Tangut Western Xia, who held the western part including western Hetao. The Khitans were succeeded by the Jurchens, forerunners of the Manchus, who set up the Jin dynasty ruling Manchuria and the north of China.

The Mongol tribes were brought together by Genghis Khan in 1206, giving rise to the Mongol Empire; the Western Xia of the Tanguts fell to it in 1227 and the Jurchen Jin in 1234. Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis, proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, with a summer capital at Shangdu (Xanadu), near today's Dolonnor. The Ongud and Khunggirad peoples dominated what is now Inner Mongolia at this time. When the Han-led Ming overthrew the Yuan in 1368 it captured parts of the region, including Shangdu and Yingchang, and rebuilt the Great Wall on its present line, which roughly follows the region's southern border (departing from it a good deal at the Hebei border). The Ming created the Three Guards, made up of Mongols. Soon after the Tumu incident of 1449, in which the Oirat ruler Esen taishi took the Chinese emperor prisoner, Mongols moved in large numbers southward from Outer Mongolia into Inner Mongolia. From then until 1635 the region served as the Mongols' political and cultural heart under the Northern Yuan.

Hohhot is a cold, dry, sunny city with big seasonal temperature swings, a good transport network to Beijing and Baotou, a substantial student population and a distinctive blend of Han, Mongol and Hui cultures. If you plan to study at Inner Mongolia Normal University, look for current programme information on the university website, since many figures here, especially the population and economic data, come from 2010 to 2012 and railway plans date from 2015 to 2017.

Inner Mongolia University (IMU) is a public university in Hohhot, the capital of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The regional government runs it, and the Ministry of Education of China co-funds it. IMU is included in Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction programme, which tells you the national government treats it as a priority institution.

Physically, the university spreads across four campuses with a combined 1,990 thousand square metres. Teaching is organised into 20 colleges containing 34 departments, plus 1 independent department for general education. One caution: the figures in this profile come from different years, and some are dated. As of February 2006, IMU offered 92 master's programmes and 59 undergraduate majors. Around 2,414 people worked there, of whom 1,303 were full-time teachers and researchers, with 744 professors and associate professors among them. Agreements for exchange and cooperation had been signed with 20 foreign universities. Check the university's own website for current numbers before you apply.

IMU was founded in 1957 in Hohhot. In 1978 the Ministry of Education designated it a national key comprehensive university, and in 1997 it took a place among the 100 universities picked for key construction and development under the former Project 211. Today it also belongs to the central government's Double First-Class Construction scheme.

Descriptions of the university disagree on the number of campuses: three separate ones, all in Hohhot, in one account and four in another, so confirm the current number with the university. The main campus sits next to Manduhai Park. Higher education in Inner Mongolia and China as a whole has been growing fast, so the university has been expanding on a large scale, with a new campus under construction in the suburbs of Hohhot.

When the campus was first laid out, builders dug an artificial lake called Rengong Hu. Staff keep it up through spring, summer and autumn, and once winter freezes the water, part of the ice serves as a skating rink. Its name changed twice. First it became Sai Hu, because sai is the Mongolian word for good. Then, for the fortieth anniversary in 1997, it became Taoli Hu: in Chinese 桃李 (taoli) is a word for intellectuals, and in Mongolian toli means mirror. The water covers 13,000 square metres, and the library looks out over it from the north of the main campus.

Nearly every college provides a handful of bilingual courses delivered in Mongolian as well as Chinese. In some majors, a bachelor's, master's or doctorate can even be earned through Mongolian-medium study, with a few compulsory Chinese-language courses always in the mix. More recently, IMU has also worked on teaching courses in Russian, Japanese and English. The College of Law is a clear example, since it put such courses on its official list in a significant curriculum reform from the mid-2000s, and many other colleges have followed.
Undergraduates are recruited from candidates sitting the nationwide university entrance examination (the gaokao system), in which a panel named by the state sets every subject's questions.
Master's students sit an entrance exam for master's programmes. A nationally appointed group sets some of the subjects, and supervisors set the rest.
Doctoral students follow the same pattern: an entrance examination with some national questions and some written by supervisors.

Foreign degree and non-degree students apply through a special procedure designed for foreigners. Instruction is available in Chinese, Mongolian, English and other languages, and it is also possible to study languages such as Russian and Japanese at IMU.

The university teaches full-time degree students, and it also has vocational and technical courses, adult education and a stream for foreign students. In 2005 the student body was 22,203, including 12,766 undergraduates and 3,191 postgraduates.

Like many Chinese universities, IMU has a very large administrative system alongside teaching and research, and it even runs some businesses under its umbrella. Teaching units were originally called departments. Near the end of the 1990s, nearly all became schools in the sense of a law school, each covering several departments, but the university's website now translates them as colleges. It is not clear whether the colleges are the same as the earlier schools or are enlarged versions of them.

The administrative side comprises the Party and Executive Affairs Office, the Regulation Inspecting Committee (including the Supervisory and Audit Office), the Organization Department, the Propaganda Department, the Office Managing Retired Staff, the Personnel Department, the Teaching Affairs Department, the Research Affairs Department, the Finance Department, the Service Department, Public Security, the Youth League committee (the Students' Affairs Office) and the Staff Union.

Three men, Bao Junchen (born January 1946), Liu Zhilan (born August 1944) and Xu Bonian (born January 1939), each became a vice-president of the regional People's Political Consultative Committee on 16 January 2003. Chen Youzun (born September 1925) also held a vice-president post on that committee.

Yang Jing, born in December 1953, chaired the region from April 2003, and Zhao Shuanglian, born in April 1957, has been vice-chairman since January 2003.

Within Inner Mongolia, no university is ranked higher. Nationally, it has appeared in the top 200 of the Best Chinese Universities Ranking every year from 2015, and the 2023 edition of that table, also known as the Shanghai Ranking, put IMU 113th in China. On the world stage, the 2026 Academic Ranking of World Universities lists it somewhere between 901st and 1000th, while the University Rankings by Academic Performance for 2026 to 2027 give a precise position of 954.
Every May, since the mid-1980s, the university holds its Cultural Festival, with a series of activities during the event.
An annual Track and Field Games takes place in spring.
Founded on 14 October 1957, the library is on the northern side of the main campus, looking across the artificial lake.

Inner Mongolia University Press began in 1985 and publishes in Chinese and Mongolian, with about 120 books a year. Since opening it has published 1,315 books, 140 of them in Mongolian and 60 in English, Japanese, Russian and other languages.

The Journal of Inner Mongolia University (Neimenggu Daxue Xuebao) comes in three versions: a Mongolian edition, a Chinese Humanities and Social Sciences edition, and a Chinese Natural Sciences edition (Acta Scientiarum Naturalium Universitatis NeiMongol, ISSN 1000-1638, domestic periodical number CN15-1052/N). They are in fact three separate journals, though Chinese publishing rules treat them as one.
For a student, much of daily life depends on the city around campus: the weather, how you get around and what you can do. The sections below introduce Hohhot, where Inner Mongolia University stands.

In the south-central region of Inner Mongolia, Hohhot has the Hetao Plateau lying to its south and the Daqing Shan range (大青山, 'Great Blue Mountains') wrapped around it on the north. A curiosity for geography fans: if you dug straight through the planet from the city you would come out near Los Menucos, a village in Río Negro Province, Argentina, about 22 kilometres (14 mi) away.

The Köppen system classes Hohhot as a cold semi-arid (BSk) climate. Expect winters that are lengthy, frigid and extremely dry; summers that are hot and somewhat humid; blustery winds, mainly in spring; and a touch of monsoon. In January the daily mean is -10.7 °C (12.7 °F), and in July it reaches 23.2 °C (73.8 °F). The annual average is 7.6 °C (45.7 °F). Precipitation totals 411 millimetres (16.2 in) a year, with July and August delivering over half.
Totals vary enormously from year to year. 1965 was a dry one with only 155.1 mm (6.11 in), while 1959, six years before, saw 929.2 mm (36.58 in), over a third of it (338.6 mm, 13.33 in) in July.

In summer, tourists come to see the Zhaohe grasslands nearby. Desertification has a downside: sandstorms hit the city almost annually. The sun shines generously throughout the year, with a monthly possible-sunshine range of 54 percent (November) to 66 percent (September) and a yearly total of 2,680 hours. The coldest official reading was -32.8 °C (-27 °F) on 6 February 1951, and the hottest was 38.9 °C (102 °F) on 30 July 2010. Unofficially, January 1930 saw -36.2 °C (-33 °F).

The urban population has grown quickly since the 1990s. The 2010 Census counted 2,866,615 people, which is 428,717 more than in 2000 and works out at an average annual growth rate of 1.63 percent over the decade. The built-up (metro) area, covering 4 urban districts, holds 1,980,774 inhabitants.

By the 2010 count, 87.16 percent of residents were Han Chinese. Go back a few decades in most Han families and you reach ancestors from Shanxi, Hebei or the north-east. Most Mongols here speak Chinese in daily life; a survey run by IMU in 1993 found just 8 percent of the Tümed Mongols, the leading tribe in Hohhot, able to speak Mongolian. Many people have mixed ancestry. The anthropologist William Jankowiak, author of Sex, Death, and Hierarchy in a Chinese City (1993), concluded that the gap between minority and Han culture in Hohhot is small. It shows mostly in minor matters such as food and art, while attitudes on ethics, status, life goals and worldview overlap heavily. A breakdown by ethnic group was published with the 2000 census.

Industry is a strength. Hohhot, Baotou and Ordos together generate over 60 percent of everything the region manufactures. Behind those two, Hohhot is third in size, with 2012 GDP of RMB 247.56 billion (growth of 11.0 percent on the year before), about 15.5 percent of the regional total. It is also the region's top shopping market, where consumers spent RMB 102.2 billion in 2012, 14.9 percent more than in 2011. The city has been a central objective of the national China Western Development project. Household names have their bases here: the Inner Mongolia Yili Industrial Group, the country's top dairy producer when measured by sales revenue, and China Mengniu Dairy Co.

As the economic centre of Inner Mongolia, Hohhot has expanded a great deal since the 1990s, with business districts growing fast in all the main districts. A new municipal government office tower in eastern Hohhot signalled that the city centre was moving east. Hailiang Plaza (海亮广场), a tower of 41 storeys at the heart of the city, became one of the city's few notable department stores for luxury goods.
Hohhot Economic and Technological Development Zone
Hohhot Export Processing Zone

Though it is a mid-sized industrial city, Hohhot's street scenes are full of minority touches because of its mixed population. In the old town, every building along the main thoroughfare Tongdao Road carries Islamic or Mongol exterior designs. Recent government initiatives have stressed the city's links with minority groups, especially by building more Mongol-themed architecture. By regulation, all street signs and public-transport announcements appear in both Chinese and Mongolian.

The older generation tends to use the Hohhot dialect, which belongs to the Jin language group found in neighbouring Shanxi and can be hard for speakers of other Mandarin varieties to follow. Newcomers, living largely in Xincheng and Saihan, use a local form of Mandarin, generally with a distinct accent and a few vocabulary items of its own.

Many faiths have deep roots in the city, and places of worship have been built or restored in large numbers over the past two decades. By the 2010s, the Old City and the Hui district between them hosted 12 Buddhist monasteries, roughly a dozen Chinese temples, six mosques, five Protestant churches and one Catholic church.

Local specialities centre on Mongol cooking and dairy products, and Hohhot is the base of the famous dairy firms Yili and Mengniu. A Mongol drink, suutei tsai (奶茶, nǎichá, 'milk tea'), is a typical breakfast for residents and visitors alike. Hot pot is a local tradition, as is shaomai, a steamed dumpling that appears on dim sum menus.

Baita International Airport (IATA code HET) is east of downtown, a car journey of roughly 14.3 km (8.9 mi). Nonstop flights serve large mainland cities such as Chengdu, Shenzhen, Shanghai, Tianjin and Beijing, along with Taichung, Hong Kong and Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia.

The city is served by the line linking Beijing and Baotou, the Jingbao Railway, which opened in 1921. There are two stations, Hohhot and Hohhot East. Beijing trains connect with destinations to the south and north-east. The famous one is the K90, an overnight service on the Hohhot-Beijing route since the 1980s, which people call the '9-0'. Going west, trains pass Baotou and continue to Lanzhou; there are also links to most big Inner Mongolian cities and to Ulaanbaatar.

The two cities are fairly close, yet the quickest conventional train to Beijing needs around six and a half hours. That is why high-speed rail was widely debated, and work on a high-speed station started in 2008. It was done in 2011, though initially only regular trains stopped there. January 2015 brought the region's first D-series (dongchezu) route from CRH, along the Baotou-Hohhot-Jining corridor. It cut the trip between Inner Mongolia's two biggest cities down to only 50 minutes and ran at up to 200 km/h (124 mph) from Hohhot to Baotou. Another high-speed link toward Zhangjiakou, plus the planned Beijing-Zhangjiakou railway, was scheduled for 2017 with a design speed of 250 km/h (155 mph). In August 2017 the section to Ulanqab (Jining) opened, and the journey time is now 40 minutes.

A 1997 expressway, originally called the Hubao Expressway, connects Hohhot and Baotou. It has since been extended eastwards via Jining and Zhangjiakou to the capital, becoming a section of the G6 Beijing-Lhasa (Jingzang) Expressway. China National Highway 110, from Yinchuan to Beijing, passes through, and Highway 209 begins in Hohhot and runs south, finishing in Guangxi. A road completed in 2006, the Huwu Highway, joins the city to its counties in the north, which used to demand a long detour through mountains. Long-distance buses run to outlying counties, to Baotou, Wuhai and Ordos, and to other parts of Inner Mongolia.

Street naming follows a rule: main routes running north to south are roads (Lu), and those running east to west are streets (Jie). The largest flyover is beside the Drum Tower (Gulou) and is named after it. Many principal streets honour Inner Mongolian leagues and cities. In the north-south group are Xing'an, Xilin Gol, Hulun Buir, Jurim (now Tongliao) and Ulaanhad (now Chifeng); the east-west group has Bayannur, Hailar, Ulaanqab and Erdos.
Getting around means buses (close to a hundred routes, at 1 yuan a ride) or taxis, which are usually green or blue and start at 8 yuan.
The Hohhot Metro is running. Line 1, the red line, covers 21.719 km (13.5 mi), and Line 2, the blue line, is longer at 27.32 km (17.0 mi).

For secondary schooling the city has Hohhot No. 1 and No. 2 Middle Schools, the Hohhot Experimental Middle School, and a middle school attached to Inner Mongolia Normal University. Hohhot hosted the 39th China Adolescents Science and Technology Innovation Contest and had already hosted it twice before.

Hohhot had no professional football team until Shenyang Dongjin F.C. moved there in 2012 and became Hohhot Dongjin. They played at Hohhot City Stadium, newly built in 2007, finished bottom of the league in 2012 and were relegated to League Two. After half a season in Hohhot in 2013, the team moved to Liaoning and used Benxi City Stadium as its home ground.

A second club arrived on 14 January 2015, when Taiyuan Zhongyou Jiayi F.C. relocated and renamed itself Nei Mongu Zhongyou F.C. Competing in China League One, it adopted Hohhot City Stadium as its home ground that year. Its origins go back to 8 October 2011, when it was founded as Shanxi Jiayi F.C.
Inner Mongolia University lists 135 programs for international students on this site: 50 bachelor, 34 master's, 15 doctoral, 36 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 135 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 12,000 to CNY 13,600 (median CNY 13,600), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 18,400 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 22,400 (median CNY 22,400), according to the university's published fee table.

135 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

inner-mongolia-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Inner Mongolia University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hohhot, register at Inner Mongolia University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Inner Mongolia University of Technology, or IMUT, sits in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region of the People's Republic of China, and it answers to the regional government rather than to Beijing. Its Chinese name is 内蒙古工业大学. The story starts in 1951, when it opened as the Suiyuan Higher Technical School. From 1958 it was the Inner Mongolia Polytechnic Institute, and in 1993 it took the name it carries today. The university runs three campuses: two in Hohhot, the regional capital, and one in the city of Ordos.

Enrolment is above 27,000 students. Engineering is the core of the place, though over the years the university has broadened into subjects such as economics and law. Degrees are offered at three levels: 72 disciplines at undergraduate level, 22 at master's level and 6 at doctoral level.

inner-mongolia-university-of-technology.h: A pioneer among engineering universities in minority regions

blocks.x: IMUT was founded in 1951, which makes it the earliest engineering university set up in a minority-nationality area after the People's Republic was established. That history gives it a noticeable role inside the national higher-education system and a strong regional focus: it trains engineers for the autonomous region and its industries.

Degree and postgraduate education began in 1984. Two years later, in 1986, the university gained the right to award master's degrees, and in 2003 it won the right to award doctorates. On the administrative side, the Graduate Office was created in 1984 and a Graduate Department followed in 1988. A Graduate Office followed in March 2001, and 2010 saw the creation of the Graduate School proper.

At doctoral level the university holds authority in 6 first-level disciplines: power engineering and engineering thermophysics, architecture, politics, mechanics, chemical engineering and technology and materials science and engineering. Another 25 first-level disciplines are authorised for master's degrees, together with 15 professional master's degrees.

The regional government has also labelled certain subjects. IMUT has 2 first-class disciplines under the autonomous region's own "Double First-Class" project, 3 advantageous and characteristic disciplines, 9 key disciplines and 4 key cultivation disciplines.

National assessment gives a sense of where the university stands. The Ministry of Education's Academic Degrees and Graduate Education Development Center ran the fourth national subject evaluation in 2017. Chemical engineering and technology came out at B-; materials science and engineering scored C, as did power engineering and engineering thermophysics; and mechanics, civil engineering and architecture were rated C-. The university says its discipline level and academic influence keep rising steadily. As with any ranking, check the university's own site for newer results.

After some 70 years of development, IMUT has built a team of graduate supervisors and a set of distinctive research platforms. It counts 80 doctoral supervisors and 639 master's supervisors. Research infrastructure includes 1 key laboratory at provincial and ministerial level under the Ministry of Education, 1 joint national-local engineering research center that the National Development and Reform Commission approved, 41 platforms for research and innovation at autonomous-region level and 17 innovation teams at the same level.

Over those decades the quality of training has improved steadily. At present 4490 doctoral and master's students are enrolled, and during the last 10 years the university has trained 217 doctoral students and 7228 master's students of various types. The Graduate School manages postgraduate teaching and study, and it also coordinates how the university builds up its disciplines.

Internally the Graduate School has five offices: Admissions, Training and Student Status Management, Degrees, a General Office, and an office for Degree Site Establishment and Quality Assessment. They handle, in order, student intake, training, degrees, building up disciplines and quality control, and general administration. In 2018 a Discipline Construction Office and a Faculty Office were added under the Graduate School.

Daily life for a student depends heavily on the surrounding city: how cold it gets, how to travel and what to do after class. IMUT's two main campuses are in Hohhot, so the following sections explain what the city is like.

Hohhot is in the south-central part of Inner Mongolia, hemmed in by the Hetao Plateau on its southern side and the Daqing Shan (大青山, "Great Blue Mountains") on its northern side. As a curiosity, the spot directly opposite Hohhot on the globe lies 14 mi (22 kilometres) from Los Menucos, a village in Argentina's Rio Negro Province.

Hohhot has a cold semi-arid climate (Köppen BSk). Expect winters that are long, cold and very dry, summers that are hot and somewhat humid, strong winds (especially in spring) and a touch of monsoon influence. Winter's low point is January, with a daily mean of -10.7 °C (12.7 °F); July is the warmest month at 23.2 °C (73.8 °F) on average, and the year as a whole averages 7.6 °C (45.7 °F).

Rainfall totals 411 millimetres (16.2 in) a year, over half of it in July and August. Years can differ wildly: 1965 brought only 155.1 mm (6.11 in), while six years earlier the city had a soaking 36.58 in (929.2 mm), with 13.33 in (338.6 mm), over a third, falling in July alone.

Summer is the tourist season thanks to the nearby Zhaohe grasslands. On the downside, desertification means sandstorms arrive almost every year now. Sunshine is plentiful all year, from a low of 54 percent of possible in November to a high of 66 percent in September, adding up to 2,680 hours of bright sun annually. Temperatures have swung between -32.8 °C (-27 °F), recorded on 6 February 1951, and a hot 102 °F (38.9 °C) on 30 July 2010; an unofficial low of -36.2 °C (-33 °F) was noted in January 1930. If you arrive from a warm country, pack seriously warm winter clothing.

The urban population has risen quickly since the 1990s. The 2010 Census put Hohhot at 2,866,615 people, which was 428,717 more than in 2000, an average annual growth of 1.63 percent over 2000-2010. The built-up urban area, covering 4 urban districts, had 1,980,774 residents.

Han Chinese make up most of the population, 87.16 percent in 2010. Look back a few decades and most Han families here have roots in Shanxi, north-east China or Hebei. Chinese is also the everyday language of most local Mongols: when Inner Mongolia University surveyed Tümed Mongols (the dominant tribe around Hohhot) in 1993, just 8 percent could speak Mongolian. For an international student this means Mandarin, not Mongolian, is the language you will need in the street. A good number of residents are of mixed ethnic origin.

In his 1993 book Sex, Death, and Hierarchy in a Chinese City, the anthropologist William Jankowiak argued that Hohhot's minority and Han cultures differ only slightly. Differences gather around small things like cuisine and art, and people share the same basic views on ethics, status, goals in life and how the world works.

Hohhot is one of Inner Mongolia's main industrial centres. Together with Baotou and Ordos, it produces over 60 percent of the region's industrial output. It is the third-largest economy in the province after Baotou and Ordos, In 2012 its GDP reached RMB 247.56 billion, 11.0 percent higher than a year before, roughly 15.5 percent of the provincewide figure. It is also the region's largest consumer market, with retail sales of consumer goods reaching ¥102.2 billion in 2012, up 14.9 percent from 2011. Hohhot has been a priority for the central government's China Western Development project, and well-known firms are based here, among them China's biggest dairy producer by sales revenue, Inner Mongolia Yili Industrial Group, and China Mengniu Dairy Co.

Since the 1990s the urban area has grown a great deal. Business districts have expanded fast in all the main districts, and a new municipal government office tower in eastern Hohhot shifted the city's centre of gravity east. Hailiang Plaza (海亮广场) is a 41-floor central tower, and it ranks among very few department stores in town known for luxury goods.

Public transport comprises nearly one hundred bus lines plus many taxis, typically green or blue. A bus ride costs 1 yuan and taxi fares start at 8 yuan.
The Hohhot Metro is open. Line 1, the red line, measures 13.5 mi (21.719 km), and Line 2, the blue line, measures 17.0 mi (27.32 km).

Hohhot had no professional football team until Shenyang Dongjin F.C. moved here in 2012 and became Hohhot Dongjin. They played at Hohhot City Stadium, newly built in 2007, finished bottom in 2012 and dropped to League Two. After half a season in Hohhot in 2013, the club moved to Liaoning and adopted Benxi City Stadium as its home ground.

Taiyuan Zhongyou Jiayi F.C. moved to Hohhot on 14 January 2015 and became Nei Mongu Zhongyou F.C. It competes in China League One and chose Hohhot City Stadium as its 2015 home. The club began life on 8 October 2011 as Shanxi Jiayi F.C.
Where a university stands influences student life nearly as much as the campus itself, so the remaining sections look at Inner Mongolia as a whole.

Our knowledge of the Mongolian Plateau's past depends largely on records written by Chinese chroniclers and historians. Until the Mongols rose in the 13th century, the Hetao region and the rest of what is now central and western Inner Mongolia were held in turn by Chinese farming settlements to the south and by a series of northern peoples: the Khitan, Jurchen, Xianbei, Xiongnu, Tujue and nomadic Mongols. In the east, the story is mainly one of changing power between Tungusic and Mongol tribes, not of conflict between nomads and Chinese farmers.

Slab Grave cultural monuments turn up in northern, central and eastern Mongolia, in Inner Mongolia, north-western China and parts of the Baikal region, and Mongolian scholars have argued that this culture was related to the Proto-Mongols.

In the Zhou dynasty, the Loufan, Linhu and Dí lived as nomads across the centre and west (the Hetao region and its surroundings), while the Donghu lived in the east. In the Warring States period King Wuling of Zhao (reigned 340-295 BC), whose state occupied parts of today's Hebei and Shanxi, expanded toward the area. He destroyed the Dí state of Zhongshan in Hebei, defeated the Linhu and Loufan and set up the Yunzhong Commandery close to modern Hohhot; he also built a long wall running across Hetao. In 221 BC Qin Shi Huang created the first unified Chinese empire and sent General Meng Tian to expel the Xiongnu, absorbing the old Zhao wall into the Qin Great Wall of China. Two commanderies, Jiuyuan and Yunzhong, were kept, with 30,000 households moved in to consolidate control, but the effort was abandoned when the Qin collapsed in 206 BC.

In the Western Han period, Emperor Wu sent General Wei Qing to retake Hetao from the Xiongnu in 127 BC and kept building settlements there for defence. That same year he created the commanderies of Shuofang and Wuyuan. Meanwhile the Xianbei controlled today's eastern Inner Mongolia and would later overtake the Xiongnu in power.

Under the Eastern Han (25-220 AD), Xiongnu who submitted to the Han were settled in Hetao and mixed with Han immigrants. Later, in the Western Jin period, a Xiongnu noble from Hetao named Liu Yuan founded the Han Zhao kingdom there, which marked the start of the Sixteen Kingdoms period, a time when the north split into numerous regimes, Han and non-Han alike (Xiongnu and Xianbei among them).

The Sui (581-618) and Tang (618-907) dynasties re-established a unified empire and, like earlier rulers, conquered Hetao and settled people there, only to abandon the effort once Tang power declined. The area, together with the rest of today's Inner Mongolia, was then taken by the Liao dynasty of the Khitans, a nomadic people from southern Manchuria and eastern Inner Mongolia. The Tangut Western Xia followed in the west, including western Hetao. The Jurchens, ancestors of the modern Manchus, later replaced the Khitans and who went on to found the Jin dynasty ruling Manchuria and northern China.

In 1206 Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes and founded the Mongol Empire. Its armies conquered the Tangut Western Xia in 1227, and the Jurchen Jin dynasty fell in 1234. Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, with a summer capital at Shangdu (Xanadu), close to present-day Dolonnor. Throughout this period the Ongud and Khunggirad peoples were the dominant groups in what is now Inner Mongolia.

The Han-led Ming dynasty overthrew the Yuan in 1368 and seized parts of Inner Mongolia, among them Shangdu and Yingchang. Ming builders restored the Great Wall to the line it follows today, which loosely tracks the southern edge of the present autonomous region, apart from a big divergence at the Hebei border, and the Ming organised the local Mongols into the Three Guards. In 1449, in the Tumu incident, the Oirat ruler Esen taishi captured the Chinese emperor, and soon afterwards Mongols moved south in large numbers from Outer Mongolia. From that point until 1635 Inner Mongolia served as the political and cultural heart of the Northern Yuan Mongols.

Inner Mongolia is officially part of North China, though its length means that sections of it fall within Northeast and Northwest China as well. Eight provincial-level neighbours border it, spread across all three regions: Gansu, Ningxia, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Hebei, Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang. That equals Shaanxi's record for the most such neighbours. The bulk of the international frontier is shared with Mongolia (which Chinese speakers sometimes call "Outer Mongolia"), and a short stretch touches Russia's Zabaykalsky Krai.

In geological terms the region is mostly the northern flank of the North China Craton, a Precambrian block that is tilted and buried under sediment. The extreme south-west reaches the edge of the Tibetan Plateau, where the autonomous region's highest peak, Main Peak in the Helan Mountains, climbs to 11,670 ft (3,556 metres) and is still rising in short bursts. The Mongolian Plateau covers most of the region, with an average altitude near 3,940 ft (1,200 metres) and a thick blanket of loess and sand. In the north, the Mesozoic Khingan Mountains have a cooler climate and more forest: mainly Manchurian elm, ash, birch and Mongolian oak with several pine and spruce species. North of Hailar District, where permafrost appears in patches, forests are almost all conifers. The southern landscape is grassland in the east and sparse vegetation in the arid west, and herding is the main way of making a living.

Beneath the deep sedimentary cover lie old, weathered rocks, which explains why Inner Mongolia is a big mining area. It holds large reserves of coal, iron ore and rare-earth minerals, and these resources have turned the region into a major industrial base.
Desertification is growing and sandstorms are frequent, which harms farming.

inner-mongolia-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Inner Mongolia University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hohhot, register at Inner Mongolia University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Jiamusi University (佳木斯大学, Jiāmùsī dàxué) is a public university run by the province of Heilongjiang, in the city of Jiamusi in the northeast of that province. It has a geographical claim to fame: because of where it sits, it is the first university in China to see the sun come up each day.

The school dates from 1947. The present institution took shape in 1995, when four schools were joined: Jiamusi Medical College (佳木斯医学院), Jiamusi Engineering College (佳木斯工学院), Jiamusi Teachers Vocational School (佳木斯师范专科学校) and the municipal Jiamusi University. Three further schools were folded in after 2000. One was Fujin Normal School (富锦师范学校). Another was the Heilongjiang Provincial Polytechnic School (黑龙江省理工学校), and the third was Jiamusi Municipal Grain Workers Secondary Vocational School (佳木斯市粮食职工中等专业学校).
Jiamusi is the only university in the city, so student life centres on this campus and on the city around it.

jiamusi-university.h: Jiamusi, the city at China's eastern edge

blocks.x: Because the city influences everyday life for students, what follows explains where Jiamusi lies, how cold its winters get, what drives its economy and how to travel to and from it.

Jiamusi sits in the east of Heilongjiang province, between latitudes 45°56′ and 48°28′ north and longitudes 129°29′ and 135°05′ east. China's easternmost point lies within its territory, yet Shuangyashan's urban area is actually further east than the city of Jiamusi itself. Five prefectures neighbour it:
Harbin, to the west
Yichun, also to the west
Hegang, to the north
Qitaihe, to the south
Shuangyashan, to the east

To the east, it also borders Russia's Khabarovsk Krai. The prefecture is mostly flat, with plains and an average elevation of 85 metres (279 ft), and is 31,258 square kilometres (12,069 sq mi) in total area. In the east of the city three great rivers come together, the Songhua, the Amur and the Ussuri, and the silt they deposited created the Sanjiang Plain.

The climate is humid continental, influenced by the monsoon (Köppen: Dwa). Winters are long, bitter and dry, whereas summers are humid and very warm. January is the coldest month, with a 24-hour monthly average of −18.0 °C (−0.4 °F), and July the warmest, at 22.5 °C (72.5 °F). Over a full year the mean is 4.0 °C (39.2 °F). Rain and snow total roughly 542.6 mm (21.36 in) each year, and June to August brings over 60% of it. A frost-free period lasts about 130 days a year. Frozen ground reaches down 1.2 m (3 ft 11 in) in a normal winter. Freezing starts in late November, and the thaw begins in late March. Extremes on record run from −41.1 °C up to 38.1 °C. For a newcomer from a warmer place, the practical lesson is simple: plan for serious winter clothing.

Jiamusi has long been a significant transit port and a distribution centre for goods, and it is the economic hub of eastern Heilongjiang. The city's GDP in 2011 rose to RMB 62.53 billion, steady growth of 14.2% on the year before, and in 2015 it stood at RMB 81.01 billion.
It is also an agricultural hub for Heilongjiang. Agriculture added RMB 18.92 billion in value in 2011, a 14.2% increase, and the city's crop production grew by 26.8%, reaching 7.3 million tons.

Industry showed strong growth that year. Enterprises of designated size or above produced gross industrial output of more than RMB 39.34 billion in 2011, which was 35.5% higher than a year earlier. Heavy industry contributed RMB 22.77 billion (up 38.7%), and light industry RMB 16.57 billion (up 31.4%). Heavy and light industry accounted for 64% and 36% of the total, respectively. The pillar industries are the processing of farm products, chemicals, construction materials, and the production and supply of electricity. Main products include cement, edible oils, fertilizer and feed. Next to cities like Daqing and Harbin, Jiamusi's industrial sector is comparatively weak.

Services overtook everything else in 2011, becoming the biggest contributor to the city's economy. Its value-added output was RMB 26.99 billion, 43.2% of the total. The consumer market was very active, and sales of consumer goods came to RMB 24.55 billion, up 18.2% on the year.

Trade with other countries is significant as well. Foreign trade value for 2011 grew by 19.6%, to RMB 3.65 billion. Exports were worth US$3.01 billion, up 6.1% on the previous year, while imports stood at US$640 million, a jump of 197.5%. The figures as published do not fit neatly together, so treat the trade totals as approximate. Russia is the largest foreign trade partner. Trade with Russia was worth US$900 million in 2011, a rise of 24.5%, representing 24.66% of all the city's foreign trade. Utilized FDI reached US$150 million in 2011, an increase of 33.5% over the previous year.

This is a transport hub in northeast Heilongjiang, where the Suijia (Suihua-Jiamusi) Railway meets the Tujia (Tumen-Jiamusi) Railway. From Jiamusi Railway Station, trains run to Harbin, Dalian, Beijing, Tianjin, Jinan and various other Chinese cities. The Harbin-Jiamusi intercity railway opened to passengers on 30 September 2018. It cut the journey between the two cities from six hours to two and a half.
The G1011 Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway and the G11 Hegang-Dalian Expressway serve the city, as do six other highways. Together they form a comprehensive highway network.
To the east of the city centre, 9 km (5.6 mi) away, is Jiamusi Dongjiao Airport. It has flights to several domestic destinations and to international ones such as Khabarovsk and Seoul.

Jiamusi Port is a significant port on the lower Songhua River, first built in 1919. It was expanded in 1937 and turned into a steel-structured port. Even so, annual throughput stayed below 120 thousand tons until the People's Republic was founded in 1949. By 2014 it had risen to around 1 million tons a year. Passenger ships operate from mid-April until early November. They go upstream on the Songhua to Harbin or Qiqihar, and downstream to Tongjiang or on to Khabarovsk, in Russia.
Students at Jiamusi University also live in a province with its own character, and a university's region shapes daily life as much as its campus. These sections cover Heilongjiang.

Ancient Chinese records and other sources say that the Sushen, the Buyeo, the Mohe and the Khitan lived in Heilongjiang. Some place names are Manchu or Mongolian. The Mongolic Donghu people were in Inner Mongolia and western Heilongjiang. The Bohai Kingdom ruled the eastern part between the 7th and 10th centuries, and then the Khitan Liao dynasty did. The Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115-1234), which later ruled much of north China, arose inside the borders of modern Heilongjiang.

As an administrative unit, Heilongjiang dates from 1683, under the Manchu Qing dynasty during the reign of the Kangxi emperor. It was made out of Jilin province's northwest, and it covered only the western part of the modern province. A military governor, the General of Heilongjiang (Manchu: Sahaliyan Ula i Jiyanggiyūn), supervised it. The Manchu word jiyanggiyūn reads the Chinese 將軍 jiāngjūn, meaning general or military leader, and is cognate with the Japanese shōgun. Under the Treaty of Nerchinsk, his authority stretched north to the Stanovoy Mountains. What is now eastern Heilongjiang stayed under the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose power reached the Sea of Japan. Han Chinese were not allowed to migrate to these deep Manchurian lands.

The Military Governor's seat was first at Heilongjiang City (also called Aigun or Heihe, or Saghalien Ula in Manchu), on the Amur river. Then in 1690 the seat was relocated to Nenjiang (Mergen), on the Nen River, and in 1699 farther south again, to Qiqihar. Supply considerations may lie behind these moves, in the view of modern historians. Nenjiang and Qiqihar are linked to southern Manchuria by a convenient waterway, the Nen River. Getting to Aigun (Heihe), in contrast, would have required a long voyage down the Sungari to its junction with the Amur and then upstream on the Amur, or a portage over the Lesser Xing'an Mountains that separate the Nen valley from the Amur valley. Qiqihar may also have had the advantage of lying where a northbound road to Nenjiang met a westbound one to Mongolia, which let its garrison defend against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

North of Aigun, the Qing had little military presence. European sources from the 18th and early 20th centuries, and Russian reports from the 1850s, put the farthest Qing advance guard post at Ulusu-Modon (Ulussu-Mudan; Chinese 乌鲁苏穆丹 Wūlǔsūmùdān), close to the famous S-shaped bend of the Amur. The post stood on the left (north) bank, which was lost to the Russians in 1860.

In 1858 and 1860 the Qing government had to give up to the Russian Empire everything lying beyond the Ussuri and Amur rivers. The Qing Empire was cut off from the Sea of Japan as a result, and Heilongjiang took on the northern and eastern borders it has now. Meanwhile the Qing opened Manchuria to Han Chinese migration, and by the early twentieth century, thanks to the Chuang Guandong, the Han had become the region's dominant ethnic group.

Heilongjiang was invaded by Japanese forces in 1931, and by 1932 the conquest was complete, with the province absorbed into Manchukuo, a puppet state of Japan. In 1945 the Soviet Army defeated the Japanese forces in Manchuria. Soviet forces helped the Chinese communists during the Chinese Civil War, and Heilongjiang was the first province to be wholly controlled by the communists. Harbin was the first major city to come under their control.

When communist rule began, Heilongjiang covered only the western part of today's province, with its capital at Qiqihar. The rest was the province of Songjiang, with Harbin as its capital. The two were merged into present-day Heilongjiang in 1954. In the Cultural Revolution Heilongjiang was also enlarged to include Hulunbuir League and a few other areas that had been in Inner Mongolia, though that has mostly been reversed since.

Heilongjiang's terrain is varied. Mountain ranges dominate much of the province. They are the Greater and Lesser Khingan Ranges, the Wanda Mountains, the Laoye Mountains and the Zhangguangcai Mountains. The highest peak is Datudingzi Mountain, standing 1,690 metres (5,540 ft) tall on the Jilin border. The Greater Khingan Range holds the largest remaining virgin forest in China and is a key area for forestry.

Flat, low-lying land lies in the east and southwest, with the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers, all tributaries of the Amur. The northern border runs along the Amur valley. Xingkai Lake (also called Khanka Lake) lies on the frontier with Primorsky Krai in Russia.

Most of the province has a humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), but in the far north the climate is subarctic (Köppen Dwc). Winters are long and bitter. In January, averages fall between −31 and −15 °C (or −24 to 5 °F). Summers are short and warm to very warm, and July averages between 18 and 23 °C (64 to 73 °F). Yearly rainfall of 400 to 700 millimetres (16 to 28 in) falls mostly in summer. Sunshine is generous, at around 2,300 to 2,650 hours annually, and in spring the Songnen Plain and the Sanjiang Plain are rich in wind energy. Eleven cities stand out as the largest: Harbin, Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi and Daqing, then Jixi, Shuangyashan, Hegang, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe.

jiamusi-university.h: Roads, rail and air across the province

blocks.x: By October 2020 Heilongjiang had a road network of 165,989 km (103,141 mi), including expressways and highways. The corridor that matters most is the Beijing-Harbin Expressway, which starts at the Heilongjiang-Jilin border and ends inside the Harbin Ring Expressway. The Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway heads northeast and connects remote counties under Harbin and Jiamusi and other major counties in the northeast. Where it nears its end, the Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off at Jiansanjiang and connects the state-owned farms of the far east, finishing near the Sino-Russian border. The Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway runs southeast to northwest and links the province's largest population centres, Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar, until it ends at the Heilongjiang-Inner Mongolia border. The Hegang-Dalian Expressway, in east Heilongjiang, runs between Hegang and the border with Jilin and helps carry lumber and coal.

Railways total 60 lines, covering around 5,300 kilometres (3,300 miles), and one section belongs to the Eurasian Land Bridge. In 2012 the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway opened. It links Harbin, the provincial capital, with Dalian in Liaoning province, passing through Changchun and Shenyang and making 23 stops. Forecasts called for 37 million passengers a year by 2020 and 51 million by 2030.

Airports of note include Jiamusi Airport, Mudanjiang Airport, Qiqihar Airport, Heihe Airport and Harbin Taiping International Airport. The last of these can handle six million passengers each year and has connections with more than 70 domestic and international cities.

A rail crossing of the Amur between China and Russia is also under way. Valery Solomonovich Gurevich, who was a vice-chairman of Russia's Jewish Autonomous Oblast, put forward the Tongjiang-Nizhneleninskoye railway bridge in 2007; it will connect Tongjiang to Nizhneleninskoye, a village in that oblast. The Chinese section was done in July 2016, and the Russian section was started in December 2016. In March 2019 the two sides were joined structurally. Several delays have affected the start of rail traffic: an estimate made in December 2019 said the end of 2020, and a later one said the third quarter of 2021.

Heilongjiang's GDP in 2022 was 1.59 trillion RMB (US$236 billion nominal), or CN¥51,906 (US$7,717 nominal) per head. The primary sector contributed ¥360 billion (22.7%), the secondary ¥465 billion (29.2%) and the tertiary ¥764 billion (48%). Steady growth has marked GDP since 2003, when it was 443.3 billion yuan. By 2007 it had reached 707.72 billion yuan, which is a 60 % increase. The private economy in 2006 was valued at RMB234 billion and was 37.6 percent of GDP; private firms paid RMB20.5 billion in tax that year. Private enterprises have led the province's growth overall, and many leading ones have started to emerge.

No other province plants as much rice, corn and soybeans. The grain area adds up to 14.37 million ha (35.5 million acres): 5.5 million ha (14 million acres) is corn and 4 million ha (9.9 million acres) is rice. Vast tracts of black soil (chernozem), among the most fertile soils, lie here. Cultivation across the black soil belt has expanded almost 100-fold since the early 20th century, and after the 1960s farming turned into a modern, heavily mechanised industry using more fertilizer. Asia's top regions for growing japonica rice include this province, which is noted for high-quality brand varieties. Cold-resistant varieties, favourable policies and climate change have all helped raise rice output significantly in recent years. Beets, flax and sunflowers are among the commercial crops.

Lumber is another contribution to China. Larch and Korean pine are the main species cut. Forests grow mostly in the Greater and Lesser Khingan Mountains, where protected animals such as the lynx, the red-crowned crane and the Siberian tiger live. Herding is based on horses and cattle, and Heilongjiang has more milk cows than any other province-level division in China.

Heilongjiang belongs to northeast China, the traditional industrial base of the country. Industry focuses on coal, petroleum, lumber, machinery and food. Because of where it lies, the province is also a key gateway for trade with Russia. Manchuria has suffered stagnation since a wave of privatization in the 1990s closed uncompetitive factories. In response, the government launched the Revitalize Northeast China campaign, which promotes the private sector as the preferred way to reform and open up.

Petroleum matters greatly, with the Daqing oilfields supplying a large part of China's needs. Graphite, gold and coal are other minerals of significance. Wind power has great potential, with a potential capacity of 134 gigawatts.

The permanent resident population stood at 30.99 million as 2022 ended, which was 260,000 lower than a year before. There were 20.52 million city dwellers and 10.47 million rural residents; urbanization therefore reached 66.2%, a rise of 0.5 percentage points. By age, 9.3% of the population was 0-14 and 17.8% was 65 or above.

Earlier counts show the trend. The 2021 Statistical Bulletin gave 31.25 million permanent residents, 460,000 fewer than in 2020. The Seventh National Population Census (2020) counted 31,850,088. The Sixth Census (2010) had counted 38,313,991, so over ten years the population fell by 6,463,903 (−16.87%), which works out to a yearly growth rate of −1.83% on average.
Detail from the 2020 census:
Women numbered 15,897,620 (49.91%) and men 15,952,468 (50.09%), giving a sex ratio of 100.35 (females = 100)
People aged 60 or over: 7,395,690 (23.22%); of those, 4,972,868 were 65 or older (15.61%)
10,952,394 people (34.39%) lived in rural areas, and 20,897,694 (65.61%) in urban ones

Rates in 2020 were 3.35‰ for births and 8.23‰ for deaths, so natural growth was −4.48‰. The province's demographic profile is one of low births, low deaths and strong population ageing, and out-migration has also contributed to continuous decline since 2014.
