Jiangnan University (江南大学) is a state university in Wuxi, in Jiangsu Province. It answers to the Ministry of Education, and the Jiangsu provincial government shares in sponsoring it. Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme both include it. Before it took its present form it was known as the Wuxi University of Light Industry, and light industry is still where its reputation rests. Biotechnology, food science, fashion design, industrial design, and mechanical, chemical and textile engineering are the subjects for which it is best known.
One of the sources of today's university was a private Jiangnan University, founded at Wuxi in 1947 by Rong Desheng, the leading national capitalist of the Republic of China period.

Higher education was reorganised in 1952, after the People's Republic was set up. At that time the engineering departments of Nanjing University (whose line goes back to the San Jiang Normal School, opened in Nanjing in 1902 and later called National Central University) were combined with engineering departments from the private Jiangnan University and from several other East China institutions, such as Fudan, Wuhan and Zhejiang universities. The combined body became the Nanjing Institute of Technology, which we now know as Southeast University in Nanjing.

Then, in 1958, the Nanjing institute's Department of Food Technology relocated to Wuxi and became the Wuxi Institute of Light Industry. It took the name Wuxi University of Light Industry in 1995. The present Jiangnan University was created in 2001 by merging that university with two smaller colleges, Jiangnan College and Wuxi Education College.

A recently finished campus of 208 hectares, with 1.05 million square metres of floor space, forms the university's home. It stands beside Lake Li, an inner lake of Lake Tai that is also a national scenic area, in southern Wuxi. The planners wanted to demonstrate an 'Eco-campus', and they designed and built it with that concept in mind.

Seventeen schools make up the university, and 48 undergraduate programmes are spread over 9 fields: science, engineering, medicine, literature, economics, management, law, education and the arts. Postgraduate study is broad. Seven postdoctoral stations exist for light industry technology and engineering, food science and technology, chemical engineering and technology, control science and engineering, environmental engineering, and textile engineering and design. Master's degrees are offered in 58 programmes and doctorates in 28.
The schools are grouped by their location on campus, which is a handy way to see what is taught.
South-west: the schools of Food Science and Technology, Biotechnology, Chemical and Material Engineering, Pharmaceutical Sciences, and the Wuxi School of Medicine.
South-east: Business, Law, Marxism, Foreign Studies, and Artificial Intelligence and Computer Science.

North-west: Textile and Clothing, Design, Mechanical Engineering, and Environmental and Civil Engineering, as well as a School of Internet of Things Engineering that was formed from the former schools of Communications and Control Engineering and of Information Engineering.
North-east: Science, Humanities and Education, and the Division of Sports.

In the 2024 Academic Ranking of World Universities, Jiangnan University came 301st to 400th among universities worldwide. QS World University Rankings for 2025 placed it 851st in the world and 275th in Asia.

The university is seen as one of the best research institutions in food science and technology anywhere. In 2025 its food science and technology programme was number one in the world in the Shanghai Ranking, URAP, U.S. News and SCImago Institutions Rankings alike. If you want to study food, fermentation or nutrition, that record counts for far more than the university's overall position.
Research is organised around several leading bases:
the State Key Laboratory of Food Science and Technology;
the National Engineering Laboratory for Cereal Fermentation Technology;
the National Engineering Research Centre for Functional Food;
Ministry of Education key laboratories for industrial biotechnology, for carbohydrate chemistry and biotechnology, for synthetic and biological colloids, and for eco-textile science and technology.

The university employs 3,393 people as faculty, among them 2,137 full-time instructors. Senior titles are held by 63.8% of the faculty, doctorates by 68.9%, and 42.1% have spent more than a year abroad.

Honours among staff include three academicians of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, 14 holders of the 'Thousand Talents Plan' award, 13 distinguished professors under the 'Chang Jiang Scholars Program', 5 winners each of the National Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars and the National Science Fund for Outstanding Scholars, a chief scientist of the '973 Program' and eight recipients of the 'Ten Thousand Talent Program'.

Across 39 countries and regions, 190 universities and research institutions have signed cooperation and exchange agreements with Jiangnan, and 28.6% of its students have gone overseas on exchanges. With the University of California, Davis, it set up a Confucius Institute devoted to the theme of Chinese food culture, said to be the first of its kind in the world.

International students have been welcome since 1964, and graduates have come from more than 80 countries. There are special scholarships for them: the 'President Scholarship', the 'Taihu Scholarship' and the 'New Student Scholarship'. In 2010 the university recruited 25 students on self-enrolled Chinese Government Scholarships.

At doctoral level, international students mainly study food science, fermentation engineering, pharmaceutical engineering, textile science, control science, chemical engineering, environmental engineering, packaging and light industry machinery, and the theory and technology of product design.
The city around the campus shapes your daily life as a student, so the sections below describe Wuxi, home of Jiangnan University.

Wuxi has had a developed economy since ancient days. A local capital-funded enterprise, the Yeqin Cotton Mill, was founded by the brothers Yang Zonglian and Yang Zonghan in 1895 beyond the city's south gate, and it was the first of its kind. Textiles, silk and grain processing grew quickly after it, and the city became a cradle of Chinese national industry and trade. Many 'firsts' and 'mosts' in modern industrial history appeared in that period, and big industrial families such as the Rongs and the Tangs came to prominence, showing the entrepreneurial spirit of local industrialists.

Private firms flourished once reform and opening up began, using the southern Jiangsu model that depends on township industry. Famous companies changed their forms at that time. Taiji Industry became in July 1993 the first private Jiangsu enterprise to list on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, and since then the group of Wuxi-based listed companies has expanded. Known as the 'Wuxi plate', it is the largest in Jiangsu and counts for more and more in the economy of the whole Yangtze River Delta.

Through the southern Jiangsu model, Wuxi became an important economic centre of eastern China and a very active commercial city. By the end of 2013, First Financial Weekly had named it one of China's 'new first-tier cities' because of steady overall strength, and the Chinese edition of Forbes ranked it fifth in mainland China's best commercial cities for 2013, first among prefecture-level cities.
These numbers come from different years, so use them for scale rather than exact comparison.

Sectors: in one year, primary industry contributed 13.365 billion yuan (up 1.1%) and secondary industry 717.739 billion yuan (up 3.6%); the three sectors stood in proportion 0.9 to 48.3 to 50.8. The earlier year's growth rate had been 2.4%.

Jobs: 158,100 new jobs appeared in cities and towns, of which 77,200 went to laid-off or unemployed people who found work again, and 31,200 to people who had struggled to get a job. Registered urban unemployment was 2.68%.

Private sector: it added 983.124 billion yuan, 3.3% more, which was 66.2% of all output (0.2 percentage points higher). Output of private industry above designated size reached 1,426.928 billion yuan (up 12.8%), while private investment fell 3.6% to 240.341 billion yuan.

Companies: 423,300 enterprises were on the register at year end, among them 36,000 state-owned and collective holding companies, 7,000 foreign-funded firms and 380,400 private firms. In addition, 660,900 households were self-employed, and 80,800 of them had registered that year.
Prices: the urban consumer price index went up 2.1% (0.4 points faster); services rose 1.0% and goods 2.9%. Factory-gate prices for producers increased 1.7% and purchase prices 3.9%.

Most recent year: 2025 GDP was 1,677.394 billion yuan, 5.1% up in constant prices, with 14.248 billion yuan from the primary sector (up 2.6%), 787.047 billion from the secondary (up 5.0%) and 876.099 billion from the tertiary (up 5.1%). Fiscal revenue of 122.5 billion yuan came third in the province, and GDP per head of 223,000 yuan came third in the country after Beijing and Shanghai.

Wuxi New District (WND) was set up in 1992, covers 220 square kilometres (85 square miles), and has grown into one of China's main industrial parks. In 2013 its GDP was 121.3 billion yuan ($19.54 billion) and its industrial output was 276.7 billion yuan, about 15% of production in the Wuxi area. Inside the district are a Hi-tech Industrial Development Zone, the Taihu International Technology Park, an Airport Industrial Park, the China (Wuxi) Industrial Expo Park, the China Wu Culture Expo Park and an International Education and Living Community.

Visitors can choose among many hotels: the Marriott at Wuxi Maoye City, a Hilton DoubleTree resort at Lingshan beside the Giant Buddha, the Kempinski, the Landison Square Hotel (with its Wu jade phoenix sculpture in the lobby), the Radisson Blu Resort at Wetland Park, the Sheraton at Binhu, the Wuxi Grand Hotel and the Wuxi Hubin Hotel.

Rail first. Wuxi Railway Station stands on the Shanghai-Nanjing Intercity High-Speed Railway, 301 km (187 miles) long, opened on 1 July 2010, which connects the city directly to Shanghai, Suzhou and the provincial capital Nanjing.

The Wuxi Metro opened Line 1 on 1 July 2014. That made Wuxi the 22nd mainland metropolitan area, and the third city in Jiangsu, to run rail transit. By January 2024, five lines were operating (Lines 1 and 2, Phase I of Lines 3 and 4, and Line S1), all underground, with 145 km of track and 97 stations. Four further lines, 4 Phase II, 5 Phase I, 6 Phase I and S2, about 120 km together, were under construction. The system had a record 1.3 million passengers on 21 January 2024 and then 1.4112 million on 16 February 2024.
For flying, Wuxi Shuofang Airport, which opened in 2004 and lies 14 km (8.7 miles) from the centre, offers direct flights to Osaka, Singapore, Taipei, Hong Kong, Beijing, Guangzhou and Shenzhen.

The main roads include China National Highway 312, which connects Shanghai to central and north-western China and runs through Wuxi, and the 274 km (170 mile) Shanghai-Nanjing Expressway (G42), opened in November 1996, that links the city with Suzhou, Shanghai, Changzhou, Zhenjiang and further Jiangsu cities. A 62.3 km (38.7 mile) expressway to Yixing connects Wuxi with that city in the same prefecture-level area.

Freight moves through Wuxi Jiangyin Port, which has 12 berths, mainly in the Shenxia Port Area, all cleared for foreign ships, on 1.5 million square metres, operated by the Dagang and Dacheng branches. The Dagang branch has a yard of 710,000 square metres, two big warehouses of 12,000 square metres (each with two 20-ton cranes) and 10 berths with a year-round depth of 15 metres at the quay. Of these, two are ocean-going berths for ships of 50,000 and 100,000 tons, and one is a 2,000-ton sea-going berth, served by 9 gantry cranes of 40 tons, so vessels up to 100,000 tons can be unloaded and cargo transferred. Four 5,000-ton inland berths, 536 metres long in total, have portal cranes and conveyor loading belts, and the port area has 7 truck scales of 120 to 150 tons and 2 gantry cranes. Storage capacity peaks at 3 million tons. The branch mostly deals in metal ore, coal and some general cargo, and offers crushing and screening of ore, producing lump and fine ore at 800,000 to 1 million tons a year. Liner services for general cargo run from Jiangyin to the Middle East, Thailand and South Korea. The Dacheng branch came into operation after it was completed in 2015.
Buses have a long history: the first line opened in 1927. In 2020 there were 297 lines totalling 5,760 km and 3,036 vehicles, carrying 191.18 million passengers over the year.

The Wuxi Sports Center, with a capacity of 30,000, opened in October 1994. It hosts the Wuxi Classic snooker tournament, which has attracted the leading names of the game. The Wuxi City Sports Park Stadium was the venue for the 2017 ITTF Asian Championships in table tennis and for the snooker World Cup in June 2019. Major League Baseball made the Wuxi Development Center, at Dongbeitang High School, its main Chinese recruitment base in 2009, and scouts go there to find the country's best players in the hope that they will turn professional in America.

The Wuxi New Sports Center is old, among other reasons, so the Wuxi Olympic Sports Center project is due to open formally in 2026. The site covers about 56.7 hectares with around 467,000 square metres of building and an investment of about 6.9 billion yuan. Plans call for a stadium of 60,000 seats, a gymnasium of 18,000 seats, a swimming pool of 2,000 seats and a public fitness centre, all built to Class A standard so that large national multi-sport events can be held. A 70,000 square metre complex for culture, shopping, sport and tourism, including commercial space and hotels, is also planned.

jiangnan-university.h: Lake Tai and the city's sights

blocks.x: In the southern Yangtze river delta, Wuxi lies on Lake Tai, which is the third-largest freshwater lake in China, and the cruises on it attract many tourists. The lake contains 72 peninsulas and peaks and 48 islets, such as Yuantouzhu, the 'Islet of Turtlehead', and Taihu Xiandao, the 'Islands of the Deities'.

Over the centuries, learned scholars and well-known figures built private gardens and parks around Wuxi. Lihu Park, in Binhu District, was built in 1927 and named for Fan Li, the politician and economist. A water Ferris wheel is the feature of the Star of Taihu Lake. The park has a long embankment lined with willows and a lakeside path crossing many small bridges and pavilions. Changguangxi Wetland Park lies on the lake's south-west shore beneath Junzhang Hill; it is a 10 km (6.2 mile) canal that joins Lihu Lake in the north and Taihu Lake in the south, and it has the Shitang Bridge and a lotus pond. Binhu District is also home to Wuxi Zoo and the Taihu Lake Amusement Park, a national AAAA site with more than 1000 animals, among them Asian elephants, leopards, chimpanzees, giant pandas and white rhinoceros, as well as an area for ecology and science exhibitions and recreation.

The Mt. Lingshan Grand Buddha Scenic Area, covering 30 hectares (74 acres) at the south-western tip of Wuxi, is dominated by an 88 metre (289 ft) bronze Buddha, the largest bronze Buddha statue in the world. In the same area are the Brahma Palace, Xiangfu Temple, the Five Mudra Mandala, a 7.2 metre (24 ft) statue of Sakyamuni known as Nine Dragons Bathing Sakyamuni, and many more Buddhist sites. West of the city at the foot of Xi Shan lies Xihui Park, opened in 1958, which holds Jichang Garden and the Dragon Light Pagoda.

Jiangnan University is a good choice if your interest is food, biotechnology, textiles or design, and it offers a modern lakeside campus in a prosperous city that is well connected by high-speed rail to Shanghai and Nanjing. Check the university's own website for current programmes, scholarships and admission requirements before applying, and remember that the economic and transport figures above come from several different years, so confirm anything that matters to your plans with the university or the city authorities.
Jiangnan University lists 202 programs for international students on this site: 52 bachelor, 46 master's, 25 doctoral, 79 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 172 taught in Chinese, 30 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,800 to CNY 16,400 (median CNY 16,400), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

199 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (13):
Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
Bioengineering
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Design Studies
Fermentation Engineering
Food Science and Engineering (Engineering)
Industrial Design
Microbiology
Pharmaceutical Engineering and Technology
Pharmacy
Sugar Engineering
Textile Engineering
Textile Science and Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

jiangnan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jiangnan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuxi, register at Jiangnan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Jiangsu Normal University is a provincial key university in the city of Xuzhou, in northern Jiangsu province. Its Chinese name is 江苏师范大学 (simplified), or 江蘇師範大學 (traditional), and the pinyin is Jiāngsū Shīfàn Dàxué. It was built through a partnership between China's Ministry of Education and the Jiangsu provincial government. The word "Normal" in its name means that teacher training is part of its tradition, although today the university teaches a very wide range of subjects.

jiangsu-normal-university.h: Early years and the move north

blocks.x: Its origins lie in Wuxi, in southern Jiangsu, where a Business Cadre School was founded in 1952. In 1956 the Ministry of Education allowed it to become a higher education institution, and it took the name Jiangsu Normal Academy. In August 1958 it moved north to Xuzhou. The following March it merged with Xuzhou Normal Academy to become Xuzhou Normal College, which was then the only undergraduate college in northern Jiangsu. In the early 1960s, thanks to a suggestion from Zhou Enlai that such a vast region needed a college, it escaped being closed during a reorganisation of the higher education system.

The Cultural Revolution was a hard period. Red Guards at one point renamed the school Huaihai College (淮海大学), and it did not take in students for six years. Recovery came quickly afterwards: it started enrolling postgraduates in 1979, and in 1981 became one of the first group of Chinese universities permitted to award master's degrees.

More mergers followed. A second teacher-training school, the Second Xuzhou Normal Academy (opened 1984), was folded into Xuzhou Normal College in 1989. Approval for full university status came from the Ministry of Education in 1996, giving the name Xuzhou Normal University, and three years later the Xuzhou Industrial College, previously run by the State Coal Bureau, was added too. The present name, Jiangsu Normal University, was adopted in 2011.
The university now has four campuses in and around Xuzhou:
Quanshan Campus (泉山校区), the main and largest one, built from 1985 onward
Yunlong Campus (云龙校区), the oldest, dating from the 1950s
Jiawang Campus (贾汪校区), in the outer suburbs of Xuzhou, which was formerly the Xuzhou Industrial College campus
Kuiyuan Campus (奎园校区), once the home of the Second Xuzhou Normal Academy

Together the four campuses cover about 122 thousand square metres, with close to a million square metres of floor space inside the buildings. (The land figure appears small next to the building area in the university's own data, so check it with the admissions office if it matters to you.)

The university employs 1358 full-time teachers. Among them are 218 professors, 445 assistant professors and 313 people with doctorates, and the staff also includes two members of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (academicians) and a committee member from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

Teaching is organised in schools, colleges and institutes. The list below gives each unit with the programmes that its entry mentions, so you can see how wide the choice is. Names are as translated in the university's materials.

School of Linguistic Sciences: language research of several kinds, from neurolinguistics (using fMRI and ERP methods) to theoretical and engineering linguistics, plus Chinese minority linguistics, the Chinese language, and teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages
School of Literature, with Chinese Language and Literature in a non-normal track and in a high-level secretarial track, as well as Chinese Language
College of Foreign Languages, offering English (normal, commercial and translation tracks), Japanese, Russian, Spanish and International Marketing
School of Educational Science, with elementary education, psychological education, preprimary education and applied psychology
Institute of Mathematical Sciences: statistics, information and computing science, and mathematics, both pure and applied

Physical and Electronic Engineering Institute: physics plus electronic subjects, namely electronics science and technology, electronic information engineering, and optical information science and technology
College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering: chemistry and applied chemistry, along with the engineering of pharmaceuticals and of the environment
College of Life Science: biology, biotechnology, and also horticulture and zoology
College of Landscape and Animal Science
School of City and Environmental Science: environmental science, geosciences, geographic information systems, and planning for towns, countryside and resources
School of Geodesy and Geomatics: remote sensing, land resource management, and the engineering of surveying and mapping
College of Mechanical Engineering: mechanics, the electronics of machinery and computer numerical control (CNC)
Electrical Engineering and Automation Institute
School of Economics: general economics together with international commerce and international economy and trade
Faculty of Management: marketing, finance, administration, logistics and the management of public enterprises
School of Law and Politics: law (including international trade law), social work, politics and administration, and ideological and political education
College of Information and Communication: advertising, plus journalism and editing for radio and television
History and Culture and Tourism Institute: history, managing tourism and managing the culture industry
Physical Culture Institute: athletic training, physical education and the science of traditional ethnic sports
Academy of Fine Arts: drawing, artistic design, and fine arts with an additional teacher-training track
Academy of Music

jiangsu-normal-university.h: Xuzhou, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Jiangsu Normal University is in Xuzhou, so the city shapes your daily life: where you go on weekends, how you travel home, and what the weather will be. This section describes the land, the weather, the people, the economy and transport links.

Xuzhou sits at the south-eastern tip of the North China Plain, in a transition zone between the alluvial fan of the Yellow River and the Huai River basin. The ground is an undulating plain on top of 10 to 60 metres (33 to 197 ft) of deep sediment deposited when the Yellow River shifted course in the past.

Limestone hills rise suddenly from the flat floodplain. They include Yunlong Mountain at 142 metres (466 ft) and, as the region's highest point, Dadong Mountain at 361 metres (1,184 ft). Geologists describe the rocks as the Xuzhou-Huaibei fold-thrust belt, on the south-eastern margin of the North China Craton.

Movement along the Tancheng-Lujiang (Tan-Lu) fault zone created the Xuzhou and Feng-Pei coalfields. In the late 1990s the proven coal reserves were 3.94 billion tonnes, more than 93% of the total for Jiangsu province.

Heavy mining left scars: fragmented land and flooding where the ground had sunk. Small mines were shut and the land was restored. In the north of Xuzhou and in Jiawang, waterlogged areas of subsidence were converted into artificial wetlands, the Jiuli Lake and Pan'an Lake, and the local environment has partly recovered.

Water in the region is shaped by two huge man-made features. One is the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal; the other is the abandoned bed of the Yellow River, a "perched river" whose bed lies 2 to 5 metres (6.6 to 16.4 ft) higher than the ground around it. It now marks the dividing line between the drainage of the Huai River and that of the Yi-Shu-Si river systems.
Because the area is low-lying, with a raised riverbed at a meandering bend, floods used to be common. Records show 59 breaks in the levees near Xuzhou between 1550 and 1855.

The ancient riverbed runs through the middle of the city today. A scenic reservoir, Yunlong Lake (5.82 square kilometres, or 2.25 sq mi), lies south-west of the centre. The Kui River drains it and flows 35.6 kilometres (22.1 mi) southward into Anhui province. This river was once one of the dirtiest feeding the Huai, and in 2005 a stretch downtown was sealed under concrete to hold in the odours. After major ecological clean-up, the covers were taken off in 2021 and the river is again an open waterway through the city.

On earthquake risk, Xuzhou lies on a fairly stable fault zone, separate from the main Tan-Lu system. Even so, old loose silt can liquefy, behaving like a liquid and making earthquake damage worse, so the city still faces some danger.

The climate is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence (Köppen Cwa): cool and dry in winter, warm in spring, long, hot and sticky in summer, and crisp in autumn. Daily temperatures average 0.7 °C (33.3 °F) in January, the coldest month, and 27.3 °C (81.1 °F) in July, the hottest, with a yearly mean of 14.9 °C (58.8 °F). Winter snow is possible but seldom heavy.

Rain is light in winter. Most of the 842.8 millimetres (33.2 in) yearly total arrives from June to August. July is the dullest month, with 44% of possible sunshine, and three months reach 54%. The year's total is 2,221 hours of bright sunshine.
At the 2020 census Xuzhou had 9,083,900 permanent residents, up 5.9% from 2010. By 2023 they made up roughly 10.6% of Jiangsu province's permanent population.

Older figures show how the city grew. The old Xuzhou Prefecture, a larger area that took in Dangshan, Xiao and the urban districts of today's Suqian, rose from 2.95 million people in 1776 to 4.34 million in 1910. It remained largely agricultural, with hardly any industry or trade, and the prefectural seat itself held only about 32,000 people in 1910. Cities grew faster in the twentieth century: the city had 171,903 residents in 1931, then 314,773 in 1947, and 333,190 when the 1953 census was taken.

Xuzhou had a GDP of RMB 890.04 billion in 2023, or RMB 98,683 per person (about US$14,000). It is the largest economy in the Huaihai Economic Zone, with the highest GDP, GDP per person and total retail sales, at RMB 444.51 billion, among that zone's member cities.

The Jiawang Coal Mine, established in 1882, started Xuzhou's modern coal industry, and for decades, up to the 1950s, it was the only place in Jiangsu with large-scale extraction. The energy crisis of the 1970s then led to a "multi-party development" approach, in which the Datun Mining Area (known as a "Shanghai Enclave") operated beside mines belonging to other regional authorities.

From the 2000s resources started to run out, and most local mines were closed. Three bodies now dominate what is left: Xuzhou Mining Group, Shanghai Datun Energy Resources and China Resources Tianneng Xuzhou Coal and Power. For larger enterprises in the sector, total assets in 2023 were 41.98 billion RMB.

Renewables entered the picture in 2006, when GCL Silicon was founded; in that same year the firm brought its first polysilicon plant in Xuzhou into service, and the site later grew into a key producer of photovoltaic materials. A new chapter began in 2024 when BYD started to build a 30 GWh sodium-ion battery factory here.

Coal mining created demand for equipment, and Xuzhou's equipment-making sector grew out of that into a modern cluster of construction machinery. XCMG, which has its headquarters in the city, was the fourth-largest construction equipment maker in the world by 2024 revenue.

By 2023 the city counted 225 specialised equipment makers above the designated size, whose yearly output included 143,167 tons of mining equipment and 729,259 tons of cranes. Beyond heavy machinery, Xuzhou has become a production base for two-wheelers, making 526,300 motorcycles in 2023.

The Yellow Pavilion (黃樓) dates to 1078, when Su Shi was Prefect of Xuzhou. He had it built to mark the finishing of the city's wall and flood defences under his leadership. The colour "yellow" carries two meanings: it stands for the element earth, which overcomes water, and it refers literally to the pounded earth (hangtu) used for the new defences and for the pavilion's foundation. The building you can visit today is a reconstruction from 1988.

Within the city, several expressways carry traffic, notably the east, north and west sections of the third ring road, the Xuzhou East Avenue expressway (城东大道快速路), and routes towards Pantang, Jiawang and Suqian. Longer-distance routes link Xuzhou to the national network.
G2 Beijing-Shanghai Expressway
G2513 Huai'an-Xuzhou Expressway
G3 Beijing-Taipei Expressway
G30 Lianyungang-Khorgas Expressway
S49 Xinyi-Yangzhou Expressway
S65 Xuzhou-Mingguang Expressway
S69 Jinan-Xuzhou Expressway
Four national highways also pass through the city:
China National Highway 104
China National Highway 205
China National Highway 206
China National Highway 311

Xuzhou is one of China's important rail hubs. Xuzhou Railway Station is where the Beijing-Shanghai railway meets the Lianyungang-Lanzhou (Longhai) railway. In the east, Xuzhoudong Railway Station is the interchange between the Beijing-Shanghai and Xuzhou-Lanzhou high-speed lines and the end of the Xuzhou-Lanzhou, Xuzhou-Yancheng and Lianyungang-Xuzhou lines. A link called the Dahu connection line joins the two stations.

Freight is a major role of the northern station, Xuzhoubei, which is the biggest marshalling yard in the China Railway Shanghai Group, handling more than 20,000 wagons per day. The city is one of 14 official assembly centers for China Railway Express, and it has combined sea and rail links to Ningbo-Zhoushan, Lianyungang, Yangshan and Qingdao ports. In 2023 it moved 54.53 million tons of freight by rail.

Xuzhou Guanyin International Airport (徐州观音国际机场) is among the three largest international airports in Jiangsu and has scheduled passenger flights to major airports across China. Until 2019 it had two terminals: the Domestic Terminal (Terminal 2) and the International Terminal (Terminal 1).
No other city in northern Jiangsu had a rapid transit system before Xuzhou opened one. These lines are running:
Line 1 (September 2019): from Xuzhoudong Railway Station to Luwo, with interchanges at Pengcheng Square (Line 2) and Xuzhou Railway Station (Line 3)
Line 2 (November 2020): from Keyunbei to Xinchengqudong, serving the Yunlong Campus of Jiangsu Normal University
Line 3 (June 2021): from Xiadian to Gaoxinqu'nan, which also stops at the Wenchang Campus of China University of Mining and Technology and the Quanshan Campus of Jiangsu Normal University
Line 6 (September 2025): runs between Xuzhoudong Railway Station and Tongshan Chinese Medical Hospital

jiangsu-normal-university.h: Jiangsu: the province behind the university

blocks.x: Student life depends on the wider province as well as the city, and Jiangsu has an unusually rich history. The account that follows starts with the earliest Chinese states and runs to the present, with an eye on why the north and the south of the province are so different.

At the dawn of Chinese civilisation the region that became Jiangsu was a long way from the cultural heartland, which lay in north-western Henan. Its inhabitants were the Huai (淮夷), an ancient people whom northern writers called barbarians. Under the Zhou, links with the centre multiplied, and in the south of the province a state called Wu emerged, one of hundreds of small polities spread across northern and central China at the time.

Wu rose to great-power status late in the Spring and Autumn period, under King Helu. It beat Qi, a leading northern state in modern Shandong, in 484 BC and then competed to be overlord of all the Chinese states. The achievement did not last: Yue, a newer state to the south in what is now Zhejiang, took over Wu in 473 BC, and in 333 BC the strong western state of Chu absorbed Yue. Finally Qin eliminated every rival and brought the country together in 221 BC.

During the Han era (206 BC to 220 AD), Jiangsu still sat far from the main centres on the North China Plain. It was governed as two provinces, called zhou: Xu in the north and Yang in the south. In the Three Kingdoms period the south of Jiangsu was the base of Eastern Wu (222 to 280). Its capital, Jianye, which later got the new name Jiankang, is the Nanjing of today.

When nomadic peoples overran the north in the fourth century, the Jin court fled to Jiankang. The migrants who streamed south swelled the cities of southern and central Jiangsu. Jiankang then served as capital for four Southern dynasties in turn, growing into China's biggest centre of trade and culture.

Reunification under the Sui in 581 pulled politics northward again. Even so, the Sui built the Grand Canal across Jiangsu, tying the Central Plains to the prosperous Yangtze Delta, and under the Tang (618-907) the court relied on southern Jiangsu for its yearly grain supply. The Song period (960-1279) brought a wealthy merchant class and a market economy, and Jiangnan, meaning southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and the surrounding region, became a trading hub. Since then Suzhou and Yangzhou have stood in the national imagination for luxury, and the region is still among the wealthiest in China.

In 1127, during the wars between the Jin and the Song, the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty gained North China. The line between the Jin in the north and the Southern Song in the south ran along the Huai River, which at that time crossed northern Jiangsu on its way to the Yellow Sea. The thirteenth century brought Mongol rule over the whole country.

After the Mongols had been expelled, the Ming dynasty arose in 1368 with its first capital at Nanjing. The lands around it, roughly equal to modern Jiangsu plus Anhui, formed Nanzhili, a name meaning "southern directly governed". A coup led by Zhu Di (who became the Yongle Emperor) sent the capital far north to Beijing, but Nanjing remained the southern capital. In the later Ming, Jiangnan was still a major commercial area, and some scholars regard its booming textile trade as an early sign of industrialisation and capitalism, a development that was ultimately cut short.
The Qing renamed Nanzhili "Jiangnan province" and then divided Jiangsu from Anhui into separate provinces in 1666; the borders of Jiangsu have changed little since that date.

Western powers began pressing into China in the 1840s, and the wealthy, trading-minded Yangtze Delta was exposed to them first. Shanghai, a modest town in Jiangsu at the time, rapidly became a cosmopolitan centre for commerce and banking, and was later separated as its own municipality. Jiangnan also played a big part in the Taiping Rebellion (1851-1864), a huge and bloody revolt that aimed to found a Christian theocracy. The movement started in far-off Guangdong and swept through much of southern China; by 1853 its leaders had taken Nanjing as their capital and given it the name Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was proclaimed in 1912, and soon afterwards warlords split the country. Control of Jiangsu moved between factions until April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek installed his government in Nanjing; before long he held most of China. The provincial administration went to Zhenjiang in 1928.

War with Japan broke this stability. When full-scale fighting began in 1937, Nanjing fell on 13 December. Over the next three months the occupying troops committed the atrocities now known as the Rape of Nanjing. The city then became the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist East China government, and Japan held most of Jiangsu until 1945.

Nanjing was once more the national capital after the war, yet civil war had by now started between the Kuomintang government and the Communist forces, which were based chiefly in the north-east. The pivotal Huaihai Campaign was fought in northern Jiangsu, the part of the province where Xuzhou lies, and the Kuomintang lost. The communists crossed the Yangtze soon afterwards and captured Nanjing. The Kuomintang retreated south and eventually reached Taipei, from where the Republic of China government today governs Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands, though it also still lays claim, technically, to Nanjing as its rightful capital. When Zhenjiang was lost, the provincial government relocated to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

The communist victory made Beijing (previously Peiping) the capital of the People's Republic, and Jiangsu was split into the Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. On 15 November 1952 the province was re-established, with Nanjing demoted to provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up first favoured Guangdong on the south coast, so Jiangsu fell behind at the start; from the 1990s the same policies were spread more evenly. Suzhou and Wuxi in the south, both next door to Shanghai, then thrived and are now among China's top ten cities by GDP, ahead of the capital Nanjing. A wide income gap between southern and northern Jiangsu has nevertheless remained, which is worth remembering for a student in the north, in Xuzhou.

jiangsu-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jiangsu Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Xuzhou, register at Jiangsu Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Located in the city of Zhenjiang, Jiangsu University (江苏大学) is a public university answerable to the Jiangsu provincial government, with joint backing from the national education ministry and the ministry for agriculture and rural affairs. It is the product of a merger in August 2001 between a technology university, a medical college and a teacher training school: Zhenjiang Medical College (镇江医学院), Jiangsu Technology University (江苏理工大学) and the Zhenjiang Teachers Vocational School (镇江师范专科学校).

The formal approval for the merger came from China's Ministry of Education in August 2001, uniting Jiangsu University of Science and Technology with the medical college and the teachers' college in the same city.

The senior partner was the former Jiangsu University of Science and Technology, a school that the State Council had listed in 1978 as one of 88 national key universities. Its family tree starts with Sanjiang Normal School of 1902. That school became Liangjiang Normal School (1906), then Nanjing Higher Normal School (1915) and National Southeastern University (1921). Further changes in 1927 and 1928 produced Disi Zhongshan University, then Jiangsu University in February 1928 and Central University a month later. In 1949 the name Nanjing University was adopted. Three years after that, its engineering college was reorganised as Nanjing Polytechnic Institute (1952). A part split off in 1960 and moved to Zhenjiang in 1961, in time becoming Jiangsu University of Science and Technology. Merging with two other colleges of the city in 2001 gave it the name Jiangsu University.
Put simply, the university dates its founding to 1902 as part of Sanjiang Normal University, and the 2001 merger gave it its present identity.

Study options total 88 undergraduate programmes, 170 master's programmes and 42 PhD programmes. They fall within 10 academic fields, which are literature, history, law, education, medicine, economics, management, science and engineering. There are also 13 post-doctoral research stations.

The university employs 5,763 staff when those at the affiliated hospital are included. Teaching faculty number 2,475, including 450 professors, and some 54% of them have doctorates while more than 24% have overseas study experience. Over 33,000 full-time students are enrolled, which includes 10,000 postgraduates. International students number 842, coming from 74 different countries. Another 10,000 or so full-time students attend Jingjiang College of Jiangsu University.

The university is organised into these schools: Medicine, Medical Technology, Pharmacy, Food and Biological Engineering, Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Material Science and Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Energy and Power Engineering, Automotive and Traffic Engineering, Electrical and Information Engineering, Computer Science and Telecommunication Engineering, Environment, and Science. In the social sciences and humanities there are Business Administration, Finance and Economics, Law, Humanities and Social Sciences, Foreign Languages, Art and Teacher's Education, and finally Jingjiang College.

Humid subtropical (Köppen: Cfa) is the climate type. Expect sticky heat in summer, a cold but moderate winter, and more rain once the East Asian monsoon arrives. The lowest temperature since 1951 is −12.0 °C (10.4 °F), although −12.9 °C (8.8 °F) was recorded unofficially on 27 January 1933, and the highest is 39.5 °C (103.1 °F).

Local speech here has an unusual history. As in Nanjing, a type of Lower Yangtze Mandarin took the place of Zhenjiang's original Wu dialects entirely, and people in nearby Changzhou, who still speak Taihu Wu, cannot follow it. The 2020 population was 3,210,418, compared with 3,114,105 in 2010, which is a change of 0.31% a year.

The city is best known for its fragrant black vinegar, Zhenjiang vinegar. A Chinese legend credits Heita, son of Dukang, the supposed inventor of alcoholic drinks. Heita left a vat of wine untouched for 21 days. When he came back it had gone off, yet he found the sour result pleasant and a good partner for food. Today's recipe is said to be 1400 years old, and the main modern producer, Jiangsu Hengshun Vinegar Industry Co., traces its history to 1840.

Other local favourites are crab cream buns, Chinkiang pork (鎭江肴肉, similar to head cheese) and pickled vegetables. There was once a local custom for the new year in which families ate a red-bean dish and left rice alone. A single bowl of beans stayed on the table for the flies, on the theory that they would then leave the household in peace during the celebrations.

A natural spring in a park at the edge of the city has been prized since the Tang period (7th-9th century) as Jiangsu's finest water for making tea, and today it is promoted as the "First Spring under Heaven".

Zhenjiang was a place of study for Sesshū Tōyō, the 15th-century Japanese master of ink-wash painting. The city's Jinshan temple appears in the story of Madame White Snake, and a replica of it was built in the garden of the Kangxi Emperor at Chengde.

Zhenjiang is conveniently placed in the Yangtze River Delta transport corridor, where the Grand Canal crosses the Yangtze, between the economic regions of Shanghai and Nanjing. Its port is the third largest on the Yangtze. It has two crossings of the Yangtze. One is the Runyang Yangtze River Bridge complex to Yangzhou, whose suspension span is one of the world's longest. The other is the Taizhou Yangtze River Bridge from Yongzhong to Taizhou, among the longest cable-stayed bridges in the world.

The Nanjing-Shanghai Railway reached Zhenjiang in 1906. After the Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge opened in 1968 the line continued to Beijing, tying the city to the political and commercial centres of China. The main station was Zhenjiang West Railway Station until it was demolished in 2004 because it created congestion in the city centre, and since then Zhenjiang Railway Station has been the principal station.

In April 2010 the Shanghai-Nanjing Intercity Rail began service, the first line with a design speed above 300 km/h (186 mph) to stop in the city. The Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway followed in 2011, and its trains stop at Zhenjiang South Railway Station. With the two lines, Shanghai is now less than an hour away and Beijing under five hours. Trains to Shanghai are frequent, about one every half hour or less.

Zhenjiang proper has no commercial airport. It does have a military field, Zhenjiang Dalu General Airport (镇江大路机场), which could one day take regional flights. The nearest international airports are Changzhou Benniu, 62 km (39 mi) from the centre, Nanjing Lukou, around an hour's drive (80 km or 50 mi) by Nanjing Provincial Highway 243, and Sunan Shuofang, roughly two hours (143 km or 89 mi) away. You can check in for flights at Lukou Airport at the New Zhenjiang Bus Station (镇江汽车新站).

Road links include the Beijing-Shanghai Expressway and China National Highway 312. City buses numbered nearly a hundred routes in 2014. All of the buses have had GPS since 2012 and are controlled from a central "smart transport network system". Together with the rail links above, this makes it simple to reach Shanghai or Nanjing from the campus city.
As of 2025 Zhenjiang is a leading city for scientific research, and it appears in the world's top 100 cities in the Nature Index.

For full-time bachelor's study there are two public institutions, Jiangsu University itself and the separate Jiangsu University of Science and Technology (江苏科技大学). Also based in the city is the Silkworm Raising Research Institute, which belongs to the Academy of Agricultural Science of China. The Shaozong Library has a collection of sayings and proverbs in 100 volumes, dating between the 7th and the 11th centuries. Senior high schools are the Jiangsu Provincial Zhenjiang No. 1 High School (江苏省镇江第一中学), the Zhenjiang High School of Jiangsu Province (江苏省镇江中学) and the Jiangsu Provincial Dagang High School (江苏省大港中学), which matters to families moving with a student.
A university's province shapes everyday life, so this is the story of Jiangsu.

In the earliest dynasties Jiangsu lay far from the heartland of Chinese civilisation, which was in the northwest of Henan, and it was inhabited by the Huai peoples (淮夷). Contact grew under the Zhou, and eventually the state of Wu arose in southern Jiangsu as one of hundreds of states across northern and central China. Wu became a great power late in the Spring and Autumn period under King Helu, and in 484 BC it beat Qi, a major northern state in modern Shandong, and competed for the position of overlord of all the Chinese states. Yue, a state that had emerged in the south in what is now Zhejiang, conquered Wu in 473 BC, and Chu from the west conquered Yue in 333 BC. Qin swept all of them away and unified China in 221 BC.

Under the Han (206 BC to 220 AD) the region was still remote from the civilised core on the North China Plain. It was split into two provinces (zhou), Xu in the north and Yang in the south. Southern Jiangsu became the base for Eastern Wu (222 to 280) in the Three Kingdoms era, with its capital at Jianye, renamed Jiankang later, which is modern Nanjing. Nomadic invasions of northern China in the 4th century led the Jin court to relocate to Jiankang, and the cities of southern and central Jiangsu swelled with people arriving from the north. Jiankang stayed capital for four Southern dynasties in turn and became China's largest commercial and cultural centre.

The Sui reunited the country in 581 and the political centre moved north again, but the Grand Canal, dug through Jiangsu, joined the Central Plains to the rich Yangtze Delta, and the Tang (618-907) relied on southern Jiangsu for yearly grain shipments. In the Song era (960-1279), when a wealthy merchant class and a market economy appeared, Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and neighbouring areas) became a trading centre. Cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou have been symbols of luxury and opulence in China since, and the region remains among the richest in the country.

During the Jin-Song wars the Jurchen Jin gained North China in 1127. A line along the Huai River, which at that time ran across northern Jiangsu into the Yellow Sea, separated Jin territory in the north from the Southern Song in the south. China then fell to the Mongols in the 1200s. In 1368 the Ming dynasty, founded after the Mongols were driven out, first made Nanjing its capital, and the regions around it, equivalent to modern Jiangsu and Anhui, were set up as Nanzhili ("southern directly governed") province. After a coup by Zhu Di, who became the Yongle Emperor, the capital went north to Beijing, though Nanjing remained the southern capital. In the late Ming, Jiangnan was still a major trading area, and some historians see signs of incipient industrialisation and capitalism in its thriving textile industry, a trend that was cut short.
The Qing changed Nanzhili into "Jiangnan province", and in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui became separate provinces. Jiangsu's borders have changed little since.

From the 1840s, as Western powers pressed into China, the wealthy trading region of the Yangtze River Delta came under growing outside influence. Shanghai, formerly an insignificant small town in Jiangsu, turned quickly into a cosmopolitan metropolis of trade and banking and was later made a separate municipality. Jiangnan was a major theatre of the Taiping Rebellion of 1851 to 1864, a vast and deadly revolt that aimed at a Christian theocracy. Starting far off in Guangdong, it moved through much of South China and by 1853 had established Nanjing as its capital, renamed Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was founded in 1912 and warlords soon tore the country apart, with Jiangsu changing hands several times. In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek established a government in Nanjing and before long controlled most of the country. The provincial administration relocated to Zhenjiang in 1928. This phase ended when the second Sino-Japanese War started on a full scale in 1937. Nanjing fell on 13 December 1937, and the atrocities of the following three months are known as the Rape of Nanjing. The city then became the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government of East China, and most of Jiangsu was under Japanese occupation until 1945.

Nanjing once more served as capital of the Republic of China when the war ended, but fighting between the Kuomintang government and Communist forces, who were mainly located in the north-east, soon turned into civil war. In northern Jiangsu the Huaihai Campaign, the decisive battle, ended with a Kuomintang defeat, and it was not long before Communist armies crossed the Yangtze and entered Nanjing. The Kuomintang retreated south and ended up in Taipei, from where the Republic of China government still administers Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands, while technically still claiming Nanjing as its rightful capital. After Zhenjiang fell, the provincial government was moved to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

Once the Communists took over, Beijing (formerly Peiping) became the capital of the People's Republic and Jiangsu was dissolved into the Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. On 15 November 1952 Jiangsu Province was re-established, with Nanjing demoted to provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up first focused on China's south coast, in Guangdong, which left Jiangsu behind, and from the 1990s it was applied more evenly. Suzhou and Wuxi, two southern Jiangsu cities next to Shanghai, have since become especially prosperous, ranking in China's top 10 by GDP and passing the provincial capital Nanjing, though the income gap between northern and southern Jiangsu stays large.

Jiangsu is flat, low-lying and densely populated, so it is one of the Chinese regions most vulnerable to climate change and rising seas. Between 1961 and 2007, observations by the Center of Climate Change in Jiangsu found that average temperature rose by 0.16 to 0.45 °C per decade, while precipitation shifted by anything from −28.7 to 37.09 mm per decade. Severe weather has intensified and happens more often. Farming, ecosystems, water supplies, transport links and the coast are all hurt, and the speed of sea level rise is far above the global average.

In early 2023 the Cross Dependency Initiative (XDI) published a climate-risk ranking of the world's regions in which Jiangsu came out as the most vulnerable, because so much industry, trade, housing and commercial property is concentrated there. The 14th five-year plan, endorsed by the National People's Congress in 2021, outlines a low-carbon transition nationally. At provincial level, Jiangsu's government aims under its own 14th plan to lower carbon dioxide output per unit of GDP by 18% and to accelerate a green, low-carbon economy. It also plans to restore damaged coastal areas such as Lianyugang and Yancheng, and to build seawalls and river floodgates to withstand rising seas.
The Han Chinese are the majority, and Hui and Manchu communities are among the minorities. Cities were home to 73.94 percent of the province's population in 2021, and rural areas to 26.06 percent.
The 2021 indicators were as follows. The birth rate was 5.65 per 1000 and the death rate 6.77 per 1000. There were 103.05 men for every 100 women, and the literacy rate was 96.94%.

Folk religion, Taoism and Chinese Buddhism predominate. Based on surveys carried out in 2007 and 2009, 16.67% of residents take part in ancestor worship and 2.64% identify as Christian. The surveys did not report on other religions, so the remaining 80.69% could be non-religious, or could follow nature deities, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, folk sects or minority faiths such as Islam. Muslims in Jiangsu numbered 130,757 in 2010.

Professional teams play in several leagues. Football clubs include Suzhou Dongwu F.C., Nantong Zhiyun F.C. and Nanjing City F.C. in the China League One, and Wuxi Wugo F.C. in China League Two. Basketball in the Chinese Basketball Association has the Jiangsu Dragons and the Nanjing Monkey King. In the Chinese Volleyball League there are the Jiangsu Zenith Steel, and baseball's China Baseball League has the Jiangsu Pegasus.

jiangxi-agricultural-university.h: Jiangxi Agricultural University at a glance

blocks.x: Jiangxi Agricultural University (JXAU; 江西农业大学, Jiāngxī Nóngyè Dàxué) can be found in the northern suburbs of Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi province. It is a key university run by the province, and among Chinese universities it was an early one, in the first group allowed to award bachelor's and master's degrees.

Seventeen colleges teach 60 academic majors. JXAU presents itself as a high-level agricultural university with distinctive character. Its strengths lie in agriculture, with a focus on biotechnology and development that is coordinated across many disciplines.

The earliest roots of JXAU go back to 1905, when Jiangxi Industrial School was set up. It is regarded as the first institution for agricultural education in Jiangxi. In 1908 the school took the name Jiangxi Higher Agricultural School, and after that it passed through a series of reorganisations and mergers. The key dates are:
1905: Jiangxi Industrial School is founded.
1908: it becomes Jiangxi Higher Agricultural School.
1940: degree-level teaching starts in earnest with National Chung Cheng University College of Agriculture, whose first principal was the botanist Hu Xiansu.
1949: the college is renamed Nanchang University College of Agriculture.

1952: agricultural and veterinary departments from Nanchang University, veterinary schools in the province, and institutions from Henan, Hunan and Guangxi are combined to make Jiangxi Agricultural College.
1958: the Jiangxi Communist Labor University Headquarters is established.
1968: it is renamed Jiangxi Communist Labor University.
1969: it is merged with Jiangxi Communist Labor University. The records for 1968 and 1969 overlap and appear inconsistent, so the university's own account of this period is the better reference.
November 1980: it takes its current name, Jiangxi Agricultural University.
Most of a JXAU student's free time is spent in Nanchang, so this part of the guide covers its position, seasons, people, economy, transport links and sights.

Nanchang sits well inland in southeastern China. The Yangtze is 130 km (81 mi) to the north. On the Gan River's right bank, the city is placed just below the point where the Jin River flows in, and from there the Gan carries on for roughly 40 km (25 mi) to the northeast before reaching Poyang Lake.
Under the Köppen system, Nanchang is humid subtropical (Cfa), and each season is distinct.
Winters are cool and brief, with the odd frost. They open fairly dry and sunny, but gradually turn damper and cloudier.
Spring starts out gloomy. From April through June, monthly rainfall tops 220 mm (8.7 in).
Summers drag on and are humid, with some of the highest temperatures among Chinese provincial capitals. Sunshine is greatest in July and August, when the sun shines for nearly 60 percent of daylight.
Autumn is mild to warm, and it is the driest part of the year.

Averaging temperatures over 24 hours gives 5.9 °C in January and 29.6 °C in July (42.6 °F and 85.3 °F). The mean for the year is 18.5 °C, or 65.3 °F. Rainfall and snow add up to around 1,704 mm (67 in). Sunshine as a share of the possible total runs from 27 percent in March up to 56 percent in August, and across the year the city gets an average of 1,809 hours. The coldest day recorded since 1951 was 29 December 1991 at -9.7 °C (15 °F), while on 23 July 1961 the thermometer climbed to a record 40.6 °C (105 °F).

Nanchang had 6,255,007 residents at the time of the 2020 Chinese census. Within that total, 5,382,162 people live in the built-up area, made up of 6 urban districts and Nanchang County, which is mostly urbanised too. Thirty-seven ethnic groups were counted across its divisions, but 99.2% are Han Chinese. The sex ratio is roughly 109 males per 100 females, and people aged above 60 make up 14.97% of the population.

The city is an agricultural centre for Jiangxi province. Grain production reached 16.146 million tons in 2000, and rice and oranges are the staples. Ford Motor Company operates a plant where the Ford Transit van is assembled under the Jiangling Motor joint venture. The industrial base is broad, covering aircraft and automobile manufacturing, metallurgy, electro-mechanics, textiles, chemical engineering, pharmaceuticals and traditional Chinese medicine, plus others. The city has grown rapidly and is placed 15th among the 20 fastest growing cities on the planet. It is seen as a place with some of the greatest potential for future development both in China and worldwide.

The 2017 gross regional product (GDP) of the city reached 500.319 billion yuan, equal to US$80.03 billion, which was 9.0% more than a year before. Primary industry contributed 19.213 billion yuan (growth of 4.0%). Secondary industry contributed 266.61 billion yuan (growth of 8.4%), and the third sector added 214.496 billion yuan (growth of 10.2%). GDP per person stood at 81,598 yuan, which converts to 12,285 US dollars using the average exchange rate of that year. Fiscal revenue for the year totalled 78.282 billion yuan, a rise of 14.3% on the previous year.

Ten years earlier the picture was much smaller. GDP in 2008 had been just 166 billion yuan (US$24.3 billion) and GDP per capita 36,105 yuan (US$5,285). Foreign trade, imports and exports combined, was worth 3.4 billion US dollars, and financial revenue added up to 23 billion yuan.
The city's development areas fall into three levels.
At national level there are three:

The Nanchang Export Processing Zone lies within the Nanchang Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. The State Council gave approval on 8 May 2006, and acceptance inspection was passed on 7 September 2007. Of a planning area of 1 km2, 0.31 km2 has been developed. Customs procedures are quick and convenient, and both this zone and the hi-tech zone (NCHDZ) enjoy special preferential policies.

The Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone (NCHDZ) began in March 1991 and is the only high-tech zone of national grade in Jiangxi. Of its 231 km2 (89 sq mi) area, 32 km2 (12 sq mi) is complete. It has natural conditions and an industrial foundation that suit electronics. On just 0.4 percent of the city's land, it brings in 25 percent of the industrial added value and 50 percent of industrial benefit and tax.
The Nanchang Economic and Technological Development Zone is the third.

At provincial level are the Nanchang Yingxiong and Jiangxi Shanghai economic and technological development zones. The city also has two special economic districts, Honggutan New District and Ganjiang New District.

Nanchang is well placed. A local saying, three rivers and five lakes, praises its surroundings. High-speed rail and air hubs tie it to three major economic circles, namely the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the cross-province corridors that serve Haixi. For China it is a comprehensive transport hub, and within Jiangxi it is the most important integrated one.

Several main lines converge in Nanchang: the Beijing-Kowloon (Jingjiu) Railway, the Shanghai-Kunming line (once called the Zhejiang-Jiangxi or Zhegan Railway), the Xiangtang-Putian line and the intercity railway to Jiujiang, which makes the city a key rail centre for southeastern China. Jiangxi and neighbouring Fujian have most of their network run by Nanchang's Bureau of Railways. The two main passenger stations are Nanchang station and Nanchang West station. CRH (China Railway High-speed) services run to Hangzhou, Changsha and Shanghai.

Opened in 1996, Nanchang Changbei International Airport (KHN) is the principal international airport. The site is in Lehua Town, around 26 kilometres to the north of the CDB area. No other airport in Jiangxi has an international route, and none is larger. Destinations on the mainland include Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Haikou. A joint military and civilian airfield also exists near Liantang, in Nanchang County.

Passenger numbers have jumped. By 2014 the airport served up to 10 international destinations and handled 7.25 million passengers, 6.3% more than the year before. A segment of that traffic, the Nanchang aviation port, passed 280,000 passengers with growth of nearly 40%, and it is regarded as an important driver of expansion that should keep up its rapid development. The annual throughput passed 10 million on 6 December 2017, making Nanchang the 31st million-grade airport in the nation. Over the whole of 2017 it handled 10.93 million passengers, 39.0% up on the previous year and an addition of 3.07 million. There were 89,000 take-offs and landings (up 35.2%), and cargo and mail amounted to 52,000 tons (up 3.3%). Big expansion and upgrading work has been going on recently so that the airport fits the Beijing-Kowloon high-speed railway and the Nanchang North Station air-rail transport hub.

Nanchang has plenty of roads. National routes include No. 105 (Beijing to Zhuhai), No. 320 (Shanghai to Kunming) and No. 316 (Fuzhou to Lanzhou). Expressway G70 passes through, and a ring expressway around the city, G70_01, was opened in 2007. Operators include the Xufang Bus Station, the Nanchang Long-distance Bus Station and the Chang'an Transport Company Limited. Coaches to places beyond Jiangxi, including Nanjing, Shenzhen and Hefei, depart from the long-distance station, while Xufang handles cities, towns and counties within the province.

Jiangxi's first urban rail system is Nanchang Rail Transit, which has carried passengers since 26 December 2015, making Nanchang the 25th mainland city to get a metro. The project was first planned in 1999 and officially started in 2009. Lines 1 and 2 together make up a first phase 50.996 kilometers in length, with Line 1 running underground. Line 1 was formally opened at the close of 2015, and Line 2's first section went into trial operation on 19 August 2017.

Water is everywhere around Nanchang, from the Fu River and the Gan River to Aixi Lake, Qingshan Lake and Elephant Lake. Shipping and trade by water are therefore central to the economy. Nanchang Port ranks as the largest port on the Gan River. From it, passengers can travel by boat to Jinggang Shan and Tengwang Pavilion, or on passenger ships to Poyang Lake and attractions such as Stone Bell Hill, Dagu Hill and the Poyang Lake Bird Protection Area.
Tengwang Pavilion is a towering structure dating back to the year 653, on the Gan River's east bank, and counted among the Four Great Towers of China.
Poyang Lake is the largest freshwater lake in China and is also known as the Migrator Birds Paradise.
The Star of Nanchang in Honggutan District held the title of the world's tallest Ferris wheel between 2006 and 2008.
Qiushui Square opened on 28 January 2004, and its group of music fountains is the largest in Asia.
The Jiangxi Provincial Museum shares a site with the Bada Shanren Exhibition Hall.
People's Park is downtown Nanchang's biggest park.

Bayi Square and Memorial in the centre of town marks the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 (Ba Yi is Mandarin for eight-one), which founded the People's Liberation Army and ultimately led to the People's Republic of China in 1949.
Bada Shanren Memorial Hall is a big artistic museum that combines sculpture with a general art museum.

For its research output, Nanchang appears on the Nature Index among the world's top 100 cities. These colleges and universities offer full-time bachelor programmes (institutions without such programmes are not listed):
Nanchang University (南昌大学)
Jiangxi Normal University (江西师范大学)
Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics (江西财经大学)
Nanchang Hangkong University (南昌航空大学)
East China Jiaotong University (华东交通大学)
East China University of Technology, Nanchang Campus (东华理工大学)
Nanchang Institute of Technology (南昌工程学院)
Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University (江西科技师范学院)
Jiangxi Manufacturing and Vocational College (江西制造职业技术学院)
Jiangxi Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医学院)
Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医药大学)
Jiangxi Agricultural University (江西农业大学)

Secondary schools in the city include the Nanchang Foreign Language School (南昌市外国语学校) and a high school attached to Jiangxi University of Technology (江西科技学院附属中学), and Nanchang International School (南昌国际学校) caters to international families.
Life as a student is affected by the surrounding province nearly as much as by the campus, and this section covers Jiangxi's history and economy.

Jiangxi is built around the Gan River valley, historically south China's chief north-south route for transport. The corridor beside the Gan was one of few routes that could be travelled easily through otherwise rugged mountains in the southeast. It carried trade and communication between the North China Plain and Yangtze valley and what is now Guangdong. This explains why Jiangxi was strategically significant for so long.

jiangxi-agricultural-university.h: From ancient kingdoms to Han commanderies

blocks.x: In the Shang dynasty period (16th to 11th centuries BC) Jiangxi lay beyond the reach of early Chinese civilization, and it was probably inhabited by the peoples known together as the Baiyue. Wu was a state in the Spring and Autumn period, and the north of Jiangxi was its western edge. In 473 BC Wu was defeated by Yue, a power based in what is now northern Zhejiang, and then Chu (from modern Hubei) took northern Jiangxi; Yue may have exerted some influence in the south. Chu overcame Yue in 333 BC, and Qin's conquest of Chu in 223 BC placed most of Jiangxi under Jiujiang Commandery, seated at Shouchun (壽春). That commandery did not work well and disappeared quickly as Qin collapsed.

Early in the Han dynasty, possibly before Xiang Yu's death in 202 BC, Yuzhang Commandery (豫章, Gan: Ì-zong) was created, the first in Jiangxi by any Chinese dynasty. The name came from the Yuzhang River (豫章江, Gan: Ì-zong Kong), as the Gan River was originally called, and this is why Gan is the province's short name. Eight counties were added in 201 to the seven Qin had set up, and three more were added in later years. Across most of the Han period, eighteen counties made up the commandery and took in most of today's province. Nanchang, Gan, Yudu and Luling were among the county seats, located where major cities stand now, though some other counties were relocated or abolished afterwards.

Emperor Wu of Han placed Yuzhang Commandery in Yangzhou Province, part of the broader creation of provinces (zhou) across China. In 291 AD, under the Western Jin, Jiangxi turned into a zhou of its own, Jiangzhou (江州, Gan: Kong-chiu). It stayed in the hands of the southern dynasties through the Southern and Northern Dynasties, and the number of zhou rose gradually. The Sui dynasty counted seven commanderies and twenty-four counties, and the Tang added a commandery and fourteen counties. Later the commanderies were dropped and turned into zhou, which are called prefectures in English rather than provinces.

The Tang also brought in circuits as a top-level division. At first Jiangxi was in the Jiangnan Circuit (the circuit south of the Yangtze). When this was split into two halves in 733, Jiangxi fell in the western one, the Jiangnanxi Circuit (western circuits south of the Yangtze), and that is the origin of the name Jiangxi.

After the Tang collapsed in 907, China entered the era of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. First Wu (吳, Gan: Ng) ruled Jiangxi and then Southern Tang (南唐, Gan: Nām-thóng), both centred on modern Nanjing, farther down the Yangtze. When the Ten Kingdoms were gone, the Jiangnanxi Circuit was restored with nine prefectures and four army districts, sixty-eight districts in all. It was divided later into thirteen circuits, and Jiangxi Province appeared for the first time, with most of present-day Guangdong included. More or less, Jiangxi had by then taken on its present borders.

Once the Qing regime had fallen, Jiangxi was among the first bases of the Communists, who enlisted many peasants for the growing people's revolution. The Nanchang Uprising broke out in Jiangxi on 1 August 1927, a key event of the Chinese Civil War. Afterwards the Communist leadership sheltered in southern and western mountains of the province to escape the Kuomintang's drive to destroy it. A government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was founded in Ruijin in 1931. Ruijin is sometimes known as the Former Red Capital (红色故都, Gan: Fūng-set Kū-tu) or simply the Red Capital. In 1935, completely surrounded by Nationalist forces, the Communists fought their way out and started the Long March to Yan'an.

Five military campaigns were mounted by the National Government against the Jiangxi Soviet area from 1930 to 1934. The ferocity of the fighting between the two parties, with purges inside the Red Army and in the post-war government, killed or drove off a huge number of people. Jiangxi's population dropped by 40%, and only 13.8 million remained in 1936.

Transport changed too. The Yuehan Railway opened in Hunan in 1936, and Jiangxi lost the key position it had on north-south routes. When the east-west Zhegan Railway entered service in 1937, it altered existing traffic patterns in the province to a large extent, and the importance of Jiujiang Port (九江港) began to fall.

In World War II, after the Doolittle Raid, locals in Jiangxi helped most of the American B-25 crews that came down in China to get to safety. They paid heavily for it. To scare the Chinese out of helping downed American airmen, the Imperial Japanese Army began the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign. At least 10,000 civilians in Jiangxi died while searching for Doolittle's men.

The Chinese Communist Party took full control of Jiangxi when the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949. That same year the provincial government of the Republic of China was evacuated to Taichung in Taiwan Province, and then dissolved itself.

Under the Third Front campaign, Jiangxi was among the main places receiving industrial investment. Its dominant crop is rice, and cotton and rapeseed are commonly grown as cash crops. Jiangxi produces more kumquats than any other province in China, especially around Suichuan County.

Mining is a big part of the provincial economy. Rich in mineral resources, the province is first in China for deposits of tungsten, copper, gold, silver, uranium, thorium, tantalum, niobium and more. Dexing is a notable mining centre for copper and Dayu County for tungsten.

The province lies right next to some of the wealthiest in China, namely Guangdong, Zhejiang and Fujian, which are sometimes accused of taking talent and capital away from it. Wages in Jiangxi are the lowest nationally and property prices the third lowest. For 2016 the nominal GDP was CNY 1.84 trillion (US$276.48 billion), or CNY 40,400 (US$6,082) per head.
