International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

jiangxi-agricultural-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jiangxi Agricultural University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanchang, register at Jiangxi Agricultural University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Jiangxi Normal University, known as JXNU (江西师范大学), is in Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi Province. As the name suggests, it has a strong teacher-training tradition, but its degrees range much wider: literature, history, philosophy, economics, management and law, plus natural science, engineering, education and the arts, are all on offer. It is run with joint backing from the Ministry of Education and the provincial government of Jiangxi, and it is included in the national Midwest University Fundamental Capacity Building Project. The province treats it as a key local university with priority for development, and it has real weight in Jiangxi's political, economic, cultural and social life.

Inside the university there are 22 colleges, plus one independent college, the College of Science and Technology. Teaching is spread over two campuses, Yaohu Lake and Qingshan Lake, which together cover 233 hectares. The library holds 3.04 million printed volumes and 3 million e-books. In the Best Chinese Universities Ranking, JXNU is placed 125th.
The idea behind the university came from the White Deer Grotto Academy on Mount Lu near Jiujiang, and its first head was Hu Xiansu. The institution has changed names several times:
1940: founded as National Chung Cheng University
1949: renamed National Nanchang University
1953: became Jiangxi Teachers College
1983: took the name Jiangxi Normal University
2003: merged with the Jiangxi Worker's University of Finance, also called the Jiangxi Banking School

The motto is "Ponder Prudently and Practice Earnestly, Be Impartial and Upright". The school tradition stresses unity and diligence, and a search for truth that leads to innovation ("Be United and Diligent, Seek Truth and Make Innovations"). The development philosophy is to build the university on quality, talent, innovation, culture and harmony. The school spirit combines patriotism and pride in the university, democracy and harmony, realism and pragmatism, and open-mindedness with innovation.

Research and teaching are organised around five postdoctoral workstations. Doctoral study covers 9 first-level disciplines and 63 second-level disciplines. At master's level there are 30 first-level disciplines and 16 professional master's programmes, and undergraduates choose from 87 bachelor's programmes. Chemistry is one of the subjects that the ESI database places in the world's top 1 per cent.

Payroll staff exceed 2,600 in total, counting teachers and administrators. More than 1,700 are full-time teachers, and over 700 hold doctorates. Of the faculty, 22.16 per cent are 35 or younger, 53.73 per cent hold senior academic rank, and 84.67 per cent have a master's degree or higher.

Links of friendship connect JXNU with more than 60 universities, spread over 17 countries or regions. Agreements on mutual credit recognition, or on exchanging staff and students, have been signed with 28 overseas universities. About twelve research teams or institutes, at home and abroad, cooperate with it on key laboratories. It operates two Confucius Institutes; the one at the University of Antananarivo in Madagascar has won the title of "Model Confucius Institute". More than 30 foreign teachers work on campus.

For overseas applicants, scholarships matter. Three scholarships can be held here: the Chinese Government Scholarship, the Confucius Institute Scholarship and the scholarship of the Jiangxi provincial government. The university adds a scholarship of its own. More than 400 international students, drawn from over 40 countries, study here every year, so you would not be the only newcomer.
In a Chinese alumni network ranking of universities by outstanding politician alumni, JXNU comes 78th. In the same network's ranking by billionaire alumni it is 126th.

Over seventy years the university has produced more than 300,000 graduates, many of whom are now mainstays of their fields. The impact on the province's schools is especially large. About 50 per cent of Jiangxi's "super rank" primary and secondary teachers, over 60 per cent of its core teachers, and above 80 per cent of the super-rank senior middle school teachers are JXNU alumni. Others have become professionals, entrepreneurs and statesmen.
Everyday life depends on the city around the campus, so the next sections turn to Nanchang: where it is, what the weather does, how the economy works, how to travel, and what to see.

Nanchang lies inland in the southeast of China, 130 km (81 mi) from the Yangtze, to the south. The city is built along the Gan River's right bank, a little below the Jin River's confluence, and about 40 km (25 mi) southwest of where the Gan flows out into Poyang Lake.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), and all four seasons are distinct. Winter is brief and cool, with the odd frost; it begins fairly sunny and dry and grows wetter and greyer. Spring starts gloomily, and April, May and June each bring over 220 mm of rain (8.7 in). Summer lasts long and is humid, with some of the highest temperatures of any provincial capital in China. July and August are the sunniest months, with sunshine close to 60 per cent of the time. Autumn is warm to mild and has the lowest rainfall of the year.

Temperatures average 5.9 °C in January (42.6 °F) and 29.6 °C in July (85.3 °F), with 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) as the mean for the year. About 1,704 mm (67 in) of precipitation falls annually. Possible sunshine goes from 27 per cent in March up to 56 per cent in August, which totals an average 1,809 sunshine hours a year. Since 1951 the coldest reading was -9.7 °C (15 °F), on 29 December 1991, and the hottest 40.6 °C (105 °F), on 23 July 1961. Plan for hot, sticky summers and for a damp spring.

At the 2020 census Nanchang had 6,255,007 residents, and 5,382,162 of them lived in the built-up area, which takes in 6 urban districts and Nanchang County, most of which is now urbanised. The prefecture contains 37 ethnic groups, but 99.2 per cent are Han Chinese. There are roughly 109 men for every 100 women, and the share of people over 60 is 14.97 per cent.

Nanchang is a regional centre for the agriculture of Jiangxi, with a grain harvest of 16.146 million tons in 2000. Staples of the local economy include rice and oranges. Ford has a factory in the city where the Transit van is assembled, as part of the Jiangling Motor joint venture. Local industry also includes aircraft and automobile manufacturing, metallurgy, electro-mechanics, textiles, chemical engineering, traditional Chinese medicine and pharmaceuticals, among other things. The city describes its growth as rapid, ranking 15th among the 20 fastest growing cities in the world, and it is considered among the cities with the greatest future potential in China and the world.

For 2017 the city's gross regional product stood at 500.319 billion yuan, or US$80.03 billion, a rise of 9.0 per cent on 2016. The primary sector added 19.213 billion yuan (up 4.0 per cent), the secondary sector added 266.61 billion (up 8.4 per cent), and the third sector, services, added 214.496 billion (up 10.2 per cent). GDP per head was 81,598 yuan, or 12,285 US dollars at the year's average exchange rate. Total fiscal revenue reached 78.282 billion yuan, which was 14.3 per cent higher than in 2016.

For comparison, in 2008 GDP was 166 billion yuan (US$24.3 billion), and per-head GDP was 36,105 yuan (US$5,285). Trade in imports and exports was worth 3.4 billion US dollars, and financial revenue added up to 23 billion yuan in total.
Nanchang's industrial planning is split between national-level zones, provincial-level zones and a special economic district.
National level: the Nanchang Export Processing Zone, the Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone, and the Nanchang Economic and Technological Development Zone.

Provincial level: two zones, one named after Shanghai (the Jiangxi Shanghai Economic and Technological Development Zone) and the Yingxiong one (Nanchang Yingxiong Economic and Technological Development Zone).
Special economic district: Honggutan New District and Ganjiang New District.

The export processing zone lies inside the Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. The State Council approved it on 8 May 2006, and it passed the national acceptance inspection on 7 September 2007. It was planned at 1 km2 and so far 0.31 km2 has been built. Customs clearance is simple and convenient, and there are special preferential policies for both the processing zone and the high-tech zone.

The High-tech Industrial Development Zone (NCHDZ) is the only national-level high-tech zone in Jiangxi and was set up in March 1991. It has 231 km2 (89 sq mi), of which 32 km2 (12 sq mi) is finished. Its natural conditions and industrial base suit the electronics industry. Using just 0.4 per cent of the city's land, it has delivered 25 per cent of Nanchang's industrial added value and 50 per cent of industrial profit and tax.

Nanchang's location is favourable and its transport is convenient. Local sayings describe it with the phrase "three rivers and five lakes", and refer to its control of the better lakes. Through high-speed rail and air hubs it connects three major economic circles: the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the inter-provincial corridors of the Haixi area. It counts as one of the country's comprehensive transport hubs and an important one within Jiangxi.

Nanchang is a big rail hub for southeastern China. The Beijing-Kowloon (Jingjiu) Railway, the Shanghai-Kunming railway (once the Zhejiang-Jiangxi or Zhegan Railway), the Xiangtang-Putian railway and the Nanchang-Jiujiang intercity railway all meet here, and the Nanchang Bureau of Railways runs much of the network in Jiangxi and neighbouring Fujian.
The two main passenger stations are Nanchang station and Nanchang West station. CRH (China Railway High-speed) services connect the city to Hangzhou, Changsha and Shanghai.

Changbei International Airport (KHN), opened in 1996, is the principal airport. You will find it at Lehua Town, 26 kilometres to the north of the CBD area. Jiangxi has no other airport with an international route. Domestic links include Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Haikou, Shanghai and Beijing. A separate military and civilian airfield is near Liantang in Nanchang County.

Changbei is also Jiangxi's largest airport. By 2014 it served up to 10 international destinations, and it handled 7.25 million passengers that year, up 6.3 per cent. One passenger segment passed 280,000, growing by nearly 40 per cent, and is cited as an important engine of growth. On 6 December 2017 annual throughput went above 10 million, making it the 31st "million-grade airport" in China. For the full year 2017 throughput hit 10.93 million, up 39.0 per cent, a gain of 3.07 million passengers. Flights numbered 89,000, up 35.2 per cent, and cargo and mail came to 52,000 tons, up 3.3 per cent. To match the Beijing-Kowloon high-speed railway and a planned airport complex hub at Nanchang North Station, big expansion and upgrade work has been under way recently.

Road infrastructure is extensive. National roads running through the city include No. 105 (Beijing to Zhuhai), No. 320 (Shanghai to Kunming) and No. 316 (Fuzhou to Lanzhou). National Highway G70 also passes through, and a ring road, G70_01, opened in 2007. Chang'an Transport Company Limited, Nanchang Long-distance Bus Station and Xufang Bus Station are the principal transport operators.
The Long-distance Bus Station runs routes to places outside Jiangxi, such as Nanjing, Shenzhen and Hefei, while Xufang Bus Station handles cities, towns and counties inside the province.

Nanchang Rail Transit, in service since 26 December 2015, is the first urban rail system in Jiangxi and made Nanchang the 25th mainland city with a metro. Planning began in 1999, and construction officially began in 2009. The first phase of Lines 1 and 2 totals roughly 51 km (the printed figure is awkward, so confirm this locally); Line 1 is underground. Line 1 opened formally at the end of 2015, and the first section of Line 2 began trial operation on 19 August 2017.

Water routes matter greatly to trade, shipping and the economy, because the city is bounded by the Gan and Fu rivers and by Elephant, Qingshan and Aixi lakes. Nanchang Port is the biggest on the Gan. Passenger boats from the port go to Jinggang Shan and Tengwang Pavilion; others sail to Stone Bell Hill, Dagu Hill, the Poyang Lake bird reserve and the lake itself.
Tengwang Pavilion: a towering pavilion from 653 on the Gan River's east bank, counted among "the Four Great Towers of China".
Poyang Lake: China's largest freshwater lake, nicknamed "the Migrator Birds Paradise".
Star of Nanchang: a Ferris wheel in Honggutan District that was the tallest in the world between 2006 and 2008.
Qiushui Square: opened on 28 January 2004, with the biggest group of music fountains in Asia.
Jiangxi Provincial Museum and the Bada Shanren Exhibition Hall.
People's Park, downtown Nanchang's biggest park.

Bayi Square and Memorial: in the city centre, it commemorates the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 (Ba Yi means "eight-one" in Mandarin), when the People's Liberation Army was founded. The story is linked to the People's Republic that emerged in 1949.
Bada Shanren Memorial Hall: a large artistic museum with sculpture and a general art museum.

Nanchang appears in the Nature Index among the world's top 100 cities by scientific research output, so you will find plenty of academic neighbours. Institutions without full-time bachelor programmes are left out of this list.

Among the comprehensive and specialist institutions with full-time bachelor programmes, Nanchang University and Jiangxi Normal University are the best known general universities. Business and economics are covered by Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics. For aviation, transport and engineering there are Nanchang Hangkong University, East China Jiaotong University and Nanchang Institute of Technology. East China University of Technology has a Nanchang campus too. Jiangxi Agricultural University serves farming and rural subjects, and two further institutions focus on medicine: the Jiangxi Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Rounding out the list are the Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University and the Jiangxi Manufacturing and Vocational College. The Chinese names of the main ones are 南昌大学, 江西师范大学 and 江西财经大学.

For younger students, options include the Nanchang Foreign Language School, the Jiangxi University of Technology High School and Nanchang International School. This is relevant if you plan to bring children.
Life in a university town also depends on its province. The sections below describe Jiangxi.

The province centres on the Gan River valley, historically south China's main north-south route. Across the otherwise rugged southeastern mountains, the Gan corridor is one of the few easy ways through. It carried traffic and trade between the Yangtze valley and North China Plain on one side and modern Guangdong on the other, which is why Jiangxi mattered strategically for so much of China's past.

Early Chinese civilisation did not reach Jiangxi in the Shang dynasty (16th to 11th centuries BC); the Baiyue peoples probably lived there. In the Spring and Autumn period, the northern part was the state of Wu's western border region. Yue, based in northern Zhejiang today, conquered Wu in 473 BC, after which Chu (centred on present-day Hubei) absorbed northern Jiangxi, while Yue may have had some influence further south. Then Chu subdued Yue, in 333 BC. When Qin overcame Chu in 223 BC, most of Jiangxi was recorded as falling under the Jiujiang Commandery, seated at Shouchun (壽春); it proved ineffective and ended not long after the fall of Qin.

At the start of the Han dynasty, perhaps before Xiang Yu's death in 202 BC, the Yuzhang Commandery (豫章) came into being; it was the first commandery a Chinese dynasty established in Jiangxi. Its name comes from the Yuzhang River (豫章江), the Gan River's former name, and "Gan" has become the province's short form. Eight counties were added in 201 to the seven inherited from Qin, and three more followed later, so through most of the Han period its eighteen counties covered much of today's Jiangxi. County seats such as Nanchang, Gan, Yudu and Luling stood where major cities are today, although other counties were later moved or abolished.

Emperor Wu of Han placed Yuzhang within Yangzhou Province, part of a drive to set up provinces (zhou) throughout the empire. Jiangxi became a zhou of its own in 291 AD, under the Western Jin, called Jiangzhou (江州). In the era of the Southern and Northern Dynasties it was ruled by the southern courts, and zhou slowly multiplied.

Under the Sui there were seven commanderies with twenty-four counties in Jiangxi; the Tang then added one more commandery and fourteen counties. Commanderies were abolished and turned into zhou, which are now rendered as "prefectures". A new top-level unit, the circuit, was a Tang invention. Jiangxi first sat in the Jiangnan Circuit, meaning "circuit south of the Yangtze". When this was divided into western and eastern halves in 733, Jiangxi was in the western half (Jiangnanxi Circuit), which is the origin of the name Jiangxi.

The Tang fell in 907, opening the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era. First Wu (吳) governed Jiangxi, followed by Southern Tang (南唐); both had their capitals in present-day Nanjing, further down the Yangtze. When the ten kingdoms ended, the Jiangnanxi Circuit was set up again with nine prefectures and four army districts, comprising sixty-eight districts. Later the territory was split into thirteen circuits and a Jiangxi Province appeared for the first time, then including most of modern Guangdong. Gradually the boundaries came close to today's.

When the Qing regime ended, Jiangxi turned into a very early Communist base, and many peasants joined the growing revolution. The Nanchang Uprising broke out there on 1 August 1927, during the Civil War. Afterwards the Communist leaders sheltered in the hills of the south and west to escape Kuomintang efforts to eradicate them. Ruijin saw the founding of the Chinese Soviet Republic's government in 1931; the town is sometimes nicknamed the "Former Red Capital" (红色故都), or just "Red Capital". Nationalist forces completely surrounded the Communists in 1935, but they broke out and set off on the Long March to Yan'an.

From 1930 to 1934 the National Government mounted five military campaigns against the Jiangxi Soviet area. The brutal fighting and purges (including internal purges of the Red Army and of the post-war government) caused many deaths or flights, and Jiangxi's population fell by 40 per cent, leaving only 13.8 million people in 1936.

In 1936 the Yuehan Railway opened in Hunan, and Jiangxi lost its key position in north-south traffic. The east-west Zhegan Railway opened in 1937 and substantially altered traffic patterns, and Jiujiang Port began to decline.

After the Doolittle Raid in the Second World War, most of the American B-25 crews who came down in China were helped to safety by Jiangxi locals, but the Gan people who helped them paid dearly. The Imperial Japanese Army started the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign to frighten Chinese from aiding downed American airmen, and in Jiangxi no fewer than 10,000 civilians died as people hunted for Doolittle's crews.

In 1949 the province came under full CCP control as the People's Republic was founded. The provincial government of the Republic moved out to Taichung, in Taiwan Province, and dissolved itself in the same year.

During the Third Front campaign Jiangxi was a big recipient of national investment in industrial capacity. Its dominant crop is rice, with cotton and rapeseed typical cash crops. Jiangxi is China's top producer of kumquats, especially in Suichuan County.

Mining is a major part of the economy. Mineral wealth is great: no province has more copper, tungsten, gold, silver, uranium, thorium, tantalum or niobium, among other deposits. Dexing is a noted copper centre and Dayu County a tungsten one.

Jiangxi lies very close to some of China's richest provinces, Guangdong, Zhejiang and Fujian, which are sometimes blamed for drawing talent and capital away. Wages here are the lowest in the country, and property prices the third lowest. Nominal GDP in 2016 was CNY 1.84 trillion (US$276.48 billion), which works out at CNY 40,400 (US$6,082) per person.
Jiangxi Normal University lists 198 programs for international students on this site: 73 bachelor, 108 master's, 14 doctoral, 3 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 189 taught in Chinese, 9 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 22,000 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

195 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (9):
Business Administration

Computer Science and Technology
Electronic Information Engineering
Environmental Geography Studies
Geography

Subject Teaching (English)

jiangxi-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jiangxi Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanchang, register at Jiangxi Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

jiangxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Jiangxi University of Chinese Medicine in brief

blocks.x: Located in Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi province in south-east China, Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医药大学) is a specialist medical university that comes under the Jiangxi provincial government. Its history begins in 1959, and its main focus is Chinese medicine and the subjects that go with it.

The university has several campuses that together cover 2,308 Chinese mu, or about 154 hectares. Published descriptions disagree on the exact number of campuses (some say four and some say two, naming Wanli and Yanming), and they also disagree on the number of students, so ask the university for current figures. International applicants are welcome to apply. Students have access to a library, housing and administrative services, among other academic and non-academic facilities.
The two campuses named most often are the following.
Wanli Campus
Yanming Campus

Programmes for international students follow two broad stages. A foundation stage comes first, with the basic medical sciences plus language and orientation courses. Hospital-based subjects follow in a clinical stage.
Anatomy and physiology
Biochemistry and pathology
Pharmacology
Community medicine
Microbiology
Forensic medicine and toxicology
Chinese language
An introduction to China
Medicine and surgery
Obstetrics and gynaecology
Paediatrics and orthopaedics
Psychiatry and anaesthesiology
Ophthalmology and otorhinolaryngology
Radiology and dermatology
Emergency medicine
Chinese, and medical Chinese

The Clinical College of Medicine offers a medicine programme to applicants in both science and arts categories, and the qualification awarded after five years is the MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery).

Training aims to give students grounding in the basic theory of medicine, basic and necessary medical knowledge, clinical medicine fundamentals, and training in humanities, science, education and professional clinical skills. Graduates should be able to use Chinese medicine for diagnosis and prevention, as well as for rehabilitation and community health services.

The core courses fall into two groups. The first group, the professional basics, takes in the basic theory of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), diagnostics, pharmacy and prescriptions. Students read the classics (the Nei Jing, the Treatise on Cold Damage and the Golden Chamber) and study febrile diseases and collation, alongside the modern sciences of anatomy, physiology, medical immunology and pathogen biology, pathology and pharmacology. The second group is clinical, and includes TCM internal medicine, surgery, gynaecology, ophthalmology, acupuncture and moxibustion, paediatrics, ENT and bone science, together with diagnostic science, internal medicine, surgery, emergency medicine, regional anatomy, bone and joint imaging, orthopaedic surgery, trauma first aid and chiropractic.

The integrated route has courses of its own. It repeats the professional basics (TCM theory, diagnostics, pharmacy, prescriptions, the classics, febrile diseases and collation, together with human anatomy, physiology, immunology, pathogen biology, pathology and pharmacology) and adds diagnostic fundamentals. After that come combined Chinese and Western medicine courses in gynaecology, ophthalmology, acupuncture, paediatrics, injury science, ENT and emergency medicine.

The university has more than 1,400 employees, not counting the Eastern Hospital. Its hospital has more than 1,600 beds. In June 2014 a new 26-storey medical complex with nearly 50,000 square metres of floor space went into use. Equipment includes a gem energy spectrum CT scanner, the first of its kind bought in the province, as well as 3.0T and 1.5T MRI machines, DR equipment, colour Doppler and many advanced ultrasound therapy devices.
Three hospitals are attached to the university.
The First Affiliated Hospital (第一附属医院)
The Second Affiliated Hospital (第二附属医院)
The Jiangxi Hospital of Heat-Sensitive Moxibustion

Over six decades the First Affiliated Hospital has become a comprehensive grade 3-A (tertiary) hospital, joining treatment to teaching, research, preventive care and rehabilitation, and acts as Jiangxi's centre for clinical care, teaching, research and health care. Its staff exceed 1300 full-time employees, and it runs 29 wards with 1600 beds and 56 clinical and technical departments, such as internal medicine, surgery, gynaecology and paediatrics. Special departments include Guo Yitang (a workshop for TCM doctors), the heat-sensitive moxibustion hospital and a department of special TCM therapy.

Its strengths in specific fields are recognised at several levels. There are 7 national key clinical disciplines, 12 key clinical disciplines and 8 key disciplines designated by the State Administration of TCM, and at provincial level 13 key disciplines and 2 top disciplines.

The Second Affiliated Hospital is in the east of Nanchang. Its origin was the 1958 hospital of a steel company in the city (Nanchang Steel Co., Ltd.), and it took its current name in May 2010. It is now a grade 2-A hospital that combines medical services with teaching, research, preventive care and community health care.
It has 270 employees and treats about 100,000 outpatients a year. To build a team of young, well-trained professionals, it has recently recruited over 40 new staff, most with master's degrees.

It operates more than 20 clinical departments. These include emergency, cardiology, neurology, gastroenterology, nephrology and respiratory medicine, general surgery, and orthopaedics and traumatology. Others are anorectal disease, neck, shoulder and lumbocrural pain (NSLP), gynaecology and obstetrics, paediatrics, acupuncture and rehabilitation, ophthalmology and otorhinolaryngology, and Guo Yitang. A community health care centre completes the list. Equipment includes SCT, DR, 4D colour ultrasound, haemodialysis machines, TCT and a chromosome image analysis system. Its signature TCM diagnosis and treatment is promoted in four areas (orthopaedics and traumatology, acupuncture and rehabilitation, anorectal diseases and NSLP), and a newer gynaecology and obstetrics department blends Western and traditional Chinese approaches. Its stated aim is to be a hospital the public is satisfied with, by offering good-quality care and community health advice.

The university's own journal is called the Journal of Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Its researchers have also published work in other areas, including studies on acupoint combinations and even a paper on operating system scheduling algorithms.

For a student, the city around the campus matters as much as the classroom: how the seasons feel, how to travel, and what there is to see. The sections below describe Nanchang, where the university is located.

The city lies inland in the south-east of China, some 130 km (81 mi) from the Yangtze River to its north. It is built on the Gan River's right bank, a little below the place where the Jin River merges with it, and roughly 40 km (25 mi) south-west of where the Gan empties into Poyang Lake.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), with four clearly different seasons. Winter is brief and cool, with the odd frost; it opens fairly bright and dry and turns progressively wetter and cloudier. Spring is gloomy from the outset, and April, May and June each get over 220 mm (8.7 in) of rain. The long humid summer is one of the hottest among Chinese provincial capitals, though July and August are also the sunniest months of the year, with sunshine nearly 60 percent of the time. Autumn is warm to mild and the driest season.

January averages 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) and July 29.6 °C (85.3 °F), with 18.5 °C (65.3 °F) as the mean for a whole year. Around 1,704 mm (67 in) of rain falls annually. In March only 27 percent of possible sunshine is received, against 56 percent in August, so the year's total is 1,809 hours. The record lows and highs since 1951 are -9.7 °C (15 °F) on 29 December 1991 and 40.6 °C (105 °F) on 23 July 1961. Expect to need an umbrella in spring and light, cool clothing in summer.

The 2020 Chinese census recorded a population of 6,255,007 in Nanchang, 5,382,162 of whom lived in the built-up area, which consists of six urban districts and Nanchang County, much of which is urbanised. Thirty-seven ethnic groups are counted in the city's divisions, though 99.2% are Han Chinese. There are about 109 men for every 100 women, and 14.97% of residents are over 60.

Nanchang is a regional hub for farm production in Jiangxi; its grain harvest was 16.146 million tons in 2000, and rice and oranges are staple products. There is a Ford Motor Company plant in the city, where the Ford Transit van is put together within the Jiangling Motor joint venture. Industry is concentrated in aircraft and car manufacturing, metallurgy, electro-mechanical goods, textiles, chemical engineering, traditional Chinese medicine and pharmaceuticals. The city is said to have grown fast enough to rank 15th among the world's 20 fastest-growing cities, and it is considered one of the places in China, and in the world, with the greatest development potential. That ranking dates from some years ago.

The city's gross regional product for 2017 came to 500.319 billion yuan (US$80.03 billion), which was 9.0% higher than a year earlier. Primary industry added 19.213 billion yuan (up 4.0%), secondary industry added 266.61 billion yuan (up 8.4%), and tertiary industry added 214.496 billion yuan (up 10.2%). GDP per person was 81,598 yuan, which is 12,285 US dollars at the average exchange rate for the year, and total fiscal revenue was 78.282 billion yuan, a rise of 14.3%.

For comparison, in 2008 the GDP was 166 billion yuan (US$24.3 billion), or 36,105 yuan (US$5,285) per person, with 3.4 billion US dollars of trade in imports and exports and 23 billion yuan in financial revenue.
#### Industrial zones
Nanchang's development areas are divided into national-level zones, provincial-level zones and special economic districts.
National-level zones:

Nanchang Export Processing Zone, in the Nanchang Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. The State Council approved it on 8 May 2006, and it passed national inspection on 7 September 2007. Its planned area is 1 km2, of which 0.31 km2 has been built. It offers simple customs clearance and special preferential policies, for both the zone itself and the Hi-Tech Zone.

The Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone (shortened to NCHDZ), set up in March 1991 and the one national-level high-tech zone in Jiangxi. It covers 231 km2 (89 sq mi), of which 32 km2 (12 sq mi) is complete. It has natural advantages and a sound base for the electronics industry. Although it uses only 0.4 percent of the city's land, it produces 25 percent of Nanchang's industrial added value and 50 percent of its industrial profit and tax.
Nanchang Economic and Technological Development Zone
Provincial-level zones:
The Jiangxi Shanghai zone and the Yingxiong zone, both economic and technological development zones
Special economic districts:
Honggutan New District and Ganjiang New District

Nanchang is well placed and well connected. A traditional saying praises it for its three rivers and five lakes. Using high-speed rail and its air hub, it links three major economic circles: the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the inter-provincial corridors of the Haixi area. It is one of China's comprehensive transport hubs and an important one within Jiangxi.

Nanchang is a major rail hub in south-eastern China. Four lines meet here: the Beijing-Kowloon (Jingjiu) Railway, the Shanghai-Kunming railway (formerly the Zhejiang-Jiangxi or Zhegan line), the Xiangtang-Putian railway and the Nanchang-Jiujiang intercity railway. Much of the rail network in Jiangxi, and in neighbouring Fujian too, is operated by the Nanchang Bureau of Railways.

Nanchang railway station and Nanchang West railway station are the city's two principal passenger stations. High-speed CRH (China Railway High-speed) trains connect Nanchang with Hangzhou, Changsha and Shanghai.

The principal airport is Nanchang Changbei International Airport (KHN), which dates from 1996. It sits in Lehua Town, 26 kilometres to the north of the central business district, and is the sole airport in Jiangxi with an international air route. Domestic flights serve Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Haikou, Shanghai and Beijing, among other cities. There is also a military and civilian airfield near Liantang in Nanchang County.

It is the largest airport in the province. In 2014 it opened up to 10 international destinations and handled 7.25 million passengers, a rise of 6.3%, with international traffic exceeding 280,000 passengers, close to 40% more, and driving much of the growth. On 6 December 2017 its annual passenger total went above 10 million, making it the 31st airport in the country to reach that level. For 2017 the total was 10.93 million, 39.0% more than the year before, an addition of 3.07 million passengers. Aircraft movements numbered 89,000, up 35.2%, and cargo and mail totalled 52,000 tons, up 3.3%. Major expansion and upgrading is under way, linked to the Beijing-Kowloon high-speed railway and the Nanchang North Station airport complex transport hub.

Roads are plentiful. Three national routes run through, linking Beijing and Zhuhai (No. 105), Shanghai and Kunming (No. 320), and Fuzhou and Lanzhou (No. 316). National Highway G70 passes through as well, and the G70_01 ring road around the city opened in 2007. The main operators are the Chang'an Transport Company Limited and two bus stations, Nanchang Long-distance and Xufang.

Coaches to cities outside Jiangxi, such as Nanjing, Shenzhen and Hefei, run from the Nanchang Long-distance Bus Station, while the Xufang Bus Station serves cities, towns and counties inside the province.

Nanchang Rail Transit, the first metro system in Jiangxi, has been running since 26 December 2015, making Nanchang the 25th city in mainland China with a metro. Planning began as early as 1999, and construction officially began in 2009. The first phase of Lines 1 and 2 totals roughly 51 kilometres, and Line 1 is underground. Line 1 opened at the end of 2015, and the first section of Line 2 began trial operation on 19 August 2017.

Rivers and lakes surround Nanchang: the Gan and Fu rivers and Elephant, Qingshan and Aixi lakes. Because of this, waterways are central to local trade, shipping and the economy. The biggest port on the Gan is Nanchang Port, from which boats reach Jinggang Shan and Tengwang Pavilion, and passenger ships also sail to Poyang Lake, Stone Bell Hill, the Poyang Lake bird reserve, Dagu Hill and other sights.
Several places stand out for visitors.
Tengwang Pavilion: a lofty pavilion on the Gan River's east bank that goes back to 653, and counts as one of the Four Great Towers of China
Poyang Lake: China's largest freshwater lake, nicknamed a paradise for migratory birds
The Star of Nanchang, in Honggutan District, which held the record as the tallest Ferris wheel in the world between 2006 and 2008
Qiushui Square: set up on 28 January 2004, with the biggest group of music fountains in Asia
Jiangxi Provincial Museum and the Bada Shanren Exhibition Hall
People's Park, the biggest park in downtown Nanchang

Two memorials deserve a note. Bayi Square and Memorial stands at the heart of the city. It commemorates the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 (Ba Yi in Mandarin means 1 August), when the People's Liberation Army was founded, a step on the road to the People's Republic in 1949. Bada Shanren Memorial Hall is a big museum and scenic site with sculpture and a general art museum.

Nanchang is a major centre of research and appears among the world's top 100 cities by scientific research output, as tracked by the Nature Index. Colleges and universities with Chinese names are given below, leaving out institutions that have no full-time bachelor programmes.
Nanchang University (南昌大学) and Jiangxi Normal University (江西师范大学)
Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics (江西财经大学), plus Jiangxi Agricultural University (江西农业大学)
Nanchang Hangkong University (南昌航空大学) and East China Jiaotong University (华东交通大学)
Nanchang Campus of East China University of Technology (东华理工大学)
Nanchang Institute of Technology (南昌工程学院)
Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University (江西科技师范学院)
Jiangxi Manufacturing and Vocational College (江西制造职业技术学院)

The university profiled here, Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医药大学), which some lists still give under its older name, Jiangxi Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医学院)

Younger students have a choice of high schools, among them Nanchang Foreign Language School (南昌市外国语学校) and the school attached to Jiangxi University of Technology (江西科技学院附属中学). Nanchang International School (南昌国际学校) is available for international families.

Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics (JUFE, 江西财经大学) is a coeducational public research university in Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi Province. It was founded in Nanchang in 1923. The Ministry of Finance of China has six affiliated business schools, and JUFE is one of them. Its teaching centres on business and management.

Two sets of results stand out. In the Best Chinese Universities Ranking for 2022, JUFE placed seventh nationwide among universities specialising in finance, business and economics, and second in East China, behind only Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. On the international stage, 2023 saw it listed among the world's top 500 universities for each of four subjects: Business, Economics, Finance and Management. In the overall Times Higher Education World University Rankings for 2023, it fell in the 1001-1200 band.
One notable graduate is Wang Wenjing, a billionaire businessman and the chairman of Yonyou.
Your daily routine will be tied to the city around the campus, so the next sections describe Nanchang's position, weather, population, economy, transport, sights and other universities.

Inland in southeastern China, Nanchang lies 130 km (81 mi) south of the Yangtze River. The city is on the Gan River's right bank, a little below where the Jin River joins it, and about 40 km (25 mi) southwest of the place where the Gan empties into Poyang Lake.
The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons.
Winter is short and cool, with occasional frosts. It begins fairly sunny and dry and gets progressively wetter and cloudier.
Spring starts out especially gloomy, and between April and June each month brings more than 220 mm (8.7 in) of rain.
Summer is long and humid, among the hottest of any Chinese provincial capital. The sunniest months are July and August, when sunshine fills nearly 60 percent of daylight hours.
Autumn is warm to mild and has the lowest rainfall of the year.

In numbers, the 24-hour average rises from 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) in January to a July figure of 29.6 °C (85.3 °F), and across the year the average is 18.5 °C (65.3 °F). Annual precipitation is about 1,704 mm (67 in). Monthly possible sunshine ranges between 27 percent in March and 56 percent in August, and the city gets an average of 1,809 hours of sunshine annually. Since 1951 the coldest day was 29 December 1991 at -9.7 °C (15 °F), and the hottest was 23 July 1961 at 40.6 °C (105 °F).

The 2020 Chinese census counted 6,255,007 people in Nanchang. Of these, 5,382,162 live in the built-up (urbanized) area, made up of 6 urban districts together with Nanchang County, which is largely urbanized. Thirty-seven ethnic groups were counted in its prefecture divisions, and 99.2% of residents are Han Chinese. There are about 109 men for every 100 women, and 14.97% of the population is aged above 60.

Nanchang is a regional hub for farming in Jiangxi, with a grain yield of 16.146 million tons in 2000, and rice and oranges are staples. Ford has a plant here, assembling the Ford Transit van within the Jiangling Motor joint venture. Industry covers aircraft and automobile manufacturing, metallurgy, electro-mechanics, textiles, chemical engineering, traditional Chinese medicine and pharmaceuticals, among other sectors. Nanchang's development has been rapid enough that it has ranked 15th among the fastest-growing 20 cities in the world, and it is considered one of the cities with the greatest potential for future growth in China and the world.

In 2017 Nanchang's gross regional product (GDP) grew 9.0% to 500.319 billion yuan (US$80.03 billion). By sector, primary industry added 19.213 billion yuan (up 4.0%), secondary industry 266.61 billion yuan (up 8.4%), and the third, with 214.496 billion yuan, rose 10.2%. Per capita GDP was 81,598 yuan, which converts to 12,285 US dollars at the average annual exchange rate. Total fiscal revenue was 78.282 billion yuan, up 14.3% on the previous year.

An earlier snapshot, 2008, shows how fast things have moved: GDP stood at 166 billion yuan (US$24.3 billion) and total financial revenue at 23 billion yuan; imports and exports were worth 3.4 billion US dollars in all, and per capita GDP came to 36,105 yuan (US$5,285).

Development zones come in three levels. The national ones are the Nanchang Export Processing Zone, the Nanchang Economic and Technological Development Zone, and the Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone (NCHDZ) is the only national-grade high-tech zone in Jiangxi and was set up in March 1991. It covers 231 km2 (89 sq mi), of which 32 km2 (12 sq mi) are completed. It has distinctive natural conditions and a solid industrial base for the electronics industry. On just 0.4 percent of the city's land, NCHDZ produces 25 percent of Nanchang's industrial added value and 50 percent of its industrial benefit and tax.

The Nanchang National Export Processing Zone sits inside NCHDZ. The State Council approved it on 8 May 2006, and it passed national acceptance inspection on 7 September 2007. Its planned area is 1 km2, of which 0.31 km2 has been built. Customs clearance is simple and convenient, and both the export zone and NCHDZ enjoy special preferential policies.

At provincial level the zones are the Jiangxi Shanghai Economic and Technological Development Zone and the Nanchang Yingxiong Economic and Technological Development Zone. The special economic districts are Honggutan New District and GanJiang New District.

Nanchang's geography is a plus for travel. It is praised in a local saying about "three rivers and five lakes", and it uses high-speed railways and aviation hubs to link three important economic circles: the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the inter-provincial traffic corridors in Haixi District. Nationally it is a comprehensive transportation hub, and inside Jiangxi it is an important integrated one.

For southeastern China, Nanchang is a key railway junction, where four lines meet: the Beijing-Kowloon (Jingjiu) Railway, the Shanghai-Kunming railway (once known as the Zhejiang-Jiangxi or Zhegan Railway), the Xiangtang-Putian railway and the Nanchang-Jiujiang intercity railway. Nanchang's Bureau of Railways runs much of the rail network of Jiangxi and neighbouring Fujian province.
The main passenger stations are Nanchang railway station and Nanchang West railway station. CRH (China Railway High-speed) trains connect the city with Hangzhou, Changsha and Shanghai.

The main international airport is Nanchang Changbei International Airport (KHN), which opened in 1996. It stands in Lehua Town, 26 kilometres north of the CDB area. It is the only airport in Jiangxi Province with an international air route, and it has links to mainland cities including Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Haikou, Shanghai and Beijing. A military and civilian airport also operates near Liantang, in Nanchang County.

Changbei is also the largest airport in Jiangxi. It reached up to 10 international destinations in 2014, when it handled 7.25 million passengers, a rise of 6.3%. International traffic there topped 280,000 passengers, up nearly 40%, a major source of growth. On 6 December 2017 annual passenger throughput passed 10 million, making it the 31st "million-grade airport" in China. For the whole of 2017 throughput reached 10.93 million, a 39.0% year-on-year increase and a net gain of 3.07 million passengers. Flights taking off and landing numbered 89,000, up 35.2%, and cargo and mail came to 52,000 tons, up 3.3%. To support the Beijing-Kowloon high-speed railway and the airport complex hub at Nanchang North Station, a large expansion and upgrade is under way.

Road infrastructure is extensive. National highways cross the city: No.105 (Beijing to Zhuhai), No.320 (Shanghai to Kunming) and No.316 (Fuzhou to Lanzhou). National Highway G70 also passes through, and a round-city highway, G70_01, opened in 2007. Bus services are run by three main operators: the Xufang Bus Station, Chang'an Transport Company Limited and the Nanchang Long-distance Bus Station.

Long-distance buses from the Nanchang Long-distance Bus Station serve cities outside Jiangxi, such as Nanjing, Shenzhen and Hefei. The Xufang Bus Station runs to cities, towns and counties within the province.

Nanchang Rail Transit, Jiangxi Province's first urban rail system, has operated since 26 December 2015, which made Nanchang the 25th mainland Chinese city to have a metro. Planners began work in 1999, and building officially started in 2009. The first phase of Lines 1 and 2 totals 50,996 kilometers, and Line 1 is underground. Line 1 opened for operation at the end of 2015, and the "First Section" of Line 2 began trial operation on 19 August 2017.

Rivers and lakes matter for trade and shipping. The city has the Gan River and the Fu River running by, along with Aixi Lake, Qingshan Lake and Elephant Lake. The biggest port on the Gan River is Nanchang Port. From it passengers can go by boat to Jinggang Shan and Tengwang Pavilion, and other passenger ships visit Poyang Lake and attractions such as Dagu Hill, Stone Bell Hill and the Poyang Lake Bird Protection Area.
Poyang Lake is China's largest freshwater lake, and has the nickname "the Migrator Birds Paradise".
A pavilion from the year 653, Tengwang Pavilion, towers over the Gan River's east bank and ranks as one of "the Four Great Towers of China".
In Honggutan District, the Star of Nanchang held the title of tallest Ferris wheel in the world between 2006 and 2008.
Qiushui Square opened on 28 January 2004 and has Asia's largest group of music fountains set to music.
People's Park is the largest park downtown, and the Jiangxi Provincial Museum shares a site with the Bada Shanren Exhibition Hall.
The Bada Shanren Memorial Hall is a big artistic scenic museum, with sculpture and a general art museum.

At the heart of the city, Bayi Square and Memorial marks the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 (Ba Yi in Mandarin), when the People's Liberation Army was founded, a step on the way to the People's Republic of China in 1949.
By scientific research output, the Nature Index puts Nanchang among the world's top 100 cities. Its higher education institutions (those without full-time bachelor programmes are left out) are:
General and teacher-training universities: Nanchang University (南昌大学) and Jiangxi Normal University (江西师范大学)

Science and engineering: East China Jiaotong University (华东交通大学), Nanchang Institute of Technology (南昌工程学院), East China University of Technology, Nanchang Campus (东华理工大学), and Nanchang Hangkong University (南昌航空大学)
Other specialists: Jiangxi Agricultural University (江西农业大学), Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University (江西科技师范学院), Jiangxi Manufacturing and Vocational College (江西制造职业技术学院)
Medicine: Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医药大学) and Jiangxi Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医学院)
Business: Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics (江西财经大学), the subject of this profile

Two high schools are Nanchang Foreign Language School (南昌市外国语学校) and Jiangxi University of Technology High School (江西科技学院附属中学). There is also an international school, Nanchang International School (南昌国际学校).
Provincial context shapes student life too, so here is a look at Jiangxi's past and economy.

At the centre of Jiangxi is the Gan River valley, long the main north-south transport route of south China. The corridor beside the river is one of the few easy routes through otherwise rugged, mountainous south-eastern terrain, and it carried the main flow of trade and communication linking northern areas (the North China Plain and Yangtze River valley) with today's Guangdong province in the south. That is why Jiangxi has been strategically important for much of Chinese history.

Under the Shang dynasty (16th to 11th centuries BC), Jiangxi lay beyond the reach of early Chinese civilization, and it was probably settled by peoples collectively called the Baiyue. In the Spring and Autumn period the state of Wu had its western frontier in the north of modern Jiangxi. After the state of Yue (centred in modern northern Zhejiang) defeated Wu in 473 BC, northern Jiangxi was taken by the state of Chu (centred in modern Hubei), and Yue may also have held some sway in the south, until Chu subjugated Yue in 333 BC. When Qin conquered Chu in 223 BC, most of the Jiangxi area was recorded as belonging to Jiujiang Commandery, located at Shouchun (壽春), but the commandery was ineffective and ended soon after the fall of Qin.

Early in the Han dynasty, possibly before Xiang Yu died in 202 BC, Yuzhang Commandery (豫章, Gan: Ì-zong) was established, the first commandery that a Chinese dynasty set up in Jiangxi. It took its name from the Yuzhang River (豫章江), the original name of the Gan River, and "Gan" has become the province's abbreviation. In 201 eight counties were added to the seven it had inherited from Qin, and three more came later. For most of the Han period its eighteen counties covered most of modern Jiangxi. County seats such as Nanchang, Gan, Yudu and Luling were on the sites of today's major cities, although other counties were later moved or abolished.

Emperor Wu of the Han placed Yuzhang Commandery under Yangzhou Province, as part of a trend to create provinces (zhou) across China. In 291 AD, under the Western Jin, Jiangxi became its own zhou, called Jiangzhou (江州, Gan: Kong-chiu). Through the Southern and Northern Dynasties, the southern dynasties kept Jiangxi, and the zhou gradually multiplied.

The Sui dynasty had seven commanderies and twenty-four counties in Jiangxi. The Tang added another commandery and fourteen counties, and commanderies were then abolished and became zhou, from then on translated as "prefectures" rather than "provinces".

The Tang introduced circuits as a new top-level division. At first Jiangxi lay within the Jiangnan Circuit ("Circuit south of the Yangtze"). In 733 that circuit was split into western and eastern halves, and Jiangxi fell in the western one, the Jiangnanxi Circuit ("Western circuits south of the Yangtze"), which is where the modern name Jiangxi comes from.

jiangxi-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: From the Five Dynasties to the Song

blocks.x: When the Tang collapsed in 907, the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period began. Jiangxi belonged first to Wu (吳, Gan: Ng) and then to Southern Tang (南唐, Gan: Nām-thóng), both based in modern-day Nanjing, farther down the Yangtze. Once the ten kingdoms had passed, Jiangnanxi Circuit came back, now made up of nine prefectures and four army districts (sixty-eight districts in total). Later still, thirteen circuits were carved out of Jiangxi and Jiangxi Province was created for the first time, including most of modern Guangdong, with something close to its modern borders.

After the Qing regime fell, Jiangxi became one of the Communists' earliest bases, and many peasants joined the growing revolution. During the Chinese Civil War the Nanchang Uprising broke out on 1 August 1927. Afterwards the Communist leadership took refuge in the mountains of western and southern Jiangxi, away from Kuomintang attempts to wipe them out. In 1931 the government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was set up in Ruijin, which people sometimes call the "Red Capital" or, in full, the "Former Red Capital" (红色故都, Gan: Fūng-set Kū-tu). Completely encircled by Nationalist forces in 1935, the Communists broke out and started the Long March to Yan'an.

Between 1930 and 1934 the National Government launched five military campaigns against the Jiangxi Soviet area. The brutal fighting between the two parties, along with purges (including inside the Red Army and in the post-war government), caused large numbers of deaths or departures. Jiangxi's population fell by 40%, to only 13.8 million in 1936.

In 1936 the Yuehan Railway opened in Hunan, and Jiangxi lost its key position in north-south traffic. A year later, in 1937, the east-west Zhegan Railway opened and altered Jiangxi's traffic patterns greatly. Jiujiang Port (九江港) began to lose importance.

After the Doolittle Raid in World War II, most of the American B-25 crews that came down in China eventually reached safety with help from Jiangxi locals. The Gan who helped them paid dearly. To frighten the Chinese out of helping downed American airmen, the Imperial Japanese Army began the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign, and at least 10,000 civilians died in Jiangxi searching for Doolittle's men.

In 1949, when the People's Republic of China was founded, the CCP took full control of Jiangxi. That year the Republican provincial government fled to Taichung in Taiwan Province, where it dissolved itself.

During the Third Front campaign, Jiangxi was a major beneficiary of investment in industrial capacity across China. Rice is the main crop, cotton and rapeseed are common cash crops, and kumquats are a specialty: Jiangxi leads China in output, above all in Suichuan County.

Mining and related industries are a big part of the economy. Mineral wealth is large: among Chinese provinces Jiangxi has the biggest deposits of niobium, tantalum, thorium, uranium, silver, gold, tungsten and copper, among others. Dexing (copper) and Dayu County (tungsten) are noted mining centres.

Jiangxi sits very close to some of China's richest provinces (Guangdong, Zhejiang and Fujian), which are sometimes blamed for drawing away its talent and capital. It has the lowest wages in China and the third lowest property prices. Nominal GDP in 2016 was CNY 1.84 trillion (US$276.48 billion). Per capita GDP was CNY 40,400, or US$6,082.

For a student of business, JUFE offers a recognised finance and economics education in a mid-sized provincial capital that is growing fast, has a metro, an international airport and high-speed rail, in a province with low property prices by national standards.
Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics lists 24 programs for international students on this site: 8 bachelor, 9 master's, 6 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 15 taught in English, 9 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 26,000 to CNY 26,000 (median CNY 26,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 34,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 34,000 to CNY 34,000 (median CNY 34,000), according to the university's published fee table.

21 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (11):
Accounting
Computer Science and Technology
Finance Studies
International Business
International Finance
International Trade
Public Administration
Public Economics and Management
Statistics
Tourism Management
Western Economics
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

jiangxi-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanchang, register at Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

jilin-agricultural-university.h: Jilin Agricultural University: what it is

blocks.x: Jilin Agricultural University (JLAU, 吉林农业大学) is a public university devoted to agriculture, in Changchun, the capital of Jilin Province in north-east China. Its founding year is 1948. Two authorities supervise it, the provincial government of Jilin and the national Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, and it counts among the institutions supported by a national scheme to build basic capacity in the western and central parts of China.

jilin-agricultural-university.h: From cadre school to agricultural university

blocks.x: The story begins with the Agricultural Cadre School (农业干部学院). It opened in Heilongjiang Province in 1948, run by the Northeast Bureau of the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee. A decade later, in 1958, it was restructured and became Changchun College of Agriculture (长春农学院). Zhou Enlai, who was premier at that point, wrote the calligraphy for its name. Only a year after that, in 1959, it received its official title of Jilin Agricultural University.

About 18,000 students study at JLAU. The university is divided into 20 colleges for undergraduates, plus a teaching department that reports directly to the university, a graduate school and nine stations for postdoctoral research.
The university's academic units are mostly built around farming, food, environment and life sciences, with a few general colleges on top. The principal ones are:
Crops and plants: the colleges of Agronomy, Horticulture, Plant Protection, and Forestry and Grassland Sciences.
Animals, medicine and life: the colleges of Veterinary Medicine, Chinese Medicinal Materials and Life Sciences.
Land, food and business: the College of Resources and Environmental Sciences, the College of Food Science and Engineering, and the College of Economics and Management.
Technology: the colleges of Engineering and Technology and of Information Technology.
Arts and languages: the colleges of Humanities and of Foreign Languages.

A student's day-to-day experience depends heavily on the surrounding city, including its weather, the transport options and the leisure available. The sections below describe Changchun, the home of Jilin Agricultural University.

Changchun occupies the central part of the great Northeast China Plain. The municipality ranges from 43° 05′ to 45° 15′ north and from 124° 18′ to 127° 02′ east. The whole municipality is large at 20,571 km2 (7,943 sq mi), while the metro area shrinks to 2,583 square kilometres (997 sq mi) and the city proper to only 159 km2 (61 sq mi).

Height above sea level is moderate across the administrative region, from 820 to 1,150 ft (250 to 350 metres). Low mountains cover a small area in the east, where Laodaodong Mountain is the tallest at 711 metres. Changchun also marks the point where the third east-west 'Europe-Asia Continental Bridge' crosses another route. Water is plentiful, with 222 rivers and lakes in the prefecture. The small Yitong River, which feeds into the Songhua River, passes through the city proper.
The climate is humid continental, shaped by the monsoon, with four seasons (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac).
Winter is long, lasting from November to March, and cold, windy but dry because of the Siberian anticyclone. The January mean is -14.3 °C (6.3 °F).
Spring and autumn are brief transitions, mostly dry and windy with a little precipitation.
Summer is hot and humid, with winds usually from the south-east thanks to the East Asian monsoon, and a July average of 23.7 °C (74.7 °F).

Winter snowfall is usually light, and most of the year's rain comes from June to August. Sunshine averages about 2,597 hours a year, with possible sunshine going from 69 percent in February down to 49 percent in July. Between 140 and 150 days are free of frost. Records show a low of -36.5 °C (-34 °F) on 4 January 1970 and a high of 100 °F (38.0 °C) on 9 July 1951. Pack seriously warm clothing for the long winter.

In 2010 the Sixth China Census found 7.677 million residents in Changchun, and a 2011 estimate suggested 7.59 million. Of them, 3.53 million lived in the urban area. Births ran at 6.08 per thousand and deaths at 5.51 per thousand, and the 2010 sex ratio was 102.10 men to 100 women.
As in most of north-east China, the Han Chinese are the main group, making up 96.57 percent of the population, with a number of minority nationalities making up the rest.

Most people speak Northeastern Mandarin, which came from a mixture of languages spoken by migrants from Hebei and Shandong. After the People's Republic was founded, fast economic growth drew huge numbers of newcomers from many places, and because these immigrants strongly influenced the speech of the urban areas, the north-eastern dialect used in the city is closer to standard Mandarin than the dialect in rural areas.
Changchun's religious life centres on Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam, and the authorities have approved 396 places for worship and religious activity. Religious buildings include these:
Buddhist and Chinese temples: Wanshou Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple, Pumen Temple, the Big Buddha Temple and Changchun Temple.
Churches: the Catholic Church, and the Christian Church on West Wuma Road.
The City Mosque.
Shamanism was once widespread in north-east China, and plenty of Manchus followed it. It, and scholarship about it, are now regarded as a significant piece of the region's cultural heritage.

Changchun hosts the Jilin Provincial Museum, which has national first-grade status. It moved here from Jilin City once the seat of the provincial government changed. The museum began in the heart of the old town, but a new building to hold its collections, which took nine years to construct, was finished in 2016 on the edge of the city, in Nanguan District close to Jingyuetan Park.

Badabu is a group of buildings that once housed eight ministries of Manchukuo: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs, and Civil Affairs. Because of their unusual mixture of Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian architecture, they have recently become a sightseeing highlight.

South-east of Changchun is Jingyuetan National Forest Park, which holds a AAAAA rating, the highest among China's tourist attractions. Each year the park stages Vasaloppet China, a cross-country ski event.

In 2010 Changchun's gross domestic product (GDP) was RMB 332.9 billion, up 15.3 percent on a year earlier. Primary industry grew 3.3 percent to RMB 25.27 billion, secondary industry grew 19.0 percent to RMB 171.99 billion, and tertiary industry grew 12.6 percent to RMB 135.64 billion.

By 2012 GDP had reached RMB 445.66 billion, 12.0 percent more than in 2011. The primary sector grew 4.3 percent to RMB 31.71 billion, the secondary sector added RMB 229.19 billion (13.1 percent up on the previous year), and the tertiary sector grew 11.8 percent to RMB 184.76 billion. GDP per head in 2012 was 58,691 yuan, or $9,338.

Cars dominate, with agricultural processing, biopharmaceuticals, photoelectronics, construction materials and energy as the other leading sectors. Changchun is the country's largest hub for automobile manufacturing and for research and development of vehicles, and its output in 2009 was 9 percent of all cars made in China. The giant of the business is the FAW (First Automotive Works) Group, the biggest vehicle producer in China, which built the first Chinese truck in 1956 and the first Chinese car in 1958. A big share of the city's south-west end is taken up by the group's factories along with their housing and services. Local brands include the Red Flag luxury marque, and FAW has joint ventures with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. During 2012 the group sold 2.65 million vehicles for sales revenue of RMB 408.46 billion (up 10.8% year on year). The city invented the national car industry, so a popular nickname is 'China's Detroit'.

Another strong sector is transport equipment and machinery. Half of China's passenger trains and a tenth of its tractors are made in Changchun. One of CRRC's main divisions, Changchun Railway Vehicles, works with Bombardier Transportation in a joint venture that builds Movia metro cars for Guangzhou, Shanghai and Tianjin.

The bulk of CRRC's bullet train carriages come out of its Changchun factory. In November 2016, CRRC Changchun showed the world's first bullet-train carriages with sleeper berths, so that high-speed trains could be used for overnight journeys across China and run in extremely cold conditions. Nicknamed Panda, the new trains run at 250 km/h and can operate at -40 degrees Celsius. They have Wi-Fi hubs, and berths that fold up into seats in the daytime.

Inbound foreign direct investment totalled US$3.68 billion in 2012, which was 19.6% more than in 2011. Coca-Cola made a US$20 million investment in 2004 to build a bottling plant inside the city's ETDZ. Every year Changchun hosts the Changchun International Automobile Fair, the Changchun Film Festival, the Changchun Agricultural Fair, an Education Exhibition and a Sculpture Exhibition.
Other large firms in Changchun are:

Yatai Group, which dates from 1993 and has been quoted on the Shanghai Stock Exchange since 1995. It has become a large conglomerate with interests ranging across property development, cement, securities, coal mining, pharmaceuticals and trading.
Jilin Grain Group, a major grain processor.
Changchun has three notable development zones.

jilin-agricultural-university.h: Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone

blocks.x: Founded as the Changchun Automotive Trade Center in 1993, this zone was reorganised in 1996 under its present name, the Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone. It lies in the south-west, beside both the Changchun Film ThemeCity and the vehicle maker China First Automobile Works Group Corporation. The area is roughly 3,229,173 square feet (300,000 square metres). Inside are an exhibition centre and five specially marked-out industrial centres. The Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center, which started operating in 1994, is China's largest wholesale center for vehicles and spare parts. The others are a resale center for used vehicles, a specialised center for industrial and commercial vehicles and a tyre wholesale center.

Located in the south of Changchun, this 49 km2 (19 sq mi) zone was one of the first 27 national advanced-technology zones in China. It contains 18 full-time universities and colleges, 11 key national laboratories and 39 research institutions at state or provincial level. Development concentrates on five industries: bio-engineering, automobile engineering, new materials, photo-electricity and information technology.

CETDZ opened in April 1993 and enjoys every preferential policy given to development zones in China's coastal open cities. In all it spans 43.52 square miles (112.72 square kilometres), and 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of that is set aside for development and use. Downtown is 5 kilometres (3 miles) away, the freight railway station is 2 km (1.2 mi) away and the international airport 15 km (9 mi). Industries given priority are automotive parts and components, photoelectric information, bio-pharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials, and projects with high technology and high added value account for more than 80 percent of production. Fixed asset investment in the zone rose to RMB 38.4 billion in 2006. It has 1,656 registered enterprises, of which 179 have foreign funding, and its industrial output reached RMB 277 billion in 2007.

jilin-agricultural-university.h: A niche: food for the skies

blocks.x: Grain is grown in large quantities nearby, and the city is a regional hub for air and rail, so Changchun has set up a specialised Aviation Food Industrialization Base. It provides prepared meals for a number of airlines and studies food science for long-haul flights, a niche area of manufacturing.

Two main stations handle passengers. Changchun railway station (长春站, or 長春站 in traditional characters) sits in the centre and serves every conventional train and some of the high-speed ones. It lies on the Beijing-Harbin Railway, on the Changchun-Hunchun intercity railway and on several other lines. Daily departures go to other places in Jilin and the north-east (Jilin City, Yanji, Harbin, Shenyang, Dalian) and to big cities elsewhere in China, among them Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. At the western edge of the built-up area, the new Changchun West railway station is mainly for Harbin-Dalian high-speed trains. A smaller third station, Changchun East in Erdao district, is on the Changchun-Tumen line.
The bus system is comprehensive, with more than 250 routes, and most buses charge 1 to 2 yuan per ride.

Few Chinese cities still run a historic tram, but Changchun does. The network started in 1941 and peaked at 6 lines and almost 53 km. Following a number of route adjustments, just a single line has survived since the 2000s. In 2014 a branch was added to reach the new West Railway Station, and the tram now operates as part of the bus system.

The city's rapid transit mixes light rail and metro lines. Service began on 30 October 2002, which made Changchun China's fifth city with rail transit. In November 2018 the network had five lines (1, 2, 3, 4 and 8) and about 100.17 kilometres of track. Four projects were under construction as of September 2019: Lines 6 and 9, an extension of Line 2 to the west and an extension of Line 3 to the east. The plan is for a network of 10 lines, 341.62 kilometres in length, by 2025.

In September 2019 the system averaged 680,400 passengers a day, and the daily peak across the network was 830,500 on 13 November 2019. The total passenger volume for 2019 was estimated at about 168 million.

Four expressways tie the city into the national network: G1 (Beijing-Harbin), G12 (Ulanhot-Changchun-Jilin-Hunchun), G25 (Changchun-Shenzhen) and S1 (Changchun-Changbaishan). The province's busiest section is the Changchun-Jilin North Highway between Jilin's two biggest cities, which acts as the backbone for social and economic contact between them.
Private cars are increasingly common and the streets are congested. Compared with other north-eastern cities, bicycles are rare, though mopeds and pedal cycles are seen fairly often.

North-east of the urban area, 31.2 kilometres (19.4 miles) away, is Changchun Longjia International Airport. Work began in 1998 with the aim of replacing the older Dafangshen Airport, which had been built for joint use in 1941. Passenger flights began on 27 August 2005, and nearby Jilin City shares the running of the airport with Changchun.

Science is a strength: the Nature Index 2024 Science Cities ranking places Changchun in the world's top 30 cities for research output. The city has 27 regular full-time institutions of tertiary education with roughly 160,000 students. Two of them, Jilin University and Northeast Normal University, are key universities in China, and Jilin University has more than 60,000 students, which makes it one of the country's largest.
