jilin-agricultural-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jilin Agricultural University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Changchun, register at Jilin Agricultural University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

jilin-international-studies-university.h: Where Jilin International Studies University sits

blocks.x: Jilin International Studies University is in Changchun, the capital of Jilin Province in northeast China. If you are weighing it up as a study destination, the city and province matter as much as the campus, since they decide your climate, your travel options and your surroundings. The sections below walk through Changchun first and then widen out to Jilin as a whole.

Changchun occupies the middle of the Northeast China Plain. The municipality extends from latitude 43° 05′ to 45° 15′ N and from longitude 124° 18′ to 127° 02' E. In total the municipality covers 20,571 km2 (7,943 sq mi). Within that, the metro area takes up 2,583 square kilometres (997 sq mi), while the city proper is a modest 159 km2 (61 sq mi).

Elevation is moderate: across the administrative region, the land lies at 250 to 350 metres (820 to 1,150 ft) above sea level. A small patch of low mountains lies in the east, and its peak, Laodaodong Mountain at 711 meters, is the highest point. The city also sits where the third east-west "Europe-Asia Continental Bridge" crosses. There are 222 rivers and lakes in the prefecture, and a small tributary of the Songhua River, the Yitong, runs through the city proper.

jilin-international-studies-university.h: Four seasons, with a long cold one

blocks.x: Changchun's climate has four seasons and is humid continental with a monsoon influence (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). The seasons differ sharply:

Winter: it lasts from November to March, and it is long, cold and windy but dry, under the sway of the Siberian anticyclone. The mean temperature in January is -14.3 °C (6.3 °F), so serious winter clothing is essential. Snowfall is normally light.
Spring and autumn: fairly short in-between seasons, usually dry and windy with a little rain.
Summer: hot and humid, with southeasterly winds from the East Asian monsoon. The July average is 23.7 °C (74.7 °F), and the bulk of the year's rainfall comes in June, July and August.

Sunshine is 49 percent of what is possible in July and rises to 69 percent in February, so a normal year brings about 2,597 hours of it. The frost-free period lasts 140 to 150 days. The coldest day on record, 4 January 1970, hit -36.5 °C (-34 °F), and the hottest, 9 July 1951, reached 38.0 °C (100 °F).

The Sixth China Census counted 7.677 million people in Changchun in 2010, and an estimate for 2011 was 7.59 million. Births ran at 6.08 per thousand people, and deaths at 5.51 per thousand. Of the total, 3.53 million live in the urban area, and the 2010 sex ratio was 102.10 men to every 100 women.
As in most of Northeast China, the Han (96.57 percent) are the dominant nationality, and a few other minority nationalities live in the city.

In terms of language, the common dialect is Northeastern Mandarin, which grew out of the mixed speech of immigrants from Hebei and Shandong. After the People's Republic was founded, quick economic growth drew large numbers of newcomers from many regions. They influenced the speech of the urban areas heavily, which is why city speakers sound closer to standard Mandarin than rural ones.

Four major religions are found in Changchun: Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam, with 396 government-approved places of worship. Religious buildings include several Buddhist and Taoist temples (Changchun Wanshou Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple, Pumen Temple, Big Buddha Temple and Changchun Temple) as well as Changchun Catholic Church, West Wuma Road Christian Church and the Changchun City Mosque. Shamanism spread across Northeast China in ancient times and many Manchus held it. Today it and the study of it are regarded as an important part of the region's cultural heritage.

Jilin Provincial Museum is a national first-grade museum. It came to Changchun from Jilin City when the provincial government moved. It used to stand in the old town centre. Nine years of construction produced a new building, finished in 2016, for the collections, on the city's edge in Nanguan District, close to Jingyuetan Park.

Badabu, the "eight ministries", is a group of buildings that once housed eight Manchukuo ministries: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs and Civil Affairs. Their unusual mix of Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian architecture has made them a recent sightseeing highlight.
Jingyuetan National Forest Park, southeast of the city, is one of China's AAAAA Tourist Attractions and holds the annual Vasaloppet China ski event.
In 2010, Changchun's gross domestic product (GDP) was RMB332.9 billion, 15.3 percent above the previous year. The sector breakdown:
Primary industry output rose by 3.3 percent, reaching RMB25.27 billion.
Secondary industry rose 19.0 percent, to RMB171.99 billion.
Tertiary industry, up 12.6 percent, came to RMB135.64 billion.

In 2012 GDP stood at RMB445.66 billion, an increase of 12.0 percent on 2011. Of this, primary industry contributed RMB31.71 billion (4.3 percent growth), secondary industry RMB229.19 billion (13.1 percent growth) and tertiary industry RMB184.76 billion (11.8 percent growth). Per-person GDP that year was ¥58,691, or $9338.

The main industries are automobiles, processing of farm products, biopharmaceuticals, photo-electronics, building materials and energy. Changchun is China's biggest centre for car manufacturing and research and development, and in 2009 it made 9 percent of the nation's vehicles. It hosts FAW (First Automotive Works) Group, the country's biggest vehicle maker, which built China's first truck in 1956 and its first car in 1958. The company's factories, housing and services take up a large share of the city's southwest. Cars built in Changchun include the Red Flag luxury marque, and the city also hosts joint ventures with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. FAW sold 2.65 million vehicles in 2012, with sales revenue of RMB 408.46 billion, up 10.8% on the year. Because it was the cradle of China's car industry, Changchun is nicknamed "China's Detroit".

Transport equipment and machinery are also leading industries. Half of China's passenger trains and a tenth of its tractors (50 percent and 10 percent) are made in Changchun. One main division of CRRC, Changchun Railway Vehicles, runs a joint venture with Bombardier Transportation which builds Movia metro cars for the metros of Guangzhou, Shanghai and Tianjin.

The CRRC factory in Changchun is where most of the company's bullet train carriages are made. In November 2016 CRCC Changchun showed the world's first bullet train carriages with sleeper berths, which makes overnight journeys across China possible. Nicknamed Panda, the new trains can handle ultra-low temperatures down to -40 degrees Celsius, run at 250 km/h, have Wi-Fi hubs, and have sleeper berths that fold into seats by day.

In 2012 the city drew US$3.68 billion of foreign direct investment, 19.6% more than the year before. An earlier example is Coca-Cola, which invested US$20 million in 2004 to build a bottling plant in the city's ETDZ.
Each year Changchun stages a film festival, an agricultural fair, an education exhibition, a sculpture exhibition and the Changchun International Automobile Fair.
Other large employers include:

Yatai Group, established in 1993 and floated on the Shanghai Stock Exchange two years later. It is now a major conglomerate in property development, cement, securities, coal mining, pharmaceuticals and trading.
Jilin Grain Group, which processes grain on a large scale.

Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone: this began as the Changchun Automotive Trade Center in 1993 and took its current name in 1996. It sits in the southwest of the city beside the Changchun Film ThemeCity and the China First Automobile Works Group Corporation, and measures roughly 300,000 square metres (3,229,173 square feet). The zone has an exhibition center plus five separate industrial centers. Among them, the Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center opened in 1994 and is China's largest wholesale market for vehicles and spare parts. Other centers cover used vehicles, industrial and commercial vehicles, and tires.

High Technology Development Zone: part of the first group of 27 state-level advanced technology zones, located in the southern part of the city across 49 km2 (19 sq mi). Within it are 18 full-time universities and colleges, 11 key national laboratories, and 39 research institutions run by the state or province. Five industries get most attention: bio-engineering, automobile engineering, new material fabrication, photo-electricity and information technology.

Economic and Technological Development Zone (CETDZ): created in April 1993, it gets all the preferential policies that apply to such zones in coastal open cities. It covers 112.72 square kilometres (43.52 square miles), and 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of this has been reserved for development and use. Downtown is 5 kilometres (3 miles) away, the freight railway station 2 km (1.2 mi) and the international airport 15 km (9 mi). Five leading industries are developed: automotive parts and components, photoelectric information, bio-pharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials. Over 80 percent of output comes from high-tech, high value-added projects. Fixed asset investment reached RMB38.4 billion in 2006, 1656 enterprises were registered (179 of them foreign-funded), and industrial output totalled RMB 277 billion in 2007.

Because Changchun is a major grain-producing base and a regional air and rail hub, it has built a specialised Aviation Food Industrialization Base. The base provides ready-made meals to several airlines and carries out food science research for long flights, so it is a niche manufacturing sector.

Changchun has two main passenger stations. The central Changchun railway station (长春站 / 長春站) handles all conventional trains and some high-speed ones, and connects to the Beijing-Harbin Railway, the Changchun-Hunchun intercity railway and several other lines. There are several departures a day to places in the province and the northeast (Jilin City, Yanji, Harbin, Shenyang, Dalian) and to major cities elsewhere, among them Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. A newer station, Changchun West, stands at the western end of the built-up area and at the western end of the built-up area, mainly serves high-speed trains of the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway. The small Changchun East railway station, in Erdao district, is on the Changchun-Tumen line.

The bus network is extensive, with over 250 routes, and a ride usually costs 1 to 2 yuan. Few Chinese cities still run a historic tram, and Changchun is among them. Opened in 1941, it had 6 lines covering almost 53 km at its height, but route adjustments left one line from the 2000s onward. A new branch opened in 2014 linking the Changchun West Railway Station, and the entire system now runs under the city bus network.

Changchun Rail Transit combines light rail and metro lines. Its first line began running on 30 October 2002, so Changchun became the fifth Chinese city to open rail transit. By November 2018 there were 5 lines (1, 2, 3, 4 and 8) covering about 100.17 kilometers. In September 2019, 4 projects were under construction: Line 6, Line 9, the Line 2 West Extension and the Line 3 East Extension. By 2025 the network is planned to have 10 lines and 341.62 kilometers of track.
In September 2019 the system carried an average of 680,400 passengers a day. The peak was 830,500 on 13 November 2019, and the estimated total for 2019 was about 168 million passengers.

The city connects to the national expressway grid via the Beijing-Harbin Expressway (G1), the Ulanhot-Changchun-Jilin-Hunchun Expressway (G12), the Changchun-Shenzhen Expressway (G25) and the Changchun-Changbaishan Expressway (S1). The province's busiest stretch is the Changchun-Jilin North Highway. It joins Jilin's two largest cities and carries the main flow of their social and economic traffic.
Private cars are increasingly common on the congested streets. Bicycles are rarer than in other northeastern cities, though mopeds and pedal cycles are fairly common.

Changchun Longjia International Airport is 31.2 kilometres (19.4 miles) northeast of the urban area. Work began in 1998 so that the airport could take the place of Changchun Dafangshen Airport, a joint-use field dating from 1941. It opened for passengers on 27 August 2005 and is operated jointly by Changchun and nearby Jilin City.

Changchun ranks among the world's top 30 cities for scientific research in the Nature Index 2024 Science Cities. It has 27 regular full-time tertiary institutions, together enrolling roughly 160,000 students. Two of them, Jilin University and Northeast Normal University, are key national universities, and Jilin University has more than 60,000 students, making it one of China's largest.

A province shapes student life as much as a campus does. Jilin has a long frontier history, rich natural resources and a distinctive blend of peoples.

In ancient times the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí (勿吉) lived in what is now Jilin, and the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo governed some of the land. Control then passed from one power to the next: the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo, Balhae, the Khitan-led Liao, the Jurchen Jin and the Mongol Yuan. In Qing times most of the land came under a military governor, the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose territory included much of what is now Primorsky Krai in Russia.

Once Primorsky Krai was given up to Russia in 1860, the authorities started inviting Han Chinese settlers into the region, mostly from Shandong. By the early 20th century the Han had become the region's main ethnic group. In 1932 Jilin was brought into Manchukuo, the puppet state set up by Japan, whose capital was Changchun (then called Xinjing), today Jilin's capital. When Japan was beaten in 1945, the Red Army took Jilin after Operation August Storm. The Soviet Union then handed the region and the rest of northeastern China to the Communists. From Manchuria as a base, the Communists went on to win the rest of China in the Chinese Civil War.

The province of 1949 was smaller. It covered only the area around Changchun and Jilin City, the capital was Jilin City, and Changchun was a separate municipality outside it. In the 1950s Jilin was enlarged to its present borders. The Cultural Revolution enlarged it again with a section of Inner Mongolia, which gave Jilin a frontier with Mongolia, an independent country, though that change was later undone.

More recently, Jilin and the rest of the heavy-industry Northeast have faced economic difficulties during privatization, which led the central government to start the "Revitalize the Northeast" campaign.

Jilin is in central northeast China, with Russia on its eastern border and North Korea to the southeast. Its area is 190,000 km2 (73,000 sq mi) and its population is 24 million. The capital, Changchun, lies 113 km (70 mi) to the west of Jilin City.

The province has 136 types of mineral, of which 70 have been mined. Around 27,000 kinds of wild plants grow here, 9,000 of them medicinal herbs, a huge resource for Traditional Chinese medicine. There are large reserves of fuels (oil, gas, coal), metals (iron, nickel, molybdenum, gold, silver) and minerals such as talc, graphite, gypsum and cement rock. Its oil shale reserves are the biggest in China.

Altitude is greatest in the southeast and falls gently toward the northwest. The Changbai Mountains cross the southeast, and Paektu Mountain, 2,744 m (9,003 ft) high, is the province's top peak. Other ranges are the Jilinhada, Zhang Guangcai and Longgang mountains.

The Yalu and Tumen rivers drain the extreme southeast and together form part of the border between China and North Korea. Rivers feeding the Liao drain the southwest. The Songhua and the Nen carry water from the north, and both end up in the Amur.

The climate is a northern continental monsoon type: winters are long and cold and summers short and warm. January averages are between -20 and -14 °C (-4 to 7 °F), and annual rainfall averages between 350 and 1,000 mm (13.8 to 39.4 in).
Besides Changchun and Jilin City, the major cities are Yanji, Siping, Tonghua, Baishan, Baicheng, Songyuan and Liaoyuan.

In 2025 the province's nominal GDP was RMB 1,497.4 billion (US$209.6 billion), and in 2025 per capita nominal GDP reached RMB 64,618 (US$9,046). GDP has been rising by double digits every year since 2003, with a 51 percent increase between 2003 and 2007. Compared with 2005, the added value and profit of large enterprises were up 19 percent and 30 percent.

Farming centres on rice, wheat, maize and sorghum. Rice grows mostly in the east, such as in Yanbian Prefecture, the Changbai Mountains supply lumber, and sheep herding is important in the west, such as around Baicheng.

Jilin has the largest shale oil reserves, and its mineral reserves rank among China's top five. It also has more kieselguhr, wollastonite, floatstone and molybdenum than most provinces. The main industries are cars, train carriages and iron alloy. It is one of China's most important commodity grain bases, and sixth in timber production. It has long been a leading pharmaceutical centre as well, with among the largest yields of ginseng and deer antlers in China, used widely in Chinese medicine.

Jilin New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone: founded in 1992 in Jilin city, with a planned area of 818 km2 (316 sq mi) of which 242 km2 (93 sq mi) is established. Leading industries are new materials, refined chemical products, combined photoelectron and mechanical products, electronics, medicine and bioengineering. Songhua Lake is only 14 km (8.7 mi) away, and the closest bus and train stations are within 3 km (1.9 mi).

Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone: founded in May 1998 in the northeast of Jilin city, and planned to cover 28 km2 (11 sq mi). Changchun is 90 km (56 mi) away, Jilin Airport 5 km (3.1 mi) and Jilin Railway Station 8 km (5.0 mi). Its major industries are bioengineering, refined chemicals, and fine processing of chemical fiber and farm products. It has four parks, for chemicals, food, textiles and medicine. The medical park specialises in traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals, small-molecule medicine, bio-pharmaceuticals and health products.

Jilin is home to Han Chinese, Manchus, Hui, Mongols and Xibe. Because the Korean Peninsula is nearby, Koreans make up around 4% of the population, and most live in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture. The Manchu were once the majority in Jilin, which was part of their historical homeland, but since they adopted Han culture and Chinese languages, Manchu is considered critically endangered. Most people in the province speak Mandarin. These population statistics exclude active-duty members of the People's Liberation Army.

Jilin shares many cultural traits with neighbouring parts of Northeast China, such as Errenzhuan and Yangge. In music, Jiju (Jilin Opera) is a traditional entertainment that Jilin has developed in its short history of migration. Jilin's ethnic Koreans have a distinct culture that is closely tied to Korea.

Studying in Changchun means living in a major university city and China's automobile capital, with good rail, air and road links. Come ready for a long, cold winter and a lively, well-connected urban setting.

jilin-normal-university.h: Jilin Normal University at a glance

blocks.x: Jilin Normal University (吉林师范大学, Jílín Shīfàn Dàxué; traditional Chinese 吉林師範大學) is located in Siping, a city in Jilin Province in northeast China. An older name, Siping Normal Institute (四平师范大学), may still turn up in documents. The university was founded in 1958 and is one of the places where teachers for Jilin Province are trained. Over recent years, seminars and classes of different kinds have helped it train upwards of 22,000 teachers.

The university has more than 920,000 square metres of land in total, with over 500,000 square metres of buildings. It is divided into 22 colleges and 2 teaching sections, and runs 27 research institutions and 117 laboratories.

The teaching staff number 1,493, of whom 994 are full-time teachers. They include 10 doctoral supervisors and 230 master's degree supervisors, and the faculty counts 212 professors and 210 associate professors. Between them they teach 55 undergraduate majors.
What surrounds a university shapes a student's life nearly as much as the campus itself, so the sections below introduce the province of Jilin, where Jilin Normal University stands.
In ancient times this was the homeland of the Xianbei, the Sushen, the Mohe, the Jurchens and the Wùjí (勿吉), and parts of it came under the rule of the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo.

Russia received Primorsky Krai in 1860, and the government afterwards invited Han Chinese settlers into Jilin, mostly from Shandong. By the early 1900s they formed the largest ethnic group in the region. Japan folded the area into Manchukuo, its puppet state, in 1932, with Changchun (then named Xinjing, and now the provincial capital) as Manchukuo's capital. When Japan was defeated in 1945, the Red Army took Jilin during Operation August Storm, and the Soviet Union passed it, along with the whole of northeastern China, to the Communists. From Manchuria as their base, the Communists later won the Chinese Civil War and took the remainder of the country.

Provincial borders have changed over time. In 1949 Jilin province was smaller, made up of just the areas around Changchun and Jilin City, with Jilin City as the capital and Changchun an independent municipality. The province was expanded in the 1950s to its present borders. In the Cultural Revolution it grew again to take in part of Inner Mongolia, which gave it a border with Mongolia, but that was later undone.

More recently, Jilin, like the rest of heavy-industry Northeast China, has faced economic difficulties linked to privatisation. The central government answered with a campaign it named "Revitalize the Northeast".

The central part of northeastern China is where Jilin lies, with Russia on its eastern border and North Korea on its southeastern one. About 24 million people live in the province, which measures 190,000 square kilometres (73,000 square miles). Changchun is the capital, 113 kilometres (70 miles) to the west of Jilin City. Other major cities are Siping, Yanji, Songyuan, Tonghua, Liaoyuan, Baishan and Baicheng.

Altitude is greatest in the southeast and falls gently toward the northwest. The Changbai Mountains, in the southeast, hold the province's highest peak, Paektu Mountain, which rises to 2,744 metres (9,003 feet). The Jilinhada, Zhang Guangcai and Longgang mountains are also part of the province.

The water systems are varied. The Yalu and Tumen rivers drain the extreme southeast, and together they form part of the border between China and North Korea. Tributaries of the Liao River drain the southwest, while the Songhua and Nen rivers drain the north and both eventually flow into the Amur.

Jilin has a northern, continental monsoon climate. Winters last long and are cold, whereas summers are warm but short. In January the average temperature runs from −20 to −14 °C (−4 to 7 °F). Annual rainfall is typically from 350 up to 1,000 mm (13.8 to 39.4 in). Be ready for severe winters, as in the rest of northeast China.

Jilin has rich mineral deposits: 136 types of mineral, of which 70 have been mined. It is also rich in resources for traditional Chinese medicine: about 27,000 kinds of wild plant grow here, 9,000 of which are medicinal herbs.

Among the province's large reserves are oil, gas and coal, iron, nickel and molybdenum, talc and graphite, gypsum and cement rock, and gold and silver. Its oil shale reserves are the largest of any province.

Nominal GDP for Jilin in 2025 came to RMB 1,497.4 billion, or US$209.6 billion. Since 2003 it has been growing at double-digit rates, and between 2003 and 2007 it rose by 51 percent. Per person, nominal GDP in 2025 climbed to RMB 64,618, equal to US$9,046. Compared with 2005, the value added and profit of large enterprises rose by 19 percent and 30 percent respectively.

The main crops are rice, wheat, maize and sorghum. Most rice is grown in the east (Yanbian Prefecture, for example). The Changbai Mountains are a significant source of lumber, and in the west, around Baicheng, herding sheep is an important activity. Jilin ranks as one of China's most important commodity grain bases and is 6th in timber production.

The province holds China's biggest shale oil reserves, and its mineral reserves are among the five largest in the country. Next to other provinces, it has especially large deposits of molybdenum, wollastonite, kieselguhr and floatstone. Cars, train carriages and iron alloy are the focus of industry.
The province has traditionally been a pharmaceutical centre. Its ginseng and deer antler yields are among the biggest in China, and both are widely used in Chinese medicine.
Several zones concentrate industry and investment:

The Jilin New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone was founded in 1992 in Jilin city. The planned area is 818 square kilometres (316 square miles), and 242 square kilometres (93 square miles) of that has been developed. Leading industries include electronics, medicine, bioengineering, new materials, refined chemical products and the integration of photoelectron and mechanical technology. Songhua Lake is only 14 kilometres (8.7 miles) away, and bus and train stations are within 3 kilometres (1.9 miles).

The Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone began in May 1998 in the northeast of Jilin city. The zone's planned area is 28 square kilometres (11 square miles). Changchun is 90 kilometres (56 miles) away, Jilin Airport 5 kilometres (3.1 miles) and Jilin Railway Station 8 kilometres (5.0 miles). Key industries include bioengineering, refined chemicals, and fine processing of both chemical fibre and farm products. It is split into four industrial parks: Chemical, Food, Textile and Medical. Health products, biological medicines, mini molecule medicine and traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals are the Medical Park's specialities.

Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone (CETDZ): the state approved it in 1993 as a state-level zone. Of its 112.72 square kilometres (43.52 square miles), 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) is reserved for development and use. At the end of 2006, 38.4 billion yuan had been invested in fixed assets, and 1,656 enterprises were registered there, 179 of them with foreign funding. The zone's regional gross product was 101.8 billion yuan, its industrial output value 233.0 billion yuan and its overall financial revenue 15.7 billion yuan.

Changchun hosts one of the largest factories where CRRC builds bullet trains. CRCC Changchun unveiled, in November 2016, carriages that were the first anywhere with sleeper berths for bullet trains, built to cope with extremely low temperatures. These "Panda" trains travel at 250 kmph, operate at −40 degrees Celsius, provide Wi-Fi hubs, and carry berths that fold up into seats during the day.

Changchun High-Tech Industrial Development Area: four roads and a single light-rail line join it with downtown. By light rail it takes twenty minutes to reach the nearest train station, Changchun Station. In 2002 it was the first area in Northeast China to qualify for ISO14001 environmental certification, and 38% of it is landscaped.

Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone: it received national-level approval as a border economic cooperation zone in 1992, and its planned area is 24 square kilometres (9.3 square miles). Inside it were created the Hunchun Sino-Russia Trade Zone (2001) and the Hunchun Export Processing Zone (2002). The location is strategic, where China, Russia and Korea meet. Seafood processing, bio-pharmaceuticals, electronics manufacture and textiles are among the industries it emphasises.

Hunchun Export Processing Zone: a 2.44 square kilometre (0.94 square mile) planned area, inside a 5 square kilometre (1.93 square mile) section of the border zone, sharing infrastructure and policies with the parent zone.

Han Chinese, Manchus, Hui, Mongols and Xibe live in Jilin. Ethnic Koreans, who make up about 4% of the population thanks to the closeness of the Korean Peninsula, live mostly in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture. The Manchu were once the majority here, since this is part of their historical homeland, but they adopted Han culture and Chinese languages, and the Manchu language is now considered critically endangered. The figures leave out members of the People's Liberation Army on active service.
Most people speak Mandarin, China's official language. Korean is widely spoken closer to the east, and some people in Qian Gorlos autonomous county speak Mongolian.

Jilin shares many cultural features with neighbouring parts of Northeast China, such as Errenzhuan and Yangge. Jilin Opera, called Jiju, is a traditional entertainment form that the province created during its relatively short history of migration. Jilin's ethnic Koreans have their own distinct culture, which is closely tied to Korea.
Jilin has several attractions:

At Ji'an you can see Goguryeo sites and tombs, among them Gungnae City, Hwando Mountain City and the pyramid-shaped Tomb of the General. They form part of a World Heritage Site called Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom.
Natural scenery draws visitors to Paektu Mountain, and in particular to Heaven Lake, which sits on the border with North Korea.
Balhae royal tombs, the Ancient Tombs at Longtou Mountain (the Mausoleum of Princess Jeonghyo is one), are in Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture.
The province has many universities and colleges. These include, in order from the best known:
Large general universities: Jilin University (吉林大学)
Teacher training: Northeast Normal University (东北师范大学), Jilin Normal University (吉林师范大学) and Changchun Normal University (长春师范大学)
Medicine and agriculture: Jilin Medical College (吉林医药学院), Jilin Agricultural University (吉林农业大学) and Jilin Agricultural Science and Technology University

Science and technology in Changchun: Changchun Institute of Technology (长春工程学院), the Changchun Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, and also Changchun University of Technology (长春工业大学) and Changchun University of Science and Technology (长春理工大学)
Other Changchun colleges: Changchun University (长春大学), Changchun Taxation College (长春税务学院) and Changchun Institute of Post & Telecommunications (长春邮政学院)
In Yanbian: Yanbian University (延边大学), along with Yanbian University of Science and Technology (延边科技大学)
Energy and elsewhere: Northeast China Institute of Electric Power Engineering (东北电力学院), Jilin College of Electrification and Beihua University
Local professional teams include:
Basketball: the Jilin Northeast Tigers, in the Chinese Basketball Association
Football: Changchun Yatai in the Chinese Super League, and Yanbian Longding in China League One

Jilin Normal University is a teacher-training institution founded in 1958, with a large campus and a broad range of undergraduate majors. It sits in a province with cold winters, rich natural resources, a strong car and rail industry, and a distinctive mix of Chinese, Manchu, Korean and Mongol cultures.
Jilin Normal University lists 41 programs for international students on this site: 20 bachelor, 20 master's, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 41 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 22,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 22,000), according to the university's published fee table.

40 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

jilin-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jilin Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Siping, register at Jilin Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

JLU, short for Jilin University, is a public university in Changchun, the capital of Jilin province in China's northeast. It reports to the Ministry of Education and is part of the national Double First-Class Construction, as well as Project 211 and Project 985, all of which single out leading universities.

It is described as a comprehensive, national key university, which in practice means a very large institution that teaches many subjects and takes part in national research priorities. Later sections give the numbers and then describe Changchun, the city where you would live.

Its origins lie in Harbin, in Heilongjiang, where it opened in 1946 under the name Northeast College of Administration. Over the decades it merged with many other institutions and changed its name repeatedly. In May 1948 the college joined Harbin University and became the Northeast Academy of Science. By November of that year the academy had moved to Shenyang in Liaoning and gone back to the name Northeast Administration College. It became Northeast People's University in 1950. During the Korean War the university was relocated to Changchun, in Jilin, and in 1958 it received the name Jilin University.

Five institutions were united in 2000 to form the current university: the earlier Jilin University, Norman Bethune University of Medical Sciences, Jilin University of Technology, Changchun Institute of Posts and Telecommunications, and Changchun University of Science and Technology, which dated from 1951. On August 29, 2004, the University of Military Logistics was merged in as well. An institute concentrating on projects of military interest was created inside the university in April 2006.
The result is a university whose structure reflects its history, with technology, medicine, communications and other fields that were once separate institutions now operating under one name.

The faculty numbers 6,657 people in total. Of them, 2,110 are professors and 1,618 act as doctoral advisors, and 43 belong to the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering (33 of those are adjunct members).

The university is organised into 47 colleges or schools, along with a number of institutions and affiliated organisations, grouped into 9 divisions. Specific names are best checked on the university's own website, because the structure is large and changes from time to time.
Rankings vary by method and are published every year, so the following gives an overall sense of where Jilin University stands rather than a fixed position.
Research output: the CWTS Leiden Ranking for 2024, based on publications from 2019 to 2022, placed Jilin University 19th in the world.
The SCImago Institutions Rankings put it 55th in the world in 2024.
In the Nature Index 2025 Annual Tables, which measure high-quality research published in 82 selected science journals, it was 15th among leading institutions globally.
The University Ranking by Academic Performance for 2024/25 put it 74th globally.
The Center for World University Rankings (CWUR) for 2025 listed it 194th worldwide and 42nd in Asia.

The differences between these positions are large because each list measures something different, such as publication counts, research quality or overall performance, so it helps to look at what each one actually tracks.
Changchun is where you would spend your time outside class, so here is a guide to its location, weather, people, economy and transport.

Changchun is in the middle of the Northeast China Plain. The municipality runs between latitudes 43° 05′ and 45° 15′ north and longitudes 124° 18′ and 127° 02' east. Altogether it covers 20,571 km2, or 7,943 sq mi. The metro areas make up 2,583 square kilometres (997 sq mi) of that, and the city proper just 159 km2 (61 sq mi).

The land is at a moderate height, between 250 and 350 metres (820 to 1,150 ft) across the administrative region. In the east, a small area of low mountains includes Laodaodong Mountain, 711 meters high, which is the highest point. The city also sits where the third east-west "Europe-Asia Continental Bridge" crosses, and the prefecture is dotted with 222 lakes and rivers. A small tributary of the Songhua River, the Yitong, runs through the city proper.

The climate is humid continental, influenced by the monsoon, with four seasons (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). Winters last from November to March and are long, cold and windy, yet dry, thanks to the Siberian anticyclone; January averages −14.3 °C (6.3 °F). The seasons either side are short periods of change, usually dry and windy but with a little precipitation. Summers are hot and humid, and the East Asian monsoon brings prevailing southeasterly winds; the July average is 23.7 °C (74.7 °F). Winter snow is usually light, and June to August bring most of the year's rain.

Sunshine is plentiful for much of the year: possible sunshine is 69 percent in February and 49 percent in July, for around 2,597 hours in a typical year. The frost-free period is 140 to 150 days. The record low is −36.5 °C (−34 °F), set on 4 January 1970, and the record high is 38.0 °C (100 °F), set on 9 July 1951. If you are coming from a warmer place, prepare for a real northern winter.

At the sixth Chinese census, in 2010, the city had 7.677 million people, and an estimate for 2011 gave 7.59 million. Births ran at 6.08 per thousand and deaths at 5.51 per thousand. The urban area was home to 3.53 million people, and the sex ratio in 2010 was 102.10 males for every 100 females.
As in most of Northeast China, the Han people form the great majority, at 96.57 percent, with several minority nationalities making up the rest.

The common dialect is Northeastern Mandarin, which grew out of a blend of languages brought by immigrants from Shandong and Hebei. Rapid economic growth after the People's Republic was founded then drew a great many migrants from elsewhere. Their influence made the northeastern dialect in urban Changchun closer to standard Mandarin than the rural version, which is helpful if you are learning Chinese.

Religious life centres on four faiths, namely Islam, Christianity, Taoism and Buddhism, and the authorities have approved 396 places for worship and religious activity. Buddhist and Taoist temples include Pumen Temple, Changchun Temple, Big Buddha Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple and Changchun Wanshou Temple. The Catholic church, the Christian church on West Wuma Road and the city mosque, all in Changchun, serve other communities. Many Manchus once practised shamanism, which circulated widely in Northeast China in ancient times, and today it and its study are an important part of the region's cultural heritage.

The Jilin Provincial Museum has the rating of a national first-grade museum. It came to Changchun from Jilin City after the provincial government moved. Its old home was in the centre of the old town, and a new building, finished in 2016 after nine years of construction, stands on the outskirts in Nanguan District, close to Jingyuetan Park.

Badabu is a group of former buildings of the eight ministries of Manchukuo: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs and Civil Affairs. Its mix of Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian architecture has recently turned it into a sightseeing highlight.
To the southeast, Jingyuetan National Forest Park is rated an AAAAA Tourist Attraction of China, and it hosts Vasaloppet China every year.
The figures below come from 2010 to 2012 and are therefore dated; use them to understand the scale and structure of the economy rather than as current statistics.

In 2010 Changchun's GDP was RMB332.9 billion, a 15.3 percent rise on the year before. The primary sector grew 3.3 percent to RMB25.27 billion; the secondary sector grew 19.0 percent to RMB171.99 billion; and the tertiary sector grew 12.6 percent to RMB135.64 billion. For 2012, GDP per capita was ¥58,691, or $9338, and total GDP was RMB445.66 billion, 12.0 percent higher than in 2011. In that year the primary sector reached RMB31.71 billion (up 4.3 percent), the secondary sector RMB229.19 billion (up 13.1 percent) and the tertiary sector RMB184.76 billion (up 11.8 percent).

Leading industries include automobiles, agricultural processing, biopharmaceuticals, photoelectronics, construction materials and energy. In 2009 Changchun produced 9 percent of China's cars, which made it the country's largest centre for automobile manufacturing, research and development.

FAW (First Automotive Works) Group is headquartered here and is China's largest vehicle producer. China's first truck, in 1956, and first car, in 1958, came from FAW. Its factories and the housing and services around them fill a large part of the city's southwest. The Red Flag luxury brand is built in Changchun, together with vehicles from joint ventures with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. FAW sold 2.65 million units in 2012 and took RMB 408.46 billion in sales revenue, up 10.8%. Because the industry started here, one of Changchun's best-known nicknames is "China's Detroit".

Transport equipment and machinery are also major industries. About half of China's passenger trains (50 percent) and 10 percent of its tractors are built in Changchun. Changchun Railway Vehicles, a main division of CRRC, has a joint venture with Bombardier Transportation making Movia metro cars for the Tianjin, Shanghai and Guangzhou metros. CRRC also builds most of its bullet-train carriages in the city. In November 2016 the factory presented bullet-train carriages with sleeper berths, a world first, which allows such trains to be used on overnight journeys. The new trains are nicknamed "Panda". They can travel at 250 km/h and run in temperatures down to −40 degrees Celsius, and each has Wi-Fi and berths that fold up into ordinary seats during the day.

Foreign direct investment in 2012 was US$3.68 billion, a rise of 19.6%. Coca-Cola opened a bottling plant in the city's ETDZ in 2004, investing US$20 million. The city holds annual events including the Changchun International Automobile Fair, the Changchun Film Festival, the Changchun Agricultural Fair, an Education Exhibition and a Sculpture Exhibition.
Other large companies in Changchun include:
Jilin Grain Group, a major grain processor.

Yatai Group, a conglomerate founded in 1993, which became a listed company on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1995. Its businesses range across property development, cement, securities, coal mining, pharmaceuticals and trading.
#### Automotive trade zone

The Changchun Automotive Trade Center started in 1993 and was re-established in 1996 as the Changchun Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone. It is in the southwest of the city, beside the Changchun Film ThemeCity and the FAW Group's China First Automobile Works, and its area is about 300,000 square metres, or 3,229,173 square feet. The zone contains an exhibition center and five industrial centers. One of these, the Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center (open since 1994), is the biggest market for vehicles and spare parts in China. The others cover used cars, industrial and commercial vehicles, and tire wholesale.
#### High technology zone

The Changchun High Technology Development Zone, one of the first 27 state-level advanced technology zones, is in the south of the city and covers 49 km2 (19 sq mi). It includes 11 key national laboratories, 39 state and provincial research institutions and 18 full-time universities and colleges, and its focus is on five industries: bio-engineering, automobile engineering, new materials, photo-electricity and information technology.
#### Economic and technological development zone

The Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone began in April 1993 and has all the preferential policies that apply to development zones in coastal open cities. It measures 112.72 square kilometres in all (43.52 square miles), and 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of that is reserved for development. The zone is 5 kilometres (3 miles) from downtown. The freight railway station is 2 km (1.2 mi) away, and the international airport is 15 km (9 mi) away.

The five leading industries are automotive parts and components, photoelectric information, bio-pharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials. More than 80 percent of output comes from high-tech and high value-added projects. By 2006 total fixed assets investment had risen to RMB38.4 billion, and of the 1656 enterprises registered, 179 were foreign-funded. Industrial output reached RMB 277 billion in 2007.

The city is both a major grain-producing base and a regional air and rail hub, so it has developed a specialised Aviation Food Industrialization Base. The base provides prepared meals to several airlines and does research in food science for long-haul flights, a niche manufacturing sector.

Two major rail stations serve passengers. Changchun railway station (长春站 in simplified Chinese, 長春站 in traditional), in the centre, takes all conventional trains and some high-speed ones, and it connects via the Beijing-Harbin Railway, the Changchun-Hunchun intercity railway and various other lines. Trains leave several times a day for cities within the province and the northeast, including Harbin, Shenyang, Dalian, Jilin City and Yanji, and for major cities across the country such as Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou.

The new Changchun West railway station is at the western end of the urbanised area and is the station mainly used by high-speed trains of the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway. Changchun East is a small station in Erdao District, on the Changchun-Tumen line.
The city has a comprehensive bus system of more than 250 routes, and most buses charge 1 to 2 yuan per ride.

Changchun is one of a few Chinese cities that keep a historic tram system. It first ran in 1941 and, at its peak, had 6 lines that covered almost 53 km. Route changes since then have left only one line from the 2000s onward, though a branch opened in 2014 to serve the new Changchun West Railway Station. The bus system now operates the trams too.

Changchun Rail Transit combines light rail and metro lines. The first line opened on 30 October 2002, which made Changchun the fifth big city in China to have rail transit. By November 2018 there were 5 lines (Lines 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8), covering about 100.17 kilometers.

By September 2019 four projects were under construction: Line 6 and Line 9, the Line 2 West Extension and the Line 3 East Extension. The plan was for a network of 10 lines and 341.62 kilometers by 2025, so the actual network may now be larger than the figures above.

The average daily passenger volume in September 2019 was 680,400, and the busiest day of the line network was 13 November 2019, with 830,500 passengers. Total passenger volume for 2019 was estimated at about 168 million.

The main expressways linking Changchun to the national network are the Beijing-Harbin Expressway (G1), the Ulanhot-Changchun-Jilin-Hunchun Expressway (G12), the Changchun-Shenzhen Expressway (G25) and the Changchun-Changbaishan Expressway (S1). The Changchun-Jilin North Highway is the busiest section in the province, linking its two biggest cities and acting as the trunk line for their social and economic communication.

Private cars are increasingly common, and the streets are congested. Compared with other cities in the northeast, bicycles are relatively rare, but mopeds and pedal-powered vehicles are fairly common.

Changchun Longjia International Airport is 31.2 kilometres (19.4 miles) northeast of the urban area. Building started in 1998 to replace Changchun Dafangshen Airport, an older airport, shared between civil and military use, that dated from 1941. Passenger service began on 27 August 2005, and nearby Jilin City and Changchun share its operation.

The Nature Index 2024 Science Cities puts Changchun among the world's top 30 cities for scientific research. Its 27 regular institutions of full-time higher education enrol about 160,000 students altogether. Two of China's key universities, Northeast Normal University and Jilin University, are here, and JLU is one of the country's largest universities, with over 60,000 students.

The city around it, Changchun, is an industrial and scientific centre known for cars and railway vehicles, with a long, cold winter, a growing rail transit network and a lively mix of museums, parks and historic buildings. Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Changchun, register at Jilin University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Jinan University, usually shortened to JNU and written 暨南大学 in Chinese, is a state-run national university based in Guangzhou, the provincial capital of Guangdong in southern China. Responsibility is shared: the Communist Party's United Front Work Department, the Ministry of Education and the Guangdong provincial government all take part in managing it. The university belongs to the national Double First-Class Construction scheme and to Project 211, and it is one of 13 institutions that Guangdong designates as High-Level Universities.

For an international applicant the most relevant thing about JNU is its long habit of welcoming students from abroad. The university presents itself as the pioneer among Chinese universities in admitting overseas students, and it ranks among the institutions in China with the biggest international enrolments. That history explains why the campus has so many services, courses and student communities built around people who did not grow up in mainland China. If you are weighing several Guangzhou universities, this tradition is probably the clearest point of difference.

jinan-university.h: A school for overseas Chinese that grew into a national university

blocks.x: The story begins in 1906, when Duanfang, then Viceroy of Liangjiang, asked the Guangxu Emperor to approve a school for the children of overseas Chinese communities. The idea was to carry education outwards and to keep emotional ties alive between China and its compatriots living abroad. The emperor agreed, and Duanfang is remembered as the founder. Jinan Academy opened in Nanjing on 23 March 1907, the first institution of its kind in China and the start of a tradition of overseas Chinese education.

Over the next decades the school moved several times. It relocated to Shanghai, took the title National Jinan University in 1927, and was evacuated to Fujian Province during the war against Japan. After 1949 the university was dissolved and its faculties were folded into other institutions, Fudan University among them. It was reopened in Guangzhou in 1958, which is why the Guangzhou campus is now its home.
The key dates, in order, are these.
1906 to 1907: Jinan Academy is proposed and then founded in Nanjing.
1918: the academy moves to Shanghai.
1927: it is renamed National Jinan University.
1941 to 1946: wartime conditions force the university to relocate to Fujian Province.
1949: the university is dissolved and its schools are absorbed by Fudan University and Jiaotong University, among others.
1958: it is re-established in Guangzhou.
1983: it becomes a national pioneer in using a credit system.
1996: it passes the preliminary review for Project 211 and enters the list of leading universities slated for priority development in the twenty-first century.
2001: new colleges open, including Journalism and Communication, Information Science and Technology, Foreign Studies, Pharmacy, Law and the International School.
2002: with State Council approval, it joins the first group of universities to run an EMBA programme.
2006: the centenary is celebrated.
2011: the Graduate School is set up.
2014: a new campus opens in the Guangzhou Higher Education Mega Center.
In short, JNU is more than a century old but has been a Guangzhou institution only since 1958, and its modern campus network was built mostly in the last twenty-five years.

The two characters of Jinan mean roughly 'reaching southward'. The phrase is drawn from an ancient Chinese historical classic, the Classic of History, where it describes teaching and customs spreading out from China to the wider world. It matched the founders' original goal of sending Chinese learning and culture south from the old capital region to communities overseas.

jinan-university.h: Where you will study: the campuses

blocks.x: JNU is spread over several sites, five in China and one in Japan. Which one you attend depends on your programme, so check the location of your college before arranging housing.
Main campus in Tianhe District, Guangzhou
College of Chinese Language and Culture, also in Tianhe District
Panyu campus in Panyu, Guangzhou
Zhuhai campus in Xiangzhou District, Zhuhai
Tourism College in Nanshan District, Shenzhen
Japan campus in Toshima, Tokyo

The university is organised into 38 colleges, which together contain 59 departments and offer 108 undergraduate majors. The source figures are not perfectly consistent, because one line also mentions 55 departments, of which 43 grant master's degrees and 19 grant doctorates, so treat the exact counts as approximate and confirm them with the university. Behind the teaching sits a research base of 182 institutes and 77 laboratories, plus 15 postdoctoral research stations.

The research profile is broad. JNU holds four national key disciplines, eight that are recognised by the State Council's Overseas Chinese Affairs Office, 20 first-level key disciplines of Guangdong Province and four second-level ones. Among its designated bases are a national key centre for humanities and social science research, a Ministry of Education base for Chinese language and literature, a national base for cultural quality education, a national base for the teaching of Chinese to foreigners, and an education base for overseas Chinese work run with the State Council office. At provincial level there is another humanities and social science research base. On the engineering side it has one national engineering centre, seven engineering centres at ministerial and provincial level, and eleven key laboratories at those levels.

There are 50,535 students in total, made up of 10,767 graduate students and 22,527 undergraduates. A further group of 13,512 comes from outside the mainland: foreign nationals, overseas Chinese, and residents of Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan. Put simply, roughly one student in four is international or of overseas origin, so you will not be an exception on campus. The current Party secretary is Sun Yu and the president is Xing Feng.

jinan-university.h: Colleges and schools you might apply to

blocks.x: The range of academic units is wide. The main ones are listed here, roughly from humanities to sciences and professional fields.
International School

Law School, which includes intellectual property

College of Life Science and Technology

International Business School

School of Environment and School of Marxism
The Jinan University and University of Birmingham Joint Institute
School of Mechanics and Construction Engineering
College of Chemistry and Materials Science
Three of these deserve a closer look for overseas applicants.

This college teaches programmes entirely in English. It was created to serve the growing number of overseas Chinese and foreign applicants, along with some high-performing students from within China. The undergraduate options include International Journalism, Food Science and Engineering, Computer Science, International Economics and Trade, Clinical Medicine, Accounting (offered with CPA Canada), Pharmacy, Public Administration, Finance, and the MBBS medical degree.

Students can also join short or long exchange and visiting arrangements with partner universities in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Germany, France, Australia and New Zealand, which is useful if you want international experience on your record.

Building on JNU's humanities tradition, the school aims to rank among China's leading business schools, combining an understanding of Chinese culture and globalisation with modern management teaching. Its MBA programmes received international AMBA accreditation in 2011.

jinan-university.h: The College of Chinese Language and Culture

blocks.x: This college holds two official designations. The Ministry of Education calls it a National Base for Teaching Chinese as a Foreign Language, and the State Council's Overseas Chinese Affairs Office calls it an Overseas Chinese Education Base. It is regarded as the leading unit in South China for Chinese as a second language and for overseas Chinese education. If your plan begins with language study, this is the natural starting point.

Its structure includes departments for second-language and foreign-learner Chinese, overseas Chinese education and applied linguistics, a pre-university department, a correspondence course department, two research bodies on overseas Chinese education, and an internet and educational technology centre.
JNU is one of China's oldest universities and sits among the Double First-Class institutions. Its own list of achievements includes the following.
It was the earliest Chinese institution to admit overseas students.
It was the first to enrol students in both the spring and autumn semesters.
It pioneered the credit system in China.
It claims the largest overseas student population of any Chinese university.
It says it is the only Chinese university with alumni who have become national leaders both in China and in other countries.

Academic exchange is a routine part of university life here. JNU has cooperation or exchange arrangements with over 180 universities and research institutes across Asia, the Americas, Europe and Oceania. One example is a Sino-Malaysian think tank formed with City University in Malaysia within the Belt and Road Initiative. The university also reports 57 regional alumni associations around the world, which can be helpful for networking and for finding graduates working in your home region.
JNU's graduates include politicians, scholars, artists and athletes from mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao and Southeast Asia. A selection follows.
Wu Xueqian, a former Chinese Foreign Minister

Jack C. K. Teng, who worked as an educator, writer, politician, diplomat and pioneer of the Olympic movement
