jinan-university.h: Living in Guangzhou: what the city offers

blocks.x: Most of your daily routine will depend on the city around the campus, meaning its climate, its economy, how people move about and what there is to see. The sections below describe Guangzhou.

The old centre of Guangzhou grew up near Baiyun Mountain on the eastern bank of the Pearl River, known in Chinese as the Zhujiang. It lies about 130 kilometres (80 miles) upstream from the point where the river meets the South China Sea, and some 300 miles below the head of navigation. The river mouth is guarded at the Humen Strait, and from there the city looked out over the fertile delta plain of the Pearl. Today's municipality covers 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 square miles) on both sides of the river, between roughly 112 degrees 57 minutes and 114 degrees 03 minutes east and 22 degrees 26 minutes and 23 degrees 56 minutes north, in the south-central part of Guangdong. The Pearl is China's fourth-largest river. Tidal flats along the estuary support intertidal ecosystems, although many have been reclaimed for farmland. Baiyun Mountain is nicknamed the city's lung.
The land rises from southwest to northeast: mountains form the city's back, and the sea lies in front. The highest point is Tiantang Peak, 1,210 metres or 3,970 feet above sea level.

Guangzhou is in a water-rich part of southern China. Rivers and channels cover about 10 percent of the municipal area, or 74,400 hectares (10.05 percent of the land area), and they soften the landscape and help keep the urban environment ecologically steady. The main waterways are the Beijiang, the northern main stream of the Dongjiang, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi, the Baini, the Guangzhou reach of the Pearl River, the Shiqiao waterway and the Shawan waterway.

The city has relatively little water that originates locally, about 7.979 billion cubic metres, of which 7.881 billion is surface water and 1.487 billion groundwater. Based on the 2010 census that works out at around 628 cubic metres per person, half the national figure, or 1.0601 million cubic metres per square kilometre. Much more water simply passes through: roughly 186.024 billion cubic metres a year, about 23 times the local supply. Of this, 159.15 billion arrives from the Xijiang and Beijiang rivers, 14.203 billion from the Dongjiang and 2.828 billion from the upper Zengjiang, and the flow concentrates in the southern districts. In the south the river network is tidal, with strong runoff. Water leaves toward the South China Sea through three outlets, Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili, into the Lingding Ocean. Over a year the flood tide brings in about 271 billion cubic metres and the ebb takes out around 408.8 billion, and the three outlets carry an annual runoff of 137.7 billion, part of which is usable fresh water.

The ground beneath the city is geologically complex and favourable to mineral formation. Forty-seven (47) kinds of mineral have been found, across 820 sites and 25 medium and large mining areas, and 18 oil deposits of medium or large size are counted among them. The main products are construction granite, cement limestone, ceramic clay, potassium, feldspar, salt, manganese, nepheline, fluorite, marble, mineral water and geothermal water. Energy and non-ferrous metal resources are scarce, scattered and small, and their grades are unstable.

Farming reflects the shift from tropical to subtropical conditions. The region is among China's richest in fruit, with tropical, subtropical and temperate species spread over 41 families, 82 genera and 174 species and totalling more than 500 varieties, among them 55 main varieties of lychee. It is regarded as the centre of origin for lychee, longan, wampee and Chinese olive. Vegetables total 15 main categories, 127 species and over 370 varieties, and the area also produces flowers, ornamental plants, grain, cash crops, livestock, poultry and aquatic products. Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first Guangzhou product to receive a geographical indication.

Although it sits just below the Tropic of Cancer, Guangzhou has a humid subtropical climate driven by the East Asian monsoon. Summers are hot, wet and sticky, and the monsoon season is long, running from April to September. Winters are mild and fairly dry. January averages 13.8 degrees Celsius (56.8 F) and July 28.9 degrees (84.0 F), giving a yearly mean of 22.4 degrees (72.3 F). Humidity averages about 76 percent, and the metropolitan area receives more than 1,950 millimetres (77 inches) of rain annually.

Sunshine is modest, 1,559 hours a year, well below nearby Shenzhen and Hong Kong, with possible sunshine going from 17 percent in March up to 51 percent in October. The most comfortable months are October to December, which are cool, breezy and moderate, and these are considered the best time to travel. Since 1951 the official range has run from 0 degrees on 11 February 1957 and again on 23 December 1999 to 39.1 degrees (102.4 F) on 1 July 2004. Older unofficial readings go lower: minus 5.0 degrees (23.0 F) on 18 January 1893, which modern meteorologists think was closer to minus 3.0 (26.6 F), and minus 0.3 (31.5 F) on 8 December 1934 at a Huangpu District station that began records in 1912. Snow last fell on 24 January 2016, 87 years after the previous fall. For planning, pack for heat and humidity in the warm half of the year and expect little cold in winter.

Guangzhou is the main manufacturing hub of the Pearl River Delta, a leading commercial and industrial region of China. Its 2021 GDP reached 2,823 billion yuan (444.37 billion US dollars nominal), second in South-Central China after Shenzhen, and GDP per head was 151,162 yuan (23,794 dollars). It counts as one of the country's most prosperous cities. The 2020 Hurun Global Rich List placed it tenth in the world and fifth in China for billionaires, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen, and the 2020 Global Financial Centers Index put it 21st worldwide and eighth in Asia and Oceania.

Looking ahead, Oxford Economics projects Guangzhou to be among the ten largest cities in the world by nominal GDP in 2035, alongside Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, with GDP per person above 42,000 US dollars by 2030. Fast industrialisation once left the city badly polluted, but green urban planning since then has made it one of the more liveable cities in China.

For students, this economic weight matters in two ways. It means a wide pool of employers, trade fairs and foreign companies close to the university, and it means the city has a long record of dealing with newcomers from other regions and countries, which is reflected in the population figures that follow.

Zhujiang New Town, covering 6.44 square kilometres in Tianhe District, is the twenty-first-century central business district and home to several financial institutions. Guangzhou is also a magnet for foreign firms: by 2018 more than 30,000 foreign-invested companies had settled there, with projects from 297 Fortune Global 500 companies and regional or global headquarters of 120 of them.

The city's best-known event is the Canton Fair, officially the China Import and Export Fair, held each April and October. First staged in spring 1957, it is China's oldest, highest-level and largest trade fair. From its 104th session it moved from the older Liuhua complex to the Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center in Pazhou, which is served by two stations on Metro Line 8, one on Line 11 and three on Tram Line THZ1. It is now organised in three phases rather than two.

Local specialities include Cantonese cuisine, one of China's best-known regional cuisines, summed up by a saying that you should 'eat in Guangzhou'. There is also Cantonese carving in jade, wood and ivory, colourful Canton porcelain developed as an export ware over about three centuries, Cantonese embroidery (one of China's four main styles), and Zhujiang Beer, a pale lager that is among the country's most successful brands.
Industrial areas and economic zones include the following.
GAC Group, the automotive company
Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone

Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone, founded in 2005 with a planned area of 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 square miles). It is in Nansha District, 54 kilometres (about a 70-minute drive) south of Baiyun International Airport, near Nansha Port and on Metro Line 4 as it is extended toward the Nansha ferry terminal. It encourages automobile assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry.

Guangzhou Free Trade Zone, founded in 1992 in eastern Huangpu District, close to the development zone and the airport. Its core activities are international trade, logistics, processing and software, and it has added AI, new materials, new energy, new mobility, information and communication technology and new transport. The area is now marketed under the name Huangpu District and also houses the Guangzhou IP Court.
Guangzhou Science City

At the end of 2024 Guangzhou had 18.978 million permanent residents, and 87.24 percent of them lived in urban areas. The 2020 census counted 18,676,605 residents on 1 November 2020, up 5,975,805 (47.05 percent) from 12,700,800 in 2010. Of these, 16,096,724 (86.19 percent) were urban and 2,579,881 (13.81 percent) rural. Migration shapes the city: 11,522,907 people were living away from their registered household location, a group that includes 9,378,825 members of the floating population, which makes Guangzhou one of China's biggest destinations for internal migrants.

For comparison, a 2014 estimate gave 13,080,500 residents with 11,264,800 in urban areas, about 1,800 people per square kilometre. The built-up area merges directly with neighbouring cities. The Pearl River Delta urban zone covers about 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 square miles) and has been estimated to hold 22 million people, counting Guangzhou's nine urban districts, Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890 thousand) and Huizhou's Huiyang District (760 thousand). With adjacent Hong Kong included the agglomeration exceeds 28 million. Strong demand for labour has created a large floating population, with up to ten million migrants living in the area for at least six months each year, and around five million of Guangzhou's residents in 2008 were migrant workers. An OECD estimate put the wider metropolitan area at 25 million in 2010.

A 2018 study of the city's growth from 1990 to 2020 describes how, in 1990, developed housing was concentrated in a small western part of Guangzhou, with farmland and forest elsewhere. From 2005 onward, residential areas spread, and by 2020 developed neighbourhoods ran from west to east, while the far south and much of the north remained mainly agricultural or wooded.

jinan-university.h: Getting around and faith in the city

blocks.x: Besides the metro, Guangzhou has sea links. High-speed catamarans run daily from the Nansha Ferry Terminal and the Lianhua Shan terminal in Guangzhou to the Hong Kong China Ferry Terminal, and also from Nansha to the Macau ferry pier in Hong Kong.

Before modern times Guangzhou had roughly 124 religious pavilions, halls and temples. Today there are Buddhist and Taoist associations, a Jewish community, and a history with Christianity, which was reintroduced to China through colonial powers.

jinan-university.h: Putting it together: is Jinan a good fit?

blocks.x: Pulling the main threads together, Jinan University offers a very international student body, a long record in teaching Chinese to non-native speakers, an English-taught International School, and a base in one of China's richest and most connected cities. Those are real advantages if you are an overseas or ethnic Chinese applicant who wants support structures that already exist rather than ones you have to invent for yourself.

There are also practical points to settle before you apply. The university is spread over several campuses in Guangzhou, Zhuhai and Shenzhen, so confirm which one hosts your college and whether you can live on it. The reported statistics about departments differ from one line to another, so ask the admissions office for current figures instead of relying on any single number. And because Guangzhou is hot and humid for much of the year but rarely cold, you can plan your wardrobe around heat rather than winter coats.

Finally, compare the International School, the College of Chinese Language and Culture and the regular Chinese-taught colleges on tuition, language requirements and scholarships, then choose the route that matches your goals and your budget.
Jinan University lists 373 programs for international students on this site: 74 bachelor, 180 master's, 92 doctoral, 27 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 354 taught in Chinese, 19 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 19,000 to CNY 29,000 (median CNY 22,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 34,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.

373 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (3):
Biology and Medicine
Business Administration
Chinese Studies (Law)

Jinan University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.
Application windows found for Jinan University:
Autumn 2026 undergraduate intake (closed): opens 15 Jan 2026, closes 31 May 2026
Deadlines can move and seats can fill earlier than the closing date, so apply as soon as your documents are ready.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

jinan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jinan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guangzhou, register at Jinan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

jingdezhen-ceramic-university.h: Jingdezhen Ceramic University: a school for porcelain

blocks.x: Jingdezhen Ceramic University (景德镇陶瓷大学) is in the city of Jingdezhen, Jiangxi Province, and is China's only higher education institution devoted to the ceramic arts. Jingdezhen has long been central to Chinese ceramics, in both the development and the production of the craft. In effect, the university is where present-day teaching methods and infrastructure meet a wellspring of age-old Chinese tradition. The artist Jackson Li is one of its better-known graduates.
Everyday life as a student depends on the city outside the campus: how hot it gets, how you travel and what you can do. Jingdezhen is described below, followed by the province of Jiangxi.

jingdezhen-ceramic-university.h: Where it is and what is under the ground

blocks.x: Jingdezhen is in the north-east of Jiangxi, next to Anhui, and the urban centre lies at the north-eastern end of the Poyang Lake Plain. Its total area is 5,256 km2, or 2,029 sq mi. The highest point reaches 1,618 m, or 5,308 ft, while the plains in the south average 200 m, or 660 ft, above sea level.

A number of cities and counties lie between Jiangxi and Anhui around it. Dongzhi, Xiuning and Qimen County in Anhui are to the north, north-west and north-east. Wannian County and Yiyang County are to the south, Boyang County is to the west, and Wuyuan County and Dexing City are to the south-east.

The prefecture's natural resources are kaolin, coal, manganese and lime. Kaolin has since turned up in many places around the world, but it was the kilns of Jingdezhen that first perfected the use of kaolin together with petuntse to make world-class hard-paste porcelain. The word 'kaolin' comes from the transcription by the French Jesuit d'Entrecolles of the local term gāolǐngtǔ (高嶺土), and the term in turn comes from Gaoling (高嶺, Gāolǐng), a village within Ehu Town in Fuliang County. For the first half of the Qing dynasty, most of Jingdezhen's kaolin came from that village.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) and shaped by the East Asian monsoon. Summers are long, humid and very hot; winters are cool and drier with the occasional cold snap. The 24-hour average temperature is 5.6 °C, or 42.1 °F, in January and 29.1 °C, or 84.4 °F, in July, and the annual mean is 17.81 °C, or 64.1 °F. Yearly precipitation averages 1,805 mm, or 71.1 in.

The city gets 1,798 hours of bright sunshine a year, with the share of possible sunshine ranging from 25% in March to 56% in August. Winter opens fairly sunny and dry but turns steadily wetter and cloudier. Spring begins especially gloomy, and every month from March to July averages over 190 mm, or 7.5 in, of rain. Summer is the sunniest season, and autumn stays warm to mild and relatively dry. Readings above 40 °C, or 104 °F, have been recorded at the top end, and minimums below −10 °C, or 14 °F, at the bottom.

Jingdezhen is an important industrial and commercial base within Jiangxi. In 2018 its GDP was 92.611 billion yuan, with the primary sector contributing 6.62%, the secondary sector 44.22% and the tertiary sector the largest slice, 49.16%.

Incomes in 2018 were ¥37,183 per head in disposable terms for urban residents, which put the city third among Jiangxi's prefecture-level divisions, after Nanchang and Xinyu. Rural residents' disposable income was ¥16,510, fourth in the province behind Pingxiang, Xinyu and Nanchang. The city's public budget revenue that year was ¥8.98555 billion against expenditure of ¥20.43550 billion.
Important industrial enterprises in the city include Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, Jingdezhen Ceramics and Jingdezhen Refrigeration Compressor.

Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, set up in 1969, belongs to the Aviation Industry Corporation of China. Most of what it sells are helicopters for the People's Liberation Army. Customers abroad include Boeing, Sikorsky and Leonardo, and Changhe makes aircraft parts for the Boeing 767-300BCF.
Another Changhe, Jiangxi Changhe Automobile Co Ltd, is a car maker owned by BAIC Group and based in the city. Output for 2019 was forecast at 53,400 vehicles.

The most famous of the local ceramics firms is Jingdezhen Ceramics Co Ltd (景德镇陶瓷股份有限公司), run as a joint venture with a French company. In February 2002 the then General Secretary of the CCP, Jiang Zemin, gave U.S. President George W. Bush a porcelain set made by the company under its Hongye (红叶) brand.
Across China, the Jingdezhen Refrigeration Compressor Company has a name for its non-Eph refrigeration compressor, of which it sells about 20% of the national market.
Jiangxi's agriculture leans heavily on Jingdezhen, where rice is widely grown. The area also produces commodity grain, pigs and cotton.

Fuliang County has large tea plantations and processing plants, and its tea is famous across China. The Tang dynasty poet Bai Juyi wrote a poem in which a woman complains that her merchant husband loved money more than family and had gone off the month before to buy tea in Fuliang, which suggests the area's tea was already celebrated a thousand years ago. Fuliang's 'Fuhong' brand tea won a golden prize at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in 1915.

Leping City, nicknamed the 'Vegetable Township of South China', grows and processes vegetables on a large scale for Jiangxi and even for the whole of China, and its output and sales matter greatly to the provincial farm economy. The figures available say that in 2007 Leping had 1.7 million hectares under cultivation, producing 620,000 tons in total (a figure that looks too big for a county-level city, so check it against local statistics). China's Agriculture Ministry named Leping a demonstration zone for 'pollution-free' vegetable production.

Jingdezhen is the most important transport hub in north-eastern Jiangxi. Historically the Chang River was the main line of communication. Porcelain went by boat downriver to Poyang Lake, joined the Yangtze at Hukou County in Jiangxi, and from there could be taken to the coast and exported. These days the city is linked with the rest of China by road, rail and air.
The city is on three main roads:
The G206, running from Yantai in Shandong to Shantou in Guangdong
The G56 Hangzhou-Ruili Highway, from Hangzhou in Zhejiang to Ruili in Yunnan
The G35, running from Jinan in Shandong to Guangzhou in Guangdong

The Anhui-Jiangxi Railway ties Jingdezhen to many key cities: Shanghai, Nanjing, Hefei, Jinan and Qingdao in the north and east, and Guangzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, Nanchang, Kunming and Guiyang elsewhere. The Jiujiang-Jingdezhen-Quzhou Railway was still under construction at the time of writing; once finished, the two lines will cross at Jingdezhen and make it an important rail hub for Jiangxi and East China. Jingdezhen Railway Station stands in the city centre, under the control of the Nanchang Railway Bureau.

The city's airport, Jingdezhen Luojia, is found at Luojian Village to the north-west, about 8 km, or 5.0 mi, from downtown. CAAC statistics show the airport handled 189,256 passengers in 2008, which ranked 81st among Chinese airports. Annual cargo and mail came to 119.8 tons and landings to 2,424, ranking 111th and 91st nationally.

Domestic destinations, with the airline code in brackets, are Xi'an (ZH), Xiamen (CA), Kunming (MU), Fuzhou (ZH), Hangzhou (MU), Chengdu (CA), Shenzhen (ZH), Guangzhou (ZH), Shanghai (ZH) and Beijing (CA). No international flights operate here. In Jiangxi only Nanchang has a larger airport.

Until the 1980s Jingdezhen had just one bus line, running 7 kilometres, or 4.3 miles, from Huang-ni-tou to Nan-men-tou. There was no taxi service, and the buses were channel-type vehicles that could carry a hundred passengers or more at a time; they were replaced at the end of the 1990s once they had reached the end of their service lives.

Today buses and taxis are the two main ways to get around. Over 20 public bus lines cross the city and countryside, and taxis are plentiful, with fares starting at ¥8 for the first 2 kilometres, or 1.2 miles.

For education there are 328 primary schools, 110 secondary schools, 4 special education schools and 4 institutions of higher education. Those four are Jingdezhen Ceramic Institute (JCI), Jingdezhen College, the Jiangxi Ceramic Arts and Crafts Vocational and Technical College (江西陶瓷工艺美术职业技术学院) and the Jingdezhen Ceramic Vocational and Technical College (景德镇陶瓷职业技术学院). One of the secondary schools, No.1 Middle School of Jingdezhen, opened in 1940 and has a reputation, compared with other Jiangxi schools, for how many of its students get into Chinese colleges.

Tourism is big business. Jingdezhen is one of Jiangxi's major tourist destinations, with 85.063 million visitors in 2018. Many attractions relate to its ceramics, including the Ancient Kiln Folk Customs Museum, a 5A attraction; another 8 are rated 4A and 14 rated 3A. From the city you can also reach well-known areas nearby, such as Lushan, Huangshan and Wuyuan. Jingdezhen has more tourist hotels than any other city in Jiangxi, including one quasi-five-star hotel and two four-star hotels, besides many three-star and other ordinary ones.
A province shapes student life nearly as much as the campus does, so here is a profile of Jiangxi.

Jiangxi is built around the Gan River valley, historically the main north-south transport route in southern China. The Gan corridor is one of the few easy routes across the mountainous, rugged terrain of the south-east, and traders and messengers used it to travel between modern Guangdong in the south and the North China Plain and Yangtze valley in the north. That is why Jiangxi has been of strategic importance for much of China's history.

During the Shang dynasty (16th to 11th centuries BC), the region was beyond the reach of early Chinese civilisation, and it was probably inhabited by the peoples known together as the Baiyue. In the Spring and Autumn period the north of modern Jiangxi was the western edge of the state of Wu. After Yue, a power in modern northern Zhejiang, conquered Wu in 473 BC, Chu (based in modern Hubei) took northern Jiangxi, and the south may have felt some Yue influence. Chu subjugated Yue in 333 BC. When Qin conquered Chu in 223 BC, most of Jiangxi was recorded as placed under Jiujiang Commandery at Shouchun (壽春), but that commandery was ineffective and ended soon after Qin fell.

At the start of the Han dynasty, possibly before Xiang Yu died in 202 BC, Yuzhang Commandery (豫章) was set up in Jiangxi, the first commandery created there by a Chinese dynasty. It took its name from the Yuzhang River, the original name of the Gan River, and 'Gan' is now the province's abbreviation. Eight counties were added in 201 to Qin's original seven, and three more later. Through most of the Han era, eighteen counties made up the commandery and took in most of modern Jiangxi. Several county seats (Nanchang, Gan, Yudu, Luling and others) were on the sites of big cities today, but other counties were moved or dropped in later centuries.

In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, Yuzhang Commandery was placed in Yangzhou Province, part of a trend of creating provinces (zhou) throughout China. In 291 AD, in the Western Jin, Jiangxi became a zhou of its own, called Jiangzhou (江州). During the Southern and Northern Dynasties it was governed by the southern ones, and zhou gradually multiplied. In the Sui dynasty Jiangxi contained seven commanderies and twenty-four counties; the Tang added one more commandery and fourteen counties; commanderies were then abolished and became zhou, now translated as 'prefectures' rather than 'provinces'.

The Tang introduced circuits as a new top-level division. Jiangxi was at first in the Jiangnan Circuit (meaning 'Circuit south of the Yangtze'), and in 733 this circuit was split into western and eastern halves. Jiangxi fell in the western half, the Jiangnanxi Circuit ('Western circuits south of the Yangtze'), which is where the modern name 'Jiangxi' comes from.

In 907 the Tang fell, and the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period began. First Wu (吳) and then Southern Tang (南唐) ruled Jiangxi, both from the area of present-day Nanjing downstream on the Yangtze. When the ten kingdoms ended, the Jiangnanxi Circuit came back, now with nine prefectures and four army districts (sixty-eight districts between them). Jiangxi was afterwards divided into thirteen circuits, and Jiangxi Province was set up for the first time with most of modern Guangdong inside it, and the area had roughly reached its modern borders.

When the Qing regime collapsed, Jiangxi turned into one of the first Communist bases, and large numbers of peasants joined the swelling people's revolution. On 1 August 1927, in the course of the Chinese Civil War, the Nanchang Uprising broke out in Jiangxi. The Communist leaders then retreated into the mountains in the south and west of the province, avoiding Kuomintang efforts to eliminate them. In 1931 the government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was set up in Ruijin, sometimes called the 'Former Red Capital' (红色故都) or just the 'Red Capital'. Surrounded completely by Nationalist forces in 1935, the Communists fought their way out and set off on the Long March towards Yan'an.

The National Government launched five military campaigns against the Jiangxi Soviet area from 1930 to 1934. The brutal fighting and purges, including internal purges of the Red Army and later of the government, caused many deaths and much flight, and the population of Jiangxi fell by 40%, to only 13.8 million in 1936.

Jiangxi lost its key place in north-south traffic in 1936, when the Yuehan Railway opened in Hunan. The east-west Zhegan Railway opened in 1937 and greatly altered traffic patterns in the province, and Jiujiang Port (九江港) started to decline.

After the Doolittle Raid in the Second World War, most of the American B-25 crews who came down in China reached safety with help from Jiangxi locals, who paid dearly for sheltering them. To scare Chinese people away from aiding downed American airmen, the Imperial Japanese Army launched the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign; no fewer than 10,000 civilians in Jiangxi lost their lives during the hunt for Doolittle's men.

The CCP gained full control of Jiangxi in 1949 with the founding of the People's Republic. Before dissolving itself that same year, the Republican provincial government left for Taichung, in Taiwan Province.

Mountains enclose Jiangxi on three sides: the Mufu, Jiuling and Luoxiao mountains in the west, the Huaiyu and Wuyi mountains in the east, while the south has the Dayu and Jiulian (九连山) mountains. Hills, ranges and valleys alternate in the southern half of the province, and the northern half is flatter and at lower altitude. Mount Huanggang (黄岗山), in the Wuyi Mountains on the Fujian border, is the top of the province at 2,157 metres, or 7,077 ft.

The dominant feature is the Gan River, which crosses the entire province from south to north and flows into Lake Poyang, China's largest freshwater lake; the lake empties into the Yangtze, which forms part of the northern border. Two important reservoirs are Wan'an, on the upper Gan, and Zhelin, on the Xiushui River in the north-west.

The climate is humid subtropical (Cfa in the Köppen classification), with winters that are short, cool and damp, and summers that are very hot and humid. Temperatures average about 3 to 9 °C, or 37 to 48 °F, in January and 27 to 30 °C, or 81 to 86 °F, in July. Annual precipitation of 1,200 to 1,900 millimetres, or 47 to 75 in, falls largely in heavy rains in late spring and summer.

Nanchang is the capital and the most densely populated city, and ranks among the large metropolises of China. It has been the hub of Jiangxi civilisation through history, taking a leading role in commerce, intellectual life, industry and politics. Ganzhou is the largest subdivision of the province.

The 2020 Chinese census put Jiangxi's population at 45.18 million, 99.73% of them Han Chinese, mainly Gan and Hakka. Ganzhou, the biggest city, has a particularly large Hakka community, and the She people are among the minorities.

In gender balance, Jiangxi and Henan are the most skewed provinces in China. A 2009 study in the British Medical Journal reported more than 140 boys for each 100 girls among children aged one to four.
Liú (刘) was Jiangxi's most frequent surname in 2019, which was true of no other province; across the country it ranks only fourth.
As of January 2015 the Yangtze had two crossings in Jiangxi, both at Jiujiang.
Jingdezhen Ceramic University lists 81 programs for international students on this site: 47 bachelor, 27 master's, 4 doctoral, 3 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 81 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 15,400), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 19,800), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 31,500), according to the university's published fee table.

81 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

jingdezhen-ceramic-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Jingdezhen Ceramic University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jingdezhen, register at Jingdezhen Ceramic University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Jinzhou Medical University (锦州医科大学, Jǐnzhōu yīkē dàxué), abbreviated JZMU, is a medical university in the city of Jinzhou in Liaoning Province, northeast China. The school was founded in 1946. Over time it grew into Jinzhou Medical College (1958), then Liaoning Medical University (2006), before taking the current name JZMU in 2016.

The campus is in the north of the city and covers 1,140,000 square metres. There are 16 teaching departments with 98 teaching offices. For hands-on work the university has 56 teaching laboratories, four comprehensive hospitals attached to it, and 169 bases where students train and practise, which suggests plenty of clinical exposure.

Altogether the university offers 21 specialised undergraduate subjects and 32 master's programs, plus a single doctoral program. Six forms of education are available: regular higher education, state-owned privately run schooling, adult learning, vocational training, online study and a track for international students.

The teaching staff number 823 full-time teachers. Of them 74 hold doctorates, 533 are associate professors and 219 are professors and chief doctors (the university's figures overlap and do not add up neatly, so ask the university for a precise breakdown). The library features a modern electronic reading room, and readers can search medical literature through MEDLINE (American) and the Chinese Medical Institute's retrieval system.

Students range from undergraduates through graduates and master's students to postgraduates. The reported total is 13,806 students, a number that includes the international students, who study in the undergraduate program taught in English. At present over 400 international students are enrolled across a wide range of medical programs.

The university is also active in academic exchange with universities abroad, for instance the University of Glasgow, and it regularly swaps scholars and specialists to deliver lectures. About 120 of its teachers have gone to study and do research in more than 20 countries.

If you are an international student, this is the unit you will deal with. The College of International Education (CIE) began in April 2004 inside the International Exchange Department (IED) of the university, which at that time was Liaoning Medical University.

The IED is the working body for academic affairs involving foreign countries. Its job is to carry out national foreign and educational policies, to follow the rules for managing foreign affairs strictly, and, in practice, to manage, guide, coordinate and serve all foreign-related work in the university. Two offices make up the IED: one handles educational administration and the other manages dormitories.

Alongside the IED stands the CIE, a parallel college sharing the same staff. It is among the youngest but most energetic departments in the university and works hard to recruit medical students from many educational backgrounds. It teaches medical courses to international students who will become medical graduates, and it also lets them learn more about Chinese society and culture.
Daily life depends on the city outside the campus gates. This part of the profile covers Jinzhou's economy, shops, transport, sights and a famous book that describes it.
The city's industry is varied. Its long-standing sectors are petrochemicals, metallurgy, textiles, pharmaceuticals and building materials.

Established in 1992, the Jinzhou Economic and Technical Development Zone was among Liaoning's earliest approved province-level zones. Its transport links are good: the seaport, the airport and several state highways are all close by.

A few Western brands have opened in town, KFC being the most prominent, as it has long had a presence in China. For groceries and household items the main stores are RT-Mart, New-Mart and Do-Do Express.

As for banks, an older description names Bank of Jinzhou (Jinzhou Yinhang) as the only one with native English speakers on staff; Bank of China, Western Union and various other services are present too. The same account adds that Visa and MasterCard cards worked only at a few large bank branches connected to those networks and nowhere else in the city. This information may be out of date, so confirm payment options before you travel and carry some other way to pay.

Air travel goes through Jinzhou Jinzhouwan Airport, which connects to China's big airports. Jinzhou has two railway stations: one serves long journeys and the other short-distance routes. The commonest ways of getting about town are walking and cycling. Taxis are everywhere, with a starting fare of 6 RMB, while buses reach all parts of the city and cost least, although they can be unreliable.

The Liaoshen Campaign Memorial (遼沈戰役紀念館 in traditional characters, 辽沈战役纪念馆 in simplified) honours the Liaoshen Campaign of 1948. The museum is large. It keeps more than 16,000 items of campaign equipment (tanks, cannons, mortars, machine guns and rifles) together with thousands of photographs and documents. Its most famous exhibit is the Panoramic Picture Hall, where a revolving circular screen recreates the entire Battle of Jinzhou.

Yiwulü Mountain stands in the west of Beizhen City, part of Jinzhou, and counts among Northeast China's three sacred mountains. Wanghai Mountain, the highest peak, rises 867 meters above sea level. Scattered along the range are attractions including Beizhen Temple, Shenshui Bridge, Cloud Pass, Lotus Stone, Wanghai Temple, the Fish Pool, and Guanyin, Sijiao and Kuangguang pavilions.

Mount Bijia is an island in the Bohai Sea south of Jinzhou with a Chinese Buddhist temple on it. Boats are the only way across for most of the day, but at low tide a natural causeway links the island with the mainland. Visitors walk over from the seafront, and locals call the causeway Tian Qiao, the 'Sky Bridge'. A tall stone pavilion on top looks like a giant pen resting on a pen holder, which is where the name Bijiashan, 'Pen Holder Mountain', comes from.

Guangji Pagoda (廣濟寺塔 or 广济寺塔) is in Guta Park in the heart of Jinzhou. The 72-meter tower has thirteen levels in an octagonal shape and is a fine example of Liao-style architecture. A peaceful temple at its foot completes the traditional Chinese scene, and early in the morning you will see locals gather there for rituals, exercise and other activities. Entry to the temple grounds is free.

A small ice park is created on the Xiaoling River in winter, open until the ice melts. Activities include skating, skating chairs and ice vehicles, ATV rides across the frozen surface and rubber tyre rides towed by vehicles.

These days the city's best-known attraction is its Night Market, normally held on summer evenings; when the weather turns colder it becomes a Morning Market instead. Come for the snacks, drinks, activities and bustle. It is on Nanning Street (南宁路).

Readers who want a literary view of the city can pick up Wild Swans: Three Daughters of China, one of the best-selling nonfiction books of the 1990s. It describes Jinzhou in some detail both before and after the 'Liberation' of China in 1949.

jinzhou-medical-university.h: Liaoning: the province behind the city

blocks.x: JZMU stands in Liaoning Province, and the wider region influences student life almost as strongly as the campus itself. What follows covers the province's history, landscape and economy.

From the 4th century BC to the 9th century AD, Han Chinese regimes mostly settled and governed Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the area belonged to the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples. Around 300 BC the state of Yan took it and set up two commanderies: Liaodong ('east of the Liao River') and Liaoxi ('west of the Liao River'). Xiangping, the Yan city that was the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today.

When the Han dynasty collapsed, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family founded a semi-independent state based in Liaodong, and it lasted until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Also known as Yan, the state sent out many maritime diplomatic and trading expeditions and left a lasting mark on Northeast Asian culture, though it was short-lived.

Once the Western Jin dynasty had ended, three Xianbei states of the Murong tribe governed Liaoning in turn (Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan). The Northern Wei captured the Yan capital in 436, and Goguryeo then occupied the Liaodong Peninsula. Eventually the Tang dynasty annexed the area, during its war with Goguryeo.

The An Lushan Rebellion broke out in the middle of the 8th century and drained the Tang of resources it needed on its frontiers, so the Bohai kingdom gradually spread into Liaodong. Liaoning was in the end conquered by the Khitan Liao dynasty, which divided the region into four circuits: the Eastern Capital (Dongjingdao), the Supreme Capital (Shangjingdao), the Central Capital (Zhongjingdao) and the Lower Capital (Xiajingdao).

The Jurchen Jin dynasty ran most of the land through the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu), and shared out the rest between the Xianping Route, the Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu) and the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206 and the region was later absorbed into the Yuan dynasty. The Yuan arrangement was complicated. The east fell under the Liaoyang Route and the Shenyang Route, both within the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. In the north, Xianping Prefecture belonged to the Kaiyuan Route. The west, including the Guangning Route, was likewise subordinate to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. Jinzhou and Chaoyang, by contrast, formed part of the Daning Route and reported to the Central Secretariat.

jinzhou-medical-university.h: The Ming frontier and the rise of the Qing

blocks.x: The Ming took control of Liaoning in 1371, only three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. Around 1442 they built a defensive wall to protect the province's farming heartland from a possible threat from the Oriyanghan Jurchen-Mongols, who were Ming tributaries, to the northwest. In 1467 and 1468 the wall was extended to cover the northeast as well, against the Jianzhou Jurchens, who would later be known as the Manchu. This 'Liaodong Wall' had the same purpose as the Great Wall but was cheaper to build. Some sections used stones and tiles, but most was simply an earth dike with a moat on each side.

Despite the wall, the Jurchens took Liaodong, the eastern part of Liaoning, early in the 17th century, many years ahead of the rest of China. Their dynasty, called Later Jin at first and then renamed Qing, had its capital at Xingjing (兴京) between 1616 and 1621. Xingjing lay outside the Liaodong Wall in what is now eastern Liaoning. The capital then moved to Dongjing, east of present-day Liaoyang, and in 1625 to Shengjing (now Shenyang). Beijing became the main Qing capital when it fell to them in 1644, yet Shengjing kept its importance as a regional capital through most of the dynasty.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning many of its people. Local Chinese were killed in the fighting or escaped to the south side of the Great Wall, and the retreating Ming armies themselves wrecked many cities. In 1661, long after the conquest, Fengtian's Civil Governor (Fuyin), Zhang Shangxian, reported that Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng were the only places east of the Liao River with any population; the others were abandoned or held a few hundred people at most. He wrote that Tieling and Fushun had 'only a few vagrants'. West of the Liao River, only Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning kept notable populations.

Resettlement began after laws passed in 1651 and 1653. The Qing court invited migrants, notably from Shandong, to come from beyond the Great Wall and fill sparsely populated Fengtian Province, which roughly corresponds to modern Liaoning. A good number of Liaoning residents today descend from those seventeenth-century settlers. For most of the Manchu period, though, the remainder of the Northeast was formally closed to Han Chinese. The Willow Palisade, built from about 1638 to about 1672, was meant to keep migrants out of today's Jilin and Heilongjiang and the adjoining parts of Inner Mongolia. It surrounded Fengtian's agricultural core, in most places lying just beyond the former Ming Liaodong Wall or reusing it, and it cut that core off from the Manchu forests to the northeast and Mongolian pasture to the northwest.

Later the Qing tried to stop the flow of migrants into Fengtian, to send some settlers back where they came from, or, failing that, to legalise them. An edict of 1704, for instance, noted that recent Han Chinese settlers had not obeyed earlier orders to leave. It told them to register properly and join a local defence group (保, bao) or return to their original homes within ten years. Ten years later another edict appeared, again reminding officials that something must be done about illegal migrants. Yet Beijing's officials never got the control they wanted: between 1683 and 1734 the population of Fengtian doubled.

Under the Qing, Manchuria was split between three generals, and the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn) governed much of what is now Liaoning. From 1860 the Manchu government began to open the region to settlers again, and before long the Han Chinese had become its largest ethnic group.

The province of Fengtian was created in the 20th century in the area that is Liaoning today. The Russo-Japanese War of 1904 and 1905 between Japan and Russia was fought largely on Liaoning soil. Port Arthur and Mukden were two of its key battles, and Mukden was the largest land battle fought up to that point. During the Warlord Era of the early twentieth century, the Fengtian clique, led by Zhang Zuolin and then his son Zhang Xueliang, controlled Liaoning. The province was first given its present name on 29 January 1929, and the Zhongdong Railway Incident happened later that year. Japan invaded in 1931, and the area fell under the Japanese-controlled puppet state of Manchukuo. After Japan was defeated in 1945, the first major battles of the Chinese Civil War, known as the Liaoshen Campaign, were fought in and around Liaoning.

Liaoning did not yet exist when the People's Republic began in 1949. There were instead two provinces, Liaodong and Liaoxi, and five municipalities (Shenyang, Lüda, which is now Dalian, Anshan, Fushun and Benxi). In 1954 these were combined as Liaoning, and in 1955 it also received parts of the former Rehe province. Liaoning also took in part of Inner Mongolia during the Cultural Revolution, but that was later reversed.

Industrialisation came early to Liaoning: first during the Japanese occupation and then at a faster pace in the 1950s and 1960s. Anshan, for example, hosts one of China's largest iron and steel complexes. That early focus on heavy industry has recently become a burden, since many large state-run enterprises have struggled. Because Liaoning and other Northeast provinces face special difficulties from their heavy industrial heritage, the central government recently began a 'Revitalize the Northeast' campaign.
You can think of Liaoning as three broad zones. The west is highland, the middle is plain and the east is hilly.

The Nulu'erhu Mountains dominate the western highlands, following roughly the line of the border with Inner Mongolia. Low hills cover the whole zone. A thin coastal plain called the Liaoxi Corridor joins the Liao River Basin with the North China Plain, finishing at the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass.

The central zone is a basin, mostly low and flat, where the Liao and Daliao rivers and their tributaries drain. In the east, the Changbai and Qianshan mountains reach out into the sea and form the Liaodong Peninsula. Mount Huabozi, the highest point in Liaoning at 1336 m, is in this zone.
The climate is continental monsoon, and annual rainfall averages between about 440 and 1130 mm. Summer is the rainy season, and the other seasons are dry.
The province's major cities are Shenyang, Dalian, Anshan, Liaoyang and Fushun, then Dandong, Jinzhou and Yingkou.

jinzhou-medical-university.h: What the province grows, mines and ships

blocks.x: Maize, sorghum and soybeans are the staple crops, along with some cotton. Dalian and its surroundings supply 75% of the apples and peaches that China exports. Local fruit specialities are apples (Dalian and Yingkou), golden peaches (Dalian), pears (Beizhen, in Jinzhou), white pears (Huludao and Suizhong), and apricots and plums (Gushan, in Dandong).

Under the ground, Liaoning has more iron, magnesite, diamond and boron than any other province-level division in China. Petroleum and natural gas are also important, and crude oil is abundant, above all in the Liaohe Oilfield. Salt is produced along the coast.
For trade, the cities of Dalian, Dandong and Yingkou have grown into major ports, serving as commercial gateways for the whole of northeast China.

Kunming Medical University (KMU), formerly Kunming Medical College, is a specialist medical university in Kunming, the capital of Yunnan Province. Today it is the biggest university in Yunnan devoted to medicine. The sections below describe how it grew, how large it is, what you can study, and what living in Kunming is like.

Medical teaching in Kunming began in 1933, when Donglu University started a specialised medicine programme. In 1937 the programme had grown enough to become a School of Medicine within Yunnan University, the successor to Donglu University. It became an independent school in 1956 and was named Kunming Medical College. In 1993 the provincial authorities listed it among Yunnan's key institutions of higher education. In 2012, after an evaluation by China's Ministry of Education, it was raised to university level and received its current name.

The campus covers 125.4 hectares (310 acres). KMU enrols about 15,000 students, of whom more than 1,400 are postgraduates, and has 6,000 staff, with over 1,150 of them professors or associate professors.

Thirteen schools make up the academic side, giving the university 15 bachelor's, 34 master's and 1 doctoral programme, and 5 research institutes sit beside them. Clinical and practical training takes place across a broad network. Besides the 9 affiliated hospitals there are 9 teaching hospitals and as many as 39 practice hospitals. Other placements include 9 forensic medicine sites, 6 sites for preventive medicine, 4 for pharmacy and 2 for optical work. In short, students can count on a stable base for studying and for practising.

The library holds nearly 100,000 books and serves as Yunnan's central hub in the national literature-sharing network, and it is a first-class repository of Chinese medical and academic literature. KMU additionally serves as a national centre for clinical medicine trials and as the provincial expert testimony centre for Yunnan.

The nine hospitals together offer over 9,800 beds, and seven carry China's Level-A Tertiary General Hospital accreditation. Each has its own role. The First Affiliated Hospital, with more than 3,000 outpatient visits a day, is the biggest general hospital in Yunnan. The Second is among the 100 best general hospitals in the country, and in Yunnan it leads on organ transplantation for people and on treating burns. The Third is the province's biggest hospital for cancer alone, and it houses three provincial cancer research centres. Dentistry is covered by the Affiliated Stomatology Hospital, which has over 100 dental chairs, modern equipment and the title of Yunnan's largest stomatology specialist hospital.

Yunnan has abundant natural resources, and KMU does extensive research on the diseases that are common or endemic in the province, constantly applying the newest diagnostic and treatment technology. Its work covers basic, applied and developmental research across many subjects and specialties, and it takes responsibility for many national and provincial key science projects and international cooperation programmes. Since 2004 more than 800 research results have won awards at national and provincial level, including national invention awards and national science and technology conference awards. KMU describes itself as a leader in medicine and health within the province.

International cooperation is an area where KMU says it has done well. Over 100 medical schools and institutions have partnerships or exchange arrangements with it, located in places as varied as Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, India, Australia, Sweden, Italy, France, Germany, the UK and the US. In addition, more than 60 overseas academics hold honorary or guest professor titles from KMU.

Teaching is organised in these schools: Basic Medical Sciences, Clinical Medicine, Clinical Oncology, Stomatology, Forensic Medicine, Nursing, Public Health, Pharmaceutical Science, Humanities and Social Science, Continuing Education, and Advanced Vocational Education and Training, plus Haiyuan College.

Beyond the schools there are research and training units: institutes for health science, neuroscience and higher medical education, a clinical skills training centre, centres for biomedical engineering and for general scientific research, and a provincial key laboratory studying the pharmacology of natural products.

The longer degrees run five or six years. Stomatology takes 6 years. Clinical Medicine, Clinical Anaesthesiology, Laboratory Medicine, Medical Imaging, Optometry, Forensic Medicine and Preventive Medicine each take 5 years.
The shorter ones last 4 years: Nursing, Pharmacology, Public Health Management, Labor & Social Security, Law (Medical Law), Rehabilitation Treatment and Aesthetic Medicine.

In the basic and laboratory sciences you can specialise in physiology or neurophysiology, in pathology and pathophysiology, in pathogenic biology, in clinical laboratory diagnostics, in biochemistry and molecular biology, or in the combined field of human anatomy, histology and embryology.

Clinical options are broad: internal medicine and surgery, pediatrics, obstetrics, ophthalmology, otolaryngology, oncology, anaesthesiology, emergency medicine, gerontology, rehabilitation and physical medicine, radiology and nuclear medicine, dermatology and venereology, and both neurology and psychiatry and mental health. Dentistry is covered under oral medicine, oral basic medicine and oral clinical medicine.

Other fields cover population and community health (including biostatistics and epidemiology, occupational and environmental health, care for mothers and children, and social medicine with public health management), health toxicology, forensic medicine, pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacology, and an integrated field that combines traditional Chinese medicine with Western practice.

The single doctoral programme is in surgery, which brings together seven disciplines. These are burns surgery, cardiac surgery, thoracic surgery, plastic surgery, orthopedic surgery, neurosurgery and general surgery.

In east-central Yunnan lies Kunming, whose administrative area covers 21,600 square kilometres (8,340 square miles). Its latitude range is 24°23' to 26°22' N and its longitude range 102°10' to 103°40' E. The area measures 140 kilometres (87 miles) at its widest from east to west, and 220 kilometres (137 miles) at its longest from north to south.

A fertile basin beside the northern shore of Lake Dian holds the city, which hills enclose on the north, west and east. It has played a central role in the communications of southwestern China for centuries. Dian, nicknamed "the Pearl of the Plateau", is Yunnan's biggest lake and China's sixth biggest freshwater lake, covering roughly 340 square kilometres (130 square miles). Elevations vary a lot across the municipality. The top is Mazong Ridge of the Jiaozi Snow Mountain in Luquan at 4,247 metres (13,934 feet); the bottom is 695 metres (2,280 feet), where the Xiao and Jinsha rivers join in Dongchuan District. The downtown sits 1,891 metres (6,204 feet) up.

Low latitude combined with high altitude, 1,888 metres (6,194 feet) up on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, gives Kunming a very gentle climate by Chinese standards. Winter is brief, cool and dry, while summer is long, mild and damp. Because the weather feels like spring all year, ideal for plants and flowers, Kunming is nicknamed the "City of Eternal Spring". In summer it hardly gets hot, going above 30 °C (86 °F) only a handful of times, although unusual snowfalls do occur in some winters. The classification is subtropical highland (Köppen Cwb). Blossoms and greenery cover the city throughout the year.

Daily mean temperature is lowest in January, at 9.3 °C (48.7 °F), and highest in June, at 20.7 °C (69.3 °F), while the daily maximum is lowest in December and highest in June. The monsoon season lasts from May to October, and the remaining months are fairly dry. The yearly average temperature is 16.0 °C (60.8 °F), annual rainfall is 991.0 millimetres (39.0 in), with nearly three-fifths between June and August, and there are 230 frost-free days. Sunshine varies from 29% of the possible total in July to 70% in February, with 2,240.9 hours a year. The record low is −7.8 °C (18.0 °F), from 29 December 1983, and the record high is 32.9 °C (91.2 °F), from 25 May 2014.

By population, the Han are 5,542,314 people (86.16%), and the minority groups combined come to 889,898 (13.84%). Some of the 26 nationalities found across Yunnan are represented in Kunming. The average resident can expect to live to 76.

The centre is organised around three main squares (Nanping, Dongfeng and Jinma Biji) and six main streets. Those streets are Beijing, Zhengyi, Renmin, Dongfeng, Jinbi and Qingnian roads. For shopping, the key streets are Zhengyi Road, Renmin Road, Qingnian Road, Guanghua Street, Jingxing Street and Nanping Street, the last of which was built over a section of Dongfeng Road. Of these, Nanping Street, Zhengyi Road and Jingxing Street are the favourites for strolling.

The modern centre is Nanping Square, west of the Panlong River, at the crossing of Nanping Street and Zhengyi Street, where the southern city wall used to run. The area is a dense shopping district full of clothes and electronics shops, ringed by new high-rises, with a preserved old quarter to the north. The earlier centre was Dongfeng Square, east of the river outside the old walls at the junction of Beijing Road and Dongfeng Road. In the morning crowds practise taijiquan and play badminton there, and on weekends amateur theatre is staged. Since the Songhua Dam was built, the Panlong River has flowed artificially and has become a kind of canal, and it takes treated sewage and wastewater from nearby pipes.

The area matters to Kunming's Hui community. Shuncheng Street, once a Muslim quarter and among the last old streets in the centre, has been knocked down for apartments and shopping centres during rapid modernisation. Nancheng Qingzhen Si, the city's new mosque, stands behind a supermarket a block north of Zhengyi Road. Its green dome and zigzag-patterned minaret can be seen from afar, and it replaces a Qing-period building on the same ground.

Just past the mosque, Jingxing Street runs west from Zhengyi Road into a district occupied by the bird and flower market, which fills the streets that join it with Guanghua Street to the north every day. Orchids and other plants collected or grown across the province are sold there.

South of the centre and of Jinbi Road, itself south of Dongfeng Road (both end at Beijing Road), two large pagodas rise. Each has thirteen storeys of whitewashed brick and is crowned by four iron cockerels. Tang-dynasty builders put up the West Pagoda between 824 and 859. They built the East Pagoda then too, but an earthquake destroyed it in 1833 and it was reconstructed in the same style in 1882. Visitors heading for the West Pagoda should walk down Dongsi Road, past a second mosque, to a small lane on the right. The East Pagoda, a slightly leaning replica, is reached from Shulin Jie, a few minutes east, in a decorative garden. Neither pagoda's temple is open to the public.

Many streets have jacaranda trees, which bloom heavily in mid to late April, especially along Jiaochang Middle Road. They are not native to Kunming. They grew from seeds swapped with Algeria and raised in the Kunming Botanical Garden, whose seeds the city then used to line its streets.

Cuihu Park, also called Green Lake Park, is a leading city park, mostly a lake surrounded by greenery, with a statue on its west side of Nie Er, who wrote the national anthem. Another memorial to Nie Er is in Xishan Park, best known for the Longmen Grottoes (a different place from the grottoes of the same name at Luoyang), with several ancient temples and the Longmen, or "dragon gate", itself.

Daguan Park is on Dian Chi at the southwestern edge of the city. The Kangxi Emperor of the Qing first laid it out, and it has since been altered and now includes a lively funfair, food stalls and shops.
The city zoo opened in 1950 next to Yuantong Park, which is known for Yuantong Temple. It houses 5,000 animals of 140 species and welcomes 3 million visitors a year.
There are more parks: Black Dragon Pool and the Botanical Gardens lie in the north of the city, the World Horti-Expo Garden in the northeast, and the Wenmiao Tea Garden in Wuhua District.

Out in the northern suburbs, the World Horti-Expo Garden was constructed for the 1999 World Horticulture Exposition, which ran between 1 May and 31 October that year and took the theme "Man and Nature - Marching Toward the 21st Century". A cable car runs from the garden to Golden Temple Park on neighbouring Mingfeng Hill. The temple there dates from 1602 (year 30 of the Wanli reign, Ming dynasty). Everything in it, from beams, pillars and arches to doors, windows, roof tiles, Buddhist figures and inscribed boards, is cast in copper, adding up to more than 200 tons, so it is the biggest copper structure in China.

Kunming's best-known and largest Buddhist temple is Yuantong, whose original structure went up over 1,200 years ago during the Tang, and it lies in a hollow at the south end of Yuantong Park. Around 12 km (7.5 mi) northwest of downtown stands Qiongzhu Si, the Bamboo Temple, dating from 639 and rebuilt over 1422-1428. Several more Buddhist temples stand alongside the road up to the Dragon Gate (龙门) in the Western Mountains.

Museums include the Yunnan Provincial Museum and the Kunming City Museum, which was redeveloped in 2014. The Yunnan Ethnology Museum opened in 1995, and the Natural History Museum of Zoology in November 2006.

For more than 30 years Kunming has been China's national high-altitude training base, and each year many Chinese and foreign athletes come to train. There are two main complexes, the Hongta Sports Center and the Haigeng National Training Center.

The Hongta (Red Pagoda) cigarette company paid US$58 million to build the Hongta Sports Center in 2000. Beside Haigeng Park, it serves mainly professionals, but members of the public can join as a sports club, and amateur football games take place each weekend. Among the facilities are around 10 football pitches (one ringed by a running track), tennis courts, a basketball court, a badminton hall, a swimming pool of 50 metres (160 feet), a gym with treadmills and weight machines, and one of the few ice hockey rinks in China. Indoors there are air hockey and pool tables, and a bowling alley is in the basement. The complex also includes a restaurant and a hotel of 101 rooms.

Ten minutes from Hongta, the Haigeng National Training Center stands on Dianchi (Lake Dian), close to the prize-winning Lakeview Golf Club and some new condominium estates. The government built it in the late 1970s purely to support high-altitude training.

Golf is a big attraction, and an hour's drive from downtown takes you to any of four courses. US Golf Digest has for six years running rated Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, in nearby Yiliang County, the best course in China and Hong Kong, and Asian Golf Monthly named it the top golf resort in Asia in 2004. The Omega China Tour stops there for its Kunming event. Foreign money has gone into Kunming golf: the US$600 million resort began in 1992 as a project headed by Keppel Land Group of Singapore, and its two courses were laid out by Jack Nicklaus and Robert Trent Jones, Jr.

More venues include Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose arena, and the Yunnan Provincial Stadium, which is where Hongta Yunnan Football Club plays. The city also has the Kunming Municipal Athletic Center, Kunming Gymnasium, Wuhua District Stadium, Lakeview Golf Villa and tennis courts in Cuihu Park. Nicklaus personally designed the Mountain Course at Spring City.

Compared with other southwestern cities, Kunming enjoys a mild climate, a big consumer market and abundant natural resources. Yunnan is one of China's major producers of agricultural goods, minerals and hydropower, and since Kunming lies at its centre the city acts as the main trading hub for much of what the province produces.

Copper, lead and zinc are the chief industries, and iron and steel production has expanded. Salt and phosphate mines near Kunming are some of China's largest, and Yunnan Copper Company Limited, based in the city, is one of the province's biggest mining firms. Starting in the late 1970s, processing of food and tobacco and the making of machinery and construction equipment were added to the list of leading industries.

The State Council designated Kunming an Open City in May 1995. Before 1995 was over, 929 enterprises funded from overseas had been approved, with total investment of $2.3 billion (including $1.1 billion of foreign capital), and more than 40 projects were worth over $9 million each.

Kunming is a centre for engineering and manufacturing machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and vehicles, heavy trucks included. It also has chemicals, plastics, cement and textile factories, and processing plants, such as tanneries, woodworking and papermaking factories, that use local farm products. A tire plant that Yunnan Tire Co. opened in Kunming in 1997 has a capacity of two million tires a year.

Two big zones operate: the Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone, focused on biological medicine, new materials, electronic information and agriculture, and the Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone, for mechanical equipment, biological science and food, information industry and software.

The National Development and Reform Commission has also recognised 30 key industrial parks in Yunnan. The largest include the Chenggong, Anning, Songming Yanglin, Dongchuan Special and Xundian Special parks, and Kunming Haikou Industrial Park.

In 2008 Kunming was home to 65 of Yunnan's Top 100 Enterprises, ranked by 2007 revenue. Hongta Group topped the list with revenues of about RMB 39.88 billion for 2007, and tobacco is still the province's largest sector.

The city's position on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau means that people travelling to or from Kunming from outside Yunnan mostly use two modes of transport, rail and air. The source text says no more about connections, so check timetables and routes before you travel.
Kunming Medical University lists 209 programs for international students on this site: 30 bachelor, 125 master's, 54 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 179 taught in Chinese and English, 29 taught in Chinese, 1 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 24,000 to CNY 35,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 40,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 45,000 to CNY 45,000 (median CNY 45,000), according to the university's published fee table.

209 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (1):
Clinical Medicine (Taught in English)

Kunming Medical University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.
