International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

kunming-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Kunming Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Kunming, register at Kunming Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Kunming University of Science and Technology, known as KUST (昆明理工大学), is based in Kunming, the capital of Yunnan Province in southwestern China. It counts among China's best hundred universities, and within Yunnan it is both the biggest institution and the sole polytechnic. Its teaching history stretches back to 1925, although it is dated officially from 1954. In early 2015 Xi Jinping, the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, visited Yunnan on an inspection tour and described KUST as "a famous university in China". All three of its campuses are in Kunming.

In size, the university runs 30 faculties (schools or colleges) and has 3,900 staff. It offers more than 300 degree programmes at bachelor, master and doctoral level to roughly 40,000 full-time students who study on campus. The range of subjects is wide: engineering and science lead, with management, economics, medicine, law, the arts, philosophy, farming and teacher education alongside. Anyone comparing figures should note that sources quote slightly different totals (for example 29 faculties in one place and 30 in another), so confirm current numbers on the university's own website.

kunming-university-of-science-and-techno.h: What the university set out to be

blocks.x: An older statement of aims described KUST's goal for 2010: that it would turn into a leading university grounded in science and engineering. For Yunnan it was meant to train skilled technical staff, carry out applied basic research and high-technology research, turn that work into industry, and advise on national social and economic planning. That date has long passed, but the aims still describe the university's character well.

Yunnan University Science Park opened as an experimental university science park in 1999 and received national university science park status in May 2001. KUST supports the park together with Yunnan University and Yunnan Normal University.

The first departments that would become KUST began admitting students to bachelor programmes early in 1925. In September 1954 the institution, then called the Kunming Institute of Technology (KIT), became an independent public institution of higher education. A merger in 1999 joined KIT with the former Yunnan Polytechnic University, and the result is today's KUST.

The programme list is broad. Across its faculties (29 in the count used here) the university teaches science, engineering, economics, administration, arts, law and education, and the degrees awarded cover doctorates (PhD), several master's types (MS, MSEng, MEng, MA) and bachelor's types (BS, BSEng, BA). Apart from regular degrees, the university offers post-doctoral places, preparatory courses, adult continuing education and vocational training, and Chinese language courses for international students. KUST is also a member of the SAP University Alliances.

The Graduate School and the Division of Life and Medical Sciences make up the biological side. The Faculty of Life Science and Technology includes the Center for Pharmaceutical Sciences and Engineering and the Center for Biotechnology and Bioengineering. A Medical School follows, with departments of Clinical Medicine and Basic Medicine.

The Faculty of Agriculture and Food brings together departments for Agricultural Mechanization, Agricultural Electrification, Agricultural Hydraulic Engineering, Food Science and Engineering, and Food Quality and Safety. Attached to this area is an Institute of Primate Translational Medicine.

Mining and metals are old strengths in Yunnan, and several faculties reflect this. The Faculty of Metallurgical and Energy Engineering covers Metallurgical Engineering, New Energy Science and Engineering, and Energy and Power Engineering.

The Faculty of Materials Science and Engineering is organised around Materials Physics and Chemistry, Metallic Material Science, Inorganic and Non-metallic Material Science, Material Process Engineering, and Gemmology and Materials Technology, with a Materials Experiment and Testing Center to support them.

Environmental Science and Engineering has three departments: Environmental Engineering, Environmental Science, and Renewable Resource Science and Technology. Separately, the Faculty of Land Resources Engineering handles Geosciences, Land Information and Mapping Engineering, Resource Exploration Engineering, and Mineral Process Engineering.

Mechanical and Electrical Engineering is a faculty of its own, containing Mechanical Engineering, Industrial Engineering and Packaging Engineering. The Faculty of Information Engineering and Automation covers Computer Science, Automation, Telecommunication Engineering and Biomedical Engineering. Electric Power Engineering is divided into Electrical Engineering and Hydraulic Engineering.

The Faculty of Civil Engineering and Mechanics offers Civil Engineering, Engineering Mechanics, Municipal Engineering and Construction Management, plus a research institute on building environments and energy engineering. Designers and planners belong to the Faculty of Architecture and City Planning, with Architecture, Urban and Rural Planning, and Landscape Architecture. Chemistry-related study sits in the Faculty of Chemical Engineering, whose subjects are Chemical Engineering, Process Equipment and Control Engineering, and Biomass Engineering.

The Faculty of Transportation Engineering has four departments: Traffic Engineering, Traffic and Transportation, Logistics Engineering and Vehicle Engineering. There is also a Faculty of Civil Aviation and Aeronautics, and one more for public security and emergency management that houses a Safety Engineering department.
The Faculty of Management and Economics teaches Business Administration, Accounting, Applied Economics, Finance, Marketing, and Management Science and Information System.

The Law School works through a set of research centres: criminal law; constitutional and administrative law; environmental and natural resources law; civil and commercial law; economic law; southeast Asian and international law (Laws of Southeast Asia and International Law); and jurisprudence theory. It is also tied to two provincial bodies, one on local legislation (Yunnan Provincial Institute for Local Legislation) and one on intellectual property development. The Southeast Asian law focus is a useful reminder of Yunnan's position next to that region.
The Faculty of Science has departments for System Science and Applied Mathematics, Electronic Science and Applied Physics, and Applied Chemistry.
The Faculty of Art and Communication includes Environmental Design, Industrial Design, Journalism and Mass Communication, Visual Communication and Fine Arts.

The School of Marxism has several teaching and research centres, covering the fundamental principles of Marxism, Sinicized Marxism, Ideological and Political Education and the Development of Modern Chinese Society. Next to them are a centre for research in philosophy and social sciences and an Education Centre of Humanistic Quality.

Languages are taught in the Faculty of Foreign Languages and Cultures, which has departments for English Language and Literature, College English Teaching, and English Teaching for Non-English Major Postgraduates, together with an MTI Education Center.
Several further units sit outside the main faculty structure.

City College, with departments including Architecture, Mechanical Engineering, Information Engineering, Civil Engineering, Art and Design, Accounting, Language Enhancement, Management and Economics, Earth Sciences, Public Foreign Language Teaching, Sports, General Core Courses, Communication Engineering, Traffic Engineering and Logistics Engineering
School of International Education
School of Continuing Education
Oxbridge College
If you are an international applicant, the School of International Education is probably the first office to contact.

Applicants come from every part of China, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan included, and KUST also holds authorisation to take international students for degrees from bachelor to PhD. This is well above the 40,000 full-time on-campus students quoted earlier, so the two numbers probably count different groups. The university runs 64 bachelor programmes, 49 master programmes and eight PhD programme areas. In addition it hosts three state-authorised post-doctoral stations. One academic subject has state-level key status, and 14 more have it at the provincial level.

Staff total about 3,844, counting both academic and non-academic posts. Nearly 1,100 hold the rank of professor or associate professor, and around 1,600 are full-time teachers. One academician of the China Academy of Engineering works for KUST, and 17 more academicians from the China Academy of Science and the China Academy of Engineering work with the university jointly.

KUST has three campuses, named Chenggong, Lianhua and Xinying, all in Kunming. Together they cover about 120 hectares, and building floor space exceeds 730,000 square meters, with many important construction projects under way.

Library holdings come to roughly 1.7 million books and periodicals, and the library is recognised as a state-level research document collection unit. For research the university has built a state-level engineering research centre and two test stations (provincial or ministerial level), along with two research and development centres, two key laboratories at provincial level and a class-A design and research institute. The full count is 32 research institutes, 13 laboratories and 13 centres.

The 2025 Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) puts KUST in the 301-400 group worldwide. In the 2024 CWTS Leiden Ranking, which is based on publications for 2019–2022, it came 282nd in the world. The Best Chinese Universities Ranking for 2025 put it second in Yunnan Province, behind Yunnan University, and 117th in the country.

The university works with more than 100 local governments, universities, research bodies and companies around the country. Its research matters a great deal to Yunnan and to southwestern China as a whole. In the last two years reported, KUST took over two-thirds of the growth in research funding across all universities in Yunnan.
Nearly 70 universities in about 30 countries are exchange and cooperation partners of KUST. Lamar University in Beaumont, Texas, is one of them.
Daily life for a student is shaped by the city outside the campus: its weather, how people travel, and what there is to do. What follows is an introduction to Kunming, the home of KUST.

Kunming lies in east-central Yunnan. The total area is 21,600 square kilometres (8,340 square miles). Latitudes 24°23' to 26°22' N and longitudes 102°10' to 103°40' E frame the territory. At its widest, from east to west, it is 140 kilometres (87 miles) across, and from north to south the greatest length is 220 kilometres (137 miles).

The city occupies a fertile basin by the northern shore of Lake Dian, with mountains on its northern, western and eastern sides. This position has made Kunming a key crossing point for communications in southwestern China. Lake Dian is nicknamed "the Pearl of the Plateau"; it is the biggest lake in Yunnan and the sixth biggest freshwater lake in China, with an area of around 340 square kilometres (130 square miles). Within the city's territory the highest point is Mazong Ridge on Jiaozi Snow Mountain in Luquan, reaching 4,247 metres (13,934 feet), while the lowest is the point in Dongchuan District where the Xiao River joins the Jinsha River, 695 metres (2,280 feet) up. The central urban area is at an elevation of 1,891 metres (6,204 feet), which is worth remembering if you come from the coast, as the altitude can take a little getting used to.

The city is on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, at an elevation of 1,888 metres (6,194 feet). Because the latitude is low and the ground is high, the weather is among the gentlest anywhere in China: winters are short, cool and dry, and summers are long, pleasant and humid. Since spring-like conditions seem to last all year and suit plants and flowers so well, it has the nickname "City of Eternal Spring". Summer heat is rare, with temperatures going above 30 °C (86 °F) only a few times, although unusual snowfall does turn up in some winters.

The climate is classed as subtropical highland (Köppen Cwb). January is the coolest month, averaging 9.3 °C (48.7 °F) over the day and night, and June the warmest, averaging 20.7 °C (69.3 °F). Daily highs are lowest in December and highest in June. Blossoms and green growth cover the city throughout the year. The monsoon season runs from May to October and the other months are comparatively dry.

Over a typical year the average temperature is 16.0 °C (60.8 °F). Rain totals 991.0 millimetres (39.0 in), and nearly three-fifths of it comes between June and August. There are 230 frost-free days. Sunshine is at its lowest in July (29% of what is possible) and its highest in February (70%), adding up to 2,240.9 hours a year. The recorded extremes are −7.8 °C (18.0 °F) on 29 December 1983 and 32.9 °C (91.2 °F) on 25 May 2014.

Han Chinese number 5,542,314 and make up 86.16% of the population. Ethnic minorities together total 889,898, or 13.84%. Some of the province's 26 nationalities live in Kunming, and average life expectancy in the city is 76 years.

Three large squares and six main streets give the centre its layout. Squares: Nanping, Dongfeng and Jinma Biji. Streets: Beijing, Zhengyi, Renmin, Dongfeng, Jinbi and Qingnian roads. Shops cluster along Jingxing Street and Guanghua Street, on Zhengyi, Qingnian and Renmin roads, and on Nanping Street, which was built on top of part of Dongfeng Road. Of these, Nanping Street, Zhengyi Road and Jingxing Street are the most popular for walking.

kunming-university-of-science-and-techno.h: The modern and the older centre

blocks.x: The modern heart of Kunming is Nanping Square, on the western bank of the Panlong River where Nanping Street crosses Zhengyi Street. The old southern city wall once stood here. Today it is a crowded, dense shopping district full of clothing and electronics shops, ringed by many new high-rise buildings, with a preserved part of the old city lying to the north.

Dongfeng Square, on the river's eastern bank outside the old city walls, where Beijing Road meets Dongfeng Road, used to be regarded as the centre. In the mornings people gather there to practise taijiquan and play badminton, and amateur theatre is performed at weekends. The Panlong River now depends on an artificial flow following construction of the Songhua Dam, so it works more like a canal, and nearby pipes discharge treated sewage and wastewater into it.

The centre matters to Kunming's Hui community. Shuncheng Street, among the last old streets in the central area, once formed a Muslim quarter, but rapid modernisation has seen it demolished for apartments and shopping centres. One block north of Zhengyi Road, behind a supermarket, rises Nancheng Qingzhen Si, the city's new mosque. The mosque's green dome and its minaret, patterned with chevrons, are visible from far off, and it stands on the site of an earlier building from the Qing dynasty.

Just beyond the mosque, Jingxing Street runs west off Zhengyi Road into the area of the bird and flower market, which fills the streets that connect it with parallel Guanghua Street to the north, every day. Many plants on sale, such as orchids, have been gathered or grown across the province.

Jinbi Road is south of Dongfeng Road, and each of them joins Beijing Road. South of Jinbi Road and the centre stand a pair of tall Chinese pagodas, both thirteen storeys of whitewashed brick with a crown of four iron cockerels. Construction of the West Pagoda took place between 824 and 859 under the Tang dynasty. An earthquake in 1833 destroyed the East Pagoda, which had been put up at the same time; it was rebuilt in 1882 in the original Tang style. For the West Pagoda, head down Dongsi Road, pass a second mosque, and look for a narrow lane on your right. The East Pagoda, a decorative and slightly leaning duplicate, stands in an ornamental garden a short walk east along Shulin Jie. The temples belonging to both pagodas are closed to visitors.

Jacaranda trees line many streets and bloom heavily in mid to late April, especially along Jiaochang Middle Road. They are not native to Kunming. Their origin is a seed exchange with Algeria: the seeds were raised in the Kunming Botanical Garden, and the city then used that stock to plant the street trees.

Among the main parks is Cuihu Park (Green Lake Park), which is largely a lake with greenery all around. A statue of Nie Er, who composed China's national anthem, stands on its western side. Xishan Park has another monument to Nie Er. It is best known for the Longmen Grottoes (not the grottoes of the same name at Luoyang), a complex of ancient temples that includes the Longmen, or "dragon gate".

On the shore of Dian Chi at the city's southwestern edge is Daguan Park. It was first laid out by the Kangxi Emperor during the Qing dynasty; since then a lively funfair, food stalls and emporiums have been added.

Kunming's zoo opened in 1950 and sits next to Yuantong Park, which is known for the Yuantong Temple inside it. The zoo is home to 5,000 animals of 140 species and attracts 3 million visitors annually. Other green spaces include Black Dragon Pool and the Kunming Botanical Gardens (north), the World Horti-Expo Garden (northeast) and, in Wuhua District, the Wenmiao Tea Garden.

The World Horti-Expo Garden, in the northern suburbs, was built for the World Horticulture Exposition of 1999. The expo ran between 1 May and 31 October that year, with the slogan "Man and Nature—Marching Toward the 21st Century". Nearby on Mingfeng Hill is Golden Temple Park, reached from the garden by cable car. Golden Temple was constructed in 1602, in the Ming dynasty's Wanli reign (its 30th year). Everything in it is copper, from the beams and pillars to arches, doors, windows, tiles, Buddhist statues and inscribed boards, and the metal weighs over 200 tons. It is China's largest copper building.

Yuantong Temple is the biggest and best-known Buddhist temple in the city. The first structure was built more than 1,200 years ago in the Tang dynasty, and the temple lies in a hollow on the south side of Yuantong Park. The Qiongzhu Si (Bamboo Temple) is about 12 km (7.5 mi) from the centre towards the northwest. It dates from 639, and was rebuilt from 1422 to 1428. On the road up to the Dragon Gate (龙门) in the Western Mountains you pass numerous other Buddhist temples.
For museums, the leading choices are the following.
Yunnan Provincial Museum
Kunming City Museum (redeveloped in 2014)
The Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology, which opened in November 2006
Yunnan Ethnology Museum (opened 1995)

Each year athletes from China and abroad travel to Kunming to train at altitude; for more than 30 years the city has served as the national base for high-elevation training in China. Two big complexes are used: the Hongta Sports Center and the Haigeng National Training Center.

The Hongta Sports Center cost US$58 million and opened in 2000, funded by the Hongta (Red Pagoda) cigarette company. It stands close to Haigeng Park and is mostly used by professionals, but it also serves as a sports club open to the public, and amateur football is played there every weekend. Facilities include about 10 football pitches (one has a running track around it), a swimming pool 50 metres (160 feet) long, a badminton hall, and courts for tennis and basketball. It has one of the few ice hockey rinks in China, a workout room with treadmills and weights, game rooms with air hockey and pool tables, and a bowling alley in the basement. A 101-room hotel and a restaurant complete the site.

Ten minutes from Hongta, beside Dianchi (Lake Dian), is the Haigeng National Training Center. The neighbourhood has the Lakeview Golf Club, which has won awards, and some newly built condominiums. The government built it in the late 1970s specifically for high-altitude training.

Golf is a major draw. Four courses lie within an hour's drive of downtown. Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, in Yiliang County close by, was rated best course in China and Hong Kong by US Golf Digest six years in a row, and in 2004 Asian Golf Monthly named it the best golf resort in Asia. The Kunming stop of the Omega China Tour takes place there.

Foreign investment has helped golf here. The "Spring City" resort is a US$600 million project, begun in 1992 when Singapore's Keppel Land Group led the investment. Jack Nicklaus and Robert Trent Jones, Jr designed its two courses.
The main venues include the following.
Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose venue
Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, whose Mountain Course was designed by Jack Nicklaus
Lakeview Golf Villa
Cuihu Park tennis courts
Kunming Municipal Athletic Center
Kunming Gymnasium
Yunnan Provincial Stadium, where Hongta Yunnan Football Club plays at home
Wuhua District Stadium

Among southwestern cities, Kunming has three things going for it: major natural resources, a large consumer market and a mild climate. Yunnan is one of the country's top producers of agricultural goods, minerals and hydroelectric power, and Kunming sits in its middle, so it works as the chief trading centre for most of what the province produces.

The main industries are copper, lead and zinc. Iron and steel production has been expanded, and some of China's largest salt and phosphate mines surround the city. One of Yunnan's biggest mining companies, Yunnan Copper Company Limited, is headquartered in Kunming. From the late 1970s food and tobacco processing and the making of construction equipment and machines joined the list.

In May 1995 Kunming won State Council approval as an Open City. By the end of that year the city had approved 929 enterprises funded from overseas, with total investment of $2.3 billion, of which $1.1 billion was foreign capital. More than 40 projects were each worth over $9 million.

Kunming is a centre for engineering and for making machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and vehicles, including heavy goods vehicles. It also has chemical works, plastics, cement and textile factories. Local farm products feed its processing plants, among them tanneries and factories for wood and paper. Yunnan Tire Co. opened a plant in Kunming in 1997 that can produce two million tires a year.

The city has two main development zones. The Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone focuses on biological medicine, new materials, electronic information and agriculture. The Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone concentrates on mechanical equipment production, biological science and the food industry, and the information industry and software.
The National Development and Reform Commission has also recognised 30 key industrial parks across Yunnan. The largest include the following.
Chenggong Industrial Park
Anning Industrial Park
Songming Yanglin Industrial Development Zone
Dongchuan Special Industrial Park
Xundian Special Industrial Park
The Kunming Haikou Industrial Park is also on the list.

Kunming was the base of 65 of Yunnan's 100 leading enterprises in 2008, a list ranked by 2007 revenue. Hongta Group led it, with revenue of about RMB39.88 billion for 2007. Tobacco is still the largest sector in the province.
Kunming lies on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau. For travel to or from places outside Yunnan the two main options are rail and air.
Kunming University of Science and Technology lists 485 programs for international students on this site: 70 bachelor, 163 master's, 41 doctoral, 211 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 485 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 26,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 19,500 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 21,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 26,000 to CNY 26,000 (median CNY 26,000), according to the university's published fee table.

485 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

kunming-university-of-science-and-techno.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Kunming University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Kunming, register at Kunming University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

lanzhou-jiaotong-university.h: Lanzhou Jiaotong University at a glance

blocks.x: Lanzhou Jiaotong University (LZJTU; in Chinese 兰州交通大学, pinyin Lánzhōu Jiāotōng Dàxué) specialises in transport and railway-related education and is based in Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in north-western China. If you are drawn to rail, civil, traffic or related engineering, this is the kind of university where those subjects sit at the centre of the curriculum rather than at the edge.

Back in 1958 the school opened under a different title, Lanzhou Railway University, with railway engineering as its purpose. Its founders were a trio: the Chinese Ministry of Railways plus two established transport universities, Beijing Jiaotong and Southwest Jiaotong. Control stayed with the ministry up to the year 2000, and the name changed to today's in 2003.
The university is organised into the following fourteen units. Together they show how far the original railway focus has widened into general engineering, business, languages and the arts.
Civil Engineering
Automatization and Electric Engineering
Electronics and Information Engineering
Mechatronic Engineering
Environmental and Municipal Engineering
Economics and Management
Traffic and Transportation
Chemical and Biological Engineering
Foreign Languages
Mathematics, Physics and Software Engineering
Architecture and Urban Planning
Art and Design
Continuing Education
International Joint Education

Teaching falls into eight broad fields, namely the sciences and engineering, economics and management, and then literature, law, art and education studies. Doctorates can be awarded in seven first-level subject areas, together with one cross-disciplinary category, and five postdoctoral research centres operate on campus.

Postgraduates on the master's route can pick from 28 first-level disciplines and 16 professional degree categories, and the provincial government treats 24 of the university's subjects as key disciplines. Undergraduates face 66 programme options, though only 65 are recruiting at present. In the Essential Science Indicators (ESI) database, work in chemistry, materials science, environmental science and several engineering fields has placed in the world's top 1%, which signals real research muscle in those areas.
The university employs 2,279 staff, of whom 1,838 are full-time teachers. These include 322 professors and 703 associate professors, and 916 of the teachers hold a doctorate.

Full-time enrolment is 30,437. The largest group is undergraduates at 22,102; next come master's students at 7,587 (915 of whom study part-time), then 804 vocational college students and 496 doctoral candidates. Another 212 are international students. Since foreigners are a small minority, expect plenty of everyday practice in Chinese.

Partnerships reach 25 countries and regions, with over 67 partner universities and institutions. Examples include Japan, Brazil, Canada, Russia, France, Spain, the United States and the United Kingdom. The most recent big project dates from 2021, when LZJTU and the University of Seville opened a Confucius Institute in Spain, with authorisation from the Chinese International Education Foundation.
For a student, daily routine is set largely by the surrounding city, from the weather to travel options and leisure. What follows is a guide to Lanzhou, where LZJTU is based.

The city is high up, at 1,600 metres (5,200 ft), and sits near the geographic centre of China in its north-west. Urban development follows the Yellow River's south bank as the water flows from west to east, and the built-up strip exceeds 20 square kilometres (7.7 square miles). The Qilian Ranges, Mount Pingliang and Mount Kongtong rise to the south and north of the city.

The city stands where the upper Yellow River leaves the mountains. It has been an important centre since early times, because it marks the southern end of the route that follows the Hexi Corridor across Central Asia. From here, travellers could reach the area around the ancient capital Chang'an (today's Xi'an, in Shaanxi) from the west and north-west, and could also head to the Qinghai Lake region along the upper Yellow River and its tributaries.

Köppen's classification puts Lanzhou in the BSk semi-arid group of the temperate zone, with hot summers and cold, very dry winters. For the urban core, the 1971 to 2000 averages run from a January daily mean of -4.1 °C (24.6 °F) up to a July mean of 23.4 °C (74.1 °F), and across all twelve months the city averages 10.9 °C (51.6 °F).

Annual rainfall is only 309 millimetres (12.2 in), nearly all of it between May and October. So little falls in winter that snow can be confined to the autumn and spring shoulders. Sunshine is decent without being plentiful: the monthly possible-sunshine figure goes from 47 percent (September) to 57 percent (April), and the year totals 2,350 hours of bright sun.

Geography works against clean air here. Lanzhou occupies a narrow, winding river valley whose mountain walls trap the air. In January 2013 a national environmental analysis from Tsinghua University and the Asian Development Bank counted the city among the ten most polluted in the world, and at one point the haze was reportedly thick enough to hide Lanshan, the mountain on the city's south side. Factories, among them petroleum processors, add emissions, and winter and spring bring heavy dust storms from the Gobi Desert.

The World Health Organization, drawing on Chinese statistics, said in 2011 that Lanzhou was the most polluted of eleven western Chinese cities. The annual average for PM10 was 150 micrograms per cubic metre, seven times the level the WHO considers safe and higher than Beijing's 121.

The authorities have since taken action, and it has mostly worked. Official figures describe thirteen heavily polluting firms with surplus capacity being shut, more than 200 of the dirtiest being halted over winter, and 78 factories relocating to an industrial park beyond the city limits. China awarded Lanzhou a climate progress title in 2015. The city that satellites once could not make out has, in recent years, brought down its Air Pollution Index faster than anywhere else in the country. The WHO's 2018 database covering 2,700 towns places Lanzhou 158th for PM2.5, at an average of 54 micrograms per cubic metre, twice the figure for Milan. Coarse PM10 dust is still high at 132 micrograms per cubic metre, partly due to sandstorms. Conditions have clearly got better, but anyone with breathing problems should still prepare for the dusty seasons.

lanzhou-jiaotong-university.h: The river and the water supply

blocks.x: Silt gives the Yellow River its muddy colour at Lanzhou. Even so, a 2008 account called the water here much better than the foul flow found a couple of hours further downstream. Recently, a few endangered Chinese giant salamanders turned up in the river around the city.

There have also been scares. Benzene in the tap water reached 20 times the national limit of 10 micrograms per litre on 11 April 2014, and officials warned residents against drinking it. Industrial chemical production was the suspected cause, as with the 2005 chemical plant explosions in Jilin. Then, in 2020, a vaccine-making facility, the Lanzhou Biopharmaceutical Plant, let bacteria escape in its exhaust air after expired disinfectant was used, causing a brucellosis outbreak that affected more than 3,000 people.

Tremors are a regular feature, though usually weak. The great quake of 1920 caused more than 100,000 deaths across Ningxia and eastern Gansu but only 42 in Lanzhou, a toll attributed to the sturdy yet flexible wooden construction of its buildings. Lanzhou was also shaken in 2008 by the Sichuan earthquake.

In the 2020 census Lanzhou counted 4,359,446 inhabitants, crossing the 4 million mark for the first time. Of these, 3,042,863 live in the metro area, a 1,112.9 square-kilometre (429.7 square-mile) zone made up of four central districts: Chengguan, Qilihe, Anning and Xigu. Honggu and the Lanzhou New Area by the airport are outside the continuous urban zone for now.

After a spell of sluggish growth, numbers jumped. Commentators point to families seeking better schools, migrant workers returning home to Gansu in retirement, improved city services and official policy.
Most visitors to Gansu and the Hexi Corridor pass through Lanzhou first, and it is the jumping-off point for heritage sites like the Bingling Temple Grottoes. In town, the main attractions are these:
Five Spring Mountain Park (五泉山公园) lies on Gaolan Mountain's northern slope. It takes its name from five springs, and it holds many Buddhist temples and old buildings.
Zhongshan Bridge (中山桥) holds the distinction of being the earliest lasting crossing of the Yellow River.
Baita Mountain Park (白塔山公园) climbs the hillside to 1,700 metres (5,600 ft). It welcomed the public in 1958, on the far side of Zhongshan Bridge.
Lanzhou Botanical Garden (兰州植物园) in Anning District grows many kinds of trees, flowers and shrubs.
Xiguan Mosque (西关清真寺) ranks among the larger mosques in China.
Xinglong Mountain (兴隆山) is thick with pine forests and dotted with colourful temples.
Lutusi ancient government site (鲁土司衙门旧址) is a big complex of old administrative buildings.
Gansu Provincial Museum (甘肃省博物馆) shows archaeological and fossil finds from Gansu, along with exhibitions on the province's history.

Lanzhou Museum (兰州市博物馆) is an important Silk Road cultural site. Its October 2017 inventory counted over 13,000 objects, from ceramics and bronzes to calligraphy, coins, jade and stonework. These include 52 national first-class relics, 78 national second-level relics and 682 national third-level relics.
Gansu Art Museum (甘肃艺术馆) offers artists a broad platform for display and exchange with the public.
Lanzhou City Planning Exhibition Hall (兰州市规划展览馆) presents the deep Yellow River culture of Lanzhou by combining indoor exhibits, architectural ideas and urban character.
Lanzhou Painted Pottery Museum (兰州彩陶博物馆) holds 250 items, 50 of them precious relics, and shows the painted pottery civilisation represented by Majiayao ware.
Gansu Science and Technology Museum (甘肃科技博物馆) uses sound, light, electricity and other modern techniques so visitors can learn about science in a pleasant atmosphere.

lanzhou-jiaotong-university.h: From poor provincial capital to industrial centre

blocks.x: Lanzhou's fortunes turned after 1949. A capital of a very poor province became the hub of a large industrial area, and the city was among the first in China to industrialise, because the First and Second Five-Year Plans targeted it.

Per-person GDP was RMB 25,566 (US$3,681) in 2008, placing Lanzhou 134th among 659 Chinese cities. The 2015 figure was RMB 57,191 (US$9,182.28), and the city sat 100th among Chinese cities for total GDP.
Chengguan district hosts the International Solar Energy Center, known as UNIDO-ISEC.

Nearby deposits include dolomite, clay, manganese, nickel, zinc, silver, gold and coal. For electricity, there is a thermal plant fed by Qinghai coal, a hydroelectric station in the Zhulama Gorge in Gansu, and, upstream on the Yellow River in the Liujia Gorge, a big multipurpose dam.

Heavy and process industries dominate: refining, petrochemicals, metallurgy, machinery, rubber and fertiliser, along with textile mills. Gansu has one of the country's biggest oil refineries, Lanzhou is the province's petrochemical centre, a pipeline ties the refinery to the Yumen fields, and local firms make oil-industry equipment.

Textiles matter, with woollen and leather goods particularly well known. Locomotives and rolling stock for north-western railways are built here, plus machine tools and mining equipment. Output of aluminium products, industrial chemicals and fertilisers is substantial, and rubber is another big sector. Gaolan, close by, supplies copper. Lanzhou has also been a centre of China's national nuclear industry since the 1960s, when its uranium enrichment plant was completed.

Farmers and herders across a wide hinterland send their crops and animals to Lanzhou for sale. Typical products are spring wheat, vegetables, beans, oilseed, melon, peaches and tobacco, and the area is also known for roses and lilies.
Lanzhou Zhongchuan Airport, the main airport, is 70 km (43 mi) north of the city and opened to the public in 1970. It has direct connections to more than 70 international and domestic destinations.

In August 2012 Lanzhou became only the second north-western city to announce a subway. Lanzhou Metro is planned as six lines totalling 207 km (129 mi). Line 1 is wholly underground and started running in June 2019; stage one of Line 2 followed in June 2023. Wulipu Station and Dongfanghong Square Station are where passengers switch between the two.

Western China's rail network revolves around Lanzhou Railway Station, which sees over 100 passenger trains begin or pass through daily and ties the western provinces to the east. Find it in Chengguan district on Huochezhan Dong Lu. The city's second big station, Lanzhou West, is where the high-speed services call.
The main station serves the following routes:

The Longhai Railway runs east (Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Lianyungang) and joins the main eastern network, with direct trains to Beijing, Shanghai and other cities. It was finished in 1953 and was the first railway to reach Lanzhou.
The Lanxin Railway leads west and north-west. Trains run straight through to Ürümqi and western Gansu, and onward links reach other parts of Xinjiang and Kazakhstan.
The Lanqing Railway takes you west and south-west, with through trains to Xining and Lhasa.
The Chongqing-Lanzhou railway runs south-east, with through trains to Guangyuan and Chongqing.
A line to the north and north-east gives direct service to Yinchuan and Baotou.
The Lanzhou-Zhongchuan Airport Intercity Railway links Lanzhou Railway Station with the airport.
The Lanhe Railway, still under construction, will reach Linxia and Hezuo.

Passenger-only high-speed lines are finished towards the east (Xuzhou-Lanzhou), the west (Lanzhou-Xinjiang) and the north (Yinchuan-Lanzhou), and they stop only at Lanzhou West Railway Station. The Sichuan-Qinghai railway, designed for top speeds of 200 to 250 km/h (120 to 160 mph), is under construction.

For freight, Lanzhou forms an important link on one route of the Eurasian Land Bridge and gives rail access westward to Qinghai, Xinjiang and Tibet. A large freight terminal was built recently to handle growing volumes, and the city has China's fourth-largest marshalling yard. Regular freight services run to Chongqing, Hamburg, Almaty and Kathmandu.

In 2016 Lanzhou ranked fourth among Chinese cities for the worst rush-hour congestion, but after an urban ring road was completed it fell to 33rd in 2017. Main routes in and out include these highways:
G75 Lanzhou-Haikou Expressway
G30 Lianyungang-Khorgas Expressway
G6 Beijing-Lhasa Expressway
G22 Qingdao-Lanzhou Expressway
G2201 Lanzhou Ring Expressway
China National Highway 212
China National Highway 213
China National Highway 312

Long-distance coaches use one of three terminals: the West station in the Xiaoxihu neighbourhood, the East station beside Lanzhou Station, and the South station by the G75 expressway terminus. City buses number 132 lines, converging on Xiguan. A well-regarded bus rapid transit system, opened in 2013, won Lanzhou an honourable mention at the Sustainable Transport Awards of 2014.
LZJTU belongs to Gansu, and the wider province influences a student's experience nearly as much as the campus. This part of the guide introduces Gansu itself.

The Song dynasty coined the name Gansu by joining the first syllables of two earlier prefectures from the Sui and Tang eras. One, Gan, was centred on the Zhangye area; the other, Su, on the Jiuquan area. In the east, Gansu forms a piece of the ground where Chinese civilisation first took shape.

Stone Age peoples lived here long ago. In the east, the Dadiwan culture, which gave up archaeologically significant objects, thrived for roughly three millennia, between about 6000 BC and about 3000 BC. Majiayao followed, rooted in the period 3100 BC to 2700 BC, and part of the Qijia culture spanned 2400 BC to 1900 BC. The Yuezhi originally inhabited the extreme west until the Xiongnu drove them away around 177 BC.

Qin, the state seen in China as the origin of the empire, emerged in Gansu's south-east near Tianshui, and the area may be part of the source of the Qin name. Excavations at Fangmatan near Tianshui produced Qin tombs and artefacts, including a map of Guixian County that is 2,200 years old.

For the empire, Gansu was a strategic frontier and a communications corridor, because the Hexi Corridor runs along the province's 'neck'. Han builders pushed the Great Wall across it and founded the garrison towns of Yangguan and Yumenguan (Jade Gate Pass, near Dunhuang), whose remains are still visible. Later, the Ming raised the Jiayuguan outpost. Beyond Yumenguan and the Qilian Mountains, in the north-western tip, nomads such as the Yuezhi and Wusun roamed and now and then entered imperial strategy.

A treaty signed at Qingshui in 823 between the Tang dynasty and the Tibetan Empire cost China much of western Gansu for a long time. Once the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed, migrating Uyghurs founded a Buddhist Yugur state in part of Gansu, the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, which survived from 848 until 1036 AD. Afterwards the Xixia (Western Xia) dynasty held large areas of Gansu and Ningxia.

Along the Silk Road, Gansu was important for trade and as a channel for culture. Murals in its temples and Buddhist grottoes, among them the Maijishan Caves and the Mogao Caves (the 'Caves of the Thousand Buddhas'), are rich in artistic and historical interest. In August 2006 an early type of paper bearing Chinese characters, dated to about 8 BC, was found at a Western Han garrison site near the Yumen pass.

The Dungan Revolt of 1862 to 1877 is linked to Gansu too, though it entered the province from neighbouring Qinghai. Qing forces included Muslim commanders such as Ma Zhan'ao and Ma Anliang, who helped to defeat the rebels. A second Dungan revolt broke out in 1895 and lasted into 1896.

Repeated earthquakes, droughts and famines meant that until recently Gansu developed far more slowly than other Chinese provinces. Its abundant mineral wealth is now turning it into an important industrial base. In 1920 a quake of magnitude 8.6 claimed about 180,000 lives, largely in present-day Ningxia, and one of magnitude 7.6 in 1932 killed 275.

From 1927 to 1930 came the Muslim Conflict in Gansu, aimed at the Guominjun. By 1940 the Muslim general Ma Buqing effectively ran Gansu, even though Ma Hongbin served as acting provincial chairman. Ma Buqing had earlier based himself in Liangzhou District of Wuwei, where he held sway over 15 million Muslims. Nationalist soldiers entered Xinjiang through Gansu and brought it under Nationalist control, and Tienshui saw a Japanese-Chinese air fight.

Because Xinjiang bordered the Soviet Union, Gansu was open to Soviet penetration, and it carried Soviet supplies into the Republic of China throughout the Second Sino-Japanese War. A road from Dihua (Ürümqi) ended at Lanzhou. The Chinese Air Force guarded the province from several bases, one of which was Gonxingdun Aerodrome. From summer 1939 the Yumen Laojunmiao oil wells supplied most of wartime China's domestic petrol, with a wartime output of 250,000 tons of crude. Plans also named Lanzhou and Lhasa as the ends of a new railway. After the war, the Kuomintang Islamic insurgency of 1950 to 1958, an extension of the Civil War, touched Gansu and several other provinces.

The province is large: 454,000 square kilometres (175,000 square miles), with the bulk of its land higher than 1,000 metres (3,300 ft). It is squeezed between the Loess Plateau and the Tibetan Plateau. Going round the border, Mongolia's Govi-Altai Province lies north-west, Xinjiang west, Sichuan south, Shaanxi east, and Inner Mongolia and Ningxia north. The Yellow River crosses the southern part. China's geographical centre also falls inside Gansu, where a monument at 35°50′40.9″N 103°27′7.5″E marks the spot.

Gansu contains a stretch of the Gobi Desert and small pieces of the Badain Jaran and Tengger deserts. Most of the Yellow River's water comes from Gansu, and the river passes straight through Lanzhou; the Wuwei area is in the Shiyang River Basin instead. Mountains dominate the south, belonging to the Qilian range, while the north is flat. At the very western end, the Altyn-Tagh reaches the province's highest altitude of 5,830 metres (19,130 ft).

The Hexi Corridor, a natural land passage some 1,000 kilometres (620 mi) long from Lanzhou to the Jade Gate, lies within the province, bounded by the Gobi Desert on the north and the Qilian Mountains on the south.

Continental conditions, either semi-arid or arid (Köppen BSk or BWk), prevail across most of Gansu. Summers range from warm to hot and winters from cold to very cold, though day and night differ so much that afternoon highs often stay above 0 °C (32 °F) in midwinter. High-altitude districts have a subarctic climate (Dwc), where winter lows can touch -40 °C (-40 °F). Rain and snow are scarce and mostly summer events. It is so dry in winter that lasting snow cover appears only high up, and in the south-west the snow line can sit at 5,500 metres (18,040 ft).

Services have been Gansu's biggest economic sector since 2014, and tourism is growing in importance. On the education side, Lanzhou University, the only Class A Double First Class university in China's north-west, is in the province.

lanzhou-university.h: Lanzhou University: an overview for applicants

blocks.x: In Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu province in north-west China, you will find Lanzhou University (兰州大学), a public university under the Ministry of Education. It has been included in Project 211, in Project 985 and in the Double First-Class Construction programme, which means it has long been among the universities that the state backs most strongly. In the north-west, it is widely regarded as the leading university.

The university was founded in 1909 and teaches undergraduate and graduate students across four campuses. Three of them are in the centre of Lanzhou, and the fourth is in Yuzhong County, about 30 miles from the main campus. China's first national bases for training talent in basic arts and science subjects included one at Lanzhou. The university also took part from the start in the national innovation experiments for college students, and it is among just 19 Chinese universities piloting special programmes for top students in basic disciplines.

Current enrolment is 20,686 undergraduates, 15,081 master's students and 5,326 doctoral students. It offers 99 undergraduate majors, 16 of which are national characteristic majors. Nationally recognised units number 10 teaching teams, 6 talent training bases and 52 first-class undergraduate major construction sites.

lanzhou-university.h: From a law school to a research university

blocks.x: Lanzhou University traces its roots to 1909, when a Gansu school of law and politics opened as its forerunner. It was renamed Sun Yat-sen University of Lanzhou in 1928, and from 1945 it was National Lanzhou University. After 1949 it took the name Lanzhou University, and it was named one of China's 14 key universities.

Medical education began in 1932 with a medical college and its hospital. Two bodies merged into the university later: a Gansu research institute on grassland ecology in 2002, and the medical college itself in 2004.

Observers rank it among China's leading institutions of higher education, and as the best university in the north-west. In 1981 it was among the first universities authorised to enrol candidates for bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees. The 2017 Double First-Class Construction round gave it Class A status.

Four fields have doctoral programmes counted among the best ten in China: physics, chemistry, atmospheric sciences and geography. Highly ranked programmes also exist in biology, botany, mathematics, history, media, ecology, information science and Chinese literature. Basic science stands out, and the university is within the top 1% of the Essential Science Indicators index. As a concrete example of its research, a gamma shutdown sensor developed at Lanzhou University was part of the landing system of the Chang'e 4 lunar probe.
Three main laboratories and an analytical testing facility have been approved by the Chinese Ministry of Education as being of high importance to the nation.

Founded in 1991 with the approval of China's Planning Commission, the Laboratory of Arid Agroecology works on the ecology of dry-land farming. It is the only laboratory in the Ministry of Education's system devoted to this topic. Funding from a World Bank loan, along with authority to confer bachelor's, master's, doctoral and post-doctoral degrees, has helped it develop strongly.

The Laboratory of Applied Organic Chemistry, opened in December 1987, was in the first group of state key laboratories approved by the Planning Commission and and welcomes visiting scholars and scientists from China and abroad. It is a principal training ground for organic chemists. Its research looks at organic molecules with special functions, and in particular basic research on active organic molecules.

Set up by the Ministry of Education in 1993, the Open Laboratory of Applied Magnetism studies the applications of magnetism, mainly perpendicular magnetic recording. It also carries out research and development on new magnetic materials with commercial uses. Mössbauer spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance spin-echo spectroscopy and general magnetic testing are used to examine the microscopic structure and overall magnetic behaviour of materials. Its main equipment includes a vibrating sample magnetometer, a high-pressure Mössbauer spectroscope and a magnetron sputtering system, among other items. It also supports materials science and condensed matter physics research. The staff comprises 24 professional researchers and technicians, four of them doctoral advisers.

Construction of the Analytical Testing Center began in 1982, paid for by the first World Bank loan for developing universities. It has more than 20 major instruments, among them a high-resolution mass spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer, an X-ray quadrupole diffractometer, a laser Raman spectrometer and an FT-IR spectrometer. Its main job is determining and analysing the structure of matter. Graduate students also do experiments here that lead to master's and PhD degrees, and members of the public can use its testing service. Since 1992 it has held approval from the State Technology Superintendency to inspect chemical and mining goods that are imported or exported.

Different sources describe the campuses slightly differently, so check the university's website for the current arrangement. One account gives two campuses: the oldest in the middle of Lanzhou (Chengguan District) and the main campus in Yuzhong County. A further campus connected with the Belt and Road policy, to the north of the city, was being built.

The university has 6 national bases for training research and teaching personnel in fundamental disciplines, and runs 35 more institutes. It hosts a national key laboratory in applied organic chemistry and three Ministry of Education key laboratories, covering arid and grassland ecology, the environment of west China, and magnetism and magnetic materials. There is also a Ministry of Agriculture key laboratory on grassland agro-ecosystems.

The Academic Ranking of World Universities placed Lanzhou University among the world's top 500 in 2007, one of the Project 985 universities to manage this. Research from Lanzhou is widely cited in international journals; for 2008 to 2017 it came 26th among Chinese universities in citations per paper.

Later rankings show where it stands now. In 2023 the ARWU placed it in the 201–300 band, with Chemistry and Atmospheric Science in the global top 100 by subject. U.S. News & World Report's Best Global Universities for 2025–2026 put it 460th in the world, 116th in Asia and 62nd in China. QS's 2020 world ranking put it in the 751–800 band. League tables use different methods and change every year, so use them as rough guides only.

lanzhou-university.h: Living in Lanzhou: the city around the campus

blocks.x: A student's life depends a lot on the city beyond the campus. The sections that follow introduce Lanzhou and explain what to expect from its setting, air, climate and transport.

Lanzhou stands at 1,600 metres above sea level (about 5,200 feet), in what is geographically the north-western centre of China. Its built-up area runs along the southern bank of the Yellow River, which flows west to east through the city, and the metropolitan area spans over 20 square kilometres of urban land. To the south and north rise the Qilian Ranges, Mount Pingliang and Mount Kongtong.

The city lies on the upper Yellow River, where the river leaves the mountains. It has been a centre since early times because it is the southern end of the route that leads across Central Asia by way of the Hexi Corridor. From here, one can reach the area around the ancient capital Chang'an (modern Xi'an) in Shaanxi from both the west and north-west, and the Qinghai Lake region by way of the upper Yellow River and its tributaries.

The temperate-zone climate here is semi-arid (Köppen BSk), meaning hot summers and cold winters that are very dry. Using 1971–2000 averages for the urban core, the mean temperature runs from −4.1 °C in January to 23.4 °C in July, and the annual mean is 10.9 °C. Rainfall is only 309 millimetres a year (12.2 inches), and almost all of it falls between May and October. Snow is so scarce in the dry winters that it sometimes falls only in autumn and spring. Sunshine is 47 percent of the possible total in September and 57 percent in April; it is generous but not abundant, adding up to 2,350 hours a year.

Lanzhou sits in a narrow, curving river valley hemmed in by mountains, which blocks the free flow of air. An environmental analysis by Tsinghua University and the Asian Development Bank, published in January 2013, listed Lanzhou as one of the world's ten most air-polluted cities. At times the mountain on the south side of the city, Lanshan, could not be seen. The city has many factories, some of them processing petroleum, and winter and spring bring large dust storms from the Gobi Desert. Two years earlier, in 2011, the World Health Organization had used Chinese statistics to report that Lanzhou had the poorest air of eleven cities in western China. The annual mean PM10 of 150 micrograms per cubic metre was seven times the WHO's safe level and worse than Beijing's 121.

Since then the authorities have acted, and the measures have largely worked. They closed thirteen polluting enterprises with excess capacity, suspended over 200 highly polluting enterprises in winter, and relocated 78 industrial enterprises to a park beyond the city. China gave Lanzhou its climate progress title in 2015. Once a city that satellites could barely detect through the haze, it has cut its Air Pollution Index faster than any other Chinese city in recent years. By the 2018 WHO database, out of 2,700 towns listed, Lanzhou had the 158th highest PM2.5 level, averaging 54 micrograms per cubic metre (twice Milan's). The larger PM10 particles stay high, at 132 micrograms per cubic metre, partly because of sandstorms.

Heavy silt gives the Yellow River its muddy colour at Lanzhou, though in 2008 the water here was described as far cleaner than the fouled flow two hours downstream. Several endangered Chinese giant salamanders have turned up in and near the river in recent years. In April 2014, officials told residents to avoid tap water for a time after benzene in the supply measured 20 times the national limit of 10 micrograms per litre, with industrial chemical production suspected. Water and air quality are worth checking with local sources before you arrive.

Earthquakes occur regularly in Lanzhou, though they are usually weak. A major earthquake in 1920 killed over 100,000 people across Ningxia and eastern Gansu, yet the toll in Lanzhou itself was 42, and this low number has been credited to the strong but flexible wooden buildings in the city. The city also felt the Sichuan earthquake of 2008.

The 2020 Chinese census put the number of Lanzhou residents above 4 million for the first time, at 4,359,446. Of these, 3,042,863 lived in the built-up metro area, which is 1,112.9 square kilometres across four central districts (Chengguan, Qilihe, Anning and Xigu). Honggu District and Lanzhou New Area, around the airport, are still separate from the conurbation. After a period of slow growth, the rise has been marked, which people explain by families seeking better schooling, retired migrant workers coming back to Gansu, better services and government policy.

lanzhou-university.h: Things to see in and around Lanzhou

blocks.x: Lanzhou is the main transport and tourism gateway to Gansu and the Hexi Corridor, with access to historical sites such as the Bingling Temple Grottoes. In the city itself the following are worth knowing:
Five Spring Mountain Park (五泉山公园), on the north side of Gaolan Mountain, is known for its five springs and many Buddhist temples, with a number of ancient buildings.
The first permanent bridge over the Yellow River is Zhongshan Bridge (中山桥).
Baita Mountain Park (白塔山公园) opened in 1958 across from that bridge; it was built against the hillside at a height of 1,700 metres (about 5,600 feet).
Lanzhou Botanical Garden (兰州植物园), in Anning District, grows many kinds of trees, flowers and other plants.
Xiguan Mosque (西关清真寺) is among the larger mosques in China.
Xinglong Mountain (兴隆山) is covered by dense pine forest, with colourful temples scattered across it.
The Lutusi ancient government site (鲁土司衙门旧址) is a large complex of old government buildings.
Gansu Provincial Museum (甘肃省博物馆) shows archaeological and fossil finds from the province and exhibitions on its history.

Lanzhou Museum (兰州市博物馆) counts as a significant Silk Road cultural site. In October 2017 its collection exceeded 13,000 pieces: pottery, porcelain, bronzes, calligraphy, coins, jade, stoneware and more. The relics are graded nationally as 52 first-class, 78 second-class and 682 third-class.
Gansu Art Museum (甘肃艺术馆) offers artists a wide display space and a platform for outside exchange.
Lanzhou City Planning Exhibition Hall (兰州市规划展览馆) presents Lanzhou's deep Yellow River culture, mixing indoor exhibits, architectural ideas and urban character.
Lanzhou Painted Pottery Museum (兰州彩陶博物馆) has 250 items, including 50 precious relics, and shows the painted-pottery civilisation represented by the Majiayao culture.
Gansu Science and Technology Museum (甘肃科技博物馆) applies high-tech displays using light, sound and electricity, so visitors learn about modern science in an enjoyable way.

lanzhou-university.h: From poor provincial capital to industrial centre

blocks.x: Since 1949 Lanzhou has gone from being the capital of a poverty-stricken province to the centre of a major industrial region. Lanzhou was among the earliest Chinese cities to industrialise, and the First and Second Five-Year Plans both concentrated on it.

GDP per person stood at 25,566 RMB (US$3,681) in 2008, which placed Lanzhou 134th among 659 cities. By 2015 per-person GDP had risen to 57,191 RMB (US$9,182.28) and the city took 100th place for total GDP.
Chengguan District is home to the International Solar Energy Center (UNIDO-ISEC).

Mineral resources include dolomite, clay, manganese, nickel, zinc, silver, gold and coal. For power, a thermal plant burns coal brought from Qinghai, while a hydroelectric station works at Zhulama Gorge in Gansu and a large multipurpose dam stands in Liujia Gorge on the Yellow River above the city.

Major industries are petrochemicals, an oil refinery, machinery, metallurgy, textiles, rubber processing and fertiliser. Gansu has one of the country's largest oil refineries, and Lanzhou is the centre of the province's petrochemical industry. A pipeline links the refinery to the Yumen fields, and the city also makes equipment for the oil industry.

Textiles are a major sector, particularly woollen and leather goods. The city also builds locomotives and rolling stock for the north-western railways, plus machine tools and mining equipment. It produces aluminium products, industrial chemicals and fertilisers on a large scale, and has a big rubber industry. Copper is mined nearby at Gaolan. In addition, the city has been a centre of China's nuclear industry since the 1960s, after completion of its uranium enrichment plant.

Farm produce and livestock from a large surrounding region are collected and sold in Lanzhou. Crops include spring wheat, vegetables, beans, oil crops, melons, peaches and tobacco, and the area is also known for roses and lilies.
The city's main airport, Zhongchuan, lies 70 kilometres (43 miles) to the north and opened to the public in 1970. More than 70 international and domestic destinations are served directly.

In August 2012 Lanzhou became the second city in north-west China to announce a subway line. The planned Lanzhou Metro network has six lines running 207 kilometres (129 miles). Line 1, entirely underground, opened in June 2019, and the first stage of Line 2 followed in June 2023. Two interchange stations, Wulipu and Dongfanghong Square, let passengers switch between the lines.

Lanzhou Railway Station is a major rail hub of western China, found in Chengguan District on Huochezhan Dong Lu, and more than 100 passenger trains start from or pass through it each day. It joins the western provinces to the east. The second main station is Lanzhou West, with high-speed services. Rail links from Lanzhou Railway Station include:

The Longhai Railway runs east through Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Lianyungang and links with the eastern network, so direct trains reach Beijing, Shanghai and other cities. It was the first line into Lanzhou, finished in 1953.
The Lanxin Railway goes west and north-west; direct trains serve western Gansu and Ürümqi, with further connections to other parts of Xinjiang and to Kazakhstan.
The Lanqing Railway heads west and south-west, with direct trains to Xining and Lhasa.
The Chongqing–Lanzhou railway lies to the south-east and has direct trains to Guangyuan and Chongqing.
A line to the north and north-east serves Baotou and Yinchuan directly.
Lanzhou–Zhongchuan Airport Intercity Railway between the station and the airport
Lanhe Railway to Linxia and Hezuo, under construction at the time of writing

New passenger-only high-speed lines have been built to the east (Xuzhou–Lanzhou), the west (Lanzhou–Xinjiang) and the north (Yinchuan–Lanzhou). They call only at Lanzhou West. A further line, the Sichuan–Qinghai railway, was under construction, designed for speeds of 200 to 250 km/h (120 to 160 mph).

One of the Eurasian Land Bridge routes passes through Lanzhou, and the city also gives rail access further west to Tibet, Xinjiang and Qinghai. A big freight terminal was built recently to handle rising volumes, and the marshalling yard is the fourth largest in China. Regular freight trains run to destinations such as Hamburg, Kathmandu, Almaty and Chongqing.
In 2016 Lanzhou ranked fourth among Chinese cities for the worst rush-hour traffic, but after an urban ring road was completed it dropped to 33rd in 2017. Main roads and expressways include:
G2201 Lanzhou Ring Expressway
G22 Qingdao–Lanzhou Expressway
G6 Beijing–Lhasa Expressway
G30 Lianyungang–Khorgas Expressway
G75 Lanzhou–Haikou Expressway
China National Highways 212, 213 and 312

Long-distance coaches use three major stations in the urban area: West (in the Xiaoxihu neighbourhood), East (beside Lanzhou Station) and South (near where the G75 expressway ends). Within the city there are 132 local bus lines centred on Xiguan. The bus rapid transit system, opened in 2013, is well regarded, and it earned an honourable mention in the 2014 Sustainable Transport Awards.
