Lanzhou University of Technology (兰州理工大学, Lánzhōu Lǐgōng Dàxué), often shortened to LUT, is a science and engineering university in Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in northwest China. It is a good fit if you want applied engineering and technology in a region where heavy industry, energy and the Silk Road past all meet.

lanzhou-university-of-technology.h: From a technical school to a university

blocks.x: The roots go back to 1919, when the institution opened as Ganzhou Technical School. The big changes came in 1958. First the school became Lanzhou Polytechnic Institute, and in the same year it joined forces with Gansu Communication College under the name Gansu University of Technology.

Its range of subjects grew again in 1965. Three specialties came over from the Northeast Heavy-Machine Building Institute and a fourth from the Beijing Machine-Building Institute; before the move, all four belonged to China's First Machine-Building Industry Ministry. After the State Council reorganisation of 1998, responsibility for the university passed to the provincial and central governments together. In May 2003, with Ministry of Education approval, it received its present name, Lanzhou University of Technology.
LUT stands in Qilihe District, within the city of Lanzhou. It has two campuses, with a total site of 2430 acres and floor space of 2,220,000 square metres.

The institution has twenty-one colleges and departments. Study options include sixty-five undergraduate programmes, eighty-six master's programmes and twenty-six doctoral programmes. On the research side there is one national key laboratory, twelve provincial engineering research centres and fifteen engineering research centres run jointly with industry. Fifteen academic disciplines are classed as important at provincial level, and together they give the university a recognisable academic character of its own.

There are 2,309 faculty members in all. Of these, 1,570 are full-time lecturers, 890 hold the rank of professor or associate professor, and 130 supervise doctoral students. The student body is 27,599 full-time students, including 3,878 postgraduates.

The university has 279 international students from 35 countries. It runs overseas exchange schemes in 2+2 and 1+2+1 formats, in cooperation with partner universities abroad. In a 2+2 route you would normally spend two years at each institution; check the current partner list and conditions with the international office.
Much of student life is shaped by the city beyond the gates, so the sections that follow cover what to expect from Lanzhou: the setting, the weather, the air, transport and sights.

lanzhou-university-of-technology.h: A river city in the northwest

blocks.x: The city's altitude is 1,600 m (about 5,200 ft), and it lies close to the geographical centre of China. Its urbanised area (given as over 20 square kilometres, or 7.7 sq mi) runs along the south bank of the Yellow River, which flows through from west to east. Hills and mountains enclose it. On the south and north sides you find the Qilian Ranges along with Mt. Pingliang and Mt. Kongtong.

The city grew up on the upper Yellow River at the point where the river leaves the mountains. That position made it a regional centre early on. It marks the southern end of the route that crosses the Hexi Corridor toward Central Asia, and it controls approaches to the ancient capital district around Chang'an (today's Xi'an, in Shaanxi) from both west and northwest. Through the upper Yellow River and its tributaries it also gives access to the area around Qinghai Lake.

Lanzhou is in the temperate zone with a semi-arid climate (Köppen BSk): summers are hot and winters are cold and very dry. Using 1971 to 2000 averages for the urban core, the January daily mean is -4.1 °C (24.6 °F) and the July mean reaches 23.4 °C (74.1 °F); the whole-year mean sits at 10.9 °C, or 51.6 °F.

Rain totals only 309 millimetres (12.2 in) a year, and nearly all of it falls between May and October. Winters are so dry that snow may be limited to autumn and spring. Sunshine is plentiful without being exceptional: possible sunshine runs from 47 per cent in September to 57 per cent in April, and the annual total is 2,350 hours.

lanzhou-university-of-technology.h: A city that cleaned up its air

blocks.x: This section deals honestly with an issue many applicants ask about. Lanzhou sits in a narrow, curving valley, and the hills around it hold air in place instead of letting it move on. A January 2013 environmental analysis from Tsinghua University and the Asian Development Bank listed Lanzhou as one of the world's ten worst cities for air pollution. Reports said the smog sometimes hid Lanshan, the mountain on the south side of town. The city is also home to many factories, among them petroleum processing plants, and gets big dust storms from the Gobi Desert, particularly in winter and spring.

In 2011 the World Health Organization, using Chinese statistics, reported the worst air quality of eleven western Chinese cities for Lanzhou. Its annual mean PM10 level of 150 micrograms per cubic metre was seven times the WHO safe level, and higher than Beijing's 121.

Since then the authorities have acted, with largely successful results. Thirteen polluting enterprises with excess capacity were shut down, more than 200 heavy polluters stopped work over winter, and 78 factories moved out to an industrial park beyond the city limits. China's climate progress title went to Lanzhou in 2015. A city that satellites once could hardly pick out has, in recent years, brought down its Air Pollution Index faster than anywhere else in the country. The WHO's 2018 database covers 2,700 towns, and Lanzhou comes 158th for PM2.5, averaging 54 micrograms per cubic metre (roughly twice Milan's level). Coarse PM10 stays high at 132 micrograms per cubic metre, partly because of sandstorms.
In practice this means: expect better air than the old headlines suggest, but check daily readings and keep a mask for dusty spring days.

lanzhou-university-of-technology.h: The river and the tap water

blocks.x: The Yellow River carries a heavy load of silt where it passes Lanzhou, so it looks muddy. Even so, the water here is better than the foul outflow that barely counted as water two hours downstream in 2008. In recent years several endangered Chinese giant salamanders have turned up in or near the river within Lanzhou.

Two incidents are worth knowing. On 11 April 2014 officials advised people to stop drinking from the tap. Benzene had reached 20 times the national limit of 10 micrograms per litre, and industrial chemical production was the suspected cause, similar to what happened after the 2005 Jilin chemical plant explosions. And in 2020 a brucellosis outbreak affected over 3,000 people after the Lanzhou Biopharmaceutical Plant, a vaccine producer, accidentally released the bacteria into the air through exhaust because expired disinfectant had been used.

Earthquakes strike Lanzhou regularly, though mostly at low intensity. A great quake in 1920 killed over 100,000 people across Ningxia and eastern Gansu, yet just 42 died in Lanzhou itself, which has been credited to the strong but flexible wooden buildings of the time. The city was also shaken by the 2008 Sichuan earthquake.

Lanzhou passed 4 million inhabitants for the first time in the 2020 census, with 4,359,446 people. Of these, 3,042,863 live in the metro or built-up area, which spans 1,112.9 square kilometres (429.7 sq mi) and is made up of four central districts: Chengguan, Qilihe, Anning and Xigu. Two other areas, Lanzhou New Area by the airport and Honggu District, have not yet merged into the urban area.

Growth picked up sharply after a slower period. Suggested reasons are better schooling for children (a draw for parents), migrant workers coming home to Gansu in retirement, better city services and government policy.

Lanzhou is the main transport and tourism gateway to Gansu and the Hexi Corridor, and it gives access to historic sites such as the Bingling Temple Grottoes. Closer to the university, these places stand out:
Five Spring Mountain Park (五泉山公园), on the north side of Gaolan Mountain, known for its five springs and its many Buddhist temples with ancient buildings.
Zhongshan Bridge (中山桥), the first permanent bridge across the Yellow River.
Baita Mountain Park (白塔山公园), set against the hills at an elevation of 1,700 m (5,600 ft); it opened in 1958 across from Zhongshan Bridge.
Lanzhou Botanical Garden (兰州植物园) in Anning District, with a large range of trees, flowers and other plants.
Xiguan Mosque (西关清真寺), counted among the larger mosques in China.
Xinglong Mountain (兴隆山), covered in thick pine forest and dotted with colourful temples.
The former Lutusi government offices (鲁土司衙门旧址), a large group of old official buildings.
Gansu Provincial Museum (甘肃省博物馆): archaeological and fossil finds from Gansu, plus exhibitions on the province's history.

Lanzhou Museum (兰州市博物馆): an important Silk Road cultural site. As of October 2017 it held more than 13,000 items, such as pottery, porcelain, bronze, calligraphy, coins, jade and stoneware, including 52 national first-class, 78 national second-level and 682 national third-level cultural relics.
Gansu Art Museum (甘肃艺术馆): a broad display space and platform where artists meet the public.
Lanzhou City Planning Exhibition Hall (兰州市规划展览馆): presents the deep Yellow River culture of Lanzhou through indoor displays, architectural ideas and urban features.
Lanzhou Painted Pottery Museum (兰州彩陶博物馆): 250 items, among them 50 precious relics, illustrating the painted-pottery civilisation represented by Majiayao pottery.
Gansu Science and Technology Museum (甘肃科技博物馆): uses sound, light, electricity and other high-tech methods so visitors can learn about modern science in a relaxed setting.

lanzhou-university-of-technology.h: From poor provincial capital to industrial centre

blocks.x: Lanzhou's transformation since 1949 has been striking: once the capital of a very poor province, it is now at the centre of a big industrial area. The First and Second Five-Year Plans concentrated investment here, which made it one of China's earliest industrialised cities. GDP per capita was RMB 25,566 (US$3,681) in 2008, 134th among 659 Chinese cities. By 2015 it had risen to RMB 57,191 (US$9,182.28), and Lanzhou ranked 100th among Chinese cities for total GDP. The UNIDO-ISEC (International Solar Energy Center) has its base in Chengguan District.

The local mineral list covers coal, gold, silver, zinc, nickel, manganese, clay and dolomite, and water power is a further asset. A coal-fired power station takes its fuel from Qinghai. There is also a hydroelectric station in the Zhulama Gorge (Gansu), and upstream of Lanzhou the Liujia Gorge on the Yellow River carries a big multipurpose dam.

Main sectors are textiles, rubber processing, fertiliser, refining, petrochemicals, machinery and metallurgy. One of the country's biggest refineries is in Gansu, and Lanzhou anchors the province's petrochemical industry. The refinery receives crude by pipeline from the Yumen fields, and the city also manufactures oil-industry equipment.

The textile trade is large, with woollen and leather goods especially well known. The city builds locomotives and rolling stock for railways in the northwest, as well as machine tools and mining equipment. Aluminium goods, industrial chemicals and fertilisers are produced at scale, rubber is a big industry, and copper is mined nearby at Gaolan. Since the 1960s, when the Lanzhou uranium enrichment plant was completed, Lanzhou has also been among the centres of China's nuclear power industry. For an engineering student, this concentration of heavy industry means local internships and employers are within easy reach.

The city acts as a collection point and market for farm produce and livestock drawn from far around. Crops include spring wheat, vegetables, beans, oil-bearing crops, melons, peaches and tobacco, and flowers such as roses and lilies are grown too.
Lanzhou Zhongchuan Airport, the city's main airport, lies 70 km (43 mi) to the north. It began public service in 1970 and offers direct links to more than 70 international and domestic destinations.

Lanzhou announced a subway in August 2012, the second city in northwest China to do so. The Lanzhou Metro is planned as six lines totalling 207 km (129 mi). Line 1 is fully underground and opened in June 2019; the first stage of Line 2 came in June 2023. You can switch between the two lines at Wulipu or Dongfanghong Square stations.

Lanzhou Railway Station (Huochezhan Dong Lu, Chengguan District) is a key rail hub of western China, linking the western provinces with the east; over 100 passenger trains begin or pass through every day. The second main station, Lanzhou West, handles the high-speed services. From the main station, the rail connections are:

The Longhai Railway going east to Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Lianyungang, where it joins the main eastern network (direct trains to Beijing and Shanghai among others). It opened in 1953 as the first line ever to reach Lanzhou.
The Lanxin Railway, heading west and northwest, with through trains to western Gansu and Ürümqi and onward connections inside Xinjiang and to Kazakhstan.
The Lanqing line, running west and southwest to Xining and Lhasa.
The Chongqing-Lanzhou line, running southeast to Chongqing and Guangyuan.
A northbound and northeastern route to Yinchuan and Baotou.
An intercity link between the main station and the airport (Lanzhou-Zhongchuan Airport Intercity Railway).
The Lanhe Railway to Linxia and Hezuo, still under construction.

Dedicated high-speed passenger lines are finished to the east (Xuzhou-Lanzhou), west (Lanzhou-Xinjiang) and north (Yinchuan-Lanzhou). They all call only at Lanzhou West Station. Another line, the Sichuan-Qinghai railway, is still being built; it is designed for 200 km/h (120 mph) up to 250 km/h (160 mph).

For freight, the city is a key link on one route of the Eurasian Land Bridge and opens the way by rail to Qinghai, Xinjiang and Tibet. A large new freight terminal copes with rising volumes, and the marshalling yard is the fourth biggest in China. Scheduled freight runs to Chongqing, Hamburg, Almaty and Kathmandu.
In 2016 Lanzhou ranked fourth among Chinese cities for the worst rush-hour congestion, but by 2017, after an urban ring road was completed, it had dropped to 33rd. Major routes include:
G75 Lanzhou-Haikou Expressway
G30 Lianyungang-Khorgas Expressway
G6 Beijing-Lhasa Expressway
G22 Qingdao-Lanzhou Expressway
G2201 Lanzhou Ring Expressway
China National Highways 212, 213 and 312

Long-distance coaches use three main stations in the urban area. The West station is in the Xiaoxihu neighbourhood, the East station is by Lanzhou Station, and the South station stands close to where the G75 expressway ends. City buses run on 132 lines with Xiguan as the main hub. The bus rapid transit system, which opened in 2013, won the city an honourable mention at the Sustainable Transport Awards of 2014.
Where a university sits in its province shapes daily life almost as much as the campus itself, so here is a short portrait of Gansu.

Gansu is a compound name that first appeared under the Song dynasty. It joins the names of two prefectures of the Sui and Tang periods: Gan (in the Zhangye area) and Su (in the Jiuquan area). Its eastern portion helped give rise to ancient Chinese civilisation.

In prehistoric times Gansu was home to Neolithic cultures. In the east, the Dadiwan culture (the source of significant archaeological finds) thrived between roughly 6000 BC and 3000 BC. Majiayao settlements date to 3100-2700 BC, and the Qijia culture took hold in part of the province during 2400-1900 BC. The Yuezhi lived in the far west of Gansu until the Xiongnu drove them out around 177 BC.

The State of Qin, seen as the state that founded the Chinese empire, grew out of southeastern Gansu, specifically the Tianshui area, and the Qin name may partly come from there. Qin tombs and objects have been excavated at Fangmatan near Tianshui, including a 2,200-year-old map of Guixian County.

For the empire, Gansu worked as a strategic frontier and a communications link, since the Hexi Corridor follows the province's "neck". Han rulers carried the Great Wall across the corridor and set up the key fort towns of Yangguan and Yumenguan (the Jade Gate Pass near Dunhuang), whose ruins survive. Ming builders added the Jiayuguan outpost. Beyond Yumenguan and the Qilian Mountains, in the far northwest, lived nomads such as the Yuezhi and the Wusun, who now and then featured in imperial geopolitics.

Under the Qingshui treaty, agreed in 823 by the Tibetan Empire and Tang China, much of western Gansu was lost for a long period. Later, when the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed, Uyghurs who migrated from it set up a Buddhist Yugur state in part of Gansu, the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom (848 to 1036 AD). The Xixia (Western Xia) dynasty also held most of Gansu and Ningxia.

Along the Silk Road, Gansu was economically significant and also a route for cultural exchange. Temples and Buddhist grottoes such as the Mogao Caves ("Caves of the Thousand Buddhas") and the Maijishan Caves hold murals that tell us a lot about art and history. Archaeologists working near the Yumen pass in August 2006 found, at a Western Han garrison site, an early kind of paper with Chinese characters, dated to about 8 BC.

The Dungan Revolt of 1862 to 1877 began from this province. On the Qing side were Muslim generals, among them Ma Zhan'ao and Ma Anliang, who helped crush the rebels; the uprising had spread into Gansu from Qinghai next door. Another Dungan revolt followed in 1895 to 1896.

Earthquakes, droughts and famines meant that Gansu's economic progress lagged well behind other provinces until recently. Its abundant mineral resources have since allowed it to start developing into an important industrial centre. A magnitude 8.6 quake in 1920 killed about 180,000 people, mostly in what is now Ningxia, and a magnitude 7.6 quake killed 275 in 1932.

Between 1927 and 1930 came the Muslim Conflict in Gansu, directed against the Guominjun. By 1940 the acting chairman of the province was the Muslim general Ma Hongbin, but another Muslim general, Ma Buqing, was effectively in charge of Gansu; he had earlier based himself in Liangzhou District, Wuwei, and controlled 15 million Muslims. Kuomintang soldiers reached Xinjiang by way of Gansu, bringing it under their control, and Tienshui in Gansu saw an air battle between Japanese and Chinese planes.

Via Xinjiang, Gansu was exposed to Soviet influence, and during the Second Sino-Japanese War it was a corridor for Soviet supplies sent to the Republic of China; a road from Dihua (Ürümqi) ended at Lanzhou. The Chinese Air Force defended Gansu from several bases, including the Gonxingdun Aerodrome. Starting in summer 1939, the Yumen Laojunmiao oil wells gave wartime China most of its domestic petrol, producing 250,000 tons of crude in those years. A new railway was meant to reach Lanzhou and Lhasa. Later, the Kuomintang Islamic insurgency (1950 to 1958) extended the Chinese Civil War into several provinces, Gansu among them.

The province measures 454,000 square kilometres (175,000 sq mi), and the large majority of it is over 1,000 m (3,300 ft) high. Gansu lies between two plateaux, the Tibetan and the Loess. Its neighbours are Mongolia (Govi-Altai Province) in the northwest, Inner Mongolia and Ningxia in the north, Shaanxi in the east, Sichuan in the south and Xinjiang in the west. The south of Gansu is crossed by the Yellow River. China's geographical centre lies in the province too, at the Center of the Country Monument (35°50′40.9″N, 103°27′7.5″E).

Part of the Gobi Desert lies in Gansu, with small parts of the Badain Jaran and Tengger deserts. Most of the Yellow River's water comes from Gansu, and the river flows straight through Lanzhou, while the area around Wuwei belongs to the Shiyang River Basin. The south is very mountainous (part of the Qilian Mountains) and the north is flat. The highest point, 5,830 metres (19,130 ft), is in the Altyn-Tagh in the far west.

Inside the province is the Hexi Corridor, a natural land passage of roughly 1,000 kilometres (620 mi) from Lanzhou to the Jade Gate. Desert (the Gobi) bounds it on one side, to the north, and the Qilian Mountains on the south.

Climate across Gansu is mostly continental and semi-arid to arid (Köppen BSk or BWk). Summers are warm to hot and winters cold to very cold, but day-night temperature swings are so wide that afternoon highs can stay over 0 °C (32 °F) all winter. At extreme altitude a few areas turn subarctic (Dwc) and winter nights can fall as low as -40 °C (-40 °F). Limited rainfall mainly arrives in summer. Snow cover stays on very high ground only, because winters are dry, and in the southwest the snow line can be 5,500 metres (18,040 ft) up.

Since 2014 services have been the largest economic sector in Gansu, and tourism is becoming more important. On the education side, Lanzhou University, in the province, is the northwest's single class A Double First Class university.
Lanzhou University of Technology lists 121 programs for international students on this site: 19 bachelor, 31 master's, 23 doctoral, 48 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 89 taught in Chinese, 32 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 24,000 to CNY 28,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.

119 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (11):
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Chemical Process Machinery
Civil Engineering
Control Science and Engineering
Cultural Heritage Conservation Science and Technology
Manufacturing Systems Information Engineering
Materials Science and Engineering
Mechanical Engineering
Mechatronic Engineering
Power Engineering and Engineering Thermophysics
Refrigeration and Cryogenic Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

lanzhou-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Lanzhou University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Lanzhou, register at Lanzhou University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Liaoning Normal University, known as LNU (simplified Chinese 辽宁师范大学, traditional 遼寧師範大學, pinyin Liáoníng Shīfàn Dàxué), is in Dalian, in Liaoning Province. It is a comprehensive university whose strongest identity is teacher training, and it runs the biggest teacher-education college in the province.

The university opened in August 1951, soon after the People's Republic of China was founded, as part of a push to rebuild the way teachers were trained. Under the new shifan (师范) system, selected further and higher education institutions were set up specifically to produce future teachers, and students were attracted by tuition waivers, stipends and fellowships. The normal universities stood at the top of this system and were the only institutions through which senior high school teachers could qualify. Liaoning had two of them: LNU and Shenyang Normal University, which was founded in the same year.

LNU currently has 22 schools plus a School of Graduate Studies. Research-degree authority is broad: doctorates can be awarded in 32 secondary disciplines, master's degrees in 27 primary disciplines, 118 disciplines for the master's degree and 11 specialties, and there are six centers for post-doctoral studies. At provincial level it holds four first-class characteristic disciplines (all primary disciplines) and nine key secondary disciplines.

The university offers 72 undergraduate programmes, including 5 major orientations. Six of these have special status at national level and 9 at provincial level; 4 are provincial pilot majors for comprehensive undergraduate reform, 3 are provincial pilot majors for reforming the engineering education model, and 1 is a province key support major.
The list of teaching honours is long, and it helps to see it as a whole:
Courses: one excellent course at national level, 16 at provincial level, 4 for graduate students and 12 open video courses at provincial level.
Textbooks: 9 planned textbooks at national level and 7 at provincial level.
Teaching teams: 2 at national level and 7 at provincial level.
Renowned teachers: 1 at national level and 13 at provincial level, with 5 academic leaders at provincial level.
Talent-training platforms: 1 provincial innovation zone for talent training and 7 bases for most-needed talent.
Basic education curriculum reform awards: 2 at national level and 5 at provincial level.
Education practice construction projects: 1 national and 5 provincial.
Entrepreneurship and innovation projects: 17 national and 60 provincial.
Teaching achievement prizes in higher education: 2 national and 51 provincial, plus 2 teaching achievement prizes in basic education.

Research facilities include a marine biopharmaceutical engineering technology research center recognised by the NDRC. On the research side LNU counts 7 provincial-level key laboratories and 4 provincial university key laboratories, one provincial engineering technology research center, a humanities and social science research base under the Ministry of Education (1) plus 6 key bases in those fields, 9 research bases of other kinds and 5 provincial university innovation teams.

Among the staff, 3 teachers have been named New Century Excellent Talents by the Ministry of Education, and 43 have been named University Excellent Talents by Liaoning's Department of Education. Over the 11th Five-Year Plan period, staff finished 869 research projects, published more than 400 books and 6701 academic papers (579 of them in SCI, 100 in EI, ISTP or SSCI), received approval for 297 patents and won 448 research awards.

Exchange with the wider world is a priority: LNU has ties with 85 universities and research institutions across 16 countries and areas. Partnerships include an Italian study center named for Matteo Ricci and Martino Martini, run with the University of Macerata; a Japanese study and research center named Omori and sponsored by the Japanese International Exchange Center; the LNU-MSU School of International Business; a Film & Television Art College set up with Hong Kong and Japanese enterprises; a biopharmaceuticals research and development center (LNNU) with Britain's Ulster University; an international professional school with HCC; and two Confucius Institutes, at Miami University and at Milan University.

Honours include awards for model construction and ideological and political work, for juvenile education, for social practice and for research on juvenile delinquency. It was one of the first model universities for the national standardisation of language and characters, an excellent group in that field, and a national excellent Putonghua testing center. It has also been rated a leading advanced unit for student mental health education, school roll management and ideological and political work, and has won numerous provincial and municipal awards.

On the west side of Dalian, LNU stands along Huang He Road (黄河路). Huang He Road splits the main campus into a southern and a northern section. The published figures give 116 areas of land and a total of 350,000 square meters of buildings, and the libraries hold 1.33 million books. A second campus on Western Hill is close to the main campus.

liaoning-normal-university.h: Missouri State University programme on campus

blocks.x: The LNU-MSU College of International Business is a joint college. Its Missouri State University China Campus is housed in LNU's northern campus. Students can take a 2-year Associate of Arts in General Studies or a 4-year Bachelor of Science in General Business.
Student life depends on the city around the campus: the weather, the transport and the things to do. The sections below describe Dalian.

Dalian is one of China's most intensively developed industrial regions. Administratively it joins two parts: Dalian itself, and the smaller Lüshunkou, further down the Liaodong Peninsula, which used to be the city of Lüshun and appears in Western and Russian history as Port Arthur. In older sources, Dalniy (also spelled Dalney), the Russian-planned city on the south shore of Dalian Bay, lay 25 miles (40 kilometers) from Port Arthur, now called Lüshunkou, literally "Lüshun Port".

Dalian sits on Korea Bay, north of the Yellow Sea, about halfway along the Liaodong peninsula at the narrowest point of its neck (isthmus). Its coastline measures 1,184 mi (1,906 km), and it administers most of the peninsula along with around 260 islands and reefs nearby. It lies south-south-west of the Yalu River, and the harbor entrance forms a sub-bay called Dalian Bay.

Dalian's climate is humid continental with monsoon influence (Köppen Dwa): summers are warm and wet because of the East Asian monsoon, and winters are cold, windy and dry under the huge Siberian anticyclone. Its position on the Liaodong Peninsula delays every season except winter by roughly a month. January averages -3.3 °C (26.1 °F) over 24 hours and August 24.8 °C (76.6 °F); the annual mean is 11.8 °C (53.2 °F). Annual rainfall averages 22.8 in (580 millimeters), concentrated in summer and varying greatly from year to year. The sea keeps day-to-night swings small, with an annual mean daily range of only 6.66 °C (12.0 °F). Sunshine runs from 45% of the possible in July to 66% in March, adding up to 2,625 hours of bright sunshine a year. Since 1951 the record low is -21.1 °C (-6 °F), on 4 January 1970, and the record high 99 °F (37.3 °C), on 7 August 2026.
The 2010 census counted 6.69 million people in Dalian. At the end of 2014 the registered household population was 5.943 million, which was 29,000 more than a year earlier.

Dalian's GDP has grown by double-digit percentages every year since 1992. In 2014 growth was 5.8% and GDP reached RMB 765.56 billion, which works out at RMB 109,939 per person. In the National Bureau of Statistics' nationwide appraisal Dalian comes eighth among Chinese cities for overall strength. The leading industries are electronics, machine manufacturing, and petrochemicals with oil refining.

The area began as an agricultural and aquaculture region. Once a ferry opened between Yantai and Lüshun in the early 20th century, farmers and fishers from Shandong, on the other side of the Yellow Sea, started to settle here during the Chuang Guandong era.

liaoning-normal-university.h: Heavy and light industry, and distribution

blocks.x: The city had shipbuilding and locomotive works even before and throughout the Second Sino-Japanese War; those companies later became Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Company and Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Works (DLoco). After WWII Dalian emerged as a key centre for heavy and light industry, with firms such as Wafangdian Bearing Co., Dalian Chemical Group and Dalian Heavy Industry Co., and for distribution, with the Dashang Group as an example.

Dalian Port is a major gateway for international trade: it is linked by trade and shipping with over 300 ports across 160 countries and regions and has over 100 container routes, international and domestic. The oil-tanker harbor, the largest by tonnage in China, was completed in 1976 at the end of a pipeline from the Daqing oilfields. Dalian is China's 6th largest port, and In AAPA world port rankings Dalian was 8th busiest worldwide by cargo tonnage in 2012 and 12th busiest container port by total TEUs handled in 2013. As a result the city is a significant centre for oil refining, diesel engineering and chemical production.

Dayaowan Port (大窑湾港, Dàyáowān Gǎng) is a newer port, completed in 1993 too; it lies on the Dagushan (大孤山) Peninsula in the northern suburbs and specialises in handling mining and oil products for export and import. Add the railway stations (Dalian and Dalian North), Dalian International Airport and the expressways to Shenyang (Shenda), Changchun (Changda) and Harbin (Hada) in the north and to Dandong in the east, and Dalian becomes an important distribution hub.

The central government has given Dalian many advantages, including the 1984 "open-city" title that lets it attract large amounts of foreign investment (see Special Economic Zone). In Jinzhou District the Development Zone attracted a wave of Japanese firms (Toshiba, Sanyo Electric, Nidec, Mitsubishi Electric and Canon), and then South Korean, American and European companies such as Pfizer. Intel announced in 2007 that it would build a semiconductor fabrication facility (a fab) in the Development Zone; it was Intel's first fab on an entirely new site since 1992 and started operating in October 2010. Car makers with plants in the city are BYD Automobile (a production base for BYD K9 electric buses), Dongfeng Nissan Passenger Vehicle Company and Chery.
The city has further zones: Dalian Hi-Tech Industrial Zone, Dalian Free Trade Zone, Dalian Export Processing Zone and Dalian Economic and Technological Development Zone.

Dalian is the financial centre of Northeast China. All five of China's major banks have Dalian branches: Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, Industrial & Commercial Bank of China and Bank of China. The former Dalian City Commercial Bank, now Bank of Dalian, handles processing for the Dalian Mingzhu IC Card used on public transport, among other duties, and it has opened branches in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenyang as well as five other cities.

Founded in 1993, Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE) is Northeast China's sole futures exchange, and the futures business has developed rapidly. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has approved 19 listed futures products. They include agricultural goods (corn, corn starch, soybeans, soybean meal, soybean oil, RBD palm olein, polished round-grained rice and eggs), chemicals and plastics (linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polypropylene (PP), ethylene glycol (EG) and ethenylbenzene (EB)), and fiberboard, blockboard, metallurgical coke, coking coal and iron ore. Options on soybean meal, corn and iron ore are also traded. In 2019 DCE recorded trading volume of 1,331 million lots and turnover of RMB 68.92 trillion, and the U.S. Futures Industry Association (FIA) listed it as the world's 11th largest exchange by volume for that year.

Dalian has stressed IT development since the 1990s, especially in the Hi-Tech Zone and the Software Park in the western suburbs close to Dalian University of Technology. The High-Tech Zone is a hub for high-tech industries with over 4,700 enterprises, 80 of them Fortune Global 500 companies. Chinese IT firms including Neusoft Group, Hisoft and DHC are based there, as are American, European, Indian and Japanese ones: Cisco, Hitachi, Oracle, Accenture, Sony, Panasonic, Ericsson, HP, Dell, IBM, Infosys and Wipro. There are nine professional business incubators (a hi-tech business incubator and animation and software incubators among them), which have incubated over 400 companies. The "Lüshun South Road Software Industry Belt" plan, including Dalian Software Park Phase 3, is now in progress.
Intel's Fab 68 is in Dalian. Plans were unveiled on 26 March 2007 and it started working on 26 October 2010; it was Intel's first chip fabrication plant in East Asia.

Dalian attracts plenty of domestic tourists and also overseas visitors, notably from Russia, Japan and South Korea, thanks to its mild climate, many beaches and its place in modern Chinese history. Famous beaches include Jinshitan Golden Coast (金石滩黄金海岸), Fujiazhuang (付家庄), Bangchuidao (棒棰岛), Xinghai Park (星海公园), Xinghai Bay (星海湾) and Xiajiahezi (夏家河子). In 2007 it was one of three cities, with Hangzhou and Chengdu, honoured as "China's best tourist city" by the National Tourism Administration and the UN World Tourism Organization.
Zhongshan Square (中山广场), laid out by Russians in the 19th century and known for the classical buildings around it, which the Japanese erected in the 20th century's first half.

Laohutan Ocean Park, whose attractions include the World of Birds, the Coral Aquarium and the Polar Region Marine Animals World, where the white whale and dolphin show is a major draw. Nearby is Tigers Sculpture Square, whose tiger is the emblem of Tiger Beach (老虎滩, Lǎohǔtān), and a retired Anshan-class destroyer, the Taiyuan, which is open to visitors.
Xinghai Square (星海广场, "Square of the Sea of Stars") on Xinghai Bay, which went up in 1998 to mark Dalian's 100th anniversary and is described as the world's largest city square.
Dalian Natural History Museum and Heishijiao Geological Park
Sunasia Ocean World
Dalian Forest Zoo

Bangchuidao Scenic Area, a carefully maintained park that served as a State Guesthouse from 1960 and is now open to visitors, with upgraded facilities: Chinese and Western style villas, lavish greenery, a hot spring, a golf course, a recreation center, and tennis and badminton courts, as well as Bangchuidao beach. From the beach you can see Bangchui Island (棒棰岛, Bàngchuí Dǎo), named for an islet shaped like a Bangchui, an ancient washing tool. During its years as a State Guesthouse it hosted numerous Chinese and foreign leaders and high-profile officials, among them Henry Kissinger, Boris Yeltsin, Gerhard Schröder, Juan Antonio Samaranch, Kim Jong Un, Xi Jinping, Hu Jintao, Jiang Zemin, Deng Xiaoping and Zhou Enlai.
Dalian Sightseeing Tower
Donggang Music Fountain
Fujiazhuang Beach

liaoning-normal-university.h: Jinzhou District and the Development Zone (northern suburbs)

blocks.x: Dahei Mountain

Jinshitan National Holiday Resort and Discoveryland (金石滩, Jīnshítān, "Golden Pebble Beach"). The resort has an eastern and a western peninsula, open ground between the two and a Golden Coast beach 10 mi (16 kilometers) long. Attractions are the Golden Pebble Waxworks Museum, Geological Museum and Coastal National Geopark; Golden Rock Park and Wanfuding Park; Discoveryland Theme Park; the China Martial Arts Hall and the Mao Zedong Badge Exhibition Hall; the Model Movie & TV Art Center; the Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort; the International Vehicle Campsite; equestrian and hunting facilities (an Equestrianism Base and a Hunting Club); and a convention center and resort plus two golf courses, Golden Pebble Golf Club and Golden Gulf Golf Course. The Dalian International Beach Carnival, the International Winter Swimming Festival and the Grape Festival are held in Jinshitan every year.

The Discoveryland Theme Park (发现王国, also "the Discovery Kingdom") opened in 2006 and was the work of Romero Petrilli VanRell Associates, who worked on a Disney theme park. The area quoted for it, 470,000 sq mi (1,217,294 km2), cannot be right for a theme park, so treat that figure as a typing error and ask the park for the real size.
Lüshun Museum
Lüshun Railway Station

Shuishiying Meeting Place, Hill 203 and East Jiguan Mountain (东鸡冠山): the Battle of Lüshun in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) saw its fiercest fighting here, and the ceasefire treaty was signed at this site.

The Japanese and Russian Prison Site Museum, Lüshun. Russians built the prison in 1902 and the Japanese later enlarged it; during World War II it held people of various nationalities who opposed the Japanese invasion. An Jung-geun, the Korean independence activist who assassinated Itō Hirobumi, was held in the prison and killed there.
Lüshun Snake Museum and, nearby, the Snake Island and Bird Port reserve at Lüshun
Hengshan Temple (横山寺) and Longwangtang Cherry Blossom Park. The temple, near Longwangtang Reservoir (龙王塘水库), goes back to the Han dynasty; it was rebuilt in 2003.
Pulandian District: Anbo Hotspring and Ski Course (安波温泉滑雪场)
Wafangdian: Changxing Island International Golf Course
Zhuanghe: Buyun Mountain Hot Spring (步云山温泉) and the Bingyu Valley Scenic Area
Changhai County: the islands of Changhai County

Dalian has many hot spring hotels. Notable ones are in Lüshunkou District (Laotieshan Hot Spring Hotel and Tianmu Hot Spring Hotel), Jinshitan (Tang Dynasty Hot Spring Resort), Wafangdian (Minghu Hot Spring Hotel) and Ganjingzi District (Chengyuan Hot Spring Villa).

Skiing is increasingly popular. Well-known resorts are in Ganjingzi District (Linhai Ski Resort, and Dalian Happy Snow World near the airport), Pulandian District (Anbo Ski Resort) and Wafangdian (Minghu Ski Resort and Minghu International Skiing Holiday Village).
Cycling is less common in Dalian than in many Chinese cities, because the roads are hilly. Local law also bans motorcycles in the downtown core, so there are few of them there.

The city has a thorough bus network and an efficient metro. In March 2023 the metro had three underground lines (1, 2 and 5) and three overground lines (3, 12 and 13), while new lines and extensions, among them Line 4 and Line 7, were being built. The new rail system is meant to link the whole city in future. The Dalian Tram is the second-oldest tram system in China, and most public transport can be paid for with the Mingzhu IC Card (明珠卡).
China Daily named Dalian the most liveable city in China in 2006.

Four theaters are well known: Hongji Grand Stage stages Beijing Opera; Dalian People's Culture Club is mostly for music; the Working People's Theater, or Doudou Grand Stage (工人剧院/豆豆大舞台), is mainly for Errenzhuan; and there is also the Development Area Grand Theater (开发区大剧院).
One research center in the city is the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics.

Liaoning Technical University (LNTU), also called Liaoning University of Engineering and Technology (辽宁工程技术大学, traditional 遼寧工程技術大學, pinyin Liáoníng Gōngchéng Jìshù Dàxué), is spread over three campuses. Two are in Fuxin, Liaoning, and the third is in Huludao, also in Liaoning. The provincial government and the State Administration of Work Safety run it together.
This profile starts with the university and then covers Fuxin, where most students will live, followed by the history, geography and economy of Liaoning province.

LNTU is counted among China's national key universities. The State Council gave it "key university" status in 1978, along with 87 other higher education institutions. It could award master's degrees from 1981 and doctoral degrees from 1993, and in 1999 it was permitted to set up a research mobile station for engineering master's degrees. It is also approved to enrol international students.

Six broad fields are taught or researched: law, economics, management, liberal arts, science and engineering. The 14 colleges and departments include Mechanical Engineering, Resources and Environment Engineering, Electronics and Information Engineering, and Business Administration, along with a Vocational College and a Department of Mechanics and Engineering. Undergraduate and higher vocational study together offer 58 majors.

Enrolment stands at over 29,000 students, with a further 3,000 mature students. At research level the university offers 17 majors for doctoral degrees, 41 for master's degrees and 11 for engineering master's degrees, and it has three post-doctoral disciplines. Its strengths in national assessment are one key national subject and nine at provincial or ministerial level, and it has eight key laboratories at ministerial level plus one national laboratory.

Teaching is carried out by about 200 professors, 400 associate professors and 400 senior lecturers, and a further 200 people with doctorates or postgraduate status are working toward doctoral degrees.

Library holdings exceed 1.1 million books, and 2,000 periodicals in Chinese and other languages are available. LNTU has relationships with over ten overseas universities and research institutes, particularly in Germany and the United States.

liaoning-technical-university.h: Fuxin: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Fuxin is where two of LNTU's three campuses are, so this section describes its economy, schools, roads and railways.

Fuxin is a mining centre in a farming region, and its main products are coal and agate. It is nicknamed China's "Agate City": about half of the country's known agate deposits are here, and the city produces more than 90% of the nation's agate products.

Coal is central to the economy but over-mined and in short supply. As the mines run dry, the city is looking for other industries, and one measure has been to develop part of Fuxin as a "Special Economic Zone" to attract foreign investment.

Fuxin was named in 2001 as the first resource-exhausted city in mainland China. In 2020 its "cabbage-priced" housing drew attention, much as housing in Hegang, Heilongjiang, had been very cheap for years. Reports from China Business Network and Securities Times said many homes, even fully furnished ones, cost less than 75 dollars per square metre. For international students this means living costs for housing in the city are likely to be low, although the figure comes from press reports on the property market rather than a survey of rents.

During 2009 Fuxin approved 25 foreign-funded enterprises and 2 joint ventures, with contracted funds of over US$143 million in total. Foreign direct investment that year came to US$64.12 million, 24% more than the year before and 17% above the province's target. Seven projects were each contracted at over ten million dollars.

Foreign direct investment has helped new key industries to grow in place of mining. Wind power led, supplying more than 70% of the total FDI in 2009 and becoming the main focus of the city's foreign investment.
Liaoning Technical University
Fuxin College

China National Highway 101, which runs from Beijing to Shenyang, serves Fuxin, and the G25 Changchun-Shenzhen Expressway links the city to the national trunk highway system. The G2512 Fuxin-Jinzhou Expressway connects Fuxin to Jinzhou.

By rail, many trains join Fuxin to large cities in the north and northeast, including Beijing, Tianjin and Shenyang. A direct train now also runs between Shanghai and Fuxin, connecting the city to the booming east coast.
A university's province shapes student life as much as its campus does, and Liaoning has been a frontier between peoples for over two thousand years.

liaoning-technical-university.h: Early states, from Yan to Tang

blocks.x: Han Chinese governments mostly settled and ran Liaoning from the 4th century BC to the 9th century AD. Before the 3rd century BC it was home to the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples, and the state of Yan took the area about 300 BC. Yan divided the region into two commanderies. One, Liaodong, lay to the east of the Liao River, and the other, Liaoxi, to its west. Xiangping, the Yan city that was Liaodong's centre, stood where Liaoyang is today. After the Han dynasty collapsed, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family ran a semi-independent state in Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Even though that state, also called Yan, was brief, it sent many maritime diplomatic and trading missions and had a lasting effect on Northeast Asian culture. When the Western Jin ended, the Murong Xianbei states (Former, Later and Northern Yan) governed Liaoning. Northern Wei captured the Yan capital in 436 and the Liaodong Peninsula went to Goguryeo, before the Tang annexed it in the Goguryeo-Tang War.

The An Lushan Rebellion in the mid 8th century drained Tang resources from its frontiers, and the Bohai state slowly pushed into Liaodong. The Khitan Liao dynasty later took Liaoning and split it into four circuits: Eastern Capital (Dongjingdao), Supreme Capital (Shangjingdao), Central Capital (Zhongjingdao) and Lower Capital (Xiajingdao).

Under the Jurchen Jin, the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu) covered most of the land. What was left went to Xianping, to the Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu) and to the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it later became part of the Yuan dynasty. Under the Yuan the east was split between the Liaoyang and Shenyang Routes under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; the north was Xianping Prefecture in the Kaiyuan Route; the west, including the Guangning Route, also came under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; while the Daning Route, answering to the Central Secretariat, included the Jinzhou and Chaoyang regions.

liaoning-technical-university.h: The Ming and the Liaodong Wall

blocks.x: The Ming Empire controlled Liaoning from 1371, three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. Around 1442 it built a defensive wall to protect the province's farmland from a possible threat from the northwest, the Oriyanghan (a Jurchen-Mongol people who paid tribute to the Ming). In 1467 and 1468 the wall was extended to cover the northeast too, against the Jianzhou Jurchens, who would later be known as the Manchu. This "Liaodong Wall" was meant to do the same job as the Great Wall of China but was built more cheaply: stones and tiles went into some sections, but most of it was only an earth bank with a moat on each side.

Nevertheless the Jurchens captured Liaodong, meaning eastern Liaoning, at the start of the 17th century, long ahead of the collapse of the rest of China. They called their dynasty Later Jin at first and renamed it Qing later. From 1616 to 1621 their capital was Xingjing (兴京), outside the Liaodong Wall in what is now eastern Liaoning. It moved to Dongjing, east of present-day Liaoyang, and then in 1625 to Shengjing, now Shenyang. After Beijing fell to the Qing in 1644 the main capital moved there, but Shengjing continued to be an important regional capital for most of the Qing period.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning a great part of its population. Many Chinese residents were killed in the fighting or fled south past the Great Wall, and the retreating Ming forces themselves destroyed many cities. A report in 1661 by Zhang Shangxian, the civil governor (Fuyin) of Fengtian Province, shows how bad the damage was. Besides Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, he said, the cities east of the Liao River were empty or held only a few hundred residents; in his words, "Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants." Only Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning, west of the Liao, still had sizeable populations.

Starting with laws of 1651 and 1653, the Qing government in the second half of the 17th century recruited migrants, especially from Shandong, south of the Great Wall, to settle the thinly populated Fengtian Province (roughly today's Liaoning). A lot of Liaoning residents today are descended from those settlers. Han Chinese were still officially barred from settling in the rest of the Northeast through most of Manchu rule. The Willow Palisade, built from about 1638 to about 1672, was meant to keep them out of what are now Jilin, Heilongjiang and neighbouring parts of Inner Mongolia. It enclosed the farmland of Fengtian, running outside the old Ming wall for the most part or reusing it, and it kept that farmland apart from Manchu woodland to the northeast and from pastures used by Mongols to the northwest.

In time the Qing attempted to stop migrants coming to Fengtian, to send some settlers back to where they came from, or, if that failed, to give them legal status. An edict of 1704 noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave, and told them either to register properly and join a local defence group (保, bao) or to go back to their original homes within ten years. A decade later another edict again reminded officials of the need to deal with illegal migrants. Whatever the policy, the result fell short of what Beijing hoped for: the population of Fengtian actually doubled from 1683 to 1734.

Three generals governed Manchuria during the Qing, with most of modern Liaoning in the hands of the General of Shengjing (in Manchu, Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn). From 1860 the Manchu government began allowing migration again, and soon Han Chinese were the region's dominant ethnic group.

A province called Fengtian was set up in the early 1900s on what is now Liaoning. In 1904 and 1905, Russia and Japan fought a war, and Liaoning saw many of its decisive fights, among them Port Arthur and Mukden; the latter was the largest land battle fought up to that time. Later, in the Warlord Era, Liaoning belonged to the Fengtian clique led by Zhang Zuolin and then by his son Zhang Xueliang. The province got its present name on 29 January 1929, and the Zhongdong Railway Incident happened later that year. Japan invaded in 1931, and the region became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the first big battles of the Chinese Civil War, the Liaoshen Campaign, took place in and around Liaoning.

Liaoning did not yet exist when the People's Republic began in 1949. The area was Liaodong and Liaoxi provinces plus the municipalities of Anshan, Benxi, Fushun, Shenyang and Lüda (now Dalian). In 1954 all of them were merged as "Liaoning"; part of Rehe province was added in 1955, and for a time during the Cultural Revolution some Inner Mongolian land was included, though that was later undone.

Industrialisation came early to Liaoning, under Japanese occupation at first and with greater force through the 1950s and 1960s. Anshan, for example, has one of China's largest iron and steel complexes. That early emphasis on heavy industry has recently become a burden, because many large state-run enterprises have run into difficulties. In recognition of the special problems of Liaoning and other northeastern provinces with a heavy-industry heritage, the central government launched a "Revitalize the Northeast" campaign.
Geographically the province falls roughly into three bands. Hills lie to the east, a plain fills the middle, and uplands rise in the west.

West: The Nulu'erhu Mountains, which run roughly along the border with Inner Mongolia, dominate the highlands, and low hills cover the whole region. Between the Liao River Basin and the North China Plain runs a thin coastal lowland called the Liaoxi Corridor, which terminates at the Shanhai Pass of the Great Wall.
Centre: A mostly flat, low-lying basin drained by the Liao, the Daliao and their tributaries.
East: The Changbai and Qianshan Mountains, whose far ends enter the sea as the Liaodong Peninsula. The province's highest point, Mount Huabozi (1336 m), is in this region.
The climate is continental monsoon, with rainfall of around 440 to 1130 mm a year. Summer is rainy and the other seasons are dry.
Among the province's principal cities are Shenyang and Dalian, then Anshan, Fushun, Liaoyang, Dandong, Jinzhou and Yingkou.

Liaoning has the biggest and richest provincial economy in Northeast China. Its nominal GDP in 2017 was 2.39 trillion yuan (about US$354 billion), the 14th largest of China's 31 provinces, and each person produced on average 54,745 yuan (US$8,108). Of the three northeastern provinces, Liaoning is first by both total GDP and GDP per head.

In 2008 Liaoning had the highest GDP growth among the "G8x8" regions, the eight sub-national units with the highest GDP in each of the top eight GDP nations. Preliminary figures showed GDP growth of 13.1 percent in 2009, the fastest of any province. Growth has since slowed: 3% in 2015, then a 1.3% contraction in the first quarter of 2016.

Leading industries are petrochemicals, metallurgy, electronics and telecommunications, and machinery. Nationally, it ranks among the top three producers of pig iron, steel and metal-cutting machine tools. Raw materials are another strength: mining, quarrying, the smelting and rolling of ferrous metals, and oil and gas extraction are all highly significant. Equipment and machinery manufacturing is also a key business, centred on Shenyang and Dalian, where Shenyang Machine Tool Co. Ltd., Daxian Group Co. Ltd. and Shenyang Jinbei Co. Ltd. lead their sectors. Light industry is mainly textiles and clothing: cotton and wool spinning, chemical fibre, knitting, silk, and the making of garments and textile machinery.

Liaoning's industrial base is broad, taking in shipbuilding, machinery, electronics, metal refining, petroleum, chemicals, construction materials and coal. Services (the tertiary industry) were 34.5 percent of GDP in 2008. Plans call for continued restructuring of large and medium-sized state enterprises, and a focus on four pillars of the economy, which are electronics, machinery, metallurgy and petrochemicals. Liaoning is also where the Li Keqiang index began, an alternative measure of economic performance used where official GDP figures are doubtful.

Maize, sorghum and soybeans are the chief crops, and cotton is also grown. The area around Dalian produces three-quarters of the apples and peaches that China exports. Named local fruits include Dalian's golden peaches, apples from both Dalian and Yingkou, Beizhen pears (Jinzhou) and white pears from Huludao and Suizhong, and apricots and plums from Gushan, a district of Dandong.

Liaoning has more iron, magnesite, diamond and boron than any other province-level division in China, and it is an important source of oil and natural gas. Salt is produced on the coast. Crude oil is abundant too, especially in the Liaohe Oilfield.

The coastal waters produce a great variety of seafood. Dalian supplies abalone, sea cucumber, scallops, prawns, crabs and sea urchins; Dandong supplies fish, Yingkou jellyfish and Panjin clams. Both the home market and neighbouring export markets buy these products, though how well known each is abroad differs. Dalian, Dandong and Yingkou have been built up as major ports and as the economic gateways to northeast China.

LNTU suits students interested in mining, resources, environmental engineering and related technical fields, in a region that is cold and industrial rather than glamorous. Fuxin offers low-cost living and a growing focus on wind power, and Liaoning's big ports and cities, Shenyang and Dalian above all, are within reach by road and rail.

Liaoning University, shortened to LNU (辽宁大学, Liáoníng Dàxué), is a public university in Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning Province. It opened in 1948. The provincial government of Liaoning and the national Ministry of Education support it jointly, and it is included in the Double First-Class Construction as well as Project 211. Those two schemes mark it as one of the universities that receive extra backing from the state.

The university in its current form was born in September 1958, when Shenyang Normal College, Shenyang Institute of Russian and the Northeast Institute of Finance and Economics were merged into one. Marshal Zhu De personally wrote the calligraphy for the university's name. Altogether the university holds 143 hectares (350 acres). That figure includes the Puhe Campus and the Liaoyang Foreign Languages College as well as the university proper, and buildings provide 600,000 square metres of floor space.

Teaching is organised into fifteen colleges, which I have grouped by theme. The business and economics group has the College of Economics, the College of Business Administration and the Asia-Australia College of Business. The humanities and social science group has these colleges:
Liberal Arts
Philosophy and Public Administration
International Relations
Law
Foreign Languages
Radio, Film and Television
Science and technology are covered by the College of Chemical Science and Engineering and the College of Information Science and Technology. The remaining three colleges serve other student groups:
The College of Higher Professional Techniques
The College of Adult Education
The College of Foreign Students
A fifteenth college trains self-study students in the humanities and professional techniques.
In addition, five faculties are at college level: those of Physics, Mathematics, History, Environment Science and Life Science.

Altogether the choice is forty-three undergraduate disciplines, plus fifty-three at master's level (which include the MBA and JM). Doctoral authority covers a PhD in theoretical economics, a first-level discipline, and nine more doctorates in second-level disciplines, and the university also has three post-doctoral mobile stations.

World economy and national economy are its two national key disciplines. The Ministry of Education has also designated a base for training personnel in the basic national economy, a key humanities research base, and a research centre on the comparative economic system. Eleven more disciplines hold province-level key status, and there is one test and detection centre.
Full-time faculty number 1,116, and 614 of them are professors or associate professors. The student body is 18,700 strong and includes undergraduates, graduate students and international students.

Formal relationships for academic cooperation and exchange link LNU to more than forty universities and research institutions in fourteen countries. Since its founding it has educated over a hundred thousand full-time students for China, and over 5,000 foreign students from forty-two countries have studied there, including students from Thailand, South Korea, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, Russia, Japan and the United States.

The library building has 18,500 square metres of floor space and modern equipment. Its 1.6 million-plus volumes include over 300 kinds of rare, treasured books, which the United Nations has confirmed as exclusive holdings of this library. On campus there are also a history museum, with more than two thousand art treasures, and a museum of natural history, with eleven thousand biological specimens.
Zhang Yumao, a literary scholar
Wu Bing'an, an ethnologist who specialises in folklore and popular culture
Everyday life for a student depends on the city outside the campus gates: its weather, its transport and its entertainment. The sections that follow introduce Shenyang.

Shenyang is in the centre of Liaoning Province, between 41° 11' and 43° 02' N and between 122° 25' and 123° 48' E. The western part of the administrative area lies on the Liao River system's alluvial plain, and the eastern part is wooded hinterland of the Changbai Mountains. Heights run from 7 m (23 ft) at the lowest point to 414 m (1,358 ft) at the highest, and the urban area averages 45 m (148 ft).

The main urban area stretches north of the Hun River. This was once the biggest tributary of the Liao River itself, and local people often call it the city's "mother river". Around the central city run three artificial rivers, joined by channels to make one unbroken waterway. On the south and south-east side is the South Canal (南运河); to the north and north-east is the Xinkai River (新开河), once called the North Canal; and on the west is the Weigong River (卫工河), which used to be the Weigong Nullah.

Linear parks and gardens line the South Canal, which is its best-known feature. Engineers made the canal out of the former Wanquan River (萬泉河, "ten thousand springs river"), an old water source for the original city that also appears under the names Little Shen River (小瀋水) and Wuli River (五里河, "five-li river"). Smaller rivers support the outer areas, among them the Xi River (细河), the Puhe River (蒲河) and the Mantang River (满堂河). All of these flow into the Hun at three places: on the south-east, the due south and the south-west of the city. A canal on the east side, Huishan Nullah (辉山明渠), once emptied into the lower Xinkai River but has disappeared, filled in by urban construction.

Shenyang has many parks, and the South Canal Linear Parks (南运河带状公园) are the best known. They follow the river for 14.5 km (9.0 mi) through the southern parts of the Dadong, Shenhe and Heping Districts, with 6 large parks and 18 riverside gardens spread over some 1,400,000 m² (350 acres). Flowers include roses, apricots, bladder cherry, honeylocust, natal lily, scarlet sage, morning glory and black-eyed-Susan, and there are wide green areas of peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, weeping willow, pine and black locust. No other planted open space in the city is as large. It is a key contributor to Shenyang's 40-percent "greening ratio" and to the title of "national forest city", awarded in 2005.

Air quality is a concern. The Shenyang Environmental Protection Bureau says winter coal burning at boiler stations for hydronic district heating produces 30 percent of the city's air pollution. In the winter of 2013 to 2014 the city burned 16 million metric tons of coal, and half of that went to heating. Other major sources were construction dust (20 percent), vehicle exhaust (20 percent), industry (10 percent) and dust from outside the city (20 percent), mostly yellow dust from the Gobi Desert. The Bureau described air quality as "slowly improving".

The climate is humid continental, influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac): summers are hot and humid because of the monsoon, and winters are cold and dry because of the Siberian anticyclone. The four seasons are clearly different. In July and August together, close to half of the year's rain falls.

January is the coldest month, with a mean of −11.4 °C (11.5 °F), and July the warmest, with 24.9 °C (76.8 °F); the whole year averages 8.6 °C (47.5 °F). Given how severe the winters are, the frost-free period of 183 days is long. The city gets 2,421 hours of bright sunshine a year, and July is the least sunny month (42 percent of the possible total) while February is the sunniest (64 percent). The lowest temperature recorded is −33.1 °C (−28 °F) and the highest 38.4 °C (101 °F). Pack serious winter clothing.

p Shenyang has 9.07 million people, and 85.12% of them live in urban areas. The city is ethnically and culturally varied, with 38 of China's 56 recognised groups represented. Han Chinese are the majority at 91.26 percent. The 37 minority groups run from the Manchu, Korean and Hui, through the Xibo, Mongolian, Zhuang, Miao, Tujia and Dong, to groups such as the Daur, Bai, Uyghur, Tibetan and Yi. They also include Taiwanese Aboriginal People and the She, Bouyei, Yao, Akha, Kazakh, Dai, Li, Shui and Nakhi, plus the Jingpo, Kyrgyz, Tu, Mulao, Qiang, Maonan and Gelao, and finally Russians, Evenks, Tatars, Oroqen, Nanai and Lhoba.
Few of these groups are native to the Shenyang area; the Manchus and the Xibe are among the exceptions. The city has many temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship.

As one of China's key industrial centres, Shenyang is the core city of the Shenyang Economic Zone, which has the status of a New Special Reform Zone. The city has concentrated on heavy industry, mainly machine tools, aerospace, defence and heavy equipment, and lately also on software, automotive products and electronics. Its heavy industry dates back to the 1920s and was already well developed by the time of the Second World War, and the first five-year plan (1951 to 1956) saw many factories built in Tiexi district. By the 1970s, Shenyang stood alongside Shanghai and Tianjin as one of the three top industrial centres in the country, and at one point there was talk of making it a direct-controlled municipality.

The planned economy fell out of favour after the 1980s, and that changed the picture. Heavy industry slowly shrank, state-owned factories went bankrupt and hundreds of thousands of workers lost their jobs, turning Shenyang into a "rust belt" city. More recently the economy has revived markedly, thanks to the national "Revitalize Northeast China" campaign and to fast growth in software and vehicle manufacturing. Investment subsidies are offered to multinational corporations that open an office or headquarters here.

The service sector has been growing, particularly in banking. Foreign banks operating in Shenyang include HSBC (Britain), United Overseas Bank (Singapore), Bank of East Asia (Hong Kong), the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ (Japan) and Hana Bank (South Korea). A count in 2006 found 1,063 banks and bank branches and 144 insurance-related companies, and the city aimed to bring in 30 foreign banks and 60 other financial institutions, not banks, by 2010. These figures are old, so treat them as history.

The Economist Intelligence Unit's Access China White Paper of November 2010 put Shenyang in a group of six it called the CHAMPS, with Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan and Pingdingshan, as part of a profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China.

Three development zones help drive investment: the Shenyang Economic & Technological Development Zone, the Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone and the Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone.

Large industrial firms have their headquarters here. Brilliance Auto, a major Chinese carmaker, also has most of its plants in Shenyang. Among others, Shenyang Aircraft Corporation makes planes for civilian customers and for the PLAAF, China's largest software company is Neusoft Group, and its biggest machine tool manufacturer is Shenyang Machine Tool Group. General Motors, Tyco International and Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation are enlarging their operations in the city. GDP per head in 2009 reached 78,490 yuan, third highest among Liaoning's 58 cities and counties.

Shenyang is the main transport hub of Northeast China. It offers flights, trains, a subway (five lines at the time these figures were compiled), buses throughout the city and a large network of streets and expressways. The largest terminal in the region is Terminal 3 at Shenyang Taoxian International Airport. A tram system opened in the south of the city in 2013.

The north-east's railway hub is Shenyang, with eight lines connecting it to Fushun, Harbin, Changchun, Dalian and Beijing. The Qinhuangdao-Shenyang high-speed railway, the first line in China built only for passengers, is the main route for travellers through the Shanhai Pass. Early in 2007 trains running at 200 km/h (120 mph) brought the Beijing journey down to roughly 4 hours, almost a third of what it had been. At the end of 2012 the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway opened, giving trains of up to 300 km/h (190 mph) between Shenyang and Harbin, Changchun and Dalian.
There are two main stations: Shenyang North in Shenhe District, and Shenyang station in Heping District.

The history of Shenyang North Railway Station (沈阳北站, Shěnyáng Běi Zhàn) begins in 1927, when the warlord Zhang Zuolin ordered a terminal for the Jingfeng Railway to compete with the Shenyang Railway Station, which the Japanese were running at that time. The original building, now a listed heritage building, was first called the Fengtian City Station (奉天城站) and stood about 1 km (0.62 mi) south-west of the present site. Until 1946 the station went by the name Liaoning General Station (遼寧總站), and people still call it the "Old North Station". The current "New North Station" Main Station Building (主站房) was begun in 1986 and went into use in December 1990. It has since become one of the five key rail hubs in China, with the nickname "Northeast's No. 1 Station" (东北第一站).

High-speed rail brought more passengers and a need for more floor area, so in 2011 the station started a big expansion, the "North Station Transport Hub Reconstruction Project" (北站交通枢纽改造工程). The northern side of the tracks, in Huanggu District, gained a "North Square" (北广场) and a new "Sub-Station Building" (子站房) of three floors. In the original Main Station Building, which has 16 floors, the former waiting lounge was replaced by a large elevated concourse bridging the tracks, and a roof with no pillars, the biggest of its kind in mainland China, domes the platforms. Outside the main building, the old South Square (南广场) became a multi-level complex. Its two upper levels work as a raised drop-off zone like those at airports, the ground level handles the buses, and below ground are three levels with shopping malls, parking, taxi pick-up and a connection to Subway Line 2. If ever needed, the underground area can quickly be turned into an air raid shelter.

The other main station, Shenyang Railway Station (沈阳站, Shěnyáng Zhàn), has more than a century of history. Russian builders put it up in 1899 on the eastern side of the South Manchurian Railway, naming it Fengtian Station (奉天站, Fèngtiān Zhàn). After the Russo-Japanese War the Japanese enlarged it and gave it the name Fengtian Yam (奉天驛, Fèngtiān Yì), used until the Second World War ended. In 1945 to 1950 it became Shenyang South Railway Station (瀋陽南站, Shěnyáng Nán Zhàn), also simply the "South Station" as opposed to the North Station, and locals still say that today. This causes confusion, because the real Shenyang South railway station is now in the suburbs, where Hunnan meets Sujiatun.

These days the station serves regular-speed passenger services. It is being refurbished, with a large archway and a new terminal; until the work is finished, travellers reach the platforms by routes under and over the ground. In 2010 the station added a West Station Building (西站房) and a West Square (西广场) on the west side of the tracks. The old East Station Building (东站房) is protected on the provincial heritage list.
A freight link began in 2011: a direct container train now runs daily from Leipzig in Germany to Shenyang, carrying car parts across Siberia over 11,000 km (6,800 mi) in 23 days.
The city's main airport is Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, in Hunnan District. It is among eight major airline hubs, and is the 23rd busiest airport in China.

Shenyang also has three further airports, which the public cannot use. The oldest is the East Pagoda Airport (东塔机场), in Dadong District, which opened in the 1920s and stopped operating in the 1980s, though in 2013 someone proposed relocating and reopening it at Xinmin. In Huanggu District, the Beiling Airport (北陵机场) serves test flights by Shenyang Aircraft Corporation. The Yuhong Airport (于洪机场), in Yuhong District, is strictly military, used by the Northern Theater Command's local garrisons.

Shenyang natives have their own dialect, a version of Northeastern Mandarin that formed in the early Qing period. It resembles other north-eastern dialects and Putonghua, the standard national Mandarin, yet it counts as a kind of Dongbeihua and contains a great deal of vocabulary absent from the official language.

Errenzhuan and Yangge, two folk dances of the north-east, draw big audiences in Shenyang. Near Middle Street, the Big Stage Theatre (大舞台剧场) is well known for Errenzhuan and for comedy skits by Zhao Benshan and his students. With so many popular comedians living in the city, Shenyang is recognised across China as a stronghold of comedy.

The city is the base of several performing arts groups, including Liaoning Ballet, the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China and the Liaoning Song and Dance Ensemble. Zimei, Na Ying and the pianist Lang Lang are among the artists who come from Shenyang.
Liaoning University lists 108 programs for international students on this site: 48 bachelor, 45 master's, 15 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 91 taught in Chinese, 17 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.

108 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
