The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

liaoning-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Liaoning University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shenyang, register at Liaoning University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

liaoning-university-of-technology.h: Liaoning University of Technology: the basics

blocks.x: Liaoning University of Technology (辽宁工业大学, Liáoníng Gōngyè Dàxué) was formerly called Liaoning Institute of Technology. It stands in Jinzhou, a city in Liaoning province in northeast China. The university dates from 1951 and is run by the province. Engineering is its main subject area, but students can also study science, the liberal arts, economics and management.

Roughly 14,000 students study for undergraduate degrees and 578 are postgraduates. Teaching is organised in 20 colleges and faculties, which together cover 38 undergraduate specialities and 20 at postgraduate level. Staff number 1,278, among them 780 full-time teachers. For international contacts, the School of International Education manages exchange programmes with more than 20 foreign universities.

Student life depends on the city around the campus. This section covers the local economy, how to get around, and what to see and do in Jinzhou, and it will help you decide whether you want to explore on foot, by bike or by taxi on weekends and holidays.
Jinzhou's industries are varied. The long-established ones are petrochemicals, metallurgy, textiles, pharmaceuticals and building materials.

A development zone for the economy and technology was set up in Jinzhou in 1992. It ranked among the earliest provincial-level zones approved by Liaoning. Transport links are good, with easy access to Jinzhou Seaport, the airport and several state highways. This matters mostly to companies, but it also shows that the city is well connected to the rest of Liaoning and to the coast.

liaoning-university-of-technology.h: Shops, banks and paying for things

blocks.x: Some Western chains have opened in the city, most notably KFC, which has had a presence in China for many years. For food and everyday goods, the main retailers are RT-Mart, New-Mart and Do-Do Express. Bank of Jinzhou (Jinzhou Yinhang) was, when the information was written, the only bank in the city with native English-speaking staff. Western Union and Bank of China are also available, as are many other banking services. Visa and MasterCard are not generally accepted in Jinzhou, with the exception of a few large bank branches connected to those networks, so plan your payments accordingly and bring a way of paying that works locally. Since this information may be out of date, confirm the current situation after arriving.

Jinzhou Jinzhouwan Airport has flights to major airports in China. The city has two railway stations: long trips leave from one, and the other handles shorter routes. The most common ways to travel within the city are on foot and by bicycle. Taxis are everywhere, with fares starting at 6 RMB per trip. Buses cover the whole city and are the cheapest option, although they are not always dependable.

liaoning-university-of-technology.h: Things to see in and near Jinzhou

blocks.x: Liaoshen Campaign Memorial (辽沈战役纪念馆): this big museum is dedicated to the 1948 Liaoshen Campaign. More than 16,000 items of military hardware are on show, from rifles and machine guns to mortars, cannons and tanks, alongside thousands of photographs and papers. The most famous exhibit is the Panoramic Picture Hall, where a rotating circular screen reproduces the whole Battle of Jinzhou.

Yiwulü Mountain: in the west of Beizhen City within Jinzhou, this is counted among the three sacred mountains of Northeast China. The main peak, Wanghai Mountain, rises to 867 metres above sea level. Tourist sights are spread through the range, among them temples (Beizhen and Wanghai), a bridge (Shenshui), pavilions (Guanyin, Sijiao and Kuangguang), and natural features including the Fish Pool, Lotus Stone and Cloud Pass.

Mount Bijia: a Buddhist temple stands on this Bohai Sea island, which lies to the south of Jinzhou. For much of the day you need a boat to reach it, but when the tide goes out a natural causeway links it to the mainland. Visitors can then walk across from the seafront, and locals call this natural wonder Tian Qiao, or Sky Bridge. A tall stone pavilion at the summit looks like a giant pen resting in a pen holder, which is where the name Bijiashan, Pen Holder Mountain, comes from.

Guangji Pagoda (广济寺塔): in Guta Park at the centre of Jinzhou, this 72-metre pagoda has thirteen levels in an octagonal shape and is a fine example of Liao-style architecture. A quiet temple beneath it completes a traditional Chinese scene. In the early morning you can watch locals gather for rituals, exercise and other activities, and entry to the temple grounds is free.

Winter ice park: in cold weather a small ice park appears on the Xiaoling River and remains for as long as the water stays frozen. You can skate, sit on skating chairs or vehicles, drive an ATV across the ice, or hold on to a rubber tyre while a vehicle tows you.

Night Market: Jinzhou is best known today for its night market on Nanning Street (南宁路). It usually runs on summer evenings and turns into a morning market in colder seasons. You can try snacks and drinks, join in activities and soak up the busy atmosphere.

Wild Swans: Three Daughters of China, one of the bestselling non-fiction books of the 1990s, includes detailed descriptions of Jinzhou, both from the period before the 1949 Liberation and from the years after it.
Knowing the province's past helps you understand why northeast China feels the way it does.

liaoning-university-of-technology.h: Early states, from Yan to Tang

blocks.x: Between the 4th century BC and the 9th century, Han Chinese governments mostly settled and ruled Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived there. Around 300 BC the state of Yan conquered the area and set up two commanderies, with the Liao River as their dividing line: Liaodong to its east and Liaoxi to its west. Xiangping, the Yan city at the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today.

When the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family built a semi-independent state centred on Liaodong, which lasted until Cao Wei beat it in 238. That state, also called Yan, sent many maritime diplomatic and trading missions, and its short life still left a lasting mark on the culture of Northeast Asia. Once the Western Jin ended, three Xianbei states of the Murong tribe governed Liaoning in turn (Former Yan, Later Yan, then Northern Yan). Northern Wei captured the Yan capital in 436, and the Liaodong Peninsula passed to Goguryeo. Later the Tang dynasty annexed the region in the Goguryeo-Tang War.

The An Lushan Rebellion of the mid 8th century drained Tang resources away from the frontiers, and Bohai gradually spread into Liaodong. Eventually the Khitan Liao dynasty conquered Liaoning. Under the Liao, it was divided into four circuits: the Eastern Capital (Dongjingdao), Supreme Capital (Shangjingdao), Central Capital (Zhongjingdao) and Lower Capital (Xiajingdao) Circuits.

Most of the territory was run as the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu) under the Jurchen Jin dynasty, with the remainder shared among three more routes: Xianping, Northern Capital (Beijinglu) and Supreme Capital (Shangjinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206 and it was eventually folded into the Yuan dynasty. The Yuan arrangements were complicated. In the east, the Liaoyang and Shenyang Routes answered to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat, and the same was true of the western area including Guangning Route. The north was under Xianping Prefecture, part of Kaiyuan Route. Jinzhou and Chaoyang took a different line, belonging to the Daning Route, which reported to the Central Secretariat.

The Ming took Liaoning in 1371, only three years after driving the Mongols out of Beijing. A defensive wall went up around 1442 to protect the province's farmland from a possible threat from the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group in the northwest who were Ming tributaries. In 1467 and 1468 the wall was lengthened to cover the northeast as well, against raids by the Jianzhou Jurchens, the people who later became known as Manchus. This Liaodong Wall had the same purpose as the Great Wall of China but was cheaper to build. Stone and tile were used in a few places, but mostly it was just an earth bank with a moat on each side.

The wall did not stop the Jurchens, who took Liaodong (eastern Liaoning) early in the 17th century, long before they conquered the rest of China. They called their dynasty Later Jin at first, and renamed it Qing later. From 1616 to 1621 its capital was Xingjing (兴京), outside the Liaodong Wall in what is now eastern Liaoning. It then shifted to Dongjing, just east of present-day Liaoyang, and finally in 1625 to Shengjing, which is now Shenyang. After the Qing took Beijing in 1644 the main capital moved there, but Shengjing remained an important regional capital for most of the Qing era.

The conquest cost Liaoning a great deal of its population. Many Chinese residents were killed in the fighting or escaped to the south of the Great Wall, and retreating Ming troops destroyed numerous cities. Even in 1661, Zhang Shangxian, who served as Fengtian Province's civil governor (Fuyin), reported that apart from Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city east of the Liao River was empty or had just a few hundred people left. In his words, Tieling and Fushun had only a few vagrants. In the west, only Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning still had significant populations.

From the second half of the 17th century, beginning with laws of 1651 and 1653, the Qing government recruited settlers from south of the Great Wall, especially from Shandong, to populate Fengtian Province, which roughly matches today's Liaoning. Many present-day Liaoning families trace their ancestry to these 17th-century settlers. For most of the Manchu era the rest of the Northeast, meaning present-day Jilin, Heilongjiang and neighbouring parts of Inner Mongolia, was officially off-limits to Han Chinese. Migration there was blocked by the Willow Palisade, built between about 1638 and 1672. It enclosed Fengtian's agricultural heartland. In most places it either ran a little beyond the former Ming Liaodong Wall or made use of it, and it divided Fengtian from Mongol pastureland in the northwest and Manchu forests in the northeast.

Later the Qing tried to halt the flow of migrants into Fengtian, to make some go back, or, failing that, to legalise them. An edict of 1704 noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave. It told them either to register properly and join a local defence group (保, bao), or to return to their home provinces within ten years. A decade later, naturally, another edict again raised the problem of illegal migrants. Officials in Beijing found the restrictions less effective than they hoped, and the population of Fengtian doubled between 1683 and 1734.

Three generals governed Manchuria under the Qing, and the one in charge of most of present-day Liaoning was the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn). From 1860 the Manchu government began to open the region to migration again, and Han Chinese soon became its main ethnic group.

Fengtian province was created in the 20th century on the land that is Liaoning today. Liaoning was the setting for much of the Russo-Japanese War (1904 to 1905). Among its decisive battles here were Port Arthur and Mukden, and the latter was the largest land battle that had ever been fought. In the Warlord Era the Fengtian clique, headed by Zhang Zuolin and then his son Zhang Xueliang, held power. The province first got its present name on 29 January 1929, and the Zhongdong Railway Incident happened later that year. Japan invaded in 1931, and Liaoning was made part of Manchukuo, a puppet state under Japanese control. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the first major battles of the Chinese Civil War, the Liaoshen Campaign, took place in and around Liaoning.

Liaoning did not yet exist when the People's Republic was founded in 1949. The territory consisted of the provinces of Liaodong and Liaoxi and five municipalities (Shenyang, Anshan, Fushun, Benxi and Lüda, now called Dalian). They were combined as Liaoning in 1954, and bits of the old Rehe province came in 1955. A part of Inner Mongolia was also attached during the Cultural Revolution, but that was undone afterwards.

Industrialisation came early to Liaoning. It began during Japanese occupation and accelerated greatly in the 1950s and 1960s. Anshan, for instance, has one of China's largest iron and steel complexes. Recently that early emphasis on heavy industry has become a burden, because many large state-owned enterprises have run into financial trouble. Because Liaoning and the other Northeast provinces face particular difficulties as a result of their heavy-industry heritage, the central government has launched a Revitalize the Northeast campaign.

liaoning-university-of-technology.h: The land and climate of Liaoning

blocks.x: A simple way to picture Liaoning is as a trio of belts: high ground to the west, lowland in the centre, and hill country to the east.

West: the Nulu'erhu Mountains dominate, running roughly along the border with Inner Mongolia, and low hills cover the whole area. The Liaoxi Corridor, a narrow coastal strip of plain, connects the Liao River Basin with the North China Plain and finishes at Shanhai Pass, where the Great Wall meets the sea.
Centre: a largely flat and low-lying basin, whose rivers include the Liao and Daliao together with their tributaries.
East: here the Changbai and Qianshan Mountains run on into the sea to form the Liaodong Peninsula. Mount Huabozi, at 1336 m the province's highest point, belongs to this region.
Liaoning has a continental monsoon climate, with annual rainfall between about 440 and 1130 mm. Summer is the rainy season and the other seasons are dry.
The main cities are Shenyang and Dalian, followed by Anshan, Fushun, Liaoyang, Dandong, Yingkou and Jinzhou, where the university stands.

Liaoning has the biggest and richest provincial economy in Northeast China. Nominal GDP in 2017 was 2.39 trillion yuan (about US$354 billion), the 14th largest of China's 31 provinces, and per capita GDP came to 54,745 yuan (US$8,108). It leads the three Northeast provinces in both total GDP and per capita GDP.

In 2008, Liaoning had the fastest GDP growth among the G8x8, the eight sub-national regions with the highest GDP in the world's top eight GDP countries. Preliminary statistics showed growth holding at 13.1 percent in 2009, still the highest of any province. Since then the pace has slowed: the economy grew 3 percent in 2015 and shrank 1.3 percent in the first quarter of 2016.
Liaoning is also where the Li Keqiang index originated, an alternative measure of economic performance used when official GDP figures are considered unreliable.

The leading industries are petrochemicals, metallurgy, electronics and telecommunications, and machinery. For pig iron, steel and metal-cutting machine tools the province is one of China's top three producers. It counts as a key raw-materials base for the country, and its mining and quarrying, ferrous metal smelting and pressing, and oil and gas extraction all carry great weight.

Equipment and machinery manufacturing is another strength, with Shenyang and Dalian as the industrial centres. Well-known leaders in their fields include Shenyang Machine Tool Co. Ltd., Shenyang Jinbei Co. Ltd. and Daxian Group Co. Ltd. Light industry concentrates on textiles and clothing: cotton and wool spinning, chemical fibre, knitting, silk, garments and textile machinery.

In 2008 services contributed 34.5 percent of GDP. Going forward, the province intends to continue restructuring its large and medium-sized state enterprises and to build up four pillar industries, namely machinery, electronics, metallurgy and petrochemicals.

Maize, sorghum and soybeans are the main crops, and cotton is also grown. The Dalian region supplies three quarters of China's exported apples and peaches. Fruit is varied by place. Dalian is known for golden peaches and, with Yingkou, for apples. Pears come from Beizhen (in Jinzhou), while Huludao and Suizhong grow white pears. Gushan in Dandong produces apricots and plums.

No other province-level region of China has as much iron, magnesite, diamond or boron as Liaoning. It is also an important source of oil and natural gas, with large crude oil deposits, particularly in the Liaohe Oilfield, and salt is produced along the coast.
Dalian, Dandong and Yingkou are developed as major ports and as economic gateways to the whole of Northeast China.

liaoning-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Liaoning University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.

After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jinzhou, register at Liaoning University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Liaoning University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, often abbreviated LNUTCM (辽宁中医药大学), is a medical university in Liaoning Province, in northeast China. Its main campus lies in Huanggu District of Shenyang, the provincial capital. A branch campus operates in Dalian and a further campus in Benxi, so students should check which site their programme uses before they plan housing or travel.

The institution opened in 1958 as the Liaoning College of Traditional Chinese Medicine (辽宁中医学院). It was created by joining a provincial school of traditional Chinese medicine with the provincial hospital of the same specialty. In 2006 the college was renamed and became Liaoning University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

The university was in the first group of Chinese institutions approved to award master's degrees and to enrol foreign students. For an international applicant, that long experience with overseas students is a reassuring detail, though you should still ask the international office about current course language, fees and visa steps.

Your daily experience as a student depends on the city around the campus: its weather and air, how you move about, what the local economy is like, and what you can enjoy on days off. The following sections introduce Shenyang, where the main campus is located.

liaoning-university-of-traditional-chine.h: Where Shenyang lies and what it looks like

blocks.x: Shenyang is in the middle of Liaoning Province, between latitudes 41° 11' and 43° 02' N and longitudes 122° 25' and 123° 48' E. The land is varied. Flat alluvial land belonging to the Liao River system occupies the western part of the municipality, and forest-covered hinterland of the Changbai Mountains fills the east. Elevation tops out at 414 m (1,358 ft), drops to just 7 m (23 ft) at the lowest point, and averages 45 m (148 ft) across the urban area.

The main built-up area lies north of the Hun River. This was once the largest tributary of the Liao proper, and local people often call it the city's "mother river". Three man-made rivers ring the central area and are linked by channels into one continuous waterway: the South Canal (南运河), curving round the south and southeast; the Xinkai River (新开河), formerly called the North Canal, covering the north and northeast; and the Weigong River (卫工河), formerly the Weigong Nullah, to the west.

Of the three, the South Canal is the most famous, thanks to the chain of parks and gardens built beside it. Engineers made it by straightening the former bed of the Wanquan River (萬泉河, 'ten thousand springs river'), a stream that supplied the old city with most of its water and had other names too: Little Shen River (小瀋水) and Wuli River (五里河, 'five-li river'). Smaller rivers such as the Xi River (细河), the Puhe River (蒲河) and the Mantang River (满堂河) support the system at the edges, and water flows into the Hun River at three spots: the southeast, due south and the southwest of the city. A further canal on the east side, the Huishan Nullah (辉山明渠), used to empty into the lower Xinkai River but no longer exists, because urban construction reclaimed the land.

Parks are a feature of the city, and the most celebrated are the South Canal Linear Parks (南运河带状公园). Running 14.5 km (9.0 mi) along the river, they pass through the south of three districts (Dadong, Shenhe and Heping). In all there are 6 big parks and 18 gardens by the water, together about 1,400,000 m2 (350 acres) in size. Planting includes roses, apricots, bladder cherries, honeylocusts, natal lilies, scarlet sage, morning glories and black-eyed Susans, plus wide stretches of peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, weeping willow, pine and black locust trees. This is the biggest continuous area of planted open space in Shenyang. It adds a great deal to the city's greening ratio of 40 percent and helped Shenyang earn the title "national forest city" in 2005.

The local environmental protection bureau reports that burning coal in boiler stations for winter district heating produces about 30 percent of Shenyang's air pollution. In the winter of 2013–2014 the city used 16 million metric tons of coal, and half of it went on heating. Other main sources were dust from building sites (20 percent), exhaust from vehicles (20 percent), emissions from industry (10 percent) and dust from outside the city (20 percent, mostly yellow dust blown from the Gobi Desert). The bureau described the air quality as "slowly improving". Those figures are from the early 2010s, so look for newer data if this matters to you.

Shenyang has a humid continental climate influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). Summers are hot and humid because of the monsoon, and winters are cold and dry because of the Siberian anticyclone. The four seasons are clearly distinct, and almost half of the year's rain falls in July and August.

The coldest month is January, with a mean of −11.4 °C (11.5 °F); the warmest is July at 24.9 °C (76.8 °F). Over twelve months the mean is 8.6 °C (47.5 °F). Frost-free days number 183, a long time given how hard the winters are. Bright sunshine totals 2,421 hours a year, with the monthly share of possible sunshine between 42 percent in July and 64 percent in February. Extremes have reached −33.1 °C (−28 °F) at the cold end and 38.4 °C (101 °F) at the hot end. Bring genuinely warm winter clothing.

The city has 9.07 million residents, and 85.12% of them live in urban areas. It is ethnically and culturally mixed, with 38 of China's 56 recognised ethnic groups present. Han Chinese are the majority at 91.26 percent. The remaining 37 are minority groups, which I list in loose batches below.
Among the larger communities are the Manchu, Korean and Hui, then Xibo, Mongolian, Zhuang, Miao and Tujia
Also counted: Dong, Daur and Bai, together with Uyghur, Tibetan, Yi, She and Taiwanese Aboriginal People
More: Bouyei, Yao, Akha, Kazakh, Dai, Li, Shui and Nakhi
Further groups include Jingpo, Kyrgyz, Tu, Mulao, Qiang, Maonan and Gelao, as well as Russians
The smallest are the Evenks, Tatars, Oroqen, Nanai and Lhoba

Most of these groups come from elsewhere; only a few, notably the Manchus and the Xibe, are native to the Shenyang area. Many temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship are found across the city.

liaoning-university-of-traditional-chine.h: From heavy industry to rust belt and back

blocks.x: This is one of China's important industrial cities, and it anchors the Shenyang Economic Zone, which has the status of a New Special Reform Zone. Heavy industry has long been the backbone: aircraft and space equipment, machine tools, heavy machinery and defence products. More recently the city has moved into software, vehicles and electronics. The roots go back to the 1920s, and by the time of the Second World War factories were already well established. In the years of the first five-year plan (1951–1956) a large number of new plants were built in the Tiexi district.

At its height in the 1970s Shenyang ranked with Shanghai and Tianjin among the top three industrial centres in China, and for a time there was talk of making it a directly-controlled municipality. When the planned economy lost favour after the 1980s, heavy industry slowly declined and Shenyang became a "rust belt" city; state-owned factories went bankrupt and left hundreds of thousands out of work. Even so, the local economy has bounced back a good deal lately, thanks to Beijing's "Revitalize Northeast China" campaign plus fast growth in software and car manufacturing. Multinational companies that open offices or headquarters in Shenyang can receive investment subsidies.

Services, banking especially, have grown. Foreign banks present in Shenyang include Hana Bank of South Korea, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ of Japan, the Bank of East Asia of Hong Kong, Singapore's United Overseas Bank and HSBC of Britain. The city counted 1,063 banks and branches along with 144 insurance-related companies in 2006. Its goal, set for 2010, was to bring in 30 foreign banks and 60 financial institutions that are not banks.

A report by the Economist Intelligence Unit (its Access China White Paper, November 2010) placed Shenyang in a group of six it called CHAMPS, which stands for Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang; the paper looked at the 20 emerging cities it saw as most important in China.
The city has three development zones.
Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone
Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone
Shenyang Economic & Technological Development Zone

Many large industrial firms are headquartered here. Brilliance Auto, a leading Chinese carmaker, has most of its plants in Shenyang. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation builds civilian aircraft and aircraft for the PLAAF. Neusoft Group is China's largest software company, and Shenyang Machine Tool Group is the country's biggest machine tool maker. Tyco International, General Motors and the Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation are enlarging their Shenyang operations.
In 2009 the GDP per capita was 78,490 yuan, which ranked third among the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning Province.

Shenyang is the transport hub of Northeast China. It has air and rail links, a subway (five lines at the time the source was written, so check for any newer lines), a dense network of streets and expressways, and buses across the city. The biggest terminal in northeast China is Terminal 3 of Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, and a new tram network was built in the city's south in 2013.

Rail links from Shenyang go to Beijing, Dalian, Changchun, Harbin and Fushun by eight railways. The Qinhuangdao–Shenyang high-speed railway, the first passenger-only line in China, forms the main passenger corridor through the Shanhai Pass. From early 2007 a fast train running at 200 km/h (120 mph) shortened Beijing–Shenyang travel to roughly 4 hours, nearly a third of what it had been. Then, in late 2012, the Harbin–Dalian high-speed railway began operating; its trains reach 300 km/h (190 mph) and tie Shenyang in with Harbin, Changchun, Dalian and other large northeastern cities.
Two main stations serve the city: Shenyang North in Shenhe District and Shenyang Station in Heping District.

Known in Chinese as 沈阳北站 (Shěnyáng Běi Zhàn), this station had a different name until 1946: Liaoning General Station (遼寧總站). Some still say "Old North Station". The earliest building is now a protected heritage structure. When finished it was called Fengtian City Station (奉天城站), and the warlord Zhang Zuolin had it built in 1927 as the terminus of the Jingfeng Railway, roughly 1 km (0.62 mi) southwest of the present site, so as to compete with the Japanese-run Shenyang Railway Station of that time.

The current "New North Station" is a different structure: its main building (主站房) was begun in 1986 and opened for use in December 1990. It grew into one of the five most important rail hubs in the country, nicknamed "Northeast's No. 1 Station". In 2011 a huge enlargement started, called the North Station Transport Hub Reconstruction Project, because high-speed rail had pushed passenger traffic up and more floor area was needed. On the Huanggu District side, north of the railway, there is now a three-storey sub-station building and a North Square. The waiting lounge of the original 16-storey main building has moved to a big raised concourse above the tracks, and a pillar-free roof, the largest in mainland China, covers the platforms. The old South Square (南广场) in front of the main building became a multi-level complex: two upper levels form a raised drop-off area like an airport's, a large ground-level area handles buses, and three underground levels hold shopping malls, car parks, taxi pick-up and the interchange with Subway Line 2. The underground city can also be rapidly converted into an air raid shelter if necessary.

The other main station, 沈阳站 (Shěnyáng Zhàn), has more than a century of history. Russian builders put it up in 1899 beside the South Manchurian Railway's eastern side under the name Fengtian Station (奉天站). Following the Russo-Japanese War it was expanded by the Japanese and called Fengtian Yam (奉天驛) until the Second World War ended. From 1945 to 1950 it carried the name Shenyang South Railway Station (瀋陽南站), shortened to "South Station" as opposed to the North Station. Many locals still use that nickname today, which can confuse visitors: the official Shenyang South railway station is a separate one, in the suburbs where Hunnan meets Sujiatun.

These days it handles ordinary-speed passenger trains. Refurbishment, with a big archway and a new terminal, is in progress, and until it ends passengers reach the platforms by detours above and below ground. In 2010 the western side gained a new building and a square, known as the West Station Building and West Square. The old east building has a place on the provincial list of protected heritage sites.
Since 2011 a direct container train has run each day between Leipzig in Germany and Shenyang, hauling car parts across Siberia. The distance is 11,000 km (6,800 mi) and the trip takes 23 days.
Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, in Hunnan District, serves the city. It ranks as the 23rd busiest airport in China and is counted among eight major airline hubs.

Three other airports in the city are closed to the public. The oldest, East Pagoda Airport (东塔机场) in Dadong District, dates from the 1920s and went out of service in the 1980s, though a 2013 proposal suggested moving it to Xinmin and reopening it. Test flights by Shenyang Aircraft Corporation use Beiling Airport (北陵机场), in Huanggu District. Finally, military garrisons of the Northern Theater Command alone use Yuhong Airport (于洪机场) in Yuhong District.

Native Shenyang people speak the Shenyang dialect, a version of Northeastern Mandarin that developed in the early Qing dynasty. It is close to other northeastern dialects and to Putonghua, the national standard, but it belongs to the Dongbeihua family and has plenty of vocabulary that is not in the official language. If you already speak standard Mandarin you will follow most of it, but expect some local words.

Errenzhuan and Yangge, two folk dances of the northeast, enjoy great popularity here. Near Middle Street, the Big Stage Theatre (大舞台剧场) is famous for Errenzhuan shows and for comic sketches performed by Zhao Benshan and his students. Thanks to the many comedians based in Shenyang, the city has a national reputation as a stronghold of Chinese comedy.

Performing arts groups based in Shenyang include the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China and Liaoning Ballet, as well as an ensemble for song and dance from the province. The pianist Lang Lang, Zimei and Na Ying are among the artists who come from the city.
A university's province affects student life as much as its campus does. These sections cover Liaoning, from its long history to its farming.

liaoning-university-of-traditional-chine.h: Early rulers, from Yan to Tang

blocks.x: For about a thousand years, from the 4th century BC to the 9th century AD, Han Chinese governments mostly settled and ran Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived there. The state of Yan took the area around 300 BC and organised it into two commanderies: Liaodong, meaning east of the Liao River, and Liaoxi, to its west. The Yan city of Xiangping, centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today.

After the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family built a semi-independent state around Liaodong, which lasted until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Also called Yan, this short-lived state sent many maritime diplomatic and trade missions and left a lasting mark on Northeast Asian culture. Once the Western Jin dynasty ended, the Murong tribe of the Xianbei ruled Liaoning through three states, named Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan. In 436 Northern Wei took the Yan capital and Goguryeo took over the Liaodong Peninsula, until the Tang dynasty annexed the region in the Goguryeo–Tang War.

The An Lushan Rebellion, which began in the middle of the 8th century, drained Tang resources away from the frontiers, and the Bohai slowly pushed into Liaodong. In the end the Khitan Liao dynasty conquered Liaoning and divided it into four circuits: Eastern Capital (Dongjingdao), Supreme Capital (Shangjingdao), Central Capital (Zhongjingdao) and Lower Capital (Xiajingdao).

The Jurchen Jin dynasty ran most of the area as the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu), while the remaining land was shared by the Xianping Route, a Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu) and a Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it later became part of the Yuan dynasty. In the east, the Liaoyang Route and Shenyang Route came under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. The north fell under the Xianping Prefecture of the Kaiyuan Route, and the west, including the Guangning Route, was likewise subordinate to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. Jinzhou and Chaoyang were placed in the Daning Route, which answered to the Central Secretariat.

liaoning-university-of-traditional-chine.h: The Ming period and its wall

blocks.x: The Ming empire took control in 1371, only three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. A defensive wall was built around 1442 to protect the province's farming heartland from a possible threat in the northwest, the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group that paid tribute to the Ming. In 1467 and 1468 the wall was extended to guard against attacks from the northeast by the Jianzhou Jurchens, who would later be called the Manchu people.
Called the "Liaodong Wall", it served much like the Great Wall of China but was a cheaper design. Some sections used stone and tile, but most of it was just an earth dike with a moat on each side.

liaoning-university-of-traditional-chine.h: The Jurchen and the Qing capital

blocks.x: In spite of the Liaodong Wall, the Jurchens conquered eastern Liaoning (Liaodong) early in the 17th century, many years ahead of their takeover of the rest of China. Their dynasty, first called "Later Jin" and then Qing, put its capital at Xingjing (兴京) from 1616 to 1621. Xingjing lay outside the wall in what is now eastern Liaoning. The capital moved to Dongjing, east of present-day Liaoyang, and in 1625 to Shengjing, which is modern Shenyang. After the Qing took Beijing in 1644 the main capital moved there, but Shengjing stayed an important regional capital for most of the Qing era.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning much of its population. Fighting killed many Chinese residents and others escaped to the south of the Great Wall; retreating Ming forces themselves wrecked many cities. In 1661, long after the conquest, Fengtian's civil governor (Fuyin) Zhang Shangxian reported that east of the Liao River only Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng were inhabited in any real sense, while the other cities stood empty or held a few hundred people at most. In his words, "Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants". Across the river to the west, just Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning kept sizeable populations.

In the second half of the seventeenth century, beginning with laws of 1651 and 1653, the Qing authorities invited settlers from the area south of the Great Wall, mainly Shandong, to populate Fengtian Province, a thinly settled area that roughly matches modern Liaoning. Many people in Liaoning today can trace their family to those settlers. For most of the Manchu era the rest of the Northeast (now Jilin, Heilongjiang and nearby parts of Inner Mongolia) remained officially off limits to Han Chinese. The Willow Palisade (c. 1638 – c. 1672) was built to keep migrants out. It enclosed Fengtian's farming heartland and mostly ran either beside the former Ming wall or along the same line, separating the farmland from the Manchu forests in the northeast and Mongol grazing lands in the northwest.

Later the Qing government tried to halt the flow of migrants into Fengtian, or to send some settlers back to where they came from, or, if that failed, to legalise them. An edict of 1704 noted that recent Han Chinese settlers had not obeyed earlier orders to leave, and told them either to register properly and join a local defence group (保; bao) or to go back to their home areas within ten years. Ten years on, another edict appeared, reminding officials that something had to be done about illegal migrants. The restrictions were never as effective as the officials in Beijing wanted, and between 1683 and 1734 the population of Fengtian doubled.

During the Qing period three generals governed Manchuria, and much of present-day Liaoning fell to the one at Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn). The Manchu government started reopening the region to migration in 1860, and Han Chinese soon became the dominant group.
Liaoning grows mostly maize, sorghum and soybeans, with some cotton. Around Dalian, farms supply three-quarters of the apples and peaches that China exports.

Local fruit varies by area: Yingkou and Dalian for apples, Dalian again for golden peaches, Jinzhou's Beizhen district for pears, Huludao and Suizhong for white pears, and Gushan, in Dandong, for apricots and plums.
