Ludong University (鲁东大学) is a public university run by the province of Shandong and based in the coastal city of Yantai. Its story starts in 1958 with the opening of Yantai Teachers Speciality School (烟台师范专科学校). A new name came in 1984, Yantai Normal University (烟台师范学院), which is better translated 'Yantai Normal College', and in 2006 the institution was granted full university status. Today it teaches 48 majors across the arts and sciences.

ludong-university.h: Yantai: the city around the campus

blocks.x: A student's day-to-day experience depends heavily on the surrounding city. This part of the profile explains where Yantai is, how its landscape and weather work, how it earns its living, what universities and transport links it has, and which places are worth visiting.

Yantai stretches along the northern shore of the Shandong Peninsula, just south of the point where the Bohai Sea meets the Yellow Sea, and it lies opposite the southern coast of Liaoning. The terrain is reported as roughly 36.62% mountains, 39.7% hills, 50.23% plain and 2.90% basin. These percentages add up to more than 100, so treat them as a rough indication of a landscape that mixes all four types, and not as exact shares.

Urbanised land in the prefecture amounts to about 2,643.6 km2. Qixia City is the only county-level area that is wholly inland. Everything else touches the sea, and Changdao consists entirely of islands. The prefecture's coastline measures 909 kilometres (565 mi) in total.

Hilltops in the hilly parts generally rise 100 to 300 metres (330 to 980 ft). Mountain peaks average about 500 metres. The area's top elevation is reached on Mount Kunyu (崑嵛山), whose summit is 922.8 metres above sea level (3,028 ft).
The prefecture has 121 rivers longer than 5 kilometres (3.1 mi). The biggest are the Wulong (五龙河), Dagu (大沽河), Dagujia (大沽夹河), Wang (王河), Jie (界河), Huangshui (黃水河) and Xin'an (辛安河).

The climate here is shaped by the monsoon. Which Köppen category Yantai falls into depends on the cold-month threshold chosen. Using the 0 °C (32 °F) isotherm it counts as hot-summer humid continental (Dwa), whereas the -3 °C (27 °F) isotherm makes it humid subtropical (Cwa). In practice summers are hot, humid and rainy, and winters are cold and dry. Temperatures recorded since 1951 range from -12.8 °C (9 °F) to 38.4 °C (101 °F), though an unofficial reading of -15 °C (5 °F) was noted on 10 January 1931.

Yantai is now Shandong's second-largest industrial city after Qingdao, although agriculture is still the region's biggest industry. The area is famous across China for a particular apple variety and for Laiyang pears, and the city is home to Changyu, which is China's biggest and oldest winery for grapes.

The economy is one of the liveliest and most varied in the province. Fishing, fruit growing (above all apples) and light manufacturing were its traditional mainstays, and the city has since become a modern industrial base. It is strong in equipment manufacturing, petrochemicals, cars, electronics and pharmaceuticals, and new high-tech sectors are growing. Longkou, a county-level city within Yantai, is well known across China for cellophane noodles.

A big coal-fired plant near Yantai port generates most of the city's power. It burns bituminous coal and has coal gasification equipment to reduce pollution. Efforts to shift northern China from coal to gas led to supply shortages, so in 2017 Beijing adopted a revised scheme to convert half of the north to clean winter heating. In the Yantai area, the city of Haiyang was expected to cover all its heating needs in winter with nuclear energy from 2021; check how far that has actually gone.

Two zones matter most. First is the Yantai Economic and Technological Development Area, one of the earliest national-level development zones the state approved. It has 115,000 residents and a planned size of 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi). It occupies the end of the Shandong Peninsula by the Yellow Sea and touches the downtown. Both the port and Yantai Railway Station (not the same as Yantai South Railway Station) are only 6 kilometres away.

Second is the Yantai Export Processing Zone, YTEPZ, which was among the first 15 such zones the State Council approved. Its total construction area is 4.17 km2, with 3 km2 in the initial zone. After several years the zone is finished: its infrastructure is complete, with 120,000 m2 of standard workshops and 40,000 m2 of bonded warehouses. A good investment environment has brought in companies from places such as Japan, Korea, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Sweden, the United States and Canada, along with Chinese firms.

Higher education in Yantai includes Yantai University, Ludong University and the Shandong Institute of Business and Technology. Two outside institutions, China Agricultural University and Binzhou Medical College, also have campuses in the city.

For international families, Yantai has a Korean international school, the Korean School in Yantai. Between 1881 and 1951 the city also had Chefoo School, a missionary school founded for the education of foreign children.

Flying: Yantai Penglai International Airport runs regular flights to China's main airports and to Seoul, Osaka and Hong Kong. Rail: the Lancun-Yantai railway terminates in the city. Shandong's first intercity high-speed railway, the Qingrong line, is now open, and on it the quickest Qingdao-Yantai trains take about 1 hour 15 minutes instead of about 4 hours 30 minutes.
Penglai City, about 80 km from downtown Yantai, is home to the Dan Cliffs (丹崖), where tradition says the Eight Immortals set off for the Conference of the Magical Peach.

Yangma Island lies in the north of Muping District and is large. The island's climate is pleasant, neither bitterly cold in winter nor scorching in summer, so it suits leisure and holidays and is nicknamed 'the Maldives of China'. Its history is long. Tradition says that Emperor Qin Shi Huang kept royal horses here during a tour to the east, hence the name 'Royal Horse Island', which became Yangma Island.

Ludong University is in Shandong, and a university's region influences student life nearly as much as its campus does. The sections below describe the province: its long history, climate, geology and economy.

ludong-university.h: From prehistory to the first states

blocks.x: People have lived in Shandong, on the eastern margin of the North China Plain, for a very long time. A chain of Neolithic cultures flourished there: Houli (around 6500 to 5500 BC), Beixin (5300 to 4100 BC), Dawenkou (4100 to 2600 BC), Longshan (3000 to 2000 BC) and Yueshi (1900 to 1500 BC).

Control by the Shang and Zhou dynasties reached western Shandong in varying degrees. In the east lived the Dongyi, whom people on the Central Plain looked down on as barbarians. In 567 BC the state of Qi annexed the Dongyi state of Lai, and the Dongyi slowly adopted Chinese ways.

Regional states grew powerful during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. Shandong held two: Qi, whose capital was Linzi, and Lu, whose capital was Qufu. Lu was the birthplace of Confucius and yet was a small state that Chu, to its south, eventually swallowed up. Qi stayed a major power the whole time and ruled cities such as Jimo, Linzi and Ju.

Qi fell to the Qin dynasty, which created the first centralised Chinese state in 221 BC. Under the following Han dynasty the area of modern Shandong was divided into commanderies, supervised by two inspectorates (刺史部): Qingzhou (青州) in the north and Yanzhou (兗州) in the south. During the Three Kingdoms period it formed part of Cao Wei, the kingdom that governed the north.

The Western Jin dynasty briefly reunited the country, but nomadic invaders from the north then overran the north, including Shandong. In the following century or so power over the province passed from one regime to another: Later Zhao, Former Yan, Former Qin, Later Yan, Southern Yan, the Liu Song, and last the Northern Wei, the first of the Northern dynasties. Shandong remained under Northern rule through the rest of the Northern and Southern dynasties.

The Buddhist monk Faxian came ashore at Laoshan, at the southern edge of the Shandong peninsula, in 412 AD. His next stop was Qingzhou, where he edited and translated the scriptures he had carried home from Pakistan and India.

Unity returned under the Sui in 589, then the Tang (618 to 907) presided over another golden age. In the early Tang, Shandong was part of an administrative unit called Henan Circuit. Later China broke into warlord factions in the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period; the Five Dynasties, which included Shandong, were all in the north.

China was reunified under the Song in the late tenth century. Outlaw bands active in Shandong in Song times inspired the folk tales behind the classic novel Water Margin. A notable archaeological find was made in 1996 at Qingzhou, where more than two hundred buried Buddhist statues came to light. Some are early painted figures, and the likely reason for their burial was the persecution of Buddhism by Emperor Huizong, who preferred Taoism.
The Jurchen Jin dynasty took northern China from the Song in 1142. The Jin organised Shandong as the Shandong East Circuit and Shandong West Circuit, which is the earliest use of its modern name.

The Ming dynasty formed the province that we know today as Shandong. It was bigger then, reaching into eastern Liaoning (Liaodong). The capital was transferred from Qingzhou to Jinan in 1376, and for seven hundred years since, Jinan has been the provincial capital.

Emperor Yongle made Beijing the national capital in 1421. Shipping grain by canal then became important, and Jining and Linqing, on the Grand Canal, prospered. Later, however, the Little Ice Age (about 1550 to 1770) reduced harvests and brought repeated famine. The imperial court's harsh policies made it worse and peasant revolts erupted again and again.

In 1633 two Ming generals, Kong Youde and Geng Zhongming, brought their troops from Dengzhou to Liaodong and surrendered to the Manchu Qing; they later took part when Qing forces entered China proper. White Lotus Society uprisings in Shandong grew more intense by 1640. Zhu Datian was sent by the Ming court to crush the rebellion, and the province's population fell sharply a second time.

A powerful earthquake, with an estimated magnitude of 8.5 and an epicentre just northeast of Linyi, devastated Dengzhou and its surrounding prefecture, and it is claimed that somewhere between 43,000 and 50,000 foreigners and locals died.

ludong-university.h: The late Qing and foreign powers

blocks.x: Once China lost the First Opium War, Western influence kept growing, and a coastal province such as Shandong felt it keenly. After the Second Opium War the Qing opened Chefoo (Yantai) to trade, and Western countries moved in with consulates, missionaries, Christian schools and factories. Because Shandong was strategically important, each power wanted influence there. During the 1880s it became the supply and training base of the Beiyang Fleet, which had its headquarters at Weihaiwei. Japan's Imperial Navy defeated the fleet disastrously in 1894, and Japanese influence started to spread into the province. Then, in 1897, the killing of two German Catholic missionaries at Juye in Heze caused the Juye Incident, and the Qing court had to cede Qingdao to the German Empire. Russian pressure led Weihaiwei to be given to Britain in 1898.

Another development was migration. After Russia annexed Outer Manchuria in 1860, the Qing government dropped its ban on settlement and encouraged people from Shandong to move into the part of Manchuria that remained Chinese. Many Shandong people left in search of better opportunities, heading for Northeast China, the Russian Far East and Korea. In Northeast China (Manchuria) they helped build up population and agriculture, working in farming, construction and mining. About 200 thousand Chinese labourers lived in the Russian Far East before the Soviets deported and killed them, and 95% of them were from Shandong.
The Boxer Rebellion began in Shandong and the province became one of its centres. To put it down, the general Yuan Shikai was made governor in 1899 and kept the job for three years.

Germany took charge of the peninsula in 1898, forcing a lease of Jiaozhou Bay and its port of Qingdao. Developing the area was a high priority for the Germans, who invested more than 200 million marks in first-class harbour facilities, with berths, heavy machinery, rail yards and a floating dry dock. Private companies opened mines, banks, factories and railways around the province.

Japan took over German possessions in Qingdao and Shandong during the First World War. At Versailles in 1919 these passed to Japan instead of going back to China, and the public anger this caused, known as the Shandong Problem, sparked fierce student protests in the May Fourth Movement. The US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations approved reservations to the treaty, one of which was 'to give Shantung to China', but the treaty with reservations failed to pass. In 1922 Shandong returned to China after American mediation at the Washington Naval Conference, with Weihai following in 1930.

Chinese rule came back during the Republic's Warlord Era, with control first going to the Zhili clique. After the Second Zhili-Fengtian War in 1924, however, the Fengtian clique, based in the northeast, took over. In April 1925 it placed Zhang Zongchang, known as the 'Dogmeat General' and called China's 'basest warlord' by Time, in charge as military governor. His rule lasted until the Northern Expedition removed him in 1928. His successor was Han Fuju, loyal to Feng Yuxiang at first but afterwards a supporter of Chiang Kai-shek's Nanjing government. He also removed the eastern warlord Liu Zhennian, 'King of Shandong East', and with that he ruled the whole province.

When Japan invaded China in 1937, a conflict that later joined the Pacific theater, Han Fuju was appointed Deputy Commander in Chief of the 5th War Area and given the task of defending the lower Yellow River valley. But he left his base, and when Japanese troops crossed the Yellow River about 600,000 ethnic Chinese civilians left Jinan, leaving behind only elderly people too old to travel. Soon afterward he was executed for ignoring orders.

During the occupation, resistance went on in areas the Japanese did not hold, notably in Muslim peasant villages. By 1945 communist Red Army forces had taken parts of Shandong, and over four years of civil war they extended their control until the Kuomintang, the Republic of China's government, was driven from Shandong and eventually to Taiwan. One decisive moment was in May 1947, in the Yimeng Mountains of central Shandong, when the Communists' East China Field Army wiped out the Nationalist 74th Corps in the Menglianggu Campaign; many regard that corps as the best unit in the National Revolutionary Army. In 1948 the Communists seized Weixian, called the 'fortress of central Shandong', in the Battle of Weixian.

The People's Liberation Army marched into Qingdao on 2 June 1949, once the Nationalist 11th Pacification District and the US forces had left, and made the city part of Shandong. That August (the 12th) the PLA's Third Field Army also won the Changshan Islands Campaign, so the Communists held the whole province.

Shandong's climate is temperate and humid continental (Köppen Dwa), with a humid subtropical edge (Cwa) toward the south. Typical summers are hot, reaching about 35 °C, and rainy, except on the eastern Jiaodong Peninsula, where highs are about 28 °C, and on Mount Tai, where they are about 20 °C. Winters are cold and dry. Expect average temperatures of -9 to 1 °C (16 to 34 °F) in January and 18 to 28 °C (64 to 82 °F) in July. Rainfall totals 550 to 950 mm a year (22 to 37 in), and because of the monsoon most of it falls during the summer.

In geological terms Shandong forms part of the Eastern Block of the North China craton. Since the Mesozoic its crust has thinned in a way that is unusual for a craton, going from about 200 km thick to as little as 80 km (120 mi to 50 mi), and this led to widespread volcanic activity in the Tertiary.

Fossils are plentiful in some of its rock formations. Zhucheng, in the southeast, has yielded many dinosaur fossils. The discovery there in 2008 of roughly 7,600 dinosaur bones, belonging to Zhuchengtyrannus, Ankylosaurus and other genera, may be the largest such collection ever found in one place.

Shandong's economy has long relied on fishing. By 2014 the province produced more than 9 million tons of aquatic products worth ¥360 billion, and over 12 million mu (about 800,000 hectares) was used for aquaculture. Sea cucumbers, kelp, prawns, flounder, sole, clams and Chinese mitten crabs lead the marine side, while fresh-water farming is quickly developing local specialties like softshell turtles, loach, icefish and Siniperca chuatsi.

Sporting events held in Shandong include the 2002 Table Tennis World Cup, the 2004 AFC Asian Cup, the 2007 A3 Champions Cup, the sailing events of the 2008 Summer Olympics and Paralympics, the 2009 National Games of China, the 2011 Sudirman Cup, the 2012 Badminton Asia Championships and the 2012 Asian Beach Games.
Ludong University lists 117 programs for international students on this site: 62 bachelor, 54 master's, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 116 taught in Chinese, 1 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 14,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.

117 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (1):
Physics
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

ludong-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Ludong University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Yantai, register at Ludong University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

minzu-university-of-china.h: Minzu University of China at a glance

blocks.x: Minzu University of China (MUC for short) is a public university run at national level and based in Beijing. Its supervising body is the National Ethnic Affairs Commission, a unit within the United Front Work Department of the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee. Three government schemes for leading universities list it: Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction.

The university's special field is the study of China's ethnic minorities, and it is ranked first in China among universities in that area. Its stated goal is to be among the best universities of its kind anywhere in the world at preserving and promoting the cultures of all ethnic groups. With strong government backing it has grown quickly over the years. Its reputation is particularly high in ethnology and anthropology, the economics of ethnic and regional development, religion studies, history, dance and the fine arts.

In Chinese, the name means roughly central ethnic university, which signals a national institution devoted to serving minority peoples. The older English name rendered the Chinese word for the ethnic groups as nationalities, a term taken from German and Russian Marxist writing. On 20 November 2008 the university adopted a new official English name. The reasons reported were a worry that the word central might suggest a university in the geographic middle of China (as it does for the South-Central University for Nationalities), and that the old wording did not sound good. The renaming of Renmin University is cited as a precedent.

The new name hides the university's ethnic focus, but what students mostly noticed was something else: it made their nickname, the village, out of date. The Chinese word for village is 村 (pinyin cūn), whose pinyin spelling resembles the old English abbreviation CUN, and villages carry homely, friendly associations in mainland Chinese culture.

The story begins during the Chinese Civil War, when the Chinese Communist Party opened a Nationalities Institute at its base in Yan'an in October 1941. During 1950 to 1952 it was combined with other departments of ethnic languages and sociology, some of which came out of Peking University and Tsinghua University. The Central Institute for Nationalities that emerged was founded in 1951 and held its formal opening on 11 June 1952, with a big park-like site on Beijing's outskirts as its campus.

Both the Yan'an and the Central institutes aimed to train cadres, or officials, for minority regions, and to give a liberal arts education to promising minority students. Those cadres were to serve as a link between their home communities and the government, and the institute's research was, and is, expected to back the ethnic affairs commission's policies. In the early years the institute took part in the sensitive work of dividing the country's vast population into official ethnic groups. That ended with the Cultural Revolution, when regular teaching became almost impossible.

In 1999 it received key university status under Project 211, a scheme meant to pick out 100 Chinese universities to lead in the twenty-first century. From 2004 it joined Project 985, the national effort to bring 39 universities up to world-class standing. As part of that programme the campus has been almost completely rebuilt.

Meanwhile Haidian has gone on developing as Beijing's main university district. Today the campus is a neighbour of the National Library of China and of Zhongguancun, the technology district that the local press nicknames China's silicon valley. A large parcel of land in Beijing's Fengtai district was acquired in 2006, so a second campus there is a likely future development.
In 2001 the People's Daily called the university China's top academy for ethnic studies. The Shanghai Ranking puts it first in China among universities that began as ethnic minority institutions.

Because the university concentrates on arts and humanities, and especially on subjects connected with minorities, it tends to sit lower in global rankings. It is in the 301-350 band in the QS Asia University Rankings and in the 271-280 band among BRICS countries in the QS BRICS rankings. On the world stage, it makes the top 2000 in the U.S. News & World Report Best Global Universities list, in the CWUR table (Center for World University Rankings), and in RUR, CWTS Leiden and University Ranking by Academic Performance lists. Positions shift from year to year, so check the latest editions.

Each of the 56 recognised minority groups has a fixed quota, so that all are represented among students. In 2011 the university took gaokao scores (the National Higher Education Entrance Examination) from the mid-400s upward, which is under the 50th percentile and was among the lowest bars for any Beijing university. A Chinese university may, at its own discretion, accept a student whose score is just under the cutoff, and minimum scores have sometimes been lowered to allow in students from the groups with fewest admissions. Those numbers are old and entry standards change every year, so treat them only as a rough indication and ask the university for current requirements.

To help minority students enrol, the university offers remedial courses. One is a one-year tutorial that goes back over the final year of senior secondary school, and another is a set of Chinese language classes for catching up. Separate bridging programmes also pick out high-achieving minority pupils at secondary schools and bring them to Minzu University to get ready for admission to Beijing's very top universities; tuition for these is paid by the government.
Among the students and staff linked with the university are the following.
Arken Abdulla, a pop singer-songwriter who performs in Uyghur and Mandarin Chinese
Kahar Barat, a Uyghur-American historian
Fei Xiaotong, a sociologist and anthropologist
D. O. Chaoke, an Evenki linguist
Han Geng, a Mandopop singer and actor
Song Zuying, a Miao singer whose repertoire spans classical Chinese and Western songs, and who sang at the 2008 Summer Olympics closing ceremony
Ulan Tuya (born 1983), a Chinese singer and songwriter
Zhang Chengzhi, a writer who once sat in on a class in Kazakh
Kao Chin Su-mei, a Taiwanese Aboriginal actress and singer, who has been a legislator in Taiwan's Legislative Yuan for the Highland Aborigines constituency
Mi Na, a contemporary artist

A student's daily routine is shaped by the city beyond the gates, including its seasons, its transport and its attractions. The sections below introduce Beijing, the home of this university, starting with how it looks and where it sits.

Three building styles dominate urban Beijing. First comes the architecture of imperial China, whose finest examples are the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple, the Temple of Heaven and the enormous Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), which remains the emblem of the People's Republic. The second is sometimes called the Sino-Sov style, which is boxy and sometimes poorly built, and which dates from the 1950s to the 1970s. The third is thoroughly modern, seen above all in the central business district (CBD) in east Beijing, with buildings such as the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Early in the twenty-first century the city saw a huge amount of construction in many modern styles by international designers, most strongly in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s design mixes with a neofuturistic look, blending old and new. The tallest building in Beijing is the 528-metre China Zun. Two Beijing towers have taken the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) prize for the best tall building overall since 2007: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. The prize goes to a single building worldwide each year.

Then there are the siheyuan, courtyards surrounded by buildings. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are normally linked by alleys called hutongs. Hutongs mostly run straight from east to west, so that doors face north and south, which is good Feng Shui. Their width varies, and some are so narrow that only a few people can pass at once. Once they were found all over Beijing, but they are disappearing quickly because entire blocks of hutongs are being cleared for tower blocks. People who lived in them have the right to apartments at least equal in size to their old homes. Many still say that the neighbourly feeling and street life of the hutongs cannot be recreated, and the properties are often owned by the government.

Beijing lies at the northern edge of the North China Plain, which is roughly triangular and opens to the south and east. Mountains to the north, north-west and west protect the city and northern China's farmland from the desert steppe. In the north-west of the municipality, notably in Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, and Xishan (the Western Hills) frame the west. The Great Wall in the north of the municipality was built along this rugged terrain to defend against raids from the steppe. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, is the highest point in the municipality at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma all belong to the Hai River system and run towards the south-east. Miyun Reservoir, high on the Chaobai, is the biggest reservoir in the municipality. The city is also where the Grand Canal to Hangzhou ends in the north (the canal was built more than 1,400 years ago for transport), and the northern end of the South-North Water Transfer Project, which brings water from the Yangtze basin and was built in recent years.

The urban area stands on plains in the south-central part of the municipality, at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, and takes up a fairly small but growing part of the municipality. Ring roads spread outward in circles: the Second Ring Road runs where the old walls stood, while the Sixth connects satellite towns around the suburbs. Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square are in the centre, just south of the Forbidden City, which was the emperors' residence. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, home to China's current leaders. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tiananmen and the Square and is the main east-west axis of the city.
People often say Beijing has grown outward like a pancake (tan da bing), from the old inner city to the edge, and this pattern is frequently blamed for some of the city's urban problems.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (BSk). Summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon, and winters are brief but cold and dry under the influence of the huge Siberian high-pressure system. In spring, sandstorms can blow in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe while temperatures climb quickly and the air stays dry. Autumn, like spring, is a transition season with little rain.

Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest period has been early August and the coldest early January. China's seasonal standard marks the start of spring in Beijing on 26 March, with summer beginning 20 May, autumn 13 September and winter 31 October. Because March and September have been warming faster, and May and October more slowly, autumn is usually shorter than spring.

For the 1991 to 2020 period, the average yearly temperature in the urban area is between 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) and 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Daily minimums average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily maximums 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). In the lower-lying suburbs the yearly average is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In the hills and mountains, yearly averages range from 0 °C (32 °F) to 10 °C (50 °F), dropping as altitude rises. The daily average is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) in January and 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July.

Rainfall averages about 528.0 mm (20.79 in) a year, or 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and close to three-quarters of it comes between June and August. Winter months are the sunniest by share of possible hours, at 62% in January and February, while July is the lowest at 42%; overall there are 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year. Since 1951 the lowest temperature was -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, and the highest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), on 24 July 1999. In practice that means a dry, cold winter, a hot, wet summer and short, pleasant spells in spring and autumn.

Beijing has long had environmental problems. Between 2000 and 2009 the urban area quadrupled in size, which raised emissions and also changed the local weather: surface albedo, wind speed and near-surface humidity went down, while ground and air temperatures, vertical air mixing and ozone went up. Because of urbanisation and the burning of fossil fuels, serious air pollution affects the city and the health of many residents. In 2013 heavy smog hit Beijing and much of northern China, affecting 600 million people. That episode turned air pollution into a major economic and social issue nationwide. The city government responded by announcing reduction measures, including a drop in coal's share of the energy mix from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017. At national level, heavily polluting vehicles were ordered off the roads from 2015 to 2017, and the shift of the energy system to clean sources was stepped up.
#### Where the pollution comes from

Joint research by American and Chinese scientists in 2006 found that much of Beijing's pollution is carried in from surrounding cities and provinces, and that 35 to 60% of the ozone on average comes from outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin in particular have a strong effect on the capital's air, partly because summer winds blow mostly from the south and south-east and the mountains to the north and north-west trap the air.

About 40% of the city's PM 2.5 comes from burning coal, which is also the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. From 2012 the city began switching coal-fired power stations to natural gas, aiming to keep yearly coal use under 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons: 73% for heating and electricity and the remainder for industry. Plenty of pollutants also come from neighbours. Tianjin's coal use was forecast to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, and Hebei burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, with only 30% of it for electricity and a large part for steel and cement. Coal-mining regions in Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000, and Shandong's power plants add to the load. The four biggest coal-consuming provinces are, in order, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia. These are older figures and projections, so look for current data.

Four large coal-fired plants once supplied the city with electricity and winter heat. The first to go was Gaojing Thermal Power Plant, in 2014; two others followed in March 2015, and Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, the fourth, was scheduled to close in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was a cut of 13 million tons in coal use, with a ceiling of 15 million tons for 2015.
#### Cleaning the air for big events

Nearly US$17 billion was spent preparing for the 2008 Summer Olympics to meet promises to clean up the air. It assembled a fleet of 3,800 buses powered by natural gas, among the biggest in the world, and was the first Chinese city to demand the local counterpart of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The government sometimes uses cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air before large events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to deal with drought. Lately it has turned more to short-term factory shutdowns and stricter limits on cars. The brief clear spells called APEC blue and parade blue, around the APEC China 2014 summit and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade, are examples. Air quality improved dramatically during and before those events and then slipped back to unhealthy levels soon after.

The first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed most industry and many businesses; a red alert, the top level, followed later that month. In November 2016 the city's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting older cars would be banned from the roads when red alerts are in force in the city or nearby regions.
#### Recent improvement

There has been real progress since a war on pollution was declared in 2014. Fine particulates fell by 35% in 2017 and dropped further by 2020, chiefly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting factories in the Beijing area were cleaned up. The annual PM2.5 average reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the cleanest since 2013, and 2024 saw just two days of heavy pollution, the fewest on record and 96.6 percent below the 58 days of 2013.
#### Reading the numbers

Because pollution levels are high, different sources report them differently. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) publishes daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city, and the US Embassy in Beijing has posted hourly figures for fine particulates (PM2.5) and ozone on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants by different criteria, so the BJEPB figures and its health impact assessments are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog is harmful. It clearly affects rates of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, hospital visits and even death. Students with asthma or similar conditions should check air quality apps and keep masks handy on bad days.
#### Dust storms

Dust from eroding deserts in northern and north-western China brings seasonal dust storms to the city, and the Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain artificially to fight them and reduce their effects. No fewer than eight storms struck in just the first four months of 2006. One storm in April 2002 dumped almost 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing before travelling on over Japan and Korea.

Mudanjiang Normal University sits in a city whose weather, location and economy will shape your student years. This section starts with the city, then looks at the schools in Mudanjiang, and finishes with Heilongjiang province.

Mudanjiang covers longitudes 128°02' to 131°18' E and latitudes 43°24' to 45°59' N, in the southeast of Heilongjiang province. It is the southernmost prefecture in the province. Four other prefectures border it:
Harbin, to the west
Jixi, to the northeast
Qitaihe, to the north
Yanbian in Jilin, to the south

To the east lies Russia's Primorsky Krai. The prefecture has an average elevation of 230 metres (755 ft), and most of the land is mountains and hills. The Changbai Mountains begin to rise in the east, and the central area is part of the Hegu Basin. Suifenhe City, on the Russian border, is the lowest part at 86.5 metres (283.8 ft). The summit of the prefecture is Zhangguangcai mountain, which stands 1,686.9 metres (5,534 ft) high.

The climate is monsoon-influenced humid continental (Köppen Dwa). Summers are hot and humid, winters are very cold and dry, and spring and autumn are short. Even so, winters here are much milder than across most of the province, because the basin setting shields the city from the worst of the biting wind.

January averages -16.7 °C (1.9 °F) and July 22.3 °C (72.1 °F), and over the whole year the mean works out at 4.78 °C (40.6 °F). Nearly three fifths of the yearly rain arrives between June and August. Possible sunshine rises from 46 percent in July to 62 percent in February and March, adding up to 2,368 hours of bright sun a year. The coldest day on record was 3 January 1963 at -38.3 °C (-37 °F), and the hottest was 24 July 1998 at 38.4 °C (101 °F).

Expect a serious winter, so good thermal clothing is essential, followed by a warm, humid summer. Because the basin shelters the city, Mudanjiang's winters are gentler than in much of the rest of the province, though you will still want a heavy coat, gloves and insulated boots from late autumn.

In 2010 the city's GDP grew 18.5 percent to RMB 78.1 billion, the fourth highest in Heilongjiang after Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar. Tourism and light manufacturing are the main supports of the local economy. Key industries include parts for the car industry, papermaking, forestry, petrochemicals, new materials, pharmaceuticals and energy. Foreign trade jumped 71.8 percent to US$9 billion in 2010, which was three quarters of the entire province's total. These figures are more than a decade old, so treat them as background rather than current data.
Five zones concentrate investment:
A development zone aimed at trade with Russia (the Mudanjiang to Russia zone)
The Sino-Russian Information Industrial Garden
The Jiangnan economic and technological development area
A bioindustry development zone
The Heilongjiang Northern Pharmaceutical Technological Development Zone

By rail: Mudanjiang is a railway hub in the east of the province, where the Binsui (Harbin-Suifenhe) and Tujia (Tumen-Jiamusi) lines cross. From Mudanjiang Railway Station, trains reach Beijing, Jinan, Dalian, Harbin, Changchun and other Chinese cities.

By air: Mudanjiang Hailang International Airport is the second-largest international airport in Heilongjiang, but it is currently closed for renovation and handles no flights. Check its status before you plan travel.
By road: the G11 Hegang-Dalian Expressway and the G10 Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway connect the city to the national highway network.
The available information about education in the city mixes together several institutions, so the details below are best checked with the schools themselves.

This is a provincial institution of higher education in Heilongjiang. Its origins go back to a branch of Northeast Agricultural College at Nenjiang, opened in September 1958 and shut in 1964. A new institution, Bei'an Teachers' College, was created on that closed branch's foundations, and the State Council gave its approval in January 1965. During 1964, the Bei'an college moved onto the old Ning'an County Breeding Farm and became Heilongjiang's Ning'an Teachers' College. In December 1970 the provincial Revolutionary Committee authorised its expansion into Mudanjiang Teachers College.

The college has since developed to offer master's degrees, and it is a comprehensive teacher-training institution with full-time undergraduates, international students and adult education, totalling over 22,000 students. The campus covers 1.05 million square metres, with nearly 390,000 square metres of buildings, and is classed as a provincial garden-style unit. It recruits students from all over China and has 15 secondary colleges. The college became Mudanjiang Normal University in 2015, with the college name giving way to the university name. In a Soft Science ranking of China's best universities, published on 26 February 2023, Mudanjiang Teachers College was placed 459th.

A separate institution, Mudanjiang University, dates from 1983 and was among the first 100 local universities established nationwide. It has three parts: the main campus, the Hailin campus and an industrial park training base. The site is 500,000 square metres, with 186,000 square metres of buildings. Fixed assets are worth 450 million yuan, teaching equipment is worth 90 million yuan and the library holds 644,800 books. More than 10,000 students attend, in 10 secondary schools and 43 majors. Two majors have central government support as key construction projects, and six have provincial financial support. The school has 104 laboratories and training bases on campus and 125 off campus. Three majors, mechatronics, animation design and production, and computer information security storage, have been designated national backbone teacher-training bases by the Ministry of Education.

Known locally as Mudanjiang Yizhong, this is the province's first demonstration high school. It was founded in September 1945 as Mudanjiang Municipal High School and took its present name in 2001. In September 2007 it moved as a whole to a new campus of 218,000 square metres, with a built area of 93,000 square metres, 73,000 square metres of green space and 70,000 square metres for sport. In 2009 it received a national award as an experimental school under the National 100 High School Construction Project, and in 2011 it was chosen to pilot provincial science projects. Figures from February 2015 show 359 teaching staff. Of these, 123 held master's degrees, 8 were special teachers and 144 were senior teachers, and 107 served as academic leaders or core teachers at national, provincial or city level. Student numbers were above 5,200.

mudanjiang-normal-university.h: An early history of peoples and dynasties

blocks.x: Ancient Chinese records and other sources say Heilongjiang was home to peoples such as the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan. The Mongolic Donghu lived in Inner Mongolia and the west of Heilongjiang, and some local names come from Manchu or Mongolian. Between the 7th and 10th centuries, the Bohai Kingdom ruled the east of the province, and the Khitan Liao dynasty followed. The Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115 to 1234), which later governed much of northern China, rose within the borders of present-day Heilongjiang.

Heilongjiang first appeared as an administrative unit in 1683, under the Manchu Qing dynasty during the reign of Kangxi, when it was separated from the northwestern corner of Jilin province. At that time it took in only the western part of the present province. Its ruler was the General of Heilongjiang (Sahaliyan Ula i Jiyanggiyūn in Manchu), also translated as Military Governor. The word jiyanggiyūn is the Manchu form of the Chinese 將軍 (jiāngjūn), a military leader or general, and is cognate with the Japanese shōgun. Under the Treaty of Nerchinsk, his power extended north to the Stanovoy Mountains. The east of what is now Heilongjiang remained subject to the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose authority stretched to the Sea of Japan. Han Chinese were not allowed to settle in these remote parts of Manchuria.

The governor's first seat in 1683 was Heilongjiang City (also called Aigun or Heihe, or Saghalien Ula in Manchu) on the Amur. By 1690 the seat had shifted to Nenjiang (Mergen), beside the Nen River, and in 1699 it moved again, farther south, to Qiqihar. Historians believe supplies drove these moves. The Nen River offered Nenjiang and Qiqihar an easy waterway to southern Manchuria, but supplying Aigun required either a long voyage down the Sungari River to where it meets the Amur and then upstream to Heihe, or carrying goods overland through the Lesser Xing'an Mountains from the Nen valley to the Amur valley. Qiqihar may also have been attractive because it stands where a road north to Nenjiang meets a road west to Mongolia, so its garrison could defend against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

The Qing kept little military presence north of Aigun. European sources of the 18th and early 20th centuries, and Russian reports from the 1850s, put the farthest Qing advance guard post at Ulusu-Modon (Ulussu-Mudan; 乌鲁苏穆丹, Wūlǔsūmùdān), near the famous S-shaped bend of the Amur. This post stood on the left (north) bank and was lost to the Russians in 1860.

Under pressure in 1858 and 1860, the Qing government handed everything beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers to the Russian Empire. The Qing were thereby cut off from the Sea of Japan, and Heilongjiang acquired the northern and eastern borders it has now. Around the same time the Qing opened Manchuria to migration by Han Chinese. By the early 20th century, thanks to the mass movement known as Chuang Guandong, Han Chinese had become the main ethnic group in the region.

Japanese forces invaded Heilongjiang in 1931 and completed their conquest of it in 1932, when it became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army defeated the Japanese in Manchuria in 1945, and in the Chinese Civil War Soviet forces helped the communists. Heilongjiang became the first province fully under their control, and Harbin was the first major city they held.

When communist rule began, Heilongjiang covered only the western part of today's province and had Qiqihar as its capital. The rest was Songjiang province, with its capital at Harbin. In 1954 the two were merged to form present-day Heilongjiang. During the Cultural Revolution the province was enlarged with the Hulunbuir League and other areas that had been in Inner Mongolia, but most of that change has since been reversed.

Heilongjiang has varied terrain. Mountain ranges dominate much of it: the Greater Khingan and Lesser Khingan Ranges, the Zhangguangcai Mountains, the Laoye Mountains and the Wanda Mountains. The highest summit, on the boundary with Jilin, is Datudingzi Mountain (1,690 metres, or 5,540 ft). The Greater Khingan Range holds the largest remaining virgin forest in China and is important to its forestry industry.

In the lower, flatter east and southwest, the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers flow, and each of them feeds into the Amur, which itself forms the valley along the northern boundary. On the Russian side lies Primorsky Krai, and Xingkai Lake (also known as Khanka Lake) straddles the frontier with it.

Across most of the province the climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), although the far north is subarctic (Dwc). The long, bitter winters give January averages of -31 to -15 °C (-24 to 5 °F), whereas the short summers are warm to very warm, with July averaging 18 to 23 °C (64 to 73 °F). Between 400 and 700 millimetres (16 to 28 in) of rain falls each year, much of it in summer. Sunshine is plentiful, about 2,300 to 2,650 hours a year, and in spring the Songnen and Sanjiang plains offer abundant wind energy.
Among the major cities, apart from Mudanjiang itself, are Harbin, Qiqihar, Daqing, Jiamusi, Heihe, Hegang, Jixi, Qitaihe, Yichun and Shuangyashan.

By road: as of October 2020 the province has 165,989 km (103,141 miles) of expressways, highways and other roads. The Beijing-Harbin Expressway is the main route into Heilongjiang, running from the Jilin border to the Harbin Ring Expressway. The Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway heads northeast, linking remote counties in the jurisdiction of Harbin, Jiamusi and elsewhere in the northeast. The Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off it at Jiansanjiang near the end, joining many state-owned farms in the far east before it ends near the Russian border. The Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway crosses southeast to northwest and connects Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar before reaching the Inner Mongolia border. The Hegang-Dalian Expressway helps move lumber and coal between Hegang and the Jilin border in the east.

By rail: the province has 60 lines, about 5,300 kilometres (3,300 miles) in all, among them part of the Eurasian Land Bridge. The high-speed line between Harbin, the provincial capital, and Dalian in Liaoning opened in 2012 and passes through Changchun and Shenyang, with 23 stops. Forecasts expected 37 million passengers annually by 2020, rising to 51 million by 2030.

By air: main airports are Harbin Taiping International, Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi and Heihe. Harbin International can handle six million passengers a year and flies to over 70 cities at home and abroad.

Valery Solomonovich Gurevich, vice-chairman of Russia's Jewish Autonomous Oblast, proposed the Tongjiang-Nizhneleninskoye railway bridge in 2007. It crosses the Amur and links Tongjiang with Nizhneleninskoye, a village in that oblast. The Chinese section was finished in July 2016, and work on the Russian section began that December. The two sides were structurally joined in March 2019. Opening to trains has been postponed several times, with estimates moving to the end of 2020 in December 2019 and then to the third quarter of 2021.

Heilongjiang's GDP in 2022 was 1.59 trillion RMB (US$236 billion nominal), or CN¥51,906 (US$7,717 nominal) per head. The primary sector contributed ¥360 billion (22.7 percent), the secondary sector ¥465 billion (29.2 percent) and the tertiary sector ¥764 billion (48 percent).

GDP has grown steadily since 2003, from 443.3 billion yuan to 707.72 billion in 2007, a 60 percent rise. Private business reached RMB 234 billion in 2006, 37.6 percent of GDP, and private firms paid RMB 20.5 billion in tax that year. Private enterprise has led the province's overall growth, and many leading private firms are emerging.

Heilongjiang has China's biggest plantations of rice, corn and soybeans, covering 14.37 million hectares (35.5 million acres) of grain, including 4 million hectares (9.9 million acres) of rice and 5.5 million hectares (14 million acres) of corn. Huge areas of black soil (chernozem), among the most fertile of all soils, lie within its borders. Farming in this black-soil belt has expanded nearly a hundredfold since the early 1900s, and after the 1960s agriculture was modernised through heavy mechanisation and greater fertiliser use. The province is one of Asia's leading producers of japonica rice, known for high-quality brands. Cold-resistant varieties, supportive policies and climate change have all helped raise rice output sharply in recent years. Other commercial crops include beets, flax and sunflowers.

The province is also a major source of timber, especially Korean pine and larch. Most forest grows in the Greater and Lesser Khingan Mountains, where protected animals including the lynx, the red-crowned crane and the Siberian tiger make their home. Herding centres on horses and cattle, and Heilongjiang has more milk cows than any other province-level division in China.

As part of northeast China, long the country's industrial heartland, Heilongjiang concentrates on food, machinery, timber, coal and petroleum. Its position makes it a gateway for trade with Russia. A wave of privatisation in the 1990s closed uncompetitive factories, and Manchuria has since suffered from stagnation. The government responded with the Revitalize Northeast China campaign, which promotes private business as the preferred way to carry out reform and opening up.

Petroleum matters greatly, with the Daqing oilfields a major national source. Gold, graphite and coal are further valuable minerals. The wind resource is also large: the province could in theory support 134 gigawatts of generating capacity.

Most residents are non-religious or follow Chinese folk religions, Taoism among them. Many Manchu people practise Manchu shamanism, and Chinese Buddhism and Tibetan Buddhism are both important. Culturally, Heilongjiang belongs to the fairly uniform culture of northeast China, known in Mandarin as Dongbei.
Heilongjiang leads China in promoting winter sports and the winter-sports industry, for example by pushing bandy as an Olympic sport. Events and leagues connected with the province include:
the 2009 Winter Universiade
the 2018 Bandy World Championship, Division B
the Asia League Ice Hockey
