nanchang-hangkong-university.h: What kind of university this is

blocks.x: Nanchang Hangkong University (南昌航空大学, Nánchāng Hángkōng Dàxué), sometimes translated as Nanchang Aeronautics University and abbreviated NCHU, stands in Nanchang, the city where China's first domestically built aircraft was produced. It began as an engineering school and has grown into a multidisciplinary university. Aeronautics and national defence are its signature strengths, and two supervisors share oversight: the provincial government of Jiangxi and the national Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

The teaching staff numbers more than 1,200 professional teachers. The current student body totals about 21,000 registered students: roughly 19,000 undergraduates, 1,095 postgraduates and over 1,200 vocational students. The university says it puts all-round student development and educational quality first, and it keeps experimenting with teaching methods. The result it points to is a graduate employment rate that is the highest among universities in Jiangxi Province.

For a prospective international student, the main thing to take from this profile is that NCHU is a technical, industry-linked institution. If your interests lie in materials, testing, aerospace manufacturing, electronics or similar engineering fields, it deserves a close look.
The university builds on engineering as its strongest area and on majors with an aviation flavour. Ten of its disciplines are ranked as key disciplines by the province of Jiangxi:
Materials: Materials Processing Engineering, Materials Science, and Material Physics and Chemistry
Measurement and control: Measuring and Testing Technologies and Instruments, Control Theory and Control Engineering, and Optical Engineering
Aerospace and environment: Manufacturing Engineering of Aerospace Vehicle and Environmental Engineering
Computing and the humanities side: Computer Applied Technology, and Ideological and Political Education

Among those ten, Manufacturing Engineering of Aerospace Vehicle holds the status of a top-priority discipline in the province, and Environmental Engineering is recognised as a key discipline for national defence.

NCHU hosts nine key laboratories or research centres at provincial or ministerial level. Four of them serve the national aviation and defence sectors or the education ministry, and five are provincial:
The Ministry of Education's Key Laboratory of Nondestructive Test
A defence-industry laboratory on light alloy fabrication science and technology, answering to the national defence-industry science commission
A key laboratory for aeronautical detection and evaluation, linked to the China aviation industry
A key laboratory for hot working of aerial materials, also linked to the aviation industry
A provincial research centre for materials science and engineering
A provincial key university laboratory for corrosion and protection
A provincial research centre for testing technology and control engineering
A provincial research centre for university ideological and political theory course education
A provincial promotion centre for rapid prototyping productivity

Three provincial key bases support links with business and research. Two are demonstration bases for cooperation among industry, study and research, one in computing and information technology and one in materials science and technology. The third is a sports-culture research base recognised by the State Sport General Administration.

nanchang-hangkong-university.h: Majors that carry national or provincial status

blocks.x: Three majors have been designated national specialty majors. They are Metallic Materials Engineering, Instrumentation and Measurement Technology, and Electronic Information Engineering.

Provincial brand status goes to twelve majors. Some overlap with the national group (metallic materials, instrumentation and measurement, electronic information). The others are material forming and control, environmental engineering, mechanical design and manufacturing, and automation. The list is completed by electronics science and technology, flight vehicle manufacturing, computer science and technology, and two non-engineering subjects, English and Economics.

Flight vehicle manufacturing and optical engineering are also National Defense Key Construction majors. Separately, the province gives specialty-major status to four programmes: environmental engineering, electronics science, computer science and, once more, flight vehicle manufacturing.

There are four provincial teaching teams, in Metallic Materials Engineering, Non-Destructive Testing Technology, the Engineering Training Center and Applied Chemistry. The university also runs two national experimental teaching demonstration centres, one for engineering training and one for college physics, plus eight provincial ones.

International cooperation is part of the picture. NCHU keeps long-term partnerships with institutions in eight countries: Japan, Canada, Ukraine, Britain, Australia, France, Finland and South Korea. Overseas teachers and experts also visit to teach during the year. Ask the international office which partners currently offer exchange places.

Over recent years NCHU has gathered a long list of honours. Within the aviation industry it has been named a unit that contributed significantly to the industry's 40th anniversary, an advanced unit overall, and an advanced unit for its cultural and ideological progress and cohesion project. At the provincial level in Jiangxi it has been recognised as a civilised unit, an advanced grass-roots Party organisation, an advanced unit in afforestation, an advanced unit in campus construction, and an advanced unit for Party building and ideological and political work. It has also received national awards as a "National Model Staff Family" and a "National Advanced Unit in Military Training".

Much of student life depends on the city outside the campus gates: what the weather does, how you get around and what you can see on a day off. The sections that follow describe Nanchang, the home of Nanchang Hangkong University.

Nanchang is an inland city in the southeast of China, roughly 130 km (81 mi) from the Yangtze, to the south. The Gan River runs beside it, and Nanchang occupies the right-hand bank just below the spot where the Jin River flows in. Poyang Lake, where the Gan ends, is some 40 km (25 mi) to the northeast.
The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), and the four seasons are distinct. Here is how the year typically runs.
Winter is short and cool, with occasional frost. It starts fairly sunny and dry, then becomes steadily wetter and cloudier.
Spring begins especially gloomy. Rainfall passes 220 mm (8.7 in) in every month from April through June.

Summer is long and humid. It features some of the highest temperatures among Chinese provincial capitals, and the sunniest time is July and August, when the sun shines nearly 60 percent of the daylight hours.
Autumn is warm to mild, and it has the lowest rainfall of the year.

In figures, January averages 5.9 °C and July 29.6 °C, and across the whole year the mean temperature is 18.5 °C. Total precipitation is about 1,704 mm (67 in) annually. March is the dullest month (27 percent of possible sunshine) and August the brightest (56 percent), producing an annual total of 1,809 sunshine hours. Since 1951 the lowest temperature recorded was −9.7 °C on 29 December 1991, and the highest 40.6 °C on 23 July 1961.

The 2020 Chinese census recorded 6,255,007 residents in Nanchang. Of that total, 5,382,162 live in the urbanised area, which combines 6 urban districts with Nanchang County (itself mostly urbanised). The census counted 37 ethnic groups in the city's administrative divisions, but 99.2% of residents are Han Chinese. The ratio is about 109 men to every 100 women, and people over 60 make up 14.97% of the population.

Nanchang serves as a regional centre for farming in Jiangxi: grain output reached 16.146 million tons in 2000, and rice and oranges are staple products. Industry covers aircraft building, car manufacturing, metallurgy, electro-mechanics, textiles, chemical engineering, traditional Chinese medicine and pharmaceuticals, among others. Ford has a plant in the city that builds the Ford Transit van under the Jiangling Motor joint venture. One claim made for the city is that it ranks 15th among the 20 fastest-growing cities in the world, and it is described as one of the places in China with the most room to grow. That last statement is a general assessment rather than a measured result.

More recent official figures for 2017 show gross regional product (GDP) of 500.319 billion yuan, about US$80.03 billion, which was 9.0% higher than in the previous year. The primary industry contributed added value of 19.213 billion yuan (up 4.0%), the secondary industry 266.61 billion yuan (up 8.4%) and the tertiary sector 214.496 billion yuan (up 10.2%). GDP per head was 81,598 yuan, which equals 12,285 US dollars at the annual average exchange rate. Fiscal revenue for the year reached 78.282 billion yuan, which was 14.3% more than before.

An earlier snapshot is useful for comparison. Back in 2008 the economy was far smaller, at 166 billion yuan (US$24.3 billion) or 36,105 yuan (US$5,285) a head. Trade in goods came to 3.4 billion US dollars of imports and exports, and the financial revenue total was 23 billion yuan.
The city's economic planning is organised around several zones, from national down to provincial level.
National level: an export processing zone, a high-tech industrial development zone (NCHDZ) and an economic and technological development zone, all named for Nanchang
Provincial level: the Jiangxi Shanghai zone and the Yingxiong zone, both economic and technological development areas
Special economic districts: Honggutan New District and Ganjiang New District

The Export Processing Zone sits inside the high-tech zone. The State Council approved it on 8 May 2006, and it passed national acceptance inspection on 7 September 2007. It was planned to cover 1 km2, of which 0.31 km2 had been built. Customs clearance there is simple and convenient, and the zone and the high-tech zone both have special preferential policies.

The Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone (NCHDZ) is the only national-grade high-tech zone in Jiangxi, set up in March 1991. It covers 231 km2 (89 sq mi), of which 32 km2 (12 sq mi) has been completed. It has favourable natural conditions and an industrial base well suited to the electronics industry. Using only 0.4 percent of the city's land area, it generates 25 percent of Nanchang's industrial added value and 50 percent of its industrial benefit and tax.

Nanchang's position makes travel easy. It is praised in a traditional phrase as a city of "three rivers and five lakes". High-speed rail and air connections tie it to three major economic circles: the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the inter-provincial corridors of the western Taiwan Strait region (Haixi). It is one of the country's comprehensive transport hubs and the main integrated hub within Jiangxi.

The city is a key railway centre for southeastern China. Four lines meet here: the Beijing–Kowloon (Jingjiu) Railway, the Shanghai–Kunming railway (once called the Zhejiang–Jiangxi or Zhegan Railway), the Xiangtang–Putian railway and the Nanchang–Jiujiang intercity railway. Nanchang's Bureau of Railways runs much of the rail network in Jiangxi and the neighbouring province of Fujian.
Nanchang railway station and Nanchang West railway station handle most passengers. China Railway High-speed (CRH) trains link the city to Hangzhou, Changsha and Shanghai.

Nanchang Changbei International Airport (KHN) opened in 1996 and is the city's chief international airport. It sits in Lehua Town, 26 kilometres to the north of the CBD area, and it is the only airport in Jiangxi with an international route. Domestic links include Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Haikou, Shanghai and Beijing. A separate military and civilian airfield is located near Liantang in Nanchang County.

Changbei is the biggest airport in Jiangxi. In 2014 it offered up to 10 international destinations and handled 7.25 million passengers, a rise of 6.3%. International traffic topped 280,000 passengers, up nearly 40%, and became an important source of growth. On 6 December 2017 annual throughput passed 10 million, making it the 31st "million-grade" airport in the country. For the whole of 2017 it handled 10.93 million passengers, up 39.0% (a net gain of 3.07 million), with 89,000 flights, up 35.2%, and 52,000 tons of cargo and mail, up 3.3%. Major expansion and upgrading is being carried out to fit with the Beijing–Kowloon high-speed railway and the planned airport complex at Nanchang North Station.

Highways reach the city from several directions. National roads No. 105 (Beijing to Zhuhai), No. 320 (Shanghai to Kunming) and No. 316 (Fuzhou to Lanzhou) cross it, along with National Highway G70, and an orbital highway around the city, G70_01, opened in 2007. Bus and coach services come from three main operators: Chang'an Transport Company Limited, plus the long-distance and Xufang bus stations.

Coaches leaving from the Nanchang Long-distance Bus Station go to places beyond the province (Nanjing, Shenzhen and Hefei, for example), whereas Xufang Bus Station covers destinations within Jiangxi: cities, towns and counties.

Jiangxi's first urban rail network, Nanchang Rail Transit, has run since 26 December 2015, and the city was the 25th in mainland China to get a metro. Planning began in 1999 and building officially started in 2009. The first phase covers Lines 1 and 2, and its length is printed as 50,996 kilometres, which cannot be right for a single city, so check the operator's site for the real figure. Line 1, which is underground, opened at the end of 2015, and the first section of Line 2 began trial operation on 19 August 2017.

The city is on the Gan River and close to the Fu River and to Elephant, Qingshan and Aixi lakes, so waterways matter for trade, shipping and the economy. Nanchang Port is the largest on the Gan River. Travellers can take boats from here to Jinggang Shan and Tengwang Pavilion, and passenger ships also sail to Poyang Lake, Stone Bell Hill, Dagu Hill, the Poyang Lake Bird Protection Area and other attractions.
When you want a break from lectures, these are the main sights in and around the city.
Tengwang Pavilion, a towering pavilion dating from 653 on the Gan River's eastern bank, ranked as one of China's Four Great Towers.
Poyang Lake, the biggest freshwater lake in China, also called the "Migrator Birds Paradise".
The Star of Nanchang in Honggutan District, which was the tallest Ferris wheel in the world from 2006 to 2008.
Qiushui Square, opened on 28 January 2004, home to Asia's largest music fountain group with music.
Jiangxi Provincial Museum, which includes the Bada Shanren Exhibition Hall.
People's Park, the largest green space in the downtown area.

Bayi Square and Memorial, in the middle of the city, commemorating the birth of the People's Liberation Army in the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 (Ba Yi means "eight-one" in Mandarin). The uprising is linked to the story that led to the People's Republic of China in 1949.
Bada Shanren Memorial Hall, a large artistic museum complex with sculpture and a general art museum.

Nanchang is a significant centre of learning. The Nature Index, which follows research output, lists it among the world's 100 leading cities for science. The list below covers institutions with full-time bachelor programmes; those without are left out.
General and teacher-training universities: Nanchang University (南昌大学) and Jiangxi Normal University (江西师范大学)
Business and finance: Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics (江西财经大学)

Engineering and technology: Nanchang Hangkong University (南昌航空大学, this one), East China Jiaotong University (华东交通大学), Nanchang Institute of Technology (南昌工程学院) and the Nanchang campus of East China University of Technology (东华理工大学)
Agriculture: Jiangxi Agricultural University (江西农业大学)
Medicine: Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医药大学), also listed under an older name as Jiangxi Institute of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江西中医学院)
Other: Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University (江西科技师范学院) and Jiangxi Manufacturing and Vocational College (江西制造职业技术学院)

Secondary schools mentioned include Nanchang Foreign Language School (南昌市外国语学校) and the high school attached to Jiangxi University of Technology (江西科技学院附属中学), and the city has Nanchang International School (南昌国际学校) as an international school. Families moving with a student may find that useful.
The province outside the campus gates affects a student's life almost as much as the university itself does. The sections below describe Jiangxi.

nanchang-hangkong-university.h: A corridor between north and south

blocks.x: Jiangxi is built around the valley of the Gan River, which for centuries was the main north-south transport route of southern China. The valley is one of the few easy passages through the rough mountains of the southeast. Merchants and messages moved along it between the north (the North China Plain and the Yangtze valley) and what is now Guangdong in the south. That gave Jiangxi great strategic importance across much of Chinese history.

nanchang-hangkong-university.h: Early states and the Han commandery

blocks.x: During the Shang period (16th to 11th centuries BC) the area was beyond the reach of early Chinese civilisation, and it was probably home to peoples known together as the Baiyue. In the Spring and Autumn period, northern Jiangxi formed the western edge of the state of Wu. After the state of Yue, centred in northern Zhejiang, conquered Wu in 473 BC, northern Jiangxi passed to Chu, a state centred on what is now Hubei, while Yue may have kept some influence in the south. Chu subdued Yue in 333 BC. When Qin conquered Chu in 223 BC, most of Jiangxi was recorded as falling under Jiujiang Commandery, based at Shouchun (壽春), but that administration was ineffective and ended soon after Qin collapsed.

The early Han dynasty set up Yuzhang Commandery (豫章) in Jiangxi, possibly before Xiang Yu died in 202 BC, and it was the first commandery created there by a Chinese dynasty. It took its name from the Yuzhang River, the original name of the Gan River, and the "Gan" abbreviation for the province comes from that river. In 201 BC eight counties were added to the seven inherited from Qin, with three more established later. For most of the Han era its eighteen counties took in the greater part of today's province. Several county seats, such as Nanchang, Gan, Yudu and Luling, were on the sites of present-day cities, although other counties were moved or abolished over the centuries.

Emperor Wu of the Han assigned Yuzhang Commandery to Yangzhou Province, in line with a wider move to create provinces (zhou) across China. In 291 AD, under the Western Jin, Jiangxi became a zhou of its own called Jiangzhou (江州). The Southern and Northern Dynasties era left Jiangxi under the southern courts, and the count of zhou crept up.

Under the Sui, Jiangxi was divided into seven commanderies and twenty-four counties. The Tang added one more commandery and fourteen counties, and then abolished commanderies, turning them into zhou, which are called prefectures from this point on in English.

The Tang also introduced circuits as the top administrative level. Jiangxi first lay inside the Jiangnan Circuit, meaning the circuit south of the Yangtze. That circuit was divided into a western and an eastern half in 733, and Jiangxi fell in the western one, the Jiangnanxi Circuit. The modern name Jiangxi comes from this.

After the Tang collapsed in 907, China entered an age of rival states, the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. Jiangxi was first part of Wu (吳) and then of Southern Tang (南唐), both based in modern Nanjing, downstream on the Yangtze. After the ten kingdoms, the Jiangnanxi Circuit was set up again with nine prefectures and four army districts, sixty-eight districts in total. It was later divided into thirteen circuits, and Jiangxi Province was created for the first time, covering most of present-day Guangdong too. By then Jiangxi had more or less taken on its modern borders.

When the Qing regime fell, Jiangxi became one of the earliest Communist bases, and many peasants were recruited to the growing revolution. The Nanchang Uprising broke out on 1 August 1927, in the middle of the Chinese Civil War. Communist leaders afterwards sheltered in the hills of southern and western Jiangxi, away from the Kuomintang's efforts to wipe them out. In 1931 the government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was founded in Ruijin, sometimes called the "Former Red Capital" or simply the "Red Capital". Surrounded by Nationalist forces in 1935, the Communists broke out and began the Long March towards Yan'an.

The National Government mounted five military campaigns against the Jiangxi Soviet area from 1930 to 1934. The violent fighting between the two parties, including purges inside the Red Army and the cleansing of government afterwards, killed or drove away so many people that Jiangxi's population fell by 40%, to 13.8 million in 1936.

When the Yuehan Railway opened in Hunan in 1936, Jiangxi lost its central role in north-south travel. The east-west Zhegan Railway opened in 1937 and altered the traffic pattern a great deal, and Jiujiang Port began to lose its importance.

During the Second World War, after the Doolittle Raid, most of the American B-25 crews who came down in China reached safety with local help in Jiangxi. The locals who helped paid dearly: the Imperial Japanese Army launched the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign to frighten Chinese people out of helping downed airmen, and at least 10,000 civilians in Jiangxi died while searching for Doolittle's men.

The province came fully under Communist Party control when the People's Republic was founded in 1949. The Republican provincial government evacuated to Taichung in Taiwan Province and dissolved itself that same year.

During the Third Front campaign, Jiangxi was a major target for new industrial capacity. Rice is the dominant crop, with cotton and rapeseed as common cash crops, and the province leads China in kumquats, especially in Suichuan County.

Mining is a major part of the economy. No other province has more copper, tungsten, gold, silver, uranium or thorium in the ground, and it also leads for tantalum, niobium and more. Dexing is known for copper and Dayu County for tungsten.

The province borders some of China's richest areas (Guangdong, Zhejiang and Fujian), and they are sometimes blamed for drawing talent and capital away. Jiangxi has the lowest wages in the country and the third-lowest property prices. Nominal GDP for 2016 stood at CNY 1.84 trillion (US$276.48 billion), equal to CNY 40,400 (US$6,082) per person. For a student, low living costs are a practical plus, though as the figures here come from 2016, treat them as a general indication only.
Nanchang Hangkong University lists 34 programs for international students on this site: 10 bachelor, 24 master's programs.

By language of instruction: 22 taught in Chinese, 12 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.

34 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (12):
Aeronautical Engineering
Aerospace Manufacturing Engineering
Civil Engineering
Computer Science and Technology
Control Theory and Control Engineering
Electronics and Communication Engineering
Environmental Science and Engineering (Engineering)
Management Science and Engineering
Management Science and Engineering (Engineering)
Materials Science and Engineering
Optical Engineering
Software Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanchang-hangkong-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanchang Hangkong University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanchang, register at Nanchang Hangkong University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Nanchang University (NCU, 南昌大学) is a public university in Nanchang, the capital of Jiangxi province. It belongs to the provincial system, and the Jiangxi Provincial People's Government and China's Ministry of Education sponsor it together, an arrangement that gives it backing from both local and national authorities. NCU is included in Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction programme, two national schemes that single out priority universities.

nanchang-university.h: From medical school to comprehensive university

blocks.x: Several earlier institutions feed into NCU's history, and it helps to see them as a chain of founding dates:
1921: Jiangxi Public Medical School.
1937: National Chung-Cheng Medical College.
1940: National Chung-Cheng University.
1958: Jiangxi University and Jiangxi Polytechnic College, both founded in the same year.

The big turning point came in 1993, when Jiangxi University and Jiangxi Polytechnic University (the two 1958 institutions) merged and took the new name Nanchang University. The Ministry of Education chose NCU for Project 211 in 1997, and it has stayed among mainland China's top 100 national key universities ever since. In 2004 the Jiangxi provincial government and the Ministry of Education signed an agreement to develop the university jointly. In 2005 Jiangxi Medical College was folded into NCU as its Faculty of Medicine, though it kept its own name.

Earlier mergers left NCU with four campuses. The main one is Qianhu Campus, within Nanchang, which covers 300 hectares. All undergraduates live and study there, as do most postgraduates, most research institutes and laboratories, and most faculty and staff. Much of the research also happens on the Qingshanhu Campus.

The undergraduate catalogue lists more than 82 programmes, grouped under 12 of China's academic disciplines. The arts, management, medicine, agriculture, engineering and science are among them, as are history, literature, education, law, economics and philosophy. Over 35,000 full-time students are enrolled on these courses.

Postgraduate study sits with the Graduate School, which handles over 20 doctoral-level programmes (PhD and MD) as well as 175 master's programmes for a student body approaching 15,000. Eight fields have post-doctoral status approved by the Ministry of Education. Four are engineering related (materials, food, mechanical, and chemical engineering and technology), and the rest are clinical medicine, biology, environmental science and engineering, and management science and engineering. Joint programmes with overseas partners also exist, and the university's website lists the current exchange arrangements.
NCU consists of the Graduate School plus five major faculties. The structure below reflects how the university presents itself.
The Faculty of Humanities includes Art and Design, Foreign Languages, Journalism and Communication, and a general School of Humanities.
The Faculty of Social Sciences takes in Law, Marxism, Tourism Studies, Sports and Physical Education, Management, Economics and Management, and Public Policy and Management, each as its own school.

Science and Technology (Division I) groups Software, Information Science and Technology, Mechanical Engineering, Material Science and Technology and a School of Sciences that covers mathematics, chemistry, physics and related subjects.
Science and Technology (Division II) groups Life Sciences, Food Science and Technology, Civil Engineering and Architecture, and a school that joins environmental science with chemical engineering.
Jiangxi Medical College, which is also known inside the university as the Faculty of Medicine.
The medical side has several schools of its own:
School of Basic Medical Sciences
School of Public Health
School of Pharmacy
School of Nursing
School of Dentistry, linked with Jiangxi Dental Hospital
School of Ophthalmology and Optometry
The First, Second, Third and Fourth Clinical Medical Schools, each tied to the corresponding affiliated hospital of Nanchang University
A joint programme in biomedical sciences offered together with Queen Mary University of London and Jiangxi Medical College
The Center for Laboratory Animal Science

As a public research university, NCU does most of its research on the Qianhu and Qingshanhu campuses. Money arrives from national and provincial sources: the Natural Science Foundation and the Social Science Fund of China, the education and science ministries, and Jiangxi's own education and science departments. On that basis, over 50 key laboratories and research centres at national or provincial level are in operation, alongside 60 basic training centres and professional labs. Jiangxi Medical College adds a strong research focus of its own and works closely with 13 highly ranked affiliated hospitals around the province, which act as the main teaching hospitals for its students.
The list below shows which subjects have received national recognition.
World-class discipline, under the Ministry of Education's Double First Class University Plan: Material Science and Technology.
National key disciplines: Food Science, and Materials Physics and Chemistry.
National key discipline in incubation: Materials Process Engineering.
Nine clinical specialties are nationally key: neurology, cardiology, burn surgery, pain medicine, vascular surgery, emergency medicine, critical care, respiratory medicine and gastroenterology.

In the Essential Science Indicators (ESI), six areas reach the world top 1%: pharmacology and toxicology, materials science, engineering, clinical medicine, chemistry, and agricultural science including food science.
Representative centres of excellence include:
A branch of the State Key Laboratory for food science and technology is hosted at NCU.
Three national engineering research centres focus respectively on silicon-based LEDs, on bioengineered drugs and related technologies, and on efficient biotransformation of agricultural products.
A Ministry of Education key laboratory studies the environment and resource use of Poyang Lake.

Other research units are the Institute for Advanced Study, the Institute of Life Science, the Institute of Translational Medicine, the Human Aging Research Institute and the Institute of Space Science and Technology.
Rankings differ by method, so it is wise to look at several. The figures below are the ones available for NCU.

Worldwide: 201 to 300 in the 2024 Academic Ranking of World Universities (the Shanghai Ranking); 451st in the 2025 World University Rankings of the Center for World University Rankings (CWUR); and 537th in the 2025 U.S. News and World Report Best Global University Ranking.
Mainland China: the university normally falls within the top 100 of nearly 3,000 institutions in most domestic and international tables.
Jiangxi Province: first in every regional ranking.

The teaching staff number 4,624, including 1,556 associate and full professors. Many have been honoured for teaching or research by education, health and science ministries or by the provincial government. The breakdown is long, but it shows the calibre of the faculty:
Academy membership: five academicians belong to the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering, and one is a foreign academician.
Young-scholar schemes: four hold the Distinguished Young Scholars award of the National Natural Science Fund, and five are Yangtze Scholars.
State Council expertise: one staff member sits on the Discipline Evaluation Group of the Academic Degrees Committee.
Experts: five are National Young and Middle-aged Experts with Outstanding Contributions, and the Ministry of Health picked one as an outstanding expert.
Teaching and medical honours: one is a National Prominent Teacher, and two have won the Bethune Award.

Talent projects: five belong to the first or second level of the National Hundred, Thousand and Ten Thousand Talents Project, three are National Thousand Talents recipients, ten are New Century Excellent Talents and four are exclusively employed Jinggang Scholars.
Allowances: 93 receive special payments from the State Council or the provincial government.

Across its library network, NCU counts 2.65 million printed books, 1,338 periodicals (foreign-language titles included) and more than 1 million e-books. The special collections include 61,400 rare books, and 93,000 volumes are in foreign languages. A total of 34 subscribed online libraries and databases are available, such as SCI, EI, INSPEC, ISTP, AIP/APS, ELSEVIER and PQDD. Add multimedia CDs, interactive videos and teaching materials, and users have plenty of choice for study and research.

To give students practical experience, there are nine big multi-purpose training labs. Their topics run from linguistics and mechanics to networking, computing, electronics, physics, chemistry, biology and engineering. Beyond these, the university provides 216 internship bases and 47 professional research labs.

The University Science Park hosts more than 100 start-ups, and in 2004 this incubator earned recognition as a National University Science Park. NCU has more recently launched a School of Innovation and Entrepreneurship, which gives students and professors training and workshops on setting up companies and on management and operations skills.
ZTE Software Technology (Nanchang) Co., Ltd. began in 2005 as a partnership of NCU and ZTE, one of the country's top suppliers of communication equipment.

Lattice Power (Jiangxi) Co., Ltd., founded in 2006, is a world-leading producer of silicon-based LED products. It grew out of the work of Prof. Fengyi Jiang's research team, who won a First Class State Technological Invention Award in 2015.

Kuangda Biotechnology (Nanchang) Co., Ltd., founded in 2009, is a world-leading producer of vegetable drinks fermented with lactic acid bacteria. It grew from the work of two professors, Mingyong Xie and Tao Xiong, who were given a Second Class State Science and Technology Progress Award in 2016.

NCU puts a high value on international work, with regular exchanges involving over 30 universities and institutions in more than 20 countries. It has opened three Confucius Institutes abroad. Poitiers in France came first: it was France's first and Europe's second. The other two are in Spain, with Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha, and in Indonesia, with Hasanuddin University.

A long relationship with the University of Abertay Dundee in the United Kingdom brings together master's education: every year a cohort of School of Software undergraduates is admitted to Abertay to study for a computer science master's. Another milestone came in summer 2012, when NCU and Queen Mary University of London decided to create the joint biomedical sciences programme. Other partners are found in Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Australia, New Zealand, the USA, Germany, Ireland and elsewhere.

Two offices matter most if you are coming from abroad. The International Education Center, also called the International Exchange College, is the main administrative body for international students. Its remit covers admissions, housing, Chinese-language testing through the HSK, tracking of academic progress and exams, and checking the quality of the training. The separate International Affairs Department helps local students and staff with international activities, oversees the international students managed by the International Exchange College, and deals with approaches from foreign institutions that wish to set up joint academic programmes, schools, departments or centres.

A student's daily experience depends a great deal on the surrounding city: its weather, its transport and its attractions. The sections that follow introduce Nanchang, the home of Nanchang University.

The city is inland, in the south-east of China, about 130 km (81 mi) from the Yangtze, to its south. Its position is on the Gan River's right-hand bank, just after the Jin River joins, and some 40 km (25 mi) south-west of where the Gan empties into Poyang Lake.
Four clearly separate seasons shape the year, under a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa).
Winter is brief and cool, with now and then a frost. It opens fairly sunny and dry but steadily turns wetter and cloudier.
Spring is particularly gloomy, and each month from April to June sees over 220 mm (8.7 in) of rain.
Summer lasts long and feels humid, and temperatures rank near the top among Chinese provincial capitals. The sunniest time is July and August, when the sun shines nearly 60 percent of the time.
Autumn is warm to mild and has the lowest rainfall of the year.

Average daily temperature climbs from 5.9 °C (42.6 °F) in the coldest month, January, to 29.6 °C (85.3 °F) in July, with a yearly average of 18.5 °C (65.3 °F). Around 1,704 mm (67 in) of precipitation falls annually. March has the lowest possible-sunshine share, 27 percent, and August the highest, 56 percent, for 1,809 hours of sunshine a year. Records since 1951 show a low of -9.7 °C (15 °F) on 29 December 1991 and a high of 40.6 °C (105 °F) on 23 July 1961. In practice, expect hot, sticky summers and damp, grey stretches in spring.

The 2020 census counted 6,255,007 residents. Of these, 5,382,162 live in the built-up urban area, made up of 6 urban districts and Nanchang County, which is largely urbanised. The prefecture is home to 37 ethnic groups, although 99.2% of people are Han Chinese. There are about 109 men for every 100 women, and 14.97% of the population is aged over 60.

Nanchang is a regional centre for farm production in Jiangxi, with rice and oranges as staples, and it produced a grain harvest of 16.146 million tons in 2000. Industry is varied: aircraft and automobile manufacturing, metallurgy, electro-mechanics, textiles, chemical engineering, traditional Chinese medicine and pharmaceuticals all play a part. Ford has a plant in the city assembling the Ford Transit van through the Jiangling Motor joint venture. Nanchang is often described as ranking 15th among the 20 fastest-growing cities in the world and as one of the cities with the greatest development potential in China, a claim worth treating as a general indication rather than a precise measure.

The city's 2017 gross regional product reached 500.319 billion yuan (US$80.03 billion), a 9.0% increase over 2016. The primary sector added 19.213 billion yuan (up 4.0%) and the secondary sector 266.61 billion yuan (up 8.4%), while the tertiary sector, listed as 'the three industries', added 214.496 billion yuan (up 10.2%). GDP per person was 81,598 yuan, which converts to 12,285 US dollars at the average exchange rate for the year. Total fiscal revenue was 78.282 billion yuan, a rise of 14.3%.

For comparison, 2008 output was 166 billion yuan (US$24.3 billion), equal to 36,105 yuan (US$5,285) per head. Trade in imports and exports reached 3.4 billion US dollars, and financial revenue stood at 23 billion yuan.
Nanchang has several zones for business, and they fall into three levels.
National-level zones: the Nanchang Export Processing Zone, the Nanchang National High-tech Industrial Development Zone and the Nanchang Economic and Technological Development Zone.
Provincial-level zones: two economic and technological development zones, Jiangxi Shanghai and Nanchang Yingxiong.
Special economic districts: Honggutan New District and GanJiang New District.

The Nanchang National Export Processing Zone lies inside the Nanchang Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone. The State Council approved it on 8 May 2006, and it passed its national acceptance inspection on 7 September 2007. It has a planned area of 1 km2, of which 0.31 km2 is built, and it offers simple, convenient customs clearance and special preferential policies, shared with the hi-tech zone (NCHDZ).

NCHDZ is the only national-grade high-tech zone in Jiangxi and was set up in March 1991. It covers 231 km2 (89 sq mi), of which 32 km2 (12 sq mi) is finished. Its natural conditions and industrial base suit the electronics industry. Using just 0.4 percent of the city's land, the zone produces 25 percent of the industrial added value and 50 percent of the industrial profit and tax for Nanchang.

Nanchang's location and transport links are its advantages. It is often praised with a poetic phrase that refers to 'three rivers and five lakes', and it uses high-speed rail and air hubs to connect three major economic circles: the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the inter-provincial corridors of the Haixi area. It is one of China's comprehensive transport hubs and an important integrated hub for Jiangxi.

Nanchang is a key rail hub for south-eastern China. Four lines meet here: the Beijing-Kowloon (Jingjiu) Railway, the Shanghai-Kunming railway (formerly the Zhejiang-Jiangxi or Zhegan Railway), the Xiangtang-Putian railway and the Nanchang-Jiujiang intercity railway. The Nanchang Bureau of Railways runs much of the network in Jiangxi and neighbouring Fujian. The city's main passenger stations are Nanchang railway station and Nanchang West railway station, and CRH (China Railway High-speed) services link Nanchang with Hangzhou, Changsha and Shanghai.

The main international airport, Changbei (KHN), was built in 1996 in Lehua Town, 26 kilometres north of the central business district area. It is Jiangxi's largest airport and its only one with an international route, and flights go to mainland cities including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Haikou. A military and civilian airport also exists near Liantang in Nanchang County.

By 2014 the airport served up to 10 international destinations and handled 7.25 million passengers, up 6.3%. International traffic topped 280,000 passengers, a rise of almost 40%, and is a key growth driver. On 6 December 2017 annual throughput passed 10 million, making it China's 31st million-passenger airport. For the whole of 2017 the airport handled 10.93 million passengers (up 39.0% on the year, a net gain of 3.07 million), about 89,000 flight movements (up 35.2%) and 52,000 tons of cargo and mail (up 3.3%). Large-scale expansion is under way to fit in with the Beijing-Kowloon high-speed railway and the planned Nanchang North Station airport transport hub.

Several national roads cross Nanchang: No. 105 runs between Beijing and Zhuhai, No. 320 between Shanghai and Kunming, and No. 316 between Fuzhou and Lanzhou. The G70 national expressway also passes through, and a ring expressway around the city, G70_01, has been open since 2007. Bus services are operated mainly by Chang'an Transport Company Limited, plus the two stations named below. The Long-distance Bus Station covers routes outside Jiangxi, for example to Nanjing, Shenzhen and Hefei, while the Xufang Bus Station serves cities, towns and counties inside the province.

Nanchang Rail Transit, the first urban rail system in Jiangxi, has run since 26 December 2015, making Nanchang the 25th city on the mainland with a metro. Planning began in 1999 and the project officially started in 2009. Line 1, mostly underground, opened at the end of 2015, and the first section of Line 2 began trial operation on 19 August 2017. The combined length of the first phases of both lines is sometimes quoted as 50,996 kilometres, which is clearly a typographical slip, so check the transit operator's website for the actual figure.

Water is woven through the city: the Gan and Fu rivers and Elephant, Qingshan and Aixi lakes are all nearby, so shipping, trade and the wider economy depend on waterways. Nanchang Port, the biggest on the Gan, offers boat trips to Jinggang Shan and Tengwang Pavilion. Some passenger ships also go to Poyang Lake, Stone Bell Hill, Dagu Hill, the bird reserve at Poyang Lake and other sights.
Tengwang Pavilion, which rises high above the Gan River's eastern shore, goes back to 653 and counts as one of the Four Great Towers of China.
Poyang Lake, China's largest freshwater lake, is nicknamed the 'Migrator Birds Paradise'.
The Star of Nanchang in Honggutan District was the tallest Ferris wheel in the world from 2006 to 2008.
Qiushui Square, opened on 28 January 2004, has the biggest music fountain group in Asia.
The Jiangxi Provincial Museum and the Bada Shanren Exhibition Hall.
People's Park, the largest park in the downtown area.

Bayi Square and Memorial stands at the heart of Nanchang. It honours the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 (Ba Yi in Mandarin), which marked the start of the People's Liberation Army and ultimately led to the People's Republic of China being founded in 1949.
Bada Shanren Memorial Hall is a large art complex, combining sculpture with a general art museum.
These colleges and universities are in the city (institutions without full-time bachelor's programmes are not listed):
Nanchang University itself (南昌大学)

Families with younger children will find a few options too: Nanchang Foreign Language School (南昌市外国语学校), a high school attached to Jiangxi University of Technology (江西科技学院附属中学), and Nanchang International School (南昌国际学校).

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanchang-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanchang University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.

Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.

Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanchang, register at Nanchang University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

NAU, or Nanjing Agricultural University (南京农业大学), is a public university based in Nanjing, which is Jiangsu Province's capital city. It reports to the Ministry of Education, which sponsors it jointly with the Jiangsu Provincial Government, and it holds both Project 211 and Double First-Class Construction status.

NAU's story starts in 1902 with the Agriculture Section of Sanjiang Teacher's College (三江师范学堂), a teacher-training school. The direct predecessors were two agricultural colleges, one in the private Jinling University and one in the National Central University. Jinling University opened a four-year agricultural department in 1914, China's first four-year institution of higher agricultural education, and in 1930 that department grew into the College of Agriculture of Jinling University.

After the People's Republic was founded in 1949, the private Jinling University's agriculture college turned into a public one under the same university name, and the National Central University's college became part of the National University of Nanjing. Its first chairman was Jin Shanbao, an expert in wheat genetic breeding. During the 1960s the State Council named the college one of the country's two key agricultural colleges and universities.

In January 1972 the school moved to Yangzhou and combined with Jiangsu Agricultural College of northern Jiangsu to form a single Jiangsu Agricultural College. Classes came back to the original site in February 1979, when the State Council approved reopening Nanjing Agricultural College, which was placed under the Ministry of Agriculture among the national key universities.

The Ministry of Education approved a new name in July 1984, Nanjing Agricultural University. In December 1998 NAU formally joined the national "Project 211" group of key universities, and in February 2000 it moved from the Ministry of Agriculture to direct management by the Ministry of Education.
The university groups its colleges into faculties.
Plant Science covers the College of Agriculture, the College of Plant Protection and the College of Horticulture.
Animal Science covers the College of Veterinary Medicine, the College of Animal Science & Technology, the College of Prataculture and the College of Aquaculture.
Biology and Environment includes the College of Life Sciences and the College of Resources & Environmental Sciences.
Food and Engineering covers the College of Engineering, the College of Food Science & Technology and the College of Information Science & Technology.

Social Science brings together the College of Economics & Management, the College of Public Administration, the College of Humanities & Social Sciences, the College of Finance and the College of Rural Development.
General education is delivered by the College of Foreign Studies, the Department of General Education on Political Science and the Department of Physical Education.
The flagship laboratory is the State Key Laboratory for Crop Genetics and Germplasm Innovation (作物遗传与种质创新国家重点实验室), which is a national-level facility. Other facilities, listed by focus, are:
Soybean Improvement
Meat Quality and Safety Control
Information Agriculture
Crop Genetics & Germplasm Enhancement
National Key Engineering Center for Organic-based Fertilizers
NAU also publishes academic journals:
Horticulture Research
Chinese Agricultural Education
Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Medicine
Journal of Nanjing Agricultural University
Journal of Nanjing Agricultural University (Social Science)
Institution of Chinese Agricultural Civilization

nanjing-agricultural-university.h: Why the history matters for you

blocks.x: The timeline above shows how long NAU has specialised in agriculture, and how often its administrative home has changed: a teacher's college section in 1902, two separate agricultural colleges, a merger in Yangzhou in 1972, a return to Nanjing in 1979, and university status in 1984. Since 2000 it has been run directly by the Ministry of Education and co-sponsored with the Jiangsu Provincial Government.

nanjing-agricultural-university.h: The city of Nanjing for agricultural students

blocks.x: Because NAU is an agricultural university, the land, water and farming of the Nanjing region matter more here than at most universities. The rest of this profile goes through the city with that in mind, starting with the countryside and ending with weather and transport.

Nanjing is a significant base for grain and commercial agriculture in China. The leading cash crops are rice, cotton, tea, bamboo, hemp, silkworm cocoons, fruit and medicinal herbs, and because the water on both sides of the Yangtze is so fertile, it is also an important base for freshwater fisheries.
Nanjing's combined agricultural output in 2019, counting forestry, animal husbandry and fishery, was valued at 47.250 billion yuan, 4.8% more than in 2018. The breakdown was:
farming proper: 24.077 billion yuan
fishery: 15.389 billion yuan
services supporting the four sectors: 3.333 billion yuan
animal husbandry: 2.435 billion yuan
forestry: 2.017 billion yuan

Two broad kinds of soil exist in the Nanjing area. The natural ("zonal") soils are yellow-brown in the north and centre of the city, and red in the south along the Anhui border. The soils shaped by human farming are mostly paddy soil, together with some yellow Gang soil and soil from vegetable gardens. Their distribution follows the lie of the land and the way water moves across it, and they sort into three kinds of terrain: low mountains and hills, hills, and flat plain. A second national soil survey, carried out between 1980 and 1987, identified 7 soil types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species in Nanjing, over a total of 416,300 hectares.

Few Chinese regions have as many plants as Nanjing. Its vegetation is complex. Natural cover divides into 7 types: coniferous forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, forest mixing deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved trees, bamboo, shrubland, grassland and aquatic vegetation. Cultivated vegetation takes in field and vegetable crops, orchards, economic forests and green belts. Seven species are rare and endangered plants under national key protection: Pterocarpus sinensis, Ming Codonopsis, Chinese Allium chinense and Sphaerocarpus sinensis are examples.

The animal record is just as detailed. There are 795 insect species in 125 families and 11 orders, and 99 fish species in 22 families and 12 orders. Land vertebrates in the wild total 327 species in 29 orders and 90 families, including 243 bird species (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 mammal species (8 orders, 22 families). Nine species receive national first-level protection, including the White Shoulder Eagle and the Oriental White Crane. Another 65 are protected at the second level, for example the little swan, the Chinese tiger, the swallowtail and the finless porpoise. Jiangsu Province lists 125 key protected animals, and 35 species are endangered.

Nanjing has plenty of mineral resources. Among 49 types discovered are lead, zinc, iron, copper, strontium, ferrosulfide, gypsum, clay, limestone and dolomite, and 31 of them have proven reserves. The minerals gather in 4 metallogenic belts, the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur polymetallic belt, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt. Iron and sulfur reserves account for 40 percent of those held in all of Jiangsu, and strontium reserves are the largest in East Asia and Southeast Asia. In total, over 40 kinds of minerals are found.

Covering 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 sq mi), Nanjing is large. The city lies in the heart of the lower Yangtze drainage area, inside the Yangtze River Delta, one of the biggest economic zones in China. The Yangtze runs past its west and then its north, and the Ningzheng Ridge encloses the north, east and south. To other cities: Shanghai is 270 kilometres (170 mi) to the east-southeast, Beijing 900 kilometres (560 mi) to the north-northwest, Luoyang 650 kilometres (400 mi) to the northwest and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) to the west-southwest.

Flowing from Jiujiang in Jiangxi through Anhui and Jiangsu, the Yangtze reaches the East China Sea. The lower basin has a northern part, the Huai River basin, and a southern part, the Zhe River basin, and the Grand Canal links them east of Nanjing. Locals call the surrounding area the Xiajiang (下江, Downstream River) region: Jianghuai culture dominates in the north and Jiangzhe in the south. It is also well known as Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, South of the Yangtze).

Next to Nanjing are Yangzhou (northeast), Zhenjiang (east) and Changzhou (southeast). Its western boundary is Anhui, where it touches five prefecture-level cities. Xuancheng is to the southwest, Ma'anshan, Chaohu and Wuhu are to the west, and Chuzhou lies to the northwest.

The humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) is influenced by the East Asian monsoon. Seasons are distinct and damp all year; summers are very hot and muggy, winters cold and damp, with spring and autumn of reasonable length. Nanjing is traditionally counted with Chongqing and Wuhan as one of the Yangtze's "Three Furnaces" because summer heat never lets up. Yet between mid-June and the end of July comes the plum blossom blooming season and the meiyu, East Asia's rainy season (literally "plum rain"), with gentle rain and dampness. Winter winds are from the northeast.

Even so, Nanjing is cold for its latitude. At 32°04'N it has winters like London's (51°30'N) or colder, with a January 2 °C colder than London's, and its winter is 7 °C colder than that of Savannah, Georgia, which has the same humid subtropical climate on the US East Coast.

The average for January is 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the record low for a day was -14.0 °C (6.8 °F) on 6 January 1955. Summer's prevailing wind is from the southeast; July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F) and the record high for a day was 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on 13 July 1934. Days with precipitation above 0.1 mm number 112.9 in a typical year, and in 1957 there were as many as 160. Yearly precipitation averages 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in).

Late summer and early autumn can bring typhoons, though they are uncommon. The year's mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F), and the 24-hour monthly average lies between 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), the January figure, and the July figure of 28.4 °C (83.1 °F). Since 1951 the extremes have been -14.0 °C (7 °F) on 6 January 1955 and 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959. Precipitation arrives on 113 days of the year on average, with 1,144 millimetres (45 in) of rain. Bright sunshine totals 1,932.4 hours a year, with monthly possible sunshine at 37 percent in June and 48 percent in both August and October.

In early December 2013 smog covered a stretch of central and eastern China some 1,200 kilometers (750 mi) long, beginning on 2 December and over Zhejiang, Shanghai, Anhui, Jiangsu, Shandong, Hebei and Tianjin. With little cold air moving, slow-moving air masses laden with industrial emissions let pollutants build into a thick smog layer. Central and southern Jiangsu were heavily affected, Nanjing and its surroundings most of all: the AQI was at "severely polluted" level for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials blamed calm winds, car exhaust under low air pressure, and coal-fired district heating in north China, while the prevailing winds drove low-lying air masses with factory emissions, mostly SO2, towards the east coast.

Nanjing sits on the lower Yangtze, which crosses the city diagonally from southwest to northeast over about 93 kilometers, more than 300 kilometers from the sea. The Qinhuai River, known as the mother river of Nanjing, flows from south to north through the main urban area into the Yangtze. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake lie in the city centre like two pearls, open to the public, and water covers about 11% of the area. Almost all the waterways belong to the Yangtze system; the exception is the group of rivers entering Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake in the north of Liuhe District, part of the Huai River system. The Yangtze system comprises the Qinhuai River system south of the river, the Chuhe River system to the north, a riverside system of small tributaries on both banks, the West Taihu Lake system to the east of Gaochun, and a system of two lakes, Gucheng and Shijiu. Groundwater is plentiful and of excellent quality, and Pukou Pearl Spring is especially renowned, while Jiangning Tangshan and Pukou Tangquan are long-established hot spring areas.

Purple Mountain, covered in deciduous and coniferous forest, preserves several historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel is being built on the Yangtze so that vessels of 50,000 DWT from the East China Sea can reach Nanjing.

No other inland port in China is as large as the Port of Nanjing, which handled 191,970,000 t of cargo in 2012. The port area stretches 98 kilometers (61 mi) with 64 berths, 16 of them for ships above 10,000 tonnes. It is the biggest container port on the Yangtze too: the Longtan Containers Port Area, with a one-million-container capacity, opened in March 2004 and reinforced its leading regional position. In 2010 it had six public ports and three industrial ports. A 12.5-meter-deep channel lets 50,000-ton ocean ships come straight to the port, and ships of 100,000 tons or more can arrive after reducing their load during the Yangtze's high tide. CSC Jinling runs a large shipyard.

nanjing-agricultural-university.h: Bridges and tunnels over the Yangtze

blocks.x: In the 1960s the first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge was finished, and at that time it was the only bridge over the lower Yangtze in eastern China. It stood for national pride and was an important symbol of modern China: Chinese engineers designed and built it, after surveys by other nations failed and after the country had relied on Soviet expertise and then turned it down. It was begun in 1960 and opened in 1968. The two tiers carry road and rail, 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) long on the upper deck, with about 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) over the water. Since then the city has added four more bridges and four tunnels.

The crossings are a mix of bridges and tunnels. Reading downstream, the bridges are Dashengguan (the Third Bridge), the Fifth Bridge, the First Bridge, Baguazhou and Qixiashan. The tunnels are the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道) and the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel.
The six bridges, by opening year, are:
1968: Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (First Nanjing Yangtze Bridge), longest span 160 m
1997: Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge (Second), longest span 628 m
2005: Nanjing Dashengguan Yangtze River Bridge (Third), longest span 648 m
2012: Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge (Fourth), longest span 1,418m
2020: Nanjing Jiangxinzhou Yangtze River Bridge (Fifth), longest span 600 m
2023: Nanjing Xianxin Yangtze River Bridge, longest span 1,760 m

The 2010 census gave Nanjing a population of 8.005 million, and the OECD put the encompassing metropolitan area at 11.7 million. Official statistics estimated 8.11 million for 2011, of whom 6.47 million lived in the urban area. Births stood at 8.86 percent and deaths at 6.88 percent, and there were 107.31 men to every 100 women.

Like most of eastern China, Nanjing is officially mainly Han, at 98.56 percent, and 50 other official ethnic groups make up the rest. In 1999 a count found 77,394 residents in minorities, and the large majority, 64,832, were Hui, who accounted for 83.76 percent of the minority population. Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) were the next largest groups. Most minority residents lived in Jianye District, where they made up 9.13 percent of the population.

Nanjing is the transport hub of eastern China and the downstream Yangtze area, and its land, water and air links form a three-dimensional system. As in most other Chinese cities, most people travel by public transport. As of October 2014 the Yangtze was crossed by four bridges and two tunnels, connecting districts north of the river to the city centre on the south bank.

Nanjing combines a long agricultural tradition with a modern, well-connected city. If you plan to study agriculture here, you will have fertile land, plenty of water and a strong farming economy on your doorstep, along with a climate of hot, humid summers and cold, damp winters.
