Nanjing Forestry University, known as NJFU (南京林业大学), is a public university run at provincial level, based in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu. Because it is run through the Jiangsu provincial system rather than directly by the national education ministry, it is classed as provincial. It also belongs to the national Double First-Class Construction programme, which backs selected universities and disciplines, a good sign for a university that specialises in one field.

NJFU's roots lie in the forestry departments of two older Nanjing institutions, Jinling University and Central University. The institution in its own right was created in 1952 as Nanjing Forestry College, formed by merging forestry departments that came from three other places: Hubei Agricultural College, Nanchang University and Wuhan University. In 1972 it became the Nanjing Technological College of Forest Products, and the current name has been used since 1985.

In other words, this is a university built around forestry from its very first day, and the sections on Nanjing's rivers, forests, plants and wildlife below make more sense when you read them with that in mind.

Daily life for a student is shaped by the city around the campus: its weather, how people move about and what there is to see. The sections below introduce Nanjing, the city that hosts Nanjing Forestry University, and then widen out to Jiangsu Province.

The city has a land area of 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 sq mi). It lies at the heart of the lower Yangtze drainage area, within the Yangtze River Delta, which is among China's biggest economic zones. The Yangtze passes the west of the city and then bends along its north side, and a belt of hills called the Ningzheng Ridge encircles the north, east and south.

Some distances show where it sits in the country. Shanghai is 270 kilometres (170 mi) to the east-southeast of it, which is to say Nanjing lies to Shanghai's west-northwest. Beijing is 900 kilometres (560 mi) to the north-northwest, Luoyang 650 kilometres (400 mi) to the northwest, and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) to the west-southwest.

The river system around it is worth understanding. The Yangtze flows downstream from Jiujiang in Jiangxi, through Anhui and Jiangsu, and out to the East China Sea. North of the lower Yangtze lies the Huai River basin, and south of it the Zhe River basin, and the Grand Canal east of Nanjing links the two. Locals and historians call the surrounding area Xiajiang (下江, "Downstream River"). Jianghuai predominates in its northern part and Jiangzhe in its southern part, and the region as a whole is also known as Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, "South of the Yangtze").

Three Jiangsu cities border Nanjing: Yangzhou lies northeast, Zhenjiang east and Changzhou southeast. The western boundary is shared with Anhui Province, and five of its prefecture-level cities touch Nanjing. Chuzhou is to the northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan to the west, and Xuancheng to the southwest.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), shaped by the East Asian monsoon. The year has four distinct seasons, and dampness is a feature of all of them. Summers are very hot and muggy and winters are cold and damp, with spring and autumn lasting a fair length of time between them. With Chongqing and Wuhan, Nanjing is one of the traditional "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze for its persistent summer heat. Between mid-June and late July, however, comes the plum blossom season, which is also the meiyu, East Asia's rainy season (the word means "plum rain"), with gentle rain and damp air. A northeast wind dominates in winter and a southeast wind in summer.

For all that "furnace" reputation, Nanjing is cold for its latitude. Winter temperatures match or fall below London's: January in Nanjing, at 32°04'N, is 2 °C colder than January in London at 51°30'N. Against Savannah, Georgia, on the humid subtropical US east coast, the winter here is 7 °C colder. Bring warm clothes.
The key numbers are these:
January averages 3.1 °C (37.6 °F). The record low for a single day is −14.0 °C (6.8 °F), reached on 6 January 1955.

July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F). The highest daily maximum is 43.0 °C (109.4 °F), recorded on 13 July 1934. Another record series covering the period since 1951 gives a high of 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959, and a low of −14.0 °C (7 °F) on 6 January 1955.
The annual mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F).
Rain of more than 0.1 mm falls on 112.9 days a year, about 113 on average, and the most ever recorded in a year was 160 days in 1957.
On average 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in) of precipitation falls in a year.
Sunshine is limited. The share of possible sunshine is lowest in June (37 percent) and highest in August and October (48 percent), and the year total is 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine.
Typhoons are unusual but can arrive in late summer and early autumn.

Nanjing has plenty of natural resources, including more than 40 kinds of minerals. Iron and sulfur reserves account for 40 percent of Jiangsu's total, and its strontium reserves are the largest in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water is also plentiful, from the Yangtze and from groundwater, and there are natural hot springs too, at Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou.

In the heart of the city, Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are open to everyone and easy to reach. Purple Mountain, covered in deciduous and coniferous forest, preserves a range of historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel in the Yangtze is under construction so that ships of 50,000 DWT can sail between the East China Sea and Nanjing.

Students should know that smog can be a problem. A dense smog wave started on 2 December 2013 across central and eastern China, over a stretch of around 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) passing over Tianjin, Hebei, Shandong, Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and also Zhejiang. Little cold air was moving, and slow-moving air masses carrying industrial emissions let pollutants build up in a thick layer. Central and southern Jiangsu, particularly Nanjing and its surroundings, were hit hard: the air quality index stood at "severely polluted" for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to a lack of wind, car exhaust under low air pressure and coal-fired district heating in northern China. Prevailing winds pushed low-lying air masses full of factory emissions, mostly SO2, towards the east coast.

Two soil groups cover Nanjing: zonal soil and cultivated soil. Zonal soil is yellow-brown in the north and centre of the city, and red in the south along the Anhui border. Cultivated soil, created by farming, is mostly paddy soil, plus smaller areas of yellow Gang soil and of vegetable garden soil. Soil patterns follow the terrain and water conditions, and the land divides into low mountain and hilly areas, hilly areas and plains. The second national soil survey, run from 1980 to 1987, sorted Nanjing's soil into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species across 416,300 hectares.

Nanjing sits on the lower Yangtze, which crosses the city diagonally from southwest to northeast over about 93 kilometres, more than 300 kilometres from the river mouth. The Qinhuai River, which people call the mother river of Nanjing, flows from south to north through the main urban area and then enters the Yangtze. Two lakes, Xuanwu and Mochou, are likened to pearls set in the main city. Water covers about 11% of the city's area.

Most of the river and lake network belongs to the Yangtze system. Only the rivers that run into Baoying Lake and Gaoyou Lake, in the north of Liuhe District, are part of the Huai system. Within the Yangtze system there are several sub-systems: the Qinhuai to its south and the Chuhe to its north, a riverside network of small streams, a two-lake system formed by Gucheng Lake and Shijiu Lake, and the West Taihu Lake system to the east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and of excellent quality, and the Pukou Pearl Spring is especially well known. The hot spring areas at Jiangning Tangshan and Pukou Tangquan have a long history.

Nanjing is also a major port. China's largest inland port is the Port of Nanjing, which handled 191,970,000 t of cargo in 2012. Its 64 berths are spread along a port area 98 kilometres (61 mi) in length, and 16 are for ships above 10,000 tons. It is the biggest container port on the Yangtze too: in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area opened as a base with a capacity of one million containers. By 2010 the port operated three industrial ports and six public ones. A 12.5-metre-deep channel lets 50,000-ton ocean ships come straight to the port, and vessels of 100,000 tons or more can arrive after lightening their load at high tide on the Yangtze. CSC Jinling has a large shipyard here.

This is especially relevant for a forestry university. Nanjing is one of the plant-rich regions of China, and its vegetation is varied. Natural vegetation falls into seven types. These are coniferous forest, bamboo forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, mixed forest of deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved trees, shrubland, grassland and aquatic plants. Planted vegetation includes field crops, vegetables, commercial woodland, orchards and green belts. The state gives key protection to seven rare and endangered plant species, among them Pterocarpus sinensis, Ming Codonopsis, Chinese Allium chinense and Sphaerocarpus sinensis.
Wildlife is just as varied:
795 species of insects from 125 families in 11 orders.
99 species of fish from 22 families and 12 orders.
327 species of land vertebrates in 29 orders and 90 families, including 243 bird species (56 families and 17 orders) and 47 mammals from 8 orders and 22 families.

First-level national protection covers nine wild animals, for example the White Shoulder Eagle and the Oriental White Crane. Another 65, including the little swan, Chinese tiger, swallowtail and finless porpoise, have second-level protection. The province lists 125 key protected animals, and 35 species are endangered.

Nanjing's mineral wealth is considerable. 49 types of mineral have been found, such as limestone, gypsum, clay, dolomite and ferrosulfide as well as iron, copper, lead, zinc and strontium, and 31 of them have proven reserves. Deposits cluster in four metallogenic belts, including the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen belt of iron, copper and sulfur, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt.

Getting over the Yangtze matters a great deal in Nanjing. The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, completed in the 1960s, was then the only bridge across the lower Yangtze in eastern China. It was a source of national pride and an emblem of modern China, because Chinese engineers designed and built it themselves after other countries' surveys had failed and after China had first relied on, then rejected, Soviet expertise. Work began in 1960 and traffic started in 1968. The bridge has two levels for road and rail. Its upper deck is 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) long, of which about 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) span the river itself.

Four further bridges and four tunnels have since been added. Going downstream, the crossings are Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge and the Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge.
The main road bridges, in order of opening, are:
Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (First Bridge), opened 1968, longest span 160 m
Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge (Second Bridge), opened 1997, longest span 628 m
Nanjing Dashengguan Yangtze River Bridge (Third Bridge), opened 2005, longest span 648 m
Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge (Fourth Bridge), opened 2012, longest span 1,418 m
Nanjing Jiangxinzhou Yangtze River Bridge (Fifth Bridge), opened 2020, longest span 600 m
The Nanjing Xianxin Yangtze River Bridge, which opened in 2023 with a longest span of 1,760 m

When the 2010 census was taken, Nanjing had 8.005 million people, and the OECD put the wider metropolitan area at 11.7 million. Official figures for 2011 gave the city 8.11 million, with a birth rate of 8.86 percent and a death rate of 6.88 percent. The urban area held 6.47 million, and there were 107.31 men for every 100 women.

Han people form the overwhelming majority, 98.56 percent, as in most of eastern China, and 50 other officially recognised ethnic groups are present. In 1999 there were 77,394 residents of officially defined minorities. The Hui were by far the largest group with 64,832 people, or 83.76 percent of the minority population. The second and third largest were the Manchu with 2,311 people and the Zhuang with 533. Most minority residents lived in Jianye District, where they made up 9.13 percent of the population.

Nanjing is one of the country's important grain and commercial agriculture bases. Major cash crops include rice and cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea and bamboo, as well as fruit and medicinal materials. The fertile waters on both banks of the Yangtze also make it a key freshwater fishery base.

Taken together, farming, forestry, livestock and fishery produced 47.250 billion yuan in 2019, an increase of 4.8% over 2018. Within that, farming produced 24.077 billion yuan, fishery 15.389 billion, animal husbandry 2.435 billion and forestry 2.017 billion, while related services contributed 3.333 billion yuan. For a forestry student, it is notable that forestry itself is a small slice of the city's primary output.

Nanjing is the transport hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze region. Its three-dimensional system runs over land, over water and through the air. Most residents, like people in other Chinese cities, depend chiefly on public transport. In October 2014 the Yangtze was spanned by four bridges and two tunnels, connecting the city centre on the south bank with the districts to the north.
A university's surroundings influence student life nearly as much as the campus itself, so here is a short account of Jiangsu, the province where NJFU is located.

nanjing-forestry-university.h: From ancient states to the Song

blocks.x: In the earliest Chinese dynasties, what is now Jiangsu lay far from the centre of Chinese civilisation in northwest Henan, and it was the home of an ancient people called the Huai barbarians (淮夷). Under the Zhou dynasty contact grew, and the state of Wu emerged in southern Jiangsu among the hundreds of states of northern and central China. As the Spring and Autumn period was ending, Wu became a great power under King Helu. In 484 BC it beat Qi, a major northern power in what is now Shandong, as part of a struggle to become overlord of all the states. Wu itself was subdued in 473 BC by Yue, a state to the south in modern Zhejiang, and Yue was in turn conquered in 333 BC by the powerful western state of Chu. In 221 BC Qin finally swept the other states away and unified China.

The Han dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD) governed Jiangsu, still distant from the North China Plain heartland, as two zhou: Xu Province north and Yang Province south. Next, during the Three Kingdoms period, southern Jiangsu served as the base of Eastern Wu (222 to 280). Its capital, Jianye, was later renamed Jiankang and is the Nanjing of today. In the 4th century nomads invaded and overran northern China, so the Jin imperial court relocated to Jiankang, and migrants from the north crowded into the cities of southern and central Jiangsu. Jiankang served as the capital of four successive Southern dynasties and became China's largest commercial and cultural centre.

When the Sui dynasty reunified the country in 581, the political centre moved north once more. Even so, builders cut the Grand Canal through Jiangsu so that the Central Plains would be joined to the thriving Yangtze Delta, and the Tang dynasty (618 to 907) depended on southern Jiangsu for yearly grain deliveries. The Song dynasty (960 to 1279) brought a wealthy merchant class and an emerging market economy, and Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and neighbouring areas) became a trading centre. From then on, cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou stood for opulence and luxury in China, and the region is still among the richest in the country.

nanjing-forestry-university.h: Ming, Qing and the Taiping years

blocks.x: In 1127 the Jurchen Jin dynasty won control of North China in the Jin-Song wars. The Huai River, which once ran through northern Jiangsu to the Yellow Sea, became the border between the Jin in the north and the Southern Song in the south. In the thirteenth century the Mongols took over China. After they were driven out, the Ming dynasty, founded in 1368 after the Mongols were driven out, first placed its capital in Nanjing, and the areas around it, matching today's Jiangsu and Anhui, formed Nanzhili province ("southern directly governed"). Zhu Di, later the Yongle Emperor, seized power in a coup and moved the capital to distant Beijing, although Nanjing kept the status of southern capital. In the late Ming, Jiangnan remained a major trade centre. Some historians see in its flourishing textile industry the beginnings of industrialisation and capitalism, a trend that was cut short.
The Qing dynasty renamed Nanzhili as "Jiangnan province", and in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui were separated into distinct provinces. Jiangsu's borders have been largely stable since.

Foreign powers began pushing into China in the 1840s, and the wealthy, commercial Yangtze River Delta met Western influence more and more. Shanghai, at first a small and unremarkable Jiangsu town, rapidly turned into a metropolis of trade and banking with a cosmopolitan character, and was later separated off as an independent municipality. Jiangnan also features strongly in the Taiping Rebellion (1851 to 1864), a huge and deadly uprising that tried to found a Christian theocracy in China. It started far away in Guangdong and spread through much of South China. By 1853 the rebels had made Nanjing their capital, renamed Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was founded in 1912 and warlords soon tore the country apart. Jiangsu changed hands several times, until April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek established a government at Nanjing, and soon brought most of the country under his control. In 1928 the provincial government relocated to Zhenjiang. The second Sino-Japanese War, which became full-scale in 1937, interrupted this arrangement, and Nanjing fell on 13 December 1937. Japanese forces committed atrocities in the three months that followed, known as the Rape of Nanjing, and the city then became the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government of East China. Most of Jiangsu remained occupied by Japan until 1945, when the war ended.

Postwar, Nanjing once more served as the capital of the Republic of China. But the Kuomintang government was now at war with Communist forces who were based mostly in Northeast China. The Huaihai Campaign, fought in northern Jiangsu, proved decisive and ended in defeat for the Kuomintang, and the Communists then crossed the Yangtze and captured Nanjing. The Kuomintang retreated south and ended up in Taipei, from where the Republic of China government still administers Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands, while technically continuing to claim Nanjing as its de jure capital. After Zhenjiang was captured, the provincial government moved to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

Beijing (formerly Peiping) became the capital of the People's Republic after the Communist takeover, and Jiangsu was divided into the Sunan and Subei Administrative Regions. The province was reconstituted on 15 November 1952, with Nanjing relegated to the position of provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up first concentrated on Guangdong on the south coast, which left Jiangsu behind, and was applied more evenly across China from the 1990s. Suzhou and Wuxi, two southern Jiangsu cities close to Shanghai, have since become very prosperous. They rank among China's top 10 cities by gross domestic product and have overtaken the provincial capital, Nanjing. The income gap between northern and southern Jiangsu remains large.

NJFU is a specialist, forestry-centred university with provincial backing and a place in the Double First-Class Construction. It stands in a historic, well-connected city with hot, humid summers and cold winters, a major river port, rich green spaces and plant life, and a long record as a capital.
Nanjing Forestry University lists 164 programs for international students on this site: 78 bachelor, 58 master's, 28 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 82 taught in Chinese and English, 80 taught in Chinese, 2 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,500 to CNY 16,500 (median CNY 16,500), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 27,000 to CNY 27,000 (median CNY 27,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 31,000 to CNY 31,000 (median CNY 31,000), according to the university's published fee table.

164 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (2):
Forestry
Resources and Environment
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanjing-forestry-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanjing Forestry University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Nanjing Forestry University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Nanjing Medical University (NJMU, also written NMU; 南京医科大学) is a public university in Nanjing, in Jiangsu province. The Jiangsu provincial government is its supervising body, and it is included in the Double First-Class Construction scheme.

Its story begins in Zhenjiang in 1934, and the school moved to Nanjing in 1957. The campus network now consists of Jiangning and Wutai, the two main campuses, each of which provides apartments for international students.

An English-taught MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery) programme has been available since 2005, with approval from the PRC's Ministry of Education (MOE). That makes the university directly relevant for students from abroad who want to train in medicine in English.

The school was founded in 1934 as National Jiangsu Medical College. When it relocated to Nanjing in 1957, it was renamed Nanjing Medical College. The college introduced six-year programmes in 1962, making it one of the earliest Chinese medical universities to do so. Approval for master's and doctoral degrees came in 1981. In 1993 it became Nanjing Medical University, and today it is counted among the leading medical universities in China.

In 2020 the university had two campuses. Wutai, the main campus, covers 8 hectares. Jiangning is the New Campus, at 87 hectares, which makes it almost 11 times the size of Wutai. Wutai remains the centre for clinical teaching and research.

NJMU offers bachelor's, master's and PhD degrees, and it also has post-doctoral research programmes. Its structure comprises one independent school, Kangda College, together with 16 secondary schools. Most of these concentrate on medicine, public health or other fields of health care. The medical and health schools are:
School of Basic Medical Sciences
First School of Clinical Medicine
Second School of Clinical Medicine
Third School of Clinical Medicine
Fourth School of Clinical Medicine
Gulou School of Clinical Medicine
School of Public Health
School of Stomatology
School of Pharmaceutical Sciences
School of Nursing
School of Medical Policy and Management

Four others serve different purposes: the School of International Education, the School of Higher Vocational and Technical Education, the School of Continuing Education and the College of International Studies.
Clinical training depends on hospitals. NMU has 24 affiliated hospitals and about 50 teaching hospitals, spread over Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shandong provinces.

The register lists over 1,400 faculty members, of whom 175 are associate professors and 117 are full professors. Supervision of master's programmes is handled by 812 people and of doctoral programmes by 185. The university's own description of its strengths names the following:
nine Jiangsu Specially-Appointed Professors
six winners of the China National Funds for Distinguished Young Scientists
five recipients of funds from the Ministry of Education's New Century Excellent Talent Support Program
two global experts recruited under the national Thousand Talent Program
one academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering
one Chang Jiang Scholar Distinguished Visiting Professor
one winner of the National Award for Distinguished Teachers
three State-Level Teaching Teams and one Innovation Team of the Ministry of Education

An international exchange and cooperation programme sends instructors abroad for study and work. Partners include medical schools and scientific research institutions in France, Japan, Germany, Australia, the United States of America and Britain. The count of foreign students passed 500 by 2014. In addition, NMU takes part as a partner in the Alliance for Health Policy and Systems Research, which is part of the World Health Organization.

nanjing-medical-university.h: Nanjing: the city that surrounds the campus

blocks.x: How you live as a student depends largely on the city, so these sections explain where Nanjing is, what each season feels like, what the land and water offer, who lives there and how people get around.

Land area in Nanjing totals 2,548 sq mi, or 6,598 square kilometres. It lies at the centre of the area drained by the lower Yangtze, within the Yangtze River Delta, which is one of China's largest economic zones. On its western side and then its northern side, the city is skirted by the Yangtze, and the Ningzheng Ridge wraps around the remaining north, east and south edges. Some distances show where it stands. Luoyang is 650 kilometres (400 mi) to the northwest, Beijing 900 kilometres (560 mi) to the north-northwest, Shanghai 270 kilometres (170 mi) to the east-southeast, and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) to the west-southwest.

The Yangtze leaves Jiujiang in Jiangxi and runs through Anhui and Jiangsu before emptying into the East China Sea. In the lower part of the basin, the Huai River basin occupies the northern side and the Zhe River basin the southern side; the Grand Canal, east of Nanjing, joins the two. Locals refer to the region as Xiajiang (下江, Downstream River), where the north is mainly Jianghuai and the south mainly Jiangzhe. It is equally well known by the names Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, South of the Yangtze).

Within Jiangsu the city's neighbours are Zhenjiang to the east, Yangzhou to the northeast and Changzhou to the southeast. In the west it touches Anhui, with five prefecture-level cities along the border. These are Chuzhou (northwest), Xuancheng (southwest) and Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan (west).

nanjing-medical-university.h: A hot, damp city with surprisingly cold winters

blocks.x: Nanjing's humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) is shaped by the East Asian monsoon. Damp conditions occur all through the year, and each of the four seasons is clear. Summers are muggy and very hot, winters damp and cold, and spring and autumn last long enough to enjoy. Because of its fierce summers, Nanjing is traditionally named alongside Chongqing and Wuhan as one of the Yangtze's Three Furnaces. The plum blossom season runs from the middle of June to late July, and that is also when meiyu, the plum rain of East Asia, arrives with mild rain and humidity. In winter the wind blows mostly from the northeast.

Given the Three Furnaces reputation, many students are surprised by how cold the winters get at this latitude. Nanjing lies at 32°04′N, London at 51°30′N, yet January in Nanjing is 2 °C colder than January in London, and winter temperatures in general are similar or lower. Savannah, Georgia, on the US east coast, shares the humid subtropical climate type, but Nanjing's winter is 7 °C chillier than Savannah's.

Some figures: the January average is 3.1 °C (37.6 °F). Its coldest daily minimum on record was −14.0 °C (6.8 °F), on 6 January 1955. July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F) under a prevailing southeast wind, and the hottest daily maximum reached 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on 13 July 1934. On average 112.9 days a year have precipitation above 0.1 mm, and 1957 holds the record for the most such days, at 160. Over a whole year, precipitation averages 1,144 millimetres, or 45.0 in.

Late in summer and early in autumn, typhoons can occasionally arrive, though they are uncommon. The yearly mean temperature comes to approximately 16.4 °C (61.5 °F). By month, the 24-hour average is lowest in January (3.1 °C, or 37.6 °F) and highest in July (28.4 °C, or 83.1 °F). On the 1951 to present record, a low of −14.0 °C (7 °F) occurred on 6 January 1955, and a high of 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959. Rain falls on around 113 days annually and adds up to 1,144 millimetres (45 in). The share of possible sunshine is lowest in June at 37 percent and highest in August and October at 48 percent. In all, the city gets 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine a year.

Starting on 2 December 2013, thick smog spread over central and eastern China across roughly 1,200 kilometers (750 mi). It covered Tianjin, Hebei, Shandong, Anhui, Jiangsu, Shanghai and Zhejiang. Cold air was not moving through, and slow air masses carrying industrial emissions let pollutants collect in a dense layer. The worst hit were central and southern Jiangsu, particularly Nanjing and the area around it. The AQI index showed severely polluted conditions for five days running and heavily polluted ones for nine. Officials pointed to calm winds, vehicle exhaust under low air pressure, and the coal-fired district heating of north China as causes. Winds in the region carried low air masses full of factory emissions (mostly SO2) toward the east coast.

More than 40 minerals have been found in Nanjing. The city has 40 percent of the iron and sulfur reserves of Jiangsu province, and in strontium its reserves are the first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. There is also plenty of water, whether from the Yangtze or from groundwater. Hot springs exist in places, for example Tangquan in Pukou and Tangshan in Jiangning. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake sit in the middle of the city, and the public can reach both easily. Purple Mountain, with its deciduous and coniferous forest, protects a range of historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel on the Yangtze is also being built, which is meant to let vessels of 50,000 DWT sail in from the East China Sea.

Altogether 49 mineral types have been discovered, including limestone, clay, gypsum, dolomite, ferrosulfide, strontium, zinc, lead, copper and iron, and 31 of them have proven reserves. Most deposits sit in four metallogenic belts. The belts are named Jiangpu-Liuhe (iron and copper), Ningzhen (a polymetallic belt of iron, copper and sulfur) and Ningwu (iron and copper).

Nanjing's soils are of two main kinds, zonal and cultivated. In the north and centre the zonal soil is yellow-brown, and in the south, near the Anhui border, it is red. Soil created by cultivation is chiefly paddy soil, with a little vegetable garden soil and yellow Gang soil. The pattern follows the shape of the land and its hydrology, in three groupings: low mountains and hills, hills, and plains. A second national soil survey between 1980 and 1987 sorted Nanjing's soil into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species, on a total of 416,300 hectares.

Across Nanjing the Yangtze flows on a diagonal from southwest to northeast. The stretch inside the city is about 93 kilometers, and the river mouth is over 300 kilometers away. Locals call the Qinhuai River the mother river of Nanjing. It flows north through the central urban area before it joins the Yangtze. Two lakes, Mochou and Xuanwu, are compared to pearls set in the heart of the city. About 11% of the city is covered with water. Nearly all the rivers and lakes belong to the Yangtze system, with the exception of the rivers in the north of Liuhe District that run into Baoying Lake and Gaoyou Lake, which form part of the Huai River system. The Yangtze system includes a number of sub-systems: Qinhuai (south of the river), Chuhe (north of it), riverside streams that feed in from either side, the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun, and the pair of lakes called Gucheng and Shijiu. Groundwater is plentiful and excellent in quality, with the Pukou Pearl Spring particularly renowned. Spring areas with long histories include Tangquan in Pukou and Tangshan in Jiangning.

No inland port in China is bigger than Nanjing's, which handled 191,970,000 t of cargo in 2012. The port area extends 98 kilometers (61 mi) and has 64 berths, of which 16 take ships above 10,000 tons. It leads the Yangtze for containers too, and in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area opened, with capacity for a million containers, which strengthened its lead. By 2010 it ran nine ports, six of them public and three industrial. A 12.5-meter-deep Yangtze channel lets 50,000-ton ocean ships come straight to the port, and ships of 100,000 tons or more can arrive as well once load has been reduced, during high tide on the river. A large shipyard belongs to CSC Jinling.

Plant life in Nanjing is abundant and varied. Its vegetation falls into 7 natural types: bamboo forest, shrub, grass, aquatic vegetation, coniferous forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, and mixed deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved forest. Cultivated vegetation covers field and vegetable crops, orchards, green belts and economic forests. National key protection applies to seven rare and endangered plants such as Ming Codonopsis, Chinese Allium chinense, Pterocarpus sinensis and Sphaerocarpus sinensis.

Wildlife is varied as well. Insects are represented by 795 species belonging to 125 families and 11 orders, and fish by 99 species in 22 families and 12 orders. The terrestrial wild vertebrates total 327 species in 29 orders and 90 families. Birds account for 243 species (56 families, 17 orders) and mammals for 47 species (22 families, 8 orders). Under first-level national protection are 9 species, for example the White Shoulder Eagle and the Oriental White Crane. Another 65 get second-level protection, among them the finless porpoise, the little swan, the Chinese tiger and the swallowtail. Jiangsu Province lists 125 species as key protected, and 35 species are endangered.

nanjing-medical-university.h: Bridges and tunnels over the Yangtze

blocks.x: Opened in 1968 after construction began in 1960, the Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge was, at that time, the one and only bridge spanning the lower Yangtze in eastern China. After other nations' surveys failed, and after depending on Soviet expertise and then rejecting it, Chinese engineers designed and built it themselves, so it was a matter of pride and a powerful symbol of modern China. The design has two tiers, for road and rail. The upper deck is 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) long, and around 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) of it crosses the river. Since that time, the city has added four bridges and four tunnels. Reading the crossings in order downstream, first comes the Dashengguan Bridge, then the Third Bridge and the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge. Next are the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道) and the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, followed by the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the First Bridge and the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel. The Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge and the Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge come last.
Opening years and longest spans of the bridges:
1968: Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (the First Nanjing Yangtze Bridge), longest span 160 m
1997: Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge (the Second), longest span 628 m
2005: Nanjing Dashengguan Yangtze River Bridge (the Third), longest span 648 m
2012: Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge (the Fourth), longest span 1,418 m

The 2010 census found a total population of 8.005 million for the City of Nanjing, and the OECD's estimate for the metropolitan area at the time was 11.7 million. Births were 8.86 percent and deaths 6.88 percent. The urban area held 6.47 million. For every 100 women there were 107.31 men.

Han people make up the great majority, 98.56 percent, which is typical of eastern China, and there are 50 other officially recognised ethnic groups. A 1999 count found 77,394 residents from officially defined minorities. Of that number the Hui were by far the biggest group at 64,832, or 83.76 percent of the minority population, while the Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) came second and third. Jianye District had most of the minority residents, accounting for 9.13 percent of its population.

The city is one of China's significant bases for agriculture and for commercial grain. Medicinal materials, fruits, bamboo, tea, hemp, silkworm cocoons, cotton and rice are the cash crops grown. The Yangtze's fertile waters on both banks also make Nanjing an important freshwater fishing base in China.

Agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery together produced 47.250 billion yuan in 2019, 4.8% more than the previous year. The agricultural part was 24.077 billion yuan, forestry 2.017 billion yuan, animal husbandry 2.435 billion yuan, fishery 15.389 billion yuan, and the services serving these industries 3.333 billion yuan.

Eastern China and the downstream Yangtze area rely on Nanjing as a transport hub, where land, water and air links make up a three-dimensional system. Most citizens, as in other Chinese cities, depend mainly on public transport. As of October 2014 the Yangtze was crossed by four bridges and two tunnels, tying the districts north of the river to the centre of the city on the south bank.

Nanjing Medical University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.
Application windows found for Nanjing Medical University:
Autumn 2026 MBBS intake (closed): opens 1 Jan 2026, closes 30 Jun 2026
Deadlines can move and seats can fill earlier than the closing date, so apply as soon as your documents are ready.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanjing-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanjing Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Nanjing Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

nanjing-normal-university.h: A quick portrait of the university

blocks.x: Nanjing Normal University, often shortened to NJNU (and written NNU in some of its English-language material), is a public university in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu Province. Its Chinese name is 南京师范大学, pronounced Nánjīng Shīfàn Dàxué. It belongs to the provincial system, but the Ministry of Education and the Jiangsu government jointly support it, and it holds a place in both the Project 211 group and the Double First-Class Construction programme, two national schemes that single out universities for extra investment.

Figures dating from 2020 show a large and varied institution. The university teaches on three campuses in Nanjing, called Xianlin, Suiyuan and Zijin, and it is organised into 28 colleges and schools. At that time the roll counted 18,369 undergraduates, plus 12,564 postgraduates; 1,525 of the postgraduates were working toward doctorates. Those numbers will have moved since, so check the university's own website for the current picture.

For an international applicant, the practical meaning is this: NJNU is a mid-sized comprehensive university with a particular strength in education, humanities and social science, backed by public funding and a campus layout that mixes a historic garden site with a big modern suburb.
NJNU has two ancestral lines, and both are worth knowing because they explain why the university carries such an unusual historical weight.

The first line begins in 1902 with Sanjiang Normal School, a teacher-training college. "Sanjiang" was a Qing-dynasty administrative name covering what today is roughly Jiangsu, Jiangxi and Anhui. Over the decades that school was renamed again and again. It was Liangjiang Advanced Normal School, then National Nanjing Higher Normal School, then National Southeastern University. Later titles included National 4th Sun Yat-sen University and National Jiangsu University, before it became National Central University and finally Nanjing University.

The second line starts earlier, in 1888, with Nanking Academy. It grew into the Private University of Nanking in 1910, and it holds the distinction of being the earliest Chinese institution officially called a "university" in English. It was also registered with education authorities in New York State. Then, in 1951, the Private University of Nanking joined with the Private Ginling College and the two were reorganised as the National University of Nanking.

The national reorganisation of higher education in 1952 reshaped everything. Selected schools and departments from Nanjing University and the University of Nanking were separated out and combined into Nanjing Normal College, which settled on the old Ginling College site. The new college then swapped some academic departments with Soochow University in Suzhou, so that both institutions ended up with a stronger, more coherent set of disciplines.

The college took the title of Nanjing Normal University in 1984. Twelve years later, in 1996, the Ministry of Education put it among the first universities placed on the original Project 211 list of key national universities. The year 2000 brought a merger with a power-engineering polytechnic (Nanjing Polytechnic of Power Engineering), which had been run nationally under the Ministry of Chemical Industry. Today the university also sits inside the Double First-Class scheme.
In short, this is a school with more than a century of roots in teacher education that expanded into a full arts-and-sciences university after 1952, and later added engineering through a merger.

The university spreads across both urban and suburban Nanjing. That is a useful setting for a student: Quacquarelli Symonds ranked Nanjing in 2019 as one of the world's strongest student destinations, and the city has been one of China's Four Great Ancient Capitals and is today the provincial capital of Jiangsu.

The Suiyuan campus lies at 122 Ninghai Road in Gulou District. It stands on the land of the old Ginling College, and the state protects it nationally as an important heritage location. Its classical Chinese buildings give it a very different feeling from the newer parts of the university.

The Xianlin campus, at 1 Wenyuan Road in Qixia District, is the university's centre of gravity. It sits inside Xianlin University City, opened in 2001, and is the newest and the largest of the three, spread over 346.7 hectares. The grounds are divided into east, west, north and south zones, and most undergraduates study here. At its heart stands the main library, funded by a donation from Zhu Jingwen, which is the biggest single-building library in Jiangsu Province.

The Zijin campus, at 78 Bancang Street in Xuanwu District, was the home of the power-engineering polytechnic that merged with NJNU in 2000. Two engineering schools (electrical and automation, and energy and mechanical) used to teach there, but they relocated to the expanded Xianlin campus in 2019.
When you apply, confirm which campus your programme uses; the answer for most undergraduates is Xianlin.

Since separating from the teacher-training college of Nanjing University, NJNU has grown into a research university in the arts and sciences with a number of highly ranked subjects. The Ministry of Education's 2012 subject evaluation put it third nationally for education. Geography and Marxism studies each took sixth place, and foreign languages and literatures came seventh. Psychology and fine arts each placed ninth, and law was thirteenth.
There were 28 colleges and schools in 2020. They span education, humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, engineering and the arts:
Education and teacher training: Teacher Education, Education Science, Psychology, Sports Science and Physical Education, and the Honors College

Humanities and social sciences: Ginling College, International College for Chinese Studies, Public Administration, Business, Law, Marxism, Chinese Language and Literature, Foreign Languages and Cultures, Journalism and Communication, Social Development, and the Social Development Academy
Natural sciences: Mathematical Sciences, Physics and Technology, Chemistry and Materials Science, Geography, Life Sciences

Engineering and technology: Energy and Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Automation, Computer Science and Electronic Information (which also serves as the School of Artificial Intelligence), Environment, Marine Science and Engineering, Food and Pharmaceutical Engineering
Arts: Music and Fine Art

If you are a future applicant from abroad, note the International College for Chinese Studies in this list; that is typically the first place to look for Chinese-language and Chinese-culture study for foreign students.

As of 2020 the university ran undergraduate degrees in 74 majors, research master's degrees in 41 disciplines, professional master's degrees in 25 disciplines and doctoral degrees in 26 disciplines, and it hosted 22 post-doctoral research centres. A further 29 of its undergraduate programmes had been named National First-class Undergraduate Programmes by the Ministry of Education.

The research record in recent years includes the following national funding wins. Social science: 32 key projects financed by the National Social Science Fund, and 7 key philosophy and social-science research projects backed by the Ministry of Education. Science and technology: 2 National Science and Technology Support Projects, 4 projects from the 973 Program (the National Basic Research Program), 1 from the 863 Program (the State High-Tech Development Plan) and 28 key projects supported by the National Natural Science Foundation.

The university has also signed a cooperation pact with Purple Mountain Observatory and the Nanjing branch of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. It covers frontier work in earth and space science, staff exchange and joint postgraduate training. One tangible result: on 4 July 2021, asteroid number 216446, which the observatory had discovered, received the name "NNU Star", after approval by the IAU body responsible for naming small bodies.

The ARWU world list for 2023 placed NJNU somewhere between 401 and 500. Domestically, the 2021 CUAA table put it 41st in the overall ranking and 20th for humanities and social sciences. Just above it in that subject table were Shanghai Jiao Tong (18th) and China University of Political Science and Law (19th); just below came Zhongnan University of Economics and Law (21st), Jinan University (23rd) and Xi'an Jiaotong (26th).

By September 2021 the Essential Science Indicators (ESI) database, a widely cited measure of academic influence, placed NJNU in the world's top 1% in ten fields. The percentages show how close to the top each field sits:
Computer Science, in the top 0.99%
Social Sciences (general), top 0.88%
Mathematics, top 0.78%
Geosciences, top 0.70%
Plant and Animal Science, top 0.61%
Environment and Ecology, top 0.54%
Materials Science, top 0.48%
Agricultural Sciences, top 0.45%
Engineering, top 0.29%
Chemistry, which is the highest of the ten at top 0.28%
Rankings differ by method and by year, so treat them as a rough guide and not as a verdict.
NJNU has partnerships with universities overseas that let students earn two degrees or an extra qualification. A selection:
Accounting or finance: two bachelor's degrees, partner Macquarie University (Australia)
Computer science: two bachelor's degrees, partner University of Queensland (Australia)
Education: two bachelor's degrees, partner Tohoku University (Japan)
Education: two bachelor's degrees, partner University of Strathclyde (UK)
Electrical engineering: two bachelor's degrees, partner Northumbria University (UK)
Law: two bachelor's degrees, partner Hokkaido University (Japan)

An extra fifth-year LL.M. (Master of Laws) in partnership with UC Riverside (US)
A matching fifth-year LL.M. with Swansea University (UK)
Entry conditions, tuition and availability for each arrangement are not given here, so ask the university directly before planning around one.

The campus has 180 recognised student organisations and clubs. Anyone with a new idea can start one. Founding an organisation that also admits off-campus students needs the agreement of the relevant departments and the approval of the university's Party Committee, and the staff of the Youth League Committee are there to point students towards existing groups and advise on setting up new ones.
A few examples show the range:

Astronomy Club. A university-level academic society founded in September 2009. It has steadily improved its observation equipment, grown its membership and widened its activities, and it now owns five telescopes: one reflector, one catadioptric (a mirror-and-lens design), and three refractors.

G-Mix Dancing Club. A group of women at the university started this dance association in October 1999 to raise students' artistic skills. The members practise together a minimum of three sessions weekly, and each semester invites professional instructors for lessons.

Guangyu Chinese Opera Club. Founded in September 2003, it covers several opera traditions, including Beijing, Kun, Yue, Huangmei and Yu opera. Weekdays are for practising singing, Saturdays for performance training and Sundays for watching different operas together, with a lecture each semester. The club aims to carry on opera culture while enriching campus life.

HOLA Ballroom Dance Club. Dance enthusiasts set it up in 2015 for social dancing. It teaches Latin and ballroom styles, mainly the International Latin dances (cha-cha, rumba, samba, paso doble and jive), at beginner and intermediate levels, so you need no previous experience. Members train weekly for shows and contests at the university and around Nanjing.

The Xianlin Sports Center covers 23,000 square metres and is easy to reach: six public bus routes run straight to it, and Metro Line 2 stops a few miles away. It contains two main halls. Hall A is the competition venue and includes a yoga room, dance room, VIP fitness centre and showers. Hall B is the comprehensive training hall, with a warm-water indoor swimming pool, a badminton court, basketball and volleyball courts, a table-tennis room, a weight-training room for men, a martial-arts room, a gymnastics hall, an indoor plastic running track and two outdoor swimming pools. The centre has hosted many national and international sports competitions and arts performances. After the Tenth National Games were held successfully, in line with the National Fitness Program the exercise rooms opened to Nanjing residents too, except during teaching and team training.

At Suiyuan, students and members of the public exercise in the sports centre after class and on holidays. The School of Sports Science and Physical Education runs training programmes open to the public, intended to improve social interaction and to ease the pressure caused by an uneven spread of gym facilities. Three halls are open to outsiders there: badminton, table tennis and basketball.

A great deal of your daily experience as a student will come from the city around the campus: the weather, the way people travel and the things to do. The sections below describe Nanjing, the home of Nanjing Normal University.

nanjing-normal-university.h: Where Nanjing sits on the map

blocks.x: Nanjing covers 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 square miles). It occupies the middle of the lower Yangtze's drainage area, within the Yangtze River Delta, which ranks among China's biggest economic regions. The Yangtze passes the western edge of the city, then turns to run along its northern side, while the Ningzheng Ridge forms a ring of hills on the north, east and south.

The distances to other places give a sense of position. Nanjing is 650 kilometres (400 miles) southeast of Luoyang, 900 kilometres (560 miles) south-southeast of Beijing, 270 kilometres (170 miles) from Shanghai in the west-northwest direction. Chongqing lies 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) away in the opposite sense, to the west-southwest of Nanjing.

From Jiujiang in Jiangxi the river flows on through Anhui and Jiangsu before reaching the East China Sea. In the lower basin, the Huai River basin lies to the north and the Zhe River basin to the south, and the Grand Canal east of Nanjing links the two. Locals call the surrounding area the Xiajiang (下江, "downstream river") region; Jianghuai culture is the main influence in the north and Jiangzhe in the south. The region also goes by the names Dongnan (the Southeast) and Jiangnan (south of the Yangtze).

Inside Jiangsu, the neighbouring cities are Yangzhou (northeast), Zhenjiang (east) and Changzhou (southeast). The western boundary is also a provincial one: it touches Anhui, and five Anhui prefecture-level cities border Nanjing. They are Chuzhou in the northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan in the west, and Xuancheng in the southwest.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), driven by the East Asian monsoon. Four distinct seasons occur, and damp air is the norm in every month. Summers are very hot and muggy and winters are cold and damp, while spring and autumn last a fair length of time. Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing are traditionally called the "Three Furnaces" along the Yangtze because of their stubborn summer heat. The stretch between mid-June and late July is plum-blossom time, when the meiyu ("plum rain") arrives with gentle rain and humidity. Northeast winds prevail in winter and southeast winds in summer.

The "furnace" label can mislead newcomers, because winters here are surprisingly cold for the latitude. Nanjing's winter temperatures are about the same as London's or lower, and its January averages 2 °C colder than London's, even though Nanjing lies at 32°04'N and London at 51°30'N. Compared with the humid subtropical American East Coast, a Nanjing winter runs 7 °C colder than one in Savannah, Georgia. Pack warm clothing for the cold months.

January averages 3.1 °C (37.6 °F). The lowest temperature ever logged was −14.0 °C (6.8 °F), on 6 January 1955. The average July temperature is 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), and one record puts the highest daily temperature at 43.0 °C (109.4 °F), reached on 13 July 1934. Another record series since 1951 gives a maximum of 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959, so the sources disagree on the extreme high. Annual mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F).

Rain falls on about 112.9 days a year (days over 0.1 mm), with a record of 160 days in 1957, and yearly precipitation averages 1,144 millimetres (45.0 inches). Typhoons are unusual but can arrive in late summer and early autumn. Possible sunshine hours range by month from 37 percent in June up to 48 percent in August and October; in total the city gets 1,932.4 hours of bright sun a year.

Nanjing has more than 40 kinds of minerals; its iron and sulfur reserves account for 40 percent of those in Jiangsu, and its strontium reserves are the largest in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water is plentiful, from the Yangtze and from groundwater, and the city has natural hot springs such as Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou.

Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake lie in the city centre and anyone can visit them, and Purple Mountain, wooded with broadleaf and conifer species, shelters a number of historic and cultural landmarks. A deep-water channel on the Yangtze was under construction at the time of writing, intended to let 50,000 DWT ships sail in from the East China Sea.

Air pollution deserves mention. A thick smog began on 2 December 2013 across central and eastern China and stretched about 1,200 kilometres (750 miles), reaching Tianjin, Hebei and Shandong in the north and Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang further south. Little cold air movement, slow air masses carrying industrial emissions and mainly sulfur dioxide pollution built a heavy layer over the region. Central and southern Jiangsu were hit worst, especially around Nanjing, where the air quality index stood at "severely polluted" for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to calm winds, car exhaust under low pressure and coal-fired district heating in northern China, with prevailing winds pushing factory emissions towards the east coast. This was one event and conditions change, so check current air-quality readings when you plan your stay.

Soils fall into two broad groups. The natural, zonal group is yellow-brown across the north and centre and red in the far south near Anhui, and while the cultivated soil, shaped by farming, is mainly paddy soil with some yellow Gang soil and vegetable-garden soil. The pattern follows the terrain and water conditions and falls into low mountain and hill areas, hill areas and plains. The second national soil survey (1980 to 1987) divided the soils into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species across 416,300 hectares.

The Yangtze crosses the city diagonally from southwest to northeast over a stretch of about 93 kilometres, and the city is more than 300 kilometres from the river mouth. The Qinhuai River comes up from the south, flows north through the main built-up area and joins the Yangtze; it is known as Nanjing's "mother river". Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are described as two pearls set into the city. Water now covers about 11% of the city's area.

Nearly all rivers and lakes belong to the Yangtze system. The exception is a few streams in northern Liuhe District that drain to Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake, which are part of the Huai system. The Yangtze system itself has several parts: the Qinhuai on the south bank, the Chuhe on the north bank, riverside streams feeding in from both sides, a pair of lakes (Shijiu and Gucheng) and the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and its quality excellent; the Pukou Pearl Spring is especially famous, and the Tangshan area in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou are long-established hot-spring areas.

The Port of Nanjing is China's largest inland port, handling 191,970,000 tonnes of cargo in 2012. The port runs 98 kilometres (61 miles) along the river and has 64 berths, 16 of which take ships above 10,000 tonnes. It is also the biggest container port on the Yangtze: in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area opened with a capacity of one million containers. By 2010 the port operated six public and three industrial harbours. The river's 12.5-metre-deep waterway lets 50,000-tonne ocean-going ships reach the port directly, and ships of 100,000 tonnes or more can arrive after unloading part of their cargo at high tide. CSC Jinling operates a large shipyard here.

Nanjing is among the places in China with rich plant life. Natural vegetation comes in seven types. There are conifer woods and deciduous broadleaf woods, along with mixed stands of deciduous and evergreen broadleaf trees, then bamboo groves, scrub, grassland and water plants. Planted vegetation covers field crops, vegetables, commercial forests, orchards and green belts. Seven species are under national key protection as rare or endangered; they include Sphaerocarpus sinensis and Pterocarpus sinensis, together with Chinese Allium chinense and Ming Codonopsis.

Wildlife is varied too: 795 species of insects from 125 families in 11 orders, 99 species of fish from 22 families and 12 orders, and 327 species of land vertebrates from 29 orders and 90 families. Within that total are 243 bird species (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 mammal species (22 families, 8 orders). Nine animals get top-level national protection, for instance the Oriental white crane and the white-shouldered eagle. Another 65 have second-level status; the little swan, Chinese tiger, swallowtail butterfly and finless porpoise are examples. Jiangsu also protects 125 key species and lists 35 endangered ones.

Nanjing has discovered 49 kinds of minerals, from metals such as iron, copper, lead and zinc to strontium, ferrosulfide, dolomite, limestone, gypsum and clay, and 31 of them have proven reserves. The deposits cluster in four metallogenic belts, among them the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen belt of iron, copper and sulfur, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt.

Nanjing's first Yangtze bridge was finished in the 1960s; at that point it was the sole bridge across the lower Yangtze in the east of the country. It became a source of national pride and a symbol of modern China, since Chinese engineers designed and built it after foreign surveys failed and after relying on, then rejecting, Soviet expertise. Work began in 1960 and traffic started in 1968. It is a two-level road and rail bridge, 4,600 metres (15,100 feet) long on the upper deck, of which about 1,580 metres (5,180 feet) cross the river itself.

Four additional bridges and four tunnels have followed. Moving downstream, the crossings are the Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel, the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel, the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Baguazhou Bridge and the Qixiashan Bridge. The six numbered bridges with their opening years and longest spans:
First Bridge (Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge): opened 1968, longest span 160 m
Second Bridge (Baguazhou): opened 1997, longest span 628 m
Third Bridge (Dashengguan): opened 2005, longest span 648 m
Fourth Bridge (Qixiashan): opened 2012, longest span 1,418 m
Fifth Bridge (Jiangxinzhou): opened 2020, longest span 600 m
Xianxin Bridge: opened 2023, longest span 1,760 m

The 2010 census counted 8.005 million people in the city of Nanjing, and the OECD then estimated the wider metropolitan area at 11.7 million. Official statistics for 2011 gave 8.11 million, with 6.47 million in the urban area. Recorded rates were 8.86 percent for births and 6.88 percent for deaths, and there were 107.31 men for every 100 women.

The Han make up 98.56 percent of the population, which is typical of eastern China, and 50 other official ethnic groups are also present. A 1999 count found 77,394 residents from minority groups, and most of them (64,832, or 83.76 percent of the minority total) were Hui. The Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) were the second and third largest groups. Most minority residents lived in Jianye District, where they made up 9.13 percent of the population.

Nanjing is an important grain and commercial farming base for China. Rice and cotton are the leading cash crops, followed by silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea, bamboo, fruit and medicinal herbs, and the fertile waters on both sides of the Yangtze make it a significant freshwater fishing base too.

In 2019 the total output of agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishing was 47.250 billion yuan, up 4.8% on the year before. Farming contributed 24.077 billion yuan, forestry 2.017 billion, livestock 2.435 billion, fishing 15.389 billion and related services 3.333 billion.

Nanjing is a transport hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze region, with a land, water and air network that works in three dimensions. As in most Chinese cities, public transport is how most people travel. By October 2014 the city had four bridges and two tunnels across the Yangtze, linking the districts north of the river to the centre on the south bank. For a student, that means the metro and buses are the sensible way to reach campus and explore the city.
Nanjing Normal University lists 393 programs for international students on this site: 79 bachelor, 104 master's, 80 doctoral, 130 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 337 taught in Chinese, 56 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,600 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 19,900), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,200 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 18,200), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 24,000 to CNY 45,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.

393 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
