nanjing-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanjing Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Nanjing Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Nanjing University, often shortened to NJU, is a state university with a presence in two Jiangsu cities, Nanjing and Suzhou. The Ministry of Education sponsors it and it is formally affiliated to the ministry. Its membership of Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme marks it as a national priority, and it sits in the C9 League, a group of nine elite Chinese research universities.

The institution began in 1902 as Sanjiang Normal School. Over the following decades it was renamed repeatedly: first Nanjing Higher Normal School, later National Southeastern University, then National Central University. The name Nanjing University arrived in 1950, and the University of Nanking was merged into it two years later, in 1952.

NJU is spread over four sites. The Gulou campus is in the middle of Nanjing, the Xianlin campus is in the north-east of the city, and the Pukou campus is in Nanjing's Pukou District. The fourth site is in a different city altogether: Suzhou. When you apply, check which campus hosts your chosen programme, since the sites are far apart.

Teaching staff, counting part-time appointments, include more than twenty Nobel laureates. Fifteen of its academic disciplines carry the national Double First-Class label, which is a sign of breadth as well as depth.

nanjing-university.h: The motto and where it came from

blocks.x: The official motto reads, in English, "Sincerity with Aspiration, Perseverance with Integrity". In characters it is 诚朴雄伟 励学敦行 (simplified) or 誠樸雄偉 勵學敦行 (traditional), pronounced chéng pǔ xióng wěi lì xué dūn xíng. The opening half, "Sincerity with Aspiration", comes from the period when the university was National Central University. The second half, "Perseverance with Integrity", borrows from classical Chinese sayings.

The history of the motto has several steps. It started with Li Ruiqing, head of Liangjiang Higher Normal School, which was NJU's ancestor. He inscribed a proverb about vegetable roots: whoever can chew them can achieve great things (嚼得菜根 做得大事). Decades later, under National Central University, President Luo Jialun officially made "Sincerity with Aspiration" the motto. After the People's Republic was founded in 1949 the university went through repeated reorganisations and mergers, and for a long time no official motto existed. The present wording was adopted at the centenary celebrations in 2002, after wide consultation among staff and students, under President Jiang Shusheng.
Nanjing Higher Normal School first used the song in 1916. Jiang Qian wrote the words, and Li Shutong (also known as Hong Yi) composed the tune.
Several rankings are worth knowing, although every list uses its own method.
As of 2025, an aggregate of the four most closely followed rankings (THE, ARWU, QS and US News) gave NJU these positions: 68th worldwide, 14th in Asia, and 7th within China.
The Times Higher Education table for 2027 puts it 59th globally, 13th in Asia and 7th in China.
Shanghai's Academic Ranking of World Universities for 2026 lists it 70th worldwide, 12th in Asia and 6th in China.

For research output, the 2025 Nature Index annual table placed it 6th among universities in China and in the Asia-Pacific, and 7th among universities worldwide. It has been in the Nature Index's world top 20 universities every year since 2016.

Across ARWU, QS, THE and U.S. News & World Report, NJU consistently lands inside the global top 150. Older tables tell a similar story. In the combined THE-QS list for 2007 it was fourth in China (behind Peking, Tsinghua and Fudan), seventeenth in Asia and 125th worldwide. By the 2011 Times Higher Education table it had improved to 120th in the world, sixteenth in Asia and, again, fourth in China. In 2017 it fell in the 91 to 100 band of THE's World Reputation Ranking, QS ranked it 114th overall, and its QS Graduate Employability placing was 101st worldwide.

The domestic Netbig table, compiled by a higher-education publisher since 1999, kept NJU in the top three until 2005 and in the top five in its latest edition. The Academic Ranking of World Universities, produced since 2003 by Shanghai Jiao Tong University, has put it between second and seventh in China.

Since the national entrance examination was restored in 1977 after the Cultural Revolution, NJU has produced more alumni elected to the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering than any other university, over a period of more than 30 years.

The record goes back further. In 1931 the Republic of China held its first examination for senior civil service posts, seen as a revival of the imperial examination. One hundred candidates were chosen, all men, and 25 of them were NJU graduates, including the top scorer (zhuangyuan), Chow Bangdao, who later headed China Medical College and served as Political Deputy Minister of Examination. Peking University was second with 8 graduates. In the second round in 1933 women also passed, and half of them came from NJU. So did the top scorer, Lee Hsuehteng, a law graduate who became Chief Justice of the ROC Supreme Court. In the first 60-odd years of the Republic of China, a quarter of its Chief Justices were alumni of National Central University, the forerunner of NJU.
In natural science, including mathematics, Academia Sinica elected 53 academicians for the first time, and 28 of them had studied or taught at NJU.

nanjing-university.h: Nanjing, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Student life depends heavily on the city: its climate, how you move around and what you can do there. The sections below describe Nanjing, home of Nanjing University.

The city covers 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 square miles) in the heart of the lower Yangtze drainage area. It belongs to the Yangtze River Delta, which is among the largest economic zones in China. The Yangtze passes the west side of the city and then the north side, and the Ningzheng Ridge curves around the north, east and south. To place it on the map, Luoyang is 650 kilometres (400 miles) to the north-west, Beijing 900 kilometres (560 miles) to the north-north-west, Shanghai 270 kilometres (170 miles) to the east-south-east, and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) to the west-south-west. Shanghai is the nearest of the big cities, which is handy for trips.

Below Jiujiang in Jiangxi, the Yangtze continues through Anhui and Jiangsu before reaching the East China Sea. Two river basins flank the lower Yangtze: the Huai River basin to the north and the Zhe River basin to the south. The Grand Canal, east of Nanjing, joins the two. The Nanjing area is called the Xiajiang (下江, "Downstream River") region, in which Jianghuai culture dominates the north and Jiangzhe the south. It is also well known by the names Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, "south of the river").

Among its neighbours inside Jiangsu are Yangzhou (north-east), Zhenjiang (east) and Changzhou (south-east). Anhui Province forms the western border, and five of its cities touch Nanjing: Chuzhou in the north-west, Xuancheng in the south-west, and Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan along the west.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) and is driven by the East Asian monsoon. Expect four clear seasons, with moisture in the air all year round, scorching and muggy summers, cold and wet winters, and spring and autumn of decent length. Together with Chongqing and Wuhan, the city has long been named one of three "Three Furnaces" on the Yangtze because summer temperatures stay so high. Yet between mid-June and the end of July the plum-blossom season arrives with the meiyu, East Asia's rainy season (the word literally means "plum rain"), which brings light showers and extra dampness. A north-east wind blows in winter.

Despite that reputation, winters are cold for the city's latitude. They match or undercut London's, and a Nanjing January is 2 °C colder than London's even though Nanjing is at 32°04'N and London at 51°30'N. Compared with Savannah, Georgia, on the humid subtropical east coast of the USA, Nanjing's winter is 7 °C colder.
The numbers are as follows.
The January average is 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the coldest daily minimum ever noted was −14.0 °C (6.8 °F) on 6 January 1955.
A south-east wind dominates the summer. July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), and the highest daily maximum recorded was 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on 13 July 1934.
There are 112.9 days a year with more than 0.1 mm of precipitation (about 113 on average), and the maximum was 160 in 1957. Annual rainfall averages 1,144 millimetres (45.0 inches).
The annual mean temperature is roughly 16.4 °C (61.5 °F).
Looking only at records since 1951, the range is from the −14.0 °C (7 °F) of 6 January 1955 up to 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959.
Sunshine, as a share of what is possible, varies from 37 per cent in June to 48 per cent in August and October, which totals 1,932.4 hours of bright sun in a year.
Typhoons are unusual but can arrive in late summer and early autumn. Pack for damp cold in winter, because it feels colder indoors than the thermometer suggests.

Nanjing is well supplied with natural resources, including more than 40 types of minerals. Iron and sulfur reserves account for 40 per cent of the provincial total in Jiangsu, and its strontium reserves are the largest in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water is plentiful, whether from the Yangtze or from underground. Natural hot springs also exist, among them Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou.

Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake lie in the middle of the city, where the public can easily reach them. Purple Mountain is covered in both deciduous and coniferous woodland that protects various historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel is being built on the Yangtze so that Nanjing can take 50,000 DWT vessels coming from the East China Sea.

On 2 December 2013 a dense bank of smog formed across central and eastern China, across roughly 1,200 kilometres (750 miles), touching Tianjin and Hebei, Shandong, Jiangsu and Anhui, and also Shanghai and Zhejiang. Little cold air was moving, and slow air masses carried industrial emissions, so pollutants built up into a thick layer. Central and southern Jiangsu were badly affected, particularly Nanjing and its surroundings, where the air quality index (AQI) stayed at "severely polluted" for five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to the lack of wind, vehicle exhaust under low air pressure, and the coal-fired district heating of northern China. Prevailing winds pushed low-lying masses of factory emissions, mostly SO2, toward the east coast.

Two kinds of soil dominate: zonal soil and cultivated soil. Zonal soil is yellow-brown in the northern and middle parts of the city, and red in the south near the Anhui border. Cultivated soil, which farming created, is mainly paddy soil, with smaller amounts of yellow Gang soil and soil from vegetable gardens. Where each kind occurs depends on relief and water conditions, and the city divides into low mountain and hill land, hill land and plain. A national soil survey carried out between 1980 and 1987 (the second such survey) sorted Nanjing's soils into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species across 416,300 hectares.

Nanjing sits on the lower Yangtze, which crosses the city diagonally from south-west to north-east over a stretch of about 93 kilometres, more than 300 kilometres from the river mouth. The Qinhuai River, called the "mother river" of Nanjing, runs from south to north through the main urban area before joining the Yangtze. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are set in the urban core like two pearls. Water makes up about 11 per cent of the city's area.

Almost all of the city's waterways belong to the Yangtze system. The exception is the group of streams in the north of Liuhe District that feed Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake, which fall in the Huai system. Within the Yangtze system there are several parts: the Qinhuai system on the south bank, the Chuhe system on the north bank, the small-river riverside network draining into both sides, the paired lakes Shijiu and Gucheng, and the West Taihu Lake system in the east of Gaochun. The city has rich groundwater of very high quality, with the Pukou Pearl Spring the best known. The Tangshan area of Jiangning and the Tangquan area of Pukou have enjoyed hot springs for a very long time.

The Port of Nanjing is the biggest inland port in China. Cargo handled in 2012 amounted to 191,970,000 tonnes. The port area stretches 98 kilometres (61 miles) and has 64 berths, 16 of them for ships over 10,000 tonnes. Nanjing is also the largest container port on the Yangtze: in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area, with a capacity of one million containers, opened and strengthened the city's lead in the region. By 2010 the operation comprised six public and three industrial ports. A 12.5-metre-deep channel in the Yangtze lets ocean ships of 50,000 tonnes reach Nanjing directly, and ships of 100,000 tonnes or more can arrive too if they lighten their load during the river's high-tide period. CSC Jinling operates a large shipyard.

Nanjing has abundant plant resources and many kinds of plants. Seven natural vegetation types are present: conifer woods, deciduous broad-leaved woods, mixed woods of deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved trees, bamboo groves, scrub, grassland and water plants. Planted vegetation takes the form of field crops, vegetables, economic forests, orchards and green belts. Seven plants, including Sphaerocarpus sinensis, Chinese Allium chinense, Ming Codonopsis and Pterocarpus sinensis, are rare or endangered species under national protection.

Among wildlife, the city has 795 species of insects from 125 families in 11 orders, and 99 species of fish from 22 families in 12 orders. Land vertebrates number 327 species from 29 orders and 90 families. Of these, 243 are birds (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 are mammals (22 families, 8 orders). Nine species get first-level national protection (the Oriental White Crane and White-shouldered Eagle are examples), 65 get second-level protection (including the little swan, the Chinese tiger, the swallowtail and the finless porpoise), 125 are key protected animals in Jiangsu Province, and 35 are endangered.

The city has 49 discovered types of mineral resources, for instance strontium, ferrosulfide, dolomite, limestone, gypsum, clay and the metals iron, copper, lead and zinc, and 31 of them have proven reserves. They concentrate in four metallogenic belts: the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur polymetallic belt, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt. The source text breaks off before naming the fourth, so look for an official survey if you need it.

The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge was completed during the 1960s, and back then no other bridge spanned the lower Yangtze anywhere in eastern China. It meant a great deal beyond transport: Chinese engineers planned and built it on their own, after other countries' surveys had failed and after the country had relied on Soviet expertise and then dropped it, so people saw it as a proud emblem of a modernising China. Work began in 1960 and the bridge opened in 1968. It has two levels, one for road and one for rail, and its upper deck is 4,600 metres (15,100 feet) long, of which about 1,580 metres (5,180 feet) cross the river itself.

Since then the city has added four further bridges and four tunnels. In order going downstream, the crossings are the Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge and the Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge.

Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge, the Second Bridge: opened 1997, longest span 628 m.

In the 2010 census the city of Nanjing had 8.005 million inhabitants, and the OECD put the larger metropolitan area at 11.7 million. Official figures for 2011 estimated the city at 8.11 million, with a birth rate of 8.86 per cent and a death rate of 6.88 per cent. Within the built-up area lived 6.47 million people, and the city's male-to-female ratio was 107.31 to 100.

Like most of eastern China, Nanjing is overwhelmingly Han in its official makeup (98.56 per cent), with 50 other recognised ethnic groups. In 1999 there were 77,394 residents from official minorities. By far the biggest group was the Hui, with 64,832 people, or 83.76 per cent of the minority population. Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) were second and third. Most minority residents lived in Jianye District, where they were 9.13 per cent of the population.

Nanjing is one of China's significant bases for grain, both for farming and for trade. Rice, cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea, bamboo, fruit and medicinal herbs are the leading cash crops. The fertile waters on both banks of the Yangtze also make it one of the country's important freshwater fishing bases.
For 2019, the combined output value of agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fisheries was 47.250 billion yuan, up 4.8 per cent on the previous year. The breakdown was as follows.
Agriculture: 24.077 billion yuan
Forestry: 2.017 billion yuan
Animal husbandry: 2.435 billion yuan
Fisheries: 15.389 billion yuan
Support services for these sectors: 3.333 billion yuan

Nanjing is the main transport hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze region. Land, water and air links together form a three-dimensional transport system. As in most Chinese cities, most residents rely mainly on public transport. In October 2014 four bridges and two tunnels crossed the Yangtze, joining the districts north of the river to the city centre on the south bank.
Nanjing University lists 52 programs for international students on this site: 51 bachelor, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 52 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 21,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.

52 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

NUAA (南京航空航天大学), whose full name is Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, is known in Chinese shorthand as Nanhang, is a public university in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu Province. It is supervised by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, so its identity is closely tied to China's aviation, space and defence industries. Three national designations apply to it: Project 211, the Double First-Class Construction plan, and the "Seven Sons of National Defence", a group of universities with a defence-technology background.

nanjing-university-of-aeronautics-and-as.h: From aviation college to national university

blocks.x: Its first incarnation, in October 1952, was the Nanjing College of Aviation Industry. Four years later, in 1956, it became the Nanjing Aeronautical Institute, and in 1993 it took the name it carries today.

nanjing-university-of-aeronautics-and-as.h: Where you will study: the campuses

blocks.x: NUAA works across three campuses, with a fourth, an international campus, still being developed in the Jiangbei New District of Nanjing. Each has a Chinese nickname that you will hear in conversation. The Ming Palace campus (Minggugong) is simply called "Headquarters". The Jiangjun Road campus (将军路) is "Jiangning Campus". The third, Tianmu Lake, is known as "Liyang Campus".

This campus lies in Nanjing's Qinhuai District. Zhongshan East Road runs along its southern edge, Ruijin Road along the north and Mido Street on the east. It occupies ground where the imperial palace of the Ming Dynasty once stood, and the site of the Imperial Temple on that land is now the location of the present campus garden. A stream that used to be the old imperial river, the Royal Belt River, cuts through the grounds. Two rows of stately French sycamores add to the setting, and the Jiangsu Aviation and Aerospace Museum is on the premises as well.

The Jiangning campus is in Nanjing's Jiangning District, with Baijia Lake on its eastern side and General Mountain and Cuiping Mountain on the west. The Nanjing Airport Expressway divides it into an eastern and a western half, joined by flyovers and culverts. The west side contains 22 residential halls, 7 instructional buildings, 5 dining establishments and 1 engineering training facility. On the east side you will find thirteen residential buildings, four cafeterias and three instructional buildings.

Tianmu Lake is in the south of Liyang, a county-level city southeast of Nanjing. Four roads frame it: Meilingyu Avenue in the north, East Binhe Road in the south, South Street in the east and South Yanshan Road in the west. It covers 969 acres, with a total construction area of about 530,000 square meters planned.

Research is organised around a handful of flagship facilities, which are listed here by field. Two State Key Laboratories concern flight itself:

The programme count is large: 46 at undergraduate level, 127 at master's level and 52 at doctoral level. Two first-level disciplines hold national key status, Aerospace Science & Technology and Mechanics. Nine second-level disciplines hold the status too. Four are mechanics subjects (Fluid Mechanics, Solid Mechanics, Engineering Mechanics, and General and Fundamental Mechanics). The other five are Mechanical Manufacture & Automation, Aircraft Design, Man-Machine and Environmental Engineering, Manufacturing Engineering of Aerospace Vehicle, and Aerospace Propulsion Theory & Engineering.

Other tiers of recognition exist as well. Eight disciplines are designated key by the national defence science and technology commission (the Commission of National Defense Science, Technology and Industry), among them Technology of Micro Air Vehicles and Tele-Communication & Information Systems. Ten more, such as Mechanical Design and Theory and Navigation Guidance & Control, are key disciplines of Jiangsu Province. Four disciplines were specially created for "Changjiang Scholar Award" professors: Engineering Mechanics, Aircraft Design, Manufacturing Engineering of Aerospace Vehicle and Mechanical Manufacture & Automation. NUAA also runs 12 postdoctoral programmes, including Aerospace Science & Technology.

Large-scale recruitment of foreign students started around 2005, after the College of International Education was set up. The first full-time international undergraduates that year came from neighbouring countries such as Nepal and Pakistan and studied Aerospace Engineering. Over 400 international students have graduated since that time, in Software Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, International Business and Aerospace Engineering. More than 470 undergraduates from 40 countries are enrolled now, including Nepal, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh in South Asia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Sri Lanka, Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and Kenya, Ghana and Nigeria.

Postgraduate international students have also been admitted for some years, and dozens of master's and PhD students have graduated across different specialties. Scholarships are available to outstanding international students at both levels, under government schemes that include the China Government Scholarship and the Distinguished International Students Scholarship.

Exchange students visit too. Under exchange and summer programmes with universities in Australia, Canada, France and Germany, dozens of students come every year to study at undergraduate or postgraduate level.

International students have helped raise NUAA's research profile abroad. In 2018, a paper by a Pakistani doctoral student of Distinguished Professor Liu Sifeng was cited by the Nature Index and later indexed in Essential Science Indicators, the database of the world's top 1% most highly cited publications.
NUAA's engineering record gives a sense of what its students and staff work on:
In 2014 the university produced three Unmanned Ornithopters.
An aircraft designed by NUAA engineering students took first place at the American Helicopter Society's 33rd annual Student Design Competition in 2016.
The university has produced many highly cited scientific papers, some of which Nature Index has picked up.
Faculty, students and research staff have built over 40 drones (unmanned aerial vehicles, UAVs) for China since the university was founded.

In 2017 the AG600 "Kun dragon" (Kun Long), designed as the world's largest amphibious aircraft, made its first successful test flight. Its other developer was the China Aviation Industry General Aircraft Co., Ltd., which worked on it alongside the NUAA Innovation Center, and NUAA contributed work that included the engine cooling systems.

NUAA's own academic output includes the following titles. Grey Systems: Theory and Applications is one, and the university's Transactions and its Journal (both titled "Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics") are the general ones; two more cover specialist fields:
Journal of Date Acquisition and Processing
Journal of Vibration Engineering

Several well-known people are linked to NUAA. Among teachers and scholars: Liu Sifeng is internationally known for his expertise in Grey Relational Analysis and Grey System Theory; Jeffrey Yi-Lin Forrest teaches mathematics, systems science, economics and finance at Slippery Rock, in the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education (SSHE), is a guest professor at Nanhang, and founded and presides over the IIGSS (International Institute for General Systems Studies); Ye Peijian is a renowned Chinese aerospace scientist; and Çetin Kaya Koç is a cryptographic engineer. Here are alumni from industry and public life:
In aircraft design: Wu Guanghui, who designed the COMAC C919 airliner; Huang Lingcai, behind the AVIC AG600; and Wu Ximing, chief designer of the Z-10, Z-11 and Z-19 helicopters
In industry: Lin Zuoming, who chairs the Board of AVIC and is also a politician, and Hu Wenming, formerly head of China State Shipbuilding Corporation
In government: Liu Weiping, Governor of Gansu Province, and Lü Zushan, Governor of Zhejiang Province
In the arts: Chen Duling, an actress

The weather, the way you travel and the places you spend your free time will shape your years at NUAA almost as much as the classroom. The sections below introduce Nanjing, the city around the university.

Within the Yangtze River Delta, Nanjing's land area is 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 sq mi), set in the heart of the lower Yangtze River basin, within the Yangtze River Delta, one of China's largest economic zones. The Yangtze passes the city's west side and then its north side, while the Ningzheng Ridge curves around the north, east and south. Distances give a sense of position. Shanghai is 270 kilometres (170 mi) to the east-southeast, Beijing lies 900 kilometres (560 mi) to the north-northwest, Luoyang is 650 kilometres (400 mi) away to the northwest, and Chongqing is 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) to the west-southwest.

Starting at Jiujiang in Jiangxi, the Yangtze runs on through Anhui and then Jiangsu before it reaches the East China Sea. In the lower basin the Huai River basin lies to the north and the Zhe River basin to the south, with the Grand Canal east of Nanjing connecting them. People call the surrounding area the Xiajiang (下江, Downstream River) region, where Jianghuai culture dominates in the north and Jiangzhe in the south. It is also known as Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, South of the Yangtze).

Yangzhou borders it on the northeast, then comes Zhenjiang on the east, and Changzhou on the southeast. To the west, Nanjing meets Anhui Province and five of its prefecture-level cities: Chuzhou in the northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan in the west, and Xuancheng in the southwest.

nanjing-university-of-aeronautics-and-as.h: Climate: hot summers, surprisingly cold winters

blocks.x: The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) and is shaped by the East Asian monsoon. The year has four distinct seasons, and dampness lasts through all of them. Summers are very hot and muggy, winters cold and damp, and spring and autumn are reasonably long. The city is traditionally counted, with Chongqing and Wuhan, among the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze because of its constant summer heat. From mid-June to the end of July the plum blossom blooming season brings the meiyu, the East Asian rainy season (literally "plum rain"), with spells of gentle rain and humidity. Winter's prevailing wind is from the northeast.

For all that furnace reputation, winters surprise newcomers. For its latitude (32°04'N) Nanjing is cold: in winter it is about as cold as London, or colder, which sits at 51°30'N, and January is 2 °C colder than in London. Compared with Savannah, Georgia, on the humid subtropical US East Coast, Nanjing's winter is 7 °C colder. Pack warm clothes.

January averages 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the lowest daily minimum ever recorded was -14.0 °C (6.8 °F) on 6 January 1955. In summer the prevailing wind comes from the southeast, July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), and the record daily maximum was 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on 13 July 1934. Rain of more than 0.1 mm falls on 112.9 days a year on average, with a record of 160 days in 1957, while 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in) of precipitation falls in an average year.

Typhoons are unusual but can arrive in late summer and early autumn. Over the year the mean is near 16.4 °C (61.5 °F), and the 24-hour average swings from a July high of 28.4 °C (83.1 °F) down to a January low of 3.1 °C (37.6 °F). Since 1951 the extremes have been -14.0 °C (7 °F) on 6 January 1955 and 40.7 °C (105 °F) on 22 August 1959. Precipitation falls on about 113 days of the year, totalling 1,144 millimetres (45 in). Between 37 percent (June) and 48 percent (August and October) of possible sunshine is received each month, so the city gets 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine a year.

Nanjing has a rich endowment of natural resources, including more than 40 kinds of minerals. Iron and sulfur reserves amount to 40 percent of the totals in Jiangsu province, and its strontium reserves rank first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water is plentiful too, from the Yangtze and from groundwater, and there are natural hot springs too, at Tangquan in Pukou and Tangshan in Jiangning.

In the middle of the city, open to the public, are Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake. Purple Mountain, covered in deciduous and coniferous forest, shelters a variety of historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel is also being built in the Yangtze so that Nanjing can take vessels of 50,000 DWT arriving from the East China Sea.

Pollution has been a concern. A thick wave of smog began across central and eastern China on 2 December 2013, stretching roughly 1,200 kilometers (750 mi) over seven provincial-level areas: Tianjin, Hebei, Shandong, Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang. Little cold air was moving, and slow air masses loaded with industrial emissions trapped pollutants in a dense layer. Central and southern Jiangsu were badly hit, Nanjing especially: its air quality index read "severely polluted" for five days running and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to calm winds, vehicle exhaust in low air pressure and north China's coal-fired district heating; the prevailing winds pushed low air masses carrying factory emissions (mostly SO2) towards the east coast.

Two broad kinds of soil occur: zonal soil and cultivated soil. In the north and centre of the city the zonal soil is yellow-brown, while red soil lies in the south along the Anhui border. Farming has created cultivated soil, mainly paddy soil, alongside some vegetable garden soil and yellow Gang soil. How soils are distributed follows the rise and fall of the land and the water conditions, and falls into three groups: low mountain and hilly areas, hilly areas, and plains. A national soil survey carried out from 1980 to 1987, the second of its kind, divided Nanjing's soil into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species across a total of 416,300 hectares.

The Yangtze crosses Nanjing diagonally from southwest to northeast. Its course through the city is about 93 kilometers, and the sea entrance is more than 300 kilometers away. From south to north the Qinhuai River rushes through the main urban area before meeting the Yangtze, and it is known as Nanjing's mother river. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are described as two pearls set in the main city. Water covers about 11% of the city. Almost everything belongs to the Yangtze system; only the rivers that run into Baoying Lake and Gaoyou Lake, in the north of Liuhe District, are part of the Huai River system, whereas the rest of the waterways are Yangtze water. The Yangtze system includes the Qinhuai River system south of the Yangtze, the Chuhe River system to its north, a riverside system of small streams joining from both banks, the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun, and a two-lake system made up of Gucheng Lake and Shijiu Lake. Groundwater is abundant and of excellent quality, and the Pukou Pearl Spring is especially famous. Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou are long-established hot spring areas.

China's biggest inland port is the Port of Nanjing, which in 2012 handled 191,970,000 t of cargo. Its port area runs 98 kilometers (61 mi) and has 64 berths, 16 of them for ships over 10,000 tonnes. It is also the biggest container port on the Yangtze: in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area opened with a one-million-container capacity, which strengthened Nanjing's lead in the region. As of 2010 it ran six public ports and three industrial ports. With a 12.5-meter-deep waterway, 50,000-ton ocean ships can come straight to the port, and vessels of 100,000 tons or more can reach it too, after reducing their load, at high tide on the Yangtze. CSC Jinling has a large shipyard here.

Plant life is varied: Nanjing is among China's regions with abundant plant resources. Natural vegetation falls into 7 types: bamboo forest, shrub, grass and aquatic vegetation, along with three kinds of woodland (coniferous, deciduous broad-leaved, and mixed deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved). Cultivated vegetation covers field crops, vegetable crops, economic forests, orchards and green belts. Among rare and endangered plants under key national protection are seven species, such as Ming Codonopsis, Pterocarpus sinensis, Sphaerocarpus sinensis and Chinese Allium chinense.

Insects are the largest wild animal group, with 795 species from 125 families in 11 orders, and 99 species of fish from 22 families in 12 orders. Terrestrial wild vertebrates number 327 species from 29 orders and 90 families; of these 243 are birds (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 are mammals (8 orders, 22 families). Nine species, among them the Oriental White Crane and the White Shoulder Eagle, enjoy first-level national protection. Sixty-five get second-level protection, for example the little swan, the Chinese tiger, the swallowtail and the finless porpoise. Jiangsu Province lists 125 key protected animals, and 35 species are endangered.

So far 49 types of mineral have been found, such as limestone, dolomite, gypsum, clay, strontium, ferrosulfide and the metals iron, copper, lead and zinc. Reserves are proven for 31 of them. Most are concentrated in 4 metallogenic belts: the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur polymetallic belt, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt.

Nanjing's bridges are part of its story. The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, finished in the 1960s, was then the only bridge over the lower Yangtze in eastern China. It was a point of national pride and a symbol of modern China: it was designed and built by Chinese engineers, after other nations' surveys failed and after the country first relied on and then rejected Soviet expertise. Work began in 1960 and traffic opened in 1968. It has two tiers, for road and rail; the upper deck spans 4,600 metres (15,100 ft), of which about 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) cross the river itself. Four more bridges and four tunnels have followed. Counting from the upstream end, the bridge crossings are the Dashengguan, Third, Fifth, First, Baguazhou and Qixiashan bridges. Tunnels are interleaved with them: the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道) and the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel.
The bridges, with their opening years and longest spans, are:
Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge (First Nanjing Yangtze Bridge): opened 1968, longest span 160 m
Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge (Second): opened 1997, longest span 628 m
Nanjing Dashengguan Yangtze River Bridge (Third): opened 2005, longest span 648 m
Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge (Fourth): opened 2012, longest span 1,418m
Nanjing Jiangxinzhou Yangtze River Bridge (Fifth): opened 2020, longest span 600 m
Nanjing Xianxin Yangtze River Bridge: opened 2023, longest span 1,760 m

In the 2010 census Nanjing had 8.005 million inhabitants, and the OECD put the wider metropolitan area at 11.7 million at that time. An official estimate for 2011 gave the city 8.11 million people, 6.47 million of them in the urban area. The death rate stood at 6.88 percent against a birth rate of 8.86 percent, and there were 107.31 men for every 100 women.

As in most of eastern China, the Han nationality predominates officially (98.56 percent); another 50 official ethnic groups account for the remainder. A count in 1999 found 77,394 residents in officially defined minorities, and the vast majority, 64,832, were Hui, who made up 83.76 percent of that minority population. Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) were the second and third largest groups. Most minority residents lived in Jianye District, where they made up 9.13 percent of that district's residents.

Nanjing is an important agricultural and commercial grain base for China. The main cash crops include rice, cotton, tea, bamboo, hemp, silkworm cocoons, fruit and medicinal herbs, and thanks to the fertile waters on both sides of the Yangtze it is also a significant freshwater fishery base.

Combined output from agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery came to 47.250 billion yuan in 2019, which was 4.8% higher than the previous year. Agriculture contributed 24.077 billion yuan, fishery 15.389 billion, animal husbandry 2.435 billion, forestry 2.017 billion, and the service industry for all four sectors 3.333 billion.

Nanjing is the transport hub of eastern China and the downstream Yangtze area, with a three-dimensional system that combines land, water and air links. As in most Chinese cities, public transport is how most people travel. Since October 2014 the Yangtze has been crossed by four bridges and two tunnels which connect the northern districts to the downtown area on the south bank.

For a student, the practical points are straightforward. Expect a very hot, humid summer, a wet early summer, and a winter colder than the latitude suggests. Expect, too, a big, well-connected river city with mineral and water wealth, a major inland port and an agricultural base.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanjing-university-of-aeronautics-and-as.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, abbreviated NJUCM (南京中医药大学), is a public university in Nanjing, the provincial capital of Jiangsu. It belongs to the Jiangsu provincial system and is included in the Double First-Class Construction, the national scheme for strengthening selected universities and subject areas.

NJUCM dates from 1954, which makes it one of the earliest universities of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) in China, and it claims first place among the country's universities that focus entirely on traditional Chinese medicine. In 2018 it had close to 20,000 students on its three campuses, Xianlin, Hanzhongmen and Taizhou, and the student body includes international students. Its teaching covers 33 undergraduate programmes, 7 master's programmes and 4 doctoral programmes.

The university was established in 1954. It has used several names, and tracing them shows how the institution grew from a training school into a full university. It began as the Jiangsu Traditional Training School (江苏省中医进修学校, Jiāngsū Shěng Zhōngyī Jìnxiū Xuéxiào), then turned into a provincial TCM school, the Jiangsu Provincial School of Traditional Chinese Medicine (江苏省中医学校). After that came a spell as a branch of Jiangsu New Medical College (江苏新医学院), described in the records as its branch library, then as Nanjing Traditional Chinese Medicine College (南京中医学院, Nánjīng Zhōngyī Xuéyuàn). The present name, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, has been in use since 1995.
NJUCM stands in a famous old city, an ancient capital with a long and varied history. It operates three campuses, which have different ages and locations, so check which one your programme uses.

The Xianlin campus is the newer one, opened in 2002. Its buildings cover 418,253 square metres and house teaching rooms, laboratories, libraries, offices, student dormitories and other facilities. The Taizhou campus is the most recent, having opened in 2020. The Hanzhongmen campus is the oldest of the three, located in central Nanjing.
Xianlin: 138 Xianlin Road, in Nanjing's Qixia District
Hanzhongmen: 282 Hanzhong Road, in Nanjing's Gulou District
Taizhou: 6 Kuangshi Road, in the Pharmaceutical High tech District of Taizhou

The university is organised into 17 schools and institutes, and it is linked to a number of hospitals and companies. As a leading TCM institution it has built up both clinical research and teaching. Two libraries together hold more than a million printed volumes, which places them among the largest collections of Chinese-medicine books anywhere.

The first library was set up in 1954 and was then called the library of the Jiangsu Traditional Chinese Medicine Training School. The current Jingwen Library on the Xianlin Campus opened in 2005 thanks to a generous gift from Dr. Chu Ching-wen, a prominent educational industrialist.

The holdings are impressive. There are more than 3,000 kinds of ancient book in over 40,000 volumes, which is about 40% of the ancient Chinese medicine books that survive today. Readers get open access every year to 1,056 kinds of printed journals in Chinese and foreign languages, along with 21,000 kinds of journals overall, and database resources of 96 kinds. Another thing to note is the electronic collection of about 1 million books, again in Chinese and foreign languages.

The library aims to become a distinctive university library that combines knowledge services with research, placing resources, technology and service at the centre, and it works to promote practical use of Chinese medicine literature.
Clinical training uses a very large network of affiliated hospitals, mostly across Jiangsu. In Nanjing and the immediate region they include:
Two hospitals that carry the university's own name, the Affiliated Hospital and the Second Affiliated Hospital
The Nanjing TCM Hospital, Bayi Hospital and Nanjing General Hospital
Two integrated Chinese and Western medicine hospitals, one run for the city (Nanjing) and one for the province (Jiangsu)
The Gulou Clinical Medicine School of Integrated Chinese and Western Medicine

Across other Jiangsu cities there are TCM hospitals attached to the university in Changzhou, Wuxi, Suzhou, Taizhou, Nantong, Yangzhou, Xuzhou, Yancheng, Jiangyin, Kunshan, Changshu, Jiangyan, Zhangjiagang, Lianyungang, Zhenjiang, Wujin, Taicang, Huai'an, Suqian and Rugao. Clinical medicine schools of integrated Chinese and Western medicine also operate in Wuxi, Nantong and Lianyungang, and Xuzhou Central Hospital is a further affiliate. Beyond Jiangsu, the university is also linked to Hebei Yiling Hospital.
The university is associated with three pharmaceutical companies:
SZYY Group Pharmaceutical Limited
Wai Yuen Tong
Jiangsu Kanion Pharmaceutical

nanjing-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: What the numbers mean for you

blocks.x: Some of this section's figures help with planning. With nearly 20,000 students across three campuses, NJUCM is mid-sized, and since each campus has its own address, it is wise to confirm early where your programme is taught. Xianlin, opened in 2002, holds the modern teaching and research facilities, while the Taizhou campus, opened in 2020, is in a different city altogether, in the Pharmaceutical High tech District.

The very large hospital network is a real attraction for clinical training. Besides the city's own TCM hospitals, there are partner hospitals in around twenty other Jiangsu cities, so a student's clinical placement may involve travel within the province.

Readers interested in historical medical texts should note the library's ancient-book collection, which represents 40% of the surviving ancient Chinese medicine books, and the open-access journals and databases that come with it.
Programmes are delivered through these schools and institutes, which give a sense of what you can study:
Basic Medicine, and three Clinical Medicine schools (First, Second and Third)
Medicine and Life Sciences, and Integrative Medicine
Pharmacy and Nursing
Health Economics and Management, and Psychology
Information Technology
Foreign Languages and International Education
Humanities and Political Education
The International Jingfang Institute
The Graduate School and the School of Continued Education

NJUCM was among the first advanced Chinese medicine institutions that the Ministry of Education authorised to recruit international students, and also students coming from Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. It broke new ground in 1993 by teaming up with RMIT University in Australia to run a Bachelor programme in Chinese Medicine. Eight overseas Chinese Medicine Centers have been created one after another in Oceania, Europe and America, and three of them, the Sino-Australia, Sino-Switzerland and Sino-France centers, have been recognised as national-level overseas Chinese medicine centers.

The university works hard to build understanding of Chinese medicine abroad, especially through its Confucius Institute and overseas centres. On 20 June 2010 it set up a leading Chinese Medicine Confucius Institute together with RMIT University of Australia. It maintains extensive contacts with more than 90 countries and regions, and has formal partnerships with universities, government agencies and academic organisations in over 30 countries and regions.

The World Health Organization designated NJUCM a Collaborating Center for Traditional Medicine on 5 August 1983, and the current term is its 9th in a row. Its terms of reference have two parts. One is to support the WHO's work in raising public awareness and sharing knowledge of traditional medicine, so that it is more available, accessible and affordable in member states. The other is to back the WHO's efforts to encourage communication and cooperation on traditional medicine, both inside countries and across borders, so that regional and global networks grow stronger.

The university's international pages are organised under headings such as annual reports on WHO collaboration, short collaboration news, links with government, exchange between universities, academic exchange, the Confucius Institute and joint projects.
Chen Guangcheng, a civil rights activist
Lang Yongchun, a Chinese television host

What a student's daily life is like depends heavily on the city, on how it feels through the seasons and on transport and things to do. This part describes Nanjing, home of Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine. NJUCM is a medical university, and several details here, such as medicinal crops, hot springs and rich plant life, connect nicely with that.

Nanjing is the transport hub of eastern China and of the area downstream on the Yangtze, with land, water and air services forming a three-dimensional network. Public transport carries most citizens, as in other Chinese cities. In October 2014 four bridges and two tunnels crossed the Yangtze, joining the districts on the north bank to the city centre on the south side.

nanjing-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Bridges and tunnels over the Yangtze

blocks.x: In the 1960s the first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge was completed. At that time it was the single bridge spanning the lower reaches of the Yangtze in eastern China. It was a matter of national pride and a symbol of modern China, as Chinese people designed and built it after foreign surveys failed and after the country had relied on Soviet expertise and then turned it down. Construction ran from 1960 to 1968, when it opened. It carries both road and rail on two levels: the upper deck is 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) long, including a river section of about 1,580 metres (5,180 ft).

Later came four more bridges and four tunnels. In order downstream, the crossings are Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge and the Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge.

First Bridge (Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge): opened 1968, longest span 160 m
Second Bridge (Baguazhou): opened 1997, longest span 628 m

At the 2010 census Nanjing had 8.005 million inhabitants, and the OECD thought the surrounding metropolitan area held 11.7 million. The official count for 2011 was 8.11 million. Urban residents numbered 6.47 million. The city's birth rate was 8.86 percent, its death rate 6.88 percent, and there were 107.31 men to every 100 women.

The Han nationality accounts for 98.56 percent of the population, which is typical for eastern China, and 50 other official ethnic groups also live in the city. A 1999 count found 77,394 people in officially defined minorities. Of these 64,832 were Hui, which is 83.76 percent of the total, with the Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) in second and third place. Jianye District had the highest concentration of minority residents, who made up 9.13 percent of its people.

Nanjing is a significant base for grain and commercial agriculture in China. The main cash crops are rice and cotton, tea, hemp, bamboo, silkworm cocoons, fruit and medicinal materials. Thanks to the rich waters on both sides of the Yangtze, it is also an important freshwater fishing base.
For 2019 the combined output value of agriculture, forestry, livestock and fishing came to 47.250 billion yuan, a 4.8% increase on the year before. The breakdown was:
Farming: 24.077 billion yuan
Fishery: 15.389 billion yuan
Livestock: 2.435 billion yuan
Forestry: 2.017 billion yuan
Services supporting these sectors: 3.333 billion yuan

The city covers 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 sq mi) of land. It lies in the central part of the lower Yangtze drainage area, inside the Yangtze River Delta, which counts as one of the largest economic zones in the country. The Yangtze runs past the city's west and then its north, and a ring of hills, the Ningzheng Ridge, closes in around the north, east and south.

From Nanjing, Shanghai is 270 kilometres (170 mi) away to the east-southeast, Beijing 900 kilometres (560 mi) to the north-northwest, Luoyang 650 kilometres (400 mi) to the northwest and Chongqing 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) to the west-southwest.

As for the river itself, it flows downstream out of Jiujiang in Jiangxi, crossing Anhui and Jiangsu before reaching the East China Sea. North of the lower Yangtze lies the Huai River basin, with the Zhe River basin on the southern side, and the Grand Canal east of Nanjing links the two. Known as Xiajiang (下江, the "Downstream River" region), the area has a northern Jianghuai part and a southern Jiangzhe part. It also carries the names Dongnan (东南, "the Southeast") and Jiangnan (江南, "South of the Yangtze").

Neighbours inside Jiangsu are Yangzhou in the northeast, Zhenjiang in the east and Changzhou in the southeast. Anhui lies on the west, with five prefecture-level cities touching Nanjing: Chuzhou (northwest), Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan (west) and Xuancheng (southwest).

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), and the East Asian monsoon influences it. Four seasons are clearly marked and the air is damp year-round. Summers bring heat and mugginess, winters are cold and wet, and spring and autumn last a reasonable time. Together with Chongqing and Wuhan, Nanjing has long been counted among the "Three Furnaces" on the Yangtze because of its steady summer heat. Between mid-June and the end of July the plum blossoms bloom and the meiyu, the East Asian rainy season (literally "plum rain"), brings a stretch of light rain and damp conditions. The northeast wind blows mostly in winter.

Remarkably, Nanjing is cold for its latitude. Its winter temperatures are about the same as London's or lower: its January is 2 °C colder than London's, though Nanjing is at 32°04'N and London at 51°30'N. Savannah, Georgia, on the US east coast shares the humid subtropical climate, yet Nanjing's winter is 7 °C colder.
Numbers to remember:
January averages 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the lowest daily minimum, −14.0 °C (6.8 °F), was recorded on 6 January 1955.
A southeast wind blows in summer. July averages 28.4 °C (83.1 °F), and the highest daily maximum, 43.0 °C (109.4 °F), was reached on 13 July 1934.
Days with more than 0.1 mm of precipitation numbered 112.9 on average, with a peak of 160 days in 1957. Annual precipitation averages 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in).

The annual mean temperature is about 16.4 °C (61.5 °F). Looking only at the period since 1951, the extremes were a low of −14.0 °C (7 °F) in January 1955 and a high of 40.7 °C (105 °F) in August 1959.
Sunshine hours total 1,932.4 a year. Possible sunshine is 37 percent in June at the low end and 48 percent in August and October at the high end.
Typhoons are rare, but they can appear late in summer and early in autumn.

Central and southern Jiangsu suffered badly, Nanjing and its surroundings above all: the AQI stayed at "severely polluted" for five days straight and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials put the blame on calm air, vehicle exhaust under low air pressure, and coal-fired district heating in the north of China. Winds pushed low air masses carrying factory emissions, mainly SO2, toward the east coast.

Nanjing has abundant natural resources, including over 40 kinds of minerals. Iron and sulfur reserves are 40 percent of Jiangsu's, and strontium reserves rank first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Water resources are rich too, from both the Yangtze and underground, and natural hot springs include Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou. These hot spring areas have a long history.

The city's lakes, Xuanwu and Mochou, sit in the centre and are readily open to the public. Forests of deciduous and coniferous trees cover Purple Mountain, where various historical and cultural sites are preserved. A deep-water channel is being built in the Yangtze so that Nanjing can take vessels of 50,000 DWT coming from the East China Sea.

Soil and mineral details are as follows. Zonal soil (yellow-brown in the north and centre, red in the south near the Anhui border) and cultivated soil (mostly paddy, with some yellow Gang and vegetable garden soil) are the two main groups. The soil varies with terrain and hydrology across low mountain and hilly areas, hilly areas and plains. In the second national soil survey of 1980 to 1987, Nanjing's soil fell into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species over 416,300 hectares.

Underground, 49 types of mineral have been discovered, among them clay, gypsum, limestone, dolomite and ferrosulfide as well as iron, copper, lead, zinc and strontium, and 31 of them have proven reserves. They are concentrated in four metallogenic belts, such as the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur belt and the Ningwu iron and copper belt.

Over about 93 kilometres the Yangtze runs on a diagonal through the city, southwest to northeast, and the sea is over 300 kilometres away. The Qinhuai River flows south to north through the main urban area into the Yangtze and is called Nanjing's mother river. Xuanwu and Mochou lakes are two pearls in the main city, and water covers around 11% of the area.

Almost all of the water network belongs to the Yangtze system; only rivers entering Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake, in northern Liuhe District, drain to the Huai. The Yangtze system comprises the Qinhuai network south of the river and the Chuhe north of it, a riverside system of small streams, the two lakes Shijiu and Gucheng, and the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and of excellent quality, and the Pearl Spring at Pukou has a special reputation.

The Port of Nanjing is the biggest inland port in China, with 191,970,000 t of cargo in 2012. It spans 98 kilometres (61 mi) of port area with 64 berths, 16 of which handle ships above 10,000 tons. It is also the biggest container port on the Yangtze: the Longtan Containers Port Area, a base able to handle one million containers, opened in March 2004. In 2010 the port consisted of six public and three industrial ports. A 12.5-metre waterway allows 50,000-ton ocean ships to reach the port directly, and larger ships of 100,000 tons or more can also get in at high tide once they have reduced their load. CSC Jinling runs a large shipyard.

Nanjing has a rich diversity of plants. Seven natural vegetation types occur here. Coniferous and bamboo forest are two; others are deciduous broad-leaved forest and mixed broad-leaved forest with both deciduous and evergreen trees; the rest are shrub, grass and aquatic vegetation. Cultivated vegetation consists of field crops, vegetables, commercial woods, orchards and green belts. Ming Codonopsis, Pterocarpus sinensis, Chinese Allium chinense and Sphaerocarpus sinensis are among seven rare and endangered plant species under national key protection.

Among the wildlife are 795 insect species in 125 families and 11 orders, 99 fish species in 22 families and 12 orders, and 327 species of land vertebrates in 29 orders and 90 families. Of the vertebrates, 243 are birds (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 are mammals (8 orders, 22 families). Nine species have first-level national protection, among them the White Shoulder Eagle and the Oriental White Crane. Sixty-five more are in the second level, including the finless porpoise, swallowtail, Chinese tiger and little swan. The province names 125 key protected animal species, and 35 are endangered.

NJUCM combines a 1954 founding and a clear identity as a TCM university with a large clinical network, an unusually rich library, and international programmes backed by WHO and Australian partnerships. Nanjing offers it a historic, well-connected setting, with hot summers, cold winters and plenty of green space.

Before you apply, it is worth reading the climate figures again. Nanjing's winters are colder than many newcomers expect, with January averaging 3.1 °C, while July averages 28.4 °C and feels very humid. The plum rain season in June and July adds more dampness, so lightweight rain gear and warm layers are both useful.

nanjing-university-of-posts-and-telecomm.h: About Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications

blocks.x: The Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications (NJUPT; 南京邮电大学) is a provincial public university in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. It is affiliated with the Province of Jiangsu. The university is part of the Double First-Class Construction.

Established in 1958, the history of the Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications can be traced to the training class for the cadres of the General Postal Administrations during the wartime in 1942. Thereafter, it underwent a series of name and structural changes, including the Posts and Telecommunications Training Department of Shandong University (山东大学邮电专科部) and Shandong Postal School (山东邮政专科学校). Zhao Zhigang, Chief of the then Wartime General Postal Administration, served concurrently as the head teacher of the training class and the principal of the school in succession during the period from 1942 to 1947. In 1948, the school was formally named the East China Posts and Telecommunications School at Yidu (now called Qingzhou), affiliated to the East China General Administration of Posts and Telecommunications. It then moved from Jinan, Shandong to Nanjing, Jiangsu in August 1949.

In December 1950, it was chronologically enlarged into the Nanjing School of Posts and Telecommunications under the direct control of the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, the East China School of Posts and Telecommunications, the Nanjing Institute of Posts and Telecommunications, and the Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications. After the reform of the leadership system of national universities in February 2000, the Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications started to be jointly administered by both the central and the provincial government, with the provincial government playing the principle role. In March 2013, the university merged with the Nanjing College for Population Management (南京人口管理干部学院).

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Nanjing, where Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications is located.

Nanjing, with a total land area of 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 sq mi), is situated in the heartland of the drainage area of the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, and in the Yangtze River Delta, one of the largest economic zones of China. The Yangtze River flows past the west side and then the north side of Nanjing City, while the Ningzheng Ridge surrounds the north, east and south sides of the city. The city is 650 kilometres (400 mi) southeast of Luoyang, 900 kilometres (560 mi) south-southeast of Beijing, 270 kilometres (170 mi) west-northwest of Shanghai, and 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) east-northeast of Chongqing. The Yangtze flows downstream from Jiujiang, Jiangxi, through Anhui and Jiangsu to the East China Sea. The northern part of the lower Yangtze drainage basin is the Huai River basin and the southern part is the Zhe River basin. They are connected by the Grand Canal east of Nanjing. The area around Nanjing is called Xiajiang (下江, Downstream River) region, with Jianghuai dominant in the northern part and Jiangzhe dominant in the southern part. The region is also well known as Dongnan (东南, South East, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, and River South, South of Yangtze).

Nanjing borders Yangzhou to the northeast; Zhenjiang to the east; and Changzhou to the southeast. On its western boundary is Anhui, where Nanjing borders five prefecture-level cities: Chuzhou to the northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu, and Ma'anshan to the west and Xuancheng to the southwest.

Nanjing has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) and is influenced by the East Asian monsoon. The four seasons are distinct, with damp conditions seen throughout the year, very hot and muggy summers, cold, damp winters, and in between, spring and autumn are of reasonable length. Along with Chongqing and Wuhan, Nanjing is traditionally referred to as one of the "Three Furnaces" along the Yangtze River for the perennially high temperatures in the summertime. However, the time from mid-June to the end of July is the plum blossom blooming season in which the meiyu (rainy season of East Asia; literally "plum rain") occurs, during which the city experiences a period of mild rain as well as dampness. The northeast wind prevails in winter.

Despite being called one of the "Three Furnaces", Nanjing has a cold climate for its latitude. Nanjing's winter temperatures are similar to, or lower than, those of London, and Nanjing's January is 2 °C colder to London's January, despite the fact that Nanjing is on 32°04'N and London is on 51°30'N. Comparing to the East coast of USA which has the same humid subtropical climate, Nanjing's winter is 7 °C colder than the winter of Savannah, Georgia.

The average temperature in January is 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the extreme daily minimum temperature is −14.0 °C (6.8 °F), which occurred on January 6, 1955. The southeast wind prevails in summer, with an average temperature of 28.4 °C (83.1 °F) in July and an extreme daily maximum temperature of 43.0 °C (109.4 °F), which occurred on July 13, 1934. The number of precipitation days greater than 0.1 mm was 112.9 days, and the extreme maximum annual precipitation days were 160 days in 1957. The average annual precipitation is 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in).

Typhoons are uncommon but possible in the late stages of summer and early part of autumn. The annual mean temperature is around 16.4 °C (61.5 °F), with the monthly 24-hour average temperature ranging from 3.1 °C (37.6 °F) in January to 28.4 °C (83.1 °F) in July. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −14.0 °C (7 °F) on January 6, 1955, to 40.7 °C (105 °F) on August 22, 1959. On average precipitation falls 113 days out of the year, and the average annual rainfall is 1,144 millimetres (45 in). With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 37 percent in June to 48 percent in August and October, the city receives 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine annually.

Nanjing is endowed with rich natural resources, which include more than 40 kinds of minerals. Among them, iron and sulfur reserves make up 40 percent of those of Jiangsu province. Its reserves of strontium rank first in East Asia and the Southeast Asia region. Nanjing also possesses abundant water resources, both from the Yangtze River and groundwater. In addition, it has several natural hot springs such as Tangshan Hot Spring in Jiangning and Tangquan Hot Spring in Pukou.

Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are located in the center of the city and are easily accessible to the public, while Purple Mountain is covered with deciduous and coniferous forests preserving various historical and cultural sites. Meanwhile, a Yangtze River deep-water channel is under construction to enable Nanjing to handle the navigation of 50,000 DWT vessels from the East China Sea.

A dense wave of smog began in the central and east parts of China on December 2, 2013, across a distance of around 1,200 kilometers (750 mi), including Tianjin, Hebei, Shandong, Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang. A lack of cold air flow, combined with slow-moving air masses carrying industrial emissions, collected airborne pollutants to form a thick layer of smog over the region. The heavy smog heavily polluted central and southern Jiangsu Province, especially in and around Nanjing, with its AQI pollution Index at "severely polluted" for five straight days and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials blamed the dense pollution on lack of wind, automobile exhaust emissions under low air pressure, and coal-powered district heating system in north China. Prevailing winds blew low-hanging air masses of factory emissions (mostly SO2) towards China's east coast.

There are mainly two types of soil in Nanjing: zonal soil and cultivated soil. The zonal soil is yellow-brown soil in the northern and central areas of Nanjing, and red soil in the southern part of the border with Anhui. The cultivated soil formed by human-made farming is mainly paddy soil, and there are some yellow Gang soil and vegetable garden soil. The distribution of soil presents a certain law with the undulation of topography and hydrological conditions, which can be divided into three categories: low mountain and hilly area, hilly area and plain area. According to the second national soil survey from 1980 to 1987, the soil in Nanjing is divided into 7 soil types, 13 subtypes, 30 soil genera and 66 soil species, with a total area of 416,300 hectares.

Nanjing is located at the lower reaches of the Yangtze River. The Yangtze River runs diagonally across the city from southwest to northeast. It is about 93 kilometers long and more than 300 kilometers away from the sea entrance. The Qinhuai River rushes from south to north, passes through the main urban area, and joins the Yangtze River. It is known as the mother river of Nanjing. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are like two pearls embedded in the main city. The water area of the city now accounts for about 11%. The river and lake water system mainly belongs to the Yangtze River system, and only the rivers that flow into Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake in the northern part of Liuhe District belong to the Huai River system. The Yangtze River system includes the Qinhuai River system in the south of the Yangtze River, the Chuhe River system in the north of the Yangtze River, the riverside system formed by small rivers that flow into the river on both sides of the river, the two lakes system composed of Shijiu Lake and Gucheng Lake, and the West Taihu Lake system in the east of Gaochun. The groundwater resources are abundant and the water quality is excellent, and the Pukou Pearl Spring is particularly famous. Jiangning Tangshan and Pukou Tangquan are hot spring areas with a long history.

The Port of Nanjing is the largest inland port in China, with annual cargo tonnage reached 191,970,000 t in 2012. The port area is 98 kilometers (61 mi) in length and has 64 berths including 16 berths for ships with a tonnage of more than 10,000. Nanjing is also the biggest container port along the Yangtze River; in March 2004, the one million container-capacity base, Longtan Containers Port Area opened, further consolidating Nanjing as the leading port in the region. As of 2010, it operated six public ports and three industrial ports. The Yangtze River's 12.5-meter-deep waterway enables 50,000-ton-class ocean ships directly arrive at the Nanjing Port, and the ocean ships with the capacities of 100,000 tons or above can also reach the port after load reduction in the Yangtze River's high-tide period. CSC Jinling has a large shipyard.

Nanjing is one of the regions with abundant plant resources and a wide variety of plants in China. The vegetation types are complex, including 7 types of natural vegetation including coniferous forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, mixed deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved forest, bamboo forest, shrub, grass and aquatic vegetation. Cultivated vegetation includes field crops, vegetable crops, and economic forests, orchards and green belts. Seven species such as Sphaerocarpus sinensis, Chinese Allium chinense, Ming Codonopsis, and Pterocarpus sinensis are national key protected rare and endangered plants. Among wild animals, there are 795 species of insects belonging to 125 families of 11 orders. There are 99 species of fish belonging to 22 families and 12 orders. There are 327 species of terrestrial wild vertebrates belonging to 29 orders and 90 families, 243 species of birds belonging to 56 families of 17 orders, and 47 species of mammals belong to 8 orders and 22 families. Among all animal species, 9 species of wild animals under national first-level protection, such as the Oriental White Crane and White Shoulder Eagle, 65 species of wild animals under the second-level protection, such as the little swan, Chinese tiger and swallowtail, and finless porpoise, and 125 key protected animals in Jiangsu Province Species, 35 species of endangered animals.

In the 1960s, the first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge was completed, and served as the only bridge crossing over the Lower Yangtze in eastern China at that time. The bridge was a source of pride and an important symbol of modern China, having been built and designed by the Chinese themselves following failed surveys by other nations and the reliance on and then rejection of Soviet expertise. Begun in 1960 and opened to traffic in 1968, the bridge is a two-tiered road and rail design spanning 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) on the upper deck, with approximately 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) spanning the river itself.  Since then four more bridges and four tunnels have been built.  Going in the downstream direction, the Yangtze crossings in Nanjing are: Dashengguan Bridge, Third Bridge, Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), Line 10 Metro Tunnel, Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), First Bridge, Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge and Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge.

Nanjing is rich in mineral resources. The discovered minerals include 49 types of iron, copper, lead, zinc, strontium, ferrosulfide, dolomite, limestone, gypsum, and clay, among which 31 are of proven reserves. Nanjing's minerals are mainly concentrated in 4 metallogenic belts, namely the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper metallogenic belt, Ningzhen iron, copper, and sulfur polymetallic metallogenic belt, Ningwu iron, copper.

At the time of the 2010 census, the total population of the City of Nanjing was 8.005 million. The OECD estimated the encompassing metropolitan area at the time as 11.7 million. Official statistics in 2011 estimated the city's population to be 8.11 million. The birth rate was 8.86 percent and the death rate was 6.88 percent. The urban area had a population of 6.47 million people. The sex ratio of the city population was 107.31 males to 100 females.

As in most of eastern China, the official ethnic makeup of Nanjing is predominantly Han nationality (98.56 percent), with 50 other official ethnic groups. In 1999, 77,394 residents belonged to officially defined minorities, among which the vast majority (64,832) were Hui, contributing 83.76 percent to the minority population. The second and third largest minority groups were Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533). Most of the minority nationalities resided in Jianye District, comprising 9.13 percent of the district's population.

Nanjing is one of China's important agricultural and commercial grain bases. The main cash crops are rice, cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea, bamboo, fruits, medicinal materials, etc. Due to the fertile water quality on both sides of the Yangtze River, it is also one of China's important freshwater fishery bases.

In 2019, the total output value of Nanjing's agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry, and fishery was 47.250 billion yuan, an increase of 4.8% over the previous year. Among them, the agricultural output value was 24.077 billion yuan, the forestry output value was 2.017 billion yuan, the animal husbandry output value was 2.435 billion yuan, the fishery output value was 15.389 billion yuan, and the agricultural, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery service industry output value was 3.333 billion yuan.

Nanjing is the transport hub in eastern China and the downstream Yangtze River area. Different means of transport constitute a three-dimensional transport system that includes land, water and air. As in most other Chinese cities, public transport is the dominant mode of travel for the majority of citizens. As of October 2014, Nanjing had four bridges and two tunnels over the Yangtze River, linking districts north of the river with the city center on the south bank.
