NJUST (南京理工大学), formally the Nanjing University of Science and Technology, is a public university in Nanjing's Xuanwu district, Jiangsu Province. Administratively it comes under China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, and the Ministry of Education and the Jiangsu provincial government also sponsor it. NJUST is in Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction scheme, two national programmes for strengthening leading universities.

nanjing-university-of-science-and-techno.h: A military engineering school that moved south

blocks.x: NJUST's roots go back to 1953, when it began as the Department of Artillery Engineering at the People's Liberation Army's Institute of Military Engineering in Harbin. From the start its stated purpose has been to serve national strategies and social progress. The campus moved to Nanjing in 1962, the university changed names several times, and the present name was settled in 1993. The inscription on the school badge dates from September 1998 and was written by Jiang Zemin, at that time both China's president and head of the Communist Party as its general secretary. The ministry that oversees NJUST has been the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology since June 2008.

nanjing-university-of-science-and-techno.h: What and how you can study

blocks.x: The university is multidisciplinary: its fields run from engineering and science to liberal arts, law, education, economics, business and management, supported by many centers, institutes, programs and administrative offices. Teaching and research run at undergraduate and postgraduate levels across 15 schools, which together offer 70 undergraduate majors, 116 master's programs and 49 doctoral programs, with 14 post-doctoral research stations. NJUST is also counted among the "Seven Sons of National Defence".

Under Project 211, NJUST was made a National Key University in 1995. A graduate school received the Ministry of Education's approval in 2000, and in 2011 it was authorised to build a 985 Advantage Discipline Innovation Platform. The Ministry of Education included it in the state's Double First-Class Construction in September 2017. As of June 2018 the university listed its colleges and schools, which you can find on its official website.

Unlike many Nanjing universities, NJUST has a single main campus. It stands in Xiaolingwei, Xuanwu District, by the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum and Purple Mountain, which lie to its north, and covers 3,118 mu (207.87 ha). The single-campus layout keeps teaching, laboratories and student life in one place. Check the university website for the latest campus maps and list of schools. Two related institutions exist outside it: Zijin College of NJUST, founded in 1998 in Xianlin University City in Nanjing, and Taizhou Institute of Science and Technology, a branch institute of NJUST started in June 2004 in Taizhou, Jiangsu.

Student life depends on the city around the campus, so the following sections describe Nanjing: its place on the map, its weather, its rivers and its people. The figures below come from different years, from 2010 up to 2023, so treat them as a snapshot rather than a current report.

Nanjing occupies 2,548 sq mi (6,598 square kilometres) of land at the centre of the lower Yangtze drainage area, inside the Yangtze River Delta, one of China's biggest economic zones. The Yangtze passes first along the west of the city and then along the north, while the Ningzheng Ridge forms a ring on the north, east and south sides. For orientation, Nanjing is 400 mi (650 kilometres) south-east of Luoyang, 560 mi (900 kilometres) south-south-east of Beijing, 170 mi (270 kilometres) west-north-west of Shanghai and 750 mi (1,200 kilometres) east-north-east of Chongqing.

Downstream from Jiujiang in Jiangxi, the Yangtze crosses Anhui and Jiangsu on its way to the East China Sea. The lower basin has a northern half, the Huai River basin, and a southern half, the Zhe River basin, which the Grand Canal links east of Nanjing. The surrounding area is called the Xiajiang (下江, "Downstream River") region; Jianghuai culture dominates its north and Jiangzhe its south. The region is also widely known as Dongnan (东南, the Southeast) and Jiangnan (江南, "south of the Yangtze").

Yangzhou lies to Nanjing's north-east, Zhenjiang to the east and Changzhou to the south-east. In the west the boundary is with Anhui, which supplies five prefecture-level neighbours: Chuzhou (north-west), Xuancheng (south-west) and, further west, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan.

The East Asian monsoon influences Nanjing's humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa). Seasons are distinct and the air is damp all year; summers are very hot and muggy, winters cold and damp, and spring and autumn are of reasonable length. Together with Chongqing and Wuhan, the city is traditionally known as one of the Yangtze's "Three Furnaces" because summer heat there is so persistent. Mid-June to the end of July, however, is meiyu, the East Asian rainy season (literally "plum rain"), when the plum blossoms bloom and the city has mild rain and dampness. Winter winds mainly come from the north-east.

In spite of the "Three Furnaces" label, Nanjing is cold for its latitude. Its winter temperatures match or fall below London's: January is 2 °C colder than London's January, though Nanjing is at 32°04'N and London at 51°30'N. Against the US East Coast, which shares a humid subtropical climate, Nanjing's winters are 7 °C colder than those in Savannah, Georgia. In practice that means a damp, cold winter that can surprise newcomers from warmer countries. Pack proper winter clothing.

The average January temperature is 3.1 °C (37.6 °F), and the lowest daily minimum on record is -14.0 °C (6.8 °F), from January 6, 1955. Summer brings south-east winds, a July mean of 28.4 °C (83.1 °F) and a record daily maximum of 43.0 °C (109.4 °F) on July 13, 1934. Days with at least 0.1 mm of precipitation average 112.9 a year, and the record was 160 days in 1957. The average annual precipitation is 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in).

Typhoons seldom come but can arrive late in summer or early in autumn. Annual mean temperature is roughly 16.4 °C (61.5 °F). Since 1951 the lowest reading is -14.0 °C (7 °F), on January 6, 1955, and the highest 105 °F (40.7 °C), on August 22, 1959. It rains on about 113 days each year. Sunshine is only 37 percent of the possible in June and 48 percent in August and October, so the year totals 1,932.4 hours of bright sunshine.

More than 40 kinds of minerals are found in Nanjing. Its reserves of iron and sulfur amount to 40 percent of those of Jiangsu province, and its strontium reserves rank first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Both the Yangtze and groundwater supply plenty of water, and the city has natural hot springs: Jiangning's Tangshan and Pukou's Tangquan.

Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake lie in the city centre and are easy for the public to reach. Purple Mountain, with deciduous and coniferous forests, protects many historical and cultural sites. A deep-water channel is being built in the Yangtze River so that Nanjing can handle 50,000 DWT vessels coming from the East China Sea.

On December 2, 2013 a thick smog began to spread over central and eastern China across roughly 750 mi (1,200 kilometers), taking in Zhejiang, Shanghai, Anhui, Jiangsu, Shandong, Hebei and Tianjin. Cold air hardly moved, and slow air masses loaded with industrial emissions let airborne pollutants build up into a heavy layer. Central and southern Jiangsu suffered most, especially around Nanjing, where the AQI pollution index read "severely polluted" five days in a row and "heavily polluted" for nine. Officials pointed to the lack of wind, vehicle exhaust under low air pressure and north China's coal-powered district heating, and prevailing winds carried low-lying air masses with factory emissions (mostly SO2) towards the east coast. That episode is a reminder to check daily air-quality readings in winter.

Two kinds of soil dominate Nanjing, zonal and cultivated. Zonal soil is yellow-brown in the north and centre and red along the southern edge where the city meets Anhui. Soil shaped by human farming is chiefly paddy soil, with patches of yellow Gang soil and vegetable garden soil. How the soils are distributed follows the relief and the water conditions, and can be grouped into three areas: plain, hills, and low mountains with hills. The second national soil survey (1980-1987) divided Nanjing's soils into 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species over 416,300 hectares in total.

Nanjing lies on the lower Yangtze, which crosses the city diagonally from south-west to north-east. About 93 kilometers of the river lie within the city, and the sea entrance is more than 300 kilometers away. From south to north the Qinhuai River flows through the main urban area into the Yangtze; people call it the mother river of Nanjing. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake sit in the main city like two pearls, and water covers about 11% of the city's area. Nearly all rivers and lakes belong to the Yangtze system, the exceptions being rivers feeding Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake in northern Liuhe District, which are part of the Huai River system. The Yangtze system itself has five parts: the Qinhuai River system south of the Yangtze; the Chuhe River system to its north; a riverside system of small streams entering from both banks; a two-lake system of Shijiu Lake and Gucheng Lake; and the West Taihu Lake system in eastern Gaochun. Groundwater is abundant and of excellent quality, with the Pukou Pearl Spring being particularly famous, and the hot spring areas of Jiangning Tangshan and Pukou Tangquan have a long history.

China's biggest inland port is the Port of Nanjing, which moved 191,970,000 t of cargo in 2012. Its 98 kilometers (61 mi) of port area contain 64 berths, 16 of which take ships above 10,000 tons. It is also the largest container port on the Yangtze: in March 2004 the Longtan Containers Port Area opened as a base able to handle one million containers, reinforcing Nanjing's leading position. As of 2010 the port consisted of six public ports and three industrial ports. A 12.5-meter-deep waterway in the Yangtze lets ocean ships of 50,000 tons sail straight to Nanjing Port, and ships of 100,000 tons or more can also reach it after reducing their load during the river's high tide. CSC Jinling runs a large shipyard here.

Nanjing has abundant plant life of great variety. Natural vegetation falls into 7 types: coniferous forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, mixed forest of deciduous and evergreen broad-leaved trees, bamboo forest, shrubland, grassland and aquatic vegetation. Crops, vegetables, orchards, economic forests and green belts make up the cultivated vegetation. Seven species are rare and endangered plants under national key protection, among them Pterocarpus sinensis, Sphaerocarpus sinensis, Chinese Allium chinense and Ming Codonopsis.

Among wild animals recorded are 795 species of insects (125 families, 11 orders), 99 species of fish (22 families, 12 orders) and 327 species of land vertebrates (29 orders, 90 families). The vertebrates include 243 bird species in 56 families and 17 orders, and 47 mammal species in 8 orders and 22 families. Nine wild species have first-level national protection, for example the Oriental White Crane and the White Shoulder Eagle; 65 have second-level protection, including the finless porpoise, swallowtail, Chinese tiger and little swan; 125 are key protected species in Jiangsu Province; and 35 species are endangered.

Nanjing's first Yangtze River Bridge, completed in the 1960s, was then the only bridge over the Lower Yangtze in eastern China, and it was a source of pride and an important symbol of modern China: Chinese engineers designed and built it themselves after foreign surveys had failed and after China had relied on, then turned away from, Soviet expertise. It was begun in 1960 and opened to traffic in 1968 as a two-tier road and rail bridge. The upper deck runs 15,100 ft (4,600 metres), of which about 5,180 ft (1,580 metres) crosses the river itself. Four more bridges and four tunnels have followed. Moving downstream, the city's Yangtze crossings are Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel (南京长江隧道), the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel (南京扬子江隧道), the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge and Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge. The main road bridges, in order of opening, are:
Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, also called the First Nanjing Yangtze Bridge: opened 1968, longest span 160 m
Nanjing Baguazhou Yangtze River Bridge, the Second: opened 1997, longest span 628 m
Nanjing Dashengguan Yangtze River Bridge, the Third: opened 2005, longest span 648 m
Nanjing Qixiashan Yangtze River Bridge, the Fourth: opened 2012, longest span 1,418m
Nanjing Jiangxinzhou Yangtze River Bridge, the Fifth: opened 2020, longest span 600 m
Xianxin Yangtze River Bridge in Nanjing, which opened in 2023 with a longest span of 1,760 m

Altogether 49 types of mineral have been found (they include clay, gypsum, limestone, dolomite, ferrosulfide, strontium, zinc, lead, copper and iron), and 31 of them have proven reserves. They cluster mainly in 4 metallogenic belts: the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur polymetallic belt, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt; the name of the fourth belt appears to be incomplete in the available data, so check geological sources for the full name.

In the 2010 census the City of Nanjing had a total population of 8.005 million, and the OECD put the surrounding metropolitan area at 11.7 million at the time. An official estimate for 2011 was 8.11 million. The urban area held 6.47 million people. The birth rate stood at 8.86 percent and the death rate at 6.88 percent, and men outnumbered women with a sex ratio of 107.31 males to 100 females.

Officially, Nanjing is mostly Han Chinese (98.56 percent), as in most of eastern China, and 50 other official ethnic groups live there. In 1999 there were 77,394 members of officially defined minorities, the vast majority of them (64,832) Hui, who made up 83.76 percent of the minority population. Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) were the next largest groups. Most minority residents lived in Jianye District, accounting for 9.13 percent of that district's population.

Nanjing is a significant base for grain farming and agricultural trade in China. Its chief cash crops are fruits, tea, bamboo, hemp, silkworm cocoons, cotton and rice, as well as medicinal materials. Fertile water along both banks of the Yangtze makes it a major freshwater fishery base too.

In 2019 the combined output value of farming, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery was 47.250 billion yuan, up 4.8% on the previous year. Agriculture accounted for 24.077 billion yuan, fishery for 15.389 billion, animal husbandry for 2.435 billion and forestry for 2.017 billion, with 3.333 billion more from the services that support these industries.

Nanjing is the transport hub of eastern China and the downstream Yangtze area, with a three-dimensional system of land, water and air links. As in most Chinese cities, most residents travel by public transport. By October 2014 the city had four bridges and two tunnels across the Yangtze, connecting the districts on the north side of the river to the downtown area south of it; the list above includes later crossings, so counts differ by date.
Nanjing University of Science and Technology lists 83 programs for international students on this site: 36 bachelor, 32 master's, 14 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 79 taught in Chinese, 4 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 24,000 to CNY 36,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 36,000 to CNY 44,200 (median CNY 36,000), according to the university's published fee table.

82 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (3):
Applied Chemistry
Chemical Engineering
Computer Science and Technology
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanjing-university-of-science-and-techno.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanjing University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Nanjing University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

nanjing-university-of-the-arts.h: Nanjing University of the Arts in brief

blocks.x: Nanjing University of the Arts, abbreviated NUA and also called the Nanjing Arts Institute (the Chinese name is 南京艺术学院), is a university which awards bachelor's and postgraduate degrees across the fine arts, design and neighbouring creative disciplines. If you are an applicant looking for a place in the arts rather than in engineering or business, this is the Nanjing option to read about.

The institution did not start in Nanjing. Its history begins in 1912 with Shanghai Chinese Art College. In 1930 that school took the name Shanghai Academy of Fine Arts. In 1952 a number of institutions were amalgamated, and the outcome was East China Arts College, located in Wuxi. The college moved to Nanjing in 1958 and adopted its present name in 1959. One piece of cultural heritage is worth noting: Cai Yuanpei wrote the words of the school song. The university has partnership programmes with the University of Dayton and with Hokuriku University, which can matter if you are interested in exchange.
Getting there is simple. The Caochangmen/NUA/JSSNU station on the Nanjing Metro serves the campus, so you can reach the university by rail without needing a car or a long bus ride.

nanjing-university-of-the-arts.h: Where you will be living: Nanjing

blocks.x: Choosing a university means choosing a city, and daily life will be shaped by Nanjing's position, weather, rivers and transport more than by any prospectus. The following sections give you a practical picture.

Nanjing covers about 6,598 square kilometres (roughly 2,548 square miles) in the heartland of the lower Yangtze River drainage area, which lies inside the Yangtze River Delta, one of China's biggest economic zones. West of the city the Yangtze flows by, and then it turns around the north; the Ningzheng Ridge forms a ring on the north, east and south sides.

The city's position relative to other well-known places gives you a feel for the geography. It is 650 km southeast of Luoyang, 900 km south-southeast of Beijing, 270 km west-northwest of Shanghai, and 1,200 km east-northeast of Chongqing. In miles that is about 400, 560, 170 and 750.

The great river arrives from Jiujiang in Jiangxi, crosses Anhui and Jiangsu and ends in the East China Sea. North of the lower Yangtze basin lies the Huai River basin, and south of it the Zhe River basin; the Grand Canal east of Nanjing connects the two. Local usage calls the surrounding region Xiajiang, meaning the downstream river region, in which Jianghuai influence is strongest in the north and Jiangzhe influence in the south. It is also known as Dongnan (the Southeast) and Jiangnan (south of the river).

Around Nanjing you will find Yangzhou northeast, Zhenjiang east and Changzhou southeast. Anhui Province lies along the western edge. Five of its cities share a border with Nanjing, namely Chuzhou in the northwest, Xuancheng in the southwest, and Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan in the west. These are the places most likely to appear on weekend trips and train timetables.

The climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa) and follows the East Asian monsoon. Four seasons are clear, humidity stays high year-round, summer is extremely hot and sticky, winter is cold and damp, and the two shoulder seasons last a decent time. The city shares with Chongqing and Wuhan the traditional nickname 'Three Furnaces' of the Yangtze, a reference to long summer heat. Between mid-June and the end of July the plum blossom season brings the meiyu, literally 'plum rain', a stretch of gentle rain and moist air. Winter winds come mostly from the northeast.

Do not underestimate the cold. Considering how far south Nanjing is (32 degrees 04 minutes north, against London's 51 degrees 30 minutes), it is a cold place: winter temperatures match London's or fall below them, and the January average is 2 degrees C lower than London's. In comparison with Savannah, Georgia, which has a similar climate class on the American east coast, a Nanjing winter is 7 degrees C colder.

The numbers are these. In January the mean is 3.1 C (37.6 F); in July it rises to 28.4 C (83.1 F); over twelve months the mean comes to roughly 16.4 C, or 61.5 F. The lowest temperature on record is -14.0 C (6.8 F), reached on 6 January 1955, and the highest is 43.0 C (109.4 F) on 13 July 1934; since 1951, readings have ranged between -14.0 C on that January day and 40.7 C (105 F) on 22 August 1959, which is a slightly different record period. Southeast winds are typical in summer. Precipitation of more than 0.1 mm falls on 112.9 days in an average year (the record is 160 days, in 1957), and the annual total is 1,144 mm, or 45.0 inches. Sunshine is moderate: the share of possible sunshine is lowest in June at 37 percent and highest in August and October at 48 percent, and the city gets 1,932.4 hours of bright sun in a year. Typhoons are rare but possible in late summer and early autumn.

Air quality is a fair question for any student. On 2 December 2013 a heavy blanket of smog formed over central and eastern China, for roughly 1,200 km (750 miles), covering Tianjin and Hebei in the north, Shandong, Jiangsu and Anhui in the middle, and Shanghai and Zhejiang on the coast. Windless conditions, slow air masses carrying industrial emissions and a lack of cold air trapped the pollution. Central and southern Jiangsu suffered most, and in and around Nanjing the air quality index showed 'severely polluted' for five days in a row and 'heavily polluted' for nine. The causes named by officials were still air, exhaust from cars under low pressure and coal-burning district heating in northern China, with prevailing winds carrying low-lying factory emissions, mostly sulphur dioxide, toward the coast. That was one episode, but it is sensible to check current conditions when you plan your stay.

nanjing-university-of-the-arts.h: Rivers, lakes and the inland port

blocks.x: Nanjing sits on the lower Yangtze, which crosses the city on a diagonal from southwest to northeast. The city's own stretch of the river is about 93 km long, and the river mouth lies more than 300 km away. The Qinhuai River flows from south to north across the central urban area to meet the Yangtze, and locals call it the mother river. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are often compared to two pearls set in the city. About 11% of the municipal area is water. The systems that matter belong almost entirely to the Yangtze; the exception is a group of rivers in northern Liuhe District that empty into the Gaoyou and Baoying lakes, which belong to the Huai system. That Yangtze family includes the Qinhuai system south of the river, the Chuhe system on the north bank, a riverside network of small streams, the Shijiu Lake and Gucheng Lake pair, and the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and good, and the Pukou Pearl Spring is especially well known. The hot spring areas of Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou have been used for a long time.

The city is also a major working harbour. Nanjing Port ranks first among China's inland ports: 191,970,000 tonnes of cargo passed through in 2012. The waterfront stretches 98 km and has 64 berths, of which 16 can take vessels over 10,000 tonnes. It is the largest container port on the Yangtze, strengthened in March 2004 by the opening of the Longtan Containers Port Area, built for one million containers. In 2010 it ran six public and three industrial port areas. With a 12.5 m deep channel, 50,000-ton ships can sail right up, and ships of 100,000 tons or more can arrive after lightening their load at high tide. CSC Jinling runs a large shipyard.

The city has more than 40 kinds of minerals; the city holds 40 percent of the province's iron and sulfur, and its strontium reserves are the biggest in East and Southeast Asia. Found minerals total 49 types, among them iron, copper, lead, zinc, strontium, iron sulphide, dolomite, limestone, gypsum and clay, with 31 having proven reserves. Four mineral belts hold most of them: the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur belt, and the Ningwu iron and copper belt. Water is rich in two senses, from the river and from underground, and the hot springs have already been mentioned. A deep-water channel on the Yangtze was being built to bring 50,000 DWT ships from the East China Sea. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake sit in the middle of the city and welcome the public, and Purple Mountain, covered in conifers and broadleaf woodland, protects many historical and cultural sites.

Two kinds of soil dominate. Natural zonal soil is yellow-brown in the north and centre and red in the south near the Anhui border. Soil shaped by farming is mainly paddy soil, with some yellow Gang soil and vegetable-garden soil. Their distribution follows relief and water, and the land is divided into low mountains, hills and plains. The national soil survey of 1980 to 1987 recognised 7 types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species across 416,300 hectares.

Vegetation is varied. Seven natural types are present: conifer forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, mixed forest, bamboo, scrub, grassland and water plants, with field crops, vegetables, orchards, economic forests and green belts added by people. The national list of protected rare plants includes seven found here: Pterocarpus sinensis, Ming Codonopsis, Chinese Allium chinense, Sphaerocarpus sinensis and three more. Wildlife records list 795 insect species (125 families, 11 orders), 99 fish species (22 families, 12 orders) and 327 land vertebrates (29 orders, 90 families), including 243 birds (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 mammals (8 orders, 22 families). Nine animals, the Oriental White Crane and the White Shoulder Eagle among them, receive the top level of national protection; 65, including the little swan, Chinese tiger, swallowtail and finless porpoise, receive second-level protection; and Jiangsu lists 125 key species with 35 endangered species.

Nanjing's first Yangtze bridge was completed in the 1960s and, at the time, was the only fixed link across the lower Yangtze in eastern China. China was proud of it: Chinese engineers designed and built it after outside surveys had failed and after the project had first drawn on Soviet expertise and then rejected it. Building started in 1960 and the bridge opened in 1968. It carries road traffic on top and trains below; the upper deck is 4,600 metres (15,100 feet) long, and about 1,580 metres (5,180 feet) of it is over the river proper. The years since have seen four more bridges and four tunnels.

Going downstream, the crossings are the Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel, the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel, the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Baguazhou Bridge and the Qixiashan Bridge. The bridges by order of opening are:
First Bridge: 1968, longest span 160 m (this seems small for such a bridge, so verify before using it).
Baguazhou Bridge, the Second: 1997, 628 m.
Dashengguan Bridge, the Third: 2005, 648 m.
Qixiashan Bridge, the Fourth: 2012, 1,418 m.
Jiangxinzhou Bridge, the Fifth: 2020, 600 m.
Xianxin Bridge: 2023, 1,760 m.

Transport in the city more generally is excellent. Nanjing is the hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze area, and land, water and air connections work together as one system. As in most Chinese cities, most people travel by public transport. By October 2014 four bridges and two tunnels connected the northern districts to the downtown area on the southern bank.

In the 2010 census, 8.005 million people lived in the city, and the OECD estimated that the wider metropolitan area held 11.7 million. The official 2011 estimate was 8.11 million. Of those, 6.47 million lived in the urban area. Births ran at 8.86 percent and deaths at 6.88 percent. There were 107.31 men for each 100 women.

Nanjing follows the usual eastern pattern: 98.56 percent of people are Han, and 50 other official ethnic groups make up the rest. The 1999 figure for minority residents was 77,394, and the Hui accounted for 64,832 of them, which is 83.76 percent. Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) came second and third. Jianye District had the most minority residents, who were 9.13 percent of its population.

Agriculture is still important. The area is a significant base for grain and commercial crops, and typical cash crops include rice, cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea, bamboo, fruit and herbal medicine plants. Fertile water on both banks of the Yangtze also makes it an important freshwater fishing area. In 2019 total output from farming, forestry, animal husbandry and fishing came to 47.250 billion yuan, 4.8% more than a year earlier. By sector: agriculture 24.077 billion yuan, forestry 2.017 billion, animal husbandry 2.435 billion, fishery 15.389 billion and services to these industries 3.333 billion.

A university shapes your life, but so does the region it belongs to. NUA belongs to Jiangsu Province, and this section sets out the long background that explains why Jiangsu looks the way it does today.

nanjing-university-of-the-arts.h: Early states and the southern capitals

blocks.x: In the earliest Chinese dynasties, what is now Jiangsu lay far from the centre of Chinese civilisation in the northwest of Henan, and it was home to an ancient group called the Huai barbarians. During the Zhou dynasty contact grew, and the state of Wu emerged in southern Jiangsu as one of hundreds of states then spread over northern and central China. Late in the Spring and Autumn period, King Helu made Wu a great power, and in 484 BC it beat Qi, a major northern state in present-day Shandong, as it competed to be overlord of all the Chinese states. In 473 BC the state of Yue, which had arisen to the south in modern Zhejiang, conquered Wu. Chu, a strong power from the west, then took Yue in 333 BC. In the end Qin removed all rivals and unified China in 221 BC.

During the Han era (206 BC to 220 AD) Jiangsu remained remote from the North China Plain, and two provinces shared it: Xu in the north and Yang in the south. Southern Jiangsu then served as the base of Eastern Wu (222 to 280) in the Three Kingdoms age; Wu's capital Jianye, renamed Jiankang later, stands where Nanjing is now. Nomadic invasions of northern China in the 4th century pushed the Jin court south to Jiankang, and cities of southern and central Jiangsu swelled with migrants from the north. Jiankang remained the capital of four Southern dynasties in succession and became the largest centre of trade and culture in China.

The Sui dynasty reunited the country in 581, and political power shifted north again, but the Grand Canal was dug through Jiangsu to join the Central Plains with the rich Yangtze Delta. The Tang dynasty (618 to 907) depended on southern Jiangsu for its yearly grain deliveries. In the Song dynasty (960 to 1279) a wealthy merchant class and an emerging market economy appeared, and Jiangnan, meaning southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and adjoining areas, became a centre of trade. From that point cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou stood for luxury and splendour in Chinese eyes, and the region is still one of the wealthiest parts of the country.

nanjing-university-of-the-arts.h: Division, Ming rule and Qing borders

blocks.x: In 1127 the Jurchen Jin dynasty took control of North China during the Jin-Song wars. The Huai River, which then ran across north Jiangsu to the Yellow Sea, marked the line between the Jin in the north and the Southern Song in the south. The Mongols took China in the 13th century. The Ming dynasty, founded in 1368 after the Mongols were driven out, first placed its capital in Nanjing, and the lands around the city, covering today's Jiangsu and Anhui, formed Nanzhili province (the name means 'southern directly governed'). Zhu Di, later the Yongle Emperor, seized the throne in a coup and moved the capital far north to Beijing, though Nanjing remained the southern capital. In the late Ming, Jiangnan was still a leading trade area. Some historians read the booming textile industry of the time as the start of industrialisation and capitalism, though the trend was cut short.
The Qing dynasty renamed Nanzhili as Jiangnan province, and in 1666 split Jiangsu and Anhui into separate provinces. Jiangsu's borders have changed little since.

From the 1840s, Western powers pushed into China, and the wealthy trading region of the Yangtze Delta felt their influence more and more. A small town in Jiangsu, Shanghai, quickly turned into a metropolis of commerce, banking and international life, and later became a municipality in its own right. Jiangnan also features strongly in the Taiping Rebellion of 1851 to 1864, a huge and deadly uprising that aimed to set up a Christian theocracy. The uprising started far away in Guangdong, moved through much of the south, and in 1853 its leaders took Nanjing as their capital and renamed it Tianjing, or 'Heavenly Capital'.

The Republic of China was founded in 1912 and warlords soon fragmented the country. Jiangsu changed hands several times. In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek set up a government at Nanjing and before long most of the country came under his authority. In 1928 the provincial government moved to Zhenjiang. The full-scale second Sino-Japanese War began in 1937, and on 13 December 1937 Nanjing fell. The atrocities committed by the occupying Japanese over the next three months are remembered as the Rape of Nanjing. Afterwards Nanjing served as the base of a collaborationist East China government headed by Wang Jingwei, and Japanese forces held most of Jiangsu until 1945.

With peace, Nanjing once more became the Republic of China's capital, yet the Civil War between the Kuomintang government and the Communist forces, based mainly in the northeast, had begun. The Huaihai Campaign, which decided the contest, took place in the north of Jiangsu and ended in Kuomintang defeat. The Communists crossed the Yangtze and took Nanjing. The Kuomintang retreated south and ended up in Taipei, from where the Republic of China government still administers Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands, while technically still claiming Nanjing as its legal capital. After the fall of Zhenjiang the provincial government relocated to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

After the Communist takeover, Beijing (then called Peiping) became the capital of the People's Republic and Jiangsu was dissolved into the Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. On 15 November 1952 Jiangsu Province was re-established and Nanjing was reduced to the rank of provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening-up policy began with the southern coast, in Guangdong, and Jiangsu lagged behind at first; from the 1990s the measures were applied more evenly across the country. Suzhou and Wuxi, two southern Jiangsu cities next to Shanghai, have since grown extremely rich: they are among China's top 10 cities by gross domestic product and have outstripped the provincial capital of Nanjing. Income differences between north and south Jiangsu remain large.
NUA offers an arts-focused education in a historic and well-connected city, in a province that is among the richest in China.

Two practical points follow from everything above. First, plan for Nanjing's real winters: indoor heating arrangements and warm clothing deserve as much thought as your portfolio, because January temperatures sit close to London's and sometimes below. Second, think about regional travel from the start. The Yangtze bridges and tunnels, the metro, the neighbouring cities of Zhenjiang, Yangzhou and Changzhou, and fast routes to Shanghai give an arts student plenty to visit on weekends. Check the university's own website for current programmes, entry requirements and exchange partners before you apply, and remember that the figures quoted in this profile come from different years, so they describe the general picture rather than today's exact numbers. Ask the admissions office about anything that affects your visa, fees or accommodation.

Nankai is a state-funded research university found in Tianjin and run under the Ministry of Education. It sits inside China's flagship programmes for top universities, namely Project 211, Project 985 and the current Double First-Class initiative, so it belongs to the small group of institutions the central government backs most heavily.

The school began as a privately founded institution in 1919, set up by Yan Xiu and Zhang Boling. The wartime years of 1937 to 1945 pushed it into a famous partnership with Peking University and Tsinghua University, and in December 2000 the Ministry of Education and the Tianjin municipal government agreed to develop it jointly.

The people connected with Nankai give a good sense of its weight. Zhou Enlai, who became the first Premier of New China, studied here. So did the mathematician Shiing-Shen Chern, while the Nobel physicists Chen Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee are counted among its alumni and faculty. Philosophy professor P.C. Chang taught here and later became vice-chair of the UN body that wrote the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

nankai-university.h: A private school with foreign money, 1919 to 1937

blocks.x: Nankai opened without any government funding. Its backing came from foreign charitable money and local business people, so it started small: only 96 students spread over three departments covering liberal arts, science and business. A distinctive feature was that many courses used foreign curricula and textbooks and were taught in English.

The Nankai Institute of Economics followed in 1927 and quickly became one of the best-known research centres of its kind in China. It was the first non-foreign body to compile a Chinese Consumer Price Index.

By 1937 the school had grown into a university with three colleges, 13 departments and two research institutes, although it still counted just 429 students and 110 staff. Its reputation was strong enough to earn it the nickname 'The North Star of Higher Learning'.

In July 1937, during the war with Japan, bombing wrecked the campus. Roughly two-thirds of the buildings were lost, including the library. Several artefacts, among them the university bell, were taken and are still held in Japanese museums.

A month later Nankai teamed up with Peking University and Tsinghua University in a joint wartime institution, first called the National Changsha Provisional University. It relocated to Kunming and took the name National Southwestern Associated University, the wartime institution still remembered in China by its short name Xinan Lianda. After the war Nankai went back to Tianjin in 1946 and was reorganised as a national university. It then had 16 departments grouped into four schools: Liberal Arts, Science, Engineering, and a combined school for Political Science and Economics.

After the People's Republic was founded, Nankai was restructured into a comprehensive university leaning towards arts and sciences, offering 14 departments plus three professional specialties. Normal academic life stopped during the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976. In 1976 the devastating earthquake at nearby Tangshan, on the edge of Tianjin, damaged buildings on campus to varying degrees.

In February 1978 the State Council revived the system of national key colleges, and Nankai was named the first of them. After 1980 new specialties and institutes arrived. On the arts side, applied finance programmes appeared and the School of Economics reopened in 1983, while the sciences gained interdisciplinary and high-technology fields.

Nankai was one of the first Chinese universities to welcome American students, in the 1980s. In 1989 local public security officials ordered two Americans to leave, amid political tension over the pro-democracy demonstrations. By the late 1980s the range had widened to take in management and art as well as the humanities and the natural, applied and life sciences.

Several structural changes followed. Tianjin Foreign Trade College merged into Nankai in 1994. TEDA College was created in 1999 together with the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area. The 2000 agreement with the city government came next, and it brought an experimental cooperation scheme with Tianjin University in which each school stays independent but works closely with the other. In 2002 Nankai, the Shenzhen government and UC Berkeley jointly set up a Financial Engineering College in Shenzhen.

Leadership news from later years shows how the university sees itself. In May 2006 President Rao Zihe reopened 15 of the 21 college dean posts to fresh appointments, aiming to strengthen teaching. In February 2015, when official voices called for universities to be purged of Western textbooks and other ideological influences, President Gong Ke publicly disagreed, saying he could not accept calls for academics to be cleansed and that such thinking belonged to 1957 or 1966. Prospective students will find that a good illustration of the debates around university life in China.
Indian students have also used Nankai as a study destination, and some have funded their studies through international exchange schemes such as the Swami Vivekananda Scholarship.

nankai-university.h: Where you will study: the three campuses

blocks.x: Nankai spreads across three campuses in and around Tianjin. The land area is given as 456.1 (the unit is missing in the original data; it appears to be hectares) and the built floor space as 136.8 hectares. Because the university's own figures are not fully clear, check the current numbers on its website.

Balitai in Tianjin's Nankai district has been the university's home since 1919. On the humanities and social side you will find literature, foreign languages, economics and business, together with an Institute of Japan Studies. The natural sciences are covered by mathematics, physics, chemistry and life sciences. Named in full, the units are the College of Foreign Languages, School of Literature, Business School, School of Economics, Institute of Japan Studies, School of Mathematical Sciences, College of Life Sciences, College of Chemistry and Institute of Physics. The list of ten colleges is given, but only nine names appear, so ask the admissions office where a particular subject is taught.

Jinnan opened in September 2015 in the Jinnan area and now accommodates fourteen colleges. Medicine and pharmacy are based here, as are law, finance, philosophy, history, Chinese language and culture, and tourism and service management. So are the technical colleges for software, computing and control, electronics and optics, and materials. The Zhou Enlai School of Government is here too. Their full names are the School of Medicine, College of Pharmacy, Law School, School of Finance, Faculty of Philosophy, College of History, College of Chinese Language and Culture, College of Tourism and Service Management, College of Software, College of Computer and Control Engineering, College of Electronic Information and Optical Engineering, School of Material Science and Engineering, and the Zhou Enlai School of Government.
The TEDA campus lies in the Binhai New Area and is home to two research institutes, one for biological sciences and biotechnology and one for applied physics.
In short, your subject decides which campus you live on, so find out early which site your programme uses.

Nankai teaches the arts, medical and life sciences, technology, natural sciences and humanities, and describes its balance between sciences and liberal arts as roughly even. It operates a two-semester calendar. The first term runs from early September to early January, and the second from early February to early July. That leaves a winter break of about a month and a summer break of about two months.

The figures it publishes show the scale. In 2013 it had 22 colleges and schools, with 79 bachelor's, 231 master's and 172 doctoral programmes, around 12,000 undergraduates and 11,000 graduate students, and about 10 percent international students. In 2018 the totals were 80 undergraduate programmes, 231 master's, 172 PhD programmes and 28 postdoctoral research stations, with 24,525 full-time students. The teaching staff numbered 1,986 full-time members, including 214 professors and 805 associate professors. These numbers are several years old now, so treat them as a guide and confirm current ones with the university.

International applicants have several funding routes to investigate. The Nankai University Scholarship and the Tianjin Government Scholarship come from the university and city, the Chinese Government Scholarship and the Confucius Institute Scholarship from national bodies, and there is a CSC scholarship aimed at American students. Exchange activity runs through the International Office, and the university reports partnerships with over 300 institutions abroad. Examples include a Chinese-language programme for elementary schools in the United States, launched in 2009, and the Study International programme of 2010, which set a target of sending 100,000 Americans to study in China within four years. Its first participants reached Nankai in autumn 2010.

Nankai received an invitation in 2012 to join the Global University Leaders Forum as its 35th member. The group already included Yale, Harvard and Oxford, which tells you the company the university keeps.

Another figure gives more than 200 partner universities and institutions for research exchange. Honorary professorships have been awarded to former South Korean president Kim Dae Jung and to Henry Kissinger, once US Secretary of State, as well as to Nobel laureates: Reinhard Selten, Robert A. Mundell, Samuel Chao Chung Ting, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang. Robert F. Engle, winner of the 2003 economics Nobel, became an honorary professor in November 2016.

Many other scholars and entrepreneurs hold visiting professorships. In 1987 Dr. Heng-Kang Sang returned from America and established the College of Economic and Social Development. Mathematics is a particular strength, and Nankai counts as one of the world's best-known mathematics centres. Shiing-Shen Chern built what is described as the largest mathematics institute in the world by office area. The university has opened nine Confucius Institutes abroad, and its scientists have contributed to a number of notable advances.

Nankai usually places in China's top ten, with 2017 and 2018 as exceptions. Several older results are on record. Renmin University's June 2011 list of 50 leading Chinese universities put it tenth, and so did the 2011 Netbig ranking. The 2013 QS World University Rankings had it 62nd in Asia and 11th in China, Wu Shulian's 2012 first-class university ranking placed it eighth, and the 2013 CWTS Leiden Ranking put it 53rd in the world and first in China. More recently, the Nature Index Global 2025 placed it 16th in the world and 12th in China.
Undergraduates choosing a major will want to know that mathematics, chemistry, history, business and economics are regarded as some of the best programmes in the country.
In 2018 the university enrolled 24,525 full-time students: 13,067 undergraduates, 8,162 master's students and 3,296 doctoral students. Of these, 1,902 were international students.

Campus life is only part of the picture, since the city shapes your daily routine: the weather, the way you get around and what you can do on weekends. This part of the profile describes Tianjin.

Tianjin lies on the west shore of the Bohai Gulf, with Shandong and Liaoning on the opposite side of the water. Beijing is 120 kilometres (75 miles) to the northwest. Hebei province surrounds the city on every side except the east, where the Bohai Sea forms the boundary. In coordinates, the municipality covers longitude 116°43' to 118°04' E and latitude 38°34' to 40°15' N, adding up to 11,860.63 square kilometres of land and water.

It has 153 km of coastline and 1,137.48 km of land border. At its northern end, the Grand Canal (which connects the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers) terminates in Tianjin. Most of the land is flat and swampy near the coast, with tidal flats on the coastal plain, though hills appear in the northern part, where the Yan Mountains extend into Tianjin. The highest point is Jiuding Peak in Ji County on the Hebei border, at 1,078.5 metres.

The Hai River forms inside the municipality where the Ziya, Daqing and Yongding Rivers and the North and South Grand Canals meet, and it reaches the sea in Tanggu District. The Beidagang Reservoir (Dagang District) lies to the south and the Yuqiao Reservoir (Ji County) to the north.

Tianjin has a semi-arid climate (Köppen BSk, bordering on Dwa and Cwa) with four distinct monsoon-influenced seasons. Winters are cold, windy and dry because of the Siberian anticyclone, and summers are hot and humid. Spring is dry and breezy, and sandstorms from the Gobi Desert sometimes blow in and can last several days.

The average temperature is about 13.3 °C over the year, ranging from -2.8 °C in January to 27.2 °C in July. Records from the main weather station, in Xiqing District, show a low of -22.9 °C and a high of 41.1 °C. Sunshine totals 2,460 hours a year, with the share of possible sunshine running from 45 percent in July to 61 percent in March and April. Annual rainfall is 521 millimetres, and nearly three-fifths of that comes in July and August. Some parts of the municipality count as humid continental.
Pack for a proper winter, and expect a dry, windy spring.

In May 2014 the city introduced rules to cut pollution. On severe pollution days they allow measures such as halving the number of vehicles on the road, stopping construction and manufacturing, closing schools and halting large outdoor events. In the past, flights have been grounded and highways closed. Professional athletes from abroad have said the air has interfered with sport and was thick enough to taste. Check the current situation before you arrive, as conditions may have changed since these measures were introduced.

nankai-university.h: The Tianjin economy and what it means for graduates

blocks.x: Tianjin's industries include petrochemicals, textiles, car manufacturing, machinery and metalworking. Airbus has run an assembly plant for its A320 series jets in the city since 2009. In 2010 the world's fastest supercomputer, Tianhe-1A, was installed at the National Supercomputing Center in Tianjin. For 2009 the city reported GDP of 750.1 billion yuan, which works out at 62,403 yuan per head. These figures are old, so use them for a sense of scale only.
Several special zones explain why the city draws so much investment.

Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA): one of the first state-level development zones, created on 6 December 1984 with State Council approval. It enjoys national preferential policies for attracting domestic and foreign investment into modern technology industries, and its administrative commission manages it with provincial-level economic and administrative powers on behalf of the city government.

Tianjin Export Processing Zone: one of the first 15 such zones approved by the State Council, on 27 April 2000. It is a sealed zone where customs officers supervise everything moving in and out, and it benefits from central government incentives for processing and trade enterprises. It lies northeast of TEDA with a planned area of 2.54 square kilometres, and a permanent wall separates it from the rest of the city.

Tianjin Airport Economic Area: an international logistics zone a joint venture of Binhai International Airport and the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone, located inside the airport's air-freight area. Its companies handle sorting, storage, distribution, processing and exhibitions, and it is under construction as the largest air-freight base in northern China.
Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone: northern China's sole free trade zone, which the State Council approved in 1991. It is 30 km from the city proper, under 1 km from the wharf and 38 km from the airport.

Tianjin Tanggu National Marine High-Tech Development Area: set up in 1992 and raised to national level in 1995, it is the sole national high-tech zone focused on marine technology. At the close of 2008 it was home to 2,068 companies in five industries, among them new materials, oil products, modern machinery and electronic information.

Tianjin Nangang Industrial Zone: a base for heavy and chemical industry and a harbour, part of Tianjin's strategy of two cities and two harbours, with a circular-economy approach. The planned area is 200 square kilometres, of which 162 square kilometres is land.

About 40 percent of the municipality is farmland, and wheat, rice and maize are the main crops. The municipality's oil reserves are put at roughly a billion tonnes, with oilfields in Dagang District. Salt is another product, and Changlu ranks among China's salt-making areas. Geothermal energy is a further resource, and deposits of manganese and boron were first discovered in China beneath Tianjin. Tianjin Electric Power Utility builds, runs and maintains the electricity network.

The Binhai New Area sits where the Beijing-Tianjin city belt meets the belt around the Bohai Sea. It serves as a gateway to North, Northeast and Northwest China and is the closest departure point for the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

At the end of 2009 the municipality had 12.28 million people, of whom 9.8 million held Tianjin hukou, the local residence registration. Of the permanent residents, 5.99 million lived in urban districts and 3.81 million in the countryside. Growth picked up afterwards, and by the end of 2013 the population was 14.72 million. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 15.4 million in 2010.

Most residents are Han Chinese, but people from 51 of China's 55 minority groups live in the city. The largest minorities are Hui, Korean, Manchu and Mongol communities. The figures exclude active-duty members of the People's Liberation Army.

nankai-university.h: Concession-era streets and the old city

blocks.x: The city mixes European architecture from the 19th and early 20th centuries with modern glass-and-concrete buildings, and much colonial architecture is protected even while redevelopment goes on.

The history behind it is a hard one. Behind the architecture lies a painful chapter. Western powers seized this port city in the 19th century after a quarrel involving a British ship, using armed gunboats to defeat Chinese forces. The Treaty of Tianjin of 1856 handed European nations nine concessions beside the Hai River, where they could trade and sell opium. Each concession ran as a self-contained enclave, with French châteaus and towers in one and German red-tiled Bavarian villas in another. Violence flared at a French orphanage in the Tianjin Incident of 1870, and again during the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, when foreign forces demolished the walls of the old city so they could watch the residents. Most of what remained of the old city was cleared in 2000 and 2001, sparing only a handful of historic buildings, for example the Tianjin Temple of Confucius.

Sightseers now walk the old concession streets, located west and south of the central railway station and south of the Hai River. The downtown on the south bank is French, with châteaus; the British mansions are east of it, and German-style buildings survive still further to the east and south.

Tianjin has three national nature reserves. Baxianshan has kept much of its original forest ecology thanks to long-term minimal human interference. In Jizhou District, the Middle-Upper Yuan Geologic reserve has been accepted by the International Union of Geological Sciences as a worldwide reference section of rock strata. The Ancient Coast and Wetlands reserve contains three characteristic shell ridges, which document how the sea withdrew and the Tianjin plain took shape.

Culturally, Tianjin holds two World Heritage listings: a stretch of the Grand Canal between Beijing and Hangzhou, and the Great Wall at Huangyaguan in the north of Jizhou District. Ancient Culture Street, a national 5A tourist attraction, is centred on the Tianhou Temple, the oldest surviving historic building group in the city and an important northern site of Mazu worship. Yangliuqing Town, famous for its New Year paintings, is a designated China Historical and Cultural Town.

Inside the city, Chinese, European and modern buildings stand together along the Haihe River. Its 'one bridge, one scene' lighting turned the river into a landmark, and it impressed overseas guests at gatherings such as the World Economic Forum. Time magazine ranked the Binhai Library, in Binhai New Area, number one among its World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018, in August of that year.

Museums have a long history in Tianjin, starting in the reforming years of the late Qing. The Musée Hoangho Paiho, set up in 1914 by the French Jesuit and naturalist Émile Licent, ranks among the earliest museums in China and made real contributions to palaeontology, geology, archaeology and museum studies.

Today there are three national first-class museums. The Tianjin Museum covers history and art and traces itself to a museum established in 1918. The Natural History Museum, a big multi-subject collection spanning zoology, botany, palaeontology and geology, descends from the Hoangho Paiho. At Water Park, the Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall remembers China's first premier and his wife, both of whom were students in Tianjin.

The National Maritime Museum of China opened in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City in May 2019 as the country's first national, comprehensive public maritime museum. Other themed halls include the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall.

Entry fees to city parks and squares were dropped from 2008 onwards as part of an upgrading programme, so they are free to visit. Large urban parks include Tianjin Zoo, Water Park, Zhongshan Park, People's Park, Central Park, Hedong Park, Haihe Music Park, Meijiang Park, Ergong Park, Nancuiping Park, Xigu Park, Five Great Avenues Park, Shuixi Park (formally opened in October 2018) and Beining Park. The last of these started in 1906 as a plantation built by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi, and was later given the name Ningyuan from its motto, 'Without tranquility, one cannot reach far.'

In Binhai New Area the main parks are Aircraft Carrier Park, Shell Ridge Wetland Park, Haigang Park, Taifeng Park, Ziyun Park, Haihe Bund Park and two waterfront ones, South Embankment Coastal Trail Park and East Embankment Park.

Since 2011 the city has planned and built 16 suburban parks in and around Tianjin and Binhai New Area, with more natural, rural scenery than the city parks. The first two, Beiyunhe in the north and Xiqing in the southwest, went under construction in 2012. In 2014 all 16 were brought in the ecological red line, covering a core area of 66,855 hectares.

Street lighting first arrived in 1902, and by the 1930s the lit streets had earned Tianjin the nickname 'Northern City That Never Sleeps.' The nightscape is now part of specialised urban planning. In central districts, the lighting follows a fishbone layout: the Haihe is the main axis, its continuations (the North Canal and South Canal) extend it, and lesser roads branch off. This lit waterfront is now a leading tourist route and has played a part in the SCO Tianjin Summit, the 13th National Games and the Summer Davos Forum.
