nanning-normal-university.h: Nanning Normal University and the place it calls home

blocks.x: Nanning Normal University is located in Nanning, the capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China. For international students, the city and region around a campus matter as much as the classroom, because they set the weather, the food, the languages you will hear and the places you can reach at weekends. This overview therefore starts with Nanning itself, from its skyline to its metro, and then widens out to Guangxi as a whole.

nanning-normal-university.h: A green city with a tall landmark

blocks.x: The highest building in Nanning is the Guangxi China Resources Tower, which stands 402.7 metres (1,321 feet) tall. It is 22nd on the list of China's tallest buildings, and in Guangxi and south-western China it is surpassed only by buildings in Chongqing. Nanning is nicknamed the Green City (绿城), thanks to parks full of lush tropical growth, and it is counted among the most heavily planted cities in the country.

Recently the city has begun a citywide beautification campaign meant to clean the streets and improve Nanning's image. Part of it has been to cut back on street-side food sellers who lack proper licences and to limit parking on busy roads. The programme has had some early success, but the authorities accept that long-term effort is needed to make the improvements last.

nanning-normal-university.h: Where Nanning sits and what the land is like

blocks.x: Nanning is in the south of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, only 160 kilometres (99 miles) from the Vietnamese frontier. The administrative area is 22,293 square kilometres (8,607 square miles). The city occupies a hilly basin whose elevation ranges from 70 to 500 metres (230 to 1,640 feet), and Qingxiu Mountain overlooks the southern edge of town.

The climate is warm and humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), close to the subtropical monsoon type (Köppen Cwa), and the temperature over a whole year averages 22.3 °C (72.1 °F). In summer it is hot and sticky; the 24-hour average in July, the warmest month, is 28.5 °C (83.3 °F). Mild, dry winters bring a January mean of 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), the lowest of the year. From May to October rain falls most often and relative humidity stays consistently over 60 percent; over a year about 1,286 millimetres (50.6 inches) of rain falls.

The city is free of frost for all but three or four days a year, and snow is virtually unknown. It has fallen only twice since 1900, in December 1975 and again in January 2016, and neither time did it lie on the ground. The coldest reading on record is -2.1 °C (28 °F), on 12 January 1955, and the hottest 40.4 °C (105 °F), on 9 May 1958. Sunshine ranges between 15 percent of possible hours in March and 51 percent in September, and totals 1,579 hours over the year. Expect grey, damp stretches in spring and strong heat in midsummer.

Warm weather gives Nanning rich biodiversity: a large number of animal species and above 3,000 kinds of plants. The Jaba flower, an evergreen shrub, is the official city flower, and the almond tree, the backbone species for greening and landscaping around the city, is the city tree.

nanning-normal-university.h: How the city earns its living

blocks.x: In 2015 Nanning's GDP was 341 billion RMB, with output of about US$7,844 per person. Exports were worth US$10 billion in 2007, and fixed-asset investment from abroad came to 34.3 billion RMB. Six development zones and industrial parks operate in the city, and three of them alone produced 6 billion RMB, which is above 8 percent of the whole city's GDP. There are plentiful mineral resources, among them gold, silver, iron, manganese, aluminium, indium, coal, quartz, marble and granite, and a third of the mineral types found in China are found around Nanning. One of the zones is the Nanning Economic and Technological Development Area.

The Nanning Rail Transit (NNRT) is planned to have nine lines in all. Line 1 opened in June 2016 and Line 2 in December 2017, and Lines 3 and 4 followed, in 2019 and 2020. Line 1 runs between the east and the west of the city and joins its political and financial centre to its academic and research district, so it is handy for students.
Air passengers use Wuxu International Airport, Nanning's airport.

Nanning has two main stations: Nanning station and the newer Nanning East station, which is the principal stop for high-speed trains. A third, Nanning North, was scheduled to open in 2023 alongside the Guiyang-Nanning high-speed railway. The old station is a junction on the Nanning-Kunming, Nanning-Guangzhou and Hunan-Guangxi lines. A high-speed link to Pingxiang, on the Vietnamese border, is planned as part of a goal of connecting the Pan-Pearl River Delta and south-east China more closely with ASEAN countries.

Some high-speed service began at the end of 2013, on the Hunan-Guangxi line and on the route from Nanning to Beihai and its Fangchenggang branch. Guangxi also sits at a crossing point of the Guangzhou-Guiyang high-speed line.

The highways around Nanning are China National Highways 210, 322, 324 and 325 and these expressways: G72 Quanzhou-Nanning, G7201 Nanning Ring, G7211 Nanning-Youyiguan, G75 Lanzhou-Haikou and G80 Guangzhou-Kunming.

At the 2020 census Nanning had 8,741,584 people, of whom 5,293,359 lived in the built-up area covering six urban districts (Wuming District was not yet joined to it). The Zhuang live in close-knit communities within the city, as do 35 ethnic groups altogether, such as the Han, Yao, Hui, Miao, Dong and Man peoples.

Within Guangxi, Nanning leads in education, culture, health, science and technology. Facts reported about its cultural life include 54 research institutes belonging to its districts, ten colleges plus 50 trade schools, 62 mass cultural organisations, 13 performing groups, 8 cinemas, 285 film-projection units, over 70 karaoke venues and more than 1000 newsstands, with bookshops and cultural markets found everywhere.

The city has both its own dishes and food from other parts of China and abroad, and traditional food culture is easy to find along most streets. Nanning cooking resembles Cantonese and Southeast Asian styles. Restaurants offer Guangdong, Sichuan, Hunan and Jiangsu food, and Japanese, Thai and Western cooking too.

Rice noodles are the local favourite. The best known are Laoyou rice noodles, whose name means old friends: they start with a stir-fry of chilli pepper, sour bamboo shoots, fermented black beans and garlic, to which pork, broth and noodles are added. The sour, spicy taste suits breakfast, lunch or dinner, and it is cheap street food. Guilin rice noodles and hand-made noodles are also well liked, and lemon duck is a dish that began in Nanning.

Guilin, famous worldwide for its hills, is near, as are the minority villages of northern and western Guangxi and the border with Vietnam to the south. In the city, you can visit the Guangxi Museum, People's Park (with Zhenning Fort), Mount Qingxiu, Yangmei Ancient Town and the Guangxi Medicinal Herb Botanical Garden, as well as Nanhu Park, Shishan Park and the zoo.

Guangxi's earliest people were a patchwork of tribes that the Chinese named the Baiyue, or Hundred Yue. The region became Chinese territory for the first time under the Qin. In 214 BC a Han Chinese general called Zhao Tuo took most of southern China in the name of the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, shortly before the emperor's death. Civil war broke out, and Zhao used it to found his own kingdom at Panyu, which was called Nanyue (Southern Yue). It was sometimes a vassal of the Han and sometimes independent, and it extended settlement and Chinese ways of life under its own slogan of harmonising and gathering the Hundred Yue (和集百越). It ended in 111 BC, when the Han empire advanced southwards.
The name Guangxi goes back to a Wide province (廣州) of Eastern Wu, the state that held south-eastern China in the Three Kingdoms period. One of its commanderies was Guilin.

nanning-normal-university.h: From the Tang to the Yuan

blocks.x: In the Tang period the Zhuang backed the kingdom of Nanzhao in Yunnan under Piluoge, and in two campaigns, 751 and 754, that kingdom beat back imperial armies. Guangxi ended up divided into a Zhuang-dominated western part, beyond Nanning, and a Han-dominated eastern part.

When Nanzhao collapsed, Liu Yan set up the Southern Han at Xingwangfu, in modern Guangdong. It barely controlled Guangxi, suffered from instability, and the Song absorbed it in 971. The Song gave the name that survives today, governing the area as the Guangnanxi Circuit (West Southern Expanse). His independent state did not last, however, and a Song general with tattoos, Di Qing, brought Guangxi back to Chinese rule.

The Mongol Yuan conquered the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan in 1253 and destroyed the Southern Song after the Battle of Yamen in 1279. They did not treat Lingnan as a subject territory or a military district; they made Guangxi (Western Expanse) a regular province.

The area stayed turbulent. The Ming responded by setting its different local groups against each other, and in 1465 a clash between Zhuang and Yao at Big Rattan Gorge reportedly left 20,000 dead. Across the Ming and Qing periods the powerful Cen family, Zhuang by ethnicity, ruled parts of Guangxi as hereditary local chiefs (tusi) confirmed by the emperors.

The Qing did not interfere until they imposed direct rule in 1726, but the 1800s brought incessant unrest: a revolt by the Yao in 1831, the Jintian Uprising of January 1851, which opened the Taiping Rebellion, and the Da Cheng Rebellion of April 1854. Events in Guangxi contributed to the outbreak of the Second Opium War in 1858, which in turn legalised foreign involvement inland. The Guangxi Army fought hard in the Sino-French War of 1884. It achieved little inside Vietnam, yet on 23 March 1885 it threw the French back from Chinese soil at the Battle of Zhennan Pass, today's Friendship Pass.

Following the Wuchang Uprising, Guangxi seceded from the Qing state on 6 November 1911. Governor Shen Bingdan first stayed in office but was later removed by a mutiny under General Lu Rongting. Lu's Old Guangxi clique took over Hunan and Guangdong too, and took a leading part in the war to protect the republic against Yuan Shikai, who wanted to restore an emperor. The loyalty of the Zhuang made the Self-Government Army cohesive, though unwilling to venture far from its home provinces. Quarrels with Sun Yat-sen ended in defeat in the Guangdong-Guangxi War of 1920 and 1921, a short occupation by Cantonese forces under Chen Jiongming, and years of disorder and banditry. Eventually the Guangxi Pacification Army of Li Zongren created the New Guangxi clique, run by Li together with Huang Shaohong and Bai Chongxi.

A victory over Wu Peifu in Hunan won the Pacification Army the names Flying Army and Army of Steel. When Sun Yat-sen died, Li crushed a revolt by Tang Jiyao and then took part in the Northern Expedition, through which the Republic of China established its authority over other warlords. His force was among the few Kuomintang units largely free of Communist influence. In the People's Republic, Guangxi is remembered as well for the Baise Uprising of 1929, a Communist revolt under Chen Zhaoli and Deng Xiaoping that failed.

A women's unit, the Guangxi Women's Battalion, was formed in 1937 when Soong Mei-ling urged women to back the war with Japan; estimates of its strength range from 130 to 500 or 800 students. Because it lies so far south, Guangxi was never taken in the civil war; it became part of the People's Republic in December 1949, two months after the republic was founded.

Guangxi gained a small coastal strip of Guangdong in 1952 (Qinzhou, Lianzhou, which is now Hepu County, Fangchenggang and Beihai), giving it a sea outlet; this was undone in 1955 and restored in 1965, so Guangxi is the one autonomous region without a land-locked position. Heavy industry grew a little in the 1960s and 1970s, yet the region stayed mainly a scenic holiday area, and even the 1990s boom seemed to bypass it. Now industry is growing and cash crops are becoming more important, and GDP per head has risen as Guangdong's industries shift production to cheaper-labour areas in Guangxi. In the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War, Guangxi's communities supported the People's Liberation Army with food, housing and logistics, and local militia built roads, bridges and trenches and looked after the wounded.

Guangxi has Yunnan on its west, Guizhou on its north, Hunan on its north-east and Guangdong on its east and south-east, while Vietnam and the Gulf of Tonkin lie to the south-west and south. The "Guang" in its name is the same character as in Guangdong (广, or 廣 in traditional script), reflecting how near they are.
Hills and mountains cover big areas. Here is how the main ranges are arranged:
Part of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau occupies the north-west.
Across the north run the Fenghuang and Jiuwan ranges, as well as the Duyao Mountains.
The Nanling Mountains make the north-eastern border, with the Yuecheng and Haiyang ranges branching away from them.
Near the middle are the Da Ming and Da Yao ranges, and the Duyang Mountains pass through the west.
The Yunkai Mountains lie along the south-eastern edge.

The highest peak is Kitten Mountain, in the Yuecheng range, at 2,141 metres (7,024 feet). Karst terrain, with sheer mountains and huge caverns, accounts for 37.8 percent of the land, and about a quarter of the region is forest.

Rivers drain to different places. The Qin and Nanliu rivers run to the Gulf of Tonkin, a number of tributaries feed the Xiang River in neighbouring Hunan, and the Xi River system crosses Guangxi to the south-east on its way to the South China Sea. On the Vietnamese border, the Ban Gioc-Detian waterfall (Dé Tiān Pùbù in pinyin) marks the dividing line between the two countries.

Nanning, Liuzhou, Guilin and Beihai are the biggest cities, and the towns of Longmen, Sanjiang and Yangshuo are well known. The Xi River system supplies waterways to the Pearl River Delta. Beihai, Qinzhou and Fangchenggang are the key seaports on the short Gulf of Tonkin coast, and the Pinglu Canal was built to connect the Xi River system to coastal Guangxi. In total, the region has seven airports, serving Guilin, Nanning, Liuzhou, Beihai, Wuzhou, Baise and Hechi.

The regional climate is subtropical. Summers, lasting April to October, are long, hot and humid, and winters are mild with rare snow. The yearly average varies from 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) in some places to 23.5 °C (74.3 °F) in others; in January temperatures are normally 4 to 16 °C (39 to 61 °F), and in July 27 to 32 °C (81 to 90 °F). Rain-bringing monsoon winds make annual precipitation high, between 1,080 millimetres (43 inches) in the drier parts and 1,730 millimetres (68 inches) in the wettest. Monsoon winds blow from the south-south-west between late April and early October, with the heaviest rain from May to August. In the far south, typhoons coming off the South China Sea can occasionally produce microbursts between July and September.

The Han are the largest group. Most live along the southern coast and in the east, and their main subgroups speak Yue and Southwestern Mandarin varieties. In the south, people speak Qinzhou Yue, and in the east Goulou Yue; Pinghua is the speech of Nanning and Guilin; and Hakka-speaking areas are found in Luchuan and Bobai counties and some places near the Vietnamese border.

More than 16 million Zhuang live in Guangxi, making this the home of China's largest minority, with over 90 percent of all Zhuang living in the region, mostly in the middle and the west. Large numbers live in the Nanning, Liuzhou, Chongzuo, Baise, Hechi and Laibin areas. The county-level city of Jingxi has the highest share: a 2021 publication of the Guangxi government states that 99.7 percent of its people are Zhuang.

Other sizeable indigenous groups are the Yao, Miao, Kam, Mulam, Maonan, Bouyei, Gin, Yi, Sui and Gelao, along with the Hui. Smaller communities include Tibetans, Mongols, Koreans, Manchus, Hlai and Tujia.

Guangxi has remarkable linguistic variety. Alongside Chinese varieties such as Guiliu Mandarin and Yue, many people speak Zhuang, Vietnamese (Kinh), Hmong, Mien, Nuosu, Kam, Sui, Gelao, Mulam, Maonan, Bunu or Lajia.

Nanning is a green, warm, humid southern city with a growing metro, good rail links and a distinctive food culture, set in a region whose Zhuang and other peoples have shaped its history and daily life. For the latest information on Nanning Normal University's programmes, admissions and services for international students, consult the university's own website.
Nanning Normal University lists 132 programs for international students on this site: 54 bachelor, 75 master's, 3 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 132 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 11,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 13,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 14,000 (median CNY 14,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.

127 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

nanning-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nanning Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanning, register at Nanning Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Nantong University (南通大学) is a public university run at provincial level, located in the city of Nantong in Jiangsu Province. The Province of Jiangsu is its parent, and the money comes jointly from the Ministry of Transport and the Jiangsu Provincial People's Government. Its earliest predecessor was set up in 1912. The university occupies 4,000 acres, with 800 thousand square meters devoted to school buildings.

It is a comprehensive university built by the Jiangsu Provincial Government together with the Ministry of Transport. Its three founding components were the Nantong Normal College, Nantong Engineering College and Nantong Medical College. Teaching is spread over four campuses: Qixiu, Zhongxiu, Qidong and the new campus.

Nearly 34 thousand full-time students are enrolled, among them 1,550 graduates and 300 overseas students. The 84 undergraduate programmes rest on nine major disciplines: engineering, science, medical science, management, economics, law, literature, history and education.
For international medical applicants, one detail stands out: the university is accredited and approved by the MCI (Medical Council of India) and the WHO (World Health Organization).

"Bridging China and the West, Striving for the Best" is the motto of the university. Its mission is to ensure that learning is meant for use, and that use should suit the local community, and the value it stands for is "Beautiful Morality and Pure Science".
The university publishes its own set of statistics, which differ somewhat from the figures above:
Faculty and staff: 3,152, of whom 1,549 are senior faculty
Undergraduates: about 40,000
Postgraduates: about 2,700
Overseas students with academic degrees: 750
Affiliated hospital: 1
Undergraduate programmes: 106
Doctor stations: 3
Doctoral degree programmes in level I academic disciplines: 3
Master's degree programmes in level I academic disciplines: 22
Majors for professionals' master's degrees: 12
Cuaa.Net ranking among universities in China: 100

Nantong University has thirteen schools and one institute. Technical and engineering fields are taught in the School of Mechanical Engineering, the School of Transportation and Civil Engineering, the School of Chemistry and Chemical Industry, the School of Information Science and Technology and the Institute of Traffic. Health fields are served by the School of Medicine and the School of Pharmacy. The remaining schools are the School of Science, the School of Education Science, the School of Chinese Culture and Literature, the School of Foreign Language, the School of Art, the School of Politics and the School of International Education.
Student life depends on the city, so the next sections describe how Nantong looks, feels, works and connects to the rest of China.

Nantong is in central Jiangsu, on the northern bank of the Yangtze River estuary. The Yellow Sea borders it to the east and the Yangtze to the south. The ground is mainly alluvial deposit, a major part of the Yangtze River Delta plain, and it is mostly flat apart from isolated outcrops of bedrock such as Langshan Hill.

The land was formed by the gradual build-up of delta sediment and sandbanks. Its southeastern areas, among them Haimen and Qidong, joined the mainland around the 19th century. A dense network of waterways, belonging to the Yangtze and Huai River systems, crisscrosses the area. Mineral resources on land are limited, but the city has a long coastline and extensive intertidal mudflats.

Humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) is the climate, and each of the four seasons is distinct. In winter it is chilly and damp. Cold northwesterly winds from the Siberian high can push night temperatures below freezing, although snow is fairly rare. Summers are hot and humid, with frequent downpours and sudden thunderstorms. January averages 3.6 °C (38.5 °F) for a day, and July 27.9 °C (82.2 °F); across a whole year the mean is 16.2 °C (61.2 °F). Plum rains arrive in June and early July, which is the wettest stretch of the year.
Culturally, the Song-era Xuanmiao Temple and the Nantong Museum are the main sites.

Nantong's scenery centres on the Hao River, nicknamed the Emerald Necklace of Nantong, which encircles the city over 15 km (9.3 mi) in total length and lines most of the city's scenery. Among popular sites is Langshan ("Wolf Hill"), about 110 meters high, which has a Buddhist temple on top dedicated to a Song dynasty monk. Sailors pray to him for protection at sea because of his legendary power over water demons.

In 1557 a local hero defended the city from Japanese pirates, and the Cao Gong Zhu Memorial Temple honours him. Shuihuiyuan Garden, or Water Garden, is unlike any other Chinese classical garden because it was made in the Hui style. Several notable people are buried in it. They include Wen Tianxiang, a national hero of the Nansong dynasty, and Luo Binwang, who wrote poetry under the Tang. Another is Zhang Jian, late-Qing scholar, modern industrialist and champion of education.

Nantong has grown rapidly over the last 25 years, like most cities in the Yangtze River Delta, and its growth is usually put down to its advantageous position just north of Shanghai. The Sutong Bridge is expected to tie Nantong more closely to Shanghai, cutting the trip between them from three hours to one.

On the river the shipping corporation Cosco runs a big port and ship repair yard. This is Cosco (Nantong) Shipyard Co., Ltd, the group's first shipyard, beside Nantong's busy port. Its 1120 m of coastline hold two floating docks, one of cape size and one of panamax size, and roughly 150 vessels are handled each year. Another yard, run by Nantong Mingde Heavy Industries, went bankrupt in 2014, and Minde's parent company, Jiangsu Sainty Marine Corporation, was due to end operations in 2017.
Local manufacturers cover several sectors. Textiles dominate the list:
Nantong Suzhong Textile Co. Ltd., which makes yarn and thread
Nantong Printing and Dyeing Co. Ltd., a textile processor
Nantong Taierte Clothing Co. Ltd., working in textile production and processing
Nantong No.2 Yarn-dyed Weaving Mill, producing cloth and garments
Empire Clothing Co. Ltd., maker of garments for men, women and children
Non-textile businesses include:
Nantong Fujitsu Microelectronics Co Ltd
Nantong Xiaoxing Transformer Co., Ltd., supplying electric transformers
Nantong Freezing Equipment Factory, which produces food-industry refrigeration and quick freezing equipment
Nantong General Pharmaceutical Factory, which makes tablets, capsules, injections and other pharmaceutical materials

Nantong Xingdong International Airport is in Xingdong town, Tongzhou District, 9.8 kilometers northeast of the city centre and 120 kilometers from Shanghai. It serves Nantong and nearby areas. Terminal 2 was finished in 2014, a step towards handling international flights, and the first of these took off on 26 May 2023, to Hong Kong.

Two bridges cross the Yangtze to the south. The Chongming-Qidong Yangtze River Bridge, finished in 2011, carries the G40 Shanghai-Xi'an Expressway from Qidong to Chongming Island. Finished in 2008, the Sutong Yangtze River Bridge carries the G15 Shenyang-Haikou Expressway from Nantong to Changshu and is counted among the world's longest cable-stayed bridges.

At Hai'an, in the northwestern part of Nantong Prefecture, two railways intersect: Nanjing-Qidong (Ningqi) and Xinyi-Changxing (Xinchang). Since 2020 the Nantong-Shanghai railway has run south to Suzhou and Shanghai, crossing the Yangtze on the Hutong Yangtze River Bridge, which opened at the same time.

The busiest stations at the moment are Nantong Railway station and Hai'An railway station. East of Nantong railway station the Nanjing-Qidong line is single-track, so Electrified Multiple Unit trains cannot run beyond Nantong; At Qidong railway station, 4 round-trip "K" trains call each day. Rudong county reaches the national rail network through a line from Hai'an, and trains leave daily for Nanjing. The first line of Nantong Metro opened in 2022.

The comprehensive university here is Nantong University, which came out of a merger of three older institutions: the Nantong Engineer College, Nantong Medical College and Nantong Normal College. In 2007 it counted 21 schools and around 22,000 registered students.

Nantong has a remarkable record of educational pioneering. It was home to China's earliest school for training teachers, and also to its first folk museum (the Nantong Museum), its first school of industrial textile manufacturing, its first embroidery school, its first drama school and its first school for deaf and blind pupils. Much of this traces to one man, Zhang Jian, who started Nantong Normal College, the first normal school of modern China. He built museums, libraries and theaters too, and turned the city into an important cultural centre.

Secondary schools include Nantong Middle School and Nantong No.1 Middle School (this list is incomplete), and for international families there is the Nantong Stalford International School (http://en.ntsis.com/).
The province you live in shapes your experience as much as the campus does. Jiangsu's history, people, environment and sport are covered below.

nantong-university.h: From ancient states to the Song

blocks.x: In the earliest Chinese dynasties, what is now Jiangsu was far from the centre of Chinese civilization, which lay in the northwest of Henan, and it was home to an ancient ethnic group, the Huai barbarians (淮夷). The Zhou dynasty brought more contact, and in time the state of Wu emerged in southern Jiangsu, one of hundreds of states then spread across northern and central China. Late in the Spring and Autumn period, under King Helu of Wu, Wu became a great power. In 484 BC it defeated Qi, a major northern power in modern Shandong, and contested the position of overlord over all the Chinese states. Yue, which had emerged in what is now Zhejiang to the south, subjugated Wu in 473 BC, and Chu, a powerful state from the west, subjugated Yue in 333 BC. Finally, in 221 BC, Qin eliminated every other state and unified China.

Under the Han dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD), Jiangsu remained distant from the North China Plain, where civilization was centred. It was split between two zhou (provinces), Yang Province in the south and Xu Province in the north. Southern Jiangsu then became the heartland of the Eastern Wu (222 to 280) in the Three Kingdoms era, with a capital called Jianye, which was later renamed Jiankang and is now Nanjing. Nomadic invaders overran northern China in the 4th century, and the Jin imperial court fled to Jiankang. Migrants from the north poured into the cities of southern and central Jiangsu. Four Southern dynasties in turn kept their capital at Jiankang, which grew into China's biggest centre of commerce and culture.

The Sui dynasty united the country in 581 and the political centre shifted north again, yet engineers built the Grand Canal across Jiangsu so that the Central Plains stayed linked to the wealthy Yangtze Delta. The Tang dynasty (618-907) relied on southern Jiangsu for yearly grain deliveries. In the Song dynasty (960-1279), which saw a wealthy mercantile class and an emerging market economy, Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and neighbouring areas) became a trading centre. After that, big cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou were seen as synonyms for opulence and luxury in China, and the region is still among the richest parts of the country.

North China fell under the Jurchen Jin dynasty in 1127, during the Jin-Song wars. The Huai River, once flowing across north Jiangsu into the Yellow Sea, then divided the Jin territory in the north from the Southern Song in the south. By the thirteenth century the Mongols ruled China. In 1368 the Ming dynasty was founded after driving out the Mongols, and at first it put its capital in Nanjing. The regions around Nanjing, equivalent to today's Jiangsu and Anhui, were named Nanzhili province (literally "southern directly governed"). Zhu Di, later the Yongle Emperor, seized power in a coup and then the capital moved to Beijing, far north, though Nanjing remained the southern capital. In the late Ming, Jiangnan remained an important trading region, and some historians see in its flourishing textile industry the first signs of industrialization and capitalism, a trend that was aborted.
The Qing dynasty turned Nanzhili into "Jiangnan province", and in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui were split into separate provinces. Jiangsu's borders have mostly stayed stable since.

From the 1840s, as Western incursion into China began, Western influence reached the rich, commercial Yangtze River Delta more and more. A small, unremarkable Jiangsu town, Shanghai, shot up into a metropolis of trade, banking and cosmopolitanism before being separated off as its own municipality. Jiangnan also featured strongly in the Taiping Rebellion (1851-1864), a massive and deadly uprising whose aim was a Christian theocracy in China. Starting in the far south, in Guangdong province, the rebellion spread through much of South China. Nanjing became its capital by 1853, and the rebels called the city Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was founded in 1912, and warlords soon tore the country apart. Control of Jiangsu passed between several hands until Chiang Kai-shek, in April 1927, established a government at Nanjing and soon brought most of China under his control. In 1928 the provincial government moved to Zhenjiang. The second Sino-Japanese War, which began on a full scale in 1937, interrupted this arrangement. Nanjing fell on 13 December 1937, and over the next three months the occupying Japanese committed atrocities that are remembered as the Rape of Nanjing. The city then became the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government of East China, and most of Jiangsu stayed under Japanese occupation until the war ended in 1945.

After the war Nanjing again served as the capital of the Republic of China. By then, however, civil war had erupted. The Kuomintang government faced Communist forces who were based further north, mostly in Northeast China. In northern Jiangsu came the decisive Huaihai Campaign, which the Kuomintang lost, and soon the Communists had crossed the Yangtze and captured Nanjing. The Kuomintang fled south and ended up in Taipei, from where the Republic of China government still administers Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands, though it also continues, technically at least, to claim Nanjing as its rightful de jure capital. After Zhenjiang was captured, the provincial government moved to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

Following the Communist takeover, Beijing (formerly Peiping) became the capital of the People's Republic, and Jiangsu was dissolved into the Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. Jiangsu Province was re-established on 15 November 1952, with Nanjing reduced to the status of provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up first concentrated on Guangdong on the south coast, which soon left Jiangsu behind; from the 1990s the policies were applied more evenly across China. Suzhou and Wuxi, two southern Jiangsu cities close to Shanghai, have since grown especially prosperous. They are among China's top 10 cities by gross domestic product and have overtaken the provincial capital, Nanjing. The income gap between northern and southern Jiangsu is still large.

Flat land, low altitude and dense population leave Jiangsu highly exposed; it is among the Chinese regions most vulnerable to climate change and the rising seas that come with it. For 1961 to 2007, figures from Jiangsu's Center of Climate Change show that the province warms on average by 0.16 to 0.45 °C every 10 years, while total precipitation changes by by amounts between -28.7 mm and 37.09 mm every 10 years. Extreme weather has become stronger and more common, and agriculture, ecosystems, water resources, transport and the coastline all suffer. Sea levels are rising much faster than the world average.

In early 2023 the Cross Dependency Initiative (XDI) published a ranking of climate change risk for global regions that placed Jiangsu as the most vulnerable in the entire world, the reasons given being its wide industrial, trade, residential and commercial development.

National policy is addressing this. The 14th five-year plan, which the National People's Congress endorsed in 2021, sets the general direction and steps for a low-carbon transition. For its part, the Jiangsu government aims under that plan to cut carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 18% and to speed up a green, low-carbon economy. It also intends to restore damaged coastal areas such as Lianyugang and Yancheng, and to build resilience against rising seas with seawalls and river floodgates.

Most residents are ethnic Han Chinese, and there are also Hui and Manchu minorities. In 2021, 73.94 percent of people in the province lived in urban areas and 26.06 percent in rural areas. Indicators for 2021:

nantong-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Nantong University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

ningbo-university.h: Ningbo University: what to know first

blocks.x: Ningbo University, known as NBU (宁波大学), is a public university funded by the city. It stands in the Jiangbei area of Ningbo, a port city in Zhejiang province, and answers to the Ningbo Municipal People's Government. It also belongs to the national Double First-Class Construction programme, which marks it out as a university the state wants to build up.
Academician Zhu Zhaoxiang was the founding president, in office between September 1985 and September 1988. Academician Yan Luguang later led the university, from 1999 to 2004.
For outside perspective, the 2024 Academic Ranking of World Universities placed NBU in the 401 to 500 band worldwide and 78th within China.
Your daily life as a student will depend on the city as much as on the campus, so the next parts describe Ningbo and then the province of Zhejiang.

Ningbo spans longitudes 120°55' to 122°16' E and latitudes 28°51' to 30°33' N. The East China Sea and the Zhoushan Archipelago lie to the east. On the north is Hangzhou Bay, and across it the cities of Jiaxing and Shanghai. Shaoxing borders it to the west and Taizhou to the south.

The land area is 9,816 square kilometres (3,790 square miles), and the city also administers 9,758 square kilometres (3,768 square miles) of ocean. Its coastline totals 1,562 km (971 miles): 788 km (490 miles) on the mainland and 774 km (481 miles) around islands. Together that is one third of the whole provincial coastline. The city administers 531 islands, adding up to 524 square kilometres (202 square miles).

Ningbo's built-up core is wedged between the ocean and low mountains in the southwest, and the ground in between is coastal plain and valley. The Yongjiang River splits the central business district in two. Two peninsulas stand out. In Beilun District, the Chuanshan Peninsula (穿山半岛) contains the most easterly point on the Zhejiang mainland, and in Xiangshan County there is the Xiangshan Peninsula (象山半岛). Heading north from Mount Tiantai, the Siming Mountains (四明山) cross Yuyao, Haishu and Fenghua, where they peak at 979 metres (3,212 ft).
Tidal flat ecosystems exist next to the city, although farmers have reclaimed large stretches for agriculture.

Ningbo's humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) brings four clear seasons: hot, humid summers and cool, cloudy, dry winters with the occasional fall of snow. Across the year the average is 17.6 °C (63.7 °F), from a January mean of 5.8 °C (42.4 °F) up to 29.1 °C (84.4 °F) in July. The coldest reading since records began in 1951 was -8.8 °C (16 °F), on 12 January 1955, and the hottest was 42.1 °C (108 °F), on 8 August 2013. Annual rainfall averages 1,430 mm (56 in). June brings the Asian monsoon's plum rains, and humidity peaks then as well.

Typhoon effects are felt from August to October, with about 1.8 storms a year on average, although the city is not often hit directly. A 2012 OECD study placed Ningbo among the 20 cities in the world most exposed to flooding made worse by human-caused climate change. In response, the city is one of those in China adopting sponge-city strategies to reduce the effects of climate change.

Plan for hot humid summers and a rainy June, and keep an eye on forecasts in late summer and early autumn. Winters are chilly rather than freezing, though damp, cloudy days can make them feel colder than the thermometer suggests, so bring warm layers and a good umbrella.

Ningbo is an important port, about 220 kilometres (140 miles) south of Shanghai, and exports have been part of its economy since the 7th century. It is now a major exporter of electrical goods, textiles, food and industrial tools. Private business is especially strong, accounting for 80 percent of GDP in 2013.

For a long time Ningbo was somewhat cut off from other big cities. That changed in 2007 when the Hangzhou Bay Bridge opened, cutting the drive to Shanghai from four hours down to about two and a half. Today Ningbo works as the economic centre of the southern Yangtze River Delta and appears on lists of China's most competitive cities.

Trade in 2009 came to US$60.8 billion, 10.4 percent below 2008. Exports were worth US$38.65 billion, 16.6 percent lower, while imports of US$22.16 billion rose 3.1 percent. The economy grew 9.26 percent in 2013, to 712.89 billion yuan, equal to US$115.12 billion. Output per person in 2009 was US$10,833, around three times the national average. All of these figures are some years old. They are included to show how large and trade-driven the local economy is, and current statistics are available from the city's own publications.

Several major development zones in and around the city have drawn a lot of foreign investment. More than 60 financial institutions, domestic and foreign-invested, run operations in Ningbo, and over 10,000 foreigners have been attracted to the city. City authorities offer favourable policies that encourage investment in creative industries, information services, manufacturing, strategic new industries and international trade.

Ningbo Economic and Technological Development Zone: in the northeast behind Beilun Port, 27 km (17 miles) from the city centre. For 20 years it has provided the overall framework for large-scale building, and it is close to both Ningbo Lishe International Airport and Ningbo Port. ExxonMobil, DuPont and Dow Chemical are among its investors.

Ningbo Daxie Development Zone: approved in 1993, covering 5.92 square kilometres (2.29 square miles). After more than ten years of building it has a base for transshipping energy products, liquid chemicals and containers.

Ningbo National Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone: founded in 1999 and promoted to national level in January 2007. It lies 10 km (6.2 miles) from the international airport and 18 km (11 miles) from the port. It acts as a technical innovation base for the Yangtze River Delta, and encouraged industries include chemicals, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, raw material processing and research and development.

Ningbo Free Trade Zone: one of 15 such zones authorised by the State Council and Zhejiang's only one. Created in 1992, it covers 2.3 square kilometres (0.89 square miles) in the middle of China's mainland coastline, south of the Yangtze River Delta. Its 2008 industrial output reached 53.33 billion yuan, a rise of 19.8 percent over 2007.
Nordic Industrial Park: a wholly foreign-owned industrial estate, one of the earliest in China, with a Scandinavian management team.
Ningbo Advertising Park: a national-level pilot park in the Southern Business District, where financial incentives have brought in more than 300 related firms.

Ningbo has a long history and a prosperous present, and that gives visitors a great deal to explore. The attractions below are grouped by district and follow those recommended by the municipal culture and tourism authorities, so you can plan weekend trips around the area you live in.

Moon Lake Park (Yuehu Park) is a reservoir dug in the Tang dynasty, in 636 CE, at the heart of the district. The park contains the lake, small islands and many ancient buildings and sites, as follows.

Tianyi Pavilion, built in 1516, is one of the most popular and famous sights in Ningbo. It is the oldest library still standing in Asia and ranks among the world's three oldest private libraries. The books it holds start in the 11th century, among them printed and handwritten Confucian classics, rare local histories and registers of those who succeeded in the imperial examinations. These days Tianyi Pavilion means the entire museum complex. The Ming-dynasty house of Fan Qing, who first owned the library, forms part of it (also dated to 1516), with a classical garden and a private opera stage. A mahjong (麻將) museum is included as well, because Ningbo is regarded as where the game began.
Other Haishu sites include the following.

He Ancestral Temple (賀祕監祠): commemorates He Zhizhang (659 to 744 CE), a Tang poet who gave himself the nickname Siming Crazy Guest, Siming being a mountain by Ningbo. It was finished in the Song dynasty, in 1144, and repaired in the Qing in 1865.

Ancient Korean Embassy: built under the Northern Song to receive Korean envoys and merchant groups. War destroyed it in 1130. In 1984 it was declared a protected cultural relic site, and today it works as a display on how Ningbo and Korea have been connected.

A literary trail: Qu You, a novelist born in Ningbo, wrote Peony Dengji (牡丹燈記) for his collection Jiandeng Xinhua. In Japan it is known as Botan Dōrō, or Tales of the Peony Lantern. It tells of love between a ghost and a living man in the days of Fang Guozhen, around Moon Lake. The scholar Koyama Issei, from Japan, worked out that many of its settings, such as Xuanmiao Temple, Zhenming Ridge, Central Lake East Bridge and Central Lake Temple, match real places in geography and architecture. Japan turned the story into one of its three celebrated Kaidan tales.

Drum Tower Complex (Haishu Tower): all that survives of a Tang-dynasty city gate tower. In the Republic period a six-metre Romanesque bell tower was placed on top, and the commercial area around the base has been reconstructed in the old style.
Chenghuang Temple (Ningbo County Temple): a temple of the City God, of great age, in the central shopping district.

Tianfeng Pagoda: a nationally protected relic, Song-style brick-and-wood tower typical of Jiangnan. Hexagonal and seven storeys above ground with seven more below, no other old structure in the city is taller, and it is a landmark valued for its age, design and relics. It was first built in 695 CE under the Tang (618 to 907 CE).
Tianyi Square: a well-known shopping complex in the busy old downtown, named after the Tianyi Chamber, Asia's oldest private library.
Nantang Old Street: an old riverside commercial street of folk crafts, souvenir shops and small restaurants. It used to host local fairs and flea markets and was renovated as a tourist site in 2013.
Liangzhu Cultural Park: a theme park about the Butterfly Lovers, one of China's four great folk tales, often called the oriental Romeo and Juliet.
Baiyun Manor: an old academy where Huang Zongxi (黃宗羲), also named Taichong, gave lectures. He was an outstanding historian, writer and thinker who lived across the late Ming and early Qing.
Tashan Weir: an ancient dam from the Tang dynasty.
Ningbo Wulongtan Scenic Resort (or Five-dragon Pools): counted among Ningbo's Ten New Sceneries, with a national AAAA rating.
Xiaowen Street: an ancient street in Haishu's old town, named after the filial Song-dynasty son Yang Qing (杨庆).

Ningbo Museum (also called Yinzhou Museum or Ningbo Historic Museum) focuses on regional history and traditional customs. Its architect, Wang Shu, won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2012, the first Chinese national to do so, and this building is seen as his masterpiece. It also served as the key location when Liu Cixin's science-fiction novel Three Bodies was adapted for television in 2023.
Romon U-Park is one of the world's largest urban indoor theme parks.

Ningbo Eastern New Town is a newly built district with a carefully planned central business district, including two 400-metre skyscrapers, headquarters of many listed companies and government offices. It has several museums, galleries and shopping centres, among them the Ningbo Urban Planning Exhibition Center, Yinzhou Park and the Southern CBD. Hankyu, the Japanese department store, opened its first branch abroad here in 2021 (the Ningbo Hankyu Commercial Complex), and the new library in the Eastern New Town dates from 2018.
Dongqian Lake is Zhejiang's largest natural freshwater lake. The first written mention dates to the West Jin dynasty, and sights around the lake include these.
Little Putuo: an island in the lake, with temples that a Song-dynasty prime minister named Shihao had built.
Yuefei Temple: a Song-dynasty shrine in memory of Yuefei.

Southern Song Dynasty Rock Carving Park: this site was honoured with a national best-project award for conserving cultural relics, presented jointly by two Chinese architecture and cultural-heritage bodies.
Fuquan Mountain: a hill where visitors find a tea-culture theme park.
Ningbo Ocean World: an aquarium that includes a sea-life theatre.
Ningbo Wildlife Park: formerly Ningbo Youngor Zoo, a 4A-level scenic area inside the Dongqian Lake Tourist Resort and one of the largest wildlife parks in China by water area.
Ningbo Hanling Old Street: a very old street, thousands of years in age, formerly known as Hanling City, where the word city meant a bazaar.
Qita Temple: a downtown Zen Buddhist complex that dates back to its consecration under the Tang.

Tianhou Temple: formerly a temple of Mazu, the Empress of Heaven, used by Fujianese merchants as a guild hall called Qing'an Huiguan. Nineteenth-century visitors admired it: S. Wells Williams thought it Ningbo's loveliest spot, and John Thomson ranked it among the finest temples in China. The Chinese Civil War destroyed the structure. It has since been reconstructed, with many of its original artworks, as a museum of maritime affairs and folk customs for east Zhejiang.
Temple of King Ashoka: a Buddhist temple whose origins lie in the Western Jin, in 282 AD.
Tiantong Temple: it belongs to the group known as the Five Chan Buddhism Temples, and Japanese Sōtō Buddhism (曹洞宗) traces its beginnings here.
Ningbo Sakura Park (Zhongxing Sakura Park): created to mark the friendship between Ningbo and its partner city Nagaoka, in Japan, with cherry trees.

Ningbo is part of Zhejiang, so the province's past is part of your background reading. Much of what is now ordinary local geography, from the canals to the coastal cities, grew out of the events described here. This outline moves from the earliest settlers to the end of the Tang.

Zhejiang's oldest known culture is Kuahuqiao, an early Neolithic community in the Hangzhou area from about 6000 to 5000 BC. After that come the Hemudu culture, beginning around 5500 BC, and the Liangzhu culture, which started about 3400 BC. Both are Neolithic cultures of Zhejiang.

In the second millennium BC, the Shang civilisation did not reach this region, which was home to peoples gathered under the name Dongyue. The kingdom of Yue turns up in written records from the Spring and Autumn period, which place it in northern Zhejiang. The Shiji traces its rulers to Yu the Great, founder of the Xia. A poem called the Song of the Yue Boatman (越人歌, Yuèrén Gē, meaning a song by a man of Yue) was put into Chinese characters and written down by authors in northern or inland China, in Hebei and Henan, around 528 BC. Because it had to be transliterated, it shows that Yue speech could not be understood by northern and inland Chinese. Other pieces of the Yue picture include the Sword of Goujian, which carries bird-worm seal script, and Yuenü (越女), the Lady of Yue, a swordswoman from the kingdom. The state of Chu favoured Yue as a means of limiting the rise of Wu.

King Goujian rescued Yue from its early defeats and took over the rival's lands in 473 BC. He then moved the royal capital from the Mount Kuaiji area, near today's Shaoxing, to Wu's old capital, present-day Suzhou. Chu, now without a southern enemy, turned directly on Yue and destroyed it in 333 BC. In 222 BC the Qin Empire annexed the territory and made it a commandery called Kuaiji, which was at the outset administered from Wu, in Jiangsu.

Kuaiji Commandery was where Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu began their revolt against Qin, which at first revived the kingdom of Chu before losing to the Han. In the Later Han, power returned to the settlement beneath Mount Kuaiji. The Minyue hinterland, however, was barely governed, and its Yue people mostly kept their own political and social ways.

Warlords named Yan Baihu and Wang Lang ruled Zhejiang when the Han fell, until Sun Ce and Sun Quan beat them and ended up founding the Kingdom of Wu. The Wu court shifted from Kuaiji to Jianye, now Nanjing, but the rulers continued to develop the region, and they gained from waves of refugees leaving the chaos in the north. Kilns were built for industry, and trade extended to Manchuria and Funan in southern mainland Southeast Asia.

Zhejiang was part of Wu (229 to 280), called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, the most economically developed of the Three Kingdoms (220 to 280). Romance of the Three Kingdoms says that Zhejiang's navy was the best equipped. In the story, Wei (魏) and Shu (蜀) were short of supplies and avoided meeting Wu head on. When they did fight, they depended heavily on camouflage and deception to capture arrows, bows and other Wu military stores.

Nanjing, then Jiankang, remained prominent, but Qiantang, the old name of Hangzhou, was still one of three major southern centres paying large taxes to the northern imperial capitals. Jiankang and Chengdu were the other two. Qiantang was promoted and renamed Hangzhou in 589.

After Wu fell and the Wu Hu uprising shook the Jin dynasty (266 to 420), many elite northern families had worked with non-Chinese rulers and conquerors. Some lost privileges and took refuge south of the Yangtze, and some may have settled near Hangzhou. The clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), chancellor of Shu Han and a man of the Central Plain, is one example. It gathered in a suburb of Hangzhou prefecture and formed Zhuge Village, where every villager carries the surname Zhuge. The village kept itself apart from the surrounding communities for centuries, and has only recently become public knowledge. That hints that a few of the most powerful northern refugees might have settled south of the Yangtze. Yet Zhejiang is hilly and short of farmland, so most refugees probably went to other southern regions where land was fertile and cities offered resources: Hunan, Jiangxi and Anhui, southern Jiangsu and eastern Fujian, regions with looser, less organised local government. Where individuals settled probably depended on their northern social rank and military power. The remnant Jin state and the Southern dynasties competed with certain Han elites from the Central Plain and from south of the Yangtze.

Throughout the Six Dynasties (220 or 222 to 589) and under the Sui and Tang, Zhejiang, the heart of the Jiangnan region of the Yangtze Delta, stayed the richest area. Once it belonged to the Sui, its wealth supported that dynasty's wish to expand in both directions, above all into Korea and Vietnam. To make this possible the Sui repaired and extended the canals that grew into the Grand Canal of China. The canal carried grain and other resources from Zhejiang on a regular basis, passing through the major city Hangzhou, its hinterland along the Zhe River and the Hangzhou Bay shore, and then Suzhou, before reaching the North China Plain.

Defeat in the Korean war brought down the Sui and put the Tang in power, beginning a golden age that lasted for centuries. Zhejiang was an important economic base in the Jiangnan East Circuit and was seen as particularly prosperous. The Grand Canal kept working throughout the Tang, carrying grain and materials north to the plain and to the empire's major cities. When the Tang disintegrated, the regional kingdom of Wuyue took in the greater part of Zhejiang.

Professional teams in the province include two Chinese Basketball Association sides, the Zhejiang Golden Bulls and the Bayi Rockets, who play in Ningbo. In football, Zhejiang Professional F.C. plays in the Chinese Super League.
