Ningbo University of Technology (宁波工程学院, Níngbō Gōngchéng Xuéyuàn) is a provincial university run in Ningbo, a port city in Zhejiang Province, eastern China. It describes itself as comprehensive, although its name and history show a strong engineering orientation.

The existing campus spans 428,015.77 square metres, of which 204,000 square metres is floor area for buildings. A new campus is also being built, with a much larger area of 914,791.894 square metres. The university is now located in Jiangbei District, having earlier been based in Haishu District, so older maps and articles may still show the former address.

The institution opened in 1983 under the name Ningbo College. Fourteen years later, in 1997, the national Ministry of Education granted it recognition as a National Exemplary Engineering College. In 2004 the ministry gave a further accreditation, allowing it to run full-time four-year undergraduate programmes.
These counts look dated, so ask the university for the current numbers when you apply.
No details are supplied, and it is mentioned here only for completeness.

Life on campus depends on the surrounding city. Ningbo is a large coastal city with a very long trading history, so the sections below explain where it is, what the weather does, how the economy works and what to see in your free time.

On a map, the city is found between 28° 51' and 30° 33' north and between 120° 55' and 122° 16' east. Its eastern side meets the East China Sea and the Zhoushan Archipelago. In the north is Hangzhou Bay, and across the bay lie Jiaxing and Shanghai. Shaoxing borders it to the west and Taizhou to the south.

The land area is 9,816 square kilometres (3,790 sq mi) and its maritime territory is a further 9,758 square kilometres of sea (about 3,768 square miles). Coastline totals 1,562 km (971 mi): 788 km (490 mi) on the mainland and 774 km (481 mi) around islands. Together that equals one-third of the entire coast of Zhejiang. The city administers 531 islands that cover 524 km2 (202 sq mi).

The city proper is squeezed between the sea and low mountains in the southwest, with a coastal plain and valleys in the middle. The Yongjiang River cuts through the central business district. Two peninsulas matter on the map. The Chuanshan Peninsula (穿山半岛) lies in Beilun District and includes the easternmost point of mainland Zhejiang, and the Xiangshan Peninsula (象山半岛) is in Xiangshan County. Rising to 979 m (3,212 ft), the Siming range (四明山) stretches northward from Mount Tiantai across Yuyao, Haishu and Fenghua.
Tidal flat ecosystems lie next to the city, although big stretches have been reclaimed for farming.

By the Köppen system Ningbo is humid subtropical (Cfa), and all four seasons are distinct. Summers are hot and humid. Winters are chilly, cloudy and dry, with a little snow now and then. The mean annual temperature is 17.6 °C (63.7 °F); January is the coolest month at 5.8 °C (42.4 °F) and July the warmest at 29.1 °C (84.4 °F). Records since 1951 show a cold extreme of -8.8 °C (16 °F), set on 12 January 1955, while on 8 August 2013 the mercury reached 42.1 °C (108 °F).

Rainfall averages 1,430 mm (56 in) a year. June is the plum-rain month, when the Asian monsoon brings steady rain and humidity is at its highest. Typhoon season runs from August to October. The city is touched by an average of 1.8 storms each year, although direct hits are uncommon. Flooding is a concern: a 2012 OECD report ranks Ningbo inside a global top 20 for flood risk linked to human-driven climate change, and the city is among those in China putting "sponge city" strategies in place to reduce the effects.
For newcomers: pack for muggy summers and an umbrella in June, and be ready for the occasional typhoon warning in late summer.

ningbo-university-of-technology.h: A port that long faced inward

blocks.x: Ningbo is an important port 220 kilometres (140 mi) south of Shanghai, and its export trade goes back to the 7th century. Today it ships electrical goods, textiles, food and industrial tools. Private business is unusually strong; it accounted for 80 percent of GDP in 2013.

For a long time the city was rather cut off from other large centres. That changed in 2007 with the Hangzhou Bay Bridge, which trimmed the road journey to Shanghai by an hour and a half, from four hours down to two and a half. Today it serves as the southern Yangtze River Delta's economic hub, and rankings count it among the most competitive cities in China.

2009: output fell 10.4 percent from the 2008 level to US$60.8 billion. Exports shrank 16.6 percent to US$38.65 billion, whereas imports grew 3.1 percent to US$22.16 billion. Per-capita output of US$10,833 was roughly triple the national average.
2013: growth of 9.26 percent lifted the total to US$115.12 billion, or 712.89 billion yuan.

Several important development zones in and around the city have drawn plenty of foreign money. More than 60 financial institutions, domestic and foreign-funded, operate in Ningbo, and over 10,000 foreigners have been attracted to live there. Incentives from the municipal government target creative industries, information services, manufacturing, new strategic industries and international trade.

Ningbo Economic and Technological Development Zone: northeast of the city behind Beilun Port, 27 km (17 mi) from the centre, and close to both the port and Ningbo Lishe International Airport. After twenty years it provides the framework for large-scale development. ExxonMobil, Dupont and Dow Chemical are among its investors.

Ningbo Daxie Development Zone: approved in 1993 and covering only 5.92 square kilometres (2.29 square miles). Over ten-plus years it has built up the industrial and logistics base for moving energy products, liquid chemicals and containers.

Ningbo National Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone: founded in 1999 and raised to national level in January 2007, 10 km (6.2 mi) from the airport and 18 km (11 mi) from the port. It is a technical innovation base for the Yangtze River Delta, with biotech and pharmaceuticals, chemical production and processing, the processing of raw materials and R&D as favoured sectors.

Ningbo Free Trade Zone: one of 15 such zones authorised by the State Council and the only one in Zhejiang. It began in 1992, covers 2.3 square kilometres (0.89 square miles), and lies midway along the mainland coast at the south of the Yangtze River Delta. In 2008 it turned out RMB 53.33 billion of industrial output, a 19.8 percent rise on 2007.
Nordic Industrial Park (NIP): an early example of a wholly foreign-owned industrial park in China, managed by a Scandinavian team.
Ningbo Advertising Park: a national-level pilot park in the Southern Business District, where financial incentives have drawn over 300 related firms.
Ningbo's long history and prosperity left it with rich tourist resources. The list below follows the city's districts and uses attractions recognised by the municipal culture and tourism authority.
Moon Lake Park (Yuehu Park): a Tang-dynasty reservoir (636 CE) at the heart of the district, dotted with islets and old buildings.

Tianyi Pavilion: among the city's best-known attractions. Dating from 1516 CE, it is Asia's oldest surviving library and ranks with the 3 oldest private libraries anywhere. Its holdings start in the 11th century and include woodblock and handwritten editions of Confucian classics, scarce local histories and rosters of men who passed the imperial exams. The name now covers the whole museum complex, which includes the Ming-dynasty mansion of the first owner, Fan Qing (1516 CE), a traditional garden, an old private theatre for Chinese plays, and a Mahjong (麻將) museum, because the game is said to have originated in Ningbo.

He Ancestral Temple (賀祕監祠): honours the Tang poet He Zhizhang (659 CE to 744 CE), nicknamed by himself the "Siming Crazy Guest". Completed in 1144 CE under the Song, it was restored in 1865 CE in the Qing period.

Ancient Korean Embassy: built in the Northern Song to receive Korean envoys and trade missions. War destroyed it in 1130 CE, and it became a protected site in 1984. Today it is a showroom for the history of ties between Ningbo and Korea.

Moon Lake literary spots: Zhenming Ridge, Xuanmiao Temple, Central Lake Temple and the Central Lake East Bridge. The Ningbo-born writer Qu You set his tale Peony Dengji (牡丹燈記, Japanese Botan Dōrō, also known as Tales of the Peony Lantern) at Moon Lake, in the Fang Guozhen period. It is a ghost-and-human love story. The Japanese scholar Koyama Issei matched several places in the story to real sites, and the tale became one of three Kaidan stories in Japan.

Drum Tower, also called Haishu Tower: all that survives of a Tang city-gate tower. A six-metre Romanesque bell tower was added at the top in the Republic period, and the shops around its base are rebuilt in traditional style.
Chenghuang Temple, known too as Ningbo County Temple: an ancient City God temple amid the downtown shopping district.

Tianfeng Pagoda: a national protected site and the tallest ancient structure in town, a six-sided Song-style brick-and-wood tower typical of Jiangnan. It looks like seven storeys above ground, with another seven below. First built in 695 CE in the Tang dynasty (618 to 907 CE).
Tianyi Square: in the busy old downtown with a famous shopping complex, named for Tianyi Ge, Asia's oldest private library.
Nantang Old Street: a riverside street of folk-craft shops, souvenir stores and small restaurants, once used for fairs and flea markets and renovated as a tourist site in 2013.
Liangzhu Cultural Park: a theme park about the Butterfly Lovers, one of four great Chinese folktales, often called the Oriental Romeo and Juliet.
Baiyun Manor: an old academy where the late-Ming and early-Qing thinker and historian Huang Zongxi (黃宗羲, style name Taichong) lectured.
Tashan Weir: a Tang dam.
Wulongtan Scenic Resort (Five-dragon Pools): one of Ningbo's Ten New Sceneries and a national AAAA scenic area.
Xiaowen Street: an old street named for Yang Qing (杨庆), a filial son of the Song era.

Ningbo Museum: also called the Yinzhou Museum or Ningbo Historic Museum, it presents local history and customs and is a masterwork of Wang Shu, who in 2012 became the first Chinese citizen to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize. It is also the main location for the 2023 TV adaptation of Liu Cixin's Three Bodies.
Romon U-Park: one of the world's largest urban indoor theme parks.

Ningbo Eastern New Town: a recently developed district with a planned business centre, two skyscrapers of 400 m, corporate headquarters, government offices, museums, galleries and shopping malls. Within it you will find the Urban Planning Exhibition Center, Yinzhou Park and the Southern CBD, along with the new city library that opened in 2018 and the Ningbo Hankyu complex, which came in 2021 as the Japanese department store Hankyu's first branch overseas.

Dongqian Lake: Zhejiang's largest natural freshwater lake, first recorded in the West Jin dynasty. Around it are Little Putuo (an island with Song temples built by the prime minister Shihao), Yuefei Temple (in memory of Yuefei), Taogong Island (where the folklore couple Fanli and Xishi lived), the Southern Song Dynasty Rock Carving Park (honoured with a national best-project award for cultural relics conservation), Fuquan Mountain, which hosts a theme park devoted to Chinese tea, and the Ningbo Ocean World aquarium with its ocean theatre. The former Youngor Zoo, now Ningbo Wildlife Park, is a 4A scenic area within the lake resort and counts among the biggest wildlife parks in China measured by water area. Ningbo Sakura Park (Zhongxing Sakura Park) was created to mark the sister-city link with Nagaoka, Japan.
Hanling Old Street: an ancient street once called Hanling City, where "city" meant bazaar.
Qita Temple: a Zen Buddhist complex first consecrated in the Tang dynasty, downtown.

Tianhou Temple: formerly a Mazu temple used as the Qing'an Huiguan guild hall of Fujianese merchants. S. Wells Williams called it the most beautiful place in Ningbo in the 19th century and John Thomson counted it among China's most beautiful temples. The original was destroyed in the Chinese Civil War, and the rebuilt complex, with many original artworks, now serves as the museum of maritime affairs and folk customs for eastern Zhejiang.
Temple of King Ashoka: Buddhist, first founded in the Western Jin (282 AD).
Tiantong Temple: counted among the "Five Chan Buddhism Temples", it is where Japan's Sōtō school (曹洞宗, Sōtō-shū) of Buddhism traces its roots.

ningbo-university-of-technology.h: Zhejiang: the province behind the city

blocks.x: A university's region shapes daily life almost as much as the campus does, so a short history of Zhejiang follows.

In the Hangzhou area, the Kuahuqiao culture, an early Neolithic settlement, flourished around 6000 to 5000 BC. Zhejiang also hosted the Hemudu culture (from 5500 BC) and the Liangzhu culture (from 3400 BC).

During the second millennium BC the region lay outside the main sphere of Shang civilisation, and its people were known collectively as Dongyue. The kingdom of Yue appears in records of the Spring and Autumn period, based in northern Zhejiang. The Shiji claims its rulers descended from Yu the Great, founder of the Xia. The "Song of the Yue Boatman" (越人歌, Yuèrén Gē), written down in Chinese around 528 BC by authors in Hebei and Henan, shows that Yue speakers could not understand northern dialects. The Sword of Goujian, inscribed in bird-worm seal script, survives from the period, and Yuenü (越女), "the Lady of Yue", was a famed swordswoman. To check Wu's rise, Chu chose to build up Yue.

King Goujian recovered from early defeats and annexed Wu's land fully in 473 BC. The Yue kings moved their capital from the Mount Kuaiji area near today's Shaoxing to the old Wu capital at present-day Suzhou. In 333 BC Chu destroyed Yue. The Qin Empire absorbed the area in 222 BC and created Kuaiji Commandery, initially governed from Wu in Jiangsu.

Kuaiji Commandery was the first power base of the rebellion led by Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu against Qin, which restored the kingdom of Chu for a time before the Han overcame it. In the Later Han period, control returned to the settlement beneath Mount Kuaiji, but the Minyue hinterland was nominally ruled and its Yue inhabitants kept their own structures.

After the Han collapsed, warlords Yan Baihu and Wang Lang held Zhejiang until Sun Ce and Sun Quan defeated them and founded the Kingdom of Wu. Though the court moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (now Nanjing), the Sun rulers kept developing the region and gained from refugees fleeing northern turmoil. Kilns were set up and trade reached Manchuria and Funan in mainland Southeast Asia.

Wu (229 to 280), or Eastern Wu, was the most economically advanced of the Three Kingdoms (220 to 280). Romance of the Three Kingdoms depicts Zhejiang with the best-equipped navy, and says Wei (魏) and Shu (蜀) avoided direct clashes with Wu, relying on camouflage and deception to take its arrows and bows.

Although Nanjing (then Jiankang) dominated, Qiantang, the old name of Hangzhou, remained one of three major southern centres providing tax revenue to the north, the others being Jiankang and Chengdu. It was promoted and renamed Hangzhou in 589.

Once Wu had fallen and the Wu Hu rose against the Jin dynasty (266 to 420), many elite northern families had cooperated with the non-Chinese rulers. Some lost status and fled south of the Yangtze, and a few settled around Hangzhou. The clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), chancellor of Shu Han, formed Zhuge Village (Zhege Cun) in the suburbs, where every villager bears the surname Zhuge. It has kept itself apart for centuries and was only recently publicised. Since Zhejiang is mountainous with little farmland, most refugees probably went further, to southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, where land was richer and regional governments looser.

Through the Six Dynasties (220 or 222 to 589), the Sui and the Tang, Zhejiang remained one of the richest areas, forming the core of Jiangnan, the Yangtze River Delta. After the Sui absorbed it, the wealth funded ambitions in Korea and Vietnam and drove the building of the network that became the Grand Canal. The Canal carried grain and resources from Zhejiang through Hangzhou, its hinterland along the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay, and from Suzhou to the North China Plain. The failed Korean war led to Sui's fall to the Tang, who ruled over a golden age. Zhejiang, part of the Jiangnan East Circuit, stayed prosperous, and the Canal kept moving grain north. As the Tang broke up, Zhejiang formed most of the territory of the kingdom of Wuyue.

In basketball, the Chinese Basketball Association has two professional teams in the province, the Zhejiang Golden Bulls and the Bayi Rockets, who are based in Ningbo. In football, Zhejiang Professional F.C. competes in the Chinese Super League.

Ningbo University of Technology is an engineering-minded provincial university in a prosperous trading port with mild, wet weather, excellent historic sights and a deep regional history. Confirm the staff and student figures and the campus move to Jiangbei with the university before you apply.

ningbo-university-of-technology.h: What stands out about the university

blocks.x: The most useful fact for an applicant is the university's engineering identity. It started life as Ningbo College in 1983, received national recognition as an exemplary engineering college in 1997, and was approved for full-time four-year undergraduate teaching in 2004. That timeline makes it a relatively young institution, built up over four decades rather than inherited from the 19th or early 20th century.

Two points deserve a check with the university directly. The first is the campus location: sources mention both Haishu District and Jiangbei District, and a new site of 914,791.894 square metres is under construction. The second is the headcount, since roughly 700 staff and 8,000 students come from an older description.

ningbo-university-of-technology.h: Why Ningbo suits an engineering university

blocks.x: The city's strengths line up well with the subjects an engineering college teaches. Ningbo exports electrical products, textiles, food and industrial tools. Its private sector produced 80 percent of GDP in 2013. It has a port, an airport and several development zones in chemicals, energy transshipment, biotechnology, logistics, advertising and international trade. For an engineering student that means a visible industrial environment right outside the campus, even though the source does not describe any formal links between the university and these firms.

The economy has also been shaped by geography. Because Ningbo was once somewhat remote from other large cities, the Hangzhou Bay Bridge of 2007 mattered a great deal: it brought Shanghai within about two and a half hours by road.
Hot, humid summers, with July averaging 29.1 °C.
A rainy spell in June, called the plum rains.
A typhoon season from August to October, with 1.8 storms on average each year, rarely a direct hit.
Cool, cloudy, dry winters, averaging 5.8 °C in January, with occasional snow.
Rain of about 1,430 mm a year overall.
The attractions listed above fall into several themes.
History and books: Tianyi Pavilion, Tianfeng Pagoda, the Drum Tower and the Ancient Korean Embassy site.
Religion and philosophy: Qita Temple, Tiantong Temple, the Temple of King Ashoka and Tianhou Temple.
Water and nature: Moon Lake, Dongqian Lake, Wulongtan and the Ningbo Wildlife Park.
Modern city life: Eastern New Town, the Ningbo Museum, the new library and the Hankyu complex.

Zhejiang's story begins with Neolithic cultures such as Kuahuqiao, Hemudu and Liangzhu. It then passes through the kingdom of Yue, Qin and Han rule, the Eastern Wu of the Three Kingdoms, the Six Dynasties, and the Sui and Tang, when grain from the region moved north along the Grand Canal. The point for modern students is that this province has been a wealthy, outward-looking heartland of Jiangnan for well over a thousand years, and Ningbo, a trading port since the 7th century, fits that pattern.
Ningbo University of Technology lists 26 programs for international students on this site: 21 bachelor, 5 master's programs.

By language of instruction: 23 taught in Chinese, 3 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.

26 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (2):
Intelligent Construction
International Business
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

ningbo-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Ningbo University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Ningbo, register at Ningbo University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Ningxia Medical University (NXMU, Chinese: 宁夏医科大学; pinyin: Níngxià Yīkē Dàxué), previously known as Ningxia Medical College, is a medical school located in Yinchuan City, Ningxia Province, China.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Yinchuan, where Ningxia Medical University is located.

Yinchuan lies in the middle of the Yinchuan Plain. It is sheltered from the deserts of Mongolia by the high ranges of the Helan Mountains to its west. The Yellow River runs through Yinchuan from southwest to northeast. The average elevation of Yinchuan is 1,100 meters (about 3,608 feet). The urban center of Yinchuan lies about halfway between the Yellow River and the edge of Helan Mountains.

Yinchuan has a cold desert climate (Köppen BWk) with an annual rainfall of 194 mm (7.64 in). Yinchuan has distinct seasons, with dry, cold winters, late springs and short hot summers. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from −6.8 °C (19.8 °F) in January to 24.4 °C (75.9 °F) in July, with the annual mean at 10.1 °C (50.2 °F). Diurnal temperature variation tends to be large due to the aridity, which also partly contributes to the sunny climate; with monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 58 percent in January to 67 percent in November, the city receives 2,761 hours of bright sunshine annually. There are 158 frost-free days.

As of 2019, 72.43% of the city's population is Han Chinese, 25.79% is Hui, and 1.78% are other ethnic minorities. Of the city's six county-level divisions, all have a super-majority of Han Chinese people sans the county-level city of Lingwu, which is majority Hui.

Of the city's population, 79.05% live in urban areas as of 2019. This proportion is highest in Xixia District, where 91.28% of the population lives in urban areas, and is lowest in Lingwu, where 58.22% of the population lives in urban areas.

As of 2025, Yinchuan had a GDP of CN¥303.353 billion (US$42.469 billion) and a GDP per capita of CN¥104,100 (US$10,917). In 2010, Yinchuan was designated as the site for the China-Arab States Cooperation Forum. At the national level, Yinchuan hosts the China-Arab States Expo, to function as a commercial link between China and Arab States. Yinchuan has an aircraft tire plant owned by Singapore-based Giti Tire.
Yinchuan classifies itself as a smart city, where modern technology is employed such as facial recognition for public transport payments, connected trash bins and digital citizen service centres.

Until the 1950s, the Yellow river, which is navigable downstream as far as Baotou in the Inner Mongolian autonomous region and upstream to Zhongwei and Zhongning, was the chief communication link. Yinchuan still has a river port at Hengcheng, about 15 km (9.3 mi) to the east.

Since 1958, the city has been served by Yinchuan railway station on the Baotou–Lanzhou railway integrating it in the Chinese railway network. The Taiyuan–Zhongwei–Yinchuan railway opened in 2011. Since the opening of the Yinchuan–Zhongwei high-speed railway in 2019, Yinchuan is also served by high-speed train services.

Yinchuan is the first Chinese city to implement a monorail beyond demonstrational use, transporting visitors around the Yinchuan International Flower Expo park. The BYD Skytrain based system entered operation in September 2017.
Highways link the city to Baotou along the river, to Lanzhou in Gansu province to the southwest, to Wuwei in Gansu to the west, and to Xi'an in Shaanxi province to the southeast.
China National Highway 110, 109, 211 and 244
G69 Yinchuan–Baise Expressway
G85 Yinchuan–Kunming Expressway
G1816 Wuhai–Maqên Expressway
G2004 Yinchuan Ring Expressway

In Q1 2018, Yinchuan ranked first in traffic congestion severity in China. According to research by AutoNavi, and the Planning and Research Institute of the Ministry of Transport, this was caused by numerous construction works and the poor structure of the road network, rather than pure traffic volume. After reorganization of the road network and bottleneck intersections, congestion has reduced.
It is served by Yinchuan Hedong International Airport. It is 25 km (16 mi) from Yinchuan and has flights to Beijing, Chengdu, Dunhuang, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Xian, and Zhengzhou.

Although most residents are Han Chinese, Yinchuan is a center for the Muslim Hui people, who constitute slightly over a quarter of the population. Hui Muslims play a vital role as being middlemen in trade between the Middle East and China, and the China-Middle East trade has become increasingly important to the country. Consequently, the national government has started constructing a $3.7 billion Islamic theme park called "World Muslim City" in Yinchuan. Unlike Uyghurs, who faces far more restrictions in religious freedoms, Hui Muslims generally do not seek independence from China and have a cultural affinity to the Han, and are far more assimilated into mainstream Chinese life.

A number of cultural festivals are celebrated in Yinchuan. These include an Internet Film Festival, a Car and Motorcycle Tourism Festival, and an International Poetry Festival. Until 2000, Yinchuan was also the traditional host of an August festival celebrating the harvesting of Goji berries (a major product of Ningxia).
The city's attractions include the Sand-lake, the Western Xia tombs, and the China Western film Studios.
Sand Lake is a lake in a desert 35 miles north of Yinchuan with birds, reeds, lotus and fish.

The Western Xia Imperial Tombs are 15.5 miles west of Yinchuan on east side of Mt. Helan. Since June 1972, nine imperial tombs and 253 lesser tombs have been unearthed, which are as grand as Ming Tombs in Beijing. With a total area of more than 19.3 square miles, it is unique among royal burials.

China West Film Studio, which has been famed as "One Superb in China, and Treasure of Ningxia Province", is at the eastern foot of the magnificent Helanshan Mountain, 25 kilometers from the railway station of Yinchuan City, and 48 kilometers from Hedong Airport. It produced The Herdsman, Red Sorghum, Lover's Grief over the Yellow River, New Dragon Gate Inn, Ashes of Time, A Chinese Odyssey, the television series Qiao's Grand Courtyard, and nearly one hundred other films. In 2018, John Cena lived for five months in Yinchuan while working on a film, Hidden Strike, with Jackie Chan.
There are two pagodas in Yinchuan that are part of the "Eight Famous Scenery of Ningxia": one is the Haibao Pagoda in the northern suburb and the other is the Chengtiansi Pagoda in the west.
Parts of the Great Wall are near the city.
Ningxia Medical University is in Ningxia, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Ningxia.
The earliest human activity in Ningxia can be traced back to 30,000 years ago, with remains of the Shuidonggou culture found in Lingwu.

As a frontier zone between nomadic pastoralists and sedentary farmers, Ningxia was a frequent seat of war and incursions by non-Chinese tribes. Ningxia and its surrounding areas were incorporated into the Qin as the Beidi Commandery as early as the 3rd century BC. To pacify the region, the imperial government established military colonies to reclaim land. In addition, horse pasturages were founded under the Imperial Stud to safeguard the supply of army horses, as early as the Western Han dynasty (206 BC – AD 9). Throughout the Han dynasty and the Tang dynasty there were several large cities established in the region. The Liang Province rebellion at the end of the Han dynasty affected Ningxia.

By the 11th century the Tangut people had established the Western Xia dynasty on the outskirts of the then-Song dynasty. Jews also lived in Ningxia, as evidenced by the fact that in 1489, after a major flood destroyed Torah scrolls in Kaifeng, a replacement set was sent to the Kaifeng Jews by the Ningbo and Ningxia Jewish communities.

It then came under Mongol domination after Genghis Khan conquered Yinchuan in the early 13th century. Muslims from Central Asia also began moving into Ningxia from the west. By the late 17th century, Ningxia had become a weaving centre, producing many early Chinese carpets. The Muslim Dungan Revolt of the 19th century affected Ningxia.

In 1914, Ningxia was merged with the province of Gansu. In 1928, it became a separate province. Between 1914 and 1928, the Ma clique ruled the provinces of Qinghai, Ningxia and Gansu; General Ma Hongkui was the military governor of Ningxia and had absolute authority in the province. The Muslim conflict in Gansu, which lasted from 1927 to 1930, spilt over into Ningxia. In 1934, warlord and National Revolutionary Army general Sun Dianying attempted to conquer the province, but was defeated by an alliance led by the Ma clique.

From 1950 to 1958, a Kuomintang Islamic insurgency resulted in fighting throughout Northwest China, including Ningxia. In 1954, the Chinese government merged Ningxia with Gansu, but in 1958 Ningxia formally became an autonomous region of China. In 1969, Ningxia received a part of the Inner Mongolian Autonomous Region, but this area was returned in 1979.

A number of Chinese artifacts dating from the Tang dynasty and Song dynasty, some of which had been owned by Emperor Zhenzong, were excavated and then came into the hands of Ma Hongkui, who refused to publicize the findings. Among the artifacts were a white marble tablet from the Tang dynasty, gold nails, and bands made out of metal. It was not until after Ma Hongkui died that his wife went to Taiwan in 1971 from America to bring the artifacts to Chiang Kai-shek, who turned them over to the Taipei National Palace Museum.

Present-day Ningxia is one of the nation's smallest provincial-level units and borders the provinces of Shaanxi and Gansu and the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. At 3556 meters above sea level, Aobaogeda (敖包疙瘩) in the Helan Mountains is the highest point in Ningxia.

Ningxia is a relatively dry, desert-like region and features a diverse geography of forested mountains and hills, table lands, deserts, flood plains and basins cut through by the Yellow River. The Ningxia ecosystem is one of the least studied regions in the world. Significant irrigation supports the growing of wolfberries, a commonly consumed fruit throughout the region. Ningxia's deserts include the Tengger Desert in Shapotou.

The northern section, through which the Yellow River flows, supports the best agricultural land. A railroad, linking Lanzhou with Baotou, crosses the region. A highway has been built across the Yellow River at Yinchuan.

On 16 December 1920, the Haiyuan earthquake, 8.6 magnitude, at 36.6°N 105.32°E﻿ / 36.6; 105.32, initiated a series of landslides that killed an estimated 200,000 people. Over 600 large loess landslides created more than 40 new lakes.

It was reported that approximately 34 percent (33.85 million mu; 22,600 km2) of the region's total surface consisted of grassland. This figure is down from approximately 40 percent in the 1990s. The grasslands are spread over the dry desert-steppe area in the northeast (which forms a part of the Inner Mongolian steppe region), and the hilly pastures located on the semi-arid Loess Plateau in the south. It is ascertained that the grasslands of Ningxia have been degraded to various degrees. Scientists debate the extent to which this degradation occurs over space and time. Historical research has also found limited evidence of expanding grassland degradation and desertification in Ningxia. A major component of land management in Ningxia is a ban on open grazing, which has been in place since 2003. The ecological and socio-economic effects of this Grazing Ban in relation to the grasslands and pastoralists' livelihood are contested. The ban stipulates that animal husbandry be limited to enclosed pens and no open grazing be permitted in certain time periods set by the Autonomous Region's People's Government.

The region is 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) from the sea and has an arid continental climate on the north to humid continental climate to the south, with average summer temperatures rising to 17 to 24 °C (63 to 75 °F) in July and average winter temperatures dropping to between −7 and −15 °C (19 and 5 °F) in January. Seasonal extreme temperatures can reach 39 °C (102 °F) in summer and −30 °C (−22 °F) in winter. The diurnal temperature variation can reach above 17 °C (31 °F), especially in spring. Annual rainfall averages from 190 to 700 millimetres (7.5 to 27.6 in), with more rain falling in the south of the region.
Ningxia is rich in mineral resources with proven deposits of 34 kinds of minerals, much

of which located in grassland areas. In 2011 it was estimated that the potential value per capita of these resources accounted for 163.5 percent of the nation's average. Ningxia boasts verified coal reserves of over 30 billion tons, with an estimated reserve of more than 202 billion tons, ranking sixth nationwide. Coal deposits are spread over one-third of the total surface of Ningxia, and mined in four major fields in the Helan and Xiangshan mountains, Ningdong and Yuanzhou (or Guyuan). The region's reserves of oil and natural gas can be found in Yanchi and Lingwu County, and are ideal for large-scale development of oil, natural gas and chemical industries. Ningxia leads China in gypsum deposits, with a proven reserve of more than 4.5 billion tons, of which the rarely found, top-grade gypsum accounts for half of the total deposits. The Hejiakouzi deposit in Tongxin County features a reserve of 20 million tons of gypsum with a total thickness of 100 meters. There is a considerable deposit of quartz sandstone, of which 17 million tons have been ascertained. In addition, there are phosphorus, flint, copper, iron, barite, other minerals and Helan stone – a special clay stone.

Rural Ningxia was for long an officially designated poverty area, and remains on the lower rungs of the developmental ladder. Its nominal GDP in 2023 was 569.65 billion yuan (US$79.75 billion) and its per capita GDP 77,981 yuan (US$10,917). It comprises 0.41% of the national economy.

Similar to other areas, Ningxia has seen a gradual decline of its peasant population due to rural–urban migration. Despite this, the great majority (62.8 percent) was still agricultural at the time of the survey. Animal husbandry is important for the regional economy. In the main pastoral county, Yanchi, it is even the leading industry when specified for the primary sector. The dominant grazing animals are sheep and goat. In the (semi-)pastoral regions, herders engage in a mixed sedentary farming operation of dryland agriculture and extensive animal husbandry, while full nomadic pastoralism is no longer practiced. Since a cattle breeding plan was implemented in 2002, the province has become one of China's main dairy production areas.
Ningxia is the principal region of China where wolfberries are grown. Other specialties of Ningxia are licorice, products made from Helan stone, fiddlehead and products made from sheepskin.

Ningxia wines are a promising area of development. The Chinese authorities have given approval to the development of the eastern base of the Helan Mountains as an area suitable for wine production. Several large Chinese wine companies including Changyu and Dynasty Wine have begun development in the western region of the province. Together they now own 20,000 acres of land for wine plantations and Dynasty has ploughed 100 million yuan into Ningxia. In addition, the major oil company China Petroleum and Chemical Corporation has founded a grape plantation near the Helan Mountains. The household appliance company Midea has also begun participating in Ningxia's wine industry. Vineyards have been set up in the region.
Ningxia was a major recipient of China's investment in industrial capacity during the Third Front campaign.

Yinchuan Economic and Technological Development Zone was established in 1992. Spanning 32 km2 (12 sq mi), it has an annual economic output Rmb23.7 billion (25.1% up) (US$3.5 billion). Major investors are mainly local enterprises such as Kocel Steel Foundry, FAG Railway Bearing (Ningxia), Ningxia Little Giant Machine Tools, etc. Major industries include machinery and equipment manufacturing, new materials, fine chemicals and the animation industry.

Desheng Industrial Park (in Helan County) is a base for about 400 enterprises. The industrial park has industrial chains from Muslim food and commodities to trade and logistics, new materials and bio-pharmaceuticals that has 80 billion yuan in fixed assets. Desheng is looking to be the most promising industrial park in the city. It achieved a total output value of 4.85 billion in 2008, up 40 percent year-on-year. The local government plans to cut taxes and other fees to reduce the burden on local enterprises. The industrial output value reached 2.68 billion yuan in 2008, an increase of 48 percent from a year earlier.

Islam is the Majority religion in Ningxia, followed by 54% of the population. The Han Chinese practise Chinese folk religions, Taoism, Confucianism and Chinese Buddhism. Christianity is the religion of 1.17% of the province's population. In 2014, there were 7,268 mosques in Ningxia, which is about one per 920 residents.

One of Ningxia's main tourist spots is the internationally renowned Xixia Tombs site located 30 km (19 mi) west of Yinchuan. The remnants of nine Western Xia emperors' tombs and two hundred other tombs lie within a 50 km2 (19 sq mi) area. Other famous sites in Ningxia include the Helan Mountains, the mysterious 108 stupas, the twin pagodas of Baisikou and the desert research outpost at Shapotou. A less visited tourist spot in Ningxia is the Mount Sumeru Grottoes (须弥山), which is among the ten most famous grottoes in China.

Ningxia Medical University is on the Ministry of Education's list of universities approved to enrol international students in English-taught MBBS (Clinical Medicine) programs for 2026-27. Universities that are not on the annual list may not recruit English-taught MBBS students, so confirm the current list before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

ningxia-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Ningxia Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Yinchuan, register at Ningxia Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Known as NXU (宁夏大学), Ningxia University serves the region as a public institution located in Yinchuan, capital of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. The autonomous region owns it, and the cost of running it is split between the regional authorities and the national Ministry of Education. National schemes it participates in include Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction initiative.

The school was founded in 1958. Late in 1997 it absorbed Ningxia Institute of Technology together with Yinchuan Normal College, a college that already contained Ningxia Education College. In February 2002 it combined with Ningxia Agricultural College, and the merged institution became the Ningxia University that exists today.

NXU now runs three campuses. Its workforce is above 2,600 people, and more than 50 per cent of those are formal teaching staff. Over half of these teachers hold titles at the intermediate or senior level, and 52 per cent hold a master's or doctoral degree. The State Council pays special allowances to 15 of the teachers, while another 17 were selected for the national "Hundreds, Thousands, Tens of Thousands Experts Project". The university enrols over 15,000 undergraduates and more than 1,300 graduate students, and over 600 students are in minority preparatory programmes.

Teaching is arranged through residential colleges (Shuyuan). A college supervises at least one academic division (Xuebu), and under each division sit several schools (Xueyuan), the bodies that actually run undergraduate degrees.

NXU is regularly ranked first among universities in the Ningxia region. Since 2016 it has stayed inside the top 300 nationwide on the Best Chinese Universities Ranking, which is also called the "Shanghai Ranking". As of 2025 that table placed it 134th in China. The Academic Ranking of World Universities for 2026 puts it in the 901st band worldwide, and the University Rankings by Academic Performance for 2026-2027 give it 943rd in the world. These are different tables with different methods, so treat the numbers as signals rather than a single verdict.
Student life depends a lot on the city around the university: the weather, getting around and what to do. The sections below explain Yinchuan.

The city occupies the centre of the Yinchuan Plain. A tall wall of mountains, the Helan range, lies to its west and protects it from the Mongolian deserts. The Yellow River crosses the city from south-west to north-east. Average elevation is 1,100 metres (about 3,608 feet), and the urban centre lies about halfway between the river and the foot of the Helan Mountains.
The climate here is cold desert (Köppen BWk), with annual rainfall of just 194 mm (7.64 inches). The seasons are distinct: winters are dry and cold, spring comes late, and summers are short and hot.
Over 24 hours, January averages −6.8 °C (19.8 °F) and July averages 24.4 °C (75.9 °F). The annual mean is 10.1 °C (50.2 °F).
The air is so dry that temperatures swing widely between day and night, and dryness helps keep skies sunny.
Possible sunshine ranges between 58 per cent in January and 67 per cent in November, adding up to 2,761 sunny hours a year.
There are 158 frost-free days a year.
In practice you will want warm winter clothes, sun protection and moisturiser.

As of 2019, 72.43 per cent of the city's residents are Han Chinese, 25.79 per cent are Hui and 1.78 per cent belong to other ethnic minorities. The city has six county-level divisions. Five of them have a Han Chinese super-majority, and the exception is the county-level city of Lingwu, where the Hui are the majority.
In 2019, 79.05 per cent of the population lived in urban areas. Xixia District has the highest share, with 91.28 per cent urban, and Lingwu has the lowest at 58.22 per cent.

In 2025 the city produced a GDP of CN¥303.353 billion (about US$42.469 billion), which works out at CN¥104,100 (US$10,917) per resident. The city was named the home of the China-Arab States Cooperation Forum in 2010, and it also hosts the national China-Arab States Expo, which acts as a business link between China and the Arab world. A Singapore-based firm, Giti Tire, owns an aircraft tyre plant here.
Yinchuan describes itself as a smart city, using technology such as facial recognition for paying public transport fares, connected rubbish bins and digital citizen service centres.

Before the 1950s the Yellow River was the main communication route. It can be navigated downstream as far as Baotou in Inner Mongolia and upstream to Zhongwei and Zhongning. A river port remains at Hengcheng, roughly 15 km (9.3 miles) east of town.

The railway reached Yinchuan in 1958, when its station opened on the Baotou-Lanzhou line and tied the city into the national network. Another connection, the Taiyuan-Zhongwei-Yinchuan line, followed in 2011, and since 2019 the Yinchuan-Zhongwei high-speed line has carried fast trains.

No Chinese city had used a monorail for anything beyond demonstration until Yinchuan did so. The system, a BYD Skytrain that started running in September 2017, takes visitors round the grounds of the Yinchuan International Flower Expo park.
By road, Baotou is reached along the river, and Lanzhou (south-west) and Wuwei (west) are both in Gansu, while Xi'an in Shaanxi lies to the south-east. The main routes are:
China National Highways 110, 109, 211 and 244
the G69 Yinchuan-Baise Expressway
the G85 Yinchuan-Kunming Expressway
the G1816 Wuhai-Maqên Expressway
the G2004 Yinchuan Ring Expressway

In the first quarter of 2018, Yinchuan ranked top in China for severity of traffic congestion. Research by AutoNavi and the Ministry of Transport's Planning and Research Institute blamed this on many construction projects and a badly structured road network, not simply on the number of vehicles. Congestion has eased since the road network and bottleneck junctions were reorganised.
The airport, Yinchuan Hedong International, sits 25 km (16 miles) out of town. Its routes include Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, along with Chengdu, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Dunhuang.

Han Chinese are the majority, but Yinchuan is also a centre for the Hui, a Muslim people who make up slightly more than a quarter of the population. The Hui have long acted as go-betweens for commerce linking the Middle East with China, and that trade matters more and more to the country. With this in mind, the national government has started building "World Muslim City", an Islamic theme park in Yinchuan costing US$3.7 billion. The Hui have a cultural closeness to the Han and are widely integrated into mainstream Chinese life.

Yinchuan celebrates a number of festivals: an Internet Film Festival, an International Poetry Festival and a Car and Motorcycle Tourism Festival. An August festival for the goji berry harvest (goji being a major Ningxia product) was traditionally held in the city too, up to the year 2000.
Three well-known attractions are the China Western film studios, the Western Xia tombs and Sand Lake.
Sand Lake is a desert lake 35 miles north of Yinchuan, where visitors find birds, reeds, lotus and fish.

The Western Xia Imperial Tombs stand 15.5 miles to the west, on the eastern flank of Mount Helan. Excavations since June 1972 have unearthed nine imperial tombs and 253 smaller ones, comparable in grandeur with the Ming Tombs in Beijing. Covering more than 19.3 square miles, the site is unlike any other royal burial ground.

China West Film Studio carries the praise "One Superb in China, and Treasure of Ningxia Province". The studio lies at the foot of Helanshan, on its eastern side, 25 kilometres from Yinchuan railway station and 48 kilometres from Hedong Airport. Its credits include Red Sorghum, The Herdsman, New Dragon Gate Inn, Ashes of Time, A Chinese Odyssey and Lover's Grief over the Yellow River, as well as the TV series Qiao's Grand Courtyard and close to a hundred other titles. In 2018 the actor John Cena spent five months in Yinchuan filming Hidden Strike with Jackie Chan.
Two of the "Eight Famous Scenery of Ningxia" are pagodas. One is Haibao Pagoda, in the north of the city, and the other is Chengtiansi Pagoda, in the west.
Stretches of the Great Wall lie near the city.
Where a university sits matters almost as much as the university itself. This part covers Ningxia as a whole, beginning with its history.
Traces of the Shuidonggou culture found at Lingwu show that people were active here about 30,000 years ago.

Ningxia was a frontier between nomadic herders and settled farmers, so it saw frequent warfare and raids by non-Chinese tribes. By the 3rd century BC it and the surrounding lands had been taken into the Qin state as the Beidi Commandery. To pacify the area the imperial government set up military colonies to bring land into cultivation. Horse farms run by the Imperial Stud existed in the region as early as the Western Han (206 BC to AD 9), to keep the army supplied. Several big cities were built here during the Han and Tang dynasties. At the close of the Han, unrest in the Liang Province rebellion reached Ningxia as well.

The Tangut people established the Western Xia dynasty around the 11th century, on the margins of the Song realm. Jews lived in Ningxia too: after a great flood destroyed Torah scrolls in Kaifeng in 1489, the Jewish communities of Ningbo and Ningxia sent a replacement set to the Kaifeng Jews.

Genghis Khan took Yinchuan in the early 13th century, and the region came under Mongol rule. Muslims from Central Asia began to arrive from the west. By the end of the 17th century Ningxia was a weaving centre, producing many of China's earliest carpets. The 19th-century Dungan Revolt, a Muslim uprising, affected it as well.

Ningxia was absorbed by Gansu in 1914 and returned as a province of its own in 1928. During those fourteen years the Ma clique controlled Qinghai, Ningxia and Gansu together, with General Ma Hongkui holding total authority as Ningxia's military governor. A Muslim conflict in Gansu between 1927 and 1930 spread to Ningxia. Sun Dianying, a warlord and general in the National Revolutionary Army, tried to seize the province in 1934, but an alliance headed by the Ma clique defeated him.

An Islamic insurgency linked to the Kuomintang caused fighting across Northwest China, Ningxia among it, between 1950 and 1958. In 1954 the government placed Ningxia inside Gansu once more, yet 1958 saw it formally turned into an autonomous region. A piece of Inner Mongolia was assigned to it in 1969 and returned in 1979.

Some Chinese artefacts from the Tang and Song dynasties, a few once owned by Emperor Zhenzong, were dug up and ended up with Ma Hongkui, who would not make the discoveries public. Among the objects were gold nails, metal bands and a Tang-dynasty tablet carved from white marble. Only after Ma Hongkui died did his wife travel from America to Taiwan, in 1971, and give the objects to Chiang Kai-shek, who passed them to the National Palace Museum in Taipei.

Ningxia today is one of the smallest provincial-level units in the country. Its neighbours are Shaanxi and Gansu, with the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region beyond. Its highest point is Aobaogeda (敖包疙瘩) in the Helan Mountains, at 3,556 metres above sea level.

The region is relatively dry and desert-like, yet its geography is varied: forested mountains and hills, plateaus, deserts, flood plains and basins crossed by the Yellow River. Its ecosystem is among the least studied in the world. Heavy irrigation supports wolfberries, a fruit eaten across the region, and the deserts include the Tengger Desert at Shapotou. The northern section, which the Yellow River crosses, holds the best farmland. A railway connects Lanzhou with Baotou through the region, and a highway bridge crosses the Yellow River at Yinchuan.

A magnitude 8.6 quake, the Haiyuan earthquake, struck on 16 December 1920 (36.6°N 105.32°E). It triggered a chain of landslides in which an estimated 200,000 people died, and over 600 large loess landslides formed more than 40 new lakes.

Reports say that roughly 34 per cent of the region (33.85 million mu, or 22,600 km2) is grassland, down from about 40 per cent in the 1990s. The grassland lies in two zones: dry desert-steppe in the north-east, an extension of the steppe of Inner Mongolia, and hilly pasture on the semi-arid Loess Plateau down south. The grasslands have been degraded to varying degrees, though scientists argue over how far this happens in space and time, and historical research has found only limited evidence of spreading degradation and desertification.

A central part of land management is a ban on open grazing, in place since 2003. Livestock farming must take place in enclosed pens, and open grazing is not allowed during periods set by the regional people's government. The ban's ecological and socio-economic effects on grasslands and herders' livelihoods are disputed.

The sea is 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) away. Arid continental weather prevails in the north, humid continental in the south. In July the average is 17 to 24 °C (63 to 75 °F); in January it sinks to between −7 and −15 °C (19 and 5 °F). The most extreme days reach 39 °C (102 °F) in summer and fall to −30 °C (−22 °F) in winter, and in spring especially the difference between day and night can pass 17 °C (31 °F). Yearly rainfall is 190 to 700 millimetres (7.5 to 27.6 inches), and the south gets more.

Ningxia is well endowed with minerals, with 34 kinds of proven deposits, many in grassland areas. A 2011 estimate said the potential value of these resources per person was 163.5 per cent of the national average.

Coal: verified reserves exceed 30 billion tons, and the estimated total is more than 202 billion tons, sixth in China. Coal underlies a third of the region and is worked in four main fields, which are in the Helan and Xiangshan mountains, at Ningdong, and at Yuanzhou (Guyuan).
Oil and natural gas: reserves lie in Yanchi and in Lingwu County and are well suited to big oil, gas and chemical industries.

Gypsum: China's leading reserve, proven at over 4.5 billion tons, half of it rare top-grade material. The Hejiakouzi deposit in Tongxin County holds 20 million tons with a total thickness of 100 metres.
Quartz sandstone: 17 million tons confirmed.
Others: phosphorus, flint, copper, iron, barite and Helan stone, a special clay stone.

Rural Ningxia was officially designated a poverty area for a long time, and it is still low on the development ladder. In 2023 it recorded a nominal GDP of 569.65 billion yuan (about US$79.75 billion), equal to 77,981 yuan (US$10,917) a head. That makes up 0.41 per cent of the national economy.

As elsewhere, rural-to-urban migration is steadily thinning the farming population, yet at the time of the survey the great majority (62.8 per cent) was still agricultural. Livestock matters to the regional economy, and in Yanchi, the main pastoral county, it is actually the leading primary-sector industry. Sheep and goats dominate. In pastoral and semi-pastoral districts, herders combine settled dryland farming with extensive livestock rearing, and fully nomadic herding is no longer practised. A cattle breeding plan launched in 2002 helped turn the region into one of China's main dairy areas.
Ningxia is China's principal wolfberry-growing region. Other specialities are licorice, Helan stone products, fiddlehead ferns and sheepskin goods.

Wine looks like a promising growth area. The authorities have approved the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains as suitable for wine production. Big Chinese producers such as Changyu and Dynasty Wine have begun operating in the west of the province. Between them they hold 20,000 acres of vineyard land, and Dynasty alone has put 100 million yuan into Ningxia. Sinopec (China Petroleum and Chemical Corporation) established a grape plantation close to the Helan Mountains, and the appliance maker Midea has also taken part. Vineyards have been planted across the region.
Airports: besides the Hedong International Airport at Yinchuan, there are Zhongwei Shapotou, Guyuan Liupanshan and, for the north, Wuhai Airport.
Highways: China National Highways 109, 110, 211, 307, 309 and 312.
Bridge: the Taole Yellow River Expressway Bridge (陶乐黄河大桥).
Railways: the Baotou-Lanzhou railway and the Baoji-Zhongwei railway (宝中铁路).

Islam is the main faith in Ningxia, practised by 54 per cent of the people. Han Chinese follow Chinese folk religion, Taoism, Confucianism and Chinese Buddhism, and 1.17 per cent of the province's residents are Christian. A count in 2014 found 7,268 mosques in Ningxia, which is roughly one per 920 residents.
Ningxia University lists 212 programs for international students on this site: 76 bachelor, 121 master's, 15 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 212 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 12,800 to CNY 128,000 (median CNY 12,800), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 12,800 to CNY 160,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.

212 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.
