North China Electric Power University (华北电力大学), known as NCEPU, is a public institution with its main campus in Beijing. Its supervising body is the Ministry of Education, and three kinds of sponsor share the cost: a council formed by 12 giant state-owned power corporations, the China Electricity Council, and the Ministry itself. That last group shows how closely the university is tied to China's energy industry. NCEPU is a member of Project 211 and of the Double First-Class Construction.

Polytechnic subjects are the university's focus. Apart from the main campus in Beijing, a branch campus operates at Baoding, in Hebei Province. The roughly 3,000 full-time faculty and staff serve a student body of about 20,000 undergraduates plus 7,000 at graduate level.

Formally NCEPU reports to China's Ministry of Education. It is on the official list for the Double First Class University Plan (the successor to Project 211) and bears the title "Predominant Discipline Innovation Platform". It is currently a key university built jointly by the Ministry of Education and its University Council, on which seven large enterprises sit. They are China Power Investment Corporation, China Guodian Corporation, China Huadian Corporation, China Datang Corporation, China Huaneng Group, China Southern Power Grid Co., Ltd., and State Grid Corporation of China.

In 1958 the Beijing Institute of Electric Power was founded. A move to Baoding, Hebei province, in 1970 brought a new name, North China Institute of Electric Power. The Beijing Power Engineering and Electronics Institute joined the school in 1995 (a merger), and the present name dates from then. Its main campus returned to Beijing in 2006, though Baoding still hosts a branch campus.
The main campus today is in Zhuxinzhuang, Changping District, right next to the Badaling Expressway, and the setting is attractive.

NCEPU counts as a key university and has more than 40 years of history behind it. Graduates come out of programmes in the social sciences, economics, management and engineering technology. One older description gives over 8,500 students, with more than 600 of them at graduate and doctoral level. That does not fit the much larger enrolment in the opening profile, so treat it as outdated and check the university's own website for current figures.

The university groups its teaching into departments and schools. Departments cover foreign languages, law and politics, finance and accounting, economics and trade, computer science and technology, automation, information engineering, thermal power engineering, electric power engineering, and mathematical and physics science.
Schools, which show how the institution has become a broad, energy-focused university, are:
Science and Technology
Foreign Language
Mathematical and Physical Science
Human and Social Science
Environment Engineering and Science
Control and Computer Engineering
Economics and Management
Nuclear Science and Engineering
Renewable Energy
Energy and Power Engineering
Electrical and Electronic Engineering
(Each of these is a school in its own right.)

Above degree level, NCEPU has a centre for post-doctoral studies with one post-doctoral project programme. It runs 24 bachelor's degree programmes, 17 master's degree programmes and 7 doctoral programmes. It is authorised to admit overseas students. In the library, 11,000 square metres of floor space (120,000 sq ft) house a collection of over one million volumes.

Ministerial key subjects number five: power plant thermal power engineering, technological economics, industrial automation, theoretical electric engineering and power system and its automation. Three ministerial key laboratories are also based here, namely State Monitoring and Fault Diagnosis in Electric Device, Power System Intelligence Protection and Control, and Industrial Process Simulation and Control.

The university has built cooperative links with universities and institutes in over 20 countries and regions, for example Taiwan, Japan, Russia, France, the United States and Britain. Exchange places abroad include the University of Strathclyde, the University of Bath, UC Berkeley, Purdue and Illinois Tech. Another tie is its founding membership of the Cooperation Consortium that unites Beijing's High Technology Universities, a leading academic association among universities in northern China.

north-china-electric-power-university.h: Beijing: the city you would live in

blocks.x: How you experience student life depends on the city beyond the gates: weather, transport and leisure. The sections below look at Beijing, where NCEPU has its main campus.

Beijing's urban areas are dominated by three architectural styles. The first is the imperial Chinese tradition, with the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and, perhaps most famously, Tian'anmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace, still the best-known symbol of the People's Republic of China. The second is the "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to the 1970s, with boxy and at times poorly built structures. The third is far more modern: the east of the city, in the Beijing CBD, shows it best, with the new CCTV Headquarters, and it also appears at the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

From about 2000 onward Beijing expanded quickly with new construction in a range of modern styles by international designers, most strongly in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s design and neofuturistic architecture sit together, old beside new. China Zun, at 528 metres, is the tallest building in Beijing. Since 2007, the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for the best overall tall building has gone to a Beijing building twice: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. That award goes to just one building in the world each year.

Siheyuans are Beijing's courtyards enclosed by buildings, and notable large ones include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Narrow lanes called hutongs normally join the courtyards. Most run straight from east to west, so the doors open to the north and south, which is considered good Feng Shui. Widths differ, and in some hutongs the lane is so narrow that only a few people on foot can pass at one time.

These siheyuans and hutongs used to be everywhere in the city, but they are disappearing quickly because entire city blocks are being replaced by high-rises. Former hutong residents have the right to apartments in the new buildings, at least as large as what they gave up. Many residents complain that hutong community spirit and street life are impossible to replace; the properties are often government owned.

The city is on the northern edge of the North China Plain, an area shaped roughly like a triangle that spreads out to the south and east. Mountains in the north, northwest and west shield both the city and northern China's farming heartland from the desert steppes that press in. Yanqing District and Huairou District, in the northwest of the municipality, are mainly covered by the Jundu Mountains, and Xishan, the Western Hills, mark the west. The Great Wall crosses the northern municipality on rugged ground and was built as protection from nomad raids out of the steppes. On the Hebei border in the Western Hills lies Mount Dongling, with a height of 2,303 metres (7,556 ft), the municipality's high point.

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are among the big rivers in the municipality. All are tributaries within the Hai River system and run towards the southeast. Miyun Reservoir, on the Chaobai's upper reaches, is the municipality's biggest. Beijing is also where the Grand Canal to Hangzhou ends in the north; it was built more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route. In addition, the South-North Water Transfer Project, built in the last decade, brings water from the Yangtze River basin to the city.

Beijing's urban core sits on plains in the south-central municipality, between 40 and 60 metres (130-200 feet) up, and it covers a fairly small but growing portion of the municipal area. Concentric ring roads define its spread. Following the old city walls is the Second Ring Road; satellite towns in the suburbs connect via the Sixth. Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square form the centre, immediately south of the Forbidden City where emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, residence of the country's current leaders, is to the west of Tian'anmen, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between Tiananmen and the Square, serves as the principal east-west axis.
People often say Beijing "spreads like a pancake" (tan da bing) outward from the old centre to its fringe, and that way of growing is frequently blamed for the city's urban problems.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa) and borders on a cold semi-arid monsoonal climate (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid, while the large Siberian anticyclone shapes winters that are brief, cold and dry. Spring brings sandstorms that blow in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, together with quick warming and generally dry weather. Autumn resembles spring as a transitional season with very little rain or snow.

The hottest stretch of the year in Beijing, based on 2001 to 2026, falls in early August, and the coldest in early January. China's standard seasonal division starts winter on 31 October, autumn on 13 September, summer on 20 May and spring on 26 March. Warming has been faster in March and September and slower in May and October lately, so autumn is generally shorter than spring.

For 1991 to 2020 the yearly average temperature in the urban area is between 12.9 °C and 13.3 °C (55.2 °F to 55.9 °F). The daily minimums average 7.7 °C to 8.4 °C (45.9 °F to 47.1 °F), and the daily maximums 18.5 °C to 18.9 °C (65.3 °F to 66.0 °F). In the lower parts of the suburbs the yearly average is 11.5 °C to 13.0 °C (52.7 °F to 55.4 °F); minimums there are 5.9 °C to 8.0 °C (42.6 °F to 46.4 °F), and maximums 18.2 °C to 18.7 °C (64.8 °F to 65.7 °F). In the mountains the yearly average is from 0 °C to 10 °C (32 °F to 50 °F) and goes down with altitude.
In January the daily average is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F); in July it reaches 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

Beijing receives about 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of precipitation a year, although Haidian and Chaoyang get 584.2 mm (23.00 in). Close to three-quarters falls in the months of June to August. The proportion of possible sunshine is lowest in July at 42% and highest in January and February at 62%, so the year brings 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine. The coldest day since 1951 was 22 February 1966, at -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F); the hottest was 24 July 1999, at 41.9 °C (107.4 °F).

Environmental trouble has a long history in Beijing. From 2000 to 2009 the built-up area grew fourfold. That sharply raised emissions from human activity, and it fundamentally altered the local weather, even setting emissions aside. At the surface, albedo, wind speed and humidity decreased, whereas ozone, vertical air dilution and temperatures of the ground and nearby air increased. The combination of urbanisation and pollution from fossil fuels has left the city regularly hit by serious environmental problems that damage the health of many residents.

In 2013 a severe smog episode covered Beijing and most of northern China, and 600 million people were affected overall. That "pollution shock" made air pollution a significant economic and social worry across China. Afterwards the Beijing government announced measures to lower air pollution, among them bringing coal's share down to 10% in 2017 from 24% in 2012. At the national level, the government ordered the removal of heavily polluting vehicles between 2015 and 2017 and put more effort into shifting the energy system toward cleaner sources of energy.

A 2006 study carried out jointly by American and Chinese researchers found that much pollution reaching the city originates in the surrounding cities and provinces. About 35% to 60% of ozone, on average, can be linked to sources beyond Beijing. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality strongly affect Beijing's air quality, in part because summer airflow tends to come from the south and southeast, and in part because of the mountains north and northwest of the city.

Coal burning provides about 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5, and it is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide too. From 2012 the city began switching its coal-fired power stations to natural gas, with an aim of limiting annual coal use to 20 million tons. Beijing's coal use in 2011 was 26.3 million tons, with 73% going to heating and power generation and industry taking the remainder. Neighbouring regions emit a large share of the air pollutants. Coal use in nearby Tianjin was expected to go from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Hebei Province used over 300 million tons in 2011, which is more than all of Germany, with only 30% going to power generation and much of the rest into steel and cement. Plants in the coal-mining areas of Shaanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000, plus those in Shandong, add to the pollution in Beijing. By coal consumption, the Chinese provinces ranked first to fourth are Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

Four large coal-fired power plants once supplied the city with electricity and winter heat. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant, the first, was shut down in 2014 and two others closed in March 2015. The last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to close in 2016. The city planned to cut 13 million tons of coal use from 2013 to 2017 and to cap consumption at 15 million tons in 2015. These targets come from earlier years, so look for recent figures to see how things stand today.

Almost US$17 billion went into cleaning the city's air before the 2008 Summer Olympics, in order to keep promises made about air quality. During the Games Beijing introduced numerous measures. It stopped work at every construction site, shut many factories in Beijing for good and temporarily stopped industry in neighbouring regions, closed some gas stations, and halved motor traffic through an odd-even scheme based on licence plate numbers. Bus and subway fares came down, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. A fleet of 3,800 natural gas-powered buses was also put together, one of the world's largest, and Beijing was the first Chinese city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Cloud seeding is one tool the authorities sometimes use to make rain showers more likely and clear the air before large events, as ahead of the parade for the 60th anniversary in 2009, as well as against drought. Recently they rely more on temporarily closing factories and tighter controls on cars. Examples are "APEC blue" and "parade blue", the brief periods during and just ahead of the 2015 China Victory Day Parade and APEC China 2014. Air quality improved a lot in these periods but returned to unhealthy levels shortly afterwards.

The first smog alert in Beijing came on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing most of the city's industry and many commercial businesses. A second smog "red alert" followed later that month. In November 2016 the environmental protection bureau said that, from 2017, highly polluting old cars would be forbidden to drive whenever smog "red alerts" were issued in the city or surrounding regions.

Pollutants have measurably dropped in recent years, since a "war on pollution" was announced in 2014. Beijing recorded a 35% drop in fine particulates in 2017, and a further drop by 2020. The biggest reasons were replacing coal-fired power with gas and cleaning up the polluting factories in the Beijing area. In 2022 the average concentration of PM2.5, the main airborne fine particulate matter, came down to 30 micrograms per cubic meter, giving the city its best air quality since 2013. Only two days of heavy pollution occurred in 2024, the lowest count ever and 96.6 percent below the 58 days recorded in 2013.

Different sources publish different readings because pollution in Beijing is high. On its website, the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) reports daily levels from 27 monitoring stations in the city. The American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly PM2.5 (fine particulate) and ozone on Twitter. The BJEPB and the US Embassy measure different pollutants using different criteria, so the pollution levels and health impact the BJEPB reports are often lower than the Embassy's.

Smog is dangerous and harmful to the people who live in the city. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on how often people in Beijing get cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Breathing heavily polluted air can lead to cardiovascular and respiratory problems, visits to emergency rooms, and even death.

Dust blown from eroding deserts in northern and northwestern China produces seasonal storms that trouble Beijing. The Beijing Weather Modification Office at times induces rain by artificial means to combat the storms and lessen their impact. Eight or more struck during January to April 2006. In April 2002 a single storm left nearly 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it went on to Japan and Korea.
North China Electric Power University lists 30 programs for international students on this site: 10 master's, 10 doctoral, 10 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 15 taught in Chinese, 15 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 35,000 to CNY 35,000 (median CNY 35,000), according to the university's published fee table.

30 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (5):
Business Administration
Control Science and Engineering
Electrical Engineering
Power Engineering and Engineering Thermophysics
Renewable Energy and Clean Energy
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

north-china-electric-power-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. North China Electric Power University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at North China Electric Power University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

north-china-university-of-technology.h: North China University of Technology at a glance

blocks.x: North China University of Technology, known in Chinese as 北方工业大学 and often shortened to NCUT, is a public university in the Shijingshan district on the western side of Beijing. It belongs to the city rather than to a national ministry: the Beijing municipal government is both its supervising authority and its main source of funding. For an international applicant this matters in a practical way, because the university's priorities are closely tied to the needs of the capital and its industries.

The institution traces its roots to a vocational school set up in the Beiping period in 1946. Today it describes itself as a multi-disciplinary university with ten colleges, thirty undergraduate majors, twelve teaching and experimental centres and nine research and design institutes. It has also been admitted to a national programme that promotes the training of excellent engineers, which signals that engineering education remains the core of its identity. These headline figures come from older university descriptions and may have changed, so check the current numbers on the university's own website before you apply.

north-china-university-of-technology.h: From a vocational school to a municipal university

blocks.x: The story of NCUT is a long chain of renamings, each reflecting a change in who ran the school and what the country needed from it. It helps to know this chain, because it explains why the university is strong in engineering, metallurgy and electronics and why it keeps a practical, industry-facing character.

In 1946 two men, Shen Jianshi and Chen Guangxi, pushed through the creation of a higher vocational engineering school in Beiping that carried a national title. Its first recruitment of students started at the end of April. Early conditions were modest: after talks with officials from the education and economic affairs ministries, the school borrowed a former Japanese ironworks near Xizhimen as a temporary site. It reported at the time to the education ministry of the national government and counted as a state institution.

In early 1950 the school moved to a site known as Prince Alcohol House. On 1 January 1951 it was given the new name Beijing Heavy Industry School, along with a new seal. In the same period a committee overseeing China's geological industry planning asked the school to set up an exploration department on its behalf.

On 8 December 1952 a Beijing Machinery Manufacturing School was announced, and a separate steel-focused school appeared in Beijing alongside it, supervised by the steel bureau inside the heavy industry ministry. In 1955 a State Council decision put the school directly under the Ministry of Heavy Industry. On 6 October 1959, following central guidelines for colleges and technical secondary schools, the Ministry of Metallurgical Industry handed the Beijing metallurgical college over to the Shijingshan Iron and Steel Company, which was itself under that ministry. This is the origin of the university's link with Shijingshan, the district where it still stands.

In 1978 the State Council approved the creation of the Beijing College of Metallurgical Mechatronics. In May 1979 the college established a Department of Metallurgy and a Department of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering. Between 1980 and 1983 the Ministry of Metallurgical Industry commissioned it to run six training courses for the leading cadres of colleges and universities in the metallurgy system. In 1984 it came under the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Corporation, and in 1985, with State Council approval, it took the name North China University of Technology that it still carries.
Several milestones followed:
December 1993: the university became part of the fifth batch of institutions in China authorised to award master's degrees.

1998: the school became a school built together by the national government and Beijing city, with Beijing doing most of the managing. It set a service direction of being based in Beijing, serving the whole country, serving the non-ferrous metal industry and helping the capital's economy and society grow.
June 1999: after careful assessment by Beijing's education commission, the school received permission to offer higher vocational and technical education.
2002: a Graduate Department was formally established and set up to work alongside the scientific research department.
October 2011: the university was chosen for the second batch of the Ministry of Education's outstanding engineer education and training programme.
December 2012: the State Council's degree committee cleared it to join a national doctoral training scheme created for special national needs.
2015: the school put large-scale enrolment and training into full effect.
February 2017: two new institutes were founded, one for control engineering and one for sponge city and underground space research.

Teaching is organised into thirteen units. The engineering side is made up of the schools of Civil Engineering, Mechanical and Materials Engineering, Electronic and Information Engineering and Electrical and Control Engineering, with a separate School of Computer Science. Creative and built-environment study sits in the School of Architecture and Art, while business and the social sciences are covered by the School of Economics and Management and the School of Humanities and Law. There is also a School of Sciences, a School of Marxism and a School of Continuing Education. Finally, two units are aimed at an international audience: the International School and the Brunel London School.

Those last two are the places to ask first about programmes and exchanges designed with overseas students in mind. Programme availability and teaching languages change, so confirm details with the university.

NCUT's research record is described in older university material, and the numbers in that material are not consistent from one version to the next, so treat the figures below as indicative only. In general terms, the university has taken on projects funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and by major national and Beijing programmes, including the 863 plan and the science and technology support plan. It reports finishing over 1000 cooperative projects with companies, having more than 70 results formally appraised at provincial or ministerial level and holding over 70 national patents. It also lists more than 220 monographs or translations, more than 50 provincial or ministerial awards and a count of 490 high-level papers in the major indexes in 2010, about seven times the 2006 figure. During the 11th Five-Year Plan period it says it won 21 awards at or above provincial and ministerial level, among them three national science and technology progress awards, three provincial or ministerial first prizes and one Lu Xun prize for literature. Some other numbers about publication totals and research funding are unclear or inconsistent, so they are not repeated here; the university's website has the current figures.
On the teaching side, figures given for the end of 2012 describe a university with a solid quality-assurance record:
3 national-level specialty construction points and 5 Beijing-level ones
2 national high-quality courses and 10 Beijing top-quality courses
A national base for cultural quality education of college students
1 excellent teaching team at the Beijing municipal level
1 national experimental teaching demonstration centre (the comprehensive engineering training centre) and 5 municipal-level experimental teaching demonstration centres in Beijing
Teaching achievement prizes, including three first prizes at the Beijing municipal level
13 teaching materials selected under the national 11th Five-Year Plan and 21 at Beijing municipal level

The teaching staff included a national-level outstanding teacher, seven Beijing famous teachers, five local high-level talents, 12 city-level innovation teams and 81 municipal backbone teachers in the young and middle-aged group. Again, these are snapshot numbers from 2012 and are best used to gauge the scale of the faculty rather than as current statistics.

Sport has a surprising profile at NCUT. Since 1998 the college baseball team has won seven national championships and the softball team two. The baseball team toured Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan and other places in 2000. The men's basketball and volleyball squads and the women's table tennis team have likewise reached the podium again and again in Beijing university competition. The university chairs the baseball and softball branch of the China University Sports Association, and it holds the qualification to recruit high-level athletes in those two sports.

Students also do well in academic contests. Prizes have come from the national electronics design contest for undergraduates, the Challenge Cup inventions competition, citywide maths and physics contests, a national English contest for college students and many other events. Added together, these have produced well over 2000 special, first, second and third prizes. For a prospective student who likes to test their skills in competitions, this is a good sign of the culture.

Every year NCUT sends students to partner universities across Europe, the Americas, Japan and elsewhere; the usual figure given is more than 340. Between 2007 and 2010, 374 students went abroad to study, and in 2010 alone 148 went to partner institutions for exchange study or joint training programmes. At the same time the university enrolled more than 190 long-term foreign students and received more than 220 teachers from friendly foreign universities for visits, lectures, academic exchange and short-term study. These numbers are more than a decade old; ask the international office for up-to-date figures and a list of current partners.

Graduates who have gone on to found well-known companies include Wang Zhongjun of the film and media group Huayi Brothers Media, Liu Donghai of Digitong Energy Technology, and Yongqiang Qian, who started the education company New Oriental. That entrepreneurial streak is something prospective students can take as encouragement.

north-china-university-of-technology.h: Living in Beijing: what to expect outside the campus gates

blocks.x: A university degree is only part of the experience. NCUT's students also live in China's capital, a city of imperial monuments, rapid modern building, four very different seasons and an air-quality story that every newcomer should understand. This part of the profile walks through the weather first, then the lie of the land, the look of the city and finally the environment.

Beijing sits on the boundary between a humid continental and a cold semi-arid climate (classed Dwa and BSk in the Köppen system). The East Asian monsoon makes the summers hot and sticky, whereas winters are short, cold and dry because of the huge Siberian high-pressure system to the north. Spring tends to arrive quickly and dryly, and sometimes with sandstorms that sweep in from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe. Autumn is another in-between season with very little rain. Looking at records from the last couple of decades, the warmest stretch falls in early August and the coldest in early January.

Under China's official seasonal calendar, spring begins in Beijing on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. In recent years March and September have warmed faster and May and October more slowly than they once did, so autumn now feels briefer than spring.
Figures for 1991 to 2020 help you picture daily conditions:

In the built-up urban area the yearly mean is about 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Average daily lows run 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and average daily highs 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).
In the lower suburbs the yearly mean is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F).
Mountain districts range from 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), getting colder the higher you go.
January averages −2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).
Annual rainfall is roughly 528.0 mm (20.79 in) overall, rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in the Haidian and Chaoyang districts, and nearly three-quarters of it arrives between June and August.
The city gets about 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine a year; July is the dullest month at 42% of possible sunshine, while January and February are the sunniest at 62%.
Records since 1951 stand at −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), reached on 22 February 1966, and 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), reached on 24 July 1999.
In practice, that means serious winter coats, a sturdy umbrella for summer storms and breathable clothing for the humid months.

Geographically the city is perched on the northern rim of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that stretches away to the south and east. Hills and mountains curve around the north, northwest and west, acting as a barrier against desert steppe and sheltering the farmland of northern China. The Jundu Mountains fill the northwest, particularly Yanqing and Huairou, and the Western Hills form the western skyline. Along the rugged northern edge of the municipality runs the Great Wall, which was built to keep nomadic raiders from the steppe out. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills right on the Hebei border, is the highest point of all at 2,303 metres (7,556 feet).

Water is limited but important. The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma rivers belong to the Hai River system and head southeast, and the largest reservoir is Miyun, on the upper Chaobai. Beijing also marks the northern terminus of the Grand Canal that reaches Hangzhou, which has been in use for more than 1,400 years, and it receives water through the South–North Water Transfer Project, which brings supplies from the Yangtze basin and was built in the last ten years or so.

The built-up core occupies a relatively small portion of the municipality, on flat land that lies 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level, but it keeps expanding outward. Ring roads wrap the centre like ripples: the Second Ring Road marks the line of the former city walls, and the Sixth Ring Road ties in satellite towns. The heart of Beijing is Tian'anmen Square with the gate beside it, immediately south of the Forbidden City, where emperors once lived. Zhongnanhai, the compound where today's national leaders live, lies to the west. Chang'an Avenue slices between the gate and the square and serves as the capital's principal east–west line. Commentators say Beijing has grown outward from the old centre in a pattern nicknamed tan da bing, or spreading like a pancake, and they often blame this form for many of its urban problems.
You will notice three very different looks as you travel around the city.
Imperial heritage. The Gate of Heavenly Peace at Tian'anmen is the most famous emblem, and the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Temple of Heaven belong to the same tradition.
Mid-century blocks. Between the 1950s and the 1970s many buildings went up in a Soviet-influenced manner that people call Sino-Soviet style. They are generally boxy, and some were not built well.

Contemporary towers and venues. Around the central business district in the east you will see the new CCTV Headquarters, while the National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts stand elsewhere in the city.

Since the early 2000s the construction boom has brought designers from around the world, especially to the CBD. The tallest building today is the China Zun at 528 metres. Two Beijing buildings have won the CTBUH award for the world's best tall building of the year, a prize that goes to a single building annually: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. At the 798 Art Zone, old 1950s factory design and futuristic style are blended together, which makes it a popular place for an afternoon out.

The older way of living is the siheyuan, a set of buildings arranged around a courtyard. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are two of the more impressive examples. Courtyards are joined by narrow lanes called hutongs. Most of these lanes run east to west, so that doorways open to the north or south, a choice that follows feng shui practice. Some are wide enough for a car, while others allow only a handful of walkers at a time. Both the courtyards and the lanes were once everywhere, but entire blocks are being replaced by tall apartment buildings. People who lived in hutongs have the right to flats at least as large as their old homes, though many say that the close community and the street life of the lanes are impossible to recreate. A large share of these properties are owned by the government.
Every student should read this part, because air quality is one of the main daily considerations in Beijing. The news is mixed but, in recent years, quite positive.

north-china-university-of-technology.h: Why the air became a problem

blocks.x: The city has struggled with environmental problems for a long time. Its built-up area grew fourfold in the years 2000 to 2009. That growth raised emissions, and it also changed the local meteorology: wind speed, surface humidity and reflectivity near the ground fell, while temperatures, ozone and the stagnation of the air increased. Together with the burning of fossil fuels, this regularly produced serious pollution and health problems among residents.

A major turning point came in 2013, when severe smog blanketed Beijing and much of northern China, affecting around 600 million people. The episode made clean air a top economic and social issue for the country. Beijing's government responded with measures such as cutting coal from 24% of its energy in 2012 to 10% by 2017, while the central government required the removal of highly polluting vehicles from 2015 to 2017 and speeded up the shift to cleaner energy.

Studies carried out jointly by American and Chinese scientists in 2006 concluded that a great deal of Beijing's pollution is imported. Between 35% and 60% of its ozone, on average, originates outside the city boundary. Shandong and Tianjin exert a particularly strong influence, helped along by southerly and southeasterly winds in summer and by the mountains that trap air to the north and northwest.

Burning coal is responsible for about 40% of Beijing's PM2.5 and is the dominant source of nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide. Since 2012 the city has been switching coal-fired power stations to natural gas, and it set an aim of limiting yearly coal use to 20 million tons. The city burned 26.3 million tons in 2011, with 73% going to heat and power and the rest to industry. Much pollution blows in from neighbours. Tianjin's consumption was projected to grow from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015, and Hebei burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, more than Germany did in total, with only 30% for power and much of the remainder for steel and cement. The coal-producing regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000, add to the burden together with Shandong. Those four provinces, in the order Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, are the top four coal users in China.

Four big coal-fired plants once supplied both power and winter heating to the capital. Gaojing was closed in 2014, two others shut in March 2015 and the Huaneng plant was scheduled to follow in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was to remove 13 million tons of coal demand and to hold annual use at 15 million tons in 2015.

north-china-university-of-technology.h: What has been done about it

blocks.x: Preparations for the 2008 Summer Olympics led to spending of almost US$17 billion on clean-air work. While the Games were on, the authorities stopped building work everywhere, closed numerous factories for good and paused industry in nearby provinces for a time. The city also put 3,800 natural-gas buses on the road, one of the biggest fleets of its kind anywhere, and was the first in China to demand the Chinese version of the Euro 4 standard.

For major occasions, officials have also used cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air, as before the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to ease droughts. More recently the focus has shifted to shutting factories for short periods and tightening limits on cars. This produced the brief spells of clean sky called APEC blue and parade blue, around the 2014 APEC meeting in China and the 2015 Victory Day parade. Conditions were excellent during and before those events but returned to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, which shut most industry and commerce, and another red alert followed later that month. Under rules announced by the environmental protection bureau in November 2016, heavily polluting older cars are barred from the roads from 2017 whenever red alerts are declared in the city or in nearby regions.

The efforts have paid off. After the war on pollution began in 2014, fine particulates dropped by 35% in 2017 and then fell further to 2020, thanks mainly to replacing coal with gas and cleaning up industrial plants around the capital. The yearly mean for PM2.5 reached 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the cleanest result since 2013, and in 2024 there were only two heavy-pollution days. That is the lowest on record and 96.6% fewer than the 58 days of 2013.

Readings differ depending on who publishes them. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau posts daily data from 27 monitoring stations on its site, while the US Embassy has published hourly PM2.5 and ozone levels through social media. The two organisations track different pollutants against different standards, and as a result the Chinese bureau's numbers, and the health effects they imply, have often looked milder than the embassy's.

The health risk is real. Polluted air is directly tied to higher illness rates from heart and breathing conditions in Beijing, and prolonged exposure to heavy smog may lead to emergency hospital visits or worse. Most residents check an air quality app before going out, and masks are common on bad days.

In spring, dust from the eroding deserts of northern and northwestern China creates storms that hit the city. The municipal Weather Modification Office will sometimes trigger rain to fight them. During just the first four months of 2006, at least eight occurred, and one storm in April 2002 left about 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it drifted on to Japan and Korea. Students arriving for a spring term should be ready for a few hazy days.

Northeast Agricultural University, known as NEAU (Chinese name 东北农业大学), is a public university in Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang Province in China's far northeast. It opened in 1948 and is counted among the country's key agricultural universities. Two government bodies sit above it: the Heilongjiang Provincial People's Government and the national Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Day-to-day funding comes from the provincial education department. NEAU is also a member of Project 211 and of the Double First-Class Construction programme, which recognise it among the institutions the state wants to build up.

For international applicants, the main point is that this is a specialist university with deep roots in farming, food and the life sciences, set in a region that is one of China's great agricultural heartlands.

In 1948 the university started life as the Northeast Agricultural Institute (东北农学院), and by January 1950 it had been renamed Harbin Agricultural Institute (哈尔滨农学院). Then, in October of the same year, Shenyang Agricultural Institute (沈阳农学院) merged with it, and the earlier name, Northeast Agricultural Institute, was brought back.

A further merger came in February 1994, when the institute joined the Heilongjiang Institute of Agricultural Administration (黑龙江省农业管理干部学院). The combined body was given its present name, Northeast Agricultural University.

Most of what a student needs to know about daily life depends on the city around the campus: its weather, how people travel, and how they spend free time. The sections below describe Harbin, the home of NEAU.

northeast-agricultural-university.h: Where Harbin is and what the land looks like

blocks.x: Harbin is the capital of Heilongjiang and lies in the south of the province. The whole prefecture covers 53,068 square kilometres (20,490 square miles), a vast territory that runs from latitude 44° 04' to 46° 40' N and from longitude 125° 42' to 130° 10' E. It occupies the southeast corner of the Songnen Plain, one of the main sections of the great Northeastern Plain, and the city centre stands on the southern bank of the Songhua River in its middle stretch. Because the outline of Heilongjiang resembles a swan, Harbin is nicknamed "the pearl on the swan's neck".

Its neighbours are Daqing on the west, Suihua on the northwest, Yichun on the north, Jiamusi and Qitaihe on the northeast and Mudanjiang on the southeast, while Jilin Province touches the southwest edge. The main urban area is flat and low, averaging about 150 metres (490 feet) above sea level. Mountains and uplands fill the ten county-level divisions in the east, and the far east of the prefecture has large wetlands, mostly in Yilan County, close to the southwest margin of the Sanjiang Plain.

By the Köppen classification, Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Dwa). It lies north of 45 degrees latitude and is affected by the Siberian high, so it is famous for cold weather and a long winter, and "Ice City" is a nickname it has earned. Winters are dry, freezing and often sunny, with little snowfall: the January average over 24 hours is just −17.3 °C (0.9 °F). Spring and autumn are short, with changeable winds between the extremes. Summers can turn hot, and July averages 23.7 °C (74.7 °F). This is also the wet season: more than half of the 539 millimetres (21.2 inches) of annual precipitation arrives in July and August. Overall there are about 99 days with rain or snow.

Over the full year the average comes to 5.2 °C (41.4 °F). December is the dullest month, with 45 percent of possible sunshine, and September the brightest at 60 percent, which adds up to 2,340 hours of bright sun in a year. Record lows of around −41 to −43 °C (about −42 to −45 °F) have been quoted for the city's weather station, and highs have approached 39 °C (about 103 °F), so you should plan for a very wide seasonal range. Because different sources give slightly different record figures, the local meteorological service has the exact values.

Harbin has also adapted its planning to a changing climate. Planners use sponge-city thinking, and the Qunli stormwater park is an example: it catches rainwater, cleans it and holds it, while keeping the natural wildlife habitat intact.

northeast-agricultural-university.h: What the cold means for new arrivals

blocks.x: If you come from a warm country, the first winter is the biggest adjustment. Expect weeks of deep freezing weather, dry air and clear skies rather than heavy snowfall, and plan for proper winter clothing from the day you arrive. The upside is a short, pleasant spring and autumn and a warm summer, and a city that has turned its cold into a local festival and a tourist attraction.

No other city in Heilongjiang has a bigger economy than Harbin. Its GDP reached RMB 501.08 billion in 2013, up 8.9 percent on the year before, and RMB 575.12 billion in 2015. In 2012 the primary, secondary and service sectors contributed 11.1, 36.1 and 52.8 percent respectively. Trade in goods (imports plus exports) amounted to US$5,330 million at the end of 2012, and the working population was 3.147 million that year. These numbers are from the early to mid 2010s, so check current statistics if you need up-to-date values.

The black earth (chernozem) around Harbin is among the most nutrient-rich in China. That makes it excellent for grain and for crops used in textiles, and the city is a national base for commodity grain and a good location for agricultural businesses. For an agriculture university, this is a natural setting for field study and industry contacts.

Harbin also has light industry, textiles, medicine, food processing, aircraft, cars, metallurgy, electronics, building materials and chemicals, which together form a fairly complete industrial system. Prominent local employers are the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory, Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and Harbin Electric Company Limited. Power equipment is a leading trade: hydro and thermal generating equipment made in Harbin accounts for one third of China's installed capacity. Platts reported that in 2009-10 Harbin Electric took second place worldwide by steam-turbine market share, tied with Dongfang Electric and just short of Shanghai Electric. The Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, whose business is research, development, production and sale of medicines, is the second-biggest pharmaceutical company in China by market value.

In finance, Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank are among the largest banks in the northeast and are both headquartered in the city; in 2011 the latter placed fourth among Chinese city commercial banks on a competitiveness measure. On the retail side, the Qiulin Group runs Harbin's biggest department store.

Every year since 1990, Harbin has hosted its International Trade and Economic Fair. By the 2013 statistics, exhibitors and visitors numbering over 1.9 million, coming from 80-plus countries and regions, had taken part, and contracts worth more than US$100 billion had been concluded. The city is also one of the main destinations for foreign direct investment in Northeast China, which stood at US$980 million in 2013. At the 18th regular meeting of the Chinese and Russian prime ministers (Li Keqiang and Dmitry Medvedev) in October 2013, it was agreed that the fair would be renamed the "China-Russia EXPO" and co-sponsored by China's Ministry of Commerce, the Heilongjiang government and two Russian ministries (Economic Development, and Industry and Trade).
Several zones concentrate particular industries.
Harbin Economic and Technology Development Zone (national level): telecommunications equipment, chemicals, car assembly, electronics, textiles and medical supplies.
Harbin High and New Technological Development Zone: biology, medicine, electronics, IT and optical-mechanical-electrical integration.
Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (provincial level): car assembly, electronics manufacturing, heavy industry and industrial instruments.
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (provincial level): trading and distribution, food and drink processing, medical equipment, shipping and logistics.
Harbin Port.

The Songbei Economic Development Zone is in Songbei District and has a planned area of 5.53 square kilometres. It encourages electronics assembly and food and beverage processing. Regional and provincial offices of big companies such as China Datang Corporation, China Netcom and China Telecom have moved in, making it a cluster of local headquarters. Two research hubs, the Harbin Science and Technology Innovation Center and the Harbin International Agricultural Science and Technology Innovation Center, are also here. Thanks to such institutes, Harbin ranked ninth among 50 big Chinese cities for scientific and technological innovation ability in a 2006 competitiveness ranking, and sixth among Chinese cities by volume of scientific and technological results.

The Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone is one of China's 90 national economic development zones. It was set up in 1991 and was given national status by the State Council in April 1993. Its boundaries have been reorganised several times (the high-tech zone was merged into it and later split off again), and today its centralised parks cover 18.5 square kilometres, divided into the Nangang and Haping Road parks. The Yingbin Road Hi-tech Park, 12.2 square kilometres in size, formerly belonged to it but has been run by the High and New Technology zone since 2009.

Nangang Park is meant for incubating high-tech projects, enterprise research bases and service industries such as finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture and entertainment, and it is where big-name companies and their local branches have their offices.
Yingbin Road Park concentrates on high-tech incubation and industrial development.

Haping Road Park is a broad industrial base for projects in car and car-parts manufacturing, medicines, food, electronics and textiles, with car assembly and raw-material processing especially encouraged.

Another national zone, the High and New Technology Industry Development Zone, is one of 56 such zones across China. It began as a provincial-level zone in 1988 and gained national status from the State Council in 1991. Its built-up area totals 23.9 square kilometres, in two parts: the Science and Technology Innovation Town and the High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

The 2020 census counted 10,009,854 people in Harbin, a fall of 5.62 percent from the previous decade. The built-up area, which includes all urban districts except Acheng and Shuangcheng (not yet urbanised), had 5,282,083 residents. 70.61 percent of people live in urban areas and 29.39 percent in rural areas.

The age profile is relatively old, with 10.46 percent of residents under 14 and 14.65 percent over 65. Men make up 50.02 percent and women 49.98 percent. The birth rate, at 6.95 births per 1,000 people, is below the national average of 12.13.
Han Chinese are the large majority (93% in 2000). Among minorities are the Manchu, Hui and Mongol peoples, and there is a small Russian community; the 2020 census gives a detailed breakdown.

Harbin's religious map reflects its history. Its Catholic community falls under a missionary pre-diocesan body, the Apostolic Administration of Harbin. The city also contains a former cathedral of the Eastern Catholic Russian exarchate, and another building, the heavily damaged Church of the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, once housed Russian soldiers from the Outer Amur Military Region who were garrisoned here. Muslims form a small share (0.4% in 2000); the Daowai Mosque in Harbin is the largest mosque in Heilongjiang. The city once had a small Jewish community centred on Zhongyang Main Street, where many European Jewish refugees lived.

Harbin's culture grows out of Han traditions blended with Manchu and Russian influences, and this mix can be seen in the architecture, food, music and customs. On 22 June 2010 the city was named a UNESCO City of Music in the Creative Cities Network.

Harbin is a favourite domestic destination, especially in winter when large ice sculpture displays appear. It also has a big indoor ski park inside the Wanda Harbin Mall, with six slopes up to 500 metres (1,600 feet) long. The 2023-2024 winter season brought 87 million visitors, most of them from elsewhere in China. The city is also known for European-style architecture, including Central Street, Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Baroque-style complex of Lao Daowai (Old Town).

northeast-agricultural-university.h: Winter culture and the ice festival

blocks.x: Harbin is the northernmost major city in China, and the Siberian anticyclone strongly affects it. Winter daily temperatures average −19.7 °C (−3.5 °F), which differs from the January figure above because the two measure different periods; yearly minimums colder than −25.0 °C (−13.0 °F) are not unusual. Because of this cold, the city is known as "Ice City", and from December to March ice and snow sculptures in many styles fill it.

Since 1985 the city has held its international ice and snow sculpture festival. The official opening date is 5 January, but in practice many works are on show earlier. There are two main exhibition areas. On Sun Island (Taiyang Dao, a AAAAA-rated recreation area across the Songhua River) you will find enormous snow sculptures. The separate "Ice and Snow World" opens each night, with sculptures lit from inside and out, and features full-size illuminated buildings made from crystal-clear ice blocks, 2 to 3 feet thick, taken from the Songhua River. Building the exhibition takes 15,000 workers 16 days, and every early December ice cutters harvest 120,000 cubic metres (4.2 million cubic feet) from the frozen surface of the river as raw material. Parks and main avenues in the city also have ice buildings, large snow sculptures, ice slides, and festival food and drink.

Other winter pursuits include alpine skiing at Yabuli, snowmobile driving, winter swimming in the Songhua River, and the traditional ice-lantern display in Zhaolin Garden, first held in 1963. Harbin's snow carving and ice recreations are known across the country and particularly popular in Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore. Together with the Sapporo Snow Festival in Japan, the Quebec Winter Carnival in Canada and Norway's Holmenkollen Ski Festival, it is reckoned one of the world's four largest winter festivals of ice and snow.

Each November Harbin also dispatches ice artists to the US as a showcase for the craft. Over 100 craftsmen are needed to build ICE!, a yearly indoor display of Christmas-themed ice carvings held in Nashville, Tennessee, Grapevine, Texas, Kissimmee, Florida and National Harbor, Maryland.
Heilongjiang Television (HLJTV) is the regional broadcaster, with seven channels and a satellite channel for other provinces.
Harbin Television (HRBTV) is the municipal station, with five specialised channels.
Long Guang (Dragon Broadcast) is the province-wide radio group, once known as Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, and offers seven channels including one in Korean.
Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS) offers music, news, traffic, economy and city life for Harbin and nearby areas including Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.

For a student, Harbin offers a large provincial capital of about ten million people, a strong farming and food base that suits an agricultural university, a lively industrial and trade scene with a strong Russia connection, and a winter season that is both a challenge and a highlight. Population, GDP and trade figures quoted above come from different years and may have changed, so the city government's own statistics pages give the latest picture.
A university's surroundings shape student life as much as its campus does, and NEAU sits in Heilongjiang. The following sections look at the province as a whole.

Ancient records say that the land of today's Heilongjiang was home to peoples such as the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan. In Inner Mongolia and the west of the province lived the Mongolic Donghu, and some place names are Manchu or Mongolian. Between the 7th and 10th centuries the Bohai Kingdom held the east, and the Khitan Liao dynasty followed. The Jurchen, who founded the Jin dynasty (1115-1234) and later ruled much of the north, emerged from lands inside the modern province.

Heilongjiang was set up as an administrative unit in 1683, under the Kangxi Emperor of the Manchu Qing dynasty, carved out of the northwest of Jilin Province. At first it covered only the west of today's province and was overseen by the General of Heilongjiang (also translated as Military Governor), whose authority, under the Treaty of Nerchinsk, extended up to the Stanovoy Mountains in the north. The east stayed under the General of Jilin, whose reach extended to the Sea of Japan. These Manchurian lands were closed to Han Chinese migrants.

The governor's seat was first at Heilongjiang City (Aigun, also called Heihe) on the Amur River, but moved to Nenjiang on the Nen River in 1690 and then south to Qiqihar in 1699. Historians think supplies drove the moves: Nenjiang and Qiqihar are linked to southern Manchuria by the convenient Nen waterway, whereas reaching Aigun meant sailing down the Sungari to the Amur and back up, or hauling goods over the Lesser Xing'an Mountains. Qiqihar was also well placed at a crossroads between a northbound road and a westbound one to Mongolia, so its garrison could guard against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

Qing military presence north of Aigun was thin. European sources from the 18th and early 20th centuries, and Russian reports from the 1850s, put the farthest Qing outpost at Ulusu-Modon, near the famous S-shaped bend of the Amur, on the north bank, which was lost to Russia in 1860.

Two treaties, in 1858 and 1860, forced the Qing court to give the Russian Empire all the land beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers. The loss cut China off from the Sea of Japan and gave Heilongjiang the northern and eastern borders it has today. Around the same time Han Chinese were allowed to settle in Manchuria, and the mass movement known as Chuang Guandong made them the largest group in the region by the early twentieth century.

Japanese forces invaded in 1931 and completed their conquest of the province in 1932, when it became part of the Japanese-backed state of Manchukuo. In 1945 the Soviet Army defeated the Japanese in Manchuria, and in the civil war that followed the Soviets backed the Chinese communists. Heilongjiang was the first province fully under communist control, and Harbin the first major city.

At the start of communist rule, Heilongjiang covered only the west of the present-day province, with Qiqihar as its capital; the rest was Songjiang Province, whose capital was Harbin. The two were merged into today's Heilongjiang in 1954. During the Cultural Revolution the province was enlarged with the Hulunbuir League and other parts of Inner Mongolia, though most of that change has since been reversed.

The province has varied terrain. Large parts are covered by mountain ranges including the Greater and Lesser Khingan Ranges, the Zhangguangcai Mountains, the Laoye Mountains and the Wanda Mountains. The highest summit, Datudingzi Mountain (1,690 metres, 5,540 feet), is on the border with Jilin. In the Greater Khingan Range stands the biggest surviving primeval forest in China, a mainstay of the forestry sector.

The flatter, lower east and southwest are crossed by the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers, all tributaries of the Amur, and the northern border runs along the Amur valley. Xingkai Lake (Khanka Lake) lies on the frontier with Russia's Primorsky Krai.

Most of the province is humid continental (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), while the far north turns subarctic (Dwc). Winters last long and are harsh, with January averages somewhere between −31 and −15 °C (−24 to 5 °F). Summers are brief but warm to very warm, averaging 18 to 23 °C (64 to 73 °F) in July. Yearly rainfall measures 400 to 700 millimetres (16 to 28 inches) and is concentrated in the summer months. Sunshine is plentiful, about 2,300 to 2,650 hours a year, and in spring the Songnen and Sanjiang plains offer abundant wind energy.
Big cities besides the capital Harbin include Qiqihar, Daqing, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi, Jixi, Hegang, Shuangyashan, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe.

Counting every class of road, expressways and highways included, Heilongjiang had 165,989 km (103,141 miles) as of October 2020. The most important corridor is the Beijing-Harbin Expressway, which starts at the Jilin border and ends inside the Harbin Ring Expressway. The Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway heads northeast and ties together remote counties under Harbin, Jiamusi and others in the northeast. Near its end, the Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off at Jiansanjiang and serves state-owned farms in the far east before finishing near the Russian border. The Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway runs southeast to northwest and connects major population centres, including Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar, ending at the Inner Mongolia border. The Hegang-Dalian Expressway, in the east, carries timber and coal between Hegang and the Jilin border.

The province has hosted or taken part in several sporting events, among them the 2009 Winter Universiade, the 2018 Bandy World Championship (Division B) and the Asia League Ice Hockey. Winter sport is a natural fit for the climate, and it adds to the sense that people here have learned to enjoy the cold rather than simply endure it.

Heilongjiang combines a long frontier history, big rivers and forests, and some of the most fertile farmland in China. Its harsh winters shape everything from architecture to leisure, while its road network and expressway corridors tie Harbin to the rest of the northeast. Anyone planning a study period at NEAU should treat the region as part of the course: the land, the weather and the farming economy are exactly what an agricultural university is built around.
