northeast-electric-power-university.h: Northeast Electric Power University at a glance

blocks.x: Northeast Electric Power University, or NEEPU (东北电力大学, Dōngběi Diànlì Dàxué), is a public university in Jilin City, in Jilin Province. The provincial government sponsors it and the Province of Jilin is its home authority. Its focus is engineering, above all anything to do with electric power, and it teaches about 19,000 full-time students.

The university was formed in Changchun in 1949 and moved to Jilin City in 1955. If you are looking at power systems, electrical engineering or energy, it is a specialist choice in China's northeast rather than a general university.

The starting point was the Changchun Electrical Machinery Advanced Professional School of 1949, described as the very first electrical engineering school established under the new Republic of China, and NEEPU developed out of it. In 1955 it left Changchun for Jilin City. By 1958 it had become an undergraduate institution of higher learning under the name Jilin Electric Power Institute.

In 1978 it was renamed the Northeast China Institute of Electric Power Engineering. At that stage the national Ministry of Electric Power was its supervising body. Since 2000 it has been run on a joint-building model, shared between the central and local governments. In December 2005 the Ministry of Education approved a further new name, Northeast Dianli University. Finally, in 2016, the English name became Northeast Electric Power University. If you meet the older English names in documents, they all refer to the same institution.

Where you live decides most of your daily routine, so the next sections describe Jilin City: its location, weather, the environmental incidents in its recent past, sights, sport, schools and how to travel.
Jilin City is in the middle of Jilin Province, between 125° 40' and 127° 56' east and between 42° 31' and 44° 40' north. Its neighbouring prefectures are:
Harbin in Heilongjiang, to the north
Changchun and Siping, to the west
Yanbian, to the east
Liaoyuan, Tonghua and Baishan, to the south

The city lies among hills close to the Songhua River. Four well-known mountains surround it: North Mountain on the west, Long Tan Mountain on the east, Zhuque Mountain on the north and Turtle Mountain on the south. Together with the Songhua River they are said to form a bagua within the Taiji pattern. The best-known peak is North Mountain (Beishan), home to several Buddhist temples, which the Qianlong Emperor is said to have visited.

The climate is humid continental and influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Dwa), with four seasons. Winter is long, running from November to March, and it is cold and windy but dry because of the Siberian anticyclone; the January mean is -15.4 °C (4.3 °F). Spring and autumn are brief in-between seasons, usually dry and breezy with a little precipitation. Summer turns hot and humid, and the East Asian monsoon brings a southeasterly wind most of the time, and the July average is 23.3 °C (73.9 °F). Winter snow is usually light, and most of the year's rain is packed into June, July and August. Pack heavy winter clothes.

A string of explosions struck Jilin City's petrochemical plant No. 101 on 13 November 2005, and six people died. The Songhua River suffered serious pollution as roughly 100 tons of benzene and nitrobenzene compounds poured in. Benzene once registered at 108 times the safe level set nationally. Downstream cities such as Harbin, Songyuan and Khabarovsk cut off their water supplies for nearly a week. The pollution went on to the Amur (Heilong) River, a major boundary between China and Russia, and in the aftermath Chinese leaders had to offer Russia an apology about how the matter was dealt with.

During the summer 2010 China floods, Jilin was among the worst-hit regions, with heavy rain and landslides. On 28 July 2010 the floods swept several thousand barrels of toxic chemicals from two Jilin chemical plants into the Songhua River; the contents included trimethylsilyl chloride and hexamethyldisiloxane, and each barrel held around 170 kg of a poisonous substance. Some barrels were reported to explode on contact with water. By the late afternoon of 1 August, 6,387 barrels had been taken out of the river. Officials said tests showed the river water was still safe to drink.

Three PLA soldiers in Jilin drowned as they helped clear barrels and fight the flood. On 28 July, a breach in the Dahe Dam (Changshan Township) let out 4 million m3 of water; five villages below the dam were wiped out and 40 people were dead or missing. Across Jilin prefecture the floods left over 100 dead or missing. After the Songhua climbed to double its usual level, work crews started on fifty-one small reservoirs that had been damaged, and reinforced river embankments in the province.

Winter brings tourists to Jilin City for the spectacular rime ice (雾凇, 霧凇) on the trees along the Songhua, the one river hereabouts that stays unfrozen all winter. The rime appears each year in January and February. Water vapour rising from the warm river meets the cold night air of about -20 °C (-4 °F) and crystallises on willow branches.
Places to visit include:
The Meteorite Museum, which holds the largest stony meteorite from a documented meteorite fall.
North Hill (Beishan) Park, northwest of the city.
Dragon Pool Mountain Park.
Songhua Lake, southeast of the city.

Another sight is Wulajie Old City (乌拉街, also spelt Wulakai; 44°05′N 126°28′E), a walled town from the Qing dynasty in Longtan District. It stands on the Sungari's east bank, downstream from the city's main urban zone, and served as the point where local products were collected for the imperial court. Back in 1682, Ferdinand Verbiest ranked Wulajie (Ula) as the province's most illustrious city, and the Kangxi Emperor visited in person to enjoy sturgeon fishing. Today a nearby state school is among the very few in China to teach some Manchu.

The winter calendar offers skiing, skating, sledding and snowboarding, and many people also swim in winter, which is widely practised. Resorts for skiing are Beidahu, Lake Songhua, Zhuque Hill, Wujiashan and North Hill (北山滑雪场); swimmers have the Filibiin swimming resort.

Secondary schools on the list are Ararsame Second High School, Jilin Yuwen High School and the city's No. 1 High School. Higher education in town includes Beihua University, Jilin Medical College, Jilin Agriculture University and the Jilin Institute of Chemical Technology, plus Northeast Dianli University, the previous name of NEEPU.

Jilin's own Ertaizi Airport (IATA: JIL, ICAO: ZYJL) once handled both commercial and military flights. Commercial services all moved, by 3 October 2005, to Changchun Longjia International Airport when that opened, and Ertaizi ended its commercial operation. Longjia is roughly 76 km (47 mi) from Jilin City and flies to many destinations, and China Southern Airlines offers a few direct international links from Changchun.

Jilin railway station sits on the Changchun-Tumen Railway's east-west mainline, which gives easy access to many places in China, including Beijing, Tianjin, Dalian, Jinan and Hangzhou. Trains to Harbin, Changchun and Shenyang are frequent and convenient, using the Harbin-Dalian high-speed rail and its Changchun to Jilin branch. On the roads, China National Highway 202 and the G12 Hunchun-Ulanhot Expressway serve the city.
A university's province shapes daily life nearly as much as the campus, so these sections look at Jilin Province.

northeast-electric-power-university.h: Peoples and powers of the past

blocks.x: Early inhabitants included the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí (勿吉), and parts of the area came under Buyeo and Goguryeo. Many rulers followed: the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo again, Balhae, then the Liao of the Khitan, the Jin of the Jurchen and the Yuan of the Mongols. Under the Qing, the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn) administered much of it, with a territory that reached across most of today's Russian Primorsky Krai.

Russia took over the Primorsky Krai area in 1860, after which the government began opening the land to Han Chinese migrants, most of them from Shandong. By the early 20th century the Han had become the largest ethnic group. Japan folded the area into its puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932 and made Changchun (known then as Xinjing), today's provincial capital, the state's capital. When Japan was beaten in 1945, Operation August Storm ended with the Red Army taking Jilin. The Soviets passed the region, and the rest of the northeast, to the Communists, who used Manchuria as the base from which they went on to win the rest of China in the Civil War.

In 1949 the province was smaller, covering only the area around Changchun and Jilin City, with its capital at Jilin City, while Changchun was an independent municipality. By the 1950s its borders had grown to what they are now. Another expansion in the Cultural Revolution added part of Inner Mongolia and so created a frontier with independent Mongolia, but this was later undone.

More recently Jilin, like the rest of China's heavy-industry northeast, has faced economic difficulty during privatisation. This led the central government to launch a campaign called "Revitalize the Northeast".

Jilin is in the central part of northeast China and borders Russia to the east and North Korea to the southeast. The province covers 190,000 km2 (73,000 sq mi) and has 24 million inhabitants. Its capital, Changchun, is west of Jilin City by 113 km (70 mi). Of 136 mineral types found, 70 have been extracted. Resources for traditional Chinese medicine are plentiful too, with roughly 27,000 sorts of wild plant including 9,000 medicinal herbs. Big reserves exist of coal, oil, gas, iron, nickel, molybdenum, gold, silver, talc, graphite, gypsum and cement rock, and no other province has as much oil shale.

Altitude is greatest in the southeast and falls gradually to the northwest. The Changbai Mountains run through the southeast and include Paektu Mountain, the province's top summit (2,744 m, or 9,003 ft). The Jilinhada, Zhang Guangcai and Longgang ranges are further highlands.

In the far southeast the Yalu and Tumen rivers take the water away, and they also help form the China-North Korea border. Liao River tributaries serve the southwest. Up north, the Nen and Songhua rivers both end in the Amur. Winters are long and cold and summers short and warm, as in a northern continental monsoon climate; January averages -20 to -14 °C (-4 to 7 °F), and annual rain is 350 to 1,000 mm (13.8 to 39.4 in). Cities of note: Changchun, Jilin City, Siping, Songyuan, Baicheng, Baishan, Tonghua, Liaoyuan and Yanji.

Jilin's nominal GDP in 2025 added up to RMB 1,497.4 billion, or US$209.6 billion. GDP has been climbing at double-digit rates from 2003, growing 51 per cent between 2003 and 2007. Per-head nominal GDP rose to RMB 64,618 (US$9,046) in 2025. Large enterprises, measured against 2005, saw their incremental value go up 19 per cent and profit 30 per cent.

Main farm products are maize, rice, wheat and sorghum; rice grows chiefly in the east (the Yanbian area, for example), while the Changbai Mountains supply a good deal of lumber. In the west, such as Baicheng, people herd sheep. Resource-wise, no Chinese province holds more shale oil, and its mineral wealth is among the top five nationally; kieselguhr, wollastonite, floatstone and molybdenum are especially plentiful. The industrial core is automobiles, rail carriages and iron alloy. As a major commodity grain base, Jilin also takes sixth place for timber output. A long reputation as a pharmaceutical centre rests on ginseng and deer antler yields that are among the largest in China and widely used in Chinese medicine.

The Jilin New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone was founded in 1992 in Jilin City. Its planned area is 818 km2 (316 sq mi), of which 242 km2 (93 sq mi) is established. Key industries are new materials, refined chemicals, an optoelectronics-and-machinery mix, electronics, medicine and bioengineering. Songhua Lake is only 14 km (8.7 mi) away, and bus and train stations are within 3 km (1.9 mi).

A second zone, the Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone, was founded in May 1998 in the city's northeast. It plans 28 km2 (11 sq mi) in total, lying 90 km (56 mi) from Changchun, with Jilin Airport 5 km (3.1 mi) off and the railway station 8 km (5.0 mi) away. Its work covers refined chemicals, bioengineering, and fine processing of chemical fibre and farm products. Four industrial parks make it up (Chemical, Food, Textile and Medical), and the Medical park specialises in traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals, small-molecule medicine, biopharmaceuticals and health products.

With state approval in 1993, the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone (CETDZ) gained state-level status. The area is 112.72 km2 (43.52 sq mi), and 30 km2 (12 sq mi) of that is reserved for development. Through the end of 2006, fixed-asset investment came to 38.4 billion yuan. Registered businesses numbered 1656, 179 of them foreign-funded, and the zone produced 101.8 billion yuan of gross regional product, 233.0 billion yuan of industrial output and 15.7 billion yuan of financial revenue.

One of the biggest CRRC bullet-train factories is in Changchun. The world's first bullet train carriages with sleeper berths and the ability to run in extremely low temperatures were unveiled there in November 2016. These "Panda" trains reach 250 kmph, work at -40 degrees Celsius and have Wi-Fi hubs; their berths fold up into seats by day.

Four roads and a light-rail line connect the Changchun High-Tech Industrial Development Area to downtown, and Changchun Station is twenty minutes off by light rail. In 2002 it became Northeast China's first area to win ISO14001 environmental certification, and 38 per cent of it is landscaped.

In 1992 the Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone was approved at national level, with 24 km2 (9.3 sq mi) planned. Inside it were set up the Sino-Russia Trade Zone (2001) and the Export Processing Zone (2002). Its position is strategic, at the meeting point of Chinese, Russian and Korean borders, and its industries include seafood processing, electronics manufacturing, biopharmaceuticals and textiles. The Export Processing Zone, within a 5 km2 (1.93 sq mi) area, plans 2.44 km2 (0.94 sq mi) and shares infrastructure and policies with the larger zone around it.

Residents are Han Chinese, Manchu, Hui, Mongol and Xibe. Ethnic Koreans, about 4 per cent of the people (the peninsula is nearby), live mostly in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture. Manchus were once the majority in Jilin, which belongs to their historical homeland, but as they took on Han culture and Chinese languages, the Manchu language is now critically endangered. Population figures exclude active-service members of the People's Liberation Army.

Jilin belongs to Northeast China and shares much of its culture with neighbouring regions, including forms such as Errenzhuan and Yangge. Jiju, or Jilin Opera, is the province's own musical and theatrical tradition, shaped during its fairly short history of migration. Jilin's ethnic Koreans have their own culture, which keeps close ties with Korea. Most people in the province speak Mandarin, the official language, but near the east many speak Korean, and some people in Qian Gorlos autonomous county speak Mongolian.

At Ji'an there are Goguryeo sites and tombs, among them Hwando Mountain City, Gungnae City and the pyramid-like Tomb of the General; they form part of the World Heritage listing for the Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom. Scenery draws visitors to Paektu Mountain, above all Heaven Lake on the North Korean border. Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture holds the Ancient Tombs at Longtou Mountain, royal tombs of Balhae that include the Mausoleum of Princess Jeonghyo.
Jilin has many other institutions, which helps if you want to compare options or plan further study. Those named include:

In Changchun: Changchun Institute of Technology, Changchun Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, Changchun Institute of Post and Telecommunications, Changchun Taxation College, Changchun University, Changchun Normal University, Changchun University of Technology, Changchun University of Science and Technology, Northeast Normal University and the large Jilin University (吉林大学).

Elsewhere in the province: Beihua University, the Jilin College of Electrification, Jilin Agricultural Science and Technology University, and also Jilin Normal University, Jilin Agricultural University and Jilin Medical College.
In Yanbian: Yanbian University and Yanbian University of Science and Technology.
Finally, Northeast China Institute of Electric Power Engineering is NEEPU's earlier name.
Northeast Electric Power University lists 74 programs for international students on this site: 43 bachelor, 22 master's, 9 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 74 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 19,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 19,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 28,000 (median CNY 23,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 28,000 to CNY 28,000 (median CNY 28,000), according to the university's published fee table.

31 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

northeast-electric-power-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Northeast Electric Power University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jilin City, register at Northeast Electric Power University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

northeast-forestry-university.h: Northeast Forestry University at a glance

blocks.x: Northeast Forestry University (NEFU, 东北林业大学), a public institution in Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang in China's far north-east, reporting to the Ministry of Education. Three bodies share in building it: the education ministry itself, the provincial government of Heilongjiang, and the national forestry and grassland authority. It belongs to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction programme. If you are interested in forests, wildlife, wood science, ecology or landscape design, this is one of the best-known places in China to study them, and it is set in a region that holds the country's biggest state-owned forests.

NEFU was founded in 1952, and it grew out of the forestry department at Northeast Agricultural College, combined with other forestry teaching staff brought together at that time. Accounts of exactly which institutions contributed differ, so check the university's own history page if you need the detail. What is clear is that NEFU is one of China's three oldest centres for forestry teaching and research.

northeast-forestry-university.h: The home campus and its forests

blocks.x: The main campus in Harbin covers more than 136 hectares (about 336 acres) and holds teaching buildings, research laboratories and practice sites. Harbin is the centre of China's largest area of state-owned forest, so the location suits the subject. Students also learn in the field at two experimental forestry centres: the Maoershan Experimental Forestry Center, set inside Maoershan National Forest Park, and the Liangshui Experimental Forestry Center, which sits within Liangshui National Nature Reserve. Counting these sites, the university's land adds up to 33,000 hectares (about 81,545 acres).

Day-to-day living is compact. The campus has fifteen dormitories and a single dining hall. With more than 20,000 undergraduates enrolled, the density of people on campus is higher than at many other Chinese universities, which is worth bearing in mind when you think about housing and space.

northeast-forestry-university.h: A forestry-led university with wide range

blocks.x: Forestry is the leading field, but NEFU is multidisciplinary. It has a distinctive specialisation in forest engineering and also covers the forestry-related sides of agriculture, science, engineering, economics, management, the humanities and law. Sixteen colleges and two departments carry out the teaching.

The degree structure is broad. There are five post-doctoral research programmes, four first-level and thirty-two second-level doctoral programmes, and ten first-level and seventy-five second-level master's programmes. Three kinds of special-discipline master's degree cover nine fields, and fifty-seven programmes lead to a bachelor's degree.

National and provincial recognition is extensive. The state has designated two of its fields as national first-level key disciplines, and another two as national second-level ones. The State Forestry Administration has authorised six key disciplines, Heilongjiang Province has authorised two key discipline groups, four provincial first-level key disciplines and fifteen provincial subordinate ones. The National Planning Commission and the Ministry of Education approved NEFU to run national training centres for life science and technology, and the university also operates teaching and research centres for basic sciences, with biology in particular, approved by the Ministry of Education.

On the research side, the university runs a key national observation station for science (the Maoershan forest ecosystem station), three Ministry of Education key laboratories, four State Forestry Administration laboratories and 49 research institutions. Within the university there are nine practice sites, among them the Maoershan and Liangshui centres, and 180 further training bases outside the university.

northeast-forestry-university.h: Living in Harbin: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Student life depends heavily on the city, in particular its winter weather, its economy and its events. The sections below describe Harbin, where NEFU is located.

Harbin is the capital of Heilongjiang and lies in the south of the province. The municipality covers 53,068 square kilometres (about 20,490 square miles). It is located where the Songnen Plain, a large part of the Northeastern Plain, ends in the south-east, and the city centre stands on the southern bank of the Songhua River's middle reach. Because Heilongjiang's outline looks like a swan, Harbin is nicknamed the "pearl on the swan's neck".

Administratively it is large, spanning latitudes of 44° 04′ to 46° 40′ N and longitudes of 125° 42′ to 130° 10′ E. Its neighbours are Yichun in the north, Jiamusi and Qitaihe in the north-east, Mudanjiang in the south-east, Suihua in the north-west and Daqing in the west, while Jilin province borders it on the south-west. The central area is low and flat, at an average height of some 150 metres (about 490 feet). The ten county-level divisions in the east, however, are mountains and uplands, and the far east of the area has broad wetlands, mainly in Yilan County at the south-western edge of the Sanjiang Plain.

Harbin has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa). The Siberian high and the city's latitude, above 45 degrees north, bring cold weather and a long winter. The nickname "Ice City" fits: winters are dry and bitterly cold, and the January average over 24 hours is only −17.3 °C (about 1 °F), though precipitation is light and skies are often sunny. Spring and autumn are short transitions with changeable winds. Summer heat is possible, with a July mean of 23.7 °C (about 75 °F). That is also when most rain falls: more than half of the 539 millimetres (about 21.2 inches) of annual precipitation arrives in July and August.

Possible sunshine is realised at 45 percent in December and 60 percent in September, adding up to 2,340 hours of bright sun a year, and some form of precipitation occurs on about 99 days. The yearly average is 5.2 °C, or 41.4 °F. The lowest temperature on record is −42.6 °C, with −41.1 °C logged at the official station in January 1931, while the highest, 39.2 °C (103 °F), was reached on 4 June 2001. An unofficial reading of 41.0 °C was taken in July 1907 (about 105.8 °F).

Harbin's planners have used "sponge city" ideas to limit the effects of climate change. In the Qunli stormwater park, for example, rain is gathered, filtered and stored, while natural habitat is protected.

The 2020 census counted 10,009,854 people in Harbin, which was 5.62 percent fewer than a decade earlier. The built-up area includes all urban districts except Acheng and Shuangcheng, which are not yet urbanised, and holds 5,282,083 people. Overall 70.61 percent of residents live in urban areas and 29.39 percent in rural ones.

The age profile skews older, with 10.46 percent of residents aged under 14 against 14.65 percent over 65. Males are 50.02 percent and females 49.98 percent. The birth rate of 6.95 per thousand people is below the Chinese average of 12.13.

Most people are Han Chinese (93 percent in 2000). The minorities include Manchu, Hui and Mongol people, and there is a small Russian community. The 2020 census gave a detailed breakdown by ethnic group.

Religious life is varied. Harbin's Catholics are cared for by its Apostolic Administration, a missionary jurisdiction that predates a full diocese, and the city also holds the former cathedral of an Eastern Catholic body, the Russian Catholic Apostolic Exarchate. A church dedicated to the Iver Icon of the Mother of God, now badly damaged, was once used by Russian troops of the Outer Amur Military Region who were stationed in the city. Muslims were a small share of residents, 0.4 percent in 2000, and the Daowai Mosque is the largest mosque in Heilongjiang. There was also a small Jewish community around Zhongyang Main Street, which sheltered many Jewish refugees from Europe.

Harbin has the biggest economy in Heilongjiang. Its GDP was RMB 501.08 billion in 2013, up 8.9 percent on the previous year, and RMB 575.12 billion in 2015. In 2012 the three sectors stood in the proportion 11.1:36.1:52.8, trade in imports and exports came to US$5,330 million, and the working population was 3.147 million. These are older figures, so look up the latest statistics if the economy matters for your plans.

The chernozem soil around Harbin is among the most nutrient-rich in China, which makes it valuable for growing food and fibre crops. As a result Harbin is a base for commodity grain production and a good place for agricultural business.

Many industries operate here, including light industry, textiles, medicine, food, aircraft, motor vehicles, metallurgy, electronics, building materials and chemicals, together forming a fairly complete industrial system. Among the key enterprises are the Northeast Light Alloy Processing Factory, Harbin Aircraft Industry Group and Harbin Electric Company Limited. Power equipment is a core industry: the hydro and thermal power equipment made here accounts for a third of China's installed capacity. Industry analysts at Platts ranked Harbin Electric the world's second-largest producer of steam turbines for 2009–10, tied with Dongfang Electric and a little behind Shanghai Electric. In medicine, Harbin Pharmaceutical Group, which researches, develops, makes and sells drugs, is China's second-biggest drug company by market value.

Harbin has staged a yearly trade and economic fair since 1990. By 2013 the total attendance of exhibitors and visitors had passed 1.9 million, drawn from more than 80 countries and regions, and the contracts signed were worth over US$100 billion. Harbin is a major destination for foreign direct investment in the north-east, with US$980 million used in 2013. After a meeting of the Chinese and Russian prime ministers in October 2013, Li Keqiang and Dmitry Medvedev agreed that the fair would be renamed the "China-Russia EXPO", co-sponsored by China's Ministry of Commerce and the Heilongjiang government on one side, and on the other side by two Russian ministries: Economic Development, and Trade and Industry.

Two of the largest banks in the north-east, Longjiang Bank and Harbin Bank, have their headquarters in the city. In 2011 Harbin Bank came fourth for competitiveness among China's city commercial banks. In retail, Qiulin Group owns Harbin's biggest department store.
Harbin Economic and Technological Development Zone (a national zone) concentrates on telecommunications equipment, chemicals, car production and assembly, electronics, textiles and medical equipment.
The High and New Technological Development Zone of Harbin works in biology, medicine, electronics, IT and the combination of optics, machinery and electrics.
Harbin Pingfang Automobile Industrial Zone (a provincial zone) specialises in vehicle production and assembly, electronics assembly, heavy industry, instruments and industrial equipment.
Harbin Limin Economic Development Zone (a provincial zone) is mainly about trading and distribution, food and beverage processing, medical supplies, and shipping, warehousing and logistics.
Harbin Port is the city's river port.
Harbin Songbei Economic Development Zone is described below.

The Songbei zone lies in Songbei District, and it is planned to cover 5.53 square kilometres. It promotes electronics assembly and manufacturing plus food and drink processing. Regional and provincial offices of big companies such as China Telecom, China Netcom and China Datang Corporation have moved in, forming an early cluster of local headquarters. Regional research centres in the zone include an international agricultural science and technology innovation centre and a Harbin innovation centre for science and technology. Helped by such institutes, Harbin placed ninth out of 50 major Chinese cities for scientific and technological innovation ability in 2006, and sixth for the quantity of scientific and technological achievements. That ranking dates from 2006 and may have changed.

HETDZ, the economic and technological zone, is among 90 national economic development zones in the country. It began in June 1991 and won national status from the State Council in April 1993. A merger in December 2012 brought the high-tech development zone into it, although that zone had previously been split off in 2009. Its centralised parks add up to 18.5 square kilometres, split between the Nangang park and the Haping Road park. A third, the Yingbin Road Hi-tech Centralized Park (12.2 square kilometres), used to belong to HETDZ but has been managed by the high-tech industry zone since 2009.

Each park has its own role. The Nangang Centralized Park is designated for incubating high-tech projects and for company research and development bases, together with services such as finance, insurance, catering, tourism, culture and entertainment, and it hosts the headquarters and branches of large well-known companies. Yingbin Road Centralized Park is mainly about incubating high-tech projects and developing high-tech industry. Haping Road Centralized Park offers a general industrial base for investments in motor vehicles and parts, medicines, foodstuffs, electronics and textiles, and car production and assembly and raw-material processing are the encouraged industries.

Harbin's zone is one of China's 56 national high and new technology zones. It started in 1988 at provincial level and was upgraded to national status by the State Council in 1991. Its built-up area totals 23.9 square kilometres and has two parts, the Science and Technology Innovation Town and the High-tech Industrial Development Zone.

Han culture forms the base of local life, blended with Manchu and Russian influences, and the mix shows in architecture, food, music and customs. On 22 June 2010 UNESCO made Harbin a City of Music within its Creative Cities Network.

Harbin is a popular domestic destination, especially in winter, when large ice sculpture displays are on show. It also has a big indoor ski park inside the Wanda Harbin Mall, with six ski slopes up to 500 metres long. In winter 2023–2024, 87 million visitors came, mostly from other parts of China. Harbin is also known for European-style architecture such as Saint Sophia Cathedral, Central Street and the baroque buildings of Lao Daowai, the Old Town.

Harbin is the northernmost of China's major cities, in the north of the north-east. The Siberian anticyclone has a direct effect here, so the average daily temperature through winter is −19.7 °C, and yearly lows beneath −25.0 °C are nothing out of the ordinary. This freezing weather earns the "Ice City" label, and from December to March ice and snow sculptures in many styles decorate the city.

The ice and snow sculpture festival, an international event, has been held since 1985. It officially opens on 5 January, though many sculptures appear earlier. They are found throughout the city, but two areas are the main venues. Giant snow sculptures stand on Sun Island (Taiyang Dao), a top-rated AAAAA recreation area across the Songhua River from the city. The separate "Ice and Snow World" opens every night with the lights on, lighting the displays from inside and out. Its full-size illuminated buildings are made from blocks of crystal-clear ice, two to three feet thick, cut straight from the Songhua River. Building the exhibits takes 15,000 workers 16 days, and in early December ice artisans saw 120,000 cubic metres of ice from the frozen river for the sculptures. Several parks and main avenues add to this with huge ice buildings, snow sculptures, ice slides and festival food and drink. Related winter activities include skiing at Yabuli, snowmobile driving and winter swimming in the Songhua, as well as the traditional ice-lantern display in Zhaolin Garden, which began in 1963. The art of snow carving and ice recreation has a reputation across China and in countries such as Korea, Japan, Thailand and Singapore.
It ranks as one of the world's four biggest winter festivals, alongside Sapporo's in Japan, the Quebec Winter Carnival in Canada and Norway's Holmenkollen ski festival.

Every November the city sends teams of ice artists to the United States to promote the craft. More than 100 artisans create ICE!, an annual indoor display of Christmas-themed ice carvings, at National Harbor in Maryland, in Nashville, Tennessee, in Kissimmee, Florida and in Grapevine, Texas.

HLJTV, Heilongjiang Television, is the regional broadcaster, with seven channels and one satellite channel reaching other provinces. The municipal station, Harbin Television (HRBTV), has five specialised channels. For radio, the group called Long Guang (Dragon Broadcast), once the Heilongjiang People's Broadcasting Station, covers the whole province with seven channels, one of them in Korean. Harbin People's Broadcasting Station (HPBS) airs music, news, traffic, economy and local-life programmes for Harbin and nearby areas such as Daqing, Suihua and Fuyu.

northeast-forestry-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Northeast Forestry University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Harbin, register at Northeast Forestry University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

northeast-normal-university.h: Northeast Normal University at a glance

blocks.x: Northeast Normal University, or NENU (东北师范大学), is a public university in Changchun, the capital of Jilin Province, and it belongs to the family of "normal" universities, the Chinese term for institutions that specialise in training teachers. It reports to the Ministry of Education and is jointly funded by the ministry and the Jilin Provincial People's Government. It was selected for Project 211 and is part of the Double First-Class Construction, two national programmes that direct extra support to leading universities.

NENU is administered directly by the Ministry of Education. Under the 211 Project it was picked as a university that deserved priority in development. Its land in Changchun adds up to 1,500,000 square metres, of which the main campus has 800,000 and the new campus has 700,000.

The story starts with Northeast University, which was founded in February 1946 in Benxi, Liaoning Province, as the first comprehensive university that the Communist Party established anywhere in the north-east of China. The school moved to Changchun in 1949, and in 1950 it was given its present name, Northeast Normal University.
NENU is organised into 19 schools, offers 56 undergraduate specialties and has a graduate school with 145 master's specialties and 77 doctoral specialties. The units are these:
Psychology; Education (a faculty); Politics and Law
Economics and Business
Chinese Language and Literature; History and Culture; Foreign Languages
Music and Fine Arts
Mathematics and Statistics; Computer Science and Software
Physics, Chemistry and Life Science
Urban and Environmental Science
Physical Education and Media Science
The International Relations Institute and the Marxism Research Institute
IHAC, the Institute for the History of Ancient Civilizations

The academic strength is summarised in a handful of figures. Nine faculties may award doctoral degrees, and 11 disciplines have post-doctoral research and development stations. The national higher education authorities recognise five key disciplines. Six disciplines are part of the key-discipline construction projects run under the Tenth Five-Year Plan and the 211 Project, and 18 more are key subject programmes at provincial level in Jilin.

Three disciplines act as national bases for personnel training and research in the fundamental arts and sciences. The Ministry of Education has designated two of the disciplines as humanities and social science key research bases, and has authorised eight laboratories and research centres. There are several national training programmes and institutes as well, such as the PSCSJ (a preparatory school for Chinese students heading to Japan).

Full-time teachers number 1,297. That figure includes 354 professors and 429 associate professors, and 272 of the staff supervise doctoral students. Academic honours run from the top: the faculty includes an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, another of the Third World Academy of Sciences, and 11 people serving on the State Council's Academic Degree Committee.
Further honours are listed below:
Yangtze River Scholar Program: five professors
Ho Leung Ho Lee Prize: one recipient
National Outstanding Youth Fund: four recipients
National outstanding young and middle-aged specialists: five
The "One Hundred Experts Program" (a talent scheme at national level organised by the Chinese Academy of Sciences): three professors
A personnel construction programme sponsored by the Ministry of Education: 25 teachers
Two state-level renowned teachers, together with 14 on the Guiding Committee for Higher Education Instruction and 13 outstanding individuals within the education system
There are 22,221 full-time students at NENU. They include 15,191 undergraduates, 6,599 master's and doctoral students, and 431 international students.

For NENU, education and teaching are "the foundation of school setting". It has also developed an educational concept built on two mottoes: "BE DILIGENT AND CREATIVE IN STUDIES" and, alongside it, "BE EXEMPLARY IN VIRTUE". It reports that the quality of its students has risen steadily, that it has a high reputation in basic education, and that society has evaluated it positively. In 2004 the State Council named it a "National Advanced Unit for Job-Hunting", one of just four universities honoured nationwide that year, so graduate employment is evidently a strength.
NENU calls scientific research "the basis of institution strengthening", and gives it great weight. In 2013 its natural science research and education placed 18th among all universities in China.
Ma Jun, a historian and professor
Daily life outside the classroom depends on the city: the weather, transport and what there is to do. This section describes Changchun, where NENU is based.

Changchun lies in the middle of the Northeast China Plain, between latitudes 43° 05′ and 45° 15′ N and longitudes 124° 18′ and 127° 02′ E. The whole municipality has an area of 20,571 km2 (7,943 sq mi). Inside it, the metro area measures 2,583 square kilometres (997 sq mi), while the city proper is much smaller at 159 km2 (61 sq mi).

The land is at a moderate elevation, from 250 up to 350 metres (820 to 1,150 ft) across the administrative region. A small area of low mountains rises in the east, and the highest point there is Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres. Changchun also sits at a crossing point of the third east-west "Europe-Asia Continental Bridge". In the prefecture are 222 rivers and lakes. One of them, the Yitong River, is a small branch of the Songhua, and it passes through the city proper.
Changchun's climate has four seasons and is a monsoon-influenced humid continental one (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). The seasons differ a great deal:
Winter lasts from November to March. It is long, cold and windy but dry, because of the Siberian anticyclone, and January averages −14.3 °C (6.3 °F). Snowfall is usually light.
Spring and autumn are fairly short transitions, with some precipitation but usually dry and windy weather.
Summer is hot and humid. The East Asian monsoon brings southeasterly winds, and the July average is 23.7 °C (74.7 °F). June to August is when most of the year's rain falls.

On sunshine and frost: the share of possible sunshine goes from 49 percent in July up to 69 percent in February, and in a typical year the city sees about 2,597 hours of sun, with 140 to 150 frost-free days. The coldest recorded day was 4 January 1970 at −36.5 °C (−34 °F), and the hottest was 9 July 1951 at 38.0 °C (100 °F). If you come from a warm country, you will need serious winter clothing.
Births ran at 6.08 per thousand against deaths at 5.51 per thousand. Within the urban area there were 3.53 million people, and the sex ratio in 2010 was 102.10 men to 100 women.
Han people make up 96.57 percent of the population, as is usual in northeast China, and several minority nationalities live there as well.

Northeastern Mandarin is the common dialect. It developed from a mixture of languages brought by immigrants from Hebei and Shandong. After the People's Republic was founded, quick economic growth attracted huge numbers of migrants from many places, and they influenced speech in the urban areas, so the northeastern dialect there is closer to standard Mandarin than the rural version.

Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam are the four main religions, and 396 places for worship and religious activities are approved by the government. Among the Buddhist and Taoist temples are Changchun Wanshou Temple, Baoguo Prajna Temple, Baiguo Xinglong Temple, Pumen Temple, the Big Buddha Temple and Changchun Temple. Christians and Muslims worship at the Catholic Church, the Christian Church on West Wuma Road and the city mosque.
Shamanism spread across Northeast China in ancient times, and many Manchus believed in it. Today shamanism and its study are an important part of the region's cultural heritage.

Changchun is home to the Jilin Provincial Museum, rated a national first-grade museum. It was transferred from Jilin City when the provincial government changed seat, and at first stood in the old town centre. In 2016, nine years after building began, a new home for its collections was finished on the city outskirts, in Nanguan District close to Jingyuetan Park.

The Badabu buildings once housed eight ministries of Manchukuo: Public Safety, Justice, Economy, Communications, Agriculture, Culture and Education, Foreign Affairs and Civil Affairs. Their architecture blends Chinese, Japanese and Manchurian features, and they have lately become a sightseeing highlight.
To the southeast lies Jingyuetan National Forest Park, one of China's AAAAA Tourist Attractions, which hosts Vasaloppet China every year.

In 2010 Changchun's gross domestic product (GDP) was RMB332.9 billion, up 15.3 percent on the year. The primary sector grew by 3.3 percent and produced RMB25.27 billion. The secondary sector grew faster, by 19.0 percent, to RMB171.99 billion, and services rose 12.6 percent and reached RMB135.64 billion.

By 2012, GDP per capita was ¥58,691 (about $9338), and total GDP was RMB445.66 billion, 12.0 percent more than in 2011. In that year the primary sector produced RMB31.71 billion (up 4.3 percent), the secondary sector RMB229.19 billion (up 13.1 percent) and services RMB184.76 billion (up 11.8 percent).

The city's leading industries are automobiles, agricultural processing, biopharmaceuticals, photoelectronics, building materials and energy. Changchun is China's largest centre for automobile manufacturing, research and development, and it made 9 percent of the country's cars in 2009. It is home to the biggest vehicle maker in China, FAW (First Automotive Works) Group, which produced China's first truck in 1956 and its first car in 1958. FAW's factories, along with the housing and services around them, take up a large part of the south-west end of the city. Red Flag, the luxury marque, is built in Changchun, along with models from joint ventures with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. FAW sold 2.65 million vehicles in 2012, bringing in RMB 408.46 billion, a rise of 10.8% from 2011. Changchun is the birthplace of the Chinese auto industry, and one of its best-known nicknames is "China's Detroit".

Transport equipment and machinery are also major industries. Half of China's passenger trains (50 percent) and a tenth of its tractors (10 percent) come from the city. CRRC's Changchun Railway Vehicles division has a joint venture with Bombardier Transportation, which builds Movia metro cars for the Guangzhou, Shanghai and Tianjin metros.

Most of CRRC's bullet train carriages are produced at the Changchun factory. The company showed off in November 2016 the first bullet train carriages in the world with sleeper berths, making overnight high-speed journeys across China possible. The "Panda" trains, as they are nicknamed, travel at 250 km/h, work in temperatures as low as −40 degrees Celsius, offer Wi-Fi, and have berths that turn into seats during the day.

In 2012 foreign direct investment in the city reached US$3.68 billion, up 19.6%. In 2004 Coca-Cola invested US$20 million in a bottling plant inside the city's ETDZ. Each year the city hosts the Changchun International Automobile Fair, the Changchun Film Festival, the Changchun Agricultural Fair, an Education Exhibition and a Sculpture Exhibition.
Two other large companies are based in Changchun:

Yatai Group was created in 1993 and went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange two years later. It has grown into a major conglomerate with interests in property development, cement, securities, coal mining, pharmaceuticals and trading.
Jilin Grain Group processes grain on a large scale.
Three zones concentrate the city's industry and technology.

northeast-normal-university.h: Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone

blocks.x: A trade centre for the motor industry was founded in 1993 and, in 1996, was re-established with its current title, the Changchun Automotive Economic Trade and Development Zone. In the southwest of the city, it is next to First Automobile Works and the Changchun Film ThemeCity. The area is about 300,000 square metres (3,229,173 square feet) and holds an exhibition centre plus five dedicated industrial centres. One of them, the Changchun Automobile Wholesale Center, started up in 1994 and is China's largest wholesale market for vehicles and spare parts. Another deals in used cars. The remaining two are a specialist centre for industrial and commercial vehicles and a wholesale market for tires.

Among the first 27 state-level advanced technology development zones in China, this one is in the southern part of the city and spreads over 49 km2 (19 sq mi). Inside it are 18 full-time universities and colleges, 11 national key laboratories and 39 research institutions at state or provincial level. Development focuses on five industries: bio-engineering, automobile engineering, new materials, photo-electricity and information technology.

The CETDZ was established in April 1993, and the policy benefits given to the development zones of coastal open cities apply to it. It covers 112.72 square kilometres (43.52 square miles), with 30 square kilometres (12 square miles) of that reserved for development and use. Downtown Changchun is 5 kilometres (3 miles) away; the freight railway station is 2 km (1.2 mi) away and the international airport is 15 km (9 mi) away.

Five leading industries are developed here: automotive parts and components, photoelectric information, bio-pharmaceuticals, fine food processing and new building materials. More than 80 percent of the zone's output comes from high-tech and high value-added projects. Fixed-asset investment reached RMB38.4 billion in 2006, and the zone's 1,656 registered enterprises include 179 foreign-funded ones. Industrial output totalled RMB 277 billion in 2007.

Because it is a major grain-producing base and a regional air and rail hub, Changchun has also built an Aviation Food Industrialization Base. It supplies prepared meals to several airlines and does food science research for long-haul flights, a niche in manufacturing.

Two main passenger stations serve the city. The central Changchun railway station (长春站) handles all conventional trains and some high-speed ones, and connects to the Beijing-Harbin Railway, the Changchun-Hunchun intercity railway and several other lines. Trains leave there every day for places in the province and the northeast (Harbin, Shenyang, Dalian, Yanji and Jilin City among them) and for large cities elsewhere, among them Guangzhou, Shanghai and Beijing.

The newer station, Changchun West, sits at the western end of the built-up area, and it is used mostly by high-speed trains of the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway. Changchun East railway station is small, in Erdao District, on the Changchun-Tumen line.
More than 250 bus routes make up a comprehensive bus system, and most rides cost 1 to 2 yuan.

Changchun is one of the few Chinese cities that kept a historic tram system. It opened in 1941 and at its peak had 6 lines covering almost 53 km. After several route changes only one line has remained since the 2000s, and a new branch opened in 2014 to link the new Changchun West Railway Station. The bus system's operator now runs the entire tram network.

Changchun Rail Transit combines light rail and metro lines. Its first line opened on 30 October 2002, which made Changchun the fifth Chinese metropolitan city with rail transit. By November 2018 there were 5 lines (1, 2, 3, 4 and 8) covering about 100.17 kilometres.

Work was in progress in September 2019 on four more projects: Lines 6 and 9, and extensions of Line 2 to the west and Line 3 to the east. The plan is that 10 lines totalling 341.62 kilometres will make up the network by 2025. Daily ridership averaged 680,400 in September 2019, and the peak daily figure was 830,500 on 13 November 2019. Total passengers in 2019 were estimated at about 168 million.

National expressways link Changchun with the rest of the country: the Beijing-Harbin Expressway (G1), the Ulanhot-Changchun-Jilin-Hunchun Expressway (G12), the Changchun-Shenzhen Expressway (G25) and the Changchun-Changbaishan Expressway (S1). The busiest stretch in the province is the Changchun-Jilin North Highway, which joins Jilin's two biggest cities and carries their social and economic traffic.
Private cars are increasingly common on busy city streets. Bicycles are comparatively rare next to other northeastern cities, but mopeds and pedal cycles of other kinds are fairly common.

Changchun Longjia International Airport lies north-east of the urban area, 31.2 kilometres (19.4 miles) away. It was begun in 1998 as a replacement for Changchun Dafangshen Airport, an older airfield for joint use that dated from 1941. Passenger service started on 27 August 2005, and Changchun and nearby Jilin City share its operation.

In the Nature Index 2024 Science Cities, Changchun is one of the top 30 cities in the world for scientific research. The city has 27 regular institutions of full-time tertiary education, with an enrolment of around 160,000 students. NENU and Jilin University are the two key universities, and Jilin University, with more than 60,000 students, is one of China's largest.
Teacher training: Changchun Normal University and Jilin Engineering Normal University
Science and technology: Changchun University of Science and Technology and Changchun Institute of Technology
Medicine: Changchun University of Chinese Medicine
Arts: Jilin College of the Arts

A private option for languages, Jilin Huaqiao Foreign Languages Institute, offering bachelor study in foreign languages, international trade management and didactics

For families who come with children, secondary schools in the city include:
The high school attached to NENU, and the middle school affiliated with Jilin University
The Second experimental school of Jilin Province

Changchun Foreign Languages School

NENU is a university with a teacher-training tradition, about 22,000 students and the backing of both the national and the provincial governments. Its home city, Changchun, offers very cold winters, a strong industrial base in cars and trains, good rail and air links, and a large student population. When you compare universities, consider which campus, programme and climate suit you best.

Travel to Changchun, register at Northeast Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Northeastern University, usually shortened to NEU and known in Chinese as Dongbei Daxue, is a public university in Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning Province in north-east China. It belongs to the national tier of institutions run under the Ministry of Education, and its costs and direction are shared between that ministry, the national defence-industry administration (SASTIND), the Liaoning provincial government and the Shenyang municipal government. That broad backing is one reason it sits among the country's best-supported universities.

For a prospective international student, the label that matters most is the university's place in China's priority programmes. NEU has been part of Project 211 and Project 985, the two long-running national drives to build leading universities, and it is included in the current Double First-Class Construction plan. In practical terms, this means steady state funding, strong laboratories and a reputation that employers across China recognise, especially in engineering, metallurgy, automation and materials.

The story begins in the early 1920s. In 1921 the provincial assembly of Fengtian, the old name for the Shenyang region, approved a proposal to bring together the resources of the neighbouring provinces of Jilin and Heilongjiang and found a university. The goal was to keep local talent at home and to strengthen education in the north-east. The university opened its doors in April 1923, with Wang Yongjiang, who was then acting governor of Fengtian, as its first president. It started with two parts: a school of literature and law, housed in a former literature school, and a school of science and engineering, housed in a former higher normal school in Shenyang.

The years that followed were turbulent, and the university's path says a lot about its character. In August 1928 General Zhang Xueliang took over as president. The following year, 1929, he commissioned a university song, with words by Liu Bannong and music by Zhao Yuanren; the composer Lv Yuan later adapted and polished it. In 1931 Japanese forces took control of Shenyang, and the university was forced into exile. By October that year it had restarted its teaching in Beiping, the name then used for Beijing.

Wartime displacement continued. In 1936 the engineering school moved to Xi'an and set up a branch there, and in January 1937 an acting president was appointed by the national government. By June 1937 the whole school had moved to Xi'an. In the spring of 1938, as air raids on Xi'an intensified and the situation worsened, the university moved again, this time to Santai in Sichuan. Only after the war ended did the community return home: in May 1946 the staff and students came back to Shenyang.

Around 1949 the old university was reorganised. Its engineering school and part of its science school became the core of an engineering college focused on metallurgy and located in the Nanhu area of Shenyang, which is still the heart of the university today. Accounts of the exact administrative changes in that period are not always consistent, so if you need a precise chronology, the university's own history pages are the best reference. A later milestone came in 1997, when Shenyang Gold College was folded into NEU, widening its range of disciplines.
In short, NEU combines a 1920s founding and a long record of resilience with a modern identity as a research-focused engineering university.

NEU is best known for engineering and industrial technology. It hosts two national key laboratories, one devoted to rolling and automation and the other to the integrated automation of process industries. Beyond these, it runs 4 national engineering or technology research centres, 12 key laboratories, engineering centres and strategic research bases under the Ministry of Education, and 57 key laboratories, engineering centres and engineering laboratories supported by Liaoning Province.

The faculty also includes senior scholars. Five full-time members of the Chinese Academy of Engineering or the Chinese Academy of Sciences work at NEU: Wen Bangchun, Chai Tianyou, Wang Guodong, Feng Xiating and Tang Lixin. For a graduate applicant, the useful point is that supervisors with this level of standing, together with so many specialised laboratories, give you access to serious equipment and projects in fields such as steel rolling, process control and rock engineering.

northeastern-university.h: Where you will study: the campuses

blocks.x: As of January 2024 the university operates 4 campuses, three in Shenyang and one in Qinhuangdao in Hebei Province. Knowing which one your programme uses is an important part of planning, because the distances between them are considerable.

Nanhu Campus is the historic main campus, facing the Hun River from its south side, with Nanhu Lake to its north. It covers roughly 2.03 million square metres, with around 1 million square metres of buildings, so it feels like a small town in its own right.

Hunnan Campus is the newer site, at 195 Chuangxin Road in Hunnan District, about 16 kilometres from Nanhu. It covers 890,000 square metres, with a planned building area of 970,000 square metres. At the time of the information available, 15 buildings were in use, among them the first teaching building, the library, the information centre, and buildings for life sciences, humanities and management, and architecture. There is also a gymnasium, five student dormitory blocks, a student life service centre, an energy and power centre and a central substation. Because the university is still developing this site, check its website for which faculties are based here now.

Shenhe Campus, in the south-east of the city near the Hunnan development zone and 6 kilometres from Nanhu, used to be the home of the Basic College. Once the Hunnan campus was finished, regular students stopped studying there. Since 2015 it has hosted the School of Continuing Education, which runs adult education and vocational training.

Qinhuangdao Campus sits in Haigang District of Qinhuangdao, on the Hebei coast, and covers about 530,000 square metres. Figures reported for it include 849 faculty members, among them 283 senior professionals and 265 supervisors of master's and doctoral students. It combines a branch of the university's graduate school, a joint Chinese-foreign teaching institution and eight colleges, and offers 36 undergraduate majors spanning the arts, sciences, business and technical fields. It shares doctoral and master's resources with the main university and has its own master's programmes in optical engineering and ethnology. As staffing numbers change from year to year, treat these figures as a snapshot.

International league tables place NEU comfortably in the upper tier of world universities. In 2025 the ARWU list (the Shanghai ranking) put it in the 201-300 band globally. The same year the U.S. News Best Global Universities ranking listed it at number 445 in the world, number 111 in Asia and number 58 in China. Rankings differ in method and change annually, so use them as one input alongside programme-level strengths, and check current positions before you apply.
For more detail on admissions, programmes and international student services, the university's official website is the place to look.

A student's daily life depends heavily on the city outside the campus gate: the weather, the way you travel, the food and the things to do. This part introduces Shenyang, the home of Northeastern University, so you know what to expect before you arrive.

northeastern-university.h: The lie of the land and its rivers

blocks.x: Shenyang sits in the middle of Liaoning Province, between about 41° 11' and 43° 02' north and 122° 25' and 123° 48' east. The terrain changes as you travel across the city's administrative area. The west is flat land deposited by the Liao River network, while the east rises into forested country that forms the hinterland of the Changbai Mountains. The highest point stands 414 metres (1,358 ft) over the sea, and the lowest point is a mere 7 metres (23 ft), with the built-up urban area averaging 45 metres (148 ft). In everyday terms, the city is flat and easy to cycle or walk around.

The central districts lie north of the Hun River, which was once the largest tributary of the Liao and is affectionately called the city's mother river. Three man-made rivers wrap around the centre and are linked by channels into one continuous waterway: the South Canal to the south and south-east, the Xinkai River (the former North Canal) to the north and north-east, and the Weigong River to the west. The South Canal is the best known, thanks to the string of linear parks and gardens beside it. It was dug along the former bed of the Wanquan River, whose name means ten thousand springs; it was also called the Little Shen River or the Wuli River, and it was a main water source for the old city.

Smaller rivers such as the Xi, the Puhe and the Mantang reinforce this system on the outskirts, and they flow into the Hun at three points on the south-east, south and south-west of the city. A canal on the east side, the Huishan Nullah, once drained into the lower Xinkai River but no longer exists, because the land was reclaimed for building.

Shenyang has plenty of parks. The best known are the South Canal Linear Parks, a 14.5 km (9.0 mi) ribbon through the southern parts of the Dadong, Shenhe and Heping districts. Together they hold 6 big parks and 18 riverside gardens over about 1,400,000 square metres (350 acres). Planting includes roses, apricots, bladder cherries, honey locusts, natal lilies, scarlet sage, morning glories and black-eyed Susans, with wider green areas of peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, weeping willow, pine and black locust trees. This is the largest stretch of planted open space in the city, and it made a significant contribution to Shenyang's 40 percent greening ratio and helped the city win the title of national forest city in 2005.

Air quality is the less pleasant side of the picture. The city's environmental protection bureau has reported that coal burned in winter by boiler stations for district heating accounts for 30 percent of local air pollution. During the winter of 2013-2014 the city used 16 million metric tons of coal, and half of that went on heating. Building-site dust adds 20 percent, traffic fumes another 20 percent, factories 10 percent, and dust carried in from outside the city a further 20 percent, mostly yellow dust from the Gobi Desert. The bureau described air quality as slowly improving. Those figures date from over a decade ago, so check recent readings and bring a good mask for the heating season if you are sensitive.

Shenyang has a humid continental climate shaped by the monsoon (Koppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). Summers are hot and humid because of the monsoon, and winters are dry and cold because of the Siberian anticyclone. The four seasons are clearly distinct, and nearly half the year's rain falls in July and August.

Average temperatures swing from a January low of -11.4 °C (11.5 °F) to a July high of 24.9 °C (76.8 °F), giving a yearly mean of 8.6 °C (47.5 °F). The frost-free period lasts 183 days, which is long for a place with such harsh winters. The city gets 2,421 hours of bright sunshine a year, with July seeing 42 percent of the possible total and February 64 percent. The record range runs from -33.1 °C (-28 °F) up to 38.4 °C (101 °F). If you come from a warm country, plan for a proper down coat, thermal layers and waterproof boots from late autumn; buildings are heated, so indoors is comfortable.

Shenyang has a population of about 9.07 million, and 85.12% of residents live in urban areas. Counts change with each census, so look at recent official statistics if you need a precise number. The city is ethnically varied: 38 of China's 56 recognised ethnic groups live here. The Han Chinese majority makes up 91.26 percent of the population, and the other 37 groups include the Manchu, Korean, Hui, Xibo, Mongolian, Zhuang, Miao, Tibetan, Uyghur and Russian communities, among many smaller ones. Most of these communities come from elsewhere; only a few, notably the Manchu and the Xibe, are native to the Shenyang area.
The city has many temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship, so students of different faiths will find somewhere to go.

Locals speak the Shenyang dialect, a variety of Northeastern Mandarin that took shape in the early Qing dynasty. It is close to other north-eastern speech and to standard Mandarin (Putonghua), but it belongs to the Dongbei family and has many words you will not find in the official language. If you have learned standard Mandarin, you will be understood, though you may need a few weeks to tune your ear to the local flavour.

Shenyang is one of China's important industrial centres and the central city of the Shenyang Economic Zone, a special reform zone for the region. Its traditional strength is heavy industry, particularly aircraft, machine tools, large equipment and the defence sector, and more recently software, vehicles and electronics. Heavy industry took root in the 1920s and was well established before the Second World War. In the first five-year plan (1951-1956), many factories were built in the Tiexi district. By the 1970s Shenyang ranked among China's top three industrial centres next to Shanghai and Tianjin, and for a time was considered for promotion to a directly administered municipality.

The story then turned. After the 1980s, as the planned economy lost favour, heavy industry gradually declined and Shenyang became a classic rust belt city, after hundreds of thousands of workers lost their jobs when state factories failed. In recent years, however, the economy has revived considerably, helped by the national campaign to revitalise Northeast China and by fast growth in software and car manufacturing. Subsidies for investment have been offered to multinational companies that set up offices or headquarters here. For students of engineering, computing or industrial management, that mix of old industry and new technology is a real advantage.

Services, particularly banking, have also grown. Foreign banks with a presence include Hana Bank of South Korea, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ of Japan, the Bank of East Asia of Hong Kong, United Overseas Bank of Singapore and HSBC of Britain. In 2006 the city counted 1,063 banks and branches plus 144 insurance-related firms, and local goals then were 30 foreign banks and 60 non-bank financial institutions by 2010. These are old targets, so they show the direction of travel rather than today's totals. In November 2010 the Economist Intelligence Unit's Access China white paper named Shenyang one of the CHAMPS, a group of emerging cities (with Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan and Pingdingshan) in its list of 20 rising Chinese cities.
The city has three development zones, which are where many companies and research parks are concentrated:
Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone
Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone
Shenyang Economic and Technological Development Zone

Several big industrial names are headquartered here. Brilliance Auto, a major Chinese carmaker, has most of its plants in Shenyang. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation builds civilian aircraft as well as aircraft for the PLAAF. Neusoft Group is described as China's biggest software company, and Shenyang Machine Tool Group as its largest machine tool maker. Tyco International, General Motors and the Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation were once reported to be growing their operations here, though company plans change. For comparison of living standards, the city's GDP per capita was 78,490 yuan in 2009, third among the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning at that time; later figures will be higher, so look for the latest data.

Shenyang is the transport hub of Northeast China. It has air and rail links, a subway (five lines at the time of the information available, with more being added), a large network of streets and expressways, and buses across the city. The biggest air terminal in the north-east is Terminal 3 at Taoxian International Airport, and a tram network opened in the south of the city in 2013.

Shenyang is the north-east's railway hub. Eight rail lines radiate from the city towards Beijing, Dalian, Changchun, Harbin and Fushun. The Qinhuangdao-Shenyang high-speed line is the main passenger corridor through the Shanhai Pass and was China's first railway built just for passengers. From early 2007 a 200 km/h (120 mph) fast service shortened the trip between Beijing and Shenyang dramatically, to around 4 hours. The Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway came into use at the end of 2012, linking Shenyang to the other big north-eastern cities at up to 300 km/h (190 mph). Since 2011 a daily container train has also hauled car parts some 11,000 km (6,800 mi) from Leipzig in Germany across Siberia to Shenyang in about 23 days.

There are two main stations: Shenyang North in Shenhe District and Shenyang Station in Heping District. Locals often have their own names for them, which can confuse newcomers, so always check the Chinese characters on your ticket.

Shenyang North was called the Liaoning General Station before 1946, and people still call it the Old North Station. The original building, now a listed heritage building, opened in 1927 about 1 km (0.62 mi) south-west of the current site, at the end of the Jingfeng Railway; it was built on the orders of a regional military leader to rival the Shenyang station then run by the Japanese. Work on the main building of today's New North Station began in 1986, and it opened in December 1990. It grew into one of the five key rail hubs of the country and earned the nickname the Northeast's No. 1 Station. In 2011 a large rebuilding project began to cope with the growth in passengers after high-speed trains arrived. The station now has an extra three-storey sub-station building and a North Square on the Huanggu District side of the tracks. The waiting hall in the original 16-storey main building has moved to a big elevated concourse bridging the tracks, under a pillar-free roof that is the largest of its kind on the mainland and domes the platforms. The South Square outside the main building became a multi-level complex, with an elevated drop-off area in the style of an airport, ground-level bus stops, and a three-level underground city with shops, parking, taxi pick-up and an interchange with Subway Line 2. The underground space is designed so it could be quickly turned into a civil-defence shelter.

Shenyang Station is over a century old. Russian builders put it up in 1899 beside the eastern flank of the South Manchurian Railway as Fengtian Station, and the Japanese enlarged it after the Russo-Japanese War. Between 1945 and 1950 it was known as Shenyang South Station, or simply South Station, in contrast to North Station, and many locals still use that name, even though the real Shenyang South station is now at the suburban junction of Hunnan and Sujiatun. Today the station handles regular-speed services and is being refurbished with a grand arch and a new terminal, so access to platforms may be rerouted underground and overhead while building continues. A new West Station Building and West Square opened on the west side in 2010, and the old East Station Building is on the provincial protected heritage list.

Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, in Hunnan District, counts as one of China's eight main airline hubs, ranked 23rd for traffic nationwide. Three other airports exist in the city, none open to the public. East Pagoda Airport in Dadong District is the oldest; it opened in the 1920s and was retired in the 1980s, although relocating and reopening it in Xinmin was proposed in 2013. Beiling Airport in Huanggu District is used for test flights by Shenyang Aircraft Corporation, and Yuhong Airport in Yuhong District serves the local Northern Theater Command garrisons for military purposes only.

Two folk dances from the north-east, Errenzhuan and Yangge, are very popular here. The Big Stage Theatre near Middle Street is well known for Errenzhuan and Chinese comedy sketches performed by Zhao Benshan and his students. With so many comedians based in the city, Shenyang is recognised nationally as a stronghold of Chinese comedy, so a night out may well involve a live comic show.

The city is also home to performing arts groups such as an acrobatic troupe, a song and dance ensemble and a ballet company. Well-known artists from Shenyang include Zimei, Na Ying and the pianist Lang Lang.

In short, Shenyang offers a solid industrial economy, excellent rail links, strong seasonal contrasts and a lively performance culture, which together make it a distinctive place to spend your student years.
Northeastern University lists 218 programs for international students on this site: 81 bachelor, 77 master's, 60 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 172 taught in Chinese, 46 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
