International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

northeastern-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Northeastern University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shenyang, register at Northeastern University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Northwest A&F University, usually shortened to NWAFU (Chinese name 西北农林科技大学, which translates roughly as Northwestern Agricultural and Forestry Science and Technology University), is a national public university in Yangling District, part of Xianyang in Shaanxi Province. It reports to China's Ministry of Education and is enrolled in three national flagship schemes: Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction. For an international applicant, that combination is the clearest sign that the central government treats it as a priority institution in agriculture and forestry.

The Yangling campus has deep roots. A school was founded here in 1934 by Yang Hucheng (楊虎城), a general who commanded the Northwest Army under the Kuomintang. Yangling therefore has been an education town for far longer than the current university has existed.

The present university was created by combining seven separate organisations. The State Council approved the plan in response to a joint proposal from the Ministry of Education and the Shaanxi provincial government, and its reply granted a start-up fund of 600,000,000 RMB, with outlines of later investment and staffing arrangements. The opening ceremony took place on 11 September 1999, when Vice Premier Li Lanqing led a central government delegation to Yangling and announced the new university.
Leadership is shared between a president and a Communist Party Committee secretary, which is the normal arrangement in Chinese universities. The presidents so far have been:
September 1999 to August 2003: Mr. Chen Zongxing (陈宗兴)
August 2003 to January 2011: Professor Sun Wuxue (孙武学)
January 2011 to July 2017: Professor Sun Qixin (孙其信)
December 2017 to the present: Professor Wu Pute (吴普特)
The Party Committee secretaries have been:
September 1999 to August 2003: Professor Sun Wuxue (孙武学), who later became president
August 2003 to May 2013: Professor Zhang Guangqiang (张光强)
May 2013 to August 2015: Dr. Liang Gui (梁桂)
August 2015 to the present: Mr. Li Xingwang (李兴旺)

northwest-af-university.h: Where it appears in the rankings

blocks.x: NWAFU belongs to the Project 985 group, a club of 39 well-regarded Chinese universities. International league tables place it as follows:
Times Higher Education World University Rankings, 2017: in the 801-1000 band worldwide
The 2025 Best Global Universities list from U.S. News & World Report: 288th overall
Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), 2025: in the 201-300 band
Nature Index Research Leaders, 2025, which measures research output in leading journals: 230th among academic institutions worldwide
Read together, these tell you the university is a strong research institution, with its reputation concentrated in particular fields rather than spread evenly.

Within China, NWAFU is counted among the top three agriculture universities for both research and teaching quality. Its research is especially dominant in agricultural biology: wheat breeding, insect science, managing agricultural resources, gardening and fruit crops, crop protection, food science (with a particular reputation for enology, the study of wine), forestry and veterinary medicine. It is also respected for agricultural water conservancy, agricultural economics and management, agricultural mechanics and information engineering, and research into the history of ancient agriculture.

The subject tables sharpen the picture. In 2025, Agricultural Science was ranked third in the world in both the U.S. News & World Report global rankings and ARWU, while Plant and Animal Science came eighth in the world in ARWU. A student who wants a career in crops, food or land management would find few better-placed universities in China.

Daily life for students depends heavily on the town around the campus: how easy it is to travel, what the economy looks like and what you can visit on a free weekend. This section covers Yangling itself.

Yangling is home to the university's main campus. Its other defining feature is the Yangling Agriculture Hi-Tech Industrial Zone, which won national hi-tech zone status from the State Council in 1997. The zone is about 82 kilometres (51 miles) east of Xi'an, and the Xi'an Xianyang International Airport lies 70 kilometres (43 miles) from it. For students, those distances are the practical measure of how long an arrival journey from the airport will take.
Tai Bai Mountain (太白山) is the nearest well-known natural destination, roughly 35 to 40 kilometres from Yangling district, which makes it a realistic trip for a weekend.
A university's province shapes student life as much as its campus does. Shaanxi offers an unusually rich historical backdrop, a varied landscape and a modern economy built on energy and technology.

Shaanxi is regarded as one of the cradles of Chinese civilisation. Between the Zhou and Tang dynasties, a period of over 1,100 years, thirteen dynasties made their capitals here. Its main city and present capital, Xi'an, is one of China's four great ancient capitals and the eastern end of the Silk Road, the trade route that carried goods onward to Europe, Arabia and Africa.
The timeline is long and eventful:
After the Qin dynasty collapsed, the area was briefly ruled as the Three Qins. This gave the province one of its two abbreviations, 秦 (Qin); the other is 陝 (Shaan).

Liu Bang then took the region in the struggle known as the Chu-Han Contention. The Han dynasty pushed the Northern Silk Road westward for exploration and for military reasons. This route lies furthest north of all the Silk Roads and measures about 2,600 kilometres (1,600 miles): it left Xi'an, crossed the Wushao Ling Pass to Wuwei, and emerged at Kashgar before joining up with ancient Parthia.
The kingdom of Northern Xia, led by the Xiongnu, had its capital at Tongwancheng (407-431).
Shaanxi was also a contested frontier between the Northern Song and the Tangut-led Western Xia. Western Xia found the frontier fort of Luōwùchéng (罗兀城) in 1071, but Song took it in 1081.

Shaanxi became a province under the Ming, when the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission was founded in 1376. Its area also took in today's Gansu, Ningxia and part of Qinghai, and travellers from Central and West Asia mostly came into China through it.

On 23 January 1556 one of history's most devastating earthquakes struck near Hua Shan in the southeast. An estimated 100,000 people died, and emigration and famine cut the regional population by an estimated 830,000.
When the short-lived Jiangxi Soviet ended, Mao Zedong and the Chinese Communists began the Long March, which brought them to the Shaanxi Soviet at Yan'an.

The administrative story also runs deep. The Northern Song set up the Shaanxi Lu (circuit) in 997, governed from modern Xi'an. In 1286 the Yuan dynasty organised Shaanxi Province under a Branch Secretariat. Once the Qing dynasty took power, Gansu was separated from Shaanxi, though one Viceroy of Shaan-Gan governed both.

Near Xi'an, in Lantian County in the northwest of the province, researchers found the Lantian Man site. The hominin fossils there date back about one million years, and Lantian Man is classed as a subspecies of Homo erectus. You can see the fossils at the Shaanxi History Museum in Xi'an, which is an easy cultural outing for students based in the region.
Shaanxi stretches a long way from north to south, so its terrain changes a great deal:
The far north, next to Inner Mongolia, belongs to the Ordos Desert.
The centre of the province is the Loess Plateau.
The Qin Mountains (Qinling) run east to west through the south-central area, and south of them the climate is subtropical.
Between the plateau and the mountains lies the Wei River Valley, also called Guanzhong, one of the cradles of early Chinese civilisation. This is the area where Yangling and Xi'an are found.

Going clockwise, Shaanxi borders Shanxi (east and northeast), Henan (east), Hubei (southeast), Chongqing (south), Sichuan (southwest), Gansu (west), Ningxia (northwest) and Inner Mongolia (north). It shares first place with Inner Mongolia for the number of provincial-level neighbours.

The wide span of latitude produces several climates. Under the Köppen system, the north, including the Loess Plateau, is cold arid (BWk) or cold semi-arid (BSk), meaning bitter, parched winters, dry spring and autumn seasons, and muggy hot summers. Guanzhong is mostly semi-arid, with a few humid subtropical (Cwa) pockets, so winters range from cool to cold and summers are hot and humid, often with an early heatwave. The south is far more humid, with milder winters and long, hot, humid summers. Across the province yearly average temperatures fall from about 8 to 16 °C (46 to 61 °F). In January the range is -11 to 3.5 °C (12.2 to 38.3 °F); in July it is 21 to 28 °C (70 to 82 °F). Pack for real winter cold if you study in the Guanzhong area.
Besides Xi'an, the other cities to know are:
Baoji
Hanzhong
Lintong
Tongchuan
Xianyang
Yan'an
Ankang

Around the mid-19th century the province sold animal skins, wine, liquor and musk abroad, and bought in European animal skins, watches, Chinese-language books and cloth. Moneylending was common, and Shaanxi businesspeople took part in the loan business in Guangzhou. In the Third Front campaign the province was a major recipient of national investment in industrial capacity.

Today the two largest industries are fossil fuels and high technology. Output in 2009 put the province third in China for coal, natural gas and crude oil. It also hosts some of Western China's best universities and research institutes, which helps explain its big role in aircraft and aerospace: it supplies over 50% of the R&D and manufacturing equipment behind China's home-built commercial aviation.

The numbers give a sense of scale. In 2011 nominal GDP came to 1,239 billion RMB (US$196.7 billion) and GDP per capita to 21,729 RMB (US$3,179), which placed Shaanxi 17th nationally. Over the first six months of 2019 the province produced 1,162.557 billion yuan of output, 5.4% more than a year earlier. The primary industry added 55.319 billion yuan (up 4.5%), the secondary industry 557.935 billion yuan (up 4.2%) and the tertiary industry 549.303 billion yuan (up 6.8%).

northwest-af-university.h: Development zones that offer jobs and internships

blocks.x: Shaanxi has a cluster of state-approved industrial zones. They matter to students because they are where graduate employers and research partners are concentrated.

Baoji Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone: set up in 1992 and given national hi-tech zone status by the State Council; its long-range plan covers 40 km2 (15 sq mi). It is served by Xi'an Xianyang International Airport and National Highway 310. Industries include auto parts, electronics, IT, pharmaceuticals, bioengineering and new materials.

Shaanxi Xi'an Export Processing Zone (XEPZ): approved by the State Council on 21 June 2002 and put into operation on 5 April 2004. It was northwest China's earliest state-level export processing zone, and one of seven pilot zones offering bonded logistics. It operates under the Administrative Committee of the Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone, which the city government has authorised to exercise economic and administrative power there. It is a special economic zone with more than 40 domestic and foreign enterprises, and its main industries are aviation, machinery, electronics and new energy.

Western Triangle: a newer economic area joining three major urban economies in the west: Xi'an, Chongqing and Chengdu. Adding Xi'an is expected to speed regional growth and help the city make more of its high-technology sector.

Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone: founded in 1993 and recognised as a national zone in 2000. Highways cross it, and the airport at Xi'an Xianyang is a 20-minute trip away. Its four pillar industries are automotive, electronics, food and new materials, and more than 1,700 enterprises have moved in.

Xi'an High-tech Industrial Development Zone: opened in 1991 as a national high-tech zone and a pivotal location for high-tech investment in central and northwest China. National highways surround it, it is 30 minutes from the airport, and it ranks among China's top three high-tech zones.

Xi'an Software Park: launched in December 1998 as the city's specialist park for large-scale software and service outsourcing. It holds national status as a Torch Program software industry base, a national software industry base, a national software export base and a demonstration area for service outsourcing, making it one of four parks in China with these "double bases". It houses 90% of Xi'an's software and outsourcing enterprises. By the end of 2008 it had nearly 780 companies, 170 of them foreign-funded, and over 71,000 employees.
Yangling Agriculture Hi-Tech Industrial Zone: the zone next to the university, described above, approved in 1997, 82 km (51 mi) from Xi'an and 70 km (43 mi) from the airport.

The population is overwhelmingly Han Chinese, apart from some Hui communities in the northwest by the Ningxia border. The central Guanzhong region, where the capital Xi'an stands, is more populous than the northern (Shaanbei) and southern (Shaannan) parts.

The main traditions are Chinese folk religion, Taoism and Chinese Buddhism. Surveys in 2007 and 2009 found that 7.58% of people take part in ancestor veneration and 1.57% identify as Christian. No figures were given for other groups, so the remaining 90.85% could be non-religious or follow nature deities, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, folk sects or Islam in small communities. Local Christian sites include the Catholic Church in Shaanxi, the Catholic church in Zhifang (demolished in 2017) and the Golden Lampstand Church (destroyed in 2018).
Shaanxi's cultural heritage includes:
Shaanxi cuisine, a good reason to try the local food
Qinqiang, the province's representative folk opera
Shaanxi shadow play
Xintianyou, a local folk song style
Xi'an has its own cultural and religious traditions, which are well worth reading about before you go.

Professional sport in Shaanxi includes basketball teams in the Chinese Basketball Association system: the Shaanxi Wolves in the National Basketball League (NBL) and the Shaanxi Red Wolves in the Women's Chinese Basketball Association (WCBA).

northwest-af-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Northwest A&F University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Yangling, register at Northwest A&F University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Northwest Normal University, called NWNU for short (Chinese name 西北师范大学, pinyin Xiběi Shifàn Dàxué), is a public university in Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in north-west China. Chinese central government has given it the power to award associate, bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees in over 80 subject areas. Its name points to its origin in teacher education, and that remains its reputation, even though today it also teaches many other disciplines.

NWNU is a key institution run jointly by the Gansu provincial government and the Ministry of Education, and it is counted among the 14 universities of western China that receive special state support. The family tree starts in 1902 with the Normal School of the Metropolitan University, which later became National Beiping Normal University. Japan's invasion after the 'July 7 Incident' of 1937 scattered Beijing's schools. Beiping Normal University was folded together with National Beiping University and the Beiyang Engineering Institute into a new body called Northwest Union University, while the normal university carried on as an attached normal school. In 1939 it became independent again with a new title, the National Northwest Normal Institute, and in 1941 it relocated to Lanzhou. Before 1958 it was one of just six major normal institutes under direct control of the education ministry.

Control passed to Gansu Province in 1958, and the institute was renamed Gansu Normal University. In 1981 it went back to the name Northwest Normal Institute, and in 1988 it was renamed Northwest Normal University, the name it has used since.

The university has had a particular mission in preparing teachers for China's minority regions. A teacher training centre for northwest ethnic minorities was created in 1985 and reports directly to the education ministry; it is run under the arrangement 'Two Plaques, One Leading Board'. In 1987 a Tibetan teachers' training centre, under the State Council, was added. With the ministry's support NWNU has gone on to create many more institutes. Examples are centres for elementary curriculum reform and for the development of minority education in the northwest, a national base for training vocational and physical education teachers, a base for training mentors, a laboratory working on eco-environmental macromolecule materials, and a base for Chinese language and culture education.

Support from the State Council's Overseas Chinese Affairs Office and from Gansu itself paid for 25 more research institutes, including ones for cultural development and educational development in Gansu, and 4 key labs at provincial level. Altogether the university now has 26 colleges and one independent institute, 70 departments and 2 teaching departments, 160 teaching and research centres and 41 experimental labs.

NWNU's grounds total 960 hectares, and 729 hectares belong to the new campus. The campus also has 3,600 hectares set aside as green land and compensation land for construction. Buildings add up to 820 thousand square metres of floor space, with 395.8 thousand of it in teaching and support buildings.

The value of teaching equipment may reach 20,534 million yuan, and the library has a collection of more than 3.49 million volumes. On the technical side, the university runs networks for distance learning, for managing teaching affairs, for computers across the campus, for communications and for cable television.

About 180,000 students have completed their studies since the university became independent, and it draws students from 31 provinces, cities and autonomous regions. A separate count of 35,200 recent graduates divides into 5,600 postgraduates and doctors, 16,900 undergraduates and 12,700 adult-education students. Those two totals are of different scale, probably covering different periods, so ask the university for up-to-date numbers. It has so far launched 5 successive reform programmes for undergraduate teaching.

Altogether 2,547 people work as teaching staff. Of those, 1,303 teach full time, and the full-time group includes 292 professors and 716 associate professors; 410 hold doctorates and 624 hold postgraduate degrees. There are 3 academicians among them, 101 doctoral supervisors and 696 supervisors of master's students. Honours include one 'National Distinguished Teacher' and one 'Yangtze River Scholar', two national teaching teams, and an innovation team recognised by the education ministry. More than 380 outside experts hold special or part-time professorships, ten of them academicians of the Chinese Academy of Sciences or of the Academy of Engineering. Many well-known scholars have taught here over the years, among them Li Zheng, Li Jinxi, Yuan Dunli, Dong Shouyi, Li Jianxun, Hu Guoyu, Lv Sibai, Kong Xianwu, Chang Shuhong, Chen Yong, Huang Zhou, Peng Duo, Guo Jinxi, Cheng Guodong, Xue Qunji, Li Bingde, Jin Baoxiang, Jin Shaoying and Nan Guonong.

Since 1982 NWNU has belonged to the first group of institutions that the State Council allowed to grant bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees. Six postdoctoral centres cover pedagogy, Chinese literature, histology, mathematics and chemistry. At doctoral level the university holds authority in 7 first-level disciplines (pedagogy, chemistry, Chinese language and literature, histology, mathematics, physics and geography), 50 second-level disciplines and one specialty. For master's degrees it has 32 first-level disciplines, 157 second-level ones and 11 specialties. Two disciplines are national key disciplines, 16 are key at provincial level and 33 at university level, and an innovation team is backed by the Ministry of Education. Undergraduates can choose from 66 specialties, from English, art and bioscience to geography, physics, chemistry, mathematics and applied mathematics, and Chinese language and literature.

More than 120 universities have established links with NWNU. It has founded research institutes and international bodies in over 40 countries, plus Taiwan and Hong Kong, hosted over 50 large academic conferences and taught more than 1,100 students from overseas. In partnership with the University of Khartoum in Sudan and with Moldova's Free International University, it runs 2 Confucius Institutes.
The family of schools attached to the university includes an educational group, two middle schools (No. 1 and No. 2), a primary school and a kindergarten.

Three graduates are worth knowing about. Lydia H. Liu teaches comparative literature at Columbia University and received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1997. Du Yaxiong is an ethnomusicologist whose research covers ancient Chinese music theory and the folk music of minority peoples. Li Xi has served on the Standing Committee of the 20th Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party.
Your daily routine as a student depends on the city around the campus, so the following pages look at Lanzhou, the home of Northwest Normal University.

At 1,600 metres (about 5,200 feet) above sea level, Lanzhou lies at the geographical centre of north-west China. The built-up city runs along the south side of the Yellow River, which crosses it from west to east, and spans over 20 square kilometres (some 7.7 square miles). Several mountain ranges flank it north and south: the Qilian Ranges, Mt. Pingliang and Mt. Kongtong.

Lanzhou stands on the upper Yellow River where it comes out of the mountains, and it has mattered since ancient times as the southern end of the road through the Hexi Corridor into Central Asia. It also controls approaches to the old capital region around Chang'an (today's Xi'an, in Shaanxi) from west and north-west, and to the Qinghai Lake area by way of the upper river and its tributaries.

Lanzhou has a temperate, semi-arid climate (Koppen BSk), meaning hot summers and cold, extremely dry winters. In the urban core the 1971 to 2000 averages run from -4.1 C (24.6 F) in January up to 23.4 C (74.1 F) in July, while the whole year averages 10.9 C (51.6 F). It rains little, 309 mm (12.2 in) in a year, and nearly all of that falls between May and October. Winters can be so dry that snow only comes in autumn and spring. The sun is out generously but not abundantly: possible sunshine rises from 47 percent in September to 57 percent in April, giving 2,350 hours of bright sunshine annually.

Environmental problems have been a big part of Lanzhou's recent story. The city sits in a narrow, bending river valley, and the surrounding mountains keep the air from moving. A national environmental analysis published in January 2013 by Tsinghua University and the Asian Development Bank placed it among the ten most polluted cities in the world for air. Reports say that haze was so thick at times that residents could not make out Lanshan, the mountain on the south side of the city. Many factories, including oil-processing plants, add to the pollution, and strong dust storms from the Gobi Desert hit the city, mainly in winter and spring. In 2011 the World Health Organization, using Chinese data, found the worst air of eleven cities in western China in Lanzhou: its annual mean PM10 of 150 micrograms per cubic metre was seven times the WHO safe level and higher than Beijing's 121.

Since then the authorities have taken action, and it has largely worked. The report cites the closure of 13 polluting firms with excess capacity, the winter suspension of over 200 heavily polluting firms and the relocation of 78 industrial firms to a park outside the city. Lanzhou received China's climate progress title in 2015. Satellites once could not see the city through the haze, and now it has cut its Air Pollution Index faster than any other Chinese city. In the WHO's 2018 database of 2700 towns, Lanzhou stood 158th for fine particles (PM2.5) at an average of 54 micrograms per cubic metre, which is double the level of Milan. Coarse PM10 particles are still high, at 132 micrograms per cubic metre, in part because of sandstorms.

The Yellow River in Lanzhou is muddy because it carries a lot of silt. Still, a 2008 comment held that water here was far better than the 'fetid outflow that barely passes for water two hours downstream'. In recent years the endangered Chinese giant salamander has been found in and around the river at Lanzhou.

Two events show the risks. On 11 April 2014 city officials told people not to drink tap water: benzene reached 20 times the national limit of 10 micrograms per litre, and industrial chemical production was suspected, as in the Jilin chemical plant explosions of 2005. And in 2020, more than 3,000 people caught brucellosis after bacteria escaped in exhaust air from the Lanzhou Biopharmaceutical Plant, a vaccine maker, because an expired disinfectant had been used.

Earthquakes are regular in Lanzhou, but mostly weak. The huge quake of 1920 killed over 100,000 people in Ningxia and eastern Gansu, yet only 42 deaths occurred in Lanzhou, a low figure credited to the sturdy but flexible wooden construction of the time. The 2008 Sichuan earthquake was also felt in the city.

By the 2020 census Lanzhou had 4,359,446 residents, passing 4 million for the first time, and 3,042,863 of them lived in the built-up area of 1,112.9 square kilometres (429.7 square miles) in four central districts: Chengguan, Qilihe, Anning and Xigu. Lanzhou New Area, by the airport, and Honggu are not yet physically joined to the city. After a period of slow growth the rate rose quickly. Explanations include families moving for children's schooling, retired migrant workers coming home to Gansu, better city services and government policy.
As the main gateway to Gansu and the Hexi Corridor, Lanzhou is the starting point for historic sites such as the Bingling Temple Grottoes. Within the city, visit:
Five Spring Mountain Park, on the north slope of Gaolan Mountain, which has five springs and many Buddhist temples with ancient buildings.
Zhongshan Bridge, the earliest permanent bridge across the Yellow River.
Baita Mountain Park, which lies across the bridge, on high ground of 1,700 m (5,600 ft), and opened in 1958.
Lanzhou Botanical Garden, in Anning District, with a rich selection of trees, flowers and other plants.
Xiguan Mosque, among the bigger mosques of China.
Xinglong Mountain, thick with pine forest and sprinkled with brightly coloured temples.
The Lutusi ancient government site, a large group of old official buildings.

Lanzhou's museums cover history, art and science. The Gansu Provincial Museum displays finds from archaeology and fossils in Gansu, along with history exhibitions. The Lanzhou Museum is a significant Silk Road cultural site with more than 13,000 items as of October 2017, among them pottery, porcelain, bronzes, calligraphy, coins, jade and stone objects; 52 are national first-class relics, 78 second-class and 682 third-class. The Gansu Art Museum is an exhibition and exchange platform for artists. The Lanzhou City Planning Exhibition Hall explains Lanzhou's Yellow River culture through indoor displays, architectural ideas and urban features. The Lanzhou Painted Pottery Museum shows 250 pieces, 50 of them precious relics, representing the painted pottery culture of Majiayao. The Gansu Science and Technology Museum relies on sound, light, electricity and similar technology to make learning about science enjoyable.

Since 1949 Lanzhou has gone from the capital of a poor province to the centre of a significant industrial region, and it was among the first Chinese cities to industrialise, as a key location under the First and Second Five-Year Plans. In 2008 GDP per head was 25,566 RMB (US$3,681), placing it 134th out of 659 Chinese cities; by 2015 it was 57,191 RMB (US$9,182.28), and the city ranked 100th by total GDP. A UN-linked body, the International Solar Energy Center (UNIDO-ISEC), has its base in Chengguan district.

Local minerals are coal, gold, silver, zinc, nickel, manganese, clay and dolomite. Power comes from a thermal plant that burns coal from Qinghai, a hydroelectric station at Zhulama Gorge in Gansu, and a large multipurpose dam at Liujia Gorge on the Yellow River upstream of the city.

Lanzhou's main industries are textiles, rubber processing, fertiliser, refining, petrochemicals, machinery and metallurgy. Gansu has one of China's biggest refineries, and the city leads the province in petrochemicals; a pipeline brings oil from the Yumen fields, and the city makes oil-industry equipment too. Textiles are a big business, especially woollen and leather goods. Factories build locomotives and rolling stock for northwestern railways as well as machine tools and mining equipment. Large quantities of aluminium goods, industrial chemicals and fertiliser are produced, rubber is a major industry, and copper is mined nearby at Gaolan. Lanzhou has also been a centre of China's national nuclear industry since the 1960s, when its uranium enrichment plant was finished.

Farm produce and livestock from a large surrounding area are gathered and sold in Lanzhou. Crops include spring wheat, vegetables, beans, melons, peaches and tobacco, as well as oil-bearing crops, and flowers such as roses and lilies.

Zhongchuan Airport, the main airport of Lanzhou, is 70 km (43 mi) to the north and has operated for the public since 1970. More than 70 domestic and international destinations can be reached directly from it.

In August 2012 Lanzhou declared that it would build a subway, the second city in north-west China to do so. The Lanzhou Metro network is planned as six lines totalling 207 km (129 mi). Line 1 is completely underground and opened in June 2019; the first phase of Line 2 followed in June 2023. Passengers change between the lines at Wulipu and Dongfanghong Square stations.

Lanzhou's main station, on Huochezhan Dong Lu in Chengguan district, is a key rail junction for western China and ties the western provinces to the east; more than 100 passenger trains begin or pass through each day. The second main station, Lanzhou West, handles the high-speed trains. From the main station, conventional lines run in several directions:
East on the Longhai Railway, which reached Lanzhou first, in 1953, towards Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Lianyungang, with through trains on to Beijing and Shanghai.
West and north-west on the Lanxin Railway, with trains to Urumqi and the west of Gansu, and connections elsewhere in Xinjiang and to Kazakhstan.
West and south-west on the Lanqing Railway, which serves Xining and Lhasa.
South-east on the Chongqing-Lanzhou line, to Chongqing and Guangyuan.
North and north-east, to Yinchuan and Baotou.
The intercity link between the station and Zhongchuan Airport.
The Lanhe Railway to Linxia and Hezuo, still under construction.

High-speed trains that carry only passengers now run east (Xuzhou-Lanzhou line), west (Lanzhou-Xinjiang line) and north (Yinchuan-Lanzhou line), and all of them stop at Lanzhou West only. The Sichuan-Qinghai railway, with a design speed of 200 to 250 km/h (120 to 160 mph), is under construction.

Freight matters too. Lanzhou is a link on one Eurasian Land Bridge route and gives rail access to Qinghai, Xinjiang and Tibet. A large new freight terminal handles growing volumes, and the city's marshalling yard is the fourth largest in China. Scheduled freight services run to Chongqing, Hamburg, Almaty and Kathmandu.

Lanzhou's rush hour traffic ranked 4th worst among Chinese cities in 2016, but an urban ring road helped to cut that to 33rd by 2017. Major routes include the G75 Lanzhou-Haikou, G30 Lianyungang-Khorgas, G6 Beijing-Lhasa and G22 Qingdao-Lanzhou expressways, the G2201 ring expressway, and national highways 212, 213 and 312.

For coach travel there are three main stations in the city: West (Xiaoxihu), East (next to the railway station) and South (near where the G75 expressway ends). Inside the city 132 bus lines operate, with the main interchange at Xiguan. The bus rapid transit system opened in 2013 and received an honourable mention at the 2014 Sustainable Transport Awards.

NWNU is a teacher-training university with a long history and a broad set of programmes in a city that is a gateway to the north-west. Check the university's own website for current programmes and admission requirements, and check Lanzhou's current air quality before you travel.

northwest-university.h: Xi'an as a place to study

blocks.x: What a student needs to know about daily life largely comes down to the city outside the campus: its weather, how people move around and what happens there. The next sections introduce Xi'an.

Xi'an stands in the south-central area of Shaanxi Province, on the Guanzhong Plain, a flood plain formed by eight rivers and streams that run around it. To the south the city runs up to the base of the Qin Mountains on their northern side, which are called Qinling in Chinese, and to the north it follows the banks of the Wei River. About 100 kilometres (62 miles) east is Hua Shan, one of China's five sacred Taoist mountains, and not far to the north begins the Loess Plateau.

The setting has been prized for over two thousand years. At the start of the Han dynasty, the adviser Zhang Liang urged the emperor Liu Bang to make Guanzhong his capital. He described the plain as lying behind the Xiao mountain and Hangu Pass, linked to Gansu and Sichuan, a fortress stretching for thousands of miles with rich harvests, in the words of an old saying a heavenly land. As a result Guanzhong came to be called the Nation of Heaven.

Xi'an has a temperate climate under the influence of the East Asian monsoon, sitting on the border between humid subtropical and hot-summer humid continental types. In the Wei River valley, summers are hot and humid, winters cold and dry, and springs and autumns dry. Most rain arrives between July and late October. Snow falls from time to time in winter but rarely lies for long, dust storms often blow in March and April as the city warms up fast, and summer brings frequent short thunderstorms.

Monthly mean temperatures run from about freezing in January to 27.0 degrees Celsius (80.6 F) in July, and the annual mean is 14.08 degrees (57.3 F). Since 1951 the lowest reading was minus 20.6 degrees (minus 5 F) on 11 January 1955, and the highest at the current station in Jinghe was 42.3 degrees (108 F) on 15 July 2025. Another station recorded 42.9 degrees (109 F) on 17 June 2006, and an unofficial minus 25.0 degrees (minus 13 F)) was noted at a northern-suburb station in January 1930. So bring serious winter clothing and plan for hot summers.

A little-known fact about the area is that China's official time comes from near here. The Shaanxi Astronomical Observatory was founded in 1966. A 1975 geodetic report decided the country's geodetic origin should sit in central mainland China to reduce measurement bias, and Lintong, a town close to Xi'an, was selected. From 1986 onward Chinese Standard Time has been set by the National Time Service Center, an institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences that works on time and frequency. It generates and maintains the national standard time scale and broadcasts time and frequency signals. During the 1970s and 1980s it set up its own universal and atomic time scales and radio dissemination methods, meeting the needs of science and the national economy.

The Seventh National Census in 2020 recorded 12,952,907 permanent residents in Xi'an. Men made up 51.07 percent and women 48.93 percent. By age, 15.65 percent were 0 to 14, 68.33 percent were 15 to 59, 16.02 percent were over 60, and 10.9 percent were over 65. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 12.9 million in 2010, of which 5,740,000 were urban.

Many parts of the city can be explored on foot, and underpasses and overpasses have been added in busy commercial, residential and educational areas, especially around the Bell Tower shopping and entertainment district, to keep pedestrians safe. A bike-sharing network began in 2013 and now has 52,000 bikes, which more than 200,000 people use daily. Taxis are plentiful, yet many residents still commute on the city's 270 official bus routes, served by more than 7,800 buses carrying over 4 million passengers on an average day. A fast-growing subway adds more than 1.5 million rides per day. More than 2 million cars are registered in the city, so congestion is a regular urban problem.
The metro opened in stages, and the lines currently described are as follows.

Line 2 runs north to south from North Railway Station to Weiqu Nan. It was the first line open to the public (16 September 2011), with operations starting on 28 September 2011. It is 19.9 kilometres (12.4 miles) in length and has 17 stations.
Line 1 opened on 15 September 2013 and runs west to east with 19 stations between Houweizhai and Fangzhicheng.
Line 3 runs from Baoshuiqu in the north-east to Yuhuazhai in the south-west and opened on 8 November 2016.

Line 4 follows a course roughly alongside Line 2 (east of it, except in the north), starting at the north square of the North Railway Station and ending at Hangtianxincheng, and opened on 26 December 2018.
Line 5 opened on 28 December 2020 and is 41.6 kilometres long with 31 stations between Matengkong and Chuangxingang.
Line 16 opened on 27 June 2023, and is 15.03 kilometres long with 9 stations from Qinchuangyuanzhongxin to Shijingli.

Four further lines, including an extension of Line 1, are under construction. The network reaches many famous sights: Banpo Museum (Line 1, Banpo Station), the Bell and Drum Towers and the city fortifications ((Line 2) and the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda (Lines 3 and 4), Daming Palace National Heritage Park (Line 4) and the Shaanxi History Museum (Lines 2, 3 and 4). First trains leave at 6:00 on Lines 1 to 4. Last departures are at 23:00 on Lines 3 and 4, 23:30 on Line 1 and 23:50 on Line 2.

Xi'an North Railway Station, a few miles north of the centre, serves high-speed trains. It is on the Zhengzhou to Xi'an high-speed line, part of the Xuzhou to Lanzhou route, which was begun on 25 September 2005 and opened on 6 February 2010. The line made flying between the two cities uncompetitive, and all passenger flights stopped within 48 days of regular service. The station itself, started on 19 September 2008 and opened on 11 January 2011, had 34 platforms and was the largest railway station in north-western China when it opened. Trains on the Datong to Xi'an line (which links to Beijing North), the Xi'an to Chengdu line and the Yinchuan to Xi'an line call there as well.

Xi'an Railway Station sits just north of the old walled city and serves as the main conventional-rail hub in Shaanxi. It covers 597,000 square metres (6,430,000 square feet), with six passenger platforms and 11 passenger tracks, and handles 112 services and about 80,000 people daily. Direct trains run to Beijing, Zhengzhou, Lanzhou, Baoji and Mount Hua. Two large stations, Xi'an East and Xi'an South, are being built for new high-speed lines such as Xi'an to Chongqing and Wuhan to Xi'an. The city's other stations are Xi'an West, Yinzhen, Sanmincun and Fangzhicheng.

Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (code XIY) is the main airport and the largest in north-western China. It lies 25 miles north-west of central Xi'an and 8 miles north-east of Xianyang. The chief carriers are China Eastern, Hainan Airlines and China Southern. Terminal 3 and a second runway opened on 3 May 2012, and Terminal 5, started in 2022, was completed in September 2024. As well as most Chinese cities, the airport has flights to several big overseas cities, among them Tokyo, Seoul, London, Paris and Sydney.

Under China's Western Development policy, Xi'an was made a priority for accelerated development, with emphasis on IT, advanced materials, aerospace, energy and chemical engineering. Between 1997 and 2006 the output of the city's modern service industry grew by an average of 13 percent a year, compared with 0.74 percent for traditional services, taking it from 8.113 billion to 25.85 billion US dollars. In 2020 the research network known as Globalization and World Cities ranked Xi'an as a Beta minus city, meaning global second tier, and the Global Financial Centres Index put it among the world's top 100 financial centres.

Important sectors are equipment manufacturing, tourism and service outsourcing. Manufacturing produced 36.5 billion yuan, 44.5 percent of the city's total. Xi'an is also one of China's four ancient capitals, so, Xi'an draws visitors to the Terracotta Army, the city wall and Famen Temple. In 2019 tourists exceeded 300 million and earned 314.6 billion yuan, revenue grew on average by 36.4 percent a year, and foreign exchange earnings of 530 million in 2009 were growing at about 35.8 percent a year.

Xi'an was among the first Chinese cities to build a service-outsourcing sector, with over 800 companies and an output above 23 billion yuan in 2008. Jobs in the sector doubled between 1997 and 2006, from 60,000 initially, and computer consulting jobs doubled from 16,000 to 32,000 jobs. Because software outsourcing is so important, a Software New Town was planned for completion by 2015 with 30 billion yuan of investment. Other major exports are lighting equipment and car parts, major imports are mechanical and electrical goods, and the largest trading partner is the United States.

Industry is concentrated in Xi'an's Economic and Technological Development Zone. The city is a pioneer of China's software industry, and the Xi'an Software Park inside the Xi'an Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone had attracted over 1,085 companies and 106,000 employees by 2012. One account describes a large pool of inexpensive talent from some 100 local universities, producing about 3,000 computer graduates a year, paid roughly 120 US dollars a month, half the wage for the same job in Beijing. That figure is dated, so treat it as historical rather than current.

Xi'an's International Trade and Logistics Park spans roughly 35 square miles and was conceived as a model of logistics-based urban growth. It functions as a large dry port and rail container centre, and more China-Europe freight trains leave from, or come back to, Xi'an than to any other city.

The city teamed up with China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation in November 2006 to create an industrial base in Xi'an for aerospace science and technology. It focuses on the civil space industry: manufacturing of equipment, software and outsourced services, new materials and solar photovoltaic power. Beyond its core area it was meant to cover Xi'an and the Guanzhong region and then extend into the north-west and south-west. The target was total output of 2.8 billion US dollars by 2012, with 10 to 20 brand products with their own intellectual property and five to eight with global competitiveness.

After an initial aerospace centre was launched in Shanghai in 2008, China began building another civil aerospace centre in Shaanxi. On 26 December 2007 the State Development and Reform Commission signed off the plan for a national civil aerospace industrial base at Xi'an. Covering 23 square kilometres (8.9 square miles), it concentrates on satellites, new materials, energy, IT and other civil applications.
Xi'an once had well-known professional teams, but each has since relocated and renamed itself.
In the Chinese Jia-A League, Shaanxi National Power relocated to Ningbo, taking the name Ningbo National Power in 2004.
In the Chinese Football Association Super League, Shaanxi Baorong Chanba relocated to Guiyang, taking the name Guizhou Renhe in 2012.
In the Chinese Basketball Association, Shaanxi Dongsheng relocated to Foshan, becoming the Foshan Dralions in 2010.
A university's province matters as much to student life as its campus, so the following sections turn to Shaanxi.

northwest-university.h: One of the cradles of Chinese civilisation

blocks.x: Thirteen feudal dynasties placed their capitals in Shaanxi over over 1,100 years, from the Zhou to the Tang. Xi'an, the present capital, is one of China's four great ancient capitals and the eastern end of the Silk Road, which continues onward to Europe, Arabia and Africa. After the Qin dynasty collapsed, the area was briefly ruled as the Three Qins, and that is the source of one of the province's two abbreviations, Qin (秦), the other being Shaan (陝). Liu Bang later took it during the Chu-Han contest. Under the Han, the Northern Silk Road was extended for exploration and military aims. The northernmost of the Silk Roads, about 2,600 kilometres (1,600 miles) long, it linked Xi'an westward across the Wushao Ling Pass to Wuwei, and on to Kashgar, then to ancient Parthia.

Later chapters include the Xiongnu-led Northern Xia (407 to 431), which placed its capital at Tongwancheng, and a border dispute between the Northern Song and the Tangut-led Western Xia, in which Western Xia founded the Luowucheng frontier fort in 1071 and Song captured it in 1081. Under the Ming, the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission was set up in 1376, with authority that also included modern Gansu, Ningxia and part of Qinghai, and the majority of visitors from Central and West Asia came in China through Shaanxi.

On 23 January 1556 one of history's deadliest earthquakes struck near Hua Shan in south-eastern Shaanxi, killing an estimated 100,000 people, while emigration and famine reduced the regional population by about 830,000. The collapse of the short-lived Jiangxi Soviet set off the Long March, which carried the Communists under Mao Zedong to the Shaanxi Soviet at Yan'an.

Administratively, the Northern Song created the Shaanxi Lu circuit, governed from today's Xi'an, in 997, and the Yuan set up Shaanxi Province governed by a Branch Secretariat in 1286. Once the Qing took power, Gansu was separated from Shaanxi, yet the two provinces remained under the Viceroy of Shaan-Gan.

Prehistory is represented by the Lantian Man site in Lantian County, north-western Shaanxi near Xi'an, where hominin fossils about one million years old were found. Scientists treat Lantian Man as a Homo erectus subspecies, and the fossils are shown at the Shaanxi History Museum in Xi'an.

The province includes the Ordos Desert in the far north on the Inner Mongolia border, the Loess Plateau in the centre, the Qin Mountains running east to west through the south-central area, and a subtropical zone south of the Qinling. Between the plateau and the mountains sits the Wei River Valley (Guanzhong), one of the cradles of early Chinese civilisation. Going clockwise, Shaanxi touches Shanxi (east and north-east), Henan (east), Hubei (south-east), Chongqing (south), Sichuan (south-west), Gansu (west), Ningxia (north-west) and Inner Mongolia (north), tying with Inner Mongolia for the largest number of provincial-level neighbours.

Because the province spans a wide range of latitude, climates vary. The north, including the Loess Plateau, is cold arid or cold semi-arid, where winters are cold and very dry, spring and autumn are dry, and summer is hot and humid. Guanzhong is mostly semi-arid, with a few humid subtropical pockets, winters that are cool to cold and hot, humid summers with early heatwaves. The south is much more humid and subtropical, with milder winters and long summers that are hot and humid. Annual means are roughly 8 to 16 degrees Celsius (46 to 61 F), January averages range from minus 11 to 3.5 degrees (12.2 to 38.3 F), while July runs from 21 to 28 degrees (70 to 82 F). Other cities beyond Xi'an include Ankang, Yan'an, Xianyang, Tongchuan, Lintong, Hanzhong and Baoji.

By the middle of the 1800s the province was selling animal hides, wine, spirits and musk, and its merchants were active in moneylending, including in Guangzhou. It imported European skins, watches, Chinese books and cloth. During the Third Front campaign it received substantial investment in industrial capacity.

Fossil fuels and high technology are today the two biggest industries. In 2009 the province was third in the country for output of coal, natural gas and crude oil. With some of western China's leading universities and research institutes, it has a major role in aircraft and aerospace, producing over half of the research and manufacturing equipment used by the country's home commercial aircraft sector. Nominal GDP in 2011 was 1,239 billion yuan (196.7 billion US dollars) and per-person GDP was 21,729 yuan (3,179 dollars), 17th in China. In the first half of 2019 total output reached 1,162.557 billion yuan, up 5.4 percent: primary industry added 55.319 billion yuan (up 4.5 percent), secondary 557.935 billion (up 4.2 percent) and tertiary 549.303 billion (up 6.8 percent).

Baoji Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone was set up in 1992 and approved by the State Council as a national high-tech zone, with a long-term planned area of 40 square kilometres. It is near Xi'an Xianyang Airport and National Highway 310, and hosts auto parts, electronics, IT, pharmaceuticals, bioengineering and new materials.

The Shaanxi Xi'an Export Processing Zone was approved by the State Council on 21 June 2002 and began operating on 5 April 2004. It was the north-west's first state-level export processing zone and one of seven pioneer zones in China with bonded logistics. It is run by the Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone's administrative committee, acting as a special economic zone. More than 40 domestic and foreign firms have settled there, and the key industries are aviation, machinery, electronics and new energy.
Shaanxi's cultural identity includes the following.
Shaanxi cuisine
Qinqiang, the representative folk opera of the province
Shaanxi shadow play
Xintianyou, a local folk song tradition
The culture and religion of Xi'an itself add to this, and are a good reason to explore the city beyond the classroom.

northwest-university.h: Reading this profile as an applicant

blocks.x: The facts that matter most to a newcomer are these: Xi'an is large, with nearly thirteen million permanent residents; it has a growing metro, two major railway stations and a big international airport; and it is a centre of aerospace, software and tourism industries as well as one of China's four ancient capitals.

Seasonally, expect hot, humid summers, cold dry winters, dust storms in March and April, and most of the rain between July and late October. If you are comparing universities in different cities, those conditions and the scale of the city may weigh as heavily as any single course on your shortlist. Check the university's own international admissions pages for programme lists, tuition, accommodation and visa guidance before you apply.
Northwest University lists 165 programs for international students on this site: 63 bachelor, 62 master's, 40 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 148 taught in Chinese, 17 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 22,500 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 80,000 (median CNY 21,600), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 37,500 (median CNY 32,500), according to the university's published fee table.

165 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (17):
Area Studies
Biology
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Chemistry
Computer Science and Technology
Cultural Relics Conservation Technology
Ecology
Geography

Geology

The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

northwest-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Northwest University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Xi'an, register at Northwest University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: Northwestern Polytechnical University at a glance

blocks.x: Northwestern Polytechnical University, known as NWPU or NPU (西北工业大学), is a public university for science and engineering based in Xi'an, in China's Shaanxi Province. Its supervising body is the industry and information technology ministry, and the university has been admitted to three national programmes for leading institutions, namely the Double First-Class Construction plan and Projects 985 and 211. Its reputation rests above all on aeronautics, astronautics and marine engineering, which are the fields the university was merged together to serve.
This profile explains where the university came from, how its three campuses differ, what it teaches and how it ranks, who its alumni are, and then what Xi'an is like as a place to live and study.
NWPU was formed from three earlier institutions, each created in response to a different national emergency or need.

northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: Wartime engineering schools in the north-west

blocks.x: In 1938, with Japan invading China, numerous eastern universities fled the occupied zone for the interior, then called "Free China". Four engineering colleges ended up in Shaanxi: the engineering faculties of Beiping University and of National Northeastern University, the National Beiyang Engineering Institute, and a private school, Jiaozuo Engineering Institute. Together they became the National Northwestern Engineering Institute. It was based at Hanzhong, a city ringed by mountains. After Japan's surrender, the institute moved in 1946 to Xianyang.

northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: The aeronautics institute from the east

blocks.x: In 1952 China wanted its aeronautics research brought together in one place. Aeronautical engineering departments from the former National Central University (later Nanjing University), from Jiaotong University and from Zhejiang University were moved to Nanjing and combined as the East China Aeronautics Institute. In 1956 it moved to Xi'an and took the name Xi'an Aeronautics Institute, which became the second of NWPU's forerunners.

In 1957 the two institutes just described, Northwestern Engineering and Xi'an Aeronautics, were combined, and NPU was the result. From the start the new university focused its research on defence technology in aeronautics, astronautics and marine engineering.

northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: The military engineering institute from Harbin

blocks.x: The third forerunner arrived in 1970. Relations with the Soviet Union had worsened, and the Harbin-based military engineering institute of the People's Liberation Army, close to the Sino-Soviet frontier, was dismantled and its departments dispersed. Its Department of Aeronautical Engineering moved to Xi'an and joined the two existing parts of NPU.

The university is under sanctions from the United States and Taiwan because of its links with the PLA. In 2022 Chinese official bodies and commercial cybersecurity companies blamed a cyberattack on NWPU to the US National Security Agency. Applicants should know this background, since NWPU's defence connections shape how it is viewed abroad.

In total NPU's campuses cover about 4.58 square kilometres. The Youyi Campus in Beilin District, Xi'an, takes up about 0.8 km2, the Chang'an Campus in Chang'an District, Xi'an, about 2.6 km2; the third, Taicang in Suzhou, Jiangsu, measures roughly 1.18 km2.

People call Youyi the old campus. West Youyi Road and South Laodong Road divide it into south, west and north parts. It holds teaching facilities, housing for staff and students, stadiums, support facilities and a kindergarten, plus the primary and middle schools that are affiliated with NPU.

Chang'an is called the new campus and is split into east and west halves by Dongxiang Road. It has many new administrative and teaching buildings, laboratories and sports facilities, and it is the main base for NPU's undergraduate education. In other words, a first-year undergraduate should expect to be here.

The Taicang Campus sits on the border between Suzhou and Shanghai. It was under construction, with operations due to start in September 2021. It will have 10 schools, among them the School of Artificial Intelligence, the School of Flexible Electronics and the School of Business, with room for around 10,000 students.

Construction continues at both Xi'an campuses. The central government has invested 1.58 billion CNY, about US$252.8 million, in NPU's infrastructure, with the help of the industry ministry mentioned above and the earlier national defence science and technology commission. More than 20 projects were under way at the same time. Youyi's share includes rebuilding old and unsafe apartments after the earthquake, and a first new student apartment block. Chang'an's includes a new library, a high-tech experimental research centre, two infrastructure plans (I and II), and buildings for materials science and for innovation, science and technology.

NPU has strong research capacity in engineering. The State Council named it a National Key University in 1960. During the seventh and eighth Five-Year Plans it was among 15 National Key Developing Universities, it joined Project 211 in the ninth plan and Project 985 in the tenth. Since it was founded it has trained more than 150,000 senior technicians and researchers for China's defence industry and wider economy. NPU produced the first PhD graduates in China in six disciplines. Its former students include 30 PLA generals, six winners of the national TOP 10 Outstanding Youth Elite honour, and over 30 fellows of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) or the Chinese Academy of Engineering (CAE).
NPU is listed as one of China's "Seven Sons of National Defence", and is also a member of the SAP University Alliances.

For 2026, NWPU falls inside the top 200 in two global tables, ARWU (Academic Ranking of World Universities) and in U.S. News & World Report's Best Global Universities. Within China, Shanghai Ruanke's Best Chinese Universities Ranking put it 25th in 2022, and among engineering universities it came tenth. Some of its subjects were also graded in the Ministry of Education's third round of discipline evaluations.

The university hosts seven State Key Laboratories and, below them, 28 key laboratories run at provincial or ministerial level. Such laboratories focus on particular research areas and are government funded. The State Key Laboratories cover these areas:
Materials science
Chemistry
Mathematics and physics
Geography
Biotechnology
Information technology
Engineering
Medicine

The Education Experimental School, also called the Honors College, has special standing in NPU. It began as the Education Reform Class of 1985 and became a school in its own right in 2001. The idea is that the university's strongest students get its best resources and become leaders in their fields later.

The structure is 15 academic schools, the Honors College, an independent school, a joint school and several administrative schools. It offers 58 undergraduate programmes, 117 master's programmes, 67 doctoral programmes and 14 postdoctoral programmes. Nationally recognised strengths include 2 first-level and 7 second-level National Key Disciplines, plus 2 National Key (to cultivate) Disciplines, and the university can award doctorates in 21 first-level disciplines and master's degrees in 31. Research infrastructure adds the 7 State Key Laboratories, 28 key laboratories at provincial or ministerial level, and 19 engineering research centres at that level.

The alumni list mixes senior public officials, academics and entrepreneurs.

Two faculty members are singled out. Hu Peiquan founded both the engineering mechanics department and the university's journal. Chuah Hean Teik advises the university as a consultant professor; he previously served as president and chief executive of Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman.

northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: Xi'an: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life for an NWPU student depends on Xi'an itself, so the following sections cover the city's setting, weather, population, transport, economy and sport.

Xi'an occupies a flood plain, built up by eight rivers and streams, in the Guanzhong Plain of central-southern Shaanxi. The Qin Mountains (Qinling) rise at the city's southern edge, and the Wei River runs along its north. To the east, some 100 km (62 mi) away, is Hua Shan, among the five sacred Taoist mountains, and the Loess Plateau lies not far to the north.

At the start of the Han dynasty, the strategist Zhang Liang urged Emperor Liu Bang to make Guanzhong his capital. His argument, in the original (关中左崤函，右陇蜀，沃野千里，此所谓金城千里，天府之国也), was that the plain sits behind Mount Xiao and Hangu Pass, links Gansu and Sichuan, forms an iron citadel that stretches for a thousand miles and yields rich harvests like a heavenly kingdom. Since then Guanzhong has been known as the "Nation of the Heaven".

Xi'an has a temperate climate shaped by the East Asian monsoon, and under the Köppen system it sits on the line between humid subtropical and hot-summer humid continental (Cwa/Dwa). In the Wei River valley, summers are hot and humid, winters cold and dry, and spring and autumn dry. Most rain falls from July to late October. Snow falls from time to time in winter but seldom lies for long. Dust storms are common in March and April as the city heats up fast, and summer brings frequent short thunderstorms.

The annual mean is 14.08 °C (57.3 °F); across the months, the daily average climbs from roughly freezing in January to a July figure of 27.0 °C (80.6 °F). Since 1951 the coldest reading was -20.6 °C (-5 °F) on 11 January 1955, and the warmest at the current station in Jinghe was 42.3 °C (108 °F) on 15 July 2025. Another station recorded a higher 42.9 °C (109 °F) on 17 June 2006, and an unofficial low of -25.0 °C (-13 °F) was noted at a station in the northern suburbs in January 1930.

Near Xi'an is the institution that sets the time for the whole country. The Shaanxi Astronomical Observatory was founded in 1966. A 1975 national geodetic report called for the origin point to lie in central mainland China, which would keep measurement bias to a minimum, and the town of Lintong (临潼), near Xi'an, was selected. Since 1986 Chinese Standard Time has been set from here. The National Time Service Center (NTSC), part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, works mainly on time and frequency: it produces and maintains the national standard time scale and broadcasts time and frequency signals. During the 1970s and 1980s it set up independent universal-time and atomic-time scales and ways of distributing them by low- and high-frequency radio, which together meet the needs of science and the national economy.

The Seventh National Census in 2020 counted a registered (hukou) population of 12,952,907 in the city. Men were 51.07% and women 48.93%. By age, 15.65% were 0 to 14, 68.33% were 15 to 59, 16.02% were over 60, and 10.9% were over 65. For the wider metropolitan area, the OECD estimated a 2010 population of 12.9 million, of whom 5,740,000 lived in urban parts.

Many parts of Xi'an are easy to get around on foot. Underpasses and overpasses have been built in busy commercial, residential and educational areas, above all around the Bell Tower shopping and entertainment districts, so that pedestrians can cross safely and conveniently.

Bike sharing arrived in 2013; today 52,000 shared bikes are in service, ridden by more than 200,000 people every day. There are plenty of taxis, yet many residents still travel to work on the 270 official municipal bus routes. Those routes use more than 7,800 buses, and total daily bus ridership averages above 4 million, and the fast-growing subway adds more than 1.5 million commuters daily. The city has more than 2 million registered cars, so traffic jams are a familiar problem.

Line 2 runs north to south from the North Railway Station to Weiqu Nan. It was the first line open to the public, on 16 September 2011, with operations starting on 28 September 2011. It is 19.9 kilometres (12.4 miles) long and has 17 stations.
Line 1 opened on 15 September 2013 and runs west to east between Houweizhai and Fangzhicheng, with 19 stations.
Line 3 goes from Baoshuiqu in the northeast to Yuhuazhai in the southwest and opened on 8 November 2016.

Line 4 opened on 26 December 2018. For most of its length it lies just east of Line 2, and it connects Hangtianxincheng in the south with the North Railway Station's north square (Beikezhan, Beiguangchang).
Line 5 began service on 28 December 2020. Its 41.6 kilometres and 31 stations link Matengkong with Chuangxingang.
Line 16 opened on 27 June 2023. It is 15.03 kilometres long with 9 stations, from Qinchuangyuanzhongxin to Shijingli.
Four more lines were under construction, one of them an extension of Line 1.

The metro serves many of the best-known sights: Banpo Museum (Banpo Station, Line 1), the Bell and Drum Tower and the Fortifications of Xi'an (both Line 2), the Shaanxi History Museum (Lines 2, 3 and 4), Line 4's Daminggong National Heritage Park and the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, which is on Lines 3 and 4.

For timetables, the first trains on Lines 1, 2, 3 and 4 leave at 6:00. The last departure is 23:00 on Lines 3 and 4, 23:30 on Line 1 and 23:50 on Line 2. On 30 December 2008 a fire at one station was put out within an hour with all workers evacuated safely, and 66 hours later, on 2 January, another fire broke out at a different Line 2 station.

Xi'an North railway station lies a few miles north of the centre and handles the high-speed trains of the Zhengzhou-Xi'an High-Speed Railway, which is part of the Xuzhou-Lanzhou high-speed railway. Work on that line began on 25 September 2005 and it opened on 6 February 2010; flying between Zhengzhou and Xi'an could not compete, and within 48 days of regular high-speed service starting every passenger flight linking the pair of cities had been cancelled. The station itself, with 34 platforms, was the largest in Northwest China when it opened on 11 January 2011, after construction began on 19 September 2008. Other high-speed lines using it are Xi'an-Chengdu and Yinchuan-Xi'an, along with the Datong-Xi'an line, which gives a connection to Beijing North.

Xi'an railway station, just north of the walled city, is the main hub for conventional trains in Shaanxi. The site covers 597,000 square metres (6,430,000 square feet), with 11 passenger tracks and 6 platforms, and 112 services carry 80,000 people daily. Destinations on direct trains include Lanzhou, Baoji, Mount Hua, Beijing and Zhengzhou. Two large stations, Xi'an East and Xi'an South, were being built for new high-speed lines such as Xi'an-Chongqing and Wuhan-Xi'an. Other city stations are Xi'an West, Yinzhen, Sanmincun and Fangzhicheng.

Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (XIY) is the city's main airport and the biggest in north-western China. It lies 25 miles northwest of central Xi'an and 8 miles northeast of central Xianyang. Hainan Airlines, China Southern and China Eastern are the chief carriers. Terminal 3 and the second runway opened on 3 May 2012, and Terminal 5, started in 2022, was finished in September 2024. Besides most Chinese cities, it flies to international destinations that include Tokyo, Seoul, London, Paris and Sydney.

The national strategy for developing the west picked out Xi'an for faster growth, especially in IT, aerospace, advanced materials, energy and chemical engineering. Between 1997 and 2006, output value in its service industry grew at an average of 13 percent a year, against 0.74 percent for traditional services, a climb from US$8.113 billion up to US$25.85 billion. Then in 2020 a world-cities research network (GaWC) called Xi'an a Beta- city, meaning global second tier, and the same year the Global Financial Centres Index ranked it within the world's best 100 financial centres.

Key industries are equipment manufacturing, tourism and service outsourcing. Manufacturing brings in RMB 36.5 billion annually, which is 44.5 percent of the total for the city. Xi'an is one of China's four ancient capitals, and sites like the Terracotta Army, the City Wall and the Famen Temple make tourism important as well: in 2019 over 300 million visitors came, spending RMB 314.6 billion in total. Revenue grows on average 36.4 percent a year; foreign-exchange earnings, at 530 million in 2009, grow about 35.8 percent a year.

It was one of the first service-outsourcing cities in China, with over 800 companies, and in 2008 the sector's output went beyond RMB 23 billion. Between 1997 and 2006 its workforce doubled from a base of 60,000, while jobs in computer consulting rose from 16,000 to 32,000. Because software outsourcing matters so much, the city planned a Software New Town with 30 billion RMB of investment, due for completion in 2015. Lighting equipment and car parts are major exports, mechanical and electrical products are the main imports, and the largest trading partner is the United States.

Thirty-five square miles or so are taken up by Xi'an's international trade and logistics park, planned as a pattern for urban growth built on logistics. As a dry port and rail container hub it is important, and more China-Europe Freight Train services start or end in Xi'an than in any other city.

The main industrial area is an economic and technological development zone. The Jiangcungou site, which had been China's biggest landfill, shut in 2019. Xi'an was early to build a software industry, and by 2012 its Software Park, inside the Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone (XDZ), had drawn over 1,085 companies and 106,000 employees by 2012. One description says the city draws on a large and inexpensive talent pool from the roughly 100 universities in the area, producing around 3,000 computer graduates a year, each earning about $120 a month, half the pay for comparable work in Beijing.

The city teamed up in November 2006 with the national aerospace science and technology corporation to found an aerospace science and technology industrial base, concentrating on the civil space industry: equipment manufacturing, software and outsourcing, new materials and solar photovoltaics. The core area was to be extended to Xi'an and Guanzhong, and an expansion zone to reach other parts of the north-west and south-west. The target was total output of US$2.8 billion by 2012, with 10 to 20 brand products with their own intellectual property and 5 to 8 with global competitiveness.

Following the first aerospace centre in Shanghai in 2008, China began building a second civil aerospace centre in Shaanxi. Planning for a National Civil Aerospace Industrial Base in Xi'an received the go-ahead from the State Development and Reform Commission on 26 December 2007. Spread over 23 km2 (8.9 sq mi), it will specialise in satellites, new materials, energy, IT and other civil technologies. For a student of aeronautics or astronautics at NWPU, this local industry is a real advantage.
Xi'an has hosted professional teams that later moved elsewhere:
Jia-A League football: Shaanxi National Power, which relocated to Ningbo in 2004 and was renamed Ningbo National Power
Chinese Super League football: Shaanxi Baorong Chanba, relocated to Guiyang in 2012 and renamed Guizhou Renhe
Basketball (CBA): Shaanxi Dongsheng, which moved to Foshan in 2010 and became the Foshan Dralions

northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: What this means for an applicant

blocks.x: Taken together, the facts point to a university that is strongest where engineering meets national defence and aerospace, with its undergraduate teaching centred on the Chang'an Campus and a growing presence in the Yangtze delta through Taicang. The city beyond the gate is large and well connected, with a growing metro, high-speed rail, an international airport, and a local economy in which aerospace, software and tourism all play a part. Students should check which campus their programme is based on, since the three sites are in different cities.
Northwestern Polytechnical University lists 151 programs for international students on this site: 14 bachelor, 44 master's, 31 doctoral, 62 non-degree programs.
