northwestern-polytechnical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Northwestern Polytechnical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Xi'an, register at Northwestern Polytechnical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

ocean-university-of-china.h: A marine university with a century behind it

blocks.x: Ocean University of China, often shortened to OUC and known in Chinese as Zhongguo Haiyang Daxue (中国海洋大学), is a state-funded institution based in Qingdao, a port city on the Shandong coast. It reports to the Ministry of Education and belongs to the national schemes that pick out leading Chinese universities: the 211 and 985 programmes, plus the Double First-Class Construction initiative. Students and staff commonly call it "Haida", a short form you will hear constantly on campus.

Although it teaches a wide spread of natural sciences, social sciences and engineering, its reputation rests above all on marine science and fishery science. If you are interested in oceans, coasts, aquatic biology or related fields, this is one of the first names in China that comes up. The university marked its hundredth anniversary on 25 October 2024 with a large celebration.

ocean-university-of-china.h: From a private college to a national ocean university

blocks.x: The story starts in 1924, when the institution opened as Private Qingdao University (私立青岛大学) on the grounds of the old German Bismarck Barracks. Wealthy donors paid for most of it. The early years were unsettled because the country was torn by internal conflict, and the college was folded into Shandong University under a regional warlord administration. When that administration fell in August 1928, Shandong University stopped operating for a while. In 1930 it came back as Shandong University's Qingdao arm (国立山东大学(青岛)), teaching literature and science through two colleges.

Growth followed. By 1936 there were 411 students. In 1937, with a Japanese occupation looming, staff and students left for Sichuan and were absorbed by other schools there. After the Second World War the Qingdao division resumed as a branch of Shandong University, expanded to five colleges and counted 2,366 students by 1951. Later in that decade its medical courses and hospitals were detached to form the Qingdao Medical School, which later became part of Qingdao University.

The decisive reshaping came in 1959, and it explains why the university is now so ocean-focused. Marine science departments from several universities, among them Fudan University and Xiamen University, were relocated to Qingdao. The college left Shandong University's supervision and came directly under the Ministry of Education as the Shandong College of Oceanography (山东海洋学院). In October 1960 it was named one of the National Key Universities, a status that meant generous backing. The next renaming came in January 1988, to Ocean University of Qingdao (青岛海洋大学); to mark it, Deng Xiaoping personally wrote the new name in his own calligraphy. Since October 2002 it has carried its present name, Ocean University of China.

ocean-university-of-china.h: Campuses and where you will live and study

blocks.x: OUC has more than one campus, and the oldest is the most photogenic. Yushan Campus (鱼山校区) occupies the former Bismarck Barracks on a hill overlooking the sea, in the old German-concession area of Shinan District. Its German-style buildings date from the early 1920s and are widely regarded as beautiful, which makes this a memorable place to start a degree. The neighbourhood around it is a favourite with visitors, with several churches and the Zhan Qiao pier close by.

Fushan campus, beside Qingdao University, is much the smallest section. Most departments now sit on the newest campus in Laoshan District, which opened in autumn 2006. Across all sites the university covers more than 733,000 square metres of land, with about 230,000 square metres of floor space. When you apply, ask the admissions office which campus your college and programme use, because they are quite different in setting and in distance from the old city centre.

Since 1994 the university has had dual oversight, shared between the State Education Commission and Shandong's provincial government. It joined Project 211 in June 1997 and is one of the 39 universities in Project 985.

OUC was among the first institutions that the State Council's Academic Degree Committee authorised to award doctoral, master's and bachelor's degrees, and it can confer every academic title, including professorships and doctoral supervision. The figures reported for its current offer are 69 undergraduate programmes spread across 22 colleges and departments, 13 first-level and 80 second-level doctoral programmes, 34 first-level and 192 second-level master's programmes, and 12 post-doctoral research stations. Counts like these shift as programmes are added or merged, so use the university's own admissions pages for the latest list.

The research base is substantial. Two national key disciplines (covering ten sub-disciplines) and 20 key disciplines designated by the province anchor its academic profile. Research laboratories include seven attached to the Ministry of Education, nine to Shandong Province and four to Qingdao Municipality, plus three Ministry of Education engineering research centres and two provincial ones. A national marine science and technology laboratory in Qingdao, led by OUC with an estimated investment of one billion yuan, was described as under construction. The university also runs a national base for training talent in basic research and teaching in oceanology and marine chemistry.

Reported enrolment is about 39,500 students, of whom more than 8500 are doctoral and master's students and around 900 are international students. The staff number about 2,800, more than half of them professors or lecturers, among them three Chinese Academy of Sciences academicians, five from the Chinese Academy of Engineering and over 250 doctoral supervisors. A hundred and five professors receive special State Council allowances, and nine have been honoured as young or middle-aged experts with outstanding contributions to the state. The well-known modern writer Wang Meng is a professor at OUC and honorary dean of its College of Literature, Journalism and Communication. These numbers come from different years and are best treated as approximate; the university's own website has the current counts of students, international students and staff.

The university describes its aims as pushing reform in teaching, staying focused on its specialist strengths and meeting social and economic needs. Its guiding school motto, "Unity, Diligence, Practicality and Creativity", is meant to shape a distinctive study culture.

Practical marine work is helped by its own research vessel, the Dongfanghong 2 (东方红2号), a 3500-ton ship about 96 metres long and 15 metres wide that is counted among the most advanced research ships in China. Its multi-subject surveys span geophysics, geology, biology, chemistry, physics, meteorology and hydrology, and students also join voyages for practical fieldwork.

On land there are dozens of laboratories, an audio-visual education centre, a computer centre and an analysis and testing centre. The library holds more than 1.9 million printed books, about 1.1 million e-books and over 30,000 Chinese and foreign journals. The university publishes the Journal of Ocean University of China in natural science and social science editions, and its campus network has over 3,000 user terminals linked to CERNET, China's education and research network.

OUC is described as the source of a very large share of China's marine science research and publication. It also advises on practical coastal development in Shandong, for example on port construction at Rizhao and Dongying. It runs 27 research institutions. Particularly productive ones include a UNESCO-linked Chinese centre for marine biotechnology, a national marine science research centre in Qingdao and a marine development studies centre. Not everything is about the sea: some centres study humanities topics, such as the German Studies Center.

OUC has exchange and cooperation links with more than 140 universities and research bodies in over 20 countries or regions, and 105 of them have signed formal cooperation agreements. Each year the university holds international gatherings on marine science and other subjects, and joint education arrangements have produced programmes such as the Sino-German Initiative in Marine Sciences master's.

A Sino-Australian research centre devoted to coastal management (SARCCM), with a multidisciplinary focus, is hosted by UNSW Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy. OUC also takes an active part in the University of the Arctic, a cooperative network centred on the circumpolar north that brings together over 200 universities, colleges and other bodies interested in Arctic education and research.

Rankings change every year, but for reference the Academic Ranking of World Universities placed OUC in the 301-400 band globally and 56th in China in 2025, and the QS rankings listed it 297th in Asia that year. Check the latest tables before drawing conclusions, since methods and results vary.
Much of daily student life depends on the city, so the sections below explain Qingdao in practical terms: where it is, what the weather does, how people earn a living and how you get around.

Qingdao sits on the southern shore of the Shandong Peninsula (Schantung-Halbinsel in German). On the northeast it borders Yantai, on the west Weifang and on the southwest Rizhao, three other prefecture-level cities. Its territory covers 10,654 square kilometres (4,114 square miles), stretching from about 35°35' to 37°09' north and 119°30' to 121°00' east. The built-up parts are fairly flat, but mountains rise within the city limits and nearby, and the highest point reaches 1,133 metres (3,717 ft) above sea level. By land type, 15.5 percent is highland, with foothills 25.1 percent, plains 37.8 percent and low-lying areas 21.7 percent. The coastline is 730.64 kilometres (454.00 miles) long, and five significant rivers, each longer than 50 kilometres (31 miles), flow through the region.

In terms of seasons, Qingdao has a four-season, monsoon-influenced temperate climate that falls in the zone between the Köppen Cwa type (subtropical) and the Dwa type (continental), both humid. The sea moderates almost everything, so maritime features are strong too, shaped by the southeast monsoon and by ocean currents and water masses.

Winter runs from cool to cold, with wind but little rain, and January averages 0.2 °C (32.4 °F). Summers are hot and humid, yet very hot days are uncommon, and August averages 25.6 °C (78.1 °F). Being on a peninsula by the sea, spring arrives about a month later than in most inland parts of China, and the yearly gap between day and night temperatures is a mere 6.3 °C (11.3 °F). Autumn, by contrast, is milder than inland Shandong. Sea temperature reaches its high of about 25 °C (77 °F) around late August, so swimming is possible for roughly two months either side of that. Over a whole year the mean comes to 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Records since 1951 run from -15.9 °C (3 °F), logged on 7-8 January 2021, up to 38.9 °C (102 °F) on 15 July 2002. Colder unofficial readings exist too: -16.9 °C (1.6 °F), and -16.4 °C (2.5 °F) at the official station on 10 January 1931. For planning, pack for cool, windy winters and mild, humid summers. Sunshine, measured as a share of the hours it could possibly shine, ranges from 38 percent of possible hours in July to 59 percent in October, adding up to about 2,261 hours a year.

One summer nuisance deserves a mention. Beaches can be hit by heavy algal blooms; as the algae rot they release hydrogen sulfide with a strong rotten-egg smell. Sea lettuce blooms, partly linked to the farming of seaweed in Jiangsu Province, prompted officials in 2013 to announce a large-scale algae disaster.

About 10 million people live in Qingdao, of whom roughly 6.2 million are in the urban area and an estimated 5 million in other cities under Qingdao's administration. The reported annual birth rate is about 10.15 per thousand (around 76,507 births) and the death rate 6.32 per thousand. The 2021 yearbook put the permanent population in 2020 at 10.1057 million, up 182,700 on the year before. Compared with other big Chinese cities, living standards here rank near the top, helped by a strong export economy and comparatively high family incomes.

Qingdao also has a large Korean community. Around 2009 an estimated 100,000 Koreans worked, studied and lived here, second in China only to Beijing at about 200,000. For an international student, that means Korean food, shops and services are easy to find.

Shandong is a major economic region of eastern China, and much of its recent growth has been concentrated in Qingdao. Reported figures show how quickly the city developed: per-capita GDP was CN¥52,895 (about US$7,616) in 2008 and CN¥161,200 (about US$23,000) in 2024. Total GDP reached CN¥1200.15 billion in 2018, though it dipped slightly in 2019. In 2006 the World Bank named Qingdao one of six "golden cities", from among 120 Chinese cities that were assessed for investment climate and government effectiveness. Some early-2000s GDP numbers quoted for the city are inconsistent, so rely on current official statistics for exact comparisons.

Internationally, Qingdao is best known for Tsingtao beer, brewed since 1903 by a German-British venture the Chinese beer that is most famous abroad. The city also hosts the household appliance maker Haier and the electronics company Hisense, and the guitar brand Epiphone opened a factory there in 2002.

In 1984 one district was named by the national government as a special zone for economic and technology development (SETDZ), and the entire city then went through fast-tracked growth in manufacturing and services. Heavy foreign investment has flowed in, especially from South Korea and Japan, and the port acts as a hub for both local and international trade. On the primary side, the city has an estimated 200 square kilometres (50,000 acres) of farmland, and its twisting coastline provides rich stocks of fish, shrimp and other marine resources. Wind power generation is among the strongest in the region. For a graduate, this mix of ports, manufacturing and international trade means a city with plenty of employers who deal with the world.
Development is organised around several named zones.
Qingdao West Coast New District

Qingdao is well connected by road, sea, air and rail, and it has a growing metro. The roads are heavy with expressways, the airport is newly built, and fast trains reach the capital in under three hours. That matters if you plan to travel home during breaks or explore Shandong.
The Qingdao area has about 1,145 km (711 miles) of roads, and nearly 500 km (310 miles) of that is expressway. Several national expressways start or pass through the city:

The G2011 Qingxin Expressway is a spur route from Qingdao to Xinhe in Pingdu. Provincial expressways include:

S19 Longqing Expressway (Longkou to Qingdao)
S21 Xinwei Expressway (Xinhe to Weifang)
S24 Weiqing Expressway (Weihai to Qingdao)

G308 (Qingdao to Shijiazhuang)
G309 (Rongcheng to Lanzhou)

ocean-university-of-china.h: Bridge and tunnel across the bay

blocks.x: On 30 June 2011 Qingdao opened Haiwan Bridge, at that moment the longest span across water on Earth. It is 42.5 km (26.4 miles) long, linking Qingdao with Huangdao and Hongdao, and it passed Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, the earlier record-holder, by almost 4.8 km (about three miles). It rests on more than 5,000 pillars, cost about 10 billion yuan (roughly 1.5 billion US dollars), took four years to build and came from a design by the Shandong Gausu Group. At least 10,000 workers in two teams worked around the clock, building from opposite ends. The crossing cuts the trip between central Qingdao and the sprawling suburb of Huangdao by 30 minutes. The Jiaozhou Bay Tunnel opened that same day and carries public buses, adding another convenient link between the two sides.

The seaport, operated by Qingdao Port International, ranks among the busiest anywhere. It has cooperative ties with 450 ports in 130 countries and is a link in the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road initiative. Yearly cargo handling first went beyond 100 million tons in 2003, with 3.41 million twenty-foot equivalent units of containers. By 2011 it ranked sixth in the world for total cargo volume with 372,000,000 metric tons, equal to 366,000,000 long tons or 410,000,000 short tons, and in 2016 it was eighth worldwide by container count. Adjacent ports such as Dongjiakou belong to the same system.
Passenger ferries run to Japan and Korea. The Orient Ferry links Qingdao with Shimonoseki in Japan, the New Golden Bridge II sails to Incheon and the Blue Sea Ferry to Gunsan in South Korea.

Qingdao Jiaodong International Airport lies 39 km from the city centre. It opened on 12 August 2021 to replace Qingdao Liuting International Airport. Thirteen domestic and international airlines serve it on 94 routes, 12 of them international or regional.

Rail building picked up speed from the late 1990s. Qingdao is the terminus of the Jinan-Qingdao high-speed railway, the Qingdao-Jinan passenger railway and the original Qingdao-Jinan line. The city has major stations at Qingdao, Cangkou, Dagang and Qingdao North, while Sifang station no longer takes passengers. High-speed D- and G-series trains reach 300 km/h (190 mph) along the Jinan-Qingdao stretch and serve Tianjin, Jinan, Hefei, Shanghai and Beijing. The quickest Qingdao to Beijing service, G206/G205, takes 2 hours 58 minutes. On conventional lines you can also reach Zhengzhou, Xi'an, Chengdu, Lanzhou, Jining, Jinan and Beijing.

ocean-university-of-china.h: Local buses, taxis, metro and tram

blocks.x: Public transport in Qingdao is well developed. As of 2012 the public bus fleet comprised 5283 large and medium buses, including compressed natural gas buses, and 136 trolleybuses. All of them can be paid for with the contactless Qingdao public transport IC card (青岛卡); later every operator moved to the Qingdaotong card, with the West Coast New Area's Zhenqing bus company the last to adopt it in 2019. Non-air-conditioned buses cost 1 yuan, apart from the tunnel bus, and road passenger transport approaches 737 million trips a year. The "Ri-Xin Bus" public transport brand is known across China. Taxi operators include Yiqing, Zhongqing, Jiaoyun and Huaqing.

The metro is expanding quickly and the published figures differ by date. In August 2009 the government declared it would spend over 29 billion yuan on the subway before 2016. Line 3, the first to open, began service on 16 December 2015, with 54.7 km (34.0 miles) built for about 29.2 billion yuan (about US$4.3 billion). The 2009 announcement had put the budget at US$4.2 billion. Early plans envisaged eight lines totalling 231.5 km (143.8 miles) in the city centre and some suburbs. A later description gave an operating length of 243 km, or 151 miles, on the West Coast Line, the Oceantec Valley Line and Lines 8, 6, 4, 3, 2 and 1. A different account, dated February to March 2023, said seven lines were open (Lines 11 and 13 had joined 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8), with 315 km of operation and 146 stations, tenth in China and second among northern cities, and that 10 lines or extensions were under construction totalling 188 km, expected to be finished by 2028. The long-term plan has 19 lines with 872 km in total, and the approved third-phase plan has 13 lines with 503 km. Because these numbers vary, check the Qingdao Metro website for the current map.

The Qingdao Tram, officially a modern tram demonstration line in Chengyang District, opened in 2016. Management and operation sit with the rail bus company of the Qingdao Public Transport Group, and the system has just one line.

ocean-university-of-china.h: Look and feel of the city

blocks.x: Qingdao's centre has a surprisingly large number of German-style buildings, even though the German leased-territory period lasted only 16 years, from 1898 to 1914. The blend of German and Chinese architecture, together with the German roots and the sizeable Korean expatriate population, gives the city an atmosphere that is noticeably its own. A traditional saying pictures the city as red tiles, green trees, a blue sky and a blue sea. Many former foreign-style areas are well preserved. New districts are being rebuilt on a large scale, but the old city, most of all in western Shinan District, still has many traditional buildings.

Beer lovers have a yearly date in the calendar: the city's international beer festival began in 1991 and is held each August or September. In 2014 Qingdao also staged a major international horticultural fair, the Qingdao International Horticulture Expo. Qingdao has served as a filming location for several movies:

Ocean University of China lists 259 programs for international students on this site: 69 bachelor, 114 master's, 76 doctoral programs.

Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,500 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 23,500), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 31,000 to CNY 31,000 (median CNY 31,000), according to the university's published fee table.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

ocean-university-of-china.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Ocean University of China may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Qingdao, register at Ocean University of China by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Peking University, usually shortened to PKU, is a public institution in Beijing's Haidian district. It answers to the Ministry of Education, which also provides its funding. Several national programmes mark its top-tier status in China, namely the Double First-Class Construction scheme, Project 985 and Project 211. It also belongs to the C9 League, the informal group of China's leading research universities.

For anyone comparing Chinese universities, the history is a good place to start. The Imperial University of Peking, as it was first called, opened its doors in 1898 under a royal charter issued by the Guangxu Emperor. That makes it the second-oldest university in the country, after Tianjin University, which dates from 1895. In May 1912 the Republic of China's government ordered the institution renamed, and Peking University became its name. In 1952, after the People's Republic was established, a nationwide reorganisation of universities and departments merged Yenching University into PKU. Beijing Medical University followed in April 2000.

Today the university has eight faculties. Health Science, Interdisciplinary Studies, Economics and Management, Social Sciences, Humanities, Engineering, Informatics and Sciences each form one. Beneath the faculties are six affiliated hospitals, 24 research entities and a total of 55 schools and departments. Its staff in 2024 counted 54 academicians from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, 20 members of the World Academy of Sciences, and 16 academicians from the Chinese Academy of Engineering.

The idea for a national university grew out of national shock. China lost the Sino-Japanese War, and thinkers including Yan Fu, Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao argued that education had to be reformed. The minister Li Duanfen suggested in June 1896 that the capital should have a university. The Guangxu Emperor gave his approval on 11 June 1898, as one step of the Hundred Days' Reform, and so the Imperial University of Peking came into being. Its Chinese name, Jingshi Daxuetang, can be translated as the Capital Grand Study Hall. The formal founding followed on 3 July 1898, once the emperor had accepted the royal charter that Liang wrote. The minister Sun Jianai was put in charge of carrying it out.

The new institution had a double role. It was the country's leading place of higher learning, and it was also its highest educational authority. Its first president was William Alexander Parsons Martin. The reform movement was short-lived, though. When the conservative Empress Dowager Cixi took power on 21 September, most of the reforms were reversed. The university survived with narrower goals and a smaller scope. When it opened on 31 December, only 160 students enrolled, well short of the 500 planned. Teaching covered mathematics, astronomy, physics, botany and zoology, and the laboratories had modern equipment.
The Xinhai Revolution brought a new name in 1912, Government University of Peking, and then in 1919 the school became the National University of Peking.

peking-university.h: Cai Yuanpei and the May Fourth years (1916-1927)

blocks.x: The university's character was shaped by Cai Yuanpei, a noted scholar who took over as president on 26 December 1917. Under him PKU grew into the largest institution of higher learning in the country, with 14 departments and more than 2,000 students. Inspired by the German tradition of academic freedom, he brought in faculty governance and democratic management. He also hired a deliberately mixed faculty. Leading voices of the progressive New Culture Movement taught there. Lu Xun, Hu Shih, Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Liu Bannong, Ma Yinchu and Liang Shuming were all on the staff. Prominent conservatives such as Gu Hongming and Huang Kan were on the staff too. Cai defended freedom of thought and the independence of education, and resigned several times to protest government policy and interference.

The university is also tied to a famous day of protest. On 1 May 1919, several PKU students heard that the Treaty of Versailles would let Japan take over Germany's colonial rights in Shandong province. A meeting was quickly organised at PKU, joined by representatives of other Beijing universities. The result was the march of 4 May, when students from thirteen universities walked to Tiananmen. They protested the treaty terms and urged the Beiyang government to refuse to sign. Three officials, whom the protesters believed were collaborating with Japan, were also named in calls for immediate resignation. They were Cao Rulin (Minister of Transportation), Zhang Zongxiang (ambassador to Japan) and Lu Zongyu (Minister of Currency). Some demonstrators were beaten or arrested, and protesters set fire to Cao Rulin's home. Afterwards, students, workers and merchants across almost every major Chinese city stopped work and refused to buy Japanese goods. Under heavy public pressure the government released the detained students and dismissed the three officials, and China's delegates in Paris declined to sign the treaty.

peking-university.h: War, politics and the later twentieth century

blocks.x: In the Second World War years (1938-1946), PKU staff joined colleagues from Tsinghua University and Nankai University to create the National Southwestern Associated University. It was based in Kunming, Yunnan. The period was highly productive and left a lasting mark on Chinese intellectual life and on postwar reconstruction.

Writing groups at PKU and Tsinghua took part in the political campaign known as Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius (1973 to 1976), publishing commentaries under the pen name Liang Xiao. It reads like a person's name, but it is a homophone for the Chinese words meaning two schools.
The 21st century has brought a steady run of recognitions and new units:

October 2015: Tu Youyou, an alumna and professor, won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her discovery of artemisinin, a drug that has saved millions of lives, was a major contribution to the global fight against malaria.

20 February 2017: a contract with the Open University created an Oxford presence, comprising the HSBC Business School's Oxford Campus, the Peking University Oxford Center and the Shenzhen Oxford Innovation Center.

29 June 2020: PKU and Moscow State University jointly lead the newly founded Sino-Russian Mathematics Center. Other Chinese units and Russian bodies, St. Petersburg University among them, helped build it, drawing on the Double First-Class alliance in mathematics.
2 April 2021: a Nanchang Innovation Research Institute attached to PKU was inaugurated.
15 July 2021: the School of Integrated Circuits began its life at PKU.
6 September 2021: a new campus at Changping opened and welcomed its first teachers and students.
30 September 2021: the Lanyuan Centre was launched. Its first dean is Ke Yang, who teaches in the School of Clinical Oncology and is a foreign academician of the American Academy of Medical Sciences.

October 2021: computer science was promoted from a department to a full School of Computer Science. The honorary president is Yang Fuqing, who belongs to the Chinese Academy of Sciences as an academician.

2022: PKU and The Lancet set up a commission on healthy ageing in China. Its purpose is to move the debate beyond the risks of an ageing population, towards the opportunity that comes from freeing up the intellectual and working abilities of older people and of the whole of Chinese society.

June 2022: when the International University Sports Federation (FISU) published its first Healthy Campus list, PKU was the only Chinese university with platinum certification. It took part in 4 projects, which made it China's single representative among 130 projects worldwide.

March 2025: the former Faculty of Information and Engineering was divided into a Faculty of Informatics and a Faculty of Engineering. The engineering faculty also gained two new schools, Mechanics and Engineering Science, and Advanced Manufacturing and Robotics.

peking-university.h: The campus and PKU's other sites

blocks.x: The main campus occupies the former grounds of imperial gardens from the Qing dynasty, and it still feels like a traditional Chinese garden. There are old-style houses, pagodas, landscaped gardens and several historic buildings. Talbot Hamlin, an American architect and art historian, designed some of the buildings erected between 1919 and 1922. You can enter through the East, West or South gates. The West Gate is the best known, mainly for the murals painted on its ceiling. Weiming Lake lies in the north of the campus, ringed by walking paths and small gardens.

There are museums on campus too, notably the Arthur M. Sackler Museum of Art and Archaeology and the Museum of University History. Items on display include burial objects excavated in Beijing, thousands of years old, from the tombs of royalty of the Warring States period. Visitors can see ritual pottery vessels, intricate jewellery, and human remains arranged in the burial style of that era.
Beyond the main campus there are other sites you may hear about:
The medical side of the university, the Health Science Center (PKUHSC), is found on Xueyuan Road next to other colleges.
During the Third Front construction programme, PKU opened a branch in Hanzhong, Shaanxi.
The Shenzhen Graduate School opened in 2001 in the northwest of Shenzhen city.

peking-university.h: Shenzhen Graduate School in more detail

blocks.x: The Shenzhen Graduate School was set up in September 2001 in partnership with the Shenzhen Municipal Government. It stands in Shenzhen's University Town, next to the Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen) campus and to Tsinghua's international graduate school in the same city. Wen Hai, a well-known Chinese economist and vice-president of PKU, is its current chancellor. Among the research schools based there are the School of Transnational Law and the HSBC Business School. A strategic agreement with the Shenzhen government, dated 29 August 2016, commits PKU to developing the graduate school further. The plan is to build a brand-new campus near the existing one and to launch undergraduate programmes.

The university has 55 schools and departments, offering 137 undergraduate majors, 59 master's programmes and 59 doctoral programmes. Alongside basic research it carries out applied research. It reports 420 research institutions. Of these, 7 are State Key Laboratories, 5 are National Engineering Research Centers and 1 is a National Laboratory. The library holds 8 million items and is the largest university library in Asia. Its ceremony for the 120th anniversary took place on 24 October 2018 in the Yingjie Overseas Exchange Center.
PKU also shares the running of the Wallace H. Coulter Department of Biomedical Engineering with Emory University and Georgia Tech.

Over the past century, PKU alumni have led other major Chinese universities. Luo Jialun led Tsinghua, Yuan Baohua led Renmin University, Qian Sanqiang headed Zhejiang University, Zhang Zhirang was president at Fudan, Teng Weizao at Nankai, and Guan Weiyan at the University of Science and Technology of China, with many more besides.

In 2025, the QS Asia University Rankings put PKU first among all Asian universities.

In the 2025 QS World University Rankings it came 14th globally and first in Asia. Times Higher Education (THE) in 2025 gave it 13th place worldwide and 2nd in Asia, and its indicators for the teaching environment and the research environment stood at 9th and 6th in the world.

The 2023 QS edition listed it first in Asia and 12th worldwide. Under the Three University Missions Ranking it was first in the Asia-Pacific and 15th globally. U.S. News and World Report, as of 2026, lists it 19th worldwide, 3rd across the Asia-Pacific and 2nd inside China.

Employability is covered by the THE Global Employability University Ranking 2025, where graduates from PKU placed 2nd in Asia and 11th across the world. The same year it was 11th for world reputation in THE's tables. In 2024 it was 7th among universities in the SCImago Institutions Rankings, and in November 2024 Clarivate Analytics placed it 12th in the world for Highly Cited Researchers.

peking-university.h: The National School of Development and business education

blocks.x: The National School of Development, formerly the China Center for Economic Research, is counted among China's five most influential think tanks. Justin Yifu Lin and colleagues started the school's MBA in 1998, named the Beijing International MBA (BiMBA). The Quacquarelli Symonds TopMBA ranking for 2014-2015 put it within the six best MBA programmes in Asia Pacific. In Forbes's view it is China's second most valuable full-time MBA, after CEIBS, and Bloomberg Business counted it among the best business schools in Asia.

peking-university.h: Studying at PKU as an international student

blocks.x: About 7,000 international students study at PKU in a typical year. The student body is truly global: North America, South America, Asia, Australia, most of Western Europe and many African countries are all represented. At the main campus, international students live in the dormitories at Shaoyuan Garden and Zhongguanyuan Global Village.

The partnership with Waseda University in Japan is the most developed of PKU's links in Northeast Asia. It started with an academic agreement in 1982 and has grown since 2003 into dual-degree programmes and joint research. Under the PKU-Waseda project, selected PKU undergraduates spend their third year at Waseda in Japan and return to Beijing for the fourth. Waseda sends many exchange students to PKU in the other direction. At graduation, a student holds two bachelor's degrees, each issued by a different university. Joint master's training and dual doctoral degrees also exist. Offering dual degrees at all three levels, bachelor's, master's and doctoral, is rare anywhere in the world.
Cornell University: an agreement signed in 2005 established a major at Cornell in China and Asia-Pacific Studies. Its students must spend a semester at PKU while doing internships.
Yale University: a joint undergraduate programme began in 2006, with students living and studying for a semester overseas alongside the host institution's own students.

The School of International Studies has launched joint degree programmes with Seoul National University, the University of Tokyo, Paris School of International Affairs and the London School of Economics.
Stanford University has a joint research centre and a base for its students and scholars, the Stanford Center at Peking University, in the Lee Jung Sen Building.
The HSBC Business School offers joint degrees with both the Chinese University of Hong Kong and the University of Hong Kong.

PKU's partnership with Freie Universität Berlin dates to 1981, and with the Higher School of Economics to 2015. Washington University in St. Louis joined in 2019, through the McDonnell International Scholars Academy.

peking-university.h: Global Excellence Strategy and art research

blocks.x: On its 121st founding anniversary, PKU unveiled the Global Excellence Strategy, a blueprint for building its international presence during what it calls the Fourth Industrial Revolution. The strategy aims to deepen international cooperation, overcome obstacles to development, gather resources from around the world and encourage collegial ties. The strategy is framed around the English word CLOUDS, a nod to the cloud era. C is for creativity and L for leadership, O for openness, U for uniqueness, D for diversity and S for shaping.

PKU has also joined art-research projects with partners abroad. One is the Center for the Art of East Asia (CAEA), run with the University of Chicago, and another is a digital art and design department created with UNESCO.

peking-university.h: Beijing: the city around the campus

blocks.x: A PKU student lives in the capital as much as on campus. The sections below describe what the city looks like, how it is laid out, what the seasons are like and what you should know about the air before you arrive.

Three architectural layers sit on top of one another in Beijing. The oldest is the imperial one. Its showpiece is Tian'anmen, the massive Gate of Heavenly Peace that has become the emblem of the People's Republic, and the same layer includes the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City. Next comes the so-called Sino-Sov style, which dates from the 1950s to the 1970s. Its buildings tend to be boxy and in some cases badly constructed. The most recent layer is thoroughly modern. The east of the city, around the Beijing CBD, has the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere you will find the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the start of the 21st century the construction boom has been tremendous, with designers from many countries contributing styles of their own, above all in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone you can see 1950s design blended with a neofuturistic look, old and new together. China Zun, at 528 metres, is the tallest building in the city. Beijing has won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building twice since 2007: the Linked Hybrid took it in 2009 and the CCTV Headquarters in 2013. Only a single building in the entire world is given this award in any year.

Beijing's traditional housing is the siheyuan, a set of buildings arranged around a courtyard. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are two of the grander ones. Alleys called hutongs join the courtyards together. For good Feng Shui they usually run straight from east to west, which leaves doorways facing north or south. Their width varies, and the narrowest allow only a few people to walk through together. Siheyuans and hutongs used to be everywhere, but they are vanishing quickly because entire blocks of them are demolished to make way for high-rises. People who lived in hutongs may take apartments in the new buildings, with floor space no smaller than their previous homes. Many of them nevertheless say that the neighbourly feeling and street life of the hutongs cannot be recreated. Often the old properties belong to the government.

The municipality occupies the northern fringe of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that stretches away to the south and east of Beijing. Hills and mountains rise to the north, northwest and west. They act as a barrier, protecting both the capital and the farmland of northern China from the desert steppe beyond. In the northwestern part of the municipality, notably Yanqing District and Huairou District, the Jundu Mountains dominate the landscape, and the western edge is framed by the Western Hills, also called Xishan. The Great Wall crosses the northern part of the municipality, built on difficult terrain to keep out nomadic raiders from the steppe. At 2,303 metres (7,556 ft), Mount Dongling is the top of the municipality. It lies in the Western Hills, right on the border with Hebei.

Rivers such as the Chaobai, the Yongding and the Juma flow southeast, and all of them are tributaries within the Hai River system. The largest reservoir in the municipality is Miyun Reservoir, on the upper reaches of the Chaobai River. Two large waterworks end in Beijing. One is the Grand Canal, which runs to Hangzhou and was constructed more than 1,400 years ago for transport. The other is the South-North Water Transfer Project, built during the past decade to bring water north from the Yangtze River basin.

Urban Beijing lies in the south-central plains of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres above sea level (130 to 200 feet). It is a modest fraction of the municipality's total area, although it keeps growing. Ring roads spread outward from the centre in concentric circles. Where the old city walls once stood, you now find the Second Ring Road, while the Sixth Ring Road ties together suburban satellite towns. At the heart of the city are Tian'anmen and the square of the same name, directly south of the Forbidden City, where emperors once lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, where China's present leaders live. Chang'an Avenue, passing between the gate and the square, is the principal east-west axis. Beijing grew outward from the old centre to its edges in a way that people often liken to a pancake spreading across a pan (tan da bing). That sprawl is commonly given as one cause of the city's urban problems.

The climate is classed as humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), a short step from a monsoonal cold semi-arid climate (Köppen: BSk). Hot, humid summers come with the East Asian monsoon. The Siberian anticyclone, a huge high-pressure system, shapes winters that are cold, dry and short. Springs can bring sandstorms that cross the Mongolian steppe from the Gobi Desert, with rapid warming and mostly dry weather. Autumn is another season of transition and has very little rain.

Looking at the period from 2001 to 2026, early August is the hottest time of the year and early January the coldest. By the official Chinese calendar of the seasons, spring begins on 26 March, then summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. March and September have been warming faster lately, and May and October more slowly, so autumn generally comes out shorter than spring.
These are the main averages for 1991 to 2020:

In the urban area the yearly mean temperature falls between 12.9 and 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Typical daily lows are 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and typical daily highs 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).
In the lower-lying suburbs the yearly mean ranges from 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F). Daily lows are 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and daily highs 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F).
In the mountains the yearly mean is anywhere from 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F), dropping as you climb.
The mean daily temperature in January is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F), against 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July.

Roughly 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of rain or snow falls in a year, but Haidian and Chaoyang get more, at an average of 584.2 mm (23.00 in). Close to three-quarters of the total comes between June and August. The sun shines for 42% of the possible hours in July and 62% in January and February, adding up to 2,490.5 hours of bright sunshine annually. Since 1951 the lowest temperature recorded was -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, and the highest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), on 24 July 1999.

Desert erosion in the north and northwest of China produces dust storms that visit the city seasonally. The Beijing Weather Modification Office will sometimes trigger rain by artificial means to reduce their impact. Eight storms or more occurred in just the first four months of 2006. One storm in April 2002 deposited nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing and then carried on to Japan and Korea.

peking-university.h: Beijing's air quality: what changed and why

blocks.x: Air quality is the topic that most newcomers ask about. Beijing has struggled with environmental problems for a long time, though conditions have improved a good deal lately.

The built-up area quadrupled in size from 2000 to 2009. That brought a sharp rise in emissions from human activity, and it also altered the local meteorology considerably. Wind speed, humidity near the surface and surface albedo all fell, whereas ground temperatures, near-surface air temperatures, ozone and the vertical dilution of air all increased. Rapid urbanisation, plus pollution from burning fossil fuels, gave Beijing grave environmental problems that harmed the health of many inhabitants. A thick smog blanketed Beijing and most of northern China in 2013, hitting a total of 600 million people. This pollution shock turned air quality into a major economic and social concern across the country. Beijing's authorities then announced a package of measures. One was to lower coal's share of the energy mix, from 24% in 2012 down to 10% in 2017. At national level the government told owners of heavily polluting vehicles to take them off the road between 2015 and 2017, and stepped up the shift to clean energy.

peking-university.h: Pollution from beyond the city limits

blocks.x: A joint study by American and Chinese researchers in 2006 concluded that neighbouring cities and provinces produce a large share of Beijing's pollution. About 35 to 60% of the ozone, on average, can be traced to sources outside Beijing. Tianjin Municipality and Shandong Province have what researchers describe as significant influence on the capital's air. The reasons include the southerly and southeasterly airflow that prevails in summer and the mountains that lie to the north and northwest.

Burning coal is responsible for roughly 40% of the PM 2.5 in Beijing, and it is also the main source of nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012, and it intends to limit coal use to 20 million tons a year. Beijing used 26.3 million tons in 2011; 73% went to heating and power generation and the balance to industry. Many of the pollutants originate in nearby regions. Tianjin's coal use was projected to climb from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million in 2015. Hebei Province used more than 300 million tons in 2011, which exceeds the total for Germany. Only 30% of Hebei's coal went to power generation, and a substantial portion went to steel and cement production. Power plants in coal-mining regions (Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000) and in Shandong add to Beijing's pollution too. Ranked by coal consumption, the provinces of Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia occupy first to fourth place respectively.

Four large coal-fired plants once provided Beijing with electricity and with heat for the winter. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was the first to shut, in 2014. Two others closed in March 2015, and Huaneng Thermal Power Plant was due to follow in 2016. Plans for 2013 to 2017 called for a 13 million ton cut in coal consumption, with a cap of 15 million tons in 2015.

Beijing spent nearly US$17 billion on cleaning the air ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, to keep its promises. Throughout the Games it put a number of schemes into effect. All construction sites stopped work, some gas stations closed and so did many Beijing factories, permanently. Industry in neighbouring regions was shut for a time. Drivers could use their cars only on odd or even days depending on licence plates, which halved traffic, while bus and subway fares were lowered, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. A fleet of 3,800 natural gas buses, one of the largest anywhere, was assembled. Beijing was the first Chinese city to demand the Chinese version of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The authorities have also used cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air ahead of big occasions, for instance the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. Lately they have preferred other tools, namely temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars. This produced the short stretches called APEC blue and parade blue, in the run-up to and during APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. Air quality then improved dramatically, but slid back to unhealthy levels soon after each event.

Beijing's first smog alert was issued on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing most industrial and commercial businesses in the city. A second red alert followed later the same month. An announcement by the environmental protection bureau in November 2016 set a new rule for 2017: old cars with high emissions may not be driven whenever a smog red alert applies in the city or nearby regions.

The war on pollution, declared in 2014, has led to real reductions. Fine particulates fell by 35% in Beijing in 2017, and there was more progress by 2020. Two steps did most of the work: natural gas took the place of coal for power, and polluting industrial plants in the Beijing area were cleaned up. By 2022 the annual average of PM2.5 had come down to 30 micrograms per cubic meter, the best level since 2013. Heavy pollution occurred on only two days in 2024, a record low and a 96.6 percent drop from 58 days in 2013.

Different sources give different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily figures from 27 monitoring stations on its website. Separately, the American Embassy in Beijing posts hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures on Twitter. Because the two measure different pollutants against different standards, the BJEPB tends to report lower pollution and a smaller health impact than the embassy does. Smog does harm people. It affects the rates of illness from cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing directly, and breathing a lot of polluted air can cause heart and lung problems, emergency visits to hospital, and even death. If you are sensitive to air quality, look at a live reading before heading out.

peking-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Peking University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Peking University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Qingdao University (abbreviation: QDU/QDU Med school; Chinese: 青岛大学) is a key provincial research university located in Qingdao, Shandong, China.

The university was first established in 1985. In 1993, the former Qingdao University, Qingdao Medical College, Shandong Textile Engineering College, and Qingdao Normal College, merged to form the new Qingdao University. At present, QDU is one of the best comprehensive universities in Shandong Province, recognized as a member of the national "Excellent Engineer Education and Training Program."

With a strong profile in Medical Sciences, Textile and Design, Business, and liberal arts, QDU serves 35,000 full-time undergraduate students, 9,800 graduate students, and 1,600 international students.

In 1985, Qingdao University was established, with the educational goal of "high level distinctive university," and disciplines of arts, science, engineering, business and many other subjects. School construction and development were supported financially by the central government, and also academically supported by Nankai University, Tianjin University, University of Science and Technology of China, and Shandong University. In 1993, Qingdao University merged Shandong Textile Engineering Institute (山东纺织工学院), Qingdao Medical College (青岛医学院) and Qingdao Normal College (青岛师范专科学校).

Qingdao University consists of 25 faculties and departments as well as a graduate school. Courses are offered in 11 main Academic disciplines: Philosophy, Economics, Law, Literature, History, Natural sciences, Engineering, Management, Medicine, Education and Military sciences. There are 104 Undergraduate degree programs, 209 master's degree programs, 127 Doctoral degree programs, and 15 post-doctorate mobile stations. In addition, there are 7 professional master's degree programs in Law, Business Management, Engineering, Clinical Medicine, Public Health, Dentistry and Public Administration respectively.

In July 2025, a dormitory security guard at Qingdao University was found unconscious due to heatstroke in his duty room and was later pronounced dead despite emergency medical treatment. According to Chinese Business View, multiple university departments are still investigating the incident. The logistics office, student affairs office, and general duty office have shifted responsibility among themselves; the campus hospital stated it had not been notified, while the university's security and safety management departments confirmed an investigation is underway. Online posts claim the guard lived frugally, cared for stray cats, wore clothes left behind by graduates, and had reportedly not been paid for several months.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Qingdao, where Qingdao University is located.

Qingdao is located on the south-facing coast of the Shandong Peninsula (German: Schantung-Halbinsel). It borders three prefecture-level cities, namely Yantai to the northeast, Weifang to the west, and Rizhao to the southwest. The city occupies an area totaling 10,654 km2 (4,114 sq mi), and stretches in latitude from 35° 35' to 37° 09' N and in longitude from 119° 30' to 121° 00' E. The populated sections of the city are relatively flat while mountains spur up within city limits and nearby. The highest elevation in the city is located 1,133 meters (3,717 ft) above sea level. Of the total area of Qingdao, 15.5% is highland, while the foothill, plain, and lowland areas constitute 25.1%, 37.8%, and 21.7%, respectively. The city has a 730.64-kilometer (454.00 mi)-long coastline. Five significant rivers exceeding 50 kilometers (31 mi) in length can be found in the region.

Qingdao has a temperate, four-season, monsoon-influenced climate that lies in the transition between the humid subtropical (Köppen: Cwa) and humid continental (Köppen: Dwa) regimes. Due to the direct regulation of the marine environment, the city is influenced by the southeast monsoon and the currents and water masses from the ocean, so it also has significant maritime climate characteristics. Winters range from cool to cold and windy, but are generally dry, with a January average of 0.2 °C (32.4 °F). Summer is generally hot and humid, but very hot days are rare, with an August average of 25.6 °C (78.1 °F). Due to its proximity to the coast and location on a peninsula, compared to most inland areas of China, its spring is delayed by one month, and the annual diurnal temperature variation is only 6.3 °C (11.3 °F); conversely, its fall is milder than inland areas in Shandong. The water temperature peaks at about 25 °C (77 °F) in late August. Thus, swimming is possible for two months on either side. The annual mean temperature is 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −15.9 °C (3 °F) on 7 and 8 January 2021 to 38.9 °C (102 °F) on 15 July 2002; unofficial readings have reached a record low of −16.9 °C (1.6 °F) or for the official weather station there, −16.4 °C (2.5 °F) on 10 January 1931. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 38 percent in July to 59 percent in October, the city receives 2,261 hours of bright sunshine annually.

During the summer months, the beaches of Qingdao are afflicted by massive algal blooms. The decomposing algae release large amounts of hydrogen sulfide gas, which produces an offensive "rotten egg" odor. Sea lettuce blooms, which are partially caused by seaweed farming in Jiangsu Province, led local officials to declare a "large-scale algae disaster" in 2013.

Of the 10 million residents of Qingdao, 6.2 million reside in the Qingdao urban area. Another estimated 5 million live in other cities under Qingdao's jurisdiction. The annual birth rate is calculated around 76,507, with a birth rate of 10.15 per year per thousand, and a death rate of 6.32, both calculated on an annual basis. Living standards are among the highest of leading Chinese cities due to the strong export economy and relatively high family wages.

There is a large Korean community in Qingdao. By 2009, there were approximately 100,000 Koreans working, studying and living in Qingdao, which makes Qingdao the second in terms of Korean population in China, following Beijing which has about 200,000 Koreans.
According to the 2021 Qingdao Statistical Yearbook, the permanent resident population of Qingdao in 2020 was 10.1057 million, an increase of 182,700 people compared to the previous year.

In recent years, an important region in Eastern China, Shandong Province has seen substantial change in its economic landscape. Much of this development has been concentrated in Qingdao. Qingdao has seen rapid development. With an annual growth rate of 18.9 percent in 2006, the city's GDP reached 42.3 billion, ranking first in Shandong Province and tenth out of China's top 20 cities. GDP per capita comprised CN¥52,895 (US$7,616) in 2008. In 2024, Qingdao's GDP per capita comprised CN¥161,200 (US$23,000).

In 2006, Qingdao was ranked one of six "golden cities" by the World Bank, out of 120 Chinese cities assessed on factors including investment climate and government effectiveness. In 2018, Qingdao's GDP reached CN¥1200.15 billion, though it shrank a little in 2019.

Internationally, Qingdao is perhaps best known for its Tsingtao Brewery, founded by a German-British joint venture in 1903 that produces Tsingtao beer, the best-known Chinese export beer. It is also home to Haier, a large white goods manufacturer, and Hisense, a major electronics company. In 2002 guitar manufacturers Epiphone opened a factory in Qingdao.

In 1984 the Chinese government named a district of Qingdao a Special Economic and Technology Development Zone (SETDZ). Along with this district, the entire city had gone through fast-tracked development of secondary and tertiary industries. Qingdao has been the recipient of large foreign investment and its port is a hub for local and international trade. South Korea and Japan in particular made extensive investments in the city.

In terms of primary sector industries, Qingdao has an estimated 50,000 acres (200 km2) of arable land. Qingdao has a zigzagging pattern coastline, and thus possesses an invaluable stock of fish, shrimp, and other sea resources.
Qingdao's wind power electricity generation performs at among the highest levels in the region.

On 30 June 2011, the longest bridge over water opened in Qingdao. The bridge, Haiwan Bridge, is 26.4 miles (42.5 km) long and connects Qingdao to Huangdao and Hongdao. The bridge is almost three miles (4.8 km) longer than the previous record-holder, the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in the American state of Louisiana. Haiwan Bridge is supported by more than 5,000 pillars and costs about 10 billion yuan which is about 1.5 billion dollars. The bridge was designed by the Shandong Gausu Group and the construction lasted for four years. Haiwan Bridge cut the commute between the city of Qingdao and the sprawling suburb of Huangdao by 30 minutes. At least 10,000 workers toiled in two teams around the clock to build the bridge, which was constructed from opposite ends.
On the same day, the Jiaozhou Bay Tunnel opened. The tunnel brought much convenience to people by supporting public buses and making transport between the two areas more convenient.

Qingdao (official name: Qingdao port international co. ltd.) hosts one of the world's busiest seaports. Cooperative relations have been established with 450 ports in 130 countries worldwide. The port of Qingdao is part of the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. In 2003, the annual cargo handling capacity exceeded 100 million tons for the first time. The number of containers reached 3.41 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) of cargoes.

By 2011, the port had become the world's sixth-busiest by Total Cargo Volume, having handled 372,000,000 metric tons (366,000,000 long tons; 410,000,000 short tons) of cargo in that year. As of 2016, it was the 8th in the world in terms of TEUs (Twenty Foot Equivalent Units).

The Orient Ferry connects Qingdao with Shimonoseki, Japan. There are two ferry lines connecting Qingdao with South Korea. The New Golden Bridge II operates between Qingdao and Incheon, and the Blue Sea Ferry operates between Qingdao and Gunsan.
Qingdao port also includes a number of large adjacent ports including Dongjiakou.

Qingdao Jiaodong International Airport, located 39 km (24 mi) away from the city center, is served by 13 domestic and international airlines that operate 94 routes, 12 of which are international and regional. The airport opened on August 12, 2021, as a replacement for Qingdao Liuting International Airport.

Qingdao's railway development picked up during the late 1990s. It is at the start of the Jinan–Qingdao high-speed railway, the Qingdao–Jinan passenger railway and the original Qingdao–Jinan railway. Qingdao's city proper has some major railway stations, including Qingdao railway station, Cangkou railway station, Dagang railway station and Qingdao North railway station. Sifang railway station is now closed to passengers.

D and G series high-speed trains travel on the Jinan–Qingdao high-speed railway and reach speeds of 300 km/h (190 mph) on the Jinan-Qingdao Section. Services go to Beijing, Shanghai, Hefei, Jinan and Tianjin. The fastest train between Qingdao and Beijing is G206 / G205, which takes 2 hours and 58 minutes.
Domestic rail lines connect Qingdao with many cities in China, including Beijing, Lanzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Jinan and Jining.

Qingdao's public traffic owns 5283 large and medium-sized buses, CNG buses as of 2012. There are also 136 trolleybuses as of 2012. All of the buses and trolleybuses can be accessed using the Qingdao Public Traffic IC Card (青岛卡), which uses radio frequencies so the card does not have to physically touch the scanner. After that, all public transportation companies use Qingdaotong Card, the last company that started to use this card is the Zhenqing bus company located in The West Coast New Area of Qingdao (original Huangdao Distinct) in 2019.

Non air-conditioned buses cost 1 yuan (excluding the tunnel bus), The volume of road passenger transport approaches 737 million per year. The Public Transport Brand of 'Ri-Xin Bus (日新巴士)' is also known in China.
There are several taxi companies in Qingdao including Yiqing Company, Zhongqing Company, Jiaoyun Company, and, Huaqing Company.

After getting the approval from the State Council, the government announced on 18 August 2009 that Qingdao is ready to spend more than 29 billion yuan ($4.2 billion) before 2016 on its subway construction. Construction of 54.7 km (34.0 mi) of subway line 3 was completed before 2016 with a total investment of 29.2 billion yuan ($4.3 billion). Metro Line 3 is the first line in function and opened on 16 December 2015. In the long term, the city plans to build eight subway lines in downtown and some suburban districts, which account for 231.5 km (143.8 mi) in future. The system has an operating length of 243 km (151 mi), lines in operation including Line 1, Line 2, Line 3, Line 4, Line 6, Line 8, the Oceantec Valley Line, and the West Coast Line.

As of February 24, 2023, according to the approved network plan of Qingdao City, there are 19 long-term plans for Qingdao Metro, with a total length of 872 kilometers; The third phase construction plan has been approved, with a total of 13 lines and a total length of 503 kilometers, ranking ninth in the national approved mileage level; Seven lines have been opened and operated, including Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11, and 13, with an operating mileage of 315 kilometers. As of March 2023, there are 146 operating stations, ranking tenth in China and second in northern cities; There are 10 lines under construction (including extension lines), including the West Extension and Phase II of Line 2, Line 5, Phase I and Phase II of Line 6, Phase II of Line 7, South Section and Branch of Line 8, Phase I of Line 9, and Phase I of Line 15. The total length under construction is 188 kilometers, and it is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

The Qingdao Tram (official name: Modern tram demonstration line) of Chengyang District, Qingdao, is a tram system operating in Chengyang District, Qingdao, China. It opened in 2016. The Qingdao Public Transport Group Rail Bus Co., Ltd. is responsible for operation and management. The system is only composed of 1 tram line.

There are a large number of German-style buildings in Qingdao's city center, a remarkable fact considering the German leased-territory period only lasted 16 years (1898–1914). The unique combination of German and Chinese architecture therein, combined with German demographic roots and a large Korean expatriate population, gives Qingdao a rather distinct atmosphere. An old saying described Qingdao as a city of "red tiles green trees, blue sky, and blue sea." A larger number of areas in former foreign styles are well preserved. Although the new city area is under large-scale reconstruction, the old city area (especially the western part of Shinan District) still retains many traditional buildings.
