qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: Qingdao University of Science and Technology at a glance

blocks.x: QUST, as the university is usually shortened, is a public university run by Shandong province and based in the coastal city of Qingdao. It began as a school for the chemical and rubber trades and has since grown into a broad institution that awards degrees in science, technology, the humanities, business, management, medicine, law and the arts.

The university is spread across several sites: two in Qingdao itself (the districts of Sifang and Laoshan), one in Gaomi, a county-level city that belongs to Weifang, and one in Jinan, the provincial capital. For an applicant, the practical point is that the campus you are assigned to depends on your college, so it is worth checking this before you apply.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: From a Shenyang vocational school to a full university

blocks.x: The story starts in the north-east. The site of the future university was a Catholic school, Shenyang Wenhui Middle School (沈阳文会中学), which had been teaching since 1876. In 1950 the regional government of the Northeast turned those premises into the Shenyang Light Industry Vocational School (沈阳轻工业高级职业学校). Church-run schooling was about to end, so an arrangement was made beforehand and the teachers and pupils simply carried over into the new institution. The higher-education section concentrated on what the country needed at the time, namely chemistry, papermaking and rubber manufacture, while the former middle school carried on beneath the new school. The first three vocational classes started in October 1950 with 128 students altogether.

Shenyang was only a first stop. The Ministry of Light Industry resolved in December 1954 to move the whole school to Qingdao, where the local rubber industry was short of skilled people. Teachers, students and equipment travelled from Liaoning to Shandong, and that September (1956) the school reopened as the Qingdao Rubber Industry School (青岛橡胶工业学校). In those years the site lay on the edge of the city and was hardly built up at all.

In 1958 it became Shandong College of Chemical Industry (山东化工学院), passing under the direct control of the Ministry of Chemical Industry and gaining the right to award bachelor's degrees. The Cultural Revolution then hit hard: by 1968 only three subjects survived, namely Rubber Products, Chemical Machinery and Rubber Machinery, study was cut to two years, and from 1972 students had to be recruited from among workers, peasants and soldiers (工农兵学员). Things improved in 1977, when the Gaokao, the national entrance examination, was restored as the route into higher education; 443 new undergraduates joined that year.

Postgraduate recruitment in technical fields was authorised in 1980, and distance learning followed in 1981 with an intake of 91. In 1985 the name changed to Qingdao Institute of Chemical Industry (青岛化工学院). Many students and staff saw this as a step down and disliked it, yet the worry proved unfounded and the institution kept developing. Through the following years the range of subjects widened steadily. By 1993 there were six faculties, among them Foreign Languages and Computer Science, with about 3,963 students and 17 bachelor's courses.

The move towards a comprehensive university gathered pace in 2001, when the college absorbed the Qingdao Arts and Crafts School (青岛工艺美术学校) and enrolment reached 10,747. The largest change came in 2002: full university status was granted, together with the name it still bears, Qingdao University of Science and Technology. The new Laoshan campus welcomed its first students that September. Further milestones were the College of Communication and Animation and extra language majors in the School of Foreign Languages (2006), the third campus in Gaomi (2009), which took the university beyond Qingdao for the first time, and the start of work in 2014 on an affiliated school in Laoshan district (青岛科技大学附属学校).

In short, this is a seventy-year story of a specialist technical school widening its remit step by step, and that history explains why chemistry, rubber and materials remain the university's strongest areas today.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: What you can study and how the university is rated

blocks.x: Shandong designates nine provincial key universities (山东省属重点高校), and QUST is one of them. In 2013 it was placed 45th among engineering universities in mainland China, and in 2011 it joined the first national Excellent Engineers Education and Training Plan (卓越工程师教育培养计划). Its campuses together cover roughly 700,000 square metres, and the reported value of fixed assets is 2,200 billion yuan; that figure looks very large, so check it against the university's own publications. The library, which has been collected since 1950 across five branches, now occupies about 50,000 square metres and holds over 2.4 million volumes, digital ones included.

On the degree side, the university has three first-level and 22 second-level doctoral programs, four postdoctoral research stations, 20 first-level and 125 second-level master's programs, plus 68 undergraduate programs. The best-known fields are chemistry and materials science. The university hosts two Ministry of Education key laboratories, one for rubber and plastics and one for eco-chemical engineering, and postdoctoral work is available in these areas. International companies have set up joint research centres with it as well; one example is the LANXESS Rubber Research Center Qingdao.
Five majors carry the national distinctive label (国家级特色专业), shown here in reverse of the usual catalogue order:
Process Equipment and Control Engineering
Mechanical Engineering and Automation
Polymer Materials and Engineering
Applied Chemistry
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Those five also hold provincial brand status (省级品牌特色专业), and so do these:
English Language Studies
Business Administration
Electronic Information Engineering
Automation
Materials Chemistry
A useful extra: the university is an authorised test centre for the TOEIC English test and for the CELI Italian exam, so you can sit these without travelling elsewhere.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: The campuses and the colleges on each

blocks.x: Which campus you study on matters a good deal, because they differ in age, size and surroundings. Here they are in turn.

The oldest campus is in the Sifang district, close to the eastern end of the Jiaozhou Bay Bridge. Its main building dates from 1956 and is admired for its style, which draws on the Soviet architecture fashionable then. Most of the core majors that define the university still sit here. Next to the campus is a cluster of high-end chemical and rubber businesses known as Rubber Valley (橡胶谷), and the university's science park is alongside.
You will find it at 53 Zhengzhou Road in Qingdao, Shandong Province. Teaching units here, reversed from the university's own ordering:
College of Adult Vocational Education 成教学院高职学院
College of Environment and Safety Engineering 环境与安全工程学院
College of Materials Science and Engineering 材料科学与工程学院
School of Polymer Science and Engineering 高分子科学与工程学院
College of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering (化学与分子工程学院)
College of Chemical Engineering (化工学院)

Laoshan is the biggest campus by area and opened in 2002. It stands near well-known sights, among them Mount Lao (崂山) and Shilaoren Beach (石老人海水浴场), which is a pleasant bonus for anyone who likes the sea and hiking. The colleges added during the change into a comprehensive university are here, along with the main administration and the library. The southern section, Nanyuan (南苑), was complete within a few years of the opening; the northern section, Beiyuan (北苑), came into use in 2012 and is still growing.
The street address is 99 Songling Road, Qingdao, Shandong Province. The units here, again in reverse:
College of Automation and Electronic Engineering (自动化与电子工程学院)
College of International Cooperation (国际合作学院)
Sino-German Technology College (中德科技学院)
Department of Sports (体育教学部)
Law School (政法学院)
College of Marxism (马克思主义学院)
College of Communication and Animation (传播与动漫学院)
College of the Arts (艺术学院)
College of Economics and Management (经济与管理学院)
School of Foreign Languages (外国语学院)
School of Information Sciences and Technology (信息科学技术学院)
College of Mathematics (数理学院)
College of Electromechanical Engineering (机电工程学院)

The Gaomi campus hosts branches of several main faculties, chiefly in economics, chemistry and computing. Associate-degree courses are also taught there, with 22 majors on offer. About 4,000 students and 260 teachers are based in Gaomi, and, as in Laoshan, building work is continuing. The address is 1 Xingtan West Street, Gaomi, Shandong Province, and the Chinese name is 青岛科技大学高密校区.
For the Jinan campus the only detail available here is its address: No. 80 Wenhua East Road, Jinan City, Shandong Province.

The strongest international link is with the University of Paderborn in Germany, which led to the Sino-German Technology College on the Laoshan campus. Students who meet the requirements set by the two universities and by the German academic exchange service DAAD can finish their bachelor's studies at one of several German universities and may continue to a master's there. Across the whole university, agreements exist with more than 60 educational institutions spread over 16 countries and territories. Those that exchange teachers with QUST include:
Kangnam University (South Korea)
Kongju National University (South Korea)
Tambov State Technical University (Russia)
Institute of the Pacific United (New Zealand)
Regensburg University of Applied Sciences (Germany)
City University of Hong Kong (Hong Kong, China)

Few Shandong universities do this, but QUST sponsors a professional football side directly, known as QUST F.C. It has competed in China League Two and got as far as the quarter-finals in 2009. A second team, the Qingdao Sea Eagles (青岛海之鹰足球俱乐部), is also under the university's management and plays in the local Qingdao league. In addition, many enterprises, mostly in rubber and plastics, are affiliated with the university, which signals close contact between study and industry.
Three names stand out among the people linked with the university:
Wang Zhongyu (born 1933), who graduated in 1953 and was later governor of Jilin Province between 1989 and 1992
Mo Yan (born 1955), novelist and short-story writer and the 2012 Nobel Prize in Literature laureate, a visiting professor since 2011
Wang Tianpu (born 1962), president of Sinopec Corporation, who took a Bachelor of Engineering in 1985
Daily life for a student depends heavily on the city outside the gates: the weather, how you get around and what you can do in your free time. The sections that follow describe Qingdao.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: Where Qingdao sits and what the land is like

blocks.x: The city looks south from the coast of the Shandong Peninsula. Its neighbours, all prefecture-level cities, are Yantai (north-east), Weifang (west) and Rizhao (south-west). The city covers 10,654 square kilometres (4,114 sq mi) between latitudes 35° 35' and 37° 09' N and longitudes 119° 30' and 121° 00' E. Built-up areas are fairly flat, but mountains rise inside the city limits and nearby, the highest point being 1,133 metres (3,717 ft). By terrain, 15.5% of the area is highland, 25.1% foothills, 37.8% plains and 21.7% lowland. The coastline is 730.64 km (454.00 mi) long, and five major rivers longer than 50 km (31 mi) flow through the region.

The climate is temperate with four seasons and a monsoon influence, sitting where the humid subtropical type (Cwa in the Köppen scheme) shades into the humid continental type (Dwa). The sea moderates the weather, bringing south-east monsoon winds and ocean currents, so the maritime character is strong. Winters are cool to cold, windy and mostly dry, and January averages 0.2 °C, or 32.4 °F. Summers are hot and humid but seldom extreme, with August averaging 25.6 °C, or 78.1 °F.

Because the city is on a peninsula by the sea, spring arrives about a month later than in most inland parts of China, and the temperature swing between day and night comes to just 6.3 °C, or 11.3 °F, across the year. Autumn, in contrast, is milder than in inland Shandong. In late August the sea peaks at roughly 25 °C, or 77 °F, which makes swimming possible for about two months either side. Over a whole year the mean temperature is 13.3 °C, or 55.9 °F.

Records since 1951 run from a low of −15.9 °C, or 3 °F, on 7 and 8 January 2021 up to a high of 38.9 °C, or 102 °F, on 15 July 2002. Informal readings have gone lower, down to −16.9 °C or 1.6 °F, while the official station recorded −16.4 °C or 2.5 °F on 10 January 1931. Sunshine as a share of the possible total is lowest in July (38 percent) and highest in October (59 percent), and the year as a whole brings 2,261 hours of bright sun.

One summer drawback to know about: the beaches are sometimes hit by large algal blooms. As the algae rot they give off hydrogen sulfide, which smells like rotten eggs. Blooms of sea lettuce, which seaweed farming in Jiangsu Province is partly blamed for, prompted officials in 2013 to speak of a 'large-scale algae disaster'.

About 10 million people live in Qingdao, 6.2 million of them in the urban area and an estimated 5 million in the other cities under its administration. The birth rate is 10.15 per thousand people (around 76,507 births a year) and the death rate 6.32 per thousand. Living standards rank among the highest of China's leading cities, helped by a strong export economy and comparatively high family wages. The statistical yearbook for 2021 puts the permanent resident population in 2020 at 10.1057 million, up by 182,700 on the year before.

There is also a large Korean community. Around 2009 roughly 100,000 Koreans worked, studied and lived in Qingdao, the second-biggest Korean population in China after Beijing with about 200,000. International students may find Korean shops and restaurants easy to come by as a result.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: How the city earns its living

blocks.x: Shandong Province has become an important part of eastern China, and much of its recent transformation has centred on Qingdao. Growth hit 18.9 percent in 2006, taking GDP to 42.3 billion, the highest in the province and tenth in a ranking of China's twenty leading cities. In 2008 GDP per head stood at CN¥52,895, about US$7,616, and by 2024 the figure was CN¥161,200, about US$23,000. The World Bank assessed 120 Chinese cities in 2006 for investment climate and government effectiveness and named Qingdao one of six 'golden cities'. GDP reached CN¥1200.15 billion in 2018, then dipped slightly in 2019.

The best-known name abroad is Tsingtao Brewery, started in 1903 by a German-British joint venture, whose beer is China's most recognised export brew. The city also hosts Haier, a major maker of household appliances, and Hisense, a leading electronics company, and Epiphone opened a guitar factory there in 2002.

In 1984 the national government named one district of Qingdao a Special Economic and Technology Development Zone (SETDZ), and the whole city went through fast-tracked growth in manufacturing and services. It has attracted a lot of foreign investment, particularly from South Korea and Japan, and its port is a hub for local and international trade. In farming and fishing terms, the city has an estimated 50,000 acres (200 km2) of arable land, and its zigzagging coast gives it a rich stock of fish, shrimp and other marine resources. Wind power generation is among the strongest in the region.
Industrial areas in the city include:
Qingdao University Industrial Zone
Qingdao High-tech Industrial Zone
Qingdao Free Trade Zone
Qingdao Special Economic and Technological Development Area
Qingdao West Coast New District

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: Moving around and leaving the city

blocks.x: Qingdao is well connected by road, sea, air and rail, and has a growing metro. The notes below cover each mode.
Roads in the Qingdao area total 1,145 km (711 mi), and close to 500 km (310 mi) of that is expressway. These national expressways start in the city or run through it:
G22 Qinglan Expressway, running from Qingdao as far as Lanzhou in Gansu
G2011 Qingxin Expressway, a spur route linking Qingdao with Xinhe in Pingdu, Shandong
G20 Qingyin Expressway, from Qingdao to Yinchuan in Ningxia
G18 Rongwu Expressway, from Rongcheng in Shandong to Wuhai in Inner Mongolia
G15 Shenhai Expressway, from Shenyang in Liaoning to Haikou in Hainan
Provincial expressways also begin in or cross the city:
S24 Weiqing Expressway, between Weihai and Qingdao
S21 Xinwei Expressway, between Xinhe and Weifang
S19 Longqing Expressway, between Longkou and Qingdao
S16 Rongwei Expressway, between Rongcheng and Weifang
National highways that serve the city are the G204 (Yantai to Shanghai), G206 (Yantai to Shantou), G308 (Qingdao to Shijiazhuang) and G309 (Rongcheng to Lanzhou).

The Haiwan Bridge opened on 30 June 2011 as the longest bridge over water anywhere. Its length is 42.5 km, or 26.4 miles, and it ties Qingdao to Huangdao and Hongdao. The earlier record belonged to the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana, which the new bridge exceeds by almost three miles (4.8 km). Over 5,000 pillars support it, and the cost was about 10 billion yuan, roughly 1.5 billion dollars. The Shandong Gausu Group drew up the design, and construction lasted four years, with at least 10,000 workers in two teams building around the clock from opposite ends. Commuters going between the centre and the sprawling suburb of Huangdao now save half an hour each way.
The Jiaozhou Bay Tunnel opened the same day. It carries public buses and makes crossing between the two shores of the bay easier.

The official name of the port operator is Qingdao Port International Co. Ltd., and the port is one of the busiest in the world. It has working ties with 450 ports in 130 countries, and it forms one link in the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. Annual cargo handling passed 100 million tons for the first time in 2003, when containers reached 3.41 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU). In 2011 the port ranked sixth worldwide by total cargo volume, having moved 372 million metric tons that year (about 366 million long tons, or 410 million short tons), and in 2016 it stood eighth in the world for TEU. Several large neighbouring ports, including Dongjiakou, belong to the same port complex.

Passenger ferries cross to Japan and Korea. The Orient Ferry sails to Shimonoseki, Japan; the New Golden Bridge II runs to Incheon in South Korea; and the Blue Sea Ferry goes to Gunsan, also in South Korea. For a student from either country, this offers an alternative to flying.

Qingdao Jiaodong International Airport lies 39 km (24 mi) from the city centre. The airport opened on August 12, 2021, taking over from Qingdao Liuting International Airport. Thirteen airlines, domestic and foreign, operate 94 routes from it, and 12 of those routes are international or regional.

Rail development accelerated from the late 1990s. Qingdao is the end of the Jinan-Qingdao high-speed railway, the Qingdao-Jinan passenger railway and the original Qingdao-Jinan railway. Major stations in the urban area are Qingdao, Cangkou, Dagang and Qingdao North; Sifang station is closed to passengers. High-speed D and G series trains on the Jinan-Qingdao line travel at up to 300 km/h (190 mph) and call at Tianjin, Hefei, Shanghai, Jinan and Beijing. For the capital, the G206 and G205 are the fastest services, taking 2 hours and 58 minutes. Ordinary rail lines tie Qingdao to Jining, Jinan, Zhengzhou, Xi'an, Chengdu, Lanzhou and Beijing, among other places.

As of 2012 the public bus fleet comprised 5283 large and medium buses running on compressed natural gas, plus 136 trolleybuses. Every bus and trolleybus accepts the contactless 青岛卡, the Qingdao Public Traffic IC Card, which only needs to be held near the reader. All public transport operators now use the Qingdaotong card; the last to adopt it, in 2019, was the Zhenqing bus company in the West Coast New Area (the former Huangdao district). Buses without air-conditioning cost 1 yuan (the tunnel bus excepted), and road passenger transport approaches 737 million trips a year. The 'Ri-Xin Bus' (日新巴士) brand is also well known across China. Taxi firms include Yiqing, Zhongqing, Jiaoyun and Huaqing.

The metro is growing fast. The State Council gave its approval, and on 18 August 2009 the city declared it would invest over 29 billion yuan (US$4.2 billion) in subway construction before 2016. Line 3, the first to function, opened on 16 December 2015; its 54.7 km (34.0 mi) were completed before 2016 for a total of 29.2 billion yuan (US$4.3 billion). Longer term, eight lines are planned for downtown and some suburban districts, adding up to 231.5 km (143.8 mi). One description credits the network with 243 km (151 mi) in operation across Line 1, Line 2, Line 3, Line 4, Line 6, Line 8, the Oceantec Valley Line and the West Coast Line.

A more recent description dates from February 24, 2023. The approved network plan then held 19 long-term lines of 872 kilometres in total. Phase three had been approved, with 13 lines and 503 kilometres, which put the city ninth nationally for approved mileage. Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11 and 13 were carrying passengers over 315 kilometres, and in March 2023 the system had 146 stations, tenth in China and second among northern cities. Ten lines or extensions were under construction, 188 kilometres in all, namely the west extension and phase two of Line 2, Line 5, phases one and two of Line 6, phase two of Line 7, the southern section and a branch of Line 8, and the first phases of Lines 9 and 15; everything is expected to be finished by 2028. The two accounts differ, so treat the exact line list as a snapshot and check the metro operator's current map.

There is also a tram, officially the modern tram demonstration line, in Chengyang District. It opened in 2016 and consists of a single line. Management belongs to the rail bus subsidiary (Rail Bus Co., Ltd.) of the Qingdao Public Transport Group.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: The look and feel of the old town

blocks.x: Qingdao has many German-style buildings in its centre, which is striking given that the German leased-territory period lasted only 16 years (1898-1914). A blend of German and Chinese architecture, together with the German roots of the city and a large Korean expatriate community, gives Qingdao a distinctive atmosphere. An old saying called it the city of 'blue sea, blue sky, green trees and red tiles.' Many areas in former foreign styles have been well preserved. Although the new city is being heavily rebuilt, the old quarter, above all the west end of Shinan District, still has plenty of traditional buildings.
Every August or September since 1991 the city has held its International Beer Festival. In 2014 it also hosted the Qingdao International Horticultural Exposition, a large international fair.
Qingdao has served as a backdrop for several films:
The Wandering Earth 2 (流浪地球2), 2023
A Little Red Flower (送你一朵小红花), 2020
The Great Wall (长城), 2016
A Better Tomorrow 2018 (英雄本色2018), 2016
Ocean Heaven (海洋天堂), 2010
Underdog Fight II (硬汉 II), 2013
Underdog Fight (硬汉), 2008
Beauty Remains (美人依旧), 2005

Names tied to Qingdao include Gao Fenghan (高凤翰), Xiao Hong (萧红), Ma Jun (马军), Duanmu Hongliang (端木蕻良), Ma Jian (马建) and Xiao Jun (萧军). Zou Chenglu (邹承鲁), Erin Pizzey, Toshiro Mifune and Malcolm H. Wiener were born in the city, and the diplomats James R. Lilley and Li Zhaoxing (李肇星) are listed too, as are the businessman Zhang Ruimin (张瑞敏) and the American football kicker Long Ding.

From film, television and music, the list covers Bai Baihe (白百合), Victoria Song (宋茜, of f(x)), Tang Guoqiang (唐国强), Huang Zitao (黄子韬, musician and actor), Xia Yu (夏雨), Li Cunxin (李存信), Huang Bo (黄渤), Ren Jialun (任嘉伦), Chen Hao (陈好), Ni Ping (倪萍), Huang Xiaoming (黄晓明), and Fan Bingbing (范冰冰, born in Qingdao) together with Fan Chengcheng (范丞丞), her younger brother.

Sports names include the table tennis players Zhang Jike (张继科) and Chen Meng (陈梦), the archer Zhang Juanjuan (张娟娟), the chess grandmaster Bu Xiangzhi (卜祥志), and the footballers Hao Haidong (郝海东) and Wang Dong (王栋, a midfielder for Qingdao Huanghai).
Qingdao University of Science and Technology lists 157 programs for international students on this site: 70 bachelor, 73 master's, 10 doctoral, 4 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 154 taught in Chinese, 2 taught in English, 1 taught in Not listed. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 17,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 8,000 to CNY 28,600 (median CNY 20,500), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 10,000 to CNY 28,600 (median CNY 28,600), according to the university's published fee table.

156 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (2):
Chemistry
Mechanical Engineering
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

qingdao-university-of-science-and-techno.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Qingdao University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Qingdao, register at Qingdao University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Qinghai Minzu University is also known in English as Qinghai University for Nationalities. Its Chinese names are 青海民族大学 in simplified characters and 青海民族大學 in traditional characters, and its pinyin is Qīnghǎi Mínzú Dàxúe. It sits in Xining, the capital of Qinghai Province. The institution dates from December 1949, which makes it the first university of higher education ever opened in Qinghai.

Student life depends a great deal on the city outside the campus gates, including its weather, its transport links and its leisure options. The sections below introduce Xining, home of the university.

The city lies in the east of Qinghai Province, beside the Huangshui River, and its four urban districts together cover 343 km2 (132 sq mi). Geographically it occupies the eastern rim of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, along the upper Huangshui, at an average altitude of roughly 2,200 metres (7,200 ft). Newcomers should expect thinner air than they are used to. Xining is the political, economic and cultural centre of the province.

People have lived in this area for about 2,100 years. In the Western and Eastern Han dynasties its growing agriculture drew attention, and its economic and military value was recognised. In ancient times it was a hinge between the Central Plains and western China, and a link on the Silk Road. That role continues: it is still a key rail and road connection to the interior of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

Xining is nicknamed the Summer Resort Capital of China because its summers stay cool. Its climate sits on the border between cold semi-arid (Köppen BSk) and dry-winter humid continental (Dwb), shaped by dryness and altitude. Nights are cool or cold all year round, and the gap between daytime and night-time temperature frequently reaches or passes 15 °C (27 °F), so layers are always useful.
Some figures to plan around:
Daily averages swing between -7.9 °C (17.8 °F) at the coldest, in January, and a July peak of 17.5 °C (63.5 °F).

Over twelve months the mean works out at 6.0 °C (42.8 °F). Judged against the rest of Qinghai that is mild, since the city is low in elevation, and it makes Xining one of the warmer places in the province.

Rain comes mostly between May and September, and the city is often dry and sunny. Sunshine as a share of the possible total is lowest in September (49 percent) and highest in November (67 percent), and over a year it adds up to 2,540 hours of bright sunshine.
The coldest reading on record is -26.6 °C (-16 °F), and the hottest 36.5 °C (98 °F).
Dry winters mean there is very little snow on the ground.

The World Bank put US$1 billion into river treatment around Xining in 2007, covering Sanxian County's anti-flood project, and added a further US$1 billion for infrastructure. Qinghai has put heavy investment into the Huangshui Main River and the Nanchuan River, covering 24.5 km (15.2 mi). Work on a 40 km (25 mi) stretch of river and 10 flash flood relief channels is still waiting because equipment is lacking. Sanxian County has its own backlog: 80 flash flood relief channels and a 108.4 m (356 ft) river course are still untreated.

World Health Organization figures from 2011, drawing on Chinese statistics, ranked Xining's air second worst among eleven western Chinese cities, with an annual mean PM10 of 141 ug/m3. Beijing's level was lower, at 121. It is worth knowing if you are sensitive to pollution.
In 2015 per-capita GDP stood at 49,200 RMB (US$7,897). Traditional strengths include salt, milk, meat, fur, wool spinning and textiles, alongside light processing.

The Xining Economic & Technological Development Zone (XETDZ) won state-level approval in July 2000. Planned to cover 4.4 km2 (1.7 sq mi), it is on the eastern side of the city, 5 km (3.1 mi) out of downtown. It was the first national-level zone of its kind on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, created as part of the national strategy of developing the west.

Transport access is good. The Xining-Lanzhou expressway connects to the zone, and two main roads, the widest in the city, run through it. Xining Airport is 15 km (9.3 mi) off, and the railway station just 4 km (2.5 mi).
The zone focuses on several groups of industries:
Chemicals drawn from salt lake resources, nonferrous metals, and petroleum and natural gas processing
Special medicines, foods and biochemicals that use local plateau plants and animals
New products serving the environment and ecology, plus high technology, advanced materials and IT
Services including logistics, banking, real estate, tourism, hotels, catering, agency work and international trade

The 2020 census counted 2,467,965 people in the prefecture-level city of Xining, up from 2,208,708 in 2010. Of these, 1,954,795 live in the built-up (metro) area of 5 urban districts. The local government currently administers four districts, three counties and the national economic and technological development zone. With more than two million residents, Xining was the first city on the upper Yellow River to reach a population in the millions.

About 37 nationalities live in Xining, though only four are numerically significant: Han, Hui, Monguor (Tu) and Tibetan. Local customs are shaped by Tibetan, Monguor, Muslim and Han influences. In the 2010 census, Han Chinese were 74.04 percent of the city's population. The main minorities were Hui at 16.26 percent, Tibetans at 5.51 percent and Tu at 2.6 percent. As the name Minzu (nationalities) suggests, this variety is part of the university's own setting.

Kumbum Monastery (Ta'er Monastery), in the southwest of the city, is one of six famous monasteries of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, also called the Yellow Hat Sect. Hundreds of monks live there.
Dongguan Mosque, in the city zone, has a history of over 600 years and is among the best-known mosques in northwest China, with splendid and varied towers, walls and halls.
Beishan Si (North Mountain Temple) is a Taoist site and a unique religious structure.
Xining has more than 300 Christian meeting points, and the pre-diocesan Apostolic Prefecture of Xining serves the Catholic minority.
Xining has three universities in all:
Qinghai University
Qinghai Normal University
Qinghai University for Nationalities
For families who want English-language schooling, Xining International Academy is a private international school.

The city fills a fertile basin among mountains, in the Huangshui valley; the Huangshui flows into the Yellow River and works as a river port. About 200 km (120 mi) separates Xining from Lanzhou, Gansu's capital, to the east. The route between them was long the principal trade path from northern China into Tibet and the Qaidam Basin. Modern highways now follow those old routes.

Xining station has been linked since 1959 to China's rail network by the Lanzhou-Qinghai Railway. The line was afterwards extended past Qinghai Lake via Haiyan into the Qaidam area and on to Golmud, and in 2006 reached Lhasa, Tibet, as the Qinghai-Tibet Railway.

The Lanzhou-Xinjiang High-Speed Railway, which opened in December 2014, is the second major line. At first it offered fast trains only to Lanzhou, Urumqi and the stops between them. On 9 July 2017, the opening of the Baoji-Lanzhou high-speed railway tied it into the national high-speed network.
In many Chinese cities conventional and high-speed trains use separate stations, but Xining railway station handles both. A passenger can therefore change here, for instance from Xinjiang to Tibet.
Xining Caojiapu International Airport offers regular passenger flights. Destinations include Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Chengdu, plus Kunming, Xi'an and Wuhan.
These routes serve the city:
China National Highway 214
China National Highway 227
China National Highway 315
G6 Beijing-Lhasa Expressway
The surrounding province affects daily life nearly as much as the campus itself, and Qinghai is large, high and culturally varied.

Bronze Age Qinghai was inhabited by nomadic tribes with close ties to other Central Asian peoples; they farmed and herded animals, and their way of life is called the Kayue culture. The Han dynasty held the eastern part about 2,000 years ago. The land later became a battlefield, as the Tang and the Central Plain dynasties after them repeatedly fought Tibetan tribes here.

Around the mid-3rd century CE, a nomadic people related to the Mongolic Xianbei settled the grasslands near Qinghai Lake (Koko Nur) and founded the Tuyuhun Kingdom. The 7th century brought attacks from two sides, the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty, both hoping to control Silk Road trade. Tibetan King Songtsen Gampo prevailed and settled the shores of Tso ngon, also called Lake Go or Kokonor Lake. Military conflict had badly weakened the Tuyuhun, who were absorbed into the Tibetan Empire. Under Trisong Detsen and Ralpacan the empire spread beyond Tso ngon and until 848 held a vast area to the north and east, Xi'an included.

As the Tibetan Empire broke up, local powers rose while Western Xia to the north and the Song dynasty to the east competed for influence. These ranged from the military rule of the Guiyi Circuit to a Tibetan tribal confederacy and finally the Tibetan theocratic kingdom of Tsongkha. The Song dynasty defeated Tsongkha, the Kokonor kingdom, in the 1070s. When the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty administered Tibet, the territory around the headwaters of the Ma chu (Machu River, the Yellow River) and the Yalong (Yangtze) rivers was called Amdo, though it was split into administrative divisions different from Tibet proper.

After the Yuan fell, the early Ming briefly controlled most of Qinghai, but it was gradually lost to the Khoshut Khanate that the Oirats founded. Most of Qinghai's Salar people now live in Xunhua Salar Autonomous County. They had migrated there from Samarkand in 1370. Han Pao-yuan, who led the four upper clans, was given the office of centurion by the Ming, and his clans adopted Han as a surname. The Ming gave the same office to Han Shan-pa, chief of the four lower clans, whose people took the surname Ma.

Khoshut Mongols held much of present-day Qinghai from 1640 to 1724, when Qing armies conquered it. Xining, today's provincial capital, began to serve as an administrative centre, although officially the city was in Gansu, inside the "Tibetan frontier district". Also in 1724, Nian Gengyao proposed an ordinance of 13 articles on governing Qinghai effectively (青海善后事宜十三条), and the Central Government adopted it to gain complete control.

Under the Qing the governor served as the Emperor's viceroy, yet local ethnic groups kept considerable autonomy. Many chiefs held on to their traditional authority and took part in local government. The Dungan Revolt (1862-1877) wrecked the Hui Muslim community in Shaanxi, and the main Hui population moved to Gansu and Qinghai. A second revolt followed in 1895, with various Muslim peoples across Qinghai and Gansu rebelling against the Qing.

After the Qing fell in 1911, the Chinese Muslim warlord Ma Qi controlled the region until the Republic of China's Northern Expedition consolidated central rule in 1928. In July and August 1912, General Ma Fuxiang had been "Acting Chief Executive Officer of Kokonur", in effect governor of the area that later became Qinghai. Qinghai Province was created in 1928. Ma Qi became military governor; his brother Ma Lin succeeded him, and then Ma Qi's son Ma Bufang took over.

In 1932 Tibet invaded, hoping to seize southern parts of Qinghai after a dispute over a monastery in Yushu. Ma Bufang's army defeated the Tibetan forces. American journalist John Roderick described Ma Bufang as a socialist and friendly compared with the other Ma Clique warlords, and reports call him good-humoured and jovial, unlike the brutal Ma Hongkui. Qinghai stayed relatively untouched while much of eastern China suffered through the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Chinese Civil War.

Ma Bufang raised the political prominence of the Hui and Salar by recruiting heavily for his army from counties where they were the majority. He began a state-run, state-controlled industrialisation project, creating educational, medical, agricultural and sanitation programmes that the state ran or supported. The state paid for food and uniforms in every school, public or private, and roads and a theatre were built. It also controlled the whole press and allowed independent journalists no freedom.

When the 1949 revolution approached Qinghai, Ma Bufang abandoned his post, flew to Hong Kong and travelled overseas, never returning to China. On 1 January 1950 the Qinghai Province People's Government was proclaimed, pledging loyalty to the new People's Republic of China. Apart from small changes to suit the terrain, the new state left the province's territory intact. Opposition to Communist rule persisted through the Kuomintang Islamic insurgency of the Hui (1950-58), which spread beyond Hui areas into the Tibetan south. In 1949 Hui were 15.6% of Qinghai's people, a share exceeded only in Ningxia. Even so, the state denied them the autonomous townships and counties that Chinese law entitled them to, until the 1980s.

Qinghai lies on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau and is the largest province by area in China, not counting autonomous regions. The Yellow River starts in the south of the province, and the Yangtze and the Mekong rise in the southwest. The Riyue Mountain divides the province into a pastoral zone in the west and an agricultural zone in the east.

The Sanjiangyuan National Nature Reserve holds the headwaters of the Yellow, Yangtze and Mekong rivers and was created to protect them. It has 18 subareas, each made up of three zones with different levels of strict management.

China's biggest salt water lake is Qinghai Lake, and globally it ranks second. Further large lakes are Lake Hala in the Qilian mountains, Gyaring and Ngoring at the Yellow River's source, Lake Donggi Cona, and numerous salt lakes across the west. In the northwest, the resource-rich Qaidam basin sits at 3000 to 5000 meters above sea level, and roughly a third of it is desert.

Qinghai averages about 3000 m in elevation. Its mountain ranges include the Tanggula and Kunlun ranges, and the highest peak is Bukadaban Feng at 6860 m. Because it is so high, winters are quite cold, and harsh at the highest elevations, summers are mild and temperatures swing widely between day and night. Yearly mean temperature falls between roughly -5 and 8 °C (23 to 46 °F). January readings run -18 to -7 °C (0 to 19 °F), while in July they reach 15 to 21 °C (59 to 70 °F). Strong winds and sandstorms are common from February to April. Most rain falls in summer, and with very little in winter and spring, much of the province stays semi-arid or arid.

Qinghai has a population of 5.6 million and more than 37 recognised ethnic groups. Han people are 50.5% and ethnic minorities 49.5%. In 2010, the largest groups after the Han were Tibetans at 20.7%, Hui at 16% and Tu (Monguor) at 4%, along with some Mongol and Salar communities. Han Chinese are the majority in the northeast and in the cities of Xining, Haidong, Delingha and Golmud.

Hui communities cluster in Xining, Haidong, and Minhe, Hualong and Datong counties. Huzhu County is mostly Tu and Xunhua County mostly Salar, and Tibetans and Mongols are scattered thinly through the rural west. Four Muslim groups live in the province (Hui, Salar, Dongxiang and Bao'an), and Hui traders dominate wholesale business.

The Han mostly follow Chinese folk religion, which includes Taoist and Confucian traditions, or Chinese Buddhism. The many Tibetans practise Tibetan Buddhism or the traditional Bön religion, and the Hui are Muslim. A 2004 Chinese General Social Survey put Christians at 0.76% of the province, and a 2010 survey found 17.51% follow Islam.

Historically, Xining was from September 1848 the seat of a short-lived Latin Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of Kokonur (also spelt Khouhkou-noor or Kokonoor), a pre-diocesan missionary jurisdiction. It was suppressed in 1861, and no incumbents are recorded.

Qinghai Minzu University gives you a degree in a city of high altitude, cool summers and rich cultural mixing, linked by rail and air to the rest of China. Expect dry, sunny weather, cold winters and a community where Han, Hui, Tibetan and Tu traditions all matter.
Qinghai Minzu University lists 44 programs for international students on this site: 3 bachelor, 19 master's, 22 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 44 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,800 to CNY 14,800 (median CNY 14,800), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.

44 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

qinghai-minzu-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Qinghai Minzu University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Xining, register at Qinghai Minzu University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Qinghai University, abbreviated QHU (青海大学, Qīnghǎi Dàxué), is the leading provincial public university of Qinghai and stands in Xining, the provincial capital on the Tibetan Plateau. The Province of Qinghai is its home authority, and the Qinghai provincial government shares sponsorship with China's Ministry of Education. National programmes recognise it twice over, through Project 211 and through the Double First-Class Construction drive, which gives it a place among the few western universities with central-government support.

QHU was founded in 1958. The university's own July 2020 figures describe a sizeable institution. There are 15 colleges and 26 departments. Over 27,000 students are taught by 4,615 staff. On the academic side it lists 5 doctoral authorization points, 57 master's authorization points and 40 master's fields. The undergraduate major count is given as 67 in one place and 69 in another, so ask the admissions office for the current number if it matters to your plans.

qinghai-university.h: Where it stands and how it started

blocks.x: Among the universities of Qinghai Province, QHU is the one on the Tibetan Plateau at Xining, and its opening year was 1958. Its grounds take up over 2,692 acres (10.89 km2), spread across five districts. In April 2018 the count stood at 14 professional research institutes, 15 colleges and 26 departments, offering 69 undergraduate majors.

Staff in April 2018 totalled 4,615. The figure includes 2,565 medical and full-time scientific research personnel and 1,467 full-time teachers; 329 of those teachers are doctorate holders, and 87 per cent have a master's degree or higher.

Seven academicians who hold dual posts work with the university, alongside one full academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Four specially appointed professors come under the Ministry of Education's "Changjiang Scholars Award Program". Two winners of the National "Outstanding Youth Fund" have been picked for national schemes (the "Ten Thousand Talents Program", the "National Hundreds and Thousand Talents Project" and the "New Century Excellent Talents Support Program"). In all, 20 people count as talents at national level, and 31 draw the State Council's "Special Allowance".

Prizes won by staff are varied: the National Innovation Award; a science and technology innovation award from Hong Kong's Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation; a young teacher award from the Fok Ying Tung Education Foundation; a contribution award for innovative talents from the Chinese overseas Chinese community; and in basic medicine, awards from the Three World National Academy of Sciences, described as the only prize of its kind. Eleven people have won awards in this last group. Beyond these, over 30 people are recognised national or provincial teaching teachers, outstanding teachers or educators, and more than 60 are provincial outstanding experts or technical professionals. Qinghai's "135" plans list 9 team projects, and there are over 160 high-level talents and provincial leaders in natural science and engineering technology. A Ministry of Education Innovative Team Development Plan includes one team, a second team is a "National University Huang Danian Teacher Team", and 16 research teams carry the title "Qinghai Province Talent Highland".
The people behind these honours, by category:
The one academician is Wang Guangqian, who is supported by Tsinghua University.
Xiao Lu is the university's single Top Young Talent in the Organization Department's "Ten Thousand Talents Program".
Two winners of the National Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars: Chen Wenguang and Mei Shengwei.

Of the 31 State Council Special Allowance experts, those named are Wei Dengbang, Tie Shengnian, Tang Daocheng, Geng Paili, Gerili, Yu Hongxian, Zhou Qingping, Zhang Yongcheng, Zhang Dengshan, Zhang Caijun, Chen Gang, Du Dezhi, Li Jie, Li Lirong, Chi Dezhao, Xu Cunhe, Liu Qingyuan, Liu Hongxing, Liu Shujie, Daga, Deng Yong, Wen Shaodun, Wang Chunying, Wang Jianjun, Wang Jian, Mao Xuerong, Ma Xiaogang and Ma Yushou, with others besides.
Liu Yujiao and Du Dezhi were both selected for the New Century Talent Project (2 people).
Qi Delin is the one person in the Ministry of Science and Technology's Innovative Talent Promotion Plan.
Gree Li and Du Dezhi are counted as National Outstanding Professional and Technical Talents (2 people).
Greeley and Du Dezhi won the Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation award from Hong Kong (2 winners).
Chen Yonghua and Zhang Hongyan hold the Fok Ying Tung Education Foundation Young Teacher Award (2 people).

The July 2020 tally of disciplines is as follows: one world-class discipline under construction, two domestic first-class disciplines, one first-class discipline at provincial level, two national key disciplines and sixteen provincial key disciplines. For degree rights, QHU has 5 doctoral authorization points, 17 at first-level master's, 136 at second-level master's, and 9 professional master's categories spanning 50 fields, together with a single post-doctoral research mobile station.
The discipline in the world-class construction scheme is ecology.
Two disciplines are national key ones, counting those still in cultivation: altitude medicine within internal medicine, and breeding and genetics of crops.

The provincial key list is long. On the farming side it takes in agronomy, horticulture, animal science, animal medicine and grassland science. Engineering is represented by civil engineering, water conservancy and hydropower, mechanical manufacturing and automation, and chemical engineering and technology. In health, basic medicine, preventive medicine and Tibetan medicine appear. Business administration and regional economics round it out, with others too.
The first-level doctoral programme is in crop science.
At second level, doctoral study is open in ethnic (Tibetan) medicine, high-altitude internal medicine, pasture genetics and farming, plus crop genetics and breeding and crop cultivation and farming.

At first-level master's level the fields are crop science, forestry, grassland science, landscape architecture, basic medicine, business administration, mechanical engineering, water conservancy engineering, geological resources and engineering, and chemical engineering and technology.
The pattern is easy to read. QHU is strongest where the plateau itself matters: ecology, grassland and crop science, high-altitude and Tibetan medicine, and the engineering of water and resources.

Teaching quality is documented too. As of July 2020 the university counted 6 sites for national characteristic professional construction, 4 national teaching teams, 5 national first-class majors, 9 national excellence plan projects and one each of the following: a national talent training model innovation experimental zone, a national experimental teaching demonstration center, a national quality bilingual demonstration course, a national off-campus practice education base for college students and a national comprehensive professional reform project. Online, there are 3 national quality video open courses and 1 national quality online open course. Highlights:
Subjects designated national specialties: economics, resource exploration engineering, preventive medicine, Tibetan medicine, grassland science and chemical engineering technology.
The national teaching teams are in basic medicine and in Tibetan medicine.
Its national excellent course is Tibetan Medicine and Pharmacology.
The national experimental teaching demonstration center covers Tibetan medicine.
Management is the national bilingual teaching demonstration course.
The Agricultural Products Quality and Safety Risk Assessment Laboratory (Xining), under the Ministry of Agriculture, is a key laboratory.
A Ministry of Education pilot reform project explores new ways of training Tibetan medicine talent in Tibetan areas.

Provincial demonstration centres for experimental teaching cover Tibetan medicine, basic medicine, biological science, chemistry and chemical engineering, and electrical and electronic work, with more besides. Provincial quality courses are spread across many subjects. Medicine and science are represented by Basic Traditional Chinese Medicine, Tibetan Medicine Prescriptions, Immunology, Pathology, Epidemiology, Internal Medicine, Botany, Analytical Chemistry and Livestock Anatomy and Histology. Engineering and computing courses include soil mechanics and basic engineering, civil engineering materials, automatic control theory, Engineering Training, basic programming and Computer Basics. The list continues with College English, Enterprise Strategic Management, statistics and others.

Within China, counterpart support comes from Tsinghua University, Northwest A&F University, East China University of Science and Technology and the China University of Geosciences (Beijing). Overseas, QHU has set up good working relations with well-known universities, for example MIT in the United States, Kochi University (Japan) and Oakland University (New Zealand). Universities in more than 20 countries and regions have signed exchange and cooperation agreements: Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US are among them.

A joint key laboratory for plateau medicine was created in 2014 with the University of Utah, and a new round of "Three Brothers" cooperation began that year among Tsinghua University, Auckland University and Qinghai University. Two alliances, one led by QHU (the "Qinghai-Utah Technology Innovation Alliance") and a US partner called the "Utah-Qinghai Industrial Technology Innovation Strategic Alliance", entered the Sino-US Green Partnership and were written into a ten-year framework for energy and environmental cooperation between the two countries. The work covers medicine, the salt-lake chemical industry and the ecological environment.

The university's website, as of October 2017, says it has joined the "121" dual-degree programme of the China Educational International Exchange Association (CEAIE), and signed agreements under the "China Talent Training Program" run by the China Education Exchange Center (CCIEE). Routes for study abroad and exchange now exist with universities in Britain, New Zealand, Turkmenistan, Taiwan and the United States. Progress has been reported in joint training of students abroad, the China Scholarship Council's high-level university graduate programme, status as a Chinese government scholarship institution, the admission of international students, and student exchanges with Taiwan. For overseas applicants, the Chinese government scholarship status is the most relevant of these.

By the end of 2017 the library's paper holdings came to 1.67 million documents, 880,000 of them belonging to the school's own collection. Subjects run to over a dozen: science, engineering and agriculture, then literature, history, classics, philosophy and law, and finally education, management and medicine. It subscribes to 77 well-known domestic and foreign databases and has 800,000 kinds of e-books and nearly 48,000 kinds of e-journals.

Among its academic journals are the Journal of Qinghai University and the Journal of Qinghai University Medical College, as well as periodicals for animal husbandry and veterinary medicine and for agriculture and forestry science and technology in Qinghai. The Journal of Qinghai University is a general natural-science journal that started in January 1983 under the title Journal of Qinghai Institute of Technology; it took its present name in 1988 after the university's name changed. The facilities are well equipped, notably in science and technology.

Statistics on the school's website (June 2016) report 1,452 research projects of different levels in recent years, backed by 470 million yuan. Of them, 289 are national-level, taken from schemes such as the National Natural Science Foundation, the National Philosophy and Social Science Foundation, the 863 high-tech programme, the 973 basic research programme and the Science and Technology Support Plan. Completed work totals 790 projects, yielding 488 results, which include 10 and 32 rated internationally advanced in two categories, and 35 new plant varieties.

Honours total: one National Science and Technology Progress Award (plus a second prize), two National Teaching Achievement Awards, two Ministry of Education first prizes for Science and Technology Progress, two Major Contribution Awards for Science and Technology in Qinghai, 35 provincial science and technology progress awards and 13 provincial awards in philosophy and the social sciences. Staff have published over 7,900 academic papers at home and abroad, including 3 in Science and Nature. A building and development plan for the 21st century has been drawn up and is being carried out.

Qinghai University regularly ranks first among universities in Qinghai. Since 2019 it has been among the top 300 in the Best Chinese Universities Ranking, also called the "Shanghai Ranking", and in 2023 that ranking placed it 205th in China. In the global University Rankings by Academic Performance for 2023 to 2024 it came 1373rd.
Student life depends a great deal on the city around the campus, so here is what to expect from Xining: the setting, climate, air, economy, people, religion and transport.

Xining sits in the east of Qinghai, beside the Huangshui River. Its four urban districts add up to 343 km2 (132 sq mi). The city lies at the plateau's eastern edge and the Huangshui's upper reaches, roughly 2,200 m (7,200 ft) up on average, and it is Qinghai's centre for politics, business and culture.

People have lived in the region for about 2,100 years. Under the Western and Eastern Han dynasties, Xining attracted attention for its developing agriculture and its economic and military value. In antiquity it was a vital pivot between the Central Plains and the west of China, and a link in the Silk Road. Today it is still a significant rail and road junction toward the interior of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

Cool summers have earned Xining the title "Summer Resort Capital of China". By classification the climate is cold semi-arid at the margin (Köppen BSk), or dry-winter humid continental (Dwb); dryness and altitude shape it. Nights are cold or cool all year, and day-to-night swings often reach or pass 15 °C (27 °F).

January averages -7.9 °C (17.8 °F) over 24 hours and July 17.5 °C (63.5 °F); across the year it is 6.0 °C (42.8 °F), warm by Qinghai standards given the low elevation. Most rain comes between May and September, but sunny, dry days are frequent. Possible sunshine varies from 49 per cent in September to 67 per cent in November, adding up to 2,540 hours a year. The recorded extremes are -26.6 °C (-16 °F) and 36.5 °C (98 °F). Because winters are dry, snow cover is very thin.

The World Bank lent US$1 billion in 2007 for river treatment in Xining, including a flood-prevention project in Sanxian County, and added another US$1 billion for infrastructure. Large sums have been invested by Qinghai in the main Huangshui and the Nanchuan River, 24.5 km (15.2 mi) in all. Still, treatment of a 40 km (25 mi) stretch of river and of 10 flash-flood relief channels is on hold for lack of equipment. In Sanxian County a river course (given as 108.4 m, or 356 ft, long) and 80 flash-flood relief channels still need work.

A 2011 World Health Organization report, using Chinese statistics, ranked Xining second worst for air quality among eleven western Chinese cities, with an annual mean PM10 of 141 micrograms per cubic metre. That was worse than Beijing's 121. Check current readings, since conditions can differ from year to year.
In 2015 per-capita GDP was 49,200 RMB, or US$7,897. Local industry is built on salt, milk, meat, fur, wool spinning and textiles, along with light processing.

qinghai-university.h: The Economic and Technological Development Zone

blocks.x: The state approved the Xining Economic and Technological Development Zone (XETDZ) in July 2000. Its planned area is 4.4 km2 (1.7 sq mi) in the east of town, 5 km (3.1 mi) from the centre. As the plateau's first zone at national level, it was built to carry out the strategy of developing the west.

Transport is convenient: the Xining-Lanzhou expressway connects to it and two main roads, the broadest in the city, run through it. The railway station is 4 km (2.5 mi) away and the airport 15 km (9.3 mi). Four lines of business are promoted:
salt-lake-based chemicals, along with non-ferrous metals and oil and gas processing;
medicines, foods and biochemicals that use animals and plants of the plateau;
products for ecological and environmental protection, plus high-tech, new-material and IT products;
services such as logistics, banking, property, tourism, hotels, catering, agency work and international trade.

The 2020 census gave the prefecture-level city of Xining 2,467,965 people, up from 2,208,708 in 2010. Of them, 1,954,795 live in the built-up (metro) area made up of 5 urban districts. Local government covers four districts, three counties and a national economic and technological development zone. Xining, with over two million inhabitants, was the earliest city along the upper Yellow River to reach millions.

About 37 nationalities live in Xining, though only Han, Hui, Monguor (Tu) and Tibetans are numerous. Local customs reflect Tibetan, Monguor, Muslim and Han influences. In the 2010 census, Han Chinese were 74.04 per cent of the population, with the main minorities being Hui (16.26 per cent), Tibetans (5.51 per cent) and Tu (2.6 per cent).

In the southwest of the city stands Kumbum Monastery (Ta'er Monastery), home to hundreds of monks and counted among the six famous monasteries of the Gelug (Yellow Hat) school. The Dongguan Mosque, with over 600 years of history, is in the city zone and ranks among the best-known mosques of northwest China, with fine and varied towers, walls and halls. Beishan Si (North Mountain Temple) is a unique Taoist site. Christians have more than 300 meeting points in the city, and the Catholic minority is served by the Apostolic Prefecture of Xining, which predates a diocese.

Higher education in the city comprises Qinghai Normal University, Qinghai University for Nationalities and QHU itself. Families may be interested that an English-language school, Xining International Academy, also operates here.

qinghai-university.h: Getting to Xining and around it

blocks.x: The city occupies a fertile basin among mountains, in the Huangshui valley; this river, a tributary of the Yellow River, works as a river port. Xining is around 200 km (120 mi) to the west of Lanzhou (Gansu's capital) along what was historically the principal trade route between northern China and both Tibet and the Qaidam Basin. Today's highways follow those paths.

Xining station has been linked to China's rail network by the Lanzhou-Qinghai Railway since 1959. That line was later extended into the Qaidam area through Haiyan, near Qinghai Lake, to Golmud, and in 2006 on to Lhasa in Tibet (see the Qinghai-Tibet Railway).

A second main line is the Lanzhou-Xinjiang High-Speed Railway, which opened in December 2014. At first it gave high-speed service only to Lanzhou and Urumqi, with points between, but the opening of the Baoji-Lanzhou high-speed railway on 9 July 2017 connected it to the national high-speed network.

Unlike many Chinese cities, where ordinary and high-speed trains use separate stations, Xining railway station handles both kinds. It is therefore a handy transfer point, for example for someone travelling from Xinjiang to Tibet.
Scheduled passenger flights from Xining Caojiapu International Airport reach big Chinese cities: Wuhan, Xi'an, Kunming, Chengdu, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Beijing.
Main roads serving Xining include China National Highways 214, 227 and 315 and the G6 Beijing-Lhasa Expressway.
