Qiqihar University (QQHRU; 齐齐哈尔大学, pinyin Qíqíhār Dàxué) is a public university run by the Province of Heilongjiang. It sits in Qiqihar, in the west of Heilongjiang in northeastern China, and the provincial government pays for it.

For a prospective student it helps to know three things up front. The university is a regional institution created by combining older colleges. Its campus is built around a lake. And the city and province are cold-winter, industrial and agricultural parts of China's northeast, so this profile spends time on the climate, economy and transport as well as the university itself.

qiqihar-university.h: How the university was formed and what the campus is like

blocks.x: Qiqihar University was established in 1996 by merging two colleges: Qiqihar Light Industry College (founded 1952) and Qiqihar Normal College (founded 1958). The merging did not stop there. Keshan Normal College came in later, and so did two provincial vocational schools, one for commerce and trade and one for the chemical industry, both in Heilongjiang.

The campus lies beside Labor Lake in Qiqihar and covers 1.25 square kilometres, with 720,000 square metres of buildings. Its nickname is "The Round Lake University". Honours include "Garden University" and "Provincial Model Unit", both awarded by the CPC committee for Heilongjiang and by the provincial government.
Qiqihar has many schools: four elementary schools lead into 8 high schools run by the city or its counties. Two universities are located here, Qiqihar University and its medical school.

The land under the city's administration totals 42,289 square kilometres (16,328 sq mi). Heights above sea level range between 100 and 500 metres and average 146 metres, although a regional figure gives the typical range as 200 to 500 m (660 to 1,600 ft). The city stretches along the middle and lower Nen River in the heart of the Songnen Plain, next to the Greater Khingan Range and the Hulunbuir Prairie.
Its neighbouring prefecture-level cities and regions are:
Baicheng, Jilin, to the south
Daqing, to the east
Heihe, to the north
Suihua, to the northeast
Hulunbuir, Inner Mongolia, to the west
Hinggan League, Inner Mongolia, also to the west

Distances from the metropolitan area help to place it. Harbin, the provincial capital, is 359 km (223 mi) away. Closest of the four is Daqing at 139 km (86 mi); Baicheng is 282 km (175 mi) off, and Suihua is farther at 328 km (204 mi).

The four seasons are distinct, and the climate type is humid continental with monsoon influence and cold winters (Köppen Dwa). Expect a long, very cold, dry winter, when January's 24-hour mean sits at -18.1 °C (-0.6 °F). Between the extremes, spring and autumn are short, mild and quick to pass. July is very warm and humid at 23.3 °C (73.9 °F) on average, and over the whole year the mean is 4.38 °C (39.9 °F).

Rainfall averages 415 millimetres (16.3 in) a year, with more than two-thirds from June to August. Sunshine is generous, at 2,839 hours of bright sun over the year; July has the lowest possible-sunshine share (56%) and February the highest (73%). The coldest day on record was 8 January 1956 at -39.5 °C (-39 °F), the hottest 26 June 1980 at 42.1 °C (108 °F). Unusually, for so cold a city, it has never seen a reading of -40 degrees (Celsius or Fahrenheit, which coincide there) or below.

In the Seventh national census the population was 4,067,489. Ten years earlier the Sixth national census (2010) had found 5,367,003 people, so the city lost 1,299,514 residents, which is 24.21% and works out as an annual rate of -2.73%. Men numbered 2,044,598 (50.27%) and women 2,022,891 (49.73%). The sex ratio, with women as 100, went from 102.00 in 2010 to 101.07.

The city is heavily industrial, with manufacturing at its core. In 2009 its 95 large equipment-manufacturing enterprises held 30.6 billion yuan in total assets, 46.5% of the assets of all the city's industrial enterprises above the designated size. The workforce they employed, reported as 5.2 million, was 45.6% of the employment in those larger firms. Income from the main business reached 25.57 billion yuan. Industrial added value was 8.05 billion yuan, with 1.96 billion yuan in profit and 1.03 billion yuan paid in tax. Against the year before, the growth rates were 2.9% (income), 3% (added value), 19.6% (profit) and 22.3% (tax), and the shares of the city's larger industrial enterprises were 40.6%, 40%, 44.3% and 31.7% respectively.

For everyday needs, the city has 23 hospitals. Retailers with a presence include Walmart, RT-Mart, Suning Commerce Group and GOME Electrical Appliances. Being a large city, it hosts many banks as well: for example Agricultural Bank of China, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, China Construction Bank and Bank of China.
Two attractions are close to the city: the Zhalong Nature Reserve and Longsha park.
Domestic flights use Qiqihar Sanjiazi Airport, 13 km (8.1 mi) from downtown, with daily departures for Shanghai, Guangzhou, Beijing and other large cities.

Qiqihar is well connected by train. Qiqihar Railway Station sends trains to Harbin and Beijing, and also to Xi'an, Hangzhou, Dalian and several other big cities. Two lines cross at Ang'angxi district: the Harbin-Manzhouli Railway and the Qiqihar-Bei'an Railway. A newer intercity railway between Harbin and Qiqihar, opened on 17 August 2015, runs fast trains often and a few of them go straight through to Beijing.
The Nen River carries freight.

qiqihar-university.h: Heilongjiang: the province around the campus

blocks.x: A university's province shapes student life as much as its campus does, so here is a closer look at Heilongjiang, covering its past, landscape, economy, population and culture.

qiqihar-university.h: Early peoples and the creation of the province

blocks.x: Ancient Chinese and other records say that peoples such as the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan lived in Heilongjiang, while the Inner Mongolia and the west of Heilongjiang were home to the Mongolic Donghu, and some local names derive from Manchu or Mongolian. From the 7th to the 10th century the Bohai Kingdom controlled the east, with the Khitan Liao dynasty afterwards. The Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115 to 1234) later ruled a large part of northern China, yet it first rose inside what is now Heilongjiang.

Heilongjiang became an administrative unit in 1683, under the Kangxi emperor in the Manchu Qing period, taken from northwestern Jilin province. This first Heilongjiang covered only the western part of today's province. Its overseer was a military governor, titled the General of Heilongjiang in Manchu (Sahaliyan Ula i Jiyanggiyūn). That word is the Manchu rendering of the Chinese 將軍 (jiāngjūn), "general" or "military leader", and is related to the Japanese shōgun. In line with the Treaty of Nerchinsk, his power stretched north to the Stanovoy Mountains. Today's eastern Heilongjiang belonged instead to the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn), whose reach went all the way to the Sea of Japan. These deep Manchurian lands were closed to Han Chinese settlement.

qiqihar-university.h: Why the capital moved to Qiqihar

blocks.x: The Military Governor's first seat in 1683 was Heilongjiang City (also called Aigun or Heihe, and Saghalien Ula in Manchu) on the Amur River. Within seven years, in 1690, the seat went to Nenjiang (Mergen), also on the Nen River, and then in 1699 it came south again to Qiqihar. Modern historians suggest supply was the reason. Nenjiang and Qiqihar are linked to southern Manchuria by the convenient Nen River waterway, whereas to reach Aigun (Heihe) you had to go all the way down the Sungari to its junction with the Amur and back up that river, or haul goods overland over the Lesser Xing'an Mountains separating the two valleys. Another plus for Qiqihar could have been its position where the road north to Nenjiang met the road west to Mongolia, letting its garrison guard against both the Russians and the Ölöt Mongols.

The Qing had little military presence north of Aigun. European sources from the 18th and early 20th centuries and Russian reports from the 1850s put the farthest Qing outpost at Ulusu-Modon (Ulussu-Mudan; 乌鲁苏穆丹, Wūlǔsūmùdān), near the famous S-shaped bend of the Amur. That post stood on the left (north) bank and passed to the Russians in 1860.

qiqihar-university.h: Borders, migration and the twentieth century

blocks.x: In 1858 and again in 1860 the Qing had to hand the Russian Empire every territory beyond the Amur and Ussuri, so the empire lost its access to the Sea of Japan and Heilongjiang acquired the northern and eastern borders it has now. Manchuria was opened at that time to Han Chinese migration, and through the Chuang Guandong movement the Han had become the dominant ethnic group by the early 20th century.

Japanese forces invaded Heilongjiang in 1931 and had completed their conquest of the province by 1932, when it became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army beat the Japanese in Manchuria in 1945 and supported the communists in the civil war that followed. Heilongjiang was the first province to fall entirely under communist control, and Harbin was their first major city.

At the start of communist rule, Heilongjiang covered only the western part of today's province, with Qiqihar as capital, and the rest was Songjiang province with its capital at Harbin. In 1954 the two were merged to make today's Heilongjiang. The province also grew during the Cultural Revolution to include Hulunbuir League and other areas formerly in Inner Mongolia, though that has mostly been undone.

Heilongjiang has varied terrain. Much of it is mountainous, including the Greater and Lesser Khingan Ranges and the Zhangguangcai, Laoye and Wanda Mountains. Datudingzi Mountain, at 1,690 metres (5,540 ft) on the border with Jilin, is the tallest. The Greater Khingan Range holds China's biggest remaining virgin forest and is important for the country's forestry.

The flatter, lower east and southwest have the Muling, Naoli, Songhua, Nen and Mudan Rivers, all of them flowing into the Amur, which itself forms the valley along part of the northern border. On the Russian border, next to Primorsky Krai, is Xingkai Lake, also called Khanka Lake.

Most of the province is humid continental (Köppen Dwa or Dwb), but the far north is subarctic (Köppen Dwc). January is long and bitterly cold, averaging between -31 and -15 °C (-24 to 5 °F); July is warm to very warm but short, at 18 to 23 °C (64 to 73 °F). Rain totals 400 to 700 millimetres (16 to 28 in) a year, falling mainly in summer, and there are around 2,300 to 2,650 hours of sun, and in spring the Songnen and Sanjiang Plains offer abundant wind energy.
The largest cities are Harbin and Qiqihar, then Mudanjiang, Jiamusi, Daqing, Jixi, Shuangyashan, Hegang, Qitaihe, Yichun and Heihe.

Its road network was 165,989 km (103,141 mi) long as of October 2020, counting expressways, highways and other roads. The main corridor into the province is the Beijing-Harbin Expressway, running from the Heilongjiang-Jilin border to the Harbin Ring Expressway. The Harbin-Tongjiang Expressway goes northeast to link remote counties under Harbin, Jiamusi and others in the northeast. Near its end, the Jiansanjiang-Heixiazi Island Expressway branches off at Jiansanjiang to serve state-owned farms in the far east, ending near the Sino-Russian border. Another main corridor, the Suifenhe-Manzhouli Expressway, runs southeast to northwest through Mudanjiang, Harbin, Daqing and Qiqihar before reaching the border with Inner Mongolia. To carry lumber and coal in the east, the Hegang-Dalian Expressway links Hegang with the Jilin border.

The rail system has 60 lines totalling about 5,300 kilometres (3,300 miles); part of the Eurasian Land Bridge is among them. The Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway, finished in 2012, links Harbin to Dalian in Liaoning via Changchun and Shenyang with 23 stops. Forecasts were for 37 million passengers annually by 2020 and 51 million by 2030.

Main airports are Harbin Taiping International, Qiqihar, Mudanjiang, Jiamusi and Heihe. The Harbin airport has a capacity of six million passengers yearly and flies to more than 70 cities at home and abroad.

Valery Solomonovich Gurevich, vice-chairman of Russia's Jewish Autonomous Oblast, proposed the Tongjiang-Nizhneleninskoye railway bridge in 2007. The bridge over the Amur will connect the village of Nizhneleninskoye, in the Oblast, to Tongjiang. The Chinese part was finished in July 2016 and work on the Russian part started in December 2016. The two sides were structurally joined in March 2019. Opening has been put back more than once: the December 2019 estimate was the end of 2020, then the third quarter of 2021.

Heilongjiang's GDP for 2022 came to 1.59 trillion RMB, which is US$236 billion at nominal rates, and per-person GDP was CN¥51,906 (US$7,717 nominal). By sector, services contributed ¥764 billion (48%), industry ¥465 billion (29.2%) and primary industry ¥360 billion (22.7%). The economy has grown steadily from 2003, when it was 443.3 billion yuan, to 707.72 billion yuan in 2007, a rise of 60%. The private economy was worth RMB234 billion in 2006, 37.6 percent of GDP, and private enterprises paid RMB20.5 billion in tax that year. Private firms have led the province's growth, and many strong ones are emerging.

No other province grows more rice, corn or soybeans. In all, grain covers 14.37 million ha (35.5 million acres); rice occupies 4 million ha (9.9 million acres) of that, and corn takes up 5.5 million ha (14 million acres). It has huge areas of black soil (chernozem), among the most fertile soils. Cultivation of the black soil belt has grown almost 100-fold since the early 20th century, and after the 1960s farming became heavily mechanised with more fertiliser. The province is one of Asia's leading producers of japonica rice, known for high-quality brands, and cold-resistant varieties, favourable policies and climate change have lifted production in recent years. Beets, flax and sunflowers are also grown.

Lumber is another important product, chiefly Korean pine and larch from the Greater and Lesser Khingan Mountains, where protected species such as the Siberian tiger, red-crowned crane and lynx live. Herding centres on horses and cattle, and the province has more milk cows than any other province-level division in China.

Heilongjiang belongs to the Northeast, China's traditional industrial base, with industry built on coal, petroleum, lumber, machinery and food. It is also a gateway for trade with Russia. After privatisation closed uncompetitive factories in the 1990s, Manchuria stagnated, and the government responded with the Revitalize Northeast China campaign, which favours the private sector as the route to reform and opening up.

Petroleum is of great importance, with the Daqing oilfields a key national source. Coal, gold and graphite are other minerals, and the province has big wind-power potential, with a possible capacity of 134 gigawatts.

At the end of 2022 Heilongjiang had 30.99 million permanent residents, 260,000 fewer than the year before. The urban population was 20.52 million and the rural population 10.47 million, which puts urbanisation at 66.2% (an increase of half a percentage point). Children aged 0 to 14 made up 9.3% and people aged 65 and over 17.8%. The 2021 Statistical Bulletin gave a permanent population of 31.25 million, 460,000 fewer than in 2020.
The Seventh National Population Census (2020) counted 31,850,088, down 6,463,903 (-16.87%) from 38,313,991 in 2010, an average annual rate of -1.83%. The 2020 breakdown:
Sex: 15,952,468 men (50.09%) against 15,897,620 women (49.91%), a sex ratio of 100.35 with women as 100
Ages 60 and over: 7,395,690 (23.22%), of whom 4,972,868 were 65 or older (15.61%)
Place of residence: 20,897,694 in cities and towns (65.61%), 10,952,394 in the countryside (34.39%)

The 2020 figures were 3.35 births and 8.23 deaths per thousand people, so natural growth was -4.48 per thousand. The province combines low birth and death rates with a very old population, and out-migration has pushed the total down continuously since 2014.

Most residents have no religion or follow Chinese folk religion, including Taoism. Many Manchu people practise Manchu shamanism, and Chinese and Tibetan Buddhism have a notable presence. Culturally, Heilongjiang belongs to the fairly uniform culture of Northeast China, called "Dongbei" in Mandarin.
Heilongjiang leads China in promoting winter sports and the winter sports industry, and it is campaigning for bandy to become an Olympic sport.

Qiqihar University offers a lakeside campus in a quiet, industrial, cold-climate city, with good rail and air links. Bring clothing for temperatures that sit well below freezing for much of the winter, and expect warm, humid summers with most rain in June to August.

Practical points to remember: the city's population has been shrinking, Harbin is the nearest provincial hub (359 km away) and the intercity high-speed line makes the trip straightforward, and the Zhalong Nature Reserve and Longsha park are the local places to spend a free afternoon. Most international applicants will find the winters the biggest adjustment, so plan your wardrobe and your arrival date with that in mind.
Qiqihar University lists 76 programs for international students on this site: 3 bachelor, 73 master's programs.

By language of instruction: 51 taught in Chinese, 25 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.

Renmin University of China, usually shortened to RUC, sits in Beijing's Haidian district and is run as a public institution. It reports to the Ministry of Education, which shares the funding with the Beijing Municipal People's Government. For a student weighing options, it helps to know that RUC belongs to the national Project 211 and Project 985 groups and to the Double First-Class Construction programme, which together mark it as one of the state's priority universities.

Its reputation rests mostly on the social sciences, law, business and the humanities, and the sections below explain where it came from, what it teaches, where you would live and study, and what the surrounding city is like.

renmin-university-of-china.h: From a wartime school to a national key university

blocks.x: Renmin's roots go back to 1937, when the Chinese Communist Party opened Shanbei Public School (陕北公学) in the north of Shaanxi. Its declared aim was to educate huge numbers of revolutionary cadres who could meet the needs of the wartime struggle against Japan's invasion. Over the following years the school changed its name twice, first to North China United University and later simply North China University.
Several institutions came together in 1950 to form one Renmin University of China. Four years on, in 1954, it was designated a national key university, the youngest of the six given that status.

Presidents over the decades have included Wu Yuzhang, Cheng Fangwu and Guo Yingqiu, followed by Yuan Baohua, Huang Da and Li Wenhai, and then Ji Baocheng and Chen Yulu. Lin Shangli holds the post in 2022.

The figures below describe RUC as of 2022, and the university's own website will have the current numbers. There are 25 schools, 13 research institutes and a graduate school. Undergraduates can choose among 63 specialties, and 8 more specialties are open to students taking a second bachelor's degree. Master's candidates have 149 specialties to pick from, doctoral candidates have 100, and the university holds 33 national key disciplines.

The library covers 26,000 square metres, with 15 reading rooms and a dedicated economics hall, and it offers more than 2,000 seats, so finding somewhere quiet to study during exam season is realistic.

Outside China, RUC has built links with 125 universities and research institutions in 32 countries and regions, which is why it often acts as a meeting point for academics and cultural exchange between China and the rest of the world.
Most of the schools fall into a few families, and seeing them grouped makes the structure easier to follow.

The economics and business side includes the schools of Economics, Finance, Business, Agricultural Economics and Rural Development, Labor and Human Resources, Statistics, and Public Administration and Policy.

For law, politics and society there are Law, International Studies (with departments of International Politics, Foreign Affairs and Politics), Marxism Studies, and Sociology and Population Studies (covering sociology, social work, demography and psychology).

The humanities and communication cluster contains Chinese Classics, History, Philosophy, Literary Studies, Arts, Journalism, Education, and Teaching Chinese as a Foreign Language. The Foreign Languages school has separate departments for English, French, German, Japanese, Russian and Spanish.

Technical and applied fields are smaller but present: Information, Information Resource Management, Environment and Natural Resources, and Science, which includes physics and chemistry departments. The School of Continuing Education serves adult learners.
Two institutes complete the picture, the Institute of Qing History and the Sino-French Institute.

RUC has also set up a number of policy and thematic centres. In 2015 it established the China Academy of Financial Inclusion, a government think-tank charged with working out how financial services can reach more people in China. On 25 October 2017 it opened a research centre on Xi Jinping Thought, described as the first of its kind, and on 25 May 2024 it launched the Research Center for Shiology, directed by Liu Guangwei, who founded Shiology and leads the World Shiology Forum.

Founded in 2005 and based in Beijing, the Rural Reconstruction Center studies both the theory and the practice of rebuilding rural communities. Its activities include campaigning for fair trade, coordinating green energy projects that link cities and countryside, and promoting fairer education.

renmin-university-of-china.h: Where you would study: four campuses

blocks.x: Renmin currently operates two campuses, is building a third, and no longer uses a fourth.

Most schools, departments and institutes are based at No.59 Zhongguancun Street in Haidian district. The campus is known across Beijing for its English Corner. Every Friday evening people gather near the east gate, around Qiushi Garden, to practise spoken English, so it is an easy way to meet local students and residents.

About 1,165 international students live and study here, and many of them come from South Korea. South Koreans are numerous enough that the canteen for international students prints a Korean menu alongside the regular Chinese one.

RUC's second active campus is in Suzhou Industrial Park in Jiangsu province, in the east of the country. It houses the RUC Sino-French Institute (IFC Renmin), which has 900 Chinese and international students. Several Chinese and Sino-foreign master's programmes from different RUC faculties are taught on the same grounds under the RUC International College. It forms part of Dushu Lake Higher Education Town in Suzhou, a cluster of internationally oriented graduate schools that also includes Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University and a joint graduate school run by Southeast University with Monash.

The university is building what will become its future main campus in Lucheng, in Tongzhou district east of central Beijing, provisionally called the Eastern Campus. It lies in the same town that the Beijing municipal government is relocating to. The source text expected completion by the end of 2017, which is clearly out of date, so ask the university about the present status before you plan around it.
The former main campus stands east of the Forbidden City in Dongcheng district. The land still belongs to the university, but it is no longer used for teaching.

renmin-university-of-china.h: Motto, values and the school song

blocks.x: RUC's motto is to seek truth from facts. Its spirit is summed up as building scholarship that serves ordinary people and helps run the country, and the aim for graduates is to be a model for the nation and a pillar of society. Its guiding idea is a focus on people and on humanistic values, which is the meaning behind the three parallel 人 characters ("person") in the seal-script emblem.

The school song has had many versions over the decades. Yan'an produced the first one in 1937, for the Northern Shaanxi school. A second came that same year in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei border region for North China Associated University. Zhengding in Hebei gave rise to another in 1948 for North China University, and later still Wu Yuzhang, Cheng Fangwu and Ji Baocheng each wrote a separate Renmin University song.

Ji Baocheng's piece became the official anthem in 2007, taking over from an older song that had been used since 1980 and carried heavy political overtones. Ten years later, in 2017, the original Northern Shaanxi school song was named as the one that represents the university.

Rankings need careful reading here. In 2022 Renmin and Nanjing University became the first Chinese institutions to withdraw from all international rankings. They were chosen as pilots for a new domestic system meant to reflect Chinese characteristics, and more Chinese universities are expected to follow as the country works toward its own benchmark for elite institutions. So the newest international figures may not be repeated by the university itself.

Earlier results give a sense of its standing. A 2015 list compiled by the Chinese University Alumni Association and China Education Center put RUC fifth among all Chinese universities. In the 2014 edition of the Times Higher Education world table, it came fifth within China, with Peking, Tsinghua, USTC and Fudan ahead of it. The same table had it 13th among emerging economies, 32nd in Asia and within the top 250 worldwide.

QS's 2020 table put it inside the global top 300 on two measures, academic reputation and employer reputation. Its graduates are in demand both in China and overseas, and the 2022 QS Graduate Employability Rankings gave it a position in the 181-190 range worldwide.

In the Ministry of Education's most recent discipline assessment, RUC took first place nationally in 9 fields. These are theoretical and applied economics, law, political science, sociology, journalism and statistics, plus business management and public administration. Beyond that, it counts 25 national key disciplines, which puts it fifth in the country. Its 13 national key humanities and social science research bases are the most of any Chinese university, and so are its 6 national teaching and research bases in basic arts subjects. Few Chinese universities offer as many social science and humanities majors. When undergraduate majors in 92 professional categories were ranked in 2022, 25 of Renmin's majors were the best in China, 48 placed in the top 5, and 57 in the top 10.

Subject tables from QS in 2021 put RUC in the world's top 100 for both Arts and Humanities and Social Sciences and Management. Within that, it was in the top 40 for philosophy, the top 80 for social sciences and management, and the top 51 for law and legal studies.

The Financial Times counts the Renmin Business School among the world's top 50. Its global MBA comes 38th, the Executive MBA 43rd, and its executive education programmes 11th, which is the highest in Asia. U.S. News & World Report, as of 2026, gave Renmin third place in China and Asia and eleventh place worldwide for economics and business.

The Academic Ranking of World Universities in 2024 listed RUC 9th in the world for public administration, 31st for finance, 43rd for library and information science, 51st for both management and statistics, and 76th for business administration and for economics.
Looking at who has taught and studied here shows what kind of university Renmin is. The roles below are as they were recorded, so some may have changed.

Huang Da is emeritus professor of finance and served as president from 1991 to 1994. Several well-known scholars teach or have taught in the School of International Studies: Jin Canrong, Shi Yinhong, Song Xinning (a Jean Monnet Professor) and Zhang Ming, as well as Manuel Pérez García, who was an associate professor there from 2013 to 2017. Liu Xiaofeng teaches in the School of Liberal Arts, and Mao Shoulong and Zhang Kangzhi in public administration.

Pan Suiming, a scholar of sexology, and Zhou Xiaozheng both teach sociology and population studies. Wang Liming is a civil law specialist who was dean of the School of Law from 2005 to 2009, and Zeng Xianyi, a legal historian, was dean from 1990 to 2005 and is now emeritus. Wen Tiejun is professor and dean of Agricultural Economics and Rural Development. In finance and economics, Wu Xiaoqiu is a professor in the School of Finance, Yang Ruilong is professor and dean of the School of Economics, and Baron von Pfetten has been a visiting professor there.

Wu Shuqing, an economist, led Peking University from 1989 to 1996. Liu Yu works as a political scientist at Tsinghua University, and Zhao Tingyang, a political philosopher, belongs to the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).

Han Xu was ambassador to the United States from 1985 to 1989. Liu Yandong became the highest-ranking woman in Chinese politics and the only woman on the Politburo. Ma Kai chaired the National Development and Reform Commission from 2003 to 2008. Xiao Yang was chief justice at the country's highest court, serving 1998 to 2003 and then 2003 to 2008. Xie Feng was Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs from 2021 to 2023 and is now ambassador to the United States.

Wang Ju-hsuan was labor affairs minister for the Republic of China (Taiwan) from 2008 to 2012. Chen Yulu spent 2015 to 2022 as a deputy governor of the People's Bank of China and now heads Nankai University. You Quan ran the United Front Work Department between 2017 and 2022, and Grace Mugabe was Zimbabwe's First Lady from 1996 to 2017. Liu He is a Politburo member and vice premier who also directs the party's central commission on financial and economic affairs. Zhou Dan became known as the first openly gay lawyer on the mainland to speak publicly for LGBT rights.

Duan Yongping founded Subor (Xiao Ba Wang, 小霸王) and BBK (Bu Bu Gao, 步步高). Hu Shuli founded the business magazine Caijing and is its editor-in-chief. Banking leaders include Pan Gongsheng, executive vice president of the Agricultural Bank of China, Xiang Junbo, its chairman from 2009, and Xiao Gang, chairman of Bank of China from 2003. Zhang Lei founded and leads Hillhouse Capital Group, and Liu Qiangdong founded JD.com.

Bob Fu took part in organising the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and later founded ChinaAid, which gives legal help to dissidents. Zeng Jinyan, a human rights activist, was among Time's 100 in 2007 and is the wife of Hu Jia, who received the Sakharov Prize in 2008. Zhang Zhixin was jailed and put to death for criticising the idolisation of Mao during the Cultural Revolution.

Wang Xiaobo is a modern writer who has been popular and influential among young Chinese readers, and he was married to the sociologist and sexologist Li Yinhe. Zhang Jie graduated in 1960, and her work has won many prizes.

Olympic champions include the divers Lin Yue, Huo Liang and Li Ting (10 m platform), Sang Xue (10 m platform), Peng Bo and Wu Minxia (3 m springboard), and Guo Jingjing, who won gold in the 3 m springboard and the synchronised springboard at the 2004 Summer Games. Wang Junxia won a gold and a silver medal on the track at the 1996 Olympics and has held the women's 10,000 m record since 1993 with 29:31:78. Vivian Kong of Hong Kong won Olympic gold in women's individual épée fencing, and Liang Yan played for the national women's volleyball team.

The list also names the historian Dai Yi, Shi Yan, a farmer who started China's first Community Supported Agriculture farm, and two American soldiers, James Veneris and Samuel David Hawkins, who were captured in the Korean War and chose to defect to China at the armistice.

Many respected universities abroad have exchange and cooperation agreements with Renmin. In North America they include Columbia, Princeton, Yale, Chicago, Michigan, Rutgers, McGill, Carleton, Queen's and Boston College Law School. Partners in Europe are LMU Munich, Geneva, King's College London and Queen Mary, and in Asia there are Singapore Management University and Waseda. A donation in January 2010 shows how close some ties are: Zhang Lei, who studied at Renmin and at the Yale School of Management, gave Yale US$8,888,888, the largest gift from an alumnus the school had received.
It also belongs to three networks: the Worldwide Universities Network, the Beijing-Hong Kong Universities Alliance and the Asia-Pacific Association for International Education.

A few specific programmes are worth knowing. Labor and Human Resources keeps up an exchange with Rutgers, linking Renmin to the Huamin Research Center and the Rutgers School of Social Work, and each year since 2010 students and teachers from both sides have visited one another. There is a joint Double Masters in Asian and International Affairs run by International Studies with King's College London. Renmin students also travel abroad for events like the annual National Model United Nations in New York. Back in Beijing, the Culture Plaza on campus is home to the University of Chicago Center, which has operated since September 2010.

Distinguished guests visit as well. In January 2008, on a state visit, Gordon Brown (then prime minister of Britain) joined Premier Wen Jiabao at Renmin for a conversation with students, scholars, athletes and entrepreneurs.

Families who relocate with a student may find the university's own schools relevant. Its affiliated high school in Beijing has sister-school ties with Phillips Academy in Massachusetts, Phillips Exeter in New Hampshire and Punahou in Honolulu. The affiliated primary school, also in Beijing, is paired with a Mandarin-language immersion school of the magnet type in Houston, in Texas.

A university is only part of the experience. Daily life depends on the city around it, so the next sections cover Beijing's buildings, landscape, weather and air, which is what students ask about most before they arrive.

Three architectural styles dominate central Beijing. The first is the traditional imperial style, which you can see at the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the huge Tian'anmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace. The second is the so-called Sino-Soviet style of the 1950s to the 1970s, with boxy buildings that were sometimes poorly built. The third is the modern architecture that stands out in the Beijing CBD in the east, such as the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the early 21st century the city has seen enormous construction, with designs by international architects especially visible in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s industrial design sits alongside neofuturistic style. The tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. Twice since 2007 a Beijing tower has taken the CTBUH's top skyscraper prize: the Linked Hybrid complex in 2009 and CCTV Headquarters in 2013. The honour goes to just one building worldwide each year.

Older housing is built around siheyuans, courtyards enclosed by buildings. Grand examples include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are joined by alleys called hutongs, which generally run east to west so that doors face north and south, a choice made for good Feng Shui. Some alleys are so narrow that only a few people can pass at once. These neighbourhoods were once everywhere, but entire blocks are being replaced by high-rises. Residents are entitled to flats at least as big as their old homes, yet many say the community feeling and street life cannot be replaced, and the properties are often owned by the government.

renmin-university-of-china.h: Shape and setting of the city

blocks.x: Geographically, Beijing is placed where the North China Plain, a rough triangle opening southward and eastward, reaches its northern limit. Ranges on three sides, north, northwest and west, protect the city and the agricultural heartland behind it from the encroaching desert steppe. In the northwest, especially in Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, while the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs across the northern part of the municipality along rugged ground, built to keep out nomadic raiders. The highest point is Mount Dongling in the Western Hills, on the border with Hebei, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The main rivers, including the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, belong to the Hai River system and flow southeast. Miyun Reservoir on the upper Chaobai is the largest reservoir in the municipality. The city is also where the Grand Canal to Hangzhou begins, a transport route dug more than 1,400 years ago, and the destination of the South-North Water Transfer Project, a recent scheme that moves water up from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up urban area lies on plains in the south-central part of the municipality at 40 to 60 metres (130-200 ft) above sea level, a small but growing share of the total area. Ring roads radiate outward in concentric circles. The Second Ring marks where the old city walls stood, while the Sixth connects satellite towns in the suburbs. At the very centre are Tian'anmen and its square, immediately below the Forbidden City where the emperors once lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, where China's current leaders live, and Chang'an Avenue, passing between Tiananmen and the square, is the main east-west axis. People often say the city has grown outward like a pancake (tan da bing), and this sprawl is a common explanation for its urban problems.

Four seasons are clearly marked in Beijing. Technically the climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and sticky, and the huge Siberian high-pressure system brings cold, dry winters that do not last long. In spring, dust can arrive from the Gobi across the Mongolian steppe while temperatures climb quickly and the air stays dry. Autumn resembles spring as a season of change with very little rain. Looking at 2001 to 2026, the warmest stretch fell in early August and the coldest in early January.

By the official Chinese definition, the seasons begin on these dates: spring on 26 March, summer on 20 May, autumn on 13 September and winter on 31 October. In recent years March and September have warmed faster, and May and October more slowly, so autumn tends to be briefer than spring.

For the urban area, the yearly mean over the period 1991 to 2020 is between 12.9 and 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Typical daily minimums run 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and typical daily maximums 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). Out in the low-lying suburbs, yearly means are slightly cooler, 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with minimums from 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums from 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). The mountains are colder again, from 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F) on average, dropping as the land rises.

The mid-winter month of January has a daily mean of −2.7 °C (27.1 °F), whereas July reaches 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Annual precipitation is roughly 528.0 mm (20.79 in), and the districts of Haidian and Chaoyang, where many campuses are found, get a little more at 584.2 mm (23.00 in). Nearly three-quarters of it comes in June, July and August. Sunshine is limited by cloud to 42% of the possible total in July but reaches 62% in January and February, giving 2,490.5 bright hours a year. The recorded extremes since 1951 are −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F) on 22 February 1966 and 41.9 °C (107.4 °F) on 24 July 1999.
Practically, pack serious winter clothing for a dry, freezing January, and expect hot, damp weather from June to August with most of the year's rain.
Air quality is a fair question for any international student, and the record shows both a hard past and real recent improvement.

The built-up area of Beijing grew to four times its former size between 2000 and 2009. More buildings meant more emissions, and the expansion also changed local meteorology: surface albedo, wind speed and humidity near the ground went down, while temperatures, ozone and the mixing of air upward went up. Urban growth plus the burning of fossil fuels left the city with a repeated health problem. The worst episode came in 2013, when heavy smog hit Beijing and most of northern China, touching 600 million people. After that shock, air pollution became a major economic and social worry nationally. The Beijing government set out to lower coal's share of its energy mix, from 24% in 2012 to 10% in 2017, and from 2015 to 2017 the national government ordered the heaviest-polluting vehicles removed and pushed harder for a clean energy system.

A 2006 study by American and Chinese researchers working together showed that a large part of Beijing's pollution is carried in from nearby cities and provinces. Between 35 and 60% of the ozone, on average, originates outside the city. Shandong and Tianjin have a significant influence, partly because summer winds usually come from the south and southeast and mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Coal is the biggest single contributor, responsible for around 40% of PM 2.5 in the city and most of its nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012 and wants to hold annual coal use to 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, of which 73% went to heat and electricity and the remainder to industry. The surrounding regions matter just as much. Tianjin's use was forecast to climb from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million by 2015. Hebei burned over 300 million tons in 2011, more than the whole of Germany, with only 30% of that going to power generation and a large share used to make steel and cement. Plants in the mining areas of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000, add to the burden, as do those in Shandong. Among provinces, Shandong uses the most coal, followed by Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

The city once relied on four large coal-fired plants for electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant shut in 2014, two others closed in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to stop during 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was to take 13 million tons off annual coal use, and to keep the total at 15 million tons in 2015.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, almost US$17 billion went on cleaning the air. Bus and subway fares were lowered, new subway lines opened and high-emission vehicles banned. The city put together 3,800 gas-powered buses, one of the largest fleets of its kind anywhere, and was the first Chinese city to adopt the national equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Cloud seeding has occasionally been used to bring rain and wash the air before big occasions, for example the 2009 parade for the 60th anniversary, and also against drought. More recently the authorities rely on temporary factory closures and tougher traffic restrictions, as with the short-lived "APEC blue" around APEC China 2014 and "parade blue" before the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. The air improved dramatically during those events and fell back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The first smog alert ever issued in Beijing came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed down most industry and commerce, with a "red alert" following later the same month. A November 2016 announcement by the city's environmental protection bureau added a rule: starting in 2017, old cars that pollute heavily may not be driven whenever a red alert covers the city or neighbouring areas.

Readings have come down since a "war on pollution" was announced in 2014. Fine particulates dropped by 35% in 2017 and declined further by 2020, thanks mainly to replacing coal with natural gas and cleaning up polluting factories. In 2022 the yearly average for PM2.5 fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the city's best result since 2013. The year 2024 saw just two days of heavy pollution, the fewest ever recorded and 96.6 percent below the 58 days counted in 2013.

Figures differ by source. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily readings from 27 monitoring stations on its website, and the US Embassy reports hourly fine-particle (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. The two bodies measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the BJEPB's numbers, and the health effects it reports, are often lower than the Embassy's. Either way, smog does harm: it clearly raises the rates of heart and lung disease in the city, and heavy exposure can lead to respiratory and cardiovascular trouble, hospital emergency visits and even death. Students with asthma or other conditions should check current readings and think about a good mask.

Deserts in the north and northwest of China are eroding, and the dust they release comes to Beijing as seasonal storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office occasionally triggers rainfall to limit the damage. Eight or more storms struck from January to April 2006 alone, and one in April 2002 left close to 50,000 tons of dust on the city on its way to Japan and Korea.

Deadlines can move and seats can fill earlier than the closing date, so apply as soon as your documents are ready.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

renmin-university-of-china.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Renmin University of China may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Renmin University of China by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Shaanxi Normal University, abbreviated SNNU (Shaanxi Shifan Daxue in Chinese), is a state-run university in the Chang'an District of Xi'an, the capital of Shaanxi province. It answers to the Ministry of Education and is included in both Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction programme. A normal university is traditionally a teacher-training institution, though like most of its kind SNNU now teaches a broad range of subjects, as the list of colleges below shows.

Its present form dates from 1960, when two earlier institutions, Xi'an Teachers College and Shaanxi Teachers College, were joined into one provincial university. In 1978 responsibility passed from the province to the national Ministry of Education, a change that signals the higher status the university had by then reached.

For a prospective international student, this profile does three jobs: it shows you how SNNU's academic units are arranged, it explains the city of Xi'an in some detail (weather, population, transport, economy and sport), and it describes the province of Shaanxi, whose history is among the longest in China.

shaanxi-normal-university.h: Xi'an: the setting for your studies

blocks.x: Student life at SNNU is largely about the city, so this section explains Xi'an as a newcomer would want it explained.

Xi'an sits on the Guanzhong Plain, a flood plain that eight rivers and streams have built up in the south-central stretch of Shaanxi. To the south the city meets the northern slopes of the Qin Mountains (Qinling), and to the north it reaches the banks of the Wei River. The sacred Taoist peak of Hua Shan, one of five, is some 100 kilometres (62 miles) to the east, and the Loess Plateau begins not far to the north.

The richness of this plain was recognised at the very start of the Han dynasty. Zhang Liang, the chief of staff, advised Emperor Liu Bang to make Guanzhong his capital. As the advice is traditionally quoted, the region is backed by Mount Xiao and Hangu Pass, links Long (Gansu) with Shu (Sichuan), and amounts to an iron castle stretching for a thousand miles with harvests rich enough to be called the land of heaven. Ever since, Guanzhong has been nicknamed the Nation of Heaven.

The climate is temperate under the East Asian monsoon. Climatologists place Xi'an on the border between humid subtropical and hot-summer humid continental (Cwa/Dwa). In the Wei River valley summers are hot and humid, winters cold and dry, and spring and autumn dry. Most rain falls from July until late October. Snow comes now and then in winter but seldom lies for long. In March and April, when the city warms quickly, dust storms are common, and in summer there are frequent brief thunderstorms.

Average temperatures hover near freezing in January and reach 27.0 degrees C in July, with a yearly mean of 14.08 degrees C. Since 1951 the readings have swung from minus 20.6 degrees C (11 January 1955) to 42.3 degrees C (15 July 2025, at the present station in Jinghe). Another station recorded 42.9 degrees C on 17 June 2006, and an unofficial low of minus 25.0 degrees C was noted at a suburban station in January 1930. A student should plan for proper winter clothing, a mask or scarf for dusty spring days, and light clothes for the summer.

In 1966 the Shaanxi Astronomical Observatory was founded. The 1975 national geodetic origin report said the reference point should lie in central mainland China to keep measurement bias small, and Lintong, a town near Xi'an, was selected. From 1986 Chinese Standard Time has been set by what is now the National Time Service Center (NTSC), part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. This institute carries out research and services on time and frequency: it produces and maintains the national time scale and sends out time and frequency signals. In the 1970s and 1980s it also built independent scales of universal time and atomic time, and low- and high-frequency radio dissemination methods, to serve science and the national economy.

The 2020 national census counted 12,952,907 permanent residents (by registered household). Men were 51.07 per cent and women 48.93 per cent. By age, 15.65 per cent were 0 to 14, 68.33 per cent were 15 to 59, 16.02 per cent were over 60 and 10.9 per cent over 65. The OECD estimated in 2010 that the metropolitan area had 12.9 million inhabitants, of whom 5.74 million lived in urban parts.

Much of the city is pleasant to explore on foot. Planners have added underpasses and overpasses in the commercial, residential and university districts, most of all in the lively shopping area by the Bell Tower, so that walkers can cross roads safely. Bike sharing started in 2013; the fleet is 52,000 bicycles and over 200,000 people ride them daily. Taxis are plentiful, but many residents commute by the 270 official bus routes, served by more than 7,800 buses that carry over four million passengers on an average day. A fast-growing metro adds more than 1.5 million riders a day. With over two million registered cars, traffic jams are a frequent complaint.

Line 2 was the first to open to the public, on 16 September 2011 (services began 28 September), running 19.9 kilometres and 17 stations from the North Railway Station in the north to Weiqu Nan in the south. Line 1, which opened on 15 September 2013, is the west-east route: 19 stations link Houweizhai with Fangzhicheng. Line 3 runs from Baoshuiqu in the northeast to Yuhuazhai in the southwest and opened on 8 November 2016. Line 4 came into service on 26 December 2018. It starts at the north square of the North Railway Station and ends at Hangtianxincheng, following Line 2 on the eastern side for most of its length. Line 5, which opened on 28 December 2020, is 41.6 kilometres long with 31 stations between Matengkong and Chuangxingang. Line 16 started on 27 June 2023 and covers 15.03 kilometres with nine stations from Qinchuangyuanzhongxin to Shijingli. Four more lines, including an extension of Line 1, are being built.

The network reaches many famous sights: the Banpo Museum (Line 1, Banpo Station), the Bell and Drum Tower and the city wall fortifications (Line 2), the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda (Lines 3 and 4), the Daminggong heritage park (Line 4) and the Shaanxi History Museum, which has three lines nearby (2, 3 and 4).

Trains start at 6:00 on Lines 1 to 4. The last departures are at 23:00 on Lines 3 and 4, 23:30 on Line 1 and 23:50 on Line 2. Two fires on Line 2 are recorded: one on 30 December 2008, put out within an hour with all workers safely evacuated, and another at a different station 66 hours later, on 2 January.

Xi'an North railway station, a few miles north of the centre, is the high-speed hub on the Zhengzhou-Xi'an line, a section of the Xuzhou-Lanzhou high-speed railway. Building of that line started on 25 September 2005 and it opened on 6 February 2010; within 48 days of regular service all passenger flights between Zhengzhou and Xi'an stopped because they could not compete. The station itself was begun on 19 September 2008 and opened on 11 January 2011. With 34 platforms it was the largest in northwest China when it opened. It also serves the Datong-Xi'an line (which connects to Beijing North), the Xi'an-Chengdu line and the Yinchuan-Xi'an line.

Xi'an railway station, just north of the walled old city, is the principal hub for conventional trains in Shaanxi. It covers 597,000 square metres, has six passenger platforms and 11 passenger tracks, and handles 112 services and 80,000 people a day. Direct services include Beijing, Zhengzhou, Lanzhou, Baoji and Mount Hua. Two big stations, Xi'an East and Xi'an South, are under construction for new high-speed routes such as Xi'an-Chongqing and Wuhan-Xi'an. Other stations are Xi'an West, Yinzhen, Sanmincun and Fangzhicheng.

Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (XIY) is the largest airport in northwest China, about 25 miles northwest of the city centre and 8 miles northeast of Xianyang. The main carriers are China Eastern, Hainan Airlines and China Southern. Terminal 3 and a second runway opened on 3 May 2012, and Terminal 5, started in 2022, was completed in September 2024. As well as most Chinese cities, it has flights to Tokyo, Seoul, London, Paris and Sydney.

Xi'an was a prime target for the China Western Development policy, and was pushed to develop fields such as IT, new materials, aerospace, energy and chemical engineering. Between 1997 and 2006 its new-economy service sector grew about 13 per cent a year, compared with 0.74 per cent for traditional services, taking output from 8.113 to 25.85 billion US dollars. The Globalization and World Cities Research Network ranked Xi'an a Beta-minus (second-tier global) city in 2020, and it was among the world's top 100 financial centres in that year's Global Financial Centres Index.

The key sectors are equipment manufacturing, tourism and service outsourcing. Manufacturing had annual output of 36.5 billion yuan, 44.5 per cent of the total. Being one of China's four ancient capitals, Xi'an offers the Terracotta Army, the city wall and Famen Temple, which makes tourism a major industry. In 2019 over 300 million tourists generated 314.6 billion yuan; income grows by an average 36.4 per cent a year, and foreign-exchange earnings, 530 million in 2009, by about 35.8 per cent.

It was also one of the first Chinese cities for service outsourcing, with more than 800 companies and output above 23 billion yuan in 2008. Between 1997 and 2006 jobs in outsourcing doubled from 60,000, while the computer consulting workforce rose from 16,000 to 32,000. A Software New Town with 30 billion yuan of investment was planned for completion in 2015. The city also exports lighting equipment and car parts and imports mechanical and electrical goods; its biggest trading partner is the United States.

A model for growth driven by logistics, the Xi'an International Trade and Logistics Park occupies roughly 35 square miles and works as an inland port and rail container centre. No other city sends or receives as many China-Europe freight trains.

The principal industrial district is the Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone. Separately, China's former largest rubbish tip, at Jiangcungou, shut in 2019. Xi'an is a software pioneer: by 2012 the Xi'an Software Park inside the Xi'an Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone had attracted over 1,085 companies and 106,000 employees. One description credits this to the large pool of low-cost talent from some 100 local universities, producing about 3,000 computer graduates a year at roughly 120 dollars a month, half the pay for the same job in Beijing.

A joint venture between the city and the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, set up in November 2006, produced the civil space industry base. Its business lines cover equipment, outsourced software and services, new materials and solar power. The base would serve Xi'an and the Guanzhong region first and then reach other parts of north-west and south-west China. The target was total output of 2.8 billion US dollars by 2012, with 10 to 20 brand products carrying their own intellectual property and five to eight that could compete worldwide. Shanghai launched an initial civil aerospace centre in 2008, and China is building a second one in Shaanxi, whose plan had received the go-ahead from the State Development and Reform Commission on 26 December 2007 as the national civil base at Xi'an. The site, 23 square kilometres, is meant for civilian satellites, materials, energy and IT.
Xi'an has lost its best-known professional teams to other cities. They were:
In the Chinese Jia-A League, Shaanxi National Power, which moved to Ningbo in 2004 and became Ningbo National Power.
In the football Super League, Shaanxi Baorong Chanba, which moved to Guiyang and became Guizhou Renhe in 2012.
In the Chinese Basketball Association, Shaanxi Dongsheng, which moved to Foshan and became the Foshan Dralions in 2010.
A province leaves its mark on students as surely as the campus does, so here is a brief outline of Shaanxi.

Shaanxi is counted among the cradles of Chinese civilisation. Thirteen dynasties placed their capitals here across a stretch of over 1,100 years that ran from the Zhou era into the Tang. Xi'an, today's provincial capital, is one of China's four great ancient capitals and the eastern end of the Silk Road, which led on to Europe, Arabia and Africa.

When the Qin dynasty fell, the area was briefly ruled as the Three Qins, which is the source of the province's abbreviation Qin; the other abbreviation is Shaan. Liu Bang then took it during the Chu-Han Contention. The Han dynasty pushed the Northern Silk Road westwards for exploration and for military reasons. This was the most northerly Silk Road, about 2,600 kilometres (1,600 miles) long. Starting from Xi'an, it crossed the Wushao Ling Pass to reach Wuwei, and came out at Kashgar before meeting ancient Parthia.

The Xiongnu-led state of Northern Xia (407-431) had its capital at Tongwancheng. The Northern Song and the Tangut-led Western Xia later disputed the frontier inside Shaanxi. The Luowucheng fort was established by Western Xia in 1071, and Song captured it in 1081. Administrative changes continued: the Northern Song set up the Shaanxi Lu (circuit) governed from today's Xi'an in 997, and the Yuan created Shaanxi Province under a Branch Secretariat in 1286. Under the Ming, the province was formed in 1376 with a Provincial Administration Commission whose area also included present Gansu, Ningxia and part of Qinghai. Travellers from Central and West Asia mostly came into China by way of Shaanxi then. After the Qing took power Gansu was separated, though both provinces were still under the Viceroy of Shaan-Gan.

One of history's deadliest earthquakes struck near Hua Shan in southeast Shaanxi on 23 January 1556, killing about 100,000 people and reducing the regional population by an estimated 830,000 through emigration and famine. In the twentieth century the Long March, which began when the Jiangxi Soviet ended, took Mao Zedong and the Communists to a new base, the Shaanxi Soviet at Yan'an.

At Lantian County, northwest of Xi'an, fossils of Lantian Man were found. They date from about a million years ago and scientists consider them a subspecies of Homo erectus. They are displayed in the Shaanxi History Museum in Xi'an.

shaanxi-normal-university.h: Terrain and weather across the province

blocks.x: In the north, along the Inner Mongolia border, lies part of the Ordos Desert. The Loess Plateau fills the centre, the Qin Mountains run east to west through the south-central part, and south of them the climate is subtropical. Between the plateau and the mountains lies the Wei River Valley, Guanzhong, an early cradle of Chinese civilisation.

Moving clockwise, Shaanxi touches Shanxi (east and northeast), Henan (east), Hubei (southeast), Chongqing (south), Sichuan (southwest), Gansu (west), Ningxia (northwest) and Inner Mongolia (north). Only Inner Mongolia borders as many provincial-level units.

Because it spans so many degrees of latitude, Shaanxi has varied climates. The north, including the Loess Plateau, is cold arid (BWk) or cold semi-arid (BSk), with cold, very dry winters, dry spring and autumn and hot, humid summers. Guanzhong is largely semi-arid, with some humid subtropical (Cwa) pockets; winters there range from cool to cold and summers are hot, damp and often open with heatwaves. The south is far wetter, in the humid subtropical zone, where winters are gentler and the summer is long, hot and humid. Annual means run from roughly 8 to 16 degrees C, with January between minus 11 and 3.5 degrees C and July between 21 and 28 degrees C. Besides Xi'an, Shaanxi's cities are Ankang, Baoji, Hanzhong, Lintong, Tongchuan, Xianyang and Yan'an.

By the middle of the nineteenth century, musk, wine, liquor and animal skins were Shaanxi's exports, while European skins, watches, cloth and Chinese-language books came in. Money lending was common, and Shaanxi merchants took part in the Guangzhou loan trade. Later, during the Third Front campaign, the province received heavy investment in industrial capacity.

Fossil fuels and high technology are now the largest industries. In 2009 Shaanxi ranked third in China for coal, natural gas and crude oil. The province hosts several leading universities and institutes of western China, and it is therefore a key player in aircraft and aerospace: over half of the R&D and manufacturing equipment used by the country's home-built commercial aviation comes from here. Nominal GDP in 2011 was 1,239 billion yuan (196.7 billion dollars), or 21,729 yuan (3,179 dollars) per person, 17th among Chinese provinces. In the first half of 2019, output reached 1,162.557 billion yuan, 5.4 per cent up on a year earlier: 55.319 billion yuan from primary industry (up 4.5 per cent), 557.935 billion from secondary industry (up 4.2 per cent) and 549.303 billion from tertiary industry (up 6.8 per cent).

Two economic zones are worth knowing. Baoji Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone was set up in 1992 and approved by the State Council as a national high-tech zone, with a long-term planned area of 40 square kilometres. It is served by Xi'an Xianyang airport and National Highway 310, and its firms make auto parts, electronics, IT products, medicines and bioengineering goods, as well as new materials. The Shaanxi Xi'an Export Processing Zone (XEPZ) won State Council approval on 21 June 2002 and began operating on 5 April 2004. It is the northwest's first state-level export processing zone, and one of seven pioneers in China given a bonded-logistics role. The Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone's administrative committee runs it as a special economic zone, with over 40 enterprises, domestic and foreign, whose main businesses are aviation, machinery, electronics and new energy.

Cultural highlights of Shaanxi include its food, shadow-puppet theatre, the folk art called Xintianyou and Qinqiang, which is the province's emblematic folk opera. Xi'an has its own religious and cultural traditions as well.

Taken together, the facts make Xi'an a city of strong contrasts: a place of ancient capitals, the Silk Road and the Terracotta Army, and also a hub of software, aerospace and logistics with a growing metro. If you study at SNNU, expect cold dry winters, a hot summer and dusty spring days. Check the university's own website for current programmes, campus facilities and the services offered by the International College of Chinese Studies, because the numbers quoted here come from different years.

The city statistics above are drawn from different years. Forecasts, such as the 2012 aerospace targets or the Software New Town planned for 2015, have long since passed, so you should treat them as history of what planners aimed for rather than as present facts. The metro is also changing: lines that were still being planned or built when the figures were gathered may be open by the time you arrive, and the airport's newest terminal only finished in 2024. Look up current timetables, fares and campus maps on official sites before you travel, and ask the university which campus, dormitory and classroom buildings your programme will use.

Because Xi'an is one of the four ancient capitals and also a modern technology centre, many students spend free time visiting the Bell and Drum Tower, the city wall, the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda or the Shaanxi History Museum, all of which are named in the metro description above and are reachable on the lines mentioned.

shaanxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: About Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine

blocks.x: Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine is a public medical university based in Xianyang, Shaanxi Province, China.

The university operates two campuses: the North Campus in Xianyang, the historic ancient capital of China, and the South Campus in the West Xi'an New District along the Dan River, with a combined area of approximately 796,675.3 square meters.
Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine (SUCM) is focused on advancing Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), with a mission to preserve China's ancient medical heritage while driving modern innovation.

In 1952, the Northwest Chinese Medicine Training School (西北中医进修学校) was founded in Xi'an with approval from the Ministry of Health of the Central People's Government. In 1959, it became Shaanxi College of Chinese Medicine (陕西中医学院). The university relocated to its current campus in Xianyang in 1961. In 2015 the university was formally renamed to the Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine (陕西中医学院).

Recognized as one of China's premier traditional Chinese medicine institutions, the university was designated as one of the eight key TCM universities by the central government in 1978. The university became one of the first institutions approved by the Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council to grant master's degrees in TCM in 1981.
In 1990, the university became one of the first institutions approved by China's Ministry of Education to admit international students.

In 2019, the university established a partnership with the Grigore T. Popa University of Medicine and Pharmacy (UMF) in Iasi, Romania through an agreement with Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine, aiming to promote TCM education and cultural exchange.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the university mobilized over 4,500 medical staff and volunteers to support outbreak response efforts in Wuhan, Shanghai, Inner Mongolia, Xi'an, Xinjiang, and Tibet.
In 2025, Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine took part in an Arab-China International Forum on Traditional Medicine in Cairo, Egypt.
The university is currently listed under the World Directory of Medical Schools.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Xianyang, where Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine is located.

Xianyang sits in the central part of the Guanzhong Basin in Shaanxi Province. The terrain steps down from north to south, with distinct elevation gradients and clear topographic boundaries. The Loess Plateau and adjacent plains dominate the landscape. The highest point within the city is Shimen Mountain in the northeast, reaching 1,826 m, while the lowest point lies at the Qīnghé exit in Dacheng Town, Sanyuan County, at 366 m.

The northern part is part of the southern edge of the Loess Plateau, generally delineated by the Jing River. The southwest features loess hills and ravines, while the northeast consists of eroded loess gullies and low-to-mid hills. The central and southern parts form the Wei River Plain, a flat and largely erosion-free segment of the Guanzhong Plain. This basin is further divided into the Jing–Wei alluvial plain and the loess plateau, arranged in descending terraces from north to south.

Surface water is primarily composed of river runoff and groundwater. All rivers belong to the Wei River tributary of the Yellow River. The main tributaries within Xianyang are the Qishui, Xinhe, Fenghe, Jinghe, and Shichuan rivers, with the Jinghe being the most significant, forming two major drainage systems: Jinghe and Wei River. Groundwater is richer in the south and poorer in the north. Prolonged drought and over-extraction of groundwater have led to the drying of some rivers and ponds, and a continuous decline in groundwater levels. Although there is substantial transit water, its utilization remains challenging due to uneven distribution of surface and groundwater.

Xianyang is one of the top 200 cities in the world by scientific research outputs, as tracked by the Nature Index. Xianyang is home to the main campus of Northwest A&F University (NWAFU), one of the world's top universities in agriculture science related-fields, and a member of "Project 985" club which is an organization of 39 reputable universities in China.
