Before the Ming dynasty, most of the Han population in the region practiced Buddhism or Taoism, while the Hui people adhered to Islam. Catholicism was introduced into the area in the late Ming and early Qing dynasties. Following the First Opium War in 1840, both Catholicism and Protestantism spread across the counties of Xianyang, eventually becoming two of the most widely followed and influential religions in the area.

During the Cultural Revolution of 1966–1976, all religious activities in the region were forcibly suspended. After the Third Plenary Session of the 11th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party in 1978, religious properties such as churches and temples were returned to religious organizations, and religious activities were gradually restored.
Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine is in Shaanxi, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Shaanxi.

Shaanxi is considered one of the cradles of Chinese civilization. Thirteen feudal dynasties established their capitals in the province during a span of more than 1,100 years, from the Zhou dynasty to the Tang dynasty.

The province's principal city and current capital, Xi'an, is one of the four great ancient capitals of China and is the eastern terminus of the Silk Road, which leads to Europe, the Arabian Peninsula, and Africa.

The region was briefly governed as the Three Qins after the fall of the Qin dynasty. This is the origin of one of Shaanxi's two abbreviations, 秦 (Qin), the other being 陝 (Shaan). Then it was conquered by Liu Bang during the Chu-Han Contention. Under the Han dynasty, the Northern Silk Road was expanded to advance exploration and military purposes to the west. This Northern Silk Road is the northernmost of the Silk Roads and is about 2,600 kilometres (1,600 mi) in length. It connected the ancient Chinese capital of Xi'an to the west over the Wushao Ling Pass to Wuwei and emerging in Kashgar before linking to ancient Parthia.
The Xiongnu-led kingdom Northern Xia (407–431) set its capital in Tongwancheng.
The Northern Song dynasty and the Tangut-led Western Xia contested their border in Shaanxi. Western Xia found the Luōwùchéng (罗兀城) frontier fort in 1071 but was taken by Song in 1081.

Under the Ming dynasty, Shaanxi was established with the founding of the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission in 1376, whose administration also included the modern provinces of Gansu, Ningxia, and part of Qinghai. During this dynasty, most visitors from Central and West Asia entered the country via Shaanxi.

One of the most devastating earthquakes in history occurred near Hua Shan in southeastern Shaanxi on 23 January 1556, killing an estimated 100,000 people and causing a regional reduction in population by an estimated 830,000 due to emigration and famine (see 1556 Shaanxi earthquake).
The end of the short-lived Jiangxi Soviet signaled the beginning of the Long March by Mao Zedong and the Chinese Communists to the Shaanxi Soviet at Yan'an.

The administrative evolution of Shaanxi: The Northern Song established the Shaanxi Lu (circuit), governed from modern Xi'an in 997. The Yuan dynasty established Shaanxi Province (Yuan dynasty), governed by a Branch Secretariat in 1286. After the founding of the Qing dynasty, Gansu was split from Shaanxi, but both provinces were governed under the Viceroy of Shaan-Gan.

The Lantian Man site, with hominin fossils from approximately one million years ago, was found in Lantian County in northwestern Shaanxi province, near the city of Xi'an. Scientists classify Lantian Man as a subspecies of Homo erectus. The fossils are displayed at the Shaanxi History Museum, Xi'an, China.

The geography of the area is described as being part of the Ordos Desert in the north along the border with Inner Mongolia, the Loess Plateau in the central part of the province, the Qin Mountains (Qinling) running east to west in the south central part, and subtropical climate south of the Qinling. In between the Loess Plateau and the Qinling lies the Wei River Valley, or Guanzhong, a cradle of early Chinese civilization.

Going clockwise, Shaanxi borders Shanxi (E, NE), Henan (E), Hubei (SE), Chongqing (S), Sichuan (SW), Gansu (W), Ningxia (NW), and Inner Mongolia (N). In terms of number of bordering provincial-level divisions, Shaanxi ties Inner Mongolia.

Due to its large span in latitude, Shaanxi has a variety of climates. Under the Köppen climate classification, the northern parts, including the Loess Plateau, have either a cold arid (Köppen BWk) or cold semi-arid (Köppen BSk), with cold and very dry winters, dry springs and autumns, and hot, humid summers. The area known as Guanzhong is mostly semi-arid, though there are a few areas with a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa), with cool to cold winters, and hot, humid summers that often see early-season heatwaves. The southern portion is much more humid and lies in the humid subtropical zone, with more temperate winters and long, hot, humid summers. Annual mean temperature is roughly between 8 and 16 °C (46 and 61 °F), with January temperatures ranging from −11 to 3.5 °C (12.2 to 38.3 °F) and July temperatures ranging from 21 to 28 °C (70 to 82 °F).
Besides the provincial capital of Xi'an, other cities include: Baoji, Hanzhong, Lintong, Tongchuan, Xianyang, Yan'an and Ankang.

As of the mid-19th century, Shaanxi exported animal skins, wine, liquor, and musk. Money loans were also common, with Shaanxi business people involved in the Guangzhou loan business. Shaanxi commonly imported European animal skins, watches, Chinese language books, and cloth.
Shaanxi was a major recipient of China's investment in industrial capacity during the Third Front campaign.

The fossil fuel and high technology sectors compose the two largest industries in Shaanxi province. During 2009, the province ranked third in China for production of coal, natural gas and crude oil. As the home of several of the leading universities and research institutes in Western China, Shaanxi province also plays a major role in China's burgeoning aircraft and aerospace industries, producing more than 50% of the R&D and manufacturing equipment for the country's domestic commercial air industry. Nominal GDP for 2011 was 1,239 billion RMB (US$196.7 billion) and GDP per capita was 21,729 RMB (US$3,179), ranking 17th in the PRC.

In the first half of 2019, Shaanxi's total production value reached 1,162.557 billion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 5.4%. The added value of the primary industry was 55.319 billion yuan, an increase of 4.5%; the second industry was 557.935 billion yuan, an increase of 4.2%; the tertiary industry was 549.303 billion yuan, an increase of 6.8%.

Established in 1992, Baoji Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone was approved as a national hi-tech zone by the State Council. It has a long-term planned area of 40 km2 (15 sq mi). The transportation system around the zone includes Xi'an-Xianyang International Airport and National Highway 310, and industries operating within the zone include auto parts, electronics, IT, pharmaceuticals and bioengineering industries and new materials.

Shaanxi Xi'an Export Processing Zone (XEPZ) was approved on 21 June 2002 by the State Council for its establishment and was put on 5 April 2004. As the first state-level export processing zone in northwest China, XEPZ has become one of the seven pioneer EPZs with the function of bonded logistics in China. XEPZ is under the leadership of the Administrative Committee of Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone (XETDZ), which is designated by Xi'an municipal government to exercise economic and administrative power within the zone. XEPZ is a special economic zone. By now, there are more than 40 enterprises home and abroad settled in XEPZ. The pillar industries feature aviation, machinery, electronics and new energy.

The Western Triangle is a new economic zone composing the three major city-level economies of Western China: Xi'an, Chongqing and Chengdu. It is believed that the addition of Xi'an to the Triangle will spur economic growth in the region and allow the city an opportunity to capitalize on the commercial potential of its high-technology industries.

shaanxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone

blocks.x: Established in 1993, Xi'an Economic and Technology Development Zone was approved as a national zone in 2000. The zone is 20 minutes from Xi'an Xianyang International Airport, and national highways pass through. It has formed four pillar industries: automotive, electronics, food, and new materials industries. So far, the zone has attracted more than 1,700 enterprises.

Xi'an HTDZ opened its gates in 1991. It was established as a "pivotal location" for investment by high-tech industry companies in central and northwest China. Established in 1991, Xi'an Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone is a national high-tech zone. It is surrounded by national highways and it is 30 minutes from Xi'an-Xianyang International Airport. Furthermore, it is ranked in the top three high-tech zones in China.

Xi'an Software Park, established in December 1998, is the professional park for Xi'an to develop scale software and service outsourcing industries. The park has been appraised as a software industry base under the National Torch Program, national software industry base, national software export base, city demonstrational area of national service outsourcing base. It is one of the four parks with "double bases" of software in China. Xi'an Software Park assembles 90% of enterprises engaging in software and service outsourcing in Xi'an. There were nearly 780 companies, of which foreign-funded enterprises account for 170, and over 71,000 jobholders in the park by the end of 2008.

Yangling Agriculture Hi-Tech Industrial Zone was approved as a national-level hi-tech development zone by State Council in 1997. It is 82 km (51 mi) from Xi'an to the east and 70 km (43 mi) from Xi'an Xianyang International Airport.

Nearly all the people in Shaanxi are ethnic Han Chinese, with pockets of Hui population in the northwestern region (adjacent to Ningxia). Shaanxi province is one of the centers of ancient Chinese civilization. The central part of Shaanxi, known as Guanzhong, where the provincial capital Xi'an is located, is more populous compared to the others (Shaannan and Shaanbei).

The predominant religions in Shaanxi are Chinese folk religions, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism. According to surveys conducted in 2007 and 2009, 7.58% of the population believes and is involved in ancestor veneration, while 1.57% of the population identifies as Christian. The reports didn't give figures for other types of religion; 90.85% of the population may be either irreligious or involved in worship of nature deities, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, folk religious sects, and small minorities of Muslims.

Shandong Normal University, written 山东师范大学 in simplified Chinese and 山東師範大學 in traditional characters (pinyin: Shāndōng Shīfàn Dàxué), goes by the English abbreviation SDNU. It is based in Jinan, the capital of Shandong Province in eastern China. After the People's Republic was founded, it became one of the first higher education institutions to open in the province, which makes it an established name for anyone interested in teacher education and the humanities in this part of China.

Teacher training in Shandong has roots reaching back to 1902, but the university in its own right was set up in 1950. Until 1981 it was called Shandong Normal College (山东师范学院). A new campus received its first students in 2005. In November 2012 SDNU joined the first group of Shandong "famous universities with characteristics", a provincial scheme that aims to train graduates with applied skills. Then in 2020 the province chose it as one of its high-level universities to be built into a first-class university.

Teaching takes place on two campuses, Qianfoshan and Changqinghu. Land holdings add up to just under 3,850 mu (around 2.56 million square meters) and the buildings offer roughly 1.35 million square meters of floor space. The student body has over 34,000 full-time Chinese students, and more than 200 international students are enrolled, so international students are a small minority and you should expect a mostly Chinese-speaking campus.

SDNU employs 2,831 staff in total. Of these, 2,119 are full-time teachers, with 417 full professors and 878 associate professors. The faculty includes 8 dual academicians. Another 54 people have been chosen for national talent programmes such as the "10,000 people plan", the Changjiang scholars (youth scholars included) and the national outstanding youth scheme. Within that group, 22 hold the national honorary title National Excellent Teacher, and 96 receive special State Council allowances. Two teaching teams also earned a national award named after Huang Danian, given to model college teacher teams.

Two of SDNU's research centres, the Qilu Culture Research Centre and the Elementary Teaching Courses Research Centre, are the only humanities key research centres that China's Ministry of Education (MOE) has set up at provincial universities. The university publishes six international academic periodicals. One of them, China Population Resources & Environment, is the sole journal in China devoted to sustainable development.

Partnerships link SDNU with 158 institutions in 32 countries and regions. Starting in 2011, foreign instructors have regularly come in to give two-week special courses in English on web and media topics, through its School of Communications. The Ministry of Education approved SDNU in 1983 to recruit international students and to host international students on China scholarships, and it is also an approved HSK exam centre. Since that approval, graduates from abroad number over 5,000.

Lu Youquan, education theorist
Everyday student life depends on the city beyond the campus, so here is an overview of Jinan: weather, economy, getting about, sport, and then the wider province of Shandong.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), and each of the four seasons is clearly marked. Expect a dry spring with nearly no rain, a hot wet summer, a crisp autumn, and a cold, dry winter that brings little snow. Mean annual temperature is 14.9 °C (58.8 °F), and precipitation totals 734 millimetres (28.9 in); summer gets most of that, and the amount differs greatly from year to year. The driest and coldest month is January: the mean is −0.3 °C (31.5 °F) and rainfall equivalent is 5.0 millimetres (0.20 in). July is the hottest, with a mean of 27.4 °C (81.3 °F). Sunshine ranges from 40% of the possible total in July to 58% in May, giving 2,226 hours a year.

Mountains lie to the south, so temperature inversions happen often, on about 200 days a year. Add comparatively high rainfall for northern China and hills around the city on three sides, and summers can feel especially oppressive; local people have even suggested Jinan as a fourth "furnace" city, in addition to the traditional Three Furnaces. Records from 1951 onward show a low of −19.7 °C (−3 °F) recorded on 17 January 1953 and a high of 42.5 °C (109 °F) recorded on 24 July 1955.

In 1852 the Yellow River moved to a new channel just north of Jinan, and a railway hub was built. Together these events turned the city into a leading market for agricultural goods from the rich farmland to its north. Trade in farm produce led to textiles and clothing, flour mills and oil presses, and then factories making paper, cement and matches. Large iron and steel works and chemical plants followed around Jinan in the 1950s; the metal works turn out pig iron and ingot steel as well as finished steel products. In the 1970s Sinotruk located its headquarters and its truck and construction vehicle factories in the city.

shandong-normal-university.h: Economic rankings and output over time

blocks.x: Jinan has for a long time held third place in Shandong Province. Before the 2019 merger with Laiwu City it had moved past Yantai to become the province's second largest economy.

National Bureau of Statistics yearbook data show total economic output of 256.3 billion yuan in 2007, divided among primary, secondary and tertiary industry at 5.9%, 45.2% and 48.9% respectively. The 2008 GDP of 301.7 billion yuan put Jinan sixth among provincial capitals. Guangzhou was far ahead at 821.5, then Hangzhou at 478.1, Wuhan with 396.0, Chengdu with 390.1 and Nanjing with 377.5.

The 2009 GDP reached 335.0 billion yuan, 11.3% up on 2008, which placed Jinan 21st nationally and 7th among provincial capitals. Those placed above it, counting provincial capitals and municipalities together, were Shanghai at 1,490.09 and Beijing at 1,186.59, then Guangzhou at 911.27 and Tianjin at 750.08. Next came Chongqing at 652.87 (569.74 if only its urban core is counted), after which Hangzhou had 508.8 and Wuhan had 456.0. Chengdu reached 450.26, Shenyang 435.9, Nanjing 423.02 and Changsha 374.5. Just below Jinan was Zhengzhou, at 330.0.

By 2011 GDP was 440.629 billion yuan, up 10.6% year on year, and per resident it came to 64,331 yuan (up 8.9%), or about 9,960 US dollars. In 2016 it reached 653.61 billion yuan, 7.8% higher, with 90,999 yuan per permanent resident (up 6.5%), equal to 13,700 US dollars at the average exchange rate that year.

The 2022 total was 1,202.75 billion yuan, up 3.1% at constant prices. The primary sector added 42.05 billion yuan (growth of 3.1%), the secondary sector added 418.02 billion (3.2% growth) and services added 742.67 billion (3.0%), so the structure was 3.5:34.8:61.7. For 2024 GDP was 1,352.76 billion yuan, 5.4% higher at constant prices, made up of 44.0 billion from primary industry (up 3.6%), 451.92 billion from secondary (up 5.8%) and 856.84 billion from tertiary (up 5.2%), a ratio of 3.3:33.4:63.3. In short, services now make up nearly two thirds of the local economy.
Several large industrial enterprises operate in Jinan today, in two broad groups.

Heavy industry: the energy group, the electric power corporation, the heavy industry group, the iron and steel group and the gold group, all in the Shandong name, together with the China National Heavy Duty Truck Group, the Jinan branch of Sinopec and the Shandong Hi-Speed Group
Light industry: Inspur Group, and the appliance maker Joyoung

Jinan High-tech Industrial Development Zone was founded in 1991 and was among the first zones of this kind approved by the State Council. On the city's eastern side, its planned area totals 83 km2 (32 sq mi): with a central district of 33 km2 (13 sq mi), a 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi) export processing district, and a further 40 km2 (15 sq mi) of eastern extension. Firms attracted to it include LG, Panasonic, Volvo and Sanyo. It became a member of the world science and technology association in 2000 and opened a China-Ukraine High-tech Cooperation Park, and the Qilu Software Park became a sister park to the one in Bangalore, India.
Jinan Export Processing Zone is in the eastern suburbs, east of the High-tech zone and north of the Jiwang highway. It lies 9 km (5.6 mi) from the Jiqing Highway and 18 km (11 mi) from Jinan Airport.

In the 2020 Chinese census Jinan had 9,202,432 residents, including the recently merged Laiwu City. The built-up (metro) area includes 6 of the 10 urban districts, because Jiyang, Zhangqiu, Laiwu and Gangcheng are not yet joined to the urban area, and it was home to 5,452,335 people. Most are of Han ethnicity.

Two major railways cross at Jinan. The Jinghu Railway from Beijing to Shanghai is the main north–south rail line in eastern China, and in Jinan it meets the Jiaoji Railway, which runs east to the seaport of Qingdao. The Hanji Railway adds a link westward to Handan in Hebei Province.
Within the province, towns on the Jinghu line are Dezhou, Tai'an, Jining and Zaozhuang. Along the Jiaoji line you find Zibo, Weifang and Qingdao, and the Hanji line serves Yancheng and Liaocheng.

In the central area you can use Jinan railway station, Jinan East or Daminghu, the last of which stands beside Daming Lake. High-speed trains on the Beijing–Shanghai line call elsewhere, at Jinan West railway station in Huaiyin District, in the western suburbs. Public service there began on 30 June 2011, and it is expected to grow into a major hub, with fast west–east lines to Taiyuan, Shijiazhuang and Qingdao. Jinan East only opened in 2018. Another station, Jinan North, is planned.
Jinan Metro construction began in 2013 and the system officially opened in 2019. Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8, the Jiyang Line and SkyShuttle Line 1 now operate, with 140 stations altogether.

China National Highways 104, 220 and 309 are the major roads. As Jinan is a hub for both road and rail, its Coach Terminus has one of the heaviest passenger flows in China: up to 92,000 passengers a day on peak days and about 42,000 on quiet ones.

The airport, Jinan Yaoqiang International, lies in Yaoqiang Subdistrict of Licheng District, around 33 km (21 mi) to the northeast of the centre; that is where its name comes from. Expressways take you to downtown. Its domestic network covers many large cities, and among its overseas destinations are Seoul, Osaka and Bangkok, Singapore, Helsinki, Paris and Los Angeles.

Regular city buses come in air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned versions, and the air-conditioned routes carry a K before the route number. Since 2018 most lines have air conditioning, including some without the K. Together they make up over 200 routes covering the whole city.

Shandong Hi-Speed Kirin is Jinan's best-known sports team. Its home league is the Chinese Basketball Association (CBA), which it joined in 1995; the 2012–13 season took it to the final, losing 4–0 to the Guangdong Southern Tigers.

In football the best-known club is Shandong Taishan, which competes in the Chinese Super League, the top level. The club has never left the top flight since the league went professional in 1994. Its honours are five league titles, eight Chinese FA Cups and a single Chinese FA Super Cup. Back in 2004 Jinan was among four Chinese cities that hosted the AFC Asian Cup.

China's National Games, the premier national sporting event, were held in Jinan in 2009. They were the first major multi-sport event in the country after the Beijing Olympics of 2008, with the Jinan Olympic Sports Center as the main stadium.

Jinan has, from 2014, hosted the national winter swimming festivals at Daming Lake, and from 2016 these have been run jointly with the International Winter Swimming Association (IWSA). During the 2019–20 season it staged the 8th Winter Springs-swimming International Invitational.
Your university sits in a province with a very long history, so a short overview of Shandong is useful context.

Over thousands of years a succession of Neolithic cultures flourished in Shandong, at the eastern end of the North China Plain. The earliest was Houli (c. 6500–5500 BC), followed by Beixin (c. 5300–4100 BC), then Dawenkou (c. 4100–2600 BC), Longshan (c. 3000–2000 BC) and finally Yueshi (c. 1900–1500 BC).

The Shang and Zhou dynasties held western Shandong with varying strength, while the east belonged to the Dongyi peoples, regarded by those of the Central Plain as barbarians. In 567 BC the state of Qi annexed the Dongyi state of Lai, and from then on the Dongyi became gradually sinicized.

As regional states accumulated power during the Spring and Autumn and the Warring States eras, two stood out here: Qi with its centre at Linzi, and Lu with its centre at Qufu. Lu is renowned as Confucius's home, yet it was fairly small and was eventually annexed by Chu, its neighbour to the south. Qi, by contrast, stayed a major power throughout, controlling cities such as Jimo, Linzi and Ju.

shandong-normal-university.h: From the Qin to the Song

blocks.x: In 221 BC the Qin dynasty defeated Qi and set up the first centralised Chinese state. The Han who followed them created several commanderies in today's Shandong, overseen by two inspectorates (刺史部): Qingzhou (青州) in the north and Yanzhou (兗州) in the south. In the Three Kingdoms period the area belonged to Cao Wei, the northern kingdom ruling northern China.

Following that period, a short spell of unity under the Western Jin gave way to invasions by nomadic peoples from the north, and northern China, Shandong included, was overrun. During the next hundred years or so the land changed hands repeatedly: Later Zhao took it first, then Former Yan, Former Qin, Later Yan and Southern Yan, and then the Liu Song dynasty. The final owner was the Northern Wei, the first of the Northern dynasties that ruled during the era of Northern and Southern dynasties, and Shandong remained with the north from then on.

The Buddhist monk Faxian landed in 412 AD at Laoshan, which sits at the southern edge of the Shandong peninsula, and went on to Qingzhou, where he edited and translated the scriptures he had brought from Pakistan and India.

Unity returned under the Sui in 589, and the Tang dynasty (618–907) then oversaw another golden age for China. In its early decades Shandong was run as a part of the Henan Circuit, one of the empire's political divisions. Later the country broke up under warlords, producing the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, in which Shandong belonged to the Five Dynasties, which were all northern.

Late in the tenth century the Song dynasty reunited China. Water Margin, a classic novel, was based on folk tales about outlaw bands active in Shandong under the Song. In 1996 a major archaeological find was announced at Qingzhou: over two hundred buried Buddhist statues, including early examples of painted figures. They are believed to have been buried because Emperor Huizong, who favoured Taoism, suppressed Buddhism.

The Song were forced in 1142 to give the north of China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty. Under Jin, Shandong was administered in two parts, East and West Circuits, and this was the first time the name Shandong was used.

The Ming dynasty created the modern province of Shandong, which had more territory then, including the eastern part of Liaoning (Liaodong). In 1376 the provincial capital moved from Qingzhou to Jinan, and Jinan has stayed the capital for seven centuries since.

After the capital was moved to Beijing by Emperor Yongle in 1421, grain shipped along the Grand Canal made Jining and Linqing, two cities on that waterway, prosper. Later the Little Ice Age (roughly 1550–1770) reduced harvests and brought famine year on year; together with harsh imperial policies, this triggered peasant rebellions again and again.

Two Ming generals, Kong Youde and Geng Zhongming, took their troops from Dengzhou to Liaodong in 1633 and went over to the Manchu Qing, later taking part in the Qing advance into China proper. Meanwhile, peasant risings under the White Lotus Society were strengthening in Shandong by 1640. The Ming court sent Zhu Datian to put down the revolt, which again caused Shandong's population to fall sharply.

One source also mentions an earthquake of estimated magnitude 8.5 with its epicentre just northeast of Linyi, which devastated Dengzhou and its prefecture and is claimed to have caused somewhere from 43,000 to 50,000 deaths, among foreigners and locals alike. The details given are unclear, so treat the account with caution.

shandong-normal-university.h: The land and coast of Shandong

blocks.x: The province sits where the North China Plain ends, along the lower Yellow River, and a peninsula carries it out into the sea. To the north is the Bohai Sea; its land neighbours are Hebei (northwest), Henan (west) and Jiangsu (south), and the Yellow Sea wraps round the northeast, east and southeast. A short border with Anhui sits between Henan and Jiangsu.

The northwest, west and southwest of the province belong to the vast North China Plain, while the centre is more mountainous, with Mount Tai the most famous peak. In the east, the hilly Shandong Peninsula reaches into the sea, and the Miaodao Archipelago to its north marks the boundary between the Bohai Sea (west) and the Yellow Sea (east). The province's highest point is Jade Emperor Peak, 1,545 metres (5,069 ft), and this is also the summit of the Mount Tai Ranges.

The Yellow River passes through the west, and since 1855 it has always flowed into the sea along the northern coast. Within Shandong the river runs on a raised embankment, higher than the land beside it, which splits the west of the province into the Hai He basin to the north and the Huai River basin to the south. The Grand Canal of China enters Shandong from the northwest and exits in the southwest, and Weishan Lake is the biggest lake in the province. Altogether the coastline measures 3,000 kilometres (1,900 mi), with a rocky shore of cliffs, bays and islands. Laizhou Bay is the southernmost of the Bohai Sea's three bays and borders the northern shore from Dongying to Penglai; the far smaller Jiaozhou Bay is the one that Qingdao surrounds. At the northern tip of the peninsula the Miaodao Islands stretch out, separating the Bohai from the Yellow Sea.
Jinan is the economic and cultural centre of the province, and Shandong's economic strength has also helped modern coastal cities grow at Qingdao, Weihai and Yantai.
The province also has professional teams in several leagues.
Basketball (CBA): Shandong Hi-Speed Kirin and the Qingdao Eagles
Football, top level (Chinese Super League): Qingdao Hainiu and Qingdao West Coast, together with Shandong Taishan
Football, second level (China League One): Qingdao Red Lions
Shandong Normal University lists 79 programs for international students on this site: 18 bachelor, 38 master's, 22 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 62 taught in Chinese, 17 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,400 to CNY 28,700 (median CNY 19,400), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 21,200 to CNY 34,600 (median CNY 29,900), according to the university's published fee table.

79 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shandong-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shandong Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jinan, register at Shandong Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Shandong University, often shortened to SDU and written 山东大学 in Chinese, is a public institution based in Jinan, the capital of Shandong Province. It reports to China's Ministry of Education, which puts it in the national tier of universities rather than the purely provincial one. It was a member of both Project 211 and Project 985, the two earlier national funding programmes, and today it belongs to the Double First-Class Construction scheme that replaced them.

Within Shandong it is generally treated as the leading university, and nationally it sits comfortably among the well-regarded names. Its biggest selling point for applicants is range. SDU teaches in every major field of study apart from military science, which makes it a classic comprehensive university: whether you lean towards medicine, engineering, law, literature or pure science, there is probably a school that fits.

The research numbers back this up. As of 2024, twenty of its subject areas sit in the top 1% worldwide in the ESI (Essential Science Indicators) tables, and five of those reach the top 0.1%. On the international side, the university also holds cooperation agreements: it has signed them with over 300 universities and institutions, spread across more than 30 countries and regions.

Two details about its structure are worth knowing before you read further. First, the university runs eight campuses in total (a later section on campuses describes the individual sites in more detail), and all but two are in Jinan; the other two are in Weihai and Qingdao. Second, its official founding date is tied to a college opened in Jinan in November 1901, even though some of its medical and science traditions trace back even earlier to missionary schools on the coast. The next section tells that story.

shandong-university.h: Where the story starts: academies and mission schools

blocks.x: SDU's history is really the story of several institutions that were folded into one over about a century. It helps to meet the main ancestors one at a time.

The oldest root is a traditional academy. The Luoyuan Academy was created in Jinan in 1733 by edict of the Qing ruler known as the Yongzheng Emperor. Yue Jun, who was governor of Shandong at the time, was given 1,000 taels of silver, roughly 37 kg, to get it going. The name means "source of the Luo", a reference to its first site close to the Baotu Spring. Its job was instruction in the Chinese classics, and its pupils were the sons of gentry families.

Many well-known scholars were linked to it, among them Bi Yuan (1730 to 1797), Sang Tiaoyuan (1695 to 1771), Shen Qiyuan (1685 to 1763), He Shaoji (1799 to 1873), Kuang Yuan (1815 to 1881), Wang Zhihan (1821 to 1850), Liu Yaochun, Zhu Xuedu (1826 to 1892) and Miao Quansun (1844 to 1919).

The academy also figures in a tense episode of 1881. Two American Presbyterian missionaries, John Murray and Stephen A. Hunter, tried to buy land beside the academy to build a chapel. On 13 July 1881 literati from the academy incited a violent attack on that property. The affair, called the Jinan Missionary Incident, created real diplomatic friction between the Qing court and the United States. After the incident the academy was rebuilt in 1896 and became the largest of its kind in Shandong. In 1901, five years later, it was replaced by the newly created Imperial Shandong College, which took over the site. That plot, on Spring City Road, is now occupied by the Provincial Bureau of Statistics.

A different strand begins on the north-eastern coast of the Shandong Peninsula. The first spark came with Calvin W. Mateer and his wife Julia Brown Mateer, American Presbyterian missionaries who landed in early January 1864 at the freshly opened treaty port of Dengzhou (Tengchow in the older spelling), in the Penglai area. Getting there had been an ordeal. They left New York on 3 July 1863, sailed via Africa's southern tip to Shanghai, and were wrecked off the coast at Yantai at the very end.

In autumn 1864 the couple opened a primary school for boys, called the Mengyang Educational Society, in a Guanyin temple. The temple had been sold to them because nobody could pay for its maintenance. It began with six boarders and two day pupils. By 1869 it had grown to take 30 boarders and was split into primary and high school sections, and the high school took the name Wenhui Guan.

Eighteen years of school-level teaching passed before 1882, the year the Tengchow College of Liberal Arts got its formal status. By 1889 it enrolled 100 students. Its six-year curriculum was strongly mathematical and scientific: algebra, geometry with conic sections, trigonometry, surveying, navigation, analytical geometry, mathematical physics, calculus and astronomy. Religion was just as central, in the classroom and in everyday life. The college earned a reputation for academic excellence, and one fact shows how high it stood. W. A. P. Martin once recruited thirteen young professors to teach Western subjects at the Imperial University of Peking, the ancestor of today's Peking University; twelve of them were Tengchow graduates.
Not long after, in 1884, British Baptists opened the Tsingchow Boys' Boarding School in Qingzhou, another town in northern Shandong but inland from the coast.

The American and British missions decided in 1902 to combine their educational efforts. They set up an arts college in Weifang, a theological college in Qingzhou and a medical college in Jinan. In 1909 these three colleges were merged into Shantung Protestant University, later renamed Shantung Christian University, with Jinan chosen as the home of the combined institution. The name by which it is best remembered, Cheeloo University, was an informal title that the school council approved officially in 1915. The name derives from "Qilu", a poetic nickname for Shandong that combines two ancient states once found there: Qi, which lasted from 1046 BC to 221 BC, and Lu, from the 10th century BC to 256 BC.

One notable faculty member was Henry Winters Luce (1868 to 1941), whose son, the publisher Henry R. Luce, founded TIME, Fortune and Life. Luce led the early fundraising for the Jinan campus, which is now SDU's Baotuquan Campus, and between 1912 and 1915 gathered 300,000 dollars from American donors. The Chicago architects Perkins, Fellows and Hamilton designed its buildings. Luce became vice-president in 1916 but resigned a year later, feeling that the then president, J. Percy Bruce, did not back his hope of a university with major national influence.

Medicine became Cheeloo's trademark. From 1914 to 1936 it built and then enlarged Cheeloo Hospital as a leading teaching hospital for Chinese medical education. Then came a wave of consolidation under Samuel Cochran, who served as dean and acting university president. From 1916 to 1923, four other medical schools were brought to Jinan and absorbed into the Cheeloo School of Medicine. The four were Nanking University's medical department, a Hankow medical school, a women's medical college serving North China, and the older Peking Union Medical College.

The university also drew Chinese writers and thinkers. Lao She, famous for Rickshaw Boy (a novel) and Teahouse (a play), lectured at Cheeloo between 1930 and 1934. Until 1937 he went on teaching at other universities, including National Shandong University in Qingdao.

War and politics then intervened. In 1937 Japanese forces took northern China in the Second Sino-Japanese War, and Cheeloo relocated to Sichuan, teaching from the Chengdu campus of West China Union University. Back in Jinan the hospital kept running, staffed mostly by Westerners. For the rest of the war, Japan's military occupied the entire campus, using it to accommodate roughly 1,200 patients and 600 officers. The end came in the Korean War years (1950 to 1953), when Beijing came to view Christian schools as instruments of what it called "American imperialism" and closed them. Cheeloo ceased to exist in 1952. Its School of Medicine was joined with Shandong Provincial Medical College and also the Norman Bethune Medical College of East China, making Shandong Medical College; that name became Shandong Medical University in 1985.

The idea of a modern national university in Shandong came from Yuan Shikai, who was then provincial governor. He led the modernisation of the army in the last years of the Qing, and his control of a powerful force plus his own ambitions later helped bring the Republic of China into being, and then helped push it towards rule by warlords. He had held the governorship since December 1899, sent there to put down the Boxer Uprising and to calm foreign diplomats who wanted decisive action.

In 1901, the year the uprising formally ended, Yuan sent the Guangxu Emperor a draft charter for the university and asked Li Yukai, who was magistrate at Penglai, to begin the groundwork. The Boxer Protocol had been signed on 7 September 1901, and the emperor approved the charter in November. With that, Imperial Shandong University became China's second modern national university. Only one predecessor exists: the Imperial Capital University of 1898, which later turned into Peking University. Its charter then became a template for later imperial universities. Today the original charter is held in Taipei's National Palace Museum, having been taken there as the Kuomintang withdrew when the Chinese Civil War ended.

Yuan wanted Western learning to play a prominent role. Following the precedent of W. A. P. Martin's appointment at the capital university three years earlier, he invited the American Presbyterian missionary Watson McMillan Hayes (1857 to 1944), at that moment president of Tengchow College, to organise the new institution and act as its president. Hayes reached Jinan in July 1901. He started the preparations, launched the province's first successful daily paper, and won from the Qing court a Sunday holiday, which meant classes did not run on Sundays from day one. A dispute about compulsory worship of Confucius by the students then arose. By the end of 1901, Hayes had quit, together with six Chinese Christian colleagues he had brought along. His later years were spent teaching in a Presbyterian theological class in Chefoo (now Yantai) and carrying on missionary and teaching work around Shandong, until 1944, when he died in a Japanese internment camp at Wei County (present-day Weifang).

The college opened on 13 November 1901 in a ceremony attended by Yuan himself. Teaching took place in the old Luoyuan Academy premises, which had been expanded and refurbished in 1896. For the first term 299 students applied. Just 120 of them cleared the first examination, and the final intake was 100 students. The initial faculty had 50 members, including some from overseas, and later grew to 110. More than 20 subjects were taught, from Chinese classics and history to social sciences, natural sciences and a foreign language. The course initially lasted three years and was later extended to four. The first president was Zhou Xuexi.

Name changes followed. In 1904 the college moved to a new site in the Ganshi Qiao area, south-west of Jinan's old centre, and became the Shandong Institution of Higher Learning. In 1911 it was renamed the School of Higher Learning.

Qingdao supplies another chapter. At the time the city belonged to the German leased territory of Kiautschou Bay, and its first modern academic institution was a German-Chinese school officially titled "Advanced School of Special Sciences of a Special Type", a mouthful chosen deliberately. It opened on 25 October 1909, about eleven years after the German lease began. The Germans took a more cooperative line towards the Chinese government over this school than they had in taking the territory. The sinologist Otto Franke led the negotiations. Governor Oskar von Truppel strongly resisted any Chinese influence, but Franke's collaborative plan won firm support from Admiral von Tirpitz and the German envoy in Beijing.

The school operated under German naval administration yet was recognised and financed by the Chinese government. The awkward name was chosen at China's insistence, with "special" signalling a status above other provincial universities and below the Imperial College in Beijing. Locals called it the "Hainan School", after an old name for Qingdao. There was a preparatory level, six years long and five from 1911, for students aged 13 to 15, followed by an upper school. Pupils studied German and Chinese, history, geography, mathematics and a range of sciences (physics and chemistry, plus natural history, zoology, botany and health), along with drawing, music and sport. Engineering and the natural sciences were taught entirely in the Western manner, while the humanities mixed Chinese and European approaches. Religion was not taught, because the Chinese authorities asked for it to be excluded. Student numbers rose to about 400 by 1914, and the school built up a German library of about 5,000 volumes and a Chinese one of about 8,000. Its work stopped when the First World War broke out in 1914 and was never restarted.

Control of Qingdao passed from Japan back to China in 1922. In August 1924 a new private institution, Qingdao University, appeared, led by Gao Enhong, the city's governor. The earlier German-Chinese school was not mentioned at the opening, and no foreign teachers were hired for the time being. The university occupied the former Bismarck barracks, built for German troops in 1903 while Qingdao belonged to the German concession. Teaching leaned towards business administration and engineering, and four years of study led to a bachelor's degree. One student, Luo Ronghuan, later became a marshal in the People's Liberation Army.

Its fortunes turned in 1924 when the Zhili clique of warlords, who had ruled Shandong since the Japanese handover, unexpectedly lost to the Fengtian clique in the Second Zhili-Fengtian War. Gao Enhong had to resign and money dried up. The Fengtian clique made the warlord Zhang Zongchang ruler of Shandong. He was an illiterate former bandit known for ruthlessness, brutality and flamboyant antics, and in 1926 he ordered six schools to be combined into a provincial Shandong University in Jinan.

Through the Northern Expedition the Kuomintang government in Nanjing regained northern China, Shandong included, in 1928. Planning for a state university in the province soon began, and that August the government decided the provincial institution should give way to a national one. The National University of Qingdao formally opened on 21 September 1930 and was renamed National Shandong University in 1932. It also used the old Bismarck barracks. Its chancellor, Yang Zhensheng, took Peking University as his model and aimed for an "inclusive", "scientific and democratic" academic atmosphere. His appointments were impressive. They included Lao She, Wen Yiduo, Shen Congwen and Liang Shiqiu from the literary world, plus two scientists: Wang Ganchang, a nuclear physicist who taught there between 1934 and 1936, and the embryologist Tong Dizhou. Zang Kejia, a poet who would later help edit Chairman Mao's selected poems, was Wen Yiduo's student in Qingdao for four years from 1930.

shandong-university.h: War and the civil war years (1937 to 1949)

blocks.x: Full-scale war began with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in July 1937, and by November National Shandong University had to leave Qingdao. It went first to Anqing in Anhui and soon after to Wanxian in Sichuan, now Wanzhou District of Chongqing. Books, equipment and administrative files travelled in separate shipments and suffered heavy losses. Classes restarted in Wanxian in spring 1938 but the Ministry of Education soon stopped them, and teachers and students were sent to the National Central University, which had moved from Nanjing to Chongqing the previous year. Its books and equipment went into storage in Chongqing, divided among the National Central Library, the vocational school of the same national-central name, and the National Central University. In spring 1946, after the war, it returned to Qingdao.

Part of the Qingdao campus served as headquarters for American forces between 1945 and May 1949: first the U.S. Sixth Marine Division (disbanded 31 March 1946), then the Western Pacific unit of the U.S. Fleet Marine Force. In 1947 students protested over the Su Mingcheng Incident: an American sailor had killed a rickshaw puller after a quarrel.

Meanwhile the Communist side was building its own institutions. Before Japan surrendered, in 1944, the Chinese Communist Party's Central China Bureau resolved to create Huazhong Construction University on the basis of its party school, in Xinpu in Xuyi County on the Jiangsu and Anhui border; in August 1945 it moved to Qingjiang. That same month the Communist-led Shandong Anti-Japanese People's Government started a Shandong University at Linyi, capital of its base area. People called it Linyi Shandong University to distinguish it from the nationalist one. In early 1946 Peng Kang, president of Huazhong Construction University, brought his teachers and students into Linyi Shandong University.

Japan withdrew and the Communists and Kuomintang fought the Chinese Civil War. In summer 1948 the party's East China Bureau decided to merge the Linyi university with Huazhong Construction University as East China University in Weifang. After Jinan fell to the Communists the university moved there in November. Orders came in winter 1950, after the Kuomintang and the US Navy pulled out of Qingdao, to relocate to that city, and there it was merged into Shandong University in 1951.

East China University was absorbed in 1951, and that year the university also issued its Journal of Shandong University. A year later, with Cheeloo dissolved, its medical school went to Shandong Medical College. Soviet teachers worked at the university until the Sino-Soviet split. In October 1958 the university went back from Qingdao to Jinan, first using the Hongjialou Campus. The marine sciences stayed in Qingdao, and later became Shandong Ocean University. A new Central Campus was begun in 1959. That was a Great Leap Forward year, and also the year of a serious Yellow River flood. On 10 October 1960 Shandong University was placed on the list of National Key Universities.

The Cultural Revolution was a severe interruption. Early June 1966 brought strikes that closed Jinan's schools, with teachers "struggled against", and the university came to a standstill. On 29 July 1970 the provincial Revolutionary Committee decided to split it up. Arts subjects moved to Qufu, where they were joined to Qufu Normal College under the name Shandong University. Biology went to the Tai'an-based Shandong Agricultural College, and what remained of the sciences became a separate Shandong Science and Technology University. From 1971 workers and peasants were meant to benefit from a new admissions policy: applicants were put forward "by the masses", then needed sign-off from both the political leadership and the university itself. By 1976, 3,267 students admitted this way had completed courses of two or three years. Premier Zhou Enlai heard about the reorganisation in 1973 and, although already terminally ill with bladder cancer, ordered a return to the earlier structure. All of the committee's changes were reversed in early 1974.

The Weihai Campus was founded in 1984, and Shandong Medical College became Shandong Medical University in 1985. SDU grew rapidly from 1986 to 1996. Its structure in 1997 comprised 14 colleges and 45 schools, with 56 undergraduate, 57 master's and 17 doctoral programmes on offer.

The year 2000 brought a double merger, taking in both Shandong Medical University and Shandong University of Technology. From the medical university came the old Cheeloo campus, which became the West Campus and was renamed Baotuquan Campus in 2009. The technology university's site became the South Campus, renamed Qianfoshan Campus in 2009. In 2003 construction began on a large valley campus south of Jinan, first called the New South Campus and now Xinglongshan, meant for first- and second-year undergraduates.

One public controversy is worth mentioning for balance. Reports surfaced in July 2019 that male foreign students were each given three Chinese "buddies", mostly women, to help with life in China. The application form for the programme even mentioned wanting foreign friends "of the opposite sex". The university apologised, but denied that male international students were matched with three female local students, and blamed "insufficient checks" for wording it described as "improper expression". The affair prompted complaints that foreign students receive too many privileges.

shandong-university.h: How SDU performs in the rankings

blocks.x: Rankings are only one way to look at a university, but several place SDU in a strong position, and they show where its strengths are. The Academic Ranking of World Universities was first published in 2003, and That first edition listed SDU among its top 500, one of the Project 985 universities to do so. In the joint THE-QS World University Rankings of 2005 it was placed joint 282nd globally. In 2010 the Chinese University Alumni Association (CUAA) ranked it 14th among China's Top 100 universities, with the 11th highest score for teaching. On engineering, a 2008 assessment from a Chinese management-and-science research centre (the Research Center of Management and Science in China) put SDU's programmes 15th nationally.

Research output is where it shines. For the last ten years SDU has stayed among the top 10 universities in China by the number of papers indexed in the Science Citation Index, and the university is judged particularly strong in medicine, physics and mathematics. Mines ParisTech counts alumni who run Fortune Global 500 companies, and in that ranking SDU is number one inside China.
More recent results point the same way:
The 2024 CWTS Leiden Ranking placed it 15th in the world on publications from 2019 to 2022.
The SCImago Institutions Rankings for 2024 position it 59th among universities worldwide.
Nature Research's Nature Index 2025 Annual Tables, which track high-quality articles in 82 selected science journals, list it 18th.
The Shanghai Ranking (ARWU) places it somewhere between 101st and 150th.
Under CWUR's 2025 world table it is 168th globally and 36th within Asia.

shandong-university.h: How the university is run and what it teaches

blocks.x: At the top, SDU is led by a president (xiaozhang) supported by vice presidents who each handle a specific area such as research or international exchange. Directors (chuzhang) lead the central offices, which cover areas like finance, personnel, research and international affairs. Below this level the academic work is divided into 31 faculties, which the university calls schools (xueyuan), plus a graduate school. A dean (yuanzhang) leads each school, and a school can be broken into departments with their own chairpersons.

Teaching is grouped into 11 main disciplines. Philosophy, economics and law come first, then literature, history and the natural sciences, and the list ends with engineering, management, medicine, education and military science. Students choose from 104 undergraduate degree programmes, 209 master's programmes and 127 doctoral programmes. Seven professional master's degrees are offered on top of that: public health, dentistry, clinical medicine, law, engineering, business management and public administration.
The student body was about 57,500 full-time students in 2009, including 14,500 postgraduates and more than 1,000 foreign students. Keep in mind that this figure dates from 2009.

Research is organised on a large scale. The university reports 34 key academic disciplines at national, provincial or ministerial level. It runs two national key laboratories and 21 provincial or ministerial ones, plus a national engineering and technology promotion centre and 10 provincial technology research centres. On the basic-research side it has three national bases for scientific research and personnel development, and a further three national bases for fundamental science personnel development. The Ministry of Education has approved three of its social science key research bases. Academics include 23 members (adjuncts counted) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Healthcare teaching relies on 12 teaching hospitals and three general hospitals, one of them Qilu Hospital, and the library has more than 3,550,000 items.

shandong-university.h: The schools you can choose from

blocks.x: The following schools and programmes are listed, which gives a quick idea of the breadth on offer, including the two honour colleges and the general programme:

Engineering: Civil Engineering; Electrical Engineering; Energy and Power Engineering; Mechanical Engineering; Materials Science and Engineering; Control Science and Engineering; Environmental Science and Engineering; Information Science and Engineering; Chemistry and Chemical Engineering; plus the School of Macroelectronics
Computing and mathematics: the School of Computer Science and Technology, the School of Mathematics and System Sciences, and the School of Physics
Medicine and life sciences: Medicine, Dentistry, Nursing, Pharmacy, Public Health and Life Science
Business, law and social sciences: Business Administration, Economics, Law, Political Science and Public Administration, Philosophy and Social Development, Marxist Theory Education
Humanities and arts: Foreign Languages and Literature, History and Culture, Literature and Journalism, Journalism, Fine Arts
Other units: Physical Education and International Education (both schools), the honour colleges Taishan College and Nishan College, and a General Study Program

SDU says it has seven campuses in total, although the introduction counts eight; both numbers appear in the university's own description, so ask the admissions office which sites your programme uses. All but two are in Jinan, and together the Jinan sites cover 3.8 km2. One of the other two is in Qingdao and one in Weihai. Where you live and study depends heavily on your school, so the notes below cover each site.

Building started in 1959, roughly a year after the university came back to Jinan from Qingdao, and the timing was dramatic: the Great Leap Forward, the Great Chinese Famine and a devastating Yellow River flood in July 1959 all coincided. The Mingde Building here houses central administration. The site also has student dormitories, a large dining hall and the main library. A university hotel, the Academic Exchange Center (known as Xueren Dasha), is also here. Streets inside the campus carry names taken from Confucian concepts.

Nine schools teach here: economics, history and culture, Marxism-Leninism, life sciences, environmental engineering, information science and engineering, chemistry and chemical engineering, mathematics and system science, and literature with journalism and communication.

This campus takes its name from Hongjialou Square and lies just north and east of it, next to the Sacred Heart Cathedral. The first building dates from 1936, when Franciscan sisters from the Jinan archdiocese put it up for their Yifan Girls' Middle School. That school merged with Liming Middle School in 1948, and the site then went to the Shandong Agricultural Institute until the institute left for Tai'an in 1958. October 1958 saw the university return from Qingdao, and this became its first campus in Jinan. Law, Fine Arts, and Foreign Languages and Literature are taught here today.

This was Cheeloo University's home, established in 1909, and it is the campus with the strongest sense of history. The designers were Perkins, Fellows and Hamilton of Chicago, a firm renowned for Prairie School campus buildings. They wanted a Chinese flavour, but took the roof profile to be the single defining mark of Chinese architecture. Consequently the roofs look Chinese while the buildings below lack the wooden Dougong brackets and similar supports that traditionally accompany them.

Among the historic buildings are Bergen Science Hall (chemistry and biology classes used to be held there), Mateer Science Hall (once the home of physics and physiology) and McCormick Hall. The Alumni Gate, completed on 17 June 1924, used to be the main way in. Medicine, pharmacy, dentistry, nursing and public health are all located here, so the health sciences remain where they have always been taught.

This site opened in 1949 for Shandong University of Technology and became SDU's when the two merged in July 2000. It measures about 420,000 square metres and is still given over to engineering. Teaching here covers civil, electrical, mechanical and power engineering, materials science, computing, and control science, with physical education as the exception. Its roads honour famous engineers and inventors from China and abroad.

The newest campus in Jinan is also the biggest, at around 769,000 square metres. Work started in March 2003 and the first facilities opened in August 2004. First- and second-year students from nine departments live and study here, and it includes a Student Associations Activity Center of about 2,000 square metres. If you start as an undergraduate, you may well spend your first two years here.

Computer science and the Software College are based on this site. Work began in July 2001, and the area today comes to about 267,000 square metres, where over 3,000 students live. Neighbouring it is a group of commercial software firms, including the CIIIC (China International ICT Innovation Cluster), with whom the campus pools educational resources. For students aiming at a software career, that proximity is attractive.

Founded in 1984, this campus covers around 1 million square metres, making it the largest. Thirteen departments teach here. Korean studies, business, law, and journalism and communication are among them, as are art, ocean science and information engineering. The list continues with electrical and mechanical engineering, space science and physics, mathematics and statistics, international education, and vocational and technical training. An interdisciplinary research body, the Weihai Institute for Interdisciplinary Research, was also established on this campus. Just to the west stands SDU's own Academic Center, which works as a hotel and conference venue on the beach.

The building programme began in March 2011, and the first phase was formally opened in September 2016. The site lies north of Xingshizhuang Village in Aoshanwei Town, part of Jimo, north-east of Qingdao, right next to Aoshan Bay and the coastal highway. Altogether about two million square metres are planned, 43 percent of it for the first stage. Once finished the campus should hold 30,000 students; early plans spoke of recruiting a first class of 5,000 freshmen in autumn 2013, and the construction budget was put at 800 million yuan (about 124 million US dollars).

The architects want a blend of Chinese and Western styles, with many buildings echoing Qingdao's German colonial red roofs and other details. New York's Perkins Eastman drew up the master plan, and there is a pleasing link to the past: its co-founder Bradford Perkins is a grandson of Dwight H. Perkins, whose practice designed Cheeloo's Jinan campus. Plans give the campus a research role in advanced science and engineering, stressing contact with high-tech industry and with partners abroad. The whole scheme is intended to spread SDU across the province, as the University of California does for that state, only under closer central control.

SDU has built a network for educational cooperation, with exchange agreements with over 70 universities in over 50 countries. It is also linked as a sister school to American middle and junior high schools, Scofield Magnet Middle School among them.

Overseas academics visit in three patterns. In 2009 there were 160 short-term visitors (stays under a month), 70 medium-term (under six months) and 80 long-term (more than six months). Thirty of the 80 long-term staff teach languages: Russian, Spanish, German, French, Korean, Japanese and English. The others work in fields including biology, chemistry, physics, philosophy, law, Chinese classics and traditional philosophy, and international politics and economics.

Every year about 1,500 international students from around 40 countries enrol, and during any semester more than 1,000 are on campus. Asia and Africa supply most of them, though Europe, Canada, Australia and the United States are represented too. Since 1980 the university has welcomed over 10,000 students from more than 60 countries. Chinese language and culture are the favourite subjects, followed by economics and medicine. SDU also takes part in short-term exchange programmes, which bring approximately 2,500 international visitors a year.

A joint urban research centre was founded in 2006 with the US-based University of Cincinnati, and each side has a presence on the other's campus. SDU's partnership with Virginia Tech produced an International Laboratory, opened in August 2010 inside the Central Campus's Integrated Research Building. Its subject is biophysics and engineering analysis of model biological systems taken from the diversity of life in China. SDU also takes part in the Study China Programme, which is coordinated by the University of Manchester and paid for by the UK government department then responsible for business, innovation and skills.
For students interested in research, the following are the main facilities. State-level units include:
National Glycoengineering Research Center
A national engineering laboratory for coal-fired pollutant emission reduction
The State Key Laboratory for Crystal Materials
The State Laboratory for Microbial Technology
Ministry of Education key laboratories cover these topics:
Colloid and Interface Chemistry
Liquid Structure and Heredity of Materials
Experimental Teratology
Cardiovascular Remodelling and Function Research
Cryptologic Technology and Information Security
Power System Intelligent Dispatch and Control
The Ministry of Health supports a Key Laboratory for Otolaryngology. In the humanities and social sciences the Ministry of Education recognises four key research bases:
Center for Ancient Chinese Philosophy and Zhouyi
Institute for Contemporary Socialism
Institute for Literary Theory and Aesthetics
Center for Judaic and Inter-Religious Studies
There are three national research institutes, for Crystal Materials, Microbiology, and Infrared and Remote Sensing Technology. Provincial research centres in Shandong are a long and varied list:
Geotechnical and Structural Engineering Research Center
Risk Analysis and Random Calculus Laboratory
Institute for Social Studies, Science and Religion
A group working on number theory
A group working on high energy physics
Oriental Archaeology Research Center
Economic research: the Center for Economic Research
Health: the Center for Health Management and Policy
Regional studies: Centers for European Studies and for Japanese Studies
Center for Space Thermal Science
Modern Logistics Research Center
Institute of ECIWO Biology
A second Key Laboratory for Otolaryngology
Medical students will spend time in the affiliated hospitals. Three are described in detail.

Qilu Hospital began as Cheeloo University's hospital. Harold Balme (1878 to 1953), a British doctor from London's King's College Hospital, supervised the work that began in 1914. He later became Cheeloo's third president, serving from 1921 to 1927. On 27 September 1915 the first building, known today as the Republican Building, was opened by Shandong's military governor, Jin Yunpeng. Around twenty years afterwards the hospital transferred to a new building finished in 1936, and the old one went to Cheeloo's School of Medicine. Qilu Hospital now has capacity for 1,800 beds, and each year it treats over 1.9 million outpatients. It offers pediatrics, neurosurgery, general surgery, otolaryngology, obstetrics and gynecology, hematology, cardiology and internal medicine, among other things. The address is 107 Wenhua West Road, Jinan.

With around 2,431 beds, the Second Hospital of Shandong University is larger still, and offers neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery and internal medicine. It is affiliated with the university but run by the National Medical Department. You will find it at 247 Beiyuan Street, Jinan.
Dental students have the Stomatology Hospital, founded in 1977. It has 105 staff, four research centres and two laboratories, and sits at 44 Wenhua West Road in Jinan.

The motto, chosen in May 2002, can be translated as "Noble in Spirit, Boundless in Knowledge" (xue wu zhi jing, qi you hao ran in Chinese). For branding the university also uses "Soul of the mountains, spirit of the sea", a nod to Shandong's character as a mountainous peninsula. Visitors to the south gate, which is the Central Campus's main entrance, see an inscription that describes the mission: "Preparing talents for the world; Striving for the prosperity and strength of the country". The calligraphy is a reproduction of Mao Zedong's own. He wrote the characters in March 1964, after the Great Leap Forward and before the Cultural Revolution, in the address on a thank-you note to Gao Heng, an SDU professor who had sent him books and articles.

The university has two songs. The official anthem has lyrics by Cheng Fangwu, revised by a group of people, with music by Zheng Lvcheng. A separate "Song of Shandong University" has words by Qiao Yu, who also wrote the lyrics of My Motherland, and music by Gu Jianfen, both natives of Shandong.

The logo is built on the characters for mountain (shan, also the abbreviation of Shandong) and big, or university (da). Mountain and sea are merged in the design. They recall two sayings: that a path leads up the mountain of books, with diligence as the way, and that the sea of learning has no end, with hard work as the boat. The same image stands for the university's mountain-and-sea spirit.
The university has had these presidents, in order:
Tang Shaoyi, 1901
Zhou Xuexi (also 1901), who went on to serve two terms as finance minister for the Republic of China
Wang Shoupeng, head of the provincial university in Jinan, 1926 to 1927
Yang Zhensheng, head of the national university in Qingdao, 1930 to 1932
Zhao Taimou, also at the Qingdao national university, 1932 to 1936 and again 1946 to 1949
Lin Jiqing, acting head in Qingdao, 1936 to 1946
Hua Gang, heading the Qingdao university, 1951 to 1955
Chao Zhefu, Qingdao, 1956 to 1958
Cheng Fangwu, first president after the return to Jinan, 1958 to 1974
Wu Fuheng, 1979 to 1984
Deng Conghao, 1984 to 1986
Pan Chengdong, 1986 to 1997
Zeng Fanren, 1998 to 2000
Zhan Tao, 2000 to 2008
Xu Xianming, 2008 to 2013
Zhang Rong, 2013 to 2017
Fan Liming, 2017 to 2022
Li Shucai, 2022 to the present
The roll of people linked with SDU is heavy on writers and scientists. Writers and humanities scholars:
Lao She (1899 to 1966), best known for Rickshaw Boy and Teahouse
Feng Yuanjun (1900 to 1974), writer and scholar of classical Chinese literature and literary history
Gao Heng (1900 to 1986), a pioneer in modern readings of the I Ching; he exchanged letters with Mao Zedong
Ji Xianlin (1911 to 2009), a polymath: linguist, paleographer, historian and writer
Jin Xuefei (born 1956, pen name Ha Jin), who writes in English and won the American National Book Award in 1999
Liang Shiqiu (1903 to 1987), writer and translator, who put the complete works of Shakespeare into Chinese, as well as Orwell's Animal Farm
Lydia H. Liu, a Guggenheim Fellow in 1997, who studies comparative literature at Columbia University

Ma Ruifang (born 1949), author and scholar who studied the works of Pu Songling

Shen Congwen (1902 to 1988), writer who combined vernacular and classical Chinese techniques
Wang Tongzhao (1897 to 1957), a novelist and poet who wrote Mountain Rain and led the Chinese Department
Wen Yiduo (1899 to 1946), poet and scholar influenced by Western models, whose collections include Hongzhu (Red Candle) and Sishui (Dead Water)
Zang Kejia (1905 to 2004), poet and chief editor of Poetry magazine, who also helped edit Chairman Mao's selected poems
James Veneris (1922 to 2004), an American who defected during the Korean War and became an English professor
Scientists, mathematicians and scholars in other fields:
Peng Shige (born 1947), mathematician known for work on stochastic analysis and on financial mathematics
Tong Dizhou (1902 to 1979), an embryologist who became a vice president at the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Wang Ganchang (1907 to 1998), nuclear physicist and student of Lise Meitner, a principal contributor to China's nuclear deterrent
Wang Pu (1902 to 1969), who studied under Lise Meitner too, a nuclear physicist and founder of the School of Physics

Zhou Ming-Zhen (1918 to 1996), paleontologist who worked on early tertiary mammals

Public life:
Luo Ronghuan (1902 to 1963), Marshal of the People's Liberation Army and security chief on the Long March
