shandong-university.h: Living in Jinan: what to expect

blocks.x: Daily life as a student is shaped far more by the city around you than by the campus gates. The weather, the way people travel and what there is to do all matter. The sections that follow describe Jinan, the home of SDU's main campuses.

In climate terms Jinan is humid continental (Köppen type Dwa), and the four seasons are clearly separated. Spring is dry and almost rainless, summer is hot and wet, autumn is crisp, and winter is cold and dry with little snow. Pack accordingly: you will want both summer clothes and a proper winter coat.
Here are the main figures:
Average annual temperature: 14.9 °C (58.8 °F).
Annual precipitation: 734 millimetres (28.9 in). Most falls in summer, and totals swing widely between years.
January: the coldest and driest month, averaging −0.3 °C (31.5 °F), with just 5.0 millimetres (0.20 in) of precipitation in rain equivalent.
July is the hottest month, averaging 27.4 °C (81.3 °F).
Sunshine: 2,226 hours of bright sunshine a year, with monthly possible sunshine running from 40% in July to 58% in May.
Records since 1951: the coldest day was 17 January 1953 at −19.7 °C (−3 °F), and the hottest was 24 July 1955 at 42.5 °C (109 °F).

The geography adds a twist. Because mountains lie to the south, about 200 days of the year see a temperature inversion. Rainfall is high by northern Chinese standards, and combined with mountains that wrap around the city on three sides, it produces particularly oppressive summers. For this reason Jinan has been named as a candidate for a fourth "furnace" alongside the traditional Three Furnaces of China. Expect sticky heat in July and August.

Jinan's rise as a commercial centre started in 1852, when the Yellow River moved into a new bed just north of the city. Together with the later arrival of a railway hub, this made Jinan a major market for farm produce from the fertile regions to the north.

Trade in farm goods then encouraged related industry: clothing and textiles, flour milling, oil pressing and factories for paper, cement and matches. The 1950s added large iron and steel works and chemical plants around the city; the metal plants turn out pig iron, ingot steel and finished steel. In the 1970s Sinotruk set up its headquarters and factories for trucks and construction vehicles in Jinan.

Jinan has long held third place in Shandong Province by economic output. It passed Yantai to take second place in the province before Laiwu City was merged into it in 2019. The following figures show how fast it has grown:
2007: total output reached 256.3 billion yuan. Agriculture (the primary sector) made up 5.9% of it, industry (secondary) 45.2% and services (tertiary) 48.9%.

2008: GDP came to 301.7 billion yuan, which was sixth among provincial capitals. The five ahead of it were Guangzhou (821.5), then Hangzhou, which scored 478.1, Wuhan on 396.0, Chengdu on 390.1 and finally Nanjing, with 377.5.

2009: GDP rose 11.3% on the previous year to 335.0 billion yuan. That was 21st in the country. Counting provincial capitals alone it was 7th. For comparison, the larger provincial capitals and municipalities were Shanghai (1,490.09 in the same units), Beijing at 1,186.59 and Guangzhou at 911.27. Tianjin followed with 750.08, and Chongqing with 652.87 (of which 569.74 is for its urban core). Behind them were Hangzhou at 508.8, plus Wuhan (456.0), Chengdu (450.26), Shenyang (435.9), Nanjing (423.02) and Changsha (374.5). Zhengzhou, at 330.0, was just behind Jinan.
2011: GDP of 440.629 billion yuan, up 10.6%. Averaged per permanent resident, this meant 64,331 yuan (up 8.9%), roughly 9,960 US dollars.
2016: GDP of 653.61 billion yuan, up 7.8%. Per resident, the figure was 90,999 yuan, a rise of 6.5%, which equals 13,700 US dollars at the year's average exchange rate.

2022: GDP of 1,202.75 billion yuan, up 3.1% at constant prices. By sector, farming and related primary industry added 42.05 billion yuan (growth of 3.1%), secondary industry 418.02 billion (3.2%) and the tertiary sector 742.67 billion (3.0%). The three sectors stood in the ratio 3.5:34.8:61.7.

2024: GDP of 1,352.76 billion yuan, up 5.4% at constant prices. Primary industry contributed 44.0 billion yuan (+3.6%), the secondary sector 451.92 billion (+5.8%) and the tertiary sector 856.84 billion (+5.2%). In ratio terms that is 3.3:33.4:63.3.

Reading across these years, you can see a steady shift away from industry and towards services, which in the 2024 figures supply close to two thirds of output. For a graduate, that tilt suggests the city's job market leans toward service-sector work, though industry remains substantial.
Large industrial enterprises in Jinan include these heavy-industry names:
Sinopec's Jinan branch
Shandong Hi-Speed Group
Shandong Iron and Steel Group
Shandong Heavy Industry
The China National Heavy Duty Truck Group
Shandong Gold Group
Shandong Electric Power Corporation
Shandong Energy Group
In light industry the notable names are Inspur Group and Joyoung.

Two zones are worth knowing about, particularly for students in technical fields. The State Council approved the Jinan High-tech Industrial Development Zone in 1991, among the earliest zones of this type. East of the city, it is planned over 83 km2 (32 sq mi) in three parts. The core area is 33 km2 (13 sq mi), the export processing district is 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi), and an eastern extension adds another 40 km2 (15 sq mi). Volvo, LG, Panasonic and Sanyo have all located firms here. International links followed in 2000. That year the zone became a member of the world science and technology association and opened a China-Ukraine High-tech Cooperation Park. Its Qilu Software Park is a sister park to one in Bangalore, India.

The Jinan Export Processing Zone is in the eastern suburbs, east of the High-tech Zone and north of the Jiwang highway. It is 9 km (5.6 mi) from the Jiqing Highway and 18 km (11 mi) from Jinan Airport.

shandong-university.h: How many people live in Jinan

blocks.x: In the 2020 Chinese census the total population, counting Laiwu City which was merged in recently, was 9,202,432. The built-up metro area, made up of 6 of the 10 urban districts (four districts, Jiyang, Zhangqiu, Laiwu and Gangcheng, are not yet part of the conurbation), had 5,452,335 inhabitants, most of whom are of Han ethnicity.
Jinan is a transport hub, which is good news if you plan to travel at weekends and during holidays.

The city sits where two major railways cross. The Jinghu Railway from Beijing to Shanghai is the principal north-south line of eastern China, and in Jinan it meets the Jiaoji Railway, which links the city with the port of Qingdao in the east. The Hanji Railway goes west to Handan in Hebei Province.
On the Jinghu line, trains reach Dezhou, Tai'an, Jining and Zaozhuang from Jinan. The Jiaoji line reaches Zibo, Weifang and Qingdao, and the Hanji line goes to Yancheng and Liaocheng.

Three stations serve the centre: Jinan station, Jinan East and Daminghu, which is next to Daming Lake. Fast trains on the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line use Jinan West, which lies away from the centre, in Huaiyin District on the western edge. Public service there began on 30 June 2011, and the station is expected to grow into a hub, with high-speed lines going to Qingdao in the east and, to the west, Taiyuan and Shijiazhuang. Jinan East opened in 2018. A further station, Jinan North, is planned.
The Jinan Metro was started in 2013 and formally opened to the public in 2019. Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8, the Jiyang Line and SkyShuttle Line 1 now operate, with a total of 140 stations.

City buses come in air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned versions, and the air-conditioned routes carry a K before the number. From 2018 most lines are air-conditioned, including some without the K, and more than 200 routes cover the whole city.

Roads are busy too. Major expressways include China National Highways 104, 220 and 309. As Jinan is a junction for both road and rail, its main coach terminus is among the busiest in China. Counts reach 92,000 passengers in a day at peak periods, and about 42,000 on quiet days.

Jinan Yaoqiang International Airport is about 33 km (21 mi) north-east of the centre, in Yaoqiang Subdistrict of Licheng District, which gives it its name. Expressways link it to the city centre. Domestic routes link it with many major Chinese cities, and international routes include Seoul, Osaka, Bangkok, Singapore, Paris, Helsinki and Los Angeles.

Sports are a good way to meet locals. Jinan's best-known basketball team is Shandong Hi-Speed Kirin, which has competed in the CBA, the Chinese Basketball Association, since 1995. In the 2012-13 season it reached the final but lost 4-0 to the Guangdong Southern Tigers.

Football fans follow Shandong Taishan Football Club, the city's most famous team. It plays in the top tier, the Chinese Super League, and has done so in every season since the league turned professional in 1994. Its trophy cabinet holds five top-division titles, eight FA Cups and a single FA Super Cup. In 2004, Jinan was one of four host cities in China for the AFC Asian Cup.

In 2009 the city hosted the National Games of China, the country's premier national sports event and the first big multi-sport event in China after the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The Jinan Olympic Sports Center was the principal venue. A quirkier tradition dates from 2014: national winter swimming festivals take place at Daming Lake, and since 2016 the organisers have worked jointly with the IWSA (International Winter Swimming Association). The 2019-20 season brought the 8th Winter Springs-swimming International Invitational to the city.

Taken together, SDU offers a very wide choice of subjects, a long record in medicine and the sciences, campuses in Jinan, Weihai and Qingdao, and a large community of international students. Jinan adds good transport links, a strong industrial and technology base, and four distinct seasons.

shandong-university.h: Points to weigh when you apply

blocks.x: Think about which campus your programme uses before anything else, because the campuses differ greatly in character. Engineering students will be at Qianfoshan, health science students at the historic Baotuquan site, and software students at the Qilu Software College Campus beside the technology cluster. Undergraduates in nine departments spend their first two years at Xinglongshan in the mountain valley south of Jinan. Those who study in Weihai or Qingdao will live on the coast instead, and neither city is Jinan.

It also helps to remember that several figures in this profile, such as student numbers and visitor counts, come from 2009, and that the rankings quoted come from different years and methods. Treat them as a general picture, and confirm the latest numbers with the university when you apply.
Finally, expect to adapt to the climate. Jinan's summers are hot and humid and its winters are cold and dry, with temperatures averaging −0.3 °C in January and 27.4 °C in July.

Everyday life for students at SDUST is lived in Qingdao, so this part of the guide looks at the city's setting and weather, its people and economy, the ways of getting around and some of its character.

Qingdao faces south on the coast of the Shandong Peninsula (known in German as Schantung-Halbinsel). Three prefecture-level cities border it. Rizhao lies to the southwest, Yantai to the northeast and Weifang to the west. The city has an area of 4,114 sq mi (10,654 km2), between latitudes 35° 35' N and 37° 09' N and longitudes 119° 30' E and 121° 00' E. Settled districts are relatively flat, but mountains spring up both inside the city limits and near them. The top elevation, 1,133 meters (3,717 ft) over sea level, is found there. Looking at the land by type, 15.5% is highland, 25.1% foothill, 37.8% plain and 21.7% lowland. The coastline is 730.64 kilometers (454.00 mi) long, and five major rivers, each over 50 kilometers (31 mi), run through the area.

Qingdao has a temperate four-season climate that the monsoon influences, sitting where the humid subtropical regime (Köppen: Cwa) gives way to the humid continental regime (Köppen: Dwa). The ocean exerts direct control, through the southeast monsoon and through ocean currents and water masses, which means the city has strong maritime characteristics. Cool-to-cold, windy and generally dry winters bring a January mean of 0.2 °C (that is, 32.4 °F). Summers are hot and humid for the most part, but very hot days are rare, and August averages 25.6 °C (78.1 °F). Because the city is by the coast on a peninsula, spring arrives about one month later than in most inland regions of China, and across the year the swing between day and night temperatures is only 6.3 °C (11.3 °F). Autumn works the other way and is milder than in the inland parts of Shandong.

The sea warms up to about 25 °C (77 °F) at its peak in late August, so swimming is possible for two months before and after. The average temperature for the year works out at 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Records since 1951 start with a low of −15.9 °C (3 °F) on 7 and 8 January 2021, while the high was 38.9 °C (102 °F), recorded on 15 July 2002. Unofficial readings go lower still, to −16.9 °C (1.6 °F), and the official weather station logged −16.4 °C (2.5 °F) on 10 January 1931. In July the possible sunshine share is at its lowest, 38 percent, and in October its highest, 59 percent; the annual total is 2,261 hours of bright sunshine.

The summer beaches have one drawback. Large algal blooms plague them, and as the algae rot they release hydrogen sulfide with an offensive smell, much like rotten eggs. In 2013 officials declared a large-scale algae disaster over sea lettuce blooms, which seaweed farming in Jiangsu Province helped to cause.

Of the 10 million people living in Qingdao, 6.2 million are in the urban area, and another 5 million or so live in the other cities under its jurisdiction. Roughly 76,507 babies are born in a year, which is 10.15 per thousand, set against a death rate of 6.32 per thousand, both annual figures. A strong export economy and relatively high family wages mean residents enjoy living standards that count among the best of China's leading cities. The Qingdao Statistical Yearbook for 2021 gives 10.1057 million permanent residents in 2020, an increase of 182,700 over the previous year.

A large Korean community lives here. Around 100,000 Koreans were working, studying and living in Qingdao by 2009. That made it China's second-largest Korean population centre, behind Beijing with roughly 200,000.

Shandong Province has changed its economic landscape substantially in recent years, and much of the change has happened in Qingdao, which has grown quickly. In 2006 growth of 18.9 percent a year took GDP to 42.3 billion, which was first in Shandong and tenth among China's leading 20 cities. In 2008 GDP per capita came to US$7,616 (CN¥52,895), and by 2024 it was US$23,000 (CN¥161,200). The World Bank listed Qingdao in 2006 as one of six golden cities among 120 assessed Chinese cities, looking at factors such as the investment climate and the effectiveness of government. GDP in 2018 came to CN¥1200.15 billion, falling back slightly in 2019.

Abroad, the city is probably best known for Tsingtao Brewery, which began as a German-British joint venture in 1903 and makes China's most famous export beer, Tsingtao. Two big companies are based here as well: Hisense, a major electronics company, and Haier, which makes white goods on a large scale. The guitar maker Epiphone started a factory in the city in 2002.

In 1984 the central government gave one Qingdao district the status of Special Economic and Technology Development Zone (abbreviated SETDZ). Secondary and tertiary industries across the city then went through accelerated growth. Qingdao has received large foreign investment, with South Korea and Japan investing heavily, and its port serves as a hub of local and international trade.

For primary industries, Qingdao has around 50,000 acres (200 km2) of farmland. The coast zigzags, which gives the city a very valuable supply of fish, shrimp and other seafood. Its wind power output is among the highest in the region.

Four provincial expressways start in or cross the city. They are the S16 Rongwei Expressway from Rongcheng to Weifang, the S19 Longqing Expressway from Longkou to Qingdao, the S21 Xinwei Expressway from Xinhe to Weifang and the S24 Weiqing Expressway from Weihai to Qingdao.

Among the National Highways that go through or start in Qingdao are G204 (from Yantai to Shanghai), G206 (Yantai to Shantou), G308 (Qingdao to Shijiazhuang) and G309 (Rongcheng to Lanzhou). Of these, G308 is the one that begins in Qingdao.

shandong-university-of-science-and-techn.h: Haiwan Bridge and the bay tunnel

blocks.x: A new record was set for the longest bridge over water when Haiwan Bridge opened in Qingdao on 30 June 2011. It joins the city with Huangdao and Hongdao over a distance of 26.4 miles (42.5 km), almost three miles (4.8 km) beyond the previous record holder, the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana, USA. The bridge stands on more than 5,000 pillars. It cost about 10 billion yuan, or about 1.5 billion dollars. The Shandong Gausu Group was the designer, and building lasted four years. At least 10,000 workers toiled round the clock in two teams that started at opposite ends and worked toward each other. Haiwan Bridge saves 30 minutes on the trip from downtown Qingdao to sprawling Huangdao. The Jiaozhou Bay Tunnel was opened on that very day. It carries public buses and makes travel between the two areas easier.

One of the world's busiest seaports belongs to Qingdao (its official name is Qingdao Port International Co. Ltd.). It has set up cooperative relationships with 450 ports in 130 countries and forms a component of the Maritime Silk Road of the 21st Century. Cargo handling capacity topped 100 million tons a year for the first time in 2003, with containers numbering 3.41 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU). Total cargo volume made it the world's sixth-busiest port in 2011, with a volume of 372,000,000 metric tons, or 366,000,000 long tons and 410,000,000 short tons, that year. By 2016 it was eighth in the world measured in TEUs. Dongjiakou and other big adjacent ports form part of the same port.

Sea links reach Japan and South Korea. The Orient Ferry connects the city with Shimonoseki in Japan. To South Korea there are two ferry lines: the New Golden Bridge II serves the Incheon route, and the Blue Sea Ferry runs to Gunsan.

Qingdao Jiaodong International Airport lies 39 km (24 mi) from downtown. It is used by 13 domestic and international airlines on 94 routes, and 12 of those routes are international or regional. It opened on August 12, 2021, taking over from Qingdao Liuting International Airport.

Rail development in Qingdao accelerated in the late 1990s. The city is the starting point for the Jinan-Qingdao high-speed railway, the Qingdao-Jinan passenger railway and the original Qingdao-Jinan railway. Its main stations include Qingdao railway station, Qingdao North, Cangkou and Dagang, whereas Sifang station has been closed to passenger traffic.

High-speed D and G series trains use the Jinan-Qingdao high-speed railway, where they can reach 300 km/h (190 mph) between Jinan and Qingdao. They serve Beijing, Shanghai, Hefei, Jinan and Tianjin. G206 / G205 is the quickest between Qingdao and Beijing, with a journey of 2 hours and 58 minutes. Other domestic lines tie Qingdao to places like Jinan, Jining, Zhengzhou, Xi'an, Chengdu, Lanzhou and Beijing.

shandong-university-of-science-and-techn.h: City buses, taxis and the metro

blocks.x: As of 2012 the public bus network had 5283 CNG buses of large and medium size, and 136 trolleybuses. A single contactless smartcard, written 青岛卡 in Chinese and called the Qingdao Public Traffic IC Card, works on every bus and trolleybus because it relies on radio frequencies and does not need to touch the scanner. All public transport operators now use the Qingdaotong Card, and the Zhenqing bus company, based in Qingdao's West Coast New Area (originally Huangdao District), joined as the last one in 2019. A bus without air conditioning costs 1 yuan, though the tunnel bus is different. Passenger numbers by road approach 737 million per year, and the Ri-Xin Bus (日新巴士) public transport brand is also known nationally. Yiqing, Zhongqing, Jiaoyun and Huaqing are among the taxi companies.
On 18 August 2009, with State Council approval, the government announced that over 29 billion yuan ($4.2 billion) would go into subway construction before 2016.
The first line to open was Line 3, on 16 December 2015. It was completed before 2016, covering 54.7 km (34.0 mi) at a total outlay of 29.2 billion yuan ($4.3 billion).

The long-term idea was eight lines downtown and in certain suburbs, with 231.5 km (143.8 mi) still to come. One account puts operating length at 243 km (151 mi), spread across the West Coast Line, the Oceantec Valley Line and Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8.

As of 24 February 2023 the approved network plan had 19 long-term lines adding up to 872 kilometers. The plan for third-phase construction has been approved as well, with 13 lines of 503 kilometers, ninth in the country by approved mileage.

Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 11 and 13, seven in all, had opened by then, giving 315 kilometers in operation. As of March 2023 the 146 operating stations placed Qingdao tenth in China and second among northern cities.

Ten lines (extensions included) were under construction. They cover Line 5, Phase I of Lines 9 and 15, the West Extension and Phase II of Line 2, Phases I and II of Line 6, Phase II of Line 7, and the Line 8 branch and south section. The 188 kilometers involved are due for completion by 2028.

In Chengyang District runs the Qingdao Tram, officially the modern tram demonstration line. It opened in 2016 and consists of a single tram line. Management is the responsibility of Rail Bus Co., Ltd., a unit of the Qingdao Public Transport Group.

The centre of Qingdao has many buildings in the German style, which is striking given that the German leased-territory period ran for only 16 years (1898-1914). German and Chinese architecture combine here, and together with the German origins of part of its population and a sizeable Korean expatriate community they give the city a rather distinctive feel. One old saying portrays it as red tiles, green trees, blue sky and blue sea. Many areas built in foreign styles of the past have been kept in good condition. Although the new city is being rebuilt on a large scale, the old city retains many traditional buildings, notably in the west of Shinan District.

Shandong University of Technology, abbreviated SDUT and known in Chinese as 山东理工大学, is based in Zibo, a city in Shandong province. Engineering sciences are its main focus, and it has been teaching since 1956.

The school opened in June 1956 under the name Shandong Institute of Technology (山东工程学院). Even in the Cultural Revolution years it stayed open as one of just 13 institutions in Shandong that taught undergraduates. In 1990 its scope widened into a polytechnic institution, and in 2001 it joined forces with several other colleges and became a full university with the name it carries today.

SDUT is spread over two campuses, and both lie in Zibo's Zhangdian District. Between them they take up roughly 2.4 million square metres of land, with 1.3 million square metres of floor space in buildings. Students can expect 268 lecture halls equipped with multimedia technology and 21 laboratories. On the same grounds sits the headquarters of Shandong's Research Institute of Engineering and Technology, which suggests a link between teaching and applied research.

shandong-university-of-technology.h: Who studies here and what they can choose

blocks.x: Enrolment is large: 34,000 full-time undergraduates and 5,300 postgraduates. Undergraduates choose from 21 subjects arranged into nine categories, namely art, pedagogy, history, law, literature, management, economics, science and engineering.

At master's level there are 14 engineering subjects and five in agricultural extension, along with two professional degrees: an MBA (Master of Business Administration) and an MF (Master of Finance). For international applicants, SDUT teaches at bachelor's, master's and doctoral level, with courses from the arts to mechanical engineering and from Chinese philology to economics. It has 12 doctoral programmes, each concentrating on a different area of engineering and technology.

shandong-university-of-technology.h: Zibo: the city beside your campus

blocks.x: Daily life as a student is shaped by the city around the campus, so here is some background on Zibo, where SDUT is located: the land, the weather, the people and what the place is famous for.

Zibo is in the middle of Shandong province. Mount Tai is its neighbour to the south, and the Yellow River runs along its northern side. East of it are the coastal cities Qingdao, Yantai and Weihai, and Jinan, the provincial capital, lies to the west.

The city sits where the mountains of central Shandong give way to the North China Plain. Medium-sized mountains cover the south, hills fill the centre, and the north slopes down into flat land. The proportions are 42% mountains, 29.9% hills and 28.1% plains. Water is relatively plentiful: the Yihe River begins in the southern mountains and the Yellow River crosses the north. The usable groundwater reserve is given as 1.24 tons a day, a figure that looks small and unclear in its original form, so treat it with care.

Zibo lies in the warm temperate zone with a semi-humid, semi-dry continental climate. As elsewhere in the province, there are four distinct seasons, with January the coldest month and July the hottest. The growing season lasts 180 to 220 days, and sunshine totals between 2542.6 and 2832.6 hours a year. Precipitation averages 640.5 mm (25.2 inches) a year.

The seventh national census, at 00:00 on 1 November 2020, put Zibo's resident population at 4,704,138, with 2,102,819 men and 2,078,441 women. The male-to-female ratio was 101.17, the death rate 5.92% and the birth rate 8.81%, which gave a natural growth rate of 2.90% that year. Density came to 704.15 people per square kilometre. Note that these male and female figures do not add up to the total, so a careful reader should check the latest official statistics.

In the fourth national census, over 99 percent of residents were Han Chinese. The remaining population includes 44 minority nationalities, among them the Hui, Manchus, Mongols and Koreans. Only Mongols and Manchus number more than 1,000 people. Jinling Hui town, at the meeting point of Zhangdian and Linzi, is one of just four towns in Shandong named after an ethnic minority.

For 2008, the disposable income per person was 17,629 yuan for urban residents, up 11.2% on the year before, and 7,364 yuan for rural residents, up 13.9%. The Engel's coefficients, which show how consumption is structured among urban and rural residents in China, come to 32.1% for urban households and 35.6% for rural ones. These are older figures, so treat them as a snapshot rather than a current picture.

The Zibo dialect keeps classical northern Chinese features but has its own character. Low vowels are pronounced particularly far back in the mouth, and a retroflex consonant is missing in most areas, with the exception of some parts of Linzi District. In sentence construction it is not very different from Mandarin; small differences show up in how people ask questions and how they express the likelihood of actions.

By administrative district, the dialect falls into three main groups. Huantai, Zhangdian and Zhoucun lie along the transport route linking Jinan and Weifang and have a mild Mandarin accent, something between the accents of Beijing, Jinan, Qingdao and Zichuan. Boshan has its own accent, which comes from the traditional centre of Zibo prefecture. Zichuan has a distinct accent too, with plenty of colloquial expressions.

Zibo's food belongs to the wider family of Shandong cooking, though strictly speaking Zibo cuisine is not a true branch of Lu cuisine (Shandong cuisine), whereas Boshan cuisine is. Boshan restaurants are found only in Zibo and the places near it. Among the local snacks are Sauced Mutton, Vegetable Pancake, Shi Ha Ma Dumpling and Zhou Cun Pancake. Heartier dishes include pork feet stewed alongside Chinese cabbage, lotus root and kelp, and a hotpot built on pork intestine and fried beancurd. Bean-curd Case is a fried bean-curd shell filled with meat and vegetables.
In early 2023 the city's outdoor barbecue restaurants became a viral sensation on social media and drew millions of visitors.

Five-Voiced Drama is a local theatre form that began in central Shandong and used to be very popular there. The name comes from the usual cast of four or five performers; the shows are known for lovely singing tunes and lively lyrics, and the straightforward performance and local flavour set it apart from other Chinese drama. Well-known plays include Wang Xiao Gan Jiao (Salesboy) and Wang Erjie Si Fu (Lonely lady). No other professional troupe in the country performs it apart from the Zibo Five-voiced Drama Troupe, and it has been given the status of "National Intangible Cultural Heritage".

Boshan coloured glaze is a celebrated craft of Shandong and has a long history. In the Hongwu era of the Ming, servants of the emperor founded an "Out Factory" producing coloured glaze for imperial use, for instance the "blue and green curtain". Folk production was growing, too, as the Ming drew to a close. During the Jingtai years, enamel material was made in four big kilns on Xi Yejie Street. Boshan masters of the Jiajing period and just before it made pearl light, pearl rejecting, bed-curtain hooks and mosquito net hooks, and over time a coloured glaze trade formed. In 1617 (the 46th year of Wanli), a group led by Sun Yanshou founded the first coloured glaze guild, in Yanshan Town. Besides selling locally, makers shipped the products to Beijing and southern China.
These titles show how the city has been recognised nationally:
Historical and Cultural City (1994), conferred by the State Council of P.R. China
Best Tourism City in China (2001), conferred by the National Tourism Administration of P.R. China
National Garden City (2005), granted by the Ministry of Construction of P.R. China
National Hygienic City (2006), awarded by the P.R. China commission for the National Patriotic (Public) Health Campaign

Zibo has many historic and cultural sites. Visitors who want to understand its long history and Qi culture should start with the Linzi Museum of Ancient Chariots and the Zibo Museum of Ceramics, then the Zibo City Museum and the Museum of the History of the State of Qi, then take in the Zhoucun Ancient Commercial Town and, in Zhoucun, the Thousand Buddha Temple. Yuanshan National Forest Park, in the southwest of Baoshan District, is another good stop. It has a stretch of the Qi State's Great Wall, a folk garden, Dinosaur Valley and a grass skiing field. Built in the era of the Spring and Autumn and the Warring States, the wall is more than 2,500 years old.

In 2023 the barbecue craze, which had caught on across the internet, made Zibo a favourite destination over the May Day holiday. A study of travel vlogs found the city portrayed as affordable, welcoming and peaceful.

Under the Han and Tang dynasties the Silk Road thrived, famed for trade and cultural contact between East and West. The Shandong area, Zibo above all, was a major centre of silk supply, and the city is still an important producer of silk and light textiles in China, with products well regarded at home and overseas.

More than 50 types of mineral have been found in the city. With big, high-quality and widely distributed reserves, Zibo supplies much of Shandong's pottery clay, chemical limestone, coal clay, bauxite, iron and coal, among others. Northern Zibo also has petroleum and natural gas. The city grew first as a mining centre, and it is now upgrading its technology and changing its industrial structure.

Environmental improvement has been a steady effort since 2002. Authorities closed small coal mines and chemical factories that polluted, and every major plant was told to install sewage disposal in order to limit air and soil pollutants. Today three municipal sewage plants in Zibo satisfy the Grade-A1 standard of China's Integrated wastewater discharge standard (GB 8978-1996).

Zibo's total industrial output in 2008 reached 532 billion RMB. GDP that year was 231.7 billion yuan RMB, ranked below Qingdao, Yantai, Jinan and Weifang in the province. Agriculture, industry and services made up 3.5%, 64.8% and 31.7% of GDP respectively.

By 2017 GDP had reached 478.13 billion yuan RMB, and the city held the same place in the provincial ranking, just behind Qingdao, Yantai, Jinan and Weifang. The shares were 3.1% for agriculture, 52.1% for industry and 44.8% for services, so the economy has moved towards services. Street food vendors were encouraged in Zibo in 2023, and that policy worked so well that Beijing, Moscow, Ottawa and Shenzhen, among others, treated it as a model.

Zibo is an important traffic hub in Shandong. The Jiaoji, Zhangbo, Zidong and Xintai railways cross here, and the Jiqing and Binlai expressways run through the city and link every county and district. Jinan Yaoqiang International Airport is 70 km (43 mi) from the city centre, while Qingdao Liuting International Airport is 210 km (130 mi) away and the Qingdao Seaport 260 km (160 mi).

There are 37 railway stations, large and small, in service. Zibo Railway Station, on the Jiaozhou-Jinan and Zibo-Dongying lines, is one of the busiest in the province, and as of 1 July 2009 it had 103 trains stopping every day. On a multiple unit train from Zibo, Jinan is 1 hour away, Qingdao 2 hours and Beijing 4 hours.

Jiqing Expressway links Jinan in the west with Qingdao in the east via Zibo. Starting at Binzhou, Binlai Expressway meets the Jiqing route to the northwest of downtown Zhangdian and then heads south towards Laiwu.

National Highway 309 begins at Rongcheng in Shandong and finishes in Lanzhou, Gansu Province, passing through six provinces over 2,208 kilometres. National Highway 205 starts at Shanhaiguan in Hebei province and ends at Shenzhen, covering 3160 kilometres through eight provinces.

Buses provide local mass transit. More than 2,500 large and medium diesel and CNG buses serve over 250 routes. Using a "Qikatong" card in the downtown area gets passengers a 10% to 40% discount. The city is restructuring its public transit system for more efficient management and more professional service, and full-electric buses and taxis have joined daily operations.

Zibo has been honoured nationally as a "technology-intensive area", a "cultural model city" and a city that is "advanced" in "invigorating itself through science and technology". In 2008 there were 443,000 pupils in grades 1 to 9, taught under the compulsory system in 169 middle schools and 379 primary schools. School districts follow both neighbourhoods and administrative districts. There are 42 high schools, including Shandong Zibo Experimental High School.

Zibo has 14 institutions of higher education. Wanjie Medical College and Shandong University of Technology are the only ones able to award bachelor's degrees, and the remainder are vocational universities. SDUT also runs postgraduate and PhD programmes. Key majors, more than 30 in all, range from logistics and textile and clothes to biological pharmacological science, electronics and informatics and mechanics, and each year the system can supply local firms with 30,000 specialised technical personnel.
A university's surroundings matter to student life at least as much as its buildings, so the sections below introduce Shandong.

On the North China Plain's eastern edge, Shandong hosted a succession of Neolithic cultures over thousands of years: Yueshi (c. 1900-1500 BC), Longshan (c. 3000-2000 BC), Dawenkou (c. 4100-2600 BC), Beixin (c. 5300-4100 BC) and Houli (c. 6500-5500 BC).

shandong-university-of-technology.h: Shang, Zhou and the warring states

blocks.x: The Shang and Zhou dynasties held western Shandong with varying strength, while eastern Shandong was the home of the Dongyi peoples, whom people in the Central Plain regarded as barbarians. The Dongyi gradually became sinicized after the state of Qi absorbed the Dongyi state of Lai in 567 BC.

Power passed to regional states in the Spring and Autumn and the Warring States eras. Shandong held the state of Qi, centred on Linzi, and the state of Lu, centred on Qufu. Lu is famous as Confucius' home, but it was fairly small and was eventually absorbed by its southern neighbour Chu. Qi stayed a major power through the entire era and ruled cities such as Jimo, Linzi and Ju.

Qin conquered Qi in 221 BC and built China's first centralised state. Under the Han that came afterwards, today's Shandong was divided into commanderies overseen by two inspectorates (刺史部): in the south the Yanzhou Inspectorate (兗州), in the north the Qingzhou Inspectorate (青州). When the Three Kingdoms period came, Shandong was part of Cao Wei, the northern kingdom.

The Western Jin dynasty briefly reunited the country, but northern China, Shandong included, was then overrun by nomadic invaders from the north. For about the following century Shandong passed from one power to another: first the Later Zhao, then Former Yan, Former Qin and Later Yan, followed by Southern Yan and the Liu Song dynasty, and at the end the Northern Wei, which was the first of the Northern dynasties in the Northern and Southern dynasties period. For the remainder of that era Shandong stayed under the Northern dynasties.

Faxian, a Chinese Buddhist monk, landed in 412 AD at Laoshan, which is on the southern edge of the Shandong peninsula. From there he went to Qingzhou, where he edited and translated scriptures brought back from India and Pakistan.

The Sui dynasty restored unity in 589, and the Tang (618-907) led the next golden age. At first Shandong was administered as part of the Henan Circuit (a political division). Afterwards China split among warlord factions, giving rise to the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era, during which Shandong was part of the Five Dynasties, which were all in the north.

Reunification came again under the Song dynasty in the late tenth century. Outlaw bands who were active in Shandong during Song times gave rise to folk tales, and these became the classic novel Water Margin. A major archaeological find came in 1996 at Qingzhou, where more than two hundred buried Buddhist statues came to light. Some are early painted figures, and they are thought to have been buried because Emperor Huizong, who favoured Taoism, repressed Buddhism.

The Jurchen Jin dynasty took northern China from the Song, who had to cede it in 1142. Jin rule split Shandong into a Shandong East Circuit and a Shandong West Circuit, and this was the first time the current name appeared.

It was the Ming dynasty that created the modern province, which then also reached into eastern Liaoning (Liaodong). Jinan replaced Qingzhou as capital in 1376 and has stayed the provincial capital for seven centuries since.

Jining and Linqing, both on the Grand Canal, flourished from the development of canal grain transport once Emperor Yongle had shifted the capital to Beijing in 1421. Then came the Little Ice Age (roughly 1550-1770): crop yields fell, famine returned year after year, and together with the imperial court's harsh policies this set off continuous peasant rebellions.

Kong Youde and Geng Zhongming, two generals of the Ming, took their troops from Dengzhou in Shandong to Liaodong in 1633 to surrender to the Manchu Qing, and they later joined the Qing army as it entered China proper. White Lotus Society uprisings in Shandong grew more intense by 1640, and the Ming court sent Zhu Datian to suppress the revolt; Shandong's population again fell sharply.

An earthquake of estimated magnitude 8.5, centred a little to the northeast of Linyi, it devastated Dengzhou and the surrounding prefecture. Estimates of the dead run from 43,000 to 50,000, foreigners and locals alike. No date is given for this event here, so check a dedicated history source for when it happened.

Shandong sits at the North China Plain's eastern edge, along the lower Yellow River, and extends into the sea as the Shandong Peninsula. Its neighbours are the Bohai Sea and Hebei in the north and northwest, Henan in the west, Jiangsu in the south, and the Yellow Sea on the northeast, east and southeast. A short border with Anhui lies between Henan and Jiangsu.

The northwest, west and southwest belong to the big North China Plain. The centre is more mountainous, and Mount Tai stands out. The east is the hilly Shandong Peninsula reaching out to sea, and the Miaodao Archipelago to its north marks the boundary between the Bohai Sea (west) and the Yellow Sea (east). Shandong's highest point is Jade Emperor Peak, 1,545 metres (5,069 ft), also the high point of the Mount Tai Ranges.

The Yellow River has entered the sea off Shandong's northern coast since 1855, after crossing the west of the province. It flows along a levee higher than the land around it, splitting western Shandong between a northern part in the Hai He watershed and a southern part in the Huai River watershed. China's Grand Canal comes in from the northwest and exits in the southwest. Weishan Lake is the province's largest lake.

Shandong's coast measures 3,000 kilometres (1,900 mi). Cliffs, bays and islands mark the rocky shoreline of the peninsula. Between Dongying and Penglai on the northern coast is Laizhou Bay, the southernmost of the Bohai Sea's three bays. The much smaller Jiaozhou Bay is enclosed by Qingdao. The Miaodao Islands extend north from the tip of the peninsula, dividing the Yellow Sea from the Bohai Sea.
Jinan is the economic and cultural centre of the province, and the strength of the provincial economy has produced modern coastal cities at Qingdao, Weihai and Yantai.
Professional teams based in Shandong play in these leagues:
Chinese Basketball Association: Shandong Hi-Speed Kirin and Qingdao Eagles
Chinese Super League: Qingdao West Coast, Qingdao Hainiu and Shandong Taishan
China League One: Qingdao Red Lions
Shandong University of Technology lists 157 programs for international students on this site: 74 bachelor, 68 master's, 14 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 149 taught in Chinese, 8 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 13,600 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 14,600), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 17,600 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 18,600), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 23,600 to CNY 26,000 (median CNY 24,800), according to the university's published fee table.

157 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

Agricultural Engineering

The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shandong-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shandong University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Zibo, register at Shandong University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

shanghai-conservatory-of-music.h: A conservatory with nearly a century of history

blocks.x: The Shanghai Conservatory of Music, often shortened to SHCMusic, is a public music college owned by the Shanghai municipal government. It takes part in China's Double First-Class Construction scheme and its founding date is 27 November 1927. Within China and abroad it is known as a leading place to study music.

Its parent was the National Conservatory of Music (Guoli yinyueyuan, 国立音乐院), set up by Cai Yuanpei on 27 November 1927. Dr. Xiao Youmei, also spelled Shio Yiu-mei, was the first director and designed the course of study, basing it on what he had learnt as a graduate of the Leipzig Conservatory of Music. The creation of the school was a landmark in the history of modern music teaching in China, and it soon counted as the foremost place to learn Western music in the country. Teachers came from as far away as Russia and France, and several of the first professors were Russian emigres who had left Russia for China to escape the civil war of 1918 to 1922.
The school changed its name several times:
1929: National Training School of Music
1943: Branch of the National Conservatory of Music
1945: Shanghai National Training School of Music
Early 1950s: the Shanghai and Huadong branches of the Chinese Conservatory of Music
1956: the present name, Shanghai Conservatory of Music

Four departments make up the conservatory, covering six disciplines and 23 sub-disciplines. Some are traditional, others recently developed. Besides teaching, it supports a high-level research institute for music, a large specialist library, a museum of Asian instruments rated first-class and an unusual music publishing house.

Younger musicians are catered for as well. A six-year secondary school (opened in 1953) and a three-year elementary section (opened in 1956) prepare stronger candidates for degree-level study, so the conservatory has a self-contained system running from music and general schooling right up to tertiary level.

Three art centres bring together teaching, performance and research: the Zhou Xiaoyan International Opera Center, the International String Academy and the International Piano Art Center. The conservatory runs six performing groups, namely its symphony orchestra, a New Ensemble, a string quartet, a percussion ensemble, a national (Chinese traditional) music orchestra and a choir. For a student, these ensembles are the practical way to turn lessons into stage experience.

Close ties with top conservatories and celebrated musicians are a feature of the school. Partner schools are found in the US and Japan, in Australia, and across Europe, including France, Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, the UK and Russia. Well-known international figures have held honorary or guest professorships, such as the violinists Isaac Stern, Itzhak Perlman and Pinchas Zukerman, the cellists Yo-Yo Ma and Mstislav Rostropovich, the pianist Leon Fleisher, the conductors Seiji Ozawa and Simon Rattle, and Yuri Shishkin.
Besides the music departments, there are a general education unit, a School of Marxism, and the Secondary Professional Music School affiliated with the conservatory.

The 2021 Best Chinese Universities Ranking put it fourth among arts-focused universities nationwide and first in the "Music and Dance" subject. A common view is that no music or arts school in China carries more prestige.

QS's 2022 world ranking for Performing Arts placed the conservatory 43rd globally and second in China, with only Beijing's Central Academy of Drama ahead. The 2024 QS subject rankings put it 10th in the world in Music and 30th in Performing Arts. Rankings differ in method and change yearly, so treat them as a guide and look at current tables when you apply.
Twelve people have led the conservatory since it opened. This list gives their terms:

The faculty includes 50 professors and 120 associate professors, and there are around 1,200 students. That small student body relative to the number of senior teachers suggests a lot of individual attention, though you should confirm class sizes with the department you apply to.
The conservatory highlights these people connected to its past and present:

He Luting (1903-1999), composer, graduate and former president. The main concert hall on campus now carries his name.

shanghai-conservatory-of-music.h: Shanghai: the city around the conservatory

blocks.x: Most of what matters for daily life comes from the city. Shanghai is huge, fast, expensive and very well connected, and the following sections explain how it looks, what it costs and how to move around.

Shanghai is a coastal city at the mouth of the Yangtze. The river flows along its northern edge, Hangzhou Bay lies to the south, and the East China Sea opens up to the east. Its ground was built up from the Yangtze's natural silt and, in recent times, from reclamation projects. The soil is sandy, so skyscrapers need deep concrete piles to stop them from sinking into the soft ground. The municipality has provincial status and governs the estuary and many nearby islands. Its neighbours are Zhejiang, which lies south, and Jiangsu, which wraps around the west and north. The northernmost part is Chongming Island, which grew during the 20th century until it became mainland China's second-biggest island.

The city is built on an alluvial plain, and its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land are almost entirely flat; average height above sea level is only four metres (13 feet). Tidal flat habitats around the estuary have been reclaimed for farming. The few hills, such as She Shan, are in the south-west, and the highest point is the peak of Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, at 103 metres (338 feet). Water is everywhere in the form of rivers, canals, streams and lakes, since Shanghai belongs to the basin that drains into Lake Tai.

Downtown is split by the Huangpu River, a man-made branch of the Yangtze dug in the Warring States era at the command of Lord Chunshen. The historic core grew up on the west bank (Puxi), where Suzhou Creek, a link to Lake Tai and the Grand Canal, enters the river, while the Lujiazui financial district was developed on the east bank (Pudong). Building Pudong International Airport destroyed local wetlands along the eastern shore, and this was partly offset by protecting and enlarging a nearby shoal, Jiuduansha, as a nature reserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), and the four seasons are clearly distinct. The average annual temperature is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) downtown and 16.2-17.2 °C (61.2-63.0 °F) in the suburbs. Winters are mild to cold and damp, and Siberian north-westerly winds can bring freezing nights. Snow falls on average 4.7 days a year, and the ground is snow-covered 1.6 days. Summers are hot and humid with occasional downpours and thunderstorms, and 21 days a year reach 35 °C (95 °F) or higher. Typhoons can hit in summer and early autumn.

Locals and visitors tend to prefer autumn, which is typically dry and bright, and spring, which brings changeable and often wet weather. Sunshine is weakest in June, at only 28% of what is possible, and strongest in August at 46%. Across twelve months the sun shines brightly for 1,754 hours. Using China's standard seasonal division, the averages for 2001 to 2025 give a start to spring of 9 March, to summer of 15 May, to autumn of 5 October and to winter of 4 December. A hot stretch lasts about three weeks (19 July to 8 August) when the mean temperature stays above 30 °C (86.0 °F).

Weather records at Xujiahui go back to 1951. The lowest temperature there was -10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977, although a cold spell on 19 January 1893 reached an unofficial -12.1 °C (10.2 °F). On two days, 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022, the highest ever reading of 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) was recorded. Even the warmest night, 13 August 2010, never fell below 32.1 °C (89.8 °F). Xujiahui averaged 19.43 °C (67.0 °F) in 2025, which is 1.93 °C warmer than the 1991 to 2020 norm, with an average daily high of 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and daily low of 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

Along the Huangpu, the Bund displays a row of early 20th-century buildings in different styles. The HSBC Building is neoclassical, while the Sassoon House (today part of the Peace Hotel) is Art Deco. It has been renewed several times: first in 1986, with a new promenade by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren, and again before the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic was rearranged.

Foreign influence shaped much of the city's growth, above all that of Britain, France and the United States. A building boom in the 1920s and 1930s left a good many Art Deco landmarks. Among the architects, László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak resident of the city between 1918 and 1947, designed the Park Hotel and two entertainment venues, the Grand Cinema and the Paramount. The Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel and Broadway Mansions are the work of Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, two more leading Art Deco architects, and the Austrian C.H. Gonda was responsible for the Capitol Theatre.

Look out for the shikumen (石库门, "stone storage door"), the typical old-style Shanghai home. Built of grey brick on two or three floors, each house has a small front yard sealed by a heavy wooden door in a stone arch. Rows of them share straight lanes called longtangs (弄堂). Stalinist or Soviet neoclassical architecture also appears, mostly dating from the first two decades of the People's Republic, which began in 1949, until relations with the USSR broke down towards the end of the 1960s; Soviet advisers had come to help China build up its economy. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

Count the buildings of 150 metres or higher and Shanghai has 206, seventh among world cities. Famous examples are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, and above all the Shanghai Tower. Completed in 2015, it now stands highest in China and ranks third among the world's skyscrapers. Close by, at the northern tip of Lujiazui, stands the Oriental Pearl Tower, 468 m (1,535 ft) high. Many areas of the former foreign concessions are well kept, and despite heavy redevelopment the Old City keeps traditional buildings, for example the Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan-style garden.

Finance and innovation make Shanghai a global player, while at home it leads in commerce, trade and shipping, and its container port is the busiest on earth. Widen the lens to Greater Shanghai, which reaches Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou, and in 2022 its metropolitan product was estimated at nearly RMB 13 trillion (US$1.9 trillion). In 2020 the economy of Shanghai alone was estimated at US$1 trillion on a PPP basis, making it China's most productive metro area and among the ten biggest in the world. Its six biggest sectors, namely shops and retail, finance, IT, property, machinery and cars, together make up roughly half of GDP.

Shanghai's 2025 output was worth CN¥5.67 trillion. In dollars that is US$814 billion nominal, or US$1.66 trillion adjusted for purchasing power, and it makes up 4% of China's total GDP. Divide by population and each resident accounts for CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). For individual earnings in 2022, residents had an average disposable income of CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) each year, and urban employees earned CN¥212,476 (US$31,589) on average. It is among China's wealthiest cities and, as an Economist Intelligence Unit study found in 2023, the priciest place to live on the mainland. A Julius Baer report on global wealth and lifestyle went further for 2021, naming it the world's costliest city for a luxurious lifestyle. Plan your budget carefully.

Foreign trade in 2023 (imports plus exports) came to CN¥7.73 trillion, or US$1.07 trillion, which is 18.5% of the national total. Forbes ranked Shanghai fifth for number of billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projected its nominal GDP at US$1.3 trillion in 2035, first in China and among the world's top five cities. As of August 2024 it was fourth in the world, and second in Greater China after Beijing, by number of Fortune Global 500 companies. Between 1992 and 2008, before the global financial crisis, it grew at double-digit rates in nearly every year, which made it one of the fastest-developing cities anywhere.

Shanghai is eighth in the world and third in Asia in the Global Financial Centres Index. Technology is another strength, with a lively start-up community serving both Chinese and global markets, and a 2021 ranking put it second to New York as a fintech powerhouse. The Shanghai Stock Exchange, valued at US$4.02 trillion in 2019, is China's largest and the world's fourth largest. For six key commodities (rubber, copper and zinc among them) the Shanghai Futures Exchange saw the world's biggest trading volume in 2009. At the end of 2017 the city had 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Shanghai remains one of China's main industrial bases for domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Its manufacturing rests on several zones: Hongqiao, Jinqiao (an export processing zone), Minhang and the high-tech zone at Caohejing. Baosteel Group, China's biggest steelmaker, is based here, as is the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, China's largest shipbuilding base, and the Jiangnan Shipyard, one of the country's oldest shipbuilders. SAIC Motor, one of China's three largest carmakers, partners strategically with Volkswagen and General Motors and ranked 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

Visitors bring in a great deal of money. During 2017 the city welcomed 318 million Chinese tourists, a 7.5% increase, and 8.73 million from abroad, which was 2.2% more. No other city on earth earned as much from tourism that year. The International Congress and Convention Association counted 82 international meetings hosted in 2018, a jump of 34% on the 61 of 2017. In 2023 the city had 57 hotels rated five stars and 52 rated four, with 1,942 travel agencies serving them. Official ratings cover 144 tourist attractions, and a further 34 count as red (revolutionary heritage) sites. The 2023 figures show 3.64 million tourists (4.8 times 2022), bringing in tourism income of CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), up 98.5%, and 2.41 million of the visitors were foreign, a 5.2-fold increase.

A milestone arrived in September 2013, when the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone opened. Nothing like it had existed on the mainland before, and a package of reforms accompanied it to attract overseas capital. That year, The Banker noted, no other place in Asia-Pacific attracted as much foreign direct investment into financial services. By October 2019 the zone had grown to 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi); only Hainan's is larger on the mainland. It merges four earlier bonded areas: the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, the logistics park beside it, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area and the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Duty is not charged on commodities inside, and they skip customs clearance.

In 2023 Shanghai had 24,874,500 residents, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) held a local hukou, meaning they were registered there. In 2022, 89.3% lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. Of China's four municipalities, Chongqing has the bigger population if you count the whole administrative area, yet since Chongqing's urban population is much smaller, Shanghai is generally treated as the country's largest city. The OECD estimates the metropolitan population at 34 million.

The municipal statistics bureau counts roughly 157,900 foreign residents. Japanese citizens are the biggest group at 28,900, followed by Americans (21,900) and Koreans (20,800). The true total is probably well above these figures. The city also draws internal migrants, who account for 40.3% (9.8 million) of residents.

People registered in the city live 83.18 years on average, longer than in any other mainland city. This brings population ageing: 17.4% (4.3 million) of registered residents were 65 or older in 2021. In 2017 the government imposed population controls, and the population fell by 10,000 by year's end.
Shanghai has metros, buses, ferries and taxis, all payable with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

The Shanghai Metro includes subway and light metro lines and reaches every core urban district and nearby suburbs. As of 2025 it has 19 metro lines (not counting the maglev and the Jinshan railway), 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 miles) of line in service, the longest in the world. Its daily ridership record is 13.3 million, set on 8 March 2019. The Shanghai maglev, which opened in 2004, was the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world and is the fastest, running at up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

Tram history began in 1908 with the first line. Seventeen years later, 328 tramcars served 14 routes operated together by Chinese, French and British companies; all were taken into state ownership in 1949. From the 1960s lines were removed or replaced by trolleybuses or buses, and the final line was pulled up in 1975. Trams came back in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began running in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the most extensive bus network in the world, which includes the oldest continuously operating trolleybus system. By 2019 it had 1,575 lines covering 8,997 kilometres (5,590 miles), run by several companies. In 2024, 30,900 taxis operated in the city and carried 134 million passengers.
Shanghai Conservatory of Music lists 136 programs for international students on this site: 14 bachelor, 58 master's, 24 doctoral, 40 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 136 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 32,000 to CNY 32,000 (median CNY 32,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 40,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 48,000 to CNY 48,000 (median CNY 48,000), according to the university's published fee table.

136 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shanghai-conservatory-of-music.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shanghai Conservatory of Music may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai Conservatory of Music by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

shanghai-international-studies-universit.h: Shanghai International Studies University at a glance

blocks.x: Shanghai International Studies University goes by SISU, and sometimes SHISU. It is a public university in Shanghai. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and the Ministry and the Shanghai Municipal People's Government fund it jointly. SISU is included in Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction, two national schemes for strengthening leading universities. Its starting date is December 1949.

Soon after the People's Republic of China came into being in 1949, the East China Bureau of the Chinese Communist Party Central Committee (中共中央华东局) and the Shanghai Municipal government agreed that a higher education institute for Russian studies should be set up. Its purpose was to produce capable diplomats and translators who could work on international affairs. Mayor Chen Yi supported the plan, and in December 1949 the new school, the Shanghai Russian School (上海俄文学校), formally opened. Its first president was Jiang Chunfang, who was first chief editor of the Encyclopedia of China and among the best-known Russian translators in China.

An English department was added in 1950, and the college was absorbed as the foreign language school of the East China People's Revolution University (called 华东人民革命大学 in Chinese). In April 1951 a department of oriental language and literature started up, and teaching began in languages such as Burmese, Vietnamese and Indonesian.

A nationwide reorganisation of higher education institutes started in China in 1952. The oriental language department was folded into Peking University, and the college took the name Shanghai Russian College, specialising in the Russian language. Following its expansion in 1956 the institution was commonly called Shanghai Foreign Language Institute (上海外国语学院). In 1963 the State Council approved it as a national key university, its departments then taught Spanish, Arabic, Japanese, German, French, English (re-established) and Russian.
A small but notable detail comes from 1964: Vicki Garvin began working at the institute (SFLI) and so became the first African American college teacher in China.

In 1994 the Ministry of Education approved a new name, Shanghai International Studies University (上海外国语大学). The same year it became among the first group of colleges and universities to be supervised together by the national Ministry of Education and the Shanghai Municipality. SISU passed the evaluation for what was then Project 211, run by the Ministry of Education, in 1996. Later the Chinese central government's Double First Class University Plan took it in.

The figures below are a mix of years, so check the latest tables if you need current numbers. In 2016 the QS World University Rankings put SISU at 651-700 worldwide. In QS BRICS 2016 it stood 76th, and it was 142nd in the Asian edition of the QS university rankings. In the QS ranking by subject as of 2025, its linguistics was 95th. In the widely used Best Chinese Universities Ranking, among universities specialising in language teaching and research, it placed first in East China and second nationwide.
Altogether there are 33 master's programmes. Thirty are research programmes, and three are taught programmes.

SISU offers 12 doctoral programmes. Eight are in language-related fields: Arabic, Asian and African languages and literatures, English, French, German, Japanese, Russian, and Translation Studies. The others are International Relations, International Politics, Diplomacy, and Foreign Linguistics and Applied Linguistics. (Strictly, the language doctorates also cover literature, as their titles show.)

SISU's Graduate Institute of Interpretation and Translation, abbreviated GIIT, holds top marks from AIIC (the International Association of Conference Interpreters), and it is the sole Asian university on AIIC's list of the 15 best professional schools of conference interpreting worldwide.
Partnerships link SISU with 286 universities and institutions in 55 countries and regions. Its teaching takes place on two campuses: Hongkou District has one, and Songjiang District the other.
This campus lies in the centre of Shanghai and covers 16.9 hectares.
The Songjiang campus sits in Shanghai's Songjiang New District and takes up 53.3 hectares.
Alumni include business leaders, diplomats, journalists and an actress:
Wei Zhe, who was CEO of Alibaba

Zhang Jianmin, China's Consul General in San Francisco (People's Republic of China)
Zhou Shuchun, the editor-in-chief of China Daily

Li Linsi, who once advised Chiang Kai-shek on diplomacy
