Joan Chen, a Chinese American actress who is also a film director, screenwriter and producer

Where you study affects daily life as much as the university itself: how you travel, what you spend, what the weather is like and what you can do. The sections below introduce Shanghai, the city around SISU. They begin with transport, since many students judge a campus by how easily they can get about.

Metros, buses, ferries and taxis make up Shanghai's public transport, and you can pay for all of them with a Shanghai Public Transport Card. The Shanghai Metro combines subway and light-metro lines, running into every core urban district and nearby suburban ones. Since 2025 it has had 19 lines, not counting the maglev train and the Jinshan railway, with 508 stations on 808 kilometres (502 mi) of line, the world's longest network. The record for a single day's ridership is 13.3 million, from 8 March 2019. The Shanghai maglev train started service in 2004 as the first commercial high-speed maglev anywhere, and it is also the fastest, operating at up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

Trams first ran in the city in 1908. By 1925 Chinese, French and British companies together operated 14 routes with 328 tramcars, until all were nationalized in 1949. During the 1960s the lines were taken up or replaced with trolleybus and motorbus routes, and the final tram line was removed in 1975. A rubber-tyred tram, the Zhangjiang Tram, brought trams back in 2010, and the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began running in Songjiang District in 2018.

The bus network is the most extensive in the world, and it includes the world's oldest trolleybus system that is still working. By 2019 it counted 1,575 lines and 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi) in total, with several companies as operators. For taxis, 30,900 were in service in 2024, and they carried 134 million passengers that year.

At the end of 2023 the city's population was 24,874,500, of whom 14,801,700, or 59.5%, held a Shanghai hukou, which means local registration. A 2022 figure shows 89.3% living in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. By the number of people in the full administrative area, Shanghai is second among China's four municipalities after Chongqing, yet people generally regard it as China's largest city, because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller. The OECD gives the metropolitan area an estimated 34 million people.

The Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau counts about 157,900 foreign residents. Of these, 28,900 are Japanese, 21,900 are American and 20,800 are Korean. The real foreign population is probably well above that. Shanghai also draws many migrants from within China: 9.8 million people, or 40.3% of the city's residents, come from other regions.

People in Shanghai live longer than elsewhere. Life expectancy for registered residents is 83.18 years, the highest among mainland Chinese cities. One result is an ageing population: in 2021, 4.3 million people, 17.4% of those registered, were 65 or over. In 2017 the Chinese government brought in population controls for the city, and the population shrank by 10,000 by the end of that year.

Shanghai stands at the mouth of the Yangtze on China's east coast. The Yangtze lies north, Hangzhou Bay south and the East China Sea east of it. Natural deposits from the Yangtze, along with modern land reclamation, created the ground it stands on. The soil is sandy, so skyscrapers need deep concrete piles to stop them sinking into the soft earth. As a municipality at provincial level, it administers the estuary plus many islands nearby. Zhejiang province adjoins it on the south, and Jiangsu on both the west and north. Chongming Island marks the northernmost point of the municipality; it has become the second-largest island in mainland China because it grew in the 20th century.

The city sits on an alluvial plain, so almost all of the 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land is flat, with an average height of four metres (13 feet). The tidal-flat ecosystems that existed around the estuary have been reclaimed for farming. In the southwest there are a few low hills, She Shan among them, and the highest spot is on Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, at 103 metres (338 feet). Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are plentiful here, because the land belongs to the Lake Tai drainage basin.

shanghai-international-studies-universit.h: The Huangpu and its two banks

blocks.x: The Huangpu River divides the downtown area. Lord Chunshen ordered it dug in the Warring States period as an artificial tributary of the Yangtze. Puxi, on the west bank near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, was the old heart of the city; that creek leads to Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. On the east bank, Pudong, the Lujiazui financial district was built. When Pudong International Airport was built, local wetlands along the eastern shore were lost, and the damage has been partly balanced by protecting and enlarging the nearby shoal of Jiuduansha as a nature preserve.

Shanghai's climate is humid subtropical (Köppen: Cfa). Downtown the annual average temperature is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F), against 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F) in the suburbs. There are four seasons. Winters range from mild to cold and are damp; winds from the northwest that come from Siberia can bring night-time temperatures below freezing. Snow falls on 4.7 days a year on average, and 1.6 days see snow lying on the ground. Summers are hot and humid, and downpours or thunderstorms come now and then. About 21 days a year reach 35 °C (95 °F) or more, and typhoons can threaten the city in summer and early autumn.

Spring (changeable and often rainy) and autumn (generally sunny and dry) are the most pleasant seasons. Sunshine is 28% of the possible total in June, the lowest, and 46% in August, the highest, and the city has 1,754 hours of bright sunshine a year. By China's seasonal division and figures from 2001 to 2025, the calendar runs like this: spring from 9 March, summer from 15 May, autumn from 5 October, winter from 4 December. Across the three weeks of 19 July to 8 August, temperatures average over 30 °C (86.0 °F).

Records at the Xujiahui weather station go back to 1951. The record low on 31 January 1977 was -10.1 °C (13.8 °F); a colder, unofficial value of -12.1 °C (10.2 °F) had occurred on 19 January 1893. The record high, 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), occurred twice, once on 21 July 2017 and again on 13 July 2022. The warmest night on record at Xujiahui had a minimum of 32.1 °C (89.8 °F), on 13 August 2010.
Xujiahui's mean temperature in 2025 was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), 1.93 °C above the 1991-2020 average. Typical highs by day reach 23.66 °C (74.6 °F), while typical lows at night fall to 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

Along the bank of the Huangpu stands the Bund, a row of early 20th-century buildings in different styles, ranging from the Art Deco Sassoon House (today a part of the Peace Hotel) to the neoclassical HSBC Building. The area has been revitalised on a number of occasions. A new promenade by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren was added in 1986. The second revival came before the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic flow was reconfigured.

Much of the city's development testifies to the imperial presence of Britain, France and the United States. During the building boom of the 1920s and 1930s Shanghai acquired a number of Art Deco buildings. The Hungarian-Slovak architect László Hudec, resident in the city from 1918 to 1947, designed Art Deco buildings including the Paramount, the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, also leading Art Deco architects, were responsible for the Metropole Hotel, the Broadway Mansions and the Peace Hotel; the Austrian C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

Typical homes are called shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men, meaning "stone storage door"). These are grey brick houses of two or three storeys, with a front yard guarded by a heavy wooden door within a stone arch. The houses connect and line up along straight alleys called longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). There is also Soviet neoclassical, or Stalinist, architecture, put up mainly after the People's Republic was founded in 1949 and before the late-1960s Sino-Soviet Split, a period in which Soviet personnel arrived to help China develop a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

Shanghai has 206 buildings of 150 m or more, which puts it seventh in the world for skyscrapers. They include the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center. At the moment the Shanghai Tower, completed in 2015, is China's tallest building and the world's third tallest. Close by, at the north end of Lujiazui, is the Oriental Pearl Tower, 468 m (1,535 ft) high. Many former foreign concession districts are well preserved. Even with constant redevelopment, the Old City still has traditional buildings and designs, for example the Yu Garden, an elaborate garden in the Jiangnan style.

Globally the city is a centre for finance and innovation, and nationally it is central to commerce, trade and transport. Its port, the Port of Shanghai, is the busiest container port in the world. In 2022 the nominal gross metropolitan product of the Greater Shanghai area, covering Huzhou, Zhoushan, Jiaxing, Ningbo, Nantong, Wuxi and Suzhou as well as the city, was estimated at nearly 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion). The city's economy was estimated at $1 trillion (PPP) as of 2020, which is the most productive metro area in China and among the ten largest metropolitan economies worldwide. Shanghai's six largest industries are automotive manufacturing, machine manufacturing, real estate, IT, finance and retail, and together they account for about half the city's GDP.

By 2025 GDP was CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion nominal; $1.66 trillion PPP), which is 4% of China's GDP, and GDP per capita was CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal; US$66,944 PPP). In 2022 people had a disposable income averaging CN¥79,610 per person (US$11,836) annually, and urban employees earned an average salary of CN¥212,476 (US$31,589). Shanghai is therefore one of China's wealthiest cities, and the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2023 study named it the most expensive city to live in on the mainland. Prospective students should plan their budgets accordingly. The Julius Baer Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report also found Shanghai the world's most expensive city for a luxurious lifestyle in 2021.

Trade totalled CN¥7.73 trillion in 2023 (imports and exports together), or US$1.07 trillion, representing 18.5% of the national total. Forbes ranked Shanghai fifth for the number of billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projects nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion in 2035, which would be first in China and put Shanghai among the world's top 5 major cities by GRP. In August 2024 it held fourth place worldwide, and second place in Greater China (Beijing was first), for its number of Fortune Global 500 companies. In the past two decades it has been among the world's fastest-developing cities, with double-digit GDP growth recorded in almost every year from 1992 to 2008, just before the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai is a global financial centre, third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a major base for China's and the world's technology industry, with a big startup ecosystem; in 2021 it was ranked second in the world as a Fintech powerhouse, after New York City. The Shanghai Stock Exchange had US$4.02 trillion of market capitalization in 2019, making it the biggest in China and the fourth largest globally. On the Shanghai Futures Exchange in 2009, trading in six key commodities (rubber, copper and zinc among them) was the largest anywhere. Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions by the end of 2017, and 251 of them were foreign-invested.

As a leading industrial centre, Shanghai matters a great deal to China's domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Industrial zones form the backbone of its secondary sector: the Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone, the Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, the Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone and the Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone. The city is home to Baosteel Group, China's largest steelmaker, the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, China's largest shipbuilding base, and the Jiangnan Shipyard, one of China's oldest shipbuilders. In cars, SAIC Motor, a Shanghai company, ranks among China's three largest auto groups and has strategic partnerships with General Motors and Volkswagen; the Fortune Global 500 list for 2023 placed it 84th.

Domestic tourist numbers grew 7.5% in 2017 to 318 million, and overseas visitors grew 2.2% to 8.73 million; Shanghai that year earned more from tourism than any other city in the world. The International Congress and Convention Association recorded 82 international meetings in Shanghai in 2018, up 34% from 61 in 2017. Hotels numbered 57 at five-star level and 52 at four-star level in 2023; the city also had 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions and 34 red tourist attractions. The 2023 tourist total was 3.64 million, 4.8 times the 2022 figure, producing CN¥177.12 billion, or US$24.53 billion, of value, 98.5% more than a year earlier. Foreign tourists numbered 2.41 million, which was a 5.2-fold increase.

Mainland China's first free-trade zone, the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, opened in September 2013, with several reforms to encourage foreign investment. The Banker reported that in 2013 Shanghai received more financial sector foreign direct investment than anywhere else in the Asia-Pacific region. As of October 2019 only the Hainan Free Trade Zone is larger by land area; Shanghai's covers 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) and integrates four bonded zones that were already there: Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park and Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone. Goods entering the zone need no customs clearance and pay no duty.

After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai International Studies University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

shanghai-jiao-tong-university.h: Shanghai Jiao Tong University at a glance

blocks.x: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, known everywhere as SJTU, is a state university in Shanghai under the Ministry of Education. It holds the national designations Project 211 and Project 985, takes part in the Double First-Class scheme, and sits in the C9 League, a small circle of China's leading research universities. The school began as Nanyang Public School in 1896, joined the Jiao Tong University group in 1921, and took its present name in 1959. The organisation today is large: 33 schools, plus 23 directly affiliated units and 5 enterprises of its own, and on the medical side 12 affiliated hospitals together with 2 medical research institutes.
For an international student, that scale means a very broad campus network, with strong engineering and a large medical side. The history below explains why the university is built the way it is.

shanghai-jiao-tong-university.h: A school founded for modernisation, 1896 to 1920

blocks.x: Nanyang Public School opened in 1896, which makes it one of the earliest modern universities in China. Sheng Xuanhuai asked the Qing government to allow it in October of that year; the Guangxu Emperor approved the plan in December, and Sheng became the first president. Sheng belonged to the Westernization Movement. He wanted to weaken the imperial examination system and promote Western academic methods and a more practical kind of education, so the new school concentrated first on business and political science in support of the Self-Strengthening Movement and the nation's development.

Administrative control changed hands often in the following years. In 1905 commerce officials took over and gave it the title High Industrial School. Two years later, in 1907, responsibility moved to the posts and communications authorities, and a long new name followed: the Shanghai High Industrial School of the Postal Transmission Department. Then came a brief spell, 1911 to 1912, as Grand Nanyang University. Once the Republic of China existed (1912), the communications ministry became the owner and the name changed again, to Shanghai Special Industrial School.

Tang Wenzhi served as president from 1907 to 1920, and during these years the curriculum followed the Western model of engineering education. Civil, mechanical and electrical engineering programmes grew, a 4-year traffic management programme was introduced, and new courses in industrial economy and factory management appeared. Specialised courses replaced general education, and experiments and practical work became the priority.

Because the university lacked qualified teachers of its own, foreign instructors, mostly Americans, made up about half of the faculty in specialised subjects from 1908 to 1920, and Americans led both the Civil Engineering and Electrical Engineering departments. By the 1920s, though, many Chinese scholars returning from study abroad had taken their places.

On 25 May 1949 the People's Liberation Army took the western part of Shanghai, and Jiao Tong University gradually restarted its work. Classes resumed on 2 June, and on 15 June the Shanghai Military Commission formally took charge. On 20 August the Science College of Jinan University was merged in, with its students moving to the campus by 9 September. After the People's Republic was founded, December 1950 saw new majors in automotive engineering, civil engineering, highway management and construction equipment. In March 1951 (the 1st) the telecommunication management department gained the word 'engineering' in its name. The faculties were then regrouped on 28 July 1952 around mechanical, electrical and shipbuilding fields, and on 21 August the mechanical engineering department of the former East China Traffic College joined the university.

Several steps followed in the mid-1950s. On 25 December 1954 Peng Kang, the Party Secretary, announced a presidential responsibility system. The Shipbuilding College was expanded on 7 January 1955 and placed directly under the first machinery ministry, and on 29 and 30 January the shipbuilding department of Dalian Institute of Technology sent its teachers and students across. On 22 June 1955 the academic structure moved from two-year specialist courses to five-year degrees, and the two-year route was phased out by July. By 29 June the telecommunication and automotive programmes had been transferred to Chengdu and Changchun respectively.

Postgraduate education started in 1956: on 13 March the university began discussions on admitting its first graduate cohort in fields such as mechanical engineering, metallurgy and electrification. Growth continued: in 1958 the university counted 5,000 students in 6 departments and 15 majors. That March, Nanyang College of Technology and the Shanghai Shipbuilding Institute were formally absorbed.

shanghai-jiao-tong-university.h: The move to Xi'an and the split

blocks.x: A committee meeting on 24 and 25 May 1955 decided to follow central government instructions and relocate the university. An office to prepare the move was opened in Xi'an on 20 August, and the plan itself was made public on 24 November. A delegation inspected the Xi'an site in January 1956. The move began in earnest in 1957 after the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee agreed on 22 June, but a week later the university changed course and decided to run campuses in both cities, with only some departments moving. Many civil engineering teachers and students went west that September. On 31 July 1959 the Xi'an campus became a separate institution, Xi'an Jiaotong University, and the Shanghai campus was renamed Shanghai Jiaotong University. If you search for Jiao Tong in China, remember that these are two different universities.

Leadership became shared in 1961 between three bodies: a national defence science and technology commission, the education ministry and the Shanghai city Party committee. The branch campus on Minyan Road went to Shanghai Institute of Technology on 10 June of that year, and the preparatory department followed on 10 January 1962. Eight departments, including shipbuilding, radio engineering and electrical engineering, formed the structure adopted on 29 August 1962. From 1970 the university answered to the Sixth Ministry of Machinery Industry. In 1978 applied mathematics, applied physics and engineering mechanics came back as departments, and civil engineering was rebuilt in 1985. Minhang Campus opened officially in 1987. An agricultural college in Shanghai merged into SJTU in 1999. Finally, in 2005 the former Shanghai Second Medical University and the old SJTU were joined to make the institution you see now.

shanghai-jiao-tong-university.h: The end of the Michigan partnership

blocks.x: One recent development is relevant to anyone interested in exchange programmes. Five SJTU students who had joined an exchange at the University of Michigan faced charges in the United States in 2024, accused of offences linked to espionage after they were caught in military exercises at Camp Grayling in which Taiwanese forces took part. Michigan ended its partnership with SJTU in January 2025. This followed other US universities ending links with Chinese partners, notably Georgia Tech and Tianjin University, and UC Berkeley and Tsinghua University, in 2024 and 2025. If you plan to apply through a joint programme, check whether the partnership still operates.
Daily life for students depends on the city around the campus, so the next sections cover Shanghai's land, weather, buildings, economy, people and transport.

Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary on China's east coast. It is bounded by the river to the north, by Hangzhou Bay to the south, and by the open sea, the East China Sea, to the east. Natural deposits from the Yangtze and modern land reclamation formed the ground. The soil is sandy and soft, so skyscrapers need deep concrete piles to keep them from sinking. The provincial-level municipality manages the estuary and many islands around it, and it shares borders with Zhejiang to the south and with Jiangsu to the west and north. Chongming Island marks its northernmost point, and after expanding during the 20th century it is the second-largest island in mainland China.

The city stands on an alluvial plain. Of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land, nearly all is flat, with a mean height of just 4 metres (13 feet). Tidal flats around the estuary have mostly been turned into farmland. A few hills, such as She Shan, rise in the southwest, and the highest point is the summit of Dajinshan Island, 103 metres (338 feet), in Hangzhou Bay. Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are everywhere, and Shanghai's abundance of water comes from its place in the drainage basin of Lake Tai.

The Huangpu River divides downtown into two halves. It is a man-made tributary of the Yangtze, dug on the order of Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. The old city grew on the Puxi side, the west bank, close to the point where Suzhou Creek enters; that creek gives a link to Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. On the east bank, Pudong, planners later built the main financial district, Lujiazui. Pudong International Airport destroyed some wetlands on the eastern shore, and the loss was partly balanced by turning a nearby sandbar, Jiuduansha, into a protected and growing nature reserve.

Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen Cfa). The average annual temperature is 17.5 C (63.5 F) downtown and 16.2 to 17.2 C (61.2 to 63.0 F) in the suburbs. All four seasons are distinct. Winters are mild to cold and damp, and northwest winds from Siberia can bring night temperatures below freezing. In an average year there are 4.7 days of snowfall and 1.6 days of snow cover. In summer the heat comes with humidity, with sudden downpours or thunderstorms now and then; about 21 days each year are 35 C (95 F) or hotter. Typhoons can threaten the city in summer and early autumn.

Spring is changeable and often rainy, and autumn is usually sunny and dry, so those are the most pleasant times. Sunshine is limited: possible sunshine is 28% in June and 46% in August, and the annual total is 1,754 hours. China's official way of dividing the seasons gives these average start dates for 2001 to 2025: spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October, winter on 4 December. Between 19 July and 8 August, the three hottest weeks, the average temperature is over 30 C (86.0 F). At the Xujiahui weather station, the lowest temperature since 1951 was -10.1 C (13.8 F), on 31 January 1977 (an unofficial -12.1 C, 10.2 F, was recorded on 19 January 1893). The record high is 40.9 C (105.6 F), reached on 21 July 2017 and again on 13 July 2022. The highest daily minimum ever recorded there was 32.1 C (89.8 F) on 13 August 2010.
Recent data show warming. Xujiahui averaged 19.43 C (67.0 F) in 2025, which was 1.93 C above the 1991 to 2020 average. Daily highs average 23.66 C (74.6 F), while daily lows average 16.44 C (61.6 F).

The Bund, on the bank of the Huangpu, displays a row of early 20th-century buildings, ranging from the neoclassical HSBC Building to the Art Deco Sassoon House, today part of the Peace Hotel. The area has been refreshed more than once. A new promenade by Paulus Snoeren, a Dutch architect, was added in 1986, and there was another renovation before the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic was reorganised.

Much of the city's character reflects the presence of Western powers, mainly Britain, France and the United States. A construction boom in the 1920s and 1930s left several Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in the city from 1918 to 1947, was responsible for the Paramount and also for the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel. Two other leading Art Deco figures were Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, who created the Metropole Hotel, Broadway Mansions and the Peace Hotel. The Capitol Theatre was the work of the Austrian C.H. Gonda. Another common local form is the shikumen ('stone storage door') house: typically two- or three-storey grey brick homes with a front yard guarded by a heavy wooden door set in a stone arch. These houses stand side by side along straight alleys called longtang. There is also a Soviet-style, neoclassical or Stalinist, strand. Most of it was built in the years after 1949, when the People's Republic was founded, and before the Sino-Soviet Split of the late 1960s ended the era when Soviet staff were present to help develop a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

The city has 206 buildings above 150 m, which puts it seventh in the world for skyscrapers. Well-known towers are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, and the tallest of all is the Shanghai Tower, finished in 2015; it is highest in China and third highest worldwide. The Oriental Pearl Tower, 468 m (1,535 ft) high, rises close by at the northern end of Lujiazui. Many districts of the former foreign concessions have been kept in good condition, and, despite heavy redevelopment, the Old City still has traditional architecture and design, notably the Yu Garden, a rich Jiangnan-style garden.

Shanghai is a leading world city for finance and innovation, and a centre across China for commerce, trade and shipping; its port is the busiest container port anywhere. The wider Greater Shanghai region, which takes in Suzhou, Ningbo, Wuxi, Nantong, Jiaxing, Huzhou and Zhoushan, generated a nominal gross metropolitan product of close to 13 trillion RMB (about $1.9 trillion) in 2022. In 2020 the Shanghai economy was estimated at $1 trillion in purchasing power terms, the most productive metropolitan area in China and among the ten biggest in the world. Retail, finance, IT, real estate, machinery and automobile manufacturing are its six largest industries and about half of GDP.

In 2025 Shanghai's GDP was CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion nominal, $1.66 trillion in PPP), 4% of China's total, and GDP per capita was CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). Incomes show the wealth: in 2022 residents had average disposable income of US$11,836 a head (CN¥79,610), and workers in urban units earned an average of US$31,589 (CN¥212,476) a year. The other side of this is cost. The Economist Intelligence Unit found in 2023 that Shanghai is the priciest mainland city to live in, and in 2021 Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report named it the costliest city on earth for a luxury lifestyle. Budget carefully.

Foreign trade totalled US$1.07 trillion (CN¥7.73 trillion) in 2023, which was 18.5% of everything China traded. Forbes put Shanghai fifth for billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projected that its nominal GDP would hit US$1.3 trillion in 2035, first in China and among the top five cities in the world. By August 2024 only three cities in the world, and only Beijing in Greater China, had more Fortune Global 500 companies. Growth has been rapid; GDP rose by double digits in nearly every year between 1992 and the 2008 financial crisis.

The city is a global financial centre: third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a hub of China's technology industry with a large startup scene, and in 2021 it ranked second in the world as a fintech powerhouse, after New York. In 2019 the market capitalisation of the Shanghai Stock Exchange was US$4.02 trillion, the biggest in China and the fourth biggest in the world. Six key commodities, including rubber, copper and zinc, all had the world's highest trading volumes on the Shanghai Futures Exchange in 2009. By the end of 2017, there were 1,491 financial institutions in the city, 251 of them foreign-invested.

As a main industrial centre, Shanghai plays a big part in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Industrial zones such as the Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone, the Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, and Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone, together with the Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, form the backbone of the secondary sector. The city is the home of Baosteel Group, China's biggest steelmaker, Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, the largest shipbuilding base, and Jiangnan Shipyard, one of the oldest. SAIC Motor, one of China's three largest automotive groups, is based here and has strategic ties to both General Motors and Volkswagen, and it ranked 84 on the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

In 2017 domestic tourist numbers rose 7.5% to 318 million and overseas visitors rose 2.2% to 8.73 million, and Shanghai earned more from tourism than any other city in the world. The International Congress and Convention Association recorded 82 international meetings in 2018, up 34% from 61 in 2017. Facilities in 2023 included 57 five-star hotels and 52 four-star hotels, along with 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated attractions and 34 'red' tourist sites. The 2023 tourism count was 3.64 million visitors, 4.8 times the 2022 figure, bringing in US$24.53 billion (CN¥177.12 billion), a rise of 98.5%. Foreign tourists numbered 2.41 million, a 5.2-fold rise.

The mainland's first free-trade zone began in Shanghai in September 2013 and came with reforms designed to encourage foreign investment. A magazine called The Banker reported that, in 2013, no other city in the Asia-Pacific region attracted as much foreign direct investment in financial services. As of October 2019 the zone covered 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 square miles), second only to Hainan among mainland free-trade zones, and it joined four bonded areas: the Yangshan port area, the Pudong airport zone, and the Waigaoqiao zone and its logistics park. Goods entering are free of duty and customs clearance.

At the end of 2023 Shanghai had 24,874,500 inhabitants, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) held a local hukou. In 2022, 89.3% lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural areas. By total administrative area it is the second largest of China's four municipalities after Chongqing, but because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller, Shanghai is generally regarded as the largest city. The OECD puts the metropolitan population at about 34 million.

The official count of foreign residents is about 157,900, and it includes Japanese (28,900), Americans (21,900) and Koreans (20,800); the real total is probably far higher. It is also a city of internal migrants: 40.3% (9.8 million) of residents come from other parts of China.

Registered residents live to 83.18 years on average, the longest life expectancy of any mainland city, and the result is an ageing population. By 2021, 4.3 million people, or 17.4% of those registered, were aged 65 and above. National population controls in 2017 led to a fall of 10,000 residents by the end of that year.

Shanghai's public transport includes metro, buses, ferries and taxis, and a single Shanghai Public Transport Card can pay for them. The Shanghai Metro combines subway and light metro lines and reaches every core urban district and nearby suburbs. In 2025 it had 19 lines (not counting the maglev and the Jinshan railway), 508 stations and 808 km (502 miles) of track, the longest network in the world. Daily ridership hit a record 13.3 million on 8 March 2019. The Shanghai maglev, opened in 2004, is the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world and the fastest, running at up to 430 km/h (270 mph).

The buses form the world's most extensive network, including the world's oldest trolleybus system still in continuous operation, with 1,575 lines and 8,997 km (5,590 miles) of routes by 2019, run by several companies. In 2024 there were 30,900 taxis, and they carried 134 million passengers.

Trams first ran in Shanghai in 1908. Chinese, French and British firms together operated 14 routes and 328 tramcars by 1925, and the state took them all over in 1949. During the 1960s the lines were gradually dismantled or converted to trolleybus and bus routes, and the last was taken out in 1975. The city brought trams back in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began operating in Songjiang District.

SJTU combines a long history, a large and mixed set of schools and hospitals, and a location in China's most international city. Check the university's own website for current admission rules, partnerships and campus details before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shanghai-jiao-tong-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shanghai Jiao Tong University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai Jiao Tong University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

SHMTU, also written SMU (上海海事大学), belongs to the city of Shanghai. The municipal government supervises it, with the national Ministry of Transportation as co-sponsor. Its academic range is wide, spanning science, law, literature, economics, management and engineering, but its standing is highest in maritime, shipping and transport education, a speciality in which it is counted among the leading Chinese universities.
The chain of institutions that led to today's university is long, and the dates show how often it was reorganised.

It started in 1909 with a shipping section in Shanghai Industrial College. Two years later, in 1911, the Ministry of Post and Transport ran a merchant marine college with a navigation section, and by 1912 that had turned into the Wusong (Woosung) Merchant Marine School. The school was moved under the Ministry of Transport as Wusong Merchant Marine College in 1929, still with navigation alone, and a marine engineering section was added in 1930.

During the war years the college relocated. In 1939 it was the Chongqing National Merchant Marine College and had added a ship building section, giving it three. By 1943 it had been absorbed into Chongqing National University of Transport, which kept navigation and marine engineering but turned the ship building section into a Ship-Building Engineering Department. Back in Wusong in 1946 as the Wusong National Merchant Marine College, it taught navigation and marine engineering, and in 1948 it began short-term advanced training in telecommunications.

Postwar changes continued. A merger in 1950 joined the college to Jiaotong University's department of shipping management and produced the Shanghai Nautical College. It taught marine navigation in a Navigation Department, marine engineering in a Marine Engineering Department, and radio communication at associate-baccalaureate level. In 1951 a Harbor Engineering Department was added, offering waterway transportation and port management, and in 1953 the college merged with the Northeast Navigation College.

The present institution stems from decisions in 1958 and 1959. In 1958 the Ministry of Communications decided to bring maritime education back to Shanghai and set up Shanghai Maritime University, and in 1959 the ministry founded Shanghai Maritime Institute. The institute formally became Shanghai Maritime University in 2004.

The Ministry of Communications created SMU in 1959. Since 2000 the Shanghai municipality has been its main administrator, and the city and ministry jointly build it up. SMU offers 35 bachelor's programmes and 12 associate-degree programmes. The state has authorised it to give master's degrees in 30 programmes and doctorates in seven.

The Ministry of Communications and the city have both named a set of courses as key specialties. Those about transport and engineering are Port Machinery Electronics Engineering, Delivery Means Utilization Engineering, Logistics Management and Engineering, Mechanical Design and Theory, Power Electronics and Electrical Drive, and Communications and Transport Planning and Management. Industrial Economics and International Law are also on the list. For bachelor's study, Shanghai singles out Maritime Law, Customs Logistics, and International Trade and Economics as key disciplines to develop further. SMU received an "A" in the Ministry of Education's 2004 evaluation of undergraduate teaching.

Nearly 15,000 full-time students attend SMU. More than 10,000 are working toward a bachelor's degree and over 2000 toward a master's. For decades the university has trained people for the shipping industry, and it has sent over 40,000 graduates into shipping companies, public institutions and government departments.

Shanghai's government supports international students here with scholarships, mostly for graduate study. The categories are a full scholarship (Class A), a half scholarship (Class B) and a limited one (Class C). Terms change, so confirm the current rules with the university.
Another option is an MSc in International Transport and Logistics, taught at SMU as an offshoot of the World Maritime University.

Shanghai stands at the mouth of the Yangtze on the east coast, with the river to its north, Hangzhou Bay to its south and the East China Sea to its east. The ground was made by the Yangtze's deposits and, more recently, by land reclamation, so the soil is sandy. Builders have to sink deep concrete piles under skyscrapers to stop them sinking into the soft ground. The municipality, which has the same rank as a province, governs both the estuary and numerous islands around it. Zhejiang is its neighbour to the south, and Jiangsu borders it on the west and north. Its northernmost point is on Chongming Island, which grew in the 20th century to become China's second-largest island on the mainland.

Shanghai is built on an alluvial plain, and almost all of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land is flat, with an average height of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flats around the estuary have mostly been reclaimed for farming. Hills are few, and they lie in the southwest, She Shan being one. The city's top elevation is on Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, where the peak reaches 103 metres (338 feet). Water is everywhere: rivers, canals, streams and lakes make the area famous for its water resources, which belong to the Lake Tai drainage basin.

Downtown is split by the Huangpu River, a tributary of the Yangtze that was dug by human hands on the order of Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. Puxi, the west bank, is where the old city grew up, close to where Suzhou Creek enters the Huangpu and connected the city with Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. The financial heart, Lujiazui, was built on the opposite side, in Pudong. Some eastern wetland was lost to Pudong International Airport, and the damage was partly made up for by protecting and expanding the nearby Jiuduansha shoal as a nature reserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen: Cfa), with four distinct seasons. The average annual temperature is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) downtown and 16.2-17.2 °C (61.2-63.0 °F) in the suburbs. Winter is cold and damp, though not extreme, and cold northwesterly winds blowing from Siberia can push nights below freezing. On average there are 4.7 days of snowfall and 1.6 days of snow cover a year. Summers are hot and humid, with occasional downpours and thunderstorms, and 21 days a year reach or pass 35 °C (95 °F). From summer into early autumn the city can be hit by typhoons.

Spring and autumn are generally the best seasons. Spring can be changeable and rainy, while autumn is typically sunny and dry. Monthly possible sunshine is lowest in June, at 28%, and highest in August, at 46%, totalling 1,754 hours a year. Using China's official seasonal definition and data for 2001 to 2025, the seasons start on these dates: 9 March for spring, 15 May for summer, 5 October for autumn and 4 December for winter. Between 19 July and 8 August, a period of three weeks, temperatures average over 30 °C (86.0 °F).

The weather station at Xujiahui has logged a lowest temperature since 1951 of −10.1 °C (13.8 °F), on 31 January 1977; an unofficial reading of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) dates back to 19 January 1893. The top reading is 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), reached twice, on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022. A night in August 2010 (13 August) set the record for the warmest daily minimum, at 32.1 °C (89.8 °F). Xujiahui's 2025 mean was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), 1.93 °C warmer than the 1991-2020 average, and daily highs averaged 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) while lows averaged 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund runs along the Huangpu and is lined with early 20th-century buildings in styles from the neoclassical HSBC Building to Sassoon House, an Art Deco building that is now part of the Peace Hotel. It has been revived more than once. The Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren designed a new riverside walkway in 1986, and before the 2010 Expo a second renewal restored the Waibaidu Bridge, a century old, and changed how traffic flows.

Much of the city's character reflects the presence of the Western powers, mostly Britain, France and the United States. The construction boom of the 1920s and 1930s left many Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who made his home in the city between 1918 and 1947, was behind the Paramount, the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel. The Broadway Mansions, Metropole Hotel and Peace Hotel came from Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, two more leading Art Deco architects, and the Austrian C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

One common house type is the shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men), meaning "stone storage door". Typically it is a grey brick house of two or three floors, with a small front yard behind a heavy wooden door in a stone arch. Rows of them connect along straight lanes known as longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). The city also has Soviet neoclassical (Stalinist) buildings, put up mainly between 1949, when the People's Republic was founded, and the Sino-Soviet Split in the late 1960s, a time when Soviet advisers were in China to help build a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is an example.

Only six cities have more skyscrapers than Shanghai, which has 206 buildings that are 150m or taller. The best known are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, and the Shanghai Tower, completed in 2015, is now the tallest in China and third tallest in the world. At the northern tip of Lujiazui, the Oriental Pearl Tower is a short way off, at 468 m (1,535 ft). Large parts of the former foreign concessions survive in good condition, and although redevelopment has been intense, the Old City still has traditional architecture such as the Yu Garden, an elaborate garden in the Jiangnan style.

Finance and innovation are global strengths of Shanghai, and trade, commerce and transport are national ones. The Port of Shanghai handles more containers than any other port. For 2022, the output of Greater Shanghai (Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou included) was put at almost 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion) in nominal terms. In 2020 the economy of the city itself was estimated at $1 trillion measured by PPP, the most productive metropolitan area in China and one of the ten biggest in the world. Half of the city's GDP comes from six industries: retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing and automobiles.

In 2025 the city's GDP was 5.67 trillion yuan, which is $814 billion nominal or $1.66 trillion on a PPP basis, and that is 4% of the national total. GDP per person was 228,280 yuan (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). During 2022, disposable income averaged 79,610 yuan (US$11,836) per resident per year, and people employed in urban units earned on average 212,476 yuan (US$31,589). In 2021 a wealth and lifestyle report from Julius Baer named it the planet's most expensive place for a lavish lifestyle. International students should budget accordingly.

Shanghai's trade in goods came to 7.73 trillion yuan (US$1.07 trillion) in 2023, which was 18.5% of China's total. It stood fifth by billionaire count on Forbes's 2022 list. A forecast by Oxford Economics has nominal GDP at US$1.3 trillion by 2035, first in China and among the top five cities in the world for gross regional product. As of August 2024 only three cities hosted more Fortune Global 500 companies, and within Greater China just Beijing had more.
Growth in the city was in double digits in almost every year from 1992 until the financial crisis of 2008, and across the past two decades Shanghai has been among the world's fastest-growing cities.

Shanghai is a global financial centre, third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a major base for Chinese and global technology and has a large startup scene. In 2021 it was ranked the world's second Fintech powerhouse, after New York City.

At the end of 2019 the Shanghai Stock Exchange stood at US$4.02 trillion in market value, the largest in China and fourth in the world. Six commodities, among them zinc, copper and rubber, were traded at the Shanghai Futures Exchange in 2009 in volumes that ranked first worldwide. By the end of 2017 the city had 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Manufacturing and heavy industry are pillars of the city's role in China. Its secondary sector rests on industrial zones at Hongqiao, Minhang, Jinqiao and Caohejing, which are, respectively, an economic and technological development zone, another such zone, an export processing zone and a high-tech development zone. The city is home to Baosteel Group, the biggest steelmaker in China, the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, the country's largest shipbuilding base, and the Jiangnan Shipyard, one of its oldest shipbuilders. SAIC Motor is based in Shanghai, one of China's three largest car makers, with strategic partnerships with Volkswagen and General Motors, and it ranked 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

In 2017, domestic visits to the city rose 7.5% to 318 million and overseas visits rose 2.2% to 8.73 million, and Shanghai earned more from tourism than any other city in the world. The International Congress and Convention Association recorded 82 international meetings in Shanghai in 2018, up 34% from 61 in 2017. As of 2023 there were 57 five-star hotels and 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated attractions and 34 "red" tourist attractions. Tourism in 2023 recovered strongly: 3.64 million tourists, 4.8 times the 2022 figure, generated 177.12 billion yuan (US$24.53 billion), 98.5% more than the previous year, and foreigners numbered 2.41 million, a 5.2-fold rise.

The Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, launched in September 2013, was the mainland's first, and it brought in various reforms to attract investors from abroad. The Banker reported that Shanghai took in more foreign direct investment in finance than anywhere else in the Asia-Pacific in 2013. Since October 2019 it has covered 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi), the second biggest by area on the mainland after the Hainan zone, by merging four bonded areas that already existed (Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, the Waigaoqiao logistics park, Yangshan Free Trade Port and the Pudong Airport zone). Goods coming into the zone pay no duty and skip customs clearance.

In 2023 Shanghai had 24,874,500 residents, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) held a local hukou registration. In 2022, 89.3% of the population lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural areas. Of China's four municipalities, Shanghai has the second-largest population in its whole administrative area, after Chongqing. Even so, people generally treat Shanghai as the largest Chinese city, since Chongqing's urban population is far smaller. The OECD estimates the metropolitan area's population at 34 million.

The city's statistics bureau counts about 157,900 foreign residents, including 28,900 from Japan, 21,900 from the US and 20,800 from Korea, but the true number of foreigners is likely a lot higher. The city also draws many domestic migrants: 40.3%, or 9.8 million, of residents come from other parts of China.

Life expectancy for registered residents is 83.18 years, the highest of any city on the mainland, and that has contributed to an ageing population. In 2021, 4.3 million people, or 17.4% of registered residents, were 65 or over. The central government introduced population controls for Shanghai in 2017, and the population fell by 10,000 by the end of that year.
Public transport consists of the metro, buses, ferries and taxis, all of which can be used with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

The Shanghai Metro mixes subway and light metro lines and reaches every core urban district and nearby suburbs. As of 2025 it runs 19 lines, excluding the maglev and Jinshan railway, serving 508 stations along 808 kilometres (502 mi), the longest system on Earth. Daily ridership peaked at 13.3 million on 8 March 2019. The maglev, opened in 2004, is the first commercial high-speed maglev anywhere and also the fastest, with a maximum operating speed of 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

The city's first tram line opened in 1908, and by 1925 Chinese, French and British firms were jointly running 328 tramcars on 14 routes. The state took them all over in 1949. Starting in the 1960s the lines were taken up or substituted with trolleybus and bus services, and 1975 saw the last of the old network taken out. A new generation arrived with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram in 2010, followed in 2018 by the Songjiang Tram, which has steel wheels and serves Songjiang District.

No bus network in the world is bigger, and it includes the oldest trolleybus system still running without a break. By 2019 several companies were operating 1,575 lines with a combined length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi). Taxis numbered 30,900 in 2024 and took 134 million passengers during the year.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shanghai-maritime-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shanghai Maritime University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai Maritime University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

shanghai-normal-university.h: A first look at the university

blocks.x: Shanghai Normal University, often shortened to SHNU (written 上海师范大学 in Chinese), is a publicly funded research university located in Shanghai. It began as a teacher-training institution and has grown into a broad, comprehensive university, although teacher education and the liberal arts remain the areas people associate with it most strongly.

The Shanghai municipal government counts it among the city's three key local universities, together with Shanghai University and the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology. That label means it receives strong backing from the city. The university is also built jointly by the Ministry of Education and the Shanghai authorities, and it takes part in the city's wider programme of education reform.

A few national schemes are worth knowing about if you are comparing universities. SHNU appears on the list of institutions under Plan 111 and on the list for the national programme that sends graduate students abroad with public funding for high-level university construction. It is also one of the Chinese institutions approved to host international students on Chinese Government Scholarships, which matters directly if you intend to apply for that kind of funding. Beyond the mainland, the university is one of sixteen members of the Shanghai-Hong Kong Universities Alliance.
In short, SHNU is a city-backed, teaching-minded university with a long tradition in education, humanities and the arts, and with a formal route for foreign students to receive scholarship support.

shanghai-normal-university.h: From teachers' college to normal university

blocks.x: The story starts in 1954, when the institution opened as Shanghai Teachers Training College. Two years later it was divided into a pair of institutions, called Shanghai No. 1 Teachers College and Shanghai No. 2 Teachers College. They were reunited in 1958 under the name Shanghai Teachers College.

The following decades brought several changes of name and merger. Accounts of the middle period are not fully consistent about the exact sequence, so treat the details below as an outline rather than a precise timeline. What is clear is that for part of the 1970s the institution carried the title Shanghai Normal University, having taken in four other schools, that it went back to the name Shanghai Teachers College in 1978, and that it became Shanghai Teachers University in 1984. In October 1994 it merged with Shanghai Teachers College of Technology, creating a new Shanghai Teachers University. In May 2003 the official English name of the new university became Shanghai Normal University.

Between September 1997 and August 2003 the university took several other bodies under its wing one after another. These were Shanghai Teacher Training College; Shanghai Tourism Institute; Shanghai Xingzhi Art School; and the Department of Human Sanitation and Health that belonged to Huangling Teacher School. This explains why the university today has such a mixed list of colleges, from arts and tourism to engineering.

The campus also hosts a number of teacher-development units, including the Shanghai Teachers Training Center, a separate training centre for college teachers, and the editorial office of a journal that collects academic abstracts in the liberal arts.

Two dates stand out for postgraduate study. In 1981 SHNU was in the first group of Chinese universities allowed to award master's degrees, and in 1986 it obtained the right to admit doctoral candidates. For a prospective research student, that means the university has been training postgraduates for several decades, not just a few years.

Reported enrolment is roughly 20,000 undergraduates and 8,000 graduate students, together with 2700 students from abroad. Student numbers change from year to year, so the university's own admissions pages are the place to check current totals.

SHNU says it has exchange and cooperation links with 311 universities and cultural or academic institutions in 40 countries and regions. Ten Chinese-foreign jointly run degree programmes are supported with partners from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Russia and France. Dual-degree arrangements with American universities include the University of Dayton, Colorado State University, the University of Georgia, the University of Wyoming, Chapman University and the University of Kansas.

The university uses Confucius Institutes as a platform for international work. The aim, as the university describes it, is to promote Chinese language learning and, through it, trade and economic ties between China and other countries.

The first overseas institute linked to SHNU was set up at Fukuyama University in Japan in April 2008. Talks followed with the University of Botswana and Kent State University. The institutes at Fukuyama University, the University of Botswana and the University of Missouri have since begun classes, and teachers from SHNU have been sent to teach there. In the university's own words, these institutes serve as a bridge for friendship and cultural exchange across Asia, Africa and America.
