At undergraduate level the university offers 88 majors across 11 subject categories. These are agriculture, art, economics, education, engineering, history, law, literature, management, philosophy and science. The Ministry of Education has given the Chinese Language and Literature major a special status for training and research, and the study of ancient Chinese literature is one of four key national bases.

Several majors have received extra recognition from the city. In 2005 the Shanghai Municipal Education Commission started its Undergraduate Educational Highland project and picked five SHNU programmes as key ones. They are English, Film and TV Communication, Teacher Education, Chinese Language and Literature, and MICE Economy (meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions).

At postgraduate level the university lists 6 primary and 46 secondary disciplines that can lead to a doctorate, 9 mobile post-doctoral research centres and 203 master's programmes. The university says several of its fields carry weight among scholars: history, philosophy, psychology, pedagogy, astrophysics, computational mathematics and Chinese language and literature. It also names fields that draw interest from the wider public, namely art, advertising, tourism management, rare earth materials, plant functional genes and the MICE economy.

Research bases add to this picture. Among universities run by a city, only SHNU's Urban Culture Research Center has been approved by the Ministry of Education as a key humanities research base. Municipal key laboratories work on galaxies and cosmology, and three e-research institutes cover comparative linguistics, computational science and urban culture. In total, the university counts one national key major subject and 11 key major subjects at city level.

The university has 2,917 faculty and staff, of whom 1,920 are full-time teaching faculty, and 1105 of the teachers hold doctorates. About 200 further people work part time, among them 20 foreign teachers on long-term contracts and five professors of academician level who were hired specially.

SHNU describes research as a priority. In the "past four years" referred to in its own summary, it reports 1756 research projects, including 137 at national level and 312 at provincial or ministerial level, supported by 380 million yuan of funding that has grown every year. The exact period behind that phrase is not stated, so it is best to read the figures as a rough indication of scale.

For the period from 2005 to 2008, the figures are more specific. Faculty worked on 233 liberal-arts projects at provincial level or above, 48 of them financed through the National Philosophy and Social Sciences Foundation. In science and engineering there were 216 projects, including 88 supported by the National Natural Science Foundation and some sub-projects of the national "863" and "973" programmes. In the same four years, 67 achievements won municipal or higher awards. On the humanities side these came from national and Shanghai awards for educational science, for humanities and social sciences, and for philosophy and social sciences.

Two science results are singled out. Research on amorphous alloys and their catalytic function won a first prize in the Ministry of Education's natural sciences awards, and a study of cosmic dynamics won a first prize in the Shanghai science and technology progress awards of 2005. SHNU also filed 287 patent applications in this period, of which 108 were granted, and registered 20 pieces of computer software.
Because several of these statistics are many years old, they should be seen as history rather than a current scorecard.

Several rankings put the university in context. In 2015, nine of its subjects appeared in the QS subject rankings, and its mathematics ranked among the world's top 100 in the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU). Chemistry, mathematics, materials science and engineering have entered the top 1% in Essential Science Indicators (ESI).

On social sciences publishing, a Ministry of Education analysis placed SHNU 28th across China for output in the Chinese Social Sciences Citation Index (CSSCI) in 2018. Within Shanghai it came 4th; only Fudan University, East China Normal University and Shanghai Jiaotong University were ahead. That year, authors from SHNU published 476 papers in this index, including 26 in leading social science, literature and history journals, plus 42 papers in SSCI and A&HCI journals.

For overall rankings, the university was 84th among mainland Chinese institutions in the 2019 Best Global Universities list from U.S. News & World Report and 50th in the QS Asia ranking for 2019 within mainland China. In the 2023 ARWU it stood in the 801-900 band worldwide. Rankings change every year and use different methods, so use them as one input rather than the deciding factor.

SHNU has two main campuses, Xuhui and Fengxian, which together cover more than 1.53 million square metres. Total floor area is 650,000 square metres, of which 67,000 is classroom space, 239,000 is student dormitory space, and 60,000 is indoor laboratory and fieldwork space.

Two central libraries hold 3.25 million books, 21 electronic databases and four collections of rare or important reference materials. Fixed assets across the university are valued at 1.27 billion yuan, with 315 million yuan of that in teaching facilities and research equipment.
Knowing that there are two campuses is practical: check carefully which campus your college and your accommodation are on before you plan your daily travel.
Where you study shapes daily life as much as the classroom does. The next sections describe the city around Shanghai Normal University: its setting, weather, buildings, economy, people and transport.

Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary on China's east coast. The Yangtze River forms the northern edge, Hangzhou Bay is on the southern side, and the East China Sea opens up eastward. The ground was formed by silt deposited by the Yangtze and by modern land reclamation, which gives it soft, sandy soil. Skyscrapers have to be built on deep concrete piles so that they do not sink.

Shanghai is a provincial-level municipality that governs the estuary along with a good number of the islands around it. Zhejiang borders it southward, while Jiangsu lies to the west and also to the north. Its most northerly spot is on Chongming Island, which grew during the twentieth century until only one island on the mainland coast was bigger.

The city stands on an alluvial plain and almost all of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land is flat, with an average height of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flats once surrounded the estuary but were reclaimed for farming. Only a handful of hills, among them She Shan, rise in the southwest. The city's top elevation, 103 metres (338 feet), is on Dajinshan Island out in Hangzhou Bay. Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are everywhere, since Shanghai belongs to the Lake Tai drainage basin.

The Huangpu River divides the downtown. It is an artificial tributary of the Yangtze, dug on the orders of Lord Chunshen during the Warring States era. The old core of the city grew on the west bank (Puxi), close to where Suzhou Creek enters the river; the creek connects with the Grand Canal and Lake Tai. The financial district of Lujiazui was built on the east bank, in Pudong. Pudong International Airport destroyed some local wetlands on the eastern shore, and the damage has been partly offset by protecting and enlarging Jiuduansha, a shoal close by that now serves as a nature reserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen: Cfa), and all four seasons are clearly marked. The average annual temperature is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) in the downtown area and 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F) in the suburbs.

Winters range from cool to cold and are damp. Cold northwesterly winds blowing from Siberia can bring night temperatures below freezing, and the city sees an average of 4.7 days of snowfall and 1.6 days of snow cover a year. Summers are hot and humid, with the occasional downpour or thunderstorm, and 21 days a year on average reach or pass 35 °C (95 °F). Typhoons can affect the city in summer and early autumn.

Spring is pleasant but changeable and often rainy, and autumn is usually sunny and dry, so these are the most comfortable seasons. Annual bright sunshine totals 1,754 hours. In terms of the share of possible sunshine, June is the dullest month at 28% and August the brightest at 46%.

The official seasonal calendar for 2001 to 2025 starts spring on 9 March and summer on 15 May, with autumn following on 5 October and winter from 4 December. Across the three weeks from 19 July to 8 August, temperatures average over 30 °C (86.0 °F), so anyone arriving in high summer should expect real heat.

Since 1951 the lowest reading was −10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977, and the highest was 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), seen twice at the Xujiahui weather station, on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022. A colder, unofficial figure of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) dates back to 19 January 1893. The highest daily minimum ever recorded at Xujiahui was 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) on 13 August 2010.
Xujiahui averaged 19.43 °C (67.0 °F) in 2025, which was 1.93 °C above the 1991 to 2020 average. Its average daily high was 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and its average daily low was 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund, on the bank of the Huangpu, is lined with early twentieth-century buildings in different styles. The neoclassical HSBC Building is one; the Art Deco Sassoon House, today within the Peace Hotel, is another. The riverfront has been renewed more than once. A new promenade designed by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren came in 1986, and a second makeover took place ahead of the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic was reorganised.

Much of Shanghai's older architecture reflects the period of Western influence, especially Britain, France and the United States. A building boom in the 1920s and 1930s left many Art Deco buildings behind. The Hungarian-Slovak architect László Hudec, resident from 1918 to 1947, designed the Paramount, the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner were responsible for the Metropole Hotel, the Broadway Mansions and the Peace Hotel, while the Austrian C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

A very typical piece of local housing is the shikumen (石库门), meaning "stone storage door": grey-brick houses of two or three storeys with a front yard behind a heavy wooden door set in a stone arch. They stand side by side along straight lanes called longtangs (弄堂). The city also has Soviet-style neoclassical buildings, mostly built between 1949 and the Sino-Soviet split of the late 1960s, when Soviet personnel helped with development. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is an example.

Shanghai has 206 buildings taller than 150 metres, which makes it seventh in the world for skyscrapers. Well-known towers are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center. The Shanghai Tower was completed in 2015, and it stands as China's tallest building and the world's third tallest. Nearby, at the northern end of Lujiazui, is the 468 m (1,535 ft) Oriental Pearl Tower. Many streets in the former foreign concessions are well preserved, and, despite heavy redevelopment, the Old City still keeps traditional design, as in the Yu Garden, a Jiangnan-style garden.

Shanghai serves as a world centre for finance and new ideas and as a national hub for trade, commerce and transport, with the busiest container port anywhere. The wider metropolitan area takes in Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou as well, and it produced a nominal gross metropolitan product of almost 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion) in 2022. In 2020 the city economy was estimated at $1 trillion in purchasing-power terms, which made it China's most productive metro area and placed it among the world's ten biggest metropolitan economies. Six industries (retail, finance, IT, property, machinery and car manufacturing) together account for about half of GDP.

In 2025, Shanghai's GDP was CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion nominal, $1.66 trillion in PPP), about 4% of China's total, with GDP per person at CN¥228,280, which is US$32,840 at market rates or US$66,944 in PPP terms. For 2022, disposable income per resident averaged CN¥79,610 a year (US$11,836), and urban employees earned CN¥212,476 on average (US$31,589).

For a student the key point is cost. A 2023 study by the Economist Intelligence Unit rated Shanghai the most expensive city to live in on the Chinese mainland, and a 2021 Julius Baer report called it the world's most expensive city for a luxurious lifestyle. Budget accordingly for housing and daily spending, and compare costs on the university's website.

Trade is huge. In 2023 the combined value of imports and exports was CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), 18.5% of the nation's total. Forbes ranked Shanghai fifth for billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projected a nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, which would be first in China and among the world's top five city economies. In August 2024 the city ranked fourth in the world, and second in Greater China after Beijing, for the number of Fortune Global 500 companies. Between 1992 and 2008, growth was in double digits in almost every year, until the global financial crisis; Shanghai was among the fastest-growing cities in the world over those two decades.

Shanghai is a global financial centre, third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a large hub for technology and a home to many start-ups, and in 2021 it was ranked the second fintech powerhouse after New York.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange was worth US$4.02 trillion in market capitalisation in 2019, which made it China's largest exchange and the fourth largest globally. Trading in 2009 placed six key commodities (rubber, copper and zinc among them) first in the world by trading volume on the Shanghai Futures Exchange. By the end of 2017 the city had 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Shanghai is one of China's main industrial centres, with heavy industry and manufacturing. The secondary sector rests on several industrial zones: the Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone, the Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, and the Hongqiao and Minhang economic and technological development zones.

Large employers include China's biggest steelmaker, Baosteel Group, the largest shipbuilding base in China, Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and the Jiangnan Shipyard, one of the country's oldest. The car maker SAIC Motor, based in the city, is one of China's three biggest automotive groups and has partnerships with Volkswagen and General Motors. It ranked 84th on the Fortune Global 500 in 2023.

Tourism figures swing widely from year to year, so look at them as a snapshot. In 2017 domestic visitors rose 7.5% to 318 million and overseas visitors rose 2.2% to 8.73 million, and Shanghai was the highest-earning tourist city in the world. In 2018 it hosted 82 international meetings, a rise of 34% from 61 in 2017. By 2023 the city had 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels, along with 1,942 travel agencies. It also listed 144 rated tourist attractions plus 34 red tourist attractions. The 2023 total of 3.64 million tourists was 4.8 times the 2022 figure and brought in CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), a rise of 98.5%, while foreign visitors reached 2.41 million, a 5.2-fold increase.

The Shanghai Free-Trade Zone opened in September 2013 as the first of its kind on the Chinese mainland, with reforms meant to encourage foreign investment. The Banker reported that in 2013 Shanghai drew the largest volume of financial-sector foreign direct investment in Asia-Pacific. As of October 2019 it was the second-largest free-trade zone on the mainland by land area, after Hainan, covering 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi). It brought together four bonded areas that already existed: the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, and the Waigaoqiao free trade zone along with its logistics park. Goods entering the zone do not pay duty or go through customs clearance.

At the end of 2023, Shanghai had 24,874,500 residents, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) held local hukou registration. In 2022, 89.3% of people lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. Among China's four directly administered municipalities it is second to Chongqing by total administrative population, but it is usually regarded as the biggest Chinese city because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller. The OECD estimates the metropolitan area at 34 million.

The city's statistics bureau counts about 157,900 foreign residents. Japanese citizens are the largest group at 28,900, followed by 21,900 Americans and 20,800 Koreans, though the real number of foreign citizens is probably much higher. Shanghai also attracts people from elsewhere in China: 40.3%, or 9.8 million, of residents come from other regions.

Life expectancy for the registered population is 83.18 years, the highest of any mainland Chinese city, and this has produced an ageing population: in 2021, 17.4% (4.3 million) of registered residents were 65 or older. In 2017 population controls were introduced, and the population fell by 10,000 by the end of that year.
Public transport combines the metro, buses, ferries and taxis, and all of them can be paid for with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

The Shanghai Metro mixes subway and light-metro lines and reaches every core urban district and nearby suburbs. As of 2025 it runs 19 lines, excluding both the maglev and the Jinshan railway, with 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of track, the longest network in the world. A record 13.3 million journeys were made in one day on 8 March 2019.
The Shanghai maglev opened in 2004. It was the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world and is the fastest, reaching 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph) at top speed.

The first trams ran in 1908. A joint effort by Chinese, French and British firms had put 328 tramcars on 14 routes by 1925, and all were nationalised in 1949. From the 1960s they were removed or replaced by trolleybuses and buses, and the last line disappeared in 1975. The tram returned in 2010 as the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram opened in Songjiang District.

The bus network is the most extensive in the world, and includes the world's oldest continuously operating trolleybus system. By 2019 it had 1,575 lines covering 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi), run by several companies. In 2024, 30,900 taxis carried 134 million passengers.
In practice, you can reach most of the city by metro, and buses and taxis fill the gaps, so a student living near either SHNU campus will find it straightforward to explore.

shanghai-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shanghai Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.

SHOU, or Shanghai Ocean University, is a state-funded research university in Shanghai whose specialities are aquaculture, marine science and marine engineering. It is part of the Double First-Class Initiative. Its sponsors are the Ministry of Natural Resources, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs and the Shanghai Municipal Government, which share responsibility for it.

The university began in 1912 as the Jiangsu Provincial Fisheries School, set up by Zhang Jian and Huang Yanpei, and it has stayed focused on higher education in fisheries ever since. It became Shanghai Fisheries College in 1952, and in 2008 it took its present name, Shanghai Ocean University.
Roughly 12,098 undergraduates and 5,700 graduate students are enrolled. There are 14 colleges, and they teach at both undergraduate and graduate level.

shanghai-ocean-university.h: What SHOU is known for academically

blocks.x: They are Agricultural Sciences, Biology and Biochemistry, Engineering, Environment and Ecology, and Plant and Animal Science. The university also started a journal, Aquaculture and Fisheries, in 2016, together with Elsevier and KeAi Publishing, and it was the first fisheries science journal in English published on the mainland.

shanghai-ocean-university.h: Fields of study at a glance

blocks.x: The subject list below is grouped by area.

Aquaculture and Fisheries: ichthyology; breeding and propagation of aquatic animals; fish genetic resources and germplasm conservation; and the nutrition, feed science, disease prevention and control of fish.
Fisheries Engineering and Resource Management: fishing gear technology and methods; fisheries machinery and engineering; conservation and management of fisheries resources.
Fisheries Policy and Economics: fisheries law and policy, and fisheries economics.
Marine Environmental Science and Ecology: marine ecology, and seaweed cell engineering.
Life Sciences and Biotechnology: biotechnology.
Food Science and Technology: food science and engineering, plus refrigeration and cryogenic technology.

In 2023 the Academic Ranking of World Universities put SHOU in the 800-900 range. In 2021 U.S. News and World Report listed it at 499th among Asia's best universities. Nationally, the Best Chinese Universities Ranking placed it first for marine fisheries science and technology. For anyone planning a career in fisheries or aquaculture, that last result is probably the most relevant.
SHOU has two sites in Shanghai. The main campus is in Pudong, at Lingang. The second is in Yangpu, on Jungong Road. Ask the university which site your college uses.

Daily life for a student depends on the city, so the remaining sections cover Shanghai itself: how it is laid out, the weather, the architecture, the economy, who lives there and how to travel around.

Shanghai stands on the Yangtze Estuary, halfway along China's east coast. The river runs along its northern edge, the East China Sea is on its east, and Hangzhou Bay lies to the south. The land has been made partly by the river's own sediment and partly by reclamation projects. Soft, sandy soil means that skyscrapers are built on deep concrete piles so they will not sink.

Shanghai is a municipality ranked at the level of a province. It governs the estuary and many islands, with Zhejiang as its southern neighbour and Jiangsu bordering it on the west and north. Chongming Island marks its northern limit and has been the second-largest island in mainland China since it grew in the twentieth century.

Because the city stands on an alluvial plain, nearly all of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 sq mi) is level, with an average height of four metres (13 feet). Where tidal flats once supported natural ecosystems around the estuary, farmland now lies. Hills are scarce. She Shan, in the southwest, is one, and the highest spot of all is on Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, at 103 metres (338 feet). The region is rich in water, with rivers, canals, streams and lakes, as part of the Lake Tai drainage basin.

shanghai-ocean-university.h: The Huangpu River and the two halves of the city

blocks.x: The Huangpu divides the downtown. It was dug as an artificial tributary of the Yangtze during the Warring States period on the orders of Lord Chunshen. West of the river is Puxi, the historic centre, near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, which connected the city to the Grand Canal and Lake Tai. East of the river is Pudong, where the Lujiazui financial district was built. Pudong International Airport's construction destroyed some wetlands on the eastern shore, and the damage has been partly balanced by protecting and enlarging the nearby shoal of Jiuduansha as a nature reserve.
Shanghai's climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa). Yearly averages are 17.5 degrees Celsius (63.5 F) downtown and between 16.2 and 17.2 degrees (61.2 to 63.0 F) in the suburbs.

Winter: cold and damp, though not harsh by northern standards. Northwesterly winds from Siberia can take overnight temperatures below zero. Snow falls on 4.7 days of a typical year and covers the ground on 1.6 days.
Spring: pleasant, but unsettled and often rainy.
Summer: hot and humid, with the occasional downpour or thunderstorm. In a normal year, 21 days reach at least 35 degrees (95 F). Typhoons threaten the city in summer and early autumn.
Autumn: generally sunny and dry, which makes it the best season along with spring.

June is the least sunny month, with 28 percent of possible sunshine, and August the sunniest, with 46 percent; together they add up to 1,754 hours of bright sun over the year. Official seasonal start dates, averaged over 2001 to 2025, are 9 March for spring, 15 May for summer, 5 October for autumn and 4 December for winter. From 19 July to 8 August the three-week average is above 30 degrees (86.0 F).

The Xujiahui weather station recorded its coldest day since 1951 on 31 January 1977, at minus 10.1 degrees (13.8 F), though an unofficial minus 12.1 degrees (10.2 F) had been noted on 19 January 1893. The hottest days were 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022, with 40.9 degrees (105.6 F). Its highest daily minimum, 32.1 degrees (89.8 F), came on 13 August 2010. The annual mean in 2025 was 19.43 degrees (67.0 F), which is 1.93 degrees warmer than the 1991-2020 average, with highs averaging 23.66 degrees (74.6 F) and lows 16.44 degrees (61.6 F).

Along the Huangpu runs the Bund, lined with early twentieth-century buildings of several styles, including the neoclassical HSBC Building and the Art Deco Sassoon House, which is today part of the Peace Hotel. Two rounds of renewal have been carried out. In 1986 the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren gave it a new promenade. The second round came before the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and the traffic arrangements changed.

The imprint of Britain, France and the United States on the city is visible. Many Art Deco buildings date from the construction boom of the 1920s and 1930s. The architect Laszlo Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in Shanghai between 1918 and 1947, designed several, among them the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema and the Paramount. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, also prominent in the style, designed the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel and the Broadway Mansions, and the Austrian C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

Shikumen ("stone storage door") houses are a very common type. They are grey-brick houses, usually two or three floors high, with a stone arch at the front yard in which a heavy wooden door provides protection. Rows of connected houses are laid out along straight lanes called longtang. Soviet neoclassical, or Stalinist, buildings also exist. Most date from the period between 1949, when the People's Republic was founded, and the late 1960s Sino-Soviet split, when Soviet personnel were in China to assist with building a communist state. One example is the Shanghai Exhibition Center.

There are 206 buildings of 150 metres or more in Shanghai, the seventh-largest group of skyscrapers in the world. Among them are the Jin Mao Tower, the Shanghai World Financial Center and the Shanghai Tower, which opened in 2015 and is the tallest in China and the third tallest anywhere. At the northern tip of Lujiazui, close to them, stands the Oriental Pearl Tower (468 m, or 1,535 ft). The former foreign concessions have many well-preserved areas, and in spite of fast redevelopment the Old City keeps its traditional buildings, such as Yu Garden, a rich example of a Jiangnan garden.

This is a city where finance and innovation meet national commerce, trade and transport, and its container port is the busiest in the world. In nominal terms, Greater Shanghai (Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou are included) made a gross metropolitan product of nearly 13 trillion RMB (US$1.9 trillion) as of 2022. The economy was estimated at US$1 trillion in PPP in 2020, making it the most productive metro area in China and one of the ten largest in the world. Six industries are the biggest, namely retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing and car manufacturing, and they provide about half of GDP.

The city's GDP in 2025 was CN¥5.67 trillion (US$814 billion nominal, or US$1.66 trillion in PPP), which is 4 percent of China's total. Per head that is CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). Disposable income per head averaged CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) in 2022, and urban-unit employees had an average annual salary of CN¥212,476 (US$31,589). For luxury living, Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report named it the most expensive city in the world in 2021. If you plan to study here, this should shape your budget.

The value of imports and exports in 2023 was CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), 18.5 percent of the national total. Forbes counted more billionaires in only four other places in 2022. Oxford Economics expects Shanghai's nominal GDP to reach US$1.3 trillion in 2035, first in China and good enough to put it among the top five major cities worldwide by gross regional product. In August 2024 it had the fourth-largest number of Fortune Global 500 companies of any city, and the second-largest in Greater China after Beijing. Double-digit GDP growth in nearly every year from 1992 to 2008, before the global financial crisis, makes it one of the fastest-developing cities of the past two decades.

Shanghai ranks third in Asia and eighth in the world in the Global Financial Centres Index. It also hosts a large part of the Chinese and world technology industries and a big startup scene, and it was rated the world's second Fintech powerhouse in 2021, after New York City.

As of 2019, the Shanghai Stock Exchange's market capitalisation was US$4.02 trillion, the biggest in China and fourth in the world. For six key commodities, rubber, copper and zinc among them, the Shanghai Futures Exchange had the largest trading volume anywhere in 2009. The city had 1,491 financial institutions at the end of 2017, and 251 of them were foreign-invested.

Heavy industry and manufacturing are central to the city's role. Its secondary sector rests on four zones: Hongqiao and Minhang (both economic and technological development zones), Jinqiao (export processing) and Caohejing (high-tech).

Baosteel Group is China's biggest steelmaker, the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group is the country's biggest shipbuilding base and Jiangnan Shipyard is one of its oldest yards, and all are based here. SAIC Motor, based in Shanghai, is among China's three largest car groups. Volkswagen and General Motors are its strategic partners, and it was 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

Visitor numbers in 2017 were 318 million domestic tourists, up 7.5 percent, and 8.73 million from overseas, up 2.2 percent. That year Shanghai earned more from tourism than any other city in the world. The International Congress and Convention Association recorded 82 international meetings held in the city in 2018, up 34 percent from 61 in 2017.

As of 2023 there were 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions and 34 red tourist attractions. The source also gives 3.64 million tourists for 2023, a 4.8-fold rise on 2022, bringing in CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), 98.5 percent more than the year before, and it says foreign tourists reached 2.41 million, a 5.2-fold rise. Those numbers are much lower than the 2017 figures, so check a current source before relying on them.

In September 2013 Shanghai opened mainland China's first free-trade zone, with reforms meant to encourage foreign investment. The Banker said that for 2013 no other place in the Asia-Pacific received a bigger amount of foreign direct investment in financial services. Hainan's is the only mainland free-trade zone with more land than Shanghai's, as of October 2019, which has 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi). It was formed by merging four bonded zones already in place, which were the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, and the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone and Free Trade Logistics Park. Goods that enter it do not pay duty or go through customs clearance.

In 2023 Shanghai had 24,874,500 residents, of whom 14,801,700, or 59.5 percent, held a local hukou, meaning they were registered locally. By 2022, 89.3 percent lived in cities and towns and 10.7 percent in the countryside. Chongqing is larger by administrative area, which makes Shanghai the second largest of China's four municipalities, but Shanghai is normally regarded as China's largest city because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller. The OECD estimates 34 million people in the metropolitan area.

The Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau says there are about 157,900 foreign residents. Japanese number 28,900, Americans 21,900 and Koreans 20,800. The real figure is likely far higher. Newcomers from within China are many too: 9.8 million people, or 40.3 percent of residents, came from other regions.

shanghai-ocean-university.h: Long lives and an older population

blocks.x: People registered in Shanghai live 83.18 years on average, the highest figure of any mainland city. The flip side is an ageing population, with 4.3 million registered residents (17.4 percent) aged 65 or over in 2021. In 2017 population controls were introduced for the city and the total fell by 10,000 by the end of the year.
Metros, buses, ferries and taxis make up the public transport system, and all of them accept the Shanghai Public Transport Card.

Subway and light metro lines make up the Shanghai Metro, which serves every core urban district and the suburbs beside it. In 2025 it had 19 lines (the maglev and the Jinshan railway are not counted), with 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of track, making it the longest metro network in the world. Daily ridership peaked at 13.3 million on 8 March 2019. The maglev train began running in 2004 as the first commercial high-speed maglev, and it remains the fastest, at up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

Trams started in 1908. By 1925 Chinese, French and British companies together ran 328 trams on 14 routes, and all of them became state-owned in 1949. From the 1960s the lines were pulled up or replaced with trolleybuses and buses, and the final tram line was removed in 1975. A new tram era started in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram, followed in 2018 by the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram in Songjiang District. For visitors, the metro is the easiest way to move around.

No city has a bigger bus network, and it includes the oldest trolleybus system still running continuously. In 2019 it had 1,575 lines totalling 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi), and several companies operate them. Taxis numbered 30,900 in 2024, and they carried 134 million passengers that year.
In summary, SHOU gives you an unusual specialisation in marine and fisheries subjects in a vast, wealthy city with excellent transport, but you should plan carefully for living costs.

Shanghai University (SHU) is a municipal public university in Shanghai, China. It is owned by the Shanghai Municipal People's Government. The university is part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction.
Shanghai University traces its historical origins to a university of the same name founded in Shanghai on 23 October 1922.

The present-day institution was established in 1994 through the merger of Shanghai University of Technology, Shanghai University of Science and Technology, the former Shanghai University, and Shanghai Institute of Science and Technology.

The university's three principal campuses are located in Baoshan District, Yanchang in Jing'an District, and Jiading District. The main university library is on the Baoshan campus. The university library system holds more than four million volumes.

Shanghai University is a comprehensive, research-intensive university whose teaching and research cover the humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, engineering, business, law and the arts. It offers undergraduate and postgraduate education and operates a number of research institutes.

Shanghai University jointly operates the SILC Business School with the University of Technology Sydney. The school was founded in 1994 and was among the earlier Sino-foreign joint business schools established in China.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shanghai, where Shanghai University is located.

Shanghai is located on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south, and the East China Sea to the east. The land is formed by the Yangtze's natural deposition and modern land reclamation projects. It has sandy soil, and skyscrapers have to be built with deep concrete piles to avoid sinking into the soft ground. The provincial-level Municipality of Shanghai administers the estuary and many of its surrounding islands. It borders the provinces of Zhejiang to the south and Jiangsu to the west and north. The municipality's northernmost point is on Chongming Island, the second-largest island in mainland China after its expansion during the 20th century.

Shanghai is located on an alluvial plain and the vast majority of its 6,340.5-square-kilometre (2,448.1-square-mile) land area is flat, with an average elevation of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flat ecosystems exist around the estuary, but they have been reclaimed for agricultural purposes. The city's few hills, such as She Shan, lie to the southwest; its highest point is the peak of Dajinshan Island (103 metres or 338 feet) in Hangzhou Bay. Shanghai has rivers, canals, streams, and lakes, and it is known for its rich water resources as part of the Lake Tai drainage basin.

Downtown Shanghai is bisected by the Huangpu River, a man-made tributary of the Yangtze created by order of Lord Chunshen during the Warring States period. The historic centre of the city was located on the west bank of the Huangpu (Puxi), near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, connecting it with Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. The central financial district, Lujiazui, was established on the east bank of the Huangpu (Pudong). Along Shanghai's eastern shore, the destruction of local wetlands due to the construction of Pudong International Airport has been partially offset by the protection and expansion of a nearby shoal, Jiuduansha, as a nature preserve.

Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cfa), with an average annual temperature of 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) for downtown areas and 16.2–17.2 °C (61.2–63.0 °F) for suburbs. The city experiences four distinct seasons. Winters are temperate to cold and damp—northwesterly winds from Siberia can cause nighttime temperatures to drop below freezing. Each year, there are an average of 4.7 days with snowfall and 1.6 days with snow cover. Summers are hot and humid, and occasional downpours or thunderstorms can be expected. On average, 21 days meet or exceed 35 °C (95 °F) annually. In summer and the beginning of autumn, the city is susceptible to typhoons.

The most pleasant seasons are generally spring, although changeable and often rainy, and autumn, which is usually sunny and dry. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 28% in June to 46% in August, the city receives 1,754 hours of bright sunshine annually. According to China's seasonal division standard, from 2001 to 2025, Shanghai enters spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October, and winter on 4 December. The average temperature for the three weeks from 19 July to 8 August is above 30 °C (86.0 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977 (unofficial record of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was set on 19 January 1893) to 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022 at a weather station in Xujiahui. It also has 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) as the highest ever daily minimum temperature at Xujiahui on 13 August 2010.

In 2025, the average temperature of Xujiahui was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), which was 1.93 °C higher than the average from 1991 to 2020. The average daily high temperature is 23.66 °C (74.6 °F), and the average daily low temperature is 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund, located by the bank of the Huangpu River, is home to a row of early 20th-century architecture, ranging in style from the neoclassical HSBC Building to the Art Deco Sassoon House (now part of the Peace Hotel). The area has been revitalized several times: the first was in 1986, with a new promenade by the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren. The second was before the 2010 Expo, which includes restoration of the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and reconfiguration of traffic flow.

Much of the city’s development attests to the imperial presence of Western powers, namely Britain, France and the United States.Shanghai's construction boom during the 1920s and 1930s caused the city to have several Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in the city between 1918 and 1947, designed Art Deco buildings such as the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema, and the Paramount. Other prominent Art Deco-style architects are Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, who designed the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel, and the Broadway Mansions; and Austrian architect C.H. Gonda, who designed the Capitol Theatre. One common architectural element is the shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men, "stone storage door") residence, typically two- or three-story gray brick houses with the front yard protected by a heavy wooden door in a stylistic stone arch. Each residence is connected and arranged in straight alleys known as longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). Shanghai also has Soviet neoclassical architecture or Stalinist architecture: most were erected between the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 and the Sino-Soviet Split in the late 1960s when Soviet personnel came to China to aid in the development of a communist state. An example of Soviet neoclassical architecture in Shanghai is the Shanghai Exhibition Center.

Shanghai has 206 buildings 150m+ making it the seventh city in the world with the most skyscrapers. Some of Shanghai's skyscrapers include the Jin Mao Tower, the Shanghai World Financial Center, and the Shanghai Tower, which was completed in 2015 and is currently the tallest building in China and the third tallest in the world. The Oriental Pearl Tower, at 468 m (1,535 ft), is located nearby at the northern tip of Lujiazui. Many areas in the former foreign concessions are well-preserved. Despite rampant redevelopment, the Old City retains traditional architecture and designs, such as the Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan style garden.

The city is a global centre for finance and innovation, and a national centre for commerce, trade, and transportation, with the world's busiest container port—the Port of Shanghai. As of 2022, the Greater Shanghai metropolitan area, which includes Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan, and Huzhou, was estimated to produce a gross metropolitan product (nominal) of nearly 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion). As of 2020, the economy of Shanghai was estimated to be $1 trillion (PPP), ranking the most productive metro area of China and among the top ten largest metropolitan economies in the world. Shanghai's six largest industries—retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing, and automotive manufacturing—comprise about half the city's GDP.

As of 2025, Shanghai had a GDP of CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion in nominal; $1.66 trillion in PPP) that makes up 4% of China's GDP, and a GDP per capita of CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 in nominal; US$66,944 in PPP). In 2022, the average annual disposable income of Shanghai's residents was CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) per capita, while the average annual salary of people employed in urban units in Shanghai was CN¥212,476 (US$31,589), making it one of the wealthiest cities in China, but also the most expensive city in mainland China to live in according to a 2023 study by the Economist Intelligence Unit. According to Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report, Shanghai was the most expensive city in the world for living a luxurious lifestyle in 2021.

In 2023, the city's imports and exports reached CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), accounting for 18.5% of the national total. In 2022, Shanghai was ranked fifth-highest in the number of billionaires by Forbes. Shanghai's nominal GDP was projected to reach US$1.3 trillion in 2035 (ranking first in China), making it one of the world's top 5 major cities in terms of GRP according to a study by Oxford Economics. As of August 2024, Shanghai ranked 4th in the world and 2nd in Greater China (after Beijing) by the largest number of the Fortune Global 500 companies.

In the last two decades, Shanghai has been one of the fastest-developing cities in the world; it has recorded double-digit GDP growth in almost every year between 1992 and 2008, before the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai is a global financial center, ranking third in Asia and eighth globally on the Global Financial Centres Index. Shanghai is also a large hub of the Chinese and global technology industry and home to a large startup ecosystem. As of 2021, the city was ranked as the 2nd Fintech powerhouse in the world after New York City.

As of 2019, the Shanghai Stock Exchange had a market capitalization of US$4.02 trillion, making it the largest stock exchange in China and the fourth-largest stock exchange in the world. In 2009, the trading volume of six key commodities—including rubber, copper, and zinc—on the Shanghai Futures Exchange all ranked first globally. By the end of 2017, Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions, of which 251 were foreign-invested.

As one of the main industrial centres of China, Shanghai plays a key role in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Several industrial zones—including Shanghai Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, and Shanghai Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone—are backbones of Shanghai's secondary sector. Shanghai is home to China's largest steelmaker Baosteel Group, China's largest shipbuilding base Hudong–Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and one of China's oldest shipbuilders, the Jiangnan Shipyard. In auto manufacturing, the Shanghai-based SAIC Motor is one of the three largest automotive corporations in China, and has strategic partnerships with Volkswagen and General Motors. The company ranked 84 on the Fortune Global 500 list in 2023.

In 2017, the number of domestic tourists to the city increased by 7.5% to 318 million, while the number of overseas tourists increased by 2.2% to 8.73 million. In 2017, Shanghai was the highest earning tourist city in the world. According to the International Congress and Convention Association, Shanghai hosted 82 international meetings in 2018, a 34% increase from 61 in 2017. As of 2023, it had 57 five-star hotels, 52 four star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions, and 34 red tourist attractions. In 2023, Shanghai had 3.64 million tourists, a 4.8-fold growth compared to 2022. It generated CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion) in value, a 98.5% increase from the previous year. The number of foreign tourists reached 2.41 million, with a 5.2-fold increase.

In September 2013, the city launched the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone—the first free-trade zone in mainland China. It introduced several reforms to incentivize foreign investment. The Banker reported that Shanghai attracted the highest volumes of financial sector foreign direct investment in the Asia-Pacific region in 2013. As of October 2019, it is the second largest free-trade zone in mainland China in terms of land area (behind Hainan Free Trade Zone) covering an area of 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) and integrating four existing bonded zones—Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, and Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Commodities entering the zone are exempt from duty and customs clearance.

As of 2023, Shanghai had a population of 24,874,500, including 14,801,700 (59.5%) hukou holders (registered locally). As of 2022, 89.3% of Shanghai's population lives in urban areas, and 10.7% live in rural areas. Based on the population of its total administrative area, Shanghai is the second largest of the four municipalities of China, behind Chongqing, but is generally considered the largest Chinese city because the urban population of Chongqing is much smaller. According to the OECD, Shanghai's metropolitan area has an estimated population of 34 million.

According to the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau, about 157,900 residents in Shanghai are foreigners, including 28,900 Japanese, 21,900 Americans, and 20,800 Koreans. The actual number of foreign citizens in the city is probably much higher. Shanghai is also a domestic immigration city—40.3% (9.8 million) of the city's residents are from other regions of China.

Shanghai has a life expectancy of 83.18 years for the city's registered population, the highest life expectancy of all cities in mainland China. This has also caused the city to experience population aging—in 2021, 17.4% (4.3 million) of the city's registered population was aged 65 or above. In 2017, the Chinese government implemented population controls for Shanghai, resulting in a population decline of 10,000 people by the end of the year.
Shanghai has a public transportation system comprising metros, buses, ferries, and taxis, which can be accessed using a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

Shanghai's rapid transit system, the Shanghai Metro, incorporates subway and light metro lines and extends to each core urban district as well as neighboring suburban districts. As of 2025, there are 19 metro lines (excluding the Shanghai maglev train and Jinshan railway), 508 stations, and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of lines in operation, making it the longest network in the world. On 8 March 2019, it set the city's daily metro ridership record with 13.3 million. Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev train is the first and the fastest commercial high-speed maglev in the world, with a maximum operation speed of 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

The first tram line in Shanghai was opened in 1908. By 1925, there were 328 tramcars and 14 routes operated by Chinese, French, and British companies collaboratively, all of which were nationalized in 1949. Since the 1960s, tram lines were either dismantled or replaced by trolleybus or motorbus lines; the last tram line was demolished in 1975. Shanghai reintroduced trams in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram. In 2018, the steel wheeled Songjiang Tram started operating in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the world's most extensive bus network, including the world's oldest continuously operating trolleybus system, with 1,575 lines covering a total length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi) by 2019. The system is operated by multiple companies. As of 2024, 30,900 taxis were in operation in Shanghai, which carried 134 million passengers that year.

shanghai-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shanghai University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

shanghai-university-of-finance-and-econo.h: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics in brief

blocks.x: SUFE, the Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, is a publicly funded university in Shanghai with a specialist focus on finance and economics. It reports to the Ministry of Education and has been included in two national schemes, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction. If your goal is a career in banking, accounting, economics or business, the combination of a specialised university and a major financial city is the main reason to look at SUFE.

The university began in 1917 as a business programme inside the Nanjing Advanced Normal School. Four years later, in 1921, the programme was relocated to Shanghai, where it turned into the Shanghai University of Commerce.

The institution kept changing over the following decades. A rename in 1928 made it the Central University's School of Commerce. It broke away from the Central University in 1932 and ran independently as the National Shanghai College of Commerce. The year 1950 brought the name Shanghai College of Finance and Economics, and since 1985 it has used its present name.
Rankings are a useful guide when you are comparing universities, but they measure different things, so it is worth noting which list each figure comes from.

Netbig, a Chinese ranking, gave SUFE first place in its 'finance and economics' category five times: in 2003, 2004, 2005, 2007 and 2008. In the 2021 edition of the Best Chinese Universities Ranking, it was rated the best of China's universities that specialise in finance, business and economics.

For Tilburg University's Economics Schools Research Ranking covering 2016 to 2020, SUFE came 41st worldwide and 3rd across Asia, and within mainland China only Peking University was ahead of it, so SUFE was 2nd.

QS (Quacquarelli Symonds) places it 144th among BRICS universities and within the top 350 in Asia. In QS subject tables it is in the top 64 worldwide for economics and econometrics and in the top 101 for accounting and finance.

The Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) put SUFE in the 701 to 800 band overall in 2022. In its 2023 subject rankings SUFE was in the top 43 worldwide for finance and the top 76 for economics. It was in the top 101 for management, public administration and statistics, in the top 201 for business administration and for hospitality and tourism management, and in the top 401 for political sciences.
U.S. News and World Report lists it 34th in the world for business and economics, with 10th place in Asia and 7th in China.
In short: SUFE is much stronger in its specialist subjects than in broad whole-university tables, which is exactly what you would expect from a focused institution.

shanghai-university-of-finance-and-econo.h: Studying in Shanghai: the city behind the campus

blocks.x: Life at SUFE means life in Shanghai. The notes below follow the things a new student usually asks about first: how expensive the city is, how to get around, what the weather is like, and what kind of place it is.

shanghai-university-of-finance-and-econo.h: Cost of living and the economy

blocks.x: Shanghai is rich. Its economy is closely tied to finance, innovation and trade, and it hosts the world's busiest container port. The Greater Shanghai area, a region that also includes Ningbo, Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Jiaxing, Huzhou and Zhoushan, had an estimated gross metropolitan product of nearly 13 trillion RMB (about $1.9 trillion) in 2022. Estimates for 2020 put the city's economy at $1 trillion on a purchasing-power basis, the most productive metropolitan area in China and one of the top ten in the world. The six biggest sectors are retail, finance, information technology, real estate, machinery and car manufacturing, and together they make up about half of the city's output.

The 2025 GDP of the city was $814 billion in nominal terms (CN¥5.67 trillion), or $1.66 trillion adjusted for purchasing power, which is 4% of China's total. Per person, that is CN¥228,280, or US$32,840 nominal and US$66,944 on the PPP measure. Disposable income per head averaged US$11,836 (CN¥79,610) in 2022, and the average annual pay in urban employment was US$31,589 (CN¥212,476). These numbers go with high prices: the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2023 study ranked Shanghai as the priciest city on the Chinese mainland, and Julius Baer's wealth report listed it as the world's most expensive for a luxury lifestyle in 2021. A student budget should be planned with that in mind.

Trade is huge. Foreign trade in 2023 was worth US$1.07 trillion (CN¥7.73 trillion), or 18.5% of the national total. Forbes ranked the city fifth for billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projected a nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, the highest in China and in the world's top five. In August 2024 the city stood fourth worldwide, and second in Greater China, in the count of Fortune Global 500 company headquarters, behind Beijing. From 1992 to 2008 the economy grew by double digits in almost every year, until the 2008 financial crisis; it has been one of the world's fastest-growing cities of the past two decades.

The Global Financial Centres Index puts Shanghai third in Asia and eighth in the world. The technology sector and startup scene are large, and in 2021 the city was second only to New York as a fintech powerhouse. At the end of 2017 it had 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested. The Shanghai Stock Exchange, with US$4.02 trillion in market capitalisation in 2019, is the biggest in China and the fourth biggest in the world. On the Shanghai Futures Exchange in 2009, rubber, copper and zinc were among six commodities with the highest trading volumes anywhere. For an economics or finance student, these institutions are on your doorstep.

The Shanghai Free-Trade Zone opened in September 2013 as the first one on the mainland, with reforms intended to attract foreign investment. The Banker magazine reported that no other Asia-Pacific city attracted more foreign direct investment into financial services in 2013. By October 2019 the zone covered 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 square miles), making it second to Hainan in size, and it brought four existing bonded zones together: the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone and its Logistics Park, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area and the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Goods in the zone avoid duty and customs clearance.

Shanghai is also an industrial city. Zones such as Hongqiao, Jinqiao, Minhang and Caohejing support its manufacturing sector. The largest steelmaker in China, Baosteel Group, is here, as are Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group (China's biggest shipbuilding base) and Jiangnan Shipyard, which is among the oldest. SAIC Motor, one of the three largest Chinese carmakers, works with Volkswagen and General Motors and was number 84 in the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

Tourism is another pillar. In 2017 domestic visitors grew 7.5% to 318 million and foreign visitors 2.2% to 8.73 million, and Shanghai earned more from tourism than any city in the world that year. In 2018 the city held 82 international meetings, up 34% from 61 in 2017, as counted by the International Congress and Convention Association. Hotels and agencies are plentiful: 57 five-star hotels, 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist sites and 34 red tourist sites by 2023. Recovery after 2022 was sharp. In 2023 the city had 3.64 million tourists, 4.8 times the 2022 level, who generated US$24.53 billion (CN¥177.12 billion), up 98.5%, and the 2.41 million foreign tourists among them were 5.2 times as many as the year before.

A Shanghai Public Transport Card works across metro, buses, ferries and taxis. The metro runs on subway and light-metro lines and reaches every core district as well as the neighbouring suburbs. By 2025 there were 19 lines, not including the maglev and the Jinshan railway, with 508 stations over 808 km (502 miles), the longest network on earth. The single-day ridership record is 13.3 million, set on 8 March 2019. Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev is the world's first commercial high-speed maglev and the fastest, with a top speed of 430 km/h (270 mph).

Buses make up the largest network in the world and include the oldest trolleybus system in continuous service. In 2019 it had 1,575 lines with 8,997 km (5,590 miles) of routes, operated by several companies. There were 30,900 taxis in 2024, carrying 134 million passengers that year.

Trams have a history here too. A line opened in 1908, and by 1925 Chinese, French and British firms were running 14 routes with 328 cars together until nationalisation in 1949. The lines were removed or replaced with trolleybus and bus services from the 1960s onward, and the final line disappeared in 1975. The Zhangjiang Tram, which has rubber tyres, brought trams back in 2010, and in 2018 the Songjiang Tram, with steel wheels, began running in Songjiang District.

Shanghai is on the east coast, at the Yangtze Estuary. North of it flows the Yangtze, to the south lies Hangzhou Bay, and to the east is the East China Sea. The land comes from river sediment and from modern reclamation, so it is sandy and soft, and tall buildings stand on deep concrete piles. As a provincial-level municipality it administers the estuary and numerous islands, and it borders Zhejiang (south) and Jiangsu (west and north). The northernmost part is Chongming Island, which has grown to become the second-largest island in mainland China.

Almost all of the 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land is flat alluvial plain, at an average of about four metres (13 feet) above sea level. Former tidal flats around the estuary have been converted for farming. Hills are rare, such as She Shan in the southwest, and Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay has the highest point at 103 m (338 ft). Rivers, canals, streams and lakes abound because the city lies in the Lake Tai basin.

Downtown is split by the Huangpu River, an artificial tributary of the Yangtze ordered by Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. West of the river is Puxi, the historic centre, near where Suzhou Creek enters; the creek leads towards Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. East of the river is Pudong, location of the financial district Lujiazui. When Pudong International Airport was built it destroyed coastal wetland, and the shoal of Jiuduansha was protected as a nature reserve and allowed to expand to make up part of the loss.

The climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa). Annual mean temperature is 17.5 C (63.5 F) downtown and 16.2 to 17.2 C (61.2 to 63.0 F) in the suburbs. Winter is mild to cold but always damp, and winds from Siberia out of the northwest can bring freezing nights. Snow falls on 4.7 days a year and lies on the ground on 1.6. Summers are hot and humid with the occasional downpour or thunderstorm; 21 days a year reach 35 C (95 F) or more. Typhoon risk exists in summer and early autumn.

Spring and autumn are best. Spring is variable and often wet, while autumn is generally sunny and dry. Sunshine is lowest in June, at 28% of the possible total, and highest in August at 46%, adding up to 1,754 hours across the year. Using the national definition of the seasons, the averages for 2001 to 2025 were these: winter starts 4 December, autumn 5 October, summer 15 May and spring 9 March. From 19 July to 8 August the mean temperature stays above 30 C (86.0 F). At Xujiahui, the lowest reading since 1951 was -10.1 C (13.8 F), recorded on 31 January 1977, with an unofficial -12.1 C (10.2 F) back on 19 January 1893; the highest was 40.9 C (105.6 F), twice, on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022; and the highest overnight low was 32.1 C (89.8 F) on 13 August 2010. The year 2025 was warm: Xujiahui averaged 19.43 C (67.0 F), which is 1.93 C above the 1991 to 2020 mean. Typical daily highs are 23.66 C (74.6 F) and typical lows 16.44 C (61.6 F). Pack for both ends of the range.

The Bund, on the Huangpu River bank, preserves a line of early 20th-century buildings. One end of the stylistic range is the neoclassical HSBC Building and the other the Art Deco Sassoon House, now a section of the Peace Hotel. Paulus Snoeren, a Dutch architect, redesigned the promenade in 1986. A second revival came before the 2010 Expo, which included repairing the Waibaidu Bridge, a century old, and changing the traffic layout.

Western powers, particularly Britain, France and the United States, left their mark on the city. The building boom of the 1920s and 1930s produced a stock of Art Deco architecture. Designers include László Hudec (a Hungarian-Slovak in Shanghai from 1918 to 1947, with the Park Hotel, Grand Cinema and Paramount), Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner (Peace Hotel, Metropole Hotel, Broadway Mansions), and the Austrian C.H. Gonda (Capitol Theatre). The shikumen house, with its 'stone storage door', is typical: grey brick, two or three storeys, a small yard behind a wooden gate in a stone arch, arranged in connected rows along straight lanes (longtang). The Soviet or Stalinist neoclassical style, found for instance in the Shanghai Exhibition Center, mostly dates from the period between 1949 and the break between China and the Soviet Union (the Sino-Soviet Split) in the late 1960s, when Soviet staff were in China to help build a communist state.

Shanghai has 206 buildings of 150 m or more, seventh most in the world. Among them are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, and also the Shanghai Tower, completed in 2015, which stands as the highest building in China and ranks third worldwide. At the northern end of Lujiazui you will see the Oriental Pearl Tower, 468 m (1,535 ft) tall. Large parts of the former foreign concessions are well preserved, and the Old City keeps traditional buildings in spite of fast redevelopment, for example the Yu Garden, a detailed Jiangnan-style garden.

In 2023 the population was 24,874,500, and 14,801,700 of them (59.5%) held local hukou registration. In 2022, 89.3% were urban dwellers and 10.7% rural. Chongqing has a larger administrative area population, so Shanghai is the second-largest of the four municipalities, but because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller, Shanghai is usually considered the biggest Chinese city. The OECD suggests about 34 million in the metropolitan area.

About 157,900 foreigners are officially counted (28,900 Japanese, 21,900 Americans, 20,800 Koreans), although the actual figure is probably higher. Domestic migrants are 40.3% of residents, about 9.8 million.

Life expectancy for registered residents is 83.18 years, the highest in mainland China, which has brought population ageing: 4.3 million people, 17.4%, were 65 or older in 2021. After population controls in 2017 the city shrank by 10,000 by the end of the year.

SUFE offers a specialised programme in a city where finance, trade and technology are part of daily life. Before applying, check the university's own website for current programmes, admission rules, tuition and accommodation, and treat the rankings above as snapshots from different years rather than a permanent verdict. Think too about the practical side of Shanghai: a high cost of living, a metro that reaches almost everywhere, hot humid summers and damp, cold winters. A student who prepares for those four things will settle in much faster and spend more time on studies and on the city's financial world.
