shanghai-university-of-international-bus.h: Shanghai: the setting for your studies

blocks.x: You will spend much of your time in the city, so this section describes Shanghai: its land, its weather, its architecture, its economy, its people and its transport.

Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary on China's east coast. Water surrounds it on three sides: the East China Sea on the east, Hangzhou Bay on the south and the Yangtze to the north. The ground is made up of silt deposited naturally by the Yangtze, plus land reclaimed in modern times. Because the soil is sandy and soft, tall buildings need deep concrete piles to keep from sinking. As a provincial-level municipality, Shanghai administers the estuary and a number of nearby islands. Zhejiang province is its southern neighbour, and Jiangsu lies to the west and north. The northernmost point is on Chongming Island, which grew during the 20th century into the second-largest island in mainland China.

The city stands on an alluvial plain, so almost all of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land is flat. The average height is just four metres (13 feet). Around the estuary there used to be tidal flat ecosystems, which farmers have since reclaimed. The few hills, including She Shan, are to the southwest. The highest point, 103 metres (338 feet), is the peak on Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay. Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are plentiful, and the city is famous for its water resources since it belongs to the Lake Tai drainage basin.

The Huangpu River divides downtown in two. This artificial tributary of the Yangtze was created on the orders of Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. The old centre grew up on the western side (Puxi), close to where Suzhou Creek, a link to Lake Tai and the Grand Canal, meets the river. On the eastern side (Pudong) stands Lujiazui, the principal financial district. When Pudong International Airport was built, wetland along the east coast was lost; to partly compensate, the nearby shoal called Jiuduansha has been protected and expanded as a nature reserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Downtown averages 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) across the year and the suburbs 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F), and there are four clear seasons. Winters range from mild to cold and are damp, and northwesterly winds from Siberia can push night temperatures below freezing. Snow falls on 4.7 days of a typical year and lies on the ground for 1.6 days. Humid, hot summers bring occasional downpours or thunderstorms. An average of 21 days a year reach or pass 35 °C (95 °F). Typhoons can affect the city in summer and early autumn.

Spring, although changeable and often wet, and autumn, usually sunny and dry, are generally the nicest seasons. Possible sunshine goes from 28 percent in June to 46 percent in August, for 1,754 hours of bright sunshine in a year. China's seasonal standard puts the start of spring at 9 March in Shanghai (averaged over 2001 to 2025), with summer from 15 May, autumn from 5 October and winter from 4 December. The hottest stretch lasts three weeks, from 19 July to 8 August, when the mean temperature is higher than 30 °C (86.0 °F).

The Xujiahui weather station has recorded some striking numbers. The lowest official reading since 1951 came on 31 January 1977, when it fell to -10.1 °C (13.8 °F), though an unofficial -12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was reported on 19 January 1893. At the other end, 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) was reached twice, on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022. On 13 August 2010 the night never cooled below 32.1 °C (89.8 °F), the warmest minimum ever noted there. For 2025, Xujiahui's mean of 19.43 °C (67.0 °F) was 1.93 °C warmer than the 1991 to 2020 norm, made up of an average daily high of 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and an average daily low of 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).
Pack for a damp, cold-ish winter and a very humid summer, and keep spring and autumn for exploring.

shanghai-university-of-international-bus.h: The Bund and the architecture of the concessions

blocks.x: The Bund runs beside the Huangpu River and is lined with buildings from the early 20th century. They range from the neoclassical HSBC Building to the Art Deco Sassoon House, today part of the Peace Hotel. Refurbishment has happened twice. A new promenade by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren came first, in 1986. Ahead of the 2010 Expo came a second round, which saw the hundred-year-old Waibaidu Bridge restored and traffic rearranged.

The influence of Britain, France and the United States, the Western powers that were present here, can be seen across much of the city's development. In the 1920s and 1930s a building boom added a number of Art Deco buildings.
László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak resident of the city from 1918 until 1947, was behind Art Deco works such as the Paramount, the Grand Cinema and the Park Hotel.
Two more leading Art Deco architects, Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, were responsible for the Metropole Hotel, the Broadway Mansions and the Peace Hotel.
C.H. Gonda, an Austrian, designed the Capitol Theatre.

The shikumen (石库门, from the Shanghainese meaning stone storage door) is a common local housing type. These are typically two- or three-storey grey brick houses whose front yard is closed off by a heavy wooden door set in a stone arch. Rows of such houses are linked together along straight alleys known as longtangs (弄堂).

The city also has Soviet neoclassical or Stalinist buildings. Most were built in the years after the People's Republic was founded in 1949 and before the Sino-Soviet split of the late 1960s, when Soviet personnel came to China to help it develop as a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

The skyline contains 206 buildings of at least 150 metres, so only six cities in the world have more skyscrapers. The best known are the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, along with the Shanghai Tower, which opened in 2015 and is China's tallest building and the third tallest anywhere. The 468 m (1,535 ft) Oriental Pearl Tower stands close by, at the north end of Lujiazui. Many districts that were once foreign concessions have been well preserved. Even with rampant redevelopment, the Old City keeps traditional architecture and design, for example the Yu Garden, an elaborate garden in the Jiangnan style.

Finance and innovation make Shanghai important worldwide, while within China it is a leading centre for trade, commerce and transport. The Port of Shanghai handles more containers than any other port. Estimates for 2022 put the nominal output of Greater Shanghai at almost 13 trillion RMB (US$1.9 trillion). That wider area takes in Huzhou, Jiaxing, Nantong, Ningbo, Suzhou, Wuxi and Zhoushan. A 2020 estimate valued the city's economy at US$1 trillion (PPP), the most productive metropolitan area in China and one of the world's ten largest. Six sectors, namely machine manufacturing, automotive manufacturing, real estate, finance, retail and IT, generate about half of the city's GDP.

The 2025 GDP figure is CN¥5.67 trillion (US$814 billion nominal, US$1.66 trillion PPP), 4 percent of China's total, and GDP per head is CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). For 2022, disposable income per resident averaged CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) annually, and people working in urban units earned an average of CN¥212,476 (US$31,589) a year. Shanghai is one of China's wealthiest cities, but the Economist Intelligence Unit found in a 2023 study that it is also the priciest mainland city to live in, and in 2021 the Julius Baer bank's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report called it the most expensive city on earth for a luxurious way of life. Budget carefully, and ask the university about typical student living costs.

Trade in 2023 (imports plus exports) amounted to CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), which was 18.5 percent of everything China traded. Forbes put Shanghai fifth for billionaires in 2022. A study by Oxford Economics expects nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, the highest in the country and enough to put it among the five leading cities worldwide by gross regional product. In August 2024 Shanghai ranked fourth in the world, and second in Greater China after Beijing, for headquarters of Fortune Global 500 companies.
For two decades Shanghai ranked among the fastest-growing cities anywhere. GDP rose by double digits in nearly every year from 1992 until the financial crisis of 2008.

The Global Financial Centres Index ranks Shanghai third in Asia and eighth worldwide. The city is also a major centre of technology, for China and internationally, and has a large community of startups. As for financial technology, it came second only to New York City in a 2021 ranking.

Market capitalisation on the Shanghai Stock Exchange stood at US$4.02 trillion in 2019. That made it the largest exchange in China and the fourth largest globally. Six key commodities (among them copper, rubber and zinc) saw the world's highest trading volumes on the Shanghai Futures Exchange in 2009. By the end of 2017, 1,491 financial institutions were based in the city, and 251 of those had foreign investment.

As one of China's main industrial centres, Shanghai is important for domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Industrial zones form the backbone of the secondary sector: Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, and the Minhang and Hongqiao economic and technological development zones. Baosteel Group, China's largest steelmaker, is based here, as is the country's largest shipbuilding base, Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and one of its oldest shipbuilders, the Jiangnan Shipyard. One of China's three largest car groups, SAIC Motor, is based in the city and has strategic partnerships with General Motors and Volkswagen. It held 84th place in the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

In 2017 domestic visitors rose 7.5 percent to 318 million and overseas visitors rose 2.2 percent to 8.73 million, and Shanghai was the world's highest-earning tourist city. The International Congress and Convention Association counted 82 international meetings in the city in 2018, up 34 percent from 61 the year before. The 2023 inventory included 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated attractions and 34 red tourism sites. Visitor numbers in 2023 rebounded to 3.64 million, 4.8 times the 2022 level, and brought in CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), a rise of 98.5 percent. Among these were 2.41 million foreign tourists, a 5.2-fold increase.

September 2013 saw the launch of the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, a first for the mainland, along with reforms to attract foreign investors. The Banker magazine reported that for 2013 Shanghai received more foreign direct investment in finance than anywhere else in Asia-Pacific. By October 2019 the zone was the mainland's second largest by land area, behind only Hainan, at 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 square miles). It merged four bonded areas that already existed: Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone and the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park. Customs clearance and duty are not required for goods coming into the zone.

In 2023 Shanghai had 24,874,500 residents, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5 percent) held local hukou registration. In 2022, 89.3 percent lived in urban areas and 10.7 percent in rural areas. Counting the whole administrative area, Shanghai is the second-largest of China's four municipalities after Chongqing, but it is usually regarded as China's largest city, because Chongqing's urban population is far smaller. The OECD estimates that the metropolitan area has 34 million people.

Official statistics from the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau count about 157,900 foreign residents, including 28,900 Japanese, 21,900 Americans and 20,800 Koreans. The true number of foreign citizens is probably much higher. Shanghai also draws people from other parts of China, and 40.3 percent (9.8 million) of its residents come from other regions.

People registered in the city can expect to live 83.18 years, longer than in any other mainland city, which also means the city is ageing: 17.4 percent (4.3 million) of registered residents were 65 or older in 2021. In 2017 the government introduced population controls for Shanghai, and the population fell by 10,000 by the end of that year.
A Shanghai Public Transport Card lets you use the public system: metros, buses, ferries and taxis.

The Shanghai Metro combines subway and light metro lines and reaches every core urban district and neighbouring suburban districts. As of 2025, 19 lines are in operation (the maglev and the Jinshan railway are counted separately), serving 508 stations over 808 kilometres (502 miles). No other metro network in the world is longer. A daily ridership record of 13.3 million was set on 8 March 2019. The maglev train, which started running in 2004, was the world's first commercial high-speed maglev, and it is still the fastest, reaching 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

Shanghai's first tram line began operating in 1908. Chinese, French and British companies together ran 14 routes with 328 tramcars by 1925, and everything was nationalised in 1949. From the 1960s the lines were taken up or replaced by trolleybuses and motor buses, and the last line was removed in 1975. The rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram brought trams back in 2010, and a steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began running in Songjiang District in 2018.

Shanghai has the most extensive bus network in the world, including the oldest trolleybus system still in continuous service. By 2019 it had 1,575 lines covering 8,997 kilometres (5,590 miles), run by several companies. In 2024, 30,900 taxis were operating in the city, carrying 134 million passengers that year.

shanghai-university-of-political-science.h: A note on the school and its name

blocks.x: Run by the Shanghai municipal government, the Shanghai University of Political Science and Law is a public college. Despite "University" in its English title, it has not yet been given formal university status, so you may see it described as a college in official documents.

Its history is short and clear. From 1993 to 2004 it functioned as the Law School of Shanghai University. In 2004 it was registered as a legal entity in its own right and became independent of Shanghai University.

shanghai-university-of-political-science.h: Why the city matters to your studies

blocks.x: A law and politics student in Shanghai is studying in China's most international big city, with deep links to finance, trade and government. The notes below follow what a newcomer asks first: who lives here and what does it cost, how do I get about, what is the weather, and what is there to see.

Shanghai's resident population was 24,874,500 in 2023. Of these, 14,801,700 people (59.5%) held local hukou, meaning that they are registered as residents of the city. In 2022, 89.3% lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. Shanghai is the second most populous of China's four direct-controlled municipalities if you count the whole administrative area, after Chongqing. Even so, most people regard it as the country's biggest city, because the part of Chongqing that is truly urban is far smaller. The OECD gives the metropolitan area an estimated 34 million inhabitants.

The city's statistics bureau recorded roughly 157,900 foreign residents. Japanese nationals number 28,900, Americans 21,900 and Koreans 20,800. The real number of foreigners is probably much larger. Shanghai also attracts many people from elsewhere in China: 40.3% of residents, or 9.8 million, were born in other regions.

For people registered in Shanghai, life expectancy is 83.18 years, which is the highest of any mainland city. One consequence is an ageing population: in 2021, 4.3 million registered residents, or 17.4%, were 65 or older. The government brought in population controls in 2017, and by the end of that year the population had dropped by 10,000.

Shanghai is rich, and it is expensive. Its 2025 GDP was CN¥5.67 trillion, which is about US$814 billion at nominal rates and US$1.66 trillion adjusted for purchasing power, around 4% of national output. GDP per head was CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). Take income in 2022: disposable income averaged CN¥79,610 per resident (US$11,836), while salaried staff in urban units averaged CN¥212,476, or US$31,589, over the year. The Economist Intelligence Unit's 2023 study found no mainland Chinese city more expensive for everyday living, and in 2021 a report on global wealth and lifestyle by Julius Baer ranked it first worldwide for the cost of a luxurious life. Student budgets here need careful planning, especially for housing.

Worldwide, Shanghai counts as a hub of finance and innovation. At home it leads in trade, commerce and transport, and its port handles more containers than any other. Greater Shanghai means the city plus Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou, and its gross metropolitan product in 2022 was estimated at almost RMB 13 trillion (US$1.9 trillion). The 2020 estimate for the city's own economy was US$1 trillion on a PPP basis, which made it the most productive metropolitan area in China and one of the ten biggest in the world. About half of the city's GDP is produced by only six sectors. They are retail, finance, IT, property, machinery making and the car industry.

Trade figures are huge. Goods coming in and going out of the city added up to CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion) in 2023, and that equals 18.5% of all Chinese trade. Forbes put Shanghai fifth worldwide for billionaires in 2022. A study by Oxford Economics forecasts nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, the highest in China and putting Shanghai among the five biggest city economies. By August 2024 it was home to the fourth-largest number of Fortune Global 500 companies anywhere, and the second-largest in Greater China after Beijing. For two decades the city has grown at extraordinary speed, with double-digit growth in nearly every year between 1992 and 2008, until the global crisis of 2008.

Shanghai takes eighth place globally, and third in Asia, in the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a major technology hub, both for China and for the world, with a big start-up ecosystem; in 2021 only New York ranked above it as a fintech powerhouse. The Shanghai Stock Exchange was worth US$4.02 trillion at the end of 2019, the largest exchange in China and the fourth largest in the world. Rubber, copper, zinc and three further key commodities recorded the largest trading volumes anywhere in 2009 on the Shanghai Futures Exchange. At the end of 2017 there were 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested. For a student of law or politics, this concentration of institutions means many legal and regulatory employers within one city.

Shanghai is still one of China's main industrial centres, important in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. The secondary sector rests on zones including Hongqiao, Jinqiao, Minhang and Caohejing, each with its own economic or technological focus. The city is home to Baosteel Group, the biggest steelmaker in China, to the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group (the largest shipbuilding base), and to the Jiangnan Shipyard, among the country's oldest. SAIC Motor, based here, is one of China's three largest car companies, partners with Volkswagen and General Motors, and was 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500.

Visitor numbers climbed in 2017: domestic tourists rose by 7.5% to 318 million and overseas visitors by 2.2% to 8.73 million, and no city earned more from tourism that year. The International Congress and Convention Association reports 82 international meetings in Shanghai in 2018, up 34% on the 61 held in 2017. As of 2023 Shanghai offered 1,942 travel agencies, hotels at the top end (57 with five stars, 52 with four), and 144 officially graded attractions, plus another 34 "red" sites tied to revolutionary history. Another figure for 2023: 3.64 million tourists, 4.8 times the number a year earlier, who spent value worth CN¥177.12 billion (about US$24.53 billion), 98.5% more than before. Of those visitors 2.41 million were foreign, a rise of 5.2 times on the year before.

September 2013 saw the opening of a free-trade zone, the earliest of its kind on the mainland, together with reforms meant to bring in overseas investment. As of October 2019 it spread across 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi), and only Hainan's zone had more land among those on the mainland. It brings together four earlier bonded zones: Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area and the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Goods in the zone are free of duty and of customs clearance.
Shanghai's public transport covers metros, buses, ferries and taxis, and you can use a single Shanghai Public Transport Card to pay for them.

Subway and light-metro lines make up the Shanghai Metro, which reaches all the core urban districts and also the suburbs next to them. It is the longest system on earth: in 2025 it runs 508 stations on 19 lines, with 808 kilometres (502 mi) of track in use. The maglev and the Jinshan railway are counted separately. A record 13.3 million rides were made in a single day on 8 March 2019. The maglev opened in 2004 and is the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world and also the fastest, running at up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

Shanghai's first tram ran in 1908. Seventeen years later 328 cars worked 14 routes, run in partnership by Chinese, French and British firms, and the state took them all over in 1949. From the 1960s the lines were either dismantled or replaced with trolleybuses or ordinary buses, and the last line was torn up in 1975. Trams came back in 2010 with a rubber-tyred line in Zhangjiang, and in 2018 a steel-wheeled one opened in Songjiang District.

No city has a bigger bus network. By 2019 it had 1,575 lines covering 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi), several companies operate it, and it includes the world's oldest trolleybus system that has run without a break. During 2024 the city's 30,900 taxis carried 134 million passengers.

Shanghai's climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Downtown the annual mean is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F), and the suburbs are slightly cooler at 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F). Four distinct seasons occur. Winter is mild to cold and damp; north-westerly winds from Siberia can take night temperatures below freezing. Snow falls on 4.7 days a year on average, and lies on the ground on 1.6 days. Summers are hot and humid, with downpours and thunderstorms from time to time, and 21 days a year reach or pass 35 °C (95 °F). Typhoons can hit in summer and early autumn.

Spring is variable and often rainy, but together with autumn, which is typically sunny and dry, it is the best time of year. Sunshine peaks at 46% of the possible total in August and dips to 28% in June, so the year brings 1,754 hours of bright sunshine. Seasons in the standard Chinese calendar for 2001 to 2025 begin on these dates: spring 9 March, summer 15 May, autumn 5 October, winter 4 December. In the hottest three weeks, from 19 July to 8 August, the mean temperature is over 30 °C (86.0 °F).

If you want the extremes: the weather station at Xujiahui has logged data since 1951. Its coldest day was 31 January 1977 at -10.1 °C (13.8 °F), though a colder, unofficial figure of -12.1 °C (10.2 °F) dates from 19 January 1893. The hottest was 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), recorded on both 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022. The warmest night on record, 13 August 2010, still stayed at 32.1 °C (89.8 °F). Looking at 2025, the Xujiahui annual mean of 19.43 °C (67.0 °F) was 1.93 °C higher than the 1991 to 2020 norm. A typical day peaks around 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and falls to about 16.44 °C (61.6 °F) overnight.

Shanghai occupies the Yangtze Estuary on the east coast. The Yangtze runs on the north side, Hangzhou Bay on the south and the East China Sea on the east. The land comes from the river's silt and from modern reclamation. Because the soil is sandy and soft, tall buildings have to be supported on deep concrete piles so that they do not sink. As a municipality ranked equal to a province, Shanghai administers the estuary along with many islands near it. Zhejiang is its neighbour on the south; Jiangsu lies on the other sides, to the west and north. At the far north lies Chongming Island, which expanded through the 20th century and is today the mainland's second biggest island.

Located on an alluvial plain, the city is overwhelmingly flat across 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles), at an average height of four metres (13 feet). The tidal flats near the estuary have been reclaimed for farming. Hills are rare. She Shan is one of the few, in the south-west, and the city's top elevation is on Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, 103 metres (338 feet) high. The area is rich in rivers, canals, streams and lakes, since it belongs to the Lake Tai drainage basin.

The Huangpu River, an artificial tributary of the Yangtze ordered by Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period, cuts downtown in two. On the western bank (Puxi), the old centre of the city took shape near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, a waterway that connects with Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. Lujiazui, the central financial district, was built on the eastern bank (Pudong). When Pudong International Airport was built, local wetlands were lost on the eastern shore. To make up in part, the nearby shoal of Jiuduansha has been protected and enlarged as a nature reserve.

The Bund, along the Huangpu waterfront, is a stretch of early 20th-century architecture in mixed styles. At one end of the range sits the neoclassical HSBC Building; at the other is the Art Deco Sassoon House, which now belongs to the Peace Hotel. It has been renewed more than once. The first was in 1986, when Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren designed a new promenade. The second came before the 2010 Expo, with restoration of the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and a new traffic layout.

Shanghai's development largely reflects the presence of Western powers, notably Britain, France and the United States. The boom of the 1920s and 1930s left a number of Art Deco buildings. The Hungarian-Slovak László Hudec worked and lived in Shanghai between 1918 and 1947, and his Art Deco designs include the Park Hotel and the Grand Cinema as well as the Paramount. Two other leading architects of the style, Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, designed the Peace and Metropole hotels and Broadway Mansions. The Capitol Theatre was the work of the Austrian C.H. Gonda.

Typical housing is the shikumen (石库门, "stone storage door"; also written 石庫門 and in Wugniu as zaq-khu-men). These are houses of two or three storeys in grey brick, with a front yard behind a heavy wooden door in a decorative stone arch. They stand in connected rows along straight alleys called longtangs (弄堂). A further strand is Soviet neoclassical (Stalinist) architecture. It dates mainly from the years after the People's Republic was founded in 1949 and ends with the split with the USSR late in the 1960s; during that time Soviet staff came over to assist China's development as a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is a typical case.

Shanghai is a city of towers. Only six other cities have more buildings of 150 metres or higher, and Shanghai counts 206. Famous ones are Jin Mao and the World Financial Center, and the tallest of all is the Shanghai Tower, which opened in 2015 as China's highest building and the third highest in the world. At 468 m (1,535 ft), the Oriental Pearl Tower rises beside them where Lujiazui ends in the north. Walk through the former foreign concessions and you will find many streets carefully preserved. Redevelopment has been intense, but the Old City still keeps traditional design, with the Yu Garden, a detailed Jiangnan-style garden, as the prime example.

The Shanghai University of Sport (SUS) is a municipal public university in Yangpu, Shanghai, China. It is affiliated with the City of Shanghai. The university is part of the Double First-Class Construction.
The school was founded in 1952.

SUS was established in November 1952 by the merger of departments of Physical Education from East China Normal University, Nanjing University and Ginling College. Wu Yunrui, the first president of SUS, devoted himself to the advanced values and notions of physical education.

SUS was formerly under the direct governance of the General Administration of Sport of China and began to be jointly constructed and managed in 2001 by the General Administration of Sport of China and Shanghai Municipal Government.
Shanghai University of Sport consistently ranks the best in China among universities specialized in sport in the recognized Best Chinese Universities Ranking.
As of 2025, Shanghai University of Sport ranks #1 in Asia and #23 in the world according to "Global Ranking of Sport Science Schools and Departments" released by Shanghai Ranking.

In over 60 years of construction and development, SUS has grown into a multi-disciplined university with six categories of education: management, science, literature, medicine and arts featured with sport science. SUS has established a complete education system covering bachelor, master and doctoral programs and set up a mobile station for post-doctoral research in sport science.

SUS has more than 4000 full-time undergraduate students on campus, 1000 postgraduate students, 1400 overseas students, 1400 adult students, and more than 700 teaching and administration staff, among whom 82 are professors and 170 associate professors.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shanghai, where Shanghai University of Sport is located.

Shanghai is located on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south, and the East China Sea to the east. The land is formed by the Yangtze's natural deposition and modern land reclamation projects. It has sandy soil, and skyscrapers have to be built with deep concrete piles to avoid sinking into the soft ground. The provincial-level Municipality of Shanghai administers the estuary and many of its surrounding islands. It borders the provinces of Zhejiang to the south and Jiangsu to the west and north. The municipality's northernmost point is on Chongming Island, the second-largest island in mainland China after its expansion during the 20th century.

Shanghai is located on an alluvial plain and the vast majority of its 6,340.5-square-kilometre (2,448.1-square-mile) land area is flat, with an average elevation of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flat ecosystems exist around the estuary, but they have been reclaimed for agricultural purposes. The city's few hills, such as She Shan, lie to the southwest; its highest point is the peak of Dajinshan Island (103 metres or 338 feet) in Hangzhou Bay. Shanghai has rivers, canals, streams, and lakes, and it is known for its rich water resources as part of the Lake Tai drainage basin.

Downtown Shanghai is bisected by the Huangpu River, a man-made tributary of the Yangtze created by order of Lord Chunshen during the Warring States period. The historic centre of the city was located on the west bank of the Huangpu (Puxi), near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, connecting it with Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. The central financial district, Lujiazui, was established on the east bank of the Huangpu (Pudong). Along Shanghai's eastern shore, the destruction of local wetlands due to the construction of Pudong International Airport has been partially offset by the protection and expansion of a nearby shoal, Jiuduansha, as a nature preserve.

Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cfa), with an average annual temperature of 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) for downtown areas and 16.2–17.2 °C (61.2–63.0 °F) for suburbs. The city experiences four distinct seasons. Winters are temperate to cold and damp—northwesterly winds from Siberia can cause nighttime temperatures to drop below freezing. Each year, there are an average of 4.7 days with snowfall and 1.6 days with snow cover. Summers are hot and humid, and occasional downpours or thunderstorms can be expected. On average, 21 days meet or exceed 35 °C (95 °F) annually. In summer and the beginning of autumn, the city is susceptible to typhoons.

The most pleasant seasons are generally spring, although changeable and often rainy, and autumn, which is usually sunny and dry. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 28% in June to 46% in August, the city receives 1,754 hours of bright sunshine annually. According to China's seasonal division standard, from 2001 to 2025, Shanghai enters spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October, and winter on 4 December. The average temperature for the three weeks from 19 July to 8 August is above 30 °C (86.0 °F). Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −10.1 °C (13.8 °F) on 31 January 1977 (unofficial record of −12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was set on 19 January 1893) to 40.9 °C (105.6 °F) on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022 at a weather station in Xujiahui. It also has 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) as the highest ever daily minimum temperature at Xujiahui on 13 August 2010.

In 2025, the average temperature of Xujiahui was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), which was 1.93 °C higher than the average from 1991 to 2020. The average daily high temperature is 23.66 °C (74.6 °F), and the average daily low temperature is 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

The Bund, located by the bank of the Huangpu River, is home to a row of early 20th-century architecture, ranging in style from the neoclassical HSBC Building to the Art Deco Sassoon House (now part of the Peace Hotel). The area has been revitalized several times: the first was in 1986, with a new promenade by the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren. The second was before the 2010 Expo, which includes restoration of the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and reconfiguration of traffic flow.

Much of the city’s development attests to the imperial presence of Western powers, namely Britain, France and the United States.Shanghai's construction boom during the 1920s and 1930s caused the city to have several Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in the city between 1918 and 1947, designed Art Deco buildings such as the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema, and the Paramount. Other prominent Art Deco-style architects are Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, who designed the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel, and the Broadway Mansions; and Austrian architect C.H. Gonda, who designed the Capitol Theatre. One common architectural element is the shikumen (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men, "stone storage door") residence, typically two- or three-story gray brick houses with the front yard protected by a heavy wooden door in a stylistic stone arch. Each residence is connected and arranged in straight alleys known as longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). Shanghai also has Soviet neoclassical architecture or Stalinist architecture: most were erected between the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 and the Sino-Soviet Split in the late 1960s when Soviet personnel came to China to aid in the development of a communist state. An example of Soviet neoclassical architecture in Shanghai is the Shanghai Exhibition Center.

Shanghai has 206 buildings 150m+ making it the seventh city in the world with the most skyscrapers. Some of Shanghai's skyscrapers include the Jin Mao Tower, the Shanghai World Financial Center, and the Shanghai Tower, which was completed in 2015 and is currently the tallest building in China and the third tallest in the world. The Oriental Pearl Tower, at 468 m (1,535 ft), is located nearby at the northern tip of Lujiazui. Many areas in the former foreign concessions are well-preserved. Despite rampant redevelopment, the Old City retains traditional architecture and designs, such as the Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan style garden.

The city is a global centre for finance and innovation, and a national centre for commerce, trade, and transportation, with the world's busiest container port—the Port of Shanghai. As of 2022, the Greater Shanghai metropolitan area, which includes Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan, and Huzhou, was estimated to produce a gross metropolitan product (nominal) of nearly 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion). As of 2020, the economy of Shanghai was estimated to be $1 trillion (PPP), ranking the most productive metro area of China and among the top ten largest metropolitan economies in the world. Shanghai's six largest industries—retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing, and automotive manufacturing—comprise about half the city's GDP.

As of 2025, Shanghai had a GDP of CN¥5.67 trillion ($814 billion in nominal; $1.66 trillion in PPP) that makes up 4% of China's GDP, and a GDP per capita of CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 in nominal; US$66,944 in PPP). In 2022, the average annual disposable income of Shanghai's residents was CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) per capita, while the average annual salary of people employed in urban units in Shanghai was CN¥212,476 (US$31,589), making it one of the wealthiest cities in China, but also the most expensive city in mainland China to live in according to a 2023 study by the Economist Intelligence Unit. According to Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report, Shanghai was the most expensive city in the world for living a luxurious lifestyle in 2021.

In 2023, the city's imports and exports reached CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), accounting for 18.5% of the national total. In 2022, Shanghai was ranked fifth-highest in the number of billionaires by Forbes. Shanghai's nominal GDP was projected to reach US$1.3 trillion in 2035 (ranking first in China), making it one of the world's top 5 major cities in terms of GRP according to a study by Oxford Economics. As of August 2024, Shanghai ranked 4th in the world and 2nd in Greater China (after Beijing) by the largest number of the Fortune Global 500 companies.

In the last two decades, Shanghai has been one of the fastest-developing cities in the world; it has recorded double-digit GDP growth in almost every year between 1992 and 2008, before the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai is a global financial center, ranking third in Asia and eighth globally on the Global Financial Centres Index. Shanghai is also a large hub of the Chinese and global technology industry and home to a large startup ecosystem. As of 2021, the city was ranked as the 2nd Fintech powerhouse in the world after New York City.

As of 2019, the Shanghai Stock Exchange had a market capitalization of US$4.02 trillion, making it the largest stock exchange in China and the fourth-largest stock exchange in the world. In 2009, the trading volume of six key commodities—including rubber, copper, and zinc—on the Shanghai Futures Exchange all ranked first globally. By the end of 2017, Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions, of which 251 were foreign-invested.

As one of the main industrial centres of China, Shanghai plays a key role in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Several industrial zones—including Shanghai Hongqiao Economic and Technological Development Zone, Jinqiao Export Economic Processing Zone, Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, and Shanghai Caohejing High-Tech Development Zone—are backbones of Shanghai's secondary sector. Shanghai is home to China's largest steelmaker Baosteel Group, China's largest shipbuilding base Hudong–Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and one of China's oldest shipbuilders, the Jiangnan Shipyard. In auto manufacturing, the Shanghai-based SAIC Motor is one of the three largest automotive corporations in China, and has strategic partnerships with Volkswagen and General Motors. The company ranked 84 on the Fortune Global 500 list in 2023.

In 2017, the number of domestic tourists to the city increased by 7.5% to 318 million, while the number of overseas tourists increased by 2.2% to 8.73 million. In 2017, Shanghai was the highest earning tourist city in the world. According to the International Congress and Convention Association, Shanghai hosted 82 international meetings in 2018, a 34% increase from 61 in 2017. As of 2023, it had 57 five-star hotels, 52 four star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions, and 34 red tourist attractions. In 2023, Shanghai had 3.64 million tourists, a 4.8-fold growth compared to 2022. It generated CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion) in value, a 98.5% increase from the previous year. The number of foreign tourists reached 2.41 million, with a 5.2-fold increase.

In September 2013, the city launched the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone—the first free-trade zone in mainland China. It introduced several reforms to incentivize foreign investment. The Banker reported that Shanghai attracted the highest volumes of financial sector foreign direct investment in the Asia-Pacific region in 2013. As of October 2019, it is the second largest free-trade zone in mainland China in terms of land area (behind Hainan Free Trade Zone) covering an area of 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) and integrating four existing bonded zones—Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, and Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Commodities entering the zone are exempt from duty and customs clearance.

As of 2023, Shanghai had a population of 24,874,500, including 14,801,700 (59.5%) hukou holders (registered locally). As of 2022, 89.3% of Shanghai's population lives in urban areas, and 10.7% live in rural areas. Based on the population of its total administrative area, Shanghai is the second largest of the four municipalities of China, behind Chongqing, but is generally considered the largest Chinese city because the urban population of Chongqing is much smaller. According to the OECD, Shanghai's metropolitan area has an estimated population of 34 million.

According to the Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau, about 157,900 residents in Shanghai are foreigners, including 28,900 Japanese, 21,900 Americans, and 20,800 Koreans. The actual number of foreign citizens in the city is probably much higher. Shanghai is also a domestic immigration city—40.3% (9.8 million) of the city's residents are from other regions of China.

Shanghai has a life expectancy of 83.18 years for the city's registered population, the highest life expectancy of all cities in mainland China. This has also caused the city to experience population aging—in 2021, 17.4% (4.3 million) of the city's registered population was aged 65 or above. In 2017, the Chinese government implemented population controls for Shanghai, resulting in a population decline of 10,000 people by the end of the year.
Shanghai has a public transportation system comprising metros, buses, ferries, and taxis, which can be accessed using a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

Shanghai's rapid transit system, the Shanghai Metro, incorporates subway and light metro lines and extends to each core urban district as well as neighboring suburban districts. As of 2025, there are 19 metro lines (excluding the Shanghai maglev train and Jinshan railway), 508 stations, and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of lines in operation, making it the longest network in the world. On 8 March 2019, it set the city's daily metro ridership record with 13.3 million. Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev train is the first and the fastest commercial high-speed maglev in the world, with a maximum operation speed of 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

The first tram line in Shanghai was opened in 1908. By 1925, there were 328 tramcars and 14 routes operated by Chinese, French, and British companies collaboratively, all of which were nationalized in 1949. Since the 1960s, tram lines were either dismantled or replaced by trolleybus or motorbus lines; the last tram line was demolished in 1975. Shanghai reintroduced trams in 2010 with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram. In 2018, the steel wheeled Songjiang Tram started operating in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the world's most extensive bus network, including the world's oldest continuously operating trolleybus system, with 1,575 lines covering a total length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi) by 2019. The system is operated by multiple companies. As of 2024, 30,900 taxis were in operation in Shanghai, which carried 134 million passengers that year.
Shanghai University of Sport lists 66 programs for international students on this site: 22 bachelor, 19 master's, 11 doctoral, 14 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 59 taught in Chinese, 7 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 22,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 22,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 33,000 to CNY 33,000 (median CNY 33,000), according to the university's published fee table.

66 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (5):
Human Movement Science
Journalism and Communication Studies
Psychology
Sports Education and Training
Sports Management
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shanghai-university-of-sport.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shanghai University of Sport may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai University of Sport by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Among Shanghai's leading medical universities is this one, formally Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine. You may also see it called Shanghai University of Chinese Medicine or Shanghai Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Its history can be traced back to 1916, so it counts among the first four colleges of Chinese medicine founded in China. In the 2026 Shanghai Ranking of Chinese Medicine Universities it came second.
The institution has grown by stages.
1917: a school of Chinese medicine opened in the city, and it later became a junior college.
1956: following the founding of the People's Republic, it was raised to college level.
1975: foreign students sat their first acupuncture class at the college.
1985: a newly founded academy of traditional Chinese medicine in Shanghai was merged into the university.
1993: the school adopted its present Chinese-medicine university name.
2003: a museum of traditional Chinese medicine opened under the university.
2015: it was one of five founding members of an alliance for building world first-class universities of traditional Chinese medicine.
2017: it joined the Double First-Class Construction list, both as a university and for specific disciplines.
2026: it was placed second in the national ranking of Chinese medicine universities compiled in Shanghai.
The date of 1916 is given as the origin of the school, while the school itself was founded in 1917, so check the university's own history page if you need an exact date for official use.

The 1975 acupuncture class is worth noting for international readers. It shows that teaching traditional Chinese medicine to people from abroad has been part of this university's work for around fifty years.
The university awards bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees. The programmes named are listed here by level.
At doctoral level: Traditional Chinese Medicine, Chinese Materia Medica and Integrative Medicine
At master's level: History of Science and Technology, and Medical Technology

At bachelor's level there are twelve programmes. The flagship is a five-year course in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Closely related are Acupuncture and Tuina, Clinical Integrative Medicine and Chinese Materia Medica, and a joint China-UK course covers Pharmaceutical Science. Further health and care subjects are Nursing, Preventive Medicine, Food Safety and Nutrition, Rehabilitation Therapy, and Hearing and Speech Rehabilitation. The remaining two are Bio-engineering, centred on TCM informatics and engineering, and Public Administration, centred on health management.
Entry requirements, teaching language and fees vary by programme, so use the university's international admissions pages for those details.

Clinical training takes place in affiliated hospitals, nine of them at present, which between them treat 19.3 million patients a year. One of the nine is run by the city of Shanghai and specialises in Chinese medicine, and another, Guanghua, practises Chinese and Western medicine together.
Longhua Hospital
Shuguang Hospital
Yueyang Integrative Medicine Hospital
Shanghai Municipal Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Putuo Hospital
Shanghai TCM-Integrated Hospital
Shanghai Seventh People's Hospital
Guanghua Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Hospital
Baoshan Hospital
The university also operates medical centres abroad, in the Czech Republic, Malta, Morocco and the United States among other countries.
The campus is at 1200 Cai Lun Road, in Zhangjiang Hi-Tech Park in Shanghai's Pudong New Area, and occupies 35 hectares.

By 2025 the university had 9,073 students and 1,300 faculty members. Three of the faculty are academicians of the Chinese Academy of Sciences or the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Three subjects rank in the ESI top 1 percent. In the U.S. News and World Report Best Global Universities list it stands at 1449th overall and 45th in pharmacology and toxicology.
Sixty-plus medical institutions in 30 countries and regions work with the university on patient care, teaching and research.

The university's publications are four journals: Chinese Medicine and Culture, the Journal of Acupuncture and Tuina Science, the Shanghai Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine, and its own university journal. Its museum of traditional Chinese medicine sits on the same campus.

shanghai-university-of-traditional-chine.h: Shanghai, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Day-to-day life depends mostly on the city, so the next sections cover Shanghai: land, weather, buildings, economy, population and transport.

Midway along China's east coast, Shanghai occupies the mouth of the Yangtze. Water surrounds it on three sides: the river itself in the north, the open East China Sea eastward, and Hangzhou Bay along the south. River silt and modern reclamation created the land. Because the soil is sandy and soft, tall buildings must rest on deep concrete piles so that they do not sink. The Municipality of Shanghai has provincial rank and governs the estuary along with many islands around it. Zhejiang adjoins it to the south and Jiangsu to the west and north. Chongming Island, its northernmost point, grew in the twentieth century and is now the second-largest island in mainland China.

Alluvial ground underlies Shanghai, so nearly all of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 sq mi) of land is flat, at about four metres (13 feet) above sea level on average. Reclamation for agriculture has covered the tidal flat ecosystems around the estuary. Hills are few. She Shan is one, in the southwest, and the highest point is the top of Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, at 103 metres (338 feet). Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are plentiful, and the area is known for its water resources as part of the Lake Tai drainage basin.

The Huangpu River divides downtown Shanghai. This waterway was cut by hand as a branch of the Yangtze, on the instruction of Lord Chunshen in the Warring States period. The oldest part of Shanghai grew on the west bank (Puxi), near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, which linked the city with the Grand Canal and with Lake Tai. The main financial district, Lujiazui, was developed on the east bank (Pudong). Wetlands on the eastern shore were lost when Pudong International Airport was built, but the loss has been partly offset by protecting and enlarging a nearby shoal, Jiuduansha, as a nature reserve.

Shanghai's climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa). The yearly average is 17.5 degrees Celsius (63.5 F) downtown and 16.2 to 17.2 degrees (61.2 to 63.0 F) in the suburbs, and the four seasons are distinct.

Winter is temperate to cold and damp, and cold winds from Siberia in the northwest can push night temperatures under freezing. Snow falls on an average of 4.7 days a year and lies on the ground on 1.6.
Summer is hot and humid with the occasional downpour or thunderstorm. In an average year 21 days reach at least 35 degrees (95 F). Typhoons can reach the city in summer and early autumn.
Spring tends to be pleasant but changeable and often wet, while autumn is generally sunny and dry, so these are the best seasons overall.

Sunshine is 28 percent of the possible total in June and 46 percent in August, and over a year the city gets 1,754 hours of bright sun. China's seasonal standard puts the start of spring on 9 March, of summer on 15 May, of autumn on 5 October and of winter on 4 December, as averaged for 2001-2025. For three weeks, 19 July to 8 August, the mean temperature is higher than 30 degrees (86.0 F).

At the Xujiahui weather station the coldest reading since 1951 was minus 10.1 degrees (13.8 F), on 31 January 1977, although an unofficial minus 12.1 degrees (10.2 F) is credited to 19 January 1893. Heat peaked at 40.9 degrees (105.6 F) twice, on 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022, and 13 August 2010 saw the highest overnight minimum ever measured there, 32.1 degrees (89.8 F). In 2025 the average at Xujiahui was 19.43 degrees (67.0 F), 1.93 degrees above the 1991-2020 mean. The typical daily high is 23.66 degrees (74.6 F) and the daily low is 16.44 degrees (61.6 F).

Along the Huangpu waterfront the Bund presents a row of early twentieth-century buildings, that mix the neoclassical (the HSBC Building) with Art Deco (Sassoon House, now a wing of the Peace Hotel). The district has been refreshed twice. In 1986 the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren designed a fresh promenade for it, and before the 2010 Expo the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic was reorganised.

Western powers, above all Britain, France and the United States, left a visible mark on much of the city's growth. Many Art Deco buildings came out of the boom years of the 1920s and 1930s. Laszlo Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak who lived in Shanghai from 1918 to 1947, designed several, among them the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema and the Paramount. Two more leading Art Deco architects, Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, were behind Broadway Mansions, the Metropole Hotel and the Peace Hotel, and C.H. Gonda, an Austrian, was the designer of the Capitol Theatre.

Shikumen, meaning "stone storage door", are a typical residential style: grey brick houses of two or three floors whose front yards are shut off by a stout wooden door framed in a stone arch. They are joined in rows along straight lanes called longtang. The city also has Soviet neoclassical (Stalinist) buildings, most dating from 1949, when the People's Republic began, until the Sino-Soviet split of the late 1960s, a time when Soviet personnel were in China to help build a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is one example.

Among world cities Shanghai ranks seventh for skyscrapers, with 206 buildings of 150 metres or more. The Jin Mao Tower, Shanghai World Financial Center and Shanghai Tower are among them. Shanghai Tower, completed in 2015, is currently the tallest building in China and third highest on Earth. Next door, where Lujiazui ends in the north, stands the 468 m (1,535 ft) Oriental Pearl Tower. Many districts of the former foreign concessions are well preserved. Redevelopment has been intense, yet the Old City keeps traditional architecture and design, as in Yu Garden, an elaborate Jiangnan-style garden.

Finance, innovation, commerce, trade and transport all come together in Shanghai, and its container port is the busiest in the world. In 2022 the output of Greater Shanghai, a metropolitan area that also includes Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou, was put at close to 13 trillion RMB (about US$1.9 trillion) at nominal rates. In 2020 the economy was put at US$1 trillion in PPP terms, which made it the most productive metro area in China and one of the world's top ten. Retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing and automotive manufacturing are the six biggest industries and together account for about half of GDP.

The city's GDP for 2025 was CN¥5.67 trillion (US$814 billion nominal, US$1.66 trillion PPP), which is 4 percent of China's total, and GDP per head was CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). Disposable income in 2022 averaged CN¥79,610 per resident (US$11,836), and people employed in urban units earned CN¥212,476 (US$31,589) on average over the year. It is among the richest cities in China, yet a 2023 Economist Intelligence Unit study found it the costliest city to live in on the mainland. Julius Baer's Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report called it the most expensive city in the world for a luxurious lifestyle in 2021. Students should budget with that in mind.

In 2023 the city handled CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion) in imports and exports, 18.5 percent of the national total. Forbes ranked Shanghai fifth for billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projects nominal GDP of US$1.3 trillion by 2035, the highest in China, placing Shanghai among the world's five leading cities by gross regional product. In August 2024 it ranked fourth in the world, and second in Greater China behind Beijing, by number of Fortune Global 500 companies. For two decades the city has been among the fastest-developing in the world, recording double-digit GDP growth almost every year from 1992 until 2008, when the financial crisis struck.

Shanghai is eighth in the world and third in Asia in the Global Financial Centres Index. It is a major base for the Chinese and world technology industries too, with a big startup ecosystem. As of 2021 it ranked as the world's second Fintech powerhouse, after New York City.

In 2019 the Shanghai Stock Exchange's market capitalisation was US$4.02 trillion, the highest in China and fourth in the world. During 2009 the Shanghai Futures Exchange led the world in trading volume for six key commodities, among them rubber, copper and zinc. At the end of 2017 there were 1,491 financial institutions in Shanghai, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Manufacturing is central to Shanghai: it is one of China's main industrial centres and has a big role in domestic manufacturing and heavy industry. Four zones carry the secondary sector. They are Hongqiao (economic and technological development), Minhang (also economic and technological development), Jinqiao (export processing) and Caohejing (high-tech).

Baosteel Group makes more steel than any other Chinese company and has its base in Shanghai. The city also hosts China's largest shipbuilding base, the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, and the Jiangnan Shipyard, which is among the oldest in the country. In the car industry, SAIC Motor, based here, is one of China's three largest automotive corporations. Its strategic partners are Volkswagen and General Motors, and Fortune placed it 84th on the Global 500 for 2023.

In 2017 domestic visitors to Shanghai rose by 7.5 percent to 318 million, and overseas visitors rose by 2.2 percent to 8.73 million. That year Shanghai was the highest-earning tourist city in the world. The International Congress and Convention Association recorded 82 international meetings in the city in 2018, a 34 percent rise from 61 in 2017.

As of 2023 the city had 57 five-star hotels and 52 four-star hotels, along with 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated attractions and 34 red tourism sites. The source also reports 3.64 million tourists for 2023, a 4.8-fold jump over 2022, spending which produced CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), up 98.5 percent from the year before. Foreign visitors reached 2.41 million, 5.2 times as many as before. Those 2023 totals look small beside the 2017 totals above, so treat them with caution and check a current tourism source.

Mainland China's first free-trade zone, the Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, was launched in September 2013 with reforms meant to attract foreign investment. By October 2019 only the Hainan Free Trade Zone was larger on the mainland by land area. Shanghai's covers 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) by combining four bonded areas that already existed. Those were the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area, and two at Waigaoqiao, namely the Free Trade Zone and the Free Trade Logistics Park. Imported goods entering the zone are not charged duty and do not need customs clearance.

In 2023 Shanghai had 24,874,500 inhabitants, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5 percent) held a local hukou, meaning they were registered locally. In 2022, 89.3 percent of residents lived in urban areas and 10.7 percent in rural areas. By total administrative area it is the second largest of China's four municipalities, after Chongqing, but it is usually regarded as China's largest city because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller. The OECD estimates the metropolitan area at 34 million people.

The city's statistics bureau counts about 157,900 foreign residents, among them Japanese (28,900), Americans (21,900) and Koreans (20,800), but the true total is probably much higher. The city also attracts people from within China, with 9.8 million residents, or 40.3 percent, coming from other regions.

Registered residents live 83.18 years on average, the longest of any mainland city. The result is an ageing population: in 2021, 4.3 million registered residents, or 17.4 percent, were 65 or older. The Chinese government brought in population controls for Shanghai in 2017, and by the end of that year the total had dropped by 10,000.
Shanghai's public transport includes metro, buses, ferries and taxis, all of which can be used with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

Subway and light metro lines make up the Shanghai Metro, which serves every core urban district as well as neighbouring suburbs. In 2025 the network had 19 lines in service, not counting the maglev and the Jinshan railway, plus 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 mi) of track. No other metro in the world is longer. Ridership peaked at 13.3 million on 8 March 2019. The maglev opened in 2004; it was the first commercial high-speed maglev anywhere and is still the fastest, running at up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

The city's first tram line opened in 1908. Chinese, French and British companies were jointly running 328 tramcars on 14 routes by 1925, and all of them were nationalised in 1949. From the 1960s the lines were either dismantled or replaced with trolleybus and motorbus services, and the last tram line was taken away in 1975. Trams returned in 2010 as the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began operating in Songjiang District.

The bus network is the most extensive in the world and includes the oldest trolleybus system still in continuous operation. By 2019 it ran 1,575 lines over 8,997 kilometres (5,590 mi), operated by a number of companies. The city had 30,900 taxis in 2024, which together carried 134 million passengers during the year.
In summary, this university offers a focused course of study in traditional Chinese medicine in a large, wealthy, well-connected and expensive city.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shanghai-university-of-traditional-chine.h: How to apply, step by step

Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
