Travel to Shanghai, register at Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Shantou University (汕头大学, Shàntóu Dàxué, often abbreviated STU) is a comprehensive university in Shantou, in eastern Guangdong Province. The State Council approved its creation in 1981, and it belongs to the provincial Project 211 group of key universities. Backing comes from three sources: the national education ministry, the Guangdong provincial government, and a charitable foundation set up by the Hong Kong businessman Li Ka-shing. Shantou is described as the sole public university in China to enjoy long-term funding from that foundation, and the only higher-education institution anywhere in the Chaoshan region.

The foundation has pledged HK$5.4 billion in total, a sum that also covers the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, and by 2012 HK$4.2 billion of it had been handed over. Also in June 2012, the education ministry, the provincial government and the foundation signed a three-way deal to develop STU jointly, with the goal of an internationally respected and nationally leading university. Relations between the foundation and the university's management have changed over the years, and the foundation no longer keeps an office on campus, so if funding arrangements matter to you, read the university's current information.

Since 2001 the university has pursued a far-reaching internationalising reform. Overseas-trained academics were recruited as provost, vice-president and deans, and curriculum design, teaching, resource management and personnel systems were all reworked. The aim was to make the university a testing ground for higher-education reform in China. There are also plans to bring the Medical College onto the main campus and to build a globally advanced curriculum around life science.
Many senior national and provincial figures have visited the campus over the years, which reflects the support the project has enjoyed at central, provincial and municipal levels.
Here are the key steps in order:

1981: founding approved. Students first arrive in 1983, the year formal permission was granted (26 August) and the Shantou Medical Vocational School was merged in and renamed Shantou University Medical College.
1 January 1984: the foundation stone is laid.
20 June 1986: Deng Xiaoping meets Li Ka-shing in Beijing and suggests STU should develop in a freer way and gradually become a national key university.
10 February 1987: the University Council is established. The official inauguration ceremony follows on 8 February 1990.
1991: STU is included among universities admitting students above the first-round undergraduate cut-off score.
1993: authorisation to run master's programmes. 1998: authorisation to offer doctoral programmes.
2001: comprehensive educational reform begins, along with a financial reform called Sunshine Finance, and a Preclinical Medicine Center for postdoctoral research is set up.

2002: Pathology and Pathophysiology are approved as a National Key Discipline; the credit-system reform and English Enhancement Program begin; a system-based integrated medical curriculum is introduced.
2006: the EIP-CDIO engineering reform begins. 2007: the annual-salary system for faculty is reformed.
2008: the Ministry of Education allows STU to admit master's students by recommendation without an exam, and the residential college pilot starts with the founding of Veritas College.
2009: the Guangdong government designates STU a pilot for becoming a self-governing university.

2011: its plan for self-governance and medical education reform becomes the Guangdong Pilot Project of Comprehensive Educational Reform, and an Integrative Thinking core curriculum is designed for the freshmen entering that year. The Business School's BBA gains accreditation (see below).
2012: every undergraduate must take a community-service course, and the tripartite agreement is signed.
2013: the Ministry of Education lists STU as a mainland partner in the exchange programme for faculty and students between Hong Kong and mainland universities.

STU has an honorary chairman of its council, Li Ka-shing, and an honorary president, Xu Dixin. Chairs of the council, presidents and party secretaries have changed over time, so consult the university website for the current office-holders.

Shantou University stands at the foot of Sangpu Mountain, on about 1.26 square kilometres, with total floor space of roughly 455,500 square metres. Several notable buildings and spaces are worth knowing about.

The library, which cost about 200 million RMB and was paid for by the Li Ka Shing Foundation, opened in 2009. It has a reputation as Asia's loveliest campus library. It was designed by Ray Chen, and a Great Hall of Reading lies at its core. The building has an area of 21,000 square metres, 1,500 seats and 27 seminar rooms, plus an exhibition room, lecture hall, conference centre and student lounge. Wi-Fi covers the whole library to allow easy access to online journals. It was a pioneer in China in using UHF RFID technology for book circulation, sorting and stock-checking. Holdings come to more than 1,743,000 volumes or items. Its Chaoshan Literature Collection forms part of CADAL, a national digital-library project backed by three central government bodies, whose full name is the China Academic Digital Associative Library. Near the entrance stands a statue called Looking up, Looking down by the British sculptor Zadok Ben-David.

In June 2006 a bronze series called Living World by the Taiwanese sculptor Ju Ming was installed beside the campus reservoir; the lower part of the cylindrical building that houses it works as a half-open reservoir operations room.

The Great Hall (the auditorium) covers over 5,600 square metres and seats 1,798, with modern lighting, audio-visual equipment and air conditioning. Block A, the new administration building, was opened on 28 June 2012; it occupies 5,545 square metres of ground and has 16,319 square metres of floor space. The Academic Conference Center, designed by William Chang Suk Ping, has over 50 rooms and halls.

Work on the sports arena project began with a ceremony on 29 June 2012. The park was designed to cover 60,868.6 square metres with 52,127.4 square metres of buildings, including a 6,000-seat multi-use arena (nicknamed High Park), a swimming hall, fitness and training areas, a meeting hall, a 200-room hotel and parking for 200 vehicles. The Li Ka Shing Foundation was to fund the full cost, estimated at 350 million RMB, and completion was scheduled for 2015. It was intended to support the university's whole-person education approach. Because these were plans as published at the time, check with the university to see what is open now.

STU is organised into colleges and schools covering most major fields: Liberal Arts, Science, Engineering, Medicine, Law, Business (the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business), the Cheung Kong School of Journalism and Communication, the Cheung Kong School of Art and Design, the School of Continuing Education, the residential Veritas College and the English Language Center. Another summary adds a Graduate School to the count of ten colleges and schools. Below are the details that stand out.

Shantou's engineering college was the first in China to join the CDIO initiative (Conceive, Design, Implement, Operate). It uses an adapted EIP-CDIO model, where EIP means Ethics, Integrity and Professionalism. The decision to adopt CDIO came in 2005 after study of the approach, local needs and Canada's engineering reform experience, and in 2006 STU became the first Chinese CDIO member. In 2010 the Ministry of Education chose it for the first group in its Outstanding Engineer Education Program.

The Law School's teaching philosophy goes by the acronym PLEASE, which stands for Professor, Language, Edited textbook, Activities, Disciplines and Employment. Courses use a bilingual or English-immersion format. The Alternative Dispute Resolution programme in particular has accreditation from a Hong Kong body, the International Administration Centre. The Public Administration curriculum is designed to prepare professionals for international public administration projects.

The Business School is building a teaching model that combines theory, craft and technique. Its curriculum emphasises advanced economic and management theory and practice plus analysis of successful Chinese enterprises. It has a Chinese (especially Chao-Shan) Business Case Bank and practice and innovation bases for students, so that classroom theory, vocational training and hands-on experience support one another. In 2011 its Bachelor of Business Administration programme was accredited under EFMD's EPAS scheme, the first such accreditation of its kind in Asia.

The Medical College uses a system-based integrated teaching model, with English-immersion courses in clinical medicine, medical ethics, research and innovation. Note that medical graduates seeking to practise abroad should check recognition rules directly with the relevant regulator. For example, the United Kingdom's General Medical Council keeps a register of overseas medical qualifications it does not accept, and it has listed this college on that register. Rules vary by country and can change, so confirm the position with the relevant authority before you apply.

The school took its inspiration from the journalism programmes at Columbia University and the University of Missouri. Its curriculum aims to be grounded in basics yet practical, with an international outlook and plenty of hands-on work. Teaching follows the widely used Platform Module system, with small groups and a mix of English-immersion and bilingual courses, and a four-year Journalistic English discipline is in development. Peter Arnett, a journalist who has won a Pulitzer Prize, has been a teacher there since 2007.

Veritas College was founded in July 2008 as a residential college. It was the first full-range undergraduate residential college in mainland China, and it houses students from many different majors under one roof as part of the university's whole-person education approach. The School of Continuing Education and the Cheung Kong School of Art and Design complete the list.

The ELC was founded in 2003 (it is dated May 2002 in other descriptions of the English Enhancement Program, so the exact date varies). It provides English training for all students on the main campus. The core is a two-year sequence of compulsory courses, with electives for specialised skills such as debate, speech and academic writing, and the ELC organises many co-curricular activities. The English Enhancement Program is aimed at university-wide students who want to pass the national CET exam.

STU offers a full range from bachelor's to doctoral study, including a seven-year master's programme in Clinical Medicine. It lists 1 National Key Discipline, 3 postdoctoral programmes, 1 doctoral programme at first-level discipline and 25 at second-level, 10 first-level and 84 second-level master's programmes, and 6 professional master's degrees. Research facilities include 1 National Key Laboratory and 5 Provincial Key Laboratories. There are also 2 national pilot sites for innovative-talent training, 7 National Distinctive Programs, 4 Provincial Branded Programs, and professorships under the Cheung Kong Scholars scheme.

One profile gives the staff at 5,113 and the student body at over 9,450, with nearly 70,000 graduates so far. Those numbers are from earlier years, so look at the university's website for current figures. Students are recruited from all over the country, including Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan.

Research centres include a Ministry of Education-funded Artificial Intelligence Manufacturing Technology Laboratory, the molecular pathology division of the National Key Discipline, a tumour pathology institute, the province's marine biology laboratory and its image-processing key laboratory, a CAD/CAM Center, wind-tunnel and structural engineering labs, an FMS laboratory, and an institute for artificial intelligence and pattern recognition.

In 2011 the university won 70,308,100 RMB in research funding, 45.8 percent more than the year before. Fifty-four projects won a combined 27,547,000 RMB from the country's two main national science and social-science funds, and funding at national level grew by over 60 percent. A December 2012 analysis by China's institute for scientific and technical information found that the journals carrying work by STU staff had an average impact factor that climbed from 1.92 (2007) to 2.59 (2011), a historic high. STU topped the table for citations in a 2012 ranking of Chinese universities' Nature and Science papers, and in the same year it won provincial major-project money for the cultural industry for the first time.

The university makes full use of the foundation's support and its overseas contacts. Thanks to that backing it is one of only a few mainland universities giving full scholarships to exchange students from abroad. Nearly 20 partner universities, in the US, UK, France, Japan, Russia, Australia and Germany among others, take part in undergraduate and graduate exchanges.
Du Gangjian, a former dean of the law school, is one of the university's notable figures.

shantou-university.h: Shantou: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Here is a look at Shantou, where daily life will happen.

Shantou lies in eastern Guangdong, between roughly 23 degrees 02 minutes and 23 degrees 38 minutes north and 116 degrees 14 minutes and 117 degrees 19 minutes east. The Tropic of Cancer runs through the city's north, where a monument marks it, the easternmost one in mainland China, at 23 degrees 26 minutes north, 116 degrees 35 minutes east. The highest point in the city's jurisdiction is Mount Dajian on Nan'ao Island, at 587 metres (1,926 feet). On the mainland, the highest is Mount Lianhua in Chenghai District, at 562 metres (1,844 feet). Three rivers, the Han, the Rong and the Lian, reach the sea at the city. Hong Kong lies 301 kilometres (187 miles) to the south-west.

The climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cwa) and shaped by the monsoon: expect brief, mild winters and a lengthy, sticky, hot summer. Winter opens sunny and dry, then grows steadily wetter and greyer. Spring is mostly overcast. Summer brings the heaviest rain but is much sunnier, with 8.2 days a year of rainfall of 50 mm (1.97 inches) or more, and autumn is sunny and dry.

Over the year, the average temperature moves between 14.7 degrees Celsius (58.5 F) in January and 29.1 degrees (84.4 F) in July, and the yearly mean is 22.58 degrees (72.6 F). Annual rainfall is about 1,618 mm (64 inches), around 60 percent of it from May to August. Sunshine ranges from 28 percent of the possible total in March to 58 percent in July and October, adding up to 1,979 hours a year. Since 1951 the record low is 0.3 degrees (33 F) on 29 December 1991, though an unofficial reading of minus 0.6 degrees (31 F) was noted on 18 January 1893, and the highest recorded temperature is 38.9 degrees (102 F). The takeaway is a warm place with mild winters, where you need only a light jacket in the coolest weeks and rain gear from late spring through summer.

Shantou's economy is mid-sized by Guangdong standards. Manufacturing makes up a large and growing share of jobs, with canned food, garments, printing, plastics and toys among the main products. Toys are the leading export, worth about 400 million US dollars a year. The electronics maker Canaton Calculator Co. is a multinational based in the area. In Chaoyang District, the town of Guiyu is a major electronic-waste recycling centre, which has raised environmental and health concerns among international organisations. In 2017 the city's GDP was about 230 billion yuan (roughly US$35.4 billion). A very large tax-fraud case, put at around 32.3 billion yuan, was uncovered in 2000.

Shantou Free Trade Zone covers 2.34 square kilometres (0.90 square miles) in the south of the city. The State Council approved it and it was founded in January 1993, entering formal use in December that year after customs inspection. Its development covers export processing, warehousing, international trade, finance and the information industry. The goal is a modern international zone open to the outside world, learning from free trade zones elsewhere.

Few places in China are as crowded as Shantou. The former Chaoyang City was the most populous county-level unit in the country, at 2.4 million people. Shantou governs six districts and one county directly, and its six urban districts contain 5,330,764 residents.

Together with neighbouring Jieyang and Chaozhou, Shantou forms the Chaoshan administrative metropolitan area. The area spans 10,404 square kilometres (4,017 square miles), and the 2020 census recorded 13,648,232 permanent residents. The built-up area, spread over 11 districts plus Puning city and Raoping county, housed 12,543,024 people in 2020. That makes it effectively China's fifth-largest built-up area, after the Guangzhou-Shenzhen Pearl River Delta megacity, the Shanghai-Suzhou-Wuxi-Changzhou conurbation, Beijing and the Hangzhou-Shaoxing agglomeration.

Most residents are Teochew people. Teochew belongs to the Southern Min family, which is also spoken across the strait in Taiwan and in nearby southern Fujian. A Hakka minority, popularly called Half-Hakka, lives mostly in Chaoyang and Chaonan districts; they use Teochew in daily life and keep Teochew customs. Mandarin-medium schooling has made most people, especially the young, fluent in Mandarin, and Cantonese television and labour migration to the Pearl River Delta have made Cantonese a common third language among younger people. Teochew is likely to be what you hear in shops and on the street.

Government figures indicate that some 2.16 million overseas Chinese trace their roots to Shantou, with large Teochew populations in Thailand and Cambodia that make up a majority of Thai Chinese and Chinese Cambodians. That explains the unusually large number of direct flights between Bangkok and Shantou. The Teochew presence is also strong in Singapore and Malaysia. Johor Bahru, at the southern tip of Malaysia, is nicknamed Little Swatow, because most of its Chinese residents are Teochew, and they are also the second-largest Chinese group in Singapore.

The Guangdong Education Bureau oversees education across the province. The city is known for four schools below university level: Jinshan Middle School, Number One Middle School, the Experimental School and Yuhuai Senior High School. Besides STU, higher education in the city includes the following institutions:
GTIIT, the Guangdong Technion-Israel Institute of Technology
A Shantou college run by South China University of Technology
Shantou Polytechnic
Shantou Radio and TV University
Sports venues in the city include the following.
Haibin Stadium in Jinping District
Zhengda Stadium in Longhu District
A swimming and diving hall in Haojiang District
A youth football court at Shantou Times Square downtown
Fitness square and tennis courts at Xinghu Park in Longhu District
Shantou Citic Golf Club, 27 holes, in Haojiang District
Shantou Jinfeng Sports Park in Longhu District, with golf, basketball and football facilities

Shantou offers a mid-sized, warm and very distinctive Teochew-speaking city, a campus with strong foundation backing and international ambitions, and a long list of English-language and exchange options. For current fees, entry requirements and programme availability, always rely on the university's own website.

Several terms in this profile are worth unpacking if you are new to Chinese higher education. Project 211 is a national scheme that backed a group of leading universities, and STU's place in the provincial version of it marks it as a key institution within Guangdong. A National Key Discipline is a subject area that the national education authorities have singled out for special support, and Shantou lists Pathology and Pathophysiology, approved in 2002, as its example. Cheung Kong in the names of several schools is the name of the donor's business group.

The statistics for staff and students come from earlier years, as do the sports-park, library and administration-building details, which were written when those projects were new or still planned. The university's own website will give you today's totals, programme lists and facilities. Rankings for citations and journal impact factors are likewise snapshots, and their methods vary.

shantou-university.h: Daily life in a Teochew city

blocks.x: Daily life in Shantou differs from the big Pearl River Delta cities because the local language, food culture and customs are Teochew rather than Cantonese. Most students will find Mandarin works everywhere, especially with younger people, but being aware of the local speech will make the city friendlier. The climate means a long, humid summer: plan for light clothing and rain protection from May to August, when about 60 percent of the year's rain falls, and for pleasant, dry weather in autumn.

Travel connections reflect the city's overseas links. The direct flights to Bangkok, and the strong Teochew communities in Thailand, Cambodia, Singapore and Malaysia, mean that students from those countries may find familiar speech and culture here. Hong Kong is about 301 kilometres away, so it is reachable for a longer weekend trip.

The wider Chaoshan region, which joins Shantou with Jieyang and Chaozhou, has over 13.6 million permanent residents, so in practice you will live in a large metropolitan area even though Shantou itself is a mid-sized economy by Guangdong standards. Industries such as toys, garments, plastics and printing explain the city's commercial character, and the free trade zone points to its trade orientation.

Check which programmes are taught in English, how the exchange scholarships work for your nationality, and whether your intended degree is recognised in the country where you plan to work afterwards, especially for medicine and law. Shantou University Medical College (SUMC; simplified Chinese: 汕头大学医学院; traditional Chinese: 汕頭大學醫學院), shortly "Shantou Medical College" or "Swatow School of Medicine", is the medical school of Shantou University in eastern Guangdong Province of China. With a history traced back to 1924, the college is now a public medical school with over ten affiliated and teaching hospitals, integrating medical teaching, research and treatment.

In 1924, the Chaozhou Obstetrics Training Institute was established. It subsequently underwent several developments and name changes: Shantou Obstetrics School, Shantou Municipal Senior Midwifery Vocational School, Shantou Municipal Senior Midwifery Technical School, Shantou Municipal Health Technical School, Guangdong Provincial Seventh Health School, Shantou Health School, Shantou Junior Medical College, etc.
In 1977, the program Bachelor of Medicine started instruction.
In September 1983, with the approval of the State Council of China, the school became the Medical College of Shantou University.
In 1984, the Journal of Shantou University Medical College (汕头大学医学院学报
) was founded.
In 1989, the First Affiliated Hospital of Shantou University Medical College was founded.
In 2010, program Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (M.B.B.S.) start running.
In 2015, program Master of Medicine started running.
In 2023, the Affiliated Cancer Hospital became the first Grade III Class A oncology hospital in eastern Guangdong.
In 2026, the first public dental hospital in eastern Guangdong was established by Shantou University Medical College.
Shantou University Medical College offers programs for undergraduate, master and doctoral degrees, including
Bachelor of Medicine (5 years).
Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (M.B.B.S., 5 years).
Master of Medicine (8 years).
As of March, 2026, there are 5,578 full-time students enrolled in the medical college, including 3,643 undergraduates, 1,711 master's students, 176 doctoral students, and 48 international students.
The hospitals of Shantou University Medical College includes
5 directly affiliated hospitals (First Affiliated Hospital, Second Affiliated Hospital, Mental Health Center, Affiliated Cancer Hospital, and Shantou International Eye Center),
1 dental hospital,

and 10 clinical colleges (Shenzhen Pediatric Clinical College, Luohu Clinical College, Yuebei Clinical College, Longgang Maternal and Child Health Clinical College, Peking University Shenzhen Clinical College, Meizhou Clinical College, Longgang Clinical College, Longgang Third People's Hospital Clinical College, Bao'an Clinical College, and Xiaolan Clinical College).

among which, the First Affiliated Hospital of Shantou University Medical College is a large comprehensive 3A hospital with 1,816 beds. In 2017, the hospital set up the first international medical department in east Guangdong province. It has the largest resort home in the country.

Shantou University Medical College currently has 526 full-time faculty members, including 6 professors who were selected for the 2025 list of the world's top 2% of scientists. It is among the first batch of pilot schools for the National Excellent Physician Education and Training Program and in the Guangdong Province's High-Level Key Discipline Construction Project.
In academic research, the college published 51 papers listed in Nature Index for the Time frame of 1 April 2025 - 31 March 2026, including 36 in Health sciences.
The college's Clinical Medicine has been among the top 1% of ESI globally for 13 consecutive years since 2012.

The college has international cooperation and exchange with 77 higher education and research institutions in 17 countries and regions, including Canada, the Netherlands, Italy, Australia and Hong Kong.
The college hosts the Journal of Shantou University Medical College (汕头大学医学院学报
), with sections covering basic medicine, clinical medicine, surveys and research, technical methods, case reports, and reviews.

Under the personal advocacy and care of Mr. Li Ka-shing, the college established the first college student palliative care volunteer team in the country and won the gold medal in the "First China Youth Volunteer Service Project Competition".

Medical degrees obtained from Shantou University Medical College are acceptable to the provincial/territorial medical regulatory authorities in Canada, and graduates of this college are eligible to apply for ECFMG Certification in the United States of America.
However, as of August 2026, the United Kingdom's General Medical Council (GMC) lists Shantou University Medical College on its official register of "Overseas medical qualifications we do not accept."

Shantou, 515031, Guangdong Province,

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shantou, where Shantou University Medical College is located.

Shantou is located in eastern Guangdong with latitude spanning 23°02′33″ – 23°38′50″ N and longitude 116°14′40″ – 117°19′35″ E; the Tropic of Cancer passes through the northern part of the city, and along it there is a monument, in fact the easternmost in mainland China, at 23°26′33″N 116°35′20″E. The highest peak in the city's administration is Mount Dajian (大尖山) on Nan'ao Island, at 587 m (1,926 ft); the highest peak on the geographic mainland is Mount Lianhua (莲花山), at 562 m (1,844 ft) in Chenghai District. The city is located at the mouths of the Han, Rong (榕江), and Lian Rivers.
Shantou is 301 km (187 mi) northeast of Hong Kong.

Shantou has a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa), with short, mild to warm winters, and long, hot, humid summers. Winter begins sunny and dry but becomes progressively wetter and cloudier. Spring is generally overcast, while summer brings the heaviest rains of the year though is much sunnier; there are 8.2 days annually with 50 mm (1.97 in) of rainfall. Autumn is sunny and dry. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 14.7 °C (58.5 °F) in January to 29.1 °C (84.4 °F) in July, and the annual mean is 22.58 °C (72.6 °F). The annual rainfall is around 1,618 mm (64 in), about 60% of which occurs from May to August. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 28% in March to 58% in July and October, the city receives 1,979 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from 0.3 °C (33 °F) on 29 December 1991 (unofficial record of −0.6 °C (31 °F) was set on 18 January 1893) to 38.9 °C (102 °F) on 11 July and August 8, 2026.

Shantou's economy is medium by Guangdong standards. Manufacturing accounts for a large and increasing share of employment, with canning, garments, lithography, plastic, and toys being some of the principal products. Toy manufacturing is the city's leading export industry, with 400 million U.S. dollars' worth of exports each year. Canaton Calculator Co. is a multinational electronic devices manufacturing company.
Guiyu, a populous town in Chaoyang District, is the biggest electronic waste site on earth. Health-environmental issues incurred have concerned international organizations such as Greenpeace.

In 2000, the biggest tax fraud in the history of the People's Republic of China was uncovered, estimated worthy of 32.3 billion yuan. In 2017, the analyzed data of Shantou GDP is approximately 230 billion yuan(US$35.4 billion).

With an area of 2.34 km2 (0.90 sq mi), Shantou Free Trade Zone lies at the south part of Shantou city. It was ratified by the State Council of the People's Republic of China and founded in January 1993, and it formally came into use on December of the same year after its supervision installations were checked and accepted by the General Administration of Customs. It has been comprehensively developing export processing, storage, international trade, finance and information industry. Its goal is to establish a modernized international zone that is open to overseas by drawing experience from international free trade zones.
Shantou is one of the most densely populated regions in China. Former Chaoyang City was China's most populous county-level administrative region, with 2.4 million inhabitants.
Shantou has direct jurisdiction over six districts and one county, and the six urban districts of Shantou have a population of 5,330,764.

With it and the surrounding cities of Jieyang and Chaozhou, the administrative metropolitan area known as Chaoshan covers an area of 10,404 km2 (4,017 sq mi), and had a permanent population of 13,648,232 as of the 2020 census. Nevertheless, its built-up area spread on 11 districts, Puning city and Raoping county was home to 12,543,024 inhabitants as of 2020 census.
This is de facto the fifth built-up area of China after Guangzhou-Shenzhen Pearl River Delta megacity, Shanghai-Suzhou-Wuxi-Changzhou conurbation, Beijing and Hangzhou-Shaoxing agglomeration.

Most residents are linguistically Teochew people. Teochew is a variant of Southern Min (Hokkien-Taiwanese) spoken in the neighbouring Southern Fujian and Taiwan. There are also Hakka, popularly known as Half-Hakka (半山客), living mainly in Chaoyang District and Chaonan District, although they speak Teochew on a daily basis and practise Teochew culture. The Mandarin-medium education system, widely promoted throughout China, has made most people, especially younger generations, speak Mandarin fluently. Cantonese language TV and labor migrations to the Pearl River Delta has also made Cantonese widely spoken as a third language by the younger generations.

Governmental statistics show that 2.16 million overseas Chinese have roots in Shantou, with significant populations of Teochew people residing in Thailand and Cambodia, which constitute a majority of Thai Chinese and a majority of Chinese Cambodians. This is demonstrated by the unusually high number of international direct flights between Bangkok and Shantou. In addition, there are at least two Teochew-speaking air hostesses on board each China Southern flight between Shantou and Bangkok. The Teochew presence, furthermore, is evident in Singapore and Malaysia; Johor Bahru, a coastal city situated at the latter's southernmost tip, is known as 'Little Swatow', due to the majority local Chinese populace is dominantly Teochew and as well as the second largest group of the local Chinese population in Singapore.
Education is overseen provincewide by the Guangdong Education Bureau.

Shantou University Medical College is in Guangdong, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Guangdong.

The Neolithic era began in the Pearl River Delta (珠江三角洲) 7,000 years before present (BP), with the early period from around 7000 to 5000 BP (c. 5050–3050 BC), and the late period from about 5000 to 3500 BP (c. 3050–1550 BC). In coastal Guangdong, the Neolithic was likely introduced from the middle Yangtze River area (Jiao 2013). In inland Guangdong, the Neolithic appeared in Guangdong 4,600 years before present (BP). The Neolithic in northern inland Guangdong is represented by the Shixia culture (石峽文化), which occurred from 4600 to 4200 BP (c. 2650–2250 BC).

Originally inhabited by a mixture of tribal groups known to the Chinese as the Baiyue ("Hundred Yue"), the region first became part of China during the Qin dynasty. Under the Qin Dynasty, Chinese administration began and along with it, reliable historical records about the region. After establishing the first unified Chinese empire, the Qin expanded southwards and set up Nanhai Commandery at Panyu, near what is now part of Guangzhou. The region was later controlled by an independent kingdom known as Nanyue between the fall of Qin and the reign of Emperor Wu of Han. The Han dynasty administered Guangdong, Guangxi, and northern Vietnam as Jiaozhi Province; southernmost Jiaozhi Province was used as a gateway for traders from the west—as far away as the Roman Empire. Under the Wu Kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period, Guangdong was made its own province, the Guang Province, in 226 CE.

Canton was a prosperous port city along a tropical frontier region beset by disease and wild animals, but rich in oranges, banyan, bananas, and lychee fruits. They traded slaves, silk and chinaware with Persians, Brahmans and Malays in exchange for their renowned medicines and fragrant tropical woods. Shi'a Muslims who had fled persecution in Khorasan and Buddhists from India lived side by side in the thriving town each erecting their own houses of worship. A foreign quarter sprang up along the river where many traders of diverse backgrounds including Arabs and Singhalese took up residence.

The port's importance declined after it was raided by Arabs and Persians in 758 and the foreign residents were at times troubled by the corrupt local officials, sometimes responding violently. During one incident in 684, for example, a merchant vessel's captain murdered a corrupt governor who had used his position to steal from the merchant.

Together with Guangxi, Guangdong was made part of Lingnan Circuit (political division Circuit), or Mountain-South Circuit, in 627 during the Tang dynasty. The Guangdong part of Lingnan Circuit was renamed Guangnan East Circuit (廣南東路) in 971 during the Song dynasty (960–1279). "Guangnan East" (廣南東) is the source of the name "Guangdong" (廣東; 广东).

As time passed, the demographics of what is now Guangdong gradually shifted to (Han) Chinese dominance as the populations intermingled due commerce and state-organized colonization from the late 3rd century BCE, which resettled large numbers of northern soldiers, civilians, and convicts/exiles.Wen, Bo; Li, Hui; Lu, Daru; et al. (2004). "Genetic evidence supports demic diffusion of Han culture". Nature. 431 (7006): 302–305. doi:10.1038/nature02878..). From the fall of the Han dynasty onwards, it shifted more abruptly through massive migration from the north during periods of political turmoil and nomadic incursions. For example, internal strife in northern China following the rebellion of An Lushan resulted in a 75% increase in the population of Guangzhou prefecture between the 740s–750s and 800s–810s. As more migrants arrived, the local population was gradually assimilated to Han Chinese culture or displaced.

As Mongols from the north engaged in their conquest of China in the 13th century, the Southern Song court fled southwards from its capital in Hangzhou. The defeat of the Southern Song court by Mongol naval forces in The Battle of Yamen 1279 in Guangdong marked the end of the Southern Song dynasty (960–1279).
During the Mongol Yuan dynasty, large parts of current Guangdong belonged to Jiangxi. Its present name, "Guangdong" was given in early Ming dynasty.

Since the 16th century, Guangdong has had extensive trade links with the rest of the world. European merchants coming northwards via the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, particularly the Portuguese and British, traded extensively through Guangzhou. Macau, on the southern coast of Guangdong, was the first European settlement in 1557.

In the late 18th century and early 19th century, coastal Guangdong came to be severely afflicted by pirates, notably those of the Guangdong Pirate Confederation, around the Pearl River delta particularly. These were suppressed through a joint effort between the Portuguese Navy and Qing forces, however.

Later in the 19th century, the opium traded through Guangzhou triggered the First Opium War, opening an era of Western imperialists' incursion and intervention in China. In addition to Macau, which was then a Portuguese colony, Hong Kong was ceded to the British, and Kouang-Tchéou-Wan (modern day area of Zhanjiang) to the French.

Due to the large number of people that emigrated out of the Guangdong, and in particular the ease of immigration from Hong Kong to other parts of the British Empire (later British Commonwealth), many overseas Chinese communities have their origins in Guangdong and/or Cantonese culture. In particular, the Cantonese, Hakka, Teochew dialects have proportionately more speakers among overseas Chinese people than Mandarin-speaking Chinese. Additionally, many Taishanese-speaking Chinese emigrated to Western countries, with the results that many Western versions of Chinese words were derived from the Cantonese dialects rather than through the mainstream Mandarin language, such as "dim sum".   Some Mandarin Chinese words originally of foreign origin also came from the original foreign language by way of Cantonese. For example, the Mandarin word níngméng (simplified Chinese: 柠檬; traditional Chinese: 檸檬), meaning "Lemon", came from Cantonese, in which the characters are pronounced as lìng mung. In the United States, there is a large number of Chinese who are descendants of immigrants from the county-level city of Taishan (Toisan in Cantonese), who speak a distinctive dialect related to Cantonese called Taishanese (or Toishanese).

During the 1850s, the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, whose leader Hong Xiuquan was born in Guangdong and received a pamphlet from a Protestant Christian missionary in Guangdong, was allied with a local Guangdong Red Turban Rebellion (1854–1856). Because of direct contact with the West, Guangdong was the centre of anti-Manchu and anti-imperialist activity. The generally acknowledged founder of modern China, Sun Yat-sen, was also from Guangdong.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shantou-university-medical-college.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shantou University Medical College may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shantou, register at Shantou University Medical College by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Shanxi University, often shortened to SXU (山西大学), is a public university based in Taiyuan, the capital city of Shanxi Province. It is run at provincial level, answering to the Shanxi government, and it has a place in China's Double First-Class Construction scheme. It is also one of the country's older modern universities, and its story is bound up with the first steps of Western-style higher education in China.

SXU descends from the Shansi Imperial University (山西大学堂), a name sometimes spelt in the older romanisation as Shansi University. Preparations were led in 1901 by Cen Chunxuan, who was governor of Shanxi at the time. On May 8, 1902 the institution formally took on a College of Western Studies, led by Timothy Richard, a Baptist missionary from Wales, whose job was to teach Western technologies. For that reason 1902 counts as the official founding year. Government money paid for much of the work, and one of the early funding sources was an amount returned by the British government out of the Boxer Indemnity after the Boxer Protocol; it went toward the College of Western Studies.

Two other pioneers began teaching Western technology at about the same time: the Northern Grand School (later Tianjin University) and the Metropolitan Grand School (later Peking University). These three together launched modern higher education in China.

Following the Xinhai Revolution, the Shansi Imperial University became "Shanxi University" in 1912. In 1918 it was called "National Shanxi University" (国立山西大学), and in 1931 it took the simpler name again. The Second Sino-Japanese War, which began in 1937, forced it out of Taiyuan. Its law school relocated to Pingyao, the liberal arts college to Yuncheng, and the engineering and physics department and the president's office to Linfen. Japanese troops occupied those towns as well, so teaching stopped until 1938, when the university was rebuilt at Sanyuan in Shaanxi (陕西). It then moved once more, to Yichuan. A typhus epidemic there led to a return to Shanxi (山西) in 1943, at Jixian Nancun, the province's temporary wartime capital, which was renamed KeNanPo, "overcoming the suffering". Only in 1946, once the war had been won, did the university finally go back to Taiyuan.

In 1952 the Ministry of Education ordered a reorganisation that combined the liberal arts and science departments into Shanxi Normal College. The law school went to Renmin University of China in Beijing, and the engineering department was dissolved, with its pieces going to three institutions: Taiyuan University of Technology, Northwestern Polytechnical University and the University of Science and Technology Beijing. In 1959 the university was rebuilt on Wucheng Street in Taiyuan. By 1998 it was regarded as a key university of the province, and in May 2005 it became a university co-developed by the central education ministry and the Shanxi provincial authorities.
The one graduate named among notable alumni is Wu Weihua.
Because campus life is shaped by the city outside it, this part describes Taiyuan itself.

Taiyuan sits on the Fen River at the northern end of the river's fertile upper basin, right at the centre of Shanxi. From east to west it spans 144 km (equal to 89 miles), and from north to south 107 km (66 miles). It controls the main north–south route through the province, and also the major natural passages through the Taihang Mountains, which lead toward Hebei on one side and northern Shaanxi on the other.

Mineral resources are plentiful. The local list includes gold, copper, mica, gypsum, phosphorus, quartz, graphite, limestone, bauxite, silica, marble, iron and coal. Output of coal, iron, silica and marble is high. Gujiao, a satellite city to the west, produces more metallurgical coal than anywhere else in China. Among trees, conifers dominate, notably pine, white pine, spruce and cypress.

The climate is described as warm temperate and continental with monsoon influence, and technically it counts as cold semi-arid (Köppen BSk). Winter is long, dry and cold. Summer is hot and humid, while spring and autumn are short and windy. Dry and wet seasons are clearly separate. In spring the air is dry and dust storms come now and then, followed by early summer heat waves, and most rain arrives in July and August. Because of the dryness, daytime and night-time temperatures differ widely for most of the year, apart from summer. The city is moderately high above sea level, which makes it far cooler than cities of similar latitude such as Shijiazhuang.

Monthly 24-hour mean temperatures climb from −4.7 °C in January (23.5 °F) to 24.3 °C in July (75.7 °F), and the year averages 10.9 °C, or 51.6 °F. Possible sunshine reaches 51 percent in July and 61 percent in May, and the annual total is 2,493 hours. Since 1951 temperatures have ranged between −25.5 °C and 39.4 °C (−13.9 °F to 102.9 °F). A cold reading of −29.5 °C (−21.1 °F) on 7 January 1930 is unofficial. For a student, the message is simple: bring proper winter clothing.

The municipality has an area of 6,988 km2, equal to 2,698 square miles. In 2007 it had 146,700 hectares of forest and 422.5 km2 of grassland (163.1 square miles), and by 2015 forest covered 21.69% of the six urban districts.

The city has had serious air pollution, particularly during the 1990s and the first ten years of the 2000s, and at one point it appeared on a list of the world's ten most polluted cities. Conditions have steadily improved as people have become more aware of the problem and as stricter, more detailed rules have been enforced. Taiyuan set up a "coal-free zone" in 2017, covering 1,460 km2, where most individuals and organisations may not buy, sell, store, carry, burn or otherwise use coal. The zone was enlarged a little in 2019 by the city government, to 1,574 km2.

At the time of the 2020 census, the prefecture of Taiyuan had 5,304,061 residents spread across 6,959 km2 (2,687 sq mi). A total of 4,529,141 of them were in the six urban districts, which cover 1,460 km2 (560 sq mi).

Taiyuan's economy has grown steadily, matching China's wider expansion during the 2010s. The city's GDP in 2018 was 388.450 billion yuan, more than twice the 2010 value. Disposable income per person was reported at 31,031 yuan in 2018, which was 7.2% higher than in 2017. Foreign trade in 2015 consisted of imports worth 4,085.130 million USD and exports worth 6,592.250 million USD. Looking further back, 2007 output was 3.9 billion yuan in the primary sector, 105.2 billion in the secondary sector and 132.2 billion in the tertiary sector. One quarter of the coal mined in China comes from Shanxi, and Taiyuan is where the China Taiyuan Coal Transaction Center operates; it started trading in 2012.
Taiyuan is an important transport hub in northern China, with highways to neighbouring provincial capitals, and air routes to most major Chinese cities and a few abroad.

The Taiyuan Metro began operating in 2020. Line 2 has been running since December 2020 and Line 1 followed in February 2025. The city began replacing its fleet of 8,000 taxis with all-electric cars in early 2016, starting with the BYD e6.
The main airport is Taiyuan Wusu International Airport. Domestic flights go to Beijing, Shanghai, Dalian and other large cities, and there are some international flights.
Roads of national importance include the G5, G55, G2001, G307, G108, G208 and the G20, which includes the Shitai Expressway.

Fast trains run on several high-speed lines, among them the Datong–Xi'an, the Taiyuan–Jiaozuo and the Shijiazhuang–Taiyuan. The 600 km (370 mi) journey from Taiyuan to Beijing takes less than three hours on a high-speed train. The main station is Taiyuan South. A conventional line, the Taiyuan–Zhongwei–Yinchuan railway, was opened in 2011 and provides a direct connection westward: to western Shanxi, to northern Shaanxi and to Ningxia and beyond.
The Chinese Basketball Association's Shanxi Loongs play home games at Riverside Sports Arena. A football club called Shanxi Metropolis, now defunct, once used the Shanxi Sports Centre Stadium.

Modern Taiyuan has few old buildings left in the middle of the city. What remains of the old town lies to the west of the central station, to the north of Fudong Street and near Wuyi Road. Places worth visiting include:
Shanxi Museum on West Binhe Road in the downtown area, one of China's biggest museums.
The twin towers of Yongzuo Temple, southeast of the centre. They appear on the city's emblem and are seen as the symbol of Taiyuan.
Yingze Park, Longtan Park and Chongshan Monastery, all in the middle of the city and popular with visitors.
Jinci Temple and Christ's Church, Jinyuan, in Jinyuan District in the south. The district also holds the Flying Bridge Across the Fish Pond, built in the Song dynasty.

The Tianlongshan Grottoes on the West Mountain range in western Taiyuan, carved gradually across centuries from the northern Qi dynasty onward. Thousands of Buddhist statues and artworks were made there, but the site is damaged now, with many sculptures missing, and a lot of the missing pieces are now displayed in museums around the world. In 2013 researchers at the University of Chicago began the Tianlongshan Caves Project, which studies and digitally records the caves and sculptures.
The Longshan Grottoes, a complex of Taoist caves not far from Tianlongshan. Its eight main grottoes were carved between 1234 and 1239, during the Yuan dynasty.
A region has as much influence on student life as the campus itself, so the next parts cover the whole province.

During the Spring and Autumn period (c. 770 – c. 481 BC) the state of Jin occupied the territory of today's Shanxi. It broke into three, Han, Zhao and Wei, in 403 BC, a date that many take as the traditional start of the Warring States period (c. 473 – 221 BC). Qin conquered all three by 221 BC and founded the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC).

Bingzhou was the name given to the area under the Han (206 BC – AD 220). During the Sixteen Kingdoms period (304–439), when northern nomads invaded, Shanxi passed through the hands of Former Qin, Later Zhao, Former Yan and Later Yan. Then came the Xianbei kingdom of Northern Wei (386–534), which kept one of its early capitals in what is now Datong, in northern Shanxi, and ruled nearly all northern China.

The Tang dynasty (618–907) had its origin in Taiyuan. Under the Tang and afterwards, the region was known as Hédōng (河東), meaning "east of the (Yellow) river". Wu Zetian, who became one of the very few female rulers of China, was born in Shanxi in 624.

In the early years of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era (907–960), Shanxi supplied rulers for three of the five dynasties, and it contained the only one of the Ten Kingdoms in the north. Li Cunxu, military governor of Hedong, overthrew Later Liang (907–923) and founded the second dynasty, Later Tang (923–936). Shi Jingtang, another governor of Hedong, overthrew Later Tang to set up Later Jin, the third, and Liu Zhiyuan, a further governor of Hedong, founded Later Han, the fourth, once the Khitans had destroyed Later Jin. When Later Zhou, the fifth, appeared, the Hedong governor of that moment, Liu Chong, rebelled and made Northern Han an independent state, one of the Ten Kingdoms, covering northern and central Shanxi.

In return for military help, Shi Jingtang gave the Khitans a strip of northern China. This area, the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, took in part of northern Shanxi, and since it lay on the south side of the Great Wall it was a problem for Song defences against the Khitans for the next hundred years. Later Zhou, the final dynasty of the five, was founded by a Han Chinese named Guo Wei, a former Assistant Military Commissioner serving the Later Han court, which Shatuo Turks governed. He seized power by a military coup against the Turkic emperor, but the new dynasty did not last, and the Song conquered it in 960.

In the first decades of the Northern Song (960–1127), the sixteen ceded prefectures stayed contested between the Song and the Liao. The Southern Song abandoned all of North China, Shanxi included, in 1127 to the Jurchen Jin (1115–1234), following the Jingkang Incident in the Jin-Song wars. The Mongol Yuan divided China into provinces yet did not create a Shanxi province, because it counted Shanxi as part of the empire's heartland. The name Shanxi, and roughly its modern borders, date from the Ming (1368–1644), matching the land and borders of the Tang-period Hedong Commandery.

During the Qing (1644–1911), the province reached north beyond the Great Wall to include part of Inner Mongolia, among it the area of modern Hohhot, where it overlapped with the jurisdiction of the Eight Banners and the Guihua Tümed banner. Trade and banking flourished there for centuries, and the wealth of "Shanxi merchants" became proverbial. UNESCO-listed Pingyao, a city that is very well preserved, still shows many signs of that Qing-era economic importance. The commercial strength was still clear in the late Qing: after the Boxer Uprising, Empress Dowager Cixi stayed in Shanxi during her flight to the west, and local officials and merchants made large financial contributions.

Shanxi lies on a plateau. Higher ground rises in the east (the Taihang Mountains) and the west (the Lüliang Mountains), and a series of valleys runs through the middle, carrying the Fen River. Mount Wutai (Wutai Shan) in the northeast is the highest peak, given as 3,058 m in one account and 3061.1 m in another for its main summit, Yedoufeng, the tallest in northern China, so the exact height depends on the measurement. Most of the northern boundary with Inner Mongolia follows the Great Wall. Along part of the southern border, the Zhongtiao Mountains keep Shanxi apart from the Yellow River where it runs east to west, and Mount Hua is in the southwest.

From east to west the province is 385 km wide (239 mi), and from end to end 682 km long (424 mi). Its total area is 156,700 km2, or 60,500 square miles, which is 1.6% of China. The Yellow River marks the western border with Shaanxi. Two of its tributaries, the Fen and the Qin, run north to south and drain most of the province, and the Sanggan and Hutuo, which feed the Hai River, drain the north. The biggest natural lake is Xiechi, a salty one close to Yuncheng in the southwest.

Shanxi's shape is a parallelogram that stretches from southwest to northeast. Loess covers a good part of the typical mountain plateau, which is higher in the northeast and lower in the southwest. The inside of the plateau is rolling, valleys cut across it in every direction, and landforms are complex and varied, including mountains, hills, terraces, plains and rivers. Mountains and hills take up 80.1% of the area; plains and river valleys account for the other 19.9%. Most of the province is higher than 1,500 metres.

This inland province at mid-latitudes has a temperate continental monsoon climate. January averages are below freezing, while July averages run at roughly 21–26 °C. Winter is long, dry and cold, summer is warm and humid, and spring is very dry with a risk of dust storms. It is among the sunniest regions in China, and heat waves in early summer are common. Annual mean temperatures fall between 4.2 and 14.2 °C, generally dropping as you move south to north and from basin floors up to high mountains. Rainfall is given as roughly 350 to 700 millimetres a year (14 to 28 inches) in one account and as 358 to 621 mm in another for the whole province, so published figures vary. About 60% of it falls from June to August, and terrain has a strong influence on where it falls. The four seasons are clear, rain and heat arrive together, sunshine is ample, and there are big differences in temperature between north and south, winter and summer, day and night.

shanxi-university-of-chinese-medicine.h: About Shanxi University of Chinese Medicine

blocks.x: Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine is a public medical university based in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, China.
The university has two campuses in Taiyuan and Jinzhong and has four affiliated hospitals which serve as teaching and patient care sites using traditional Chinese medicine.
Shanxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine traces its origins to 1978, when a Traditional Chinese Medicine program was established under Shanxi Medical College (山西医学院中医大学).

In 1986, the program began operating independently, and in 1989, it was officially established as a public university named Shanxi College of Traditional Chinese Medicine (山西中医学院) with the approval of the former State Education Commission. The university was authorized to confer master's degrees in 2000 and began enrolling graduate students in 2001.
In 2017, it was renamed Shanxi University of Chinese Medicine (山西中医药大学) with the approval of the Ministry of Education. In 2024, it was granted the authority to confer doctoral degrees.

Today, it is a key university in Shanxi Province, jointly supported by the provincial government and the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine. It is also one of the first pilot institutions in the Ministry of Education's Excellence in Doctor (TCM) Education and Training Program and serves as a model university for innovation and entrepreneurship education reform in the province.

In 2019, the university and seven other Chinese medical schools were removed from the World Directory of Medical Schools, limiting the scope of practice of its graduates to traditional Chinese medicine.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Taiyuan, where Shanxi University of Chinese Medicine is located.

Taiyuan lies on the Fen River in the north of its fertile upper basin. The city is located at the center of the province, with an east–west span of 144 km (89 mi) and a north–south span of 107 km (66 mi). It commands the north–south route through the province as well as important natural lines of transportation through the Taihang Mountains to Hebei in the east and to northern Shaanxi in the west.

Taiyuan is abundant in natural resources such as coal, iron, marble, silica, bauxite, limestone, graphite, quartz, phosphorus, gypsum, mica, copper, and gold. It boasts high production of coal, iron, silica, and marble. The western satellite city of Gujiao is the largest production site of metallurgical coal in China. The tree population in Taiyuan is dominated by coniferous forest, which includes pine, white pine, spruce, and cypress.

Taiyuan belongs to the warm temperate continental monsoon climate, with long, dry, and cold winters, hot and humid summers, short and windy spring and autumn, and distinct dry and wet seasons. The city experiences a cold semi-arid climate (Köppen climate classification BSk). Springs are dry, with occasional dust storms, followed by early summer heat waves. Most of the year's rainfall is concentrated in July and August. Due to this aridity, there tends to be considerable diurnal variation in temperature, except during the summer. The weather is much cooler than comparable-latitude cities such as Shijiazhuang, due to the city's moderately high altitude. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from −4.7 °C (23.5 °F) in January to 24.3 °C (75.7 °F) in July, while the annual mean is 10.9 °C (51.6 °F). Monthly sunshine ranges from 51 percent in July to 61 percent in May, with 2,493 hours of sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −25.5 °C (−13.9 °F) to 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), though an unofficial record low of −29.5 °C (−21.1 °F) was noted on 7 January 1930.

The municipality of Taiyuan is 6,988 km2 (2,698 sq mi). It had a forest area of 146,700 hectares and total grassland area of 422.5 km2 (163.1 sq mi) in 2007. The forest area coverage rate in the six urban districts increased to 21.69% in 2015.

Taiyuan has suffered from severe air pollution, especially in the 1990s and the first decade of the 21st century, and it was once listed among the ten most air-polluted cities in the world. Air quality has been gradually improving, with increasing public awareness of air quality control and stricter and more detailed rules for pollution being applied. The city has taken action to combat air pollution, creating a "coal-free zone" of 1,460 km2 in 2017. This zone prevents most people and organizations from buying, selling, storing, transporting, burning, or using coal. In 2019, the Taiyuan City Government expanded the size of this zone slightly, to a total of 1,574 km2.
As of the 2020 census, Taiyuan prefecture had a total population of 5,304,061 inhabitants on 6,959 km2 (2,687 sq mi), of whom 4,529,141 lived in the six urban districts on 1,460 km2 (560 sq mi).

Consistent with China's economic expansion throughout the 2010s, Taiyuan's economy has seen steady growth. In 2018, the city's GDP was worth 388.450 billion yuan, more than double what it was in 2010. Disposable income per capita was reported to be 31,031 yuan in 2018, a 7.2% increase from 2017. In 2015, Taiyuan imported 4,085.130 million USD worth of goods and exported the equivalent of 6,592.250 million USD. Taiyuan's primary, secondary, and tertiary industries were worth 3.9 billion yuan, 105.2 billion yuan, and 132.2 billion yuan, respectively, in 2007. Shanxi produces a quarter of China's coal, and Taiyuan is the location of the China Taiyuan Coal Transaction Center, which began trading in 2012.
Taiyuan is a major transportation hub in northern China, with highways linking neighboring provincial capitals, and airlines to most other major Chinese cities and some international ones.
The Taiyuan Metro opened in 2020. Line 1 launched in February 2025, while Line 2 has been operating since December 2020.
In early 2016, the city began the conversion of all its 8,000 taxis to purely electric vehicles, initially using the BYD e6.
The city's primary airport is Taiyuan Wusu International Airport, which accommodates domestic airlines to major cities such as Beijing, Shanghai, and Dalian. International flights are also available.
Taiyuan has a number of major roads, such as the G5, G20 (including Shitai Expressway), G55, G2001, G307, G108, and G208.

Major high-speed railways passing through Taiyuan include the Shijiazhuang–Taiyuan, Datong–Xi'an, and Taiyuan–Jiaozuo. By high-speed rail, the travel time between Taiyuan and Beijing is less than three hours, on a distance of 600 km (370 mi). The city's main train station is Taiyuan South railway station. The conventional-speed Taiyuan–Zhongwei–Yinchuan railway, opened in 2011, provides a direct connection with western Shanxi, northern Shaanxi, Ningxia, and points further west.
The Shanxi Loongs of the Chinese Basketball Association play at Riverside Sports Arena. The defunct football club Shanxi Metropolis played at the Shanxi Sports Centre Stadium.

Taiyuan is a modern city with only a few historic buildings remaining in the centre. The remnants of old Taiyuan can be found west of the central station, north of Fudong Street, and close to Wuyi Road.
One of the main tourist destinations is Shanxi Museum, located on West Binhe Road, in downtown Taiyuan, which is among the largest museums in China.
The twin towers in Yongzuo Temple, which are featured on the city's emblem, are regarded as a symbol of Taiyuan. The temple is southeast of the city centre.
Chongshan Monastery, Longtan Park, and Yingze Park, in the city centre, are popular tourist destinations.

Jinci Temple and Christ's Church, Jinyuan, are both located in the Jinyuan District of southern Taiyuan. The district is also home to the Flying Bridge Across the Fish Pond, built during the Song dynasty.

Along the West Mountain range in western Taiyuan are the Tianlongshan Grottoes, which were gradually built over centuries, beginning in the northern Qi dynasty. They contain thousands of Buddhist statues and artwork. The grottoes exist in a damaged state, with many of the sculptures missing. Many of them are housed in museums around the world. Researchers at the University of Chicago initiated the Tianlongshan Caves Project in 2013, to pursue research and digital imaging of the caves and their sculptures.
Not far from the Tianlongshan Grottoes are the Longshan Grottoes, a Taoist cave complex. The main eight grottoes were carved in 1234–1239, during the Yuan dynasty.
Shanxi University of Chinese Medicine is in Shanxi, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Shanxi.

In the Spring and Autumn period (c. 770 – c. 481 BC), the state of Jin was located in what is now Shanxi. It underwent a three-way split into the states of Han, Zhao, and Wei in 403 BC, a traditional date sometimes taken as the start of the Warring States period (c. 473 – 221 BC). By 221 BC, all of these states had fallen to the state of Qin, which established the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC).
The Han dynasty (206 BC – AD 220) ruled Shanxi as Bingzhou.

During the invasion of northern nomads in the Sixteen Kingdoms period (304–439), several regimes including the Later Zhao, Former Yan, Former Qin, and Later Yan continuously controlled Shanxi. They were followed by Northern Wei (386–534), a Xianbei kingdom, which had one of its earlier capitals at present-day Datong in northern Shanxi, and which went on to rule nearly all of northern China.

The Tang dynasty (618–907) originated in Taiyuan. During the Tang dynasty and after, present day Shanxi was called Hédōng (河東), or "east of the (Yellow) river". Empress Wu Zetian, one of China's only female rulers, was born in Shanxi in 624.

During the first part of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (907–960), Shanxi supplied rulers of three of the Five Dynasties. Among the Ten Kingdoms, it was the only one located in northern China. Shanxi was initially home to the jiedushi (commander) of Hedong, Li Cunxu, who overthrew the first of the Five Dynasties, Later Liang (907–923) to establish the second, Later Tang (923–936). Another jiedushi of Hedong, Shi Jingtang, overthrew Later Tang to establish the third of the Five Dynasties, Later Jin, and yet another jiedushi of Hedong, Liu Zhiyuan, established the fourth of the Five Dynasties (Later Han) after the Khitans destroyed Later Jin, the third. Finally, when the fifth of the Five Dynasties (Later Zhou) emerged, the jiedushi of Hedong at the time, Liu Chong, rebelled and established an independent state called Northern Han, one of the Ten Kingdoms, in what is now northern and central Shanxi.

Shi Jingtang, founder of the Later Jin, the third of the Five Dynasties, ceded a piece of northern China to the Khitans in return for military assistance. This territory, called the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, included a part of northern Shanxi. The ceded territory became a major problem for the Song dynasty's defense against the Khitans for the next 100 years because it lay south of the Great Wall.

The later Zhou, the last dynasty of the Five Dynasties period was founded by Guo Wei, a Han Chinese, who served as the Assistant Military Commissioner at the court of the Later Han which was ruled by Shatuo Turks. He founded his dynasty by launching a military coup against the Turkic Later Han Emperor however, his newly established dynasty was short-lived and was conquered by the Song dynasty in 960.

In the early years of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), the sixteen ceded prefectures continued to be an area of contention between the Song dynasty and the Liao dynasty. Later the Southern Song dynasty abandoned all of North China, including Shanxi, to the Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115–1234) in 1127 after the Jingkang Incident of the Jin-Song wars.The Mongol Yuan dynasty administered China into provinces but did not establish Shanxi as a province, since Shanxi was regarded as part of the core region of the empire. Shanxi only gained its present name and approximate borders during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) which were of the same land area and borders as the previous Hedong Commandery of the Tang dynasty.

During the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), Shanxi extended north beyond the Great Wall to include parts of Inner Mongolia, including what is now the city of Hohhot, and overlapped with the jurisdiction of the Eight Banners and the Guihua Tümed banner in that area. For centuries, Shanxi served as a center for trade and banking. The "Shanxi merchants" were once synonymous with wealth. The well-preserved city and UNESCO World Heritage Site Pingyao shows many signs of its economic importance during the Qing dynasty. This commercial strength remained evident into the late Qing period: following the Boxer Uprising, Empress Dowager Cixi resided in Shanxi during her westward flight, during which substantial financial contributions were presented by local officials and merchants.

Soon after the Chinese Communist Revolution, Mao Zedong assigned Kang Sheng to carry out land reform in Shanxi. Kang encouraged the populace to have numerous farmers from a variety of socioeconomic backgrounds denounced as "landlords", beaten, arrested, and executed. In some areas of the province as many as one in five residents were denounced as landlords, and his program was copied throughout the rest of the new People's Republic of China. Shanxi became the site of Mao's "model brigade" of Dazhai: a utopian communist scheme in Xiyang County that was supposed to be the model for all other peasants in China to emulate. If the people of Dazhai were especially suited for such an experiment, it is possible that decades of Yan's socialist indoctrination may have prepared the people of Shanxi for Communist rule. After the death of Mao, the experiment was discontinued, and most peasants reverted to private farming under the reform and opening up.

Beyond land reform and the Dazhai campaign, the early decades of the People's Republic of China saw Shanxi transformed into one of the country's primary bases for coal production and heavy industry, a role reinforced during successive phases of socialist industrialization and national defense planning.

During the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), political upheaval and institutional disruption significantly affected the province's administrative, educational, and industrial systems, Shanxi was affected by the "Destroy the Four Olds" campaign, though the full extent of damage to the province's cultural heritage remains unquantified. During the preceding Great Leap Forward, timber from some historic buildings had been stripped for use as fuel in backyard furnaces, though the scale is difficult to assess precisely. Notable incidents of destruction during the decade include: the demolition of the Shun Emperor Mausoleum in Yuncheng; the smashing of a pair of stone lions approximately six meters tall before the Yuncheng Guan Yu Temple, with the five cubs carved on the body of the female lion shattered; the destruction of Buddhist and Luohan statues within the Yuqing Chan Courtyard at Sima Guang's tomb in Xiaxian County; and the near-total destruction of over a hundred temples and historic sites within Taiyuan, from which the director of the provincial museum was able to salvage only a small number of clay sculpture fragments. Mount Wutai's Buddhist community was also devastated: before the Cultural Revolution, the mountain housed approximately 304 monks and nuns, of whom 239 were forcibly relocated to their home regions and 36 were sent back under supervised labor; of 124 temples that had existed before the Cultural Revolution, only 63 remained by 1977, with fewer than ten in relatively intact condition. In 1969, two temples on Mount Wutai, the Wulang Temple and Jingang Cave, both originally founded in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt during the Ming and Qing, were razed with explosives to make way for a villa for Lin Biao, with their architecture, statuary, and cultural artifacts destroyed entirely and their monks expelled.

Following the introduction of economic reforms in the late 1970s, Shanxi experienced slower diversification compared with coastal regions, as its economy remained heavily dependent on coal and state-owned enterprises. In the 1990s and 2000s, the rapid expansion of coal extraction brought both economic growth and serious challenges, including industrial accidents, environmental degradation, and governance issues. In the mid-2010s, Shanxi became the focus of a large-scale anti-corruption campaign that reshaped the province's political leadership. Since then, provincial authorities have pursued economic restructuring and diversification, though structural constraints associated with resource dependence continue to pose challenges.

Shanxi encompasses a wide range of ecosystem types, including forests, grasslands, wetlands, desert and semi-desert areas, agricultural landscapes, and urban ecosystems. According to official surveys, Shanxi is home to approximately 2,743 species of terrestrial wild plants and 543 species of terrestrial wild animals. Representative protected animals found in Shanxi include the brown-eared pheasant (Crossoptilon mantchuricum), which is endemic to northern China, as well as the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), golden snub-nosed monkey (Rhinopithecus roxellana), leopard (Panthera pardus), sika deer (Cervus nippon), forest musk deer (Moschus berezovskii), and Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra). These species are distributed across forested mountain regions, river systems, and associated habitats.
Shanxi has eight civil airports, 147,700 km of highways, including 6,446 km of expressways. Total railway track in operation is 6,489 km, including 1,347 km of high-speed rail.
The population is mostly Han Chinese with minorities of Mongol, Manchu, and the Hui.
In 2004, the birth rate was 12.36 births/1,000 population, while the death rate was 6.11 deaths/1,000 population. The sex ratio was 105.5 males/100 females.
