Shenyang Aerospace University, usually shortened to SAU, is a public university in Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning province in Northeast China. Its name tells you the focus: it trains people for China's military and civil aviation industries, and aviation and space engineering give the campus its character.

The university used to be called Shenyang Institute of Aeronautical Engineering (SYIAE). On 18 March 2010 the Ministry of Education approved the new name, so you may still meet the old one in older documents and references.

SAU opened in 1952. In its early decades it answered to the national bodies that ran the aircraft and space industries, first the Ministry of Aeronautical & Astronautical Industry, then the China General Corporation of Aeronautical Industry that succeeded it.

Since 1999 the university has been run by the Liaoning provincial government. It is jointly owned with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, and it is the only university that has this particular arrangement with both the ministry and the province. It is also one of eight universities that were built up by the former national defence ministry together with local governments, and it is the only university in Liaoning that specialises in aeronautical and astronautical engineering.
For a prospective student, this history explains why the university sits so close to the aviation sector: its founding purpose, its owners and its regional role all point in the same direction.

Aeronautics and astronautics are the signature subjects, but SAU is a multi-disciplinary university. Engineering is the centre of gravity, and around it you will find science, liberal arts and management.

The university is organised into 17 schools. It employs more than 900 lecturers, of whom about 400 are professors or associate professors, and it teaches roughly 20,000 full-time students. That is a mid-sized campus with a strong senior teaching body.

A university is more than its buildings, and for most students the day-to-day experience is shaped by the city: the weather, the way you get around, what there is to do in the evenings. The sections below introduce Shenyang before turning to the wider region of Liaoning.

Shenyang lies in the middle of Liaoning province, between latitudes 41°11' and 43°02' N and longitudes 122°25' and 123°48' E. The land changes character across the city's administrative area. The western districts rest on the flat alluvial plain built by the Liao River system, while the east climbs into forested country, the hinterland of the Changbai Mountains.
Heights vary more than you might expect for a plains city. The city's top elevation is 414 m (1,358 ft), the bottom is a mere 7 m (23 ft), and the built-up area sits at an average of 45 m (148 ft).

The main urban area lies on the north bank of the Hun River, which was once the biggest tributary of the Liao itself and which locals often call the city's mother river. Three man-made waterways wrap around the centre and link up into one continuous loop: the South Canal (南运河) along the southern and southeastern edge, the Xinkai River (新开河), formerly the North Canal, on the northern and northeastern side, and the Weigong River (卫工河) closing the loop in the west.

The South Canal is the best known, thanks to the string of linear parks and gardens beside it. Engineers made it by canalising the former bed of the Wanquan River (萬泉河, meaning 'ten thousand springs'), a stream that in earlier times was also named the Little Shen River (小瀋水) or the Wuli River (五里河, 'five-li river') and supplied the old city with water.

Smaller rivers strengthen the system at the edges: the Xi River (细河), the Puhe River (蒲河) and the Mantang River (满堂河). All of them empty into the Hun River at three separate places around the south side of the city. A fourth channel on the east side, the Huishan Nullah (辉山明渠), used to drain into the lower Xinkai River but has disappeared because the land was reclaimed for building.

Green space is one of the city's selling points. The most famous example is the South Canal Linear Parks (南运河带状公园), a ribbon 14.5 km (9.0 mi) long that follows the canal across the south of Dadong, Shenhe and Heping Districts. It combines 6 large parks with 18 riverside gardens, together covering about 1,400,000 m2 (350 acres).

The planting is varied. Flower beds hold roses, apricot, bladder cherry and honeylocust, together with natal lily, scarlet sage and morning glory plus black-eyed-Susan, while the wider greenery takes in ginkgos, weeping willows and pines, with black locusts, peach, pear and crabapple trees among them. This is the largest area of vegetated open space in the city. It contributes strongly to Shenyang's 40-percent greening ratio and helped the city win the title of national forest city in 2005.

Air quality is the less comfortable side of the story, and it is better to know about it in advance. The Shenyang Environmental Protection Bureau attributes 30 percent of the city's air pollution to coal burned in winter by the boiler stations that supply district heating. In the winter of 2013–2014 the city used 16 million metric tons of coal, and half of that went on heating. The remaining sources are construction dust (20 percent), vehicle exhaust (20 percent), industry (10 percent) and dust arriving from outside the city (20 percent, mostly yellow dust from the Gobi Desert). The Bureau describes the trend as slowly improving.

The climate is humid continental with a monsoon influence (classified Köppen Dwa and Trewartha Dcac). The monsoon makes summers hot and humid, whereas the Siberian anticyclone makes winters cold and dry. The four seasons are clearly separate, so pack for real winter and real summer.

The numbers give a sense of the range. January is the coldest month, averaging −11.4 °C (11.5 °F), and July the warmest at 24.9 °C (76.8 °F), so the year as a whole averages 8.6 °C (47.5 °F). On record the thermometer has fallen as low as −33.1 °C (−28 °F) and climbed to 38.4 °C (101 °F). Nearly half of the year's rain falls in July and August.

Sunshine totals 2,421 hours a year, and July is the dullest month, with 42 percent of possible sunshine, against 64 percent in February, so the coldest months are often bright. The frost-free period lasts 183 days, which is a respectable length given how severe the winters are.

Around 9.07 million people live in Shenyang, and 85.12% of them are in urban areas. The city is a varied place, with 38 of China's 56 recognised ethnic groups present. Han Chinese make up 91.26 percent of residents. The other 37 groups, in no particular order, are Lhoba, Nanai, Oroqen, Tatars, Evenks, Russian, Gelao, Maonan, Qiang, Mulao, Tu, Kyrgyz, Jingpo, Nakhi, Shui, Li, Dai, Kazakh, Akha, Yao, Bouyei, She, Taiwanese Aboriginal People, Yi, Tibetan, Uyghur, Bai, Daur, Dong, Tujia, Miao, Zhuang, Mongolian, Xibo, Hui, Korean and Manchu.

Most of these communities came from elsewhere, though a few, notably the Manchus and the Xibe, are native to the area. The city also has many temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship, which reflects the mix.

Shenyang is one of the major industrial centres of China, and it anchors the Shenyang Economic Zone, which has the status of a New Special Reform Zone. The city built its name on heavy industry, above all aerospace, defence, machine tools and heavy equipment, and has lately added software, vehicles and electronics. This matters for an aerospace student, because the local economy contains the kind of employers that the university's courses point towards.

shenyang-aerospace-university.h: From heavy industry to rust belt and back

blocks.x: The first heavy industry appeared in the 1920s, and by the time the Second World War broke out the sector was firmly established. Tiexi district then received a wave of new factories under the first five-year plan (1951–1956). By the 1970s Shenyang ranked among China's top three industrial centres alongside Shanghai and Tianjin, and at one stage it was considered for promotion to a directly administered municipality.

Things changed when the planned economy lost favour after the 1980s. Heavy industry shrank, state-owned factories went bankrupt, hundreds of thousands of workers lost their jobs, and Shenyang became a rust belt city. In recent years the economy has recovered markedly, helped by the central government's 'Revitalize Northeast China' campaign and by fast growth in software and car manufacturing. Multinational companies that open offices or headquarters in the city receive investment subsidies.

Services, particularly banking, are growing. Foreign banks present in the city include Hana Bank of South Korea, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ of Japan, the Bank of East Asia of Hong Kong, United Overseas Bank of Singapore and Britain's HSBC. In 2006 Shenyang hosted 1,063 banks and branches and 144 insurance-related firms, and its target for 2010 was 30 foreign banks plus 60 financial institutions that are not banks.

In its November 2010 Access China White Paper, the Economist Intelligence Unit placed Shenyang in a group of six it calls the CHAMPS, made up of Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang itself, drawn from its ranking of China's top 20 emerging cities. The city's GDP per capita in 2009 was 78,490 yuan, third among the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning.
Business activity is concentrated in three development zones:
Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone
Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone
Shenyang Economic & Technological Development Zone

Several large firms are headquartered locally. Brilliance Auto, a leading Chinese car maker, also keeps most of its plants here. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation builds aircraft for civilian customers and for the PLAAF. Neusoft Group is China's biggest software company, and Shenyang Machine Tool Group is the country's largest machine tool maker. Foreign and joint-venture names such as Tyco International, General Motors and the Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation are all expanding their presence.

Shenyang is the transport hub of Northeast China. It has air and rail links, a subway system that currently has five lines, a dense grid of streets and expressways, and buses across the city. A tram network opened in the south in 2013. The biggest airport terminal in the whole northeast is Terminal 3 at Shenyang Taoxian International Airport.

Rail is the city's strongest card. Eight separate lines tie Shenyang to Beijing, Dalian, Changchun, Harbin and Fushun. The Qinhuangdao–Shenyang high-speed line, the first railway in China built only for passengers, is the main passenger corridor through the Shanhai Pass. A 200 km/h (120 mph) service introduced in early 2007 cut the trip to Beijing nearly threefold, to about 4 hours. The Harbin–Dalian high-speed railway, open since late 2012, reaches 300 km/h (190 mph) and links Shenyang to Harbin, Changchun and Dalian.
There are two main stations, Shenyang North in Shenhe District and Shenyang station in Heping District.

Shenyang North (沈阳北站, Shěnyáng Běi Zhàn) was called the Liaoning General Station (遼寧總站) until 1946 and is affectionately known as the 'Old North Station'. The first building, originally the Fengtian City Station (奉天城站), was completed in 1927 at the terminus of the Jingfeng Railway, roughly 1 km (0.62 mi) to the southwest of where the station now stands. Warlord Zhang Zuolin ordered it so as to rival the Japanese-run Shenyang station. That building is now listed as heritage. The present 'New North Station' main building was begun in 1986 and opened in December 1990. It became one of China's five most important rail hubs and earned the nickname 'Northeast's No. 1 Station' (东北第一站).

In 2011 a large rebuilding scheme began, known as the North Station Transport Hub Reconstruction Project, because high-speed trains had pushed passenger numbers beyond the old floor space. On the Huanggu District side of the tracks it created a North Square and a 3-storey Sub-Station Building. The waiting hall of the original 16-storey main building moved onto a large elevated concourse over the rails, and a pillar-free roof, the largest in mainland China, covers the platforms. The South Square (南广场) was rebuilt as a multi-level complex with an airport-style drop-off on two raised levels, a ground-level bus area, and a three-level underground city holding shops, parking, taxi pick-up and the interchange with Subway Line 2, which could also be turned quickly into an air raid shelter.

Shenyang station (沈阳站) is more than 100 years old. Russians built it in 1899 beside the South Manchurian Railway on its eastern side, and it was called Fengtian Station (奉天站). After the Russo-Japanese War the Japanese enlarged it and renamed it Fengtian Yam (奉天驛), a name that lasted until the end of the Second World War. From 1945 to 1950 it was known as Shenyang South Railway Station (瀋陽南站), or just the 'South Station' as opposed to the North Station. Locals still use that name, even though the real Shenyang South station is now at the suburban junction of Hunnan and Sujiatun.

Today this station handles ordinary-speed passenger trains. A big archway and a new terminal are being added, and until the work ends passengers reach the platforms by detouring below and above ground. In 2010 the western side gained a West Station Building and a West Square, while the old East Station Building has provincial heritage protection.

Freight links reach far beyond China as well. Since 2011 a container train has run every day with car parts from Germany: the journey from Leipzig crosses Siberia, covers 11,000 km (6,800 mi) and takes 23 days to reach Shenyang.
Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, in Hunnan District, serves the city. It counts as one of eight major airline hubs in China and ranks 23rd for traffic nationwide.

Three other airfields exist in Shenyang but none is open to the public. The oldest, in Dadong District, is East Pagoda Airport, which opened in the 1920s and went out of use in the 1980s, although a 2013 proposal suggested moving and reopening it at Xinmin. Test flights for Shenyang Aircraft Corporation use the Beiling Airport in Huanggu District, and military garrisons of the Northern Theater Command alone use the Yuhong Airport in Yuhong District.

Local people speak the Shenyang dialect, a form of Northeastern Mandarin that took shape in the early Qing dynasty. It is close to other northeastern speech and to standard Putonghua, but it counts as part of Dongbeihua and has plenty of vocabulary you will not find in the national standard. Students who have learned textbook Mandarin should expect to tune their ear.

Locals love two northeastern folk dances, Errenzhuan and Yangge. Near Middle Street, the Big Stage Theatre has a famous programme of Errenzhuan and comic sketches by Zhao Benshan and his students. Because so many comedians are based in the city, Shenyang has a national reputation as a stronghold of Chinese comedy.

The city is home to numerous performing arts organisations, including the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China, the Liaoning Song and Dance Ensemble and the Liaoning Ballet. Well-known artists born in the city include Zimei, Na Ying and the pianist Lang Lang.
Shenyang Aerospace University sits in Liaoning, and the history and economy of a province shape student life too. What follows is a short tour of how Liaoning came to be.

shenyang-aerospace-university.h: Early rulers, from Yan to Tang

blocks.x: Between the 4th century BC and the 9th century, Han Chinese governments mostly settled and ruled Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC the area was home to the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples, and around 300 BC the state of Yan conquered it and created two commanderies, Liaodong ('east of the Liao River') and Liaoxi ('west of the Liao River'). The Yan city of Xiangping, the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today.

When the Han dynasty collapsed, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family kept a semi-independent state, also called Yan, centred on Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. It sent many maritime trade and diplomatic missions and left a lasting mark on Northeast Asian culture despite its brevity. After the Western Jin dynasty ended, three Murong-led Xianbei states ruled Liaoning in turn, called Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan. In 436 Northern Wei took the Yan capital and Goguryeo took over the Liaodong Peninsula, and the Tang dynasty later annexed the region in the Goguryeo–Tang War.

The An Lushan Rebellion in the mid 8th century drained Tang resources away from the frontiers, and the Bohai state slowly spread into Liaodong. Liaoning eventually fell to the Khitan Liao dynasty, which split it into four circuits named for capitals: Dongjingdao (Eastern), Shangjingdao (Supreme), Zhongjingdao (Central) and Xiajingdao (Lower).

Jurchen Jin administrators placed most of the land in the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu); smaller shares went to the Xianping Route, Shangjinglu (the Supreme Capital Route) and Beijinglu (the Northern Capital Route). Genghis Khan conquered Liaoning in 1206, and it passed into the Yuan dynasty. The east fell under the Liaoyang Route and Shenyang Route of the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat, the north under Xianping Prefecture of the Kaiyuan Route, and the west, including the Guangning Route, also answered to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat. Jinzhou and Chaoyang belonged to the Daning Route, which reported to the Central Secretariat.

shenyang-aerospace-university.h: Ming rule and the Liaodong Wall

blocks.x: In 1371, just three years after the Mongols were pushed out of Beijing, Liaoning came under Ming control. Around 1442 it built a defensive wall to guard the farming heartland against the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group and Ming tributaries to the northwest. In 1467–1468 builders lengthened it to cover the northeast too, this time against attacks by the Jianzhou Jurchens, the people later known as the Manchus.
The Liaodong Wall served a similar purpose to the Great Wall but was cheaper to build. Some stretches used stone and tile, yet most of it was simply an earth bank with a moat on each side.

The wall did not stop the Jurchens. Early in the 17th century they seized Liaodong, eastern Liaoning, decades ahead of their conquest of the remainder of China. Their dynasty, styled Later Jin before it became the Qing, set up its capital at Xingjing (兴京) in 1616–1621, outside the Liaodong Wall in the east of today's province. The capital moved to Dongjing, east of present-day Liaoyang, and finally in 1625 to Shengjing, which is now Shenyang. When Beijing fell to the Qing in 1644 the main capital moved there, but Shengjing stayed an important regional capital for most of the Qing period.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning much of its population. Many residents died in the fighting, others escaped to the south side of the Great Wall, and a number of cities were wrecked by Ming troops as they withdrew. As late as 1661 Zhang Shangxian, Civil Governor (Fuyin) of Fengtian Province, reported that apart from Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city east of the Liao River was either empty or held only a few hundred people. In his words, 'Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants'. On the far bank, to the west, just Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning still had sizeable populations.

From laws issued in 1651 and 1653 onward, the Qing government recruited settlers from south of the Great Wall, especially from Shandong, to fill the thinly peopled land of Fengtian Province, which corresponds roughly to modern Liaoning. Many Liaoning families today trace their roots to those seventeenth-century newcomers.

Officially, however, the remainder of the Northeast stayed off limits to Han Chinese through most of Manchu rule. To keep people out of today's Jilin, Heilongjiang and neighbouring Inner Mongolia, the authorities raised the Willow Palisade (c. 1638 – c. 1672). It encircled Fengtian's farmland, mostly just beyond the earlier Ming Liaodong Wall or along its line, and cut the cultivated land off from Manchu forest in the northeast and Mongol pasture in the northwest.

Later the government tried to halt the flow of settlers into Fengtian, send some back, or at least legalise those who stayed. An edict of 1704 noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave and told them to register and join a local defence group (保, bao) or return home within ten years. Ten years on, another edict appeared reminding officials that illegal migrants still needed attention. Beijing never got the results it wanted, and in the half-century to 1734 the population of Fengtian doubled, counting from 1683.

Qing Manchuria was divided among three generals. Much of modern Liaoning was in the hands of the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn). Settlement was reopened by the Manchu government from 1860, and soon afterwards Han Chinese were the dominant group in the region.
Liaoning's main crops are maize, sorghum and soybeans, and cotton is grown too. Dalian and its surroundings provide three-quarters of the apples and peaches that China exports.

Local fruit is a point of pride. Dalian and Yingkou are known for apples, and Dalian also for golden peaches. Pears are a speciality of Beizhen in Jinzhou, white pears are grown at Huludao and Suizhong, and Gushan in Dandong is the place for apricots and plums.
Shenyang Aerospace University lists 59 programs for international students on this site: 39 bachelor, 18 master's, 2 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 45 taught in Chinese, 14 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 26,000 to CNY 26,000 (median CNY 26,000), according to the university's published fee table.

59 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shenyang-aerospace-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shenyang Aerospace University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shenyang, register at Shenyang Aerospace University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Shenyang Jianzhu University (Chinese: 沈阳建筑大学; pinyin: Shěnyáng Jiànzhú Dàxué) is a university in Shenyang, Liaoning, China under the provincial government.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Shenyang, where Shenyang Jianzhu University is located.

Shenyang ranges in latitude from 41° 11' to 43° 02' N and in longitude from 122° 25' to 123° 48' E, and is located in the central part of Liaoning province. The western parts of the city's administrative area are located on the alluvial plain of the Liao River system, while the eastern part consists of the hinterlands of the Changbai Mountains, and is covered with forests. The highest point in Shenyang is 414 m (1,358 ft) above sea level and the lowest point only 7 m (23 ft). The average elevation of the urban area is 45 m (148 ft).

The city's main urban area is located to the north of Hun River, formerly the largest tributary of the Liao River proper and often locally referred as the city's "mother river". The central urban area is surrounded by three artificial rivers — respectively the South Canal (南运河) from the south and southeast, the Xinkai River (新开河, formerly the North Canal) from the north and northeast, and the Weigong River (卫工河, formerly the Weigong Nullah) from the west, all interconnected by channels as a continuous waterway. The South Canal in particular, famous for the series of linear parks and gardens along it, was canalized from the old course of the Wanquan River (萬泉河; 'ten thousand springs river'), historically also called the Little Shen River (小瀋水) or Wuli River (五里河; 'five-li river'), which was a principal water source for the old city. These are reinforced on the peripheries by smaller rivers such as Xi River (细河), Puhe River (蒲河) and Mantang River (满堂河), and drains into the Hun River at three different locations on the southeast, due south and southwest side of the city. There was also previously another canal on the east side called Huishan Nullah (辉山明渠) that drains into Xinkai River's lower section, but is now no longer existent due to land reclamation from urban constructions.

Shenyang has many parks, among the most famous are the 14.5 km (9.0 mi) South Canal Linear Parks (南运河带状公园) situated along the homonymous river traversing the southern parts of Dadong, Shenhe and Heping Districts. It comprises 6 large parks and 18 riverside gardens covering an area of approximately 1,400,000 m2 (350 acres), with exotic variety of vegetations such as rose, apricot, bladder cherry, honeylocust, natal lily, scarlet sage, morning glory and black-eyed-Susan, and extensive greenspaces of peach, pear, crabapples, ginkgos, weeping willows, pines and black locusts. It is the largest stretch of vegetated urban open space in Shenyang, contributing significantly to the city's 40-percent "greening ratio", and was instrumental in the city being awarded the "national forest city" title in 2005.

According to the Shenyang Environmental Protection Bureau, winter usage of coal by boiler stations for hydronic district heating is the source of 30 percent of the air pollution in Shenyang. Half of the 16 million metric tons of coal consumed by the city during the winter of 2013–2014 were used for heating. Other major factors include dust from construction sites (20 percent), vehicle exhaust (20 percent), industrial emissions (10 percent) and extraterritorial dust (20 percent, mostly yellow dust from Gobi Desert). However, air quality was described by the Bureau as "slowly improving".

Shenyang has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac) characterised by hot, humid summers due to the monsoon, and dry, cold winters due to the Siberian anticyclone. The four seasons here are distinctive. Nearly half of the annual rainfall occurs in July and August. Monthly mean temperatures range from −11.4 °C (11.5 °F) in January to 24.9 °C (76.8 °F) in July, for an annual average of 8.6 °C (47.5 °F). The frost-free period is 183 days, which is long considering the severity of the winters. The city receives 2,421 hours of bright sunshine annually; monthly percent of possible ranges from 42 percent in July to 64 percent in February. Extreme temperatures range from −33.1 °C (−28 °F) to 38.4 °C (101 °F).
See or edit raw graph data.

Shenyang has a population of 9.07 million, 85.12% of which reside in urban areas. Ethnically and culturally diverse, Shenyang has 38 of China's 56 recognized ethnic groups, including the Han Chinese majority that make up 91.26 percent of Shenyang's population. The 37 minority groups are Manchu, Korean, Hui, Xibo, Mongolian, Zhuang, Miao, Tujia, Dong, Daur, Bai, Uyghur, Tibetan, Yi, Taiwanese Aboriginal People, She, Bouyei, Yao, Akha, Kazakh, Dai, Li, Shui, Nakhi, Jingpo, Kyrgyz, Tu, Mulao, Qiang, Maonan, Gelao, Russian, Evenks, Tatars, Oroqen, Nanai and Lhoba. Most of these groups are not native to the Shenyang area; a few, such as the Manchus and the Xibe, are.
Shenyang has numerous temples, mosques, churches and other religious places of worship.

Shenyang is an important industrial center in China and is the core city of the Shenyang Economic Zone, a New Special Reform Zone. It has been focused on heavy industry, particularly aerospace, machine tools, heavy equipment and defence, and recently on software, automotive and electronics. The heavy industry started in the 1920s and was well developed before the second world war. During the first five-year plan (1951–1956) many factories were built in Tiexi district. At its peak in the 1970s, Shenyang was one of the top three industrial centers in China alongside Shanghai and Tianjin, and was at one time being considered for upgrading to a direct-controlled municipality. However, as the planned economy fell out of favor after the 1980s, the heavy industry had declined gradually and the city became a rust belt city, with hundreds of thousands of people laid off from bankrupted state-owned factories. Nonetheless, the economy of the city has revived significantly in recent years, thanks to the central government's "Revitalize Northeast China" campaign and the rapid development of software and auto manufacture industries. Investment subsidies are granted to multinational corporations (MNCs) that set up offices or headquarters in Shenyang.

The services sector—especially banking—has been developing in Shenyang. Shenyang has several foreign banks, such as South Korea's Hana Bank, Japan's Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ, Hong Kong's Bank of East Asia, Singapore's United Overseas Bank and the Britain-based HSBC. In 2006, the city hosted a total of 1,063 banks and bank branches and 144 insurance-related companies. By 2010, it aims to attract 30 foreign banks and 60 non-bank financial institutions.

The city has been identified by the Economist Intelligence Unit in the November 2010 Access China White Paper as a member of the CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), an economic profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China.
Shenyang has three development zones:
Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone
Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone
Shenyang Economic & Technological Development Zone

Numerous major industrial companies have their headquarters in Shenyang. Brilliance Auto is a major Chinese automobile manufacturer, and most of its production plants are also located in Shenyang. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation produces airplanes for civilian use as well as for the PLAAF. Neusoft Group is the biggest software company in China. Shenyang Machine Tool Group is the largest machine tool manufacturer in China. Tyco International, General Motors and Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation are expanding their operations in Shenyang.
The GDP per capita of the city of Shenyang is 78,490 yuan in 2009 (ranked 3rd out of all 58 cities and counties in Liaoning province).

As the transport hub of Northeast China, Shenyang is served by air, rail, a currently Five-line subway system and an extensive network of streets and expressways, with bus services throughout the city. Terminal 3 at Shenyang Taoxian International Airport is the largest terminal in northeast China. A new tram network system was built in the city's south in 2013.

Shenyang is the railway hub of Northeast China. Eight railways connect Shenyang with Beijing, Dalian, Changchun, Harbin and Fushun. The city is also served by the Qinhuangdao–Shenyang high-speed railway, the main passenger transport corridor in and out across the Shanhai Pass, and the first passenger-specific railway line in China. In early 2007, a 200 km/h (120 mph) high-speed train decreased travel time between Beijing and Shenyang by almost three-fold to around 4 hours. The Harbin–Dalian high-speed railway opened in late 2012 and connects Shenyang with other major cities in Northeast China such as Harbin, Changchun and Dalian at speeds of up to 300 km/h (190 mph).
Shenyang has two major railway stations: the Shenyang North railway station in Shenhe District, and the Shenyang railway station in Heping District.

The Shenyang North Railway Station (Chinese: 沈阳北站; pinyin: Shěnyáng Běi Zhàn) was formerly the Liaoning General Station (遼寧總站; Liáoníng Zǒngzhàn) before 1946, and colloquially known as the "Old North Station". The original station building (now an MHCSPNL-listed heritage building), initially named the Fengtian City Station (奉天城站; Fèngtīan Chéng Zhàn) at the time of completion, was built in 1927 at the terminal point of Jingfeng Railway, about 1 km (0.62 mi) southwest of the current station site, on the orders of warlord Zhang Zuolin to compete with the then Japanese-administered Shenyang Railway Station. The Main Station Building (主站房) of the current "New North Station" began construction in 1986 and was commissioned for operation in December 1990, and became one of the five most important railway hubs in China, earning itself the nickname "Northeast's No. 1 Station" (东北第一站). In 2011, a huge expansion project known as the "North Station Transport Hub Reconstruction Project" (北站交通枢纽改造工程) was initiated in response to the growing demand of floor area posed by the increasing passenger traffic after introduction of the high-speed rail service. The station now has an additional 3-storey "Sub-Station Building" (子站房) and a "North Square" (北广场) on the northern (Huanggu District) side of the railways, while the old waiting lounge in the original 16-storey Main Station Building is now relocated to a large elevated concourse that bridges over the rail tracks, with a pillar-less roof (the largest in mainland China) doming the platforms. The original South Square (南广场) outside the Main Station Building was rebuilt into a multi-levelled complex, with two above ground forming an elevated airport-style drop-off zone and a large ground-level area for bus stops, as well as a three-level underground city providing shopping malls, parking lots, taxi pick-up and interchange with Subway Line 2, while also capable of rapid conversion into an air raid shelter if needed.

The Shenyang Railway Station (Chinese: 沈阳站; pinyin: Shěnyáng Zhàn) has a history of more than 100 years. It was built by the Russians in 1899 on the eastern side of the South Manchurian Railway and was named the Fengtian Station (Chinese: 奉天站; pinyin: Fèngtiān Zhàn) at the time. It was later expanded by the Japanese after the Russo-Japanese War and renamed to Fengtian Yam (Chinese: 奉天驛; pinyin: Fèngtiān Yì) until the end of the World War II. Before adopting its current name, the station was known as the Shenyang South Railway Station (Chinese: 瀋陽南站; pinyin: Shěnyáng Nán Zhàn) or simply the "South Station" (in contrast to the forementioned "North Station") between 1945 and 1950, a name the locals still use colloquially to present days (though the current Shenyang South railway station is actually at the suburban junction between Hunnan and Sujiatun). Today, the station focuses on regular-speed passenger service and is being refurbished with a large archway and new terminal, reducing access to the boarding platforms by rerouting customers under and over ground while construction is completed. The station was expanded in 2010 with the addition of a new West Station Building (西站房) and a West Square (西广场) on the western side of the railways. The old East Station Building (东站房) is currently on the provincial protected heritage list.
Since 2011, a daily direct container rail service has carried automotive parts 11,000 km (6,800 mi) from Leipzig, Germany to Shenyang through Siberia with a 23-day transit time.
The city is served by the Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, located in Hunnan District. It is one of the eight major airline hubs and the 23rd busiest airport in China.

There are three other airports in Shenyang, none of them open to public. The East Pagoda Airport (东塔机场) in Dadong District is the oldest airport in Shenyang, opened in 1920s and retired in the 1980s, though there has been proposals in 2013 to relocate and reopen it in Xinmin. The Beiling Airport (北陵机场) in Huanggu District is used by Shenyang Aircraft Corporation for test flights. The Yuhong Airport (于洪机场) in Yuhong District is commissioned for military use only by the local Northern Theater Command garrisons.

People native to Shenyang speak the Shenyang dialect, a variant of Northeastern Mandarin. The dialect was formed in the early period of the Qing dynasty. It is similar to the other Northeastern dialects and also to the national standard of Mandarin, Putonghua, but is known as a form of Dongbeihua and has a wide range of vocabulary that is not part of the country's official language.

Two northeast folk dances, Errenzhuan and Yangge, are very popular in Shenyang. The Big Stage Theatre (大舞台剧场) near Middle Street is famous for its Errenzhuan and Chinese comedy skit performances by Zhao Benshan and his students. Due to the popularity enjoyed by many Shenyang-based comedians, the city is nationally recognized as a stronghold of Chinese comedy.

Shenyang is home of many performance art organizations, such as Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China, Liaoning Song and Dance Ensemble, and Liaoning Ballet. Many artists are from Shenyang, such as Zimei, Na Ying and the pianist Lang Lang.
Shenyang Jianzhu University is in Liaoning, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Liaoning.

From 4th century BC to 9th century, Liaoning was predominantly settled and administered by Han Chinese regime. Prior to 3rd century BC, Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples inhabited Liaoning and later, the state of Yan conquered the area around 300 BC. Two commanderies, Liaodong ("east of the Liao River") and Liaoxi ("west of the Liao River"), were established within the Liaoning region. The Yan city of Xiangping, the center of Liaodong, was located on the site of the present Liaoyang city. As the Han dynasty fell, warlord Gongsun Du and his family established and maintained a semi-independent state based in Liaodong, until it was defeated by Cao Wei in 238. The state, also known as Yan, conducted numerous maritime diplomatic and trade expeditions, and had a lasting influence on Northeast Asian culture despite being short-lived. After the end of Western Jin dynasty, Liaoning was ruled by Xianbei states of the Murong tribe – Former Yan, Later Yan, and Northern Yan. In 436, as Northern Wei seized the Yan capital, Liaodong Peninsula was taken over by Goguryeo. The Tang dynasty annexed the region during the Goguryeo–Tang War.

In the mid 8th century the An Lushan Rebellion broke out, which greatly drained Tang's resources away from its frontiers, and the Bohai gradually expanded into Liaodong. Eventually, Liaoning was conquered by the Khitan Liao dynasty; during the Liao dynasty, the region was divided among the Eastern Capital Circuit (Dongjingdao), the Supreme Capital Circuit (Shangjingdao), the Central Capital Circuit (Zhongjingdao), and the Lower Capital Circuit (Xiajingdao).

Under the Jurchen Jin dynasty, most of the area was administered by the Eastern Capital Route (Dongjinglu), while the rest was divided among the Xianping Route, the Supreme Capital Route (Shangjinglu), and the Northern Capital Route (Beijinglu). In 1206, Liaoning was conquered by Genghis Khan, and later was incorporated into the Yuan dynasty, during the eastern part of the region belonged to the Liaoyang Route and Shenyang Route under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; the northern area was under the Kaiyuan Route’s Xianping Prefecture; the western area, including Guangning Route, was also subordinate to the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat; while the Jinzhou and Chaoyang regions were part of the Daning Route under the Central Secretariat.

The Ming Empire took control of Liaoning in 1371, just three years after the expulsion of the Mongols from Beijing. Around 1442, a defense wall was constructed to defend the agricultural heartland of the province from a potential threat from the Jurchen-Mongol Oriyanghan (who were Ming's tributaries) from the northwest. Between 1467 and 1468, the wall was expanded to protect the region from the northeast as well, against attacks from Jianzhou Jurchens (who were later to become known as the Manchu people). Although similar in purpose to the Great Wall of China, this "Liaodong Wall" was of a lower-cost design. While stones and tiles were used in some parts, most of the wall was in fact simply an earth dike with moats on both sides.

Despite the Liaodong Wall, the Jurchens conquered Liaodong, or eastern Liaoning, in the early 17th century, decades before the rest of China fell to them. The Jurchen dynasty, styled "Later Jin" before being renamed to Qing, established its capital in 1616–1621 in Xingjing (兴京), which was located outside of the Liaodong Wall in the eastern part of the modern Liaoning Province. It was moved to Dongjing (east of today's Liaoyang, Liaoning), and finally in 1625 to Shengjing (now, Shenyang, Liaoning). Although the main Qing capital was moved from Shengjing to Beijing after it fell to the Qing in 1644, Shengjing retained its importance as a regional capital throughout most of the Qing era.

The Qing conquest of Liaoning resulted in a significant population loss in the area, as many local Chinese residents were either killed during fighting, or fled south of the Great Wall, many cities being destroyed by the retreating Ming forces themselves. As late as 1661, the Civil Governor (Fuyin) of Fengtian Province, Zhang Shangxian reported that, outside of Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang, and Haicheng, all other cities east of the Liao River were either abandoned, or hardly had a few hundred residents left. In the Governor's words, "Tieling and Fushun only have a few vagrants". West of the Liao, only Ningyuan, Jinzhou, and Guangning had any significant populations remaining.

In the latter half of the seventeenth century (starting with laws issued in 1651 and 1653), the imperial Qing government recruited migrants from south of the Great Wall (notably, from Shandong) to settle the relatively sparsely populated area of Fengtian Province (roughly corresponding to today's Liaoning). Many of the current residents of Liaoning trace their ancestry to these seventeenth century settlers. The rest of China's Northeast, however, remained officially off-limits to Han Chinese for most of the Manchu era. To prevent the migration of Chinese to those regions (today's Jilin and Heilongjiang, as well as the adjacent parts of Inner Mongolia), the so-called Willow Palisade was constructed (c. 1638 – c. 1672). The Palisade encircled the agricultural heartlands of Fengtian, running in most areas either somewhat outside the old Ming Liaodong Wall, or reusing it, and separating it from the Manchu forests to the northeast and the Mongol grazing lands to the northwest.

Later on, the Qing government tried to stop the migrants flow to Fengtian or even to make some settlers return to their original places of residence – or, failing that, to legalize them. For example, an edict issued in 1704 commented on the recent Han Chinese settlers in Fengtian having failed to comply with earlier orders requiring them to leave, and asked them either to properly register and join a local defense group (保; bao), or to leave the province for their original places within the next ten years. Ten years later, naturally, another edict appeared, reminding of the necessity to do something with illegal migrants ... In any event, the restrictive policy was not as effective as desired by the officials in Beijing, and Fengtian's population doubled between 1683 and 1734.

During the Qing Dynasty, Manchuria was ruled by three generals, one of whom, the General of Shengjing (Mukden i Jiyanggiyūn) ruled much of modern Liaoning. In 1860, the Manchu government began to reopen the region to migration, which quickly resulted in Han Chinese becoming the dominant ethnic group in the region.
Main agricultural products of Liaoning include maize, sorghum, and soybeans. The region around Dalian produces three-quarters of China's exported apples and peaches. Cotton is also produced.

Liaoning's fruits include apples from Dalian and Yingkou, golden peaches from Dalian, pears from Beizhen of Jinzhou, white pears from Huludao and Suizhong, and apricots and plums from Gushan of Dandong.

shenyang-jianzhu-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shenyang Jianzhu University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.

shenyang-ligong-university.h: Shenyang Ligong University at a glance

blocks.x: Shenyang Ligong University (SYLU, sometimes written SLU) is a provincially run university in Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning Province in north-east China. Its campus is in the Hunnan New District, a newer part of the city. In practical terms this means you would study in a modern, purpose-built setting rather than in the old centre, so it is worth looking at transport links to the city before you choose accommodation.

It has since become a multidisciplinary university known mainly for engineering, with additional strengths in science, management, economics, law and the arts. Its character is shaped by a connection to national defence. It recruits students from across the country, although its main contribution is to the development of Liaoning Province.

The leadership's stated ambition is to become a high-level university for teaching and research, with its own distinctive features, a national reputation and a place among the first rank of universities in Liaoning. That goal is expressed with plenty of enthusiasm and an innovative, enterprising spirit, and it tells prospective students that the university is still building its profile.

International cooperation is a visible part of the profile. The university reports stable partnerships with 65 universities in 11 countries, including Russia, Finland, Japan, Germany, Canada, Britain and the US. Nine institutes belonging to the national science academies of Russia and Belarus have helped it build four advanced laboratories. Joint degree programmes have also been run with partners in Russia, Canada, the USA, the UK and elsewhere.

The Russian connection is the strongest. Working with Russia's Tomsk State University, the university set up a Confucius Institute, and the link grew when the Pushkin Russian Language Center opened. China's Ministry of Education has approved that center as a national hub for Russian. If you are interested in Russian language or in joint study with Russian institutions, this is a notable advantage.

Research facilities include a national base for Sino-Russian scientific and technological cooperation, a total of six engineering research centres at provincial level and three provincial innovation teams. Over a five-year period it took on 1,760 research projects, of which 146 were at national level, including 19 under the 973 or 863 programmes and 26 funded by the National Natural Science Foundation. Awards include one national prize and 30 provincial ones. Researchers published 3,874 papers, 1,215 of them indexed in SCI, EI and ISTP, along with 288 books. In addition, 444 patents were granted, 44 of which are for inventions. The university says its greatest research strength is in machinery manufacturing, energy and environmental protection, electronic information, automatic control and the production of new materials. These numbers describe an earlier five-year period and have certainly moved on, so ask the university for a current summary.
The university sets out the following focus areas, which show the practical, industry-oriented nature of the work.

Machinery manufacturing: flexible manufacturing systems, automatic assembly and detection, numerical-control machine tools and machining, industrial robots, machining at ultra-high precision, special machining, fast cutting, combined milling and cutting, monitoring and control of machining processes, structural and functional design of cars and motorcycles, fault diagnosis, dynamic balancing, mould design and manufacture, and CAD and CAM applications.

Energy and environmental protection: an energy-saving crude oil heater using radiation without pressure, a microprocessor-controlled sprinkler system for farm irrigation, coal that fixes sulphur and is made from household waste, energy-saving speed control through frequency conversion, environmental protection engineering design and management, equipment and techniques for the treatment, analysis and monitoring of water and smoke pollution, and a process for treating wastewater containing heavy metals.

Electronics and information: bar-code technology, magnetic card and IC card production, development of intelligent detection equipment, applications of infrared detection, theory of interference resistance and stability in detection systems, computer control systems, theory and use of discrete event dynamic systems, speed regulation, electronic devices, computer networks, and software and hardware development.

New materials and chemical engineering: cementing compounds and sealants, bonding technology with adhesives, building materials that save energy, how to make composites and what their properties are, testing of foundry plaster and aluminium alloy, brightness of aluminium alloy handrails for estate cars, process and material for pistons in car air-conditioners, high-strength die-cast aluminium, aluminium alloy materials, new cast iron for car brakes, materials and manufacturing methods for engine covers, and industrial lubricants.

Casting techniques and equipment: ultrasonic casting, sand reclamation, die-casting of large and intricate thin-walled parts, an expert system for blanking die design, an argon refining device, numerical simulation of casting, improved solid moulds for diesel engines, and casting engineering with CAD, CAE, CAPP and expert systems.

Management engineering: corporate identity design, asset valuation, enterprise development strategy, sustainable development for cities and companies, building modern enterprise systems for large and medium state-owned firms, innovative development of small and medium-sized businesses, management strategy for firms, strategic studies of the local economy and technology, consulting, and rural land protection.

shenyang-ligong-university.h: Shenyang: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Day-to-day life for a student depends heavily on the city around the campus, so the following sections describe Shenyang, its land, rivers, parks, climate, people, economy, transport and culture.

The city lies at the heart of Liaoning Province, between latitudes 41°11′ and 43°02′ north and longitudes 122°25′ and 123°48′ east. Its western districts rest on a floodplain built by the Liao River system, while the east is wooded land that belongs to the Changbai Mountains hinterland. The highest point is 414 metres (1,358 feet) above sea level and the lowest only 7 metres (23 feet), with an average urban elevation of 45 metres (148 feet).

The built-up core lies north of the Hun River, which used to be the Liao's biggest tributary and which locals often call the mother river. Around the centre run three artificial waterways. The South Canal (南运河) curves round the south and south-east; to the north and north-east is the Xinkai River (新开河), previously the North Canal; and to the west is the Weigong River (卫工河), once known as the Weigong Nullah. Channels connect them into a continuous waterway. The South Canal is especially famous for the string of linear parks and gardens along its banks. It was made by canalising the former course of the Wanquan River (萬泉河, meaning ten thousand springs), which went by other names too, the Little Shen River and the Wuli River (五里河, five-li river), and supplied most of the old city's water.

On the outskirts, smaller rivers reinforce the system, such as the Xi, Puhe and Mantang, and drain into the Hun at three points on the south-east, south and south-west sides of the city. There used to be a further canal on the east side, the Huishan Nullah (辉山明渠), which drained into the lower part of the Xinkai River, but it no longer exists because of land reclamation for urban construction.

Shenyang has many parks, and the best known are the South Canal Linear Parks (南运河带状公园), which stretch 14.5 km (9.0 miles) along the canal through the southern parts of the Dadong, Shenhe and Heping districts. Altogether there are six big parks and eighteen gardens by the water, totalling roughly 1,400,000 square metres (350 acres). Flowers and shrubs such as roses, apricots, bladder cherry, natal lily, scarlet sage and black-eyed Susan share space with wide groves of peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, willow, pine and locust trees. This is the largest continuous stretch of green urban space in the city and a major part of the city's 40 percent greening ratio, which helped it earn the title of national forest city in 2005.

The Shenyang Environmental Protection Bureau says that coal burned by boiler stations for district heating in winter causes 30 percent of the city's air pollution. In the winter of 2013 to 2014, the city used 16 million metric tons of coal, and half of that went on heating. The rest comes from building-site dust at 20 percent, exhaust fumes at 20 percent, factories at 10 percent and dust blown in from outside, also 20 percent, mostly yellow dust from the Gobi Desert. The bureau described air quality as slowly improving, so it is worth checking an air quality app during winter.

Shenyang's climate is humid continental with a monsoon influence (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac). The monsoon brings hot and humid summers and the Siberian high brings dry, cold winters, with four clearly separate seasons. Close to half the year's rainfall comes in July and August. The mean temperature is −11.4 °C (11.5 °F) in January and 24.9 °C (76.8 °F) in July, with 8.6 °C (47.5 °F) as the yearly figure. Considering how harsh winter gets, a frost-free season of 183 days is surprisingly long. Sunshine adds up to 2,421 hours annually, with possible sunshine at 42 percent in July and 64 percent in February. The temperature has ranged between −33.1 °C (−28 °F) and 38.4 °C (101 °F).

The city is home to 9.07 million people, and 85.12% of them are city dwellers. The city is ethnically and culturally varied, with 38 of China's 56 recognised ethnic groups, including the Han majority at 91.26 percent of the population. Among the 37 minorities, the largest ones include the Manchu, Korean, Hui, Xibo and Mongolian peoples. The full list also covers the Zhuang, Miao, Tujia, Dong, Daur, Bai, Uyghur, Tibetan, Yi, Taiwanese Aboriginal People, She, Bouyei, Yao, Akha, Kazakh, Dai, Li, Shui, Nakhi, Jingpo, Kyrgyz, Tu, Mulao, Qiang, Maonan, Gelao, Russian, Evenk, Tatar, Oroqen, Nanai and Lhoba groups. Most of these groups did not originate in the Shenyang area, though a few, including the Manchus and the Xibe, did. Religious life is visible, with plenty of temples, mosques and churches around the city.

shenyang-ligong-university.h: From heavy industry to a new mix

blocks.x: As one of China's important industrial centres, Shenyang anchors the Shenyang Economic Zone, designated a New Special Reform Zone. Heavy industry has been its speciality, above all aerospace, machine tools, heavy equipment and defence, and lately software, vehicles and electronics have joined in. The sector began in the 1920s and was well established before the Second World War. In the first five-year plan, 1951 to 1956, a great many factories rose in the Tiexi district. In the 1970s, at its height, Shenyang was among the top three industrial centres of China together with Shanghai and Tianjin, and it was at one point considered for upgrading to a directly administered municipality.

From the 1980s the planned economy lost favour and heavy industry shrank gradually. The city turned into a rust-belt centre, as hundreds of thousands of people lost jobs when state-owned factories went bankrupt. The economy has since recovered a good deal, helped by the national Revitalize Northeast China campaign and by rapid growth of software and car manufacturing. Subsidies for investment are offered to multinationals that open offices or base their headquarters in the city.

Services, especially banking, have been growing. Foreign banks present include Hana Bank of South Korea, Japan's Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ, the Bank of East Asia of Hong Kong, Singapore's United Overseas Bank and Britain's HSBC. In 2006 it counted 1,063 banks and branches along with 144 firms in insurance, and the stated goal for 2010 was 30 foreign banks and 60 non-bank financial institutions. The Economist Intelligence Unit, in a November 2010 white paper called Access China, listed Shenyang with five other cities (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan and Pingdingshan) as the CHAMPS group in a study of 20 emerging Chinese cities.
The city has three development zones: the Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone, the Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone and the Shenyang Economic and Technological Development Zone.

Many large industrial companies have headquarters in Shenyang. Brilliance Auto, a major Chinese car maker, has most of its plants there. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation builds civilian aircraft and planes for the PLAAF. Neusoft Group is China's biggest software company, and Shenyang Machine Tool Group is the country's largest machine tool maker. Tyco International, General Motors and Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation have been expanding their operations in the city. Output per head in 2009 was 78,490 yuan, which ranked third of the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning.

Shenyang is the transport hub of north-east China, with air and rail links, a subway system that had five lines at the time of the description, a wide network of streets and expressways, and buses across the city. Terminal 3 at Taoxian International Airport is the biggest in the north-east, and the south of the city got a new tram network in 2013.

The north-east's main rail junction is Shenyang, where eight lines reach out to Beijing, Dalian, Changchun, Harbin and Fushun. It is also served by the Qinhuangdao–Shenyang high-speed line, the principal passenger route through the Shanhai Pass and China's first railway built only for passenger trains. From early 2007, trains running at 200 km/h (120 mph) shortened the trip between Beijing and Shenyang by nearly two thirds, to about 4 hours. Late in 2012 the Harbin–Dalian high-speed line opened, tying Shenyang to Harbin, Changchun and Dalian with a top speed of 300 km/h (190 mph).
The two main stations are Shenyang North in Shenhe District and Shenyang station in Heping District.

Shenyang North (沈阳北站), once known as the Liaoning General Station before 1946 and called the Old North Station by locals, has a history linked to the warlord Zhang Zuolin. The original building, now listed as heritage, was first named Fengtian City Station. It was completed in 1927 at the terminus of the Jingfeng Railway, roughly 1 km (0.62 miles) south-west of where the station is now, and it was built in order to rival the Shenyang station that the Japanese then administered. The main building of the current New North Station was begun in 1986 and opened in December 1990, and it became one of China's five most important rail hubs, earning the nickname Northeast's No. 1 Station. A big expansion called the North Station Transport Hub Reconstruction Project started in 2011, in response to rising passenger numbers after high-speed rail began. It added a 3-storey sub-station building and a North Square on the Huanggu District side of the tracks. The old waiting area inside the 16-storey main building was moved to a large elevated concourse over the tracks, and a pillar-free roof, the biggest in mainland China, covers the platforms. The South Square outside the main building was rebuilt as a multi-level complex with an airport-style drop-off zone on two upper levels, a ground-level area for buses, and a three-level underground city holding shops, car parks, taxi pick-up and the interchange with Subway Line 2. The underground space is designed so that it can be converted quickly into a shelter against air raids.

Shenyang station (沈阳站) is more than 100 years old. It was built by the Russians in 1899, alongside the eastern edge of the South Manchurian Railway, and was first named Fengtian Station. The Japanese expanded it after the Russo-Japanese War and named it Fengtian Yam until the end of World War II. Between 1945 and 1950 it was known as Shenyang South Railway Station or just the South Station, as distinct from the North Station, and locals still say it, even though the real Shenyang South station is now out in the suburbs where Hunnan meets Sujiatun. These days the station deals with conventional-speed passenger trains, and a refurbishment is adding a large arch and a new terminal; until it is finished, passengers reach the platforms by detours above and below ground. A new West Station Building and a West Square were added on the west side in 2010, and the old East Station Building is on the provincial list of protected heritage.
For freight, a daily direct container train has run since 2011 from Leipzig in Germany to Shenyang through Siberia, carrying automotive parts over 11,000 km (6,800 miles) in 23 days.

Shenyang Taoxian International Airport in Hunnan District serves the city. Of China's eight main airline hubs it is one, and it ranks as the 23rd busiest airport in the country. Three other airports in Shenyang are closed to the public: East Pagoda Airport in Dadong District, the oldest in the city, which opened in the 1920s and was retired in the 1980s (a 2013 proposal suggested moving it to Xinmin and reopening it); Beiling Airport in Huanggu District, which the Shenyang Aircraft Corporation uses for test flights; and Yuhong Airport in Yuhong District, used only by the local garrisons of the Northern Theater Command.

Local people speak the Shenyang dialect, a branch of Northeastern Mandarin formed in the early Qing dynasty. It is similar to other north-eastern dialects and to standard Putonghua, but as a type of Dongbeihua it includes many words that standard Chinese does not, which is something to expect when you chat with local classmates.

Folk dance and song of the north-east, notably Errenzhuan and Yangge, are much loved here. Near Middle Street, the Big Stage Theatre (大舞台剧场) is known for Errenzhuan and for comic sketches by Zhao Benshan and his students. With so many comedians living in the city, Shenyang has a national reputation as a stronghold of Chinese comedy.

Several performing arts groups are based here, such as the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China, Liaoning Ballet and the Liaoning Song and Dance Ensemble. Well-known artists from the city include Zimei, Na Ying and the pianist Lang Lang.
