Shenyang Normal University, abbreviated SYNU, is written 沈阳师範大学 in simplified characters and 瀋陽師範大學 in traditional ones, and pronounced Shěnyáng Shīfàn Dàxué. It is a broad-based university in Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning Province in north-east China. The Liaoning provincial government governs it. Despite the word 'normal' in its name, which points to its roots in teacher training, the university now teaches a wide range of subjects.
The university began in 1951 as Northeastern Education College. Its name has changed several times since then.
1951: Northeastern Education College.
1953: Shenyang Teacher's College.
1965: Liaoning First Teachers' College.
1978: back to Shenyang Teacher's College.
2001: the present name, adopted when Shenyang Teacher's College merged with Liaoning Educational College.
The university is a non-profit organisation.

Teaching is organised into 18 colleges and 30 departments. Education has a prominent place: the Liaoning Provincial Basic Education Teaching Research Training Center works together with the College of Educational Science. Other colleges deal with software and information science, information technology, foreign languages, drama, and arts and design, and there is an International Commercial College as well. Overall, students can choose from 47 bachelor's programmes, and 31 more lead to a master's degree.

The range of research is wide. Units doing it include an institute of entomology (the study of insects), an institute studying educational economics and administration, and a school for human resource development and administrative science. Apart from standard undergraduate study, SYNU runs part-time programmes for adults working towards a master's, and it provides courses designed for students from overseas.

One college, the College of International Business (CIB, 國際商學院), was created with an American partner, Fort Hays State University (FHSU). About half of SYNU's foreign teachers work there, and its tuition is the highest of any college in the university, so check the fees carefully if it interests you.
CIB offers two degree routes:

Double degree: in partnership with FHSU, graduates receive two qualifications, one from FHSU and one from SYNU. Part of the course content comes from FHSU and is delivered inside the CIB building by Cooperating Teachers acting as intermediaries, and the rest is taught by the Chinese side of CIB.
Single degree: the whole course is taught by CIB's Chinese side, and the only qualification is one from SYNU.

The 2001 merger with Liaoning Educational College led to a move from the former urban site to a fresh campus in Shenyang's northern suburbs. Its postal address is still given as Huanggu District (皇姑區), although the site is actually at the border between Yuhong District (於洪區) and Shenbei District (瀋北新區). Land for the campus, 300 acres (1.2 km2) with 793,000 square metres of floor space, was taken from three former villages, North Sitaizi (北四臺子), Zhengliang (正良) and Guoqi (郭七).

The neighbourhood is much less developed than older parts of Shenyang but is changing quickly. The old village of Zhengliang (正良), for instance, has been flattened without leaving any trace, and a new residential area, Xin Zheng Liang Cun (正良新村), is planned for the same spot. The campus is the site of the largest statue of Confucius, and the libraries hold over 1.5 million volumes.

For a student, much of daily life depends on the city around the campus, including the climate, ways of getting around and things to do. The sections below describe Shenyang, the city where Shenyang Normal University is based.

shenyang-normal-university.h: Where Shenyang is and how its land lies

blocks.x: The city occupies the centre of Liaoning province, between 41° 11' and 43° 02' north and between 122° 25' and 123° 48' east. Its western districts lie on the flat alluvial land of the Liao River system, whereas the east is forested hinterland of the Changbai Mountains. Altitude varies from 7 m (23 ft) at the lowest spot to 414 m (1,358 ft) at the highest, and the built-up area averages 45 m (148 ft).

Downtown Shenyang stands on the north side of the Hun River. Once the biggest tributary of the Liao itself, it is affectionately called the city's 'mother river'. The centre is ringed by three man-made rivers that channels join into a single waterway. The South Canal (南运河) curves around the south and south-east, the Xinkai River (新开河, formerly the North Canal) around the north and north-east, and the Weigong River (卫工河, formerly the Weigong Nullah) round the west.

Of the three, the South Canal is the most celebrated, because a chain of parks and gardens follows it. It was converted from the former Wanquan River (萬泉河, meaning 'ten thousand springs river'), a stream that had been the old city's principal water source and was also known as the Little Shen River (小瀋水) or the Wuli River (五里河, 'five-li river'). Along the outskirts, smaller waterways give extra support: the Puhe River (蒲河), the Mantang River (满堂河) and the Xi River (细河). The system empties into the Hun River in three places, on the south-east, south and south-west sides. An eastern canal named Huishan Nullah (辉山明渠) used to run into the lower Xinkai River but no longer exists, as urban construction reclaimed its land.

Parks are one of the city's strengths, and the best known are the South Canal Linear Parks (南运河带状公园). They follow the canal for 14.5 km (9.0 mi) through the south of the Dadong, Shenhe and Heping districts, in a system of 6 big parks and 18 riverside gardens that spread over roughly 1,400,000 m2 (350 acres). Roses, apricot, bladder cherry, honeylocust, natal lily, scarlet sage, morning glory and black-eyed Susan are some of the flowering plants, and large green areas are planted with peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, weeping willow, pine and black locust. This is the largest area of planted open space in the city. It contributes a great deal to Shenyang's 40-percent greening ratio and played a key role in the city winning the 'national forest city' title in 2005.

Shenyang's Environmental Protection Bureau traces 30 percent of local air pollution to winter coal, which boiler stations burn to supply district heating. During the 2013 to 2014 winter the city consumed 16 million metric tons of coal, and half went to heating. Other sources were construction-site dust at 20 percent, exhaust from vehicles at 20 percent, outside dust at 20 percent (mainly yellow dust blowing from the Gobi Desert) and emissions from industry at 10 percent. The Bureau calls the trend 'slowly improving'.

Classified as monsoon-influenced humid continental (Köppen Dwa, Trewartha Dcac), the climate gives hot, humid summers courtesy of the monsoon and dry, cold winters courtesy of the Siberian anticyclone. All four seasons are distinct. July and August alone deliver close to half of the year's rain.

In January the monthly mean is -11.4 °C (11.5 °F), and in July it is 24.9 °C (76.8 °F), with 8.6 °C (47.5 °F) as the average for the year. Winters are harsh, yet frost-free days number 183, a long period by comparison. Bright sunshine totals 2,421 hours a year, and the monthly possible-sunshine figure moves between 64 percent (February) and 42 percent (July). Recorded extremes are -33.1 °C (-28 °F) at the cold end and 38.4 °C (101 °F) at the hot end.

Population stands at 9.07 million, and 85.12% of people live in urban areas. Culturally the city is diverse: 38 of China's 56 recognised ethnic groups are represented, with Han Chinese forming 91.26 percent of residents. Among the other 37 groups, the Manchu, Korean, Hui, Mongolian and Zhuang are among those you may hear about most, and the full list also covers the Russian, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uyghur, Tibetan, Tatar and Evenk peoples, Taiwanese Aboriginal People, and Xibo, Miao, Tujia, Bouyei, Yao, Dai, Dong, Daur, Bai, Yi, She, Akha, Li, Shui, Nakhi, Jingpo, Tu, Mulao, Qiang, Maonan, Gelao, Oroqen, Nanai and Lhoba groups. Few of these peoples originate in the Shenyang region, though the Manchu and Xibe do. Many temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship serve the religious communities.

Industry is central to the city's identity. Shenyang is the main city of the Shenyang Economic Zone, designated a New Special Reform Zone. Heavy industry has been its focus, led by defence, aerospace, heavy equipment and machine tools, and recently software, cars and electronics have been growing.

Heavy industry arrived in the 1920s and was highly developed by the time the Second World War began. Between 1951 and 1956, under the first five-year plan, many new factories went up in Tiexi district. By the 1970s the city stood, with Shanghai and Tianjin, among China's top three industrial centres, and officials once thought about making it a direct-controlled municipality. The decline came after the 1980s, when the planned economy lost favour: heavy industry shrank, state-owned factories went bankrupt, hundreds of thousands of workers lost their jobs, and Shenyang turned into a rust-belt city. Recovery has been significant lately, thanks to the central government's 'Revitalize Northeast China' campaign and rapid growth in software and car making. Multinational companies opening offices or headquarters here are given investment subsidies.

Services, banking above all, are on the rise. Overseas lenders with a presence include HSBC (Britain), Hana Bank (South Korea), United Overseas Bank (Singapore), the Bank of East Asia (Hong Kong) and the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ (Japan). A 2006 count found 1,063 banks and branches in the city, plus 144 insurance-related firms, and the aim for 2010 was to draw in 30 overseas banks along with 60 financial institutions that are not banks. In its November 2010 Access China White Paper, the Economist Intelligence Unit put Shenyang in a group of six it called CHAMPS, with Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan and Pingdingshan, to illustrate the economic profile of China's top 20 emerging cities.
The city has three development zones:
Shenyang Finance and Trade Development Zone
Shenyang High-Tech Industrial Development Zone
Shenyang Economic and Technological Development Zone
Many large industrial companies have headquarters in Shenyang:
Brilliance Auto, a major Chinese carmaker with most of its plants in Shenyang.
Shenyang Aircraft Corporation, which builds civilian aircraft and aircraft for the PLAAF.
Neusoft Group, the biggest software company in China.
Shenyang Machine Tool Group, China's largest machine tool maker.
Foreign groups such as General Motors, Tyco International and the Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation, all of which are enlarging their operations here.
GDP per person in 2009 was 78,490 yuan, third among the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning province.

Shenyang functions as the transport hub for the whole of Northeast China, with flights, trains, a subway (five lines when this was written), a broad network of streets and expressways, and buses everywhere in the city. The largest terminal in the north-east is Terminal 3 of Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, and in 2013 a new tram system began operating in the south.

Eight railways meet here, tying Shenyang to Fushun, Harbin, Changchun, Dalian and Beijing, which makes it the rail centre of the north-east. The Qinhuangdao-Shenyang high-speed railway, China's first line carrying only passengers, forms the main route across the Shanhai Pass. A high-speed train introduced in early 2007 runs at 200 km/h (120 mph) and shortened the trip to Beijing by almost two thirds, to about 4 hours. Later, in late 2012, the Harbin-Dalian high-speed railway opened. Trains there can reach 300 km/h (190 mph), and the line joins Shenyang to Dalian, Changchun and Harbin.
Two major stations serve the city: Shenyang North in Shenhe District and Shenyang railway station in Heping District.

Shenyang North Railway Station (沈阳北站, Shěnyáng Běi Zhàn) is known colloquially as the 'Old North Station' and, until 1946, bore the name Liaoning General Station (遼寧總站, Liáoníng Zǒngzhàn). Its original building, which is now a listed heritage structure, opened as Fengtian City Station (奉天城站, Fèngtīan Chéng Zhàn). The warlord Zhang Zuolin ordered it in 1927, at the terminus of the Jingfeng Railway and roughly 1 km (0.62 mi) south-west of where the station stands now, as a rival to the Japanese-run Shenyang Railway Station. Building of the Main Station Building (主站房) at the 'New North Station' started in 1986 and came into use in December 1990. It became one of China's five most important rail hubs, and the nickname 'Northeast's No. 1 Station' (东北第一站) followed.

Rising passenger numbers after the arrival of high-speed trains meant more floor area was needed, and in 2011 a huge project to rebuild the transport hub (北站交通枢纽改造工程) got under way. It added a three-storey Sub-Station Building (子站房) and a North Square (北广场), both on the northern side of the tracks in Huanggu District. The waiting hall of the original 16-storey Main Station Building has been moved to a wide raised concourse bridging the rails, beneath a pillar-free roof, the biggest of its kind in mainland China, which arches over the platforms. The old South Square (南广场) by the Main Station Building was rebuilt as a multi-level complex. Its two upper levels act as an elevated, airport-style drop-off, with a large ground-level area for buses, and beneath it lies a three-level underground city with malls, parking, taxis and an interchange with Subway Line 2. In an emergency it can quickly be turned into an air-raid shelter.

The second main station is Shenyang station (沈阳站, Shěnyáng Zhàn), which is more than 100 years old. It was built by Russians in 1899 beside the eastern side of the South Manchurian Railway, and the name at that time was Fengtian Station (奉天站, Fèngtiān Zhàn). After the Russo-Japanese War the Japanese expanded it and renamed it Fengtian Yam (奉天驛, Fèngtiān Yì), a name it kept until the end of the Second World War. From 1945 to 1950 it was the Shenyang South Railway Station (瀋陽南站, Shěnyáng Nán Zhàn), or simply the 'South Station' as opposed to the North Station, and locals still use that name today, even though the actual Shenyang South railway station is now at the suburban junction of Hunnan and Sujiatun. Today the station handles regular-speed passenger trains. It is being refurbished with a large archway and a new terminal, and while work goes on, passengers are rerouted under and over ground to reach the platforms. In 2010 a new West Station Building (西站房) and West Square (西广场) opened on the west side of the tracks, and the old East Station Building (东站房) is on the provincial protected heritage list.
Since 2011 a freight service, a container train that runs daily, has hauled automotive parts from Leipzig in Germany to Shenyang, a distance of 11,000 km (6,800 mi) across Siberia that takes 23 days.
The airport is Shenyang Taoxian International Airport, in Hunnan District. It is among China's eight major airline hubs and ranks 23rd for traffic.

Three other airfields lie within the city, none for public use. The oldest, East Pagoda Airport (东塔机场) in Dadong District, opened in the 1920s and was retired in the 1980s, though a 2013 proposal suggested moving and reopening it in Xinmin. Test flights for Shenyang Aircraft Corporation use Beiling Airport (北陵机场) in Huanggu District, and the Northern Theater Command garrisons alone use Yuhong Airport (于洪机场) in Yuhong District, for military purposes.

People from Shenyang speak the Shenyang dialect, a variety of Northeastern Mandarin that took shape in the early Qing dynasty. It is close to other north-eastern dialects and to standard Mandarin (Putonghua), but as a form of Dongbeihua it has many words that the official language does not include.

Two folk dances from the north-east, Errenzhuan and Yangge, are very popular. The Big Stage Theatre (大舞台剧场) near Middle Street is famous for Errenzhuan and for Chinese comedy sketches by Zhao Benshan and his students. Many comedians based in Shenyang are popular, and the city is nationally recognised as a stronghold of Chinese comedy.

The performing arts have a strong base, with groups such as Liaoning Ballet, the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China and the Liaoning Song and Dance Ensemble. The city has also produced well-known performers, among them the pianist Lang Lang, Na Ying and Zimei.
Shenyang Normal University lists 134 programs for international students on this site: 58 bachelor, 75 master's, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 132 taught in Chinese, 2 taught in Chinese and English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 18,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 18,000), according to the university's published fee table.

134 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

shenyang-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Shenyang Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shenyang, register at Shenyang Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Shenyang University of Technology (沈阳工业大学, Shěnyáng Gōngyè Dàxué, abbreviated SUT) is a university in Shenyang, the main city of Liaoning Province in north-east China, and it is run by the provincial government. The rest of this profile focuses on what a student needs to know about the city and the province, because daily life depends so much on what lies beyond the campus gate. For details of SUT's own departments, courses, fees and campus, the university's website is the place to look.

Shenyang lies in the middle of Liaoning, between roughly 41 degrees 11 minutes and 43 degrees 02 minutes north and between 122 degrees 25 minutes and 123 degrees 48 minutes east. The western part of the city's area is flat alluvial land belonging to the Liao River system, and the east rises into forested country at the edge of the Changbai Mountains. Heights vary from 7 metres (23 feet) at the lowest point to 414 metres (1,358 feet) at the highest, with an average of 45 metres (148 feet) across the urban area.

The built-up core lies north of the Hun River, which used to be the largest tributary of the Liao and is affectionately called the mother river of the city. Around the central districts runs a ring of three artificial waterways joined by channels: the South Canal on the south and south-east, the Xinkai River (once called the North Canal) on the north and north-east, and the Weigong River on the west. The South Canal is the best known thanks to the chain of park strips and gardens lining it; it was made by canalising the old Wanquan River, whose name means ten thousand springs, which was also known as the Little Shen River or the Wuli River and used to be the principal water source of the old city. Smaller rivers support the outer edge: the Xi, the Puhe and the Mantang, which feed into the Hun at three points to the south-east, due south and south-west. A fourth canal, the Huishan Nullah on the east side, drained into the lower Xinkai River but has disappeared under urban development.

Shenyang has plenty of parks. The most famous are the South Canal Linear Parks, which run 14.5 kilometres (9.0 miles) across the southern stretches of three districts (Dadong, Shenhe and Heping). They consist of six large parks and eighteen riverside gardens covering about 1,400,000 square metres (350 acres). The flowerbeds hold roses, scarlet sage, natal lily, morning glory and black-eyed Susan, mixed with apricot, bladder cherry and honeylocust, while wider green areas are planted with peach, pear, crabapple, ginkgo, weeping willow, pine and black locust trees. This is the largest continuous belt of planted open space in the city, it contributes strongly to a greening ratio of 40 percent, and it helped Shenyang earn the title of national forest city in 2005.

Air quality in winter deserves a mention. The local environmental protection bureau attributes 30 percent of the city's air pollution to coal burned by boiler stations for district heating. Of the 16 million tonnes of coal used in the winter of 2013-2014, half went to heating. The remainder was split between construction-site dust and traffic exhaust (20 percent each), dust arriving from beyond the city, mainly yellow dust off the Gobi Desert (also 20 percent), and factory emissions (10 percent). The bureau described the situation as slowly improving. These figures are from several years ago, so look at current air-quality readings before you arrive, and consider a mask for the worst days.

The climate type is humid continental with a monsoon influence (Koppen Dwa; Trewartha Dcac). The monsoon makes summers hot and sticky, while a Siberian high-pressure system brings dry, bitterly cold winters. The four seasons are distinct, and nearly half of all rain falls in July and August.

January is the coldest month, averaging minus 11.4 degrees Celsius (11.5 F), and July the warmest at 24.9 degrees (76.8 F); across the whole year the mean is 8.6 degrees (47.5 F). The frost-free period lasts 183 days, which is a lot for a place with such severe winters. Sunshine totals 2,421 hours a year, and the monthly share of possible sunshine swings between 42 percent (July) and 64 percent (February). Recorded extremes run from minus 33.1 degrees (minus 28 F) to 38.4 degrees (101 F). In short, you need serious winter clothing for the cold season and light, breathable clothes for the humid summer.

Shenyang's population is about 9.07 million, and 85.12 percent live in urban areas. It is an ethnically varied place: 38 of China's 56 officially recognised ethnic groups are represented, though the Han Chinese majority makes up 91.26 percent of residents. The 37 minorities include the Manchu, Korean, Hui, Mongolian and Xibo communities, which are among the larger ones, and the Zhuang, Miao, Tujia, Dong, Daur, Bai, Uyghur, Tibetan and Yi. Smaller groups are the Taiwanese Aboriginal peoples, She, Bouyei, Yao, Akha, Kazakh, Dai, Li, Shui, Nakhi, Jingpo, Kyrgyz and Tu, as well as the Mulao, Qiang, Maonan and Gelao, and finally Russians, Evenks, Tatars, Oroqen, Nanai and Lhoba. Most are not originally from the Shenyang area, but a few, such as the Manchu and the Xibe, are. Temples, mosques, churches and other places of worship can be found across the city.

Native residents speak the Shenyang dialect, a form of Northeastern Mandarin that took shape in the early Qing period. It is similar to other north-eastern dialects and to standard Mandarin (Putonghua), but it belongs to what people call Dongbeihua and includes plenty of vocabulary that standard Mandarin lacks. If your Mandarin is textbook-style, expect to adjust your ear a little.

Errenzhuan and Yangge, two folk dances of the north-east, are hugely popular here. The Big Stage Theatre, near Middle Street, is famous for Errenzhuan and comedy sketches performed by the comedian Zhao Benshan and his students. Because of the many popular comedians based in the city, Shenyang has a national reputation as a stronghold of Chinese comedy. Performing groups based here include the Shenyang Acrobatic Troupe of China, Liaoning Ballet, and an ensemble for song and dance. Well-known artists from the city are the singers Zimei and Na Ying, along with the pianist Lang Lang.

shenyang-university-of-technology.h: From heavy-industry giant to a reviving centre

blocks.x: Shenyang is one of China's important industrial centres and the core of the Shenyang Economic Zone, a designated New Special Reform Zone. Its traditional strength is heavy industry: aerospace, machine tools, heavy equipment and defence, with software, cars and electronics added more recently. The industrial base dates to the 1920s and was already mature before the Second World War. During the first five-year plan (1951-1956), Tiexi District was filled with new factories. In the 1970s Shenyang ranked with Shanghai and Tianjin as one of the country's three leading industrial cities, and there was even a time when it was considered for upgrading to a municipality under central control.

After the 1980s, as the planned economy lost favour, heavy industry gradually shrank and the city became a rust-belt example, with hundreds of thousands of workers laid off from bankrupt state-owned factories. In recent years the economy has recovered markedly, helped by the central government's drive to Revitalize Northeast China, plus fast growth in software and car making. Subsidies are offered to multinationals that open offices or headquarters in the city.

Services, banking above all, have grown. Overseas lenders with a presence include HSBC from Britain, Hana Bank from South Korea, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ from Japan, the Bank of East Asia from Hong Kong and Singapore's United Overseas Bank. Counting 2006, there were 1,063 banks and branches in the city, plus 144 firms connected with insurance, and local planners hoped to bring in 30 foreign banks and 60 other financial firms by 2010. These are old targets, so use them for context rather than as current data.

A November 2010 Economist Intelligence Unit white paper on China grouped Shenyang with Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan and Pingdingshan under the label CHAMPS, in a profile of 20 emerging Chinese cities. GDP per head in 2009 was 78,490 yuan, third among the 58 cities and counties of Liaoning.
Business is concentrated in three development zones, which specialise in different fields:
A finance and trade zone
A high-tech industrial zone
An economic and technological development zone

Many major companies are headquartered here. Brilliance Auto, a large Chinese carmaker, has most of its plants in the city. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation builds civil aircraft as well as planes for the air force. Neusoft Group is described as China's biggest software company, and Shenyang Machine Tool Group as the country's largest machine-tool maker. Tyco International, General Motors and the Michelin Shenyang Tyre Corporation have been expanding their operations in the city. For an engineering or technology student, this mix of industry and software is a real asset when looking for internships.

shenyang-university-of-technology.h: The transport hub of the north-east

blocks.x: Shenyang is the north-east's transport hub, with air and rail links, a subway system (five lines at the time of writing), a dense network of streets and expressways, and buses across the city. A tram network opened in the south in 2013. Terminal 3 at the Taoxian airport is the biggest in the whole north-east.

The city is the region's railway hub. Eight railway lines connect it to Beijing, Fushun, Dalian, Changchun and Harbin. It is also on the Qinhuangdao-Shenyang high-speed line, the main passenger corridor through the Shanhai Pass and the first dedicated passenger railway in China. In early 2007, trains running at 200 km/h (120 mph) brought the Beijing-Shenyang journey down to roughly 4 hours, a threefold cut. The Harbin-Dalian high-speed line, opened in late 2012, joins Shenyang to Harbin, Changchun and Dalian at up to 300 km/h (190 mph).
The city has two principal stations. Shenyang North is in Shenhe District, and Shenyang station is in Heping District.

Shenyang North was called the Liaoning General Station before 1946 and is still nicknamed the Old North Station. The original building, now a heritage-listed structure, was first named Fengtian City Station and built in 1927 at the end of the Jingfeng Railway, about 1 kilometre (0.62 miles) south-west of today's site. It was built on the orders of the warlord Zhang Zuolin to rival the Shenyang station then run by the Japanese. Construction of the current New North Station's main building began in 1986 and it opened in December 1990, becoming one of China's five most important railway hubs and earning the nickname Northeast's No. 1 Station. Rising passenger numbers after high-speed rail arrived led to a large rebuilding scheme, the North Station Transport Hub Reconstruction Project, begun in 2011. It added a three-storey Sub-Station Building and a North Square on the Huanggu District side of the tracks. The waiting hall in the original 16-storey main building was moved to a large elevated concourse over the tracks, and the platforms sit under a pillar-free roof, the largest in mainland China. The South Square was rebuilt as a multi-level complex, with an elevated, airport-style drop-off zone, a ground-level bus area and a three-level underground city holding shops, parking, taxi pick-up and the link to Subway Line 2. The underground space can also be converted quickly into an air-raid shelter if needed.

Shenyang station has over a century of history. Russian builders put it up in 1899 beside the South Manchurian Railway, on its eastern side, and named it Fengtian Station. After the Russo-Japanese War the Japanese enlarged it and used the name Fengtian Yam until the end of the Second World War. Between 1945 and 1950 it was known as Shenyang South Station, or simply South Station, as opposed to the North Station, and locals still use that name today, even though the actual Shenyang South station is now at the suburban boundary between Hunnan and Sujiatun. Today it handles mainly ordinary-speed passenger trains. A big archway and new terminal are under construction, so passengers are routed above and below ground to the platforms in the meantime. In 2010 it gained a West Station Building and West Square, and the old East Station Building is on the provincial heritage register.
A freight service has run daily since 2011, carrying containers of car parts from Leipzig, Germany, across Siberia to Shenyang: a distance of 11,000 kilometres (6,800 miles) covered in 23 days.

The main airport, Taoxian International, is located in Hunnan District, is one of eight big airline hubs, and is the country's 23rd busiest airport. Three other airports exist in the city but are closed to the public. East Pagoda Airport in Dadong District opened in the 1920s and closed in the 1980s, though a 2013 proposal suggested moving and reopening it in Xinmin. Beiling Airport, in Huanggu District, serves test flights for the aircraft maker, and Yuhong Airport, in Yuhong District, is reserved for military garrison use.
Student life also depends on the province around the campus, so here is a brief history of Liaoning and its agriculture.

From the 4th century BC to the 9th century, the Han Chinese were the main settlers and administrators in Liaoning. Before the 3rd century BC, the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples lived there, and around 300 BC the state of Yan took over. Yan set up two commanderies named for their position relative to the Liao River: Liaodong in the east and Liaoxi in the west. The Yan city of Xiangping, the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is now. When the Han dynasty fell, a family led by Gongsun Du set up a semi-independent state based in Liaodong, which lasted until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Also called Yan, it sent out many sea missions for diplomacy and trade, and although it was short-lived it left a lasting mark on North-east Asian culture. After the Western Jin, the Murong clan of the Xianbei ruled Liaoning through three successive states called Former, Later and Northern Yan. In 436, when Northern Wei took the Yan capital, the Liaodong Peninsula passed to Goguryeo, and the Tang later absorbed the region in the Goguryeo-Tang War.

The An Lushan Rebellion in the middle of the 8th century drained Tang resources from the frontier, and the Bohai gradually spread into Liaodong. The Khitan Liao dynasty later conquered Liaoning and split it into four circuits named for capitals: Eastern, Supreme, Central and Lower.

The Jurchen Jin ran most of the area as the Eastern Capital Route, with smaller parts in the Xianping, Supreme Capital and Northern Capital routes. Genghis Khan conquered the region in 1206 and it was absorbed into the Yuan dynasty, which governed it in several pieces. The eastern area was assigned to the Liaoyang and Shenyang routes and the western area, including Guangning Route, was under the same Liaoyang Branch Secretariat, while the north fell to Xianping Prefecture within Kaiyuan Route. Jinzhou and Chaoyang belonged to Daning Route, answerable to the Central Secretariat.

shenyang-university-of-technology.h: The Ming and the Liaodong Wall

blocks.x: The Ming took control in 1371, three years after the Mongols were driven out of Beijing. Around 1442 a defensive wall went up to protect the province's farming heartland from a possible threat from the Oriyanghan Jurchen-Mongols, who were Ming tributaries, in the north-west. In 1467-1468 it was extended to guard against attacks from the Jianzhou Jurchens in the north-east, who would later be known as Manchu. It served a similar purpose to the Great Wall but was cheaper to build: some stretches used stone and tile, but mostly it was an earth embankment with a moat on each side.

Despite the wall, the Jurchens captured Liaodong in eastern Liaoning in the early seventeenth century, well before the rest of China fell to them. Their dynasty, first styled Later Jin and later renamed Qing, set up its capital from 1616 to 1621 at Xingjing, outside the wall in what is now eastern Liaoning, relocated to Dongjing (east of modern Liaoyang), and settled in 1625 at Shengjing, the city we now call Shenyang. After the main capital moved to Beijing in 1644, Shengjing stayed important as a regional capital for most of Qing rule.

The Qing conquest emptied much of Liaoning. Local people were killed in the fighting or escaped to the south, beyond the Great Wall, and retreating Ming troops themselves wrecked many towns. A report from 1661 by Fengtian's civil governor, Zhang Shangxian, said that east of the Liao only Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng were really inhabited; other towns were deserted or had a few hundred people, and Tieling and Fushun, he wrote, held just a few vagrants. On the western bank, only Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning still had large populations.

Laws passed in 1651 and 1653 began a programme in which the Qing recruited settlers, notably from Shandong, to populate the thinly settled Fengtian Province, which roughly matches today's Liaoning. A large share of Liaoning residents today descend from these seventeenth-century newcomers. The rest of the north-east stayed officially closed to the Han for most of the Manchu era. The so-called Willow Palisade, built from about 1638 to about 1672, was meant to prevent migration into what is now Jilin and Heilongjiang and the neighbouring parts of Inner Mongolia. It surrounded Fengtian's farmland, either running just outside the old Ming wall or reusing it, and divided that farmland from Manchu forest in the north-east and Mongol pasture in the north-west.

Later the government tried to stop the flow of migrants into Fengtian, to send some back, or else to give them legal status. An edict of 1704 noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave, and told them to register and join a local defence group (bao) or leave within ten years. A decade later another edict again raised the problem of illegal migrants. The restrictions were less effective than Beijing wished, and between 1683 and 1734 Fengtian's population still doubled.

Under the Qing, Manchuria was ruled by three generals, and the General of Shengjing governed much of today's Liaoning. From 1860 the Manchu government began opening the region to settlers again, and Han Chinese soon became the dominant group.

Liaoning's main crops are maize, sorghum and soybeans, and cotton is grown too. Dalian's surroundings supply three-quarters of the apples and peaches that China exports. Local fruit specialities include Dalian and Yingkou apples, Dalian golden peaches, Beizhen pears from Jinzhou, Huludao and Suizhong white pears, and the apricots and plums of Gushan, Dandong.

Shenyang offers a large, industrial, historically rich city with strong rail links, a cold winter and a distinctive regional culture and humour. shenyang-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Shihezi University, abbreviated SHZU, is a public university in the city of Shihezi, in Xinjiang. It dates from 1996 and is tied to the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC, or simply "the Corps"), a body that co-funds it with the Ministry of Education. Two national programmes for leading universities, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction, include SHZU. Its home city is nicknamed the Garden City and lies on the Manas River, below the northern slopes of the Tianshan range.

SHZU was formally created in September 1996 by combining four earlier colleges: Shihezi Medical College (established 1949), Shihezi Agricultural College (1959), the XPCC Vocational College of Economics (1959) and the XPCC Vocational College of Education (1960). That heritage explains why the university is strong in practical fields such as agriculture, medicine and economics.

shihezi-university.h: What and how you can study

blocks.x: Ten broad fields make up the curriculum: history and law, education, sciences, literature and arts, management, economics and trade, engineering, medicine and agriculture, taught across 23 colleges.
The degree offer is as follows:
10 doctoral programmes
60 master's programmes
97 bachelor's programmes
1 pre-university senior middle school programme
five specialties for serving teachers who want master's degrees
two post-doctoral scientific work stations, plus four post-doctoral mobile stations
SHZU has also set up graduate education bases jointly with Peking University and Tianjin University, and it runs a programme in culture-oriented quality education.

Government bodies back the research facilities. Three ministries and regional bodies, namely the Ministry of Agriculture, the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region (XUAR) and the XPCC, support eleven disciplines. Three key laboratories were built jointly with the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Science and Technology as well as the XPCC, which also backs two laboratories of its own. There are two more key bases for art and scientific research and 24 graduate schools and research centres in all. Through these, SHZU has grown into an important research base for both the XPCC and the XUAR.

In the Best Chinese Universities Ranking (also called the Shanghai Ranking), SHZU came 138th in China and second in Xinjiang, behind Xinjiang University. In the global Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) it was in the 901-1000 band.

Altogether 2,600 people work for the university, among them 1,894 full-time teachers. The teachers include 355 professors, 706 associate professors and two academicians from the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Fifty-eight have won outstanding-achievement awards at national or provincial level, and 81 receive special government subsidies as distinguished experts. A group of over 10 foreign experts and teachers joins the staff yearly.

The student body of about 41,000 comes from 31 provinces and regions. Undergraduates number 22,462, postgraduates 6482, and there are 415 international students whose home countries include India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Kazakhstan, Russia and the United States. (Another section of the source puts the student number at about 40,000 and calls SHZU the second-largest university in Xinjiang.)

Land area is 1,802,000 square metres. Of that, 1,214,000 square metres is covered by buildings and 184,100 square metres by laboratories. The library has 3,000,000 books and journals in Chinese and foreign languages. It was selected as Xinjiang's single model project for university digital libraries under State High-tech Project 863, and the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has a book collection point here.

Food processing and textiles now lead the economy of Shihezi. A rail line to Ürümqi and Wusu bypasses the city, and its good road network came from a United Nations economic development project. Textile mills employ most people, though shifts in the global textile trade have made employment rise and fall. Because Shihezi serves the farms around it as a hub, its future is bound to theirs; sugar beet grows nearby, and since the 1990s cotton farming has expanded quickly until it now dominates. A polysilicon factory run by Daqo New Energy Corp., among the world's biggest producers of the material, is also located in the city.

Shihezi can be reached by China National Highway 312 and by two railways, the Northern Xinjiang line and the Second Ürümqi-Jinghe line. Its airport, Shihezi Huayuan, was rebuilt from May 2012 and reopened on 26 December 2015.

Shihezi lies in Xinjiang, a region where many cultures have met for thousands of years. The history below runs from the earliest settlers to the middle of the twentieth century. It touches on subjects that are still being researched, so treat the early sections as a summary of current scientific thinking rather than final answers.

Scientists who study ancient DNA say that the first people of the Xinjiang area descended from two groups, Ancient North Eurasians and Northeast Asians. In the Bronze Age a further stream of genes arrived, tied to the westward-to-eastward spread of early Indo-Europeans, and the population became varied. By the Iron Age, herders from the Steppe were mixing more with Northeast Asians. In the north and east of Xinjiang the people looked genetically closer to Northeast Asia, whereas in the south they were closer to Central Asia.

A major study ran from 2009 to 2015 on 92 people buried at the Xiaohe Cemetery, looking at markers in their Y chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA. The fathers' lines turned out to be almost entirely European in origin. The mothers' lines were much more mixed, with East Eurasian and West Eurasian ancestry and a few Indian or South Asian lines. As centuries passed the West Eurasian maternal lines faded and East Eurasian ones took over, and women brought in from Siberian communities by marriage erased the diversity that had marked the earlier Xiaohe people.

The conclusion is that the Tarim people were diverse from the beginning, the outcome of long mixing among Ancient North Eurasians, South Asians and Northeast Asians. Their mummies have been found at Loulan, at the Xiaohe tombs and at Qäwrighul, all in the western Tarim Basin. Scholars used to think the mummies spoke Tocharian or another Indo-European language. Newer evidence suggests instead that the earliest ones came from a separate group, unrelated to the Indo-European herders, that spoke an unidentified language, perhaps one with no relatives. Anthropologists labelled many of the bodies Caucasoid, but sites in the basin hold both "Caucasoid" and "Mongoloid" remains, which suggests that newly arrived nomads from the west met farming communities in the east.

The Yuezhi, Saka and Wusun were nomadic tribes. They were probably part of the Indo-European-speaking migration that reached the Tarim Basin well before the Xiongnu or the Han Chinese. Emperor Wu of Han (who ruled from 141 to 87 BC) took the western Tarim Basin from the Xiongnu, who had been its previous overlords. At that time the basin was home to Tocharians, who spoke an Indo-European language, at Turfan and Kucha; Saka peoples, based in the Shule and Khotan kingdoms; Tibeto-Burmese groups, notably relatives of the Qiang; and Han Chinese. Some linguists argue that Paleosiberian languages, for instance in the Uralic and Yeniseian families, left a strong mark on Tocharian.

The Yuezhi are well documented in the region's history. The oldest known mention is in the Guanzi (管子), written by the Chinese chancellor Guan Zhong, and dates to 645 BC. He described the Yúshì (禺氏, also written Niúshì, 牛氏), a people of the north-west who sent jade to China from mountains in Gansu that carried the same name, Yushi. Archaeology backs up the claim that jade came from the Tarim Basin for a very long time. The tomb of Fuhao of the Shang dynasty contained over 750 jade objects, and every one came from Khotan, in present-day Xinjiang. From at least the middle of the first millennium BC the Yuezhi were trading jade, and their chief customers were the rulers of agricultural China.

The Western Regions was the Chinese name for the Tarim and Dzungaria areas, which the Northern Silk Road passed through. Early in the Han dynasty the Xiongnu, a strong nomadic people, dominated them. In the 2nd century BC Emperor Wu prepared for war against these nomads and sent Zhang Qian west to find out about the little-known kingdoms there and to propose an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. China won the war and took over a strategic belt of land reaching from the Ordos and the Gansu corridor to Lop Nor. This split the Xiongnu from the Qiang in the south and gave China direct access to the Western Regions. Zhang Qian then went as envoy to the region's states, a start to several decades of struggle that China won in the end.

Chinese economic and cultural influence spread along the Silk Road in the 100s BCE. In 60 BCE the Han created the Protectorate of the Western Regions (西域都護府) in 60 BCE, with its centre at Wulei (烏壘) near present-day Luntai, to oversee the area as far as the Pamir Mountains. The protectorate was lost in the civil war fought against Wang Mang (AD 9 to 23) and came back under Han control in 91 through the work of General Ban Chao.

At the start of the 4th century the Western Jin was overwhelmed by nomadic invaders from the north. After that a series of short-lived states governed north-western China: Former Liang, Former Qin, Later Liang and Western Liáng. Each tried, with differing success, to hold on to the protectorate. Once the Northern Wei empire had reunited the north, it controlled the south-eastern part of what is now Xinjiang. The west was run by local states (Shule, Yutian, Guizi and Qiemo), and Gaochang, the remains of the Northern Liang state that once ruled part of Gansu, held the middle, around Turpan.

The Tang dynasty sent a chain of military expeditions against the Western Turkic Khaganate and the southern oasis states that were its vassals. Emperor Taizong started the campaigns by annexing Gaochang in 640. Karasahr, close by, was taken in 644, and Kucha was conquered in 649. To govern the area the Tang founded the Protectorate General to Pacify the West (安西都護府), the Anxi Protectorate, in 640.

The Anshi Rebellion nearly destroyed the Tang. Taking advantage, Tibet attacked along a front that ran from Xinjiang to Yunnan, occupied the capital Chang'an for 16 days in 763, and by the end of the century held southern Xinjiang. In the same period the Uyghur Khaganate controlled northern Xinjiang, a large part of Central Asia and Mongolia.

Tibet and the Uyghur Khaganate lost power in the middle of the 9th century. After that, western Xinjiang fell to the Kara-Khanid Khanate during the tenth and eleventh centuries, a league of Turkic tribes that included Karluks, Chigils and Yaghmas. After the Kirghiz wrecked the Uyghur Khaganate in Mongolia in 840, Uyghur groups settled in Qocha (Karakhoja) and Beshbalik, near modern Turfan and Ürümqi. Foreign overlords ruled their state in eastern Xinjiang, which survived until the 13th century. The Uyghurs there were Manichean to begin with and later became Buddhist, while the Kara-Khanids turned to Islam.

Another group arrived in 1132: survivors of the Liao dynasty, escaping a rebellion by the Jurchens next to them in Manchuria. They established the Qara Khitai (Western Liao), an empire that governed the Kara-Khanid and Uyghur lands of the Tarim Basin for the following hundred years. Khitan and Chinese were the main languages of administration, with Persian and Uyghur also in use.

The change of religion deserves a closer look. The land that is now Xinjiang (the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria) first belonged to Tocharians, speakers of an Indo-European language, and to Iranian Sakas; both groups followed Buddhism or Zoroastrianism, and Tocharian speakers lived in the Turfan and Tarim basins, where the Caucasian mummies were found. The conversion of the Kara-Khanids, who held Kashgar, made the area Muslim in the 10th century. Around the middle of that century the Turkic Muslim Karakhanid ruler Musa attacked the Saka Buddhist Kingdom of Khotan, and about 1006 the Karakhanid leader Yusuf Qadir Khan took Khotan.

When Genghis Khan had united Mongolia and begun to move west, the Uyghur state around Turpan and Urumchi pledged loyalty to him in 1209. It paid taxes and sent soldiers, and its rulers kept their kingdom. In 1218 the Qara Khitai fell to the Mongols. Xinjiang became a stronghold of Ögedei Khan, then of Kaidu, his descendant, and their branch of the Mongol family held off the Yuan dynasty until its rule ended.

The Yuan and the Chagatai Khanate struggled for the region in the Mongol period, and the Chagatai controlled most of it. In the middle of the 14th century the Chagatai Khanate broke up. Several Persianised Mongol khans then ruled a politically divided land: from Moghulistan (helped by local Dughlat emirs), from Uigurstan (later Turpan) and from Kashgaria. Wars among these khans were frequent, and they also fought the Timurids of Transoxiana in the west and, in the east, the Oirats, who were heirs of the Chagatai line in Mongolia and China. Then, in the 17th century, a Dzungar empire spread across most of the region.

The Dzungars were Mongols, a name for the shared identity of several Oirat tribes, and their khanate was among the last great nomadic empires. It spread across Dzungaria, from the western end of the Great Wall of China to modern eastern Kazakhstan, and from northern Kyrgyzstan today to southern Siberia. The empire lasted from the early 17th century to the mid-18th, and after its fall the Chinese gave most of the region the name "Xinjiang".

The Tarim Basin's settled Turkic Muslims were originally under the Chagatai Khanate, whereas the Dzungar Khanate belonged to nomadic Oirat Mongols who were Buddhists. In the early 17th century the Naqshbandi Sufi Khojas, who claimed descent from Muhammad, took power from the Chagatayid khans in the Tarim Basin. The Khojas divided into the Afaqi (White Mountain) and Ishaqi (Black Mountain) factions, who competed for power. After the Ishaqi's victory, the Afaq Khoja turned for help in 1677 to Tibet's leader, the 5th Dalai Lama, who in turn called on Buddhist followers within the Dzungar Khanate to act. The Dzungars took the Tarim Basin in 1680 and made the Afaqi Khoja their puppet. Later, Turfan's Uyghurs, whose ancestors had been Buddhist but who were now Muslim, held that "infidel Kalmuks" (the Dzungars) had built the Buddhist monuments of the area.

The Qing had controlled Xinjiang for a century by the 1860s, having seized it from the Dzungar Khanate in 1759; the Oirats who made up its population became victims of genocide. Because most of the region is semi-arid or desert, it did not attract Han settlers other than traders, and other peoples, such as the Uyghurs, moved in.

A rebellion by Hui Muslims and other Muslim peoples, the Dungan Revolt, ran from 1862 to 1877 across Shaanxi, Ningxia, Gansu and Xinjiang. Reports put the death toll at 20.77 million from fighting and migration, and many refugees starved. Thousands of refugees from Shaanxi escaped to Gansu, and some of them formed battalions in the east of the province with the aim of recapturing their lands. As the Hui rebels got ready to attack Gansu and Shaanxi, Yakub Beg, a commander from the Kokand Khanate who was either Uzbek or Tajik, left the khanate in 1865 after the Russians took Tashkent. He made Kashgar his base and soon ruled Xinjiang. He promoted trade and built caravanserais, canals and other irrigation works, yet his rule was considered harsh. On 16 May 1877 an army under General Zuo Zongtang, advancing rapidly on Kashgaria, recaptured it.

The Qing turned Xinjiang ("new frontier") into a regular province in 1884, following the reconquest from Yakub Beg in the late 1870s. This made it part of China proper and ended the older names Zhunbu (準部, Dzungar Region) and Huijiang (Muslimland). Afterwards many Uyghurs left the south for the fertile north and east of Xinjiang, sometimes helped by the Qing authorities.

After the Soviet Union invaded, the Xinjiang War of 1937 left the province under the control of Sheng Shicai, a Han warlord from the north-east. For a decade he governed with Soviet backing and adopted many Soviet policies on ethnic groups and security. The Soviets kept a military base there and posted a number of military and economic advisers. Sheng had invited some Chinese Communists to Xinjiang, Mao Zedong's brother Mao Zemin among them, but in 1943 he had all of them executed for fear of a plot. In 1944 the Soviets told Chiang Kai-shek, then President and Premier of China, that Sheng planned to defect to them, and Chiang moved him in 1945 to Chongqing as Minister of Agriculture and Forestry. During the Ili Rebellion, Uyghur separatists backed by the Soviets founded the Second East Turkestan Republic (ETR) in the Ili region, and the Kuomintang held on to most of the remaining territory.

sichuan-agricultural-university.h: Sichuan Agricultural University at a glance

blocks.x: Sichuan Agricultural University (usually abbreviated SCAU, and sometimes SAU) is an agriculture-focused public university based in Ya'an, Sichuan. It belongs to the provincial system. The Ministry of Education and Sichuan's provincial authorities share the job of sponsoring it, and it takes part in two national schemes: Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction.
Farming and forestry subjects are the heart of the university. Its registered office and main campus are in Ya'an, and it runs three campuses in all, divided between Ya'an and Chengdu.

The origin lies in the last years of the Qing Dynasty, a time when the country believed that better schooling would make it stronger. Sichuan's governor, Xu Handu, asked the imperial court for permission to open a secondary-level agricultural school in the province. In 1906, the 32nd year of the Guangxu reign, the Sichuan Provincial Agricultural School (四川通省农业学堂) was founded in Chengdu. Its home was a disused warehouse on the right-hand side of the Baochuan Bureau, within Houzaimen. No agricultural school had existed in Sichuan before, and this one is the historical root of the present university.

Teaching started on June 1, 1906, and the official opening took place on September 12. Governor Xiliang spoke to the gathering. He reminded his audience that Sichuan has vast tracts of rich farmland and was famed in antiquity as a land of plenty. It had once rivalled the rest of the world through profits from silk, but clung to old methods, and the profits gradually drained away. For that reason, he argued, farming education had to be promoted in order to prepare for renewing the farm economy.

At the start, the school ran preparatory and undergraduate courses in three fields, agriculture, forestry and silk farming (sericulture). It transferred in April 1910 to a newly built campus on the agricultural experimental field near Wangjianglou, beyond the east gate of Chengdu.

The 1911 Revolution brought a change: with the Sichuan Military Government's approval, the school was retitled Sichuan Higher Agricultural School (四川高等农业学校) and with college-level and secondary-level departments. It took the name Sichuan Public Agricultural School (四川公立农业专门学校) and began undergraduate courses in agriculture and sericulture.

Then, in August 1927, it was merged with five other specialised schools to create Public Sichuan University (公立四川大学). Four of its partners were the public schools of law and politics, of industry, of foreign languages and of national studies, each prefixed "Sichuan Public". The agricultural school turned into the university's College of Agriculture. The provincial government decided in 1931 that engineering and agricultural sciences should be separated into colleges of their own, and the agricultural one became Sichuan Provincial Agricultural College (四川省立农学院).

A further merger came in July 1935, when that college and the agricultural college of Chongqing University were absorbed by National Sichuan University (国立四川大学) to form its College of Agriculture. Development accelerated. Yang Kaiqu was appointed dean in November 1937. During a survey of Chinese higher education in 1943, the British scientist and historian of science and technology Joseph Needham, a biochemist, described agriculture as the strongest subject at Sichuan University, a strong vote of confidence in its College of Agriculture of the time.

sichuan-agricultural-university.h: Reorganisation and the move to Ya'an

blocks.x: When China restructured higher education in 1952, some departments were sent elsewhere, but others arrived. Majors in agronomy, forestry, animal husbandry and veterinary science came in from four institutions: Southwest Agricultural College, the agricultural college of Yunnan University, Chuanbei University and Xichang Technical College. This strengthened the college's foundation.

In 1956 the college relocated from Chengdu to Ya'an, where it became a school in its own right: Sichuan Agricultural College (四川农学院). Its founding ceremony in Ya'an took place on September 5, 1956. Guests included Deng Xihou, who was vice governor of the province, Zhao Mengming from the Provincial Agriculture Department, Kang Naier of the Provincial Higher Education Bureau, and local Party and government leaders. The school then counted 1,134 students and 515 members of faculty and staff, of whom 205 taught full time. In 1959 it launched three-year master's courses covering rice growing, corn breeding, feeding livestock, breeding poultry, and veterinary obstetrics and gynecology. The Cultural Revolution then halted them until 1978.

By the time college entrance exams returned in 1977, the college had six departments: forestry, horticulture, agricultural chemistry, agricultural machinery, agriculture, and a combined one for animal husbandry and veterinary medicine. Students could choose from nine majors. These were tea science, soil chemistry, agricultural economics, plus agriculture, animal husbandry, veterinary medicine, horticulture, forestry and agricultural machinery.
The later milestones are:
June 1985: the provincial people's government agreed to rename the school Sichuan Agricultural University (四川农业大学), and doctoral recruitment began that year.

June 14, 1999: the State Development Planning Commission admitted it to the "211 Project", to be built up during the "Ninth Five-Year Plan" period. That put it among the first group of key universities in the scheme.
July 2010: the university's Chengdu Scientific Research Institute was dissolved and turned into the Chengdu Campus.
October 2010: the Chengdu campus formally opened for use.
September 2017: SCAU was one of the first group of universities selected for the national "Double First-Class Construction".
The three sites cover roughly 300 hectares (740 acres) in total.
The Chengdu campus lies in Chengdu's Wenjiang District and holds a number of colleges and research institutes.

The Ya'an campus, in Yucheng District, is part of the fabric of Ya'an city. At over 200 hectares (490 acres), it is about a third of the whole city's area. The Fenjiang River splits it into an old campus and a new one.
The Dujiangyan campus, in the Chengdu-administered city of Dujiangyan, provides general and specialist undergraduate programs.

The university has 26 colleges, along with 4 research institutes (centers) and 2 state key laboratories. Ten major disciplines are covered: art, law, education, literature, medicine, management, economics, engineering, science and of course agriculture.
The degree-granting powers are broad:
8 post-doctoral research stations
Doctoral degrees in 11 first-level and 49 second-level disciplines, and in 1 category of professional doctorate
Master's degrees in 20 first-level and 100 second-level disciplines, and in 16 categories of professional master's degree
76 majors open to undergraduate enrollment
4 disciplines recognised as national key or key cultivation disciplines, and 20 key at ministry and provincial level

Rankings give some context. In the fourth national discipline evaluation round (2017), the university's overall score placed it 7th among Chinese agricultural and forestry universities and 4th among universities in Sichuan. ESI (Essential Science Indicators) puts nine of its fields in the world's top 1%. They are chemistry, engineering, microbiology and sociology, together with agricultural science, plant and animal science, biology and biochemistry, molecular biology and genetics, and environmental science and ecology.

On the Chengdu Campus you will find agriculture-related colleges (Agronomy, Animal Science and Technology, Veterinary Medicine, Forestry, Horticulture, Resources, Grassland Science and Technology) as well as Environmental Sciences, Landscape Architecture, Economics, Management and Marxism, along with an International College. The same campus has the Rice Research Institute, the Triticeae Research Institute, the Maize Research Institute, the Animal Nutrition Institute and the State Key Laboratories.
At the Ya'an Campus the following are based:
Colleges of Science and of Life Science
Colleges of Food Science and of Information Engineering
College of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering
College of Water Conservancy and Hydropower Engineering
College of Literature and Law, and College of Arts and Sports
College of Distance and Continuing Education
The Dujiangyan Campus accommodates the College of Architecture and Urban-Rural Planning, the College of Civil Engineering, the College of Tourism and the Business School.
The city around the campus decides much of your daily life, from weather to transport to leisure. This part introduces Chengdu, where several SCAU units are located.

Chengdu sits on a wide plain at an elevation of between 450 and 720 meters (1,480 and 2,360 feet). Along its northwest edge are the steep Longmen Mountains, and on the west the Qionglai range, which rises above 3,000 m (9,800 ft). Peaks there include Xiling Snow Mountain at 5,164 m (16,942 ft) and Miao Jiling, which stands at 5,364 m (17,598 ft). The western highlands also hold a large primeval forest with abundant wildlife and a giant panda habitat. In the east are the low Longquan Mountains and, bordering them, the hills of the middle Min River, an area where several rivers come together. Chengdu has long been known as "the Abundant Land", thanks to its fertile soil, favourable climate and the ingenious Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

In geographic terms, the city is on the Chengdu Plain, at the Sichuan Basin's western rim, and flat land is the main terrain type. The prefecture lies between latitudes 30° 05' and 31° 26' N, and longitudes 102° 54' and 104° 53' E. Measured east to west it spans 192 kilometers (119 mi), and south to north 166 km (103 mi), and its administered land is 12,390 km2 (4,780 sq mi). Its neighbours are Deyang (northeast), Ziyang (southeast), Meishan (south) and Ya'an (southwest), while the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture lies to the north.

Central Chengdu stands about 500 m (1,600 ft) above sea level and has several rivers, including the Jin, the Fu and the Sha. The landscape beyond the urban zone is more varied. Eastward you meet the Penzhong Hills (盆中丘陵) and the Longquan Mountains (龙泉山脉); westward the Qionglai Mountains climb to 5,364 m (17,598 ft) in Dayi County. The prefecture's highest place is Daxuetang, a name shared with Miaojiling, on Xiling Snow Mountain in Dayi County, and it is 5,364 meters high. The lowest is 359 meters, on the riverbank where the Tuojiang River flows out near Jianyang City.

Chengdu's climate is monsoon-influenced humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa). It is largely mild, and the air is humid throughout the year. Each of the four seasons is clear-cut, and the moderate rainfall mostly arrives in the warmer months, softening both hot summers and cold winters. Because the Qin Mountains (Qinling) far to the north deflect icy Siberian winds, winters are short and gentler than in the Lower Yangtze region. In January the daily mean temperature is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F). Snowfall is uncommon, though frost occurs on a few occasions each winter.

Summer is hot and sticky, but not as extreme as in Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing, the three "Three Furnaces" cities of the Yangtze basin. Daily averages across July and August hover near 25 °C (77 °F), and afternoons can touch 33 °C (91 °F). The prolonged heat typical of much of eastern China seldom occurs. Most rain falls in July and August, with little in the cool months.

Chengdu is among the cloudiest cities nationally, with less sunshine over a year than much of Northern Europe. The share of possible sunshine is 15 percent in December, climbing to 32 percent in August, for a yearly total of 1006 hours of bright sunshine. In general, March and April days are sunnier and warmer than those in October and November. Over a whole year the mean is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F), and the lowest and highest readings on record are -6.5 °C (20 °F) and 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).
Several milestones created today's Chengdu:

1988: the Implementation Plan for a Gradual Housing System Reform in Cities and Towns marked the start of housing reform across urban China. Over 20 property companies were founded in Chengdu, the first stage of its real estate growth.

The 1990s: a thorough clean-up of the Funan River helped the environment. The scheme earned the UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour in 1998, and in 2000 a "Local Initiative Award" from the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives.

From 1997: construction began on a project named Five Main Roads & One Bridge, with three roads for the east and two heading south. It created the Eastern and Southern sub-centers and so steered where people wanted to live, with many buildings going up east and south of the 2nd Ring Road. Renovation of the Shahe and Jin Rivers drew people to live beside them too. People joked that Chengdu's map should be redrawn every three months.

Late 1990s to early 2000s: a speculative housing boom. Dozens of commercial property projects arrived in 2000. While boosting the market, the government gave citizens large subsidies for a period to encourage home ownership, and housing became a commodity.

The New Century Global Center, which as of February 2026 is the third-largest building on Earth by floor area, stands in the city. The building is 100 meters (330 ft) tall, with a footprint of 500 by 400 meters (1,600 by 1,300 ft), and total floor area comes to 1,700,000 square meters (18,000,000 sq ft). It contains shops, cinemas, offices and hotels, a water park with an artificial beach and wave machine, and a Mediterranean-style village that includes a big 5-star hotel and an ice rink, with a parking area of 15,000 spaces.

Chengdu had 20,937,757 residents in the 2020 census. The metropolitan area proper, made up of the 12 urban districts and Guanghan City (which belongs to Deyang), had 16,045,577. It is Sichuan's largest city and China's fourth largest. By 2021 the figure was 21,192,000, and Chengdu had added more people than any other Chinese city. An estimate by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) gave the metropolitan area 18.1 million people in 2015.
China Daily placed Chengdu fourth among China's most livable cities in 2006.
Chengdu has a rich literary heritage, and its roll of writers includes:
Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, the two great masters of Fu, a literary form mixing descriptive prose with verse
Li Bai, regarded as the finest poet of the Tang, and Du Fu, the finest of the Song
Yang Shen'an, a celebrated scholar of the Ming dynasty
Guo Moruo and Ba Jin, who are well known as modern authors

Chang Qu, a Jin dynasty historian from Chengdu, compiled the Record of Hua Yang State, the earliest local historical record. Under the Later Shu Kingdom, the Chengdu poet Zhao Chongzuo edited the first anthology of Ci poetry in Chinese history, titled Among the Flowers. Meng Chang, Later Shu's king, composed the first Spring Festival couplet. It reads, roughly, that a harvest year receives celebrations and good festivals point to long springs.
More recently, Chengdu was chosen in 2021, ahead of Winnipeg in Canada, to host the 81st World Science Fiction Convention, which was held in 2023.

In the Five Dynasties period, the Chengdu painter Huang Quan and fellow artists founded the Fine-Brush Flower-and-Bird Painting School. The "Hanlin Painting Academy" of that era was the earliest royal academy in the country.

Muslims have lived in Sichuan since the Tang dynasty (618-907), and there are 12 mosques in Chengdu, among them the Huangcheng Mosque in the middle of the city, which dates from the 16th century. The city also has official, Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations, and a number of its churches operate underground.

On the Catholic side, the Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan, now the Diocese of Chengdu, was founded on 15 October 1696. Its first Apostolic Vicar was Artus de Lionne, a French missionary with the Paris Foreign Missions Society.

Protestant history in the city goes back to 1890, when the Canadian Methodist Mission was looking for extra stations in Asia. In February 1891, at a meeting, Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart proposed Chengtu as the site of its first mission. Hart had earlier served as Superintendent for Central China of the New York Methodist Mission Society, and between 1866 and 1888 he had built western hospitals and boys' and girls' schools at missions on the Yangtze and Gan Rivers. It was proposed that he should lead the party. He arrived in Chengtu on 9 May 1891, and two weeks later bought a house that he divided into living space and a dispensary for the missionary staff who would follow.

The mission's first headquarters opened its doors on 24 June 1892, and more than 1,000 local people attended. Only a few came to the first Methodist service the next Sunday. On 3 November 1892 the first western dispensary in Sichuan took in sixteen patients. The mission grew so popular that in spring 1893 it moved to larger premises close to Chengtu's East Gate, where a hospital and the city's first Methodist church, Sï-Shen-Tsï, were built. Rioters razed both in 1895, and the staff escaped to Chongqing and later to Shanghai. Dr. Hart travelled to Peking to demand redress, and Sichuan Viceroy Liu Ping Chang paid the full compensation. The compound was rapidly rebuilt but destroyed again in the riots of 1901. After the second reconstruction, later missionaries moved the boys' and girls' schools to a larger site south of the city and expanded them, and in 1914 the Divinity College was dedicated as Hart College. The college was part of the West China Union University (now Sichuan University) and of the West China School of Medicine, called Huaxiyida. In the Cultural Revolution the Sï-Shen-Tsï church was taken out of use and put in the care of the neighbouring Chengdu City Second People's Hospital, which turned the chapel into a kindergarten and an office for its equipment department. It was given back to the church in 1984.

In recent years there has been tension with the authorities. In December 2018 they tried to shut the Early Rain Covenant Church, an underground congregation of 500 people led by Pastor Wang Yi. More than 100 of its members were arrested, and the pastor and his wife were among them. Police raided the church's kindergarten and its theological college, and shut down its media channels. Before being detained, a member named Li Yingqiang said that the church's meetings would carry on even if only five people were left, since the faith was genuine, and that suffering for it was worth the cost. Police reportedly told one member that the church had been ruled an illegal organisation. Chinese media were barred from covering the story, though video that reached Western social media appeared to show arrests and injuries allegedly caused by police. A photograph of the detention warrant of a Ms. Jiang indicates that the leaders face the charge of "inciting subversion of state power", for which the maximum sentence is 15 years.
A Chabad Jewish Center was founded in Chengdu in 2012. It moved five times before it found a permanent site in Wuhou District.

A popular saying puts Shu opera above every other performance art in the world, a saying that reflects the standing of Sichuan opera and of Zaju, an old comic art that combined dancing, singing, poetry and miming. The city's first opera, titled "Bullfighting," dates from the Warring States period. The Shu Kingdom's royal court, in the Three Kingdoms era, saw the first opera with a detailed plot, and the earliest clearly documented Zaju in China was performed in Chengdu as well. Archaeologists have excavated tombs of witty Han dynasty poets in Chengdu. Sichuan opera is still known for face-changing masks and fire breathing.
Chengdu's native tongue is the Chengdu dialect, a variety of Sichuanese. It has had a notable effect on Chinese stand-up comedy and rap music.

Hot chilies and Sichuan peppercorns define the cuisine of Sichuan. Well-known dishes include Dan Dan Mien, Mapo doufu and Chengdu hot pot, with peppercorns used in both the noodles and the tofu dish. A 2006 Los Angeles Times piece labelled Chengdu "China's party city" because of its easygoing way of life. Though its population is under half of Shanghai's, it has more teahouses and more bars. In 2023 it had over 30,000 teahouses, plus 3,566 licensed bars, nightclubs and dance halls. A statistical report from 2019 had already shown more bars than Shanghai, the most of any Chinese city. Tea culture here is more than a thousand years old and goes back to the days when Chengdu began the Southern Silk Road. UNESCO has formally named it a "City of Gastronomy".

Teahouses are found all over the city. Some are elaborate and traditional, furnished with bamboo, while others are plain and modern. They serve jasmine, longjing and biluochun teas, and customers go there for mahjong, a massage or an ear cleaning. The bigger ones often stage live entertainment such as Sichuan opera.

Chengdu is equally known for hot pot, a traditional Sichuan meal in which vegetables, fish and/or meat are cooked in a bubbling, spicy broth. It suits a group of friends and is loved by locals and visitors alike, and you can find hot pot restaurants all over the city.
In 1992 the Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone was set up, and it is now the Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park.
The main highways around Chengdu are:
National Highway G5, linking Beijing and Kunming
National Highway G42, from Shanghai to Chengdu
National Highway G76, from Xiamen to Chengdu
National Highway G93, the Chengdu-Chongqing Ring
National Highway G4202, the Chengdu Ring

For applicants interested in agriculture, forestry, animal science or related subjects, SCAU offers a long-established programme, a national top-10 position among agricultural universities, and the choice of living either in compact Ya'an or in the large, lively city of Chengdu.
Sichuan Agricultural University lists 141 programs for international students on this site: 36 bachelor, 61 master's, 44 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 141 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 12,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 12,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.

141 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

sichuan-agricultural-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Sichuan Agricultural University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.
