Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chengdu, register at Sichuan Agricultural University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Sichuan International Studies University (SISU, 四川外国语大学) is a public research-focused university located in Chongqing, in southwest China. Despite the word Sichuan in its name, it is based in Chongqing, which was part of Sichuan Province until 1997. Among Chinese students it is known simply as Chuānwài (川外). It is counted among the first four higher education institutions in the country that specialise in foreign languages.

SISU presents itself as the flagship for foreign language teaching and information consultancy in the southwest. The most recent Wu Shulian ranking of Chinese universities puts it fourth among its peers, the universities specialising in international studies across China. For a language student, that is a useful signal: it is not the largest name in the field, but it is a recognised one.

The university started in the spring of 1950 as the Russian Training School of the Southwest Military University of the People's Liberation Army (PLA). (Different sources give April or May 1950 for the founding; the university itself can confirm the exact date.) It is the only university specialising in foreign languages in southwest China. Because it has a close connection with China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, it counts among the few schools that the ministry targets for recruitment.
The development of SISU is usually marked by six important dates:

April 1950: the PLA's Russian Training Corps was founded under the name of the Southwest University of Military and Political Sciences. Deng Xiaoping, Liu Bocheng and He Hong, along with other founding figures of the People's Republic of China.
January 1951: renamed the Russian Training Brigade of the PLA's Senior Infantry School No. 2.
November 1952: renamed the Russian Department of the Southwest People's Revolutionary University.
March 1953: renamed Southwest Russian College.
May 1959: renamed Sichuan Institute of Foreign Languages.
May 1990: renamed Sichuan International Studies University.
These stages show a clear path from a Russian-only military course to a broad modern language university.

Most Chinese students arrive after studying a liberal arts curriculum only in high school. The university has 12,000 registered students, with 8,000 of them on four-year and three-year undergraduate programmes, 2,500 in adult and continuing education, and the remainder on short-term training courses.

SISU employs 1,366 staff, including 929 full-time faculty. Of the teaching staff, 49.33% have senior professional titles and 48.22% have doctoral degrees. The university counts 184 recognitions of high-level talent. These include State Council Special Allowance holders, National Outstanding Educators and National Model Teachers, plus members of the Ministry of Education's Foreign Language Teaching Advisory Board, experts at provincial and ministerial level who have contributed outstandingly, and academic leaders with their reserve candidates, scholars on the Chongqing Talents Program, Bayu Scholars, and Chongqing Model Educators.

The language list is wide. Programmes cover 23 languages. Among the European ones are English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Romanian and Ukrainian. The Asian and Middle Eastern ones are Japanese, Korean, Thai, Vietnamese, Malay, Burmese, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, Hebrew and Arabic.

The curriculum has also gained non-language specialties for instance law and finance. There are also pedagogy, sociology, journalism, advertising and international politics, and Chinese language education for foreigners.

Several master's programmes are available, such as those in the language and literature of Russian, English, French, German and Japanese, and Comparative Literature and World Literature, among others. The university also offers doctoral programmes.

The main campus stands in Shapingba (Chongqing) at the foot of Mount Gele and beside the Jialing River, and it covers 770,000 square metres. It has won recognition as a "Garden Institution" from the city government of Chongqing in recognition of its greenery.

The university runs more than 110 teaching laboratories. It has created three municipal-level experimental teaching demonstration centres in Chongqing. The three are a foreign language laboratory centre, an integrated communication skills lab centre and a centre for simulating diplomacy and international affairs.

The library holds about 1.3 million printed volumes, written in 22 languages. Its digital collection has 1.85 million e-books and 64,460 e-journal titles with over 1 million volumes in total, and access to 99 academic databases.
The main academic units are listed below. Some language colleges carry two names, because they are also part of the Chongqing College of Multi-languages.
College of Online and Continuing Education
MOE Training Centre for Overseas Study
School of International Studies
Department of Physical Education
College of Language Intelligence, also called the College of General Education)
College of International Law and Sociology
College of International Education
College of Finance and Economics
School of International Business and Management
School of Journalism and Communication
College of Chinese Languages and Culture
School of International Relations
School of Marxism
Eastern Languages and Cultures College (also part of Chongqing College of Multi-languages)
Western Languages and Cultures College (part of Chongqing College of Multi-languages)
College of Russian Studies
College of Japanese Studies
College of German Studies
College of French Studies
School of Business English
College of Translation and Interpreting
School of English Studies

SISU has exchange and cooperation ties with over 140 universities and institutions in more than 30 countries and regions. It operates two joint education programmes approved by the Ministry of Education: a Sino-Australian programme in Business English and a Sino-French programme in Logistics Management. Together with partners it set up three Confucius Institutes: one with the N. A. Dobrolyubov State Linguistic University in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia; another with Togo's University of Lomé; and a third with an education service centre in the United States, the East Central Ohio Educational Service Center. A Confucius Classroom was also opened in Ecuador, at the Siyuan Academia de Lengua China.

In recent years it has been active in joint talent training from bachelor's through master's to doctoral level, plus faculty development programmes, research collaboration and international recruitment. It enrols over 400 international students a year on average and welcomes over 70 foreign experts and teachers for long or short stays. Every year it each year more than 100 of its teachers and over 600 of its students go overseas on exchange and teaching programmes. For international applicants, this means you would join a campus where foreign students and teachers are a regular presence.

sichuan-international-studies-university.h: Chongqing: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life depends on the city itself: its weather, how people travel and the things to do. We now describe Chongqing.

Chongqing is in the subtropics, in the transition zone between the Sichuan Basin and the middle and lower Yangtze plain. The monsoon is frequent, and late spring and early summer often bring rain at night. This "night rain in the Ba Mountains" appears in poems throughout Chinese history, including Li Shangyin's "Written on a Rainy Night, Sent to the North". The territory measures 470 kilometres (290 miles) at its longest from east to west and 450 kilometres (280 miles) at its widest from north to south. On the east it neighbours Hubei and Hunan, on the north Sichuan and Shaanxi, and on the south Guizhou.

The municipality covers a big area laced with rivers and mountains. The Daba Mountains rise to the north, Wu Gorge to the east, with the Wuling range to the southeast and the Dalou range to the south. The land slopes down from north to south toward the Yangtze valley, with a large mass of mountains and hills and steep slopes at various heights. Karst scenery is common, with stone forests, clusters of peaks, limestone caves and valleys in many places. The Longshuixia Gap (龙水峡地缝), with its Three Natural Bridges, is a popular tourist attraction.

The Yangtze crosses the entire area from west to east, over 665 kilometres (413 miles), cutting through the Wu Mountains in three places to form the famous Three Gorges: Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling. The Jialing River comes from the northwest, flows via the "Jialing Lesser Three Gorges" (Libi, Wentang and Guanyin), and joins the Yangtze in Chongqing.

The central urban area, known as Chongqing proper, stands on mountains and is partly surrounded by the Yangtze and Jialing. Its terrain has mountains and rivers, forests and springs, waterfalls, gorges and caves. Li Bai, the Tang dynasty poet, drew inspiration from this natural scenery and wrote an epigram about it. Zhongliang (中梁山) and Tongluo (铜锣山) are the mountains that roughly mark the western and eastern limits of the urban area. Several high mountains lie outside the centre, including Wugong Ling Mountain in Jiangjin, at 1,709.4 metres (5,608 feet).

The climate of Chongqing is a monsoonal humid subtropical one (Köppen Cwa), close to an ordinary humid subtropical climate (Cfa). Relative humidity is very high for most of the year, above 75% in every month. Together with Wuhan and Nanjing, the city is counted among the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze, with long summers that are some of China's hottest and most humid and in July and August the urban area sees highs of 34 °C (93 °F). Winters are short and rather mild, but damp and overcast.

Because the city is in the Sichuan Basin, its yearly sunshine is among the lowest in the country, only 983 hours, less than much of northern Europe. In the city proper, the possible sunshine share is a mere 5% in January and reaches 43% in August. The lowest temperature since 1951 was −1.8 °C (29 °F), logged 11 January 1955, and the highest was 43.7 °C (111 °F), logged 18 and 19 August 2022.

With more than 100 days of fog a year, Chongqing is called the "Fog City" (雾都). In spring and autumn a thick fog layer covers it for 68 days a year. In the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937 to 1945) this unusual weather may have helped protect the city from falling to the Imperial Japanese Army.

The 2020 national census counted 32,054,159 people in Chongqing, roughly 2.27% of China's total, which makes it the world's most populous city proper. The OECD estimated in 2010 that the metropolitan area around the central urban district had 17 million people. In 2020 Chongqing overtook Shanghai to become China's biggest municipality in urban population. By 2021 an estimated 70.4% of residents were urban and 29.6% rural, and in 2024 the urban population was 23.01 million.

The census recorded 50.55% of residents as male and 49.55% as female (the two figures add up to slightly more than 100, so treat them as approximate). By age, 15.91% were 0 to 14, 62.22% were 15 to 64 and 21.87% were 65 or older. For highest level of education, 15.41% had college, 15.96% high school, 30.58% middle school and 29.89% elementary school.

The main religious traditions are Chinese Buddhism, Taoist traditions and Chinese folk religions. Surveys from 2007 and 2009 showed 26.63% of the population following Chinese ancestral religion and 1.05% identifying as Christian. The reports gave no figures for other types of belief, so 72.32% may be either non-religious or else take part in nature deity worship, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or folk sects. For 2010 Chongqing had 9,056 Muslims.

Chongqing received heavy funding for industrial capacity under the Third Front campaign. The government has made a major effort to turn the city into an economic, trade and financial centre for the region and to use it as a platform for developing China's western interior. It is urbanising fast. Statistics suggest that new construction added around 137,000 square metres (1,470,000 square feet) of usable floor space every day to meet demand for homes, shops and factories. For this reason on 14 March 1997 Chongqing was split from Sichuan Province and became a municipality of its own, to speed up its development and, through it, that of China's poorer western regions (see the China Western Development strategy). The 2000s found it established as a key industrial area of the west.

In 2022 the nominal GDP of Chongqing reached US$433 billion (CN¥2.91 trillion), about 2.41% of China's GDP, ranking 16th among province-level units. Its three sectors contributed as follows: the primary sector (farming and similar activity) produced CN¥201.21 billion, equal to US$29.92 billion. Secondary industry came to CN¥1.169 trillion (US$173.86 billion), and the tertiary sector, mostly services, to CN¥1.542 trillion (US$229.3 billion). GDP per person was US$13,479 nominal (CN¥90,663), 10th in the country.

The Economist Intelligence Unit's November 2010 Access China White Paper named Chongqing as one of six cities grouped as CHAMPS, a group made up of Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang, part of a profile of the 20 leading emerging cities in China.

Because of its geographic remoteness, Chongqing and Sichuan have long been important military bases for weapons research and development. Industry in Chongqing is varied, but its exports are small compared with eastern China, because of its inland position. Instead, factories make goods for local consumers: cars, machinery, chemicals, textiles, electronics, sports equipment and processed food.

Chongqing is China's third-largest centre for motor vehicle production with the world-leading motorcycle output of any Chinese centre. In 2007 annual capacity was one million cars plus 8.6 million motorcycles. Leading makers include Changan Automotive Corp (China's fourth-biggest automaker) and Lifan Hongda Enterprise, and Ford Motor Company has three plants in the city. The municipality is also one of nine leading iron and steel producers in China and one of its three major aluminium producers. Among the important manufacturers are Southwest Aluminum (西南鋁業) and Chongqing Iron and Steel Company (重庆钢铁股份有限公司), Asia's largest aluminium plant.
Farming remains significant, with rice and fruit, especially oranges, as the main produce.

Chongqing is rich in resources, with big deposits of coal and natural gas, and over 40 kinds of minerals, among them strontium and manganese. Coal reserves are about 4.8 billion metric tons. The The largest inland gas field in China, the Chuandong Natural Gas Field, holds around 270 billion cubic metres, more than a fifth of the national total. The city has China's largest strontium reserve (China has the world's second-biggest strontium deposit), and the Xiushan area produces manganese, though the mining industry has been criticised as heavily polluting and unsafe.

A 10-million-ton refinery run by CNPC (parent company of PetroChina) is planned for Chongqing to process crude oil imported through the Sino-Myanmar pipelines. The pipeline, not finished at the time of the source, would run from Sittwe on Myanmar's west coast via Kunming in Yunnan to Chongqing, and supply China with fuel sourced in Africa, the Middle East and Myanmar.

Chongqing has recently tried to climb the value chain by shifting toward high-technology and knowledge-intensive industries, with new development zones, the Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ) being one). By promoting favourable policies that favour the electronics and IT sectors, the local government hopes to build a 400-billion-RMB high-technology manufacturing hub that will surpass the automotive sector and provide 25% of exports.

Chongqing has also put large sums into infrastructure to draw in business. Road and rail links to the rest of China have been expanded and improved, which reduces logistics costs. The Three Gorges Dam nearby, the largest in the world, supplies power to Chongqing and lets oceangoing ships reach its Yangtze River port. These improvements have attracted many foreign direct investors in sectors from cars to finance and retail, including Ford and Mazda in vehicles, banks such as HSBC, Standard Chartered, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, ANZ and Scotiabank, and retailers Wal-Mart, Metro AG and Carrefour.
Chongqing has several economic and technological development zones:
Liangjiang New Area, which contains the Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center, China's biggest of its type
Jianqiao Industrial Park, in Dadukou District
Chongqing Export Processing Zone
Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ)
Chongqing Hi-Tech Industry Development Zone
Chongqing Economic & Technological Development Zone
Chongqing Chemical Industrial Park
Chongqing belongs, with Chengdu and Xi'an, to the West Triangle Economic Zone.

Since it became a national-level municipality in 1997, Chongqing has hugely expanded its infrastructure. With railways and expressways built to the east and southeast, it is a major transport hub in southwest China. In October 2014 there were 31 bridges over the Yangtze in the municipality, including over a dozen in the urban core. Apart from the first two, built in 1960 and 1977, all were finished after 1995.

Public transport includes the metro, intercity railway, a bus system found everywhere and the world's largest monorail network. In May 2007 the municipal government announced an ambitious plan: Chongqing would spend RMB 150 billion across 13 years to complete a network combining underground metro lines with heavy monorail.

As of 2017 there were four lines. The first is the 14-kilometre (8.7 mi) CRT Line 1, a conventional subway. Next is the 19-kilometre (12 mi) heavy monorail called CRT Line 2 (up to Phase II). Line 3 is a heavy monorail that links the airport and the south of downtown. Line 6 runs from Beibei, a district in the far north, into downtown. Late in 2017 Line 5 opened.

The plan called for CRT to have six lines and one loop line by 2020, adding 363.5 kilometres (225.9 mi) of track to the 2012 network and 93 new stations on top of the 111 stations that existed in 2012. By 2050 Chongqing is meant to have 18 lines. These are planning targets, so look at an up-to-date transit map before you travel.

Chongqing is the only city in China to have kept public aerial tramways. There used to be three: the Jialing River Tramway, the South Mountain Tramway and the Yangtze River Tramway. Only the Yangtze River Tramway still operates, and it is now a Class 4A tourist attraction. It is 1,160 metres (3,810 feet) long, joins the north and south shores of the Yangtze, and carries about 10,000 passengers a day.

Chongqing railway station, in Yuzhong, is reached by Metro Lines 1 and 3 (Lianglukou station). It is the city's oldest station, close to the Jiefangbei central business district, and handles mostly long-distance trains. A big renovation is planned, so many services have moved to Chongqing North.
Chongqing North railway station handles many long-distance and high-speed trains to Chengdu, Beijing and other cities. Finished in 2006, it has a link to the metro.
Chongqing West railway station, in Shapingba, handles many long-distance and high-speed services to many cities. It was completed in 2018.

Shapingba railway station, near the Shapingba central business district, can be reached from Shapingba metro station, which serves Lines 1 and 9 and the Loop line. Many local and regional trains and was completed in 2018. The main campus is also in Shapingba, so this district is worth knowing for transport.
The newest, Chongqing East railway station, began operating in 2025.

Rail freight heads to Chongqing in large volumes, with improved handling facilities, and subsidies and incentives that have led many factories to relocate or be built in the city have greatly increased rail traffic. It is a major regional rail hub, with these lines:
Lanzhou-Chongqing railway, going to Gansu Province
Chongqing-Lichuan railway, going to Hubei Province
Suining-Chongqing railway, going to Sichuan Province
Chongqing-Huaihua railway, going to Hunan Province
Xiangyang-Chongqing railway, going to Hubei Province
Sichuan-Guizhou railway, to Guiyang in Guizhou Province
Chengdu-Chongqing railway, to Chengdu in Sichuan Province

The Chongqing People's Broadcast Station is the city's biggest radio station. Chongqing TV is the only TV network at municipal level, said to rank fourth among China's television stations. It broadcasts many locally oriented channels and can be seen on many TV sets across China.
Sichuan International Studies University lists 98 programs for international students on this site: 41 bachelor, 44 master's, 12 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 97 taught in Chinese, 1 taught in Chinese and English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 15,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.

98 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

sichuan-international-studies-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Sichuan International Studies University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chongqing, register at Sichuan International Studies University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Sichuan University, usually shortened to SCU, is a state-run comprehensive university in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province in south-west China. It sits under the Ministry of Education, which also provides its funding, and it belongs to the group of institutions picked out for national investment under Project 211, the Project 985 scheme and the Double First-Class Construction programme. For an international applicant, that combination of central-government backing and wide subject coverage is the main reason SCU appears on so many shortlists.

The university in its present form is quite young, even though its roots are old. Chengdu University of Science and Technology merged with the older Sichuan University in 1994 to create Sichuan Union University, which took the name Sichuan University again in 1998. In 2000 West China University of Medical Sciences was folded in as well, and that final merger produced the institution you would apply to today.

Sichuan University is among the oldest modern universities in China. Today's institution grew from three main strands: the school that became National Sichuan University in 1931, a technical college that grew into Chengdu University of Science and Technology (usually called CUST), and a medical school whose origins lie with West China Union University. The 1896 founding date is the one given by the International Association of Universities, and the mergers of 1994 and 2000 then shaped what exists now. The sections below follow each strand in turn.

The direct ancestor of the modern university is the Sichuan Chinese and Western School. In 1895 Lu Chuanlin, who was governor of Sichuan at the time, asked the Guangxu Emperor for permission to open a modern school in Chengdu that would teach Chinese and Western learning side by side. The school welcomed its first students on 18 June 1896. English and French were on the timetable from the start, with mathematics added a year later, and the school was run in a modern way: teaching was divided by subject and progress was tracked with something close to a credit system.

Over the next few years the school absorbed older Chengdu academies. In 1902 it joined Zunjing Academy, a Qing-period institution, and the combined body became the Sichuan Provincial University Hall. Before that year ended it was renamed again, as Sichuan Provincial Capital Higher School. Jinjiang Academy, another Qing-dynasty foundation, was brought in during 1903. These academies count as part of the university's family tree, but both the university itself and the World Higher Education Database treat 1896 as the date its modern story starts.

sichuan-university.h: Republican years and National Sichuan University

blocks.x: After the 1911 Revolution and the creation of the Republic of China, the Provincial Higher School was renamed Sichuan Government Higher School. In 1916 another reorganisation moved its staff, students and property into Sichuan Higher Normal School, which in turn became National Chengdu Higher Normal School.

Changes to higher education during the 1920s split that normal school. National Chengdu University was set up in 1926 from part of it, offering humanities, sciences and law, while the teacher-training side grew into National Chengdu Normal University. Separately, in 1927 five provincially run specialist schools in agriculture, engineering, law and politics, foreign languages and Chinese studies were consolidated as Public Sichuan University. Its colleges were literature (Chinese and foreign), law and politics, engineering, and agriculture.

On 9 November 1931 Public Sichuan University, National Chengdu University and National Chengdu Normal University were united under one name, National Sichuan University. That gave Chengdu a single comprehensive state university, and over the following years it added colleges covering agriculture, engineering, law, the sciences, the humanities and teacher training.

War badly interrupted this progress. Chengdu was a target for Japanese bombers during the Second Sino-Japanese War, and on 27 July 1939 bombs hit the campus, wrecking or damaging many buildings. To keep students and staff safe, the university moved to Mount Emei that same year and carried on teaching there. It came back to Chengdu in 1943 and settled in the area that is now the Wangjiang Campus. By 1949 it had six colleges and 25 academic departments.

sichuan-university.h: West China Union University and medical education

blocks.x: A second line of descent, which joined only in 2000, starts with West China Union University, which Protestant missionary societies from the United States, Canada and Britain set up in Chengdu, and it opened in 1910 with 11 students. The 1911 Revolution interrupted its work, but the arts and sciences programme reopened in 1913, and a medical faculty began teaching in 1914. Medicine and dentistry went on to become the heart of the university's academic life.

When the Communist party took control of Chengdu in 1949, the new people's government assumed responsibility for this privately run university, and in 1951 it became West China University. The central government's national reshuffle of higher education in the early 1950s then sent its non-medical departments to other institutions, while its medical and health programmes became the foundation of Sichuan Medical College in 1953. That college gained university status in 1985 and took the name West China University of Medical Sciences.

sichuan-university.h: Reshaping after 1949 and the engineering branch

blocks.x: In September 1950 National Sichuan University formally became Sichuan University, and soon afterwards it went through heavy reorganisation as part of a national overhaul of Chinese higher education. The 1950s reforms followed the Soviet model of specialised institutions: professional faculties were taken out of comprehensive universities and departments were shuffled between campuses. As a result, Sichuan University changed from a broad comprehensive university into one centred mostly on the humanities and basic sciences.

The reshuffle also created a second, engineering line of descent. Sichuan University's former College of Engineering broke away in August 1954 as the independent Chengdu Engineering College, teaching mechanical, electrical, civil and hydraulic engineering among other fields. A year later, in 1955, it took in the Sichuan Chemical Engineering College, itself assembled from engineering and chemical resources across south-west China as departments were moved around. In 1978 the merged college became Chengdu University of Science and Technology, known as CUST, one of the country's designated national key universities.

SCU was itself named a national key university in 1960. The Cultural Revolution hit it as hard as the rest of Chinese higher education, and its archives show that regular student admissions stopped for most of the years between 1967 and 1976. Teaching and degree study expanded again once the reform era began in 1978.

By the late 1980s Chengdu had three large neighbouring institutions: Sichuan University, CUST and West China University of Medical Sciences. Their strengths complemented each other, with the first leading in humanities and sciences, the second in engineering and the third in medicine. When they were later merged, the push came from another national restructuring, this time in favour of large multidisciplinary universities.

sichuan-university.h: The mergers that made today's university

blocks.x: Sichuan University and CUST were merged in April 1994 into Sichuan Union University. It was one of the best-known early cases of the wave of mergers in Chinese higher education during the 1990s. Researchers who study these reforms point out that joining large institutions can be hard, with difficulties in administration, in institutional identity and in how academic work is organised, and the Sichuan University and CUST combination became an important example in discussions of that process.
The new Sichuan Union University joined the Project 211 programme in its first phase, in 1996, and in December 1998 the Education Ministry approved reviving the name Sichuan University.

The final big merger took place in September 2000. The State Council and the Ministry of Education approved a union of Sichuan University with West China University of Medical Sciences; the new Sichuan University replaced both older bodies, which stopped existing as separate legal entities. What had been the medical university now forms the West China Medical Center, and it keeps alive the medical and dental heritage that began at West China Union University.

Put simply, the two mergers combined three academic cultures: humanities and sciences from Sichuan University, engineering and applied sciences from CUST, and health sciences from West China University of Medical Sciences. Together they make up the multidisciplinary university of today.

SCU is a comprehensive research university under the direct control of China's Ministry of Education. Its teaching falls into 13 broad disciplinary categories, ranging from literature, science and engineering to medicine, economics and management, and on to law and history, philosophy, education, the arts, agriculture and interdisciplinary studies. In 2026 the university counted 37 schools and departments organised by discipline, with the Overseas Education College alongside them.

SCU has been part of each of China's national programmes for building leading universities: Project 211, Project 985 and later the Double First-Class Construction. When the first Double First-Class discipline list came out, six SCU disciplines made it: mathematics, chemistry, basic medicine, stomatology, nursing and materials science and engineering. Those same six stayed the core disciplines in the second construction cycle, so they are a good guide to where the university is strongest.

Undergraduate study at SCU combines subject training with general education and interdisciplinary courses. As reported by the Ministry of Education in 2021, the university then had 64 nationally recognised first-class undergraduate courses, and small-class, inquiry-based teaching had spread across much of the undergraduate curriculum. National training bases for foundational subjects have covered chemistry, mathematics, biology, basic medicine, and Chinese language and literature. By 2025 the ministry described the university as expanding doctoral and interdisciplinary training in artificial intelligence, medical technology, new energy, new materials and carbon-neutral technologies.

Medicine is taught through the West China Medical Center, which inherits the legacy of West China Union University. Five units do the teaching: the schools of Basic Medical Sciences and Forensic Medicine, Clinical Medicine, Stomatology, Public Health and Pharmacy, each carrying the West China name. Clinical training and medical research are tied to four hospitals: West China Fourth Hospital, West China Hospital of Stomatology, West China Second University Hospital and the flagship West China Hospital.

In February 2026 the university listed 37 schools and academic departments organised by discipline, together with the Overseas Education College, the unit for international students. Its academic directory also includes specialised research, interdisciplinary and joint-education units beyond these schools. The schools fall broadly into four groups:
Humanities and social sciences
Natural sciences
Engineering and interdisciplinary fields
Medicine and health sciences, gathered in the West China Medical Center

Beyond the schools there are the Sichuan University-Pittsburgh Institute, the College of Excellent Engineers and other joint or specialised programmes. There are also research institutes that recruit graduate students yet sit outside the discipline-based schools; examples cover frontier medical science, religious studies, nuclear science and technology, and atomic and molecular physics.

Research at SCU reaches across the natural sciences, engineering and medicine as well as the humanities and social sciences. For 2026 it listed a single national major science-and-technology infrastructure facility, along with 19 further national-level platforms (national laboratories, engineering research centres, clinical research centres and engineering laboratories). Four more national platforms had just been organised, and four others serve the social sciences.

The university hosts three national key laboratories, covering biotherapy, oral disease prevention and control, and the protection and governance of mountain rivers. The oral-disease one started life in 2007 as a State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases and received its present name when it was reorganised in 2023.

A large share of the output is biomedical and clinical. National clinical and translational research platforms run by the West China medical bodies address oral disease, biotherapy and clinical medicine. Engineering and physical-science work clusters around materials, polymers, chemistry and chemical engineering, plus water resources, biomedical engineering, electronics and energy.

A flagship project is the Sichuan arm of the national major science and technology infrastructure for translational medicine, a multi-site facility centred on biotherapeutic translational medicine. Part of it stands on the Huaxi Campus of West China Hospital and the rest is placed at other sites around Chengdu. The clinical-research core at the hospital opened in 2021, followed by the university's biotherapy translational-medicine building. Separately, an integrated Carbon Resource Neutrality research platform investigates turning waste carbon products into green materials and fuels.

The Nature Index tracks articles in a chosen set of applied, health, natural and social-science journals. Over the rolling year from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 it ranked SCU 12th in the world and 11th in China on research output share, with chemistry and health sciences accounting for much of it. Other editions of the index put the university 8th among universities in China and the Asia-Pacific region and 9th among universities worldwide.

In national terms, SCU belongs to the top tier of Project 985 and is one of just two western Chinese universities (Xi'an Jiaotong University is the other) counted among the leading 15 comprehensive research universities in the country. It also holds first place in south-west China, a region of Chongqing, Sichuan, Guizhou, Yunnan and Tibet that is home to over 180 million people.

On the international side, SCU stands out among Chinese universities for reputation: the Times Higher Education world reputation table placed it at No.61 globally as of 2022. For 2026 the Academic Ranking of World Universities put it 77th globally, 15th in Asia and 10th in China, while U.S. News listed it 139th among its best global universities. The 2025 CWTS Leiden Ranking has it 4th worldwide on total publications and 9th for publications within the top 1% of their fields, 2020-2023. Rankings measure different things and change every year, so treat these figures as a snapshot and check the latest editions before you decide.
Rankings measure different things and change every year, so treat these figures as a snapshot and check the latest editions before you decide.

SCU is spread over four campuses named Wangjiang, Huaxi, Jiang'an and Meishan. Three of these are in Chengdu, while Meishan is in the neighbouring city of the same name. Together the university reports a campus area of 8,050 mu, about 5.37 km2 (1,330 acres). Academic units are spread across the four campuses rather than run as four separate universities, so which campus you live on depends mainly on your school.

Wangjiang, in Chengdu's Wuhou district, is where the university's administration sits. Its role as the main campus began in the Republican era, with the move there in the 1940s, and the site has kept growing. Engineering and natural-science teaching and research, along with much of the humanities and social sciences, is based here. You will find the Liberal Arts and Sciences Library, the Engineering Library, laboratories, engineering research buildings, offices, sports facilities and student residences.

Some of the oldest buildings enjoy heritage protection. The State Council's seventh batch of nationally protected Major Historical and Cultural Sites, announced in 2013, includes SCU's early buildings dating from 1913 to 1954: historic structures at Huaxi and the former administrative building at Wangjiang.

Huaxi Campus, historically called Huaxiba, is the main base of the West China Medical Center, also in Wuhou. It began as West China Union University's campus and still has many early 20th-century buildings; these historic structures are part of the nationally protected group mentioned above. Here you find the West China schools of basic medical sciences and forensic medicine and of pharmacy, plus other medical teaching and research facilities, while the clinical, stomatology and public-health institutions are located in the Huaxi area and at nearby hospital sites. The Medical Library, especially strong in medicine and stomatology, is on this campus.

The medical complex works hand in hand with four main teaching hospitals: the Fourth Hospital, the Stomatology hospital, the Second University Hospital and West China Hospital itself, all with the West China name. Alongside the medical center's schools and laboratories, they supply clinical teaching, biomedical research and specialist care.

Jiang'an is in Shuangliu, another part of Chengdu. Construction got under way in the early 2000s, and students arrived in September 2003. The plan centres on landscaped waterways and open spaces, and the campus serves as a main base for undergraduates and general education. It has the Jiang'an Library, laboratory buildings, teaching complexes, a gymnasium, athletic grounds, halls of residence and a landscaped waterway that runs for almost one kilometre.

The Jiang'an Library, finished in 2005, covers roughly 272,000 sq ft (25,300 m2). It is a general library serving foundational study and humanities and social-science research. Several schools use the campus for teaching, administration or research, among them humanities and arts units and interdisciplinary and engineering programmes, and the Institute for Disaster Management and Reconstruction, a joint venture with Hong Kong Polytechnic University, is also located here.

Meishan is the university's newest campus, and the first one beyond Chengdu, in the Dongpo district of Meishan city. The Ministry of Education approved it in December 2020; a construction agreement between the university and Meishan's city government followed in January 2021, and first-phase building started in 2023. The first students and staff moved in during September 2025.

Phase one has about 3,700,000 sq ft (340,000 m2) of floor space in more than 20 buildings. These include Dongpo Academy, a library, a gymnasium, teaching halls, and research buildings for new materials, smart energy and smart water engineering. The campus is meant for advanced research, interdisciplinary teaching, technology transfer, continuing education and cooperation between the university and local government.

Wangjiang is the administrative centre and houses a broad mix of humanities, social-science, science and engineering units. Huaxi is where medical and health-sciences teaching and research is concentrated. Jiang'an carries much of the undergraduate teaching and also hosts academic and interdisciplinary units. Meishan, in use since 2025, is growing mainly into a base for technology transfer, advanced training, interdisciplinary research and university-region partnerships.

The library system was formed when the libraries of the former Sichuan University, CUST and West China University of Medical Sciences were combined. Four main branches exist: two at Wangjiang (Liberal Arts and Sciences, and Engineering), the Medical Library at Huaxi, and the Jiang'an Library. Historic holdings range from Chinese thread-bound books and rare editions to local Sichuan materials, newspapers and periodicals from before 1949, and specialist engineering and medical collections.

The Sichuan University Museum traces back to an antiquities museum that West China Union University set up in the early 20th century. Today it holds over 80,000 historical and cultural objects, plus extensive zoological, botanical, ethnographic and archival collections. A newly built museum, with more than 650,000 sq ft (60,000 m2) of floor space, of which around 110,000 sq ft (10,000 m2) is exhibition space, started trial operation in 2023, and the Sichuan Provincial Cultural Heritage Administration announced in May 2024 that it had been designated a National First-Class Museum. Elsewhere on campus you can find a university-history exhibition, medical and dental history displays, art and cultural spaces, and memorials to alumni and key events.

Because SCU was formed from several predecessors, the people associated with it include alumni and teachers from National Sichuan University, from CUST and its forerunners, and from West China Union University together with its medical successors.

Zhu De, a military commander and politician, one of the People's Liberation Army's Ten Marshals who later led the National People's Congress as chairman of its Standing Committee; the university and People's Daily name him as a graduate by way of its predecessor institutions.
Guo Moruo, a poet, writer, historian and archaeologist, linked to the predecessor schools and counted among the notable alumni.
Ba Jin, the novelist and essayist whose books include Family.
Jiang Zhuyun, a Communist revolutionary remembered as "Sister Jiang"; she studied at National Sichuan University, which commemorates her in a memorial and historical exhibition.
Dai Bingguo, a diplomat who served as State Councillor from 2008 to 2013; he studied Russian and graduated from the Department of Foreign Languages in 1964.
Jung Chang, the British-Chinese author of Wild Swans, who studied English at SCU before she left for postgraduate study in Britain in 1978.

Zhang Xingdong, who works on biomedical materials; he is a member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a foreign member of the US National Academy of Engineering, graduated in 1960 and later became a professor at the university.
Meng Daqiao, a nuclear-materials scientist and Academy of Sciences member, who took his Department of Chemistry degree in 1980 and his doctorate from the university in 2002.

Zhao Ermi, a herpetologist elected to the Chinese Academy of Sciences, who began in 1947 in the biology department at West China Union University, graduated in 1951 and later became professor and doctoral supervisor at SCU.
Zhang Lan, educator and political figure, first president of National Chengdu University, one of the main predecessors of National Sichuan University.

Wu Yuzhang, a revolutionary, historian and educator who was president of Chengdu Higher Normal School, an SCU predecessor, from 1922 to 1924 and later became the first president of Renmin University of China.

Ke Zhao, a mathematician and Academy of Sciences member who was SCU's professor, president and later honorary president; his research covered number theory and combinatorics, and the Erdos-Ko-Rado theorem carries his name alongside Paul Erdos and Richard Rado.

Xu Xi, a polymer scientist elected to the Chinese Academy of Sciences, who taught successively at the Chengdu Institute of Technology, CUST, Sichuan Union University and then SCU, and who pioneered polymer-materials teaching and research in China.
Liu Yingming, a mathematician and Academy member who joined in 1963 and later served as vice president, dean of the graduate school and director of the Institute of Mathematics.
Zhang Xingdong, whose research helped make biomaterials a major field at the university and who joined the Chinese Academy of Engineering in 2007.
Zhao Ermi, whose posts included professor and doctoral supervisor at SCU as well as researcher at the Chengdu Institute of Biology, which belongs to the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Day-to-day student life depends heavily on the city around the campus: its landscape, its weather, its transport and its leisure options. The rest of this overview describes Chengdu.

Chengdu stands on a broad plain between 450 and 720 meters (1,480-2,360 ft) above sea level. To the north-west rise the steep Longmen Mountains, and to the west the Qionglai range, which tops 3,000 m (9,800 ft) and includes Miao Jiling, 5,364 m high (17,598 ft), and Xiling Snow Mountain at 5,164 m (about 16,942 ft). The western uplands also hold a large primitive forest, rich in wildlife and home to giant pandas. Low Longquan Mountains lie east of the city, and on the west side are the hills of the middle Min River, a spot where several rivers meet. Chengdu has been called "the Abundant Land" since ancient times, owing to fertile soil, a favourable climate and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

More precisely, the city sits on the western rim of the Sichuan Basin, on the Chengdu Plain, so flat land dominates. The prefecture spans latitude 30° 05' to 31° 26' N and longitude 102° 54' to 104° 53' E, measuring 119 mi (192 kilometers) east to west and 103 mi (166 km) north to south, and 4,780 sq mi (12,390 km2) of land are under its administration. Its neighbours are Deyang to the north-east, Ziyang to the south-east, Meishan to the south, Ya'an to the south-west and, to the north, Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture. The urban area, at 500 m (1,600 ft), has a few rivers, among them the Jin, Fu and Sha.

Away from the city centre the terrain becomes more varied. The Longquan Mountains and the Penzhong Hills lie to the east, and the Qionglai Mountains to the west climb to 17,598 ft (5,364 m) in Dayi County, which is also the highest point: Daxuetang, also called Miaojiling, on Xiling Snow Mountain, at 5,364 meters. The lowest is the riverbank where the Tuojiang River leaves Jianyang City, at 359 meters.

Chengdu has a humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon (Köppen Cwa), warm for most of the year with high humidity throughout. There are four distinct seasons, and moderate rainfall falls mainly in the warm months, so neither the summers nor the winters feel extreme. Far to the north, the Qin Mountains (Qinling) block much of the cold Siberian wind, which makes the short winter milder than in the Lower Yangtze region. January averages 5.9 °C (42.6 °F). Snow is rare, but there are a few frosty spells each winter.

Summer is hot and humid, yet it does not reach the level of Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing, the "Three Furnaces" cities that all sit in the Yangtze basin. Across July and August the 24-hour mean is about 25 °C (77 °F), and afternoon highs can occasionally reach 33 °C (91 °F); the long, sustained heat common across eastern China is unusual. Rain is most frequent in July and August and scarce in the cooler months.

Be ready for grey skies. Chengdu is among the least sunny cities in China, getting less sun than much of Northern Europe: 1006 hours of bright sunshine a year, with possible sunshine at 15 percent in December and 32 percent in August. Spring (March-April) is generally sunnier and warmer during the day than autumn (October-November). Annual mean temperature is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F); the record range runs from a low of -6.5 °C (20 °F) up to 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).

sichuan-university.h: How the city has been built up

blocks.x: Housing reform helped drive Chengdu's growth. A 1988 national plan for gradually reforming the housing system in cities and towns kicked off urban housing reform across China, and more than 20 real estate firms were set up in Chengdu, the first step in its property development.

The 1990s brought environmental work too, notably a sweeping clean-up of the Funan River. It earned the UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour Award in 1998, and in 2000 the "Local Initiative Award" from International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives.

Work on the Five Main Roads and One Bridge project started in 1997: three roads for the east and two heading south. This created the base for the Eastern and Southern sub-centers and set the direction of residential growth, with new buildings clustering east and south of the 2nd Ring Road. Cleaning up the Shahe River, along with the Jin River scheme, likewise drew residents to live beside both waterways. People said that Chengdu's map had to be redrawn every three months.

Property speculation boomed from the late 1990s into the early 2000s, with dozens of commercial real estate projects appearing in 2000. As the government built up the property market, it urged citizens to buy their own homes and offered considerable subsidies for a time, so housing became a commodity.

The New Century Global Center, which as of February 2026 is the world's third-largest building by floor area, stands in the city. It rises 100 meters (330 ft) and measures about 1,600 by 1,300 ft (500 by 400 meters), giving 18,000,000 sq ft (1,700,000 square meters) of floor space. Inside are shops, cinemas, offices and hotels, a water park with an artificial beach and waves, and a Mediterranean-style village that includes a large 5-star hotel, plus an ice rink and a 15,000-space car park.

China's 2020 census counted 20,937,757 people in the municipality; 16,045,577 of them live in the metropolitan area proper, which covers the 12 urban districts and Guanghan City (administered by Deyang). It is Sichuan's largest city and the fourth largest in China. A 2021 estimate of 21,192,000 means Chengdu gained more residents than any other Chinese city. By the OECD's estimate, the metropolitan area held 18.1 million people in 2015.
China Daily ranked Chengdu the fourth most livable city in China back in 2006, and the city has a reputation for a relaxed way of life that students tend to enjoy.

Many of China's most important literary figures have links to Chengdu. Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, both masters of the Fu form of descriptive prose and verse, lived here, as did the poets Li Bai and Du Fu, towering figures of Chinese verse, and Yang Shen'an, a noted Ming-dynasty scholar. In modern times the city produced Guo Moruo and Ba Jin. Chang Qu, a Jin-dynasty historian of the city, compiled the Record of Hua Yang State, the earliest local history. Under the Later Shu Kingdom, the poet Zhao Chongzuo edited Among the Flowers, China's first anthology of Ci, and King Meng Chang is credited with the first Spring Festival couplet, which wishes for a harvest year that welcomes celebration and for festivals that herald long springs.
In 2023 the city staged the 81st World Science Fiction Convention, having won the 2021 site-selection vote against Winnipeg in Canada.

In painting, the Five Dynasties-era Chengdu artist Huang Quan helped found, together with fellow painters, the school of fine-brush flower-and-bird painting. The Hanlin Painting Academy of the day was China's earliest royal academy.

Locals say Shu opera has no rival anywhere, a nod to Sichuan opera and Zaju, an old comic form of dance, song, poetry and mime. The city's first opera, called "Bullfighting", dates to the Warring States period, and the first detailed one was staged at the Shu Kingdom's royal court during the Three Kingdoms period. China's first clearly recorded Zaju was performed in Chengdu as well, and tombs of witty Han-dynasty poets have been excavated here. Face-changing masks and fire breathing are still hallmarks of Sichuan opera.

The local language is the Chengdu dialect, a form of Sichuanese, which has had a strong influence on Chinese comedy and rap music. Standard Mandarin will get you through university, but a few local phrases go down well.

Islam arrived in Sichuan as early as the Tang dynasty (618-907), and Chengdu now has 12 mosques; Huangcheng Mosque in the city centre dates from the 16th century. Congregations here are official, Roman Catholic and Protestant, with some meeting as underground churches. The Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan, today the Diocese of Chengdu, was established on 15 October 1696 with Artus de Lionne of the Paris Foreign Missions Society as its first Apostolic Vicar.

The Protestant story links directly to the university. The Canadian Methodist Mission was searching for further stations in Asia in 1890, and in February 1891 Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart recommended Chengtu for the first one. Hart, previously Superintendent for Central China at the New York Methodist Mission Society, had built western hospitals and schools for boys and girls at missions along the Yangtze and Gan Rivers between 1866 and 1888, so he was proposed to lead the group. He arrived in Chengtu on 9 May 1891 and two weeks later bought a house, which he divided into living quarters and a dispensary for missionary staff arriving later.

The first Protestant Mission Headquarters opened its doors on 24 June 1892, welcoming over 1,000 people from the community. Only a handful came to the first Methodist service the following Sunday, and the first western dispensary in Sichuan took in sixteen patients on 3 November 1892. The mission grew so popular that a larger plot near Chengtu's East Gate was acquired in spring 1893; it became home to the city's first Methodist church (Si-Shen-Tsi Methodist Church) and hospital. Rioters wrecked both in 1895, and the staff withdrew to Chongqing and later Shanghai. Dr. Hart travelled to Peking to demand redress, and full compensation was collected from Sichuan Viceroy Liu Ping Chang. The compound was rebuilt quickly, but the riots of 1901 destroyed it again, and it went up a second time. Afterwards the Boys' and Girls' Schools were moved and enlarged on land south of the city, and in 1914 the Divinity College was dedicated as Hart College. It was part of West China Union University, the forerunner of today's Sichuan University and of the West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida).

During the Cultural Revolution the church building fell out of use and was passed to Chengdu City Second People's Hospital next door; the hospital turned the chapel into a kindergarten and an office for its equipment department. It was handed back to the church in 1984.

Religious life in China is closely regulated, and visitors should be aware of that. In December 2018 the authorities tried to close the Early Rain Covenant Church, an unregistered congregation of about 500 members led by Pastor Wang Yi. More than 100 members were detained, including the pastor and his wife. The church's kindergarten and theological college were searched by police, and Chinese media were barred from covering what happened. The church's leaders were charged with inciting subversion of state power, an offence carrying up to 15 years. A Chabad Jewish Center was founded in Chengdu in 2012 and, after moving five times, found a permanent home in Wuhou District.

Sichuan cooking is defined by spicy chilies and Sichuan peppercorns. Mapo doufu, Chengdu hot pot and Dan Dan Mien are famous local dishes; Mapo doufu and Dan Dan Mien both use Sichuan peppers. In 2006 the Los Angeles Times labelled Chengdu "China's party city" because of its carefree lifestyle. Tea houses and bars are everywhere: the city has more of both than Shanghai even though its population is under half as big. In 2023 Chengdu counted over 30,000 teahouses and 3,566 legally registered bars, nightclubs and dance halls, and a 2019 statistical report showed it had more bars than Shanghai, the most of any city in China. Tea culture here goes back more than a thousand years to the days when it marked the start of the Southern Silk Road. UNESCO has officially named Chengdu a "City of Gastronomy".

Tea houses are everywhere, from ornate traditional places with bamboo furniture to plain modern rooms. They serve jasmine, longjing and biluochun teas, and people go to them to play mahjong, have a massage or even have their ears cleaned. Some of the larger ones put on live shows such as Sichuan opera.

Hot pot is the dish most visitors remember. It is a traditional Sichuanese meal in which vegetables, fish or meat are cooked in a boiling, spicy broth, ideal for a gathering of friends and popular with locals and tourists alike. Hot pot restaurants can be found all over the city.
The Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park was established in 1992 under the name Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone. Major highways serving the city are:

National Highway G42 Shanghai-Chengdu
National Highway G76 Xiamen-Chengdu
