International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

sichuan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Sichuan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chengdu, register at Sichuan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

The name Soochow University is shared by several institutions, and the spellings Soochow and Suzhou are easy to mix up. Before you apply, or when you read an old reference, make sure you have the right school. Four are worth telling apart:
Soochow University (1900-1952), written 東吳大學 in Chinese, a Methodist university in Suzhou, Jiangsu, that no longer exists.
Soochow University in Taipei (東吳大學), a private university in Taiwan.
Soochow University in Suzhou (苏州大学), a provincial public university in Jiangsu, China. This is the one this CAS profile covers.
Suzhou University in Anhui (宿州学院), a provincial public college in Suzhou, Anhui.

In short, the university described here belongs to the city of Suzhou in Jiangsu Province, in the Yangtze River Delta. The rest of this page explains that city, its surroundings and the province, because the place where you live will shape your studies as much as the campus does.

Suzhou is a prefecture-level city in the south-east of Jiangsu Province, at 31°18'6.1" N, 120°34'51.9" E, in the Yangtze River Delta, which counts among the world's most dynamic economic regions. The city sits on the Lake Tai Plain, a fertile basin of river-deposited soil. Lake Tai (Taihu), at 2,578 km² the third-largest freshwater lake in China, borders it to the south-west, and the Yangtze marks the north. The city covers 8,657.32 square kilometres. Most of Lake Tai's surface falls inside Suzhou's boundary. Rivers, lakes and mudflats take up 36.6% of the land, which supports the city's reputation as a "Jiangnan water town", meaning a place south of the Yangtze known for its watery scenery.

The ground is low and flat, and plains make up 53.7% of the area. Suzhou belongs to two main natural regions, the Yangtze River Delta Plain and the Taihu Lake Plain, which divide into four smaller zones: the plain and sandbars along the Yangtze coast, the Suxi plain (Suzhou and Wuxi), the hilly area around Lake Tai and its shores, and the Yangcheng-Dianmao lowland.

Everywhere the terrain slopes very gently from west to east. Plains lie 3 to 4 metres above sea level, and the areas near Yangcheng Lake and Wujiang sink to roughly 2 metres. Some low mountains and hills are scattered about, 100 to 350 metres high, mainly in the western hills and on islands in Lake Tai. The main peaks are:
Qionglong Mountain, 342 metres, the highest
Nanyang Mountain, 338 metres
Misty Peak on West Dongting Mountain, 336 metres
Qizi Mountain, 294 metres
Moli Peak on East Dongting Mountain, 293 metres
Yushan Mountain, 262 metres
Tan Mountain, 252 metres
Tianping Mountain, 201 metres
Lingyan Mountain, 182 metres
Yuyang Mountain, 171 metres

soochow-university.h: Rivers, lakes and the "Venice of the East"

blocks.x: A dense web of rivers, canals and clustered lakes is what the old city is known for. Which lake is where? Taihu (太湖) and Caohu (漕湖) are western; Dianshan (淀山湖) and Chenghu (澄湖) lie east; Kuncheng (昆承湖) is northern; and three lakes sit in the centre, namely Yangcheng (阳澄湖), Jinji (金鸡湖) and Dushu (独墅湖). The Yangtze and the Grand Canal run through the north of the city. Water from Lake Tai goes north into the Yangtze and east through the Dianmao wetlands (淀泖地区) into the Huangpu River; the Grand Canal comes in from the west at Wangting (望亭) and leaves to the south at Shengze (盛泽). In the past the "Three Rivers" (三江) emptied straight into the sea, but now they join the Huangpu River (黄浦江), which produces Suzhou's three main water systems.

With so many waterways, Suzhou is called the "Water Capital", the "Aquatic City" and the "Jiangnan Water Town". Marco Polo, charmed by the city in the 13th century, described it as the "Venice of the East" in his travels.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with four seasons. Expect hot, sticky summers and cool, grey, damp winters with the odd snowfall. Winds from Siberia arrive from the north-west in winter and can bring nights below freezing; in summer, winds from the south or south-west can push the thermometer past 35 °C (95 °F). The yearly average is 17.2 °C (63.0 °F). Records at Wuzhong District, kept since 1951, show a high of 41.0 °C (105.8 °F) on 7 August 2013 and a low of -9.8 °C (14.4 °F) on 16 January 1958. Pack for both damp cold and heavy heat.

Most residents are Han Chinese. Mandarin is the language of broadcasting and teaching, but many people also speak the local dialect, Suzhounese, which belongs to the Wu family of languages. There are American and European expatriates, plus a large Korean community. The Industrial Bank of Korea estimated 15,000 Koreans in the municipality in 2014, when 850 Korean companies operated in the city. Korean children formed the biggest group at the Suzhou Singapore International School.

Manufacturing is the base of the economy, and from 2020 it has been the largest in China. Its sectors include iron and steel, IT and electronic equipment, and textiles. The service sector is also well developed, thanks mainly to tourism, which brought in RMB 152 billion in 2013. In that year the city's GDP passed RMB 1.3 trillion, up 9.6 per cent on the year before.

Suzhou is one of China's leading destinations for foreign investment, helped by closeness to Shanghai and lower operating costs. The city government has introduced measures to attract foreign direct investment into factories (pharmaceuticals, electronic goods, cars) and services (banking, logistics, research). One measure is a preferential tax policy for limited-partnership venture capital firms in the Suzhou Industrial Park. Altogether Suzhou is Jiangsu's economic, industrial, commercial and logistics centre, and an important hub of finance, culture, art, education and transport.
In 2013, the city produced 1,311,200 tonnes of grain, a fall of 2.9 per cent. Grain supply was kept secure by building commodity grain bases, wholesale grain markets and reserve systems.

Silk is part of the city's identity. Raising silkworms and reeling silk are old local trades, which made Suzhou one of China's key silk bases. Weaving and dyeing centred here from the Song and Yuan periods, and by the Ming dynasty people praised its silk as the "clothing of the world".

No other joint venture between the governments of China and Singapore is as large as the Suzhou Industrial Park, which sits next to Jinji Lake on the eastern side of the Old City. It began as a signing: Vice Premier Li Lanqing (for China) and Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew (for Singapore) put their names to the agreement on 26 February 1994, and the project, first called the Singapore Industrial Park, started on 12 May of that year. The park's jurisdiction covers 288 km² (111 sq mi), of which the China-Singapore cooperation area is 80 km² (31 sq mi), planned for 1.2 million residents.

Inside it you will find the Dushu Lake Science and Education Innovation District of Suzhou, a cluster of universities and other higher education bodies. Soochow University has a presence there, as does Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University. It is also a popular place to live for foreigners working in Suzhou and for the "new Suzhou" residents who move in to find work.

Suzhou Industrial Park Export Processing Zone: approved by the government in April 2000, with a planned area of 2.9 km² (1.1 sq mi), inside the China-Singapore park. All of its infrastructure is of a high standard.

Suzhou New District: created in 1990 and upgraded to a national-level hi-tech industrial zone in November 1992. Registered capital of the foreign-invested firms reached US$13 billion by the end of 2007, with US$6.8 billion actually paid in. It now hosts over 1,500 foreign firms, and about 40 Fortune 500 companies have started 67 projects there.

Three parallel railways run along the Shanghai-Nanjing corridor, and Suzhou sits on it. The main station, close to downtown, is one of the most heavily used passenger stations in the country. Two lines serve it: the Beijing-Shanghai railway, mostly with conventional trains to stations all over China, and the Shanghai-Nanjing intercity railway, whose high-speed D and G trains run frequently, mainly between Shanghai and Nanjing. The quickest G train gets you to Shanghai railway station in only 25 minutes, and to Nanjing in under an hour.

A few kilometres to the north, Suzhou North station is on the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed railway, opened in 2011, with high-speed trains to Beijing, Qingdao and other places. Other stops on the same two lines serve places within the prefecture-level city such as Kunshan. Between Suzhou and Kunshan South, Suzhou Industrial Park station is important for people who live in or visit that area. The northern part of the prefecture, including Zhangjiagang, Changshu and Taicang, was the last to get a rail link, when the Shanghai-Suzhou-Nantong railway arrived in 2020.

The Nanjing-Shanghai Expressway connects Suzhou and Shanghai. Alternatives are the Yangtze Riverine Expressway and the Suzhou-Jiaxing-Hangzhou Expressway. The Suzhou Outer Ring, finished in 2005, links the surrounding county-level cities of Taicang, Kunshan and Changshu, and China National Highway 312 also goes through the city.

On the Yangtze's right bank, the city's port moved 428 million tons of freight and 5.86 million TEU of containers in 2012. That volume made it the world's busiest inland river port, whether measured by cargo weight or by containers.

For flights, the nearest airport with commercial service is Wuxi Shuofang Airport, 20 km from central Suzhou, in the neighbouring city of Wuxi. A city terminal opened in 2023 gives connections to Shanghai Hongqiao and Shanghai Pudong international airports and has its own IATA code, SZO.

Nine metro lines operate now and another is being built, under a master plan of nine independent lines. The first two opened on 28 April 2012 (Line 1) and 28 December 2013 (Line 2). Then came Line 4 in 2017, Line 5 in June 2021, and Line 11 in June 2023, which connects through to Line 11 of the Shanghai Metro. The three newest lines all started in 2024: Line 6 in June, Line 8 in September and Line 7 in December.

Two tram routes serve the Suzhou New District. Buses reach every part of the city and charge flat fares, usually 1 yuan for a bus without air conditioning and 2 yuan with it. A bus rapid transit network, the Suzhou BRT, opened in 2008. It is 25 km (16 mi) long and has 5 lines that use raised busways and dedicated bus lanes.

The Suzhou Dongwu football club plays in China League One, the second tier of Chinese professional football. The Suzhou Industrial Park Sports Arena, with 13,000 seats, was one of the venues of the 2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup.
Suzhou's traditions are among its biggest attractions. This is what to look for.

Opera and storytelling: Kunqu opera began in the Suzhou area, as did the much later Suzhou Opera. Suzhou pingtan is a local style of ballad-singing and storytelling, combining songs accompanied by the pipa and sanxian with spoken passages in dialect.
Silk: through China's imperial era, Suzhou silk stood for top quality, and the city supplied silk to ancient royal families. By the 13th century it was already the centre of the lucrative silk trade.

Song brocade: the Song-style brocade of Suzhou is counted among China's three famous brocades, with Nanjing's Yun brocade and Sichuan's Shu brocade. Made of silk, it is thin but strong, with bright colours, fine patterns and a soft feel. Production goes back to the Five Dynasties and flourished in the Song dynasty, after the government moved south and the country's political and cultural centre shifted to the Yangtze area.
Food: Suzhou cuisine (苏帮菜) is part of Jiangsu cuisine and includes Yangcheng Lake hairy crab and squirrel fish.

Handicrafts: a long list, from embroidery and fans to Chinese musical instruments, scroll mounting, lanterns, mahogany furniture, jade carving and silk tapestry. Jiangenxutang Studio is known for traditional painting pigments, and Taohuawu Studio for New Year wood-block prints. Paintings, calligraphic art, silk hand embroidery and wedding gowns complete the picture.
Suzhou is also where "Jasmine" comes from, a song performed by Chinese singers and actresses countless times at important meetings and celebrations. Jasmine is a symbol of Suzhou, as is Lake Tai.

Suzhou's gardens have an ancient history. The first one belonged to the king of Wu in the Spring and Autumn period, around 600 BC. More than 200 gardens existed in the 16th to 18th centuries. They were built to the style of Chinese painting, so each view is like a picture, and each whole garden is like a huge painting. The largest private garden today is the Humble Administrator's Garden, built in the 16th century for Wang Xianchen, an imperial censor.

Suzhou embroidery is one of the "Four Famous Embroideries", along with those of Hunan, Sichuan and Guangdong. The Suzhou method uses fine silks and gold thread. Sculpture, Song brocade, and jade and rosewood carving are other local crafts. Suzhou embroidery is recognised as cultural heritage, and many craftspeople are using intangible cultural heritage resources to improve technique and to engage better in the economy.

Relics from many periods fill the city's museum, among them revolutionary records, stone carvings, folk customs, drama and verse, embroidery, silk cloth, garden items, coins and Buddhist objects. A separate centre for silk weaving technique, run under the city's cultural authorities, passes on the living heritage of Song brocade and kesi weaving. Master artisans work with apprentices in a workshop that is partly open for visitors to watch, so these demanding skills are kept alive.

Suzhou ranks 33rd among cities for scientific output in the Nature Index for 2025. Postgraduate institutions here include the Southeast University-Monash University Joint Graduate School. The Suzhou Dushu Lake Higher Education Town hosts several more, such as the joint graduate school of the National University of Singapore and Fudan, and the Nanjing University Graduate School.

To the earliest dynasties, whose core was in north-western Henan, Jiangsu was a remote place inhabited by an ancient people known as the Huai barbarians (淮夷). Under the Zhou, contact increased, and a state called Wu emerged in southern Jiangsu, one among hundreds of states then scattered over northern and central China. Towards the end of the Spring and Autumn period Wu rose to be a great power under King Helu, and in 484 BC defeated Qi, a major northern power in what is now Shandong, in a contest for leadership over all the Chinese states. The state of Yue, which had risen to the south in present-day Zhejiang, conquered Wu in 473 BC. In 333 BC the powerful western state of Chu conquered Yue in turn. Finally Qin swept all rivals away and unified China in 221 BC.

The Han dynasty ruled from 206 BC to 220 AD. Jiangsu stayed far from the North China Plain heartland and was split between Xu Province in the north and Yang Province in the south. Later, when China divided into three kingdoms, the southern part of the region was the core of Eastern Wu (222 to 280), with a capital at Jianye, which became Jiankang and is today's Nanjing. When nomads overran northern China in the 4th century, the Jin court moved to Jiankang, and the cities of southern and central Jiangsu swelled with migrants from the north. Jiankang remained the capital through four Southern dynasties and became China's biggest commercial and cultural centre.

When the Sui reunited the country in 581, politics shifted back north, but the Grand Canal was dug through Jiangsu to join the Central Plains to the prosperous Yangtze Delta. The Tang (618-907) depended on southern Jiangsu for yearly shipments of grain. In the Song dynasty (960-1279), when China saw a wealthy merchant class and a growing market economy, Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and neighbouring areas) became a trading centre. From then on, major cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou stood for opulence and luxury, and the region is still one of China's richest.

In 1127 the Jurchen Jin dynasty took control of North China in the Jin-Song wars. The Huai River, which once crossed north Jiangsu to reach the Yellow Sea, marked the boundary between the Jin north and the Southern Song south. The Mongols took over China in the 13th century. The Ming dynasty, founded in 1368 after the Mongols were driven out, first made Nanjing its capital, and the surrounding regions, which correspond to Jiangsu and Anhui today, were named Nanzhili ("southern directly governed"). After a coup by Zhu Di (later the Yongle Emperor) the capital moved far north to Beijing, though Nanjing remained a southern capital. In the late Ming, Jiangnan was still a major trading area, and some historians see in its thriving textile industry a first sign of industrialisation and capitalism, although the trend was cut short.
The Qing renamed Nanzhili as "Jiangnan province", and in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui were separated into two provinces. Jiangsu's borders have mostly stayed the same since then.

From the 1840s, as Western powers pushed into China, the wealthy, commercial Yangtze Delta met outside influence more and more. Shanghai, once an ordinary small Jiangsu town, rapidly became a cosmopolitan metropolis of trade and banking and was eventually separated as its own municipality. Jiangnan also had a big role in the Taiping Rebellion (1851-1864), a huge and deadly uprising that tried to found a Christian theocracy. It started far to the south in Guangdong, swept through much of South China, and by 1853 had made Nanjing its capital under the name Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

China became a republic in 1912, then fell into the hands of rival warlords, and Jiangsu passed from one to another. In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek set up a government in Nanjing and soon controlled most of the country; the Jiangsu provincial government settled in Zhenjiang in 1928. That period of order ended when the Second Sino-Japanese War went full-scale in 1937. Nanjing fell on 13 December 1937, and the occupying forces' atrocities during the following three months are remembered as the Rape of Nanjing. Wang Jingwei's collaborationist East China government then made its seat in the city, and Japan held most of Jiangsu until 1945.

Peace did not bring calm. Nanjing again served as the Republic's capital, but the Kuomintang government was now fighting a civil war against Communist forces based mainly in the Northeast. The Huaihai Campaign, the decisive battle, took place in northern Jiangsu; the Kuomintang lost, and Communist troops soon crossed the Yangtze to occupy Nanjing. The defeated government retreated south and finally reached Taipei. From there the Republic of China still governs Taiwan, the Pescadores and neighbouring islands, and it also still formally lays claim to Nanjing as the lawful capital. With Zhenjiang lost, the Jiangsu provincial government for a time operated from Shengsi County, in Zhejiang.

Once the Communists had taken over, Beijing (then Peiping) became capital of the People's Republic and Jiangsu was split into two administrative regions, Subei and Sunan. The province was recreated on 15 November 1952, with Nanjing as its capital rather than a national one. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up favoured the Guangdong coast at first, so Jiangsu fell behind; from the 1990s the policies were spread more evenly. Two southern cities close to Shanghai, Suzhou and Wuxi, have done particularly well since, ranking in China's top ten by GDP and overtaking Nanjing. A wide income gap between north and south Jiangsu persists.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

soochow-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Soochow University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.

South China Agricultural University, usually shortened to SCAU (华南农业大学), is a provincial public university devoted mainly to agriculture and the life sciences. It sits in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong, and answers to the Guangdong provincial government rather than to a national ministry. It also belongs to the national Double First-Class programme, the government scheme that backs selected universities and subjects in building world-class standing. If you are weighing up agricultural, food, veterinary or biological studies in southern China, this is one of the best-known names in the region.

south-china-agricultural-university.h: A university with more than a century of roots

blocks.x: SCAU's story begins long before its current name, and the sequence of milestones below shows how a small experimental station became a major university.
1909: Guangdong established an agricultural experiment station together with an affiliated institute of agriculture. This is the earliest root the university traces.
1917: The station's educational side became the Guangdong Provincial Public Agricultural School, which began offering agriculture as a four-year degree subject.
1924: The school was absorbed into Guangdong University as its College of Agriculture.
1926: The college was renamed the College of Agriculture of National Sun Yat-sen University.

1931: Sun Yat-sen University prepared a new campus at Shipai and took in roughly 3.5 square kilometres of land in the northern part of that district. The agricultural college grew quickly once it had this space.

1952: China reorganised its universities nationwide. South China Agricultural College (华南农学院) was created by combining agricultural schools and departments from institutions in two provinces, among them Lingnan University, Guangxi University and what had been National Sun Yat-sen University.
1979: The institution was named one of China's national key universities.
1984: It took its present name, South China Agricultural University.
2000: During the wider reform of how higher education was managed, control passed to the Guangdong provincial government.
2015: Guangdong listed it among its high-level universities under cultivation.
2022: It joined the Double First-Class group of universities.

In short, the university is the product of several mergers and name changes, and its agricultural identity has stayed constant through all of them. Applicants should note that the 1952 merger drew on institutions from more than one province, which explains why SCAU has such broad strengths across southern China's farming and forestry traditions.

The university is organised into 26 colleges and departments. It offers 95 undergraduate programmes, 107 master's programmes and 60 doctoral programmes. Beyond these, applicants can choose among nine professional master's courses, and veterinary medicine has its own professional doctorate. For an international student this breadth matters: even though the name says agriculture, you will find neighbouring fields in the same university, which can make it easier to change direction or to take a cross-disciplinary master's or doctorate.

Published rankings are a snapshot of one year, so treat the figures below as dated and check the current tables before relying on them. In the 2016 QS World University Rankings by subject, SCAU was placed in the 50th to 100th band for agriculture and forestry. In the 2017 US News Best Global Universities list it stood at 962nd overall, where the agricultural sciences subject came 177th and plant and animal science came 228th. These numbers tell you that the university's reputation is strongest in its specialist subjects, more than in overall comparisons with large comprehensive universities. Later editions may differ, and the university's own website is the place to look for current standings.

south-china-agricultural-university.h: Guangzhou: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life as a student depends heavily on the city, so this part of the profile explains Guangzhou, where SCAU is based: its position, its resources, its weather, its economy and its people.

The old town of Guangzhou grew up near Baiyun Mountain on the eastern bank of the Pearl River, known in Chinese as the Zhujiang. It lies roughly 130 kilometres from the point where the river meets the South China Sea, and far further downstream from the head of navigation. The location gave the city command of the fertile Pearl River Delta, with the Humen Strait guarding its route to the sea. The older figures put the distance to the sea at about 80 miles and the distance to the head of navigation at about 300 miles. Today the municipality spreads over 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 square miles) astride the river, between roughly 112°57′ and 114°03′ east and 22°26′ and 23°56′ north, in south-central Guangdong. The Pearl is the fourth-longest river in China. Tidal flats line its estuary and support intertidal ecosystems, although many of those flats have been reclaimed for farming over time. Baiyun Mountain is affectionately called the city's "lung" (市肺) by locals, because it offers green space inside an urban area.

Heights increase from the southwest toward the northeast: hills and mountains run along the rear of the city while the coast fronts the sea. The summit of Tiantang Peak, at 1,210 metres (3,970 feet), is the municipality's top elevation.

south-china-agricultural-university.h: Natural wealth: water, farmland and minerals

blocks.x: Guangzhou has 47 types of minerals and 820 ore fields, and figures given for large and medium mining areas and deposits vary between sources, so the exact counts should be treated as approximate. Building granite and cement limestone head the list, followed by ceramic clay, potassium, albite, salt, manganese, nepheline, syenite, fluorite, marble, and both ordinary and thermal mineral water. Anything useful for energy or for non-ferrous metals is thin on the ground, patchy and unreliable in grade. Because Guangzhou lies in the water-rich south, rivers and waterways take up about 10 percent of its land area, and they help keep the local ecology steady and the scenery pleasant.

Water is worth a closer look, because it shapes the city's agriculture. The city's water surface covers about 74,400 hectares, around 10.05 percent of the land area. The main rivers are the Beijiang, the northern main stream of the Dongjiang, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi, the Baini, the Guangzhou reach of the Pearl River, and the Shiqiao and Shawan waterways. Guangzhou has comparatively little water of its own but receives a very large flow passing through from upstream rivers, mainly the Xijiang, Beijiang and Dongjiang systems. The published volume figures for rainfall, groundwater and inflow are inconsistent, so they are left out here. In the south, the river network is affected by tides. The Pearl River reaches the sea through three main outlets, Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili, into the Lingding estuary, so the tides bring in large volumes of water, part of which is usable as fresh water.

For a student of agriculture, the local farming landscape is a draw in itself. Crops here show the transition from tropical to subtropical conditions. Guangzhou is one of the richest areas in China for fruit trees, with tropical, subtropical and temperate types, spanning 174 species from 82 genera in 41 families and more than 500 varieties in total. Lychee alone has 55 principal varieties, and the area is regarded as a centre of origin for lychee, longan, wampee and Chinese olives. Vegetables are also a strength, with 15 main categories, 127 species and over 370 varieties. The farm sector additionally covers flowers (cut and potted), ornamental seedlings, medicinal and edible blossoms, lawn turf, cereals, cash crops, animal husbandry, aquaculture and wild fauna. Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first local product in Guangzhou to be protected by a geographical indication.

south-china-agricultural-university.h: Climate and the best time of year

blocks.x: The classification here is humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa), under East Asian monsoon influence, even though the city sits only a little to the north of the Tropic of Cancer's line, on its south side. Expect wet, hot, sticky summers with a punishing heat index, and mild, fairly dry winters. Monsoon conditions last a long time, from April through September. Average monthly temperatures run from 13.8 °C (56.8 °F) in January up to 28.9 °C (84.0 °F) in July, and the annual mean is 22.4 °C (72.3 °F). Relative humidity averages about 76 percent and the metropolitan area receives more than 1,950 millimetres of rain a year.

Sunshine is limited: only 17 percent of the possible total in March, rising to 51 percent in October, which adds up to about 1,559 hours of bright sun a year, clearly fewer than in nearby Shenzhen or Hong Kong. The months from October into December are cool, windy and very comfortable, and are often named as the best time to visit. Since 1951 the thermometer has recorded lows of 0 °C (32 °F) on two dates, 11 February 1957 and 23 December 1999, and a high of 39.1 °C (102.4 °F) on 1 July 2004. Unofficial older readings exist too: a low on 18 January 1893 of −5.0 °C (23.0 °F), which modern meteorologists think was nearer −3.0 °C (26.6 °F), and a −0.3 °C (31.5 °F) reading on 8 December 1934 at a Huangpu District station whose records began in 1912. Snow is extremely rare, and the latest fall, on 24 January 2016, came 87 years after the one before. Pack for heat, humidity and rain rather than for winter.

Think of Guangzhou as the chief factory floor of the Pearl River Delta, itself one of China's leading commercial and manufacturing regions. Output in 2021 came to 2,823 billion yuan (US$444.37 billion in nominal terms), the second-biggest economy in South-Central China after Shenzhen, with 151,162 yuan (US$23,794) per person. Few Chinese cities are considered richer. The Hurun Global Rich List 2020 ranked it tenth in the world for billionaires and fifth in China, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Oxford Economics projected that by 2035 it would be among the ten largest cities in the world by nominal GDP, alongside Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, with per-person GDP above US$42,000 by 2030. The 2020 Global Financial Centres Index put it 21st worldwide and eighth in Asia and Oceania. Projections like these are estimates, and you should check newer figures if they matter to you.
Rapid industrialisation once gave Guangzhou a reputation as a polluted place. Green urban planning has since changed that picture and it is now counted among the more liveable big cities in China.
The city's newest downtown is Zhujiang New Town, a 6.44 square kilometre district in Tianhe that serves as its 21st-century business centre. Several financial firms keep their headquarters there.

The Canton Fair, officially the China Import and Export Fair, takes place every April and October. It began in the spring of 1957 and is the longest-running, highest-level and largest trade fair in China. From its 104th session it moved from the older Liuhua complex to the Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center in Pazhou, which can be reached via Metro Line 8 (two stops), Line 11 (one stop) and the tram line THZ1 (three stops). Since that session, the fair has been run in three phases instead of two. If you are in the city during these months, expect crowded hotels and transport around Pazhou.

Cantonese food is one of the best-known regional cuisines in China, summed up by the saying "Eat in Guangzhou" (食在廣州). Local craft traditions include Cantonese carving in jade, wood and ivory (the last of which is controversial), Canton porcelain developed over about three centuries for export and valued for its colourful look, and Cantonese embroidery, which is one of the four major embroidery styles in China. Zhujiang Beer, a pale lager, is among the country's most successful brands.
These are the areas that concentrate Guangzhou's industry and many graduate jobs:
The automobile maker GAC Group, one of the city's best-known employers.
The Economic and Technological Development Zone of Guangzhou.

The Nansha Export Processing Zone, opened in 2005 in Nansha District with a planned area of 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 square miles). Car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry are its priorities. It is 54 kilometres (34 miles), or a 70-minute drive, south of Baiyun International Airport and close to Nansha Port, and Metro Line 4 was being extended to the Nansha ferry terminal.

The Guangzhou Free Trade Zone, created in 1992 in eastern Huangpu District next door to the development zone and also near the airport. International trade, logistics, processing and software are its core, and newer sectors such as new energy, AI, new mobility, new materials, information and communication technology and new transport are being added. The area is now branded as Huangpu District, and the city's IP Court is based there.
Guangzhou Science City.

A China Briefing article reported that, by 2018, foreign investors had set up over 30,000 companies in the city. Among the Fortune Global 500 firms, 297 ran projects here and 120 had put a headquarters, or a regional one, in Guangzhou. That is useful context if you hope for internships or international employers within reach of campus.

At the end of 2024 Guangzhou had a permanent resident population of 18.978 million, with an urbanisation rate of 87.24 percent. The Seventh National Population Census recorded 18,676,605 permanent residents on 1 November 2020, which was 5,975,805 or 47.05 percent more than the 12,700,800 counted in 2010. City dwellers made up 86.19 percent, which is 16,096,724 people, and rural residents 13.81 percent, or 2,579,881.

Migration is a defining feature. In 2020, 11,522,907 residents were living away from where their household was registered, and 9,378,825 of them belonged to the floating population. That puts Guangzhou among China's largest destinations for migrants. For a newcomer, this means a city where almost everyone arrived from somewhere else, and where it is normal to be a stranger. An earlier estimate for 2014 gave 13,080,500 residents, 11,264,800 of them urban, at around 1,800 people per square kilometre, so figures differ by year and definition and the latest official numbers are the ones to use.

Guangzhou's urban sprawl runs straight into those of its neighbours. Taken together, the continuous built-up zone of the Pearl River Delta spans around 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 square miles) and is thought to house 22 million people. That tally covers Guangzhou's nine urban districts, Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890 thousand) and Huizhou's Huiyang District (760 thousand). Adding adjacent Hong Kong lifts the agglomeration past 28 million. Strong growth and heavy demand for labour created a huge floating population of workers from elsewhere, as many as 10 million of whom spend at least half the year in the area. In 2008 such workers numbered around five million among the city's own permanent residents. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 25 million people as of 2010.

A 2018 study by Gong and colleagues tracked development between 1990 and 2020. In 1990, built-up residential districts were almost all packed into a small part of western Guangzhou, with other areas dominated by farmland and forest. From 2005 onward, housing spread to other parts, and by 2020 developed residential areas stretched from the west to the east of the city. The far south and large parts of the north remain mainly agricultural or wooded with very little housing.

If you plan weekend trips, note that high-speed catamarans sail every day from the Nansha and Lianhua Shan terminals in Guangzhou to the China Ferry Terminal in Hong Kong, and from Nansha to the pier in Macau. On the faith side, roughly 124 temples, halls and pavilions of various religions stood in the city in earlier times. Now the Buddhist Association is joined by a Taoist Association and a Jewish community, and Christianity has a long local history.

south-china-agricultural-university.h: Guangdong: the province behind the campus

blocks.x: Guangdong has been China's main window on the sea for centuries, and that history still colours the food, the language and the attitude of the people you will meet.
Student life is shaped by the province as much as by the campus, so here is a summary of Guangdong.

Archaeologists date the Neolithic in the Pearl River Delta to about 7,000 years ago. The early phase ran from around 7000 to 5000 years before present (roughly 5050 to 3050 BC) and the late phase from about 5000 to 3500 (roughly 3050 to 1550 BC). On the coast the new way of life probably arrived from the middle Yangtze, a conclusion published in 2013. Inland it showed up about 4,600 years ago, and in the north the Shixia culture represents it, lasting from 4600 to 4200 years ago (about 2650 to 2250 BC).

Many tribal peoples, grouped by the Chinese under the label Baiyue ("Hundred Yue"), lived here at first. The region entered China under the Qin dynasty, which started administration and with it dependable written records. Having created the first unified empire, the Qin expanded south and placed a commandery called Nanhai at Panyu, close to today's Guangzhou. An independent kingdom, Nanyue, then ruled the area from the Qin collapse until Emperor Wu of the Han. The Han governed Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam together as Jiaozhi Province, and its far south was an entry point for merchants from the west, some from as far as the Roman Empire. Later, in 226 CE, the state of Wu in the Three Kingdoms era made Guangdong a separate province called Guang.

Canton, as Guangzhou was long known abroad, was a busy port on a tropical frontier, rich in oranges, bananas, banyan trees and lychees. Merchants traded silk and porcelain with Persian, Indian and Malay visitors in exchange for medicines and fragrant tropical woods. Buddhists from India and Muslims from Khorasan lived side by side and built their own places of worship, and a foreign quarter formed beside the river where Arab and Sinhalese traders settled. The port's importance fell after raids in 758, and foreign residents were at times troubled by local officials; an incident in 684 is recorded as one example.

In 627, under the Tang, Guangdong and Guangxi were placed in the Lingnan Circuit (the "Mountain-South Circuit"). In 971, under the Song dynasty (960-1279), the Guangdong part was renamed Guangnan East Circuit (廣南東路), and the name "Guangdong" (廣東, 广东) comes from "Guangnan East". Under the Yuan, large parts of what is now Guangdong belonged to Jiangxi, and the present name was fixed in the early Ming.

Over the centuries the population became predominantly Han Chinese, through trade, intermarriage and state-organised settlement from the late third century BCE, which brought soldiers, civilians and exiles from the north. After the Han dynasty fell, larger waves came from the north during times of turmoil. Unrest after the An Lushan rebellion, for example, raised the population of Guangzhou prefecture by 75 percent between the 740s-750s and the 800s-810s. As more settlers came, local peoples were gradually absorbed into Han culture or pushed aside.

In the 13th century, as the Mongols conquered China, the Southern Song court fled south from Hangzhou. Its defeat by Mongol naval forces at the Battle of Yamen in Guangdong in 1279 ended the Southern Song dynasty.

From the 16th century, Guangdong had wide trading links overseas. Portuguese and British merchants in particular sailed north across the South China Sea and through the Malacca Straits to trade at Guangzhou. On the southern shore, Macau became the first European settlement, in 1557. Then, in the late 18th and early 19th centuries pirates troubled the Pearl River delta coast, until Portuguese naval and Qing forces together suppressed them.

In the 19th century opium trading through Guangzhou led to the First Opium War and opened a period of Western pressure on China. Besides Macau, then Portuguese, Hong Kong passed to the British and the area now called Zhanjiang to the French.

Many people left Guangdong, and migration from Hong Kong into the British Empire and later the Commonwealth was easy, so a lot of overseas Chinese communities have Guangdong or Cantonese roots. Cantonese, Hakka and Teochew are proportionally more common among overseas Chinese than Mandarin. Many Taishanese speakers also went to Western countries, so some Western versions of Chinese words come from Cantonese rather than Mandarin, such as "dim sum". Some Mandarin words of foreign origin also came through Cantonese; the word for lemon, níngméng (柠檬), is one example. In the United States, many Chinese Americans descend from migrants from Taishan, who speak a distinct dialect related to Cantonese.

Guangdong's closeness to foreign influence made it a hotbed of anti-Manchu and anti-imperialist movements. In the 1850s the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, whose leader Hong Xiuquan came from the province and first met a missionary's Christian pamphlet there, joined forces with the local Red Turban Rebellion (1854-1856). Sun Yat-sen, generally acknowledged as the founder of modern China, was a Guangdong native too.

In 2024 about 75.9 percent of Guangdong's population lived in cities and 24.1 percent in the countryside. Most residents are Han Chinese, but the Han population is so varied linguistically that the province is called a "treasure trove of regional languages" (方言寶庫). The largest group are the Cantonese, with sizeable Hakka and Teoswa communities east of the Pearl River Delta. The province also holds a few small minority communities: Mien, She, Hmong, Li and Zhuang. Expect to hear Mandarin on campus and Cantonese in much of the surrounding city. In summary, SCAU offers a specialist agricultural education in a large, warm, wet and very international southern city, and applicants should check the university's own website for current programmes, fees and rankings.
