South China Normal University, or SCNU, is a provincial public university in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong. It is a normal university, meaning it grew out of teacher education, but it now teaches across a wide range of fields. The Guangdong provincial government and the Ministry of Education sponsor it together. SCNU belongs to Project 211 and, since 2017, to the national Double First-Class Construction programme.

The university presents itself as distinctive for the combination of teaching and research. Fields covered range from philosophy and economics through law, education, literature and history to science, technology and management, and one description adds agriculture, medicine and art. An elementary school and a middle school are attached to it.

The school has been renamed and relocated several times in some eighty years, but the university points out that through every change it kept going. Its tradition is to research advanced learning and train professional talent for society. It also carries forward the revolutionary spirit of its predecessor, Southern University: loyalty, unity, simplicity and humility, hard work and courage, and seeking truth from facts. The motto urges hard struggle, careful scholarship, a search for truth and for innovation, and being a good example to other people.

SCNU dates from 1933, when it was called the Guangdong Provincial Teacher's College of Xiangqin University. Project 211 membership came in 1996. In 2015 the Guangdong provincial government and the Ministry of Education began jointly building and supporting it, and in 2017 SCNU was admitted to the Double First-Class Construction.

More than 30 schools and colleges make up the university, offering 84 undergraduate programmes, over 200 graduate programmes and over 100 doctoral programmes. Enrolment in 2017 was 24,894 undergraduates, 7,553 postgraduates and 842 doctoral candidates, and some 1,000 international students from over 100 countries are on campus long-term every year. There are 1,979 full-time teachers, over half of whom tutor postgraduates or supervise doctorates. The university also operates dozens of state key laboratories and engineering research centres, and its current president is Dr. Wang Enke.
SCNU has four campuses in three cities.
Shipai campus, the main campus, in Tianhe District, Guangzhou
The HEMC campus, in the Guangzhou Higher Education Mega Center, Panyu District, Guangzhou
Nanhai campus, in Nanhai District, Foshan
Shanwei campus, in the Chengqu district of Shanwei
Your campus depends on your school, so check the university's admissions office for where your programme is taught.
The lists below are organised by campus, and the university may have changed names or moved units since the information was compiled.

Shipai holds the units for teacher education and the humanities: Education, Special Education, Politics and Administration, Marxism, History and Culture, Foreign Studies, International Culture, Fine Arts and Tourism Management. Science and technology units are there too: Mathematical Sciences, Life Sciences, Geography, Computer and Psychology, as well as the School of Information Technology in Education.

Other Shipai units include research bodies such as the Institute of Optoelectronic Materials and Technology, the College of Biophotonics, the Institute for Brain Research and Rehabilitation and the South China Research Center for Applied Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Studies. Adult and international education sit in the College of Continuing Education, the Phoenix International School and the School of Internet Education, and there is also a school for professional development and research on primary and secondary education.

Arts, law and business subjects: the School of Literature, Economics and Management, Law, Politics and Public Administration, Physical Education and Sports Science, Music, Tourism Management, and Entrepreneurship.

Natural science and engineering: the Schools of Physics and Telecommunications Engineering, Chemistry, Environment, and Information and Optoelectronic Science and Engineering, together with the South China Academy of Advanced Optoelectronics, the Institute of Quantum Matter, the Academy of Environment, the Institute for Science, Technology and Society, and four units that have no official English translation: the Academy of Front-line Physics Science, the Department of Physics, the South China Nuclear Science Computing Center, and the Academy of Future Technology.

Nanhai's units cover technology and business: the International Business College, the School of Artificial Intelligence, the School of Electronic Science and Engineering (also called the School of Microelectronics), the RSB Digital Business Institute and the SCNU Aberdeen Institute of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence.

Xingzhi College, the School of Data Science and Engineering, the Department of General Education, the School of Materials and New Energy, the College of Vocational and Technical Education, the School of Basic Education, the School of Business and the School of Creative Design.

Teaching and research support comes from the Network Center, the Research Resources Center, the Journal of South China Normal University, the university archives and libraries, the Center of Teachers' Learning and Development and the Center of Education and Development. Affiliated bodies are the SCNU hospital, a kindergarten, a primary school and a high school.
The university has multi-purpose libraries on three campuses, together holding more than 3.74 million books.
Shipai: built in 1998, with 29 thousand square metres of floor area, around 1.83 million books and 1,700 reading seats
HEMC: built in 2004, with 39 thousand square metres, around 1.12 million books and 1,800 seats
Nanhai: built in 2002, with 14 thousand square metres, around 0.61 million books and 1,100 seats
As of 2023, the Academic Ranking of World Universities placed SCNU in the 400-500 range. The 2026-2027 U.S. News Best Global Universities listing puts it at 514th in the world.

The campus has over 120 student associations in five areas: theory and study, society and practice, academic and technological work, entertainment and sport, and personal interests. Among them are English and psychology societies, the Huayun society for Han Chinese clothing, the Hai Pengzi literature association, and martial arts and guitar clubs.

Each campus has its own canteens. On Shipai they are Tao Yuan, Yong Yuan and Qin Yuan. On the HEMC campus they are Han Yuan and Nan Yuan, and on Nanhai there is Xi Yuan, which was renamed to that name in 2017.

south-china-normal-university.h: Guangzhou, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Because most of daily life happens in the city, the rest of this profile describes Guangzhou: its geography, resources, climate, economy, people and transport.

The oldest part of the city stood near Baiyun Mountain on the Pearl River's (Zhujiang's) eastern bank. From there the river mouth on the South China Sea lay some 80 miles (130 km) off, and the head of navigation about 300 miles upriver. This position gave control of the rich alluvial plain of the Pearl River Delta, whose route to the sea was guarded at the Humen Strait.

Today the city extends over 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 sq mi) astride the river, from 112 degrees 57 minutes to 114 degrees 03 minutes east and 22 degrees 26 minutes to 23 degrees 56 minutes north, in south-central Guangdong. The Pearl is the fourth-largest river in China. Intertidal ecosystems survive on tidal flats along the estuary, although many flats have been reclaimed as farmland. Baiyun Mountain is nowadays nicknamed the city's "lung".
Ground level climbs from the southwest to the northeast, with mountains forming the city's backbone and the sea on its front. The highest point is Tiantang Peak, rising to 1,210 metres (3,970 feet).

Guangzhou lies just south of the Tropic of Cancer, yet its climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cwa), under the influence of the East Asian monsoon. Summer brings rain, heat, high humidity and a high heat index, while winter is mild and relatively dry. The monsoon season lasts a long time, from April until September.

In January the monthly average is 13.8 degrees Celsius (56.8 F), and in July it is 28.9 degrees (84.0 F); across the year the mean is 22.4 degrees (72.3 F). The months from October to December are mild, cool and windy, and are the best time to visit. Humidity averages around 76 percent and the urban area gets over 1,950 mm (77 in) of rain annually.

Sunshine is limited. Possible sunshine climbs from 17 percent in March to 51 percent in October, and the 1,559 hours of bright sun a year are far fewer than in neighbouring Shenzhen and Hong Kong. Official extremes since 1951 are 0 degrees (32 F), seen on 11 February 1957 and again on 23 December 1999, and 39.1 degrees (102.4 F) on 1 July 2004. An unofficial low of minus 5.0 degrees (23.0 F) was noted on 18 January 1893, but modern meteorologists think the true figure was about minus 3.0 degrees (26.6 F). The Huangpu District station, whose records start in 1912, logged an unofficial low of minus 0.3 degrees (31.5 F) on 8 December 1934. Snow last fell in the city on 24 January 2016, 87 years after the previous fall. In practice, expect warm, damp weather for much of the year and very little cold.

Mineral wealth is varied. The ground holds 47 kinds of mineral, 820 ore fields and 18 large or medium oil deposits. Chief among them are granite, limestone for cement, ceramic clay, potassium, albite, rock salt, mirabilite, nepheline, syenite, fluorite and marble, together with mineral water and geothermal water. The city lies in southern China's water-rich belt, and rivers and streams occupy 10 percent of its land, beautifying the scenery and keeping the local ecology steady.

Another description of the geology gives more detail. The structure is rather complex and suits the formation of minerals: 47 kinds, counting subspecies, found at 820 sites, with 25 large and medium-sized mining areas. Building granite, cement limestone, ceramic clay, potassium, sodium feldspar, salt, manganese, nepheline orthoclase, fluorite, marble, mineral water and thermal water are the main ones. Energy minerals and non-ferrous metals are scarce, scattered, small in scale and uneven in grade. These facts matter mostly to industry rather than to students.

Local water is limited, while water flowing through from elsewhere is plentiful, which is the defining feature of the city's supply. Water surfaces cover 74,400 hectares, 10.05 percent of the land. The main watercourses are the Beijiang, the Dongjiang north main stream, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi River, the Baini River, the Pearl River's Guangzhou reach, the Shiqiao Waterway and the Shawan Waterway. The Beijiang and the Dongjiang pass through the city and merge with the Pearl River before reaching the sea.

Dividing by the 2010 census population gives 1.0601 million cubic metres per square kilometre and 628 cubic metres per person, half the national per-capita level. Inflow from upstream amounts to 186.024 billion cubic metres, which is 23 times the local total, and it is concentrated mostly in the south and in Zengcheng District. The Xijiang and Beijiang supply 159.15 billion cubic metres of it, the Dongjiang's north main stream 14.203 billion, and the upper Zengjiang 2.828 billion.

Tides strongly affect the river network in the south, which has large flows. The Pearl River reaches the Lingding Ocean and then the South China Sea through three major outlets south of the city: Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili. Per year the incoming tide amounts to 271 billion cubic metres and the outgoing tide to 408.8 billion, and the three outlets discharge 137.7 billion cubic metres of runoff. The tide carries in a lot of water each year, and part of it is fresh water that people can use.

Farming here reflects the transition between tropical and subtropical zones. The region is among China's richest for fruit trees, with tropical, subtropical and temperate groups, adding up to 41 families, 82 genera, 174 species and over 500 varieties. Lychee alone accounts for 55 main varieties. Lychee, longan, wampee (yellow skin) and black and white olives all began or diversified here. For vegetables the area is prized for quality and range: 15 major categories, 127 species and more than 370 varieties. Flowers on sale include cut flowers, foliage and branches, potted flowers, bonsai, bedding plants, ornamental seedlings, edible and medicinal flowers, and lawns. Grain, cash crops, livestock, poultry, aquatic products and wild animals are also produced, and Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first Guangzhou variety to win geographical-indication protection.

The Pearl River Delta is one of China's leading commercial and industrial regions, and Guangzhou is its main manufacturing centre. The city's 2021 GDP was 2,823 billion yuan (US$444.37 billion nominal), second only to Shenzhen in South-Central China, and GDP per capita stood at 151,162 yuan (US$23,794). It counts as one of China's most prosperous cities.
Counting billionaires, the 2020 Hurun Global Rich List puts it tenth worldwide and fifth in China, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen.

Oxford Economics projects that by 2035 it will be one of the ten biggest cities in the world by nominal GDP, together with Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, and that its nominal GDP per head will pass US$42,000 in 2030.

The 2020 Global Financial Centers Index has it 21st worldwide, just ahead of Amsterdam and behind Washington, D.C., and eighth across Asia and Oceania after Shanghai, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, Beijing, Shenzhen and Dubai.
Rapid industrialisation once made it a rather polluted city, but green urban planning has made it one of the more livable cities in China.
Zhujiang New Town is Guangzhou's 21st-century central business district, covering 6.44 km2 in Tianhe District. Several financial institutions have their headquarters there.

The Canton Fair, whose formal name is the China Import and Export Fair, takes place each April and October under the Ministry of Trade. It started in spring 1957 and matters a great deal to the city. In China no other trade fair has such a long history, such a high level or such a large scale. With its 104th session the fair left the older Liuhua complex for the new Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center in Pazhou, which has two stations on Line 8, one on Line 11 and three on Tram Line THZ1. Since then it has been staged in three phases instead of two. If you visit in those months, expect hotels and transport to be busy.

Cantonese cuisine ranks among the best known and most popular in China, and the saying goes simply "Eat in Guangzhou". Cantonese carving covers jade, wood and, controversially, ivory. Canton porcelain evolved over three centuries into a leading export ware and is now noted within China for its colourful style. Cantonese embroidery ranks as one of China's four principal embroidery traditions, and Zhujiang Beer, a pale lager, is among the country's most successful brands.
GAC Group is a major local manufacturer.
Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone.

Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone, set up in 2005, is planned to cover 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 sq mi). It is in Nansha District, 54 km (34 miles) south of Baiyun International Airport, a drive of 70 minutes, and it is close to Nansha Port. Encouraged industries are car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry. Metro Line 4 is being extended to the Nansha Ferry Terminal.

Guangzhou Free Trade Zone opened in 1992 on the eastern side of Huangpu District, beside the Economic and Technological Development Zone and only a short distance from Baiyun Airport. Businesses there work in international trade, logistics, processing and software, and newer sectors are being added: new energy, AI, new mobility, new materials, information and communication technology and new transport. The area has been renamed for marketing purposes and is now promoted as Huangpu District. It also houses the Guangzhou IP Court.
Guangzhou Science City.

Many international firms use Guangzhou as a base. China Briefing reports that by 2018 over 30,000 foreign-invested companies had settled there, among them 297 Fortune Global 500 companies with projects in the city and 120 with headquarters or regional headquarters.
At the end of 2024 Guangzhou's permanent resident population was 18.978 million, with an urbanisation rate of 87.24 percent.

In the Seventh National Population Census, 18,676,605 permanent residents were counted on 1 November 2020. Compared with 12,700,800 in 2010, the city had grown by 5,975,805 people, or 47.05 percent. Urban residents made up 86.19 percent (16,096,724 people) and rural residents 13.81 percent (2,579,881).

Migration shapes the city. The 2020 census found 11,522,907 people living somewhere other than their registered household location, including 9,378,825 floating-population members, so Guangzhou stands out as one of China's biggest destinations for migrants.

south-china-normal-university.h: Earlier estimates and the wider region

blocks.x: In 2014 the population was estimated at 13,080,500, of whom 11,264,800 lived in urban areas, a density of about 1,800 per km2. The built-up area of Guangzhou itself runs into several neighbouring cities. Across the Pearl River Delta Economic Zone, a built-up area of about 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 sq mi) holds an estimated 22 million people. That figure covers Guangzhou's nine urban districts and then Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890,000) and Huizhou's Huiyang District (760,000). Add Hong Kong and the agglomeration exceeds 28 million. Rapid growth and strong labour demand have created a huge floating population of migrant workers, and up to 10 million migrants stay in the area at least six months each year. Around five million permanent Guangzhou residents were migrants in 2008. The OECD put the wider metropolitan area at 25 million as of 2010. For a student, this means a big, mixed, fast-moving city where almost everyone is from somewhere else.

Gong and colleagues published a study in 2018 of how Guangzhou developed from 1990 to 2020. In 1990, residential districts were almost all in one small section of western Guangzhou, with only a few small communities elsewhere, surrounded by farmland and woodland. After 2005 more areas filled in, and by the 2020 map developed neighbourhoods stretched from west to east. The far south and large parts of the north were still mostly farmland and woodland with very few built-up communities.

Ferry travel to Hong Kong and Macau is possible by fast catamaran every day. Boats leave from Nansha Ferry Terminal and from Lianhua Shan Ferry Terminal in Guangzhou for the Hong Kong China Ferry Terminal, and there is also a link from Nansha to the Macau Ferry Pier in Hong Kong, which makes weekend trips to those cities practical.

In the past Guangzhou had roughly 124 religious pavilions, halls and temples. Today it has a Buddhist Association and also a Taoist Association and a Jewish community, and it has a history of Christianity, which colonial powers reintroduced to China.

In summary, SCNU offers study in one of China's largest and most prosperous cities, with campuses in Guangzhou and nearby Foshan and Shanwei, a warm humid climate and the benefits of a strong regional economy.
South China Normal University lists 121 programs for international students on this site: 22 bachelor, 35 master's, 25 doctoral, 39 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 121 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 17,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 19,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 19,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

121 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

south-china-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. South China Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guangzhou, register at South China Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

south-china-university-of-technology.h: South China University of Technology: the basics

blocks.x: South China University of Technology (SCUT) is a publicly funded university in Guangzhou, the capital city of Guangdong province in southern China. The Ministry of Education supervises it, and the Guangdong provincial government shares in sponsoring it. As with many of the country's top universities, three national schemes have included it: Double First-Class Construction, Project 985 and Project 211. For an international student, that combination points to a well-funded, research-oriented engineering university.

In 1952 a nationwide reshuffle of higher education created the South China Institute of Technology (华南工学院), the forerunner of today's university. The new institute gathered engineering schools and departments from leading universities across five provinces of central and southern China. Among them were the old National Sun Yat-sen University, Lingnan University, Hunan University, Guangxi University and South China Joint University, plus four more.
The main milestones since then are listed below.
1960: designated a National Key University and put under the direct administration of the Ministry of Education
1988: renamed South China University of Technology
1995: selected under Project 211 as one of the universities China would invest in heavily for the 21st century

1999: given an excellent grade in the Undergraduate Teaching Assessment, which put it among the first Excellent Universities of Undergraduate Education nationwide; that same year, with approval from the technology and education ministries, a national science park opened
2000: approval to set up a Graduate School
2001: joined Project 985, whose support went to 39 national universities
2017: placed in Class A of the Double First-Class scheme, a group of 36 universities

Rankings are only one way of judging a university, and different tables use different methods and subject weightings, but together they show the broad picture. The 2013 Leiden Ranking measured the share of each university's publications that are among the top 10% in their fields. On that measure SCUT stood 138th worldwide and 11th in Asia. Within China, excluding Hong Kong, it was 5th, after Nankai University, Hunan University, the University of Science and Technology of China and Lanzhou University.
In the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), the trend has been strongly upward.
2014: 301-400. In 2015, subject tables ranked its engineering/technology and computer science 48th, mathematics in the 151-200 band and chemistry in the 101-150 band

QS ranked it 392nd in the world for 2023. U.S. News is similar in direction: its Best Global Universities list had SCUT at 448th in 2015, 394th in 2017 and 219th in 2023. Newer editions will have appeared since, so check current tables.

SCUT's graduates and staff have made their mark in several fields. Because the university trains many engineers and architects, you will notice that business and design feature strongly. They are grouped below by field.
Cheng Siwei, a Vice Chairman of China's National People's Congress
Chen Ding, who won the 20 kilometres walk at the 2012 Summer Olympics
He Jingtang, head of the SCUT School of Architecture and a member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, who led the design of the widely admired China Pavilion for Shanghai Expo 2010
Thomas Hou, a professor of applied and computational mathematics (the Charles Lee Powell chair) at the California Institute of Technology
Rong Baisheng, architect and civil engineer
Yao Zhenhua, founder of Baoneng Group
Li Dongsheng, chief executive of TCL Corporation
Zhang Zhidong, a former chief technology officer of Tencent
He Xiaopeng, who co-founded UCWeb Inc. and served as its president
Robin Zeng, the founder and president of CATL
Daily life as a student depends on the city beyond the campus gate, including the weather, local transport and things to do. The rest of this profile covers Guangzhou, the home of SCUT.

Historically the town grew up by Baiyun Mountain, on the Pearl River's (Zhujiang) eastern bank. It was about 80 miles (130 kilometres) from where the river joins the South China Sea, and some 300 miles downstream of the head of navigation. Its position gave it command of the fertile alluvial Pearl River Delta, with the route to the sea defended at the Humen Strait.

The modern city covers 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 square miles) and straddles the river between longitudes 112° 57′ and 114° 03′ east and latitudes 22° 26′ and 23° 56′ north, in the south-central part of Guangdong. The Pearl is China's 4th-largest river, which gives some sense of how big the delta around Guangzhou is. Tidal flats along the estuary support intertidal ecosystems, although many have been reclaimed for farming. Locals now call Baiyun Mountain the lung of the city (市肺).
The ground rises from south-west to north-east, with mountains making up the city's backbone and the sea at its front. Tiantang Peak, the city's top, stands at 1,210 metres (3,970 feet).

Guangzhou lies in the water-rich south of China, so rivers, streams and other waterways take up roughly 10% of the land area, a large share for a major city. They add to the scenery and help keep the city's environment steady. In total, the water surface is 74,400 hectares, which is 10.05% of the land area.

The pattern of supply is unusual: there is relatively little local water but plenty that passes through. The main rivers include the Beijiang, the Dongjiang North Mainstream, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi, the Baini, the Pearl River Guangzhou Reach, the Shiqiao Waterway and the Shawan Waterway. The Dongjiang and Beijiang flow through Guangzhou and join the Pearl River on the way to the sea. Local water resources average about 7.979 billion cubic metres. Based on the permanent population in the 2010 census, that gives 1.0601 million cubic metres per square kilometre, or 628 cubic metres per person, half the national per-person average. In contrast, the water passing through the city from upstream is about 186.024 billion cubic metres, 23 times the local total. Most of it is concentrated in the southern Wanghe and Zengcheng districts. The Xijiang and Beijiang rivers contribute about 159.15 billion cubic metres, the Dongjiang adds 14.203 billion through its north mainstream, and 2.828 billion arrives from the upper reaches of the Zengjiang. The component figures in published summaries do not always add up exactly, so treat them as approximate.

The southern river network is under tidal influence, with high runoff and strong tides. The Pearl River's three main outlets, Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili, run into the Lingding Ocean and out to the South China Sea south of the city. Each year the incoming tide brings 271 billion cubic metres, the outgoing tide takes 408.8 billion, and the three outlets together discharge a net 137.7 billion cubic metres. Tides bring in large amounts of water, part of which is usable fresh water.

Farming reflects Guangzhou's position between the tropics and subtropics. Few places in China have such a wealth of fruit trees. Tropical, subtropical and temperate kinds all grow here, covering 41 families, 82 genera and 174 species and more than 500 varieties, among them 55 main varieties of lychee. The area is where lychee, longan, wampee and Chinese olives originated and diversified. Vegetables are also prized for quality and variety, with 15 principal categories, 127 species and over 370 varieties. The flower trade includes cut flowers, foliage and branches, potted plants, bonsai, ornamental seedlings, edible and medicinal flowers and lawns. Staple grains, cash crops, livestock, poultry, seafood and wild animals complete the picture, and Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first Guangzhou product to gain geographical indication protection.

On minerals, the geology is complex and favourable to mineral formation. Forty-seven kinds of minerals have been found (the count includes subspecies), across 820 sites and 25 large and medium mining areas. (Another summary mentions 18 large and medium oil deposits.) Principal deposits include granite for building, cement limestone, ceramic clay, potassium, sodium feldspar, salt, manganese, nepheline orthoclase, fluorite and marble, plus mineral and thermal spring water. Deposits of energy minerals and non-ferrous metals are in short supply, scattered, small and of unstable quality.

Guangzhou sits just south of the Tropic of Cancer and has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa) driven by the East Asian monsoon. Summer is rainy, hot and sticky, and the heat index is high, while winter is gentle and fairly dry. The monsoon lasts a long time, April to September. The coldest month, January, averages 13.8 °C (56.8 °F) and the warmest, July, 28.9 °C (84.0 °F), with 22.4 °C (72.3 °F) across the year. From October to December the weather is mild, cool and windy, which makes it the most pleasant time to travel.

Relative humidity is about 76 percent, and the metropolitan area gets over 1,950 millimetres (77 in) of rain a year. Sunshine is limited. March gets only 17 percent of possible sun and October 51 percent, which comes to 1,559 hours a year, considerably fewer than neighbouring Shenzhen and Hong Kong.

Since 1951 the official range has run from a low of 0 °C (32 °F), reached on both 11 February 1957 and 23 December 1999, up to a high of 39.1 °C (102.4 °F) on 1 July 2004. Older unofficial readings vary: one of -5.0 °C (23.0 °F) on 18 January 1893 is now thought by modern meteorologists to have been closer to -3.0 °C (26.6 °F), and a station in Huangpu District that began recording in 1912 logged -0.3 °C (31.5 °F) on 8 December 1934. The most recent snowfall in the city was on 24 January 2016, 87 years after the one before it. Most of the time, then, you will need only light clothing, an umbrella and something warmer for the occasional cooler winter day. Snow is so rare that it makes the news.

Manufacturing in the Pearl River Delta, a top commercial and industrial region, is centred on Guangzhou. Its 2021 GDP was ¥2,823 billion (US$444.37 billion in nominal terms), second only to Shenzhen in South-Central China, and ¥151,162 (US$23,794) per person. The city counts among the wealthiest in the country.

The Hurun Global Rich List 2020 put the city 10th in the world for billionaires and 5th in China, after Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Oxford Economics forecasts that Guangzhou will be one of the ten biggest cities in the world by nominal GDP in 2035, together with Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, and that nominal GDP per head will pass $42,000 in 2030. As a financial centre, the 2020 Global Financial Centers Index ranked it 21st worldwide, which is between Washington, D.C. and Amsterdam, and 8th in Asia and Oceania, with Shanghai, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, Beijing, Shenzhen and Dubai ahead of it.
Fast industrialisation once made Guangzhou a fairly polluted city, but after green urban planning was introduced it is now counted among China's most liveable cities.
#### Zhujiang New Town
The newest downtown is Zhujiang New Town, the 21st-century central business district. It occupies 6.44 km2 of Tianhe District, and several financial institutions have their headquarters there.
#### Canton Fair

The Canton Fair, officially the China Import and Export Fair, takes place each April and October under the Ministry of Trade. It started in spring 1957 and is a major event in the city; it is China's oldest, highest-level and largest trade fair, so hotels and transport can be busy while it runs. The 104th session was the first in a new venue, the Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center (广州国际会展中心) at Pazhou, replacing the older complex at Liuhua. Visitors can reach it by two Line 8 metro stations, a Line 11 station or three stops on Tram Line THZ1. Also from the 104th session, the fair has run in three phases instead of two.
#### Local specialities
Cantonese cuisine is one of China's best-known regional styles, and a saying simply tells people to eat in Guangzhou (食在廣州). Local crafts and products include the following.
Cantonese carving, in jade, wood and (a controversial material) ivory
Canton porcelain, an export ware developed over the past three centuries and known in China for its very colourful style
Cantonese embroidery, one of China's four main embroidery styles
Zhujiang Beer, a pale lager and one of the country's most successful brands
#### Industrial zones
Major industrial names and areas in the city include the following.
GAC Group
Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone

Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone, founded in 2005, with a planned area of 1.36 square kilometres (0.53 square miles) in Nansha District. Car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry are the industries it promotes. The zone is 54 kilometres (34 miles) south of Baiyun International Airport (about 70 minutes by road), beside Nansha Port, and Metro Line 4 was being extended to the Nansha Ferry Terminal.

Guangzhou Free Trade Zone, founded in 1992 in the east of Huangpu District, near the Economic and Technological Development Zone and also very near Baiyun Airport. Its target industries are software, processing, logistics and international trade. The area has lately been rebranded and is promoted under the Huangpu District name, with newer sectors being added, including AI, new energy, new materials, new transport and mobility, and information and communication technology. The Guangzhou IP Court is also based here.
Guangzhou Science City
#### Foreign business
International companies have come in large numbers.
At the end of 2024 Guangzhou had a permanent resident population of 18.978 million, with an urbanisation rate of 87.24%.
#### The 2020 census

The Seventh National Population Census put the permanent resident population at 18,676,605 on 1 November 2020. Compared with 12,700,800 in 2010, that is 5,975,805 more residents, a 47.05% increase. Urban areas held 86.19% of the population (16,096,724 people) and rural areas 13.81% (2,579,881).

Migration remains central to the city's make-up. The census counted 11,522,907 people living somewhere other than their registered household location, including 9,378,825 in the floating population, which confirms Guangzhou as one of China's biggest destinations for migrants.

An older estimate for 2014 was 13,080,500 people, with 11,264,800 in urban areas, and a density of about 1,800 people per km2, though the 2020 census figures above are much higher. The built-up area of Guangzhou proper joins directly with several other cities. The Pearl River Delta Economic Zone's built-up area covers about 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 square miles) and is thought to hold 22 million people, counting Guangzhou's nine urban districts, Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890,000) and Huizhou's Huiyang District (760,000). If the neighbouring Hong Kong Special Administrative Region is counted as well, the total passes 28 million. The fast-growing economy needs many workers and so has produced a huge floating population of migrants: as many as 10 million spend at least half of each year in the area. For 2008, about five million of the people counted as permanent residents of Guangzhou were migrant workers.
#### The wider metropolitan area
The OECD estimated that the surrounding metropolitan area had 25 million people as of 2010.
#### How the city has spread

A 2018 study by Gong and colleagues followed Guangzhou's growth between 1990 and 2020. In 1990 nearly all developed residential districts lay in one small part of western Guangzhou, and elsewhere there were only small pockets of housing among farmland and forest. From 2005 to 2020, other districts began to develop more housing. By the 2020 map, developed residential areas stretched from the west of the city to the east, while the far south and large parts of the north were still mainly farmland and forest with very little housing.

south-china-university-of-technology.h: Getting to Hong Kong and Macau by sea

blocks.x: Fast catamaran ferries sail every day from Guangzhou's Nansha and Lianhua Shan ferry terminals to the China Ferry Terminal in Hong Kong. Nansha Ferry Terminal also has a service to the Macau Ferry Pier in Hong Kong. Both cities are within easy reach for a weekend trip or a visa run.

Before the modern era Guangzhou had about 124 religious pavilions, halls and temples. Today, besides the Buddhist Association, the city has a Taoist Association and a Jewish community, and it has a history with Christianity, which was reintroduced to China by colonial powers.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

south-china-university-of-technology.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. South China University of Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Guangzhou, register at South China University of Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Southeast University, usually shortened to SEU, is a state-funded institution in Nanjing, the capital of Jiangsu Province. It reports to China's Ministry of Education, and it carries three of the best-known national labels in Chinese higher education: Projects 211 and 985, plus the Double First-Class scheme. For an international applicant, that combination tells you the university sits among the country's heavily funded research universities, with engineering as its signature strength.

The roots of the school go back to 1902, when Sanjiang Teachers College opened as a modern institution on ground once occupied by the Ming Guozijian. The name changed many times afterwards. In 1921 it became National Southeast University, the second national university in China. In 1928 it was renamed National Central University and treated as the flagship of the nation. After the Civil War ended Nationalist control of Nanjing, it was renamed National Nanking University in August 1949. The name Southeast University came back in May 1988.

southeast-university.h: A century of names and mergers

blocks.x: The story is long and full of renamings, so it helps to follow it in stages.

southeast-university.h: The imperial school on the site

blocks.x: The campus ground was originally the home of the first Guozijian (Imperial Academy) of the Ming dynasty. The Imperial Academy had travelled with the capital from one dynasty to the next, yet the idea began with the Wu Emperor of the Jin dynasty, and he drew on the royal schools of the Three Kingdoms era, among them one that Sun Xiu of Wu founded at Nanjing in the year 258. Building a modern college on this site was therefore a deliberate statement about continuity in Chinese learning.

southeast-university.h: Sanjiang and Liangjiang normal colleges, 1902 to 1911

blocks.x: By the end of the 19th century the Qing state was under strain from unrest at home and pressure from abroad. Anti-foreign violence in 1899, known as the Boxer Uprising, and the invasion that followed it by eight allied powers persuaded the court to reform education. In 1901 a reform programme began, and in 1902 the 'Imperially Authorized School Regulations' were issued under the leadership of Zhang Baixi, starting a national school system. Later that year, on 30 May, Liu Kunyi, who governed the Liangjiang region as viceroy, sent a paper to the court proposing a normal college in Jiangning, which is today's Nanjing. In February 1903 his successor Zhang Zhidong put forward a plan for Sanjiang Normal College and sent Miao Quansun to Japan to study how such schools worked. Miao was later named inspector of the college and took charge of preparing the project. The college opened formally in September 1903.

Because the original name caused confusion and a number of disputes, it was changed in 1905 to Liangjiang Normal College. Li Ruiqing became principal the next year. He shut down the junior teacher-training courses, added general and professional subjects, and started the first painting course in China. By 1907 the college had departments of Geography and History, Chinese and Foreign Languages, Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry, and Agriculture. When the Xinhai Revolution broke out at the end of 1911, the college almost closed.

Governor Han Guojun chose Jiang Qian as principal on 15 July 1914 and asked him to establish Nanjing Higher Normal School on the same site. Jiang hired Guo Bingwen, a scholar educated in the United States, as dean of teaching and Chen Rong as adviser, and sent both of them to Europe to study education systems and recruit teachers. The school officially opened on 10 September 1915. A step that still stands out today came in December 1919, when it admitted 8 women as regular students and 50 more as visiting students, which made it the first school in China to teach women and men together. A Polytechnic Faculty was added in 1916.

Guo Bingwen became president of the southern division in September 1918. On 7 April 1920 he proposed a Preparatory Committee for Southeast University, and in September he applied to the State Council and the Ministry of Education for permission to found the university, which was approved that December. The Board was formed on 6 June 1921 with Guo as president, and teaching started that September. That December the school council agreed that Nanjing Higher Normal School would become part of the new university. By 1923 it had grown to include arts and sciences, education, engineering, agriculture and business, offering more than 20 lines of study across 5 subject areas. Its Engineering School, created in 1921, grew out of the earlier Polytechnic Faculty.

southeast-university.h: Hohai and National Central University, 1924 to 1949

blocks.x: Two mergers came next. In 1924 the engineers of the new university teamed up with a water-engineering school called Hohai Engineering School, and the result, led by president Mao Yisheng, was National Hohai Technology University. By 1927 that body and some further schools had been absorbed with the original university into National Central University, a name it kept until 1949.

southeast-university.h: The 1949 change and the Nanjing Institute of Technology

blocks.x: The People's Liberation Army entered Nanjing in April 1949, and a military committee for the city assumed control of the university. On 8 August 1949 it received the name National Nanjing University, and in October 1950 it became simply Nanjing University.

In 1952 the People's Republic began a nationwide reorganisation of its colleges. In Nanjing, the changes mostly involved Nanjing University and the University of Nanking. The Nanjing Institute of Technology was created on the old National Central University site by combining the Engineering School of Nanjing University (then the largest school there) with the engineering departments of the University of Nanking, including its Chemistry and Electrical Machine departments. Later still, related subjects arrived from Jiaotong, Zhejiang, Shandong, Xiamen and Fudan universities and from private Jiangnan University.

In June 1988 the Nanjing Institute of Technology took the name Southeast University and began its change from a technical institute into a comprehensive university with technology at its core. A small note for readers searching online: since 2000 the old name Nanjing Institute of Technology has been used by a different institution, so do not mix the two up. In 2000 Nanjing Railway Medical College, the Nanjing Higher Institute of Transportation and the Nanjing Geological School were all merged into SEU. Later sections of the profile say 2001 for the same merger, so if the exact year matters for an official document, check the university's own website.

SEU is one of 32 universities administered directly by the national education ministry, a group generally seen as the top tier in China. Roughly 16,000 undergraduates and 10,000 graduate students study here, spread over more than 30 schools and departments. Admission is very competitive. For undergraduate places it normally takes the top 2% of high school students from across the country, and for graduate study it takes the top 5% of undergraduates. Most students are placed in engineering or other large schools: Mechanical Engineering, Energy and Environmental Engineering, Information Science and Engineering, Civil Engineering, Computer Science and Engineering, Economics and Management, and Transportation Engineering. The remaining students join smaller units such as Automation, Electronic Science and the Department of Physics.

The university employs around 5,600 faculty members. The list of distinctions is long: 8 members of the Chinese Academy; 25 Changjiang Scholars; 31 national young researchers of distinction; 57 outstanding researchers recognised by the Department of Education; one fellow and 9 members of the State Degree Committee; and 7 seats on the expert committee of the '863 Projects', the second-highest count in the country.

SEU offers 64 undergraduate programmes, 206 master's programmes, 109 doctoral programmes and 15 postdoctoral research sites. In the most recent official ranking summary, 6 programmes were placed in the top 5 nationwide and 6 more in the top 10, with the School of Biomedical Science and Engineering in first place. The facilities behind that record are substantial. SEU counts 10 national first-class academic programmes with 6 more in the pipeline, plus 3 National Research Labs, a National Professional Lab, a pair of National Engineering Research Centers and 7 Department of Education first-class labs.
Money has followed that capability. In 2006 research funding reached 600 million yuan, 7th in the country, and by 2010 it exceeded 1.1 billion yuan, which placed 11th nationwide.

SEU counts itself among China's twenty leading universities for research and development. More than 20 national or provincial institutes and a set of key research bases operate under its roof. During the past ten years its staff have finished over 1000 projects, and more than 500 of those earned science and technology prizes at national, provincial or city level. Its Architecture Design and Research Institute is among the few design institutes in the country with first-class status and has taken on major commissions. Zhongda Hospital, which belongs to the university and dates from 1935, carries the Ministry of Public Health's 'Class A Grade 3' rating.
The ranking figures come from different years, so treat them as snapshots and check current tables before you apply.
In 2007 the university was placed 443rd among world universities.
In 2010 Nature Publishing Index (China) ranked it 8th among domestic research institutes.
QS tables for 2010 had it 87th among all Asian universities and 76th for engineering and IT in Asia, with a worldwide band of 301st to 350th in that subject.
In 2016 the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) placed it between 201st and 300th, and 20th in the ARWU engineering field ranking.
In the 2017 national ranking compiled by Wu Shulian, SEU came 14th in China, part of a group of 22 other universities counted as the country's top tier.
By the 2020 ARWU, the global band had improved to 101st to 150th, with a national rank of 7th to 13th.
The direction of travel is upward, which is what matters when you compare it with other engineering-focused universities.

southeast-university.h: Campuses and where you will study

blocks.x: SEU has three main campuses. Sipailou, in Xuanwu District, and Dingjiaqiao, in Gulou District, are inside Nanjing city. Jiulonghu is in the suburbs, in Jiangning District.

Sipailou, at 2 Sipailou, is the flagship and was inherited from National Central University. Dingjiaqiao holds the School of Medicine, which was formed when Nanjing Railway Medical College joined SEU.

Jiulonghu was founded in 2005 and is now where most undergraduates and master's students study. Once it opened, Sipailou became mainly the home of the university's most important research institutes and administration. Jiulonghu sits at the southern end of the Jiangning Technology Development District, bounded by Suyuan Avenue on one side, Shuanglong Street on another and Jiyin Street to the north, and is around 20 kilometres from Sipailou. It covers 3749 mu, has a total building area of 574 thousand square metres, and was built with an investment of 1.6 billion yuan. The design builds on the university's own culture, joins teaching and research on one site, mixes Chinese and Western styles, and aims for a green and lively community.

One more campus belongs to the history. In 1988 a Pukou campus across the Yangtze River opened, mainly for first-year and second-year students. In 2008 it was separated from SEU and taken over by Cheng Xian Institute. The profile elsewhere says its authority passed to Chengxian College in 2005, so the dates are not consistent between sources. The 2001 merger brought in a railway medical college, a transport college and a geology school, all from Nanjing.
The university teaches through a wide network of schools. Engineering and science units include the following.

For business, language, arts and social subjects there are the Schools of Economics and Management, Foreign Languages, Humanities, Law and Art. The alumni and staff list is mixed and not always clearly dated, but it gives a good picture of what graduates go on to do.

The alumni list names Chiang Kai-shek, President of the Republic of China; Huang Wei, vice chairman of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and a former Vice Minister of Construction; and Dio Wang, an Australian senator.

The first name on the list is Chien-Shiung Wu, the physicist known as the 'Oriental Marie Curie', whose beta-decay experiments showed that symmetry is not conserved in the weak interaction. Zhengxu Zhao is chief scientist of space mission visualization and control, a professor, and a Fellow of the British Royal Society of Arts. Harry Shum (Shen Xiangyang) is a computer scientist who became Executive Vice President of Artificial Intelligence and Research at Microsoft; another entry for him describes him as a Microsoft senior vice president and a youth-category judge for the National Natural Science Foundation.

Yung Ho Chang (Zhang Yonghe) holds an architecture prize from the American Academy of Arts and teaches in the Department of Architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Cheng Taining is chief architect at a Chinese engineering corporation and heads an architectural design institute that bears his name. The musician Li Zhi was banned in the People's Republic of China for references to the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre.
Most day-to-day student life happens in the city around the campus, so the climate, transport and local habits matter. The sections below describe Nanjing, the home of Southeast University.

The city spreads over 6,598 square kilometres (2,548 sq mi) in the lower Yangtze basin, within the Yangtze River Delta, which ranks among China's biggest economic regions. Water frames it on two sides: the Yangtze runs past the west and then bends along the north, and a range called the Ningzheng Ridge encloses the remaining sides. For orientation, Beijing is 900 km away to the north-northwest, Shanghai 270 km to the east-southeast, Luoyang 650 km to the northwest and Chongqing 1,200 km to the west (these are approximate distances of 560, 170, 400 and 750 miles).

Upstream, the great river travels from Jiujiang in Jiangxi across Anhui and Jiangsu before reaching the East China Sea. The Huai River basin lies to the north of the lower Yangtze basin and the Zhe River basin to the south, with the Grand Canal linking them east of Nanjing. The region around the city is called Xiajiang (Downstream River), with the Jianghuai culture dominant in the north and Jiangzhe in the south. People also know it as Dongnan (the Southeast) and Jiangnan (south of the Yangtze).

Neighbouring places are easy to remember. On the Jiangsu side, Yangzhou lies to the northeast, Zhenjiang to the east and Changzhou to the southeast. Across the provincial border in Anhui, five cities touch Nanjing: Chuzhou in the northwest, Wuhu, Chaohu and Ma'anshan in the west, and Xuancheng in the southwest.

Nanjing has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen Cfa) shaped by the East Asian monsoon. The seasons are distinct and the air is damp all year. Summers are very hot and muggy, winters are cold and damp, and spring and autumn are reasonably long. With Chongqing and Wuhan, the city is traditionally one of the 'Three Furnaces' along the Yangtze because of its summer heat. From mid-June to the end of July comes the meiyu or 'plum rain' season, a spell of mild rain and dampness during plum blossom time. Northeast winds prevail in winter and southeast winds in summer.

The winters surprise many newcomers. For its latitude Nanjing is cold: winter temperatures are about the same as London's or lower, and January is 2 degrees C colder than January in London even though Nanjing is at 32 degrees 04 minutes north and London at 51 degrees 30 minutes north. Compared with the humid subtropical east coast of the United States, winter in Nanjing is 7 degrees C colder than in Savannah, Georgia. Pack warm clothing.
Here are the figures:
Temperature: January averages 3.1 C (37.6 F), July 28.4 C (83.1 F), and the whole year about 16.4 C (61.5 F).
Extremes: a low of -14.0 C (6.8 F) on 6 January 1955, and a high of 43.0 C (109.4 F) on 13 July 1934. Another figure gives 40.7 C (105 F) on 22 August 1959 as the extreme since 1951.
Rain: 112.9 days a year with more than 0.1 mm, with a record of 160 days in 1957; a typical year brings 1,144 millimetres (45.0 in) of precipitation.
Sunshine: monthly possible sunshine runs from 37 percent in June to 48 percent in August and October, for 1,932.4 hours a year.
Typhoons are rare but can occur in late summer and early autumn.

A thick wave of smog began on 2 December 2013 across about 1,200 kilometres (750 mi) of central and eastern China, taking in Tianjin, Hebei, Shandong, Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang. Little cold air movement, together with slow air masses carrying industrial emissions, trapped pollutants over the region. Central and southern Jiangsu were hit hard, and Nanjing's air quality index stayed at 'severely polluted' for five days in a row and 'heavily polluted' for nine. Officials pointed to calm winds, car exhaust under low air pressure and the coal-fired district heating of northern China, and noted that prevailing winds pushed low-lying air carrying factory emissions, mostly SO2, toward the east coast. This was a particular event, so check the current air quality when you plan your stay.

The Yangtze crosses Nanjing diagonally from southwest to northeast. Its stretch within the city is about 93 kilometres long, more than 300 kilometres from the sea entrance. The Qinhuai River runs south to north through the main urban area into the Yangtze and is called the mother river of Nanjing. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are described as two pearls set in the city, and open water covers about 11% of the municipal area. Almost everything belongs to the Yangtze system; only rivers flowing into Gaoyou Lake and Baoying Lake in northern Liuhe District belong to the Huai system. The Yangtze system takes in the Qinhuai system south of the river, the Chuhe system north of it, the riverside system of small streams, the two-lake system of Shijiu Lake and Gucheng Lake, and the West Taihu Lake system east of Gaochun. Groundwater is plentiful and of excellent quality, with the Pukou Pearl Spring particularly famous, and Jiangning Tangshan and Pukou Tangquan are old hot spring areas.

Nanjing has the biggest river port in China, which handled 191,970,000 tonnes of cargo in 2012. Its shoreline is 98 kilometres (61 mi) long with 64 berths, 16 of which take ships above 10,000 tonnes. It is also the biggest container port on the Yangtze; the Longtan Containers Port Area, with a capacity of one million containers, opened in March 2004. As of 2010 it was split into six public and three industrial port areas. A 12.5-metre-deep channel lets 50,000-ton ocean ships arrive directly, and vessels of 100,000 tons or more can come after reducing their load during the Yangtze's high tide. CSC Jinling operates a large shipyard here.

Nanjing is rich in natural resources, including more than 40 kinds of minerals. Iron and sulfur reserves account for 40 percent of Jiangsu's total, and strontium reserves rank first in East Asia and Southeast Asia. The discovered minerals cover 49 types, including iron, copper, lead, zinc, strontium, iron sulphide, dolomite, limestone, gypsum and clay, and 31 of these have proven reserves. They cluster in 4 metallogenic belts: the Jiangpu-Liuhe iron and copper belt, the Ningzhen iron, copper and sulfur belt and the Ningwu iron and copper belt. The city also has hot springs, such as Tangshan in Jiangning and Tangquan in Pukou, and a Yangtze deep-water channel was being built so that 50,000 DWT ships could come from the East China Sea. Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake are in the middle of the city and open to everyone, while Purple Mountain has deciduous and coniferous forest and preserves many historical and cultural sites.

There are two main soil types. Zonal soil is yellow-brown in the north and centre of the city and red along the southern border with Anhui. The cultivated soil made by farming is mostly paddy soil, with some yellow Gang soil and vegetable garden soil. Soil patterns follow terrain and water conditions and fall into three zones: low mountain and hilly areas, hilly areas and plains. The second national soil survey of 1980 to 1987 sorted Nanjing's soil into 7 soil types, 13 subtypes, 30 genera and 66 species, with a total area of 416,300 hectares.

Nanjing has abundant and varied plant life. Natural vegetation falls into 7 types, running from conifer woods and deciduous broad-leaved woods through mixed broad-leaved forest, bamboo groves and shrubland to grassland and water plants. Farmed and planted land adds field crops, vegetables, orchards, economic forests and green belts. Seven rare plants, including Sphaerocarpus sinensis, Chinese Allium chinense, Ming Codonopsis and Pterocarpus sinensis, are under national protection.

For animals, records 795 insect species from 125 families and 11 orders, 99 fish species from 22 families and 12 orders, and 327 terrestrial wild vertebrates from 29 orders and 90 families. Of these, 243 are birds (56 families, 17 orders) and 47 are mammals (8 orders, 22 families). Nine species, among them the Oriental White Crane and the White Shoulder Eagle, hold top-level national protection, while 65 others, including the little swan, the Chinese tiger, the swallowtail and the finless porpoise, are protected at the second level. There are also 125 key protected species in Jiangsu and 35 endangered species.

Nanjing's first Yangtze bridge, finished in the 1960s, was at that time the lone fixed crossing of the lower Yangtze in eastern China. Chinese engineers designed and built it themselves after foreign surveys failed and after Soviet help had been used and then set aside, so it became a source of pride and a symbol of modern China. Work started in 1960 and traffic began in 1968. The structure has a road deck above a railway deck; the upper deck is 4,600 metres (15,100 ft) long, of which about 1,580 metres (5,180 ft) span the water. Since then the city has added four more bridges and four tunnels.

In downstream order, the crossings are the Dashengguan Bridge, the Third Bridge, the Fifth Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the Nanjing Yangtze River Tunnel, the Line 10 Metro Tunnel, the Nanjing Yangtze Tunnel, the First Bridge, the Yanziji Yangtze River Tunnel, the Baguazhou Bridge and the Qixiashan Bridge. The bridge list with opening years and longest spans is:
First Nanjing Yangtze Bridge: opened 1968, longest span 160 m (the figure looks odd for the span of such a bridge, so verify before quoting it).
Baguazhou Bridge (Second): opened 1997, 628 m.
Dashengguan Bridge (Third): opened 2005, 648 m.
Qixiashan Bridge (Fourth): opened 2012, 1,418 m.
Jiangxinzhou Bridge (Fifth): opened 2020, 600 m.
Xianxin Bridge: opened 2023, 1,760 m.

By October 2014 the city had four bridges and two tunnels linking the districts north of the river with the centre on the south bank. Nanjing serves as the transport hub for eastern China and the lower Yangtze region, with land, water and air links forming one system. As in most Chinese cities, public transport is the main way most residents travel.

At the 2010 census, Nanjing had 8.005 million people. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 11.7 million at that time. Official figures for 2011 put the city at 8.11 million, with a birth rate of 8.86 percent and a death rate of 6.88 percent. The urban area held 6.47 million people, and there were 107.31 men for every 100 women.

Like most of eastern China, Nanjing is overwhelmingly Han (98.56 percent), though it officially counts 50 other ethnic groups too. In 1999, 77,394 residents belonged to minorities, and the Hui were by far the biggest group with 64,832 people, or 83.76 percent. Manchu (2,311) and Zhuang (533) followed. Most of them lived in Jianye District, where they accounted for 9.13 percent of residents.

Nanjing is an important farming and grain trade base. Typical crops are rice and cotton, silkworm cocoons, hemp, tea, bamboo, fruit and medicinal plants, and the fertile water on both sides of the Yangtze makes it an important freshwater fishing base. In 2019 the output of agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery together was 47.250 billion yuan, up 4.8% on the previous year. Agriculture contributed 24.077 billion yuan, forestry 2.017 billion, animal husbandry 2.435 billion, fishery 15.389 billion and related services 3.333 billion.

southeast-university.h: What this means for your plans

blocks.x: Choosing SEU means choosing a research-focused engineering university with a long history, three campuses, a strong national standing and an easy rail and river location in one of eastern China's most important cities. Before you apply, confirm programme names, campus locations and admission rules on the university's official website, because the details change from year to year.

southeast-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Southeast University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.

After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Nanjing, register at Southeast University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Southern Medical University (南方医科大学) is a public medical university run by the government of Guangdong Province. Its home is Baiyun District in Guangzhou, the provincial capital in southern China. For most of its life it was a military school, and that history still explains a good deal about how it is organised. In 2004 the whole institution moved out of the armed forces and into civilian hands, and today it belongs entirely to the Guangdong Provincial People's Government.

The campus sits at the foot of Baiyun Mountain, one of the best-known green spaces in Guangzhou. The main campus and a second campus in the southern suburbs together cover close to one square kilometre. The grounds are planted with rows of trees and flower beds that bloom through much of the year, so the place feels more like a garden than a typical urban block. The university has also grown beyond Guangzhou: a further site, the Shunde Campus, now operates in Foshan.

southern-medical-university.h: From army school to civilian university: the long history

blocks.x: The story of Southern Medical University is really the story of two military medical schools that were eventually joined together. It is easiest to follow them one at a time and then see how they ended up as a single provincial university.

southern-medical-university.h: The first strand: a wartime medical school

blocks.x: The oldest roots go back to August 1951. The Korean War had created an urgent need for medical staff, so the Northeast Military Region of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) decided to set up its own medical school. It was built around the PLA's Second Army Hospital in Qiqihar and formally opened on 30 October 1951 under the Health Department of the region's Logistics Department. Li Ziping, a deputy head of that department, became the first president.
Over the next decade the school changed name and level several times, which is typical of Chinese institutions that began in the military.

January 1953: following a Central Military Commission order to standardise all military medical schools, the name became PLA No. 11 Army Medical Secondary School, offering a two-year course that produced military medical assistants for troop health care.
May 1954: an army-wide reshuffle of medical secondary schools upgraded it to PLA No. 11 Army Medical School. Its three-year course trained second-level military doctors.

18 January 1956: the school was placed under the PLA's General Logistics Department, and that March it and its hospital were taken from the Shenyang Military Region and brought under the same department.

June 1958: the school was handed to civilian administration, under the national Ministry of Health, although some sources say it went to the Heilongjiang provincial government instead. It joined forces with No. 2164 Hospital and was renamed Qiqihar Medical College, now a proper higher-education institution, with the course stretched from three years to five.

January 1962: the college and its hospital went back under the General Logistics Department and were renamed PLA Qiqihar Medical College. The three-year course was now mainly for serving military officers who were already in post.
21 October 1966: it became simply the PLA Military Medical College.

southern-medical-university.h: Moving south: Changsha and then Guangzhou

blocks.x: In August 1969 the General Logistics Department told the school, with the centre's approval, to leave Qiqihar and occupy an old PLA Engineering Corps Academy site in Changsha, Hunan Province, and the relocation began on 3 October 1969. The stay was short. On 4 February 1970 Premier Zhou Enlai approved a different plan: the State Council and the Central Military Commission gave the college the empty campus of Jinan University at Shipai in Guangzhou, which had been shut down. The college kept its name, moved into the Jinan site, and was run for a time by the Guangzhou Military Region. That is when the institution became a Guangzhou university.

That April the Guangzhou Military Region's health school was folded into it. Then, on 24 July 1975, Central Military Commission Document No. 95 took the college away from the Guangzhou Military Region and returned it to the General Logistics Department. To bring its title into line with other institutions it became the First Military Medical University of the PLA, the name by which it was officially known from then on.

southern-medical-university.h: Growth as the First Military Medical University

blocks.x: The next two decades were a period of steady expansion.
1976: a Department of Traditional Chinese Medicine was established.

February 1978: the PLA No. 103 Hospital, previously under the Fuzhou Military Region, was brought in as the university's Second Affiliated Hospital, known to the public as Zhujiang Hospital. The university's original hospital became its First Affiliated Hospital, which the public knows as Nanfang Hospital.

1978: the original Jinan University reopened. Ye Jianying lent his support that April, and the Central Military Commission approved a fresh campus location for the university at Qilinkang, on the north-eastern edge of Guangzhou. In the same year the programme was set at four years and the university began recruiting students from across the country.
1979: the university was named a national key institution, the course was lengthened to five years, and master's students were enrolled for the first time.
February 1980: Ye Jianying personally wrote the university's name in his own calligraphy.
November 1992: the military region's health school joined the university once more, this time as its Nursing Department.
June 1993: the Nursing Department's site and most of its staff went back to the Guangzhou Military Region, where they were reorganised as the PLA Guangzhou Medical College.
July 1999: that Guangzhou Medical College was absorbed back into the university.
2004: China picked the university as one of just eight pioneering institutions to trial a medical degree lasting eight years.

southern-medical-university.h: The second strand: the Guangzhou military health school

blocks.x: The health school that kept moving in and out of the university has a history of its own. It was created in October 1964 in Chigang, Guangzhou, by combining the region's nursing school with the medical training units of three hospitals (the Military Region General Hospital, PLA No. 163 Hospital and PLA No. 303 Hospital). Its name was PLA Guangzhou Military Region Health School.
April 1970: it was absorbed into the Military Medical College.

August 1974: it split off again as the PLA Guangzhou Military Region Medical School, answerable to the Military Region's logistics department. Its main campus had training, political and administrative departments, and a single teaching hospital, PLA No. 197 Hospital.
July 1986: it was renamed the PLA Guangzhou Military Region Health School.
November 1992: it merged into the First Military Medical University as the Nursing Department.
July 1999: as the armed forces reformed their schools and structures, it was fully merged into the university, which ended the back-and-forth.

The decision came in November 2003. The Central Military Commission, meeting at the 15th All-Army Conference on Military Academies, chose to hand the entire First Military Medical University to local civilian management, as part of a larger overhaul of military structures. The formal paperwork followed on 29 May 2004, when the two General Offices (State Council and Central Military Commission) issued Document No. 40 (2004), concerning the transfer of four military institutions that also included the Quartermaster University. For this university, it meant passing to Guangdong Province and operating as an independent civilian institution.

A handover ceremony took place in the university auditorium on 24 August 2004. The university was transferred in full to the Guangdong provincial government and took the name Southern Medical University.
In short, the school began in a Heilongjiang military hospital in 1951, passed through Changsha, and put down roots in Guangzhou from 1970. It has been a civilian university only since 2004.

The university teaches clinical medicine at bachelor's and master's levels. Its programmes cover Western medicine, traditional Chinese medicine, economics and a range of medical-related fields. For language support, Chinese students take basic English, and international students take basic Mandarin Chinese. If you are an international applicant, that Mandarin teaching matters, because clinical training in China is carried out largely in Chinese.

Both the World Health Organization and the Medical Council of India recognise the university. Applicants from India in particular tend to check this, since it affects whether a foreign medical degree can later be registered at home. You should still confirm current recognition status directly with the relevant bodies and with the university's admissions office before you apply.

Leadership has changed many times, reflecting the many name changes above. This list covers the military era first, with titles as the school stood at each point.

Li Ziping opened the story in 1951 as first head of the Northeast Military Region Medical School. Wang Yizhi took over in March 1953 and presided as the school passed through its secondary-school and army-medical-school phases and became Qiqihar Medical College in Heilongjiang; he additionally held the post of Nenjiang Prefecture commissioner, and later led the PLA Qiqihar Medical College. Ruan Hanqing was in charge of that college and then of the Military Medical College until September 1970. After him, Zhao Yunhong ran the Military Medical College from September 1970 to June 1975, and then the First Military Medical University from July 1975 to June 1990.
Four major generals followed:

Yang Genyuan, August 1991 to March 1996
Bai Shuzhong, March 1996 to August 1998
Li Kang, August 1998 to June 2004
Zheng Muming, likewise a major general, held the top job for the last two months of that era (June to August 2004), overseeing the changeover to Southern Medical University.
