southern-medical-university.h: Living in Guangzhou: what the city offers a student

blocks.x: Daily life for an international student depends heavily on the city around the campus, including its climate, how people move about, and what the economy and community are like. The sections below explain Guangzhou, where Southern Medical University stands.

Guangzhou's original settlement stood close to Baiyun Mountain, on the eastern side of the Pearl River (Zhujiang in Chinese). The river's mouth on the South China Sea is about 130 kilometres (80 miles) away, and the head of navigation is some 300 miles upstream. From that spot the city controlled the fertile alluvial Pearl River Delta, and its sea access was guarded at the Humen Strait.

The modern city spreads across 7,434.4 square kilometres (2,870.4 square miles) on both banks of the river, in south-central Guangdong between longitudes 112° 57′ and 114° 03′ east and latitudes 22° 26′ and 23° 56′ north. The Pearl ranks fourth among China's rivers by size. Along the estuary, tidal flats support intertidal ecosystems, though farmland reclamation has taken over many of them. Locals call Baiyun Mountain the city's "lung" (市肺), a nod to its role as green space in a dense urban region.

The ground climbs gradually from the southwest toward the northeast, with hills at the back of the city and the ocean at its front. Tiantang Peak is the high point, standing 1,210 metres (3,970 feet) above sea level.

Guangzhou sits in the water-rich south, and water covers about 10 per cent of its land area (74,400 hectares, or 10.05 per cent). The main watercourses include the Beijiang, the northern mainstream of the Dongjiang, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi River, the Baini River, the Guangzhou reach of the Pearl River, the Shiqiao Waterway and the Shawan Waterway. The Beijiang and Dongjiang flow through the city and join the Pearl River on the way to the sea. These rivers shape the landscape and help keep the local environment stable.

The water picture has an unusual feature: the city has relatively little local water but a lot of water passing through. Local resources average 7.979 billion cubic metres in total, of which 7.881 billion are surface water and 1.487 billion are groundwater. Using the 2010 census population, that works out to 1.0601 million cubic metres per square kilometre, or 628 cubic metres per person, about half the national per-capita figure. Water flowing in from upstream is far larger, at 186.024 billion cubic metres, which is 23 times the local total. This transit water is concentrated in the southern Wanghe and Zengcheng areas. Some 159.15 billion cubic metres is diverted from the Xijiang and Beijiang, 14.203 billion from the Dongjiang's northern mainstream, and 2.828 billion arrives from the upper Zengjiang.

The southern river network lies in the tidal zone, with heavy runoff and strong tides. South of the city the Pearl River empties through three outlets (Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili) into the Lingding Ocean and on to the South China Sea. In a year, 271 billion cubic metres flow in on the high tide and 408.8 billion flow out on the ebb, while river runoff through the outlets totals 137.7 billion. The tides bring in a large amount of water each year, part of which is fresh and usable.

Farming around Guangzhou shows the shift from tropical to subtropical conditions, and the area is one of the richest in China for fruit. Fruit trees from the tropical, subtropical and temperate zones add up to more than 500 varieties (174 species, 82 genera and 41 families), among them 55 main kinds of lychee. It is the home region and centre of variety for lychee, longan, wampee (yellow skin) and black and white olives. Vegetables are a strength too: more than 370 varieties from 127 species across 15 main groups.

Flower growing is another trade, covering cut blooms, foliage and branches, pot plants, bonsai, bedding plants, seedlings, edible and medicinal flowers and turf. Rice and other grain, cash crops, livestock, poultry, fisheries and wildlife complete the farm picture. Zengcheng Simiao rice is notable as the first Guangzhou product to receive a geographical-indication protection.

The geology is fairly complex and favourable to mineral formation. Surveys have recorded 47 mineral types (subspecies included) at 820 sites, with 25 sizeable mining areas. Granite for building, limestone for cement and ceramic clay lead the list, followed by potassium, sodium feldspar, salt, manganese, nepheline orthoclase, fluorite and marble, plus mineral and thermal spring water. A separate figure mentions 18 oil deposits of medium or large size. Fuels and non-ferrous metals are in short supply, thinly spread, small and uneven in quality, so the region's wealth does not rest on mining.

Guangzhou has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa), driven by the East Asian monsoon, even though the city lies only just below the Tropic of Cancer. Summer brings rain, heat and heavy humidity; winter is mild and comparatively dry. The monsoon lasts a long time, from April through September.
January averages 13.8 °C (56.8 °F), July averages 28.9 °C (84.0 °F), and the whole-year mean is 22.4 °C (72.3 °F).
Humidity sits near 76 per cent, and the metropolitan area gets over 1,950 millimetres (77 inches) of rain a year.
Possible sunshine ranges from 17 per cent in March to 51 per cent in October. Total bright sunshine is 1,559 hours a year, noticeably less than in nearby Shenzhen and Hong Kong.
October to December is mild, cool and breezy, and is regarded as the best time to visit.

Since 1951 the thermometer has never dropped below 0 °C (32 °F), a mark touched on 11 February 1957 and again on 23 December 1999, and the hottest day reached 39.1 °C (102.4 °F) on 1 July 2004. Unofficial figures go lower: −5.0 °C (23.0 °F) on 18 January 1893, which modern meteorologists believe was really closer to −3.0 °C (26.6 °F), and −0.3 °C (31.5 °F) on 8 December 1934 at the Huangpu District station that opened in 1912. The most recent snowfall came on 24 January 2016, 87 years after the one before it.
For planning: expect heat, damp and rain for much of the academic year, pack for humidity, and treat the autumn months as the most comfortable.

Within the Pearl River Delta, one of China's leading commercial and industrial regions, Guangzhou is the chief centre of manufacturing. Its 2021 GDP was ¥2,823 billion (about US$444.37 billion nominal), second in South-Central China behind Shenzhen, and GDP per person was ¥151,162 (US$23,794 nominal). It is counted among the most prosperous cities in China.

Some comparisons help to place it. The Hurun Global Rich List 2020 put Guangzhou 10th globally and 5th within China (after Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen) for its count of billionaires. Oxford Economics forecasts a top-ten place worldwide by nominal GDP by 2035, alongside Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, with nominal GDP per head above US$42,000 by 2030. On the 2020 Global Financial Centers Index it came 21st overall, sandwiched between Washington, D.C. and Amsterdam, and 8th for Asia and Oceania, trailing Shanghai, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, Beijing, Shenzhen and Dubai.
Rapid industrialisation once made Guangzhou a rather polluted city. Since green urban planning was introduced, it is now counted among the most livable cities in China.

Zhujiang New Town is Guangzhou's central business district for the 21st century. It covers 6.44 square kilometres in Tianhe District, and a number of financial institutions have their headquarters there.

Every April and October the Ministry of Trade stages the Canton Fair (formally the China Import and Export Fair). The first edition took place in spring 1957, and it remains the country's longest-running, top-level and largest trade fair, a major moment in the city's calendar. Starting with the 104th session it left the older Liuhua complex for the newly built Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center (广州国际会展中心) at Pazhou. Getting there is easy by public transport: two Line 8 stations, one Line 11 station and three stops on Tram Line THZ1 serve it. The fair now runs in three phases rather than two.
Guangzhou is known for crafts and food that you will meet during your stay.
Cantonese cuisine is one of the most famous regional cuisines in China, and a saying holds simply that one should "Eat in Guangzhou" (食在廣州).
Cantonese carving works in jade, wood and (a point of controversy) ivory.
Canton porcelain took shape over roughly three centuries as an export product, and is recognised across China for its vivid colours.
Cantonese embroidery counts as one of China's four principal embroidery traditions.
Zhujiang Beer is a pale lager and a notably successful Chinese brand.
Several development areas anchor the city's industry.
GAC Group, the automobile maker
Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone

Guangzhou Nansha Export Processing Zone, founded in 2005 with a planned area of 1.36 square kilometres in Nansha District. Encouraged industries include car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry. It lies 54 kilometres (34 miles) south of Baiyun International Airport, about a 70-minute drive, and close to Nansha Port. Metro Line 4 is being lengthened to reach Nansha Ferry Terminal.

Guangzhou Free Trade Zone, founded in 1992 in eastern Huangpu District, next to the Economic and Technological Development Zone and very near Baiyun Airport. It concentrates on global trade, logistics, processing and software. The area has lately been rebranded under the Huangpu District name, and it is bringing in newer sectors: new energy, AI, new mobility and transport, new materials and information and communication technology. The Guangzhou IP Court is based here too.
Guangzhou Science City

The city is a hub for international business. China Briefing reported that by 2018 over 30,000 foreign-funded firms had set up in the city, among them 297 Fortune Global 500 companies running projects and 120 that keep a headquarters or regional headquarters in Guangzhou.
At the end of 2024 Guangzhou had 18.978 million permanent residents, and 87.24 per cent of them lived in urban areas.

The Seventh National Population Census put the permanent population at 18,676,605 on 1 November 2020. That was 5,975,805 more than in 2010 (12,700,800), a rise of 47.05 per cent. Urban residents numbered 16,096,724 (86.19 per cent) and rural residents 2,579,881 (13.81 per cent).

Migration is a big part of the picture. The census counted 11,522,907 people living away from their registered household location, among them 9,378,825 in the floating population, which makes Guangzhou one of the largest migrant-receiving cities in China. For an international student, this means a city used to newcomers from other places.

An earlier estimate, from 2014, was 13,080,500 people, of whom 11,264,800 lived in urban areas, giving a density of around 1,800 people per square kilometre. Guangzhou's built-up core runs straight into several neighbouring cities. The Pearl River Delta Economic Zone, built up over about 17,573 square kilometres (6,785 square miles), is thought to house 22 million people across Guangzhou's nine urban districts, Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890,000) and Huizhou's Huiyang District (760,000). Add neighbouring Hong Kong and the cluster tops 28 million. A booming economy hungry for labour has drawn a very large floating population: as many as 10 million migrants live in the zone for six months or more a year, and in 2008 roughly five million of Guangzhou's permanent residents were migrant workers.
The OECD estimated that the surrounding metropolitan area had a population of 25 million in 2010.

A study by Gong and colleagues in 2018 traces Guangzhou's development from 1990 to 2020. In 1990, built-up residential districts were almost entirely confined to a small part of western Guangzhou, with the rest of the city mostly farmland and forest and only scattered housing. From 2005 to 2020 other districts developed more residential communities, and by the 2020 map there were developed communities running from the west to the east of the city. The far south and large parts of the north still remain mainly farmland and forest, with very little housing.

southern-medical-university.h: Ferries to Hong Kong and Macau

blocks.x: High-speed catamarans sail daily from Guangzhou's Nansha and Lianhua Shan ferry terminals to the China Ferry Terminal in Hong Kong, and Nansha also has a service to the Macau Ferry Pier in Hong Kong.

In earlier times the city had around 124 religious pavilions, halls and temples. Today, besides the Buddhist Association, the city has a Taoist Association and a Jewish community, and it also has a history with Christianity, which was reintroduced to China by colonial powers.

SUSTech, short for the Southern University of Science and Technology, is a public university that belongs to the city of Shenzhen in Guangdong Province. The Shenzhen Municipal People's Government owns and funds it. More than 10,000 students were enrolled in 2022, and the university belongs to China's Double First-Class Construction programme. It is a young institution in a young city, so for students who want a modern, research-minded campus in southern China, it deserves a close look. Keep in mind that its history is short, and judge it on current programmes and facilities rather than long tradition.

SUSTech opened in 2010. That year the Ministry of Education had not yet allowed it to admit ordinary high school graduates, so it took in home-educated students instead. This made it the second university to try to boost home-grown talent and innovation and to develop a culture of university education in China. Once it won the needed permission, it began to admit regular high school graduates in later years, like other universities. Its home, Shenzhen, is a fast-growing technology capital.

The campus is large, covering 1,978,980 m2 in Shenzhen's Nanshan District, and combines contemporary architecture with watercourses and avenues of trees. The university has pledged to follow environmentally friendly policies and says its goal is zero carbon emissions.
Different league tables rate SUSTech as follows.
Times Higher Education (2022 survey): placed within mainland China's top ten and 162nd worldwide; its Asia rank was 19th, and in the Young University Rankings it was 13th
Academic Ranking of World Universities, also called the "Shanghai Ranking": a world position of 101-150th, 19th in Asia and 11th within China
THE Young Universities Rankings 2021: China's top young university
THE Global University Employability Ranking 2021: 158th

In the 2021 Nature Index Young Universities table (the Leading 150 Young Universities), SUSTech came second in the world. In the Annual Nature Index Table 2025 it was 22nd in the world and 16th in the Asia-Pacific region. This index measures research output in leading science journals, so it is a useful sign of research strength.

Undergraduates in the School of Medicine can choose Biomedical Sciences or Clinical Medicine. Teaching mixes basic science with clinical practice, using small classes and problem-based learning. A joint medical school with King's College London opened in Shenzhen in 2021, with formal approval from China's Ministry of Education. Anyone on the clinical medicine programme graduates with a King's College London degree alongside the SUSTech Bachelor of Medicine, and no period of study in the United Kingdom is required to get it.

They could be offered places that remain if the list is not filled once all prioritised applicants have been placed. Check the current UK rules with the relevant authorities before you plan around this route.
Everyday life for a student depends on the city outside the campus gates, so this section covers Shenzhen's history, weather, economy, people, buildings and transport.

Historically the city occupies about the same area as Bao'an County. When the Opium Wars ended, the county's southern part passed to British Hong Kong, leaving the village of Shenzhen right at the frontier. Its railway station was the final stop on the mainland section of the Kowloon–Canton Railway. The economy kept growing, and the place had become a city by 1979.

Shenzhen lies in the Pearl River Delta. Hong Kong borders it on the south, Huizhou on the north and northeast, Dongguan on the north and northwest, Lingdingyang and the Pearl River on the west, and Mirs Bay on the east. The provincial capital, Guangzhou, is roughly 100 kilometres (62 mi) to the northwest. The city is long and narrow: east to west it stretches 81.4 kilometers, whereas the shortest north–south distance is just 10.8 kilometers.

At the end of 2017 Shenzhen had a resident population of 12,528,300, of whom 4,472,200 were registered residents, though the real population within the administrative area exceeded 20 million. Shenzhen belongs to the built-up area of the Pearl River Delta, where 44,738,513 people live across 9 municipalities (Macau among them).

More than 160 rivers or channels pass through the city, and 24 reservoirs inside its limits hold a combined 525 million tonnes. Among the notable rivers are the Shenzhen River, the Maozhou River and the Longgang River.

The city is roughly one degree south of the Tropic of Cancer, yet thanks to the Siberian anticyclone its climate is warm and humid subtropical (Köppen Cwa), influenced by the monsoon. Mild, relatively dry winters are partly due to the nearby South China Sea; frosts almost never happen. The dry start to winter turns steadily more humid and cloudy. Fog appears on 106 days a year, mostly in winter and spring. March is when skies are cloudiest (only 27 percent of possible sunshine), rain increases sharply from April, and the wet season lasts into late September or early October. October is the sunniest month at 53 percent, and over the year the city gets 1,853 hours of bright sunshine.

The monsoon is strongest in summer, which is also very hot and humid. Even so, real heat is rare, with only 2.4 days at 35 °C (95 °F) or higher. Heavy downpours are likely, though, so a good umbrella is worth having. On 9.7 days a year the rain totals 50 millimetres (2.0 inches) or more, and on 2.2 days it totals at least 100 mm (3.94 in). The last part of autumn is dry. Yearly precipitation averages about 1,933 mm (76 in), part of which comes with typhoons that hit from the east in summer and early autumn. On the temperature record, the lowest reading is 0.2 °C (32 °F), on 11 February 1957, and the highest 38.7 °C (102 °F), on 10 July 1980.

Shenzhen was the first Special Economic Zone (SEZ), set up by Deng Xiaoping, who was then China's paramount leader. The city was first reorganised in April 1979 as a Special Export Zone, intended to create a good investment environment and import advanced technology and management know-how, and became a Special Economic Zone when it was renamed in May 1980.

Nominal GDP for 2022 stood at 3.24 trillion RMB, which converts to HK$2.87 trillion. That passed neighbouring Hong Kong (HK$2.11 trillion) and Guangzhou (2.88 trillion RMB, or HK$2.68 trillion), and it makes Shenzhen the third largest city economy in China, behind Shanghai and Beijing. Between 2016 and 2017 its GDP grew 8.8%, faster than Hong Kong's 3.7% and Singapore's 2.5%. The Shenzhen Stock Exchange (SZSE), with a market capitalisation of US$2.5 trillion on 30 November 2018, is the world's 8th largest exchange.

In the Global Financial Centres Index for 2021, Shenzhen came 8th in the world for competitiveness and size, and 6th in Asia & Oceania; five cities (Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore, Beijing and Tokyo) ranked above it in that region. A research network on globalization and world cities classed it, in 2020, as an Alpha- (global first-tier) city. Forbes reports that only four cities have more billionaires. A study by Oxford Economics projects its nominal GDP to be among the ten largest of any city in 2035, alongside Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, and expects nominal GDP per capita to pass US$57,000 in 2030, the highest in mainland China and similar to Tokyo and Seoul.

The 21st Century Maritime Silk Road includes Shenzhen. It leads from China's coast down to the southern tip of India, then via the Suez Canal into the Mediterranean and up to the Upper Adriatic and Trieste, a northern Italian hub with rail lines onward to Central Europe and the North Sea. Counting Fortune Global 500 headquarters inside city limits in August 2023, Shenzhen ranked seventh worldwide and third in China, after Beijing and Shanghai.

In 2020 Shenzhen's total permanent population was 17,560,000, and 5,874,000 of them (33.4 percent) held a local hukou (local registration). The youthfulness of the city shows in the figures: only 5.36 percent of residents were over 60. Life expectancy was nevertheless 81.25 in 2018, among China's top twenty cities. Men outnumber women 130 to 100, the widest gap of any Guangdong city, and the birth rate is high by Chinese standards, at 21.7 babies per 10,000 people among 13.44 million residents in 2019. Measured over its entire administrative area, Shenzhen ranks as China's fifth most populous city proper. The Pearl River Delta Metropolitan Region also includes Guangzhou and Dongguan, Foshan and Zhongshan, Zhuhai and Huizhou, and both Hong Kong and Macau. It is described by the World Bank as the largest urban area in the world, with 78 million people at the 2020 census.

Before the SEZ was founded in 1980, the area's inhabitants were mainly Hakka and Cantonese. Once the zone existed, newcomers poured in from elsewhere in Guangdong (Teochew as well as Hakka and Cantonese). Others came from southern and central provinces, among them Hunan and Guangxi, Jiangxi, Sichuan and Henan. Most settled in so-called urban villages, chengzhongcun (城中村, meaning 'village in the city'); Baishizhou in Nanshan District is one. The city also has a significant Korean minority in Nanshan and Futian Districts, whose roots lie with workers who came for South Korean firms that set up in the city at the start of China's reform and opening up.

Shenzhen's population overshot the 14.8 million target set for 2016 to 2020, and on 25 May 2021 the city's justice bureau announced it would make hukou harder to obtain. Registered residents rose by 2.178 million (58.9 percent) between 2015 and 2020, and the permanent population grew by 7,136,088 (68.46 percent) between 2010 and 2020, an average of 5.35% a year.

Local government religious affairs officials say that Buddhism and Taoism are the two principal faiths. Protestant and Catholic churches and mosques are found in every district, and Shenzhen is also where the Holy Confucian Church, founded in 2009, has its headquarters.

The original local communities, before the Special Economic Zone, fell into Cantonese-speaking and Hakka-speaking groups, both cultural and linguistic sub-ethnic groups native to Guangdong. Cantonese took two local forms: standard Cantonese, and the Weitou dialect, which several villages south of Fuhua Road spoke, as do a few Hong Kong villages (two or three) on the far side of the Shenzhen River. That fits with the area having been settled by people who went south with the Southern Song court in the late 13th century.

Newcomers from other regions have reshaped the linguistic landscape, and the city has moved towards Mandarin: the central government promotes it as a national common language, and most out-of-province immigrants and their children speak it natively. More recently, though, more people speak several languages, since young people of Mandarin-speaking migrant families absorb the local culture from friends, television and other media. The South China Morning Post reports that some residents, both Cantonese and non-Cantonese, have tried to bring Cantonese back as a part of Shenzhen culture, even though Mandarin is heard everywhere.

The Guardian called Shenzhen "the world leader completing new skyscrapers" in 2019. Only Hong Kong has more buildings above 150 meters: Shenzhen had finished 297 as of July 2021. In 2016 it completed more skyscrapers than the whole United States and Australia combined, and the boom continues, with more than 85 skyscrapers being built across the city in 2021, the most of anywhere in the world. Most were designed by architects from Hong Kong or abroad in a modern style, although in the last decades of the 20th century functionalism was the leading style among the towers.

The most prominent examples are the Guomao Building (160 metres, 525 ft), Shun Hing Square (384 metres, 1,260 ft), KK100 (441.8 metres, 1,449 ft), China Resources Headquarters (392 metres, 1,286 ft), and the 599 metre (1,965 ft) Ping An Finance Centre, which is the second tallest in China and fifth tallest anywhere in the world. The Ping An Finance Centre was finished in 2015 and was meant to be unique and elegant in its surroundings, representing the history and achievements of its main tenant, Ping An Insurance.

Several historical buildings follow traditional Chinese architecture. Hakka walled villages, among them Crane Lake and Gangeng, can be visited in Longgang District. Like other villages of this type, they are laid out with heavy grey walls, narrow lanes and courtyards. Nantou (or Xin'an), a historic town in Nanshan District, still has a few Ming-era buildings, including the Guandi Temple, although modern construction has replaced most traditional ones. Chiwan, also in Nanshan, has the tomb of Zhao Bing, the final Southern Song emperor, and the Tianhou Temple, commissioned by Zheng He, as an offering to the sea goddess Mazu to keep the Ming treasure fleet safe. Old coastal defence forts survive inside the city boundaries too, for example Dapeng Fortress and Chiwan Left Fort.
A recent landmark is the Marisfrolg Pavilion, in Longhua District, finished in 2023 with a design inspired by an insect exoskeleton.

Shenzhen is the second largest transport hub in Guangdong and in South China, after the provincial capital Guangzhou. Its public transport is extensive, covering rapid transit, buses and taxis, and you can use most of it with a Shenzhen Tong card or with QR codes generated through WeChat mini programs. Shenzhen is known as the first major city in the world to run only electric buses and taxis, and by 2023, 70% of cars in the city were electric.

Shenzhen has its own airport, Shenzhen Bao'an International, and is also close to Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA). Bao'an is 35 kilometres (22 miles) from the city centre, and it is the main hub for Shenzhen Airlines and Donghai Airlines (passenger) and for Jade Cargo International, SF Airlines and UPS Airlines (cargo). In 2018 it handled 49,348,950 passengers, 355,907 aircraft and 1,218,502.2 of cargo, which made it China's 5th busiest airport for passengers and 4th busiest for aircraft and cargo. Passengers with tickets can also reach HKIA's Skypier by ferry from the Shekou Cruise Centre or the Fuyong Ferry Terminal, and coaches link Shenzhen with HKIA as well.

The Shenzhen Metro is the city's rapid transit system. In 2022 it had 419 kilometres (260 miles) of route on 12 lines with 290 stations. The plan for 2030 is 8 express and 24 non-express lines with a total of 1142 kilometres of track. Average daily ridership in 2021 was 5.99 million passengers, and the metro also runs a tram system in Longhua District.

Intercity trains stop at seven stations: Futian, Guangmingcheng and Pingshan, plus Shenzhen East, North and West, and the one simply named Shenzhen, which is also known as Luohu Railway Station. Three high-speed lines pass through. One is the Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong Express Rail Link, another is the Beijing–Guangzhou high-speed railway, and the last is the Xiamen–Shenzhen railway, which is one section of the Hangzhou–Fuzhou–Shenzhen passenger railway. For visitors from Hong Kong or Guangzhou, the express link is usually the fastest option. Two older, non-high-speed lines also run through the city: the Beijing-Kowloon Railway and the Guangzhou-Shenzhen Railway, which makes up one part of the Kowloon–Canton railway.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

southern-university-of-science-and-techn.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Southern University of Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shenzhen, register at Southern University of Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

SWJTU (西南交通大学) is a science and engineering university in Chengdu, Sichuan, run at national level and answerable to the Ministry of Education. Its status as a national key university comes with joint backing from the Ministry of Education, the Sichuan provincial and Chengdu municipal governments, and China Railway Corporation. Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme both include it.

southwest-jiaotong-university.h: A school with a very long railway tradition

blocks.x: The university dates from 1896 and counts among China's leading engineering universities. People call it the birthplace of China's railway engineers, and it is where teaching in modern transport, mining, metallurgy and civil engineering first took root in the country. Over time the institution has carried different titles, such as Tangshan Institute of Railway, Tangshan Jiaotong University and the Imperial Chinese Railway College. For anyone who wants a career in rail, bridges or tunnels, that heritage is the main reason to look at SWJTU.

SWJTU regularly appears among the better universities in China. In 2016 the Times Higher Education Asia University Rankings placed it in the 181 to 190 range, and its position in that year's THE table for BRICS and emerging economies was 161. The university was in the first group admitted to the Double First Class University Plan, the successor to Project 211, which gives it Chinese state Double First Class status. So far, 57 fellowships, in the United States and at the China National Academy of Sciences, have gone to its staff and former students.
Three graduates show the university's strengths.
Mao Yisheng was an expert in bridge construction and a social activist.
Tung-Yen Lin was a structural engineer, best known as a pioneer in making the use of prestressed concrete standard practice.

Jianyou Cao was among the earliest contributors to railway electrification in China, a member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, an expert in electric power systems and the founder of the university's school of electrical engineering.

A student's everyday experience depends on the surrounding city, meaning its climate, its transport and what there is to enjoy. This part introduces Chengdu, where Southwest Jiaotong University is based.

Chengdu stands on a broad plain, between 450 and 720 metres (1,480 to 2,360 feet) above sea level. To the north-west the steep Longmen Mountains rise, and the Qionglai Mountains border it on the west. Those western ranges rise above 3,000 m (9,800 ft); two of their peaks are Miao Jiling at 5,364 m (17,598 ft) and Xiling Snow Mountain at 5,164 m (16,942 ft). The western highlands shelter a big primeval forest, rich in living species, which is also giant panda habitat. Lower country lies to the east, where the Longquan Mountains stand beside the hills of the middle Min River, a landscape of converging rivers. Since ancient times Chengdu has been called "the Abundant Land", thanks to its fertile soil, benign climate and the ingenious Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

Chengdu occupies the Chengdu Plain at the west of the Sichuan Basin, and most of its land is flat. It lies between 30° 05' and 31° 26' N and between 102° 54' and 104° 53' E, 192 kilometres (119 miles) across from east to west and 166 km (103 miles) from south to north, which adds up to 12,390 km2 (4,780 sq mi) under its administration. Bordering it are Deyang (north-east), Ziyang (south-east), Meishan (south), Ya'an (south-west) and, to the north, the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture.

The urban area, about 500 m (1,600 ft) above sea level, has a few rivers, including the Jin, Fu and Sha Rivers. Outside the city proper the landscape grows more varied. The Penzhong Hills (盆中丘陵) and the Longquan Mountains (龙泉山脉) lie to the east, and to the west the Qionglai Mountains peak at 5,364 m (17,598 ft) within Dayi County. That peak, Daxuetang or Miaojiling on Xiling Snow Mountain, is the top of Chengdu's territory (5,364 metres). The bottom is 359 metres, at a riverbank where the Tuojiang River leaves Jianyang City.

Chengdu's climate is humid subtropical, influenced by the monsoon (Köppen Cwa). It is mostly warm, and humidity is high all year. The four seasons are clear, and moderate rainfall, mainly in the warm months, softens both the heat of summer and the cold of winter. Far to the north, the Qin Mountains (Qinling) shelter the city from chilly Siberian winds. As a result winter is short and gentler than in the Lower Yangtze area.
January: the daily mean is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F). Snow is rare, but there are some frosty spells each winter.

Summer: hot and damp, yet milder than Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing, which together with it share the Yangtze basin and are known as the "Three Furnaces". In July and August the mean over 24 hours is near 25 °C (77 °F), and afternoons occasionally hit 33 °C (91 °F). Prolonged heat of the kind seen across much of eastern China seldom occurs.
Rain: it falls most in July and August, and very little falls in the cooler months.

Sunshine: Chengdu has one of the lowest yearly sunshine totals in the country, below much of Northern Europe. Possible sunshine ranges from 15 per cent in December to 32 per cent in August, giving 1,006 hours of bright sunshine a year. Daytime in spring (March to April) is usually brighter and warmer than in autumn (October to November).
Over the year the average is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F). Readings have ranged between a low of −6.5 °C (20 °F) and a high of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).
Expect grey skies and damp, so if you need strong sunshine for your mood, bring a plan.

southwest-jiaotong-university.h: How the city has been rebuilt

blocks.x: A policy paper of 1988 on gradual housing-system reform in cities and towns launched China's wholesale reform of urban housing. In Chengdu, over twenty property companies were founded, and that marked the opening stage of the city's real estate development.

The 1990s brought a comprehensive renovation of the Funan River, another boost to Chengdu's environment. The Funan River Comprehensive Improvement Project earned a UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour in 1998 and, in 2000, a "Local Initiative Award" from the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives.

In 1997 work began on a scheme called Five Main Roads & One Bridge. Of the five roads, three went to the east of the city and two to the south, forming the base of Chengdu's Eastern and Southern sub-centres. Those sub-centres steered residents to move east and south, and numerous buildings went up beyond the 2nd Ring Road on those sides. The renovation of the Shahe River, together with the Jin River project, also began a trend of living beside both rivers. People joked that the map of Chengdu needed updating every three months.

Speculation drove a housing boom between the late 1990s and the early 2000s, and in 2000 dozens of commercial property projects appeared. As the property market was promoted, the government urged citizens to buy their own homes and gave substantial subsidies for a certain period, so houses came to be treated as commodities.

The New Century Global Center, which as of February 2026 ranks third in the world by floor area, stands in Chengdu. The building is 100 metres (330 ft) high, 500 by 400 metres (1,600 by 1,300 ft) on the ground, and has 1,700,000 square metres (18,000,000 sq ft) of floors. It contains retail outlets, cinemas, offices and hotels, as well as a water park that has a man-made beach and waves, a skating rink, a large 5-star hotel set in a Mediterranean-style village, and space for 15,000 vehicles.

In the 2020 census the municipality held 20,937,757 people. Of these, 16,045,577 lived in the metropolitan core, made up of 12 urban districts and Guanghan City (administered by Deyang). Sichuan's largest city, Chengdu is also fourth largest in China. By 2021 the population was 21,192,000, and no other Chinese city added as many residents.
The OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) put the wider Chengdu metropolitan area at 18.1 million residents in 2015.
China Daily ranked Chengdu as China's fourth most livable city in 2006.

A good deal of China's major literature has links to Chengdu. Writers connected to the city include the poets Li Bai and Du Fu, two of China's most eminent; Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, who were masters of the fu, a form blending description with verse; the Ming scholar Yang Shen'an; and, in modern times, Guo Moruo and Ba Jin. Local history writing began with Chang Qu of the Jin dynasty, who put together the Record of Hua Yang State, the earliest of its kind. During the Later Shu Kingdom the poet Zhao Chongzuo compiled Among the Flowers, which was the first Ci anthology anywhere in China. The king of Later Shu, Meng Chang, wrote the very first Spring Festival couplet: "A harvest year accepts celebrations, good festivals foreshadow long springs."
The 81st World Science Fiction Convention was held in Chengdu in 2023, after the city beat Winnipeg in Canada in the 2021 site vote.

In the Five Dynasties period the Chengdu painter Huang Quan joined others in founding a school of fine-brush flower-and-bird painting. The "Hanlin Painting Academy" of that time was China's first royal art academy.

Muslims have lived in Sichuan since the Tang dynasty (618 to 907), and 12 mosques stand in Chengdu. Huangcheng Mosque, in the middle of the city, dates from the 16th century. The city has official Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations, and some underground churches too.

The Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan, now the Diocese of Chengdu, was created on 15 October 1696. The Paris Foreign Missions Society sent Artus de Lionne, a Frenchman, to serve as the first Apostolic Vicar.

Protestant missionary history in Chengdu started in 1890, when the Canadian Methodist Mission wanted further stations in Asia. In February 1891 a meeting heard a recommendation from Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart, formerly Superintendent of the Central China mission of the New York Methodist Mission Society, that its first station be Chengtu. The meeting also proposed that he lead the party that would found it, because between 1866 and 1888 he had set up missions on the Yangtze and Gan Rivers with Western hospitals and schools for boys and girls. He arrived in Chengtu on 9 May 1891 and bought a house a fortnight later, dividing it into homes and a dispensary for the staff who would join him.

The first Protestant Mission Headquarters in Chengtu opened on 24 June 1892, welcoming more than a thousand local visitors. A first Methodist service followed on the next Sunday, but only a few people came. Sichuan's first Western dispensary began work on 3 November 1892, treating sixteen patients on day one. So many people came that, in the spring of 1893, the mission obtained a bigger site by Chengtu's East Gate, and there the city's first Methodist church (the Sï-Shen-Tsï Methodist Church) and a hospital were built. Rioters tore both down in 1895, driving the missionaries to Chongqing and later Shanghai. Dr. Hart went to Peking to demand redress, and Sichuan's Viceroy, Liu Ping Chang, paid the full amount. The compound went up again quickly but was destroyed once more in the riots of 1901, after which it was rebuilt a second time. Later missionaries shifted the boys' and girls' schools to a larger place just south of the city and, in 1914, named the Divinity College Hart College. It joined the West China Union University, now Sichuan University, and the West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida). In the Cultural Revolution the Sï-Shen-Tsï church building stopped being used as a church and was put under the management of Chengdu City Second People's Hospital next door, which turned the chapel into a kindergarten and an office for its equipment department. The hospital returned the building to the church in 1984.

Religious activity is tightly regulated in China. One example came in December 2018, when the authorities moved against the Early Rain Covenant Church, an unregistered congregation of about 500 people whose pastor was Wang Yi. More than 100 members, the pastor and his wife included, were detained. Officials raided the church's kindergarten and theological college and closed its media channels. A member, Li Yingqiang, declared before his own arrest that the congregation would keep meeting even if only five remained, since their faith was real. Reports say police told one member the church was now deemed an illegal organisation. Domestic media could not report on these events, while video and photographs that spread on Western social media showed arrests and what were said to be injuries caused by police. A photograph of a detention warrant for a Ms. Jiang indicates that the leaders were accused of "inciting subversion of state power", for which the maximum sentence is 15 years.
A Chabad Jewish Center was set up in Chengdu in 2012 and, after moving five times, found a permanent home in Wuhou District.

Sichuan opera and Zaju, an old comic form mixing dancing, singing, verse and mime, are summed up by a proverb: "Shu opera towers above all other performances in the world". Chengdu's earliest opera, "Bullfighting", was written back in the Warring States era. The first detailed opera was performed at the Shu Kingdom court during the Three Kingdoms period, and the first Zaju whose performance is clearly recorded in China was also staged here. Archaeologists have excavated the tombs of Han-dynasty poets known for wit. Today the art is best known for face-changing masks and fire breathing.

People in Chengdu speak the Chengdu dialect, a form of Sichuanese. It has been an influence on Chinese comedy and rap music. International students usually learn standard Mandarin, but you will hear the local dialect everywhere.

Chilies and peppercorns give Sichuan cooking its character. Mapo doufu, Dan Dan Mien (noodles) and Chengdu hot pot are among the famous dishes, and the first two both use Sichuan pepper. The Los Angeles Times called Chengdu "China's party city" in 2006, citing its relaxed way of life. Compared with Shanghai, Chengdu has more tea houses and more bars even though it has fewer than half as many people. Records for 2023 show over 30,000 teahouses, plus 3,566 bars, nightclubs and dance halls that were legally registered, and a 2019 statistical report made Chengdu the Chinese city with the greatest number of bars, ahead of Shanghai. Tea culture here is more than a thousand years old, going back to when the city was where the Southern Silk Road began. UNESCO has recognised and named Chengdu a "City of Gastronomy".

You will find tea houses on every side, whether elaborate old-style rooms with bamboo furniture or simple modern ones. Jasmine, longjing and biluochun are typical teas. Customers drop in for mahjong, a massage or an ear cleaning, and the larger houses stage live shows such as Sichuan opera.

Hot pot is a Chengdu speciality and a traditional Sichuan dish: vegetables, fish or meat cooked in a boiling, spicy broth. It suits a gathering of friends and appeals to locals and tourists alike. Hot pot restaurants are found all over the city.
The Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park was created in 1992 under the name Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone.

National Highway G42, Shanghai to Chengdu
National Highway G76, Xiamen to Chengdu
National Highway G93, the Chengdu-Chongqing ring route
National Highway G4202, the Chengdu Ring

Southwest Medical University (SWMU; Chinese: 西南医科大学), formerly Luzhou Medical College (泸州医学院), is a public medical university in the city of Luzhou, Sichuan, China.

The school was first established in 1951 as Southern Sichuan Doctors' School (川南医士学校). In 1958, the school was renamed as Luzhou Specialist School of Medicine (泸州医学专科学校). In 1978, it was authorized to grant bachelor's degrees and changed its name to Luzhou Medical College (泸州医学院).

In 2015, Luzhou Medical College was authorized to change its name to Sichuan Medical University (四川医科大学). However, the well-known West China Medical Center of Sichuan University, which was famously known as "Sichuan Medical College" (四川医学院) from 1953 and 1985, protested that the new name was too similar to its former name. In 2016, the school changed its name again to Southwest Medical University.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Luzhou, where Southwest Medical University is located.

Luzhou is situated in the southeast region of Sichuan province, at the intersection of Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou and Chongqing, at longitude 105° 08' 41"E ~106° 28'E and latitude 27° 39' N ~ 29° 20'N. A prefecture-level city of Sichuan with a registered population of 4.8 million, Luzhou is 267 km (166 mi) away from Chengdu, the provincial capital. It is adjacent to Chongqing in the east, borders Guizhou and Yunnan provinces in the south, Yibin City and Zizhong City in the west, Chongqing and Neijiang in the north. The city governs 7 administrative divisions, including 3 districts (Jiangyang, Longmatan, Naxi) and 4 counties (Lu, Hejiang, Xuyong, Gulin).

Owing to its position in the southern peripheral area of Sichuan Basin and the connective region with Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, Luzhou is characterised by river valleys, hills, and level lands in the north and highland areas, and by mountains, sheer valleys, and rushing rivers in the south. Fishing and agriculture are the primary industries in the northern area, and forest and mineral resources are primary in the southern part of the region. Luzhou's lowest point is 203 metres (666 ft), at the surface of Yangtze river in Jiucengyan, Hejiang county, while the highest point is located at the peak of Liangzi mountain, Xuyong County, reaching 1,902 metres (6,240 ft). Luzhou is also a region covered by rivers. The Yangtze river flows through the whole area from west to east, covering a total course of 133 kilometres (83 mi), and the maximum flood level was 18.68 metres (61.3 ft) during the past 30 years. Other rivers converge here, such as Tuo River, Yongling River, Chishui River, and Laixi River.
Covering an area of 12,246.87 square kilometres (4,728.54 sq mi), it is 121.64 kilometres (75.58 mi) wide from east to west and 181.84 kilometres (112.99 mi) long from south to north.

Luzhou has a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) and is largely mild, except during the summer, and humid, with four distinct seasons and ample rainfall: winters are short, mild, and comparatively dry, while summers are long, hot, and humid. Within the prefecture, annual mean temperatures range from 17.1 to 18.5 °C (62.8 to 65.3 °F). In the urban area, monthly daily average temperatures range from 7.6 °C (45.7 °F) in January to around 27 °C (80.6 °F) in July and August, with August being slightly warmer. The diurnal temperature variation is 6.1 °C (11.0 °F) and is lowest during winter. Snow is rare here. The annual precipitation in the prefecture ranges from 748.4 to 1,184.2 millimetres (29.46 to 46.62 in), 70% of which occurs from May to September. Sunshine is quite low, with only 1200 to 1400 hours per year, and the frost-free period is lengthy, lasting 300 to 358 days.

Luzhou has always been a hub of economic activities in the tri-province border area of Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou.  Food, liquor, and chemicals production, along with construction equipment manufacturing are the most important industries of the local economy.  In 2006, Luzhou's total GDP reached 33.11 billion yuan (7,819 yuan per capita).

Luzhou is a center of liquor production, particularly baijiu. Luzhou Laojiao (Chinese: 泸州老窖; lit. 'Luzhou Old Fermentation Pit') and Gulin Langjiu (Chinese: 古蔺郎酒) are the two best known brands with national and international reputation.

Luzhou is a manufacturing center of hydraulic trucks, cranes and excavators in China. Among the cities along the Yangtze River, Luzhou is the second largest producer of hydraulic trucks, after Shanghai.

The chemical industry, particularly natural gas production, is also important to Luzhou's economy. At present, Luzhou has developed a national chemical industry system covering production, education, scientific research, design, machine and architecture. A group of national large scale enterprises have been established and achieved a globally advanced level. Lutianhua enterprise is the most extensive carbamide and oil chemical production base in China, producing fatty acid, fatty amine, synthetic ammonia, and carbamide. Its annual output of carbamide is 1.24 million tons and 0.9 million tons of synthetic ammonia. It is one of the 500 largest national enterprises. Tianhua Co, Ltd is a key enterprise which brings in 0.3 million tons of synthetic ammonia and 0.6 million tons of carbamide, processing two sets of chemical fertilizer devices with world technical levels. Luzhou Chemical Factory participates in military and civil chemical production. State-owned Torch Chemical Factory is the only producer of "801". It gained the national quality golden award, surpassing the America Standard.

Luzhou is a tourist destination; specific scenic spots include Yuchan in Luxian county, Fobao in Hejiang county, Mt. Fangshan in Jiangyang county, the lychee and longan orchard along the Yangtze River and Tuojiang River, and many others. With the official approbation of the National Ministry of Forestry, Fobao Forest Park became a National Forestry Park and was classified as an "AAA" tourist attraction in 2001 by the National Tourism Administration.

Luzhou and Xuyong county have national cultural significance. The Luzhou Old Fermentation Pit (Luzhou Laojiao, 泸州老窖) and Dragon Head Bridge are listed as key protected cultural relics of the nation. There are more than ten protected historical relics in Sichuan Province, including the site of the Battle of Chishui River. This site was chosen as the "National Demonstration Base for Patriotic Education" by the Central Propaganda Ministry in 2001.

The Sci-tech Park of Luzhou Laojiao is a national industry tourism demonstration spot and Luzhou Zhangba Longan Orchard is a national agricultural tourism spot. Other scenic areas nearby include Leshan, Yibin, Zigong and Chongqing, such as the Bamboo Forest, Mt. Simianshan in Chongqing and Sidong Channel in Guizhou Province.

Luzhou is a key comprehensive development zone in the upper Yangtze River and Sichuan province as well as an important production base for rice, fruit such as litchi and longan, cured tobacco, poultry, tea, and traditional Chinese medicine ingredients.

The Sichuan Pilot Free Trade Zone (FTZ) officially launched on 1 April 2017, forms part of a third batch of government-endorsed pilot FTZs. All told, the zone covers an area of 119.99 km2 and consists of three sub-zones: The Chengdu Tianfu New Area (90.32 km2 inclusive of the Chengdu High-Tech Comprehensive Bonded Area 4 (Shuangliu Park) (4 km2) and the Chengdu Airport Bonded Logistics Centre (Type B) (0.09 km2)), the Chengdu Qingbaijiang Railway Port Area (9.68 km2 inclusive of the Chengdu Railway Bonded Logistics Centre (Type B) (0.18 km2)), and the Chuannan Lingang Area (19.99 km2 inclusive of the Luzhou Port Bonded Logistics Centre (Type B) (0.21 km2)).

The Chuannan Lingang Area will focus on developing a range of high quality professional services, including shipping logistics, port trade, education and medical support. As part of its remit, it will also look to nurture the advanced manufacturing industries, as well as looking to take a lead in a number of other sectors, including equipment manufacturing, medicine and food/beverages. Furthermore, it will play a key role in the development of an integrated transport hub, which will provide streamlined connections between the Chengdu-Chongqing city cluster and Yunnan and Guizhou, its southerly neighbours.

Expressways connecting to Chengdu and Chongqing were completed in the 1990s.  Railroads and an airport provide additional links to several cities in China.  The city has four bridges over the Yangtze which form part of Sichuan's overland corridor to the South China Sea.

The G76 Xiamen-Chengdu Expressway connects Luzhou to Chengdu and Guiyang, the G93 Chengdu Ring Expressway connects Luzhou to Chongqing, and the G4215 Chengdu-Zunyi Expressway connects Luzhou to Chengdu and Zunyi. Other main highways include G321, G353 Heze-Baoji, the national highway and several provincial highways.

Luzhou is served by a freight-only branch. A passenger service briefly operated but was cancelled in 1995. A new railway station served by multiple high-speed lines has opened on June 28, 2021, with links to Chengdu and various other cities.

Luzhou is an important inland port serving as a transshipment point for goods heading to cities deeper into Sichuan such as Chengdu. Making it the largest river port in Sichuan on the upper Yangtze, with the capability to load and unload container ships. The Luzhou International Container Pier handled over 500,000 containers in 2016.

Luzhou Lantian Airport was built in 1945 and initially provided an air route between China and India for the US Air Force during World War II. Services were suspended in the 1960s, but later it was used for training purposes by the Chinese Air Force. Major renovations and expansions were completed in January 2001, and now the airport serves direct flights to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Kunming, Guiyang, Shenzhen, Xiamen, Hangzhou, Haikou, Changsha, Nanning, Xi'an, Daocheng Yading Airport, Lanzhou, Lijiang, Nanjing, Wuhan and Zhengzhou.
The new Luzhou Yunlong Airport opened in September 2018, and all services were transferred from Lantian to the new location, 11 km north of the city.
Luzhou White Cake: Luzhou White Cake is one of the traditional specialty snacks of Luzhou, Sichuan, made primarily from glutinous rice.

Luzhou Piglet Cake: Piglet Cake is one of the traditional snacks of Luzhou. The outer skin is made of glutinous rice flour, and the filling is usually savory ingredients such as pickled mustard greens and pork.

Gulin Spicy Chicken: Gulin Spicy Chicken is one of the representative dishes of Gulin County, Luzhou City. It uses chicken, chili peppers and Sichuan peppercorns as the main ingredients. It has a spicy and fragrant flavor and has a typical Sichuan cuisine style.

Hejiang Grilled Fish: Popular in Hejiang County, Hejiang grilled fish is made with freshwater fish from the Yangtze River basin. After being grilled over charcoal, it is cooked with chili peppers, broad bean paste and other seasonings, resulting in a rich flavor.

Luzhou Red Soup Mutton: Luzhou red soup mutton is a common winter delicacy in Luzhou. It is made by simmering mutton with chili peppers and spices. The soup is bright red and spicy and fragrant, which is a characteristic of southern Sichuan cuisine.

Southwest Medical University is in Sichuan, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Sichuan.

The Sichuan Basin and adjacent areas of the Yangtze watershed were a cradle of indigenous civilizations dating back to at least the 15th century BC, coinciding with the Shang in northern China. The region had its own distinct religious beliefs and worldview. The earliest excavated culture found therein is the Baodun culture (c.2700–1750 BC) excavated in the Chengdu Plain.
The most important native states were those of Ba and Shu.
Ba stretched into Sichuan from the Han Valley in Shaanxi and Hubei down the Jialing River as far as its confluence with the Yangtze at Chongqing.

Shu occupied the valley of the Min, including Chengdu and other areas of western Sichuan. The existence of the early state of Shu was poorly recorded in the main historical records of China. It was, however, referred to in the Book of Documents as an ally of the Zhou. Accounts of Shu exist mainly as a mixture of mythological stories and historical legends recorded in local annals such as the Chronicles of Huayang compiled in the Jin dynasty (266–420), and the Han-dynasty compilation Chronicle of the Kings of Shu. These contained folk stories such as that of Emperor Duyu who taught the people agriculture and transformed himself into a cuckoo after his death.

The existence of a highly developed civilization with an independent bronze industry in Sichuan was excavated in 1986 at a small village named Sanxingdui in Guanghan, Sichuan. This site, believed to be an ancient city of Shu, was initially discovered by a local farmer in 1929 who found jade and stone artifacts. Excavations by archeologists yielded few significant finds until 1986 when two major sacrificial pits were found with spectacular bronze items as well as artifacts in jade, gold, earthenware, and stone. This and other discoveries in Sichuan contest the conventional historiography that the local culture and technology of Sichuan were undeveloped in comparison to the technologically and culturally "advanced" Yellow River valley of north-central China.

The rulers of the expansionist state of Qin, based in present-day Gansu and Shaanxi, were the first strategists to realize that the area's military importance matched its commercial and agricultural significance. The Sichuan basin is surrounded by the Hengduan Mountains to the west, the Qin Mountains to the north, and Yungui Plateau to the south. Since the Yangtze flows through the basin and then through the perilous Three Gorges to eastern and southern China, Sichuan was a staging area for amphibious military forces and a haven for political refugees.

Qin armies finished their conquest of the kingdoms of Shu and Ba by 316 BC. Any written records and civil achievements of earlier kingdoms were destroyed. Qin administrators introduced improved agricultural technology. Li Bing, engineered the Dujiangyan irrigation system to control the Min River, a major tributary of the Yangtze. This innovative hydraulic system was composed of movable weirs which could be adjusted for high or low water flow according to the season, to either provide irrigation or prevent floods. The increased agricultural output and taxes made the area a source of provisions and men for Qin's unification of China.

Sichuan was subjected to the autonomous control of kings named by the imperial family of the Han dynasty. During the 11 years hiatus between 25 and 36 AD, Sichuan was controlled by the Chengjia Kingdom. Following the declining central government of the Han dynasty in the second century, the Sichuan basin, surrounded by mountains and easily defensible, became a popular place for upstart generals to found kingdoms that challenged the authority of Yangtze Valley emperors over China.

In 221, during the partition following the fall of the Eastern Han – the era of the Three Kingdoms – Liu Bei founded the southwest kingdom of Shu Han (蜀漢; 221–263) in parts of Sichuan, Guizhou, and Yunnan, with Chengdu as its capital. Shu-Han claimed to be the successor to the Han dynasty.

In 263, the Cao Wei of North China conquered the Kingdom of Shu-Han as a step on the path to reuniting China. Salt production became a major business in Ziliujing District. During the Six Dynasties period of Chinese disunity, Sichuan began to be populated by non-Han ethnic minority peoples, owing to the migration of Gelao people from the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau to the Sichuan basin.

Sichuan came under the firm control of a Chinese central government during the Sui dynasty, but it was during the subsequent Tang dynasty that Sichuan regained its previous political and cultural prominence for which it was known during the Han. Chengdu became nationally known as a supplier of armies and the home of Du Fu, who is sometimes called China's greatest poet. During the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763), Emperor Xuanzong of Tang fled from Chang'an to Sichuan which became his refuge. The region was torn by constant warfare and economic distress as it was besieged by the Tibetan Empire.

In the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, Sichuan became the heart of the Shu kingdom with its capital in Chengdu. In 925, the kingdom was absorbed into Later Tang but would regain independence under Meng Zhixiang who founded Later Shu in 934. Later Shu would continue until 965 when it was absorbed by the Song.
The Ming dynasty defeated Ming Yuzhen's Xia polity which ruled Sichuan.

During the Ming dynasty, major architectural works were created in Sichuan. Buddhism remained influential in the region. Bao'en Temple is a well-preserved 15th-century monastery complex built between 1440 and 1446 during the Zhengtong Emperor's reign (1427–64). Dabei Hall enshrines a thousand-armed wooden image of Guanyin and Huayan Hall is a repository with a revolving sutra cabinet. The wall paintings, sculptures, and other ornamental details are masterpieces of the Ming period.

In the middle of the 17th century, the peasant rebel leader Zhang Xianzhong (1606–1646) from Yan'an, Shaanxi Province, nicknamed Yellow Tiger, led his peasant troop from north China to the south and conquered Sichuan. Upon capturing it, he declared himself emperor of the Daxi dynasty (大西王朝). In response to the resistance from local elites, he massacred a large number of people in Sichuan, killing around one in three people. As a result of the massacre as well as years of turmoil during the Ming-Qing transition, the population of Sichuan fell sharply, requiring massive resettlement of people from the neighboring Huguang Province (modern Hubei and Hunan) and other provinces during the Qing dynasty.

Chengdu Export Processing Zone (Chinese: 成都出口加工区; pinyin: Chéngdū chūkǒu jiāgōng qū)) was ratified by the State Council as one of the first 15 export processing zones in the country in April 2000. In 2002, the state ratified the establishment of the Sichuan Chengdu Export Processing West Zone with a planned area of 1.5 km2 (0.58 sq mi), located inside the west region of the Chengdu Hi-tech Zone.

SWPU (西南石油大学) is a provincially affiliated public university whose main base is Chengdu, in Sichuan. Its sponsors are shared among the Ministry of Education, the Sichuan government and three major state energy groups: the CNPC, Sinopec (China Petroleum & Chemical) and CNOOC (the offshore oil company). It also sits within the Double First-Class Construction programme. The school dates from 1958.

SWPU operates in Chengdu and in Nanchong. The original campus is in Nanchong, and the main campus is in Chengdu. Combined, they cover about 200 hectares (490 acres), with more than 900,000 square metres of floor space.

southwest-petroleum-university.h: How the name and owner changed

blocks.x: The school opened as Sichuan Petroleum Institute. In 1970 it became Southwest Petroleum Institute, and in 2005, once it gained university status, it took its present name. Governance moved back and forth over the decades, as the timeline shows.
1958 to 1962: Sichuan Petroleum Institute, run by the Sichuan provincial government.
1962 to 1970: still Sichuan Petroleum Institute, now under the national Ministry of Petroleum Industry.
1970 to 1978: renamed Southwest Petroleum Institute and returned to the Sichuan provincial government.
1978 to 1988: Southwest Petroleum Institute under the Ministry of Petroleum Industry.
1988 to 1998: under China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC).
1998 to 2000: under CNPC (Group).
2000 to 2005: Southwest Petroleum Institute under the Sichuan provincial government again.
2005 onward: Southwest Petroleum University, run by the Sichuan provincial government.
In short, ever since 2000 the university has been co-managed by Sichuan Province and CNPC, and the Education Ministry and two other energy companies joined as sponsors.

There are 18 schools and departments, which offer 60 bachelor's programmes between them. Among Chinese universities it was in the first group to be authorised for all three degree levels, bachelor's, master's and doctoral. A graduate school at provincial level offers three post-doctoral research programmes, and the university teaches 23 doctoral programmes and 85 master's programmes, with oil and gas engineering as its one key discipline.

Three fields hold national key status, all in the petroleum chain: exploitation, drilling, and storage and transportation, each in its engineering form.
