The provincial and ministerial tier includes seven laboratories and 25 research and technical centres, one being a centre for well-completion techniques that was built with assistance from the United Nations. Canada's government supported a training centre run jointly with China for natural gas exploration and exploitation (the Sino-Canadian Training Center). On the national tier, a key laboratory studies reservoir geology and recovery for oil and gas and covers three key disciplines. Further facilities under the Ministry of Education are a key laboratory for oil and gas equipment, a research centre on natural gas exploitation engineering and another on oilfield petrochemical engineering. Readers can use two large libraries holding more than two million volumes.

Since 2001 SWPU has taken part in over 6,121 scientific programmes and obtained 783 million RMB in research funding. It has won 95 provincial or ministerial prizes, and 495 patents have been approved, of which 184 are invention patents.

Students come from all over China. Every autumn it enrols over 5,000 new undergraduates and over 1,000 new master's and doctoral candidates. Full-time enrolment is above 32,498: 26,490 undergraduates, 3,801 postgraduates, 715 PhD students and 8 international students. Alumni number more than 100,000 since the founding. Over the last ten years more than 94 percent of graduates have found work each year.
By September 2025 the staff totalled 2,769, among them 394 with senior professional titles and 709 with associate senior titles.
Note the international student figure of just 8; the university is mainly a domestic institution, so international applicants should ask about support, language of teaching and housing.

Cooperation agreements link SWPU with universities and research bodies in countries such as Canada, France, Germany, India, Japan, Russia, the UK and the US. A concrete example is a 2+2 degree programme with the University of Leeds in the UK.

southwest-petroleum-university.h: Chengdu: the city around the main campus

blocks.x: Most of a student's daily experience comes from the city, so this part describes Chengdu: its terrain, weather, growth, population, culture and food.

The Chengdu Plain, at 450 to 720 metres (1,480 to 2,360 feet) above sea level, forms the western rim of the Sichuan Basin, and the city sits on it. Mountains close it in on the western side. To the northwest are the steep Longmen Mountains, and in the west the Qionglai Mountains rise above 3,000 m (9,800 ft). Peaks there include Miaojiling at 5,364 m (17,598 ft) and Xiling Snow Mountain at 5,164 m (16,942 ft). The highlands also shelter a big primeval forest with abundant wildlife, which is home to giant pandas. East of the city are the low Longquan Mountains and the hills of the middle Min River, an area where several rivers converge.
Ancient people called Chengdu "the Abundant Land" because of its fertile soil, kind climate and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

In numbers, the prefecture spans latitudes 30° 05' to 31° 26' N and longitudes 102° 54' to 104° 53' E. Measured across, it stretches 192 kilometres (119 miles) from east to west and 166 km (103 miles) from south to north, taking in 12,390 square kilometres (4,780 square miles). The neighbouring areas are Deyang to the northeast, Ziyang to the southeast, Meishan to the south, Ya'an to the southwest and, in the north, the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture. The urban area, at about 500 m (1,600 ft), has a few rivers, three of them the Jin, Fu and Sha. Away from the city centre the terrain gets more complicated, with the Longquan range (龙泉山脉) and the Penzhong Hills (盆中丘陵) to the east and the Qionglai range to the west, reaching 5,364 m in Dayi County.

The highest point is Daxuetang, another name for Miaojiling, on Xiling Snow Mountain in Dayi County at 5,364 metres. The lowest is a riverbank at 359 metres, where the Tuojiang River leaves Jianyang City.

In climate terms Chengdu is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence (Köppen Cwa): mostly warm, and humid throughout the year. There are four clear seasons, and moderate rain falls mainly in the warm months, which softens both the heat of summer and the cold of winter. The Qinling (Qin) Mountains far to the north block cold Siberian winds, so the short winter is milder than along the lower Yangtze. January averages 5.9 °C (42.6 °F). Snow is rare, though each winter has a few frosty spells.

Summers are hot and sticky but not as extreme as in the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze basin: Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing. In July and August the daily mean is around 25 °C (77 °F) and afternoon highs can hit 33 °C (91 °F), though long spells of heat like those in much of eastern China are unusual. Rain is concentrated in July and August, and there is very little in cooler months.

The city is one of the cloudiest in China. Its sunshine total, just 1006 hours a year, is less than in much of northern Europe, and possible sunshine runs between 15 percent in December and 32 percent in August. March and April days are usually brighter and warmer than those of October and November. Average temperature over the year is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F); the record low is -6.5 °C (20 °F) and the record high 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).

China's urban housing reform got under way with a 1988 plan for gradual reform of the housing system in cities and towns. In Chengdu over 20 property companies were founded, the first stage of its real estate development.

In the 1990s the thorough restoration of the Funan River was a major environmental step. UN-Habitat gave it a Scroll of Honour Award in 1998, and the international council for local environmental initiatives (ICLEI) followed in 2000 with its Local Initiative Award.

Work on the Five Main Roads and One Bridge scheme started in 1997: three of the roads ran to the east and two to the south. They laid the groundwork for eastern and southern sub-centres, which steered residents in those directions, and lots of buildings went up beyond the 2nd Ring Road on the east and south sides. Renovation of the Shahe River and the Jin River drew more people to live beside them. People joked that the map of Chengdu needed updating every three months.

A speculative housing boom came around the turn of the millennium, with dozens of commercial property projects in 2000 alone. As the property market grew, the government gave substantial subsidies for a time to encourage citizens to buy their own homes, and houses became commodities.

One landmark is the New Century Global Center, which as of February 2026 is the third-largest building in the world by floor area. It is 100 metres (330 ft) tall and measures 500 by 400 metres (1,600 by 1,300 ft), with 1,700,000 square metres (18,000,000 sq ft) of floor space. Inside are retail outlets, cinemas, offices and hotels, a water park with an artificial beach and waves, a skating rink, a Mediterranean-style village that includes a big five-star hotel, and car parking for 15,000.

The 2020 census counted 20,937,757 people in the municipality, of whom 16,045,577 live in the metropolitan area proper, defined as the 12 urban districts and Guanghan City (administered by Deyang). It is Sichuan's biggest city and the fourth biggest in China. In 2015 the OECD estimated the metropolitan population at 18.1 million.
China Daily named Chengdu the country's fourth most livable city in 2006.

Chengdu has produced or hosted some of China's most important literature. Among the figures are Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, masters of Fu, a blend of descriptive prose and verse; the poets Li Bai and Du Fu (the source assigns them to the Tang and Song dynasties respectively); the Ming scholar Yang Shen'an; and the modern writers Guo Moruo and Ba Jin. The Jin-period historian Chang Qu wrote the Record of Hua Yang State, the earliest local history. In the Later Shu Kingdom the poet Zhao Chongzuo compiled Among the Flowers, China's first Ci anthology, and King Meng Chang of Later Shu is credited with the first Spring Festival couplet, which promises that a year of good harvests will welcome celebrations and that happy festivals herald long springs.
Chengdu staged the 81st World Science Fiction Convention in 2023, after winning the 2021 site-selection vote against Winnipeg, Canada.

In the Five Dynasties period the Chengdu painter Huang Quan and others began the Fine-Brush Flower-and-Bird Painting School. At the time there was also a "Hanlin Painting Academy", the first royal academy of its kind in China.

Islam has been present in Sichuan since the Tang dynasty (618 to 907), and Chengdu has 12 mosques. Huangcheng Mosque in the centre dates from the 16th century. Chengdu also has official, Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations, and some are underground.
The Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan, now the Diocese of Chengdu, was set up on 15 October 1696, with Artus de Lionne of the Paris Foreign Missions Society as its first vicar.

Protestant history begins in the late 19th century. The Canadian Methodist Mission wanted new stations in Asia in 1890, and Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart proposed Chengtu as the first in February 1891. He had previously built Western hospitals and schools on the Yangtze and Gan Rivers from 1866 to 1888. Hart arrived on 9 May 1891 and two weeks later bought a house, which he divided into living quarters and a dispensary. The first Protestant mission headquarters opened its doors on 24 June 1892 with over 1,000 local people attending. The first Methodist service followed on Sunday with only a few worshippers, and on 3 November 1892 the first Western dispensary in Sichuan opened, treating sixteen patients. The mission grew popular enough that a larger site near the East Gate was acquired in spring 1893, where the Sï-Shen-Tsï Methodist Church and a hospital were built.

Rioters destroyed those buildings in 1895, and mission staff fled to Chongqing and later Shanghai. Hart went to Peking to seek redress, and the Sichuan Viceroy Liu Ping Chang eventually paid full compensation. The compound was rebuilt, then destroyed again in the riots of 1901, and rebuilt a second time. Later missionaries moved the boys' and girls' schools to the south of the city and enlarged them, and in 1914 the Divinity College was dedicated as Hart College, one of the parts of West China Union University. That university is now Sichuan University, and the West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida) is part of it. When the Cultural Revolution came the church was no longer used for worship; the Chengdu City Second People's Hospital next door was put in charge, turning the chapel into a kindergarten and an equipment office. The building went back to the church in 1984.

The Early Rain Covenant Church was an underground congregation of about 500 members led by Pastor Wang Yi, and in December 2018 the authorities tried to close it. Over 100 members, among them Wang and his wife, were detained; officers also raided its kindergarten and theological college and shut its media outlets. Domestic media were forbidden to report on it. For international students, this is a reminder that religious activity in China is regulated and that you should learn the rules before you arrive.
In 2012 a Chabad Jewish Center was founded, moved five times, and eventually settled permanently in Wuhou District.

A local proverb praises Sichuan opera as unmatched anywhere ("Shu opera towers above all other performances in the world"). The city's first opera, "Bullfighting", dates from the Warring States period, and the Shu royal court of the Three Kingdoms period staged the first detailed opera. The earliest well-documented Zaju, an old comic drama of dance, song, poetry and mime, was likewise performed in Chengdu, and tombs of witty Han-dynasty poets have been dug up there. Face-changing masks and fire breathing remain the signature of Sichuan opera.
People in Chengdu speak the Chengdu dialect, which belongs to Sichuanese and has had a strong influence on comedy and rap in China.

Sichuan cuisine is known for spicy chilies and peppercorns. Well-known dishes include Chengdu hot pot, Mapo doufu and Dan Dan Mien noodles, the last two both flavoured with Sichuan pepper. The Los Angeles Times called Chengdu "China's party city" in 2006, for its carefree lifestyle. Despite having under half Shanghai's population, it has more teahouses and bars. Figures for 2023 show over 30,000 teahouses, plus 3,566 legally registered venues of the bar, nightclub and dance-hall kind, and a statistical report of 2019 already put it ahead of Shanghai as the city with the most bars in China. Tea drinking here goes back over a thousand years, since Chengdu was where the Southern Silk Road began. UNESCO has named Chengdu a "City of Gastronomy".

Teahouses are everywhere, from ornate traditional ones with bamboo furniture to plain modern ones. The teas include jasmine, longjing and biluochun. People go to play mahjong, get a massage or have their ears cleaned, and some bigger teahouses stage live shows such as Sichuan opera.

Hot pot is the city's other great speciality. It is a Sichuanese dish of vegetables, fish or meat cooked in a boiling, spicy broth, ideal for gatherings of friends, and it draws locals and tourists alike. Hot pot restaurants are all over Chengdu.
Founded in 1992 under the name Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone, the Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park is a national-level park for technology businesses.
National expressways serving Chengdu include G5 Beijing-Kunming, G42 Shanghai-Chengdu, G76 Xiamen-Chengdu, G93 Chengdu-Chongqing Ring and G4202 Chengdu Ring.

SWPU is a specialist oil and gas university with a heavy industry connection, in a city that offers a mild climate, relaxed social life and famous food. Check the current number of international students, the language of instruction and the campus assigned to your programme, because the university spans Chengdu and Nanchong.

Taken together, the figures describe a university with a clear industrial purpose. Its three national key disciplines all belong to the oil and gas supply chain, its sponsors include the three big state energy companies, and more than 94 percent of graduates have been employed every year for the past decade. For someone who wants a career in petroleum or related engineering, that is a strong fit. For someone who wants a broad, international campus, the low count of international students (8) and the Chengdu-Nanchong split are points to discuss with the admissions office.
Mild winters with a January mean of 5.9 °C, rare snow and a few frosts.
Warm, humid summers, with a July and August mean near 25 °C and highs of about 33 °C.
Plenty of cloud: only 1006 hours of sunshine a year.
A relaxed social scene built around teahouses, hot pot and Sichuan opera.
Southwest Petroleum University lists 17 programs for international students on this site: 11 master's, 6 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 17 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

17 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (11):
Business Administration
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Civil Engineering
Computer Science and Technology
Control Science and Engineering
Environmental Science and Engineering
Geological Resources and Geological Engineering
Geology
Materials Science and Engineering
Mechanical Engineering

The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

southwest-petroleum-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Southwest Petroleum University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chengdu, register at Southwest Petroleum University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Southwest University, known as SWU, is a public comprehensive university in Beibei, a district of Chongqing. The Ministry of Education is its supervising body, and the money comes jointly from the Chongqing Municipal People's Government, the Ministry of Education itself and the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. It belongs to the Double First-Class Construction group of universities. It also sits within Project 211, although a later description in the same material says the 211 Project has been abolished, and universities in the Double First Class plan are the ones that now get preferential support from the central government for development and construction. Check the university's own website for the current wording.

SWU is large. Counting everyone, it has more than 80,000 students, and about 50,000 of them are full-time. Each year it also hosts a good number of international students, who pursue bachelor's, master's or doctoral degrees as well as other advanced study.

Today's university was created in July 2005. China's Ministry of Education approved the merger of Southwest Agricultural University with Southwest China Normal University, and each partner had a history of more than 100 years. Before they merged, the two were next-door neighbours, with only a wall between their grounds. They had a long relationship too, because both shared one ancestor, West China Union University (founded 1906). Another account gives the origin more simply, as a school set up in the Qing dynasty in 1906 under the name West China University, which developed mostly once the Republic of China had come into being.

Among comprehensive universities supervised by the Ministry of Education, this was counted a key institution. It started as Southwest Teachers College, created in 1950 from several mergers that included the Sichuan Provincial Educational College and the former National Women's Teachers College. Southwest China Normal University became its name in 1985.

Southwest Agricultural College was founded in 1950, and Xianghui College, the Western China University and the Sichuan Provincial Educational College all fed into it. Two of the dates reported for later stages are hard to reconcile. One says that in 1979 the State Council authorized it as a national key university and that the college was reshaped into Southwest Agricultural College, while another says it was raised to Southwest Agricultural University in 1958. The year 2001 brought two additions: the Citrus Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agriculture and the Sichuan Animal Husbandry and Veterinary College. That started a new phase for Southwest Agricultural University, whose strengths ran across teaching, pedagogy, psychology, agronomy and agriculture.

southwest-university.h: What SWU teaches and what it is known for

blocks.x: The university covers a wide spread of disciplines: management, agriculture, engineering, science, history, literature, pedagogics, law, economics and philosophy. Its offering comes to 97 bachelor's programs, 159 master's programs, 9 postdoctoral programs and 66 doctoral programs, along with 40 national key disciplines.

Nationally, SWU is best known for the methods of teaching and for agricultural studies. Pedagogics, psychology and agriculture have a clear lead in China, and its research on the silkworm genome is among the best in the world. Substantial creative research has been done in several areas: zero tillage cultivation, the silkworm genome, how minorities in southwestern China are educated and how they behave psychologically, and the study of how humans perceive time.

Hanhong College takes its name from the motto of the university. It runs SWU's Undergraduate Top Talent Training Plan. It opened in November 2011, and in July 2018 the School of Innovation and Entrepreneurship took it in.

The college pools the best teaching resources from across the whole university. Its educational philosophy is summed up as a solid foundation, strong quality, the promotion of individuality and the pursuit of innovation. Talent is developed through what it calls one system and three modernizations, namely a tutorial system plus globalization, personalization and internationalization. The aim of the model is to produce innovative top talents who have sound personalities, excellent physical fitness and a drive for excellence.

About 400 students are enrolled. Its classes include the Yuan Longping Class for science and engineering, and the Wu Mi Class, which is for liberal arts. Both began in 2011 as pilots for training top-notch talents in basic disciplines. In 2014 the experimental class Shen Nong Class was added to train outstanding agricultural and forestry talents.

Students receive the best teachers and teaching conditions, together with independent classrooms, libraries and activity rooms. The college offers a Hanhong College Special Scholarship and international exchange visiting programs. Students are encouraged to join projects, laboratories and teams early on, and they get scientific research training. Separate indicators govern how master's degree students are recommended and exempted. The proportion of graduates who go on to further study stays above 80% each year, and more of them are studying at first-class universities at home and abroad every year.

SWU began enrolling international students in the 1950s, and its location, Chongqing, is described as the central city of the Western China Development Project. The Ministry of Education designated it as one of the universities that may enrol students on Chinese Government Scholarships.

International students there study a range of subjects. The most common choices are Chinese martial arts, fine arts, agriculture, food sciences, life sciences, Chinese minorities studies, business in China, economics, psychology, pedagogy and Chinese language. Those who qualify may compete for a Chongqing Mayor Scholarship or the SWU Excellent Overseas Students Scholarship. For every overseas student on a long programme, the university also pays a share of an integrative insurance that covers medical care and accidents.

The staff includes 300 professional researchers as well as 2,650 full-time teachers. Of the academic staff, 113 are PhD supervisors and 513 are master's degree tutors, and the ranks include 739 associate professors (associate research fellows) and 349 professors (research fellows). More than 50,000 students attend.

The campus has three libraries, the north section library, the south section library and the central library. Built in 2005, the central library is both the newest and the biggest. By January 2014 the university library held 3,800,000 volumes in total.
Buildings on campus mentioned for visitors include:
the Art Gallery
the Soccer Court
the Thirty-third Teaching Building
the Basketball Building
the Eighth Teaching Building
the Life Science Building
Daily life depends on the city that surrounds the campus. What follows covers Chongqing's landscape, weather, people, economy and transport, and finishes with local media.

Chongqing lies in the subtropics, where the Sichuan Basin meets the plain along the middle and lower Yangtze. Monsoon conditions are common, and rain tends to fall in the night during late spring and early summer. Chinese poets have written about this for centuries as the Ba Mountain night rain; Li Shangyin wrote one such poem, a letter to the north composed on a rainy night. The territory stretches 470 km (290 mi) across at its longest point, east to west, and 450 km (280 mi) at its widest, north to south. Its neighbours are Hubei and Hunan on the east side, Guizhou on the south side, and Sichuan and Shaanxi on the north side.

Rivers and mountains crisscross a large area. The Daba Mountains stand in the north. In the south are the Dalou Mountains, with the Wuling Mountains to the southeast and the Wu Gorge to the east. From north to south the land falls toward the Yangtze valley, and most of it is a great mass of mountains and hills with steep slopes at different elevations. Karst scenery is widespread: stone forests, clusters of peaks, limestone caves and valleys appear in many places. One tourist attraction is the Longshuixia Gap (龙水峡地缝) with its Three Natural Bridges. The Yangtze runs west to east through the whole territory for 665 km (413 mi). On its way it slices through the Wu Mountains three times, creating the famous Three Gorges, which are Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling. Coming from the northwest, the Jialing River passes through the Jialing Lesser Three Gorges (Libi, Wentang and Guanyin) before meeting the Yangtze at Chongqing.

The central urban area, called Chongqing proper, stands on mountains, with the Yangtze and the Jialing wrapping around part of it. In terms of terrain, the area holds forests, springs, waterfalls, gorges, caves, mountains and rivers. This scenery inspired an epigram by Li Bai, the Tang dynasty poet. Tongluo Mountain (铜锣山) to the east and Zhongliang Mountain (中梁山) to the west roughly mark where the urban area ends. Beyond the centre are some tall mountains, for instance Wugong Ling in Jiangjin, at 1,709.4 m (5,608 ft).

southwest-university.h: A city of heat, damp and fog

blocks.x: The climate is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence (Köppen Cwa), and it comes close to the ordinary humid subtropical type (Köppen Cfa). Humidity is very high nearly all year, and no month falls below 75%. The cities of Wuhan, Nanjing and Chongqing are traditionally grouped as the Three Furnaces along the Yangtze. Summers in Chongqing are long and rank among the hottest and muggiest in China, with urban highs of 34 °C (93 °F) reached in July and August. In contrast, winters are short, fairly mild, damp and cloudy.

One result of being inside the Sichuan Basin is very little sun. At only 983 hours a year, Chongqing has one of the lowest totals in China, lower than many places in Northern Europe. In the city proper the possible sunshine percentage is a mere 5% in January and rises to 43% in August. The record low since 1951 is -1.8 °C (29 °F), set on 11 January 1955. On 18 and 19 August 2022 the record high of 43.7 °C (111 °F) was reached.

Fog gives the city its nickname, the Fog City (雾都). Over 100 days a year are foggy, including 68 days in spring and autumn when thick fog covers the city. This weather may have helped to keep the Imperial Japanese Army from overrunning Chongqing in the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945).

Chongqing counted 32,054,159 people in the 2020 national census, which was about 2.27% of the national total and made it the most populous city proper anywhere. It surpassed Shanghai in 2020 as the municipality in China with the most urban residents. About 70.4% of the population was urban in 2021 against 29.6% rural, and 23.01 million lived in urban areas in 2024.

Looking at age, 15.91% were aged 0-14, 62.22% were 15-64 and 21.87% were 65 or over. People's highest level of education was college for 15.41%, high school for 15.96%, middle school for 30.58% and elementary school for 29.89%.

The main religions are Chinese folk religion, Taoism and Chinese Buddhism. Surveys from 2007 and 2009 found 26.63% following Chinese ancestral religion and 1.05% identifying as Christian. No other religions were reported separately. The other 72.32% could be irreligious, or could worship nature deities or follow Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or folk religious sects. A count in 2010 found 9,056 Muslims in Chongqing.

In the Third Front campaign, Chongqing was one of the main places where China built up its industrial capacity. Authorities have worked hard to make the municipality the economic, trade and financial hub of its region, and to use it as a base for developing the western interior. Its urbanisation is fast. On 14 March 1997 Chongqing was separated from Sichuan province and given municipality status of its own, so that it could grow faster and help the poorer western areas of China (under the China Western Development strategy). It had become a significant industrial area in the west of the country by the 2000s.

In 2022, nominal GDP reached US$433 billion (CN¥ 2.91 trilion), which was around 2.41% of the national total and 16th among all province-level units. The breakdown by sector: primary industry US$29.92 billion (CN¥201.21 billion), secondary industry US$173.86 billion (CN¥1.169 trillion) and tertiary industry US$229.3 billion (CN¥1.542 trillion). Nominal GDP per head, at US$13,479 (CN¥90,663), was 10th highest nationally. In its November 2010 Access China White Paper, the Economist Intelligence Unit included Chongqing in CHAMPS, a profile of the 20 leading emerging cities in China. CHAMPS stands for Shenyang, Pingdingshan, Maanshan, Anshan, Hefei and Chongqing.

Chongqing and Sichuan are both hard to reach, and that has long made them key bases for weapons research and development. The industries are diverse, but the export sector is small, unlike eastern China, since the location is inland. Instead, factories supply local markets with goods like cars, processed food, chemicals, textiles, machinery, electronics and sports equipment.

China's biggest motorcycle production centre and its third largest centre for motor vehicles is Chongqing. In 2007 annual capacity was 8.6 million motorcycles and 1 million cars. Changan Automotive Corp, the fourth biggest Chinese automaker, is one leading producer, along with Lifan Hongda Enterprise, and Ford Motor Company has 3 plants. Chongqing is counted among China's nine largest producers of iron and steel, and it also ranks as one of the three major aluminum producers in the country. Notable makers include Southwest Aluminum (西南鋁業), Asia's biggest aluminum plant, and Chongqing Iron and Steel Company (重庆钢铁股份有限公司). Farming still matters, mainly rice and fruit such as oranges.

southwest-university.h: Minerals, energy and the next industries

blocks.x: Natural resources are rich. There is a lot of coal and natural gas, plus more than 40 other minerals including strontium and manganese. Coal reserves total about 4.7×109 long tons (5.3×109 short tons), which is 4,800,000,000 metric tons. China's largest inland gas field is the Chuandong Natural Gas Field, with about 270 billion m3, over a fifth of the national total. The city has China's largest strontium reserve, and China itself holds the second biggest strontium deposit in the world. Xiushan is where manganese is mined. Critics have called mining heavily polluting and unsafe. CNPC, the parent of PetroChina, plans to run a 10 million ton refinery in Chongqing for crude oil brought through the Sino-Myanmar pipelines. When finished, that pipeline will start at Sittwe on the west coast of Myanmar and pass through Kunming in Yunnan on the way to Chongqing, supplying fuel sourced in Myanmar, Africa and the Middle East.

There has recently been an effort to climb the value chain with high-technology, knowledge-intensive industries, and it has led to new development zones, among them the Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ). By promoting favourable policies for electronics and information technology, the local government hopes to build a 400 billion RMB high-technology manufacturing hub. This would overtake the car industry and make up 25% of exports.

Chongqing has also put a great deal of money into infrastructure that attracts investors. Upgraded and extended roads and railways connect the city to the rest of China and reduce the cost of logistics. The nearby Three Gorges Dam, the largest in the world, provides electricity and allows ocean-going ships to come up the Yangtze to Chongqing's port. These improvements have brought in many foreign direct investors across sectors from cars to banking and retail, including Ford, Mazda, Wal-Mart, Carrefour, Metro AG, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, Scotiabank, ANZ Bank, HSBC and Standard Chartered Bank, among other multinational corporations.
Several zones are set aside for economic and technological development:
Chongqing Economic and Technological Development Zone
Chongqing Chemical Industrial Park
Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ)
Jianqiao Industrial Park, located in Dadukou District
Chongqing Hi-Tech Industry Development Zone
Chongqing Export Processing Zone
Liangjiang New Area, which includes the Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center, China's biggest of its kind
Along with Chengdu and Xi'an, Chongqing forms the West Triangle Economic Zone.

Since the city was promoted in 1997 to national-level municipality, its infrastructure has grown dramatically. Expressways and railways built toward the east and southeast have made Chongqing a main transport hub for southwestern China. As of October 2014, 31 bridges spanned the Yangtze in the municipality, and over a dozen were in the urban core. The first two were built in 1960 and 1977, and every other one dates from 1995 or after.

Chongqing has an extensive metro, intercity rail, buses everywhere and the world's largest monorail network. Under a plan made public in May 2007, 13 years and 150 billion RMB are set aside for a system that blends underground metro lines and heavy monorail.

As of 2017, four lines were in operation. Line 1 is conventional subway, 14 km (8.7 mi) in length, while Line 2 is a heavy monorail of 19 km (12 mi) through its Phase II. Line 3, also a heavy monorail, connects the southern part of downtown to the airport. Beibei, a district far to the north, is linked to downtown by Line 6, and Line 5 started service in late 2017. By 2020, the plan said, the network would have 1 loop line and 6 lines, which meant 363.5 km (225.9 mi) of new track to the 2012 network and 93 stations to the 111 open in 2012. By 2050 the target is 18 lines.

No other city in China has kept its aerial tramways in public service. Chongqing had three: the Yangtze River, Jialing River and South Mountain tramways. Only the Yangtze River Tramway still runs, and it counts as a Class 4A tourist attraction. Its 1,160 m (3,810 ft) span connects the south and north banks of the Yangtze, with about 10,000 passengers on an average day.
Five stations matter most.

Chongqing railway station is in Yuzhong, reached via Lianglukou Metro station on Lines 1 and 3. It is the oldest in the city, close to the Jiefangbei CBD in the centre, and handles mainly long-distance trains. A big renovation is planned, which is why a lot of its services have moved to Chongqing North.
Chongqing North railway station, completed in 2006 and linked to the metro, has numerous long-distance and high-speed trains to Chengdu, Beijing and more.
Chongqing West railway station in Shapingba was completed in 2018 and has many long-distance and high-speed services to numerous cities.

Shapingba railway station, near the Shapingba CBD, was also completed in 2018. Lines 1 and 9 and the Loop line stop at Shapingba metro station, from which it is reached. Local and regional trains are its main business.
Chongqing East railway station was opened in 2025.

Chongqing is a big destination for freight, and handling facilities continue to improve. Subsidies and incentives have moved and created many factories there, so rail traffic has soared. As a regional hub it has links on the following railways:
Chengdu-Chongqing railway (Chengdu, Sichuan Province)
Sichuan-Guizhou railway (Guiyang, Guizhou Province)
Xiangyang-Chongqing railway (Hubei Province)
Chongqing-Huaihua railway (Hunan Province)
Suining-Chongqing railway (Sichuan Province)
Chongqing-Lichuan railway (Hubei Province)
Lanzhou-Chongqing railway (Gansu Province)

The biggest radio station is the Chongqing People's Broadcast Station. Chongqing TV is the one television network at municipal level, and people say it is the fourth-largest station in China. Its channels are mostly aimed at local viewers, though many TV sets across China can receive it.

southwest-university-of-political-scienc.h: About Southwest University of Political Science and Law

blocks.x: The Southwest University of Political Science and Law (SWUPL) is a municipal public university in Yubei, Chongqing, China. It is affiliated with the City of Chongqing, and co-funded by the Chongqing Municipal People's Government and the Ministry of Education.
The university was founded in 1953 as Southwest College of Political Science and Law.

Southwest University of Political Science and Law (SWUPL) developed from the Department of Political Science and Law at Southwest University of People's Revolution which was founded in 1950, with Marshal Liu Bocheng as the university president.

In 1953, SWUPL was officially established through merging the Political Science and Law departments of Chongqing University and Sichuan University, the Law departments of Chongqing Finance and Economy College, and of Guizhou University and Yunnan University.

In 2000, the administration of the university was transferred from the Ministry of Justice to the Chongqing municipality, thus creating a system of co-administration between the central and local government.

In 2003, it was approved as one of the first universities to grant doctoral degree of first-level legal discipline. In 2004, it established one post-doctorate mobile station of Law. In 2007, SWUPL was awarded as "excellent undergraduate education" by Ministry of Education.
In 2008, SWUPL became a university co-administrated by Ministry of Education and Chongqing Municipality.
SWUPL became the first University in Chongqing co-administered by the Ministry and Municipality on October 24, 2012.

The university has three campuses, the main in Yubei, the other two in Shapingba and Baoshenghu, covering a total area of 209 hectares (520 acres). There are 14 schools, including School of Civil and Commercial law, School of Economic Law, Law School, School of Administrative Law, School of International Law, School of Criminal investigation, School of Marxism, School of Juris Master, School of Management, School of Politics and Public Administration, School of Journalism and Communication, School of Foreign Languages, School of Applied Law, and School of Economics.

It offers 20 bachelor's programs, 37 master's programs of sub-disciplines, 4 professional master's programs and 10 doctoral programs of sub-discipline, and 2 national key disciplines.  The university has postdoctoral center for legal research and 6 provincial key bases for humanity and social science research.  It has 1421 faculty and staff members, among which 1157 are full-time. It has 5159 postgraduates and 18591 undergraduates.  The university's library has over 4,200,000 books.
The university consists of Shapingba, Yubei and Baoshenghu Campuses in Chongqing municipality.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Chongqing, where Southwest University of Political Science and Law is located.

Chongqing is located in the subtropics, situated in the transitional area between the Sichuan Basin and the plain on the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze. Its climate features frequent monsoon conditions, often raining at night in late spring and early summer. The city's "night rain in the Ba Mountains" features in poems throughout Chinese history, including "Written on a Rainy Night—A Letter to the North" by Li Shangyin. Its territory is 470 kilometers (290 mi) from east to west at its longest, and 450 kilometers (280 mi) from north to south at its widest. It borders Hubei and Hunan to the east, Sichuan and Shaanxi to the north, and Guizhou to the south.

Chongqing covers a large area crisscrossed by rivers and mountains. The Daba Mountains stand in the north, the Wu Gorge in the east, the Wuling Mountains in the southeast, and the Dalou Mountains in the south. The area slopes downward from north to south towards the Yangtze valley, and features a large massif of mountains and hills, with steep sloping areas at different heights. Karst landscape is common in this area, and stone forests, numerous collections of peaks, limestone caves and valleys can be found in many places. The Longshuixia Gap (Chinese: 龙水峡地缝), with its Three Natural Bridges, has made the region a popular tourist attraction. The Yangtze River runs through the whole area from west to east, covering a course of 665 kilometers (413 mi), cutting through the Wu Mountains at three places and forming the well-known Three Gorges: the Qutang, Wuxia and Xiling gorges. Coming from northwest and running through "the Jialing Lesser Three Gorges" of Libi, Wentang and Guanyin, the Jialing River joins the Yangtze in Chongqing.

The central urban area of Chongqing, called Chongqing proper, is built on mountains and partially surrounded by the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. With its special topography, Chongqing's topography includes mountains, rivers, forests, springs, waterfalls, gorges, and caves. The Tang dynasty poet Li Bai was inspired by the natural scenery and wrote this epigram.

The Zhongliang (中梁山) and Tongluo (铜锣山) mountains roughly form the eastern and western boundaries of Chongqing's urban area. Several high mountains are situated outside central Chongqing, including the 1,709.4-meter (5,608 ft)-high Wugong Ling Mountain in Jiangjin.

Chongqing has a monsoonal humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa), bordering on an ordinary humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) and for most of the year experiences very high relative humidity, with all months above 75%. Known as one of the "Three Furnaces" of the Yangtze River, along with Wuhan and Nanjing, its summers are long and among the hottest and most humid in China, with highs of 34 °C (93 °F) in July and August in the urban area. Winters are short and somewhat mild, but damp and overcast. The city's location in the Sichuan Basin causes it to have one of the lowest annual sunshine totals nationally, at only 983 hours, lower than much of Northern Europe; the monthly percent possible sunshine in the city proper ranges from a mere 5% in January to 43% in August. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −1.8 °C (29 °F) on 11 January 1955 to 43.7 °C (111 °F) on 18 and 19 August 2022

Chongqing, with over 100 days of fog per year, is known as the "Fog City" (Chinese: 雾都); this is because in the spring and fall, a thick layer of fog enshrouds it for 68 days per year. During the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), this special weather possibly played a role in protecting the city from being overrun by the Imperial Japanese Army.

According to the 2020 national census, Chongqing has a population of 32,054,159, accounting for around 2.27% of the national total. This makes it the most populous city proper in the world. As of 2010, the metropolitan area encompassing the central urban area was estimated by the OECD to have, a population of 17 million.

In 2020, Chongqing surpassed Shanghai as China's largest municipality by urban population. As of 2021, 70.4% of Chongqing's population is estimated to be urban, and 29.6% rural. As of 2024, Chongqing had an urban population of 23.01 million.

The Census also lists the male percentage as 50.55% and the female percentage as 49.55%. In terms of age distribution, of the total population, 15.91% were age 0–14, 62.22% were 15–64, and 21.87% were 65 and over. Of the population's highest education level achieved, 15.41% were college, 15.96% were high school, 30.58% were middle school, and 29.89% were elementary school.

The predominant religions in Chongqing are Chinese folk religions, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism. According to surveys conducted in 2007 and 2009, 26.63% of the population practices Chinese ancestral religion, while 1.05% of the population identifies as Christian.

The reports did not give figures for other types of religion; 72.32% of the population may be either irreligious or involved in worship of nature deities, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, or folk religious sects.
In 2010, there were 9,056 Muslims in Chongqing.
Chongqing was a major recipient of China's investment in industrial capacity during the Third Front campaign.

There has been a massive government push to transform Chongqing into the region's economic, trade, and financial center and use the municipality as a platform to open up the country's western interior to further development. Chongqing is facing rapid urbanization. For instance, statistics suggest that new construction added approximately 137,000 square meters (1,470,000 sq ft) daily of usable floor space to satisfy demands for residential, commercial and factory space. Thus, Chongqing was separated from Sichuan province and made into a municipality in its own right on 14 March 1997 in order to accelerate its development and subsequently China's relatively poorer western areas (see China Western Development strategy). By the 2000s the city had become an important industrial area in western China.

As of 2022, Chongqing's nominal GDP was US$433 billion (CN¥ 2.91 trilion), about 2.41% of the country's GDP and ranked 16th among province-level administrative units; the municipality's primary, secondary and tertiary industries were worth CN¥201.21 billion (US$29.92 billion), CN¥1.169 trillion (US$173.86 billion) and CN¥1.542 trillion (US$229.3 billion) respectively. Its nominal GDP per capita was US$13,479 (CN¥90,663) and ranked 10th in the country.

Chongqing has been identified by the Economist Intelligence Unit in the November 2010 Access China White Paper as a member of the CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), an economic profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China.

Traditionally, due to its geographic inaccessibility, Chongqing and Sichuan have both been important military bases in weapons research and development. Even though Chongqing's industries are diversified, unlike eastern China, its export sector is small due to its relatively disadvantageous inland location. Instead, factories producing local-oriented consumer goods such as processed food, cars, chemicals, textiles, machinery, sports equipment and electronics are common.

Chongqing is China's third largest motor vehicle production center and the largest for motorcycles. In 2007, it had an annual output capacity of 1 million cars and 8.6 million motorcycles. Leading makers of cars and motorbikes includes China's fourth biggest automaker; Changan Automotive Corp and Lifan Hongda Enterprise, as well as Ford Motor Company, with the US car giant having 3 plants in Chongqing. The municipality is also one of China's nine largest iron and steel producers in China as well as one of its three major aluminum producers. Important manufacturers include Chongqing Iron and Steel Company (重庆钢铁股份有限公司) and Southwest Aluminum (西南鋁業), which is Asia's largest aluminum plant.
Agriculture remains significant. Rice and fruits, especially oranges, are the area's main produce.

Natural resources are also abundant with large deposits of coal, natural gas, and more than 40 kinds of minerals such as strontium and manganese. Coal reserves total approximately 4,800,000,000 metric tons (4.7×109 long tons; 5.3×109 short tons). Chuandong Natural Gas Field is China's largest inland gas field with deposits of around 270 billion m3 – more than 1/5 of China's total. Has China's largest reserve of strontium (China has the world's 2nd biggest strontium deposit). Manganese is mined in the Xiushan area. Although the mining sector has been denounced as heavily polluting and unsafe. Chongqing is also planned to be the site of a 10 million ton capacity refinery operated by CNPC (parent company of PetroChina) to process imported crude oil from the Sino-Myanmar pipelines. The pipeline itself, though not yet finished, will eventually run from Sittwe (in Myanmar's western coast) through Kunming in Yunnan before reaching Chongqing and it will provide China with fuels sourced from Myanmar, the Middle East and Africa. Recently, there has been a drive to move up the value chain by shifting towards high technology and knowledge intensive industries resulting in new development zones such as the Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ). Chongqing's local government is hoping through the promotion of favorable economic policies for the electronics and information technology sectors, that it can create a 400 billion RMB high technology manufacturing hub which will surpass its car industry and account for 25% of its exports.

The city has also invested heavily in infrastructure to attract investment. The network of roads and railways connecting Chongqing to the rest of China has been expanded and upgraded reducing logistical costs. Furthermore, the nearby Three Gorges Dam, which is the world's largest, supplies Chongqing with power and allows oceangoing ships to reach Chongqing's Yangtze River port. These infrastructure improvements have led to the arrivals of numerous foreign direct investors (FDI) in industries ranging from car to finance and retailing; such as Ford, Mazda, HSBC, Standard Chartered Bank, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, ANZ Bank, Scotiabank, Wal-Mart, Metro AG and Carrefour, among other multinational corporations.
The city includes a number of economic and technological development zones:
Chongqing Chemical Industrial Park
Chongqing Economic & Technological Development Zone
Chongqing Hi-Tech Industry Development Zone
Chongqing New North Zone (CNNZ)
Chongqing Export Processing Zone
Jianqiao Industrial Park (located in Dadukou District)
Liangjiang New Area
Liangjiang Cloud Computing Center (the largest of its kind in China)
Chongqing itself is part of the West Triangle Economic Zone, along with Chengdu and Xi'an.

Since its elevation to national-level municipality in 1997, the city has dramatically expanded its infrastructure. With the construction of railways and expressways to the east and southeast, Chongqing is a major transportation hub in southwestern China.

As of October 2014, the municipality had 31 bridges across the Yangtze River including over a dozen in the city's urban core. Aside from the city's first two Yangtze River bridges, which were built, respectively, in 1960 and 1977, all of the other bridges were completed since 1995.
Public transport in Chongqing consists of metro, intercity railway, a ubiquitous bus system and the world's largest monorail network.

According to the Chongqing Municipal Government's ambitious plan in May 2007, Chongqing is investing 150 billion RMB over 13 years to finish a system that combines underground metro lines with heavy monorail.

As of 2017, four metro lines, the 14-kilometer (8.7 mi) long CRT Line 1, a conventional subway, and the 19-kilometer (12 mi) long heavy monorail CRT Line 2 (through Phase II), Line 3, a heavy monorail connects the airport and the southern part of downtown. Line 6, runs between Beibei, a district in the city's far north to downtown. Line 5 opened in late 2017.

It was planned that by 2020, CRT would consist of 6 lines and 1 loop line, adding 363.5 kilometers (225.9 mi) of road and railway to the 2012 transportation infrastructure, and 93 new metro stations would be added to the 111 stations in place in 2012. By 2050 Chongqing would have 18 lines.

Chongqing is the only Chinese city that has kept public aerial tramways. There were three aerial tramways in Chongqing: the Yangtze River Tramway, the Jialing River Tramway and the South Mountain Tramway, of which the Yangtze River Tramway is the only one still operating, now considered a Class 4A tourist attraction. The 1,160-meter (3,810 ft)-long tramway connects the southern and northern banks of the Yangtze River, carrying about 10,000 passengers a day.
Major stations in Chongqing:

Chongqing railway station in Yuzhong, accessible via Metro Lines 1 & 3 (Lianglukou Metro station), is the city's oldest railway station and located near the Jiefangbei CBD in the city center. The station handles mostly long-distance trains. There are plans for a major renovation and overhaul of this station, thus many services have been transferred to Chongqing North railway station.

Chongqing North railway station is a station handling many long-distance services and high-speed rail services to Chengdu, Beijing and other cities. It was completed in 2006 and is connected to Metro Line.
Chongqing West railway station is in Shapingba, a station handling many long-distance services and high-speed rail services to many cities, completed in 2018.

Shapingba railway station is in Shapingba, near Shapingba CBD, accessible via Shapingba metro station on Lines 1, 9 and the Loop line. It handles many local and regional train services. It was completed in 2018.
Chongqing East railway station opened in 2025.

Chongqing is a major freight destination for rail with continued development with improved handling facilities. Due to subsidies and incentives, the relocation and construction of many factories in Chongqing has seen a huge increase in rail traffic.
Chongqing is a major rail hub regionally.
Chengdu–Chongqing railway (to Chengdu, Sichuan Province)
Sichuan–Guizhou railway (to Guiyang, Guizhou Province)
Xiangyang–Chongqing railway (to Hubei Province)
Chongqing–Huaihua railway (to Hunan Province)
Suining–Chongqing railway (to Sichuan Province)
Chongqing–Lichuan railway (to Hubei Province)
Lanzhou–Chongqing railway (to Gansu Province)

The Chongqing People's Broadcast Station is Chongqing's largest radio station. The only municipal-level TV network is Chongqing TV, claimed to be the fourth-largest television station in China. Chongqing TV broadcasts many local-oriented channels, and can be viewed on many TV sets throughout China.

SWUFE (西南财经大学), short for Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, is a state-run university in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan Province. Its specialities are finance, economics and business. The Ministry of Education oversees it, and the Sichuan provincial government helps pay for it. Nationally it belongs to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction scheme.
A milestone came in December 2014, when SWUFE's School of Business Administration won European Quality Improvement System accreditation, the first business school in Western China to do so.

southwestern-university-of-finance-and-e.h: A university with a long road to Chengdu

blocks.x: The story begins in 1925 in Shanghai. A group of students and scholars led by Zhang Shouyong left St. John's University after the May 30th Movement and set up Kwang Hua University. The Second Sino-Japanese War and the Japanese advance across the mainland led the university to shift its headquarters to Chengdu in 1938. Many leading universities from eastern China made the same journey west after the Republic of China shifted its capital from Nanjing to Chongqing.

Once the Second World War was over, the main body returned to Shanghai (1946), leaving the Chengdu campus as a branch. That very year the Chengdu branch split off as an independent private institution named Chenghua University. The Shanghai university was later merged with others and is now part of East China Normal University.

After the founding of the People's Republic, Chenghua University, in 1952, absorbed the economics and business departments of 16 other universities and colleges, emerging as the Sichuan Institute of Finance and Economics. From 1961 to 1978 the school was known as Chengdu University. The central bank, the People's Bank of China, ran it from 1980 until 2000, when the Ministry of Education assumed control. It was under the central bank, in 1985, that the university acquired its current name.

National recognition came in stages. SWUFE joined Project 211 in 1995. In 2011 it was added to Project 985's extension, the 985 Innovative Platforms for Key Disciplines Project. Then, in 2017, three bodies (the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance and the National Development and Reform Commission) published the Double First-Class lists. SWUFE appears on the list of Double First-Class development universities, and applied economics is one of the disciplines selected for the same status.

SWUFE has two campuses in different parts of Chengdu. Liulin, the main campus, was founded in 2004 in Wenjiang; it spreads over about 107 hectares (264 acres). Guanghua, founded in 1938, is in Qingyang and is smaller, at about 47 hectares (116 acres). Ask which campus your program uses before you arrange housing.

In the Best Chinese Universities Ranking for 2024, SWUFE came fourth in the country among universities specialising in finance, business and economics, and first in Western China, a region of almost 300 million people. U.S. News & World Report has it third in China, fourth in Asia and seventeenth in the world for Business and Economics.

Several widely cited international league tables treat it as one of China's best for economics and business subjects: the Shanghai Ranking, U.S. News, URAP and the NTU Ranking. In 2025 URAP rated it number one in Asia and eighth worldwide for Economics and Business, while the QS World University Rankings listed it at 373rd in Asia the same year.

The 2023 Academic Ranking of World Universities also gives strong subject results. SWUFE is in the world's top 32 for Finance and top 45 for Economics, and sits within the top 76 for Management and the top 101 for Business Administration.

Three research bodies stand out. The Institute of Financial Studies (IFS), established on 29 July 2010, researches international finance and the course of financial development in China. It is directed by Philip H. Dybvig, who is well known for the Diamond-Dybvig model, published in 1983 with Douglas W. Diamond.

The China Household Finance Survey (CHFS) center is a non-profit research body that the university's Research Institute of Economics and Management founded in 2010. Within a few years it had become an academic survey institute holding detailed micro data in three databases: the finances of private Chinese households, small and micro businesses, and the governance of communities. Registered users can obtain CHFS data to support academic and policy work.
The Institute of Western China Economic Studies supervises doctoral research in three fields: demography, agricultural economics, and the economics of population, resources and the environment.

The library dates from 1952 and occupies a building of 50,000 square metres (540,000 sq ft). Its digital collection has reached two million items, making it the largest library in southwest China. In May 2002 a Translation Center was added to handle overseas communication and to edit and publish an English version of SWUFE's The Economist.

Opened in 1998, the Money and Securities Museum was one of the earliest museums to show genuine financial objects such as banknotes and coins, securities, certificates and cards from planned and market economies alike. Its hall of 700 square metres (7,500 sq ft) has displayed over 60,000 items.

International applicants should note that SWUFE delivers four bachelor's programs and two master's programs wholly in English. Thousands of foreign students, drawn from more than a hundred countries, have been trained on them.

Partnerships reach 130 universities, financial institutes and companies in 36 countries and regions. Partner countries include the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan, Canada, Australia, Brazil, Chile, Austria, Israel, Portugal, Russia, Slovenia and the Netherlands.

Campus life is organised around about 100 student associations, not counting those sponsored by companies. They cover five domains: thinking and theory, scholarship and technology, culture and the arts, sport and fitness, and public welfare with practice and communication. Examples are the Research on Philosophy Club, a Model UN group, the Starting Point Drama Club, Hip-pop, the Green Development Association, the Oracle Club and the career magazine Pre Guide for Career.

Among former students the university lists the following. The banking and government world is well represented. Jiang Chaoliang governed Jilin Province and earlier chaired Agricultural Bank of China. Li Ruogu led the Exim Bank of China as chairman and president. Liu Jiayi, now Secretary of the CPC's Shandong Provincial Committee, formerly headed the National Audit Office as Auditor General. Shang Fulin, previously Chairman of the China Banking Regulatory Commission, is Vice Director of the CPPCC's Economic Policy Committee. Wei Hong was Governor of Sichuan. Others include Yang Rong, a Chinese-born automotive businessman, and Zhang Zhan, a former lawyer and citizen journalist.

southwestern-university-of-finance-and-e.h: Chengdu as a place to live and study

blocks.x: Everyday life depends heavily on the city: the weather, how people get about, what to eat and what to do after class. The rest of this profile describes Chengdu, the city around SWUFE's campuses.

Chengdu stands on a wide plain at 450 to 720 metres (1,480 to 2,360 feet) above sea level. The city sits at the western rim of the Sichuan Basin, on the Chengdu Plain, so most of the terrain is flat. The prefecture runs from latitude 30° 05' to 31° 26' N and longitude 102° 54' to 104° 53' E, The prefecture stretches 192 kilometres (119 mi) across from east to west, and 166 km (103 mi) from south to north, administering a land area of 12,390 km2 (4,780 sq mi). Around it are Deyang (northeast), Ziyang (southeast), Meishan (south), Ya'an (southwest), and, to the north, the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture.

The built-up area sits at about 500 m (1,600 ft) and has several rivers, among them the Jin, Fu and Sha. Beyond the urban area the land gets more complicated. Eastward you meet the Longquan Mountains (龙泉山脉) and the Penzhong Hills (盆中丘陵). High, steep Longmen Mountains lie to the northwest. In the west the Qionglai range tops 3,000 m (9,800 ft); its peaks include Miaojiling at 5,364 m (17,598 ft) and Xiling Snow Mountain at 5,164 m (16,942 ft). The western uplands are also home to extensive primeval forest with abundant wildlife, and to giant panda habitat.

East of the city the low Longquan Mountains meet the hill country of the middle Min River, an area where several rivers converge. The highest spot in the whole prefecture is Daxuetang, another name for Miaojiling, in Dayi County's Xiling Snow Mountain, at 5,364 metres. The lowest is 359 metres up on the bank where the Tuojiang River flows out through Jianyang City. Since ancient times Chengdu has been called the Abundant Land, because of its fertile soil, favourable climate and the innovative Dujiangyan Irrigation System.

Chengdu has a humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon (Köppen Cwa). It is mostly warm and always humid, with four clear seasons. Moderate rain, falling chiefly in the warm months, takes the edge off both sweltering summers and freezing winters. Far to the north the Qin Mountains (Qinling) shelter the city from cold Siberian winds, which is why its short winter is gentler than winter in the Lower Yangtze. In January the daily mean is 5.9 °C (42.6 °F); you will rarely see snow, although frost does arrive for a few periods each winter.

Summer is hot and humid, but it does not match the 'Three Furnaces' cities of Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing in the same river basin. The 24-hour mean in July and August is about 25 °C (77 °F), and afternoons can touch 33 °C (91 °F). Heat that lingers for weeks, as in much of eastern China, seldom occurs. July and August are also the wettest months, while the cooler months get hardly any rain.

Sunshine is scarce. Chengdu's yearly total is one of the lowest in China, below that of much of Northern Europe. Possible sunshine is just 15 percent in December and reaches only 32 percent in August, which amounts to 1,006 hours of bright sunshine over the year. Daytime spring weather (March and April) tends to be sunnier and warmer than autumn (October and November). The yearly mean temperature is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F) and temperatures have ranged between -6.5 °C (20 °F) and 39.4 °C (102.9 °F). A student arriving from a sunnier climate should expect plenty of grey, humid days.

Chengdu's modern building boom has a clear starting point. A national plan of 1988 for gradual housing reform in cities and towns launched housing reform across urban China, and more than 20 property companies promptly opened in Chengdu, the first step in the city's real estate development.

Cleaning up the environment was the next step. A sweeping 1990s overhaul of the Funan River won a UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour in 1998, and in 2000 it received the Local Initiative Award of the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives.

Road building came next. The Five Main Roads and One Bridge project started in 1997: three roads for the east and two for the south, which created the base for the city's Eastern and Southern sub-centers. Those sub-centers set the direction in which residents chose to live, and a flood of buildings appeared east and south of the 2nd Ring Road. Cleaning up the Shahe and Jin rivers also made the riverbanks popular places to live. At one point people joked that Chengdu's map would need redrawing every quarter.

The late 1990s and early 2000s brought a speculative housing boom, and dozens of commercial developments appeared in 2000 alone. To stimulate the market, the state offered sizeable subsidies for a time to people buying their own homes. Houses had become commodities.

The city's best-known giant is the New Century Global Center, listed as the world's third-largest building by floor area as of February 2026. It stands 100 metres (330 ft) high on a footprint of 500 by 400 metres (1,600 by 1,300 ft), giving a floor area of 1.7 million square metres (18 million sq ft). Inside are retail outlets, cinemas, offices and hotels, as well as a water park with an artificial beach and waves, an ice-skating rink, parking for 15,000 vehicles and a Mediterranean-style village built around a large 5-star hotel.

Chengdu is the biggest city in Sichuan and the fourth biggest in China. The 2020 census recorded 20,937,757 residents in the municipality. The metropolitan area, defined as the 12 urban districts together with Guanghan City (part of Deyang), accounted for 16,045,577 of them. By 2021 the total had risen to 21,192,000, and Chengdu gained more people than any other Chinese city. For reference, the OECD put the metropolitan population at 18.1 million in 2015.
China Daily named Chengdu the fourth most livable city in China in 2006. The city's cultural heritage runs deep, as the sections below show.

Some of China's most important literature has Chengdu roots. Famous figures linked to the city include Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, masters of the Fu, a mix of descriptive prose and verse; Li Bai and Du Fu, two of China's most eminent classical poets; the Ming scholar Yang Shen'an; and the modern writers Guo Moruo and Ba Jin. History writing began early here: Chang Qu, a Jin dynasty historian, wrote the earliest local chronicle, the Record of Hua Yang State. Under the Later Shu Kingdom the poet Zhao Chongzuo edited Among the Flowers, which was the first anthology of Ci poetry in Chinese history, and the king himself, Meng Chang, is credited with the first Spring Festival couplet: 'A harvest year accepts celebrations, good festivals foreshadow long springs.'
In modern times the city staged the 81st World Science Fiction Convention in 2023, having beaten Winnipeg, Canada, in the 2021 site-selection vote.

Chengdu also has a place in art history. In the Five Dynasties period the local painter Huang Quan and his colleagues began the school of fine-brush flower-and-bird painting. The Hanlin Painting Academy of that time was the earliest royal art academy in China.

southwestern-university-of-finance-and-e.h: Sichuan opera, language and daily speech

blocks.x: Local pride in the stage is summed up in a proverb that Shu opera towers above every other performance in the world. It speaks to the achievements of Sichuan opera and of Zaju, an ancient comic drama blending dance, singing, poetry and mime. The city's first opera, 'Bullfighting', was composed in the Warring States period, and in the Three Kingdoms period the royal court of the Shu Kingdom staged the first detailed opera. The first clearly documented Zaju in China was also performed in Chengdu, and archaeologists have dug up tombs of witty Han dynasty poets here. Face-changing masks and fire breathing remain Sichuan opera's trademarks.
People in Chengdu speak Chengdu dialect, a variety of Sichuanese, and it has left a mark on Chinese comedy and rap music.

The signature of Sichuan cooking is hot chili and numbing peppercorns. Mapo doufu, Dan Dan Mien and Chengdu hot pot are the famous local dishes, and Sichuan pepper goes into the first two. UNESCO has recognised Chengdu as a City of Gastronomy. Hot pot is a traditional Sichuanese dish in which vegetables, fish or meat cook in a boiling, spicy broth. It is ideal for sharing with friends, loved by residents and visitors, and hot pot restaurants are scattered across the city.

Tea has been part of Chengdu life for over a thousand years, back to when the city was the departure point of the Southern Silk Road. Tea houses are found everywhere, from richly decorated traditional ones with bamboo furniture to plain modern ones. Menus feature jasmine, longjing and biluochun. Customers come to play mahjong, get a massage or have their ears cleaned, and some of the larger houses stage live shows such as Sichuan opera.

The city has a laid-back image: in 2006 the Los Angeles Times labelled it the country's 'party city' for its carefree way of life. It has more tea houses and bars than Shanghai even though its population is less than half as large. Figures for 2023 show over 30,000 tea houses and 3,566 licensed bars, nightclubs and dance halls, and a 2019 statistical report put Chengdu ahead of Shanghai for bars, making it the Chinese city with the most.

Islam has a long history in Sichuan, going back to the Tang dynasty (618 to 907). Chengdu has 12 mosques, and the Huangcheng Mosque in the middle of the city dates to the 16th century. There are official Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations as well, and some of the churches operate underground.

Catholic organisation goes back to 15 October 1696, when the Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan (today the Diocese of Chengdu) was founded. Its first Apostolic Vicar was Artus de Lionne, a French missionary from the Paris Foreign Missions Society.

The Protestant story begins a few centuries later. The Canadian Methodist Mission wanted more stations in Asia in 1890, and at a meeting in February 1891 Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart proposed Chengtu (the then spelling) for its first one. Hart had earlier overseen the New York Methodist Mission Society of Central China and had built western-style hospitals and schools for boys and girls at missions along the Yangtze and Gan Rivers between 1866 and 1888, so it was suggested that he lead the party. He arrived in Chengtu on 9 May 1891 and, two weeks later, bought a house and divided it into living space and a dispensary for the missionaries who would come after him.

On 24 June 1892 the first Protestant mission headquarters in the city opened its doors with over 1,000 townspeople present. The first Methodist service, the following Sunday, drew only a handful. The first western-style dispensary in Sichuan began work on 3 November 1892, with sixteen patients coming for treatment. It proved so popular that a bigger plot near the East Gate was obtained in spring 1893, and on it were built the Sï-Shen-Tsï Methodist Church, the city's first Methodist church, and a hospital.

Both buildings were wrecked by rioters in 1895, and the staff fled to Chongqing and then Shanghai. Hart went to Peking to press for redress, and Sichuan Viceroy Liu Ping Chang paid the full compensation. The compound went up again quickly but was destroyed once more during the 1901 riots, and was rebuilt a second time. Missionaries who came later moved the boys' and girls' schools to a larger site just south of the city, and in 1914 the Divinity College there was dedicated as Hart College. It became part of West China Union University, which is now Sichuan University, and of the West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida). The Cultural Revolution left the Sï-Shen-Tsï church building unused. The nearby Chengdu City Second People's Hospital took charge of it and turned the chapel into a kindergarten and an office for its equipment department, returning it to the church only in 1984.

Relations between unregistered congregations and the state can be tense. In December 2018 the authorities moved against the Early Rain Covenant Church, an unregistered congregation of some 500 people led by Pastor Wang Yi. Over a hundred members, including the pastor and his wife, were detained, and the church's kindergarten and theological college were searched and its media outlets closed. Police reportedly told one member that the church had been declared an illegal organisation. Chinese media were barred from reporting, and the leaders appear to have been charged with 'inciting subversion of state power', for which the maximum sentence is 15 years. Accounts reaching foreign social media included video and photographs, and coverage inside China was restricted.
A Chabad Jewish Center was established in 2012; it moved five times before settling permanently in Wuhou District.
A business zone that began in 1992 as the Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone is now the Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park.
Five national highways reach Chengdu. G5 runs Beijing to Kunming, G42 links Shanghai and Chengdu, G76 links Xiamen and Chengdu, G93 forms the Chengdu-Chongqing Ring, and G4202 is the Chengdu Ring.
Southwestern University of Finance and Economics lists 205 programs for international students on this site: 36 bachelor, 60 master's, 42 doctoral, 67 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 164 taught in Chinese, 41 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

205 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
