The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

southwestern-university-of-finance-and-e.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Southwestern University of Finance and Economics may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Chengdu, register at Southwestern University of Finance and Economics by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Sun Yat-sen University, known by its initials SYSU (Zhongshan Daxue in Chinese), is a state-run university based in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province in the far south of China. Its parent body is the Ministry of Education, and its funding is shared between that ministry, the national defence science and technology authority (SASTIND) and the Guangdong provincial government. In national terms it belongs to the leading tier: it has been part of Project 211 and Project 985 and now sits within the Double First-Class Construction programme.

The school dates from 1924 and bears the name of Sun Yat-sen, the man who led the revolution that created the Republic of China. Its home base, called the South Campus, is in Guangzhou's Haizhu District, on land that once belonged to Lingnan University (established 1888). Across the whole university there are five campuses in three cities (Guangzhou, Zhuhai and Shenzhen) and ten affiliated hospitals. A centennial conference on 12 November 2024 marked the hundredth anniversary and unveiled a set of future initiatives.

If you are an overseas applicant, the take-away is that SYSU is big, research-driven and spread over several sites, with medicine as a particular strength. Before you accept an offer, find out which campus your programme uses. The rest of this profile covers the university's history, rankings, structure, campuses and alumni, and then the city of Guangzhou.

Today's SYSU did not grow in a straight line. Over the decades more than a dozen colleges were merged into it, split off from it or reorganised around it. The name itself came out of a wave of universities that tried to teach in line with Sun Yat-sen's political ideas. The latest big combination happened in 2001, when the separate medical university carrying the Sun Yat-sen name was brought into the main university and turned into its College of Medical Science.

Sun Yat-sen opened National Kwangtung University in Canton (the old Western spelling of Guangzhou) in 1924. He chose the motto and wrote it out by hand: a five-part call to study widely, ask precisely, think carefully, judge clearly and act sincerely. When he died, the government set up under the first Communist-Nationalist alliance ordered on 17 July 1926 that the university be renamed National Sun Yat-sen University as a tribute.

In 1926 there were really four universities with that title. The Canton one is the ancestor of SYSU. The Wuhan one became Wuhan University and the Hangzhou one became Zhejiang University. The one in Nanjing was the forerunner of three later institutions: National Central University, Southeast University and Nanjing University. A fifth was intended for Zhengzhou, but it was called Henan Provincial Sun Yat-sen University, and it is now Henan University.

During the 1930s the Canton university had seven schools: education, medicine, agriculture, engineering, law, science and arts. In 1935, alongside Peking and Tsinghua, it opened one of the first graduate schools in China and began recruiting postgraduates. The prefix National disappeared in 1949, leaving the plain name Sun Yat-sen University. Across the 1950s the government redrew the map of Chinese higher education, and SYSU came out as a leading comprehensive university built around arts and sciences.

The medical side has a long story. One forerunner, the Pok Tsai Medical School of 1866, is said to be the first place in China to teach Western medicine, and Sun Yat-sen both studied there and carried out revolutionary activity. In 1936 that school became the medical college of Lingnan University. Another forerunner was the Kung Yee Medical School and Hospital, founded in Canton in 1908. The government took over Kung Yee in 1925 and made it the medical department of National First Sun Yat-sen University.

After 1953, when the medical colleges of Sun Yat-sen and Lingnan universities were combined into the College of Medicine of South China, the Guangdong Guanghua College of Medicine came in (1954). The school was renamed more than once: Guangzhou College of Medicine, then Sun Yat-sen College of Medical Science, and in 1985 Sun Yat-sen University of Medical Science. It turned into a multi-school medical university working at national level, with strong output in medical genetics, eye disease, tumour research, parasitology, kidney medicine, transplantation, infectious liver disease, biomedical engineering and molecular medicine. The 2001 merger brought it back under the SYSU umbrella.

Lingnan University was a private college founded in 1888 in Guangzhou by Dr Andrew Happer with a group of American missionaries. Its first name was Canton Christian College. A medical centre linked to the same circles had been created by the female medical missionary Mary H. Fulton (1854-1927), sent out by the Presbyterian Church (USA) mission board and supported by a Brooklyn congregation, the Lafayette Avenue Presbyterian Church, whose minister was David Gregg. Its two parts were the Hackett Medical College for Women, which was China's first women's medical college, and the David Gregg Hospital for Women and Children. The college opened formally in 1902 with a four-year course. In late 1932 the Chinese government took over its registration and control, and by 1936 the centre had joined with Guangzhou Hospital and Lingnan to make up the Sun Yat-Sen Medical College.

The communist authorities ordered Lingnan to be merged into Sun Yat-sen University in 1953. Some Lingnan people went to Hong Kong, started the Lingnan School in Wan Chai in 1967, moved it to Tuen Mun in the mid-1990s and renamed it Lingnan University in 1999. In Guangzhou, a new Lingnan College appeared inside SYSU in 1988 and is regarded today as one of China's best schools for economics and management.

Every major global league table places SYSU among China's best, though the number depends on the year and the publisher. Back in 2015 it was seventh in China in the Times Higher Education table, sixth in the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) and eighth in U.S. News. The 2011 Times Higher Education list had it at 171 worldwide and fifth in China, and that publisher's reputation survey put it at 151 in the world. The QS graduate employability table gave it 191.

Newer results are from 2026. ARWU lists it 62nd worldwide, tenth in Asia and seventh in China. U.S. News has it 74th in the world, fifteenth in Asia and eighth in China, while the Center for World University Rankings shows 81st in the world, thirteenth in Asia and seventh in China. The 2025 Leiden Ranking from CWTS puts the university seventh worldwide for the number of publications and twenty-sixth for papers in the top one per cent of their fields between 2020 and 2023.

The Nature Index records high-quality science papers by affiliation and updates monthly. In the 2024 results, SYSU was the seventh-best university in Asia Pacific and eighth among universities worldwide for research output.

Some earlier measures are still cited. From January 2003 to February 2013, the Essential Science Indicators database showed SYSU with fifteen subject areas in the top one per cent for citations. Only Peking University did better among Chinese universities; SYSU shared second place with Fudan, Shanghai Jiao Tong and Zhejiang. Those fields were chemistry, clinical medicine, physics, biology and biochemistry, materials science, molecular biology and genetics, engineering, plant and animal science, environment and ecology, pharmacology and toxicology, neuroscience and behaviour, mathematics, microbiology, agriculture and general social sciences.

A second measure, the Nature Publishing Index, counts articles and reviews in Nature and its sister journals during a rolling year. Between 7 January 2013 and 30 June 2014 SYSU stood fifth among Chinese universities. If you hope to build a research career, note that the university runs 39 postdoctoral research stations.

The academic structure has been revised repeatedly. Since the end of 2022 there are three levels, namely the university, its faculties, and the schools or departments within them. Right now there are 65 schools and directly affiliated teaching units, grouped under seven faculties: Humanities, Social Sciences, Economics and Management, Natural Sciences, Engineering, Information Science and Technology, and Medicine. The units are scattered across all five campuses, so an offer letter should always be read together with the campus location.

Lingnan (University) College, the business and economics school that descends from the missionary university, has carried accreditation from AACSB, EQUIS and AMBA since 2015. These three together are often called triple accreditation, and they are an international quality signal for management programmes.

SYSU says it has the biggest group of affiliated hospitals of any Chinese university. The roster comprises the First Hospital (into which the Fourth Hospital has been absorbed), the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital (known as the Second), the Third Hospital, the Fifth Hospital in Zhuhai, the Sixth Hospital for gastrointestinal and anal disease, the Cancer Center, the Stomatologic Hospital, the Ophthalmologic Center, and the Seventh and Eighth Hospitals in Shenzhen. The eight general hospitals together with the Cancer Center and the eye centre are rated Grade 3A, the highest grade in China.

The First Affiliated Hospital opened in 1910 as the Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Public Institution of Medicine. It is the most comprehensive hospital in the system and among the largest in China, and a national list puts it second among general hospitals.

The Memorial Hospital (Second Hospital) goes back to 1835, when the American Peter Parker founded an eye hospital in Canton. It began with eye disease, then widened its scope, and was later known as the Canton Hospital.

The Cancer Center is a top-grade Class A hospital. It was listed as a national key subject in 2001, became a World Health Organization Collaborating Center for cancer research in 1980, and has been a sister institution of MD Anderson Cancer Center at the University of Texas since 2003. In 2004 it opened a shared laboratory with Sweden's Karolinska Institutet for immunotherapy, molecular virology and cancer epidemiology. National rankings place it first among cancer hospitals.

The Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center was China's first leading eye hospital and acts as the last stop for the hardest eye cases in the country. Treatment, teaching, research and prevention of blindness all happen there, and it counts among the twenty biggest general eye centres in the world. Since 2006 it has housed the State Key Laboratory of Ophthalmology, which is unique in China, and national rankings give it first place among eye hospitals.

The university library system is one of the largest in the country, with over six million paper volumes (periodicals included) in December 2012. In June 2005 Harvard College Library gave SYSU the 158,000 volumes of its Hilles Library. The collection took a century to assemble. It concentrates on humanities and social science, chiefly in English, with some titles in other Western languages.

SYSU also publishes 25 academic journals. They include Acta Scientiarum Naturalium Universitatis Sunyatseni, the university journal in its social science and medical editions, Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology, Modern Clinical Nursing, New Medicine, Chinese Journal of Nervous and Mental Diseases, Chinese Journal of Cancer and Eye Science. A number of them are published in Chinese.

Since 2006 SYSU has opened five Confucius Institutes with partners overseas: at Ateneo de Manila University, at the Autonomous University of Yucatan, at the University of Cape Town, in Indianapolis with Indiana University-Purdue University Indianapolis, and in Lyon with the universities Lyon 2 (Lumiere) and Lyon 3 (Jean Moulin).
SYSU occupies 6.17 square kilometres (2.38 square miles) in total. Three campuses are in Guangzhou, one is in Zhuhai and one is in Shenzhen. They differ a lot in size, age and subject focus.
Guangzhou South Campus (Haizhu District): 1.17 square kilometres, the historic centre, with mainly science and humanities.
Guangzhou North Campus (Yuexiu District): 0.39 square kilometres, mostly medical sciences.

Guangzhou East Campus: 1.13 square kilometres in Xiaoguwei, Panyu, in the northern part of the Guangzhou Higher Education Mega Center (University City). The provincial government built that centre as part of a drive to develop Guangdong through science and education, and the first students arrived in September 2004.

Zhuhai Campus: 3.48 square kilometres at Tang Jia Wan, Zhuhai. First- and second-year students in certain arts, natural science and medical programmes study there, together with students from the School of Network Education and Continuing Education.
Shenzhen Campus: 3.217 square kilometres in Guangming District, Shenzhen. Building started in 2016 and it welcomed students in September 2018, so it is the newest site.

At least 36 billionaires have graduated from SYSU since 2017, making it first in South Central China and seventh in the country by that measure. The people listed here show how wide its alumni reach is, across politics, finance, science, art and sport.

George Chann, painter in the Chinese-American community
Fang Fenglei, banker who held a senior post at China International Capital Corporation and chaired Goldman Sachs China

Xu Yinchuan, once the world champion of xiangqi, Chinese chess

Yingying Zhang, who studies photosynthesis and crop yields

sun-yat-sen-university.h: Guangzhou: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Most of your daily life as a student depends on the city rather than the campus alone, so here is a briefing on Guangzhou: its land, weather, economy and people.

Guangzhou began close to Baiyun Mountain, on the eastern side of the Pearl River (Zhujiang). The old town was around 130 kilometres inland from the South China Sea and some 300 miles downstream of the head of navigation. From there it controlled the fertile river-delta plain, with the Humen Strait protecting the route to the sea. Now the city's 7,434.4 square kilometres straddle the river, between longitudes 112 degrees 57 minutes and 114 degrees 03 minutes east and latitudes 22 degrees 26 minutes and 23 degrees 56 minutes north, in the south centre of Guangdong. The Pearl is China's fourth-largest river. Mudflats line its estuary, although many have been drained for agriculture. Baiyun Mountain is called the city's lung (shifei in Chinese), the green space that lets a huge city breathe.
Terrain climbs from the southwest toward the northeast, with mountains behind and the sea in front. Tiantang Peak, at 1,210 metres, is the high point.

With so many rivers and channels, water covers about a tenth of the land: 74,400 hectares, or 10.05 per cent. Major waterways include the Beijiang, the north mainstream of the Dongjiang, the Zengjiang, the Liuxi, the Baini, the Guangzhou reach of the Pearl, the Shiqiao and the Shawan. The Beijiang and Dongjiang pass through the city and merge with the Pearl before reaching the sea.

Locally generated water is modest but what flows through the city is plentiful. The local total is 7.979 billion cubic metres, of which 7.881 billion is surface water and 1.487 billion groundwater. Based on the 2010 census, that works out to 1.0601 million cubic metres per square kilometre and 628 cubic metres per person, about half the national average. Water in transit is 23 times larger, at 186.024 billion cubic metres, and it is concentrated in the south and in Zengcheng District. Of that, 159.15 billion cubic metres is brought in from the Xijiang and Beijiang, 14.203 billion from the Dongjiang into its north mainstream, and 2.828 billion from the upper Zengjiang. The southern river network is strongly tidal. The Pearl leaves through three mouths (Humen, Jiaomen and Hongqili) into the Lingding Ocean and out to the South China Sea. The yearly flood tide brings 271 billion cubic metres and the ebb tide 408.8 billion, while the three mouths discharge 137.7 billion; a share of the tidal water is usable fresh water. The source figures are not entirely consistent, so quote them only as rough guides.

Guangzhou's geology is intricate, and 47 kinds of minerals have been recorded at 820 sites, among them 18 large and medium-sized oil deposits. Common ones are building granite, cement-grade limestone, ceramic clay, potassium, sodium feldspar, salt, mirabilite, manganese, nepheline syenite, fluorite, marble, mineral water and hot-spring water. Fuel and non-ferrous metals are short and thinly scattered, with unstable grades.

Because the climate sits between tropical and subtropical, farming is varied. Guangzhou is among the richest fruit regions in China, with temperate, subtropical and tropical species: 41 families, 82 genera, 174 species and over 500 varieties, including 55 main lychee types. It is the original home of several lychee, longan, yellow skin and olive varieties. Vegetables cover 15 categories, 127 species and 370-plus varieties. Cut flowers, potted plants, bonsai, seedlings, edible and medicinal flowers, lawns, grain, cash crops, livestock, poultry, fish and wild animals are all part of local production, and Zengcheng Simiao rice was the first Guangzhou product to receive protection as a geographical indication.

Though just south of the Tropic of Cancer, Guangzhou is humid subtropical (Koppen Cwa) under the East Asian monsoon. Expect hot, humid, wet summers and mild, fairly dry winters. The monsoon lasts from April to September. January averages 13.8 degrees C and July 28.9 degrees C, with a yearly mean of 22.4 degrees C. From October to December the weather is mild, breezy and cool, which makes it the most comfortable season for visitors. Humidity averages around 76 per cent and urban rainfall tops 1,950 millimetres a year.

The sun does not shine often: possible sunshine is 17 per cent in March and 51 per cent in October, and the total of 1,559 hours is clearly below Shenzhen or Hong Kong. Official extremes since 1951 reach down to 0 degrees C (11 February 1957 and 23 December 1999) and up to 39.1 degrees C (1 July 2004). Unofficial older readings include minus 5 degrees C on 18 January 1893, a figure modern meteorologists think was actually closer to minus 3, and minus 0.3 degrees C at a Huangpu District station on 8 December 1934. The last snow fell on 24 January 2016, 87 years after the snowfall before it. In short, bring light clothes, an umbrella and a plan for humidity; winter coats are rarely needed.

Guangzhou is the chief manufacturing centre of the Pearl River Delta, one of the country's strongest commercial and industrial belts. Its 2021 GDP was 2,823 billion yuan (444.37 billion US dollars), the second-biggest in South-Central China behind Shenzhen, or 151,162 yuan (23,794 dollars) per person. It is seen as one of China's richest cities. Hurun's 2020 Global Rich List put it tenth worldwide for billionaires and fifth in China, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Oxford Economics expects it to join Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen in the world's top ten by nominal GDP in 2035, with GDP per head above 42,000 dollars by 2030. It was 21st in the 2020 Global Financial Centers Index, between Washington, D.C. and Amsterdam, and eighth across Asia and Oceania. Fast industrial growth once left the city fairly polluted, but green planning has made it one of the more liveable Chinese cities today.
Zhujiang New Town is the twenty-first-century business district, 6.44 square kilometres in Tianhe District, with many financial firms headquartered there.

Each April and October the Canton Fair (China Import and Export Fair) takes place under the Ministry of Trade. Started in spring 1957, it is the oldest, biggest and highest-level trade fair in China. From the 104th session it left the older Liuhua complex for the new Guangzhou International Convention and Exhibition Center in Pazhou, reachable by two Line 8 stations, one Line 11 station and three stops on Tram Line THZ1. It has also run in three phases instead of two since then.

Local specialities include Cantonese food, one of China's best-known cuisines (the old saying is to eat in Guangzhou), carvings in jade, wood and, controversially, ivory, Canton export porcelain with its bright colours, Cantonese embroidery, one of China's four main embroidery traditions, and Zhujiang Beer, a successful pale lager.

Notable industry sites are the carmaker GAC Group, the Guangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone and Guangzhou Science City. The Nansha Export Processing Zone started in 2005 on 1.36 square kilometres in Nansha District and encourages car assembly, biotechnology and heavy industry; it lies 54 kilometres, or 70 minutes' drive, south of Baiyun International Airport near Nansha Port, and Metro Line 4 is being extended to the Nansha ferry terminal. The Guangzhou Free Trade Zone was set up in 1992 in eastern Huangpu District, next to the development zone and the airport, for trade, logistics, processing and software. The district is now marketed under the Huangpu name and has added new energy, AI, new mobility, new materials, communications technology and transport, and it houses the Guangzhou IP Court.

For business, Guangzhou is an international crossroads: by 2018 it had more than 30,000 foreign-invested firms, among them 297 Fortune Global 500 companies with projects and 120 using the city for their headquarters or regional headquarters.

Guangzhou had 18.978 million permanent residents at the end of 2024, and 87.24 per cent live in urban areas. At the Seventh National Census (1 November 2020) the count was 18,676,605, an increase of 5,975,805 (47.05 per cent) on the 12,700,800 of 2010, with 16,096,724 city dwellers (86.19 per cent) and 2,579,881 rural residents (13.81 per cent). The census also found 11,522,907 people living away from their registered home, 9,378,825 of whom belong to the floating population, which makes Guangzhou one of China's largest destinations for migrants.

A 2014 estimate gave 13,080,500 people, including 11,264,800 urban residents, about 1,800 per square kilometre. The city's built-up area blends into neighbouring cities. The built-up Pearl River Delta zone covers about 17,573 square kilometres and about 22 million people, taking in nine Guangzhou urban districts, Shenzhen (5.36 million), Dongguan (3.22 million), Zhongshan (3.12 million), most of Foshan (2.2 million), Jiangmen (1.82 million), Zhuhai (890,000) and Huiyang District of Huizhou (760,000). Adding Hong Kong takes the total above 28 million. Because the economy is growing fast and needs workers, up to 10 million migrants live in the zone for at least six months each year, and around five million of Guangzhou's residents in 2008 were migrant workers. The OECD put the wider metropolitan area at 25 million in 2010.

Research by Gong and colleagues (2018) followed the city's growth from 1990 to 2020. In 1990 built-up housing areas were almost entirely in a small slice of western Guangzhou, surrounded by farms and forest. From 2005 other districts expanded, and the 2020 map shows continuous housing from west to east, while the south and much of the north remain farmland and forest.

High-speed catamarans run every day from the Nansha and Lianhuashan ferry terminals to the Hong Kong China Ferry Terminal, and from Nansha to the Macau ferry pier in Hong Kong, handy for a weekend trip.

Before modern times Guangzhou had around 124 religious halls, pavilions and temples. It now has Buddhist and Taoist associations, a Jewish community and a Christian history dating from the colonial period.

sun-yat-sen-university.h: Questions to settle before you accept an offer

blocks.x: A university with five campuses in three cities is really several study environments under one name. The facts above suggest a short checklist. First, ask which campus will host your programme and for how many years, because the figures differ widely: the Guangzhou South Campus is 1.17 square kilometres and mostly science and humanities, the North Campus is a compact 0.39 square kilometres focused on medicine, the East Campus sits inside University City, the Zhuhai Campus spreads over 3.48 square kilometres and takes some first- and second-year students, and the Shenzhen Campus has been open only since September 2018. Second, if your field is medicine, nursing, ophthalmology or cancer research, look at which affiliated hospital is attached to your programme, because the network is large and its members are specialised. Third, if you are interested in management or economics, check whether your course is taught at Lingnan College, since its AACSB, EQUIS and AMBA accreditation is a recognised mark of quality.

Remember also that the university has changed its structure as recently as the end of 2022. Programme names, schools and even campus assignments can shift, so the official website of SYSU and its admissions office are the final authority, not an overview like this one. The rankings quoted here come from different years and different organisations, which is why they disagree in detail while agreeing in broad terms: SYSU consistently appears among the top ten Chinese universities.

Guangzhou is a warm, wet, busy and international city. The monsoon season of April to September brings heat, humidity and heavy rain, so waterproofs and light, quick-drying clothes are sensible. Autumn, from October to December, is the pleasantest period, and a first visit to the campus is best planned then. Snow is almost unknown, so you will not need winter equipment.

Because the Guangzhou area merges with Shenzhen, Dongguan, Foshan, Zhongshan, Jiangmen, Zhuhai and Huizhou into one very large urban belt, a student can easily find a wide range of neighbourhoods, jobs and cultural experiences nearby. The same fact means crowds: the metropolitan area holds around 25 to 28 million people, and migrants make up a large share of residents, so you will be one of many newcomers rather than a rare outsider. The Canton Fair, the business district at Zhujiang New Town and the thousands of foreign-invested companies also mean there is a steady flow of international visitors, and that can help students who want exposure to trade and commerce.

Finally, the Zhuhai and Shenzhen campuses give students access to two other coastal cities, and the ferry links from Nansha and Lianhuashan to Hong Kong and Macau make short trips possible during breaks. Whichever campus you land on, take time to read the local transport details on the official university pages before you travel.

Several numbers in the city section come from different years, and some do not agree with each other, for example the two descriptions of mineral sites and the water statistics. Population figures also vary by source: the permanent population was 18,676,605 in the 2020 census and 18.978 million at the end of 2024, while older estimates of 13 million or so describe the city as it was in 2014. When you plan a budget, a visa or housing, rely on current official announcements from the university and the Guangzhou authorities, and treat the statistics here as a way of understanding scale and character rather than as exact current data.

taiyuan-university-of-technology.h: A science and engineering university in Shanxi

blocks.x: Taiyuan University of Technology (太原理工大学, known as TYUT) is a public university in Taiyuan, the capital of Shanxi Province, specialising in science and engineering. The Shanxi provincial government funds it and it belongs to the province. It is also part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction, two national schemes that single out leading universities.

The university traces its beginnings to the Western Learning School of the Shanxi Grand Academy, set up in 1902 and counted among the earliest modern universities in China. After more than a hundred years it has grown into a comprehensive university whose core is engineering, joined by the sciences and supported by a number of other disciplines.

TYUT has 23 colleges. They offer 84 undergraduate disciplines, 34 master's programmes, 15 doctoral programmes and 13 postdoctoral research centres. The student body numbers more than 30,000 undergraduates and 7,779 master's and doctoral students. The university has three national key disciplines, 13 provincial key disciplines and 12 provincially supported ones, which lead its research.

The workforce totals 3549 teaching and administrative staff, with 2178 of them full-time teachers. Among them are three members of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, one member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (an academician in each case), 244 supervisors of doctoral students and 1254 teachers with senior professional and technical titles. These counts date from a particular year, so ask the university for the latest.

The university's own periodicals include its flagship journal and a papers series named after the university, along with Coal Conversion, Shanxi Coal, the Journal of Systematic Dialectics and a social science journal.

Its guiding principle is to pursue practicality, create originality and serve the locality. More than 100,000 graduates have entered the workforce, and in 2004 the Ministry of Education named it an Excellent University for Undergraduate Education.

Research is strong in both technology development and applied science. TYUT twice in a row led a national 973 research project as the principal scientific unit, and it has also taken part in a national 863 high-tech project. Ministries and the province have given it a total of 434 prizes. One young teacher, Dou Yinke, was chosen to join China's 21st scientific expedition to Antarctica. Tiancheng Scien-tech Cooperation Ltd, the university's company, is the only one in the province that has been listed on the stock market.

More than 30 partner universities abroad work with TYUT, based in the US, Japan, Britain, Australia, Canada, Russia, Germany, France, India and Norway, to name some, and dozens of institutions in Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland collaborate with it on teaching and research.

Taiyuan stands on the Fen River, at the northern end of the river's fertile upper basin, in the middle of the province. It spans 144 km (89 miles) from east to west and 107 km (66 miles) from north to south. It controls the main north-south route through Shanxi and key natural passes: through the Taihang Mountains east into Hebei, and west towards northern Shaanxi.

The area is rich in minerals. Coal, iron ore, marble and silica are produced in large amounts, and there are also deposits of bauxite, limestone, graphite, quartz, phosphorus, gypsum, mica, copper and gold. To the west, the satellite city of Gujiao is the biggest source of metallurgical coal in China. Among trees, conifers dominate, including pines (among them white pine), spruce and cypress.

Taiyuan has a warm-temperate continental monsoon climate. It is classed as cold semi-arid (Koppen BSk): winters are long, dry and cold, summers hot and humid, spring and autumn short and windy, and the dry and wet seasons are clearly separated. Springs are dry and may bring dust storms, followed by early heat waves in summer. Most rain falls in July and August. Because of the dryness, temperatures swing widely between day and night, except in summer. The moderately high altitude keeps the city noticeably cooler than other cities at similar latitudes such as Shijiazhuang.

Average temperatures run from minus 4.7 degrees Celsius (23.5 F) in January up to 24.3 degrees (75.7 F) in July, and the yearly mean is 10.9 degrees (51.6 F). Sunshine accounts for 51 percent of possible hours in July and 61 percent in May, adding up to 2,493 hours a year. Since 1951 the temperature has ranged from minus 25.5 degrees (minus 13.9 F) to 39.4 degrees (102.9 F), and an unofficial minus 29.5 degrees (minus 21.1 F) was reported back on 7 January 1930, and that earlier reading is not part of the official series. Pack warm winter clothing and expect dry air, with some wind in spring.

taiyuan-university-of-technology.h: Land cover and the city's size

blocks.x: The municipality covers 6,988 square kilometres (2,698 square miles). In 2007 it had 146,700 hectares of forest and 422.5 square kilometres (163.1 square miles) of grassland, and forest cover in the six urban districts reached 21.69 percent by 2015.

Taiyuan suffered serious air pollution, particularly in the 1990s and the 2000s, and at one point appeared on lists of the world's ten most polluted cities. The situation has gradually improved as the public has become more aware and rules have become stricter and more detailed. In 2017 the city created a coal-free zone of 1,460 square kilometres, where most individuals and organisations may not buy, sell, store, carry, burn or use coal; in 2019 the city government widened it slightly, to 1,574 square kilometres. It is still sensible to check air-quality readings during the heating season.

The 2020 census counted 5,304,061 residents in the prefecture, which covers 6,959 square kilometres (2,687 square miles). The six urban districts, covering 1,460 square kilometres (560 square miles), were home to 4,529,141 of those people.

Taiyuan's economy grew steadily through the 2010s, in line with the national picture. Its GDP was 388.450 billion yuan in 2018, more than twice the 2010 figure. Disposable income per person was 31,031 yuan in 2018, up 7.2 percent on 2017. In 2015 the city imported goods worth 4,085.130 million US dollars and exported goods worth 6,592.250 million. Looking at sectors in 2007, agriculture was worth 3.9 billion yuan, industry 105.2 billion and services 132.2 billion. Coal is central: the province produces a quarter of the nation's output, and a coal trading exchange (the China Taiyuan Coal Transaction Center) began operating in the city in 2012.
Taiyuan is a significant transport hub in northern China. Highways link it to neighbouring provincial capitals, and flights serve most major Chinese cities and some overseas destinations.

The metro began operating in 2020, with Line 2 starting in December that year; Line 1 followed in February 2025. In early 2016 the city started replacing all of its 8,000 taxis with fully electric cars, beginning with the BYD e6, so most taxis you take may be electric.
Taiyuan Wusu International Airport is the main airport. Domestic services reach major cities including Beijing, Shanghai and Dalian, and there are some international flights.
Major roads include the G5, the G20 (with the Shitai Expressway), the G55, the G2001, the G307, the G108 and the G208.

High-speed lines through Taiyuan include Shijiazhuang-Taiyuan, Datong-Xi'an and Taiyuan-Jiaozuo. The 600 km (370 miles) to Beijing takes less than three hours by high-speed train. The main station is Taiyuan South. A conventional-speed railway, Taiyuan-Zhongwei-Yinchuan, opened in 2011 and provides a direct connection towards the west, serving western Shanxi, northern Shaanxi and Ningxia.

Basketball fans can watch the Shanxi Loongs, a Chinese Basketball Association team, at the Riverside Sports Arena. A former football club, Shanxi Metropolis, used to play at the Shanxi Sports Centre Stadium but no longer exists.

taiyuan-university-of-technology.h: Sights in and around the city

blocks.x: Taiyuan is mostly modern, with only a few historic buildings left in the centre. The surviving pieces of the old town are found near Wuyi Road and Fudong Street, to the north of that street and west of the central station.
The Shanxi Museum, on West Binhe Road downtown, is one of the largest museums in China and a main attraction.
The twin towers of Yongzuo Temple, southeast of the centre, appear on the city emblem and are seen as a symbol of Taiyuan.
Three central landmarks draw many visitors: Chongshan Monastery, and the parks of Longtan and Yingze.
In Jinyuan District, in the south, are Jinci Temple and Christ's Church, plus the Song-dynasty Flying Bridge Across the Fish Pond.

The Tianlongshan Grottoes lie along the West Mountain range. They were built up over centuries starting under the Northern Qi and contain thousands of Buddhist statues and works of art. The caves are damaged, and many sculptures are missing, with a number now held in museums around the world. In 2013 researchers at the University of Chicago began the Tianlongshan Caves Project to study and digitally image the caves and their sculptures.
Nearby, the Longshan Grottoes form a Taoist cave complex, and the eight main grottoes were carved between 1234 and 1239, in the Yuan dynasty.
Student life depends on the surrounding province too, so here is an outline of Shanxi's history.

In the Spring and Autumn period (about 770 to 481 BC), the state of Jin occupied what is now Shanxi. In 403 BC it split three ways into Han, Zhao and Wei, which some historians treat as the opening of the Warring States era (about 473 to 221 BC). By 221 BC all those states had fallen to Qin, which founded the Qin dynasty (221-206 BC).

The Han dynasty (206 BC to AD 220) governed Shanxi as Bingzhou. In the Sixteen Kingdoms period (304-439), when northern nomads invaded, control passed through several regimes, among them Later Zhao, Former Qin and the two Yan states. After them came the Xianbei kingdom of Northern Wei (386-534), whose early capital included Datong in the north of the province, and which later governed almost the whole of northern China.

The Tang dynasty (618-907) began in Taiyuan. From then on, Shanxi was known as Hedong, meaning east of the Yellow River. Shanxi was the birthplace, in 624, of Wu Zetian, who is among the very few women to have ruled China.

In the opening part of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (907-960), three of the five ruling houses came from Shanxi, and the single northern state among the Ten Kingdoms was also there. Military governors of Hedong brought down and founded dynasties in turn. Li Cunxu overthrew Later Liang (907-923) to found Later Tang (923-936). Shi Jingtang then overthrew Later Tang to found Later Jin, and Liu Zhiyuan founded Later Han once the Khitans had brought Later Jin down. When the fifth dynasty, Later Zhou, rose, the Hedong governor Liu Chong rebelled and set up his own state, Northern Han, in northern and central Shanxi, one of the Ten Kingdoms.

In return for help from the Khitans, Shi Jingtang handed them a slice of the north called the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, partly in northern Shanxi. Since the land lay on the Chinese side of the Great Wall, it caused the Song headaches over defence for roughly a century. Later Zhou's founder, Guo Wei, was an ethnic Han who had held a post under the Later Han, then led by Shatuo Turkic rulers, and took the throne by force. The dynasty was short-lived: the Song conquered it in 960.

In the early Northern Song (960-1127), the ceded prefectures stayed contested between the Song and the Liao. In 1127, after the Jingkang Incident in the Jin-Song wars, the Southern Song gave up all of north China, Shanxi included, to the Jurchen Jin (1115-1234). The Mongol Yuan did not make Shanxi a province, since they treated it as part of the empire's core. Only under the Ming (1368-1644) did it receive its present name and roughly its present borders, which matched those of the Tang-era Hedong Commandery.

Under the Qing (1644-1911), the province reached north beyond the Great Wall into Inner Mongolia, covering the area of modern Hohhot and overlapping with the territory of the Eight Banners and the Guihua Tumed banner. For centuries Shanxi was a hub of trade and banking, and its merchants were famous for their wealth. The well-preserved city of Pingyao, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shows how important the Qing-era economy was. That strength remained visible in the late Qing: when the court fled west after the Boxer Uprising, Empress Dowager Cixi stayed in Shanxi, and local officials and merchants gave large financial contributions.

After the founding of the People's Republic, land reform was carried out in Shanxi, and the county of Xiyang's Dazhai was promoted as a model farming brigade for the rest of the country; after the end of the Mao era, this model was discontinued, and the reform and opening-up policy let most farmers go back to working their own land. Shanxi also became one of the country's main bases for coal and heavy industry, a role reinforced through successive industrialisation and defence-planning phases.

The Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) disrupted the province's administration, schools and industry, and the Destroy the Four Olds campaign damaged its heritage, though the full extent is not measured. Heritage had also suffered in the preceding Great Leap Forward, when wood from some old buildings fed backyard furnaces, although how much is hard to say. Recorded losses include a mausoleum for the legendary Shun in Yuncheng, a pair of tall stone lions at the Guan Yu Temple in the same city, and over a hundred temples and sites in Taiyuan itself. Mount Wutai's Buddhist community was badly affected: the mountain had around 304 monks and nuns, of whom 239 were sent back to their home areas and 36 to supervised labour, and of 124 earlier temples just 63 survived into 1977, with under ten in fairly intact condition.

After economic reform began in the late 1970s, Shanxi diversified more slowly than the coastal regions because it relied heavily on coal and state-owned firms. Rapid coal expansion in the 1990s and 2000s brought growth but also problems, including industrial accidents, environmental damage and governance issues. Since then provincial authorities have been working on restructuring and diversifying the economy, although dependence on resources remains a structural challenge.
Shanxi has eight civil airports and 147,700 km of highways, of which 6,446 km are expressways. The rail network in service measures 6,489 km, of which 1,347 km is high-speed line.

Most residents are Han Chinese, with Mongol, Manchu and Hui minorities. Figures from 2004 gave a birth rate of 12.36 and a death rate of 6.11 per 1,000 inhabitants, with 105.5 men for every 100 women.

For a student, Taiyuan offers a university with a long engineering tradition, a cold, dry climate, improving air quality, good rail links to Beijing, and rich history close by. Details such as staff counts, programme numbers and transport lines change over time, so consult the university's own website for the latest.

taiyuan-university-of-technology.h: How to read the university's figures

blocks.x: Some terms need a short explanation. Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction are national programmes that give extra support to selected universities, so being included signals that the national authorities regard TYUT as a key institution in its field. The 973 and 863 projects mentioned in the research section are national research programmes, one for basic research and one for high technology. A national key discipline is a subject recognised for special support at national level, while a provincial one is recognised at the level of Shanxi.

The numbers of colleges, programmes, staff and students were recorded at specific times and are likely to have moved on. The same applies to the economic figures, the metro lines and the taxi programme. If you are comparing universities, treat them as a guide to scale and ask the university for the most current data.

Taiyuan is a dry, high-altitude city, so winters are bitterly cold and spring can be dusty and windy. Bring warm layers, lip balm and moisturiser, and keep an eye on the air-quality reports, especially in winter when heating raises pollution. Autumn and early summer are typically the most comfortable seasons, while July and August bring most of the rain.

Transport is straightforward for a city of this size: the new metro lines, plentiful electric taxis, an airport with domestic and some international flights, and a high-speed link to Beijing in under three hours. The surrounding province is full of heritage, from the merchant-banker town of Pingyao to the Buddhist cave temples near the city, so weekend trips can be rewarding and are easy to plan.

the-central-academy-of-drama.h: The Central Academy of Drama in a nutshell

blocks.x: The Central Academy of Drama (中央戏剧学院, Zhōngyāng Xìjù Xuéyuàn) is China's national public drama school, located in Beijing and run under the Ministry of Education. It belongs to the Double First-Class Construction programme. For anyone who dreams of acting, directing, stage design or writing for the theatre in China, it is the most famous address in the country. Chinese opinion holds it to be the country's top drama school. In the QS World University Rankings for Performing Arts (2021 edition) it came second in Asia and thirty-second worldwide.

The school's origins reach back to 1938. Mao Zedong, who was then Chairman of China, personally named the school, designed its emblem and wrote the characters for it. Today's academy resulted from merging earlier schools and took final shape in April 1950, under its first president, Ouyang Yuqian.

It absorbed three predecessors. One was the drama department of the Lu Xun Art Academy, a 1938 foundation in Yan'an. Another was the art school at North China University. The third was the National Drama College, founded in Nanjing in 1935.

The renaming from National Academy of Drama to "Central Academy of Drama" won formal approval from the Central People's Government's Government Affairs Council in January 1950, and the founding meeting followed on 2 April. At first the academy had a double task, teaching and also producing new work. So it opened with general courses lasting a year, soon added two-year undergraduate courses, and gave training to professional cadres at provincial and military level or higher, in order to lift professional standards. Its first units included an opera department, a drama department, a stage art department, general subjects, a dance and sports cadre training class and the Cui Chengxi dance research class.

From the summer of 1953 the departments began to recruit undergraduates from across the country. To make that possible the academy reorganised its professional structure and teaching system in a major way. It abolished the Opera Department. Out of the old Drama Department it created separate Performance, Directing, Stage Art and Drama Literature departments, and it also set up teaching and research groups for physical education, vocal music and other subjects.

As of October 2022, the academy has 16 undergraduate teaching units. Among them are the Humanities Department, the Basic Teaching Department and the Ideological and Political Theory Teaching and Research Department. The curriculum offers 11 undergraduate majors, divided into 27 major directions (international projects are not included in that count).

Plenty of famous performers and directors studied here. Gong Li, Zhang Ziyi, Jiang Wen, Wang Xingyue, Zhao Jinmai and Li Landi are some of them. The lists below show the entrance year, not the year of graduation, so a name under 1996 means that person began study that year.

The oldest names in the record entered in the 1950s and 1960s: Jin Yaqin (1950), Zheng Zhenyao (1954), Yan Shunkai (1959) and Wen Xingyu (1960). Then came Chen Baoguo and Guo Lianwen in 1974, and Chen Daoming in 1979.

The 1980s produced a remarkable run of screen stars. Jiang Wen, Lü Liping and Yue Hong entered in 1980, and Ni Dahong in 1982. The 1984 group includes Zhang Hanyu and Wu Xiubo. In 1985 the roll lists Gong Li, Jia Hongsheng, Wei Zi and Chen Wei. Chen Zhihui entered in 1986, and in 1987 Hu Jun and Xu Fan arrived.
