Your daily life as a student depends on the capital around the academy: how the city looks, where it sits, what the weather does and how clean the air is. The following sections describe Beijing, home of the Central Academy of Drama.

Three building styles define urban Beijing. First comes the imperial tradition, best shown by the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and above all the massive Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the People's Republic's trademark building. Second is the "Sino-Sov" manner of the 1950s to 1970s: boxy structures that are sometimes poorly built. Third is a far more modern group, visible above all in the Beijing CBD in the east (where the new CCTV Headquarters stands) and in other spots like the National Center for the Performing Arts and the Beijing National Stadium.

Since the start of the 21st century Beijing has seen a huge wave of construction, with international designers contributing various modern styles, especially in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone mixes 1950s industrial design with neofuturistic touches, so old and new stand together there. The tallest building in the city is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing towers have taken the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which honours the best tall building overall, twice since 2007: the Linked Hybrid in 2009 and CCTV Headquarters in 2013. The prize goes to one building worldwide each year.

A siheyuan is a courtyard home, with buildings around an open yard. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Alleys called hutongs link these courtyards together. Hutongs generally run straight from east to west, so doorways face north or south, which is considered good for Feng Shui. Their widths vary, and some are so tight that only a few pedestrians can squeeze through at once.

Once found everywhere in Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are vanishing quickly as whole blocks are replaced with high-rise buildings. Hutong residents have the right to move into new apartments at least as large as their old homes. Many still say that the traditional community feeling and street life cannot be replaced, and the properties concerned are often owned by the government.

Beijing sits on the northern edge of the North China Plain, a roughly triangular lowland that opens to the south and east. To the north, northwest and west, mountains protect the city and northern China's farming heartland from the advancing desert steppe. The Jundu Mountains dominate the northwest of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou districts, and the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall in the north of the municipality was built on this rugged terrain to hold off nomadic raiders from the steppe. Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, is the municipality's highest point at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Major rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma all belong to the Hai River system and flow southeast. The Miyun Reservoir, upstream on the Chaobai, is the municipality's largest reservoir. Beijing is also the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, built more than 1,400 years ago as a transport route, and of the South-North Water Transfer Project, built in the past decade to bring in water from the Yangtze River basin.

The urban area occupies a fairly small but growing part of the municipality, on plains in the south-centre at 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. Ring roads radiate outward in concentric circles. The Second Ring Road traces where the old city walls stood, and the Sixth Ring Road links the satellite towns of the suburbs. Right at the heart, directly south of the Forbidden City (where China's emperors once lived), are Tian'anmen and its Square. West of Tian'anmen lies Zhongnanhai, where the current leaders live, and Chang'an Avenue, which passes between Tiananmen and the Square, is the city's main east-west axis.
The way Beijing has grown outward from its old core is commonly called "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), and people often blame this pattern for urban problems.

The climate is humid continental (Köppen Dwa), shading into a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid, while the huge Siberian anticyclone shapes winters that are short, cold and dry. In spring, sandstorms can blow in from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, together with fast warming and generally dry weather. Autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with little rain. From 2001 to 2026 the hottest time of year in Beijing has been early August and the coldest early January.

Under the Chinese seasonal standard, the calendar runs like this: spring from 26 March, summer from 20 May, autumn from 13 September, winter from 31 October. March and September have warmed faster lately while May and October have warmed more slowly, so autumn tends to be shorter than spring.

Here are the 1991 to 2020 normals. In the urban area, the year-round mean runs between 12.9 and 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F). Nights average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and afternoons reach 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). Low-lying suburbs are a little cooler: the mean is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). In the mountains, temperatures fall as altitude rises, and the yearly mean sits between 0 and 10 °C (32 to 50 °F).

In January the daily mean is -2.7 °C (27.1 °F), and in July, 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Yearly precipitation is around 528.0 mm (20.79 in) on average, rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and about three-quarters of it comes between June and August. Possible sunshine ranges from 42 per cent in July to 62 per cent in January and February, giving 2,490.5 hours of sunshine a year. Since 1951 the lowest reading has been -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), on 22 February 1966, while the highest was 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), on 24 July 1999.

the-central-academy-of-drama.h: Why the city struggles with pollution

blocks.x: Environmental problems in Beijing have a long history. Between 2000 and 2009 the urban area quadrupled, which not only greatly increased human emissions but also altered the local weather, even without counting those emissions. Near the ground, humidity, wind speed and surface albedo declined; ground and near-ground air temperatures, vertical air dilution and ozone all increased. Urban growth together with pollution from burning fossil fuel means that Beijing is often hit by serious environmental trouble that harms many residents' health.

In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and most of northern China, affecting 600 million people altogether. This "pollution shock" turned air pollution into an important economic and social concern across China. The Beijing government then announced anti-pollution measures, such as cutting coal's share of energy from 24 per cent in 2012 to 10 per cent by 2017. Nationally, heavily polluting vehicles were ordered off roads between 2015 and 2017, and the switch to clean energy sources was stepped up.

the-central-academy-of-drama.h: Where the dirty air comes from

blocks.x: American and Chinese researchers working together in 2006 found that a large part of Beijing's pollution is imported from neighbouring cities and provinces: between 35 and 60 per cent of ozone, on average, is traced to sources outside the city. Shandong Province and Tianjin both strongly affect Beijing's air, partly because summer winds blow mainly from the south or southeast and the mountains lie to the north and northwest.

Nearly US$17 billion went on keeping promises to clear the air before the 2008 Summer Olympics. For the Games' duration, many air improvement schemes were introduced. Construction sites stopped work, many Beijing factories were closed for good, industry in neighbouring regions was shut temporarily, and some gas stations closed. It also assembled a fleet of 3,800 buses running on natural gas, among the largest anywhere, and was the first Chinese city to demand the national equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Coal burning produces about 40 per cent of Beijing's PM 2.5 and is the main source of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012 and aims to limit coal use to 20 million tons a year. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73 per cent of it for heating and power and the rest for industry.

Much of the pollution comes from the neighbouring regions. Coal use in Tianjin was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. In 2011 Hebei burned more than 300 million tons, which exceeds the whole of Germany, with just 30 per cent used for power and much of the rest for steel and cement. Beijing's air is also affected by power stations in Shandong and in the coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where consumption has tripled since 2000. Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces for coal consumption.

Beijing once had four major coal-fired power plants providing electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant shut in 2014 and two others in March 2015; the final one, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was set to go in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was to reduce coal use by 13 million tons, holding it to 15 million tons in 2015.

Sometimes the authorities seed clouds to raise the chance of rain showers and clear the air before major events, such as the parade for the 60th anniversary in 2009, or to fight drought. Lately, however, they have relied more on temporary factory closures and tighter restrictions on cars. The results were "APEC blue" and "parade blue": brief clear spells during and immediately before the APEC China 2014 summit and the China Victory Day Parade of 2015. Air quality improved dramatically around those events but returned to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, which closed most industry and commercial business in the city. A "red alert" followed later that month. The city's environmental protection bureau announced in November 2016 that from 2017 old, high-polluting cars could not be driven whenever a smog red alert is in force, whether in the city or in nearby regions.

Measurable falls in pollutants followed the declaration of a "war on pollution" in 2014. Fine particulates dropped 35 per cent in 2017 and fell further by 2020. The main causes were switching from coal power to natural gas and cleaning up polluting factories around Beijing. The yearly average PM2.5 concentration dropped to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024 Beijing had just two days of heavy pollution, a record low and 96.6 per cent below 2013's total of 58 days.

Because pollution is high, different sources report different numbers. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) website gives daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city, and the US Embassy in Beijing posts hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants by different criteria, so the BJEPB readings and health impacts are often lower than the embassy's. Smog harms the population: air pollution has a direct and significant effect on cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart problems, emergency visits and even death. Check an app each morning, and wear a mask on the worst days.

Desert erosion in northern and northwestern China produces seasonal dust storms that trouble Beijing. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rainfall artificially to fight them and reduce their effects. No fewer than eight such storms came in just the first four months of 2006. One storm in April 2002 left nearly 50,000 tons of dust over the city and then carried on toward Korea and Japan.
The Central Academy of Drama lists 24 programs for international students on this site: 6 bachelor, 2 master's, 1 doctoral, 15 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 24 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 36,000 to CNY 36,000 (median CNY 36,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 42,000 to CNY 42,000 (median CNY 42,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 46,000 to CNY 46,000 (median CNY 46,000), according to the university's published fee table.

23 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

the-central-academy-of-drama.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. The Central Academy of Drama may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at The Central Academy of Drama by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Tiangong University (天津工业大学, literally "Tianjin Industrial University") is a public university that belongs to the municipality of Tianjin. The city government sponsors it. It stands in Xiqing District and belongs to the Double First-Class Construction programme. Until 2019 it used the English name Tianjin Polytechnic University, even though its Chinese name had not changed, so older documents and rankings may use that title.

Its origins lie in 1958, when it opened as the Hebei Textile Institute (河北纺织工学院). Reorganisations followed, and the present Chinese name has been used since 2000. At present the university is made up of fourteen colleges and has two campuses within Tianjin. Hedong District holds the original campus, and the newer one is in Xiqing.
The schools fall into engineering, science, social science and arts groups:
Textiles and materials: School of Textiles Science and Engineering, and School of Materials Science and Engineering

Engineering and technology: Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Automation, Electronics and Information Engineering, Environmental and Chemical Engineering, and Computer Science and Technology
Science: School of Science and School of Life Sciences
Business, law and humanities: Economics, Management, Laws and Humanities
Arts: School of Arts
International and graduate education: School of International Education, which handles overseas students, and the School of Graduate
If you are an international applicant, the School of International Education is the natural first point of contact.

Life as a student depends on the city outside the campus: how cold or hot it gets, how you travel and what you can do in your free time. The following sections introduce Tianjin, the home of Tiangong University.

Tianjin sits on the western shore of the Bohai Gulf, with the provinces of Shandong and Liaoning on the opposite side of the water. Beijing is the neighbour 120 kilometres (75 miles) to the northwest. Except for its eastern edge, which is the Bohai Sea, the city is wrapped on all sides by Hebei Province. Its latitude range is 38°34′ to 40°15′ north, its longitude range is 116°43′ to 118°04′ east, and it covers 11,860.63 square kilometres (4,579.41 square miles) in all.

The coastline is 153 km (95 mi) long and the land border 1,137.48 kilometres (706.80 miles). The Grand Canal of China, which connects with the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, has its northern terminus at the city. Most of the municipality is flat, and the ground is marshy near the sea, with tidal flats along the coastal plain next to the city. In the north, though, there are hills where the Yan Mountains reach into Tianjin. The top of the municipality is Jiuding Peak (九顶山), found in Ji County along the northern boundary with Hebei, which rises 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft).

Five waterways come together inside the municipality to form the Hai River: the Ziya (子牙河), Daqing (大清河) and Yongding rivers, and the North and South Grand Canals. The Hai reaches the sea without leaving the municipality, at Tanggu District. The main reservoirs are Yuqiao Reservoir, in Ji County in the north, and Beidagang Reservoir, in Dagang District in the south.

Tianjin has a semi-arid climate. Under the Köppen system it is BSk, bordering on Dwa and Cwa. As elsewhere in East Asia, the monsoon shapes four distinct seasons, so winters are cold, windy and dry (thanks to the Siberian anticyclone) while summers are hot and humid. Spring is dry and windy, and sometimes sandstorms blow in from the Gobi Desert and can last for days.

January is the coldest month, averaging −2.8 °C (27.0 °F), and July the hottest, at 27.2 °C (81.0 °F); the whole year averages 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Xiqing District, where the university's newer campus stands, hosts the main weather station, and its record temperatures are a low of −22.9 °C (−9 °F) and a high of 41.1 °C (106 °F).

Sunshine runs at 45% of the possible total in July and 61% in March and April, which amounts to 2,460 hours a year. Annual precipitation is 521 millimetres (20.5 in), and nearly three-fifths of it falls in July and August alone. The city therefore belongs to the semi-arid zone, while some parts of the municipality are humid continental instead (Köppen BSk and Dwa, in that order).

In May 2014 the city government passed new rules aimed at reducing pollution. On severe days the measures include cutting the number of vehicles allowed on the road by half, stopping construction and manufacturing, closing schools and cancelling large outdoor events. In the past, flights have been grounded and highways closed too. Foreign professional athletes living in Tianjin have commented that the air interferes with sport, and one said it was thick enough to "taste". Check the current air-quality index before outdoor exercise.

The main industries are petrochemicals, textiles, car manufacturing, machinery and metalworking. EADS Airbus has an assembly plant in the city for the Airbus A320 series airliners, working since 2009. Tianhe-1A, then the fastest supercomputer on earth, was installed in 2010 at the city's National Supercomputing Center. For 2009 the city's GDP was ¥750.1 billion, which is RMB ¥62,403 per head.
Several zones concentrate investment and trade.

Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA). It dates from 6 December 1984, when the State Council approved it as one of the earliest state-level economic and technological development zones. State preferential policies let it attract domestic and foreign investment for new technology-based modern industries. It is run by an administrative commission on behalf of the Tianjin government, and the commission has provincial-level administrative and economic management powers.

Tianjin Export Processing Zone. Approval from the State Council came on 27 April 2000, making this one of the first fifteen such zones in China. It is a closed, special zone in which Customs officials constantly supervise goods coming in and going out, and the central government gave it preferential policies to attract processing and trade firms. Northeast of TEDA, it is planned to cover 2.54 km2 (0.98 sq mi). The published area for its first phase is 1 square metre (11 sq ft), an evident misprint, so ask for the correct number. A permanent wall separates the export processing area from the rest.

Tianjin Airport Economic Area. Investment in the Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone came from two partners, the Port Free Trade Zone and the airport (Tianjin Binhai International Airport), and the zone is located within the airport's air-freight district. Domestic and foreign air-freight logistics companies there handle sorting, warehousing, distribution, processing and exhibitions, and it is being developed into the largest air-freight base in northern China.

Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone. No other free trade zone exists in northern China. The State Council gave its approval in 1991. Distances: 30 km (19 mi) to the city proper, less than 1 km (0.62 mi) to the wharf, and 38 km (24 mi) to the airport.

Tianjin Tanggu National Marine High-Tech Development Area. Set up in 1992, it was promoted in 1995 by the State Council to a national-level high-tech area, and it is the only one of that level devoted to marine technology. As of late 2008, 2,068 corporations were operating in the zone across five industries, including new materials, oil manufacturing, modern machinery and electronic information.

Tianjin Nangang Industrial Zone. A base for heavy and chemical industry and for harbour activity, it forms part of Tianjin's "dual-city, dual-harbor" development strategy and aims at a circular economy. The zone is planned at 200 km2 (77 sq mi), with 162 km2 (63 sq mi) of that on land.
Around 40% of the municipality's area is farmland, and the crops that matter most economically are maize, rice and wheat.

Oil deposits amount to about 1 billion tonnes, and Dagang District has oilfields. Salt is another industry, and Changlu Yanqu is one of the salt-producing areas of China. Geothermal energy is a further resource, and the manganese and boron deposits under Tianjin were the first discovered anywhere in China. The Tianjin Electric Power Utility is in charge of building, delivering and maintaining electricity supply.

The Binhai New Area (TBNA) is positioned at the meeting point of two urban belts, the Beijing-Tianjin belt and the Circum-Bohai belt. It serves as an entrance to three regions: the north, the northeast and the northwest of China. Being in the middle of Northeast Asia, it is also the closest starting point for the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

The end of 2009 saw 12.28 million people in Tianjin, 9.8 million of whom held a Tianjin hukou (permanent residence registration). Urban areas had 5.99 million of the permanent residents and rural areas 3.81 million. Recently the city has moved back to population growth, and by the end of 2013 it had 14.72 million people.
The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 15.4 million people in 2010.

Han Chinese make up most of the population. People from 51 of the 55 minority ethnic groups of China live in Tianjin, and the larger minorities are the Hui, Koreans, Manchus and Mongols. These figures leave out active-duty members of the People's Liberation Army.

The city mixes nineteenth- and early twentieth-century European buildings with modern Chinese structures of concrete and glass. Redevelopment continues, but much of the colonial architecture is protected.

The history behind it is a hard one. Foreign powers took over the port in the nineteenth century. A quarrel over a British ship led to a fight in which armed gunboats defeated Chinese forces, and the Treaty of Tianjin (1856) gave Europeans nine concessions on the Hai River for trade, opium included. Each enclave was self-contained, so the French built châteaus and towers and the Germans built red-tiled Bavarian villas. Trouble broke out at a French orphanage in the Tianjin Incident (1870), then once more at the time of the Boxer Rebellion (1900), when foreigners pulled down the old city walls so that they could keep an eye on residents.

The old city was mostly torn down in 2000 and 2001, with a handful of historic buildings surviving; the Tianjin Temple of Confucius is one. Sightseeing now centres on the old concession districts. They lie south of the Hai River and south and west of the central station. French châteaus form the downtown area south of the river, British mansions are to the east, and German-style buildings are found farther east and south.

Tianjin has three national nature reserves. Baxianshan has kept most of its original forest ecology because people have interfered very little over a long time. In Jizhou District, the Middle–Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve has been accepted by the geological sciences' international union (IUGS) as a worldwide standard stratigraphic section. Third is the Tianjin Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve, whose three classic shell ridges clearly record the plain's change from sea floor to land.

Two World Cultural Heritage sites represent the cultural landscape: the Great Wall at Huangyaguan, in the north of Jizhou District, and the section of the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal that crosses Tianjin. Another attraction is Ancient Culture Street, rated 5A nationally, with the Tianhou Temple at its core. That temple complex is the oldest historic group of buildings in the city and a major site in northern China for the cult of Mazu. Yangliuqing Town, known for its New Year paintings, bears the title "China Historical and Cultural Town".

Along the Haihe River in the urban area, buildings on both banks combine Chinese, European and modern styles, producing a distinctive skyline. At night, each bridge is lit in its own way ("one bridge, one scene"), and the river has become a landmark that international visitors came to see during big events like the World Economic Forum. Binhai Library, in Binhai New Area, won first place in Time magazine's 2018 list of the "World's 100 Greatest Places", announced in August of that year.

Museums in Tianjin go back to the reforms of the late Qing. The French Jesuit priest and naturalist Émile Licent founded the Musée Hoangho Paiho in 1914; it was among China's first museums and made a significant contribution to paleontology, geology, archaeology and museology.

National first-class status belongs to three museums. First, the Tianjin Museum, a general history and art museum that traces its roots to an institution of the same name from 1918. Second, the Tianjin Natural History Museum, a large museum of zoology, botany, paleontology and geology, which descends from Musée Hoangho Paiho. Third, at Water Park, a memorial hall for Zhou Enlai, the People's Republic's first premier, and his wife Deng Yingchao, who both studied in Tianjin in their youth.

The National Maritime Museum of China, which opened in May 2019 within the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, is the first comprehensive national maritime museum in the country meant for public visitors. Specialised exhibition halls offer more cultural and scientific experiences, among them the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall.

Starting in 2008, the city improved its parks and squares a little at a time, and ended entrance fees. Now anyone can enter freely. Among the main urban parks are Water Park and the zoo, People's Park and Central Park, and Zhongshan, Hedong and Xigu parks. Others are Nancuiping, Shuixi, Beining, Meijiang and Ergong, plus Haihe Music Park and Five Great Avenues Park. Beining Park started life in 1906 as a plantation created by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi; it was later renamed "Ningyuan" after a motto saying that without tranquility one cannot reach far. Shuixi Park opened formally in October 2018.

Binhai New Area has its own set of major parks. They are Haihe Bund, Taifeng, Ziyun and Haigang parks, the Shell Ridge Wetland Park, the East Embankment Park, the South Embankment Coastal Trail Park and the Aircraft Carrier Park.

A programme of 16 suburban parks, in and around the city proper and Binhai New Area, has been planned and built since 2011. They have more natural scenery and a rural character than the urban ones. Work began in 2012 on Beiyunhe Suburban Park in the north and Xiqing Suburban Park in the southwest. By 2014 all 16 had been brought within the ecological redline, with a core area of 66,855 hectares in total.

Street lighting arrived in Tianjin in 1902, and by the 1930s its lit streets had won it the nickname "Northern City That Never Sleeps". Night lighting is now part of specialised urban planning. Central districts follow a "fishbone" lighting pattern along the Haihe River and the canals that continue it (North Canal and South Canal). The Haihe forms the spine and smaller roads branch from it like ribs. This lit riverside is a leading tourist route, and it figured prominently in the Summer Davos Forum, the 13th National Games and the SCO Tianjin Summit.
One middle school is named for families with children: Tianjin No. 7 Middle School.

tianjin-foreign-studies-university.h: Tianjin Foreign Studies University: a quick introduction

blocks.x: TFSU (天津外国语大学) specialises in foreign languages and is a public university under municipal control in Tianjin. It is attached to the city of Tianjin, and the Tianjin Municipal People's Government provides its funding.

TFSU's earliest ancestor dates from 1964, when it was called Tianjin Foreign Languages Vocational School. Ten years later, in 1974, five units came together as the Tianjin Foreign Languages College: that vocational school, a separate Tianjin Foreign Languages School, the Japanese Department from Tianjin Teachers College, and from Hebei University the departments of Chinese and of Foreign Languages. The college gained accreditation to grant master's degrees in 1981. It became Tianjin Foreign Studies University in 2010, and a partnership agreement with the University of Aberdeen was approved in May 2026.

tianjin-foreign-studies-university.h: Tianjin: a port city beside Beijing

blocks.x: A language student lives in the city, not just on campus. The sections below therefore cover Tianjin's geography, weather and air quality, its economy, its people and what there is to see.

The Bohai Gulf's west coast is where Tianjin stands, with the provinces of Shandong and Liaoning on the far side of the water. To reach the capital, Beijing, you travel about 120 kilometers (75 mi) northwest. On all sides but the east, the municipality is surrounded by Hebei, and the Bohai Sea is its eastern boundary. In latitude Tianjin spans 38° 34' to 40° 15' N, and in longitude 116° 43' to 118° 04' E. Its total area is 4,579.41 sq mi (11,860.63 square kilometers).

The municipality has a 153 km (95 mi) coastline and a land border of 706.80 miles (1,137.48 kilometers). It is the northern terminus of China's Grand Canal, a waterway that connects to both the Yellow River and the Yangtze. Generally the municipality is level, and it becomes swampy close to the coast, where tidal flats lie along the coastal plain beside the city. In the north the Yan Mountains enter Tianjin, making the ground hilly. Its highest point is Jiuding Peak (九顶山) in Ji County, right on the Hebei border, whose altitude is 3,538 ft (1,078.5 m).

The Hai River begins within the municipality where five waterways meet: the Daqing River (大清河), the Ziya River (子牙河), the Yongding River, and the North and South Grand Canals. It continues to the sea, and its mouth is in Tanggu District, also inside the municipality. There are two notable reservoirs. Yuqiao Reservoir is in Ji County in the north, and Beidagang Reservoir is in Dagang District in the south.

Technically Tianjin has a semi-arid climate. In the Köppen system that is BSk, with neighbouring Dwa and Cwa types close by. As elsewhere in East Asia, four seasons are marked and the monsoon plays a role. The Siberian anticyclone gives winters that are cold, windy and dry, while the monsoon season makes summers hot and humid. Spring tends to be dry and windy. Sandstorms from the Gobi Desert sometimes arrive then and can continue for days.

Averaging over 24 hours, the month of January comes in at −2.8 °C (27.0 °F) and July at 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). The mean temperature for the whole year is 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). At the chief weather station, in Xiqing District, the temperature has swung between −22.9 °C (−9 °F) and 41.1 °C (106 °F). The proportion of possible sunshine is 45% in July and goes up to 61% in March and April, and annual sunshine for the city totals 2,460 hours. Rain and snow total 521 millimeters (20.5 in) per year, and almost three-fifths of that arrives in July and August alone. So the city as a whole falls within the semi-arid band, although some parts of the municipality are humid continental (Köppen Dwa).

In May 2014 the city's administration put new laws in place to try to reduce pollution. On days when pollution is severe, the measures cut traffic by half, stop building and factory work, shut schools and halt large-scale outdoor activities. Earlier, flights were grounded and highways were closed too. Some professional sportsmen who were born abroad have commented on the air in Tianjin, saying it hampers sport and is thick enough that one can taste it.

Tianjin has industries in petrochemicals, textiles, cars, machinery and metalworking. EADS Airbus manufactures here, in a plant that has assembled airliners of the Airbus A320 series since 2009. For 2010, the National Supercomputing Center of Tianjin was home to the world's fastest supercomputer, Tianhe-1A. In 2009 the city produced a GDP of ¥750.1 billion, or RMB ¥62,403 per head.

The State Council approved TEDA, and it began on 6 December 1984 as one of the earliest state-level economic and technological development zones. Its task is to draw in domestic and foreign investment to build modern, technology-led industries, and it enjoys national preferential policies. TEDA's Administrative Commission belongs to the Tianjin Municipal Government and governs the zone for it, with administrative and economic management powers at the level of a province.

Approved on 27 April 2000, this enclosed special zone is one of the 15 earliest export processing zones that the State Council authorised. Goods moving in or out are under constant control by Customs officials. The central government has granted the zone preferential policies, hoping to attract processing and trading businesses. Its planned area, northeast of TEDA, is 2.54 km2 (0.98 sq mi). A published figure for the first-phase area, given as 1 square meter (11 sq ft) wide, can't be right, so please ask the zone for up-to-date numbers. A permanent wall divides export processing land from the rest.

Investment by Tianjin Binhai International Airport and by Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone built the Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone. It sits in the airport's air cargo area. Both Chinese and foreign air cargo logistics firms there sort, warehouse, distribute, process and exhibit goods. Construction of northern China's largest air cargo base is under way.

In 1991 the State Council approved the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone, and today no other free trade zone exists in northern China. From the city proper it is 30 km (19 mi) away. The wharf is under 1 km (0.62 mi) distant, while Tianjin Binhai International Airport is 38 km (24 mi) away.

The State Council upgraded this zone, established in 1992, to national-level status in 1995. It is the only national-level high-tech area that concentrates on marine technology. At the end of 2008 it hosted 2,068 corporations in 5 industries, namely new materials, oil manufacturing, electronic information and modern machinery manufacturing, plus one more.

Nangang combines a heavy and chemical industry base with a harbor. It fits the dual-city, dual-harbor strategy for spatial development in Tianjin and is meant to be a circular economy. In total it is planned to cover 200 km2 (77 sq mi), and the land part is 162 km2 (63 sq mi).

TBNA, the Tianjin Binhai New Area, is found at the point where two city belts meet, the Circum-Bohai one and the Beijing-Tianjin one. It serves as a gateway to North China, to Northeast China and to Northwest China. In the middle of Northeast Asia, it is the closest departure point of the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

Roughly 40% of the municipality is farmland. In economic terms wheat, rice and maize are the crops that count most. Underground there is about 1 billion tonnes of petroleum, and Dagang District holds the oilfields. Salt is also produced, with Changlu Yanqu as one of the production areas in China. Another resource is geothermal energy. Boron and manganese deposits beneath Tianjin were China's first discoveries of those minerals. Electricity is built, delivered and maintained by Tianjin Electric Power Utility.

Tianjin's municipal population was 12.28 million at the end of 2009, and 9.8 million of that held Tianjin hukou (permanent residence) and lived in the city. Among permanent residents, 5.99 million were in urban areas and 3.81 million in rural ones. The population has begun to grow again in recent years, reaching 14.72 million by the end of 2013. In 2010 the OECD put the population of the metropolitan area around it at 15.4 million. None of these counts includes People's Liberation Army personnel in active service.
Han Chinese form the majority. The city is home to people from 51 of the 55 minority ethnic groups, and the larger minority populations are Mongol, Manchu, Korean and Hui.

Nineteenth-century and early twentieth-century European architecture sits alongside modern Chinese buildings of concrete and glass. Redevelopment goes on, yet much colonial-era architecture remains protected.

How did the European quarters arise? In the nineteenth century Western powers took the port city after a dispute about a British ship. Gunboats overcame Chinese forces, and in the Treaty of Tianjin (1856) Europeans obtained nine concessions beside the Hai River, in which to trade and sell opium. Every enclave was self-contained, with the French putting up châteaus and towers and the Germans Bavarian villas with red tiles. Tensions flared in 1870, in the Tianjin Incident at a French orphanage, and again in the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, when foreigners tore down the old city walls so they could watch the residents.

Most of the old city was pulled down in 2000-2001. A few historic buildings survive, the Tianjin Temple of Confucius being one. Today's visitors go to the former concession streets, which lie to the south of the Hai River and to the south and west of the central station. The French châteaus make up the downtown area on the south side of the river. To the east are British mansions, and German-style buildings remain further east and south.

Three national nature reserves lie within Tianjin. Baxianshan has kept most of its original forest ecology, since people have long left it largely alone. In Jizhou District, the Middle-Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve has been accepted by the International Union of Geological Sciences as a standard global stratigraphic section. The third, the Tianjin Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve, has three typical shell ridges that record in detail how the sea retreated and the land of the Tianjin Plain formed.

Cultural landscapes include two World Cultural Heritage sites. One is the Tianjin stretch of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal. The other is a section of the Great Wall at Huangyaguan, in the north of Jizhou District. The Tianhou Temple is the heart of Ancient Culture Street, a national 5A tourist attraction. This is the oldest surviving group of historical buildings in Tianjin and an important site in northern China for Mazu culture. Yangliuqing Town, known for its Yangliuqing New Year Paintings, is a China Historical and Cultural Town.

Along both banks of the Haihe River in the urban area stand traditional Chinese, European and modern buildings together, and over time this mix has created a cityscape of its own. At night the river's lighting, one bridge and one scene, has made it a famous landmark. For international visitors it has become a leading sight during large events such as the World Economic Forum. Time magazine ranked Binhai New Area's Tianjin Binhai Library first on its list of the World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018, in August of that year.

Museums in Tianjin go back to the late Qing reform era. Émile Licent, a French Jesuit priest and naturalist, founded the Musée Hoangho Paiho in 1914. It was among the earliest museums in China, and it played an important part in the development of paleontology, geology, archaeology and museology.
Today the city has three national first-class museums:
The Tianjin Museum covers history and art. Its origins go back to a museum founded in 1918.
The Tianjin Natural History Museum covers several disciplines (zoology, botany, paleontology and geology) in a large building, and it descends from the Musée Hoangho Paiho.

Water Park is the site of the Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall. The People's Republic's first premier, Zhou Enlai, and Deng Yingchao, his wife, are remembered there, and both of them studied in Tianjin in their youth.

The National Maritime Museum of China opened in May 2019 in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, the first national, comprehensive museum of its kind in China to be open to the public. The Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall are other specialised and themed exhibition halls.

City parks and squares have been improved step by step since 2008, and the entrance fees were removed so that anyone can enter. Urban parks of note include Haihe Music Park, Water Park, Tianjin Zoo, Central Park, People's Park, Zhongshan Park, Nancuiping Park, Shuixi Park, Meijiang Park, Ergong Park, Hedong Park, Xigu Park, Five Great Avenues Park and Beining Park. Beining Park started life as a plantation set up in 1906 by Zhou Xuexi, an industrialist. Afterwards it took the name Ningyuan from its motto: one cannot reach far without tranquility. Shuixi Park opened officially in October 2018. Binhai New Area's main parks are Aircraft Carrier Park, Haigang Park, Shell Ridge Wetland Park, East Embankment Park, South Embankment Coastal Trail Park, Haihe Bund Park, Taifeng Park and Ziyun Park.

Since 2011, sixteen suburban parks have been planned and built in the surroundings of the city and of Binhai New Area. These parks have more natural scenery and rural features than urban parks do. Work began in 2012 on two of them, with the Beiyunhe Suburban Park going up in northern Tianjin and the Xiqing Suburban Park in the southwest. All sixteen were brought under the ecological redline by 2014, with a combined core area of 66,855 hectares.

Street lighting was first installed in Tianjin in 1902. In the 1930s its illuminated streets earned the city a nickname, the Northern City That Never Sleeps. The nightscape now forms part of specialised urban planning. Lighting in the central districts takes a fishbone shape along the Haihe River and its extensions, the North Canal and the South Canal, with the Haihe as the main axis and secondary roads branching away. The Haihe nightscape is a major tourist route, and it has played an important role at events including the SCO Tianjin Summit, the 13th National Games and the Summer Davos Forum.

Tianjin Medical University, or TMU (天津医科大学, Tiānjīn Yīkē Dàxué), is a public university that specialises in medicine and is based in Tianjin. It belongs to the city of Tianjin, and the funding is shared three ways, by the National Health Commission, the Ministry of Education and the Tianjin Municipal People's Government. It is part of two national schemes, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction, which bring extra national support for research and teaching.

The school opened its doors in 1951 under the name Tianjin Medical College, and it was the very first medical institution to win State Council approval. Its first president was Hsien-I Chu, a well-known endocrinologist. A merger in December 1993, approved by the State Education Council, joined Tianjin Medical College with the Tianjin Second Medical College, and the combined body took the name Tianjin Medical University.

Two milestones on the academic side are worth knowing. The State Council Academic Degree Committee accredited the university in 1981 to award bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees, and in 1988 it received permission to run a seven-year medical programme. For prospective international students, it is also helpful that the university appears in the International Medical Education Directory (IMED).

The university occupies 400,000 square metres. It employs 7,493 staff, among them 6,610 professionals, and 1,468 of those hold senior posts. Enrolment is 8,515 students: 5,127 undergraduates studying for bachelor's degrees, 494 on junior-college courses and 1,940 postgraduates. The postgraduates divide into 347 doctoral students (MD and PhD) and 1,593 master's students (MSc). More than 954 international students are counted separately, so the community has a clear international presence.

The university library has 510 thousand volumes and subscribes to 3 thousand kinds of journal; the Ministry of Health named it a Central Library. A computer network that includes Internet access supports medical education, distance medical education, e-mail and document transmission, among other services.

TMU has eight departments covering 15 specialties. They include clinical medicine and anaesthesiology, but also the integration of traditional Chinese and Western medicine and medical humanities. For clinical training, it has 6 university hospitals (these are its affiliated hospitals), 11 clinical colleges and more than thirty teaching hospitals.

TMU has both state-level and local-level key disciplines. The one that holds national status combines traditional Chinese and Western medicine in clinical surgery. Eight more are local-level key disciplines:
Oncology
Cardiovascular diseases
Neurology
Urinary surgery
General surgery
Medical imaging
Nuclear medicine
Endocrinology, including metabolic disease

Three further disciplines have local-level key development status: microbiology and immunology, ophthalmology and stomatology. Nine research institutions support this work, together with a Key Laboratory of the Ministry of Health and nine of that ministry's Clinical Pharmacology Centers. Over the past decade roughly three hundred medical studies passed formal appraisal and eleven won national prizes.

Several scholarships are available: the People Scholarship, the Zhu Xianyi Scholarships, the Chen Lude Nursing Scholarship, the Wang Kechang Scholarship, the Science and Engineering Scholarship, the Tianjin Takeda Scholarship and the Jianxuyunzhu Medical Scholarship. Ask the admissions office which of them are open to international applicants, since eligibility is not spelled out here.

The International Education College looks after foreign students. On 21 December 2007 TMU marked ten years since it first admitted a group of foreign students to its English-taught programme. It now has the largest foreign student body, with students from over 24 countries. Most newcomers arrive in the autumn, but some applicants start in spring so as to get an early start on Chinese.

Every student has to learn Chinese. Students need it to speak with patients on hospital rounds and in clinical training, and simply to get around, which is why it sits inside the medical syllabus for the opening two years. Plan on serious language study from the first week.

The Cancer Institute and Hospital (TMUCIH) is known as the birthplace of oncology in China, and across five decades it has grown into one of the largest cancer centres in the country. The hospital goes back to 1861, when it was founded as the "London Christian Church Hospital". In 1952 the oncologist Jin Xian-Zhai opened the first tumour ward there. By 1972 it had become a specialised cancer hospital with 341 beds, and in 1977 it founded the Institute of Cancer Research, which started with 8 departments. Now it counts among China's major bases for preventing and treating cancer, and for training and research.

The university is building what is intended to be the biggest cancer centre in Asia for prevention, treatment and research. Construction began on 27 June of a comprehensive centre of 93,000 square metres at the hospital. Once finished, the hospital is expected to have 1,800 beds, to see up to 500,000 outpatients and to perform more than 20,000 operations each year.

The plan is to bring basic cancer science, patient care and advanced training together. Seven clinical research centres are to be built, with the goal of a "seamless interconnection" between treating patients and doing science, and the centre hopes to make a breakthrough in joining the two.

A formal agreement on 7 June 2006 linked the hospital with the M. D. Anderson Cancer Center of the University of Texas. It expands joint work in clinical care, teaching and translational cancer research, and it grew out of contacts between doctors and scientists on both sides over more than a decade. The two institutions describe a shared mission to end cancer worldwide, and the agreement provides a structure for joint programmes in scientific discovery, advanced treatment, education and prevention.
A Swedish tie followed in 2009. Karolinska University Hospital's Center for Molecular Medicine and TMU agreed to create a joint Sino-Swedish Center for Molecular Medicine.
In all, TMU has over 50 partner universities across more than 16 countries, and 108 guest professors come from famous research institutes worldwide, for instance Johns Hopkins University.
A great deal of daily life is shaped by the surrounding city, meaning its weather, its transport and its leisure options. Here is Tianjin.

Tianjin is on the western shore of the Bohai Gulf, facing Shandong and Liaoning across the water. Beijing, 120 km (75 mi) to the north-west, is a neighbour. Hebei surrounds Tianjin on every side except the east, where the Bohai Sea forms the border. The city lies between latitudes 38° 34' and 40° 15' N and longitudes 116° 43' and 118° 04' E, and covers 11,860.63 km² (4,579.41 sq mi).

The coastline is 153 km (95 mi) long and the land border measures 1,137.48 km (706.80 mi). The Grand Canal of China, which ties into the Yellow River and the Yangtze, ends at Tianjin on its northern side. Terrain is mostly flat and marshy near the coast. Up north the Yan Mountains push into the municipality and make hills, while tidal flats occupy the coastal plain beside the city. Jiuding Peak (九顶山), 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft) tall and located in Ji County on the Hebei border, is the municipality's high point.

The Hai River forms inside the municipality, where five waterways meet: the Ziya River (子牙河), the Daqing River (大清河), the Yongding River, the North Grand Canal and the South Grand Canal. It flows out to the sea within the municipality, in Tanggu District. Two reservoirs store water: Yuqiao Reservoir, up north in Ji County, and Beidagang Reservoir, down south in Dagang District.

By the Köppen system Tianjin has a semi-arid climate (BSk), bordering on Dwa and Cwa. As elsewhere in East Asia, there are four seasons shaped by the monsoon. The Siberian anticyclone makes winters cold, windy and dry, and the summer monsoon makes summers hot and humid. Spring is dry and breezy, and sandstorms from the Gobi Desert sometimes blow in and may last for days.

Averaged over a day, January is the coldest month at −2.8 °C (27.0 °F), July the warmest at 27.2 °C (81.0 °F), and the whole year averages 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). The weather station in Xiqing District, the main one, has recorded a low of −22.9 °C (−9 °F) and a high of 41.1 °C (106 °F). Bright sunshine totals 2,460 hours annually, with a monthly share of possible sunshine from 45% (July) up to 61% (March and April). Yearly precipitation is 521 mm (20.5 in), and almost three-fifths of it comes in July and August. That puts the city in the semi-arid zone, although some parts of the municipality are classed as humid continental.

In May 2014 the city government passed new rules intended to reduce pollution. On severe days they allow measures such as taking half the vehicles off the roads, stopping construction and manufacturing, closing schools and halting large outdoor events. In the past flights have been grounded and highways closed. Some foreign-born professional sportsmen have spoken about the air, saying it gets in the way of exercise and is thick enough to "taste". If you have asthma or other breathing issues, ask your doctor before you go.

The main industries are petrochemicals, textiles, car manufacturing, mechanical engineering and metalworking. EADS Airbus makes aircraft here, and its assembly plant for the A320 series has been running since 2009. As of 2010 the fastest supercomputer on Earth, Tianhe-1A, was housed in Tianjin, at the National Supercomputing Center. In 2009 the city's GDP was ¥750.1 billion, or RMB ¥62,403 per person.

TEDA, the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area, received State Council approval on 6 December 1984 and was one of the earliest national zones of its kind. It enjoys national preferential policies, because its job is to attract domestic and foreign investment into modern, technology-led industries. TEDA's administrative commission is part of the Tianjin Municipal Government, which uses it to run the zone with provincial-level administrative and economic management powers.

The Tianjin Export Processing Zone was among the first 15 such zones the State Council approved, and the approval date was 27 April 2000. It is a special enclosed area in which customs officials constantly supervise goods going in and out. The central government gave it preferential policies to attract firms in processing and trade. It lies north-east of TEDA, with a planned area of 2.54 km² (0.98 sq mi), and a permanent wall divides the export processing area from the rest. (The published figure for the first-phase area is clearly a misprint, so ignore it.)

Tianjin Binhai International Airport and the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone together invested in the Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone. It occupies the airport's air cargo area and is home to Chinese and foreign firms handling sorting, warehousing, distribution, processing and exhibitions. Work continues on what will be the biggest air cargo base in the north of the country.

No other free trade zone exists in northern China. Approved by the State Council in 1991, it lies 30 km (19 mi) from the city proper, less than 1 km (0.62 mi) from the wharf, and a 38 km (24 mi) trip from the airport.

tianjin-medical-university.h: Tanggu National Marine High-Tech Development Area

blocks.x: The Tanggu Marine High-Tech Development Area began in 1992, and in 1995 the State Council raised it to national level. Specialising in marine technology, it is the sole national high-tech area with that focus. At the close of 2008 it had 2,068 corporations and 5 industries, among them electronic information, modern machinery, oil manufacturing and new materials.

Nangang is a base for heavy and chemical industry with a harbour. It belongs to Tianjin's "dual-city, dual-harbor" strategy for spatial development and is a circular-economy zone. The overall planned area is 200 km² (77 sq mi), and 162 km² (63 sq mi) of that is land.

Around 40% of the municipality is farmland, where the most valuable crops are maize, rice and wheat. Under the ground, Tianjin has petroleum deposits of about 1 billion tonnes, with oilfields in Dagang District. Salt is another industry, and Changlu Yanqu is one of China's salt-producing areas. Geothermal energy is a further resource. Manganese and boron deposits found beneath Tianjin were the first in China. Tianjin Electric Power Utility builds, delivers and maintains the city's electricity.

The Tianjin Binhai New Area (TBNA) sits where the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt meets the Circum-Bohai City Belt. As a gateway to the north, north-east and north-west of China, and the centre of Northeast Asia, it is the nearest point from which to start the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

At the end of 2009 Tianjin Municipality had 12.28 million people, of whom 9.8 million held a Tianjin hukou, meaning permanent residence registration. Of the permanent residents, 3.81 million lived in the countryside, and 5.99 million lived in urban areas. Population has recently turned upward: by the end of 2013 it reached 14.72 million. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 15.4 million in 2010.

Most residents are Han Chinese, and members of 51 of China's 55 minority groups live in Tianjin. The larger minority communities are the Hui, Koreans, Manchus and Mongols. These counts leave out active-duty members of the People's Liberation Army.
The city mixes European architecture of the 19th and early 20th centuries with modern Chinese buildings of concrete and glass. Redevelopment goes on, but much colonial-era building is protected.

In the 19th century Western powers took the port after an incident over a British ship, defeating Chinese forces with armed gunboats. Under the Treaty of Tianjin (1856), European countries obtained nine concessions beside the Hai River in which to trade and sell opium. Each was a self-contained enclave. French builders favoured châteaus and towers, while Germans preferred red-tiled Bavarian villas. Violence flared at a French orphanage in the Tianjin Incident of 1870, and again in 1900, in the Boxer Rebellion, when foreigners pulled down the old city walls so they could keep watch on residents.

Demolition in 2000 and 2001 cleared most of the old city, sparing only a few historic buildings, among them the Tianjin Temple of Confucius. Visitors now come for the former concession streets. These lie south of the Hai River and south and west of the central station. South of the river, the downtown is French in style. Further east are British mansions, then German-style buildings to the east and south.

Three national nature reserves lie within Tianjin. Baxianshan has kept most of its original forest ecology because people have interfered with it so little for so long. The Middle-Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve, in Jizhou District, has earned recognition from the International Union of Geological Sciences as a global standard stratigraphic section. As for the Tianjin Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve, its three typical shell ridges show clearly how the sea withdrew and the Tianjin Plain became land.

For cultural landscapes, Tianjin has two World Cultural Heritage sites. One is the Huangyaguan Great Wall, in the north of Jizhou District; the other is the Tianjin stretch of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal. Ancient Culture Street, a national 5A tourist attraction, is built around the Tianhou Temple, the oldest surviving historical building complex in the city and an important northern Chinese site for Mazu culture. Yangliuqing Town is known for Yangliuqing New Year Paintings and holds the title "China Historical and Cultural Town".

In the urban area, traditional Chinese, European and modern buildings stand together on both banks of the Haihe River, creating a distinctive cityscape. The nightscape, built on the idea of "one bridge, one scene", has made the river a landmark and a leading sightseeing spot for international visitors during big events like the World Economic Forum. One more distinction: Time magazine, in August 2018, listed the Binhai Library in the Binhai New Area at number one in its "World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018".

Museums began in Tianjin in the last years of the Qing, the era of reform. In 1914 the naturalist and French Jesuit priest Émile Licent established the Musée Hoangho Paiho, among the first museums in China, which played a major role in palaeontology, geology, archaeology and museology.

Three national first-class museums exist today. First, the Tianjin Museum is a general museum of history and art whose origins lie in a museum founded in 1918. Second, the Tianjin Natural History Museum is large and multidisciplinary, with zoology, botany, palaeontology and geology, and it descends from the Musée Hoangho Paiho. Third, at Water Park, the Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall honours Zhou, who became the People's Republic's first premier, and his wife Deng, who both studied in Tianjin as young people.

The National Maritime Museum of China opened in May 2019 in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, as the country's first national, comprehensive museum of the sea open to the public. Other specialised exhibition halls include the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall.
Tianjin has been upgrading its parks and squares since 2008, and it dropped entrance fees so that anyone can visit free. The main urban parks are grouped below:
Central Park, Zhongshan Park, Ergong Park, Meijiang Park and Haihe Music Park
Beining Park, Shuixi Park, Nancuiping Park, Tianjin Zoo and Water Park
Xigu Park, Five Great Avenues Park, Hedong Park and People's Park

Beining Park started life as a plantation laid out in 1906 by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi. Its later name, "Ningyuan", comes from a motto: "Without tranquility, one cannot reach far." Shuixi Park opened officially in October 2018. In Binhai New Area, the notable parks include Aircraft Carrier Park, Haigang Park, Shell Ridge Wetland Park, Haihe Bund Park, Taifeng Park, Ziyun Park, East Embankment Park and the South Embankment Coastal Trail Park.

From 2011 on, the city has planned and constructed 16 suburban parks around the city and Binhai New Area, which are more natural and rural in feel than the urban ones. The first works began in 2012, at Beiyunhe Suburban Park in the north and Xiqing Suburban Park in the south-west. By 2014 the 16 parks lay within the ecological redline, covering a core area of 66,855 hectares in total.

The first street lamps went up in 1902. By the 1930s the lit-up streets had given Tianjin a nickname, the "Northern City That Never Sleeps". Night lighting is now part of dedicated urban planning. Central districts use a "fishbone" layout: the Haihe and its continuations, the North Canal and South Canal, form the spine, and side roads branch from it. The lit Haihe is a leading tourist route and has been part of the Summer Davos Forum, the SCO Tianjin Summit and the 13th National Games.
