Tianjin Normal University (TNU) (Chinese: 天津师范大学; pinyin: Tiānjīn shīfàn dàxué) is a public research university founded in 1958 in Tianjin, China. In 2017–2018, Chinese University Alumni Association (CUAA) ranks Tianjin Normal University 3rd in normal universities in north China.
Tianjin Normal University was founded in 1958.

In April 1999, with the approval by the Ministry of Education, Tianjin Municipal Committee of the CPC and Tianjin Municipal Government decided to found the new Tianjin Normal University by integrating the old Tianjin Normal University, Tianjin Teachers' Training Academy, and Tianjin Educational Institute.
In 2001, the first Confucius Institute in Africa opened as a collaboration between Tianjin Normal University and Kenya's University of Nairobi.

Approaved by Tianjin Municipal Government in March 2003, the construction project of the new campus of TNU was officially initiated. TNU now has 23 colleges, 1 independent college, 49 research institutes, and 87 specialties for undergraduates (including 56 specialties for 4-year students and 31 for 2-year students). Offering programs at various levels and in many disciplines, the university has developed a unique system of education, with a series of pre- and in – service training courses and different levels of education for different purposes: for academic degrees, for diplomas or simply for training. The programs offered have already covered 8 of the 11 academic disciplines for undergraduates. TNU also boasts the "Psychology and Behavior Research Center", one of the one hundred major humanities and social sciences research centers under the Ministry of Education, Tianjin research lab of modern Pedagogical techniques, a key lab of water environment and water resources and a research center for politics and humanistic social science. It also has an affiliated middle school and an affiliated primary school.
The Ba Li Tai Campus is situated on Wei Jin Road in the heart of downtown Tianjin. It now hosts international students studying in Tianjin Normal University who take Chinese as the second language.

Tianjin Normal University's Xi Qing Campus is situated on West Bin Shui Avenue. The campus hosts 23 colleges and 50 research organisations and 87 undergraduate departments. 20,540 full-time students currently study at Tianjin Normal University.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Tianjin, where Tianjin Normal University is located.

Tianjin is located on the west coast of the Bohai Gulf; the provinces of Shandong and Liaoning are located across those waters. The city is bordered by Beijing, which is 120 kilometers (75 mi) to the northwest. Tianjin is surrounded on all sides by Hebei, with the exception of its eastern border, which is the Bohai Sea. With a latitude ranging from 38° 34' to 40° 15' N and a longitude ranging from 116° 43' to 118° 04' E, the total area of the city is 11,860.63 square kilometers (4,579.41 sq mi).

The city has 153 km (95 mi) of coastline and 1,137.48 kilometers (706.80 mi) of land border. It is located at the northern end of the Grand Canal of China, which connects with the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers. The municipality is generally flat and is swampy near the coast; however, it has hills in the north, where the Yan Mountains enter Tianjin. Tidal flats occur on the coastal plain adjacent to the city. The highest point in the municipality is Jiuding Peak (九顶山) in Ji County on the northern border with Hebei; the mountain has an altitude of 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft).

In the Tianjin Municipality, the Hai River forms at the confluence of the Ziya River (子牙河), Daqing River (大清河), Yongding River, North Grand Canal, and South Grand Canal; it enters the Pacific Ocean within the municipality as well as in Tanggu District. Reservoirs include the Beidagang Reservoir in the south (in Dagang District) and the Yuqiao Reservoir in the north in Ji County.

Tianjin has a semi-arid climate (using the Köppen system, the city has a BSk climate bordering on Dwa and Cwa). As in other areas of East Asia, the city has a four-season, monsoon-influenced climate; it also has cold, windy, and dry winters due to the Siberian anticyclone and hot, humid summers due to the monsoon season. Spring in the city is dry and windy; the season sometimes consists of sandstorms blowing in from the Gobi Desert, which are capable of lasting for several days. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from −2.8 °C (27.0 °F) in January to 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July, with an annual mean of 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Extreme temperatures in the city at the main weather station in Xiqing District have ranged from −22.9 °C (−9 °F) to 41.1 °C (106 °F). With the monthly percentage of the possible amount of sunshine ranging from 45% in July to 61% in March and April, the city receives 2,460 hours of sunshine annually. Having an annual total precipitation of 521 millimeters (20.5 in), with nearly three-fifths of it occurring in July and August alone, the city lies within the semi-arid climate zone, although parts of the municipality are humid continental (Köppen BSk/Dwa, respectively).

In May 2014, the city's administration enacted new laws in an attempt to lower the city's pollution levels. These measures included several methods to restrict pollution on days when is severe, such as by halving the number of vehicles allowed on roads, halting construction and manufacturing activity, closing schools, and halting large-scale outdoor activities.
In the past, flights have also been grounded and highways have been closed.
Foreign-born professional sportsmen have made statements regarding Tianjin's air quality, citing it as an impediment to athletic activity and being thick enough to "taste".

Industries include petrochemical industries, textiles, car manufacturing, mechanical industries, and metalworking. EADS Airbus is one of the manufacturers in the city, and has opened an assembly plant for its Airbus A320 series airliners; the plant has been operational since 2009. As of 2010, the fastest supercomputer in the world, Tianhe-1A, has been located at the National Supercomputing Center of Tianjin. The city's GDP in 2009 was ¥750.1 billion, with a GDP per capita of RMB ¥62,403.

As one of the first state-level economic and technological development zones, the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA) was founded on December 6, 1984, with the approval of the State Council. It is given state preferential policies with the task of attracting domestic and foreign investment to develop new technology-oriented modern industries. As an affiliated organization of the Tianjin Municipal Government, the Administrative Commission of Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area exercises unified administration of TEDA on behalf of the Tianjin Municipal Government and has provincial-level administrative and economic management rights.

The Tianjin Export Processing Zone is one of the first 15 export processing zones approved by the State Council, having been approved on April 27, 2000. This area is a special enclosed zone. where Customs officials conduct constant administration for commodities transported into and out of the zone. The central government granted the special economic zone preferential policies to attract enterprises in the business of processing and trade to invest in the zone. The Tianjin Export Processing Zone is located to the northeast of TEDA and has a planned area of 2.54 km2 (0.98 sq mi). The area developed in the first phase is 1 square meter (11 sq ft) wide. A permanent wall is built to separate the export processing and non-export processing zones.

The Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone is jointly invested by the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone and Tianjin Binhai International Airport. It is located inside the airfreight area of Tianjin Binhai International Airport. It has domestic and foreign airfreight logistics enterprises engaged in sorting, warehousing, distribution, processing, and exhibition. It is in the process of constructing the largest airfreight base in northern China.

The Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone is the only free trade zone in northern China. The zone was approved for establishment in 1991 by State Council. It is 30 km (19 mi) from Tianjin city proper, less than 1 km (0.62 mi) away from the wharf, and 38 km (24 mi) away from Tianjin Binhai International Airport.

tianjin-normal-university.h: Tianjin Tanggu National Marine High-Tech Development Area

blocks.x: The Tianjin Tanggu Marine High-Tech Development Area was established in 1992 and was upgraded to the national-level high-tech development area by the State Council in 1995. It is the only national-level high-tech development area specializing in developing the marine technology industry. By the end of 2008, the zone had 2,068 corporations and 5 industries there, including those for new materials, oil manufacturing, modern machinery manufacturing, and electronic information.

The Tianjin Nangang Industrial Zone is a heavy and chemical industry base and harbor, a part of the"dual-city, dual-harbor" space development strategy of Tianjin, and a zone with a circular economy. The total planned area of Nangang Industrial Zone is 200 km2 (77 sq mi), of which the terrestrial area is 162 km2 (63 sq mi).
Farmland takes up about 40% of Tianjin Municipality's total area. Wheat, rice, and maize are the most economically important crops.

Tianjin Municipality has deposits of about 1 billion tonnes of petroleum, with Dagang District containing oilfields. Salt production is also one of the city's industries, with Changlu Yanqu being one of China's salt production areas. Geothermal energy is another resource of Tianjin. Deposits of manganese and boron under Tianjin were the first to be found in China.
Tianjin Electric Power Utility constructs, delivers and maintains electrical power services.

The Tianjin Binhai New Area (TBNA) is located at the juncture of the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt and the Circum-Bohai City Belt. It is the gateway to North China, Northeast China, and Northwest China. Lying in the center of Northeast Asia, it is the nearest point of departure of the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

At the end of 2009, the population of Tianjin Municipality was 12.28 million, of which 9.8 million owned and lived in Tianjin hukou (permanent residences). Among permanent residents of Tianjin, 5.99 million lived in urban areas, while 3.81 million lived in rural ones.  Tianjin has recently shifted to population growth; its population had reached 14.72 million as of the end of 2013.
The encompassing metropolitan area was estimated by the OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) to have, as of 2010, a population of 15.4 million.

The majority of Tianjin residents are Han Chinese. People from 51 out of the 55 minor Chinese ethnic groups live in Tianjin. Minorities with higher populations in the city include Hui, Korean, Manchu, and Mongol people.
The graph above excludes members of the People's Liberation Army in active service.

The city blends nineteenth- and early twentieth-century European architecture with modern Chinese concrete-and-glass structures. While redevelopment continues, much colonial architecture is protected.

In the nineteenth century, Western powers seized the port city after a dispute over a British ship. Armed gunboats defeated Chinese forces, and the Treaty of Tianjin (1856) granted Europeans nine concessions along the Hai River to trade and sell opium. These enclaves were self-contained: the French built châteaus and towers, Germans red-tiled Bavarian villas. Tensions erupted in the Tianjin Incident (1870) at a French orphanage and again during the Boxer Rebellion (1900), when foreigners demolished the old city walls to monitor residents.
The old city was largely demolished in 2000–2001, leaving only a few historic buildings, such as the Tianjin Temple of Confucius.

Today, the former concession streets south and west of the central station and south of the Hai River draw visitors. The French châteaus form the downtown south of the river, British mansions lie east, and further east and south, German-style buildings remain.

Tianjin contains three national nature reserves. Among them, Baxianshan has largely preserved its original forest ecology due to long-term minimal human interference. The Middle–Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve in Jizhou District has been recognized by the International Union of Geological Sciences as a standard global stratigraphic section. The Tianjin Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve features three typical shell ridges, clearly documenting the geological evolution from marine retreat to land formation on the Tianjin Plain.

In terms of cultural landscapes, Tianjin hosts two World Cultural Heritage sites: the Huangyaguan Great Wall in the northern part of Jizhou District and the Tianjin section of the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal. Ancient Culture Street is a national 5A tourist attraction, with the Tianhou Temple as its core structure. It is the oldest existing historical building complex in Tianjin and a significant northern Chinese site representing Mazu culture. Yangliuqing Town is renowned for Yangliuqing New Year Paintings and has been designated a "China Historical and Cultural Town".

Within the urban area, both banks of the Haihe River feature a mixture of traditional Chinese, European, and modern architecture, gradually forming a distinctive cityscape. The "one bridge, one scene" illuminated nightscape along the Haihe has made the river a famous landmark and a prominent sightseeing destination for international visitors during major events such as the World Economic Forum.
In August 2018, Time magazine ranked the Tianjin Binhai Library in Binhai New Area first on its "World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018" list.

Tianjin's museum tradition began during the late Qing reform era. In 1914, the French Jesuit priest and naturalist Émile Licent established the Musée Hoangho Paiho, one of China's earliest museums, which played a key role in paleontology, geology, archaeology, and museology.

Currently, Tianjin has three national first-class museums: Tianjin Museum, Tianjin Natural History Museum, and the Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall. The Tianjin Museum is a comprehensive history and art museum, tracing its origins to the Tianjin Museum established in 1918. The Tianjin Natural History Museum is a large, multidisciplinary natural history museum covering zoology, botany, paleontology, and geology, originating from the Musée Hoangho Paiho. The Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall, located at Water Park, commemorates the first premier of the People's Republic of China, Zhou Enlai, and his wife Deng Yingchao, who studied in Tianjin during their youth.

In May 2019, the National Maritime Museum of China in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City opened as China's first national, comprehensive, and public-oriented maritime museum. Tianjin also hosts specialized and thematic exhibition halls such as the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall, and Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall, providing cultural and scientific experiences for residents and visitors.

Since 2008, Tianjin has gradually upgraded city parks and squares, removing entrance fees and making them freely accessible to the public. Major urban parks include Water Park, Tianjin Zoo, Nancuiping Park, Shuixi Park, Beining Park, Meijiang Park, Ergong Park, Zhongshan Park, Haihe Music Park, Central Park, People's Park, Hedong Park, Five Great Avenues Park, and Xigu Park. Beining Park was originally a plantation built in 1906 by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi and was later renamed "Ningyuan" for its motto "Without tranquility, one cannot reach far." Major parks in Binhai New Area include Haihe Bund Park, Taifeng Park, Ziyun Park, South Embankment Coastal Trail Park, East Embankment Park, Shell Ridge Wetland Park, Aircraft Carrier Park, and Haigang Park. Shuixi Park officially opened in October 2018.

Since 2011, Tianjin has planned and constructed 16 suburban parks in and around the city and Binhai New Area. Compared with urban parks, suburban parks feature more natural landscapes and rural characteristics. Construction of the Beiyunhe Suburban Park in northern Tianjin and the Xiqing Suburban Park in the southwest began in 2012. By 2014, the 16 suburban parks were incorporated into the ecological redline, with a total core area of 66,855 hectares.

Tianjin first installed street lighting in 1902. By the 1930s, the city's illuminated streets had earned it the nickname "Northern City That Never Sleeps." Currently, the city's nightscape is incorporated into specialized urban planning. In the central districts, lighting forms a "fishbone" pattern along the Haihe River and its extended sections (North Canal and South Canal), with the main axis along the Haihe and secondary roads radiating from it. The Haihe nightscape has become a major tourist route and has played an important role in events such as the Summer Davos Forum, the 13th National Games, and the SCO Tianjin Summit.

tianjin-university.h: A quick portrait of Tianjin University

blocks.x: Tianjin University, usually shortened to TJU (Chinese name 天津大学), is a state-run research university based in the port city of Tianjin. It answers to China's Ministry of Education, which also provides its funding. The university belongs to the Double First-Class scheme and to the older Projects 211 and 985, the three best-known government programmes for backing leading universities. For a prospective international student, that combination is a reliable sign that the university is among the state's priority institutions for research money and graduate training.

The university is best known as an engineering powerhouse. It began life in 1895 as Peiyang University (北洋大學), created under an imperial charter signed by the Guangxu Emperor, and it is often described as the oldest modern university in China. The idea behind it was practical: train people in engineering and mining so that the country could modernise, then widen the offer to science, business, law, the humanities and more. Adopting Western teaching models was a deliberate break with the past, and the school became a symbol of that turn.

After the founding of the People's Republic of China the institution was renamed Tianjin University in 1951. Today it counts among the biggest multidisciplinary engineering universities in China, and back in 1959 it was among the 16 institutions that were first designated national key universities by the central government.

tianjin-university.h: From a college in 1895 to a national key university

blocks.x: The story starts with Sheng Xuanhuai, who sent a memorial to the Guangxu Emperor asking permission to open a modern higher-education institution in Tianjin. Approval arrived on 2 October 1895, and the new school, first called the Peiyang Western Study College, was set up by Sheng together with the American educator Charles Daniel Tenney. It grew into Peiyang University and became the first institution in China to offer four-year modern degree programmes. Its founders took leading American universities as their model and hoped to strengthen the nation by training people with up-to-date scientific and technical knowledge.

Its influence on later Chinese higher education is a point of pride. In the early years, undergraduates had the right to move directly into graduate programmes at Harvard and Yale, with no entrance examination to pass. The law school was a pioneer too. Regarded as China's earliest and finest, it was later merged into Peking University, which gained a fresh start from it. Peiyang's aeronautics department was likewise separated off and grew into what is now Beihang University. After the 1949 revolution and the restructuring of universities, Peiyang University took the name Tianjin University in 1951.
The following dates give a sense of how steadily the university has expanded its teaching, research and campuses.
1895 Peiyang University is founded.
1900 China's first modern diploma is awarded to a graduate.
1907 The institution becomes a comprehensive university, bringing engineering together with arts, law and teacher education.
1935 Graduate students enrol for the first time, and the first master's degree follows in 1937.
1951 It merges with the Hebei Institute of Technology and is renamed Tianjin University.
1958 A first library building of 14,423 square metres is established.
1959 It is named among the initial 16 National Key Universities.
1981 The first PhD students enrol; the graduate school opens in 1984; the first doctoral degree is conferred in 1985.
1995 The university marks its 100th anniversary.
1999 A National University Science Park is built to help move research into industry.
2000 It joins the first batch of universities under Project 985.
2009 The bachelor's programme in chemical engineering is accredited by the Institution of Chemical Engineers (IChemE).
2010 The plan for a new campus is launched, and in 2015, for the 120th anniversary, the new Peiyang Park campus is completed.
2013 The university's chemical science and engineering co-innovation centre is chosen as one of 14 initial collaborative innovation centres under the "2011" programme.
2017 and again in 2021 the university appears on China's list of world-class universities and disciplines under construction.

As of 2023 the university reports six national key disciplines, plus 17 that hold key status at municipal level. Its graduate-level offer is broad: 12 first-level and 49 second-level disciplines award doctorates, 87 award master's degrees, and 17 engineering fields award the master of engineering. It also runs the MBA and the MPA (public administration). Supporting this are 15 postdoctoral research programmes, one national engineering research centre, two national centres that promote scientific and technological achievements, and seven engineering R&D centres and open laboratories at ministry level. The number of state key laboratories is given as four in one account and five in another, so check the university's own website if that detail matters to you. In June 2001 an expert panel from the Ministry of Education judged that the university had completed all the construction targets set under Project 211 for the Ninth Five-Year Plan period.

tianjin-university.h: Laboratories, patents and links with industry

blocks.x: Across campus there are more than 80 laboratories, 110 research institutes and 15 experimental research and engineering development centres. The reported record, covering the decades since China's reform and opening up, includes hundreds of prize-winning projects. Of these, 70 earned a top national honour (the Natural Science Award, the Invention Award or the Science and Technology Progress Award), while a further 510 received progress awards from the Ministry of Education or from provincial and ministerial bodies. There are 393 patent applications listed, of which 278 were granted. These figures date from earlier years, so treat them as a snapshot of strength rather than a current tally.

In 2001 the university's Science and Technology Park became one of 22 university science parks in China. The university describes a research system that runs from basic research through applied work to development, and says its funding from the National Natural Science Foundation has regularly been the highest among engineering universities. It works with many large and medium-sized companies, and its research funds reached RMB 280 million in 2000.

Among the former Project 985 universities, Tianjin University is one of those that has made it into the world top 500. In 2024, the Aggregate Ranking of Top Universities, which combines the three most closely watched league tables (THE, ARWU and QS), placed it 172nd in the world. Tianjin University was among the first Chinese universities to look for cooperation with outside organisations. It keeps relations with higher-education institutions and transnational companies around the world, and with regional governments such as Hebei, Jilin, Xinjiang, Tibet and Chongqing. It has signed cooperation agreements with over 20 multinational firms, and with 80 universities spread across 28 countries, for academic exchange, joint research and joint training.

Distinguished visitors have been appointed honorary or guest professors. Among them are Herbert A. Simon, Nobel laureate from Carnegie Mellon University; Gerald Vizenor, an emeritus professor of American literature at the University of New Mexico, whose novel Griever: An American Monkey King in China draws on Tianjin University as a setting; and the physicist Yang Zhenning, based at the State University of New York. In recent years the university has also sponsored or run over a dozen major international conferences, which open more doors for exchange. On 27 October 2012 it joined the University of South Australia to set up the China-Australia Centre for Sustainable Urban Development.

tianjin-university.h: Life in Tianjin: why the city matters

blocks.x: Day-to-day student life depends heavily on the city around the campus. The next sections explain the geography, weather, economy, people and sights of Tianjin, so you know what to expect when you arrive.

tianjin-university.h: Where Tianjin sits and what the land is like

blocks.x: Tianjin lies on the western shore of the Bohai Gulf. Shandong and Liaoning are across the water. Beijing is its neighbour to the northwest, about 120 kilometres (75 miles) away, while Hebei Province wraps around the rest of the municipality except on the east, where the Bohai Sea forms the boundary. The municipality stretches between latitudes 38° 34' and 40° 15' N and longitudes 116° 43' and 118° 04' E, and covers 11,860.63 square kilometres (4,579.41 square miles).

It has 153 kilometres (95 miles) of coastline and a land border of 1,137.48 kilometres (706.80 miles). The city is at the northern end of the Grand Canal of China, which links the Yellow and Yangtze rivers. Most of the municipality is flat, and it turns swampy near the sea, with tidal flats along the coastal plain. Hills appear only in the north, where the Yan Mountains reach into Tianjin. The highest point is Jiuding Peak (九顶山) in Ji County on the Hebei border, at 1,078.5 metres (3,538 feet).

Water is important here. The Hai River takes shape from five waterways: the Yongding River, the North and South Grand Canals, the Daqing River (大清河) and the Ziya River (子牙河). It reaches the sea within the municipality, at Tanggu District. Two notable reservoirs are Beidagang in the south (Dagang District) and Yuqiao in the north (Ji County).

Under the Köppen system, Tianjin is classed as semi-arid (BSk), bordering on other types. It has four seasons shaped by the monsoon. Winters are cold, windy and dry because of the Siberian anticyclone, and summers are hot and humid. Spring is dry and breezy, and sandstorms from the Gobi Desert sometimes blow in and can last several days, which is worth knowing if you have asthma or allergies.

Daily average temperatures peak at 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July and bottom out at −2.8 °C (27.0 °F) in January, and the year as a whole averages 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Extremes recorded at the main station, in Xiqing District, stretch from a low of −22.9 °C (−9 °F) to a high of 41.1 °C (106 °F). July is the dullest month, with 45% of possible sunshine, whereas March and April reach 61%; over twelve months the city enjoys 2,460 hours of sun. Rain totals 521 millimetres (20.5 inches) a year, and close to three-fifths of that comes in July and August.

In May 2014 the city administration passed new rules to cut pollution. On days of severe smog the measures include cutting road traffic by half, stopping construction and manufacturing, closing schools and halting large outdoor events. In the past, flights have been grounded and highways closed. Some professional athletes from abroad have commented that the air can hamper outdoor sport. If you are sensitive to air quality, pack a good mask and check daily readings during the colder months.

Tianjin's traditional industries are petrochemicals, textiles, car manufacturing, machinery and metalworking. Airbus has run an assembly plant there for its A320 family of airliners since 2009. The National Supercomputing Center in Tianjin housed Tianhe-1A, which in 2010 was the fastest supercomputer in the world. In 2009 the city's output stood at ¥750.1 billion, which works out at RMB 62,403 for each resident. These are older figures, and the economy has changed since, so look at current statistics if you need up-to-date numbers.
Several special zones explain why the city has attracted so many companies.

Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA). Founded on 6 December 1984 with State Council approval, it is one of the first state-level zones of its kind. It receives national preferential policies so that it can attract Chinese and foreign investment in modern technology industries. A management commission acts for the municipal government and holds provincial-level administrative and economic powers.

Tianjin Export Processing Zone. This is one of the first 15 such zones approved by the State Council, on 27 April 2000. It is a closed, customs-supervised area northeast of TEDA with a planned area of 2.54 square kilometres (0.98 square miles), and it is separated from the surrounding territory by a permanent wall. Its purpose is to attract processing and trade businesses.

Tianjin Airport Economic Area. The free trade zone at the port and the Binhai airport jointly invested in a logistics zone that sits within the airport's freight area. It hosts domestic and foreign air-freight firms handling sorting, storage, distribution, processing and exhibitions, and it is working to become northern China's largest air-freight base.

Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone. Approved by the State Council in 1991, it is the sole free trade zone of its kind in northern China. It lies 30 kilometres (19 miles) from the city proper, less than a kilometre from the wharf and 38 kilometres (24 miles) from the airport.

Tianjin Tanggu Marine High-Tech Development Area. Founded in 1992 and raised to national level in 1995, it is the only national high-tech zone that specialises in marine technology. By the end of 2008 it hosted 2,068 companies across five industries, including new materials, oil equipment, modern machinery and electronic information.

Tianjin Nangang Industrial Zone. A base for heavy and chemical industry and a harbour, it forms part of the city's "dual-city, dual-harbour" development strategy and is meant to follow a circular economy. Planned area is 200 square kilometres (77 square miles), of which 162 square kilometres (63 square miles) is land.

Tianjin Binhai New Area (TBNA). It sits where the Beijing-Tianjin city belt meets the Circum-Bohai belt, and acts as a gateway to North, Northeast and Northwest China. It lies in the centre of Northeast Asia and is the nearest departure point for the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

Farmland covers about 40% of the municipality, and wheat, rice and maize are the main crops. Beneath the surface lie roughly 1 billion tonnes of petroleum, with oilfields in Dagang District. Salt production is also an industry, and Changlu Yanqu is one of China's salt areas. Geothermal energy is a further resource, and deposits of manganese and boron beneath Tianjin were the first found in China. Electric power is supplied and maintained by Tianjin Electric Power.

At the end of 2009 the municipality had 12.28 million residents, of whom 9.8 million held Tianjin hukou (permanent residence). Urban districts housed 5.99 million of those permanent residents, and the countryside 3.81 million. After a recent shift towards growth the population reached 14.72 million by the end of 2013. The OECD estimated a metropolitan area population of 15.4 million as of 2010. The census figures leave out active-duty members of the People's Liberation Army.
Most residents are Han Chinese, but people from 51 of China's 55 minority groups live in the city. The larger minority communities are the Hui, Korean, Manchu and Mongol peoples.

Tianjin blends European buildings from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with modern Chinese concrete-and-glass towers. Redevelopment continues, but much of the colonial-era architecture is protected. The European look has a difficult history behind it. During the nineteenth century, Western powers seized this port following a quarrel over a British vessel; gunboats overcame the Chinese defenders, and under the 1856 Treaty of Tianjin Europeans obtained nine concession areas beside the Hai River, where they could trade and sell opium. Each concession was a self-contained enclave. The French put up châteaus and towers, while the Germans built red-tiled villas in Bavarian style. Unrest flared at a French orphanage in the Tianjin Incident of 1870 and again during the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, when foreigners pulled down the old city walls so that they could keep an eye on the local population.

The walled old city was largely torn down in 2000 and 2001, so only a handful of historic buildings remain, for instance the Tianjin Temple of Confucius. For sightseeing, head for the former concession streets that lie to the south and west of the central station and across the Hai River to the south. French châteaus make up the downtown area on the river's southern bank, British mansions stand to the east, and German-style houses survive further east and south.

Three national nature reserves lie within Tianjin. Baxianshan has hardly been touched by people over the years, so its forest ecology is largely intact. In Jizhou District, the Middle-Upper Yuan reserve is a geological site that the International Union of Geological Sciences has accepted as a global standard rock-layer reference. A third reserve protects the ancient coastline and wetlands, where three classic shell ridges show how the sea retreated and the Tianjin Plain came into being.

On the cultural side, Tianjin has two World Heritage sites. One is the Huangyaguan section of the Great Wall in the north of Jizhou District, the other the part of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal that runs through the city. A national 5A tourist area, Ancient Culture Street, is organised around the Tianhou Temple, which is the oldest surviving group of historic buildings in Tianjin and a key northern site for the cult of Mazu. Yangliuqing Town is known for its New Year paintings and carries the title "China Historical and Cultural Town".

Inside the city, the banks of the Haihe River combine traditional Chinese, European and contemporary buildings, and the "one bridge, one scene" night illumination has made the river a landmark that international guests admire, for example when the World Economic Forum is held. Time magazine, in August 2018, put the Tianjin Binhai Library (in Binhai New Area) at the top of its list of the World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018.

Tianjin's museum tradition goes back to the late Qing reform period. The French Jesuit priest and naturalist Émile Licent started the Musée Hoangho Paiho in 1914. It ranks among the earliest museums in China and played a leading role in palaeontology, geology, archaeology and the study of museums themselves.

There are now three national first-class museums in the city. The Tianjin Museum covers history and art and can be traced back to an earlier museum founded in 1918. Next comes the Tianjin Natural History Museum, which spans zoology, botany, palaeontology and geology and descends from Licent's institution. Third is the memorial hall for Zhou Enlai, China's first premier, and his wife Deng Yingchao, which stands at Water Park; both of them studied in Tianjin in their youth. A newer attraction, the National Maritime Museum of China, opened in May 2019 inside the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, and is billed as the country's first comprehensive national maritime museum aimed at the public. The city also has specialised halls, including the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Tianjin Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall.

From 2008 onward Tianjin has gradually improved its city parks and squares and scrapped admission charges, which means you can walk in for nothing. The central city's best-known green spaces are Water Park, the zoo, Nancuiping, Shuixi (which opened in October 2018), Beining, Meijiang, Ergong, Zhongshan, Central Park, People's Park, Hedong, Xigu, Haihe Music Park and Five Great Avenues Park. Beining Park started in 1906 as a plantation created by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi, and was later given the name "Ningyuan" from his motto that without tranquillity one cannot reach far. Binhai New Area has its own set, among them Haihe Bund, Taifeng, Ziyun, Shell Ridge Wetland, Aircraft Carrier and Haigang parks, plus the South Embankment coastal trail park and East Embankment park.

A second group of 16 suburban parks has been planned and built since 2011 around the city and Binhai New Area. They offer wilder, more rural scenery than the downtown parks. Construction started in 2012 on the Beiyunhe park in the north and the Xiqing park in the southwest, and by 2014 the whole set had been placed under the ecological redline, protecting a core area of 66,855 hectares.

Street lamps first appeared in Tianjin in 1902, and by the 1930s its bright streets had won the city the nickname "Northern City That Never Sleeps". Nowadays night lighting is written into urban planning. Across the central districts the scheme follows a "fishbone" layout: the main spine runs along the Haihe River and its continuations (the North Canal and South Canal), and smaller roads branch off it. The Haihe evening scene is a leading tourist route, and it has served as a backdrop for the Summer Davos Forum, the 13th National Games and the SCO Tianjin Summit.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

tianjin-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Tianjin University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Tianjin, register at Tianjin University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Tianjin University of Finance and Economics (天津财经大学), shortened to TUFE, is a state-run university located in Tianjin, a major port city. It opened in 1958 and ranks among the first Chinese institutions to teach applied economics and business administration. If you are weighing business, accounting or finance programmes in northern China, it is a specialist institution well worth a look.

In its first years the school depended heavily on teachers from Nankai University's business school as well as other professors across the north. This was a result of the national reorganisation of higher education after the People's Republic was founded. Since 1 October 1969 the university has come under the municipal government of Tianjin.

The campus is home to over 11,000 undergraduates and 1,300 graduate students. There are 117 professors and 226 assistant professors (the figure is given in the university's own wording and may refer to associate-level staff, so confirm titles with the university).

A complete ladder of study runs from doctorates to bachelor's degrees. Fields covered are economics and business, management, law, science with engineering, education, and literature plus art. TUFE grants bachelor's and master's degrees across 33 areas, while its doctoral degrees are limited to statistics, accounting and finance. The Ministry of Education permits TUFE to run MBA programmes. As early as 1987 it was in the first group approved by the State Council's Academic Degree Committee to run educational programmes with foreign universities and to award foreign degrees.

Another strength is professional accountancy. TUFE teaches the course content for Chinese Certified Public Accountants (CPA), and it hosts an exam centre of Britain's Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA), plus a test centre for the Cambridge English Certificate.

Another description gives forty majors, grouped under seven headings (economics, management, science, law, humanities, pedagogics and engineering). The university enrols every kind of student: those working for doctorates, masters, bachelor and associate degrees, adult trainees and overseas students. Teaching is organised in 12 schools and departments; examples are International Economics and Trade, Banking, Accounting and Statistics, along with Law, Languages, Art and Information. Specific majors named include:
Accounting subjects: Auditing, Financial Accounting, International Accounting and Certified Public Accountant
Statistics, and Ventures Management
Finance and trade: International Banking, Monetary and Banking, and International Trade
Other options: English Language and Literature, Business Japanese, E-commerce, Art Design and Business Law
The different counts quoted for majors (33 areas, forty majors) probably reflect different ways of counting, so check the current prospectus.

The main campus is at 25 Zhujiang Road in Hexi District, Tianjin, and most departments and research centres are located there. A second campus, Machangdao, is in the central district, close to the Tianjin Institute of Foreign Languages. The land area is given as 800,000 m2, with 455,600 m2 of floor space. Another passage gives 80 hectares and 400,000 square meters of floor space, so the sources do not agree exactly.

History is concentrated on the 'west campus', where the First Classroom Building and the Old Library stand. The 'east campus' feels newer, with the main library, fresh classroom blocks and several large multi-purpose buildings. Library holdings are in Chinese and other languages. For their own research, students can read current issues of most major economics journals, for example the American Economic Review, the Journal of Finance and the Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Rooms in the student apartments normally hold two or four people, and the apartment area includes gyms and a branch library. Basketball is the most popular sport, helped by the women's basketball team, which has been national champion several years running.
The International Exchange Center is a multi-purpose building that houses a cafeteria, accommodation and classrooms.

International exchange is something the university has pursued for many years. Over time it has made contacts with over 50 universities and research institutes in around 20 countries and regions. The list takes in North America (the United States and Canada), Australia and New Zealand, Asian partners (Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, India) and European ones: Great Britain, plus France, Sweden, Russia, Germany, Belgium and Greece. To date more than 1,000 overseas students have come, with students from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan counted among them, and many have taken doctoral, master's or bachelor's degrees.
A university is more than its buildings, so this section describes the city: its position, weather, air, economy, people and sights.

The Bohai Gulf's western shore is where Tianjin lies, facing Shandong and Liaoning across the water. The capital, Beijing, is 120 kilometers (75 mi) away to the northwest. On every side but the east, where the Bohai Sea provides the border, Tianjin is encircled by Hebei. Its territory spans latitudes 38° 34' to 40° 15' N and longitudes 116° 43' to 118° 04' E, and the area comes to 11,860.63 square kilometers (4,579.41 sq mi).

There are 153 km (95 mi) of coast and 1,137.48 kilometers (706.80 mi) of land boundary. As the northern terminus of the Grand Canal of China, Tianjin connects through it to the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers. Flat land dominates the municipality, with swamp close to the sea; in the north, though, the foothills of the Yan Mountains rise, and tidal flats run along the coastal plain beside the city. Jiuding Peak (九顶山), standing at 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft) in Ji County on the border with Hebei, is the highest point.

Five waterways come together inside the municipality to form the Hai River: the Ziya River (子牙河), the Daqing River (大清河), the Yongding River and the North and South Grand Canals. The river's mouth, where it enters the Pacific, is also in Tianjin, in Tanggu District. Two reservoirs are worth noting: Beidagang in the south (Dagang District) and Yuqiao in the north (Ji County).

In Köppen terms the climate is semi-arid (BSk, close to Dwa and Cwa). As elsewhere in East Asia, the monsoon shapes four seasons. The Siberian anticyclone brings cold, windy, dry winters; the monsoon season brings humid heat in summer. Spring tends to be windy and dry, and now and then sandstorms from the Gobi Desert blow through for days at a time.

January is the coldest month, averaging −2.8 °C (27.0 °F) day and night, while July averages 27.2 °C (81.0 °F); the whole year averages 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Readings at Xiqing District's main weather station have swung between −22.9 °C (−9 °F) and 41.1 °C (106 °F). Sunshine ranges between 45% of what is possible (July) and 61% (March and April), giving 2,460 hours across the year. Rain and snow total 521 millimeters (20.5 in) annually, with nearly three-fifths of that in July and August. Overall the city is in the semi-arid zone, although other parts of the municipality are classed as humid continental (Köppen Dwa).

tianjin-university-of-finance-and-econom.h: Air quality and the response to smog

blocks.x: In May 2014 the city government passed new rules to bring pollution down. The measures apply on days when pollution is severe: only half the usual number of vehicles may be on the roads, construction and factory work stop, schools close and big outdoor events are called off. In the past flights were also grounded and highways closed. Foreign professional sportsmen have commented on the air, calling it an obstacle to athletic activity and saying it is thick enough to "taste". It is good to be realistic about this before you arrive.

Petrochemicals, textiles, cars, machinery and metalworking are the main industries. The aircraft maker EADS Airbus has an assembly plant here for its A320 series, running since 2009. The world's fastest supercomputer in 2010, Tianhe-1A, sat in the National Supercomputing Center of Tianjin. The city produced ¥750.1 billion of GDP in 2009, which is RMB ¥62,403 per person.

TEDA, the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area, came into being on 6 December 1984 after the State Council approved it; it was among the very first state-level zones of its kind. It enjoys preferential state policies, and its task is to attract investment from China and abroad for modern technology-driven industries. It is part of the Tianjin Municipal Government, and its Administrative Commission runs TEDA on the government's behalf with provincial-level powers over administration and economic management.

The State Council approved 15 export processing zones at first, and the Tianjin one, approved on 27 April 2000, was among them. Customs officers keep constant watch over goods that enter or leave this closed special zone, and the central government offered preferential policies to draw in firms engaged in processing and trade. It sits northeast of TEDA, and the plan calls for 2.54 km2 (0.98 sq mi). A permanent wall divides the export processing area from the rest.

Within the air freight area of Tianjin Binhai International Airport is the Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone, funded jointly by the airport and the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone. Domestic and foreign air freight logistics firms there handle sorting, warehousing, distribution, processing and exhibitions, and the zone is in the middle of building northern China's biggest air freight base.

Northern China's only free trade zone is the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone, which the State Council approved in 1991. Distances: 30 km (19 mi) to the city proper, less than 1 km (0.62 mi) to the wharf, and 38 km (24 mi) to Tianjin Binhai International Airport.

Founded in 1992 and promoted to national level by the State Council in 1995, the Tianjin Tanggu Marine High-Tech Development Area is unique as the one national high-tech zone specialising in marine technology. In late 2008 it was host to 2,068 corporations in 5 industries: new materials, oil manufacturing, modern machinery and electronic information, among others.

Nangang Industrial Zone is a heavy industry and chemical base with its own harbour. It belongs to the city's "dual-city, dual-harbor" development strategy and works on circular economy principles. The planned total is 200 km2 (77 sq mi), and 162 km2 (63 sq mi) of that is dry land.
About 40% of the municipality is farmland, and wheat, rice and maize are the leading crops economically.

Below ground there are about 1 billion tonnes of petroleum deposits, and Dagang District has oilfields. Salt is another local industry, since Changlu Yanqu is one of China's salt-producing areas, and geothermal energy is also available. The manganese and boron found under Tianjin were the first of those minerals to be discovered in China. Tianjin Electric Power Utility builds, delivers and maintains electricity services.

Binhai New Area (TBNA) lies at the meeting point of the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt and the Circum-Bohai City Belt. It serves as an entrance to the north, northeast and northwest of China. Because it is in the middle of Northeast Asia, it is the closest departure point to the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

At the end of 2009 Tianjin Municipality had 12.28 million inhabitants, 9.8 million of whom held Tianjin hukou (permanent residence). Of the permanent residents, urban areas held 5.99 million and rural ones 3.81 million. Population has since grown, reaching 14.72 million at the end of 2013. An OECD estimate (the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) put the wider metropolitan area at 15.4 million people in 2010. These figures exclude members of the People's Liberation Army on active service.
Most residents are Han Chinese. Members of 51 of China's 55 minority groups live in Tianjin, and the largest minorities are the Hui, Korean, Manchu and Mongol peoples.

Tianjin mixes European architecture from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with modern Chinese concrete-and-glass buildings. Redevelopment goes on, but most colonial buildings are protected.

The port was taken over by Western powers during the 1800s following a dispute about a British ship. Gunboats overcame the Chinese defenders, and under the 1856 Treaty of Tianjin Europeans received nine concessions along the Hai River, where they could trade and sell opium. Each concession was a world of its own, with French châteaus and towers in one and red-tiled Bavarian-style villas built by Germans in another. Unrest broke out in 1870 at a French orphanage (the Tianjin Incident) and again in 1900, in the Boxer Rebellion, when foreigners knocked down the old city walls to keep an eye on the residents.

In 2000–2001 most of the old city was torn down, leaving a handful of historic buildings, including the Temple of Confucius. Today's visitors head for the former concession streets, found to the south and west of the central station and south of the Hai River. French châteaus make up the downtown area south of the water; the British mansions are to the east; and farther east and south the German-style buildings survive.

Tianjin has three national nature reserves. Baxianshan, thanks to minimal human interference over a long time, has largely kept its original forest ecology. The Middle–Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve (Jizhou District) is accepted by the International Union of Geological Sciences as a worldwide reference stratigraphic section. In the Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve, three typical shell ridges show plainly how sea gave way to land on the Tianjin Plain.

Two sites of World Cultural Heritage status add cultural interest: the Great Wall at Huangyaguan, in the north of Jizhou District, and the section of the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal that passes through Tianjin. Ancient Culture Street, a national 5A tourist attraction, centres on the Tianhou Temple, which is Tianjin's oldest surviving historical building complex and an important northern Chinese site of Mazu culture. Yangliuqing Town is known for its New Year Paintings and has the title "China Historical and Cultural Town".

In the urban area the banks of the Haihe River combine traditional Chinese, European and modern buildings and gradually form a distinctive skyline. Lit at night in a "one bridge, one scene" style, the river is a famous landmark, and international guests at big events like the World Economic Forum often come to see it. Time magazine named the Tianjin Binhai Library, in Binhai New Area, number one in its "World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018" ranking in August 2018.

Tianjin's museum tradition goes back to the reform years at the end of the Qing. One of China's first museums, the Musée Hoangho Paiho, was started in 1914 by Émile Licent, a French Jesuit priest and naturalist, and it played a big part in paleontology, geology, archaeology and museology.

Three museums in the city hold national first-class rank. First is the Tianjin Museum, covering history and art, which goes back to a museum set up in 1918. Second, the Natural History Museum is a large, multi-subject institution with zoology, botany, paleontology and geology, and it descends from the Musée Hoangho Paiho. tianjin-university-of-science-and-techno.h: Founding as a light industry college

blocks.x: In 1958 the school opened as the Hebei Institute (河北轻化工学院) of Light Industry. It was among the four earliest colleges in China to offer undergraduate courses in light industry, and the Ministry of Light Industry supervised it. The State Council ordered a reorganisation of higher education in 1959, and as a result Tianjin University handed over most of the teachers and experimental equipment of its Pulp and Paper Department.
1959: most staff and equipment of Tianjin University's Pulp and Paper Department transferred in.

1964: staff and facilities followed from two other institutes, first the fermentation engineering department of Beijing's light industry institute and then the plastics moulding and processing department from Wuxi's institute of the same kind.
1968: the new name was Tianjin Institute of Light Industry (天津轻化工学院).
1971: Tianjin University moved its entire Pulp and Paper Department across.
1972: the Ministry of Light Industry's Tanggu Salt Industry College and the Salt Chemistry Department of Beijing's Institute of Light Industry were merged and put under the school's control.

2002: the Ministry of Education gave its approval, and the name became Tianjin University of Science and Technology.
In short, the university's roots lie in paper, fermentation, plastics and salt chemistry, which gives it a very applied industrial character.

The coast measures 153 km (95 mi) and the land border 1,137.48 kilometres (706.80 miles). The northern end of China's Grand Canal, which joins the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, is at Tianjin. Spring is dry and windy, and sometimes sandstorms blow in from the Gobi Desert and can last several days.

In May 2014 the city administration passed new rules to cut pollution. On days when pollution is severe, they include cutting by half the vehicles permitted on the roads, stopping construction and manufacturing, closing schools and halting large outdoor activities. In the past, flights have been grounded as well and highways shut. Foreign-born professional sportsmen have commented that the air quality hinders athletic activity and is thick enough to "taste". If you have breathing difficulties, ask current students about the situation on bad days.

Petrochemicals, textiles, cars, machinery and metalworking are among Tianjin's industries. EADS Airbus has been assembling its Airbus A320 series airliners in the city since 2009. On heavy-pollution days, they call for roughly half of vehicles to stay off the road, a stop to building and factory work, school closures and an end to large-scale outdoor activities. As a student you should keep an eye on daily air-quality readings, particularly in winter, and consider a good mask for the worst days. The city's environmental authorities publish current information if you want to check before travelling.

Heavy and light industry both matter: petrochemicals, textiles, vehicles, machinery and metalworking. The Airbus A320 series is assembled in a plant run by EADS Airbus, in operation since 2009. In 2010 the National Supercomputing Center of Tianjin housed Tianhe-1A, then the fastest supercomputer in the world, but such rankings change fast. For 2009, GDP stood at ¥750.1 billion, which is ¥62,403 per person. Because these are older numbers, current data should be taken from the city statistics office, and the same goes for the other economic figures in this section, which mix several different years.

Around 40% of the land is farmland, and the main crops are maize, rice and wheat. Beneath the surface lie roughly 1 billion tonnes of petroleum, and Dagang District holds the oilfields. Salt is made too, and Changlu Yanqu is among China's salt-producing areas. Geothermal energy is another resource, and the manganese and boron found beneath Tianjin were China's first discoveries of those minerals. Tianjin Electric Power Utility builds, delivers and maintains the city's electricity supply.
#### Development zones

The Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA) opened on December 6, 1984 with State Council approval, among the earliest state-level zones of its kind. State preferential policies help it attract domestic and foreign investment into modern, technology-based industry. The municipal government delegates powers to its Administrative Commission, which has provincial-level authority over administration and economic management.

The Tianjin Export Processing Zone, approved on April 27, 2000, was one of the first 15 in the country. Customs officers supervise goods entering and leaving this special enclosed zone all the time, and a permanent wall divides it from the rest. Preferential central government policies encourage processing and trade firms to invest. The zone is planned to cover 2.54 km2 (0.98 sq mi) and lies northeast of TEDA.

The Airport Economic Area contains the Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone, which the Port Free Trade Zone and Binhai International Airport invested in together. It sits within the airport's air freight area and hosts sorting, storage, distribution, processing and exhibition businesses, both Chinese and foreign. The zone is building what will be the biggest air freight base in northern China.

No other free trade zone exists in northern China besides the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone, which the State Council approved in 1991. It is 30 km from the city proper (19 mi), under 1 km from the wharf (0.62 mi) and 38 km (24 mi) from Binhai International Airport.

Founded in 1992, the Tianjin Tanggu National Marine High-Tech Development Area was promoted by the State Council to national level in 1995 and is the single national high-tech area dedicated to the marine technology industry. At the end of 2008 there were 2,068 companies in 5 industries: electronic information, modern machinery manufacturing, oil manufacturing and new materials, among others.

Nangang Industrial Zone is a base for heavy and chemical industry, with a harbour, part of the "dual-city, dual-harbor" development strategy, and also a circular-economy zone. Its planned area is 200 km2 (77 sq mi) with 162 km2 (63 sq mi) of land.

Binhai New Area (TBNA) lies where the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt meets the Circum-Bohai City Belt. From here you reach the north, northeast and northwest of China. It sits at the heart of Northeast Asia and is the closest starting point for the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

Tianjin Municipality had 12.28 million residents at the end of 2009. Of them, 9.8 million held Tianjin hukou (permanent residence) and lived in the city, with 5.99 million of the permanent residents in urban areas and 3.81 million in rural ones. The population has recently begun growing, and it reached 14.72 million at the end of 2013. In 2010 the OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 15.4 million. All of these are older figures, and a recent census will give updated totals.

Most residents are Han Chinese. Tianjin is home to people from 51 of China's 55 minority groups, and the largest minorities are the Hui, Korean, Manchu and Mongol peoples. Serving members of the People's Liberation Army are not counted in these figures.

European buildings of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries stand beside modern Chinese concrete-and-glass structures. Redevelopment is continuing, yet much of the colonial architecture is protected.

In the nineteenth century, a dispute over a British ship gave Western powers a pretext to take the port; their gunboats defeated Chinese forces. A later treaty gave Europeans nine concessions on the Hai River to trade, including in opium. Each enclave was self-contained, with French châteaus and towers and German red-tiled Bavarian villas. A French orphanage was the scene of the 1870 Tianjin Incident, and tension flared again in the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, when foreigners knocked down the old city walls to keep an eye on the residents. In 2000–2001 most of the old city was demolished, and few historic buildings remain, one being the Tianjin Temple of Confucius.

Today's visitors head for the old concession streets, which are south and west of the central station and south of the Hai River. The French châteaus make up the downtown district south of the river, with British mansions to the east, and German-style buildings further east and south.

The municipality has three national nature reserves. Baxianshan has kept most of its original forest ecology because of long-term low human disturbance. The Middle–Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve, in Jizhou District, has been accepted as a global standard stratigraphic section by the world geological sciences union (IUGS). A third reserve, the Ancient Coast and Wetlands one, has three typical shell ridges, which show clearly how the Tianjin Plain changed from sea to land as the water withdrew.

There are two World Cultural Heritage sites: the section of the Great Wall at Huangyaguan, in northern Jizhou District, and the stretch of the Grand Canal (Beijing to Hangzhou) that runs through Tianjin. Ancient Culture Street, built around Tianhou Temple, is a national 5A tourist attraction. The temple is the oldest surviving group of historic buildings in Tianjin and a key northern site for Mazu culture. Yangliuqing Town, known for the New Year paintings that carry its name, is officially a "China Historical and Cultural Town".

In the city centre the two banks of the Haihe River mix traditional Chinese, European and modern buildings, step by step forming a distinctive skyline. Lights along the river, with "one bridge, one scene", have made it a landmark and a main sightseeing route for international guests at big events like the World Economic Forum. In August 2018, Time magazine put the Binhai Library, found in Binhai New Area, at number one in its list of the "World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018".

Museums began in the late Qing reform era. Émile Licent, a French Jesuit priest and naturalist, founded the Musée Hoangho Paiho in 1914, one of the earliest in China, and it played an important role in palaeontology, geology, archaeology and museology.

At present three museums are national first-class. The Tianjin Museum covers history and art and traces its origins to a museum set up in 1918. The Natural History Museum is a large, multidisciplinary museum of zoology, botany, palaeontology and geology, and it grew out of the Musée Hoangho Paiho. The third is the memorial hall at Water Park for Zhou Enlai, first premier of the People's Republic, and his wife Deng Yingchao, who both studied in Tianjin when young.

The National Maritime Museum of China opened in May 2019 in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, the first comprehensive national maritime museum meant for the general public. There are also thematic halls, such as the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall, the Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Science and Technology Museum.

The city has been upgrading parks and squares since 2008 and has removed entrance fees so that anyone can use them. Among urban parks are Water Park, the zoo, Nancuiping, Shuixi, Meijiang, Ergong, Zhongshan, Hedong and Xigu, as well as People's Park, Five Great Avenues Park, Central Park and the Haihe Music Park. Beining Park began in 1906 as a plantation built by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi. It was later renamed "Ningyuan" after a motto that says one cannot reach far without tranquility. Shuixi Park formally opened in October 2018. In Binhai New Area the main parks are Haihe Bund, Taifeng, Ziyun, Haigang, Shell Ridge Wetland, Aircraft Carrier, South Embankment Coastal Trail and East Embankment.

Since 2011 the city has planned and built sixteen suburban parks, in the surroundings of Tianjin and of Binhai New Area. Compared with city parks, these have more natural scenery and a rural character. Construction began in 2012 on the Xiqing Suburban Park in the southwest and the Beiyunhe Suburban Park in the north. By 2014 all 16 were part of the ecological redline, with a combined core area of 66,855 hectares.

The first street lighting in Tianjin dates from 1902, and by the 1930s its illuminated streets had earned it the label of a "Northern City That Never Sleeps". Today night lighting is part of specialised urban planning. In the central districts, lights form a "fishbone" pattern, with the Haihe as the main axis and side roads branching off it, along the river and its continuations, the North and South Canals. The Haihe's night view is a leading tourist route. It has been used for events including the 13th National Games, the Summer Davos Forum and the SCO Tianjin Summit.
Tianjin No. 7 Middle School is one of the city's middle schools. Families moving to Tianjin with children can ask the local education bureau about school places.

tianjin-university-of-technology-and-edu.h: About Tianjin University of Technology and Education

blocks.x: The Tianjin University of Technology and Education (TUTE; 天津职业技术师范大学; lit. 'Tianjin Vocational and Technical Normal University') is a municipal public vocational university in Hexi, Tianjin, China. It is affiliated with the City of Tianjin, and co-sponsored by the Tianjin Municipal People's Government, the Ministry of Education, and the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security.

In February 1979, in order to meet the needs of teachers in the development of technical education, the Central People's Government established the "Tianjin Technical Teachers College" (天津技工师范学院) based on the "Tianjin Labor Bureau Technical School" (天津市劳动局技工学校) and "Tianjin Fifth Machine Tool Factory" (天津市第五机床厂). The school was placed under the State General Administration of Labor (国家劳动总局).
In October 1983, the school was renamed "Tianjin Vocational and Technical Teachers College" (天津职业技术师范学院) with the approval of the Ministry of Labor and Human Resources.

In February 2000, with the approval of the General Office of the State Council, the school was transferred from the central government sponsorship to the central and local co-sponsorship, with main management responsibility in the City of Tianjin.
In May 2004, the school was renamed "Tianjin Engineering Teachers College" (天津工程师范学院) with the approval of the Ministry of Education.
In March 2010, the school was approved by the Ministry of Education to be renamed "Tianjin Vocational and Technical Normal University" (天津职业技术师范大学).

In 1993, TUTE began to recruit foreign students. In 2006, TUTE was allowed to enroll students with Chinese Government Scholarship. There were also "Principal Scholarship" to reward excellent overseas students.

In 2008, TUTE established its International School. In charge of the enrollment, cultivation, and management of overseas students. It became one of the fastest growing schools in Tianjin for overseas students. During the past few years, TUTE has also cooperated with schools from the United States, Japan, South Korea, Britain, and Australia.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Tianjin, where Tianjin University of Technology and Education is located.

Tianjin is located on the west coast of the Bohai Gulf; the provinces of Shandong and Liaoning are located across those waters. The city is bordered by Beijing, which is 120 kilometers (75 mi) to the northwest. Tianjin is surrounded on all sides by Hebei, with the exception of its eastern border, which is the Bohai Sea. With a latitude ranging from 38° 34' to 40° 15' N and a longitude ranging from 116° 43' to 118° 04' E, the total area of the city is 11,860.63 square kilometers (4,579.41 sq mi).

The city has 153 km (95 mi) of coastline and 1,137.48 kilometers (706.80 mi) of land border. It is located at the northern end of the Grand Canal of China, which connects with the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers. The municipality is generally flat and is swampy near the coast; however, it has hills in the north, where the Yan Mountains enter Tianjin. Tidal flats occur on the coastal plain adjacent to the city. The highest point in the municipality is Jiuding Peak (九顶山) in Ji County on the northern border with Hebei; the mountain has an altitude of 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft).

In the Tianjin Municipality, the Hai River forms at the confluence of the Ziya River (子牙河), Daqing River (大清河), Yongding River, North Grand Canal, and South Grand Canal; it enters the Pacific Ocean within the municipality as well as in Tanggu District. Reservoirs include the Beidagang Reservoir in the south (in Dagang District) and the Yuqiao Reservoir in the north in Ji County.

Tianjin has a semi-arid climate (using the Köppen system, the city has a BSk climate bordering on Dwa and Cwa). As in other areas of East Asia, the city has a four-season, monsoon-influenced climate; it also has cold, windy, and dry winters due to the Siberian anticyclone and hot, humid summers due to the monsoon season. Spring in the city is dry and windy; the season sometimes consists of sandstorms blowing in from the Gobi Desert, which are capable of lasting for several days. The monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from −2.8 °C (27.0 °F) in January to 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in July, with an annual mean of 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Extreme temperatures in the city at the main weather station in Xiqing District have ranged from −22.9 °C (−9 °F) to 41.1 °C (106 °F). With the monthly percentage of the possible amount of sunshine ranging from 45% in July to 61% in March and April, the city receives 2,460 hours of sunshine annually. Having an annual total precipitation of 521 millimeters (20.5 in), with nearly three-fifths of it occurring in July and August alone, the city lies within the semi-arid climate zone, although parts of the municipality are humid continental (Köppen BSk/Dwa, respectively).

In May 2014, the city's administration enacted new laws in an attempt to lower the city's pollution levels. These measures included several methods to restrict pollution on days when is severe, such as by halving the number of vehicles allowed on roads, halting construction and manufacturing activity, closing schools, and halting large-scale outdoor activities.
In the past, flights have also been grounded and highways have been closed.
Foreign-born professional sportsmen have made statements regarding Tianjin's air quality, citing it as an impediment to athletic activity and being thick enough to "taste".

Industries include petrochemical industries, textiles, car manufacturing, mechanical industries, and metalworking. EADS Airbus is one of the manufacturers in the city, and has opened an assembly plant for its Airbus A320 series airliners; the plant has been operational since 2009. As of 2010, the fastest supercomputer in the world, Tianhe-1A, has been located at the National Supercomputing Center of Tianjin. The city's GDP in 2009 was ¥750.1 billion, with a GDP per capita of RMB ¥62,403.

As one of the first state-level economic and technological development zones, the Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA) was founded on December 6, 1984, with the approval of the State Council. It is given state preferential policies with the task of attracting domestic and foreign investment to develop new technology-oriented modern industries. As an affiliated organization of the Tianjin Municipal Government, the Administrative Commission of Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area exercises unified administration of TEDA on behalf of the Tianjin Municipal Government and has provincial-level administrative and economic management rights.

The Tianjin Export Processing Zone is one of the first 15 export processing zones approved by the State Council, having been approved on April 27, 2000. This area is a special enclosed zone. where Customs officials conduct constant administration for commodities transported into and out of the zone. The central government granted the special economic zone preferential policies to attract enterprises in the business of processing and trade to invest in the zone. The Tianjin Export Processing Zone is located to the northeast of TEDA and has a planned area of 2.54 km2 (0.98 sq mi). The area developed in the first phase is 1 square meter (11 sq ft) wide. A permanent wall is built to separate the export processing and non-export processing zones.

The Tianjin Airport International Logistics Zone is jointly invested by the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone and Tianjin Binhai International Airport. It is located inside the airfreight area of Tianjin Binhai International Airport. It has domestic and foreign airfreight logistics enterprises engaged in sorting, warehousing, distribution, processing, and exhibition. It is in the process of constructing the largest airfreight base in northern China.

The Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone is the only free trade zone in northern China. The zone was approved for establishment in 1991 by State Council. It is 30 km (19 mi) from Tianjin city proper, less than 1 km (0.62 mi) away from the wharf, and 38 km (24 mi) away from Tianjin Binhai International Airport.

Tianjin Electric Power Utility constructs, delivers and maintains electrical power services.

The Tianjin Binhai New Area (TBNA) is located at the juncture of the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt and the Circum-Bohai City Belt. It is the gateway to North China, Northeast China, and Northwest China. Lying in the center of Northeast Asia, it is the nearest point of departure of the Eurasian Continental Bridge.
