The city faces the Bohai Gulf on its western shore, and across the water lie Shandong and Liaoning. Beijing is 120 kilometres (75 mi) to the northwest. The municipality is ringed by Hebei on every side except the east, where it meets the Bohai Sea. It lies between latitudes 38° 34' and 40° 15' N and longitudes 116° 43' and 118° 04' E, and it covers 11,860.63 square kilometres (4,579.41 square miles).
Its coastline is 153 km (95 mi) long and its land boundary 1,137.48 kilometres (706.80 mi). The Grand Canal, which connects with the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers, has its northern terminus in Tianjin.

The municipality is mostly flat and swampy near the coast, with tidal flats on the coastal plain next to the city. Only the north has hills, where the Yan Mountains extend into the municipality. Its summit, Jiuding Peak (九顶山), stands in Ji County on the Hebei border and reaches 1,078.5 m (3,538 ft).

Five waterways meet inside Tianjin to create the Hai River: the Ziya (子牙河), the Daqing (大清河), the Yongding and the North and South Grand Canals. It flows out to the sea in Tanggu District, also within the municipality. Reservoirs include Yuqiao, in Ji County in the north, and Beidagang, in the south at Dagang District.

Tianjin is semi-arid (Köppen BSk, bordering on Dwa and Cwa), and as elsewhere in East Asia it has four seasons shaped by the monsoon. Winters are cold, windy and dry because of the Siberian anticyclone, and summers are hot and humid when the monsoon arrives. Spring is dry and windy, and Gobi Desert sandstorms sometimes blow in and last for several days.

January is the coldest month, averaging -2.8 °C (27.0 °F), and July the warmest at 27.2 °C (81.0 °F), with a yearly mean of 13.3 °C (55.9 °F). Readings at Xiqing District's main station have gone as low as -22.9 °C (-9 °F) and as high as 41.1 °C (106 °F). Possible sunshine is 45% in July and 61% in March and April, and the city gets 2,460 hours of sunshine a year. Annual precipitation is 521 millimetres (20.5 in), with nearly three-fifths falling in July and August alone. The city is therefore classed semi-arid, although some of the municipality counts as humid continental.

In May 2014 the city government passed new rules to bring down pollution. On days when pollution is severe, they cut the number of vehicles allowed on the road in half, stop construction and manufacturing, close schools and halt large outdoor events. In the past, flights have been grounded and highways closed. Foreign professional sportsmen have spoken about the air, saying it hinders athletic activity and is so thick they can "taste" it. Anyone with breathing problems should consider this before choosing the city.

Tianjin's industries include petrochemicals, textiles, car making, machinery and metalworking. EADS Airbus has an assembly plant for its A320 series airliners, running since 2009. As of 2010, the world's fastest supercomputer, Tianhe-1A, was based in Tianjin at its National Supercomputing Center. GDP in 2009 came to ¥750.1 billion, or ¥62,403 per head.

Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area (TEDA): founded on 6 December 1984 with State Council approval, among the first state-level zones of this kind. It enjoys state preferential policies in order to draw domestic and foreign investment and build technology-oriented modern industry. Its administrative commission acts for the municipal government and holds provincial-level administrative and economic management powers.

Tianjin Export Processing Zone: on 27 April 2000 it became part of the first batch of 15 such zones nationwide. Customs staff constantly regulate whatever goes in or out of this special enclosed area, and central government gives it preferential policies to bring in processing and trading companies. Northeast of TEDA, it is planned to cover 2.54 square kilometres (0.98 square miles). A permanent wall divides the zone from non-export areas.

Tianjin Airport Economic Area (the Airport International Logistics Zone): the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone and Binhai International Airport invested in it together, and it lies in the airport's cargo area. Domestic and foreign air freight companies there do sorting, warehousing, distribution, processing and exhibition work, and it is being built into northern China's largest air freight base.

Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone: approved by the State Council in 1991, it remains the single free trade zone in northern China. Distances: 30 km (19 mi) to the urban centre, less than 1 km (0.62 mi) to the wharf, and 38 km (24 mi) to the airport.

Tianjin Tanggu National Marine High-Tech Development Area: founded in 1992 and upgraded to national level by the State Council in 1995, the only national-level high-tech area specialising in marine technology.

Tianjin Nangang Industrial Zone: a base for heavy industry and chemicals, with a harbour, that forms part of Tianjin's "dual-city, dual-harbor" spatial strategy and is run as a circular-economy zone. The planned area is 200 km2 (77 sq mi), 162 km2 (63 sq mi) of it land.

Binhai New Area (TBNA): placed where the Beijing-Tianjin City Belt meets the Circum-Bohai City Belt, it serves as a gateway to northern, northeastern and northwestern China. It also sits in the middle of Northeast Asia, and is the closest starting point of the Eurasian Continental Bridge.

Farmland makes up about 40% of the municipality's area, with wheat, rice and maize the most important crops. Tianjin has about 1 billion tonnes of petroleum deposits, and Dagang District has oilfields. Salt production is another industry, Changlu Yanqu being one of China's salt-producing areas, and geothermal energy is a further resource. The first manganese and boron deposits ever found in China lie under Tianjin. Electricity services are built, delivered and maintained by Tianjin Electric Power Utility.

At the end of 2009 the municipality had 12.28 million people, of whom 9.8 million held Tianjin hukou (permanent residence). Of the permanent residents, 3.81 million were rural and 5.99 million urban. Population growth has picked up recently, reaching 14.72 million by the end of 2013. The OECD estimated that the metropolitan area had 15.4 million people in 2010. Most residents are Han Chinese, and people from 51 of China's 55 minority groups live in the city, with the larger minorities being Hui, Korean, Manchu and Mongol. The population figures exclude active-duty members of the People's Liberation Army.

Walking through Tianjin means passing from nineteenth- and early twentieth-century European façades to modern towers of glass and concrete. Redevelopment continues, yet a lot of the colonial-era architecture is protected.

The story behind it begins in the 1800s. After a quarrel over a British vessel, Western powers took the port: gunboats overcame Chinese forces, and under the Treaty of Tianjin of 1856 Europeans received nine concessions beside the Hai River, where they were allowed to trade and to sell opium. Each enclave was self-sufficient. French residents put up châteaus and towers, and Germans built red-roofed villas in the Bavarian manner. Two episodes show how tense things became. In 1870, the Tianjin Incident broke out at a French orphanage. In 1900, during the Boxer Rebellion, foreign troops pulled down the old city walls so they could watch the population. The old walled city itself was largely levelled in 2000 and 2001; among the few historic buildings left is the Tianjin Temple of Confucius.

If you want to see the foreign quarters today, head for the former concession streets located west and south of the central station and south of the river. The French area, with its châteaus, makes up the downtown south of the Hai, British mansions are to the east, and German-style buildings are found further east and south.

Tianjin has three national nature reserves. In Baxianshan, little human interference over a long period has left the forest ecology largely intact. In Jizhou District the Middle-Upper Yuan Geologic National Nature Reserve is accepted by the International Union of Geological Sciences as a global reference section of rock strata. The Tianjin Ancient Coast and Wetlands National Nature Reserve displays three typical shell ridges, which show clearly how the plain turned from sea floor into land as the sea retreated.

Cultural landmarks include two World Heritage sites, namely the Huangyaguan section of the Great Wall in northern Jizhou District and the Tianjin stretch of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal. Ancient Culture Street, a national 5A attraction, is built around Tianhou Temple, the oldest surviving group of historic buildings in the city and an important northern site for the cult of Mazu. Yangliuqing Town is known for its New Year paintings and carries the title "China Historical and Cultural Town".

Along the Haihe River in the city, both banks combine traditional Chinese, European and contemporary architecture, producing a skyline that is unmistakably Tianjin. Lighting on the "one bridge, one scene" principle makes the river glow at night, and it has become a headline sight for international visitors, for instance during the World Economic Forum. In August 2018 Time magazine's "World's 100 Greatest Places of 2018" put Tianjin Binhai Library, in Binhai New Area, at number one.

The city's museum tradition dates to the late Qing period of reform. A French Jesuit and naturalist, Émile Licent, set up the Musée Hoangho Paiho in 1914, one of the earliest museums in China, and it contributed to paleontology, geology, archaeology and museum studies.
Today three museums hold the highest national grade:
Tianjin Museum, a general history and art museum that traces itself to an earlier Tianjin Museum from 1918.
Tianjin Natural History Museum, a large museum covering zoology, botany, paleontology and geology, which evolved from the Musée Hoangho Paiho.
Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall, beside Water Park, honouring China's first premier and his wife, both of whom studied in Tianjin as young people.

The National Maritime Museum of China opened in May 2019 in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City and is described as the country's first national, comprehensive museum of the sea for the public. Visitors can also see the Tianjin Science and Technology Museum, the Urban Planning Exhibition Hall and the Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall.

From 2008 the city began renovating its parks and squares and dropped entrance charges, making them free for everyone. In the urban area these are Water Park, the zoo, Nancuiping, Shuixi, Beining, Meijiang, Ergong, Zhongshan, Haihe Music, Central, People's, Hedong, Five Great Avenues and Xigu parks. Beining Park began in 1906 as a plantation owned by the industrialist Zhou Xuexi, and was later renamed "Ningyuan" after a motto he favoured: "Without tranquility, one cannot reach far". Shuixi Park only opened in October 2018.

Binhai New Area has its own set: Haihe Bund Park, Taifeng Park, Ziyun Park, the South Embankment Coastal Trail Park, East Embankment Park, Shell Ridge Wetland Park, Aircraft Carrier Park and Haigang Park.

Beyond these, officials planned and built 16 suburban parks around the city and Binhai New Area from 2011 onward. These are wilder and more rural in feel than the city parks. Beiyunhe Suburban Park (north) and Xiqing Suburban Park (southwest) were both started in 2012, and by 2014 all 16 were placed inside the ecological redline, with core area totalling 66,855 hectares.

The first street lamps appeared in 1902. By the 1930s the brightly lit streets had given Tianjin the nickname "Northern City That Never Sleeps". These days night lighting is covered by dedicated urban planning. In central districts the pattern resembles a fishbone: a main spine follows the Haihe and its continuations, the North Canal and South Canal, and secondary routes branch from it. The riverside night view is a leading tourist route and a backdrop to occasions including the Summer Davos Forum, the 13th National Games and the SCO Tianjin Summit.

tianjin-university-of-traditional-chines.h: Bringing it together for an applicant

blocks.x: This is a municipal public university devoted to traditional Chinese medicine, financed jointly by national and city bodies. Its home city is a large port municipality, only 120 kilometres from Beijing. The weather brings cold, dry winters, humid summers and sometimes sandy springs, and the pollution rules show that air quality can be an issue. In return you get colonial-era architecture, free parks, good museums and a river that is attractive at night. For anything specific to the university, such as programmes, campuses and admissions, consult its official website.
Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine lists 48 programs for international students on this site: 6 bachelor, 23 master's, 15 doctoral, 4 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 37 taught in Chinese, 11 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 31,000 to CNY 41,000 (median CNY 31,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 43,000 to CNY 53,000 (median CNY 43,000), according to the university's published fee table.

48 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (5):
Acupuncture and Tuina
Medicinal Chemistry
Pharmaceutics
Pharmacology
Traditional Chinese Pharmacology
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

tianjin-university-of-traditional-chines.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Tianjin, register at Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Tibet University (西藏大学 in Chinese, meaning University of Tibet; sometimes shortened to UTibet or TU) is a public university in Lhasa, the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region, and is run at regional level. Funding comes from two sources, the Ministry of Education and the regional authorities. It has been included in Project 211 and in the Double First-Class Construction programme.

It ranks among China's national key universities, and no other university in the autonomous region is larger. Its department of Tibetan studies has an international reputation, and most of its students are ethnic Tibetans, so the university keeps its attention on local communities and local culture.
There are four campuses in Lhasa: Na Jin, He Ba Lin, the Financial School campus and the Medical School campus.

The earliest ancestor of the university was a set of informal classes started in 1951 by the cadre school of the Tibet Military District. The school was renamed Tibet Local Cadre School in 1956, and in 1961 a Tibetan Administrative Cadre School was formed on its foundations, headed by Ngapoi Ngawang Jigme. October 1965 brought another new name, Tibetan Teacher Training School, and in 1966 it took in 755 children of farmers and herdsmen. A further change came in 1975, when it became the Tibetan Teacher Training College, with teaching in three groupings: politics and language, maths and physics, and the arts with physical education. A Department of Tibetan Language was merged in during 1982.

The State Council gave formal approval in May 1983 for a University of Tibet, with the existing teachers college in Lhasa as its base. It was officially founded on 20 July 1985, counted as one of 43 projects to assist Tibet. Eight departments were running by 1989, alongside a department for Tibetan language training. Subjects ranged from Tibetan language and literature to political history, art and Tibetan medicine, and from maths and science, chemistry and biology to economics and management.

After 1999 a series of other institutions were absorbed, which broadened its range of departments. Those joining included the region's art school, the regional finance school, the Tibet Medical College and the medical department of the Tibet Institute for Nationalities. The last big merger took place in March 2001: with Ministry of Education approval, the university combined with an agricultural and animal husbandry college (Tibet College of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry), and the result is today's Tibet University.
In December 2008 the university became a beneficiary of Project 211, and in 2017 the central government included it in the Double First-Class University Plan.

tibet-university.h: Student life and who studies here

blocks.x: Estimates of enrolment vary between roughly 7,500 and 8,000 students, so check the university's own site for the current number. Nearly 20% of students are in the Department of Tibetan Studies, which has a high reputation and attracts international students as well as local ones, even though most teaching is in Chinese. Every student must pass a Tibetan language examination before graduating.
Foreign students have been welcome since 1993. International students may study Tibetan as a foreign language, and some courses, such as Tibetan music and fine arts, are open to them.

Tibet University is consistently the top-ranked university in the Tibet Autonomous Region. Since 2020 it has been among the top 300 universities in China in the Best Chinese Universities Ranking (the Shanghai Ranking), which placed it 189th in China in 2022. The University Ranking by Academic Performance for 2024 to 2025 put it 2023rd in the world.
Teaching is divided among 14 colleges. The numbers add up as follows, by area of study.
Humanities and sciences: the College of Letters, the College of Science and the College of Engineering
The College of Medicine and the College of Arts
Business: the College of Economics and Management and, separately, the College of Finance and Economics
The College of Foreign Languages
Public affairs and teaching: the College of Political Science and Law and the College of Education
The College of Information Science and Technology
The College of Marxism, the College of Ecology and Environment, and the Institute of Chinese National Community

For a student, what matters about daily life is largely the city outside the campus: its air, weather, transport and things to do. What follows is an introduction to Lhasa, the city that the university calls home.

Lhasa stands on the central Tibetan Plateau, roughly 3,600 m up (11,800 ft), with surrounding peaks that rise to 5,500 m (18,000 ft). At this height the air holds only about 68 percent of the oxygen found at sea level, so new arrivals should expect to feel the altitude and give themselves time to adjust.

The Lhasa River, also called the Kyi River or Kyi Chu, is a tributary of the Yarlung Zangbo (Brahmaputra) and flows along the south side of the city. Tibetans in the area call it the merry blue waves. The river is 315 km (196 mi) long; it begins among the snow-capped summits and ravines of the Nyainqêntanglha range and ends at Qüxü, where it joins the Yarlung Zangbo, and the surrounding landscape is very beautiful. To the north are marshlands, which are mostly uninhabited. The roads in and out run east and west, while the roads to the north are less developed.
#### Chengguan District

Chengguan District sits along the middle section of the Lhasa River, where the ground slopes upward on both banks. Measured across, it is 28 kilometres (17 mi) from east to west, and from north to south it stretches 31 kilometres (19 mi). Its neighbours are Doilungdêqên District on the west, Dagzê County on the east, Lhünzhub County on the north and, to the south, Gonggar County in Lhoka (Shannan) Prefecture.

Chengguan stands 3,650 metres (11,980 ft) up and has an area of 525 square kilometres (203 sq mi); only 60 square kilometres (23 sq mi) of that is built-up urban land. Its average yearly temperature is 8 °C (46 °F), and rainfall is 300 to 500 millimetres (12 to 20 in), mostly between July and September.

Chengguan District is the administrative name for the inner urban area of a prefecture-level city, which in this case is Lhasa. Beyond the urban area the district is mostly mountainous with hardly any rural population. In administrative rank it equals a county. It was founded on 23 April 1961 and has 12 subdistricts that are entirely urban.

The high elevation gives Lhasa a cool, semi-arid climate (Köppen BSk), close to both a monsoon-influenced subtropical highland type (Cwb) and a humid continental type (Dwb). Winters are frosty and summers mild, but the sheltered valley protects the city from extreme cold, heat and strong winds.

The sun shines for 53 percent of possible hours in July and 84 percent in November, close to 3,000 hours over the year, and for that reason Tibetans sometimes name Lhasa the sunlit city. The coldest month is January, with an average of 0.6 °C (33.1 °F). June and July are the warmest, both averaging 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) over the day, although nights tend to be warmer in July. The annual mean works out at 9.9 °C (49.8 °F). Extremes run from -16.5 °C on 17 January 1968 to 30.8 °C on 24 June 2019 (2 to 87 °F).

Yearly precipitation totals 458 millimetres (18.0 in), most of it in July, August and September. December is by far the driest month, with a mere 0.3 millimetres (0.01 in), while August is the wettest, at 133.5 millimetres (5.26 in). Many people think summer is the best season, since rain tends to come at night and the days are still sunny. Pack layers: the sun is strong, but evenings are cold in most months.

An old reference work, the eleventh edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica (1910 to 1911), estimated that about 30,000 people lived in and around Lhasa, counting the lamas. A census taken in 1854 had found 42,000, but numbers are known to have fallen sharply after that. The same work noted roughly 1,500 Tibetan laymen as residents and about 5,500 Tibetan women, as well as around 2,000 Chinese in permanent households. The city also housed traders from Nepal and Ladakh (roughly 800), plus small numbers from Bhutan, Mongolia and other places. It observed with interest that the Chinese community had a crowded cemetery, looked after with care in its own tradition, and that metalworkers and mechanics were supplied by the Nepalese of the time.

Several Western travellers became famous in the early 20th century for journeys to Lhasa, including Francis Younghusband, Heinrich Harrer, Alexandra David-Néel and William Montgomery McGovern. At that time the city was the heart of Tibetan Buddhism, and nearly half of the people living there were reported to be monks. That share may be overstated, since it could include monks from monasteries in the surrounding area who travelled in for festivals and did not live in the city.

Most of the Chinese population before 1950 were merchants and officials. In the Lubu quarter lived the descendants of Chinese vegetable growers, some of whom married Tibetan women. Their ancestors reached Lhasa in the 1840s to 1860s, after a Chinese official took up the post of Amban.

Estimates for the middle of the 20th century differ. One writer says the city held about 10,000 people in 1959, plus some 10,000 monks at the Drepung and Sera monasteries. Another source, Hugh Richardson, wrote that in 1952 Lhasa had some 25,000 to 30,000 people, or 45,000 to 50,000 if one included the large monasteries on its edge.

The whole prefecture-level city has 521,500 people, a figure that includes known migrants but leaves out military garrisons. Of these, 257,400 live in the urban area (100,700 of them migrants) and 264,100 outside it. Nearly half of the prefecture's people live in Chengguan District, which contains the urban area, the actual city.

Ethnic Tibetans, Han, Hui and other groups live in the urban area. It was taken in November, a time when many Han people working seasonally in sectors like construction would have been away, and it excluded military personnel. A 2011 book suggested that as many as two out of three city residents are non-Tibetan, while the government states that the district overall remains 63% ethnic Tibetan. By 2014, half of the Han people in Tibet were living in the district, and schools often taught in two languages or entirely in Chinese. These numbers are from different years and sources, so use them as rough guides.

Lhasa's development relies on competitive industry and a feature economy. To keep population growth and the environment in balance, tourism and services are being promoted as the main future drivers. Many rural residents still farm and herd in traditional ways, and Lhasa has long been the hub of the Tibetan trading network. Chemical and car-making plants operated in the area for many years and caused heavy pollution, a situation that has improved recently. Nearby mines produce copper, lead and zinc, and experiments continue with new mining methods and geothermal heat extraction.

Farming and herding are regarded as of a high standard, with highland barley and winter wheat the main crops. The area is rich in water resources, geothermal heat, solar energy and mines. Electricity is widely available, and both machines and traditional methods are used to make textiles, leather, plastics, matches and embroidery. Traditional handicrafts have advanced considerably.

The expectation is that heavily polluting industries will fade as tourism and services expand, helping build a healthier ecosystem. Soil erosion, soil acidification and vegetation loss are among the environmental problems being addressed. Tourism now brings major business, drawing on the Potala Palace, the Jokhang, the Norbulingka Summer Palace, the large monasteries nearby, the Himalayan landscape and the many wild plants and animals of the high Central Asian plateau. Visitor numbers fell sharply in 2008 after unrest in the region, but the industry was recovering by 2009. The authorities have set an ambitious target of 10 million visitors by 2020, mostly domestic tourists. Not everyone is comfortable with the pace of change: UNESCO has voiced concern over the decline of Lhasa's traditional cityscape as renovation takes place near historic landmarks including the Potala Palace.
#### Hotels

Lhasa has a number of hotels. The Lhasa Hotel, a four-star property, is in the western suburbs to the north-east of Norbulingka. It opened in September 1985 and is the leading CITS property in Tibet. It can accommodate about 1000 guests in more than 450 rooms (suites), every one with air conditioning, a mini-bar and other basics, and some in traditional Tibetan decor. Holiday Inn managed it from 1986 to 1997, and it is the subject of a book titled The Hotel on the Roof of the World. Also worth knowing is the historic Banak Shöl Hotel at 8 Beijing Road, which is noted for its wooden verandas.
#### Notable businesses

Close to Tibet University, south of Yanhe Dong Lu, is the Lhasa Carpet Factory, which makes traditional Tibetan rugs for export around the world. A modern plant with about 300 workers, it is Tibet's largest rug producer. Women traditionally wove and men spun, but now both work on the rugs.

The Lhasa Brewery Company opened in 1988 on the northern edge of the city, south of Sera Monastery. At an altitude of 11,975 feet (3,650 m), it is described as the highest commercial brewery anywhere, and it turns out 85 percent of Tibet's beer today. The five-storey brewery cost an estimated US$20 to 25 million, and by 1994 it produced 30,000 bottles a day with some 200 workers. The Carlsberg group has strengthened its position in the Chinese market since 2000 with investment and expertise, and it has invested in the brewery, greatly improving the plant and working conditions and enlarging the premises to cover 62,240 square metres (15.3 acres).

A few night spots stage cabaret in which singers perform in Chinese, Tibetan and English, while dancers in traditional Tibetan dress trail long, flowing cloth from their arms. A number of small bars play live music, though their drinks lists are usually short and their customers mostly foreign tourists.

A local tradition of music and dance is Duihuan (སྟོད་གཞས་). In most of Tibet the traditional form uses a single instrument, but in Lhasa it uses four: the Zainianqin and Yangqin, along with the Jinghu, a bamboo flute and stringed bells that keep the rhythm. Musicians play, pull, strum and sing together.

Lhasa has two universities, Tibet University and the Tibet Tibetan Medical University, and three specialist colleges cover teacher training (Lhasa Teachers College), police training (Tibet Police College) and vocational and technical education (Tibet Vocational and Technical College).

The main university of the autonomous region is Tibet University (Tibetan: བོད་ལྗོངས་སློབ་གྲྭ་ཆེན་མོ་), with its campus in Chengguan District, east of the centre. A forerunner dates from 1952, and the university proper was founded in 1985 with Chinese government funding. Enrolment is around 8000. As a comprehensive university it holds the top academic position in the region, and it is a Project 211 member and a recipient of Double First-Class Construction support.

Lhasa has had rail service since 2006, when the Qinghai-Tibet Railway opened to passengers. At 5,072 metres above sea level, it is the highest railway in the world. Xining, capital of Qinghai Province, is the line's other main city, some 2,000 km (1,200 mi) from Lhasa, and from Xining passengers can continue across China's extensive railway system. Five trains arrive and depart at Lhasa railway station daily. Train Z21 takes 40 hours 53 minutes from Beijing West and reaches Lhasa at 13:03 every day, In the other direction, Z22 leaves Lhasa at 15:30 and arrives in Beijing West at 08:20 on the third day, after 40 hours 50 minutes. Other services connect Lhasa with Chengdu and Chongqing, Lanzhou and Xining, and Guangzhou and Shanghai, among further cities. Timetables may have changed, so check before booking.

Altitude sickness is a risk for passengers, so extra oxygen is pumped through the ventilation system and is available at each berth through a flap the passenger can open, and personal oxygen masks can be requested. Soft sleeper cabins have 64 seats per train, each with an electrical socket for devices.

Lhasa has been linked by rail to Shigatse, Tibet's second-largest city, since 2014. A third line, the Sichuan-Tibet railway, links Lhasa to Nyingchi County and the interior, finishing at Chengdu, and building began in June 2015.

For rail onward through South Asia, the nearest large Indian station is New Jalpaiguri at Siliguri in West Bengal, though extending India's network into Sikkim should make connections easier. There are early plans to link Lhasa with Kathmandu. A Chinese Tibetan spokesperson said in 2015 that an extension to Kathmandu, with a tunnel under Mount Everest, was expected to be finished by 2020; plans like this change, so treat that date with caution and check for updates.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

tibet-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Tibet University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Lhasa, register at Tibet University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Tongji University is a state-run institution in Shanghai and reports directly to China's Ministry of Education. Three flagship national funding schemes cover it: Project 211, along with Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction drive. For an applicant, that membership signals that the central government treats it as one of its priority universities for investment.

The school was founded in 1907 by German doctors working in Shanghai. Today it describes itself as having more than 2,815 scholars, among them 27 of whom belong to one of China's two national academies (sciences or engineering). The structure covers 29 colleges, plus 11 hospitals and 7 primary and secondary schools attached to it, so it is a very large academic family rather than a single faculty.
In short: a German-rooted, nationally backed, engineering-strong university in China's biggest city.

Tongji's story begins in 1907, when the German government joined forces with Erich Paulun, Oscar von Schab and Paul Krieg, all German physicians, to open a medical school for Chinese students, called Deutsche Medizinschule für Chinesen in German. The school was tied to the Tongji Hospital that the doctors had set up in the city, an initiative that came from Paulun. The word Tongji is the Shanghainese approximation of the German word deutsche, and it also carries a meaning of crossing the river in the same boat, which is to say working together.

Engineering was added to the curriculum, and in 1912 it was renamed to reflect its two fields, as a German medical and engineering school for Chinese students in Shanghai. Between 1923 and 1924 it became formally a Chinese university, called Tongji University, and in 1927 it became National Tongji University.

When the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937 to 1945) broke out, the campus could not stay in Shanghai. It moved first to Zhejiang Province, then on to Jiangxi and Yunnan, and finally to Sichuan. The university only returned to Shanghai in 1946. Few institutions in China have as strong a story of persistence as this one.

tongji-university.h: Reform, mergers and the Tongji Model

blocks.x: After a period of reorganisation, the State Council authorised Tongji, among the first universities to receive this permission, to start a graduate school. Entry into Project 211 brought substantial government money. In 1995 it was put under joint sponsorship by the Shanghai city government and the State Education Commission.

The next stage was consolidation. In 1996 Tongji merged with the Shanghai Institute of Urban Construction and the Shanghai Institute of Building Materials. The State Council praised this combination as the "Tongji Model" for reforming how Chinese higher education is organised. Then in April 2000 the larger Tongji took in Shanghai Railway University too. Today Tongji is a comprehensive university whose programmes span science, engineering, medicine, the arts, law, economics and management.
For readers who like dates, the main steps are below, starting from the most recent.

August 2026: the university announced that it would end its system of long-term (tenured-style) employment, a decision that caused public controversy. This is a recent development, so check the university's own news pages for the current position.
November 2010: a cooperation deal with Portugal's Instituto Superior Técnico turned IST into Tongji's Portuguese Campus.

July 2005: Tongji signed with the Milan and Turin polytechnics (Politecnico di Milano and Politecnico di Torino) to build a Sino-Italian University Campus in Shanghai, with a Sino-Italian House. A year on came PoliTong, a joint engineering project leading to two bachelor's degrees.
2002: Tongji was added to Project 985.
April 2000: merger with Shanghai Railway University, itself the product of a May 1995 union of the Shanghai Railway College with the Shanghai Railway Medical College.
August 1996: absorbed two Shanghai schools, the Institute of Urban Construction and the Institute of Building Materials.
November 1995: entered Project 211.
October 1995: it was declared a joint project of the former State Education Commission and Shanghai's municipal government.
December 1978: with the State Council's approval, relations with Germany resumed and Tongji became a channel for cultural, technological and scientific exchange between China and Germany.
February 1972: the Marine Geology Department from East China Normal University joined it.

1952: the Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry departments of its College of Science went to Fudan University, while Machinery, Electrical Engineering and Ship Manufacture moved to Shanghai Jiaotong University. In return Tongji received civil engineering and architecture teaching from Saint John's University in Shanghai, as well as units from several other institutions.

1951: the Biology Department of the College of Science went to East China Normal University, while the Medical School and the Survey Department of the College of Engineering moved to Wuhan in Hubei Province.
September 1949: the College of Literature and Arts and the College of Law were merged into Fudan University.
June 1949: the Shanghai Military Control Commission took over the university.
August 1946: the College of Science grew into a College of Literature and Science and returned to Shanghai.
April 1946: the university moved back to Shanghai.
1945: a College of Law was set up.
October 1940: it settled at Lizhuang, near Yibin in Sichuan.
Winter 1938: Kunming, in Yunnan, became its base.
September 1937: the Second Sino-Japanese War forced a move to the south.
August 1927: renamed National Tongji University.
May 20, 1924: the government counted it among China's earliest national universities.
March 1922: new name, Tongji Medical and Engineering University.
October 1907: the Tongji German Medical School opened its doors.
These entries show how often the university was split up and rebuilt. If you meet older alumni or older textbooks, they may refer to departments that now belong to other Shanghai universities.

Tongji registers more than 50,000 students across every level of study, from certificate and diploma courses up through bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees, and including postdoctoral placements. Over 4,200 academics teach or research here. Six of them sit in the Chinese Academy of Sciences and seven in the Chinese Academy of Engineering, and the staff includes 530-plus full professors and 1,300 associate professors.

The range of courses is wide: 81 bachelor's degrees, 151 master's programmes, 58 doctoral programmes and 13 postdoctoral mobile stations. Research is a national priority here, and the university hosts five state key laboratories and engineering research centres.

tongji-university.h: What it is best known for

blocks.x: Tongji's reputation rests on Civil Engineering and Architecture. Civil Engineering, Architecture and Transportation Engineering are described as ranking first in the People's Republic of China, and the architecture programme is said to be by far the hardest in the country to enter. If you are an international applicant in those fields, expect strong competition and plan your portfolio or academic record accordingly.

The university actively encourages cooperation and exchange abroad. Its ties cover education, science, technology and economics, and reach Germany, France, Spain, Austria, Switzerland, Finland, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia and Japan, and several joint international programmes have been created in recent years. In 2006 it enrolled 1,829 international students; that figure is dated, so ask the international office for the latest number. Formal strategic partners include Ecole des Ponts ParisTech and two technical universities, Darmstadt and Graz (Technische Universität).

Tongji celebrates its Anniversary Day on May 20. The history behind the date is a little tangled. The German Medical School opened in Shanghai on June 3, 1907, and a ceremony took place on October 1 of that year. The anniversary was first fixed at May 18, the day in 1924 when the Wusong campus opened, and ceremonies were held on that date in 1925 and 1926. At a staff meeting on January 19, 1931, it was decided to move the date to May 20, two days later, after the nation had mourned the death of the politician Chen Yingshi (Chen Qimei) with flags at half-mast. Since then May 20 has been the day.

The university holds the title of State-level Garden Unit for Excellent Afforestation, so expect green grounds. It has five campuses within Shanghai, together covering 2,460,000 square metres. The Siping Campus is on Siping Road and the West Campus is on Zhennan Road. Gonghexing Road is home to the North Campus, and Wudong Road to the East Campus. Out in Jiading District, the Jiading Campus occupies a spot within Shanghai International Automobile City, in Anting. Note that the East Campus was sold in 2009 to the Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, so it is no longer Tongji's. The campuses still in use are:

Daily life as a student is shaped less by the campus than by the city around it: the weather, how you travel and what you can do in your free time. Next we look at Shanghai, Tongji's home.

Shanghai stands on the estuary of the Yangtze on China's east coast. The Yangtze borders it on the north side, Hangzhou Bay on the south side, and the East China Sea on the east. The ground was built up by river deposits and by modern land reclamation. It is sandy and soft, which is why tall buildings need deep concrete piles to stop them sinking. As a provincial-level municipality, Shanghai administers the estuary and many nearby islands. Zhejiang Province is its neighbour on the south, and Jiangsu on the west and north. The northernmost point of the municipality is on Chongming Island, which, after twentieth-century expansion, is the second-largest island in mainland China.

The city is on an alluvial plain. Of its 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles) of land, nearly all is flat, at an average height of four metres (13 feet). Tidal flats once ringed the estuary, though farmland has replaced them. The few hills, such as She Shan, are in the southwest, and the highest point is the summit of Dajinshan Island in Hangzhou Bay, at 103 metres (338 feet). Rivers, canals, streams and lakes are everywhere, and water is abundant, since the area belongs to the Lake Tai drainage basin.

The Huangpu River splits downtown Shanghai in two. It is a man-made tributary of the Yangtze, dug during the Warring States period on the orders of Lord Chunshen. On the west bank, called Puxi, the historic core developed near the mouth of Suzhou Creek, which ties the city to Lake Tai and the Grand Canal. The financial district, Lujiazui, was built on the east bank, called Pudong. On the eastern shore, wetlands were lost when Pudong International Airport was built, and this loss has been partly made up by turning the neighbouring Jiuduansha shoal into a protected, expanding nature preserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Downtown averages 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) over the year, and suburbs run slightly cooler at 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F). The four seasons are clearly separate. Winters are cool to cold and damp, and northwesterly winds from Siberia can push night temperatures below freezing. Snow falls on 4.7 days of an average year, and settles on the ground for 1.6 days. Summers are hot and sticky, with occasional downpours and thunderstorms, and 21 days a year reach or pass 35 °C (95 °F). Typhoons can threaten the city in summer and early autumn.

Spring is generally pleasant, though changeable and often wet, and autumn is typically sunny and dry. Possible sunshine goes from 28% in June up to 46% in August, and the city gets 1,754 hours of bright sun a year. By China's seasonal definition, for 2001 to 2025 spring begins 9 March, summer 15 May, autumn 5 October and winter 4 December. For the three weeks between 19 July and 8 August the mean is over 30 °C (86.0 °F), so summer arrivals should be ready for the heat.

Since 1951 the temperature has ranged from a low of −10.1 °C (13.8 °F), recorded 31 January 1977 (an unofficial −12.1 °C, or 10.2 °F, was logged earlier, on 19 January 1893), to a high of 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), reached at the Xujiahui weather station on two dates, 21 July 2017 and 13 July 2022. The warmest night on record there was 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) on 13 August 2010.
For 2025, Xujiahui averaged 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), 1.93 °C above the 1991 to 2020 average. Daily highs averaged 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and daily lows 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).

Along the Huangpu, the Bund holds a line of early twentieth-century buildings. Styles vary, from the neoclassical HSBC Building to Art Deco's Sassoon House, today part of the Peace Hotel. The waterfront has been renewed several times, beginning in 1986 with a new promenade designed by the Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren, and again before the 2010 Expo, when the century-old Waibaidu Bridge was restored and traffic was reorganised.

Much of the city's built heritage reflects the presence of Western powers, mainly Britain, France and the United States. The building boom of the 1920s and 1930s left many Art Deco structures. Between 1918 and 1947 the Hungarian-Slovak László Hudec lived in the city and designed Art Deco landmarks such as the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema and the Paramount. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner, also prominent in the style, were behind the Peace Hotel, the Metropole Hotel and Broadway Mansions, while the Austrian architect C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

One typical local form is the shikumen house (石库门; 石庫門; Wugniu: zaq-khu-men, meaning "stone storage door"). It is usually a grey-brick building of two or three storeys, whose front yard is closed off by a heavy wooden door in a stone arch. Rows of these houses are connected along straight alleys called longtangs (弄堂; lon-daon). The city also has Soviet neoclassical, or Stalinist, architecture, mostly put up from 1949, when the People's Republic was founded, until the Sino-Soviet Split of the late 1960s. Soviet specialists had come to help establish a communist state. The Shanghai Exhibition Center is an example.

With 206 buildings of 150 metres or more, Shanghai is the seventh city in the world for skyscrapers. The best known are the Jin Mao Tower, the Shanghai World Financial Center and the Shanghai Tower. The last was finished in 2015 and is the tallest building in China and the world's third tallest. Next to them, at the northern tip of Lujiazui, the Oriental Pearl Tower rises 468 metres (1,535 feet). In spite of heavy redevelopment, many former foreign concession areas are well preserved, and the Old City keeps traditional architecture, such as Yu Garden, an elaborate garden in the Jiangnan style.

The city serves as a world centre for finance and innovation and as a national centre for commerce, trade and transport. Its Port of Shanghai handles more containers than any other port. For 2022 the wider Greater Shanghai area, which adds Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou, was estimated to generate nearly 13 trillion RMB in gross metropolitan product (US$1.9 trillion, nominal). In 2020 the city's economy was estimated at US$1 trillion on a PPP basis, making it China's most productive metro area and among the top ten metropolitan economies globally. Six sectors lead (retail, finance, IT, real estate, machine manufacturing and the car industry) and together they account for about half of the city's GDP.

In 2025 Shanghai's GDP was CN¥5.67 trillion (US$814 billion nominal; US$1.66 trillion PPP), about 4% of China's total, and GDP per head of CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal; US$66,944 PPP). In 2022, residents had an average disposable income of CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) each, while employees of urban units earned CN¥212,476 (US$31,589) a year on average. That makes Shanghai one of the wealthiest Chinese cities, yet a 2023 Economist Intelligence Unit study also found it the priciest place in mainland China to live. A 2021 report on wealth and lifestyle from Julius Baer called it the world's most expensive city for a luxury lifestyle. Students should budget carefully for rent in particular.

Trade in 2023 (imports plus exports) came to CN¥7.73 trillion, or US$1.07 trillion, which is 18.5% of the national total. Forbes ranked Shanghai fifth for number of billionaires in 2022. Oxford Economics projected that its nominal GDP would reach US$1.3 trillion by 2035, first in China and within the world's top five cities by gross regional product. As of August 2024 it ranked fourth in the world, and second in Greater China after Beijing, for the number of Fortune Global 500 companies. For two decades it ranked among the world's fastest-developing cities, with double-digit GDP growth in nearly every year from 1992 to 2008, before the 2008 financial crisis.

The city is a global financial centre, third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a large hub of China's and the world's technology industry, with a large start-up ecosystem, and in 2021 only New York ranked higher as a fintech powerhouse. In 2019 the Shanghai Stock Exchange had a market capitalisation of US$4.02 trillion, the largest in China and fourth in the world. On the Shanghai Futures Exchange, the volume traded in 2009 in six key commodities, including rubber, copper and zinc, was the highest globally. At the end of 2017 Shanghai had 1,491 financial institutions, 251 of them foreign-invested.

Heavy industry and manufacturing matter greatly in Shanghai, one of the nation's main industrial hubs. Its secondary sector rests on zones including Hongqiao (Economic and Technological Development Zone), Jinqiao (Export Economic Processing Zone), Minhang (Economic and Technological Development Zone) and Caohejing (High-Tech Development Zone). Baosteel Group, China's largest steelmaker, the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, China's largest shipbuilding base, and the Jiangnan Shipyard, one of China's oldest shipbuilders, are all here. In cars, SAIC Motor is among China's three biggest automotive groups, partners strategically with both Volkswagen and General Motors, and ranked 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500 list.

In 2017, domestic visitors rose 7.5% to 318 million and overseas visitors rose 2.2% to 8.73 million, and Shanghai was the highest-earning tourist city in the world that year. The International Congress and Convention Association recorded 82 international meetings in 2018, rising 34% from 61 the year before. By 2023 there were 57 five-star and 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated tourist attractions and 34 red tourist attractions. The year 2023 saw 3.64 million tourists, 4.8 times the 2022 level, who brought revenue of CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), 98.5% more than in the previous year, and foreign visitors reached 2.41 million, a 5.2-fold increase. These figures come from different years and categories, so treat them as indicators of scale rather than a single consistent series.

September 2013 saw Shanghai launch mainland China's first free-trade zone, with reforms meant to encourage foreign investment. The Banker reported that during 2013 Shanghai received more financial-sector foreign direct investment than anywhere else in Asia-Pacific. By October 2019 the zone, at 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 square miles), was the mainland's second largest after Hainan. It merges four bonded areas that existed before: the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area and the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Goods entering the zone do not pay duty or go through customs clearance.

In 2023 the city had 24,874,500 residents, 14,801,700 of them (59.5%) holding local hukou registration. In 2022, 89.3% lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. By total administrative area Shanghai is the second-largest of China's four municipalities after Chongqing, but because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller, Shanghai is generally seen as China's largest city. The OECD estimates the wider metropolitan area at 34 million people.

The Shanghai Municipal Statistics Bureau counts around 157,900 foreign residents. Of these, Japanese number 28,900, Americans 21,900 and Koreans 20,800, though the real number of foreign citizens is probably much higher. Shanghai also draws people from the rest of China: 40.3% (9.8 million) of its residents come from other regions, so as a newcomer you will find yourself among many others.

tongji-university.h: Long lives and an ageing city

blocks.x: Registered residents can expect to live 83.18 years, the longest in any mainland city. One result is an ageing population: 17.4% (4.3 million) of the registered population in 2021 was aged 65 or over. In 2017 the central government introduced population controls for Shanghai, and by the end of the year the population had declined by 10,000.
Public transport covers metro, buses, ferries and taxis, and all can be used with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

The Shanghai Metro combines subway and light metro lines and reaches every core urban district and neighbouring suburbs. As of 2025 it had 19 lines (leaving out the maglev and the Jinshan railway), 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 miles) of line in operation, the longest network in the world. A daily ridership record of 13.3 million was set on 8 March 2019. The Shanghai maglev, opened in 2004, was the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world and is also the fastest, reaching up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph) in service.

Trams started in 1908 with a first line. In 1925 the city had 328 tramcars across 14 routes, operated jointly by Chinese, French and British firms; all were taken into state hands in 1949. From the 1960s the lines were taken up or replaced by trolleybus and bus routes, and the last was removed in 1975. The Zhangjiang Tram, rubber-tyred, brought trams back in 2010, and in 2018 the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram began running in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the most extensive bus network in the world, and the world's oldest continuously running trolleybus system is part of it. By 2019 there were 1,575 lines over 8,997 kilometres (5,590 miles), operated by multiple companies.
There were 30,900 taxis in service in 2024, and they carried 134 million passengers that year.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

tongji-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Tongji University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
