Tsinghua University, written 清华大学 in Chinese and Qīnghuá Dàxué in pinyin (often shortened to THU), is a state-run research university in Beijing's Haidian district. It answers to the Ministry of Education, which also provides its funding. For applicants, the useful shorthand is that it belongs to the C9 League of leading Chinese universities and sits inside the national Double First-Class Construction scheme, the successor to the older Project 211 and Project 985 programmes.

The campus lies in the north-west of the capital, on land that was once the imperial gardens of the Qing dynasty. Today the university is organised into 22 schools and 59 departments, and its faculties run from the natural sciences and engineering through the humanities, law and medicine to history, philosophy, economics, management, teacher education and the arts.

Since opening in 1911, Tsinghua has trained graduates who became prominent in science, engineering, government, business and scholarship. The Nobel physics laureate Yang Chen-Ning is one of them, as are the Chinese leaders Zhu Rongji, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping.

Tsinghua's story runs through a century of Chinese upheaval. The sections below follow it from a school funded by American money to a comprehensive university that now sits at the top of many international tables.

tsinghua-university.h: A scholarship school from a war settlement (1911 to 1949)

blocks.x: The university was born out of the turmoil that followed the Boxer Rebellion, a rising against outside influence over the country. Once an alliance of foreign powers, the United States among them, had put down the revolt, the Qing court had to pay indemnities to the victors. The American Secretary of State, John Hay, argued that the US$30 million assigned to the United States was too high. After lengthy talks with the Qing ambassador Liang Cheng, President Theodore Roosevelt won approval from Congress in 1909 to cut the payment by US$10.8 million, provided the money went to scholarships for Chinese students studying in America.

That fund paid for Tsinghua College (清華學堂, Qīnghuá Xuétáng), which opened on 29 April 1911 on the grounds of a former royal garden in Beijing. Its job was to prepare the students whom the government intended to send to the United States. The YMCA recruited its science teachers in America, and graduates went straight into American schools as juniors. The school's motto, "Self-Discipline and Social Commitment", comes from a 1914 talk by the scholar and teacher Liang Qichao, who drew on the I Ching to describe the ideal gentleman.

The school grew into a full university step by step. It launched its own four-year undergraduate course and a research institute for Chinese studies in 1925, and in 1928 it took the name National Tsinghua University.

War then forced a move. As Japan invaded, many Chinese universities left their campuses. In 1937 Tsinghua joined Peking University and Nankai University to create a joint wartime institution, the National Changsha Temporary University, in Changsha, Hunan. That body later moved to Kunming in Yunnan and became the National Southwestern Associated University. The Tsinghua part returned to Beijing when the Second World War ended.

tsinghua-university.h: Reshaping under the People's Republic (1949 onward)

blocks.x: The communist victory in the Civil War in 1949 and the founding of the People's Republic split the Tsinghua community. The then president, Mei Yiqi, and many professors left for Taiwan with the retreating Nationalist government. In 1955 they started the National Tsing Hua Institute of Nuclear Technology there, and it grew into National Tsing Hua University in Taiwan. That institution is separate from, and independent of, the Tsinghua in Beijing, a point worth remembering when you read about the two names.

In 1952 the Communist Party reorganised higher education along Soviet lines, giving each institution one field of specialism, such as the social sciences or the natural sciences. Tsinghua was slimmed down into a polytechnic centred on engineering and the natural sciences.

A year later, in 1953, Tsinghua became the first university to set up a political counselor scheme, following a 1952 instruction from the Ministry of Education to pilot such posts. Recent graduates who were also Party members acted as counselors, looking after the student body and its organisations and often serving at the same time as secretaries of the Communist Youth League. After Deng Xiaoping backed it, the scheme spread to other universities and was firmly institutionalised throughout the country during the 1990s and 2000s.

During the Third Front construction campaign, Tsinghua opened a branch in Mianyang, in Sichuan province. In 1966 its researchers played a key part in moving China from vacuum-tube computers to fully transistorised ones.

The Cultural Revolution, from 1966 to 1976, brought enormous social and political instability. Many students walked out of their classrooms at Tsinghua and elsewhere, and some joined the Red Guards. With teachers persecuted or unable to teach, the university shut down completely. It admitted students again only in 1978, after the Cultural Revolution had ended, and then began to regain its influence in Chinese public life. During the 1973 to 1976 campaign known as Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius, writing groups at Tsinghua and Peking University circulated commentaries under the pen name "Liang Xiao", which sounds like the Chinese for "two schools".

The 1980s brought a different direction. Tsinghua moved past the polytechnic model to a multidisciplinary system in which different schools work together. Under it Tsinghua revived or created the Academy of Arts and Design, the School of Public Policy and Management, the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, the School of Life Sciences, the School of Sciences, the School of Economics and Management and the Law School.

International partnerships followed. The MIT Sloan School of Management (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) became a partner of Tsinghua's School of Economics and Management in 1996. By 1997 the two had launched a joint degree, the Tsinghua-MIT Global MBA. Then, in 1998, working with Temple University's Beasley School of Law, Tsinghua became the first Chinese university to offer a Master of Laws (LLM) in American law.

Xi Jinping, who now leads the Chinese Communist Party and the country as General Secretary, studied chemical engineering here and graduated in 1979. Hu Jintao, a former General Secretary and paramount leader, took a degree in hydraulic engineering in 1964. The campus also draws guest lecturers of world renown, among them Henry Paulson, Carlos Ghosn, Henry Kissinger, Tony Blair and Bill Clinton.

One incident is worth a mention. In November 2010 a fire broke out in the historic Tsinghua Xuetang while it was being renovated; open flames had been used on site against the rules. Nobody was hurt, but the blaze destroyed the wooden roof, the floors and the stairs in the building's eastern wing, an extension that dated from the late 1910s. Restoration followed quickly and was complete before the university's centenary.

The scale of the institution is now considerable. As of 2026 it has 22 schools and 59 departments, 41 research institutes, 35 research centres and 167 laboratories, of which 15 are national key laboratories. Through its colleges, graduate and professional schools and institutes it offers over 82 bachelor's programmes, 80 master's programmes and 90 doctoral programmes. It also operates Tsinghua University Press, a publisher of textbooks, academic journals and other scholarly works. In September 2006 the renowned Peking Union Medical College took the new name "Peking Union Medical College, Tsinghua University", but the pair are technically still separate institutions.

In 2014 Tsinghua opened Xinya College, a residential college in the liberal arts tradition, set up as a pilot for reforming undergraduate education. It follows American and European models and blends general with professional education. Its core curriculum covers Chinese and Western literature and the study of civilisations, and it requires physical education and foreign languages. Most Tsinghua undergraduates must pick a major when they enter, but Xinya students decide at the end of their first year, which leaves room to try several fields first.

December 2014 saw the creation of an Advisory Committee of Undergraduate Curriculum, or ACUC, the first student-run body in mainland China through which students take part in running their school. When the Tsinghua University Academic Committee came into formal existence on 8 July 2015, its charter said that undergraduate decisions must be put to students via the ACUC. A new wave of academic reform began and has continued since. It has brought in a GPA grading system, writing classes, critical thinking classes and second foreign language classes, and it requires undergraduates to be able to swim before they graduate. Other changes include class cross-registration with Peking University so the two institutions can complement each other's general education, lower fees for withdrawing from classes and for transcripts and certificates, and adjusted rules for co-terminal graduate admission.

Another landmark came in 2016 with Schwarzman Scholars, founded with an endowment of almost US$400 million from Steven Schwarzman, who chairs and runs the Blackstone Group, together with other multinational companies and global figures. Each year the programme picks 100 to 200 scholars from around the world for a one-year, fully funded master's course in leadership meant to prepare future global leaders. The intake is split 40% from the United States, 20% from China and 40% from the rest of the world. Scholars live at Schwarzman College, a residential building made for the programme and designed by Robert A. M. Stern, who drew on traditional British colleges and Chinese courtyard houses. It is among China's earliest academic buildings to win LEED gold certification. Residential rooms occupy floors three to five, and the basement levels hold the facilities.

Spending in 2016 reached RMB 13.7 billion, or US$3.57 billion in purchasing power parity terms, the largest budget of any Chinese university. In 2018 the Financial Times reported links between the university and cyber-espionage. During 2024 Tsinghua said its president's office had been absorbed by the Chinese Communist Party committee of the university, which from then on would run it directly.

For a prospective student, the key facts are the breadth of the offer and the strength of the networks around it. This part covers the degree portfolio, how hard it is to get in, how research is funded and organised, and where Tsinghua stands in the major rankings.

Tsinghua carries out research on a large scale. Another count of its offer lists 51 bachelor's, 139 master's and 107 doctoral programmes, taught through 20 colleges and 57 departments covering medicine, law, social sciences, arts and literature, engineering and science.

Beyond the C9 League, the university belongs to several international groupings. One is the Association of Pacific Rim Universities, a body of 50 leading Asian and American institutions. Another is the McDonnell International Scholars Academy, run from Washington University in St. Louis, with 35 premier universities worldwide. A third, with 17 top regional institutions, is a research network called the Association of East Asian Research Universities. On energy, Tsinghua sits in the Low Carbon Energy University Alliance (LCEUA) with the University of Cambridge and MIT, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

tsinghua-university.h: How hard is it to get in

blocks.x: Entry to Tsinghua is intensely competitive at every level. Chinese undergraduates are admitted through the gaokao, the national college entrance exam, in which candidates can name Tsinghua among their preferred choices. Selectivity differs from province to province, but because so many high-school students sit the exam every year, the overall acceptance rate is far below 0.1% of all test takers.
The graduate schools are also very demanding: only around 16% of MBA applicants are accepted each year.

Most research at Tsinghua is paid for by government money from national programmes and special projects. In science and technology these sources provide over 2 billion yuan, which supports more than 1,400 projects a year. State investment in science and technology is expected to rise, and Tsinghua's research budget is projected to grow with it.

In 2007 the university received security clearance to carry out classified research of military interest. Every year it also hosts the Intellectual Property Summer Institute, run with the Franklin Pierce Law Center in Concord, New Hampshire.

Its research units fall into three kinds: those approved by the government, those set up independently by the university, and those created jointly with independent legal entities outside the university. On 31 December 2022 there were 428 university-level research institutions in operation.

On the Times Higher Education tables, Tsinghua is first in China, first in the whole Asia-Oceania region and first among emerging countries. Its industry income, research and teaching indicators place it 1st, 5th and 7th in the world respectively. In the THE World Reputation Rankings it is the most reputable Chinese university, 8th globally and 1st in Asia-Pacific.
UNITAR, the UN Institute for Training and Research, issued a 2020 ranking called WURI (World's Universities with Real Impact), and Tsinghua came 10th among global innovative universities in it.

The QS tables tell a similar story. Tsinghua has led the regional QS BRICS University Rankings since the list was created in 2013. Employers value its graduates: the QS Graduate Employability Rankings 2017 placed it 3rd worldwide, and 1st across the whole Afro-Eurasia and Oceania region. In 2020 it stood 15th in the QS World University Rankings, and 6th globally and 1st in Asia for graduate employability.

The 2026 to 2027 edition of the Best Global Universities list from U.S. News and World Report has Tsinghua 6th worldwide and 1st in Asia-Pacific. In the Academic Ranking of World Universities (the "Shanghai Ranking") it holds 18th place globally, and first place across Asia and Oceania. Combining the four best-known rankings (THE, ARWU, QS and US News), the BlueSky Ranking of University Rankings put Tsinghua 12th worldwide and best in Asia-Pacific for 2025/2026.

The SCImago Institutions Rankings for 2024 put Tsinghua 3rd among the world's universities. Nature Research's Nature Index 2025 Annual Tables place it 6th globally for high-quality publications in the natural sciences.

Across the sciences as a whole, the 2025 CWTS Leiden Ranking has it 2nd in the world, behind only Harvard, by the number of publications in the top 1% of their fields. For highly cited researchers, Clarivate Analytics (November 2024) listed it 2nd in Afro-Eurasia and Oceania behind CAS, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and, globally, 4th behind CAS, Harvard and Stanford.

Subject tables show where the university is strongest. In the 2021 Times Higher Education subject rankings Tsinghua was 6th in the world for Education, 7th for Clinical, pre-clinical and Health, 11th for Business and Economics, 12th for Computer Science, 13th for Life Science, 17th for Engineering and Technology, 18th for Physical Science, 33rd for Social Science, 37th for Law and 40th for Arts and Humanities. These are long-standing strengths.

Engineering is the clearest case. Since 2015 Tsinghua has been ahead of MIT at the top of the U.S. News and World Report Best Global Universities list for Engineering. As of 2024 it also held first place worldwide in nine subjects: Material Science, Environment/Ecology, Environment Engineering, Engineering, Energy and Fuels, Computer Science, Chemistry, Chemical Engineering and Artificial Intelligence.

The same 2024 U.S. News results put Tsinghua in the global top 10 for Water Resources, Physics, Physical Chemistry, Optics, Nanoscience and Nanotechnology, Meteorology and Atmospheric Sciences, Mechanical Engineering, Green and Sustainable Science and Technology, Geosciences, Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Condensed Matter Physics and Civil Engineering.

In 2020's ARWU Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, Tsinghua is in the world's top five for Transportation Science and Technology, Energy Science and Engineering, Nanoscience and Nanotechnology, Mechanical Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Civil Engineering, Instruments Science and Technology and Telecommunication Engineering. It is in the global top 10 for Water Resources, Environmental Science and Engineering, Materials Science and Engineering, Computer Science and Engineering, and Electrical and Electronic Engineering.

tsinghua-university.h: A closer look at schools and departments

blocks.x: Tsinghua is large enough that each school has its own character and history.
The Department of Industrial Engineering (Tsinghua IE) is built around three institutes, listed here:
Operations Research and Data Science
System Operation and Digital Management
Human Factors and Human-System Interaction
Alongside these, the department runs three multidisciplinary, application-driven centres at university level, each created with an outside partner:
The Institute of Quality and Reliability, set up with the State Administration for Market Regulation
The Institute of Industrial Culture, set up with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology
The Smart Logistics and Supply Chain Management Center, set up with Jiaozhou City in Qingdao, Shandong Province

The Department of Mathematical Sciences (DMS) dates from 1927. It was merged with the mathematics department of Peking University in 1952, became the Department of Applied Mathematics in 1979, and took its present name in 1999.

Today it has three institutes. Pure Mathematics has 27 faculty members, Applied Mathematics and Probability and Statistics has 27, and Computational Mathematics and Operations Research has 20. The department teaches about 400 undergraduates and 200 graduate students.

This unit started in 1960 under a longer title, Precision Instrument and Machine Manufacturing, as an independent department carved out of Machine Manufacturing. It received its current name in 1971. Its dean describes the mission as backing national development while improving the well-being of ordinary people.

Four units lead the research: the Center for Photonics and Electronics, the Navigation Technology Engineering Research Center, the Institute of Instrument Science and Technology and the Institute of Opto-electronic Engineering. On top of these the department hosts three key laboratories. They are the Key Lab of High-accuracy Inertial Instrument and System, the State Key Lab of Precision Measurement Technology and Instruments, and the State Key Laboratory of Tribology. It has two national engineering research centres as well, the CIMS one and the Optical Disk National Engineering Research Center.
Here is what each of the four units does.

Institute of Opto-electronic Engineering (IOEE): founded in 1958, it won state authorisation to award PhDs in 1981 and approval for a post-doctoral research site in 1988. Topics studied range from birefringent frequency-splitting lasers and binary optics (both theory and components) to optical information processing, precision metrology and opto-electronic instruments. Its scientists include Professor Kegong Zhao, who used to head the Chinese National Institute of Metrology, and Guofan Jin, a professor who is an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering.

Institute of Instrument Science and Technology: it is the core institute of the State Key Lab for Precision Measuring Technology and Instrument Science. It has advanced equipment and has worked in every major area of modern instrument science. By 2012 it had produced more than 1,500 publications and over 100 patents and had collected many significant awards.

Engineering Research Center for Navigation Technology: a comparatively young unit, founded in 2000 with the aim of excellence in high-accuracy inertial instruments and navigation technology and in MEMS inertial sensors, and of training future scientists and engineers in inertial technology. Further interests are electro-mechanical control systems of high precision, including how they are applied, and MEMS inertial sensors together with the systems built from them. As of 2012 it occupied 2,900 square metres, about 550 of them clean rooms, with over 50 million RMB (US$7.56 million) of equipment.

Center for Photonics and Electronics: it focuses on advanced photonic and laser technology, with 200 square metres of clean-room space and highly modern laser equipment. Its research spans solid-state lasers, fibre lasers, active optics and laser detection. More than 100 of its scientific papers have appeared, 40 of them indexed by SCI, and it holds 18 national patents, and regularly exchanges visits and holds conferences with foreign scholars.

Within the State Key Laboratory of Tribology (SKLT) there is a central laboratory plus four sub-laboratories. Among its honours are 25 awards from Chinese ministries or provinces, two National Natural Science Awards, two National Invention Awards, two National Excellent Science Book Awards and one National Award for Science and Technology Progress. From abroad it received the STLE's Edmond E. Bisson Award in 2003 and the 2008 PE Publishing Prize from the editor and editorial board of the Journal of Engineering Tribology. In 2005 China's Ministry of Education recognised it as one of its creative groups, and in 2007 the National Natural Science Foundation of China did the same for it as a creative research group. A Tribology Science Fund attached to its key laboratory partners with that Foundation to finance projects across many kinds of applied science and technology.

It teaches two disciplines, optical engineering and the instrumental science and technology of precision instruments and mechanology. It provides more than 40 undergraduate courses and 25 graduate courses. Six teaching laboratories or centres play a major role in undergraduate and graduate education:
The Teaching Lab of Manufacturing Engineering
The CAD Teaching Centre
The Engineering Graphics Teaching Laboratory
The Creative Machine Design Teaching Laboratory
The Experimentation Teaching Center for Measurement and Control Technology
The Teaching Laboratory of Optics and Length Measurement

The School of Life Sciences began in 1926 as the Department of Biology, with the botanist Qian Chongshu as its first dean. In the national reorganisation of the early 1950s the department was absorbed into other universities, Peking University among them, and Tsinghua had no biological research for nearly 30 years.

The decision to bring the department back was taken in June 1984, and it reopened in September. Peking University's biology department, the Institute of Biophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and many other institutions and biologists gave valuable help. It took its present name in September 2009. As of 2013 the dean was Dr. Wang Hongwei (王宏伟), a structural biologist and foreign associate of the US National Academy of Sciences. The school has 129 professors and staff and around 600 undergraduates, including candidates in the joint MD programme with Peking Union Medical College.

tsinghua-university.h: Medicine and Peking Union Medical College

blocks.x: The Rockefeller Foundation founded Peking Union Medical College in 1917, modelled on American medical education. In 2001 Tsinghua started a medical school of its own, which merged in 2006 with the college, now "Peking Union Medical College, Tsinghua University".

Its medical course is among the most competitive in the country: it takes 90 students a year into an 8-year MD programme. Students spend the first 2.5 years on premedical education at Tsinghua and then move to Peking Union Medical College for the last 5.5 years of clinical medicine, basic medical education and research.
The School of Economics and Management traces its roots to 1926, when Tsinghua founded its Faculty of Economics.

Opened in April 2002, the Tsinghua School of Journalism and Communication (TSJC) grew out of communication studies that sat inside the Chinese Language and Literature department. Its creation coincided with the media gaining ever more influence on world affairs in an age of fast globalisation. Research fields are Business Journalism, Media Operation and Management, New Media Studies, Film and Television Studies and International Communication, all grounded in academic research on journalism and communication theory.

The school aims to use Tsinghua's wide academic base for the benefit of Chinese and international media, to build a first-rate discipline in the field, to train capable professionals and to explore advanced ideas in journalism and communication. It also offers a two-year graduate course on international business journalism, backed by Bloomberg L.P. and by the ICFJ (International Center for Journalists); it trains gifted students and media professionals worldwide in financial media and corporate communication.

Five research-oriented centres carry out its academic work: Cultural Industry Studies, Media Management Studies, Film and Television Studies, New Media Studies and International Communications Studies, each organised as its own Center.

The roots of law at Tsinghua lie in the years of Tsinghua College (1911 to 1929); in that period large numbers of students went abroad to Western universities to read law. Those who graduated from places such as Columbia, Yale and Harvard went on to matter in law and diplomacy. The well-known legal scholars Xiang Zhejun (向哲浚), Mei Ju'ao (梅汝璈), Pu Xuefeng (浦薛凤), Kung Chuan Hsiao (萧公权), Wang Huacheng (王化成), Yan Shutang (燕树棠) and Tuan-Sheng Ch'ien, as well as the diplomat Tang Yueliang (唐悦良), either went through Tsinghua College or travelled abroad after passing its exams.

The School of Law was set up in 1929, after Tsinghua College became Tsinghua University. Its teaching then concentrated on international affairs and Chinese law, with political science and economics also on the syllabus. It developed greatly until the Japanese army reached Beijing in 1937. Graduates of that period include Lou Bangyan (楼邦彦), Gong Xiangrui (龚祥瑞) and Wang Tieya (王铁崖).

In 1952, as government policy turned Tsinghua into an engineering university, the law school was closed and its faculty sent elsewhere, among them Peking College of Political Science & Law (the forerunner of the China University of Political Science & Law) and Peking University. There was no formal law school at Tsinghua until 1995, although law courses had been taught again since the early 1980s.

Formal re-establishment of the law department came on 8 September 1995. On 25 April 1999, the university's 88th anniversary, it became the "School of Law". The new school resembles the old one and works to give its students an international dimension. Thanks to its faculty and students it is now among China's leading law schools, and from 2011 onward the QS World University Rankings have consistently placed it first or second in mainland China.

Tsinghua and the Shenzhen Municipal Government jointly founded the Graduate School at Shenzhen to train top-level professionals and carry out scientific and technological innovation. It is directly affiliated with Tsinghua in Beijing, and since 18 October 2003 its campus has stood in Shenzhen's University Town. The academic divisions are:
Division of Life Science and Health
Division of Energy and Environment
Division of Information Science and Technology
Division of Logistics and Transportation
Division of Advanced Manufacturing
Division of Social Sciences and Management
Division of Ocean Science and Technology

Studying at Tsinghua means living on one of the most admired campuses in China. This part describes the buildings and who designed them, the museums, the famous alumni, and the many canteens where students eat every day.

The campus sits in the north-west of Beijing, in Haidian district. Forbes in 2010 gathered architects and campus designers, whose verdict named it among the most beautiful university campuses in the world, and it was the only Asian university on that list.

Many architects shaped the site. Several of the best-known buildings were drawn by Henry Killam Murphy (1877 to 1954), an American who had studied at Yale: the Grand Auditorium, the Roosevelt Memorial Gymnasium, the Science Building and the Old Library's eastern side. Yang Tingbao was responsible for the Old Library's middle and western sections, along with the Observatory, the Life Sciences building and Mingzhai, one of the student dormitories. The Aviation Hall, the Chemistry Hall and the Mechanical Engineering Hall were Shen Liyuan's work, while Zhuang Jun did the West Dormitories, Zhaolan Yuan and the Civil Engineering Hall. T. Chuang, who graduated from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1914, helped lay out the grounds, with Neoclassical and Palladian influences. Zhang Bo designed the Shengyinyuan, and further twentieth-century Chinese architects (Guan Zhaoye, Wang Guoyu, Zhou Weiquan and Li Daozeng) each contributed various buildings.
One part of the university lies elsewhere: the Institute of Nuclear and New Energy Technology has its own campus in a northern suburb of Beijing.

The Tsinghua History Museum has a construction area of 5,060 square metres. Its old documents, pictures, artworks, maps, graphics, videos and music tell the story of the university and honour the people who built it up. The university also has its own art museum, the Tsinghua University Art Museum, whose collection has come from the Academy of Arts and Design since 1956.

Tsinghua has produced notable graduates above all in politics, scholarship and industry. Forbes has called it China's "power factory" because of the number of senior Chinese politicians it has trained.

In politics the list is led by Xi Jinping, China's present general secretary and president, and Hu Jintao, who held both posts before him. Other senior figures include Zhu Rongji (former premier), Wu Bangguo (former chairman of the National People's Congress) and Huang Ju (former first vice premier), along with Wu Guanzheng, Zhou Xiaochuan (once governor of the People's Bank of China), Lou Jiwei (former finance minister), General Sun Li-jen, Liang Qichao and others. Since 2016, Tsinghua graduates with political prominence have outnumbered those of other famous universities by a disproportionate margin.
In the sciences and scholarship, the graduates named include:
Yang Chen Ning, Nobel laureate in Physics, honoured for his work with Tsung-Dao Lee on parity nonconservation in weak interactions
Shiing-Shen Chern, mathematician and Wolf Prize winner
Min Chueh Chang, biologist
Zhou Peiyuan, theoretical physicist
Zhang Yuzhe, astronomer
Leslie Ying, biomedical engineer
Qingyan Chen, mechanical engineer
Fei Xiaotong, anthropologist
Wu Wenzao, sociologist and ethnologist
K. C. Hsiao, political scientist
Pan Guangdan, sociologist

Business is another strength. No other Chinese university has educated more billionaires, and as of 2017 Tsinghua counts 152 of them among its alumni. They include Zhang Zetian (e-commerce), Xu Hang (medical devices), Jiang Bin (chairman of Goertek, components) and Sun Hongbin (real estate), plus others.
In the arts and letters, alumni include the author Qian Zhongshu, Wen Yiduo, the painter Xinyi Cheng, Chen Yinke, the historian and poet Wang Guowei and the architect Xu Tiantian.

Political commentators use the term Tsinghua clique for Communist Party politicians who are Tsinghua graduates. They belong to the fourth generation of Chinese leaders and are said to hold reformist and cautiously pro-democratic views; a number studied in the United States after Tsinghua, and some are said to have been inspired by Hu Yaobang's ideals of reform. Their rise to power in the PRC began at the Chinese Communist Party's 17th National Congress in 2008.
Food is a daily part of campus life, and Tsinghua has a large network of dining halls with their own names and stories. They fall into student canteens, staff canteens and specialty halls.

The largest student hall is the Zijingyuan Canteen in the north-east corner of the campus, within the Zijing Student Apartments zone. It has five floors (one of them a basement), a building area of 11,671 square metres, and room for over 3,500 diners at once.
The Taoliyuan Canteen covers 9,696 square metres on four floors (including one basement level) and began formal service on 6 August 2004.

The Qingfenyuan Canteen started out in March 1957 as the "Seventh Canteen". Its name comes from the stone inscription "清芬挺秀、华夏增辉", and it was renamed Qingfenyuan in December 2006 to inspire future generations to keep striving. The replacement was built where the former Qingfenyuan and Qing Qing fast-food area had stood, and it began serving at the close of November 2015. Its position, south-east of where Xuetang Road crosses Zhishan Road, lies along a path students use between lessons. It has four floors and about 8,600 square metres of usable space, with seats for over 1,900.

The Tīngtaoyuan Canteen was completed in July 1981 and was originally the "Tenth Canteen". It stands where Xuetang Road meets Zhishan Road, covers more than 2,000 square metres over two levels and holds over 1,000 diners. It lies east of the Wan quan River, with a hundred willows to the west and a gently winding lawn and bamboo clusters to the south-west. Diners can watch the rippling water and hear the rustling pines in a breeze, which is why it was renamed Tīngtaoyuan in 2006.
The Rongyuan Canteen opened on 8 January 2013 inside the School of Finance at Wudaokou. It is the only canteen there, with a building area of 1,286 square metres on two floors.

The Dingxiangyuan Canteen, formerly the "Fourteenth Canteen", was completed in January 1987. It has 1,300 square metres of usable space and seats over 580. Its name comes from white lilac, one of the campus flowers, and suggests that although the hall is modest in size, its food is as pure, elegant and fragrant as lilac.
The Wenxinyuan Canteen, at the south-west corner of the Guanchouyuan Canteen, has been in use since 2001. It serves halal food in a clean, pleasant setting and holds over 100 people at a time.
The Shuangqingyuan Canteen began trial operation on 16 August 2021 near the off-campus Shuangqing Apartments, so that nearby students and staff can eat conveniently.

The Guanchouyuan Canteen, formerly the Tsinghua University Dining Plaza, is on the north side of the West-Grand Sports Field. It has 13,250 square metres over three floors and seats about 3,000. It is a large all-round hall offering full Chinese meals, Western cuisine and specialty snacks. Its name has a long background. In 1707 the third son of the Kangxi Emperor built the Xichun Garden (now the Gong-zi-Ting), which held 150 mu of fertile fields. The Qianlong Emperor later put up the Guanchou Building by the fields and wrote poems more than once in praise of farm work. The canteen now stands beside those former imperial farmlands, and its name is meant to remind Tsinghua's teachers and students of the hardship of tilling and the labour of farmers.

The Teachers' Restaurant is on the third floor of the Qingfenyuan Canteen. It opened officially on 21 March 2016, seats about 400 and is designed as a comfortable, well-served space where faculty can talk over academic matters.
The Zhilanyuan Dining Hall lies north-east of the Zijing Apartments. It has a building area of 2,500 square metres over two floors, serves halal meals and can seat about 800 diners.

Qingqing Fast Food is in the basement of the Qingfenyuan Dining Hall, with about 340 square metres of space and room for roughly 400 diners. Its idea is convenience, speed, nutrition and hygiene to suit a busy modern life, serving Western-style fast meals quickly to students, faculty and staff.
Qingqing Leisure Dining, in the basement of the Taoliyuan Dining Hall, belongs to the same "Qingqing series" and gives students somewhere to chat, relax or read.
Qingqing Yonghe sits on the north side of the first floor of the Guanchouyuan Dining Hall and holds 112 people at a time.

tsinghua-university.h: Beijing: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life for a Tsinghua student is shaped by the capital itself: what it looks like, how the land lies, what the weather does through the year and how clean the air is. The sections here cover each of these in turn.

Beijing's buildings fall into three broad families. First comes imperial China's traditional building style. Its best-known examples are the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and, above all, Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), which is still the People's Republic's signature landmark. The second is a style sometimes called "Sino-Sov", built between the 1950s and 1970s, whose structures tend to be boxy and in some cases poorly built. The third is thoroughly modern, seen most clearly in the Beijing CBD in the east, with the new CCTV Headquarters, and elsewhere in the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Early in the twenty-first century the city saw enormous growth in new construction, with international designers contributing many modern styles, above all in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone blends 1950s design with neofuturistic touches, mixing old and new. The tallest building in Beijing is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing towers have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award for best overall tall building since 2007: the CCTV Headquarters in 2013 and, earlier, the Linked Hybrid in 2009. That award goes to just one building in the world each year.

Older residential Beijing is made of siheyuans, courtyards ringed by buildings. Grand specimens include Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. The courtyards are linked by lanes called hutongs, which are normally laid out straight along an east-west line, giving doorways a north or south aspect that is thought lucky in Feng Shui. Their widths vary, and some are so narrow that only a few pedestrians can pass at once. Once found everywhere in Beijing, siheyuans and hutongs are vanishing quickly as whole blocks of them give way to high-rises. Hutong residents are entitled to apartments at least as large as their old homes, yet many complain that hutong street life and neighbourly community can never be replaced. These properties are often owned by the government.

On the north side of the broadly triangular North China Plain, open to the south and east, lies Beijing. Mountains to the north, north-west and west protect the city and the farming heartland of northern China from the desert steppes. In the north-west of the municipality, especially Yanqing and Huairou districts, the Jundu Mountains dominate, while the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall crosses the northern part of the municipality along the rugged ridges, built to guard against raiders from the steppes. Mount Dongling is the municipality's top point at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft); it belongs to the Western Hills and sits on the Hebei border.

The main rivers, including the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma, all belong to the Hai River system and flow south-east. The largest reservoir in the municipality is the Miyun Reservoir, on the upper Chaobai. Beijing is also the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, dug more than 1,400 years back to move goods, and of the South-North Water Transfer Project, put up within the last ten years to carry water from the Yangtze basin.

The urban area occupies a relatively small but growing share of the municipality, on the plain in the south-central part, lying 40 to 60 metres (130 to 200 feet) above sea level. Ring roads radiate outward in concentric circles. The innermost, the Second Ring Road, traces where the old city walls stood, and the Sixth Ring Road ties together satellite towns in the suburbs. At the centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, with the Forbidden City, once home to China's emperors, just to the north of them. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, where the current leaders live. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tian'anmen and the Square and forms the main east-west axis.
Growth from the old inner city to the urban edge gets the nickname "spreading like a pancake" (tan da bing), a pattern frequently blamed for Beijing's urban problems.

Under the Köppen system Beijing counts as humid continental (Dwa), and it sits near the boundary of monsoonal cold semi-arid (BSk). Summers are hot and humid because of the East Asian monsoon, while winters are short, cold and dry, shaped by the huge Siberian anticyclone. In spring the Gobi Desert can send sandstorms across the Mongolian steppe towards the city, along with fast warming and generally dry conditions. Autumn, like spring, is a transitional season with minimal rainfall. Records for 2001 to 2026 put the hottest spell in early August and the coldest in early January.

Under China's seasonal division standard, the seasons start on 26 March (spring), 20 May (summer), 13 September (autumn) and 31 October (winter). Because March and September have warmed faster in recent years and May and October more slowly, autumn is generally shorter than spring.
The figures for 1991 to 2020 are as follows.
Urban area: the annual mean runs from 12.9 to 13.3 °C (55.2 to 55.9 °F), with daily lows of 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily highs of 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F).
Low-altitude suburbs: annual mean of 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F); lows of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F); highs of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F).
Mountain areas: 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F) as a yearly mean, getting colder at higher altitude.

January's mean daily temperature is −2.7 °C (27.1 °F); July's is 27.2 °C (81.0 °F). Yearly rainfall comes to about 528.0 mm (20.79 in), rising to 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three-quarters of it arrives between June and August. Sunshine, as a share of what is possible, varies from 42% in July up to 62% in January and February, adding up to 2,490.5 hours of bright sun in a year. The record low since 1951 is −27.4 °C (−17.3 °F), set on 22 February 1966, and the record high is 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), reached on 24 July 1999. In practical terms, a student should pack for both a hot, wet summer and a cold, dry winter.

Air quality is the topic about Beijing that prospective students ask about most often. The picture has changed a good deal, so this section sets out the causes of the problem, the measures taken and the recent improvement.

tsinghua-university.h: Why the city struggled with its environment

blocks.x: Beijing has a long record of environmental trouble. Between 2000 and 2009 the built-up area quadrupled. That not only raised emissions sharply but also changed the local weather: surface albedo, wind speed and near-surface humidity fell, while ozone, vertical air dilution and temperatures at the ground and just above it all climbed, even leaving human emissions aside. Urbanisation combined with the burning of fossil fuels often causes serious problems and ill health for many residents. In 2013 heavy smog covered Beijing and most of northern China, affecting 600 million people in all. That "pollution shock" turned air quality into a major economic and social worry in China. The Beijing government then announced steps to cut it, for example cutting coal's share from 24% (2012) to 10% (2017); the national government, for its part, had the worst-polluting vehicles taken off the road from 2015 to 2017 and stepped up the shift to clean energy.

Joint research by American and Chinese scientists in 2006 found that much of the city's pollution blows in from neighbouring cities and provinces. Between 35 and 60% of ozone, on average, originates beyond the city limits. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality are named as having a notable effect on the capital's air, partly because of the summer winds from the south and south-east and the mountains blocking the north and north-west.

Burning coal accounts for around 40% of PM 2.5 in the city and is the main origin of nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations to natural gas since 2012, and wants yearly coal use capped at 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73% of it for heating and power and the rest for industry. A lot of the pollution is emitted by neighbours. Coal use in Tianjin was expected to rise from 48 to 63 million tons between 2011 and 2015. Hebei Province alone burned more than 300 million tons in 2011, which exceeds the whole of Germany, and only 30% went to power generation, with a large share going into steel and cement. Power stations in Shandong and in the coal-mining areas of Shaanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shanxi, where coal use has tripled since 2000, add to the problem too. By coal consumption, Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia rank first to fourth among Chinese provinces.

Four large coal-fired plants once supplied the city's electricity and winter heating. The first, Gaojing Thermal Power Plant, closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to close in 2016. Over 2013 to 2017 the plan was to reduce coal use by 13 million tons, with a ceiling of 15 million tons for 2015.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, and to keep its promises to clean the air, Beijing spent nearly US$17 billion. It cut bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It also assembled 3,800 natural gas buses, one of the largest such fleets in the world, and became the first Chinese city to require the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

The authorities also sometimes seed clouds to make showers more likely, to clear the air before large events such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and to fight drought. More recently they have relied more on temporary factory closures and tighter limits on cars, as with "APEC blue" and "parade blue", the short spells during and just before APEC China 2014 and the 2015 China Victory Day Parade. Air quality improved dramatically at those times, only to slip back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

On 8 and 9 December 2015 Beijing issued its first smog alert, which shut most industry and commercial business in the city, and another "red alert" followed later that month. Under an announcement by the city's environmental protection bureau in November 2016, highly polluting old cars have been banned from the roads from 2017 whenever a smog red alert is issued in the city or neighbouring regions.

Pollutants have fallen measurably since the "war on pollution" was declared in 2014. Fine particulates dropped 35% in 2017 and fell further by 2020, mainly because coal power was replaced with natural gas and polluting industrial plants in the Beijing area were cleaned up or removed. Beijing's annual average concentration of PM2.5 fell to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best figure since 2013. In 2024 the city had only two days of heavy pollution, its lowest number on record and a decrease of 96.6 percent from 58 days in 2013.

Many sources publish pollution readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website, and the American Embassy in Beijing reports hourly fine particulate (PM2.5) and ozone levels on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants against different criteria, so the pollution levels and health impacts reported by the BJEPB are often lower than those reported by the US Embassy.

The health risk is real. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on the rate of cardiovascular and respiratory disease in Beijing, and heavy exposure can cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems, emergency room visits and even death.

Each season, dust blown from eroding deserts in northern and north-western China brings storms to Beijing. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes makes rain artificially to combat them and lessen the damage. In January to April 2006 alone, no fewer than eight storms struck, and in April 2002 a single one dropped nearly 50,000 tons of dust onto the capital before heading for Japan and Korea.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

tsinghua-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Tsinghua University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at Tsinghua University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: Who UCAS is and how it is organised

blocks.x: UCAS (中国科学院大学), formally the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, has its headquarters in the Shijingshan district of Beijing. It is a public university and belongs to the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), the country's leading scientific research body. It is on the list of institutions under the Double First-Class Construction scheme.

UCAS is unusual because it does not have to sit in one place. Colleges and schools exist across the country, side by side with CAS institutes and in the same locations, and an institute typically takes on an additional nameplate to become one. Behind this network are more than 110 CAS institutes in over 20 cities. The university is headquartered in Beijing, where it has 4 campuses, and adds 5 branches, located in Lanzhou, Guangzhou, Wuhan, Chengdu and Shanghai.

Founded in 1978, UCAS was the first graduate school in China to receive ratification from the State Council. Its graduates include the country's first doctoral graduate in science, first in engineering, first woman to earn a doctorate and first person to hold two doctorates. For the 20th anniversary in 1998, President and Communist Party General Secretary Jiang Zemin wrote an inscription for the school. It calls for revitalizing China through science and education, with emphasis on developing and nurturing talented people.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: From graduate school to independent university

blocks.x: The institution's development can be followed through its names:
1978: it began in Beijing as the graduate school of USTC (the University of Science and Technology of China), the first of its kind in the country.
1986: USTC opened a second graduate school at its main campus in Hefei, Anhui, so the Beijing one was relabelled USTC Graduate School (Beijing).
2000: the name changed to CAS Graduate School, tying it to the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
2005: GUCAS, short for Graduate University of CAS, became the official English name.
2012: a further renaming produced UCAS, the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the institution became an independent legal entity.

2014: UCAS began recruiting undergraduate students. On 7 November that year it formally took part in activities of the C9 League, a group of elite Chinese universities known for comprehensive, leading education, although it was not an official member.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: How degrees work for CAS institutes

blocks.x: UCAS runs its own undergraduate and graduate programmes at its campus in Beijing. There is a second role as well. CAS has given the authority to register student status and issue graduate degrees, for the institutes under it, to two universities, USTC and UCAS, and CAS decides which one handles each institute. Graduate students at most CAS research institutes are registered at UCAS and graduate with UCAS degrees. A few selected institutes send their students to USTC instead, and those students receive USTC degrees. Those who study at the institutes need not be physically on the campus of the university that issues their degree.

One rule is worth remembering if you plan to do research here. Graduate students at institutes where UCAS issues the degree must name UCAS as their affiliation in everything they publish. A student who does not will find the degree application set aside.

Because UCAS is part of the Double First-Class University Plan drawn up by China's central government, it receives national attention, and several rankings place it near the top of Chinese universities.

Center for World University Rankings (CWUR): in the 2026 edition UCAS is 41st in the world and third in China, after Tsinghua University and Peking University. CWUR presents itself as a leading consultancy. Governments and universities turn to it for policy advice, strategic insight and consulting that aim to improve educational and research outcomes.
NTU Rankings 2019: 18th, and first in China.

Nature Index: the 2023 edition names UCAS first among Chinese and Asia-Pacific universities for research output, and second in the world behind only Harvard. The Nature Index records which institutions the authors of high-quality scientific articles belong to, and each month it publishes research output broken down by institution and by country.
CWTS Leiden Ranking 2025: 12th in the world, counting scientific publications from 2020 to 2023.
U.S. News and World Report Best Global University Ranking, as of 2025: 54th worldwide, ninth across Asia and fifth within China.
Times Higher Education World Reputation Rankings: in the 61st to 70th band worldwide, so internationally it ranks among the Chinese universities with the strongest reputations.

The 2025 U.S. News ranking also broke results down by subject, and a long run of UCAS subjects made the global top 100. Among the physical and earth sciences are chemistry, physical chemistry, physics, condensed matter physics, optics, geoscience, meteorology and atmospheric sciences, environment and ecology, and water resources. The life sciences are represented by biology and biochemistry, cell biology, microbiology, molecular biology and genetics, pharmacology and toxicology, plant and animal science, agricultural science, food science and technology, and biotechnology and applied microbiology. On the engineering side there are chemical, civil, mechanical and electrical and electronic engineering, plus engineering in general, energy and fuels, materials science, polymer science, nanoscience and nanotechnology. Finally, artificial intelligence and computer science are on the list.

UCAS's teaching staff are drawn from the research professors of CAS. Since the Nature Index began in 2014, the Nature Research team has consistently ranked CAS as the top research institute in the world. On that basis UCAS can reasonably claim to be the strongest graduate school in China, and one of the strongest anywhere.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: Students and a star named after UCAS

blocks.x: Graduate education is the university's main focus, but it added undergraduates in 2014. The 2015 figures were 664 undergraduates and 44,464 graduate students.

Foreign students can reach UCAS through its departments and through CAS research institutes nationwide, which between them cover many specialties and research fields. Four routes are available: a Master Program, a PhD Program, a Program for Regular Visiting Students and a Program for Senior Visiting Students.

There is also a small distinction in space. The asteroid 189018 Guokeda carries the university's name. The official naming citation (M.P.C. 111803) was published by the Minor Planet Center, with a date of 25 September 2018.
Where you live matters as much as where you study. UCAS is in Beijing, so the following sections describe the setting, the weather, the city's form and its air.

Beijing is at the northern limit of the North China Plain, a triangular lowland that opens toward the south and east. To the north, northwest and west the land is mountainous. These ranges guard the capital and the farming region of northern China against the desert steppe. In the northwest of the municipality, and especially in Yanqing District and Huairou District, the Jundu Mountains are the main feature. Xishan, the Western Hills, mark the west. Along the northern part of the municipality runs the Great Wall, which was laid out over rough terrain to protect against attacks from nomads on the steppe. The municipality's highest peak is Mount Dongling, 2,303 metres (7,556 ft) high, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

Water is drawn from several sources. The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma rivers all form part of the Hai River system, and they flow toward the southeast. On the upper Chaobai lies Miyun Reservoir, the biggest in the municipality. Beijing marks the northern end of the Grand Canal that runs south to Hangzhou, a transport route built more than 1,400 years ago. It is also the endpoint of the South-North Water Transfer Project, which has been built over the last decade to supply water from the Yangtze River basin.

The built-up area lies in the south-central plains at a height of 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet). Compared with the whole municipality it is quite small, but it keeps expanding. Ring roads circle the centre, one outside another. Where the old city walls once stood, the Second Ring Road now runs, and out in the suburbs the Sixth Ring Road ties the satellite towns together. At the middle are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square. Just to their north is the Forbidden City, where China's emperors used to live. Zhongnanhai, where the country's present leaders reside, is west of Tian'anmen. Chang'an Avenue passes between Tiananmen and the square and serves as the main east-west axis. People often say Beijing has expanded outward like a pancake (tan da bing), a pattern that is regularly cited as one cause of the city's urban problems.

Visitors will notice that Beijing's architecture falls into three broad groups. Imperial-era buildings come first, with Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace), the Temple of Heaven, the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Forbidden City among the best known. Tian'anmen remains the symbol of the People's Republic. There are also the Sino-Sov structures of the 1950s to 1970s, which tend to be boxy and are sometimes described as poorly constructed. The third group is modern, and the Beijing CBD in eastern Beijing is its main centre. It includes the new CCTV Headquarters. Further examples elsewhere include the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

The 21st century has seen enormous growth in construction, with styles imported from designers around the world, above all in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone sets 1950s buildings beside neofuturistic ones. China Zun, 528 metres tall, is Beijing's highest building. Twice since 2007 the CTBUH has picked a Beijing structure as its overall best tall building: the Skyscraper Award went to the Linked Hybrid (2009) and then to the CCTV Headquarters (2013). Just one building a year, worldwide, gets it.

Siheyuans are courtyards enclosed by buildings. Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling are fine large examples. Alleys known as hutongs link them. Most hutongs run straight east to west, which means that doors face north and south, a feature thought to bring good Feng Shui. Some are extremely narrow, letting only a few people walk through at one time. They were once found throughout the city, but are being lost rapidly, because the replacement of whole hutong blocks with tall buildings is under way. Residents have the right to apartments in the new buildings, at least as large as the homes they had before. Many say that community spirit and street life of the hutongs are impossible to replace. The properties are often owned by the government.

Beijing's climate is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa) but it comes close to a monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes the summers hot and humid. Winters are cold, dry and brief, as the vast Siberian anticyclone dominates. Dust from the Gobi Desert can blow in over the Mongolian steppe in spring, and temperatures climb fast with generally dry conditions. Autumn resembles spring as a transitional season with little rainfall.

From 2001 to 2026, the hottest part of the year in Beijing was early August and the coldest was early January. Under the national standard for dividing the seasons, the dates when Beijing's seasons start are 26 March for spring, 20 May for summer, 13 September for autumn and 31 October for winter. In recent years March and September have warmed up more quickly, while May and October have warmed more slowly, so autumn tends to be the shorter season of the two.

Beijing once had four big coal-fired power stations supplying electricity and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was shut in 2014 and two more were shut in March 2015. The remaining one, the Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was set to close in 2016. The city planned to cut 13 million tons of coal consumption between 2013 and 2017, and to hold it to 15 million tons in 2015.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: The Olympics and other big days

blocks.x: Nearly US$17 billion was spent on cleaning up the city's air for the 2008 Summer Olympics. For the Games, the city introduced several air improvement schemes. It stopped work at all construction sites, closed some gas stations, shut many Beijing factories for good and shut industry in neighbouring areas temporarily. Odd and even licence plate days halved the traffic. Fares on buses and the subway were reduced, new subway lines opened, and vehicles with high emissions were banned. Beijing put together a fleet of 3,800 natural gas buses, among the largest in the world, and it was also China's first city to require the Chinese equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

Rain-making by cloud seeding has been used by the government before major events, such as the parade marking the 60th anniversary in 2009, and also against drought. Recently there is more emphasis on temporary factory closures and extra limits on cars, as in the cases known as APEC blue and parade blue, short periods around the 2015 China Victory Day Parade and the APEC China 2014 summit. Air quality got much better during and just before these events, then went back to unhealthy levels soon afterwards.

The city issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, which closed most industrial and commercial businesses, and a smog red alert came later that month. In November 2016, the environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017, whenever a smog red alert is issued in the city or neighbouring regions, old cars that pollute heavily may not be driven.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: Improvement and how to read the figures

blocks.x: The war on pollution declared in 2014 has brought measurable reductions. In 2017 fine particulates fell 35% and they fell further by 2020. Two changes did most of the work: natural gas took over from coal for power, and polluting industrial facilities around Beijing were cleaned up. The annual average concentration of PM2.5, the main fine airborne particulate, was down to 30 micrograms per cubic meter in 2022, which was the city's best result since 2013. In 2024 there were just two days of heavy pollution, the fewest ever recorded and 96.6 percent down on the 58 days in 2013.

Because of how serious the pollution has been, there are many different readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) publishes daily readings from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website, and the American Embassy in Beijing posts ozone and fine particulate (PM2.5) figures every hour on Twitter. The BJEPB and the embassy measure different pollutants using different criteria, so BJEPB numbers for pollution and its health effects are often lower than the embassy's. Smog is harmful and dangerous to the population. Air pollution has a direct and significant effect on how often people in Beijing suffer from cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Large doses of polluted air can lead to respiratory and cardiovascular problems, visits to emergency rooms and even death.

university-of-chinese-academy-of-science.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. University of Chinese Academy of Sciences may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at University of Chinese Academy of Sciences by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Chengdu, capital of Sichuan, is where this public institution stands, and it is known everywhere by its abbreviation, UESTC (its full English name is University of Electronic Science and Technology of China). Four partners back it: the Ministry of Education, which it reports to, plus the industry and IT ministry (MIIT), Sichuan's provincial government and the Chengdu city authorities. It also belongs to China's three elite-university schemes, namely Project 211, Project 985 and Double First-Class Construction.

Premier Zhou Enlai personally directed that the university be set up, in 1956. Electronics teaching from three older schools supplied its first departments. First came Jiaotong University, which later split into the two institutions now called Shanghai Jiao Tong and Xi'an Jiaotong. Next was Nanjing Institute of Technology, today's Southeast University. The last was the South China Institute of Technology, which is now South China University of Technology. In its present form UESTC is a research university of wide scope. Electronics sits at the centre, engineering is the biggest area of study, and management, humanities and medicine are added as distinctive strands.

Four campuses make up the university: Qingshuihe, Shahe, Jiulidi and Yongning. Its own total for built-up area is 1,490 km2 (370,000 acres), but the later figure of 16.6 km2 for three Chengdu campuses seems a better guide to real size. More than 40 schools teach 65 undergraduate majors, 13 of which hold national-level featured status. In 2022 about 3,800 faculty taught over 42,000 students.

The story below follows the university from its founding to its present standing, and it is worth knowing because the dates explain why UESTC is regarded as a national flagship in electronics and information science.

The first students arrived in summer 1956 at CIRE, the Chengdu Institute of Radio Engineering, and no earlier Chinese university had concentrated purely on electronic and information science and technology. The departments that formed it were lent by three well-established universities: Shanghai Jiao Tong, Southeast (then called Nanjing Institute of Technology) and South China University of Technology. The state counted it among its key universities from the 1960s onward, a clear sign of the priority given to the field.
The main steps after the founding can be set out in order. The list that follows is a quick reference for students who want to understand how the university's status has risen.
1988: CIRE adopted the name it still uses, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China.
1997: Project 211, the national Education Revival Project, picked it as one of its 100 leading key universities.
2000: it moved into the Ministry of Education university system and became a national key university reporting directly to the ministry.
2001: it became one of 39 research-intensive Chinese universities to receive special Project 985 funding aimed at building world-class institutions.
2007: the Qingshuihe campus opened for use.
2017: it was placed in the Double First-Class University Plan as a Class A university.

Today UESTC reports more than 3,800 faculty members. Among them are 8 academicians of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Chinese Academy of Engineering, 325 full professors and 483 associate professors. The staff also includes 21 IEEE Fellows, 121 recipients of the Thousand Talents Program and 15 scholars on Elsevier's highly cited list. For an applicant, these figures say that the senior teaching and research body is large and well recognised internationally, especially in electrical and information fields.

UESTC describes itself as a research university built on the Stanford model, with electronics at the centre of a broad programme. It covers all six National Key Disciplines that China defines for electronic and information science and technology, alongside many other subjects. Several of its schools were reorganised in 1984 and again in 2018, so you may see slightly different names on older documents.

university-of-electronic-science-and-tec.h: How UESTC is measured and where it excels

blocks.x: Applicants often ask how a Chinese university is judged. There are two layers. Domestic assessment is led by the China Discipline Evaluation, and international comparison relies on the ARWU, QS and THE tables, which are the three most established and influential global rankings.

The China Discipline Evaluation, or CDE, is the Ministry of Education's official review of discipline quality across 14 domains and 113 first-level disciplines, and it is one of the most important yardsticks for Chinese universities. It has been carried out roughly every five years since 2002. In the fourth round, grades run from A+ for the top 2 percent, through A (2% to 5%), A- (5% to 10%), B+ (10% to 20%), B (20% to 30%), B- (30% to 40%), C+ (40% to 50%) and C (50% to 60%), down to C- (60% to 70%).
