Daily life for a student depends heavily on the city outside the campus gate: what the weather does, how you move around, and what you do with free evenings. The sections below describe Chengdu, the home of UESTC, starting with the land it stands on.
Chengdu lies on a wide plain at 450 to 720 metres (1,480 to 2,360 feet) above sea level, on the western rim of the Sichuan Basin. Almost all of the terrain is flat.

Mountains wall the plain in. Steep Longmen ridges stand north-west of the city, and the Qionglai range to the west tops 3,000 m (9,800 ft). Among its summits are Miaojiling, 5,364 m (17,598 ft) high, and the 5,164 m (16,942 ft) Xiling Snow Mountain. Vast primeval forest, teeming with species and a giant panda habitat, covers part of the western highlands. East of the city are the low Longquan Mountains and the hilly edge of the middle Min River, where several rivers converge. Chengdu has been called the Abundant Land since antiquity, for its fertile soil, favourable climate and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System, a notable engineering work.

On the map, Chengdu prefecture covers latitudes 30° 05' to 31° 26' N and longitudes 102° 54' to 104° 53' E. Its extent is 192 kilometres (119 mi) from east to west by 166 km (103 mi) from south to north. The land area it administers comes to 12,390 km2 (4,780 sq mi). Deyang lies to the north-east, Ziyang to the south-east, Meishan to the south, Ya'an to the south-west, and, to the north, the autonomous prefecture of the Ngawa Tibetan and Qiang peoples. Rivers cross the urban area, which sits at around 500 m (1,600 ft); the Jin, Fu and Sha are three of them.

Further out, the landscape is less simple. In the east are the Longquan Mountains and the Penzhong Hills, and the western Qionglai range peaks at 5,364 m (17,598 ft) within Dayi County. The prefecture's highest point is Daxuetang (Miaojiling), on Xiling Snow Mountain in that county. Its lowest is 359 metres, at the riverbank where the Tuojiang River leaves Jianyang City.

The climate is humid subtropical with a monsoon influence (Koppen Cwa). It is mostly mild, humid all year and has four well-defined seasons. Rain is moderate and falls chiefly in the warmer months, taking the edge off both summer heat and winter cold.

Winter is short. The Qinling range far to the north blocks much of the cold Siberian wind, so the season is gentler than in the Lower Yangtze region. January averages 5.9 °C (42.6 °F). Snow is rare, though each winter brings a few frosty spells.

Summers are hot and muggy, yet they do not match the 'Three Furnaces' cities of Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing, all in the Yangtze basin. July and August have a daily mean around 25 °C (77 °F), and afternoons may reach 33 °C (91 °F). Heat that lingers for weeks, as in much of eastern China, rarely occurs. The wettest spell is July and August, and the cooler months stay quite dry.

Dull skies are common. Chengdu receives some of the lowest yearly sunshine of any Chinese city, less than much of Northern Europe: only 1006 hours of bright sunshine a year. The share of possible sunshine goes from 15 percent in December up to 32 percent in August. Spring days in March and April are normally warmer and sunnier than those of October and November.
The annual average temperature is 16.9 °C (62.4 °F), with a recorded low of -6.5 °C (20 °F) and a high of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F).

university-of-electronic-science-and-tec.h: How the city has been built and rebuilt

blocks.x: Chengdu looks the way it does because of a few decisive decades of change. The notes below trace the main steps and are helpful if you wonder why parts of the city feel new.

A key date is 1988, when a national plan for gradual housing reform in cities and towns launched urban housing reform across China. Chengdu soon had more than 20 property companies, which was the beginning of its real estate sector.

Cleaning up the Funan River was the main environmental project of the 1990s. In 1998 it received a UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour Award and, two years later, the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives' Local Initiative Award.

Work on the Five Main Roads and One Bridge project started in 1997. Three of the roads ran to the east, two to the south, and together they formed the base of the city's Eastern and Southern sub-centres. Residents followed, moving east and south, and many blocks appeared near the 2nd Ring Road in those directions. Projects on the Shahe and Jin Rivers also made riverside living fashionable. Change was so rapid that people said the map had to be redrawn every three months.

A speculative housing boom ran through the late 1990s and early 2000s, and in 2000 dozens of commercial property projects appeared. The government supported the market by giving buyers sizeable subsidies for a set period, so that homes became ordinary commodities.

A notable building is the New Century Global Center, which as of February 2026 ranks third in the world by floor area. Standing 100 metres (330 ft) high and 500 by 400 metres (1,600 by 1,300 ft) across, it has 1,700,000 square metres (18,000,000 sq ft) of space. The complex combines retail, cinemas, offices and hotels with a water park featuring an artificial beach and waves, plus a Mediterranean-style village that includes a big 5-star hotel, an ice rink and 15,000 parking spaces.

No city in Sichuan is bigger than Chengdu, and only three in China are. The 2020 census recorded 20,937,757 people in the municipality, 16,045,577 of them in the metropolitan area (the 12 urban districts and Guanghan City, which is under Deyang). By 2021 the total was 21,192,000, a bigger gain than any other Chinese city. The OECD's 2015 estimate for the metropolitan area was 18.1 million.

Chengdu has a strong reputation for being pleasant to live in. China Daily ranked it the fourth most livable city in the country in 2006. The notes below cover its writers, art, faith, theatre, language and food.

Much of China's important literature has a link to Chengdu. Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong, both masters of the fu form (a blend of descriptive prose and verse), lived here, as did the poets Li Bai of the Tang and Du Fu, honoured as the finest of their era. Yang Shen'an was a well-known Ming scholar from the city, and Guo Moruo and Ba Jin are famous modern writers.

The city's written records are among the oldest locally. Chang Qu, a historian of the Jin dynasty, produced the Record of Hua Yang State, the earliest local history. A poet from the Later Shu Kingdom, Zhao Chongzuo, edited the collection Among the Flowers, China's first anthology of Ci. And The first Spring Festival couplet came from Meng Chang, king of Later Shu, and it says that a harvest year welcomes celebrations while good festivals foreshadow long springs.
In 2023 the city staged the 81st World Science Fiction Convention, having beaten Winnipeg in the 2021 vote.

In the Five Dynasties period, the Chengdu painter Huang Quan and his peers founded the Fine-Brush Flower-and-Bird school. At the time, the Hanlin Painting Academy here was the earliest royal art academy in China.
Chengdu is home to several faiths, and its religious history is varied.

Muslims have been in Sichuan since the Tang dynasty (618 to 907). There are 12 mosques in Chengdu, and the Huangcheng Mosque in the city centre dates from the 16th century. Official, Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations all exist, some of them as underground churches.
The Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of Szechwan, today the Diocese of Chengdu, was set up on 15 October 1696, with Artus de Lionne of the Paris Foreign Missions Society as its first Apostolic Vicar.

Protestant work began with the Canadian Methodist Mission, which in 1890 wanted additional stations in Asia. In February 1891, Dr. Virgil Chittenden Hart, formerly in charge of Central China work for the New York Methodist Mission Society, urged Chengtu as the first station. His name came up to lead the party, given that between 1866 and 1888 he had built Western hospitals and boys' and girls' schools at the missions he founded along the Yangtze and Gan Rivers. He reached Chengtu on 9 May 1891. A house bought two weeks later was split into quarters and a dispensary for staff arriving afterwards.

The first Protestant Mission Headquarters opened its doors on 24 June 1892, with more than 1,000 local people attending. The first Methodist service, the following Sunday, drew only a handful. The first Western dispensary in Sichuan began work on 3 November 1892 and saw sixteen patients. The site grew so popular that a bigger one near the East Gate was acquired in spring 1893, and there the city's first Methodist church (Si-Shen-Tsi) and hospital were built.

Things then went badly. Rioters razed the church and hospital in 1895 and staff retreated to Chongqing, then Shanghai. In Peking, Hart demanded redress, and Sichuan Viceroy Liu Ping Chang eventually paid compensation in full. Rebuilding was fast, but the riots of 1901 wrecked the compound again, and it was rebuilt a second time. Later missionaries shifted the boys' and girls' schools to a bigger site south of the city. In 1914 the Divinity College was dedicated as Hart College, a unit of the West China Union University, today's Sichuan University and its West China School of Medicine (Huaxiyida). The Cultural Revolution ended worship at Si-Shen-Tsi church. Its management passed to the Chengdu City Second People's Hospital close by, which turned the chapel into a kindergarten and an office for its equipment department until returning it to the church in 1984.

The most recent event dates to December 2018, when the Early Rain Covenant Church, an underground congregation of about 500 under Pastor Wang Yi, faced an official attempt at closure. Police detained over 100 members, the pastor and his wife among them, raided its kindergarten and theological college and closed its media operations. Church member Li Yingqiang declared, before his own arrest, that even with five people remaining the worship would go on, because the faith was real. Reports say a member was informed the church counted as an illegal organisation. Chinese media were not permitted to cover the matter, but video that reached Western social media appeared to show the arrests, with photos alleged to show injuries caused by police. One detention warrant photographed online seems to charge church leaders with inciting subversion of state power, an offence with a ceiling of 15 years in prison.
Jewish life has a small presence as well. A Chabad Jewish Center opened in 2012, and after five moves it settled in a permanent home in Wuhou District.

A proverb claims that Shu opera is the best show on earth, and it reflects how highly Sichuan opera and Zaju, an old comic form that blends dancing, singing, poetry and miming. In Chengdu the first opera, called 'Bullfighting', dates from the Warring States period. During the Three Kingdoms period the first detailed opera played at the Shu royal court. China's earliest firmly recorded Zaju was likewise performed here, and archaeologists have dug up tombs of witty Han dynasty poets. Visitors to Sichuan opera still see its famous face-changing masks and fire breathing.

The everyday language is Chengdu dialect, a variety of Sichuanese. It has had a notable influence on Chinese comedy and rap music. Students who study Mandarin will still find it easy to get by, but you may hear the local accent often.

Sichuan cuisine is known for fiery chilies and numbing peppercorns. Famous dishes are Mapo doufu, Chengdu hot pot and Dan Dan noodles, and Mapo doufu and Dan Dan noodles both include Sichuan pepper. UNESCO has recognised Chengdu as a City of Gastronomy.

The Los Angeles Times gave Chengdu the nickname 'China's party city' in 2006, a nod to its carefree way of living. Shanghai has over twice the population, yet Chengdu has more tea houses and bars. In 2023 it counted above 30,000 teahouses, and 3,566 bars, nightclubs and dance halls were legally registered. A 2019 statistical report showed more bars than Shanghai, the most of any Chinese city. Its tea culture is more than a thousand years old and reaches back to when the city served as the departure point of the Southern Silk Road.

Tea houses are everywhere, from ornate traditional places with bamboo furniture to plain modern ones. The menu includes jasmine, longjing and biluochun teas. People go there to play mahjong, get a massage or have their ears cleaned, and some bigger houses stage live shows such as Sichuan opera.

Hot pot is the dish most visitors associate with Chengdu. It is a traditional Sichuan meal in which vegetables, fish or meat are cooked in a boiling, spicy broth. It suits a group of friends, appeals to residents and tourists alike, and restaurants serving it can be found across the city.
One economic zone of note is the Chengdu National Cross-Strait Technology Industry Development Park, which started life in 1992 under the name Chengdu Taiwanese Investment Zone.

UIBE (对外经济贸易大学) is a public university in Beijing's Chaoyang district; the English name is University of International Business and Economics. It reports to the Ministry of Education, which shares the funding with the Ministry of Commerce. It belongs to Project 211 and to the Double First-Class Construction programme, two national schemes that single out leading Chinese universities.

Accreditation is one of its main selling points. No other finance and economics university in China holds all four of EQUIS, AACSB, CAMEA and AMBA, as UIBE does. Looking only at the AACSB, EQUIS and AMBA trio, it is among 15 mainland universities that have them, and it was the fifth to earn all three. If you want a business degree whose quality is recognised abroad, those labels are worth noting.

Teaching centres on economics, finance, international business, management, law, foreign languages and international relations, and UIBE is counted among China's leading places to study business and finance. The Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation created it in Beijing in 1951.

university-of-international-business-and.h: From a cadre school to a national university

blocks.x: The institution opened in 1951 as the Senior Business Cadre School. By 1953 it had become Beijing Foreign Trade College. A year later it absorbed the foreign trade major of Renmin University of China's Department of Trade and was formally set up as the Beijing College of Foreign Trade. Its current name arrived in 1984.

In June 2000 came a major merger. The China Finance Institute joined the university, forming a new and larger UIBE managed directly by the Ministry of Education. Then, in December 2010, that ministry and the Ministry of Commerce agreed to build the university jointly, which explains why two ministries stand behind it today.
One recent change matters if you read older material: the campus UIBE ran in Israel shut in 2024, after relations between China and Israel worsened during the Gaza conflict.

UIBE is arranged as a group of schools and research institutes. Subjects range from trade, finance and business administration to law, languages, public administration and information technology. The details below show how wide the offering is.

Among the main academic units is the School of International Trade and Economics, where teaching and research focus on international trade and international finance. It consists of seven departments and ten research centers.

A 2001 merger created the China School of Banking and Finance: UIBE's own banking and finance school joined the old China Institution of Finance, once attached to the People's Bank of China. Bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees are offered in finance and related fields, and the school has around 1,500 students once international and part-time graduate students are counted.

Starting life in 1982 as the Department of International Business Management, the School of Business is now one of the larger schools here. You can study accounting, marketing, management, human resource management or finance, and certain courses are delivered in English with textbooks from the United States. As of May 2014 it was a member of the AACSB and of EQUIS, the European Quality Improvement System.
Founded in 1984, the School of Law concentrates on legal teaching and research, above all international law, and holds a key discipline in that area approved by the state.

The School of Foreign Studies traces its roots to the Beijing Foreign Trade College of 1954. Twelve languages have their own departments here: Arabic, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Persian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Vietnamese and Modern Greek. The Sino-Italian Language Training Centre is based in the school too. A prospective international student will care more about the School of International Education, which supports foreign students on degree and non-degree courses, among them Chinese language and Business Chinese.

Daily life for a student depends heavily on the city, so this part introduces Beijing, home to UIBE. It covers what the city looks like, how the land is laid out, the weather, and the air pollution that has long been Beijing's biggest environmental worry.

Three architectural styles dominate the urban area. The first is imperial: the traditional buildings of old China, with Tian'anmen (the Gate of Heavenly Peace) the best-known emblem of the People's Republic. Also in this group are the Temple of Heaven, the Forbidden City and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second is the so-called "Sino-Sov" style of the 1950s to the 1970s, whose buildings tend to be boxy and sometimes badly built. The third consists of modern buildings, most conspicuously in the Beijing CBD in the east, where the new CCTV Headquarters stands, but also elsewhere in the form of the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the start of the twenty-first century the city has seen enormous growth in new construction, with international designers contributing a variety of modern styles, especially in the CBD. At the 798 Art Zone, 1950s industrial design and neofuturistic architecture sit side by side, blending old and new. The tallest building is the 528-metre China Zun. The CTBUH Skyscraper Award for the best tall building of the year goes to just one building in the world annually, and Beijing has taken it twice since 2007, with the Linked Hybrid building (2009) and then the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

Siheyuans are courtyard houses with buildings around a central yard; grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. They are joined by narrow lanes called hutongs. Hutongs typically run straight, east to west, which puts doorways on the north and south sides, a layout thought to bring good Feng Shui. Their width varies, and some are so tight that only a few pedestrians can pass at once. Siheyuans and hutongs were once everywhere, but entire blocks are being replaced by high-rises. Hutong residents have the right to move into new apartments at least as large as their old homes, though many say the community spirit and street life of the lanes cannot be recreated, and the properties are often owned by the government.

Beijing stands at the northern edge of the North China Plain, which is roughly triangular and opens to the south and east. Mountains to the north, north-west and west protect the city and the farmland of northern China from the desert steppe beyond. The Jundu Mountains dominate the north-west of the municipality, particularly Yanqing and Huairou districts, while the Western Hills (Xishan) frame the west. The Great Wall runs along the rugged northern part of the municipality, built to keep out nomads from the steppe. The highest point is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

Rivers such as the Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are tributaries of the Hai River system and flow south-east across the municipality. Its largest reservoir, Miyun, sits on the upper stretch of the Chaobai. Two big water-related projects end in Beijing: the Grand Canal, a transport route more than 1,400 years old that leads south to Hangzhou, and the South-North Water Transfer Project, built over the past decade to carry water north from the Yangtze basin.

The built-up area lies on the plain in the south-centre of the municipality, 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) above sea level. It takes up a relatively small share of the municipal area, but the share is growing. Ring roads radiate outward in concentric circles. The innermost, the Second Ring Road, follows where the old city walls stood, and the outermost, the Sixth, ties in the satellite towns of the suburbs. At the centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, directly south of the Forbidden City, where the emperors lived. West of Tian'anmen is Zhongnanhai, home of the current national leaders. Chang'an Avenue, which passes between Tian'anmen and the square, is the city's main east-west axis.
People often say Beijing has grown "like a pancake" (tan da bing), spreading outward from the old centre to the fringe, and this pattern is frequently blamed for the city's urban problems.

The classification is humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to a monsoon-influenced cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). The East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and humid, whereas the great Siberian anticyclone makes winters short, cold and dry. Spring brings rapid warming and mostly dry weather, and sandstorms can arrive from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe. Autumn is, like spring, a transition season with very little rain.

For 2001 to 2026 the hottest period has been early August and the coldest early January. Using the national standard for the seasons, Beijing's spring begins 26 March, its summer 20 May, its autumn 13 September and its winter 31 October. Because March and September have been warming faster and May and October more slowly in recent years, autumn is generally shorter than spring.

The averages for 1991 to 2020 are these. In the urban area the annual mean temperature is between 12.9 °C (55.2 °F) and 13.3 °C (55.9 °F), with daily minimums of 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 to 47.1 °F) and daily maximums of 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 to 66.0 °F). In the lower suburbs the annual mean is 11.5 to 13.0 °C (52.7 to 55.4 °F), with minimums of 5.9 to 8.0 °C (42.6 to 46.4 °F) and maximums of 18.2 to 18.7 °C (64.8 to 65.7 °F). Mountain areas are colder still, averaging 0 to 10 °C (32 to 50 °F) and dropping as altitude increases. January averages -2.7 °C (27.1 °F) and July 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

About 528.0 mm (20.79 in) of rain falls in a year, or 584.2 mm (23.00 in) in Haidian and Chaoyang, and nearly three quarters of it arrives between June and August. Possible sunshine is lowest in July (42%) and highest in January and February (62%), for 2,490.5 hours of bright sun a year. Since 1951 the coldest day was 22 February 1966 at -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), and the hottest was 24 July 1999 at 41.9 °C (107.4 °F).

Beijing has struggled with environmental problems for a long time. Between 2000 and 2009 the urban area grew to four times its size. That raised human emissions and changed the local weather too: albedo, wind speed and humidity near the surface dropped, while ground temperature, near-surface air temperature, the mixing of air vertically, and ozone all went up. Urban growth together with pollution from burning fossil fuels often causes serious environmental trouble and health problems for many residents.

The heavy smog of 2013, which affected 600 million people across Beijing and most of northern China, became a turning point. Following that "pollution shock", poor air became a big economic and social issue nationwide. Beijing announced steps to cut it, including lowering coal's share of its energy mix from 24% (2012) to 10% (2017), while the central government told the worst-polluting vehicles to leave the roads in the years 2015 to 2017 and pushed harder to switch the energy system to clean sources.

A joint study by American and Chinese researchers in 2006 found that a large part of Beijing's pollution is imported from nearby cities and provinces; between 35% and 60% of the ozone, on average, originates outside the city. Shandong Province and Tianjin were singled out as having a "significant influence on Beijing's air quality", partly because summer winds usually blow from the south or south-east and the mountains lie to the north and north-west.

Coal accounts for about 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and for most of its nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations to natural gas since 2012, aiming to hold annual coal burning to 20 million tons. In 2011 it burned 26.3 million tons, 73% for heating and power and the rest for industry. A lot of the city's pollutants are carried in from neighbouring areas. Coal use in Tianjin was expected to rise from 48 million tons in 2011 to 63 million in 2015. Hebei burned over 300 million tons in 2011, which is more than the whole of Germany; just 30% of it fed power generation and a good deal went to steelmaking and cement. The coal-mining regions of Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi, where use has tripled since 2000, add pollution through their power plants, as does Shandong. Among Chinese provinces, coal consumption ranks Shandong first, then Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia.

Beijing itself had four large coal-fired power plants providing electricity and winter heating. The Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was closed in 2014, two more closed in March 2015, and the last, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was due to close in 2016. The plan for 2013 to 2017 was to take 13 million tons off coal use, with a ceiling of 15 million tons in 2015.

For the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent on cleaning up the air. During the Games, Beijing halted work on all construction sites, shut many factories permanently, temporarily closed industry in neighbouring regions and shut some petrol stations. Car traffic was cut by half through an odd-and-even licence plate system, public transport fares were lowered, new subway lines were opened and high-emission vehicles were banned. Beijing also built up a fleet of 3,800 buses running on natural gas, among the largest anywhere, and was China's first city to require the local counterpart of the Euro 4 emissions standard.

The authorities have sometimes used cloud seeding to make rain more likely and clear the air ahead of large events, such as the 60th anniversary parade in 2009, and also to fight drought. More recently they have relied more on temporary factory closures and tighter vehicle restrictions. The results were nicknamed "APEC blue" and "parade blue": short spells of unusually clean sky around the 2014 APEC meeting in China and the 2015 Victory Day Parade. In both cases the air quality improved dramatically, then fell back to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing issued its first smog alert on 8 and 9 December 2015, closing most industry and commercial business in the city, and a second "red alert" came later that month. In November 2016 the city's environmental protection bureau announced that from 2017 highly polluting old cars would be barred from driving whenever red alerts were issued in the city or neighbouring regions.

Real progress has followed the "war on pollution", declared in 2014. Fine particulates fell by 35% in 2017, with further reductions by 2020, mainly because natural gas replaced coal power and polluting industrial plants were cleaned up. Average PM2.5 concentration dropped to 30 micrograms per cubic metre in 2022, the best since 2013. In 2024 there were only two heavily polluted days, a record low and a 96.6 percent fall from the 58 of 2013.

Because pollution is such a concern, several sources publish readings. Twenty-seven monitoring stations across the city report daily figures, published by the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB). Separately, the American Embassy reports PM2.5 and ozone every hour on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants using different criteria, so the BJEPB's pollution levels and health impact are often lower than the embassy's.

Smog is harmful. Air pollution directly affects how often people in Beijing suffer cardiovascular and respiratory disease, and prolonged heavy exposure can mean breathing and heart trouble, hospital emergency visits and even deaths. If you have asthma or other conditions, take this seriously and check the daily air-quality figures.

Erosion of the deserts in northern and north-western China sends seasonal dust storms into Beijing, and the city's Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain to reduce their effects. January to April 2006 saw no fewer than eight. In April 2002 a single dust storm deposited nearly 50,000 tons of dust on Beijing before passing on to Japan and Korea.

The University of Jinan (UJN, 济南大学) is a public university in Jinan, the capital of Shandong province. Funding is shared between the Ministry of Education and the provincial government of Shandong, which also oversees it. Two national schemes involve UJN: the 111 Plan and the Outstanding Engineer Education and Training Program. Bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees can all be awarded here, and the university may nominate its best students to skip the usual graduate entrance exam, a useful route if you plan to continue to a master's.

The university began life as the Shandong Institute of Building Materials, set up in Zibo, Shandong, in 1948. The institute received approval in 1983 to move to Jinan, the provincial capital. Then in 2001, after joining forces with three colleges, it was formally renamed the University of Jinan. Shao Guifang, then Vice Governor of Shandong, and Lü Fuyuan, then Vice Minister of Education, unveiled the nameplate together.

Three campuses make up the university, and together they occupy over 2.43 million square metres, which is 243 hectares or 600 acres. Buildings total 1.02 million square metres of floor space. The university puts the value of its fixed assets at 2.14 billion yuan, of which teaching facilities represent 370 million yuan.

The library building covers 63,000 square metres and is equipped with a digital system and a search system for information. On the shelves and online there are more than 4.6 million books, both printed and electronic, along with 4,200 kinds of Chinese and foreign periodicals and 23,000 kinds of electronic journals. The campus network is also linked to the China Education and Research Network.

UJN has 24 schools and 2 post-doctoral research centres. At doctoral level it awards degrees in 3 first-level disciplines (26 disciplines in all), and at master's level in 20 first-level disciplines (144 in all). Counting majors, the university lists 92 for a bachelor's degree and 6 for a master's. Subjects cover ten broad areas, including art, management, medicine, technology, science and history, as well as literature, education, law and economics. The full-time student body of undergraduates, postgraduates and foreign students totals 35,916.
The university's guiding words are diligence, rigorousness, unity and creativity.

At the centre of the emblem is the character 济, the first syllable of the city's name, drawn in the seal script fashionable under the Qin dynasty. The shape also suggests a boat on water: water is a signature of Jinan's geography, and sharing one boat expresses the university's spirit of working together. Three colours have set meanings. Red is for passion, green for youth and blue for breadth, all of which reflect the university's view of education. The year 1948, when the university was born, is shown on the emblem too.
UJN has 1,981 full-time teachers. The senior ranks include 305 professors and 707 associate professors, and 841 teachers hold a doctoral degree.

Altogether 54 disciplines and research bases are classed as key at national or provincial level. Within that group, the Shandong provincial government manages one key national laboratory, and the Ministry of Education oversees one engineering research centre. Provincial-level assets are 14 discipline bases, 10 laboratories and 14 engineering research centres. Another 4 key laboratories were funded through Shandong's Twelfth Five-Year Plan, and 8 social science research bases have the approval of the provincial government.
The university has built up a long list of recognised programmes and courses:
4 national-level distinctive specialties and 16 at provincial level
5 national-level quality courses and 53 provincial-level top-grade courses
2 national exemplary bilingual courses and 2 national quality public audio and video courses
6 specialties training Outstanding Engineers
9 specialties backed jointly by the university and industry partners
5 provincial experimental teaching centres

In recent years its teachers have led 6 national and 55 provincial teaching and research projects. They have also produced 8 textbooks under national guidance and collected 3 national awards and 75 provincial awards for their teaching results and research.

Students have done well in competitions as well, including the 'Challenge Cup' Extracurricular and Academic Contest and the China Undergraduate Mathematical Contest in Modeling. They have won 3,133 provincial or national awards, among them 48 first prizes and 125 second prizes at national level.

On the research side, the university has handled 347 national projects, with money coming from the 973 and 863 programmes, the national science and technology support programme and the country's natural science and social science foundations, plus 814 projects at provincial level. It has earned 238 national and provincial prizes for its results, among them a second prize in technological invention and three second prizes in science and technology progress at national level. It owns 666 national patents. Researchers have had 4,799 papers indexed in SCI, EI or ISTP and have published 214 academic works, translations or textbooks. Eight journals are also sponsored by UJN, for example China Powder Science and Technology, the Journal of University of Jinan and a journal on cancer prevention and treatment.

UJN promotes open education and works actively with partners around the world. Research institutes are among its partners, and exchange arrangements exist with 77 universities worldwide, for example in Brazil, Japan, Australia, France, Germany, Britain, Canada, America and Congo.

university-of-jinan.h: Staff abroad and visitors at home

blocks.x: International work includes building up the international experience of the teaching staff. Roughly a hundred teachers and academic leaders are sent abroad every year, to developed countries including Britain, Germany, Australia, Canada and the United States, to do joint research, take further study or attend academic conferences. The university also hosts such events itself and has succeeded with ten influential international conferences and bilateral forums. Examples are the first international conference on advanced materials and a recent one on the design and application of intelligent systems. Hiring abroad is another strand: more than 300 overseas teachers and scholars, coming from Germany, France, Britain, America and other countries, have been invited to lecture, teach or research, and dozens of internationally celebrated scholars have served as visiting or emeritus professors.

For students coming the other way, UJN is a host for foreign students on Chinese government and provincial government scholarships and via the Confucius Institute. In total it has accepted more than 2,100 international students, whose home countries include Pakistan, Ghana, Indonesia, South Korea, Spain, France, Britain, Australia and the USA, and it has developed a thorough education system with its own character for overseas students. In 2017 more than 700 regular international students were enrolled. Meanwhile, UJN follows an international outlook of going out, and each year it sends hundreds of its own students to well-known foreign universities for exchange, short courses and practice, so they develop a global view and become more competitive.

The university also develops education jointly with foreign partners. Aiming at internationalisation, UJN brings in more quality educational resources by working with partner universities in South Korea, Britain, Canada, Australia and the USA, and four undergraduate programmes are now run jointly with foreign universities. This cooperation lets UJN take on advanced curriculum design and teaching content and methods from abroad, supports the internationalisation of its disciplines, and produces creative graduates with good international communication skills.

UJN also cares about promoting the Chinese language worldwide. It follows guidance from the Confucius Institute Headquarters and the provincial Education Department, sending teachers and volunteers abroad to teach Chinese, for instance in Thailand, Ethiopia, the Republic of Congo and South Korea. Three Confucius Institutes have been established as a result: one in the Republic of Congo, one in South Dakota and one in the City and County of Denver, both of the latter in the United States.
Daily life for a student depends heavily on the city around the campus, including its weather, transport and leisure options. The sections below describe Jinan, home of the University of Jinan.

Four distinct seasons shape life in Jinan, which falls into the humid continental (Köppen Dwa) climate zone. Spring brings dry weather with almost no rain, summer is hot and wet, autumn is crisp, and winter is cold and dry with only light snowfall. Temperatures average 14.9 °C (58.8 °F) over the year. Annual precipitation is 734 millimetres (28.9 in), concentrated in summer and quite variable year to year.

The coldest, driest month is January, with a mean of -0.3 °C (31.5 °F) and just 5.0 millimetres (0.20 in) of rainfall equivalent. The hottest is July, at a mean of 27.4 °C (81.3 °F). Possible sunshine is lowest in July (40%) and highest in May (58%), and over a year the city gets 2,226 hours of bright sun.

Because of the mountains to the south, temperature inversions occur on roughly 200 days each year. Rainfall is high by northern Chinese standards, and with hills on three sides of the city, summers feel particularly oppressive. This is why Jinan has been named as a candidate to join the Three Furnaces of China as a fourth. Records kept since 1951 show a low of -19.7 °C (-3 °F) on 17 January 1953 and a high of 42.5 °C (109 °F) on 24 July 1955, so bring clothes for both a cold winter and a very hot summer.

Two changes shaped Jinan's early economy: the Yellow River moved to a new bed just to the north in 1852, and a railway hub arrived. Together they made the city a leading market for the produce of the fertile farming regions north of it. Agricultural trade then led to textile and clothing manufacture, flour mills, oil presses, and factories making paper, cement and matches. Big iron and steel works and chemical plants appeared around the city in the 1950s, and the metal works turn out pig iron, ingot steel and finished steel. Sinotruk, maker of trucks and construction vehicles, chose Jinan for its headquarters and factories in the 1970s.

Jinan has long been third in Shandong's economy, and before merging with Laiwu City in 2019 it had overtaken Yantai to become the province's second largest. The figures below show how output has grown:
2008: GDP reached 301.7 billion yuan. Five provincial capitals were ahead, with Guangzhou (821.5), Hangzhou (478.1), Wuhan (396.0), Chengdu (390.1) and Nanjing (377.5), which placed Jinan sixth.

2009: GDP rose 11.3% to 335.0 billion yuan, which was 21st in the country and seventh among provincial capitals. The cities above it included Shanghai at 1,490.09, Beijing at 1,186.59, Guangzhou at 911.27, Tianjin at 750.08, Chongqing at 652.87 (569.74 for its urban core), Hangzhou at 508.8, Wuhan at 456.0, Chengdu at 450.26, Shenyang at 435.9, Nanjing at 423.02 and Changsha at 374.5, while Zhengzhou, at 330.0, was behind.
2011: GDP of 440.629 billion yuan, up 10.6%, or 64,331 yuan per permanent resident (up 8.9%), equal to 9,960 US dollars.
2016: GDP of 653.61 billion yuan, up 7.8%, or 90,999 yuan per permanent resident (up 6.5%), equal to 13,700 US dollars at the average exchange rate for the year.

2022: GDP came to 1,202.75 billion yuan, growing 3.1% at constant prices. Added value was 42.05 billion yuan from the primary industry (3.1% growth), 418.02 billion from the secondary (3.2%) and 742.67 billion from the tertiary (3.0%), so the structure was 3.5 : 34.8 : 61.7.

2024: GDP reached 1,352.76 billion yuan, 5.4% more than the previous year at constant prices. Primary industry contributed 44.0 billion yuan (growth 3.6%), secondary 451.92 billion (5.8%) and tertiary 856.84 billion (5.2%), a structure of 3.3 : 33.4 : 63.3. Services keep taking a bigger share.
Jinan's large-scale industrial enterprises are grouped as follows.

In heavy industry the list includes Sinopec's Jinan branch and the China National Heavy Duty Truck Group, as well as many Shandong-based groups: Energy, Electric Power, Heavy Industry, Iron and Steel, Gold and Hi-Speed.
In light industry, Inspur Group and Joyoung are the best-known names.

Established in 1991, the high-tech zone east of the city was one of the earliest approved by the State Council. Its planned size is 83 km2 (32 sq mi): a central area of 33 km2 (13 sq mi), an export processing district of 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi) and an eastern extension of 40 km2 (15 sq mi). Firms such as Volvo, LG, Panasonic and Sanyo have been attracted. In 2000 the zone became a member of the world science and technology association and opened a cooperation park for high technology with Ukraine, and its Qilu Software Park has Bangalore's software park in India as a sister park.

Out in the eastern suburbs, beyond the high-tech zone and to the north of the Jiwang highway, is the Jinan Export Processing Zone. Jiqing Highway is 9 km (5.6 mi) from it, and Jinan Airport is 18 km (11 mi) away.

The 2020 census put the total population, including the recently merged Laiwu City, at 9,202,432. The built-up (metro) area, made up of 6 of the 10 urban districts, held 5,452,335 people, most of them Han Chinese. Jiyang, Zhangqiu, Laiwu and Gangcheng are not yet joined to the urban area.

Two main railway routes cross at Jinan. One is the Jinghu Railway between Beijing and Shanghai, the chief north-south spine of eastern China's railways. The other, the Jiaoji Railway, runs east from Jinan to the port of Qingdao, while the Hanji Railway goes west to Handan, in Hebei Province.

Inside Shandong, trains on the Jinghu line connect Jinan with Tai'an, Zaozhuang, Dezhou and Jining. Zibo, Weifang and Qingdao are reached on the Jiaoji line, and Yancheng and Liaocheng on the Hanji line.

Three stations serve the centre: the main Jinan railway station, Daminghu railway station beside Daming Lake, and Jinan East, which opened in 2018. For the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed railway you need Jinan West, away from the centre in Huaiyin District, in the suburban west. It opened to the public on 30 June 2011 and is turning into a future hub, with high-speed lines running west to east towards Taiyuan, Shijiazhuang and Qingdao. A further station, Jinan North, is planned.
Construction of the metro began in 2013, and service started in 2019. At present Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 run, along with the Jiyang Line and SkyShuttle Line 1, for a total of 140 stations.

Major roads include China National Highways 104, 220 and 309. As a hub for both road and rail, Jinan has a coach terminus with one of the highest passenger flows in the country. On the busiest days it counts as many as 92,000 passengers, and on quiet days about 42,000.

Jinan Yaoqiang International Airport is about 33 km (21 mi) north-east of the centre, in Yaoqiang Subdistrict of Licheng District, which gives the airport its name. Expressways connect it to central Jinan. Flights serve many large Chinese cities. Abroad, the destinations include Seoul, Osaka, Bangkok, Singapore, Helsinki, Paris and Los Angeles.

City buses are either air-conditioned or not, and air-conditioned routes have a K before the route number. Since 2018 most routes are air-conditioned, including some without the K. More than 200 routes cover the whole city.

Basketball: Shandong Hi-Speed Kirin is the best-known team in the city. They have been in the Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) since 1995. In the 2012 to 2013 season they reached the final but lost 4 to 0 to Guangdong Southern Tigers.

Football: Shandong Taishan Football Club is the most famous football team. It plays in the Chinese Super League, the top tier, and has done so every season since the league turned professional in 1994. Taishan has won five top-division titles, eight Chinese FA Cups and one Chinese FA Super Cup. Jinan was also one of four Chinese host cities for the 2004 AFC Asian Cup.

Big events: in 2009 Jinan hosted the National Games of China, the highest-level national sports event in the country and the first major multi-sport event in China after the Beijing Olympics of 2008. The main venue was the Jinan Olympic Sports Center.

Winter swimming: since 2014 the city has been the site of China's national winter swimming festivals at Daming Lake, organised since 2016 together with the International Winter Swimming Association (IWSA). In the 2019 to 2020 season Jinan held the 8th Winter Springs-swimming International Invitational.

university-of-jinan.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. University of Jinan may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jinan, register at University of Jinan by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

UNNC is the short name of the University of Nottingham Ningbo China, a cooperative university run jointly by Chinese and foreign partners, in the city of Ningbo, Zhejiang Province. Founded in 2004, it grew out of a tie-up between Zhejiang Wanli University and Britain's University of Nottingham. In China, the Ministry of Education treats UNNC as an independent legal entity, while the University of Nottingham regards it as one of its own campuses. Put simply, you get a Chinese-registered university with a British parent.

Nottingham's Chinese partner was the Wanli Education Group, the operator of Zhejiang Wanli University, which worked in the Ningbo Higher Educational Zone. The two sides signed an agreement on founding the campus in October 2003 and a further joint venture deal in March 2004. Soon afterwards China's Ministry of Education granted official approval, making UNNC the first joint-venture university in China to gain legal status as an independent campus.

university-of-nottingham-ningbo-china.h: The first students and the campus

blocks.x: Teaching started in September 2004 with 254 students, all from Zhejiang province, in the first cohort, who began in temporary premises inside Zhejiang Wanli University. Work on a purpose-built campus of 144 acres had started in April 2004 and was ready for the second intake in September 2005. John Prescott, the British Deputy Prime Minister, formally opened it on 23 February 2006; he was joined by State Counsellor Chen Zhili and Zhou Ji, China's education minister, among the guests.

At the end of 2012 Britain's higher education quality watchdog, the QAA (Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education), came to UNNC to assess quality. The QAA's report, published in May 2013, found UNNC's academic standard and student quality in line with those at Nottingham in the UK. English is the language of teaching, and graduates are awarded University of Nottingham degrees. In June 2024 UNNC also signed an agreement with the Zhejiang international communication center.

UNNC has also been the subject of public discussion. In December 2007 the founding Provost, Ian Gow OBE, wrote an article for a discussion paper called "British Universities in China", subtitled "The Reality Beyond the Rhetoric". Drawing on his time as founding Provost, he warned British universities that lasting strategic alliances would need a much better grasp of Chinese higher-education policy, especially as China was becoming a major educational hub and a power in research and development. Vice-Chancellor Colin Campbell then issued a statement distancing the university from Professor Gow's view and criticising a Guardian article for misreading it, and the Guardian later published another response.

In 2018, Stephen Morgan, associate provost since 2016, was taken off the management board after criticising the Chinese Communist Party's 19th National Congress and Party-backed initiatives within the university, though he stayed on the faculty. If questions of academic freedom matter to you, read the university's own statements and independent reporting before applying.

The campus is in Yinzhou District, in the Ningbo Higher Education Park, a zone planned specially for universities; it also holds shared public amenities, among them a stadium and the city library. The site covers 887 mu, roughly 59 hectares or 140 acres. Students arrived in 2004, and John Prescott, Deputy Prime Minister of the UK, held the official inauguration in February 2006. Architecturally the campus takes its cue from the University of Nottingham's University Park campus in England: buildings in British style, landscaped gardens and a lake at the centre.
Day-to-day life depends on the city outside the gates, so these sections describe Ningbo: its position, weather, economy and sights.

Ningbo lies between latitudes 28° 51' and 30° 33' N and longitudes 120° 55' and 122° 16' E. It is bounded by the East China Sea and the Zhoushan Archipelago on the east, by Hangzhou Bay on the north (across which lie Jiaxing and Shanghai), by Shaoxing on the west and by Taizhou on the south. The city has 3,790 sq mi (9,816 square kilometers) of land and 3,768 sq mi (9,758 km2) of ocean territory, and a total coastline of 971 mi (1,562 km): 490 mi (788 km) on the mainland and 481 mi (774 km) on islands, together one-third of the whole provincial coastline. The city administers 531 islands, which add up to 202 sq mi (524 km2).

Ningbo proper is wedged between the sea and low south-western mountains; plain and valleys fill the gap, and the central business district is split by the Yongjiang River. Two peninsulas stand out: Chuanshan (穿山半岛), in Beilun District, where mainland Zhejiang's easternmost point lies, and Xiangshan (象山半岛), in Xiangshan County. Heading north from Mount Tiantai, the Siming Mountains (四明山) pass through the Haishu and Fenghua Districts and Yuyao City in the municipality and top out at 3,212 ft (979 m). Tidal flat ecosystems lie next to the city, although large parts have been reclaimed for farming.

Köppen classes Ningbo's climate as humid subtropical (Cfa), with four distinct seasons. Expect a hot, humid summer and a chilly, cloudy, dry winter in which snow occasionally falls. January is the coolest month, averaging 5.8 °C (42.4 °F), and July the warmest at 29.1 °C (84.4 °F), with 17.6 °C (63.7 °F) as the annual mean. Over the record since 1951 the low was -8.8 °C (16 °F), recorded on 12 January 1955, and the high 108 °F (42.1 °C) on 8 August 2013.

Annual rainfall averages 56 in (1,430 mm). June brings the Asian monsoon's plum rains, and relative humidity peaks then. Typhoon effects reach Ningbo between August and October, with an average of 1.8 storms a year, though direct hits are uncommon. A 2012 OECD study put Ningbo among the top 20 cities in the world most at risk of flooding from human-caused climate change, and the city is among those in China adopting sponge city strategies to reduce the impact.

Ningbo, an important port city, lies 140 mi (220 kilometers) south of Shanghai, and its export business dates back to the 7th century. Electrical goods, textiles, food and industrial tools are the main exports now. A well-developed private sector generated 80 percent of the city's GDP in 2013.

For a long time Ningbo was somewhat cut off from other major cities. When the Hangzhou Bay Bridge opened in 2007, the highway journey to Shanghai fell to two and a half hours, from four. Ningbo now acts as the economic hub of the southern Yangtze River Delta and counts as one of China's most competitive cities.

A few numbers: 2009 saw economic activity of US$60.8 billion, 10.4 percent less than 2008, with exports at US$38.65 billion (16.6 percent lower) and imports at US$22.16 billion (3.1 percent higher). Growth in 2013 was 9.26 percent, taking the economy to 712.89 billion yuan, or US$115.12 billion. Output per head in 2009 was US$10,833, roughly triple the national average.
#### Foreign investment

Several important development zones in and around Ningbo have drawn considerable foreign investment. More than 60 financial institutions, domestic and foreign-invested, operate in the city, and over 10,000 foreigners have been attracted to live here. Preferential policies from the municipal government aim to draw investment into creative industries, information services, manufacturing, new strategic industries and international trade.
#### Development zones

Economic and Technological Development Zone (Ningbo): in the north-east behind Beilun Port, 17 mi (27 km) from downtown. For twenty years it has been the main framework for big construction projects and for creating a good investment climate. The port and Ningbo Lishe International Airport are close, and ExxonMobil, Dow Chemical and Dupont are among its investors.

Daxie Development Zone (Ningbo): approved in 1993 and covering 2.29 sq mi (5.92 km2). More than ten years of construction have given it the industrial and logistical base to handle transshipment of containers, liquid chemicals and energy.

National Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (Ningbo): founded in 1999 and raised to national level in January 2007. It is 6.2 mi (10 km) from Ningbo International Airport and 11 mi (18 km) from Ningbo Port, and serves as a key technical innovation base for the Yangtze River Delta. Encouraged sectors are research and development, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, chemical production and processing, and raw material processing.

Ningbo Free Trade Zone: one of 15 zones the State Council has authorised, and Zhejiang Province's only one. Set up by the State Council in 1992 on 0.89 sq mi (2.3 km2), it lies midway along mainland China's coast, south of the Yangtze River Delta. Its industrial output value in 2008 was RMB 53.33 billion, 19.8 percent more than in 2007.
Nordic Industrial Park (NIP): one of China's earliest industrial parks owned entirely by foreign investors, in Ningbo and run by a Scandinavian management team.
Ningbo Advertising Park: a national-level pilot park in the Southern Business District; financial incentives have brought in over 300 firms in the field.

A long history and a prosperous economy have given Ningbo a wealth of things to visit. The main attractions below, grouped by district, follow the list kept by the municipal tourism, culture, radio and television bureau.

Yuehu Park, or Moon Lake Park, sits in the middle of Haishu District around a reservoir that was dug in the Tang dynasty, in 636 CE. Besides the lake and a few small islands it is home to many ancient Chinese buildings and historical sites, described below.

Tianyi Pavilion, also called Tianyi Chamber, ranks among Ningbo's best-known sights. It was built in 1516 CE and is the oldest surviving library in Asia and counted among the 3 oldest private libraries anywhere. Its holdings reach back to the 11th century and include woodblock-printed and hand-copied editions of the Confucian classics, scarce local histories and lists of successful imperial examination candidates. The name now stands for an entire museum complex. It takes in the Ming-dynasty mansion (1516 CE) that belonged to the library's first owner, Fan Qing, together with a traditional Chinese garden and an old private theater for Chinese plays, and it also contains a Mahjong (麻將) museum since Ningbo is thought of as where the game began.

Honouring the poet He Zhizhang (賀知章, 659 CE-744 CE), who lived in the Tang dynasty and styled himself the "Siming Crazy Guest" (Siming being a mountain near Ningbo), the He Ancestral Temple (賀祕監祠) dates from the Song dynasty (finished in 1144 CE) and was mended in the Qing (1865 CE).

The Ancient Korean Embassy was put up in the Northern Song dynasty to host Korean envoys and trading groups. Fighting destroyed it in 1130 CE; in 1984 the site was declared a cultural relics protection unit, and it now serves as a showroom for the history of Ningbo's relations with Korea.

A ghost story links four Moon Lake locations: Xuanmiao Temple, Zhenming Ridge, Central Lake East Bridge and Central Lake Temple. The Ningbo-born novelist Qu You set a tale, Peony Dengji (牡丹燈記; in Japanese Botan Dōrō, and as 怪談牡丹燈籠 it is known in English as Tales of the Peony Lantern), in his collection Jiandeng Xinhua, telling of love between a ghost and a man in the Fang Guozhen period at Moon Lake. The Japanese scholar Koyama Issei matched these four places to the geography and architecture in the story, and the tale became one of three Kaidan stories adapted in Japan.

Haishu Tower, part of the Drum Tower Complex, is all that survives of a Tang-dynasty city gate tower. In the Republic period a six-meter-high Romanesque bell tower was added at the top, and the buildings of the commercial area at its foot have been reconstructed in traditional style.
Chenghuang Temple, known as Ningbo County Temple, is an ancient City God temple in the heart of the downtown shopping area.

Tianfeng Pagoda is a nationally protected cultural relic and a classic Song-style brick-and-wood loft tower of a type found only in Jiangnan. The hexagonal landmark is the tallest ancient structure in town: it looks like a tower of seven stories but has seven more below ground, and it is prized for its age, its architecture and the artifacts found in it. Building began in 695 CE under the Tang dynasty (618-907 CE).
Tianyi Square is a lively spot in the old downtown, with a well-known national shopping complex that takes its name from the Tianyi Ge (Chamber), Asia's oldest private library.

Along the river, Nantang Old Street offers shops selling folk arts and crafts, souvenirs and local snacks in small restaurants. It used to be where local fairs and flea markets took place, and a 2013 renovation turned it into a visitor attraction.
Liangzhu Cultural Park is a theme park built around the tale of the Butterfly Lovers, one of China's four folklores and often called the oriental Romeo and Juliet.

Baiyun Manor was the ancient academy where Huang Zongxi (黃宗羲) lectured. Huang, whose style name was Taichong, was an eminent thinker, writer and historian at the end of the Ming and start of the Qing.
Tashan Weir is an ancient dam from the Tang dynasty.
Wulongtan Scenic Resort, also known as Five-dragon Pools, is rated National AAAA as a scenic area and numbers among Ningbo's Ten New Sceneries.
Xiaowen Street is an ancient street in Haishu's old town, named after Yang Qing (杨庆), a son of the Song dynasty remembered for his filial devotion.

university-of-nottingham-ningbo-china.h: Yinzhou District, where UNNC is located

blocks.x: Ningbo Museum (also Yinzhou Museum or Ningbo Historic Museum) presents local history and traditional customs. Its architect, Wang Shu, was in 2012 the first Chinese citizen ever to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize, and and the museum is regarded as his masterwork. It was also the principal location for the 2023 television adaptation of Liu Cixin's science fiction novel Three Bodies.
Romon U-Park is among the largest urban indoor theme parks on Earth.

Ningbo Eastern New Town is a recently developed part of the city with a carefully designed CBD (two 400m skyscrapers, the headquarters of many listed companies and government offices) and various museums, galleries and shopping centers. They include the Urban Planning Exhibition Center; the Hankyu Commercial Complex, which opened in 2021 as the first overseas store of the well-known Japanese department store Hankyu; the New Ningbo library, which opened its doors in 2018; and Yinzhou Park with the Ningbo Southern CBD.

Dongqian Lake is Zhejiang's largest natural freshwater lake. West Jin dynasty writings give its earliest historical mention, and the shores hold several scenic and historical sights. Little Putuo is a lake island with temples that a Song-dynasty prime minister named Shihao had built. Yuefei Temple was built in the Song dynasty to commemorate Yuefei. On Taogong Island, folklore says, Fanli and Xishi once lived. The Southern Song Dynasty Rock Carving Park received a "National Cultural Relics Conservation Best Project Award" from two bodies, the China Cultural Relics Conservation Foundation and the China National Architecture Research Association. Fuquan Mountain has a Chinese tea theme park.
Ningbo Hanling Old Street has a history of thousands of years and used to be called Hanling City, where "city" meant a bazaar.
In downtown Ningbo, Qita Temple is a Zen Buddhist temple complex first consecrated in the Tang dynasty.

Tianhou Temple was dedicated to Mazu as the "Empress of Heaven" and was once the guild hall (Qing'an Huiguan) of merchants from Fujian. In the 19th century S. Wells Williams considered it the loveliest place in Ningbo and John Thomson counted it among the loveliest temples in China, but the original building was lost during the Chinese Civil War. The reconstruction reuses many original works of art, and the building is now the East Zhejiang Maritime Affairs and Folk Customs Museum.
Temple of King Ashoka is a Buddhist temple founded in the Western Jin dynasty (282 AD).
Tiantong Temple is counted among the "Five Chan Buddhism Temples" and is where the Japanese Buddhist Sōtō school (曹洞宗, Sōtō-shū) began.
Ningbo Ocean World is an aquarium with an ocean theater.
Ningbo Wildlife Park, used to be called Ningbo Youngor Zoo and is now a 4A-level scenic area inside the Dongqian Lake Tourist Resort and one of China's largest wildlife parks measured by water area.
Ningbo Sakura Park (Zhongxing Sakura Park) was created to mark the friendship between Ningbo and its sister city Nagaoka in Japan.

USTB (北京科技大学) is a state-run institution in Beijing's Haidian District, answering to the Ministry of Education. It counts among the universities in China's Project 211 and its Double First-Class Construction drive. Until 1988 it carried a different name, Beijing Steel and Iron Institute (北京钢铁学院), which tells you a lot about its roots: this is a school built around metals, materials and engineering.

USTB was set up in 1952 by joining five earlier colleges together, and its first name was the Industrial Institute of Steel and Iron of Beijing (北京钢铁工业学院). In 1960 it became Beijing Steel and Iron Institute, and only in 1988 did it take the name it uses today. A further milestone came in 1997, when USTB was placed in the first tier of China's 211 Project, the national effort to develop 100 world-class universities for the 21st century.

Today USTB is made up of 38 schools. Study options number 48 at bachelor level, 121 at master level and 73 at doctoral level, along with 16 postdoctoral research areas. Its large departments cover physics, chemistry, engineering, economics and English, and one of the biggest is Materials Science and Engineering. The student body is about 14,000 undergraduates plus roughly 14,000 PhD and graduate students. Inside Materials Science and Engineering alone, about 500 are undergraduates and roughly 200 more are on assorted postgraduate courses.

Because the university began as an iron and steel school, its materials science department is among the strongest anywhere and is well known internationally, especially for physical metallurgy and the metal physics of microstructures in structural and functional materials. If metals, materials or process engineering is your field, this is a very natural address.
The academic units are listed below. The first group is teaching schools, followed by research laboratories, centres and institutes.
National Center for Materials Service Safety

university-of-science-and-technology-bei.h: The campus and its Olympic legacy

blocks.x: The site covers 803,900 m2 in Haidian District by the Fourth Ring Road, in the zone of Beijing where most of the leading higher-education institutions are concentrated. On the eastern side stands the USTB Gymnasium, one of four university venues in Beijing used for the 2008 Summer Olympics. It hosted judo and taekwondo at the 29th Olympic Games and wheelchair basketball and wheelchair rugby at the 13th Paralympic Games.

Students live in dormitories that were newly built and finished in 2005. After the Games, the main hall of the gymnasium became a space for indoor physical education, fitness training, sports contests and artistic performances, and the comprehensive gymnasium serves for swimming classes and as an aquatic park. In short, you get good sports facilities on your doorstep.

university-of-science-and-technology-bei.h: A long record with international students

blocks.x: The university is a participant in the Chinese Government Scholarship Program, and foreign students have been enrolling since 1954. Over two thousand of them, coming from 74 countries and regions, have studied or researched on campus, so you would be in good company.

USTB turns up within the top 500 of several international league tables: QS, ARWU (the Academic Ranking of World Universities), U.S. News & World Report, CWTS Leiden and the Center for World University Rankings. In the 2023 edition of ARWU, nicknamed the Shanghai Ranking, it sat in the 201-300 group. In U.S. News's 2024 global table it was 381st overall and 89th among Asian institutions.

Within Beijing it is regarded as a leading engineering research centre, and Chinese academics respect its metallurgy and materials science teaching in particular. Every year from 2018, ARWU has named it number one in the world for Metallurgical Engineering.

A few recent results show where the research energy lies. A metaverse project for self-driving vehicles, "Jiu Lu", was launched by the university. Two SCCE papers from USTB were rated excellent by the national science and technology association (CAST). USTB took 23 prizes in the 2022 metallurgy science and technology awards, and has five State-level science and technology prizes.
