university-of-science-and-technology-bei.h: Living in Beijing: what the city is like

blocks.x: Where you live matters almost as much as where you study. Day to day, a student at USTB will feel the city's weather, its air, its streets and its skyline long before thinking about its history. The sections below walk through Beijing as a place to live: how it looks, how the land lies, what the seasons do, and how the air quality has changed.

Walk across Beijing and you will meet three architectural layers. The oldest is imperial: the huge Tian'anmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace), still the best-known symbol of the People's Republic, sits alongside the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Imperial Ancestral Temple. The second layer is the so-called "Sino-Sov" look of the 1950s to 1970s, when blocky, sometimes badly built structures went up. The third is the modern skyline, concentrated around the Beijing CBD in the east of the city, where you find the new CCTV Headquarters, and also seen at the Beijing National Stadium and the National Center for the Performing Arts.

Since the start of the 21st century the city has seen an enormous wave of construction, much of it by international designers and most visible in the CBD. The 798 Art Zone is a good place to see the old and the new side by side, mixing 1950s industrial design with neofuturistic touches. The tallest building in town is the 528-metre China Zun. Beijing towers have twice won the CTBUH Skyscraper Award, which goes to a single best tall building in the whole world each year: first the Linked Hybrid (2009), then the CCTV Headquarters (2013).

Then there are the siheyuans, courtyard homes built around an open yard. Grand examples include the Prince Gong Mansion and the Residence of Soong Ching-ling. Courtyards are linked by narrow lanes called hutongs, which usually run east to west so that doors open to the north and south, a layout chosen for good Feng Shui. Some are wide, others so tight that only a few people can squeeze through together. Both used to be everywhere, but entire blocks are being swapped for high-rises. Hutong residents are entitled to new apartments at least as large as their old homes, yet many say the neighbourly street life cannot be rebuilt, and the properties are often owned by the government. If you want to see this old fabric, go sooner rather than later.

Geographically, Beijing is perched where the North China Plain, a rough triangle of flat land, ends in the north; the plain stretches away south and east of the city. To the north, northwest and west, mountains act as a screen, keeping the desert steppes away from the farmland of northern China. In the northwest, notably in Yanqing District and Huairou District, the Jundu Mountains take over, and the Western Hills (Xishan) form the western backdrop. The Great Wall runs along the rugged northern terrain; it was built there to hold off raiders from the steppe. The highest point in the municipality is Mount Dongling, in the Western Hills on the Hebei border, at 2,303 metres (7,556 ft).

The Chaobai, Yongding and Juma are the main rivers, all belonging to the Hai River system and all flowing southeast. The largest reservoir is Miyun Reservoir on the upper Chaobai. Two great waterworks end or begin here: Beijing is the northern end of the Grand Canal to Hangzhou, a transport route more than 1,400 years old, and it receives Yangtze basin water through the South-North Water Transfer Project, built within the last decade.

The built-up city occupies a modest but growing share of the municipality, on flat land 40 to 60 metres (130-200 feet) above sea level in the south-central part. Its shape is a set of nested ring roads. The innermost, the Second Ring Road, traces where the old walls stood, while the Sixth Ring Road, far out, links the satellite towns around the edge. At the very centre are Tian'anmen and Tian'anmen Square, just south of the Forbidden City, once home to the emperors. West of Tian'anmen lies Zhongnanhai, where China's current leaders live. Chang'an Avenue slips between Tiananmen and the Square and serves as the main east-west axis.

People call this steady outward sprawl from the old core a pancake spreading (tan da bing), and it is often blamed for the city's urban problems, including the long journeys you may face between campus and the centre.

Climatically, the city is classed as humid continental (Köppen: Dwa), close to the monsoonal cold semi-arid type (Köppen: BSk). In practice: the East Asian monsoon makes summers hot and sticky, while the huge Siberian anticyclone makes winters brief, cold and dry. Spring can bring sandstorms from the Gobi Desert over the Mongolian steppe, with fast warming and dry air. Autumn is a transition season with very little rain. Between 2001 and 2026 the hottest time was early August and the coldest early January.

Under China's official seasonal definitions, spring starts here on 26 March, followed by summer from 20 May, autumn from 13 September and winter from 31 October. Because March and September have recently warmed faster, and May and October more slowly, autumn is generally the shorter season compared with spring.

Now the numbers, taken over the period 1991-2020. Across the urban area, the yearly mean temperature is 12.9 °C at the low end and 13.3 °C at the high end (55.2 and 55.9 °F). Nights average 7.7 to 8.4 °C (45.9 and 47.1 °F), and afternoons 18.5 to 18.9 °C (65.3 and 66.0 °F). Lower suburban land is slightly cooler: yearly means run 11.5-13.0 °C (52.7 and 55.4 °F), with night averages of 5.9-8.0 °C (42.6 and 46.4 °F) and daytime highs of 18.2-18.7 °C (64.8 and 65.7 °F). Up in the mountains the yearly mean sits anywhere from 0 °C (32 °F) to 10 °C (50 °F), falling as the altitude climbs. The average January day sits at -2.7 °C (27.1 °F), while July averages 27.2 °C (81.0 °F).

Rainfall is limited. The municipality gets roughly 528.0 mm (20.79 in) in a year, though Haidian and Chaoyang see more, 584.2 mm (23.00 in), and nearly three-quarters of the total arrives between June and August. Skies are often bright: 2,490.5 sunshine hours annually, and the proportion of possible sun is lowest in July (42%) and highest in January and February (62%). Records since 1951 show a low of -27.4 °C (-17.3 °F), set on 22 February 1966, and a high of 41.9 °C (107.4 °F), set on 24 July 1999. Pack for real cold in winter and real heat in summer.

Beijing has struggled with pollution for a long time, and prospective students are right to ask about it. The story today is one of clear improvement, but it helps to understand how the problem arose and what has been done.

The urban footprint of Beijing quadrupled during 2000-2009. Emissions climbed as a result, and the local meteorology shifted as well: wind speed, humidity and surface albedo near the ground declined, while temperatures, ozone and the trapping of air under a lid grew. Sprawl plus the burning of fossil fuels gave the city lasting environmental trouble and health problems for many residents. Then came 2013, when dense smog blanketed Beijing and most of northern China and touched 600 million people. This "pollution shock" turned clean air into a national economic and social priority. The city responded by trimming coal from 24% of its energy mix in 2012 to 10% by 2017, while the central government demanded the withdrawal of heavy-polluting vehicles over 2015-2017 and accelerated the move to clean energy.

American and Chinese scientists working together in 2006 concluded that a large part of the city's dirty air is imported from surrounding cities and provinces: between 35% and 60% of ozone, on average, starts outside Beijing. Shandong Province and Tianjin Municipality matter most, since summer breezes tend to blow from the south and southeast and the ranges north and northwest of the city stop the air from clearing.

Coal is the main culprit. It accounts for about 40% of Beijing's PM 2.5 and is the biggest supplier of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. The city has been switching its coal-fired power stations over to natural gas since 2012, and wants yearly coal use held at 20 million tons or less. In 2011 the figure was 26.3 million tons, of which 73% went to heat and electricity and the balance to industry. Yet much of what Beijing breathes is made elsewhere. Tianjin's coal burn was forecast to grow from 48 to 63 million tons across 2011-2015. In 2011 Hebei Province consumed above 300 million tons, a bigger amount than the whole of Germany, and just 30% of it fed power generation, with a large part going to steelmaking and cement. Coal-mining regions such as Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Shaanxi (whose consumption is three times its 2000 level) plus Shandong also send emissions Beijing's way. Among Chinese provinces, coal consumption is highest in Shandong, then Shanxi, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, in that order.

Inside the city limits there were once four big coal plants supplying power and winter heating. Gaojing Thermal Power Plant was the first to go, in 2014; two others stopped in March 2015; the final one, Huaneng Thermal Power Plant, was scheduled to stop in 2016. The plan for 2013-2017 was a cut of 13 million tons in coal burned, with a ceiling of 15 million tons set for 2015.

Ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics, nearly US$17 billion was spent to deliver on promises of cleaner air. It also cut bus and subway fares, opened new subway lines and banned high-emission vehicles. It put together 3,800 natural-gas buses, among the largest such fleets anywhere, and became the first Chinese city to demand the equivalent of the Euro 4 emission standard.

For major events the authorities have at times seeded clouds to bring rain and wash the air, for instance ahead of the parade marking the 60th anniversary in 2009, and also to fight drought. Lately the preferred tools are temporary factory shutdowns and heavier traffic limits. They created the short-lived "APEC blue" and "parade blue" skies around the APEC China meeting of 2014 and the military parade for Victory Day in 2015. Air quality improved sharply for those days, then slipped back to unhealthy levels soon after.

Beijing's very first smog alert came on 8 and 9 December 2015 and closed down most industry and commerce; a second "red alert" was declared later in December. The environmental protection bureau said in November 2016 that from 2017, old high-emission cars may not be driven whenever a smog red alert covers the city or adjoining areas.

A declared "war on pollution" in 2014 has produced measurable gains. Fine particulates dropped by 35% during 2017 and went lower again by 2020, chiefly because gas took over from coal for power and dirty factories were cleaned up or removed. By 2022 yearly PM2.5 averaged 30 micrograms per cubic metre, the cleanest since 2013. Just two heavily polluted days occurred in 2024, a record low and a 96.6 percent fall from the 58 days of 2013. Expect much cleaner skies than a decade ago, though winter smog is not entirely gone.

Because of the pollution history, several sources publish readings. The Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau (BJEPB) posts daily data from 27 monitoring stations around the city on its website. The American Embassy in Beijing reports hourly PM2.5 and ozone figures on Twitter. The two measure different pollutants by different criteria, so the BJEPB numbers and the health impact they suggest are often lower than the Embassy's. It is sensible to check both.

Smog is a genuine health risk. It measurably raises illness rates from heart and lung disease in the city, and heavy exposure can cause breathing and heart trouble, hospital visits and even deaths, so a mask and an air-quality app are worth having on bad days.

Dust eroded from deserts in northern and northwestern China brings seasonal dust storms. The Beijing Weather Modification Office sometimes induces rain to fight them and soften their effect. There were at least eight such storms in just the first four months of 2006, and in April 2002 a single storm left almost 50,000 tons of dust on the city before it carried on to Japan and Korea. If you arrive in spring, expect a few hazy, gritty days.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

university-of-science-and-technology-bei.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. University of Science and Technology Beijing may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Beijing, register at University of Science and Technology Beijing by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

university-of-science-and-technology-lia.h: University of Science and Technology Liaoning in outline

blocks.x: University of Science and Technology Liaoning, sometimes shortened to USTL, stands in Anshan, a steel city in Liaoning Province in north-east China. It describes itself as the earliest university of metallurgy established in China. It began as an institution run directly by the national metallurgy ministry and is now a first-class key university of Liaoning Province. Its engineering focus is clear, though it also teaches science, economics, management, literature, law and art, which makes it a multidisciplinary university overall.

The university has been picked for several national and provincial programmes. They include the Ministry of Education's programme for training excellent engineers, the national project on new engineering research and practice, the list of institutions that host students on Chinese government scholarships, and a Liaoning provincial pilot for credit-system management and for transformation and development. It has the right to recommend its own students for postgraduate study, and it has a National University Science and Technology Park. For an international student, the scholarship-host status is particularly worth noting.

The roots go back to 1948, when the idea of a school for iron and steel in Anshan took shape (鞍山钢铁学院). A decade later, in 1958, it was set up properly as AIIST, short for Anshan Institute of Iron and Steel Technology, and put under the central government's ministry for the metallurgical industry. Postgraduate recruitment began in 1980, and in 1983 the university gained the right to award master's degrees.
The later changes came quickly:
1994: a local advanced vocational college in Anshan joined the institute.
1998: supervision passed from the national metallurgy ministry to the Liaoning provincial government.
1999: three provincial colleges, those of food industry, metallurgical industry and construction material industry, along with their campuses, were brought into AIIST.
2002: it became Anshan University of Science and Technology, or ASUST.
2006: the Ministry of Education approved the present name, University of Science and Technology Liaoning, and that same year the university gained the power to confer doctorates.

In February 2021 the university reported grounds of over 1.84 million square metres. It lists 19 colleges and 59 undergraduate majors, plus a graduate offer of 3 first-level doctoral programmes, 13 second-level doctoral programmes, 14 first-level master's programmes, 47 second-level master's programmes and 8 professional master's degrees. A different description gives the university 15 faculties, 35 undergraduate programmes, 11 high-level special professional programmes and 35 graduate programmes. These counts clearly vary with the date and the way they are counted, so confirm the current numbers on the university's own website. Enrolment is given as around 18,000 students.

Several undergraduate subjects have national key status: metallurgy, inorganic non-metallic materials, automation and network engineering. The computer and software engineering department is rated by the province as a key computing department, and in a ministry evaluation the software engineering field landed somewhere between 60th and 80th nationwide.

university-of-science-and-technology-lia.h: Anshan, the city behind the university

blocks.x: The rest of this profile describes Anshan, because a student's day-to-day experience depends on the place around the campus: the weather, the transport links and what the local economy looks like.

Anshan lies north of the Liao River plains. The west and centre of the city are broad, flat land, while the south-east edge turns hilly and mountainous, ending at the Qian Mountains, where the well-known Qianshan National Park is found. Minerals are abundant underground, including iron ore, coal, magnesite, talc and jade. The western plains are fertile and well suited to agriculture, with arable land covering 24,480 hectares (60,500 acres), which is 26.4% of the whole territory. The area is famous for Nanguo pears (南果梨), nicknamed the king of pears. In the Ming dynasty, Anshan was a travel stop with inns for people passing through on official business.

Anshan's climate is humid continental with a monsoon influence (Köppen Dwa). The monsoon brings hot, sticky summers, whereas the Siberian high produces long, cold, dry winters, and the four seasons are clearly distinct. Roughly half the annual rain falls in July and August. In January the daily average is −7.6 °C (18.3 °F); in July it is 25.9 °C (78.6 °F); across the year the figure is 10.6 °C (51.1 °F). You can expect a lot of sun, with 2,595.4 hours annually, and humidity averages 55%, from a low of 44% in April to 71% in July and August. The coldest recorded temperature is −26.9 °C (−16.4 °F), and the hottest 38.2 °C (100.8 °F).

The local economy matters for internships, graduate jobs and daily life, and in Anshan that means steel and the industries that grew around it. The history below shows why the university was founded here.

university-of-science-and-technology-lia.h: Why Anshan became a steel city

blocks.x: The north-east is one of the country's main industrial regions, and Anshan ranks among its key sites. The city sits amid no less than a quarter of China's iron and coal resources, which has earned it a reputation as China's capital of iron and steel. Before the steel industry arrived, Anshan was a fairly small and unimportant town. As the mills grew, so did the city, and spin-off industries developed next to the steelworks until the whole area became a heavy-industry hub.

university-of-science-and-technology-lia.h: From a joint venture to Angang

blocks.x: A joint Chinese-Japanese venture, the Anshan Zhenzing Iron Ore Company Unlimited, began operating in 1918. After Japan occupied northeast China in 1931, the mills became a monopoly owned by Japan, and Anshan became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo, with further industry developing around the mills. As a strategic industrial hub in World War II, the city was bombed continually by the Allies.

The numbers show how big the works became. In 1931 and 1932, Manchuria as a whole made 1,000,000 tonnes of processed iron, and nearly half of that came from Shōwa Steel in Anshan. By 1938 output had risen to 7,000,000 tonnes. In 1941 the Shōwa Steel Works could produce 1,750,000 tonnes of iron bars and 1,000,000 tonnes of processed steel, and by 1942 its total capacity stood at 3,600,000 tonnes, which put it among the world's major iron and steel centres.

Soviet forces looted the plant in 1945. The Republic of China government repaired part of it, but it was destroyed again in the Chinese Civil War, which the Communist forces won. The mills were repaired once more, and the Anshan Iron and Steel Company, known as Angang, was founded in 1948. From that year to 2001 its output added up to 290 million tons of steel, 284 million tons of pig iron and 192 million tons of rolled products. Angang was China's largest steel producer until a new steel plant opened in Shanghai. Today it comprises three steelworks with 13 rolling mills and supporting plants making coke, refractory materials and machinery for steelmaking. Annual capacity is 10 million tons each of pig iron and steel, plus 9.5 million tons of rolled steel. About a quarter of China's iron ore reserves, roughly 10 billion tons, lie in Anshan, so the city will remain a significant steel producer for a long time.

The south and south-east of Anshan hold magnesite reserves equal to a quarter of the world's total. The city also has the largest talcum reserve on the planet, a full third of world supply. Xiuyan is known for its jade; the largest single piece ever discovered came from there, and today it is carved as a Buddha and draws many visitors.

A five-year plan drawn up by the Anshan government in 2000 aimed to make the city a strong, modern industrial base that also has a lively tourism sector. The targets were a city GDP of 100 billion RMB by 2005 and a modern industrial city built by using advanced technology to transform traditional industries. Attracting foreign investment was another central goal, and the government expected foreign investment assets of around 80 billion RMB by 2005. In November 2010 the Economist Intelligence Unit's Access China White Paper placed Anshan among the CHAMPS, a six-city group made up of Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Maanshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang, in a study of the 20 top emerging cities in China. The cultural sociologist Michael B. Griffiths has also documented how businesses can reach Anshan's consumers.
The city is diverse for an industrial centre in the north-east, with a large Manchu community and many people who came for work in the steel industry.

Anshan prefecture has 3,584,000 residents, of whom 519,400 are ethnic Manchu, reflecting the long rule of northeast China by that group. Most live in or near the Xiuyan Man autonomous area inside the prefecture. Towards the end of the Qing period large numbers of Han people headed to the north-east looking for jobs, and this continued into the twentieth century. As Anshan grew into a large industrial centre during and after World War II, its population soared and newcomers soon outnumbered the Man. The last census recorded 48 ethnic groups in Anshan. Han people number 3,020,500, and after them and the Man come the Hui, with 23,400, and the Chaoxian, with 10,000. The Hui are spread widely, while most Chaoxian live in Tiexi (West district) and Qianshan district.

The 2010 census gave the city a population of 3.65 million. The two neighbours, Anshan and Liaoyang, have grown towards one another so that there is hardly any farmland to see between them, and the urban districts of both cities together hold 2.17 million inhabitants.

The city splits into several districts. Tiedong, in the east, has 452,900 people, and Tiexi, in the west, has 311,600; the railway lines running north to south through the city separate the two. The north-western part of the city is dominated by Angang's huge steelworks. Lishan district houses 425,600 people, and Qianshan district's suburbs have 366,200. Within the prefecture, the subordinate city of Haicheng has 1,181,100 people and the neighbouring town of Tai'an has 354,700.

There is no river or sea port in Anshan. A military airfield close by, Anshan Teng'ao Airport (AOG), also handles domestic commercial flights: five routes to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu and Nanjing, each with a daily flight all year round. It is 15 km (9 miles) south-west of the centre. A city terminal in Tiexi district, on Qianshan Road, supplements the small airport building; travellers can buy tickets and check in there, and then ride a coach to the airport. The nearest other major airports are Shenyang Taoxian International (SHE), about 90 km (56 miles) north, and Dalian Zhoushuizi International, about 270 km (170 miles) south. These flight details are dated, so check current schedules.

The road network starts with the Shenyang–Dalian Expressway beside the city (a section of the G15 from Shenyang to Haikou), an eight-lane tolled road paid for with private money and the first of its type in mainland China. A few kilometres north of the city the Liaozhong Ring Expressway (G91) links Benxi in the east with the Jingshen Expressway (G1) in the west. The Panhai and Danxi expressways, which combine to make the G16, run through the counties of Haicheng and Xiuyan, linking them with Yingkou and Panjin to the west and with Dandong to the east. Long-distance coaches go to all the main cities in the province and to Beijing.

By rail, the city connects to Beijing, Dalian, the north-eastern provinces of Jilin and Heilongjiang and eastern Inner Mongolia, and there is even a slow direct train to Hong Kong. Since December 2012 the Harbin–Dalian High-Speed Railway has served Anshan West and Haicheng West stations, linking Dalian in the south with Shenyang, Changchun and Harbin in the north-east. This line was hailed as the first alpine high-speed railway in the world: it runs at its full 300 km/h in summer but is held to 200 km/h in winter. High-speed trains also run through Anshan to Beijing, and Tai'an county is served by a separate high-speed line between Shenyang and Beijing.

Within the city, people mostly travel by bus and taxi. A single tram line once ran along Zhonghua Avenue past the main gate of Angang, but it has been closed and the rails removed. Because the city centre is flat, cycling is popular, and almost every road has a wide bicycle lane on each side, often protected from motor traffic by a kerb island.
Anshan is only one part of Liaoning, and the province has a long and layered past. A short tour helps you read the place names and cultural mix you will meet during your stay.
The province around the university has a long story, and it explains why Liaoning is a mix of cultures.

university-of-science-and-technology-lia.h: From the Yan state to the Tang

blocks.x: From the 4th century BC to the 9th century, Han Chinese governments mostly settled and ruled Liaoning. Earlier, before the 3rd century BC, the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples were the inhabitants. About 300 BC the state of Yan took the area and created two commanderies, Liaodong to the east of the Liao River and Liaoxi to the west. Xiangping, the Yan city that served as the centre of Liaodong, stood where Liaoyang is today. When the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family kept a semi-independent state, also called Yan, in Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Though it was short-lived, it carried out many diplomatic and trading voyages by sea and left a lasting influence on culture in north-east Asia. Once the Western Jin ended, the Murong tribe's Xianbei states governed Liaoning, namely Former Yan, Later Yan and Northern Yan. When Northern Wei captured the Yan capital in 436, Goguryeo took the Liaodong Peninsula; later the Tang annexed the region during the war between Goguryeo and Tang.

The An Lushan Rebellion in the mid-8th century drained Tang resources away from the frontiers, and the Bohai state slowly spread into Liaodong. In time the Khitan Liao dynasty conquered Liaoning and split it among the Eastern, Supreme, Central and Lower Capital Circuits. The Jurchen Jin dynasty administered most of it as the Eastern Capital Route and divided the remainder among the Xianping, Supreme Capital and Northern Capital Routes. Genghis Khan conquered the region in 1206, and it was later brought into the Yuan dynasty: the east belonged to the Liaoyang and Shenyang Routes under the Liaoyang Branch Secretariat, the north to Xianping Prefecture of the Kaiyuan Route, and the west, including the Guangning Route, was also under the Liaoyang secretariat, while the Jinzhou and Chaoyang areas came under the Daning Route and the Central Secretariat.

The Ming took control of Liaoning in 1371, only three years after the Mongols were driven from Beijing. Around 1442 a defensive wall went up to protect the province's farmland from a possible threat from the Oriyanghan, a Jurchen-Mongol group that was a Ming tributary, in the north-west. Between 1467 and 1468 it was extended to shield the region from the north-east, against the Jianzhou Jurchens, who later became known as the Manchus. This Liaodong Wall had a similar purpose to the Great Wall but a cheaper design: some parts used stone and tile, but most of it was an earth bank with a moat on each side.

Yet the wall did not hold: early in the 17th century the Jurchens seized Liaodong (eastern Liaoning), many years before they conquered the rest of China. Their dynasty, first styled Later Jin and later renamed Qing, placed its capital at Xingjing (兴京), outside the Liaodong Wall in the east of the modern province, between 1616 and 1621. It then shifted to Dongjing, which lay east of present-day Liaoyang, and in 1625 to Shengjing, now Shenyang. After the Qing captured Beijing in 1644 the main capital went there, but Shengjing remained a significant regional capital through most of Qing rule.

The Qing conquest cost Liaoning much of its population. Many local Chinese either died in the fighting or escaped to the area south of the Great Wall, and retreating Ming troops themselves wrecked a lot of cities. As late as 1661 Zhang Shangxian, the civil governor of Fengtian Province, reported that apart from Fengtian City (Shenyang), Liaoyang and Haicheng, every city east of the Liao River was abandoned or had only a few hundred residents. He wrote that Tieling and Fushun had no more than a few vagrants. Across the Liao to the west, just Ningyuan, Jinzhou and Guangning still had sizeable populations.

From the 1650s, beginning with laws in 1651 and 1653, the imperial government actively recruited settlers from beyond the Great Wall, many of them from Shandong, to fill the sparsely populated Fengtian Province, which broadly matches today's Liaoning. Many people in Liaoning today trace their ancestry to these seventeenth-century settlers. Officially, the remainder of the north-east stayed closed to Han Chinese through most of the Manchu era. To stop migration there, covering today's Jilin and Heilongjiang and neighbouring Inner Mongolia, the Qing built the Willow Palisade between about 1638 and 1672. It circled the farmland of Fengtian, running slightly outside the old Ming wall or following it in places, and separated it from the Manchu forests in the north-east and the Mongol grazing land in the north-west.

Later the government tried to stop migrants entering Fengtian, to send some back, or if that failed to legalise them. An edict of 1704, for instance, noted that recent Han settlers had ignored earlier orders to leave and told them to register and join a local defence group (保, bao) or return home within ten years; ten years on, another edict appeared reminding officials of the need to deal with illegal migrants. The restrictions did not work as well as Beijing hoped, and the population of Fengtian still doubled from 1683 to 1734. Under the Qing, Manchuria had three generals, and the General of Shengjing was the one who governed most of present-day Liaoning. The Manchu authorities began to reopen the region to migrants in 1860, and soon Han Chinese made up the main ethnic group.
Liaoning is not only about steel and history; farmland and orchards are important too, and local fruit appears in markets everywhere.

The principal crops in Liaoning are maize, sorghum and soybeans, and cotton is grown too. Around Dalian, farms grow three-quarters of the apples and peaches that China exports. Specialities by place include apples from Dalian and Yingkou, golden peaches from Dalian, Beizhen pears from Jinzhou, white pears from Huludao and Suizhong, and Gushan apricots and plums from Dandong.

university-of-science-and-technology-of-.h: About University of Science and Technology of China

blocks.x: The University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) is a public university in Hefei, Anhui, China. It is owned by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and co-funded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the Ministry of Education of China, and the Anhui Provincial Government. It is part of Project 211, Project 985, and the Double First-Class Construction.

The university was founded in Beijing by the Chinese Academy of Sciences in September 1958. In the beginning of 1970, the university moved to Hefei during the Cultural Revolution. The university has 13 schools, 11 national research platforms, 8 science-education integration colleges, and 5 joint cooperative institutes with local governments. The university is a member of the C9 League.

The university was founded in Beijing by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) in September 1958. The director of CAS, Guo Moruo was appointed the first president of USTC. USTC's founding mission was to develop a high-level science and technology workforce, as deemed critical for the development of China's economy, defense, and science and technology education. The establishment was hailed as "A Major Event in the History of Chinese Education and Science." CAS has supported USTC by combining most of its institutes with the departments of the university. In 1959, USTC was listed in the top 16 national key universities, becoming the youngest national key university.
At the beginning of 1970, the university moved to Hefei during the Cultural Revolution.
In 2012, USTC and the National University of Defense Technology signed a strategic agreement to cooperate on quantum computing research at a ceremony attended by Pan Jianwei and Yang Xuejun.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Hefei, where University of Science and Technology of China is located.

Hefei is located 130 kilometres (81 mi) west of Nanjing in south-central Anhui. Chao Lake, a lake 15 km (9 mi) southeast of the city, is one of the largest fresh water lakes in China. Though the lake has unfortunately been polluted with nitrogen and phosphorus in recent decades, the situation is improving due to efforts by both the government and the people.

Hefei features a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons. Hefei's annual average temperature is 16.6 °C (61.9 °F). Its annual precipitation is just slightly over 1,000 millimetres (39 in), being heavier from May through August. Winters are damp and cold, with January lows dipping just below freezing and January averaging 2.8 °C (37.0 °F). The city sees irregular snowfalls that rarely turn significant. Occasional cold spells from Siberia that usually happen during winter months such as December, January, February. Sometimes November and March which can bring snow and heavier snowfall. (Springs are generally relatively pleasant if somewhat erratic. Summers are hot and humid, with a July average of 28.6 °C (83.5 °F). In the months of June, July, August, and often September, daily temperatures can reach or surpass 37 °C (99 °F) with high humidity levels being the norm. Autumn in Hefei sees a gradual cooling and drying. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 35 percent in March to 50 percent in August, the city receives 1,868 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −20.6 °C (−5 °F) on 6 January 1955, to 41.1 °C (106 °F) on 27 July 2017.

Air quality typically diminishes in May and June when the city is blanketed by smog caused by the smoke generated as farmers outside the city burn their fields in preparation for planting the next crop.
As of 2021, the GDP of Hefei is CN¥1,141.28 billion. The GDP per capita of the city is ¥121,187 (US$18,784), ranking within the top 20 of cities in China.
As of 2023, the GDP of Hefei is CN¥1,267.38 billion.
In 2025, Hefei produced 1.37 million electric vehicles, equivalent to nearly one in every 12 electric vehicles made in China.
Hefei's city government is highly engaged in business, both through state-owned enterprises and investment. This approach has helped drive economic growth and re-structure the cities economic base.

In 2008, the local government spent US$3.5 billion for a controlling ownership stake in BOE Technology (Jingdongfang). BOE Technology subsequently grew to be one of the world's leading manufacturers of semiconductor products for telecommunications. It is also the world's largest manufacturer of liquid crystal displays, organic light-emitting diodes, and flexible displays. As of at least 2024, BOE has three production lines in Hefei, and its presence has helped Hefei attract further business in the electronics supply chain and contributed to Hefei's development as one of the main centers for the optoelectronic industry in China.
In 2008, Hefei invested heavily in iFlytek, a voice-recognition technology firm spun off from USTC.

The local government invested heavily in NIO in order to integrate it with Hefei Changan Automobile, a legacy enterprise from the Third Front construction. NIO was on the brink of bankruptcy in 2020 when Hefei obtained a 25% stake in the company in exchange for RMB 7 billion. NIO moved its headquarters to Hefei, where the government helped it obtain loans from local banks to expand its supply chains. As of 2022, NIO is China's most successful electric vehicle manufacturer. The local government has also invested in the ChangXin Memory Technologies, which is China's largest and the world's fourth-largest DRAM maker.

Hefei has been identified by the Economist Intelligence Unit in the November 2010 Access China White Paper as a member of the CHAMPS (Chongqing, Hefei, Anshan, Ma'anshan, Pingdingshan and Shenyang), an economic profile of the top 20 emerging cities in China.
Hefei was identified by The Economist in December 2012 as the world's No.1 fastest growing metropolitan economy.
Hefei has supported the growth of the chip industry in the city and has become one of the biggest sites for the manufacture of memory chips (DRAM).

Hefei has been the provincial capital since 1945 (before it was Lihuang, which is today's Jinzhai) and is a natural center of transportation, being situated to the north of Chao Lake and standing on a low saddle crossing the northeastern extension of the Dabie Mountains, which form the divide between the Huai and Yangtze rivers. From Hefei there is easy water transport via the lake to the Yangtze River opposite Wuhu.

There are two main train stations in Hefei. The newest one is Hefei South railway station (Hefeinan station, 合肥火车南站) where most high-speed trains pass through. The alternative station is Hefei railway station (合肥火车站) which is smaller and older.

There are some small stations such as Feidong Station (肥东火车站), Feixi Station (肥西火车站), Shuijiahu Station (水家湖火车站), Chaohu Station (巢湖火车站), Chaohu East railway station (Chaohudong station; 巢湖火车东站), Hefeibeicheng Station (Hefei Northtown Station 合肥北城火车站), Lujiang Station (庐江火车站) and so on. These stations are mostly located in small towns and connect commuters with the main city.

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport replaced the old Hefei Luogang International Airport and started its operation on 30 May 2013, 00:00. This new domestic aviation hub is located in Gaoliu Village situated in the northwestern part of Hefei City. The first arriving flight was China Eastern Airlines flight MU5172 from Beijing Capital International Airport. The first departing flight was China Eastern Airlines MU5468 to Shanghai Pudong International Airport.

Hefei Xinqiao International Airport provides scheduled passenger service to major airports in China and other international cities. Destinations include Hong Kong, Macao, Singapore, Taipei (Taoyuan, Songshan), Kaohsiung, Taichung, Seoul, Cheongju, Yangyang, Jeju, Osaka, Nagoya, Shizuoka, Okayama, Boracay Island, Bali Island, Frankfurt, Siem Reap, Bangkok, Phuket Island and Krabi Island.

Hefei Metro is a rapid transit rail network under construction that will eventually serve both urban and rural areas of Hefei. As planned, Line 1 covers a total distance of 24 kilometres (15 miles) starting from Hefei Railway Station. It was inaugurated in December 2016.

In February 2013, Metro Line 2 also began its construction. It is being built alongside the Changjiang Dong Road, Changjiang Zhong Road and Changjiang Xi Road, which is a major passenger corridor in the east–west direction. It will pass through the city center area and connect to a transit point where passengers will be able to take the shuttle bus to Hefei Xinqiao International Airport. The Line 2 was opened on 26 December 2017.

In November 2015, Metro Line 3 construction began. Line 3 was opened on 26 December 2019. Line 3 connects the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone and the Economic Technology Development District, from the vocational education town to the university town. In 2016, Metro Line 4 construction began and was subsequently opened on 26 December 2021. Line 4 connects the New Station Exploitative-experimental Zone and the High Technology Development District. In 2017, Metro Line 5 construction began. The south part of Line 5 was opened on 26 December 2020. Line 5 connects Binhu New District and the Beicheng (North city) New District. The north part of Line 5 is expected to open at the end of 2022.

Alongside Line 1, Line 2, Line 3, Line 4 and Line 5, Hefei is also planning to build other 12 metro lines, 4 lines of intra-metropolitan rail transit (to Lu'an, Huainan, Lujiang and Chaohu) and 3 lines of tram and hopefully accomplish the project by 2030.
There is an extensive public bus system in the city, including eight bus rapid transit lines. There are several commuter lines which only run at designated time or having a large interval.

USST (上海理工大学), short for the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, is a public university run by the city of Shanghai. It sits in the Yangpu district and is paid for out of the municipal government's budget, so its fortunes are closely tied to those of the city around it. For an international applicant, that connection matters: the university trains people for the industries that Shanghai itself depends on, especially engineering, manufacturing and management.

The roots of the school go back more than a century. One strand runs through Hujiang University, founded in 1906. The other begins with a German medicine and engineering school that opened in 1907. After the founding of the People's Republic these two lines were reshaped separately. Both strands were reorganised in the early 1950s. Hujiang University turned into the Shanghai Institute of Mechanical Engineering, which took the name East China University of Technology in 1994, and the National Shanghai Advanced Mechanical Vocational School became Shanghai Mechanical College. The two merged in 1996 to form today's university, and in 1998 the former Ministry of Machinery Industry handed control to the Shanghai municipal government.

The oldest strand of the campus story starts with American Baptists. The Northern and Southern Baptist communities in the United States bought 26.5 acres of land in late 1905 and built a college there, first called the Shanghai Baptist College and Seminary. Its first president was a missionary named John Thomas Proctor, who was appointed by the trustees in August 1906 at a meeting held in Moganshan. Proctor also taught history and philosophy, and he stayed in post until the autumn of 1910, when Dr. F. J. White took over as acting president.

Chinese staff came into leadership gradually. Mr. Tong Tsing-En was the first Chinese professor. Dr. Herman C. E. Liu became the first Chinese president and held the post from 1928 until 1938. Anyone walking around the oldest part of the campus today is looking at the physical legacy of this period.

university-of-shanghai-for-science-and-t.h: From two schools to one university

blocks.x: The modern university is the product of a merger between East China University of Technology and the Shanghai Institute of Mechanical Technology. The first of these grew out of Shanghai Industry School, which was set up on the former Hujiang University campus (the older institution ran from 1906 to 1952) after the People's Republic was established. The second traces itself to the German medical school, called Deutsche Medizinschule, created in 1907. For a long stretch, between 1960 and 1994, the school operated as the Shanghai Institute of Mechanism (上海機械學院).

In May 1996 the two institutions were joined and USST was born. The English name explains its own history: it begins with "University of Shanghai", which was the name of one of its predecessors, as a deliberate nod to where it came from.

The 1998 handover to Shanghai followed a principle of joint building by the central and local governments, with day-to-day management resting with the municipality. That turned USST into what the sources describe as a new-style municipal institution of higher learning. In July 2003 a reorganisation of Shanghai's universities brought two further schools under its wing, one for medical apparatus and instruments and one for publishing and printing training. These turned into USST's colleges of the same two subjects, which explains why a university known for engineering also has a strong publishing school.

university-of-shanghai-for-science-and-t.h: What kind of university it is

blocks.x: USST is multidisciplinary, but engineering is clearly its backbone. Beside that it teaches management, commerce, the arts, science and medicine. Its degrees are organised under six headings, namely the sciences, engineering, economics, management, the arts and medicine.

The figures below are from 2016, so treat them as a snapshot and check the university's own website for current numbers. At that point USST had 18 colleges or schools plus one teaching faculty. Inside these sat 44 research institutes, 26 research centres and 3 research associations. Full-time enrolment was 24,600 students, made up of 17,400 undergraduates and 7,200 candidates for master's and doctoral degrees.

On the academic side, the university listed 19 specialties and 54 bachelor majors, along with four post-doctoral research stations. Five disciplines could award a Ph.D., and 91 second-level disciplines could award master's degrees, with a further 10 engineering and MBA categories. At municipal level it had a key discipline, and it counted three key disciplines recognised by the Shanghai Education Committee and seven that had been key disciplines under the former Machinery Ministry.

Other parts of the university's own description give slightly different counts, for example 30 research institutes and 12 research centres in a later passage, which suggests the numbers have been updated over time. Prospective students should ask the admissions office for the latest figures.

On the research side USST has one national key discipline, one state key laboratory linked to a National Engineering Research Center, and a National University Science Park, plus many provincial-level research platforms. Named centres include the Economic Management Experiment Center, the Modern Publishing and Printing Center and an experiment centre for energy and power engineering. Three National Experimental Teaching Demonstration Centers are also based here.

For undergraduates, the more relevant point is that the university has built a good number of training bases. These include a state-level base for student innovation, a national base for continuing education of professional and technical personnel, and an experimental teaching demonstration center in Shanghai.

Three research areas are repeatedly described as among the best in China: power engineering with engineering thermophysics, optics, and the combined field of management science and engineering. Because society needs engineers who can work across boundaries, the university has also been developing new cross-disciplinary areas. These include advanced manufacturing and high-end equipment, biomedical engineering, new optoelectronic devices and electrical test and control technology, micro-nano frontier materials, and energy saving and environmental protection technology.

The university has put effort into raising its competitiveness in science and technology, with a mix of basic and applied research. It has been involved in major national programmes, among them the 863 Program (the national high-tech R&D programme) and the 973 Program (key basic research), as well as provincial research projects.

The record in recent years includes one Second Prize of the State Science and Technology Progress Award and 17 provincial science and technology awards. Funding from bodies such as the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the National Social Science Foundation and the national scientific instruments project has supported some 220 major projects. Researchers have published 4 papers in the Nature family of journals and hold more than 400 authorised patents.

The science park and the technology transfer centre have also been rated well. The park came 6th nationally in 2011 and earned a Class A (Excellent) grade, and a national evaluation a year later called the Technology Transfer Center excellent and placed it 7th in the country.

USST has 1,098 full-time teaching staff. Of these, 415 hold senior technical and professional titles, including 111 professors and 282 associate professors. The staff includes 50 doctoral advisers and 280 master's advisers. Since 2004 the staff have produced 1,041 academic papers and books a year, and twenty-one teachers have won provincial or ministerial prizes.

The main campus lies in the north-east of downtown Shanghai, beside the Huangpu River. It is next to Fuxing Island and Gongqing Forest Park, with plenty of trees and red-walled buildings. A distinctive feature is the number of old buildings: USST has more historic buildings than any other university in Shanghai. The campus was first built between the 1900s and the 1940s and is now listed by the Shanghai Municipal Government as heritage architecture.

Thirty-one individual buildings (one of them at the Fuxing Road campus) appear on the list of outstanding historic buildings in Shanghai, and ten on the campus have been placed on the cultural relics protection list by the Yangpu District Government. Most of them are in a late Romanesque style or a simplified Gothic Revival style, built in masonry.
The university operates from six campuses:
Jungong Road Campus, the main campus
Jungong Road South Campus, which used to belong to Shanghai Ocean University
Jungong Road No. 1100, the former Shenjiang Foundation Institute campus
Nanhui campus, home of the Shanghai Publishing and Printing Higher College
Yingkou Road Campus, where the Shanghai Medical Instrumentation College is based
Fuxing Road campus, which houses the Sino-British College
When you apply, check which campus your programme uses, as they are spread across the city and teaching units are not all on the main site.
The university groups its teaching into a set of colleges and schools. The main ones are listed here, followed by the colleges that work with foreign partners.
School of Mechanical Engineering
School of Energy and Power Engineering
School of Optical-Electrical and Computer Engineering
School of Materials Science and Engineering
School of Environment and Architecture
School of Engineering and Technology
School of Medical Instruments and Food Engineering
Institute of Photonic Chip
Business School
College of Foreign Languages
School of Social Science
College of Communication and Art Design
Shanghai Publishing and Printing College
School of Music
College of Science
College of Basic Science

Shanghai College of International Education
Rankings vary by who produces them, and the figures below come from several different years, so they are best read as a rough picture of where USST sits rather than an exact position.

Domestic results are good for a municipal university. Among the 63 universities and colleges in Shanghai it was in the top 10 in 2016. Nationally it sat in the top 1% in 2015, and in 2016 it was counted among the 40 strongest universities for scientific and technological research.

On the Shanghai Ranking's Best Chinese Universities list for 2020, USST was 89th nationwide and 9th within Shanghai. The Wu Shulian table for 2019 gave it 75th place nationally and 7th locally. CUAA's 2020 table, one of the best-known domestic rankings, put it at 79th nationally and 9th in the city.

Subject results come from the China Discipline Ranking of the Ministry of Education in 2012, the only national table the Ministry approves. There USST's optical engineering was 10th, power engineering and engineering thermophysics 13th, biomedical engineering 16th, food science and engineering 25th, and management science and engineering 28th. Humanities and social science fields also did well: communication studies 23rd, public management 29th, applied economics 45th, and foreign languages and literatures (foreign linguistics included) 40th.

The Academic Ranking of World Universities (the Shanghai Ranking's global table) placed USST in the 401-500 band in 2023. Its 2018 subject tables put mechanical engineering at 201-300 and four other fields at 301-400: electrical and electronic engineering, chemical engineering, and energy science with engineering.

In the U.S. News Best Global Universities ranking for 2020, USST came 225th among Asian institutions and 87th among those in China. In U.S. News subject tables it was 424th for engineering, 313th for materials science, and 582nd and 629th in chemistry-related subject entries. An earlier 2017 U.S. News result had its materials science at 347th in the world and 8th in China. The QS rankings in 2020 placed it in the 351-400 band within Asia's top 500.

The Business School is accredited by AACSB, the Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business (a body that accredits business schools worldwide), and is one of just 20 business schools in China that belong to it. If you are considering management studies, that is a useful credential.

USST has links with more than 110 universities in over 20 countries, among them Australia, Germany, the United States, Canada and Japan, as well as Switzerland, Russia and Hong Kong, China. Two partnerships stand out for foreign students.

The best-known of its overseas ventures is the Sino-British College (SBC), based in central Shanghai on the Fuxing Road campus. It is an international university college set up jointly by USST and nine British universities:
Sheffield Hallam University
The University of Salford
Manchester Metropolitan University
Liverpool John Moores University
The University of Huddersfield
The University of Bradford
Leeds Metropolitan University
The University of Leeds
The University of Sheffield

SBC became a fully licensed university college on 1 September 2006. No other higher-education institution in Shanghai holds a Ministry of Education licence to run complete degree programmes with several overseas universities at the same time, an arrangement known as the "1 to N Model". Courses can be taught entirely in Shanghai or combined with a period of study abroad, and graduates receive degrees from one of the British partner universities.

The Shanghai-Hamburg College, also called the Sino-German College, was founded in September 1998. It belongs to the programme of cultural exchange between the sister cities Shanghai and Hamburg. The college follows the German model of training engineers (FH) and draws on German teachers and teaching resources. The aim is to supply skilled people for Sino-German industry and, in particular, for German multinational companies working in China. Graduates are meant to be internationally minded, practical professionals who understand German engineering and technology and can handle cross-cultural communication.

There are three bachelor's programmes, each four years of full-time study: international economics and trade, electrical engineering and automation, and machinery manufacturing and automation. Year one is mostly intensive German with Chinese and German teachers, and students must pass the Goethe-Institut's German as a foreign language exam (DaF) and the TestDaF run by the TestDaF-Institut.

Later, professors from Hamburg University of Applied Sciences teach a third of the specialist subjects in German, using original German teaching materials. In the internship semester, 10% of the strongest students are sent to German companies such as Airbus, Lufthansa Technik, Siemens and Philips, and other students find placements in German domestic firms or joint ventures.

The alumni list covers literature, politics, science, business and entertainment, which gives a sense of how far the institution's reach extends. These names are those commonly associated with the university or its predecessors.
Xu Zhimo (徐志摩), a leading romantic poet of twentieth-century Chinese literature
Peggy Lam Pei Yu-dja (林贝聿嘉), GBS, OBE, a politician and activist in Hong Kong who heads the Family Planning Association there; she is a cousin of the architect I. M. Pei
Li Gongpu (李公朴), a social activist and patriot who is regarded as a democrat in modern Chinese history
Chu Fu-Sung (朱抚松), a Republic of China politician who served as foreign minister between 19 December 1979 and 22 April 1987
Meng Jianzhu (孟建柱), a senior economist and politician who sits on the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party and is secretary of the Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission
Li Daoyu (李道豫), a Chinese diplomat who once served as the PRC's ambassador to the United States
Xu Kuangdi (徐匡迪), a politician and scientist; he was Shanghai's mayor between 1995 and 2001 and later a vice-chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference
Huang Qifan (黄奇帆), mayor of Chongqing and a Central Committee member of the Chinese Communist Party
Min Naiben (闵乃本), a crystal physicist, academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and winner of the National Natural Science Award
Arnold Fu (伏彩瑞), who graduated from the Department of English at USST and founded Hujiang.com (沪江网), serving as its CEO
Dai Jun (戴军), a Chinese singer, television host and actor

Much of what makes student life work is the city around the campus: the weather, how you move around, and how much things cost. The sections below describe Shanghai, the home of USST, from landscape to economy to public transport.

Shanghai lies on China's east coast at the mouth of the Yangtze. To the north runs the Yangtze, to the south lies Hangzhou Bay, and the East China Sea forms the eastern edge. The ground was built up by river sediment and by modern land reclamation, so the soil is sandy and soft; tall buildings have to rest on deep concrete piles to keep from sinking. As a provincial-level municipality, Shanghai administers the estuary and many islands near it. Zhejiang province is its southern neighbour and Jiangsu lies to the west and north. Its northernmost point is on Chongming Island, which, after expanding during the twentieth century, is the second-largest island in mainland China.

The city is built on an alluvial plain. The land area is 6,340.5 square kilometres (2,448.1 square miles), and almost all of it is flat; the average height above sea level is just four metres (13 feet). Tidal-flat habitats once lined the estuary but have been reclaimed for farming. The few hills, such as She Shan, are in the south-west, and the city's top elevation, 103 metres (338 feet), is on Dajinshan Island out in Hangzhou Bay. Water is everywhere: rivers, canals, streams and lakes make Shanghai famous for its water resources, which belong to the Lake Tai basin.

The Huangpu River divides the downtown area. It is a man-made branch of the Yangtze that Lord Chunshen ordered dug in the Warring States era. The old city centre developed on the western side (Puxi), near the point where Suzhou Creek enters the river and connects to Lake Tai and the Grand Canal, whereas the financial district, Lujiazui, was built on the eastern side (Pudong). Building Pudong International Airport destroyed some coastal wetland, and this loss has been partly offset by protecting and enlarging the nearby shoal of Jiuduansha as a nature reserve.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen: Cfa) and the four seasons are clearly marked. Downtown averages 17.5 °C (63.5 °F) over the year, while the suburbs run slightly cooler at 16.2 to 17.2 °C (61.2 to 63.0 °F). Winters are cold and damp, and northwesterly winds from Siberia can push night temperatures below freezing. On average there are 4.7 days of snowfall and 1.6 days of snow cover a year. Summers are hot and humid, with the occasional downpour or thunderstorm; an average of 21 days a year reach or exceed 35 °C (95 °F). Late summer and early autumn bring a risk of typhoons.

For comfort, spring and autumn are the best seasons. Spring is changeable and often rainy, while autumn is typically sunny and dry. Sunshine is lowest in June, at 28% of the possible total, and highest in August at 46%, which gives 1,754 hours of bright sun a year. By China's seasonal definitions, the 2001-2025 averages put the start of spring on 9 March, summer on 15 May, autumn on 5 October and winter on 4 December. Across the three weeks between 19 July and 8 August the average temperature stays above 30 °C (86.0 °F).

Records since 1951 show a low of -10.1 °C (13.8 °F), on 31 January 1977; an unofficial reading of -12.1 °C (10.2 °F) was taken back on 19 January 1893. The high is 40.9 °C (105.6 °F), reached at the Xujiahui weather station on 21 July 2017 and again on 13 July 2022. Xujiahui also logged the warmest night ever, when the temperature never fell below 32.1 °C (89.8 °F) on 13 August 2010. The 2025 average there was 19.43 °C (67.0 °F), 1.93 °C above the 1991-2020 norm; the typical daily high is 23.66 °C (74.6 °F) and the typical low is 16.44 °C (61.6 °F).
In practice: pack for damp cold in winter, expect a sticky summer, and treat typhoon season as part of the calendar.

Shanghai is a city you can read through its buildings. Start on the Bund, the riverside strip along the Huangpu. Its early twentieth-century buildings range between two styles, with the neoclassical HSBC Building at one end and, at the other, the Art Deco Sassoon House, today part of the Peace Hotel. The waterfront has been given a fresh look twice. A promenade by Dutch architect Paulus Snoeren appeared in 1986, and a second makeover came before the 2010 Expo, restoring the century-old Waibaidu Bridge and rerouting traffic.

Much of what you see reflects the presence of Western powers, chiefly Britain, France and the United States. The building boom of the 1920s and 1930s left many Art Deco buildings. László Hudec, a Hungarian-Slovak architect resident in the city between 1918 and 1947, designed the Park Hotel, the Grand Cinema and the Paramount. Clement Palmer and Arthur Turner were behind the Peace and Metropole hotels as well as the Broadway Mansions, while the Austrian C.H. Gonda designed the Capitol Theatre.

Among residential styles, the shikumen (石库门, "stone storage door") house is the best known: usually a two- or three-storey grey-brick home whose front yard is guarded by a heavy wooden door set in a stone arch. These houses are linked together and arranged along straight alleys called longtangs (弄堂). The city also has Soviet neoclassical, or Stalinist, buildings, mostly built after 1949 and before the Sino-Soviet split at the end of the 1960s, a time when Soviet specialists arrived to help China develop its communist system; the Shanghai Exhibition Center is an example.

The modern skyline is just as striking. With 206 buildings above 150 metres, Shanghai ranks seventh in the world for skyscrapers. Landmarks include the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center. Tallest of all is the Shanghai Tower, completed in 2015, which is China's highest building and the third highest anywhere. Close by, at the northern end of Lujiazui, rises the 468 m (1,535 ft) Oriental Pearl Tower. In spite of heavy redevelopment, many former foreign concession areas are well preserved, and the Old City keeps its traditional character, including the Yu Garden, an elaborate garden in the Jiangnan style.

Shanghai works as a worldwide centre for finance and innovation and as China's centre for commerce, trade and shipping; its Port of Shanghai handles more containers than any other port. Counting neighbouring cities (Suzhou, Wuxi, Nantong, Ningbo, Jiaxing, Zhoushan and Huzhou), the Greater Shanghai area produced an estimated gross metropolitan product of close to 13 trillion RMB ($1.9 trillion, nominal) in 2022. By 2020 the city economy was put at $1 trillion in purchasing-power terms, the most productive metro area in China and one of the ten largest in the world. About half of GDP comes from six sectors: retail, finance, IT, property, machine manufacturing and car manufacturing.

In 2025 Shanghai's GDP stood at CN¥5.67 trillion, which is $814 billion nominal or $1.66 trillion in PPP and about 4% of the national total; per person that means CN¥228,280 (US$32,840 nominal, US$66,944 PPP). Per resident, disposable income in 2022 averaged CN¥79,610 (US$11,836) a year, and those working in urban units earned an average CN¥212,476 (US$31,589). The city is therefore among China's richest, but a study published by the Economist Intelligence Unit in 2023 also found it the priciest place to live on the mainland, and the Global Wealth and Lifestyle Report from Julius Baer judged it the most expensive city on earth for a luxury lifestyle in 2021. For a student, the lesson is to budget carefully for housing and daily costs.

Trade is huge. Total imports and exports in 2023 came to CN¥7.73 trillion (US$1.07 trillion), 18.5% of the national figure. Forbes put Shanghai fifth for billionaires in 2022, and Oxford Economics expects nominal GDP to hit US$1.3 trillion by 2035, which would be the highest in China and place the city in the world's top five by that measure. In August 2024 it was fourth worldwide for Fortune Global 500 companies, and second in Greater China behind Beijing. Growth has been dramatic, too: GDP rose by double digits in nearly every year from 1992 until the 2008 financial crisis.

Shanghai ranks third in Asia and eighth worldwide on the Global Financial Centres Index. It is also a major centre of China's and the world's technology industry, with a large startup scene; in 2021 only New York ranked above it as a fintech powerhouse.

At US$4.02 trillion in 2019, the market capitalisation of the Shanghai Stock Exchange made it the biggest exchange in China and the fourth biggest worldwide. On the Shanghai Futures Exchange, trading volume in six key commodities (rubber, copper and zinc among them) was the highest in the world in 2009. At the end of 2017 there were 1,491 financial institutions in the city, 251 of which had foreign investment.

Shanghai remains one of China's main industrial centres, with an important role in manufacturing and heavy industry. The secondary sector rests on several zones: Hongqiao, Minhang, Jinqiao (an export processing zone) and Caohejing (a high-tech zone), each with its own economic and technological development status. Local companies include Baosteel Group, China's largest steelmaker; Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding Group, the country's largest shipbuilding base; and the Jiangnan Shipyard, one of its oldest shipbuilders. In cars, SAIC Motor is among China's three biggest groups, partnered with both Volkswagen and General Motors, and it was 84th on the 2023 Fortune Global 500 list. For engineering students at USST, this industrial base is the likely source of internships and jobs.

Visitors flock here. During 2017 domestic tourist numbers grew 7.5% to 318 million and overseas arrivals grew 2.2%, reaching 8.73 million; Shanghai earned more from tourism that year than any other city. The International Congress and Convention Association counted 82 international meetings in 2018, a 34% jump on the 61 of 2017. The 2023 inventory was 57 five-star hotels, 52 four-star hotels, 1,942 travel agencies, 144 rated attractions and 34 red tourism sites. Also in 2023, tourist arrivals numbered 3.64 million, 4.8 times the 2022 total, and spending produced CN¥177.12 billion (US$24.53 billion), a rise of 98.5%. Of the visitors, 2.41 million were foreign, 5.2 times more than before.

The Shanghai Free-Trade Zone, opened in September 2013, was a first for the mainland and came with reforms meant to attract foreign investors. As of October 2019 its area of 240.22 square kilometres (92.75 sq mi) made it the mainland's second-largest zone, after Hainan. It brings together four existing bonded zones: the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, the Waigaoqiao Free Trade Logistics Park, the Yangshan Free Trade Port Area and the Pudong Airport Comprehensive Free Trade Zone. Goods entering the zone do not pay duty and are exempt from customs clearance.

The 2023 population was 24,874,500, of whom 14,801,700 (59.5%) were hukou holders, meaning registered locals. In 2022, 89.3% of the population lived in urban areas and 10.7% in rural ones. Across its whole administrative area Shanghai is the second-largest of China's four municipalities after Chongqing, though it is generally seen as the biggest Chinese city because Chongqing's urban population is much smaller. The OECD estimates the metropolitan area at 34 million people.

Foreign residents are an important part of the picture. Official statistics count about 157,900 of them, among whom Japanese (28,900), Americans (21,900) and Koreans (20,800) form the largest groups, though the real number is probably much higher. Shanghai also draws migrants from within China: 40.3% (9.8 million) of residents come from other regions of the country.

Life expectancy for the registered population is 83.18 years, the highest of any city in mainland China. One consequence is an ageing population: in 2021, 17.4% (4.3 million) of registered residents were aged 65 or over. In 2017 the government introduced population controls for Shanghai, and the population fell by 10,000 by the end of that year.
Shanghai's public transport includes the metro, buses, ferries and taxis, and you can pay for them with a Shanghai Public Transport Card.

The Shanghai Metro combines subway and light metro lines and reaches every core urban district and the neighbouring suburbs. By 2025 the system had 19 lines (the maglev and Jinshan railway are counted separately), 508 stations and 808 kilometres (502 miles) of track, the longest network anywhere. Its busiest day so far was 8 March 2019, with 13.3 million trips. The Shanghai maglev opened in 2004 and was the first commercial high-speed maglev in the world; it runs at up to 430 kilometres per hour (270 mph).

Shanghai's first tram line dates from 1908. Seventeen years later, 328 tramcars ran on 14 routes shared among Chinese, French and British operators, until nationalisation in 1949. Beginning in the 1960s the lines were removed or replaced by trolleybus and motorbus services, and the final tram line went in 1975. A modern revival began with the rubber-tyred Zhangjiang Tram in 2010, followed in 2018 by the steel-wheeled Songjiang Tram in Songjiang District.

Shanghai has the most extensive bus network in the world, and the oldest trolleybus system still running continuously. By 2019 there were 1,575 lines with a combined length of 8,997 kilometres (5,590 miles), operated by several companies. In 2024 there were 30,900 taxis in service, and they carried 134 million passengers that year.
University of Shanghai for Science and Technology lists 85 programs for international students on this site: 45 bachelor, 26 master's, 14 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 85 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,200 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 3,000 to CNY 35,000 (median CNY 35,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 35,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.

84 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

university-of-shanghai-for-science-and-t.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. University of Shanghai for Science and Technology may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Shanghai, register at University of Shanghai for Science and Technology by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Wenzhou Medical University, usually shortened to WMU (温州医科大学, Wēnzhōu Yīkē Dàxué), is a public university owned and funded at provincial level. It is based in the city of Wenzhou in Zhejiang province, on China's southeast coast. As the name suggests, it is a health-sciences institution, so most applicants come here to study medicine or a closely related field.
The university teaches through 15 schools, which fall into a few natural groups.
Clinical and medical schools:
School of Basic Medical Sciences
School of the 1st Clinical Medical Sciences
School of the 2nd Clinical Medical Sciences
School of Stomatology
School of Ophthalmology and Optometry
School of Mental Health
Other health and science schools:
