The university's own description speaks of 15 schools, yet 17 names appear above, so confirm the current structure with the admissions office before you apply.

Medical students learn on the wards of the university's affiliated hospitals. These are the First Affiliated Hospital, the Second Affiliated Hospital together with the Yuying Children's Hospital, the Eye Hospital and the Dental Hospital, all of Wenzhou Medical University. Specialist eye and dental hospitals are especially useful if you intend to specialise in ophthalmology, optometry or stomatology.
In the 2021 Academic Ranking of World Universities, WMU appeared in the 501 to 600 band worldwide. That is one data point from a single year, and rankings change, so look at the latest edition.

wenzhou-medical-university.h: Wenzhou, the city around your campus

blocks.x: Where you live affects your studies as much as the lecture halls do. The rest of this profile first covers Wenzhou itself, then Zhejiang province.

Wenzhou occupies the southeastern corner of Zhejiang. The East China Sea is its eastern boundary, Fujian province is next door to the south, Lishui lies to the west and northwest, and Taizhou meets it on the north and northeast. The municipality includes 12,110 square kilometres (4,680 square miles) of land and 8,649 square kilometres (3,339 square miles) of sea.

Low mountains and hills dominate Wenzhou, with plains and offshore islands playing a smaller role. The ground tilts from southwest down to northeast, and ranges such as the Donggong, Kuocang and Yandang cross it. Baiyunjian, in Taishun, is the highest peak at 1,611.3 metres (5,286 ft). The city has over 150 rivers, 714 or so islands and a coastline of 502 km (312 miles). Other figures put the mainland shoreline at roughly 514 km (319 miles), so the exact length depends on how it is measured.

Geographers divide Wenzhou into four zones. Moving from west to east you cross medium and low mountains first, then a middle belt of hills, low mountains and basins. After that come plains and tidal flats, and finally the island zones along the coast. Wenzhou sits where the mountains of southern Zhejiang meet the sea.
#### The mountain ranges

Three systems shape the highlands. The Kuocang Range crosses most of Yongjia County after it enters Wenzhou, dividing the Ling River basin from the Ou River basin and running into the Northern Yandang Mountains. Along the Zhejiang-Fujian border lies the Donggong Range, whose branches separate the Feiyun from the Xiaoxi, a feeder of the Ou. The Northern Yandang Mountains mark the Yongjia-Yueqing line and keep the Nanxi River apart from the coastal rivers flowing east. The Southern Yandang Mountains are a leftover branch of the Donggong system. They come in from Fu'an in Fujian and reach from Taishun toward the west of Ouhai. In their area, the Feiyun and Ao rivers have cut basins of different sizes among the hills. Altogether 17 peaks in the city top 1,000 metres (3,300 ft).
#### The eastern plains
The plains in the east are threaded with waterways, such as the Wenrui, Ruiping, Pingcang and Liulehong river networks. Each plain has its own location and size:

Yueqing Plain: north of the Ou River estuary, running from the Northern Yandang foothills to Yueqing Bay and from Dajing Town southward to the estuary's north bank; about 330 square kilometres (130 square miles).
Yongjia Plain: on the lower Ou River's north bank next to the Yueqing Plain; about 145 square kilometres (56 square miles).

Wenrui Plain: between the Ou River's south bank and the Feiyun River's north bank, made up of the Sanxi, Coastal, Zhuangyuan, Wutian, Xianyan and Xincheng plains; about 543 square kilometres (210 square miles).
Ruiping Plain: along the lower Feiyun River and the south bank of its estuary, including Xiangjiang and Mayu in Rui'an and Wanquan in Pingyang; about 229 square kilometres (88 square miles).
Taoshan Plain: along the Feiyun's north bank and the lower Jinchao Harbour, covering Taofeng, Tongxi and Chaoji; about 75 square kilometres (29 square miles).
Beigang Plain: along the middle and lower Ao River in Pingyang County, taking in the Ao River Plain plus the Xiaojiang, Mabu and Shuitou plains; about 183 square kilometres (71 square miles).
Jiangnan (Nangang) Plain: south of the Ao River, covering Longgang City and the northeast of Cangnan County; about 297 square kilometres.
#### Coast, bays and islands

Wenzhou's coast is deeply indented, with plenty of bays and tidal inlets and many islands close to shore. The best-known inlets are Wenzhou Bay, Yueqing Bay, Dayu Bay and Yanpu Bay. Islands lie in strings or clusters, forming archipelagos called Dongtou, Dabei, Beiji, Nanji and Qixing.

Tidal flats are extensive. The largest continuous area begins below the Ou estuary and continues down the coast as far as Pipamen in Cangnan County. Elsewhere, flats lie outside river mouths and in the shallow sea near shore. Yueqing Bay holds big flats inside the bay itself. Lingkun Island is ringed by flats, which formed because the surrounding shorelines weaken the currents. Among the Dongtou islands there are smaller patches between the islands and in nearby shallows, often tied to reefs and shoals. Cangnan County adds sizeable flats in its sheltered Dayu and Yanpu harbours.

Wenzhou has been creating new land from the sea. The Wenzhou Peninsula Project began in April 2003 and aims to connect the Dongtou Islands to the mainland. The Wenzhou Oufei Project is the biggest single reclamation scheme in the whole country. Since 2012, about 448 square kilometres (173 square miles) have been reclaimed, which accounts for most of the recent expansion of the city's land. The tidelands were consolidated using vacuum preloading, on a planned scale of 323.4 square kilometres.

There have been environmental objections. Scholars have criticised damage to waterbird habitat. Rapid city growth and reclamation along the East China Sea flyway squeeze and fragment the stopover and wintering sites that migrating birds depend on. Wenzhou and other coastal cities host 66 threatened bird species, about 50.77 percent of the threatened birds recorded in China, so the coastal wetlands matter. The city has also seen widespread, long-lasting land subsidence in coastal urban areas, linked in part to reclamation on soft marine mud and to heavy development.

Geologically, Wenzhou lies in the northeast of the South China fold belt. Two fault depressions, Taishun-Wenzhou and Huangyan-Xiangshan, dominate its structure. In the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods an intense phase of tectonic activity called the Yanshanian episode caused big volcanic eruptions, intrusions of magma and faulting. Faults running north-northeast produced basins. During the Cretaceous these filled mostly with river and lake sediments, with occasional lava flows, forming small volcanic-sedimentary basins including Xianyan, Fanshan and the Shanmen-Wencheng-Taishun basins, where red clastic rocks are common.

The oldest rocks at the surface are lightly metamorphosed layers of the Lower Jurassic Fengping Formation. Older strata from before the Mesozoic are mostly missing, apart from scattered Upper Palaeozoic metamorphosed clastic rocks and marble. Quaternary deposits lie mainly along the coast and riverbanks, as coastal sediment and river alluvium.

Minerals are a minor part of the story. By 2022, the city had registered 19 kinds of solid mineral across 37 occurrences on land. Non-metallic minerals dominate, and the main ones are alunite and pyrophyllite along with stone and aggregate for construction. Building stone includes K-feldspar granite, granodiorite and dolerite, and tuff is the commonest source rock for aggregate. Ten types are mined, mainly construction aggregate, with smaller output of pyrophyllite, fluorite and decorative stone, plus limited use of geothermal resources and mineral water. Officially there are 55 mining licences, split into 45 for solid-mineral mines (39 of them aggregate quarries) and 10 for geothermal or mineral-water sites. A further 9 exploration licences cover fluorite, pyrophyllite, lead, silver, beryllium, illite and geothermal prospects. So much alunite lies underground that the city sometimes styles itself the world's alunite capital.

Three river systems drain Wenzhou: the Ou, the Feiyun and the Ao. All flow east into the East China Sea, and together they make up three of Zhejiang's eight major river systems. More than 150 rivers and streams exist in the city, and the eastern plains have an especially dense network.

The Ou River is Zhejiang's second-largest. Its source is Guomaojian, on Baishanzu's northwestern slopes where Longquan meets Qingyuan. From there it flows 388 km (241 miles), draining 17,859 square kilometres (6,895 square miles), to the East China Sea. Wenzhou contains only the lower course, about 78 km (48 miles) in length with a catchment of 4,066 square kilometres (1,570 square miles). Beyond Meiao the channel widens sharply, from narrow stretches to 500-3,000 metres (1,600-9,800 ft), and a delta harbour area develops near the estuary. The Nanxi River enters from the left bank and runs into Wenzhou Bay. The total fall from source to mouth is roughly 1,250 metres (4,100 ft). Tides dominate the lower river: they reach about 90 km (56 miles) inland, averaging 3.92 metres (12.9 ft) and peaking at 5.7 metres (19 ft).

The Nanxi River is the biggest tributary of the lower Ou. It rises at Luoling on the south side of the Kuocang Range in northwestern Yongjia and flows north to south through central Yongjia. The main channel runs for 139.92 km (86.94 miles) across a basin of 2,490 square kilometres (960 square miles), and the Nanxi joins the Ou at Qingshuibu.

The Feiyun River is Zhejiang's fourth-largest and Wenzhou's second. The river starts in Zhongxi Village, part of Jingnan Township in Jingning She Autonomous County, passes Taishun, Wencheng and Rui'an and reaches the sea. Its main channel is 198.7 km (123.5 miles) long, draining 3,713.9 square kilometres (1,433.9 square miles). The estuary is about 3,000 metres (9,800 ft) wide, and the tide reaches about 59 km (37 miles) upstream, with a mean range of 4.5 metres (15 ft) and a maximum of 6.2 metres (20 ft).

The Ao River is Zhejiang's eighth-largest and Wenzhou's third. Its source is close to Guiku, below Wudi Mountain, in Wencheng's Shanxi Town. The main channel measures 82 km (51 miles), and the basin covers 1,542 square kilometres (595 square miles).

On the coastal plains the water system is built around tanghe, which are canalised waterways, along with distributary channels and drainage ditches. In the north, the Yongle Plain network covers the Yueqing towns of Hongqiao, Lecheng and Liushi and also Wuniu in Yongjia. Further south, the Wenrui tanghe network collects the flow of several mountain streams. Its main canal is about 36 km (22 miles) long and reaches the East Gate of Rui'an's urban area from Xiaonanmen in Lucheng. Next comes the Ruiping system, whose trunk channel used to be known as the Jiangnan Canal: it covers 17 km (11 miles) between Rui'an and the county seat of Pingyang, via Wuqiao and Sunqiao. Finally, the Nangang Jiangnan river network, built around the Hengyang distributary channel, serves the Nangang and Jiangnan plains.

Wenzhou's climate is humid subtropical, and the winter and summer monsoons alternate clearly. You can expect hot summers, mild winters, four distinct seasons and a lot of rain. Yearly average temperatures range between 17.3 and 19.4 °C (63.1 to 66.9 °F), and yearly rainfall between 1,113 and 2,494 mm (43.8 to 98.2 inches), depending on the location. January averages 4.9 to 9.9 °C and July 26.7 to 29.6 °C. Severe cold and extreme heat are rare. Late spring and early summer bring the meiyu, or plum-rain, season, and typhoons peak between July and September. Frost is absent for about 241 to 326 days of the year, and sunshine adds up to between 1,442 and 2,264 hours annually.

Rain is highly seasonal, with about two thirds of the annual total falling in the flood season. Flooding clusters in the meiyu period (May and June) and the typhoon season (July to September), when intense downpours can quickly cause flash floods in the mountains. Typhoons come mainly in summer and autumn. In very active years Wenzhou may be hit five to seven times, with damaging wind and heavy rain.

Drought also returns from time to time. Midsummer drought is the commonest and the most harmful, followed by autumn drought, and a midsummer drought that continues into autumn can seriously affect farming and daily life. Midsummer droughts tend to follow a long spell under the western Pacific subtropical high, while autumn and winter droughts more often occur when strong continental high pressure brings northerly winds and little warm, moist air. Hail occasionally falls, mostly in the mountains and in the warm season.
For a student, the practical points are to prepare for wet early summers and keep an eye on typhoon warnings between July and September.

Tourism in Wenzhou is mostly domestic. In 2023 the city logged about 56.84 million domestic tourist trips, bringing in roughly 76.5 billion yuan. Overseas tourism is small: about 91,000 inbound visitors, spending about 36.19 million US dollars.

There are three national-level scenic areas, the Yandang Mountains, the Nanxi River and Baizhangji-Feiyun Lake, with a combined 1,637.39 square kilometres (632.20 square miles). The province recognises eight further scenic areas, which together cover 254.26 square kilometres (98.17 square miles). Their names are Yaoxi, Xianyan, Zeya, Dongtou, Zhailiao Stream, the Nanji Islands, Radon Springs-Jiufeng and the Maritime-Yucang Mountains.
Because the province you study in colours everyday life, this section turns to Zhejiang and its past.

An early Neolithic community, the Kuahuqiao culture, existed in what is now the Hangzhou area between roughly 6000 and 5000 BC. The Neolithic Hemudu culture began in 5500 BC and the Liangzhu culture in 3400 BC, and both belonged to Zhejiang.

Throughout the second millennium BC, the area now called Zhejiang lay outside the main reach of Shang civilisation. Peoples collectively called the Dongyue lived there instead. Records from the Spring and Autumn period mention the kingdom of Yue, which they place in northern Zhejiang, and the Shiji says its rulers descended from Yu the Great, the founder of the Xia. A famous poem, the Song of the Yue Boatman (越人歌, Yuèrén Gē), was written down in Chinese by authors in northern or inland China, in Hebei and Henan, around 528 BC. It shows that the Yue spoke a language that northern and inland Chinese could not understand. The Sword of Goujian carries bird-worm seal script, and Yuenü, the Lady of Yue, was a swordswoman of the state. The state of Chu encouraged Yue in order to hold back the growth of Wu.

Under King Goujian, Yue recovered from early setbacks and absorbed its rival's territory in 473 BC. The kings then moved their centre of power away from Mount Kuaiji (today's Shaoxing) to Wu's former capital, now Suzhou. With no southern rival left to turn on, Chu attacked Yue directly and destroyed it in 333 BC. The Qin Empire annexed the lands in 222 BC and organised them as a commandery named after Kuaiji in Zhejiang, though its first headquarters were in Wu, in Jiangsu.

Kuaiji Commandery was the first power base of the rebellion of Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu against Qin. It at first restored the kingdom of Chu, but ultimately lost to the Han. In the Later Han period the settlement below Mount Kuaiji took charge again. Its power over the inland Minyue region was little more than nominal, though, and the Yue people there largely kept their own political and social arrangements.

After the Han empire collapsed, Zhejiang was held by the warlords Yan Baihu and Wang Lang until Sun Ce and Sun Quan defeated them and eventually founded the Kingdom of Wu. The Wu court moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (now Nanjing), yet they continued to develop the region and gained from refugees fleeing chaos in the north. Kilns were set up for industrial production, and trade stretched to Manchuria and Funan in southern mainland Southeast Asia.

During the Three Kingdoms period (220 to 280), Zhejiang belonged to Wu (229 to 280), also called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, the economically strongest of the three states. The novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms says Zhejiang had the best-equipped navy. In the story, Wei and Shu lacked materials and avoided fighting Wu head on, relying on camouflage and trickery to seize Wu's arrows, bows and other military supplies.

Jiankang (Nanjing) kept its prominence, but Qiantang, as Hangzhou was formerly called, was still among the three biggest southern cities supplying heavy tax revenue to the northern imperial centres. The other two were Jiankang and Chengdu. Qiantang was upgraded and renamed Hangzhou in 589.

After Wu fell and the Wu Hu uprising shook the Jin dynasty (266 to 420), many elite families in the north worked with non-Chinese rulers and conquerors. Some lost status and took shelter south of the Yangtze, and some may have settled near Hangzhou. One example is the clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), a chancellor of Shu Han from the Central Plain, which gathered in the suburbs of Hangzhou prefecture and formed Zhuge Village, where all villagers share the surname Zhuge. The village isolated itself from its neighbours for centuries and has only recently become widely known. That hints that a few powerful elite refugees from the Central Plain may indeed have fled south. However, Zhejiang is mountainous and short of farmland, so most refugees probably settled in places beyond it with fertile land and urban resources, chiefly southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, where regional government was less organised. Where refugees ended up probably depended on their rank and military strength in the north. The remnant Jin state and the southern dynasties contended with Han elites who came both from the Central Plain and from south of the Yangtze.

Zhejiang lay at the heart of Jiangnan, the Yangtze River Delta, and remained the wealthiest area through the Six Dynasties (220 or 222 to 589) and the Sui and Tang eras. After joining the Sui empire, its riches paid for that dynasty's plans of expansion to north and south, particularly towards Korea and Vietnam. To move supplies, the Sui repaired and enlarged the waterways that became the Grand Canal of China. Grain and other goods went by boat from Zhejiang, via Hangzhou and its hinterland along the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay, and then from Suzhou on to the North China Plain.

The failed Korean war brought about the Sui overthrow by the Tang, who oversaw a golden age lasting centuries. In the Tang empire's Jiangnan East Circuit, Zhejiang was an important economic hub, seen as especially prosperous. Through the Tang the Grand Canal kept carrying grain and materials to the northern plain and the imperial cities. When the Tang broke apart, most of Zhejiang formed the regional kingdom of Wuyue.

Zhejiang hosts several professional teams. In the Chinese Basketball Association, the province has the Zhejiang Golden Bulls, and the Bayi Rockets play in Ningbo. In football, Zhejiang Professional F.C. competes in the Chinese Super League.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

wenzhou-medical-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Wenzhou Medical University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wenzhou, register at Wenzhou Medical University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Wenzhou University (WZU) is a public university in the coastal city of Wenzhou, in Zhejiang province. It is run by the city rather than by the central government: the owner is the Wenzhou Municipal People's Government. For international applicants this tells you what kind of institution to expect, namely a large local university closely tied to its home city and region, not one of the national flagship universities.

WZU in its present form was created by merging two earlier institutions. One was Wenzhou Normal College, which opened in 1956. The other was the earlier Wenzhou University, which had been founded in 1984. The history is short and the university's own site is the place to find a fuller account of the changes since the merger.

The two main campuses lie in Chashan University Town, a district of Wenzhou ringed by green hills and rivers. Together the campuses occupy 1.7 square kilometres (about 420 acres), and the buildings have a floor area of 820,000 square metres. The library holds around 1.59 million volumes.

Staff numbers are 1,950 in total, counting teachers, administrators and support workers. The full-time teaching force is 1,310 people, among whom are 167 professors and 448 associate professors. A further 181 act as supervisors for master's and doctoral candidates, and 201 appear under the heading of academics. These categories overlap and are counted in different ways, so ask the university for a precise breakdown if it matters for your plans.
The full-time student body numbers 24,960.

Day-to-day student life is shaped by the city around the campus, so the sections that follow describe Wenzhou, covering its landscape, weather, rivers and visitor attractions, and then the wider province of Zhejiang.

Wenzhou lies in the south-east of Zhejiang. The East China Sea forms its eastern edge, Fujian province lies to the south, Lishui is a neighbour to the west and north-west, and Taizhou meets it to the north and north-east. The municipality has a land area of 12,110 square kilometres (about 4,680 square miles) plus 8,649 square kilometres of sea (some 3,339 square miles).

Low mountains and hills dominate the terrain, with plains and offshore islands in supporting roles. The ground falls from the south-west towards the north-east, and mountain ranges cross it, the best known being the Yandang, Kuocang and Donggong ranges. Baiyunjian, in Taishun, is the top summit at 1,611.3 metres (about 5,286 feet) above sea level. Rivers criss-cross the eastern plains in a dense net; the Ou, Feiyun and Ao rivers are the main drainage systems. In all there are more than 150 rivers, about 714 islands, and a coastline of around 500 kilometres (roughly 312 miles).

The climate is humid subtropical, with clear seasons and plenty of rain. Depending on the location, the mean temperature over a year is between 17.3 and 19.4 °C (63.1 to 66.9 on the Fahrenheit scale) and rainfall totals 1,113 to 2,494 millimetres (roughly 43.8 to 98.2 inches).

Wenzhou sits between the mountains of southern Zhejiang and the East China Sea shore, so very different terrain lies close together. Geographers divide it into four belts. Middle and low mountains fill the west; basins, hills and low mountains make up the centre; plains and tidal flats occupy the east; and island groups lie off the coast. The Ou, Feiyun and Ao rivers form the three big drainage systems, and their valleys follow the main channels and tributaries.

In the Southern Yandang Mountains, the Feiyun and Ao rivers have cut a string of basins and valleys of various sizes, which join the surrounding low hills. Three mountain systems account for the relief. First, the Kuocang Range enters Wenzhou and spreads over a large part of Yongjia County, where it forms the divide between the Ling and Ou rivers before meeting the northern Yandang hills. Second, the Donggong Range follows the provincial border with Fujian, and its spurs separate the Xiaoxi, which feeds the Ou, from the Feiyun. Third, the Yandang mountains of the north mark the line between Yongjia and Yueqing and keep the Nanxi River apart from the streams that run straight to the coast. Their southern counterpart is a surviving branch of the Donggong system that comes in from Fu'an in Fujian and reaches from Taishun towards western Ouhai. Seventeen peaks in the municipality top 1,000 metres (3,300 feet), and the highest of them is the 1,611.3-metre Baiyunjian in Taishun County.
Waterways thread through the eastern plains, among them the Pingcang, Liulehong, Wenrui and Ruiping networks. The main plains and their approximate areas in square kilometres are listed below.
The Yueqing Plain covers about 330 (about 130 square miles) and lies north of the Ou estuary, running from the hill foot in the west down to Yueqing Bay
The Yongjia Plain measures about 145 (about 56 square miles) on the north bank of the lower Ou, next to Yueqing

The Wenrui Plain, at about 543 (about 210 square miles), sits between the Ou's south bank and the Feiyun's north bank, and combines six smaller plains: Xincheng, Xianyan, Wutian, Zhuangyuan, the Coastal plain and Sanxi
The Ruiping Plain, about 229 (about 88 square miles), occupies the lower Feiyun and the south side of its estuary, taking in Xiangjiang and Mayu in Rui'an and Wanquan in Pingyang
The Taoshan Plain, about 75 (about 29 square miles), follows the Feiyun's north bank and the lower Jinchao Harbour tributary, including Taofeng, Tongxi and Chaoji
The Beigang Plain, about 183 (about 71 square miles), extends beside the mid and lower Ao in Pingyang County and includes Shuitou, Mabu and Xiaojiang plus the Ao River Plain itself
The Jiangnan Plain, also known as Nangang, spans about 297 square kilometres (115 square miles) south of the Ao and takes in Longgang and north-eastern Cangnan County

The coast is deeply indented, with the mainland shoreline given as roughly 514 kilometres (about 319 miles), although the city's earlier figure of about 502 kilometres shows that the exact length depends on how it is measured. Bays and tidal inlets are numerous. The principal bays are Dayu, Yanpu, Wenzhou and Yueqing. Near-shore islands cluster in chains and groups, forming archipelagos named Qixing, Nanji, Beiji, Dabei and Dongtou.

Wide tidal flats border the coast. The biggest continuous area begins just south of the Ou estuary and runs on down the coast until the Pipamen area in Cangnan County. These flats sit off river mouths and spread over shallow seas near the shore. Inside Yueqing Bay there are large flats, while around Lingkun Island a ring-like shoreline and weak water movement have created circular ones. Close to the Dongtou Archipelago, small patches lie between islands and in shallow water, often attached to reefs and shoals. Sizeable flats also fill the sheltered harbours of Dayu and Yanpu in Cangnan.

Work on the Wenzhou Peninsula Project started in April 2003 with the aim of tying the Dongtou Islands to the mainland. A second scheme, the Oufei Project, is the largest single reclamation project anywhere in China. Land gained from the sea since 2012 totals 448 square kilometres (about 173 square miles), which is most of the city's recent land growth. Engineers dried the tideland using vacuum preloading, and the planned size was 323.4 square kilometres.

Academics have criticised the damage to coastal habitat for waterbirds. Fast urban growth and land reclamation along the migratory route beside the East China Sea compress and fragment the main resting and wintering areas. Coastal cities such as Wenzhou are home to 66 threatened bird species, about 50.77% of those at risk in China. Land subsidence has also been widespread and long-lasting, particularly in coastal urban districts, and it has been linked in part to reclamation on soft marine sediment and the intensity of building that followed.

Geologically the city belongs to the north-eastern South China fold belt, where two fault depressions shape the structure: Huangyan–Xiangshan and Taishun–Wenzhou. In the Jurassic and Cretaceous, the intense Yanshanian tectonic episode caused big volcanic eruptions, intrusions of magma and faulting. Along north-north-east trending faults, a series of fault-bounded basins formed. In the Cretaceous they filled mainly with river and lake sediments, interrupted by volcanic outpourings, leaving many small mixed volcanic and sedimentary basins, with red clastic rocks widespread in places like Fanshan, Xianyan and the Shanmen–Wencheng–Taishun group. The oldest exposed rocks are lightly metamorphosed layers of the Lower Jurassic Fengping Formation. Strata older than the Mesozoic are mostly absent, except for scattered Upper Palaeozoic metamorphosed sandstones and marble. Quaternary deposits lie chiefly along the coast and riverbanks, as coastal sediments and river alluvium.

A 2022 count found 19 kinds of solid mineral in 37 onshore deposits. Non-metallic minerals dominate, with alunite, pyrophyllite and construction stone as key resources. Building stone mostly comes from granodiorite, dolerite and K-feldspar granite, and tuff is the most widespread rock used as aggregate. Ten of the mineral types are mined, mainly aggregate, with smaller operations for pyrophyllite, fluorite and decorative stone and limited use of geothermal heat and mineral water. Mining licences number 55: 45 for solid minerals (39 of them aggregate quarries) and 10 covering geothermal and mineral-water sites. Nine exploration licences target geothermal resources, illite, beryllium, silver, lead, pyrophyllite and fluorite. So much alunite lies underground that Wenzhou occasionally describes itself as the "Alunite Capital of the World".

The Ou, the Feiyun and the Ao are the three main river systems, and all run east to the East China Sea. Together they make up three of the eight major river systems of the whole province. More than 150 rivers and streams cross the municipality, most densely on the eastern plains.

The Ou is the second-longest river in Zhejiang. It starts at Guomaojian on the north-western slopes of Baishanzu, on the line between Longquan and Qingyuan, and flows 388 kilometres (about 241 miles) over a drainage area of 17,859 square kilometres before it reaches the sea. Wenzhou holds mainly the lower course, some 78 kilometres in length draining 4,066 square kilometres (1,570 square miles). Below Meiao the channel opens up from narrow reaches to between roughly 500 and 3,000 metres wide, and near the estuary a deltaic harbour area forms. On the left bank the Nanxi River enters and carries on into Wenzhou Bay. Overall the Ou falls about 1,250 metres (4,100 feet) from source to mouth. Tides strongly affect it, up to about 90 kilometres inland, and the average tidal range is 3.92 metres, reaching 5.7 metres at most.

The Nanxi is the biggest tributary joining the lower Ou. Rising at Luoling on the south slope of the Kuocang Range, in north-west Yongjia, it flows north to south through the middle of Yongjia and meets the Ou at Qingshuibu. Its main channel measures 139.92 kilometres and its basin 2,490 square kilometres.

Fourth in Zhejiang and second in Wenzhou, the Feiyun starts at a village called Zhongxi, in Jingnan Township of Jingning She Autonomous County, then passes through Taishun, Wencheng and Rui'an on its way to the sea. Its main channel runs for 198.7 kilometres, draining an area of 3,713.9 square kilometres (1,433.9 square miles). The estuary is about 3,000 metres wide, the tide penetrates about 59 kilometres upstream, and the tidal range averages 4.5 metres with a peak of 6.2 metres.

The Ao comes eighth in the province and third in the city. Its source is at the foot of Wudi Mountain, close to Guiku in Shanxi Town, Wencheng, and from there it travels to the East China Sea. Over 82 kilometres (51 miles) of main channel, the Ao drains a basin of 1,542 square kilometres (595 square miles).

Across the coastal plains, rivers are arranged as tanghe, which are canalised waterways, together with distributaries and drainage ditches. One of them, the Yongle network, is found in Yueqing (near Liushi, Lecheng and Hongqiao) and in Yongjia's Wuniu district. Another, the Wenrui tanghe network, gathers the water of numerous mountain streams; its principal canal is about 36 kilometres (22 miles) long, between Lucheng's Xiaonanmen and the eastern gate of Rui'an town. The Ruiping tanghe network has a main channel formerly named the Jiangnan Canal, which covers 17 kilometres (11 miles) between Rui'an and the county seat of Pingyang via Wuqiao and Sunqiao. The Nangang Jiangnan network is built around the Hengyang distributary channel and spreads across the Nangang and Jiangnan plains.

The city's humid subtropical climate swings between a winter monsoon and a summer monsoon. Expect hot summers, mild winters, four clear seasons and heavy rain. Over the year the mean temperature stays between 17.3 and 19.4 °C, with January averaging 4.9 to 9.9 °C and July 26.7 to 29.6 °C. Severe cold and fierce heat are both unusual. Annual rainfall is 1,113 to 2,494 millimetres. The late spring and early summer bring the meiyu, or "plum-rain", season, and July to September is when typhoons most often arrive. Frost-free days number roughly 241 to 326 a year, and sunshine adds up to about 1,442 to 2,264 hours.

Rainfall follows a strong seasonal pattern, and around two thirds of the annual total arrives during the flood season. The risk of floods is highest in the meiyu weeks of May and June and again from July to September, when typhoons can dump intense rain that triggers flash floods in the hills. Typhoons are mainly a summer and autumn event; in a particularly active year Wenzhou may be hit five to seven times by damaging wind and rain. Drought returns periodically too. Midsummer drought is both the most common type and the most damaging, with autumn drought next. If a midsummer dry spell lasts into autumn, farming and everyday life suffer considerably. Prolonged dominance of the western Pacific subtropical high often lies behind the midsummer type, whereas autumn and winter droughts usually appear when strong continental high pressure brings northerly winds and little warm, humid air. Hail falls now and then, mostly on high ground in the warmer months.
For a student, the practical points are a rainy early summer, a typhoon season to keep an eye on, and mild winters compared with northern China.

Domestic visitors dominate Wenzhou's tourism. In 2023 the city counted around 56.84 million domestic tourist visits, with domestic tourism income of roughly 76.5 billion yuan. International tourism is limited, with around 91,000 visitors from abroad earning about 36.19 million US dollars.

Three scenic areas hold national-level status: Baizhangji–Feiyun Lake, the Nanxi River and the Yandang Mountains, with 1,637.39 square kilometres (632.2 square miles) between them. A further eight have provincial status. They are the Maritime–Yucang Mountains, Radon Springs–Jiufeng, the Nanji Islands, Zhailiao Stream, Dongtou, Zeya, Xianyan and Yaoxi, covering 254.26 square kilometres (98.17 square miles) in all.

wenzhou-university.h: The wider setting: Zhejiang through the ages

blocks.x: A university's province affects student life as much as its campus does, so this part gives a historical overview of Zhejiang.

Around 6000 to 5000 BC, people lived at Kuahuqiao, an early Neolithic site in the Hangzhou area. Zhejiang also saw the Neolithic Hemudu culture (beginning around 5500 BC) and the Liangzhu culture (beginning around 3400 BC).

In the second millennium BC, the area of modern Zhejiang stood outside the main influence of Shang civilisation. Its people were known collectively as the Dongyue. The kingdom of Yue appears in records from the Spring and Autumn period, and the chronicles place it in northern Zhejiang. The Shiji says its rulers descended from Yu the Great, the founder of the Xia. A text called the "Song of the Yue Boatman" (越人歌, Yuèrén Gē) was written down in Chinese around 528 BC by authors in northern or inland China, in Hebei and Henan. The song indicates that the Yue spoke a language that northerners and inland Chinese could not follow. The Sword of Goujian carries an inscription in bird-worm seal script, and Yuenü, "the Lady of Yue", was a swordswoman from this state. To restrain the growing kingdom of Wu, Chu followed a policy of strengthening Yue.

King Goujian led Yue back from early setbacks, and in 473 BC it absorbed all the lands of its rival. Afterwards the Yue rulers shifted their centre away from the original base near Mount Kuaiji (now Shaoxing) to the old Wu capital at what is now Suzhou. With no southern power left to use against Yue, Chu confronted it directly and destroyed it in 333 BC. The Qin Empire annexed the former Yue lands in 222 BC and organised them into a commandery named after Kuaiji in Zhejiang, though at first it was headquartered in Wu, in Jiangsu.

Kuaiji Commandery was the first power base for the rebellion of Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu against Qin. It briefly restored the kingdom of Chu, but in the end the Han prevailed. When the Later Han ruled, control came back to the town below Mount Kuaiji, but the Han hold on the Minyue interior was only nominal, and the Yue people there mostly kept their own political and social ways.

Once the Han fell, Zhejiang came under the warlords Wang Lang and Yan Baihu, until Sun Ce and Sun Quan defeated them; Sun Quan later established the Kingdom of Wu. The court was moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (present-day Nanjing), yet the new rulers went on developing Zhejiang and profited from refugees escaping the chaos in the north. Industrial kilns were built, and merchants traded as far afield as Manchuria and Funan in what is now southern mainland Southeast Asia.

During the Three Kingdoms era (220–280), Wu (229–280), also called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, was the wealthiest of the three states. The classic novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms credits Zhejiang with the finest naval force. In its story, Wei and Shu lacked resources and shunned head-on fighting with Wu, relying on camouflage and trickery to capture Wu's bows and arrows.

Nanjing (then called Jiankang) stayed prominent, but Qiantang, the former name of Hangzhou, was still one of three large southern centres that paid tax revenue to the northern imperial heartland. Chengdu and Jiankang were the others. Qiantang was promoted and renamed Hangzhou in 589.

When Wu collapsed, and unrest followed from the Wu Hu risings against the Jin dynasty (266–420), sent many elite northern families south of the Yangtze, and some probably settled near Hangzhou. A village in the Hangzhou area where everyone bears the surname Zhuge is often cited as a descendant community of the family of Zhuge Liang (181–234), who served as chancellor of Shu Han; it kept itself apart from its neighbours for centuries. Given Zhejiang's mountains and shortage of farmland, though, most refugees probably went to other parts of southern China with more fertile land, among them southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui. Where they went depended on their social status and military strength in the north.

As the core of Jiangnan, the Yangtze River Delta, Zhejiang was the richest region through the Six Dynasties period (220 or 222–589), and it stayed that way under the Sui and the Tang. Once inside the Sui empire, its riches were used to fund campaigns to the north and south, notably in Korea and Vietnam. To move supplies, the Sui rebuilt and lengthened the waterways that grew into China's Grand Canal. Grain and other goods travelled up the canal from Zhejiang's main centre, Hangzhou, together with its hinterland on the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay, and from Suzhou, to the North China Plain. The failed Korean war brought the Sui down and the Tang took over, presiding over a golden age lasting centuries. Zhejiang was an important economic centre of the Jiangnan East Circuit and was considered especially prosperous. The Grand Canal stayed effective throughout the Tang, moving grain and goods north. As Tang power broke apart, the regional kingdom of Wuyue took shape on most of Zhejiang's land.
Professional teams based in the province include:
In the Chinese Basketball Association, the Zhejiang Golden Bulls and the Bayi Rockets (in Ningbo)
In football, Zhejiang Professional F.C. plays in the top-flight Chinese Super League.

wenzhou-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Wenzhou University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wenzhou, register at Wenzhou University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Wuhan Sports University (武汉体育学院; 武漢體育學院), whose Chinese name literally means Wuhan Institute of Physical Education and is often shortened to 武体, is a provincial public institution for sport education and research in Wuhan, Hubei. It has two English identities: 'Wuhan Sports University' is the label used for teaching and training, while 'Wuhan Institute of Physical Education' appears in research-related communication. Responsibility is shared between the Hubei provincial government and the national sports authority, the General Administration of Sport of China. The institute is also a member to the Wuhan Institute Group (WIG), a grouping of ten ministerial or provincial higher education institutions in the city.

Four campuses make up the university: Donghu (Zhuodaoquan), Canglong Island, Donghu High-tech Zone (Baoxie) and Wudang Mountain. On 30 September 2024 the full-time enrolment stood at 15,209 students, a figure that leaves out correspondence junior college and undergraduate programs. By level, the students are 11,907 undergraduates, 2,585 master's candidates, 205 doctoral candidates, 469 junior college students and 43 international students, so foreign students are still a very small group here. Separately, an affiliated College of Sports Science and Technology teaches almost 6,000 students, and two Grade A tertiary hospitals work with the university, one directly affiliated and one on an operational basis.

The undergraduate offer is 24 programs across sport, the arts, the humanities, management, science and engineering; three of them are national-level distinctive programs and four are provincial-level brand programs. Research capacity includes 6 provincial or ministerial laboratories and 2 provincial collaborative innovation platforms. Two periodicals come from the university as well: the Journal of Physical Education, indexed by RCCSE, and the Journal of Wuhan Institute of Physical Education, indexed by CSSCI.

wuhan-sports-university.h: How the institute came to Wuhan

blocks.x: The roots lie in the Zhongnan Institute of Physical Education, which was created in 1953 in Nanchang, Jiangxi. It moved to its present location in Wuhan in 1955 and in February 1956 was renamed Wuhan Institute of Physical Education, or WIPE. Until 2001 the National General Administration of Sports alone supervised it; since then it has answered jointly to that body and the Hubei provincial government.

A turning point came in 1985, when WIPE opened its first arts major, Sport Management. Sport economics, sport English and sport psychology came afterwards, and the most recent addition is Sport Advertising. This growth is a fair example of the continuing reform of Chinese higher education, which aims to turn the specialised schools modelled on the Soviet Union into comprehensive institutions.

Wuhan Sports University holds a solid place in China's sport education and research scene. It is best known for research on sport education and on computational sport science, and for helping to develop elite athletes.

Two rankings give an outside view. One is a global listing of sport science schools and departments, which put the university in the top 200 worldwide in 2023; the other is the XYH 2023 China Physical Education University Ranking, where it came fourth nationally.
Fifteen teaching units share the work (8 colleges, 2 faculties, 3 departments and 2 schools), and the list below runs from the smallest support departments up to the core sport colleges:

An overseas route has existed since 2006 through a 3+1 cooperative education programme with the University of the West of England (UWE): participants study in Wuhan for three years and then spend the final year at UWE. The first 15 students from the 2006 intake went to UWE in the autumn semester of 2009.

WIPE has mainly focused on undergraduate teaching. Its graduate school was famous during the 1980s but increasingly lost ground to Beijing Sports University. Still, in 2006 the institute gained the authority to confer doctoral degrees.

At the end of 2024 (31 December) the university's buildings covered 657,862.91 square metres, of which 16,907.16 square metres are office space and 640,955.75 square metres are for other uses. The official vehicle fleet numbers 21. Two are for the top leadership, eight for emergency support and three for specialised technical use, and the remaining eight are mainly non-motor vehicles, for example electric two-wheelers used on campus patrols and electric refuse trucks. Its equipment includes 83 general units or sets each priced above 500,000 yuan and 32 special units or sets each above 1 million yuan.

Staff total 812, with over 500 professional teachers and trainers. Of these, over 60 hold the rank of professor or national trainer, 165 are associate professors, and ten experts draw a special allowance from the State Council and the provincial government. Ten more have been named Hubei Outstanding Contributions Experts and three are visiting professors under the Chutian Scholar scheme. A foreign name also appears: Prof. Walter Brehm, who leads the Sport Institute at Germany's University of Bayreuth, accepted a visiting professorship in October 2009.
The campus offers a full set of indoor and outdoor sports buildings and classroom blocks, plus advanced research facilities, and the library holds more than 800,000 volumes.

The indoor pool was built in 1984 and has been in use since 1986, serving both the public and competition. Its water is kept at a constant temperature. At the time it was the largest pool in China fitted with solar heating, which in the original design could warm 70 tons of water a day. The university's swimming teaching and research section oversees it, although a private contractor runs it, particularly in summer. Swimmers have competed here at various levels, including in fin swimming, a less publicised discipline, and results have been remarkable, with 10 world champions among them, and 6 world records, 4 Asian records and 5 national records have been set in the pool.

Local media have recently criticised hygiene rules at swimming pools in the city, including this one, claiming that the water was not properly treated and that visitors' health certificates, which the law requires, were not carefully checked. One employee answered that the pool had limited funds and could not pay for a doctor, adding that by the usual practice in the industry, swimming does not call for a health certificate. Check current arrangements for yourself if you plan to use the pool.
What students need to know about everyday life largely depends on the city around campus: its weather, its transport and what there is to do. Here is Wuhan.

wuhan-sports-university.h: Rivers, lakes and the three towns

blocks.x: Wuhan lies in east-central Hubei, between latitudes 29° 58' and 31° 22' N and longitudes 113° 41' and 115° 05' E, where the Han River joins the Yangtze. The site is the eastern edge of the Jianghan Plain, on the middle stretch of the Yangtze.

The urban area has three parts, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, together known as the 'Three Towns of Wuhan'. The name takes 'Wu' from the first and 'Han' from the other two, and the cities were merged in 1927, creating Wuhan. Rivers separate the three districts, and bridges join them, including the 'First Bridge', one of the earliest modern bridges in China. To orient yourself: Wuchang is on the south-eastern side of the Yangtze; Hankou lies north of the Yangtze and also north of the Han; and Hanyang is west of the Yangtze and south of the Han.

Terrain is uncomplicated: the middle is low and flat, the south hilly, and the Yangtze and Han wind through. The She River joins the Yangtze in Huangpi District. Wuhan covers 8,494.41 square kilometres, or 3,279.71 sq mi, that is mostly alluvial plain, dotted with hills and a great many lakes and ponds. A quarter of the urban territory is water, the highest share among China's major cities. Nearly 200 lakes lie within the city. East Lake (33 km2) and Tangxun Lake are the biggest in China that sit wholly inside a city's limits.

South Lake and Sand Lake are also popular, while Liangzi Lake, in the south-east of Jiangxia District, covers more surface than any other lake in Hubei. The highest points in Wuhan are twin peaks of 872.5 metres at the boundary of Huangpi District and Xiaogan City. Within the city boundary you can also find Mount Luojia (珞珈山) in Wuchang District, and, in Hongshan District, Mount Yujia (喻家山/瑜珈山) and Mount Hong (洪山).

Wuhan has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons and plenty of summer rain. The summers are famously humid, with dewpoints often at or above 26 °C, or 79 °F. Wuhan, Chongqing and Nanjing were once called the 'Three Furnacelike Cities' of the Yangtze for their hot summers, but recent data suggest Wuhan has dropped out of the hottest tier; today's 'New Four Furnacelike Cities' are Nanchang, Hangzhou, Fuzhou and Chongqing.

The shoulder seasons are generally mild; winter is cool, dry for the most part, with occasional snow. January averages 4.1 °C, or 39.4 °F, over 24 hours and July 29.3 °C, or 84.7 °F. Rainfall comes to just under 1,320 mm, or 52 in, a year, most of it falling between April and July. The annual mean is 17.4 °C, or 63.3 °F, and the frost-free period lasts from 211 to 272 days. In sunshine terms, January achieves only 30 percent of the possible total and August 53 percent, and the city proper gets 1,783 hours of bright sun annually. The lowest temperature on record is −18.1 °C, or −1 °F, reached on January 31, 1977, and the highest is 39.7 °C, or 103 °F, reached on July 27, 2017 and again on August 18, 2022; an unofficial reading of 41.3 °C, or 106 °F, dates from August 10, 1934.

Until the 21st century Wuhan was mainly agricultural. From 2004 the city became a focal point of the Rise of Central China Plan, a policy aiming to turn lagging inland economies into hubs for advanced manufacturing.

Steel has been the backbone of local industry since 1890. In 2010 the car industry for the first time outproduced Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO) in GDP terms. Dongfeng-Citroen Automobile Co., Ltd. is headquartered in the city, which hosts five carmakers in total: SAIC-GM, Dongfeng Honda, Dongfeng Renault, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Citroën.

By 2016 investors from more than 80 countries had set up 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises in Wuhan, and a combined $22.45 billion USD in capital. France is especially prominent: roughly 50 French firms, Renault and PSA Group among them, work in Wuhan, which represents more than one third of all French investment in China and the largest amount for any single Chinese city.

Wuhan is a major national centre for the economy, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. Main industries include optic-electronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, bio-engineering, new materials and environmental protection, and the emerging industries it promotes include energy-efficiency technology and renewable energy. As of 2021 the Global Financial Centres Index lists Wuhan among the 100 leading financial centres worldwide.
Five major zones are worth knowing, listed by date of establishment.

First comes the Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone, a national zone incorporated in 1993, now about 10-25 square km with plans to reach 25-50. Activities it promotes are telecommunications equipment, heavy industry, food and beverage processing, chemicals, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, and automobile production and assembly.

The Wuhan Export Processing Zone, created in 2000, sits inside that development zone. It is planned to cover 2.7 square kilometres, or 1.0 square mile, and the first 0.7 square kilometre, or 0.3 square mile, has been built.

The Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone, or East Lake High-Tech Development Zone (ELHTZ), is a national-level high-tech zone. Its core industries are optical electronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, with software outsourcing and electronics encouraged too. It is China's biggest production centre for optoelectronic products, with leading firms such as Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable, the country's largest maker of fibre-optic cable, and Fiberhome Telecommunications. It is also the development centre of China's laser industry, home to HGTECH and Chutian Laser.

Inside the Donghu zone is the Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park, a joint development of the East Lake zone and Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. It has a planned area of 0.67 square kilometres, or 0.26 square miles, and total floor area of 6,000,000 square meters, or 65,000,000 square feet. It is 8.5 km, or 5.28 mi, from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km, or 29.02 mi, from Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Biolake was established in 2008 in the Optics Valley of China, in the East Lake New Technology Development Zone. It covers 15 km2, or 5.8 sq mi, and has six parks (bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical device and medical health), designed so that research and living space sit side by side.

No city in Central China has more people, and few in the whole country do. At the time of the Seventh Census of China, in 2020, 12,326,500 people lived in Wuhan, which was 2.5411 million, or 25.97%, more than at the 2010 census. The decade 2010-2020 was the fastest growth in the history of the census, averaging 2.34% a year, and it was the first time the city's population passed 10 million. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 19 million in 2010.

A study from November 2019 used night-time lighting and land cover data as proxies to examine urban development, and found that socioeconomic activity in Wuhan is highly concentrated compared with the spread of the built-up area.

A 2017 survey found that 79.2% of residents are either non-religious or follow worship of gods and ancestors, and 0.9% are Taoists. Buddhism has 14.7% of residents, Protestantism 2.9%, Islam 1.6%, Catholicism 0.3%, and a further 1.6% belong to other religions that were not specified.

The Wuhan Railway Hub, one of the four key hubs in China, is run by China Railway Wuhan Group. Hankou station (in Hankou), Wuchang station (in Wuchang) and Wuhan station (in a newly developed part of Hongshan District, east of the lake) are the three main ones. Since they are miles from each other, a traveller must always check which station a train uses.

The original Hankou Station was the end of the Jinghan railway from Beijing, and Wuchang Station was the end of the Yuehan railway to Guangzhou. Once the First Yangtze Bridge was built and the two lines became the Jingguang railway, trains from both stations could run in all directions, unlike cities such as New York or Moscow where each terminal serves a particular direction.

On April 1, 2009 the Hefei-Wuhan high-speed railway opened, bringing high-speed service between Wuhan and Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai, and a handful of daily trains cover the Shanghai trip in less than six hours. Most of those express trains left from Hankou station as of early 2010.

Construction of the new Wuhan station, with 11 platforms on the north-eastern outskirts, began in 2006. It opened in December 2009, when China introduced its second high-speed train, running from Guangzhou to Wuhan. Billed as the fastest in the world, it reaches 394 km/h, or 244.82 mph, and cut the journey between the two cities from ten and a half hours to three. The service now continues north to Beijing. As of 2011 the new station is mainly used by Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, and most regular trains to other places still use Hankou and Wuchang.

Builders are working on a number of lines in the Wuhan Metropolitan Area intercity network. When complete it will join the three main stations to outer districts, distant suburbs, and the neighbouring cities Huanggang, Huangshi, Xiaogan and Xianning. The Xianning branch was first to carry passengers, at the end of 2013, and the line towards Xiaogan opened on December 1, 2016; the opening of the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway on November 29, 2019 took that route on to Shiyan.

Freight is handled at Wuhan North, the big freight station and classification yard, which has 112 tracks and over 650 switches. It is in Hengdian Subdistrict of Huangpi District, 20 km, or 12 mi, north of Wuhan Station and 23 km, or 14 mi, from Hankou Station.

The Wuhan Metro belongs to and is run by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd. It now has 11 lines, 282 stations and 435 km, or 270 mi, of route. Line 1 opened on July 28, 2004, making Wuhan the seventh city in mainland China with a rapid transit system, after Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian. Line 2 followed on December 28, 2012 as the first underground metro line to cross the Yangtze. Crossing the Yangtze and Han rivers had long been the bottleneck of traffic in Wuhan, and the metro eased that considerably. With 1.22 billion passengers in 2019, it was the sixth-busiest system in mainland China. Growth is rapid, with several lines or sections under construction, and the city government promised at least two lines or sections would open every year. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic the entire system was shut between January 23 and March 27, 2020.
Trams are the newest mode. The Auto-city T1 Line started on July 28, 2017, and the systems that exist or are planned are:
The Old Hankou Streetcar, a loop line around Hankou
Optics Valley trams, T1 and T2, running south and east of Guanggu Circle (Guanggu Guangchang) in south-eastern Wuchang since January 18, 2018
Auto-city trams on Lines T1, T2, T6 and T8, serving the Wuhan Economic Development Area in the far west of Hanyang; only T1 was running as of 2017
Buses, including trolleybuses, also serve the city. The trolleybus system has run since 1958, and its first route, route 1, still operates.

The Port of Wuhan makes the city a major hub for shipping in central China, serving local people and cargo. Because it stands on the Yangtze, Wuhan has a long ferry tradition: modern steamboat services started in 1900, and in 1937 a train ferry began carrying rail cars from Hankou to Wuchang. Numbered stops around the city let passengers get on and off, and there is a night-time tourist ferry. Today the Wuhan Ferry Company runs the boats, and in 2010 it purchased ten new vessels in place of ships that had been in service for 29 years.

wuhan-sports-university.h: What this means for a prospective student

blocks.x: Put simply, the university offers a sport-focused education with a strong emphasis on teaching, and its home city adds a large, well-connected urban setting. Expect warm, humid summers and cool winters, plenty of water and green hills close to the campuses, and several railway stations, so double-check which one you need on arrival. Because the university's own figures change from year to year, confirm course details, fees and campus assignments, particularly for international programs, directly with the admissions office before you apply.
Wuhan Sports University lists 54 programs for international students on this site: 14 bachelor, 13 master's, 9 doctoral, 18 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 54 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 24,000 to CNY 24,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 34,000 to CNY 34,000 (median CNY 34,000), according to the university's published fee table.

54 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

wuhan-sports-university.h: How to apply, step by step

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).

Wuhan Textile University, known by the abbreviation WTU and in Chinese as 武汉纺织大学, is a public institution based in Wuhan, the capital of Hubei Province. Unlike many Chinese universities that sit on one large site, WTU is spread over three campuses in different parts of the city. Nanhu is the original campus, Yangguang is the largest and serves as the main campus, and Donghu was inherited from a former finance college that joined the university. Together they cover more than 2,400 mu of land (a mu is a traditional Chinese land unit, roughly one fifteenth of a hectare) and hold over 700,000 square metres of building space.

wuhan-textile-university.h: What kind of university it is

blocks.x: WTU is built around engineering, but it is broader than its name suggests. Alongside textiles and clothing, which are its signature strengths, it teaches science, art and design, economics, management, languages, law and a number of cross-disciplinary subjects. For a prospective student this means you can find a fashion or design route, a hard-engineering route, or a business route under one roof.

The university describes itself with several official labels. Hubei Province has put it on the list of universities backed by its provincial "First-class Disciplines Development Initiative", and it is counted among China's top ten fashion universities. It has taken part in the national programme to strengthen the capacity of universities in the central and western regions, and it runs the Outstanding Engineer Education and Training Program. It is also a base under the "111 Program", a national scheme for bringing overseas talent into university disciplines.

On the international side, WTU sits inside four networks. AUTEX links European and other textile universities; IFFTI brings together institutes focused on fashion technology; two further groupings tie it to partner universities along the Belt and Road and in central and eastern Europe: a textile university alliance named after the Belt and Road, and the 17+1 higher education alliance between China and the CEEC countries. For a student, such networks matter mainly through exchange places, shared projects and visiting speakers in textiles and fashion.

Undergraduates choose from 68 majors. Postgraduate study is available too: the university is authorised to grant doctorates in 2 first-level disciplines and master's degrees in 16, and it offers professional master's degrees in 15 categories. It is also proud of a milestone: it was the first provincially run university in Hubei to produce an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering from among its own staff.
As of April 2026, the university reports nearly 27,000 full-time students taught by a staff of over 2,400, including both teachers and administrators.

wuhan-textile-university.h: How WTU developed, from 1958 to today

blocks.x: The university has a layered past. Several schools founded in the late 1950s were split, merged and renamed over six decades, and the present institution is the product of that history. Reading it in order helps explain why the campuses and the subject mix look the way they do.

Two ancestors appeared in 1958. One, the Wuhan Institute of Textile Technology, opened at Sancenglou in Wuchang under Wuhan's municipal government. The other was a Hubei Light Industry School at Mafangshan, again in Wuchang, answering to the provincial light industry bureau. The textile institute was suspended in 1962. The light industry school paused during the Cultural Revolution and restarted teaching in 1970.

A major reshuffle came in 1978, when the national education authorities approved splitting the light industry school into four. The textile side produced two schools, an institute of textile technology in Wuhan and a separate textile industry school for Hubei. The light industry side likewise produced an institute and a school. Only the Wuhan textile institute counted among those the State Council had specifically approved for rebuilding, and it reported to the Ministry of Textile Industry. Twenty years later, in 1998, the arrangement changed again: the central government and Hubei Province began to manage it jointly.

In 1999 it took the name Wuhan University of Science and Technology. The earlier description we have notes it had been called Wuhan Institute of Technology before it gained university status, so you may meet that name in older documents. In 2002 Hubei Foreign Trade School, which dated from 1958, was merged in. In 2006 the provincial government placed Hubei College of Finance and Economics under its temporary management. The institution took its current name, Wuhan Textile University, in 2010, and the finance college was formally merged into it in 2011. That merger is the origin of the Donghu Campus.
2012: included in the first national round of the capacity-building project for universities in central and western regions.
2015: moved entirely into the first tier of undergraduate admissions and passed the Ministry of Education's undergraduate teaching audit.
2016: launched the Birmingham Institute of Fashion and Creative Arts, the first Sino-foreign cooperative education institution at degree level in Hubei.
2018: selected as a first-class discipline construction university in Hubei, with Textile Science and Engineering named a provincial first-class discipline.
2019: recognised by the Ministry of Education as a base for passing on excellent traditional Chinese culture.
2020: a cloth five-star red flag designed at the university reached the lunar surface aboard Chang'e-5 and was unfurled there.

2021: a big year. Professor Xu Weilin joined the Chinese Academy of Engineering as an academician, the first for any provincial university in Hubei to grow its own. Work was also approved on a State Key Laboratory focused on new textile materials and advanced processing, and a heat-resistant elastic seal from the university helped the Tianwen-1 Mars landing.
2022: Textile Science and Engineering became a key first-class discipline among Hubei's provincial universities.
2023: confirmed as a "111 Program" base, and the campus museum of textile science and technology was opened to the public.
2024: Textile Science and Engineering, and Design, both gained the right to award doctorates.

WTU teaches through twenty-one academic units. Most are schools, and the university also has a physical education department. The names below are shortened to the subject, grouped the way a student might think about them.

The Birmingham Institute of Fashion and Creative Arts, the Sino-foreign partnership
Innovation and Design
Fashion (the garment school)
