International students should note the School of International Education, which is usually the first point of contact for admissions and visas; confirm the details on the university's own website. The English names above are the university's own translations, and its site also lists the Chinese names if you need them for forms.

By April 2026 the university had completed or was running over 1,000 research projects. These include national key R&D programmes as well as work funded by the two national science foundations, one for natural science and one for social science. Its awards include one First Prize and three Second Prizes of the National Science and Technology Progress Award, plus two Second Prizes of the National Technological Invention Award. In the humanities and social sciences it has collected one Second Prize and two Third Prizes in the national outstanding research achievements for Chinese universities, and more than ten of its artworks have been chosen for national art exhibitions.

What makes WTU memorable is its role in space missions. It contributed the fabric flag carried by Chang'e-5, supplied a second flag made of basalt fibre for Chang'e-6, and developed the heat-resistant elastic seal fitted to the Mars lander. The university's own list notes that its data runs to December 2022 and is not exhaustive, so treat the figures as indicative and check its website for newer numbers.

wuhan-textile-university.h: International links and students from abroad

blocks.x: Partner institutions abroad span four continents. In Britain, the university has agreements with Manchester and with Birmingham City University. In Australia they are Monash and RMIT (the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology). Others are Hanyang University in South Korea, Gadjah Mada University in Indonesia and, in the United States, the Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT). Cooperation takes several forms: joint degree programmes, exchange semesters, short training workshops, joint research and staff exchanges.

More than 500 international students from 64 countries and regions study here. The university is also an approved provider of foreign-aid training commissioned by China's Ministry of Commerce. Across 115 courses it has trained about 3,200 government officials and technical specialists drawn from nearly 100 countries.

wuhan-textile-university.h: Finding your way around the three campuses

blocks.x: Knowing which campus your school uses is important, because they are far apart.

You will find it at No. 1 Fangzhi Road in Hongshan District. This is the university's main teaching hub and the base for most creative subjects: media and communication, fashion, innovation and design, the Birmingham institute, Marxism studies, and international education.

The address is No. 1 Yangguang Avenue, Jiangxia District. It is the second big teaching base. Chongzhen and Chongli buildings are here, together with the administration offices, the main library and the textile museum.

Its address is No. 1 Yuguang Village, Liyuan, East Lake, in Wuchang District. It was inherited from the old finance and economics college of Hubei. We have no information on which schools teach here now, so ask the university before arranging housing.

The university names a long list of graduates and associated academics. It stresses that the selection is partial and in no particular order. Read it as an indication of how far the university's reach goes, from laboratories and design studios to boardrooms.

Xu Weilin is an expert in textile and polymer materials and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering. He also serves as WTU's Party Secretary, and holds vice-chair posts at the China Textile Engineering Society and the Hubei Association for Science and Technology.

Hu Jinlian teaches at City University of Hong Kong with posts in both biomedical engineering and materials science. Her many honours include fellowships in the USA's National Academy of Inventors, the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry and Textile Institute, and the Hong Kong Institution of Textiles and Apparel. She was the first chair of Hong Kong Health Science and Technology Park and is an executive vice chairman of the Hong Kong Federation of Invention and Innovation. Colleagues call her the founder of shape memory fibers.
Qin Xiaohong is a Fellow of the China Textile Engineering Society, and a professor, doctoral supervisor and dean of Donghua University's College of Textiles.

Li Li supervises doctoral students as an associate professor in Hong Kong Polytechnic University's Institute of Textiles and Clothing. She designs functional clothing and smart wearables and is regarded as a leading international scholar of fabric and fashion design.
Xia Zhigang is a professor supervising master's students in WTU's own textile school, and directs the Key Laboratory of Yarn and Functionalization in the Textile Industry.

Lü Yonggang is a professor and doctoral supervisor at Chongqing University. He is deputy chairman and secretary-general of the Chinese Society of Microcirculation's hemorheology committee, and associate editor of the journal Medical & Biological Engineering & Computing.

Yan Zhanglian designed the official logo that represents Wuhan as a UNESCO City of Design. He belongs to the International Council of Graphic Design Associations (ico-D), sits on the international jury of Italy's A' Design Award, and has won the Asia Graphic Design Biennale grand prize, a Graphis Poster Annual silver award in the USA and several Italian design prizes. He is a visiting professor at WTU and is considered one of China's top international poster designers.

Ye Youtian was invited to create visuals for the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics stamps and won a GDC Gold Award, which is China's leading graphic design prize. He teaches at Hubei Institute of Fine Arts as an associate professor and master's supervisor.

Zhang En won the 30th China Top Ten Fashion Designer award and is creative director of the haute couture house NUNU NONO. She has designed for Paris Fashion Week, the Cannes Film Festival and state guest ceremonies.

Zhang Wenhui used to be chief womenswear designer at Shanghai Tang, the Hong Kong luxury label with a Chinese-style look. Singers and actresses such as Karen Mok and Lin Chi-ling have been her clients. She is now an associate professor and master's supervisor at WTU.

Liu Yong has twice received the Golden Summit Award, China's top fashion design prize, and twice been named one of China's Top Ten Fashion Designers. He created the formal clothing that national leaders wore at APEC and founded the womenswear brand NAERSI.
Huang Liyong won the 19th China Top Ten Fashion Designer title, runs the independent label EYMOOD and teaches at WTU as an associate professor and master's supervisor.
Cheng Si started the jewellery label WELLEN and lectures in jewellery design at Sichuan Normal University.

Li Jianquan leads two companies as chairman and general manager: Winner Medical and PurCotton Technology. He founded the medical dressing branch of the national chamber of commerce for light industrial products and arts-crafts imports and exports, and is a vice chairman of the China Cotton Association. The 2025 Hurun China Rich List placed him 443rd, with RMB 15 billion.
Sun Ying'an sat in the 11th National People's Congress and chairs Hubei Xiaomian Industrial Group, where he is also the legal representative.
Zhang Dinghong is the chairman and legal representative of Zhongbonong Animal Husbandry Technology.

Qiao Dewei is the legal representative of the Dynagreen Environmental Protection Group. In 2008 he received the honorary title "Republic Innovation Entrepreneur", given for the 30th anniversary of reform and opening-up.
Lü Shigan chairs two Shenzhen firms, Tongli Southern Elevator Sales and Zhenyin Investment Development, and is a vice chairman of the Hubei Chamber of Commerce in Shenzhen.
Cai Xueyuan is chairman and general manager at Shenzhen Yuanxing Technology.
Sun Jiajun chairs the Jiangsu Huarui Fashion Group.
Fan Mengdi is a national level I volleyball athlete who organised the 2017 China High-End Sports Industry Forum.
Yin Shiyi is a deputy secretary of the Qingdao municipal committee of the Communist Youth League.
Remember that these are only some of the people the university chooses to highlight, and titles change, so check anything important independently.

wuhan-textile-university.h: Living in Wuhan: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life as a student depends heavily on the city: how it looks on the map, what the weather does, how you travel and what the local economy offers. Here is what an incoming student should know about Wuhan.

wuhan-textile-university.h: Where Wuhan is and how it is laid out

blocks.x: Wuhan lies in the east-central part of Hubei, between latitudes 29°58' and 31°22' N and longitudes 113°41' and 115°05' E. It stands where the Han River meets the Yangtze, at the eastern end of the Jianghan Plain and along the Yangtze's middle reaches.

The city is really three old towns joined together: Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, together nicknamed the "Three Towns of Wuhan". The modern name combines "Wu" from Wuchang with "Han" from Hankou and Hanyang, and the merger happened in 1927. Rivers separate the three, and bridges connect them, among them the "First Bridge", one of the first modern bridges in China. In practical terms:
Wuchang is on the south-eastern side of the Yangtze, across the river from both Hankou and Hanyang.
Hankou is north of the Yangtze, and also north of the Han River, which separates it from Hanyang.
Hanyang is west of the Yangtze and south of the Han River.

The terrain is gentle: low and flat through the middle, with hills in the south, and the two big rivers winding through. The She River joins the Yangtze in Huangpi District. The city administers 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 square miles) of land, most of it alluvial plain dotted with hills, lakes and ponds. Water takes up a quarter of the urban area, the highest share among major Chinese cities. Wuhan has nearly 200 lakes. East Lake (33 square kilometres) and Tangxun Lake are the largest lakes lying wholly inside a Chinese city.

Other lakes include South Lake and Sand Lake, and Liangzi Lake, in the south-east of Jiangxia District, is the largest lake in Hubei by surface area. The highest ground in Wuhan is a pair of peaks on the boundary between Huangpi District and Xiaogan, 872.5 metres above sea level. Hills inside the urban area include Mount Luojia in Wuchang District and Mount Hong and Mount Yujia in Hongshan District.

Wuhan has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four clear seasons and plenty of summer rain. Summers are notably sticky, with dewpoints often reaching 26 °C (79 °F) or higher. Wuhan has long been grouped with Chongqing and Nanjing as one of the "Three Furnacelike Cities" of the Yangtze, although recent data suggests that it has slipped out of the very hottest group, now represented by Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang. Spring and autumn are mild. Winter is cool and fairly dry, with the occasional snowfall.

Some figures: the average temperature is 4.1 °C in January and 29.3 °C in July, with an annual mean of 17.4 °C. Rainfall comes to just under 1,320 mm (52 inches) a year, most of it between April and July. The frost-free period runs 211 to 272 days. Possible sunshine ranges from 30 percent in January to 53 percent in August, giving the city about 1,783 hours of bright sunshine a year. The record low is -18.1 °C (31 January 1977) and the record high is 39.7 °C (27 July 2017 and again 18 August 2022), with an unofficial 41.3 °C reported on 10 August 1934. Pack light, breathable clothes for summer and a proper coat for winter.

Wuhan stayed largely agricultural until the 2000s. Since 2004 national policy has treated it as a centre of the plan to raise Central China, a programme meant to build advanced manufacturing in poorer inland economies. Steel has anchored local industry since 1890. In 2010, for the first time, the car industry's contribution exceeded that of the Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO). Five carmakers operate in the city: Dongfeng Honda, Citroën, SAIC-GM, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Dongfeng Renault, and Dongfeng-Citroën is headquartered there.

By 2016, Wuhan had drawn investment from more than 80 countries, with 5,973 foreign-invested firms and a combined capital injection of US$22.45 billion. Around 50 French firms, among them Renault and PSA Group, are based here. That accounts for more than a third of all French investment in China, and it is the highest concentration in any Chinese city. Wuhan is a major centre for trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. Its leading industries are optoelectronics, car manufacturing, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, biological engineering, new materials and environmental protection, and the emerging list includes energy-efficiency and renewable energy. In 2021 it ranked in the top 100 financial centres of the Global Financial Centres Index.
Several zones, listed here in the order they were established, show where jobs and internships may come from.

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone: a national-level zone formed in 1993, currently about 10 to 25 square kilometres with plans to grow to 25 to 50. It encourages car assembly, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, chemicals, food and beverage processing, heavy industry and telecom equipment.

Wuhan Export Processing Zone: created in 2000 inside the development zone, planned at 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile), of which the first 0.7 square kilometre (0.3 square mile) has been built.

Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone (East Lake High-Tech Zone): a national-level high-tech zone built on optoelectronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, with software outsourcing and electronics encouraged. It is China's largest production centre for optoelectronic products, home to Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable (the country's largest fibre-optic cable maker) and Fiberhome Telecommunications, and it is the centre of China's laser industry with companies such as HGTECH and Chutian Laser.

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park: located inside the Donghu zone and co-developed by the zone's authority and Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. The planned area is 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles) with 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet) of floor space. It is 8.5 km (5.28 miles) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 miles) from Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Wuhan Biolake: a biotechnology base founded in 2008 in the Optics Valley of China, covering 15 square kilometres (5.8 square miles) with six parks (bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical device and medical health), designed for both research and living.

Wuhan is the most populous city in Central China. The 2020 census counted 12,326,500 residents, up 25.97 percent (2.5411 million) from 2010, which was its fastest decade of growth and the first time the city passed 10 million. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 19 million in 2010. A study from November 2019 using night-time light and land-cover data found that Wuhan's concentration of social and economic activity is high compared with its physical spread.

A 2017 survey found that 79.2 percent of residents are non-religious or follow worship of gods and ancestors (of which 0.9 percent are Taoists); 14.7 percent are Buddhist, 2.9 percent Protestant, 0.3 percent Catholic and 1.6 percent Muslim, and a further 1.6 percent follow other faiths.

China Railway Wuhan Group runs the Wuhan Railway Hub, one of China's four key rail hubs. Three main stations serve the city: Hankou, Wuchang, and Wuhan station in the newer district east of East Lake (Hongshan District). They are many miles apart, so always check which station your ticket names.

Historically Hankou Station ended the Jinghan line from Beijing and Wuchang Station ended the Yuehan line to Guangzhou. After the First Yangtze Bridge joined them into the Jingguang railway, trains from both stations could go in every direction, unlike New York or Moscow where stations tend to serve particular directions.

High-speed rail arrived with the Hefei-Wuhan line on 1 April 2009, connecting Wuhan with Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai, and a number of daily trains reach Shanghai in under six hours; by early 2010 most of these left from Hankou. The new Wuhan station, begun in 2006 on the north-eastern edge, has 11 platforms and opened in December 2009 together with the Guangzhou-Wuhan high-speed service, which can reach 394 km/h (about 245 mph) and cut the journey from ten and a half hours to three. Service was later extended north to Beijing. As of 2011 the new station mainly handles Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, while most conventional trains still use Hankou and Wuchang.

Intercity lines for the Wuhan metropolitan area are meant to link the three main terminals with outer districts and nearby cities of Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang and Xiaogan. The Xianning line opened at the end of 2013, the Xiaogan line on 1 December 2016, and the latter was extended to Shiyan with the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway on 29 November 2019. For freight, Wuhan North station in Hengdian Subdistrict of Huangpi District has 112 tracks and over 650 switches, 20 km (12 miles) north of Wuhan station and 23 km (14 miles) from Hankou.

The metro belongs to Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd. and currently has 282 stations on 11 lines, with a total route length of 435 km (270 miles). Line 1 opened on 28 July 2004. At that point only six mainland cities already had a metro (Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian), so Wuhan was seventh. Line 2 opened on 28 December 2012 and was the first underground line to cross the Yangtze. Because crossing the Yangtze and the Han had long been the bottleneck of local traffic, the metro eased the problem considerably. It carried 1.22 billion passengers in 2019, the sixth-busiest in mainland China. The city government promised that at least two lines or sections would open each year. During the COVID-19 pandemic the whole network stopped from 23 January to 27 March 2020.

Trams began on 28 July 2017 with the Auto-city T1 line. Built or planned systems include a set of Auto-city routes (T1, T2, T6 and T8) serving the economic development area at the far western end of Hanyang; two Optics Valley lines (T1 and T2) south and east of Guanggu Circle in south-eastern Wuchang, which opened on 18 January 2018; and the Old Hankou Streetcar, a loop around Hankou.

Buses, including trolleybuses, fill in the local network. The trolleybus system dates from 1958 and its first route, number 1, still runs. Wuhan is a central China hub for river and maritime shipping, and the Port of Wuhan handles both local passengers and cargo. Ferries have a long history on the Yangtze: modern service started in 1900 with steamboats, and in 1937 a train ferry began carrying railway cars from Hankou to Wuchang. Today numbered stops dot the shoreline, there is a tourist ferry at night, and the Wuhan Ferry Company runs the service. In 2010 it bought ten new ships to replace vessels that had served for 29 years.

Wuhan University, widely called WHU, is a public university in Wuhan, the capital of Hubei Province. It is run and funded by China's Ministry of Education, which places it in the central tier of national universities, and it belongs to three national programmes: Project 985, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction scheme. These labels mark it out as one of the country's priority institutions.

The story starts in 1926, when a group of six schools in Wuchang were combined into a single institution, National Wuchang Sun Yat-sen University (a name also rendered National Second Sun Yat-sen University). Four of the six were Hubei provincial schools, of medicine, legislation and liberal arts, and one more was a commercial university. The other two were National Wuchang University and a private school, Wuchang Zhonghua University. The merged university had an undergraduate department with six areas of study, namely preparatory courses plus medicine, economics, law, science and liberal arts. Below that it had 17 departments and two institutes.

National Wuhan University was established by the Nanjing National Government in 1928, built on the older institution. It opened with colleges of liberal arts, law, science and engineering. The Communist Party took charge of it in 1949 and the word National disappeared from the name, leaving Wuhan University, which is how it is known now.
2009: the university's School of Information Management reached a cooperation deal with Denmark's Royal School of Library and Information Science.

2013: WHU joined Duke University (USA) and the city government of Kunshan in setting up Duke Kunshan University. Undergraduate teaching there began in 2018 with its first intake. The agreement linking Wuhan and Duke is scheduled to end in 2028. During May 2025 two chairmen of U.S. House of Representatives committees urged Duke to pull out, pointing to national security worries. Anyone considering that programme should follow the news and check directly with both universities.
Reports often call the episode the Wuhan University Library controversy.

2026: WHU founded a joint institute with Britain's Durham University. This is its first Sino-foreign joint institute that sits within the university itself instead of being a legally separate body. Its undergraduate courses last four years and lead to a double degree, one awarded by each partner.

wuhan-university.h: The campus and its cherry trees

blocks.x: Many of the older, elegant campus buildings were designed by F. H. Kales (1899-1979).

The campus is famous for its cherry blossom, which has a complicated history. The first cherry trees were put in the ground in 1939, in the Second Sino-Japanese War, by Japanese troops who hoped they would ease the homesickness of their soldiers. The trees were kept after the war ended, in spite of the link to the occupation. More trees came in 1972, as a gesture marking the normalisation of relations between China and Japan: Premier Zhou Enlai was given a batch and passed 20 of them to WHU. The university's website also mentions later gifts: one in 1983 from Wang Mingquan, a biology professor who had studied in Kyoto, and another from a Japanese delegation in 1992.

As of 2024, the student body included 29,488 full-time undergraduates, 24,126 full-time students working on master's degrees, more than 10,000 doctoral students, and 3,007 students from abroad. There were 3,940 faculty members. Such a large international community means English-speaking students will not be alone, though you should ask about language requirements for your programme.
Different rankings measure different things, so it helps to see several side by side.
U.S. News & World Report (2026-2027): 85th in the world, 18th in Asia, 10th in China.
Academic Ranking of World Universities (2026): 77th in the world, 15th in Asia, 11th in Greater China, a region defined as Mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan.
Times Higher Education (2025): 122nd in the world and 8th in China. Each ranking uses its own method, so treat them as a rough guide rather than a verdict.
QS World University Rankings (2026): 165th in the world, 9th in China.
Nature Index 2026: 18th in the world and 15th among universities in the Asia-Pacific region.
CWTS Leiden Ranking 2025: 16th in the world for total publications, and 31st for publications among the top 1% in their fields in 2020-2023.
Beyond the academic rankings, 29 billionaires had graduated from WHU as of 2017, which put it ninth in the country on that measure.

wuhan-university.h: Wuhan, the city around the university

blocks.x: Studying at WHU means living in Wuhan, so the rest of this profile is about the city: how to get around, what the climate is like, what kind of economy it has and how it is laid out.

China Railway Wuhan Group runs the Wuhan Railway Hub, counted among the four key hubs in the national network. Wuhan has three main passenger stations that are miles apart: Hankou (in Hankou), Wuchang (in Wuchang) and Wuhan station, which is in a newly built district in Hongshan, east of East Lake. When you book, make sure you know which one your train uses.

Historically, Hankou was where the Jinghan line from Beijing stopped, and Wuchang was where the Yuehan line from Guangzhou stopped. Once the First Yangtze Bridge connected them as the Jingguang railway, trains from both stations could head in any direction. That is unlike New York or Moscow, where each station tends to serve one direction.

High-speed travel began on 1 April 2009, when the Hefei-Wuhan line opened and linked the city to Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai. Several trains a day reach Shanghai in under six hours; in early 2010 most of them left from Hankou. Work on the new Wuhan station, with 11 platforms on the north-eastern outskirts, started in 2006. It opened in December 2009 alongside China's second high-speed train, from Guangzhou, advertised as the fastest in the world able to reach 394 km/h (244.82 mph). It cut the journey between Guangzhou and Wuhan from ten and a half hours to three, and the service has since continued north to Beijing. As of 2011 the new station mostly handled Wuhan-Guangzhou trains, while most conventional trains to other places still used Hankou and Wuchang.

New intercity rail lines are being built around Wuhan. Once finished, they are meant to tie the three main stations to outer districts and suburbs, and to the neighbouring cities Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang and Xiaogan. The line to Xianning started carrying passengers at the end of 2013, and the Xiaogan line followed on 1 December 2016. On 29 November 2019 the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway extended that route as far as Shiyan.

For goods, the main station and marshalling yard is Wuhan North, in Hengdian Subdistrict of Huangpi District. It has 112 tracks and more than 650 switches, and is 20 km (12 miles) from Wuhan station and 23 km (14 miles) from Hankou.

A company, Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd., both owns and operates the metro. The present network totals 282 stations across 11 lines, running a combined 435 km (270 mi). The opening of Line 1 on 28 July 2004 made Wuhan the seventh mainland Chinese city with a metro; Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian were earlier. Line 2, opened on 28 December 2012, was the first underground line to pass beneath the Yangtze. This matters because getting across the Yangtze and Han rivers had been the main bottleneck for traffic, and the metro has eased it greatly. In 2019 the system carried 1.22 billion passengers, making it the sixth busiest in mainland China. More lines and sections are under construction, and the city government has promised the public that at least two will open each year. The entire network was out of service between 23 January and 27 March 2020 because of COVID-19.
Trams arrived on 28 July 2017, when the Auto-city T1 Line began. Systems under construction or planned are:
Auto-city trams: four routes (T1, T2, T6, T8) for the economic development area in the far west of Hanyang. Only T1, which opened in 2017, was working at the time of the information we have.
Optics Valley trams: a pair of routes, also called T1 and T2, running south and east from the Guanggu Circle in south-eastern Wuchang. They have been in service since 18 January 2018.
Old Hankou Streetcar: a loop line around the city of Hankou.

Buses cover the rest of the city, including trolleybuses that have run since 1958; the first route, number 1, is still in service. On the water, Wuhan is a key river and maritime hub in central China, and the Port of Wuhan provides both local services and shipping. Ferries have long operated along the Yangtze: steam-boat ferry service dates from 1900, and a train ferry took rail cars from Hankou to Wuchang from 1937. Numbered stops let people get on and off around the city, and there is a ferry for tourists at night. The Wuhan Ferry Company currently runs the service. It purchased ten new ships in 2010 to replace those that had served for 29 years.

The city is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa), with four distinct seasons and plenty of summer rain. Humidity is the main complaint: dewpoints regularly hit 26 °C (79 °F) or more. For years Wuhan, Chongqing and Nanjing were the "Three Furnacelike Cities" of the Yangtze, but recent data show Wuhan is no longer in the top group of hot summer cities. A newer list of four "furnaces" names Chongqing along with Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang. Spring and autumn are mostly mild, and winter is cool, quite dry and occasionally snowy.

Temperatures average 4.1 °C (39.4 °F) in the coldest month, January, and 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) in July, the hottest, with a yearly mean of 17.4 °C (63.3 °F). Rain falls mostly from April to July, totalling just under 1,320 mm (52 in). Frost-free days number between 211 and 272. Sunshine runs from 30 percent of the possible amount in January to 53 percent in August, a total of 1,783 hours for the urban area. The lowest temperature recorded was -18.1 °C (-1 °F) on 31 January 1977; the highest was 39.7 °C (103 °F) on 27 July 2017 and again on 18 August 2022, and an unofficial 41.3 °C (106 °F) was reported on 10 August 1934.

Wuhan stands in the east-central part of Hubei, at 29°58' to 31°22' N and 113°41' to 115°05' E, where the Han River flows into the Yangtze. It lies on the eastern edge of the Jianghan Plain and on the middle reaches of the Yangtze.

Wuhan is really a union of three towns, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, known collectively as the "Three Towns of Wuhan". The name was made from "Wu" in Wuchang plus "Han" in the other two, and the cities were merged in 1927. Rivers run between them, and bridges tie them together; the "First Bridge" ranks among the earliest modern bridges built in China. To orient yourself:
Wuchang is south-east of the Yangtze, which separates it from Hankou and Hanyang.
Hankou is north of the Yangtze, which divides it from Wuchang, and north of the Han, which divides it from Hanyang.
Hanyang is west of the Yangtze, which separates it from Wuchang, and south of the Han, which separates it from Hankou.

The terrain is uncomplicated: flat and low in the middle with hills to the south, and the Yangtze and Han rivers twisting through. The She River joins the Yangtze in Huangpi District. Wuhan's land area is 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 sq mi), mainly alluvial plain scattered with hills and with a huge number of lakes and ponds. A quarter of the urban area is water, the highest share of any major Chinese city. Of nearly 200 lakes, East Lake (33 km²) and Tangxun Lake are the largest within a city anywhere in China.

Also notable are South Lake and Sand Lake, while Liangzi Lake in southeast Jiangxia District is the biggest lake in Hubei by surface area. At 872.5 metres, twin peaks where Huangpi District meets Xiaogan City are the highest points. Hills within the city include Mount Luojia in Wuchang District, and Mount Hong and Mount Yujia in Hongshan District.

Wuhan is Central China's most populous city and one of the largest in the country. The 2020 census, China's seventh, recorded 12,326,500 residents, an increase of 2.5411 million (25.97%) on 2010. It was the fastest decade of growth since census-taking began, at 2.34% a year, and the first time the city passed 10 million. The OECD estimated that the wider metropolitan area held 19 million people in 2010. A 2019 study using night-time lighting and land cover data as stand-ins found that socioeconomic activity is highly concentrated in Wuhan compared with how far the city has spread physically.
Buddhists make up 14.7%, Protestants 2.9%, Catholics 0.3% and Muslims 1.6%; another 1.6% follow other religions.

Wuhan was mostly agricultural until the 21st century. From 2004 it became a focus of the Rise of Central China Plan, which seeks to turn less developed inland economies into advanced manufacturing hubs. Steel has been central to local industry since 1890. In 2010 car manufacturing for the first time surpassed the Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO) in contribution to GDP. The city hosts five car manufacturers (Dongfeng Honda, Citroën, SAIC-GM, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Dongfeng Renault), and the headquarters of Dongfeng-Citroën Automobile Co., Ltd. is also here.

By 2016, investors from over 80 countries had set up 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises in Wuhan, bringing US$22.45 billion in capital. About 50 French companies operate in the city, Renault and PSA Group among them. Put together, they represent more than a third of French investment in China, more than in any other Chinese city.

Wuhan is a key centre of the economy, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. Its main industries are optoelectronics, automobiles, iron and steel, new pharmaceuticals, biological engineering, new materials and environmental protection, and emerging industries include energy efficiency and renewable energy. The Global Financial Centres Index ranked it among the world's top 100 financial centres in 2021.
In order of founding, the main zones are as follows.

Wuhan Economic and Technological Development Zone. A national-level zone incorporated in 1993. It now covers about 10-25 km² (4-10 square miles) and aims to grow to 25-50 km². It encourages car production and assembly, biotechnology and drugs, chemicals, food and drink processing, heavy industry and telecom equipment.
Wuhan Export Processing Zone. Created in 2000 inside the development zone, planned to cover 2.7 km² (1.0 square mile); the first 0.7 km² (0.3 square mile) is already finished.

Wuhan Donghu New Technology Development Zone (East Lake High-Tech Development Zone). A national high-tech zone whose core industries are optoelectronics, telecommunications and equipment manufacturing, with software outsourcing and electronics also encouraged. It is China's biggest production centre for optoelectronic products, with leading companies such as Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable, the largest optical-fibre cable maker in China, and Fiberhome Telecommunications. It is also the development centre of China's laser industry, with HGTECH and Chutian Laser based there.

Wuhan Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park. Inside the Donghu zone and jointly developed by it and Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. It is planned to be 0.67 km² (0.26 sq mi) with 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 sq ft) of floor area, 8.5 km (5.28 mi) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 km (29.02 mi) from Wuhan Tianhe Airport.

Wuhan Biolake. This industrial base dates from 2008 and lies in the East Lake zone at the heart of China's Optics Valley. Its 15 km² (5.8 sq mi) contain six parks for bio-innovation, bio-pharma, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical devices and medical health, so that research and living can sit side by side.

wuhan-university.h: What this means for a new student

blocks.x: Taken together, the facts above describe a large, research-heavy university in a big inland city. The city has a long metro network that already crosses the rivers, and high-speed trains reach Guangzhou in about three hours and Shanghai in under six, with a service on to Beijing. The weather asks for some preparation: damp heat in summer, a cool and fairly dry winter, and rain concentrated between April and July. If you plan to apply, confirm current admission rules, language requirements and tuition on the university's own website, because the figures quoted here come from a range of years and some, such as the rail and metro data, will already have moved on.
Wuhan University lists 829 programs for international students on this site: 112 bachelor, 209 master's, 177 doctoral, 331 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 752 taught in Chinese, 77 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 24,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 23,000 to CNY 50,000 (median CNY 28,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 46,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.

815 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

Application windows found for Wuhan University:
Autumn 2026 undergraduate intake (closed): opens 1 Oct 2025, closes 30 Jun 2026
Deadlines can move and seats can fill earlier than the closing date, so apply as soon as your documents are ready.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

wuhan-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Wuhan University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at Wuhan University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

wuyi-university.h: Which Wuyi University do you mean?

blocks.x: The name Wuyi University is shared by two different institutions in China, and applicants sometimes mix them up. Check the location before you shortlist one.
Wuyi University (五邑大学) sits in Jiangmen, in Guangdong province.
Wuyi University (武夷学院) is in Wuyishan, in Fujian province.
This profile covers the Fujian one, so everything below describes Wuyishan and the province of Fujian around it.

wuyi-university.h: Living in Wuyishan: getting in and out

blocks.x: For a student, most of daily life is shaped by the city outside the campus gates, and the first practical question is how to travel. Wuyishan has its own airport, which handles flights into the area. By rail, the Hengfeng–Nanping line and the Hefei–Fuzhou high-speed line both run through the city, so you can reach larger Fujian cities and neighbouring provinces without much trouble.

Locally there is also the Wuyi Tram. This 26.4-kilometre line has ten stations and has carried passengers since 2021 between Nanpingshi Railway Station and the Wuyishan scenic area. It is still growing: by July 2025 a second line was being built, a third was in the planning stage, and an extension of roughly 42 kilometres to the existing route was also under way.

A university's province shapes student life almost as much as the campus does, so it is worth knowing Fujian properly. The sections below cover its landscape, climate and transport first, then a long history that explains why the province feels so distinct from the rest of China, and finally its tourism.

Fujian is a rugged province. Locals have a proverb (八山一水一分田) that splits the land into 80% hills and mountains, 10% water and 10% fields, and it is not far off. Higher ground lies in the northwest, where the Wuyi Mountains mark the boundary with Jiangxi. Fujian is the most heavily forested provincial-level region in China, with forest covering 62.96% of its area in 2009, and its highest summit is Mount Huanggang in the Wuyi range, at 2,157 metres.

The east of the province faces the East China Sea, the south faces the South China Sea, and the southeast looks across the Taiwan Strait, which is about 180 kilometres wide and separates Fujian from Taiwan. The coast is jagged, full of bays and islands. The larger islands include Quemoy (Kinmen), Haitan Island and Nanri Island. Kinmen and Matsu, along with a few small islands in the strait, are administered by the Republic of China. Meizhou Island holds a special place in the worship of Matsu, the goddess who protects Chinese sailors.
The Min River and its tributaries run through much of the north and centre, with the Jin and the Jiulong as other notable rivers. Because the terrain is so uneven, cliffs and rapids are common.

Underground, Fujian sits on a number of faults created where the Asiatic and Philippine Sea plates collide. Two of them, the Changle-Naoao and Longan-Jinjiang zones, move 3–5 mm every year, and either might trigger a serious earthquake one day.

Expect a subtropical climate. Winters are gentle: January temperatures average roughly 7–10 °C (45–50 °F) along the shore, and 6–8 °C (43–46 °F) up in the hills. Summers run hot, with Pacific typhoons a constant threat. Rainfall totals 1,400–2,000 millimetres (55–79 in) per year, so expect a humid, green setting.
Fujian's mountains, and its long habit of trading by sea, meant that land links developed slowly. The road, rail and air networks are summarised below.

Highways in the province totalled 54,876 kilometres (34,098 miles) in 2012, and 3,500 kilometres (2,200 miles) of that was expressway. Recent flagship projects include the Zhangzhou-Zhaoan Expressway, costing US$624 million, and the Sanmingshi-Fuzhou expressway, at US$1.40 billion. The 12th Five-Year Plan, for 2011 to 2015, set the goal of doubling the expressway network to 5,500 kilometres (3,400 mi).
Railways reached Fujian late because of the terrain and the old reliance on ships. The first connections to Jiangxi, Guangdong and Zhejiang opened in 1959, 2000 and 2009 respectively.

Four separate lines cross the northwestern border into Jiangxi as of October 2013. The oldest is Yingtan–Xiamen, dating from 1957. Hengfeng–Nanping followed in 1998, then Ganzhou–Longyan in 2005, and most recently the high-speed Xiangtang–Putian route in 2013. Toward Guangdong in the west, the Zhangping–Longchuan line (2000) gained a fast partner in late 2013: the Xiamen–Shenzhen high-speed railway, called the Xiashen Line, which forms the bottom stretch of China's Southeast Coast High-Speed Rail Corridor. Two other sections of that corridor, Wenzhou–Fuzhou and Fuzhou–Xiamen, went into service in 2009 and tie Fujian to Zhejiang at speeds up to 250 km/h (155 mph).

Within the province, coast and interior are joined by Nanping–Fuzhou (opened 1959), Zhangping–Quanzhou–Xiaocuo (2007) and Longyan–Xiamen (2012). Hoping to attract Taiwanese investors, Fujian aims to expand its rail length by 50 percent, to 2,500 km (1,553 mi).

The main airports are Fuzhou Changle International, Xiamen Gaoqi International, Quanzhou Jinjiang International, Nanping Wuyishan, Longyan Guanzhishan and Sanming Shaxian. As of 2011 Xiamen could handle 15.75 million passengers. Fuzhou can handle 6.5 million passengers a year plus more than 200,000 tons of cargo, with direct flights to 45 destinations. International routes go to Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and Japan.

wuyi-university.h: The story of Fujian: early settlement and the first kingdom

blocks.x: Fujian's past is long and layered. The following parts follow it from the Stone Age through to the twentieth century, since many of today's place names, surnames and trading ties come from these events.

Archaeology from 2011 pushes Fujian's entry into the Neolithic back to the middle of the 6th millennium BC. Pingtan Island, about 70 kilometres (43 mi) southeast of Fuzhou, holds the Keqiutou site (7450–5590 BP), where excavators recovered numerous tools made of stone, shell, bone and jade, as well as pottery, some of it thrown on a wheel. Spinning wheels turned up too, and they are firm proof that people wove cloth. In the Fuzhou suburbs, the Tanshishan site (曇石山, 5500–4000 BP) straddles the Neolithic and Chalcolithic ages; round, semi-underground houses lay in its lower layer. Nearby Huangtulun (黃土崙, around 1325 BC) is already a Bronze Age site.

Researcher Tianlong Jiao (2013) dates the coastal Neolithic to about 6,000 B.P. Few people lived there then. They survived chiefly by hunting and fishing, with limited cultivation. Four major cultures developed on the coast, and the oldest came from the north, out of coastal Zhejiang.
Keqiutou culture (壳丘头文化): about 6000 to 5500 BP, or 4050 to 3550 BC.
Tanshishan culture (昙石山文化): about 5000 to 4300 BP, or 3050 to 2350 BC.
Damaoshan culture (大帽山文化): about 5000 to 4300 BP.
Huangguashan culture (黄瓜山文化): about 4300 to 3500 BP, or 2350 to 1550 BC.

Away from the sea, the interior had two Neolithic cultures that looked nothing like the coastal four. One was Niubishan (牛鼻山文化), which flourished 5000 to 4000 years ago. The other was Hulushan (葫芦山文化), dated 2050 to 1550 BC.

The kingdom of Minyue once stood in Fujian, and its name is a compound. Mǐn (闽 or 閩; bân in Pe̍h-ōe-jī) probably began as a tribal name related to 蛮/蠻 (mán). Yuè points to the northern State of Yue in Zhejiang, which existed in the Spring and Autumn period. Yue's ruling family escaped to Fujian in 306 BC when Chu swallowed their homeland, which is why the two names were joined. The region's chief river is also called Mǐn, but the tribal name probably predates it.

The Qin, the first unified imperial state in China, removed the King of Minyue and set up a paramilitary province, Minzhong Commandery. Minyue stayed a kingdom in practice until a Qin emperor formally ended its status.

Civil war followed the Qin collapse, pitting the warlords Xiang Yu and Liu Bang against each other. Minyue's king, Wuzhu, backed Liu with soldiers, and the bet paid off: Liu won and became the founder of the Han. In 202 BC Liu rewarded him by recognising Minyue again as a tributary kingdom with its own ruler. Wuzhu could build a walled capital at Fuzhou and a few other strongholds in the Wuyi Mountains, which excavations have uncovered lately. The kingdom reached past modern Fujian into eastern Guangdong, eastern Jiangxi and southern Zhejiang.

Wuzhu's successors stayed aggressive, mounting a series of attacks on the neighbouring kingdoms of Guangdong, Jiangxi and Zhejiang, mainly in the 2nd century BC. Han power was spreading south, and it halted these raids. To end the danger, the Han emperor launched a campaign: huge armies closed in on Minyue from four directions, over land and by sea, in 111 BC. Fuzhou's leaders surrendered rather than face hopeless fighting, and Fujian's first kingdom came to a sudden end.

Afterwards the territory belonged to a far bigger unit, Yang Province (Yangzhou), whose seat was Liyang (歷陽), which is He County in Anhui today. The Han collapsed late in the 2nd century AD, opening the Three Kingdoms age. Sun Quan, who founded the Kingdom of Wu, devoted almost 20 years to bringing the Shan Yue, a mountain-dwelling branch of the Yue people, under control.

wuyi-university.h: Migrants from the north: Jin to Tang

blocks.x: From the 4th century onward, waves of newcomers from the north changed Fujian again and again.

Aristocrats were the first to arrive in numbers. At the start of the 4th century the Western Jin fell, and northern China sank into civil conflict and revolts by tribes from the north and west. Refugees came mostly from eight central Chinese clans: Chen (陈), Lin (林), Huang (黄), Zheng (郑), Zhan (詹), Qiu (邱), He (何) and Hu (胡). Chen, Lin, Huang and Zheng are still Fujian's four most widespread family names.

Despite this boost in population, the mountains kept Fujian isolated from its neighbours, so the economy lagged. Settlement stayed thin compared with the rest of China, and Western Jin created just two commanderies and sixteen counties. Like Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou and Yunnan, Fujian was frequently used as a destination for banished convicts and dissenters. Later, during the Southern and Northern Dynasties, Fujian lay inside the southern realms of Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang (with Western Liang) and Chen, all of which governed the territory below the Yangtze.

Under the Sui and Tang, still more migrants made Fujian their home. The Sui again placed it within Yang Province. In the Tang era it formed one piece of the large Jiangnan East Circuit, governed from Suzhou, and contained around 5 prefectures and 25 counties.

The Tang dynasty (618–907) was another golden age for China and brought a boom to Fujian's culture and economy, with Fuzhou's institutions growing in step. In its later years, political upheavals in the Chinese heartland pushed even larger numbers of northerners into northern Fujian.

The fall of the Tang broke China into the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, and Fujian again offered refuge to a second major wave of settlers. Three brothers, Wang Chao, Wang Shengui and Wang Shenzhi, led them and established the independent Kingdom of Min, ruled from Fuzhou. Quarrels inside the royal house followed the founder's death, and Southern Tang soon swallowed the kingdom. Wuyue, to the north, took some northern districts too, Fuzhou among them. Under Min, meanwhile, Quanzhou was becoming a busy seaport.

A separate story unfolded in the south. The warlord Liu Congxiao held Quan Prefecture (now Quanzhou) and Zhang Prefecture (now Zhangzhou, sometimes known as Nan Prefecture, 南州) as a de facto independent ruler, while professing loyalty to Southern Tang. Its second emperor, Li Jing, formalised this in 949 by creating the Qingyuan Jiedushi post for him. From 960 the circuit also paid nominal respect to Song, which had itself become Southern Tang's nominal superior.

Liu's nephew and adopted son, Liu Shaozi, took over for a short time before being deposed by two officers, Zhang Hansi and Chen Hongjin. Zhang's rule was brief, since Chen pushed him out. By 978 Song was determined to bring all Chinese lands together, and Chen concluded that independence could not last, so he offered the circuit to Song's Emperor Taizong, closing the chapter on Qingyuan as a self-governing entity.
A new Fujian Circuit was formed in 985, and it was the earliest use of the name Fujian for any administrative region.
Many Chinese sailed from Fujian's big ports to Vietnam's Red River Delta, where settlers founded Trần port and Vân Đồn. People from Fujian and Guangdong went to the coastal port of Vân Đồn to trade.

A noteworthy chapter of this migration took place in the Lý and Trần dynasties. Numerous families surnamed Trần (陳) left what is now Fujian or Guangxi for Vietnam, where they lived on the coast and southeast of the capital. Vietnam's Trần clan claims descent from Trần Tự Minh (227 BC), a Qin general in the Warring States age. He belonged to the native Mân, a Baiyue group spread across southern China and northern Vietnam, and he also fought for King An Dương Vương of Âu Lạc against the Qin invasion. Later ancestors named in the genealogy include Trần Tự Viễn (582 – 637) of Giao Châu and Trần Tự An (1010 – 1077) of Đại Việt. Around the close of the 11th century, the heirs of a fisherman, Trần Kinh, whose home was Tức Mạc village in Đại Việt, wed into the royal Lý family, and that union led to the Trần dynasty of Vietnam being founded in 1225.

The Trần filled official posts in Vietnam, and the name shows up in the examination records and official rosters of both the Trần and Lý courts. In the Vân Đồn district, where Chinese from Fujian, Guangxi and Guangdong had settled, their dress, food and speech mixed with Vietnamese customs.
Back in Fujian, pirates called the Pi-she-ye, from Taiwan or the Visayas in the Philippines, attacked the province in 1172.
The last imperial dynasties brought rebellion, sea bans and a new link with Taiwan.

With the Yuan in power, Fujian was folded into Jiangzhe province, run from Hangzhou. Between 1357 and 1366, Quanzhou's Muslim community joined the Ispah Rebellion, marched north and even captured Putian and Fuzhou, until the Yuan broke the uprising. Quanzhou's foreign trade never recovered, nor did its open, cosmopolitan feel, because outsiders had been killed or expelled.

The Yuan officer who ended the Ispah Rebellion, Chen Youding, went on governing Fujian even once the Red Turban Rebellion erupted. Soldiers of Zhu Yuanzhang (the Hongwu Emperor), later the Ming founder, beat him in 1367.

The Ming made Fujian a full province, with Fuzhou as the capital. Early on, Changle near Fuzhou served as the base where Zheng He's naval voyages were prepared and supplied. Progress after that suffered badly from a prohibition on maritime trade. Although it ended in 1550, rival harbours at Guangzhou, Hangzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai had by then overtaken the region. Chinese forces eventually destroyed the huge Wokou pirate fleets. No In (Lu Ren 鲁认) wrote a description of Ming Fujian, and Quanzhou's Ming records mention the Pisheya.

Refugees poured in at the turn from Ming to Qing, and the Kangxi Emperor imposed yet another sea-trade ban lasting 20 years, aimed at Koxinga's exiled Ming regime on Taiwan. Coastal residents were ordered inland to starve Koxinga's loyalists of supplies, and that policy gave rise to a myth that the Manchus feared water.

The refugees did not add much to the workforce, since many carried on to prosperous areas of Guangdong. The Qing took Taiwan in 1683 at the Battle of Penghu and absorbed it as Taiwan Prefecture, part of Fujian. Han settlers then moved there in far greater numbers, and most people in Taiwan today descend from southern Fujian's Hokkien. For a while the two shared one province, Fujian-Taiwan-Province, and from 1885 they were separate provinces.

After the First Sino-Japanese War, the Qing handed Taiwan to Japan under the Treaty of Shimonoseki in the 1890s. Japan then signalled in 1905–1907 that it wanted Fujian inside its sphere of influence, needing French loans while dodging the Open Door Policy. French lenders agreed only if Japan honoured Open Door principles and left China's territory intact.

The Xinhai revolution toppled the Qing and brought Fujian under the Republic of China. Between 1918 and 1920, Chen Jiongming ran an anarchist enclave, the Constitution Protection Region of Southern Fujian. A short-lived breakaway Fujian People's Government appeared in 1933, but Republic of China forces took the province back in 1934. In World War II Japan blockaded its coast from the sea.

Fujian is rich in sights. It counts four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among the highest tallies in China. For a student at Wuyi University, that means exceptional places to visit during breaks, starting with the Wuyi Mountains on your doorstep.

xian-jiaotong-university.h: Xi'an Jiaotong University at a glance

blocks.x: Xi'an Jiaotong University, usually shortened to XJTU (西安交通大学), is a public research university in Xi'an, the capital of Shaanxi province in north-west China. It reports to the Ministry of Education, which also funds it. For a prospective international student the headline is simple: XJTU belongs to the small group of Chinese universities that have been included in every major national drive to build world-class institutions. These are Project 211, Project 985 and the current Double First-Class Construction programme, where it sits in the stronger "Class A" tier. It is also one of the nine members of the C9 League, China's informal group of leading research universities.

On the research side, the research base includes state key laboratories (five of them), state special laboratories (four) and a pair of state engineering research centres. Eight teaching hospitals are affiliated with the university, and two of those rank inside China's top 100. Another role is leading the University Alliance of the Silk Road, a worldwide network of universities created as part of the Belt and Road Initiative. The alliance aims to build educational cooperation, and through it economic growth, in countries along the old Silk Road and among key partners further afield.

The story begins in 1896 in Shanghai, where the imperial government, acting on an edict from the Guangxu Emperor, created the Nanyang Public School (南洋公学) under its Business and Telegraphs Office. It opened with four parts: teacher training, foreign-language studies, and both a middle and a high school. The official who had proposed the idea to the emperor, Sheng Xuanhuai, became its first head. Today he is seen as the founder, sharing that credit with the missionary educator John Calvin Ferguson.

xian-jiaotong-university.h: A long series of owners and names

blocks.x: Over the following decades the institution changed hands and names many times. Commerce officials took it over in 1904, and a year later it was renamed Imperial Polytechnic College under the Commerce Ministry. Control moved again in 1906, this time to posts and telegraphs, with another new name (Shanghai Industrial College). With the founding of the Republic of China, the Ministry of Communications became its owner, and the name changed yet again: Government Institute of Technology under that ministry.

A School of Management was added in 1918. In 1920 the institute merged with two other colleges and took the name Nan Yang College of Chiao Tung. The Ministry of Education took charge in 1938 and the institution became National Chiao Tung University (国立交通大学).

The Second Sino-Japanese War forced the university to improvise. It moved into the French Concession in Shanghai, and in 1940 a state-run branch of Jiaotong University was opened in Chongqing. In 1941, to keep the Wang puppet government from taking control, the Shanghai school carried on under the name Private Nanyang University. The Wang government seized the Shanghai school in 1942, so the Nationalist education authorities chose the Chongqing branch to act as the main seat of Jiaotong University. A graduate school was added in 1943. When the war ended, the Chongqing headquarters returned to Shanghai and merged with the Shanghai school, and in 1946 the name of the state-run Jiaotong University was restored.

When the Kuomintang was defeated in 1949, part of the faculty went to Taiwan with Chiang Kai-shek, and in 1958 they founded a National Chiao Tung University on that island, a separate institution with a shared name. The institution that stayed in Shanghai became simply Chiao Tung University, a change that reflected the principle of public ownership for all universities under the new socialist state. In the 1950s mainland China introduced the pinyin romanisation system, and the English name changed to Jiao Tong University.

A national strategy adopted in 1956 called for most of Jiao Tong University to relocate to Xi'an, in Shaanxi (交通大学西迁). Partway through the move, national priorities shifted and people questioned whether it was still necessary. By then most of the equipment, staff, faculty and students had already arrived and the Xi'an campus had begun to operate, so the university tried running two campuses at once. Running two campuses turned out to be hard, and sending the Xi'an side back east was no longer realistic. So the State Council approved a split, and from 31 July 1959 the two campuses were separate universities. Xi'an took the name Xi'an Jiaotong University; the Shanghai campus became Shanghai Jiao Tong University.

The new Xi'an university was put straight onto the list of National Key Universities, and it was later among the handful built up under the Seventh and Eighth Five-Year Plans. A merger approved in 2000 added Xi'an Medical University and a finance and economics institute from Shaanxi, which explains why XJTU today has a sizeable medical school and strong economics and finance programmes.

XJTU has been included in every major state effort to create world-class universities. Those are Project 211, Project 985, the C9 League and, most recently, the top tier of Double First-Class Construction. An agreement in March 2025 with the Shaanxi International Communication Center aims to provide it with a steady supply of graduates.

XJTU employs more than 5,500 faculty and staff. The academic staff includes twelve academicians of the Chinese Academy of Engineering (nine of them also hold membership of the Chinese Academy of Sciences), 38 Changjiang Scholars (the Yangtze River scholarship) and 25 recipients of the Distinguished Young Scholars fund run by the National Science Fund. Teaching is recognised too. Five staff hold national teaching awards, 142 belong to the education ministry's programme for promising young talent called the New Century Program, and 547 draw government stipends given for outstanding service to the country.

About 30,000 students study here, and half of them, around 15,000, are graduate students. The university offers 84 undergraduate majors, 200 master's disciplines and 115 doctoral disciplines. The Chinese government has designated eight of these as first-order key disciplines.

Teaching and research are spread over four campuses, called Xingqing, Yanta, Innovation Harbor and Qujiang, and together they spread across over 250 hectares. The Qian Xuesen Library, on the Xingqing campus, has a collection of five million books. It subscribes to about 4,100 print journals and 30,000 electronic ones, and offers over a million e-books. The library's IT system is tied into the campus network, the national education network CERNET and the Internet, so students can reach most resources from their own devices.

xian-jiaotong-university.h: The Special Class for the Gifted Young

blocks.x: Set up in 1985, the Honors Youth Program (西安交大少年班) takes in 140 high school freshmen a year. Their first stage is spent at one of three schools: the school affiliated with XJTU, Suzhou High School-SIP or Tianjin Nankai High School. Students who pass can come to XJTU without taking the Gaokao. If they then finish the undergraduate programme successfully, a master's place at XJTU follows without the Postgraduate Admission Test. This route is aimed at very young Chinese students, so it is not an entry path for most international applicants.

XJTU's Internet Education School dates from 2001, when the Ministry of Education chose 15 experimental universities to pioneer distance education. The university works on this together with several leading Chinese universities. Its involvement extends to numerous nationwide pilots. One was the education ministry's demonstration of internet education delivered by satellite and ground networks. Another was a real-time teaching system, a key project of the Tenth Five-Year Plan. A third strand covered National Science Fund research on personalised, interactive virtual collaborative learning and on personality mining in e-learning.

XJTU is counted among China's elite universities, given its Double First-Class status, its C9 membership and its role in the Silk Road alliance. It is the only C9 university in western China. Sichuan University is the only other western institution that regularly places among the country's top 15 comprehensive research universities. In 2025 XJTU stood among China's ten leading comprehensive research universities and was first in the west, a region home to nearly 300 million people.

For 2026, the Academic Ranking of World Universities placed XJTU at 79th, U.S. News & World Report's Best Global Universities ranking placed it 129th, and the Center for World University Rankings put it 124th. Rankings change from year to year and each uses its own method, so treat these as a snapshot and check the latest editions.

Employers in China and abroad value XJTU graduates. In 2017 the QS Graduate Employability Rankings placed the university 101st in the world. Times Higher Education's world reputation table lists it between 176th and 200th, which marks it out as one of the best-regarded Chinese universities abroad.

For research output, the 2025 Nature Index placed XJTU twentieth among Asia-Pacific universities and 32nd worldwide. In the Leiden Ranking from CWTS (2025 edition), covering 2020 to 2023, it came eighth globally for the sheer number of publications and thirtieth for papers in the top 1% of their fields.

Xi'an was the key trading city on the ancient Silk Road, which makes it a natural base for a university alliance tied to the "One Belt, One Road" policy. The principal at the time, Shuguo Wang, started the project, and forums have been held since 2015. The alliance itself was formed in 2015 and sits at the centre of the university's lively research and exchange programme.

Some partnerships exist outside the alliance. One links XJTU to Washington University in St. Louis via the McDonnell International Scholars Academy. On 9 September 2019 the XJTU-POLIMI Joint School opened, a collaboration between XJTU and the Polytechnic University of Milan.

Many renowned scholars studied at XJTU. Among them are Tsien Hsue-shen and Wu Wenjun, along with Huajian Gao, Zhigang Suo and Tony Jun Huang. The list continues with Changqing Chen, Xi Chen and Xi Yao, then Yilu Liu, and also Xu Guangxian, Zhang Guangdou and An Wang. Another is Shouren Ge, known in English as Ernest S. Kuh.
The alumni body also includes entrepreneurs in China and abroad. Examples are:
Zhou Hongyi, who founded the internet security company Qihoo and chairs it; he came through the Special Class for the Gifted Young
Haitao Zheng, named to MIT Technology Review's TR35 list in 2005, also a graduate of the Special Class for the Gifted Young
Ge Honglin, chief executive of Aluminum Corporation of China (Chalco)
Kate Wang, a Chinese businesswoman and billionaire

xian-jiaotong-university.h: Living in Xi'an: why the city matters

blocks.x: Daily life as a student depends heavily on the surrounding city, meaning its weather, how you travel and what it offers. The sections below describe Xi'an, the home of XJTU.

Xi'an occupies the Guanzhong Plain, in the south and centre of Shaanxi, on low ground that was built up by eight rivers and streams around it. Its southern edge touches the foot of the Qin Mountains (Qinling), and the Wei River runs along the north. About 100 km to the east is Hua Shan, among the five sacred mountains of Taoism, while the Loess Plateau begins not far to the north.

When the Han dynasty began, its adviser Zhang Liang urged Emperor Liu Bang to site the capital in Guanzhong. In his words, the plain lay beyond Mount Xiao and Hangu Pass and reached to Long (Gansu) and Shu (Sichuan). He called it an iron castle spanning a thousand miles, a land with harvests as rich as heaven's own. From that comparison the region earned the nickname "Nation of the Heaven".

Xi'an has a temperate climate influenced by the East Asian monsoon. By the Köppen classification it falls on the border between humid subtropical and hot-summer humid continental (Cwa/Dwa). In the Wei River valley, summers are hot and humid, winters are cold and dry, and spring and autumn are dry. Most of the year's rain arrives between July and late October. Snow falls occasionally in winter but rarely lies for long. Dust storms are common in March and April while the city warms up quickly, and the summer months bring frequent but short thunderstorms.

Monthly mean temperatures run from about freezing in January up to 27 °C in July, and the year as a whole averages roughly 14 °C. Since 1951 the coldest reading was minus 20.6 °C, on 11 January 1955, and the hottest at today's station in Jinghe was 42.3 °C on 15 July 2025. A different station once measured 42.9 °C on 17 June 2006, and a suburban station in the north logged an unofficial minus 25 °C back in January 1930. In practice, pack for a proper winter and for hot, humid summer weeks.

A small piece of trivia that is also a real piece of national infrastructure: the Shaanxi Astronomical Observatory was founded in 1966. In 1975 a national report on the country's geodetic origin argued that the reference point should lie in the middle of the mainland to limit measurement bias, and the town of Lintong (临潼) near Xi'an was selected. Chinese Standard Time has been set from this site since 1986. The National Time Service Center, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, works mainly on time and frequency services and research. It generates and maintains the national standard time scale and sends out time and frequency signals. In the 1970s and 1980s it built its own universal-time and atomic-time scales and set up radio broadcasting of time signals on low and high frequencies, enough to serve uses from science to the wider economy.

The Seventh National Census of 2020 recorded 12,952,907 permanent residents. Males made up 51.07% and females 48.93%. By age, 15.65% were between 0 and 14, 68.33% between 15 and 59, 16.02% were over 60, and 10.9% were over 65.

The OECD estimated that the Xi'an metropolitan area had a population of 12.9 million as of 2010, of whom 5,740,000 lived in urban areas. The two sets of figures use different definitions of the city, so expect numbers to vary depending on what is counted.

Large parts of Xi'an are easy to cover on foot. In many commercial, residential and educational districts, and especially in the shopping and entertainment areas around the Bell Tower, pedestrian underpasses and bridges make crossing the road safer and easier.

Bike sharing started in 2013, and the network now lists some 52,000 bicycles with more than 200,000 riders daily. Taxis are plentiful, yet many people still commute on the 270 municipal bus routes, which use over 7,800 vehicles and average more than four million passengers each day. The rapidly growing subway adds more than 1.5 million commuters daily. With over 2 million registered cars in the city, traffic jams are a common complaint. These figures come from a mix of years, so the city's transport authorities have the up-to-date numbers.

The first line to open to the public was Line 2, on 16 September 2011, with regular operation starting on 28 September. It goes north-south between the North Railway Station and Weiqu Nan, over 17 stations and 19.9 kilometres. Line 1 came on 15 September 2013, connecting Houweizhai in the west with Fangzhicheng in the east through 19 stations.

Line 3 runs from the north-east (Baoshuiqu) to the south-west (Yuhuazhai) and opened on 8 November 2016. Line 4 mostly follows Line 2 on its eastern side, apart from the northern end. Opening to the public on 26 December 2018, it connects the north square of the main North Railway Station (Beiguangchang) with Hangtianxincheng in the south. Line 5, opened on 28 December 2020, links Matengkong and Chuangxingang along 41.6 kilometres with 31 stops.

Line 16 followed on 27 June 2023, with nine stations over 15.03 kilometres between Qinchuangyuanzhongxin and Shijingli. The network was still growing, with four more lines (one of them an extension of Line 1) being built.

The subway passes many of the city's best-known sights. Banpo Museum is at Banpo Station on Line 1, the Bell and Drum Tower and the city's fortifications are on Line 2, and the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda is served by Lines 3 and 4. The Daminggong National Heritage Park is on Line 4, and the Shaanxi History Museum can be reached from Lines 2, 3 and 4.

For timings, the first metro on Lines 1, 2, 3 and 4 leaves at 6:00. The last departure is at 23:00 on Lines 3 and 4, 23:30 on Line 1 and 23:50 on Line 2. Schedules may change, so check the operator before relying on them.

Xi'an North railway station lies a few miles north of the city centre. It serves high-speed trains running on the Zhengzhou–Xi'an line, itself a section of the longer Xuzhou–Lanzhou route. Building began on 25 September 2005 and trains began on 6 February 2010. Flying between the two cities could not compete: within 48 days of regular rail service, every passenger flight on that route had stopped.

With 34 platforms it was the biggest station in the north-west when it opened on 11 January 2011, after work that started on 19 September 2008. Its other routes include the Datong–Xi'an high-speed line (which connects onward to Beijing North), plus the Xi'an–Chengdu and Yinchuan–Xi'an lines.

The older Xi'an station stands immediately north of the walled old city and is the principal hub for regular (non-high-speed) trains in the province. The site covers 597,000 square metres, with six passenger platforms and eleven tracks, and about 80,000 travellers use its 112 services every day. Direct trains reach Beijing, Zhengzhou, Lanzhou, Baoji and Mount Hua among other places.

Two large stations, Xi'an East and Xi'an South, were being built for new high-speed lines such as Xi'an–Chongqing and Wuhan–Xi'an. Smaller stations in the city are Xi'an West, Yinzhen, Sanmincun and Fangzhicheng.

Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (code XIY) is the main airport for the city and the largest airport in north-western China. It lies 25 miles north-west of the city centre and 8 miles north-east of the centre of Xianyang. Most flights are operated by China Eastern, Hainan Airlines and China Southern. Terminal 3 and the second runway opened on 3 May 2012, and Terminal 5 was begun in 2022 and finished in September 2024.
As well as connecting to most Chinese cities, the airport serves several major international destinations, among them Tokyo, Seoul, London, Paris and Sydney.

xian-jiaotong-university.h: From western development to a service economy

blocks.x: National policy to develop the west made Xi'an a priority for faster investment, particularly in IT, advanced materials, aerospace, energy and chemical engineering. From 1997 to 2006 the city's service-industry output expanded at an average of 13 percent a year, against just 0.74 percent for traditional services, growing from US$8.113 billion to US$25.85 billion.

In 2020 researchers at the GaWC network classed Xi'an as a Beta- city (second tier globally), and the Global Financial Centres Index put it among the world's best 100 financial centres in the same year.

Equipment manufacturing, tourism and service outsourcing are the city's important industries. Manufacturing reached RMB 36.5 billion in annual output, a share of 44.5 percent of the whole city economy. Since Xi'an is one of China's four ancient capitals, cultural sites like the Terracotta Army, the City Wall and the Famen Temple make tourism a major business as well. More than 300 million tourist visits in 2019 brought in RMB 314.6 billion. Revenue grew by an average of 36.4 percent annually, and income from foreign currency (530 million in 2009) grew by about 35.8 percent a year. These growth rates describe an earlier period, so do not assume they still hold.

Among China's first outsourcing cities, Xi'an has more than 800 firms in the sector, which produced over RMB 23 billion in 2008. Jobs in outsourcing doubled between 1997 and 2006 from a starting point of 60,000, and computer consulting doubled too, from 16,000 positions to 32,000. Because software outsourcing matters so much, the city planned a Software New Town, scheduled for completion in 2015 with 30 billion RMB of investment. Lighting equipment and automobile parts are other major exports, mechanical and electrical products are the main imports, and the United States is the city's largest trade partner.

Covering some thirty-five square miles, the Xi'an International Trade and Logistics Park was planned as a model for urban growth built on logistics. It works as a large dry port and rail container centre, and no other city sees more China-Europe freight trains start or finish their journeys.
The main industrial district is the Economic and Technological Development Zone. The Jiangcungou landfill, once China's biggest, shut in 2019.

The growing economy supports a software industry in which Xi'an has been a pioneer in China. By 2012 the Xi'an Software Park, inside the Xi'an Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone, had attracted over 1,085 companies and 106,000 employees. One older description of the local labour market said that the 100 universities in the area produce around 3,000 computer graduates a year, who earned about $120 a month, half the pay for equivalent work in Beijing. That figure comes from an earlier time and salaries have almost certainly changed.

A joint venture formed in November 2006 between the city and the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation created an industrial base for aerospace science and technology. Its main concern is civil space business, covering equipment manufacture, software and outsourced services, new materials and solar photovoltaics.

The base was meant to reach beyond its core area to cover Xi'an and the Guanzhong region, with an expansion zone extending to other parts of the north-west and south-west. Targets for 2012 were US$2.8 billion in total output, between 10 and 20 branded products with their own intellectual property, and 5 to 8 that could compete globally. After a first civil aerospace centre was launched in Shanghai in 2008, China began building another one in Shaanxi, with planning approved by the national development and reform commission on 26 December 2007. The National Civil Aerospace Industrial Base in Xi'an covers 23 km2 and concentrates on satellites, new materials, energy, IT and other civilian uses.
Several professional teams once based in Xi'an have since relocated:
In the old Jia-A football league, Shaanxi National Power moved to Ningbo and was renamed Ningbo National Power in 2004
In the top-flight Chinese Super League, Shaanxi Baorong Chanba, relocated to Guiyang and renamed Guizhou Renhe in 2012
In the Chinese Basketball Association, Shaanxi Dongsheng went to Foshan and became the Foshan Dralions in 2010
