Xiangtan University (XTU; 湘潭大学) is a public university in Xiangtan, a city in Hunan province in central-southern China. Its status is provincial: it belongs to Hunan, and three partners share the funding. They are SASTIND (the national defence science and technology authority), the Ministry of Education, and the provincial government of Hunan. The university takes part in the Double First-Class Construction programme. For an international student, that combination points to a mid-sized regional university with national backing, located outside the capital city of Changsha.

Xiangtan University was founded in 1958 at the suggestion of Mao Zedong, in Xiangtan County, the place where he was born and grew up. Operations stopped in 1959 by order of the provincial government, and it was 1974 before the university resumed running.

The Best Chinese Universities Ranking, commonly called the "Shanghai Ranking", placed Xiangtan University first in Xiangtan and fourth in Hunan as of 2025. It is the only one of the province's top five that is not based in Changsha. In the same year the Academic Ranking of World Universities put it in the 701–800 band worldwide.

In 2017 Times Higher Education placed the university in its 800–1000 band. It has also appeared inside the global top 1,000 in several international league tables, including those compiled by ARWU, THE and the Center for World University Rankings (CWUR).

For research, the 2024 CWTS Leiden Ranking put Xiangtan University 575th in the world on publications from 2019 to 2022, and the 2025 Nature Index tables placed it among the leading 350 universities globally for high-quality research publications in the natural sciences. Rankings vary with the method and the year, so the university's own site has the current positions.

xiangtan-university.h: Living in Xiangtan: why the city matters

blocks.x: A student's days are shaped by the city around the campus, so this section turns to Xiangtan itself and then to the province of Hunan.
The city is found along the lower part of the Xiang River.

The climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot summers and winters that are cool to cold, cloudy and damp, with occasional light snow. The annual mean temperature across the administrative area is 17.4 °C. January is the coolest month at an average of 5.1 °C, and July the hottest at 29.1 °C.

At the 2010 census Xiangtan had 2,748,552 residents. The built-up area (two urban districts plus Xiangtan County) accounted for 1,877,919 of them, and if you add the four neighbouring urban districts of Zhuzhou, the combined built-up area reaches 2,933,069 people. A Chinese Cities Brand Value Report presented in 2007 at the Beijing Summit of China Cities Forum named Xiangtan one of the ten most livable cities in China.

In 2006 the city's nominal GDP reached ¥42.2 billion (US$6.2 billion), a rise of 13.2% year on year, equal to ¥15,455 (US$2,265) per head. Those figures are old, so look up current statistics for planning purposes.

The city is famous for lotus seed and soy sauce. Locals also enjoy chewing areca nut (槟榔, bīngláng), even though the nut is not grown in the area: most of the raw fruit comes from Hainan and is processed locally. The habit goes back some 400 years, to a time when people chewed it to ward off epidemics, and today it is common to see people chewing it across Hunan. In 2003 the area's areca nut industry reached sales of ¥800 million.
Roads, river and rail connect Xiangtan well. A shuttle bus runs to Changsha Huanghua International Airport.

Shaoshan, in Xiangtan, draws many visitors because it is the birthplace of Mao Zedong, chairman of the Chinese Communist Party and, from 1949 to 1976, the paramount leader of the People's Republic. Local people also like Zhaoshan, a small wooded mountain in the city.

A professional tennis player grew up and trained in Xiangtan. In 2002 and 2003 the city's stadium hosted the army-linked Bayi football team, then playing in the top-flight Jia League (today's Chinese Super League).

The province around the university matters as much as the campus itself, because Hunan sets the tone for food, language, transport and the jobs available after graduation. The following sections introduce its past, its landscape, its economy and its everyday culture.

Long ago, Hunan's primeval forests were occupied by the forebears of the present-day Yao, Dong, Tujia and Miao. The area appears in written Chinese history from about 350 BC, as part of the Zhou world. Qin overcame Chu in 278 BC and took control of the region, which later became the Changsha Kingdom under the Han dynasty. Over the following centuries Han Chinese farmers kept moving in from the north. They pushed out or absorbed the original inhabitants, cleared forests and began growing rice in valleys and plains. Part of that colonisation of the lowlands involved building and maintaining river dikes against floods, and numerous small villages in Hunan are still named after the Han families that settled them. Migration peaked in the Eastern Jin, the Sixteen Kingdoms and the Northern and Southern dynasties, periods when non-Han groups ruled most of the north amid constant disorder.

In the era of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, Hunan was the base of an independent regime called Ma Chu. Under later dynasties, migrants from the north kept coming, some escaping the Yuan (Mongol) invasions. The Red Turban risings against the Yuan began in Hunan in the fourteenth century.

Until the Qing, Hunan was joined with Hubei as the province of Huguang, and then it became a province in its own right. Early foreign visitors thought the people conservative and hostile to outsiders, yet were impressed by their keenness and stubbornness. One Qing prince regent called the Hunanese turbulent and pugnacious, and in the eighteenth century Jesuits working in China counted Hunan as the part of the country hardest to enter.

Hunan's place on the Yangtze made it an important communications centre. It was also a leading centre of scholarship and Confucian thought, centred on the Yuelu Academy in Changsha, and the Imperial Highway between north and south crossed it. Its fertile land yielded such large grain surpluses that it helped feed other parts of China. By the nineteenth century the population had climbed so far that the province was overcrowded and prone to peasant revolts. Some, for example the Miao Rebellion that lasted from 1795 to 1806, came from ethnic tension. The Taiping Rebellion started in Guangxi in 1850 and moved into Hunan, then east along the Yangtze valley; in 1864 the Xiang Army, raised in Hunan and led by Zeng Guofan, entered Nanjing to crush it.

In 1920 famine swept Hunan and killed an estimated two million civilians. This set the stage for the Autumn Harvest Uprising of 1927, led by the Hunan native Mao Zedong, which set up a brief Hunan Soviet. Communist guerrillas held out in the mountains along the Hunan–Jiangxi border until 1934; under pressure from Nationalist (Kuomintang) troops they then set out on the Long March towards bases in Shaanxi. With the Communists gone, the Nationalists went on to fight Japan in the Second Sino-Japanese War, holding Changsha until it fell in 1944. That fall came as Japan carried out Operation Ichi-Go, a plan to seize the Yuehan Railway running from Wuchang to Guangzhou. After Japan's defeat in 1945, Hunan was relatively untouched by the civil war, and in 1949 the Communists came back as the Nationalists retreated south.
Because it was Mao's home province, Hunan backed the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976). After his death in 1976, Hunan lagged behind most provinces in taking up the reforms of Deng Xiaoping.

Other first-generation Communist leaders also came from Hunan. Liu Shaoqi became President of China; Ren Bishi and Hu Yaobang served as party secretaries-general; Peng Dehuai, He Long and Luo Ronghuan became marshals; and the list goes on with Wang Zhen, one of the "Eight Elders", Xiang Jingyu, the first woman on the party's central committee, Senior General Huang Kecheng, and the veteran diplomat Lin Boqu. In more recent times, Zhu Rongji, a former premier, is also a native of Hunan.

The province sits south of the Yangtze, roughly midway along the river, between 108° 47′ and 114° 16′ east and 24° 37′ and 30° 08′ north. It covers 211,800 square kilometres, or about 81,800 square miles, and ranks tenth in size among provincial-level divisions. Mountains and hills ring the east, south and west of the province: the Wuling Mountains in the north-west, the Xuefeng Mountains in the west, the Nanling Mountains in the south and the Luoxiao Mountains in the east. Mountains and hills take up over 80% of Hunan and plains less than 20%. The highest point is Lingfeng (酃峰), at 2,115.2 metres above sea level.

In the north, the Xiang, Zi, Yuan and Lishui rivers all flow into Lake Dongting, and from there on to the Yangtze. The centre and north form a U-shaped basin open to the north, with Lake Dongting in the middle, and most of the province lies in the basins of these four Yangtze tributaries. Lake Dongting is the province's largest lake and the second largest freshwater lake in China. The Xiaoxiang region and Lake Dongting feature again and again in Chinese poems and paintings, above all in the Song dynasty, when they were associated with officials dismissed unjustly.

The name Changsha means "long sands", and in the Tang dynasty it was a busy ceramics centre; tea bowls, ewers and other products were turned out in large numbers and sent to coastal Chinese cities to be exported. An Arab dhow from the 830s, known today as the Belitung Shipwreck, was found off the small Indonesian island of Belitung with a cargo of more than 60,000 pieces; the recovered cargo is now kept in Singapore.

Climatically, the province is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Winters are short, cool and damp; summers are very hot and humid; and rain is plentiful. Average temperatures are 3 to 8 °C (37 to 46 °F) in January and about 27 to 30 °C in July, with precipitation of 1,200 to 1,700 millimetres (roughly 47 to 67 inches) a year. Geologists have named the Furongian Epoch of the Cambrian Period after Hunan, since "Furong" (芙蓉) is Mandarin for "lotus" and Hunan is known as the "lotus state".

Measured by economic size, Hunan is China's tenth-ranked province. Within Central China only Henan and Hubei are larger, and in South Central China it follows Guangdong, Henan and Hubei, while among inland provinces it is fourth, behind Sichuan, Henan and Hubei. For 2025 nominal GDP was about US$790 billion (CN¥5.53 trillion), placing Hunan among the world's 20 biggest sub-national economies, and GDP at purchasing-power parity was above US$1.62 trillion. Per-person nominal GDP passed ¥84,583 (US$11,900, or US$24,804 in PPP terms), third in South Central China after Guangdong and Hubei. In 2020 the nominal figure was US$605 billion, bigger than Poland's economy (the world's 22nd largest), Thailand's (second in ASEAN) or Nigeria's (Africa's biggest).

Around the middle of the nineteenth century, Hunan's exports were rhubarb, musk, honey, tobacco, hemp and birds. Ramie is grown in quantity around Lake Dongting, and tea is another significant crop, which shows how farming long shaped the province before industry took over. During the Third Front campaign the province was among the biggest recipients of national investment in industrial capacity.

Lately Hunan has become a key centre for steel, machinery and electronics, a trend helped by manufacturers shifting from coastal Guangdong and Zhejiang. Stibnite is mined around Lengshuijiang, which makes it one of China's main sources of antimony. Hunan is also home to world-scale builders of construction machinery such as concrete pumps and cranes: Sany Group (a major world player), Zoomlion and Sunward. Liuyang is the world's top centre for making fireworks.

The Changsha National Economic and Technical Development Zone, founded in 1992, is east of Changsha. Its total planned area is 38.6 square kilometres, and the area in use is 14 square kilometres. National Highways G319 and G107 and the Jingzhu Highway pass nearby, and the zone is very close to downtown and the railway station, and 8 km from the airport. The main industries are high technology, biotechnology and new materials.
Changsha National New and Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone.

Chenzhou Export Processing Zone, set up in 2005 with State Council approval, is Hunan's single export processing zone. The planned production area is 3 square kilometres. The zone aims to develop export-oriented high-tech industries in electronic information, precision machinery and new materials. Infrastructure there is good, and firms in the zone benefit from preferential tax policies covering exemption, guarantees and refunds. When the Eleventh Five-Year Plan ended, trade through the zone had topped US$1 billion and it supported more than 50,000 jobs; the stated ambition is to become one of the best export processing zones in China.

The Zhuzhou National New and Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone, also founded in 1992, has a planned 35 square kilometres next to National Highway G320. Biotechnology, food processing and heavy industry are its main industries. In 2007 the zone signed a cooperation agreement with Beijing Automobile Industry, one of China's biggest carmakers, which is setting up a manufacturing base there.

The 2000 census counted 64,400,700 people in Hunan, in forty-one ethnic groups, an increase of 6.17% (3,742,700) from 1990. Han Chinese made up 89.79% (57,540,000) and minorities 10.21% (6,575,300). The minorities include Tujia, Miao, Dong, Yao, Bai, Hui, Zhuang and Uyghur people, among others.
Minority languages are spoken in several prefectures:
In the Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, Qo Xiong and Tujia
Huaihua: Qo Xiong, Dong, Hm Nai and Hmu
Shaoyang: Maojia, Hm Nai, Pa-Hng and Badong Yao
Yongzhou: Mien and Biao Min
Chenzhou: Dzao Min

Roughly 5,000 Uyghurs live in Taoyuan County and elsewhere in the Changde area, where Hui and Uyghurs have intermarried. Unlike Uyghurs in Xinjiang, they eat pork and follow other Han Chinese customs such as ancestor worship at graves. Mandarin Chinese is their native language and they do not speak Uyghur, though some Uyghurs from Xinjiang visit them out of curiosity or interest.

The religious landscape is mainly Chinese Buddhism, Taoist traditions and folk religion. Survey results from 2007 and 2009 show 0.77% of people calling themselves Christian and 20.19% practising ancestor veneration. Other faiths were not counted, so the other 79.04% could be non-religious or follow nature deities, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism or folk sects. In 2010 there were 118,799 Muslims in Hunan.

Culture is a sizeable part of the provincial economy. In 2022 cultural and related industries produced added value of ¥250.65 billion (US$37.27 billion), or 5.27% of the province's GDP. Of that, cultural services made up ¥150.20 billion (US$22.33 billion), cultural manufacturing ¥78.28 billion (US$11.64 billion) and cultural wholesale and retail ¥22.17 billion (US$3.30 billion).

The 2023 cultural infrastructure was extensive. Hunan had 655 art groups, 149 public galleries and cultural centres, 148 public libraries, 180 museums and memorial halls and 108 radio and television stations. Cable TV counted 5.853 million users and 27.441 million fibre-optic broadband households were linked to cable. Radio reached 99.43% of the population and television 99.77%. The province protects 137 national and 410 provincial items of intangible cultural heritage. Publishers brought out 12,078 book titles, 235 periodicals and 44 newspapers, with total print runs of 590 million books, 80 million periodicals and 500 million newspapers.

Hunan's dialects are complex. They include Xiang, Southwestern Mandarin, Gan and Hakka, along with local varieties whose classification is still undecided, such as Xiangnan Tuhua and Waxiang. In minority areas many people speak their own language as well as Chinese.

If you like heat, Hunanese food is for you: chili peppers, garlic and shallots appear almost everywhere, producing the distinctive dry-and-spicy (干辣, gānlà) flavour. Dishes such as smoked cured ham and stir-fried spicy beef show it well. Huaguxi, a regional style of Chinese opera, is very popular across the province.

The Beijing–Guangzhou high-speed railway crosses the province. In sport, Hunan Billows F.C. plays in China's League One (the second tier of football under the Chinese Football Association), and other clubs play in the Hunan Football League. For a student, the high-speed line is the most useful point here, since it makes trips to Changsha and beyond quick and easy.

Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,000 to CNY 14,000 (median CNY 14,000), according to the university's published fee table.

Xidian University (西安电子科技大学, literally Xi'an Electronic Science and Technology University) is a public university in Xi'an, the capital of Shaanxi province. It reports to the Ministry of Education, which shares funding with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; the other co-funders are the State Administration for Science, Technology and Industry for National Defence (SASTIND) and the China Electronics Technology Group Corporation. It is included in the Double First-Class Construction scheme and in Project 211.

The university's identity is built around electronics and information. Its teaching and research concentrate on those fields, though it also offers programmes in engineering, computer science, management, economics, the liberal arts and the social sciences.

Xidian is on the list of China's National Key Universities managed by the Ministry of Education. Over 31,000 students study here. That total breaks down into 21,650 undergraduates, 9,293 on master's courses and 1,779 working towards doctorates. Undergraduate courses cover engineering, science, management and economics, with master's and PhD study above them. Seven National Key Disciplines belong to the university.
The university describes the number of its schools in two ways, 17 in one place and 18 in another, so ask the admissions office for the current structure.

xidian-university.h: What the official descriptions say about its standing

blocks.x: Several national labels apply. Xidian has a National Advantage Discipline Innovation Platform, belongs to the Project 211 and Double First-Class groups, is one of 56 universities with a Graduate School and one of 35 with a national demonstration School of Software. It presents itself as a training base for IT professionals and a centre for high-level research and innovation.

Inside the university there are 4 state key laboratories, 5 Ministry of Education key laboratories, 17 provincial key laboratories and 15 university-level research institutes and centres. The academic offer adds up to 40 doctoral programmes, 77 master's programmes and 50 bachelor's programmes, on top of those 7 national key disciplines. Its recognised strengths, both in China and overseas, are in teaching and research on communication networks, signal and information processing, information security, and microelectronics and mechatronics. In China's 2012 national assessment of first-level disciplines, information and communication engineering came second and electronic science and technology came fourth.

Xidian was in the 401 to 500 range of the 2020 Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU). Subject-level results also exist, in the 2021 ARWU global subject rankings and in the 2020 national and global subject rankings from U.S. News & World Report. Those tables are not reproduced here, so look them up directly if a particular subject matters to you.

Teaching and research here focus on four areas: signal and information processing, wireless broadband, information systems security and communications engineering. Enrolment is large, with over 3,800 undergraduates, around 2,000 students on master's courses and 300 doctoral candidates. The school has two departments, Information Engineering and Communications Engineering, and runs a national demonstration centre for experimental teaching in communication and information engineering.

The faculty numbers 311. One is a member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, two hold the title of National Famous Teacher and three are designated National Experts with Outstanding Contribution. Three of the university's national key disciplines are anchored in this school: circuits and systems, electromagnetic field and microwave technology, and signal and information processing. Four departments teach here, covering electronic engineering, electronic and information engineering, information countermeasures, and intelligent science and technology.

The school dates from 1995, which makes it one of the earliest dedicated computer science schools in the country. On the Academic Ranking of World Universities it holds eighth place in China and sits within the top 100 globally. Five departments cater for students: one for computer science and technology, and the others for networks, the Internet of Things, digital media, and data science with big data.

Six departments make up this school. They teach industrial design, mechanical design and manufacturing, electronic packaging technology, plain automation, electrical engineering with automation, and measurement and control technology with instrumentation.

The Ministry of Education has named it a national base for teaching integrated circuit specialists, and Microelectronics and Solid-State Electronics is a National Key Discipline. The school runs 2 undergraduate programmes, 5 master's programmes and 2 doctoral programmes, with around 1,800 undergraduates and 850 postgraduates. Two departments teach Microelectronics Science and Engineering and Integrated Circuit Design and Integrated System. A longer description of the school also names departments for micro-circuits and devices, integrated system engineering and integrated circuit engineering.
It includes laser technology, the Radio Wave Institute, applied physics, an optoelectronic technology experiment centre and a physics experiment centre.
The departments here are information management and information systems, business administration, industrial engineering, finance and electronic commerce.
This school brings together applied mathematics and computing science with probability and statistics, operations research and control, and, perhaps surprisingly, psychology.

xidian-university.h: Humanities and Arts, and Foreign Languages

blocks.x: Humanities and Arts covers politics, philosophy, Chinese language, history and art. Foreign Languages offers English language and literature, foreign linguistics and applied linguistics, and translation.
Life Science and Technology: biomedical engineering and biological technology.
Aerospace Science and Technology: detection, guidance and control.
Software: software engineering, at master's and PhD level.
Advanced Materials and Nanotechnology: material physics and chemistry, plus master's programmes in material science and applied chemistry.
Four themes guide research: telecommunications, processing of signals and information, computer science and engineering, and microelectronics including IC design.
Four State Key Laboratories exist: Radar Signal Processing, Integrated Services Network, Antennas and Microwave Technology, and Wide Bandgap Semiconductor Technology.

Five more laboratories carry the Ministry of Education's key-laboratory label. One studies intelligent perception and image understanding, another electronic equipment structure, and another materials and devices based on wide bandgap semiconductors. The remaining two address electronic information countermeasures with simulation technology, and ultra-fast circuit design together with electromagnetic compatibility.

The 17 provincial key laboratories range widely. Security is one cluster: system and network security, plus computer network information security. Communications is another: wireless communications, microwave communication techniques, and wireless physics. Hardware and materials are well represented too, with new semiconductor materials and instruments, intelligent materials and sensors, general-purpose electronic device measurement, computer peripherals and instruments, and electro-mechanics. Others deal with electric system integration design, electronic countermeasures, biomedical engineering, mathematical modelling, software systematic engineering, highly reliable microcircuit techniques, and laser instruments with optical information processing.
Notable alumni include:
Liu Chuanzhi, founder of Lenovo
Zhang Rongqiao, chief designer of the Tianwen-1 Mars mission
Hu Lijiao, who once headed the People's Bank of China as governor
Gou Zhongwen, a politician who directs the State General Administration of Sports
Shumin Zhai, computer scientist and ACM Fellow
Zhong Lin Wang, physicist
Lai Xuejia, cryptographer
Robert Qiu, electrical engineer and entrepreneur
Ling Li, writer
Ning Cai, an electrical engineer, has taught at the university.
The city shapes daily life, so this part explains Xi'an: where it is, what the weather does, how people move around, and what the local economy looks like.

Xi'an sits on the Guanzhong Plain in the south-centre of Shaanxi, on a flood plain formed by eight rivers and streams around it. The Qin Mountains (Qinling) rise at the city's southern edge, and the Wei River runs along its north. To the east, 100 km (62 miles) away, stands Hua Shan, one of Taoism's five sacred mountains, while the Loess Plateau begins not far to the north.

The location was prized very early. When the Han dynasty began, the emperor Liu Bang was advised by his chief of staff Zhang Liang to choose Guanzhong as his capital. Zhang described the plain as lying behind Mount Xiao and Hangu Pass, linking Gansu (Long) with Sichuan (Shu), and as an iron castle stretching for a thousand miles whose rich harvests made it like heaven's own country (关中左崤函，右陇蜀，沃野千里，此所谓金城千里，天府之国也). Ever since, Guanzhong has been known as the Nation of the Heaven.

The East Asian monsoon influences Xi'an's temperate climate, which the Köppen system places on the border between humid subtropical and hot-summer humid continental (Cwa/Dwa). Summers in the Wei valley are hot and humid, and winters are cold and dry. Spring and autumn are dry. Most rain falls from July to late October. Snow does fall now and then in winter but seldom stays long, and dust storms are common in March and April as the city warms up fast. Summer also brings frequent short thunderstorms.

In January the average temperature hovers around freezing, and in July it reaches 27.0 °C (80.6 °F); the yearly mean is 14.08 °C (57.3 °F). Since 1951 the coldest day was 11 January 1955 at -20.6 °C (-5 °F), and the hottest was 15 July 2025 at 42.3 °C (108 °F), recorded at the current station in Jinghe. Another station once recorded 42.9 °C (109 °F), on 17 June 2006. An unofficial low of -25.0 °C (-13 °F) was noted in January 1930 at a station in the northern suburbs.

Xi'an has an unusual role in national timekeeping. The Shaanxi Astronomical Observatory was founded in 1966. A 1975 geodetic report stated that the country's geodetic origin was to lie in central mainland China, to keep measurement bias as small as possible, and A town close to Xi'an, Lintong (临潼), was selected. China's standard time (CST) has been set from here since 1986. The National Time Service Center (NTSC), part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, works on time and frequency services and research: producing and maintaining the national time scale and broadcasting time and frequency signals. During the 1970s and 1980s it developed its own universal and atomic time scales and ways to broadcast them by low-frequency and high-frequency radio, meeting the needs of science and the national economy.

The Seventh National Census in 2020 recorded 12,952,907 permanent residents in the city. Men made up 51.07 percent and women 48.93 percent. By age, 15.65 percent were 0 to 14, 68.33 percent were 15 to 59, 16.02 percent were over 60, and 10.9 percent were over 65. The OECD estimated the metropolitan area's population at 12.9 million in 2010, with 5,740,000 of them urban.

Many parts of Xi'an are easy to cover on foot. Underpasses and overpasses make crossing safer and easier in commercial, residential and educational areas, especially around the shopping and entertainment streets near the Bell Tower.

A bike-sharing network began in 2013 and now has 52,000 bicycles, used by more than 200,000 people a day. Taxis are plentiful, but many residents still go to work on the city's 270 municipal bus routes, which run over 7,800 buses and carry more than 4 million passengers a day on average. A fast-growing subway system adds to that, with over 1.5 million rides daily. There are over 2 million registered cars, so traffic jams are a common problem.

Line 2 runs north to south between North Railway Station and Weiqu Nan, 19.9 kilometres (12.4 miles) and 17 stations. As the first line to open, it admitted the public on 16 September 2011 and began regular operations on 28 September 2011.
Line 1 runs west to east between Houweizhai and Fangzhicheng with 19 stations and opened on 15 September 2013.
Line 3 goes from Baoshuiqu in the northeast to Yuhuazhai in the southwest and opened on 8 November 2016.

Line 4 opened on 26 December 2018. Its route runs largely alongside Line 2, on the eastern side, apart from the north end. The northern terminus is outside the North Railway Station's north square (Beikezhan, or Beiguangchang), and the southern terminus is Hangtianxincheng.
Line 5, opened on 28 December 2020, is the longest here at 41.6 kilometres. Its 31 stations stretch between Matengkong and Chuangxingang.
Line 16 opened on 27 June 2023. It is 15.03 kilometres with 9 stations, from Qinchuangyuanzhongxin to Shijingli.
Four more lines, including an extension of Line 1, are being built.

The subway also reaches many famous places. For Line 2 these are the Bell and Drum Tower and the Fortifications of Xi'an. Line 1's Banpo Station serves the Banpo Museum. Lines 3 and 4 both stop by the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, Line 4 goes to the Daminggong National Heritage Park, and the Shaanxi History Museum can be reached on Lines 2, 3 and 4.

Lines 1, 2, 3 and 4 start running at 6:00. The last train leaves at 23:00 on Lines 3 and 4, 23:30 on Line 1 and 23:50 on Line 2. A fire on 30 December 2008 was put out within an hour and all workers got out safely, and another fire broke out at a different Line 2 station on 2 January, 66 hours later.

Xi'an North railway station lies a few miles north of the centre and handles high-speed trains on the Zhengzhou-Xi'an High-Speed Railway, part of the Xuzhou-Lanzhou high-speed line. Construction of that railway started on 25 September 2005 and it opened on 6 February 2010. It made flying between Zhengzhou and Xi'an uncompetitive, and all flights between the two cities stopped within 48 days of regular high-speed service. The station itself was begun on 19 September 2008 and opened on 11 January 2011, and with 34 platforms it was the largest in Northwest China at that time. It also serves the Datong-Xi'an high-speed railway (connecting to Beijing North), the Xi'an-Chengdu high-speed railway and the Yinchuan-Xi'an high-speed railway.

Xi'an railway station is just north of the walled city and is the main hub for conventional trains in Shaanxi. The station occupies 597,000 square metres (6,430,000 square feet) and has six platforms for passengers, eleven passenger tracks, 112 daily services and about 80,000 travellers a day. Among the places with direct trains are Beijing, Lanzhou, Zhengzhou, Baoji and Mount Hua.
Xi'an East and Xi'an South were being built for new high-speed lines such as the Xi'an-Chongqing and Wuhan-Xi'an routes.
Other stations are Xi'an West, Yinzhen, Sanmincun and Fangzhicheng.

Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (XIY), the largest in northwest China, lies 25 miles northwest of the city centre and 8 miles northeast of central Xianyang. The main airlines are China Eastern, Hainan Airlines and China Southern. Terminal 3 and the second runway opened on 3 May 2012, and Terminal 5, started in 2022, was finished in September 2024. Besides flights to most Chinese cities, there are routes to Tokyo, Seoul, London, Paris and Sydney.

The central government's drive to develop western China made Xi'an a priority for rapid growth. Favoured sectors included aerospace, chemical engineering, energy, advanced materials and information technology. Between 1997 and 2006 the newer service industry expanded by an average of 13 percent annually, compared with only 0.74 percent for traditional services, taking its output from US$8.113 billion to US$25.85 billion.

The Globalization and World Cities Research Network gave Xi'an a Beta- rating (global second tier) in 2020, and the same year the Global Financial Centres Index put it in the world's top 100 financial centres.

Equipment manufacturing, tourism and service outsourcing lead. Manufacturing produced RMB 36.5 billion a year, 44.5 percent of the city total. Xi'an was one of four ancient capitals of China, and cultural attractions such as the Terracotta Army, the City Wall and the Famen Temple make tourism another pillar. More than 300 million visits were recorded in 2019, bringing in RMB 314.6 billion in all. Revenue has grown by an average of 36.4 percent per year, and earnings in foreign exchange (530 million in 2009) by around 35.8 percent.

The city was an early adopter of service outsourcing in China and has more than 800 firms in the field. Sector output topped RMB 23 billion in 2008. Jobs in outsourcing doubled between 1997 and 2006 from 60,000, and jobs in computer consulting doubled from 16,000 to 32,000. Because software outsourcing matters so much, the city planned a Software New Town, to be finished in 2015 with 30 billion RMB of investment. Lighting equipment and car parts are major exports, mechanical and electrical products the main imports, and the United States is the biggest trading partner.

Logistics is a growing area. The International Trade and Logistics Park, about thirty-five square miles in size, was planned as a model for urban growth driven by logistics. It works as a big dry port and rail container centre, and no other Chinese city sends or receives as many China-Europe freight trains.
The chief industrial area is the Xi'an Economic and Technological Development Zone. The Jiangcungou landfill, which closed in 2019, was China's largest.

Xi'an is a pioneer of China's software industry. By 2012 the Xi'an Software Park, inside the Xi'an Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone, had attracted over 1,085 companies and 106,000 employees. One description of the city refers to a large pool of cheap labour from the area's 100 universities, producing about 3,000 computer graduates a year, each earning around $120 a month, half the pay for a comparable job in Beijing. That wage figure is dated, so treat it as an indication of the past rather than a current salary guide.

Space technology has its own industrial base. The city joined the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation in November 2006 to set up the Xi'an Aerospace Science and Technology Industrial Base, which aims at the civil space sector: new materials, solar photovoltaics, equipment manufacturing, and software and service outsourcing. The core zone is meant to extend across Xi'an and the Guanzhong region, with an expansion zone touching Northwest and Southwest China. Targets included industry output of 2.8 billion US dollars by 2012 and 10 to 20 own-brand products with intellectual property rights, of which 5 to 8 should be competitive worldwide.

China began building a second civil aerospace centre, in Shaanxi, after the first one started up in Shanghai in 2008. Planning for the Xi'an National Civil Aerospace Industrial Base had received approval from the State Development and Reform Commission on 26 December 2007. When complete it will occupy 23 square kilometres (8.9 square miles), devoted to satellites, new materials, energy, IT and other civil technologies.
Xi'an has lost its best-known professional clubs to other cities, as these three moves show.
In the Jia-A football league, Shaanxi National Power relocated to Ningbo in 2004 and took the name Ningbo National Power.
In the Super League, Shaanxi Baorong Chanba went to Guiyang in 2012, where it became Guizhou Renhe.
In basketball's CBA, Shaanxi Dongsheng moved to Foshan in 2010 and was renamed Foshan Dralions.
Xidian University lists 63 programs for international students on this site: 20 bachelor, 25 master's, 18 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 35 taught in English, 28 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 30,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 40,000 to CNY 40,000 (median CNY 40,000), according to the university's published fee table.

63 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

xidian-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Xidian University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Xi'an, register at Xidian University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Xinjiang Normal University, or XJNU, is a state university in the region of Xinjiang in the north-west of the People's Republic of China, with its home in Urumqi. In Uyghur it is شىنجاڭ پىداگوگېكا ئۇنىۋېرسىتېتى (Shinjang Pidagogéka Uniwérsitéti), and in Chinese 新疆师范大学 (Xīnjiāng Shīfàn Dàxué). The Ministry of Education gave its approval in December 1978. Two older institutions fed into it: the Ürümqi First Normal School and a Xinjiang teacher training department. As with other normal universities in China, teacher education was where it started.
Among its graduates is Gulchehra Hoja, a journalist.

xinjiang-normal-university.h: Urumqi: the city around the campus

blocks.x: Student life depends on the city, and Urumqi is unlike most Chinese cities. It is remote, high, dry and far from the sea, and its seasons and daylight hours differ from what students from the east or from abroad may expect. The pages below explain what to anticipate.

xinjiang-normal-university.h: The most distant city from the sea

blocks.x: Urumqi has the biggest population of any city in western China, and the Guinness Book of Records lists it as the major city farthest from any sea. The nearest coast is roughly 2,500 kilometres (1,600 miles) away. Karamay and Altay, both in Xinjiang, are actually nearer to the Eurasian pole of inaccessibility, but Urumqi is the largest city close to it. Its administrative area is 10,989 square kilometres (4,243 square miles), at an average elevation of 800 metres (2,600 feet).

Local geographers marked a spot in the south-western suburbs (Urumqi County), at 43 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds north and 87 degrees 19 minutes 52 seconds east, as the 'centre of Asia' in 1992. A monument was erected there during the 1990s, and visitors still come to see it.

Two deserts, the Gurbantünggüt to the north and the Taklamakan to the south, enclose the Urumqi region. Even so, several small rivers fed by snow on the Tian Shan bring water. The main Tian Shan range is south of the city, in Urumqi County, and Bogda Shan is east of it, in Dabancheng District.

Nearly half of China's glaciers, 20,000 in all, are in Xinjiang, and global warming has reduced them by 21 to 27 percent since the 1950s. Tianshan Glacier No. 1 feeds the Urumqi River and is the largest glacier close to a major city anywhere in China; it has by now broken into two smaller glaciers.

As population and economic activity increase, the region needs more water than nature supplies. In the 2000s the Irtysh-Urumqi Canal was dug to deal with shortages. Its trunk finishes at 'Reservoir 500' (44 degrees 12 minutes north, 87 degrees 49 minutes east), in the far north-east of the suburbs, where Midong District meets Fukang City. Next to the reservoir, on the western side, planners were developing a new industrial zone in 2009, called Ganquanbao Industrial Park or Industrial New City 500, that relies on it. Water then spreads through a network of canals in lower Midong District.

Urumqi straddles two climate types: humid continental (Koppen Dfa; Trewartha Dcac) and cool semi-arid (Koppen BSk; Trewartha BSac). Seasonal contrast is huge. July is very warm to hot, averaging 24.2 C (75.6 F) over a day, while January averages a frigid -12.2 C (10.0 F), and the whole year comes to 7.8 C (46.0 F). Summers receive a little more rain than winters, but you are much more likely to see sun in the warm months, and the air is driest then. At 33 percent of possible sunshine in December and 75 percent in September, the annual total comes to 2,643 hours. Rain and snow add up to about 365 mm (14.4 in). The record low since 1951 is -41.5 C (-42.7 F), recorded on 27 February 1951, and the record high is 42.1 C (107.8 F), on 1 August 1973. Bring proper winter clothing.

Air pollution put Urumqi on the Blacksmith Institute's 2007 list of the world's worst polluted places, along with Linfen and Lanzhou. A year later, in 2008, the Toronto Star named it among the top ten worst places in the world to live, citing sulphur pollution. In winter, heavy haze is extremely common and it frequently interrupts flights. Officials thought that energy-hungry industry and an old coal-burning heating system were the main reasons for the severe winter smog.

Fudan University's Department of Environmental Science and Engineering reported that in the winter of 2007 the average PM2.5 concentration was 12 times the American standard and the TSP concentration 3 times China's national ambient standard. Sulphur dioxide from factories, mixed with the city's own man-made aerosols and with soil dust blown in from outside, gave the high sulphate readings that explain much of the pollution. Check current air quality for the season in which you plan to arrive.

Because the whole country keeps one time, Urumqi's sun lags China Standard Time (UTC+8) by 2 hours and 10 minutes. Early January sunrise is at 09:45, and sunset falls between 18:45 and 19:10. Around March and September the sun comes up near 08:00 and goes down near 19:45. In June it rises about 06:25 and stays up until 21:45. Daily routines and class hours therefore feel different from eastern China.

Ever since the Qing conquest the city has had many peoples. Early on, the Manchus lived at Gongning Cheng and the Han Chinese at Dihua, while the Hui, Uyghurs and others occupied suburban districts. The Muslims settled south of the walled city of Dihua; the walls were later torn down, but the area is still where most Muslims live.

Population counts give a sense of scale. In 1787 a census found 114,348 Hui and Han in the prefectures of Zhenxi (including Barkol and Hami) and Urumqi. Within the city, there were 39,000 residents in the 1880s and 50,000 in the early 1900s. A 1908 description names Uyghurs (then called Turkis), Chinese, Manchus and a few Mongols, with Uyghurs thought to be a quarter of the total.

After the People's Republic began, Han people were actively resettled in Xinjiang. In 1960 Urumqi counted 477,321 Han Chinese and 76,496 Uyghurs. By the 2000 census the city had 2,081,834 inhabitants, at 174.53 per square kilometre (452.3 per square mile), and an estimate for 2021 gives 4.544 million.

Urumqi is a leading industrial centre in Xinjiang: it generates, with Karamay and Korla, 64.5 percent of all industrial output there. It is also the region's biggest consumer market, with ¥41.9 billion of consumer goods sold at retail in 2008, 26 percent above 2007. By 2025 GDP stood at CN¥465.8 billion (US$65.2 billion), or about CN¥112,485 (US$15,748) per person. The central government's China Western Development project has treated the city as a main target.

Every year since 1991 the city has held a trade fair for domestic and foreign markets, the Urumqi Foreign Economic Relations and Trade Fair. In 2011 it was raised in status to become the first China-Eurasia Expo, and at its 17th session delegates came from the Ministry of Commerce and the China Council for Promotion of International Trade.

The largest property developer and strongest private company in Xinjiang is Xinjiang Guanghui Industry Investment Group, with interests in energy and motor vehicles. Its headquarters, the China CITIC Bank Mansion on North Xinhua Road, is 229 metres (751 feet) high, which makes it the tallest building in Urumqi, Xinjiang, north-western China and Central Asia. Zhongshan Road (Sun Yat-sen Road) has been ranked as one of China's ten best-known shopping streets since 2005. It remains the electronics heart of the city, with the biggest computer and phone market in Xinjiang: Baihuacun, Cyber Digital Plaza and Fountain Plaza.

Growth of the urban area since the 1990s reflects the city's role as the region's economic hub, with business districts springing up around all the main districts. The old city is in the south, though building in the north began in the late 1980s, and when the municipal government's new office tower opened at Nanhu Square, Nanhu Road, in 2003, the city's centre of gravity moved north. Since there was no subway, the city started building viaducts for the Outer Ring Road in 2003, which eased traffic a lot. Shopping, business and entertainment cluster around Youhao Road, where the local company Youhao Group, named after the street, holds much of the retail market. A luxury department store, Maison Mode Ürümqi, has traded since 2008 and is one of very few of its kind. The Urumqi Economic and Technological Development Zone, in the northern district of Toutunhe, leads in steel, machinery, biochemistry and other industrial innovation.
Urumqi Tianshan International Airport is the biggest airport in Xinjiang and a hub of China Southern Airlines. It is the only airport in China with flights from Afghanistan and Tajikistan.

City traffic was the target of Urumqi's Bus Rapid Transit, which began in August 2011 with 930 million yuan of investment. Nine lines run today: BRT1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, plus the branch lines BRT61 and BRT71.

The metro began service on 25 October 2018 with the northern section of Line 1, and the southern section opened on 28 June 2019. This underground line runs 27.615 km (17.2 miles) and has 21 stations, joining the airport with Santunbei downtown. Plans foresee 7 lines of 211 km (131 miles) in all, and Lines 1 and 2 are first, with a projected cost of 31.24 billion yuan.

Urumqi is the rail centre of Xinjiang. It has two principal stations: Urumqi South, the old main station, and the newer Urumqi station, opened in July 2016. The Lanzhou-Xinjiang high-speed line has run to Lanzhou since late 2014 and stops at both.

Regular lines also come in. Urumqi is the terminus in the west for the Lanxin line (from Lanzhou) and the Wuzhun line (to Dzungaria), and in the east for the Beijiang (Northern Xinjiang) line and the Second Urumqi-Jinghe line. The Lanxin and Beijiang lines form a segment of the Trans-Eurasian Continental Railway, a route from Rotterdam that crosses the Kazakhstan border at the Alataw Pass, reaches Urumqi, and continues to Lanzhou and Lianyungang.
Main roads are China National Highways 216, 312 and 314. Note that many northern and western roads normally close in early October and stay closed until winter ends, so plan trips around that.

xinjiang-normal-university.h: Xinjiang: the region behind the city

blocks.x: XJNU is in Xinjiang, and the surrounding region influences student life as much as any campus. These sections give the long historical background.

The first people in the area we now call Xinjiang descended from Ancient North Eurasians and Northeast Asians. In the Bronze Age, more gene flow arrived that is linked with early Indo-European expansion, and the population became mixed. Iron Age samples show stronger mixing between steppe herders and northeast Asians; the north and east of Xinjiang are closer to northeast Asians, the south closer to Central Asians.

Scientists examined 92 individuals from the Xiaohe Cemetery from 2009 to 2015 for Y chromosome and mitochondrial markers. Almost all paternal lines were of European origin, but maternal lines varied, with East Eurasian and West Eurasian types and a few Indian or South Asian ones. West Eurasian maternal lines gradually gave way to East Eurasian lines, and marriage with Siberian women reduced the original variety.

The Tarim people were thus always diverse, with a complex mix of Ancient North Eurasian, South Asian and Northeast Asian ancestry. Mummies have been found in the western Tarim Basin at Loulan, at the Xiaohe tombs and at Qäwrighul. Earlier theories called them Tocharian or other Indo-European speakers, but recent evidence suggests the oldest mummies were from a separate group, unrelated to Indo-European herders, whose language is unknown and was probably an isolate. Anthropologists have labelled many mummies Caucasoid, though some sites hold remains of both 'Caucasoid' and 'Mongoloid' type, showing that western nomads newly arrived met farming communities of the east.

Nomads like the Yuezhi, Saka and Wusun probably belonged to a wave of Indo-European speakers that reached the Tarim Basin long before the Xiongnu or the Han. The Han emperor Wu (141 to 87 BC) took the western basin from the Xiongnu, who had controlled it before him, and the people he found were varied: Indo-European Tocharians around Turfan and Kucha, Saka people centred on the Shule Kingdom and the Kingdom of Khotan, a number of Tibeto-Burman groups (above all peoples related to the Qiang), and also Han Chinese. Some linguists think Tocharian absorbed much from Palaeosiberian languages such as Uralic and Yeniseian.

Records of the Yuezhi exist. In 645 BC the Chinese chancellor Guan Zhong mentioned them first, in his work the Guanzi, writing about the Yushi (or Niushi), a north-western people that brought jade to China from the Yushi mountains close by in Gansu. Archaeology shows that jade from the Tarim Basin was supplied for a very long time: the tomb of Fuhao of the Shang dynasty held more than 750 jade objects, every one from Khotan in present-day Xinjiang. From about the middle of the first millennium BC the Yuezhi traded jade, with the rulers of agricultural China as chief buyers.

Today's Xinjiang is made up of the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria. The first settlers were Indo-European Tocharians and Iranian Sakas, and they practised Buddhism and Zoroastrianism. Tocharian languages were spoken around Turfan and in the Tarim Basin, and mummies of European appearance have been found there. In the 10th century the region became Muslim, after the Kara-Khanid Khanate, whose rulers held Kashgar, converted to Islam. About the middle of that century, a Turkic Muslim Karakhanid ruler named Musa attacked the Saka Buddhist kingdom of Khotan, and in about 1006 another Karakhanid leader, Yusuf Qadir Khan, conquered it.

After Genghis Khan had brought Mongolia under one rule and started westward, the Uyghur state around Turpan and Urumchi submitted in 1209 and supplied taxes and soldiers. In exchange its rulers could keep governing their kingdom. By 1218 the Qara Khitai had fallen to the Mongol Empire. Xinjiang became a stronghold of Ögedei Khan, and afterwards of his descendant Kaidu, and that branch of the Mongol family stopped the Yuan dynasty from reaching the region until the end of its rule.

During the Mongol Empire the Yuan and the Chagatai Khanate competed over the region, and the Chagatai held most of it. The Chagatai Khanate broke into smaller khanates in the mid-14th century, and a number of Persianised Mongol khans governed the divided territory. They came from Moghulistan, helped by local Dughlat emirs, from Uigurstan (later Turpan) and from Kashgaria, and they fought each other, the Timurids of Transoxiana in the west and the Oirats in the east, meaning the successor Chagatai regime based in Mongolia and China. The Dzungars then built an empire over most of the region in the 17th century.

Several Oirat tribes together formed the Mongol Dzungars, who maintained one of the last nomad empires. Their khanate covered Dzungaria and extended from the Great Wall's western end to what is now eastern Kazakhstan, and from northern Kyrgyzstan to southern Siberia. The Chinese gave most of the region the name Xinjiang after the Dzungar empire, which had existed from the early 17th century to the middle of the 18th, collapsed.

The Turkic Muslims who farmed the Tarim Basin had first been under the Chagatai Khanate, while the Buddhist Oirat Mongols of Dzungaria, a nomadic people, ran the Dzungar Khanate. In the early 17th century Naqshbandi Sufi Khojas, who claimed descent from Muhammad, displaced the Chagatayid khans in the Tarim Basin. Two Khoja groups competed: the Afaqi (White Mountain) and the Ishaqi (Black Mountain). When the Ishaqi won, the Afaq Khoja turned in 1677 to the 5th Dalai Lama, the Tibetan leader, and asked for help. The Dalai Lama in turn urged his Buddhist followers within the Dzungar Khanate to act, and in 1680 the Dzungars took the Tarim Basin and set up the Afaqi Khoja as their puppet. Turfan's Uyghurs, descendants of earlier Buddhists but by then Muslim, believed that the 'infidel Kalmuks', meaning the Dzungars, had built the Buddhist monuments of their area.

XJNU is a normal university founded in 1978 in a city with an unusual location, dramatic seasons and a long and mixed history. Check the university's own website for current programmes, admission and campus details, and be prepared for long winters, late winter sunrises and the air quality issues described above. Many of the figures in this profile are from different years, so treat them as a general picture and confirm anything that affects your plans, such as transport links, visa matters and accommodation, with the university directly.
Xinjiang Normal University lists 31 programs for international students on this site: 12 bachelor, 17 master's, 2 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 31 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 14,400 to CNY 14,400 (median CNY 14,400), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 17,600 to CNY 19,200 (median CNY 17,600), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 25,000 (median CNY 25,000), according to the university's published fee table.

31 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. xinjiang-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Xinjiang Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.

Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Urumqi, register at Xinjiang Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Xinjiang University, usually shortened to XJU, is a comprehensive public university in Ürümqi, the capital of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in north-west China. It is regarded as a key university at national level. It sits under the regional administration, with money coming jointly from the national education ministry and the regional authorities, and it has a place in both Project 211 and the current Double First-Class programme.

The university dates back to 1924 and is generally seen as the highest-ranking institution in Xinjiang academically. In the domestic Best Chinese Universities Ranking, which is often called the Shanghai Ranking, it was placed first in the region and 129th in the country. It is one of only two universities in Xinjiang to have joined the national 211 Project, which gives an idea of how central it is to higher education in the region.

The story begins in 1924, when the Xinjiang Russian and Law School was set up; it is regarded as the ancestor of today's university. In 1935 it became Xinjiang College, and the name Xinjiang University was adopted in 1960. The campus lies in the southern part of Ürümqi. On 30 December 2000 the old Xinjiang University merged with Xinjiang Engineering Institute to form the university as it stands today. The university says that in its first 78 years it produced 65,000 graduates, a figure from the early 2000s that has certainly grown since.

Students come from a number of ethnic groups, and that mix is part of the character of the place. If you are considering applying, it is worth asking the international office about the languages used for teaching in your chosen programme.

XJU is made up of fourteen schools covering a broad span of fields: sciences, engineering, law and economics, management, the arts and history. Intellectual property became a new major in 2013. Classes are spread over three sites: a Main Campus plus separate North and South campuses.

The available figures list 3 doctoral programmes, 46 master's programmes and 75 undergraduate majors. Research institutes cover economics, demography, mathematical theory and applied chemistry, along with arid ecology, architectural design, Altaic studies and the culture of Central Asia. Another institute, the Minorities Folklore Research Center, was set up by Rahile Dawut. Those interests in arid ecology and in Central Asian and Altaic studies fit the surroundings, since the campus is near deserts, mountains and the borders of Central Asia.

Different league tables say different things, and the position depends on the method. As noted, the domestic Best Chinese Universities Ranking puts XJU 129th in China. Internationally, the numbers are as follows:
Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU): between 601st and 700th
University Rankings by Academic Performance, 2024 to 2025: 695th in the world
Center for World University Rankings, 2025: 1017th in the world
U.S. News Best Global Universities, 2024: 1317th globally and 448th in Asia
CWTS Leiden Ranking, 2025: 438th in the world and 193rd in Asia, based on publications from 2020 to 2023
Nature Index Research Leaders, 2025: among the leading 450 institutions worldwide for the quality of natural science publications
Taken together, these tables place XJU somewhere within the top 1500 universities in the world. Rankings change each year, so look at the most recent versions.

An unusual fact for the end of this section: an asteroid, number 192450, was named Xinjiangdaxue in honour of the university. The Minor Planet Center published the naming citation on 25 September 2018.
Alumni include Tashpolat Tiyip and Yang Gang. Among the people who have taught there are Rahile Dawut, Tashpolat Tiyip, Ibrahim Muti'i and Wushour Silamu.

xinjiang-university.h: Ürümqi, the city you would live in

blocks.x: Ürümqi is the regional capital and the largest city of western China. Understanding the setting is important, because the city's remote location, its extreme seasons and its air quality in winter will all affect your daily life.

xinjiang-university.h: A long way from the sea

blocks.x: The Guinness World Records lists Ürümqi as the world's most landlocked city, with the closest coast roughly 2,500 kilometres (1,600 miles) off. That is because no other major city lies nearer to the Eurasian pole of inaccessibility, even though Karamay and Altay, both inside Xinjiang, lie closer still to it. The administrative area covers 10,989 square kilometres (4,243 square miles) and the average elevation is 800 metres (2,600 feet).

Local geography experts declared a spot in the south-western suburbs (Ürümqi County) to be the center point of Asia in 1992, and a monument was raised there during that decade. The coordinates are 43°40′52″N, 87°19′52″E, and visitors still come to see it.

Desert surrounds the area, with the Gurbantünggüt to the north and the Taklamakan to the south, but several small rivers run down from the snow-capped Tian Shan and keep the area watered. The Tian Shan's central range lies to the south in Ürümqi County, while Bogda Shan stands to the east in Dabancheng District.

Xinjiang is home to 20,000 glaciers, nearly half of China's total. Since the 1950s they have shrunk by 21 to 27 percent because of global warming. Tianshan Glacier No. 1 feeds the Ürümqi River. No other major Chinese city has a bigger glacier close by, yet it has already split in two.

As the population and economy of the area expand, the demand for water has outpaced what nature supplies. To ease the shortage, the Irtysh–Ürümqi Canal was built during the first decade of this century. The main channel ends at a storage lake named Reservoir 500 (500水库) in the far north-eastern suburbs, where Midong District meets Fukang City, at about 44°12′N, 87°49′E. In 2009 a new industrial area, Ganquanbao Industrial Park, also known as Industrial New City 500, was under development to the west of the reservoir and counted on it for water. From there, canals distribute water through the lower part of Midong District.

The city sits at the meeting point of a humid continental climate (Köppen Dfa) and a cool semi-arid one (Köppen BSk). Seasonal swings are huge. Summers go from very warm to hot, and in July a typical day averages 24.2 °C (75.6 °F). Winters are bitterly cold, with January days averaging −12.2 °C (10.0 °F). Over the whole year the mean is 7.8 °C (46.0 °F). Summer is a little wetter than winter, yet the hotter months bring far more clear skies and the lowest humidity. December sees 33 percent of possible sunshine and September 75 percent, which adds up to 2,643 hours of sun annually. About 365 millimetres (14.4 inches) of precipitation falls in a year. Since 1951 the lowest reading has been −41.5 °C (−42.7 °F), on 27 February 1951, and the highest 42.1 °C (107.8 °F), on 1 August 1973. Winter clothing for this climate needs to be serious.

In 2007 the Blacksmith Institute included Ürümqi, together with Linfen and Lanzhou in China, in its list of the world's worst polluted places because of air pollution. In 2008 the Toronto Star named Ürümqi one of the world's ten worst cities to live in, pointing to sulphur pollution. Heavy winter haze is very common and often disrupts air travel. Officials have blamed the severe winter pollution chiefly on energy-intensive industries and an outdated coal-fired heating system.

Researchers in Fudan University's environmental science department reported that winter 2007 average levels of PM2.5 were twelve times the US standard, and total suspended particles were three times the Chinese national limit (12 and 3 times respectively). Industrial sulphur dioxide, mixed with local human-made aerosols and with soil dust blown in from beyond the city, was the main source of the high sulphate concentration, one of the leading causes of the heavy pollution. These figures are from 2007 and conditions may have changed; check current air quality data before planning your winter term.

China has just one time zone, so Ürümqi, which is far in the west, runs 2 hours and 10 minutes behind where the sun would otherwise suggest, using China Standard Time (UTC+8). Sunrise in early January comes as late as 09:45, with sunset between 18:45 and 19:10. Around March and September the sun comes up near 08:00 and goes down near 19:45. June days are the longest: up at about 06:25, and still shining until 21:45. Expect late mornings and long summer evenings.

Ever since the Qing conquest the city has had a mixed population. At first, Manchus settled in Gongning Cheng and Han Chinese in Dihua, while the Hui, Uyghurs and others lived in outlying districts. Muslims settled south of the walled city of Dihua, and they are still concentrated there even though the walls have gone.

An eighteenth-century count, from 1787, found 114,348 Hui and Han people across Ürümqi and the Zhenxi prefectures (which took in Barköl and Hami). The city proper held 39,000 residents in the 1880s and 50,000 by the early 1900s. A description of 1908 mentions Uyghurs, who were then called Turkis, plus Chinese, Manchus and a few Mongols, and puts the Uyghur share at about a quarter. Under the People's Republic an active programme to resettle Han people in Xinjiang began, and by 1960 the city had 477,321 Han Chinese and 76,496 Uyghurs.
The 2000 census recorded 2,081,834 inhabitants, a density of 174.53 per square kilometre (452.3 per square mile). The 2021 estimate was 4.544 million.

Ürümqi is one of the main industrial centres of Xinjiang. Together with Karamay and Korla it accounts for 64.5 percent of the region's industrial output. It is also the biggest consumer market in the region, with retail sales of ¥41.9 billion in 2008, up 26 percent on 2007. As of 2025 the city's economy is put at CN¥465.8 billion, which is US$65.2 billion, and output per head at around CN¥112,485 (US$15,748). Ürümqi has been a central target of the China Western Development project.

A trade fair on foreign economic relations has taken place in Urumqi annually since 1991. It became the first China-Eurasia Expo in 2011, and its purpose is to promote domestic and overseas markets. The 17th edition drew delegates from China's commerce ministry and from the council that promotes international trade.

Xinjiang Guanghui Industry Investment Group is the biggest real estate firm and the most powerful private company in the region, and works in energy and cars. Its headquarters, the China CITIC Bank Mansion, stands in a CBD on North Xinhua Road. At 229 metres (751 feet) it is the tallest building in Ürümqi, Xinjiang, north-western China and Central Asia. Another landmark is Zhongshan Road (中山路, also called Sun Yat-sen Road), which since 2005 has ranked among the ten most famous shopping streets in China. It is where the city's electronics trade is centred, with the biggest computer and phone markets in the region: Baihuacun, Cyber Digital Plaza and Fountain Plaza.

As the economic centre of Xinjiang, the city's urban area has grown since the 1990s, with CBDs springing up around the main districts. The old city is mostly in the south, but development in the north began in the late 1980s, and the new Municipal Government office tower at Nanhu Square on Nanhu Road, completed in 2003, signalled that the centre had moved north. With no subway at that time, the city began building viaducts for the Outer Ring Road in 2003, easing traffic. Youhao Road and the surrounding neighbourhood form the main district for business, shopping and entertainment, and the local firm Youhao Group holds a large share of retail. Maison Mode Ürümqi, open since 2008, is one of the very few well-known luxury department stores. Up in Toutunhe District, the Ürümqi Economic and Technological Development Zone is a main centre for steel, machinery, biochemistry and other new industry.
Tianshan International Airport is Xinjiang's biggest and acts as a hub for China Southern Airlines. It is also China's only airport to receive flights from Afghanistan and Tajikistan.

Ürümqi launched its Bus Rapid Transit service in August 2011, spending 930 million yuan to ease urban traffic. There are nine routes: BRT1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 61 (a branch of 6), 7 and 71 (a branch of 7).

The metro opened on 25 October 2018 with the northern section of Line 1, and the southern section followed on 28 June 2019. Line 1 is entirely underground. It runs 27.615 km (17.2 miles) with 21 stations between the airport and Santunbei in downtown. The full plan is for 7 lines covering 211 km (131 miles); Lines 1 and 2 were to be built first at an estimated 31.24 billion yuan.

Ürümqi is the main rail hub in Xinjiang and has two principal stations: the older Ürümqi South (once simply Ürümqi railway station) and the Ürümqi railway station that opened in July 2016. The Lanzhou–Xinjiang High Speed Railway stops at both and has run since the end of 2014 between Ürümqi and Lanzhou.

Conventional lines also serve the city. Four conventional lines meet here. The Lanxin (Lanzhou–Xinjiang) and Wuzhun (Ürümqi–Dzungaria) lines end in Ürümqi at their western ends, while the Beijiang (Northern Xinjiang) and the second Ürümqi–Jinghe line end at their eastern ends. Two of them, Beijiang and Lanxin, form part of the Trans-Eurasian Continental Railway. That route starts in Rotterdam, crosses the Kazakhstan border at the Alataw Pass, reaches Ürümqi and continues to Lanzhou and Lianyungang.

The main roads are China National Highways 216, 312 and 314. Many roads leading north and west usually close in early October and do not reopen until winter ends, which is worth remembering if you plan to travel by road.
A student's life depends on the surrounding region as much as on the campus, so here is some background on Xinjiang as a whole.

Genetic studies suggest that Xinjiang's first inhabitants had Ancient North Eurasian and Northeast Asian ancestry. Later gene flow in the Bronze Age, tied to the spread of early Indo-Europeans, produced a mixed population. Iron Age samples show a growing blend of Steppe herders and Northeast Asians: the north and east of Xinjiang were closer to Northeast Asians, and the south closer to Central Asians.

From 2009 to 2015 researchers tested the remains of 92 individuals buried at the Xiaohe Cemetery, looking at male-line (Y chromosome) and female-line (mitochondrial) DNA. The male lines turned out to be almost entirely of European origin, while the female lines were diverse, with East Eurasian and West Eurasian lineages and a smaller number from India and South Asia. Over time West Eurasian female lineages were replaced by East Eurasian ones, and marriage to women from Siberian communities reduced the earlier diversity of mitochondrial lineages. In short, the Tarim population was always varied, a product of a complicated history of mixing among groups of Ancient North Eurasian, South Asian and Northeast Asian ancestry.

Mummies have turned up in the west of the Tarim Basin, at Loulan, Qäwrighul and the Xiaohe tomb complex. They were once thought to be speakers of Tocharian or another Indo-European tongue, but more recent evidence suggests the earliest of them came from a separate population with no link to Indo-European herders, probably speaking a language with no known relatives. Anthropologists labelled many of them Caucasoid, though sites around the basin also contain Mongoloid remains, which points to meetings between western nomads who had just arrived and farming villages in the east.

The Yuezhi, Saka and Wusun were nomadic peoples who probably formed part of an Indo-European-speaking migration that settled the Tarim Basin well before the Xiongnu or the Han Chinese arrived. When the Han dynasty under Emperor Wu (who reigned 141 to 87 BC) took the western Tarim Basin from the Xiongnu, it was home to many peoples: Tocharians who spoke an Indo-European language in Turfan and Kucha, Saka peoples around Shule and Khotan, Tibeto-Burman groups (particularly relatives of the Qiang) and Han Chinese. A few linguists believe Tocharian absorbed a lot from Paleosiberian languages, such as the Uralic and Yeniseian families.

Yuezhi culture is recorded in the region. The earliest reference dates to 645 BC, when the Chinese chancellor Guan Zhong wrote in the Guanzi about a people from the north-west who provided jade to China from mountains in Gansu. Archaeology confirms that the Tarim Basin was a long-term source of jade: over 750 jade pieces found in Fuhao's Shang dynasty tomb all originated at Khotan, in today's Xinjiang. By the middle of the first millennium BC the Yuezhi were trading it, mostly to the rulers of farming China.

Modern Xinjiang is made up of the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria. Its early people were Indo-European Tocharians and Iranian Sakas, who followed Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Tocharian speakers lived around Turfan and the Tarim, where the mummies were found. Islam arrived in the 10th century, when the Kara-Khanid rulers who held Kashgar converted. In the middle of the century a Turkic Muslim Karakhanid ruler named Musa attacked the Buddhist Saka kingdom of Khotan, and Yusuf Qadir Khan, another Karakhanid leader, took the city around 1006.

When Genghis Khan had unified Mongolia and begun to move west, the Uyghur state around Turpan and Urumchi swore allegiance in 1209, sending taxes and soldiers and keeping its own rulers in return. His empire overcame the Qara Khitai in 1218. Ögedei Khan held Xinjiang as a stronghold, and afterwards his descendant Kaidu controlled it; that line of the family kept the Yuan emperors out until the end of its rule.

During the Mongol era the Yuan dynasty and the Chagatai Khanate competed to rule the region, and the Chagatai controlled most of it. In the mid-14th century the Chagatai Khanate split into smaller states, leaving a divided region run by several Persianized Mongol khans, in Moghulistan (with local Dughlat emirs helping), in Uigurstan, later called Turpan, and in Kashgaria. They fought each other, the Timurids of Transoxiana in the west and the Oirats in the east. In the 17th century the Dzungars built an empire across much of the region.

The Dzungars came from a group of Oirat tribes and built one of history's last nomadic empires, which lasted from the early 17th century to the mid-18th. Their khanate included Dzungaria and stretched from the western Great Wall to what is now eastern Kazakhstan, and from northern Kyrgyzstan up to southern Siberia. After it fell, China gave most of the region the name Xinjiang.

The settled Turkic Muslims of the Tarim Basin had first been ruled by the Chagatai Khanate, whereas the nomadic Buddhist Oirat Mongols of Dzungaria ran the Dzungar Khanate. In the early 17th century Naqshbandi Sufi Khojas, who claimed descent from Muhammad, took over from the Chagatayid khans in the Tarim Basin. Two rival Khoja groups, the Afaqi (White Mountain) and the Ishaqi (Black Mountain), fought each other. After the Ishaqi won, the Afaq Khoja asked the 5th Dalai Lama in 1677 to step in, and the Dalai Lama called on his Dzungar Buddhist followers to act. The Dzungars conquered the Tarim Basin in 1680 and made the Afaqi Khoja their puppet ruler. Later, the Uyghurs of Turfan, who had become Muslim after a Buddhist past, believed the Buddhist monuments in their land had been built by the infidel Kalmuks, as they called the Dzungars.
Xinjiang University lists 80 programs for international students on this site: 12 bachelor, 39 master's, 28 doctoral, 1 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 63 taught in Chinese, 17 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 18,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 25,000 to CNY 30,000 (median CNY 28,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 30,000 to CNY 35,000 (median CNY 33,000), according to the university's published fee table.

80 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (11):
Applied Mathematics
Chemical Engineering and Technology
Chemistry
Computational Mathematics
Computer Science and Technology
Mechanical Engineering
Pharmacy
