Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics
Pure Mathematics
Resources and Environment (Engineering)
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

xinjiang-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Xinjiang University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Urumqi, register at Xinjiang University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Xuzhou Medical University  (simplified Chinese: 徐州医科大学; traditional Chinese: 徐州醫科大學; pinyin: Xúzhōu Yīkē Dàxué) is a provincial medical university located in Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province, China.

The university was established in 1958 as Xuzhou branch, Nanjing Medical College initially. In 1959, Xinhailian Medical Academy was merged into the branch, which was independent and renamed Xuzhou Medical College in the next year. In 2000, Xuzhou Health Vocational School was merged into the college. With the approval of Ministry of Education, the college was formally renamed Xuzhou Medical University in 2016.
The university has a good reputation for its anesthesiology education as one of the medical colleges to establish independent department of anesthesiology first in 1987.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Xuzhou, where Xuzhou Medical University is located.

Xuzhou is situated at the southeastern extremity of the North China Plain, serving as a geographical transition zone between the Yellow River's alluvial fan and the Huai River basin. The landscape comprises an undulating plain underlain by 10–60 metres (33–197 ft) of deep alluvial deposits from historical Yellow River migrations.

This terrain is punctuated by limestone inselberg (isolated rock hills) that rise abruptly from the floodplain, including Yunlong Mountain [142 metres (466 ft)] and the region's highest point, Dadong Mountain [361 metres (1,184 ft)]. Geologically, these formations constitute the Xuzhou–Huaibei fold-thrust belt at the southeastern margin of the North China Craton.

Tectonic activity along the Tancheng–Lujiang (Tan-Lu) fault zone led to the formation of the Xuzhou and Feng-Pei coalfields. By the late 1990s, the region's proven coal reserves reached 3.94 billion tonnes—accounting for over 93% of Jiangsu province's total.

Intensive coal mining has caused landscape fragmentation and subsidence-induced flooding. Through the closure of small-scale mines and ecological restoration—including the conversion of waterlogged subsidence areas in northern Xuzhou and Jiawang into the Jiuli Lake and Pan'an Lake artificial wetlands—the local environment has partially recovered.

The regional hydrology is defined by two major man-made waterways: the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal and the Abandoned Course of the Yellow River. Functioning as a "perched river" with its bed elevated 2–5 metres (6.6–16.4 ft) above the surrounding terrain, the abandoned course now acts as a drainage divide between the Huai and Yi-Shu-Si river systems.

Due to its low-lying topography, the elevated riverbed, and its location at the meandering transition, the region was historically plagued by floods; records indicate 59 levee breaches near Xuzhou between 1550 and 1855.

While the ancient riverbed now bisects the city proper, Yunlong Lake, with a water area of 5.82 square kilometres (2.25 sq mi), serves as a scenic reservoir to the southwest. Its outlet, the Kui River, flows southward  for 35.6 kilometres (22.1 mi) into Anhui province. Historically one of the most polluted tributaries in the Huai River basin, a downtown section of the river was encased in concrete in 2005 to contain odorous emissions. Following extensive ecological remediation, these covers were removed in 2021, restoring the waterway as an open-air corridor.

While situated on a relatively stable fault zone independent of the main Tan-Lu system, the urban area remains at risk due to historical loose silt deposits that are prone to liquefaction, which can cause the ground to behave like a liquid and intensify earthquake damage.

Xuzhou has a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa), with cool, dry winters, warm springs, long, hot and humid summers, and crisp autumns. The monthly daily average temperature ranges from 0.7 °C (33.3 °F) in January to 27.3 °C (81.1 °F) in July; the annual mean is 14.9 °C (58.8 °F). Snow may occur during winter, though rarely heavily. Precipitation is light in winter, and a majority of the annual total of 842.8 millimetres (33.2 in) occurs from June thru August. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 44% in July to 54% in three months, the city receives 2,221 hours of bright sunshine annually.

In the 2020 census, Xuzhou recorded a permanent population of 9,083,900, an increase of 5.9% from 2010. By 2023, its permanent population accounted for approximately 10.6% of the total population of Jiangsu province.

Historically, the population of Xuzhou Prefecture (which then included present-day Dangshan, Xiao counties, and the urban districts of Suqian) grew from 2.95 million in 1776 to 4.34 million in 1910. Despite this growth, the region remained predominantly agricultural with minimal industrial or commercial activity; in 1910, the urban population of the prefectural seat was only approximately 32,000. Urbanization accelerated in the 20th century: the city's population reached 171,903 in 1931, 314,773 in 1947, and 333,190 in the 1953 Census.

As of 2023, Xuzhou's GDP reached RMB 890.04 billion, with a per capita GDP of RMB 98,683 (c. US$14,000). The city serves as the largest economy of the Huaihai Economic Zone, recording the highest GDP, per capita GDP, and total retail sales (RMB 444.51 billion) among the region's member cities.

Xuzhou's modern coal industry originated with the establishment of the Jiawang Coal Mine in 1882. Until the 1950s, it remained the only site of industrial-scale coal extraction in Jiangsu province. Driven by the 1970s energy crisis, a "multi-party development" model emerged, involving the Datun Mining Area (a "Shanghai Enclave") alongside mines operated by other regional authorities.

Since the 2000s, resource depletion led to the closure of most local mines, with the sector consolidating under three major entities: Xuzhou Mining Group, Shanghai Datun Energy Resources, and China Resources Tianneng Xuzhou Coal and Power. As of 2023, the industry's total assets for above-scale enterprises reached 41.98 billion RMB.

The transition to renewables began in 2006 with the establishment of GCL Silicon. In the same year, the company commissioned its first polysilicon facility in Xuzhou, which subsequently developed into a major production site for photovoltaic materials. In 2024, BYD began building a 30 GWh sodium-ion battery plant in Xuzhou.

The demands of coal mining anchored Xuzhou's equipment manufacturing sector, which evolved into a modern construction machinery cluster. XCMG, headquartered in Xuzhou, ranked fourth globally among construction equipment manufacturers by 2024 revenue.

As of 2023, the city's specialized equipment manufacturing sector comprised 225 enterprises above designated size. Annual output for major products included 143,167 tons of mining equipment and 729,259 tons of cranes. In addition to heavy machinery, Xuzhou has developed into a production base for two-wheelers, with annual motorcycle output totaling 526,300 units in 2023.

The Yellow Pavilion (黃樓) was built in 1078 during Su Shi's tenure as the Prefect of Xuzhou to commemorate the completion of the city's wall fortification project under his leadership. The name "Yellow" carries a dual significance: it symbolically represents the element of earth, which conquers water and literally refers to the pounded earth (hangtu) used in the construction of the new defenses and the pavilion's foundation. The current structure is a reconstruction dating to 1988.

Xuzhou has many urban expressways: Xuzhou 3rd Ring Road expressways (east, north and west), Xuzhou East Ave. expressway (城东大道快速路), Xuzhou-Pantang expressway, Xuzhou-Jiawang expressway and Xuzhou-Suqian expressway etc.
G2 Beijing–Shanghai Expressway
G2513 Huai'an–Xuzhou Expressway
G3 Beijing–Taipei Expressway
G30 Lianyungang–Khorgas Expressway
S49 Xinyi–Yangzhou Expressway
S65 Xuzhou–Mingguang Expressway
S69 Jinan–Xuzhou Expressway
China National Highway 104

Xuzhou is a major railway hub in China. Xuzhou Railway Station is the junction of the Beijing–Shanghai and Lianyungang–Lanzhou (Longhai) railways. Xuzhoudong Railway Station, located in the east, serves as the interchange between the Beijing–Shanghai and Xuzhou–Lanzhou high-speed railways; it also functions as the terminal for the Xuzhou–Lanzhou, Xuzhou–Yancheng, and Lianyungang–Xuzhou lines. The two stations are linked via the Dahu connection line.

Xuzhoubei Railway Station, located in the north, is the largest marshalling yard of the China Railway Shanghai Group, handling over 20,000 wagons daily. As one of 14 designated China Railway Express assembly centers, Xuzhou maintains sea-rail intermodal connections to the ports of Ningbo-Zhoushan, Lianyungang, Yangshan, and Qingdao. In 2023, the annual rail freight volume reached 54.53 million tons.

Xuzhou Guanyin International Airport is one of the three biggest international airports in Jiangsu Province, it serves the area with scheduled passenger flights to major airports in China. Xuzhou Guanyin International Airport (徐州观音国际机场) has two terminals until 2019. Domestic Terminal (Terminal 2) and International Terminal (Terminal 1).
Xuzhou is the first city in Northern Jiangsu to operate a rapid transit system.
Line 1 (Sep 2019): Xuzhoudong Railway Station – Luwo. Interchanges at Pengcheng Square (L2) and Xuzhou Railway Station (L3).
Line 2 (Nov 2020): Keyunbei – Xinchengqudong. Serves JSNU Yunlong Campus.
Line 3 (Jun 2021): Xiadian – Gaoxinqu'nan. Serves CUMT Wenchang Campus and JSNU Quanshan Campus.
Line 6 (Sep 2025): Xuzhoudong Railway Station – Tongshan Chinese Medical Hospital.
The Grand Canal flows through Xuzhou, and the navigation route extends from Jining to Hangzhou.
Luning oil pipeline, which originates from Linyi county of Shandong to Nanjing, passes through Xuzhou.
Xuzhou Medical University is in Jiangsu, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Jiangsu.

During the earliest Chinese dynasties, the area that is now Jiangsu was far away from the center of Chinese civilization, which was in the northwest Henan; it was home of the Huai barbarians (淮夷), an ancient ethnic group. During the Zhou dynasty more contact was made, and eventually the state of Wu appeared in southern Jiangsu, one of the many hundreds of states that existed across northern and central China at that time. Near the end of the Spring and Autumn period, Wu became a great power under King Helu of Wu, and defeated in 484 BC the state of Qi, a major power in the north in modern-day Shandong province, and contest for the position of overlord over all states of China. The state of Wu was subjugated in 473 BC by the state of Yue, another state that had emerged to the south in modern-day Zhejiang province. Yue was in turn subjugated by the powerful state of Chu from the west in 333 BC. Eventually the state of Qin swept away all the other states, and unified China in 221 BC.

Under the reign of the Han dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD), Jiangsu was removed from the centers of civilization in the North China Plain, and was administered under two zhou (provinces): Xu Province in the north, and Yang Province in the south. During the Three Kingdoms period, southern Jiangsu became the base of the Eastern Wu (222 to 280), whose capital, Jianye (later renamed to Jiankang), is modern Nanjing. When nomadic invasions overran northern China in the 4th century, the imperial court of the Jin dynasty moved to Jiankang. Cities in southern and central Jiangsu swelled with the influx of migrants from the north. Jiankang remained as the capital for four successive Southern dynasties and became the largest commercial and cultural center in China.

After the Sui dynasty united the country in 581, the political center of the country shifted back to the north, but the Grand Canal was built through Jiangsu to link the Central Plains with the prosperous Yangtze Delta. The Tang dynasty (618–907) relied on southern Jiangsu for annual deliveries of grain. It was during the Song dynasty (960–1279), which saw the development of a wealthy mercantile class and emergent market economy in China, that Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai, and adjacent areas) emerged as a center of trade. From then onwards, major cities like Suzhou or Yangzhou, would be synonymous with opulence and luxury in China. Today the region remains one of the richest parts of China.

The Jurchen Jin dynasty gained control of North China in 1127 during the Jin-Song wars, and Huai River, which used to cut through north Jiangsu to reach the Yellow Sea, was the border between the north, under the Jin, and the south, under the Southern Song dynasty. The Mongols took control of China in the thirteenth century. The Ming dynasty, which was established in 1368 after driving out the Mongols who had occupied China, initially put its capital in Nanjing. Regions surrounding Nanjing, corresponding to Jiangsu and Anhui today, were designated as Nanzhili province (literally "southern directly governed"). Following a coup by Zhu Di (later, the Yongle Emperor), however, the capital was moved to Beijing, far to the north, although Nanjing kept its status as the southern capital. In late Ming, Jiangnan continued to be an important center of trade in China; some historians see in the flourishing textiles industry at the time incipient industrialization and capitalism, a trend that was however aborted.
The Qing dynasty converted Nanzhili to "Jiangnan province"; in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui were split apart as separate provinces. Jiangsu's borders have been for the most part stable since then.

With the start of Western incursion into China in the 1840s, the rich and mercantile Yangtze River Delta was increasingly exposed to Western influence. Shanghai, originally an unremarkable little town of Jiangsu, quickly developed into a metropolis of trade, banking, and cosmopolitanism, and was split out later as an independent municipality. Jiangnan also figures strongly in the Taiping Rebellion (1851 – 1864), a massive and deadly rebellion that attempted to set up a Christian theocracy in China; it started far to the south, in Guangdong province, swept through much of South China, and by 1853, had established Nanjing as its capital, renamed as Tianjing (天京 "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was established in 1912, and China was soon torn apart by warlords. Jiangsu changed hands several times, but in April 1927, Chiang Kai-shek established a government at Nanjing; he was soon able to bring most of China under his control. The provincial government moved to Zhenjiang in 1928. This was however interrupted by the second Sino-Japanese War, which began full-scale in 1937; on December 13, 1937, Nanjing fell, and the combined atrocities of the occupying Japanese for the next three months would come to be known as the Rape of Nanjing, after which it became the seat of the collaborationist government of East China under Wang Jingwei, and most of Jiangsu remained under Japanese occupation until the end of the war in 1945.

After the war, Nanjing was once again the capital of the Republic of China, though now the Chinese Civil War had broken out between the Kuomintang government and Communist forces, based further north, mostly in Northeast China. The decisive Huaihai Campaign was fought in northern Jiangsu; it resulted in Kuomintang defeat, and the communists were soon able to cross the Yangtze River and take Nanjing. The Kuomintang fled southward and eventually ended up in Taipei, from which the Republic of China government continues to administer Taiwan, Pescadores, and its neighboring islands, though it also continues to claim (technically, at least) Nanjing as its rightful de jure capital. Later on, after the capture of Zhenjiang, the provincial government was then relocated to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

After the communist takeover, Beijing (formerly Peiping) was made capital of the People's Republic, while Jiangsu was dissolved into Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. On November 15, 1952, Jiangsu Province was reconstituted and Nanjing was demoted to be the provincial capital. The reform and opening up of Deng Xiaoping initially focused on the south coast of China, in Guangdong province, which soon left Jiangsu behind; starting from the 1990s they were applied more evenly to the rest of China. Suzhou and Wuxi, two southern cities of Jiangsu in close proximity to neighboring Shanghai, have since become particularly prosperous, being among the top 10 cities in China in terms of gross domestic product and outstripping the provincial capital of Nanjing. The income disparity between northern and southern Jiangsu however remains large.

Due to its flat terrain, low altitude, and dense population, Jiangsu is one of the most vulnerable regions in China to climate change and its ensuing sea level rise. According to the data collected by the Center of Climate Change in Jiangsu from 1961 to 2007, on average, the province experiences an temperature increase between 0.16 and 0.45 °C per 10 years and total precipitation change between -28.7 and 37.09 mm per 10 years. Extreme weather have become stronger and more common. Jiangsu's agriculture, ecosystem, water resource, transportation, and coastline are all negatively impacted. The speed of sea level rise exceeds the world's average by a large margin.

Specifically, a ranking on climate change risk of global regions released in early 2023 by the Cross Dependency Initiative (XDI) puts Jiangsu as the most vulnerable of the entire world. Jiangsu is at more risk due to its extensive industrial, trade, residential, and commercial development.

In response to climate disturbance across the country, the fourteenth five-year plan, endorsed by the National People's Congress in 2021, indicates the general direction and various steps towards a low-carbon transition. On a provincial level, the Jiangsu government aims to achieve an 18% carbon dioxide decrease per unit GDP and accelerate the development of a green, low-carbon economy, as indicated in the 14th five-year development. The province also plans to recover the damaged coastal regions such as Lianyugang and Yancheng, and improve resilience against rising sea level by implementing seawalls and river floodgates.

Yanbian University (YBU; 延边大学) sits in Yanji, the main city of Yanbian in Jilin Province, in northeast China. Jilin's provincial government supervises this public university, and the Ministry of Education co-funds it. The Double First-Class Construction scheme and Project 211 both include it. What makes the place special is its Korean-Chinese character, and the sections below explain Yanji, the university's standing and the province of Jilin.

At least eleven large Chinese cities have Korean communities, yet the one in Yanji is the biggest of all. Results of the 2000 census had not yet been made public when the source was written, but estimates then put Koreans at somewhere between a third of the city and more than half. Chinese and Korean are both treated as "official languages" here, and every official sign appears in two languages.

yanbian-university.h: Life in a small, young city

blocks.x: With around four hundred thousand residents, Yanji is small by Chinese standards. Shanghai, by comparison, has nearly twenty million. It is also young. Development came only in the 1800s, and the status of regional capital followed after the Second World War. Tourism and overseas investment have grown recently and made Yanji notably prosperous. Steel-and-glass buildings are common, and the wide avenues are conspicuously clean and well kept.

Transport and trade define modern Yanji. North Korea does almost 40% of its international business with China, its largest trading partner, and much of the cross-border enterprise is based in Yanji. Other countries have also started to work with Yanji's business groups, and more than five hundred joint ventures with foreign partners are currently running. South Korea and Taiwan have provided much of the recent investment, which has helped considerably to build up tourism.

Tourism is promoted through an annual event, the North China Travel Fair, held every year from 1996. With over a thousand exhibits from partners within China and overseas, it ranks as one of the biggest fairs of this type in China. Another regular fixture since 2000 is a three-day exposition each year, the Tumen River Area International Investment & Business Forum.

Yanji's role in trade across the borders with North Korea and Russia explains why it was given a national pilot zone for cross-border e-commerce. The zone uses a workforce that speaks both Chinese and Korean, and the city's logistics strengths, to help small and medium-sized Northeast Asian businesses sell online.

Yanbian University was founded in 1949 as a comprehensive university and offers eleven programmes of study, four of them at doctoral level. Full-time teaching staff number over 1,400, and more than sixteen thousand students are enrolled. One graduate, who majored in Korean, is Zhang Dejiang, who served as deputy secretary of the Yanji Municipal Committee from 1983 to 1985 and later became a Vice-Premier in Beijing.

Official titles accumulate around the university. The state counts it as a "double first-class" university under construction, a key "211 Project" university, and a key university for the development of the west. Backing comes from two joint partnerships: the provincial people's government of Jilin with the Ministry of Education, and the same provincial government with the National Ethnic Affairs Commission.

Yanji has other institutions as well. A technical research college, the Yanbian University of Science and Technology, dates from 1990, and the Yanbian Medical College is also in town. For families, the Yanbian International Academy is the local school for foreign children, and the Korean International School in Yanbian is a school for Koreans.

Two television channels made locally are entirely in Korean, and others from North and South Korea can be picked up freely. Korean cooking is very popular and available everywhere. A Korean folk festival in Yanji each September brings together traditional music, dance, painting and sport. Karaoke is a popular pastime, and the city even has a growing underground beatboxing scene, which the filmmaker Liu Feng documented in Yan Bian Box (2007).

Long ago, the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí (勿吉) lived in Jilin, and the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo controlled parts of it. After that the region came under many powers in sequence: the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo and Balhae, followed by the Khitan Liao, the Jurchen Jin and the Mongol Yuan. Under the Qing, a military governor called the General of Jilin (Girin i Jiyanggiyūn) held most of the region, and his domain stretched to what is now Russia's Primorsky Krai.

Russia received the Primorsky Krai area in 1860, and the government then began opening the rest to Han Chinese migrants, most of them from Shandong. Han Chinese were the main ethnic group by the start of the 20th century. Manchukuo, a puppet state created by Japan, took in the area in 1932, and Changchun (then called Xinjing), the capital of Jilin today, became its capital. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the Red Army took Jilin in Operation August Storm. The Soviet Union handed the region and the rest of northeast China to the Communists, and Manchuria was the base from which they conquered the rest of the country in the Chinese Civil War.

The province was smaller in 1949, covering only the area around Changchun and Jilin City, with Jilin City as capital and Changchun a separate municipality. It was expanded to its present borders in the 1950s. During the Cultural Revolution it grew again to include part of Inner Mongolia, which gave it a border with Mongolia, but that was later reversed.

More recently Jilin and the rest of heavy-industry Northeast China have faced economic difficulties as industry was privatised, which led the central government to start a campaign called "Revitalize the Northeast".

Jilin sits in the heart of northeast China. Russia lies to the east and North Korea to the southeast. Some 24 million people live in the province, which measures 190,000 km2 (73,000 sq mi). Its capital is Changchun, 113 km (70 mi) west of Jilin City.

yanbian-university.h: Resources beneath and above the ground

blocks.x: The ground holds 136 kinds of minerals, 70 of which are already being extracted. Large reserves exist of gold and silver, nickel, molybdenum, iron, coal, oil, gas, talc, graphite, gypsum and cement rock, and Jilin's oil shale reserves are the largest in the country. Plants are another asset. Roughly 27,000 wild plant species and 9,000 medicinal herb species are recorded, which is why Jilin is so important for traditional Chinese medicine.

The land is high in the southeast and slopes slowly down to the northwest. Paektu Mountain, at 2,744 m (9,003 ft), is the province's highest peak and belongs to the Changbai Mountains of the southeast. The Jilinhada, Zhang Guangcai and Longgang ranges are also found here.

In the far southeast the Yalu and Tumen rivers drain the land and between them mark part of the frontier with North Korea. The southwest is drained by Liao River tributaries, while in the north the Songhua and Nen rivers carry water that ends up in the Amur.

Jilin has a northern continental monsoon climate. The winters are long and cold and the summers short and warm. January temperatures average from −20 to −14 °C (−4 to 7 °F). Annual rainfall varies between 350 and 1,000 mm (13.8 to 39.4 in). Among the main cities are Changchun, Jilin City, Siping, Liaoyuan, Tonghua, Baishan, Songyuan, Baicheng and Yanji.

Jilin's nominal GDP in 2025 totalled RMB 1,497.4 billion, which is US$209.6 billion, and works out at RMB 64,618 (US$9,046) for each person. Since 2003 growth has been at double-digit rates, adding up to 51 percent between 2003 and 2007. Large enterprises raised their added value by 19 percent and their profit by 30 percent from the 2005 level.

Farmers mostly grow maize, sorghum, wheat and rice, and the east, Yanbian Prefecture included, is the main rice area. Timber comes in quantity from the Changbai Mountains, and herding sheep is a major activity in the west, around Baicheng. Jilin ranks among China's key commodity grain bases and is sixth in timber production. Its resources include the country's largest shale oil reserves and one of its five biggest mineral stocks, with more kieselguhr, wollastonite, floatstone and molybdenum than most provinces. Manufacturing is concentrated on cars, railway carriages and iron alloys.
Pharmaceuticals are a traditional strength. Jilin produces some of the largest harvests of ginseng and deer antler in China, both used a great deal in Chinese medicine.

Jilin City hosts the New and Hi-tech Industry Development Zone, which started in 1992. Of a planned 818 km2 (316 sq mi), 242 km2 (93 sq mi) is developed. It concentrates on new materials, refined chemicals, the combination of photoelectronics and machinery, electronics, medicine and bioengineering. It is 14 km (8.7 mi) from Songhua Lake, with bus and train stations 3 km (1.9 mi) or less away.

May 1998 saw the founding of a second zone, the Jilin Economic and Technological Development Zone, in the northeast of the city. Its planned size is 28 km2 (11 sq mi). Changchun is 90 km (56 mi) distant, the airport 5 km (3.1 mi) and the railway station 8 km (5.0 mi). Chemicals, bioengineering, chemical fibre finishing and farm products are the leading industries, spread over four parks (chemical, food, textile and medical). The medicine park specialises in traditional Chinese pharmaceuticals, small-molecule drugs, biopharmaceuticals and health products.

Changchun's Economic and Technological Development Zone (CETDZ) gained state-level status with state approval in 1993. Its area is 43.52 sq mi (112.72 km2), of which 12 sq mi (30 km2) was designated for use and development. Fixed-asset investment there had reached 38.4 billion yuan at the end of 2006. In the zone were 1656 registered enterprises, including 179 funded from abroad. It generated regional gross product of 101.8 billion yuan, industrial output of 233.0 billion yuan and financial revenue of 15.7 billion yuan.

Changchun also has one of CRRC's largest bullet-train factories. In November 2016 CRRC Changchun revealed the first bullet-train carriages in the world with sleeper berths that could also run in extremely cold conditions. Their nickname is Panda. They travel at 250 kmph and operate at −40 degrees Celsius, and they carry Wi-Fi hubs and sleeping berths that fold into seats in the daytime.

The Changchun High-Tech Industrial Development Area connects to downtown by four roads and a light-rail line, so Changchun Station is only twenty minutes away by rail. In 2002 it was the first area in the northeast to meet the ISO14001 environmental standard, and green landscaping covers 38% of it.

National-level approval for the Hunchun Border Economic Cooperation Zone came in 1992, and it was planned to cover 24 km2 (9.3 sq mi). It lies at the meeting point of the Chinese, Russian and Korean borders, and its key sectors include seafood processing, electronic products, bio-pharmaceuticals and textiles. Within it were created the Hunchun Sino-Russia Trade Zone in 2001 and the Hunchun Export Processing Zone in 2002. Inside the larger zone, the processing zone sits in a 5 km2 (1.93 sq mi) area. Its planned size is 2.44 km2 (0.94 sq mi), and it relies on the same infrastructure and policies as the larger zone.

Residents belong to several groups: Han Chinese and Manchu, Hui, Mongol and Xibe. The Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture is home to most of the Korean population, who make up about 4% of the province because the Korean Peninsula is so close. Manchus formerly made up the majority, as this is part of their historical region, but since the Manchu people took up Han culture and Chinese languages their own language has become critically endangered.
Mandarin, the national official language, is spoken by most people. In the east, many speak Korean, and some residents of Qian Gorlos autonomous county use Mongolian.

The culture of the province is close to that of other parts of the Northeast, including art forms such as Errenzhuan and Yangge. Jiju, also called Jilin Opera, is a traditional form of entertainment that Jilin developed over its relatively short migrant history. The ethnic Koreans keep a separate culture that remains closely linked to Korea.

Goguryeo sites and tombs at Ji'an, such as Gungnae City, Hwando Mountain City and the pyramid-shaped Tomb of the General, form part of a World Heritage Site whose listed name refers to ancient Koguryo capital cities and tombs. Paektu Mountain, above all its Heaven Lake on the North Korean border, is a popular scenic destination. Longtou Mountain in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture is the site of royal tombs of the Balhae, among them the Mausoleum of Princess Jeonghyo.

Yanbian is only one of many higher education institutions in Jilin. The leading names are Jilin University (吉林大学) and Northeast Normal University (东北师范大学). Medical and agricultural education are covered by Jilin Medical College (吉林医药学院), Jilin Agricultural University (吉林农业大学) and Jilin Agricultural Science and Technology University. Teaching-oriented and technical colleges include Beihua University, the Jilin College of Electrification, Changchun University (长春大学), Changchun Normal University (长春师范大学) and Jilin Normal University (吉林师范大学). In engineering and science, the options are the Changchun Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, Changchun Institute of Technology (长春工程学院), Changchun University of Technology (长春工业大学), and the university of science and technology in the same city (长春理工大学). Specialist schools include the Changchun Taxation College (长春税务学院), the Changchun Institute of Post & Telecommunications (长春邮政学院) and the Northeast China Institute of Electric Power Engineering (东北电力学院). Besides Yanbian University (延边大学), Yanji also has Yanbian University of Science and Technology (延边科技大学).
Basketball's Chinese Basketball Association includes the Jilin Northeast Tigers. In football the Chinese Super League side is Changchun Yatai, and Yanbian Longding competes in China League One.

Yangtze University (长江大学) is a public university in Jingzhou, in China's Hubei Province. It belongs to the provincial system, and the Hubei Provincial People's Government is its main sponsor.

The university came into being in 2003 through the merger of four institutions: the Jingzhou Teachers College (荆州师范学院), the Jianghan Petroleum Institute (江汉石油学院), the Hubei Provincial Healthcare Workers Medical College (湖北省卫生职工医学院) and the Hubei Agricultural College (湖北农学院). That mix explains why the university covers petroleum, farming, teacher education and medicine side by side.

Within Hubei's higher-education sector, Yangtze University is the biggest comprehensive university offering the full range of disciplines. It is counted as a Key University of Hubei Province, as one of the universities picked for the National Education Power Project, and as one of the province's Domestic First-class Construction Universities. Building it is a joint effort: the Hubei Provincial People's Government is joined by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs and by three oil majors, China National Offshore Oil Corporation, China Petroleum & Chemical Corporation and China National Petroleum Corporation.

yangtze-university.h: Where it is and what it is known for

blocks.x: The university is based mainly in Jingzhou, a historic cultural city along the Yangtze River's middle reaches, with a second site in the form of the Wuhan Campus. Its record of operation reaches back to 1936. It has distinctive strengths in petroleum science and technology, flood disasters and wetland agriculture, and the study of Jing Chu culture.

Academically, five disciplines have reached the global top 1% in ESI: agricultural science, earth science, clinical medicine, engineering, and botany and zoology, and in the number of disciplines selected the university stands at the top among provincial universities.

The faculty totals 3,107, of whom 2,361 work full-time. Those full-time teachers include 338 professors and 867 associate professors. A total of 2,143 hold master's or doctoral degrees, and 1,057 of them have PhDs. In all, 293 teachers have been chosen for talent projects and have received expert titles at provincial and ministerial level, and 51 of these carry national talent titles. Supervision capacity is 151 doctoral supervisors and 1,217 master's supervisors on the regular staff, plus 64 part-time doctoral and 868 part-time master's supervisors.

Yangtze University may recruit students at every level from undergraduate to PhD. It operates 3 post-doctoral research stations, may award the PhD in 3 first-level programmes, academic master's degrees in 37 first-level disciplines and professional master's degrees in 22 programmes. There are 110 undergraduate programmes, of which 25 are national first-class and 24 provincial first-class, spread over 11 main disciplines (science, engineering, agriculture and medicine, plus economics, management, law, education, literature, history and art).

Current enrolment is 33,405 full-time undergraduates and 7,132 full-time master's and doctoral students, along with over 500 international students. Across its history the university has produced more than 500,000 trained professionals in all fields.

The university says it follows an open-education policy. It cooperates with 55 leading petroleum and petrochemical companies as well as 160 governments and local enterprises at county level and above, and for this it has been named a National Demonstration Institution for industry-university-research cooperation education and as an innovation base for petroleum postgraduates in Hubei Province. It launched an alliance for training internationalised language-service talent along the Belt and Road, set up with enterprises, and it takes part in 12 university alliances, one of them the association linking universities of China and Central and Eastern Europe.

More than 100 institutions in countries such as the US, UK, Ireland, South Korea, Japan, Russia, Australia, Sri Lanka and the Czech Republic work with the university, with regular exchanges of students and scholars and joint research. Examples:
A civil engineering undergraduate education project, run with Ireland's Shannon University of Technology.
A Toxicology Joint Laboratory with a university in Hradec Kralove in the Czech Republic (the source text spells the name "Heradz Klalove").
A centre for garden plant resources and germplasm innovation, set up with Seoul University (South Korea) and the University of Calgary (Canada).
A plant stress biology research center created with Australia's University of Tasmania.
It has also been selected as an implementing unit of the CSC's international cooperation and training programme for innovative talents.

yangtze-university.h: What this means for international applicants

blocks.x: The Ministry of Education has authorised it to take high school graduates from Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau. It can enrol recipients of the Chinese government scholarship for international students (CSC) and runs a test centre for the HSK, the New Chinese Proficiency Test. Its international students come from 69 countries on 6 continents (examples: Pakistan, Nepal, Ghana, Papua New Guinea, Morocco, Indonesia, Colombia, Brazil, Russia, Canada, France and the United States), and 51 of those countries are along the Belt and Road. Because some details in the university's English descriptions are not consistent, confirm admission and scholarship rules on its official website before you apply.

Daily life for a student depends on the city around the campus, so the next sections describe Jingzhou. Most of the figures below date from the 2010 census, the later 7th census and the year 2019, so read them as background and look up newer releases if you need current numbers.

The 2010 census gave the prefecture-level city of Jingzhou 5,691,707 inhabitants, a density of 405 per km2. The municipal government's 7th census found a slightly smaller population: an estimated 5,231,180 people living in roughly 1,833,292 households. Of these residents, 2,664,658 (50.94 percent) were male and 2,566,522 (49.06 percent) female, a sex ratio of 103.82 males per 100 females. People with a university education numbered 534,914. Since 2010 that group has grown from 6,828 to 10,225 per 100,000 people, the average length of schooling for those aged 15 or over has gone up from 8.81 to 9.29 years, and illiteracy has fallen from 4.41 percent (251,100 people) to 2.79 percent (145,900). In the Shashi and Jingzhou districts, average schooling for people aged 15 and over is longer than 10 years.

In 2019 Jingzhou's GDP was ¥251.648 billion, up 7.5% on the year. The primary sector produced 17.3% of it, the secondary sector 37.1% and the tertiary sector 45.6%. Most growth in 2019 came from the secondary and tertiary sectors, which rose 8.1% and 8.8%. Disposable income per resident was ¥26,543, up 9.8%. City dwellers averaged ¥35,910 (up 10.2%) and rural residents ¥18,893 (up 9.2%).
#### Farming

In 2019 the combined value of Jingzhou's farming, forestry, animal husbandry and fishing came to ¥76.645 billion. Output included 4.5117 million tons of grain, 3.1332 million tons of vegetables, 433 thousand tons of vegetable oil and 38,000 tons of cotton. In the same year 2.9777 million pigs and 63.9012 million poultry were slaughtered, and aquaculture yielded 1.1195 million tons, of which 45.77% (512.4 thousand tons) was shrimp and crabs.
#### Industry and construction

In 2019 light industry output fell 2.3% while heavy industry output rose 17.0%. By ownership, the state-owned economy shrank 3.4%, the collectively owned economy grew 2.4% and the privately owned economy grew 7.2%. Construction is one of Jingzhou's most prominent industries, earning ¥29.877 billion in 2019, and the city has 385 construction firms.
#### Retail, insurance and foreign trade

Consumer retail sales reached ¥144.735 billion in 2019, a yearly growth of 11.5%. Insurance premium revenue came to ¥16.293 billion, up 15.0%, made up of ¥12.213 billion in personal insurance and ¥4.08 billion in property insurance, up 12.7% and 22.3% on 2018. Insurers paid out 5.171 billion in compensation, 1.8% more than the year before. Foreign trade totalled 1.697 billion USD, 6.8% lower than in 2018, with imports at 0.335 billion USD and exports at 1.363 billion USD.

Many remains survive from the age of the Chu State: five ruined Chu cities, 73 Chu Culture sites and over 800 ancient tombs, 18 of them royal tombs of Chu kings. There are Three Kingdoms sites too, notably the Huarong Path and the Wulin Battlefield, the setting of the Battle of Red Cliffs.

Jingzhou's city walls date from a rebuilding in 1646, rise 30 ft (9 metres) and are 33 ft (10 metres) thick, and run for 6.32 mi (10.17 kilometres) around the city. Gates, watchtowers and battlements alike have been kept in good repair. Most of the towers that stood on top of the imposing gates were damaged or rebuilt; only the Chaozong Tower, rebuilt in 1838 on the Gongji Gate, is left.

At the Jingzhou Museum you can see a well-preserved male corpse about 2,000 years old and Warring States period silk and lacquerware. In 2016 a bronze Statue of Guan Yu, 58 meters tall and weighing 1,197 tons and designed by Han Meilin, was built in Jingzhou; it was dismantled in 2021 and is awaiting relocation to Dianjiangtai.
Jingzhou has distinctive breakfast foods, including its own style of guokui, a Chinese flatbread, and its own style of rice noodles.

Jingzhou had 1,243 schools in 2019, attended by about 707,300 students. By type, that is 587 kindergartens (140,300 children), 396 primary schools (308,500), 123 general junior high schools (146,000), 53 general secondary schools (82,800), 15 secondary vocational schools (28,600) and 8 special education schools (1,151). About 53,400 faculty staff the system. Beyond schools, Jingzhou has 8 public libraries holding 1.382 million books and 176 cultural institutions employing 1,168 people.
Jingzhou Railway Station, on the Wuhan-Yichang Railway, offers regular passenger services in both directions, to Wuhan and to Yichang. Other links:
Jingmen-Shashi Railway (freight only)
Jingzhou Shashi Airport, in Shashi district
G50 Shanghai-Chongqing Expressway
G55 Erenhot-Guangzhou Expressway
China National Highway 207
China National Highway 318
A university's province shapes student life nearly as much as the campus, so these sections turn to Hubei and its past.

Sophisticated Neolithic cultures flourished in Hubei. In the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BC) the area belonged to the strong State of Chu. Nominally a tributary of the Zhou dynasty, Chu emerged from the Chinese civilisation that had appeared in the north some centuries earlier, but it mixed northern and southern culture in a way of its own. It grew into a powerful state that dominated much of the Yangtze's middle and lower stretches, reaching north onto the North China Plain.

During the Warring States period (475-221 BC), Qin, an upstart state in the north-west (in what is now Guanzhong, Shaanxi), began expanding outward and Chu emerged as its chief opponent. In the wars between them, Chu kept losing ground: first its hold on the Sichuan Basin, then, in 278 BC, its core territory, roughly modern Hubei. Qin hunted down the last of the Chu regime in 223 BC, after it had fled east while Qin was uniting China.

Qin founded the first unified dynasty in China in 221 BC. The Han dynasty followed in 206 BC and created the province (zhou) of Jingzhou across today's Hubei and Hunan. Under both dynasties, farmland in Hubei was extended and a system of river dikes protected fields from summer floods.

Towards the close of the Eastern Han dynasty, early in the 3rd century, Jingzhou belonged to the regional warlord Liu Biao. When he died in 208 his successors surrendered his realm to Cao Cao, the powerful warlord who had taken nearly all of north China. In the Battle of Red Cliffs (208 or 209), however, the warlords Sun Quan and Liu Bei forced Cao Cao out of Jingzhou. Liu Bei took the province and put Guan Yu in charge of Xiangyang (modern Xiangyang, Hubei) to protect it. After conquering Yizhou (the Sichuan Basin), though, he lost Jingzhou to Sun Quan, and for several decades it was part of the Wu Kingdom of Sun Quan and his successors.

Nomadic peoples from the north pushed into the region at the start of the 4th century (the Five Barbarians' rebellion and the Disaster of Yongjia), beginning nearly three centuries in which a nomad-ruled but increasingly Sinicized north faced a south ruled by Han Chinese. Hubei stayed under southern rule throughout, until the Sui dynasty unified China in 589. The Tang dynasty took over from the Sui in 617 and later split today's Hubei among three circuits, with Huainan Circuit in the east, Shannandong Circuit in the west and Jiangnanxi Circuit in the south. After the Tang fell apart in the early 10th century, regional regimes took over the area: Jingnan held the centre, Yang Wu and then its successor Southern Tang the east, the Five Dynasties the north, and Shu reached Shizhou (施州), which lies in modern Enshi and its Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture.

In 982 the Song dynasty brought the region back together and placed most of Hubei under Jinghu North Circuit, a fuller version of the present name. Mongol conquest came in 1279, and the Mongols formed the province of Huguang, covering parts of Guangdong and Guangxi as well as Hubei and Hunan.

The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) expelled the Mongols in 1368. Its Huguang province was smaller, almost exactly equal to modern Hubei plus Hunan. Hubei was geographically outside the centres of Ming power, and in the final years of the dynasty rebel armies under Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng ravaged it several times. The Manchu Qing dynasty took much of the region in 1644 and soon divided Huguang into Hubei and Hunan, though it kept a Viceroy of Huguang in post. Among the best-known viceroys was Zhang Zhidong (in office 1889-1907), whose modernising reforms turned Hubei, and Wuhan especially, into a prosperous commercial and industrial centre. South-east of Wuhan, the Huangshi/Daye area developed into a major centre of mining and metallurgy.

yangtze-university.h: Revolution, war and the Cultural Revolution

blocks.x: In 1911 the Wuchang Uprising took place in what is now Wuhan; it began the Xinhai Revolution, which brought down the Qing dynasty and established the Republic of China. Wuhan was the seat of a left-wing Kuomintang government under Wang Jingwei in 1927, which was later absorbed by Chiang Kai-shek's government in Nanjing. In World War II Japan conquered and occupied the eastern parts of Hubei, while the west stayed under Chinese control.

Rival Red Guard factions fought each other in Wuhan during the 1960s Cultural Revolution. The worst episode was in July 1967: the Wuhan Incident, or "July 20th Incident", when two hostile groups waged an armed struggle over control of the city at the peak of the upheaval. Later in the decade, the Sino-Soviet border conflicts raised fears of nuclear war, and Xianning prefecture in Hubei was chosen to host Project 131, an underground military command centre.

The 1954 Yangtze River Floods hit the province, and Wuhan above all, severely. Big dam projects followed. The Gezhouba Dam on the Yangtze near Yichang was started in 1970 and finished in 1988, and the Three Gorges Dam, upstream, was started in 1993. Over the next years millions of people in western Hubei were resettled by the authorities to clear space for the dam. Smaller dams have also been built on the Yangtze's tributaries.

Planned for Dafanzhen in Tongshan County, Xianning, the Xianning Nuclear Power Plant would house a minimum of four AP1000 pressurized-water reactors, each of 1,250 megawatts (MW). Site work began in 2010, and the plan was for construction of the first reactor to start in 2011 and for it to go online in 2015. As of 2018, however, building of the first phase had still not started.

The first COVID-19 case of the pandemic was identified in the city of Wuhan on 1 December 2019. The SARS-CoV-2 virus was formally identified in January 2020, after which local and national authorities created large quarantine zones across Hubei, above all in Wuhan, the epicentre. Fifteen cities were partly or fully locked down, directly affecting 57 million people. After serious outbreaks in many other countries, the World Health Organization declared a pandemic in March 2020. In Hubei, the lockdown on most cities was lifted after more than eight weeks.

Han Chinese are the main ethnic group in Hubei, and a sizeable Miao and Tujia population lives in the south-west, particularly in the Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture. Chinese officials started relocating 330,000 residents of Hubei and Henan provinces on 18 October 2009, people whose homes would be affected by the Danjiangkou Reservoir on the Han river, part of the larger South-North Water Transfer Project.

In Hubei the leading faiths are Chinese folk religion, Taoist traditions and Chinese Buddhism. Surveys from 2007 and 2009 found that 6.5% of the population believes in and takes part in ancestor cults, while 0.58% identify as Christian, down from 0.83% in 2004. These reports gave no figures for other kinds of religion, so the other 92.92% could be non-religious or take part in worship of nature deities, Confucianism, Buddhism, Taoism or folk sects.
Yangtze University lists 458 programs for international students on this site: 152 bachelor, 274 master's, 32 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 229 taught in Chinese, 229 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.

Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

yangtze-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Yangtze University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Jingzhou, register at Yangtze University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Yangzhou University (YZU in short) goes by 扬州大学 in simplified characters, 揚州大學 in traditional ones and Yángzhōu Dàxué in pinyin. It is a state-run institution in the city of Yangzhou, Jiangsu Province. It teaches both undergraduates and graduate students. Unlike universities founded as a single college, it was assembled in 1992 by combining six local colleges.
The merger was agreed by the Jiangsu provincial government in 1988 and carried out in 1992. The colleges brought together were:
Jiangsu Agriculture College (江苏农学院)
Yangzhou Teachers' College (扬州师范学院)
Yangzhou Institute of Technology (扬州工学院)
Yangzhou Medical College (扬州医学院)
Jiangsu Water Conservancy College (江苏水利工程专科学校)
Jiangsu Commerce College (江苏商业专科学校)
That mixture explains why the university is broad. Farming, teacher training, engineering, medicine, water works and commerce all feed into one campus system.

In September 2015 the Jiangsu provincial government and the national Ministry of Education jointly issued a document called the Opinions on the Co-construction of Yangzhou University. Under it the university became a "provincial and ministerial co-construction" institution, meaning that both levels of government share responsibility for developing it.

Undergraduates can choose among 92 programmes across 11 disciplines, taught in 26 schools. The source does not list the schools by name, so look at the university's English website for the current list.

yangzhou-university.h: Yangzhou, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Daily life for students depends on the city, so the next parts explain Yangzhou's land and water, its weather, how to travel in and out, and what makes it culturally special.

Yangzhou stands on a plain just north of the Yangtze River. The Grand Canal, also called the Jing-Hang Canal, passes through the prefecture from north to south. Its modern channel skirts the eastern side of the main urban area, while the old route goes through the city centre. Other notable waters in the prefecture-level city are the Baoshe, Datong and Beichengzi rivers, the Tongyang and Xintongyang canals, and Baima, Baoying, Gaoyou and Shaobo lakes.

The urban core itself is laced with canals and small lakes. The historic centre, the former walled city, is ringed by waterways: the Old Grand Canal is its eastern and southern boundary, on the north side the City Moat Canal connects the Old Grand Canal with Slender West Lake, and on the west the Erdaohe Canal descends from that lake to the Lotus Flower Pond (Hehuachi). From the pond, a short channel called the Erdaogou returns to the Old Grand Canal. The result is a loop: in principle a small craft can leave the lake, pass along the Erdaohe, cross the pond and rejoin the old canal.

The climate is subtropical monsoon with changeable, humid winds. The year splits into about four months of winter and four months of summer, with spring and autumn each lasting about two months. There are roughly 240 frost-free days and about 1,912 hours of sunshine in an average year.

Temperatures average 16.2 °C (61.2 °F) over the year. Daytime highs average 20.7 °C (69.3 °F) and night-time lows 12.4 °C (54.3 °F). January is the coolest month, with a mean of 2.8 °C (37.0 °F), and July the warmest, at 28.4 °C (83.1 °F).

Yearly precipitation is 1,099.9 mm (43.30 in), and summer brings 59.1% of it. People call the stretch from mid-June to mid-July the "plum rain season", since that is when plums ripen. Over the years from 1951, the coldest day was 6 January 1955 at -17.7 °C (0 °F), and the hottest was 14 August 2022, when 40.6 °C (105 °F) was reached in that summer's national heatwave.
For a student: bring warm clothes for a cold, damp winter and light, breathable ones for humid summers, and expect a wet spell around late June.

Only one bridge complex takes traffic over the Yangtze at Yangzhou: Runyang. Its suspension span ranks among the longest in the world, and it carries the G4011 Yangzhou-Liyang Expressway on the way to Zhenjiang.

Yangzhou Taizhou International Airport opened in 2012 for Yangzhou and neighbouring Taizhou and is in Jiangdu district. Before then, travellers flew from Nanjing Lukou International Airport, over 100 km (62 mi) distant and a trip of one hour 40 minutes from downtown Yangzhou. The city has more than 10 airline ticket offices, and flights are available domestically and internationally, with more than 20 domestic and 10 international airlines mentioned.

Passenger trains did not serve Yangzhou before 2004. Construction of Yangzhou Railway Station started in 2003 and finished a year later. It stands on the western outskirts, on the Nanjing-Qidong railway, and offers direct service to the provincial capital and to major cities in other directions, including Xi'an, Wuhan and Guangzhou. An overnight Z-series express goes to Beijing. High-speed D-series trains were later added on the same line.

A second station, Yangzhou East railway station, entered service on 11 December 2020 when the Lianyungang-Zhenjiang high-speed railway opened fully. That line, designed for 250 km/h (160 mph), links southern and northern Jiangsu. A further high-speed line, Shanghai-Nanjing-Hefei, designed for 350 km/h, is being built and should pass through Yangzhou East.

About 11.5 km (7.1 mi) south of downtown, Yangzhou harbour sits where the Beijing-Hangzhou Canal flows into the Yangtze. Average water depth is 15 to 20 metres. The State Council approved it as a first-grade open state harbour in 1992, and General Secretary Jiang Zemin wrote its name in calligraphy. It has become a comprehensive inland port handling passengers, freight, containers and port trade, and serves as the main distribution centre for northern Jiangsu, eastern Anhui and southeast Shandong. Dozens of cargo types move through it, from steel and timber to grain, cotton, coal, minerals, machinery and light-industry goods, as well as containers. Passenger services run upstream to Nanjing, Wuhu, Jiujiang, Huangshi and Wuhan, and downstream to Nantong and Shanghai. A few well-known luxury international liners also moor there. The harbour has boosted exports and the local economy.

The G2 Beijing-Shanghai Expressway runs through Yangzhou. A widening project from March 2020 to June 2023 took the Yangzhou stretch from four lanes to eight, giving more capacity and better links between northern and central Jiangsu and the Shanghai and Zhejiang area.

Coaches link Yangzhou with nearby cities frequently in the daytime. Several bus stations are on the outskirts. Most buses from Nanjing (departing from Nanjing West Bus Station) and Zhenjiang (from the station next to Zhenjiang Railway Station) arrive at Yangzhou South Bus Station, a few kilometres southwest of the downtown. Intercity service mostly ends in the early evening, so plan late arrivals carefully.

Yangzhou has a large network of public bus routes. Taxis began operating in 1982 and grew fast after 1993. There are over 40 companies with 1,571 vehicles in total. Taxi stands were set up at key stations and hotels, eight firms offer round-the-clock phone booking, and the municipal construction department has strengthened management through training on law, professional ethics and safety.

Urban rail was proposed in a 2014 city plan with two lines. The first was to cross the city east to west, beginning at Yangzhou Railway Station, going via the old centre and today's Yangzhou East station, and ending in Jiangdu District; the second was to go north to south. Another project is already being built: the intercity railway linking Nanjing, Yizheng and Yangzhou, also known as Nanjing Metro Line S5. As of June 2026 its first elevated section in Nanjing was finished and two stations had been topped out.

For tourists, the Tianma travel agency, which belongs to the Yangzhou Tourist Bureau, runs sightseeing buses with a guide on each. Starting from the railway station, it makes eight stops near sights including Daming Temple, Slender West Lake, the Imperial Dock, Siwang Pagoda, Wenchang Pagoda and Shita Temple. The public transit company also runs three special tourist lines, numbers 1, 2 and 5. Number 1 leaves the bus station and serves Slender West Lake, Shigong Temple, Ge Garden and He Garden, whereas number 5 begins at the same place and reaches Crane Temple, Wenchang Pagoda, the lake, Five-Pavilion Bridge and Pingshan Hall. On the water, a scenic route around Slender West Lake joins the Imperial Dock, Yichun Garden, Hong Garden, Dahong Bridge, Xiaojinshan, Diaoyutai, Five-Pavilion Bridge and the 24 Bridge, finishing at Daming Temple and Pingshan Hall.

The Yangzhou dialect (扬州话) represents Lower Yangtze Mandarin and is close to the court language of the Ming and Qing, which rested on the Nanjing dialect. Even so, it differs noticeably from modern Standard Chinese, and the two are only moderately mutually intelligible. Dialect has also worked as a marker of regional identity and politics on both sides of the Yangtze. When Yangzhou was a rich trading centre it counted as part of Jiangnan, famed for wealth, despite lying north of the river. When the wealth faded, it came to be seen as part of Jiangbei, the "backwater".

In its heyday, with prosperity and imperial favour, storytelling and painting thrived. The inventive painter and calligrapher Shitao spent the 1680s in Yangzhou and returned in 1697, staying until his death in 1707, and a later circle of artists, the Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou, is celebrated across China.

Yangzhou storytelling (扬州评话) is an old folk art, comparable to Xiangsheng, the comic performance tradition. It emerged as a stage art in the Ming dynasty. Performers narrate a historical story in the local dialect, using texts that artists have edited. The best-known performer was Wang Shaotang, whose best-loved cycles centre on four heroes, each in ten chapters: Wu Song (武十回), Song Jiang (宋十回), Lu Junyi (卢十回) and Shi Xiu (石十回).
Yangzhou is the hometown of Jiang Zemin, former Communist Party General Secretary and President of China, who grew up here; his middle school faces the public notary's office.

The city is known for carved lacquerware and jade, and also for public bath houses, jadeware, embroidery and paper-cut arts. It has a well-known toy industry too, particularly stuffed animals, and visitors from nearby cities come for good-quality, inexpensive toys. In 2006 the city received the Habitat Scroll of Honour.

Yangzhou's own school of cooking, called Huaiyang (淮扬菜) and also known as the Weiyang school, produces some of China's most creative dishes. Along with Sichuan, Cantonese and Shandong cooking, it counts as a distinctive style of its own.

The city turns up repeatedly in Chinese writing. Li Bai, the Tang poet (c. 700 to 762), composed a farewell piece titled "Seeing Meng Haoran off to Yangzhou from Yellow Crane Pavilion". In it, the speaker's old friend says goodbye at the pavilion in the west and sets off down the river for Yangzhou amid the mist and flowers of spring. The lonely sail and its shadow fade into the blue emptiness, until only the Yangtze is visible, flowing toward the far horizon.

Du Mu wrote famous lines too. He says that after ten years he has woken from a "Yangzhou dream", his only gain being a fickle name in the "green mansions". Those "green mansions" or "green lofts" (qinglou) were the pleasure quarters that Yangzhou became known for.
Lin Daiyu, a central character of the Qing novel Dream of the Red Chamber, is a native of Yangzhou.

The best-known attractions are Slender West Lake and the old residences inside the moated town, for instance the Wang Residence and Daming Temple. Many well-kept gardens in the local style add to the appeal, and Guangling District holds most of the old town. By June 2024 the city's heritage listing comprised 454 city- and county-level buildings, 50 at provincial level and 24 at national level.

This long, narrow lake winds through the western edge of the city and takes its name from Hangzhou's famous West Lake. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Nearby is Geyuan Garden (个园), noted for bamboo and rockeries that represent the four seasons. A bank planted with weeping willows crosses the lake, and halfway along it you reach the Five-Pavilion Bridge, which carries five covered terraces, one on each corner and one in the middle.

Within the lakeside park you will find Xu Garden, Small Gold Mountain (Xiao Jinshan), and the White Dagoba of Lianxing Temple, a copy of the one at Beijing's Beihai Park. There is also the Fishing Platform (Diaoyutai), where the Qing emperor Qian Long liked to relax. A local story says he was so delighted with his luck at fishing here that he ordered extra stipends for the town. In fact, the source adds, local swimmers had been lurking in the water and fastening fish to his hook.

On Shugang Hill in the northwest, the temple now called Fajing Temple was formerly known as Daming Temple. The first temple was built in the Liu Song dynasty (420 to 479), and a nine-storey pagoda, the Qilingta, was added in the Sui dynasty (589 to 618). A recent addition is the Jianzhen Memorial Hall, built by Tang-dynasty methods and paid for with donations from Buddhist groups in Japan.

During Qian Long's 1765 visit he disliked the name Daming, which literally means "Great Ming", worried it could stir longing for the Ming dynasty, which his Manchu forebears had brought down. He had it renamed Fajing Temple. The temple was badly damaged in the Taiping Rebellion (the source dates this to the early 20th century, which does not fit the rebellion's usual dates, so treat the timing with caution), and what stands now was rebuilt in the 1930s.

The writer Ouyang Xiu built this hall when he was prefect of Yangzhou in the Song dynasty, just west of Fajing Temple. Seen from here, the mountains beyond the Yangtze to the south form a level line at the height of your eyes, which gave rise to the name Flat Hills Hall. His student Su Dongpo also served as prefect when he moved to Yangzhou, and he built a hall directly behind his teacher's, called Guling Hall.
A university's region influences daily life nearly as much as the campus itself. This brief history of Jiangsu helps explain why Yangzhou has such a rich culture.

yangzhou-university.h: From the earliest dynasties to the Song

blocks.x: In the earliest Chinese dynasties, the Jiangsu area lay far from the centre of Chinese civilisation in northwestern Henan, and was home to the Huai Yi (淮夷), an ancient ethnic group. Contact grew in the Zhou dynasty, and the southern part of today's Jiangsu saw the rise of the state of Wu. It grew powerful under King Helu towards the end of the Spring and Autumn period, and in 484 BC it defeated Qi, a major northern power in modern Shandong, and challenged for overlordship of all the states. Yue, from modern Zhejiang to the south, subjugated Wu in 473 BC, and Chu, from the west, conquered Yue in 333 BC. Qin swept all rivals away and unified China in 221 BC.

Han rule (206 BC to 220 AD) divided Jiangsu between two provinces, Xu to the north and Yang to the south. The Three Kingdoms period made southern Jiangsu the heartland of Eastern Wu (222 to 280); its capital Jianye, later Jiankang, is present-day Nanjing. Nomadic invasions of northern China in the 4th century pushed the Jin court south to Jiankang, and migrants poured into southern and central Jiangsu, swelling its cities. Four Southern dynasties in turn ruled from Jiankang, which grew into the largest commercial and cultural hub in China.

After the Sui united the country in 581, power shifted back north, yet the Grand Canal was dug across Jiangsu, tying the rich Yangtze Delta to the Central Plains. The Tang (618 to 907) relied on southern Jiangsu for yearly grain deliveries. Under the Song (960 to 1279), which saw a wealthy merchant class and an emerging market economy, Jiangnan (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai and neighbouring areas) became a trading centre. From then on, cities such as Suzhou and Yangzhou stood for opulence and luxury in China, and the region is still among the richest parts of the country.

The Jurchen Jin dynasty took control of North China in 1127 in the Jin-Song wars. The Huai River, which then cut through northern Jiangsu to the Yellow Sea, marked the border between the Jin in the north and the Southern Song in the south. Mongol rule over China followed in the 13th century. The Ming, founded in 1368 after the Mongols were expelled, first made Nanjing its capital. The regions around it, corresponding to Jiangsu and Anhui today, became Nanzhili province ("southern directly governed"). After Zhu Di (later the Yongle Emperor) seized power in a coup, the capital moved far to the north, to Beijing, though Nanjing remained the southern capital. In the late Ming, Jiangnan continued as a trade hub, and some historians see an early form of industrialisation and capitalism in its flourishing textile industry, a trend that was cut short.
The Qing turned Nanzhili into "Jiangnan province", and in 1666 Jiangsu and Anhui were separated as provinces. Jiangsu's borders have stayed largely stable since.

Western incursion from the 1840s exposed the prosperous, mercantile Yangtze Delta to foreign influence. Shanghai began as an unremarkable small Jiangsu town, but it soon became a cosmopolitan metropolis of trade and banking and was later separated off as a municipality of its own. Jiangnan also featured strongly in the Taiping Rebellion (1851 to 1864), a vast and deadly uprising that sought to found a Christian theocracy. Starting in far-off Guangdong, it moved through much of South China, and in 1853 its leaders seized Nanjing and renamed it Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital").

The Republic of China was founded in 1912, and warlords soon tore the country apart. Jiangsu changed hands several times. In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek set up a government at Nanjing and brought most of China under his control, and in 1928 the provincial government moved to Zhenjiang. The second Sino-Japanese War, which began on a full scale in 1937, interrupted this. Nanjing fell on 13 December 1937, and the occupation's atrocities over the next three months became known as the Rape of Nanjing. The city then became the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government of East China, and most of Jiangsu stayed under Japanese occupation until 1945.

After the war, Nanjing was again the capital, but the Chinese Civil War had begun between the Kuomintang government and the Communists, based mostly in the northeast. Northern Jiangsu was the battleground of the decisive Huaihai Campaign, which the Kuomintang lost. The Communists crossed the Yangtze and took Nanjing. The Kuomintang fled south and ended up in Taipei, from where the Republic of China government still administers Taiwan, the Pescadores and nearby islands, while still technically claiming Nanjing as its rightful capital. After Zhenjiang fell, the provincial government relocated to Shengsi County in Zhejiang.

Once the Communists took over, Beijing (formerly Peiping) became capital of the People's Republic, and Jiangsu was split into the Subei and Sunan Administrative Regions. On 15 November 1952 Jiangsu Province was re-established and Nanjing became the provincial capital. Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening-up first concentrated on Guangdong on the south coast, which left Jiangsu behind, but from the 1990s such policies spread more evenly. Suzhou and Wuxi, two southern Jiangsu cities close to Shanghai, are now among the ten richest cities in China by GDP and have overtaken the provincial capital Nanjing. The income gap between northern and southern Jiangsu is still large.

Yangzhou University offers a broad range of subjects and a convenient base in a historic canal city with good rail links to Nanjing and beyond. Check the list of schools and the current programme details on the official website before applying.

If you are planning a journey to Yangzhou, the options fit together like this. Fly into Yangzhou Taizhou International Airport, which opened in 2012, or into Nanjing Lukou, about an hour and 40 minutes away. Take the train to Yangzhou Railway Station on the western outskirts or to Yangzhou East, which opened on 11 December 2020. Come by coach to Yangzhou South Bus Station, but note that intercity coaches mostly stop running in the early evening. Once in town, rely on buses and taxis, since urban rail was still only at the planning stage.

Yangzhou's character comes from its position on the Grand Canal. Grain and goods moved along the waterway for centuries, merchants grew rich, and artists, storytellers and cooks followed the money. That is why a modern visitor finds gardens, poetry associations, a distinct dialect and a famous cuisine in a city that is otherwise quite compact.

Yanshan University (燕山大学) is a provincial public university in Qinhuangdao, Hebei, China. It is affiliated with the Province of Hebei.
In 2023, it has a student population of 40,000 and a staff population of 3,200 (2,058 are teachers, including 568 professors and 678 associate professors).

The origin of Yanshan University can be traced back to the Harbin Institute of Technology (Harbin Sino-Russian Industrial School), founded in 1920. In 1958, the Department of Heavy Machinery of Harbin Institute of Technology and its related specialties moved to the strategic industrial town of Fulaerji, Qiqihar in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province and was renamed the School of Heavy Machinery of the Harbin Institute of Technology.

The School of Heavy Machinery of the Harbin Institute of Technology gained independence in 1960 and was renamed as the Northeast Heavy Machinery Institute. Later, in 1961, it merged with the Shenyang College of Heavy Machinery and the Lanzhou Petroleum Industry Institute. In 1978, it was recognized as one of the 88 key national institutions for higher education. From 1984 onwards, some of the departments and staff of the Northeast Heavy Machinery Institute started moving southward to Qinhuangdao, a coastal city in Hebei Province.
The Northeast Heavy Machinery Institute completely migrated to Qinhuangdao in 1997. It was accredited by the former State Education Commission to adopt the present name of Yanshan University.
In the 2018 "World Robot Contest-Inclusive Robot Challenge" sponsored by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the scientific research team of YSU won the first prize.

In 2023, based on the volume and citations on published research papers, engineering, materials science, chemistry, and computer science of YSU are among the top 1% of ESI (Essential Science Indicators by Clarivate) rankings worldwide.

YSU played a role in the design and production of Comac C919, as well as contributing to the design of the Shenzhou spacecraft, the Chinese high-speed rail, and the commissioning and design of FAST(Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope).

Qinhuangdao and Toledo established sister city ties in 1985, leading to a partnership between Yanshan University (YSU) and the University of Toledo (UToledo) since 1986. In 2008, they established the Confucius Institute at UToledo to promote Chinese culture and education. About 30,000 students took Chinese courses, with cultural activities reaching 100,000 locals. Managers from both universities participated in important events, and more than 200 people engaged in two-way exchange delegations. In 2016, YSU's School of Humanities and Law and UToledo's Law School signed a cooperation agreement. A master program and a health care training program were also established.
