Ding Xuexiang, director of the General Office of the Chinese Communist Party, member of the 19th Party Politburo and member of the Secretariat of the Chinese Communist Party.

Prof. Zifeng Li's 2021 research, titled Advancing Newtonian Physics by Upholding a Materialist Perspective on Spacetime and Energy-Matter, aimed to challenge Einstein's theory of relativity but faced skepticism due to the established verification of the theory. His work was recommended for Hebei Province Science and Technology Award despite facing several unsuccessful grant applications. Furthermore, the academic community have questioned the integrity of Prof. Li's research practices. Reportedly, Prof. Zifeng Li steadfastly rejects relativity, using his position to promote his theories in class. Allegedly, students who disagreed were unfairly graded, leading to a severe teaching incident. YSU criticized Li, imposing a 3-year undergraduate teaching suspension in 2017.
The Yanshan University campus covers an area of 820 acres with a total construction area of nearly one million square meters.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Qinhuangdao, where Yanshan University is located.

Qinhuangdao sits on the northwest coast of the Bohai Sea and borders Tangshan to the southwest, Chengde to the northwest, and Liaoning to the northeast. Its administrative area ranges in latitude 39° 24' to 40° 37' N and in longitude from 118° 33' to 119° 51' E, and has a total area of 7,812.4 km2 (3,016.4 sq mi).

Since the elevation of Tianjin to a provincial-level municipality, Qinhuangdao is the chief port of Hebei. The Qin emperor Qin Shi Huang is said to have sought immortality on an island in Haigang District but did not find it.
Qinhuangdao has three main developed areas:

Beidaihe: A summer seaside resort for senior government officials. Many political decisions affecting China are made here, making it the equivalent to resorts in Maine or Camp David in Maryland, United States.
Haigang: the harbor city. Qinhuangdao proper. Home of Yan Shan University, the leading university in NE Hebei province.
Shanhaiguan: a popular tourist destination, featuring the eastern end of the Great Wall.
Qinhuangdao's Olympic Sports Centre Stadium was used as an Olympic Competition Venue (Football Preliminary) during the 2008 Summer Olympics.

Qinhuangdao has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa), with four distinct seasons. Winters are cold and dry due to the Siberian high, which often causes winds to blow in from the northwest, minimising the oceanic influence: the monthly daily average temperature in January is −5.6 °C (21.9 °F), colder than Beijing's −2.7 °C (27.1 °F). Summers are hot and humid due to the East Asian Monsoon, often allowing onshore flows; summer is also when the coast moderates the weather the most: the average temperature in July here is 24.7 °C (76.5 °F), as compared to 27.2 °C (81.0 °F) in Beijing. As measured by daily mean temperature, July and August are equally warm, averaging 24.7 °C (76.5 °F). The annual mean is 10.6 °C (51.1 °F), and 70% of the annual precipitation falls from June to August. Extreme temperatures have ranged from −26.0 °C (−14.8 °F) on 6 January 2010 to 40.0 °C (104.0 °F) on 15 June 2017.

Qinhuangdao Port is a strategically important port and is the largest coal shipping port in the country, much of which is shipped to power plants elsewhere in China. With recent expansion, its capacity has reached 209 million metric tons. The harbor is adding a further six berths to add capacity and is increasingly being invested in by other port operators, such as South Africa's Port of Richards Bay, who have announced plans to invest US$150 million to increase capacity by at least 28 percent.

China is the world's third largest coal exporter, and Qinhuangdao is expected to handle much of the nation's coal exports. Rail links from Shanxi (China's largest coal producer) to Qinhuangdao Port are being upgraded, which should allow for Qinhuangdao to ultimately increase its throughput to 400 million tonnes of coal per annum from its current level of about 250 million tons by 2015. In 2018, the updated railway reached a record annual throughput of 451 million tons.

Other Chinese and foreign service suppliers are moving to Qinhuangdao to support this. China Ocean Shipping (Group) Co, China's biggest shipping company, expects US$49 billion of spending on ports over the next five years as the industry tackles bottlenecks created by the nation's unprecedented economic boom.
Qinhuangdao is on the Jingshen Expressway which links Beijing with Shenyang, Liaoning. The city is served by Qinhuangdao Beidaihe Airport.
The Qinhuangdao Wildlife Park was opened in 1995 and is China's second largest wildlife park.

Yanshan University is in Hebei, and the region around a university shapes student life as much as the campus does. The following sections describe Hebei.

Peking Man, an early population of Homo erectus, lived at Zhoukoudian in present-day Fangshan District of Beijing, near the modern Hebei border, several hundred thousand years ago; published estimates commonly range from about 700,000 to 200,000 years ago. Neolithic findings at the prehistoric Beifudi site date to 7000 and 8000 BC.

Many early Chinese myths are set in the province. Fuxi, one of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, is said to have lived in present-day Xingtai. The mythical Battle of Zhuolu, won by the Yellow Emperor, Yan Emperor, and their Yanhuang tribes against the Chiyou-led Jiuli tribes, took place in Zhangjiakou and started the Huaxia civilization.

During the Spring and Autumn period (722–476 BC), Hebei was under the rule of Yan in the north and Jin in the south. Also during this period, a nomadic people known as Dí invaded the plains of northern China and established Zhongshan in central Hebei. In the Warring States period (403–221 BC), Jin was partitioned and much of its territory in Hebei went to Zhao.

The Qin dynasty unified China in 221 BC. The Han dynasty (206 BC – 220 AD) ruled the area under two provinces, You Prefecture in the north and Ji Province in the south. At the end of the Han dynasty, most of Hebei was under the control of warlords Gongsun Zan in the north and Yuan Shao further south. Yuan Shao emerged as the victor of the two, but he was defeated by Cao Cao in the Battle of Guandu in 200. Hebei came under the rule of the Kingdom of Wei, established by the descendants of Cao Cao.

After the invasions of northern nomadic peoples at the end of the Western Jin dynasty, chaos ensued in the Sixteen Kingdoms and the Northern and Southern dynasties. Because of its location on the northern frontier, Hebei changed hands many times and was controlled at various times by Later Zhao, Former Yan, Former Qin, and Later Yan. The Northern Wei reunified northern China in 440 but split in 534, with Hebei coming under Eastern Wei; then the Northern Qi, with its capital at Ye near modern Linzhang, Hebei. The Sui dynasty again unified China in 589.

During the Tang dynasty (618–907), the area was officially called Hebei for the first time. The Great Yan State was established in Hebei from 756 to 763 during the An Lushan Rebellion. After the rebellion, Lulong Jiedushi retained its autonomy from Tang during most of the 9th century. During the late Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, Lulong was fragmented among several regimes including the short-lived Yan. It was eventually annexed in 913 by Li Cunxu, who established the Later Tang (923–936). Emperor Gaozu of the Later Jin dynasty ceded much of northern Hebei to the Khitan Liao dynasty. This territory, called the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, became a weakness in the Chinese defense against the Khitans for the next century because it lay within the Great Wall.

During the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), the sixteen ceded prefectures continued to be an area of contention between Song China and the Liao dynasty. Later, the Southern Song dynasty abandoned all of North China, including Hebei, to the Jurchen Jin dynasty after the 1127 Jingkang Incident of the Jin–Song wars. Hebei was heavily affected by the flooding of the Yellow River; between 1048 and 1128, the river ran directly through the province rather than to its south.
The Mongol Yuan dynasty divided China into provinces but did not establish Hebei as a province. Instead, the area was directly administrated by the Secretariat at the capital Dadu.

During the Ming dynasty, what is now Hebei was first constituted as Beizhili, when the capital of China was located at Nanjing along the Yangtze River. The Ming Yongle Emperor renamed Beiping as Beijing in 1403, and formally moved the capital there from Nanjing in 1421. The region known as Beizhili was composed of parts of the modern provinces of Hebei, Henan, Shandong, including the provincial-level municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin.

The Qing dynasty came to power in 1644 and centralized its capital in Beijing. Southern Zhili was reconstituted as the province of Jiangnan, while Northern Zhili simply became known as Zhili, or Directly Ruled. The northern borders of Zhili extended deep into Inner Mongolia and overlapped in jurisdiction with the leagues of Inner Mongolia.

In the 18th century the borders of Zhili were redrawn and spread over Hebei, as well as what is today Beijing, Tianjin, and the provinces of Hebei, western Liaoning, northern Henan, northern Shandong, and Inner Mongolia.

The Qing dynasty collapsed in 1912 and was replaced by the Republic of China (ROC). In a few years, China descended into a civil war, with regional warlords vying for power. Since Zhili was so close to the capital of Beijing, it was the site of the Zhiwan War, the First Zhifeng War, and the Second Zhifeng War. With the success of the Northern Expedition in 1926 and 1927 by the Kuomintang, the capital was moved from Beijing to Nanjing. The ROC assigned portions of northern Zhili province to its neighbors in the north and renamed the remainder to Hebei, reflecting the relocation of the capital and its standard provincial administration.
During World War II, Hebei was under the control of the Reorganized National Government of the Republic of China, a puppet state of the Empire of Japan.

The founding of the People's Republic of China saw several changes. The region around Chengde, previously part of Rehe Province (historically part of Manchuria), and the region around Zhangjiakou, previously part of Chahar Province (historically part of Inner Mongolia), were merged into Hebei. This extended its borders northwards beyond the Great Wall. Meanwhile, the city of Puyang was carved away, causing Hebei to lose access to the Yellow River. The city became part of the short-lived Pingyuan Province before eventually being annexed into Henan.

The capital was also moved from Baoding to the new city of Shijiazhuang, and, for a short period, to Tianjin. On July 28, 1976, Tangshan was struck by the Tangshan earthquake, one of the deadliest earthquakes of the 20th century; the official death toll was about 242,000, though some estimates are considerably higher. There were a series of smaller earthquakes in the following decade.

Today, Hebei, along with Beijing and Tianjin municipalities which it includes, make up the Jing-Jin-Ji megalopolis region. With a population of 130 million, it is about six times the size of the New York metropolitan area and is one of the largest megalopolis clusters in China. Beijing had also unloaded some of its non-capital functions to the province with the establishment of the Xiong'an New Area, which integrates the three municipalities.

Hebei is the only province in China to contain plateaus, mountains, hills, shorelines, plains, and lakes. Most of central and southern Hebei lies within the North China Plain. Western Hebei rises into the Taihang Mountains (Taihang Shan), while the Yan Mountains (Yan Shan) runs through northern Hebei. Beyond the mountains are the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. The highest peak is Mount Xiaowutai in Yu County in the northwest of the province, with an altitude of 2,882 m (9,455 ft).

Hebei borders the Bohai Sea on the east. The Hai River watershed covers most of the province's central and southern parts; the Luan River watershed covers the northeast. Excluding manmade reservoirs, the largest lake in Hebei is Baiyangdian, located in Anxin County, Baoding.
Major cities in Hebei include Shijiazhuang, Baoding, Tangshan, Qinhuangdao, Handan, and Zhangjiakou.

Hebei has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate. Its winters are cold and dry, while its summers are hot and humid. Temperatures average −16 to −3 °C (3 to 27 °F) in January and 20 to 27 °C (68 to 81 °F) in July. The annual precipitation ranges from 400 to 800 mm (16 to 31 in), concentrated heavily in summer.

Yantai University (烟台大学) is a key state university on the Shandong coast, in the city of Yantai. It belongs to the first group admitted to the province's Famous University Project, and it opened in 1984 with help from two members of the C9 League, Peking University and Tsinghua University.

Main-site figures from June 2022: the Laishan District campus covered 2,100 mu (about 140 hectares) and had 1,019,800 square metres of floor space. Teaching and research equipment there was worth 602 million yuan. A second campus, the Development Zone Science and Education Park, is in Yantai's Bajiaowan Central Innovation District and covers more than 1,000 mu of land.

Altogether there are 23 schools and 75 research institutes, and 58 undergraduate majors take new students. Master's degrees can be awarded in 23 first-level disciplines and 14 professional master's categories. There are 1,726 full-time teaching staff, and the university's full-time undergraduates, graduate students and international students add up to over 30,000.

Yantai University was founded in July 1984 as a modern comprehensive university on the Yantai coast. It was paid for by a generous bequest from Zhang Chengxian (张承先), who also served as its first president.
The motto is "to be honest, modest and natural". The coat of arms shows a dolphin and ocean flows, which stand for intelligence and an open mind. Most students are from Shandong itself.

The 21 faculties offered 49 programmes in 2008, in subjects from arts, law, science and education to management, medicine, music and engineering, and also continuing education and international culture. As well as students, the community uses the library, which has 1,680,000 physical books and 700,000 electronic items.

The university exchanges regularly with academic institutions in Britain, Canada, Norway, Australia, Korea, Germany and America. About 500 international students accept places every year. Some teachers on the staff come from Britain, Canada and the US, and some international students come to study Chinese.

You will find the campus right by the sea. Buses 7 and 10 reach downtown in about 25 minutes and both terminate outside the railway station, near one of the city's several long-distance bus stations. The former Coal College, now Shandong Institute, is another institution nearby, within a 15-minute walk of the north gate.

yantai-university.h: Yantai, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Day-to-day life depends largely on the city, so this section looks at Yantai: its geography, weather, economy, other universities, transport and attractions.

Yantai is on the northern coast of the Shandong Peninsula, below the meeting point of the Bohai Sea and the Yellow Sea, facing the southern coast of Liaoning across the water. The source breaks the terrain down as shown below, but the shares add up to well over 100 percent, so treat them as approximate and ask the university or the city for better ones.
36.62% mountainous
39.7% hilly
50.23% plain
2.90% basin

The built-up part of the prefecture is roughly 2,643.60 km2 (1,020.70 sq mi). Only Qixia City, a county-level unit, has no coast, and the rest all do, with Changdao made up entirely of islands. The coastline is 909 kilometres (565 mi) long.
Hill summits are typically 100 to 300 metres (330 to 980 ft), and mountain peaks average 500 metres (1,600 ft). The highest point is the top of Mount Kunyu, at 922.8 metres (3,028 ft).
There are 121 rivers longer than 5 kilometres (3.1 mi). The seven largest are the Wulong, Dagu, Dagujia, Wang, Jie, Huangshui and Xin'an rivers.

Monsoons shape the climate. In Koppen terms Yantai is hot-summer humid continental (Dwa) when the 0 degree Celsius (32 F) isotherm is the test, but humid subtropical (Cwa) when the minus 3 degree (27 F) isotherm is the test. Hot, humid, rainy summers alternate with cold, dry winters. Since 1951 recorded temperatures have ranged from minus 12.8 degrees (9 F) to 38.4 degrees (101 F), and an unofficial minus 15 degrees (5 F) was reported on 10 January 1931.

Yantai ranks second among Shandong's industrial cities, behind Qingdao, even though agriculture is the biggest industry in the region overall. It is famous across China for one variety of apple and for the Laiyang pear, and it is home to Changyu, the oldest and largest grape winery in the country.

Its economy is among the most dynamic and diverse in the province. Fishing, fruit (apples above all) and light manufacturing were its traditional trades. Today it is a modern industrial base whose strengths include equipment manufacturing, petrochemicals, cars, electronics, pharmaceuticals and emerging high-tech fields. Longkou, a county-level city, is known all over China for its cellophane noodles.

A big coal-fired power plant near the port provides most of Yantai's energy. It burns bituminous coal and has coal gasification technology to reduce pollution. Attempts to switch northern China away from coal and towards natural gas resulted in shortages, and in 2017 the central government adopted a different plan: change half of northern China over to clean energy for winter heating. Haiyang, a city in the Yantai prefecture, was expected to meet all of its winter heating needs from nuclear power by 2021.

The Yantai Economic and Technological Development Area, among China's first state-level zones of its kind, has 115,000 residents and a planned area of 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi). It is at the end of the Shandong Peninsula, looking out to the Yellow Sea and adjoining downtown Yantai. Yantai Port is only 6 kilometres away and so is Yantai Railway Station (the main station, not Yantai South).

Another zone is the Yantai Export Processing Zone, or YTEPZ, one of the first fifteen that the State Council cleared. Construction there covers 4.17 km2 (1.61 sq mi), starting with an initial 3 km2 (1.2 sq mi), and the work has been completed after some years. Finished infrastructure includes 120,000 m2 (1,300,000 sq ft) of standard factory space and 40,000 m2 (430,000 sq ft) of bonded warehousing. Because the investment climate is good, firms from Japan, Korea, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Sweden, the US and Canada operate there, along with Chinese firms.

yantai-university.h: Other places to study in Yantai

blocks.x: Three prominent higher education institutions are in the city.
Yantai University
Ludong University
Shandong Institute of Business and Technology

Binzhou Medical College and China Agricultural University have campuses in the city too. Yantai also has a Korean international school, and in the past it had Chefoo School, a missionary school for foreign children that ran from 1881 to 1951.
Yantai Penglai International Airport has scheduled flights to major Chinese airports and to Seoul, Osaka and Hong Kong. The Lancun-Yantai railway ends in the city.
Shandong's first intercity high-speed line, the Qingrong Intercity Railway, is open and has cut the fastest Qingdao-Yantai journey from about 4 hours 30 minutes to about 1 hour 15 minutes.

Yangma Island lies in northern Muping District and is spacious. Its mild climate, without harsh winter cold or fierce summer heat, makes it a good place for leisure and holidays, and it is nicknamed the Maldives of China. The island is old, too. Tradition says that Emperor Qin Shi Huang kept royal horses there during a tour of the east, so it was called "Royal Horse Island", which is where the name comes from.
A university also belongs to a region, so the rest of this profile summarises the history of Shandong.

Long before written history, the eastern end of the North China Plain, where Shandong lies, supported a chain of Stone Age societies. Archaeologists name five: Houli (roughly 6500 to 5500 BC), Beixin (roughly 5300 to 4100 BC), Dawenkou (roughly 4100 to 2600 BC), Longshan (roughly 3000 to 2000 BC) and Yueshi (roughly 1900 to 1500 BC).

Control by the Shang and Zhou dynasties was uneven and reached the west of the province in varying degrees. The east belonged to the Dongyi, a people the Central Plain's inhabitants saw as outsiders. When the state of Qi took over the Dongyi state of Lai in 567 BC, the Dongyi slowly adopted Chinese ways.

Real power passed to regional states during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, and two of them lay in Shandong. One was Qi, with its capital at Linzi, and the other was Lu, with its capital at Qufu. Lu was the home of Confucius but was small, and its southern neighbour Chu eventually annexed it. Qi stayed a major power for the whole era and ruled cities that included Jimo, Linzi and Ju.

yantai-university.h: Qin, Han and the age of division

blocks.x: The Qin dynasty defeated Qi in 221 BC and founded the first centralised state in Chinese history. The Han dynasty after it divided what is now Shandong into commanderies under two inspectorates: Qingzhou in the north and Yanzhou in the south. In the Three Kingdoms era the province was part of Cao Wei, the northern kingdom that ruled northern China.

A short-lived unification under the Western Jin gave way to invasions by nomadic peoples from the north. They overran northern China, and Shandong with it. In roughly a century control changed hands many times: it went to the Later Zhao, then the Former Yan, the Former Qin, the Later Yan, the Southern Yan and the Liu Song dynasty, and finally to the Northern Wei, the first of the Northern dynasties in the Northern and Southern dynasties era. Shandong stayed with the Northern dynasties until that era ended.

A well-known visitor arrived in 412 AD. The Buddhist monk Faxian came ashore at Laoshan, on the south side of the peninsula, and travelled to Qingzhou. There he worked on editing and translating the scriptures he had carried home from India and Pakistan.

The Sui brought unity back in 589, and the Tang (618-907) presided over the golden age that followed. For much of its early period Shandong was administered in Henan Circuit, one of the empire's political divisions. When the empire later fell apart into warlord factions, this produced the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, and Shandong lay inside the Five Dynasties, all of which were based in the north.

China was reunified under the Song dynasty in the late tenth century. Water Margin, a classic novel, grew out of folk tales about outlaw bands in Shandong in Song times. At Qingzhou in 1996 more than two hundred buried Buddhist statues were found, an important archaeological discovery. Some are early painted figures, and they were probably buried because Emperor Huizong, a supporter of Taoism, repressed Buddhism.
In 1142 the Song had to give northern China up to the Jurchen Jin dynasty. The Jin ruled Shandong as two units, an East Circuit and a West Circuit, and that was the first use of the present name.

It was the Ming dynasty that created the province in its modern form, and at that time its territory was larger, taking in eastern Liaoning (Liaodong). The provincial capital was shifted from Qingzhou to Jinan in 1376, and Jinan has remained the capital for some seven hundred years.

Once Emperor Yongle made Beijing the capital in 1421, grain shipments on the Grand Canal made Jining and Linqing prosperous. During the Little Ice Age, from about 1550 to 1770, harvests fell and famine came back year after year. The imperial court's harsh policies made matters worse, and peasant uprisings kept breaking out.

Two Ming generals, Kong Youde and Geng Zhongming, led troops from Dengzhou in Shandong to Liaodong in 1633 to surrender to the Manchu Qing, and later they fought in the Qing army as it entered China proper. By 1640 peasant risings under the White Lotus Society were growing stronger in Shandong. The Ming court sent Zhu Datian to suppress them, and the population shrank sharply once more.

A major earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.5 and centred just northeast of Linyi, wrecked Dengzhou and the area around it. Local people and foreigners were among the dead, and claims of the number of deaths range from 43,000 to 50,000.

yantai-university.h: The late Qing period and the foreign powers

blocks.x: The First Opium War defeat left China open to Western influence, and Shandong, as a coastal province, felt it keenly. When the Second Opium War ended, the Qing court allowed Chefoo (modern Yantai) to be used as a trade port, and Western powers built consulates, missions, Christian schools and factories there. The province's strategic position made every power want a share. During the 1880s it served as a supply and training base for the Beiyang Fleet, which had its headquarters at Weihaiwei. Japan's navy crushed the Beiyang Fleet in 1894, and from then Japan began to extend its reach into Shandong. Another blow came three years later when two German Catholic missionaries were killed at Juye, in Heze. That was the Juye Incident, and as a result the Qing government had to hand Qingdao over to the German Empire. Britain received Weihaiwei in 1898, a result of Russian Empire pressure.

There was also movement of people. Russia annexed Outer Manchuria in 1860, and the Qing government cancelled its ban on settlement and encouraged people from Shandong to go to what remained of Manchuria. Large numbers left for the Russian Far East, Korea and Northeast China to find better opportunities. Many put down roots in Northeast China, also known as Manchuria, and made a major contribution to its population and farming by working in agriculture, construction and mining. Before the Soviets expelled and killed many of them, roughly 200 thousand Chinese labourers were in the Russian Far East, and 95 percent came from Shandong.

The Boxer Rebellion began early in Shandong, which became one of its main centres. Yuan Shikai, a Qing general, took over as governor in 1899 to put the uprising down, and he kept the post for three years.

Germany gained control of the peninsula in 1898 by leasing Jiaozhou Bay and the port of Qingdao under threat of force. Development was a top priority for the Germans. They invested over 200 million marks in a world-class harbour, with berths, heavy machinery, rail yards and a floating dry dock, and private firms opened mines, banks, factories and railways across the province.

During the First World War Japan seized the German holdings in Qingdao and across Shandong. The Treaty of Versailles in 1919 handed them to Japan and did not restore Chinese sovereignty. Anger spread across China, and the "Shandong Problem" fuelled the fierce student demonstrations of the May Fourth Movement. The US Senate's Committee on Foreign Relations approved treaty reservations that included "to give Shantung to China", although the treaty with those reservations was not ratified. Shandong did return to Chinese control in 1922, after the United States mediated at the Washington Naval Conference, and Weihai followed in 1930.

Right after the Communist government took power, parts of western Shandong were used to form Pingyuan Province, which did not last. Shandong briefly gained the prefectures of Xuzhou and Lianyungang as well. Its borders have mostly stayed the same as today's.

Shandong was badly hit by the Great Chinese Famine of 1959 to 1962, when about six million people starved. A confrontation known as the "Qingdao Incident" took place on 25 August 1966, pitting cadres and workers against students from three major local universities, and it marked the start of the Cultural Revolution in Shandong.

Mao died in 1976 and the era of constant political campaigns ended. Reform and Opening Up began in 1978, and Shandong, particularly its eastern coast, grew fast economically. For the first time in 1986, the value that the province's township and village enterprises produced was greater than that of agriculture.

Several firsts followed. Shandong was the first province in China where every household had electricity, in 1996. In 1999 Zhanhua County, which was the last county in the province that the state officially classed as poor, was declared free of poverty. In 2004 Shandong passed Guangdong in industrial output and profits and for the first time was the top province in China for industrial strength.
Summer 2008: sailing at both the Olympic Games (the 29th) and the Paralympic Games (the 13th) was hosted by Qingdao, which was a partner city of Beijing.
2009: the National Games of the People's Republic (the 11th) were hosted by Jinan.

Mid-July 2010 (the 16th): during a China visit by Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany, the two countries agreed to support a Sino-German Ecopark within the economic and technological development zone at Qingdao.
2011: official approval was given to the development plan of the Shandong Peninsula Blue Economic Zone.
Early June 2014 (the 3rd): the State Council officially approved Qingdao West Coast New Area, a national-level area in Huangdao District.
Later, in August 2019, the State Council approved a pilot free trade zone for Shandong, made up of three areas in Jinan, Qingdao and Yantai.
Forecasts for 2020 put the peninsula's urban agglomeration at over 103 million people, with 67 million living in urban areas.
In short, Yantai University sits in a historic, populous and industrial province, in a coastal city that is among its strongest economies.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

yantai-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Yantai University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Yantai, register at Yantai University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Yunnan Agricultural University (Chinese: 云南农业大学) is in Kunming, Yunnan, China.

It was initially established in Kunming in 1938 (1938) as the 'School of Agricultural' at Yunnan University. Separated from Yunnan University in 1958, the School of Agriculture was renamed 'Kunming Agriculture and Forestry College' (KAFC). The formal title, Yunnan Agricultural University, was adopted in 1971 because of the merger between KAFC and Yunnan Agriculture Working University (YAWU). It has been developed as a key university of Yunnan Province since 1993.

In 2001, YAU became one of the two biological science experts training bases in Yunnan Province. YAU is now a comprehensive university offering programs in agriculture, science, arts, engineering, education, and administration.
Yunnan Agricultural University consists of 15 schools.
School of Agriculture and Biotechnology
School of Animal Science and Technology
School of Economics and Trade
School of Engineering
School of Tobacco Science
School of Plant Protection
School of Ornamental and Horticulture
School of Resources and Environment
School of Water Resources, Hydraulics, and Architecture
School of Science and Information
School of Food Science and Technology
School of Physical Education
School of Foreign Languages
School of Humanities and Social Science
School of Continuing Education

As of January 2025, the university offers 74 undergraduate programs, including 6 national-level characteristic programs, 13 national-level first-class programs, and 2 programs accredited by the China Engineering Education Accreditation. Additionally, it features 7 provincial-level characteristic programs, 8 provincial-level key development programs, 5 provincial-level brand programs, 24 provincial-level first-class programs, and 3 Sino-foreign cooperative education programs. It boasts 8 provincial-level first-class disciplines, 7 first-level doctoral programs, and 27 second-level doctoral programs; 17 first-level master's programs and 71 second-level master's programs.

The university campus, covering an area of 130 hectares, is in Heilongtan Park (Black Dragon Pool Park), one of the scenic spots to the north of Kunming. The area of the campus building is about 250,000 square meters. YAU provides facilities for teaching and research projects.

The university library has 630,000 volumes and many other journals. The campus has been networked to improve its teaching and working effectiveness and efficiency. In 1998, YAU was awarded as a Civilized University by Yunnan Provincial Government.

There are 1,198 faculty and staff members at YAU, of whom 51 are professors and 162 are associate professors. 113 faculty members are master's degree advisors, and 6 professors are appointed as the doctoral degree advisors by other universities. 11 outstanding faculty members have been selected as the major academic leaders in the New Century Science and Technology Projects in Yunnan Province. 10 faculty members have been awarded the outstanding science experts by Yunnan Province. 21 teachers have been honored as outstanding teachers in the province.
As of January 2025, the university has over 32,000 full-time students, more than 17,000 students enrolled in higher education continuing education programs, and 393 international students.
Li Zhengyou, professor, the "father of high-altitude hybrid rice".

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Kunming, where Yunnan Agricultural University is located.

Kunming is located in east-central Yunnan province. Its administrative area is located between latitudes 24°23' and 26°22' N, and longitudes 102°10' and 103°40' E, with a total area of 21,600 square kilometres (8,340 square miles). Its widest stretch from the east to the west amounts to 140 kilometres (87 miles) while its longest stretch from the north to the south amounts to 220 kilometres (137 miles).

Situated in a fertile lake basin on the northern shore of the Lake Dian and surrounded by mountains to the north, west, and east, Kunming has always played a pivotal role in the communications of southwestern China.  Lake Dian, known as "the Pearl of the Plateau", is the largest lake in Yunnan and the sixth largest freshwater lake in China.  It has an area of approximately 340 square kilometres (130 square miles). Kunming's highest point is Mazong Ridge of the Jiaozi Snow Mountain in Luquan with an elevation of 4,247 metres (13,934 feet), and its lowest point is the joint of the Xiao River and the Jinsha River in Dongchuan District, with an elevation of 695 metres (2,280 feet). Its downtown area is 1,891 metres (6,204 feet) above sea level.

Located at an elevation of 1,888 metres (6,194 feet) on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau with low latitude and high elevation, Kunming has one of the mildest climates in China, characterized by short, cool, and dry winters and long, pleasant, and humid summers. With its perpetual spring-like weather which provides the ideal climate for plants and flowers, Kunming is known as the "City of Eternal Spring". The weather has seldom reached high temperatures in summer, only exceeding 30 °C (86 °F) on a handful of occasions. However, freak snowfalls occur in occasional winters. Controlled by a subtropical highland climate (Köppen Cwb), the monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 9.3 °C (48.7 °F) in January to 20.7 °C (69.3 °F) in June, with daily high temperatures reaching their lowest point and peak in December and June, respectively. The city is covered with blossoms and lush vegetation all-year round. The period from May to October is the monsoon season and the rest of the year is relatively dry. The city has an annual mean temperature of 16.0 °C (60.8 °F), rainfall of 991.0 millimetres (39.0 in) (nearly three-fifths occurring from June to August) and a frost-free period of 230 days. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 29% in July to 70% in February, the city receives 2,240.9 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extreme temperatures in the city have ranged from −7.8 to 32.9 °C (18.0 to 91.2 °F) on 29 December 1983 and 25 May 2014 respectively.

The population of Han is 5,542,314, accounting for 86.16%; the population of all ethnic minorities add up to 889,898, accounting for 13.84%. Some of the 26 nationalities in the province live in Kunming, and the average life expectancy of the city's population is 76 years old.

The city center has three major squares and six major streets: Jinma Biji Square, Nanping Square and Dongfeng Square are the main squares, while Beijing Road, Zhengyi Road, Renmin Road, Dongfeng Road, Jinbi Road, and Qingnian Road are the main streets. Jingxing Street, Guanghua Street, Zhengyi Road, Nanping Street (built on top of a section of Dongfeng Road), Qingnian Road, and Renmin Road are the main commercial areas in Kunming; the most popular pedestrian streets are Nanping Street, Zhengyi Road, and Jingxing Street.

Kunming's modern city center is Nanping Square on the west bank of the Panlong River, at the intersection of Nanping Street and Zhengyi Street. This area is where Kunming's southern city wall once stood. This area is a crowded and dense modern shopping precinct packed with clothing and electronics stores. Surrounding the area are plenty of new high-rises, along with an area of preserved old city to the north. The area formerly considered the city center is Dongfeng Square, located on the east bank of the Panlong River outside of the old city walls at the intersection of Beijing Road and Dongfeng Road, where in the mornings there are crowds doing taijiquan and playing badminton. Weekend amateur theatre is also performed in the square. The Panlong River has had an artificial flow ever since the construction of the Songhua Dam, and the river has been developed into what is effectively a canal. The river receives treated sewage and wastewater from surrounding pipes.

The center is an area of importance to Kunming's Hui population, with Shuncheng Street, one of the last old streets in the center of the city, previously forming a Muslim quarter. Under Kunming's rapid modernisation, however, the street has been demolished to make way for apartments and shopping centers. Rising behind a supermarket one block north off Zhengyi Road, Nancheng Qingzhen Si is the city's new mosque, its green dome and chevron-patterned minaret visible from afar and built on the site of an earlier Qing edifice.

Running west off Zhengyi Road just past the mosque, Jingxing Street leads into a corner of the city that consists of Kunming's bird and flower market convening daily in the streets connecting it with the northerly, parallel to the Guanghua Street. The market offers many plants such as orchids that have been collected and farmed across the province.

Jinbi Road runs south of Dongfeng Road. Both of them connect to Beijing Road. Two large Chinese pagodas rise south of Jinbi Road and the city center, each a solid thirteen stories of whitewashed brick crowned with four iron cockerels. The West Pagoda was built between 824 and 859, during the Tang dynasty; its original counterpart, the East Pagoda, was built at the same time, but was destroyed by an earthquake in 1833 and rebuilt in the same Tang style in 1882. South down Dongsi Road, past another mosque, the entrance to the West Pagoda is along a narrow lane on the right. The East Pagoda is a more cosmetic, slightly tilted duplicate standing in an ornamental garden a few minutes' walk east on Shulin Jie. The temples associated with both pagodas are closed to the public.

Many streets are lined with Jacaranda trees, which can be seen blooming abundantly in mid to late April, particularly on Jiaochang Middle Road. The trees are not native to Kunming, but originate from seeds exchanged with Algeria, which were grown in the Kunming Botanical Garden. Seeds from the botanical garden were then used by the city to plant the trees along streets.

Cuihu Park (Green Lake Park) is one of Kunming's major parks and is predominately a lake surrounded by greenery. Located in the west side of the park is a statue of Nie Er, the composer of China's national anthem.

Another monument to Nie Er is located in Xishan Park, most well known for the Longmen Grottoes (not to be confused with the identically named grottoes in Luoyang), containing several ancient temples and the titular Longmen ("dragon gate").

Daguan Park lies on Dian Chi in Kunming's southwestern limits. Originally laid out by the Kangxi Emperor in the Qing dynasty, it has been modified over the years to include a noisy funfair, food stalls and emporiums.
Kunming's zoo, founded in 1950, is adjoined to Yuantong Park, known for the Yuantong Temple within. The zoo houses 5,000 animals from 140 species and receives 3 million visitors a year.
Other parks in Kunming include Black Dragon Pool and the Kunming Botanical Gardens in the north, the World Horti-Expo Garden in the northeast, and Wenmiao Tea Garden in Wuhua District.

The World Horti-Expo Garden is located in the northern suburbs of Kunming and was built for the 1999 World Horticulture Exposition, which ran from 1 May to 31 October 1999. It had the theme of "Man and Nature—Marching Toward the 21st Century". Golden Temple Park, located on Mingfeng Hill nearby, is connected by cable car to the World Horti-Expo Garden. Constructed in 1602 (the 30th year of the Wanli reign period of the Ming dynasty), all of its beams, pillars, arches, doors, windows, tiles, Buddhist statues, and horizontal inscribed boards are made of copper, weighing more than 200 tons. It is the largest copper building in China.

Yuantong Temple is Kunming's major Buddhist temple. It is Kunming's largest and most famous temple with the original structure being first constructed more than 1,200 years ago during the Tang dynasty. The temple sits in a depression on the southern side of Yuantong Park. Northwest about 12 km (7.5 mi) from the city center is the Qiongzhu Si (Bamboo Temple) built in 639 and rebuilt in 1422 to 1428. Numerous Buddhist temples line the road to the Dragon Gate (龙门) in the Western Mountains.
Notable museums in Kunming include:
Yunnan Provincial Museum
Kunming City Museum (redeveloped in 2014)
Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology (opened in November 2006)
Yunnan Ethnology Museum (opened 1995)

Every year, many Chinese and international athletes come to Kunming for high-altitude training. The city has been China's national high-elevation training base for more than 30 years. There are two major training complexes, Hongta Sports Center and Haigeng National Training Center.

Hongta Sports Center was built in 2000 by Hongta (Red Pagoda) cigarette company, at a cost of US$58 million. Located near Haigeng Park, the complex is mostly used by professional athletes, but also acts as a sports club for the general public. Every weekend, it hosts amateur football matches. Aside from about 10 football pitches, including one surrounded by a running track, Hongta also has a 50-metre (160-foot) swimming pool, a badminton gymnasium, tennis courts and a basketball court. It also has one of China's few ice hockey rinks, and a workout room with treadmills and weightlifting machines. There are also game rooms for air hockey; also pool tables and a basement bowling alley. The complex comes complete with a 101-room hotel and restaurant.

Haigeng National Training Center is located ten minutes away from Hongta on Dianchi (Lake Dian) near Kunming's award-winning Lakeview Golf Club and new condominium developments. This complex dates from the late 1970s and was built by the government specifically to specialize in high-altitude training.

Golf is a major attraction in Kunming. There are four golf courses within an hour's drive of downtown. For the last six years , Spring City Golf and Lake Resort in nearby Yiliang County has reigned as the best golf course in China and Hong Kong according to US Golf Digest. In 2004, it was named Asia's best golf resort by Asian Golf Monthly. It hosts the Kunming Leg of the Omega China Tour.

Kunming has attracted foreign investment in golf course development. "Spring City" Golf Resort is a US$600 million project that began as an investment led by Singapore's Keppel Land Group in 1992. Jack Nicklaus and course designer Robert Trent Jones, Jr designed the two courses.
Major sports facilities include:
Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose venue
Golf: Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, its 'Mountain Course' was designed by Jack Nicklaus
Lakeview Golf Villa
Cuihu Park tennis courts
Kunming Municipal Athletic Center
Kunming Gymnasium
Yunnan Provincial Stadium, home to Hongta Yunnan Football Club
Wuhua District Stadium

Kunming has three economic advantages over other cities in southwest China: significant natural resources, a large consumer market and a mild climate. Due to its position at the center of Yunnan, one of China's largest producers of agricultural products, minerals and hydroelectricity, Kunming is the main commercial hub for most of the province's resources.

Kunming's chief industries are copper, lead and zinc production. Its iron and steel industry has been expanded. Salt and phosphate mines around Kunming are some of the largest in China. Yunnan Copper Company Limited, based in Kunming, is one of Yunnan's largest mining corporations. From the late 1970s, Kunming's main industries also came to include food and tobacco processing and the manufacture of construction equipment and machines.

In May 1995, the State Council approved Kunming as an Open City. By the end of 1995, the city had approved 929 overseas-funded enterprises with a total investment of $2.3 billion including $1.1 billion of foreign capital. More than 40 projects each had an investment of more than $9 million.

Kunming is a center of engineering and the manufacture of machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and automobiles (including heavy goods vehicles). It has a chemical industry, and plastics, cement works and textile factories. Its processing plants, which include tanneries, woodworking and papermaking factories, use local agricultural products. In 1997, Yunnan Tire Co. opened a tire plant in Kunming, with a capacity to produce two million tires per year.

Kunming has two major development zones, Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone (biological medicine, new materials, electronic information, agriculture) and Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone (mechanical equipment production, biological science and food industry, information industry, software).
There are also 30 key industrial parks promulgated and recognized by National Development and Reform Commission in Yunnan Province. The largest include:
Chenggong Industrial Park
Anning Industrial Park
Songming Yanglin Industrial Development Zone
Dongchuan Special Industrial Park
Xundian Special Industrial Park
Kunming Haikou Industrial Park.

As of 2008, Kunming is home to 65 of the Top 100 Enterprises in Yunnan Province. The top 100 enterprises were based on their revenues for 2007. Hongta Group, with revenues of some RMB39.88 billion for 2007 topped the list. The tobacco sector remains the largest sector in the province.
Kunming is situated on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau. Rail and air are the main two methods to travel to or from Kunming from outside Yunnan.
Yunnan Agricultural University lists 138 programs for international students on this site: 71 bachelor, 55 master's, 12 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 138 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 6,000 to CNY 6,000 (median CNY 6,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 8,000 to CNY 8,000 (median CNY 8,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 10,000 to CNY 10,000 (median CNY 10,000), according to the university's published fee table.

138 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.
