After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Kunming, register at Yunnan Agricultural University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
Yunnan Minzu University (YMU; 云南民族大学) is a provincial public university in Kunming, Yunnan, China. It is affiliated with the Yunnan Provincial People's Government.
Established on August 1, 1951 (1951-08-01), the university was founded in part to instruct government leaders to assist minority ethnic groups of Yunnan to ensure their political rights.

The school was renamed Yunnan Minzu University (YMU) on April 16, 2003. Subsequent university goals have included the need to cultivate professional support for ethnic groups to ensure political, economic and cultural development and to foster international outreach.

Yunnan Minzu University has established cooperative relations with 26 universities in 10 nations, including Baylor University and University of Virginia, USA; University of Bergen, Norway; and La Trobe University, Australia.
Since its establishment, the university has received over 20,000 students and scholars from over 80 countries, visiting to study or to conduct academic exchanges and scientific research.
In February 1993, Yunnan Provincial People's Government ranked the institute as a key university of the province.
Research includes three key disciplines: Languages & Literature of Minority Ethnic Groups, Ethnic Ancient Books Studies, and National Economy.
Instruction includes five key courses on the provincial level: An Outline of Ethnology, The Socialist Construction of China, Theories & Policies Concerning Ethnic Groups, and Organic Chemistry
Research institutions resident at the university:
The Academy of Ethnic Studies and the Visual Anthropology Study Center
Academy of Languages & Literature of Minority Ethnic Groups
Academy of national Economy under the administration of the Department of Economic Management
The Ethnic Law Study Center and the Ethnic Theories Study Center
The Southeast Asia Studies Center

YMU has a staff of more than 870, of which 428 are teachers and more than 60 are professional researchers, with 36 being full professors and 215 associate professors. The honorary professors of the institute include Ji Xianlin and Zhou Yiliang, council members of the National Board of Education, Dai Ruwei, Ding Xiaqi and Yan Luguang, academicians of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Liu Yaohan and Xu Qingzhang, nationally recognized educators of China.

YMU has a land area of nearly 27 hectares and a floor area of 139,976 square meters. The institute has ample facilities for teaching. Its library include 710,000 books, over 2,000 journals and magazines, and a rare collection of ancient texts for ethnic studies including the Beiye Scriptures and the Dongba Scriptures.

Also associated with the university is the book center which the Asian Foundation established in China, including 41,557 books donated by the foundation. The museum inventory includes valuable ethnic relics (30,000 pieces) enabling local and foreign research.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Kunming, where Yunnan Minzu University is located.

Kunming is located in east-central Yunnan province. Its administrative area is located between latitudes 24°23' and 26°22' N, and longitudes 102°10' and 103°40' E, with a total area of 21,600 square kilometres (8,340 square miles). Its widest stretch from the east to the west amounts to 140 kilometres (87 miles) while its longest stretch from the north to the south amounts to 220 kilometres (137 miles).

Situated in a fertile lake basin on the northern shore of the Lake Dian and surrounded by mountains to the north, west, and east, Kunming has always played a pivotal role in the communications of southwestern China.  Lake Dian, known as "the Pearl of the Plateau", is the largest lake in Yunnan and the sixth largest freshwater lake in China.  It has an area of approximately 340 square kilometres (130 square miles). Kunming's highest point is Mazong Ridge of the Jiaozi Snow Mountain in Luquan with an elevation of 4,247 metres (13,934 feet), and its lowest point is the joint of the Xiao River and the Jinsha River in Dongchuan District, with an elevation of 695 metres (2,280 feet). Its downtown area is 1,891 metres (6,204 feet) above sea level.

Located at an elevation of 1,888 metres (6,194 feet) on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau with low latitude and high elevation, Kunming has one of the mildest climates in China, characterized by short, cool, and dry winters and long, pleasant, and humid summers. With its perpetual spring-like weather which provides the ideal climate for plants and flowers, Kunming is known as the "City of Eternal Spring". The weather has seldom reached high temperatures in summer, only exceeding 30 °C (86 °F) on a handful of occasions. However, freak snowfalls occur in occasional winters. Controlled by a subtropical highland climate (Köppen Cwb), the monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 9.3 °C (48.7 °F) in January to 20.7 °C (69.3 °F) in June, with daily high temperatures reaching their lowest point and peak in December and June, respectively. The city is covered with blossoms and lush vegetation all-year round. The period from May to October is the monsoon season and the rest of the year is relatively dry. The city has an annual mean temperature of 16.0 °C (60.8 °F), rainfall of 991.0 millimetres (39.0 in) (nearly three-fifths occurring from June to August) and a frost-free period of 230 days. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 29% in July to 70% in February, the city receives 2,240.9 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extreme temperatures in the city have ranged from −7.8 to 32.9 °C (18.0 to 91.2 °F) on 29 December 1983 and 25 May 2014 respectively.

The population of Han is 5,542,314, accounting for 86.16%; the population of all ethnic minorities add up to 889,898, accounting for 13.84%. Some of the 26 nationalities in the province live in Kunming, and the average life expectancy of the city's population is 76 years old.

The city center has three major squares and six major streets: Jinma Biji Square, Nanping Square and Dongfeng Square are the main squares, while Beijing Road, Zhengyi Road, Renmin Road, Dongfeng Road, Jinbi Road, and Qingnian Road are the main streets. Jingxing Street, Guanghua Street, Zhengyi Road, Nanping Street (built on top of a section of Dongfeng Road), Qingnian Road, and Renmin Road are the main commercial areas in Kunming; the most popular pedestrian streets are Nanping Street, Zhengyi Road, and Jingxing Street.

Kunming's modern city center is Nanping Square on the west bank of the Panlong River, at the intersection of Nanping Street and Zhengyi Street. This area is where Kunming's southern city wall once stood. This area is a crowded and dense modern shopping precinct packed with clothing and electronics stores. Surrounding the area are plenty of new high-rises, along with an area of preserved old city to the north. The area formerly considered the city center is Dongfeng Square, located on the east bank of the Panlong River outside of the old city walls at the intersection of Beijing Road and Dongfeng Road, where in the mornings there are crowds doing taijiquan and playing badminton. Weekend amateur theatre is also performed in the square. The Panlong River has had an artificial flow ever since the construction of the Songhua Dam, and the river has been developed into what is effectively a canal. The river receives treated sewage and wastewater from surrounding pipes.

The center is an area of importance to Kunming's Hui population, with Shuncheng Street, one of the last old streets in the center of the city, previously forming a Muslim quarter. Under Kunming's rapid modernisation, however, the street has been demolished to make way for apartments and shopping centers. Rising behind a supermarket one block north off Zhengyi Road, Nancheng Qingzhen Si is the city's new mosque, its green dome and chevron-patterned minaret visible from afar and built on the site of an earlier Qing edifice.

Running west off Zhengyi Road just past the mosque, Jingxing Street leads into a corner of the city that consists of Kunming's bird and flower market convening daily in the streets connecting it with the northerly, parallel to the Guanghua Street. The market offers many plants such as orchids that have been collected and farmed across the province.

Jinbi Road runs south of Dongfeng Road. Both of them connect to Beijing Road. Two large Chinese pagodas rise south of Jinbi Road and the city center, each a solid thirteen stories of whitewashed brick crowned with four iron cockerels. The West Pagoda was built between 824 and 859, during the Tang dynasty; its original counterpart, the East Pagoda, was built at the same time, but was destroyed by an earthquake in 1833 and rebuilt in the same Tang style in 1882. South down Dongsi Road, past another mosque, the entrance to the West Pagoda is along a narrow lane on the right. The East Pagoda is a more cosmetic, slightly tilted duplicate standing in an ornamental garden a few minutes' walk east on Shulin Jie. The temples associated with both pagodas are closed to the public.

Many streets are lined with Jacaranda trees, which can be seen blooming abundantly in mid to late April, particularly on Jiaochang Middle Road. The trees are not native to Kunming, but originate from seeds exchanged with Algeria, which were grown in the Kunming Botanical Garden. Seeds from the botanical garden were then used by the city to plant the trees along streets.

Cuihu Park (Green Lake Park) is one of Kunming's major parks and is predominately a lake surrounded by greenery. Located in the west side of the park is a statue of Nie Er, the composer of China's national anthem.

Another monument to Nie Er is located in Xishan Park, most well known for the Longmen Grottoes (not to be confused with the identically named grottoes in Luoyang), containing several ancient temples and the titular Longmen ("dragon gate").

Daguan Park lies on Dian Chi in Kunming's southwestern limits. Originally laid out by the Kangxi Emperor in the Qing dynasty, it has been modified over the years to include a noisy funfair, food stalls and emporiums.
Kunming's zoo, founded in 1950, is adjoined to Yuantong Park, known for the Yuantong Temple within. The zoo houses 5,000 animals from 140 species and receives 3 million visitors a year.
Other parks in Kunming include Black Dragon Pool and the Kunming Botanical Gardens in the north, the World Horti-Expo Garden in the northeast, and Wenmiao Tea Garden in Wuhua District.

The World Horti-Expo Garden is located in the northern suburbs of Kunming and was built for the 1999 World Horticulture Exposition, which ran from 1 May to 31 October 1999. It had the theme of "Man and Nature—Marching Toward the 21st Century". Golden Temple Park, located on Mingfeng Hill nearby, is connected by cable car to the World Horti-Expo Garden. Constructed in 1602 (the 30th year of the Wanli reign period of the Ming dynasty), all of its beams, pillars, arches, doors, windows, tiles, Buddhist statues, and horizontal inscribed boards are made of copper, weighing more than 200 tons. It is the largest copper building in China.

Yuantong Temple is Kunming's major Buddhist temple. It is Kunming's largest and most famous temple with the original structure being first constructed more than 1,200 years ago during the Tang dynasty. The temple sits in a depression on the southern side of Yuantong Park. Northwest about 12 km (7.5 mi) from the city center is the Qiongzhu Si (Bamboo Temple) built in 639 and rebuilt in 1422 to 1428. Numerous Buddhist temples line the road to the Dragon Gate (龙门) in the Western Mountains.
Notable museums in Kunming include:
Yunnan Provincial Museum
Kunming City Museum (redeveloped in 2014)
Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology (opened in November 2006)
Yunnan Ethnology Museum (opened 1995)

Every year, many Chinese and international athletes come to Kunming for high-altitude training. The city has been China's national high-elevation training base for more than 30 years. There are two major training complexes, Hongta Sports Center and Haigeng National Training Center.

Hongta Sports Center was built in 2000 by Hongta (Red Pagoda) cigarette company, at a cost of US$58 million. Located near Haigeng Park, the complex is mostly used by professional athletes, but also acts as a sports club for the general public. Every weekend, it hosts amateur football matches. Aside from about 10 football pitches, including one surrounded by a running track, Hongta also has a 50-metre (160-foot) swimming pool, a badminton gymnasium, tennis courts and a basketball court. It also has one of China's few ice hockey rinks, and a workout room with treadmills and weightlifting machines. There are also game rooms for air hockey; also pool tables and a basement bowling alley. The complex comes complete with a 101-room hotel and restaurant.

Haigeng National Training Center is located ten minutes away from Hongta on Dianchi (Lake Dian) near Kunming's award-winning Lakeview Golf Club and new condominium developments. This complex dates from the late 1970s and was built by the government specifically to specialize in high-altitude training.

Golf is a major attraction in Kunming. There are four golf courses within an hour's drive of downtown. For the last six years , Spring City Golf and Lake Resort in nearby Yiliang County has reigned as the best golf course in China and Hong Kong according to US Golf Digest. In 2004, it was named Asia's best golf resort by Asian Golf Monthly. It hosts the Kunming Leg of the Omega China Tour.

Kunming has attracted foreign investment in golf course development. "Spring City" Golf Resort is a US$600 million project that began as an investment led by Singapore's Keppel Land Group in 1992. Jack Nicklaus and course designer Robert Trent Jones, Jr designed the two courses.
Major sports facilities include:
Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose venue
Golf: Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, its 'Mountain Course' was designed by Jack Nicklaus
Lakeview Golf Villa
Cuihu Park tennis courts
Kunming Municipal Athletic Center
Kunming Gymnasium
Yunnan Provincial Stadium, home to Hongta Yunnan Football Club
Wuhua District Stadium

Kunming has three economic advantages over other cities in southwest China: significant natural resources, a large consumer market and a mild climate. Due to its position at the center of Yunnan, one of China's largest producers of agricultural products, minerals and hydroelectricity, Kunming is the main commercial hub for most of the province's resources.

Kunming's chief industries are copper, lead and zinc production. Its iron and steel industry has been expanded. Salt and phosphate mines around Kunming are some of the largest in China. Yunnan Copper Company Limited, based in Kunming, is one of Yunnan's largest mining corporations. From the late 1970s, Kunming's main industries also came to include food and tobacco processing and the manufacture of construction equipment and machines.

In May 1995, the State Council approved Kunming as an Open City. By the end of 1995, the city had approved 929 overseas-funded enterprises with a total investment of $2.3 billion including $1.1 billion of foreign capital. More than 40 projects each had an investment of more than $9 million.

Kunming is a center of engineering and the manufacture of machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and automobiles (including heavy goods vehicles). It has a chemical industry, and plastics, cement works and textile factories. Its processing plants, which include tanneries, woodworking and papermaking factories, use local agricultural products. In 1997, Yunnan Tire Co. opened a tire plant in Kunming, with a capacity to produce two million tires per year.

Kunming has two major development zones, Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone (biological medicine, new materials, electronic information, agriculture) and Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone (mechanical equipment production, biological science and food industry, information industry, software).
There are also 30 key industrial parks promulgated and recognized by National Development and Reform Commission in Yunnan Province. The largest include:
Chenggong Industrial Park
Anning Industrial Park
Songming Yanglin Industrial Development Zone
Dongchuan Special Industrial Park
Xundian Special Industrial Park
Kunming Haikou Industrial Park.

As of 2008, Kunming is home to 65 of the Top 100 Enterprises in Yunnan Province. The top 100 enterprises were based on their revenues for 2007. Hongta Group, with revenues of some RMB39.88 billion for 2007 topped the list. The tobacco sector remains the largest sector in the province.
Kunming is situated on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau. Rail and air are the main two methods to travel to or from Kunming from outside Yunnan.
Yunnan Minzu University lists 84 programs for international students on this site: 22 bachelor, 59 master's, 3 doctoral programs.

By language of instruction: 84 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 11,000 to CNY 20,000 (median CNY 11,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 13,000 to CNY 15,000 (median CNY 13,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 17,000 to CNY 17,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.

84 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

yunnan-minzu-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Yunnan Minzu University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Kunming, register at Yunnan Minzu University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Yunnan Normal University (云南师范大学, abbreviated YNNU) is a public teacher-training university in Kunming, the capital of Yunnan Province in south-west China. "Normal" in the name is the traditional Chinese term for a university that specialises in training teachers. YNNU is a provincial institution that is supported jointly by the Yunnan provincial government and by the national Ministry of Education.

The roots go back to the Second World War. In 1937, once war had broken out, three leading northern universities, namely Peking, Tsinghua and Nankai, moved south to Kunming and merged into the National Southwest Associated University. Its parts included schools of humanities, science, engineering, and business and law, and a Teachers College. The Teachers College itself dates from 1938.

When the war ended, the three founding universities went back to their home cities in the north in 1946. The Teachers College did not. It stayed in Kunming as an independent school under the name National Kunming Teachers College. The word "National" was dropped in 1950, and in 1984 the school received its present name, Yunnan Normal University.

The campus covers 2,847 mu, which is about 469 acres. The university is organised into 26 schools and over 40 research centres and institutes. More than 30,000 full-time students work towards degrees, and a further 18,000-plus are enrolled in continuing education. For an international applicant, these figures mean a large, busy institution; check the university's own admissions site for the programmes taught in English or Chinese for foreigners.

yunnan-normal-university.h: Kunming, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Life as a student is shaped by the city as much as by the lecture halls. Kunming has an unusually gentle climate, a strong Buddhist and Muslim heritage, plenty of parks, and a growing industrial economy. The sections below describe what you will find.

Kunming sits in the east-central part of Yunnan. On the map, its administrative area runs from 24°23' to 26°22' north and from 102°10' to 103°40' east, and adds up to 21,600 square kilometres (8,340 square miles). The area is 140 km (87 miles) across at the widest point east to west, while north to south it stretches 220 km (137 miles).

Kunming's urban core occupies fertile lakeside land at the north end of Lake Dian, with mountains rising to its north, west and east. Because of this position the city has long been a pivot for transport and communication across the south-west. Lake Dian, nicknamed "the Pearl of the Plateau", is the biggest lake in Yunnan and the sixth biggest freshwater lake in China, with a surface of about 340 square kilometres (130 square miles).

The heights vary a lot across the municipality. The highest point is Mazong Ridge in the Jiaozi Snow Mountain at Luquan, at 4,247 metres (13,934 feet). The lowest is 695 metres (2,280 feet), where the Xiao River meets the Jinsha River in Dongchuan District. The downtown area sits at 1,891 metres (6,204 feet). Newcomers from low-lying places may feel the altitude for the first few days.

Two things shape the weather: Kunming is close to the tropics, and it stands about 1,888 metres (6,194 feet) up on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau. The result is among the gentlest climates anywhere in China. Winters are short, cool and dry; summers are long, pleasant and humid. The year-round spring-like weather is ideal for plants and flowers, so the city is called the "City of Eternal Spring", and blossoms and greenery are present in every season. Summer temperatures seldom climb high, and they have passed 30 °C (86 °F) only a handful of times. Occasionally a winter brings a freak snowfall.
The official classification is subtropical highland (Köppen Cwb). Here are the key figures.
Temperature by month: January is the coolest at an average of 9.3 °C (48.7 °F); June is the warmest at 20.7 °C (69.3 °F). The daily high bottoms out in December and peaks in June.
Annual mean temperature: 16.0 °C (60.8 °F).
Rain: 991.0 millimetres (39.0 inches) in a year, nearly three-fifths of it between June and August. Monsoon weather lasts from May through October; dry conditions prevail for the remaining months.
Frost-free period: 230 days.
Sunshine: 2,240.9 hours annually. July is the dullest month, at 29% of possible sunshine, and February the brightest, at 70%.
Extremes: -7.8 °C (18.0 °F) on 29 December 1983 and 32.9 °C (91.2 °F) on 25 May 2014.
Dress in layers: sunny days feel warm, but mornings and evenings can be cool, and the wet months call for an umbrella.

Han Chinese number 5,542,314 in Kunming, making up 86.16% of the population, while all the ethnic minorities together number 889,898, or 13.84%. Some of Yunnan's 26 officially recognised nationalities live in the city. The average life expectancy of Kunming residents is 76 years.

Downtown Kunming is organised around three big squares (Jinma Biji, Nanping and Dongfeng) and six main roads. The roads are Beijing, Zhengyi, Renmin, Dongfeng, Jinbi and Qingnian. Shopping is concentrated along Jingxing Street, Guanghua Street, Zhengyi Road, Qingnian Road, Renmin Road and Nanping Street, the last built on top of a stretch of Dongfeng Road. Locals like strolling on three of these in particular: Nanping Street, Zhengyi Road and Jingxing Street.

The modern centre is Nanping Square, beside the Panlong River's western bank and at the junction of Nanping and Zhengyi streets. This is where the old southern city wall once ran. Today it is a crowded shopping precinct of clothing and electronics stores, surrounded by new high-rises, and a preserved portion of the old town lies to its north.

Before Nanping took over, the city's heart was Dongfeng Square, across the Panlong River to the east, outside the old walls, where Beijing Road crosses Dongfeng Road. In the morning, crowds do taijiquan and play badminton there, and at weekends amateur theatre is staged. The Panlong itself has been fed artificially since the Songhua Dam was built, so it now works almost as a canal, taking treated sewage and wastewater from surrounding pipes.

The centre also matters to Kunming's Hui Muslim community. Shuncheng Street, among the last old lanes downtown, was formerly a Muslim quarter, though fast modernisation has swept it away in favour of apartments and malls. The city's new mosque, Nancheng Qingzhen Si, stands behind a supermarket one block north of Zhengyi Road. Its green dome and chevron-patterned minaret can be seen from far away, and it occupies the site of an earlier Qing-dynasty building.

Jingxing Street runs west from Zhengyi Road just beyond the mosque. It leads to the daily bird and flower market that spills into the streets connecting it to Guanghua Street, the parallel road to the north. Many of the plants on sale, such as orchids, were gathered or farmed across the province.

Two big Chinese pagodas rise just south of Jinbi Road, outside the centre. Each has thirteen levels of white-painted brick, and each carries four iron cockerels on top. Construction of the West Pagoda took place between 824 and 859, in the Tang era. Its twin to the east dated from the same time, but a quake in 1833 destroyed it, and it was put up again in 1882 in the Tang manner. To reach the West Pagoda, go south along Dongsi Road, pass another mosque, and look for the narrow lane on the right. The East Pagoda is a slightly tilted, mainly decorative copy in an ornamental garden a few minutes' walk east along Shulin Jie. The temples that go with both pagodas are closed to visitors.

Many streets in Kunming are lined with jacaranda trees, which bloom richly in mid to late April, especially along Jiaochang Middle Road. They are not native to the area. The city grew them from seeds exchanged with Algeria, first raised in the Kunming Botanical Garden, and later used those seeds to plant the street trees.
Cuihu Park (Green Lake Park) is mostly a lake ringed by greenery. A statue of Nie Er, who composed China's national anthem, stands on its west side.

Xishan Park carries another monument to Nie Er. It is best known for the Longmen Grottoes, which hold several ancient temples and the "dragon gate" itself. They are not the same as the grottoes with the same name at Luoyang.
Daguan Park lies on Dian Chi, at Kunming's south-western edge. The Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty originally laid it out, and later changes have added a noisy funfair, food stalls and shops.
Kunming's zoo, founded in 1950, adjoins Yuantong Park, which is known for the Yuantong Temple inside. The zoo keeps 5,000 animals of 140 species and draws 3 million visitors a year.
Further options: Black Dragon Pool and the botanical gardens (both in the north), the World Horti-Expo Garden in the north-east, and a tea garden at Wenmiao in Wuhua District.

In the northern suburbs, the World Horti-Expo Garden was created for the 1999 World Horticulture Exposition. That event lasted six months, from 1 May until 31 October, and its slogan was "Man and Nature" looking ahead to the 21st century. A cable car links it to Golden Temple Park on nearby Mingfeng Hill. The temple was built in 1602, the 30th year of the Wanli reign in the Ming dynasty. Everything in it, from beams and pillars to doors, windows, tiles, Buddha statues and inscribed boards, is copper, with a total weight of over 200 tonnes, which makes it the biggest copper building in China.

If you visit only one temple, make it Yuantong, the largest and most famous Buddhist temple in Kunming. The original structure dates back over 1,200 years to the Tang dynasty. It lies in a depression at the south end of Yuantong Park. About 12 km (7.5 miles) north-west of the centre is the Qiongzhu Si, or Bamboo Temple, built in 639 and rebuilt between 1422 and 1428. Many more Buddhist temples line the road to the Dragon Gate in the Western Mountains.
Museums worth knowing:
Yunnan Provincial Museum
Kunming City Museum, redeveloped in 2014
The Natural History Museum of Zoology, which opened in November 2006
Yunnan Ethnology Museum, opened in 1995

Athletes from China and abroad come to Kunming each year for high-altitude training, and the city has been the national high-elevation training base for more than three decades. There are two big training complexes.

The Hongta Sports Center was paid for by the Hongta (Red Pagoda) tobacco company, which spent US$58 million to open it in 2000. It stands near Haigeng Park. Professionals use it most, yet it also operates as a sports club for the public and hosts amateur football every weekend. The complex has about ten football pitches (one with a running track around it), a 50-metre (160-foot) swimming pool, a badminton hall, tennis courts and a basketball court. It has one of China's few ice hockey rinks, a gym with treadmills and weights, games rooms with air hockey and pool tables, and a bowling alley in the basement. A hotel with 101 rooms and a restaurant complete the site.

Haigeng National Training Center is ten minutes' drive from Hongta, beside Dianchi near the award-winning Lakeview Golf Club and some new condominium blocks. The government built it in the late 1970s to specialise in altitude training.

Golf is a major attraction, with four courses less than an hour's drive from downtown. The most famous is Spring City Golf and Lake Resort in neighbouring Yiliang County. The older material we have says US Golf Digest ranked it the best course in China and Hong Kong six years running, and that Asian Golf Monthly named it the best golf resort in Asia in 2004. It hosts the Kunming stage of the Omega China Tour. The resort is a US$600 million project that began in 1992 with investment led by Singapore's Keppel Land Group, and two courses were designed by Jack Nicklaus and Robert Trent Jones, Jr. These claims are dated, so treat them as background.
Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose venue
Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, whose Mountain Course was designed by Jack Nicklaus
Lakeview Golf Villa
The tennis courts in Cuihu Park
Kunming Municipal Athletic Center
Kunming Gymnasium
Yunnan Provincial Stadium, where Hongta Yunnan Football Club plays
Wuhua District Stadium

Three things set Kunming apart from other south-western cities: abundant natural resources, a big consumer market, and a gentle climate. Because it is at the centre of Yunnan, which is one of China's largest producers of farm goods, minerals and hydroelectric power, it acts as the commercial hub for most of the province's resources.

Copper, lead and zinc are its chief industries, and the iron and steel sector has been enlarged. The salt and phosphate mines around the city are among China's largest, and Yunnan Copper Company Limited, based here, is one of the province's biggest mining firms. From the late 1970s food and tobacco processing and the making of construction equipment and machinery joined the list. The city is also a centre of engineering and of making machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and vehicles, including heavy trucks. It has chemical plants, plastics, cement works and textile mills, and its processing factories (tanneries, woodworking, papermaking) use local farm products. In 1997 Yunnan Tire Co. opened a plant in Kunming able to make two million tyres a year.

In May 1995 the State Council designated Kunming an Open City, and within the year the city had approved 929 overseas-funded enterprises with total investment of US$2.3 billion, of which US$1.1 billion was foreign capital, and over 40 projects each had investment above US$9 million.

Two main zones operate. The Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone focuses on biological medicine, new materials, electronic information and agriculture. The Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone focuses on mechanical equipment, biological science and food, information industry and software.
Beyond these, the National Development and Reform Commission has recognised 30 key industrial parks in Yunnan. Among the largest are:
Chenggong Industrial Park
Anning Industrial Park
Songming Yanglin Industrial Development Zone
Dongchuan Special Industrial Park
Xundian Special Industrial Park
Kunming Haikou Industrial Park

A 2008 ranking of Yunnan's 100 biggest enterprises by 2007 revenue placed 65 of them in Kunming. Hongta Group led the list with revenue of about RMB 39.88 billion in 2007, and tobacco remains the largest sector in the province. These figures date from 2008, so look for newer data if you need it.

Kunming lies on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, and trains and planes are the two main ways to reach it from outside Yunnan. The sources give no further detail on routes, so check current timetables when you plan your journey.

yunnan-normal-university.h: Yunnan: the wider region and its past

blocks.x: A university's province shapes student life as much as its campus does. Yunnan has one of the longest and richest histories in China, as the sections below show.

The Yuanmou Man was a Homo erectus fossil found by railway engineers in the 1960s. It is considered the oldest known hominid fossil in China, from about 1.7 million years ago. By Neolithic times, settlements existed near Lake Dian whose people made stone tools and put up simple wooden buildings.

Around the 3rd century BC, the area around present-day Kunming was called Dian. A general from the state of Chu named Zhuang Qiao (庄蹻) came in from the upper Yangtze and proclaimed himself "King of Dian". He and his followers brought a wave of Chinese influence, which began a long tradition of migration and cultural expansion into Yunnan.

When Qin Shi Huang united China in 221 BC, his power spread south and Yunnan received commanderies and counties. The existing "Five Foot Way" road in Sichuan was extended south as far as modern Qujing in eastern Yunnan. The Han dynasty conquered Dian in 109 BC during its southern campaigns, and Emperor Wu sent General Guo Chang (郭昌) south, who eventually created the Yizhou commandery. By then farming in Yunnan had improved a lot. People used bronze tools and ploughs and kept cattle, horses, sheep, goats, pigs and dogs. Anthropologists link them to the people known today as the Tai, who lived in tribal groups, sometimes under exiled Chinese leaders.

In the Three Kingdoms era, Nanzhong was the collective name for a region covering today's Yunnan together with western Guizhou and southern Sichuan. With the central government fragmenting, Yunnan became more autonomous and local tribal structures gained strength. In AD 225 the famous statesman Zhuge Liang led three columns into Yunnan to subdue the tribes. His seven captures of a local magnate called Meng Huo became legendary in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

In the 4th century nomadic peoples overran much of northern China. The Cuan (爨) clan arrived in Yunnan during the 320s. Cuan Chen (爨琛) proclaimed himself king and ruled from the area of Lake Dian, then called Kunchuan, and the clan governed eastern Yunnan for over four hundred years afterwards.

International trade crossed Yunnan too. An old overland route before the Tang dynasty ran from Yunnan through the Irrawaddy region of Burma to Bengal. The region was home to peoples who were not fully under Tang control, so although the route was ancient it saw little use before the Tang, and Chinese efforts to control it were disrupted when Nanzhao rose.

Before the 8th century many local tribes, clans and cultures lived in Yunnan. Six small realms called "zhao" arose around Lake Erhai, in the Dali area. Their names were Mengzi (蒙巂) and Yuexi (越析), then Langqiong (浪穹) and Dengdan (邆赕), and finally Shilling (施浪) and Mengshe (蒙舍). "Zhao" (诏) is an indigenous, non-Chinese word meaning "king" or "kingdom". Mengshe lay south of the other five, which is why the enlarged state was called Nanzhao, the Southern Kingdom.

By the 730s Nanzhao controlled the Erhai Lake area. In 738 its fourth king, Piluoge, brought western Yunnan together, and the Tang court recognised him as the king of Yunnan. Thirteen Nanzhao kings governed from Dali across more than two centuries, acting as a buffer state between the Tang dynasty and the Tibetan Empire.

By the 750s Nanzhao controlled all of Yunnan and had become a possible rival of Tang China, so clashes followed. Hostilities started in 750, when Nanzhao captured Yaozhou, the largest Tang town in all of Yunnan. A year later Xianyu Zhongtong (鮮于仲通), who commanded Jiannan (in modern Sichuan), led an expedition against it. Nanzhao's king Geluofeng treated the earlier clash as a personal matter and wrote to Xianyu seeking peace, but Xianyu held the envoys and refused. Facing Tang armies, Nanzhao turned to the Tibetan Empire. The Tubo and Nanzhao agreed to be "fraternal states" and Geluofeng received the title zanpuzhong, or "younger brother". Thanks to this alliance Xianyu's army of 80,000 men was shrunk to a quarter of its size.

Tang tried again. A new expedition in 753 also failed. In 754 more than 100,000 Tang troops reached the Dali plain and met only another slaughter. By the end of the 8th century Tang was no longer a serious threat.

Nanzhao kept expanding for decades. In 829 it suddenly raided Sichuan and reached Chengdu, and when it withdrew it took hundreds of Sichuan people, skilled artisans among them, to Yunnan. In 832 it seized the capital of the Pyu kingdom in upper Burma, and it also attacked the Khmer people of Zhenla. By then it was probably the strongest kingdom in mainland Southeast Asia and took an active part in the region's many-sided politics.

In 859 Nanzhao took Bozhou, deepening the conflict with Tang. The Tang governor of Annam recovered Bozhou the next year, but while his army was there, Nanzhao, helped by native peoples, occupied Hanoi. When Tang forces came back, Nanzhao withdrew from Hanoi but attacked and looted Yongzhou. In the winter of 862 it invaded Annam again with over 50,000 men, in alliance with local groups. Reports say Tang lost over 150,000 soldiers, killed or captured, in the two Annam battles. Tang won in Hanoi in autumn 866 and soon drove out all Nanzhao forces, but it could no longer attack Nanzhao. While losing in Annam, Nanzhao still raided Sichuan occasionally: Shilong (世隆), the eighth king and first emperor of Nanzhao, invaded in 869, and another attack came in 874.

The once-powerful empire vanished. In 928 Yang Ganzhen (楊干貞) took the Dachanghe throne, made the qingpingguan Zhao Shanzheng emperor of Datianxing (大天興), and in 929 abolished Zhao Shanzheng and made himself emperor of Dayining (大義寧).
Yunnan is also famous among palaeontologists. Two examples:
Yunnanozoon, a possible chordate from the Lower Cambrian
Jingshanosaurus, a long-necked prosauropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic
Yunnan Normal University lists 183 programs for international students on this site: 56 bachelor, 111 master's, 14 doctoral, 2 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 183 taught in Chinese. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 15,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 15,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 17,000 to CNY 170,000 (median CNY 17,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for doctoral programs ranges from CNY 19,000 to CNY 21,000 (median CNY 21,000), according to the university's published fee table.

183 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

yunnan-normal-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Yunnan Normal University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Kunming, register at Yunnan Normal University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Yunnan University, usually shortened to YNU (the Chinese name is 云南大学), is a public university in Kunming, the capital of Yunnan Province in south-west China. Students and locals call it "Yunda": "Yun" comes from Yunnan and "da" from daxue, the Chinese word for university, which is the same pattern many Chinese universities use for their nicknames.

The university belongs to the province but is jointly funded by the Yunnan Provincial People's Government and the national Ministry of Education. It sits inside two national programmes that channel extra money and attention to selected universities, Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction, and it also appears on the list of key universities supported under the "China Western Development" plan. For an international applicant that combination means a school with real national backing, in a region the government is actively investing in.
Classes started in April 1923, a few months after the founding in December 1922. The school was run privately at first and carried another name, and it has been renamed six times in all.

The university was established on 8 December 1922 by General Tang Jiyao, the military strongman who ran Yunnan in the 1920s. The first students were admitted on 20 April 1923. The original name was "Dong Lu University", where "Dong Lu" can be rendered as "Eastern Road" or "Eastern Land". Of its six name changes over roughly eight decades, the current one dates from 1934.

The institution gained its reputation during the Second World War. Because Kunming was far from the main fighting, many leading Chinese scholars, especially from Beijing and Nanjing and many of them holding doctorates from respected American universities, moved south to escape the northern war zone. Most of them taught at the newly formed National Southwestern Associated University, known as "Lianda", but a number ended up at Yunnan University for a variety of reasons. They found a school with a noticeable French flavour: its president held a doctorate from the Sorbonne, and the university built a name for research on the French language and French civilisation. That tradition still shows today. In 2011 its school of foreign languages was honoured as a "Chevalier des Palmes Académiques", the French academic decoration often described as the knighthood of the academic palm.

The most influential figure of this era was the mathematician Professor Xiong Qinglai, who served as president from 1937 to 1947. Under him the university was reorganised on the academic model of Tsinghua University. A remarkable group of teachers joined during these years, including Fei Xiaotong, Chu Tunan, Chen Xingshen, Hua Luogen, Yan Jici, Feng Youlan and Lü Shuxiang. Together they made the school a broad, comprehensive university with some influence at home and abroad. By 1946 it had five faculties and 18 departments, and a standard English-language reference work, the Concise Encyclopædia Britannica, named it as one of fifteen top-ranking Chinese universities.

In the early 1950s the government reorganised higher education across the whole country, and every university was affected. Most of Yunnan University's departments were cut, and by 1958 only two faculties and six departments remained. Like all Chinese universities, it then lived through a hard decade from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s, including the Cultural Revolution. Conditions improved a great deal once the reform era opened in the late 1970s, and the university has been rebuilding and expanding since.

The main campus stands in the heart of Kunming, a city famous for its gentle weather. The site is 426,669 square metres, with 350,000 square metres of that built up as teaching, library and research space. The campus faces Green Lake Park, where Siberian black-headed gulls spend their winters, and ginkgo trees give it shade. Cherry and plum trees ring the grounds, and Yuantong Hill is right next door, with a zoo known for rare animals and birds.

Because the city centre offers little room to grow, the university opened a second main campus at Chenggong, about 45 minutes from the original site by bus or subway. The first academic year there was 2010 to 2011, and it has grown considerably since.

Donglu Campus (东陆校区) is the old campus in the city centre, next to Cuihu Lake (Green Lake). Plenty of older buildings and monuments survive there, such as the Huize building, and it is being kept as the centre of graduate study.
Chenggong Campus (呈贡校区) is the new campus in Kunming's University Town, in the Chenggong district. The first undergraduates moved in around 2009. It is much larger than the Green Lake campus.
Lijiang Culture and Tourism College (丽江文化旅游学院) used to be a branch campus of the university; it is in Lijiang.
The practical point for a newcomer: check which campus your programme is based on before you book accommodation, since the two are a long commute apart.

Two libraries serve the university: an older one at Donglu and a newer, larger one at Chenggong. Together they hold over 1.2 million books, including rare copies of historically valuable works, and borrowing, cataloguing, access and public searching are all managed through a computerised network.

There is also a good-sized herbarium. It is believed to rank second in age within Yunnan, behind the Kunming Institute of Botany's. Its focus is the pteridophytes (ferns and their relatives) of China, especially the south-west, and Chu Weiming has directed it for many years.
The university also has its own kindergarten, a secondary school and a foreign-language secondary school attached to it.
Today Yunnan University is a national key university. A large academic staff teaches a broad curriculum spanning the liberal arts, law, the sciences, technology, economics and management.

Enrolment on campus stands at 19,872. The full-time undergraduates number 9,919, and postgraduates total 2,853, made up of 94 doctoral candidates, 684 master's candidates, 1,842 on advanced postgraduate courses, 170 on specialist law programmes and 63 in the advanced class for teachers. Another 7,100 take night-class and correspondence programmes. These numbers are dated, so confirm current enrolment on the university's own website.

Staff total 2,372, of whom 1,981 are specialised professionals: 222 full professors, 409 associate professors and 987 full-time instructors. Altogether 683 instructors hold a doctorate or a master's degree.
The university is organised into the schools, colleges and institutes below, which I have grouped by subject area so they are easier to scan. Under the humanities and social sciences:
Humanity and Liberal Arts
Foreign Languages
International Cultures
International Relations
Law
Public Management
Economy
Business Administration and Tourism Management
Tourism and Culture, based in Lijiang
Development Research (an institute)
Under science, engineering and medicine:
Life Science
Earth Sciences
Ecology and Environment
Materials and Energy
Information
Software Engineering
Medicine
Other units:
The International College of Modern Design Arts
The School of Occupational Technology
The School of Adult Education
There is also the Institute for Palaeontology, which grew out of the Yunnan Key Laboratory for Palaeobiology.

The units above contain upwards of 30 teaching departments and divisions that offer 65 majors, each a four-year bachelor's course. The university additionally operates 25 research institutes, 16 development and research centres, ten research offices and four service centres focused on teaching.

Three subjects, History, Biology and Mathematical Science, are designated to train national-level teaching and research talent. Yunnan University has asked the Ministry of Education to approve a state-level experimental base for all-round liberal arts training, and it already operates a state base where professional teachers are trained.

In terms of degree authority, the university holds forty-eight master's conferring points, four doctoral ones, one post-doctoral mobile station and three specialised degree points (law, occupational education and MBA). Two key state-level discipline groups are being built up, along with sixteen key provincial disciplines. A state-level centre for new product development and a Ministry of Education key laboratory also belong to it.

Research has mattered from the beginning, and staff keep a close eye on international developments. Ecology stands out: the Institute of Ecology and Geobotany wrote textbooks on classifying plant communities and on plant ecology that are used nationwide. "Geobotany" is the Russian and continental European name for the study of how a region's plants are distributed geographically; English-speaking countries say phytogeography.

The university press has put out more than two million volumes of scholarly work. Ideological Frontier, its social-science journal, holds the "Kernel National Periodical" title, and the natural-science Academic Journal of Yunnan University has been rated an excellent journal among China's key universities.

Shares in the university's Science and Technology Corporation were listed on the Chinese stock markets on 27 April 1998. This made Yunnan University the eighth of over 1,000 Chinese higher-education institutions to own a high-tech company that issues shares.

Its main product, the Yunda-120 growth regulator, has been used on 67 billion square metres of cultivated land. The corporation started as a research group with a little over 10,000 yuan in funds and grew in a short time into a listed company valued at more than 10 billion yuan.

Another company, the Biological Technology Corporation of Yunnan University, was China's first enterprise to hold independent intellectual property rights in single-clone antibody research. Two of its products, a contraceptive test paper and a sterility test paper, helped shape the national standards.

The Yunnan University Fund sits on the council of the Fund of Universities and Colleges of China as an acting member. Close to seventy directors, both Chinese and overseas, belong to it, and they have attracted scholars who push forward the reform, building and development of the university.

In recent years Yunda has built exchange relationships at different levels with more than 50 universities and research organisations in over twenty countries and regions, among them the United States, Great Britain, Russia, Japan and Australia.
The university regularly comes first in its own province and inside the national top 100. For a sense of its global standing, three international tables are useful:
Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), 2025: 301st to 400th worldwide.
CWTS Leiden Ranking, 2024 edition: 527th in the world, based on publications from 2019 to 2022.
Nature Index 2024 Annual Tables: among the top 250 research universities globally for high-quality natural science publications.
In short, it is the leading university of its province, a solid national performer and a respectable name in global research tables.
Daily life for a student mostly depends on the city outside the gate: its weather, its transport and the things to do. The sections below introduce Kunming.

Kunming is in the east-central part of Yunnan, at 24°23' to 26°22' north and 102°10' to 103°40' east. The municipal area covers 21,600 km² (8,340 sq mi) and measures 140 km (87 mi) across at its widest, east to west, and 220 km (137 mi) from north to south at its longest.

The city lies in a fertile basin beside the northern shore of Lake Dian, hemmed in by mountains on the north, west and east, and it has long been a hinge for travel and trade in the south-west. Dian is known as "the Pearl of the Plateau". It is the largest lake in Yunnan and ranks sixth among China's freshwater lakes, with an area of roughly 340 km² (130 sq mi).

The terrain is varied. Mazong Ridge, on the Jiaozi Snow Mountain in Luquan, is the highest spot at 4,247 m (13,934 ft). The lowest is in Dongchuan District, where the Xiao River joins the Jinsha River, at 695 m (2,280 ft). Downtown sits at 1,891 m (6,204 ft). If you arrive from the coast, expect thin air and give yourself a few days to adjust.

The city sits on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau at 1,888 m (6,194 ft). A low latitude and a high altitude together give it one of China's gentlest climates, with winters that are short, cool and dry and summers that are long, mild and humid. Plants and flowers flourish in the permanent spring-like weather, hence the nickname "City of Eternal Spring", and greenery and blossom cover the city all year.

Hot summers are unusual: the thermometer has gone beyond 30 °C (86 °F) only on a few occasions. A few winters bring surprise snowfalls. The climate is classed as subtropical highland (Köppen Cwb). Over a full day, the average temperature rises from a January figure of 9.3 °C (48.7 °F) to 20.7 °C (69.3 °F) in June. Daily highs are lowest in December and highest in June.

The monsoon runs May to October, and the other months are drier. Mean annual temperature is 16.0 °C (60.8 °F), and yearly rainfall of 991.0 mm (39.0 in) falls mostly in summer, nearly three-fifths between June and August. Frost-free days number 230 a year. Sunshine, as a share of what is possible, is lowest in July (29%) and highest in February (70%), adding up to 2,240.9 sunny hours in a year. The coldest day on record, 29 December 1983, hit −7.8 °C (18.0 °F), and the hottest, 25 May 2014, reached 32.9 °C (91.2 °F).

Han Chinese number 5,542,314, or 86.16% of the population, while all ethnic minorities together add up to 889,898, or 13.84%. Some of the province's 26 nationalities live in Kunming, and average life expectancy in the city is 76 years.

Downtown has three big squares, Jinma Biji, Nanping and Dongfeng, and six main roads: Beijing, Zhengyi, Renmin, Dongfeng, Jinbi and Qingnian. Shoppers head for Jingxing Street, Guanghua Street, Zhengyi Road, Qingnian Road, Renmin Road and Nanping Street, which was built over a stretch of Dongfeng Road. For a walk without traffic, the favourites are Jingxing Street, Nanping Street and Zhengyi Road.

The modern centre is Nanping Square, where Nanping Street crosses Zhengyi Street, beside the Panlong River's western bank. The old southern city wall used to run here. Now it is a packed shopping district of clothes and electronics stores, surrounded by new towers, with a preserved old quarter lying north of it.

Dongfeng Square was once seen as the centre. It lies across the Panlong River to the east, outside the old walls, where Beijing Road meets Dongfeng Road. Early in the morning crowds practise taijiquan and play badminton, and amateur actors perform at weekends. Ever since the Songhua Dam went up, the Panlong has had an artificial flow, so it acts more like a canal, and pipes from the surroundings feed it treated sewage and wastewater.

This district also matters to Kunming's Hui people. Shuncheng Street, a Muslim quarter and among the final old streets of the central city, was pulled down for flats and shopping centres as the city modernised quickly. The city's new mosque, Nancheng Qingzhen Si, stands one block north of Zhengyi Road behind a supermarket, built over an earlier Qing-era mosque; its green dome and minaret with a chevron pattern can be seen from far off.

Walk west from Zhengyi Road past the mosque and Jingxing Street takes you to the part of town where a bird and flower market fills the connecting streets every day, north of and parallel to Guanghua Street. Orchids and other plants gathered and farmed all over the province are sold there.

Jinbi Road is south of Dongfeng Road, and both meet Beijing Road. Further south, beyond the centre, two big Chinese pagodas stand. Each has thirteen levels of whitewashed brick and four iron cockerels on top. The West Pagoda dates from the Tang dynasty, 824 to 859. Its twin, the East Pagoda, was built simultaneously, collapsed in an 1833 earthquake and was rebuilt in the Tang style in 1882. For the West Pagoda, walk south on Dongsi Road, pass a second mosque, and look for a narrow lane to your right. The East Pagoda, slightly tilted and more ornamental, is a replica in a landscaped garden, a short walk east on Shulin Jie. Visitors cannot enter the temples that belong to either pagoda.

Jacaranda trees line many streets and flower heavily in the second half of April, most visibly along Jiaochang Middle Road. They did not originate in Kunming. The seeds came from Algeria in an exchange, were raised in the Kunming Botanical Garden and then supplied to the city for roadside planting.
Cuihu Park, also called Green Lake Park, is one of the main parks, largely a lake with greenery around it. A statue of Nie Er, who composed China's national anthem, stands on the western side.

A second Nie Er monument is in Xishan Park. The park's best-known feature is the Longmen Grottoes, which are unrelated to the Luoyang grottoes of the same name; they hold several ancient temples and the "dragon gate" that gives them their name.
Daguan Park is on Dian Chi, at the south-western limit of the city. The Kangxi Emperor had it laid out in the Qing era, and since then it has picked up a loud funfair, food stalls and emporiums.

The zoo opened in 1950 and shares a boundary with Yuantong Park, whose Yuantong Temple is its claim to fame. Around 5,000 animals of 140 species live there, and it welcomes some 3 million visitors annually.
More green space can be found at the Kunming Botanical Gardens and Black Dragon Pool (north), the World Horti-Expo Garden (north-east) and Wenmiao Tea Garden (Wuhua District).

In the northern suburbs, the World Horti-Expo Garden was created for the 1999 World Horticulture Exposition, held from 1 May to 31 October 1999. Its theme was "Man and Nature—Marching Toward the 21st Century". A cable car runs from the garden to Golden Temple Park on neighbouring Mingfeng Hill. The Golden Temple was built in 1602, in the 30th year of the Ming dynasty's Wanli reign. Every beam and pillar, arch, door, window, tile, Buddhist statue and plaque is made of copper, and the whole weighs over 200 tons, making it China's biggest copper building.

The largest and most famous Buddhist temple in Kunming is Yuantong Temple, whose first buildings are over 1,200 years old, dating to the Tang dynasty. It lies in a dip at the south end of Yuantong Park. Roughly 12 km (7.5 mi) to the north-west of downtown, the Qiongzhu Si (Bamboo Temple) was built in 639 and rebuilt between 1422 and 1428. In the Western Mountains, plenty of Buddhist temples stand beside the road up to the Dragon Gate (龙门).
Yunnan Provincial Museum
Kunming City Museum (redeveloped in 2014)
Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology (opened November 2006)
Yunnan Ethnology Museum (opened 1995)
These four are the notable museums worth putting on a weekend list.

Kunming has been China's national base for high-altitude training for over 30 years, so every year it attracts Chinese and foreign athletes who want to train in thin air. Two major complexes serve them. One is Hongta Sports Center, the other is Haigeng National Training Center.

The Hongta Sports Center was paid for by the Hongta (Red Pagoda) cigarette company, which spent US$58 million on it in 2000. Next to Haigeng Park, it mostly serves professionals but also works as a public sports club, hosting amateur football every weekend. Facilities include roughly 10 football pitches (one with a running track around it), badminton and basketball courts, tennis courts, and a swimming pool of 50 m (160 ft). It has one of the few ice hockey rinks in China, a gym with treadmills and weights, game rooms for air hockey and pool tables, and a bowling alley in the basement. A restaurant and a 101-room hotel complete the complex.

Ten minutes from Hongta, on Dianchi (Lake Dian), is Haigeng National Training Center, near the prize-winning Lakeview Golf Club and some new apartment developments. It dates from the late 1970s, when the government built it purely for high-altitude training.

Golf is another big attraction. Four courses lie within an hour's drive of downtown. In nearby Yiliang County, Spring City Golf and Lake Resort has been rated the best course in China and Hong Kong by US Golf Digest for the last six years, and Asian Golf Monthly named it Asia's best golf resort in 2004. The Omega China Tour holds its Kunming round there. The project cost US$600 million and began in 1992 as an investment led by Keppel Land Group of Singapore. Jack Nicklaus and Robert Trent Jones, Jr designed its two courses.
Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose venue
Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, whose Mountain Course was designed by Jack Nicklaus
Lakeview Golf Villa
Cuihu Park tennis courts
Kunming Municipal Athletic Center
Kunming Gymnasium
Yunnan Provincial Stadium, where Hongta Yunnan Football Club plays
Wuhua District Stadium
That list covers the main public sports facilities in the city.

Compared with other south-western cities, Kunming has three strengths: a mild climate, great natural resources and a big consumer market. Yunnan is one of China's top producers of agricultural goods, minerals and hydroelectric power, and Kunming, at its centre, is the main trading hub for those resources.

Copper, lead and zinc production are the leading industries, and iron and steel output has been enlarged. Some of China's largest salt and phosphate mines are close to the city. Based in Kunming, Yunnan Copper Company Limited is among the province's biggest mining firms. From the late 1970s, food and tobacco processing, plus the making of building equipment and machines, joined the main industries.

The city is also strong in engineering, turning out machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and vehicles (including heavy goods vehicles), along with chemicals, plastics, cement and textiles. Tanneries, woodworking plants and papermaking factories turn local farm produce into goods. A tire plant opened in Kunming in 1997 under Yunnan Tire Co., able to make two million tires a year.

The State Council made Kunming an Open City in May 1995. Before the year ended, 929 overseas-funded enterprises had been approved, with total investment of $2.3 billion, of which $1.1 billion came from foreign capital. More than 40 projects had investments above $9 million each.

Kunming has two major development zones. The Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone focuses on biological medicine, new materials, electronic information and agriculture. The Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone focuses on mechanical equipment production, biological science and the food industry, and information industry and software.
The National Development and Reform Commission has recognised 30 key industrial parks across Yunnan Province. Some of the largest are listed here:
Chenggong Industrial Park
Anning Industrial Park
Songming Yanglin Industrial Development Zone
Dongchuan Special Industrial Park
Xundian Special Industrial Park
Kunming Haikou Industrial Park

In 2008, 65 of Yunnan's Top 100 Enterprises, ranked by 2007 revenue, were based in Kunming. The Hongta Group led with about RMB39.88 billion in 2007 revenue, and tobacco is still the province's biggest sector. These figures are old, so use them only as background.
Kunming lies on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, and rail and air are the two main ways to reach it from outside Yunnan.
