yunnan-university-of-finance-and-economi.h: About Yunnan University of Finance and Economics

blocks.x: The Yunnan University of Finance and Economics (YUFE; Chinese: 云南财经大学) is a provincial-level university in Kunming, Yunnan province, China focusing on fields related to commerce and management.

YUFE was established as the Yunnan Financial Cadres Training School in early 1951. Its goal was to train Communist Party officials in basic financial and accounting management skills. In 1958 the school was combined with four other training institutions to become the Yunnan Institute of Finance and Trade (YIFT). During the Cultural Revolution the school was shuttered for seven years, not fully resuming operation until 1978. The following year the provincial government announced a plan to transform YIFT into a full-fledged institution of higher education, extending its offerings to four-year bachelor's degrees.

In 1998, the People's Government of Yunnan Province announced a plan to merge the Yunnan Economic Management Cadres College with the Yunnan Institute of Finance and Trade. In 1999 the institution was awarded full university status, and renamed the Yunnan University of Finance and Economics.

It is a comprehensive university with programmes in economics, management, law, philosophy, liberal arts, natural science and engineering education. The university is accredited to offer bachelor's degrees, Master's degrees and Doctoral degrees.

The university has a total of 17 teaching departments, including the School of Finance, School of Business Administration, and the International Business School. It has a total 28 undergraduate specialties. This also consist of eight provincial key disciplines and four provincial key subjects.

YUFE has four first class disciplines in theoretical economics, applied economics, management, science, engineering and business administration. YUFE also has 40 other second-class disciplines for which the university can confer master's degrees.

The university has over 34,000 full-time students (undergraduate and graduate). The total number of students is approximately 24,000, including part-time students, foreign students and mature age students.

The faculty of YUFE comprises over 2,144 faculty members including 1,400 full-time lecturers. Among them, there are more than 300 professors or associate professors and 70 Doctors.  YUFE also hired 10-20 foreign expert teachers who teach English language classes and business classes in English.

As of 2024, Yunnan University of Finance and Economics ranked # 4 in Southwestern China region and # 29 nationwide among universities specialized in finance, business, and economics in the Best Chinese Universities Ranking.

YUFE's main campus in Kunming covers 1021 mu (68 hectares) with about 634,000 square meters of floor space. The Kunming campus library has a collection of 1.4 million items. In 2019 the university founded a branch campus of 1257 mu (84 hectares) in the nearby city of Anning.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Kunming, where Yunnan University of Finance and Economics is located.

Kunming is located in east-central Yunnan province. Its administrative area is located between latitudes 24°23' and 26°22' N, and longitudes 102°10' and 103°40' E, with a total area of 21,600 square kilometres (8,340 square miles). Its widest stretch from the east to the west amounts to 140 kilometres (87 miles) while its longest stretch from the north to the south amounts to 220 kilometres (137 miles).

Situated in a fertile lake basin on the northern shore of the Lake Dian and surrounded by mountains to the north, west, and east, Kunming has always played a pivotal role in the communications of southwestern China.  Lake Dian, known as "the Pearl of the Plateau", is the largest lake in Yunnan and the sixth largest freshwater lake in China.  It has an area of approximately 340 square kilometres (130 square miles). Kunming's highest point is Mazong Ridge of the Jiaozi Snow Mountain in Luquan with an elevation of 4,247 metres (13,934 feet), and its lowest point is the joint of the Xiao River and the Jinsha River in Dongchuan District, with an elevation of 695 metres (2,280 feet). Its downtown area is 1,891 metres (6,204 feet) above sea level.

Located at an elevation of 1,888 metres (6,194 feet) on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau with low latitude and high elevation, Kunming has one of the mildest climates in China, characterized by short, cool, and dry winters and long, pleasant, and humid summers. With its perpetual spring-like weather which provides the ideal climate for plants and flowers, Kunming is known as the "City of Eternal Spring". The weather has seldom reached high temperatures in summer, only exceeding 30 °C (86 °F) on a handful of occasions. However, freak snowfalls occur in occasional winters. Controlled by a subtropical highland climate (Köppen Cwb), the monthly 24-hour average temperature ranges from 9.3 °C (48.7 °F) in January to 20.7 °C (69.3 °F) in June, with daily high temperatures reaching their lowest point and peak in December and June, respectively. The city is covered with blossoms and lush vegetation all-year round. The period from May to October is the monsoon season and the rest of the year is relatively dry. The city has an annual mean temperature of 16.0 °C (60.8 °F), rainfall of 991.0 millimetres (39.0 in) (nearly three-fifths occurring from June to August) and a frost-free period of 230 days. With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 29% in July to 70% in February, the city receives 2,240.9 hours of bright sunshine annually. Extreme temperatures in the city have ranged from −7.8 to 32.9 °C (18.0 to 91.2 °F) on 29 December 1983 and 25 May 2014 respectively.

The population of Han is 5,542,314, accounting for 86.16%; the population of all ethnic minorities add up to 889,898, accounting for 13.84%. Some of the 26 nationalities in the province live in Kunming, and the average life expectancy of the city's population is 76 years old.

The city center has three major squares and six major streets: Jinma Biji Square, Nanping Square and Dongfeng Square are the main squares, while Beijing Road, Zhengyi Road, Renmin Road, Dongfeng Road, Jinbi Road, and Qingnian Road are the main streets. Jingxing Street, Guanghua Street, Zhengyi Road, Nanping Street (built on top of a section of Dongfeng Road), Qingnian Road, and Renmin Road are the main commercial areas in Kunming; the most popular pedestrian streets are Nanping Street, Zhengyi Road, and Jingxing Street.

Kunming's modern city center is Nanping Square on the west bank of the Panlong River, at the intersection of Nanping Street and Zhengyi Street. This area is where Kunming's southern city wall once stood. This area is a crowded and dense modern shopping precinct packed with clothing and electronics stores. Surrounding the area are plenty of new high-rises, along with an area of preserved old city to the north. The area formerly considered the city center is Dongfeng Square, located on the east bank of the Panlong River outside of the old city walls at the intersection of Beijing Road and Dongfeng Road, where in the mornings there are crowds doing taijiquan and playing badminton. Weekend amateur theatre is also performed in the square. The Panlong River has had an artificial flow ever since the construction of the Songhua Dam, and the river has been developed into what is effectively a canal. The river receives treated sewage and wastewater from surrounding pipes.

The center is an area of importance to Kunming's Hui population, with Shuncheng Street, one of the last old streets in the center of the city, previously forming a Muslim quarter. Under Kunming's rapid modernisation, however, the street has been demolished to make way for apartments and shopping centers. Rising behind a supermarket one block north off Zhengyi Road, Nancheng Qingzhen Si is the city's new mosque, its green dome and chevron-patterned minaret visible from afar and built on the site of an earlier Qing edifice.

Running west off Zhengyi Road just past the mosque, Jingxing Street leads into a corner of the city that consists of Kunming's bird and flower market convening daily in the streets connecting it with the northerly, parallel to the Guanghua Street. The market offers many plants such as orchids that have been collected and farmed across the province.

Jinbi Road runs south of Dongfeng Road. Both of them connect to Beijing Road. Two large Chinese pagodas rise south of Jinbi Road and the city center, each a solid thirteen stories of whitewashed brick crowned with four iron cockerels. The West Pagoda was built between 824 and 859, during the Tang dynasty; its original counterpart, the East Pagoda, was built at the same time, but was destroyed by an earthquake in 1833 and rebuilt in the same Tang style in 1882. South down Dongsi Road, past another mosque, the entrance to the West Pagoda is along a narrow lane on the right. The East Pagoda is a more cosmetic, slightly tilted duplicate standing in an ornamental garden a few minutes' walk east on Shulin Jie. The temples associated with both pagodas are closed to the public.

Many streets are lined with Jacaranda trees, which can be seen blooming abundantly in mid to late April, particularly on Jiaochang Middle Road. The trees are not native to Kunming, but originate from seeds exchanged with Algeria, which were grown in the Kunming Botanical Garden. Seeds from the botanical garden were then used by the city to plant the trees along streets.

Cuihu Park (Green Lake Park) is one of Kunming's major parks and is predominately a lake surrounded by greenery. Located in the west side of the park is a statue of Nie Er, the composer of China's national anthem.

Another monument to Nie Er is located in Xishan Park, most well known for the Longmen Grottoes (not to be confused with the identically named grottoes in Luoyang), containing several ancient temples and the titular Longmen ("dragon gate").

Daguan Park lies on Dian Chi in Kunming's southwestern limits. Originally laid out by the Kangxi Emperor in the Qing dynasty, it has been modified over the years to include a noisy funfair, food stalls and emporiums.
Kunming's zoo, founded in 1950, is adjoined to Yuantong Park, known for the Yuantong Temple within. The zoo houses 5,000 animals from 140 species and receives 3 million visitors a year.
Other parks in Kunming include Black Dragon Pool and the Kunming Botanical Gardens in the north, the World Horti-Expo Garden in the northeast, and Wenmiao Tea Garden in Wuhua District.

The World Horti-Expo Garden is located in the northern suburbs of Kunming and was built for the 1999 World Horticulture Exposition, which ran from 1 May to 31 October 1999. It had the theme of "Man and Nature—Marching Toward the 21st Century". Golden Temple Park, located on Mingfeng Hill nearby, is connected by cable car to the World Horti-Expo Garden. Constructed in 1602 (the 30th year of the Wanli reign period of the Ming dynasty), all of its beams, pillars, arches, doors, windows, tiles, Buddhist statues, and horizontal inscribed boards are made of copper, weighing more than 200 tons. It is the largest copper building in China.

Yuantong Temple is Kunming's major Buddhist temple. It is Kunming's largest and most famous temple with the original structure being first constructed more than 1,200 years ago during the Tang dynasty. The temple sits in a depression on the southern side of Yuantong Park. Northwest about 12 km (7.5 mi) from the city center is the Qiongzhu Si (Bamboo Temple) built in 639 and rebuilt in 1422 to 1428. Numerous Buddhist temples line the road to the Dragon Gate (龙门) in the Western Mountains.
Notable museums in Kunming include:
Yunnan Provincial Museum
Kunming City Museum (redeveloped in 2014)
Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology (opened in November 2006)
Yunnan Ethnology Museum (opened 1995)

Every year, many Chinese and international athletes come to Kunming for high-altitude training. The city has been China's national high-elevation training base for more than 30 years. There are two major training complexes, Hongta Sports Center and Haigeng National Training Center.

Hongta Sports Center was built in 2000 by Hongta (Red Pagoda) cigarette company, at a cost of US$58 million. Located near Haigeng Park, the complex is mostly used by professional athletes, but also acts as a sports club for the general public. Every weekend, it hosts amateur football matches. Aside from about 10 football pitches, including one surrounded by a running track, Hongta also has a 50-metre (160-foot) swimming pool, a badminton gymnasium, tennis courts and a basketball court. It also has one of China's few ice hockey rinks, and a workout room with treadmills and weightlifting machines. There are also game rooms for air hockey; also pool tables and a basement bowling alley. The complex comes complete with a 101-room hotel and restaurant.

Haigeng National Training Center is located ten minutes away from Hongta on Dianchi (Lake Dian) near Kunming's award-winning Lakeview Golf Club and new condominium developments. This complex dates from the late 1970s and was built by the government specifically to specialize in high-altitude training.

Golf is a major attraction in Kunming. There are four golf courses within an hour's drive of downtown. For the last six years , Spring City Golf and Lake Resort in nearby Yiliang County has reigned as the best golf course in China and Hong Kong according to US Golf Digest. In 2004, it was named Asia's best golf resort by Asian Golf Monthly. It hosts the Kunming Leg of the Omega China Tour.

Kunming has attracted foreign investment in golf course development. "Spring City" Golf Resort is a US$600 million project that began as an investment led by Singapore's Keppel Land Group in 1992. Jack Nicklaus and course designer Robert Trent Jones, Jr designed the two courses.
Major sports facilities include:
Tuodong Sports Center, a multi-purpose venue
Golf: Spring City Golf and Lake Resort, its 'Mountain Course' was designed by Jack Nicklaus
Lakeview Golf Villa
Cuihu Park tennis courts
Kunming Municipal Athletic Center
Kunming Gymnasium
Yunnan Provincial Stadium, home to Hongta Yunnan Football Club
Wuhua District Stadium

Kunming has three economic advantages over other cities in southwest China: significant natural resources, a large consumer market and a mild climate. Due to its position at the center of Yunnan, one of China's largest producers of agricultural products, minerals and hydroelectricity, Kunming is the main commercial hub for most of the province's resources.

Kunming's chief industries are copper, lead and zinc production. Its iron and steel industry has been expanded. Salt and phosphate mines around Kunming are some of the largest in China. Yunnan Copper Company Limited, based in Kunming, is one of Yunnan's largest mining corporations. From the late 1970s, Kunming's main industries also came to include food and tobacco processing and the manufacture of construction equipment and machines.

In May 1995, the State Council approved Kunming as an Open City. By the end of 1995, the city had approved 929 overseas-funded enterprises with a total investment of $2.3 billion including $1.1 billion of foreign capital. More than 40 projects each had an investment of more than $9 million.

Kunming is a center of engineering and the manufacture of machine tools, electrical machinery, equipment and automobiles (including heavy goods vehicles). It has a chemical industry, and plastics, cement works and textile factories. Its processing plants, which include tanneries, woodworking and papermaking factories, use local agricultural products. In 1997, Yunnan Tire Co. opened a tire plant in Kunming, with a capacity to produce two million tires per year.

Kunming has two major development zones, Kunming High-tech Industrial Development Zone (biological medicine, new materials, electronic information, agriculture) and Kunming Economic and Technology Development Zone (mechanical equipment production, biological science and food industry, information industry, software).
There are also 30 key industrial parks promulgated and recognized by National Development and Reform Commission in Yunnan Province. The largest include:
Chenggong Industrial Park
Anning Industrial Park
Songming Yanglin Industrial Development Zone
Dongchuan Special Industrial Park
Xundian Special Industrial Park
Kunming Haikou Industrial Park.

As of 2008, Kunming is home to 65 of the Top 100 Enterprises in Yunnan Province. The top 100 enterprises were based on their revenues for 2007. Hongta Group, with revenues of some RMB39.88 billion for 2007 topped the list. The tobacco sector remains the largest sector in the province.
Kunming is situated on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau. Rail and air are the main two methods to travel to or from Kunming from outside Yunnan.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: Zhejiang Gongshang University at a glance

blocks.x: Zhejiang Gongshang University (浙江工商大学) is a public university in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang Province in eastern China. Its Chinese name literally means "Zhejiang Industrial and Commercial University", which tells you where its strengths traditionally lie. It is run by the province of Zhejiang rather than directly by the national government.

The university reported two items of recent news in 2026. It said that its nine micro-majors were registered in the Ministry of Education's "Double Thousand Plan", and it noted publications by its faculty in the Journal of the American Statistical Association and the Journal of Business & Economic Statistics. If you want to judge the current teaching and research profile, those details are worth following up on the university's own website.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: Why Hangzhou matters to a student

blocks.x: Student life depends as much on the city outside the gate as on the campus. The sections below describe Hangzhou in detail: its geography, weather, population, belief traditions, economy, scenery and culture. After that comes a longer look at the province of Zhejiang and its past.

Hangzhou lies in the northwest of Zhejiang Province. It is where the Grand Canal of China, which stretches all the way to Beijing. It occupies the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. As a sub-provincial city, its administrative area stretches west to the mountainous edge of Anhui, while to the east it reaches the coastal plain beside Hangzhou Bay. The downtown was built around the eastern and northern shores of West Lake, which is a little north of the Qiantang River.

The Qiantang is the largest river in Zhejiang. Each year, from the 15th to the 18th of the eighth lunar month, the Qiantang Tide arrives. It is known as the "Biggest Tide in the World". The largest tidal bore anywhere rushes up the river through Hangzhou, reaching as high as 12 metres (39 feet).

Hangzhou has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) and four distinct seasons. Summers are long, very hot and humid. Winters are chilly, cloudy and rather drier, with snow now and then. The yearly mean temperature is 17.0 °C (62.6 °F), and monthly daily averages run between 5 °C (41.0 °F) for January and 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) for July. Annual rainfall averages 1,438 mm (56.6 in).

In June the city feels the plum rains that the Asian monsoon brings. Typhoon storms can hit in late summer, in August and September, but they seldom strike Hangzhou directly. They usually hit the coast farther south, in Zhejiang, and reach the city as strong winds and stormy rain.

Since 1951 the temperature has gone from a low of −9.6 °C (15 °F), reached 6 February 1969, to a high of 41.9 °C (107 °F), reached 3 August 2024. Readings outside the official record were as low as −10.5 °C (13 °F), recorded in 29 December 1912 and again 24 January 1916, and as high as 42.1 °C (108 °F) on 10 August 1930. Possible sunshine ranges between 30% in March and 51% in August, giving 1,709.4 hours of sun in a year.
In practical terms: expect heat and humidity in July and August, damp weather in the plum rain month, and a cold, grey winter without the extreme freezing found farther north.

In 2023 the permanent population was 12.522 million (counting Xiaoshan and Yuhang), of whom 10.543 million, or 84.2%, were urban residents. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 13.4 million people as of 2010, though other sources give a figure of more than 21 million. That metropolitan area takes in other major cities, namely Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou.
For registered residents, life expectancy was 83.18 years in 2021, one of the highest in China.

In 1848, in the Qing era, one description called Hangzhou the "stronghold" of Islam in China, with several mosques bearing Arabic inscriptions. A Hui man from Ningbo told an Englishman the same about Zhejiang, comparing Hangzhou's many mosques with his own small congregation of about 30 families in Ningbo. Two notable mosques stand in the city today: the Phoenix Mosque and the New Hangzhou Great Mosque.

Hangzhou was an important centre of Chinese Jewry as late as the later 16th and early 17th centuries, and it might even have been where the Kaifeng Jewish community began. There used to be a synagogue in Ningbo and one in Hangzhou, but no traces of either can now be found, and the only Jews known in China lived in Kaifeng. Two of the "Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism" were from Hangzhou as well. The Immaculate Conception Cathedral is among the oldest Catholic churches in China, going back 400 years to the Ming dynasty. Christians in the city experienced persecution in the early 21st century.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: Temples and pagodas around West Lake

blocks.x: Many temples stand near West Lake. Lingyin Temple (Soul's Retreat), roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) to the west of the lake, dates from AD 326, the first year of Xianhe under the Eastern Jin Dynasty. It is about 1,700 years old, the earliest famous temple in Hangzhou, and is thought to be the city's most ancient Buddhist temple, though it has been destroyed and rebuilt many times. Yue Fei Temple on the lake's northwest shore was built in 1221, during the Song Dynasty, to remember General Yue Fei, who died as a result of political persecution. Other sites include the Jingci Temple and two pagodas, Baochu and Leifeng. The Liuhe Pagoda standing on Yuelun Hill on the north shore of the Qiantang River, and Hupao Temple (虎跑寺) are further religious sites.

Hangzhou has grown quickly since it opened up in 1992. It began as an industrial city with a mix of light industry, farming and textiles, and it is regarded as a significant coastal manufacturing base and a logistics centre for China's coast. It is also a centre for e-commerce and technology. In 2001 its GDP of RMB 156.8 billion ranked second among all provincial capitals, behind only Guangzhou. By 2018 that had grown more than threefold, to RMB 1.3509 trillion, and GDP per capita rose from US$3,020 to US$21,184.

In 2019 the metropolitan area around Hangzhou produced an estimated gross metropolitan product of 3.2 trillion yuan (US$486.53 billion, nominal). That is larger than Argentina's economy (GDP US$452 billion, the 26th largest in the world) and Nigeria's (US$448 billion, the largest in Africa).

A study by PwC and the China Development Research Foundation put Hangzhou first among "Chinese Cities of Opportunity". GaWC classes it as a "Beta+" world city. It ranked 89th among world financial centres in 2018 (Global Financial Centres Index), and the Economist Intelligence Unit placed it first in its China Emerging City Rankings, which assess the growth potential of Chinese cities, in both 2021 and 2022. The Hurun Global Rich List 2020 put Hangzhou 11th globally and 6th nationally for billionaires, with Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou ahead of it. In August 2023 it hosted the tenth-largest number of Fortune Global 500 company headquarters worldwide, and the fourth-largest in China, after Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.
The city has a smart city programme and is working to digitise its economy and become a cashless city.

Several technology companies have their headquarters in Hangzhou: Geely, HikVision, DeepSeek, Ant Group, NetEase and Alibaba Group. Alibaba's new global headquarters opened in May 2024 and has of about one million square metres across seven buildings, built for 30,000 employees. Because of the internet sector, many programmers have come from other cities such as Shanghai and Beijing, have moved to Hangzhou.

New industries have grown up in medicine, information technology and heavy equipment, plus car components, household electrical appliances and electronics, telecommunications, fine chemicals, chemical fibre and food processing. Officials describe the city's key industries as "1 + 6" clusters. The "1" is the digital economy, and the "6" covers the cultural and creative economy, finance, tourism, fashion manufacturing and the making of high-end equipment. At least since 2023, the digital sector and the creative and cultural sectors.

Studies suggest that Alibaba's revenue affects the city's economic growth in one direction only: the relationship is a one-way causal link from the company's revenue to the city's growth. A 1% rise in Alibaba's total revenue could produce 0.272% growth in the city's economy over the long run.

The Hangzhou Tourism Commission began an online campaign in March 2013 on Facebook, the "Modern Marco Polo" campaign. Over the following year nearly 26,000 people from around the world applied to become Hangzhou's first foreign tourism ambassador. At a press conference held in Hangzhou on 20 May 2014, the winner announced was Liam Bates, the winner. He received a US$55,000 contract and became the first foreigner ever appointed by China's government to such an official role.

Hangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone: it became a national development zone in 1993 with State Council approval and covering 104.7 km² (40.4 sq mi). Encouraged industries are electronic information, biological medicine, machinery and household appliance manufacturing, and food processing.

Hangzhou Export Processing Zone: set up on April 27, 2000, with State Council approval, as one of the first such zones, and the sole one in Zhejiang Province. Its planned total area is 2.92 km² (1.13 sq mi), and it lies near both the Hangzhou Port and Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport.

Hangzhou Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (HHTZ): approved by the State Council as a state-level high-tech zone in March 1991. It has three parts, with the Zhijiang Sci-Tech Industrial Park and the Xiasha Sci-Tech Industrial Park as the main regions. It is among the most influential high-tech innovation and industry bases in Zhejiang. As of 2013 it hosted over 1,100 firms developing software or providing BPO services, and firms like Siemens, Nokia and Motorola have R&D centres there. In 2011 the zone's GDP rose by 13.1 percent to RMB 41.63 billion, 5.9 percent of Hangzhou's total. It calls itself the "Silicon Valley" of China, and Alibaba Group is headquartered in it. In 2023 Alibaba sped up the construction of its global headquarters in Hangzhou, with local government support, after signing a new cooperation pact with the authorities.

Despite many recent developments, Hangzhou has kept its historical and cultural heritage and its natural setting, and tourism remains important to the economy. It also has numerous skyscrapers, which makes it the 19th city in the world, and the 9th in China, by number of tall buildings.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: West Lake and the tea hills

blocks.x: West Lake, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is one of the best-loved attractions. The West Lake Cultural Landscape covers about 3,323 hectares (8,210 acres) and contains many of the city's best-known historic and scenic spots. Around the lake are cultural sites, old pagodas, and landscape such as hills and tea fields (Phoenix Mountain among them). Two main causeways cross the lake. Lying west of the lake is Dreaming of the Tiger Spring, known for its natural spring and for being close to the famous longjing tea plantations.

Parts of the Grand Canal run across Hangzhou. The Jiangnan Canal, in 610 CE, was dug out and widened along an existing channel to link Suzhou with Hangzhou. UNESCO listed the Grand Canal as a World Heritage Site in 2014. You can reach the historical sites around Gongchen Bridge by Hangzhou Metro Line 5; get off at The Grand Canal station or at East Gongchen Bridge station.

West Lake Cultural Square in Xiacheng District contains several well-known institutions: the Zhejiang Natural History Museum and the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology, as well as the Zhejiang Global Center, which is among the tallest buildings downtown at around 160 m (520 ft). Xixi National Wetland Park, in turn, protects the region's wetland ecosystem over about 10 km² (3.9 sq mi). Restoration has involved reed beds and fish ponds, and today the park shelters many kinds of birds. It also holds one temple, along with some rural dwellings of historical importance.

Qiandao Lake is an artificial reservoir in Chun'an County, which is under Hangzhou's administration. It has more islands than any other lake in China, differing widely in size and form, each with its own scenery. The Hangzhou Botanical Garden and the Hangzhou Zoo are also found here, in Xihu District.

Native residents of Hangzhou, like those in Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu, speak Hangzhou dialect, which is a Wu dialect found only in this area and different from the dialects of southern Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu. Mandarin, the official language set by the central government, is the dominant spoken language, although it cannot be understood by speakers of the Hangzhou dialect without learning it. The dialect has an estimated 1.2 to 1.5 million speakers. As an international student, you will use Mandarin in class and daily life, but you may hear the local dialect around town.

Hangzhou has several museums. The China National Silk Museum is the largest silk museum in the world, the China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆) covers tea, and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum brings together human studies, exhibitions and research with more than 100,000 cultural relics.

Many theatres stage opera such as Yue opera. There are large shows themed on the city's history and culture, including Romance of the Song Dynasty and Impression West Lake. The landscapes of Hangzhou link stories of famous figures in Chinese history with the feelings of ordinary visitors.

The city hosts the China Academy of Art, and to well-known painters, for example Lin Fengmian and Fang Ganmin, lived and worked here. The local government invests heavily in tourism and the arts, with special attention to silk, umbrellas and the hand-held folding fans of China.

Hangzhou's Ancient Book Restoration and Display Center, part of the Zhejiang Library, holds public demonstrations, held regularly, of the traditional paper repair and binding methods used to preserve ancient Chinese texts. It plays a key part in conserving cultural documents from Jiangnan.
Zhejiang Gongshang University lies in Zhejiang, and the province around a campus has as large an effect on student life as the campus itself. The sections below trace Zhejiang's long history.

Near Hangzhou, the Kuahuqiao culture was an early Neolithic settlement between 6000 and 5000 BC. Zhejiang also saw the Neolithic cultures of Hemudu, beginning in 5500 BC, and Liangzhu, beginning in 3400 BC.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: Ancient times and the Yue kingdom

blocks.x: During the second millennium BC, the area of modern Zhejiang lay outside the main sphere of influence of Shang civilisation. It was inhabited by peoples collectively called the Dongyue. The kingdom of Yue first appears in the chronicles and records of the Spring and Autumn period, and these place it in northern Zhejiang. The Shiji says its leaders descended from Yu the Great, founder of the Xia. The "Song of the Yue Boatman" (越人歌, Yuèrén Gē) was written down in Chinese characters by authors in north or inland China, in Hebei and Henan, about 528 BC. From it we learn that the Yue people spoke a language which people in northern and inland China could not understand. The Sword of Goujian carries bird-worm seal script. Yuenü (越女, "the Lady of Yue") was a swordswoman from Yue. To hold back the rise of the kingdom of Wu, Chu followed a policy of strengthening Yue.

Under King Goujian, Yue recovered from early reverses and took over the territory of its rival in 473 BC. Afterwards the Yue kings shifted their power centre away from where they began, near Mount Kuaiji (today's Shaoxing), to what had been the Wu capital, now Suzhou. Since there was no southern rival to attack, Chu faced Yue directly and destroyed it in 333 BC. The Qin Empire annexed Yue's former lands in 222 BC and organised them into a commandery named for Kuaiji, located in Zhejiang but at first headquartered in Wu, in Jiangsu.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: Zhejiang under Han and the Three Kingdoms

blocks.x: Kuaiji Commandery was the first power base of the rebellion of Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu against the Qin Empire. It first managed to bring back the kingdom of Chu, though the Han finally conquered it. During the Later Han period, control went back to the settlement beneath Mount Kuaiji, while rule over the inland Minyue area remained no more than nominal, and the Yue inhabitants largely kept their own political and social systems.

Once the Han empire was over, the warlords Yan Baihu and Wang Lang held Zhejiang until Sun Ce and Sun Quan defeated them and eventually founded the Kingdom of Wu. Although the Wu court moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (present-day Nanjing), the region continued to develop and benefited from waves of people escaping the chaos of northern China. Industrial kilns were set up, and merchants traded as far away as Manchuria and Funan, in the south of mainland Southeast Asia.

Zhejiang was part of Wu in the Three Kingdoms period. Wu (229 to 280), usually called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, had the most developed economy of the Three Kingdoms (220 to 280). In its plot shows Wei (魏) and Shu (蜀), short of materials, avoided facing Wu directly. In armed clashes with Wu, those two states relied heavily on camouflage and deception to take away Wu's military supplies, including arrows and bows.

Nanjing (then Jiankang) remained prominent, but Qiantang (the old name of Hangzhou), was still one of the three major metropolitan centres in the south that supplied large tax revenue to the imperial centres in the north. The other two were Jiankang and Chengdu. Qiantang's rank was raised in 589, and it was renamed Hangzhou.

After Wu's collapse and the upheaval of the Wu Hu uprising against the Jin dynasty (266 to 420), most of the elite Chinese families had worked alongside the northern conquerors and non-Chinese rulers. A number may have lost their social standing and fled to areas south of the Yangtze. Some refugees from the north may have settled around Hangzhou. One case is the clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), a chancellor of the Shu Han kingdom from the Central Plain in northern China, gathered in the suburbs of Hangzhou prefecture and formed an exclusive, closed community, Zhuge Village (Zhege Cun), in which all villagers have the family name Zhuge. The village has deliberately isolated itself from nearby communities for centuries, and it has only recently become known to the public. This suggests that a few powerful, elite refugees from the Central Plain may have sought shelter south of the Yangtze.

However, given Zhejiang's mountains and its shortage of farmland, most such refugees probably settled in other parts of South China, where fertile land and urban resources were available. These were mainly southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, provinces where regional governments were less cohesive and organised. Some northern refugees may have found homes in the south, depending on their rank and on the military strength they had held in the north. The remnant Jin kingdom and the Southern dynasties competed against some of the Han elites, both those from the Central Plain and those already south of the Yangtze.

As the heartland of Jiangnan (the Yangtze River Delta), Zhejiang remained the richest area through the Six Dynasties (220 or 222 to 589), the Sui and the Tang. After it was incorporated into the Sui dynasty, its wealth served Sui ambitions to expand to the both north and south, above all Korea and Vietnam. This led the Sui to restore and extend the network that grew into the Grand Canal of China. The canal regularly carried grain and resources from Zhejiang, through its metropolitan centre Hangzhou (and its hinterland along the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay's shores) and from Suzhou, on to the North China Plain.

The disastrous Korean war led to the overthrow of the Sui by the Tang, who presided over a centuries-long golden age. Zhejiang was an important economic centre in the Jiangnan East Circuit of the empire, and it was regarded as especially prosperous. Throughout the Tang, the Grand Canal kept working, bringing grain and material resources to the North China Plain and the empire's metropolitan centres. As the Tang dynasty fell apart, Zhejiang made up the greater part of the territory of a regional kingdom called Wuyue.
Professional teams based in the province include the following, grouped by league.
Chinese Basketball Association: Zhejiang Golden Bulls and Bayi Rockets (in Ningbo)
Chinese Super League: Zhejiang Professional F.C.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

zhejiang-gongshang-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Zhejiang Gongshang University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hangzhou, register at Zhejiang Gongshang University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Zhejiang Normal University, or ZJNU, is a public university in the city of Jinhua, in central Zhejiang Province. Its main campus lies right beside Shuanglong Cave, a national park. The grounds extend over more than 220 hectares and the buildings offer a total floor space above one million square metres, which makes this a large and green campus compared with many city universities.

The institution began in 1956 as Hangzhou Normal Academy and became Hangzhou Normal College in 1958. In 1962 it merged with the Zhejiang Teaching College to form Zhejiang Normal College, and in 1965 the college moved to Jinhua, where it has stayed.

Its status rose in 1980, when the college was classified as a tertiary institution, and in 1985 it became Zhejiang Normal University. From that point it widened its range of colleges, departments and undergraduate programmes. Three other institutions then merged into it: the Zhejiang Financial School in 2000, the Zhejiang School of Preschool-Teacher Education in 2001 and the Jinhua Railway Engineering School in 2004.

ZJNU is one of the province's key universities, and its core strength is teacher education alongside a number of other fields. It is organised into 18 colleges that offer 61 undergraduate programmes. Student numbers exceed 25,480 undergraduates and 4,300 postgraduates, plus 15,000 adult-education students. The staff total 2,640, including 1,460 full-time instructors. The senior ranks include an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, 650 associate professors and 260 full professors. One of the professors has received the National Outstanding Scholar title.

ZJNU holds a national designation from the Ministry of Education as a key place for training vocational-education teachers. The Ministry of Railways has also designated it a base for training locomotive engineers, which links back to the Jinhua Railway Engineering School that merged into it. Attached to the university is the Zhejiang Training Center for University and College Teachers, which runs in-service courses.

At provincial level, the university has 24 key disciplines, 6 more disciplines under key construction and 3 research bases. It has 63 master's degree programmes. Professional master's programmes include the M.Ed., MPA, MBA, MSW, MTCSOL, an MA for part-time vocational education and and a master of science in physical education.

Library holdings include more than 3,000,000 printed books and 1,850,000-plus electronic ones. The 42 laboratories fill 119,000 square metres. One is a key laboratory of the Ministry of Education, one is a national key demonstration centre for experimental teaching, and a further five are provincial key laboratories and demonstration centres.
The university has 18 colleges and schools offering 61 programmes. They can be grouped as follows.
Teacher and vocational education: Xingzhi College, the colleges of Teacher Education and of Vocational and Technical Education, and the Hangzhou College of Preschool Teacher Education

Sciences and engineering: Engineering, Geography and Environmental Sciences, Chemistry and Life Sciences, Physics and Electronic Information, plus the schools of Computer Science and Technology and of Mathematical Sciences
Humanities, languages and law: the colleges of Law and Political Science, Foreign Languages and Humanities
Business, media and arts: the colleges of Fine Arts, Music, Communication and Creative Culture, and Economics and Management
Health and sport: the College of Physical Education and Health Sciences

International and special units: Chuyang Honors College, the Institute of African Studies and the College of International Culture and Education, plus the Office of Postgraduate Teaching and Student Affairs
Another unit, Hangzhou Junior Teachers College, is located in Hangzhou, the provincial capital.

The Research Center for Light-emitting Diodes is one of the named research centres. As a measure of research output, the Nature Index follows affiliations in high-quality scientific papers and reports results for institutions and countries on a monthly basis, and you can use it to compare universities.

ZJNU says it makes a strong effort to look outward. Recent years have brought academic exchange and cooperation links with 92 universities and research institutes abroad, spread across 42 countries. In 1996 the university opened a Chinese language and culture centre in Cameroon, and in 1997 the university received authorisation to accept international students for short and long periods.

The Ministry of Education approved an education assistance and development base at ZJNU in 2004. It runs training and human-resource projects for senior education administrators who come from other continents. The university has also been authorised to run an overseas studies centre that helps self-funded students go abroad. In 2007 it was authorised to take international students who receive the Chinese Government Scholarship, and it opened Confucius Institutes in Cameroon and Ukraine.

The university's motto is "wisdom with virtue, integrity with innovation". Its stated ambition is a comprehensive university for teaching and research at a high level, with distinct features of its own.
The city around a university shapes student life: the weather, the way you travel and the places you visit. This section covers Jinhua, where ZJNU is located.

The city is in the centre of Zhejiang Province, located between 28°32′ and 29°41′ north latitude and between 119°14′ and 120°46′ east longitude. Five cities surround it. Hangzhou, the provincial capital, is on the northwest side, Shaoxing on the northeast, Taizhou on the east, Quzhou on the southwest and Lishui to the south.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons. Summers are hot and humid. Winters are chilly, cloudy and drier, and snow occasionally falls. Over the year the average temperature is 17.33 °C (63.2 °F). January is the coolest month, averaging 5.2 °C, and July the warmest, at 29.0 °C. Rainfall comes to about 1,450 millimetres (57.1 in) a year. June is also when the Asian monsoon brings the plum rains and humidity reaches its highest average.
The economy is flexible and varies from one area to another. Private business is dominant: around 90% of enterprises, and about 88% of GDP, belong to the private sector.

Jinhua has a strong civilian-owned (private) economy, and manufacturing and processing support its industry. The city's leading sectors include clothing and textiles, machinery and electronics, pharmaceuticals and chemicals, craft manufacturing, metalwork, building materials, automobile and motorcycle accessories, food processing and plastic goods.
li Yiwu is known for light-industry commodities
Yongkang makes mechanical and electric tools and parts for cars and motorcycles
Dongyang specialises in clothing, building work and magnetic materials
Jinhua Proper focuses on medicines, construction materials and industrial measures
Lanxi produces towels, cement, daily chemicals and non-ferrous metals
Pujiang is noted for textiles, locks and crystal lanterns and ornaments
Handicrafts remain active in Jinhua. Dongyang is known for wood carving and bamboo weaving, Pujiang for straw plaiting, lace making and crystal carving, and Yongkang for hardware crafts.

zhejiang-normal-university.h: Colleges and schools in the city

blocks.x: Jinhua has two main institutions of higher education. One is ZJNU, a provincial public university. The other is Jinhua University of Vocational Technology, a public university run by the city.

Thirteen major provincial key high schools are in the Jinhua area. In the city itself these are Jinhua No. 1 High School, Aiqing High School, Jinhua Tangxi Senior High School, Jinhua Foreign Language School and the school attached to ZJNU. Counties and county-level cities have their own: Pan'an High School and Wuyi No. 1 High School, Zhejiang Pujiang High School, Lanxi No. 1 High School, and Yongkang No. 1 Senior Middle School. Dongyang and Yiwu are served by Zhejiang Dongyang High School, Zhejiang Yiwu High School and Yiwu No. 2 High School.

Jinhua has been at the forefront of China-Africa education cooperation since the 1980s, driven by its colleges and universities. ZJNU started enrolling short-term international students in China in that decade. More than 8,000 African students have been trained by the university to date. Their subjects span business administration, software engineering and comparative education, as well as the Chinese language and international education in Chinese, and mechanical design, manufacturing and automation.

Jinhua ham is famous for its colour, a mix of red and white. The lean meat tastes slightly sweet, while the fat adds flavour without being too greasy. It is a good source of protein, fat, vitamins and minerals. The ham is made during the winter and matured over the summer, which lets it ferment. Eating it is traditionally associated with health benefits: it is said to nourish the stomach and kidneys, to strengthen bone marrow and to help wounds heal.
The ham has thin, bright-yellow skin and a shape like a lute. Its flesh is red and fragrant. It is said to have "four perfections", for its colour, aroma, taste and shape.

Yongkang roumaibing, or meat patties, is a traditional snack from Yongkang. Local farmers have long made meat patties as a staple dish at harvest festivals. They look coarse, yet they are held up as a perfect example of the proverb that appearances can deceive ("don't judge a book by its cover").

There are two main kinds. The thin patty, also called the triangle patty, is large and flat; it is cut into several triangles and sold with a filling of pork and dried vegetables. The thick patty is smaller and thicker, and its filling can be potato, tofu, cowpea, lotus root and so on.
Jinhua is a communications hub for southeast China between the coast and the interior, and one of the country's chief land-transport junctions. The three main stations are Jinhua, Jinhuanan and Yiwu:
Jinhua railway station
Jinhuanan railway station
Yiwu railway station

Three railways meet here: the Zhejiang-Jiangxi line, the Jinhua-Wenzhou line and the Jinhua-Qiandaohu line. The Hangzhou-Jinhua-Quzhou Expressway and the Jinhua-Lishui-Wenzhou Expressway pass through, as do National Highways 330 and 320 and other provincial roads. The cities clustered around Jinhua Proper form a "Half-an-Hour's-Ride Economic Circle". Driving from Jinhua to Hangzhou takes only about 90 minutes, and to Shanghai about 3 hours.

Jinhua Rail Transit is the city's metro. Its Jinyidong Line links the two districts of Jinhua with Yiwu and Dongyang, and it opened on 30 August 2022. Yiwu Airport flies to major cities in mainland China and to Hong Kong.
Seventeen pavilions by Chinese and foreign architects make up Jinhua Architecture Park, which stands along the Yiwu River.

The Seventh National Census in 2020 counted a permanent population of 7,050,683. The Sixth Census, in 2010, had counted 5,361,572, so over ten years the city gained 1,689,111 residents. This is growth of 31.5%, or 2.78% a year on average. The male population numbered 3,716,342 (52.71%) and the female population 3,334,341 (47.29%). The sex ratio, expressed as males per 100 females, was 111.46, which was 3.96 higher than in 2010.

zhejiang-ocean-university.h: Zhejiang Ocean University at a glance

blocks.x: Zhejiang Ocean University, often shortened to ZJOU (浙江海洋大学 in Chinese), is a public university in the city of Zhoushan, in Zhejiang province on China's east coast. As the name suggests, the sea is the thread that runs through the place: the campus sits in an island city, and much of the teaching is aimed at fisheries, shipping, naval engineering and other marine-related fields.

ZJOU in its present form dates from 1988, when two older institutions were joined together. One was Zhejiang Fishery University, which had been set up in 1958. The other was Zhoushan Junior Teachers College, which had opened in 1978. One parent therefore brought a seafaring and fisheries tradition, and the other brought teacher training.

Two later milestones mark its academic growth. The university is recorded as being approved to award bachelor's degrees in 1982, and it gained the right to run postgraduate programmes in 2005. The 1982 approval comes before the 1988 merger, so the dates as published do not sit neatly together; if you need exact dates for an application or a document, check the history page on the university's own website.

Today the university describes its strengths as being in subjects tied to seas and oceans, yet it is not a single-subject school. It teaches across science, agronomy, engineering, literature, medicine, management, education and economics, so a student interested in, say, languages or business can find a home here as well as someone planning a career in ships or fish.

Teaching is spread over a long roster of schools, colleges and centres, including several science and technology colleges and one private college. Programme names and structures change from time to time, so treat this as a map of the main units rather than a final catalogue.

In short, if your interest is in marine science, fisheries, shipbuilding, engineering, food, business or languages, there is a matching school on the list.

Day-to-day life for a student depends heavily on the city around the campus: the weather, the way people travel, and what there is to do at weekends. The next parts of this profile introduce Zhoushan, the island city where Zhejiang Ocean University is based, and then the wider province of Zhejiang.

Zhoushan is not a single piece of land but an archipelago in the sea outside Hangzhou Bay. It is the largest island group in China, made up of 3,306 reefs plus 1,390 islands. Only 103 of those islands have people living on them all year, just 58 cover more than one square kilometre (0.39 square miles), and only twelve have populations above 10,000.

The six biggest islands are all larger than 50 square kilometres (19 square miles). In the lists below, the abbreviation at the end of each entry shows which district or county governs the island: DH is Dinghai District, PT is Putuo District, DS is Daishan County and SS is Shengsi County.
Zhoushan Island (舟山岛): home to 635,595 people, covering 502.65 square kilometres (194.07 square miles), under DH and PT
Daishan Island (岱山岛): home to 111,765 people, covering 119.32 square kilometres (46.07 square miles), under DS
Liuheng Island (六横岛): home to 59,102 people, covering 109.40 square kilometres (42.24 square miles), under PT
Jintang Island (金塘岛): home to 37,321 people, covering 82.11 square kilometres (31.70 square miles), under DH
Zhujiajian Island (朱家尖岛): home to 27,981 people, covering 75.84 square kilometres (29.28 square miles), under PT
Qushan Island (衢山岛, also called 大衢岛): home to 53,016 people, covering 73.57 square kilometres (28.41 square miles), under DS
Eleven further islands are medium-sized, between 10 and 50 square kilometres (3.9 to 19.3 square miles).
Taohua Island (桃花岛): home to 10,867 people, covering 44.43 square kilometres (17.15 square miles), under PT
Greater Changtu Island (大长涂山): home to 1,750 people, covering 40.62 square kilometres (15.68 square miles), under DS
Xiushan Island (秀山岛): home to 10,106 people, covering 26.33 square kilometres (10.17 square miles), under DS
Sijiao Island (泗礁山): home to 39,008 people, covering 25.88 square kilometres (9.99 square miles), under SS
Xiazhi Island (虾峙岛): home to 11,247 people, covering 18.59 square kilometres (7.18 square miles), under PT
Dengbu Island (登步岛): home to 2,479 people, covering 16.72 square kilometres (6.46 square miles), under PT

The sea dominates the map. Zhoushan's marine territory covers 20,800 square kilometres (8,031 square miles), whereas its land area is only 1,440.12 square kilometres (556 square miles), and 183.19 square kilometres (71 square miles) of that land is under water at high tide. The territory stretches about 182 km (113 miles) from east to west and 169 km (105 miles) from north to south. It is densely populated today but has little farmland.

Zhoushan has a humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon, with four distinct seasons: a chilly, wet winter and a sticky hot summer. The surrounding East China Sea softens the extremes, particularly in summer. January averages 6.2 °C (43.2 °F), August averages 27.8 °C (82.0 °F), and the whole-year mean is 17.1 °C (62.8 °F).

The record high of 42.3 °C (108.1 °F) was set on 8 August 2013, which was 1.7 °C above the second-highest reading, so that day was an exception rather than a pattern. Rain falls all year round, and summer is the wettest season. Sunshine totals 1,823.7 hours a year. June is the dullest month at about 30% of possible sunshine, July and August reach about 53%, and later months tend to be brighter than earlier ones. For a newcomer, that means packing for damp winters and humid summers, with an umbrella useful in any month.

At the Sixth National Population Census, taken on 1 November 2010, Zhoushan Municipality had 1,121,261 residents: 588,414 men and 532,847 women, living in about 454,800 households. Han Chinese make up the overwhelming majority, at 1,109,813 people. The districts and counties were home to the following numbers: Dinghai District 464,184, Putuo District 378,805, Daishan County 202,164 and Shengsi County 76,108.

On education, roughly 10 per cent of residents (115,286) had received higher education, while 77,577 were illiterate or semi-literate. On age, there were 114,265 children aged 0 to 14 and 176,331 seniors. These figures are now well over a decade old and the population has certainly moved since then, so look at the latest statistics on official sites if you need current numbers.

Fishing was long the backbone of Zhoushan's economy, and the city is still China's largest fishery. In recent decades the economy has diversified: shipbuilding and repair, shipping, light industry, tourism and services are now the main contributors to local output.

For 2016, the municipality reported a gross domestic product of 122.85 billion yuan, which works out at about 16,013 US dollars per person, up 11.3% on the year before. Among the eleven prefecture-level cities of Zhejiang it ranked third on that per-person basis, although in total output it came last, because its population is much smaller than that of the others. The split between primary, secondary and tertiary industry was 10.6 : 39.8 : 49.6.

The port is a major asset. In 2012, Zhoushan Port alone handled 290,990 kilotons of cargo. Ningbo Port and Zhoushan Port work in practice as one port, sharing infrastructure, harbour basin and administration, and together they handled around 744,000 kilotons that year, a volume that put the combined port ahead of Shanghai as the world's busiest by cargo weight.

Household incomes in 2012 give an idea of living standards at the time. Urban residents' per-person disposable income was 34,224 yuan, a rise of 12.2% (10.3% after allowing for prices), and rural residents' per-person net income was 18,601 yuan, a rise of 12.9% (11.0% after prices). Engel's coefficients, which show the share of spending that goes on food, were 35.9% for urban and 38.1% for rural residents. Average housing space was 32.39 square metres per person in towns and 49.10 in the countryside. All of these figures are from earlier years; the university's own site and local government releases will have more recent data.

Zhoushan can be reached by air, road and water. Travel has improved a great deal since the Zhoushan Trans-Oceanic Bridges opened in 2009, which gave the islands a fixed road link to the mainland and effectively turned the archipelago into a peninsula. One thing to know is that Zhoushan was the only city in Zhejiang without a railway, because of its island geography; a line has long been planned (see below).
#### By air

Although the airport carries the name of Mount Putuo, Zhoushan Putuoshan International Airport is actually on Zhujiajian Island. Domestic routes operate from there. Passengers can fly out to Shanghai and Beijing, to Guangzhou and Shenzhen in the south, and to Xiamen, Fuzhou, Hefei, Lianyungang, Jieyang and Jinjiang. Building work began in March 1997 and the original airport was finished in August 1997, at a cost of 410 million yuan; it is rated as a 4D airfield. In 2016 it handled 800.9 thousand passengers, which placed it 86th among Chinese mainland civil airports. A new terminal and a taxiway of 2,500 by 23 metres (8,202 by 75 feet) were being built when this information was compiled, so facilities may have changed.
#### By road

The Zhoushan Trans-Oceanic Bridges (舟山跨海大桥, also called 舟山大陆连岛工程) form a key part of the Yongzhou Expressway (甬舟高速, G9211 in the national trunk highway network). Five bridges in a row link Zhoushan to Zhenhai District in Ningbo. Starting from the Zhoushan side they are Cengang (岑港大桥), then Xiangjiaomen (响礁门大桥) and Taoyaomen (桃夭门大桥), followed by the famous Xihoumen (西堠门大桥), and finally Jintang (金塘大桥). Work began in 1999 and ended in 2010, and the group is the largest bridge complex in China. Xihoumen Bridge has the second-longest central span of any suspension bridge in the world.

China National Highway 329 begins in Hangzhou and ends at Zhujiajian in Zhoushan, 292 km (181 miles) in length at the time of writing. It is the only national highway serving Zhoushan, and it is the shortest national highway running east to west. Before it reaches Zhoushan it passes through Shaoxing and Ningbo. Between the Ningbo and Zhoushan boundaries it is a ferry crossing, which is unusual for a national highway: the dock on the Ningbo side is Baifeng and the one on the Zhoushan side is Yadanshan.

Its path through Zhoushan has been changed more than once. It first ran along the southern shore of Zhoushan Island to Shenjiamen. Once the Zhujiajian Bridge was built, it was extended to Nansha Beach on Zhujiajian. As Dinghai and Lincheng grew, part of the road became ordinary city streets, and the highway moved onto Dinghai's outer ring road and the Baiquan to Shenjiamen road. A further rebuild was under way, with a new route through the middle of Zhoushan Island to form its backbone. It uses seven tunnels totalling 11,187 metres (36,703 feet) and five interchanges, at a projected cost of 5 billion yuan and a target finish date of 2015. Whether it is complete is something to confirm locally.

Within the island, Zhoushan bus rapid transit uses dedicated lanes between the urban areas of Zhoushan Island. Line One, 25 km (16 miles) long, started running on 1 October 2013 and links Dinghai with Donggang in Putuo. It has ten stops. Three are in Dinghai at the western end: Dongmen (定海东门总站), Tanfeng (定海檀枫) and Chengdong (定海城东). Xincheng then has Nanhai (新城南海) and the central terminal (新城总站), followed by Zhoushan Hospital (新城舟山医院) and Fulidao Road (新城富丽岛路). The last three are in Putuo: Puxi (普陀浦西), Chengbei (普陀城北总站) and the Donggang Gymnasium (普陀东港体育馆). Service ran from 6:30 to 20:00, with roughly 120 trips a day. The fare was a flat 2 yuan whatever the distance, a 20 per cent discount applied with a public transport IC card, and one free transfer to ordinary buses was allowed within an hour. Buses had 4G signal, and further lines were planned. Fares and timetables will have changed, so confirm on the day.
#### By rail

A railway from Ningbo to Zhoushan was under construction when this profile's information was gathered. It is planned to run 80.8 km (50.2 miles) from Ningbo Station to Zhoushan Baiquan Station with nine stations. Between Ningbo East and Jintang it would carry both passenger and freight trains, and between Jintang and Baiquan it would be passenger-only. Check current status before relying on it.
#### By sea

Two busy ferry routes, with departures every 15 minutes to an hour, join Zhoushan Main Island to Shanghai in the north and Ningbo in the south. Scheduled ships also sail to Wenzhou and Fuzhou. Smaller ferries and speedboats serve the other inhabited islands, with frequency depending on how many people live there.

The city has four scenic areas of official rank. Mount Putuo and the Shengsi Islands are national level; Taohua Island and Daishan are provincial level. Easy links to the Yangtze Delta on the mainland have helped tourism. In 2021 the city received 27.71 million visitors, about 25 times its own population, of whom 310,500 were from outside China. Tourism is an important part of the local economy; in 2012 it brought in 26.68 billion yuan.

The Mount Putuo National Scenic Area has two parts, Mount Putuo itself and the eastern coast of Zhujiajian, together covering 41.85 square kilometres (16.16 square miles). A missionary who visited in the early 1830s, Karl Gützlaff, recorded that the island then held two large temples and about 60 small ones, attended by 2,000 monks, and described it as a place that seems like a fairyland, with giant inscriptions cut into granite, many temples and a huge mausoleum.

Mount Putuo (普陀山) has older names, Meicen (梅岑山) and Baihua (白华山), and is regarded as the sacred site of Avalokitesvara (Guanyin), a Bodhisattva revered across much of East Asia. Chinese Buddhism recognises four sacred mountains; Putuo is one, and the others are Wutai, Jiuhua and Emei. Those other three are real mountains of over 1,000 metres (3,300 feet), whereas Putuo is a small island of 12.5 square kilometres (4.8 square miles). Its highest point, Peak Foding, stands 291.3 metres (956 feet) above sea level.

The island's sights are traditionally counted in threes: three grand temples (Puji, Fayu and Huiji). Tahoto Pagoda, the Yangzhi Guanyin Stele and the Nine-Dragon Caisson are the three treasures. The three rocks are Pantuo, Heart Rock and Ergui Tingfa, and the caves are Chaoyang, Chaoyin and Fanyin. It also has 88 nunneries, 128 huts and twelve celebrated scenes. Its nicknames include Buddhist Kingdom of Sea and Sky (海天佛国) and Sacred Ground of the Southern Seas (南海圣境). A Chinese saying pairs it with West Lake in Hangzhou: West Lake is the best place for combined mountain and lake views, while Putuo is the best for mountain and sea.

Zhujiajian (朱家尖), fifth in size among the archipelago's islands, is a recently developed beach resort, with striking seascapes, unspoilt beaches, dense woods, sheer cliffs, hiking hills, excellent seafood and fishing-folk culture. The Zhoushan International Sand Sculpture Festival is held every year at Nansha Beach, one of five connected beaches, around the turn of summer into autumn. On clear days Daqing Mountain offers the best outlook over the southern islands and the mainland's Chuanshan Peninsula. Adventurous visitors can try car racing, mountain biking, gliding, climbing or bungee jumping. Baishan Mountain is known for oddly shaped boulders and a Guanyin figure carved on a cliff, and the Putuo Impression performance, directed by Zhang Yimou, is staged there. Zhujiajian is also home to the Mount Putuo Buddhist Academy, and Wushitang, the Dark Stone Beach, is 500 metres (1,600 feet) long and covered in dark pebbles.

No other coastal island in Zhejiang has such a varied plant life as Taohua Island, a provincial-level scenic area: nearly 600 kinds of tree and plant grow there, among them oranges, orchids, narcissus and, now, peach trees. Film crews like it too, since it served as a set for four Chinese television serials adapted from Jin Yong's novels: The Eagle-Shooting Heroes, Demi-Gods and Semi-Devils, The Return of the Condor Heroes, and Duke of Mount Deer. Every second year since 2004, around summer, the island stages a martial arts (wuxia) culture festival named after the author, with performances and contests for fans.

Your university lies in Zhejiang province, and a region's character shapes student life almost as much as the campus does. This section gives a short tour of the province's early history, which is where much of its cultural pride comes from.

The Kuahuqiao culture, an early Neolithic community in the Hangzhou area, existed around 6000 to 5000 BC. Zhejiang was also the home of the Neolithic Hemudu culture, which began about 5500 BC, and the Liangzhu culture, which began about 3400 BC.

zhejiang-ocean-university.h: The kingdom of Yue and the early empires

blocks.x: During the second millennium BC, the area of today's Zhejiang lay outside the main sphere of Shang civilisation and was inhabited by peoples known collectively as the Dongyue. The kingdom of Yue first shows up in records from the Spring and Autumn period, and those records place it in northern Zhejiang. The Shiji says its rulers descended from Yu the Great, founder of the Xia dynasty.

Several cultural traces survive. Northern writers in Hebei and Henan recorded the Song of the Yue Boatman (越人歌, Yuèrén Gē) in Chinese characters around 528 BC; its words reveal that Yue speakers used a tongue which northerners could not follow. The Sword of Goujian carries an inscription in bird-worm seal script. Yuenü (越女), the Lady of Yue, was a swordswoman from the state. Chu, anxious about Wu's rise, backed Yue as a counterweight.

Under King Goujian, Yue recovered from early defeats and took over its rival's lands in 473 BC. The Yue kings then moved their power base away from the Mount Kuaiji homeland (modern Shaoxing) and took over Wu's old capital, which is now Suzhou. With no southern rival left to fight, Chu confronted Yue directly and destroyed it in 333 BC. The Qin Empire annexed Yue's former lands in 222 BC and set up a commandery named for Kuaiji, headquartered at first in Wu, in today's Jiangsu.

Kuaiji Commandery was the first power base for the uprising of Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu against Qin, which at first revived the kingdom of Chu but ultimately lost to the Han. The Later Han administration returned to the town beneath Mount Kuaiji, yet its hold on the inland Minyue region was barely more than a name, and the Yue inhabitants mostly preserved their own political and social order.

When the Han empire ended, parts of Zhejiang were held by the warlords Yan Baihu and Wang Lang, until Sun Ce and Sun Quan overcame them and went on to found the kingdom of Wu. Even after the court moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (present-day Nanjing), Wu kept developing the region, and refugees from the turmoil in the north arrived in numbers. Large-scale kilns were established, and merchants traded as far afield as Manchuria and Funan, in the south of mainland Southeast Asia.

Zhejiang belonged to Wu during the Three Kingdoms period. Wu (229 to 280), usually called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, was the economic leader of the three states of that era (220 to 280). In the classic novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Zhejiang is credited with the best-equipped navy, and in its story Wei and Shu, short of resources, avoided meeting Wu head on and used camouflage and deception to take Wu's arrows and bows.

Nanjing, then known as Jiankang, stayed the leading city. Even so, Qiantang (the old name for Hangzhou) was among the three big southern centres that sent tax revenue to the northern capitals, alongside Jiankang and Chengdu. It was promoted and given the name Hangzhou in 589.

Wu eventually fell, and the Jin dynasty (266 to 420) then faced the Wu Hu uprising. Amid that turmoil many elite families in the north worked with the non-Chinese rulers, while some lost status and took refuge south of the Yangtze. Some of these northern refugees may have settled near Hangzhou. One example is the clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), a chancellor of Shu Han, which gathered in a closed village in the Hangzhou suburbs, Zhuge Village (Zhege Cun), where all villagers carry the surname Zhuge. The village kept itself apart from its neighbours for centuries and has only recently become widely known. Because Zhejiang is mountainous and has relatively little farmland, however, most refugees probably went elsewhere in the south, where there was more fertile land and more urban resources: southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, where regional government was less tightly organised. Where people ended up depended on their rank and military power, and the exiled Jin court and the Southern dynasties had to compete with Han elites from both the Central Plain and the lands south of the Yangtze.

Zhejiang, as the heartland of Jiangnan (the Yangtze River Delta), was the wealthiest region through the Six Dynasties (220 or 222 to 589), the Sui and the Tang. After it came into the Sui dynasty, its wealth funded Sui ambitions to expand north and south, notably into Korea and Vietnam. This led the Sui to repair and extend the network that became the Grand Canal of China, which moved grain and other goods from Zhejiang northward. Cargo passed through Hangzhou, its hinterland beside the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay, and then Suzhou, before reaching the North China Plain. The failure of the Korean war brought down the Sui and brought in the Tang, who presided over a golden age lasting centuries. Zhejiang was an important economic centre of the Jiangnan East Circuit and was seen as especially prosperous, and throughout the Tang the Grand Canal kept moving grain and materials to the north. When the Tang broke up, most of Zhejiang became the core of a regional state called Wuyue.
