Zhejiang Ocean University lists 79 programs for international students on this site: 39 bachelor, 40 master's programs.

By language of instruction: 71 taught in Chinese, 8 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.
Annual tuition for bachelor programs ranges from CNY 16,000 to CNY 16,000 (median CNY 16,000), according to the university's published fee table.
Annual tuition for master's programs ranges from CNY 20,000 to CNY 22,000 (median CNY 20,000), according to the university's published fee table.

77 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
English-taught degree programs (8):
Aquaculture
Business English
English
Food Processing and Safety
Food Science (Engineering)
Marine Biology
Marine Chemistry
Physical Oceanography
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

zhejiang-ocean-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Zhejiang Ocean University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Zhoushan, register at Zhejiang Ocean University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, known as ZSTU, is a state-run institution of higher education in Zhejiang, an eastern Chinese province. Its Chinese name is written 浙江理工大学. The material available about the institution itself is short, so this profile gives you a fuller picture of the place where you would live and study: the city of Hangzhou, its economy and culture, and the province of Zhejiang and its past. For current details about faculties, programmes, fees and application dates, go to the university's own website.

The 2025 Academic Ranking of World Universities placed Zhejiang Sci-Tech University in the 501-600 band worldwide. That is one reference point among many, and it is best read alongside the subject-level information the university publishes.

zhejiang-sci-tech-university.h: Hangzhou, the city around the campus

blocks.x: Where you study shapes daily life as much as the classroom does, so the next sections describe Hangzhou, the setting for ZSTU, covering its geography, weather, people, work, sights and culture.

Hangzhou is in the northwest of Zhejiang province. It is where the Grand Canal, the waterway running all the way up to Beijing, comes to an end in the south, and it lies in the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. As a sub-provincial city its administrative territory reaches west into the mountains on the Anhui border and east to the coastal plain beside Hangzhou Bay. The centre of the city wraps around the eastern and northern shores of West Lake, a little north of the Qiantang River.

The Qiantang is the biggest river in Zhejiang. Each year around the 15th to 18th of the eighth lunar month the river produces the Qiantang Tide, which people often describe as the greatest tide on Earth. Its tidal bore rushes up the river through Hangzhou and can reach 12 metres (39 feet) high.

The climate is humid subtropical (Koppen Cfa) with four clear seasons. Summers are long, very hot and sticky, while winters are cold, grey and drier, with a little snow from time to time. The yearly mean temperature is 17.0 degrees Celsius (62.6 F). Monthly averages run from 5 degrees (41.0 F) in January up to 29.3 degrees (84.7 F) in July.

Rainfall averages 1,438 mm (56.6 in) a year. June brings the "plum rains" of the Asian monsoon, and in late summer, from August to September, the city is exposed to typhoon storms. Direct hits are rare. Typhoons usually come ashore on the southern Zhejiang coast and reach Hangzhou as strong wind and heavy rain.

Records kept since 1951 show a low of minus 9.6 degrees (15 F) on 6 February 1969 and a peak of 41.9 degrees (107 F) reached on 3 August 2024. Unofficial readings stretch the range further: minus 10.5 degrees (13 F) on 29 December 1912 and again on 24 January 1916, and 42.1 degrees (108 F) on 10 August 1930. Possible sunshine is 30 percent in March and 51 percent in August, and the city gets 1,709.4 hours of sunshine in a typical year. For a new arrival, that means packing for hot, humid summers and for damp, cold winter days.

Counting Xiaoshan and Yuhang, Hangzhou's permanent population stood at 12.522 million in 2023, and 10.543 million of them (84.2 percent) lived in urban areas. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 13.4 million as of 2010, although other estimates go above 21 million. That metropolitan area takes in the major cities of Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou.
Residents live long. Life expectancy among the city's registered population was 83.18 years in 2021, one of the highest figures in China.

Hangzhou has a varied religious past. In 1848, under the Qing dynasty, it was described as a stronghold of Islam in China, with several mosques bearing Arabic inscriptions. A Hui man from Ningbo told an Englishman the same about Hangzhou in Zhejiang, comparing its many mosques with his own congregation of about 30 families in Ningbo. Two mosques of note stand in the city today, the New Hangzhou Great Mosque and the Phoenix Mosque.

Jewish history is part of the story too. Until the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries Hangzhou was a major centre of Chinese Jewry, and some think the Kaifeng Jewish community began here. Hangzhou and Ningbo each once had a synagogue, but nothing of either can be found now. Among Catholics, two of the "Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism" came from Hangzhou, and the city's Immaculate Conception Cathedral is one of the oldest Catholic churches in China, dating back some 400 years to the Ming dynasty.
Many Buddhist temples lie around West Lake.

Lingyin Temple, whose name means Soul's Retreat, stands roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) to the west. It dates from AD 326, the first year of Xianhe under the Eastern Jin, which makes it about 1,700 years old and the earliest famous temple in Hangzhou. It is believed to be the city's oldest Buddhist temple, and it has been wrecked and rebuilt repeatedly.
Yue Fei Temple was built in 1221 under the Song to honour General Yue Fei, and it overlooks the lake's northwest shore.
Jingci Temple, Baochu Pagoda and Leifeng Pagoda are also close by.
Further afield, Liuhe Pagoda stands on Yuelun Hill, on the Qiantang's northern bank, and there is also Hupao Temple.

zhejiang-sci-tech-university.h: How the city earns its living

blocks.x: The city's economy has developed quickly since 1992, when it opened up further. It has a broad industrial base, from light industry and farming to textiles, and it is regarded as an important manufacturing and logistics hub for coastal China. It is also a centre for e-commerce and technology.

The numbers show how far it has come. Hangzhou's GDP in 2001 was RMB 156.8 billion, second only to Guangzhou among provincial capitals. By 2018 the total had more than tripled, reaching RMB 1.3509 trillion, while GDP per head went up from US$3,020 to US$21,184. In 2019 the metropolitan area was estimated to produce a nominal gross metropolitan product of 3.2 trillion yuan (US$486.53 billion). That puts it ahead of Argentina, with a GDP of US$452 billion, the 26th largest in the world, and of Nigeria, with US$448 billion, the biggest in Africa.
Outside studies rate the city well.
A study by PwC and the China Development Research Foundation ranked Hangzhou first among Chinese Cities of Opportunity.
GaWC classes it as a World City at the Beta+ level.
Its place in the 2018 Global Financial Centres Index was 89th.
The Economist Intelligence Unit, which measures how much Chinese cities may grow, put it top of its China Emerging City Rankings for both 2021 and 2022.
By number of billionaires, the Hurun Global Rich List 2020 had it eleventh worldwide and sixth within China, below Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou.
Counting company headquarters, it held tenth place globally for Fortune Global 500 firms as of August 2023, and fourth place nationally after Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.
The city also runs a smart city initiative, working to digitise its economy and become a cashless city.

Several technology firms have their headquarters here: Alibaba Group, NetEase, Ant Group, DeepSeek, Geely and HikVision. Alibaba opened, in May 2024, a new global headquarters of around one million square metres in seven buildings, designed for 30,000 employees. Because of this internet industry, many programmers from other cities such as Shanghai and Beijing have moved to Hangzhou.

New sectors that have grown up include medicine, IT, heavy equipment, car parts, home appliances, electronics, telecoms, fine chemicals, chemical fibres and food processing. Officials talk about "1 + 6" industrial clusters. The 1 means the digital economy, and the 6 are the cultural and creative economy, finance, tourism, fashion manufacturing and high-end equipment manufacturing. As of at least 2023, growth has been led by the digital and creative or cultural sectors.

One study found that Alibaba's total revenue has a positive effect on the city's economic growth, but that the link runs in one direction only, from the company to the city. In the long run a 1 percent rise in Alibaba's revenue could lift the city's growth by 0.272 percent.

The Hangzhou Tourism Commission ran a Facebook campaign, "Modern Marco Polo", beginning in March 2013. Within a year close to 26,000 applicants worldwide had put themselves forward as the city's first foreign tourism ambassador. A press conference on 20 May 2014 announced the winner, Liam Bates, who was given a US$55,000 contract. He was the first foreigner China's government had ever appointed to an official role of this kind.
Three zones are worth knowing.

The Economic and Technological Development Zone gained national status from the State Council in 1993 and extends over 104.7 km2 (40.4 sq mi). It promotes electronic information, biomedicine, machinery and household appliance manufacturing, and food processing.

The Export Processing Zone opened on 27 April 2000 with the State Council's approval, being among the earliest zones of its kind and the sole one approved in Zhejiang. It is planned to cover 2.92 km2 (1.13 sq mi) and lies near Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport and Hangzhou Port.

The Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (HHTZ) received State Council approval as a state-level high-tech zone in March 1991. Three parts make it up, the main ones being the Zhijiang and Xiasha Sci-Tech Industrial Parks, and it counts among the most influential bases for high-tech innovation and industry in Zhejiang. As of 2013 it hosted more than 1,100 software developers and business process outsourcing firms, and companies including Motorola, Nokia and Siemens have set up research centres there. In 2011 its GDP rose 13.1 percent to RMB 41.63 billion, 5.9 percent of the city's total. The zone calls itself the "Silicon Valley" of China. Alibaba Group is headquartered here, and in 2023 the company sped up construction of its global headquarters in Hangzhou with local government support, after signing a fresh cooperation agreement with the authorities.

Hangzhou has changed a great deal through recent urban development, yet it keeps its historical and cultural heritage and its natural setting. Tourism remains a significant part of the economy today. The city has many skyscrapers, placing it 19th in the world and 9th in China for their number.

West Lake, one of the city's favourite attractions, is listed by UNESCO as World Heritage. Its Cultural Landscape spans about 3,323 hectares (8,210 acres) and includes many of the city's best-known historic and scenic places. Around the shore stand cultural sites, historic pagodas, hills and tea fields, including Phoenix Mountain, and two major causeways cross the water.
West of the lake is Dreaming of the Tiger Spring, known for its natural spring and for being close to the famous Longjing tea plantations.

Stretches of the Grand Canal run through Hangzhou. The Jiangnan section was dug out and widened in 610 CE, following an older channel, to link Suzhou with Hangzhou, and UNESCO inscribed the whole Grand Canal as World Heritage in 2014. To see the historic sites near Gongchen Bridge, take Hangzhou Metro Line 5 to The Grand Canal station or East Gongchen Bridge station.

In Xiacheng District, West Lake Cultural Square is the site of the Zhejiang Natural History Museum, the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology and the Zhejiang Global Center, a tower of some 160 m (520 ft) that is among the tallest downtown.

Xixi National Wetland Park was created to protect the area's wetlands and is about 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi) in size. Restoration has included reed beds and fish ponds, many bird species now live there, and it also holds a temple and several historic rural houses.
Qiandao Lake is a man-made reservoir in Chun'an County, which belongs to Hangzhou. It has more islands than any other lake in China, each with its own scenery.
Hangzhou Botanical Garden and Hangzhou Zoo are both in Xihu District.

The native people of Hangzhou speak the Hangzhou dialect, a form of Wu Chinese that belongs to this area. It is not the same as the dialects of southern Zhejiang or southern Jiangsu, and the same is true of the speech of Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu generally. Mandarin is the official language set by the central government and the main language in daily use, but it cannot be understood by speakers of the Hangzhou dialect without learning it. The dialect has an estimated 1.2 to 1.5 million speakers.

Several museums are worth a visit. The China National Silk Museum is the biggest museum about silk anywhere. The China National Tea Museum is devoted to tea, and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum brings together studies of human life with exhibitions and research and holds more than 100,000 cultural relics.

Theatres across the city stage opera such as Yue opera, and large productions based on Hangzhou's history and culture include Impression West Lake and the Romance of the Song Dynasty, among others. Its landscapes are linked with stories of well-known figures from Chinese history and with the delight of ordinary visitors.

The city hosts the China Academy of Art, and its name is linked with the painters Lin Fengmian and Fang Ganmin. Local government spends heavily to promote tourism and the arts, with special attention to silk, umbrellas and Chinese hand fans.

Attached to the Zhejiang Library, the Hangzhou Ancient Book Restoration and Display Center shows the public, on a regular schedule, how old paper is mended and books are bound in the traditional way, techniques used to keep ancient Chinese texts alive. It is central to conserving Jiangnan's cultural documents.
A university sits inside a region as well as a city, so this section turns to Zhejiang, with a quick tour of its early history.

Human settlement here is very old. Near Hangzhou, the Neolithic Kuahuqiao culture dates to 6000-5000 BC. Two more Stone Age cultures followed in Zhejiang: Hemudu, beginning in 5500 BC, and Liangzhu, beginning in 3400 BC.
In the second millennium BC the land that is now Zhejiang sat beyond the main influence of the Shang civilisation. Its people were grouped under the general name Dongyue.

Yue, a kingdom set in northern Zhejiang, enters the written record in the Spring and Autumn period. The Shiji traces its rulers back to Yu the Great, who founded the Xia. A piece known as the "Song of the Yue Boatman" was transcribed into Chinese by writers in Hebei and Henan, northern or inland China, around 528 BC. It tells us the Yue people spoke a tongue that people in the north and inland could not follow. Other traces of Yue culture include the Sword of Goujian, which carries bird-worm seal script, and the legend of Yuenu, a swordswoman called the Lady of Yue. Chu, wanting to hold back the rise of Wu, chose to build up Yue.

King Goujian brought Yue back from early defeats, and in 473 BC it swallowed up the territory of its old rival completely. The royal court left its original base around Mount Kuaiji, in what is now Shaoxing, for the former Wu capital, where Suzhou stands today. With nobody left in the south to turn against, Chu dealt with Yue head on and wiped it out in 333 BC. In 222 BC the Qin Empire absorbed the land and arranged it as a commandery called Kuaiji, which lay in Zhejiang although its first headquarters was in Wu, in Jiangsu.

zhejiang-sci-tech-university.h: From Han to the Three Kingdoms

blocks.x: The Kuaiji Commandery was where Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu launched their uprising against Qin. They briefly revived the kingdom of Chu, but the Han ultimately defeated it. Under the Later Han, the settlement beneath Mount Kuaiji became the seat of control again, although Han authority over the Minyue interior was barely more than a name and the Yue people there largely kept their own political and social arrangements.

Once the Han empire collapsed, two warlords, Yan Baihu and Wang Lang, ruled Zhejiang until Sun Ce and Sun Quan beat them and went on to found the Kingdom of Wu. Its court was relocated from Kuaiji to Jianye (today's Nanjing), yet the Wu rulers went on developing Zhejiang, which also benefited from refugees running away from upheaval in the north. Kilns were built for industrial production, and trade stretched as far as Manchuria and Funan in what is now southern mainland Southeast Asia.

During the Three Kingdoms era (220-280), Zhejiang was part of Wu, also called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, which ran from 229 to 280 and was the richest of the three states. The tale shows Wei and Shu, short of resources, steering clear of open battle with Wu. When they did fight, they leaned heavily on camouflage and trickery to seize Wu's military stores, arrows and bows included.

Jiankang, as Nanjing was then known, kept its prominence. Even so, Qiantang, Hangzhou's former name, remained among the three great southern cities that sent substantial tax revenue to the imperial centres of the north; Jiankang and Chengdu were the other two. In 589 Qiantang was given higher status and renamed Hangzhou.

The Jin dynasty (266-420) was shaken by the Wu Hu uprising, and after Wu itself fell, most elite families of the old Chinese order had worked with the non-Chinese rulers and conquerors of the north. Some of them may have lost social privilege and gone south across the Yangtze. A few refugees may have settled around Hangzhou. A possible example is the Zhuge family. Its ancestor was Zhuge Liang (181-234), chancellor of Shu Han and a man of the Central Plain. His clan collected in a suburb of Hangzhou prefecture and set up Zhuge Village (Zhege Cun), a closed community in which every villager bears the name Zhuge. For centuries it has deliberately cut itself off from nearby settlements, and only in recent times did it become publicly known. That hints that a few powerful elite refugees from the Central Plain may have found shelter south of the river.

Zhejiang, however, is hilly and short of arable land, so the majority of such refugees likely settled elsewhere in the south, where there were fertile fields and urban resources. The places named are southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, where governments were less cohesive. A refugee's choice may have turned on his social standing and military strength back in the north. The remnant Jin state and the Southern dynasties struggled for position against some Han elites, both those from the Central Plain and those from south of the Yangtze.

Lying at the core of Jiangnan, the Yangtze River Delta, Zhejiang stayed the richest region through the Six Dynasties (220 or 222-589) and under the Sui and Tang. When it came under the Sui, that wealth funded Sui plans for expansion to the north and south, notably towards Korea and Vietnam. To support those plans the Sui rebuilt and enlarged the waterways that became the Grand Canal of China. Grain and other goods travelled along it from Zhejiang, via the metropolitan centre of Hangzhou and the hinterland by the Zhe River and the shores of Hangzhou Bay, and from Suzhou, up to the North China Plain.

The Korean campaign ended in disaster, which led to the Sui being overthrown by the Tang, who then oversaw a golden age that lasted for centuries. Within the Tang administration, Zhejiang was a significant economic centre of the Jiangnan East Circuit and was seen as particularly prosperous. The canal kept doing its job through the whole dynasty, carrying grain and materials north to the plain and the empire's major cities. When Tang rule broke up, most of Zhejiang's territory formed the regional kingdom of Wuyue.
If you like to follow sport while you are here, the province has professional teams in two leagues.
Chinese Basketball Association: Zhejiang Golden Bulls and, in Ningbo, the Bayi Rockets
In the Chinese Super League, the football club is Zhejiang Professional F.C.
In summary, ZSTU gives you access to one of China's most dynamic cities, with a mild-to-hot humid climate, a strong technology economy, famous lakeside scenery and a long local history.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

zhejiang-sci-tech-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Zhejiang Sci-Tech University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hangzhou, register at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

If you are putting together a shortlist of Chinese universities, Zhejiang University (ZJU) will almost certainly be on it. It is a public institution in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang Province, and it answers to China's Ministry of Education. It belongs to three national programmes designed to build world-class universities: Project 211, Project 985 and the Double First-Class Construction plan. The C9 League, an informal group of China's most research-intensive universities, counts it as a member too.

The story of the present-day institution begins in 1927, when it was founded in Sun Yat-sen's memory under the name National Third Chung Shan University, and a year later it was called National Chekiang University (NCKU). Under President Chu Kochen, who led it from 1936 to 1949, the university escaped westward to Guizhou while the Second Sino-Japanese War raged, and did not get back to Hangzhou until 1946. In 1952 it was reorganised into a university focused on engineering. The big turning point came in 1998. Three institutions that had grown out of former ZJU departments, namely Zhejiang Agricultural University, Zhejiang Medical University and Hangzhou University, merged back in, and the outcome is the comprehensive university you can apply to today.

In terms of size, ZJU runs seven faculties containing 37 colleges and schools, with roughly 140 undergraduate and 300 graduate programmes. It has seven affiliated hospitals, a museum of its own and two international joint institutes. Fifty-two of its faculty members hold seats in one of China's two national academies: Sciences, or Engineering.

On research output the university sits at the very top of the tables: the Nature Index ranked it number one worldwide for 2026 among academic institutions, and so did the Traditional Edition of the CWTS Leiden Ranking in 2025. Graduates you may have heard of include Chinese premier Li Qiang, business founders Duan Yongping and Colin Huang, and DeepSeek's founder Liang Wenfeng.

zhejiang-university.h: Qiushi Academy and the early college (1897 to 1914)

blocks.x: The oldest root of the university is Qiushi Academy, which Hangzhou's mayor, Lin Qi, set up in 1897. Education reforms in 1902 and 1904 reshaped it: it became Chekiang University in 1902 and then Chekiang Higher Institute in 1903. To organise and oversee the teaching, an American teacher was brought in as head teacher: Elmer L. Mattox, from Hangchow Presbyterian College. The institute also broke new ground, because no other provincial educational institution had previously sent students overseas to study.
Its life was short. Reforms proposed by the new republican government after the 1911 revolution were controversial, and the institute stopped taking in students in 1912 before closing in 1914.

The link back to Qiushi Academy was drawn later. It was a professor at NCKU, Chang Ch'i-yun, who in 1947 started presenting the academy as the university's origin. Republican China's education ministry later accepted that account in its yearbook.

After the institute closed, efforts to revive it failed because warlords were fighting one another. The picture changed after the Northern Expedition of July 1927, when Hangzhou fell under the control of the Kuomintang (KMT). The new authorities combined two schools, one for industry and one for agriculture (Chekiang Industrial College, Chekiang Agricultural College), on the old Qiushi Academy site and called the result National Third Chungshan University. On 1 April 1928 it was renamed Chekiang University, and later the same year it became National Chekiang University, with Jiang Menglin, who had both studied and taught at Qiushi, as its first president.

Leadership changed often in the early 1930s. Shao Peizi, another Qiushi alumnus and teacher, took over in 1929. He declined to join the KMT, relations with the government grew tense, and funding was withdrawn in 1932, which led to his resignation. The Nationalist government then appointed a KMT member, Cheng Tien-fong, and with Chiang Kai-shek's personal intervention the university started getting its money straight from the central government. Another KMT member, Kuo Zing-Yang, became president in March 1933. As the conflict with Japan escalated and many people felt the Nationalist response was soft, the government lost popularity, and the anger boiled over during the 1935 December 9 Movement, when students drove Kuo from office, claiming he had cooperated with police in detaining student demonstrators.

In April 1936 Chen Bulei recommended Chu Kochen to Chiang Kai-shek for the presidency. Chu was a scholar who had never held a political post, and Jiang Menglin presided at his inauguration. Chen's strong financial backing, together with the authority to make political appointments inside the university, let Chu bring in leading figures from two intellectual circles, the Critical Review Group and the Science Society of China.

War then arrived. In the second half of 1937, as Japanese forces advanced, the university had to leave Hangzhou, with stops at Yishan and Zunyi before the final settlement at Meitan, all of it in Guizhou Province in the southwest. During these years NCKU students took on the job of protecting Zhejiang's historical collections, including the Wenlan Pavilion's copy of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, so that Japanese troops would not seize them.

The end of the war brought both loss and rebuilding. Fei Gong, a professor at NCKU who had criticised the Nationalist government, vanished in Chongqing in March 1945, and it was later shown that the government had had him killed. Japan surrendered in September, and the government ordered Luo Zongluo and a group of fellow NCKU professors to take over the former Japanese Imperial University on Taiwan. In October, those who had sheltered in Longquan started to come back to Hangzhou, while the group in Guizhou returned in May 1946 with help from the UN's relief and rehabilitation agency (UNRRA). On the Ministry of Education's instructions, the university opened its first medical school.

Tension returned in late 1947 after the death of Yu Zisan, president of the student union, which set off strikes and protests. Chu tried to balance the students against the Nationalist government, but his relations with the students deteriorated and, at the government's request, he moved to Shanghai. He did not go on to Taiwan; instead he lived quietly inside Shanghai's Academia Sinica building, and stayed there until the Communists took over the NCKU campus in May 1949.

In August 1948 Ma Yinchu became president and promoted communist education and organisations on campus. Then, in 1950, the new education ministry told all universities to take "National" out of their names, which is how the Chinese name became the one used today, Zhejiang University. Once Ma moved on in 1949 to be president of Peking University, communist education among the staff grew into the Thought Reform, Three-anti and Five-anti Campaigns, and ZJU scholars including Su Buqing, Tan Jiazhen and Wang Guosong were targeted for political persecution.

The early 1950s brought a deep restructuring along Soviet lines, which left ZJU as an engineering-focused university with only four departments: mechanical, civil, chemical and electrical engineering. Hangchow University's engineering school joined it. The College of Agriculture split off as Zhejiang Agricultural University. The medical school was folded into Zhejiang Provincial Medical College, producing Zhejiang Medical College. Chinese Literature, Foreign Literature and Education moved into Zhejiang Teachers College, which moved to the Hangchow University campus, and the science faculty was sent to the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

In 1954 the university left Daxue Road for Yuquan. Party Secretary Liu Dan restored scientific research and teaching alongside the engineering courses. In 1963 ZJU was named one of the National Key Universities. When the Cultural Revolution broke out in 1966, teaching stopped altogether and Liu Dan lost his post following attacks on him in the People's Daily and the Zhejiang Daily. Radical groups appeared. That August, ZJU students stood up to younger red guards, mostly high-school pupils, to stop them destroying Lingyin Temple during the drive against the "Four Olds". At a 1967 meeting in Beijing with Tan Zhenlin, ZJU red guards were told that Mao Zedong wanted Jiang Hua protected. That split the red guards in Zhejiang, because a rival faction led by Zhang Yongsheng of the Chinese Academy of Art wanted Jiang Hua persecuted, and the two sides fought each other throughout the Cultural Revolution.

zhejiang-university.h: Reform, merger and expansion (1976 to today)

blocks.x: When the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976, Liu Dan came back to ZJU as honorary president, a title nobody else has held. From November 1980 the university was funded jointly by the Ministry of Education and the Zhejiang provincial government. In 1989 ZJU students, joined by those of more than ten other Hangzhou universities, gathered in Wulin Square to back the democracy movement in Beijing. When word of the massacre in Beijing reached them, protesters lay across the railway at Nanxingqiao station for three days, before talks with vice-governor Chai Songyue. At least 60 passenger trains, plus 166 freight trains, were stopped.

Lu Yongxiang was president from 1988 to 1995. He wrote "pursuing innovation" into the university motto and reformed how teaching and research were run, including the launch of the Advanced Honor Class of Engineering Education.

The university entered Project 211 in 1995. A year on, in 1997, a joint letter went to Jiang Zemin, who was then General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party. Its authors were Wang Ganchang and Bei Shizhang from Beijing, and Su Buqing and Tan Jiazhen from Shanghai, and it urged merging four universities. The State Council agreed, and in 1998 a new Zhejiang University was formed from four major universities. Counting upwards of 30,000 students and 10,000 staff, it was thought to be Asia's biggest higher education institution. Zhang Junsheng became Party secretary to oversee the merger.
Several developments followed:

2005: the university set up Zhejiang University Holding Group, later renamed Zhejiang University Yuanzheng Holding Group. By 2022 several of its companies, among them Shenghua Land, Insigma Technology and United Mechanical & Electrical, were publicly listed.
October 2005: the Hubin campus was sold to Kerry Properties for 2.46 billion yuan, to be turned into a commercial complex.
June 2012: the Ocean College was founded together with the Zhoushan municipal government.

December 2014: Edinburgh University signed an agreement to set up a joint institute on the Haining campus, and a second one was agreed in July 2015 with the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
September 2016: the new Haining campus opened.

2019 onwards: the Institute of Hainan was founded in Sanya, Hainan, in 2019. The Ningbo campus followed in November 2020. In 2021 new institutes appeared in seven Zhejiang cities: Taizhou, Shaoxing, Huzhou, Jiaxing, Wenzhou, Jinhua and Quzhou. Tech entrepreneur Colin Huang gave 100 million US dollars in March 2021 towards the Shanghai Institute for Advanced Study that belongs to the university.

Not every chapter has been smooth, and a prospective student should know the university has had public disputes. In April 2013, 53 alumni put their names to a petition opposing Lin Jianhua's appointment as new president, writing that what was needed was an upright and capable academic leader rather than a mediocre chief executive. Vice president Chu Jian, rumoured to have been behind the unusual petition, was arrested in November 2013 for bribery. His trial only came in 2017, and he received a three-year sentence that had almost been served by then. In September 2013, despite strong objections from local residents and alumni, part of the Huajiachi campus was sold for 13.67 billion yuan, the highest price ever paid for land in Hangzhou. In July 2020 the university was harshly criticised for letting a student convicted of rape stay enrolled; after public opinion turned overwhelmingly against the decision, it reviewed the case and expelled the student.

zhejiang-university.h: Campuses and where you will study

blocks.x: ZJU is spread over seven campuses: Zijingang, Yuquan, Xixi, Huajiachi, Zhijiang, Zhoushan, and the International campus in Haining, plus Ningbo. Together they cover 6.22 square kilometres, with 3.67 million square metres of floor space in school buildings. Which campus you live on depends on your faculty, so it is worth checking this early. Short profiles follow.

Zijingang is the flagship site, in the northwest of Hangzhou. It has three libraries: the Basic Library beside the east gate, the Library of Ancient Books to the south, and the Library of Agriculture and Medicine tucked into the southeast corner. To practise English informally, head for the ground-floor of the Basic Library, which turns into an English corner on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. For getting around, Hangzhou Metro's Sanba Station and Xialongwei Station lie to the east, and Zijingang Campus Zhejiang University Station is on the south side.

Bridges over the Yuhangtang River, opened in February 2022, connect the South Gate with that southern station. The big five-arched South Gate was paid for by alumni donations, but students tend to think it unsuitable for its purpose, and in a public poll in 2021 it was voted the ugliest building in China.

Yuquan is known for Zheda Road, a tree-lined road that links the main gate with the school attached to Zhejiang University, and is admired for its greenery. Alongside it is Zheda Qiushi Village (Qiushi Village), where staff and their families live. Close by are two schools: Qiushi Primary School, whose official name is the Primary School Attached to Zhejiang University, and Hangzhou No. 15 Middle School, which is the university's attached junior high. The Yuquan 1897 cafe on campus serves as an English corner on Wednesday evenings.

Before joining ZJU in 1998, the former Hangzhou University stood here. Today the campus hosts Zhejiang University Press, the Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences and the School of Art and Archaeology. The library is in the middle, and a large meadow lies between it and the south gate. Next door is Xuejun High School, once linked to Hangzhou University and counted among the top two in the city, so it is a major feeder of ZJU undergraduates. Because of that, the Xixi canteen was often crowded with school pupils.

Huajiachi is the oldest ZJU campus. It belonged to Zhejiang Agricultural University before the merger, and before the early 1950s it was the old Huajiachi campus of National Chekiang University. It is home to dentistry, agriculture and the College of Continuing Education. The name comes from a lake inside the grounds, with the library on its east shore. In 2007 the university drew up a plan to move out; a quarter of the campus was sold in 2013, and the plan is to turn the site into a lakeside park that keeps most of the old buildings.

Zhijiang stands on Yuelun Hill beside the Qiantang River and the Liuhe Pagoda. It was the main campus of Hangchow University until ZJU took it over in 1952. Today you will find here the Guanghua Law School, the James D. Watson Institute of Genome Sciences, and also an institute for advanced study that covers the humanities and social sciences. North of the Main Teaching Building stands the law school library. Several buildings are protected as national-level Major Historical and Cultural Sites. The campus became a popular tourist spot after the 2010 film Aftershock was shot there, using it to stand in for a Chinese university of the 1980s.

Opened in 2015, this is the home of the Ocean College, in Lincheng, Dinghai District, on Zhoushan Island in Zhoushan City. The college library stands in the north of the campus, with a meadow between it and the south gate. The university's only training ship, the Zijingang, is based here. Only third- and fourth-year undergraduates and postgraduates of the Ocean College study at Zhoushan; first- and second-year students take their courses at Zijingang and move over for the third year.

The Haining International Campus is in the Zhejiang city of Haining and opened in 2016. It brings together international partners and joint institutes, and students here also belong to a residential college, with Professor Lap-Chee Tsui as its first master. By the northeast shore of the central lake stands the International Campus Library, a three-storey octagonal building. Trains on the Hangzhou-Haining intercity railway call at the station named International Campus, ZJU, which opened on 28 June 2021. Located on campus are the Zhejiang University International Business School (ZIBS), plus a joint lab with Imperial College on applied data science, and two institutes run with foreign partners: the ZJE with the University of Edinburgh and the ZJUI with the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Ningbo began in September 2017 as a venture with the city government there, and the campus administration was established in September 2019. It sits on the grounds of what used to be ZJU's Ningbo Institute of Technology (NIT), which is now NingboTech University. ZJU has no branch library of its own there, but its resources can be used through the NingboTech library. South Higher Education Park Station on Ningbo Rail Transit serves it. The Polytechnic Institute of Zhejiang University opened a branch on the site in October 2016, and the Institute of Ningbo was founded within the NIT campus in June 2018. In January 2020 NIT became independent of ZJU and was renamed NingboTech University, though it stays on the same site. The School of Software Technology is also found here.

Away from its main sites but still inside Zhejiang, ZJU has a string of research institutes. In Hangzhou these are the Innovation Institute for Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, the Innovative Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, and Zhejiang University Innovation Institute International. Elsewhere in the province there are institutes at Wenzhou, Quzhou, Jinhua, Huzhou and Shaoxing, a Research Institute in Taizhou, the International Institutes of Medicine in Yiwu, and the Ocean Research Center of Zhoushan.

Beyond the province, you will find the Shanghai Institute for Advanced Study, the Institute of State System Research (the Beijing Research Center), the Hainan Institute, the Institute of Shenzhen, the Suzhou Industrial Technology Research Institute, the Changzhou Industrial Technology Research Institute and the Zhongyuan Institute in Zhengzhou.

To escape the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, the university abandoned its Hangzhou campus. Along the way it borrowed campuses at Jiande (1937), then Ji'an and Taihe Yishan (1938), and in early 1940 it reached Meitan and Zunyi in Guizhou, where it worked for seven years until peace came. A satellite campus under Zheng Xiaocang was added at Longquan, Zhejiang, in June 1939. In 2016 Dr. Ye Yongfei, from the central committee of the Chinese Kuomintang's Revolutionary Committee, suggested bringing back the Meitan campus to boost western China's economy. The local government in Zunyi formed a committee in 2018 to rally support, though in March of that year the university answered that it had nothing concrete planned.

Another vanished site is the Hubin campus, formerly Zhejiang Medical University. Most of it was pulled down in January 2007 to make way for a modern commercial complex, the Kerry Center, which connects to Fengqi Road station on the Hangzhou Metro. One part survived: the old premises of Zhejiang's High Court and the Hang County local court now serve as the Hangzhou Urban Construction Exhibition Hall.

The motto is "seeking truth" (Chinese: 求是, pinyin Qiúshì). The university council adopted it at a meeting in Yishan, Guangxi, on 19 November 1938, on the advice of President Chu Kochen. It comes from a line of Yangming thought, 君子之學，唯求其是, which says that a gentleman studies only in order to know what is right. The same two characters had named the original Qiushi Academy in 1897, and in English the sound is close to the word "truth". In Chu's view, the search is wider than hard study or laboratory experiments. Quoting the Doctrine of the Mean, he described it as broad study, careful questioning, thoughtful reflection, clear discrimination and sincere practice.

"Pursuing innovation" was added by the university council in May 1988, to match the era of reform and opening up. Explaining the change in 1992, President Lu Yongxiang said that, strictly speaking, innovation is already part of seeking truth, but people tend to read seeking truth as being practical: applying existing knowledge and analysing reality objectively, without a stress on creativity.

At the same council meeting on 19 November 1938, President Chu invited Ma Yifu, a neo-Confucian scholar then teaching at Chekiang, to write the lyrics. Ma wrote in Classical Chinese, which was hard to follow, so the anthem was not set to music until the summer of 1941, when Professor Ying Shangneng of the National Conservatory of Music was asked to compose it. A 2014 online survey run by the Ministry of Education's news office rated it the most popular university anthem.

The mascot is the Qiushi eagle. It first appeared on the seal of National Chekiang University in the 1920s and 1930s and returned in the 1990 logo. NingboTech University and Zhejiang University City College, former affiliates that became independent in December 2019, carry it in their logos as well. The present logo was approved by the university council in January 1991 and formally digitised in May 2017; its Chinese calligraphy is taken from Mao Zedong's handwriting. The flags combine the calligraphy and the logo, in red or blue on a blank flag, or in white on a blue or red one.

Chu Kochen, president of National Chekiang University from 1936 to 1949, is credited with shaping the guiding spirit of the university. In 1936 he put two questions to the incoming freshmen: what do you want to do at Zheda, and when you graduate, what kind of person do you want to be? They are carved in stone beside the main gate of the Zijingang campus and displayed in many other places. Another saying often shown on campus sets out his view of what a university is for: not to turn out specialists like engineers and doctors, but to shape just, patriotic, determined and persistent leaders who take major roles, set trends and change the destiny of the nation.

ZJU is run in line with a charter, the Zhejiang University Chapter, which the Ministry of Education approved; the present one dates from September 2014. Under it ZJU is a national university under the Ministry's management, with funding shared between the central and Zhejiang governments. The university's Communist Party Committee runs the institution, with the president responsible for decisions, and the committee must ensure academic freedom, democracy and rule by law. Since 2000 the president and party secretary have been chosen by the Chinese Communist Party's Organization Department, and both automatically count as vice-ministerial officials. The party committee elects a standing committee, which decides major questions jointly with it. The president chairs the university council, which handles teaching, research and administration, and faculty can review and advise on decisions through the faculty representative meeting. The party secretary is currently Dr. Ren Shaobo, and the president is Professor Dr. Du Jiangfeng.

There are 17 administrative departments. The Office of the Presidents sets strategic priorities to keep the university's leading position, and the Development and Planning Office plans how they are carried out. Putting strategy into practice and promoting the university abroad and at home falls to the Division of Domestic Relations and the Office of Global Engagement. The Human Resources Department recruits and supports faculty. Teaching, learning and degree awards are organised and supervised by the Graduate School and the Undergraduate School, and the Administration of Continuing Education handles training and supervision for continuing education. Which body oversees research and development depends on the subject: it is either the Sci-Tech Academy or the Academy of Humanities and Social Sciences. The Office of Laboratory and Equipment Management buys research facilities and devices, and also maintains and evaluates them, while the university's properties are managed by the Department of General Affairs and built by the Office of Capital Construction. The Medical Management Office looks after the affiliated hospitals.

The University Chapter says the university is mostly state-funded. It has been selected for several national plans for nurturing world-class universities (Project 211, Project 985 and Double First-Class Construction). In 2022 its budget of 26.1 billion yuan was the second largest in China, behind only Tsinghua. Other income comes from affiliated businesses, government subsidy, donations and other lawful sources. Alumni giving to ZJU is consistently among the highest in China; 2.38 billion yuan arrived in 2021, the fourth highest after Tsinghua, Peking and Wuhan. On 21 September 2006 the billionaires Duan Yongping, a ZJU alumnus, and Ding Lei, a Zhejiang native, gave a one-off endowment of 40 million US dollars, 30 million from Duan and 10 million from Ding, at that time the largest private one-off gift any mainland Chinese university had received. Then in 2017 a further alumni donation of 1.1 billion yuan (about 160 million US dollars) set a new record.

zhejiang-university.h: Seven faculties and what they cover

blocks.x: As a comprehensive university it spans eleven branches of learning, from philosophy, literature and history through education, science and economics, to law, management, engineering, agriculture and medicine. These disciplines are arranged in seven faculties, each containing schools. Each faculty, school and department keeps its own academic committee with separate procedures; faculty members organise the committee, a cap limits the share of people in administrative roles, and members are chosen on recommendations from within the faculty. Here is the full breakdown.
This faculty contains:
School of Humanities
School of International Studies
College of Media and International Culture
School of Art and Archaeology
Schools and colleges here are:
School of Economics
Guanghua Law School
College of Education
School of Management
School of Public Affairs
School of Marxism
The Faculty of Science was formed by combining the science departments of Hangzhou University and Zhejiang University. It includes:
School of Mathematical Sciences
Department of Physics
Department of Chemistry
School of Earth Sciences
Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
The engineering units are:
School of Mechanical Engineering
School of Material Science and Engineering
College of Energy Engineering
College of Electrical Engineering
College of Civil Engineering and Architecture
College of Chemical and Biological Engineering
Ocean College
School of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Department of Polymer Science and Engineering

Most of the key departments ZJU had before the 1998 merger ended up here. The School of Software Technology was set up in 2001 and operates in both Hangzhou and Ningbo. Places in the College of Computer Science and Technology are regarded as being among the most competitive in China. Its computer scientists concentrate on artificial intelligence, computer vision and computer graphics, areas where ZJU ranks in the worldwide top 5 on CSranking. On the national subject evaluation (CUSR), fourth round, A+ went to four subjects: Software Engineering, Optical Engineering, Control Science and Engineering, and Computer Science and Technology. Biomedical Engineering got A-. The faculty consists of:
College of Optical Science and Engineering
College of Information Science and Electronic Engineering
College of Control Science and Engineering
College of Computer Science and Technology
School of Software Technology
College of Biomedical Engineering and Instrument Science

zhejiang-university.h: Faculty of Agriculture, Life and Environment Science

blocks.x: Known as FALE, this faculty took in most of the departments of Zhejiang Agricultural University when the 1998 merger happened. Its fourth-round CUSR results were: A+ for Plant Protection, Horticulture, Agricultural Engineering and Agricultural Resources and Environment; A for Pharmacy and for Environmental Science and Engineering; and A- for Crop Science, Animal Science and Food Science and Engineering. No other faculty has as many subjects rated A-, A or A+. It comprises:
College of Life Sciences
College of Biosystem Engineering and Food Science
College of Environmental and Resource Sciences
College of Agriculture and Biotechnology
College of Animal Sciences

This faculty took in most of the departments of Zhejiang Medical University in 1998. Its roots go back to three older bodies: Chekiang Provincial Medical School (1912), then, at National Chekiang University, a Pharmaceutical Department in 1944 and a Medical School in 1945. It was based at the Hubin campus until it moved to Zijingang in 2007.

For international applicants one fact stands out: the School of Medicine is one of 45 medical schools in China that teach MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery) programmes in English. Medical doctoral students are also drawn from the Chu Kochen Honors College through the Ba Denian Medical Program, and the School of Basic Medical Sciences runs a joint undergraduate programme in biomedicine and bioinformatics on the International Campus. The School of Medicine has seven top-level hospitals. In the fourth CUSR round, clinical medicine, pharmacy and basic medicine scored A+, A and A- respectively. The faculty includes:
College of Pharmaceutical Sciences
School of Medicine
The seven hospitals attached to the School of Medicine are:
First Affiliated Hospital (the first teaching hospital)
Second Affiliated Hospital (the second teaching hospital)
Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital (the third teaching hospital)
Yiwu Hospital, formally the Fourth Affiliated Hospital (the fourth teaching hospital)
Women's Hospital
Children's Hospital
Stomatology Hospital, whose full name is Zhejiang Provincial Stomatology Hospital

Departments do the teaching and assessing and write up the details of each degree programme, which the Undergraduate School and Graduate School must approve before they begin. Those two schools also supervise and regulate teaching for quality control, and the detailed method can differ between courses and programmes. Chu Kochen Honors College and the international dual degree programmes at Haining have their own responsible committees. Chu Kochen Honors College (CKC) is the university's elite undergraduate college, named after the former president, and it selects further from top ZJU students or from the best Gaokao candidates.

To graduate, a student must fulfil credit requirements for both compulsory and elective courses. Within that, you can choose and pass whatever mix of courses you like, provided the course is open for enrolment, although some are hard to get into because class sizes are capped.

In July 2008 the university founded Qiushi College, a residential college that forms part of the School of Undergraduate. It manages dormitories including Danyang-Qingxi Hall, Ziyun-Bifeng Hall and Lantian Hall, and it offers liberal arts education to freshmen while supporting student organisations and activities. It also helps with academic matters such as choosing a major and team building. When they enrol, undergraduates are placed in a hall of Qiushi College at Zijingang, mostly based on their faculty. During the military training and education that all Chinese freshmen take, students are grouped by hall. Because first-year students are admitted by academic faculty rather than by specific subject, your major may still be undecided at first, and you belong to a hall and not to a department. You can apply for a major later or transfer during your studies, but popular majors are very competitive and extra requirements may apply, and the college is there to assist.

Chu Kochen Honors College (CKHC) was set up in May 2000 to honour Chu Kochen, and it is normally chaired by the sitting president of the university. It grew out of the Mixed Class of Engineering, which began in 1984. Its teaching tracks are the Mixed Class, the Shennong Class, the Qiushi Sciences Class, and experimental classes in medicine, engineering and the humanities and social sciences. Entry is highly selective, and its selection questions are said to be creative yet difficult. Alumni include the entrepreneur Colin Huang and the current ZJU president Wu Zhaohui. Teaching is overseen by a dedicated committee under the president. Note that during the programme, the students who fall in the bottom 15 to 20 percent by GPA are moved to non-CKHC programmes.

Dual degree programmes at the International Campus are overseen by the joint institute so that the academic requirements of both ZJU and the partner are met. For example, the University of Edinburgh's rules on progression and degree classification apply to its joint institute there, even though they are not ZJU regulations. The campus offers a limited number of electives, and students may take a course not offered by their own institute. Transfers from a Sino-foreign programme to a purely ZJU programme, or between programmes at different joint institutes, are not allowed. Moving within one joint institute is permitted, but approval may depend on class size.

ZJU is a comprehensive research university, and its work covers 12 academic disciplines (agriculture, art, economics, education, engineering and history, then law, literature, management, medicine, natural sciences and philosophy). It has about 4,191 standing faculty members, over 1,893 of them professors. Among them are 26 members of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and 27 of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, together with 164 winners of the Chang Jiang (Yangtze River) award and 154 recipients of National Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars awards. Prominent foreign academics teach there too. ZJU has 11 State Key Laboratories, among the most of any Chinese university.

There are also three State Specialized Labs, covering secondary resources chemical engineering, power electronics and biomedical sensors. Three Ministry of Education (MOE) labs add to that. One studies soft soils and geoenvironmental engineering, one covers reproductive biology and conservation genetics for endangered wildlife, and the third is the MOE-Microsoft Key Lab of Visual Perception.

The library system holds more than 7.9 million volumes, one of the largest academic collections in China. It has 6 branch libraries: Yuquan Campus Library, the Basic Library, Library of Agriculture and Medicine and Library of Ancient Books at Zijingang, the Xixi Campus Library and the Huajiachi Campus Library. Three more libraries sit inside colleges: those of the Ocean College, the Guanghua Law School and the International Campus. Zijingang is the only campus with three libraries. If a title is held in another library, you can reserve it wherever you are and collect it there.

Globally, ZJU is 24th in ARWU 2025, where it is 3rd in Asia and Oceania, 44th in QS for 2024, 39th in the Times Higher Education (THE) table for 2026 and 35th in the USNWR for 2026-2027. In 2024, on combined performance across THE, QS and ARWU, it stood 33rd worldwide, 5th in Asia and 3rd in China. In the THE World Reputation Rankings it was 50th worldwide and 7th in Asia.

In 2024 SCImago Institutions Rankings placed ZJU 5th among universities worldwide. The 2025 CWTS Leiden Ranking put it 1st in the world for the number of scientific publications in 2020-2023, and the Nature Index Annual Table 2026 placed it first globally for research output among academic institutions.

In the Essential Science Indicators (ESI) across 22 disciplines, ZJU is in the top 1% in 15 and is among the world's top 100 institutions in 4. In 2021 U.S. News & World Report listed ZJU in the global top 50 for 19 subjects. In the sciences these were Chemistry, Physical Chemistry, Condensed Matter Physics, Optics, Material Science, Polymer Science, Nanoscience and Nanotechnology, Pharmacology and Toxicology, and Plant and Animal Science. The applied and technical ones were Computer Science, Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Civil Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Energy and Fuels, Biotechnology and Applied Microbiology, Agricultural Sciences, and Food Science and Technology.

Results of the Ministry of Education's fourth China University Subject Rankings came out in 2018. ZJU got an A rating in 31 subjects, more than any other Chinese university, and A+ in 11, which put it third behind Peking and Tsinghua.
For job prospects, In the 2022 QS Graduate Employability Rankings ZJU came 35th in the world, and 71st in the Times Higher Education Global University Employability Ranking 2025.

As of June 2023, Zhejiang University had 65,821 full-time students: of whom 16,150 were doctoral candidates, 20,554 master's candidates and 29,117 undergraduates. Among them were 5,123 international students, so you would not be the only one far from home.

CC98 is a forum run by students, created in December 2002 and reached at www.cc98.org from the school intranet. It has boards for different topics, and as of March 2023 it is available only in Chinese.

Much of what makes student life good or hard is the city outside the gates: its weather, how you get around and what you can do. This part of the profile introduces Hangzhou, where Zhejiang University is based.

Northwestern Zhejiang is where Hangzhou lies, within the south-central Yangtze River Delta, and the southern terminus of China's Grand Canal, which stretches to Beijing, is here. As a sub-provincial city, its administrative area extends westward into the mountains bordering Anhui and eastward to the Hangzhou Bay coastal plain. West Lake's eastern and northern banks are where the centre of the city developed, a little north of the Qiantang River.

The Qiantang is Zhejiang's biggest river. In the eighth lunar month, from the 15th to the 18th day, the Qiantang Tide comes in, which is billed as the biggest tide in the world. The tidal bore rushes up the river through Hangzhou and can reach 12 m (39 ft) high.

Hangzhou has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with four distinct seasons. Summers are long, very hot and humid; winters are chilly, cloudy and drier, with occasional snow. Over a year the mean temperature is 17.0 °C (62.6 °F). Averages for the day are 5 °C (41.0 °F) in the coldest month, January, and 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) in the hottest, July. The city gets 1,438 mm (56.6 in) of rain on average every year, and June brings the plum rains of the Asian monsoon. In late summer, from August to September, typhoon storms affect the city, although typhoons rarely hit it directly. They usually come ashore along Zhejiang's southern coast, bringing strong winds and stormy rain to the Hangzhou area.

Since 1951 the coldest recorded day was 6 February 1969 at -9.6 °C (15 °F), and the hottest was 3 August 2024 at 41.9 °C (107 °F). Informal readings have fallen as low as -10.5 °C (13 °F) on 29 December 1912 and again on 24 January 1916, and climbed to 42.1 °C (108 °F) on 10 August 1930. Each month, between 30% (March) and 51% (August) of possible sunshine is received, which adds up to 1,709.4 hours a year.

Hangzhou's permanent population in 2023 was 12.522 million, including Xiaoshan and Yuhang, and 10.543 million of these people (84.2%) were urban residents. For the wider metropolitan area the OECD estimated 13.4 million people in 2010, although other sources suggest more than 21 million. Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou are among the major cities in it. People registered in the city had a life expectancy of 83.18 years in 2021, among the highest in China.

Hangzhou has long had a varied religious life. In 1848, under the Qing dynasty, it was described as the stronghold of Islam in China, with several mosques carrying Arabic inscriptions. A Hui man from Ningbo told an Englishman that Hangzhou was the stronghold of Islam in Zhejiang, with multiple mosques, whereas his own mosque in Ningbo served about 30 families. Two notable mosques stand in the city today, the New Hangzhou Great Mosque and the Phoenix Mosque. In the late 16th and early 17th centuries Hangzhou was an important centre of Chinese Jewry and might be where the Kaifeng Jewish community first began. A synagogue once stood in Hangzhou, and another in Ningbo, but today neither has left any visible trace. Two of the Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism came from Hangzhou, and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral of Hangzhou, about 400 years old and dating to the Ming dynasty, is among the oldest Catholic churches in China. Christians were persecuted in the city in the early 21st century.

Many temples cluster around West Lake. Lingyin Temple, meaning Soul's Retreat, lies about 2 km (1.2 mi) west of the lake. The temple dates from AD 326, the first year of Xianhe under the Eastern Jin Dynasty, giving it about 1,700 years of history. People regard it as Hangzhou's oldest Buddhist temple and its earliest famous one, and it has been destroyed and rebuilt many times. Yuefei Temple, on the northwest shore of the lake, was built in 1221 in the Song Dynasty to honour General Yue Fei, who died through political persecution. Also worth knowing are the Baochu Pagoda, Leifeng Pagoda and Jingci Temple. Across the Qiantang River, Yuelun Hill carries the Liuhe Pagoda, on the river's north bank, and the Hupao Temple (虎跑寺) is another stop.

Growth in Hangzhou has been quick ever since the city opened up in 1992. Light industry, agriculture and textiles all feature in an industrial mix, and the city is a major manufacturing base and logistics hub for the coast of China as well as an e-commerce and technology centre. RMB 156.8 billion was its GDP in 2001, second among provincial capitals after Guangzhou. By 2018 the figure had more than tripled, reaching RMB 1.3509 trillion, while GDP per capita went from US$3,020 to $21,184. The metropolitan area's nominal gross product was put at 3.2 trillion yuan ($486.53 billion) in 2019, bigger than Argentina's economy ($452 billion, 26th largest in the world) or Nigeria's ($448 billion, the largest in Africa).

The city also scores well in outside assessments. A study by PwC and the China Development Research Foundation ranked it first among Chinese Cities of Opportunity, and GaWC classifies it as a "Beta+" world city. It was 89th in the 2018 Global Financial Centres Index and first in the Economist Intelligence Unit's China Emerging City Rankings, which judge growth potential, in 2021 and again in 2022. By the number of billionaires, the Hurun Global Rich List 2020 had it 11th globally and 6th nationally, behind Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou. Counting Fortune Global 500 headquarters inside city limits, it was tenth in the world and fourth in China, behind Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen, as of August 2023. A smart city initiative is also under way, with efforts to digitise the economy and move towards a cashless city.

Hangzhou is home to the headquarters of Geely, HikVision, DeepSeek, Ant Group, NetEase and Alibaba Group. Alibaba opened a new global headquarters in May 2024, covering about one million sqm over seven buildings and housing 30,000 employees. Thanks to the internet industry, programmers have moved here from cities like Shanghai and Beijing. New industries have grown up in medicine, information technology, heavy equipment, car components, household appliances, electronics, telecommunications, fine chemicals, chemical fibre and food processing. Officials call the key industries "1 + 6" clusters, where the "1" means the digital economy and the "6" stand for finance, tourism, fashion manufacturing, high-end equipment manufacturing and the cultural and creative economy. From at least 2023 onward, it is the digital and the creative or cultural sectors that have driven growth. Studies suggest a positive effect of Alibaba Group's revenue on the city's growth, though the causal link runs in one direction only; in the long run, a 1% rise in the group's total revenue can lift the city's growth by 0.272%.

The Hangzhou Tourism Commission launched an online Facebook campaign, "Modern Marco Polo", in March 2013. Within a year nearly 26,000 applicants from around the world had put themselves forward to be Hangzhou's first foreign tourism ambassador. Liam Bates was named the winner at a press conference on 20 May 2014, taking a $55,000 contract; he was the first foreigner China's government had appointed to a role of that kind.

In 1993 the State Council approved the Hangzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone as a national zone, with an area of 104.7 km2 (40.4 sq mi). Industries it encourages are electronic information, biological medicine, food processing, and the manufacture of machinery and household appliances. On 27 April 2000 the Hangzhou Export Processing Zone was set up with State Council approval; it was among the first of its kind and is the only one in Zhejiang Province. Close to Hangzhou Port and to the Xiaoshan International Airport in Hangzhou, it has a planned area of 2.92 km2 (1.13 sq mi).

The Hangzhou Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone (HHTZ) became a state-level high-tech zone in March 1991 with State Council approval. Its three parts include two main ones, Xiasha Sci-Tech Industrial Park and Zhijiang Sci-Tech Industrial Park, and few places in Zhejiang Province have had more influence as a high-tech innovation and industry base. By 2013 over 1,100 software developers and BPO enterprises were located in it, and R&D centres had been opened by Siemens, Nokia and Motorola. The zone's GDP grew 13.1 percent in 2011, reaching RMB 41.63 billion, or 5.9 percent of Hangzhou's total. It calls itself China's "Silicon Valley" and is where Alibaba Group has its headquarters. Alibaba speeded up work on its global headquarters in Hangzhou in 2023, with local government support, after signing another cooperation agreement with the authorities.

For anyone choosing between big Chinese cities, it is worth knowing that Hangzhou has seen a lot of recent building, but it has held on to its natural setting and its historical and cultural legacy, and tourism still matters to the economy. With numerous skyscrapers, it is the 19th city in the world, and 9th in China, for their number.

Among the most popular attractions is West Lake, which has UNESCO World Heritage status. About 3,323 ha (8,210 acres) make up the West Lake Cultural Landscape, taking in some of the city's best-known historic and scenic places. The lake is ringed by cultural sites, historical pagodas, tea fields and hills such as Phoenix Mountain, and two major causeways cross the water. To the west lies Dreaming of the Tiger Spring, which is known for its spring water and for being close to the famous longjing tea plantations.

The Grand Canal passes through parts of Hangzhou. Workers dredged and widened an existing channel in 610 CE to form the Jiangnan Canal, linking Suzhou and Hangzhou, and UNESCO named the Grand Canal a World Heritage Site in 2014. For the historical sites near Gongchen Bridge, take Hangzhou Metro Line 5 and get off at East Gongchen Bridge station or The Grand Canal station.

In Xiacheng District, the West Lake Cultural Square contains the Zhejiang Natural History Museum and the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology, together with the Zhejiang Global Center, a tower of about 160 m (520 ft) that is among the tallest downtown. Xixi National Wetland Park, which covers about 10 km2 (3.9 sq mi), protects the region's wetland ecosystem; reed beds and fish ponds have been restored, many bird species live there, and the park contains a temple and several historic rural houses. Qiandao Lake, a man-made reservoir in Chun'an County under Hangzhou's jurisdiction, has more islands than any other lake in China, each different in size, shape and scenery. Xihu District is the location of both the Hangzhou Zoo and the Hangzhou Botanical Garden.

Hangzhou natives and some people elsewhere in Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu use the Hangzhou dialect. It belongs to the Wu group but is specific to this area, and it differs from the dialects of southern Zhejiang and of southern Jiangsu. Mandarin, China's official language, dominates, yet the two are mutually unintelligible; an estimated 1.2 to 1.5 million people speak the Hangzhou dialect.

Among the museums are the China National Silk Museum, which is the world's largest on silk, the China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆), and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum, where human studies, exhibitions and research are combined and over 100,000 cultural relics are held. Many theatres stage opera such as Yue opera, and large shows themed on the city's history and culture include the Romance of Song Dynasty and Impression West Lake. The scenery ties together tales of famous figures from Chinese history and the delight of ordinary visitors. The China Academy of Art is based in Hangzhou, as are painters such as Fang Ganmin and Lin Fengmian. The local government invests heavily in tourism and the arts, with emphasis on silk, umbrellas and Chinese hand-held folding fans.

Linked to the Zhejiang Library, the Hangzhou Ancient Book Restoration and Display Center holds regular public demonstrations of the traditional paper restoration and binding methods used to preserve ancient Chinese texts. It plays a key role in conserving Jiangnan cultural documents.

zhejiang-university.h: What this means for your application

blocks.x: Taken together, the facts above give a clear picture. ZJU is large, richly funded and strongly ranked: 65,821 full-time students, a 26.1 billion yuan budget in 2022, first place worldwide for research output in the Nature Index 2026, and 31 subjects rated A in the Ministry of Education's evaluation. If you apply, remember that the campus you are assigned to shapes daily life, whether that is the main Zijingang site in northwest Hangzhou, the lakeside Huajiachi grounds, the international joint-institute campus at Haining or the Ocean College on Zhoushan Island.
