zhejiang-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Zhejiang University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Hangzhou, register at Zhejiang University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

zhejiang-university-of-technology.h: Zhejiang University of Technology and its setting

blocks.x: Zhejiang University of Technology (浙江工业大学, which can be rendered in English as Zhejiang Industrial University) is a comprehensive university funded by the provincial government and based in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang in eastern China. It is affiliated with the Province of Zhejiang. This overview focuses on the place where you would live and study, because for most international students the surrounding city and province colour everyday life at least as much as the campus. It starts with Hangzhou and then widens out to Zhejiang's long history and its sporting scene.

Hangzhou stands in the north-west of Zhejiang, in the south-central stretch of the Yangtze River Delta, at the southern terminus of the Grand Canal of China, which links it to Beijing. The city's administrative area has sub-provincial rank. Its western side climbs into the mountains that border Anhui province, and its eastern side flattens into the coastal plain beside Hangzhou Bay. The central city grew up around the eastern and northern shores of West Lake and lies just north of the Qiantang River.

zhejiang-university-of-technology.h: The great tide on the Qiantang

blocks.x: The Qiantang is the biggest river in Zhejiang, and each year, from the 15th to the 18th of a lunar month that usually falls in August, it produces a spectacular tidal bore. People call it the biggest tide in the world. The surge races inland through Hangzhou and can stand up to 12 metres (39 feet) tall. Viewing it is a classic local outing, and if you arrive in the right season you can plan a trip to watch it with classmates.

The climate is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) and the four seasons are clearly separated. Summers are long, steamy and very hot; winters are cold, grey and fairly dry, with occasional snow. Over a year the mean temperature is 17.0 °C (62.6 °F), and monthly daily means span from 5 °C (41.0 °F) in January to 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) in July. Rain totals 1,438 millimetres (56.6 inches) annually, and the monsoon's plum rains arrive in June.

Typhoon season is late summer, August and September. Direct hits are rare, because storms generally make landfall further south along Zhejiang's coast, but Hangzhou still feels their strong winds and heavy rain. The official record low since 1951 is -9.6 °C (15 °F), set on 6 February 1969, and the record high is 41.9 °C (107 °F) on 3 August 2024. Unofficial readings stretch the range to -10.5 °C (13 °F), noted in December 1912 and January 1916, and 42.1 °C (108 °F) in August 1930. Sunshine amounts to 30 percent of possible hours in March, rising to 51 percent in August, and 1,709.4 hours over a whole year. Practically speaking, pack light, breathable clothes for summer and a warm coat for the damp winter, and carry an umbrella for the June rains and any late-summer storms.

Hangzhou's permanent population reached 12.522 million in 2023 (counting Xiaoshan and Yuhang), and 10.543 million of those, or 84.2 percent, lived in urban areas. For the metropolitan region as a whole, estimates differ with the boundaries used: the OECD put it at 13.4 million in 2010, but other sources say more than 21 million. The region includes Shaoxing, Jiaxing and Huzhou. People registered in the city had a life expectancy of 83.18 years in 2021, one of the highest in China.

Hangzhou has a varied religious past. An account from 1848, under the Qing, described it as the stronghold of Islam in China, with several mosques bearing Arabic inscriptions. A Hui man from Ningbo told an Englishman that Hangzhou was Zhejiang's Muslim stronghold, with several mosques, whereas his own mosque had a modest congregation of around 30 families. Of today's mosques, two stand out: the New Hangzhou Great Mosque and the Phoenix Mosque. During the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries the city was a major centre of Chinese Jewry, and it may have been where the Kaifeng Jewish community began; a synagogue once stood here, but nothing of it can now be found. Hangzhou produced two of the three men known as the Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism, and its Immaculate Conception Cathedral, about 400 years old and dating to the Ming, ranks among the oldest Catholic churches in the country.

Around West Lake there are many temples. The Lingyin Temple, or Soul's Retreat, about 2 kilometres (1.2 miles) west of the lake, was founded in AD 326, in the first Xianhe year of the Eastern Jin. It is therefore about 1,700 years old, and it is believed to be the oldest Buddhist temple in Hangzhou despite repeated cycles of destruction and rebuilding. The Yue Fei Temple on the lake's north-western shore dates from 1221 and honours General Yue Fei, who died as a result of political persecution. You can also visit Jingci Temple and the Baochu and Leifeng pagodas. The Liuhe Pagoda crowns Yuelun Hill on the Qiantang's north bank, and Hupao Temple (虎跑寺) is another site.

Since opening up in 1992, Hangzhou has developed quickly. It has long been an industrial centre, with light manufacturing, farming and textiles, and it is viewed as a key manufacturing and logistics base for China's coast. It is also a hub for e-commerce and technology. The city's output in 2001 was RMB 156.8 billion, second among provincial capitals behind Guangzhou. It had grown to RMB 1.3509 trillion by 2018, and per-capita GDP went from US$3,020 to US$21,184. For 2019 the metropolitan area's gross product was put at 3.2 trillion yuan (US$486.53 billion), bigger than Argentina's economy (US$452 billion, the 26th largest worldwide) or Nigeria's (US$448 billion, the biggest in Africa).

Rankings tend to be positive. PwC and the China Development Research Foundation placed Hangzhou first among Chinese Cities of Opportunity. GaWC classes it as a Beta+ world city, and the Global Financial Centres Index put it 89th in 2018. In the Economist Intelligence Unit's list of fast-emerging Chinese cities, which gauges potential for growth, it came first in 2021 and again in 2022. The Hurun Global Rich List 2020 had it eleventh globally for billionaires and sixth in China, following Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou. At August 2023 its limits contained the tenth-largest number of Fortune Global 500 headquarters of any city in the world, and the fourth-largest in China behind Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. The city is also pursuing a smart-city plan, digitising its economy and building towards a cashless society, so it helps to set up mobile payment soon after you arrive.

Major technology companies based here include Alibaba Group, NetEase, Ant Group, DeepSeek, Geely and HikVision. Alibaba opened a global headquarters of roughly one million square metres in seven buildings in May 2024, with room for 30,000 staff. The internet industry has also pulled in programmers from Shanghai, Beijing and elsewhere. The city has added many other industries, among them pharmaceuticals, IT, heavy equipment, vehicle parts, home appliances, electronics, telecoms, fine chemicals, chemical fibres and food processing.

Officials frame the key industries as 1 + 6 clusters. The 1 stands for the digital economy; the 6 stand for culture and creative industries, finance, tourism, fashion manufacturing and high-end equipment. Since at least 2023 the digital and creative sectors have been the main engines of growth. One study found that Alibaba's total revenue has a positive effect on the city's economic growth, but only in one direction: a 1 percent increase in the group's revenue is linked to 0.272 percent long-run growth for the city.

The Economic and Technological Development Zone gained national status from the State Council in 1993. It spans 104.7 square kilometres (40.4 square miles) and favours electronic information, biomedicine, machinery, home appliances and food processing.

The Export Processing Zone opened on 27 April 2000 following State Council approval; it was among the earliest of its type and the single one in Zhejiang. Its planned area is 2.92 square kilometres (1.13 square miles), near Hangzhou Port and Xiaoshan International Airport.

The Hi-Tech Industrial Development Zone received state-level status in March 1991. It has three parts, led by the Zhijiang and Xiasha science and technology parks, and it is among the most influential high-tech bases in Zhejiang. As of 2013 more than 1,100 software and outsourcing companies operated there, and Motorola, Nokia and Siemens have set up R&D centres. In 2011 its GDP grew 13.1 percent to RMB 41.63 billion, equal to 5.9 percent of the city's total. The zone sees itself as China's Silicon Valley, and Alibaba has its headquarters there. In 2023, after signing a fresh cooperation agreement with local authorities, Alibaba sped up the building of its global headquarters in Hangzhou with the government's backing.

The Hangzhou Tourism Commission launched an online campaign on Facebook in March 2013, called Modern Marco Polo, to appoint the city's first foreign tourism ambassador. Close to 26,000 people applied worldwide during the following year. At a press conference on 20 May 2014 a winner was announced, who received a US$55,000 contract and became the first foreigner given such an official post by a Chinese government.

Hangzhou has changed a lot recently, but it has held on to its heritage and its natural surroundings, and tourism still counts as a major part of the economy. It also has plenty of tall towers: 19th in the world and ninth in China by number of skyscrapers.

West Lake is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the city's top draws. The listed cultural landscape covers about 3,323 hectares (8,210 acres) and takes in many celebrated historical and scenic spots: historic pagodas, hills, tea fields such as those on Phoenix Mountain, and two long causeways across the water. West of the lake, Dreaming of the Tiger Spring is known for its spring and for lying beside the plantations that grow the renowned Longjing tea.

Several stretches of the Grand Canal pass through the city. In 610 CE the Jiangnan Canal was deepened and widened along an older channel so that it joined Suzhou to Hangzhou, and UNESCO added the Grand Canal to its World Heritage list in 2014. Metro Line 5 reaches the historic area around Gongchen Bridge from either The Grand Canal station or East Gongchen Bridge station. In Xiacheng District, West Lake Cultural Square houses the Zhejiang Natural History Museum, the Zhejiang Museum of Science and Technology and the Zhejiang Global Center, a tower of about 160 metres (520 feet) that is among the highest in the centre. Xixi National Wetland Park, about 10 square kilometres (3.9 square miles), was created to protect the region's wetland ecosystem. Reed beds and fish ponds have been restored, many bird species live there, and a temple and some historically important country houses stand in the park.

Qiandao Lake, a reservoir in Chun'an County which comes under Hangzhou, has more islands than any other lake in China, and each island differs in size, shape and scenery. Xihu District holds the Hangzhou Botanical Garden and the Hangzhou Zoo.

Natives of Hangzhou, like many people in Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu, speak Hangzhou dialect, a Wu dialect found only in this area and different from those of southern Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu. Mandarin is the national standard and the main language people speak, although the two are mutually unintelligible. The dialect has around 1.2 to 1.5 million speakers. Expect Mandarin in class and on the street, with local speech in the background; if you learn a few Hangzhou phrases, locals are likely to appreciate the effort.

Among the city's museums are the China National Silk Museum, which is the world's largest silk museum, the China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆) and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum, which brings together displays and research on human studies and has more than 100,000 cultural relics. Local theatres stage operas, Yue opera among them, and big productions such as Impression West Lake and Romance of the Song Dynasty are based on the city's history and culture. The scenery ties stories of famous people in Chinese history to the feelings of ordinary visitors. Hangzhou is home to the China Academy of Art and to painters such as Lin Fengmian and Fang Ganmin. The city government puts a lot of money into tourism and the arts, and it particularly promotes silk, umbrellas and folding fans.

Attached to the Zhejiang Library, the Hangzhou Ancient Book Restoration and Display Center holds regular public demonstrations in which staff mend paper and bind books by traditional methods. Its work is important for preserving cultural documents from the Jiangnan area, and the demonstrations are a quiet, interesting stop for anyone curious about traditional crafts.

The history of the province explains a lot about the city you will live in, so here is a short tour from the Stone Age to the Tang dynasty. Some of the names below echo in the region today: Wu survives in the Wu dialect, and Yue in Yue opera, both mentioned earlier, while Qiantang is still the name of the river.

The earliest known settlement near Hangzhou belongs to the Kuahuqiao culture, an early Neolithic community from about 6000 to 5000 BC. Zhejiang also saw the Neolithic Hemudu culture (from about 5500 BC) and then the Liangzhu culture (from about 3400 BC).

Through the second millennium BC, what is now Zhejiang lay beyond the reach of the Shang state, and its inhabitants were collectively called the Dongyue. Records from the Spring and Autumn period mention a kingdom of Yue in northern Zhejiang; the historian Sima Qian's Shiji says its rulers descended from Yu the Great, founder of the Xia. A short poem, the Song of the Yue Boatman, was transcribed into Chinese around 528 BC by writers living in Hebei and Henan, and its origin shows that the Yue spoke a language northerners could not follow. The famous Sword of Goujian is inscribed in bird-worm seal script, and the legendary swordswoman Yuenü, the Lady of Yue, was from this state. Chu, to the west, tried to limit the expansion of Wu by building up Yue.

King Goujian led a recovery from Yue's early defeats, and in 473 BC he took over all the territory of his rival Wu. The Yue court then shifted from the original base near Mount Kuaiji, in modern Shaoxing, to Wu's old capital, which is now Suzhou. Having no rival to the south, Yue was confronted directly by Chu, which destroyed it in 333 BC. The Qin Empire annexed its lands in 222 BC and created Kuaiji Commandery, although the administration was at first based in Wu, in Jiangsu.

zhejiang-university-of-technology.h: From Han to the Three Kingdoms

blocks.x: Kuaiji Commandery served as the first base for Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu when they rose against Qin. They restored the kingdom of Chu for a time, until it fell to the Han. During the Later Han period control returned to the town at the foot of Mount Kuaiji, while real authority over the Minyue hinterland was weak, so the Yue people living there mostly kept their own political and social systems.

When the Han empire collapsed, Zhejiang was ruled by two warlords, Yan Baihu and Wang Lang, until Sun Ce and Sun Quan defeated them and went on to found the Kingdom of Wu. Although its court moved from Kuaiji to Jianye (today's Nanjing), the Sun family carried on developing the region, which benefited from refugees fleeing chaos in the north. Kilns were established for industry, and trade extended as far as Manchuria and Funan, in southern mainland Southeast Asia. Wu, called Eastern Wu or Sun Wu (229 to 280), was the most economically developed of the Three Kingdoms (220 to 280).

Nanjing, then called Jiankang, was still the leading city, but Qiantang (the former name of Hangzhou) remained one of three major southern centres that sent tax revenue to the northern capitals, the other two being Jiankang and Chengdu. In 589 Qiantang was promoted and given the name Hangzhou.

After Wu fell and the Wu Hu rebellion shook the Jin dynasty (266 to 420), many of the northern elite had collaborated with non-Chinese conquerors. Some lost their privileges and sought refuge south of the Yangtze, and a few may have settled around Hangzhou. A well-known example is the clan of Zhuge Liang (181 to 234), chancellor of Shu Han, whose descendants are said to have gathered in a closed settlement outside Hangzhou prefecture, Zhuge Village, where all residents share the surname Zhuge. The village kept itself apart from its neighbours for centuries and has only lately become widely known. Still, because Zhejiang is mountainous and has little farmland, most refugees probably went elsewhere in the south, where fertile land and urban resources were easier to find, chiefly southern Jiangsu, eastern Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan and Anhui, where regional governments were looser. Where someone ended up depended on their social status and military strength back in the north. The remnant Jin state and the Southern dynasties competed with certain Han elites from the Central Plain and from south of the Yangtze.

Zhejiang lay at the heart of Jiangnan, the Yangtze delta, and was the richest region throughout the Six Dynasties (220 or 222 to 589) and the Sui and Tang. After the Sui incorporated it, they drew on its wealth to pursue expansion to the north and south, especially toward Korea and Vietnam. This led the Sui to restore and extend the waterway network that became the Grand Canal. Grain and other goods travelled regularly along it from Zhejiang to the North China Plain, passing through Hangzhou and its hinterland along the Zhe River and the shore of Hangzhou Bay, and through Suzhou. The failed war in Korea brought the Sui down, and the Tang replaced them and presided over a golden age lasting centuries. Zhejiang was a significant part of the Tang empire's Jiangnan East Circuit, regarded as notably prosperous, and the canal stayed effective throughout that period. When the Tang disintegrated, Zhejiang formed most of the territory of the regional kingdom of Wuyue.

Professional teams linked to Zhejiang have included the Zhejiang Golden Bulls and the Bayi Rockets, the latter in Ningbo, in the Chinese Basketball Association, and Zhejiang Professional F.C. in the Chinese Super League. Team line-ups change from season to season, so check current fixtures if you want to see a match, and treat the team details above as a general guide that may have changed.

Zhengzhou University (ZZU; 郑州大学) is a provincial public university in Zhengzhou, Henan, China. It is affiliated with the Province of Henan. The university is part of Project 211 and the Double First-Class Construction.
Zhengzhou University is the largest university in China in terms of number of students (around 73,000 students). The campus size is 433 hectares (1,070 acres).

Zhengzhou University is the first comprehensive university established by the State Council of Chinese Government in 1954. According to the State Council, a group of faculty members from Shandong University, Peking University, Jilin University and Northeast University moved to Zhengzhou. The Zhengzhou University was established by these professors in 1954.

Henan Medical University dates back to the medical education in National Fifth Sun Yat-Sen University built in 1928 (the predecessor of National Henan University founded in 1942). This national university moved into Zhengzhou in 1952 and established Henan Medical College (the first batch authorized to confer doctoral degrees) which was the fore running of the higher medical education in Henan province.
Zhengzhou University of Technology as a National Key University under the direct administration of the Ministry of Chemical Industry of China, it was founded in 1963.

The university was admitted into Project 211 in 1996. Zhengzhou University was restructured by the merger of three universities i.e., Zhengzhou University, Henan Medical University, and Zhengzhou University of Technology on July 10, 2000. The purpose of this re-establishment was to create a center of top-notch learning covering a huge range of academic disciplines, equipped with excellent research facilities so as to revolutionize higher education in Central China in general and Henan Province in particular. Since its re-establishment, Zhengzhou University has received more attention by the Chinese Ministry of Education and the People's Government of Henan Province in terms of governmental support, finances, inter institutional cooperation and research collaboration.

Zhengzhou University now has four campuses covering 1070 acres land across Zhengzhou City. The main campus covers 799 acres of land on Science Avenue and Changchun Road in North-West section of Zhengzhou City. It is one of the most beautiful campuses in China with a construction cost of more than two billion Yuan. Majority of schools and faculties are located at main campus.

The east campus is the campus of previous Henan Medical University in the city center between Zhongyuan Road and Jianshe Road. The clinical stage of medical education is held on this campus. The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, with more than 10,000 sickbeds, is the largest hospital in the world.
The south campus is the campus of previous Zhengzhou University in the city center area of Daxue Road.

The north campus is the campus of previous Zhengzhou University of Technology in the city center of Wenhua Road 97. Some of the buildings were constructed with the help of USSR. One of the most famous School: the School of Cyberspace Security is located in here. The school of Cyberspace Security has three programs for Bachelor, which are among the best in Zhengzhou University.

After years of balanced development, Zhengzhou University now is a multi-discipline institution with 12 fields, such as science, engineering, medicine, literature, history, philosophy, law, economics, management science, pedagogy, agriculture and arts. Currently there are six national key disciplines, condensed matter physics, materials processing engineering, history of ancient China, organic chemistry, chemical technology, pathology and pathophysiology; 21 first-level disciplines are authorized to confer doctoral degrees, 3 independent second-level disciplines to confer doctoral degrees, 55 first-level disciplines to confer master's degrees, as well as 24 post-doctoral research stations. There are 51 Schools and departments as well as 9 affiliated hospitals in Zhengzhou University. The number of staff is over 6,000, 4000 academic members, 37 academicians of the Chinese Academy of Science and Engineering (15 full-time, 22 part-time and 4 oversea), 747 professors, and 1,600 associate professors. In 2020, there are around 51,000 undergraduate students, 19,000 graduate students and 2,600 international students studying in Zhengzhou University.
There exist 51 schools or departments in Zhengzhou University, ranging from art and literature to social and natural science and engineering.
National Supercomputing Center in Zhengzhou

As the seventh National Supercomputing Center approved by the Ministry of Science and Technology, Zhengzhou Center is a major technology innovation platform deployed by the state in Henan during the 13th “Five-Year Plan” period. The theoretical peak computing capacity of the host system in the center is 100PFlops and the storage capacity is 100PB. The measured continuous computing performance of the host system ranks first in the world.
Zhengzhou University Luoyang Campus
Zhengzhou University Luoyang Campus is a satellite campus of Zhengzhou University located in Luoyang, Henan.

There are 17 ESI disciplines in the top 1% of the world, including clinical medicine, chemistry, materials science, engineering, pharmacology and toxicology, biology and biochemistry, molecular biology and genetics, neuroscience and behavioral science, immunology, environment and ecology, physics, social science overview, computer science, agricultural science, microbiology, plant and zoology, mathematics, etc.

Zhengzhou University has been ranked among the top 150-200 global universities by Academic Ranking of World Universities since 2023, and 203rd globally and 45th in Asia as of 2025 by the US News & World Report Best Global University Ranking.

Times Higher Education 2023 has ranked ZZU in 601-800 best global universities, while the QS World University Rankings 2025 ranked it 511 globally. The CWTS Ranking 2023 of Leiden University ranked ZZU as 50th best global university  whereas NTU World Universities Ranking 2021 ranked it 134. The QS Asia Top Universities 2022 ranked it among 220 best universities of Asia.

Featured with a solid scientific research foundation, Zhengzhou University now owns more than 330 scientific research institutions of all levels/kinds, among which are 1 National Engineering Research Center, 1 National Technology Research Promotion Center, 1 National Chemical Safety Engineering Technology Center, 1 National Research Center for Safety Evaluation of Drugs, 2 National Drug Clinical Research Bases, 3 MOE Key Labs, 2 MOE Engineering Research Center, 1 Key Research Base of College Humanities and Social Sciences sponsored by the MOE and the Province, 1 Sports Culture Research Base under the Sports Culture Development Research Center of the State Sports General Administration, 1 National Intellectual Property Training Base, 6 Henan Provincial Collaborative Innovation Centers; Provincial Key Labs, Engineering Technology Research Centers, International United Labs, Key Humanities and Social Science Research Bases, Provincial Universities and Colleges Key Principles Open Labs, Engineering Technology Research Centers, State Key Laboratory Cultivation Bases total up to 104, and provincial key scientific and research institutions total up to 125, which indicates a strong capability on basic research, application research and development of science and technology. With a total construction area of 84,000sqm, its library contains a collection of books of more than 7.971 million. The university has its own publishing house and issues 14 academic journals.

As the largest university in China, Zhengzhou University provides millions of US dollars to sponsor hundreds of applicants with full scholarship and partial scholarship to pursue their degree non-degree study in Zhengzhou University each year. This is the only Chinese university with so many scholarship seats. In 2018, about 500 newly recruited students were sponsored by various types of scholarship, such as President Scholarship, Henan Government Scholarship, Chinese Government Scholarship, Confucius Scholarship. These scholarships usually covers:
Majority part of tuition for bachelor program.
Whole tuition for master program.
Tuition, accommodation and living allowance for doctor program.

The School of International Education (SIE) is in charge of international education of Zhengzhou University. There are approximately 1,700 overseas students from 70 countries/areas, among them 80% are degree students, more than 10% are supported by full scholarship. SIE also houses a Chinese language education base (accredited by the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office of State Council) and a Chinese international promotion base of Henan Province offering a number of Chinese language programs from short term training to bachelor's and master's degree. SIE runs a Confucius School jointly with Indian Vellore Institute of Technology and a Confucius class with St Mary School in USA. Zhengzhou university in collaboration with MEDVIZZ - CEO, Dr G Bhanu Prakash to train all medical fraternities for USMLE, PLAB AND FMGE in the campus itself.

Zhengzhou University is dedicated to conducting various forms cooperation and exchanges with famous universities abroad, absorbing advanced education programs and striving to achieve the objective of internationalization.

Most of what students need to know about daily life comes down to the city around the campus: its climate, how people get around, and what there is to do. The following sections describe Zhengzhou, where Zhengzhou University is located.

Located just north of the province's centre and south of the Yellow River, Zhengzhou borders Luoyang to the west, Jiaozuo to the northwest, Xinxiang to the northeast, Kaifeng to the east, Xuchang to the southeast, and Pingdingshan to the southwest. With the land within its administrative borders generally sloping down from west to east, Zhengzhou is situated at the transitional zone between the North China Plain to the east and the Song Mountains and Xionger Mountains to the west, which are part of the greater Qinling range. The city centre is situated to the south of the middle reach of the Yellow River, where its valley broadens into the great plain. Zhengzhou is at the crossing point of the north–south route skirting the Taihang Mountains and the mountains of western Henan. The prefecture spans 34° 16' ~ 34° 58 N latitude and 112° 42' ~ 114° 14' E longitude, covering a total area of 7,567 square kilometres (2,922 sq mi), including the metropolitan area, which covers 1,284.89 km2 (496.1 sq mi), and the city centre, which occupies 709.69 square kilometres (274.0 sq mi).

A section of the Yellow River passes by the northern edges of the urban area, extending 150.4 km (93.5 mi) within Zhengzhou prefecture. However, Jialu River, a secondary tributary of the Huai River, is Zhengzhou's main urban river and flood channel. The Jialu enters Zhengzhou from Xinmi to the southwest, and turns to the southeast within the city. Mountains loom over the western counties of Gongyi and Dengfeng while the easternmost county of Zhongmu is a vast, fertile floodplain, with the counties in between being hilly transitions.

Zhengzhou experiences a monsoon-influenced, four-season humid subtropical climate (Köppen climate classification Cwa), with cool, dry winters and hot, humid summers. Spring and autumn are dry and somewhat abbreviated transition periods. The city has an annual mean temperature of 15.4 °C (59.7 °F), with the monthly 24-hour average temperature ranging from 1.0 °C (33.8 °F) in January to 27.8 °C (82.0 °F) in July. The frost-free period lasts on average 220 days. Extremes since 1951 have ranged from −17.9 °C (0 °F) on 2 January 1955, 27 December 1971 and 1 February 1990 to 43.0 °C (109 °F) on 19 July 1966.

Rainfall is primarily produced by the monsoonal low during summer; in winter, when the vast Siberian High dominates due to radiative cooling from further north, the area receives little precipitation. During the summer season, the city is also often affected by tropical depressions, which bring additional amounts of rain. The annual precipitation is about 630 millimetres (25 in). With monthly percent possible sunshine ranging from 37 percent in January to 49 percent in April and May, the city receives 1,905 hours of sunshine per year, which is around 43% of the possible total.
In 2019, there were 177 good days in Zhengzhou, an increase of 9 days year-on-year, and 48.5% of the good days reached the standard. There were 24 days of heavy pollution, 9 days less than last year.

On 20 July 2021, "The heaviest hour of rainfall ever reliably recorded in China crashed like a miles-wide waterfall over the city of Zhengzhou on 20 July, killing at least 300 people, including 14 who drowned in a subway tunnel." Although an emergency alert was issued the day before the flood, businesses and subways remained open. From 4pm to 5pm on 21 July, 7.95 inches of rain fell. A collapsed retaining wall allowed water to pour into subway tunnels. "The Chinese government now appears to be acknowledging missteps by local officials, as well as the possibility that severe weather events will become increasingly common."

Zhengzhou, along with Xi'an, Chengdu, Chongqing and Wuhan, are some of the most economically important cities in inland China. Zhengzhou is the economic center of the province and the surrounding areas such as southeastern Shanxi and southwestern Shandong. Due to its strategic location in one of the most populous areas in the world (nearly 100 million people in Henan alone) and in China's railway, road and aviation transport networks, Zhengzhou is increasingly attracting domestic and international investment as well as migrants from other areas, transforming the city into one of the largest economic centers in China. In 2018, total GDP of Zhengzhou was ¥1020 billion, ranked 17th in China. And in 2021,  total GDP was ¥1269.1 billion, ranked 16th in China. In the first half of 2026, the GDP of city was reached 777.27 billion RMB.

By the end of 2006, Zhengzhou had a total population of over 7 million, of which 2.88 million lived in rural areas. Its main products include apples, paulownia, tobacco, maize, cotton, and wheat. In addition, Zhengzhou also produces Yellow River carp, Zhengzhou watermelons, Xinzheng jujube, Xingyang dried persimmons, Guangwu Pomegranate and Zhongmu garlic, all of which are specialties that are rarely found outside the region.
Zhengzhou and the surrounding area have large reserves of coal and other minerals. Coal mining and electricity generation are traditionally important in the local economy.

Zhengzhou has been one of the major industrial cities in The People's Republic of China since 1949. The city's staple industry is textiles. Others manufactured items include tractors, locomotives, cigarettes, fertilizer, processed meats, agricultural machinery, and electrical equipment. Some high-tech companies in new material, electronics and biotechnology are also growing rapidly during the recently years, especially in the high-tech industrial park in the northwest of the city.
Yutong, China's largest bus producer.
Shaolin Bus, a well-known small-to-medium-sized bus producer.
Dongfeng Nissan, specializing in the manufacture of SUVs and pickup trucks.
Haima Automobile Zhengzhou, an automobile manufacturer specializing in manufacturing microvans and light passenger vehicles.
Zhengzhou Unique Industrial Equipment Co., Ltd., a large tractor and agricultural equipment manufacturer.
Foxconn Zhengzhou, located in Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone, is the largest smartphone production site in the world and is also known as "iPhone City".

Synear Food Holdings Limited, along with Sanquan Food, is one of the largest producers of frozen food in China. The market share is over 20% in China
BYD Auto opened one of its largest manufacturing plants in 2023, which by 2025 employed 60,000 workers.

The service industries of Zhengzhou include retail, wholesale, hospitality, finance, exhibition, transport and delivery, tourism, and education. With a number of domestic and international institutions having regional offices in the city, Zhengzhou is becoming the financial center in central China. Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange (ZCE) is one of the only four future exchanges (inc. Shanghai Futures Exchange and Dalian Commodity Exchange and China Financial Futures Exchange) in China and is becoming an important global player specialised in agricultural future exchange. Equipped with newly built facilities such as Zhengzhou International Conference and Exhibition Center. Third party logistics (3PL) in Zhengzhou has also been experiencing industrial boom during the past few years. As a transit and tourist center of Henan Province and central China, Zhengzhou is the center of Henan cuisine.
Dennis, a regional retail chain.
Henan Jianye, a large real estate developer, which owns the China Super League club Henan Jianye F.C.

The Zhengdong New Area (Chinese: 郑东新区), literally Eastern Zhengzhou New Area, similar to Hangzhou Bay New Area in Ningbo and Hangzhou Bay New Area in Ningbo, is one of dozens of major economic zones that are currently developing in various regions of China. Established in 2003 by the provincial and municipal governments, it has become the financial center of Henan province and one of the most rapidly growing areas of China.

Kisho Kurokawa, a Japanese world-renowned planner and architect, was appointed to design the overall planning scheme for Zhengdong New Area. He brought in advanced ideas including ecological city, co-existing city, metabolic city and ring city ideas. The scheme won the "Prominent Award for City Planning Design" at the first session of Annual Meeting of the World Architects Alliance in 2002. Zhengdong New Area is mainly constituted by the CBD area, the Longhu commercial and residential area, the Longzihu college area, and the Zhengzhou East railway station commercial area.
Zhengzhou New & Hi-Tech Industries Development Zone

Zhengzhou High & New Technology Industries Development Zone was established in 1988, and approved by the state Council of PRC to be a state development zone on Mar.6,1991. It was appraised to be advanced high tech zone of China respectively in 1993, 1998 and 2002. The Zone currently covers a total area of 18.6 square kilometres (7.2 square miles). An extension plan was approved by Zhengzhou Municipal Government, the various construction work started in 2004. Under the development strategy of "multiple parks in one zone", the Zone has been making great efforts to promote the development of software, information technologies, new materials, bio-pharmaceutical and photo-machinery-electronic industries.
Zhengzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone

Zhengzhou Economic and Technological Development Zone was approved as state-level development zone on 13 February 2000. The zone has a developed area of 7 square kilometres (3 square miles) Industries encouraged include Electronics Assembly & Manufacturing, Telecommunications Equipment, Trading and Distribution, Biotechnology/Pharmaceuticals, Instruments & Industrial Equipment Production, Medical Equipment and Supplies, Shipping/Warehousing/Logistics and Heavy Industry.
Zhengzhou Export Processing Area

Zhengzhou (Henan) Export Processing Zone was established on 21 June 2002 with approval by the state council. Its planned area is 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile). Zone A is located in Zhengzhou National Economic & technological Development Area and began to operate on 1 June 2004. The area of land developed is 0.893 square kilometres (0.345 square miles) at present. Zone B is located in Zhengzhou Airport Area and is adjacent to Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport on the north and it covers a planned area of 5 square km with bonded logistics zone, bonded processing zone and supporting industry zone, etc.
Zhengzhou is located in the central part of China and is a main national transport hub.

The Zhengzhou Metro is a rapid transit metro rail network serving urban and suburban districts of the Zhengzhou metropolitan area. The system started operation on 28 December 2013. As of 2026, it currently has 13 lines in operation, creating a 450 km (280 mi) long network. The first two lines (Line 1 and Line 2) were approved by the National Development and Reform Commission in Feb. 2009. Construction of the two lines started in 2009 and 2010, and were finished in 2013 and 2015 respectively. The Chengjiao Line (planned to be part of Line 9), which is now in through operations with Line 2, allows the system to serve the Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport. A total of 21 metro lines have been planned to connect all areas in Great Zhengzhou Metropolitan Area.

As of 2026, Zhengzhou Metro operates 13 lines with a total operating length of 450 km, namely Lines 1–8, 10, 12 and 14, the Suburban Line, and the Zhengxu Line. Line 6 Phase I became fully operational on 30 November 2024, when its northeast section entered initial operation, while Line 7 Phase I and Line 8 Phase I opened on 29 December 2024. Zhengzhou's updated rail transit network plan, approved by the municipal government in May 2025, envisions 22 lines totaling about 1,260 km by 2035 and 30 lines totaling about 1,600 km by 2050.

The Zhengzhou subway fares has a segmented pricing system. The starting price is 2 yuan ($0.28) for a ride of up to 6 kilometers. If the mileage exceeds 6 kilometers, the principle of "decreasing for further distances" will apply. Within the mileage of 6 to 13 kilometers, 1 yuan ($0.14) will be added for every 7 kilometers, and for 8 kilometers between 13 and 21 kilometers, 1 yuan ($0.14) will be added. For each additional 9 kilometers above 21 kilometers, an additional 1 yuan ($0.14) is added. Riders can use cash, a physical metro card, or QR code payment available on Alipay or WeChat apps to pay for the ride.
Zhengzhou has a bus system with over 5,700 bus vehicles, operated by the Zhengzhou Bus Communication Corporation (ZZB).

The operations of Zhengzhou Bus Rapid Transit commenced in 2009. The system consists of 5 main routes (B1, B2, B3, B5 and B6) with dedicated bus lanes and dozens of branch routes that serve most areas of the city.

Zhengzhou is the junction of the Longhai Railway (Lianyungang, Jiangsu–Lanzhou, Gansu) and the Beijing–Guangzhou Railway as well as a major national railway hub. The main railway station for these conventional services is Zhengzhou railway station, opened in 1904.

Zhengzhou is also on the Beijing–Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong high-speed railway and the Xuzhou–Lanzhou High-Speed Railway. The high-speed rail network provides fast train services to most major cities in China, including Beijing (2.5 hours), Guangzhou (6 hours), Xi'an (2 hours), Wuhan (2 hours), Shanghai (4 hours), Nanjing (3 hours), Hangzhou (5 hours), and Hong Kong (6.5 hours). Proposed high-speed railways from Zhengzhou to Chongqing, Hefei, Jinan and Taiyuan are under construction.
The completion of the Zhengzhou–Jinan high-speed railway, planned for 2023, will complete a star-shaped (referred to as a "米"-shaped) network of eight high-speed lines radiating out from the city.

Zhengzhou is also the hub of intercity railways in Henan. Currently there are three intercity railways from Zhengzhou: Zhengzhou–Kaifeng intercity railway, Zhengzhou–Jiaozuo intercity railway and Zhengzhou–Xinzheng Airport intercity railway are in operation.

Zhengzhou East railway station is dedicated to high-speed trains and is one of the largest in Asia and Zhengzhou Hangkonggang railway station is a new high-speed railway hub dedicated to Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone.
Zhengzhou North railway station, over 6,000 metres (20,000 ft) long and over 800 metres (2,600 ft) wide, has been described as Asia's largest classification yard.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

zhengzhou-university.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Zhengzhou University may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Zhengzhou, register at Zhengzhou University by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.

zhongnan-university-of-economics-and-law.h: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law: the essentials

blocks.x: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, usually shortened to ZUEL (中南财经政法大学, literally the Central-Southern University of Finance, Economics, Political Science and Law), is a public university in Wuhan, in China's Hubei province. The Ministry of Education is its parent body, and the Ministry of Finance and the Hubei provincial government share the funding. The university is part of Project 211 and of the Double First-Class Construction scheme. For an international student, that combination points to a university with strong state backing and a clear focus on business, economics and law. If those are your fields, ZUEL is a natural name to put on a shortlist, and the sections below explain what to expect from the university and from Wuhan.

ZUEL was formed in 2000 by combining two separate institutions: a finance and economics university (中南财经大学) and a political science and law college (中南政法学院), both carrying the Central South name. Their shared origin is Zhongyuan University, founded in 1948 in Henan and later moved to Wuhan.

In detail, Zhongyuan's finance department was joined by economics and finance departments from Wuhan University, Sun Yat-sen University and other institutions, creating an institute of finance that later became the finance and economics university. Its law department combined with law teaching from other schools to make an institute of law. Over the following decades, including the Cultural Revolution, the two institutions were merged and separated more than once, and they were finally united again to form the university that exists now.

ZUEL has 19 schools. It teaches 51 undergraduate programmes, 104 master's programmes, 57 doctoral programmes and 6 post-doctoral programmes. It also reports one national-level key humanities research base, 4 national key disciplines, 10 provincial-level key humanities research bases and 19 key disciplines at ministry and provincial level. The university is authorised to award the MBA, EMBA, JM, MPAcc, MPA and Master of Education degrees, and it enrols overseas students, together with applicants from Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao. The Association of MBAs has accredited its MBA course.

In all, more than 2,660 people work full time in teaching and administration; among them are 219 professors, 500 associate professors and 160 doctoral supervisors. On the student side, ZUEL enrols above 20,000 full-time undergraduates and 6,000 postgraduates, plus 900 doctoral and post-doctoral researchers, over 9,000 adult students and 400 international students.

ZUEL describes a group of well-regarded scholars in management, economics and law, with a reputation both in China and abroad. Over 45 professors are sponsored by the State Council, and over 65 have received the provincial title of Young Expert with Prominent Contributions to the Country (Hubei) along with an expert allowance. In the last 25 years or so, staff have completed more than 400 key projects funded at national or provincial level. Of them, 100 were national social science or natural science fund projects or Ministry of Education key projects, while 187 were key projects backed by the finance and justice ministries. Altogether the faculty has produced over 30,000 pieces of research: more than 1,300 monographs and 1,700 textbooks, 21,000 articles, and upwards of 500 publications overseas. These totals date from an earlier period, so the real numbers today are probably higher.

These 20 units make up the academic structure, from core teaching schools to those serving continuing and international education. The list below begins with the humanities and law, then moves to business and technical fields.

The campuses cover over 210 hectares and have about 800,000 square metres of floor space. The library holds more than 2.5 million volumes and offers access to national and global information retrieval systems, which is helpful if your research needs databases, for example for finance or legal study. There are eight modern stadiums, two of which have hosted major events: the National University Games, the national top-division football matches, the finals of China's college men's football tournament and an East Asian college football match. Two modern auditoriums and over 30 apartment buildings, used as student dormitories, complete the picture. The campuses are described as spacious and attractive, with lakes, trees, grass and flowers.

In the Best Chinese Universities Ranking of 2022, ZUEL was first in South Central China and fourth or better nationally among universities specialising in finance, business and economics; it was the only university outside Beijing and Shanghai in that top four. Internationally, it has been placed in the top 500 worldwide for economics and management. Rankings change from year to year, so check the latest ones before you rely on any single number, and compare them with the university's own account of itself.

ZUEL belongs to the 五院四系 (Five Colleges and Four Departments), the group of leading law institutions, and was among the first to teach law. It has considerable influence in the legal field, and its law school is regularly counted in China's top ten.

On the international side, it maintains research and exchange ties with institutions in over 20 countries and regions in Asia, Europe, America and Australia, and it says it is open to teachers, scholars and learners from around the world. International students have studied here since the 1950s. In a past statement, the university said that over 58 years it had trained more than 200,000 graduates; because that count is clearly out of date, the number of alumni is now larger, and the university's own site has the current figure.
Student life happens in the city as much as on campus, so here is an introduction to Wuhan, the home of ZUEL.

Wuhan is in the east-central part of Hubei province, at about 29°58' to 31°22' north and 113°41' to 115°05' east. The Han River flows into the Yangtze here, on the eastern side of the Jianghan Plain, along the middle reaches of the Yangtze.

The city is a union of three older towns, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, which locals call the Three Towns of Wuhan. The name Wuhan joins the first syllable of Wuchang to the Han of the other two. They merged in 1927 and now look at each other across the rivers, linked by bridges. One of them, known as the First Bridge, was among the first modern bridges built in China.
Wuchang is on the south-east side of the Yangtze, across the river from both Hankou and Hanyang.
Hankou lies on the Yangtze's northern side, and the Han River cuts it off from Hanyang.
Hanyang is on the Yangtze's western side, facing Wuchang, and on the south bank of the Han, facing Hankou.

Wuhan's terrain is easy to describe: flat and low in the centre, hilly towards the south, crossed by the Yangtze and Han. Within Huangpi District the She River empties into the Yangtze. The land area is 8,494.41 square kilometres (3,279.71 square miles), mostly alluvial plain with hills, lakes and ponds scattered across it. A quarter of the urban area is water, the highest proportion among major Chinese cities. Nearly 200 lakes lie within it. East Lake, at 33 square kilometres, and Tangxun Lake are the biggest lakes entirely inside any city in China.

Further well-known waters are South Lake and Sand Lake, while Liangzi Lake in the south-east of Jiangxia District is the biggest lake by surface area in Hubei. The highest ground in the city, 872.5 metres above sea level, is a pair of peaks on the border between Huangpi District and Xiaogan. Hills inside the urban area include Mount Luojia in Wuchang District, and Mount Hong and Mount Yujia (喻家山, also written 瑜珈山) in Hongshan District.

Wuhan is humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa). Heavy rain falls in summer, and the four seasons are clearly marked. The humid summers are notorious, with dewpoints often at 26 °C (79 °F) or more. For that reason Wuhan was traditionally named, with Chongqing and Nanjing, as one of the Three Furnace Cities of the Yangtze. Newer climate records suggest it has dropped from the top tier of hottest summer cities, and a newer grouping lists Chongqing, Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanchang instead. Spring and autumn are mostly gentle, whereas winter is cool and dry, with an occasional snowfall.

By month, average temperatures over 24 hours rise from 4.1 °C (39.4 °F) in January to 29.3 °C (84.7 °F) in July. Rainfall adds up to just under 1,320 millimetres (52 inches) per year, most of it from April to July. The mean over a year is 17.4 °C (63.3 °F), and the stretch without frost lasts between 211 and 272 days. Sunshine accounts for 30 percent of possible hours in January and 53 percent in August, so the central city sees 1,783 hours in total. The lowest temperature recorded was -18.1 °C (-1 °F) on 31 January 1977; the highest was 39.7 °C (103 °F), on 27 July 2017 and again on 18 August 2022, and an unofficial 41.3 °C (106 °F) was logged on 10 August 1934.

Before the 21st century Wuhan was mainly farmland. A national plan called the Rise of Central China, in effect since 2004, has made it a focus for turning poorer inland regions into advanced manufacturing centres. Steel has been the backbone of local industry since 1890, though in 2010 the value of automobile production passed that of Wuhan Iron and Steel Corporation (WISCO) for the first time. Car makers here include Dongfeng Honda, Citroën, SAIC-GM, DFM Passenger Vehicle and Dongfeng Renault, and Dongfeng-Citroën Automobile Co., Ltd. is headquartered in Wuhan.

Foreign companies are well represented. By 2016, businesses from over 80 countries had created 5,973 foreign-invested enterprises in the city with US$22.45 billion in capital. Roughly 50 French firms, including Renault and PSA Group, operate in Wuhan; this accounts for more than a third of French investment in China, and no other Chinese city receives as much from France.

The city is an important centre for commerce, trade, finance, transport, information technology and education. The industries it emphasises are opto-electronics, vehicles, iron and steel, new medicines, bioengineering, new materials and environmental protection, and it lists energy-saving technology and renewable energy among emerging sectors. The Global Financial Centres Index put it among the world's top 100 financial centres in 2021.
Listed by founding date, the main zones are as follows.

The Economic and Technological Development Zone is a national zone, set up in 1993. Today it covers roughly 10 to 25 square kilometres, with plans to reach 25 to 50. It welcomes vehicle assembly, biotechnology and drugs, chemicals, food and beverage processing, heavy industry and telecom equipment.

The Export Processing Zone dates from 2000 and sits within the development zone. The plan is for 2.7 square kilometres (1.0 square mile); so far 0.7 square kilometres (0.3 square miles) has been developed.

The Donghu (East Lake) New Technology Development Zone, or ELHTZ, is a national high-tech zone built on optical electronics, telecoms and equipment, with software outsourcing and electronics also encouraged. China's biggest producer of optoelectronic products is here, led by Yangtze Optical Fibre and Cable (the country's largest maker of optical fibre cable) and Fiberhome Telecommunications. The zone is also the centre of China's laser sector, with firms such as HGTECH and Chutian Laser.

The Optical Valley (Guanggu) Software Park lies within that zone and was developed with Dalian Software Park Co., Ltd. It has a planned land area of 0.67 square kilometres (0.26 square miles) and 6,000,000 square metres (65,000,000 square feet) of floor space. It is 8.5 kilometres (5.28 miles) from National Highway 316 and 46.7 kilometres (29.02 miles) from Tianhe Airport.

Biolake, a biotechnology base founded in 2008 within Optics Valley, spreads over 15 square kilometres (5.8 square miles). Its six parks, for bio-innovation, biopharmaceuticals, bio-agriculture, bio-manufacturing, medical devices and medical health, are laid out to hold both research and housing.

Central China's largest city by population, and one of the biggest in the country, is Wuhan. The seventh national census in 2020 counted 12,326,500 residents, an increase of 25.97 percent, or 2.5411 million, over 2010. That decade was Wuhan's fastest-growing since censuses began, at an average of 2.34 percent a year, and the first time its population reached 10 million. The OECD estimated the wider metropolitan area at 19 million in 2010. A 2019 analysis that used night-lights and land-cover data as proxies found that socioeconomic activity in Wuhan is highly concentrated compared with the city's physical spread.

Most residents (79.2 percent in a 2017 survey) say they have no religion or follow worship of gods and ancestors, and of these 0.9 percent are Taoists. Others follow Buddhism (14.7 percent), Protestantism (2.9 percent), Catholicism (0.3 percent), Islam (1.6 percent) or another faith (1.6 percent).

The Wuhan Railway Hub, run by China Railway Wuhan Group, is counted as one of China's four principal rail hubs. Passengers use three big stations: Hankou, Wuchang and Wuhan, the last in a newly developed district east of East Lake in Hongshan. They are miles apart, so check carefully which one your ticket names, and leave extra time to get between stations if you have to change trains.

Originally Hankou was the southern end of the Jinghan railway from Beijing, and Wuchang was the northern end of the Yuehan line from Guangzhou. After the First Yangtze Bridge connected them into the Jingguang line, both stations began handling trains for every direction, which is unlike New York or Moscow, where each station serves particular directions.

The Hefei-Wuhan high-speed line, opened on 1 April 2009, brought fast trains to Hefei, Nanjing and Shanghai, with several services a day to Shanghai taking under six hours; by early 2010 these mostly departed from Hankou. Work on the new Wuhan station, with 11 platforms on the north-eastern outskirts, began in 2006, and it opened in December 2009 along with the country's second high-speed route, Guangzhou to Wuhan. It was promoted as the world's fastest service, reaching 394 km/h (244.82 mph), and it shortened the trip between the two cities from 10.5 hours to just three. The line has since been extended to Beijing. As of 2011 the new station mainly served Wuhan-Guangzhou high-speed trains, with conventional trains to other places still stopping at Hankou and Wuchang.

An intercity network for the metropolitan area was under construction. It is meant to link the three main terminals with outer districts and suburbs and with neighbouring cities Xianning, Huangshi, Huanggang and Xiaogan. The Xianning line carried its first passengers at the end of 2013, the Xiaogan line began on 1 December 2016, and when the Wuhan-Shiyan high-speed railway opened on 29 November 2019 the service reached Shiyan. For freight, the major station and sorting yard is Wuhan North in Hengdian Subdistrict, Huangpi District, with 112 tracks and more than 650 switches. It is 20 kilometres (12 miles) from Wuhan station and 23 kilometres (14 miles) from Hankou.

Wuhan Metro belongs to and is run by Wuhan Metro Group Co., Ltd. At the time of the data given here it had 11 lines, 282 stations and 435 kilometres (270 miles) of track, and the network has probably grown since. The first line opened on 28 July 2004, making Wuhan the seventh city on the mainland with a metro (Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Changchun and Dalian came first). Line 2, opened on 28 December 2012, was the first underground line to run beneath the Yangtze. Crossing the Yangtze and Han had long caused the worst traffic delays, and the metro has eased this a lot. As a measure of how busy it is, in 2019 it carried 1.22 billion passengers, making it the sixth busiest on the mainland. The city promised to open at least two lines or sections each year. During the COVID-19 pandemic the whole system was closed between 23 January and 27 March 2020.

The first trams went into service on 28 July 2017, on the Auto-city T1 line. Other systems under construction or in planning were the Auto-city trams in the Wuhan Economic Development Area (far western Hanyang), with lines T1, T2, T6 and T8; Optics Valley trams, with T1 and T2 in the south-east of Wuchang, south and east of Guanggu Circle, which opened on 18 January 2018; and a loop line called the Old Hankou Streetcar.
Buses also serve the city, including trolleybuses, which have operated since 1958, and the very first route, number 1, is still running.

Wuhan is one of central China's chief shipping hubs, and its port handles both local and onward cargo. Ferries have crossed the Yangtze for a long time. Steamboats started modern ferry service in 1900, and in 1937 a train ferry began moving railway cars from Hankou to Wuchang. Numbered landing points around the city let people hop on and off, and there is a tourist ferry at night. Today the Wuhan Ferry Company operates these services; in 2010 it purchased ten ships to replace boats that had served for 29 years.

ZUEL is one of China's best-known specialist universities for economics, finance and law, set in a large inland city of rivers, lakes and rail links. Wuhan offers hot, humid summers, cool winters, a developing economy and a transport network that reaches across central China. For the latest admissions information, programmes and figures, check the university's own website. Several of the numbers above come from older descriptions, so treat them as a general guide to scale rather than as exact current counts, and remember that transport figures for Wuhan in particular are likely to have grown.
Zhongnan University of Economics and Law lists 50 programs for international students on this site: 50 non-degree programs.

By language of instruction: 30 taught in Chinese, 20 taught in English. English-taught programs do not require Chinese to start; for Chinese-taught programs you normally need an HSK certificate at the level the program sets.

50 of these programs are listed as open to Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC) applicants, which means a CSC award can cover tuition, accommodation, a monthly stipend and medical insurance for eligible students.
The university has not published an application window that we could confirm yet. Intake dates change every year; a CAS advisor can confirm the current window for your program before you apply.

International students at Chinese universities can fund their studies through the Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC), provincial and city government scholarships, and university scholarships. Each has its own application route and timetable, and some are applied for through your home country's Chinese embassy rather than the university.

zhongnan-university-of-economics-and-law.h: How to apply, step by step

blocks.x: The process below is the general route for international degree applicants to Chinese universities. Zhongnan University of Economics and Law may add its own forms, interviews or deadlines, which a CAS advisor confirms before you apply.
Choose a program and check its language of instruction, duration and annual tuition on the Programs tab.

Check the admission requirements: a valid foreign passport, good health, and the right previous qualification (high-school graduation for a bachelor's degree, a bachelor's degree for a master's, a master's degree for a doctorate).
Bachelor's applicants take the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA) and send the result with the application.
Prove language ability: an HSK certificate for Chinese-taught programs, or English test results (for example IELTS or TOEFL) for English-taught programs, unless you studied in English.
Prepare certified transcripts and diplomas, a physical examination form, a police clearance certificate and a study plan or personal statement where the program asks for them.
Apply online through the university's international student system, or let CAS prepare and submit the application for you, and pay the application fee.
After admission you receive an admission notice and a JW202 or JW201 form, which you take to the Chinese embassy or consulate to apply for an X1 (long-term study) visa.
Travel to Wuhan, register at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law by the date in the admission notice, and convert your entry visa into a residence permit within 30 days of arrival.
